# Volume front matter

## Series title page

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library

The complete and uniform collection of all the holy fathers, doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles at the upper margins of the individual pages indicating and identifying the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each of the fathers on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, by which it is easy for the reader to discover which fathers, and in which places of their works, commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second series

In which are published the fathers, doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# In the year of the Lord 1029

Ademar, monk of the monastery of Saint-Cybard at Angoulême.

[Col. 0009]

## Historical and bibliographical notice concerning Ademar

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores IV, 106.)

[Col. 0009A] Ademar was born of a noble Aquitanian family, which held land “in its own hereditary right,” inhabiting the estate of Cabanne or Campagne.

[Note: [Col. 0009B] “In its own hereditary right,” which is called Campagne, near the castle of Potentia: Ademar, *On the Abbots of Limoges*, in Labbe II, p. 272. In Bouquet X, p. 151, note b, *Cabanense* is written instead of *Campanense*, which I would myself consider to be the same place. For Ademar calls his father Raimundus “of Cabanne” in *History* III, 45. The town is Chabanais, on the Vienne.]

His father was Raimundus, and his grandfather Fulcherius. From Officia, niece of Turpio, bishop of Limoges, Fulcherius fathered three sons: Rotgerius, Adalbertus, and the Raimundus just mentioned, the youngest.

[Note: [Col. 0009B] “From his niece, named Officia, were born Adalbert, the dean, and Rotgerius, with Fulcherius as their father … A third, Raimundus, also, younger in birth, was the full brother of both; I, Ademar, was his son,” with Hildegard as my mother; *On the Abbots of Limoges*, loc. cit. Raimundus is called a great-great-grandson instead of a great-grandson in *History* III, 45.]

This Raimundus married Aldeard, or Hildegard, sister of noble and powerful men,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] “Most energetic leaders, strong in body and warlike in spirit,” *History* III, 45. He seems to have called those men “leaders” who possessed larger forces and commanded an army.]

Abbo, Raimundus, and Ainard, the provost, whom Ademar praises as a man of the deepest counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0010B] *History* loc. cit.; *On the Abbots of Limoges*, loc. cit. Ademar’s genealogy is as follows:]

I would scarcely believe that his father was distinguished by the title and office of count, as Rivet maintains.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] Thus Rivet, *Literary History* VII, p. 320.]

For after Jordan, the “prince” of Cabanne, was killed after the year 1000, it seems that a brother of the same name succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] *History* III, 42.]

Ademar’s parents took no part in these public affairs and seem to have led a private life on their own estate rather than holding public offices or engaging in military matters.

Ademar was born around the year 988.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] “After you had completed the council of Limoges on the fourth day of August, not without great rejoicing, I departed from you and returned to the city of Angoulême, where from my earliest youth I have spent my life in the monastery of blessed Eparchius, now at the age of forty.” *Letter on Saint Martial*, in Mabillon, *Annals* IV, p. 717. This was written in 1028.]

As a boy he was entrusted to the monastery of Saint-Eparchius at Angoulême,

[Note: [Col. 0009C] Saint-Cybard.]

and spent most of his life there. At Limoges, however, at Saint-Martial, where his uncle Adalbert held the office of dean and provost,

[Note: [Col. 0009C] “He [the abbot Guigo, who governed approximately from 973 to 990] appointed the aforesaid Adalbert his dean in the basilica of Saint-Martial,” *On the Abbots of Limoges*, loc. cit. “The renowned dean and provost Adalbert, from the monastery of Saint-Martial,” *History* III, 45.]

he was educated by his other uncle, Rotgerius.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] “Ademar, who at that time was living with his illustrious uncle Rotgerius at Limoges in the monastery of Saint-Martial,” *History* III, 46. “Rotgerius—my teacher and uncle,” *On the Abbots of Limoges*, p. 273. He is called cantor in III, 61, and in the *Annals of Limoges* under the year 1025.]

There, without doubt, he was instructed in the letters, in which he excelled,

[Note: [Col. 0010C] “Ademar, who seemed to know something of the art of grammar,” says his opponent concerning him in the letter published by Mabillon, loc. cit., p. 718.]

and imbued with love and veneration for Saint Martial.

When he was twenty-two years old and had been established in this place, he seemed one night to see an image of the Crucified One hanging in the sky.

[Col. 0011A] But the man who saw this, struck with astonishment, could do nothing except pour tears from his eyes. He always kept what he had seen hidden in his heart.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] *History* III, 46.]

After returning from there to Angoulême, he was ordained a priest.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] “Ademar, the last of the priests of Angoulême,” letter, p. 717.]

There he devoted himself to copying and composing books.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] He sent to Rohon, bishop of Angoulême, a codex of the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, which he had copied or had caused to be copied, with verses added; edited by Mabillon, *Analecta*, second edition, p. 432. Compare the remarks there concerning Amalarius’s codex. Dacherius possessed a book of the *Questions of Zachaeus the Christian and Apollonius*, written in Ademar’s own hand or at his direction; *Spicilegium* XIII, II, p. 185.]

He brought a brief history of the abbots of Limoges down to the year 1025.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] Edited by Labbe II, pp. 271–273.]

In it he recorded the principal ecclesiastical affairs of these regions.

Shortly afterward he undertook a larger work. He wrote a history from the origin of the Franks down to his own time in three books, presenting chiefly the affairs of Aquitaine.

In the first book he follows the *Deeds of the Franks*, using a codex such as I saw in the Paris library, Suppl. Lat. n. 125, formerly belonging to Baron de Crassier. [Col. 0011B] In it the text of the *Deeds* is followed by the continuation of Fredegar, and the greater *Annals of Lorsch* are added.

Ademar copied these sources almost word for word. He also drew the second book, in which he recounts the deeds of Charlemagne, and the opening chapters of the third, from the *Annals of Lorsch*. Nevertheless, he inserted some material concerning Angoulême and transmitted a few other pieces of information whose source is unknown to us, such as the account of the singers brought from Rome to Francia by Charlemagne

[Note: [Col. 0012C] II, 8.]

and the account of the order of teachers.

[Note: [Col. 0012C] III, 5.]

He himself seems to have seen the laws of Louis the Pious, of which he speaks.

[Note: [Col. 0012C] III, 2–3.]

He also cites the *Deeds of King Pippin*,

[Note: [Col. 0012C] III, 56.]

but perhaps he used this title to designate part of an annalistic work. He rejected as fabulous the history written about the head of Saint John.

[Note: [Col. 0012C] Ibid.]

He saw the acts of the holy bishops Dionysius, Saturninus, Petragorius, and others,

[Note: [Col. 0012C] Letter, p. 722. The same acts, and in addition those of Saint Marcellus and Julian of Le Mans, were cited by a cleric from Angoulême at the council of Limoges in 1031. *Councils*, edited by Labbe IX, pp. 879–880.]

but nowhere used them in his history. Nor were the chronicles of Jerome and Bede, which he possessed,

[Note: [Col. 0012C] Letter, p. 721.]

relevant to his purpose.

Later, deprived of fuller sources, he used smaller annals, which he certainly had at hand in his monastery—Aquitanian ones, and perhaps also shorter annals of Angoulême.

Nevertheless, during these later years he added much material which he seems to have received from his parents and from older monks.

[Col. 0012B] For this reason he is almost always worthy of credence in Aquitanian matters, and he was well informed about events occurring in his own time, with only minor errors committed.

With the greatest diligence he set out what had happened in the monasteries of Saint-Eparchius and Saint-Martial, and he also consulted their charters. In addition, he narrated accurately, systematically, and at length what the dukes of Poitiers and the counts of Angoulême, Périgueux, and Limoges did at home and in war.

[Note: [Col. 0012C] I append their genealogies, so that the history may be understood more clearly:]

He treats the history of the Franks, Germans, and other peoples more briefly, and does not always follow a certain chronological order; nevertheless, he nowhere departs very far from the truth.

He also took account of events in Spain,

[Note: [Col. 0013C] III, 38, 55, 70.]

Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0013C] III, 22, 32.]

and Jerusalem,

[Note: [Col. 0013C] III, 47.]

which he probably learned from pilgrims who had returned from those places.

He saw Moors captured at Narbonne and brought to Limoges. Although they seemed to bark, speaking like puppies, they nevertheless reported how they had been defeated and captured.

[Note: [Col. 0013C] III, 52.]

In the same way, he doubtless either saw many other things himself or learned them from those who had taken part in the events.

[Note: [Col. 0013C] Compare the letter, p. 721: “Bishop Gerald of Limoges, who returned from Rome fifteen years ago, also testified to us that he had happened to read a volume there.” Ibid., p. 727: “Then Gauzbert said to me: ‘On my journey, long ago at Rome, I saw a certain distinguished count, an Alamannian, whose language I could not understand except in the psalms, litanies, and readings. His chaplains used to recite the litanies of the saints before him every day around the third hour …’ Then Salgionius said: ‘And I, when we entered the sea on our way to Jerusalem, saw a certain monk named John, a very capable grammarian from the city of Reims, who was on the ship …’”

In the history of the council of Limoges held in 1031, a cleric from Angoulême likewise relates: “Several years ago, certain brothers from Mount Sinai came to this western region by the will of God. They were serious in conduct, overflowing with instruction in the Catholic faith, upright in every aspect of life, and skilled in both languages. When they had stayed with us at Angoulême for a long time, waiting for the ruler of the city, and we saw that they were thoroughly versed in Greek and Latin letters, we arranged to question them about this matter … One was named Simeon and the other Cosmas.” *Councils*, edited by Labbe IX, p. 878. It is likely that Ademar also saw them and questioned them about many things.]

He wrote these things in a fairly good style. Although he does not seem to have aimed at a polished and ornate manner of speech, he nevertheless used the Latin language fairly well

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Compare the letter, p. 719: “Speaking Latin, I compelled him to speak Latin, and, pretending not to notice him when he uttered certain barbarous expressions, I patiently concealed them from those standing around.” Compare p. 726: “For I had heard him, as I said above, corrupt Latin badly with barbarisms at Limoges.”]

and applied a certain skill to arranging his material.

For, especially at the times when he was deprived of other sources, he does not follow the manner of annalists. Rather, he generally tries to join in his narrative events connected by a certain similarity.

[Col. 0013B] It is therefore all the more regrettable that he nowhere recorded the precise years of events—a fault he also neglected in his catalogue of the abbots of Limoges.

He brought his history down to the middle of the year 1028

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Not 1029, as Rivet says, *Literary History* VII, p. 301.]

and seems to have completed it in that same year.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] He himself states in III, 45 that he wrote while Peter, abbot of Scorcière, was still alive; but it is not known in what year Peter died. Compare *Gallia Christiana* II, p. 550.]

For in August of that year

[Note: [Col. 0013D] “Until the present year of which we speak, which is 1028 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the second indiction,” letter, p. 720.]

he attended the council held at Limoges, where he found very many bishops, abbots, and clerics of Aquitaine,

[Note: [Col. 0014C] Letter, p. 717.]

as well as his parents and relatives.

[Note: [Col. 0014C] Ibid., p. 720: “Leaving aside the conversation of my most dear noble parents, who had come from far away for the festival and were waiting there for me for my benefit.”]

At the dedication of the church

[Note: [Col. 0014C] 3 August. Compare the *Annals of Limoges* under the year 1028 and the history of the council of Limoges, in Labbe, *Councils* IX, p. 888.]

he preached publicly.

[Note: [Col. 0014C] Mabillon published a fragment of the sermon delivered there, vindicated for Ademar by Baluze, *Acta Sanctorum* VI.1, p. 31. Perhaps the same text survives in Paris codex 3785: “Sayings of the venerable Ademar on the feast of Saint Martial.” *Catalogue of the Paris Library* III, p. 466.]

After returning, he sent a letter to all who had attended the council. He also addressed it “to Arnold, bishop of Redon; Theoderic, grammarian and bishop of Metz; Conegund, empress of the Romans; Cono, Caesar Augustus and emperor; William, the orthodox and most powerful duke of the Aquitanians; and John, Roman pope.”

[Note: [Col. 0014C] Letter, p. 717. He seems to have personally known many of the bishops whom he names. For in the same place he says: “I do not want you to be surprised that I have included among your names those with whom I have never yet spoken about Saint Martial—I mean only three: the pope, the emperor, and the duke of Aquitaine.”]

In this letter he tried to prove that Saint Martial had truly been an apostle,

[Col. 0014B] and he narrated the discussion which he had had on this subject with a certain Lombard named Benedict of Chiusi.

[Note: [Col. 0014D] It is useful to quote here what Benedict says about himself in the letter, p. 726: “I am the nephew of the abbot of Chiusi. He took me through many places in Lombardy and Francia for the sake of grammar; my learning has already cost him two thousand solidi, which he gave to my teachers. I have now spent nine years studying grammar and am still a scholar. We are nine scholars who study grammar together, and I am very accomplished and learned. I have two large houses full of books, and I have not yet read them all, but I meditate in them every day. There is no book in the whole world that I do not possess. Once I leave school, there will be no one under heaven as learned as I. I shall be abbot of Chiusi after my uncle’s death; indeed, I have already been elected by everyone. And if those wicked monks who have become converts had not been concerned only with hypocrisy and rusticity, and had not taken this from me, I should have been consecrated abbot long ago. I am prior of Chiusi, and I know well how to compose a sermon from a text.”

And further: “In Aquitaine there is no wisdom; everyone is rustic. If any Aquitanian learns a little grammar, he immediately thinks himself Virgil. In Francia there is wisdom, but little. In Lombardy, however, where I learned more, there is the fountain of wisdom.” Ademar thought differently about him; compare note 30 above.]

This matter is nowhere mentioned in the *History*. He would scarcely have omitted it unless he had already completed the work beforehand.

That letter shows Ademar to have been eloquent and articulate

[Note: [Col. 0015B] “For in this land no one is considered wise unless he is very eloquent,” letter, p. 727.]

steadfast

[Note: [Col. 0015B] “For I hasten willingly to contend for the truth even unto death,” letter, p. 717. Compare ibid., pp. 725ff., p. 727: “Nevertheless, one must obey God more than the Roman pope.”]

and ardent in defending his assertion,

[Note: [Col. 0015C] “Again I declare before the sight of God and of all who dwell in heaven: if it is in any way displeasing to the glory of God, or to Martial himself, or to any of the saints who have already departed this life, that he should be preached as an apostle, then at this very hour, which is almost the sixth hour of the day, at this precise moment when I write this, at this instant, at this atom, may I die bodily and live no longer. The two Masses which I celebrated this morning in honor of the life-giving cross, one willingly and the other in obedience to the necessary command and request of Abbot Amalfredus, over the body of blessed Eparchius—if, I say, this displeases God, may they not be a help to me, but may I immediately, as I write alone inside the church, at this very hour give up my soul,” ibid., p. 726.]

although his opponent maintained that he had fabricated the assertion himself.

[Note: [Col. 0015C] Ibid., p. 718: “He was the first to devise this heresy, chiefly out of a desire to flatter, so that he might please the abbot and the monks; corrupted also by money from them, he devised it without any authority from the ancients.”]

In abundant and elegant speech, with arguments not to be despised, he tries to establish his opinion, however far removed it is from the truth.

Two councils were summoned in 1031 to examine this question, one at Bordeaux and the other at Limoges. Since we do not read that Ademar attended them, Rivet suspected that he had already died.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] *Literary History* VII, p. 302. Rivet also persuaded himself that Ademar had gone to Jerusalem, because the following words are found in a codex from the Vossian Library, formerly belonging to Saint-Martial of Limoges: “This is the book of our most holy lord Martial of Limoges, from the books of Ademar the grammarian, of blessed memory. For after he had spent many years in the service of the Lord and likewise in the monastic order in the monastery of that father, intending to go to Jerusalem to the Lord’s sepulchre and not to return from there, he left to that same patron and nourisher of his many books on which he had labored; this is one of them.” *Catalogue of the Library of Leiden*, 1716, folio, p. 386; compare *Archives* VII, 137. But Ademar the historiographer was a monk of Angoulême, not Limoges.]

I too would reach the same conclusion unless perhaps the very history of the council of Limoges

[Note: [Col. 0016B] Edited by Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum* II, p. 766; *Councils* IX, p. 869.]

—which seems to me to display nearly the same style of expression, the same doctrine, and the same veneration for Saint Martial that I detect in that letter—could be attributed to Ademar.

[Note: [Col. 0016B] Rivet, *Literary History* VII, p. 347, considered Odolric, abbot of Saint-Martial, to be the author. In Paris codex n. 2469, Ademar’s sermons on Saint Martial and this history of the council are found together; compare *Catalogue of the Paris Library* III, p. 285. Rivet rightly observes that the sermons of 994, edited by Baluze, *History of Tulle*, p. 385, are not by Ademar; compare the same author, pp. 306ff., concerning other works that scholars have attributed to Ademar.]

Certainly nothing is known about Ademar’s death. It is likely to have occurred around these years, since nothing is reported about him afterward.

Those who in later times devoted themselves to recording Aquitanian affairs, such as the author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*,

[Note: [Col. 0016C] In Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum* II, p. 249. The author who wrote the miracles of Saint Genulf also used Ademar’s work; compare Mabillon, *Acta* IV, II, especially note 14, p. 230.]

generally followed Ademar’s history.

The book came into the hands of many people. From it was also excerpted the history of the Franks preserved in Vatican Library, Christian codex n. 692, twelfth century.

[Note: [Col. 0016C] Compare *Archives* VII, p. 437. It took nothing from the first book, a little from the second and the beginning of the third, but copied a large portion of III, 16–38 almost word for word.]

From this work the author of the later *Chronicle of Saint-Maixent*, or *Malleacense*,

[Note: [Col. 0016C] In Labbe II, p. 190.]

drew a very large amount of material.

Some people copied fragments; others added to the excellent work whatever seemed to be missing from it.

There exists in the Royal Library at Paris a codex, to be mentioned below, which contains Ademar’s history, partly enlarged by very numerous additions and partly extensively altered.

But nearly all the additions are utterly false.

[Note: [Col. 0016C] To mention only a few examples: in III, 19, it says that Lothair entered a monastery four years after 855, although Ademar had correctly written “after a few days”; in III, 20, it invents intolerable fables about Odo, king of the Franks; in chapter 22, misunderstanding Ademar’s words, it says that Arduino, king of Italy, died before Otto I; what it relates in the same place about King Robert and Count Hugh already seemed to others to smell of fiction; still farther from the truth are the things it records in chapter 31 concerning Saint Adalbert and Bruno. Concerning Archbishop Heribert, captured by Henry II, Ademar spoke correctly in chapter 33; after those words were deleted, the interpolator substituted other and false material.]

The interpolator invented much from his own imagination, repeatedly misunderstood Ademar’s words, and confused the chronological order.

[Note: [Col. 0016D] For example, in chapter 23 he places Bishop Fredebert falsely in the tenth century.]

He added still more material that has the flavor of poetic narration and seems to have come from poems.

[Note: [Col. 0016D] Compare what I have already cited in chapter 22 concerning Hugh and Robert; chapter 28: “with the sword which the smith Walander had forged”; and what is related there about Arnold; chapter 34 concerning Adalbert and the king of the Franks; chapter 55: “thus fulfilling the story of Thyestes as a true one.”]

Since most people attributed all these things to Ademar, he came to be regarded as a credulous and fabulous man, and his history was lamented as excessively confused by errors.

These faults, however, belong to the interpolator, who perhaps compiled this material a hundred years or more after Ademar.

He drew certain things from the *Life of Louis*,

[Note: [Col. 0017D] III, 16.]

and other things from Aquitanian annals, which Ademar himself had also possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] III, 18–19. But he joined these rather unsuccessfully to Ademar’s narrative.]

In other passages he agrees with the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] Compare III, 16, on the coinage of Angoulême with *Deeds*, chapter 13; III, 24, on relics brought back from Jerusalem; and chapters 28, 60, and 66 with *Deeds*, chapter 19 and chapter 25.]

Since the author of that work elsewhere follows Ademar’s pure text,

[Note: [Col. 0017D] Compare *Deeds*, chapter 11, with Ademar III, 20; *Deeds*, chapters 14 and 16, with Ademar III, 23, and so forth. Much of what is read in *Deeds*, chapter 25, is absent from the interpolated codex.]

I would rather suppose that certain passages were stitched onto Ademar from the *Deeds*, not that the author himself used the interpolated codex—especially since the writer of the *Deeds* also added similar material in other places to a narrative drawn from Ademar.

[Note: [Col. 0018D] Compare chapters 9 and 10, and especially chapters 25 and 26, where many new details are read about William, count of Angoulême. Only part of these occurs in the interpolated text of Ademar, although they were doubtless written by one and the same person.]

I therefore seem justified in concluding that the interpolator compiled his work not before, but after the year 1159, when it is established that the *Deeds* were written.

Since he devotes particular attention to events in the monastery of Saint-Martial at Limoges, already set out with sufficient accuracy by Ademar,

[Note: [Col. 0018D] III, 19 [20], 22, 25, 35, 43, 49, 57, and so forth.]

he should probably be thought to have lived there, and for that reason deserves somewhat greater confidence in these matters as well.

[Col. 0017B] In this edition of Ademar, my principal aim was to present first of all his complete and pure text, using chiefly a most excellent codex
1) Paris, Bibliothèque royale, no. 5927, parchment, folio, formerly belonging to J. A. Thuani. It was written in the middle of the eleventh century, with great care and in a fairly elegant style, on excellent parchment, by more than one hand. It consists of 165 folios, joined sometimes in larger, sometimes in smaller gatherings. It contains 131 chapters of Ademar’s history. I partly transcribed this book and partly collated it with the printed editions with the greatest exactness, since it contains a pure text with only very few and minor errors. [Col. 0017C] Written in Aquitaine—perhaps at Angoulême or Limoges—it seems to stand very close to the autograph. There the history is read without a title, and the individual books are not distinguished by red headings; nevertheless, an index of the chapters is prefixed, while the beginning of the second and third books is indicated by the heading of the first chapter. The same volume contains, on folio 132, a diploma of King Charles confirming the castle of Fronsac to the church of Angoulême; on folio 133, the agreement of William and Hugh, edited from this very codex by Labbeus, II, p. 135; and, from folio 140 onward, an incomplete Life of Charlemagne by Einhard. From this codex was copied:

1a) Paris, Bibliothèque royale, Suppl. Lat. no. 142, paper, fifteenth century, folio, which contains the same work and ends with the same words of Einhard. Perhaps this is the manuscript which Labbeus saw in the College of Clermont; in any case, it was certainly very similar to it.

The interpolated history is preserved in:

[Col. 0018A] 2) Paris, Bibliothèque royale, no. 5926, parchment, late twelfth century, small folio, formerly belonging to Antoine Faure, which Labbeus received from the library of Hadrian Valesius. The volume consists of seventeen and a half gatherings, marked a–r on the final folio. In gathering m, three folios are missing. Folios 1–63 contain the first two books of Ademar; folios 63–79, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne; folios 79–114, the anonymous Life of Louis the Pious; from folio 114 onward, it continues Ademar’s History from III, 16. It very frequently altered his wording even in the earlier books, following sometimes Ademar himself and sometimes the sources that he copied—the *Deeds of the Franks* and the *Annals of Lorsch* [Note: [Col. 0018D] Compare what I shall say in *Archiv*, vol. VIII.]. Thus Labbeus, observing that the complete Lives of Charles and Louis had also been inserted, thought that only the final part could be attributed to Ademar. The text, [Col. 0018B] copied with great negligence, is filled with the most atrocious errors, showing that the scribe was unskilled both in reading old books and in copying them. The form of the letters, such as I have often seen in Limousin manuscripts, seems to indicate a monk of that city, where, as I noted above, the interpolator himself also appears to have lived. In this manuscript too, which I have no doubt was derived from 1, though not copied directly from it [Note: [Col. 0018D] Compare what Pertz says about Einhard, *Patrologia*, vol. XCVI.], the history lacks a title.

3) Most of the surviving manuscripts of Ademar derive from the same exemplar, which lacked its ending, since they conclude at III, 24, with the words “the vicariate of Pillac” (and many other churches). They contain a text untainted by interpolations. I myself have seen three [Note: [Col. 0018D] Compare *Archiv*, VII, pp. 433 ff.].

[Col. 0018C] 3a) Montpellier, no. 94, parchment, twelfth century, folio, formerly belonging to the College of Troyes. It has neither titles nor a division marking the third book.

3b) Montpellier, no. 277, parchment, folio, twelfth–thirteenth century, octavo. It gives the work the title *History of the Franks* and prefixes an index of chapters to each book.

3c) Montpellier, no. 27, parchment, fourteenth century, folio. It generally agrees with 3b, but differs from it in the order of the chapters of the third book, giving 18 instead of 22.

Other manuscripts of this kind are found:

3d) At Rome, Vatican Library, no. 1795, parchment, folio, thirteenth century. (*Archiv*, V, p. 116.)

3e) At Rome, Library of the Christian Brothers, no. 905, parchment, folio [Col. 0018D] (*Archiv*, III, pp. 422–423, compared with V, p. 117). It appears to have the same order of chapters as 3b.

3f) At Bern, no. 208, parchment, thirteenth century (*Archiv*, V, p. 488).

[Col. 0019A] 4) Paris, no. 6190 [Note: [Col. 0019B] The codex seems formerly to have belonged to E. Vinet and later to Thuani; compare Besly, *History of the Counts of Poitou*, p. 199.]. Four eleventh- or twelfth-century folios containing various excerpts from Ademar were sewn onto a codex of Rodulfus Glaber; they were later expanded from the same source. Written without order, they sometimes preserve Ademar’s own words and sometimes display, in an altered style, a very different manner of narration. Although copied from a non-interpolated manuscript, they nevertheless agree in certain passages with 2 [Note: [Col. 0019B] III, 28, 34.], so that they may perhaps be reckoned among the interpolator’s own sources.

Ademar’s complete work has never been published. Pithoeus first published the second book from codex 1 (*Scriptores XII coaetanei*, Paris edition, 2, p. 6; Frankfurt edition, p. 230), suppressing Ademar’s name; from there it passed into Duchesne’s *Scriptores* (II, p. 68) and the Kulpisian *Scriptores* (3, p. 45). The same Pithoeus made public Ademar’s excerpts from codex 4 under the title “Fragment of Aquitanian History” (*Scriptores XII coaetanei*, Paris edition, 2, p. 416; Frankfurt edition, p. 517; and *Scriptores XII coaetanei*, p. 79), which Duchesne’s editions repeated, apparently expanded from Ademar’s own manuscript (*Scriptores*, II, p. 632; IV, p. 80). A short fragment of Ademar was also inserted by A. Duchesne into the collection of *Norman Histories* (p. 19). Besly printed larger passages, copied from the finest manuscript, perhaps the same one that I have designated 1 [Note: [Col. 0019B] See p. 199.], in the proofs to his *History of the Counts of Poitou* [Note: [Col. 0019B] *History of the Counts of Poitou and the Dukes of Guyenne*, by J. Besly. Paris, 1647, folio, passim.]. Peter of Saint-Romuald published a history compiled from Ademar and other sources [Note: [Col. 0019B] *Epitome of the History of the Franks, or Chronicle of Ademar of Angoulême, with Notes and Various Interpolated Additions, by Dom Peter of Saint-Romuald of Fécamp*. Paris, L. Chamhoudry, 1652, 12mo. A similar work is preserved in Paris, codex no. 6182, paper, seventeenth century: *On the Origin of the Franks from the Chronicle of Ademar, Monk of Saint-Martial*.]. Labbeus undertook his edition shortly afterward, using the three codices indicated above (1, 1a, and 2); but, through an extraordinary error, he followed the interpolated book and neglected Ademar’s complete History, [Col. 0020A] citing the Thuani manuscript only in a few isolated passages. From the first book he gave only certain excerpts; he omitted the second as though it had already been published; and at the beginning of the third he suppressed much material drawn from the *Annals of Lorsch*. A large part of Ademar’s History was taken from the editions of Labbeus and Duchesne into Bouquet’s collection (II, p. 514; V, p. 184; VI, p. 223; VII, p. 225; VIII, p. 232; X, pp. 144–164) and provided with notes.

Even in this new edition which I have undertaken, it was not necessary to publish the entire work. I have presented only what Ademar added to those larger sources or composed on his own initiative. For this purpose I read through codex 1 and copied everything worthy of remembrance from the first books. In the later books I took care to reproduce the same codex accurately, and I have always reported in the notes what I corrected [Note: [Col. 0020B] With the single exception that I considered *ae* must always be written in the genitive, since the codex is inconsistent with itself, displaying sometimes *ae* and sometimes *e*, especially in names of cities such as *Engolisme*, *Lemovice*, and so forth.]. In the codex, *a* is often written for *e*, apparently as a result of the pronunciation customary in the regions of Aquitaine—for example, *Nannetansium*, *Rotomansis*, *biannium*, *emandatio*, *commandatum*, *opulantissimam*, *amplectabatur*, *assumans*, *revertans*, *decoram*, *Engolismensam* [Note: [Col. 0020B] These have sometimes already been corrected in the manuscript: *classa*, corrected to *classe*; *Salasensam*, corrected to *Salasensem*.]. I hesitated whether to attribute these forms to Ademar, but I did not wish to admit them. I have added below what is added or altered in 2, though I have not recorded all its readings, which are often extremely false. In the margin I have tried to establish a secure chronological order; in the notes, to correct errors and explain as briefly as possible Aquitanian matters and other points worthy of remembrance.

G. WAITZ

[Col. 0019]

## The Three Books of Histories

### Book One

[Col. 0019C] 1. The beginning of the reign of the Franks, and so forth, as in the *Deeds of the Franks*.

11. (*Deeds of the Franks*, ch. 12) The following is added: At that time Saint Eparchius was born to a father named Felix, count of Périgueux; he later, filled with holiness, became the patron of the city of Angoulême.

16 [Note: [Col. 0019] Chapter 16. The words of the *Deeds* (ch. 15?) are read as follows: “Thereafter all the churches of God, acting with the authority of the Roman apostolic see according to this example, have continued to celebrate everywhere these very three-day litanies before the Lord’s Ascension.”]. (Year 508; *Deeds*, ch. 17) The following is added: In that city [Note: [Col. 0019C] Angoulême.] he caused a venerable man, Aptonius, his chaplain, to be consecrated bishop, after expelling from that same city the first bishop, an Arian Goth.

[Col. 0020C] 24. (Year 581; *Deeds*, ch. 25) The following is added: At that time Saint Eparchius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0019] “bishop and father,” with the rest erased in 1.], patron and father of Angoulême, departed to Christ on the first day of July.

29. (*Deeds*, ch. 30) The following is added: At that time Saint Gregory, archbishop of Tours, shone forth with great miracles. At the same time Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, sent by King Charibert to the city of Angoulême, consecrated the basilica of Saint Eparchius, where the saint himself had recently been buried. The venerable Gregory, bishop of Tours, was present with him; and, placing in that same basilica many relics of the blessed Bishop Martin, they dedicated it in honor of that same Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0021] *dedecaverunt*, corrected to *dedicaverunt* in 1.]. Finally, on its altar, consecrated by Saint Germanus and Saint Gregory, there are still visible the impressed marks of the holy cross. Likewise, in honor of Saint Peter, they consecrated the church of the episcopal see [Note: [Col. 0021] *e* corrected in 1.], which the aforesaid King Clovis had ordered to be begun anew, after the previous see, dedicated to Saint Saturninus, had been destroyed because the Goths had defiled it with Arian pollution. They appointed as bishop of that city a man named Mererius [Note: [Col. 0021D] Gregory of Tours, V, 37, has *Maracharius*.], who had been the king’s chaplain in Francia. For Aptonius had very recently died in Christ.

31. (Year 575; *Deeds*, ch. 32) The following is read: They assembled an army and marched against him toward [Col. 0021B] Angoulême, where he was staying because of the strength of its walls. Abandoned by his own men, he too remained with a few, but nevertheless did not hesitate to go into battle. When they came to battle eight miles from Angoulême, beside the river Charente and near the Buxus forest, Theodebert was defeated and struck down, and died there. He was gathered up by Duke Aunulf, carried to the city of Angoulême, and buried there at Saint Eparchius. Sigebert and Chilperic, meanwhile, were fighting one another in Francia. Then Chilperic …

33. (At the beginning of *Deeds*, ch. 34) The following is added: For she [Note: [Col. 0022D] Fredegund.] was a most wicked servant-girl; but because of the beauty of her face the king loved her exceedingly, continually listened to evil counsels from her, and considered her superior to all the counsellors [Col. 0021C] of the Franks.

41. (*Deeds*, ch. 42) The following is added: At that time the emperor Heraclius, victorious, brought the cross of the Lord from the temple of Chosroes, which was in Persia, to Jerusalem, and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross then took place in his city [Note: [Col. 0021] Perhaps “holy city”?]. At that time the most devout emperor Heraclius sent gifts to Dagobert and asked him to compel all the Jews throughout his kingdom to be baptized; and this was done.

49. (Year 714; *Deeds*, ch. 51) The following is read: At that time the aforesaid Pippin the Short, father of Drogo, Grimoald, and Charles Martel [Note: [Col. 0021] Charles is also called this in chapter 50 (*Deeds*, ch. 52).], seized by a violent fever, died … [lacuna] … discreet. After the aforesaid Pippin the Elder or Short had died, who was the great-grandfather of lord Emperor Charles, the Franks attacked one another in the forest of Compiègne … Then Plectrudis, wife of Pippin the Elder, began to employ guile against Charles Martel, the aforesaid Pippin’s son by another wife, Chalpaida; while he was being held in custody, he barely escaped, with God’s help.

51. ?(*Deeds*, ch. 33) He combined the narrative of the *Deeds* with that of the continuator of Fredegar: Eudo returned Chilperic to him with many gifts; and Charles Martel, after receiving Chilperic, established him as king, forgetting all the evils he had done against him, but he refused to make peace with Ragenfred [Note: [Col. 0021] *amicias* in 1.]. King Chilperic, coming from the city of Noyon [Note: [Col. 0021] *noviono* in 1.], died of illness, and reigned for six years. The Franks, however, established as their king Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, who had been raised in the monastery of Chelles, with the consent of Charles Martel. Charles, the chief, pursued Ragenfred, besieged the city of Angers, and, after ravaging the region, returned with much booty; Charles Martel himself became mayor of the palace in the kingdom of the Franks. The following year he attacked the city of Angers with great force, captured it, and, after Ragenfred had been killed, returned.

52. (Year 732; Fredegar, ch. 108) After “he returned victorious to Francia” [Col. 0022B] the following is added: From that time everyone began to call him Martel, “the Hammer,” because just as a hammer subdues all iron, so he, with God’s help, shattered every battle.

54. (Year 736; Fredegar, ch. 109) The following is added: Then King Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, died, and Charles Martel, during that same illness, ordered Theuderic’s brother Childeric to be raised to the kingship. He was foolish, as his brother had been; but the Franks could not find a better man of royal descent … [lacuna]

(Year 741; Fredegar, ch. 110) … on the condition that he would defend the Romans against the Lombards, who were inflicting much harm in the land [Note: [Col. 0021] *t. s. p.* written twice in 1.] of Saint Peter. He … [lacuna]

… [lacuna] … the most sacred order of Easter was disrupted throughout [Col. 0022C] many regions through the error and ignorance of the computists, who did not know how properly to determine the date of Easter; and in many cities Easter was celebrated either in March, April, or May … Charles … died in peace in the year 741 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0021] Missing in 2.]. In an earlier year, when there had been confusion about Easter, the Sunday of Christ’s Resurrection ought to have been 24 April, which was the final year of the nineteen-year cycle; and Palm Sunday, “Hosanna,” fell on 17 April [Note: [Col. 0021] *domina* in 2.]. Charles reigned [Note: [Col. 0021] Missing in 2.] for twenty-five years, but was not called king, because he did not permit himself to be called king, only duke of the Franks; for he honored the royal title in the boy-kings, namely Theuderic and Childeric, [Col. 0022D] although they were inept and lacking in prudence and understanding [Note: [Col. 0021] *arentibus* in 2.]. He died on 22 October, having acquired all the surrounding kingdoms, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr. Pippin the Elder [Note: [Col. 0021] “was buried,” in 2.] his father reigned for seventeen years in loyalty to the boy-kings.

56. (*Annals of Lorsch*, year 749.) … Then the Franks grieved because they did not have a prudent king, but for many years had endured foolish men of royal descent. They wished to raise Pippin the Pious to the kingship. He did not wish to consent; but, after assembling all the leading men of the Franks, he sent men to Rome on their behalf …

57. (*Annals of Lorsch*, year 753.) … Carloman … came to Francia in order to bring back to Monte Cassino the body of Saint Benedict … [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0023]

In codex 2 the following is added under the year 755: In the year 755, the often-mentioned Pope Stephen, together with the pious King Pippin, after the dedication had been celebrated at Paris in the church of blessed Denis, set out for Aquitaine and came as far as the place called Figeac [ [Col. 0023C] Figeac in the diocese of Cahors] [ [Col. 0023] *nomiatur* in c.]. There the most devout King Pippin, warned by a divine message, had built a monastery in honor of the Savior of the world, and had brought that pope with him for its consecration; but he was forestalled by a divine miracle. For, on the night preceding the day of the consecration, some people heard voices singing psalms in that same church. At daybreak, a suddenly appearing, extremely dense cloud, breathing a most pleasant fragrance [ [Col. 0023] *fraglante* in c.], covered the entire surface of the church so completely that it entirely denied entry to those who wished to enter. Around the third hour of that day, when the cloud had departed, Lord Pope Stephen, together with his fellow bishops and clergy, and the most serene King Pippin entered the church and saw that its walls and sacred altars had been consecrated by divine anointing. Greatly astonished and filled with immense joy, the aforesaid pontiff and the most merciful King Pippin gave countless thanks to God [ [Col. 0023] *redentes* in c.], and bestowed upon that church various honors, villas, estates, castles, and very many other places [ [Col. 0024C] Pippin’s diploma is forged. See Dachery, *Spicilegium*, second edition, III, p. 319; Stephani, *Gallia Christiana*, I, 43.]. In particular, they gave it the monastery of Junante [ [Col. 0024C] The valley of Zunault.], formerly built by the most powerful Frankish king Clovis, but later utterly destroyed, after the passage of many years, by excessive rains and floods; the monastery of Saint Quentin at Galliac [ [Col. 0024C] In the county and diocese of Cahors.]; and the hermits’ monastery of Conques [ [Col. 0024C] Conques, in the diocese of Rodez.], together with many other churches and most of the surrounding region. They placed these under the jurisdiction of that church and decreed by their own privileges that it should be free from every human service except the protection of the Roman pontiff. When these matters had thus been solemnly completed, Pope Stephen and the king returned to Francia.]

## Book Two

[Col. 0023]

[Col. 0023A] 1. We shall now relate the ancestry of the exalted lord King Charles the Great, whom God loved and exalted, and made a great prince and beloved by the entire Christian people throughout the whole world [Col. 0023B]. Thus [Note: [Col. 0023C] Much of what follows also derives from the *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*.], in the time of the Emperor Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0023] *Valentiani* in 1.], who was the seventh Augustus after Constantine the Great, the divine Augustus whom Saint Pope Sylvester baptized, during whose reign Saint Jerome flourished, the Franks, still pagan, first began to have kings from among themselves.

The first king of the Franks was therefore named Pharamond, son of Marcomer, an illustrious man of that people. After Pharamond, his son Clodio reigned. After Clodio, his son Meroveus reigned. After Meroveus, his son Childeric reigned. At that time Saint Eparchius arose from the city of Périgueux, the son of Felix Aureolus, count of that city. After Childeric, his son Clovis reigned; he was the first of the Frankish kings to believe in Christ, and was baptized by Saint Remigius, bishop, together with his entire army and the whole Frankish people.

After Clovis, his son Childebert reigned with his three brothers, Theuderic, Chlodomer, and Chlothar. At that time Saint Eparchius shone forth in Angoulême through his miracles, and, while Childebert was reigning, he departed in peace to the Lord after his seventieth year of life. At that time the emperor Anastasius Augustus held the imperial office. At that time Theudebert, his nephew and the son of Theuderic, reigned together with Childebert. At that time Saint Pope Gregory I, Gregory, bishop of Tours, Saint Aredius the abbot, and Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, flourished.

After Childebert, his brother Chlothar reigned; he had Saint Radegund in marriage. After Chlothar, his son Chilperic reigned with his three brothers, Charibert, Guntram, and Sigebert, who had Brunhild in marriage. After Chilperic, his son Chlothar reigned.

This Chlothar fathered Dagobert and one daughter named Blithild [Note: [Col. 0023C] Compare the *Genealogy of Saint Arnulf*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, II, 308, 313.]. From this Blithild came the lineage of lord Charles. For this Blithild, sister of King Dagobert, had as her husband a noble Frank named Ansbert, by whom she bore a son named Arnald. Arnald begot Arnulf, who later, abandoning the world, became bishop of the city of Metz. Before he became a cleric, Arnulf had a wife named Bega, daughter of Pippin the mayor of the palace, and by her he begot Ansegisel. Ansegisel [Note: [Col. 0023] *Ansegilus* in 1.] begot Pippin the Elder, the Short, who was the great-great-grandfather of lord King Charles. Pippin the Elder, duke of the Franks, begot Charles Martel. Charles Martel begot Pippin the Pious, who, raised from that line of descent, was the first whom the Franks made king, the entire lineage descended from Pharamond having been completely set aside.

Pippin the Pious begot [Col. 0025A] lord King Charles, Augustus and emperor. Lord Charles begot lord Emperor Louis. Louis begot Charles the Bald by Queen Judith. But I shall return to the succession of the kings.

After Chlothar, his son Dagobert reigned; at that time Saint Eligius, bishop, flourished. Dagobert had as mayor of the palace the excellent man Pippin, whose daughter, named Bega [Note: [Col. 0025] Added by another hand in 1; missing in 2.], the most noble man Arnulf, father of Ansegisel [Note: [Col. 0025] *Ansegili* in 1.], took as his wife. After Dagobert, his son Clovis reigned; he had Saint Balthild in marriage. At that time the body of Saint Benedict was transferred from Benevento to Francia, to the estate of Floriacum.

After Clovis, his son Chlothar reigned. After Chlothar, his brother Theuderic reigned; Ebroin was his mayor of the palace, and Saint Leodegar, bishop, flourished, whom Ebroin himself killed. At that time Pippin the Elder was mayor of the palace in Austrasia under the kings Childeric and the younger Childebert. This Pippin agreed with the noble Franks to kill Ebroin. And Pippin the Short, because King Childeric of the Austrasians had been killed by the Franks, fought against Theuderic, king of the Franks, defeated him, and later reconciled himself with him; he became mayor of the palace in Francia and waged many courageous wars against the Suebi and other peoples.

This Pippin the Short, by his wife Chalpaida, begot Charles Martel. After King Theuderic, his son Clovis reigned. After Clovis, his brother, the younger Childebert, reigned. After the younger Childebert, his son, the younger Dagobert, reigned. After Dagobert, the royal lineage declined in wisdom, and after that Dagobert his brother Daniel, an unintelligent cleric, reigned; the Franks changed his name and called him Chilperic.

This foolish Chilperic led an army against Charles Martel, who at that time was still young and was mayor of the palace and duke in Austrasia under King Chlothar. Chilperic was defeated in battle, and Charles Martel emerged victorious. Then Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, led an army to the aid of the foolish Chilperic against Charles Martel, and was defeated by him in battle. Charles Martel captured his enemy, the foolish King Chilperic; but, forgetting his malice, he restored his kingdom to him.

After the foolish King Chilperic, his kinsman, the foolish Theuderic, reigned in name only. After Theuderic, his foolish brother Childeric reigned in name only, and the entire royal lineage came to an end. After the foolish Childeric had been removed from the throne and made a cleric in a monastery, the Franks, with the counsel of Lord Pope Zachary and the counsel of the noble Romans, by God’s will, with one agreement and one purpose, raised Pippin the Pious, son of Charles Martel, as their king.

This Pippin the Pious was the father of lord Emperor Charlemagne. Thus, after [Note: [Col. 0025] Missing in 1.] Pippin the Pious, his son lord Charles reigned, whom the Romans later chose as their advocate for Saint Peter against the kings of the Lombards. Then they chose that same lord Charles as patrician of the Romans. Afterward they raised him as emperor and Augustus. By God’s generosity, lord Charles held in his power the whole land from Mount Gargano to the city of Córdoba in Spain.

Pippin the Pious, lord Charles’s father, after he had been raised to the kingship, reigned for seven years and died in the year 768 from the Incarnation of the Lord. In that same year, all the Franks, exulting with great joy, raised lord Charlemagne as their king, in the year 768 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

The years from the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Lord are reckoned as follows according to the Seventy Interpreters. From Adam to the Flood there are 2,242 years. From the Flood to Abraham, 942 years. From Abraham to Moses, 505 years. From Moses to Solomon, 489 years [Note: [Col. 0025] Thus in 1.]. From Solomon to the restoration of the Temple under Darius, king of the Persians, 542 years. From the restoration [Note: [Col. 0025] “To the restoration” in 1.] of the Temple to the coming of the Lord, according to the Septuagint [Note: [Col. 0025] The letters *ta u. q.* are missing in 1.], 548 years. From the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Lord, according to the Seventy Interpreters, there are 5,200 years.

According to the Hebrew truth they are reckoned as follows: From Adam to Noah was the first age, and it lasted 1,656 years. The second age, from Noah to Abraham, lasted 292 years. The third age, from Abraham to David, lasted 942 years. Taken together, the years of the three ages amount to 2,811.

The fourth age, from David to the captivity in Babylon, lasted 463 years. The fifth age, from the rebuilding of the Temple to the coming of the Lord, lasted 580 years. Together, from Adam to Christ the Lord, there are 3,952 years.

From the Lord’s birth to the death of Saint Martin there are 445 years. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of Clovis, king of the Franks, who was the first Christian among the Frankish kings, there are 112 years. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of Saint Eparchius, patron of Angoulême, there are 120 years.

Saint Eparchius was born in the time of Meroveus, pagan king of the Franks, who was the grandfather of Clovis, the first Christian king of the Franks, and in the time of Theodosius the Younger, the divine Augustus and emperor. He lived during the reigns of the emperors Theodosius, Marcian, Leo, Zeno, Anastasius, and Justinian, and during the reigns of the Frankish kings Meroveus, Childeric, and Clovis, as well as during the time of King Childebert of the Franks. He died in the time of Emperor Justinian and King Childebert of the Franks, in the eightieth year of his age. From the birth of Christ to the first year of Charles’s reign there are 768 years.

[Col. 0027A] 2. Therefore, in the year 768 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the very year in which King Pippin the Pious died, his two sons, lord Charles and Carloman, were raised to the kingship together on one day, namely 9 October, and so forth, as in the *Annals of Lorsch* from the year 768 onward.

(*Annals of Lorsch*, year 769.) … And from there [Note: [Col. 0027C] Angoulême.] he took … together with Launus, bishop of that city, who had been chaplain to lord King Pippin, his father, and whom King Pippin himself had made bishop of that city …

… He returned to Angoulême, where, at the request of Bishop Launus, he issued at the monastery of Saint Eparchius a charter concerning the lands that were held there without dispute, namely those along the river Touvre: Magnac, Vivonne, Vénac, Montérion, Visac, [Col. 0027B] Roullet; along the river Nizonne, the estate of Baudeau; Camilon, Chavagnac, Ulciacum, lesser Roullet, Tourriers, Sers, Tomolatum; along the river Dronne, Montville, Baziacum, Triacum, and Marlevam [Note: [Col. 0027] Thus in 2 and in Pithoeus; in 1, after erasures, a later hand wrote: “and Baziacum with its dependencies,” which Duchesne adopted.]. His chancellor Bartholomew wrote this charter, and the lord king himself confirmed it with his own hand and sealed it with his ring. At that time there was a community of canons in the monastery of Saint Eparchius. From there the glorious King Charles returned to Francia … [lacuna]

8. (*Annals of Lorsch*, year 787) … And the most devout King Charles returned and celebrated Easter at Rome with the lord apostolic. Behold, a dispute arose during the Easter festivities between the Roman and Gallic singers [Note: [Col. 0027C] Compare the Monk of Saint Gall, I, 10, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, II, 735, and the Capitulary issued at Theodonis Villa in 805, ch. 2, *Leges*, I, 131 (*Patrologia*, vols. CIV and XCVII).].

The Gauls said that they sang better and more beautifully than the Romans. The Romans said that they delivered the ecclesiastical melodies with the greatest skill, just as they had been taught by Saint Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0027C] Compare John’s *Life of Gregory*, II, 6, which continues at II, 7: “The Germans or Franks among the other peoples of Europe were notably able to learn and repeatedly relearn the sweetness of this modulation; but they were entirely unable to preserve it uncorrupted, both because of their fickleness—for they mixed some material of their own into the Gregorian chants—and because of their natural roughness. For Alpine bodies, resounding loudly with the thunder of their voices, do not properly reproduce the sweetness of the modulation they have received; the barbarian roughness of their thirsty throats, while striving by inflections and repetitions to produce a gentle melody, emits stiff sounds with a natural kind of din, as though carts were rumbling confusedly over steps, and thus, by irritating and disturbing the minds of their listeners—whom they ought to have soothed—makes them even more exasperated.”].

They said that the Gauls sang corruptly and mangled the melody by destroying it. This dispute came before lord King Charles. The Gauls, relying on the protection of lord King Charles, sharply reproached the Roman singers; the Romans, relying on the authority of their great learning, declared them fools, rustics, and ignorant men, like brute animals, and set Saint Gregory’s teaching above their rusticity.

When the quarrel between the two sides had ended, the most devout lord King Charles said to his singers: “Tell me openly which is purer and better: the living spring or its streams running far away?” They all replied with one voice that the spring, as the head and source, was purer, while its streams, the farther they withdrew from the spring, became increasingly turbid and corrupted by dirt and impurities.

Lord King Charles then said: “Return to the spring of Saint Gregory, because you have plainly corrupted the ecclesiastical melody.” Immediately lord King Charles asked Pope Adrian for singers who could correct the Franks in their chant. He gave him Theodore and Benedict, the most learned singers of the Roman church, who had been instructed by Saint Gregory; he also gave him Saint Gregory’s antiphonaries, which Gregory himself had notated in Roman notation.

When lord King Charles returned to Francia, he sent one singer to the city of Metz and another to the city of Soissons, ordering the schoolmasters of all the cities of Francia to hand over their antiphonaries to them for correction and to learn singing from them. Thus the antiphonaries of the Franks were corrected, for each person had corrupted them according to his own preference, either adding or removing material. All the singers of Francia learned Roman notation, which they now call Frankish notation, except that the Franks could not perfectly produce the tremulous, or *vinnolatae* [Note: [Col. 0028C] *Vinnolata* is a gentle, soft, and flexible sound; it is called *vinnolata* from *vinnus*, that is, a softly curled lock, Isidore, *Etymologies*, III, 19.], sliding, or cutting sounds in the chant, breaking the sounds in their barbarous natural voices in the throat rather than expressing them.

The principal school of singing remained in the city of Metz. And to the extent that Roman instruction surpasses the school of Metz in the art of song, to that same extent the Metz chant surpasses the other Gallic schools. Likewise, the Roman singers mentioned above instructed the Frankish singers in the art of organum.

[Col. 0028C] Lord King Charles also brought with him from Rome teachers of grammar and computation [Note: [Col. 0027] *Maistros* in 1.] to Francia, and ordered the study of letters to be spread everywhere. Before lord King Charles, there had been no study of the liberal arts in Gaul.

During those Easter days, envoys of Duke Tassilo came to Rome to lord King Charles … He returned gloriously to Francia, bringing with him Roman singers, highly skilled grammarians, and computists …

9. (Annals of Lorsch, year 788.) … Likewise, his son Theudo [Note: [Col. 0028C] Tassilo’s son.] was judged, and both were made monks in the monastery of Olto [Note: [Col. 0028C] That is, Fulda.], where Saint Boniface rests …

[Col. 0029A] … (Annals of Lorsch, year 808.) … the king of the Northumbrians, that is, from the island of Ireland [Note: [Col. 0029C] He writes similarly under the year 809: “But the envoys of the pope and the emperor, returning from the Irish—from a certain man of the king of Ireland.”] …

… (Annals of Lorsch, year 809.) … Count Aureolus, descended from the family of Felix Aureolus, count of Périgueux, arose …

… (Annals of Lorsch, year 814.) … Charles … was buried at Aachen in the basilica of the Mother of God, which he himself had built. His body was embalmed and placed seated on a golden throne in the vaulted part of the tomb [Note: [Col. 0029] “positum” corrected to “positus” in 1?], girded with a golden sword, holding a golden Gospel-book in his hands and on his knees, his shoulders reclining in a chair and his head honorably upright, fastened by a golden chain to the diadem. A piece of the Cross was placed in the diadem. And they filled his tomb with aromatics, spices, [Col. 0030A] balsam, musk [Note: [Col. 0029] “Musgo” in 1.], and treasures [Note: [Col. 0029] “th”; “many things in gold” in 2.]. His body was clothed in imperial garments, and his face was covered beneath the diadem with a cloth [Note: [Col. 0029] “A hair-shirt was placed against his flesh, which he always wore secretly, and over the imperial garments a golden pilgrim’s pouch was placed, which he used to carry to Rome” added in 2.]. A golden scepter and a golden shield, which Pope Leo had consecrated, were placed before him [Note: [Col. 0029] “posita sunt,” used deponently, in 2.], and [Note: [Col. 0029] “but [it was] closed and sealed” in 2.] his tomb was sealed [Note: [Col. 0029] “eis” in 1.]. No one can relate how great the mourning for him was throughout the whole earth; for even the pagans mourned him as though he were the father of the world [Note: [Col. 0029] “The greatest mourning, however, was among the Christians, especially throughout his entire kingdom. After he had been anointed with holy oil by the bishops, received the viaticum, and arranged all his affairs, commending his spirit to God, he died in peace in the year 814 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone lives and reigns, God, for ever and ever. Amen.” added in 2.]. He died in peace, anointed with holy oil and strengthened by the viaticum, in the eight hundred and fourteenth year from the incarnation of the Lord; and his most glorious son Louis reigned in his place, while our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK THREE [Note: [Col. 0029] The rubric is lacking in 1. The beginning of the book was omitted in 2. I have restored the division from 3.]

[Col. 0029]

[Col. 0029B] 1. Therefore, after the most Christian and glorious emperor Charles had died, it was announced to his son Louis in Aquitaine, etc., as in the Annals of Lorsch.

2. (Annals of Lorsch, year 816.) … After a council had been held—that is, in the tenth indiction, in the third year of his reign, in the year 816 from the incarnation of the Lord—he ordered a rule to be made for canons, excerpted from various writings of the Fathers, and decreed that it should be observed by the canons, so that, just as monks look to the book of the Rule of Saint Benedict, so the canons should read among themselves the book of the life of clerics. This book was compiled by the deacon Amalarius, at the emperor’s command, from various sayings of learned men. The emperor gave him access to the books in his palace, so that from them he might excerpt whatever seemed appropriate; and thus, together with the decrees of the bishops who were there, [Col. 0029C] the life of the clerics was strengthened. The aforementioned Amalarius wrote for the same emperor a book on the divine offices, their varieties, and the order of the psalms according to the ancient usage of the clerics …

3. (Annals of Lorsch, year 817.) … He held the customary synod at Aachen. There [Note: [Col. 0029C] See Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Laws I, 201. The Rule of the Canons [Col. 0030C] and the books of Amalarius are known to everyone.] he summoned the abbots of his kingdom and admonished them to observe the Rule of Benedict. He also brought all the abbeys back under his own authority, so that no count or bishop could disturb them. The abbots, after deciding certain chapters among themselves, read out the written text before the emperor, who personally confirmed it together with the bishops who were present …

[Col. 0030B] 4. (Annals of Lorsch, year 818.) … A few days after Easter, the conspirators were sentenced, together with King Bernard, to undergo capital punishment [Note: [Col. 0029] “The conspirator” in 1.]. When King Bernard was attacked in order that he might be deprived of his sight, he defended himself with drawn sword, killed five of the bravest Franks, and died himself, pierced by wounds. The others were blinded …

5. (Annals of Lorsch, year 819.) … The exceedingly learned monk Rabanus Magnentius, Alcuin’s teacher, presented the emperor himself with a very remarkable book on the theology of the holy Cross. Bede taught Simplicius, and Simplicius taught Rabanus, who had been received from overseas by the lord emperor Charles and made a bishop in Francia. He taught Alcuin, Alcuin instructed Smaragdus, Smaragdus taught Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, and Theodulf taught Helias the Irishman, bishop of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 0029] “Angouleme,” feminine form, in 1.]. Helias, in turn, taught Heiric; Heiric left Remigius and the monk Ucbald the Bald as heirs of philosophy.

6–10.

11. (Annals of Lorsch, year 826.) … Eroldus … was baptized and became the emperor’s godson from the font … The emperor gave him, as his godfather’s gift, one county …

12–15.

16. [Note: [Col. 0029] I have instituted the division of the chapters, partly following 3b and 3c.] In the following year [Note: [Col. 0030C] “In the year of the settlement,” from the Annals of Aquitaine, MGH II, p. 252.] (830), the Normans burned the island of Herio in June, and it was abandoned as a general monastic settlement; there the lord emperor Charles had built the monastery of Saint Philibert [Col. 0031A] [Note: [Col. 0031] At that time Louis held a general assembly in the palace of Jogentiacum [ [Col. 0031B] d’Herbauge.] in the Limousin, and in October, with great solemnity, ordered the great royal basilica of the Savior to be dedicated. The body of Saint Martial, raised in the year 830 from the incarnation of the Lord, was placed in the same month behind the altar of the Savior, in the crypt of the great window [ [Col. 0031] “Written” in c.], in the presence of the emperor himself. Then the winter was extremely severe. The emperor returned to Francia, but after a short time he was betrayed and captured by three kings, his sons—Lothar, Louis, and Pippin—and by Lothar’s order was sent to prison [ [Col. 0031] “carcem” in c.] at Saint-Medard, then to Saint-Denis. He was stripped of his imperial garments and dressed in black. While Lothar remained for a long time at Vienne, the assembled Franks drove Louis out of custody near the palace of Saint-Denis and again raised him, against his will, to the kingship. From the day on which the body of Saint Martial was placed, as stated above, in the basilica of the Savior, until the day on which the emperor was restored to his kingdom in mid-Lent, after the harshest winter, floods and excessive rains increased without interruption. From that day fair weather was restored to Francia [ [Col. 0031] “ice” in c.; “ce post detetis” (uncertain).] [ [Col. 0031B] Saint-Jean-d’Angély.]; but in Aquitaine the rains did not cease until the body of Saint Martial was again placed in its former tomb. added in 2.] Then Count Odo of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0031B] He favored Louis’s party, and his brother was William. added in 2.] engaged Count Lambert of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0031] He favored Lothar. added in 2.] in battle and was killed [Note: [Col. 0031] “They were killed together with many princes of Neustria. Lothar, returning from Vienne, wished to fight his father near the fortress of Blois; but, inferior in strength, he came to him as a suppliant, won pardon, and was restored to his former honor. Likewise Louis and Pippin received pardon from their father and were restored to their usual dignity” added in 2.]. Five years later, Count Rainold of Arbatil [Note: [Col. 0031B] Brantôme.] fought the Normans on the island of Herio in September and was put to flight (835). In the following year (836), the body of Saint Philibert was dug up from the island of Herio on 7 June and carried by the monks to Burgundy. Two years later (838), King Pippin of Aquitaine, the emperor’s son, died and was buried at Poitiers near Saint Radegund. At his father’s command he had built the monastery of Saint John the Baptist at Angeriacum [Note: [Col. 0031B] An eclipse … 840, from the Annals of Aquitaine.], the monastery of Saint Cyprian at Poitiers, [Col. 0031B] and the monastery of Brantôme [Note: [Col. 0031B] Joac.; compare the Life of Louis, chapter 47.]. He also transferred the canonical habit into the monastic habit at the monastery of Saint Eparchius at Angoulême, and appointed Abbot Martin over these monasteries. Then [Note: [Col. 0031] “Then the mournful death of Louis was represented in the air. For just as [“sio” in c.] the stars at the beginning of his reign announced joy, so, when [“e” corrected in c.] his death was approaching, they announced a sad portent. While he was first beginning to reign in Aquitaine, his father Charles [“viventes” corrected to “vivente” in c.] still living, a sign of the Cross appeared around the full moon, shining all around, on Thursday, at the first light of dawn, on the day before the Nones of June. In the same year a wondrous crown appeared around the sun on Sunday, at the fourth hour, 3 September. This signified that the Christian religion would be extended and the worship of Christ adorned through that emperor. In the final year of his reign an unusual eclipse of the sun occurred on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, and stars were seen as though it were night for a long time. This signified [“signuit” in c.] that the great lamp of Christianity—that is, the empire itself—would be extinguished and that, after his death, it would be enveloped in the darkness of tribulations. Having heard of the death of his son Pippin, the same emperor decided that Pippin’s young son Pippin should be brought up with him in Francia [ [Col. 0032B] That is, on 5 May, when the sun suffered an eclipse. In the Life of Louis I it is said to have occurred on the third day of the Greater Litanies; hence it appears that the author of the Life meant by this not Saint Mark’s Day (25 April), but the days of Rogation, that is, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday—the vigil—before the Lord’s Ascension.”]. But Count Emeno of Poitiers, against the emperor’s will, wished to raise Pippin’s son as king of Aquitaine. For this reason the emperor, moved to anger, came to Poitiers and expelled Emeno and his brother Bernard from there. He appointed as count at Poitiers Rannulf, son of Count Girard of Auvergne and nephew of William, Girard’s brother; he made Turpio count at Angoulême and placed Raterius as count over Limoges. Emeno went to his brother Turpio, while Bernard went to Count Rainald of Arbatil. The emperor also made his son Charles the Bald rule [“ignare” in c.] in Aquitaine, and took the little Pippin with him to Francia to be reared. The same emperor ordered the coinage of Angoulême and Saintes to be struck in his name. He also appointed Siguinus over Bordeaux and Landric over Saintes. In the same year in which the aforesaid eclipse of the sun occurred, the emperor fell ill at the city of Mainz and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July; he left the imperial crown and a golden sword to Lothar [ [Col. 0032B] Compare the Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême, chapter 13.], and was buried at Metz near Saint Arnulf, in the year 840 from the incarnation of the Lord.”].] there was an eclipse [Note: [Col. 0031B] See the end of the Life of Louis, chapter 51.] of the sun, and the lord emperor Louis died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 840 from the incarnation of the Lord; he was buried at Metz near Saint Arnulf. His three sons remained: Lothar the emperor [Note: [Col. 0031] “Of Italy” added in 2.], Louis, king of Germany, and Charles the Bald, king of Francia and Burgundy. Since they were quarreling among themselves over the kingdom of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0031] “And Francia” added in 2.], they engaged in battle at Fontenay [Note: [Col. 0031] “On the field of Fontenay” in 2.], which is in Burgundy. On one side Lothar came with the army of Italy; on the other, Charles and Louis with [Note: [Col. 0031] “With Germans and” added in 2.] Franks [Col. 0032B] and Aquitanians [Note: [Col. 0031] “This battle also took place in the second year after the death of their father, that is, in the year 841 from the incarnation of the Lord. After an immeasurable slaughter had been carried out, Lothar emerged victorious.” But 2.]. At first Lothar was victorious, [Col. 0033A] but suddenly Duke Warinus, arriving with the men of Toulouse and Provence, renewed the battle [Note: [Col. 0033] “He attacked Lothar, the battle grew more severe, and Lothar was put to flight and defeated. Charles and Louis divided the kingdom between themselves in equal balance. In the aforementioned battle Raterius and Girardus, both of Auvergne by birth, were killed; William became count, and Raymond became count of the Limousin.”], and Lothar was put to flight [Note: [Col. 0033B] Life of Louis, chapter 63.] [year 841].

17. In the second year after the death of the lord Louis, Charles and Louis divided the kingdom between themselves. Two years later (843), the empress [Note: [Col. 0033] That is, the empress.] [Note: [Col. 0033B] What follows—from “Deas” through “Bordeaux”—has been taken almost entirely from the Annals of Aquitaine.] came to Tours, the mother of Charles the Bald, and died; she was buried at Saint Martin. In that same year Count Rainold of Arbatil, having engaged Count Lambert of Nantes, was killed [Note: [Col. 0033] Brittany had withdrawn from the sons of Louis; therefore the Franks and Aquitanians began to fight with the Bretons. added in 2.]. In that year Nantes was captured by the Wefaldingi, and Charles first devastated Brittany with fire and sword. In the following year (844), Count Bernard of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0033] Bernard, Emeno’s brother. added in 2.] and Arveus [Note: [Col. 0033] “Arucus” in 1; manuscript of Christ Church, 692.] son of Rainold, having engaged Count Lambert [Note: [Col. 0033] “Of Nantes” added in 2.], were killed. In another year (845), Count Siguinus of Bordeaux and Saintes was captured and killed by the Normans, and Saintes was burned by the Normans, after its excellent treasures had been carried away. Charles again went into Brittany and fought Duke Nomenoius [Note: [Col. 0033] Thus in the text.], and was victorious, Nomenoius having been put to flight [Note: [Col. 0033] “In the following year the Northmen burned the island of Herio in June” added in 2.]. At this time the Normans spread throughout Aquitaine, because its dukes had fallen into wars among themselves and there was no one to resist them. The island of Herio and the monastery of Deas, Bordeaux, Saintes, Angoulême, Limoges, Paris, Tours, Beauvais, Noviomagus, Orléans, Poitiers, and countless monasteries and fortresses were burned or destroyed by them [Note: [Col. 0033] “Lucionnus was burned by them in May, and the monastery of Saint Florentius in June; afterward the city of Nantes and the monastery of Deas were burned by them.” 2.].

18. In the eighth year after the death of the emperor Louis (848) [Note: [Col. 0033] “And in the year 848 from the incarnation. Ainardus, provost of the basilica of Saint Martial, together with all the other canons, inspired by God, laid aside secular arms and changed themselves from the canonical habit into the monastic habit in the same monastery. At that time Charles the Bald held his general assembly at Limoges during Lent, together with the bishops of Aquitaine and its leading men. While Charles the Bald was seated on the royal throne, Ainardus and all the canons of Saint Martial suddenly prostrated themselves at his feet, asking him to give them permission to become monks in the same place. The king, giving thanks to God, fulfilled their request with great joy and inclined all the bishops and nobles to their will. But Bishop Stodilus of Limoges took this very badly [ [Col. 0033] “To bear” in c.] and alone remained inflexible; at length, compelled by the king, he consented, overcome by gifts. The canons did not wish [ [Col. 0033] “Wished” in c.] to have an abbot from among themselves at that time, but appointed over themselves Odo, abbot of Saint Savin [ [Col. 0033] “Of the abbot” in c.]. Josfredus, however …” 2.], Charles the Bald held a general assembly at Limoges [Note: [Col. 0033] “General” in 1.] during Lent. Before him, Ainardus, provost of the monastery of Saint Martial, laid aside his canonical habit and became a monk; [Col. 0034A] likewise all the canons of Saint Martial voluntarily changed themselves into the monastic habit, and from then on the place was governed by monks. But Josfredus the treasurer, unwilling to abandon the world, being under the protection of Bishop Stodilus [Note: [Col. 0033] “Under escort” in 2.], removed the monastery of Saint Junianus [Note: [Col. 0033B] Saint-Julien-sur-la-Vienne.] and the church of Cairo [Note: [Col. 0033] “Cairoensam” corrected to “Cairoensem” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0033B] De Queroir.] from the legal authority of Saint Martial by plunder [Note: [Col. 0033] “By wickedness and evil intent, from its right and lordship” in 2.] and caused them to withdraw on this account. Then the monks of Saint Martin at Tours, without anyone compelling them, cast off their monastic garb before the body of that same saint and put on canonical garb [Note: [Col. 0033] “This was confirmed by oaths over the body of blessed Martin.
