After they had refreshed themselves with meat, they were immediately seized by pestilence; when morning came, all were found dead in their beds, from the greatest to the least, and from …” in 2.]. But pestilence soon broke out among them [Note: [Col. 0033] “Foot” in 1.], so that they all died in a single night, and the place was thereafter occupied by the remaining canons. Charles [Note: [Col. 0033B] “Charles … Count Gauzbertus … was killed,” from the Annals of Aquitaine, from which 2 also drew notes 10*, 12*, and 13*.] devastated Brittany with fire and sword for the third time (850). When he had returned to Aquitaine, Duke Nomenoius captured and destroyed the cities of Rennes and Nantes and then returned to Brittany [Note: [Col. 0033] “Their walls and gates” in 2.]. In the following year (851), by God’s command, he died, struck by an angel. Charles entered Brittany for the fourth time and fought Erispoius, son of Nomenoius [Note: [Col. 0033] “On the eleventh day before the Kalends of September” added in 2.]; he was victorious, but lost a large part of his army together with Duke Vivianus [Note: [Col. 0033] “After he had returned” in 2.]. In the following year (852), Count Lambert of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0033] “Nannetansium” in 1.] was killed in battle by Count Gauzbertus of Maine [Note: [Col. 0033] “On the Kalends of May” added in 2, which continues: “In the same year, in September, Charles …”]. Charles also devastated Brittany for the fifth time and, having captured his nephew Pippin [Note: [Col. 0033] “Whom the Bretons had seized by treachery” added in 2.], subjected Brittany to himself, after Erispoius had been killed [Note: [Col. 0034B] This too was taken from the Annals of Aquitaine under the year 846.]. Count Rannulf of Poitiers and his kinsman Count Raino of Arbatil were put to flight while fighting the Normans at the estate of Brillac, and Count Gauzbertus of Maine was surrounded by an ambush of the men of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0033] “Nannetansium” in 1.] and killed.

[Col. 0035A] 19. Fifteen years after the battle of Fontenay, Charles was anointed king at Limoges [Note: [Col. 0035] “While his brother Lothar was emperor, Louis was made king over Francia, Aquitaine, and Burgundy in the basilica of Saint Peter, which is called the royal basilica, where the body of Saint Martial was buried [ [Col. 0035] “Entombed” in c.]; and from there …”], in the basilica of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0035C] See the Annals of Limoges, MGH II, p. 251. It was not Charles the Bald but his son; hence what the other manuscript adds appears to be false. See the Annals of Prudentius under the year 855.], and from there entered Francia (855). A few days later [Note: [Col. 0035] “Four years later” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0035C] It is universally agreed that this happened in that same year, not four years later as 2 reports.] the emperor Lothar [Note: [Col. 0035] That is, while ill, he became a monk at the monastery of Prüm because he had driven his father from the empire and held him imprisoned. 2.] became a monk because he had thrown his father into prison. After he died, a dispute over his soul appeared [Note: [Col. 0035] “Among the brothers, between evil and good angels. The holy angels said: ‘God did not send us to the emperor but to the monk; you take the emperor, and we shall take the monk with us.’ The holy angels [“Angelis” in c.] carried the soul away with them; the demons took the body and began violently to drag it from the house in full view of everyone, but they were driven away and vanished through the brothers’ prayers.” 2.] between wicked and holy angels; but the demons were frustrated. A short time later his brother, King Louis, died, and Charles the Bald was raised to the imperial dignity (876). At that time the Normans were afflicting Aquitaine most grievously [Note: [Col. 0035] “Afflicting” in 1.], and Helias the Irishman, bishop of Angoulême, died [Note: [Col. 0035C] See the Annals of Angoulême, Labbé I, p. 324.]. The monastery of blessed Eparchius was also laid waste by the attacking pagans [Note: [Col. 0035] “By the Northmen” in 2.], so that no monk lived there, and for this reason the canonical habit returned there, although it had recently departed. Turpio, having gone with King Charles to Francia and returned from there, shortly afterward engaged the Normans, killed their king, named Maurus, and was himself killed by him. His brother Emeno [Note: [Col. 0035] Emeno, formerly count of Poitiers, then count of Angoulême. 2.] became count of Angoulême; two years later [Note: [Col. 0035] “Biannium” in 1.] he fought Count Landric of Saintes, killed Landric, was carried wounded into the fortress of Rancogne [Note: [Col. 0035C] Rancogne in the manuscript of Christ Church, 692. It may be Rancogne or Rancon; compare Besly, History of the Counts of Poitiers, pp. 32, 69, and Valesius, Notes on Gaul, p. 465.], and died on the eighth day. He was buried beside the basilica of blessed Eparchius and left behind a young son named Ademar. When Charles heard this, he sent his kinsman Vulgrinus [Note: [Col. 0035] “Vulgrinum” in 1.], brother of Abbot Aldoinus, from the monastery of Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 0035] “He sent him to Aquitaine” in 2.] and appointed him over Angoulême and Périgueux; he appointed Oliba to the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0035] “To the bishopric” in 1.] [Col. 0035C] of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 0035] This Vulgrinus was often sent by Carloman and finally by his brother, the emperor Charlemagne, to the cities of Aquitaine together with royal officials to administer justice. He was already an old man when Charles the Bald made him count of the aforementioned cities. Two sons came with him from Francia, Aldoinus [ [Col. 0035] “Alduinum” in c.] and William. He also possessed the city of Agen, which he took and vindicated because of the sister of William of Toulouse, whom he had married. He held authority in these three cities for seventeen years. He fought many battles … and Odolricus. When this same Vulgrinus died … he ended his life. Vulgrinus left to his sons … and Agen. Meanwhile, Charles the Bald … or the Younger. Then the Franks conspired … 2.]. In those times Bishop Fredebertus [Col. 0036A] of Francia [Note: [Col. 0035C] Perhaps of Basel, who occurs under the year 859; Bouquet VII, p. 582. Ochs, History of Basel, p. 154.] came to Saint Eparchius and built there a church in honor of the Savior. But he could not raise the body of the blessed man, which he wished to transfer to that church. On the very day of the consecration, after the sacrifice had been completed, he peacefully fell asleep in the Lord before the altar of the Savior and was buried there before the altar by Bishop Oliba.

20. Meanwhile, when Charles the Bald departed from this world (877), his son Louis the Stammerer reigned in his place in Francia; and thereafter no one from the kings of Francia received the empire. Then the Bavarians and Alamanni, from their own people, created a king for themselves, Otto; the Lombards likewise created from their people a king, Adalbert, and afterward Harduin; and the Romans raised one of their senators, Alberic, to the kingship. His brother Octavian was ordained pope. When King Louis died, his son Charles, surnamed the Foolish or the Younger [Note: [Col. 0036C] Charles the Simple. It will escape no one that all these matters are greatly confused.], reigned in his place. At that time Vulgrinus died on the fifth day before the Nones of May (885 or 886) and was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius [Note: [Col. 0036C] The Annals of Limoges in the royal manuscript Paris 3784, which append to the Aquitanian Chronicle information drawn from the Annals of Limoges and Saint-Columba, with very little else of importance, record Vulgrinus’s death as count of Périgueux and Angoulême under the year 885 and add: “He died on the second [or third?] day before the Nones of May; he was buried at Saint Eparchius outside the city.”]. In the fifth year after him, Bishop Oliba ended his days; Anatolus was ordained bishop in his place and died in the third year of his episcopate (892) [Note: [Col. 0036C] Compare the Annals of Angoulême under the years 892 and 895.]. Vulgrinus had frequently suffered through many battles with the Normans, and for this reason he had built the fortress of Martiliacum [Note: [Col. 0036C] Commonly Marcillac, situated between the Charente and the stream that flows into it. Mastacium, now Matas, is not far from Martiliacum. See Adrien Valesius, Notes on Gaul. Bouquet.], and Mastacium, so that they might serve as defenses against the pagans. He had sent to Martiliacum Rotbertus, learned in law, and with him Rannulfus [Note: [Col. 0035] “Who had come with him” added in 2.], whom he made viscount. This Rannulfus had three sons, Lambert, Arnold, and Odolricus. [Col. 0036C] The same Vulgrinus left to his sons: to Aldoinus, Angoulême; to William, Périgueux and Agen, which he had taken [“assumans” in 1.] and vindicated because of the sister of William of Toulouse, whom he had married. Then the Franks conspired against Charles the Younger [Note: [Col. 0037] “The Foolish” in 2.], expelled him from the kingdom, and raised Odo, duke of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0037C] It is certain that Odo never held Aquitaine; what 2 adds is even further from the truth.], to the kingship [Note: [Col. 0037] “This Odo was the son of Raymond, count of Limoges, and was first made king in Aquitaine at Limoges. He ordered that the coinage of that city be struck in his name, whereas previously it had been inscribed with Charles’s name. In that city he appointed as his representative Fulcherius, a skilled woodworker, and organized the Limousin through viscounts. Likewise [he organized] Berry, and in the second year he was raised as king in Francia.” added in 2.]. At that time (888), King Rudolf of Burgundy arrived in the Limousin with a very powerful army [Note: [Col. 0037] “At Odo’s request; for he himself was defending Francia” in 2.]. Innumerable Norman forces gathered against him, and in the battle fought at a place called Ad-Destricios the pagans were destroyed almost to the last man. Those who escaped from there fled and no longer dared to hope that they could come into Aquitaine. Rudolf, giving thanks to God, for whose love he had laid down his life, returned with great triumph [Note: [Col. 0037] 2 continues: “And other bands of Northmen, devastating upper Francia, were first defeated together with Duke Bareto, then with King Astencus [ [Col. 0038C] Hasting]; after ravaging the coastal regions and laying waste the land adjoining Francia, they were defeated by the neighboring dukes of Francia. Then the city of Rouen and the cities nearby, found empty, were claimed for settlement by their dukes. These raised over themselves a king from their own people named Rollo, who established his seat at Rouen. Having become a Christian through the priests of Francia, when death was approaching and he had fallen into madness, he had one hundred Christian captives beheaded [“decollocari” in c.] before him in honor of the idols he had worshiped; finally he distributed one hundred pounds of gold among the churches of the Christians in honor of the true God, in whose name he had received baptism. Rannulf of Poitiers and Ademar, son of Emeno, were also enemies over the city of Poitiers; Ademar was striving to claim it for himself on behalf of his father Emeno. Since this Rannulf had no offspring from his lawful wife, he took a son named Eblus from a concubine. He had the greatest friendship with his kinsman William, count of Auvergne, and made a pact with Rollo, prince of Rouen, out of fear of Ademar. For this reason he was honored by King Odo more from fear than from love. And while he was constantly attending the royal court …”]. The Normans then returned and, finding the land empty, established their seat at Rouen with their prince Rollo [Note: [Col. 0037C] Also called Rollo.]. Having become a Christian, he had many captives beheaded before him in honor of the gods whom he had worshiped. He also distributed an immeasurable weight of gold among the churches of the Christians in honor of the true God, in whose name he had received baptism.

21. Count Rannulf of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0037C] Duke of most of Aquitaine. Annals of Saint-Vaast, year 889. He was the son of Bernard, margrave of Gothia, who was stripped of his honors in 878. Bouquet.] also had a son named Eblus. This Rannulf was a kinsman of the very noble William, count of Auvergne. [Col. 0037C] He had the closest friendship with him and with Rollo, prince [Col. 0038A] of the Normans. Since he was a very brave warrior, he was greatly honored by King Odo (892). While he was constantly attending the royal court, he was killed by poison [Note: [Col. 0037] “Killed” in 1 and 2.]. As he lay dying, he entrusted his young son Eblus to Saint Gerald, who was then present there, to be protected [Note: [Col. 0037] The following is added, partly repeating what was read above: “Vulgrinus, having claimed Agen because of the sister of William of Toulouse, by whom he had the two aforementioned sons, ruled Angoulême and Périgueux with great ability, Agen for twenty-six years, Angoulême and Périgueux for fifteen years, and died in the sixteenth year after the death of Lothar [ [Col. 0038C] These matters are very confused. Vulgrinus died in 885 or 886 (the Annals of Aquitaine and the Annals of Angoulême), having been promoted to the county in 866. Lothar died in 855, although the Annals of Aquitaine also wrongly place his death in 870.”].] Ademar, son of Emeno, took Santia [Note: [Col. 0037] “He joined Santia, daughter of William, son of Vulgrinus, to himself in marriage [‘soppulavit’ in c.],” in 2.] in marriage and, being very close to Aldoinus [Note: [Col. 0037] “To Aldoinus, count of Angoulême, and William, count of Périgueux,” in the manuscript of Christ Church, 692, and the Chronicle of Saint-Maixent.] and William, seemed to enjoy their honor as though he were their brother. When summoned to the palace by King Odo [Note: [Col. 0037] “He was received in the palace by the great Odo with great honor, after Rannulf’s death,” in 2.], he was advanced as count of Poitiers. Returning from the palace, Saint Gerald secretly took Rannulf’s son from Poitiers and entrusted him to William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne, to be brought up, since he was his kinsman. At that time William, having no offspring, newly established the monastery of Cluny on his own estate, which is [Col. 0038B] in Burgundy (910). Although he wished to join his sister in marriage to Saint Gerald, he was entirely unable to do so. Saint Gerald, who always led a celibate life, was often urged to marry for the sake of children and replied: “It is better,” he said, “to die without children than to leave bad heirs.” Ademar, count of Poitiers, was also a lover of the Church. Since he too had no children, he and his wife [Note: [Col. 0037] “bis duabus lineis scriptum” in 1.] Santia, looking toward the future world, granted certain properties from their own right to the churches [Col. 0038C] of Christ: to Saint Charroux [Note: [Col. 0038C] Charroux in the diocese of Poitiers.] Voerta; to Saint Martial, Moltonnum; to Saint John [Note: [Col. 0039B] Of Angeriacum; see above, note 25.] Neiriacum; to Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 0039B] Of Poitiers.] Corcolum; and to Saint Eparchius, Godorvilla. At that time Ebo of Berry began to build the monastery of Déols [Note: [Col. 0039B] Déols, or Bourg-Dieu, in the diocese of Berry; see the foundation charter in Gallia Christiana II, 43.] in honor of the Mother of God (917). His son Rudolf later completed it, gathering there a large community of monks who lived according to the rule.

### 22

In those days Hoto, king of the Bavarians, subjected the kingdom of the Lombards to himself [Note: “after the deaths of kings Adalbert and Arduino” [Editorial note: “Note the interpolator’s errors!”] added in 2]. Likewise, after Alberic, king of the Romans, had died [Note: “king of the Romans” [Editorial note: “Note the interpolator’s errors!”] added in 2], with the consent of Pope Octavian he was advanced as emperor of the Romans (962) [Note: “He attacked Rome, and the city was closed against him [or: ‘the cause was closed to him’], and a great battle took place between the Bavarians and the Romans. Otto entered the city as victor and was crowned by Pope Octavian” added in 2].

After his death (973), his son Hoto likewise ruled as emperor. When Odo, king of the Franks, died, his son Arnulf ruled in his place for a short time and then died. Charles the Younger again assumed the kingdom (898), and Bishop Arbert anointed him [Note: “Arbert, the bishop whom Ademar thrusts upon us, is fictitious and unknown to the other writers. Bouquet. What he says about Arnulf is also false.”] [Editorial addition in 2: “by the aforesaid King Charles”]. Against him the nobles of the Franks conspired a second time, expelled him from the kingdom, and appointed Duke Robert king in his place [Note: “unwillingly” added in 2].

[Note: “For they assembled in the customary manner in a field to deliberate concerning the public welfare of the kingdom. By unanimous decision, because that king was cowardly in spirit, they rejected him by throwing straw from their hands, so that he would no longer be their lord, and left him alone in the middle of the field, separating themselves from him. When they had come together among themselves, Count Hugh, the king’s friend, arrived, unaware of the reason. Once he had learned it, he said to the Franks: ‘O most valiant Franks, you have not taken good counsel, for you have dishonorably abandoned your lord. A large part of Francia is with him, and, if we abandon him in this way, evil must come upon us. But I shall attack him and stab him with a weapon. It is better that he be killed than that the messenger punish us.’ Spurring his horse, as though he intended to kill him, as soon as he reached him he gave him this counsel, saying: ‘I shall be your messenger to these Franks on your behalf, so that for one year only they may still remain under your rule; and if during that period they do not see you improve, let them depart from you with your disgrace.’ On his return he confirmed this agreement with the Franks, and they again returned to the king. During that year the king associated friends with himself, with whom after the year he could act more confidently, while the former supporters remained in their opinion. After Robert had been raised to the kingship, Charles reached Limoges with a strong band of friends, kept vigil through the night near the window of Saint Martial in prayer, drew away with him as many of the strongest warriors of Aquitaine as he could, and went through Burgundy to Emperor Otto to seek aid” added in 2.]

Thus the Franks were divided among themselves, but the greater part favored Robert. Finally, with aid summoned from Emperor Hoto, Charles returned to Francia with a large army, partly from the Germanic people and partly from Aquitaine and Francia [Note: “partly from the Germanic people, partly from Aquitaine and Francia” [“in Francia” in c.] added in 2], and Robert joined battle with him. Fulbert the count was Charles’s standard-bearer; Robert himself, however, carried his own standard, with his beard, full of gray hair, thrown out beyond his coat of mail so that he might be recognized. King Charles, threatening Fulbert, said: “Beware, Fulbert.” From this the proverb arose: “Beware, Fulbert” [Editorial variant: “the same”]. Fulbert stabbed King Robert, cleaving him through the middle of the brain, and Robert’s army was defeated.

When the war was over, Hugh, Robert’s son, surnamed Capet, arrived with a thousand horsemen and put Charles and his weary army to flight. Afterwards he came humbly to Charles and submitted to the king’s will [Editorial variant: “to the king”]. For Charles recovered the kingdom and entrusted the duchy to Hugh Capet, just as his father Robert had customarily governed it.

From the spoils Charles had taken, he sent certain things to Saint Martial, as he had vowed: namely, from the chapel of King Robert, a Gospel book of gold and silver; a precious dalmatic of crimson cloth; a silver-plated faldstool; a complete and precious priestly vestment; two books of sacred history; a precious book on computation [“computus”]; and one standard of cloth woven with gold. When King Charles himself departed this life, his son Louis ruled vigorously in his place [added in 2].

King Charles, returning from Bavaria and partly from Francia, engaged Robert in battle and killed him; recovering the kingdom (923), he entrusted the duchy to Robert’s son Hugh to govern. When Charles departed this life, Louis ruled in his place.

At that time (929), Emperor Nicephorus, while raising the young Basil and Constantine at Constantinople, invaded the kingdom of the Saracens. He captured Antioch and other extremely strong cities, restoring them to the Greek Christians [Note: “capturing them by force, from [the beginning of this note] through Tripoli” added in 2]. His empress, Basil’s mother [Note: “empress,” corrected from “emperor” in 1], fearing that he might exercise tyranny over her sons, had him deceitfully summoned while he was besieging Tripoli [Note: “For she had sent him a letter saying that barbarians had besieged Constantinople, which was entirely false” added in 2]. While he was kneeling in the palace basilica at Constantinople on Holy Saturday of Easter and pouring out prayers to God, she ordered him killed with a sword [Note: “She ordered him stabbed through by four of his servants. To all the Greek nobles she pretended that he had died suddenly of an illness” added in 2]. This deed remained concealed for a long time, until suspicious Greek satraps, exhuming his monument [Note: “carrying” in 1], found his body pierced with swords [Note: “They found the battered corpse” added in 2] (969).

### 23

Then Ademar, count of Poitiers [Note: “Ademar—buried, according to the Annals of Aquitaine, in 930”], died (930) and was buried at Poitiers beside the basilica of Saint Hilary on the fourth day before the Nones of April. William, duke of Auvergne, also died (919) [Note: See the Annals of Masiac, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, III, p. 169], and his son by Rannulf, Eblus [Note: “Eblus Manzer” [that is, “the illegitimate”] added in 2], was advanced as count jointly of Auvergne and Poitiers [Note: “by the aforesaid King Charles” added in 2].

Having taken Adela, daughter of Rollo of Rouen, in marriage [Note: William of Jumièges calls her Gerloc; but compare the charters of King Lothair in Besly, *History of the Counts of Poitiers*, pp. 252, 259], he begot by her William Caput-stupae.

After Vulgrin’s death, his son Alduin lived for thirty years. He began restoring the walls of the city of Angoulême. At that time (916), while Gunbald was exercising the episcopate [Note: “Oliba was still holding the pontificate” added in 2], the Normans, renewing their frequent incursions [Note: “incursions,” corrected from “inroads” in 1], made raids throughout the territory of the Poitevins [Note: “through Aquitaine” added in 2].

As a result, the monks of Saint Carrofo, while Vulgrin the count was still alive [added in 2], carried a precious piece of the wood of the Cross to Angoulême for safekeeping, together with various church ornaments. When the Norman attacks ceased, Alduin tried to retain the aforesaid holy wood in his city for all his days, unwilling to return what had been entrusted to him.

For this reason [Note: “Having summoned architects from Francia [‘builders’ in c.], he ordered a church to be built in honor of the Savior” added in 2], he ordered the Church of the Savior outside the walls, at the head of the basilica of Saint Eparchius, to be adorned, so that the holy wood might be placed there [Note: “Added in 2, repeating matter printed above in chapter 19: he also transferred there the body of Saint Eparchius; having summoned from Francia his kinsman Bishop Fredebert, he had that church dedicated in honor of the Savior. But he could not raise the body of the blessed man, which he wished to transfer into that church. On the very day of the consecration, after the solemn sacrifice had been performed and Mass had ended, Bishop Fredebert peacefully fell asleep in the Lord before the altar of the Savior, and Bishop Oliba buried him there before the altar. Oliba himself also died shortly afterwards, as has already been said. Count Alduin, moreover, was afflicted for many years by bodily illness.”].

For seven years he himself was afflicted with bodily illness. Among his people such a most violent famine raged that—a thing previously unheard of—one commoner sought out another to devour him; and many, killing others with the sword, fed on human flesh like wolves.

Driven by these necessities, Alduin, one year before his death, returned the precious wood to Carrofo through his son William, surnamed Iron-Cutter, together with a golden reliquary, which he himself had ordered to be constructed with gems. In it he bestowed the estate of Lubeliacum. Immediately the plague ceased; and a year later he himself died, six days before the Kalends of April [Note: “seven days before the Kalends” in 2], and was buried beside his father.

Two years after his death (918), Lambert, viscount of Martillac, and his brother Arnald were killed by Bernard in revenge for his sister Santia, whom they had attempted to kill [Note: “See above, chapter 20”].

William Iron-Cutter restored their honor to their brother Odolric, who was younger by birth, and made him his viscount, just as Rannulf had been Vulgrin’s. Finally, when his father William, who was Alduin’s brother by Vulgrin, had died, this Bernard became count of Périgord. William Iron-Cutter obtained the principality of Angoulême, and he and his kinsman Bernard held their entire honor jointly.

Nevertheless, the aforesaid Adhemar, who had Santia, Bernard’s sister, as his wife, survived Alduin by ten years [Note: More correctly, fourteen; for he died in 930]. When Santia ended her life, she was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius on the second day before the Nones of April.

### 24

At that time (940), Bishop Gunbald died and was succeeded by Fulcald. Then William Iron-Cutter and his kinsman Bernard, having gathered an assembly of nobles [Note: “assembly,” corrected from “assembled” in 1], again restored the monastic habit in the basilica of Saint Eparchius and appointed Mainard abbot of the monastery.

He built an elegant oratory at the front of the basilica of Saint Eparchius in the name of the holy Resurrection [Note: “and deposited there many precious relics, which he had brought from Jerusalem” added in 2; compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*, chapter 19].

Then Lord William [Note: “Iron-Cutter” added in 2], by his testament, granted to the same place of Saint Eparchius the following gift: the church of Saint Hilary situated in Périgord, in the vicariate of Pillac [Note: “and many other churches”; the manuscripts end in this way in 3. “The History of the Franks ends here” in 3c]; the church of Saint Eugenia situated in Saintonge, in the vicariate of Pédriac; the estate of Fradorevilla; and the estates of Dairaco, Alviniaco, and Romanorevilla with the church itself; and one mansus at Godorvilla.

He ordered that this testament be confirmed, and the following men confirmed it with their own hands; their names are: Bernard, count; Arnald, son of Bernard; Odolric, viscount; Adhemar, viscount; Arnald, son of William; and Adhemar, son of William [Note: “of that same William” added in 2].

To Saint Martial he likewise gave the church of Cantreciacum in the diocese of Angoulême, and also the church of Manauco in the Limousin with all its appurtenances and mansi [Note: “For he had no offspring from a legitimate wife. For the aforesaid Arnald and Adhemar were born to him from concubines” added in 2].

To his faithful Iterius [Note: “prince” added in 2], from the estate of Boens, he gave the cell of Fruin [Note: “cell,” corrected from “cellem” in 1] [Note: “in the territory of Angoulême” added in 2].

### 25

Meanwhile, after Duke Eblus had died [Note: “Count of Poitiers” added in 2] (935), one of his sons became a count and the other a bishop. For Eblus, with the consent of King Louis, became bishop of Limoges.

William, surnamed Caput-stupae [Note: “by the aforesaid king” added in 2], advanced as count of Auvergne, Velay [Note: In manuscript 4, *Vellatis*; elsewhere *Vellaus*; today, Le Velay], Limoges, and Poitiers, became duke of Aquitaine. He granted his brother [Note: “his Eblus,” manuscript of Christ Church 692; Saint-Maixent Chronicle, p. 202] the abbeys of Saint Hilary and Saint Maxentius, together with certain other possessions in the territory of Poitiers.

This same Eblus was a good shepherd of the Church [Note: “He also completely restored the castle of Saint Stephen, the seat of Limoges, which his predecessor Bishop Turpio had built largely from the foundations. He newly constructed the castle of Hilary” added in 2]. He built the castle of the seat of Limoges and the castle of Saint Hilary, and established canons there, because that place had abandoned its ancient monastic habitation as a result of the Norman attacks. He restored the monastery of Saint Maxentius and completed the surrounding castle. He also restored the monastery of Saint Michael in the Wilderness [Note: Saint-Michel-en-Erm] and accomplished many other praiseworthy works for the service of God.

When he died [Note: The year is uncertain], he was buried in the basilica of the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Angel. He had been the successor of Bishop Turpio, the maternal uncle of Robert, viscount of Aubusson [Note: “Robert” misspelled in 1]. [Note: “His predecessor Turpio, of a most distinguished family, uncle of Robert, viscount of Aubusson, was magnificent in the service of God and greatly honored Odo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny. At Turpio’s request, that most reverend Odo composed the Life of Saint Gerald and the highly useful book *On Contempt for the World*. In his lifetime the same bishop was distinguished by many miracles; after his death he was buried at Aubusson in the basilica of Saint Valerius. Eblus, moreover, was the thirty-ninth bishop from Saint Martial, and, to bear the episcopal burden under him, ordained the chorepiscopus Benedict, whom he had raised from childhood; he was captured” added in 2].

That Eblus was the thirty-ninth bishop from Saint Martial. He had appointed under himself the chorepiscopus Benedict, whom he had raised from childhood, to bear the burden of his office. Benedict was later captured by Elias, count of Périgord, and deprived of his eyes. For this reason Eblus was continually afflicted by excessive and unbearable grief until the day of his death [Note: “was made” in 1]; he had intended to leave Benedict as his successor.

The same Elias [Note: “son of Boso the Old of La Marche” added in 2], having joined battle with Gerald, viscount [Note: “of Limoges” added in 2], and his son Guido, emerged victorious. Afterwards, he and his brother Aldebert were captured through Guido’s treachery and thrown into custody in the castle of Montignac.

But when, at the urging of Duke William, he was about to be deprived of his eyes on account of the aforesaid chorepiscopus, by God’s mercy he escaped from custody. Not long afterward he died on the road to Rome as a pilgrim engaged in the work of God.

His brother Aldebert, kept for a very long time in the tower [Note: “in the tower,” corrected from “in” in 1] of the city of Limoges, was finally released after taking in marriage the sister of Guido, the viscount. By her he begot a son, Bernard.

### 26

At that time, while Bishop Turpio was still alive, Odo and Teotolo [Note: “Teotolo and the aforesaid Odo, while they were …” added in 2], most distinguished canons of Saint Martin, fulfilling the evangelical command, left everything, followed poor Christ in poverty, and at Cluny were clothed in the holy habit and way of life.

Afterward, by God’s will, Odo became the most holy abbot [Note: “the second after the first abbot of that same monastery. For Berno was the first and Odo the second. Teotolo” added in 2], and after him Saint Majolus. At the command of his abbot, Teotolo was unwillingly consecrated archbishop at Tours.

This most holy Odo, highly educated in liberal letters and burning with the greatest love of God, proved an energetic restorer, by example and teaching, of the apostolic rule, which is the rule of monks.

### 27

Then, after Rollo had died [Note: “count of Rouen” added in 2] (931), his son William governed in his place. Baptized from childhood, and the entire multitude of those Normans who had lived near Francia [Note: “had lived,” singular in 1] accepted the faith of Christ; abandoning their pagan language, they became accustomed to speaking Latin.

After William was treacherously killed by Arnulf, count of Flanders (943), his son Richard succeeded him. Having become a most Christian man, he built in that part of Normandy which had formerly been called the march of Francia and Brittany the monastery of Saint Michael of the Mount, where he established monks.

Likewise, he built the monastery of Fécamp [Note: Fécamp] in honor of the supreme Trinity. He himself was buried there, and there too he installed monks.

Meanwhile, when Louis, king of the Franks, was dying (954), his son Lothair, born from Queen Gerberga, ruled in his place.

### 28

At that time (951), Fulcald, bishop of Angoulême, died after having presided for twelve years [Note: “and was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius” added in 2]. Eblus succeeded him in the episcopate and himself presided for twelve years [Note: “and was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius” added in 2].

Finally, William Iron-Cutter acquired this surname because, after engaging in battle with the Normans, neither side yielding, on the following day he fought their king Storin in the customary single combat for the sake of an agreement [Note: That is, “single” [“segular” in 2]]. With an extremely hard shortened sword [Note: “a sword named D[—], which the smith Walander had forged” added in 2; compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*, chapter 19], he cut through the middle of Storin’s chest together with his cuirass in a single blow and thus ended the day with the blow; he was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius.

For thirty years the principality was held on his behalf by Count Bernard [Note: “of Périgord” added in 2; compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*, at the same place], then by his son Arnald [Note: “surnamed Borracio” added in 4. “Surnamed Boirratio, because, wearing that same garment, armored and helmeted, he attacked a diabolical wolf that was devouring men in the field and, carrying it in his hands, offered it to the soldiers to kill” added in 2; compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*], then by William Talerandus [Note: “talelerandus” in 1], then by Rannulf Bomparius, and finally by Richard the Fool.

Arnald, having taken away the estate of Salas from Saint Eparchius [Note: “Salas,” corrected from “Salasam” in 1] and granted the estate of Boens to Duke Elias, was struck by an angel and died. For this reason, at the end of his life, he granted the estate of Ajarniac to Saint Eparchius as an act of reparation [Note: “emendation,” in 1], and was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius.

After his brother William died (962), Rannulf was killed in battle by Arnald [Note: “Manzer” added in 2; compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*, which adds: “that is, an adulterine son”], the son of William Iron-Cutter. Arnald succeeded his father in the principality of Angoulême and expelled Richard the Fool (975).

After Gauzbert, brother of Count Elias, had been captured in battle, Arnald was persuaded by Duke William to hand over this enemy to him. Gauzbert was driven out at Poitiers and condemned to lose his eyes in revenge for the chorepiscopus Benedict.

[Note: “Here he began, during the conflict, to capture Gauzbert the cleric, brother of Count Elias, whom he handed over to William, son of William Caput-stupae, his lord; and, in revenge for Benedict the chorepiscopus, he consented to have Gauzbert deprived of his eyes. For after William Caput-stupae had died, and—his son William as below, where these matters are absent. In these times” added in 2.]

### 29

At this time, around 973, Aymericus, the non-monastic abbot of Saint Martial, successor of Gonsindus, died. At the end of his life he became a monk, because King Louis, fearing his tyranny, had entrusted him with the honor of Saint Martial, but had nevertheless made him swear by an oath that he would become a monk.

He had Viscount Gerald entrusted in his hands [Note: “commended,” corrected from “commanded” in 1], as well as Boso the Old of La Marche [Note: “He built the castle of Roncomus” added in 2; compare above, chapter 19, note 45].

Near the monastery of Chambon [Note: Chambon], he destroyed by force the captured castle of Canboncase, because it was troublesome to the monks’ people.

### 30

Meanwhile, after William Caput-stupae had died (963) and been buried at the church of Saint Cyprian, his son William became duke of Aquitaine in his place. He took as wife Emma, daughter of Theobald of Champagne, and begot by her a son, William.

King Lothair, however, went to Limoges and spent some time in Aquitaine. Returning from there [Note: “returning,” corrected from “revertans” in 1], he was killed by poison by his adulterous queen (985). He left behind a son, Louis, who survived him by only one year and was himself killed by a poisoned drink [Note: “by his wife, named Blanca” added in 2] (987).

His uncle Charles wished to assume the kingdom in his place, but could not, because God in his judgment chose the better man. For the Franks, having taken counsel, rejected him and chose Duke Hugh, son of Hugh, as king [Note: “For Bishop Ascelin of Laon, a week before Easter, after a banquet, deceitfully seized him while he was resting in bed; and with the consent of many, Duke Hugh, son of Hugh Capet [Editorial note: “Already above, chapter 22, note 1*, the interpolator had called Hugh the Great by this name”], was raised as king. Charles, however, was kept imprisoned at Orléans until his death, where he begot …” added in 2].

For this reason Bishop Ascelin of Laon, in Holy Week before Easter (991), on the day of the Lord’s Supper, betrayed Charles just as Judas betrayed Christ [Note: Compare Richer, IV, 47]. Charles was thrust into prison at Orléans until his death. There he begot sons [Note: “son,” corrected, apparently, to “sons” in 1], Charles and Louis, and died.

His sons were expelled by the Franks [Note: It is inferred from a charter that this happened after 1008; the charter reads: “Done in the first year of the Lord 1008, while Robert, Louis, and Carloinus are reigning,” as Bouquet observes]. They departed to the emperor of the Romans and lived with him [Note: Many have convinced themselves that the landgraves of Thuringia descended from their line].

Duke William of Aquitaine, however, rejecting the wickedness of the Franks, refused to be subject to Hugh. Hence it came about that Hugh, bringing up the Frankish army, wearied the city of Poitiers with a siege.

When Hugh withdrew in frustration, William followed him with a force of Aquitanians as far as the Loire. There, as the Franks and Aquitanians fought in a fierce battle [Note: “This battle, which took place after the siege of that same city, occurred in 955, according to Flodoard, between Hugh the Great, father of Hugh Capet, and William Caput-stupae. It may perhaps wrongly be referred here to King Hugh and the son of the aforesaid William. Bouquet. Continued.”], the ardor of both sides being tested and much blood shed in mutual slaughter, the Franks proved superior and returned.

Afterward William made peace with Hugh and his son Robert. King Hugh, reflecting upon God’s grace toward him and, as though repaying the favor, became a most merciful defender of the Church of God.

For this reason it is believed that the offspring of Charles was rejected: because, having long neglected God’s grace, it seemed more inclined to neglect churches than to raise them up.

Accordingly, King Hugh restored the monastery of Saint Dionysius, which had already corrupted its ancient monastic rule, with more fitting observance according to what was right in God’s eyes, through the agency of the venerable Abbot Odilo. He also restored several other monasteries of the saints to the adornment of their former discipline [Note: “In those days Saint Majolus, abbot of Cluny and successor of Saint Odo, departed to the Lord in the monastery of Silviniacum [Silviniacum; compare the Life of Majolus by Syrus, III, 19], which is in the territory of Auvergne. He was buried there and shone forth through miracles. Against his will, the aforesaid Odilo was chosen to succeed him, both by Odo himself and by the entire congregation” added in 2].

At the same time, a very serious war was fought between Duke William and Geoffrey, count of Anjou. But Geoffrey, driven by necessity, submitted himself to Duke William, placed himself in his hands, and received from him the castle of Loudun [Note: Loudun] together with several other holdings in the county of Poitiers as a benefice.

### 31

At that time, after Otto II had died, Otto, his son—third in fact and in name—gained possession of the empire [Note: “Cf. Richer III, 43.”]. Devoted to philosophy and thinking of Christ’s gains, so that he might return the talent doubled before the Judge’s tribunal, by God’s will he strove to convert peoples [Note: “He strove to convert peoples throughout the region, devoted to idols, to the worship of God. For he had two most revered bishops: namely, Saint Adalbert, archbishop of the city of Prague, which is in the province of Bohemia, and also Saint Bruno, bishop of the city of Osburg, which is in the province of Bavaria, a kinsman of that emperor. [Col. 0047A] He confuses Bruno, brother of Henry II, ordained in 1007 and deserving well of the conversion of the Hungarians, with another Bruno, sent to that people—perhaps the same man who died in 1009 as the apostle of the Prussians; cf. Jahrbücher I, 3, p. 166.”]. For Saint Adalbert was short in stature, while Saint Bruno was tall of body. [Apparatus: manuscript c reads *cum* (‘when/with’) in the subsequent account of the emperor’s discovery; *differendam* (‘to distinguish’) for *differentiam*; *intactu* (‘untouched’) for *intactum*; *quae* (‘which’) for *qui* (‘who’) of Gouz; *baptistmate* for *baptismate*; *coronatum* for *coronatus* (‘crowned’); *condictum* for *conditum* (‘entombed’); and *claresceret* (‘might shine’) for *clarescere* (‘to shine’).]

Whenever Saint Adalbert was present at the emperor’s court, he would go alone in the dead of night to the forest and, barefoot, carry wood on his own shoulders to his lodging, with no one knowing. Selling the wood, he prepared his own food. When, after many days, the emperor learned of this, he regarded him as a saint. One day, speaking with him as usual, he said jokingly: “A bishop such as you are ought to go and preach to the peoples of the Slavs.” Immediately the bishop kissed the emperor’s feet and said that he would begin this work. Thereafter the emperor could not turn him away from his purpose. At the bishop’s request, an archbishop was ordained for him in the city of Prague, the man whom he himself had chosen, and the emperor willingly consented.

After preparing everything necessary, he went barefoot into the province of Poland, where no one had heard the name of Christ, and began to preach the Gospel. Following his example, Bishop Bruno asked the emperor to order the consecration in his own see of a bishop whom he had chosen, named Odolriric [Note: “He was thinking of Saint Ulrich, who had already died in 973.”]. This having been done, Bruno too humbly went into the province of Hungary, called White Hungary to distinguish it from the other Hungary, Black Hungary, because its people are dark in complexion like Ethiopians. Saint Adalbert finally converted these four provinces to the faith of Christ, provinces that had been held by the ancient error of paganism: Poland, Sclavonia, Waredonia [Note: “I do not know what this name signifies. Perhaps it stands for Wenedonia?”], and Cracow.

After founding them in the faith, he went into the province of the Pincenates to preach the Lord to them. That people, exceedingly savage in its idolatry, came to him after eight days, and he began to announce Christ to them. On the ninth day, finding him engaged in prayer, they pierced him with missiles and iron weapons and made him a martyr of Christ. Then, having cut off his head, they sank his body in a great lake, while they threw his head into a field for the beasts.

But an angel of the Lord took the head and placed it beside the corpse on the farther bank. There it remained motionless, untouched, and incorrupt until merchants passed by that place in a boat. They took away the holy treasure and made Sclavonia known. When King Botesclavus of Sclavonia learned of this—he had himself been baptized by Saint Adalbert—he gave rich gifts, received the head and body with honor, built a very large monastery in his name, and many miracles began to occur through that martyr of Christ.

Saint Adalbert suffered on the twenty-fourth day of April, that is, the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

Saint Bruno converted the province of Hungary to the faith, and also another province called Russia. He baptized the king of Hungary, named Gouz, and, changing his name at baptism, called him Stephen [Note: “These matters too are greatly confused. Géza, king of the Hungarians, had a son named Stephen, baptized by Saint Adalbert; no one reports that Géza himself was called by that name. Many have shown that what is said about Bruno is false; cf. Acta Sanctorum, June VI, p. 221; September I, p. 482.”]. On the feast of the protomartyr Stephen, Emperor Otto received him from the baptismal font and permitted him to possess the kingdom in complete freedom. He gave him permission to carry the sacred lance everywhere, as was customary for the emperor himself, and granted him relics from the nails of the Lord and from the lance of Saint Maurice, placing them in his own lance [Note: “Cf. Liudprand IV, 24.”].

The aforesaid king also ordered Saint Bruno to baptize his son, giving him, as he had done for himself, the name Stephen. To this son Stephen, Emperor Otto gave in marriage the sister of Henry, later emperor. But when Saint Bruno had gone to the Pincenates and begun to preach Christ to them, he suffered at their hands as Saint Adalbert had suffered. For the Pincenates, raging with demonic fury, drew out all his entrails through a small opening in his side and made him a most valiant martyr of God [Note: “The reading *deo* is an error for *Dei*.”; cf. Thietmar VI, 58.].

The people of Russia redeemed his body for a great price and built a monastery in his name in Russia; it began to shine with many miracles. After a few days, a certain Greek bishop came to Russia and converted the half of that province that was still devoted to idols. He also made them adopt the Greek custom of growing the beard and other such practices.

Ulrich, who had succeeded Saint Bruno, migrated to the Lord and deserved to become renowned for great virtues. Therefore Bishop Bruno, his successor and brother of Emperor Henry, built a monastery outside the city of Osburg in his name. That city was called Valentina by the Romans, after the name of the emperor who first founded it.

In those days Emperor Otto was warned in a dream to raise the body of Emperor Charlemagne, who had been buried at Aachen [Note: “It is easy to understand that fables have been mixed into this account as well; cf. Thietmar IV, 29.”]. But because the passage of time had obliterated the place, it was not known exactly where he lay. After a three-day fast, he was found in the place that the emperor had learned of in his vision: seated on a golden throne within a vaulted chamber beneath the Basilica of Mary, crowned with a crown of gold and jewels, holding a scepter and a sword of the purest gold. The body itself was found incorrupt.

After it had been raised, it was displayed to the people. A certain canon of that place, Adalbert, who had an enormous and tall body, placed Charlemagne’s crown around his own head as though to measure it. He was found to have a narrower head, the crown exceeding the circumference of his head in size. He also measured his own leg against the king’s leg and was found to be shorter; immediately his leg was broken by divine power. He survived for forty years but always remained disabled.

Charlemagne’s body was entombed in the right-hand part of the basilica, behind the altar of Saint John the Baptist, and a marvelous golden crypt was constructed over it. It began to shine with many signs and miracles. Nevertheless, no solemn feast is celebrated for him, except the anniversary observance customary for the dead.

Emperor Otto sent his golden throne to King Botesclavus in exchange for the relics of Saint Adalbert the martyr [Note: “The variant *reliquis* is printed in place of *reliquiis*.”]. King Botesclavus, having received the gift, sent the emperor an arm from the body of that saint. The emperor joyfully received it, built a magnificent basilica at Aachen in honor of Saint Adalbert the martyr, and established there a community of women devoted to God. He also built another monastery in Rome in honor of the same martyr [add. 2].

Hungary, together with their king, he merited to convert to the faith of Christ.

Gerbert, an Aquitanian by birth [Note: “Born of the lowest class” [add. 2.]], a monk [Note: “From childhood” [add. 2.]] of the church of Saint Gerald of Aurillac [Note: “The following is recorded about him in the *Chronicle of Aurillac* (Mabillon, *Analecta* II, p. 240; second edition, p. 150): ‘Raymond of Cahors, a nobleman from the castle called Saura, was elected abbot. He took care to educate Gerbert [Gerlentius, first edition], a youth born in an obscure place; but since he was clever by nature, he became outstanding in letters. Having obtained permission because of his thirst for knowledge, he traveled through many kingdoms and came to the emperor’s attention. The emperor appointed him bishop of Reims, then of Ravenna, and later raised him to the highest pontificate. He did much good for the monastery and sent gifts to his companion Raymond, namely books by grammarians and commentaries on Jerome and Ambrose.’”], first traversed France and then Córdoba for the sake of philosophy [Note: “This rests solely on Ademar’s testimony.”]. Having become known to the emperor, he was given the archbishopric of Ravenna. [Note: “Having become known to King Hugh, he was given the archbishopric of Reims. Then, having again become known to Emperor Otto, he was made archbishop of Ravenna, abandoning the archbishopric of Reims. [Col. 0049] The reading *favenne* is an error for *Ravenne*. Add. 2.”]

When Pope Gregory, the emperor’s brother [Note: “Not at all; rather, the brother of Duke Otto.”], died—this occurred in 999—the same Gerbert was elevated by the emperor to be pope of the Romans because of his philosophical learning. His former name was changed, and he was called Sylvester.

The prefect of Rome, Crescentius, wishing to seize the Roman Empire from Otto, was eventually forced into the tower called Inter-celis [Note: “That is, the fortress of Saint Angelo; cf. Liudprand III, 44.”]. He held out there for a long time, but after the tower was stormed he was captured through the treachery of his wife and hanged on the gallows [Note: “By order of the emperor” [add. 2.]], and great mourning was made for him [Note: “In Rome” [add. 2.]] (998).

In those days (994), Saint Abbot Majolus of Cluny migrated to the Lord, and the aforesaid Odilo, not inferior in virtues, succeeded him. King Hugh of the Franks, a lover of the holy Church and a most devoted guardian of justice, also died (996). His son Robert ruled in his place, a man of distinguished honor and great piety, an ornament of the clergy, nourisher of monks, father of the poor, and constant worshiper of God [Note: “In humility like King David” [add. 2.]], a king not only of peoples but also of his own morals.

### 32

At the same time, around the year 1000, the rebellious Bulgarians greatly exasperated Greece, and Emperor Basil, exceedingly angered against them, bound himself by a vow to God to become a monk if he should bring them under the authority of the Greeks.

For fifteen years he struggled against them with his army [Note: “Manuscript 1 originally has *rebellantur*, corrected to *rebellantes* (‘rebelling’).”], and in two great battles he was defeated. Finally, after the Bulgarian kings Samuel and Aaron had been killed—not in an open battle but by Greek cunning—in 1014, he gained possession of all their land, demolished their strongest cities and fortresses, established Greek garrisons everywhere against them, and took most of the Bulgarian people captive.

As he had promised in his vow, he thereafter wore a monastic habit beneath his imperial dress for the rest of his life, abstaining from pleasure and meat, while outwardly he was surrounded by imperial splendor. Then, over seven years, he so subdued rebellious Iberia that everything was done according to his command (1022).

### 33

Richard of Rouen also died (996? 1002?) and was buried at Fécamp. His son Richard succeeded him [Col. 0050B]. He was very prudent and glorious in all things and proved a lover of churches.

Emperor Otto, however, perished from having drunk poison [Note: “In the region of Benevento” [add. 2.]] without sons (1002), and his kinsman Henry assumed the empire in his place [Note: “Otto’s body was brought to Rome [variant: ‘to Rome’], and he was buried there” [add. 2.]].

Indeed, Archbishop Heribert of Cologne [Note: “Heribert”] carried the scepter and crown, together with the lance of Saint Maurice, from the deceased emperor in Bavaria and, with the consent of all the bishops, handed them over to Henry. King Stephen of Hungary also, attacking Black Hungary in war, merited converting the whole land to the faith of truth by force, fear, and affection.

In those days, when Otto died in the region of Capua, he was carrying with him the scepter, crown, and sacred lance. Henry surrounded him by treachery, captured him, and stripped him of the imperial insignia [Note: “Cf. Thietmar IV, 31. Add. 2 told the story falsely.”].

### 34

At that time the aforesaid Count Aldebert of Périgord [Note: “Chapter 25”], the son of Boso the Elder by his sister Emma, the sister of the aforesaid Bernard, brought war against the city of Poitiers and emerged victorious [Note: “After inflicting great slaughter” [add. 2.]], especially because the citizens had rashly attacked him before they ought to have done so.

He also besieged the city of Tours and received its surrender, then gave it to Fulk, count of Anjou. But Fulk soon lost it through the deceitful cunning [Note: “Of the viscount” [add. 2.]] of the citizens, and Odo of Champagne recovered it again [Note: “When he was besieging it, the king of the Franks did not dare challenge him to battle, but sent him this message: ‘Who made you count?’ Aldebert sent him this reply: ‘Who made you king?’” [add. 2.; and Pithou, p. 82, from manuscript 4.]].

Duke William, abandoning the world in monastic clothing, was buried at the monastery of Saint Maxentius (993), and his son William administered the principality with great vigor after him.

Aldebert captured and destroyed the castle of Gentiacum. When William rebuilt it and Aldebert besieged it, it was destroyed a second time. While Aldebert was riding around confidently as though already victorious [Note: “Already victorious, he rode around unarmed” [add. 2.]], he was killed by an arrow and buried at Saint Carrofo. His brother Boso rose to power in his place.

[Then William, having taken in marriage Adalmode, the wife of the aforesaid Aldebert, summoned King Robert to capture the castle of Bellac, which Boso held [Note: “Boso the Elder had built the castle itself in the Limousin march” [add. 2.]]. All France, warlike, came together there [Note: “And Aquitaine” [add. 2.]], but after many days, disappointed, it withdrew with its king. Note: “This passage is supplied from manuscript 2; something appears to be missing in 1. Yet I would not attribute to Ademar matters which the Benedictines noted were less correctly stated. The words ‘having taken … Aldebert’ are absent also in 4.”]

At that time, while the castle of Wido the viscount at Procia was being besieged by the aforesaid duke [Note: “Brosse in the district of Berry; cf. Aimoin, *Miracles of Saint Benedict* II, 11 ff. Add. 2 has ‘and four other counts,’ and: ‘At Procia in the district of Berry, with five counts and an innumerable army, he attacked them in battle and, victorious, broke the siege. The counts were Duke William, Arnald, Elias, Aldebert, and Boso’ (Pithou, p. 82, from manuscript 4).”] with a strong force, Wido [Note: “With the men of Limoges” [add. 2.]] attacked the besiegers in battle and inflicted great slaughter [Note: “Manuscript 1 reads *magnum*.”] upon them, emerging victorious (around 1000), and broke the siege [Note: “The manuscript has *disrumrumbit* written over two lines.”].

### 35

Count Arnold of Angoulême, having established a dwelling for monks at the church of Saint Amantius of Buxens [Note: “Saint-Amand de Boisse; cf. *Gallia Christiana* II, 1035.”.] out of fear of God, sent there a venerable abbot named Franco. He became a monk in the hall of Saint Eparchius and was buried beside his father on the fourth day before the Nones of March [Note: “His mother” [add. 2.]].

Bishop Aldegerius of Limoges [Note: “The successor of Eblo” [add. 2.]], taking with him the more precious priestly vestments from the church of Saint Martial, left for France. There he died [around 990] and was buried at Saint-Denis. For his burial he donated the precious ornaments he had carried away from Saint Martial.

His brother Alduin succeeded him as bishop. Through the agency of Duke William, he was consecrated at Angoulême by Bishop Hugh [Note: “By Gumbald, archbishop of Bordeaux; Fronterius of Périgueux; Abbo of Saintes; and Hugh of Angoulême, who enthroned him at Limoges—first on a portable chair at the church of Saint Gerard and then in the see of Saint Martial. But Arnold …” [add. 2.]].

The aforesaid Arnold left his son William as his successor in the county of Angoulême.

Moreover, after living twelve years, Bishop Fulcald received Ranulf as his successor (964) [Note: “He seems to have been thinking of Eblo; cf. chapter 28.”]. When this bishop had held office for nine years and died [Note: “He was buried beside the basilica of Saint Eparchius, just as Fulcald was, in a tomb” [add. 2.]] (973), the aforesaid Hugh held the bishopric for twenty years (993) [Note: “He himself was buried at Saint Eparchius in a monastic habit” [add. 2.]]. After him came Grimoard, and then the lord Bishop Roho, glorious, shone forth at Angoulême (993–1017) [Note: “Then Bishop Roho—corrected from ‘Roo’” [add. 2.]; cf. the history of the Council of Limoges, 1031 (*Concilia*, ed. Labbe IX, p. 879): ‘Our bishop of Angoulême, Hugh … who migrated forty years ago, whose successor died fourteen years ago,’ etc.].

In those days the pestilence of fire broke out over the people of Limoges. The bodies of men and women were consumed beyond number by an invisible fire, and everywhere lamentation filled the earth (994).

Therefore Gosfrid, abbot of Saint Martial, who had succeeded Wigo, and Bishop Alduin, having taken counsel with Duke William, proclaimed a three-day fast for Limoges. Then all the bishops of Aquitaine gathered together at Limoges, and the bodies and relics of the saints were solemnly brought there from every direction. The body of Saint Martial, patron of Gaul, was raised from its tomb. Thereupon immense joy filled everyone, and every sickness ceased everywhere. A compact of peace and justice was mutually established by the duke and the princes [Note: The manuscript has variants including “in turn” and a corrupted form, “viciis simphoderata.”].

Bishop Alduin, however, destroyed over a period of three years the monastery of Saint Stephen at Eymoutiers [Note: “Antimonastery, Emoutiers or Eymoutier”], which Hildegarius had carefully organized with a large community of monks, and restored canons there [Note: “At the devil’s prompting” [add. 2.]]. Because of this offense, he arranged for monks subject to a rule to be gathered inside the city of Limoges, in the church of Saint Martin.

Often the same Alduin, because of the wickedness of the people [Note: “Because of the soldiers’ plundering and the devastation of the poor” [add. 2.]], established a new observance: namely, that churches and monasteries should cease from divine worship and the holy sacrifice, and that the people, as though pagan, should cease from divine praises. He judged this observance to be excommunication.

When, during Lent, the people in Evaun within his diocese were endangered by famine, so that they would not incur death from hunger, the same bishop ordered them to eat meat. All the inhabitants of that town consumed meat, for which the bishop himself afterward urged them to do penance.

His brother Wido, viscount of Limoges, while Count Boso was away in Rome, took the opportunity to build a new castle opposite the monastery of Brantôme. Soon afterward Boso returned and battle was joined [Note: “On the field of Carracio” [add. 2.]]. Boso destroyed the castle in victory, much blood was shed in that battle, and Wido, wounded, escaped by flight.

### 36

At this time Bishop Grimoard, having given gifts, requested the monastery of Saint Eparchius from Count William and claimed it for himself. He caused it to remain without an abbot for many years [Note: “He gave many of the monastery’s possessions to his relatives and to other laymen and alienated them from the place” [add. 2.]].

For all the counts of Angoulême, from the time of King Childebert, when that place was founded, are known to have been its advocates, defenders, and administrators. As their defenders’ benefice, they held the village of Banconia.

Then the aforesaid bishop gave his kinsman Aimeric, duke of Moxedania, the monastery of Tomolatense as a possession. Until then it had always belonged to the domain of the monastery of Angoulême. It is situated in the territory of Périgord and has a church in honor of the Mother of God. There, as though by hereditary right, were buried Felix Aureolus, count of Périgord, father of Saint Eparchius, and Principia, the mother of that confessor [Note: “The words ‘and of Saint Eparchius’ are absent in manuscript 2.”].

After not many years, the aforesaid Aimeric gave the place as a benefice to his dukes, who are called the Infernals. Thus the possession was entirely alienated from the ancient right of Saint Eparchius.

As time passed, the viscount Wido captured Bishop Grimoard and held him prisoner in a tower at Limoges for the sake of the monastery of Brantôme, which Wido was demanding from him as a gift. Released on Wido’s terms, Grimoard went to Rome and appealed to Pope Gerbert.

There Wido was summoned to judgment before the pope (around 1003). When the case was heard on the most sacred day of Easter, and judgment had been pronounced by the senate, it was decreed that anyone who captured a bishop should be bound by the feet to untamed horses, torn apart, and finally devoured by wild beasts [Note: The reading *legatus* is corrected to *ligatus*, “bound”].

He was immediately handed over to Bishop Grimoard for custody, to be delivered to punishment on the third day. But the two men came to an agreement, became friends, and, before the appointed day, secretly left Rome and returned to their own lands.

### 37

When Emperor Henry found the Lombards opposed to him [Note: “This is reported by Ademar alone.”], he sent King Rudolf of Burgundy [Note: “His nephew” [add. 2.]], besieged Pavia, and gave it over to fire. He built himself a palace there and compelled the rebels to serve him (1004).

When the Greek dukes invaded his territory, he organized an expedition, entered the coastal regions of Apulia, and spent many days there attacking their cities, until pestilence afflicted his army [Note: “Cf. the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, 1022.”] and he returned (1022).

In German territory he built from the foundations a city called Bamberg. Pope Benedict consecrated it in honor of the Mother of God and, as the pagan villages and towns were converted, assigned the surrounding parishes to it.

He gave gifts to the monastery of Cluny: a golden scepter, a golden orb, a golden imperial garment, a golden crown, and a golden crucifix, together weighing one hundred pounds [Note: The manuscript has the variant *pansentia*], as well as many other things. He also frequently held familiar conversations with Odilo, abbot of that place, and in his palace he honored him above all others [Note: “The *Chronicle of Saint Maxentius* (Labbe I, p. 206), which copied this passage, adds: ‘A most noble woman named Alaidis was joined to him in marriage. She built the monastery of Payerne in honor of Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God. By her he had a son, whom he named Henry after himself. In the year 1000 the empress Alaidis died.’ These statements are very far from the truth.”].

### 38

At this time Count Ermengaud of Urgell [Note: “Urgell in Catalonia”], after many victories over the Moors and Saracens, entered a final battle and inflicted an immeasurable slaughter upon the Saracens. While returning as victor [Note: “Manuscript 1 reads *egreditur*, ‘going out.’”], he encountered another army of Moors coming against him.

Pursuing it with a few of his exhausted men, he killed many of them, but he himself fell (1008?). The Saracens carried away his head as a great treasure. Having embalmed it, their king covered it with gold and always carried it with him in battles as a means of securing victory.

[Note: “Meanwhile, after the wife of Duke William had died—the woman by whom he had a son named William—the same duke married Brisca, the sister of Sancho, duke of Gascony. She bore him a son named Odo. (End of chapter 39?) The history of the Franks ends here in manuscript Christian 692.”]

### 39

Meanwhile Abbo, abbot of Saint Benedict of Fleury on the Loire, a man of the highest philosophical learning, was traveling to Gascony. Passing through Angoulême, he was entertained in November at the monastery of Saint Eparchius.

When he came to Saint Peter of La Réole [Note: “La Réole”], a church belonging to the French monastery of Saint Benedict, he was killed there in a riot of Gascons. Buried there, he began to shine forth through miracles (1004). His pastoral staff was sent back to France.

Bernard, duke of Gascony, punished the perpetrators for the murder of so great a man, handing some over to hanging and others to the flames. He also secured for the French monks of Saint Benedict, without dispute, the entire property at La Réole [Note: “Together with the church of Saint Peter” [add. 2.]], which had previously been held in dispute by those who had invaded it.

King Robert appointed Gauzlen as abbot in place of the deceased man, although the monks resisted, unwilling to have the son of a prostitute rule over them. For Gauzlen was the illegitimate son of the noblest prince of the Franks [Note: “Hugh Capet”] and had been raised from childhood in the monastery of Saint Benedict.

The aforesaid king later made him archbishop of Bourges, after the death of Archbishop Dagbert. But for five years the people of Bourges fomented a revolt and refused to admit him into the city, saying with one voice: “It is not fitting for the son of a prostitute to rule the Church.” Eventually, however, the king’s will prevailed, and by God’s providence he was received into the see (1009) [Note: “With Abbot Odilo acting as mediator” [add. 2.]].

But when Bernard, his body wasting away through evil arts, was deprived of life by feminine snares [variant: *mulieribus*, ‘by women’], Sancho, his brother, became duke of Gascony.

After the death of Duke William’s wife [Note: “Of Poitiers” [add. 2.]], by whom he had a son named William, the same duke married Brisca, sister of Sancho. She bore him a son named Odo.

### 40

At the same time, after Gosfrid, abbot of Saint Martial, died (998), and Adalbald, a man of regular virtue, succeeded him, while Wido and his brother Bishop Alduin were returning hurriedly from Jerusalem, the tomb of Saint Eparchius began to shine with innumerable miracles, more than usual.

A clear vision was also revealed to Fulcher, abbot of Saint Carrofo, and to the monks: they were to carry the holy wood of the Cross to the tomb of blessed Eparchius. This was carried out with solemn assembly. Under the direction of Raginold, abbot of Angoulême, the holy wood was received into the basilica of blessed Eparchius on the day of his feast, the first day of July.

When the things that divine mercy had ordained had been fulfilled, the monks of Saint Carrofo bade farewell to the brothers of Angoulême and returned gloriously with the holy wood [Note: “This wood of the Cross is from the Lord’s Cross, which the patriarch of Jerusalem sent to the great King Charlemagne. The emperor placed it in the same basilica that Count Rotger of Limoges founded in honor of the Savior [cf. Rotger’s charter in Mabillon, *Annales* II, p. 711]. In the ancient language of the Gauls, the place was called Carrofus because of the crossroads there—that is, the public roads for vehicles. Thereafter, out of reverence for the Cross, it pleased people to call it Saint Carrofo” [add. 2.]].

41. Finally, Count William of Angoulême, having married Girberga, sister of Count Fulk [Note: “of Anjou”; added in recension 2], had by her two sons, Hilduin and Gosfrid.

The duke of the Aquitanians, the count of Poitiers, the already mentioned William, most glorious and powerful, was beloved by everyone: great in counsel, conspicuous for prudence, most generous in giving, defender of the poor, father of monks, builder and lover of churches, and especially a lover of the holy Roman Church. From his youth he had the custom of hastening every year to Rome, to the threshold of the apostles; and in any year when he did not hasten to Rome, he made up for his devout journey by traveling to Saint James of Galicia.

Wherever he traveled, or whenever he held a public assembly, he was considered a king rather than a duke, because of the dignity and distinction of honor with which he abounded. He not only subjected all Aquitaine to his rule, so that no one dared raise a hand against him, but also kept the king of the Franks favorably disposed toward him [Note: Having the king of the Franks as his very close friend, he was honored above the other dukes in the king’s palace; recension 2.].

Indeed, he had so bound to himself by the greatest favor Alfonso, king of Spain, Sancho, king of Navarre, and also Canute, king of the Danes and the English, that every year he received their embassies with costly gifts [Note: Compare the History of the Council of Limoges, 1031, Labbe, Councils, IX, p. 882: “Seven years ago the king of the English sent royal gifts to the duke of Aquitaine, together with a book written in golden letters, in which the names of the saints were set out with images,” etc.], and he himself sent them even more valuable gifts in return.

He was so closely joined in friendship with the emperor Henry that they honored each other with gifts. Among the many gifts, Duke William sent him a huge sword of the purest gold, on which letters were inscribed reading: “Henry, emperor, Caesar Augustus.” When he came to Rome, the Roman pontiffs received him with such reverence as though he were their own Augustus, and the entire Roman senate acclaimed him as its father.

Since he had Count Fulk of Anjou entrusted to his protection, he granted him, as a benefice, Losdunum [Note: Compare chapter 30], together with several other castles in Poitevin territory, as well as the Saintonge with certain castles.

Whenever this duke saw a cleric adorned with wisdom, he honored him greatly. Thus, because of his excellence in wisdom, he appointed Rainald, surnamed Plato, a monk from the monastery of Saint Maxentius, as abbot. He also summoned from Francia Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, distinguished for his wisdom, granted him the treasurership of Saint Hilary [Note: Compare Fulbert, Letter 128, etc.], and showed him reverence in his own presence. He could scarcely ever be found without one of the bishops.

To the monastery of Saint Martial of Limoges he gave the church at Alniensis [Note: The Alniensis district, the pays of Auny], which his father had also previously given to the same monastery—namely, Anesium, which is dedicated to Saint Peter.

To the monastery of Cluny, the monastery of Saint Michael at the Clusa [Note: On Mount Cinisio] in Italy [Note: *ad* (“at”) is absent in recensions 1 and 2; Martialis Besly, p. 366], and many other monasteries of God throughout Burgundy and Aquitaine, he assigned, along the seacoast, many gifts of lands and revenues sufficient to provide abundantly for the servants of Christ.

He embraced regular monks and abbots with the greatest reverence and affection [Note: Variant: *amplectabatur*, “he embraced,” in witness 1; *honori*, “for honor,” in witness 1, instead of *honoris*, “of honor”], and relied upon their advice in administering the realm. Thus he drew Lord Odilo, abbot of Cluny, to himself with abundant gifts, seeing in him a temple of the Holy Spirit [Note: “And entrusted himself to him in submission”; added in recension 2]. He also placed several monasteries under his authority in Odilo’s care.

The same duke newly founded the distinguished monastery of Maillezais [Note: Malliacense] in Poitevin territory (1003). Likewise, together with his mother Emma [Note: Adela, who was most Christian; she was the sister of Richard, count of Rouen—Pithou, p. 80, from codex 4], sister of Odo of Champagne, he founded the great monastery of Bourgueil [Note: Burguliense] in Angevin territory, on his own estate.

In these monasteries he gathered many regular monks to offer praises to God day and night, and appointed over them, in their fervent holy vocation, the abbot Theodelin, a very strong pillar of heavenly discipline [Note: Teelinus, who had been converted from Judaism].

Certainly, many times all the Aquitanian nobles who attempted to rebel against him were either subdued or overthrown. Thus, while he was besieging Rochemcau [Note: Rocameltis], Count Boso, a neighbor of Saint Carrofus, drew up a line of battle against him with a multitude of warriors. When the battle was joined, the duke emerged victorious [Note: “First Boso, then William, conquered”; added in recension 2]; renewing the siege [Note: “And Boso having been put to flight”; added in recension 2], he captured the castle by force.

He had with him a man of great counsel, Count William of Angoulême, whose advice he relied upon above all. They always loved each other so greatly that they were, as it were, one soul in two bodies [Note: Added in recension 2].

When Count William of Angoulême was storming the castle of Blaye [Note: Blavia], he had the duke himself with him, and with great courage captured the castle. From the duke himself he received the following as a benefice [Note: “He received it as a benefice together with these possessions, namely”; recension 2]: the viscounties of Melle, Aunac, and Rochechouart; the honors of Chabanais and Confolens [Note: An honor is virtually the same as a county, viscounty, or similar authority]; also Ruffec, and many other possessions [Note: “And likewise several estates in the Alniensis district”; added in recension 2].

42. At this time Bishop Alduin, bringing Duke William with him, built the castle of Belloc [Note: Bellojocum] beside the monastery of Saint Junian, against Jordan, lord of Chabanais.

When the duke had returned, Jordan prepared himself with chosen men either to storm the castle or to defeat the bishop. The bishop gathered a great force of armed men, with the assistance of his brother Wido, and went out to meet him. A fierce battle arose in the harshness of winter. Much blood was shed [Note: “The Limoges men, together with their bishop and their viscounts, were put to flight”; added in recension 2], and the victorious Jordan returned with several nobles as prisoners.

Now secure, he was suddenly attacked from behind by an unknown soldier [Note: “Struck in the neck from behind by a soldier whom he himself had thrown down”; recension 2]. He was struck and died; and those who had been held captive by his men were immediately stabbed with weapons in his place and gave up their lives. For them there was heavier mourning than there had previously been for those who had fallen in battle.

Jordan, the bastard brother of the deceased, then held Aimeric, the bishop’s brother, bound for a long time, until the aforementioned castle was destroyed.

43. During these days Gosfrid, abbot of Saint Martial and successor of Adalbald, summoned Count Boso and, with a large military force [Note: “Going by night to Montane”; added in recension 2], brought to Limoges the body of Saint Waleric from the church which certain nobles were unjustly taking away from Saint Martial [Note: “Which the local nobles were taking away from Saint Martial”; recension 2].

There he kept the relics of that confessor [Note: “On Mount Gaudium”; added in recension 2] until the offending nobles recognized and rendered the due justice of Saint Martial. Thus, after the possession had been recovered [Note: “Not without a great ransom”; added in recension 2], the holy body was restored to the aforementioned place, and in the presence of Duke William [Note: “And Gerard, bishop of Limoges”; added in recension 2] monastic discipline was established there.

44. In these days Emma, viscountess of Limoges, went in pilgrimage around the feast of the apostles and Saint Martial to Saint Michael the Hermit. There she was captured by the Normans during the night and kept in exile across the sea for three years.

From the treasury of Saint Martial, immeasurable quantities of gold and silver were given for her ransom, together with a golden image of the holy archangel and other rich ornaments. The Normans took all these things, however, and, having broken faith, did not return the woman, until after many days Richard, count of Rouen, ingeniously secured her through envoys sent overseas and restored her, free, to her husband Wido.

45. Meanwhile, after Count Boso had been killed by the sorceries of his wife and buried at Périgueux, and after the city itself had been captured by Duke William, that same duke became guardian of his sons and grandson.

He granted the city of Périgueux to Boso’s son Elias and restored the march to Bernard, son of Hildebert [Note: The same person as Aldebert above, chapter 34; likewise Alduin and Hilduin, and Aldegarius and Hildegarius, are the same names].

Until Bernard reached manhood, he entrusted its government to two most powerful nobles, two brothers: Peter, abbot of the canons of Scotora [Note: Le Dorat], and Umbert Drutus.
