Their father, Abbo Drutus, had defended the castle of Bellac most courageously against King Robert [Note: “This Abbo, with the consent of Count Aldebert, built the castle of Mortemart on his own estate”; added in recension 2].

The march was defended most bravely by these two until Umbert died. Peter, the abbot, possessing sole authority, had as his most faithful counselor the deeply prudent provost Ainard [Note: “A priest from the monastery of Saint Peter of Scotora. This Ainard had two [brothers]”; recension 2], who had two brothers, Abbo and Raymond, exceptionally capable leaders, strong in body and warlike in spirit.

Raymond of Chabanais married their sister Aldeard, the great-grandson [Note: Great-grandson; compare the preface, note 2] of Bishop Turpio and brother of Aldebert, the renowned dean and provost from the monastery of Saint Martial. By her he fathered Ademar of Angoulême, a monk, who wrote this account [Note: *Engolismense* in recension 1; *Egolismense* in recension 2].

While the aforementioned Ainard was alive, Abbot Peter administered the state very well and suppressed those who envied his glory. But after Ainard died at Rome, his brother Raymond died at Jerusalem, and Abbo was weighed down by illness, the renowned Peter, having no faithful counselor, began to do everything according to his own rash judgment. He appeared terrible among his own people like a lion, burned his own castle of Mortemart despite the advice of his counselors, and, on this account, his relatives and the noble margraves, together with Count Bernard and Duke William, rose against him as though he were attempting tyranny. Gradually he was expelled from the power of the margraves.

After returning from Jerusalem, he retained his former dignity in the basilica of Saint Stephen at Limoges; he enjoyed extensive possessions of churches and villages inherited from his father; he commanded a great host of soldiers who held his benefices; and, freed for the most part from secular cares, he devoted himself more freely to God and possessed greater security and glory than before [Note: Nothing is known about the time of his death].

46. In these times (1010), signs in the heavens, harmful droughts, excessive rains, severe plagues, extremely grave famines, and many eclipses of the sun and moon appeared. The river Vienne [Note: Vinzenna] dried up at Limoges for three nights over a distance of two miles.

The aforementioned monk Ademar, who at that time was living at Limoges with his uncle, the renowned Roger, in the monastery of Saint Martial, awoke in the dead of night. While looking outside at the stars, he saw toward the south, high in the sky, a great crucifix as though fixed in the heavens [Note: “As though fastened into the sky”; recension 2], and the figure of the Lord hanging upon the cross, weeping with a great stream of tears [Note: “Weeping. But he who saw these things…”; recension 2].

Overcome with astonishment, he could do nothing except shed tears from his eyes. He saw both the cross itself and the figure of the crucified Christ, entirely fiery and exceedingly blood-red, for half an hour of the night, until it closed itself within the sky [Note: Variant: “until it hid itself in the sky”].

He kept what he had seen concealed in his heart until he wrote this account; and the Lord is witness that he saw these things.

47. In that year Bishop Hilduin [Note: Alduinus] compelled the Jews of Limoges to baptism, issuing a law that they must either become Christians or leave the city [Note: Variant: “from the city” (*devitate*, witness 1)]. For one month he ordered teachers of divine doctrine to dispute with the Jews, so that they might compel them to the faith [Note: “So that they might refute them from their own books”; recension 2]. Three or four Jews became Christians.

The rest of the multitude hastened to flee with their wives and children to other cities [Note: “Some even slaughtered themselves with the sword, unwilling to receive baptism”; added in recension 2].

In that same year, on 3 Kalends of October, 1010 from the Incarnation, the Lord’s Sepulchre in Jerusalem was shattered by pagans [Note: “By Jews and Saracens”; recension 2]. For the western Jews [Note: “The Saracens of Spain”; added in recension 2] sent letters to the East [Note: Compare Rodulfus Glaber, III.10, where these events are recounted more fully], accusing the Christians and reporting that the armies of the West [Note: “Of the Franks”; recension 2] had been stirred up against the eastern Saracens.

Then the Babylonian ruler whom they call the Emir [Note: That is, Cairo, and therefore Egypt], provoked to anger by the persuasion of the Saracens [Note: “Pagans”; recension 2], inflicted great suffering upon the Christians, issuing an order that any Christians under his authority who refused to become Saracens must either have their property confiscated or be killed.

As a result, countless Christians considered their possessions worthless [Note: “The rest converted to the Saracen law, and no one was found worthy of death for Christ”; recension 2]. No one, however, was deemed worthy of death for Christ except the patriarch of Jerusalem, who was killed by various tortures, and two young brothers in Egypt, who were beheaded and became renowned for many miracles.

The churches of the saints were overthrown [Note: “For the church of Saint George, which until then no Saracen had been able to violate, was then destroyed together with many other churches of the saints”; recension 2]. And, because our sins deserved it, the basilica of the Lord’s Sepulchre was demolished to the ground.

Since they could not in any way break the stone of the tomb, they piled abundant fire upon it, but it remained immovable and solid like adamant.

When they attempted to destroy the Bethlehem church, where Christ was born, a sudden flashing light appeared to them, and their entire multitude fell down and expired; the church [Note: “And thus the church of the Mother of God”; recension 2] remained unharmed.

Ten thousand armed Saracens came to destroy the monastery on Mount Sinai [Note: Sinai, where five hundred and more monks lived under the rule of an abbot and had their own bishop there; ten thousand armed Saracens came to kill the monks and destroy their dwellings and churches. As they approached, from a distance of about four miles they saw the entire mountain burning and smoking, with flames rising to heaven; recension 2]. From four miles away they saw the entire mountain burning and flames being carried up to heaven, while everything situated there, together with its inhabitants, remained unharmed.

When they reported this to the king of Babylon, both he and the Saracen people, moved to repentance, grieved deeply over what they had done against the Christians. He issued an order that the basilica of the glorious Sepulchre should be rebuilt.

Yet, once rebuilt, the basilica was no longer equal to the former one either in beauty or in size, the one which Helena, mother of Constantine, had completed at royal expense.

Immediately afterward, famine spread throughout the entire land of the Saracens for three years, and an innumerable multitude of them died of hunger, so that the streets and deserted places were filled with corpses [Note: Variant spelling: *cadeveribus*, witness 1]. Human beings became food and burial for wild beasts and birds.

The devastation of the sword followed them. For the peoples of Arabia spread throughout their land, and those who had survived the famine perished by the sword.

The king of Babylon, who had raised himself arrogantly against God, was captured by them. While still alive, he died with his belly cut open and his entrails removed [Note: “He cast his impious soul into the abyss”; recension 2]. His belly was filled with stones and sewn shut; then, with lead tied to his neck, his corpse was sunk into the sea.

48. In that year Rodulfus, bishop of Périgueux, died while returning from Jerusalem [Note: “He reported the unspeakable things he had seen there”; added in recension 2], and Arnald succeeded him.

Arnald was consecrated at Saint Benedict of Nanteuil [Note: Nanteuil] by Siguin, archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: “By Bishops Grimoard and Islo”; the latter two were the bishops of Angoulême and Saintes; added in recension 2] [Note: “During Lent”; added in recension 2].

Then Gauzbert, lord of the castle of Malemort, was captured by Eblo, viscount of Comborn, and confined in the very strong castle of Melur. By God’s will, after his own peasants stormed and immediately captured the castle [Note: “The castle having suddenly been stormed one morning in the hayfields”; recension 2], he was rescued, and the castle was destroyed [Note: “Given over to the flames”; recension 2].

He then set out for Jerusalem and died [Note: “On the return journey”; recension 2], and after his death he began to shine through miracles. For he was very devoted to the Church and conducted himself honorably.

49. Around this time Bishop Alduin, having taken the most valuable ornaments and vestments of Saint Martial, together with a great abundance of silver, because he held the abbey in his own hands, having purchased it from Wido, hastened to Rome with Duke William before Lent, leaving the monks of Saint Martial in sadness.

As soon as he departed, very many miracles began to shine forth at the tomb of Saint Martial, bringing complete joy to the monks and to all Aquitaine. For that year the most distinguished nobles of Aquitaine, Francia, and Italy celebrated Easter gloriously at Limoges, with a great multitude gathered at Saint Martial.

When the bishop returned, he resolved to destroy and enlarge the basilica of the see of Saint Stephen, which Saint Martial had dedicated. He laid out the lines for the foundations [Note: Variant: *fondamenta*, witness 1] so that he might begin the work fifteen days later.

From there he went to the aforementioned church at Agento [Note: Ahun] [Note: “From which he had expelled the monks”; added in recension 2], and there he breathed his last (1012 or 1013).

His body was brought to Limoges, kept under vigil at the cathedral, and buried at Saint Martin. His successor was his most reverend nephew, Gerald.

He was consecrated at Poitiers, at Saint Hilary, by Siguin, archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: “At Saint Hilary in November, through all the ecclesiastical orders, by Bishop Gislebert, and in the pontifical rank by Siguin, monk and archbishop of Bordeaux”; recension 2].

Gauzlen, archbishop of Bourges, could not be present, because he had not yet been received into the see of Bourges. Nevertheless, he had sent representatives from among the monks of Saint Benedict.

Bishops Gislebert of Poitiers, Arnald of Périgueux, Islo of Saintes, and Grimoard of Angoulême were also present. After the blessing [Note: “Which was performed on Sunday”; added in recension 2], Bishops Arnald and Grimoard accompanied him all the way to Limoges.

First they came together to Saint Martial and were received by the monks [Note: “Together … they led him”; the remainder is absent in recension 2]. From there the monks led them with antiphons to the church of Cairo [Note: De Queroir].

There he sat in the episcopal chair. Carried on the shoulders of the people, while the canons sang antiphons, he received the Gospel book to be read by Bishop Grimoard. Thus, continually blessing with his right hand, he was led with honor to the door of the basilica of Saint Stephen.

Grimoard handed over the church doors to him, Arnald the bell ropes; together they enthroned him in the see of Saint Martial, and Bishop Arnald intoned in a clear voice, “We praise you, O God.”

Everyone kissed the seated bishop. Then they celebrated Mass for the martyrdom of Saint Theodore, whose feast was being observed that same day [Note: The 9th or 12th of November].

For seven days he went about clothed in a consecrated stole with the vestments [Note: “With which he had been blessed”; added in recension 2] and a Roman cope, without the capsule [Note: “But with the colobium and chasuble”; recension 2], and throughout those same consecutive days he celebrated Mass [Note: “Masses at the stations of the city”; recension 2].

[Note: We must not omit that for fifteen days there was a dispute at Poitiers on his account. All the bishops objected that there was no authority of the Fathers requiring the ecclesiastical orders from doorkeeper to priest to be conferred except through the fasts of the four seasons of the year and throughout Lent, with the days of the newly clothed extending to Palm Sunday. But the will of Duke William prevailed, and he did not fear to suppress the proper authority. During these days, Losfred; recension 2.]

Then Abbot Gosfrid began to renovate the royal basilica on a grander scale (1017) [Note: Compare the Annals of Limoges for 1017 and 1018, MGH, Scriptores II, p. 254. But Ademar says in a letter published by Mabillon, Annals IV, p. 721, that Gerald had already returned from Rome in 1013; in the same place, p. 723, he reports that the ancient basilica of the Savior, which at that time threatened to collapse because of its excessive age, was demolished to the ground seven years earlier—that is, in 1021].

In the middle of Lent (1018), as a very great multitude entered the same hall with nocturnal vigils, hastening to the tomb of Saint Martial, more than fifty men and women were trampled by one another inside the church and expired. They were buried the following day.

Bishop Gerald had gone to Rome; therefore a bishop was sent by Arnald, who reconciled the church with episcopal water [Note: “After the third day”; added in recension 2].

Shortly afterward Manichaeans arose throughout Aquitaine, deceiving the people. They denied baptism, the cross, and everything belonging to sound doctrine. Abstaining from food, they appeared like monks and pretended to be chaste, but among themselves they practiced every form of lust and were messengers of Antichrist. They caused many to stray from the faith.

50. At this time William, surnamed Buccauncta, count of Mâcon [Note: Mâcon, which is in Burgundy], built a castle against the monastery of Cluny [Note: Variant: *cluniacensis*, witness 1] in order to overcome Count Hugh.

For this deed divine judgment struck him, so that thereafter he could in no way walk upright. A few days later Count Hugh suddenly captured the castle by force and leveled it to the ground.

After Abbot Gosfrid died (1019), Hugh succeeded him. But Bishop Gerald opposed him, refusing to give him consecration out of jealousy, because he could not claim the abbey for himself. Consequently, for two years there was a considerable civil uprising, until the bishop, ashamed by reason [Note: Variant: *erubescans*, witness 1], gave his consent to Lord Hugh.

The bishop, who was treasurer of Saint Hilary, was traveling to Poitiers before the feast of All Saints when he fell ill at Saint Carrofus and died within fifteen days (1020). He was buried there.

A lead tablet was placed at his head, inscribed as follows:

“Here rests Gerald, bishop of Limoges. He died on the third day before the Ides of November. He presided over this see for eight years.”

After his death Bishop Jordan succeeded him.

51. During these years Odo, lord of Dol [Note: In Brittany], captured the castle of Argenton [Note: Argentomum] by force and ingenuity and expelled its viscount, Wido.

The same Odo built a castle near Massay [Note: Masciacum], beside the monastery. King Robert attacked it but was unable to capture it, and so withdrew frustrated.

At this time the basilica of Saint Martin of Tours, begun with great splendor by Arveus, the treasurer, was completed. After the body of Saint Martin had been raised, it was consecrated with great glory in honor of the twelve apostles.

At this time also the church of Saint Peter, the cathedral of Angoulême, was dedicated by three bishops: Siguin, a monk and archbishop of Bordeaux, and Grimoard and his brother Islo [Note: The final phrase is absent in recension 2].

At that time the church of the Holy Resurrection before the basilica of Saint Eparchius was overthrown by an earthquake [Note: “By a sudden collapse”; recension 2], and a bell tower was begun there.

When the most reverend Gislebert, bishop of Poitiers, died—around 1020—and was buried at the monastery of Maillezais, Bishop Isembert succeeded him.

52. On Good Friday, after the cross had been adored, Rome was endangered by an earthquake and a violent storm.

Immediately, a certain Jew [Note: “From the Greek school”; added in recension 2] informed the lord pope that at that very hour the Jewish synagogues were mocking the figure of the Crucified One.

Pope Benedict [Note: Benedict VIII], diligently investigating and discovering the truth, immediately condemned the perpetrators of the crime to death. After they had been beheaded, the fury of the winds ceased.

At that time Hugh, chaplain of Aimeric, viscount of Rochechouart, was present with the same lord of his at Toulouse for Easter. As is always customary there at Easter, he struck a Jew with a slap, and immediately the Jew’s brain and eyes poured from his wicked head onto the ground.

He died at once, was carried from the synagogue of the Jews in the basilica of Saint Stephen, and was given burial.

At that time the Moors of Córdoba suddenly arrived by sea through the Gallic sea with a large fleet and landed at Narbonne during the night. At first light they spread out around the city with weapons.

As they themselves later told us [Note: “Afterward, as captives”; added in recension 2], their divination had promised them that they would prosper and capture Narbonne.

But the Christians received the body and blood of God from the priests, communicated, and prepared themselves for death. They attacked the Saracens in battle, won the victory, and retained them all, whether killed or captured, together with their ships and much booty.

They either sold the captives or made them serve, and they sent twenty Moors of enormous physical size as a gift to Saint Martial at Limoges.

Abbot Gosfrid kept two of them in servitude and distributed the rest among the foreign nobles who had gathered at Limoges from various regions.

Their speech was not at all Saracen-like; instead, speaking like puppies, they seemed to yelp.

53. At that time an innumerable multitude of Normans from Denmark and the region of Ireland [Note: Variant: *classa*, corrected to *classe* in witness 1] landed with an immense fleet at an Aquitanian port.

As their parents had done, they attempted to lay waste to all Aquitaine and take its inhabitants captive.

Therefore the most courageous Duke William sent word everywhere through the bishops that they should urge the people to implore the Lord’s help with fasts and litanies.

He himself gathered a strong force of chosen men and, in the month of August, with night already approaching, pitched his camp near them along the seashore.

Seeing such a great multitude, the pagans were driven by fear. Throughout the night they dug small pits all around and covered them with turf [Note: Variant: *circuitam*, witness 1], so that the unsuspecting horsemen would fall into them.

At first light, therefore, the careless army, with the duke leading the front line, loosened its horses’ reins and charged over the pagans; immediately it fell into the pits.

As the horses fell with their riders, weighed down by the weight of their armor, the pagans captured many of them. The last ranks of the army, belatedly taking care of the trick [Note: Variant: *novissi*, witness 1], leapt from their horses.

The duke himself, when his horse struck a pit, was thrown headlong. Loaded with armor, he was just about to fall into the hands of his enemies, unless God, who always protects him, had supplied him with strength and presence of mind. With a great leap he escaped and returned to his men at the swiftest pace.

The battle was immediately suspended because of the captives, so that they would not be killed; they were, after all, men of noble birth.

Since on that day victory wavered between both sides, on the following night, when the fullness of the sea offered them an opportunity, the pagans hastily leapt into their ships with the captives and, aided by the sea, escaped. They never again troubled those regions [Note: Variant: *inequitarunt*, witness 1].

For the captives, however, the duke sent immeasurable quantities of silver, weighing out silver for each man and redeeming him.

54. From childhood this duke had been educated in letters and possessed a sufficient knowledge of Scripture. He kept an abundance of books in his palace, and whenever he happened to be free from tumult, he devoted himself personally to reading.

During the longer nights he would study over his books until sleep overcame him. The emperor Louis practiced this, and so did his father, Charles the Great.

The victorious Augustus Theodosius also frequently occupied himself in the palace hall not only by reading but also by writing [Note: “For Octavian Caesar Augustus too, in the palace hall, was very frequently engaged not only in reading but also in writing; he diligently wrote down deeds and all other things” (variant *crebime* in witness c); recension 2.] [Note: Compare the account of Theodosius the Younger, Miscellaneous History XIV, edited by Muratori, p. 96].

For after reading, Caesar Augustus Octavianus himself diligently wrote by hand his own battles, the deeds of the Romans, and everything else [Note: Compare Suetonius, Life of Augustus, chapter 85].

55. In these times the aforementioned Normans, doing what their fathers had never dared to do, entered the island of Ireland—also called Hibernia—with an innumerable fleet, together with their wives and children and the Christian captives whom they had made their slaves, intending that, once the Irish had been exterminated, they themselves should inhabit that exceedingly wealthy land [Note: [Col. 0065] Witness 1 reads “opulantissimam” for “opulentissimam.”]. It has twelve cities with extensive bishoprics, one king, and its own language, but Latin letters. Saint Patrick, a Roman, converted it to the faith and was the first bishop there. It is surrounded on every side by the sea. There the winter solstitial day is scarcely two hours long, and the summer solstitial night is of the same brief duration.

Battle was therefore joined continuously for three days, and not one of the Normans escaped alive. All their wives, together with their little children, threw themselves headlong into the sea and drowned themselves. Those who were captured alive were thrown to wild beasts to be torn apart [Note: [Col. 0065] “to be lacerated” in witness 1.]. The king allowed one of the captives to live because he learned that he was a Christian, and he presented him with gifts.

King Canute of Denmark, a pagan, after the death of King Æthelred of the English (1016), seized his kingdom by treachery and took the queen of the English in marriage. She was the sister of Count Richard of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0065] “of Rouen” misspelled “rotomansis” in witness 1.]. Having become a Christian, he held both kingdoms and brought as many pagans from Denmark as he could to the faith of Christ [Note: [Col. 0065] Witness 2 adds: “His father, a pagan named Asquek [Sven Forkbeard], held only the kingdom of Denmark.”].

When Count Richard of Rouen, son of Richard, was governing the Normans, a multitude of them, armed with their duke Rodulf, attacked Rome and, with Pope Benedict conniving at it, then attacked Apulia, laying everything waste (1017). Basil therefore led an army against them, and after two or three engagements [Note: [Col. 0065] “of the battle” corrected to “of the battles” in witness 1.], the Normans emerged victorious. In the fourth engagement they were defeated and overthrown by the people of Rus’ [Note: [Col. 0066D] They appear to have been in Basil’s army.], reduced to nothing, and countless numbers were led to Constantinople, where they were tormented in prison until the end of their lives. Hence the proverb arose: “A Greek catches a hare with a cart.”

Then the road to Jerusalem was closed for three years. For, because of the anger of the Normans, whatever pilgrims were found were bound by the Greeks, taken to Constantinople, and there imprisoned and afflicted.

Likewise, the Normans, under their duke Roger, went to Spain to kill the pagans [Note: [Col. 0066D] Compare Baluzius, *Marca Hispanica*, p. 429.]. They destroyed innumerable Saracens and took many cities and castles away from them.

On his first arrival, after capturing Saracens, Roger divided each of them into pieces day by day, in the sight of the others, like a pig, cooked him in cauldrons, and served him to them as a banquet. In another house he pretended to eat with his men the remaining half of the limbs. After he had passed through all of them in this way, he carelessly allowed the last man to escape from custody, so that he might report these monstrous deeds to the Saracens [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “Thus fulfilling the story of Thyestes as a true event.”].

Consequently, struck senseless with fear, the Saracens of neighboring Spain, together with their king Musetus, sought peace from Ermessende, countess of Barcelona, and promised to pay an annual tribute. She was a widow and had joined her daughter in marriage to Roger.

After peace had been made with them, Roger began to fight against farther Spain. One day, together with only forty Christians [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “and with Peter, bishop of Toulouse” [Col. 0068C: “It is not certain whether he held office in this year.”]], he encountered five hundred chosen Saracens lying in ambush. Engaging them, he lost his brother, a bastard, and, traversing the field for the third time [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 reads: “and breaking through the opposing ranks for the third time.”], he killed more than a hundred of the enemy. He returned home with his men, and the Saracens did not dare pursue him as he fled.

56. In these days [Note: [Col. 0067C] The year 1010 is commonly assigned, but I think this is false.] the Lord deigned to glorify the times of the most serene Duke William. For in his days the head of Saint John was found by Alduin, a most illustrious abbot, in the basilica of Angoulême, inside a stone shrine shaped like a tower and resembling a pyramid [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 1 has the corrupt reading “techaxasea” for “theca saxea”; “pyramid” is corrected from “piramidis” in witness 1.] (perhaps in 1010). They say that this holy head is the actual head of John the Baptist.

Then, after Easter, Duke William returned from Rome. When he heard this, he was filled with joy and resolved that the holy head should be shown to the people. The head itself is enclosed in a silver censer, on which these letters may be read: “Here rests the head of the Lord’s Forerunner.” Yet it is by no means reliably clear by whom, at what time, or from where it was brought here, or whether it is the Lord’s Forerunner’s [Note: [Col. 0067] “is clear” is written “pater” in witness 1.].

For in the deeds of King Pippin, although lesser matters are recorded, this event—which is among the greatest—is passed over in silence, and the writing composed about it should rightly be judged by learned men to be far from worthless [Note: [Col. 0067C] Compare *Acta Sanctorum*, June IV, pp. 754 ff., where the fabulous history is printed on p. 757.]. In this frivolous page it is reported that, in the days of Pippin, king of Aquitaine, a certain Felix brought the head of Saint John the Baptist by sea from Alexandria to Aquitaine. At that time Theophilus was archbishop of Alexandria—the one whom Luke mentions at the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles, saying, “I composed the first account, O Theophilus, about all things”—and a battle was fought in the district of Alnia between King Pippin and the Walloons. The king placed the head itself upon certain soldiers who had been killed, and they were immediately restored to life [Note: [Col. 0067].

We read in the *History of the Aquitanians*—the reading is uncertain in the edition—that the head of the holy Forerunner was first found by two monks through a revelation at the place where they had arrived; afterward it was brought by the emperor Theodosius to the royal city, Constantinople, and there venerated. But, to return to the matter at hand [addition in witness 2, Col. 0067–0068].].

Thus, when the discovery of Saint John’s head was being displayed, all Aquitaine and Gaul, Italy and Spain, stirred by the report, hastened eagerly to gather there (October). King Robert of the Franks and the queen, King Sancho of Navarre, Duke Sancho of Gascony, Odo of Champagne, counts and princes, together with bishops and abbots and all the dignitaries of the lands, converged there [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 reads: “Robert, king of the Franks; Sancho, king of Navarre; and all their dignitaries converged.”].

There everyone offered precious gifts of various kinds. The aforementioned king of the Franks, having presented a basin [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 reads “a bowl”] of pure gold weighing thirty pounds and precious garments for the adornment of the church [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “of silk and woven with gold”], was reverently received by Duke William [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “at Poitiers”] and returned to France.

It seemed to surpass every happiness and glory: a gathering of singers with the relics of holy canons, monks, and others hastening from every direction to commemorate the holy Forerunner. Among these were carried the relics of the supreme prince who is the father of the Aquitanians and the first evangelizer of Gaul, namely the blessed apostle Martial, together with the relics of Saint Stephen of the see of Limoges.

When Saint Martial’s relics were brought outside his own basilica in a carriage of gold and jeweled treasures [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 1 reads “carried through” instead of “brought out.”], all Aquitaine, which had long suffered from excessive rains, was gladdened by the arrival of its father and restored to fair weather.

With the same treasures, Abbot Josfred and Bishop Gerald, together with numerous princes and an innumerable multitude, turned aside to the basilica of Saint Savior at Carrof. The monks went out to meet them with all the common people for a mile [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 1 reads “the common people” in the singular.], and, with splendid ceremonial [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “celebrating the festival”], sounding antiphons in a loud voice, they led them as far as the altar of the Savior. After Mass had been celebrated, they escorted them in the same manner.

When they had entered the basilica of the holy Forerunner, Bishop Gerald celebrated Mass there for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “before the head of Saint John”], although it was the month of October. The canons of Saint Stephen and the monks of Saint Martial sang tropes and praises alternately [Note: [Col. 0067] Witness 2 adds: “in festive fashion”]. After Mass the bishop blessed the people with Saint John’s head. Thus, rejoicing greatly over the miracles of Saint Martial that had occurred along the way, they returned on the fifth day before the feast of All Saints.

At that time Saint Leonard the Confessor was shining with miracles in the Limousin, and Saint Antoninus the Martyr in the Quercy; people streamed there from every direction.

The glorious duke, reflecting on the honor of God, summoned the most holy Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and renewed regular discipline in the monastery of Saint John. Odilo appointed Rainald abbot in place of the deceased Abbot Alduin [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “recently deceased.”]. When Rainald gave up his spirit [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “after some years”], Lord Odilo set Aimeric over the community as father in his place (about 1020).

Likewise, while the relics of Saint Eparchius were proceeding to the holy Forerunner, the staff of that confessor was carried along with them. This pastoral staff is curved at the top. In its likeness, a fiery staff shone in the sky above the relics of that same saint from the hours of night until sunrise; it was curved at the top [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 reads: “a fiery rod, likewise curved at its summit.”]. This continued until they reached Saint John’s head. After miracles had been performed by Saint Eparchius in healing the sick, they returned with joy [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 1 reads “to” rather than “by.”].

When the canons of Saint Peter of the see of Angoulême were also proceeding with the relics, their bearers, dressed in sacred tunics, crossed a deep river and felt no water, but walked as though across dry land; no sign of water appeared upon them or upon their clothing or footwear [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “Meanwhile the head … is retained,” a passage that is read below in chapter 58. It then continues: “The stone pyramid, however, is covered all around with silver-plated wooden panels, from the abundant silver offered by Sancho, king of Navarre, to the blessed Forerunner. Some time after these things had been done, it happened that …”].

It happened that the men of Saint John and of Duke William rioted in the town of Angeriac, and the duke’s provost was wounded so severely that he was near death, while his hall there was destroyed. Then wicked nobles, especially Count Fulk, who at that time was in the duke’s service at Poitiers, persuaded him during Lent to destroy Saint John’s establishment, expel the monks, and install canons [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 reads: “to expel the monastic community and bring in the violence of the canons.”].

Although the most serene prince was deeply angered by the injury done to him, he nevertheless overcame his anger and the counsels of the wicked and settled the matter peacefully, in a royal manner and with prudent reason. He was always a defender of God’s servants, and God was his helper in all things [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds here: “In these times a comet … devoured,” a passage occurring below in chapter 58.].

Then, by chance, the city of Poitiers was burned, and the duke enlarged the seat of Saint Peter, the other churches, and his palace with greater splendor [Note: [Col. 0069] “splendor” corrected from “decoration” in witness 1.].

57. Finally, after the death of the aforementioned Bishop Gerald (1020), the Limousin nobles contended over the bishopric, attempting to claim the pontificate through the heresy of simony. Then the people of the city, together with the monks and canons, performed litanies on this account, and the most prudent duke held a judicial assembly with his counselor, Count William of Angoulême, at Saint-Junian concerning the matter (1021, January). Wido the viscount and all the princes of the Limousin were present.

There, by God’s will, he chose for the honor of the bishopric Jordan, provost of the church of Saint Leonard, a man of great nobility and simplicity. Rising early from the monastery of Saint-Junian, the duke, with the two bishops Islo and Isimbert and a multitude of princes, reached the city around the sixth hour.

The entire city, rejoicing, came out to meet him, and he soon proceeded to the royal basilica [Note: [Col. 0069C] This is what he calls the church of Saint Martial; compare the *Annals of Limoges*, year 1017, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, p. 252.]. He was received by the monks [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “clad in white garments and silk cloaks”] with the book of the holy Gospels and a censer [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “also with candelabra and holy water”], as the duke was always accustomed to be received by them.

From there he heard Mass at the tomb of Saint Martial and was lodged royally beside the monastery that day. On the following day he ordered the beard of the elected man to be blessed and shaved off. Thus he led Jordan to the seat of Saint Martial in the hall of Saint Stephen and there, with the pastoral staff, clothed him freely in pontifical honor. It was the end of January, and he returned to Poitiers.

When Lent arrived, the duke went to Rome and ordered his son, the very prudent young man William, to find the bishop duly installed upon his return [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 1 reads “I ordered”]. He took care to fulfill this, and in mid-Lent [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 reads: “on the Saturday of mid-Lent”] at Angeriac, before Saint John’s head [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “he was ordained deacon and priest, and on the following Sunday”], Jordan was consecrated bishop by Bishop Islo [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “archbishop of Bordeaux”], and by Roho of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 0070C] “of Angoulême”], and by the bishops Arnold and Isimbert. He was led to Limoges by William, a count of the most illustrious character, and by Arnold, bishop of Périgueux, and was enthroned at the seat of Saint Martial (1021).

But Gauzlen, archbishop of Bourges, to whose diocese Limoges belongs [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “because he was demanding money for the laying on of hands, he was disregarded”], excommunicated the whole Limousin because Jordan had been consecrated bishop without his authority [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “A synod was held in France before King Robert, at which seven archbishops with their suffragan bishops were present on Pentecost”]. He exempted only Saint Martial’s establishment and those things that belonged to him personally, and he prohibited the bishop himself from exercising his office.

Jordan nevertheless made satisfaction and went barefoot to the see of Bourges, with one hundred clerics and monks, all likewise barefoot. There the archbishop and clergy came out to meet them and, leading them in honor, absolved what he had bound (1022) [Note: [Col. 0069] Witness 2 adds: “Although he could have given an account and cleared himself of guilt, if he had wished, before the Roman pope, namely that he had disregarded his own archbishop on account of simony.”].

58. Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0071] From “Meanwhile … devoured” this section is absent in witness 2; compare chapters 69–70, notes 4* and 6*.], after Saint John’s head had been displayed sufficiently to the people, it was kept by order of Duke William and placed again in the former pyramid, where it remains enclosed inside a silver censer suspended by little chains.

In these times a comet, like a sword broader and longer toward the north, appeared on several summer nights. Throughout Gaul and Italy, many cities, castles, and monasteries were subsequently burned by fire. Among them Carrof was accidentally consumed by flames together with the basilica of the Savior. The church of the Holy Cross at the see of Orléans, the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury, and many other places were also devoured by fire.

Duke William, always considering God’s will, restored regular discipline at Saint Carrof (perhaps in 1014), expelling Abbot Peter, a very powerful man [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 adds: “a secular man”], who had obtained his office through the heresy of simony and administered the place in a worldly manner [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 adds: “and foolishly.”]. In his place he installed Gunbald, a regular and servant of God, abbot of Saint Savin [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 adds: “He did what was right, which pleased the eyes of the Lord. Peter, having been expelled, remained at Saint Angelus in the monastery of the Limousin, struck by an exceedingly long paralysis until his death.”].

59. At that time (1022), ten canons of the Holy Cross at Orléans, who appeared more religious than the others, were proved to be Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0071C] Compare Glaber Rodulfus III.8.]. When they refused in any way to return to the faith [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 adds: “at all”], King Robert ordered them first to be deposed from the priestly rank, then expelled from the church, and finally burned by fire.

For they had been deceived by a certain peasant [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 adds: “from Périgueux”], who claimed to perform miracles and carried with him dust from dead children. If he could make someone receive it, he immediately made him a Manichaean. They worshiped the devil, who first appeared to them in the form of an Ethiopian, and afterward in the guise of an angel of light, and who brought them a great quantity of silver every day.

Obeying his words, they had secretly renounced Christ altogether. In private they practiced abominations and crimes—things whose very mention is disgraceful—while in public they deceived true Christians by pretending to be Christians themselves.

Manichaeans were likewise discovered near Toulouse, and they too were destroyed. In various parts of the West, messengers of Antichrist arose and tried to conceal themselves in hiding places; they subverted whatever men and women they could.

A certain canon of Orléans, a cantor named Theobald, who had died three years earlier in that heresy, had appeared religious [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 1 reads “as reliable men testified”; witness 2 reads “as the heretics themselves testified.”]. After his body had been examined and the truth established, Bishop Odolric ordered it removed from the cemetery and thrown out upon the road.

The aforementioned ten, together with Lisoius [Note: [Col. 0071C] Compare the *Acts of the Council of Orléans*, Bouquet X, p. 537.], whom the king had greatly loved because of the holiness he believed him to possess, were condemned to the flames. They feared no fire, confidently declaring that they would emerge unharmed from the flames. Laughing, they were bound in the midst of the fire and immediately reduced entirely to ashes, so that not even a remnant of their bones could be found.

[Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 adds: “In those days one of the princes of Angoulême, Gardrad, since he had no son, built from the foundations in the district of Saintes a monastery at Baciacum in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr [compare the letters of Fulbert, 118–126]. Gathering regular monks there, he placed the venerable Ainard as abbot. Grimoard of Angoulême and his brother Islo, bishop of Saintes, dedicated the place (perhaps in 1014). Gardrad, making a testament, assigned the place to the Roman basilica of Saint Peter, so that five solidi of silver might always be paid each year as a tribute upon the body of Saint Peter.”]

60. At that time (1021), Aimeric, prince of Rançon [Note: [Col. 0071] “of Rançon” is written “roncomensis” in witness 1.], built the castle of Fractabotum in Saintonge during the days of the Resurrection against his lord, William, count of Angoulême, while William himself was in Rome. He had promised William fidelity over the relics of the sacred footwear [Note: [Col. 0071] Witness 2 and the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium* read *sanctarum caligarum*, “of the sacred leggings.”] of Saint Eparchius.

Because he acted perjurously against him, a few days later Josfred, the son of the aforementioned count, met and stabbed him with a sword, and he surrendered his soul without delay.

Count William, together with his son Alduin, besieged the castle for a long time. After capturing it by force and taking it, he destroyed it; much later he rebuilt it and entrusted it to his son Josfred.

William, viscount of Marsillac [Note: [Col. 0072C] Compare chapter 20, note …], and his brother Odolric had long been engaged in grave discord with their brother Alduin over the castle of Rouffiac. As a result, Count William brought about peace between them, and they swore that peace and the terms of their agreement upon the body of Saint Eparchius.

Because they lied to one another and were guilty of perjury, one of them was blinded and the other two were deprived of every honor. For William and Odolric summoned Alduin to themselves by treachery during the first week of Easter, after he had dined with them and slept in their lodging. Before he could rise from bed, they seized him, cut out his tongue, and gouged out his eyes; thus they recovered Rouffiac.

When Count William returned from Rome, he resolved to avenge such impiety. Summoning Duke William, he besieged Marsillac and laid it waste by burning it. He spared the traitors’ lives and limbs but deprived them of every honor; and, after Alduin had been punished with blindness, he granted him Rouffiac.

Several years later, by order of the same count, Alduin his son rebuilt Marsillac and retained it for his own use. The same Alduin, at his father’s command, built the castle of Montignac anew.

61. At that time (1025), two monks of Saint Martial, men of the foremost rank, conspicuous for their religious devotion, illustrious in holiness, and radiant in wisdom [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 adds: “raised to the priesthood”], who loved one another above all others, sustained the whole monastery like two pillars, and shone like two candelabra [Col. 0073B], and who sat beside one another at table—Roger the cantor and Adalbert the armarius [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 reads: “the cantor, of illustrious birth, brother of the glorious dean Adalbert, the armarius”]—on the holy day of Easter both saw in a vision that they were being summoned by Christ, and in that same week they laudably reached the end of life [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 adds: “struck by a brief and severe illness.”].

A third monk, worthy of approval for his holiness [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 names him Fulcherius], and soon afterward Abbot Hugh, most steadfast in the love of God, followed them to the heavenly realms. Odolric, a most prudent man, succeeded as abbot, and Bishop Jordan consecrated him.

62. In those days (1023), in January [Note: [Col. 0073C] On January 24. On the ninth day of the same month there was also an eclipse of the moon.], around the sixth hour, a solar eclipse occurred for one hour. The moon also repeatedly suffered an affliction: now blood-red, now blue, now disappearing.

Two stars were also seen in the south, in the sign of Leo, fighting one another throughout the whole autumn: the larger and brighter one in the east, the smaller one in the west. The smaller ran as though angry and afraid toward the larger, which did not allow it to come near. Instead, striking it at a distance with a mane of rays, it drove it back toward the west.

Afterward Pope Benedict died (1024), and John succeeded him. Basil, emperor of the Greeks, ended his days (1025), and his brother Constantine ruled in his place. Arbert, bishop of Cologne, died, later becoming renowned for miracles after his death.

Emperor Henry also died without sons (1024), and at his death left the imperial insignia to his kinsman, the younger Conrad [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 expands: “He left them to his brother Bruno, bishop of the city of Osnabrück, and to the archbishop of Cologne and the archbishop of Mainz, so that they might choose … [the intervening word is now illegible in witness c; perhaps *creantes*, ‘creating’] after him as emperor. These bishops, having gathered the kingdom, proclaimed litanies and fasts [the words ‘and fasts’ cannot be read in witness c] to the Lord for this matter. Then the people chose Conrad, nephew of the deceased Emperor Henry. But the bishops, with sounder counsel, chose another Conrad, who had Henry’s niece as his wife, because he was strong in spirit and most upright in judgment. They anointed and consecrated him with the oil of consecration to royal rank at the city of Mainz, and gave him the scepter, crown, and lance of Saint Maurice. When Easter came, he advanced toward Rome with an innumerable army. Because the Roman citizens refused to open their gates, and the matter could not be brought to an end without the shedding of much human blood, Emperor Conrad did not wish the Easter festival to be stained with human blood and therefore remained at Ravenna. There the lord pope brought him the imperial crown and crowned him with his own hands as emperor of the Romans on Easter Day (1027). In the following year, on Easter Day itself, the lord Emperor Conrad ordered his son to be consecrated king at Aachen. The boy, named Henry, was of tender age when he was consecrated king (1028). Seventy-seven bishops from both Italy and Gaul were present. And thus the lord Conrad, persuaded …”].

He, having shortly afterward been brought to the point of death, entrusted to the most powerful and prudent prince Conrad the scepter, crown, and sacred lance, on the condition that, if he lived, he would return them, but if he died, Conrad himself would possess the empire. This happened by God’s will. For he recovered from his illness but was deprived of the empire.

Conrad, however, encouraged by the Roman pope [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 adds: “John”] and by all the bishops and nobles of the kingdom, assumed the empire because he showed the balance of justice.

The younger man who had given him the opportunity to rule began to oppose him through civil strife, but Conrad prevailed [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 expands: “The emperor prevailed so greatly that he captured him alive and kept him in custody for as long as he wished.”]. These events seemed to be signified by the larger and smaller stars.

The Lombards, meanwhile, rejoicing at the emperor’s death, destroyed the imperial palace that was at Pavia. Wishing to throw off the imperial yoke, many of their nobles came to the city of Poitiers to Duke William of Aquitaine, intending to make him their king.

He wisely took precautions and, together with Count William of Angoulême, entered the territories of the Lombards. He held a judicial assembly for a long time with the princes of Italy, but, finding no faithfulness in them [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 2 initially read “thus,” corrected to “faithfulness” in witness 1.], he treated their praise and honor as nothing [Col. 0074C].

On the return journey he was informed [Note: [Col. 0073] Witness 1 reads “would be informed”] that Wido, the viscount, had died. At the intercession of William, count of Angoulême, he appointed the viscount Ademarus to Limoges in place of his deceased father.

63. In these times (1022), Arveus [Note: [Col. 0075C] Compare Glaber Rodulfus III.4.], distinguished for holiness and treasurer of Saint Martin of Tours [Note: [Col. 0075] From “of Tours” onward this is absent in witness 2, which instead reads *furoris*.], died in Christ and was buried in the atrium of the central basilica at the feet of the Crucified One.

At Tours he built anew an oratory in honor of the Mother of God, where he established a community of holy women to serve God under the governance of a rule.

64. At that time Count Fulk of Anjou, since he could not openly overcome Count Arbert of Maine [Note: [Col. 0075] Witness 2 adds: “son of Hugh”], summoned him by treachery to the capitol of the city of Saintes, as though he were granting him the city itself as a benefice.

He seized Arbert, who was unsuspecting and imagined no evil, imprisoning him in the capitol by an infamous act of treachery on the second day of the first week of Lent. Fulk’s wife also tried by deceit to seize Arbert’s wife on that same day, before she heard that her husband had been captured [Note: [Col. 0075] Witness 2 reads: “before the treachery against Arbert had been heard about among them.”], but someone anticipated her and revealed the plot.

Therefore Fulk, fearing Arbert’s wife and the nobles, did not dare kill him. Instead, he guarded him most carefully in prison for two years, and the Lord rescued the innocent man from his hands.

At that time (1026) the most glorious Richard, count of Rouen, died and was buried at the monastery of Fécamp, in the basilica of the Holy Trinity. His son Richard succeeded him, but not long afterward he too was killed by poison (1028), and his brother Robert succeeded him.

65. At that time (1026), William, count of Angoulême, traveled through Bavaria to the Sepulchre of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0075C] The *Deeds of the Bishops of Angoulême*, chapter 25, adds: “For before him no one had passed through those regions, since Christianity was still new in Hungary and Slavonia.”].

Odo of Bourges, prince of Déols; Richard, abbot of Verdun; Richard, abbot of Saint Eparchius of Angoulême; his prince and counselor Gerald of Fénes; Amalfred, later abbot; and a great company of nobles accompanied him.

King Stephen of Hungary received him with every honor and enriched him with gifts. He began his journey on the first day of October (1026), reached the holy city in the first week of March (1027), and returned home in the third week of June.

On his return he turned aside through Limoges, where the entire community of monks of Saint Martial came out to meet and receive him in festive splendor. When news of his arrival reached Angoulême, all the princes—not only those of Angoulême but also those of Périgord and Saintonge—and people of every age and sex ran to meet him, filled with joy and longing to see him.

The monastic clergy of Saint Eparchius, in white garments and various ornaments, together with a great multitude of people and clerics or canons, rejoicing, went out to meet him one mile beyond the city, with praises and antiphons. All crying out in a loud voice, “We praise you, O God,” they led him onward as was customary.

Then he chose as abbot Amalfred, the monk who had been with him, from the basilica of blessed Eparchius. For Abbot Richard had died on the journey at Solombria [Note: [Col. 0076C] “Selembria”], a city of Greece this side of Constantinople, and had been buried there on the eve of Epiphany.

Bishop Roho ordained the aforementioned abbot; the count himself, Odolric abbot of Saint Martial attended with the rank of monks, as did the neighboring abbots and a very great nobility of princes.

66. In that same year the count himself was stricken with bodily illness, even to the point of death. In that year the city of Saintes was burned by impious Christians [Note: [Col. 0075] “which is painful to say” is added in 2], together with the very basilica of Saint Peter, the episcopal seat [Note: [Col. 0075] The following material is omitted, and 2 continues: “Stephen, however, remained, and, leaping out, came away unharmed in body. At that same hour he ran on foot to the tomb of blessed Eparchius to give thanks to God; there he had kept an all-night vigil on the preceding night. Then, riding back into the city, he began to recover. The wicked woman, however, was soon tortured with many torments without the count’s knowledge [ [Col. 0075] *eecruciata* in c.], but even so she did not confess; with her heart blocked by the devil, she uttered no word or sound from her mouth. Yet she was convicted by the testimony of only three women who had been involved with her in these magical practices. The women extracted from beneath the earth, before everyone, certain fantastic images made from mud [ [Col. 0075] *lino* in the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*, c. 25], already thoroughly decayed through age [ [Col. 0075] singular *putrefacta* in c.]. The count therefore spared the wicked woman and did not allow her to be tortured further, granting her life. Jerome relates this in his exposition of Daniel, and the same account is also read in the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*, c. 25. These passages agree with 2 in what follows, although they contain many more additions.”], and that place itself remained deserted from divine worship for a long time. Desiring to avenge this injury to God, the aforementioned count gradually began to be deprived of bodily strength. In the city of Angoulême, beside the church of Saint Andrew, he ordered a house to be prepared for himself near the place of divine office [Col. 0076C], and there, falling ill, he began to lie sick (in the year 1028).

There all the princes and nobles from every region continually visited him. Since some said that he was ill through magical practices—for he had ordinarily enjoyed a robust and healthy body—yet now his body was failing neither in the manner of old men nor in that of young men, a certain wicked woman was discovered to have practiced magical arts against him. Since she did not confess, the matter was entrusted to God’s judgment, so that what lay hidden as truth might be proved by the outcome of a victory between two champions. After the oaths had therefore been made, Stephen, the count’s messenger, and William, the woman’s defender, fought one another for a long time [Col. 0077A]. Stephen was victorious without injury to his body; the other, his head battered and covered with blood, stood on his feet from the third hour until the ninth, and, defeated and half-dead, was carried away in men’s arms. He lay in bed for a long time [Note: [Col. 0077] *longuo* in 1]. Even so the wicked woman did not confess; nevertheless, she was convicted by the testimony of three women who had taken part with her in these magical practices.

Jerome relates that Antiochus Epiphanes [Note: [Col. 0077] *anthiocum* with the *h* erased in 1] was driven into madness by the fantasies of sorcerers and, overwhelmed by certain delusions, died of illness. Nor is it surprising, if God permits it, that a Christian should suffer bodily illness through the illusions of sorcerers, since we know that blessed Job was struck by the devil with a severe ulcer and that Paul was buffeted by an angel of Satan. Bodily illness, which is destined to perish, is not therefore to be feared; the striking of souls is more grievous than that of bodies [Col. 0077B].

The count therefore spared the wicked woman and did not allow her to be tortured. That same Count William, however, received penance from the bishops and abbots. Having arranged all his affairs, and assigning his honor by name among his sons and his wife as it seemed best to him, he was reconciled and absolved. Throughout the whole season of Lent he regularly attended Masses and the worship of God, until, in the first week before Easter, he was fortified with holy oil and the viaticum. Having adored and kissed the wood of the cross, he gave his spirit back to God with a praiseworthy end into the hands of Bishop Roo and the priests (in the year 1028, April 6) [Note: [Col. 0077] *reddere* in 1].

For two days his body was watched over by clerics and monks [Col. 0077C] in the basilica of the seat of the apostle Peter. The whole city was filled with mourning [Note: [Col. 0077] 2 has *Planctu t. c. r. est de*, “the whole city was filled with mourning,” and the following words are absent; they are read in the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*, where there is also added: “a multitude of nobles and crowds came from everywhere, weeping”]. On Holy Sunday, April 7, his body was carried with *Hosanna*, branches, and flowers to the basilica of blessed Eparchius, and was buried there before the altar of Saint Dionysius. Two bishops buried him: Roo of Angoulême and Arnaldus of Périgueux.

At his head his son Alduin ordered a lead tablet to be placed, inscribed as follows:

> Here lies the lord and beloved William, count of Angoulême, who died in peace in the very year in which he came from Jerusalem, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, on the vigil of *Hosanna*, in the year 1028 from the Incarnation; and all his offspring lie in the place of Saint Eparchius [Col. 0078A].

[Note: [Col. 0077] Meanwhile, at Alduin’s command, the wicked women were burned by flames outside the city. But after the count had been buried, they immediately proceeded [2; *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*].]

Thus, after his burial, the bishops proceeded with the clergy and the people in a holy Sunday procession and completed the station [Note: [Col. 0077] 2 adds “solemnly”]. Hilduin, his son, succeeded William in the principate of Angoulême. At the beginning of his principate a splendid sign of joy was shown: the people passed from the grief of the burial to rejoicing, crying out to meet the Lord, “Hosanna in the highest; blessed is the kingdom of our father David,” while carrying in their hands palms of victory, branches of security, and flowers of sweetness.

The aforementioned William offered Saint Eparchius various and precious gifts for his burial [Note: [Col. 0077] “both in lands and in sons” [*silvis*, “forests,” in the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*], along with much gold and silver and other things]. Among the other gifts [ [Col. 0077] *ca* in c.] he offered a golden cross set with precious gems, weighing seven pounds; silver candelabra made in Saracen fashion [ [Col. 0077] *sarravifa* in the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*], weighing fifteen pounds [ [Col. 0077] *pensancie* in c.; 2 and the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*, which also add: “the whole forest of Veniacum, which had formerly belonged to Saint Eparchius but had later been alienated from him by the counts’ predecessors”]; much gold and silver; and he relinquished [Note: [Col. 0077] Perhaps it should be read *guerpivit*, “he relinquished”] the forest of Vasnacum. He also gave away [Note: [Col. 0077C] That is, “he abandoned” or “handed over,” from *laxare*, French *laisser*] two silver candelabra weighing three hundred solidi, and gave away [Col. 0078B] one processional golden cross set with gems.

67. On the following day [Note: [Col. 0077] 1 has “on the following day”] after his burial, the fortress of Blaye was taken from Count Alduin by treachery by his brother Josfredus. Immediately Count Hilduin went there with military force, and, quickly capturing the fortress itself, received its surrender and stationed a military guard there. He returned to Angoulême to celebrate Easter.

After his return, his brother Josfredus, during the especially important days of Good Friday, the burial, and Easter, built another new castle opposite Blaye. When Hilduin learned this, he by no means neglected the work of God, but celebrated holy Easter with great glory and joy (April 14). On the third day after the feast, having mobilized his chosen army, he went out to engage in battle; for he had heard that his brother wished to fight him and was gathering an army [Col. 0078C]. Thus he besieged the newly fortified castle [Note: [Col. 0077] 2 adds “immediately”] and awaited battle with a fierce heart.

But his brother did not dare to challenge him to combat [Note: [Col. 0077] 2 omits the words from “and afterward” through “they became friends”], seeing that he had a powerful force. After eight days, when the castle had been stormed and captured, Josfredus came to him as a suppliant. Count Hilduin immediately forgave him and agreed to peace, and they became friends. Then, as a benefice, the count granted his brother Josfredus three parts of Blaye and retained the fourth for himself; they were reconciled under suitable conditions in special affection [Note: [Col. 0077] “Then Josfredus commended his son into the hands of his brother Count Alduin because of the two castles in Saintonge, namely Archiac and Botamvilla, which have always belonged to the count of Angoulême” [*comitatum* in the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium*; *comitem* in c.]. 2 and the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium* add “of Angoulême”].

68. At that time Odolricus, abbot of Saint Martial, a man of most vigilant uprightness, came to Angoulême to Count Hilduin. He then donated to Saint Martial the church of Saint Mary in the territory of Bordeaux, together with the large island of Dordogne [Note: [Col. 0079B] Dordogne], on which it is situated. The island or church itself lies a little more than a mile from the fortress of Fronsac, which belonged to the aforesaid count as his hereditary property, together with all the surrounding lands and castles. He retained this possession by hereditary right through his most noble wife, Countess Alaizia.

His father William, returning from Jerusalem, was a good example to many princes [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 and the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium* add “nobles, middling people, and the poor”]. Immediately Isimbertus, bishop of Poitiers, Jordan, bishop of Limoges, Count Fulk, and many of the leading men [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 adds “and an infinite multitude of middling people, poor, and rich”; the *Gesta episcoporum Engolismensium* likewise] set out for Jerusalem [Col. 0079B].

69. In those days Duke William convened a council of bishops and abbots at Saint-Carrof, to extinguish the heresies that were commonly being spread by the Manichaeans. All the princes of Aquitaine were present there, and he ordered them to establish peace and to venerate the catholic Church of God [Col. 0080A].

When Siguinus, archbishop of Bordeaux, had died—around the year 1020—and Acius had been ordained after him and had died not long afterward, William, duke of Aquitaine, and Sancho, duke of Gascony, having gathered an assembly at Blaye—around the year 1027—appointed Gotefridus archbishop, a Frank by nationality [Note: [Col. 0079] *natione* in 1] and honorable in conduct. He was consecrated there [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 adds “at Saint-Romain”] by the suffragan bishops [Note: [Col. 0079] *suffraneis* in 1]. [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 adds: “For Bishop Hislo of Saintes, who had accepted that archbishopric while Acius was alive, afflicted with paralysis, and at his request, voluntarily relinquished it according to the provisions of the canons.”]

70. Sancho, king of Navarre, also, taking Gascons with him, led an army against the Saracens. Having devastated Spain, he returned with much plunder and a great triumph (in the year 1027). In that same year Alfonso, king of Galicia, ravaged the Saracens with a great assault. When one of the cities of Spain was almost surrendering to him under siege [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 omits the continuation], while he himself, having laid aside his arms, was restraining the Christians raging outside from fighting the enemy, he was wounded by his adversaries—those whom he had resolved to spare—by an arrow shot from outside the walls, and died. Thus his army returned in grief, not without great sorrow, mourning its prince [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 adds “most valiant”].

[Col. 0079]

## MEMORIAL OF THE ABBOTS OF LIMOGES OF THE BASILICA OF SAINT MARTIAL THE APOSTLE

By Ademar, monk of Saint Cybard.

(At Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, II, 271.)

[Col. 0079C] In the year 848 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eleventh indiction, on the day before the Kalends of April, in the time of Kings Lothair and Charles the Bald, in the ninth year after the death of Louis the Emperor, son of the Emperor Charlemagne, and after the battle of Fontenay, the canonical habit was changed into the monastic habit in the basilica of the Savior of the world and of his apostle Martial in the city of Limoges.

Ainardus, abbot of that place, undertook this not unwillingly but voluntarily, together with the canons themselves, under divine inspiration. Both he himself and all his canons made themselves monks in that same place, and they did not wish to appoint an abbot from among themselves [Col. 0080C], but chose as their abbot Dodo, a regular abbot of Saint Savin by name; and they became fully regular.

The first abbot of this place who had been a monk was therefore that same Dodo, and he presided for three years.

The second abbot, Abbo, presided for eleven years. In his fifth year Charles the Bald was anointed king at Limoges by Radulfus, archbishop of Bourges, and Stodilo, bishop of Limoges, together with many other archbishops and bishops of France, Aquitaine, Italy, and Burgundy. In that year the monastery of Bellolocus was founded and consecrated by Archbishop Rodulfus [Col. 0081A], and Saint Geraldus of Aurillac was born. Abbo died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

The third abbot, Benedictus, presided for fifteen years. During his pontificate the Normans first began to pour into France and Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0081D] Rather, during their second invasion]. He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. Aldo succeeded Bishop Stodilo and died on the Nones of October; he was buried in the basilica of the Savior at Limoges. After him Geilo became bishop; he died on the fourth day before the Ides of July. After him Anselmus held the bishopric.

The fourth abbot, Gonsindus, presided for eighteen years. In his second year Emperor Charles the Bald died, and his son Louis the Stammerer assumed the kingdom. After he had reigned for three years, he died, and his son Charles assumed the kingdom [Col. 0081B] [Note: [Col. 0081D] This is erroneous], from whom King Odo took the kingdom and reigned in his place. I would not place this abbot in the catalogue if he had not been clothed in the monastic habit. For, being far too secular in heart, he took many churches and lands from the basilica of the apostle Martial and uselessly granted them to secular powers. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.

The fifth abbot, Fulbertus, presided for six years. He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of February. In his fifth year King Odo died, and Charles the Younger recovered the kingdom. In that same year Anselmus, bishop of Limoges, died on the fifth day before the Ides of February and was buried in the basilica of the Savior beside the body of the aforementioned Bishop Aldo.

The sixth abbot, Fulbertus, presided for twenty years. In his sixth year Saint Geraldus died at Aurillac on the third day before the Ides of October and was buried in the monastery of the apostle Peter, which he himself had built [Col. 0081C]. In the nineteenth year of this abbot, William, duke and count of Auvergne, died; he had built the monastery of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0081D] This is entirely true, although Besly resists it and writes that this author was false, even though Besly himself, having misunderstood a passage of Flodoard, fell into error and supplied a cause of error to other very learned men [Col. 0082D].]. The same Abbot Fulbertus died on the Kalends of February.

The seventh abbot, Stephanus, presided for seventeen years. He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December. He made over the altar of the Savior a church of gold, gems, and silver, which they call the *Munera*. He made two towers in the castle of Saint Martial: one facing the Scutarii, named Orgoleta, and the other facing the Arenas, named Fustivia. This was done at the command of King Charles the Younger to repel Duke William, count of Poitiers; and he named the castle itself after his own name [Col. 0081D] *Stenopolis*, as though “the city of Stephen” [Note: [Col. 0082D] In the French Catalogue of the same abbots of Saint Martial, it is more correctly called *Stephanopolis*, and the structures are called gates, not towers].

The eighth abbot, Aimo, presided for six years. He died on the Nones of May. He was a friend of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, whom he ordered to compose the Life of Saint Geraldus. He honored Turpio, bishop of Limoges, his brother, with the greatest affection; and in the third year after Turpio’s death, that same holy Bishop Turpio died on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. From his niece Officia, by name, were born Adalbertus the dean and Rotgerius, their father being Fulcherius, in the hereditary property belonging to them by right, which is called Campanense [Col. 0082A], beside the fortress of Potentia. A third, Raimundus, younger by birth, was the full brother of both; I, Ademar, was his son by my mother Hildegard [or Aldeard].

After Abbot Aimo, the abbacy was vacant for thirty-one years without a shepherd. I do not wish to place in the catalogue of abbots the man who presided for so many years but did so little good, since this would be unjust. For, clothed in no monastic habit whatsoever but in a canonical—or rather a lay—one, he held the headship of the place for so many years, abbot in name alone. Whoever wishes to know his name: he was called Aimericus. In his tenth year the monastery of Saint Martial was burned by divine judgment. He did not fear to give all the land of this monastery and its churches both to his relatives and to other secular powers. On the third day [Col. 0082B] before his death he put on the monastic habit, fearing the perjury he had sworn to King Lothair in France when he had been appointed abbot by the king. For he swore to the king that he would become a monk, but, a mocker of God, he delayed it until death. Had the crime of his presumption not effaced him, he would have been recorded as the ninth abbot.

The ninth abbot, Guigo, presided for seventeen years. He died at Angoulême on the third day before the Kalends of October and was buried in the basilica of Saint Eparchius before the altar of Saint Stephen, since he was also abbot of that monastery. He appointed the aforementioned Adalbertus dean in the basilica of Saint Martial. In his twelfth year King Lothair came to Limoges and ordered the abbot to build the walls of the castle. After returning to France, he died a few days later, and his offspring were thereafter deprived of the kingdom [Col. 0082C]. For his brother Charles was sent to prison by Duke Hugh, and Hugh himself became king. His son Robert, a most wise and pious king, is still alive to this day.

During the rule of this abbot, the golden crypt of the apostle Martial was burned by fire in the middle of the night. A candle, insufficiently extinguished, fell among a multitude of candles; the most precious stones were then damaged by the fire, and whatever there was within the building that could burn was consumed by the flames. The books were burned, the gold and silver melted, and within fifteen days the golden crypt, with its gems, was restored anew by Josbertus, a monk and keeper of the tomb. The same Josbertus made a golden image of the apostle Saint Martial, seated above the altar, blessing the people with his right hand and holding a book of the Gospel in his left [Col. 0082D]. The aforementioned fire occurred in June, before the feast of Saint Martial.

The tenth abbot, Josfredus, presided for seven years. He died on the fifth day before the Ides of October. During his rule a fiery plague raged among the bodies of the Aquitanians, and more than forty thousand people died from that pestilence. Therefore Abbot Josfredus and the bishops of Aquitaine gathered at Limoges, raised the body of the apostle Saint Martial [Col. 0083A], and transferred it to the Mount of Joy. Then, on the day before the Nones of December, they restored it to its tomb, and the fiery pestilence ceased. From the golden image he made a golden reliquary set with gems, in which the body of Saint Martial was carried. He made two crosses of gold and gems.

The eleventh abbot, Adalbaldus, presided for nine years. He recovered the basilica of Saint Martial by royal authority. During his rule the aforementioned dean Adalbertus, a most illustrious man, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Adalbaldus died beside him in the third month, namely on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August.

The twelfth abbot, likewise Josfredus, presided for twelve years. He made a golden crown set with gems, hanging before the body of blessed Martial. He renovated the basilica of the Savior anew with magnificent workmanship [Col. 0083B]. In his third year the tomb of the Lord Jesus Christ at Jerusalem was broken open by the Saracens and Jews, as were the other churches throughout that province. Only the church of Bethlehem, where he was born, could not be broken open. For the power of God defended it and destroyed all the Saracens who had come to violate it by a most evil death: their bellies immediately burst open, and the anger of God followed against the Saracens. More than nine hundred thousand Saracens and Jews died, from hunger as well as pestilence, over three years.

That tomb was broken open on the third day before the Kalends of October, and immediately the Saracens themselves began to rebuild it, for they had been terrified by fear. In the tenth year of this abbot, on the night of Mid-Lent Sunday, while crowds were entering the old basilica of the Savior for Matins [Col. 0083C], fifty-two people were killed by the extreme pressure at the entrance of the doors. Josfredus himself died on the Nones of December.

The thirteenth abbot, Hugo, presided for six years. In France he held a conference with King Robert and Gauzlenus, archbishop of Bourges, together with many bishops and wise men of France, concerning the apostleship of Saint Martial: why some seemed to count him among the apostles and others among the confessors [Col. 0084A].

Those who counted him among the confessors did so because they did not think that there were any apostles besides the Twelve. Others did so because they did not find his name among the four evangelists. Those who held a sounder judgment after understanding the matter affirmed that he was one distinguished apostle after the Twelve, because he lived with the Twelve and deserved to receive from the Lord the same grace of apostleship that they had received.

At that council it was determined by all that he should be numbered only in the catalogue of the apostles, just as the evangelist John, who departed in peace, ought to be. For many testimonies were found from antiquity confessing him as an apostle in the litanies and in other writings throughout Gaul and Britain [Col. 0084B], Italy and Spain. Those are Hebionite heretics who do not believe in apostles other than the Twelve. For his canonical deeds, always received by the Church, sufficiently make clear the privilege of his apostleship. Without doubt he is one of the seventy-two apostles whom the Lord sent like lambs among wolves. The Greeks, and also the evangelist Luke and the apostle Paul in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, call those seventy-two apostles.

Among the wiser Greeks also, the apostle Martial is very well known. Returning from France, as soon as he learned the council’s decision, Hugo wrote Martial into the litanies among the apostles, not trusting his own argument but the ancient testimonies. From then on Martial was acclaimed an apostle by all Catholics, completely and not partially [Col. 0084C], and the Hebionites were confounded.

In the sixth year of this abbot, Rogerius, brother of the dean Adalbertus, a most illustrious man and my teacher and paternal uncle, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. On the thirty-second day after him, that same Abbot Hugo died, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. I commend their souls to you, Lord Jesus.

The following material is not by Ademar but by another monk, a certain Helias of Rofiaco, and so forth.

[Col. 0083]

The fourteenth abbot, Odolricus, presided. He acquired two leonine pallia and a smaller Gospel book of gold. He had the head of this church dedicated with great honor, and redeemed two churches, walls, and the castle [Col. 0083D]. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of October.

The fifteenth, Abbot Petrus, presided; he made the gate at Mourmelier.

The sixteenth, Mainardus, presided as abbot after him.

The seventeenth abbot of this place was the lord Ademar, of holy and venerable memory. How greatly he ennobled this place above those who had preceded him, and how he increased it in order and religion as well as in the abundance of temporal goods, cannot be fully narrated. After governing this place religiously and faithfully for fifty years and nine months, and adorning it, as has been said, with every good, he rested in peace in the year 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September [Col. 0084D], and rests in the chapter house.

The eighteenth was Bernardus, abbot.
