The nineteenth was Lord Amblardus, a man of great religious devotion and uprightness. In his time this monastery, together with the adjoining town, was burned by fire [Note: [Col. 0083] In the year 1121 the castle of Saint Martial was burned, as was its monastery with all its workshops]. He governed this monastery for twenty-eight years. He died in the year 1143. He ordered the consuls to build walls and ditches.

The twentieth was Abbot Albertus, a very religious and upright man. He governed for thirteen years and died in the year 1150, on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

The twenty-first, Lord Petrus, a man of great religious devotion and uprightness, presided for four years [Col. 0085A] and three months. He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.

The twenty-second abbot, Petrus, was a man of great religious devotion and uprightness and a strict corrector of wicked conduct. He governed for thirteen years and eight months. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of September, in the year 1164 from the Incarnation of the Lord. In that year the conflict between Henry, the most upright king of the land of England, and his sons, which had lasted nearly two years, was brought to an end, and so forth. Helias of Rofiaco, his chaplain, the writer of these events, was made a monk of this church by his good pleasure.

The twenty-third abbot, Lord Isembertus, was a very gentle and peaceful man and highly favored by the powerful. He rendered invalid, through persistent protests, the exaction that the bishop of Limoges or the canons, under the name of a confraternity, were violently demanding from the people. He governed for twenty-four years. One month before he died, he resigned pastoral care in the chapter house. When, on the appointed day for carrying out the election, Lord the abbot of Cluny, together with the priors and provosts and many others of our community, had likewise assembled, he breathed out his soul in a good confession among those who had gathered together—namely, on the night preceding the day of the election, while the community was celebrating Compline.

On the following day the election was freely held. On Monday he was honorably committed to burial, in the presence of Bishops John of Limoges and G. of Cahors, and the abbots of Cluny, the newly elected abbot of Saint Martial, Saint Peter of Solignac, Saint Augustine, and Saint Martin.

The twenty-fourth, Lord Hugo, [presided] for sixteen years.

The twenty-fifth abbot was Petrus, called de la Grissa [Col. 0086B].

The twenty-sixth was Petrus Davalacum.

[The manuscript contains a long lacuna.]

[Col. 0085] “The remaining material could not be read in the manuscript,” says Joannes Beslius, whose copy, received in good faith from the distinguished scholar Jacobus Puteanus together with several other autograph writings of that most learned author, we have reproduced.

On the third day before the Kalends of September, in the year 1066 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the city of Limoges was burned; one hundred and twenty people died in it.

Likewise, in the year 1105, on the Kalends of June, the city of Limoges was burned by the men of the castle of Saint Martial. In that conflagration the mother church of Saint Stephen was burned with all its workshops, as were likewise the monastery of Saint Mary, the church of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Maurice, Saint Trinity, Saint Genesius, and Saint Domnolenus.

[Col. 0087]

## ADEMAR’S LETTER ON THE APOSTLESHIP OF SAINT MARTIAL

(At Mabillon, *Annales*, volume IV, Appendix, p. 717.)

## NOTICE

(Mabillon, *Annales*, book LVI, no. 49)

[Col. 0087A] In this year a council was held at Limoges, as Ademar of Chabanais testifies in his apologetic letter on the apostleship of Saint Martial, which he defended against Benedict, prior of the monastery of Chiusa, in a rather harsh style.

This letter is addressed to Jordan, bishop of Limoges; Odolricus, the most learned abbot of the monasteries of blessed Martial; Rainaldus the levite; and Albericus and the other canons of the greater church of Saint Stephen; to Aimericus, Petrus, and Geraldus the dean, as well as Adelardus and the other monks of Saint Martial; to Engelricus and his brother Teotardus, canons of the church of blessed Mary, mother of the Lord, at Le Puy; to Werno the grammarian, monk of the church of the apostle Saint Peter at Bellovacum; to Geraldus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Limoges; to Rotgerius, provost of the monastery of Saint Valeria at Cambon; [Col. 0087B] likewise to Geraldus, the most learned abbot of Solignac; to Arnaldus, bishop of Rodez, and Theodericus, bishop of Metz; and also to Cunegund, empress; to Conon, or Conrad, Caesar Augustus; to William, duke of the Aquitanians; and finally to John, the Roman pope.

He says that the last three are intermingled with the others so that, if this letter should happen to reach them, they might favor his opinion. I think that the others attended the aforementioned council of Limoges, concerning which Ademar adds the following:

> “From you, indeed, not without great exaltation, after the council of Limoges had ended, I departed on the fourth day of August, returning to the city of Angoulême, where, from my earliest childhood until now, at the age of forty, I have spent my life in the monastery of blessed Eparchius.”

Moreover, he explicitly gives the year in which he was writing in the following words [Col. 0087C]:

> “For even up to the present year in which we speak, which is the year 1028 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the eleventh indiction, and from the assumption of the blessed apostle Martial the nine hundred and fifty-fourth, there are only 160 years since the monastic order in this place”—namely, Saint Martial’s—“was changed from the canonical.”

Perhaps at that time Benedict, prior of the monastery of Chiusa among the people of Turin, had come to Limoges, where he disputed against Ademar and other monks concerning the apostleship of Saint Martial. From there he went to the monastery of Buxerium in the district of Poitiers [Col. 0088A], and, remaining there throughout the month of September, held frequent conferences on the same subject, especially in the gathering of the monks of Angoulême and Brantôme who had assembled there for the feast of the Nativity of blessed Mary. He drew many over to his opinion, boasting that Ademar had been defeated and overcome by him at Limoges.

When Ademar learned this through his own people, he wrote that sharp and pointed letter against Benedict. In it he recalls what had been said and done in the Limoges debate and recounts, with much boasting, various claims made by Benedict: namely, that he was the nephew of the abbot of Chiusa; that he had studied grammar for nine years in Lombardy and France and had given two thousand solidi to his teachers; that he had two large houses filled with books of every kind [Col. 0088B]; and that, once he had left school, no one under heaven would be wiser than he.

He also claimed to be prior of the monastery of Chiusa and to be destined to become its abbot after his uncle’s death, together with many other statements of that kind, which I do not doubt Ademar at least exaggerated. Certainly Ademar himself exceeded the bounds of modesty in this letter, in which he assails Benedict with every kind of insult, calling him a Hebionite and a heretic, for the specific reason that he rejected the apostleship of Saint Martial.

Ademar asserted this so stubbornly that he says he would not obey even if the pope decided otherwise, lest he appear disobedient to God, who had made Martial an apostle. Furthermore, he maintained that this question could not be settled except in a general council of all the bishops of Gaul and [Col. 0088C] Italy together with the Roman pope.

A certain Bernardus is said to have come to Limoges with Benedict: a monk of Ravenna, skilled in the art of medicine, who agreed with Benedict. Salgionius also held the same opinion. He had become a monk after being a canon, at Angers; nevertheless, he said that, when he was going to Jerusalem, he had seen a certain monk named John, a most accomplished grammarian from the city of Rheims, who daily on the ship pronounced Martial’s name among the order of the apostles.

This is sufficient from that letter, whose autograph itself, as I believe, the distinguished Baluzius most generously shared with me.

## ADEMAR’S LETTER ON THE APOSTLESHIP OF MARTIAL

[Col. 0089]

[Col. 0089A] To the most glorious and outstanding lords and shepherds of the holy Church, JORDAN, bishop of Limoges, and ODOLRIC, most learned grammarian and abbot of the monasteries of the blessed apostle Martial; and also to the most reverend fathers, liberally instructed in philosophical studies, RAINALD, levite of the see of Limoges, ALBERIC, and all the canons of the church of the protomartyr blessed Stephen; to AIMERIC and PETER, skilled architect, and GERALD the dean, and ADALARD, as well as all the other monks of the aforesaid apostle; to ENGELRIC and his brother TEOTARD, grammarians and canons of the see of Anisianum, the church of blessed Mary, mother of the Lord; to WERNON, grammarian and monk of the church of blessed Peter the apostle at Bellac; to GERALD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Limoges, and to his entire congregation; to ROTGER, provost of the monastery of Saint Valeria at Cambon; likewise to GERALD, a most learned man and abbot of Solignac, and to all his monks; to ARNALD, bishop of Rodez; to THEODERIC, grammarian and bishop of Metz; to CONEGUND, empress of the Romans; to CONON, emperor, Caesar Augustus; to WILLIAM, orthodox grammarian and most powerful duke of the Aquitanians; to JOHN, pope of Rome: ADEMAR, the last of the priests of Angoulême, sends observance in all things of the rule of right faith, in faith, hope, and charity toward our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, according to the sound teaching of the apostles.

I do not want you to wonder that, among the names of those with whom I have never spoken, I have included three persons only—namely the pope, the emperor, and the duke of Aquitaine—concerning the apostle Martial. For if this should perhaps reach them, I wish their serenity to smile upon these true assertions.

I left you, after the Council of Limoges, on the fourth day of August, not without great rejoicing, returning to the city of Angoulême, where from my tenderest childhood until now, at the age of forty, I have spent my life in the monastery of blessed Eparchius. For I rejoiced that you had, by God’s grace, rejected the inappropriate and long-established negligence of the earlier clerics of Aquitaine, by which you treated the holy apostle of God Martial as little better than one of the modern confessors or the younger modern bishops; and that, concerning the fact that blessed Martial himself is an ancient and natural [Col. 0089D] apostle—as the ancient tradition of our fathers and the true testimony of the Greeks attest—you had recovered the truth rather than begun it.

To you four alone I now speak with particular emphasis: Bishop Jordan, Abbot Odolric, Rainald, and Aimeric. Thus, while I was rejoicing in the Lord with Abbot Amalfred, all the brethren, and Bishop Roho over the glory of the truth of the blessed apostle Martial, suddenly the ancient enemy, through his agents, clouded my heart with anxious bitterness, so that I preferred to die rather than live, and wished that I had wings like a dove, with which I might immediately fly to you [Col. 0090A] and rest.

We were imitating your custom—or rather that of the most ancient fathers—which is old, good, and praiseworthy: in the litanies and in all the daily offices, we had followed the same holy apostle. And behold, the aged serpent disturbed all these things, which had been rightly begun, or rather recovered, by authoritative men for the praise of God and the advancement of the holy Church. Everyone except me and your Gauzbert turned away from the truth.

For I hasten gladly to contend for the truth unto death, knowing that it is more useful for a scandal to arise than for the truth to be abandoned. Neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, neither angels nor principalities, neither height nor depth, nor any creature will be able to separate me from the charity and truth of God, which [Col. 0090B] is in Christ Jesus our Lord and in his apostle Martial.

Two of our number—monks in clothing and name alone, not in deeds or morals, whose names I considered it sacrilegious to insert in this work—came without a blessing from their monastery to the Limoges territory called Buxeria during this September. There they most unhappily allowed themselves to be corrupted by the ancient serpent’s poison, by a certain Lombard heretic dressed in a monastic habit but not a monk: a devil.

Nor did they heed the false prophet who came from Lombard Clusa to Aquitaine in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly is a ravenous wolf. May the archangel Michael and his angels cast him from the presence of God, so that he may not remain in the catholic Church with his dragon-king, and so that his place may no longer be found in heaven. Then may the great voice of the saints be heard in heaven—which is the present Church—saying: “Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our Lord and the authority of his Christ have come, and the glory and truth of his apostles.” Therefore, “let the heavens rejoice and those who dwell in them.”

At the Council of Limoges, indeed, the language of the wise men—which is what you are—adorned knowledge. But at Buxeria the mouth of a fool, moistened with wine—or rather with the serpent’s poison—spewed forth folly. For you, rooted and grounded in charity, patient through charity, kind, not envious, not acting wrongly, not puffed up, not ambitious, not seeking your own interests, not provoked, not thinking evil, not rejoicing over [Col. 0090D] iniquity but rejoicing with the truth, took care to reveal the truth to the people: that Martial himself is a natural apostle—not, as barking dogs say, a new one, but the most ancient, and in every respect elected by Christ after the first twelve apostles; and not merely an apostle, but also Christ’s disciple in the flesh and fellow disciple of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

For it is greater to be Christ’s disciple in the flesh than an apostle after Christ’s ascension. No knowledgeable person is unaware that there were many false apostles and apostles of the truth after Christ’s ascension who nevertheless had not been Christ’s disciples in the flesh. And although the four Evangelists are silent about him, since they treated the Lord’s deeds only in summary, nevertheless the book of his deeds, written by his disciple Aurelian, has always been received by the catholic Church and sufficiently records from the beginning the grace of his apostleship.

But a certain Lombard—more an Hebionite than a cenobite, unworthy even of his own name, and more properly to be regarded as accursed through truth than blessed through falsehood—while lodging in the church at Buxeria, did not fear to spew forth unspeakable blasphemies not only against Martial, the apostle of God, but also against the Son of God himself, in an assembly of the monks of Angoulême and Brantôme and of the priests of Limoges, who had come for the feast of the birth of Mary, the Mother of God and perpetual virgin [Col. 0091B].

And just as it is customary among the Ariomanites, Photinians, Manichaeans, and other heretics alienated from God to be exceedingly talkative and very fluent in the rolling movement of their tongues—for this alone is characteristic of heretics—so that, since they cannot overwhelm their brutish hearers with simple truth, they may at least cast them into the pit of error through marvelous and figurative chatter, while eloquence rather than wisdom is admired in them, he began shamelessly to disparage your authority before everyone.

He censured all who, at your command, had accepted apostolic prayers in honor of blessed Martial; all who recited his name in the litanies among the apostles. He declared with detestable barking that all who proclaimed him an apostle were praying in vain, and that such prayers and litanies served only for sin. He hissed, in the manner of a crafty serpent, that those who consented to this had already been condemned in soul and body.

He said that the Masses of the blessed apostle, which our venerable shepherd Odolric had ordered to be distributed to the priests, were filth and ought all to be burned in fire.

“Your Mass of such an apostle,” he said, “is filth; it is in vain, and is just as though someone placed earthly filth upon the altar. Those who recite them are heretics. Aquitaine has been defiled by such a great heresy. The bishops of Aquitaine are rustics: when they first heard of this heresy, they rose up but did not immediately summon a council, nor excommunicate the entire place of Saint Martial, nor condemn it, nor prohibit there [lacuna] sacred ministry and divine worship.

“Abbot Odolric has little understanding of letters and is poorly educated; before rustics he pretends to be wise. The monks of the holy apostle are idiots, and there is no literary wisdom in that monastery. The abbot himself and his monks have established a false apostleship for the sake of the money in which they abound, and for the sake of arrogance and pride. They are vicious and proud, believing themselves alone admirable and superior to all monastic communities, as though they were kings. They disdain to speak with others, are inhospitable, and despise everyone. They have not dared to summon a council concerning this matter, can show no authority, but secretly make a false apostle, as though they were making counterfeit money—or, to use his own word, a ‘counterfeit’ apostle.

“‘I am very learned in letters,’ he says. ‘I contradict them. I affirm that Saint Martial is not an apostle in any way. I say that his entire life is false. I maintain that he was never Christ’s disciple in the flesh, that he was in no way present at the Supper, and that he rendered the Lord no service in washing his feet. The Lord held that supper alone with the twelve alone. The words he spoke at the supper he spoke only to the eleven, when the son of perdition had gone out. Neither Mary, the Lord’s mother, nor anyone else was present there. Jesus himself put on his garments; he himself girded himself with a towel; he himself poured water into the basin; he had no servant.

“‘I will wage battle to prove that Saint Martial is not an apostle if anyone contradicts me. I was in Limoges shortly ago, when, out of fear of the bishop—that he might excommunicate them for this matter—and in order to secure his agreement with their false apostle, those monks carried that counterfeit apostle to the see.

“‘There the canons of Saint Stephen, knowing me to be very wise, secretly begged me to destroy this apostleship. In the chapter house of Saint Stephen those foolish and illiterate monks who had secretly invented this attempted to argue with me. But they immediately fell silent, ashamed and terrified, and were unable to produce any authority for me, either anywhere in the old books or in the old litanies, in which he was proclaimed an apostle.

“‘And when a certain Ademar—who appeared to know some grammatical art and who had been the first to devise this heresy, chiefly out of flattery, to please the abbot and monks, and who had also been corrupted by their money—wanted to debate with me, persuading the brutish and foolish that Martial was rightly proclaimed an apostle without any ancient authority, he became confused at my first speech, not knowing what to answer, shamefully hid himself, and fled from my wisdom. I could not see him again, because, realizing that I was wise, he feared my presence.’”

And when our men said to him, “We thought that Ademar knew how to answer a wise man, and he himself has often been accustomed to report many authorities to us showing how blessed Martial is naturally an apostle, and that if we proclaim him an apostle this does not harm us but benefits us. Therefore, following him, both as an example and out of love for the fellowship of the congregation of Saint Martial himself, we adopted the custom of commemorating him as an apostle a month ago,” he continued:

“That foolish Ademar will never dare mutter against me about this matter. Otherwise, I will struggle with him through deeds, not words; or, as in a lawsuit, I will make my champion fight his champion, and through the oaths made upon the altar my champion will have the victory.”

Most pious shepherds, you have heard the impious, false, useless, unjust, and blasphemy-filled words of the heresiarch. Hear my truth.

While I was attentively looking upon the body of the distinguished apostle of God Martial and standing beside the pontifical chair, when the hour was already approaching at which the bishop was to enter for the divine offices, and he had already been clothed in pontifical vestments, suddenly—amid no small ferocity of grief, since Stephen and Daniel the monks were distressed by that enemy of truth—they called me and led me to that Antichrist. For one who is opposed to Christ’s will and deed is an Antichrist.

I addressed him first: “You deny,” I said, “that Martial is an apostle.”

But he, who was still arguing with the brethren there in a loud voice, with bloodshot eyes and an inflated face, replied: “We were saying nothing about Saint Martial, but about certain questions concerning the Gospels.”

Stephen said to him: “You were just denying that Saint Martial was present with the Lord among the eleven apostles.”

Deeply stirred by his words, I said: “Listen. Blessed Martial truly is an apostle.”

He, drawing forth all his breath, said to me: “Explain how.”

And I said: “If it is true that he received from Christ’s own mouth, in the flesh, the power of binding and loosing—not from any other man—then he is undoubtedly a true, complete, entire, full, perfect, and natural apostle, and a great, distinguished, and glorious one.”

Unable to deny this, he said: “Certainly that is true. But I say that Christ granted that power to no one except the eleven apostles. Martial, however, was never proclaimed an apostle until yesterday, when you invented this matter.”

I replied: “Apart from the writer of his Life, who lived in the apostolic age and reveals his apostleship most brilliantly and more clearly than daylight, others after him, including our predecessors, openly proclaimed him an apostle everywhere—in responsories, hymns, and every kind of composition, as well as in many writings.”

He said: “Neither you nor he nor I should be believed; let the books be believed. Let the books come.”

I replied: “The bishop intends to enter for Mass, which I wish to hear. Moreover, the excessive density of the great crowd in this place threatens us, and a great tumult of people hostile to our disputation surrounds us. Wait for us until tomorrow, and I will produce before you the testimony of books, in which you will find him written down as an apostle from ancient times, both in the litanies and elsewhere. For books cannot come here unless they have been carried here—and I admit that this is a participle.”

Either not understanding, or deliberately lying, he reported at Buxeria that I had told him all the books had been destroyed. But *delatus* means “carried,” whereas *deletus* means “destroyed.” So contentious and malicious was he that, although he was extremely sharp in grammatical art, he would not debate Latin with me in that same place while corrupting it with ridiculous barbarisms.

For I, speaking in Latin fashion, compelled him to speak in Latin fashion; and when he uttered barbarous expressions, I concealed the matter patiently from those standing around.

When he said, “Martial is an apostolic man, not an apostle,” and I opposed him, saying, “Martial is not an apostolic man but an apostle, for he is one of the seventy-two apostles,” he responded: “Where is the authority for those men? I know of no apostles except the twelve.”

Peter the monk immediately brought an open Gospel and placed it before us, where it read: “The Lord appointed also seventy-two others”—with “apostles” understood. At once he fell silent in confusion [Col. 0094A].

Then he immediately rose and began to flee through the crowd like a guilty dog. But I seized him by the clothing on his arms and compelled him to read the passage in Mark: “Jesus summoned the twelve and began to send them out two by two.”

Taking advantage of the mention of the twelve, he said: “I seek nothing else; this is my authority,” and withdrew.

I followed him and began gently to cite among the crowd certain statements of Jerome in support of our authoritative assertion. He replied: “You speak well and reasonably, and I know how to speak with you; but I do not know how to reason with those monks, because they speak irrationally. And I tell you by God: before you arrived, we had said nothing about Saint Martial. Your monks were saying that Paul was not an apostle, and for that reason I was angry with them.”

Then I said: “Although Paul is not one of the twelve, nevertheless whoever denies that he is an apostle is a heretic.”

He replied: “That is so.”

In this way we both departed, and I was unable to see him again, although I searched for him carefully, until, when it had grown late, I encountered him after evening had already fallen.

Such was my confusion. Yet on that same day I was filled with joy through divine splendor, since I had seen the body of the apostle carried gloriously from the basilica of the see to the basilica of the Savior, and everything had gone well. Perhaps during the evening office, present with many clerics at the tomb of the apostle himself, after the apostolic psalms I was the first to utter in a loud voice these words of melody:

“Fellow citizens with the apostles and members of God’s household have arrived today, carrying peace and illuminating their native lands, to give peace to the nations and free the Lord’s people.”

I then added these words: “Let heaven exult in praises, let earth resound with joys, let sacred solemnities sing the glory of the apostles”—and so forth to the end. All the clerics present joined me in sounding out these praises with joyful and elevated voices.

When they were finished, I suddenly saw the cowl-wearing Antichrist mentioned above emerge from the dense crowd. I rejoiced, for I thought I was seeing not a wolf but a lamb. I took him by the right hand and led him to the chancel, where, setting aside the company of my most beloved noble kinsmen, who had come from far away for the feast and were waiting there for my sake, I sat down with the man whom I believed to be angelic.

I declare that I was deceived; I grieve over my imprudence, because I did not foresee a wolf in the lamb, a dragon in the fish, a serpent in the eel, a lioness in the sheep, a lion in the ram, a troglodyte in the Lombard, a Manichaean in the monk, an Antichrist in the Christian, and a devil in the man. Certainly, if I had foreseen it, I would not even have said “hail” to him. For whoever says “hail” to him, like the two brethren of ours mentioned above who were subverted by him, shares in his evil works.

As we were speaking, the monk Aimeric brought him a very ancient volume containing the Life of the holy apostle Martial. It stated that Martial was not a gentile but a Hebrew, from the illustrious tribe of the patriarch Benjamin; that Martial had been converted not to the preaching of the apostles but to that of the Lord himself; that Martial, having left father and mother, had continually adhered to the Lord’s discipleship; and that Martial had not been Peter’s disciple—for the apostles had no disciples until after Pentecost.

It stated that Martial, because he was of the same tribe as Peter, associated more familiarly with Peter than with the other apostles; that Martial obeyed Peter’s prompting in all things in service of the Lord; that Martial was present at the miracle of Lazarus; that as a young man Martial ministered to the Lord at the holy Supper; and that when the Lord entered through closed doors, at a time when Thomas was not there, Martial was present with the other apostles. There he received the power of binding and loosing not from Peter but from the Lord himself, together with the other apostles and with Peter, and received the Holy Spirit.

It stated that Martial went with the eleven to Galilee at Peter’s urging, and there received from the Lord himself, not from Peter, together with the remaining apostles and with Peter, the power to preach the Gospel to all nations; that Martial was present with the other apostles at Christ’s ascension and there received the episcopal blessing from the Lord himself, not from Peter, together with the other disciples and with Peter; and that Martial entered and departed with the other apostles until Pentecost.

At Pentecost, it stated, he received the Holy Spirit from heaven with the other apostles, acquired knowledge of all languages, and became, with the other apostles, an unconquerable witness to Christ’s resurrection.

It stated that after receiving the Holy Spirit Martial did not separate from Peter but came with him to Antioch; that, when Peter asked him as a brother—not commanding him as a disciple—Martial continually preached the word of God in Greece, both in Peter’s absence and in his presence; and that, as a perfect disciple of Christ, he was perfectly instructed by him first directly and then through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, and was fully learned in the speech of languages for reaching whatever nation he came to.

It stated that Martial came with Peter to Rome when Peter asked him as a brother, not when he commanded him as a disciple; and that Martial was sent to Gaul not at Peter’s discretion but at the Lord’s command, through the utterance of that blessed chief of the apostles.

When he had read these things through, and could not deny that Martial was truly an apostle of God—for he had been endowed by Christ himself with the grace of so many gifts together with the eleven apostles—he finally burst out, with wrinkled brow, in this false statement:

“Some people are accustomed to say that his ancient Life perished in the fire when this place burned, and that nothing of these things was written in it, except only that after the Lord’s ascension he was converted through Peter’s preaching, like many other pagans, instructed by him, and after a long time ordained bishop and sent only to the city of Limoges, just as Apollinaris was sent to Ravenna and Mark to Alexandria. They say that a certain monk of this place fabricated this Life through his flattering falsehood; therefore I do not believe it.

“Nevertheless, because this book is old, it has greater authority than it would have if it were new. For ancient authorities, even if they are false, are more readily believed by us than new ones, even if they are true.”

Then I said: “What you say—that this Life was fabricated by some unknown monk through falsehood—is incredible, impossible, and altogether empty. For even now, namely up to the present year in which we are speaking, which is the 1028th from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the eleventh indiction, and the 954th from the assumption of the blessed apostle Martial, only 160 years have passed since the monastic order in this place was changed from a canonical one.

“And this Life, in the very form in which it is read here, is found throughout the provinces of Gaul, Spain, and Britain, as well as Italy. Without doubt it was held by many churches before the burning of this place, which occurred long afterward, after the monks had entered here.

“For among so many and such great catholic men, through whom sound Gaul has always endured—and especially the Church of Limoges, which has remained entirely untouched by every heresy—what devil would have dared or been able to write such a great lie? If a lie had been written, God forbid, none of the catholics would have accepted it, and it would certainly not be heard anywhere on earth today.

“Therefore this Life is entirely truthful. Our catholic fathers accepted this Life in truth, and I believe it firmly and embrace and approve it with all affection, just as I do the four holy Gospels. Whoever denies it I declare an enemy of truth and reject as a public heretic.

“As for what you further claim—that old false authorities ought rather to be accepted than new true ones—this is a grave prejudice. Truth is always truth, and truth must never be rejected, nor falsehood accepted. Nor should we pay attention to who says something, but to what he says.

“A single boy spoke the truth and rescued from death a woman whom two elders, speaking falsely, were leading to execution. Three boys cast into the flames spoke a new truth, while an aged king affirmed an ancient falsehood.

“If we speak the truth, why are we not believed? Truly, we are believed by lovers of truth. And what wonder if lovers of truth, even though some do not understand, nevertheless believe that Martial is an apostle of truth? For ‘if you do not believe, you will not understand’; and everyone who is of the truth hears the voice of truth.

“And although the king is stronger and wine is stronger, the women called falsehoods are stronger still, and truth conquers all these things. Truth is glorious and humble, not proud.

“We do not act proudly in this matter, but with a humility pleasing to God we desire to advance, looking down upon the insolent—those whose raw ostentation led them to prefer him . . . the first rather than the later apostle in certain places. We test everything by him, hold fast to what is good, and know that what is changeable is not true. At the command of our venerable father Odolric, a man of all knowledge and every virtue, we desire to exercise in free charity whatever in this question is mature, wholesome, sound, and established.”

While we were saying these and similar things, and he himself was affirming, “If this Life is true, then Martial is without any doubt truly an apostle,” Aimeric again entered to us with an ancient Breviary from the tomb and showed him a very old text, a responsory contained in it:

“Glorious is Martial, apostle of Gaul, who planted the Church in such a way that, although he suffered many things, when he departed in peace he nevertheless left it in peace.”

To this he replied: “This too is ancient, not new, and the man who composed this composition was wise.”

We also showed him in the same volume an old sequential hymn, written in ancient letters:

“Citizens of heaven, accept him as a colleague; let all Aquitaine use him as its apostle.”

He said: “I think it is not without divine will that you proclaim him an apostle, since nearly the whole world has already learned this through the report of fame.”

I do not know what further authority I could have shown him after these three testimonies, since “every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses.” It was night, and we departed.

I dined with you, most beloved abbot, and because I wished to return to the city of Angoulême at first light the next day, you freely dismissed me. In the morning I saw that canine Lombard himself, but because of my journey I did not converse with him.

Had I known what kind of man he was, I would have waited for him at Limoges for a year, until the serpent’s head had been crushed by the rod of my reasoning. For afterward he boasted, lying back with his scaly, dragon-like neck, that he had struggled to fight me on behalf of the blessed apostle Martial and that for this reason I had fled as quickly as possible; that Bishop Jordan and his canons had rejected everything they had begun and would never again consent to this apostleship, because they had heard that he was its opponent.

With that Hebionite there came to Buxeria a certain outstanding practitioner of the medical art, Bernard by name, a monk of Ravenna. While he was conversing with me at Egolisma and, as he had heard from the aforementioned Lombard, bringing forward many similarly contradictory assertions concerning the holy apostle Martial, he asked my abbot from Ravenna: “What chief argument am I to state for saying that Martial is an apostle?” I immediately answered him: “Because he was a disciple of the Lord, like Peter, and received from the Lord himself, in the flesh, the power of binding and loosing. This is the substance of his apostleship.”

But he replied: “Benedict, prior of Clusa, a perfect grammarian, denies that he was a disciple of the Lord; rather, he says that Peter converted him and gave him the power of binding and loosing, just as bishops give it to others whom they ordain bishops. He also asserts that this Life of his, which is found in these regions, is not the earlier ancient one, but a new composition fabricated by a certain monk about a hundred years ago. He says that it is possessed in another form in Lombardy, where Martial is said to be the equal of Saint Apollinaris and of Saints Fronto, Saturninus, Dionysius, Austremonius, Hilary of Poitiers, and Martin of Tours.”

Then, having found an opportunity to mock the fool, I laughed and said: “If the Lombard were a perfect grammarian, he would not make such statements. If there is another Life that obscures this true one, it is without a doubt spurious and false, and in no way to be received by the Catholic Church; it must be abhorred by us as poison.

“Nevertheless, even if Martial were only Peter’s disciple and had received from him the power of binding [Col. 0098A] and loosing, as that Lombard falsely claims, he could still quite appropriately be proclaimed an apostle. For Jerome too, that greatest pillar of the Church, and the Venerable Priest Bede proclaim Timothy, Paul’s disciple, an apostle in their Chronicles; Paul drew him to the faith and ordained him bishop, and he also wrote two letters to him. Onesimus likewise, Paul’s disciple, is proclaimed an apostle by many Churches, and Paul himself calls Epaphroditus, whom he sent to the Philippians, an apostle.

“Mark and Luke also, evangelists and disciples of the apostles, are proclaimed apostles by many Churches. For Peter sent Mark to Alexandria without episcopal ordination. After he had first converted the province of Egypt, he was consecrated bishop by neighboring bishops, although against his will, even though he had cut off the thumb of his hand so that he would be disqualified from the priesthood. He had been converted from the tribe of Levi in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension, when the apostles were preaching.

“Thus, even if Martial were not Christ’s disciple in the flesh—which it is impious to say—nevertheless, because he first converted Aquitania, he could rightly be proclaimed an apostle. For from the city of Rome to the Pyrenees there is no other saint who converted an entire province, or who has until today been written by the ancients in the litanies in the order of the apostles, except Martial alone.

“Gerald, bishop of Limoges, who returned from Rome fifteen years ago, also testified to us that he had happened to read there a volume in which it was written how Martial first [Col. 0098C] preached Christ at Ravenna while coming into Gaul, and how, after him and a long time later, Apollinaris, an apostolic man, came there. Hence his Life also says:

“‘Accordingly, Martial, having traversed so great a stretch of the earth with his disciples and everywhere preaching the seed of the word of God, entered and came to the castle of Tulle in the territory of Limoges.’

“Jerome says that there is this distinction between apostles and apostolic men: apostles are those who first began to preach in each province. Hence he also maintains that apostles can still be made in the Church, when the signs and indications of apostleship are fulfilled—that is, if even today, or up to the end of the world, there should be some province to which no preacher had previously come, and someone who first came to it in any manner began to preach there and founded only one Church in it, he is rightly an apostle. Those preachers and bishops who come after him are apostolic men.

“For he says that apostolic men are those who came after the apostles, to spread Christianity through regions and provinces already illuminated by them, whether during their lifetime or after their death; or those whom the apostles ordained so that they might remain as their successors in the cities of that province which the apostles had preached. For this reason he calls Titus an apostolic man, because Paul left him as his vicar in the province of Crete, which Paul had first preached, so that Titus might establish presbyters or bishops throughout its cities.

“Hence the same Jerome says in his letter to the presbyter Paulinus: ‘Let bishops and presbyters,’ he says, ‘take the apostles and apostolic men as examples, and, possessing their honor, strive also to possess their merit.’ Again, in his letter to Pammachius, On the Best Kind of Translation, he says: ‘Luke, an apostolic man and evangelist, writes that Stephen, the first martyr of Christ, recounted in the Jewish assembly, and so forth.’ Again, in the same work: ‘Mark,’ he says, ‘the disciple of Peter, thus begins his Gospel: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ,”’ and so forth.

“These are what the custom of the Churches records in the order of the apostles in the litanies, and concerning them it produces psalms and an apostolic chant, as has already been said, although today many Churches fail to observe this through negligence. This is human error; understanding and correction of the error belong to the prudent. For, in remembrance of these and similar men, whose names are pronounced in the litanies in the order of the apostles, wiser ecclesiastics more appropriately recite psalms, verses, hymns, responsories, and antiphons as those of apostles rather than of confessors or martyrs.

“But Pope Gregory himself, who lived long after the time of the apostles—even though he did not personally go to the province of the English, where no preacher had previously arrived, but sent preachers—nevertheless, because they received the faith through his immense labor and assistance, is rightly called an apostle among those same English, since whatever labor the other preachers undertook after him is all attributed to him.

“If, then, Gregory deserved to be an apostle and to be proclaimed one five hundred years after the time of the first apostles, because he possesses the signs of apostleship, why is Martial not much more an apostle? He was a witness to Christ together with Peter, beginning from Jerusalem, in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth; and, being the first to illuminate Gaul, he won the whole province of Aquitania for Christ. Aquitania itself is the seal of his apostleship before the Lord, to the end of the world. Without a doubt, he founded Churches there and first established bishops in them, city by city.

“For Austremonius was not the first bishop over the Arvernians, nor Martin over the Turonians, nor Hilary over the people of Poitiers. The same is true of the other cities. Dionysius, first a disciple of Paul and afterward of Clement, was sent by him to Gaul and was the first bishop over Paris, [Col. 0099D] where there was not yet a Church. For the ancient sees—the see of Tours in honor of Saint Peter and that of Orléans in honor of Saint Stephen—had been founded by the apostle Martial; later one was changed to the honor of Saint Maurice and the other to that of the Holy Cross. Since he came after Martial, he is not proclaimed an apostle but an apostolic man.

“Although Saturninus was the foremost of the bishops of Toulouse, which prudent person says that he was the first bishop there, when his own acts are read to say that a Church had already been consecrated there, and Bede reports that he suffered martyrdom in the time of Decius? It is likewise clear that there was Christianity at Périgueux before Fronto, since his own acts teach that he was born there, cut his hair, and went to Egypt to the hermit Apollonius.

“We do not disparage these men. But whoever carefully searches out the truth can discover that Martial subjected all Aquitania to Christ as an apostle, not merely the territory of Limoges as the bishop of a single diocese. Therefore, speaking in truth as from God, before God, in Christ, we call him an apostle. The other bishops who were in Gaul after him, and who will be there to the end of the world, are apostolic men, although all bishops, whether holy or unholy, are called and are apostles, as I can plausibly demonstrate.

“For apart from this manner in which all bishops are and can be called apostles, in what sense is Apollinaris an apostle, when Peter had already begun earlier to be proclaimed in the region of Italy, whose city is Ravenna?”

The physician replied: “Behold, Martial is an apostle—but what is his apostleship?”

I answered: “Gaul in particular, because he himself was the first to enter it.”

He said: “You are lying, for Gaul belongs to Peter’s apostleship.”

And I said: “The whole world, not Gaul alone, belongs to Peter’s apostleship. For to him in particular the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the pastures of Christ’s sheep were entrusted. But his particular apostleship is Italy, because he preached it, died there, and lies there. Likewise, Gaul is Martial’s particular apostleship, because he first illuminated it by announcing the Lord Jesus Christ, and died there and lies there.

“In the same way, Spain is James’s particular apostleship, although he himself did not preach there. His body, however, was carried across the sea to Galicia by seven of his disciples, who first announced the name of Christ in Spain and buried their master’s body there. For even if Martial had no particular apostleship—which without doubt he does—nevertheless, because he received from Christ’s own mouth, in the flesh, the power of binding and loosing, he certainly would not be deprived of the name of apostle.

“Answer me, then: what is Paul’s apostleship? Show me the apostleship of Barnabas, Luke, Onesimus, Silas, and Timothy, since the Church also proclaims these men apostles.”

When he remained silent, I said: “Even if they do not have a particular apostleship, they are nevertheless rightly proclaimed apostles, because they fulfilled the office of apostles—that is, they evangelized the nations. For not all bishops possessed their own sees, nor all presbyters their own churches, nor all abbots their own monasteries. Many bishops even abandoned their own bishoprics, yet did not thereby lose the name of bishop.

“So also, some of the apostles existed without a particular apostleship, and yet they are apostles. But since, without doubt, Gaul is Martial’s particular apostleship, both by God’s appointment and by Martial’s own, there are many inviolate testimonies both from all Aquitania and from our Catholic fathers of old. Thus, in every respect, Martial is perfectly an apostle, because he received from Christ the power of binding and loosing, and entered Gaul to evangelize not by his own will, judgment, or presumption, but at the Lord’s command and under Peter’s compulsion. Moreover, what he began well, he continued even better, and he possesses a particular apostleship—that is, the grace and proclamation of faith among the peoples of Gaul for the name of Christ.

“Therefore, whoever insists that he is not an apostle must insist that no one is an apostle except the Twelve alone; he must erase Paul’s name from the litanies and from the order of the apostles, as well as the names of Barnabas, Cleopas, Mark, Luke, Timothy, Onesimus, Silas, and Judas, together with the universal invocation that says: ‘All holy apostles, evangelists, and disciples of the Lord.’ Such a person must be a Hebionite heretic. We Catholics will in no way submit to him; rather, following the footsteps of our earlier fathers, we will invoke the name of Martial in the order of the apostles.”

To this the physician said: “Benedict says that this invocation concerns no others who are not named, but is a gathering of the apostles who have already been named.”

I replied: “The devil interprets the Scriptures badly, and this heretic explains the litanies badly. The entire Catholic Church is wiser than this one heretic. If it is a gathering of those previously named, it is superfluous. If it is an invocation both of those previously named and of all those who have not been named, which is undoubtedly the truth, it is necessary—as is also the universal invocation of angels, patriarchs and prophets, the innocent and martyrs, confessors and virgins, and all the saints. Unless they are invoked in this way, they cannot be invoked individually by name.

“For besides the four evangelists there are other evangelists, as Luke himself recalls in the Acts of the Apostles: Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven deacons, baptized the eunuch of Queen Candace, and, after being carried away by the Spirit, was found at Azotus and, passing through, evangelized the cities.

“He is not the apostle Philip, as some are mistaken. He is also that Philip—not the apostle but the evangelist—who went down to the city of Samaria and preached Christ to its inhabitants; through him Simon Magus came to believe, he who had previously attached himself to Philip.

“And the apostle Paul says of the many other apostles and evangelists whom the Lord chose after his Ascension: ‘And he himself gave some as apostles, others as evangelists, others as prophets and teachers.’ Silas and Judas, apostles ordained by other apostles, are called prophets; and Paul was ordained an apostle by prophets and teachers.

“Moreover, concerning the Life of the apostle Martial, which the heretic falsely claims is not ancient, hear how Donadeus, a monk of that same apostle, although uneducated, exposed as a liar a certain foreign grammarian who was similarly misleading people ten years ago. Ingeniously, he led the man into the ancient basilica of the Savior, which at that time threatened to collapse because of its extreme age and which, seven years ago, was demolished down to the ground. He said: ‘Tell me: is this basilica old?’

“The foolish grammarian replied: ‘It was old even five hundred years ago.’

“Immediately Donadeus showed him paintings there that could scarcely be seen because of their great antiquity, and said: ‘Where do these paintings come from?’ When the man saw Martial ministering to the Lord at his command, along with the other paintings as they are read about in his Life, he was overcome with shame and, amid the laughter of all who were present, confessed his lie.”

The physician then said: “If you can show me Martial written as an apostle in one old book alone or in the litanies, I will believe you.”

When I was able to show this in many books, I gladly said: “Come to the monastery and see.”

He refused, because he had lodging far away, and the next day departed from there for other places. He also said to me: “For medical reasons I travel through many places more than other men do, and I hear this rejected by everyone and praised by no one—especially because of Benedict, the prior who is a contradictor. He asserts to everyone that, because of this, a great scandal will arise within five years from now at the place of Saint Martial, and that a great persecution will come there, because the prayers concerning him, as they recite them, are not acceptable to God.”

I replied: “O tongue fit to be cut out and devoured by dogs!”

Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, and this Lombard resists the truth. He is unable to grasp the truth; he himself does not receive the truth, and he prevents those who receive it from doing so, thereby bringing swift destruction upon himself. His hearers turn their ears away from the truth and turn instead to fables.

Simon Magus said of Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, to Nero: “These men are acting against your kingdom.” Zaroes and Arfaxat said of the apostles Simon and Thaddeus: “Enemies of the gods will come to you and subvert your laws.” Haman the Agagite said to King Ahasuerus: “There is a people of the Jews in your kingdom who keep their own laws and are hostile to yours.” The Athenians said of Paul: “He is a proclaimer of new demons.” The chief priests and Pharisees held a council against the Lord, saying: “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him.” The Jews said to Pilate: “That deceiver, while still alive, said: ‘After three days I shall rise again.’”

Satan hinders us, but we are not ashamed of the truth. May the Lord repay him according to his deeds, because he resists our words so fiercely. He has the appearance of piety but denies its power; he has zeal, but not according to knowledge.

But I, if I were consumed at this hour by fiery thunderbolts, would in no way transgress the testimonies of our holy fathers. Rather, I would cry out: “Apostle of Christ, Martial, save me!” If the entire monastery of that apostle and the whole city of Limoges were today burned with fire in every way, even then those who love him would not abandon his pure truth. Instead, they would cry out still more ardently and confidently: “By the prayers of your apostle Martial, Lord, may we be helped, so that, absolved from our sins, we may also be delivered from the dangers threatening us; through Christ our Lord.”

The words of the wise, even if they are few, should be believed rather than the opinions of the unlearned multitude. For the popular crowd knows no other authority than this, saying: “What did all those bishops, all those abbots, all those wise men who lived two hundred years ago do? We never again heard that Martial was an apostle. Why are these wise men changing this? He has enough honor.”

And so the poisonous tongue of the envious falls into blasphemy, piercing with such words. They remove him from the rank in which God placed him and make him ascend to one in which he never was; and even Martial himself is displeased by this.

O serpent’s fangs, O deaf adders, O poisoned tongue of the devil, accustomed to tearing apart the saints of God and God himself; you never cease to pervert the Lord’s straight ways; you who said in paradise, “You shall certainly not die,” and killed our first parents; you who said concerning the Son of God, “This man is a glutton and a wine-drinker,” and, “This is the son of Joseph the carpenter”; you who said through Pharaoh, “Who is the Lord, that I should heed his voice? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go”; you who said to the Son of God, “I will give you all these things if you will fall down and worship me”; you who want everyone to fall and no one to rise; you who cast Judas down from the apostleship; you who open your mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his tabernacle and those who dwell in heaven; you who caused the bodies of martyrs to be drowned, saying, “Let Christians not make martyrs for themselves”; you who said through Simon Magus of Peter, the chief of the apostles, to Nero, “This is an ignorant man, a most deceitful fisherman, endowed with no power—in his character, his birth, or anything else”; you who once proclaimed the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son and the Son lesser than the Father, and now proclaim Martial lesser than the apostles; indeed, you deny that he is Christ’s apostle.

But, heretic, envious dog, whoever you are who say this, you rightly lie against your own head: Christ was Martial’s teacher; Christ himself taught Martial; Martial labored greatly for Christ, as a true apostle.

The multitude of the wise is the health of the world. Our proclamation that Martial is an apostle is contrary to the devil and pleasing to Christ. Through the devil’s cunning, some peasants still say: “We would rather Martial be the first confessor than the last apostle.” For this reason that perverse custom was long ago introduced by foolish people, but now it has been completely cut away by the learned. The learned should be believed rather than the common people; the learned should not assent to the opinions of the common people, but the common people should assent to the mouths of the learned. For the learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars forever and ever.

Therefore we do not consider it vain to proclaim this righteousness. The earlier apostles followed in Christ’s footsteps; after the apostles came the martyrs; after the martyrs, the confessors; after the confessors, the virgins; after the virgins, the widows; after the widows, those who practice continence. How many orthodox bishops, how many Catholic fathers, how many learned lights of the Church before us read and believed the Life of Martial, even if, when they understood it, they kept silent through negligence?

How many learned men before us sang in God’s sight: “O how glorious is the most courageous soldier Martial, who, joined to the company of the apostles and having received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, exercised a privilege of honor not unlike that of the apostles,” along with much else in which he is proclaimed an apostle? And now, because of one rustic Lombard who thinks himself a grammarian, will an assembly of learned Catholics abandon the ancient truth of our fathers?

The stags of the fields could more easily feed in the sky than the holy mother Church abandon this purest truth of hers. Although foolish people formerly rejected this sound custom, they did not entirely lose it. Against their will and unknowingly, they retained part of the spark, while the learned preserved it in the litanies. From that spark the beautiful custom of truth has now shone out like the sun, with God glorifying the times of our most devout shepherd Odolric and of Bishop Jordan.

Since, therefore, we truly proclaim Martial an apostle, he rejoices, God rejoices, the angels and all his saints rejoice. The devil is saddened; heretics and the envious are saddened, and they die with their envy unless they are separated from the devil.

I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, by his coming and his kingdom; I testify also before the Holy Spirit, who invisibly entered the hearts of the apostles: if Martial himself were now visibly to appear before me and ask me, “Who do people say that I am?”, I would answer him immediately, without any hesitation, with complete confidence and readiness: “Some call you an apostolic man, some one of the bishops, some one of the unknown saints, or one of the confessors.”

And if he deigned to ask me: “But what do my abbot Odolric, my monks, and my bishop Jordan say that I am?”, I would immediately answer: “An apostle of God.”

But I, Ademar, your unworthy servant, truly believe, confess, and declare that you are truly a great, outstanding, and most noble apostle of God. May God’s wrath fall upon whoever contradicts your being an apostle, and may destruction overtake him at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who taught you himself.

Some hesitate because they do not hear your name written in the Gospels; therefore they doubt that you are an apostle. But I, believing, quietly profess that your name was omitted because you were younger, just as in the Old Testament the Hebrews were not counted except from the age of twenty years and above.

Faith, hope, and charity accompany my steps as I make my difficult ascent. I believe that whatever Peter heard secretly from Christ, together with the Twelve, you also heard at that time in the same way through Peter; and for that reason you preached Christ more confidently to the nations. Through you I rejoice to believe likewise in God and to reject all heresies; while I hope through you to arrive at the vision of the supreme Trinity and to enjoy it eternally; and through you I love the Lord Jesus Christ more dearly and more ardently.

Whoever wishes to take from me the belief in my heart and confession with my mouth that you are Christ’s apostle wishes to take faith, hope, and charity away from me, without which no one can be saved for eternity. [Col. 0105A]

I do not agree with the Lombard, who denies that you were present at Christ’s supper, and who falsely claims with his poisonous mouth that the Lord dined with only the Twelve, like a robber rather than like a most generous king. I agree with our holy fathers and with the author of your Life, and I affirm that the Lord reclined with the twelve apostles and had attendants who served him and the twelve apostles, offered them cups, and brought whatever was necessary.

I do not agree with the vainglorious Lombard, who denies that you received from Christ himself the power of binding and loosing. Rather, I firmly profess that you were exalted by Christ with the other apostles through so great an apostolic gift. Therefore I ask you, holy apostle: loose the bonds of all my sins, and bind my mind most tenaciously to you with the bonds of your sweetest love, which must never be broken.

I will never share fellowship with the Hebionite heretic and pseudo-monk, who denies that you were present at the place where the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples in fiery tongues. On the contrary, I openly testify to all peoples that not only the Twelve but also many other disciples were gathered there on Zion, and that you, filled with the Holy Spirit among them, spoke of God’s mighty works in various tongues. Together with the other apostles, you were instructed in every language and became an unconquerable witness to Christ’s Resurrection.

Therefore, through you I implore that my heart be cleansed from every error by the visitation of that Paraclete, and that the wisdom which comes from the Father of lights shine within me without end.

May the heretic swiftly perish from the face of the earth, the one who does not cease proclaiming to everyone that no one except the eleven apostles alone saw Christ’s Ascension, and that you were in no way present there.

For I, living with Christ—I who shall never die, I who shall never taste death forever, as one who believes in Christ—ascending a high mountain and raising my voice with strength, announce to every creature with complete confidence, as the truth is in Jesus: just as Bishop Aurelian testifies, whom you raised from a double death, the author of your Life says that you went with the eleven disciples into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, at Peter’s urging. There, together with Peter and the other apostles, you received from Christ himself the power to preach, teach, and baptize. Later, when the Lord ascended to the Father on the Mount of Olives, you were present there, where you deserved to receive the pontifical blessing from the Lord himself together with the other disciples.

Therefore, holy apostle, I beseech you with great anguish: make me forget earthly things, and make me sigh unceasingly toward the heaven of heavens, where Christ has gone before.

But if the Hebionite Lombard does not abandon his unbelief, let him depart from the fellowship of the orthodox, be torn away from the unity of Catholics, be cut off from the company of all the saints, and be separated from the fellowship of the blessed angels, since he is in no way a member of the company of the holy apostles.

He has threatened to accuse us before the Roman pope because of your glory and truth, and to excommunicate all Aquitania on your account. May the envious heretic be humbled in his own snare; may the Lord arise, and may the Lombard not prevail.

Let Peter rejoice in you, because you are his beloved fellow apostle. May the Roman pope share communion with your Aquitania, not excommunicate it. Peter venerates you as truly a fellow apostle; may the Roman pope not deny that you are truly an apostle. Peter calls you his dearest brother; may the pope not deny that you are Peter’s most beloved companion. Peter prayed for you on bended knees; on your account may the pope give thanks with outstretched hands.

May all Rome rejoice in you, since all your Aquitania pays tribute to Peter. But if human judgments should somehow disagree with divine ones, if it should somehow be believed that the enemies of truth deserve preference over its friends, could a corruptible pope surpass Peter, at whose prompting you obeyed Christ’s commands? Could a pope who is destined to die excommunicate you, whom Christ, ascending to the Father, deigned to bless with his own hand? Could a pope who is destined to become a worm excommunicate the Son of God, who bestowed upon you, together with the other apostles, the pontifical power of binding and loosing? Could a human pope excommunicate the Holy Spirit, who bestowed upon you, together with the other disciples, knowledge of every language? Could a frail pope excommunicate your Aquitania, which you made a coheir with Christ for eternal life? Could a pope who is dust and ashes excommunicate the Church of God, which you cleansed from idols and always preserved unharmed from every heresy? Could a pope who will become a corpse forbid your bishops from proclaiming you an apostle—those whom you, together with all Gaul, will present to Christ on the day of judgment as sheaves of your labors, to be saved in the heavenly granary?”

With these and similar words, I say to you, I would address Martial, the apostle of God, without exhaustion, if I were to behold him.

As for what some brutish and fainthearted people say—that it is a sin for us to proclaim him an apostle, and that this displeases both God and Martial—I, the true worshiper of Christ Ademar, testify before the presence of the Savior, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, and before that same undefiled and perpetual Virgin, Mary, mother of God, and before blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; and I desire that this sin rest upon me, here and hereafter, forever.

Truly, if I bore this sin, I would be altogether blessed. For this is not a sin but the greatest piety.

Again I declare before the sight of God and of all who dwell in heaven: if it is in any way displeasing to God’s glory, to Martial himself, or to any of the saints who have already departed this life, that he be proclaimed an apostle, then at this very hour—which is approximately the sixth hour of the day—at this very moment, at this instant, at this atom of time in which I write this, may I die in the body and live no longer.

Today, on the sixth day of the week, I celebrated two Masses in succession in honor of the life-giving cross over the body of blessed Eparchius: one voluntarily, the other necessarily, in obedience to the command and request of Abbot Amalfredus. If, I say, this displeases God, may they not be a help to me; rather, at once, while I write alone inside the church, may I surrender my soul at this very hour. [Col. 0107A]

Christ is everywhere.

Christ wishes me to live; it is pleasing to Christ that we proclaim Martial an apostle. For he truly is an apostle.

O elders of the fathers, to whom I write this letter, hear still with your ears the blasphemous speeches of the Lombard amid his cups. Although the apostle commands that bread be eaten in silence, this man—not in the morning chapter or in a place of sobriety, but already swollen with food, refreshed by fish, and drenched in cups of unmixed wine—repeatedly ordered the reader to be silent in the brothers’ refectory. Not from the reading itself but concerning the apostle Martial, he made very frequent speeches to the brothers at table, so mocking that, not without immense bitterness of heart, I say that he moved brothers of every age to wanton laughter and loud guffaws.

Thus for nearly forty days, through the months of August and September, at all his lunches and dinners he alternately ate and drank, blaspheming in our presence Martial, Christ’s apostle, to his own and Christ’s dishonor. His feasts were our blasphemies.

This was his frequent daily refrain:

“‘I am the nephew of the abbot of Clusa. He took me through many places in Lombardy and Gaul for the sake of grammar. My wisdom has already cost him two thousand solidi, which he gave to my teachers. I have now spent nine years studying grammar, and I am still a scholar. We are nine scholars studying grammar together, and I am a very perfectly wise man.

“‘I have two large houses filled with books, and I have not yet read all of them, but I meditate on them every day. There is no book in the whole world that I do not possess. Once I leave school, there will be no one under heaven as wise as I am.

“‘I shall be abbot of Clusa after my uncle’s death, and I have already been elected by everyone. If such wicked converts—monks who care for nothing except hypocrisy and rusticity—had not taken this from me, I would have been consecrated abbot long ago. I am the prior of Clusa, and I know well how to compose a sermon on a letter.

“‘These foolish people of Limoges say that in Gaul they proclaim Saint Martial to be an apostle and place him in the litanies before the martyrs. This is false. I spent many years in Gaul, and I never heard his name there, even in any of the services, nor in the entire litanies. Gaul knows nothing about him: it does not know whether he is an apostle, a martyr, or a confessor. No commemoration of him is made there, even on his feast day. This should never have been thought of.

“‘Who was ever so bold as to say this? Who dared proclaim Martial an apostle unless a great general council of all the bishops of Gaul and Italy, together with the Roman pope, were first assembled and it were proved there whether he is or is not an apostle? I know very well how to organize an entire council; I am so wise.

“‘And if I were the first to affirm it, then something might arise from the matter. There is no wisdom in Aquitania; everyone there is rustic. If anyone from Aquitania learns a little grammar, he immediately thinks himself Virgil.

“‘There is wisdom in Gaul, but little; for in Lombardy, where I learned more, there is the fountain of wisdom. For this reason I shall bring all Aquitania to such a hearing that none of the clerics will know how to defend himself.

“‘Either I shall go to the Roman pope because of this presumption, or I shall send him letters of the sort I know how to compose. This pope is a very harsh and savage man, excessively prone to anger and of cruel character. As soon as he hears that a new apostle has been raised up in Gaul, he will excommunicate all the bishops, Churches, and monasteries of all Aquitania, so that no sacred ministry may be celebrated there any longer until this has been completely destroyed and public penance has been performed for it by everyone.

“‘Afterward, by the authority of a decree, he will excommunicate them so that no one in the future may ever again presume to do this.’”

Therefore, when our two pseudo-monks returned from Buxetia, they immediately began groaning and saying to us: “Alas! We were badly born; we are all dead unless God has shown us mercy.” Then they began to recount to us the things I have related above, and many much greater things that they had heard from that Lombard, the devil’s trap.

But I, confident that this opposition had arisen for the sake of a greater future firmness—and because the more truth is opposed, the more it is confirmed—and at the same time making nothing of the boastful Lombard (for I had heard him, as I said above, in Limoges badly corrupting Latin with barbarisms and possessing foolish manners; indeed, I understood that he could not conceal his anger and delighted in contention against us by his defense), whether because he judged so many prudent men of the Church of Limoges to be mistaken, or because, being a solitary foreigner who had not been invited, he wished to appear a teacher to many—for it is a fault of pride to wish to teach one’s betters—and since my mind immediately turned to writing this letter to you in order to refute the madman’s errors, I carefully and minutely questioned them about all these matters, saying:

“From where do you know whether he is wiser than we are?”

“Beyond all the men we have ever seen,” he replied, “he is wise. We have never heard anyone speak throughout the whole day in such a way. Oh, how talkative he is! No hour tires him of speaking. Wherever he may be—standing, sitting, walking, or lying down—words pour from his mouth like water from the river Tigris. He governs the whole region of Buxeria like an abbot: all the monks, laymen, and clerics do nothing without his nod, for he is the chief prelate. A multitude of people and soldiers, while we were present, hurried to him as to a prince, eager to hear him speak. He burdened them all day with his words and left them completely weary, while he himself did not grow tired. Those who departed said: ‘We have never seen a grammarian so eloquent.’”

To them I replied: “It is not a multitude of eloquent men, but a multitude of wise men, that is the health of the world. A wise man makes himself known by few words. A monk should speak few and reasonable words, restrain his tongue from speaking, and, maintaining silence, not speak until questioned. If a fool keeps silent, he will be considered wise.”

Then they said: “In this land no one is considered wise unless he is very eloquent. But we are exceedingly sad about Saint Martial, for it greatly pleased us that he was proclaimed an apostle. Now, however, we must return to our customary practice. The monks of Limoges themselves, who stand before his body, will return after not many days to their former custom; they will no longer call him an apostle, but a confessor, as Benedict asserts, and this will be a great mockery before the whole world.”

To them I said: “This is the vision I dreaded last night. There were two small but exceedingly foul serpents, of a dark color, rising from a ditch that was without standing water but moist, playing and indulging themselves with one another, while their bodies remained motionless on the surface of the ditch. Certain monks watched them with admiration and laughter, looking on gladly. But I, rather cursing than fleeing because of their malignant stench, saw them hide themselves again in their holes, as though they were fleeing more swiftly. I also saw, at the top of the ditch, a third serpent, most disgracefully variegated, no more than one cubit long, swollen with excessive poison. It was sluggishly emerging halfway from a hole and vomiting poison, which exhaled an abominable stench. Those standing around said that it was the mother of the two serpents. When I began to look at it from a distance, with my nostrils closed, it, as though ashamed of my gaze, gradually crawled backward and hid in its hole.

“I understood the two serpents to be you, the two pseudo-brothers; but the third to be your Lombard teacher. I shall no longer call him Benedict, but shall judge him worthy of the name Belitonius—that is, ‘the sound of Belial’—because through his mouth the devil makes a sound. It is indeed characteristic of Satan not to admonish through charity, but to disparage through pride and to obscure the brightness of others through envy.

“But since I know that it is difficult to raise up the truth and easy to tear it down, I am in no way surprised that, for the sake of one unknown teacher, you immediately abandoned the good which, under my persuasion over a long period of time—I, who have not been unknown since childhood—you had only with difficulty begun, amid the testimony and authority of equally trustworthy men. Nevertheless, it would have been better for you not to begin the uprightness of this truth, even if known to you, than to abandon it once begun.”

## Concerning another secular monk

Know also, most illustrious men to whom I write these things, that there is another monk of the same name, though bearing the personal name Salgionius, who, although he spends some time among the regular monks of the monastery of Angeriac, is likewise, insofar as he can be, an adversary of this truth.

One day, while he was a guest at our public assembly, he heard us sing in the choir the name of Martial among the apostles in the litanies. He immediately caused the greatest tumult, murmuring, and scandal there before everyone; thereafter, in a loud voice, he pronounced him fourth in the order of confessors, although he had been proclaimed fourteenth in the order of apostles.

When I publicly rebuked him before the abbot and the brothers, he said angrily: “Are we now to say what has never been said before?”

Gauzbertus replied: “On a journey to Rome, I once saw a certain distinguished count, an Alamannian, whose language I could not understand except in the psalms, litanies, and readings. His chaplains recited the litanies of the saints before him every day around the third hour, and every day I heard them pronounce Martial among the apostles.”

Then Salgionius said: “And when we were traveling to Jerusalem and entered the sea, I saw a certain monk named John, a most accomplished grammarian from the city of Reims, who likewise pronounced Martial every day among the apostles on the ship.”

Gauzbertus said: “Unless I had heard it myself from a foreign people speaking a barbarous language, I would not believe that he was an apostle. But you, who say that you heard a similar example from foreigners, why are you an adversary?”

“Because,” he replied, “such a custom has never until now existed among us. All our bishops and abbots are sad on this account, and they wish to send letters to the Roman pope so that he may prohibit this new presumption from taking place.”

I answered: “If the pope, persuaded by the counsel of the envious, prohibits this, nevertheless one must obey God more than the Roman pope. For no pope has been given the power either to absolve or to excommunicate God’s holy apostles, or to prohibit the Church of God from doing what is good and speaking rightly.”

He said: “Why did you begin this without his permission?”

“And you,” I replied, “why did you become a monk from a canon without his permission? Was Martial not an apostle before any pope had been established in the city of Rome? Did he not come to Rome together with Peter? Was he not made an apostle by Christ in Jerusalem, and in Zion taught by the Holy Spirit the knowledge of all languages? For the law went forth not from the city of Rome but from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

“If any apostles were ordained at Rome, let them seek their apostolate at Rome. Martial was ordained an apostle in Jerusalem, where the fountain of Christianity was, where the vineyard of balsam was, where Zion, the mother of all the Churches, was. For what is read in certain Annals—‘The birthday of Martial, who was ordained by the apostles’—is similarly read concerning the apostle James: ‘The birthday of James, the brother of the Lord, who was first ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles.’ The apostles did not consecrate him, since he had been consecrated by Christ; rather, they compelled him to undertake the governance of the Church.
