“In the same way, Martial is an apostle of such great dignity that, though not consecrated by the apostles, he was appointed by unanimous agreement to undertake the governance of a province and city still unknown, but afterward shown by the Lord to Peter. Therefore Peter said: ‘Christ entrusts Limoges to you.’ ‘Christ,’ he said, ‘not I.’

“But to Clement, whom he had made a Christian from a Roman gentile, Peter entrusted the city of Rome in another manner, saying: ‘I ordain you bishop of Rome, and to you I entrust the chair of my preaching and teaching. To you I hand over the power of binding and loosing, handed down to me by the Lord, so that whatever you decree on earth concerning anything whatsoever shall be decreed in heaven.’ Then, in the midst of everyone, he laid his hand upon him while blessing him and compelled him to sit in his chair.

“This very thing is shown by an ancient antiphon: ‘Saint Martial was delegated to preach in Gaul’—understand, by the Lord, because the Lord had previously appointed Gaul for preaching and afterward commanded him to go there through Peter, who ordered him, or rather persuaded and encouraged him. In that region he first undertook to reveal salvation to the people of Limoges by word and signs.

“If you apply this antiphon to other apostles, it will properly stand in this way: ‘Saint Peter, delegated to preach to the Italians, undertook to distribute the seeds of faith to the Roman citizens at the command of the other apostles.’ ‘Saint Andrew, delegated to preach to Achaea, undertook his preaching at Patras at the persuasion of the other apostles.’

“For although, as Clement’s book says, Barnabas was the first to begin preaching to the Romans, he returned to the East without result or fruit.

“And if no mortal afterward dared to bless the chalice of the church of Orléans, which is said to have been blessed by the divine hand while Saint Euurtius the bishop was celebrating Mass, how could any mortal afterward presume to bless Martial as a pontiff, whom Christ with his own hands blessed as bishop together with the other apostles?

“And if the blessing of patriarchs has such power that, once they have blessed the beards and crowns of clerics by saying only, ‘Blessed be your beard’ or ‘Blessed be your crown,’ no further blessing by other bishops is needed, how much more did the blessing of the Lord himself—by which he blessed the apostles with raised hands—have such power that they in no way needed another consecration by any mortal?”

He replied: “The secular princes themselves condemn this.”

I answered: “Not all who heard Christ himself or his apostles speaking the word of God received it. Even now, compliance wins friends, while truth produces hatred.”

# ADEMARUS’S FRAGMENT OF A SERMON

Delivered at the Council of Limoges.

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. VIII, p. 34, no. 3.)*

It would take too long to bring forward, in full, the established testimonies of so many Fathers concerning him—that is, Saint Martial—[the passage is incomplete in the supplied text]. Yet it is enough to recall one thing from the ancient authors concerning this matter.

You certainly know—if not by sight, then by report—that most renowned Father, Saint Abbo, to whom that man of universal learning and weighty authority, Gauzlin, archbishop of Bourges, succeeded in pastoral government: a defender of orthodox faith and cultivator of Catholic piety. He went before us long ago, crowned with martyrdom, suffering after his blood had been shed by the impious. We have heard that miracles already shine at his tomb, confirmed by the testimony of truthful people. His martyrdom is also solemnly celebrated, according to the custom of the holy martyrs, in many Churches.

In this martyr, wisdom had established so great a dwelling for itself that, although learned men flourished in countless numbers in his time, his authority was nevertheless regarded above all others. Thus, throughout all Gaul and Germany, and among the English people—for there too he was exceedingly famous—whenever any question was debated, if someone said that he had heard a determination from him, no further authority was required. Everyone judged that what had been heard from the mouth of so great a man was established. In authority he surpassed others like another Solomon.

And although by residence or birth he was a Frank, he was nevertheless renowned for Roman eloquence, so that he was judged another Tullius. In councils of the Fathers, before kings and princes, he alone distinguished the matters proposed; alone, as teacher of all, he brought uncertainty to an end in a few words. All, even the most learned of the learned, hung upon his words; in his presence they placed a finger upon their mouths.

So great was he in wisdom—and, besides being supported by the seven columns of the liberal arts, full of authority and grace—that he was an ornament to the whole Church. He adorned gatherings of bishops and approved all his statements by the authority of divine Scripture. Whatever proceeded from his mouth sounded, in a certain way, not human but divine.

In one of his treatises he could not remain silent about the truth concerning Martial, saying:

“This supreme Father Martial was altogether a sufficiently mystical guest of Christ at the supper, taking the remnants of the heavenly bread. When afterward he arose and wiped the company of the disciples, he himself gladly supplied the linens. Nor did he ever shrink from the sacred fellowship, alone among that pious and timid band apart from Thomas. Indeed, when Christ sought the heavenly things, he deserved to be blessed among the ranks of those standing by.

“He did not reject the choirs of those praising him, but with them received at that time the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the many-shaped tongues. Supported by these, he finally reached Antioch with Peter as his companion, and from there the city of Rome. Leaving it, he crossed over to Gaul, of which the famous and noble province of Aquitaine is a large part. When he arrived there, he became the apostle of the whole province for all ages.”

# ADEMARUS THE MONK’S ACROSTIC

To Roho, bishop of Ecolisma.

*(In Mabillon, Analecta, new edition, p. 432.)*

> **R**eigning King, be my patron, lest the fame of this book  
> **O**wing to its titles be obscured; let it shine before you.  
> **H**ere, in the city of Egolisma, Bishop Roho composed this volume,  
> **O**utstanding and pre-eminent among all.  
> **E**cce, the volume of the Fathers shines with splendid trophies;  
> **P**eter’s order shone with glorious honour.  
> **I**ts laws, and the most illustrious trumpet of Christ’s wars,  
> **S**poke forth with fiery mouth of the holy race;  
> **C**ontending, they laid venomous water-serpents low,  
> **O** how wonderfully adorned with stoles!  
> **P**romptly, through them, ardour shone among the chief men,  
> **U**ntil their necks were subjected to God.  
> **V**enerable man, renowned for virtues, Bishop Roho, more richly adorned in conduct,  
> **S**emper beloved by me, receive these little verses.  
> **X**enia such as these I, Adhemar, have given you: why?  
> **R**ightly you should know whence I ask that what is due you be given.  
> **I**llustrious gate of blessed love, be present to me;  
> **S**o let the Furies be far away, while you are my pious portion.  
> **T**hus may Eparchius and Peter adorn you with their protection,  
> **I**n the heights, that they may carry us into the camps of heaven.

The initial letters form **ROHO EPISCOPVS XRISTI**; the marked final letters form **ADEMARVS SERVVS XRISTI**—that is, “Adhemar, servant of Christ.”

## Note

This acrostic was written by Adhemar, servant of Christ—that is, a monk—from the most noble Cabannian family, educated at Ecolisma in the monastery of Saint Eparchius. His Chronicle and Commemoration of the Abbots of the Basilica of Saint Martial survive in the second volume of Labbe’s Library.

This author flourished in the year 1030. At that time he arranged for the History of the Roman Pontiffs attributed to Damasus to be copied for Roho, bishop of Ecolisma, by Adhemar’s own work, as the verses placed above at the front of the codex testify. The codex is now preserved in the monastery of Uzerche and ends with Leo IV.

It will not be out of place to append here the title and closing formula that the same Adhemar added to a parchment codex of the church of Saint Martial at Limoges. This codex contains four books of Amalarius *On the Divine Offices*, in the title of which the following is written:

> Here begins the preface of Symphosius Amalarius the cleric, to the Emperor Louis, on the books *On the Divine Offices*.

And at the end of the codex:

> Here ends the book of the venerable priest Symphosius Amalarius, *On the Divine Offices*, which he sent to the kings Louis and Lothair, sons of Charles the Great, emperor. Adhemar, an unworthy monk, arranged for this book to be transcribed in this volume in honor of God and Saint Benedict.

I record this here because I have nowhere read the personal name **Symphosius** attributed to Amalarius, who in this same codex is called only “priest” and “cleric.”

# Doubtful Works

# THREE SERMONS OF ADEMAR, AS IT SEEMS, DELIVERED AT THE COUNCIL OF LIMOGES IN THE YEAR 994

*(In Baluze, History of Tulle, Appendix, pp. 385–400, from codex 1238 of the Albertina Library.)*

## Sermon I

Once, as your brotherhood knows, beloved, a more grievous affliction—or, so to speak, a plague of plagues—was spreading through all the territories of Limoges and through the other neighboring cities. Therefore the whole people fled to blessed Martial for the medicine of their salvation. At that time heavenly mercy was chastising that people more severely, so that the others might have fear, that they might not be disobedient to the commands of the bishops in ecclesiastical statutes, and that those who were being punished might not afterward be afflicted with eternal vengeance.

Of such people it is written: “The Lord reproves the one whom he loves; he scourges every son whom he receives.” And Paul says: “If you are without discipline, whose sons are you? Therefore you are illegitimate children and not sons.”” Likewise the prophet says: “The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death.”

It is clear that this scourging came upon the people of Limoges not for destruction but for correction, since on this account the whole Aquitanian people performed penance for their offenses. Obeying the admonitions of the priests, it became a daughter of peace, because the peace of the bishops rested upon it. For the Lord says to the apostles: “If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you.”

At the time when these things occurred, before the most sacred body of the patron of Aquitaine was carried to Mount of Joy, it happened that the metropolitan of the city of Bordeaux—that is, of the Second Aquitaine—had already arrived at the synod of Limoges. His faith must not be left unspoken.

When the sun had set and the metropolitan himself had risen from prayer before blessed Martial, he began to turn toward his lodging. But, deeply distressed by the howling of those burning and by the intolerable stench of the fire that steamed from the bodies of the wretched, he burst into groans and tears. Stretching out his hands toward the apostle’s tomb, he cried aloud:

“O shepherd and illuminator of the Aquitanians, rise to help your people. Why do you sleep while the wretched suffer? I beg you, remove such a grievous calamity; permit these infernal punishments to reign no longer beside your body.

“O Martial, mirror of virtues, O prince of the Fathers, where is what we read—that in the flesh you were a disciple of him who healed every sickness and cured every disease among the Jewish people; who took away our sorrows and bore our infirmities, by whose bruising we were healed?

“O glory of bishops, ornament of Churches, where is what we read—that at the supper you were a minister of the Savior, when he washed the feet of his disciples?

“O minister of piety, where is what is read—that you received from the Lord, together with the other apostles, the power of binding and loosing? Certainly our ancient Fathers have handed down to us that you received every gift of grace together with the other apostles.

“What shall I say, O expectation of the poor, consolation of the wretched? Do we not truly hold that the city of Bordeaux, our episcopal see, was acquired for God by you, and that the city’s ruler, through a woman baptized by you and through the laying on of your staff, was immediately cured of a most terrible disease?

“Was not the raging fire in that same city put to sleep by your staff? I ask you: even if, on account of the guilt of the people, fire goes forth from your mouth and devours your enemies, nevertheless show that you are the disciple of him who is the fountain of mercy.

“Before all who stand here I confess truthfully: unless you extinguish this flame before I depart from this city, in those who are now present; unless I see this multitude of afflicted people healed by you, my mind will no longer believe the magnificent things that I read about you, nor will I ever again seek your patronage for this city.

“In vain will you be called the Lord’s disciple by me; in vain will you be called the apostle sent by God to the western people, unless the effect of mercy accompanies you before my eyes.

“They will declare in vain that you baptized all Aquitaine and the people of Bordeaux over whom I preside, unless I obtain what I ask for the salvation of this suffering multitude.

“Your staff, which in the city of my see has until now been guarded as a precious treasure, will be considered worthless by me unless you return my heart gladdened by the healing of these people.”

When he had finished this speech, the archbishop withdrew to his lodging. Throughout the entire city, inside and outside, there was an unceasing cry of men and women groaning from pain, and an intolerable stench exhaled from the burning of their bodies.

Then, behold, at midnight a sign appeared over the basilica of Saint Peter, where the tomb of blessed Martial is believed to be. Countless people, lying awake in vigil beneath the open sky, saw a light flashing from heaven descend upon the place of the tomb. In its radiance it illuminated the whole city like the midday light of day for almost an hour.

All who were sick in the city were suddenly made well. When the pain and groaning ceased, rest and silence came upon everyone. There were seven thousand and more—men and women—who received healing at that hour of the night. Giving glory to the God of heaven, they returned unharmed to their homes.

At that very hour of the night, the bishop mentioned above, resting in bed, saw the following vision in a deep sleep. A splendid man in a shining garment stood before him and offered him a pitcher full of water, saying:

“Martial, the disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ, commands you to refresh with this water the people burning in the flames, and they will be well.”

The pontiff awoke from sleep. As he wondered to himself at such a vision and perceived that everything was quiet, he understood that the dew of mercy was being divinely sprinkled upon the people, as he also proved when morning grew bright.

At that time the plague in that region gradually began to cease, so that it became plainly evident that he who had once taught the Aquitanians the true faith on earth was now their protector in heaven.

Seven bishops were gathered together for that blessed translation, like the seven angels of the seven Churches, so that the translation of the holy teacher might be made more celebrated for us by that sacred number seven.

The seven Churches whose shepherds gathered together for the same translation were these: the sees of Bourges and Bordeaux, Saintes and Clermont, Le Puy and Périgueux, together with Angoulême.

These seven princes of the Churches, together with the metropolitan of Limoges, the leading men of the people, and the dukes of Aquitaine, decreed with the greatest firmness at that same council that the law of the Lord should be observed by all, just as the Lord testifies through the prophet, saying: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

Above all, they urged that peace and justice be observed, so that those learned in the law might justly settle disputes between one person and another; and, with the oppression of the poor and violent acts of rapacity driven far away, that peace and friendly quiet might thereafter remain in the kingdom of Aquitaine.

Those who violated the peace were to be expelled from the thresholds of the Church as guilty of lèse-majesté, excluded from the body and blood of the Lord, removed from the fellowship and conversation of the faithful, and marked with perpetual infamy, until they were reconciled again by the bishops to Mother Church through worthy satisfaction.

At that council, in accordance with the law of the Lord, they pronounced both blessing and curse: blessing upon the obedient, and curse upon the disobedient.

The other bishops of the cities of Aquitaine, once that synod had been dissolved in peace, arrived immediately, confirming what the others had confirmed and condemning what they had condemned, so that unity might remain in the peace of the Church.

They sent the decrees of this council to the bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic see. The Roman pope gratefully received them and strengthened them with apostolic authority, rejoicing greatly in the Lord over the peace of the Church and likewise over the translation of so precious a patron.

And so that these things might thereafter be remembered each year, it was decreed by common consent, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor, power, and glory for everlasting ages. Amen.

## Sermon II

At the translation of blessed Martial, which took place in the time of Lothair, as you know well, beloved, the whole people of Aquitaine, together with the bishops, elders, and princes, went up to Mount of Joy for prayer, because the sacred limbs of that same patron had first been translated there.

Thus, not inappropriately, the prophetic oracle seemed to suit those days of joy: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths, because from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

That place seems to correspond to its name. For there was a figurative—or rather a true—mountain of the Lord: the same disciple of Christ, whose sacred limbs had been translated there for a time on account of the joy of Christians. And the same man, who traced his origin through the tribe of Benjamin from the patriarch Jacob, may not inappropriately be called the house of the God of Jacob.

For he remained a house—that is, a dwelling place—of the God of Jacob. With the other apostles he followed in the flesh and loved with his whole heart him of whom we read: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.”

Of such houses of God the Lord himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

This house of the God of Israel had taught the people of Aquitaine the ways of God. Peoples once devoted to errors had begun to walk in the paths of justice.

Then, with Martial, the law went forth for them from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. In Zion, together with the other preachers, Martial had been taught every form of knowledge by the Holy Spirit in the vision of the fiery tongues. He evangelized the law of the new grace to the western peoples and, first of all, revealed to the provinces of Gaul the word of the Lord that he had learned in Jerusalem from the teacher himself, the Savior Jesus Christ.

At that gathering, which was called the Great Council, the bishops who had assembled for the same translation of the patron hastened above all to teach the way of the Lord. They urged the people to strive to walk by the way of peace and truth, not to deviate from the path of justice by following the perversity of their hearts, to obey the institutions of the Fathers rather than the suggestions of the devil, and to rejoice over the translation of the patron in such a way that they would carry away with them an amendment of their morals and actions.

Many miracles certainly shone forth at the most precious body of that apostle. Since they are sufficiently known to you, who yourselves witnessed them at the present time, it is not necessary to recount them one by one, lest the day end before the sermon does.

Yet I am pleased to recall this one thing: when the holy body was found, all the demoniacs and those afflicted with various illnesses who came to his tomb were healed. Those whom fire was devouring likewise felt relief at the same hour.

While some returned home with their health restored, many more were brought from far away, so that one could see the whole city filled within and all around outside. The mourning, cries, and stench of the sick were exceedingly burdensome to those who were well.

But when the choir of those singing psalms carried the limbs of the patron from the tomb into the Basilica of the Savior, which is called the Royal Basilica, in a golden chest, the innumerable multitude of those burning immediately obtained complete healing. All cried out, saying:

“Blessed be the name of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who through blessed Martial showed mercy to his people.”

Nor should we be silent about the fact that, when the inner vessel containing the holy body was opened, a most pleasant fragrance came forth and refreshed the nostrils of all who stood nearby with a joyful scent.

But when those same holy limbs were carried by the hands of the priests from the tomb and placed in the golden vessel where they were deposited, behold, suddenly a great earthquake occurred. The larger church, with everyone inside it, seemed to shake. Yet no one was killed. Such terror nevertheless fell upon the people that they believed they could in no way escape death.

At that same hour those who were tormented by demons were healed. It was the third hour of the day. Then, as night approached, because of the crowds rushing in, the sacred relics were secretly carried to Mount of Joy while the ministers fasted.

Just as throughout the preceding night the priests of the Lord and the bishop had labored inside at the opening of the tomb, so outside the choirs singing psalms remained awake through that same night in psalms and praises while fasting.

Those who had undertaken that terrifying work inside began it from the first hour of the night, exhausted by fasting. When the melody of the psalms had been completed and the mysteries had been celebrated at cockcrow, strengthened by the body and blood of the Redeemer, they set their hands to removing the stones.

It was therefore fitting that the divine favor inspired these Fathers to decree by common consent that this day should be celebrated annually thereafter in memory of divine praise, because on it heavenly miracles, Christian joys, and the peace and rest of the Churches had shone forth.

Afterward, so that the commemoration of this festival might be eternal, they dedicated a new church in the name of the patron at the place where his sacred limbs had rested for several days. For from Mount of Joy they were carried back to his holy tomb before the synod was concluded.

In all things blessed is Jesus Christ our Lord, now and forever. Amen.

The bishops who then assembled for the same translation are probably these: Dacbertus, archbishop; Gondebadus, archbishop; Hilduinus, primate bishop; Abbo, bishop; Grimoardus, bishop; Stephanus, bishop; Frotarius, bishop; and Gissabertus, bishop.

These things took place in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 994, when great crowds of people filled every place around the city for more than twelve miles, beneath the open sky and a serene heaven that was exceedingly delightful.

## Sermon III
How a church, once dedicated, ought not to cease from divine praises by day and by night, nor remain empty of sacred adornment, so too a Christian mind ought never to grow sluggish in the praise of God, nor persist barren of the beauty of good works. And just as it is acknowledged to be sacrilege to violate a church, so it is dangerous for anyone rashly to assault one who, having already been purified by baptism, deserves to be the house of God; for when holy men are afflicted by the wicked, God, who dwells in them, is provoked to anger. [Col. 0120B] Indeed, God is assaulted in holy men, as he himself says through the prophet: “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye.”

Whoever honors the Church, moreover, honors his mother and truly the bride of God; indeed, he plainly appears to honor Christ himself, the head of the Church. For thus it was said to the apostles: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me.” And again: “Amen, I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans than for that city which will not receive you preaching peace.”

These things seem appropriate to the joy of today’s festival, because, when each year we commemorate the dedication of this temple, which bears the Savior’s own name, we find here a fitting opportunity to speak useful words to you. Therefore, this should be noted: if homicide or any other crime is committed in a dedicated oratory, or if the temple itself is polluted by pagans or heretics, no work of God may in any way be performed there unless it has first been sanctified again with water through episcopal reconciliation. For the Apostle says: “What fellowship has light with darkness? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?”

By a similar reasoning, whoever after baptism has committed a serious offense is already unworthy of God, because he has been defiled by a capital crime, until he is again washed by the baptism of repentance and, once cleansed, is reconciled to holy communion by priestly authority. Therefore, let all who made their vows in the baptismal font guard themselves to the end as an immaculate house of God, so that their spirit and body may be preserved whole for the coming of [Col. 0120D] the Lord.

But if it should happen that someone falls grievously after the sacrament of the bath, let him earnestly strive, through repentance and confession, to be reconciled to Mother Church through examination by the priests, lest—God forbid—he appear to be the temple of the devil and be condemned with Satan’s kingdom. Rather, remaining the temple of God, let him possess the inheritance of Christ and of God.

All must also carefully consider how weighty and terrible a destruction awaits those who have been justly excommunicated by bishops. Certainly, when bishops of a diocese excommunicate churches on account of the grave offenses of certain persons, it is no longer lawful for divine worship to be performed in them until the pontiffs themselves open them again with the key of their word. Indeed, the tongues of bishops are the keys of heaven, as the Lord says to the apostles—whose place bishops now hold in the Church: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Oh, what judgment threatens those who refuse to observe the excommunication of bishops, whose authority is so great that whoever honors them honors Christ, and whoever grieves them grieves Christ! And that only two bishops can fully exercise the authority of a council with complete force, and that in councils they ought to offer one another mutual assistance in governing in peace and justice the people entrusted to them, the Lord confirms when he says: “I tell you that if two of you agree on earth about anything whatever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven; for where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

Therefore, whenever a bishop alone, having summoned the leading men of his diocese, establishes laws for the people concerning justice and peace, because he performs the embassy of Christ in Christ’s place—so that whoever hears him hears Christ and whoever despises him despises Christ—no one may disregard his commands without great peril to his soul. But whenever a bishop calls upon another bishop to share his judgment and assistance, so that there are now two, the two bishops, of one mind and sharing the same judgment, are believed to be gathered in the Lord’s name and to have the Lord in their midst as a third judge [Col. 0121C] and confirmer of their decisions. Whoever despises the authority of these two despises the one who declares that he is present in their midst.

But if at any time a trinity of bishops is present, and they agree among themselves concerning whatever matters, the three, having the Lord as a fourth in their midst, nonetheless receive from the Lord the same privilege of authority, so that whoever seeks to oppose their words is guilty before the heavenly Majesty; and therefore he will perish without doubt.

If, then, the testimony of the Lord establishes that two or three bishops possess such great power and authority that whatever they ask of the supreme Maker is done for them, how firm do you suppose is an assembly in which many bishops are now gathered in Christ’s name? Behold, today’s present council of bishops at this holy see [Col. 0121D] of Limoges is concluded in the sevenfold number, and therefore in a sacred number, so that there can be no doubt that the Lord is in their midst.

Indeed, we may appropriately say of the present council of seven bishops that the Lord now walks in the midst of seven golden lampstands and also holds seven stars in his right hand, because the seven stars are the angels—that is, the priests—of the seven Churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches: namely, this holy see of Limoges, that of Bourges, also that of Albi and Cahors, as well as Angoulême and Périgueux, together with Poitiers.

In the same sevenfold number there are the seven seals of the book sealed within and without, and the immaculate Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world has seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Who, then, could doubt that this council of seven bishops is perfect, when the Lord testifies that the gathering of two or three is most fully confirmed? “Where,” he says, “two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

Let him therefore see how great a loss he inflicts upon his soul who seeks to be disobedient to this holy council in the confirmation and observance of justice and peace. Such a man will finally be handed over by the present council to excommunication—and deservedly so: those who refuse to submit to God’s yoke, which is gentle, are handed over to Satan’s harsh power.

Plainly, just as we see churches excommunicated by their own bishops deprived of divine office until absolution, so whoever is excommunicated by his bishop is deprived of divine grace until reconciliation through worthy satisfaction. Such persons are not permitted to enter the Church or to associate with their brothers, either at a meal or in conversation. For even if they depart from this life unreconciled, their souls, having been made strangers to the fellowship of holy souls, are in the power of Tartarus, just as their bodies here have been removed from the bodily Church.

But because some appear so darkened by the swelling of pride that, after they have been excommunicated by episcopal judgment, they nevertheless enter the Church as though with permission, in contempt of the excommunication, and join themselves to some at meals and to others in conversation without the bishop’s command, let such men know that they are destroyed doubly: both for the earlier fault and for the subsequent contumacy or negligence.

Those who knowingly associate with excommunicated persons without the bishop’s consent are likewise plainly worthy of severe judgment. Once there was a just king among the English, but because he once shared a meal with his excommunicated count, despite the bishop’s warning, he suffered the just judgment of God in this life, for he was stabbed with swords in that same house.

Pope Gregory converted that people during the time of Maurice and Phocas through his disciples, and is deservedly called its apostle by that people, because through the Gospel he first begot it in Christ.

How much more, then, may Martial rightly be pronounced the apostle of the peoples of Gaul, since, at the Lord’s command through blessed Peter, he first illumined Gaul with the light of faith in the time of Claudius and Nero? He was descended from Abraham’s line, from the tribe of Benjamin, and was one of the Lord’s seventy-two disciples; and he is pronounced an apostle in the same way as Paul and Barnabas, who were not among the Twelve.

Among that same English people, for whom Gregory first planted ecclesiastical institutions, it has been established from antiquity that Martial was numbered among the other apostles. Recently, too, the king of that people sent the duke of Aquitaine, among other gifts, a book written in letters of gold, which contains Martial written in the list of blessed Peter and the other apostles. We have verified the same thing with our own eyes in other very ancient books of that people. It is therefore clear that Martial’s apostleship shone forth not only in our own times but also in antiquity; and we confidently profess that we hold it certain that Gregory confidently placed him in his institutions.

Moreover, those who are excommunicated by bishops—that is, bound—and who neglect or despise this, whenever they intrude themselves unworthily into the Church, bind themselves each time and provoke God’s anger against themselves. The Lord says to Moses: “If any outsider approaches the sanctuary, let him die.”

Now those who are bound, or excommunicated and excluded from the fellowship of the faithful because their own faults demand it, appear to be outsiders to the Church of God. Everyone who justly allows himself to be excommunicated but refuses to obey the priest is judged not faithful but unfaithful.

By what reasoning, then, does an excommunicated person presume to take part in the divine mysteries, when for him they are nothing but judgment, although for the faithful they are a remedy? For just as whoever eats and drinks the Eucharist unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body, or as whoever unworthily eats the Lord’s bread or drinks his cup is guilty of the Lord’s body and blood, so whoever enters the Church unworthily acquires judgment rather than salvation for himself, because he is guilty of the holy Church of God.

King Uzziah was struck with leprosy as an example of such persons, because he disregarded the prohibition of his pontiff and entered the Lord’s temple unworthily. He had preserved justice for many years, being descended from David, but afterward turning toward injustice, he incurred the crime of disobedience; and under the appearance of religion, in order to burn incense to the Lord, he entered the temple unworthily.

But the pontiff Azariah, together with eighty priests of the Lord, forbade the king to do what was unlawful, in the manner of one excommunicating him: “Go out, O king, from the sanctuary,” he said, “and do not despise this, for it shall not be counted to you as glory by the Lord God.” But the proud king despised the pontiff’s excommunication and began to threaten him. Therefore, immediately an earthquake occurred in the temple, and the king was struck with leprosy until the day of his death.

The emperor Theodosius feared his bishop’s excommunication, as he ought to have done. On the day of the Lord’s Nativity he did not dare to enter the church; rather, mourning in sackcloth and ashes, he remained in his chamber until, having made worthy satisfaction for his guilt, he was reconciled by the bishop. Because he always obeyed the bishops’ commands, God always deigned to grant him complete victory in every war.

To those who make light of the excommunications of bishops we also bring forward examples from the prophets. Concerning such persons, who pervert justice, the prophet says:

“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight, who justify the wicked for bribes and deprive the righteous of his justice. Therefore, just as a tongue of fire devours straw and the heat of the flame consumes it, so their root shall be like cinders, and their shoot shall rise like dust. For they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the fury of the Lord was kindled against his people; he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like dung in the midst of the streets.”

By the shaken mountains are understood clerics or lay princes. Accordingly, by prophetic authority bishops order the destroyers of peace to remain unburied, so that, according to the prophet’s sentence, their corpses may be like dung in the midst of the streets; just as, because their guilt demands it, their souls in that world are excluded from God’s kingdom, so their bodies may be separated from Christian burial.

Therefore, let everyone observe peace, if they do not wish to be excommunicated. Let them love peace and truth—that is, justice—so that, by his granting it, the Lord’s peace may be with all; he lives and reigns forever and ever.

## Around the Year of Our Lord 1029. Bernard, Scholasticus of Angers.

[Col. 0123]

## Historical and Literary Notice

*(Literary History of France, VII, 308.)*

[Col. 0123D] Bernard, whose family is otherwise unknown, had a brother apparently much younger than himself, named Robert and surnamed the Angevin, who became abbot of Cormery in Touraine (MAB. *An.*, book LX, no. 58). From this it may reasonably be conjectured that Bernard was from Anjou. He left his homeland to become a pupil of Fulbert at Chartres (MAB. ibid., vol. IV, appendix, p. 703).

While studying there, he conceived a particular devotion to Saint Faith, who had a small chapel outside the city walls [Col. 0125A], which he often visited both to pray and to write in greater quiet. The miracles that God performed at this saint’s tomb were then widely discussed. So extraordinary were the reports circulated at Chartres that Bernard could not believe them. To assure himself of the truth, he resolved to go to the source and travel to the abbey of Conques in Rouergue, where the saint’s body was preserved. It even appears that he bound himself to this by a kind of vow.

But he could not fulfill it immediately. The bishop of Angers, who at that time was Hubert of Vendôme, summoned him to entrust him with the direction of the episcopal school. Bernard took charge of it for three years and suffered greatly, being prevented on the one hand by an accumulation of affairs from fulfilling his vow [Col. 0125B], and on the other engaged with students so backward that he could make no progress through the lessons he was obliged to give them.

At last he suddenly left Angers and undertook the journey he had planned (LAB. *Bib. nov.* II, p. 544). Indeed, he made it on two different occasions. When he was at Conques (MAB., ibid. 2), he gathered all the saint’s miracles for which he could obtain reliable evidence and sent them to Fulbert, his teacher.

It is supposed that Bernard returned to Angers, where he continued to serve as schoolmaster, and that he may have been the same person as the chaplain of Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, who was named Bernard. But there is no proof of this. There is even less evidence for extending his life to 1054, the year of the death of Abbot Robert, his brother (MAB., ibid., book LX, no. 58). Perhaps that date was mistakenly taken as the end of Bernard’s life.

What is certain is that our scholastic was flourishing during the episcopate of Fulbert (I, 53, no. 42), and indeed from its beginning, around 1010. There is a considerable distance between that date and 1054.

Bernard’s principal work is his collection of the miracles of Saint Faith, printed under the care of Father Labbe (*Bibl. nov.*, p. 531), but without the author’s name, because the dedicatory epistle in which he identifies himself was missing from Labbe’s manuscript. Dom Mabillon, having unearthed it in another manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Père at Chartres, where the work is more complete [Col. 0125D] than in the printed version, made it available to the public (MAB., ibid. IV, appendix, p. 703).

Alberic of Trois-Fontaines had already informed us that the collection belonged to Bernard, scholasticus of Angers (ALB. *chr.*, part 2, p. 34). There is no agreement about the precise year in which the author began it. Some believe it was 1010, others 1012 (MAB. ibid. I, 53, no. 42; *Gall. chr. nov.*, II, p. 896). It is at least beyond doubt that he completed it before 1026, since he speaks there as though Richard II, duke of Normandy, who died in that year, were still alive (MAB., ibid., p. 544).

The collection comprises twenty-two chapters, but it is more extensive in certain manuscripts. One of this kind has already been mentioned. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* (at the place cited above) copy a passage from the work that does not appear in the printed edition. They therefore warn that they took it from manuscripts, which proves the point we are making here.

The author, for the rest, compiled this collection without selection. It appears that all miracles were acceptable to him, provided they were well attested. He was particularly concerned with this certainty, which authorized him to invite those who might doubt them to travel to the places themselves, so that they might be convinced by their own experience (MAB., *An.* IV, appendix, p. 703).

M. de Tillemont does him the justice of observing that his narratives are highly detailed and ordinarily supported by eyewitnesses (TILL., *H. E.* IV, p. 545). But he rightly observes that some are very strange, and that the penultimate one especially can only make the others suspect of fiction or illusion. Nevertheless, Bernard asserts that he learned it from a venerable abbot who knew it from the very person to whom the event had happened.

Although the work of our scholastic contains only miracles, some of them highly extraordinary, it nevertheless includes several facts useful for illuminating the civil history of that period. Consequently, the historians of Languedoc cite a long fragment of Bernard’s work among their evidence (*Hist. de Lang.*, II, appendix, pp. 6–7).

If Catel had known of it, he would not have given the wife of William, count of Toulouse, at the end of the tenth and the beginning of the eleventh century, the name Alphonse, or Delfonse (CATEL, *Com. de Toul.*, p. 104); he would have seen there that her name was Arsinde.

It is true that he was misled by a defective copy of a translation into old Gascon verse of the fifth chapter of the work in question, in which this countess is incorrectly named Delfonse. It actually reads: “A Artous Delfonse comtesse,” whereas it should read, as the historians of Languedoc point out (vol. II, appendix, p. 545): “A Arsens de Tolose comtesse.”

This translation into ancient vernacular verse, which Catel copies in full (ibid., pp. 104–107), is a further proof of our view concerning the former use of the Romance language. We are persuaded that it closely followed the publication of Bernard’s work. Indeed, one can perceive only one motive that could have led the poet to translate this chapter rather than another: the motive was to please the countess or the two sons, Raymond and Henry, whom she became the mother of through the power of Saint Faith with God.

Everything narrated in this chapter tends to announce that event. Arsinde or her sons were therefore still alive when the poet undertook his translation. It must therefore have been before the end of the eleventh century. The harshness and crudeness of the idiom he employs in his verses likewise show that our Romance language was still in its swaddling clothes.

Bernard left another work of his own composition. It is an account of a pilgrimage that he made around 1020, in the [Col. 0127A] company of several other Angevins, to Notre-Dame du Puy in Velay. Ménard, in his *Writers of Anjou*, reports a fragment of it, which he took from Father Gissey.

[Col. 0127]

## On Saint Faith the Virgin

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. II, Appendix, p. 894.)*

[Col. 0127A] In the year 303, Dacianus came to Agen, breathing threats and slaughter against the Christians. He began an atrocious persecution. The little flock of the faithful, thrown into confusion, secretly withdrew from the city and, wandering through the steep places of the wilderness and the rugged cliffs of the valleys, hid themselves in caves. The shepherd who followed the flock, Saint Caprasius, traversed all the rocky hiding places around them.

He refreshed some with divine conversations, strengthened others with alms begged from place to place, raised everyone up by his example, and prepared them for martyrdom by setting before them eternal punishments and rewards.

At last, on the day before the Nones of October, when, according to tradition, the view of the city lay open from the lofty mountain that today bears the name of Saint Vincent, and when he himself could see with his eyes in its street a splendid spectacle—namely, the virgin Faith, whose defense he was manfully undertaking, being handed over to punishments and torturers, and, after prolonged torments upon the burning gridiron, having been dismembered and roasted, receiving from an angel in the form of a dove a crown—while meanwhile she consecrated to her bridegroom Christ the remains of her life, her holocaust almost completed, he felt charity kindled within himself by the fire that consumed the virgin. Observing that the girl had gone before him, he was ashamed not at least to follow.

Returning to Agen, he first prayed to God to turn all things toward the better and to make clear to him by an unmistakable sign what he should do in that crisis; and, if indeed he had determined that he must descend into the arena, to make water immediately spring forth from a nearby rock. Without delay, at that very place and moment, a living spring miraculously burst forth, supplying abundant and perpetual water.

At the sight of the water, the heart of the designated martyr burned more and more fiercely, and he came forward for the contest in which he afterward gloriously acquitted himself. For immediately he was led before the tribunal of the governor, confessed the Christian faith, despised the threats of the judge and torturers, and at last, undefeated in his confession of Christ, died a martyr after his head was cut off, as the acts of the same saint are recounted at greater length by Surius and in the Roman Martyrology. His feast is celebrated on 20 October.

[Col. 0127]

## Book of the Miracles of Saint Faith, by Bernard the Scholastic

## Mabillon’s Notice

*(Benedictine Annals, vol. IV, book 53, no. 42, p. 114.)*

[Col. 0127D] At about this time (the year 1010), Bernard the scholastic, placed in charge of the schools of Angers, composed the book *On the Miracles of Saint Faith of Conques or Conques-en-Rouergue* and dedicated it to Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, formerly his teacher. Most of this book was published in the second volume of Labbe’s new *Bibliotheca*, but without the author’s name.

Alberic calls him Bernard in his *Chronicle* under the year 994: “Bernard, scholastic of Angers,” he says, “published for Saint Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, a little book of the miracles of Saint Faith of Conques, who suffered at Agen under the wicked Dacianus with blessed Caprasius.”

This book exists in a Chartres manuscript, fuller than the printed editions, under the following title: “Here begins the book of the miracles of the holy and most blessed virgin and martyr Faith, published by Bernard the scholastic, master of the school of Angers.” “Bernard, least of the scholastics, dedicates this book to the most holy and most learned of men, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres.”

This book was therefore written after the year 1007, when Fulbert was appointed to the see of Chartres. The author explains that the occasion for writing it arose when, while he was attending Fulbert’s school at Chartres, he often visited the church of Saint Faith outside the city, either to write or to pray, and heard many reports of miracles regularly performed in the monastery of Conques, which some dismissed as old wives’ tales. The thought then entered his mind that he should visit the place and investigate the truth of the matter for himself.

But when the bishop invited him to become master of the school of Angers, and he remained there teaching for three years, he finally set aside this office and went to Conques—not once only. There he began carefully investigating the widely reported miracles of Saint Faith, and discovered with complete certainty that they were true.

Among these he testifies that he saw a man whose eyes had been torn out by a violent burning, but had been entirely restored through the merits of Saint Faith, as the whole province bore witness. He says that he placed this miracle at the beginning of his book as the foundation of the others, in which he preserved rather the resemblance among the events than their chronological order, reporting only those that occurred in his own time and were confirmed by trustworthy men.

The author discusses these matters at greater length in the prologue to his book, which it seemed appropriate to reproduce in full. In these miracles there is frequent mention of pilgrims traveling to holy places, whom he calls *Romeos*. One such was Witbert the *Romeo*, whose torn-out eyes were restored from heaven.

In chapter 5, Arsinde, wife of William, count of Toulouse, is praised. He was the brother of that Pons who was later treacherously killed by Artald, his stepson. In chapter 8, the countess Bertilla is mentioned. There the golden majesty—that is, the statue—of Saint Marius the confessor, the equally golden majesty of Saint Amantius, also a confessor and bishop, and finally the golden majesty of Saint Faith are named.

In chapter 14, Lord Oebalius is praised, the lord of the castle called Torenne in the Limousin, together with his wife, Lady Beatrice, who had been abandoned by him through divorce. She was the sister of Richard II, duke of the Normans, as the author proves at the end of the same chapter in these words:

“About a year and a half after my second return from Conques, it happened that a particular matter required me to visit the court of Lord William, count of Poitiers. There, when I saw Lady Beatrice, sent there by her brother Richard, count of Rouen, I eagerly entered into conversation with her, and immediately began to reflect upon this miracle”—namely, that of a pilgrim divinely freed from his husband’s bonds—“whose words, agreeing in every respect with the words of the monks of Conques, could provide probable evidence, if anyone doubted the other matters they had related to me.”

In chapter 21, to prove the miracle of a soldier delivered from disordered intestinal movements, he introduces as a witness Robert, abbot of the monastery of Cantoiol, a man distinguished by venerable gray hair. These details are taken from the printed editions.

There are many more in the Chartres manuscript. Among them the author says that so many prisoners were freed through the merits of Saint Faith “that the immense quantity of iron fetters, which in the language of the region they call *bodias*, gave the monastery an immense task. For this reason, the elders decided that such a mass of iron should be beaten out and made into doors by the skill of the smiths.”

Consequently, scarcely any entrance to the church—which is threefold—remains that does not have doors made from the fetters or chains mentioned above. Concerning this three-sided church the same author writes:

“On the outside there is a threefold basilica, measured by its roofs, which inside, because of the ample passage between them, comes together into one body of a church . . . The right side is dedicated to the holy apostle Peter, the left to Saint Mary; the middle section is dedicated under the title of the holy Savior. But because this same middle section is frequented through the continual singing of psalms, the precious relics of the holy martyr were transferred there from their own place.”

The subsequent passages concern many miracles of Saint Faith performed during a procession through Auvergne. At that time an image of Saint Faith and a golden chest, said to have been given by Charlemagne, were carried through Auvergne to an estate of Saint Faith that the natives call Pisinus Mill. A cross bearing the Gospel book, holy water, and horn trumpets led the procession; these had been offered to the monastery by noble pilgrims as ornaments.

Adjacent to this estate is the castle of Aurosa, over which a certain prince named Robert presided. He was punished from heaven because he had treated badly a monk who was guardian of that estate. But enough of these matters—more than enough.

Ermengaud, count of Urgell, in his will (Marca, *Hispania*, p. 973), which he drew up in the twelfth year of King Robert, bequeathed two silver Gradual books to the monastery of Saint Faith.

## Letter of Bernard the Scholastic, Master of the School of Angers, to Lord Fulbert, Prefixed to the Book of the Miracles of Saint Faith

*(In Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 703, from a Chartres manuscript.)*

[Col. 0129]

[Col. 0129D] To the most holy and most learned of men, FULBERT, bishop of Chartres, BERNARD, least of the scholastics, offers the gift of most holy blessedness.

[Col. 0130D] When some time ago I was enjoying your sincere way of life at Chartres, it happened quite often that, whether for writing or for prayer, I visited the little church of the martyr Saint Faith, situated outside the walls [Col. 0131A] of that same city. On that account I remember that once, in the course of our conversation, we happened to mention Saint Faith and her miracles, which are continually performed by the almighty power of Christ at the place of the monastery of Conques, where her most holy body is reverently honored. Since some of these seemed to be celebrated merely by popular report, while others were regarded as unheard-of, they were rejected by faith no differently from the inventions of an empty tale. Yet, since what was true could not remain silent through God’s will, and since belief in the truth was already spreading through almost all Europe, a quiet thought gradually arose in my heart, impatient of oblivion: I should visit the martyr’s own dwelling with the same desire to learn. At last matters came to such a point that I wrote down in a little notebook the time and day of the vow I had made there, so that it might not be forgotten. Meanwhile an occasion arose for me to move to the city of Angers, after being entreated by that city’s bishop. There I remained for nearly three years, consuming the time of study, to speak truthfully, in empty trifles. I nevertheless postponed the fulfillment of my vow, waiting for a suitable opportunity; but, as successive and manifold cares occupied me, this false expectation so deceived me that, like a fish caught within a net’s meshes, the more I tried to free myself, the more heavily I became entangled in misfortunes. At last, lest I seem to be indulging my laziness under the pretext of adversity, and since I sensed that secret and almost inextricable snares were being prepared for me by diabolical fraud, while hostile craft was utterly frightening me from the good purposes I had begun, I suddenly set everything else aside [Col. 0131C] and, with the Lord leading me, reached the desired mausoleum of the glorious martyr.

When I therefore began carefully to inquire about the powers of Saint Faith, such an abundance of miracles flowed from the various narrators that, unless my mind had been ardently eager to hear them, excessive tedium would have afflicted my brain. But I myself was granted to see the very man whose eyes had been violently torn out by a profound act of vengeance and later restored with nature unharmed; and even now, while this man dictates here, I see him, and I know the whole matter, with the entire province bearing witness. I therefore think that this event should first be inserted as the foundation of the miracles and as a preface to the reading of the others—not merely sense for sense but word for word, as I hear it from his mouth—though, being no lover of brevity, I am beginning a sufficiently long narrative [Col. 0131D]. After this, because of the haste of my return, I intend to add very few miracles, while noting the more beautiful ones among the rest in the greatest brevity and with speed [Col. 0132A]. These are not older than our own age, and their witnesses are readily available; they have left behind not a fabulous but a most evident truth. With God guiding me, I have resolved to carry them with me to my homeland, so that, when given more leisure, I may make the reading more abundant for those who will read it.

When you have received these things, most learned of mortals, correct only the arrangement of the art. For whatever has been told me, although I am unlearned and inexperienced in composing correctly, I shall not be simple-minded in hearing nor readily credulous in believing. Or rather, if my ugly style seems, unequal to the subject, to have defiled the subject, then—with my goodwill toward you preserved—take for yourself, since it is evident that you alone have ascended to a higher degree of wisdom, so noble and glorious a theme, adorned with a noble and glorious style. Do not allow the truth, gnawed away by a poor style, to horrify readers and thereby cause an excellent matter to become worthless. For to have undertaken so great and remarkable a history as though the wise had been set aside is rather the insolence of an overbold person—unless the reason set forth here frees me from this charge of audacity. To put it more plainly: it is better that heavenly miracles, still new and unquestionable, should, with the truth preserved, be committed to writing in some fashion by a scholar who is wholly unlearned, than that an orator, yawning somewhere in unknown regions of the world and entertaining doubtful hope, should be awaited. Therefore I do not seem so blameworthy if I strive, according to my abilities, to make the gifts of divine grace known, since the very scarcity of writers urgently demands that I do so.

Furthermore, I warn those of you who will read this that you should not take offense at the coherence of this writing while seeking a chronological sequence [Col. 0132C]. For the urgent necessity of my return does not allow me to investigate everything thoroughly, except what must by no means be omitted without damage to the fruit of mercy. Hence, in this book—which, with God’s cooperation, I am beginning to compose *On the Miracles of Saint Faith*—it is not the order of the years that will be consistent, but the similarity of the miracles. Since I have sought these out with the utmost diligence, in their inviolable truth, and since nothing is truer, I ask you to give full-hearted credence to my account, lest afterward it be better for you to have detracted too little from the holy martyr than too much. Or rather, if the unusual novelty of this wondrous matter disturbs you, I ask your fraternity, falling prostrate before you to the ground, for this above all: in our own time, for the sake not so much of prayer as of experience, come here yourselves after my return, so that you may not rashly judge false, without experience, what you will freely proclaim true once you have experienced it [Col. 0132D].

# THE BOOK OF THE MIRACLES OF SAINT FAITH

*(In Labbe, New Library of Manuscripts, vol. II, p. 531, from an old manuscript of the Chifflet collection in the library of Byzunt, communicated by the Reverend Father Peter Francis Chifflet, theologian of the Society of Jesus.)*

## CHAPTER ONE. On Witbert, whose eyes, torn out by the roots, Saint Faith restored

[Col. 0131]

[Col. 0131D] In the Rouergue district, where most blessed Faith also rests near the village of Conques, there still lives a certain priest named Gerald. He had a kinsman and godson, named Witbert, a member of his household and an energetic manager of his property. Once Witbert had gone to Conques for the sake of the feast. After completing the customary solemn night vigil, he was returning by the same route on the following day, that is, on the very day of the solemnity, when ill fortune caused him to encounter the aforesaid master, who had secretly been stirred against him by hateful jealousy.

When the priest saw him close at hand in pilgrim’s clothing, he addressed him at first with peaceful words: “So, Witbert, I see you have become a *Romeus*”—for in that region pilgrims to the shrines of saints are called by this name. “That is so,” he replied; “yes, my lord, I am returning from the feast of Saint Faith.” Then, after asking him about the rest as though in friendship, he gave him permission to leave. But when they had gone a little way past one another, the priest—like the agents of Judaic betrayal, if indeed it is lawful to call a priest one who pollutes the priesthood by sacrilege—looked back and ordered the man to wait a little. Having caught up with him, he ordered his own men to seize him, surrounding him on both sides.

When Witbert saw this, trembling with overwhelming fear, he began to ask what crime he was being accused of. The treacherous man answered him threateningly: “You have done me harm, and you are preparing to do worse; therefore you shall pay me punishment in no other way than by satisfying me with your very eyes.” Yet he did not indicate the manner of his alleged offense more openly, apparently out of shame. For it is disgraceful for priests to bring judgment concerning their own jealousy. The cause of this evil had indeed arisen from suspicion that a woman had been violated.

But Witbert, ignorant of the matter, offered a confident defense against every kind of guilt: “Behold, my lord, if you will openly disclose the whole wrongdoing of which I am suspected, I am ready to refute it lawfully. I do not think it possible to discover how I should incur your anger or that of your faithful men.” To him the priest replied: “Let the unnecessary evasions of your defense cease, cease! The sentence was proclaimed long ago: it has been decreed that you shall be deprived of your eyes.”

But Witbert, persisting with a gladiator’s spirit and seeing that the irreparable hour of his ruin was imminent and that there was no further possibility of ransom, nevertheless added this cry, although he despaired of present safety: “My lord, I beg you, grant me pardon; and if not for my innocence, at least for the love of God and Saint Faith, for whose love I now wear the sacred clothing of a pilgrim.”

At this the grim beast, valuing neither God nor his holy martyr, snarling with the roar of savage fury, spewed out the poison of blasphemy that he had long conceived in these sacrilegious words: “Neither God nor Saint Faith will free you today. Nor will invoking them help you to depart unpunished from my hands. Nor will you take refuge in the respect due to pilgrim’s clothing, so that, although you have most wickedly wronged me, I should regard you as an untouchable and inviolable person.”

After saying this, he ordered the man to be thrown down and the innocent man’s eyes to be violently torn out. But since he could not persuade any of his men—there were only three, whose names we omit because of the ugliness of their barbarous names—to commit so great a crime, he obtained from them at least that the man be held down [Col. 0134A]. He then suddenly dismounted and, with the fingers accustomed to touch Christ’s holy body, violently tore out the eyes of his godson and carelessly threw them on the ground.

This happened with no absence of heavenly power, which does not allow human beings to be deprived of divine care, which is always near those who truly invoke it, and which executes judgment for those who suffer injury. For those who were present there at the time deserved immediately to see a snow-white dove—or, as the perpetrator of the crime himself still maintains, a magpie. This magpie or dove took up the poor man’s little eyes, smeared with fresh blood, from the ground at that very moment and, rising above the height of the mountainous land, seemed to carry them to Conques.

When the sacrilegious man saw this, however, he was moved to repentance and began to weep profusely [Col. 0134B]. One of his companions told him, though belatedly, that he was doing so in vain. He then departed and afterward either did not dare to undertake the sacred celebration of Mass because of the crime he had committed, or—and this seems more likely—entirely neglected it because of a secular matter.

Gerald’s mother, however, sympathizing with the injured innocence in intense affection, received the aforementioned Witbert into her home and most kindly supplied him with everything he needed until he became well. Witbert had also stayed with her at that time, not so much at his master’s command as to escape the cruelty which that same master, more savage than usual after receiving the wound of false jealousy in his heart, would otherwise have exercised against him.

When Witbert had finally recovered, he earned his living publicly by the art of jesting during that same year [Col. 0134C], and made such a profit from it that—as he now customarily reports—he no longer cared to have eyes; so greatly did the desire for gain and the pleasure of comfort delight him.

When a year had passed and the day of the solemnity was approaching, as he had surrendered his limbs to sleep on the day before the vigil, a little girl of indescribable elegance seemed to stand before him in a dream. Her appearance was angelic and most serene; her face was white and sprinkled here and there with rosy color. By the incomparable vigor of her countenance she surpassed all human beauty. Her size was no different from that which she is said to have had at the time of her passion: the stature of a girl, not yet advanced in age. Her garments were exceedingly ample, woven throughout with the purest gold and surrounded by delicate varieties of embroidered design. The sleeves hung down to the feet, finely gathered into the smallest folds because of their great length. A headband, wound around in a circle, gleamed with four translucent, shining pearls.

The smallness of her body, however, seems to signify nothing other than that, at the time of her passion, as we have said, she is recorded to have been young.

But, to return to what I began: the blessed girl, leaning upon the support of the bed, gently and sweetly placed her hand upon the right cheek of the sleeping man and began: “Are you sleeping, Witbert?” He replied: “Who are you, who call me?” She answered: “I am Saint Faith.” He said to her: “What has happened, lady, that you should come to me?” She replied: “Nothing else, except that I wished to see you.”

When Witbert had given thanks, Saint Faith again asked him: “Do you recognize me?” Recognizing her as though he had seen her long before, he seemed to answer: “Yes, lady, I see you very well, and I recognize you perfectly.”

“Tell me also,” she said, “how you are and how your affairs are proceeding.”

“Very well, lady,” he replied. “Fortune is favoring my affairs, and everything, by God’s grace, is going well for me.”

“And how are they going well?” she asked. “You do not see the light of heaven?”

For, as happens in dreams, he thought he saw things otherwise than they were. At this conclusion of the questioning, he remembered the loss of his eyes: “And how,” he said, “could I see, when last year, returning from your feast, I miserably lost my eyes through the violence of an unjust master?”

She replied: “He gravely offended God and greatly provoked the anger of the supreme Creator who condemned you, undeserving as you were, to the loss of your bodily members. But if tomorrow, the day that will be the vigil of my martyrdom, you go to Conques and place two candles that you have purchased—one before the altar of the holy Savior and the other before the altar where the earth containing my body has been buried—you will deserve to rejoice in the beauty of eyes restored in their entirety. For, because of the injury inflicted upon you, I moved the heavenly Judge’s mercy to compassion with a great cry, and I wearied God by the persistence of my earnest prayer until he made the fulfillment of my petition readily obtainable.”

When she had said this, she began again and again to urge him, as she was about to depart, and to exhort him insistently to go as quickly as possible. Indeed, when he hesitated over the price of purchasing the wax, she advised him: “A thousand men whom you have never seen will give you money. Moreover, so that you may carry out the present matter more easily, hurry at dawn to the church of this parish—for it was the church near which you lost your eyes, and in ancient times it was called Spariacus—and, when you hear Mass there, you will find a giver of six denarii.”

As he returned suitable thanks for this consolation, the heavenly power departed.

He immediately awoke and sought the church mentioned above. When he had explained the entire vision in order to everyone, they all regarded it as madness. Nevertheless, he did not abandon his purpose. He begged each person individually and pleaded with the surrounding crowd, seeking to borrow twelve denarii. At last a certain Hugh, stepping forward from the rest, freely extended to him from an open purse six coins and an obol; this amount exceeded what he had received in the vision.

Then, remembering the divine vision, he became more certain of the promise to come. What need is there of words? He went to the place, disclosed the vision to the elders, bought candles, placed them on the altars and kept vigil before the golden image of the most holy virgin.

Around midnight he seemed to see, in the little hollows of the eyes that had been cut from him, twin shining objects—like berries, or even larger than a laurel tree—being sent down from above and driven completely into place. Immediately confused by the reverberation, his brain was overcome, and he fell asleep in a state of stupor [Col. 0136A].

When the morning praises were being sung, he awoke because of the singing and the shouting of the psalm-singers, and seemed to perceive the shadow of shining lights and of people moving about him. Yet, because of the inward pain in his brain, almost forgetful of himself and scarcely believing that the matter was real, he thought rather that he was dreaming. At last, when the stupor that had come upon him gradually diminished, he began to discern the forms of things more clearly. Hardly returned to himself, he recalled the vision and, placing his hands upon them, touched the windows of restored light, perfectly reformed in his forehead with fleshy pupils.

Immediately, after producing witnesses, he proclaimed Christ’s immense magnificence with immense praises. There was ineffable joy, unheard-of gladness, incredible astonishment, and almost a doubtful question whether those who saw so unprecedented a miracle—especially those who had known him previously—were witnessing it in the imagination of a dream or in the truth of the event.

In the midst of this, something occurred that was ridiculous and most deserving of applause. For, being a man of the purest simplicity, an excessive trembling of fear crept into his heart. He thought that Gerald, who had earlier torn out his eyes, might have come to the public solemnity—as often happens—and might again, if he happened to meet him, rely on a larger group and tear out the newly restored beauty of his eyes. Therefore, amid the confused and mingled noise of the crowd, he secretly escaped as best he could.

He was not yet fully certain of the gift of recovered sight, so great was the wonder of the event that had seized him, when, amid the narrow passages formed by the crowds rushing toward the church, in broad daylight he encountered a donkey that had been set there. When he looked at it, he rebuked it with manly severity, saying: “Hey, you there, whoever you are, fool! Take your donkey away, so that it does not become an obstacle to travelers.”

Then, first becoming completely certain of the truth of the event, he withdrew in swift flight to a certain acquaintance of his among the soldiers. The man’s stronghold, situated on a high cliff, had been so fortified on every side by nature that it seemed inaccessible to every kind of siege engine; it was no more than sixteen miles from Conques. He therefore fled there for protection because of the valley’s impregnable defenses and, only after the monks had at length been persuaded by much pleading and had granted him considerable security, returned.

When nearly everyone, coming from both distant and nearby regions, hastened eagerly to see him as an unheard-of miracle, they rejoiced as they departed that he had granted them various benefits.

To remove all doubt from the matter, however, the often-mentioned Witbert was not healed by mercy immediately where he had been deprived of his eyes. Rather, as stated above, his recovery was deferred for an entire year; and by the art of buffoonery he was also marked out to many of his fellow provincials as blind, and then, once marked out, was finally healed in the sight of them all.

In this there was no lesser miracle than that which is read in the Gospel concerning the man born blind—and indeed it was much more marvelous, since Truth itself promised that his followers would certainly do works greater than his own, saying: “Whoever believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father” [Col. 0137A].

## CHAPTER II. On the mule restored to life

A certain soldier from the Toulouse district, named Bonus-filius—whose surviving son is still known by the same name—came to the holy place of the virgin. When he was already scarcely two miles from the village of Conques, the animal he was riding, struck by some illness or other, suddenly became lifeless.

He therefore summoned peasants and ordered them to strip the carcass of its hide. He himself, however, went forward to the holy virgin, for whose love he had undertaken the journey. Lying on the ground, he poured out prayers and expressed his vows. Finally, before the golden image of the most holy martyr, he complained about the loss of the mule. Since the mule had been exceptionally fine and almost unequaled, he had taken its loss very hard, especially because, while laboring at a good work, the powerful enemy had inflicted this injury upon him.

The solidity of his faith deserves no small praise. For when he ceased praying, the mule—whose feet the two peasants were already holding in order to skin it—drove both of them away with its kicks and, wondrous to say, sprang up with a leap restored to life. Gazing eagerly after the tracks of its fellow animals, it rushed over the summits of the mountains toward the village.

You would have seen the animal, as those who were present there have often testified to us, overflowing with the joy of recovered life in a manner appropriate to the understanding of a brute creature. Running about in the street before the church, it seemed somehow to sense the goodness of its maker and therefore to return thanks to God with frequent braying—God who gives food to the beasts and to the young ravens when they call upon him.

The peasants hurried after it, still carrying their bloodstained knives, and, though still doubtful about the mule, related the prodigy they had witnessed. And so that certain knowledge should not rest merely upon the testimony of those who saw it, but that a written record might also remove every error of uncertainty, the mule bore on both hind legs the furrows of fresh wounds, like extremely old scars, even with the hairs growing gray. At that very hour these had been restored with solid joints [Col. 0137C], and they remained as a sign of the resurrection for as long as the mule lived.

The soldier offered one gold coin to God and his holy martyr in thanksgiving and returned to his homeland, going back by the way he had come. After sending the animal back to Saint Faith, he bestowed many gifts upon her for many years thereafter.

## CHAPTER III. Another similar miracle

A certain soldier named Gerald, a man of no obscure standing, lived in the Rouergue district, in a village called Villaris, situated about six miles from Conques. Once, when he was returning from Rome, it happened that a mule, which he had borrowed from his brother Barnard, a cleric, began to fail, broken down by some defect or other.

Remembering Saint Faith, whom he regarded as nearby, he vowed to her, for the animal’s recovery, a candle as long as its tail. Yet the mule did not recover; rather, becoming much worse, it died [Col. 0138A].

When the man saw this, he sold the hide to his host. When the wicked host offered him the smallest possible price, thinking that even if he gave nothing he would still have the hide, Gerald became extremely angry. He furrowed the carcass’s side with cuts lengthwise and across, so that, when he left, his faithless host would not rejoice in possessing an intact hide.

Then, seizing the staff of his pilgrimage, piercing the dead animal’s eye with its point and striking its tail, he said furiously: “What harm would Saint Faith now suffer if, among the other gifts of healing, she also restored health to this mule and thereby acquired such a long candle for herself? Now I, wretched man, am struck by a double misfortune: I remain on foot along the roads, and I must pay my brother a hundred solidi in my homeland [Col. 0138B]—for that is the amount the two brothers had agreed between themselves for that mule, should it happen to encounter the danger of death.”

He had scarcely finished these few words when the mule came back to life and stood on all four feet with a swift leap. And so that no one might think it had sprung up from anything other than true death, at the very moment when this occurred all the marks of the mutilated skin blossomed like a painting—not now fresh with an outpouring of blood, but, as I said of the other animal, with a certain sheen like the down of something aged.

At this, the aforementioned Gerald rejoiced greatly, returned home, gave immense thanks to God and his holy martyr, and spread the novelty of the miracle everywhere. The man’s recognized nobility and faith were known to all. So that he would not seem to report anything rashly or frivolously, he kept the mule, marked with its wounds, in the present state [Col. 0138C].
