The monks themselves, as well as many others who later saw Gerald more than a thousand times, told me this.

But, to hasten toward the end of our words, what madman would henceforth doubt that human beings will rise in the future, when even animals rise in the present?

## CHAPTER IV. On the ring refused and afterward returned to Saint Faith

A certain noble matron, having heard the report of Saint Faith’s powers, prepared to go there. When she began her journey, after she had gone a little way from her threshold, she remembered that Saint Faith sought the rings of pilgrims in dreams. She therefore immediately turned back, removed her own ring from her finger, and entrusted it for safekeeping to a chambermaid whom she had summoned.

“Take this,” she said, “and keep it until I return, lest Saint Faith, if I take it to Conques, happen to ask for it and take it from me.”

She acted cleverly, as though anyone’s precaution could evade the providence of the one who foresees everything before it occurs.

What more is there to say? The woman went, paid the debt of her prayers and returned safely. On the following night, a virginal figure appeared to her in a dream. When asked, she made herself known by the name of Saint Faith, and immediately commanded in an authoritative voice that the ring be given to her. Then, when the woman pretended that she did not have the ring, the lady pointed out to her that it was the very ring she had entrusted to the chambermaid when she departed for Conques, so that she herself would not have to give it.

When morning came, the woman awoke and regarded the divine vision as a phantasm or empty dream [Col. 0139A]. But why should I linger over the outcome? Immediately the woman began to burn throughout her entire body with such an intense fever that she could scarcely endure it for one hour. After suffering in this way for three days, however, she came to herself, remembered her fault and confessed her negligence.

As soon as she ordered a horse to be saddled, intending to return to Saint Faith by the route she had previously taken, the excessive heat of the fever subsided. Thus she went away healed and returned rejoicing, considering it no small gain to exchange the ring for her health.

## CHAPTER V. On the golden sleeves

No one could retain all the miracles of this kind that the Lord has deigned to perform through Saint Faith, nor is anyone free to write down even those that have been retained. Nevertheless, I wish to append a few of those I have heard, so that I may seem neither silent through excessive reticence nor tiresome through excessive verbosity.

I know that it was said before us: “Everything rare is precious.” Therefore I write down rare things, so that, by comparison with the rest of the whole, they may be precious. Christ will therefore pardon me for knowingly passing over very many matters.

Arsendis, the wife of William, count of Toulouse—the brother of that Pons who was later treacherously killed by Artald, his stepson—had golden bracelets, or rather sleeves, since they extended continuously to the elbow, decorated with marvelous workmanship and precious gems.

Once, when she had lain alone upon her noble bed, she saw in a dream a figure pass before her in the form of a most beautiful girl. Admiring her excessive elegance, she addressed her with this question: “Tell me, lady, who do you appear to be?”

Saint Faith answered the woman who questioned her in a humble voice: “I am Saint Faith; do not doubt it, woman.”

The other replied, most earnestly entreating her: “O holy lady, why have you deigned to approach a sinful woman?”

At that moment Saint Faith disclosed to her questioner the purpose of her coming: “Give me the golden sleeves that you possess, and, when you go to Conques, place them upon the altar of the holy Savior. This is the reason why I have sought your presence.”

The prudent matron, unwilling to let such a gift go without return, answered: “O holy lady, if through you God grants me to be made fruitful with a male child, I shall gladly carry out what you command.”

Saint Faith replied: “The almighty Creator will very easily do this for his servant if you do not refuse what I ask.”

On the following day, troubled by this response, the woman diligently sought to discover in what district the village called Conques was situated. For at that time the novelty of the miracles of the people of Conques had rarely passed beyond their own borders.

When she had learned this from those who knew, she herself performed the office of a pilgrim and carried the golden little sleeves there with the greatest devotion, offering them to God and his holy martyr. There the venerable matron honorably spent several days of the Lord’s Resurrection and honored the solemnity by her presence; afterward she returned home.

In accordance with the promise of the divine vision, she conceived and gave birth to a boy. Becoming pregnant again, she bore another. Their names were Raymond, the firstborn, and Henry, the second.

These sleeves were later used up in the construction of a panel.

## CHAPTER VI. On the woman who appropriated the ring that another woman had left to Saint Faith at her death

There is a certain town adjoining the village of Conques, over which a man named Austrinus presided under the authority of the monks. Long ago we saw his successor there, but the miracle that we are beginning to relate was not earlier than our own time.

Austrinus became engaged to another woman, named Avigerna, with the ring that his wife—whose name is omitted in the manuscript—had promised to Saint Faith at her death. He regarded the words of his former wife as though she were delirious.

Afterward, however, heavenly justice condemned the finger of this insolent negligence—displayed with gold belonging to another—as an intolerable swelling of pain. A swollen pustule grew over it with such force that it covered almost the entire ring, so that the ring could not be cut through with an iron tool without damaging the finger.

When the remedies of the summoned physicians despaired of restraining the violence of the illness, and the intensity of the suffering could no longer be endured in any way, they had recourse to divine aid. A public confession of the offense was made. The weakened woman was led to the sacred mausoleum of the holy martyr.

There she kept vigil for two nights without interruption. A third night, which was Sunday, was added. During it the violence of the pain tormented the sufferer so savagely that the wretched woman’s cries did not cease throughout the whole night [Col. 0140C].

At last, when the heralds of the morning praises began to resound, a merciful visitation descended from the heavenly throne of the supreme Majesty. It did not permit such heavy crosses of punishment to rage any longer in human flesh, nor the penitent’s tears to reach despair.

For when the grieving matron happened to blow her nose, the ring mentioned above, without harming the finger, flew across the pavement with a sound like the sharpest [uncertain reading: *arcitus*] bolt from a bow.

Therefore that Sunday was celebrated with immense rejoicing by all the people of that village. They had seen their fellow countrywoman and neighbor rescued from deadly torment through Saint Faith’s aid.

Certainly many countless miracles of this kind are also reported of Saint Faith throughout the various regions of the earth—so many that no one could write them all down, or even recount them all. For it is impossible either to explain in words or to set down in writing all the great deeds of Saint Faith.

## CHAPTER VII. On the dishonest merchant

A merchant, a native of the Auvergne district, came to Saint Faith for the sake of prayer. When he saw how easy the trade in wax was—for because of the crowds of pilgrims, the wax offered by them was sold much more cheaply—he immediately recalled the knowledge of his trade and reasoned to himself:

“If I had discovered this foolishly easy profit, I could have made myself rich and stabilized my affairs! But what ignorance has delayed until now, vigilant return and frequent repetition of the journey will accomplish within a short time. Let me therefore gird myself manfully and undertake the beginning of the enterprise.”

Having decided this, he carefully assessed the seller’s many weights of wax. After counting out ten solidi, he bought a huge mass and stored it in sacks. Already rejoicing that with a small investment he would earn four times as much, he thought to himself: “Well, well—the beginning is good. What then, if I return many times?”

But we must not delay over the outcome. A handsome candle remained, which could not fit among the rest of the heap. The man of avarice pressed it against his chest in such a way that its broader part was held beneath his belt, while the narrower part projected through the opening of his garment as far as his beard.

But the avenging omnipotence of the heavenly watcher could no longer tolerate the daring of the thief concealed there. For the candle I mentioned, suddenly ignited by the heat of divine fire, began fiercely to burn the very confines in which it was enclosed, sending out vaporous flames together with a smoky whirlwind. The great beard shone with a shower of flashing sparks, while the hood above it was burned with a crackling sound.

Nor did a thread in the fabric protect the skin of his belly, since his back, too, was burning with circling flames. You would have been astonished at the horrible howls of the maddened man, the noise of his kicking, the gnashing of his teeth, the rolling of his eyes and the violent distortion of his entire body. Miserably suffering beyond endurance, he was carried headlong here and there, like a snake suddenly struck: now it gathers itself into a coiled ball, now flashes forward in a rapid movement and stretches out its twisted neck, seeking escape. Weakened and unable to flee, it again turns against its attacker, rolling its bloodshot eyes and hissing with its mouth.

No differently did this wretched man run about, hurling himself here and there, throwing himself forward and backward, now face down, now on his back. He could not breathe in any way, driven on by a greater force.

Nevertheless, the remaining thread of human understanding brought the wretched man to repentance. He immediately ran with a great cry to the tomb of the most merciful martyr and poured out all the wax there. The painful fire vanished no more slowly than the man poured it out. Nor did he complain about the loss of money, provided that he could escape the torment [Col. 0141D].

After these events, I do not think it improper to proclaim Saint Faith’s goodness laudable and marvelous in this matter also: so that the cheapness of the trade would not fail the pilgrims, she chastised the dishonesty of greed.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the boy in whom a fourfold miracle was performed
Nor do I think that this should be passed over: among the many miracles of the saints that, according to the custom of that province, are brought to councils, holy Faith shines forth in the glory of miracles as though she held the chief place. Since these miracles are numerous, we think it sufficient to record only two, lest we seem to be composing an excessively idle volume.

The most reverend Arnaldus [Col. 0142A], bishop of Rodez, had convened a synod solely for his own parishioners. From various communities of monks and canons, the bodies of saints had been brought forth in reliquary chests or golden images. The ranks of the saints had been distributed among tents and pavilions in the meadow of Saint Felix, situated about a mile from the city.

This place was especially adorned by the golden majesty of Saint Marius the confessor, the equally golden majesty of Saint Amantius, also a confessor and bishop, the golden reliquary of Saint Saturninus the martyr, the golden image of Saint Mary, the golden cross of the Holy Cross, and the golden majesty of Saint Faith. Besides these there were many other sacred relics, whose number need not be listed on the present page.

There, among the other events, the goodness of the Almighty [Col. 0142B] deemed it worthy to glorify his handmaid through a remarkable and extraordinary miracle. A boy blind and lame from birth, deaf and mute, was carried by his parents and placed beneath an image that was honorably elevated above them. After remaining there for about an hour, he obtained divine healing; and, endowed with the gift of perfect health, he rose speaking, hearing, seeing, and even walking happily with an unhindered step.

When the noise of the crowd resounded over such a prodigy, the elders of the council, who were seated somewhat farther away, began to inquire among themselves, saying: “What does this popular outcry mean?” Countess Bertilla answered them: “What else could it be, except that holy Faith is amusing herself, as she is accustomed to do?”

Then, having investigated the matter, they were all filled with both astonishment [Col. 0142C] and joy, and roused the entire assembly to divine praises, repeatedly recalling in their excessive happiness that the venerable matron had said that holy Faith was amusing herself.

## CHAPTER IX. Likewise, concerning a blind and lame man

Again, a certain blind and lame man spent the night before the image of Saint Marius the confessor, whose powers, wonderfully and widely spread abroad, are regarded as most famous by many peoples, hoping to recover his health.

When dawn was already breaking, sudden sleep fell upon him, and he seemed to hear a voice saying: “Go to holy Faith; for it has not been granted that you can be saved from your infirmity except through her merits.”

Awakened by this answer, the sick man began to crawl there with whatever strength he possessed. When he reached the place [Col. 0142D], the aid of the holy martyr—one that admits of no delay—was immediately at hand. For as soon as the man had thrust himself into the very entrance of the pavilion, his veins began to revive and his sinews to regain strength, and he deserved to be made upright from his bent condition. When the covering over his pupils was torn away, the most serene light followed the preceding discharge of blood; nor did he lack any part of health, since the hand of the heavenly physician had touched his limbs.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the man freed from hanging on the gallows through the aid of holy Faith

Among the other things about holy Faith that were still being told to me by various informants, as I eagerly investigated them with the greatest desire [Col. 0143A], this event resounded with festive and celebrated acclaim throughout the whole population. Having afterward investigated it more certainly from those who had been present at what happened, we commit it to lasting memory.

A very noble man named Adhémar, surnamed of Avalena—for that is the name of a mountainous region of the Limousin country—had among his numerous household dependents a man who had stolen some of his horses and fled. Eventually, at another time, when he happened unexpectedly to encounter him, he immediately had the man's eyes torn out and thereafter allowed him to go free.

But another man who had been associated with him by ties of companionship, although he had not been a partner in the aforesaid theft, he bound with pitiable knots as though he were guilty of an equal crime. His resistance and denial of any knowledge of the theft [Col. 0143B] did him no good. Indeed, when he appealed to holy Faith, the cruel man gave this answer:

“What else do criminals do, except that, when they are caught, they immediately call upon holy Faith as their patron? But without doubt this outcry ought to be punished by execution.”

He therefore fastened him to a horse’s running pace, drove him home, and committed him to custody in a subterranean and dark prison deep within the interior, intending to hand him over the next day to be hanged on the gallows.

What, then, was the wretched man to do? Throughout the night, fearful and anxious in that horror of darkness, he remained estranged from sleep, never ceasing to invoke God and his holy servant with whatever words he could muster.

Around midnight he saw a maiden of indescribable appearance coming toward him from the direction of the doorway. He supposed that she was a chambermaid, except that the figure surrounding her [Col. 0143C]—neither candle nor any lamp-like implement—gave forth light.

When she approached, she began, as though unaware, to ask him why he was being held in prison. After he had explained everything and then asked her name, she answered that she was holy Faith.

“And do not,” she said, “abandon what you have begun, nor entertain any distrust; but always keep both the name and the cry of holy Faith in your mouth. Nevertheless, what they have threatened you with, you will undergo tomorrow: you will go to the gallows. But the Almighty lives, and he will draw you back from the very jaws of gaping death.”

After continuing with these and similar words, the heavenly power departed. He spent the remainder of the night in great trembling because of the extraordinary vision of the divine presence. Yet, since a good power had visited him, his mind could not be thrown into confusion.

When morning came [Col. 0143D], he was led out and brought before the tribunal. But the more frequently the man named holy Faith, the more hastily the malicious mind hurried toward the gallows. They therefore proceeded to the place of execution.

It was not enough for the old man to command only his servants; he himself had to go, accompanied by a large cavalry escort. The man who was being led away bound did not cease, as he had been warned, to invoke the name of holy Faith until the path of his voice was closed by wooden nooses, his throat strangled. Then they abandoned him hanging.

When they had gone some distance on their return, they looked back and saw the gallows empty. Returning amid great commotion, they raised the man, who had been bound even more tightly, back up again.

Again, when they looked behind them as they were returning, they found the man lying on the ground beneath the gallows, having slipped free [Col. 0144A]. Some were already saying that this was the power of holy Faith, when the cruel beast angrily rebuked them with threats and reproaches and forced them to keep silent.

Then, as the story goes, he tightened the man’s throat much more harshly and savagely with newly twisted cords, and watched him hanging until he had no hesitation in believing that he was strangled.

Yet, when they had already begun to descend as they returned down the slope of the mountain, he could not endure his anxious concern without turning his grim eyes back. When he saw the miracle, he ran back and, finding the man released and unharmed, hesitated over what to do.

The others, however, unanimously and openly proclaiming the power of holy Faith, declared their lord guilty of the most wicked deed and announced that they would no longer tolerate such an outrageous crime.

Seeing, therefore, that the miracle was worthy of recognition [Col. 0144B], the old man, moved by repentance, began to beg the man’s forgiveness. The latter would not agree, but said that he would rather go to holy Faith and lay this injury before her.

Then the aforesaid Adhémar, seeing the man’s obstinacy, himself hastened to holy Faith with fifteen young men of his household, barefoot and unarmed. One might have seen the two Adhémars—for both bore that name—arguing before the sacred image as though before a tribunal: one accusing, the other confessing his sin and offering amendment.

The elders of the place intervened, however, and, prescribing the legal compensation for the attempted killing of the man, restored peace between them.

As I have said, this miracle had already been widely reported in popular accounts; afterward it was reported with the unanimous testimony of the monks. To give credibility to their words [Col. 0144C], they summoned as a witness a more mature young man, a cousin of the aforementioned Adhémar, who had come with him to Conques after his rescue from hanging.

Had I had the opportunity, I could also have seen Adhémar himself, either by waiting for him to be summoned through messengers or by extending my journey to him. They said that no more than five years had passed since this occurred and that he was still alive.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the man for whom holy Faith brought a hammer to shatter iron fetters

Again, they unanimously related to me a most extraordinary story concerning another man. He was suffering under prolonged imprisonment and continually crying out to holy Faith, when holy Faith soon appeared to him as he lay awake [Col. 0144D].

When she identified herself by the name of holy Faith, she immediately presented him with a very old hammer, covered with rough rust, and ordered him to strike his fetters with it. Then, laden with fragments of iron, he was to set out quickly for Conques.

The man carried out her instructions. By means of the passable opening in the prison, without human hindrance and relying on divine protection, he made his way directly to holy Faith. In gratitude for so great a benefit, he rendered great thanks to God and to his holy servant, not being ungrateful.

The hammer remained hanging there for about three years, so that it might serve as a visible sign of so great a miracle for pilgrims. I was greatly annoyed that they had destroyed even the hammer for a commemorative work [reading uncertain].

Wonderful to relate! Where [Col. 0145A], do you suppose, did holy Faith obtain a material hammer? But we must not measure a divine work by human reason; we must faithfully believe what occurred.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the man who, warned beforehand by holy Faith, escaped by leaping through a tower window; and concerning the miraculous donkey

I am about to relate a marvelous event, memorable for all ages and concise even for wearisome readers. I faithfully beseech God, the living fountain of wisdom, to pour the abundance of divine wisdom into the hidden chambers of my heart and to deign to irrigate the dryness of my understanding with the dew of the Holy Spirit, so that I may be able to express what is true in an appropriate and straightforward manner, and so that my judgment, straying from the right path, may not begin to deviate through empty matters from the way things truly are.

A certain soldier was being held captive [Col. 0145B] in the district of Rodez, at the fortress of Pers, under the authority of a very noble man named Amblard. Having given hostages for himself, he came secretly to holy Faith, as though he were going to attend to some other business. Then, when the appointed time had come, he returned to captivity.

How he later escaped after some time through divine visitation must now be told. But first the situation and character of that land should be recalled in a few words.

The country is mountainous everywhere, and in places so elevated with dreadful cliffs that the eye can scarcely be satisfied with the vastness of its heights. Yet among these mountains a plain happens to occur, so fertile in the production of crops that no land of rich Ceres and excellent Bacchus seemed to me more productive.

I think that this fertility came to them because the land stands higher than our regions [Col. 0145C] and is therefore more rigid through the severity of winter cold; and because it lies nearer the sun, being situated toward the southern quarter, it is consequently hotter in the summer heat. In summer, because of its nearness to the sun, it burns excessively with scorching heat. In winter, because of the elevation of the land, it stiffens under excessive cold, as in places where the South Wind rules with freer reins.

Thus, under the opposing forces of differing natural conditions, the more that land is pressed, the more thoroughly it is baked and sweats out its useless moisture. As a result, it became the parent of a richer and sweeter growth.

But because, as we have said, it differs from our soil through the irregularity of its mountains and cliffs, it happened that the structure of the aforementioned town, founded upon the solidity of an exceedingly lofty rock, rose far higher [Col. 0145D] through the spacious emptiness of the air.

The townspeople’s settlement occupied the side that appeared flatter and more suitable for habitation. It had a fortress standing on a moderate site, namely on the side where the ground plunges down in a steeper descent.

On the summit of the tower, on that same side, there was the lord’s chamber, where the lord himself, asleep with his attendants, enjoyed tranquil sleep. Outside that chamber, on the same upper floor and on the side facing the rest of the town, the captive I have mentioned was kept under the guard of three household servants, bound at the legs by a massive weight of iron.

To this man, who had long been crying out to her with lamenting cries and had almost despaired, holy Faith appeared in a bodily, visible form while his guards slept [Col. 0146A].

When he asked her who she was and she answered that she was holy Faith, she immediately added that his persistent prayers had wearied her—or rather that his prolonged cries had compelled her—and that she had come, sent by God, to release him.

“Why, then,” she said, “are you delaying so long? Break through the middle of the chamber and escape through the highest windows of the tower.”

When he began to crawl toward the voice of the woman urging him on, the anxious lord awoke and noticed the movement of clinking iron. He then roused the chambermaid and ordered her with threatening authority to compel the sluggish guards.

When she had done this [Col. 0146B], she closed the little door and withdrew into the chamber.

After several hours had passed, holy Faith appeared again and urged the man to undertake the attempt. When he immediately did so, he found the door closed and returned unsuccessfully to the empty bed.

Again the lord, awakened by the collision of iron, sent the maidservant as before. After carrying out the lord’s command, she returned and, by God’s will, left the door of the bedchamber open.

After this, when everyone had been overcome by a much heavier sleep, holy Faith appeared for the third time and reproved the man’s cowardice more harshly and severely.

When he objected that the door was an obstacle and complained bitterly that he had already been deceived twice, she said: “Do not doubt, because you will have an unobstructed path, and God will help you.”

Trusting in the Lord, he began to move himself forward as best he could. At last, with great difficulty, he penetrated the chamber and stopped at the very windows, greatly terrified by the height of the fall.

Then holy Faith, accompanying [Col. 0146C] the man whose courage was still wavering, and seemingly going before him as though preparing the way, began to encourage him manfully:

“Come,” she said, “with confidence; you will not be able to escape in any other way. In former times, likewise, the Israelite people, warring against the tribe of Benjamin in vengeance for the crime of the city of Gibeah, are said—before obtaining victory and at the prompting of a divine oracle—to have struggled through three attempts.”

At last, placed in a pitiable danger, he took courage and set his heart upon the peril. First putting his feet out through the windows, he committed his whole body to the vast precipice. Yet Sardanapalus was never more softly and pleasantly cherished by his hanging feather bed than this man was received by the hardest rock.

So greatly did divine power support him that, although nature had denied him wings, he seemed plainly to fly rather than fall.

Made more secure by this miracle, he did not hesitate to attempt a leap [Col. 0146D] into a much deeper precipice. For, rushing down from the highest cliffs upon which the fortress rested toward the lower ground, he reached the firm earth after a third leap.

It is marvelous to relate and terrifying to hear: with what audacity could the human mind ever have ventured upon so great a danger? I confess that, in recounting such things, I myself tremble all over from excessive horror.

But he who wished to glorify his holy servant through such a miracle granted this man freedom from fear of so great a precipice. Although he suffered no injury, the crashing of the battered [bodiarum; reading uncertain] nevertheless reached the ear of the sleeper during the first leap.

Awakened by this, the soldier was inflamed with excessive fury. He announced the matter to his servants, accused the guilty, called them scoundrels [Col. 0147A], and finally ordered them threateningly to pursue the fugitive as quickly as possible.

They treated their lord’s instructions as ridiculous and promised that by the next day they would, in due time, be picking up the fragments of a battered corpse.

Nevertheless, he did not yield to them. He ordered torches and lamps to be lit and commanded runners to go ahead quickly by another route, where the descent was easier, and to seize the man.

The fugitive, drinking in the glow of the torches and already hearing nearby the shouting of his pursuers, was uncertain what to do. His feet were burdened by the enormous weight of the iron, but he crawled with all the force he could toward the refuge of a small wood that God’s providence had caused nature to produce near the town. He strove to draw himself together with all his strength.

No one needed to compel him [Col. 0147B], since necessity itself commanded him; nor should his slowness be criticized, for he seemed to himself to be moving more slowly than a tortoise.

While he struggled in this anxious danger and was already gathering himself somewhat among the dense shrubs, he strangely came upon a donkey. A knotted belt served as its halter. He mounted the donkey’s back in a womanly fashion, with both legs turned to one side, preferring to consider his immediate advantage and setting aside masculine propriety.

He would certainly have been caught if that donkey had delayed the fugitive for even a moment. Never did a horse, with freer and gentler ambling, proceed more easily and regally than the donkey traversed the middle of the region toward the place where the fugitive was thought least likely to be sought.

Meanwhile, the rider [Col. 0147C], not entirely trusting to safety, repeatedly pricked up his ear, held his breath, and looked back, turning his gaze around in case he might hear or see anyone, until nearly eight miles had been completed and he felt himself sufficiently safe.

Day was already breaking, and the emerging dawn was already compelling weary mortals to return to their labor. He tied the donkey to a certain shrub; then, when he saw harder flints, he turned a little away from the path.

The iron rigidity, receiving the blows of those stones, readily yielded to its own breaking apart, like ice. But while this was being done, the heavenly donkey vanished.

When he looked back, he could see neither the animal itself nor, despite searching with all possible diligence, any trace of the animal anywhere. He recovered the belt as evidence of the miracle from the place where he had tied it.

He therefore [Col. 0147D] proceeded directly to holy Faith on foot.

Until that day no one had entered the basilica of Saint Saviour amid a more beautiful or splendid spectacle, nor had the people of Conques ever looked upon anything with greater pleasure than the sight of a noble man, whose conspicuous and tall stature, of a most handsome body, carried a heavy mass of iron on his shoulders and breaking through the surrounding crowds celebrating the feast toward the tomb—like a lion that, having broken out of prison, burdened with the great weight of chains around its neck, returns to its native refuge in the forest.

Then, in the presence of the whole people, the man laid down his burden and granted freedom to the hostile load that he had brought captive upon his neck. Returning in a happy restoration, he filled the elders and the entire people with joy at the novelty [Col. 0148A] of so great a miracle.

Afterward he satisfied the hearts of his friends, long suspended in grief, with the joy of his unexpected return. From that time his captivity brought no further sadness: neither financial loss nor bodily harm followed it.

But what, do you think, should be inferred concerning that donkey, except that it was an angel of benevolent power, manifested in the form of a humbler beast of burden? Upon such an animal the Saviour himself also sat, preferring to be carried on a lowly mount in order to humble the arrogance of worldly pomp, although he is the Lord exalted above all nations and his glory is above the exalted ones.

O the great merit of one young girl! O the admirable gift granted to one woman! O the admirable and ineffable grace bestowed upon one virgin! Her powers can no longer be recorded by pen or adequately expressed even by human speech [Col. 0148B].

For holy Faith does not wield miraculous power only there where her body rests. Rather, as I have learned from those who daily witness her powers, on land, at sea, in prison, in illnesses, in many dangers, and—as I myself have now partly proved—in various necessities, whoever calls upon her with an upright heart will find her present.

And wherever holy Faith has a name, there too she has power—to the praise and glory of Christ almighty, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns in coeternal unity, forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning a certain Raymond: how he was shipwrecked and rescued through the aid of holy Faith

[Col. 0148C] It also seems appropriate to speak of a certain Raymond, a native of the district of Toulouse, outstanding in lineage and wealth, who possessed in that same region a town that the peasants call Boschitum.

At one time he undertook a journey to Jerusalem. After traversing most of Italy, at the city known to the ancients by the name Luna, he trusted himself to the Mediterranean Sea in a prepared fleet, so that by a sea voyage he might approach the region of Jerusalem more quickly and directly.

But when they had already crossed a very great part of the sea and were cleaving the blue waters, a storm suddenly arose. The ship struck the rocks and was wrecked; broken apart, it left the captain and the rest of the crew swallowed in the whirlpools, with only two men spared—Raymond and one servant whom he had brought with him as a faithful attendant.

That servant [Col. 0148D], clinging to a very small fragment of the vessel, was cast upon the Italian shores. Believing that his master had certainly been killed by the waves of the sea, he returned to the host with whom his master, as is customary among pilgrims, had entrusted part of his money.

To whom could he more properly return it than to his master’s wife? Explaining his misfortunes to her, he also informed her of her husband’s fatal end.

For a while she pretended grief, but she did not turn the matter into heavy tears or prolonged sighs, as is customary among good women. Instead, immediately becoming an elegant observer of men, she cast an unbridled and fickle love among various kinds of beauty.

Thus she obtained the man whom she found pre-eminent among the others, as suitable as possible [Col. 0149A] for her lust. She gave him the castle and would have transferred the rest of the honor to him as well; she would even have alienated the daughters whom she had borne to Raymond from their father’s inheritance, blinded and ruined by desire, had not a certain Hugh surnamed Excafridus, an old friend of the aforementioned Raymond, placed himself in the way of the girls’ maternal wrongs.

To prevent them from being reduced to disgrace without dowries, through his authority and the exertion of all his resources he recovered and retained half of the estate, apart from the castle, augmented by revenues.

Nor was there prolonged uncertainty about marrying the maidens, since he agreed that each of the two sisters should marry one of his sons.

But to return to what came before: Raymond, embracing in the same way one of the broken ship’s beams, was driven not toward Italy but toward Africa, continually invoking the aid [Col. 0149B] of holy Faith and never removing her name from his mouth.

Three days had already passed since he had seen neither human being nor monster. So stunned and stupefied was he by the raging sea that, apart from the natural instinct for preserving life—an instinct implanted even in brute animals—he understood absolutely nothing.

Then suddenly he encountered bands of pirates coming from the region of Turlanda, equipped in a warlike fleet with nets, weapons, spears, shields, and arms of many kinds. Having long thirsted for plunder, they had on that very day cast lots and discovered that they would immediately find booty.

Accordingly, when they found and captured the man, they surrounded him with barbaric shouting and questioned him about his race and status. No one was concerned about his circumstances, since they plainly [Col. 0149C] saw that he was a shipwreck victim.

But, as I have said, the violence of the waves had made him forget himself and the stiffness had seized his limbs so completely that he scarcely remembered that he was a human being, much less could he answer their questions—especially since he had never learned either their language or their customs.

Later, after completing their voyage, they returned to their homeland. When they questioned him again, he had been somewhat restored by food and rest and answered that he was a Christian. But he entirely denied his noble birth and professional rank, falsely claiming that he had been a farmer.

They therefore placed a digging tool in his hands and ordered him to dig. Because of the excessive softness of his hands, accustomed to liberal pursuits, and his impatience with unfamiliar labor, he did not complete the task adequately. They then began to treat him wickedly and beat him brutally with whips.

Finally [Col. 0149D], unwillingly and under compulsion, he revealed himself and declared that he had formerly practiced nothing except the arts of military service.

After an immediate examination, they tested him and found him highly skilled in arms. In addition to the other expertise of this art, he was said to gather himself beneath his weapons and protect himself with his shield so skillfully that it was difficult for anyone to strike him.

They therefore enrolled him in their military ranks and frequently took him on campaigns. When he soon acquired distinguished glory and renown, they promoted him to a higher rank of honor.

Meanwhile, in a battle fought between them and the Barbarini, the Barbarini, having killed and scattered the others, carried Raymond away as a captive for the second time.

After investigating him, they too began to treat him honorably [Col. 0150A] and frequently took him into danger. At last, after being defeated by the Saracens of Córdoba, they lost him once more.

When these men had also tested the fierce and energetic soldier in various dangers, they congratulated themselves on possessing so excellent a warrior with immense happiness and joy. Indeed, everything succeeded according to their wishes and never failed when he was their companion.

Yet the unrestrained elation of sudden joy is sometimes chastised by the interruption of sudden misfortune. For when battle was joined between them and the Alabites, they were victorious but were deprived of so great a soldier.

Finally, they waged war against Count Sancho of Castile, a very powerful man and highly skilled in military affairs. Overcome through the aid of Christ, they lost not only Raymond but also an enormous number of Christian captives.

But these barbarian [Col. 0150B] names of peoples do not appear to have been used in this form by the ancients. As the knowledge of former generations has perished through the negligence and idleness of posterity, the names of many peoples have either been entirely erased by oblivion or altered by the advance of barbarism.

When Count Sancho learned that Raymond was not only a Christian but also distinguished by noble birth, he marveled at his fortunes, rewarded him with gifts of every kind, and granted him freedom together with the other Christians.

Before he departed from him, however, holy Faith appeared to him in his sleep:

“I am holy Faith,” she said, “whose name you, shipwrecked as you were, invoked so steadfastly. Go without fear, because you will recover the honor you lost.”

He therefore rose and returned to his homeland. When he was already approaching his castle and heard that his wife had married another husband [Col. 0150C], he feared appearing there openly. For that reason he hid for some time beneath the poor covering of a pauper’s dwelling, awaiting what God’s providence would determine for him. He was partly disguised by the clothing of a pilgrim and partly disfigured by age.

For three periods of five years had passed since he had gone into exile from his homeland, and for that reason every hope that he would ever return had died.

Nevertheless, one day a certain little woman who had formerly been his concubine happened by chance to assist him while he was bathing. Recognizing him from the familiar features of his naked body, she said:

“Are you that Raymond who, long ago, while traveling toward Jerusalem, was believed to have been swallowed by the sea?”

When he denied it, she continued:

“This is true, and you will not be able to conceal your presence from me, since you once lived with me.”

Finally [Col. 0150D], she hurried secretly, as discreetly as she could, to the lady of the castle and announced the unwelcome news. Thus his arrival first came to light through a vile harlot.

Overwhelmed by the return of her husband, she began to hasten toward finding some hidden and dishonorable way to bring about his death. But while devising the means of killing him was being delayed, and no sufficiently effective opportunity for the crime presented itself—for will and fortune were at odds—he was warned in a dream, withdrew from the danger, and sought protection for his life.

He would have done this somewhat earlier had holy Faith not ordered him to come by name to his own castle. But I believe that it happened by divine will so that he might fully discover his wife’s treachery.

When he learned that his daughters [Col. 0151A] had married men of distinguished rank, he sought out the father of his sons-in-law, recounted his misfortunes, and exposed his wife’s guilt.

Hugh Excafridus, with the help of faithful friends, children, sons-in-law, and fathers-in-law, restored his old friend to his estate and rank, after soon driving out his rival.

It was further decreed that he should take back his wife. This could be done according to the institutions of the ancestors, and there would be no disgrace in it: for the man who had her, as soon as he saw that a common judgment was being imposed upon him, had yielded to what was just and right and was prepared to relinquish another man’s rightful possession.

The other man, however, because of the stigma of murderous intent, rejected her from his heart, since her wicked conscience had inflicted upon him a wound greater than any violation of bodily chastity.

To supplement briefly what was said above, they also add that Raymond had received from the first pirates [Col. 0151B] a powerful herbal potion. It had been treated with magical incantations, so that those who drank from it once were dulled by such Lethean forgetfulness that they could no longer remember either their lineage or their home.

Afterward, through heavenly mercy, holy Faith appeared to him, roused him from the stupor of that forgetfulness, and restored the matter to his memory. Yet after this he still had a slower recollection, God arranging matters in such a way that, while the traces of his former correction continued to testify, others might understand from how many evils the Lord had delivered him.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning a pilgrim who was captured and bound, and suddenly freed through the aid of holy Faith
Certain pilgrims, natives of the Limousin region, were traveling to Saint Foy. They had passed by the castle of Oebalus, which is called Torenna, when a certain townsman of that place happened to meet them—a man hostile to them, named Gosbertus. He was a cleric in name only, but in conduct a worldly soldier. Having immediately found a pretext, he reduced them all to captivity. Lord Oebalus had happened to be away; his wife at that time—though shortly afterward she was abandoned by him through divorce—Lady Beatrix, on hearing this, sent word to the soldier that, if he ever wished to have her favor, he should at once let the pilgrims go and should not detain them by force within the town’s enclosure for even one hour.

But he, not daring wholly to oppose his lady’s commands, said: “I shall release these men at my lady’s order, retaining only this one, who has proved more injurious to me and whom it is difficult to let go unpunished. If this is not sufficient for her, let her know that she will not obtain what I am certain I shall never do even for Saint Foy.” And so, after dismissing the others, he ordered that this one man alone be bound in fetters, which the rustic tongue calls *bodias*. Their rivets, hammered hard with a mallet so that the connection might become impossible to undo, broke of their own accord, while the fetters themselves were also shattered into pieces. Finally, the same thing happened with a second pair of fetters, borrowed from elsewhere. The same loss befell a third pair as well, and he said: “As I see it, Saint Foy—unless I guard against her cunning—will forcibly take my enemy away from me. But I shall strive to ensure that the matter turns out otherwise than she supposes.”

Then he had the man’s arms bound tightly with coils of rope crossed before his chest in the form of a cross. After this he had each palm brought around the neck on either side and tied with extreme force between the shoulders. With bonds winding beneath the armpits, he had the belly constricted with rough knots, so tightly that the wretched man, bound by that unheard-of arrangement, was suffocating; his breath could scarcely sustain life through a narrow opening.

He then ordered twelve spearmen, whom he had found to be equally deranged, to stand constantly beside the man, shut up in an isolated room. If they saw him freed by divine power, they were immediately to cut him down, all pierced at once by a single stroke, lest he boast that he had escaped alive.

After a short interval, the wretched man, overcome by intolerable distress and thirst, could scarcely express his condition in words, so severely had the hardness of the bonds obstructed the organs of speech. Then one of the guards I mentioned, having requested water, pressed his elbows beneath the bound man’s throat so that, once his chin had been loosened, he might bring the drink to his mouth. At that moment the difficulty of the knots released itself of its own accord, with only the little cords remaining attached to the arms to which they had been fastened.

When he himself realized that he had been divinely freed, he began to flee from the place with extraordinary vigor. But immediately, at the elder’s command, the guards attacked and stabbed him with their blades. At once, however, they were so constrained by the force of divine power that they remained fixed in place: no one could move, nor could they utter a word to one another. Thus suddenly the angel of the Lord confined them, so that they remained motionless, as though they were stone images.

Only one of them, amid the distress of suffocation, uttering a muffled groan of obscene interjection, burst out with great difficulty: “Ah! He is already going on.” The others remained fixed and immobile until the man had fled to Lady Beatrix, [so that] he might take refuge in flight. The following day she assigned him guides, to accompany him until he had gone well beyond the castle’s boundaries and could take a safe road; one of them was named Peter.

At last, when he reached Conques with his companions, he gave thanks there to the Lord for his deliverance and afterward returned joyfully to his own home, leaving behind the bonds as testimony to the power which, as I have said, remained there, hanging from his arms with loosened knots.

About a year and a half after his second return from Conques, it happened that I had to visit the court of Lord William, count of Poitiers, on a certain matter. There I saw Lady Beatrix, who had been sent there by her brother Ricaredus, count of Rouen. I eagerly entered into conversation with her and immediately began to reflect upon this miracle. Her words, agreeing in every respect with the words of the monks of Conques, could provide credible evidence if anyone should doubt the other matters they had related to me.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning a young man restored to life

Having thus briefly previewed these matters, as though hastening on to others, another almost unbelievable event presents itself, which we have taken care to entrust to living pages lest it perish in silence.

The regions commonly called Ultraclusana are so named. There, a married couple remained sterile for a long time, joined in the bond of marriage but without the fruitfulness of offspring. After taking counsel, they approached the shrine of the holy virgin. As soon as they had fulfilled their vows and begun the return journey, by divine mercy the woman’s womb was made fertile; and, delivered in childbirth, she brought forth a male child.

When this son had lived, as was thought, almost three lustres, envious death overtook him, and he was brought to the end of life, to the grief of his parents. When they saw the end of their dead son, they assailed Saint Foy with various and countless complaints and demanded that she restore to them the pledge they had lost:

“What benefit, holy and glorious Lady, did you intend to give us by your gift, when you had foreseen that we would become more sorrowful through his premature fate? He was yours, since we, already despairing of offspring, obtained him; for the sake of obtaining him we sought your holy thresholds; prostrate upon the ground before your sacred tomb, we deserved to be heard in our petition; and through you, blessed mother, we obtained the desire we had long cherished.

“What benefit was it, blessed and glorious mother, for us to obtain what we sought, if we are now forced to endure the loss that has followed? Come now, blessed virgin of Christ, in your accustomed compassion, and restore to us our child alive again—the child whom indeed we received through you, when your grace made our womb fruitful. You can no less restore to us one who has been taken away than you earlier prevailed in granting one who had not been born at all, when [the Lord] had denied him. In both matters you will prove most powerful; in both you will be recognized as the most effective martyr.”

With many such complaints, irreparable grief tormented both parents beside the bier of their dead son, and, as they embraced the lifeless body, heavy sobs of sighs exhausted them. When the bearers had already taken hold of the coffin to carry it to the church for burial, the parents cried out to Saint Foy in lamentable tones and implored her with extraordinary howls to restore the gift they had lost.

As they raised these funeral cries all the way to heaven, suddenly, as though returning from a deep sleep, the young man raised his head from the bier. His face had already been covered with a shroud, but he shook it and began to wonder at the noise of those standing around. His mother, still leaning over the bier without moving away, immediately perceived that he was breathing with living breath. She quickly uncovered his face and hands and, her manner transformed, drenched her cheeks with tears of overwhelming joy.

At this sight the whole assembled crowd stood rigid, and, as heat left everyone’s bones, terror seized them as they gazed in indescribable astonishment. Finally, after he had been released from the torpor of death, his parents tried to ask whether perhaps he had been stripped of his bodily members and taken to another realm, or whether, placed in a mental ecstasy, he had remained collapsed in his limbs while still possessing bodily warmth.

He soon said that he had entirely departed from the present age and had been led to dark places, from which Saint Foy had forcibly rescued him and sent him back to draw again the breath of this sun.

And, so that both parents might become more credible witnesses in their account of so great a miracle, they brought him to Virbium, to the shrine of Saint Foy. With the whole neighborhood bearing witness, while we marveled and our faces were wet with tears of joy, they made him recount the event there.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the man who, trusting in the power of Saint Foy, made his sons pass through fire

Many among us have often been witnesses of the event whose narration we are undertaking, and we believe their accounts as we believe divine oracles.

In the region of Périgueux there was, they say, a castle called Montagrerium. A certain knight named Helias lived there, distinguished by nobility. He entered into marriages that were unfruitful and displeasing because he had no blessing of offspring. At length, hastening to the threshold of the holy martyr, he deserved to receive the desired seed of a marital womb.

This offspring came to him as a double gift. He loved the boys with such an exceptional affection that he called them not his own sons but the sons of Saint Foy. To demonstrate this, in the presence of onlookers who earnestly tried to stop him, he would make them pass with bare legs and feet through the globes of flame, through the midst of a pyre lit in her *phala* [enclosure?]. The boys hastened to carry this out with a quick leap, without suffering any injury from the fire—a marvelous sight.

Meanwhile, he resolved to bring these same boys to the holy martyr as though she were their spiritual mother. But because a harsh winter had driven all the rivers beyond their banks and violent storms were raging everywhere, the woman and the rest of his household tried to persuade him to reserve the journey for another time. He resisted all their encouragement completely, asserting that he would undertake the journey as planned and saying that no fear of the approaching storm would deter him.

Moreover, in the presence of the boys, he declared that he feared no shipwreck because of the holy martyr, but that, trusting in their companionship, he would cross the stormy swell of the waters in a small boat. He carried this out to completion, reached the threshold of the holy virgin, and, binding the boys by vows, recounted many astonishing things about them to the brothers of our holy community. After completing the solemn rites of prayer, he returned home joyful and unharmed.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning a horse’s eye restored through the power of Saint Foy

In the region of Auvergne there is a castle commonly called Murmontis. A certain knight there had a very valuable horse. As was customary, he bled it and, after the phlebotomy, tied it by its halter to a certain post. From this post projected very sharp stakes for hanging things, made long before from the branches of a cut tree.

While the horse was fastened to the post and wandered around in an unsteady motion, it threw its head upward and struck one of the stakes. The violent blow immediately tore out its eye by the root. The knight, distressed by what had happened, put the eye—which hung down as far as the jaws—back into its proper socket. At the urging of many who were standing there, he vowed a candle to the holy martyr Foy equal in length to the same horse’s [tail], and, fastening the gouged-out eye to strips of cloth, sorrowfully led the horse back to its own stable.

That horse was incomparable in speed and commendable in every equine strength. Thus it came about that, through the holy merits of Saint Foy acting as healer, the next day the horse was found so sound that it appeared never to have been afflicted by any illness. The knight reported this splendid miracle of her powers before the holy martyr, in the presence of all who were standing in the oratory.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning a dead man restored to life

It happened that a certain man named Hunaldus obtained, in the region of Toulouse, an admirable benefit from the holy martyr and experienced, both in sight and in deed, the unexpected magnificence of her powers.

He had a son whom he customarily sent to tend the herd in the pastures. One day, as evening was rising and the boy was bringing the cattle home, he negligently left one ox among the thickets, while he put the others into the cattle-yard stalls. Noticing that one animal was missing from the empty place, he returned alone through the dark shadows of night to search the pasture.

But after a large part of the night had passed, he returned sadly and sorrowfully, having sought in vain and without the ox. He did not know what to do or where to turn. Terrified by his father’s exceedingly severe temper, he dared not enter the house while his father knew of the matter, nor could he in any way tell him what had happened. At last, when everyone had gone to sleep, he secretly withdrew to his bed.

There, while he tossed his limbs, thoroughly exhausted by the search for the lost ox, he was immediately seized by such pain that he seemed almost to have been dissolved in every joint of his bones. As the pain grew exceedingly strong, he was deprived both of movement in his limbs and of the use of reason.

When morning came and his father saw him seized by such illness, he laid aside his anger and began to grieve with mournful groans over the impending death of his son. As he was shaken by great convulsions of sobbing, he implored the healing aid of Saint Foy with loud cries, asking that his son be restored to his former health.

The boy remained immobile throughout his body. Only in the very center of his chest did his father seem to perceive vital warmth, and in such a stupor of his limbs he passed nine days, the lights of his eyes extinguished.

On the tenth day, which was observed as Sunday, they saw the pupils of his eyes wasting away in death and his forehead and cheeks covered with cold sweat. They placed a hand against his left side and felt nothing living move; every sign clearly showed that all was given over to eternal sleep.

What more need be said? They prepared the funeral, placed the lifeless corpse upon a bier, and accompanied it with wailing lamentation. But when, on the following day, it was being carried to the place dug for his burial, the father, overcome by impatient love, embraced the cold body of his dead son. Wetting his eyes and entire face with continuous tears, he filled the place with bitter cries.

Amid these inconsolable groans, he repeatedly called upon Saint Foy, martyr of God, and with tearful entreaties begged her three and four times to restore his son to him, saying:

> “Virgin Foy, beloved of God, renowned light of the world,  
> who are accustomed swiftly to bring help to the afflicted,  
> hear the voice of your suppliant, most holy martyr;  
> I ask you to bring whatever aid you can to the wretched.
>
> No one who, compelled by need, has sought your gift  
> has departed empty-handed, while you held back your hand.  
> I believe—and my faith is not vain—that you have been able  
> to obtain from your heavenly Lord what I desire.
>
> Behold, my only son, my sole delight,  
> my one hope and love for the continuation of my line, has died.  
> When he has perished, how will the rest of my life, still remaining,  
> drag out its thankless delays, deprived of an end?
>
> But if, virgin of God, you are moved by any complaints of the wretched  
> and overcome by their flowing tears,  
> restore now, I beg you, to their former life  
> the limbs of the son whom we see lying asleep in death.”

While the father, leaning over the dead body, lamented with a great wail in these and many similar complaints, all who had gathered for the final funeral service, moved by the compassion of the grieving man, wet their faces with tears. With prayers mingled with weeping, they unanimously entreated the most glorious virgin Foy to look upon them with a gracious face at the invocation of her holy name.

Then immediately—and oh, marvelous to say!—

> Grim Death, apparently fleeing backward, abandoned its prey,  
> and the devouring creature vomited its plunder from its greedy throat.  
> At once he moved his head with a slow nod,  
> and turned it from side to side, his cold marrow growing warm  
> with life-giving nourishment. Suddenly, through his frozen limbs,  
> infused spirit caused the whole body to live.  
> He rose as he lay there, scarcely lifting  
> his trembling eyes. But soon he raised all his limbs together  
> and stood upon the soles of his feet,  
> the structure of his limbs upright.

From there he returned home by the divine path, accompanied by his father. At this sight everyone turned to give thanks and poured out tears of joy at so great a miracle. Glorifying the power of the holy virgin and martyr Foy, they devoted themselves and their families to her as suppliants through vows and offerings.

After returning home from the church of Saint George, where they had gone for the young man’s burial, the father and the other members of the household carefully questioned him one day about what he had seen during those nine days when, placed outside himself, he had lain like a dead man, and how, or through whose aid, he had returned to the breath of life after being carried away for burial.

Still trembling in his breast and drawing long sighs from the depths of his spirit, he immediately began to answer their questions:

“To pass over in silence for the present the other things that happened to me at the very end, I shall quickly relate them with complete certainty and without any uncertainty of falsehood. When my spirit had been released from its bodily bonds, I was handed over to certain most dreadful ministers. Under their cruel guidance I was dragged to the mouth of an enormous abyss.

“As I feared with indescribable terror that I was being thrown into its horrible chasm—and should I speak or remain silent?—behold, a man of extraordinarily splendid appearance arrived. As I learned afterward, it was clearly Michael the archangel, governor of paradise. The most glorious virgin Foy stood beside him as his companion, shining with wondrous brilliance brighter than the sun.

“When this governor of heaven saw, in the manner of executioners, those to whom I had been assigned for torture raging implacably over my punishment, he said: ‘Why, you craftsmen of evil, do you rage with such cruelty against the torment of this young man? Why are you destroying, without any compassion, a soul created by the Most High God? Cease now your grievous mutilation of him, because, with God’s permission, through this most holy virgin Foy he will be restored to his own body, rescued from your power.’

“At these words the infernal ministers, seized by intolerable fear, restrained their hands, always ready for evil, and trembling with unusual terror obeyed the heavenly messengers. Without delay, the most fortunate virgin Foy rushed with swift force through the midst of the torturers, violently snatched my soul from their hands, and thus wonderfully restored it to my body, which, as you know, was being consigned to the earth.”

After he had related in order not only the vision but also the truth of what had happened, his father and the neighbors set out for Saint Foy to give thanks.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Raimundus, who was freed from fetters and a chain

Another event, almost similar to this one, still demands the labor of the pen. Since it is found to have occurred miraculously, we have judged it worthy of being celebrated in eternal memory.

Many of you know Raimundus for his impious conduct; his genealogy also made him sufficiently distinguished, and he was supported by the pride of worldly honor. He came from a castle called Mons Pensatus and had as his father Bernardus, the first and greatest lord of that castle.

Because the castle was near the city of Cahors, he was handed over to canons to be educated in the letters of that city, intending in later years to join their society. While under their discipline, he suffered miserably from a scarcely curable epileptic illness that recurred at intervals. He therefore began to be regarded by his parents with all the more displeasure because they had no hope in him of natural ability.

At last, compelled by the very great and renowned favor of the saint’s powers, he approached the shrine of the holy virgin. Having obtained the remedy of the health he desired through her merciful kindness, he made a point of revisiting the basilica of Saint Foy the healer every year, to give thanks for the gift bestowed upon him.

His parents and relatives, pursuing him with detestable hatred out of zeal for his inheritance, captured him when they had achieved their purpose. Finally, they handed him over to a very illustrious man named Gosbertus, who was exceedingly hostile toward him because of the insults he had inflicted.

The most holy days of Lent had arrived. When they are observed in sincere devotion, with the discipline of frugal abstinence, they destroy every wrongful way of life. Raimundus spent them among many coils of fetters, in a dryness more severe than any hermit’s austerity, and found them a burden rather than a means of obtaining salvation.

His evening food was bread filthy with green mold. With no other food to assist it, and with water barely opening a passage, it could scarcely pass through the channels of his palate. Because this treatment was intolerable for his fierce strength, he lay entangled in fetters and triple chains like a Gaetulian lion, unable with any effort to turn either foot or hand in any direction.

Indeed, the chain itself was woven with strong hooks. It was tightly fastened in numerous folds around his legs and muscular arms. Passing from behind him through an opening in the stone tower to the outside, it was so secured from without by iron bars that it could be opened by no force except the consuming filing of biting saws.

Even amid these pressures, Saint Foy did not leave his lips, and not a single moment of his life passed without her being invoked.

After the shorter cycle of five weeks had ended in such mournful bitterness, the day dawned which, in memory of the Lord’s triumph, gladdens the hearts of all throughout the world with indescribable joy through palms and flowers of various kinds. The common joy of that day, spread across the regions of the earth, offered him no happiness of relief.

When almighty God saw the obstinacy of the savage torturer Gosbertus, he was moved to mercy on the following night through the intercession of the holy virgin; for mercy is always ready for those who despair of life. While sleep softened his pains, God sent the wretched man a young man flashing with marvelous brilliance. The figure addressed him in these words:

“Are you awake, Raimundus, or are you weighed down by sleep?”

In the sweetness of his dream he seemed to answer: “Who are you, lord?”

The other replied: “I am Stephen, who, having long ago been stoned by the Jews, deserved to be enrolled among the assemblies of the citizens above. I have therefore been sent to lead you more quickly to Saint Foy.”

When Raimundus asked where the magnificent virgin was, the chief martyr said: “Rise, for you are not being deceived by sleep. Follow me without delay, and you will see her of whom I speak.”

As the vision persuaded him, Raimundus seemed to follow the holy martyr who went before him. Setting him upon the bridge of the Dordogne at Conques, Stephen addressed him in honey-sweet words:

“Direct your gaze, my son, upon the summit of this cloud-bearing mountain, and behold the divine radiance. In the midst of its immeasurable splendor, the most holy virgin Foy, the illustrious martyr, shines among the hands of angels and clearly indicates what honor is owed to her for her merits.”

When he heard this, rejoicing at the exalted praise of the sacred virgin, he raised his waking eyes upward in the vision. He saw a fiery globe shining with immense brilliance. In its midst the beautiful virgin, radiant among the angels standing beside her, said:

“That place which you see is adorned with my bones. I ask you to sanctify it with your hands.”

The angelic citizens gladly obeyed the virgin’s command. Raising their shining right hands, they made the sign of the venerable cross, and through the power of that sign the entire place was filled with the grace of holiness.

While this was happening, suddenly a stormy darkness arose—a cloud-bearing whirlwind ascending from the bottom of the river. It covered the man standing on the bridge with mist, and the falling dew thoroughly soaked his clothing.

Struck with astonishment by the vision, he scarcely tore his eyes from sleep. Then, touching his clothes with his hands, he found them wet with the falling rain, just as he had felt in the vision. Feeling around him with his hands, he discovered that all the coils of his bonds had been undone. He also found the little door, strongly secured by locks and bars during the night, standing open.

Clearly recognizing that a true vision had been shown to him, he immediately—since his mind repeatedly wavered with anxious concern about whether or not to leave—strengthened by courage, leapt over the guards’ defenses in a headlong flight. He raced up the stairway and passed through the midst of the guards lying there, reaching the upper chambers.

While he stood there turning many things over in his uncertain heart, it finally came to his mind that, because of their great weight, he could not carry the machinery of the bonds to the basilica of the holy virgin. At least, he thought, he ought to carry there a chessboard hanging in the place as evidence of his escape.

Taking it, he avoided the wall at the point where it rose highest by leaping down. Uninjured, he hurried barefoot into flight. On the rough path, as his feet slipped, a woman’s figure soon appeared before him. Having taken the footwear from her right foot, she addressed him first:

“Are you that Raimundus whom Saint Foy has just freed from prison bonds?”

When he confessed that he was, she immediately offered him the shoes as aid for the road, saying: “Take these and escape from these regions as quickly as possible while the opportunity for flight is open to you.”

Considering carefully the gift and the comfort of this benefaction, Raimundus understood that she was none other than the presence of the holy virgin. But while he was reflecting on this, she suddenly vanished and was nowhere to be seen.

Strengthened by the exhortations of so great a patroness, he completed the flight he had begun. Those pursuing him could not catch him, because Saint Foy protected him. Thus rushing unseen through the midst of his enemies, he reached the city of Cahors, where he took pains to render fitting thanks to the protomartyr Stephen, as though to the guide who had gone before him on his journey.

Because he was exhausted by prolonged hunger and flight, he sent Saint Foy, in gratitude for the salvation she had granted him, the largest candle he could provide.

Finally, on the night when, through the Lord’s betrayal, both our salvation and the destruction of the Jews proceeded, he was preparing in the wardrobe of the holy martyr the reading that was to be read in the morning. Sleep overcame him, and there he rested peacefully. In the cloud of that sleep, Saint Foy appeared mingled with him like the sun shining through the morning mist, and seemed to rebuke him in words, as though somewhat angered:

“Are you so tormented by laziness that you cease during these holy days of Easter to perform before the sanctuary of my bones the customary solemnities of thanksgiving to me? Why do you delay? Cast off the knots of delay and, with the chessboard—the credible memorial of your liberation—hasten on foot to the place of Conques. There celebrate the sacrament of Easter joy.”

Moved by the grace of this vision, Raimundus broke through the weariness of sleep. He fearfully reported what had been commanded him in sleep to Geraldo, bishop of the church of Périgueux, newly entered upon his episcopal office and happening to approach the walls of Toulouse, and likewise to Bernardo, bishop of the same city of Cahors, what had been commanded him in sleep.

When they heard Saint Foy’s instructions, they ordered him to fulfill the commands by deeds and not to delay them for any intervening reason. What more need be said? Content with only one servant, he undertook the journey and carried out the commands of the authoritative virgin.

Victorious on the journey he had begun, he reached the aforesaid place burdened with the chessboard, knelt in prayer, and expressed everything he had conceived in humble murmuring. After completing the prayer, he made the sign of the holy cross upon his forehead and the place of his heart. While all present held their mouths in silence, he carefully related what had been wonderfully done for him through the holy virgin amid the pressure of the chains.

A large crowd of both sexes heard this, and among them was the son of that same Gosbertus, who happened to be there among his fellow soldiers for the sake of prayer. He stood rigid with incredible astonishment, marveling at how Raimundus could have been freed from the entanglement of so many bonds. No less astonished was Goffredus, whose playful chessboard it had been; Raimundus had rescued it and carried it there upon his own shoulders as an offering to the holy virgin in testimony of his escape.

At last, recognizing the divine power, they turned to proclaim its praises, glorifying the power of Saint Foy, which the Lord, in answer to her sacred merits, had granted her in every kind of miraculous work.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning a mule restored to life

We shall now briefly bring to your attention what, in our own time, was wonderfully accomplished on the road of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, through the most glorious servant of Christ.

In the region of Italy called Lombardy, a certain knight, Garbertus by name, from the district of Rouergue, overtook a Poitevin traveling ahead of him, a man sufficiently distinguished by birth and military excellence. After exchanging greetings, he set out on his journey in the Poitevin’s company.

As they conversed with one another about many matters, they eventually reached the great deeds of Saint Foy in their connected discussion. The man from Ruthenicum attributed no small praise to her miracles. The Poitevin received his account with immense admiration and approval.

When they arrived at an inn in the village of Saint Domninus, the Poitevin’s mule, which was especially dear to him, was seized by a very serious illness and, dying, scarcely survived until the following day.

Garbertus, remembering how many great things Saint Foy had once accomplished for such animals, asked his companion whether he had done anything to obtain a remedy for this mule. When the other replied, “Not at all,” Garbertus immediately added:

“Have you not heard what I told you yesterday about Saint Foy? Send her a gold coin devoutly, and you will immediately receive your animal back healthy.”

Without hesitation, the Poitevin produced a gold coin from his purse and gave it to Garbertus to carry to the holy virgin.

But Saint Foy, reserving her hand for a greater display of power, did nothing for the living mule and granted it no improvement in health.

What more need be said? Dawn rose and urged everyone to hasten along the road they had begun. The mule, having died, was carried out of the stable, and only the price of its hide was paid. The travelers set out sorrowfully: one had received the gold coin as a pledge of life, while the other, having lost his animal, was forced to suffer the loss.

The man from Ruthenicum, distressed with great embarrassment because of his boasting about Saint Foy’s powers, wished shamefacedly to return the gold coin he had received.

When he held it out to its giver, suddenly he heard behind him the sound of something following, like the noise of a fleeing animal and a rider urging it on. Turning his face backward, he saw at a distance the innkeeper’s mule fleeing at a tiring gallop, while the innkeeper strained with great effort to catch it.

When he saw this, Garbertus cried out to Saint Foy in astonishment and kept the gold coin he had intended to return in embarrassment.

After recovering the mule, they asked the innkeeper what had happened in the animal’s restoration. He cried out in amazement:

“O happy are you, who have such a virgin as your patroness! Through her almighty merits, not only is the salvation of your souls granted to you, but great remedies are also provided for your bodies. This holy virgin, in deed and in power, does not permit your needs to lack assistance—even in the resurrection of animals.

“This animal you see, thrown down in the street with its teeth exposed and every breath gone, she brought to life among the hands of those who were cutting it up. With a swift leap it sprang from the ground and, escaping from our hands, was restored for your use.”

When they heard this, the whole company of pilgrims burst into praises and compelled the entire air to echo Saint Foy’s name with rival voices. Then, after paying the innkeeper the price of the hide—namely, eight silver pieces—they joyfully sought the sacred thresholds of the apostles. Returning home, they paid the vowed gold coin with immense thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the soldier who was afflicted by disordered movements of the intestines
A brave soldier lived in the Arvernian district. When misfortune lay in wait for him, his internal organs, abandoning their proper position at intervals, burst forth with a great rumbling of the intestines as far as his private parts. Worn down by excessive grief, he often prayed for death, lest he should endure this condition any longer.

After a long time, having gone from being a mounted soldier to a man on foot, he addressed his wife, who knew of his illness. [a] Under the cover of her counsel, he resolved to seek from holy Faith this favor for the affliction. Although his wife resisted and raised many objections, he carried out the intention he had conceived and thus approached the holy virgin. Devoutly prostrating himself before her most sacred body, he repeatedly entreated her with tears for the purpose of his coming and poured forth especially earnest prayers to obtain healing.

On the following night [Col. 0161D], after prolonged prayer, he lay exhausted before the holy virgin’s mausoleum. He saw the holy martyr standing beside him and addressing him in a somewhat bashful manner—as is customary with virgins:

“Are you asleep?” she said.

When he replied that he was sleeping, the blessed virgin continued:
