“Know,” she said, “that until now I have not been petitioned for a matter such as this, for which you are requesting our aid, although from various illnesses I have bestowed powerful remedies (*agridia*; the term is uncertain). But so that you do not depart from here entirely without counsel, I shall briefly explain what will prove beneficial to you. You know the blacksmith who lives in your neighborhood?”

When he indicated that he knew the man well by name and appearance, the same virgin said again [Col. 0162A]:

“Without hesitation, approach him and, with all your strength, ask him to strike you a very powerful blow upon that affliction laid upon the anvil, using the greatest hammer—the one with which a glowing mass taken from the furnace is beaten. This will quickly bring you the healing you desire.”

Forewarned by these words, which seemed almost like a jest, and at once overcome with astonishment and wonder, he awoke from sleep and pondered for a long time in the depths of his heart what such a vision might mean.

At last he returned home and, with his heart resolutely prepared for death, approached the aforementioned blacksmith without anyone knowing. He secretly disclosed what had been commanded him by holy Faith. When the blacksmith heard this, he collapsed in utter distress and swore that he would never perform such a phantasmagorical deception.

“Believe me, my lord,” he said, “these are not the words of one who heals, but rather of one who mocks [Col. 0162B]. If, in your credulity, you choose to follow this advice, you may be accused of being responsible for your own death. I, however, will in no way be the author of so grave a crime; for I know beyond any doubt that by this act you would incur immediate death.”

As the blacksmith tried to excuse himself from going further, making many conjectures and citing the many fears he had—especially fear of the man’s relatives, should he end his life in agony by a blow from the hammer—the soldier immediately assured him that none of these things would happen to him.

What more need be said? The swollen coverings of the genitals were spread upon the anvil, and the diseased private parts were prepared for the final blow. But as soon as the blacksmith, raising his arms, saw the enormous weight of the hammer lifted into the air, he was shaken by unimaginable terror, fell backward, and, as though lifeless, collapsed upon the ground with a heavy crash of his limbs.

In that precipitous fall [Col. 0162C]—marvelous to relate!—all that boiling upheaval of the intestines was immediately drawn back inward, so that thereafter throughout his life it never again appeared to burst forth externally.

Thus he escaped unharmed, neither burned by cautery nor cured by a single full draught (*amystide*) of any antidote. The “game” of holy Faith, so to speak, would provide all posterity with a spectacle sufficiently joyful and astonishing. Thus that heavy burden was lifted; thus that harsh disgrace was suppressed. Thus, instead of the horror of a terrible death, he was healed and flooded with the immeasurable fullness of ineffable joy, to the praise and glory of the holy martyr.

Lest this event seem ridiculous to anyone and therefore be rejected by us as fabricated, we consider it appropriate to call publicly upon Robert, abbot of the monastery of Cantojol, a man of highly venerable and honorable old age [Col. 0162D]. From his testimony this event was made known to us, for the man who suffered it lived far away and afterward did not appear before our eyes. From his mouth, therefore, we learned what we report. He does not flatter the ears of the people with foolish adulation or fabricated buffoonery; rather, he commends whatever he utters with his mouth by its truth. Indeed, if such a reporter is doubted, God’s benefits are distrusted.

## CHAPTER XXII

### Concerning a certain matron who acted impiously against holy Faith and perished wondrously

A marvelous event occurred in the territory of Cahors. Since almighty God wished to perform a monstrous deed there for love of his virgin, we deem it worthy to insert into this account.

In the territory mentioned above [Col. 0163A] there was a certain noble matron who—either because the female sex is always said to be greedy, or certainly through diabolical prompting—desired without measure the land of the holy martyr adjoining her own fields. She drove away the monks’ plowmen, who were working the land, after subjecting them to numerous insults.

The following day she had those acres cut with her own plow and presumed to bring them under her authority. But heavenly power acted in such a way that, while she ordered the field to be removed from its boundaries and pressed the matter vigorously, she suddenly withered throughout her entire body [Col. 0164A] and, chattering with horrifying shrieks, surrendered her wretched spirit to the underworld.

The plowmen, greatly terrified by her dreadful end, abandoned the plow and fled. Scarcely able to grope their way along in their extreme agitation, they reported what had happened to their lord. He, grieving over the woman’s death, sent for the corpse and buried it in the earth. After she had been extinguished in this manner, the land of the holy martyr remained secure from everyone and afterward lay under the monks’ authority.

# 1029 A.D. SAINT FULBERT, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

[Col. 0163]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(Oudin, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 519.)

[Col. 0163B] Saint Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, the most distinguished man of his age for holiness of life and learning, was first made treasurer of the church of Saint Hilary of Poitiers through the favor of William, duke of Aquitaine, as a fragment of the *History of Aquitaine* reports. The same fact may be read in Ademar of Chabannes’ *Chronicle*. Distinguished in life and learning, and a burning lamp lit by the Lord upon the candlestick of the Gallican Church, he was made bishop of Chartres after Rodolf through the authority of Robert, the Most Christian king, to whom he was especially dear. He was consecrated by Liétheric, archbishop and metropolitan, as Fulbert himself affirms in Letter 23, addressed to him:

“I consider myself greatly indebted to you, Father, in love and fidelity, by whose hand I received blessing and sacred anointing.”

Having attained the episcopal dignity [Col. 0163C], he vigorously defended ecclesiastical liberties, as he frequently indicates in various letters that he wrote to supreme pontiffs, kings, and bishops. Some of these survive, including one to Francon, bishop of Paris, *On Extirpating Benefices from Lay Hands*. He also complains gravely to Pope John about Count Rodulf, the sacrilegious usurper of the rights of his Church, imploring apostolic assistance:

“Fulbert, the little bishop of the great and illustrious Church,” he says.

It appears that he obtained the episcopate, as we have said, through the favor of King Robert, whose cause he energetically supported against Queen Constance. This is evident from a letter to the same king, in which he complained as follows about the violence of Viscount Godfrey against the church of Chartres:

“With all the weeping of heart and mind, I bend my knees and beseech your Piety [Col. 0163D]: come to the aid of the Church of the holy Mother of God, over which you have wished us, your faithful servants, to preside as best we can, though unworthy. After God, all our consolation and relief amid the troubles that beset us depends entirely upon you [Col. 0164B].”

He asserts his humility in these words, in Letter 68 to Odilo, abbot of Cluny:

“It is fitting, Father, that you in turn assist by your sacred intercessions your own little servant, dependent upon you and looking toward you with great confidence. For I am a very wretched man, who, since I was not sufficient for my own affairs, have somehow—whether by reason or by rashness—been led into public responsibility.”

How great the friendship between him and the aforementioned Odilo was is shown by a monk of Savigny, who writes in the *Life of Odilo*:

“He judged that Odilo should be called by this name—‘Archangel of the Monks’—in his sermons and letters. That Fulbert, his intimate friend, bishop of Chartres, praiseworthy in holiness and marvelous in wisdom, at whose death the study of philosophy perished in France and the glory of priests almost fell.”

Some writers state that he was chancellor of King Robert, but this lacks documentary proof, since in reality he was rather only chancellor of the church of Chartres. Moreover, when the city and basilica burned in 1020, Fulbert laid the foundations of the church of the Mother of God and completed it with a marvelous stone vault and timbered roof. Through this distinguished work he spread the chief fame of his name among posterity, with money supplied especially by the king of the English.

We learn this from William of Malmesbury, Book II of *The Deeds of the English*, in these words:

“King Cnut, sending money to churches overseas, enriched Chartres above all, where Bishop Fulbert then flourished, most renowned for holiness and philosophy. Among the other proofs of his industry, he brought to splendid completion the church of our Lady Saint Mary, whose foundations he had laid [Col. 0164D–0165A]. He also strove to honor it as much as possible and frequently exalted it with musical melodies. Whoever hears the chants sounding forth heavenly vows will be able to infer with what love he yearned to honor the Virgin.”

Among his other works there survives a volume of letters, in one of which he gives thanks to Cnut, the most magnificent king, because he had poured out the resources of his generosity for the expenses of the church of Chartres.

He was a most devoted servant of the Most Holy Mother of God, whose praises he published in a special book; it is said that she rewarded him. For when he was seized by illness, the Virgin appeared to him in a vision and opened her sacred breasts for him to suck. Alberic, although living long after this time, bears witness to it in his *Chronicle* under the year 1022 [Col. 0165B]:

“Fulbert flourished, a bishop most renowned for holiness and philosophy. He laid the foundations of the holy church of the Mother of God and completed it with marvelous stone timbering. He is also said to have been visited by that same Mother of God during his illness and restored by her most holy milk. He burned with great love and the happiest devotion in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, as is shown by the chants he composed about her, consecrating heavenly vows. Among his other works there survives a volume of letters.”

William of Malmesbury, Book III of *The Deeds of the English*, also bears witness to the same thing when speaking of Berengar of Angers, his archdeacon and formerly his pupil at the school of Chartres:

“Berengar, although he himself corrected his doctrine, plainly could not convert all those whom he had corrupted throughout the whole world. They say that Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, foretold this—Fulbert whom the Mother of the Lord was once seen to heal, when he was ill, with the milk of her breasts. For when many people visited him as he lay near death, and the capacity of the house scarcely sufficed for the crowds arriving, he scanned Berengar with his eye among the opposing groups and judged that he should be driven out with all the force he could muster. He protested that a huge dragon stood near him and was corrupting many people, enticing them to follow it with flattering hand and alluring breath.”

Finally, he departed this life in 1029, on 10 April. In some manuscripts he is said to have died in 1028 and to have been buried in the church of Saint Peter in the Valley. He is everywhere commended as worthy of esteem for his great reputation for holiness and learning, a reputation praised by the aforementioned Glaber, by the chronicles, and by many other authors [Col. 0165D].

The following epitaph of Fulbert is found in a manuscript:

> In the year 1028 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, our father Fulbert, beloved by God and human beings and of venerable memory, died: the glory of the bishops of his age, a brilliant light given by God to the world, a supporter of the poor, a consoler of the desolate, a restrainer of plunderers and robbers, a most eloquent man and most wise in both divine books and the books of the liberal arts. For the restoration of the holy church of his diocese, which he himself had begun to rebuild from its foundations after the fire, he left a good portion of his gold and silver. He illuminated that place with the rays of discipline and wisdom and did many good things for his clergy.

[Col. 0166A] The following verses about the same man are also read:

> Whom the source of goodness granted you, O Chartres,  
> Fulbert, an excellent river of twofold learning,  
> A star among bishops, Fulbert, radiant in conduct,  
> Clothing and constant sustenance for the poor;  
> Here enclosed he lies, dust made from dust,  
> And awaits rising with the others.  
> Cultivating virtues, putting vices to death,  
> With God’s help he proved himself from childhood.  
> For twenty years, and one and a half besides,  
> He presided over your church, Virgin Mary.  
> Phoebus was about to enter Taurus  
> After seven lights had passed, when he left his grieving people.

His works were printed individually at Paris in 1608 and afterward incorporated into volume XI of the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, published in 1618. There are found 134 letters, some sermons, a canon on women’s penance, several hymns with proses [Col. 0166B], and a treatise against Jews who deny that this prophecy of the dying Jacob—“The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah,” and so forth—was fulfilled in Christ the Lord.

On these works, see Bellarmine and Labbe. As a supplement to them, we add that there is also a letter by Fulbert on the religious and prudent distribution of the goods of the Church, in volume II of Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 827 of the Paris edition.

Under the same name, Surius includes in his *Approved Lives of the Saints*, under 13 December, p. 989 in my copy, the *Life of Saint Aubert, Bishop of Cambrai*. Although Surius published it in mutilated form, the brothers of the abbey bearing his name in the city of Cambrai possess it complete, as the brothers Sammarthani write in volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, in the section on the archbishops of Cambrai, p. 233.

The sermon *On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, which appears among the works falsely attributed to Saint Augustine, in the spurious sermons, sermon 208, col. 343 of the most recent edition prepared in our time by the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur, also belongs to the same Fulbert, bishop of Chartres [Col. 0166C].

Finally, we have found an excellent treatise by him on Acts 12:1, “King Herod stretched out his hands,” and so forth, in a manuscript in the library of Longpont, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Soissons. We published it in octavo at Leiden in 1692, by Peter van der Meerche, under the title *Sacred Opuscula of Several Ancient Writers of Gaul and Belgium*, so that it might not perish with the passage of time.

The following authors discuss Saint Fulbert: Balderic, bishop of Noyon, in Book I, chapter 77 of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*; Henry of Ghent, who begins his *Catalogue* with this author and celebrates Fulbert as the most learned man of his time in the liberal arts, a religious man, and most devoted to the Blessed Virgin; Antonio Possevino, volume I of the *Sacred Apparatus*, under “Fulbert”; Robert Bellarmine and Philippe Labbe, both in their works *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Aubert Miraeus, in his notes to Henry of Ghent’s *On Illustrious Writers*; Gerardus Joannes Vossius, Book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 43, p. 341 in my copy; and the brothers Sammarthani, volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, in the section on the bishops of Chartres, p. 485. Here we have reproduced them word for word, changing only the order [Col. 0166D].

[Col. 0167]

# A SECOND NOTICE ON SAINT FULBERT

(*Literary History of France*, volume VII, p. 261.)

## § 1. The history of his life

[Col. 0167A]

Fulbert, the greatest light of the Gallican Church in his time, remains unknown with regard to his family and place of birth [Note: The different ways of pronouncing this name are the reason it is written differently in printed books and manuscripts. Instead of Fulbert, one finds Folbert, Fulpert, Ulbert, and even Umbert; sometimes with a *W*: Wulpert and Wlbert, from which Wilbert was made. Since the latter did not seem more distant than the others from the true name, this gave rise to the supposition that there were two different persons.] (MAB., *Acts*, vol. VIII, p. 686, no. 11). He himself tells us that he was not distinguished either by birth or by wealth (FULB., *Poems*, p. 51):

> But recalling that I relied neither on wealth nor blood,  
> I ascended the cathedra, lifted from poverty and filth.

Some scholars, on the basis of one passage in his writings, have inclined to make him a Roman (FLEU., *Ecclesiastical History*, book LVIII, no. 57; MAB., *Acts*, vol. VII, preliminaries, no. 43; *Annals*, book LII, no. 72). But what they cite is highly ambiguous and proves this in no way. There would be better grounds for believing him to have been from Poitou, or more generally from Aquitaine. His close ties with Duke William V, to whom these provinces were subject, provide a strong presumption; that presumption becomes nearly proof when we see Fulbert represent himself as this prince’s subject (FULB., Letter 15), calling him his master, *herus meus*. If he had named the bishop to whom he addressed his twelfth letter (Letter 12), he might perhaps have removed all difficulty on this point. It is certain that he was born and received his first education in the diocese, or even the episcopal city, of this prelate; but it seems no less certain that the letter was addressed neither to a pope nor to a bishop of Italy.

Despite the poverty of his family (his *Poem*, ibid.; HEN. GAND., *Writers*, chapter 1), Fulbert found a way to obtain good teachers, under whom he made progress in human letters and ecclesiastical sciences that was extraordinary for his time. Of his teachers, only the learned Gerbert is known (MAB., *Acts*, vol. III, p. 371, no. 9); but he is enough to establish the merit of Fulbert’s early studies. After leaving the schools of Reims, he withdrew to Chartres, perhaps prompted by Herbert, one of his fellow students, who was from that city and who, having converted from Judaism to Christianity, became one of the learned men of his century. There Fulbert opened a school that soon acquired a brilliant reputation; at that time there was none more celebrated throughout almost the whole of Europe (ANN., vol. I, pp. 420, 422; ANN., vol. IV, appendix, p. 698, no. 2; BAR., *Annals*, 1007, no. 1). People flocked there from the most distant countries—from Arles, Liège, and Cologne—as well as from the nearest places. Monks and clerics vied with one another in going to listen to the venerable Socrates who directed it (ADEL., to B., p. 438, no. 1) [Col. 0167B].

Alongside his duties as master of the schools at the church of Chartres, Fulbert also held those of chancellor. This title has misled several writers, who took occasion from it to suppose falsely that Fulbert had been chancellor to Robert, king of France (ROB., *Alternative Chronicle*, p. 74, no. 1; VOSS., *Latin History*, book II, chapter 43, p. 115, no. 2). His literary labors were not, however, without reward, although he lived in a century when letters were not generally esteemed. William, count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine (ADEM., *Chronicle*, p. 173; DU CHES., vol. IV, p. 82; FULB., Letters 103, 128), already mentioned briefly, was a learned prince and protector of men of knowledge and virtue. He summoned Fulbert to his side and overwhelmed him with honors. Among other benefits, he gave him the treasurership of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, which Fulbert retained for a long time, even after becoming bishop, but which before his death he returned into the hands of his benefactor [Col. 0168A].

Baronius believed that Fulbert had been a monk of Saint-Père in the Valley (BAR., *Annals*, 1007, no. 2; MAB., *Annals*, book LII, no. 101). But the twenty-first letter, on which he bases his opinion and which at first sight seems to support it, actually destroys it. It contains the names of all the monks who then composed that community, and Fulbert’s name is not among them. Mr. Cave, Mr. Baillet, and Father Le Long—who apparently says this on their authority—are even less acceptable when they make Fulbert abbot of Ferrières before the year 1004 (CAVE, pp. 518–519; LE LONG, *Sacred Library*, p. 736), since Rainard governed that monastery in the same capacity at least as early as 997 (MAB., ibid., book LI, no. 43).

The only true point is that Fulbert was bound by a very close friendship to the greatest abbots of his time: Saint Abbo of Fleury, Saint Odilo of Cluny, and Blessed Richard of Saint-Vanne (FULB., Letters 21, 66, 67; HUG. FL., *Chronicle*, p. 175; MAB., ibid.), and that he was always strongly attached to the monastic order [Col. 0168B].

After teaching for a long time at Chartres (TRIT., *Chronicle of Hirsau*, p. 159; *Writers*, chapter 315), and acquiring through his learning the esteem of kings, bishops, and peoples, Fulbert’s merit caused him to be elected bishop of that city upon the death of Rodolf. He was particularly indebted for his elevation to King Robert, with whom he had studied at the school of Reims (FULB., Letter 4; MAB., *Acts*, vol. III, p. 371, no. 9). Almost all historians place the beginning of his episcopate in 1007 (BAR., ibid.; VOSS., ibid.; CAVE, p. 518). Some, however, contrary to the authority of his epitaph, postpone it by nine or ten years (MAB., *Annals*, ibid.; BAIL., 10 April, p. 143; FULB., Letter 23). He was consecrated by Leoteric or Leutheric, archbishop of Sens and his metropolitan. The length of his episcopate suggests that his ordination took place toward the end of September or at the beginning of October. It is supposed that he was still young [Note: The verse that led people to believe Fulbert was still young at his ordination is the following, in which he speaks of himself:

> And he brought the young man to this point, that you might be bishop.

But he means only that Providence led him by stages from his youth to the episcopate. The proof that he was not young at that time is, on the one hand, the long period during which he taught before becoming bishop and, on the other, the advanced age to which he lived (FULB., *Poem*, ibid.; MAB., *Annals*, ibid., p. 420), although his episcopate lasted only twenty-one and a half years.] then; but the remainder of his life shows that he must have been approaching at least fifty years of age (FLEU., ibid.).

The duties of the episcopate with which he was burdened did not cause him to interrupt the public lessons he gave to his disciples (MAB., *Annals*, ibid., p. 420). He merely ceased practicing medicine and administering remedies, as he had done previously (FULB., Letters 10, 47, 113). To these two kinds of occupation was added another that required considerable time. On becoming bishop, he became the oracle of almost the whole of France (BAR., ibid.). Princes, bishops, and private persons resorted to his counsel as to a source of light [Col. 0169C]. The proof is found in the collection of his letters.

In May 1008, shortly after his ordination, he attended the council that King Robert had summoned to his palace at Chelles (COUNCILS, vol. IX, pp. 787–788), and there received public marks of the respect and veneration in which he was held. Indeed, out of honor, they wished him to subscribe immediately after the metropolitans and before eleven other bishops, several of whom, such as Adalbero of Laon, had long been bishops. It appears from this that his colleagues already regarded him as their father and teacher.

We are not informed in detail about the actions of this great bishop. One of the most memorable [Col. 0169D] was the rebuilding of his cathedral, which had been reduced to ashes in the burning of the city in 1020 (FULB., preliminary letter, p. 2). Fulbert undertook to rebuild it with a magnificence that far exceeded the resources of a bishop without patrimony. But he found abundant resources in the generosity of Cnut, king of England and Denmark, and of William, count of Poitiers, his illustrious benefactor (Letter 97, 102, 104).

His singular devotion to the holy Virgin, under whose invocation this cathedral is dedicated [Col. 0170A], led him to establish there the feast of her Nativity, whose institution was still of recent date elsewhere (CAVE, p. 518, no. 2). The same motive of piety led him to compose several proses and hymns in her praise (FULB., *Poem*, p. 50; preliminary letters 2, 3).

In place of a continuous history of the actions of our prelate, his letters provide us with many instances of his pastoral conduct. They show that he had succeeded in uniting in his person truly episcopal firmness with noble gentleness and humility without abasement. Attentive to employ one or the other with wise discretion, when obliged to use his fiery zeal to repress disorders or correct abuses, he always did so without offending the respect owed to those in authority [Col. 0170B].

He loved his prince tenderly and felt a sincere attachment to him (Letter 96). When he incurred the prince’s displeasure on one occasion, he had no rest until he had regained his friendship. To these general features, and to those supplied by his epitaphs, let us add what he himself says about the duties of a bishop, and we shall have a fairly natural portrait of him (MART., *Anecdotes*, vol. I, pp. 131–135). He could not have written otherwise than he acted; thus, in explaining what good bishops ought to be, he succeeded in painting himself.

This pious and learned prelate died, full of years and merits, on 10 or 11 April; for ancient authors assign the latter date, unless their text is corrupt. But the greatest disagreement between the ancients and moderns concerns the year of his death. Some, such as Hugh of Flavigny and Clarius, place it as early as 1027. Others place it in 1028. The majority, especially among modern writers, assign it to the following year. Some postpone it until 1031, and Raoul Glaber two years later still (FULB., ibid., preliminary matter, p. 3; MALLEA., *Chronicle*, p. 202; LAB., *New Library*, vol. I, pp. 276, 287, 315; HUG. FL., *Chronicle*, p. 175; CLAR., *Chronicle*, p. 791; GLAB., book IV, chapter 4; VOSS., ibid.).

How can the truth be discovered through so many differing opinions? Might it be determined by the day of his death? In that case, the opinion of those who assign it to 1028 amounts to the same as that of those who place it in 1029, and there is no more than one opinion. The reason is decisive: 10 April 1028 fell before Easter, according to the reckoning of the French of that time, who continued to count the year as 1028 until Easter; whereas according to our present manner of reckoning, the year 1029 had begun in January [Col. 0170D].

To obtain something more decisive regarding the true year of Fulbert’s death, we must turn to his epitaph. It is an original document, probably composed by Sigon [Note: This Sigon, successively schoolmaster and cantor of the church of Chartres, whom we have already had occasion to mention several times, is also called dean by the historian of the abbey of Saint-Florent of Saumur, who adds that he notated the responsories for the office of this saint, composed by Rainauld, master of the school of Angers.] who took care of his funeral. It states that he governed the church of Chartres for twenty-one and a half years. Of these six months, let us take two months and twenty days to complete the year 1007, in which the holy bishop was ordained; there remain twenty-one years, three months, and ten days, which, added to 1007, bring us to 10 April 1029. It is therefore to that year that Fulbert’s death must be assigned.

We willingly submit this chronological discussion, which seemed necessary to us, to the judgment of the latest supplementer of Moréri, who has tried to transfer it to the preceding year.

Fulbert was buried in the church of the abbey of Saint-Père, where several of his predecessors and other prelates had already been buried (FULB., preliminary matter, pp. 2–3; *Gallia Christiana Vetus*, vol. II, p. 486, no. 1). Two epitaphs were erected in his memory: one in prose, which is more a brief eulogy intended for insertion in the necrologies, and the other in verse [Col. 0171B].

## Prose epitaph

> In the year 1028 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the third day before the Ides of April, our father Fulbert, beloved by God and human beings and of venerable memory, died: the glory of the bishops of his age, a brilliant light given by God to the world, a supporter of the poor, a consoler of the desolate, a restrainer of plunderers and robbers, a most eloquent man and most wise in both divine books and the books of the liberal arts. For the restoration of the holy church of his diocese, which he himself had begun to rebuild from its foundations after the fire, he left a good portion of his gold and silver; he illuminated that place with the rays of discipline and wisdom and did many good things for his clergy.

## Verse epitaph

> Whom the source of goodness granted you, O Chartres,  
> Fulbert, an excellent river of twofold learning.  
> A star among bishops, Fulbert, radiant in conduct,  
> Clothing and constant sustenance for the poor.  
> Here enclosed he lies, dust made from dust,  
> And awaits rising with the others.  
> Cultivating virtues, putting vices to death,  
> With God’s help he persevered from childhood.  
> For twenty years, and one and a half besides,  
> He presided over your church, Virgin Mary.  
> Phoebus was about to enter Taurus  
> After seven lights had passed, when he left his grieving people.

To this point the church of Chartres has conferred no public cult upon this pious bishop, although it is said that his holiness was attested after his death by several miracles (TRIT., *Chronicle of Hirsau*, ibid., p. 159; BOLL., 1 April, p. 856; MAB., *Acts*, vol. VIII, preliminaries; LAB., ibid., vol. II, p. 730). Bucelin, in his *Martyrology*, calls him blessed. A great many other modern writers give him indifferently the same title or that of saint. It was in this capacity that M. de La Rochepozay, bishop of Poitiers, had him included in the litanies of the saints of his diocese [Col. 0172A].

The authors of Fulbert’s century, and those of the following centuries, are full of praise for the holiness of his life and the brilliance of his doctrine, his eminent virtue and great learning. It would be too long, and perhaps tedious, to report them here. Some may be seen at the beginning of the editions of his works, where only a portion of them has been copied.

What contributed still more to making Fulbert’s name famous was the great number of disciples whom he formed in letters and piety. There was scarcely a church in France that did not have one of his pupils. They even spread into Italy and Germany, where they carried their master’s teaching [Col. 0172B]. We have elsewhere enumerated the best known of them. To these must be added Gerard (MAB., ibid., vol. III, p. 371, no. 9), later abbot of Saint-Wandrille, one of the great ornaments of the monastic order in his century, and Bernard, master of the school of Angers (ANN., vol. IV, appendix, p. 763, no. 1), who dedicated to his master his work on the miracles of Saint Faith with this glorious title in his memory:

> To the most holy and most learned of men, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres.

One cannot better convey the great services Fulbert rendered to France in particular, both through his teaching and through the honor he brought to the priesthood of Jesus Christ, than by reporting the thought of a contemporary author (ACTS, vol. VIII, p. 686, no. 9), who has no hesitation in saying that at the death of this admirable man the love of philosophy and the glory of the episcopate seemed to have been buried with him in the tomb.

## § II. His writings

Although the Church has not inserted Fulbert’s name into its official records, he has nevertheless been placed among its Fathers and Doctors. This is a title merited by the works of his pen. As early as 1585, Papire Masson published a collection of them (CARDINAL LIBRARY, R.), printed in Paris by Dupré in a small octavo volume. But this collection contains only part of the letters of our prelate.

Twenty-three years later, that is, in 1608, Charles de Villiers, doctor of the Faculty of Theology of Paris [Col. 0172D], published in the same format another, much fuller volume, which also appeared in Paris, from the press of Thomas Blaise. This editor included everything that the manuscripts of the College of Navarre and of Messrs. Petau and Le Fèvre had supplied concerning Fulbert’s works.

From this edition, full of errors, often rather gross ones, they passed into the various *Libraries of the Fathers* of Cologne, Paris, and Lyon (BIBL. PP., vol. XVIII, pp. 1–55). Since these last editions, several other writings by our author have been recovered. We shall give an account of them after we have enumerated those that have been collected together [Col. 0173A].

*[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]*
1. At the head of all these works stands the collection of his letters, the most interesting of all his writings (p. 3–39). Only 134 are numbered there, divided into two classes; but the total should be 138, because the numbers of Letters 62, 96, 97, and 118 are repeated. They do not all belong to Fulbert, as will become clear from the following account. The editors accompanied them with some notes containing useful material, but they required fuller and more instructive annotation.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] We have arranged Fulbert’s letters according to their chronological order, while retaining and placing in brackets [Col. 0174D] the numerical designations of the earlier editions, indicated here. EDIT. PATROL.]

The first of these letters, which is the longest as well as the most important, is a doctrinal letter concerning three essential points of the Christian faith, in the author’s own terms: the mystery of the Trinity, the nature of baptism, and the truth of the mystery of the Eucharist. Fulbert explains with equal solidity and clarity what must be believed concerning these three great truths of religion. What he says about the Eucharist in particular clearly shows that Berengar, one of his disciples, had received on this point of doctrine a teaching entirely opposed to that which he later professed. It is thought that Fulbert undertook to treat the Eucharist in this letter (PAGI, year 1004, no. 3) because of the error then held on the subject by Leutheric, his metropolitan—an error or abuse [Col. 0173C] described by the historian Helgaud, who discusses it in detail (HELG. *Vit. Rob.*, p. 64). Nothing could be more judicious, more prudent, or more useful for all ages than the general principles Fulbert establishes here concerning our mysteries (Bib. PP. ibid., p. 3, 2). This letter appeared so excellent to M. du Boulay that he incorporated almost all of it into his history of the University of Paris (EGAS. BUL. vol. I, pp. 357–358). It is also printed in some editions after Paschasius Radbertus’s treatise on the Eucharist. The authors of the Office of the Blessed Sacrament likewise took from it the fifth lesson of the thirty-seventh office. Several manuscripts contain it alone, and sometimes together with the second letter [Col. 0173D] and the following titles: *On Christian Perfection*, or *On the Three Most Necessary Things for Salvation*.

The second concerns the ceremony involving the consecrated host, which was formerly given to newly ordained priests (Bib. PP. ibid., pp. 6–7). On the occasion of the differences in this ceremony from one place to another, Fulbert says excellent things about not being troubled by the diversity prevailing in discipline, provided that the faith remains the same. It is addressed to Einard, improperly called Fidnard in the printed editions.

Among the others, several are written to King Robert; one to Canute, King of England; some [Col. 0174A] to the Count of Anjou, to Richard II, Duke of Normandy, and several to William V, Count of Poitiers; most are addressed to bishops, specifically to Leutheric, Archbishop of Sens. In this letter, as in several others, Fulbert gives sound decisions on the cases submitted to him and wise advice to those who consulted him about their doubts and difficulties. In general, these letters show that Fulbert was one of the leading men of his century. They contain many facts capable of clarifying the ecclesiastical and civil history of that period. For this reason Du Chesne included as many as sixty-five of them in his collection of historians (DU CHES. vol. IV, pp. 172–197). Baronius, the editors of the Cluniac Library (Clun. Bib., pp. 349–354), and Dom Marlot proceeded likewise, printing several of them in their works. Besides the historical benefit that may be drawn from them, they contain many illuminating observations on doctrine, morals, and discipline, especially concerning impediments to marriage.

The eighth does not concern Avesgaud but Azelin, Bishop of Paris, which misled some scholars, even men of the highest distinction. The twenty-first, addressed to Abbo of Fleury, does honor to the memory of that pious and learned abbot (Bib. PP. ibid., p. 11). Fulbert was not yet a bishop when he wrote it, nor was he one when he wrote the forty-seventh, in which remedies are discussed; this shows that the letters were not printed in chronological order. The ninety-fifth, which should be the ninety-sixth, [Col. 0174C] is from King Robert to Gauslin, Archbishop of Bourges, and the next is that prelate’s reply to the king. The letter marked for the second time as the ninety-sixth, and which should be the ninety-eighth, is from Count Odo to King Robert. The one numbered 108, or rather 111 according to our method of counting, is from St. Odilo to Fulbert. The following twenty-six do not belong to our prelate, having been written after his death or in his absence, either by his chapter or by private persons.

The 116th in the printed edition belongs to Hugh of Châteaudun, Archbishop of Tours from 1003 until 1023, the year of his death. It [Col. 0174D] is addressed to a bishop of Angers, who at that time was Hubert of Vendôme. This prelate refused to observe the interdict imposed on him by his archbishop for having taken up arms and ravaged the lands of the Church of Tours, and had written to him to complain about it. Hugh sent the reply in question here and showed him, particularly by the authority of St. Gregory, that his refusal to submit made him guilty and deserving of the penalty about which he complained, even if he had not otherwise deserved it. The letter is quite well written and proves that its author was not ignorant of the rules of the Church.

Among the other letters in the second class that do not belong to Fulbert, there are two—the 118th and the 122nd—from Isembert I, Bishop of Poitiers from about 1019 until approximately 1047. One is addressed to the Bishop of Angers mentioned above, to excuse his inability to attend the dedication of his church. The other is likewise a letter of excuse, but the name of the person to whom it is addressed has been truncated. Both are written with a precision, clarity, and a certain politeness that were not then very common.

As many as twelve are counted as having been written by Hildegar, Fulbert’s disciple, as he describes himself in the heading of Letter 112. In the judgment of Dom Mabillon (*An.* I, 72), this Hildegar is none other than the famous Hildier, concerning whom we have elsewhere [Col. 0175B] given an account based on Adelmann, who knew him personally. Fulbert, with whom he closely resembled one another in manner, doctrine, and breadth of learning (Ana. vol. I, p. 421), had sent him to Poitiers to administer the affairs of his treasury of Saint-Hilaire (FULB. ep. 18, 79–81). This office did not prevent him from opening a school there, which he directed himself with the assistance of a deputy master. Hildegar eventually left Poitiers and returned to Chartres, where he held a canonry (ep. 129, 130) and was subdean of the chapter in 1040 (Conc. vol. IX, p. 939). Before his departure, however, he persuaded Raginald, dean of Saint-Hilaire, to take charge of the treasury in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] Adelmann, who later became scholasticus of Liège and Bishop of Brescia, introduces us to several of Fulbert’s disciples. He places first Hildier, a man of Chartres, highly gifted and particularly knowledgeable in medicine, philosophy, and music. A perfect imitator of his master, he copied even his mannerisms, his gaze, and the tone of his voice, and could stand comparison with him. Sigon, who excelled in music, held second place. After these, Adelmann lists Lambert and Engelbert, who taught, one in Paris and the other in Orléans, and accumulated great wealth in that profession; a certain Rainauld of Tours [Col. 0175]—this Rainauld may perhaps be the same as Raginald, who later became assistant master of the school of Saint-Martin and afterward treasurer of that same church— a cleric of the church of Saint-Martin, regarded as a learned grammarian, *valentem grammaticum* (“an able grammarian”), who had an unusual facility in speaking and writing, which made his style diffuse; a certain Girard Gilbert, or Girard Glaber, [Col. 0175D] as Dom Mabillon would have it read, who, after traveling to the Holy Land, returned to France and died beneath the walls of Verdun; a certain Vautier, a Burgundian, whose insatiable passion for learning led him to visit almost all the schools of Europe, where he acquired extensive knowledge, especially in Spain, and who, on returning to his homeland, would have adorned the Latin language had not a premature death, caused by the pitiless faction of his envious rivals, taken him away; finally, a certain Ragimbald of Cologne, whom the beauty of his genius and the reputation of his learning had made highly renowned. Adelmann includes in this enumeration only Fulbert’s principal pupils, those with whom he had studied. The famous Berengar, later scholasticus of Tours, does not appear, and one cannot say why. It is nevertheless certain that Adelmann had him as a fellow student [Col. 0176C] at Chartres, as he himself tells us elsewhere. (Spic. vol. IV, p. 543; vol. VI, p. 519.) Angelram, or Enguerran, later abbot of Saint-Riquier, and the learned Olbert, who became abbot of Gembloux, also studied under Fulbert. Disciples came to him even from the depths of Provence. Domnus, a monk of Mont-Majour, was one of them and spent nine full years at his school (MAB. *An.* vol. IV, p. 698). Among his other disciples who were from Chartres or settled there, we are told of a Peter, chancellor of the cathedral and author of several writings, and an Arnulf, cantor of the same church, who composed several hymns or responsories in honor of Saint Evroul. The agent whom Fulbert sent to Poitiers to manage the affairs of his treasury of Saint-Hilaire (FULB. ep. 18, 79, 80, 120), and who was none other than Hildegar or Hildier, brought his master’s teaching there by taking charge of directing the school [Col. 0176D] of Saint-Hilaire. Fulbert had another disciple, whose name is designated only by an E, for whom he obtained a position as scholasticus, though the place is not stated. Hugh, Bishop of Langres, who died in 1051 and was the first writer to combat Berengar’s errors, must also be counted among Fulbert’s disciples, since he had first been a cleric of the Church of Chartres. M. Du Boulay supposes that Hubert, who taught at Orléans—he meant Meung—after the middle of this century, had enjoyed the same advantage (EGAS. BUL. vol. I, p. 606); but there is no other evidence of it. The same honor is accorded, with greater certainty, to Goisbert, who was considered highly knowledgeable in medicine and became a monk at Saint-Evroul (ORD. VIT. bk. V, pp. 574, 581, 595).]

The letters belonging to Hildegar are [Col. 0176A] the 111th together with the following four, written to private friends on subjects of little interest; Letters 120, 121, 123, 127, 129, and the next one together with the last, which should be Letter 138 for the reasons already given, although it is numbered only 134. Four of these final letters were written from Poitiers to Fulbert concerning his treasury, yet they also contain various details relevant to public history. Two others were written from Chartres to Raginald, dean of Saint-Hilaire. The last concerns writings and advice that Raginald had requested from the author. In replying to his request for advice, Hildegar cites what he had learned on the subject from the mouth of Fulbert, his master, who was no longer [Col. 0176B] alive. He shows himself there to be a faithful disciple of that great man, not only on this point but also in his views concerning the Eucharist and the grace of Jesus Christ. He tells us that Raginald had a nephew named Herbert, who was then at Chartres.

As for the other letters by foreign authors joined to those of Fulbert, there are six by William, Duke of Aquitaine; another written to him by Leo, Bishop of Vercelli; and five or six from the chapter of Chartres to various persons. We have entered into this detail in order to shorten the work of those who may undertake to send this collection of letters to press again. They greatly need to be reviewed against good manuscripts. The Vatican manuscript (BAR. *An.*, 1028, no. 5), where they are found together with the letters of [Col. 0177A] Saint Sidonius, would be of great assistance in carrying out this project. Almost innumerable errors have slipped into the collection, whether through the negligence of copyists or that of printers. Some are extremely gross, even in the headings, which is more consequential and has led several writers into error. We have already given some examples and will add the following to make the matter clearer. The heading of the fifteenth letter reads as follows: “To his lord the king, Fulbert. Count of Angers.” It should read: “To his lord the king, Fulk, Count of Angers.” Those reprinted by Du Chesne are much more accurate.

Since the edition of Charles de Villiers, Dom d’Achery [Col. 0177B] has published a letter of Fulbert (Spic. vol. II, pp. 827–832) which the later editors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* could have added to the preceding letters. It is addressed to Hildegar, who had consulted our learned prelate about the administration of ecclesiastical property and the use that may in certain circumstances be made of sacred vessels. On the first point, Fulbert shows him, by the authority of the Fathers, especially St. Jerome, that one cannot exercise too much care and piety in distributing the Church’s revenues. He reinforces this with the beautiful maxim that ecclesiastical goods are the patrimony of the poor, not of those who enjoy them. Regarding the second point, Fulbert sets out the cases in which it is permissible to sell sacred vessels, according to [Col. 0177C] the canons and the teaching of St. Ambrose.

Dom Martène and Dom Durand also published another letter of Fulbert from a manuscript of Saint-Remi at Reims (MART. *Anec.*, vol. I, pp. 130–135). It was written before the preceding letter, since it is cited there. This too is a reply to Hildegar, who had often pressed his master to tell him what he thought of bishops who went to war. Fulbert proves to him, by several well-chosen passages from Scripture and the Fathers, that this occupation is unworthy of the episcopate, whatever the pretext may be. He cites Origen together with the Latin Fathers, Haimo of Halberstadt, and a capitulary of Charlemagne forbidding bishops and lower clergy to bear [Col. 0177D] arms. In citing the treatise *On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*, he attributes it to St. Cyprian. This letter is one of the finest and best written of all Fulbert’s letters. In a few words it sketches the principal duties of a bishop; in this respect he merely copied what he himself practiced.

Other letters of Fulbert may still be found buried in the obscurity of libraries. Such, for example, may be the one formerly seen in a manuscript of Saint-Martin of Tournai (SAND. *Bib. Belg.* ms. part I, p. 102), addressed to William, Abbot of Fécamp, whose opening words are: “On the knowledge of the altar, or of the walls of the church.” A diploma by the same bishop in favor of the abbey of [Col. 0178A] Marmoutier, published by M. Baluze in his notes on the councils of Narbonne, pages 77–78, may also be added to these letters.

2. (Bib. PP. ibid., pp. 37–47.) After Fulbert’s letters come ten sermons. The first two are very short and contain the initial instruction given to the faithful concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, the flight from sin, and the obligation to do penance. It is evident that the first is merely a fragment of a longer discourse. The third is a brief explanation of the origin of, and the manner in which one should celebrate, the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin. The next three concern her Nativity, whose feast Fulbert, as we have seen, established in the church of Chartres. In the second of these three, [Col. 0178B] the author gives a kind of genealogy and an abridgment of the life of this blessed Mother of God. This is why these sermons are sometimes entitled “legends” in manuscripts and even in printed editions (Voss. *Hist. lat.*, bk. II). We see that it was then entirely customary to give the parents of the Blessed Virgin the names Joachim and Anne (ch. 43, p. 115). In the third sermon Fulbert speaks judiciously about a supposed account attributed to St. Jerome, according to which the evangelist St. Matthew had composed a genealogy of the Blessed Virgin and a history of the childhood of Jesus Christ (Bib. PP. ibid., p. 40). In his criticism of it, he confines himself to saying that the Church does not recognize this purported work and that it contains untenable facts and [Col. 0178C] opinions. At the end of the sermon there is a short prayer to the Blessed Virgin in two long verses. The first of these three sermons is praised by Henry of Ghent and Abbot Trithemius among Fulbert’s other writings (HEN. GAND. *Scri.*, ch. 1; TRIT. *Scrip.*, ch. 370). Father Jean du Bois printed a considerable fragment of it in the *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, having found it on an old loose leaf (Flor. bib., part I, pp. 516–517).

The three sermons that follow in editions of Fulbert’s works are entitled “Against the Jews” (Bib. PP. ibid., pp. 42–46). But they were wrongly divided into three and given the title “sermons.” Not a word [Col. 0178D] in them indicates that they were delivered orally. They are nothing other than the treatise *Against the Jews*, which Henry of Ghent and the anonymous author of Melk attribute to our learned bishop (HEN. GAND. ibid.; MELL. *Scrip.*, ch. 93). The notice given by the first of these two bibliographers leaves no room for doubt. The author, he says, undertook it to prove, against the common opinion of the Jews, that Jacob’s famous prophecy—“The scepter shall not be taken from Judah,” etc. (Gen. 49:10)—had been fulfilled in the person of Jesus Christ. Henry of Ghent adds, correctly, that Fulbert carried out his purpose very well by employing the authority of the Holy Scriptures and the force of reasoning (HEN. GAND. ibid.).

Finally, the tenth and last sermon in the collection is [Col. 0179A] entitled: “God Is One in Three Persons” (Bib. PP. pp. 46–47), a title insufficient to announce the contents of the piece, since it concerns not only the Trinity but also the Incarnation of the Word, the other mysteries of Jesus Christ, and the necessity of doing penance. This sermon is not complete. Its exordium, and perhaps another substantial portion of the beginning, are missing. The ending also appears to be missing. For the rest, it is merely a fabric of scriptural passages, though well chosen, to which the author has added two short passages from the Fathers, one from St. Fulgentius and the other from St. Isidore of Seville.

Following the sermons are two lists of the various degrees of capital sins, together with the canonical penances then still attached to them [Col. 0179B] (Bib. PP. ibid., p. 47). One list concerns men and the other women. What follows is a detached fragment of some sermon, whether by Fulbert or another author, which a copyist inserted into his manuscript for reasons that cannot be determined, in the same position in which it appears in the printed edition. The author, whoever he may be, first shows, chiefly by using the words of St. Augustine, in what sense these two verses from the sixth chapter of the Gospel of St. John—“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” etc., and “Whoever eats my flesh,” etc.—contain a figure. He then proves, by the authority of the Council of Ephesus and Haimo, that this sacred flesh is truly the body of Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0179C] Several manuscripts attribute to Fulbert the sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, which is Sermon 208 of the appendix to the sermons attributed to St. Augustine (AUG. *Serm. app.*, p. 343). But we have shown elsewhere that it belongs to Blessed Ambrose Autpert, to whom other manuscripts also assign it.

Locrius is much better founded in crediting him with the second sermon on the Annunciation (FER. LOCR. p. 52), which is Sermon 194 of the same appendix. From it, in abridged form, the lessons of the second nocturn for the feast of the Nativity and the second day of the octave were taken in the Roman Breviary and the old Benedictine Breviary. This sermon begins with the same [Col. 0179D] words as the one on the Assumption and has borrowed several other features from it. It ends with the famous antiphon that the Church uses for the commemoration of the Blessed Virgin: “Holy Mary, help the wretched,” etc.; this has led people to regard Fulbert as the author of that prayer.

No one tells us whether the homilies found under Fulbert’s name in a manuscript of the professed house of the Jesuits at Antwerp, together with Arnauld of Boneval’s treatise on the words of Jesus Christ on the cross, differ from the sermons just discussed (SAND. ibid., p. 334), or whether [Col. 0180A] this collection contains others in addition to those that have been printed. The anonymous author of Melk, when announcing our author’s sermons against the Jews, adds that he had also composed sermons against bad Christians, an expression that implies moral sermons. None of this kind is found among Fulbert’s sermons, which are either panegyrics, instructions on our mysteries, or, finally, controversial works, if one wishes to count his treatise against the Jews among his sermons.

3. The chronicle of Maillezais, or rather of Saint-Maixent, states that Fulbert, besides his prose writings, had also left several pieces of his own composition, set to music for the divine offices (Malleas. *Chr.*, p. 205). Trithemius adds (Scrip. ch. 315; *Chr. Hir.*, vol. I, p. 159) [Col. 0180B] that he had composed hymns, various prayers, chants to the glory of God, and several other devotional pieces. Fulbert’s principal editor collected everything of this kind that he could uncover and placed it after the sermons (Bib. PP. ibid., pp. 48–53). The collection is divided into two parts. It contains hymns; sequences, both rhymed and unrhymed; litanies and other prayers; antiphons; and responsories, both on certain mysteries such as Christmas and the Trinity, and in honor of various saints. There is an invitatory, a sequence, and responsories for the office of St. Giles. This, apparently, is what led the anonymous author of Melk and certain modern writers to assert that Fulbert had composed a life of that saint.

[Col. 0180C] Among these short devotional writings are two brief prayers to God (Bib. PP. ibid., p. 51), in which the author, while revealing his origin, has left striking evidence of profound humility.

[Note: [Col. 0179] In the Vatican manuscript, the first begins with the following verse, which is missing from the printed edition (BAR. under the year 1007, no. 3):

“Angel of the great counsel, Christ, I consult you.”]

There is also a poem on the year, the months, the days, the hours, the method of finding the leap day, the epacts, and so forth, which is a kind of abridgment of the computus. This poem is followed by another, rhymed but under a single rhyme, in which Fulbert praises the nightingale. The penultimate piece in the collection is a Sapphic hymn on the Holy Spirit, in which poetic beauties worthy of a better age are revealed. The final piece, entitled “Responsory,” although it is a hymn on Easter, is found separately on page 847 of volume eight of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris edition, 1645, where it is very much out of place.

The piece entitled “Hymn of the Trinity,” which begins with the words “The Word of God,” is more complete in a manuscript of the library of the King of England (Reg. Angl. ms., p. 68, no. 17). This manuscript indicates that an entire page is missing from the printed edition.

4. Casimir Oudin, having unearthed in a manuscript from Longpont, a Cistercian abbey in the diocese of Soissons, a treatise by Fulbert on these opening [Col. 0181A] words of the twelfth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles—“King Herod used his power to mistreat certain members of the Church”—had it printed together with other short works by ancient authors, both French and Belgian. This collection was printed in 1692 at Leiden by Pierre Vander Merche, in an octavo volume.

5. Dom Bernard Pez, in the course of his literary investigations, discovered a catalogue, drawn up around the twelfth century, of books then held at the Abbey of Saint Peter of Salzburg. Among the titles of these books is the following: *Computus of Wicpert*. It has been observed that Fulbert’s name was so variously distorted that it produced the forms Ulbert and Vilbert. It is quite possible that it likewise produced [Col. 0181B] Wicpert. We therefore regard it as highly probable that this refers to a treatise on the computus composed by our prelate. Our opinion is confirmed by finding a similar treatise cited in Du Cange’s new *Glossary*, under the word *Regulares*, under Fulbert’s name. The work cited there is not the abridgment of the computus printed among his writings, since that word does not occur in it, although the word *Normales* does.

6. The reasoning just given concerning the preceding treatise must, on the same principles, be applied to a poem found in a manuscript of the abbey of Weihenstephan in Bavaria, approximately four hundred years old, under the title [Col. 0181C] *Wulpert’s Metrical Little Book on Monastic Life*. This discovery is also due to the researches of Dom Bernard Pez. The poem is in elegiac verse and begins as follows:

> You who desire to avoid the dangers of the impure world,  
> and to devote yourself to divine service,  
> you will join the black cloister with no sluggish course;  
> or leave what is yours and bear the monastic yoke.

Although there is no positive evidence that Fulbert was a monk, he was sufficiently attached to the monastic order to have invited people to enter it through this poetic piece. The expressions of the third verse just quoted seem to confirm the opinion that places it in the early years of this century, when no monasteries other than those of black-robed monks were known—something appropriate to Fulbert’s time. It is known that the Camaldolese, Carthusians, and Cistercians appeared soon afterward.

This poem gives us an occasion to introduce another on the same subject, perhaps from the same century, but of considerably greater merit than the preceding one. We might otherwise have no opportunity to mention it. This poem, containing sixty elegiac verses, is entitled *Praise of the Monastic Life* and begins with the following two lines, which will give an idea of the entire piece:

> Happy is the human flock that, following Christ’s teaching,  
> retains nothing as its own, despising wealth.

Father Sirmond, having discovered it in a manuscript [Col. 0182A] of Saint-Melaine at Rennes, gave it a place in his notes on the letters of Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme (GOFF. VIND. ep. 1, IV, note, pp. 69–71). Its author is unknown, but the poem is no less valuable in itself.

7. Demochares, in chapter 15 of *The Celebration of the Sacred Mysteries*, and M. Bellotte, canon of Laon, following him, posit a Bishop Walbert of Poitiers and attribute five sequences to him in honor of various saints. As far as is known, the Church of Poitiers never had a bishop of that name. This leads us to think that Walbert is none other than the Bishop of Chartres under discussion here. If Fulbert was transformed into Wicpert and Wilbert, he could likewise have become Walbert; [Col. 0182B] and if he was described as Bishop of Poitiers rather than of Chartres, this probably resulted from one of his sequences, which is in honor of St. Hilary, whose church Fulbert served as treasurer for a considerable time. Josse Clichtove, who compiled a collection of sequences, did not include those bearing the name Walbert.

8. Bellarmine also attributes to Fulbert a treatise *On the Variety of the Divine Offices* (BELL. *Script.*, p. 277), adding that it is printed in the third volume of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, second Paris edition. We find it neither in the first nor in the penultimate edition at that location, nor even in the Lyon edition.

[Col. 0182C] 9. Most bibliographers agree in attributing to our prelate the *Life of St. Aubert*, Bishop of Arras and Cambrai, who died in 669 (SAND. *Bib. Belg.*, p. 252; Voss. ibid.; OUD., ibid., p. 521; CAVE, p. 519). What appears to support this opinion is, first, that the work was written in his time (SUR. 13 Dec., p. 901), that is, a few years after Gerard, Bishop of Cambrai, transferred the saint’s relics to the monastery bearing his name, which he did in 1015. Moreover, the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, when it has occasion to discuss this Life, says that its author was the celebrated Doctor Fulbert, without giving him the title of bishop. Despite these plausible arguments, we find it difficult to regard it as a work of the Bishop of Chartres. [Col. 0182D] Apart from the fact that no occasion is known on which he might have lent his pen to a work of this nature, the author clearly presents himself as a cleric or monk of the region, a member of the flock of which St. Aubert had been pastor and of which he remained protector through his power with God. It is possible that this author was named Fulbert and that, possessing learning and literary talent, as the history in question appears to show, he was given the title of celebrated doctor.

Surius published this Life from a manuscript that bore no particular author’s name. Le Mire warns that it is abridged in the printed edition [HEN. GAND. ibid., note], and that it is found in fuller form in manuscripts, specifically the one belonging to the collegiate church of Saint-Aubert at Cambrai. Bollandus printed a fragment of it to provide fuller knowledge of the translation of the relics of St. Vaast (BOLL. 6 Sept., p. 801). His learned successors will one day publish it in full and will fully inform us about everything concerning it. Sanderus had seen another copy in a manuscript of the cathedral of Arras (*Bib. Belg. ms.*). This one begins with the words “The holy man of God, Aubert,” which suggests that it differs from the one that has been printed.

It may perhaps not be out of place to observe that Pitseus (*Angl. Script.*, year 980), when discussing Fuldebert or Fudebert, abbot of Pershore in the diocese of Worcester in England, and wishing to elevate him to the rank of a writer, although he probably never wrote for posterity, credits him with works that incontestably belong to Fulbert of Chartres.

[Col. 0184A] As for his manner of writing, critics agree that it is superior to that of the other writers of his time (DI PIN, *Eleventh Century*, p. 18; BAIL., 10 April, p. 144). The style of his letters, in particular, is more polished. They contain wit, elegance, and a delicacy worthy of the best centuries. M. Du Pin does not judge the poetry of our prelate nearly so favorably. He is right if he means the greater part of it. Yet some poems deserve our esteem for the beauties they contain.

Barthius (*Adversaria*, book XIX, ch. 13, pp. 655–656) admired for its precision and sweetness the hymn of Saint Martin in iambic verse, which has improperly been given the title “Prose.” The one in Sapphic verse on the Holy Spirit is no less worthy of esteem. [Col. 0184B] From Fulbert’s own century, people had taken such a liking to the hymns and proses of this prelate that they were sung publicly in the churches of England (*Anglia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 48).

[Col. 0183]

## INFORMATION FROM FABRICIUS

*Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, book VI, p. 215.

[Col. 0183B] Fulbertus, called Folbertus by the Anonymous of Melk, ch. 93, was prefect of the public school of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0183D] Launoius, *On the More Celebrated Schools*, ch. 40], teacher of many distinguished minds [Col. 0183C], among them Berengar [Note: [Col. 0183D] Anonymous of Melk, ch. 93; Trithemius, ch. 315]; thereafter chancellor and finally bishop of Chartres from the year 1007; he died in 1028. His writings, edited by Charles de Villiers, theologian, Paris, 1608, octavo, and reprinted in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1618, volume XI, and the Lyon edition, volume XVIII, with his notes, are as follows:

One hundred and eight letters, to which twenty-six letters of other authors have been appended. Of these letters of Fulbert—on which Dupin should be consulted in the *Ecclesiastical Library of the Eleventh Century*, and some of which Baronius had published under the year 1007 and following years from a Vatican manuscript—two of the most important had also appeared in the earliest Paris editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

Nine sermons, the third of which is on the Purification of Mary; the fourth, fifth, and sixth on her Nativity [Note: [Col. 0183D] Some similar material occurs in the work *On the Nativity of the Blessed Mary* among the works of Saint Jerome. See Cave]; and the seventh, eighth, and ninth against the Jews. Henry of Ghent cites this work in chapter 1. Combefisius included most of Fulbert’s sermons in the *Preaching Library*.

*The Penance of Laymen*, and *The Penance of Women*, by Fulbert, bishop.

Hymns in prose form concerning Saint Pantaleon, Saint Piat, the Nativity of the Lord, and the Holy Trinity. On the feast of Saint Giles, a Greek by nationality [Note: [Col. 0183D] The Anonymous of Melk testifies, ch. 93, that Fulbert wrote a *Life of Saint Giles*]. On the divine Martin [Note: [Col. 0184D] Compare Barthius, XIX.13, *Adversaria*], on Saint Lambert, and *For the King*.

Verses and hymns on the Blessed Virgin and on the Holy Cross; on fear, hope, and love; *On Himself* [Note: [Col. 0184D] Here the first verse is longer in Baronius under the year 1007, no. 3:

> Angel of the great counsel, Christ, I consult you,  
> My Maker, my Life.]

On signs, months, days, and hours: a compendium of computation. On the nightingale. On Saint Caraunus. *The Steps of Chastity*. Prayers to God. A hymn on Christ born, and another to the triune God. Finally, a narrative from the ancient *Lives of the Fathers*, composed in verse, about a certain man who, inexperienced, had attempted to live an eremitical life but, unable to endure it, returned to his brother and learned to be a good man when the angel could not [the object of *potuit* is unstated in the printed text].

Besides these, the following works, edited by Charles de Villiers, circulate separately:

Fulbert’s hymn for Holy Easter, beginning “Chorus of the new Jerusalem.” It appears in George Fabricius’s *Christian Poets*, p. 799; in George Cassander’s *Ecclesiastical Hymns*, p. 234 of the *Works*; and in the Paris *Bibliothecae Patrum* of Bigne, 1589, 1624, 1644, and 1654.

A letter on the religious and prudent distribution of ecclesiastical goods, in Dacherii’s *Spicilegium*, volume II, p. 827 (new edition, volume III, p. 387). Another, against soldier-bishops, in Edmund Martene’s *Anecdota*, volume I, p. 130.

A sermon for the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, in the appendix [Col. 0185A] to the sermons of Saint Augustine in the Benedictine edition, volume V, sermon 208.

*The Life of Saint Autbert* [Note: [Col. 0185A] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, ch. 77. If anyone wishes to know more extensively about Autbert, let him read the book which Fulbert, a most distinguished teacher, [Col. 0186A] entitled *The Life of Saint Autbert* at the command of Bishop Gerard]. Autbert was bishop of Cambrai and Arras. The work is found in Surius under 13 December, but mutilated. Sammarthani, volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 233, and Miraeus, in his note on Henry of Ghent, ch. 1, observed that they had read a complete copy in manuscript codices.

A treatise, or sermon, on Acts 12:1–11, edited by Casimir Oudinus in *Sacred Opuscula of Several Ancient Writers of Gaul and Belgium*, Leiden, 1792, octavo, preceded by an engraved portrait of him and an abridgment of his life, as in volume II of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, pp. 519 and following, and likewise found in [Col. 0186A] volume II of the Sammarthani *Gallia Christiana*, pp. 485 and following.

*The Book on the Sacraments of Devotion*, which some attribute to Ivo. Combefisius, on the authority of Peter Damian, assigns it to Fulbert.

Labbe, in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, p. 58, recommends from a Vatican manuscript Fulbert’s *On the Virtues* and *Sentences of the Ancients on the Supreme Good*, in trochaic rhythm, as well as verses *On Peace*. He also notes that verses *On the Pound and Its Parts* are attributed to Fulbert, though he does not know whether they were published. Charles de Villiers published the verses *On the Ounce and Its Parts* and *On the Scruple and Its Parts* in his notes on Fulbert’s letter 113, volume XVIII of the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 55.

# ALL THE WORKS THAT COULD BE FOUND OF SAINT FULBERT, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES

From a manuscript codex of the library of the Royal College of Navarre, and from those of the most distinguished men, Lord Petau, royal senator, and Nicolas Fabri; edited through the study and industry of Charles de Villiers, doctor of theology of Paris. (Under this title in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* [beginning of volume XVIII] there appear only Fulbert’s sermons, letters, and poems; we shall add the others from other sources.)

[Col. 0185]

## DEDICATORY LETTER

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Philip Hurault, bishop of Chartres, Charles de Villiers, doctor of theology of Paris, sends greetings.

Here is our Fulbert, most reverend prelate, at last roused from the tomb and brought into the light—one whom neither sluggish winter nor time, devourer of all things, could destroy. Thus, just as Pliny relates that Gaius Aelius Tubero, after holding the prefecture, was brought home from the funeral pyre (*History*, book VII, ch. 52), so whatever had not survived of this author is drawn from dust and decay and brought back to the press.

Having obtained a manuscript from the library of the Royal College of Navarre, in which many passages seemed almost worn away by age, we arranged for them to be copied and, through our labor, have succeeded in preventing so distinguished a light of virtue from remaining hidden under a bushel. Yet I will not conceal one thing in silence: I have inserted into this author certain materials drawn from the libraries of the most learned royal senator, Petau, and of Nicolas Fabri, a most distinguished man—whom I would truly call the storehouse of all antiquity—which were not present in our manuscript.

The credit for this belongs to those two most illustrious men, who brought it about that Fulbert should come to light. Nor will I hesitate to add, for their greater commendation, what is related about Phidias, the greatest of sculptors. When he had made the Pisaean image from ivory, he ordered oil to be poured around its feet, before the statue itself, so as to make it immortal (Epiphanius, book II, *Against Heresies*, ch. 64). So, I believe, the supreme God wished those two distinguished men to be anointed with the oil of his grace, so that they might bestow immortality upon this bishop.

If you are willing to admit me into this fellowship of glory, most reverend prelate, I look for—and count among good things—no reward greater than one that can be reckoned in money. Indeed, I value the Fathers of antiquity so highly that I would not wish anything of theirs to be lost. Therefore, whatever I found belonging to that ancient Father, I gathered into one collection.

Consider him, then, most reverend prelate—not, I beg you, how elegantly he speaks, but how devoutly. For if you once hear him, you will grieve that he lay hidden for so long. I believe you have read that, when it was announced to the supreme pontiff Pius II that the most distinguished bishop of Treviso was breathing his last and already held death enclosed within his breast, he exclaimed: “Then the perfect prelate is dying, to whom the rest ought to have been similar” (Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, in his *History*).

Likewise, when you hear that Fulbert lay hidden for so long, you will exclaim and will be distressed that his memory was buried beneath so long a succession of ages. For who was more distinguished than he in integrity of conduct? Who more ardent in promoting the Catholic religion? He seemed to have drunk in the practice of piety with his nurse’s milk (Seneca, *On the Happy Life*).

Yet I know that praise now costs a great expenditure of time and much annoyance to other people’s ears [Col. 0187]. “A learned man!” But our Fulbert will be content with this more rustic title, if you call him “a good man.” It has now come about that people know better how to speak than how to live. But in Fulbert’s time, do you wish to know what the liberal studies contributed? To outward things, nothing; to virtue, much.

Although his writings may seem obscure in many places, one may nevertheless detect in them some hidden piety. And if you compare this author with Ivo of Chartres, I know to which of them you will award the palm. In the former, eloquence flourishes; in the latter, piety alone. Finally, I shall say boldly that those two bishops—those two eagles—were truly *ἀεροποροῦντας* (“flying through the air”), sent by Jupiter, as the poets tell us (Claudian, preface to the panegyric on the consulship of Manlius), into this city of Chartres, as into the navel of Gaul. For, according to Caesar, it lies in the middle of Gaul (*Commentaries*, book VII, *On the Gallic War), so that they might indicate the truth, which stands in the middle, and the worship of true religion.

Let the city of Chartres now rejoice and exult, ennobled by such prelates and enriched and cultivated by so many teachers. Let that chattering prostitute fall silent—the one who spreads the poison of heresy so widely. For Fulbert is now rising and appears under your name, most reverend prelate, to silence the mouths of slanderers.

I therefore judge that he will be more pleasing to you because, as bishop of Chartres, he was given the same pastoral staff as you, and because he is called the former chancellor of King Robert of France, while you descend from the noblest ancestors, distinguished by the dignity of chancellors. Enjoy this gift, most reverend prelate, and judge it favorably. In this way, if it pleases you, you will bind me to you as your most obedient servant.

Farewell.

[Col. 0187]

## TESTIMONIES EXCERPTED FROM THE MOST TRUSTWORTHY AUTHORITIES, BY WHICH IT IS ESTABLISHED WHO FULBERT, BISHOP, WAS

### I. From Henry of Ghent’s *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*

[Col. 0187A]

Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, the most skilled in the liberal arts of his time, a religious man and most devoted to the Blessed Virgin, wrote a sermon concerning the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, in polished style, which begins: “It is an approved custom.” He also replied to the quibbles of the Jews who said that the prophecy “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah,” and so forth, had not been fulfilled in Christ, carefully refuting the Jews’ obstinacy with the authority and arguments of Scripture.

### II. From Johannes Trithemius

[Col. 0187B]

Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most learned of all the teachers of his time; a renowned poet and most subtle dialectician; presiding over the public school for many years, he raised and educated very many highly learned students. Also most holy in life, he is said to have shone with many miracles. Among other works, he is said to have written:

- One book of letters to various persons.
- One book in praise of Saint Mary.
- Hymns and various prayers, together with certain devout works.

He flourished in the time of King Henry I, around the year 1000.

### III. From an Ancient Annal of the Library of the Royal College of Navarre, in the *Life of King Robert*

[Col. 0187C]

Fulbert was first chancellor of Robert, king of the Franks, and from chancellor became bishop of Chartres. He was most honorable in life and highly distinguished in learning. He laid the foundations of the holy church of the Mother of God at Chartres and completed it with a marvelous stone structure.

And shortly afterward:

Around the year 1039, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, died. He composed a legend concerning the Nativity of the Blessed Mary and a history, and was succeeded by Theodoric.

### IV. From the Library of Sixtus of Siena

Umbertus, or Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, wrote on Genesis 49: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah,” in the year of the Lord 1000.

### V. From William of Malmesbury, book III, *On the Deeds of the English*

Berengar, although he himself corrected his doctrine, plainly could not convert all those whom he had corrupted throughout the whole world. So exceedingly harmful is it to weaken others by example or word from what is good, because perhaps another’s sin will burden you when your own has been erased.

They say that Fulbert, bishop of Chartres—whom the Mother of the Lord once appeared to heal, when he was ill, with the milk of her breasts—had foretold this [Col. 0188B]. For when many people visited him as he lay near death, and the capacity of the house scarcely sufficed for the crowds assembling, he searched with his eyes among the opposing groups, recognized Berengar, and judged that he should be expelled with all possible force. He protested that an enormous dragon was standing near him and, with seductive gestures and alluring breath, corrupting many and enticing them to follow him.

### VI. From an Ancient Annal of the Abbey of Saint Peter, situated in the Chartres valley
