Fulbert, an outstanding teacher of sacred theology, lived here in the time of King Robert, son of Hugh Capet, who began to reign in 987. This illustrious teacher and bishop, a mirror of the Church and of the Christian faith, composed many writings in praise of the glorious Virgin, including the legend read on her Nativity, which begins: “It is an approved custom.”

In his time, in the year 1020, on the night of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary and in the fourth year of his episcopate, the city of Chartres and the entire church of the Blessed Mary were burned. The same illustrious bishop rebuilt it from its foundations through his industry, labor, [Col. 0189A] and expense, as is related in the lesson of Saint Anianus, and so forth. He lies buried in the church of Saint Peter in the Chartres valley.

### VII. From William of Malmesbury, book II, chapter 11, under the year 1032 from the Incarnation

During the time of the same archbishop Ethelnoth, King Cnut, sending money to the churches overseas, enriched Chartres above all, where Fulbert, bishop, was then flourishing, renowned for holiness and philosophy. Among the other proofs of his industry, [Col. 0190A] he gave the finishing touch, with marvelous effect, to the church of our Lady Saint Mary, whose foundations he had laid. He also strove to honor it as far as he could and frequently exalted it with musical compositions.

How greatly he yearned to honor the Virgin may be inferred by anyone who hears the songs resounding with heavenly vows. Among his other little works there is a volume of letters, in one of which he gives thanks to the most magnificent King Cnut because he had poured out the resources of his generosity upon the expanded church of Chartres.

(See also Baronius, volume XI of the *Annals*, under the year 1028.)

[Col. 0189]

# THE LETTERS OF SAINT FULBERT ARRANGED IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER

(We have examined Fulbert’s letters in the editions of Duchesne and Dom Bouquet, who nevertheless omitted very many. To the one hundred and thirty-eight letters presented by the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, we add two of great importance from Martene and Galland.)

## LETTER I [formerly V]  
### Around the year 1000

[Col. 0189B]

To his holy and venerable archbishop Bonibert, Fulbert sends the service of fidelity and the blessing of the supreme Shepherd.

First, we bless the Lord, the unbegotten Father, and his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, one true Lord, who created all things; who also illumined you, most beloved Father, with great wisdom, for teaching his people, and fittingly adorned you with the beauty of holiness, so that you might provide an example of a good life.

Next, we offer you great thanks because, although unworthy and unknown, you have deigned to anticipate us with your greeting and likewise with a gift of grace. Thus you have so kindled our love for you that we wish a perpetual remembrance of you to flourish in the innermost part of our heart, so that, at least through the frequent assistance of our prayers, if no other means is available, we may strive to repay your kindness.

Our son and your faithful servant Hilduin [Note: [Col. 0189D] Hilduin is mentioned here. In an ancient chronicle from the time of King Robert we read: “Around this time, in the year 1009, the monastery of Betten was founded by Hilduin from his own resources.” This Hilduin had recently been promoted from an aged military career into the clergy and was the first abbot of that then-poor monastery] has informed us of the distinguished signs of your affection toward us, faithfully asserting that you wish to have one of our copies of Priscian. We gladly send it through him, and whatever else you may request from us, we shall send you most cheerfully, if possible; even our own presence, should you need and desire it and should we have the power, we shall offer you with the greatest obedience.

Finally, we always wish you health, asking you to greet on our behalf that new and glorious child of adoption of the supreme King—namely, King Stephen [Note: [Col. 0190D] From history it can scarcely be determined which King Stephen this was]—and to convey to his excellence [variant: your excellence] the faithful prayers of all the communities in our diocese, namely, the canons and monks.

Farewell.

## LETTER II [formerly XXI]  
### In the year 1003

To Abbo, a most beloved Father, filled with virtue and grace, Fulbert, his servant.

By what kind of return greeting should I honor you, holy abbot and great philosopher? I scarcely know how to estimate what gift I should offer in return for the holy friendship promised by the signs of your jeweled eloquence. For since you possess in your mind what is said to exist, while you perhaps disdain what is said not to exist, what could I contribute that you either do not already have or do not disdain to have?

But since something great remains beyond philosophical essences, and since certain things said not to exist become everlasting, and are therefore at times pleasing to the wise, receive, I beg you, what I offer you as having been read by both of us.

Finally, just as by sharing in what is beyond the essence of the deity you become the Lord’s own, so, in returning your greeting, I repay your friendship with an enduring disposition of fidelity. I distinguish your goodwill from mine by this difference: because of the majesty of your person, yours is called the grace shown to a lord, while mine is called the fidelity of a pupil.

Desiring, therefore, to serve your commands with the greatest modesty, I do for your student Mediolanus what you requested, and I am sending you everything you asked to have written, almost entirely set down faithfully.

While the abbot of Saint Peter was seriously ill, though still sound in mind and speech, the monk Megenardus, formerly not a little dear to me, secretly slipped away from the cloister by night and hurried to Count Theobald, who was then staying at Blois, to seek the abbacy [Col. 0190D]. The next day the count sent him back to us with envoys, who announced that he was to be received with honor as abbot by the monks and canons.

But to nearly all of us this matter was equally strange and appalling. We therefore replied that it seemed to us quite otherwise. For a man who seeks another’s abbacy through ambition while its holder is still alive, who is not elected by the brothers, and who attempts to rule over them, cannot legitimately become abbot and ought not to be received. Finally, he was neither one of our monks nor a cleric, and he had more witnesses for conducting affairs at court than for living as a monk.

Receiving this with displeasure, he rode back to the count and vehemently inflamed the young man’s anger against us. But on the fifth day after he had made his ambition public, the aforesaid abbot’s illness came to an end in death.

Our monks assembled in chapter, together with certain canons whom reason required to be admitted. We asked whether any of the brothers favored Megenardus’s undertaking [Col. 0191B]. Individually they denied it; all of them denied it. We therefore resolved that some of them should be sent to the count—who had been designated as our bishop—to announce the Father’s death and ask for permission to elect another according to the rule.

After they had been sent, behold, two others, Vivianus and Durandus: one illiterate, the other a sickly interpreter of letters; both provosts. Pretending that, for the sake of the common good, they wished to go out to their obediences, and although the monastery’s dean forbade them to go elsewhere, they nevertheless followed Megenardus. They had secretly encouraged his initial presumption and falsely claimed at Blois, in the presence of Lord Theobald, that Megenardus himself had been requested and elected by the brothers.

Delighted by their support, the count immediately presented him publicly with the pastoral staff. When the brothers who [Col. 0191C] had remained in the cloister heard this, girded with zeal for the divine law against the fraud, they drew up and signed a document of rejection, as follows:

“Let the whole Church know that we do not elect, approve, wish, or consent that Megenardus, our monk, become abbot; rather, we reject him, repudiate him, and altogether contradict it.

“We are from the monastery of Saint Peter, and our names are written here: Durandus the dean, Gaudricus, Genesius, Robertus, Isembertus, Marcuinus, Alveus, Guarnerus, Richerus, Warinus, Herbertus, Evrardus, Benedictus, Arnulfus, Gualterus, Beringerus, Herbertus, and Bernardus.

“All these men either subscribed their names or had them subscribed in my presence.”

The following day Count Theobald returned and announced in advance that he was to be received into the monastery with a procession. The monks replied that they would gladly do this if he did not bring that presumptuous man with him.

Again angered, the count nevertheless held back that day; but on the next, amid the uproar of threats, he forced his Megenardus into the monastery of Saint Peter. At his violent entrance, the holy brothers, fearing contamination through communion with him, saluted the sanctuary of the Lord and went out in tears. Knowing no other refuge, they fled to the threshold of the principal church.

There too, finding no shepherd, the sheep abandoned on both sides consoled one another with mournful cries. But the holy Mother received them in her customary compassion; your Rodulphus received them with sweet kindness. From there they went to the monastery of the holy Father Herbert [Col. 0192A], whose rich charity supplied them from his poor resources with whatever necessities he could provide.

Meanwhile, the man whose brothers had been driven out through their importunity was, as they say, made a simulated abbot by a certain Hervise, bishop of the Breton region, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the suburb of Chartres, while the clergy were absent and the people indignant. The legate of the archbishop openly objected that this should not happen, and certain monks who had remained in the place also protested, with an honest countenance, a living voice, and regular authority.

But what can reason do among the mad? Even now that man, relying on secular power, sits first upon the abbatial throne, glorying in his victory. His agents—the abbots, the bishop, and even the pope—strive by every means, through solicitation, to ensure that nothing more serious is decreed against him.

Meanwhile the humility of the expelled brothers lies defeated and confounded, and there is no prelate in Gaul whose compassionate affection is moved or whose zeal for sacred law is inflamed, so that he might rise to break the assaults of error and revive the hopes of those wasting away in grief. For the strength of Dionysius has died; the piety of Martin is nowhere to be seen. You too have abandoned us, holy Father Hilary, who once defended the unity of the Church with the sword of the Holy Spirit.

O abandoned, O mournful, O desolate Church of Gaul! What hope of salvation will remain hereafter? Where will the afflicted Christian soul find relief? This alone, or at least above all else, seemed to comfort us: that, if it should happen that the ruins of your walls could not be repaired, we might at least flee for refuge to the still-firm Capitol of monastic life. But if even this may be entered by thieves or invaded with impunity by any ambitious men, alas! have you fallen utterly?

Therefore, returning now to you, venerable Father, whom I believe—and see—to have been provided by the Lord as a helper for us, together with my lord and your faithful Rodulphus, I beg and implore you, by the sacred gifts of wisdom granted to you and by the sweetness of brotherly charity: if you can do anything, attack the enemies of the Lord, restore the brothers who have been struck down, and do not allow them to perish for lack of your support, for those for whom you believe Christ’s blood was poured out.

Farewell.

## LETTER III [formerly II]  
### In the year 1006

To his lord Einard, ever venerable to him, Fulbert, the least of servants.

Your prudent judgment—and truly your prudent judgment—knows that in ecclesiastical observances there are many matters in which the Eastern Churches and ours correspond in common practice. There are others, however, in which we have heard them differ from one another through distinct forms of worship and varied observance. Nor are there few or rare matters that some consider necessarily to be observed, while others do not regard them as so important. Yet this diversity of observance does not offend us where the unity of faith is not divided. [Col. 0192D]

Moreover, in many respects Greece differs from Spain, and the Roman and Gallican Church from those churches. But neither are we scandalized by this, if we hear that diverse observance, but not diverse faith, has always existed in Christ’s Churches. Let the queenly Church stand at her king’s right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded by variety.

But let us, following the well-trodden and widely known path of the Fathers, keep the memory of the Fathers in the rational chamber of our breast—that is, let us keep before our eyes the examples of our predecessors—and let us hold to what we know they did rationally. As for those things which they ordered through spiritual counsel, even if, through the ignorance of our weakness, we cannot fully perceive them, let us not gnaw at them with the tooth of reckless quibbling, provided that we perceive that they in no way depart from the faith. Scripture says: “Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother” (Prov. 1:8). [Col. 0193A]

A few days ago, as you may recall, you came to me in the evening and, by a sudden inquiry, disturbed me concerning the host which, shortly after being promoted to the priesthood, you had received from the bishop’s hand [Note: Here mention is made of the host that was reserved and given from the bishop’s hand to those promoted to the priesthood, so that they might consume it in daily use until the fortieth day. This custom has fallen into disuse; nevertheless, it confirms our faith against the false opinion of modern innovators who loudly insist that the consecrated host ought not to be reserved.]. [Col. 0193D] You asked what the reason was—namely, for consuming it in daily use until the fortieth day—and whom we might have as authorities for this practice. [Col. 0193B]

Had I not feared offending the priestly reverence I bear you and your wisdom, proven in every branch of learning, I would have replied modestly rather than presumptuously, humbly rather than insolently. I would have said, in short, what the unhappy little she-goat once replied to the sheep seeking wool—or, better, a woolly fleece. Or at least I might have seemed to myself to be carrying wood from level fields into a forest, or water into the sea, or, as the saying goes, attempting to teach Minerva, if I were to speak to a man in whom I profess that the whole treasure of learning is stored.

But let it be so: a matter customary to some produces familiarity in them and astonishment in others. I certainly thought that this too was so familiar to all the Churches that it would seem neither new nor absurd to anyone. [Col. 0193C] I therefore began to hesitate longer, wondering whether I still possessed that one book which I had brought from my native land among my other belongings, and in which examples of this sort were contained.

After searching for it for a long time, I did not find it—perhaps I had lent it to someone, or perhaps it had been accidentally lost through so many changes of place. Nevertheless, recalling what I remember of it, I shall not hesitate to communicate to you a few things, having first indicated the occasion on which I too once sought the reasons for this observance. For all our provincial bishops agree concerning this rite. [Col. 0193D]

In our own time, a certain man, admitted among others to the priestly rank, received a host from the bishop’s hand, just as the others did. Wrapped in parchment prepared for this purpose, he would open it for daily celebration and consume a small portion, calculated according to the number of days then passing.

It happened, however, that one day, after the mysteries had been completed, while he was carelessly gathering the vestments together with the altar cloth, he failed to exercise any care for the sacred host and, forgetful, unhappily lost the heavenly treasure. He came to the lodging, attended to what was necessary, and the day passed into the next. When the appointed hour for communion arrived, that brother, repeating the celebration, could not find the holy host. Greatly troubled and dismayed, running up and down, [Col. 0194A] he could not find even a trace of it.

When the bishop heard of the danger caused by the brother’s negligence, he imposed upon all the brothers collectively a penance for the offense. He also determined that the brother himself should be corrected by a stricter discipline of penance.

Taking this occasion, I thought I should ask the bishop whether, without violating the dignity of the order, it seemed possible to consume all at once, on the first or second day of its consecration, the sanctified bread which he saw could scarcely be consumed bit by bit over so long a period without danger—especially since he himself knew that men of this order were extremely rare who would exercise vigilant care in this matter.

He rebuked the dullness of my slow understanding and replied that what I was asking was indeed so. If, he said, the disciples whom the Lord was about to send into the world for the ministry of preaching—those still slow and doubtful disciples—could have been satisfied merely by seeing once the appearance of the risen body, then the Lord would not have suddenly withdrawn from them what they had once seen. Instead, over forty days, at times pleasing to them, he refreshed them as though with the sweetness of heavenly bread by revealing the glorified appearance of his body. [Col. 0194B]

Thus the bishop, who holds Christ’s place, distributes the Eucharist of the sacred body to priests whom he is about to send into the people entrusted to them, so that they may consume it over forty days. In this way, while they are daily refreshed by the nourishment of heavenly bread, they may keep in mind that time during which the Lord appeared to his disciples for forty days, eating with them and refreshing them with the fullness of the desired vision.

When I pressed him more earnestly, taking advantage of our familiarity, and asked whether the same mystery could be fulfilled by bread consecrated by a priest in daily celebration—whether it would be sufficient for us if it represented the Lord’s Passion, the risen body, and the appearances made to the disciples—he replied: [Col. 0194C]

“Consider, my son: just as there are many Churches throughout the world because of their different locations, yet there is one holy catholic Church because of the one faith, so there are many offerings because of the vows of those who offer them, yet there is one bread because of the unity of Christ’s body.

“For bread consecrated by a bishop and bread sanctified by a priest are transformed into one and the same body of Christ, through the hidden power of the one who performs the work. Yet in a certain manner that is said to be one thing which, having taken flesh from a virgin womb, endured the injury of the cross and, rising from the tomb, appeared to the disciples—the memory of which the bishop seems to enact in the bread supplied to priests. Another thing is accomplished sacramentally when the bishop and all priests appear to consecrate holy bread daily, through secret prayer, on the altar table under the sacrament of the flesh that has been communicated. This looks toward that which newly ordained priests receive together with the pontifical offering. [Col. 0194D]

“For the Lord’s body, raised from the dead and placed in heaven, dies no more. But this body of the sacraments dies for us daily, rises for us daily, appears, and is eaten. Nor should the minds of the faithful be troubled by doubt on this point: they hear that Christ, having once tasted death, will die no more, while they also hear that the flesh of the assumed man, seated in the glory of the Father, and the bread sanctified here are called the true body of Christ. [Col. 0195A]

“For the one and same craftsman, the Holy Spirit, through invisible operation, transforms both that flesh assumed from the Virgin and this consecrated material and virginal creation into the substance of true flesh—namely, not just any flesh, but truly Christ’s, of which he himself says: ‘Unless you eat my flesh, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John 6:54). This matter requires exposition at another time and must be contemplated with the eyes of faith.”

Let us resolve for the present only what concerns the matter at hand. This explanation is not based upon sudden or novel inventions. You know that, under Moses, the Hebrew people were supplied with manna from heaven for forty years. Moses, the people’s leader, was supported by seventy assistants—seventy men from that same people—through whom the form of priests is represented. These are the presbyters who now, in the nascent Church, assume the pontifical burden and keep watch over the peoples entrusted to their governance. [Col. 0195B]

Moreover, Moses took some of his spirit and gave it to those seventy elders, through whom he judged the people entrusted to him for forty years. This is because our leader, the Lord Jesus Christ, poured out gifts of spiritual charisms upon the disciples whom he was about to send into the world for the ministry of preaching.

After the sacrifice of the paschal Lamb, they were sustained for forty years by manna sent from heaven. That food of the Lord, which the pontiff distributes to the Church’s new worshipers to be consumed for forty days as a provision for salvation, represents that heavenly food and angelic sweetness—not through typical or shadowy figures, but through the indisputable truth of union. [Col. 0195C] He has appointed them as vicars and assistants of his pastoral care, to instruct the people entrusted to him.

Thus, while they taste this food with it before their eyes, they may contemplate that other food in their minds: the one who, having triumphed over death on the cross, ascended to the Father. While they receive the body consecrated once for them, they may experience by the taste of faith the one through whom Christ dies and rises for us daily, and through whom he promises to remain with us until the consummation of the age. [Col. 0195D]

Let these few things among many, recalled from memory and, though composed at length on the spur of the moment, recited for the present, suffice while I read through the book brought from the Roman archive containing examples of this kind. It is easy for you to infer much from a little, or at least to gather, by a sounder reasoning, what appears to have been done irrationally.

## LETTER IV [formerly XLVIII] (1006)

**Fulbert to Adalbero, a bishop more endowed with virtue than renowned for it**

We rejoice as friends in your safety. If divine kindness should so will it, we have also prepared to assist as much as we know how in the health of your faithful friend and yours, Ebal, by sending three potions of Galen and an equal number of doses of theriac diatessaron. What effect they have, and the manner of taking or preserving them, can easily be found in your dispensaries. [Col. 0196A]

We are also sending you the vulgagine you requested, although we do not advise that your age should now be wearied by such vomiting. Rather, if need be, it should be relieved by something that can often be done without danger: oxymel and radishes, or, what is more suitable for an older man, by stimulating the sluggish bowel with laxative pills. Of these we are freely offering you nearly ninety; consider all the rest of our goods to be yours. Farewell.

[Note: Fulbert excelled for his time in medical art, as he did in divine and human literature; after becoming bishop, however, he abstained from it.]

## LETTER V [formerly I] (Before 1007)

### On the three things necessary for the advancement of the Christian religion

**Fulbert, the humble, to the venerable Father and lord Adeodatus, whom he always loves**

During yesterday’s private conversations, your commanding authority compelled me to write for the edification of brothers who are still weak and newly converted. Here you have a little work of poor intellect, but not an insignificant monument of faith. In it, I ask you to consider not the ornament of eloquence but the vows of obedience, and not to judge these foolish words suitable for learned ears, lest sacred subject matter be cheapened by rustic style. Otherwise, it would have been better to remain silent about such matters than to publish something ill-formed. [Col. 0196B]

Human wisdom cannot comprehend the immeasurable height of divine counsel through the pure contemplation of knowledge. For when our mind rashly desires to raise itself beyond itself to the inaccessible vision of God’s secrets, it is thrown back by the obstacle of its weakness and confined within the narrow limits of its ignorance. It can comprehend neither what lies beyond itself nor properly assess what lies within itself. Hence it is written: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate the depths of his counsels” (Ecclus. 3:22).

The Prophet says: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12). Many who begin to scrutinize these darknesses, asserting one thing after another, have fallen into the thick and palpable darkness of errors. [Col. 0196C]

Moreover, worldly wisdom, outwardly shining through eloquence, remains inwardly empty of the wisdom of virtue. It is always seeking and never finding, because the depths of God’s mysteries are revealed not to human disputation but to the eyes of faith, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Father, I give you thanks, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

Therefore, when the human mind cannot by its own arguments examine the reasons for divine disposition, let it reverently close the eyes of erroneous disputation before what it cannot comprehend. Let it not presume to measure invisible things by visible things, or incorruptible things by corruptible things, lest, while it beats blindly against what is closed and fails to see what is concealed, it become captive to its own definitions and, following a blind understanding as its guide, fall headlong into error. [Col. 0196D]

Three things, then, have been set before us for the advancement of the Christian religion, and are equally necessary for perfected righteousness, so that the whole sum of human salvation consists in them. Without them, righteousness has the name of virtue but not the reward of virtue.

The first is to understand and firmly hold the mystery of the Trinity and the truth of the one Godhead.

The second is to know the meaning or cause of saving baptism.

The third is that in which the two sacraments of life—that is, the body and blood of the Lord—are contained [Note: The two sacraments of life, namely, those of the Lord’s body and blood. Observe, reader, these words: Do not suppose that the body and blood of Christ the Lord are truly two sacraments. For Thomas, Part III, article 2, question 73, asking whether the sacrament of the Eucharist is one or several, replies that materially there are several signs, but formally and perfectly there is one sacrament, insofar as one refreshment is perfected through them.]. [Col. 0197A]

In these three matters, many people look too carnally. Since they contemplate the carnal meaning more than the mysterious secrets of faith, they fall headlong into the destructive precipice of error and perceive neither the truth of realities nor the power of the sacraments. Thus, divided from the unity of the Church because they refuse to become disciples of truth, they become teachers of error. [Col. 0197B]

Leaving aside the light of truth, they put forward dark calumnies and attempt to adulterate the sacred Scriptures with sacrilegious words, or to cut them away through secret erasures [Note: By furtive erasures they cut them away. Heretics are accustomed to do this. Saint Hilary, in his letter to the emperor Constantius, says: “But now those polluted by the Arian and pestilential contagion do not cease, with impious mouths and sacrilegious minds, to corrupt the purity of the Gospels.” Synesius, Letter 5, calls heretics *trapezitai ponēroi*, “wicked money-changers,” τοὺς κατάπερ νόμισμα δόγμα τὸ θεῖον παραχαράττοντας—that is, “wicked money-changers who, like counterfeiters of coin, pervert and adulterate the divine doctrine.” How much more rightly did that trumpet of Roman speech and Latin eloquence, Khodanus—that is, Hilary—say to the emperor Constantius: “I am a Catholic; I do not wish to be a heretic. I am a Christian, not an Arian. It is better for me to die in this world than, under the domination of the power of some private individual, to corrupt the chaste dignity of truth.”]. [Col. 0197D]

Thus, when the Lord said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), Arius refused to understand the words as referring to unity of substance. Sabellius did not refer “we are” to the distinct properties of the persons. And when the Lord said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), Arius attributed this not to Christ’s humanity but to his divinity, and therefore ended an unworthy life by a worthy death.

Since Arius’s followers denied that the Holy Spirit is God, they erased from the Gospel the Savior’s statement, “The Spirit is God” (John 4:24), and from the Letter of John: “And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God” (1 John 4:3). [Col. 0197C]

So too Nestorius, who said that the blessed Virgin was not the mother of God but only of a man, making one person of the man and another of the deity. He did not believe that there was one Christ in the Word of God, in flesh, and in soul, but preached separately one Son of God and another son of man.

The source next refers, without a completed predicate, to the Apostle’s passage: “What appeared in the flesh was made alive in the spirit” (1 Pet. 1:18 [reference as printed]). Macedonius, by altering the apostolic text, wished to define this apostolic saying thus: “God appeared in the flesh.” And concerning what the same Apostle says, “Made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7), the source breaks off before continuing with Marcion. [Col. 0197D]

Macedonius, through an alteration of the apostolic text, wished to define that passage in this way: “God appeared in the flesh.” And concerning the same Apostle’s statement, “Made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7), he likewise imposed his interpretation. [Col. 0198A]

Marcion confessed that Christ had the appearance of a body, but not a body.

But our Lord Jesus Christ, subsisting in the unity of one and the same person from two substances and in two substances—namely, divine and human—performed wondrous things as God and endured weakness as man. Thus, while exalted works spoke of the true God, sorrowful things demonstrated the true man.

The Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19): God in Christ, the Son of God in the son of man; divinity was working in man.

Let us hear the words of the man: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Let us hear the Word of God: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Let our weakness and condition speak in Christ. “The Son of man,” he says, “has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20). Let the divine voice thunder: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). [Col. 0198B]

As man, he is hungry; as God, he feeds five thousand men. As man, he says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38); as God, he declares confidently: “No one takes my life from me” (John 10:18). As man, he hangs upon the cross; as ruler, he addresses the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Therefore, if anyone deranged in mind says that Christ and God are of one substance only, while the realities conflict with one another, he will either say that only a man descended from heaven, or that only God was crucified. But it is not so. For neither could God alone feel death, nor could man alone overcome death. With the clearest reasoning, man received death through the distinction of substances, and God conquered it. [Col. 0198C]

But the Arians, unable to distinguish the two forms, impiously referred to God what belonged to man. Holding no proper distinction between heavenly and earthly things, and unable to assign their properties to the respective parts, they divided God’s substance as far as lay within their power. While they looked only to the words of the man, they lost God for lack of the light of understanding. Following a blind understanding as their guide into precipices, they preferred to say that God was lesser rather than confess that Christ was both man and God.

For us, it is easy to discern this diversity of substances from the fact that one is the birth or nature in which, according to the Apostle, he “was made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4); another is the nature in which he was in the beginning with God; another is the nature in which he was created from the Virgin Mary and humbled upon earth; another is the nature in which, remaining without beginning, he created heaven and earth. [Col. 0198D]

[Note: Another in which he was created from the Virgin Mary. Here the word “created” is used improperly, that is, for formed or born. Thus Bede the Venerable, rightly, in Book IV on Luke: “Christ, conceived from the Virgin’s womb, drew flesh not from nothing, nor from elsewhere, but from his mother’s flesh.”]

One is the nature in which he is said to have suffered sorrow, slept in weariness, hungered from lack of food, and wept; another is that through which he is said to have healed paralytics, commanded a man who did not know how to walk to walk, stopped the flow of blood from a woman, illuminated one blind from birth, stilled swollen waves by his command, and raised the dead. [Col. 0199A]

Since these things are so, everyone who does not wish to bear the name of the Christian religion vainly—or rather, damnably—must confess that Christ, existing in two substances, is one and the same true God and true man. Thus, with the truth of both natures preserved, true faith neither confuses nor divides the true Christ in his powers and sufferings, because personal unity admits no division in him, while the truth of both natures remains without confusion. [Col. 0199B]

For one is not God and another man, but one and the same Christ, God and man. Indeed, the same Christ is God who destroyed death through his divinity. The same Son of God, who could not die in his divinity, died in the flesh—a mortal flesh received by immortal God. And the same Christ, the Son of God, having died in the flesh, rose again, because, though he died in the flesh, he did not lose the immortality of his divinity.

But we consider that enough has been said about this, according to the measure of our ability, not for just anyone, but for those whose devoted study is occupied with the Scriptures.

Our particular concern is this: since we have discovered that some people, looking too carnally upon certain matters in which the mystery of our salvation consists, regard them as empty or useless, we wish to warn them, having recalled them from the vanity of so pernicious an opinion, to assess faithfully in sacramental matters not only what is visible but also the invisible power of the mysteries. [Col. 0199C]

For what progress do we think those who come to faith make if the grace of regeneration produces no effect beyond what is enacted through visible movements?

We know, and truly know, that by our first birth we were polluted, but by our second birth cleansed; by our first birth captives, but by our second birth free; by our first birth earthly, but by our second birth heavenly; by the fault of our first birth carnal, but by the benefit of our second birth spiritual; through the former, sons of wrath, through the latter, sons of grace.

Therefore, whatever anyone conceives perversely against the reverence due to sacred baptism, let him know that it rebounds upon an insult to God, who says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). [Col. 0199D]

It is therefore a saving discipline to know the meaning or cause of baptism, as the Apostle says: “For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ” (John 6:8 [reference as printed]). To die with Christ and be buried with him tends toward this end: that we may rise with him and live with him.

But you say to me: How can what pertains to the dead be fulfilled in the living?

Our Lord Jesus Christ, commending his benefits to us for our salvation and carefully engraving in our minds the memory of his death, burial, and also resurrection, bestowed the ineffable gifts of baptism. Through them, when the end of our first origin has come, we might die with him, be buried within the sacred waters, and, having been submerged, rise again, life emerging from our sins. [Col. 0200A]

See what the craftsman of mercy does. He found for you a kind of tomb in which he knew how to bury sins without overwhelming the sinner. Thus, when a man descends into the font as into a tomb of offenses, he emerges guilty toward the harbor, while his offenses alone suffer shipwreck.

Water and the Holy Spirit are therefore joined in their causes but separated in their benefits. Water is required in the sacraments of baptism because of burial; the Holy Spirit because of eternal life. Remove the name of the Creator, and the creature has nothing it can bestow. The former imitates the likeness of death; the latter effects the reality of salvation. [Col. 0200B]

But perhaps the mind hesitates to believe what has been proposed unless it follows the authority of testimony. Hear, then, the Apostle addressing the Romans:

“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3–4).

And after saying “buried with him,” he magnificently added: “If,” he says, “we have been united to the likeness of his death, we shall also be united to that of his resurrection” (ibid. 6:5). [Col. 0200C]

Thus, just as our Lord Jesus Christ is described as having been physically buried beneath the earth in a tomb for three days and three nights, so a man is covered beneath the related element of earth after being immersed three times. In this way, through the life-giving imitation of the mystery, when he is immersed he is buried, and when he is brought forth he is raised.

In all this, observe what the water does and what the Holy Spirit does. The water, as it were, brings the dying man down into the tomb; the Holy Spirit, as it were, leads the rising man up to heaven.

Whether it is a human being or God who baptizes, reason itself makes clear. For since sins are forgiven when a sinner baptizes, and since crimes are sometimes remitted when a criminal celebrates the mystery of baptism, this man who appears to confer what he does not possess is clearly understood to be not the author of so great a gift but its minister. [Col. 0200D]

Hence the most holy Baptist himself says: “He who sent me to baptize himself said to me: Upon whoever you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

The words of the baptizing minister plainly indicate the same thing, when he declares that the sacred gifts of baptism are not arrogantly given by him but by God himself, the author, in words such as these: “The God who regenerated you from water and the Spirit, himself anoints you with the chrism of salvation.”

Therefore, those who say that people coming to our faith are specially baptized by a human being are not to be heeded. The following defective source fragment continues their claim: “or Christians first, or catechumens baptized” [Note: “Catechumens baptized.” Some words appear to be missing, and the sense is indeed not coherent. In our text the expression is *nostrum baptisma*, “our baptism.” Formerly the Fathers used it in the neuter in this way; it is also found frequently in the constitutions of Charlemagne.]. Heretics wish this to be understood of John the Baptist. [Col. 0201A]

But who would dare call him a catechumen? While still in his mother’s womb he was filled with the Holy Spirit; he merited to receive grace before life and blessing before he saw the light. Chosen by the Lord for baptism, he was sanctified by the very office of baptism. This baptism is indeed recorded as having taken place under the sacrament of the Trinity: when the Lord said, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17:5), the Father was present in the voice, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, and the Son is proved to have been present in the body.

Finally, in calling the Baptist a catechumen, they slander not us but the author of baptism himself.

Our baptism, however, was instituted by the Creator and Redeemer, who said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). [Col. 0201B]

In this mystery, the Holy Spirit is joined to the Father and the Son in inseparable fellowship. Therefore those reborn in Christ rightly believe him to be the author of life, without whom the sacraments of life cannot be celebrated at all.

He is the author of heavenly charisms, the distributor of spiritual gifts, the absolver of crimes, and the remitter of sins. When you see him loosening the constraints imposed by nature, recognize him as the author of nature. For the Holy Spirit is so completely one in power with the Father that, in comparison with him, nothing more can be ascribed to the glory or nature of the Father.

Now let us pass to the venerable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. It is as fearful to speak about as the mystery is not earthly but heavenly; it is not comparable with human judgment but wondrous; it is not to be debated but feared. [Col. 0201C]

I had judged it preferable to remain silent about it than, through rash disputation, to define anything unworthily, because the height of the heavenly mystery plainly cannot be explained by the office of a corruptible tongue.

It is a mystery to be assessed by faith, not by appearance; to be contemplated not with bodily sight but with the spirit. Its proper use has been served not by the superstitious worship of mortals but by the authority that teaches heavenly discipline—not by human doctrine but by divine institution.

Since reason, overcome by the magnitude of realities, cannot comprehend the secret of this powerful mystery, let faith hold only this: whatever God did or endured among human beings was done for the sake of preserving or restoring the human race. In this he has always loved the benefits he gave from the beginning, so that, although offended by our evils, he was always more inclined toward mercy than toward vengeance. [Col. 0201D]

Hence, intending to abolish the sentence of our condemnation which the transgression of our first parent had miserably transmitted to his descendants, he assumed the death-bearing condition of our flesh, through which, by dying, the immortal one would dissolve the cause of our captivity.

Hence too, knowing that the devil always envies the restored dignity of human origin and, by the art of his wickedness, seeks a way to turn man away from the will of his Creator and, if possible, make him liable once more to his ancient ruin, he pitied the weakness of our frailty and provided for us, against the daily offenses of our lapses, the expiations of an appeasing sacrifice. [Col. 0202A]

Since he was soon to raise to heaven, away from our sight, the body which he once offered for us as the price of redemption, he left us the saving pledge of his body and blood, so that we would not be deprived of the present protection of the body once it had been taken away—not an empty symbol of a mystery, but the true body of Christ. Through the Holy Spirit joining it together, a hidden power works invisibly in the sacred rites beneath the visible form of a creature.

Concerning this, at the hour of his Passion, he himself said to his intimates: “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26); and shortly afterward: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you” (ibid. 26:28); and elsewhere: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:55, 57). [Col. 0202B]

Strengthened by the authority of this true teacher, while we communicate in his body and blood, we boldly confess that we are transformed into his body and that he himself remains in us.

I say that he remains in us not merely through harmony of will but also through the truth of united nature. For if the Word became flesh and we truly receive the Word made flesh as food in the Lord’s meal, how should Christ not be believed to remain naturally in us? He both assumed the nature of our flesh, having been born a man, so that it became inseparable from him, and joined the nature of his flesh to the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh communicated to us.

Thus we are in God, because the Father is in Christ and Christ is in us.

Since the riches of God toward us are immeasurable in every respect, so much so that, with his majesty concealed, he put on a corruptible body for us and subjected it to insults and sufferings in order to assist the man he had assumed, what can be judged unworthy of God? He entered the Virgin’s womb; can it be judged unworthy of God if he is infused into created virginal creatures? [Col. 0202C]

Although these elements shortly before displayed the image of their simple nature, afterward, when true heavenly majesty has been infused through sanctification, what outwardly appeared to be the substance of bread and wine becomes inwardly the body and blood of Christ.

Taste, then, and see how sweet the food is, and taste it thoroughly to discover what it is like. It tastes, if I am not mistaken, like that angelic food which contains within itself the delight of a mystical flavor—not something discerned by the mouth, but tasted by the inner affection.

Stretch out the palate of faith, widen the jaws of hope, extend the inward parts of charity, and take the bread of life, nourishment for the inner person—not fermented by the baker’s craft, but the life-giving nourishment of incarnate deity. [Col. 0202D]

Take likewise the wine, not trodden by an unclean cultivator, but pressed from the winepress of the cross.

Taste, I say, the sweetness of heavenly food, but do not be repelled by the flavor of earthly origin. For the divine taste proceeds from the faith of the inner person, while Christ certainly flows through the infusion of the saving Eucharist into the inward parts of the soul that receives him.

The divine mind receives him in its pure inner chambers in that form in which, at the very recollection of the mystery, the revealing Spirit enables it to behold him as present: as an infant, or sacrificed upon the altar of the cross, or resting in the tomb, or, having trampled death underfoot, rising again, or exalted above the heavens in the glory of the Father. [Col. 0203A]

According to these forms, Christ enters the grateful dwelling of the communicant and refreshes the mind with as many fragrances of sweetness, so to speak, as the eye of the meditating person has deserved to behold him through the forms of inner revelation.

Do not think it vain when we say that Christ is formed within the inmost heart of the communicant according to the perception of the desiring soul, since you know that our fathers, traversing the solitude of the ancient desert, were refreshed by food. A fruitful rain brought them nourishment of one kind but of varied taste, and according to each person’s appetite infused delights of differing flavor, so that whatever their longing desired, the hidden dispensation of the Giver supplied in addition. Their sense of taste received what their eyes did not know, because what was seen was one thing, [Col. 0203B] while what was consumed was another.

Cease, then, to wonder: what the manna, under the shadow, signified, the revealed truth of the Lord’s body sets forth openly. In it the divine majesty mercifully stoops to our weakness, so that, in the same kind of nourishment by which human bodies are fed, it may be sensibly tasted in the body, while God brings it to perfection in the heart, as he himself says: “Whoever eats me shall live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven. It is not as your fathers ate manna in the desert and died. Whoever eats this bread shall live forever. And the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:58).

The slippery uncertainty of every doubt must now be removed far away, since the one who is the author of the gift is also the witness to its truth. For it is impious to doubt that, at his command—all things having suddenly come into being from nothing—by equal power earthly matter in the spiritual sacraments, transcending the worth of its own nature and kind, is changed into Christ’s substance, since he says: “This is my body”; and shortly afterward: “This is my blood.”

Yet human judgment cannot comprehend this possibility of God unless you examine yourself, whoever you are, and consider how you have been made from a mass of perdition into a people acquired for God, and have emerged from a vessel of wrath as a vessel of mercy. Though shortly before you were alien from life and a stranger to pardon, suddenly, initiated into Christ’s laws and renewed by the saving mysteries, you passed into the body of the Church—not by the privilege of nature, but by the price of faith. Without any addition of bodily mass, you became greater than yourself: increased by an invisible augmentation, outwardly you remain the same, but inwardly you are altogether different. Thus, from a slave you became a son; laying aside your former baseness, you suddenly put on a new dignity, so that, having become not only an heir but also the body of Christ, you might bear God in your body.

What is the price of so great a novelty, so great a dignity, so sudden a change? See everywhere the workmanship of heavenly mercy; see the wondrous sacrament of regenerating grace; and recognize in these things the commanding craftsmanship of the Word at work. By his will, the elements of the world, joined together from nothing in a mutable order into this form of the universe, testify to his incomprehensible power by the very appearance of their beauty.

If, therefore, you believe that God can do all things, it follows that you must believe this also; nor should you persist inquisitively in deciding the matter by human arguments. If he could create creatures from nothing, surely he can much more convert those same creatures into the dignity of a superior nature and transfuse them into the substance of his body.

I say “much more,” not because he would have possessed weaker power in creating things than in changing them, but because this way of speaking is customary for human opinion, though not comparable to divine reason. Therefore faith is, above all goods, of supreme merit. Let it lead you to believe; let the power of the one who consecrates strengthen you to receive.

He promises the hope of blessed immortality to those who receive worthily; he threatens judgment to the unworthy, as the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). Because of this, many, shuddering more attentively at the consciousness of their crimes, keep far away from the sacrament of life, failing to heed how terribly the Lord threatens when he says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). In view of the judgment arising from these opposing causes, the utmost vigilance must therefore be exercised, so that, having amended their conduct, they neither receive unworthily nor perniciously withdraw.

## LETTER VI [formerly VI]. (In the year 1008.)

[Col. 0204C]

R. FULBERTUS to Noto Notus.

This is what I require from you: security for my life and limbs, and that, through your counsel, I may acquire the land that you possess [or: that I possess?]. Your aid against all men, without prejudice to your fidelity toward Robert; the return of Vindonici castle for my use and that of my faithful men, who will secure it for you; the commendation of your soldiers who hold a benefice from our *casamentum* [Note: Soldiers who hold a benefice from our *casamentum*. *Casamentum* derives from *casa*, whence *casati*, servants and household dependents, and *casamentum*, a rural house. The term is approximately French. These words are found in the constitutions of Charlemagne.], without prejudice to your fidelity; justice concerning the complaint of Sanctio and Hubert, and concerning the complaints of the canons of our Church, and concerning the laws of our courts.

If you wish to do these things, I am prepared to observe the agreement that I made with you. If you do not, do not make me weary with the journey. Farewell.

## LETTER VII [formerly VII]. (In the year 1008.)

[Col. 0204D]

To his father, worthy of glory and honor, and his archbishop, LEUTHERICUS [Note: He is listed in Democharis’s tables as the sixty-second. He died in the year 1031; he had assumed the see in the year 1000. Of him the old manuscript chronicle reads as follows: “In the year 1014 King Robert sent his army with Leuthericus, archbishop of Sens, and Raynaldus, bishop of Paris, to besiege the city of Sens and capture not Bernard the tyrant, but Regnoldus, son of Fromo the count. At last it was captured through the counsel of Raynaldus, bishop of Paris.” Mention is also made of Avisgaudus, bishop of Le Mans, who is called Avisgaudus in Democharis’s tables and is the twenty-eighth.], FULBERTUS, humble bishop, together with Avisgaudus, the venerable bishop of Le Mans, sends greetings.

Knowing that you possess zeal for divine law, that you are no less willing than obliged to assist your brothers, and that you are also very powerful, we confidently seek your aid in our necessities against Hebertus, count of Le Mans, a forerunner of Antichrist, who is striving to overthrow the episcopal see of that city. For he does not allow the aforesaid bishop Avisgaudus to remain there in peace: he has seized his houses and lands, his crops and all his provisions, and even the canonical prebends of the Church.

We wish you to feel these things as vividly as we do and to drive them away with undisguised effort. So that our petition may have an easy course, we ask you to write him a warning, ordering him to restore what belongs to the aforesaid bishop and to allow him to live in peace. Otherwise, let him know for certain that he will be excommunicated by you and your suffragans from the day [Col. 0205B] on which Bishop Avisgaudus excommunicates him.

We wish your dignity’s warning to that sacrilegious man to be copied and sent to us. Farewell forever; may the angel of the great counsel, with Christ as his counselor, preserve you.

## LETTER VIII [formerly IX]. (Around the year 1008.)

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to his most beloved lord H., subdean of Tours: grace and the blessing of God.

Since I know that your affection has willingly obeyed me in many services and still desires to obey, scarcely yielding to satiety, I earnestly command and implore you to gird yourself for the case I am setting forth. There formerly lived among you a certain extortioner of honest men and distorter of laws, named Girardus. He was obliged to purchase from our servant Deodatus a horse that he had received for thirty-two solidi, twelve coins having been given as earnest. Since Deodatus expected to receive the remainder at the appointed time, that cunning man deceived him, fleeing from us to Tours and afterward sending neither the horse nor its price, although Deodatus had often asked through messengers that he do one or the other.

For this reason I am sending you one of our men, who will identify Girardus to you and, in your hearing, bring this complaint against him on Deodatus’s behalf. You should bind him by whatever law you judge appropriate if, as is characteristic of the dishonest, he should pretend not to know the matter or even deny that it is so. Thereafter, please pronounce against him the sentence that justice requires, so that he may either lawfully pay Deodatus what is his or suffer the penalties he deserves. May your vigor always flourish.

## LETTER IX [formerly X]. (Around the year 1008.)

To his father and fellow priest, FULBERTUS.

Believe me, Father, I have compounded no ointment since I entered the episcopal order. Yet a small quantity remained from a physician’s gift, and I give it to you, depriving myself of it. I ask Christ, the author of health, to make it beneficial to you. Farewell.

## LETTER X [formerly XIX]. (In the year 1008.)

[Col. 0206A]

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop, to Guntardus and Hubertus, viscounts; Roger, Bucardus, Hugo son of Hugo, Otredus, Hamelinus, Hugo son of Herbrandus, and Guismandus’s wife; and to all those who hold the *casamentum* of Saint Mary of the Church of Chartres through the gift of Bishop Reginald.

I summon and admonish you, in the name of God, Saint Mary, and myself, to come to us before the approaching Easter, either to perform our service or to render a lawful account of your *casamenta*. If you do not do so, I shall excommunicate you for your contumacy and shall impose an interdict, so that you may neither hear the divine office while alive nor receive communion, nor receive burial when dead.

Moreover, I shall place Vindocinium castle [Col. 0206B] and its territory under anathema, so that the divine office may not be celebrated there and no dead person may be buried. Thereafter I shall give the very *casamenta* that you hold to one person or to several, and I shall make no further agreement with you concerning them. May God convert you, my sons.

## LETTER XI [formerly XXIII]. (In the year 1008.)

To his most beloved father and archbishop, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, sends the support of his prayers.

I consider that I owe you much love and fidelity, Father, through whose hand I received from God blessing and sacred anointing. Hence my mind depends so entirely upon yours that whatever, for just cause, saddens or gladdens you affects me in the same way once I learn of it.

I therefore congratulate you on the sacred discoveries, and I humbly give thanks to God because he preferred to reveal them in your time. But I have received and continue to bear with displeasure what you wrote, namely that Arnulfus, a holder of land from our Church, had injured you and your people. Therefore I immediately sent my messenger to the village of Alogia, where he was then said to be, but he had gone elsewhere. His wife nevertheless sent me word that, when he returned, he would come to me at once. If, on coming, he wishes to satisfy you, you will learn this through my letter. Otherwise, beyond the deadline you set, he will not remain in our communion.

As for the simoniacal priest about whom you wrote to me, I advise that he be driven back into the diocese of the one who ordained him; or, if he remains in yours, that he be suspended from office, lest the purity of your Church be sullied by the contagion of filthy heresy. Farewell, best of Fathers; remember your son.

## LETTER XII [formerly XXIV]. (In the year 1008 or 1009.)

To his most beloved father and archbishop, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, sends the support of prayer and the service of fidelity.

I confronted my faithful man Arnulfus by reproving him for the injuries concerning which you wrote me a complaint. But he replied that he did not avoid judgment and that he was willing to come to the hearing. Therefore, at his advice and urging, we submit this entire case to your disposition, so that you may appoint a day on which you, we, and the others concerned may meet near the castle [Col. 0207A] of Ebrae, namely upon the very land of Saint Benedict over which the dispute exists.

For Arnulfus has decided to set out on campaign with Count Odo. You must therefore prescribe such a day that he can have returned from the campaign and I, freed from my own business, can come to meet you. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII [formerly XXV]. (In the year 1008 or 1009.)

To his holy and venerable lord, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERTUS, the most humble of bishops, sends the affection and service of fidelity.

Concerning your priest who was ordained by another bishop for money, I give you the following counsel on the authority of the holy canons. First, let him be degraded; then, separated from the Church, let him be subjected to severe penance for two years, so that he may strive to recover and restore through tears the degrees of honor that he had assessed at a price. afterward, if he has done penance worthily, let him be restored.

You will find what we have said sufficiently expressed elsewhere, especially in canon 9 of the Second Council of Toledo. The canons, however, forbid rebaptisms and reordinations. Therefore you shall not reordain one who has been deposed, but shall restore his degrees to him through the instruments and vestments belonging to those degrees, saying: “I restore to you the degree of doorkeeper,” and so forth, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Finally, you shall gladden him with a blessing, concluding as follows: “May the blessing of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, descend upon you, so that you may be confirmed in the priestly order and offer acceptable sacrifices for the sins and offenses of the people to almighty God, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”

## LETTER XIV [formerly XXVI]. (Around the year 1008.)

To his father and archbishop LEUTHERICUS, endowed with the greatest knowledge and holiness—would that I, God’s little one, might obtain the support of your prayers.

Because you have excommunicated our adversary Gozonus, may you receive a reward from the Lord and faithful thanks from us. In doing this you have both rendered service to the Lord and given your disciple a sign of affection. Therefore, if your dignity should ask me for this or any other matter, our humility will show itself kind and obedient to you. Farewell.

## LETTER XV [formerly XXVII]. (Around the year 1008.)

[Col. 0207D]

To his most illustrious father and archbishop LEUTHERICUS, FULBERTUS, bishop.

As pilot of the royal ship, be cautious and watchful. Earthly spirits hiss insolently. The waves of this age swell. The headlands of worldly power threaten dangers, and hypocrites lie in ambush like pirates. Amid all these things, one must steer toward the harbor of the heavenly homeland.

Do not, therefore, mix in your heart for yourself a *bitalassum*—a “double sea”—of doubt and duplicity. The Lord’s way is simple, and whoever walks simply walks confidently. If, on any occasion, you are led astray and wander from the way of divine law, you will be submerged shipwrecked in Tartarean Charybdis [Col. 0208A]. May the strong hand of the almighty Lord govern you. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI [formerly LXXIII]. (Around the year 1008.)

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, to Gauslinus, abbot: act regularly.

The bishop of Orléans, who excommunicated you, is asking his fellow bishops to do the same. But I, not unaware of your correction, granted him a postponement on the Kalends of October. Therefore now, brother, I admonish you meanwhile to submit to your bishop, as is fitting, by rereading the steps of humility even as far as the third. Or, if it seems to you that this should not be done, do not hesitate to inform us of the reason why it should not be done.

For I can find neither law nor rational argument that releases you from this yoke of subjection. But if anyone other than you claims to have found one, I would believe that this new rhetorician had fallen from heaven rather than descended from it. See that no one deceive you with empty words.

## LETTER XVII [formerly XLI]. (Around the year 1008.)

To his brother and fellow bishop Fulco, FULBERTUS.

The difficulties that have arisen from the wickedness of this age do not so greatly obstruct your present hearing that they cannot be explained to you at leisure; but I have taken care to indicate through this letter what I would say in person. You see that the defenders of the laws are few, while their attackers are many. Indeed, our lord the king, though the supreme authority of justice rests upon him, has been so surrounded by the treachery of evil men that for the present he can neither avenge himself nor assist us as he ought.

I do not say this because I wish to weaken your courage, but so that you may remember to handle your case with sound discretion. Therefore, if the abbot of Saint Benedict acknowledges his fault concerning his contempt for you and thereafter promises the subjection that is canonically owed to you, I urge and advise you to receive him. As for oaths and the other matters belonging to secular law, set them aside for love of the lord king, so that he may recognize that you pursue religion rather than secular ambition.

But if the abbot should swell with such pride that he strives to deny you even canonical subjection, I do not know how a servant of God should spare the pride that God does not spare. Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII [formerly LXXIV]. (After the year 1008.)

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to G., his cleric.

Everything good that I had presumed to hope from you truly turns entirely in the opposite direction. For I receive from you not only no counsel or aid, but you repay affection with hatred and inflict injuries upon me undeservedly. I have already complained about these matters to you twice through the words of a messenger; now, through my letters, I complain for the third time.

I grieve that you deprive yourself of service to our Church by devoting yourself to a profane life and armed military service; that you sacrilegiously retain our tithes and offerings; that you have seized the churches of our monks; and that your household retainers devastate the estates of the canons by plunder and fire. In short, I complain that all these things, as has been said, are undeservedly done to me by you, although I remember that no harm has ever come upon you through either my action or my instigation.

If there were something for which you suspected me, you ought not to inflict certain offenses for an uncertain cause. But even if I had manifestly sinned against you and you were willing to heed the counsels of Scripture, you would nevertheless endure your bishop with patience. Yet while anger disturbs the eye of discretion and greed blinds it, you neither attend carefully enough to the case nor accept the help of salutary counsel.

Therefore, after having waited sufficiently, I now announce to you that, if you do not repent and come to correction before Christmas, you will feel me pursuing the divine laws sharply, though at present you disregard me as I admonish you gently. Farewell for now.

## LETTER XIX [formerly LXXV]. (After the year 1008.)

FULBERTUS the priest to his dear D.

Do not be troubled, my son, and let your heart not fall away from love and trust in us. My soul has not abandoned you. But because you seemed less willing to trust and obey it, it concealed its expression for a little while and, after the example of the Lord, pretended to go farther away.

But now, gently recalled to the hospitality of a friend’s heart and delighted by the bread of divine Scripture that has been offered, at the breaking of that bread it lays aside every ambiguity of expression and, shining back upon you in its former appearance, grows cheerful. I therefore ask that, if you have sufficient means of transport, you visit us in person; if not, send word that what is justly owed to you be sent from us. Farewell.

## LETTER XX [formerly LXXVI]. (After the year 1008.)

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to his dear H.

The author of the signed note that you wished to send me, whether you are dealing faithfully or dishonestly in this, nevertheless gives sound advice and gently flatters. It is right that you should not abandon the Church in which you were ordained so long as you can safely dwell in it, and that you should diligently care for the sheep entrusted to you. It is flattering, too, to be called a son, to express a desire to live, and to promise a crown of grace.

Therefore, if you approve these things as faithfully offered—and by “faithfully” I mean without deceiving your soul—I do not advise you to reject them through harmful oaths. For what was done wrongly in his ordination you can neither correct nor does it now concern you in such a way that you ought to avoid your office on account of another’s fault.

Nevertheless, I warn you to discuss whatever you do in this matter beforehand with Bishop Roger, and with Lord Rudolph, who shares with you one cause and an equal penalty of exile. Farewell, assured of my friendship.

## LETTER XXI [formerly LXXVII]. (After the year 1008.)

[Col. 0210A]

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, to R. G. A., who, as they say, are still faithful.

Neither the gate of justice nor the door of mercy is closed to you with us. Nor did we make Bishop Brictius a doorkeeper who, as you report, would bar you from our inmost chambers; rather, we entrusted the preservation of both entrances to reason.

If you wish to enter through the gate of justice, defend your fault. If through the door of mercy, do penance. Otherwise reason will not admit you. Writing this briefly in reply, we believe that we are in agreement with you, since we ourselves neither transgress the boundaries of the holy Fathers nor advise you to transgress them. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII [formerly LXXVIII]. (After the year 1008.)

[Col. 0210B]

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to A., the designated bishop, whatever he may wish for himself.

By God’s grace you have been placed in such freedom of judgment and supported by such an abundance of neighboring bishops that no necessity compels you to fall into the hands of the bishop of Senlis. But lest you diminish the honor belonging to the city or Church of Châlons, you should remember that, in the ancient description of the province of Second Belgica, that city holds third place after Reims.

A word is enough for the wise. Farewell, entering through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep.

## LETTER XXIII [formerly XIV]. (After the year 1014.)

[Col. 0210C]

To Richard, venerable prince of the Normans, FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, sends greetings and the support of his prayers.

You have done much good for the church of Saint Mary, our Lady [Note: In our manuscript chronicle it is recorded: “In the year 1013 Richard, duke of Normandy, the Pious, died. He was the third Norman duke, founder of monasteries, provider for clerics, supporter of ecclesiastical persons, guardian of orphans, and defender of widows; he proved victorious in many wars.” Meanwhile, note the word *banniendo*, that is, “obliging.” In the constitutions of Charlemagne: “Let no one be summoned to a hearing,” that is, “let no one be compelled to appear for jurisdictions, judgments, or assemblies” (for this is what *placita* signifies). It seems to be derived from our French *ban* and *arrière-ban*.]. May God repay you through her intercession. For these things we too are, and may we always remain, faithful to your soul and body.

But recently an unexpected message came to you: that Baldricus, an official, had reclaimed the very land that you gave us; had forbidden our official, whom we appointed there, to exercise any authority; had also seized his property; and had imposed a new exaction upon our men, namely, ordering them to go to the mill of Saint Audoenus, reportedly five leagues distant from their dwellings.

If these things, excellent prince, were done by your command—which we very much doubt—we grieve greatly on your account and humbly ask that they be corrected. Indeed, may your prudence order your officials not to disturb our men any further, and henceforth allow us to possess the aforesaid land as we received it from your most gracious hand. May your safety and power flourish for a very long time.

## LETTER XXIV [formerly XVII]. (In the year 1015.)

[Col. 0211A]

FULBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to Count Gualeranus, Count Gualterius, and his other sons and faithful men: greetings and blessing.

Know, brothers, that King Robert does good when he helps Christians and condemns heretics. All his faithful men, together with me, ought to encourage and assist him in this, because this is his ministry, through which he ought to be saved.

Know again that the archbishop of Le Mans asked me for advice about what he should do with Raginardus the heretic, who was persecuting the Church of God. I gave him such advice as belonged to his office. Behold, I am sending you both writings: his lament and [Col. 0211B] my advice, which I gave him according to his office.

If any falsifier should say that I subsequently gave, wrote, or conveyed different advice to him, I ask you to defend me as your spiritual father, for you can confidently do so. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV [formerly XII]. (Year uncertain.)

The servant to his lord, the great prelate Fulbert: Hildegarius, the least of his people, offers whatever vigorous service of fidelity he is able to render.

From the fact, my most reverend lord, that I understand you—because of your character, which breathes the sweetest fragrance of mature holiness—to be disposed toward your subjects in such a way that you embrace the good with sincere love, extend the compassion of a devoted heart to the wicked, and shrink from hating anyone as from a most destructive plague, I derive the consolation of a great revelation.

I have been very much afraid that, because I am excessively prone to anger, I have lost your grace, if not completely, at least to some degree. For who, even when liable to more serious offenses, should despair of pardon before a man of such excellent moral character? You pity the offender rather than hate him, and one who pities is hardly difficult to move to forgiveness. Indeed, provided that he displays correction, he will receive from you a greater use of the fruit of your love.

Thus encouraged by such powerful goodness, I beg that, when you pity me for my offenses, and when I strive to renounce them and ask pardon, you may mercifully open wider the embrace of your love. Let it be far from you [Col. 0211D] to entertain the thought that I have made a perpetual surrender to the vice of anger, since, even with many people present, and also in your presence—though I owe you reverent devotion above all others—I will not cease to become angry on occasion.

Indeed, the more frequently this vice is revealed and the more openly it is rebuked by people, the more quickly, I believe, one who truly wishes to escape from it, though its captive, will be made free from it, as the Conference of Abbot Serapion teaches. Therefore, although I wish others to be angry with me, I ask you above all to do so diligently.

For I have entrusted you to be loved in the inmost heart of my soul above all mortals, as a simplicity ignorant of flattery freely acknowledges. By God’s providence I have been a servant of your discipline since childhood; I have never revealed the secrets of my conscience so fully to anyone. To others I have disclosed some things, but to you everything.

Therefore I beg you, with the face of my mind poured out in tears, not to withhold from me, out of neglect of my welfare, the necessary alms of correction or admonition. For if you do this—and may divine mercy avert it!—I shall never be broken by so great a burden of misfortune as when I see that I am thus neglected by you.

Asked to correct my little work, farewell, supreme hope of my counsel after the Lord. Amen.

## LETTER XXVI [formerly LXII]. (In the year 1016.)

To his brother Theodoricus, FULBERTUS the priest.

Your friends, as they say, wonder with you that we previously refused to ordain you; moreover, our lord the king and almost everyone else, ignorant of the reason for the omission, loudly proclaim that it was done unjustly and insultingly.

But we, who know that it was done neither unjustly nor insultingly, offer not one but several true and authoritative reasons for it, which may persuade you and them of the correctness of the decision and remove the wrongful suspicion.

One of the reasons, therefore, was this: on the day when you appeared destined to be consecrated, we had neither letters nor legates from the bishops of the province who were absent. This fact alone has such force that, even if you needed no further assistance, you nevertheless could not be regularly ordained without it. The fourth chapter of the Council of Nicaea and the nineteenth of the Council of Antioch testify that such an ordination is invalid. This reason, however, could have been corrected by granting a postponement.

The second reason was that, at the very moment when the proposed ordination was being deliberated, we saw an injunction sent by the lord pope because of the homicide of which he had heard. Even if he had not sent it, the sentence of the Apostle would still have had to be observed: not only a bishop, but also a priest and a deacon must be without accusation.

Nor should what is written most explicitly in the Council of Riez be disregarded, in these words: “Those who henceforth are not advanced to the priesthood according to the rules of the canons”—we believe it necessary to insert this, that is, those who have been detected in any crime—and so forth, “shall be subject …”

But if someone objects that one of the Fathers, after completing penance and a long period of anchoritic life, was raised to the episcopate on account of his religious devotion, the answer is that individual persons or cases do not prejudice the common and universal law. Moreover, the introduction of examples is worthless where there is no similarity either of persons or of circumstances.

Now let us consider the remaining matters. Your confession supplied us with the third reason, which deterred us most strongly from your ordination. In accordance with the capacity of our simplicity, we judged the other reasons serious, but this third one more dangerous.
