We did not wish to cite a special chapter pertaining to this reason, but this common one from the ninth chapter of the Council of Nicaea: “If some men have been promoted as priests without examination, and afterward, when examined, have confessed their sins, and, although they had not confessed, men contrary to the rule rashly laid hands upon them, the ecclesiastical order does not receive them.” For in all things the Church defends what is irreproachable.

As for the proscription of clerics who resisted, and an election extorted by fear: that is not a true election. Since election is the acceptance of one person from among several, according to the free will of judgment, how can it properly be called an election when one person is imposed by a prince in such a way that neither clergy, nor people, nor even the highest priests are allowed to turn to another?

Concerning such violence, Constantine Augustus gave the following judgment against himself and against other princes: “Whatever is obtained by princes contrary to the laws shall have no validity.” And the Council of Riez says: “Nor shall he henceforth be bishop whom neither the clergy nor the people of his own city have elected.”

Behold, we have discharged to you the reasons we promised. If they are just, they ought not to displease you. For the sake of brevity we have also added a few chapters from divine law. To establish it in the first place was the work of great counsel; afterward to violate it was the height of irreverence; to preserve it has thus far been a glory so great that whoever has lived according to it has undoubtedly been counted among the blessed.

For these reasons, not daring to lay hands upon you, since afterward we would be deprived of the power to ordain, we refused to become transgressors of the law.

O sacrilegious impiety! In the very bosom of holy Mother Church we were nearly killed by your supporters. And indeed, escaping alive was so dear to us that the loss of the plunder that followed seems slight by comparison. But since these scandals are being caused to us on your account, you must now obtain from them an end to their persecution of priests, among whom you found this favor of persecuting.

For you know what is foretold concerning the man through whom scandal comes.

Furthermore, brother, there is something we must not conceal from you: you appear to us to be greatly in error, violently invading the episcopate without regard for God. If ambition alone is condemned, what judgment will be made concerning the importunity of violence?

Nor is this all. In the very Church that was violated and has not afterward been reconciled, you presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. Whether you do these things imprudently or deliberately remains uncertain to us. If imprudently, your simplicity must be instructed; if deliberately, your presumption must be punished.

For if it is established that you know the canons and yet deliberately strive to turn a deaf ear and contradict them, you will not only fail to obtain the episcopate that you are pursuing, but you have not even retained the priesthood that you ought to have possessed. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVII [formerly XCIII]. (In the year 1016 or 1017.)

To his most excellent and beloved lord Robert, FULBERTUS, bishop of Chartres, sends the uninterrupted course of honorable service toward the end of blessedness.

Amid my many cares, concern for you, my lord, affects me greatly. When I learn that you are acting prudently, I rejoice; but when I do not, I grieve and fear.

I have therefore heard, among other things, that at the approaching solemnity of Christmas you will hold a council with the princes of the kingdom to establish peace, and I rejoice. But I have also heard that the city of Orléans has been devastated by fire, profaned by sacrileges, and condemned by excommunication, and has not afterward been reconciled. I am astonished and afraid.

How much pain do you think your faithful priests must feel, when they are to assemble there on that day for the honor of God and of you, if they are in a place where they may neither offer sacrifice nor you receive the most holy Eucharist freely?

Far be this from you, dearest lord: that in so great a solemnity you should either be deprived of the divine offices or knowingly permit them to be usurped illicitly or unworthily. I have taken care to warn you of this so that you may either have that place reconciled or remember to celebrate the solemnity where it is more suitable.

I would also like to persuade you, if I can, not to allow anger—which does not accomplish God’s justice—to prevent you from granting your bishop a truce, promising him justice, and even providing him safe conduct, if he wishes, for reconciling his churches. If he should refuse, he will be in danger, while you will sail safely in harbor.

Moreover, since you commanded me to be present then for your service, I ask to lodge at Saint Maximinus. I do not think this will be displeasing even to the monks of that place, so that, after celebrating the vigils there on Christmas night, I may be ready to serve you the following morning. Farewell always, and prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER XXVIII [formerly XXVIII]. (After the year 1017.)

[Col. 0214C]

To Leuthericus, bishop of Sens, FULBERTUS, priest of Chartres.

Although you call me “friend,” Father, I would gladly acknowledge it if you too showed yourself a friend. But when, by ordaining bishops without my counsel [Note: It is clear that at that time suffragan bishops had the right to attend and support the ordinations of the bishops of their ecclesiastical province], you diminish the dignity of the Church of Chartres, and when in the same matter you violate canon law in many ways, you injure not only me but all who cherish justice; and I myself continue to suffer much on my own account.

Yet the divine law itself in part avenges its wrong, for, while it is being set aside by you, it nullifies your works. You did this previously in the case of T.; recently you repeated it in the case of G., whom you installed as pastor in such a way that he neither knows the flock entrusted to him nor does the flock wish to receive him. Thus rejected and expelled from the borders of his bishopric, since he cannot enter openly through the door as a lawful pastor, nor climb in by another way as a thief, he attempts to break in by royal violence like a tyrant [Note: From this it is clear that our kings, although at that time they allowed elections to proceed freely, designated and nominated bishops without the participation of clergy and people].

I am not surprised that that young man could be tempted by such ambition, since either his age or what commonly accompanies that age perhaps provides him with some excuse. But you, Father, are not merely astonishing but also horrifying: neither ignorance deceives you, nor chance disturbs you, nor does any necessity compel you; rather, knowingly and almost with deliberate purpose, you voluntarily destroy yourself and others.

Nor should I keep silent about this: in your ordinations you dangerously add the lord F., bishop of Troyes, as your associate, although you do not doubt that for a certain reason he is unprepared. In this matter you plainly offend in two ways, since by encouraging him to such presumption you make him secure against repenting of his former fault.

You must therefore now come to your senses and repent of these and similar matters, if with the Apostle you believe that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living Lord. Perhaps I may seem to speak harshly; yet, as I believe, I am not acting wrongly toward you, if you are the person of whom it is said: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9:8).

Finally, at the end of this little letter I wish to ask you not henceforth—as you are accustomed to do—to make my letters public and thereby acquire enemies for me. Therefore, if you do not wish to change your practice, I nevertheless shall not for that reason cease either to speak or to write the truth. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX [formerly XL]. (Around the year 1018)

To the venerable abbot and archbishop G., honored equally for the merits of his life and doctrine, FULBERT, humble bishop, sends the glorious rewards of both offices.

If you trust in my affection, Father, as your letter indicates, be confident, for you have understood the matter correctly; your opinion does not deceive you. Accordingly, whatever you properly request from me, you easily obtain—and now, in particular, concerning an audience with the venerable priest lord T., so that he may not be deprived any longer of the opportunity for judgment.

Before God I testify that until now I delayed and discouraged him not through plotting, but through prudence, knowing that his case is one of intimate disgrace; and, like a cesspool, the more it is stirred, the more foully it stinks. Nor is it merely shameful but also dangerous, so much so that, if it comes to judgment, either he himself or his accuser will have to be degraded with great dishonor.

Foreseeing this, and turning over in my mind the Gospel saying, “Do not judge; do not condemn,” and the rest, I remained anxiously suspended in fear, waiting for the Lord to cleanse his Church from so great a disgrace through a public investigation [or: through an insult that would arise]. But now lord T.’s impatience does not allow this to happen; he persists obstinately and presses those who are piously keeping silent ever more forcefully toward judgment.

Therefore, although unconquered and compelled, I yield and set the day and place as you requested, no longer daring to leave unexamined what I think God does not wish to pass unpunished. Farewell forever.

## LETTER XXX [formerly III]. (After the year 1019)

To his most serene lord, King Robert, FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres, wishes always to remain in the grace of the King of kings.

We give thanks to your kindness because recently you sent your envoy to us. He both gladdened us by announcing your good health and, after asking us about the condition of our affairs, reported it to Your Majesty. At that time we wrote to you about the evils which Gaufridus, viscount, inflicts upon our Church [Note: A certain Gaufridus duke is mentioned in an old manuscript of the library of the royal college of Navarre in this manner: “At this time, namely under King Robert, Duke Gaufridus ravaged the county of Mont.” I think, as far as I can determine by conjecture, that “Chartres” ought to be read].

He shows clearly and abundantly that he reveres neither the Lord nor Your Excellency, since he has restored the castle of Gallardon, formerly destroyed by you. Of it we may say: “Behold, evil is spreading from the east” (Jer. 1:14) against our Church. Again, he has dared to build another at Illiers, within the estates of Saint Mary; of it too one may truly say: “Behold, evil from the west” (ibid.).

Now, as we necessarily write again about these same evils, we complain to your mercy and ask from it counsel and assistance, since we have received no help or consolation concerning these evils from your son Hugh. Because of them, pierced with inward grief, we have now revealed our sorrow to such an extent that we have ordered our bells, ordinarily accustomed to signify joy and gladness by their pealing, to cease ringing and somehow testify to our sadness; and we have caused the divine office, hitherto customarily celebrated in our Church by God’s grace with great rejoicing of heart and voice [Note: Observe here and below the usage of the period], to be conducted with voices miserably subdued and almost reduced to silence.

Therefore, with tears of heart and mind, I kneel and implore your piety: come to the aid of the holy Church of the Mother of God, over which you wished us, your faithful servants—however unworthy—to preside as best we can; for in these troubles that beset us, after the Lord, our consolation and relief depend wholly upon you.

Consider, then, how we may be freed from these things and, by beseeching Count Odo and earnestly commanding him with your royal authority, how you may turn our sorrow into joy to order these engines of diabolical instigation to be destroyed with sincere intent—or to destroy them himself—for the Lord’s sake, for the sake of your loyalty, for the honor of Saint Mary, and for love of us, who are still his faithful servants.

But if, neither through you nor through him, this almost perpetual disgrace of our place is brought to an end, what remains except to forbid the divine office to be performed throughout our entire bishopric? Then, alas, we ourselves, unwillingly and compelled by the greatest necessity, shall go into exile somewhere, no longer able to endure seeing with our own eyes the trampling down of the holy Church of God.

To prevent us from being forced to do this, we again and again entreat your mercy tearfully: do not compel me—God forbid—to confess before a foreign king or emperor that, though exiles, we found you unwilling or unable to protect the holy Church, the bride of Christ, entrusted to your care [or: entrusted to our care].

## LETTER XXXI [formerly IV]. (After the year 1019)

To his lord Robert, most kindly king, FULBERT, bishop of Chartres by the grace of God and of the king, wishes complete happiness.

After we sent you a letter through Ragenfridus, the cleric, in which we spoke of our complaint concerning the oppression suffered by our Church, we spoke with lord King Hugh, your son, asking him why he had not come to our aid in such great necessity. He humbly cleared himself before us, replying that he was far from us and therefore had no opportunity to come to our assistance; indeed, he had not even had a sufficient number of men to accompany him.

Since we do not at all distrust the truth of his explanation, we pray your clemency on his behalf: if he did not provide help to the holy Church because it was impossible for him to do so, let not your fatherly favor become foreign to your son.

In the end, the whole burden of our assistance returns to you, most beloved lord. Through your gratuitous kindness we exercise the office of bishop, and we are wholly confident that by your protection we can be rescued from the injuries of evil men. Yet we hope to be freed from the troubles now weighing upon us without great effort on your part, provided that you earnestly act, by request and entreaty, with Count Odo so that he may deliver us from them.

Furthermore, we appeal to your most serene piety on behalf of that same king, your son, who goes about sufficiently and excessively desolate. He cannot remain in your house with security or affection, nor outside it does he possess the means to live with the honor appropriate to a king. It is therefore your duty to find some good counsel and provide it for him, lest, while he lives like a stranger and exile, the reputation of your fatherly spirit perish for you.

## LETTER XXXII [formerly LXX]. (After the year 1019)

[Col. 0217C]

FULBERT, unworthy bishop, speaks hymns with the cherubim and seraphim to the ineffably dear Father and lord Odilo.

I give you as many thanks as I can conceive in my heart, holy Father, because you regard my tiresome and scarcely bearable importunity, according to my own judgment, almost as a delight; and although I owe you everything, you in turn prepare your services for me as a lord prepares them for his servant [Note: This seems to indicate that Fulbert had been a monk under Odilo].

Truly that strong and beautiful charity lives and shines here—charity which, according to the Apostle, is patient and kind, and whose vigor never fails. I am tormented, at last, by the desire to enjoy it in your presence, but for the present I am detained by grave difficulty.

For that evildoer Gaufridus, whom I had excommunicated for many crimes, uncertain whether he was desperate or turned to madness, gathered a multitude of soldiers who did not know where they were to be led, suddenly burned our estates with fire, and is devising as many snares as he can against us.

Because of this, so that so great a matter may not remain unexamined or unpunished, I must first confront Count Odo. If he disregards it, it will remain for me to seek the protection of the king and Richard. If these men too neglect to help, I see no better course remaining than to abandon this undertaking and serve Christ more secretly. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII [formerly LXXI]. (Around the same time)

To the lord abbot G., whom he continually cherishes in the bosom of his memory, FULBERT, priest of Chartres, sends an abundance of affection.

A certain pilgrim brother named Hermengaud approached us seeking consolation, with the face, speech, and clothing of a penitent. Aged, filthy, and disfigured by pallid emaciation, he complained that through his own fault he had been expelled from the paradise of your monastery and was carrying a dying soul in a weary body.

Since we accept his declaration of ruin, we cannot lack compassion or fail to plead for him. Therefore, if you are willing and if it is permitted, in the name of that Lord who is near to those who are troubled in heart, we pray you to receive with fatherly compassion this son at last returning, though late, by a second homecoming. Thus not only God’s angels but also the brothers, whose concern is more immediate, may rejoice over the converted sinner. Farewell; be mindful of yourselves and not unmindful of us.

## LETTER XXXIV [formerly CV]. (After the year 1019)

To his most beloved lord King Robert and Queen Constance, may they be most steadfast in the Lord, FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres, sends the service of loyalty and the support of his prayers, as far as he knows and can.

Having learned of your good spirits through your messenger, we were filled with great joy and gave thanks to God. While you are safe, we hope through God’s grace and yours that we too shall be well.

Since it has pleased your kindness to consult us about our situation, we write that for the present we are being pressed by many troubles inflicted upon us by Gaufridus, viscount of Châteaudun. Before the Nativity of the Lord he rebuilt the castle of Gallardon, which you formerly destroyed; and behold, on the third day after the Epiphany of the Lord he began to build another castle at Illiers, within the estates of Saint Mary.

We therefore sent our envoys to your son King Henry [read: Hugh] and to Count Odo, uncertain whether he had dared to undertake such great evils with their consent; for otherwise it is scarcely conceivable that he would attack us in this way.

But if they do not help us in such great adversities, after the Lord we look to you, so that through you we may be freed from this kind of oppression. We grieve that you are now so occupied in other regions that we cannot breathe again through your assistance.

If your son does not quickly come to our aid, know that, by common counsel among our people, the divine office will cease throughout our entire bishopric. If Count Odo is with you, advise him to help us for the Lord’s sake and for the sake of your loyalty.

## LETTER XXXV [formerly VIII]. (Around the year 1020)

To the venerable brother and fellow bishop Francon, FULBERT sends greetings.

I considered it unnecessary to transcribe and send you the long account of our old man, since you can easily grasp his entire case, if it has any substance, from my brief reply. It was as follows:

“To his brother and fellow priest in the Lord, Avisgaud, Fulbert sends greetings.

“Far be it from us, brother, to believe that what you wrote is true—that my archbishop and I made your confession public! It is not true. In writing such things you show yourself ungrateful to those who have deserved well of you, and you unjustly insult us.

“For if we knew or hoped for anything honorable in you, we faithfully made it public as a testimony to your character, especially against those who were trying to attribute your withdrawal from the bishopric to avarice, sloth, or disgrace. But if you entrusted to our faith any hidden matters that ought to be repented of, they have been carefully concealed.

“Yet if you confessed matters that had already been spread abroad by popular report, both before and afterward, we cannot conceal them.

“From your letters I have learned that you are troubled because we called you a lover of monastic life. Since I do not understand how this could harm you, I am surprised that it troubles you. Love of religious life would rather make you worthy than unworthy of the episcopal rank, if nothing else prevented it. But whether anything does prevent it, and what that might be, I do not think your discernment is unaware.

“But whether there is an impediment, or what it is that impedes, I do not think escapes your discernment. If some grave cause that you conceal stands in the way, it is this: if you wish to begin a complaint about recovering your bishopric, it is not sufficiently apparent against whom you could lawfully bring it. No one expelled you; no one seized your chair against your will. Rather, you yourself voluntarily abandoned both the episcopal care and the chair because of illness, as you said. And, as they report, you asked the king in words and writing that either Francon, then dean of the Church of Paris, or someone else, be substituted for you.

“If this is so, and Francon was consequently substituted for you—chosen by the clergy, supported by the people, appointed by the king, and confirmed with the approval of the Roman pontiff through the hand of the metropolitan of Sens—then his substitution and consecration are certainly supported also by the favor and authority of blessed Pope Gregory. In his writings, just as he taught that no bishop who did not request it should be replaced on account of any illness, so he in no way denied a successor to one who had voluntarily renounced his see.

“But you know for yourself what other reason there is why you ought to lack the bishopric. If there is none, this alone seems to us sufficient to prevent you from being entitled to recovery.

“Therefore cease listening to inquisitive instigators; cease wearying kings and prelates with tedious letters of ineffective complaint; and cease wishing to thrust yourself improperly upon the Church of Paris. As it admits, it did not rejoice to have you as its patron, nor did it grieve to lose you, since it perceived neither an advance in doctrine from your presence nor any loss from your absence.

“Farewell, and remember us.”

## LETTER XXXVI [formerly XXXIX]. (Around the year 1020)

To the venerable bishop of Bourges, G., FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres, sends increase in virtues.

I detained your envoy for a long time because Abbot Solomon was away with some monks, without whose consultation it was not proper to answer you. When they returned, I reminded them to appear for a hearing against lord Tetfridus. They replied that they were occupied with the harvest season and could not presently conduct litigation.

But at the Council of Orléans on the Ides of October, which we have arranged will take place, they will establish for you the day and place nearest to the hearing. Only return to them before the appointed deadline their brother Dodo, who is with you.

Meanwhile, some letters written in your name were presented to us, addressed to lord Arnulf, abbot of Saint Peter’s, stating that you had excommunicated our monks. I do not remember having seen any authority that permits you to do this. But if such authority exists among you, you ought to show it to us, lest, if it is not shown, they be said to have been excommunicated either rashly or not at all.

In the letters you most recently sent me, I found the following fabricated criticism of me concerning the ordination of Abbot Solomon: “We wonder by what authority it could have happened that a subordinate was placed over a prelate without a hearing.”

You should not, I think, wonder at this, because it is not what happened; rather, you should attend to what did happen. It was not done without a hearing. Nor was the subordinate Solomon placed over Tetfridus, who was still his prelate.

For lord Tetfridus, accused by his monks, as you know, of dishonor, brought a complaint before me about his disgrace. Saying that he could not endure their malice, in the presence of my hearing and of those who were with me, he permanently renounced his prelacy, asserting that he would no longer be abbot of the monks of Bonneval. Thus, after asking permission from us to depart, he went over to you.

The monks who remained at Bonneval, knowing this, chose another from among their brothers, because he appeared irreproachable, and offered him to Count Odo so that, as was customary, he might be appointed abbot by the count, and then consecrated by me [Note: Thus the counts of Chartres had the right to nominate abbots]. In the meantime he holds the place of pastor.

Therefore, if anyone accuses me of presumption in this act, let him know that I am prepared to answer and to prove it by both reason and authority. If any abbot, troubled by illness of mind or body, permanently abandons his prelacy by renouncing it, the bishop of his diocese ought to appoint another in his place. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII [formerly XXIX]. (Around the year 1020)

To the venerable bishop of Sens, Leuthericus, FULBERT, humble priest of Chartres, sends greetings.

We received a letter from you urging us to accept what the murderers of Senlis offer in order to deserve absolution. We are always prepared to obey you in matters where we ought, but for the present we ought not to do so in this matter, because it is neither just nor expedient.

That it is not just is demonstrated by the written laws. It is not expedient that the death of saints, which is precious in the sight of the Lord, should be valued cheaply among human beings. If anyone establishes such a practice, he will be guilty of the blood of all the saints who are destined to perish for the same reason. May Your Holiness always remain well and flourish.

## LETTER XXXVIII [formerly XLVI]. (Around the year 1020)

To A., illustrious bishop of Laon, FULBERT, priest of Chartres.

We complain to you, great Father, of a grave injury inflicted upon us; by the duty of charity and office, you ought to attend to such matters. The case is as follows.

When a certain subdean of our Church died, R., bishop of Senlis, asked us to give his office either to himself or to his brother. We replied that it was not suitable for him, since he was a bishop, nor for his brother, who was still immature in age and conduct.

We then chose from among our priests for that office a certain Eberard, a learned and devout man. The aforesaid R., his mother, and his brother were so envious of this action that, before many witnesses who can testify to it, they threatened the holy man terribly.

Their words were not without effect. For certain members of their household came from the city of Senlis to ours—persons so necessary to them that their absence could not have gone unnoticed even for a single day. By day they hid, but in the deep night they went out and slaughtered that holy priest, who was coming to the Church as usual, like a rabid wolf, with hooked spears [alternatively: sickle-shaped weapons] and swords, in the very atrium of the principal Church.

His clerics, who followed their master only slowly after he had set out, found him still uttering the final words of the protomartyr Stephen. Meanwhile, the executioners, unknown because of the protection of night, had already fled, and it was uncertain against whom the crime should be directed. Then certain people, suspecting R.’s house, which was near us, because of the earlier threats, found in it a servant drying his washed clothes and shoes.

From this sign an investigation was begun. When the man was pressed more forcefully to explain the reason for the washing, he confessed that he had been present at the deed in question, betrayed his companions, and explained the sequence of what had happened.

Finally, after investigating the whole matter more deeply, we discovered that it was certainly so. We discovered, I say, in the killing of that most holy priest the stain of envy, the fraud of malice, and the sacrilegious crime—a cruel, bloody, and extraordinary deed.

Now, therefore, since the evidence of so great a case is not obscure, it demands only vengeance, as you see. Since it belongs to the law to punish all evildoers for the benefit of the commonwealth, it is nevertheless necessary to drive out with greater force those who dare to act so impiously and cruelly against God and his saints.

What further evil—or at least one equally great—could be imagined? The accomplices of Korah appear plainly to have sinned much less, yet by God’s judgment the earth swallowed them alive. For although they had despised God’s saints, they had not slaughtered them.

But if the negligence or wickedness of judges leaves such men unpunished—when conspiring to do this is an insult to God and exposing his servants to slaughter—what remains except that the wrath of the supreme Judge, raging fiercely, should destroy both these men and those others with an unheard-of atrocity of death?

Therefore, for us, to whom the same Lord has entrusted the tribunals of his Church, it is supremely necessary to rouse our king and one another by every means, lest we suddenly be struck down while negligently drowsing in such indifference.

I beg you to do this, great Father, for God has given you an incomparable power of wise persuasion. At the same time I ask you, together with me, to excommunicate the aforesaid evildoers without legitimate satisfaction—although you know that they must be deprived of communion until the end. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX [formerly XLIX]. (Around the year 1020)

To the venerable bishop of Senlis, R., FULBERT, priest of Chartres by the grace of God.

[Note: This bishop of Senlis is called Roland by Demochares and is listed as the thirty-ninth.]

Since you have decided to contend in judgment rather than ask pardon, it remains for you to summon judges who, after a place and time have been fixed, may legally justify one of us against the other. We are not usurping the office of judge in this matter, as you claim we wish to do, since no one can be both advocate and judge in his own case.

Indeed, we cannot sufficiently wonder what evil it is that makes you hasten so boldly to judgment—unless, perhaps, contrary to what human nature abhors, you prefer to be condemned publicly rather than cleansed by secret satisfaction. What else does the hateful defense of an evident fault deserve in judgment?

Your guilt is indeed so clear that no form of excuse can obscure it. For the voice of the blood of your brother and priest Evrard, after it ascended to the ears of the supreme Judge, resounded violently throughout all Gaul. As we know for certain, he was killed for no other reason than the unjust slander arising from your greed. Let the judges determine whether the effect corresponds to the cause. Farewell.

## LETTER XL [formerly L]. (Around the same time)

To the venerable bishop of Senlis, R., FULBERT, priest of Chartres by the grace of God.

[Col. 0222D]

Men of our order ought not to occupy themselves with superfluous letter-writing, for many important and serious matters fall to us to settle, if we do not disregard them. Let the letter recently sent by us concerning these matters suffice; its conclusion was:

“Let the judges determine whether the effect corresponds to the cause.”

What was written there we shall either confirm by a legitimate defense, or we shall allow you to weaken and deny it, if an opportunity for counsel and judgment is granted. Otherwise, we shall be content to have warned you of what we believe you ought to correct. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI [formerly LI]. (Around the same time)

FULBERT, bishop, wishes his venerable fellow priest R. the best fulfillment of his good purpose.

[Note: That archbishop of Rouen is called Robert, son of Richard, first duke of the Normans, by Demochares.]

The woman concerning whose case you wished to consult our humility is bound by the bond of an oath. She cannot enter into marriage without the crime of perjury, unless by the consent—or after the death—of the man to whom she conditionally bound herself by such an oath. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII [formerly LII]. (Around the same time)

To the venerable archbishop of Rouen, Robert, FULBERT, humble bishop, sends whatever support his prayers can offer.

G., whose case you mentioned to me, has wearied me sufficiently and excessively by seeking new marriages. I have always resisted him, saying that it is not lawful for him to take another wife while his own wife is alive.

At last he asked me, whether cunningly or simply, either to return his fugitive wife to him or, if she resisted, to excommunicate her; otherwise, he said, he would claim that she and I were making him commit adultery.

I therefore summoned the woman concerning this matter. She replied that she would never return to him; and, since she knew for certain that her character could not accord with G.’s character, she preferred to renounce the world and become a nun, provided that Gualerannus gave her one hundred pounds of Chartres coin to take to the monastery [Note: Observe that there were Chartres coins].

In the meantime I neither prohibit nor compel that woman to become a nun, nor do I presume to force her to return to a husband whom she hates, where she would perish.

G. often sends to me asking permission to enter a new marriage; he protests—though falsely—that he has divorced her and recovered his money. I forbid him this permission until his wife has either become a nun or died. I do not know which of the two will happen first.

If, therefore, you want my advice in this matter, I advise you to do what I am doing, adding this: if you wish to handle the case with strict judgment, know that you will have from me not opposition but support.

I have not had time at present, being disturbed by the enemy’s attacks, to transcribe the canonical chapters relevant to this case. But, if God grants us safety and peace, I shall gladly write these and other matters in your service. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIII [formerly LIII]. (Around the same time)

To his dear R., FULBERT, bishop.

Occupied with many matters, I am compelled to answer you briefly as follows. The name “Church,” outside which there is no place for the true sacrifice, by its interpretation implies plurality. The priestly greeting in which we say “The Lord be with you” is likewise directed not to one alone but to several.

The verse about which you asked me also plainly requires people standing around it. Therefore, on these and similar grounds—not indeed on the authority of the canons, which I have not been able to review at present, but provisionally according to my own judgment—I advise that it is safer for you to abstain from celebrating Mass than to celebrate it without the testimony of at least two or three faithful people.

The difficulty concerning those who offer can be resolved in this way: while we sacrifice for those on whose behalf the offering is made, through our hands the sacrifice of praise is offered to God [Note: Something seems to be missing in the sense here].

For the present, be content that I have answered you thus, and farewell. If, by reading or reviewing new material, I find anything more certain about these matters, I shall write to you out of charity. But if you first discover anything of the kind, show us the same charity. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV [formerly LIV]. (Around the same time)

To the venerable archbishop of Reims, Ebalus, FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres.

Compassionating your distress, I confronted Count Odo by reproving him. At last he replied that he wished to correct the wrong he had committed against you and to help you in order to relieve the anguish of your heart—something you desire above all: that the Church of Reims may breathe again in its former dignity.

If he is willing to do this for you, I advise you to accept it, so that you may return as soon as possible, freed from hindrance, to your office.

I also suggest, although you do not need the reminder, that you devote your entire mind to restoring peace to the poor, whom their kings and princes grievously afflict.

Moreover, I learned from Bishop Beroldus that you are so weighed down by sorrow that you wish to abandon the care of the Lord’s flock. I sharply and amicably reprove this, declaring that if you do so, you have not been a pastor. Farewell; remember me, a sinner, in your prayers.

## LETTER XLV [formerly LV]. (Around the same time)

To the ever-beloved and venerable archbishop of Reims, Ebalus, FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres, asks to share in the fountain of intimate affection.

Trusting in your goodness, not in our merit, we ask you, excellent Father, to receive as known to you this dear man of ours, named Hubert. He left his homeland to learn honorable conduct and stayed with us for some time; he showed himself to us such that he deserved to be loved and honored no less than a brother born of the same mother.

Now, moved by the same purpose, he has decided to visit the monastery of blessed Remigius, which belongs to you. If he should lack your assistance in anything there, we ask that he may experience the compassion of your heart. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI [formerly LVI]. (Around the same time)

To the venerable archbishop of Rouen, Robert, FULBERT, humble bishop, sends faithful prayers.

I sympathize with you, holy Father, over the adversities you have undeservedly suffered, especially at the hands of one who ought to have placed both himself and his possessions under your loyalty.

I also grieve deeply over that man, our brother and fellow bishop while he stood firm, who has now fallen headlong into such a precipice of disgrace and crimes.

But this is also a great consolation for you, Father: although he has taken away external things, he could not take away the inner ones. By God’s grace you possess the charity with which to recall him when he errs; the bridle of canonical discipline with which to restrain him when he resists; and the rod with which to strike him.

Use these appropriately, until, having deserved absolution, he rejoices to say to you: “Your rod and your staff have themselves consoled me” (Ps. 22:4). Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII [formerly LVII]. (Around the same time)

To the venerable bishop of Liège, Roger, FULBERT of Chartres sends every service of charity.

[Note: Demochares calls this bishop Roger and lists him as the sixth in his tables.]

Since you diligently seek your scattered sheep through the labor of a long journey, we gladly observe, Father, that you do not allow the name of pastor to be nullified by negligence. Concerning the sheep watched over in our pastures—I mean brother A., the subdeacon—be confident, for by God’s grace he ruminates well and shrewdly avoids the snares of wolves.

Nor should you continue to call him a fugitive soldier, since he is carefully preparing himself to wage war before God and us against the ranks of vices. He will come to you as soon as he can; but if our humility can find favor in your eyes, we simply ask you to deign to send him back to us and commend him in your letters, so that his presence may be a pledge forever of your affection toward us and of our loyalty toward you. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII [formerly LVIII]. (Around the same time)

To the venerable bishop of Lisieux, Roger, FULBERT, bishop of Chartres, sends greetings and faithful prayers.

The priests of our canons from the churches they possess in your diocese have come to us, saying that you have forbidden them to exercise their ministry because they do not bring you the synod-payment from those churches. [Note: “Synod” is the tax that used to be paid to the bishop by clergy attending the annual synods, which they were required to attend. This payment, as is evident, was not equally approved by all bishops; indeed, most disapproved of it.] We certainly do not fail to recognize that it is legally owed to you. But our provost Tedoldus, who is also your servant, has hitherto not understood the matter correctly, having been misled by the fact that none of the churches possessed by our canons in our diocese is burdened with this obligation, because the very devout generosity of my predecessors remitted it. Yet however much charity supports that remission, and however worthy of praise it may be, it in no way prejudices your right.

We therefore beg your serenity to grant them permission to perform their office, since henceforth they are prepared either to pay you your synod-payment or, if it pleases your charity to follow the aforesaid example of the remission granted by my holy predecessors, to retain it for the necessary uses of our brothers. If I have not deserved that you do something for my sake, I hope that at some time I shall deserve it, with the help of Christ’s grace. Farewell, dearest Father, and remember me in your prayers.

## LETTER XLIX [formerly LIX]  
*(Around the same year.)*

To the venerable Francon, bishop of Paris, Fulbert, humble priest.

I grieve for you, dearest friend, when I see you apostatizing from your former virtue. Once you complained to me about your predecessor, who with sacrilegious recklessness had granted altars to laymen as benefices; now you urge me to do the same. O heaven! O earth! What should I cry out? Or in what manner worthy of your merits could I rebuke you? But for now I restrain the raging waves of my spirit, until I can torture you in person with carefully devised instruments of reproach. Farewell for the present.

## LETTER L [formerly LXI]  
*(Around the year 1020.)*

To the holy and venerable archbishop Leuthericus, Fulbert, bishop, praying that he may advance from virtue to virtue.

You appeal to us concerning our excommunicated Guido, reverend Father, saying that he wishes to be examined by episcopal judgment and cleansed through ecclesiastical satisfaction. We, however, neither undervaluing your request nor your words, reply that we gladly wish to have mercy on him, but that we are no longer concerned with his examination. For among us the episcopal—that is, canonical and decretal—judgment concerning him has already been fully rendered as concerning an open criminal, when we excommunicated him according to the authority of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers.

We say that he is manifestly guilty for the following reasons. First, because through the greed of himself, his brother, and his mother, our subdeacon was unjustly killed. Second, because he knew that an ambush was being prepared for him and did not disclose it to me. Third, because he did not drive away his ambushers, although he could have done so; indeed, by his presence he deceitfully made vacant for their reception the house from which he ought to have served our holy Church. Fourth, because he consented to his evil deed.

By these acts, therefore, he is openly proved guilty before us. Consequently, when summoned and awaited for six months, while he delayed seeking from us the remedies of confession and penitence, he rightly incurred the deserved sentence of excommunication. Since he is held liable for an unquestionable crime on these incontrovertible grounds—and many of them truly have witnesses, ready to convict anyone who resists—who would concern himself with his examination? Is it because manifest guilt requires examination? Or would he perhaps be thought examined if, by swearing that he had no guilt, he added to his guilt? But the religious scruple of priests forbids them knowingly to allow anyone to swear falsely.

Now, what purification remains for so evident a sin except confession and penitence? If he were to seek this—hearing that I am hostile to him outside the city that is hostile to him—he would still find a place with me for the love of God, whose mercy you have reminded me of; and this might perhaps at some time obtain absolution for him. But if he does not wish to do this, when you have decided to deliberate on greater and more useful matters, include this matter among them also. I shall be with you if you order me to come. If anything has been done against him, let it stand well, supported by your confirmation; if not, let it be corrected. Farewell.

## LETTER LI [formerly LXII bis]  
*(Year 1020 or 1021.)*

To the venerable Theoderic, bishop of Orléans, Fulbert, priest of Chartres, offering the service of affection without any pretense of concealment.

I congratulate your diligence, since amid many opposing difficulties you energetically undertake your duties and also courteously remind me of matters concerning me. I receive your admonition kindly; in the other matters about which you have written to me, I shall gladly obey you as is appropriate and as time permits.

Regarding the procession of our Church that has customarily been made to yours, I consulted our clerics and heard from them what I already knew very well; and I wish you yourself to accept this calmly: namely, that because they have been seized by pressing necessity—having suffered destruction [Note: That is, having been devastated and having sustained damage.] through fire, longing for the restoration of the Church, and being occupied by many other miseries—the procession is not easy at present. When prosperous means return, however, they will make it with great joy and due devotion. Farewell, together with the most blessed clergy and flock entrusted to you, and exhort them to pray to God that he may free us from our adversities.

## LETTER LII [formerly LXIII]  
*(Around the same year.)*

To his dearest brother and fellow bishop Theoderic, Fulbert.

I truly make the injury inflicted upon you my own, moved by compassion and burning with zeal against those who have insulted the sacred order. But I see that it is useful neither to you nor safe for me that our zeal should burst forth into the vengeance of excommunication. I think we must wait and use admonitions until either penitence corrects them or the sentence of the supreme Judge punishes them. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII [formerly LXIV]  
*(Around the same year.)*

To his venerable fellow bishop Odolric, Fulbert.

Concerning the case about which you wished to consult our simplicity, we find the following written in the sixth book of the *Capitula*, chapter ninety-one:

“If a man and a woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says of the man that she cannot marry him, if she can prove that this is true, let her take another, because, according to the Apostle, her husband was unable to render her the marital debt.”

As for our journey to Saint Hilary, we still have no fixed date. Live happily in Christ Jesus our Lord. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV [formerly LXXXV]  
*(Around the year 1020.)*

To his lord and king Robert, whom he loves forever, Fulbert, priest.

I beg you, my lord, not to take offense that I did not meet you in Paris last Sunday. For know with certainty that messengers deceived me, saying that you would not be there that day, but that I was being summoned for the ordination of a certain bishop whom I did not know at all. I had received neither your sacred letter nor a letter from my archbishop concerning his ordination. Therefore, if there is any fault on my part, I was misled by another’s deception. Yet remission ought to be easy before royal piety, since even before secular judges a condition of this kind is considered pardonable.

I love you with all my heart; do not reject me from your commands. Farewell.

## LETTER LV [formerly LXXXVII]  
*(Year 1020 or 1021.)*

To his dearest lord, Robert, king of the Franks, Fulbert, humble bishop, praying for an increase of holy virtue.

If all the means required for traveling about, together with the will to do so, were available to us, it would be fitting for your piety to rebuke our negligence and summon us continually to the restoration of our Church, which has been destroyed. But now that all such means are lacking, and great necessity compels us to constant labor, how could it seem worthy of your wisdom to remind either us or our clergy of any long procession? Rather, holy Father, endure our weakness, supply our need, so that God may refresh your dear soul with every blessing. Farewell in royal fashion. [Note: In French, approximately, “to conduct oneself like a king.”]

## LETTER LVI [formerly LXXXVIII]  
*(Around the year 1020.)*

To his most benevolent lord and king Robert, Fulbert, humble priest, offering whatever support his prayers can provide.

We have been told on behalf of your highness that you wish to give Lord Francon as bishop to the Church of Paris and that, for carrying this out, you desire the support of our humility. It seems to us that, if the bishop in question is a suitable cleric, highly learned, and capable in preaching—for in this matter all bishops ought to be so, no less powerful and eloquent in action—then, if the discernment of the lord archbishop of Sens and our fellow bishops has judged that this can be done canonically, you also have the consent of us, who were not called to this deliberation. For in nothing good do we strive before the Lord to oppose your will. May your excellence flourish.

## LETTER LVII [formerly XC]  
*(Year 1020.)*

To his dearest lord Robert, the humblest of bishops, Fulbert, praying for counsel and strength from the Lord.

Since I cannot visit you in person, at least I visit you by letter, my lord, asking about your fortunes and reporting some of what is happening in our regions. I still restrain most of the people of Chartres, lest they break out to your harm. But I have been unable to restrain Hereb. and Gaufr. by any prohibition. They do whatever evil they can against you and threaten what they cannot do. May the power of the Most High crush and destroy their pride!

Some of your household dependents, who have suffered injury from those same evildoers—namely Martin of Viller-Mont and his sons—turn their anger against the land of our Holy Lady, plundering our crops and other goods that lie near their territory. We endure these things without retaliation because of you, awaiting and imploring your justice.

These and many other things, my lord, greatly distress me; for bodily illness itself seemed burden enough. But I endured even more painfully the fact that, through the wicked custom of my predecessors, I was compelled to spend the Church’s resources on the provisions of unnecessary household servants, so that I could not administer the duty of hospitality and almsgiving as I ought. Now enemies seize even those resources, few as they were, wherever they can.

To these evils is added the burning of our Church. [Note: “The burning of our Church.” From the old annal of the Abbey of Saint Peter in the Valley of Chartres, that is, in the life of Saint Anianus: “In the year 1020, on the night of the Nativity, in the fourth year of Bishop Fulbert, the city of Chartres and the entire church of blessed Mary were burned; the same glorious bishop rebuilt it from its foundations through his own diligence, labor, and expense.”]

Since I have nothing with which to restore it as is fitting, I also refuse to allow myself the expenses I need. Surrounded by these and many other difficulties—which either the law of modesty or brevity forbids me to enumerate—I am considering many things, not in order to try to escape the troubles of this life, which is impossible, but so that by some labor, however arduous, I may be able to help restore the Church.

I have decided to disclose the outcome of this deliberation of mine to you, my lord, when God grants an opportunity for me to speak with you. Farewell forever.

## LETTER LVIII [formerly CI]  
*(Year 1020.)*

To the glorious duke of Aquitaine, William, Fulbert, bishop, offering the support of his prayers.

Having been asked to write something about the form of fidelity, I have briefly noted for you the following points from the authority of books. Whoever swears fidelity to his lord must always keep these six things in mind: safety, security, honor, usefulness, ease, and possibility.

Safety: that he should not cause his lord harm with regard to his body. Security: that he should not harm him with regard to his secret affairs or the fortifications by which he can remain secure. Honor: that he should not harm him with regard to his justice or other matters that seem to pertain to his honor. Usefulness: that he should not harm him with regard to his possessions. Ease or possibility: that he should not make difficult for his lord what he could easily do, nor make impossible what was possible.

It is right that a faithful man avoid these harms; but this alone does not merit an oath, for it is not enough to refrain from evil unless one does what is good.

It remains, therefore, that in these same six matters mentioned above he should faithfully provide counsel and assistance to his lord, if he wishes to seem worthy of his benefice and to be safe with respect to the fidelity he has sworn. The lord, too, ought to repay his faithful man in all these matters. If he does not, he will rightly be judged faithless, just as the other will be judged treacherous and perjured if he is caught transgressing these obligations either by acting or by consenting.

I would have written to you at greater length if I were not occupied with many other matters, including the restoration of our city and Church, which recently burned entirely in a dreadful fire. Although we cannot be wholly unmoved by this loss, we nevertheless recover our breath in hope of divine consolation and of yours.

## LETTER LIX [formerly XVI]  
*(Around the year 1021.)*

To the most devout duke of Aquitaine, William, Fulbert, humble bishop.

It is not surprising, most serene prince, if you are somewhat moved in spirit against me because I am not repaying the services owed to our most wise and holy Father Hilary and to you. For you have shown great honor and given generous fruits of your munificence, for which you seem to have received no present return.

Yet there is something that can greatly comfort you: namely, that the treasures you have spent on the restoration of the church of Blessed Mary you will receive back from her not merely intact but multiplied. For my part, although my share of the reward may be reckoned very small, nevertheless whatever I am and whatever I can do belongs to you.

If difficulties arising from the wickedness of the world obstruct my journey so that I cannot make frequent visits, and if you are weary of waiting for my delays, then, most benevolent and dearest prince, do whatever is pleasing to your soul concerning the dignity you had entrusted to me. Know with certainty that for this reason you will never find my goodwill toward you diminished.

You will learn from your envoy, namely Lord Raimon, about certain other matters that I have not wished to write. Farewell.

## LETTER LX [formerly XVIII]  
*(Year 1021, alternatively 1024.)*

To his dear Hildegarius, Fulbert, humble bishop.

I know, son, that you desire my arrival, but the restoration of the church, the king’s commands, the urgency of the plunderers, the harvest season, the difficulty of settling the case of the bishop of Limoges, and the roughness of the road delay me. I am distressed by my delays, and I would rather not have undertaken the care of Saint Father Hilary’s affairs than handle them in this way.

Yet I draw breath from this consolation: you are doing in my place what you can. I therefore beg you to press forward energetically with your undertaking, acting both in spiritual matters and in particular affairs. If you know that Provost Robert is managing our estate carelessly, bring the matter to the attention of our duke of Aquitaine, so that at his discretion Robert may either be corrected or replaced.

Greet our dear friends R., Hu., Dur., and the others, both clerics and laymen. Brother Thedoldus has died; Brother Ebrard, a monk, has escaped the schoolmaster’s rod; and I am keeping the chancellor’s tablets for you, preparing good things and promising better ones. You too, praying for us, fare well.

## LETTER LXI [formerly XXXVII]  
*(Around the year 1021.)*

To his dearest father and fellow bishop Guido, Fulbert, offering the support of his prayers.

We ask your charity on behalf of those servants of our Church who live under your authority, that you may deign to protect them and appoint for us a time after the octave of blessed Martin, and a place where our envoys may meet you, to settle their case, which remained unresolved because of the death of your predecessor [Rodulf].

We also ask that you not find it burdensome to inform us in writing why your consecration did not take place at Soissons. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII [formerly XXXVIII]  
*(Year 1021.)*

To his exceptionally beloved fellow bishop Guido, Fulbert.

The love of justice, which has filled your soul, Father, from birth, has made it blameless and cautious of excesses. I have clearly learned the truth of this both from the statements of others and from your letters.

But I do not think you have much to fear from the ordination of Ebalus, archbishop of Reims, if he is, as they say, Christian from childhood; instructed in the sacred Scriptures with sound judgment; sober; chaste; a lover of peace and charity; troubled by no crime or mark of infamy; and finally elected by the clergy and people of his city. For, as you know very well, great men such as Ambrose of Milan and Germanus of Auxerre, along with several others, because they had been such while in lay clothing, suddenly emerged among us as holy prelates.

As for the lord pope, whose displeasure you have indicated that you fear, he has no reason rightly to be angry with you if he hears that you have provided some hope of resurrection for the holy Church of Reims, which has fallen so grievously. Farewell forever, remembering me, truly your faithful friend. May those who have commended your memory to me also fare well.

## LETTER LXIII [formerly LXXIX]  
*(Around the year 1021.)*

Fulbert, the humblest of bishops, sends greetings to his Hildegarius.

Your absence often recalls how necessary you were when present. But I console myself with the thought that I have entrusted my affairs to one worthy to receive them and prepared to reward both of us. For I hope that, if you have any merits before God—and may he grant that you do—some small portion of the reward may also fall to me with you.

I shall therefore help you wholeheartedly to earn a good reward. But I hesitate to set the day of my coming to you, because I think provisions will be lacking for me there, while I am occupied with many matters in my own diocese. Meanwhile, do what I wish and believe you will do: devote yourself eagerly to reading, prayer, and the instruction of the brothers, dividing your attention between them while caring for soul and body alike, lest the vigor of the former fade because of weariness in the latter.

Concerning the faithful ordering of Saint Father Hilary’s affairs and our own, I know you do not need admonitions, provided that you beware of thieves. Arrange for the garments and other ornaments of the church that need washing, so that they may adorn the Easter celebrations in their proper brightness. Let our laurel and the whole orchard rejoice in your cultivation. Remember also that you are a vintner and a farmer.

Concerning the various number of psalms that some add during the season of fasting at each canonical hour, at the end, after the Lord’s Prayer and the chapters that follow, I find no rule. In my judgment the psalms would indeed be superfluous, unless the devotion of the psalm-singers protected them. Once the chapters have ended, after the Lord’s Prayer, when it says, “Lord, hear my prayer,” the prayer recited from the Sacramentary should immediately follow. Nevertheless, for the present, allow the Church to retain its custom.

Concerning the meaning of clerical attire, Amalarius says briefly:

“We desire to recapitulate the entire armor of clerics. The head of the cleric is uncovered at the upper part. The mind is there, where the image of God is. At the lower part it is surrounded by hair, as though by certain things belonging to present necessity. The amice is the restraint of the voice. The alb signifies the restraint of the other lower senses, while reason presides as mistress and, through the discipline of continence, binds carnal pleasure inwardly as with a belt. The shoes signify the prohibition against the feet hastening toward evil. The sandals signify the adornment of the preacher’s journey: he must neither conceal heavenly things nor long for earthly ones. The second tunic signifies the works of the mind. The chasuble signifies the pious works of the body. The stole is the yoke of Christ, which is the Gospel. The dalmatic of the deacon, that is, of the minister, signifies care for one’s neighbors. The sudarium signifies pious and pure thoughts, by which we wipe away the troubles of the soul arising from bodily weakness. The archiepiscopal pallium is the necklace of the most devoted preaching, both in the Old Testament and in the New.”

Thus far Amalarius.

I am sending you Cyprian, Porphyry, and the *Lives of the Fathers* together with the Psalter, as you requested. I also advise you that, when you have constructed your work with Donatus, you should mix in nothing of foolish levity to make it a cause for laughter, but keep everything serious. For you have become a spectacle; beware. See also that your attendants do not suffer from the nakedness of their middles.

Greet our brothers in the Lord for me, and fare well yourself. You must not bind the mouth of a priest who is giving a blessing, unless by order of his bishop; I had forgotten this. It is nevertheless prohibited by the canon of Agde.

## LETTER LXIV [formerly LXXX]  
*(Year 1021, alternatively 1024.)*

Fulbert, humble bishop, to his brother Hildegarius.

Convey from me, and from all our clergy and people, perpetual happiness with prayers to our dearest prince William, because of the alms he sent for the restoration of our church. Then tell him that we publicly proclaimed, as he himself ordered, the power of God shown through the merit of Saint John in the punishment of Gausbert, amid the exultation and joy of all who heard it.

Also tell him that I warned the archbishop of Bourges, through one of his monks, not to neglect making peace with Lord William himself and with his bishops before scandal should arise from the matter. Tell him as well that I sent him, to be explained to him, the statements of Bacharius, Bede, and Rabanus concerning Solomon’s end, about which he had raised a question.

As for the vacant prebend, and indeed every good matter, know that I place my agreement at his disposal. Moreover, know that, for your sake, I have granted pardon to Master S. As for Tigrinus, he was urging me to send you some agent to gather the crops. But I entrust all this to your care, testing and exercising you through it.

I do not wish to send you an assistant for the schools who has not yet attained maturity of age and seriousness of character. Meanwhile, make use of whatever assistance your household can provide, until we consider the matter by common counsel. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV [formerly LXXXI]  
*(Around the same year.)*

When I hear that you are doing what you ought, I rejoice, although I am anxious about the future. Therefore, while imploring the highest Good to deign to guide you, I also admonish you to remember to obey the reins of his instructions. Again I say, farewell.

You will find Bacharius’s inserted statement, as well as those of Bede and Rabanus; nevertheless, I have not been reluctant to write out here the statements of all three.

Bacharius says:

“That remarkable Solomon, who deserved to be built up for the Lord and joined to wisdom, fell into the embraces of foreign women and, ensnared in the bond of lust, polluted himself also by the error of sacrilege when he fashioned the image of Chamos, the idol of the Moabites. But because through the prophet he acknowledged the guilt of his error, is he therefore excluded from heavenly mercy? Perhaps you will say: ‘Nowhere do I read in the canon that he repented or obtained mercy.’ I do not doubt, brother, that he repented, although his repentance was not recorded in public laws. Perhaps for this reason it is judged more acceptable: he repented not before the face of the people but in the secrecy of his conscience, with the Lord as witness.

We recognize that he obtained pardon from this, because when he had been released from the body, Scripture records that he was buried among the bodies of the kings of Israel. Yet we know that this was denied elsewhere to sinful kings who remained in the perversity of their purpose until the end of their lives. And therefore, because he deserved to be buried among righteous kings, he was not excluded from pardon. But he could not have merited that pardon without repentance.”

Bede, in his treatise on the Book of Kings, chapter thirty-nine, after a few introductory remarks, says:

“Here too, if I am not mistaken, it is openly shown—would that it had not been shown!—that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry he had committed. For if he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, he would have taken care above all that the idols he had built should be removed from the holy city, and he would not have left as a scandal to fools the things he had done erroneously, although he was wise, as though they had been done wisely and correctly.”

Rabanus, speaking under the name of Isidore in his exposition of the same book, says:

“Now, what shall I say about Solomon’s other deeds, whom Holy Scripture vehemently rebukes and condemns, and concerning whose repentance or the Lord’s indulgence toward him it records absolutely nothing? Nor does anything at all occur which even in allegory signifies something good. This is a drowning that must be mourned.”

## LETTER LXVI [formerly LXXXII]  
*(Around the same year.)*

Fulbert, humble bishop, sends greetings to his H.

I waited a long time, hoping that you would come, as you had said. Now, moved by your excessive delay, I rebuke you privately. Why have you shown yourself false and ungrateful to me, when it ought to have been sweet for you to bring your father whatever food from your hunt might have been available, so that you might deserve to receive some blessing?

Do not delay any longer if you wish to rejoice in our humble favor. Farewell, and come—or write back to me what I may confidently hope from you.

## LETTER LXVII [formerly LXXXIII]  
*(Around the same year.)*

Fulbert, humble bishop of the people of Chartres, to R., steward of the holy Church of Orléans.

You act as a friend, and as a cultivator of Christian philosophy, free from envy, when you urge me to write what is useful to a cleric and highly esteem learning. Although I am ignorant of my own measure and do not presume to great things, nevertheless, remembering in what matters I can obey, I do not wish to fail in a holy exhortation.

Therefore, as you advised, I wrote what seemed to me should be done concerning that priest who was found to celebrate Mass and not communicate, in the following terms.

The cause for which he avoided the most holy Communion must be carefully investigated: whether it was heretical unbelief; or fear arising from the consciousness of a plainly mortal crime; or fear arising from consciousness of drunkenness or lust. These miserable priests either do not know that such things are mortal sins or pretend not to know, although their evil conscience reproaches them. It must also be determined whether it was weariness from celebrating many Masses; an indiscriminate fear by which the fainthearted are sometimes affected on account of light offenses; illness of a rheumatic and nauseated stomach; or an affliction of the brain damaging the mind.

If unbelief or some other plainly mortal crime is found to be the cause, he is to be deposed by canonical authority until he makes legitimate satisfaction. If, however, the desire for drunkenness or lust is the cause—since these too are deadly—he is to be removed from office and disciplined by abstinence for as long as necessary, until, having abandoned and overcome the vice through God’s grace, he seems fit to be recalled.

If the cause is weariness from frequent celebration of Masses, he is to be rebuked and excluded from Communion for an entire year, as is written in the thirteenth Council of Toledo, chapter five. If it is indiscriminate fear arising from a light offense, he seems to require correction with compassion, as is read in the *Capitulary*, book one, chapter six. If the cause is the aforementioned illness of the stomach or brain, he ought to rest from ministry until he recovers his health.

If anything other than the matters listed above is found to be the cause, it can easily be handled by reasoning through comparison with them.

Having briefly set out these points, greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ, excellent man, who continually question me and, by questioning wisely, teach well. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII [formerly LXXXIV]  
*(Around the same year.)*

To his most benevolent and dearest lord Robert, Fulbert, by the grace of God priest of the people of Chartres.

Having learned of your benevolent will and discovered that your counsel is sound, as it usually is, I obey your will and assent to your counsel. For the present I am postponing the journey I had undertaken [Note: To Poitiers, as it seems to us, rather than to Rome.] and defer its completion to the time appointed by you, if God approves.

If, therefore, you wish to deal with justice, peace, the condition of the kingdom, and the honor of the Church, here you have a small follower ready to help according to his strength. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIX [formerly XCVII]  
*(Year 1021.)*

To the most noble king of Denmark, Cnut, Fulbert, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, together with his clerics and monks, offering the support of their prayers.

When we saw the gift you had sent us, we admired both your intelligence and your religion. Your intelligence, because, although ignorant of our language [Note: By “our language” Fulbert evidently means the language of the Franks, which was called Roman because it had arisen from the purer Roman language.] and separated from us by a great distance of land and sea, you not only energetically attend to the affairs around you but also carefully inquire into those around us.

We admired your religion because, although we had heard that you were a prince of pagans, we recognize you as not only a Christian but also a most benevolent giver toward churches and servants of God.

Therefore, giving thanks to the King of kings, from whose dispensation such things descend, we ask that he himself make your kingdom prosper in you and absolve your soul from sins through his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal and consubstantial with him, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Farewell, remembering us and not forgetful of yourself.

## LETTER LXX [formerly XCVIII]  
*(Around the same year.)*

To the noble Count S., Fulbert, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, offering faithful prayers.

If you were proceeding according to the rule in choosing the bishop of your city, the support of our humility would not be lacking, in accordance with the measure of reason. But now there is a courtly—or public—rumor that the cleric whom you wish to elect has sought your favor through the whispers of promises and the birdlime of money.

They also say that, without the king’s command and the consent of the neighboring bishops, he has invaded the episcopal residence and property. If these things are true, they are not according to the rule; nor is it right for me to help you or anyone else against law and justice. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI [formerly CII]  
*(Year 1021.)*

To the most illustrious duke of Aquitaine, William, Fulbert, bishop, offering what is useful and honorable.

I would rejoice to attend your dedication devoutly, most beloved prince, if the necessity of our Church—which cannot in any way be neglected—were not holding me back. For by God’s grace, with your help, we have gone through our crypts and are striving to cover them before winter’s severity damages them.

I also wish you to know that the letters you previously sent to Bishop Azelinus have been reported to the king. He was also very saddened by the humiliation of himself that he found written there. The bishop of Bourges would have acted according to our advice, as he says, concerning the bishop of Limoges, if fear of anger had not held him back from acting canonically.

But since the king is said to be coming soon with a roar to the forest of Le Gouz [Note: Or the forest of Orléans.], which, as you know, is near the monastery of Saint Benedict, I too have decided, with God’s favor, to go there, in order to learn what disposition I shall find toward you, the king, and the archbishop, and what response I may be able to make.

What I accomplish in the meantime I shall either report to you in person or make known by letter. Farewell happily.

## LETTER LXXII [formerly CIII]  
*(Year 1021.)*

To his always dearest and beloved lord and duke of Aquitaine, William, Fulbert, humble bishop of the people of Chartres, wishing him and all that is his in this life, and eternal joys in the next.

I am distressed, excellent man, that recently, at the gathering of the king and ourselves, I had no opportunity to speak with you—not about a secular matter, but about the place of Saint Father Hilary, whose administrators your goodness wished us to be, though the wickedness of the present time does not permit it.

I therefore send you, and in your absence beg you to accept, what I wished to tell you in person then: namely, that according to the desire of your heart you should appoint another treasurer and a head official (*capitiarius*) from among the good clerics who are in your vicinity, whom a long and dangerous journey would not keep from their office, as it has until now kept me and my men away.

Please do not think me so perverse that for this reason I should seem less faithful to you. I acknowledge that I am forever a debtor in fidelity to your soul and body, because of the kindness you have shown me though I was undeserving. Know with certainty, therefore, that if the need for my ministry should press upon you or your people, and you judged it worthy to command this of me, I would come to your aid under God’s guidance—even, if I could not otherwise, in the clothing of a poor pilgrim.

I also beg your goodness to deign to make good to Raimon the loss he suffered in our service. Farewell now and always, most devout and benevolent prince. I shall never forget you.

## LETTER LXXIII [formerly CIV]  
*(Around the year 1022.)*

To the most noble and devout duke of Aquitaine, William, Fulbert, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, greetings and faithful prayers.

I have experienced, excellent prince, your benevolence toward me as sweeter in affection and more useful in effect than all the benevolence of my friends. For my other friends scarcely ever repay my merits with an equivalent return. You, however, although I am unworthy, delight in heaping free gifts upon me with astonishing abundance of charity. Nearly three years have now passed during which you have acted in this way; I would be ashamed to have accepted your gifts without recompense. I would be uncertain whether the Lord Jesus Christ and his holy mother Mary, in whose service these gifts have been expended, will repay you. Moreover, I have not lacked the desire to visit you and serve you in your region. But many difficult circumstances have stood in the way. Therefore, you may know for certain that I shall set aside every difficulty in order to undertake this task, if it should in any way be possible. In saying this, I wish to requite the marvelous sweetness of your affection toward me; for in your recent letter I read that you rejoiced that I was still alive in our regions, as though hoping someday to see me among you. I therefore beseech the Author of all good that he may grant you a long life in this world, and that he may permit me, while still alive with you and the blessed Hilary, to serve you. You asked us to send back to you Brother Hildegarius, faithful to you and to us; but he laments as though he had not for a long time drunk from the breasts of our heart. He humbly asks your serenity to allow him to be refreshed by these for a while, so that afterward, through a gentler inspiration, he may please you and your people. May you prosper, together with all your people.

## LETTER LXXIV [formerly XXX]. (In the year 1022)

To the sacred archbishop of Sens, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, sends the virtue appropriate to the excellence of his dignity.

I did not myself elect Odalric of Orléans to the episcopate, as was reported to you; rather, I consecrated him a priest after he had been elected by the clergy and people of his city. When you heard that he wished to go to Rome and be made bishop there, I dissuaded him out of regard for your honor. He himself also gladly obeyed the one who dissuaded him, at the urging of his faithful supporters, namely Rodulf and Herfrid. Occupied with many matters, I am compelled to write only briefly. I greet you as best I can in the Lord, your devoted suffragan, reverent toward your fatherhood.

## LETTER LXXV [formerly XXXI]. (Around the same year)

To his father and primate, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERT, bishop.

I give thanks for your vigilance, which provides a warning for my simplicity. Indeed, because of the illness of my indiscretion or negligence, I truly need to be warned about many things. Yet in the matter with which you are now dealing—namely, that I should not too quickly lay hands on those who are to be made bishops—I do not think a monitor is necessary. For if you had wished until now to use my counsel in this affair, as would have been proper, both our order and your own business would have proceeded differently. But I set the past aside; I derive very great hope for the future from the fact that you are now consulting holy and wise men, our father Odilo,

> **[Note: Odilo is mentioned in several places. In our old chronicle: “In the year 1020 religion flourished through famous abbots distinguished by holiness: in Burgundy, through Odilo of Cluny, renowned for his piety, and William of Dijon.” Peter Damian writes of him in his *Life*: “This saint, born in Auvergne of equestrian lineage, while still an infant suddenly suffered such torpor of all his limbs that he could scarcely walk. Left alone at the door of the basilica of the Mother of God, he could barely crawl; grasping the horns of the altar with his hands, he felt the help of divine power. He was healed of every infirmity, became a monk, and after Maiolus was made abbot.”]**

and his followers. For through their counsel I hope that you will not only escape danger to your soul, but also recover the glory and honor of this life. Farewell, remembering that I am ready to obey and assist you in every good work.

## LETTER LXXVI [formerly XXXII]. (Around the same year)
