To the venerable archbishop of Sens, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERT, the humble bishop of Chartres by the grace of God, offers the assistance of his prayers.

You see and hear, Father, how great are the fires of war blazing in our regions. Therefore I fear that it is dangerous for us to assemble at the appointed place of the synod. Let me know quickly what your prudence thinks should be done about this.

## LETTER LXXVII [formerly XXXIII]. (Around the same year)

To the venerable archbishop of Sens, LEUTHERICUS, FULBERT, the humble bishop of Chartres, from the Most High Lord: “Well done, good servant.”

Your excellency was pleased to inquire of us what should be done concerning a certain man who, by holding his own son for confirmation, became the child’s godfather—namely, whether he should be separated from his wife, the mother of that same child, or not. We think that what the holy Fathers established concerning such a case must be observed. A statute is therefore found in the Council of Leptines, chapter 7, under Pope Zachary and the rule of Prince Charlemagne, in these words:

“If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, he shall be separated from his wife and shall not take another. Likewise, the woman shall not take another man.”

Also, in the same council:

“No one shall receive his own son or daughter from the baptismal font; nor shall he marry his goddaughter or godmother, nor the woman whose son or daughter he has held for confirmation. Whenever this has occurred, they shall be separated.”

I believe this is sufficient for you: a little is enough for the wise. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII [formerly XCV]. (Around the year 1022)

Of King Robert of the Franks to Gauslinus, archbishop of Bourges.

*(See below under ROBERT, king.)*

## LETTER LXXIX [formerly XCVI]. (Around the year 1022)

Of Gauslinus, archbishop of Bourges, to Robert, king of the Franks.

*(See below under ROBERT, king.)*

## LETTER LXXX [formerly XCVII]. (Around the year 1022)

To the pious king ROBERT, FULBERT, the humble bishop, sends every expression of fidelity.

Prompted by your sacred majesty, I was asked to investigate and quickly write to you whether any history reports that blood rained from the sky, and, if this occurred, what the event might portend. I found Livy, Valerius, Orosius, and several others who report this matter. For the present, it is sufficient to produce as a witness only Gregory, bishop of Tours, on account of his religious authority.

Gregory says in the sixth book of his *Histories*, chapter 14:

> “In the seventh year of the reign of King Childebert, who was the twenty-first year of Chilperic and Guntram, in the month of January there had been rains, lightning flashes, and heavy thunder. Flowers appeared on the trees. The star that I mentioned above as a comet appeared, so that there was great blackness around it; and it shone and sparkled amid the darkness as though it had been placed inside some opening, scattering its hair. From it there issued a ray of extraordinary size, which from a distance appeared like a great smoke from a fire. It was seen in the western quarter at the first hour of the night.
>
> “On the holy day of Easter, at the city of Soissons, the sky appeared to burn, so that two fires were visible, one larger and the other smaller. After the space of two hours they came together, became one great beacon, and disappeared. In the territory of Paris, true blood fell from a cloud and landed upon the clothing of many people; it stained them with such corruption that they themselves recoiled from and rejected their own garments. This prodigy appeared in three places within the territory of that city.
>
> “In the territory of Senlis, when a certain man rose in the morning, his house appeared splashed with blood from within. There was a great plague among the people that year. Various illnesses, including the ‘melinae,’ with pustules and blisters, afflicted many people with death. Nevertheless, many escaped by taking care.
>
> “We also heard that in that year a disease of the groin raged severely in the city of Narbonne, so that there was no prospect of life once a person had been seized by it.”

Thus far Gregory of Tours.

It is therefore clear from this history and from those mentioned above that a rain of blood portends a public slaughter in the future. As for the fact that you recently heard that such blood had rained in a certain part of your kingdom, and that wherever this blood fell upon stone or human flesh it could not be washed away, whereas wherever it fell upon wood it was easily washed away: by this, three classes of human beings seem to be signified. By the stone are signified the impious; by the flesh, fornicators; and by the wood, which is neither hard like stone nor soft like flesh, those who are neither impious nor fornicators.

When the sword comes upon that people for whom this portent has been given—or the plague signified by the blood—if beforehand the hard or the soft have been changed for the better, they will not die forever in their own blood. Those in the middle, through the anguish of death or by another means, may be delivered according to the will of the most secret and excellent Judge. Farewell, most pious king.

## LETTER LXXXI [formerly XIII]. (In the year 1023)

To his most gracious lord, ROBERT the king, FULBERT, the humble priest, wishes everlasting prosperity.

Most recently I received a sacred message from your majesty, instructing me to attend, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, the conference between you and Henry,

> **[Note: An old manuscript has these words: “King Henry and King Robert confer at the Char River in the year 1023.” Gaguin, in his *Life of Robert*, writes: “The emperor Henry and Robert, king of the Franks, met at the Char River near Ensis in the year 1023 to discuss amicably the condition of the Church, the Empire, and the kingdom.”]**

not only for the sake of serving you but also for our own advantage. Therefore, while humbly expressing my gratitude to you for such an affectionate act of piety toward me, I write back that, having long been infirm, I now especially fear illness, and do not dare undertake a long journey. Nevertheless, when a more suitable time arrives, with God’s consent I shall gladly accompany you there or elsewhere, although, even if my health did not stand in the way at present, I would still need to be informed of so great a journey well in advance. Farewell and prosper.

## LETTER LXXXII [formerly XLVIII]. (Around the year 1023)

To the venerable archbishop of Tours, ARNULF, FULBERT,

> **[Note: Who this archbishop of Tours was, and by what name he was distinguished, can scarcely be determined from the records of Demochus. He had requested the pallium from the supreme pontiff, but it had been denied him. The pallium is described by Cardinal Lothair, later Innocent III, in his book *On the Office of the Mass*, as follows: “This pallium, which the greater bishops use, is woven of white wool. Above, it has a circle constricting the shoulders, with two strips hanging down on either side, and four purple crosses—front, back, right, and left. On the left there are two, and on the right one. Three golden pins are also fastened to the pallium: at the breast, above the shoulder, and behind the back; no pin is fastened over the right shoulder. Each pin contains a precious stone. Lothair interprets their significance as follows: This pallium signifies the discipline by which they ought to govern themselves and their subjects. Through it the golden necklace is acquired, which those who strive lawfully receive, concerning which Solomon says in Proverbs: ‘Hear, my son, the discipline of your father and do not forsake the law of your mother, that grace may be added to your head and a necklace to your neck.’
>
> “The pallium woven of wool, having a circle, and so forth—all these things are filled with moral mysteries and pregnant with sacramental meanings. In the wool harshness is noted; in its whiteness benevolence is signified. For ecclesiastical discipline exercises severity against rebellious and obstinate people, but displays piety toward the penitent and humble. For this reason it is made not from the wool of just any animal, but only from that of a sheep.
>
> “The circle of the pallium, by which the shoulders are constricted, is the fear of the Lord, by which actions are restrained lest they flow toward what is unlawful or relax into what is excessive.
>
> “The four crosses are the cardinal virtues—justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance—which, unless they are purpled by the blood of Christ’s cross, falsely claim the name of virtue.
>
> “The pallium is double on the left but single on the right, because the present life, signified by the left, is subject to many troubles, whereas the future life, signified by the right, is established in a single and perpetual repose.
>
> “The three pins fastened to the pallium—at the breast, over the left shoulder, and behind the back—designate the compassion of office and the strictness of judgment; [the third designation is not supplied in the printed text]. The first pricks the mind, the second through labor, and the third through terror. No pin is fastened over the right shoulder, because in eternal repose there is no thorn of affliction.
>
> “The pin is golden, but pointed below and rounded above, and contains a precious stone, because the good shepherd is afflicted on earth on account of his care for souls, but in heaven will be crowned eternally, where he will possess that precious pearl.
>
> “The fullness of pontifical office is conferred with this pallium; for before a metropolitan is adorned with the pallium, he ought neither to ordain clerics, consecrate bishops, nor dedicate churches.”

Thus far Cardinal Lothair.]

the humble bishop, always to act prudently and simply.

And now, by the grace of God, you are acting in this way, since, although not without judgment, you nevertheless seek the counsel of your brothers. We therefore reply that, if you requested the pallium from the Roman pontiff and he denied it to you without legitimate cause, there is no need on that account to abandon your ministry. If it has not yet been requested because of your delay, it is prudent to wait until it is requested, lest he be able unexpectedly to accuse you of presumption. For certain matters worthy of our reverence are contained in the privileges of the Roman Church, and because of our negligence they are not easily found in our archives. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII [formerly XV]. (In the year 1024)

Of Fulk, count of Anjou, to King Robert.

*(See below under ROBERT, king of the Franks.)*

## LETTER LXXXIV [formerly XXII]. (In the year 1024)

To the holy and universal pope, JOHN, FULBERT, the humble bishop of Chartres, sends the support of his prayers.

I give thanks to almighty God, who, according to his customary goodness, has looked upon your humility, Father, and exalted you to the highest summit of dignity, as was fitting. Therefore the whole world turns its eyes toward you, and all proclaim you alone most blessed. Holy men contemplate your greatness and rejoice that, through your likeness to them in every virtue, you imitate them. The persecutors of the Church look upon you, fearing the rod of your severity. Those who are scourged by the impious look up to you and breathe again, still hoping that a remedy of consolation remains for them.

I am one of their number, a little bishop of a great and illustrious Church. I write to you, Father, complaining of my troubles and imploring the help of your piety. There is a certain evil-doing count named Rodulf, our excessively close neighbor, who has invaded the property of our Church on an unjust pretext, killed one of our clerics with his own hands, and bound two others whom he captured by oaths. Summoned on all these matters before the king’s court, and repeatedly called before a full church, he did not deign to come to justice either for man’s sake or for God’s sake. At last he was excommunicated by us.

Now he is hastening to the threshold of Saint Peter, as though he might there receive absolution from his sins, although he refuses to come here for correction. Therefore we ask you, beloved Father, to whose care the whole Church has been entrusted, to remember to accuse and chastise him for the blood and injury inflicted upon your sons, as your prudence knows to be deserved. Nor should your holiness unjustly admit into communion one whom divine authority excludes as a pagan. Farewell, good shepherd, and keep watch over us, lest through your negligence the Lord’s flock suffer harm.

## LETTER LXXXV [formerly XCIV]. (In the year 1024)

To his most beloved lord, King ROBERT, FULBERT, the humble bishop, sends all that is fitting for a king.

It is fitting that you know the affairs of your kingdom. Let your prudence therefore know that William of Bellême (Bellême, a fortress in the Perche), having avenged his son’s treachery, has thrown him into prison, from which, he says, he will not emerge without our counsel. He reports that he is ready to do what you ordered through the monk Hildradus.

Furthermore, when Count Odo, who was then staying at Tours, learned that I had returned from your holy presence, he sent word that I should meet him at Blois two days later, in order to hear what the Roman envoys would say. But since this concerned me little, and illness also prevented me, I did not comply. The count himself also commands and earnestly begs your majesty not to rush into action to his detriment, but to send him Milo of Caprosis (Chevreuse), who can report to you the words of the Romans, of William, duke of Aquitaine, and his own. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI [formerly XX]. (Around the year 1025)

To the venerable man and fellow priest, FRANCO, FULBERT sends what belongs to true peace.

You, dearest brother, out of the abundance of your charity, honor me excessively and dignify me with praise for wisdom; but I see and acknowledge myself as I am: humble and lacking in virtue. Yet however my smallness may stand, I confess that I neither ought nor can admit this inhumanity: to hear you complaining of the afflictions of the holy Church without compassion and zeal for justice.

But because compassion, once conceived in the heart, eagerly seeks to produce consolation, while zeal seeks to inflict the wound of vengeance—and we ought nevertheless to be more ready for the former than the latter—I too, before exercising zeal against your enemies, approach you with words of consolation. I therefore ask you, brother, not to be driven by the force of your troubles into anger beyond measure. Do not perhaps break out into arms through impatience, and, once you have appropriated another’s sword, do not make your own sword go unfeared.

Again I ask you not to become, because of the great injury, sad, turbulent, and anxious, but always to delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart. I advise you to assign publicly to the support of the weak the usufruct of the altars that your predecessors handed over to laymen. Then you should threaten anyone who defrauds them of anything from it; and if anyone should fall into such fraud, he should be condemned by anathema as a thief of sacred things and a murderer of the poor.

Do not fear, I beg you, to offend people innocently for the sake of the Lord, so that you may be worthy of him. If God is for you, who is against you? God is always for you in his own cause; he is also with you, as he says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Why then are you afraid to defend God’s cause, when he himself is with you to work together with you and to protect you?

Be strong, therefore, brother, in the Lord and in the power of his might. Be strong, I say: trust and rejoice, exult and celebrate, and with an eager spirit rehearse his contest, saying with the prophet:

> “Gather together, peoples, and be conquered; gird yourselves, and take counsel, and it shall be dissipated. Speak a word, and it shall not come to pass, because God is with us” (Isaiah 8:9).

And because I know for certain that our common Lord will champion you in his own cause, I also promise that I, his servant, shall not be absent, whether to restrain the hands of your persecutors or to silence the mouths of those who contradict you. Finally, I command you to rest secure among the surrounding clergy, so long as I hear that you are not yielding to the persecutors of the Church.

As you requested, I shall meet with Gualerannus; and after the case has been examined, I shall inform you, either by word or by letter, what I think about it and what you ought to do. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVII [formerly XLII]. (Around the year 1025)

To Father and fellow bishop FRANCO, FULBERT, bishop.

I sent Gualerannus a letter of this kind:

> “Fulbert, bishop, to Gualerannus, more honor than he has deserved. I ask and admonish you, brother, to amend the offenses you have committed against the Lord, against me, and against the bishop of Paris, who lodges a complaint against you. If you do not do so before the middle of Lent, from that time onward we shall deal with you as with a man who sins gravely and refuses to amend.”

Therefore, if Gualerannus has not justified himself to you before the prescribed deadline, then exercise your ministry concerning him. Farewell at length.

## LETTER LXXXVIII [formerly XLIII]. (Around the year 1025)

FULBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to the venerable Father and fellow bishop F., that when the Lord comes he may find him watchful.

Warned by your envoy Gualerannus about pursuing justice on the day and at the place appointed by you, he replied that Count Odo had warned him under oath to undertake an expedition against Fulk around that same day. Nevertheless, he promises that within eight days after that expedition has either taken place or been abandoned, he will come to justice.

But since he has not fixed a definite time for fulfilling his promise, and since many causes of delay may arise—or at least causes that may deprive us of the opportunity to meet—we advise you, if it can honorably be done, to hasten the matter through your trusted men and to bind your **casatum** firmly to you. **[The precise sense of *casatum* is uncertain here.]** For you do not know what fortune may bring forth. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIX [formerly XLIV]. (Around the same year)

To the holy and wise man G., abbot and archbishop, F., the humble bishop, sends the affection of true love.

Let your prudence know, holy Father, that when Lord T., the abbot, departed, he left us sadness and tears—not because we would have been unable to protect his innocence, if he possessed it, but because we could neither purge nor conceal his guilt. Therefore, if under your leadership he desires to come to an examination, at the peril of his rank and to the common disgrace of priests, you ought by shrewd judgment to restrain his ineffective efforts, observing the apostolic saying: “If a person is overtaken in any offense…” and so forth (Galatians 6:1). Farewell.

## LETTER XC [formerly XLV]. (Around the same year)

To his lord Father and fellow bishop A., FULBERT sends the sum of all desirable things.

I rejoice that the signs of your office show you to be concerned: that you wish to speak with me, to put an end to our complaint, and to punish incestuous marriages. These are the marks of an earnest, just, and chaste spirit. Since you wished to appoint a day and place for carrying out these matters, let the day be the tenth day before the Kalends of March and the place Masingy. If you come, remember to bring Haimon; otherwise, inform me in good time, lest I undertake a journey involving such great labor in vain. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI [formerly LXXII]. (In the year 1025)

FULBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, sends the support of his prayers to RICHARD, abbot, and all the monks of Saint-Médard.

As long as we heard from you reports of good and wise men, we gave thanks to the Lord with rejoicing. But now, disturbed by an ominous report [the printed reading is *laeti*; perhaps *laesi* or *tacti*], we fear for your danger. For it is said that your household members violated the atrium and church of blessed Medard with bloody slaughter. It is said of you that in that same violated church you presume to offer sacrifice to God without episcopal reconciliation. If this is true, that presumption is certainly new, excessive, and to be attacked by all good people.

What evil are you beginning to contrive in the holy Church? Do you wish to assign the portions of laymen to priests and those of priests to laymen? Where are you permitted either to dedicate a church anew or to reconcile one that has been profaned? You are not even permitted to build a house of prayer without the bishop. For you have been placed entirely under the authority of the bishop who, as Jerome says, has the power to hand over a sinful monk to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.

But lest I seem to say these things relying upon slight authority, I call as my witness the great Council of Chalcedon, composed of 328 bishops and held under Pope Leo and the emperor Marcian, at which Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, was condemned. At that council the following was also decreed concerning the matters mentioned above:

> “It has pleased us that no one build or establish a monastery without the knowledge of the bishop of that city. Those who are in monasteries throughout the individual cities or estates must be subject to the bishop, devote themselves to quiet, and observe fasts and prayers, remaining in the places where they once devoted themselves to God. They shall neither communicate nor undertake any ecclesiastical or secular business, abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps they are ordered to do so by the bishop of that city because of urgent necessities.”

Again, in the same council:

> “We order that monasteries or shrines that have been established be under the authority of the bishop who is in that city, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, so that they may not withdraw presumptuously from their bishop. If anyone should dare in any way to rescind such an institution, or should refuse to be subject to his own bishop: if he is a cleric, he shall be subject to the condemnations of the canons according to the rank of his ordination; but if he is a layman or monk, he shall be deprived of communion.”

I could append many other supports for this position from the divine laws, but I remember that I am to write briefly. And, as Isidore says, just as the weapons that a soldier can appropriately carry for the occasion are sufficient for him, so a few sentences from many are sufficient for us, as the circumstances require.

Now I wish to advise you charitably to accept sound counsel: return simply to subjection to your bishop. Ask pardon for your past fault; take precaution for the future, so that through your obedience you may have rest, and through your peace we may have joy. Otherwise, know for certain that if—God forbid!—you remain in defiance against him, you will suffer serious loss at the next gathering of the bishops. Farewell.

## LETTER XCII [formerly XCII]. (In the year 1025)

FULBERT, a priest to the king and faithful to his lord, to ROBERT.

Because I received the warning late, I did not comply with your request that I meet you at Tours on the following Saturday. If there are other matters, they are being left unspoken for the present, because unspoken matters harm you less than those stated openly. Farewell now and always.

## LETTER XCIII [formerly XCVI]. (Around the year 1025)

Of Count Odo to Robert, king of the Franks.

*(See below under ROBERT, king of the Franks.)*

## LETTER XCIV [formerly XCIX]. (Around the year 1025)

FULBERT, the humble bishop of Chartres, sends greetings to Count FULK.

I grieve for you, noble man, when I hear that you are wandering astray and placing yourself in danger. I say that you are wandering astray because, although you ought to fear God, honor the saints, and defend the Church, you despise God, dishonor the saints, and invade and carry off the property of the Church. I say that you are placing yourself in danger because those who do such things have no share in the kingdom of God.

On account of these sins, the archbishop of Tours admonished all our bishops, including me, insignificant as I am, to excommunicate you. But I judged it pious first to warn you, and I beg you to have mercy on your soul and appease God. Your end is already near.

Hasten, therefore, I ask you, to be reconciled to Christ our Savior, for there is no salvation for a human being except through him. Keep this word in mind: Whoever, by confessing and repenting, brings his sins to an end before he dies will have an end to the punishment for them in the next age; but whoever does not bring his mortal sins to an end through repentance will have punishment without end.

Awaken, therefore, for your own sake, as a man who will soon die, and be reconciled to Christ, lest you die condemned by apostolic authority. Farewell, and quickly and truthfully send me word of your intention.

## LETTER XCV [formerly C]. (Around the same year)

FULBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, sends Count FULK a warning for his salvation.

The retainers who disgraced the presence of our lord the king through so terrible a crime have caused the secular judges to assert that you too are guilty of a capital offense against majesty, since afterward you offered them your protection and places of refuge. Consequently, many requested that on the holy day of Pentecost we excommunicate both you and them.

But, taking thought for your salvation, we asked for a delay of three weeks from that day, so that we might admonish you by letter. We also obtained this condition from the king: if you come to judgment, vengeance will fall not upon your lives or limbs but upon your possessions.

Therefore we warn you, before the prescribed deadline, either to bring the authors of so great a crime to judgment or to repudiate them for the honor of the king. Then clear yourself, as you promised through the abbot of Saint-Albinus, and appease the king’s mind through humble satisfaction. But if you are unwilling either to bring the guilty men to justice or to repudiate them for the sake of your lord, you will no longer have Christian communion with us.

Keep watch, therefore, as you would for your own sake, and quickly let me know what you intend. May God grant you to choose the better course of counsel.

## LETTER XCVI [formerly XI]. (Around the year 1026)

To the venerable bishop of Paris, FRANCO, FULBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, sends the gift of every prosperity.

We have delayed excommunicating that sacrilegious woman of Laon, who is plundering the property of your Church, for the following reasons. First, there was no one who would dare carry our excommunication to her. Second, it would perhaps have benefited you little or not at all if she were excommunicated in our Church without knowing it. Third, we waited for this to be done more usefully at a gathering of the bishops of our province. You too still seem to think that this should be awaited, if the serenity of your mind agrees.

As for Lisiard, your archdeacon, whom you wrote was proud and rebellious toward you, there is no need for you to consult us, since your prudence knows perfectly well what the divine law thinks about such matters; nor is it proper for us to judge anyone who is absent and whose case has not been examined.

We wish you to know that our Adeoldus of Nogent, against whom you are threatening the sentence of anathema because of the complaint that the monks of Saint-Denis have against him, says that he is ready to justify himself in an audience before you and us. Therefore, if you wish to settle this dispute quickly and justly, appoint a day on which we can meet you and the monks of Saint-Denis at Saint-Arnoul, which seems to be a more convenient place for you to assemble. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVII [formerly XXXIV]. (Around the year 1026)

LEUTHERICUS, archbishop of Sens, and FULBERT, bishop of Chartres, to the clergy of the holy Church of Paris: moderation in prosperity, fortitude in adversity, and charity everywhere.

We have heard, dearly beloved, of the injuries suffered by your bishop, and we sympathize with you from our hearts. We believe that you too feel them as faithful sons and members well joined to a good head. But we marvel that, placed in such great sorrow, you have neither come to us to seek consolation nor at least sent a letter. For your wound is not so great that no remedy of consolation can be found, nor has that true physician abandoned the Church who promised to be with all of us every day until the consummation of the age. We marvel again that you admit into communion, contrary to canonical rule, impious men who oppose divine ordinances and persist in contumacy against your pastor—a rule which it is sacrilegious for you to ignore and dangerous to violate.

But if you think that they must be retained in communion with you until they have been publicly excommunicated by your bishop, the apostle Peter corrects this opinion in the sermon delivered to the Romans concerning the ordination of Clement, in these words [Note: The sermon of Saint Peter mentioned here is apocryphal.]: “You ought, brothers, to understand certain things from among yourselves: if there are matters which your bishop, because of the plots of wicked men, cannot state more openly and plainly—for example, if he is hostile to someone on account of his deeds—you must not wait for him to tell you so, but should observe it prudently, comply with his will without being admonished, and withdraw from the one toward whom you perceive that he is hostile.”

Blessed Peter said these and many similar things in the aforementioned sermon. But, brothers, when we set such matters before you, do not suppose—God forbid!—that we suspect anything sinister about you. We are merely performing our duty when we rouse you or other brothers of ours to vigilant caution. For it was not without reason that the prophetic saying was written concerning winged creatures which touch one another by the movement of their wings. Therefore, asking that we too may mutually repay this service, we wish to stir you with the swift wing of exhortation to be diligent in the law of the Lord, devoted through love to the obedience and support of your pastor, but wisely instructed and faithfully encouraged to resist his adversaries.

Among these adversaries is one named Lisiardus, formerly indeed an archdeacon. Although he ought to have been the eye of his bishop, the dispenser of the poor, and the catechizer of the ignorant, he has apostatized from all these duties and become for his bishop like a nail in the eye, a predator of the poor, and a leader of the ignorant into error. For, hurling proud and insulting curses against his bishop, he disturbs the serenity of his vigilance; and, without consulting his bishop, he hands over to lay soldiery the tithes and altar offerings—namely, the provisions of the poor.

By doing such things, he gives the ignorant an example of error and perdition, although he ought to have offered them instruction in true knowledge. What shall we say of the oath of fidelity, which he so pollutes that he is faithful to his bishop neither in heart, nor in word, nor in deed? We do not judge rashly concerning his heart, since it has been truthfully said in the sacred poem [Note: Perhaps by Prudentius, Saint Prosper, or some other poet of approximately the same period.]:

> The inmost things of the heart shine forth from the appearance of one’s deeds.

Accordingly, if the ruin of an angel is not sufficient as an example, the destruction of the rebellious Korah shows what punishment he deserves for his contumacy. What he has earned by his treachery and insulting curse is shown by the hanging of Judas and the leprosy of Aaron’s sister. [Col. 0248C] O exceedingly wretched man, upon whom so dreadful a storm of divine vengeance hangs!

The Old Testament condemns him in these words: “Whoever curses his father shall be put to death” (Exod. 21:17). The law of Christian judges condemns him in this judgment: “If anyone inflicts any injury or unjust dishonor upon a bishop, he shall make the legal composition for his life, and everything he is seen to possess shall be joined in its entirety to the Church over which he is known to preside.” The Council of Gangra excommunicates him in chapters 7 and 8; the Council of Carthage degrades him in chapter 57, as do many other authorities.

Therefore, unwilling to diverge from the judgment of the holy Fathers, we accordingly separate him from communion, insofar as our authority permits, until he comes to his senses and, duly humbled before his bishop, makes satisfaction to him. If, however, he does not quickly come to his senses and present himself for satisfaction, let him be struck with perpetual anathema in a plenary synod.

We order you to show this letter to Lisiardus himself, so that, warned with due gravity, he may remember to escape from such dreadful dangers. For the opportunity of escape is still open, as the Lord says through Ezekiel: “If the wicked man repents of all his sins which he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and does judgment and justice, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. 18:21). And through John: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1). The Lord himself also says: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:10).

The Catholic faith is certain—for I shall use the words of blessed Fulgentius—that whenever a person does penance, however advanced in years he may be, if he renounces his former sins with his whole heart, pours out before God tears not only of the body but also of the heart on account of them, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil deeds by good deeds, he will immediately obtain forgiveness for all his sins. Yet, as Father Augustine says, the one who promised forgiveness to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the one who delays.

We also ask, brothers, that you remember to greet and console the venerable lord F., the bishop, in our name, knowing for certain that his sorrows are ours and his prosperity ours. Farewell with him.

## LETTER XCVIII [formerly XXXV]

*(Around the same year.)*

To his beloved father and fellow bishop G., FULBERT sends life and well-being.

Your cleric and our kinsman F., on coming to us, showed himself all the more welcome because he reported everything favorable about you. Therefore, now making him the bearer of our greetings, and asking your illustriousness with small gifts—if this is not burdensome—we wish that he may find that favor useful to himself which we believe he has long enjoyed with you. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX [formerly XXXVI]

*(Around the same year.)*

To his dear father and fellow bishop GUIDO, FULBERT.

Since we have not found in the divine laws a specific rule establishing the form of penance for a deacon who pretended to be a priest and presumed to celebrate Mass, we can estimate the matter by reasoning from similar cases. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were condemned by God’s judgment and punished with a horrible death because they presumed to compare themselves with Aaron the priest and usurp his office. This man, however, a Levite, unlawfully usurped the priesthood for himself in the manner of those men. Who, then, would doubt that a mortal offense has been committed in this case, when he sees that in their case it was punished by death under God’s judgment?

But since our Savior, who came to save what had perished, does not desire the death of the sinner but that he should be converted and live, mercy dictates that such men be degraded and perform penance among the laity. Yet, lest this reasoning seem to savor too much of the severity of the old law, let us set forth evidence from the new law as well.

It is read in a certain chapter: “It has very often been decreed and prohibited that the celebration of Masses should not take place at all in unsuitable places.” After some intervening material, it continues: “For just as it has not been granted that anyone other than those consecrated for this purpose by bishops should sing Masses and consecrate the sacrifices, so it is not permitted that they presume to celebrate Masses in other houses, altars, or places than those consecrated by bishops, and so forth.” At the end of the chapter: “Therefore, if anyone, after so many prohibitions, presumes to violate these decrees of apostolic and synodal authority, renewed by that authority, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank.”

We therefore see that the chapter of the new law agrees with the old, and there is no need to hesitate further about what should be done with this deacon. He must unquestionably be removed from the choir and punished with penance.

If a question arises concerning the length of his penance, we must remember the judgment that answers this question in the following way: “The canons do not establish with sufficient care a fixed measure of time for the performance of penance for each individual crime, but leave the matter rather to the judgment of the bishop, because before the Lord not the measure of time counts so much as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food so much as the mortification of vices.”

It is therefore in your hands either to shorten or to prolong his penance, according as you see him diligent or negligent in performing it. May Your Holiness prosper.

## LETTER C [formerly LXXXIX]

*(Around the year 1026.)*

To his most beloved lord and king ROBERT, FULBERT, humble bishop, sends humility in prosperity and confidence in adversity.

Concerning Lisiardus, the cleric who has seized the property of the bishopric of Meaux with offensive persistence, we offer the following advice. Command the archbishop of Sens either to visit the bishopric himself and restore it, as is proper, to your authority and his own, or, if he is prevented from doing so, let him write to the aforesaid L., in a letter composed in his own name and ours—that is, in the name of his suffragans—that he should withdraw from the place and the properties foolishly seized, and strive to make satisfaction to us for his presumption before the next feast of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. If he neglects to do this, let him henceforth be excommunicated by all of us. Farewell.

## LETTER CI [formerly XCI]

*(Around the year 1026.)*

To the most serene king of the Franks, ROBERT, FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres, sends what is fitting and beneficial.

I congratulate you, my lord, because, as a fountain of goodness ever watering others, you have entrusted me with handling God’s business as is expedient. It is fitting for you as king to command such things, and it is safe for your subjects to undertake them. But I am surprised that you said you had either placed or intended to place Count Odo in charge of my deliberation concerning what should be done about the reception of the bishop of Meaux, since for almost a year and a half I have neither seen him nor received any embassy from him concerning such a matter.

Nevertheless, if, with God’s favor, he wishes to come to us and accept my counsel, he will undoubtedly cease provoking divine vengeance against himself by tearing apart the aforesaid Church and opposing your sacred ordinances. Farewell.

## LETTER CII [formerly LX]

*(1027.)*

[Col. 0251A]

To his venerable father and fellow bishop G., FULBERT.

I am indeed carried away by my desire to attend the blessing of Henry, the royal offspring [Note: After King Robert’s death, his son Henry succeeded him; some writers say that Robert, dying, had named his younger son as heir. Queen Constance opposed this plan and acclaimed Robert’s other son as king. Odo, count of Champagne, and Baldwin, count of Flanders, together with not a few men of considerable nobility, were present in arms. In the end Robert was compelled by royal right to yield, contenting himself with the duchy of Burgundy, a most noble and wealthy territory. Paul Aemilius, *Life of Henry*.], but my adverse bodily health delays me. I would nevertheless attempt to reach the place by moderate rides, if I were not deterred by the ferocity of his mother, whose promises are sufficiently credible when her deeds provide them with confirmation.

Prevented by this difficulty, I ask your charity, most beloved, to advise the lord archbishop of Reims and the other leading men in my place not to delay the blessing of the young man mentioned above for any reason. For I hope that he will be pleasing to God and to good men. Farewell.

## LETTER CIII [formerly LXV]

*(1027.)*

[Col. 0251B]

To his most beloved fellow bishop ODOLRIC, FULBERT sends from his heart whatever a true friend should send.

First, I give you thanks, dearest friend, because you promise us your presence at the council, the assembly, and the service. In doing this, you greatly cheer us through your innate kindness. We would indeed desire to attend the council mentioned, just as I remember having told our venerable archbishop Leuthericus in your presence; but difficulties arising from the wickedness of the present time do not permit it. We ask you to make this known to him as well, so that he may not be kept waiting by our expectation.

For the present, we have no opportunity for the desired meeting with you, unless perhaps you are willing to come near Novigentum. Farewell.

## LETTER CIV [formerly LXVI]

*(Around the year 1027.)*

To his beloved O., FULBERT.

The reason I once did not send you a letter by your courier, dearest friend, was that I intended to visit you as soon as possible. Although I delayed this for a long time, I did not cease to desire it. Meanwhile, I want you to know what I know you would certainly wish to know: that, by God’s grace, I am presently in good health, spiritually intent upon serving you and bodily prepared, as no one is more faithfully prepared—except that holy archangel of monks, Odilo, with whom I do not presume in any way to compare myself.

If I were to attempt to describe how his charity affects your soul, I would fail, lest I seem to wish to narrate what cannot be narrated. A multitude of occupations, as well as the messenger’s impatience with delay, prevented me from writing more. But I ask this one thing of your kindness: when you greet our archangel in my place, put on, with monastic simplicity, the angelic cheerfulness that is available to you. Farewell, and prosper in the strength of God.

## LETTER CV [formerly LXVII]

*(Around the year 1027.)*

[Col. 0252A]

To his venerable father ODILO, FULBERT the priest, not trusting in his own merit but moved by devotion, sends the presumed support of his prayers.

I have had, and still have, a great desire to come to you. But the causes of dissension that have recently arisen in our bishopric forced me to abandon the journey I had planned. I hastened to inform you of this as soon as possible in these few lines, so that your sublimity would not meanwhile be kept waiting for my humble self.

I shall come to you sometime, if permitted, to you whom the Holy Spirit truly inhabits, in order to seek the counsel of the divine oracle. Farewell always in the Lord; again I say, farewell.

## LETTER CVI [formerly LXVIII]

*(Around the year 1027.)*

[Col. 0252B]

To the prudent and illustrious Father O., his own FULBERT.

Just as I have received liberally from another, so now I repay my thanks, at least in affection, since in deeds I cannot. For you honored me with such preparation in your letter that no more festive welcome could be expected at Solomon’s banquet amid the instruments of poets and the burning lamps of virgins [Note: “Among the instruments of poets and the burning lamps of virgins.” This is how it appears in our manuscript and in manuscript D of Padua, belonging to a most learned and respected man. In the Genoese *Catholicon* it is interpreted as follows: “*Cincendela*, from *candeo, candes*, is so called: a fillet, a kind of hornet that shines as it flies; *cicendulum* is used for a candle, for it is said to derive from *candeo*.”].

You set before me angelic manna, not without the mystical feast of doves and turtledoves. Meanwhile you poured out the nectar of charity. Having eagerly drunk it and conveyed it into the innermost places of my heart, I rejoiced to pour forth to you, Father, as a son to a father—not prophetically, like David with a good word, but panegyrically, as is customary, and in blessing, like Israel refreshed by his son.

Then, with paternal concern, you indicated that you had carefully examined the state of my health: when vital warmth gave you some sign of well-being in me, you rejoiced; when it gave a sign of illness, you grieved and feared danger. Nor did your kindness finally allow my wound to remain without a share in your treatment. Employing divine skill wonderfully, you first poured in a certain liquid like Samian wine, which would digest the stagnant humor; then another resembling olive oil, by which the entire swelling and pain would be soothed and depart.

Now, therefore, healed by your care and refreshed by your banquets, I consider it fitting that all my powers should always support the fulfillment of your will. I do not intend in any respect to disagree with your judgment, since I trust that, with the Lord, insofar as this is granted to a human being, you will and refuse the same things as he does.

Therefore, Father, it is fitting that you in turn should assist with sacred intercessions your little servant who depends upon you and looks to you with great confidence. For I am a very wretched man: although I was not sufficient for my own affairs, I have somehow—whether by reason or by rashness—been led into public responsibility. And this is certainly true, nor should you conceal it: it makes you especially indebted to me for counsel and assistance, since it was at your urging that I did not abandon this labor. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII [formerly LXIX]

To the most holy and beloved Father O., FULBERT, humble priest, sends the support of his prayers.

I wanted to meet you, Father, as I instructed through my deacon R. But my household, disturbed by some new rumor, will consent neither to my undertaking the journey at present nor to accompany me on it until they have judged that it can be done more safely.

## LETTER CVIII [formerly LXXXXVI]

*(1027.)*

To King Robert, FULBERT the priest, faithful and ready.

Having received your embassy through R., the steward of the Holy Cross, who had been sent to me, I have once again abandoned my pilgrimage. Now I wish to learn from your serenity what you desire of me in conversation, if possible, rather than through envoys or letters.

I would come to you immediately for this purpose if I could conveniently do so. But our sacred season and the discipline of our order forbid coming in arms. Coming unarmed is made impossible by the length of the road and the wickedness of the secular world. For I have O. as a serpent on the road [Note: By the letter O. we understand Odo—some perhaps Odolric, bishop of Orléans—and by the letter R. Queen Constance. Both opposed Fulbert because he supported Henry, the elder son of King Robert, against Robert, the older son whom the woman, with womanly partiality and disregarding the prerogative of age, wished to have crowned king.], and R. as a horned serpent on the path.

For the rest, let it depend upon your decision how you may now wish to make your will known to me, since I have determined that it is appropriate for me to comply with your will, provided it does you no harm. Farewell in royal fashion [Note: In French, approximately: “May you fare like a king.”].

## LETTER CIX [formerly CVI]

*(Around the year 1027.)*

[Col. 0253C]

To his most beloved lord, Bishop FULBERT, H., his faithful servant according to the Lord’s command, sends serpentine wisdom endowed with dove-like simplicity.

What I had learned from your account, most blessed Father, and from that of many others, I have recently learned from the report of Lord Berard, bishop of Soissons: namely, that you have incurred the queen’s very serious hatred because you favor her husband in establishing the elder son as king—a son whom they say is a dissembler, sluggish, and effeminate, and likely to imitate his father in neglecting the law—while they attribute the opposite qualities to his younger brother.

Many bishops also secretly criticize you, or, together with the others, regard you as a fifth hammer discordant with the four Pythagorean hammers on this matter. Therefore, insofar as I gathered from the words of the aforesaid prelate, I did not hesitate to make known to you the opinion of your fellow bishops from France concerning how this matter should be handled, so that, if it is perhaps the sounder opinion, you may not oppose it and may guard yourself against danger.

This is their opinion for settling the dispute on both sides: while the father is alive, no king should be created; but if he presses more fiercely for this to be done during his father’s lifetime, the one whom he judges better should be raised to kingship. Take care, most prudent Father, that you not be excessively just, nor improperly dissent from your holy fellow priests.

[Col. 0254A]

> A healthy man may bear the name of madman, and a just man that of unjust,
>
> If he seeks virtue itself beyond what is enough.
>
> Remember to avoid envy through excessive cultivation;
>
> Even if it does not harm, it is burdensome to endure.

May the angel of great counsel be with you in all things. May he also grant me to see your most desired face. If I perhaps address you with an insolent whisper, I ask that I may easily find a place for pardon with you, since I have erred more through ready fidelity than through wicked presumption.

## LETTER CX [formerly CVII]

*(Around the year 1027.)*

It is certain to all who know the foundations of Catholic purity that the solidity of the whole Church consists in peace, and that the mark of Christ’s discipleship is love. For just as we read that the Lord said in the Gospel, “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27), and again, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35), it is therefore clear that no one is a disciple of Christ unless he has been marked with the sign of love and peace.

This sign, however, is acquired only by those among whom there is unity of wills. Unity of wills cannot be found except among those who establish their willing and refusing according to the judgment of a single superior. Therefore the author of peace, leaving no order in the Church without the governance of a prelate, clearly indicates that human frailty and instability can be brought into unity of spirit, or preserved in peace, by no other means.

For this reason, we few brothers in the coenobium called Cella Boboni, serving God as far as we can, because we desire to possess the bond of peace and the mark of Christian discipline through unity of heart and soul, after the death of Lord Garinus, a religious abbot, chose a certain brother named Bernard, adorned with upright morals, whom we wish to preside over us in the place of a father. We wish the diversity of our opinions to be united in his decision, lest, by thinking differently, we be found strangers to Christ’s teaching.

This election was made with the counsel and authority of the lord abbot of the Monastery Major, after the death of the glorious prince Odo, from whom he had received responsibility for this matter. Having completed the election in the customary solemn manner before the assembly of monks, he also presented the aforesaid brother to the most noble Countess H., under whose authority the place itself lies, and to Stephen, her son, the count. From them he received a grant of temporal possessions belonging to the same coenobium.

Afterward he presented him to the venerable Mainard, bishop of Troyes, whose ecclesiastical authority ought to confirm an election of this kind and from whom the care of souls ought to be received, together with the abbatial blessing celebrated according to the institution of the Fathers. He most kindly agreed, and, as the ecclesiastical custom requires, completed everything, being a most prudent man and distinguished for his learning.

## LETTER CXI [formerly CVIII]

*(Around the year 1027.)*

By Odilo, abbot of Cluny, to Fulbert.

See *Patrologia*, volume CXLII, among the letters of Saint Odilo.

## LETTER CXII

*Of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, to Hildegarius: On bishops proceeding to war.*

*(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 150, from a manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims.)*

FULBERT, humble bishop of Chartres, sends greetings to HILDEGARIUS, his brother.

I had indeed resolved not to write to you, although you have often asked me to do so—not because I ought, or indeed should, deny your affection anything, but because I judged it more prudent to close the door of my tongue than to bring into the light matters that might offend many people. For this reason I have remained silent toward you until now: I did not wish to provoke against myself the envy of detractors. I know, of course, that there will be people who will turn what we are about to say, as though it had been expressed too harshly, into an insult against themselves.

But because you persist too obstinately in pressing your request and do not cease making yourself troublesome with frequent letters, I shall open to you, insofar as the Holy Spirit grants permission, what you ask. Indeed, I shall review the very things sanctioned by the authority of the holy Fathers, whose words to contradict is to reject the truth.

[Col. 0255C]

You ask what I think about bishops who, disregarding the tranquility of ecclesiastical peace, seek seditions and pursue wars. In truth, I dare not call them bishops, lest I do injury to that religious name. I shall call them tyrants instead. Occupied with warlike affairs and surrounded by a great number of soldiers, they hire mercenaries for pay, so that I know of no kings or princes of this world so thoroughly equipped according to the laws of war, maintaining the whole discipline of arms in military array, arranging troops, and setting ranks in order to disturb the peace of the Church and shed the blood of Christians, even if those Christians are enemies.

If you present them with the testimonies that the orthodox Fathers long ago issued on this subject—that they ought to devote themselves not to arms but to ecclesiastical peace, and that they have undertaken the governance of souls, not the destruction of the living—they immediately put forward claims of justice. They say that they take up arms unwillingly, that enemy hordes hang upon their necks, that swords threaten their throats, and that they seek through arms the freedom which they cannot obtain through peace.

Why, then, do they not, in accordance with the Apostle, endure injury all the more? Why do they not suffer fraud all the more? For “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10:4–5).

They ought rather to persist in prayer and accept Paul’s counsel: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19). And the Lord says to his disciples: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23). And: “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39). And: “If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also” (ibid., 40). And again: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

For we know who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. 12:19). In the Old Testament, Israel conquered the hostile army through Moses’ prayer; conversely, when he lowered his hands, victory passed to the enemies (Exod. 17:11). From this we can conclude that we fight better through patience and prayer than through swords and seditions.

The master of truth himself, whose footsteps we must follow—as the apostle John writes, “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6)—although he had the most just cause and no less power to strike down his adversaries, as he himself declared before his passion when he said that the Father would provide him, if he wished, with more than twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53); although, at his command, the whole world would have fought for him against the senseless men who had risen up against him, even though he was truly innocent and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22), nevertheless, wishing to invite us—whose weakness he considered in all things—to patience, he was led to the sacrifice like a most gentle lamb and did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

For when the faithful disciple prepared to fight for his Master and, drawing his sword from its sheath, was already engaging in battle, so that he might know that victory lies not in the sword but in God, he heard from the Master: “Put your sword back in its place; for all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:32).

Therefore blessed Augustine, in the *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, says: “The apostle Peter was permitted to go only so far as to cause pain, not to kill.” Since the holy Church has no sword except the spiritual one, and ought not to kill but to give life, Pope Nicholas bears witness, saying: “The holy Church of God is never bound by worldly laws; it has no sword except the spiritual one; it does not kill but gives life.”

And blessed Jerome, in his letter to Ageruchia, says: “Formerly it was commanded that an eye be repaid for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Matt. 5:38); now we offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us” (ibid., 39). “At that time it was said to warriors, ‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one’ (Ps. 44:4); now Peter hears, ‘Put your sword into its sheath: whoever strikes with the sword will perish by the sword’ (Matt. 26:32).”

“Bishops,” as Isidore says in his book *On Offices*, “ought to defend their position among the people not by bloodshed but by the merits of their life.” And elsewhere: “The special duty of bishops is to read the Scriptures, examine the canons, imitate the examples of the saints through vigils, devote themselves to fasts, keep peace with their brothers, tear apart none of their members, condemn no one unless he has been proved guilty, and excommunicate no one unless his case has been examined.”

Everyone of sound judgment understands how unlawfully and contrary to his rank a man who ought to devote himself to such duties rises up for the weapons of human warfare. Therefore blessed Ambrose, wishing to give priests an example of patience, writes in his letter against Auxentius concerning the handing over of the basilicas to the citizens:

> “I see that you are more disturbed than usual. But why are you disturbed? Willingly I shall never abandon you; compelled, I do not know how to resist. I shall be able to grieve, I shall be able to weep, I shall be able to groan; against the Gothic soldiers, my tears are also weapons. Such are the defenses of a priest; otherwise I ought not, nor can I, resist.”

Again, on the same matter in the same letter:

> “If property is sought, let it be seized; if my body, I shall meet them. Do you wish to drag me into chains? Do you wish to lead me to death? It is my will. I shall not fortify myself by surrounding crowds, nor shall I cling to the altars while begging for my life; rather, I shall be sacrificed more gratefully on behalf of the altars.”

Origen, also explaining the Gospel passage, “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 9:15), says:

> “The holy apostles and martyrs did not persecute; they endured persecution. They did not curse; they endured curses. They did not blaspheme; they were killed by blasphemers.”

And blessed Pope Gregory, instructing us in a certain homily how to preserve innocence, says:

> “If only we are not sufficient for the power of preaching, let us at least preserve the duty of our office through innocence of life. For in the Gospel the Lord says, ‘Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves’ (Matt. 10:16). Therefore we are sent as lambs among wolves, so that, preserving the sense of innocence, we may not possess the bite of malice. Whoever assumes the office of preaching ought not to inflict evil but to endure it, so that through his own gentleness he may calm the anger of those who rage, and, wounded himself amid the afflictions of others, may heal the wounds of sinners.”

The same pope also teaches that a bishop ought in no way to devote himself to arms, not even for a just cause. Wishing to satisfy others by his own example, he writes on this subject to the deacon Sabinianus:

> “There is one thing which you should briefly suggest to our most serene lords, the emperors: if I, their servant, had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards, today the Lombard people would have neither king, nor dukes, nor counts, but would be divided in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I am afraid to involve myself in the death of any human being.”

From this, you can clearly infer that although he was able so effectively to avenge your injuries, nevertheless, out of fear of God, he chose the shield of patience, lest he become involved in the deaths of men; whereas these men, having cast aside the fear of God, wickedly involve themselves in slaughter and gaze upon bloody carnage with defiled eyes.

The most blessed Martin, zealously fleeing such conduct, renounced the arms with which he had served under an earthly king and dedicated the first service of his faith to a purpose of gentleness and innocence. Although he had not yet attained any grade of clerical rank, he was nevertheless deservedly preferable to many bishops, and steadfastly renounced military service, saying:

[Col. 0258A] “I am a soldier of Christ; I am not permitted to fight.”

In brief, he taught that not only bishops or ministers of sacred orders must be restrained from battle, but that anyone who has once begun to serve as a soldier of Christ must also abstain altogether from the very occasions of war. When he had likewise been placed at the summit of the episcopate, he not only pursued no enemy, but often rescued even those who deserved death from impending destruction, with an immeasurable affection of charity, mindful of that commandment: “Rescue those who are being led to death.”

I do not say this in order to prevent criminals, or people unworthy of life itself, from being punished; but this is permitted to kings and the powers of the world, and to those to whom the laws have granted it. For the laws of Caesar are one thing, and the customs of ecclesiastical dignity another.

Hence the blessed Augustine says in his *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testament*:

[Col. 0258B] “Why was the sentence given? Why should the one who takes up the sword perish by the sword, except because no one is permitted to kill anyone with the sword, apart from a judge?”

And blessed Jerome, in Book III of his commentary on Ezekiel:

“Whoever strikes down the wicked insofar as they are wicked, and possesses instruments of execution in order to kill the worst offenders, is a minister of the Lord.”

And Haimo, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans:

“There are certain monstrous crimes which are judged rather by the judges of the world than by bishops and rulers of the churches, as when someone kills an apostle, a bishop, a priest, or a deacon. The kings and princes of the world condemn such offenders. Therefore the person who judges such crimes does not carry the sword without reason.”

Thus, just as bishops and ministers of sacred orders are altogether forbidden to kill anyone, so the princes of the world are permitted to do so without guilt, as Jerome testifies in Book XI of his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians:

“A judge is not the author of a crime, whether by conquering men or by killing men.”

It is therefore clear that the power of uprooting the impious from the earth has been assigned solely to the powers of the world, as the most blessed martyr Cyprian writes in the ninth category of abuse:

[Col. 0258D] “The king,” he says, “ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, destroy the impious from the earth, not allow parricides and perjurers to live, and not permit his sons to act impiously. Bishops, however, should remain steadfast in their gentleness, ecclesiastical severity, and preaching of the word of God, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables’ (Acts 6:2).”

They ought also to teach in such a way, as Jerome says, that their lives may be irreproachable. For the person whose speech is destroyed by his actions loses the authority to teach.

Therefore, let them know that they are altogether forbidden to go to war, except for certain reasons which will be made clear in the subsequent edict of King Charles:

“Charles, by the grace of God king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, and devoted defender of the holy Church, and in all things helper of the apostolic see. At the urging of all our faithful, and especially at the counsel of the bishops and the remaining priests, we altogether forbid the servants of God to carry arms, fight, or go to the army and to war, except only those who have been chosen for this on account of the divine ministry—namely, to complete the solemn celebrations of the Mass and to carry the protections of the saints: that is, one or two bishops with priestly chaplains. Each prince is also to have one priest with him who can point out sins to those confessing and impose penance.”

These men think nothing of all this; indeed, despising even the institutions of the Gospel, they often, as we have heard, with their hands still stained by a recent slaughter, dare not only to enter the church but also, in their wicked audacity, to approach the very sacraments of Christ, not discerning [or: judging rightly] the body and blood of the Lord. They plainly pay no attention to the fact that Christ himself entered the holy places once—not with another’s blood, but with his own blood—overflowing with the abundance of God’s mercies, so that, even for those persecutors of his, although unworthy of mercy, he might say to the Father: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

They ought also to remember that David, once a most powerful king, of whom the Lord says, “I have found a man after my own heart, who will do all my will” (Psalm 88:21), was nevertheless forbidden—because of the death of Uriah, the census of the people, and his frequent military expeditions—to build a temple for the Lord. Solomon, that is, the peaceful king, deserved to build it after David’s death (1 Chronicles 28).

They therefore do not fear what the Apostle says: “Whoever eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

Accordingly, Ambrose admonishes us, saying:

“See what you are doing, priest: do not touch the body of Christ with a fevered hand. First cure yourself, so that you may be able to minister.”

And blessed Jerome says in his commentary on the Psalms:

“The chosen of Israel were hindered; and now the chosen of the Church are hindered if the priests themselves do not also receive the sacrifices innocently.”

Because, therefore, they presumptuously undertake what is unlawful, by the merit of their conduct they are rightly deprived, before the eyes of the heavenly Judge, of the honor of their dignity, although they boast before men under the false name of shepherds.

Let them therefore know that they do not possess that power of binding and loosing which was granted by God to the apostles and to bishops living according to the apostolic example, according to blessed Augustine, who says in his canonical rule:

[Col. 0259D] “Only those possess the power of binding and loosing which the holy apostles possess who hold their example together with their teaching and, according to the apostolic rule, have all things in common.”

The blessed Pope Gregory likewise says in the *Dialogues*:

“Those exercise the place of Peter in binding and loosing who hold the place of holy governance in faith and conduct.”

And elsewhere:

“He rightly deserves to lose a privilege who usurps unlawful authority.”

But if they wish to cloak their iniquity by imitating any of their fellows, in order to make excuses for sins—men who may have acted as though they were religious and nevertheless did not abstain from military expeditions—even if they have drawn someone of great authority over to their position, I place greater trust in the faith of the Gospel and in the truth of the holy Fathers than in anyone barking against such true testimonies. With the Apostle, I consider it more prudent to say: “If anyone announces to you anything beyond what was delivered to you in the Gospel, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8).

He also commands that a bishop be “without blame,” not a striker.

To those who [wish] to defend themselves by the wicked example of someone else, I say briefly: let them know that individual persons or cases do not prejudice the common law and universal judgment. Let those bishops therefore be attentive to their flock; let them feed the poor of the Church and the members of the household of faith; let the cause of widows and orphans enter before them; let them clothe the naked, refresh the souls of the needy, and render the other services of fatherhood to their children.

But let them take the greatest care that they never seize and wickedly divert to other uses what the Church gathers and preserves because of the needs of the needy, lest dogs eat the bread of the children of Christ—which is entirely harmful to their souls.

You will find countless other testimonies in the divine Scriptures; but for my part I have sent you these few, in order to satisfy your desire. If you are wise, you will be able to consider much in these few things.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXIII. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, to Hildegarius

[In Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, p. 190.]

FULBERT, bishop of Chartres, sends greetings to HILDEGARIUS from him who commands greetings to Jacob.

Compelled by the brevity proper to a letter, I answer your question concisely. Jerome says concerning ecclesiastical property, in his letter to Nepotianus (Letter 52):

[Col. 0260C] “To take anything from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To have received money for distribution to the poor and then, whether through caution or timidity, to keep it from the many hungry—or, what is a crime of the utmost plainness, to take some of it away—surpasses the cruelty of all robbers.”

Likewise, to Pammachius (Letter 48): “Where the recipient is richer than the giver, it is a kind of sacrilege to give the property of the poor to those who are not poor.” Hence Isidore says: “It is a great crime to bestow the property of the poor upon the rich and, from the resources of the needy, to purchase the favor of the powerful.”

Consider, therefore, that Scripture excepts no one: neither bishop, nor abbot, nor any steward of God’s household. Whoever diverts the goods of the Church entrusted to him must understand that he is no longer a shepherd but an invader, crueler than every robber, a domestic thief and a familiar enemy.

[Col. 0260D] For he who rashly squanders on alien purposes the things he has received for distribution solely to the poor does not wish to feed the hungry multitude of the poor in the wilderness of this world; rather, with the most wicked Judas, he establishes moneybags for himself, and, like an impudent thief, carries off the things we collect for the food of the poor.

For priests ought to know that the substance of the churches belongs to the poor, not to themselves; nor should they abuse, in the manner of tyrannical extravagance, the stewardship of the needy entrusted to them. Hence Jerome says to Paulinus (Letter 13, middle):

[Col. 0261A] “What you possess is no longer yours, but a stewardship has been entrusted to you. Remember Ananias and Sapphira: they timidly kept back what was their own. Take care that you do not imprudently squander Christ’s substance—that is, that by immoderate judgment you do not give the property of the poor to those who are not poor, and that, according to the saying of a most prudent man, generosity does not perish through generosity.”

We must also consider what ought to be given to whom, as he writes a little earlier to the same man: “Beyond food, clothing, and evident necessities, never give anything to anyone, lest dogs eat the bread of the children.”

Therefore, just as it is pious and just to preserve the goods of the Church solely for the use of the poor and captives, so it is sacrilege, and foreign to Christian devotion, to distribute them according to one’s own will and for alien uses. Jerome himself also testifies to this in his commentary on Matthew:

[Col. 0261B] “All who misuse for other purposes the revenues of the temple and those things contributed for the uses of the Church, in order to satisfy their own will, are like the scribes and priests who purchase falsehood and the blood of the Savior.”

The pious care of shepherds ought therefore to know that they must do absolutely nothing with the property of churches without the counsel and consent of their subjects, since the office of administering, not the discretion of scattering, has been entrusted to their prudence.

Having said this beforehand, let us come to the vessels of the Church, about which you especially ask. For since one who appropriates any of the Church’s goods to fulfill his own will is said to incur sacrilege, you may judge how greatly he sins who has taken away vessels dedicated to the sacred mysteries.

First, if so great a need of the poor and captives presses upon us, the other things stored in the treasuries of the Church should be given away; then the vessels themselves should be broken into pieces and distributed in works of mercy. Hence Ambrose says in the book *On Duties* (Book II, ch. 28, near the beginning):

[Col. 0261C] “The Church possesses gold, not in order to keep it but to distribute it and bring aid in necessities. What use is it to preserve what helps no one? Do we not know how much gold and silver the Assyrians carried away from the temple of the Lord? Is it not better that a priest melt it down for the nourishment of the poor, if other resources fail, than that a sacrilegious enemy defile and carry it off?”

And shortly afterward: “Was Saint Lawrence told, ‘You ought not to have distributed the treasures of the Church or sold the vessels of the sacraments’? This office must be performed by someone of sincere faith and clear-sighted prudence. Certainly, if anyone turns it to his own profit, it is a crime; but if he gives it to the poor, redeems a captive, or enlarges spaces for the burial of the remains of the faithful, it is mercy. In these three kinds of case it is permitted to break, melt down, and sell even consecrated vessels of the Church.”

He seems to me to have set forth briefly what ought to be done with the property of the Church. But it is not permissible to remove sacred vessels from the Church’s custody and hand them over to anyone as a pledge, as he likewise testifies (*ibid.*):

[Col. 0261D] “Care must be taken that the symbolic form of the mystical people does not leave the Church, lest the ministry of the sacred chalice be transferred to wicked uses. Therefore, vessels which had not been consecrated were first sought within the Church; then they were broken up; finally, they were melted down and, through small disbursements distributed to the needy, served as the price of captives.”

But if new vessels, not yet consecrated, are lacking, I think that everything may piously be converted to the uses mentioned above. Accordingly, ordinary silver should first be distributed in the necessities mentioned above, as blessed Gregory says to the lord bishop of Messana (Book VI, Letter 35):

[Col. 0262A] “Your Fraternity ought to take great care that, if there is ordinary silver in your Church, it should first be spent on the redemption of captives; otherwise it is necessary for you to provide from consecrated vessels. For, just as it is altogether serious to sell ecclesiastical implements needlessly, so again it is a fault, when such necessity is pressing, to prefer even the forsaken property of the Church to its captives and to delay their redemption.”

Likewise, to Fortunatus, bishop of Fano (*ibid.*, Letter 13):

[Col. 0262B] “Just as it is blameworthy and worthy of punishment for anyone to sell consecrated vessels except in those cases prescribed by law and the sacred canons, so no rebuke or penalty is to be inflicted if they have been disposed of from piety for the redemption of captives.”

It should be noted that blessed Gregory says that it is altogether serious needlessly to sell ecclesiastical implements—that is, candlesticks, censers, and other such things—except solely in the cases prescribed by law and the sacred canons, namely, for the redemption of captives and alms for those who have absolutely nothing. Whoever spends them otherwise acts against the canons. Therefore, whoever he may be, let him know that he is unworthy of priestly dignity, according to the judgment of the same pope writing to John, bishop of Larissa (Book II, Letter 7, before the end):

[Col. 0262C] “By a definition consonant with the holy Fathers we decree that one who does not know how to obey the holy canons is worthy neither to administer sacred things nor to receive communion nor to serve at the altars.”

From the foregoing, then, as I judge, you can see that if it is altogether serious to sell without a certain necessity the lesser implements of the Church, it is sacrilege, and altogether most grave sacrilege, to sell the more excellent consecrated vessels and crosses without the most extreme need of the poor.

For this reason, let all ministers of the Church know that they ought first to furnish, by measured distribution, everything necessary to the flock over which they preside—that is, to those who are Christ’s poor, namely monks, regular canons, or any religious persons living in common—taking the greatest care

[Col. 0262D] lest through excessively prodigal superfluity there arise such a necessity as compels the expenditure of the Church’s treasures. For if they pour things out without measure, they sin, because thoughtless extravagance is the ruin of an entire household.
