But truly, after distribution in the other works of mercy, if so great a necessity arises that some vessel of the Church must be taken, it may be sold only to another Church, so that the same office may be celebrated there as before, and, from the proceeds of its sale, another may be restored in its place or the money distributed to the poor. Thus, as we have said, it may be sold or, according to the aforesaid testimonies of the holy Fathers, broken into pieces; but it is improper that it be put up as a pledge.

[Col. 0263A] For secular persons do not know how to render the reverence due to sacred mysteries, since this use has not been entrusted to them. Perhaps adulteries, fornications, and those crimes which provoke God’s wrath may occur near the chest, or in the house in which the vessels are concealed. For when we read in the history of Kings that Uzzah immediately died because he touched the ark of the Lord when the oxen were kicking; and when Leviticus commands Aaron and his sons not to permit the sons of Kohath to carry or touch the vessels of the sanctuary, lest they perhaps perish from among the Levites: how does anyone dare to give outside his Church, to any person, cleric or layman, Christ’s altar or his tomb as a pledge?

[Col. 0263B] For what is the cross except Christ’s altar? And what is the chalice except the tomb of our same Lord? Whoever therefore puts the altar and tomb up as a pledge sells Christ with Judas; and whoever accepts them as a pledge receives money from wicked Jews with the soldiers, lest they proclaim Christ’s resurrection and glory, which they had seen at the Lord’s tomb.

We also read in Daniel that the Gentile king Belshazzar, because he served drink to his concubines in the vessels which his father had taken from the temple of the Lord, suddenly saw a hand writing and learned from the interpretation of the writing that death and the division of his kingdom were impending for him.

To speak for the moment of present matters, I shall briefly offer you one example which I recently heard; I do not know whether the report has also reached you.

[Col. 0263C] A certain miracle occurred in Lesser Brittany. A money-changer kept vessels of the Church, deposited in a chest, as a pledge for himself. By chance little boys climbed upon the same chest,

[Col. 0264A] and immediately became mad; dogs too happened to climb upon it and became frenzied with rabies. Their owner perceived that this was divine vengeance, because he had accepted consecrated vessels, not to be assigned to such places or agreements, in return for money lent. Greatly terrified, he fled to the church, told everyone what had occurred, and as quickly as possible released the sacred vessels from his possession—not with less dread than the Philistines of old drove the ark of the Lord’s covenant away from themselves because of the impending disaster.

This matter so terrified the inhabitants of that land that they declare anyone who thereafter puts sacred vessels up as a pledge or accepts them as one to be more wicked than any idolater. Consider, therefore, how great a fault it is to snatch vessels from the bosom of the Church and entrust them to secular hands.

[Col. 0264B] Let the prelates of the Church therefore take care, lest, by treating negligently the things entrusted to them and the stewardship of the poor which they have undertaken, they incur injury to their own souls. For I have heard concerning certain bishops, as I remember having written to you in a certain letter, that they embrace secular arms, hire military forces for money, and pursue other things altogether unsuitable to them. Of these, it is not I but the Prophet who says: “Your princes are companions of thieves,” who wickedly squander the substance of the churches entrusted to them upon the aforementioned uses. For, despising the episcopal office, they desire the very things which they ought wholly to avoid.

Therefore, by my counsel, every prelate should, insofar as he can, cut off from himself all the occasions through which countless harms usually come upon his children and ecclesiastical property, so that, administering well, they may receive a reward from him whose place they hold and whose footsteps they ought to follow. Farewell.

## APPENDIX. Letters of the canons of Chartres, Hildegarius, William duke of Aquitaine, and many others

## LETTER CXIV [formerly CIX]

To the most illustrious H. A., archbishop of Tours, the dean and the entire congregation of the canons of Saint Mary of Chartres offer the service of their loyal obedience and the support of their prayers, with willing and devoted hearts.

[Col. 0263D] Recently, before our most blessed Father Fulbert, our bishop, as you know, had begun his journey to Rome, he enjoyed a pleasant conversation with you.

[Note: I suspect that Fulbert went to Rome with King Robert for the sake of pilgrimage. For, Paul Aemilius says in his Life of that king, when King Robert was at Rome he offered at the altar of the holy apostle, on the day before the apostle’s feast, a writing containing the antiphon *Cornelius the Centurion*. In an old manuscript chronicle: “In the year 1026, Robert, most pious king of the Franks, setting out for Rome for devotion and pilgrimage, offered the antiphon *Cornelius the Centurion* on the day before the vigil of the apostle Paul.” For he was most reverent toward the deity, devoted to liberal studies and sacred learning, and an emulator of ancient holiness. He composed certain antiphons and sacred responses, approved and received by the judgment of the whole Church; among these are *Of the Holy Spirit* and *O Constancy of the Martyrs*. They say that he composed the latter responsory when Constance, his wife, asked her husband Robert to compose some song for her sake. When he was besieging Avallon, they say that, though no one attacked or shook it, but while he was composing hymns in his tent, a great part of the walls collapsed of its own accord, as though God and the heavenly powers were showing immediate favor to their worshipper. Paul Aemilius, in his Life of Robert.] When he had returned and was one day sitting in our assembly, speaking with us about that journey, we complained that after his departure we would suffer many adversities from various people, especially from Fulcher and his nephew, together with their bands of thieves. He replied firmly and encouragingly, as he is accustomed to do in such matters:

“The good ought to bear the injuries of the wicked with equanimity. For, as you yourselves read in a certain homily of blessed Pope Gregory, no one is good who has not tolerated the wicked.”

He added that he had spoken to you about this matter, that you could also benefit him and us, and that you had promised assistance against those evildoers. If necessity pressed, he ordered us at once to seek the support of your fatherhood.

This is what we are now doing, most powerful Father, driven by various tribulations. To pass over other matters, those excommunicated men whom we mentioned above, after our most beloved father had set out on his journey, plundered our lands—which are in the charge of Herucus and Tetoldus—as though wolves breaking into sheepfolds, although we were undeserving of such treatment. Nor were the losses inflicted upon the sheep by their rabid bites enough for them; rather, they turned to devastate a certain possession of the shepherd himself called Ermenulf’s estate.

Therefore we ask you, most righteous Father, for the love of the holy Queen of queens, our Lady, whom we serve although unworthy, and also for the sake of your own most beloved man, who places great confidence in you and, on departing, entrusted us to your protection: arrange, by exerting yourself greatly with your nephew Gaudfridus, that his plunder and ours be restored, so that those wolves may not henceforth seize the property of the lord bishop and of us, or at least until he himself returns with God’s assent.

Farewell; and kindly let your suppliants learn, by sending us word, whatever you do concerning these matters.

## LETTER CXV [formerly CX] (A.D. 1022)

To the venerable LEX., bishop, HERB., and the congregation of the canons of Saint Mary of Chartres offer the greatest good wishes and the support of their prayers.

You command us, illustrious bishop, to give you the *circadae* from our churches which are in your bishopric. But we wish to make something known to your serenity: namely, that the bishops of Blessed Mary, in whose diocese we possess churches, have always shown this mark of love and reverence toward the holy Queen of queens, our Lady, that they never demanded from us, although unworthy servants of hers, the service which you require.

See, I ask you, lest we be called troublesome when we beg you, kind Father, following the honorable footsteps of the holy Fathers, not to bind us in any way by the burden of this payment, lest you yourself be noted as the first author of causing us difficulty in this respect.

Rather, moved by no small love for your own advantage, we wish you to be enrolled in the register of the benefactors of our happy order, so that, offering a perpetual sacrifice to the Lord for them and also for you, and recounting before her the benefits of your humanity, we may proclaim you worthy to be entered also in the book of heavenly life.

Furthermore, we do not think that your wide knowledge has failed to include the fact that our lord Bishop Fulbert, whom we know to be very dear to you, has gone to Rome. We mention this so that, if it should please your generosity to favor our petition, we may make it known to him when he returns; and he will greatly rejoice with you over this good and wise deed.

If we do not obtain what we ask, at least wait for us, your suppliants. We must consult him when he has returned about this matter, since our decisions depend upon his will. In the meantime, do not impose any prohibition upon our churches.

Farewell, and may you prosper in good works. Do not consider it burdensome to write back to us from the sanctuary of your heart what oracle emerges concerning these matters. Again, again, and always, farewell.

[Note: The canons of Chartres evidently at some time paid the bishop of Lisieux the *circada*, a visitation payment from their churches. The name *circada* derives from *circumeo*, “I go around.” Archbishop Hincmar of Reims frequently uses this verb in Letter 1 to Emperor Louis the Stammerer, where, in chapter 8, he urges him not to afflict the churches in that kingdom through burdensome *circadae* and through improper customary exactions imposed twenty years earlier.]

## LETTER CXVI [formerly CXI]

A friend to his friend: Hildegarius wishes Sigifridus the fulfillment of every good thing.

While you were staying with us, I believe you remember what you promised me, since I counted you among my foremost friends and was usually devoted to your services. Nevertheless, I remind you of that matter myself and ask you, according to your promise, to send me a riding horse of such a kind as it would be fitting for you to give and for us to receive.

In this I agree with those who think that friendship ought to be sought not only for its own sake but also for the benefit it provides.

May you live long, act well, and attain an eternal reward.

## LETTER CXVII [formerly CXII]

Hildegarius, disciple of Lord Fulbert, sends greetings to Sigefridus Ric., chaplain of the count.

You have deceived me for a long time, keeping no faith at all with your words. Therefore, while I grieve that I have been deceived, I am also overwhelmed with the greatest shame because of your lie. It is not fitting for so important a person to incur the disgraceful name of falsehood.

It would also be dreadful to fall into the crime of sacrilege, because, as we read, “The words of a priest are either true or sacrilegious.”

I therefore beg you, by the holy friendship which ought to exist between us, to reconcile yourself with the reputation of honorable truth by sending me, through Gauterius, formerly my monk, the horse which you rightly promised me.

If you do not do this, know that you have fallen completely from our affection. With my conscience as witness, let me say that in what I ask of you I desire not my own advantage more than yours, and at the same time your honor.

## LETTER CXVIII [formerly CXIII]

Hildegarius offers abundant good health to E., his elder, whom he honors with pure affection.

[Note: He calls the potion *iera* a sacred medicine. Physicians know what the *potio iera* is; there are several varieties. Fulbert himself explains the meaning of the name *scrupulus* in his verses on the ounce and its divisions. See below.]

You will take the *iera* potion, which the lord bishop is sending you, with warm water before twilight. On the night when you are to take it, you must not dine. That same night, place the potion in the vessel in which it is to be mixed and sprinkle it with rock salt; or, if that is unavailable, with fine salt, in the amount of one *scrupulus*.

After taking the potion, sit before the fire without any disturbance, taking every precaution against the cold. If you lie down for a short while, it will not harm you; nevertheless, I do not want you to sleep.

As soon as you feel your bowels beginning to move, walk slowly and go to the privy in this manner. If, because of the purgation, you eventually become thirsty, you must not drink at all except a little vinegar mixed with warm water, to dilute or relieve the stomach. You may do this even when thirst does not press you, when the purgation is almost calling for it.

Delay your midday meal until you feel that the cathartic no longer wishes to have any effect. When you sit at table, take care not to have too much, and do not eat anything constipating or excessively salty.

I would write more about the manner of observing these instructions, if a little were not enough for a wise person. Yet a charity which does not know how to pretend otherwise commands me to write this: may you experience the effect of this potion in such a way that you always remain in good health.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXIX [formerly CXIV]

Hildegarius to G.: transform the words into action.

[Col. 0267B] My lord, I have suffered greatly while waiting until now for news of your charitable promise. Anxious to know what your highness had decided to assign to my small self, I kept asking where the travelers whom I saw waiting by the city wall facing this way were returning from.

But when no one gave an answer on your behalf, I returned home sadly, since night had already fallen. Yet because nothing human is entirely perfect, we spare human weakness.

Nevertheless, I ask you not to rush into words of this kind of excuse, but to strive to fulfill what you promised without the embellishment of delay. Therefore, to make me more certain, I command and beg you to deign to indicate what you order me to do.

I do not want you, my lord, to hesitate with your pen while holding a good work in your mind, since, with God’s help, it will be brought to completion.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXX [formerly CXV]

[Col. 0267C]

Of William, duke of Aquitaine, to Hildegarius.

## LETTER CXXI [formerly CXVI]

The archbishop of Tours sends greetings to H., bishop HAND.

Although your letter recently directed to me deserves a reply corresponding to it, I nevertheless thought it better for the time being to postpone the responses owed to its insolence than not to attend, insofar as it concerns us, to your welfare, and, while attending to it, not to respond discreetly and humbly to certain passages of your letter.

For it is the task of physicians, even when patients are ungrateful and provoke the practitioner with insults—whether they suffer from melancholy, mania, or any other illness—to apply the remedies of their art nonetheless and to persist more attentively in curing them.

Therefore I too, although I have not professed to be a physician, being entirely inexperienced, must nevertheless, since I have been advanced to this office by the authority of my rank, correct you when you go astray. I ought to treat you, although you are ungrateful, with remedies gathered from those of the holy Fathers, and, whether you wish it or not, persist until you are cured.

But before I come to this, I wish, as I said, to address certain passages of your letter. For I think the other matters, which occupy most of it, should be passed over.

Therefore I refute with certain and incontrovertible contradiction your accusation that I acted on an ill-considered decision and rashly and without fault separated you from the divine office to which you had not been summoned. For the decision was not ill-considered when it offered you the choice of what you preferred. Had you paid proper attention, you would not have called it ill-considered. You acted ill-considerately, then, in turning yourself—as will soon become clearer—toward the worse course.

That you and your men were not rashly and faultlessly placed under interdict is attested by the remains of the vineyards in which you fixed your camp. The example thus given to others, whom you accuse so vehemently, confirms the truth of the matter. Who, even if insane, would not assert that you were summoned, since you know that letters were sent to you by me? Therefore, brother, recognize with due penitence that you were reasonably and canonically summoned because of your fault and separated from the divine office; mourn this, and through mourning return to satisfaction.

If you attempt to defend yourself by the forty-day period of summons prescribed by the canons, I know that individual cases or persons do not prejudice the law. For when I saw you turned to madness, transformed from a bishop into the leader of so many armed men, cruelly ravaging our entire country, threatening us with steel, fire, and various forms of death, and when I saw that the forty-day period of summons had done nothing to make you desist from the impending blow, I immediately set the spear of excommunication against you. I did so so that, terrified at least by its sight, you might restrain yourself and your men even for a moment, and recognize the bishop whom you had lost.

But you preferred to be pierced by that spear of excommunication rather than to restrain yourself, even for an instant, from the tyranny you had begun. As for your statement that you did this at the king’s command, I neither deny nor affirm it, nor do I understand how it lessens the matter. For whoever’s command led you to do this, you remain burdened by the same guilt as if no one had commanded you. Indeed, this single transgression is sufficient to aggravate your guilt: you presumed to begin such an undertaking against canonical authority, without consulting me, your archbishop. And what you ought not to have done even at my command, you did while acting as your own adviser.

As for your assertion that you were driven to act against Odo, you did not even cut down a vine-shoot belonging to him; rather, besides the other insults you inflicted upon your mother Church at the command of your lord Fulco, you destroyed the vineyards of the canons of Saint Maurice down to their roots. For these reasons I sent you letters of excommunication, which you call marks of audacity contrary to law and right. I sent them not because I wished to turn you back toward the course into which you had fallen, but so that you might come to your senses and desist from what you had begun, without so rashly reproving your teacher and lord.

Whether I acted discreetly or indiscreetly, let your judicial scales weigh it—you who advise others to seek a counselor. But if I had rashly and without cause hurled excommunication against you—God forbid!—you nevertheless ought to have submitted to the judgment of your pastor and ceased from the sacred celebration. Because you did not do so, and because, with proud self-counsel, you disregarded the interdict of your teacher, you prudently plunged yourself into the abyss of excommunication.

Hear what blessed Gregory says about this:

> “Whether the pastor binds justly or unjustly, the pastor’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock, lest the one who is subject to him, even if perhaps bound unjustly, should deserve the very sentence of his binding through another fault. Therefore let the pastor fear either to absolve indiscreetly or to bind. But let the one who is under the pastor’s hand fear to be bound, even unjustly, and let him not rashly reprove the judgment of his pastor, lest, although he has been bound unjustly, guilt that did not previously exist be produced by the very pride of his arrogant reproof.”

Thus far blessed Gregory. Since, then, you have been convicted by this argument, mourn again, recognizing that you have been excommunicated, and through mourning return to satisfaction.

Let it suffice that we have answered only these passages of your letter; let some idle person answer the rest. I shall pursue with brother H. the matters that are more necessary and that I promised to address.

I observe from the movements of your body various kinds of passions sprouting in your soul; unless they are confronted by some medicine before they emerge into strength, they will produce a wondrous death in your soul. But the appropriate medicine for each passion will remain unknown unless their origins and, so to speak, their roots are investigated with the most attentive discernment.

There is therefore one source and beginning of all the soul’s passions. Yet each passion receives its name according to the quality of the part of the soul that has been corrupted. The same is taught by the example of bodily diseases. If the force of a harmful humor occupies the head, the condition is called cephalalgia; if it occupies the feet, podagra; if the hands, chiragra. The discomfort of a single humor thus receives as many names as there are portions of the limbs that it occupies.

Passing, then, from visible things to invisible ones, we believe that each vice is present in the several parts of the soul. The wisest authorities have defined the soul as threefold in its powers: rational, irascible, and concupiscible.

According to the quality of the corrupted part, therefore, the infection is named after its particular pestilence. If it infects the rational part, it produces the vices of vainglory, elation, envy, pride, presumption, and heresy. If it wounds the irascible part, it gives birth to fury, impatience, sadness, acedia, faintheartedness, and cruelty. If it infects the concupiscible part, it generates gluttony, fornication, avarice, and harmful earthly desires.

I therefore perceive, brother, from the movements of your body, as I said, that your soul is bringing forth its own death. For when you displayed such pride, contempt, and presumption toward me, especially as your teacher, it is evident that the rational part of your soul has been miserably corrupted.

These three things are clearly discerned in you by definite judgments: pride, because you answer your archbishop so proudly; contempt, because you make light of his interdict—which, even if it were unjust, God forbid, ought nevertheless, as I proved above, to have been feared by you; and presumption, because, although placed under interdict justly or unjustly, you approach the sacred celebration. The judgments concerning these three things proclaim that the rational part of your soul has been corrupted, as I said. You yourself will see whether any other things are sprouting in you.

I shall provide this part of you, which I see so horribly corrupted, with something from the remedies gathered from the holy Fathers, as I promised, by which you may be recalled to health. But this treatment will benefit you nothing unless the wound by which you have been pierced unto death is first aided by the medicine of satisfaction. Once you have been healed through satisfaction, as I have said, you will immediately cut away with the sickle of discernment the tumors of pride, contempt, and presumption that I suspect have hardened within your soul.

Then, lest the wounds of that amputation, while still fresh, generate some other passion, you will burn them with the painful cautery of fear. To keep that burning from being touched by the chill of impiety, you will tend it with the warmth of charity and the oil of mercy.

If you do this, that pride by whose prompting you hurled such harsh answers at me, that contempt by which you make light of my interdict, and that presumption by which, though excommunicated, you approach the sacred celebration will perish. The rational part of your soul will return, for the greater part, to incorruption.

After this, you will combine these forms of virtue—humility, patience, and obedience—into a single honey of the divine utterances, and carefully store this antidote in the little box of your mind. Drawing from it daily nourishment for your soul, you will not only cease forever to produce these pestilences, but will also shine incorruptly, free from all the others.

In admonishing you with these words, brother, I am not puffed up with a teacher’s arrogance; I am tremblingly carrying out the duty of my prelacy. If you heed them, you will, as I believe, provide for your salvation.

But if, God forbid, you continue to neglect these matters, because they conflict with my actions [*sic*], I restrain you from this error by the Lord’s own voice, which says:

> “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matthew 23:2).

As you yourself know better, the doctrine of the Law had been entrusted to the scribes and Pharisees so that they might expound it to their hearers. Therefore the Lord said, “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat,” that is, upon the teaching of the Law. He commanded their hearers to obey their words while setting aside their deeds, when he said, “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works.” For the Pharisees destroyed by evil deeds what they taught, as the Lord subsequently added: “For they say and do not do.”

There are such men now in the Church—bishops, priests, and abbots—who teach well and live badly; and I confess that I am one of their number. Nevertheless, because I sit upon the seat of teaching and prelacy, although unworthy and inexperienced and not matching my words with my deeds, if anything good is commanded you by me as I sit upon that seat, you must observe it, as you hear in the Lord’s admonition. If you neglect it, you will openly oppose the Lord’s commands.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII [formerly CXVIII]  
*(Year 1014.)*

**Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine, to Abbot Aribertus.**

(See below under GUILLELMUS.)

## LETTER CXXIII [formerly CXVIII bis]

**Isembertus, humble priest of Poitiers, to the holy and venerable N., bishop of the Angevin people: the support of prayer and the service of fidelity.**

Since your constant affection toward me is assured, I would rejoice all the more, excellent bishop, the more frequently I could do things pleasing to you. Let your serenity therefore know that I would most gladly come to the most solemn dedication of your church, unless I were detained by the following matter: our lord Guillelmus, count, having taken counsel with the Italians, commanded me and my lords and fellow bishops Islonius and Rohos to attend to certain serious affairs of his, which we cannot in any way postpone.

For this reason, since I cannot come to visit your charity when invited, a considerable feeling of sadness has occupied my mind. But I am consoled by the hope that, through God’s grace, I shall at another time eagerly assist your affairs.

Fare well before God in fitting health.

## LETTER CXXIV [formerly CXIX]

**Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine, to Leo, bishop of Vercelli.**

(See below under GUILLELMUS.)

## LETTER CXXV [formerly CXX]

**Fulbertus to his most beloved lord, Bishop H.: every fullness of good things desired.**

The illness of our most beloved brother B. keeps me from visiting you before the grape harvest. When the opportunity arises, God willing, I shall do so most gladly. In the meantime, I ask you to let me know by letter how you are doing, how my fellow students are conducting themselves in the schools, and whether they celebrate the canonical hours better than usual.

I am sending you one of the two little books that our friend Count G. asked to have copied. Forgetfulness had hidden this book, which had been entrusted to someone, in my chest, since I thought it had already been delivered to you. If I have caused you or your people trouble by making you search for it, the fault is mine.

In my place, I beg you, greet my lord Sigo and Hiduinus: the former, my mind, and the latter, half of my soul. May all the rest of your people be safe in Christ, while the fullness of everyone’s salvation protects you.

Amen.

## LETTER CXXVI [formerly CXXI]

**Hildegarius wishes every good to Brother E.**

I want you, dearest, to write and tell me how well the scholastic office recently entrusted to you by my lord the bishop, at my request, is proceeding; how much favor you have gained with him; who soothe you and who bite you; and how safely you yourself are holding your position.

Your prosperity is my salvation; your adversity, my illness.

May you always prosper in Christ.

## LETTER CXXVII [formerly CXXII]

**Archbishop I., humble bishop: eternal salvation.**

We give great thanks to your charity, which promises to fulfill our request under a reasonable condition. We inform your greatness that we would gladly comply with this condition, but are entirely unable to do so.

We cannot send you the instructors for the journey, since they themselves are occupied with many affairs. Nor can we ask this of Count Vu., because he has departed on an expedition and, they say, will not return until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November; yet on the following day we are to dedicate our church.

We do not wish, therefore, to cause your excellence fatigue, lest, when we wish to rejoice in your presence, we should be disturbed by some inconvenience inflicted upon you along the way. If that happened, the joy of your solemnity would be turned into the greatest sorrow.

Fare well in happiness.

## LETTER CXXVIII [formerly CXXIII]  
*(Year 1024.)*

**From D. to his lord and father F. HER., whom he continually cherishes in the innermost recesses of his soul: perpetual flourishing.**

Our duke Guillelmus, most friendly toward you, is about to set out for Italy next Thursday to inquire into the matter of his son, if this can be done with his honor and safety. For the Italians have chosen him as their king, swearing to him, insofar as they are able, their good faith concerning both the granting of the kingdom of Italy and the acquisition of the Roman Empire.

For this reason the prudent father will precede the son whom I mentioned above, in order to deliberate with them. It is now for your prudence to decide whether, in his absence, you will come to us as agreed. If you come, food will not be lacking, by God’s generosity. I therefore ask you to let me know by letter whatever seems best to you.

Meanwhile, and always, may you and all your people fare well, most holy Father, sweetness and glory of our life alike.

If you pass through Bourges, speak amicably with Odo of Dôle. I found him a prudent man on the Roman journey, and I hope he will be most obedient to you if you wish any service from him. He is also our Count Guillelmus’s most faithful and familiar companion.

When Count Guillelmus called upon Count Fulco so that he might not contrive some trick against you along the roads, Fulco replied in true faith, as you thought proper, that he would contrive none. He also wished your arrival to be announced beforehand, so that he might escort you through his territory.

May God of our salvation grant you a prosperous journey.

## LETTER CXXXII [formerly CXXVII]

**Hildegarius, his faithful servant, wishes his lord Fulbert every good thing according to his desire.**

I know, Father, that the first cause of your penitence, concerning the honor undertaken on behalf of blessed Hilary, is just. Obeying your commands, therefore, since I am the least of your servants and scarcely worthy of the name of necessary assistant, I may properly say that your absence is a great inconvenience to me: I am unlearned, daily in need of your instruction, and have for a long time been deprived of service to the holy Mother of God.

Nevertheless, because you command it, I would somehow strive to endure this, and also your long delays in coming to us, provided I were certain that the church of Saint Hilary, which you are soon to visit frequently, would thereby be raised in some measure.

What grace would then proceed from this for me before God and human beings! Captivated by the hope of it, I have endured in a remarkable fashion being absent for so long from your service and being, as it were, emancipated from the service of the lady mentioned above. It would also be of great importance to me to avert a certain diminution of your reputation, which I see approaching unless you yourself preside over the position you have undertaken.

But since for more than two years you have been detained, on the one hand by pastoral concern and on the other by the discord of princes—and I do not know when the matter can be settled except by their deaths, with perhaps many other causes arising to delay you in the same way—I scarcely dare hope that you will even once revisit the borders of Poitiers and serve that excellent confessor of Christ according to your inclination.

Nevertheless, as you promise, I shall continue to hope. In your place I shall serve as best I can for the time being, praying with constant utterance and fervent pleas that the Lord may grant a happy outcome to the matter, for me and for you alike.

Tell me, Father, I beg you: what recruit has ever fought without a leader? Who has wished to trust himself to the deep sea without a rower?

Count Guillelmus, your friend, and our canons send you faithful greetings still. Jordanus, bishop of Limoges, also sends you the fullest greetings. You once offered him assistance before the archbishop of Bourges. He earnestly asks you to send him the *Life of Saint Leonard*, who, they say, rests in his episcopate. If you can find it anywhere, say graciously that this service has been placed at interest.

[Note: [Col. 0273D] The tradition was therefore uncertain.]

For my part, do not be displeased—I mean you, my lord, and also your dearest Sigo, great in upright conduct and abilities—that I send you greetings by the hundred thousand. Please do not be wearied by my writing and foolishness. I have instructed the messengers to tell you certain things, which you can hear whenever you wish.

Farewell, dearest Father.

## LETTER CXXXIII [formerly CXXVIII]

**From Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine, to Fulbertus.**

(See below under GUILLELMUS.)

## LETTER CXXXIV [formerly CXXIX]

**Hildegarius, his little servant, sends joy of perpetual salvation to his lord, Bishop Fulbertus.**

In the letter of your friend Count G. you can detect much kindness toward you, familiarity, friendship, and forbearance—qualities that I need not explain to you, who know them perfectly well. With your life and that count as companion (Latin *Vita tua ac illius comite*, an uncertain reading), you will not lose the honor you have undertaken, if you wish to retain it.

I therefore advise you not to reject him either in deed or in writing, if you understand that this would be useful to you and to the restoration of your church, and if you have both the inclination and the ability to go to him, as he requests, and to appoint a substitute for me or add a companion to me.

For I cannot endure, unless compelled by your command, either to be entirely absent or to remain away for a longer time from the services of the holy Mother of God and from yours. I long for your instruction as a stag longs for springs of water, and value it above all gold and silver, indeed above life itself.

In the meantime, good Father, I want you to tell me what reward there will be for my labor, small though it is. Will you command that, for the present, the mouth of the ox treading out the grain not be muzzled? Or, like Isaac blessing his son Jacob—prophesying with dim eyes and not seeing his son in the present—will you provide many good things for me in the future?

On the Monday after the octave of Pentecost I shall set out for you, if I can, to learn whether you are coming to the count on the feast of Saint John.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXV [formerly CXXX]

**Hildegarius sends eternal salvation to his venerable and beloved lord R., dean of Saint Hilary.**

Many thanks are owed to you on behalf of God, my lord bishop, and myself, because, as you say, you have carefully guarded the property of Saint Hilary. You thereby most certainly prove yourself his faithful friend and ours, since you have endeavored to perform the office of those whose place you occupy.

Because we are not presently permitted to hear you concerning the matters about which you questioned us, we have taken care to inform you that you should spend the thirty-five pounds, and the other sums that I left with you, on the work of Saint Hilary, following the advice of the good Duke Guillelmus, reserving no part for me.

For I can no longer involve myself in the office of Saint Hilary, since both the road is difficult for me and my lord bishop because of the wickedness of the world, which you know, and I am so tightly bound to the service of Saint Mary that I cannot be removed from it without loss or guilt.

I also think that the excellence of the Mother of God herself can, if there is any offense on my part, plead this matter before Saint Hilary. For I would not have placed that honor behind that of any inferior person; rather, as however small a fosterling of the Mother of the Lord, I have rightly devoted myself to the service of the Mother who has been exalted even above the dignity of all the archangels.

Therefore tell that most prudent duke, on behalf of my lord bishop, to entrust the place of Saint Hilary to such a rector as will be detained from its service neither by the difficulty of the journey nor by ignorance of ecclesiastical order. These are the reasons about which the vice-lord Reginald spoke to my senior bishop, and on account of which we send you this conclusion.

Now I ask your charity, which has always been very present to me, dearest friend, to greet in my name all the clergy of our sweetest and most blessed lord and father Saint Hilary, from the least to the greatest, and to offer all of them faithful prayers.

Give the count himself a hundred thousand greetings from me. I love him above all laymen, remembering him in my prayers before the Lord and continually giving him whatever thanks I can for the love and benefits he has shown me.

Likewise, I beg you, greet my lord Bishop Isembertus. The immense greatness of his goodness prevents me from saying how great has been the grace of his kindness and cheerfulness toward me.

Also do not hesitate to extend the same greeting to the count’s son, the countess, and the others, whose goodwill, although I was unworthy of it, I rejoiced in.

In short, wishing you yourself good health, I bring my letter to an end.

## LETTER CXXXVI [formerly CXXXI]  
*(Year 1029.)*

**The canons of Saint Mary of Chartres send greetings in Christ, and continued service of fidelity, to Leothericus, sacred archbishop of Sens.**

We are greatly astonished, venerable Father, that you have had such evil outcomes after such good beginnings—namely, that when we were without a pastor, you first gave your good support to the appointment of one in his place, but ultimately distorted your judgment by ordaining someone other than the man we had elected.

Lest you say that you were unaware of our election, we sent word to you through our deacons Odelier and Frotmund that we had elected A., the dean, together with letters of ours containing the same information. He seemed to us to be the kind of man whom the fourth Council of Carthage says ought to be ordained bishop.

If thereafter either the king or some of our less wise men presented another candidate to you, you ought to have considered the matter carefully and judged between us to determine whose election was sounder, as you know is most clearly indicated in the decrees of Pope Leo in these words:

> “He shall be preferred to all others whom the consent of clergy and people has concordantly requested; so that, if the votes of the parties should happen to be divided among different persons, the judgment of the metropolitan shall prefer to the other at least the one who is supported by greater efforts and merits.”

We also wish you to know that we had our election communicated to our lord the king through his monks, Hernaldus the prior and Restaldus, provost of Saint Denis. When they objected that the king wished Theodoricus to be ordained, we instructed them to tell the king not to command such a thing rashly. He should first summon us to his court, if he wished, either so that we might consent to his will or demonstrate why we disagreed.

But our lord the king, disregarding these words of ours, hastened in his violence to have the person he preferred ordained without our petition. Perhaps he had forgotten the statement of Constantine, Christian emperor, concerning the violence of princes against himself and against other rulers:

> “Whatever has been obtained by princes contrary to the laws shall have no validity.”

But, for the present, let us say no more about him. He will see whether he is acting correctly in everything and whether he will not repent after the deed.

To you, Father, we direct the course of our complaint. We deeply regret that you have neglected the care of our Church—or rather, that you have diminished your own authority—by setting aside the decree of the aforementioned Pope Leo. If you had observed it, you would certainly have acted reasonably and would have wisely provided for us as a father does for his sons.

But consider for yourself how many other decrees of the holy Fathers you have violated by violating that one. We nevertheless write to you about a few matters out of many.

It is read in the decrees of Pope Celestine:

> “Let no bishop be given to unwilling people; the consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought.”

And a little later:

> “Let the clergy have the ability to resist if they see themselves being burdened, and let them not fear to reject those whom they know to have been imposed upon them from outside. If they cannot have a first judgment concerning the one who is to govern them that is duly free, then let it at least be free.”

Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage:

> “It must also be established that, whenever we have assembled to elect a bishop, if some contradiction should arise—for such things have occurred among us—they should not, for the purpose of clearing the man to be ordained, call for only three, but two or three in addition to the number mentioned above. And in the very people over whom the man is to be ordained, the persons making the accusation must first be examined. Finally, the objections themselves must be investigated; and, once he has been cleared, he must then be ordained publicly.”

Behold how the judgments of the Fathers are violated. You wish to impose a bishop upon us against our will, and we are not granted free judgment concerning the man who is to govern us. When objections were made against the man who was to be ordained, the objections were not cleared, nor were the persons or reasons of those who objected examined.

Since these things are so, and since in this matter you have broken the canonical law in many ways, we admonish you—not by reproving or judging you, but by entreating you with the affection of sons—to be reconciled to the very law that you have offended by confessing your fault and doing penance.

You should not be ashamed to say to your close associates, who secretly fear the Lord and are well instructed in his law, that at last you have recognized that actions contrary to the statutes of the canons ought not to stand, and that those who commit them must also repent.

If the king should thereafter wish to have this strengthened by your authority, and if you see that it cannot stand without violating the canons, beware, Father, lest you add sin upon sin. Either, insofar as you can, refrain from strengthening it, or openly declare that you cannot carry it out while preserving the authority of the laws.

Finally, we humbly ask that this letter of ours not be made public. We have dared to disclose these things within the secrecy of your dear heart. But write back to us if you think there is any reasonable objection to be made against them.

May God increase in you the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, of wisdom and understanding.

## LETTER CXXXVII [formerly CXXXII]

**The clergy of Saint Mary of Chartres, their servants and brothers in the Lord, send greetings to the holy bishops G. of Beauvais, O. of Orléans, and A. of Tours.**

We complain to you, Fathers, about our archbishop and the king, who, against our will, wish to give us as bishop a certain unlearned man, as you know, unworthy of such an office. We beg your assistance: watch, as good shepherds of the Church, at his gates, lest such a man enter it—one who has not sought to enter through the door, but has climbed in by another way, like a thief and robber (John 10:1).

While you three guard the gates, know for certain that a fourth guardian is being added: Count Odo, who will never receive him into his city unless he has first been examined by your judgment, to determine whether or not he ought to be received.

Watch, therefore, with the greatest attention, and carefully investigate the matter with your wise clergy and with us, your servants, if you deign to do so. Do not be reluctant to act out of reverence for the king, as though this pertained to his loyalty. Indeed, you will be more faithful to him if you correct what needs correcting in his kingdom and compel his mind toward the same correction.

We wish you to know that A., the dean whom we had elected, has become a monk. Nevertheless, we still desire him to become our bishop, once that wolf has been rejected—the one whom you can prove to be unworthy.

We ask you to deliberate among yourselves carefully, diligently, and secretly whether this can be done, and to make the outcome of your deliberation known to us, your servants and brothers, either by letter or through a faithful messenger. In the meantime, see that these words of ours are not made public.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVIII [formerly CXXXIII]

**The canons of Saint Mary send greetings to the most holy Father O., whom they love above all abbots and who shines forth with every virtue.**

We beseech you in the name of the Holy Trinity not to favor, against law and right, the party of Theodoricus, the false bishop, nor to advise Count Odo to make peace with him against the authority of the holy canons.

God has placed you in the world as a most brilliant mirror. Take care lest you be darkened by any stain that would obscure others; shine always with the true light by which others too may be illuminated.

Farewell, most blessed Father, and write back to us what seems best to you concerning this matter.

## LETTER CXXXIX [formerly CXXXIV]

**Hildegarius, his faithful servant, to his beloved and always to-be-loved lord Rainaldus: to forget what lies behind and continually strive toward what lies ahead.**

For the sake of charity I promised to live with your nephew Herebert until the new crops are gathered, keeping him as a friend and, for the time being, as a substitute for your presence.

We are sending part of the writings that you requested be sent to you, but not all, because some are not easy to dispatch. What is being sent is both difficult to understand and absolutely necessary: concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Unless we receive these worthily and faithfully, we cannot have life.

Concerning thoughts that force themselves upon us unwillingly, our dearest father Fulbertus held this opinion: they do no harm if, in the end, they do not please the mind; they should be driven from the soul by the sign of the cross, like troublesome flies from the eyes; reason should be appointed guardian of the mind and receiver of useful things, so that, while occupied with them, the mind cannot be attacked or penetrated by useless things.

You can find many other passages agreeing with this judgment in the *Lives of the Fathers*. With Christ’s grace to help—which is necessary, since without it we can do and are nothing—they will greatly relieve your mind.

As for the rest, which is not being sent at present because it is neither so easy to put into writing nor apparently provided with a suitable carrier, I hope, God willing, to send or bring it to you when I find a suitable time and bearer.

Farewell, dearest to my soul. Know that, dead to this world, you live for Christ; live for virtue, and let the death of vices be yours. Pray for me, your servant, Father.

[Col. 0277]

## TREATISE OF SAINT FULBERT ON ACTS 12:1: “King Herod laid hands upon some of those of the Church to afflict them,” etc., composed for the Feast of Saint Peter in Chains

(Galland, *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, p. 177.) (G)*

[Col. 0277C] He who reads Holy Scripture understands it rightly when he does not neglect its modes of expression. But it is not enough to consider these modes unless one has frequented it through continual meditation. For just as, by conversing frequently with any person, we gradually perceive what sort of person he is, so too, by repeatedly studying it, we come to know the manner of Holy Scripture.

For, as we are taught by the authority of the Fathers, Scripture sometimes signifies, in its mystical sense, a virtue worthy of praise through something which it narrates as having been done reprehensibly in the historical sense. This is especially clear in what sacred History relates as having occurred concerning David and Uriah: there both Uriah’s innocent devotion signified the unbelief of the Jews, and David’s sin prefigured the great sacrament of Christ and the Church.

[Col. 0277D] It must nevertheless be understood that, in accounts of things done historically, the reasons of those acting are not altered on account of their signification. Thus nothing is diminished from a just man’s justice, even if an evil thing is signified through what he did praiseworthily; nor is the merit of justice bestowed upon an unjust man, even if some good thing is prefigured through what he did reprehensibly. David’s sin was not therefore not a sin because it prefigured that greatest good; nor was Uriah’s innocence evil because it signified the hardness of an unbelieving people.

[Col. 0278C] We have said this beforehand lest we be judged to have detracted from apostolic merits when we say that something not suited to their holiness is signified through the things narrated of them in today’s reading. For today, according to the custom of the Church, the reading from the Acts of the Apostles is recited to us, in which James, the brother of John, is said to have been killed by the sword, while the apostle Peter is also read to have been arrested and imprisoned.

[Col. 0278D] The history is altogether worthy of faith and is to be embraced with reverence even according to the letter. Yet because it is contained in the spiritual book of the Church, and because we read that the Fathers understood certain matters from it spiritually, it does not seem unfitting, while preserving the truth of the history, to show how the whole may be understood spiritually. But now let us hear the beginning.

## I. “Herod the king stretched out his hands to afflict some of those belonging to the Church” (Acts 12:1 ff.).

Whom we ought to understand as signified by the name Herod is taught us both by the meaning of his name and by the cruelty of his deed. For Herod is interpreted as “leathern” (*pelliceus*), by which name the ancient adversary of the human race is rightly designated. When the first human beings believed his suggestions, they lost the garment of immortality and received leathern tunics, signs of mortality. Since skins are ordinarily stripped from dead animals, mortality is not unfittingly represented by leathern tunics. These tunics, moreover, are read to have been made by God and put on the human beings—not because he himself created them mortal, concerning which truthful Scripture truthfully testifies, “God did not make death,” but because the very quality of the garment showed that those whom he had created for eternal life, if they kept his commandment, had become mortal after their transgression. Yet the one who properly became the author of this clothing for human beings was the one who, by a deceitful promise, persuaded them to incur the fault by which they would deserve it.

He is therefore rightly called “leathern,” at whose instigation human nature is clothed in leathern tunics signifying death. This Herod, however, is called a king because Scripture bears witness that he is king over all the children of pride; he also rules over all who are subjected to his government, directing them toward eternal death. His hands [Col. 0279C] are either the evil spirits who serve him in deception or, certainly, wicked human beings in whom, in Paul’s words, “the mystery of iniquity” is at work. For the enemy, insatiably eager for the destruction of humanity, when his own wickedness alone does not fully satisfy his desire, joins to himself either evil spirits or wicked human beings as companions, to satisfy the hunger of his malice.

He repeatedly stretches out his hands to injure the good whenever, through subordinate spirits, he injects impure desires into their hearts, or through human savagery grows cruel against them in outward harshness. What he once did against our Head, he does not cease to do continually against us, his members. Since he could not penetrate the mind of Christ by temptation, he armed his hands—namely, the Jews and the Roman soldiers—for the destruction of his flesh. So even now, whenever he is repelled from the hearts of the elect, he is inflamed by envy and set ablaze, seeking at least to destroy them bodily.

Why he rages so fiercely is disclosed when it is added: “to afflict some of those belonging to the Church.” The intention that first stirs him to contemplate the innocence of the elect is that he may either cast them down into guilt by wicked persuasion, or, when they resist his persuasions, at least prevent them from resting. The mind of the righteous longs to rest in heavenly contemplation, yet is severely afflicted by being compelled to resist the hidden ambusher in continual conflict. Although the multitude of their triumphs promises them the crown of victory, the very fact that they are compelled to fight so frequently afflicts them greatly. Knowing that human frailty is prone to fall, they are deeply apprehensive lest the enemy, who repeatedly challenges them to battle, should at some time overcome them when they fight less attentively.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that it does not say, “to afflict the Church,” but “some of those belonging to the Church.” Although he pursues all the faithful with a general hatred, those feel his harshness more grievously who resist his light desires with mature seriousness. He attacks them with all the greater ferocity the more strongly he sees them resisting. Or else Herod afflicts certain people in particular by stretching out his hands when, while others escape his temptations, he drags others to the precipices of vice.

## II. It follows: “He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.”

We receive the passion of blessed James with every reverence, believing both that he was crowned with the crown of righteousness in triumph over martyrdom and that his enemy was punished with eternal death for his cruelty. But what we have heard happened once according to the historical account, we investigate—not without reason—to discover how it happens mystically every day.

Since James is interpreted as “wrestler” and “supplanter,” and John as “the grace of God,” these two names can signify two orders within the Church: one, that of beginners, who are still fighting against the devil in the contest of faith; the other, that of those who, by the grace of God, have overcome the adversary and no longer waver through any instability of mind.

The one who wrestles is seen now above, now below. Likewise, those who wrestle against the devil before the movements of the flesh have been perfectly subdued sometimes subject him to themselves and supplant him, yet are also at times themselves supplanted by him, at least through harmful pleasure. If this harmful pleasure is not quickly restrained, the soul immediately loses the life-giving breath of righteousness, and consent is slaughtered by the sword.

Consent that follows upon pleasure is therefore rightly called a sword, because within the holy Church even those who grievously succumb to the devil’s blandishments have been conceived by the same seed of the word and reborn in the same womb of holy Mother Church together with those who, by the grace of God, are perfect in strength. Thus diversity of merit separates them, while the communion of the sacraments unites them, so to speak, by a kindred relationship of faith.

It is certainly no novelty for the word to be called seed, since Paul, when he was scattering that same word over the hearts of the Athenians, was called by them *Seminiverbius*, “seed-picker” (that is, a chatterer or collector of scraps of learning).

If, however, by the apostle’s killing we understand not the death of sin but that of the flesh, we should know that the cruel adversary, always hungering to injure the good, when he sees—as was said above—that he cannot bring about their inward death, hastens at least to slaughter bodily the one who resists him. But in whatever way he harms the elect, his savagery is especially pleasing to those who are displeased by the life of the faithful because of the faithful persons’ innocence.

## III. Hence it follows: “When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also.”

The Jews, who are interpreted as “those who confess,” whom else do they designate here except those who, according to the Apostle, “profess that they know God but deny him by their deeds”? Yet the name Jews may also be understood of unclean spirits, who likewise, when they were driven from possessed bodies in the Gospel, confessed—although unwillingly—that Christ was the Son of the living God.

Whether, then, we understand wicked human beings or unclean spirits to be designated by the name Jews, it is certainly evident that both rejoice with equal desire over the affliction of the good. Hence the same head of the wicked girds himself all the more readily to persecute the good, the more he perceives that by this he satisfies the desires of his own followers.

When a righteous person has been put to death in the flesh, the wicked party rejoices, because one has been removed from their midst who, under the shadow of his protection, defended many from the heat of malice. When a righteous person has fallen into the death of sin, the wicked rejoice all the more, because the one who has fallen seemed, by the merit of his life, to stand at a higher elevation.

But just as above, while reverently embracing the martyrdom of blessed James according to the historical account, we showed how it can be understood according to its inward meaning, so now, preserving the historical text, let us show how the arrest of blessed Peter can be understood according to the same meaning.

The very meaning of the name of the one who was arrested opens the way for us to investigate the mystery of his arrest. As nearly all of us know, Peter received his name from “rock” (*petra*). Whom, then, does this name designate except those who seem, through steadfastness of mind, to stand firmly upon the solidity of virtues? Against such people the enemy fights with all the greater ferocity, because he grieves and recognizes that through them others too are strengthened in virtue.

And because perhaps he is not strong enough to shake their firmness of mind by the first attack of temptation, he comes upon them repeatedly, like water, and breaks their hard steadfastness. For, as a certain poet says:

> “The drop hollows the stone, not by force but by falling often.”

(Ovid, *De Ponto*, Book IV.)

Divine Scripture also testifies to this: “The waters hollow out stones, and by their overflowing the earth is gradually consumed” (Job 14:19).

When, therefore, the devil leads a strong man into the snare of sin, Herod stretches out his hands, as though to arrest Peter. Here, too, the precise wording deserves our closest attention. Above, when he wished to afflict some of those belonging to the Church, he “stretched out his hands”; now, in order to arrest Peter, he “proceeded to” or “applied” them.

We should therefore know that each person distances himself less from the devil the less closely he approaches the summit of perfection. Thus, when the devil drags one of such people into guilt, he stretches out his hands, as it were, beside himself, because he draws back to himself one who had not gone far away. But when he attempts and fails to deceive someone strong and perfect in virtue, he has, so to speak, tightly clasped hands with which to arrest Peter. He applies his hands to arrest Peter because, in order to deceive anyone strong, he weaves multiple snares of deception.

No art of the crafty tempter weakens the strength of the heart so quickly as when a person arrogates to himself the power of his own strength and rejoices in private exultation. Immediately abandoned by the heavenly Protector, he does not long remain at the summit of virtue, because thereafter he is disturbed by the wind of elation. The adversary catches him as he falls from on high, dragging him, deprived of heavenly assistance, through whatever precipices of vice he can.

Herod therefore arrests Peter with hands, as it were, already applied, when he again entangles with extended snares of fraud the one who, walking along the path of virtues, had gone far away from him. If an example is sought to support this, there is no need to go farther afield. Peter himself, whose history we are examining through figurative interpretation, partly experienced in his own person what we are saying.

For the flesh of Peter was arrested by the historical Herod, while his soul had earlier been bound three times by the typological Herod in the snare of the threefold denial, like a twisted rope. Certainly, he already possessed much evidence of his strength and firmness: he had already confessed Christ as the Son of the living God; he had already heard the Truth pronounce him blessed; he had already received the surname Peter from the solidity of the unshatterable rock; he had already received the keys of the heavenly kingdom. Yet after so many and such great gifts of divine generosity, when the hour of the Lord’s passion arrived, because he presumed somewhat too greatly upon his own firmness, he was left to himself and immediately discovered what sort of man he was.

He would indeed have perished forever unless the merciful Jesus had looked upon him with the gaze of his mercy; by looking, softened him; by softening him, moved him to bitter tears; and by moving him to tears, forgiven the crime he had committed.

By this example we who are weak are clearly instructed to keep vigilant watch over ourselves. Our mind, even when endowed with the highest virtues, must always humble itself; it must always recognize with trembling that what it is does not come from itself. Otherwise, if it is carried beyond itself by the breeze of presumption, the higher it has raised itself, the more grievously it will be dashed down.

## IV. It follows: “Now the days of Unleavened Bread were at hand.”

According to the literal sense, it is clear that the apostle was arrested by Herod during the week of the Jewish Passover. The seven days following the fourteenth day of the first month, on which the lamb was sacrificed toward evening, were properly called the days of Unleavened Bread. Yet the authority of the Evangelists customarily uses “Passover” for “Unleavened Bread” and “Unleavened Bread” for “Passover,” as is readily recognized by anyone who carefully reviews their books.

We have said these few things according to the historical sense; now let us consider the inner meaning of this statement. He says: “Now the days of Unleavened Bread were at hand.” We understand the days of Unleavened Bread as the entire period extending from the coming of our Savior to the end of the world. During this time that true “Lamb who takes away the sins of the world” is sacrificed, and through his blood the faithful people are delivered from the lordship of sin.

Hence Paul also says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us celebrate, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

I did not therefore assert without purpose that the apostle’s arrest—which signifies the fall of a strong man—took place during the days of Unleavened Bread. Rather, I was signifying that although the devil’s envy against human beings began to blaze from the very beginning of human creation, he rages all the more bitterly from the time of the Lord’s incarnation, because he senses that the end of his rage is now very near.

Hence it is written: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time” (Revelation 12:12). By the names “earth” and “sea” are signified all who are carnal, because they attend only to earthly things and, like waves, leap over one another in pride. To these the devil, having great wrath, descends because, abandoning the hearts of the elect, he rests in the hearts of the reprobate. Since he considers that he can no longer return to blessedness, he gathers companions for himself—as a consolation for his own ruin—with whom he may have woe for all eternity.

## V. It follows: “When he had arrested him, he put him in prison.”

Herod puts the arrested Peter in prison when the ancient enemy, having imprisoned a righteous person through a deadly sin, hides him in the recesses of a sinful conscience. A sinful conscience is rightly called a prison, because there the inner human being is both bound by the fetters of sins and, blinded by inward night, prevented from seeing the Sun of righteousness.

## VI. It follows: “Handing him over to be guarded by four squads of soldiers.”

Among all the statements in this reading, this one is the more difficult to penetrate. Perhaps it therefore seems so hard to understand because it signifies something grave. May the Lord deign to supply us with his grace, so that we may speak about it in such a way that, if anyone among us is still held fast in the enemy’s bonds, he may hear from these squads as much as is useful; hearing, understand; understanding, grieve; grieving, groan; groaning, shudder at having been handed over to such executioners; and, shuddering, take care to escape.

Each squad has four soldiers under it. Four squads, together with the soldiers subject to them, therefore amount to twenty soldiers. Since this number is formed from five and ten—for four times five and twice ten are both twenty—it can signify the whole multiplicity of vices committed against the commandments of the Decalogue through the five bodily senses.

Perhaps, however, we are required to distinguish these squads individually, together with the attendants who serve under them. This is somewhat laborious, but we shall try to investigate it by a twofold method. In order that we may speak more openly about these squads according to the inward meaning, we must first construct them separately and then assign to each its soldiers, as reason dictates.

Let us suppose someone so completely deprived by the devil of every light of reason that, like a fool, he can say in his heart, “There is no God.” We can plainly declare of him that, through his folly, he has been delivered into the prison of unbelief. Since he does not at all believe that the goods or evils of another life exist, he directs all his concern toward seeking the goods of the present life and avoiding its evils.

Thus it happens that the devil imposes upon his soul—already shut in the prison of unbelief—four modes of disturbance, which keep it closed under harsh guard so that it cannot escape. These disturbances succeed one another in the soul of the wise person also, according to the variety of circumstances. But in the soul of the fool they are disturbances, because through them the fool is disturbed. In the soul of the wise they are called not so much disturbances as affections, because they are governed by the reason of wisdom so that they do not disturb.

The first mode of disturbance is desire; the second, fear; the third, grief; the fourth, joy. Let no one be troubled because we have not placed these modes of disturbance in the order in which the secular poet arranged them. We judge the authority of our own Scripture superior, and in it we read: “The desire for money is the root of all evils.”

Nor did those who are counted among the sages of the world arrange them in their books in the same order or call them by the same names. One of them, when discussing disembodied souls according to his own opinion, said:

> “Hence they fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice, and so forth.”

Another, whose works are read in the schools of the world, arranged them thus:

> “Drive away joys;  
> Drive away fear; and banish hope, nor let grief be present.”

Observe that what the first placed last, the second placed first; what the first placed first, the second placed second; and what the first placed second, the second, changing its position and name, placed third. Grief, which is placed fourth here, is placed third there.

It is therefore established that the fool is confined and guarded in the prison of unbelief by these four disturbances, as though by four squads. In the same passage the poet also mentioned the prison itself, saying:

> “Hence they fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice, and do not look upon the breezes,  
> Shut away in darkness and a blind prison.”

On the authority of our Scripture, then, we place desire as the first mode of disturbance, as the first squad; fear in second place; grief in third; and joy in fourth. We shall show below why joy is counted among the disturbances of the mind.

These, then, are the four squads to which the devil entrusts his captive for guarding, after first introducing him into the prison of unbelief through the door of folly. As we have said, because he believes nothing beyond what he sees with bodily eyes, empty of inward goods he slips wholly into outward things. Desire first surrounds him, so that he may possess; fear comes second, lest he lose; grief third, if he has lost; and joy fourth, if he has recovered.

Each of these squads also has its own soldiers for guarding the devil’s captive. The vices that arise, as though originally, from each disturbance are the soldiers assigned to each squad as auxiliaries for guarding the sinner.

Under the first squad, which we have called desire, the first soldier is acquisitiveness, the second accumulation, the third lack of compassion, and the fourth pleasure. Acquisitiveness rightly follows desire, because each person strives to retain more tightly what has been acquired the more he remembers having labored heavily to acquire it.

Accumulation follows acquisitiveness because, while he promises himself long stretches of life, he works intensely to increase through daily interest what has already been gained. When it happens that his possessions multiply according to his desire, his outward resources expand, but inwardly he becomes more constricted.

Hence lack of compassion is introduced in third place, because he grows more cruelly hardened toward his needy neighbor the more he believes that what he possesses can suffice for himself alone. Yet amid all this he considers that he has labored so arduously to gather his possessions in vain if he relieves his needy neighbor of their use in such a way that he himself is also deprived of their enjoyment.

Therefore, after this, because he has thrown himself entirely into the wantonness of pleasure, pleasure advances fourth in the rank of his fellow soldiers. Through it he is so dissolved in the enticements of the flesh that the saying of those devoted to pleasure rightly applies to him:

> “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die”;  
> “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither”;  
> “Let us seek everywhere signs of joy”;  
> “Let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through.”

But while the wretched soul is thus dissolved in its pleasure, it begins to fear intensely lest what delights it so greatly should suddenly be taken away. Hence fear, with its attendants, is appropriately placed as the second squad. Its first soldier is anxiety, its second instability, its third pretense, and its fourth irrationality. We have arranged these in vain unless we also explain why they have been ordered in this way.

Anxiety follows fear in the first rank because, while the mind of one who fears trembles at losing something it embraces intensely, an immeasurable variety of suspicions disturbs it. While these suspicions propose future losses to the trembling mind, they inflict upon it through thought everything that they imagine could be inflicted.

Instability accompanies anxiety. When the person weighs the things he fears suffering and considers them intolerable, he becomes effeminate through cowardice and strengthens himself with no virtue of endurance. When he foresees that he cannot withstand such dangers by the strength of virtue, he makes every effort to see whether he can at least avoid them through pretense.

Accordingly, pretense is counted after instability, because the mind shaken by fear flees from the field of confidence and hides in the corner of duplicity. After pretense, irrationality is placed, because the mind has been surrounded by so dense a cloud of disturbances precisely because, having lost the counsel proper to human beings, it does not compose itself by any moderation of reason.

Now grief, which we have called the third squad, is brought in with its company to guard the captive. Its first attendant is envy, its second bitterness, its third outcry, and its fourth cruelty.

Envy first follows grief, because when one person obtains what another has lost, the loser is inflamed against the one who has obtained it by the envy of jealousy. Bitterness follows envy, because the mind of the envious person becomes outwardly more bitter toward everyone the more, as envy burns through its inward roots, the sap of any goodness is drained away.

Outcry is also appropriately counted after bitterness, because when the embittered mind can no longer endure its own flames within, it pours them out externally with clamorous shouting. It hurls them all the higher the more dearly it loved what has been lost.

Cruelty is named as the fourth attendant in this company because the mind exasperated by grief, having long nourished its grief under the cover of envy, when it is not fully satisfied by giving voice to it through cries, eagerly strives to join acts of cruelty to cruel words. This cruelty expands through the immensity of grief until it turns the punishments of grief back upon the very person who grieves.

It often happens that people disturbed by the loss either of possessions or of loved ones, because they have neglected to soothe the wound of their grief with the medicine of reason, fall into such waves of disturbance that they either lose their common sense or cruelly lay hands upon themselves. Observe how far grief rages through its attendants: as though it were not enough to disturb the soul’s peace, it strives to drive the soul even from the dwelling place of the body.

The fourth squad remains, which the ancients called joy. It is appropriately placed after grief because, just as grief arises from something taken away, so joy arises from something acquired. But we must consider why the authority of our predecessors counted joy among those disturbances that ordinarily turn the mind away from its proper state, when the apostle Paul counted it among the fruits of righteousness, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace, and so forth.”

We should therefore understand that when joy is used in a bad sense, it is not properly but abusively so called. Thus in Isaiah (Isaiah 48:22), where our translation has, “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord,” another translation has, “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord.”

Nevertheless, when the Apostle was speaking about charity, he used this word abusively when he said, “It does not rejoice over iniquity.” Certainly, whoever rejoices over iniquity should be said not to *rejoice* (*gaudere*) but rather to exult wildly (*gestire*). For *gaudere*, “to rejoice,” belongs only to human beings, whereas *gestire*, “to exult,” belongs not only to human beings but also to irrational animals. Thus puppies are said to *gestire* when they seem to display their inward liveliness through movements of the tail or of other limbs.

In this passage, therefore, when joy is counted among the disturbances of the mind, what is to be understood is not joy properly speaking, but rather a kind of irrational exuberance. Through immoderate gladness it lifts the mind from the weight of seriousness, and it displays this same lightness through outward signs.

Since inward lightness is revealed through outwardly displayed dissolution, that dissolution is not unfittingly assigned as the first soldier of this fourth squad. When the mind does not take care to restrain inwardly conceived gladness with the bridle of seriousness, its outward movement reveals what sort of agitation lies hidden within. Through this revelation, considerable harm is inflicted upon it, because whatever remains visible in outward appearances is drawn from the springs of inward excess. The mind is therefore judged more worthless by everyone the more clearly it is found to lack the value of seriousness in its inner treasury.

The second soldier in this final line is called boasting. When the limbs are excessively dissolved through disorderly movements, the tongue too, breaking the reins of silence, is released into the unrestrained words of boasting.

Lying is counted as the third soldier, because someone who speaks boastfully about himself at length cannot fail to insert some things about which he lies. Pride follows lying and supplies material for all the vices mentioned above; in the end, it is overcome.

For just as it is written, “The desire for money is the root of all evils,” so it is also written, “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” These two statements would be greatly at odds with one another unless in some way they were one.
