But because one always accompanies the other by an indivisible progression, it is rightly asserted both that desire is the root of all evils and that pride is the beginning of every sin.

Unless the covetous person swelled up through pride, he would never hasten to blind others with an abundance of riches. And unless the proud person were driven on by the goads of desire, he would not be swept with such force toward the summit of singular power.

## VII.

But because we have treated the statement that the apostle was arrested and handed over to the squads in one way, I wish to explain it according to another meaning as well, leaving both interpretations to the judgment of anyone who may perhaps deign to read this. We who have now been enlightened by divine grace are no longer fittingly described by what the fool said in his heart: “There is no God.” And because we have despised the whole world, perhaps desire for possession no longer inflames us, fear of losing no longer troubles us, grief over what has been lost no longer crushes us, and joy over what has been recovered no longer exalts us.

Yet there are other vices that pursue us even as we flee from the world. They press upon us all the more persistently because they find in ourselves the material for their persistence. Let us therefore take one of these and, according to its meaning, discuss the four squads.

Let us suppose someone who, through the softness of his pleasure, has fallen into the filth of lust. The devil has undoubtedly arrested him, because, taking away the freedom of chastity, he has made him captive in the servitude of desire. But the arrested sinner is delivered over to prison if, after committing the crime, he hides in the recesses of his conscience.

Nor is it enough for the cruel adversary to condemn his captive to the darkness of prison; he also appoints guards over him so that he cannot escape. For the sinner whom the devil has taken captive through the crime he has committed sometimes decides to escape from his captivity through the opening of confession. But the guards appointed to him hold back the one who wishes to leave, because the obstacles of difficulty that the devil places in his way delay him so that he cannot escape.

Preserving, then, the truth of the historical account, the squads by which Peter is shut up and guarded in prison are the very obstacles of difficulty by which someone who has decided to confess his sins is prevented from confession. To make these squads more evident, it is necessary to name them and assign to each its individual soldiers.

But just as we have seen the others in their proper order, it remains now to see by what name the first is classified and by what company it is accompanied. Let the first squad, then, be called the desire to sin. Under it let its soldiers be: first, remembrance of past pleasure; second, excuse based on weakness; third, imitation of wickedness; fourth, reasoning from one’s constitution.

The desire to sin is rightly placed first of all in the order of the squads. For the one shut up in the prison of lust would hasten to leave it more quickly if he were not still pleased to sin again. But because he still desires to sin, he cannot attack through confession what he loves.

Under this first squad, the first soldier, as we have said, is remembrance of past pleasure. It is joined to its squad by a bond, both to keep watch with it over the sinner and to supply him with material for sinning again. This remembrance compels the sinner to sin again all the more forcefully the more vividly it brings before him the pleasures he experienced when he sinned.

But if remembrance of past pleasure urges the sinner to repeat his sin, why is it not placed before the desire to sin in this company? If, as we have said, it supplies the desire with the material for existing, it seems to be something greater than the desire itself.

We should know, however, that having the desire to sin is something greater than having the remembrance of sin. The former is such a vice that it can in no way be a virtue; the latter is now counted among vices in such a way that it is sometimes also counted among virtues. For the same remembrance that reminds a sinner who wishes to sin to sin again reminds a sinner who grieves that he has sinned to weep more deeply.

Or remembrance of past pleasure is placed after the desire to sin for this reason: we properly speak of remembering things that we experienced previously in some way, whereas we can desire even things of which we have no experience at all. Thus remembrance now represents to us the pleasures of the sins we have committed, while the desire to sin also drags us toward those things of which we have no knowledge through experience. Since the desire is recognized as having greater force, it was worthy to be placed first in this company.

Under it, as the second soldier, serves excuse based on weakness. Sometimes, when a sinner has committed a crime and is himself condemned by what he has done, this excuse suddenly intervenes and consoles him, as though with gentle speech. It suggests to him that it is no wonder if he consents to sin, since the very weakness of the flesh drives him toward sin.

The third soldier is called imitation of wickedness. A perverse mind that strives to cover its own guilt with the veil of its weakness also sometimes attempts to defend it by the example of another’s iniquity. By doing what deserves condemnation, it considers itself somehow less condemnable because it finds many companions in iniquity.

In the fourth rank enters the fourth soldier, called reasoning from one’s constitution. Through this reasoning the reprobate mind often leaps into such perversity that, by reasoning, it defends its guilt. It asserts that if God had not wished the two sexes to be joined, he would not have placed in the human body members suited to this act.

What, then, could be more perverse than this fourth attendant, through whom the sinner is so confined in inner darkness that he suspects the author of all righteousness of being the author of his own unrighteousness?

Another squad follows this first one. It is called shame of confession, second in order but not in cruelty. For why does the sinner hide himself in the recesses of conscience except because he is ashamed to confess what he has done?

Under this second squad serve: first, minimization of guilt; second, expectation of a long life; third, presumption of pardon; fourth, the torpor of negligence.

Minimization of guilt keeps the first watch in this company. By persuading the sinner that what has been done is either nothing or very little, it strokes with the hand of harmful consolation the mind that had already begun to grieve in a healing way. Thus, while it lessens the weight of sin in the sinner’s judgment, it ensures that the weight of judgment will at some time press upon him intolerably.

In the place of the second soldier is counted expectation of a long life, because while the mind promises itself a long span of life, it leaves the prison of its sin through the door of confession later than it ought.

This thought also sometimes nourishes the delay of confession: whenever one converts, one presumes that pardon will be granted. As it is written: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he will be saved.” Because, therefore, the sinner—flattering himself more than is right concerning divine mercy—promises himself that he will merit pardon whenever he returns, the presumption of pardon, through which confession is delayed, is not unjustly counted as the third soldier.

The fourth soldier is the torpor of negligence. While the sinner, carnally concerned for his shame, avoids confessing; while, harmfully flattering himself, he minimizes the weight of his sin; while, presuming upon divine patience, he refuses to convert, the final day suddenly overtakes him, dissolved in the torpor of negligence.

But why does a person so gently pat himself while in guilt? Why does he cover it with so many veils? Because, loving himself with private love, he does not adopt the rule of righteousness by which he should love himself.

Hence private love itself, by which a person is turned away from contemplation of rectitude, is here counted in place of the third quaternion [Col. 0290A]. In its company the first soldier is desire for reputation, the second shame at abasement, the third severity of repentance, and the fourth fear of perseverance.

In the battle line of this quaternion, desire for reputation serves first. It is joined to its commander’s aid in such a way that it is also generated by him. For whoever loves himself with private love strives with all his might to extend the reputation of his name through favorable renown. This extension of reputation obstructs the face of confession, because it is difficult—indeed impossible—for anyone still wishing to appear glorious in the estimation of others to expose his faults purely in confession.

From this soldier another is born, called shame at abasement, [Col. 0290B] because each person humbles himself in confession concerning his offenses all the more slowly the more he is pleased by the elevation of his place or rank. While he is ashamed outwardly to appear abased, he does not fear being held shameful in the sight of the inner Judge; and he fears more to appear despised among his companions than to be sent by the just Arbiter outside the company of the humble. Therefore the Psalmist instructs us by his example, saying: “I chose to be abased in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

Yet in this connection it must be understood that often neither desire for reputation nor shame at abasement holds the sinner back from confession, but rather the severity of repentance and fear of perseverance. These two are therefore counted as the two remaining soldiers, since they themselves greatly hinder the captive from being freed [the transmitted reading *ematur* is uncertain]. One arises from love of the flesh, the other from the adversary’s instigation.

The severity of repentance that frightens the sinner away from confession arises from love of the flesh. For when he silently considers within himself how much will be imposed upon him for satisfaction for his crime if he confesses, he spares the tenderness of his flesh and is held back from confession. Fear of perseverance, however, is generated by the adversary’s instigation. The adversary makes the sinner suspicious of perseverance for this reason: that he may always keep him shut up in iniquity—so that he never dares to begin a good work, fearing that he may not be able to persevere in what he has begun.

The fourth quaternion, called the depth of evils, [Col. 0290D] keeps watch last of all, so that it may drag what has been entrusted to it from the depth of wickedness into the depth of punishment. It too has four attendants assigned to guard the captive: the first is contempt, the second hardness of heart, the third impenitence, and the fourth blindness of mind.

From the depth of evils contempt first arises before them, because, as it is written: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises.” Hardness of heart is counted as the second soldier, because when the sinner, considering the enormity of his evils, pretends that he can no longer merit forgiveness, he runs through the whole field of wickedness with a mind hardened.

Hardness of heart is followed by impenitence as the third. Through it the sinner, despising the riches of divine patience, heaps sins upon sins and, according to the Apostle, stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. In place of the fourth soldier is taken blindness of mind. For it belongs to the rule of divine rectitude that the sinner who, by seeing and despising, is often plunged into guilt should at some point stumble into it even without seeing; and that he who previously lost the ability to live well through an impenitent heart should afterward lose even the ability to know well through a heart divinely blinded.

Behold into what savage custody he thrusts himself who, consenting to the enemy’s persuasions, softly yields to harmful pleasure! Behold how he makes himself no longer his own master who, by sinning, hands himself over to Satan’s power! Behold to how many and how savage guards is entrusted everyone who, concealing himself in the hiding places of his conscience, refuses to confess!

We must therefore take the greatest care never to allow wrongful pleasure to pass into consent and, advancing as far as the desire to sin, to bind us already as captives in Satan’s snares. But if we are already held captive through our softness, let us take every precaution not to be thrust back into prison. Rather, let us burn with the fervor of repentance and quickly cast off the snares of Satan that bind us, lest, if we delay too long, the path forward become all the more difficult to open as the manifold custody surrounds us on every side. But now that Peter has been thrust into prison and assigned to the quaternions, let us see what follows.

### VIII. “Desiring to bring him forth to the people after Passover.”

Behold for what purpose the devil guards his captive so carefully; behold why he consigns him to prison; behold why he assigns him so many and such great officers: namely, that he may bring him forth to the people for a spectacle after Passover.

Since Passover is called a passage, this word “passage” appropriately signifies each person’s departure from this life. We all pass through death, but it matters whether through death we pass to death or through death to life. Those pass through death to death for whom, after the death of the flesh, eternal destruction remains. Those pass through death to life for whom, after the dissolution of the body, eternal joys follow.

The devil therefore guards his captive so carefully in order to bring him forth to the people for a spectacle after Passover, because he holds the sinner in sin until death for this purpose: that, when he passes from this life, he may send him from one prison into another—from the prison of a darkened conscience into the prison of punitive Gehenna.

If we apply this captivity specifically to one who, after assuming the religious habit, falls into mortal sin, we will see that the words “to bring him forth to the people” were not added without purpose. Certainly, at that final judgment not only human beings but also good and evil angels will be brought forth. Since we know that human beings and good and evil angels will all be present at that final judgment, why is the religious person who persists to the end in the crime he has committed said to be brought forth for a spectacle to the people alone?

It seems, then, that the phrase “to bring him forth to the people” has been added to our disgrace, since we have renounced the world. For since *populus*—“people”—is derived from *populare*, and *populare* means “to lay waste,” it will certainly be a great disgrace for us who appear religious if, after passing from this life, we too are brought forth for a spectacle of derision to those who, running through the broad roads of pleasures, lay waste to their lives every day.

### IX. “And Peter was kept in prison, but prayer was made without ceasing by the Church to God for him.”

When one who is held captive by the devil either does not wish, or is unable, to get out by himself, it belongs to holy Mother Church’s piety to implore from the Lord the effect of his release. Both things must necessarily be requested from the Lord, because the sinner, shut up in the prison of sin, sometimes grows hardened through such great insensibility and is overshadowed by such great darkness that he neither feels the squalor of his prison nor sees the chains by which he is bound. Thus, the less he feels the calamity by which he is punished, the less he desires to be freed from it.

Sometimes, however, he sees his misery and longs to be rescued from it, but cannot get out because the manifold custody of the quaternions surrounds him. Yet whether he is held in prison willingly or unwillingly, it is fitting that Mother Church recognize the son whom she has begotten and, by praying for him, direct toward him the compassion of a mother’s heart.

The force with which this must be done is made clear by the wording that follows. For when it was said, “Prayer was made,” the words “without ceasing” were added, because we obtain what we ask when no difficulty in obtaining it makes us weary of prayer. Thus, even according to the literal sense, [Col. 0292C] how much the prayers benefited blessed Peter is disclosed when the text continues:

### X. “And when Herod was about to bring him forth, in that same night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains.”

If we examine somewhat more carefully, according to the literal sense, the sequence of the Apostle’s liberation, we are clearly instructed, according to the inner sense, how much the sinner owes to divine mercy.

What does it indicate that the Apostle is said to have been freed from prison when he was already about to be brought forth for a spectacle to the people, unless that divine compassion often frees the sinner from his captivity precisely when it is already near at hand that the devil will lead him, brought forth from the body, to eternal derision?

“In that same night,” he says, “Peter was sleeping.” Peter, having been seized, sleeps in the night when a strong man, having fallen into sin, closes the eyes of his mind to knowledge of himself. The night in which he sleeps is ignorance. For if he were not ignorant of himself and of what was happening around him, he would certainly open his eyes to self-examination; opening them, he would see his danger; seeing, he would feel it; feeling, he would grieve; grieving, he would groan; and groaning, he would hasten to escape. But seized Peter sleeps because he does not attend to what threatens him.

He sleeps between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Again we are compelled to investigate who these two soldiers are who surround the sleeping Peter on either side, and what the chains are that bind his hands.

Above we heard that the Apostle, sent into prison, was assigned to the custody of four quaternions; and we also showed how this may be understood specifically. But when it is said that he slept between two soldiers, it is understood that soldiers clung to him on his right and left sides. In ordinary speech, we take as “right” whatever helps us, and as “left” whatever opposes us.

Let the soldier standing at his right side therefore be the presumption of forgiveness, which above we placed as the third soldier under the second quaternion. By promising the sinner forgiveness whenever he returns, it makes him sleep securely beside it. This soldier therefore watches the sleeper’s right side, because it promises what seems to help the sinner, relaxed in the sleep of negligence, toward presumption of forgiveness.

Let the soldier standing at his left side be shame at abasement, assigned above as the second soldier to the third quaternion. Through this shame at abasement, when the sinner imagines that he will suffer some adversity, he chooses rather to rest inwardly in whatever kind of quiet he can find than to go outside and endure the shame of abasement.

The two chains with which the sleeper is bound are habit and despair, by which he is prevented from doing anything good. The chain of evil habit binds the sinner’s hands, because often, while he strives to extend himself toward a good work, he is held back by the very sins he has been accustomed to commit. The chain of despair also binds his hands, because he becomes slower for every good work insofar as he suspects that nothing good he may do can any longer benefit him.

### XI. “And guards before the door were guarding the prison.”

If we take the prison door as access to confession, the guards keeping watch before the door are those obstacles of difficulty that we already expressly named above in the description of the second quaternion. Yet it is worth lingering here briefly and expressing the misery of this captive.

Behold: because he consents to the enemy’s flattering, he has been savagely seized by that same enemy. Behold: because he delayed confessing, he has been thrust into prison! Behold: now that he has been thrust inside, the manifold custody of the quaternions is imposed upon him from outside. Behold: even within the prison itself he is bound with chains and watched by soldiers! When, then, will one escape whom such manifold custody surrounds within and without?

But where human misery is greater, there divine mercy usually shines more brightly. For the text continues:

### XII. “And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside him, and a light shone in the dwelling.”

I see that what is said—“And behold”—must be marked with the greatest care. We customarily say “behold” when we show that something has suddenly occurred beyond expectation. Hence, through the words “and behold,” sudden and inspired assistance is indicated. This often frees the captive from his captivity precisely when he himself has already despaired of being able to escape.

But let us now see who this angel is through whom the sinner is led out of his prison. He is certainly the one of whom the Prophet says: “The priest’s lips guard knowledge, and people seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). Since *angelus* is Greek and is called *nuntius* (“messenger”) in Latin, the one who announces the law is rightly called an angel.

The lips of the priest therefore guard knowledge, because the person who shows the sacred rule of leadership to the people by reading it also guards what he knows through knowledge by living it. They seek the law from his mouth because a subject hears his superior with all the greater reverence when he understands that the superior speaks not from presumption but from the certainty of knowledge. He is rightly called an angel of the Lord because, by announcing the Lord’s law, he strives for the increase of that Lord’s gains, not for his own favor.

He would no longer properly be the Lord’s angel but his own if he spoke in order that, through his voice, the Lord’s army might not grow but that he himself might appear learned and wise. Since, however, through everything he says he chiefly intends that his Lord’s army should increase, he is called the angel of the Lord of hosts.

Concerning this angel it must be carefully noted that he is said not simply to have stood but to have stood beside him. For *astare* properly means, as it were, “to stand near.” The preacher who announces the Lord’s law indeed stands before his hearer, but by no means stands beside him, when he exhorts rightly according to the rule of faith while the hearer embraces nothing of what he hears with the arm of love.

The preacher is therefore very far from the one to whom he preaches when he cannot draw near to his heart through preaching. Thus the angel does not illumine the dwelling of such a prison, because, while the sinner does not care to hear obediently what he hears, the light of holy preaching does not drive away the darkness of his conscience.

But when the angel stands beside him, the dwelling of the prison is illumined, because when holy preaching is received by an obedient heart, it makes that heart all the more clear the more closely the heart senses itself drawn near through obedience. Then the angel not only stands but stands beside him, because the voice of preaching not only resounds outwardly but also stands inwardly beside the contrite heart.

Yet the statement that the angel stood beside Peter in the prison may also signify something else. Since standing belongs to one who labors or fights, what is signified by the standing angel except the labor of repentance? The angel who is about to lead Peter out of prison therefore stands beside him, because the preacher summons the sinner to a great contest when he invites him to engage the devil through the labor of repentance.

In this contest he is also compelled to fight against himself, when he struggles against the pleasures of the sins he remembers having committed. For if there were no labor in the state of repentance, the Psalmist certainly would not have said: “I have labored in my groaning” (Psalm 6:7). The sinner labors in his groaning when, through the grief of repentance, he chastises himself for the evils he has committed.

But he labors more vigorously for the contest of this labor when, through the voice of preaching, the suffering of the Redeemer is recalled to him. Hence, appropriately, concerning the angel who bears the figure of the preacher, the text adds:

### XIII. “And striking Peter’s side, he awakened him, saying: Rise quickly. And the chains fell from his hands.”

As has already been said before us, the striking of the side signifies the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. Since, when the Redeemer’s side was opened, blood and water flowed forth—one for the price, the other for cleansing—both are rightly recalled to the converted sinner’s memory, so that, considering the dignity of the price paid for him, he may disdain to sin any further and, having been defiled after his cleansing, may be baptized again in the springs of repentance.

Or certainly, it is necessary for every penitent to depict before the eyes of his mind the anguish of the Lord’s Passion so that, following the example of the Lord, he may also prepare his own spirit to endure suffering. Hence blessed Peter himself admonishes us, saying: “Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought.”

It is as though he were saying openly: You who are sinners must shape your spirit for endurance all the more because you recognize that the one who committed no sin suffered such things. Consider, then, what and how much the Redeemer endured in his flesh for you, and only then arm yourselves through contemplation for the same patience.

Peter, however, is awakened when he is struck on the side, because the sinner is roused from the sleep of his inertia through remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. Once awakened, he is commanded to rise quickly, so that he who until then lay prostrate on the bed of iniquity may now, humbled through grace, abandon the evils he has committed.

It must be noted here that he is commanded not merely to rise but to rise quickly, because there are some who, even after the illumination of grace, sluggishly carry out the good they see through understanding. But when one rises quickly, the chains fall from his hands, because when he seizes with spiritual fervor the good he has recognized, whatever might have hindered him quickly disappears.

Above we said that the chains are evil habit and despair. Both fall quickly from the hands of the one who rises, because when, after hearing the preaching, the sinner rises without delay from the bed of his torpor, neither the habit of sinning can drag him back into sin nor despair deter him from hoping for forgiveness.

### XIV. “Then the angel said to him: Gird yourself and put on your sandals. And he did so.”

Here too, according to the literal sense, we are instructed in the virtue of discretion. To temper the cold of the night somewhat, Peter loosened his belt and let the garment with which he was clothed hang around his feet. He thus provides an example for us who are weak: when we are afflicted by human harshness or burdened by bodily weakness, we may relax something of the strictness of our commitment, so that, while we accommodate the body’s weakness in small matters, we may recover greater strength from it for exercising the contest of faith.

According to the inner understanding, however, the preacher commands the sinner to gird himself when he exhorts him to restrain the looseness of lust with the belt of chastity. The teacher of chastity girded his disciples with this belt when he said: “Let your loins be girded.”

Peter himself also admonishes us concerning this belt, saying: “Gird up the loins of your mind.”

But since a preacher teaches more appropriately when he forms his hearer through the sayings and examples of the ancients, the angel rightly commanded Peter not only to gird himself but also to put on sandals. For what is signified by the sandals with which the legs are protected except the sayings and examples of the Fathers? They guard us from the wound of sin and, warming us and kindling us toward the love of God, set us ablaze.

We put on our sandals when, from the sayings and examples of the saints, we defend the steps of our works against the wound of sin and, warmed by imitation of them, hasten with ardent desire toward our heavenly homeland.

Nor should it disturb us that the sandals are called “ours,” belonging to the Church. The sayings and examples of the Fathers are theirs, because they were displayed through them; and they are ours, because they were left to us for imitation.

It must be understood that at this point the Greek codex has not *caligas* (“boots”), but *sandalia*, which are called *soleae* in Latin. This is a type of footwear that completely covers the lower part of the foot while displaying the upper part uncovered. The Apostles used this kind of footwear, as is shown here; and bishops today use it, not without a definite symbolic reason.

The part of this footwear that is dragged along the ground signifies care for temporal matters, through which earthly assistance is supplied to subjects by their superiors. The upper part, which displays part of the foot uncovered, signifies contemplation of heavenly things, through which the superior himself is nourished by divine revelations and imparts spiritual nourishment to those entrusted to him.

The angel commanded Peter to put on these sandals because it is very fitting that one for whose liberation the Lord sends his angel should eventually attain such perfection that he is sufficient for his neighbors in both kinds of necessity.

If, however, the words “Gird yourself and put on your sandals” are referred specifically to ecclesiastical teachers, to whom it is also said, “Let your loins be girded,” and, “With your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace,” we must carefully note that he is commanded to gird himself first and to put on his sandals afterward. For one who first puts shoes on his feet for evangelizing before tightening his loins with the belt of chastity does not preserve the proper order in his conduct.

Let him first be girded and afterward put on his sandals, so that he may first restrain within himself the looseness of lust by the firmness of chastity and then, already at peace within himself, walk with feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace.

Preachers are commanded to have their feet shod so that they may show that they must always be ready to preach. A preacher is, as it were, unshod if he is not always ready to teach. When a subject asks him about some necessary question, such a preacher begins by searching for an answer, when he ought to be answering.

Peter shod the teachers of the Church with this footwear of preaching when he said: “Always ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you.”

A person reaches this perfection when, as he is instructed in the good, he reverently obeys the admonitions of his instructor. Hence Peter’s obedience follows the angel’s command, when the text says: “And he did so.”

Peter does this at the voice of the commanding angel when a hearer obeys his preacher with such devotion that he makes no delay in carrying out what is enjoined upon him. When the preacher sees his hearer carefully fulfilling what he has already learned, he is increasingly prompted to make known to him everything that leads to perfection. Hence the text continues:

### XV. “Then the angel said to him: Put your garment around you and follow me.”

What a garment is for the body, justice is for the soul. A garment covers and warms; justice likewise drives the cold of wickedness from the soul and hides from divine judgment the shameful things that sin has placed within it.

For if wickedness were not cold, the Prophet would certainly not have said under the figure of Judea concerning a reprobate mind: “The cistern makes the water cold; thus she made her wickedness cold.” And again, if justice were not a garment, the Psalmist certainly would not have said: “Let your priests be clothed with justice.”

We are priests of the Lord, since we are members of the supreme Priest and through the mortification of the flesh offer ourselves as a living sacrifice to the Lord. We are more truly clothed with justice when we omit none of the things that must be done.

It must therefore also be noted here that the angel did not say to Peter, “Put on your garment,” but “Put your garment around you.” It is possible for someone to be covered by one kind of garment on one side while appearing uncovered on another. But when we are clothed in such a way that we remain naked on no side, we are not only clothed with a garment but surrounded by it.

Whoever therefore performs certain good works while neglecting others is clothed on one side and naked on the other, because he leaves uncovered that part of himself which he neglected to cover with the veil of justice.

Peter, being led out of prison, is therefore commanded to put his garment around himself, because whoever desires to leave the prison of sins perfectly must surround himself on every side with the garment of justice, omitting none of the things that pertain to him.

But behold: the angel standing beside him has already illumined the prison in which he was held, because the light of holy preaching has shone in the sinner’s conscience. Behold: he has already risen, because he has left behind the bed of sin on which he lay. Behold: he has already girded his loins, because he has restrained the looseness of lust. Behold: he has already put on his sandals, because he has fortified the steps of his holy works with the examples of the Fathers. Behold: he has already put his garment around himself, because he has omitted none of what he has learned.

Who should now be considered imperfect, having made such progress? Yet these things are still not enough for the angel. He still presses on; he still repeats what he knows remains to be done, so that the one whose liberation he has undertaken may either be received as perfectly obedient or, if he neglects to obey, the angel may make himself free from responsibility for his condemnation.

Therefore, after saying, “Put your garment around you,” he immediately added: “And follow me.”

Peter goes after the angel once he has put his garment around him when the converted sinner clings so closely to the footsteps of holy preaching that he does not turn aside from the path of justice through any detour of temporary intention.

Whoever, after completing a good work, glories in himself rather than in the Lord does not follow his angel after putting his garment around him. For one who, through the good he does, intends something other than what he heard from the mouth of his preacher as the one thing to be desired departs far from following his angel.

The angel therefore appropriately admonished Peter to follow, because the divine word, after instructing us in everything that pertains to our salvation, also shows how we must pass beyond the desire for empty glory.

But since the things that the angel commanded Peter to do belong to such great perfection, someone may ask how these instructions of such perfection apply to a sinner still shut up in prison. The question would perhaps be appropriate if we were now dealing with a sinner still sleeping in the prison of his sin, and not rather with one whose prison the angel has already illumined and whom the Lord has already awakened through the spirit of compunction.

Everything said about perfection applies to him all the more truly the more devoutly he girds himself against it through confession. Peter therefore, while still held captive, receives commands of freedom, because the sinner even then learns through the mouth of the preacher what he must do, while he still lies hidden in the recesses of his conscience through some weakness of mind.

But now let him finally break every knot of weakness; let him follow the angel who goes before him; let him show that he has not heard the commands of perfection in vain. What is he still doing in prison, when the Lord has already sent his angel to free him?

### XVI. “And going out, he followed him, and he did not know that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought that he was seeing a vision.”

He had been surrounded by such great custody that he thought he was seeing a vision even when the angel was truly freeing him. In the human mind, hesitation about liberation is often generated by reflection on past tribulation. When a person remembers the magnitude of the dangers through which he has passed, he marvels inwardly, almost doubting, at how he could have escaped.

Hence comes the voice of the blessed martyrs through the Psalmist: “Our soul has passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.” This does not say “perhaps” because they truly doubt their liberation; rather, by the word of hesitation through which they passed, they make known something that also accords well with the mystery of its meaning.

Since we see clearly by day but grope in doubtful vision at night, what is signified by divine vision except manifest truth, and what by nocturnal vision except uncertainty? Those who, with all the darkness of corruption removed, gaze unchangeably upon the brightness of truth are therefore rightly said already to be in the day.

We, who are still held in the blindness of this exile, know in part and prophesy in part, and so we also see in part. Although we already see through faith, we do not yet see by sight. Through this vision of faith we already rejoice in hope over our liberation, yet, being anxious about the hidden disposition of the inner Judge concerning us, we cannot see our liberation clearly.

For, as it is written: “All things are kept uncertain for the future, and a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred.”

Peter therefore, even while following the angel, thinks that he is seeing a vision. Similarly, the converted sinner, although he has already left the prison because he has disclosed his faults, and although he already follows the angel because he practices the good he has learned through the preacher, must nevertheless regard all the stages of his progress as though they were a nocturnal vision. For although he now sees what he is doing, he does not know whether he will persevere in it or how he is judged inwardly.

### XVII. “And passing through the first and second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads to the city, which opened to them of its own accord.”

Above we read that Peter, after being seized, was handed over to four quaternions—that is, to twenty soldiers altogether. It may therefore be understood that those same men who had taken charge of guarding him divided themselves into two guards in order to watch him more carefully. Apart from these, we do not read that other guards were assigned to him.

Since the same men are distinguished into a first and a second guard, let us also divide these same guards according to the inner sense. But let us set aside from this division the two soldiers between whom we showed above that he slept.

With those two excluded, let us see how the others can be divided into a first and a second guard. Let us therefore take the first quaternion, which we called the desire to sin, together with its troop, as the first guard. They are rightly assigned as the first guard, because, as was said above, the sinner refuses to leave his prison for this reason: he delights in sinning again.

Let us assign the second quaternion, which is the shame of confession, together with its soldiers, as the second guard. It too is appropriately placed as the second guard, because the desire to sin first thrusts us into sin, and afterward the shame of confession keeps us in sin.

But because Peter follows the angel, he is held by neither guard. Whoever obediently listens to the preacher of truth neither repeats sin through the desire to sin nor conceals what he has committed through the shame of confession.

When he goes after the angel, he passes through both guards unharmed, because his preacher continually supplies him from the holy Scriptures with weapons by which he may defend himself against the dangers surrounding him.

Lest the desire to sin draw him into repeating sin, the preacher applies to him from Scripture the sentence: “Son, have you sinned? Do not add again, but pray for your former sins, that they may be forgiven you.” And the Apostle says: “For if we sin willfully after receiving knowledge of the truth, there remains no sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:26).

For what is it to sin willfully except to have the will to sin? This will to sin is indicated by the present-tense participle. But for one who is sinning willfully—that is, for one whose will to sin is always present—no sacrifice for sins remains, because the offering of Christ’s body confers no healing upon his sins.

Likewise, lest the sinner hide his sins through shame of confession, the preacher sets before him sentences from Scripture: “My son, do not be ashamed to confess your sins, for there is a shame that leads to sin, and there is a shame that leads to glory.” And again: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy.” And the Psalmist says: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him.”

Here the Apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved.”

When the preacher applies these and similar exhortations to his hearer, what does he do except admonish him to resist both the desire to sin and the shame of confessing—that is, teach him how he must pass through the first and second guards?

But here someone may perhaps object: how is it that, although up to this point we have treated four quaternions, now we seem to treat only two? We must therefore understand that, if we examine the matter closely, those two of which we have spoken also contain two others. And since he expounds Holy Scripture appropriately who prudently anticipates everything that can move the reader, [Col. 0300C] let us show, if we can, how in this first and second guard—which we have constructed from the first and second quaternion—two other quaternions are also included, so that, when those two have been passed, the other two likewise are passed.

For behold, we called the first quaternion the inclination to sin and placed it, together with its soldiers, in the first guard. Its first soldier, as we stated above, is the recollection of past pleasure; the second, the excuse of weakness; the third, the imitation of wickedness; the fourth, the reasoning by which one defends one’s condition. We also named the fourth quaternion the depth of evils. When the sinner has entered this, he becomes contemptuous, hardened, impenitent, and blind. Let us therefore see [Col. 0300D] how these two quaternions and their soldiers contain one another in turn, so that one, together with its soldiers, and the other, together with its own, may be overcome at the same time.

Certainly, because through the inclination to sin the sinner repeats his sin, he descends into the depth of evils; because through the recollection of past pleasure iniquity becomes sweet to him in his heart, he disdains to return from the depth of his evils; because he offers the excuse of weakness as a defense for his faults, he gradually hardens himself against the compassion of divine mercy; because, through imitation of wickedness, he observes the examples of another’s iniquity, he does not care to correct through repentance what he has done; because he tries to protect his guilt by reasoning, he is deprived, by the just judgment of God, of the light of reason that he turns toward evil. Behold, [Col. 0301A] we have set the first and second quaternions, with the soldiers of both, alongside one another, to show how they come together in this first guard. Now let us also show how, through this first guard, the sinner passes under the guidance of the angel.

Thus, when the inclination to sin has been passed, the depth of evils is also passed; for one who has no desire to sin cannot multiply sins by repeating them. When the recollection of past pleasure has been passed, contempt too is passed at the same time; for, while by a praiseworthy forgetfulness he erases former pleasures from his mind, he hastens to return to the one who endured him for so long, having set contempt aside. When the excuse of weakness has been passed, hardness of heart is also passed at the same time; for, once he has withdrawn the veil of excuse and begins to accuse himself, he immediately, [Col. 0301B] through regard for divine grace, melts the hardness of his heart in tears. When the imitation of wickedness has been passed, impenitence too is passed; for he is in no way shaped toward evil by the example of another’s wickedness, while he carefully considers what awaits the penitent. Rather, he runs toward repentance all the more swiftly because, fearing to be discovered in his evils, he is afraid.

When the reasoning by which he defends his condition has been passed, blindness of mind is also passed at the same time; for, while he does not turn the light of reason toward the defense of his fault, he sees more clearly, enlightened by grace, what he ought to follow and what he ought to avoid.

Behold, we have shown how the two quaternions, with their soldiers, come together in the first guard and how they are passed. Now let us show [Col. 0301C] how two others come together in the second guard. Let us therefore compare the second quaternion, which is called the shame of confession, with the third, which we called private love, together with their soldiers, and arrange them in the second guard as reason dictates.

But since two soldiers from the ranks of these quaternions are those between whom the captive was earlier said, symbolically, to sleep, let us pass over those two and consider the others. From the ranks of the second quaternion, one soldier keeping watch outside the prison, the remaining three are the making-light of guilt, the length of life, and the torpor of negligence. Likewise, from the ranks of the third quaternion, with one soldier left inside the prison, the remaining three are the desire for reputation, the rigor of repentance, [Col. 0301D] and the fear of perseverance.

These two quaternions therefore correspond to one another in this way. He is ashamed to confess his faults because he loves himself with private love; he makes his sin light by excuses so that, convicted as blameworthy in the estimation of others, he may not lose the reputation he desires; he avoids submitting to the rigor of repentance because he promises himself long stretches of life; and the torpor of negligence binds him because fear makes him apprehensive of the coldness of perseverance. Thus, lest it happen that he return from iniquity, he chooses rather always to remain sluggish in sin than to begin some good work in which he might not be able to persevere, when he ought both to begin from his own good will and to hope for the perfection of perseverance from God.

But now that we have compared these matters, let us see [Col. 0302A] how they may nevertheless be passed. When the shame of confession has been passed, private love too is passed at the same time; for he becomes his own adversary when, revealing his faults, he pursues himself with a salutary hatred. When the making-light of guilt has been passed, the desire for reputation is also passed; for, while he himself makes his guilt heavier, longing to please God alone, he does not care about outward reputation. When the rigor of repentance has been passed, the promise of longevity is also passed; for, while he desires to reconcile himself quickly with the one whom he offended, he does not admit the delays of deceptive postponement. When the torpor of negligence has been passed, the fear of perseverance is also passed; for, while he himself begins to do good with a fervent spirit, he presumes that, with divine assistance, he will be able to bring it to [Col. 0302B] completion.

In this way, then, these two quaternions, with their attendants, are brought into the second guard; and in this way they are passed by the converted sinner under the guidance of the angel. But since he has now left the prison, since he has passed through the first and second guards by following his guide, let us see where he has arrived.

### XVIII

“Then they came,” he says, “to the iron gate that leads to the city.”

After the sinner has left the prison of a darkened conscience, after he has passed through the first and second guards—that is, escaped the obstacles of vices that were holding him in sin—he comes to the iron gate, because the confession of sins alone is not sufficient for salvation if he does not also afflict himself, for what he has committed, through the harshness of satisfaction.

Let us see David leaving the prison and hastening toward the [Col. 0302C] iron gate. He says: “I will declare my iniquity, and I will consider my sin.” For when the sinner declares his iniquity by confessing it, he leaves the prison; but when he considers how he may satisfy God for each sin, he proceeds toward the iron gate.

The satisfaction by which we satisfy God for our sins is appropriately understood as the iron gate, because it is very hard for a person formerly devoted to soft desires, when converted to repentance, to be compelled to abandon those same desires, mortify the flesh, groan, weep, fast, renounce the world entirely, seek a withdrawn way of life, and thereafter live according to another’s direction. The satisfaction for sin is therefore rightly called the iron gate, through which a person, in order to render God reconciled to him, kills with the iron of harsh repentance whatever [Col. 0302D] he has lived carnally within himself.

Hence John the Baptist invited sinners flocking to him to approach the iron gate, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance.” To produce fruits worthy of repentance means to hasten toward the iron gate; it means to offer God such complete satisfaction that even one who remembers having committed unlawful acts must abstain from what is lawful.

The angel therefore leads Peter, brought out of prison, to this iron gate, because the divine word, after drawing us out of the prison of sin through the ministry of confession, shows how strictly we ought to appease God by satisfaction. This iron gate [Col. 0303A] leads to the city, because the narrowness of satisfaction admits us into the spaciousness of the heavenly city. When the converted sinner hastens toward the joys of that city with fervent love, no severity of any iron gate delays the steps of his desire. Thus it is rightly said:

### XIX

“Which opened of its own accord for them.”

When Peter came to the gate with the angel going before him, that same gate opened of its own accord before him; because, when the converted sinner eagerly follows the footsteps of holy preaching, everything that previously seemed difficult becomes easy for him. The one who earlier, swollen with the grossness of sins, could walk only through broad avenues of pleasure now, worn thin by the file of repentance, passes through every narrow place without difficulty.

But I see that it must be asked why it is [Col. 0303B] said, “It opened for them,” and not rather, “It opened for him.” Certainly, the angel who was leading Peter was a spirit and therefore, even if the gate had not been opened, could have passed through by the subtlety of spiritual nature. The prison too, from which he led Peter, was closed; yet when he entered it, no door is recorded as having been opened.

But someone may object that, since no entrance is recorded as having been opened when he entered, neither was one opened when he left with Peter; and therefore it should appear that he brought him out through an unopened entrance. This opinion, however, does not seem acceptable to me unless it is confirmed by some testimony of canonical Scripture. By canonical Scripture I now mean that which is contained in the canon of the books of the Old and New Testaments.

I plainly do not remember ever having [Col. 0303C] read in it that any human being clothed in a mortal body could pass with his solid body through an unopened entrance, except our Lord Jesus Christ, who, when he was born, came forth from his mother’s womb without an opened doorway, and, when he rose again, entered among the disciples with the same immortal yet true body while the doors were closed.

If anyone objects that it is recorded of a certain apostle that he entered to a certain king while the doors were closed, this example does not persuade or frighten me; for the very Scripture in which this is recorded is counted among the apocrypha by the authority of the Fathers.

It is therefore preferable to believe that the angel who entered to Peter in prison through an unopened entrance by the subtlety [Col. 0303D] of angelic nature himself opened the prison door by the power of the Lord in order to lead him out. But however he led him out, let the one who performed the deed see to that; let us return to the question before us.

We were asking why the gate is spoken of in the plural: “It opened for them,” and not rather in the singular: “It opened for him,” since this opening was evidently necessary not for the angel, who was a spirit, but only for Peter, who was clothed in a solid body.

This difficulty in the wording sends us toward an inner understanding. If we examine it somewhat more carefully, we shall immediately see how appropriately the same gate is said to have been opened for both. As we have already said above, the strong man who has fallen into sin is represented by Peter, while by the angel every preacher [Col. 0304A] of the truth is signified.

Let us now investigate how the preacher comes with the converted sinner to the iron gate, and how he passes through this gate with him. Let us see the angel hastening with his Peter toward the iron gate. And who can more truly be called an angel than the one of whom it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before you, and he will prepare your way”? When he said, “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” what else was he doing but urging his Peter—that is, converted sinners—to hasten toward the iron gate?

Let us now see whether he himself also passed through that same gate. And who did so better than he—or rather, who did so as fully as he? In indication of repentance and affliction, he wore down his body with camel’s hair; as a sign of mortifying pleasure, he wore a leather belt around his loins; as an example of singular abstinence, he despised bread and ate locusts and wild honey; as an example of a withdrawn manner of life, [Col. 0304B] he remained in the wilderness.

Let us see another angel hastening with his Peter toward the iron gate. For who is a truer angel than the one who said: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, namely Christ?” What, then, did he say to his Peter—that is, to the Gentiles whom he had led out of the prison of unbelief? “Run in such a way that you may obtain the prize; everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things.”

When he admonishes them to run so that they may obtain the prize, what is he doing with them except persuading them to hasten toward that gate which leads to the city where they are to receive the reward? When, following the example of a worldly athlete, he commands them to abstain from everything that impedes the contest, what is he doing with them except showing them how they ought to enter through the [Col. 0304C] iron gate?

Let us now see whether he himself also does what he instructs his followers to do. He says: “I therefore run not as uncertainly; I fight not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified.”

When he thus indicates that he himself runs and fights, what else does he demonstrate except that he too hastens toward the iron gate? It is therefore rightly said of this gate, “which opened of its own accord for them,” because our holy preachers, who lead us out of the prison of sins, enter the iron gate with us, since they too, in order to offer us an example of repentance, chastise their flesh, together with its vices, by harsh [Col. 0304D] affliction.

### XX

It follows: “And as they went out, they proceeded along one street, and immediately the angel departed from him.”

What is understood by “one street” except the death of the flesh? This death of the flesh is aptly called not merely a street but “one street,” because through that way the whole human race is compelled to pass. Hence in Scripture this same death is called “the way of all flesh.”

The angel, therefore, who leads Peter out of prison does not abandon him until he has proceeded along one street; because the divine word, which through the mouths of preachers shows us the way of departure from sin, remains with us in unbroken companionship until, having passed [Col. 0305A] through the death of the flesh, it presents to us the one whom it had promised.

For it is necessary that it proceed with us that far, because, even after leaving the prison, we would quickly go astray unless it showed us the road by which we ought to travel. But when we proceed along one street, the angel immediately departs from us; because, once we have seen him [perhaps *ipsum*] who is the way, the truth, and the life, we no longer need a guide.

### XXI

It follows: “And Peter, coming to himself, said: ‘Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.’”

According to the literal sense, the meaning is clear: Peter returned from that mental ecstasy into which he had been carried above himself through joy to the condition in which he had previously been, with ordinary understanding. But if, as we have begun to do, we refer these words also to the inner understanding, we perceive in them a great image of our future deliverance and taste beforehand a great sweetness of our future rejoicing in the present.

For as long as we are held in the bondage of this exile, we cannot be perfectly present to ourselves, [Col. 0305B] because we are unable to preserve, as it was created, that image and likeness which we received from the Creator, free from sin. For whenever we sin, we both exist and are present to ourselves; because, having fallen beneath ourselves through sin, we degenerate from the likeness of the one who is above us.

But when, having avoided all the dangers mentioned above, we come to the one who made us, then we also return perfectly to ourselves, because, possessing no [Col. 0305C] sin, we are as he created us. Then, secure in our deliverance, we shall break forth into a voice of rejoicing, saying:

### XXII

“Now I truly know that God sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.”

We are then truly delivered from the hand of Herod—that is, from the power of the devil—when, taken up from the place of temptation, we no longer fear his snares. We are also delivered from all the expectation [Col. 0306A] of the people of the Jews, because neither evil spirits nor wicked people, who eagerly await the affliction of the good, thereafter mock us on account of our falls.

Nor should it seem that the wording is passed over carelessly: he does not say “from expectation,” but “from all expectation.” We are brought forth for our adversaries as a spectacle for mockery as often as, by committing any crime, we provide them laughter at our expense. For one spectacle is that of anger, another of greed, another of gluttony, another of lust, another of vainglory, and another of pride.

The enemies who eagerly await our ridicule raise the guffaws of their mockery all the higher, applauding themselves, the more deeply they see us fallen. As long as we remain in this life, which is entirely temptation, [Col. 0306B] even if we avoid some of their spectacles of mockery, it is nevertheless difficult not to fall into something by which we may be exposed. Yet through God’s grace we are daily delivered when we return to the remedy of repentance.

But when we have reached that security, then we shall be perfectly delivered “from all the expectation of the people of the Jews”; for, when death has been swallowed up in the victory of resurrection, neither shall our flesh be subject externally to any corruption, nor shall any desire stimulate our mind internally.

Then we shall truly be able to say: “Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel,” and so forth. For the words “Now I truly know” are magnificently spoken, lest anyone presume that he has truly been received until he reaches “the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” For although we already know through faith that we have been freed, we do not yet [Col. 0306C] know that we have been truly freed in vision, until we are joined in eternal fellowship to the author of our freedom.

May that Angel of great counsel lead us to this knowledge of true deliverance: Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, who first delivered us through himself from darkness and the shadow of death, and daily delivers us through his angels. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0305]

## Treatise against the Jews by Saint Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres

He undertakes to prove that the notable prophecy of the patriarch Jacob—“The scepter shall not be taken from Judah,” etc.—was fulfilled in Christ Jesus.

(Edited by Charles de Villiers, theologian of Paris, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XVIII, p. 42, under the title: “Sermons against the Jews.” See the literary notice prefixed above to the works of Saint Fulbert, col. 167.)

[Col. 0305D]

### I

The sons of the Jews say: “It is not surprising if we are now captives, if we do not possess Jerusalem and have no king of our own. For we were likewise captives in Babylon on account of our sins, without possessing a king of our own, and afterward we returned to our homeland [Col. 0306D] and had kings and princes. This, then, is our hope: that something similar may still happen to us when it pleases God.”

Others say: “Perhaps in some part of the world unknown to us a multitude of Jews has been gathered which possesses a king of its own, and therefore the scepter has not yet been taken from Judah.” [Col. 0307A]

Others say that there are wise and powerful Jews in the regions who govern their households and families very well with the rod of direction, and therefore the scepter has not been taken from Judah.

To these we first reply that, if that prophecy is to be understood as they say, then the Messiah has neither come nor will come until all the Jewish heads of households are either dead or so powerless that no one among them in the world knows how, or is able, to rule his household. Since that will not happen until the day that is the end of all mortals, the Messiah will not come before that day.

But if this is so, why do we suppose that the Messiah should come on the last day, rather than merely bury all those dead whom he was hoped to heal while they were sick? Was this the expectation of the nations? [Col. 0307B]

They should not make the scepter of Judah so commonplace, nor count as many kings as there are heads of households in their nation—a thing never done before—nor imagine their patriarch so deranged that, as a very old man about to die, he would laboriously utter great absurdities with great effort, saying: “Gather together, sons,” and so forth.

Likewise, if that prophecy is to be understood in this way, what did that patriarch prophesy to his Hebrews that any Gentile could not have prophesied to the other pagans? For heads of households would not be lacking among them until the end.

Moreover, the one who expounds it in this way diminishes the majesty of the kingdom, derogates from the prophecy, and provides no certain sign of Christ’s coming except the destruction of all good things.

We reply otherwise at the outset, because they interpret this prophecy wrongly. For, by expounding the scepter of the kingdom, which is expressed in the singular, in the plural, they scatter it into the staffs [Col. 0307C] of private persons. Thus these illegitimate scepters compel the holy prophet, full of God, to be regarded as a foolish and deranged old man.

For what would Israel appear to have prophesied to his Hebrews that any Greek, Latin, or barbarian could not have prophesied to his own people? Like the first, the following interpreter plainly strives to ensure that he may perpetually escape the salvation brought by Christ’s coming.

If he should know that a king from among the Jews exists anywhere, he will deny that Christ has come because he will not think that the scepter has been taken from Judah. If he does not know of one, it will amount to the same thing: although he does not know where such a king is, he will believe that one exists somewhere, and therefore will believe that Christ has not come.

We, however, wish to reply in such a way as to demonstrate that it is of no benefit to him, for the purpose of denying Christ’s coming, whether he points to one king or several from the race of the Jews who are not kings of Judah. Once this has been demonstrated, if they should happen to point out people who exist somewhere, it will seem superfluous to deal with them.

There are therefore three things without which a kingdom cannot exist: land, namely the land in which the kingdom exists; a people who inhabit that land; and the person of an elected king who claims the land and rules the people.

The land of the kingdom about which we are speaking is the province of Jerusalem, which is called the land of Judah. The people of this land were the tribe of Judah. Its kings, until Christ, were all from the tribe of Judah.

Just as a house consists of its parts . . . [Note: [Col. 0307D] The passage is mutilated.] That is, of the land of Judah and of a king from the tribe of Judah [Col. 0308A]; and just as there is no house if its foundation, walls, or roof is missing, so there is no kingdom if its land, people, or king is missing. For where one part is absent, the whole cannot exist. And where the whole exists, all its parts must also exist.

If, therefore, when one part has been lost, the whole no longer exists, how much more is it no longer a kingdom when all its parts have been lost? The kingdom of Judah was deprived of its land from the time when that land came into the hands of foreigners. It was deprived of its people after the tribe of Judah was dispersed among all the nations. It had been deprived of its king long before.

Thus, once all its parts had been abandoned, the kingdom of Judah ceased to be a kingdom. From that time, therefore, the scepter was plainly taken from Judah, and it was declared that Christ had come.

If, then, you posit or falsely invent a single Jew—for example, Mordecai—as king in Babylonia, or indeed in Samaria, where the ten [Col. 0308B] tribes of the Jews lived and had their own king, who was called the king of Israel, he would nevertheless not be the king of Judah, but the king of Israel or of Babylonia. The prophecy has no bearing on them, for it says: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah.”

Again, the effective cause of the kings of Judah was the priests, who anointed them as kings. The Jewish people lost their priests together with the place of sacrifice; therefore they unquestionably lost the kingdom and the scepter. For where the effective cause is absent, the effect that would arise from it cannot exist in any way.

### II

Wishing to say certain necessary things against the errors of unbelievers, we begin immediately with the Jews. They say that in this respect they agree with us Catholics: that we worship one Lord, the Creator of all. But they disagree with us in that they do not acknowledge the Trinity of persons in the unity of the Godhead, that they deny Christ to be God, and that they say he has not yet [Col. 0308C] come.

Beginning our contradiction with this last point, let us proceed step by step toward the conclusion. Countless things prove that Christ has come. Among them is the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob and of the lawgiver Moses, who displayed a certain sign of his coming in the scepter of the kingdom of Judah, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

We attribute this prophecy jointly to two men for this reason: one of them uttered it, while the other transmitted it and confirmed it in writing.

The one who uttered it—that is, the holy patriarch Jacob—was at that time a resident alien [Col. 0308D] and wanderer in Egypt with his sons, and royal dignity seemed to have no connection with them except as a promise that was to be fulfilled for their descendants after them and for us.

Yet that spiritual man foresaw that a kingdom of such a kind would arise from his race as we read in Exodus, where the Lord says to his sons: “If you will hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession from among all peoples. For the whole earth is mine, and you shall be for me a priestly kingdom” (Exod. XIX, 5).

He therefore foresaw a priestly kingdom in which sacrifice would be offered to God alone, and such a kingdom as could not exist without the priesthood. Moses indicates the location of this kingdom in Deuteronomy, saying: “Take care not to offer your sacrifice in every place that you see, but [Col. 0309A] in the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes” (Deut. XII, 13). And concerning the tribe and place already chosen, the royal psalmist of God sings: “He rejected the tabernacle of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved” (Ps. LXXVII, 67).

Thus, prophesying about this and signifying the coming of the Messiah as its end, the patriarch spoke briefly, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” But the meaning of this prophecy should be understood as though it were explained in somewhat more words in the following manner:

“The house of Judah, which is now small and foreign, will one day grow into a great people and will have its homeland in the land of the Lord’s promise, together with kings or rulers from its own [Col. 0309B] race. Thereafter the governance or rule of this people will not be taken from the hand of its own race and transferred into the hand of a foreign ruler until Christ comes.”

Therefore, when you see, O Jews, the scepter of Judah transferred into the hand of a foreign king, recognize by this certain sign that Christ has come. Do not continue to expect the temporal kingdom that has passed away, but rejoice to reign eternally with the Christ who has come.

The truth of this prophecy was plainly followed by the outcome of events. After God chose for himself in the promised land the site of the priestly kingdom, as Moses had prescribed and David later sang had been done, there was no ruler among the tribe of Judah except one of legitimate descent, until the time of the foreigner Herod, who reigned at Jerusalem under Caesar Augustus after [Col. 0309C] Hyrcanus.

At that time the Lord Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah. From that time, however, the temporal scepter was taken from Judah, and the ruler from his thigh. From that time, therefore, prophetic truth establishes that Christ had come, destined to reign forever.

The cessation of the ancient sacrifice, which took place at his coming, also demonstrates that Christ had come, as Malachi had prophesied in these words: “I have no will in you, says the almighty Lord, and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has become great among the nations, and in every place a pure sacrifice is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the almighty Lord” (Mal. I, 10).

[Col. 0309D]

The predictions of other prophets abundantly agreed with this prophecy. But since the Jews were unwilling in any way to yield to them and were always eager to slaughter victims and eat their flesh, the Lord forcibly restrained their superstition, driving them out of the place of the kingdom in which alone—and never elsewhere—the law had permitted them to sacrifice.

Thus at last, unwillingly, they perceived the truth of the prediction concerning the end of their priesthood, since they had neither permission to sacrifice outside nor the power to do so within their former walls.

When the ancient priesthood, which had been instituted for a time, had passed away, a new and everlasting priesthood of Christ succeeded it. Of this the Psalmist had foretold: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

[Col. 0310A]

The change of the law also demonstrates that Christ had come. It took place when he came, as the divine Isaiah had said above in these words: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be manifest, prepared at the summit of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills; and all the nations will come to it and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us the way of salvation, and we shall enter upon it. For from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 2).

Who is so ignorant that he does not understand in these words that the mountain raised above the mountains is Christ, the king above rulers? At the coming of this king, the prophet saw that the law would go forth—not from Mount Sinai, to instruct one nation as before, but from Mount Zion, to teach the nations, as we now see has happened.

The old law was given to Moses on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the paschal lamb; the new law was inspired [Col. 0310B] in the holy apostles on the fiftieth day after the death and resurrection of the true Lamb. Of this law the holy Jeremiah also says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will confirm a new covenant over the house of Jacob, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt,” and so forth (Jer. VII, 32).

Since, therefore, the prophets had foretold that at Christ’s coming a new law would be brought by him, and since that law was long ago promulgated, it is clear that Christ, the lawgiver, had also come before then.

The most holy Daniel demonstrates not only that Christ had come, but also the time of his anointing and passion, the end of the priesthood, and the perpetual desolation [Col. 0310C] of the Jews, reckoning these matters in the person of the archangel Gabriel, who spoke to him in these words: “Seventy weeks have been shortened over your people and over your holy city, so that transgression may be finished, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be wiped away, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX, 24).

And shortly afterward: “Christ will be killed,” he says, “and his people, who will deny him, will not be his” (ibid., 26). Again, shortly afterward: “In the middle of the week victim and sacrifice will cease, and in the temple there will be the abomination of desolation, and desolation will endure until the consummation and the end” (ibid., 27).

The summary of this prophecy, insofar as it concerns the present argument, is that in the seventieth week Christ was to be anointed and killed, and the ancient priesthood was to fail. This week was being completed, and perpetual desolation was to [Col. 0310D] follow, when Tiberius, the successor of Augustus, was reigning—at the time when the Lord Jesus was baptized and crucified.

From that time, therefore, prophetic truth establishes not only that Christ had come, but also that he had been anointed and had suffered, and that the ancient sacrifice had failed, with desolation following.

The form of his humility and passion, once described piecemeal by many prophets, also indicated that Christ had come and who Christ was; and the whole of it was found together in the Lord Jesus [Col. 0311A] alone.

For example, we present part of that description: that he deigned to be born in Bethlehem, according to the prophecy of Micah; that, seated upon an ass, he came to Jerusalem; and that at the time of his passion he was clothed in a red garment. “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter and was counted among the wicked” (Isa. LIII, 7), as Isaiah had lamented.

That he was sold for thirty pieces of silver (Matt. XXVI, 15), crowned with thorns (Matt. XXVII, 29), and shut in by a stone (Lam. III, 53), as Jeremiah had mourned; that, with his palms and feet pierced, he was given gall and vinegar to drink, that his garments were divided, and that lots were cast over his tunic (Matt. XXVII, 23–24); and that he himself was placed in dark places, like those who have been dead for ages (Ps. CXLII, 3), while David lamented.

That he was struck (Matt. [Col. 0311B] XXVI, 67), spat upon (Mark XV, 19), and wounded with a lance (John XIX, 34), while Job grieved.

Such, then, is the prophets’ description of Christ’s humility and passion. Since it has been found in its entirety only in Jesus Christ our Lord, it demonstrates not only that Christ came, but that he alone is truly the Christ. Likewise, that Christ came, and who Christ was, is shown by the testimony once given by the contemporaneous prophets, such as Zechariah and Elizabeth, Simeon and Anna, whose deeds or prophecies are well known, and by John the Baptist, who said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). For when these people personally identified the Lord Jesus, they undoubtedly demonstrated not only that Christ had come, but who Christ was.

Likewise, the signs or miracles [Col. 0311C] that were performed at the birth, baptism, and passion of our Lord Jesus—as though from without, yet nevertheless by divine agency—declared not only that Christ had come, but that he truly was the Christ. Such were the visions of the angels rejoicing at his Nativity; the new star shining brightly as his sign; and the Magi coming with gifts to his cradle. These miracles so disturbed the usurping king that, in rivalry with the newborn Christ, he carried out a most savage slaughter of infants of Christ’s own age.
