Such also were the thunder of the Father’s voice and the dove-like appearance of the Holy Spirit at his baptism; and, at his death, the darkening of the sun, the trembling of the earth, and the tearing of the temple veil [Col. 0311D].

Above all these things, Christ’s works and words demonstrate that he came. By them he once refuted the unbelief of the Jews, saying: “If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done, they would not have sin” (John 15:22). By them also he strengthened the faith of the disciples of John the Baptist, saying: “Tell John what you hear and see: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized. And blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me” (Matthew 11:5). The prophets had foretold that Christ would do these and many other things. Since all these things were seen to be accomplished by our Lord Jesus Christ, they proved that he was truly the Christ.

We willingly pass over the other proofs of Christ’s coming—for example, that “their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm 18:5), and that “in him all the tribes of the earth are seen to be blessed” (Psalm 71:17), along with countless others—because we have demonstrated sufficiently and abundantly what we had set out to prove: namely, that Christ came at his appointed time [Col. 0312A].

Nor does the Jew have anything with which to object. For if he says that the scepter has not been taken away from Judah, he is plainly false, because for approximately a thousand years the tribe of Judah has been scattered in every direction, and others possess the place of its royal and priestly rule. If he says that its priesthood has not come to an end, he is clearly lying, because he has permission to offer sacrifice neither outside Jerusalem nor within it. But if he says that the covenant has not been concluded, this too is especially false, because the right of the Old Covenant does not stand without the blood of sacrifice. If he says that the number of holy Daniel was not completed at the time mentioned above [Col. 0312B], this too is readily shown to be false by chronological calculations. If he says that the one to whom the description given above applies, together with the testimony of the prophets, is not the Christ, he is shown to be false by the fact that there is no other person to whom it could apply. If he attempts to chatter against the new judges and prophets, the ancient signs and the miracles that shine around them refute him. If he does not believe that the miracles of the Nativity and the other events took place, the slaughter of the innocent and the many historical accounts convict him. Nor can he obscure Christ’s magnificent works, for they have been impressed or represented in writings, buildings, and other signs, so that they cannot disappear without the destruction of the world.

Thus, since the Jew has been convicted by so many arguments and refuted by so many testimonies of the saints, if he does not submit to the authority of the Law and the prophets, he must be expelled from the synagogue. Having now established that Christ came, when he came, and who he is, let us proceed to demonstrate that he is the true God [Col. 0312C].

We therefore establish first that Christ surpasses all other human beings. Certain things peculiar to him reveal this, as expounded by the prophets—for example, that he is a man born of a virgin, as Isaiah testifies; and that Christ is “a man free among the dead without help,” as David testifies. For no other man was born of a virgin mother, and no other rose from the dead by his own power.

Then there are other things proper to Christ, by which he surpasses every creature, such as that statement uttered with wonder by Isaiah: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). And there is David’s statement: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). For neither an angel nor any other creature of God is his arm, nor is any other creature God’s natural Son on the eternal day.

There is abundant authority among theologians concerning this divine sonship or generation. Hence the exceedingly wise king proposed this most subtle question, saying: “Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has held the spirit in his hands? Who has bound up the waters as in a garment? Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth? What is the name of his son, if you know?” (Proverbs 30:4).

From these characteristics mentioned above, which separate Christ from creation, let his divinity be demonstrated by the following reasoning. Whatever exists is either Creator or creature; therefore, whatever is not a creature is the Creator. Since Christ is the arm of God, and is not a creature, he is without doubt the Creator. Likewise, the natural son, although distinct in number from his father because he is another person, is nevertheless, by natural definition, one and the same with his father. But Christ is God’s natural Son; therefore Christ is the same as the Father, that is, he is God.

It is therefore clear that Christ is Lord because he is the arm of God, and that he is God because he is the Son of God [Col. 0313A].

In addition to these things, there are certain prophecies concerning Christ’s divinity so explicit that their treatment requires no reasoning. For they plainly acclaim him by the very name “Lord,” with praises worthy of God, although not without mentioning his humanity, by which he is believed to be both true God and man. Among these is David’s statement: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever,” and what follows (Psalm 44:7). There is also Isaiah’s statement: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His government shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

In these words of Isaiah, one must beware of the Jews’ false interpretation, by which they attempt, when disputing with simple Christians, to bend this prophecy toward the name of Hezekiah. It is certainly false, because the Hebrew text does not say, “His name shall be called Hezekiah,” which is interpreted as “Strong of the Lord,” but rather, “His name shall be called El-gibbor,” which is interpreted as “Mighty God.” The name El, that is, “God,” belongs to God alone and not to Hezekiah, to whom the other things that follow cannot apply either [Col. 0313C].

Furthermore, in David’s prophecy, along with Christ’s divinity, one must carefully observe the distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. When it says, “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Psalm 44:7–8), it speaks to the Lord’s Son. When it says, “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (ibid., 8), it speaks of God the Father. When it then adds, “with the oil of gladness” (ibid.), it signifies the Holy Spirit, who is nevertheless God, as will be demonstrated in its proper place [Col. 0313D].

## III

There is great disagreement among human beings concerning many other matters, and also concerning the confession of faith. Seeing this, the Apostle said: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).

Not only Gentiles and Jews, but even those who wish to be called Christians themselves differ greatly among one another. Some of them are Catholics; others are heretics in many ways. I, Fulbert, who set forth these things—although a sinner and an unworthy bishop—nevertheless, because I desire and profess that I am Catholic in faith, by God’s grace wish to give others, insofar as I can, a small portion of an account of my faith and of their error, an account that is sufficiently abundant within me.

First, then, concerning the Jews. They say that they agree with us in this: “We confess one God, Creator of all.” But they disagree concerning many things, and most dangerously concerning this: they do not acknowledge the Trinity of persons in the unity of divinity, and they deny that Christ is God, or say that he has not yet come. If someone were to refute them rationally concerning this last matter, or third matter, I think he would afterward have little difficulty with the rest. For once it has been proved that Christ came, he will then be able to explain to the Jew who asks what he ought to think or do concerning the remaining matters. Let us begin, then [Col. 0314A].

That Christ came is proved by the prophecy fulfilled which Moses wrote in these words: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” For the rule of the tribe of Judah was not taken from the hand of its own kindred and transferred into the hands of foreign kings until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom we Catholic Christians have accepted. But from that time onward the scepter was truly taken away from Judah and transferred into the hands of strangers belonging to our same Lord Jesus Christ.

From that time, therefore, the prophetic authority makes clear that the one who was to be sent had come, that is, Christ. Behold, we have stated our proposition concisely. Now let us briefly touch upon the historical truth by which it is confirmed: demonstrating what kind of rulers the Jewish people had from their own lineage, when they lost them, and how the loss of their rule and the coming of the Messiah coincided in the days of Herod.

After Moses, who uttered this prophecy, and Joshua, his successor, the Jewish people had rulers from their own lineage, who were called judges, until the time of Samuel the prophet. Then they had rulers called kings, likewise from their own lineage—Saul, David, and many others—until the Babylonian deportation.

Even during the deportation there was no lack of rulers and comforters from their own lineage, men filled with God and superior even to the kings, such as the prophets Jeremiah and Daniel. After the return from Babylon, they likewise had well-ordered forms of rule from their own lineage, exercised by high priests, until the time of Aristobulus, who was both high priest of the Jewish people, likewise from his own lineage, and its final king.

After conquering Jerusalem, Pompey, the Roman commander, sent this Aristobulus, bound together with his children, to Rome, leaving the high priesthood to his brother Hyrcanus [Col. 0314D]. Hyrcanus, however, was the last high priest over the entire Jewish nation by legitimate succession of lineage. Herod was the first king of the Jews from a foreign lineage, made king by decree of the senate during the reign of Augustus. At that time Christ was born in Bethlehem, in accordance with the prophecy.

Until that point, therefore—that is, until the reign of Herod and no later—the Jewish people had legitimate rulers from their own lineage. For when the kingdom of the Jews was broken up and changed, the priesthood too was broken up and changed. After Herod received the kingdom of the Jews from the Romans, he did not appoint high priests according to the ancient right, that is, by legitimate succession of lineage; instead, he indiscriminately promised the priesthoods for a time to whatever obscure persons he chose. He nowhere allowed the high priests to use the sacred garment of the high priest, which was kept sealed under a signet [Col. 0315A].

His successor Archelaus maintained this perverse custom after him. The Roman governors maintained it thereafter, until finally, after Christ’s passion, Jerusalem was destroyed and the Jewish people dispersed, and they had neither a city, nor a king, nor a high priest, nor a people. This desolation has continued without interruption down to the present day.

If these things are so—or rather, because they are so—we have consequently confirmed through history what we had concluded from the prophecy: namely, that from the time when rule was taken away from Judah, and the ruler from his thigh, the Messiah had come. Now, if the Jews have anything with which to object, let it be heard [Col. 0315B].

Some Jews customarily make threefold objections to this argument. “First,” they say, “we do not believe that Christ has come, because we do not think the scepter of rule has been taken away from Judah. For in many regions there are wealthy and capable Jews who govern their households vigorously; and because we still see such rulers, we say that the scepter has not yet been taken away from Judah, and that Christ has not yet come.”

Anyone may mock them with humorous wit and refute them by reason in this way: “O Jews, fortunate in your misfortune! If what you say is true, has not the one who ruined and scattered you blessed you abundantly and wonderfully, if, after losing one king in your homeland, you have now found or recovered so many thousands of kings in exile?”

But none of these men has been anointed with lawful or spiritual chrism; no people follows any of them, nor does he rule over a people. Therefore, none of them is or can be called a king, high priest, prophet, or ruler of the tribe of Judah. For where the efficient causes are absent, the effects of those causes cannot possibly exist.

What grief—or laughter—then, over the foolish and unhappy lot of part of the Jewish people! While they insolently and without acknowledgment think that their rule has been scattered among the multitude and applaud themselves over the number of their kings, they are proved to have no ruler at all. This argument should be sufficient for refuting the first part.

But because good causes provide us with arguments in abundance, let us not hesitate to attack them a second time by an impossible hypothesis, as follows. The prophecy of which we are now speaking either refers to such kings—that is, peasants or private individuals—or it does not. But if it does refer to them, and if, because they presently exist in this life, it is established among you that Christ has not yet come, then it will likewise be established that he will never come until all such men have been destroyed, so that no one remains in the world to rule his household.

When will that be? Unless at the consummation of the age, when all have died and there is no longer any place either for repentance or forgiveness. And what would we suppose the Messiah would come for then, except to bury the dead? Would this, then, be the expectation of the nations? Would the prophecy just given be reduced to nothing? Far from it! For it is impossible that God should lie—he who promised, at a definite time before the end of the age, to send his Christ to save the human race.

Those, therefore, are false who say that this prophecy refers to the end of such rulers as are certain to continue until the end of the age [Col. 0316A].

Having refuted them in this way, the Jews, now refuted concerning this objection, move to another, saying: “We do not believe that Christ has come, because we do not think the scepter has been taken away from Judah. For who knows whether, somewhere in the world, a multitude of Jews has been gathered together and has over it an anointed and consecrated king from its own lineage?”

We answer that none of us on either side knows or has heard in our own days of a Jewish king reigning in any region of the world. Nevertheless, if a Jew were reigning in Judaea, the scepter would still have been taken away from Judah.

For the kingdom of Judah was a kingdom distinct from other kingdoms, consisting of its own territory, called the land of Judah and Benjamin, and its own king, who came from the tribe of Judah. Just as every house consists of its own parts—foundation, walls, and roof—and if one of these is missing it cannot be a house, so the kingdom of Judah consisted of the parts mentioned above.

For whether homeland, people, or king is missing, the kingdom cannot exist. Where one part is absent, the whole cannot exist; and conversely, where the whole exists, the parts must also exist. If the name of the whole perishes when one part perishes, how much more does the whole fail to subsist when all the parts perish?

The kingdom of Judah lost its land when the land itself came into foreign hands. It lacked a people after the people had been scattered among all the nations. It had lost its legitimate king long before. Thus, after the kingdom of Judah had lost all its parts, it ceased to be a kingdom. It is therefore clear that the scepter of Judah has nothing to do with foreign kingdoms and that it was taken away from Judah’s own right [Col. 0316C].

If some fool thinks that a kingdom of Judah either is or may be called any place where a Jew reigns over Jews, he is refuted both by fact and by Scripture. When two kings reigned over the Jewish nation—one in Jerusalem over two tribes, and the other in Samaria over ten tribes—only the one who ruled in Jerusalem was called and was the king of Judah; the one who ruled in Samaria was the king of Israel.

If, therefore, the scepter of Judah does not belong to the one who rules the ten tribes of Jews in Samaria, much less will it belong to the one who is falsely represented as king of some Jews in India.

Let us say it again: the king of Judah is a man descended from the tribe of Judah, chosen and anointed with sacred chrism by a legitimate priest to rule the people who dwell in the land of Judah. Every foreign king is excluded from this definition. None of them, therefore, is king of Judah. For those who do not share a common definition cannot share a common essence [Col. 0316D].

Another conclusion follows from this, as follows. If no one could legitimately be king from the tribe of Judah unless the priest—himself likewise anointed and consecrated—consecrated him with legitimate sacred anointing, and if there was no priest among the Jewish people after they lost the chrism and were exiled from the place in which alone they were permitted to sacrifice; and if the priests who anointed kings no longer existed, then kings could not exist either. For where the efficient causes are absent, their effects cannot exist.

It follows, therefore, not only that the scepter was taken away from Judah, but that afterward it was not even possible for a king to be made there [Col. 0317A].

Now let us come to the third objection: “It is not for us so great a sign that we are now exiles and without a king, that is, a ruler, that we should therefore believe the Messiah has come. For we were similarly in Babylon, yet the Messiah did not come in any way then. Afterwards we returned to Jerusalem and had a kingdom and priesthood. This, then, is our hope: that when God is pleased, these things will once again come to us after our restoration.”

We answer that you have said that you are now exiles and without a ruler, and this is true. At that time, however, the people had been gathered together into one place in Jerusalem—that is, [Col. 0318A] the tribes of Judah and Benjamin—with their king, priests, and prophets. They had a promise given by the Lord that, after completing seventy years of repentance, they would return to their land, which the Lord had not yet handed over to foreigners for habitation, but which remained desolate, as it does now.

Now, however, your people are not gathered together as they were then; you have neither king, priests, nor prophets, nor a land reserved for you in its desolation, nor a promise given by the Lord that you will return there after seventy years as happened then. Rather, the Lord has issued the sentence that this desolation of yours is to be perpetual; this is sufficiently demonstrated in its proper place. It has already been exacted from you for approximately a thousand years and will not fail in any of what remains until the end.

# SERMONS OF SAINT FULBERT, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, TO THE PEOPLE

*(Library of the Fathers, vol. XVIII, p. 37.) (C)*

## SERMON I

[Col. 0317B]

Venerable fathers, dear brothers, children of God, we wish to recall to you something that you ought never to forget: namely, how you ought to believe and live, and, if someone has sinned, how he may recover. These are three things.

The Catholic faith is this: that we venerate one Lord in the Trinity, and the Trinity in unity. There are many, however, who cannot understand this unless they are led to it by certain likenesses. Let us therefore say something of that kind ourselves.

In the sun there are naturally three things: the sphere, brightness, and heat. The sphere of the sun is naturally shining and hot. The supreme Father is naturally wise and loving. The sphere of the sun, its radiance, and its heat are not three suns, but one sun. The supreme Father, his wisdom, and his love are not three gods, but one God. Wisdom is the Son of God; the Holy Spirit is love. The Father, therefore, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. This God, before the ages, now, and always, made all visible and invisible things [Col. 0317C].

But it is asked why God the Father wished his Son—that is, Wisdom—to become human. Let us answer as briefly as we can: certainly for the redemption of humanity, which had perished through its own fault and could not restore itself.

Before the human being sinned, he was wise and immortal, and free in his choice. Yet the devil’s cunning was so great that he deceived him and made him foolish, mortal, and fragile. How, then, after becoming foolish, fragile, and mortal, could he overcome the devil and recover by himself what he had lost, when, while still strong, he had not defended what belonged to him? Nevertheless, it was in no way impossible for the will of the Omnipotent not to be fulfilled [Col. 0317D].

## SERMON II

[Col. 0318B]

Brothers, I believe that all of us who are gathered in this present basilica are Christians through faith. Let us therefore first give thanks to God, who has deigned to call us to his faith, cleanse us from sin through the grace of baptism, and free us from the devil.

Say, “Thanks be to God,” brothers. If we had remained in the purity given to us through baptism, we would truly be happy. But we did not remain in it. Through our own fault we fell not only into sins but also into crimes, on account of which sinners are separated from the Church: such as homicides, adulteries, fornications, sacrileges, robberies, thefts, false testimonies, pride, envy, greed, prolonged anger, and habitual drunkenness.

Therefore, just as we gave thanks to God for his goodness, so let us confess ourselves guilty because of our wickedness, and let each of us say: “We are sinners.” Brothers, we truly are such before God and his saints. But his mercy is great, for he still grants us a place or time for amendment [Col. 0318C].

Let us therefore amend for the better the things in which we sinned through ignorance, according to Scripture. But if you do not know how you ought to amend, it must be explained to you.

First of all, cease from sinning. For as long as someone does not cease offending the Lord, his repentance is not fruitful; and whoever does not put an end to criminal sin in this life will not have forgiveness in the next. Therefore, as I said, it is necessary first to put an end to crime, and then to erase what has been committed through repentance, almsgiving, and prayer [Col. 0318D].

The priests will determine the measure of your repentance. The measure of almsgiving is according to your means and good will [Col. 0319A]. Christ has established the measure of prayer for us under various conditions, which you know—namely, that he should forgive us as we forgive, and so forth.

We therefore exhort you, brothers, to flee crimes, to accept eagerly the repentance imposed upon you, and to carry it out diligently. For “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

Give alms also according to your ability, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. Let us pray both for one another and for ourselves, as the Apostle says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16).

We know that many have escaped the danger of death through repentance, and others through prayer. Let us strive, brothers, to be found among such people, because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

May he strengthen our weakness who said, “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:23), our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through endless ages of ages. Amen [Col. 0319B].

## SERMON III: ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED MARY

Brothers, we wish to explain briefly to you where the solemnity of the Purification that you celebrate today began, and what the candles you offer signify.

This solemnity therefore arose from the Law. For God commanded in the Law that a woman who, having conceived by her husband, gave birth to a firstborn son should present him to the Lord in the temple on the fortieth day after his birth, together with offerings [Col. 0319C]. This day is called the Purification.

Other mothers fulfilled the commandment of Purification and offering out of necessity, because they were polluted and sinful. But when Christ was born of the most blessed Virgin Mary, she did not need legal purification, because she was clean and holy. Nevertheless, out of humility and obedience, submitting herself to the Law and obeying it although she had no need of it, she offered her Son, together with offerings, in God’s temple on the fortieth day after his birth, as happens today.

That presentation, however, was notable and glorious. For, moved by the Holy Spirit, the holy prophet Simeon and holy Anna, a widow and prophetess, came to meet him, praising and blessing the Lord at the coming of Christ, as is read in the Gospel, and presenting miracles [Col. 0319D].

For Christ, coming in the flesh, brothers, displayed at once both an example of humility and signs of divine mercy. Just as at his birth, when he lay humbly in a manger, a new star and angelic praises celebrated him in heaven, so now, when the little infant was presented in the temple, the Holy Spirit illuminated the hearts of the prophets in order to reveal his divinity hidden in the flesh.

We therefore, who adore him as true Lord and man, celebrate this day in remembrance of his Presentation in the temple, with the offering of candles. By the light of the candle we signify his divinity; by the wax, his virginal flesh. For the bee, the maker of honey and wax, is produced without the union of male and female.

It is therefore clear that Christ’s Presentation in the temple arose from obedience to the Law, and that our symbolic offering arises from the sweet and venerable memory of his presentation [Col. 0320A].

Now, knowing from what good beginnings this solemnity arose and what pious and holy meaning our offering bears, let us adorn the solemnity with divine praises and good works, and celebrate the offering with devout affection. Let us ask the most pious Mother of God to deign to make us and our gifts pleasing to her Son, and, in accordance with the likeness of our offering—which appears pure, bright, and fervent—to ask him to grant us purity of heart and body, the light of knowledge, and the fervor of faith and charity.

Thus, kindled by the gift of his grace and illuminated by the Holy Spirit, may we, with purified minds, be able to appear in the holy temple of his glory, through the same Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0320B].

## SERMON IV: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

Among Christians it is an approved custom to observe carefully the birthdays of the holy Fathers, and especially to recite in the Church the virtues attributed to them in writing, for the praise of God, from whose gift they come, and as instruction for those of lesser standing.

Among all the saints, the memory of the most blessed Virgin is celebrated all the more frequently and festively because she is believed to have found greater favor with the Lord. Hence, after certain other and more ancient solemnities of hers, the devotion of the faithful was not content without adding the solemnity of her birth, which we celebrate today.

On this day, therefore, that book which was found to have been written about her origin [Col. 0320C] and life would seem especially suited to be read in the Church, if the Fathers had not judged that it ought to be numbered among the apocrypha. But since great and wise men have judged it so, let us, reading other things that are not foreign to the subject, fulfill the ecclesiastical custom with the appropriate offices.

The blessed Mother of the Lord and perpetual Virgin Mary was foretold by oracles before she was born and designated by miracles. Born from a divinely appointed lineage, she shone forth distinguished by the privilege of her virtues; she bore the Savior, by whom she was glorified in heaven, and she never ceases to intercede for earthly human beings.

Let the narrative of the subject now follow in order. Let us first report one of the oracles mentioned above and then dispose of it briefly.

The Eternal said to the ancient [one; reading uncertain], God said to the serpent: “I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Genesis 3:15).

What is it, brothers, to crush the serpent’s head in this passage, except to overcome, by resistance, the devil’s principal suggestion—that is, lust? If it is asked which woman accomplished such a victory, she is certainly not found in the line of human generation until one arrives at the woman of whom we are speaking, the holy one among the holy.

If it is asked in what way she herself crushed the serpent’s head, surely it was in this: she sacrificed both virginity and humility to God. By preserving her virginity, she is shown to have extinguished the lust of the flesh; by humility, which makes one poor in spirit, the lust of the mind. Thus, after conquering the devil’s principal suggestion, she crushed his vicious head beneath the foot of virtue.

Yet she triumphed not only in this way, but most especially in that Wisdom incarnate from her most pure flesh says: “Reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). This, then, is the woman toward whom that divine oracle was directed; it indicated that she would one day be born and spoke of her in particular.

Having dispatched the oracle in a few words, let each of the miracles be explained in turn [Col. 0321A].

By command of the Lord, individual rods were taken by holy Moses from each of the tribes of Israel, inscribed with their names, and placed in his tabernacle. Among them, the one belonging to Aaron was found on the following day to have sprouted, blossomed, put forth leaves, and produced almonds. Knowing that this work was a great mystery, the Lord commanded that the rod be preserved as a memorial [Col. 0321B].

The children of Israel were admonished by the presence of the rod to inquire carefully what such a wondrous event signified. The divine Isaiah later disclosed this, saying: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:1).

As though his hearers were saying, “Father Isaiah, you speak obscurely; please tell us the matter plainly,” he added clarity and said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14).

Describing splendidly also the Virgin’s Son, that is, Emmanuel, he says: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His government shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end to his kingdom” (Isaiah 9:6).

What God signified through a miracle, Isaiah revealed from the hidden place through prophecy. What the prophet sang, the outcome of the event subsequently confirmed. For just as that rod fructified without a root and without any natural or artificial aid, so the Virgin Mary, without conjugal intercourse, brought forth a son—a son signified by both flower and fruit: by the flower, because of his beauty; by the fruit, because of his usefulness.

“For he is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3), and he is life-giving nourishment not only for human beings but also for angels. Having briefly affirmed this first part of the proposition, let us touch upon what follows [Col. 0321C].

Therefore the most blessed Virgin was born, as we read, of a father from Nazareth and a mother from Bethlehem—cities which the prophets had not failed to indicate as destined for the birth or dwelling of Christ. She descended from the lineage of that illustrious man of faith, Abraham, to whom the blessing of all nations in his offspring had been promised from above, and from the stock of David, whom God exalted with outstanding praise because of the virtue known to him, saying: “I have found a man after my own heart” (Acts 13:22). She derived her origin from both the royal and the priestly tribe, for she was to bear the supreme King and High Priest.

We do not say this, however, because the Lord, who came to call sinners, would have disdained to have sinners among his mother’s relatives, among whom she might appear like a beautiful lily among thorns. This chosen and distinguished woman among daughters did not receive her name by chance, or merely by her parents’ preference, as is common, but by divine providence, so that the very form of her name might also signify something great: for it is interpreted as “star of the sea.” Let us show by analogy what mystical meaning this interpretation contains.

When sailors cross the sea, they must observe this star, shining far from the highest pole of heaven, and estimate and direct their course by looking toward it, so that they may reach the harbor for which they are bound. In the same way, brothers, all Christians must, as they row amid the waves of this age, look toward this star of the sea—that is, Mary—who is close to God, the supreme pole of all things, and direct the course of their life by regard for her example. Whoever does this will not be driven about by the wind of empty glory, nor dashed against the reefs of adversity, nor swallowed up by the Scyllaean chasm of pleasures, but will safely arrive at the harbor of eternal rest.

If someone should ask here: “What, then, do you think this person was formerly like in soul, or is now, who is set before all the saints to contemplate and imitate?” we answer truthfully that she was far more perfect than our speech can demonstrate. Yet, lest we be accused of saying nothing where there is a greater abundance of things to say, leaving much and great matter to eloquent speakers, let us say at least a little about this—things that can readily be proved once heard.

First, it is right to affirm that her soul and flesh, which the Wisdom of God the Father chose and made into a dwelling for itself, were supremely pure, free from every evil and impurity, as Scripture affirms: “For wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:4). Conversely, we confidently assert that she lacked no kind of virtue, since the messenger declared that the fullness of God’s grace was in her. Although no sound-minded person doubts this on the testimony of the archangel, if anyone still seeks, with devout desire, evidence of her virtues in the words and deeds which Scripture records, such evidence will present itself all the more readily the more faithful he is in seeking.

Some of these things are clear to almost every Christian. Who, indeed, does not contemplate with joyful wonder the strength, prudence, and faith of that mature young woman in her conversation with the angel—how steadfastly she speaks, how prudently she asks questions, and how readily she believes? Who does not see, and seeing admire, her justice, by which she strove to fulfill all the commands of the divine law, leaving unfulfilled nothing that pertained to her? For example, after childbirth she did not need the legal purification which she nevertheless underwent, because she had not known a man in conceiving. Her temperance was mentioned above: through it she brought forth the lily of virginity for God in the valley of humility.

Since, then, her deeds and words are full of the virtues mentioned above, it is clear—not only from the testimony of the angel but also from the evidence of her conduct—that no virtue was lacking from the most blessed Virgin. These virtues produced in the thought and affection of her heart an ineffable harmony, which the Wisdom of God, its creator and inhabitant, delighted to hear. Outside, they shone upon the surface of her speech and actions, so that people could rightly glorify God and receive examples leading to salvation.

What greater addition, then, could have come to such a person, so great and so distinguished, for the increase of her honor, than that a virgin conceived the Son of God and a virgin gave birth to him? By this dignity she became venerable even to the orders of the holy angels. The great and mighty archangel Gabriel plainly declared this in his deed: before she became the Mother of God, because he knew that she would become so, he anticipated it by greeting her with such veneration. By this same dignity she also became commanding, through charity toward those above and through discernment toward those below.

Many written examples provide evidence of this; for the present, it is enough to recall a few. Long ago she sent a holy angel to aid the great Father Basil and raised a dead man to life, who brought to ruin his persecutor, Julian the Apostate, living wickedly; this story is very well known. She also, O former sinner Theophilus, powerfully snatched you from the very jaws of the devil when you repented and humbly invoked her. But why should we hesitate to speak briefly of the restoration of this fallen man, when it is worthwhile to hear it?

This Theophilus once held office in the district of a certain bishop of Cilicia, as a certain writing testifies. Because of his misfortunes he fell into sadness, and from there went to a certain Jewish magician, seeking his counsel and assistance. Through this intermediary he spoke with the devil, renounced Christianity, worshiped the devil, and gave him, as a pledge of his enslavement, a written document sealed with his ring.

Afterward, however, he repented of what he had done and, deeply tormented in mind, wondered what he should do and where he should turn. At last, gathering the strength of faith and hope, he fled to a church dedicated to the memory of blessed Mary, the Mother of the Lord. There, afflicted for forty days, he continually invoked her name and implored her protection with a contrite heart.

What more need be said? The Mother of Mercy looked upon him with favor. Appearing to him in a vision, she convicted him of his impiety and stirred him to confess Christ. She consoled the grieving man by promising forgiveness; and, so that he would not doubt the promise, she powerfully snatched the aforementioned document from the devil and returned it to the captive as a pledge of his freedom.

When he awoke and found it placed upon his breast, it is not easy to say how joyful he became or with what devout feeling he uttered words of exultation and confession. The Lord’s Day followed that night. On it Theophilus, as though rising from the dead with the Lord, presented himself before the bishop and the people and explained the matter as it had happened.

You would have seen the people at one moment terrified when they heard of so dreadful a crime, and at another moved to tears when they considered the penitent’s emaciated body and face. But when they heard how great and how swift a mercy he had obtained, all those who, terrified by an evil conscience, had almost fainted, breathed again with joy in the hope of forgiveness.

To conclude the matter briefly: at the bishop’s command, Theophilus burned the ill-advised document in the fire. Then, with the clergy and people supporting him, he was led to the altar. As he received the most holy Communion from the bishop’s hand into his mouth, his face shone like the sun. Afterward, having completed three days in the church with praises to the devout Mother of the Lord, through whom he had been reconciled, he rested from his labors in a blessed end.

By such deeds it is proved that the Mother of the Lord is commanding everywhere and magnificent everywhere—certainly one for whom it is easy to send holy angels into service and to cancel the agreements of the underworld at her pleasure. Through these and innumerable other benefits, whether written about or continually experienced everywhere in their effects, she is faithfully present to just and sinful people who invoke her, and she never ceases to help them.

Let the righteous therefore come to her with Basil, praising and blessing her, and without doubt they will receive the swift fulfillment of their holy desires. Let sinners come with Theophilus, striking their guilty breasts with inward tears; they too, if they truly repent, will obtain the forgiveness they desire. From their number, while we stand before you, we implore you, O chosen one, O holy and venerable Lady, O commanding one, O merciful and gracious mistress of ours, to assist and help us now, so that we may recover and possess forever the favor of your Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, one God, forever. Amen.

## SERMON V. ALSO ON THE NATIVITY OF THE VIRGIN MARY

Dearest brothers, on this day we celebrate the birthday of our glorious Lady Mary, namely, the Mother of our Redeemer. We wish to tell you briefly something about her birth, her life and end, and the assistance which she is accustomed to offer Christians, both the righteous and sinners.

She was born from the line of Abraham and of King David, to whom God made the promise that in their offspring—that is, in Christ—all the tribes of the earth would be blessed. According to the accounts and writings of the holy Fathers, she was born in the city of Nazareth, to a father named Joachim, who came from that same city, and a mother named Anna, who came from the city of Bethlehem.

Their life was simple and upright before the Lord, irreproachable and devout among human beings. They divided all their property into three portions: one they gave to the temple and its servants; another they distributed to pilgrims and the poor; the third they reserved for themselves and the needs of their household. Thus, righteous before God and poor in the eyes of men, they lived for about twenty years in a chaste marriage before the Lord, without producing children. Nevertheless, they vowed that, if God should perhaps grant them offspring, they would dedicate the child to the service of the Lord.

When so many years had run their course, an angel of the Lord was sent first to Joachim and then to Anna, announcing to them that a daughter named Mary would be born to them, such a one as had never been born before and would never be born afterward in holiness. And so it happened according to the angel’s word: the most holy Virgin Mary was born in the city of Nazareth and remained there for three years in her father’s house. Afterward, as her parents had vowed her to God, she was taken to Jerusalem and kept in the Lord’s temple until her fourteenth year, serving day and night with fasts and prayers and vowing her virginity—something no virgin had done before—and frequently engaging in conversations with angels.

Then, when she had returned to her parents’ house in the city of Nazareth, the angel Gabriel was sent to her by God, announcing to her the conception of the Son of God. Thus the Son of God was conceived in Nazareth and born in Bethlehem.

After Christ’s birth she remained with her son until the Passion of the Cross, where Christ entrusted the Virgin Mother to the virgin disciple, the apostle John. He cared for her after the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, until the end. The most holy woman was buried in the valley of Jehoshaphat, where a church was built in her honor, while Saint John was buried at Ephesus.

Later, when devout Christians wished to look upon the relics of his mother, namely, the Lord’s mother, they found the tomb empty. Looking also into the tomb of blessed John, they found nothing except manna. Christian devotion therefore believes that Christ, God the Son of God, gloriously raised his Mother and exalted her above the heavens, and that blessed John, the virgin and evangelist, who served her on earth, deserved to share her glory in heaven.

It is beyond words how much grace and glory the Lord gave his Mother. This much, however, we know with certainty: the righteous obtain more quickly through the intercession of his Mother whatever they ask of him, and sinners too have often obtained mercy. We have many examples of both, but for the present let these suffice.

## SERMON VI. ON THE BIRTH OF THE NURTURING AND UNVIOLATED VIRGIN MARY

By the love of mutual affection and at the urging of diligent exhortation, we are compelled by certain people most sacred and beloved of God to deliver some address about the most holy and indescribably beloved Virgin, namely Mary, the bride and Mother of the Lord. We are to speak of her birth—not by weaving a historical account, but by adorning it with mystical praises and rejoicing in her benefits. The whole world would be insufficient for the subject of so great a mystery, even if it were gathered into a single order.

The undertaking and its completion will therefore be a merit for those through whose entreaty the vessel reaches harbor without shipwreck. Accordingly, as we recall with bowed humility the birth of the true and eternal King and Lord of ours, so lovable and salutary to every age and every inhabitant of the earth, and commemorate its solemnity in the yearly cycle, we first judged it right to invite communities of both sexes to this divine and glorious feast with certain exhortations. Thus, since the devotion of both groups would consider it wrong not to take part in these sacred celebrations, the united prayers of all may more fully perceive the help of the same holy Virgin extended toward them.

This is a venerable feast, shining with mysteries neither insignificant nor few. It is not to be ranked with the feasts of the other saints, but is as much more excellent as it is clear that she whose luminous beginnings of birth are recited today must be preferred to all human beings.

To praise her magnificence and proclaim her glory, let such abundant praises arise as befit her who surpasses all creatures in preeminence, including the angelic dignity. Where could there ever have been found a place capable of enclosing a majesty equal to the Father, the author of all things, except the womb of Mary, foreknown before the ages? In it, indeed, all divinity was joined with humanity. He who in equality with the Father disposed all things heavenly and earthly prepared, within the narrow enclosure of a virgin, the redemption of his flesh, which was to come and had been promised.

Blessed is such a birth and origin, from whose substance such a virgin was taken, one who would remove the ancient offenses of our parents and raise up the shaken world, which lay under the harsh dominion of a cruel enemy. What, then, should we judge this birth to have been for, except that her holy chastity might become the house and reception of the Son of the Most High? For what else? Was this chastity, either before the birth or after the birth of her worthy pledge, defiled by any contamination? No burden or later succession of children broke her, as usually happens to women who have carried human offspring in their maternal wombs.

Blessed is the fault, but holy the marital union, which from the permitted marriage-bed poured forth into the world such a great, special, and singular glory.

Finally, there can be no doubt that at her conception the life-giving and ardent Spirit filled both parents with a singular gift, and that the guardianship or visitation of the holy angels was never absent from them. Rightly, therefore, the most holy parents of this holy Virgin are greatly to be praised and exalted. In all their instruction they showed themselves so great and worthy that it was entirely fitting for such an offspring to emerge from their stock—an offspring that would become an example of every kind of goodness to former ages and to those that followed.

Blessed—and happier than all other fathers—is the man who deserved to be called the father of such offspring. Blessed also is the man who was granted not many children, but one daughter, who would conceive and bring forth the one Son of God. For it was not fitting that the most holy parents of this singular Virgin should be dishonored by the propagation of many children, since they were destined to be the distinguished guardians and educators of the one Mother of the Lord.

Truly blessed and worthy of all veneration, and to be proclaimed with a kind of sacred privilege, is the mother of this holy woman, who surpassed all mothers by conceiving and bearing the one who would bear her own Creator and the Creator of all.

Rejoice and be glad, O happy woman, because you were endowed with such a daughter, by a gift which no woman before or after you deserved to surpass. How great, we think, must have been the provision of the holy angels for parents so pleasing to God from the beginning of her conception, and how great their watch over such an immense offspring! Is the Holy Spirit to be thought absent from this exceptional girl whom he had determined to overshadow with his power?

No believer doubts that the whole multitude of the heavenly hosts kept watch over her, since they had no doubt that she would be exalted above them. O Virgin, exceedingly and supremely blessed, who is worthy of no comparison and cannot be equaled in the title of chastity! Truly blessed were those ages that deserved, at their appointed time, to receive you from a consecrated womb.

If anyone carefully and diligently investigates why the earlier holy writers did not explain in detail for their faithful followers the temporal beginnings of this aforementioned Virgin’s life, so that they might make them known to all, let them know that those writers were not ignorant of the heresy that would arise on account of the distinguished and wondrous proclamation of this sacred girl. For that reason, if they brought forth anything about her origin, they decided with prudent skill to conceal it from rivals and unbelievers, lest the blind chatter of the faithless should find material with which to assail the maternal bosom of the Church through its manifold deceit.

For even the slight and subtle account—or perhaps written narrative—that they received concerning the birth of the Lord’s mother and the infancy of the Lord himself was distorted by such crafty and ingenious deceit that afterward certain ecclesiastical teachers did not recite even the true things, although they did not entirely reject them.

There does exist, however, an unusual account bearing the name of the illustrious interpreter Jerome. It reports that blessed Matthew, after publishing the Gospel, sealed with his own hand the origin of the aforementioned Virgin and the beginnings of Jesus Christ’s childhood in such obscure Hebrew letters that he did not want it exposed to the excessive and biting jaws of unbelievers. The account further says that these writings were later translated by the aforementioned interpreter into knowledge of the Latin language at the earnest request of certain people.

Because this account has not been inserted among the canons of Sacred Scripture, the unanimous assembly of the Church neither openly chooses it in recitation nor wholly rejects it in refusing to receive it, since some statements or deeds found in that series appear impossible, though the diligence of the faithful does not deny it to those who wish and love to read it.

For us and for all the children of the Church, faith and devout belief are more than sufficient—faith by which we truly confess her to be a Virgin both in her origin and in all her activity. Her father and mother in the flesh are reported to have been Joachim and Anna, names which fit them well according to their interpretation: Joachim is said to mean “preparation of the Lord,” while Anna is interpreted as “grace of God.”

What is suggested by the interpretation of these two names except the grace which they obtained together? Where can grace exist except where preparation of conscience serves? And where can preparation for action have a place except where the grace bestowed by God has gone before? Thus, two graces joined into one, by God’s will, bring forth from themselves a grace of no small consequence, greatly beneficial to all human beings.

Let these few words about the worthy remembrance of the holy parents suffice. Now let us proceed to unfold what Christ has given.

Therefore, receiving with the greatest honor and inward rejoicing the Mother of the supreme Author and Creator, strive with every effort so that the great joy of this day, while it is cultivated and honored by worldly services, may be accompanied by an interior and pure conscience through just and appropriate acts of service. Those who venerate the sacred merits of the devout, and who greatly desire in every way to take part in the feasts of the heavenly hosts, should conduct themselves at the birthdays of the saints in the present life so that they may not afterward be absent from those whose triumphs they rejoice in here.

Accordingly, at this present celebration, earnestly entreat the Queen of all prudent virgins in your prayers. She holds authority among the choirs of holy virgins; by her intercession may she make it possible for the assembly of the holy Church, which honors her on earth with the humble service it can offer, finally to rejoice with her in everlasting gladness over both her exaltation and her glory.

For this is the chief feast, in which the whole army of angels rejoices; in which the prophecies of the prophets are disclosed; in which the writings foretelling the future among the nations are also opened; in which a bride arises, joined to God without equal; and from the chaste substance of whose body light arises in darkness to drive away the clouds of ancient sins.

This, I say, is the day on which the radiant star—indeed, the inseparable light of the sea, that is, of this world—shone forth like the Morning Star, with the loveliness of its beauty, from mortal birth, upon all who are to be saved.

This is the day of joy to be honored, on which, according to the condition of the world, a virginal vessel is prepared, ineffably adorned with divine gifts as with pearls. In it the nature of God would be bodily joined with man, not according to ordinary propagation, but through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Who, I ask, anywhere throughout the earth, either before this Virgin or after her, has been able to hear that the maker of all things, possessor of heaven and earth, King of kings and Lord of lords, the Sun of Justice, the unconquerable Light, enclosed himself within the narrow enclosure of a virgin?

O great and wondrous dispensation of God—or rather, mercy! In order to renew the first-formed parent and his succession of children, who was created, as is clear, so that he might fill the number and order of the proud angels, God did not disdain to become bodily formed from heaven within a virgin’s womb. Thus he might raise up for himself a form united with us—not according to the quantity or quality of the divine substance, but according to bodily growth, joined to him without the stain of sin—and restore it from the place where both the tempter and the one who succumbed fell, expelled through their faithless violation of the commandment.

Behold, therefore, all who gather for the sacred birth of the Virgin: you bring with you all bodily senses, and perhaps you are not now lacking the inner understandings of the heart. There is no doubt that the distributor of his virtues, who has granted each of you his own gift, knows how to distribute his gifts and endowments among individuals according to each person’s labor, so that each may become his dwelling place.

As the Apostle says, one and the same Spirit accomplishes this, distributing himself among all according to the measure of graces and being found uniquely in each person.

Raise your minds, therefore, toward the feast of the present Mother, so that no dwelling of mind or body, no joy, may be found that does not resound wholly in such a glorious birth.

Let both sexes and every condition—those who rule and those who are subject—rejoice together at this celebration, because through this Virgin redemption has come to both: namely, the immaculate Lord, bodily proceeding from her womb.

Let the elders who please God rejoice, because from the court of heaven he descended into the womb of this girl, he who knows how to restore not only souls but also bodies from their ancient ruin to a better youth, according to David’s saying: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 102:5). Let them also imitate the faith of the ancient Fathers, by which it is established that they pleased God, and let it not slip from their memory that through the birth of this Virgin the return to true salvation is granted to them even at the end of their lives.

Let strong young men rejoice on this day, because today the Virgin came forth into this light, from whose hidden depths was born a young man, “more beautiful than the sons of men,” from whose lips all grace was poured forth and carried through the four quarters of the world. Let them also transform bodily strength into vigor of soul, and through the intercession of this sacred Virgin commend their youth to Christ.

Let boys and infants also rejoice at the beginning of this especially young woman, dedicating their growing limbs to Christ and Mary. They have a boy who is a servant of chastity and purity, and Mary, of singular modesty, from whose holy womb Christ’s infancy was received.

Let those who perhaps have exercised authority over the affairs of the world sing with spiritual joy on this day, because through the Virgin came the Lord of all powers, virtues, and dominions.

Let subjects rejoice, and those whom another’s yoke burdens, because at some time the Son of the Virgin—indeed, of God—will release them, if they please him, by driving unjust yokes from their necks; and the Lord will make them superior to their own superiors through the support of his Mother.

Since our address and exhortation have now reached men of every age, it seems right that our prayer should again be directed to that sex from which we know that the Lord took his bodily beginning. He transformed the mark of the first virgin’s curse into the blessing of the second Virgin—the one who, before the creation of the world, had foreknown that his Son would be born at the end of time from that same sex and would bring every joy to all.

Truly blessed and worthy of praise are the benefits of God, which he decreed would come in our times through that sex from which the first earthborn man was offered the medicine of an evil persuasion.

O Eve, then unhappy—not only because of the guilt of disobedience, but also because of the title of the curse; now, however, happy because of the abundant gift of transformation! Rejoice, mother of all, not only because you escaped the destruction of condemnation, but also because from offspring like yourself you brought forth into the world the one who mercifully freed you and your descendants from the shackles of death.

You now mock the one who once infected you with his poisonous persuasion, because you have your maker or parent as a gracious ally, who by his noble triumph drove out the insolent dominion of your enemy.

Depart now, O deceiver and inventor of the ancient crime, from the second guilty sex, because the one who sprang without carnal burden from that same order today caused his mother to come forth into the light.

May the blessing of the second Virgin, sent down from heaven, terrify you from afar—you who rejoiced in the disgrace of the first virgin. For you who rejoiced at the beginning of human creation to expel the first settlers from their happy dwelling are now bound in eternal exultation by the second man, the Son of the Virgin.

Therefore, keeping before our eyes the most holy veneration of the day of the most sacred Virgin, do not exercise your hearts in worldly joys. Fix the whole power of your mind upon those heavenly feasts of the glorious Virgin in which she is honored by the festive services of the angels with everlasting praise.

Strive to follow your Princess, as far as you are able, with festive praises and kindly deeds, so that you may be able to follow the Lamb with her “wherever he goes,” without the failure of your shining lamps (Revelation 14:4).

Today the chief and leader of virgins, foretold by the holy prophets, arises. Let all virgins rejoice with her, because a chaste girl is born who bore the lover of perfect chastity.

Blessed are those who, without the mockery of acquaintance with sin, follow this wondrous Mother of God, as far as lies within them, through the exchange of purity.

Since, then, you joyfully receive her birth, to whose fellowship you do not hesitate to believe that you belong, strive to conduct yourselves in heavenly affairs so that, after overcoming the labors of the fleeting plague, when you have arrived at the desired sight of the divine gate, you may not be rejected when you knock, as is said of the foolish virgins who were rejected by the bridegroom because of their negligence, since they neglected to have oil—that is, good works—in their vessels. Rather, may you be able to proceed with him together into the heavenly palaces, and with his blessed Mother.

Since this solemnity, fitting for all the faithful, is honored as it ought to be by all the gatherings of Catholics, it is especially to be celebrated and honored by sacred virgins, because today the glory of prudent virgins, the flower of the field, the same as the holy Church filled with the most precious pearls, the same as the lily of the valleys, the same as the humble people, has come forth into the world.

Rejoice in every way, all virgins, who know that you have been enriched with so holy and radiant a gift of God. Hope in her who became the possessor of this gift both before childbirth and after giving birth.

Magnify her by the tireless display of good conduct, because, if you preserve with sincere integrity the wholeness of soul and body which you have begun, you will rejoice with her before the presence of the Mother of the Lord, with tambourines of exultation and joy, since you will have the privilege of celebrating with her in the heavenly chambers.

Be cheerful also, girls of tender age, because you too have a girl as Lady of the angels, now entering puberty, as it were, under the first auspices. Call upon the angels to guard your purity, because she, placed in this worldly condition while still young, was already drawing their assistance to herself, with earnest prayer, as she was destined to become their queen.

Rejoice also, mature virgins, and you who have perhaps already reached the limits of old age, because for your long perseverance you will receive not only the promised rewards but also outstanding praise before the heavenly Creator.

Do not withdraw yourselves from the rejoicing of the aforementioned Mother, you married women and those bound by the marriage yoke. For he who granted the palm of integrity to his Mother and to all devout virgins joined you to one another in mutual union by the natural bond, so that, preserving the proper and genuine measure of chastity, you might bear children.

You will not be far from the gift of chastity if you raise your children not for the appetite of lust but for love of succession.

Do not despair, O men and women corrupted in whatever bodily way, because that heavenly dwelling is filled not only from the order of virgins but also from some who were not merely righteous, but even tax collectors and former sinners.

The more you see yourselves to be guilty before the majesty of the Lord, the more earnestly breathe toward the Mother of the Lord, who is full of mercy. You have before the Father as your advocate the Son of the Virgin himself; and he will be gracious toward your sins, so that you may hope for forgiveness from him and from his Mother—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Column 0331C] At your nativity, gracious Mother, be present to us,

Increasing our virtues, removing the weight of our faults.

## SERMON VII. THAT GOD IS ONE IN THE TRINITY

Moses says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). And God said: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (ibid., 3). David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6). Isaiah says: “I am the first and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens” (Isaiah 48:12–13). And shortly afterward: “And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit” (ibid., 16). Haggai says: “My Spirit will be in your midst” (Haggai 2:6). Later: “Behold, I will shake heaven and earth, and the Desired One of all nations will come” (ibid., 7). Isidore says: “Christ shone forth from the Father like brightness from light, like a word from the mouth, like wisdom from the heart.”

### That Christ was begotten by God

David says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). Solomon says in Proverbs: “Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has held the spirit in his hands? Who has bound up the waters as with a garment? Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know?” (Proverbs 30:4). Isaiah says: “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not give birth myself? says the Lord. And shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” says the Lord (Isaiah 66:9).

That he was ineffably begotten before the ages, Micah says: “His origin is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Micah 5:2). David says: “His name endures before the sun” (Psalm 71:17). Solomon says in Proverbs: “When the abysses did not yet exist, I was conceived. When the springs of waters had not yet burst forth, I was brought forth. When he prepared the heavens, I was there, arranging all things with him” (Proverbs 8:24–25, 27, 30). Isaiah says: “In his humiliation judgment was taken away. Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Job says: “From where does the wisdom of God the Father come? For it is hidden from the eyes of human beings and concealed from the birds of heaven” (Job 28:20–21).

### That he is Lord with the Father

David says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Psalm 44:7). Moses says: “God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him” (Genesis 1:27). Zechariah says: “After the glory he sent me to the nations” (Zechariah 2:8), and elsewhere: “Sing praise and rejoice, Zion, because behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me” (Zechariah 2:10).

### That he would come in humility

Isaiah said: “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon a donkey” (Isaiah 62:11; Matthew 21:5). Jeremiah says: “We have sinned against you, O hope of Israel, its savior. Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay? Why will you be like a wandering man, and one who cannot save?” (Jeremiah 14:7–9).

[Col. 0332C] That he was to be put to death, Isaiah says: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7; Acts VIII, 32). Daniel: “The man Gabriel: After seventy weeks Christ shall be put to death” (Dan. IX, 26).

That he was to rise again, David says: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Ps. XV, 9), etc. Again: “I rose, and am still with you” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 18). Hosea: “He will revive us after two days, and on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos. VI, 3).

Concerning the time of his coming, Moses—or Israel—says: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). Daniel: “While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice. He instructed me and spoke to me, saying: Daniel, now I have come forth to teach you, that you may understand. From the beginning of your prayers the word went forth; but I have come to declare it to you, because you are a man of desires. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision: Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be wiped away, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. [Col. 0333A] Know therefore and understand: From the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should again be built, until Christ the ruler, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street shall be rebuilt, and the walls, in the distress of the times. And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be put to death; and his people, who will deny him, shall not be his. And the people, together with the ruler who is to come, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed. He will confirm a covenant with many for one week. And in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease, and in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall endure until the consummation and the end” (Dan. IX, 21–27).

[Col. 0333B] “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall ascend like a young shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. There is in him neither appearance nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no aspect to attract us, and we desired him: despised and last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness; and his face was as though hidden and despised, so that we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our weaknesses and carried our pains, while we thought him as one stricken with leprosy, smitten by God and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. We all went astray like sheep. [Col. 0333C] Each turned aside into his own way; and the Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he shall be led to the slaughter; like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and he shall not open his mouth. From distress and judgment he was taken away. Who shall declare his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living. Because of the crime of my people I struck him. And he shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in weakness. If he should make his life an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Because his soul has labored, he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I shall allot him many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he delivered his soul to death and was reckoned among criminals. And he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors” (Isa. LIII)—so that they might not perish, says the almighty Lord.

Christ says: “There is joy among the angels over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV, 7). The Apostle John says this, among other things, to those already baptized: “Little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin” (1 John II, 1). And: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus [Col. 0334A] Christ the righteous; he is the propitiation for our sins” (ibid., 2). James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James V, 16). Fulgentius: “Whenever a person performs penance, however advanced in years he may be, if he renounces his former sins with his whole heart, and pours out before the Lord tears not only of the body but also of the heart because of them, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil deeds by good works, he shall obtain forgiveness for all his sins.”

Ezekiel: “If the wicked man performs penance for all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all my commandments and does justice, he shall surely live and shall not die. I shall not remember any of his iniquities that he has committed; in the righteousness that he has practiced he shall live. Is it my will that the wicked man should die? says the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his ways and live? But if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the abominations that the wicked man is accustomed to commit, shall he live? None of all his righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered; in the transgression by which he transgressed and in the sin that he committed, in these he shall die. I shall judge each one according to his ways, O house of Israel, says the Lord. Turn and do penance for all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit; and why will you die, O house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the one who dies, says the Lord God. Return and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 21–24, 30–32).

## SERMON VIII (Fragment)

Now, after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—the clearest revelation of our freedom—has shone forth, we are not burdened by the performance of those signs that we now understand, but the Lord himself and apostolic discipline have handed down a few things in place of many, and things very easy to perform and most pure in their observance. Such are the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord; when each person receives them, he recognizes, having been instructed, what they signify, so that we may venerate them not with carnal servitude but rather with spiritual freedom.

[Col. 0334D] “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” he says, “you shall not have life in yourselves.” It seems a crime or an outrage that he commands this. Therefore it is a figure, [Note: [Col. 0333] The interpretation is mystical; and note that these two words, “the heretic will say,” are not found in Petavius’s manuscript D.] he says, commanding only that we share in the Lord’s Passion and that we store gently and profitably in memory the fact that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” Here, through food and drink, he wishes at some point to signify participation in his body and members, which is the holy Church, consisting of his predestined, called, justified, and glorified saints and faithful. Of these, the first has already taken place—that is, predestination; the second and third have taken place, are taking place, and will take place—that is, calling and justification; but the fourth is now held in hope, while in reality it is still future—that is, glorification.

The sacrament of this reality—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is prepared somewhere every day, at fixed intervals of days, on the Lord’s table, and is taken from the Lord’s table: for some unto life, for others unto destruction. But the reality itself, of which it is the sacrament, is unto life for every person and unto destruction for no one who has become a participant in it.

A little later the Lord himself explains what it means to eat his body and drink his blood: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Therefore to eat that food and drink that drink is to remain in Christ and to have him remaining in oneself. [Col. 0335B] Consequently, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, plainly does not eat his flesh or drink his blood—even if he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment.

Again, a little later, Augustine, *Tractate* 26: “The sign that he has eaten and drunk is this: if he remains and is remained in, if he dwells and is dwelt in, if he clings and is not abandoned.”

## Haymo, on the Epistle to the Corinthians

The flesh that the Word of God the Father assumed in the Virgin’s womb in the unity of his person, and the bread that is consecrated in the Church, are one body of Christ. Thus this bread passes into the body of Christ, and there are not two bodies but one body. For the fullness of the divinity that was in him fills this bread; and the very divinity of the Word, which fills heaven and earth and all that is in them, fills the body of Christ, which is sanctified throughout the whole world by many priests, and makes it one body of Christ.

And just as that bread and blood pass into the body of Christ, so everyone who worthily eats it in the Church is one body of Christ, as he himself said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI, 57). Nevertheless, that flesh which he assumed, this bread, and the whole Church do not make three bodies of Christ but one body. And just as those who share in the body and blood of Christ become one body with him, so those who knowingly share in food sacrificed to idols exist as one body with the devil.

[Col. 0335D] From the Symbol of the Council of Ephesus

We must necessarily learn this also: proclaiming according to the flesh the death of the only-begotten Son of God, that is, Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the unbloody service of sacrifice.
