Thus we also approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not as though we were receiving ordinary flesh, God forbid!, nor as though we were sanctified men joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as though we possessed a divine indwelling in that manner, but as receiving flesh truly life-giving and made proper to the Word himself.

For since he exists naturally as God and is Life, because he was united to his own flesh, he declared that it is life-giving. And therefore, although he says to us: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” and so forth, we must not regard it as the flesh of merely one man from among us—for how could human flesh, according to its own nature, be life-giving?—but as flesh truly made his own, who for our sake both became and was called the Son of Man.

Pope Sylvester: “The first Adam, at the serpent’s persuasion, incurred death and, cast out of God’s paradise of delights, ate bread in labor and sweat. But the earth from which he was made was virgin. Therefore it was necessary that the second Adam should be born of a virgin, who would overcome the serpent that tempted him and free from its captivity the man whom the serpent had first conquered. For he who had been victorious over Adam in paradise became the tempter of the Lord in the desert, so that he who had conquered the eater might himself be conquered by the faster. And just as only those who have been born from the flesh of Adam encounter death, so only those who have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit find life, and they have joined Christ’s flesh and blood to their own flesh and blood—Christ who conquered the devil, restored paradise, and opened the gate of eternal life.”

## SERMON IX. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE LORD

*(Works of St. Augustine, vol. V, Appendix, Sermon 194)*

### 1. Eve’s Losses and Mary’s Benefits

Beloved, the desired day of the blessed and ever-venerable Virgin Mary is present for us. Therefore let our earth rejoice with the greatest exultation, illumined by the solemn feast of so great a Virgin. [Col. 0336C] For she is the flower of the field, from whom arose the precious lily of the valleys; through her childbirth nature is changed, and the guilt of our first parents is erased. In her, that phrase of Eve’s misfortune was cut off, in which it is said, “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. III, 16), because she bore the Lord in joy.

Eve mourned; she rejoiced. Eve carried tears; Mary carried joy in her womb, because the former brought forth a sinner, while the latter brought forth the innocent one. A virgin indeed gave birth, because she conceived as a virgin; she gave birth inviolate, because there was no lust in the conception. A miracle occurred in both respects: she was pregnant without corruption, and in childbirth she remained a virgin mother.

An angel descended from heaven, sent by God the Father, at the beginning of our redemption, to greet blessed Mary: “Hail,” the angel said to her, “full of grace, the Lord is with you.” Mary was therefore filled with grace, and Eve was emptied of guilt. Eve’s curse is changed into Mary’s blessing: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” The Lord is with you in your heart, with you in your womb, with you in your body, with you in your help.

### 2. Mary Surpasses All Praise

Rejoice, blessed Virgin: Christ the King has come from his heaven into your womb; from the bosom of the Father he deigns to descend into his mother’s womb. “Blessed are you,” he says, “among women, for you have brought forth life both for men and for women.” The mother of our race brought punishment into the world; the Mother of our Lord brought salvation into the world. Eve was the author of sin; Mary was the author of merit. Eve harmed by killing; Mary benefited by giving life. The former struck; the latter healed. For disobedience is exchanged for obedience, and faith is given in place of faithlessness.

Therefore Mary, joyful, carries the infant; exulting, she embraces her son; she carries him by whom she was carried. Nor did she, as the Sabellians imagine, find the child by chance; but after nine months had run their course, she gave birth to Christ. Let Mary now play the instruments, and amid swift movements let the drums of the woman in childbirth resound. Let joyful choirs sing together, and let sweet songs mingle in alternating melodies.

Hear, therefore, how our tambourine-player sang; for she says: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from this moment all generations shall call me blessed. Because he who is mighty has done great things for me.” The cause, therefore, of such powerful joy was a new miracle. Mary’s new childbirth surpassed Eve’s childbirth, and Mary’s song banished Eve’s lamentation.

### 3. The World’s Salvation Depends on Mary’s Consent. Mary, Mother and Virgin. She Was Wedded to God Himself. Jeremiah’s Prophecy Concerning Mary

Finally, after the presage of that blessing, while the Virgin silently struggled within herself in a debate of the mind over what sort of greeting this might be, the heavenly messenger proceeds (Luke I): “Do not be afraid, Mary; you have found grace with the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.”

But she said: “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore the Holy One who shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.”

You have now heard how this will happen; give your answer, then. Why are you troubled now? You have heard how this will happen: the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, so that you may bear a child and not lose your virginity; you shall bring forth a son and remain undefiled after childbirth.

O blessed Mary, the whole world, held captive, begs your consent; the world has made you, Lady, the pledge of its faith. Do not delay, Virgin: answer the messenger quickly with your word and receive the Son; give your faith, and experience the power. “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

Without delay the messenger departs, and Christ enters the virginal bridal chamber. Blessed Mother of God suddenly becomes pregnant, and from that moment she is proclaimed fortunate throughout all ages. She conceived at once through belief in the word, knowing nothing of a man’s embrace; her womb was filled without being polluted by any human embrace.

Thus the virgin remains a virgin when she conceives, a virgin when pregnant, a virgin when she gives birth, and a virgin after childbirth. Glorious, therefore, is that virginity, and glorious that fertility. Mary rejoices and, in her happiness, marvels that she is a mother; she rejoices that she has given birth through the Holy Spirit. She is not frightened because she has given birth unmarried; rather, she marvels with exultation because she has become a mother.

Let us therefore also rejoice, brothers, on the day of so great a Virgin, who, while she was betrothed to a carpenter, was wedded to the architect of heaven. For a son is promised to her through the visitation of the Holy Spirit. Hearing this, she rejoices and desires to become a mother. What wonder, then, if he is born without corruption who is conceived through sanctification? For it was not fitting that he who brought salvation to us should deprive his mother of the dignity of integrity. He whom earth, sea, and heaven cannot contain is received within the limbs of a single little body.

This is the new thing foretold beforehand in the prophecy of Jeremiah: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth; a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). O woman blessed above women, who knew no man at all and encompassed a man in her womb! Mary encompasses the man by giving faith to the angel, because Eve lost the man by consenting to the serpent.

### 4. The Angel’s Words to Mary. Mary’s Obedience Commended

The angel greets the maiden who knows nothing of a man’s greeting; the Virgin is frightened by the novelty of the words. To her the angel said, as we quoted above: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord.”

“Do not,” he says, “be frightened in my presence, Mother of my Lord. I have come as the minister of your conception, not to bring about the loss of your virginity; he who is to be born from you himself sent me to you. For you shall conceive and bear a son—not a man of ordinary merit, but the Savior of the whole world.

“Recall, Mary, in the book of the prophet Isaiah, the virgin whom you read would give birth (Isa. VII, 14), and rejoice and exult, because you have been deemed worthy to be that virgin. You were prefigured there as the Virgin. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit; you shall be pregnant and shall remain undefiled. You shall indeed bear a son, and you shall suffer no loss of virginity. You shall become pregnant and shall remain an always-untouched mother. You shall feel the weight of the womb and shall not lose the modesty of chastity. Your breasts shall swell, and your generative organs shall remain untouched.”

But she said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

O happy obedience, O remarkable grace, which, while humbly giving faith, caused the maker of heaven to take bodily form within her! The Lord fulfilled in her what he had long before foretold: “I desire obedience rather than sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos. VI, 6). This was true obedience, more pleasing than every sacrifice; this will was more acceptable than all offerings. By this she deserved glory, which she herself later proclaimed: “Behold,” she says, “from this moment all generations shall call me blessed.”

### 5. A Prayer to the Blessed Virgin

O blessed Mary, who could worthily offer you the due acknowledgments of gratitude and the proclamations of praise, since by your singular consent you came to the aid of the lost world? What praises can the frailty of the human race render to you, since through your sole participation it found a way to restoration?

Receive, then, whatever grateful thanks we offer, however slight and however unequal to your merits; and when you have accepted our vows, excuse our faults by praying for us. Admit our prayers into the sanctuary of being heard; bring back to us the remedy of reconciliation. Through you, let what we bring before you be excusable; let what we ask with faithful minds be obtainable. Receive what we offer; grant again what we ask; excuse what we fear.

(For you are the sole hope of sinners; through you we hope for forgiveness of our offenses, and in you, most blessed one, lies our expectation of rewards.)

Holy Mary, help the wretched, assist the fainthearted, strengthen those who weep, pray for the people, intervene for the clergy, intercede for the devout female sex. May all who celebrate your commemoration experience your assistance. Stand ready for the vows of those who ask, and grant to all the desired outcome.

May it be your constant concern to pray for the people of God, you who, blessed, were deemed worthy to bear the price of the world, which lives and reigns forever and ever.

[Col. 0339]

## ON CAPITAL SINS

### I. On the Penance of Laymen

[Col. 0339A]

If anyone kills a person voluntarily, let him do penance for seven years. If he kills one who did not deserve it, let him do penance for ten years. If he kills a deacon, let him do penance for fourteen years. If he kills a priest, let him do penance for twenty-one years.

If anyone kills a person involuntarily, let him do penance for three years. If in a public war, let him do penance for one year.

If anyone cripples a person, let him do penance for three periods of forty days. If anyone removes a principal limb from someone, let him do penance for three and a half years.

If anyone commits a sodomitical act, or has intercourse with an animal, once, let him do penance for seven years. If he has made a habit of it, let him do penance for fourteen years.

If anyone fornicates between the thighs once, let him do penance for four periods of forty days. If he has made a habit of it, for three years. If a young child is subjected to this, let him do penance for one [Col. 0339B] period of forty days. If he does it by himself, let him do penance for two periods of forty days. If he has made a habit of it, let him do penance for one year.

If anyone commits simple adultery, let him do penance for five years. If in a twofold manner, let him do penance for ten years.

If anyone commits abduction, let him do penance for three years, one of them outside the church.

If anyone corrupts a nun, let him do penance for seven years. If anyone corrupts a female relative, let him do penance for five years.

If anyone consults diviners, let him do penance for three years. If anyone proves to be sacrilegious or perjured, [Col. 0340A] let him do penance for seven years.

If anyone swears against the peace, let him do penance for one year with almsgiving, and return. If anyone hates obstinately, let him be excommunicated.

### II. On the Penance of Women

If any woman marries two brothers, let her do penance for five years.

If any woman kills her offspring or deliberately causes an abortion: if the child already lives, let her do penance for twelve years; if it does not yet live, let her do penance afterward for six years; and let her fast every Friday.

If a mother, while sleeping, suffocates her son or daughter, let her do penance for three years.

If an infant falls somewhere and dies, let the parent do penance for one year.

If an infant dies through negligence without baptism, let the parent do penance for three years, one of them outside the church, and let the parent fast every Friday.

A faithful person who has lived well departs from this life secure. A baptized person who performs penance for a time while healthy and reconciled, and afterward lives well, departs secure.

One who, placed in the final necessity, receives penance and dies—I confess that we do not deny him what he asks, but I do not presume to say that he departs in safety. Therefore I give this counsel: abandon what is uncertain and hold fast to what is certain, so that while you are healthy you may perform penance and, when dead, possess security.

[Col. 0339]

# HYMNS AND ECCLESIASTICAL POEMS OF SAINT FULBERT, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

*(Bibliotheca Patrum XVIII, 48)*

## I. HYMN OR PROSE ON SAINT PANTALEON

[Col. 0339C]

How many massacres the Christian flock endured under the impious tyranny of the former Maximian is made clear by the pages of the Scriptures as they have come down to us.

At that time a certain senator named Eustorchius lived in Nicomedia. He had a son named Pantaleon, distinguished both in bodily beauty and in intelligence.

Therefore the father, as fathers do, joyful yet solicitous, had him undertake the liberal arts, so that he would not be a beautiful lamp without light.

Then, for the sake of learning the salutary discipline, he entrusted him to Euphrosinus, Maximian’s physician; under this teacher he began to appear frequently at the palace.

The emperor, having learned of his propriety—and others subsequently attested the same—declared that a person of such character deserved to stand beside Caesar.

[Col. 0340C] Meanwhile, a certain priest in the same town, named Hermolaus, fearing the savage ruler, concealed himself in a hiding place beneath a worn-out covering.

As he often watched Pantaleon passing by, he perceived through the Spirit that he was a vessel of election and modestly invited him inside for a conversation.

He therefore asked the boy’s name, family, and studies; he asked about his sect. The boy, noting the order of the questions, carefully weighed the sequence of his answers.

He answered the first and second questions; then, explaining the rest, he said: “I study the teachings of the physician Hippocrates and of his great predecessor Aesculapius.

“We think these men are gods, who, by their living divine power, approve those things they left described, following them as they restore health to those worn down by illness.”

At this the old man Hermolaus, opening his mature lips, [Col. 0341A] did not attempt to refute everything he had said, but only what it was not unreasonable to address briefly:

“Dear son, receive my words attentively and retain them firmly in your thoughtful memory, for I believe that your teachers do not teach such things.

“We know of two medicines among Christians: one, indeed, from earthly things, and the other from heavenly things; and just as their origins differ, so too does their efficacy.

“Earthly physicians, through long experience, have learned the powers of shoots and the qualities of similar things that alter human bodies.

“Yet no one has proved so accomplished in this art that he would not find some ailments difficult to cure and others altogether incurable.

“This is testified by that man Hippocrates, and by Aesculapius, that man ‘raised from this heaven’ [an uncertain reading]; no physician is reputed greater than they.

“But Christ shines forth as the author of heavenly medicine. By a mere command he can heal the sick and recall the dead from the grave to life.

“He gave sight to one born blind after creating his eyes, and raised Lazarus from an already stinking tomb, besides other wondrous deeds beyond number.

“But what should be said about Christ, when even we, his little servants, perform every kind of wonder in his name? You too, surely, would believe that this will not be denied you.

“Therefore, dear son, gather yourself wisely, taking manifest evidence from the works, so that you may recognize which of them is to be held as God and Lord.”

The boy began to be attracted by such reasoning. Thereafter he visited the priest each day, asked many questions about Christ, and spoke even more.

One day, returning alone from his teacher, as he turned aside from the road, he saw a boy who had been killed and, beside him, the serpent that had killed him.

At this sight he was shaken for a little while and drew back; but as soon as he recovered himself, he grew ardent with lively faith and offered this first prayer to the true God:

“O Jesus, whom Christians declare able to do all things, if you deem me worthy to be joined to the company of your people, grant, I ask, what I now confidently presume to request.

“I pray, therefore, by the power of your great name, that this boy may live again and that this serpent may burst apart, so that you may be proved to be the arbiter of life and death.”

[Col. 0341D] At these words—O faith! O wondrous goodness of God!—the dead child rises, and the water-serpent is split apart; magnificent praise is poured forth to God from a pagan mouth.

“Now I bless you,” he said, “most powerful Jesus. I shall not bless you only once, O God and Lord; may you be blessed throughout all the ages.”

Then the noble young soldier of Christ ran joyfully and went to the feet of the presbyter Hermolaus, earnestly asking that he not be delayed from the sacred fountain of baptism.

## II. HYMN ON SAINT PIATUS

Born in the land of Beneventum from illustrious parents, Piatus, renowned throughout the world, was supported by holy conduct.

Soon, as a boy, he followed Christ with admirable exertions; when grown, he despised the vain glory of the world, keeping nothing of his possessions except a simple garment.

Whatever else he possessed he gave for the support of the poor. Unaware, he went to Rome, already a man, and there joined Dionysius and his holy companions.

Thus, added to the company of so many men, he shone as a light with Dionysius; with these perfected men he was to preach Christ to the Gallic people.

The celebrated Piatus set out toward Tournai, while blessed Dionysius was going to Paris.

By spreading widely the seeds of the holy word throughout Tournai, Piatus converted to Christ thirty thousand men,

besides children and a very great multitude of the second sex—women—who became worshipers of Christ, while genuine miracles of virtue shone forth among them.

He subdued the body’s harsh powers by frugality, so that, strengthened by breaking them, he would not yield to the enemy but would bravely defeat him.

But when Caesar Maximianus heard the fame of Piatus with venomous ears, he ordered him to be seized and immediately killed.

And, as the story relates, he was ready for battle and knew not how to be conquered: bound, he conquered; he conquered the scourges and every assault.

At last he was beheaded amid a joyful company of martyrs; crowned with laurels, he carried the palm to the palace of heaven.

And while the earth received the body of the glorious martyr, a fragrance of heavenly nectar was poured all around.

So that the world might not hesitate concerning the salvation of his spirit, his flesh then proved that he reigns in heaven.

## III. PROSE ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

Let new songs resound for the King who has been born, whose Father made all things and whose mother is the most holy Virgin.

Here the one who begets knows no woman; she is pregnant without a man.

The Word, begotten in the heart of the Father before the ages,

emerges embodied from the mother’s womb after the passage of time.

O wondrous begetting! O astonishing birth! O glorious offspring!

The divinity made human: thus the prophets, taught by your Spirit, foretold that you, Son of God, would be born.

[Col. 0342D] Thus, when you arise from the holy Virgin, the angels announce peace to the earth.

The elements brighten their countenances; all the saints cry out and rejoice.

As they cry “Hail,” save us also, O Deity, one simple *exousia* in three persons.

## IV. HYMN ON THE TRINITY

The lawgiver in Genesis spoke of the Word of God and the Spirit, and King David sang of them in the second psalm after the thirtieth; thus each revealed the Trinity of unity.

Solomon the wise man, together with his holy father, clearly declared that God has a Son, namely the eternal Word begotten in his heart.

The Psalmist bears witness to Moses and Isaiah that the Son with the Father is God and Lord, for nothing is begotten by God the Father except God.

After the Psalmist, Isaiah clearly taught that God would become man, as indeed he did; that dispensation brought salvation forth for us.

And that God would be born of a virgin mother, the same prophet was commanded, before Gabriel, to proclaim; moreover, such a birth befits the author of purity.

The Lawgiver and Daniel marked the time when the King awaited by the nations would come; neglected, he disastrously destroyed the Jewish people.

The prophet showed the supreme King as about to arrive poor and humble, as though already visible; before his face the proud enemy fell.

## V. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT AEGIDIUS THE ABBOT, AT MATINS: INVITATORY

[Col. 0343B]

We adore the King, author of all goodness, who adorns Saint Aegidius with gifts of grace and rewards of righteousness.

## VI. AT MATINS: LAUDS RESPONSES

Let us proclaim the Lord, who reigns always and everywhere, wondrous in his saint Aegidius.

Let us exult to God with rejoicing hearts, who adorned our patron Aegidius with the grace of holiness.

May the merits of your beloved Aegidius support us, O God, so that at last you may find us watchful.

Blessed be the universal Lord, whom blessed Aegidius blesses with us.

Let joyful praise resound to the living and true God in the miracles of his glorious saint Aegidius.

Holy confessor and our patron Aegidius, through whose merits we glorify the Lord, may we experience you interceding for us with him.

We bless you, most merciful God, who have granted us to spend the feast day of blessed Aegidius in your praise; and we earnestly beseech you that we may deserve to be joined in virtue and reward to your saints, to whom we offer honor.

## VII. PROSE AND OTHER RESPONSES

Saint Aegidius, a Greek by nation, sprang from illustrious parents; he was strong in body and keen in intellect. He grew to maturity happily and was liberally educated. In the possession of worldly goods he was not poor, but prudent generosity distributed his immense abundance.

Accordingly, amid prosperity he was not dissolved in pleasure, nor amid hardships was he overcome by the devil. Hunger, thirst, cold, and vigils he counted as delights for the love of Christ. When injured and gravely wounded, he begged forgiveness from those who afflicted him. He believed what he had learned from the true teacher: that souls are finally possessed through patience. Thus, borne upward by virtue to sublime things, he deserved to be adorned with the priestly mitre. For he obtained that saying of the wise man: in the time of anger he became reconciliation.

The faithful confessor of Christ, Aegidius, was illustrious by birth, but far more illustrious in knowledge, virtue, and action. Indeed, it is read that he was born of royal stock. Yet while still young and prepared for the liberal disciplines, he soon equaled the greatest teachers. Since neither fickleness drove the movement of his powerful intellect headlong nor laziness made it sluggish, the grace of God was not lacking to the learned and teachable boy, commending his life by every moral excellence. Already, already, he sparkled outwardly through signs, kindled like a lamp of charity. He gave a garment to a certain sick beggar, a garment with which he himself was not excessively supplied, although he still considered his tutor’s judgment something to be feared. Immediately a memorable sign appeared, by which it became evident that God was cooperating with Aegidius. For as soon as the sick man touched the garment offered to him, he simultaneously recovered his former health. When his parents had died peacefully, he made Christ heir to his patrimony, growing rich by becoming wonderfully poor, while through expenditures on temporal things he gained eternal ones. But when the virtue of the holy man could no longer remain hidden because of its greatness, many flocked to him, seeking benefits for body and soul. Nor, where the cheerful giver was present and what was to be given was abundantly available, were they frustrated of his gift. When wondrous deeds were followed by heralds of praise, he crossed the sea and deprived his native Greece of his presence, judging it unsafe to sell the treasure of a good conscience for the price of light reputation, while remaining in his homeland. It is indeed remarkable how greatly the virtue of frugality grew in him, since for a long time he abstained even from eating bread. Hence it is readily clear that, seeking neither stews nor any enticements of the appetite, he flew away to the realms above.

## VIII. Prose concerning the holy Martin

Among the Fathers of the monastic or clerical order, Martin is remarkable for the excellence of his virtue. Not just anyone among the many, but that solitary man. First, then, bishop of Tours and father of his country. Eloquence, prudent and strong temperance, indeed every holiness, adorned him; that is, charity. Christ clothes himself in the garment which Martin shares with the poor man, granting one not yet reborn signs of such great grace to behold. Soon filled with the holy Spirit by the dew-laden spring of heaven, and relying on divine power, like the mighty Apostle he refutes arisen heresies, expels demons at a command, heals leprosy by a kiss, and restores the dead by prayer. Shall I proclaim how, after fire had been snatched from heaven, he burned temples to their foundations, and by faith moved massive burdens? How he gave the blind stars, made instruments perceptible to the deaf, and fitted the lame for dances, while the mute sang before them? How many thousands of such miracles he performed elude being bound up in a reckoning, like ballast from Pontus.

## IX. Concerning Saint Lambert

A great voice of resonant praise befits you in all things: heaven’s choir is enlarged by such a companion, while earth applauds and resounds, worthy of so great a bishop. O sacred martyr Lambert, receive our vows.

## X. For the king

Prince and strength of kings, at whose command the heaven of the world revolves, the earth stands, and the ages are ordered: grant that King Robert, born of a most noble stock, may so subdue the proud and spare the subjected that, reigning here gloriously, he may once live in heaven.

## XI. Concerning the blessed Virgin

About to give birth to the King of justice, the supreme Sun,

Today Mary, Star of the Sea, has come forth to her rising:

Rejoice, faithful ones, to behold the divine light.

**Response.**

The stock of Jesse brought forth a rod, and the rod a flower,

And upon this flower the gracious Spirit rests;

The Virgin, Mother of God, is the rod; her Son is the flower.

**Response.**

At the Lord’s command, enriching our honor,

Judaea brought forth Mary, as a thorn brings forth a rose,

So that virtue might cover vice, and grace, guilt.

## XII. Concerning the holy Cross

The venerable standard of the King who governs all,

O holy Cross, shining above all the stars of heaven,

You alone bring back to those fallen through a deadly taste

The antidote of life, the everlasting fruit, hanging there;

I honor you, I confess you with reverence, I adore you prostrate.

Christ, beginning, end, resurrection, life,

Reward, light, rest, glory and crown of the saints,

The Lord made an offering for redeeming servants;

Hanging upon you [for “having been hung”], through the wood he cleansed the poisons of the wood,

Opening the gates of life that had been closed.

I am a sharer in so great a freedom, good Shepherd;

Yet, always doing evil, I have never repaid you what was worthy.

Alas! The burden of the many evils

That have accumulated for me has already surpassed the number of the thirsty sands.

But because you seek the good rather than the evil of the sinner,

And he sins more against you who, by sinning, abandons hope,

I flee to you, I entreat you, and I confess to you;

Spare me, I beg; have mercy on me, have mercy on my departed parents

And on those who are in this light.

To those who have done good, repay a hundredfold through yourself,

You who, turning sins to good, forgive them all.

Guide, sustain, guard, protect, and save

All who venerate and pray to you under this sign.

Drive pride far from us, so that all arrogance may cease,

And so that, submissive to you, we may please you with a pure heart.

Protect us continually from the breeze of boastful praise,

And grant us worthy means of offering you thanks.

Wash the stain of envy from our minds,

Pouring into us the fire of heavenly love;

Restrain the goads of anger, make us patient,

And, driving away sadness, make us retain hope amid losses.

Grant that we may flee the crime of greed,

So that we may bring you the work of acceptable piety.

Grant that we may overcome the gluttony of the belly by sobriety,

And chastely avoid the plague of lust,

So that, purified through you and strengthened through you in our powers,

We may steadfastly strive to attain the life above.

## XIII. Concerning fear, hope, and love

The first class of human beings restrains itself from forbidden things,

Either fearing punishment, or prudently seeking a reward,

Or captivated by love of virtue, which has been well approved.

Although they seem to look toward one end,

So that they may avoid vice as deadly poison,

They nevertheless differ in the equality of their merit;

Hence they do not come to united palms of victory.

The first would worship pleasure if he could do so without penalty;

But he says vehemently: “I shrink from the face of the jealous Judge

And from burning in the flames of dreadful Gehenna.”

Would the second do the same if rewards were absent?

But, while weighing true joys with vigilant judgment,

He cautiously postpones idle pleasure.

The third, sincerely good and exceptionally honorable,

Contemplates you, golden Virtue, and loves you:

Indeed, he would rather die than, while alive, be deprived of you.

Thus there are kinds arising from affection,

By which they flee things in such a way that one order differs from another.

For who, when anxious, would hesitate to prefer to fear

The secure rest of hope? Yet he himself suitably

Rises in reverence toward pre-eminent love.

Meanwhile the best Father, observing these things from on high,

Whose keen judgment is deceived by nothing,

Says: “This one is mine, this servant is a member of my household.

This one is conformed to me, this my most beloved offspring.”

Then, weighing out rewards differing according to their merits,

He grants great things to the first, greater things to the second,

And bestows the whole upon the friend of goodness alone.

## XIV. On the same subject, more briefly

Three causes make people avoid sins:

Fear of punishment, hope of reward, and love of goodness.

Although these seem to tend toward one end,

Namely, that they be free from vice, they nevertheless differ in this:

There is a servant, a soldier, or a king’s son; and so,

Fearful at the beginning, one has increase through desire,

While the sincere lover possesses the whole sum of virtue.

But if fear progresses into hope, and hope into love,

From a servant comes a soldier, and from a soldier a son.

He avoids disgrace, whether fearing blows, seeking rewards,

Or loving virtue; they differ as slave, servant,

And king; two make progress, but for the third the state is supreme.

## XV. Fulbert concerning himself

My Maker, my life, my salvation, my only confidence,

Give me counsel, resolve, and strength to pursue it,

Uncertain what I should do and at what end I should finally rest.

For I fear that, having rashly undertaken the episcopate

To preserve the sheep, I may harm them more than benefit them;

And therefore I think I should yield to better men.

But recalling that I did not rely upon wealth or blood

When I mounted the chair, lifted poor from the dunghill,

I judge that this was done by you, as is your custom,

And I would not dare to change my place unless you should indicate it.

Although my conscience, conscious of an unblemished life, gives warning,

You know, holy Father, what is more pleasing to you among these things,

And what is more useful for me. Therefore I beg your mercy

To deign to inspire this counsel in me as I slip,

And to assist me, being present, in bringing it to completion.

## XVI. The same concerning himself

Christ received you, born among the poor, to be nourished,

And nourished and increased you undeserving in such a way

That the world marvels at the gifts bestowed upon you.

For, while you were a boy, he provided excellent teachers for you,

And brought you, as a young man, to the point of becoming a bishop.

Kings, pontiffs, and peoples magnified you,

Judging you to be a prudent and sufficiently faithful servant

Of the gracious Lord. But, shamefully, you yourself, wickedly,

Were neither prudent nor faithful, as the matter makes clear.

For it shames me to recall how wickedly

You injured him and his saints, who opposed your wickedness;

Punishments scarcely any could adequately expiate.

Yet that kind Lord still awaits you

And permits you to live, if perhaps, coming to your senses,

You may destroy sloth through zeal and your guilt through merit.

Virtue is a firm willingness to obey the Lord;

Virtue is an accepted willingness to keep the middle way.

## XVII. Summary of computation concerning signs, months, days, and Nones

The sun, passing through the twelve signs, completes the year,

And traverses all the signs in periods of thirty days,

With ten hours and a half besides.

If these parts are multiplied by twelve,

They make three hundred sixty-five days and

Six hours, which plainly constitute a quarter of a day.

By this number, therefore, the sun completes its proper year.

But because it is clearer to measure the whole than a part of a day,

The company of astrologers wished to measure the year

By three hundred sixty-five days:

Three years are closed, and in the fourth one is added,

Which comes from the quarter-days of four years.

They called this the bissextile year because of this:

At that time it marks the sixth day before the Kalends of March,

Making up the years that have passed and redeeming those to come.

They distributed the sun’s days among the months in this way:

January, August, and sharp-pointed December

Have four days before the Nones, and nineteen before the Kalends;

After the Ides, thirty days, namely one more,

Have March, May, July, the balance-bearing month, October, and the even month:

Six days before the Nones and seventeen before the Kalends;

After the Ides, thirty days, and again one more,

Have June, April, and then November;

Four days before the Nones and eighteen before the Kalends;

After the Ides, thirty days;

But February, poor month,

Has four days before the Nones and sixteen before the Kalends,

And after the Ides only twenty-eight days,

But through the bissextile it rejoices in increasing itself by a ninth.

Each month counts its own Kalends,

And no month fails to count the Ides on the eighth day.

Each month has its marked normal number.

The year has concurrent numbers which, when they coincide,

Make it possible to know on which days the months rightly begin at the Kalends.

These are the normal numbers attached to the months:

Five suit March, and one does not displease April;

May has three, June doubles them for itself;

July likewise has one, while you, August, have four;

September has seven, October brings the matter in twos;

Five henceforth for November, and December repeats seven;

January desires neither three, nor February six.

[Note: March V; April I; May III; June VI; July I; August IV; September VII; October II; November V; December VII; January III; February VI.]

Another number runs concurrently with this for discovering

On which day of the month each month wishes its Kalends to fall.

See it marked for you in seven little lines.

[Note: B. I, II, III, IV; B. VI, VII, I, II; B. IV, V, VI, VII; B. II, III, III, V; B. VII, I, II, III; B. V, VI, VII, I; B. III, IV, V, VI.]

Each one of these seven little lines

Is seen to bear four sums of numbers,

And thus twenty-eight sums are counted,

Divided by a fixed method among the years.

These sums are also called solar epacts.

These concurrent numbers circulate in the years:

One in a bissextile year, two in a non-bissextile year, neither three nor four;

Six are in a bissextile year; do not [use] seven, you twin one;

Four in a bissextile year, five and six, seven elsewhere;

Six in a bissextile year, three in a common year, five separately;

Seven bissextile, four, two, and three refuse;

Five bissextile, six, seven, and one reject;

Do not join three bissextile with four or five, nor with six.

## XVIII. Concerning the nightingale

Let the golden lyre resound with bright melodies;

Let the simple string be stretched with a fifteenfold voice;

Let it now return its first sound according to the Hypodorian mode;

Let us give praise to the nightingale in instrumental song,

Singing a sweet melody as music teaches,

Without whose art no song possesses true power.

When, in the new springtime of the earth, the shoots are produced,

The woodland branches grow green all around;

When sweet fragrance blazes through the flowering grasses,

The nightingale, conscious of its sweet sound, grows joyful,

And, modulating, extending the breath of its throat,

It gives back the praises of spring and summer:

It attends night and day with a sweet-sounding voice,

Giving the sleeping rest through the intervals of its songs,

And also beautiful solace to the traveler from his labor;

The beauty of its voice is clearer than the cithara.

Every little flock of birds is overcome by its singing;

It fills the woods and all the groves with melodies,

Made exceedingly glorious by the joy of spring;

Flying, it climbs the high treetops,

And grows eager enough to whistle festive songs.

The swan yields, resounding toward the leafy shade;

The swan yields, and its own sweet melody;

The tambourine-player and the resonant flute yield to you:

For although you may seem very small in body,

All are nevertheless captivated by your melody.

No one gave your voice these sweet songs

Except the heavenly King alone, who governs all things.

## XIX. Concerning Saint Caraunus

You shine, abundantly dear Caraunus,

And you signify this by your name.

Therefore we sing joyful little lyric verses to you,

And in pious love, pious martyr,

Ask pardon for us.

Rome, proud of its titles, brought forth from its parents

This distinguished boy of powerful intellect,

Easy in spirit, handsome in appearance.

You too, martyr, ask pardon for us.

Rich meals commonly disturb the regimen of the day;

You indulge your stomach, and drunkenness troubles your mind evilly.

If you spare the feasts, either criticism or praise follows.

To keep the middle way is labor, and one must take great care

That it not produce sadness for you, as is its custom.

Therefore, if you can, avoid these meals entirely;

But if that is not permitted, recline cheerful and cautious,

And take only a little of everything prescribed for you by your rule;

Nor should many small portions add up to an excessive total.

## XX. Hymn

Honor the holy Father simply,

O company of the poor,

And honor him as much as you know through praises;

He who brings subject ages

Back to the rule from which they had strayed,

Powerful to renew as well as to create,

And who comes to the condemned through grace,

Now comes to your long labor,

Bringing aid of peace and rest.

Now the leaders, previously unaccustomed

To the reasoning of laws,

Energetically undertake what they rightly learn;

The plunderer restrains his hand, mindful of the gallows,

And, with the robber before him,

The unarmed traveler sings aloud;

The wandering vine is restrained

By Saturn’s tooth,

And the thorn-covered earth grows gentle through cultivation.

The lance rejoices, the sword rejoices

To become a plowshare;

Peace enriches the lowly and impoverishes the proud.

Hail, supreme Father; bring complete salvation

To all who love the rest of peace,

And crush with your powerful right hand

Those who desire wars,

The evil one’s sons, destined for Gehenna.

## XXI. The degrees of chastity

Chaste perfection is completed in six degrees:

First, while awake, to seek not to know wanton arousal;

Next, not to turn lascivious thoughts over in the heart for long;

Then, not even lightly to desire what one sees in appearance;

The fourth is that the sexual organ not be moved even naturally;

The fifth, at the mention of Venus, not to let the mind wander;

The last, in sleep, not to play with any phantasm.

No one seizes this for himself; the grace of Christ grants it.

Nevertheless, a long-lasting remedy of diet must be maintained:

A measured quantity of solid food, a simple half-measure of Falernian wine;

Moreover, labor, vigils, and frequent prayer,

Lest fattened flesh kill modesty when it grows weak.

He is chaste whom no desire moves while awake,

And whom no foul illusion can violate while asleep.

## XXII. Prayer to God

You who are shown to have fashioned the world from nothing

(For no matter coeval with you existed),

And who, by an easy command, at a time known to you, will dissolve it,

After it has thereafter existed for just as long.

How small is this span of ours, in which you command the ages to roll on

While wars are vigorously waged together with vices.

Show yourself always present as King with your own soldiers,

Invigorating us to fight well.

## XXIII. Other prayers

Lord, unbegotten King and Father, true essence, have mercy.

Lord, fountain of light and creator of things, have mercy.

Lord, who marked us with the likeness of your image, have mercy.

Lord, who are perfect wisdom, have mercy.

Lord, rising light, through whom all things exist, have mercy.

Lord, form of God, sharer in humanity, have mercy.

Lord, Spirit, power of life-giving life, have mercy.

Lord, life of both, in whom all things exist, have mercy.

Lord, purifier of crimes, giver of grace; because of

our offenses do not abandon us, O comforter

of the sorrowing soul, have mercy.

## XXIV. Hymn

I bring you news from above:

Christ is born, ruler of the world,

In Bethlehem of Judah, for so the prophet

Had said before.

The joyful choir of angels sings of him;

The star declares him, the princes of the East come

To celebrate worship worthy of him.

Mystical gifts:

They offer frankincense to God, myrrh to the tomb,

And gold to the fitting King;

While honoring the One, they remember the Three:

Three give three gifts.

Let us sing glory to the triune Monad,

With God the divine Father and the Son,

And also to the Spirit proceeding from both,

With faithful heart.

## XXV. Story

In the *Lives of the Fathers of old* I read something pleasing,

Yet suitable as an example, which I tell you in rhythmic form:

Abbot John, small in stature but not in virtues,

Said to his taller companion, who was with him in the desert:

“I wish to live securely like an angel,

Enjoying neither clothing nor food produced by the work of hands.”

The brother replied: “I advise you not to be hasty in your undertaking;

It may later be better for you not to have begun it.”

But he answered: “Whoever does not fight neither falls nor conquers,”

And naked entered the inner desert.

He scarcely lasted there seven days on a diet of grass;

On the eighth day hunger commanded him to return to his companion,

Who, with the door closed late in the day, sat safely in his cell.

When the younger man called in a weak voice, “Brother, open!

John, in need of help, stands at the familiar door;

Let not your compassion reject one whom necessity has reduced,”

The other replied from within: “John has become an angel.

He gazes upon the hinges of heaven and no longer cares for human beings.”

Outside, John kept watch and endured the evil night,

And performed this penance beyond his voluntary one.

When morning came, he was admitted and sufficiently scorched by words;

Thus, intent upon the crusts, he patiently accepted everything.

Refreshed, he gave thanks to the Lord and to his companion;

Then he tried to move a little rake with his languid arms,

Corrected by hardship for his excessive levity.

When he could not be an angel, he learned to be a good man.

## XXVI. Hymn

I beg you, gracious Spirit,

Temper and govern the instrument of our mind

With the plectrum of the tongue,

To whose praise we are eagerly moved.

You are the pure love of God the Father and the Son,

By which they kindly cherish one another,

And which the Creator hears to be good

Among created things.

You breathe faith and proclaim sacred laws.

Generous in grace, with pardon discovered,

Victor over errors, witness

To worthy truth.

When you come, following tears wash away guilt;

The fire of life grows warm again,

And the heart of the repentant burns

With the incense of piety.

Let us sing glory to the triune Monad,

With God the divine Father and the Son;

And to the Spirit proceeding from both,

With faithful heart.

## XXVII. Easter hymn

[Note: Rare in old breviaries during Eastertide. 2. Cassiodorus: “with the new sweetness of honey.” Bede: “of honey.” Hilary: *melum* (“melody,” Greek μέλος) is said to derive from *mel* (“honey”), because just as honey is made from different kinds of things, so melody is made from different notes; hence the Psalmist: “Sing to the Lord a new song.” 5. Compare Revelation 5. Hilary: The *Physiologus* relates that the lion revives its cub after three days by its roar; so the Father revives the Son. 7. John 5:28. Hilary and Wimpfeling: “let it resound.” 8–12. Cornelius: Tartarus is imagined to vomit out the human being as swallowed prey (Revelation 20:13), and Christ is imagined to walk as a triumphant conqueror, drawing with him a great crowd of those liberated from servitude. The poet speaks of the fathers in limbo. Hilary, by reading it in this way, makes it apply to all Christians. 14. Ludovicus: “most exalted.” 16. Cassiodorus and Hilary: “having done likewise.” 17–20. Missing in Ludeck; 21–24 missing in Fabricius. 20. “To arrange”: a military term. 21. Sebastian Brant and Hilary: “things unknown to the mind”; thus, according to Hilary, they are incomprehensible to human ability.] (*DANIEL, Thesaurus hymnologicus*, I, 221.)

The choir of the new Jerusalem

Let it bring forth the new sweetness of honey,

Celebrating with sober joys

The joy of Easter.

[5] When Christ, the unconquered lion,

Rising after the dragon has been crushed,

Awakens the dead

By making his living voice resound.

The wicked Tartarus,

Which had devoured its prey,

Spewed it back;

The liberated throngs

[Col. 0352C] follow Jesus.

He triumphs splendidly

And, worthy of his greatness,

Makes the homeland of earth and heaven

One commonwealth.

Let us, his suppliant soldiers,

Pray in song to the King himself,

That in his most glorious palace

He may arrange us.

[Col. 0352D] Throughout the ages that know no end,

Glory be to the supreme Father,

And honor with the Son

And the Spirit, the Paraclete.

# Saint Fulbert’s verses concerning the ounce, its parts, and the scruple

(Edited by Charles de Villiers, theologian of Paris, in the notes to Fulbert’s Letter 113, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XVIII, p. 55.)

## Concerning the ounce and its parts

An ounce contains twenty-four scruples:

Its half is called a *stater*, or *semiuncia*;

A third part is two *seclae*, and likewise a *duella*;

A quarter is a *siclus*, or *sicilicus*, or finally a *sikel*;

A sixth is usually called a *sextula*, and sometimes a *secla*;

An eighth is called a *drachma* [lacuna].

## Concerning the scruple and its parts

Likewise, one *scirpus* is composed of eight *calces*;

Half a scruple is an *obolus*; a quarter is a *cerates*;

From this it pleased them to make a sixth and call it a sixth;

The last is a *calx*, weighing two grains of chickpea.

# Proclamation before they say “The peace of the Lord”

Composed by Lord Fulbert against the adversaries of the Church.

(Dunod, *Histoire de Besançon* I, Documents, p. VIII.)

In a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart, before your holy altar and your most sacred body and blood, Lord Jesus, Redeemer of the world, we approach; and concerning our sins, for which we are justly afflicted, we declare ourselves guilty before you. To you, Lord Jesus, we come; prostrate before you we cry out, because the wicked and proud, trusting in their own strength, rise up against us from every side. They invade, plunder, and devastate the lands of Saint John and Saint Stephen. They force your poor worshipers there to live in sorrow, hunger, and nakedness. They also kill them with tortures and swords; they seize our goods by which we ought to live in your holy service, and which blessed souls left to this place for their salvation, and they violently take them from us as well.

This Church of yours, Lord, which you founded in ancient times and exalted in honor of Saint John the Apostle and your protomartyr Saint Stephen, sits in sadness, and there is no one to console and liberate her except you, our God. Rise up, Lord Jesus, to our aid; strengthen us and help us. Overcome those who attack us. Break also the pride of those who afflict and wish to afflict this place and us. You know, Lord, who they are and their names; their bodies and hearts were known to you before they were born. Therefore, Lord, according to your knowledge, justify them by your power; make them recognize, as pleases you, their evil deeds, and free us in your mercy. Do not despise us, Lord, as we cry to you, but for the glory of your name and your mercy visit us in peace, and rescue us from our present distress.

# Saint Fulbert’s charters

## I. For the monks of the Major Monastery of Tours

(Baluze, *Concilia Gallicana Narbonensis*, Appendix, p. 77.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Fulbert, [Col. 0354B] not indeed by my own merits but by the prevenient grace of the Redeemer, bishop of Chartres.

“We wish it to be known to all our fellow presbyters and deacons, or to all persons of either order, namely clergy and monks, both those now present and those who will succeed in future times, how the monks of Saint Martin’s Major Monastery came into our presence, humbly asking that, for the love of almighty God and of holy Mary, Mother of God, and likewise of the aforesaid confessor Martin, we should permit them to buy and permanently possess a certain church named Navoïl, belonging to the altar of the holy and most blessed Virgin Mary. This we do, with the consent of the knight Hilgodius, to whom it appears to belong by our benefice.

“Thus they buy it and claim it for themselves in perpetuity at a minimal price from a certain vassal named Robert, from his two sons Arnulf and Notbert, and from their mother. These hold the same church from Walverius, son of Gaucelin, under whose command and consent they grant it to the monks of Saint Martin under a sale, to be held by them thereafter. They therefore have [lacuna] and hold it, and without any disturbance from any bishop or any person, from this day forward the monks serving God and Saint Martin there shall securely hold and possess the aforesaid church and whatever appears to belong to it.

“This church is situated in the county of Vendôme, not far from the castle itself. The names of the witnesses who were brought forward to hear this are written below: Theoderic, the treasurer; Sigo, the precentor; Hildegarius Pupilla; Giroinus; Rainaldus, the vicedominus; Girardus Bodellus; and Gauslinus.”

## II. Concerning Jeranivillare given by precarious tenure to the knight Gradulfus, and Palisiacum given by him in compensation

Before the year 1024.

[Guérard, *Documents inédits sur l’histoire de France*, vol. I, p. 99, from the cartulary of the Abbey of Saint-Père of Chartres.]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Fulbert, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, and Magenardus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, and the community of brothers.

“We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, how a certain knight named Gradulfus came before us and humbly requested that we should grant him, under precarious tenure, a certain piece of land belonging to our aforesaid monastery, and that he should assign to our uses a certain allod of his own in compensation, on the condition that, as long as he and his wife, named Oda, in whose dowry the aforesaid allod lies, should live, they should hold both properties; but after their death both should remain to the brothers.

“We willingly agreed to his requests, with the consent of Count Odo, in whose county both lands of which we speak are situated. Our land, which he requests to have under precarious tenure, is situated in the county of Chartres and is called Jeranivillare; while the allod by which he compensates us, situated in the county of Dreux [B., Dorcasini], above the river Blaise, is called Palisiacum.

“We therefore grant our land of Jeranivillare to the aforementioned Gradulfus under precarious tenure, so that as long as he and his aforesaid wife Oda live, they may hold both; but after their death, both the land that we give and the aforesaid allod shall come peacefully and securely to the uses of the brothers. It was further agreed that this arrangement of ours should be written in two charters, one of which the aforesaid knight should have, while the other should remain with us.

“And so that this record may remain firm, we have affixed our names and subscribed the names of Count Odo and of those who were chiefly involved in this transaction:

“Sign of Fulbert, bishop. Sign of Odo, count. Sign of Magenardus, abbot. Sign of Durandus, dean. Sign of Arnulfus. Sign of Marcuinus. Sign of Richerius. Sign of Beringerius. Sign of Wadricus. Sign of Letaldus. Sign of Christopher. Sign of Gauzbertus. Sign of Guinefredus. Sign of Otbertus. Sign of Hubertus. Sign of Hubertus. Sign of Rodbertus, and of the others.”

After the death of Gradulfus and his wife Oda, the monks suffered many wrongs concerning the aforesaid lands from the relatives of those persons, who said that what their relatives had evidently held before them rightfully belonged to them. Thus, after giving an enormous sum of money, the monks at last, with God’s help, recovered the properties for their own uses.

# Life of Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, written, it seems, by Saint Fulbert

(At Surius, 13 December.)

## Prologue

The vain hope of temporal glory has often deceived many secular people, whom an immoderate desire for praise inflamed to undertake labors and endure dangers. They thought they would live after death if they extended the memory of their name to posterity, while an empty tale recited them under the triumphal titles of corruptible pomp.

Some philosophers, vainly stirred by this appearance of things and seeking the favor of popular applause, while they felt themselves weak in enduring labors, applied themselves to writing the deeds of secular men—not with comparable labor, but in shared error. Since they knew of no other life, they judged that this could profit them as a kind of fruit of blessedness, if, through the occasion of writing, they left the abilities of their ingenuity to posterity’s memory.

But concerning these things I beg my reader to ask: what did one confer upon the other, or either upon himself, through such studies? For what did the Dardanian leader or the fierce Rutulian contribute to his Maro, or this man to that one, when they gave their bodies to worms and their souls to cruel fires? A fitting, but certainly lamentable, reward for their errors!

Their intention aspired to nothing concerning true blessedness; it is clear that they sought the fruit of their labors in things from which no cause of salvation could arise for them, nor would they be useful to the memory of posterity. But since it is written, “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psalm 111), although our fragile memory is not sufficient for the glory of those whose names are written in the book of life, it is nevertheless most worthy and supremely useful to recall, for the praise of the Lord, the deeds worthy of imitation of those whose holy life will benefit readers for their edification and hearers for the emulation of virtues.

Therefore, relying not on the aid of ingenious skill but trusting that I could be helped by the grace of the Holy Spirit, I have resolved to write a few things from among the many which heavenly grace deigned to perform through blessed Autbert, for God’s praise and for the manifestation of his faithful confessor. I learned these either from the report of highly approved men or found them written here and there in sacred documents, so that his holy community might have something with which to praise the Creator as it exercises itself in divine worship on the solemn day, and something for the imitation of holy works by which it may progress.

In this matter I beg my reader: if perhaps an uncultivated style should strike ears accustomed to refinement, let him learn to grant pardon for inexperience, since I know that nothing human is perfect. Let the writer’s boldness not risk so much in his eyes as the dignity of the one commanding avails.

The curious reader ought not demand from us that the deeds of the blessed man be written in continuous order—namely, from what ancestry he was born, by what beginnings his holy childhood, or by what miracles his youth became illustrious—when he understands that the sum of his miracles and a large part of them remain hidden from our knowledge. It is indeed uncertain whether this should be attributed to the negligence of writers or ascribed to the just judgment of God, who closes up the stars as though under a seal (Job 9), while, because of the sins of the wicked, the life of the good is hidden.

# I

Therefore, taking pity on the lot of human perdition, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, having accomplished the mysteries of the Father’s dispensation and being about to return to heaven and present before the Father’s gaze the new glory of his victorious flesh, chose new cultivators for the Church at her birth, to whom the care of the new flock would be entrusted. Illuminated by the light of faith and enriched by the gift of the Holy Spirit, they would illumine with the light of truth the world darkened by the shadows of ignorance, and would constantly cut away from the field of the Church the poisonous seeds of the ancient seducer.

The first executors of this Lord’s institution were the disciples, and afterward their successors, namely, the holy teachers whom divine providence foreordained, at the end of the world’s old age, to cultivate the minds of the faithful. Receiving the spiritual talents of gifts from the supreme Master of the household and spending them at interest in the business of souls, they strove to increase them all the more zealously because they were more certain of the Rewarder’s recompense, and because they were terrified by the Gospel sentence concerning the condemnation of the slothful servant.

Among these there shone forth the holy man, Lord Autbert, a most approved priest of Christ, in the time of the illustrious Dagobert, king of the Franks. From the very years of his sacred childhood, inspired by heavenly grace, he surpassed men advanced in years by the holiness of his conduct. Finally, entrusted to literary studies and properly instructed in ecclesiastical decrees, advancing through each grade as successive increases in virtue followed, he was raised to the summit of priestly honor.

It happened, then, by the lot of mortal nature, that Albert, bishop of the see of Cambrai, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, departed from this world. Since divine action was beneficially arranging all things, Autbert, a distinguished man and worthy successor, advancing from virtue to virtue, obtained the episcopal dignity of that same see.

Moreover, the Author of human salvation, foreseeing that the ancient enemy would pursue the Lord’s flock with all the greater fury the nearer he knew the end of the age to be—since nothing remained that he could further attempt by his arts—prepared for us a strong obstacle against the power of his tyranny, giving us Autbert, namely, the most vigilant shepherd of his flock and the most faithful guardian of souls.

**[Col. 0358A]**

# II

Once established in the episcopal see, what and how great a man he was in his life there is beyond our ability to unfold. He rises higher than any speech can contain. For the animal man cannot comprehend how great he was in the eyes of the supreme Creator, with whose lovers of the world he had nothing in common except that he seemed to be constrained by the obligations of pastoral care. If he could have withdrawn from that care without offense, it is truly believed that he would have chosen the desert rather than a monastery.

He was therefore visited by peoples who streamed to him in crowds from neighboring and distant cities. Stirred by the fame of his extraordinary way of life, they eagerly thirsted to see him. Indeed, unless the difference of sex prevents it, and unless the dignity of the persons makes the comparison inappropriate, one might see the queen of the South seeking Solomon’s wisdom—that is, a king hastening to consult a bishop.

For Dagobert, who at that time ruled the monarchy of the kingdom among the Franks, once aroused by reports of the man’s most celebrated reputation, laid aside the haughtiness of royal majesty and frequently came to him. Although raised to the power of an earthly kingdom, he nevertheless desired to be instructed by the man of God concerning the acquisition of the heavenly kingdom.

When Autbert familiarly warned him about the cares of the temporal kingdom, the blessedness of the future age, the fear of judgment, and the hope of eternity, Dagobert gladly listened to him and, having heard him, did many things—not as the incestuous Herod seemed to have listened to John rebuking him, but as the faithful Hezekiah listened to Isaiah comforting him.

Yet it cannot be estimated how great a joy filled the king’s spirit because he had been judged worthy to receive such a man as his guest, to be strengthened by his blessing, and to be built up by his conversation. Therefore, lest he seem ungrateful for such great benefits, he burned inwardly with the desire to find some way of winning the holy man’s favor more abundantly.

At last he learned from one of Autbert’s household that he could earn this favor most easily in no other way than by arranging for the properties of the church of Blessed Mary, which the venerable Father himself, by God’s authority, served, to be increased from his own resources. For nothing in transitory possessions pleased the bishop except what was spent for the uses of the church.

Then the king, being a cheerful giver, donated to the brothers who served in the oratory of Blessed Mary one royal fisc as a provision for the brothers’ temporal needs. Antiquity had given it the name Oveng.

**[Col. 0358B]**

# III

But while we praise the king by exalting his gentleness, no one can so much estimate as admire how steadfast was the humility of the man of God, who amid so much royal attentiveness could not be overthrown by any temptation to vanity.

We have observed this vice excessively in many people: at the greeting or feigned flattery of a single little man, one may see them easily inflated by the spirit of boastfulness. If they were said to have acted through some appearance or false human estimate, they would undoubtedly consider themselves prophets, although they had received no gifts.

But the just man could not be cast down from the citadel of humility by any impulse of boastfulness. Even the elevation of episcopal honor itself—which for most people usually supplies fuel for pomp—provided him with more material for lowliness.

Indeed, whenever on some occasion of a miracle the shouting of the people was aroused, he tried, with a higher purpose, to restrain the crowd’s admiration, saying that the deed had not been the work of his faith but of divine power. He piously reflected that consciousness of weakness was better than the vanity of virtues, so that he seemed to say with the Apostle: “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (1 Corinthians 12).

**[Col. 0358C]**

# IV

Therefore, unless today’s solemnity of our Father reminded us to bind ourselves more attentively to the praises of the heavenly King, those whom we have heard being scandalized because they sought signs against the holy man ought to have been struck by the blow of evangelical severity, which says: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matthew 12), so that, once the vice of Pharisaic jealousy had been completely purged, they might weigh the words of evangelical faith—words spoken by the very author of signs: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14).

Thus, when the outward miracles on which formerly carnal eyes and weak hearers depended had ceased, they should at last have learned to value life, not signs—for life contributes much more effectively to the imitation of virtues than the display of bodily miracles.

In former times visible things drew the hearts of hearers toward the end of invisible things, while what was done wondrously outside made what was being accomplished within perceptible. Now, however, it is life, not signs, that must be sought, because, through God’s action, the number of the faithful has increased.

But lest anyone perhaps suppose that blessed Autbert needed this excuse for the lack of signs—that we should speak of his life rather than of his miracles—there are certainly, besides those things which he concealed to avoid boastfulness and did not allow to come to human notice, many deeds that became known to people, since they could not be hidden. From these one may estimate how great were those deeds that he performed alone, with no witness.

For Scripture says: “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Proverbs 10). Those things concerning the man of God could have been sufficient for faithful hearers as a mark of virtue which he appears to have accomplished through his imitators, because they received from him the fact that they shone through signs and miracles: trampling upon the glory of the world, avoiding the allurements of the flesh, despising possessions, and cleaving with their whole heart to the Creator alone.

**[Col. 0358D]**

# V

Since those who sought a sign from heaven received from the Lord the sign of Jonah, yet did not believe in the sign of Jonah rising from the dead through a man recalled as if from the belly of a whale, the merits of the blessed pontiff must be considered.

There was in the church of Blessed Mary, built within the walls of the see of Cambrai, a certain boy of noble lineage, born in a village called Vallis by its inhabitants, named Landelin. His parents entrusted him to blessed Autbert so that he might be renewed in the baptismal font and instructed in sacred disciplines for the salvation of their souls.

Although still held back by the weakness of tender age, he displayed in his conduct certain signs of future holiness. For this reason the ancient enemy of the human race, who from the beginning strives to resist good works, inflamed by the torches of envy, set himself against him in temptation, intending both to deprive the holy man of the fruit of his labor and to wound the boy with the blow of death.

He feared that, through the example of the boy’s way of life, many might one day be stirred to carry out the rule of righteous conduct. But from the very point at which the impure enemy aroused the audacity of his malice against blessed Autbert, he unwillingly supplied him with an opportunity for victory.

Since the boy was still being governed under the strict discipline of a prudent teacher, and no opportunity for insolence was open to him, the malignant spirit was ashamed of a victory frustrated. But when the youth grew into the strength of manhood, an age that always seems freer to dare anything, the wicked enemy immediately prepared himself with all his strength for the arts of rebellion.

He began to assault the young man’s mind with subtle temptation and to inject various unlawful thoughts. At one time he brought before him the memory of his earthly inheritance, the nobility of his lineage, the numerous dignity of his family, the glory of possessions, and the other blandishments of a more wanton life.

Some of his relatives and companions, who appeared to love him with the affection of a purer grace, while thinking they were advising the young man, attacked him more dangerously with the blows of evil persuasion. They too, driven by the same spirit, declared that his distinguished youthful appearance was unworthy of being occupied with ecclesiastical observances. Rather, he ought to imitate the courage of his ancient parents, who had acquired great worldly glory through the arts of secular military service.

As for the monastic rule, they said, it was intolerable—easy to undertake, difficult to carry out—and should be desired by no one except one whom a fearful spirit, a weaker age, or an incapacity for any honorable display of courage compelled to conquer ingloriously and remain unknown.

**[Col. 0359A]**

But, as commonly happens, every evil speech easily infects the mind of the hearer, since constant conversations and prolonged familiarity usually pour the plague into minds. Even when there is tranquility of character, just as a calm pond rises into waves when winds stir it, so a good nature is tossed about by wicked advisers.

Youth is plainly an age vulnerable to deception and is easily misled when surrounded by the snares of frauds. Even old age scarcely withstands such deceits; for even prudence is often provoked when surrounded by crafty snares.

Therefore, if more mature experience is often shaken and cannot look after itself, what wonder if an immature age could not help itself when it was pressed by such great snares?

By God’s provident dispensation, the malice of the wicked seducer was therefore permitted to prevail for a time—not for the final outcome of their common ruin, but so that God’s works and the merits of blessed Autbert might be revealed in him.

Thus it happened that the impure enemy did not restrain himself from his undertaking until he had gradually bent the unwary youth toward his own judgment.

# VI

Made softer by the blandishments of a pernicious affection, he swiftly abandoned the monastery like a horse without a bridle that has rejected its rider. Applying himself to the arms of secular warfare, he afterward devoted himself entirely to the pursuit of plunder.

To those whom he heard were willing participants in such business, he attached himself in complete intimacy, all the more inclined to crimes because confidence in impunity and the authority of his powerful lineage encouraged him.

Fearing that anxious parents might inquire after him, and that he might be found through the evidence of his name, he changed the name by which he was accustomed to be called and ordered himself to be called Maurosus.

The surname was not inappropriate to such pursuits: stripped of the white garment of ecclesiastical purity, he had put on, through his zeal for robbery, the clandestine mind of Mauritanian unbelief, and had hidden himself in the lairs of perdition.

When the man of God heard this report, he groaned over his brother’s ruin more deeply than can be expressed. He also raged in indignation at the presumption of the adversary.

Yet what could he do? He therefore resorted to the one remedy that had always been familiar to him: the remedy of prayer. With many prayers for the salvation of the erring youth, he begged the Lord to rescue the captive soul from the enemy’s snare through the regard of his gratuitous compassion, lest the unclean enemy boast over the loss of the Lord’s flock.

The holy man’s petition could not be empty, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Psalm 33).

Moreover, the lover of human salvation foresaw a fitting occasion for his servant, by which he would both fulfill the effect of the devout petition and restore the erring son to holy Mother Church.

**[Col. 0359B]**

# VII

It happened that he was preparing, as usual with his accomplices, to plunder the house of a certain rich man. When darkness had already descended and the dreadful night was growing black—the night in which they were hastening to complete their wicked deed—it happened, by God’s merciful arrangement, that one of the thieves mentioned above was overtaken by death and breathed out his spirit.

His soul, released from the prison of the body, had been dragged by the devil, as its sins demanded, into the infernal strongholds. While his companions kept watch at the funeral rites with an empty show of religion, Maurosus, deeply afflicted by grief for the dead man, gave himself a little rest from exhaustion and sorrow.

By God’s will, and with the merits of blessed Autbert assisting, the young man was permitted to see with what punishments that wretched soul was being tortured in hell and with what fires of avenging flame it was burning. It was as though, by divine will, this was given to the erring youth as an example of fear, so that from this consideration he might understand how great a punishment for his guilt threatened him, since a similar guilt accused him through his fellowship in crime.

# VIII

Overwhelmed by the terror of such a vision, the young man burned inwardly, wondering how he might escape the judgment of so strict a punishment. Yet, from considering his crime, there arose something like despair of recovery.

Then, falling to the ground, he accused himself in the words of a tearful lament. An angel of the Lord stood beside him and said:

“Why, pitiable young man? Why do you cry out? Why weary the air with fruitless tears? Why do you call insistently upon the one whom you did not fear to offend? Is this the robe that you put on at the very font of regeneration? Is this the faith of your profession that you promised to keep when you renounced Satan and his works?

“Why do you shrink from the heavenly faces whose fellow citizen you were to be, if you had listened to Autbert? Behold how the Son of God has become the devil’s slave. Was Maurosus marked with the sign, Maurosus anointed, Maurosus reborn? Autbert had secured the inscription of Landelin in the book of life with us; the devil inserts Maurosus with himself in the document of perdition.

“Know, however, that it was not lightly dealt with before the strict Judge that, to his own injury, he has borne your insolence so patiently until now; that his fugitive either escaped the hands of men with impunity or was able to avoid the snare of death.

“For a long time you would have been destined to suffer the punishment of so great a fire, unless the intercession of blessed Autbert, your advocate, had softened the Judge’s avenging anger. A fire of torment is kindled for you, but is the flame of that fire extinguished by Autbert’s tears?

“Now, at least, having experienced it, understand what you should choose: to be dragged with torment into the abyss of Gehenna, or to enjoy a heavenly dwelling with Autbert. This deliberation would have come too late, unless Autbert had acted beforehand.

“Therefore abandon the accursed fellowship of thieves and, taking up the warfare of Christ, imitate your leader Autbert. Listen to the most blessed bishop and recognize your spiritual Father, your protector, and your redeemer from eternal destruction.

“Receive from him the counsels of heavenly teaching, so that, once amended, you may deserve to recover, through his intercession, the robe that you lost.”

When he had said these things, the angel immediately disappeared.

But what and how great can we estimate Autbert to be, when he shines with the grace of virtues before angelic witnesses and yet lacks among human beings the office of due veneration?

It is full of joy that, while still a man placed on earth, he shines in merit among the citizens of the angels. Yet it is recalled with sorrow and fear that, joined to the heavenly assemblies, he is celebrated among human beings with less careful and worthy reverence.

**[Col. 0360A]**

# IX

Now Landelin, refreshed for a short while by the angel’s words but fearing that he might be slow to help himself, abandoned the company of the wicked association and hastened to the city. He carefully inquired of the guards whether the holy man was there.

Once assured of blessed Autbert’s presence, and thinking that nothing should be concealed, he was moved to repentance, prostrated himself at the saint’s feet, confessed his guilt, and asked forgiveness for his error.

Then one might have seen the prodigal son returning from a distant region and the father rushing to embrace him.
