Thus the holy man, overcome by paternal compassion, received the youth, promising forgiveness if he cleansed his past evils by turning to a better life. He told him to have no doubt that he would render an account for him: whatever offense there had been would be reckoned in place of innocence, provided that he judged the criminal associations must be wholly avoided.

The youth declared himself ready for every form of satisfaction, terrified as he was by the horror of the vision he had so recently experienced.

But the merciful father rejoiced with him in his vows and received him as a penitent, him whom he had long mourned as having departed from him. Opening to him the bosom of divine mercy, he restored him to holy Mother Church.

Under the discipline of the venerable Father, he so constrained himself by vigils and fasts, doing penance for his former deeds, that even if his tongue had remained silent, his way of life would have proclaimed that he had seen and feared the torments of hell.

The holy man therefore urged him, while he was living for a time in the monastery under secular dress, to abandon worldly affairs completely, so that he might meditate more freely on heavenly things.

When he saw him ready for everything, he cut off the hair of his head, from him whose heart he had driven away the stains. Finally, recognizing that the virtue of holiness was flourishing in him, he advanced him through the successive grades to the office of deacon.

He appeared so suited to it that it clearly became evident to everyone that he had been chosen for it by God’s grace. After a few days, when he was raising himself more and more toward the service of God, the blessed pontiff, giving thanks to God, raised him to the summit of the priesthood.

**[Col. 0360B]**

# X

Once elevated to the height of this honor, he grew to such a summit of virtues that it cannot be narrated. Having been formed by his teacher’s conduct and strengthened by the practice of a disciplined way of life, he grew weary of the urban communities and withdrew to more remote places, in deserted regions beside the waters of the Sambre.

There, appearing eminent in signs, miracles, and the practices of a devout way of life, he gathered many people to the service of the supreme Creator.

To wipe away the stain of his earlier life, he built monasteries in the places that he had prepared as refuges and shelters for robbers. He appointed ministers to carry out ecclesiastical observance, and those whom he had formerly had as companions in crime he afterward made fellow workers in the divine mysteries.

If anyone examines more carefully the sequence of his life and the fabric of his conduct, he will easily find these things, especially since the monastic dwellings he himself built are more clearly visible to those present than they can be explained by our speech.

To say nothing of the others, which might perhaps weary unsympathetic hearers, at Lobbes he built a monastery in honor of Blessed Peter the Apostle. To those who see it, this alone may suffice as evidence of distinguished labor. He also enriched it with royal gifts and filled it equally with an abundance of estates and dependents.

He assigned to it whatever the generosity of earlier kings had acquired throughout the kingdoms of the Franks, so that the congregation of brothers serving there would not lack what is considered suitable for monks.

In that place he appointed blessed Ursmar to govern the church, a man adorned with virtues and radiant with signs and miracles. The book published about his life indicates the endowment of his merits.

In the matter of the present example, who would not consider Autbert like John, when John made a secure provider for the Church from a robber, and Autbert likewise made a true priest of the Lord from a robber and impious plunderer?

But while we repeat these things for the moment, the immense mercy of the Creator presents itself for consideration: after the fall, he granted sinners the ability to come to innocence.

Likewise, according to that saying, we both believe and rejoice that he pierced the jaw of Leviathan with the bracelet of his divinity, when he opened an escape route for this man, once fallen into Leviathan’s jaws, and guarded him so that he would not fall back again.

**[Col. 0360C]**

# XI

At Athens, that most distinguished city of the Greeks, there was a certain young man born of illustrious parents, trained in literary studies, and adorned with the conduct of faith. Inspired by heavenly love, he was planning to abandon his homeland and parents and undertake the course of a long pilgrimage, so that through the expense of temporal exile he might purchase a share in the eternal inheritance.

Coming to Rome, he spent some time visiting the apostles’ oratories for the sake of prayer. One night, when his limbs were weary from the journey and he had fallen asleep, he was warned by a voice of divine command to seek the western borders of Gaul and, entering the district of Hagnon, to look for a suitable place for his dwelling, where, after building an oratory, he might await the time of his calling.

Knowing, therefore, that divine providence would always be with him, he did not fear the hardship of the difficult journey until he reached the place where he would find someone to grant him a haven for his pilgrimage and provide him with material assistance.

The following events indicate that this divine voice foretold the blessed Authertus [i.e. Autbert]. Desiring to fulfill the Lord’s command, the man of God Gislenus—for that was his name—traversed various regions, islands, and cities, and at last, by a favorable course, reached a place then called Ursdungus by the inhabitants, apparently after a bear giving birth; now it is called Cella.

This place lies about thirty miles from the city of Cambrai, where, by divine revelation, he had heard that the holy pontiff was laboring with vigilant care over Christ’s flock.

After removing harmful trees, he began to build a basilica in honor of the apostles and to exercise himself in good works.

When the devil spread the zeal of envy through the hearts of evil people, it was reported that some, as flatterers commonly do, advised the holy bishop not to allow that false teacher to remain within his territory, to the injury of his honor—that he had come to these solitudes to deceive the minds of simple people while avoiding the urban gatherings of the wise.

But the man of the Lord, recognizing that the suggestion had been composed by envy rather than reason, said: “It is not for us to judge a man without examination, nor to believe every spirit, until it is tested whether it is from God.”

**[Col. 0360D]**

# XII

A messenger was therefore sent to summon the man into the bishop’s presence, with the provisional intention that the man of God should not be saddened by any hostile impulse from the assembly.

When the blessed Gislenus was summoned, he began to give thanks to God because heavenly grace had visited him through his bishop.

Arriving at the city, he was presented to the holy bishop, who, burning with the sweetness of charity, addressed him:

“Tell us, dearest brother: of what people are you, and what is your station?”

He replied:

“I am Greek by nation, but Christian in dignity. I was born at Athens and reborn through Christ’s baptism. Thus, coming to Rome, I reached this land by God’s command, beside the river Hagna, at a place called Ursdungus. I work with my hands and desire to build an oratory for God.

“I had indeed wished to seek your holiness, to ask permission to carry out what I have begun, but your grace anticipated me, for it summoned us.”

The gracious bishop considered the man’s words and, finding nothing blameworthy, loved him. He kept him for several days through the grace of hospitality, satisfying him with bodily nourishment and with sacred conversation about the spiritual life.

Then, having given him the gift of his blessing and received permission to return, the venerable Father urged him diligently to complete what he had begun, and promised that, once the appropriate work had been completed, he himself would consecrate the oratory with the blessing of his authority.

Rejoicing at the bishop’s promise, Gislenus applied himself more ardently to the work, perceiving from the outcome of events that he had found the man whom, by divine revelation, he had heard was promised to him for the ministry of shared labor.

When he had completed, according to his ability, what was suitable for monastic use, the man of God addressed the bishop in these words:

“The time has come, Father, when the lord bishop should fulfill for his servant the gift of the promised blessing.”

The venerable Father therefore rejoiced at the man’s good endeavors. Taking with him the blessed and venerable worshiper of God Amando, and amid the great rejoicing of the surrounding people, he consecrated the monastery to the praise of the Lord and in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul.

**[Col. 0361A]**

# XIII

Nor do I think that I should pass over the following: although the spirits of heaven, when human affairs are being administered, allow themselves to be seen by only a few—and by those endowed with the purity of a more perfect life—through visions or obscure enigmas of mystical vision, many people have heard that blessed Autbert often saw angels with bodily eyes.

This should not seem extraordinary to the prudent, since the inward gaze of the mind kindled the light of bodily sight for perceiving spiritual things, while the power of self-restraint had closed that sight to lower matters.

The necessities of affairs required the venerable Father to visit his canons who served at Arras in the monastery of Blessed Mary. That place had once been famous both for the circuit of its walls and for the multitude of its citizens, but, deformed from its ancient condition by invasions of peoples, it still stands amid frequent ruins.

After dealing sufficiently for the time with matters concerning the Church, one night, as was always his custom, he rose for the time of nocturnal prayer while the brothers were still resting and continued until the dawn.

He had not yet completed the course of his prayer when he went outside, as if to refresh his limbs with some relief, temporarily suspending his prayer. Standing on the walls, he began to be stirred by movements of devout meditation: why should Vedast, enclosed for so many years beneath the turf of a poor tomb, lack the honor due to him?

The heavenly Jerusalem had already received him, rejoicing among the company of the citizens above, as a gem flashing with the splendor of virtues. From the day of his burial until the time of blessed Autbert there had been six bishops, and he was the seventh to succeed to the summit of the pontificate. Yet through all those passing years God’s precious gem remained enclosed in an underground chamber.

His tomb was not far from the right side of the altar of Blessed Mary. Although we hear that in those times there were so many distinguished confessors of Christ, exalted in merits and illustrious in virtues, more attentive even to small matters, it is undoubtedly clear that this great treasure did not lie neglected through their negligence, but that by divine judgment and by the will of blessed Vedast the execution of this task had been reserved for blessed Autbert.

His spirit therefore began to burn, wondering where the holy confessor ought to be transferred. He reflected that it would be inappropriate for two great lights to be confined within the narrow space of a single house: namely, that where the glorious memory of the Mother of God held primacy of name, the glory of such a Father should not appear dimmer.

Suddenly, as the dawn reddened, he gazed toward the east and saw in the distance, across a little river called the Trient, a splendid man holding a staff in his hand and measuring out the site of a basilica. It was as once Ezekiel, lying bodily beside the waters of Babylon, came in spirit to the land of Israel, where in visions of God he saw the Lord’s temple measured by a man’s hand.

When Autbert saw this, the Spirit revealing it, he recognized the vision as angelic. The man of God therefore understood that blessed Vedast was, with Christ’s approval, to be transferred there.

**[Col. 0361B]**

# XIV

Having been made more certain by this revelation, the blessed pontiff decided that blessed Audomar, who at that time governed the flock of the city of Thérouanne with vigilant care, should be invited to the solemn task of the translation.

Although weighed down by old age and weakened by the loss of his sight, he did not fear the labor on account of his weakened body as much as he rejoiced to fulfill the command of blessed Autbert. The love of his spirit therefore overcame the weakness of his body, and, with Christ guiding his steps, he devotedly reached the venerable bishop.

When Autbert explained what he had in mind and what had been shown to him by divine revelation, Audomar rejoiced with him over the vision and obediently girded himself for the work with fraternal zeal.

It cannot now be estimated how great a crowd of people gathered there on that day: the clergy, of course, and a common people of both sexes, not without distinction.

After the bier and everything that seemed necessary had been prepared, the tomb was opened and the antiphon begun. With great reverence they lifted the sacred treasure. Then, with crosses, candles, and every kind of ornament belonging to solemn ceremony prepared, they began, amid the great rejoicing of the people, to transfer the sacred body to the appointed place.

When they had crossed the aforementioned little river and were already approaching the urban boundaries, blessed Audomar following the footsteps of blessed Autbert step by step, he immediately recognized in himself the power of heavenly action. It was plainly shown to him how great was the merit both of the one who was being carried and of the one who followed while carrying him.

For, when the night of his long blindness had been driven away, he immediately recovered the light of his eyes—at the very place where a church was built in memory of blessed Autbert, still visible today as a testimony to the miracle.

But because the venerable Audomar considered the light of bodily eyes of little value, desiring instead the light of the heavenly citizens, he immediately obtained again through prayer the same blindness that he had voluntarily carried.

Through this display of the miracle, the power of its worker is not hidden; what remains is to seek the merit that obtained the desired virtue.

To those who examine the matter more subtly, however, there can be no doubt that, leaving aside the merits of holy Vedast, it was the faith of blessed Autbert that obtained the miracle.

Those present were astonished at the miracle’s varied outcome, but they honorably transferred the blessed body to the place designated by the angel. There the venerable bishop built a monastery and, from the resources of his bishopric, gave what was appropriate for the needs of those serving there. In proportion to the available resources, he assigned brothers to the service of divine worship.

Concerning the death of blessed Autbert—at what time his holy soul, released from the flesh, departed for the heavenly Jerusalem—nothing certain has come to our knowledge. Certain obstacles have prevented this information and have also removed the greater part of his virtues from our memory.

His holy body was buried in the church of Blessed Peter, which at that time stood outside the city walls but is now within them. There it rested until the time of Bishop Dodilo, who succeeded him as the fourteenth bishop.

When the Normans had ravaged Gaul, Dodilo transferred the holy body with great care to the church of Blessed Mary, where it rested honorably for a long time.

**[Col. 0361C]**

# XV

The emperor Otto, son of King Henry, asked Fulbert, bishop of Cambrai, to give him the bodies of the holy bishops Autbert and Gaugeric.

Fulbert, however, after taking certain men into his counsel, gave him the bodies of Theoderic, bishop of Cambrai, and another priest, adding certain parts from the body of Saint Autbert. This was done prudently, so that the city of Cambrai would not be deprived of its patrons.

The emperor rejoiced and arranged for the distinguished relics to be deposited in the monastery that he himself had built at Magdeburg.

A report had spread throughout all Germany that Saints Autbert and Gaugeric had been transferred from Gaul to Saxony. But the matter is otherwise. In our own times, Herluin, bishop of Cambrai, investigated carefully and recovered most of the body of blessed Gaugeric.

His successor Gerard solemnly consecrated, in memory of Saint Paul, the monastery where Saint Autbert rests, which Herluin had enlarged, and restored the sacred body of blessed Autbert to its own dwelling.

This occurred in the year 1010 of Christ. The place is not far from the church of the most holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary. There, for those who ask in right faith, divine benefits are granted through the intercession of blessed Autbert.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT FULBERT

**[Col. 0362A]**

## Certain Charters

Extracted from the cartulary of the abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres.

*(Guerard, Unpublished Documents on the History of France, Cartulary of Saint-Père of Chartres, vol. I, p. 116.)*
# I. Concerning Vivian, assigned to William’s servitude for the killing of a certain servant of his

[Col. 0369A]

Let it be known to all present and future that I, Arnulf, abbot, and the whole congregation of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres entrusted to me by God, subject our fellow-liber Vivian, together with his wife and all his property, to the servitude of the knight William, on account of the secret killing of a certain servant of his, whom Vivian and his wife secretly killed. We release them on this condition, that they not be killed for this crime. The sons whom they now have, however, we retain for our own use; but those whom they may beget hereafter we assign to his servitude for this abominable offense [the reading *pertitulato* is uncertain].

[Col. 0369B] Sign of Arnulf, abbot +.

# II. Concerning the allod of Hot Mountain (*Calidus Mons*)  
*(Around the year 1020.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Among Christian peoples praise of the truly Catholic and mother Church has always flourished and may it flourish forever. This is both most worthy and just, since she is our mother and the bride of Christ our Lord, whom he acquired with his precious blood. In her we are reborn through the washing of baptism, and in her we rise again from the death of the soul through the grief of repentance; and after the end of life our corpses are buried in her courtyard.

Christ founded her upon the faith which the most faithful Peter confessed when he said to the Lord: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Blessed are those who dwell there by living as Catholics, as David sang: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

Instructed and admonished by these and many other sayings of the saints and by the mysteries of Sacred Scripture, I, Hildegard, viscountess of Châteaudun, give to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres my allod of Beaumont, with its cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, and fisheries belonging thereto, with the consent and approval of my son Hugh, archbishop of Tours—namely, on the understanding that after my death I shall be buried in the monks’ cloister, so that those passing by may always pray continually for me over my tomb.

The nobles of Châteaudun whose names are written below witnessed and approved this. But if anyone of my descendants, or any other invader driven on by the devil’s goads or arrows, should use force against the monks and in any way take away the alms which I gave to Saint Peter, let him, condemned by perpetual damnation, perish with Dathan, Abiron, Annas, and Caiaphas; and let him remain anathematized by the authority of my son Hugh, the archbishop.

Hugh, archbishop; Gautfrid, his nephew; Hubert; Godeschalc, his son; Hubert, treasurer of Le Mans; Ralph, learned in law; Fulcald; Gathon; Odo Brunellus; Hubert Brunellus; Helgaud, the archbishop’s son; Helgaud the Black; Gradulf; Firmatus the canon; Frederick; Hugh the vicar; Bernard of Buslo; Junanignus, at the archbishop’s command, made this document.

# III. Concerning the church of Rescolium, given to Saint Peter by Count Richard  
*(Before the year 1024.)*

The God who is the creator of all things is wondrous in his works, since from some things he brings forth others, carrying greater things, namely, from lesser ones [Note: The words “or brings forth” (*vel perpetrat*) are written above the line in the codex]. By sincerely considering this matter inwardly, we owe him no small thanks for it, and for that matter, with heart, voice, and deed, the greatest thanks: for he not only, as we have already indicated, fosters eternal things from temporal ones, but also, by dispensing them rationally, mercifully advances them toward eternity.

Therefore, to shape faith in this perfect and most desirable joy, among the other things that instill in mortals hope of holy eternity, Truth herself says through her own mouth: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

Understanding this gift of his, and by his same prompting, I, Richard, count of the Normans, among the other things which, under his inspiration, I returned to him from his possessions, gave to the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres a certain church dedicated to his name. It is situated in the county of Évreux, in a village called Rescolium after it. I committed this matter to writing for this reason: that it might serve as an example to the generous and a testimony against the rapacious.

If anyone should oppose the aforesaid gift, then, for as long as he persists in this intention, let him be punished with human and divine malediction.

Sign of Richard, count. Sign of Robert, archbishop. Sign of Richard, brother of the count and archbishop of Rouen. Sign of Gunnor, countess. Sign of Richard, the count’s son. Sign of Robert, the count’s son. Sign of Unfrid.

The village mentioned above was once called Rescolium from the collection of goods; for there the treasury’s goods were collected or gathered. In that place, not far from the River Avre, a small wooden church dedicated to Saint Remigius stood beside a certain spring.

As time passed, however, both the village and the church were almost completely destroyed by continual wars. Then, with the approval of Count Richard, that parish was united to the parish of Saint George, whose church was not far away, and the altar of Saint Remigius was transferred by the monks to a wing of that church. It remained there until modern times, when it was built with cement and stone by a monk named Hubert [elsewhere: “until it was built larger, with cement and stone, by the modern monks”].

# IV. Concerning the church of Wadoniscurtis, given to Saint Peter by Rajenarius  
*(Before the year 1024.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, Richard, duke of the Normans, wish it to be known to all present and future that my faithful man, named Rajenarius, came into my presence with the consent of his wife, Wandelburg by name, humbly asking that, for the salvation of my soul, or for the soul of his son, whose name was Robert, or for the remission of his sins, I should grant to the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres a church in the county of Évreux called Wadoniscurtis.

Considering the just petition of so important a man, I gave my assent. I further decreed that from this day and throughout succeeding generations, none of his people, nor anyone else, should presume, with rash insolence, to impose any right of lordship or any violent intrusion contrary to the terms of this our compact.

So that this charter might rest upon firmer authority in the name of God, I subscribed it with my own hand and handed it over to my faithful men for confirmation.

Sign of Richard, count. Sign of Robert, archbishop. [Col. 0371D] Sign of Herbert, bishop. Sign of Theoderic, abbot. Sign of Robert, cleric. Sign of Rajenarius, who made this donation. Sign of Hunfred of Wetulabus.

I am completely ignorant whether the monks of that time possessed or held the aforesaid church. For I have never heard from the ancient monks that they had possessed it, nor have I ever heard any mention of it from the modern monks—so the text reads, with a double negation.

# V. Concerning the allod of Selusellae, given by Gausfrid and his son Joscelin  
*(Before the year 1024.)*

Since it remains written and established in the decrees of the ancients that if any noble layman has honored a church or monastery with some of his hereditary possessions, or has made a donation, he may in no way reclaim it either through his son or through any successor, I, Joscelin, son of Gausfrid, wish it to be known to all present and future how and for what reason, after my father’s death, I approached Lord Abbot Majenard and the whole congregation of that place concerning the possessions which my father had left and transferred to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres.

My father Gausfrid, for the salvation of his soul, assigned to Saint Peter an allod called Exclusellas, in the county of Dourdan, on the River Andura, while I was still a child and my mother was alive.

I requested this same allod, not because I wished to withdraw it from that venerable place to which it had been given, nor to possess it by any fraud, but on this condition and agreement: that as long as I live I shall pay twelve solidi as a rent at the appointed term and shall render the required service. Nor shall I ever be permitted to sell it or transfer it to anyone—to a son or to any of my relatives. Rather, as long as I breathe, it shall remain in my hand and under my dominion.

After the end of my life, so that my father’s memory may be greater and so that I may have a share in his benefaction, I give not only what my father donated, which I now hold, by the gift of Lord Abbot Majenard and the other elders, but everything belonging to it—namely, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, and woods—so that it may return to the same place from which I received it, for the use of the servants of Christ.

So that this may occur without any claim or opposition, I have taken care to commit it to writing, chiefly lest anyone should claim it for himself [the grammar is defective in the source]. I also hand it over to my lord Odo, the illustrious count, and to his nobles for confirmation, so that what has been inserted here may remain firm and unshaken for all time.

Sign of Odo, count. Sign of Berta, his mother. Sign of Agnes, his daughter. Sign of Walter, count. Sign of Gausfrid, knight. Sign of Hervé, viscount. Sign of Rodulf. Sign of Gausbert. Sign of Albert. Sign of Wasulin. Sign of Sulius. Sign of Joscelin, who ordered this charter to be confirmed. Sign of Gausfrid, his knight.

# VI. Concerning the renunciation (*guerpitio*) of the church of Ursivillaris  
*(Around the year 1024.)*

Under the eternal rule and supreme priesthood of Christ, I, Odolric, bishop of Orléans, wish the manner and conclusion of the case written in this charter to be made known to my contemporaries and successors.

The monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres had long possessed a certain church in the region of Dunois, in a place called Ursivillaris. But one of our dependent tenants, named Hilduin, together with his relatives, brought a claim against them concerning that church, saying that it belonged to our benefice and to his own holding. He also asserted that during the times of my predecessors he had pressed this claim vigorously but had been unable to obtain justice.

We therefore summoned Lord Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and Arnulf, abbot of Saint Peter, to provide us with a hearing concerning this matter. They did so once in the same village called Ursivillaris and again in the village called Castanetas.

After the dispute had been examined on both sides, we found the monks’ case supported by written evidence, witnesses, and long possession to such an extent that under no law of Christians could the aforesaid church be taken from their possession.

Therefore, since we did not wish to contend against law and what is forbidden, I, Odolric the bishop, my brother Isembard, and the aforesaid Hilduin, together with his sons and the rest of his relatives, entirely renounced the claim we had begun against the monks of Saint Peter. We agreed that they should possess their church of Ursivillaris securely and peacefully forever, as we found to be just.

I also forbade, by the episcopal authority entrusted to me by God, that any of our successors should thereafter trouble the aforesaid monks of Saint Peter with such a sacrilegious claim. If anyone should perversely choose to persist in this hateful claim, let him be struck with the anathema by which God, when angry, condemns the incorrigible. So be it, so be it.

We, who have renounced the aforesaid claim, caused our names and those of our faithful who were present to be recorded in this charter for the sake of remembrance.

Sign of Odolric, bishop of Orléans. Sign of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres. Sign of Albert, abbot. Sign of Isembard, layman. Sign of Erfred, cleric. Sign of Salonius, cleric. Sign of Bovo, dean of Saint Martin of Tours. Sign of Tescelin, cleric. Sign of Tedoin, cleric. Sign of Alberic. Sign of Hilduin, layman. Sign of Hilduin, his son. Sign of Odolric, his son. Sign of Pontelin, his nephew. Sign of Godefrid, layman. Sign of Adrold, viscount. Sign of Frederick, lay brother. Sign of Hugh Radord. [Col. 0374B] Sign of Gualo, layman.

# Praise of the Monastic Life

*(In R. P. Sirmundus, Works of Geoffrey of Vendôme, note on Book II.)*

[Col. 0373B]

Happy is the human flock that follows Christ’s teaching  
and, scorning wealth, retains nothing as its own;  
those whom holy discipline restrains under one authority,  
so that none acts according to his own desire.

Their hearts are one, their wills undivided;  
their clothing is alike, and their food is common to all,  
yet in such a way that each receives what he appears to need,  
as fragile age or weakness requires.

All luxury is absent, and the opportunity for sin is rare,  
since all fear the eyes of all.  
The common law immediately exposes visible faults,  
so that the punishment that follows may cut away the growing vice.

They flee idleness; useful labor occupies everyone,  
lest harmful thoughts enter sluggish minds.  
Nothing is confused where everything is done in order;  
everything is attended to, and nothing is neglected.

Not only life but also the order of speech is regulated:  
they distribute great matters and small alike;  
no one speaks or keeps silent except as prescribed,  
and each stands, sits, and walks according to his proper order.

[Col. 0373D]

They frequent the church threshold night and day,  
and by holy prayers help themselves and their own.

Why should I delay and try to unfold every detail in words?  
Whatever they do is a work of body or soul.

What of the fact that they dwell in such a way  
that the arrangement and number of the houses themselves are sacred  
and sufficient for their needs?  
The domestic structure presents a square form,  
with courtyards distinguished by four porticoes.

Three houses are enclosed within it, as bodily use requires,  
and a fourth is the house of the Lord.  
These provide the monks with movement, life, and a place to stand,  
where they are contained like sheep in pens.

The first house stores drink and food,  
with which the adjoining second house refreshes them.  
The third warms limbs wearied by the day’s labor;  
the fourth continually resounds with the praises of God.

I pass over many things worthy of similar treatment,  
but I shall say briefly: nothing is excessive and nothing lacking.

I compare these leaders, this senate worthy of praise—  
small in outward appearance but outstanding in conduct—  
to ants, whose industrious little troop  
carries on its body a burden greater than itself.

And, so that they may be able to lead a common life,  
they build small granaries beneath the same household gods.

I compare them to the divine bees, which, though small in body,  
bear within them great and excellent spirits;  
they store flowing honey in hexagonal cells  
and manufacture a useful and marvelous work.

They preserve discipline and domestic laws,  
and the ingenious house refreshes them all together.

[Col. 0374D]

I compare them to the stars with which the heavenly court shines,  
which illuminate the dark air through the night;  
they preserve the law once imposed upon them for ages  
and complete their customary courses and numbers.

I compare them to the heaven that solemnly revolves all things;  
indeed, I compare them to the angelic spirits,  
who continually resound “Holy” with a threefold voice,  
the same hymn that the monks chant on earth.

Thus the cherubim in heaven and the monks dwelling on earth  
render one service to the one Lord.

# Guido of Arezzo, abbot of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, between 1029 and 1034

# Historical Notice

*(In Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin Literature, vol. IV, p. 127.)*

[Col. 0375A]

Guido of Arezzo, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict and later abbot of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana in the diocese of Cagli, near Arezzo, was summoned to Rome by Pope Benedict VIII, who died in 1024 [Note: Guido himself, in his letter to Michael, a monk of the monastery of Saint Mary at Pomposa, published by Baronius under the year 1022, nos. XXI–XXII, has *abii igitur Romanum* (“therefore I went to Rome”); it is badly printed there as *Alii igitur Romanum*]. He demonstrated to that pope and to his successor, John XIX [Note: Baronius found in his manuscript the words: “While John XX governed the Roman Church, Guido published his *Micrologus* in the thirty-fourth year of his life.” But, as Pagi observed, the John who succeeded Benedict VIII calls himself John XIX in his own rescripts], his distinguished study of music. In this respect, according to Sigebert, he should be preferred to those before him: through his rule, even boys and girls learned or were taught unknown chants more easily than through a teacher’s voice or through the use of any instrument, provided that the six letters or syllables [Note: *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*, from the well-known hymn of Paul the Deacon to Saint John the Baptist:

> So that your servants may, with loosened voices, resound  
> the wonders of your deeds;  
> cleanse the guilt from polluted lips,  
> O Saint John.

> [The highlighted syllables in the Latin verse are *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*.]

See, if desired, what Johannes Weitzius wrote about that hymn of Paul in his *Heortology*, p. 263 and following, and Menagius in *Origins of the French Language*, under “Bemol,” where he also cites this distich by an unknown author:

> With heart, strings, and lofty groaning I shall bless God;  
> may UT–RE–MI–FA cause SOL–LA to loosen the lips for him.

There is also this distich by Abraham Bucholzer in his chronology at A.D. 1044:

> Why do you apply measures and song to sorrowful toil?  
> May UT relieve wretched fate and customary labors.]

were applied melodically to the six notes [Note: See the system of modern music according to Guido, or the great scale compared with the system of the ancients, in the table given by M. Meibomius in his notes to Euclid’s *Introduction to Harmonics*, p. 51, and in Sebastian Brossard’s French *Musical Dictionary*, under “Système,” p. 163 and following]. These notes, distinguished by the bending of the fingers of the left hand, make the ascending and descending pitches of the same notes present themselves to the eyes and ears across the whole octave.

For Theobald—or rather Theodaldus—bishop of Arezzo, from 1014 to 1037 [Note: Ughelli, vol. I of *Sacred Italy*, p. 415], he wrote the *Micrologus*, or two books on music. The first consists of prose; the second partly of hexameter verse and partly of trochaic rhythmic verse [Note: Vossius, *On the Mathematical Sciences*, chapter 22, §7, p. 95; Du Cange, under “Micrologus”]. Baronius published the dedicatory letter to Theodaldus at the year 1022, no. XXIII.

Domnizo also mentions him in Book I, chapter 5, of *The Life of the Duchess Matilda*, in Leibniz, vol. I of the *Brunswick Historians*, p. 641. As far as I know, Guido’s books themselves, although preserved in several manuscript libraries, have not yet seen the light of publication. M. Meibomius cites his *Micrologus* once, in connection with Gaudentius, p. 37.

The distinguished Bernard Pez, volume III, part III of the *Anecdota*, p. 618, testifies that a brief work by Guido, *On the Measurement of the Monochord*, exists in the library of Beuron. It begins: “When you first divide the monochord from G to the end into nine steps, the first step will end at A,” and so forth.

Guido himself, in a letter to Michael, a monk of Pomposa, which the aforementioned Baronius published under the year 1022, no. XXI, mentions his *Antiphonary*, revised with rules prefixed to it. Benedict VIII turned it over as though it were some kind of marvel.

For the rest, Marcus Meibomius argues, in his notes to Aristides Quintilianus, p. 240, and to Euclid, p. 51, that, apart from the musical notation, Guido changed nothing beyond the authority of the ancients and did not make their music more systematic.

Against the opinion of those who contend that Guido’s system of song is more systematic than the ancient one because the ancient systems—thirteen in Aristoxenus and only fifteen in those who followed him—contained so many sounds, whereas Guido added the greater six-note system, so that we now have twenty notes, Isaac Vossius, *On the Powers of Rhythm*, p. 91, observes that Guido followed the example of the harps and organs of his own time in arranging his scale.

“For those instruments,” he says, “were generally equipped with twenty-pipe systems, as a writer several centuries older than Guido teaches. Moreover, the number of strings or pipes—for example, twenty-one or more—is not supplied for the reason that the sounds extend beyond fifteen or perhaps sixteen; rather, the same sounds that occur below are repeated, and this for the sake of variety in the modes.”

Indeed, Nicomachus already describes twenty-eight *phthongoi* (φθόγγους), that is, tones frequently used by musicians, in Book II of his *Manual of Harmonics*, p. 39.

Just as Guido used the syllables *ut, re, mi*, and so forth, so the ancient Egyptians were accustomed to express an equal number of sounds through the seven vowels, as Isaac Vossius teaches from Demetrius’s work *On Interpretation* (Περὶ ἑρμηνείας), §17, Oxford edition. In the same way Gregory the Great initially used the seven letters of the alphabet for this purpose; when these had been traversed, whether the melody ascended or descended, it returned to the octave and corresponded to the same number, seven, of distinctions among the sounds.

Trithemius, chapter 318, attributes to this Guido a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, against Berengar. Perhaps referring to the same man, the anonymous writer of Melk calls Guido “incomparable in faith and knowledge” in chapter 80.

Gerbert says the same; Johannes Vossius likewise says, on page 95 of *On the Mathematical Sciences*, that the musical Guido was the man who, from being a monk of the monastery of Héton, or Saint Leufred, or Lodifred, among the Norman people of Évreux, became archbishop of Aversa and a cardinal of the Roman Church.

But Trithemius correctly distinguishes that Guido, or Guimund, who wrote against Berengar, from Guido of Arezzo, in addition to the anonymous writer of Melk, chapter 102; he does so also in chapter 122 and in Book II, chapter 80, of *On Illustrious Benedictines*. Nor does the chronology permit him to have been the same person as Guido of Arezzo, since the archbishop of Aversa was still alive in 1090.

One must similarly beware of Possevinus’s error, by which he confuses Guido’s musical *Micrologus* with the *Micrologus* on ecclesiastical observances, or on the proper celebration of Mass—an error already correctly noted by Pagi under the year 1022, no. 9, and by Oudinus.

# Literary Notice

*(D. Martin Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers on Music*, II, preface.)*

[Col. 0377B]

1. Guido of Arezzo is entirely worthy to inaugurate a new era of writers on music. By removing the disordered series and confusion of the ancient notes, and by means of the lines and clefs that we call the musical scale, he greatly simplified the learning and practice of musical discipline.

He himself testifies to this in the prologue of his *Micrologus*, saying that divine grace finally came to his aid when he was teaching music to boys:

“Some of them, trained through imitation by using the monochord and practicing our notes, before the space of a single month had passed, sang unknown and unheard chants at first sight so confidently that they sang them without hesitation, providing a marvelous spectacle to many.”

Anyone unable to do this, he says, should scarcely dare to call himself a musician or singer.

He therefore grieved especially for our singers, who, even if they persist for a hundred years in the study of singing, are nevertheless never able to perform even the smallest antiphon on their own. They are always learning, as the Apostle says, and never arriving at a perfect knowledge of this art.

The line that Guido called a string was the one he used to distinguish by a yellow or red color at the place where we now put the C or F clef at the beginning of the line, among the other lines that he was also the first to invent. Of these he rightly said: “Music without lines is like a well without a rope.”

In harmonic music itself, or polyphony, Guido also somewhat softened the harshness of diaphony, as it was called, which we noted in Hucbald; we demonstrated this in the musical work itself, Book III, chapter 1, no. 7.

It is therefore hardly surprising that Guido was summoned to teach music. It also accords with his period that under the year 1023, when Hermann was appointed archbishop of Bremen, Leibniz, in *Writers of Brunswick Affairs*, p. 745, and the *Chronicle of the Slavs*, as well as Albert of Stade’s *Chronicle* in nearly the same words, relate the following:

“Hermann, therefore, thinking little of everything he found in the bishopric, first brought the musician Guido to Bremen, whose industry corrected the melody and the discipline of the cloister. Only this succeeded prosperously among his works.”

Guido himself, in a letter to Michael, the monk of Pomposa, p. 43, says that he had gone into exile through far-ranging regions. Soon afterward, he says, he was persuaded by Guido, abbot of that monastery, to remain there. This was that most holy man whose body, according to Hermannus Contractus, a contemporary writer, and various other chroniclers, was glorified by many miracles. He died in 1047, less than a year before the transfer described here; Emperor Henry III, returning with great honor from Parma, where the saint had been buried, transported the body to the city of Speyer, where a distinguished church and collegiate community of canons still exist in his honor.

From the fact that Saint Guido, abbot of Pomposa, persuaded Guido of Arezzo to remain in his monastery, the authors of the *Camaldolese Annals*, vol. II, p. 43, infer that Guido of Arezzo had not been attached to the discipline of the monastery of Pomposa in the flower of his youth.

The same writers are not opposed to the opinion that our Guido was that very abbot of the monastery of Avellana who received Saint Peter Damian into monastic discipline, and perhaps also, as one who—according to Domnizo’s testimony in *The Life of Matilda*—might be blessed as both monk and hermit, concealed himself in the Camaldolese hermitage recently founded in his native land near Arezzo.

There, in 1033, Guido, at the command of Peter, the venerable hermit, dictated, requested, and obtained from Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, to whom Guido dedicated the *Micrologus*, the donation recorded by Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 389.

But since, according to those same Camaldolese annalists—who were, while they lived, very dear to me—that strict discipline was also observed in the monastery of Avellana, nothing definite can be established concerning the Camaldolese community.

They add that even today an image of Guido can be seen in the refectory of that same monastery of Avellana, with this inscription: “Blessed Guido of Arezzo, inventor of music.” The works we are publishing show that this praise can be attributed to him in more than one respect.

2. That Guido’s name soon became famous throughout Germany is demonstrated by the writings on music of Berno, abbot of Reichenau. According to Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 156, Berno excelled in musical art, writing on the rules of harmonies and tones. In measuring the monochord, beyond Boethius’s rule, but with the approval of the lesser Boethius—Guido—he placed one tone in the hypaton tetrachord, and, contrary to the practice of the elders, usefully inserted the synemmenon within that tetrachord.

This becomes clear from Berno’s prologue to his tonary addressed to Piligrim, archbishop of Cologne from 1020, according to Trithemius in the *Annals of Hirsau* under that year, until 1034, the year to which Hermannus Contractus assigns his death; Trithemius places it in 1036, while others place it in 1035.

Berno could therefore have derived the material from Guido himself. He never says that these discoveries were his own. Indeed, when mentioning the Greek gamma added to the monochord, he repeatedly states in that same prologue, or book on the rules of harmonies and tones—as Sigebert calls it—that it was added by modern writers. The anonymous writer of Melk simply calls it “an outstanding work on music,” while Trithemius, under the year 1018 in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, calls it “a distinguished volume.” Trithemius also adds that Berno wrote a book on musical instruments, which he himself was unable to see.

Perhaps the material in question is contained in the imperial library at Vienna, in the manuscript recently transferred there from the civic library. After the prologue, or first book, of the venerable Abbot Berno’s rules for the art of music, and before the tonary, it includes sections on the measurement of pipes, the organ-builder, the weighing of the cymbal, and so forth.

# Guido of Arezzo’s Short Works on Music

*(D. Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers on Music*, II, 1.)*

# Editorial Notice

Guido’s *Micrologus* on the discipline of the musical art is extremely celebrated. We publish it from a manuscript of the library of Saint Blaise, collated with two manuscripts from Saint Emmeram, one from Admont, the incomplete Ottoburanus, and the Casinensis.

His rhythmic compositions and poem on the explanation of music follow, collated from the same Saint Blaise manuscript with the same manuscripts except the Casinensis. There are also other rules of Guido concerning unknown song, repeatedly incorporated into the prologue of his *Antiphonary*.

Next comes, from the Saint Blaise manuscript alone, an *Epilogue on the Forms of the Modes and the Qualities of Chants*, divided into six chapters. Finally comes Guido’s letter to the monk Michael concerning unknown song.

At the end follows, from a Tegernsee manuscript collated with one from Melk, Guido’s *Corrective Treatise on Many Errors Made in Gregorian Chant in Many Places*, pseudonymous or at least interpolated.

# Guido’s *Micrologus* on the Discipline of the Musical Art

The academy has chosen to recall the Muses, once released,  
so that what has hitherto scarcely been held by the great may be open to the small;  
may affection destroy the blind weapon of envy.  
Truly a dreadful plague has carried away every advantage from the earth.  
I, who first fashioned these songs, have written them in order.

# Letter of Guido, Monk and Musician, to His Bishop Theodaldus  
*[Note: Of the city of Arezzo], concerning the Discipline of the Musical Art*

[Col. 0379B]

To the most illustrious and most sweet Father, most reverend lord Theodaldus, most worthy of priests and bishops in the splendor of divine fear and of all prudence, Guido, would that he were the least of his monks, offers whatever a servant and son can offer.

While I desire to carry out at least a modest measure of the solitary life, the dignity of your kindness has wished my smallness to be joined to your study of the sacred word. This is not because your Excellence lacks many great spiritual men, abundantly strengthened by the effects of virtue and fully adorned with the studies of wisdom, who can suitably teach the people entrusted to you together with you and continually and frequently cling to divine contemplation.

Rather, it is because your piety and fatherhood, taking pity on the weakness of my small mind and body, wished to strengthen it with a fortified protection, so that if anything useful should come to me from God, God might credit it to your merit.

When, therefore, discussion was being held concerning ecclesiastical usefulness, your authority ordered me to make public the practice of the musical art, in which, with God’s favor, I remember that I have labored not in vain. You did this so that, just as by God’s authority you have carried out the Church of the most blessed Donatus, bishop and martyr, over which you preside by rightful vicariate, with a remarkably splendid arrangement, so you might make the ministers of that same church conspicuous to nearly all clerics throughout the world by a privilege of the greatest honor and distinction.

Indeed, it is sufficiently marvelous and desirable that even the boys of your Church, in their zeal for singing, surpass everywhere the accomplished old men of other places. The height of your honor and merit will be greatly increased when, after the Fathers who came before, such great and such splendid renown in learning has arisen for the Church through you.

Therefore, since I neither wished nor was able to oppose your beneficial command, I offer to your most diligent fatherhood the rules of the musical art, explained by philosophers as clearly and briefly as I could—not, however, fully by the same path, nor by following their footsteps in every respect. I have cared only for what might benefit the Church’s usefulness and assist our little ones.

This study has remained hidden until now because, although it was truly difficult, it had not been humbly explained by just anyone. On what occasion I once undertook it, and with what usefulness and intention, I shall explain in very few words.

*The letter ends.*

# Here Begins His Prologue on Music

Since both my natural disposition and the imitation of good men made me diligent for the common good, I began, among my other studies, to teach music to boys.

At last divine grace came to my aid, and some of them, trained through imitation by practicing with the monochord and using our notes, before a single month had passed, sang unknown and unheard chants at first sight so confidently and without hesitation that they provided a marvelous spectacle to many.

Anyone unable to do this, however, I do not know with what face he would dare to call himself a musician or singer.

I therefore grieved especially for our singers, who, even if they persevere for a hundred years in the study of singing, are nevertheless never able to perform even the smallest antiphon by themselves. They are always learning, as the Apostle says, and never arriving at a perfect knowledge of this art.

Desiring, therefore, to devote our very useful study to the common good, I briefly touched upon, with all the brevity I could manage, certain matters from the many musical arguments which, with God’s help, I gathered over various periods—those which I believed would benefit singers.

Whatever in music contributes less to singing, or whatever among the things said cannot be understood, I judged unworthy of mention. I do not care if the minds of some grow livid with envy, so long as the discipline of others makes progress.

*The prologue ends.*

# The Chapters Begin

*[Note: This table of chapters is omitted in the other manuscripts.]*

**Chapter I.** What should someone do who is preparing himself for the discipline of music?

**Chapter II.** What are the notes, what kind are they, and how many are there?

**Chapter III.** Concerning their arrangement on the monochord.

**Chapter IV.** In what six ways are the notes joined to one another?

**Chapter V.** Concerning the octave, and why there are only seven notes.

[Col. 0382A]

**Chapter VI.** Likewise, concerning their divisions and interpretation.

**Chapter VII.** Concerning the affinity of the notes in four modes.

**Chapter VIII.** Concerning other affinities, and concerning b and [the rounded and square forms].

**Chapter IX.** Likewise, concerning the similarity of notes whose octave alone is perfect.

**Chapter X.** Likewise, concerning modes and the recognition and correction of false melody.

**Chapter XI.** Which note holds primacy in song, and why?

**Chapter XII.** Concerning the division of four modes into eight.

**Chapter XIII.** Concerning the recognition, sharpness, and gravity of the eight modes.

**Chapter XIV.** Likewise, concerning the modes and the power of music.

**Chapter XV.** Concerning suitable or composed melody.

[Col. 0382B]

**Chapter XVI.** Concerning the manifold variety of sounds and neumes.

**Chapter XVII.** That everything said is reduced to song.

**Chapter XVIII.** Concerning diaphony, that is, the rule of organum.

**Chapter XIX.** Proof of the stated diaphony by examples.

**Chapter XX.** How music was discovered from the sound of hammers.

# CHAPTER ONE. What should someone do who is preparing himself for the discipline of the musical art?

Therefore, whoever seeks our discipline should learn several chants written out in our notation, exercise his hand in the use of the monochord, and frequently meditate upon these rules, until, having learned the power and nature of the voices, he can sing unknown chants smoothly as though they were known. But because we perceive the voices—which are the first foundations of this art—more clearly on the monochord, let us first see how, in that instrument, art has distinguished them by imitating nature.

# CHAPTER TWO. What and of what kind the notes are, and how many there are [Note: [Col. 0382D] In the Admont manuscript: “On the number and measurement of the notes.”]

The notes on the monochord are as follows. First, let the Greek Γ be placed, added by modern writers. Next come the seven grave letters of the alphabet, marked with capital letters in this manner: A B C D E F G. After these, the same seven acute letters are repeated, but written with lowercase letters. Among them, however, between a and another b we place one which we make round; the other we make square. Thus: a b [♭] c d e f g. To these we add the same letters again, but in different forms, making the tetrachord of the superacute notes; in it likewise we duplicate b: a [a], b [b], [♮], c [c], d [d]. Many call these letters superfluous; we, however, preferred to have an excess rather than a deficiency.

Thus all twenty-one are formed together in this way:

Γ A B C D E F G.  
a b c d e f g.  
a [a] b [b] [♮] c [c] d [d].

Since their arrangement had either been left unmentioned by teachers or entangled in excessive obscurity, it is now explained briefly and completely, even for children.

# CHAPTER THREE. On their arrangement on the monochord

Having first attached Γ, divide the space of the string extending from it to the end into nine parts, and place the letter A at the end of the first ninth; from A all the ancients made their beginning. Likewise, having collected one ninth from A to the end, attach the letter B in the same way.

After this, return to Γ and measure to the end in four parts; at the end of the first part you will find C. By the same division into four, just as C was found from Γ, you will find in order: D with A, E with B, F with C, G with D, the acute A with E, and the round b with F.

The notes that follow are easily obtained in order as the halves of similar and corresponding divisions. For example, from B to the end, place another in the middle of the space. Likewise, C will mark another c, D another d, E another e, F another f, G another g, a another a [a], b another b [b], [♮] another [♮], c another c [c], and d another d [d]. In the same way you could proceed upward or downward indefinitely, unless the precept of the art restrained you by its authority.

Of the manifold and various divisions of the monochord I have set down one, so that when many people directed their attention to a single method, it might be accepted without hesitation—especially since it is so useful that it is easily understood and, once understood, scarcely forgotten.

Another method of division follows. Although it is less readily committed to memory, by it the monochord is arranged more quickly, as follows. When you first divide the distance from Γ to the end into nine steps, that is, sections, the first step will end at A; the second is empty; the third at D; the fourth is empty; the fifth at a; the sixth at d; the seventh at a [a]; the remaining ones are empty.

Likewise, when you divide from A to the end into nine steps, the first step ends at B; the second is empty; the third at E; the fourth is empty; the fifth [reading absent]; the sixth at e; the seventh at [♮]; the remaining ones are empty.

Likewise, when you divide from Γ to the end into four parts, the first step ends at C, the second at G, the third at g, and the fourth ends at the terminus.

From C to the end, likewise in four steps, the first ends at E, the second at c, the third at c [c], and the fourth ends.

From F, in four steps, the first ends at the round b, the second at f, and the third at c [Col. 0383D] [Note: [Col. 0383D] Ottobonian and Admont manuscripts: “A. b. Likewise the round [b]. To the end in two steps, the first ends at b [b] and the second ends. From A. d. likewise, in two steps to the end, the first ends at d [d] and the second ends.”].

From the round b, in four steps, you will find [♮] at the second; the remaining steps are empty. From the superacute a [a], in four steps, you will find d [d] at the first; the remaining steps are empty.

Let these two methods of arranging the notes suffice. The former is easiest to remember; the latter is the quickest for carrying out. In what follows, all the methods of division will become clear in brief.

# CHAPTER FOUR. The six ways in which the voices are joined to one another

When the voices have been arranged, a greater space is seen between some voices—for example, between Γ and A and between A and B—while elsewhere there is a smaller space, as between B and C and the remaining pairs. The greater space is called a tone; the smaller, a semitone, that is, half a tone—not a complete tone.

Likewise, between one voice and the third above it there is sometimes a ditone, that is, two tones, as from C to E; sometimes a semiditone, which contains only a tone and a semitone, as from D to F and in the remaining cases.

A diatessaron occurs when, between two voices in whatever manner, there are two tones and one semitone, as from A to D, from B to E, and in the remaining cases. A diapente is greater by one tone: between any two voices there are three tones and one semitone, as from A to E, from C to G, and in the remaining cases.

You therefore have six consonances of the voices: tone, semitone, ditone, semiditone, diatessaron, and diapente.

[The following is enclosed in brackets in the Admont Miscellany and the Ottobonian manuscript: “To these consonances some singers add two further kinds of interval: diapente with a semitone, as from E to c; and diapente with a tone, as from C to a. Diapason is also added. Since these are rarely encountered, we count them less often among the six. Whoever diligently investigates the origin of diapason—what it is and of what kind—will find it discussed below.”]

In no chant, whether by ascending or descending, is one voice properly joined to another by any other intervals. A seventh, diapason, is added to these; because it is rarely encountered, it is counted less often among the others. Since, according to Boethius, the whole of harmony is formed from so few clausulae, it is extremely useful to commit them deeply to memory and never cease practicing until they are fully perceived and recognized in singing. Thus, using these clausulae as certain keys, you may acquire the skill of singing more intelligently and easily.

# CHAPTER FIVE. On diapason, and why there are only seven notes

Diapason is the interval in which diatessaron and diapente are joined. Since from A to D there is a diatessaron, and from that same D to the acute a there is a diapente, from A to the other a there arises a diapason. Its character is that it has the same letter at both ends: from B to [b] a, from C to c, from D to d, and in the remaining cases.

Just as both voices are marked by the same letter, so in every respect both are considered and believed to be of the same quality and of the most perfect similarity. For just as, when seven days have ended, we repeat the same days, so that we always call the first and the eighth the same day, so we always represent and name the first and eighth voices with the same character, because we perceive them to be consonant by natural agreement—for example, D and d.

Each is lowered by a tone, a semitone, and two tones, and is likewise raised by a tone, a semitone, and two tones. Hence, when two or three singers, or as many as possible, begin and sing through any symphony in different voices according to this interval, you will marvel that you possess the same voices in different places but not different voices, and that the same chant sounds grave, acute, and superacute, yet in unison, as follows.

[Col. 0385]

Likewise, if you sing the same antiphon partly with grave sounds and partly with acute sounds, or vary it in any way according to this interval, the same unity of the voices will appear. Therefore the poet very truly said: “seven distinctions of voices,” because, even if there are or come to be more voices, this is not the addition of others but the renewal and repetition of the same ones.

For this reason we have represented all sounds, following Boethius and the ancient musicians, with seven letters, whereas certain moderns, very incautiously, have used only four signs, representing the fifth sound everywhere with the same character. Yet it is indisputably true that some sounds are wholly discordant from their fifths, such as B and F, and that no sound is perfectly consonant with its fifth. No voice is perfectly consonant with another except at the octave.

# CHAPTER SIX. On the divisions of the voices and their interpretations

To summarize much concerning the division of the monochord in a few words: diapason always runs to the end in two equal steps, diapente in three, diatessaron in four, and the tone in nine; the more numerous the steps, the shorter the interval. You will not be able to find any divisions other than these four.

Diapason is interpreted as “of all,” either because it contains all the voices beneath it, or because in ancient times eight-stringed citharas were made according to it. In this interval the first and lower voice has two spaces, while the acute voice has one, as from A to a.

Diapente is called “of five,” for there are five voices within its space, as from D to a. Its grave voice has three spaces, while its acute voice has two.

Diatessaron means “of four”; it has four voices, and its lower voice has four spaces, while the acute voice has three, as from D to G.

Remember that these three forms are called symphonies, that is, harmonious unions of voices, because in diapason different voices produce one sound. Diapente and diatessaron possess the rights of diaphonia, that is, of organum, and make the voices somewhat alike.

The tone takes its name from *intonare*, “to sound”; it assigns nine steps to the greater voice and eight to the lesser. Semitone and ditone, although they join voices in singing, do not admit any division on the monochord.

# CHAPTER SEVEN. On the four modes and the affinities of the voices

Since there are seven voices—for, as we have said, the others, namely the octave voices, are the same—it is sufficient to explain seven, which have different modes and different qualities.

The first mode of the voices occurs when a voice is lowered by a tone and raised by a tone, a semitone, and two tones, as A and D.

The second mode occurs when a voice is lowered by two tones and raised by a semitone and two tones, as B and E.

The third mode descends by a semitone and two tones, but ascends by two tones and a semitone, as C and F.

The fourth is lowered by a tone, but rises by two tones and a semitone, as D and G [Note: [Col. 0385D] Read: “as D and G,” from what follows.].

Observe that they follow one another in order: the first at A, the second at B, the third at C; likewise, the first at D, the second at E, the third at F, and the fourth at G.

Also note these affinities of the voices, constructed through diatessaron and diapente: A is joined to D, B to E, C to F, and D to G by a diatessaron among the grave voices, but by a diapente among the acute voices, as follows.

# CHAPTER EIGHT. On the other affinities of the voices, and on b and [♮]

If there are other affinities, they too have been formed by diatessaron and diapente. Since diapason contains within itself diatessaron and diapente, and holds the same letters at both ends, there is always in the middle of its space a letter which corresponds to both ends of the diapason. The letter to which it returns a diatessaron among the grave voices corresponds to that same letter by a diapente among the acute voices, as is shown in the preceding figure. And the letter to which it gives a diapente among the grave voices receives a diatessaron from the upper voices, as A, E, a.

A and E agree in descent, since both are formed by two tones and a semitone. Likewise, G, since it sounds with C and D according to the same intervals, has taken on the descent of one and the ascent of the other. C and G both rise by two tones and a semitone; D and G are both inflected by a tone and a semitone.

The round b, because it is less regular—what they call “added” or “soft”—has concord with F. It was added because F could not have concord with the fourth above it, [♮], which differs from it by a tritone. Do not join the two b forms, b and [♮], in the same neume.

In the same chant we make particular use of the soft b when F–f is continued more extensively, whether grave or acute; there it seems to create a certain confusion and transformation, so that G sounds as the first mode, a as the second, while the soft b itself sounds as the third. For this reason many have not even mentioned it.

The other [♮] was agreed to be held in common. If you wish entirely to omit the soft b, regulate the neumes in which it occurs so that, in place of F, G, a, and the soft b, you have G, a, [♮], c. Or, if the neume is such that after D, E, F in ascent it requires two tones and a semitone—which the soft b supplies—or if after D, E, F in descent it requires two tones, take a, c in place of D, E, F; these are of the same mode and possess the prescribed ascents and descents in regular form. Clearly discerning such ascents and descents between D, E, F and a, [♮], c removes the especially harmful confusion.

We have touched briefly on the similarity of the voices, because to the extent that similarity is discovered among different things, the very difference through which the confused mind could labor for a longer time is diminished. Things joined to one another are always grasped more easily when divided.

All the modes and distinctions of the modes are therefore adapted to these three voices: C, D, E. By “distinctions” I mean those which most people call *differentiae*, namely the *saeculorum amen*. It is called a *differentia* because it distinguishes or separates the plagal sections from the authentic ones; otherwise, the term is used improperly.

Thus all the other voices have some concord with these, either in descent or in ascent. None, however, presents itself as similar to another in both respects except in diapason. Whoever seeks the similarity of all these voices will be able to find it in the figure we have placed below.

# CHAPTER NINE. On the similarity in singing of the voices whose only perfect interval is diapason

The voices mentioned above, insofar as they are similar—some in ascent, such as C and G, D and a; others in descent, such as a and E, G and D; and others in both, such as C and G, E—make similar neumes. Thus knowledge of one reveals the other.

But where no similarity has been shown, or where the voices belong to different modes, one does not accept the neume or chant of the other. If you force it to accept it, you will transform it. For example, if someone wished to begin in E or F an antiphon whose beginning is in D, although these voices belong to another mode, the ear would immediately perceive how great a transformation of the chant had occurred.

In D and a, however, which belong to one mode, we can very often begin or end the same chant. I say “very often,” not “always,” because similarity is not perfect except in diapason. Wherever the arrangement of tones and semitones differs, the arrangement of the neumes must also differ. Indeed, in the voices mentioned above, which are said to belong to one mode, differences are found: D descends by a tone, whereas a descends by a ditone; and so it is in the remaining cases.

# CHAPTER TEN. On recognizing and correcting the modes and false melody

These are the four modes or tropes which, improperly, people call tones. They are separated from one another by such a natural difference that one does not give the other a place in its own position, nor does one ever transform or accept the neume of another.

Dissonance also creeps into singing through falsity when singers, departing slightly from properly measured voices by lowering or raising them, diminish or add something. This is what the defective voices of human beings do: by raising or lowering the prescribed interval more than is right, they corrupt a neume of one mode into another; or they begin it in a place that does not receive the voice; or they make certain subductions in the tritus, which are called *dieses*, although they ought not to admit them for use except when certain positions supervene.

To make this clear, we offer an example.

[Col. 0389]

It cannot be made in any sound except the third and sixth; even if it is found in another, it must be corrected completely. Not only must the diesis itself be removed, but also the root from which it improperly arose must be eradicated.

It should be noted that, because some admit [the diesis] in place of a semitone, they construct a harmony like a wagon descending over a stony road. The rules of music have therefore been loosened more than those of all the other arts, because, when some could nowhere admit themselves to the narrow path—or rather, like a full river [perhaps read: *instar*, “like”] which, when its own channel is insufficient, spreads through the crossroads—they have chosen another path wherever semitones have accumulated, fearing to enter a narrow passage lest their great height be cramped by a narrower breadth or a shorter covering.

Where they cannot escape altogether [read: *queunt*, “are able,” for *quaerunt*], they have used the diesis, imitating those who, while fearing the force of the cold, thrust themselves once against the mouth of a furnace.

This diesis, then, which, as we said above, takes the place of a semitone, must nowhere be used except in the following manner: when tritus is sung, and tetrardus is to be prolonged in protus, and then lowered again into itself—either into the same tritus or even lower. Then tritus, which stands above tetrardus or protus, must be lowered slightly. This lowering is called a diesis, and is half of the following semitone, just as a semitone is half of the following tone.

It is measured as follows. When you have made nine steps from G to the end and have found a, divide from a to the end into seven parts. At the end of the first part you will find the first diesis, between [♮] and c. The second and third steps will be empty; the fourth will occupy the place of the third diesis, likewise between [♮] and c [c].

In the same way, make the same number of steps from d to the end, and the position of the second diesis will then appear in the order described above; it will be between e and f.

Then return to the first diesis and divide to the end into four parts. The first step will again end between e and f; the second between [♮] and c [c]; the remaining steps are empty.

We warn the reader not to think that we are foolish because we omitted writing this at the beginning. We shall have these matters ready to answer after the end of the work; for now, let us return to what we began.

There are also some who, where they ought to admit a semiditone, insert a tone. An example will make this clear. In the Communion *Diffusa est gratia*, many, because it begins in F, lower it by one tone, although there is no tone below F. Thus, wherever a semitone occurs, they place it below F, which cannot be done in any way; consequently, the end of that Communion arrives at a place where there is no voice.

It must therefore be the mark of a skilled singer to know in what place and in what manner to begin any neume, so that he may either restore it according to its own mode or, if a movement is required, seek the related voices.

We call these modes or tropes by their Greek names: *protos*, *deuteros*, *tritos*, and *tetrartos*.

# CHAPTER ELEVEN. Which voice holds the primacy in singing, and why

Although every chant is made from all the voices and modes, the voice which ends the chant nevertheless holds primacy, for it sounds longer and with greater lingering. The preceding voices, which are accessible only to the trained, are adapted to it in such a way that they seem wonderfully to derive from it a kind of likeness of color.

Through the six consonances mentioned above, the other voices must agree with the voice that ends the neume. The primacy of the voice that ends the chant, as well as the ends—and even the beginnings—of all the distinctions, must adhere to it.

An exception is *Tribus miraculis*. Although the chant ends in E, it begins this antiphon on c, which lies at a diapente and semitone from E:

> It is the third day since these things were done.

Moreover, when we hear someone singing, we do not know what kind of voice his first voice is, since we do not know whether tones, semitones, or the other intervals will follow. Once the chant has ended, however, we clearly recognize the mode of the final voice from what has preceded it. When the chant has begun, you do not know what will follow; when it has ended, you see what came before. Thus the final voice is the one we perceive most clearly.

Furthermore, if you wish to join a verse, psalm, or anything else to the same chant, you must adapt it especially to the final voice, rather than returning to examine the first or the other voices.

It should also be added that carefully composed chants direct their distinctions chiefly toward the final voice. Nor is it surprising that music takes its rules from the final voice, since in the parts of grammar too we distinguish the force of meaning almost everywhere in the final letters or syllables through cases, numbers, persons, and tenses.

Therefore, since every praise is also sung at the end, we rightly say that every chant is subject to the final voice in its mode and takes its rule from the mode that sounds last.

From the final voice, a proper descent in any chant reaches down to the fifth, and an ascent reaches up to the octave, although this rule is often exceeded when we proceed to the ninth, tenth, or eleventh. Hence they established the final voices as D, E, F, and G, because the position of the monochord first provided these with the prescribed ascent and descent: below, they have one tetrachord of grave notes, and above, two of acute notes.

# CHAPTER TWELVE. On dividing the four modes into eight

Meanwhile, when chants of one mode—for example, the first—were sometimes grave and low in relation to the ending, and sometimes acute and high, verses and psalms, and anything else that, as we said, had to be adapted to the ending, could not be delivered in one and the same manner and adapted to both. What was joined to it, if grave, did not suit the acute; if acute, it disagreed with the grave.

It was therefore decided that each mode should be divided into two, namely an acute and a grave mode. Once the rules had been distributed, the acute parts would agree with the acute and the grave with the grave. Each acute mode would be called authentic, that is, authoritative and principal; the grave would be called plagal, that is, lateral and lesser.

For one who is said to stand at my side is lesser than I; otherwise, if he were greater, I would more properly be said to stand at his side.

Thus, when one speaks of authentic first mode and plagal first mode, and similarly of the others, the four modes which naturally existed in the voices became eight in the chants.

By an improper Latin usage, people say: for authentic first mode and plagal first mode, first and second; for authentic second mode and plagal second mode, third and fourth; for authentic third mode and plagal third mode, fifth and sixth; for authentic fourth mode and plagal fourth mode, seventh and eighth.

# CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On recognizing the eight modes, and their acute and grave ranges

There are therefore eight modes, like the eight parts of speech and the eight forms of blessedness. Every chant moving through them is varied by eight dissimilar voices and qualities.

For distinguishing them in chants, certain neumes were also invented. From the way these fit the chant, we recognize its mode just as we often discover whose tunic something is from the way it fits the body. For example:

> First seek the kingdom of God  
> [musical notation: Pri [Dac] mum [a] quae [a] ri [G] te [FE] re [G] gnum [FE] Dei [DD] [C F G a G a G F E F G a G F E F D.]]

As soon as we see this neume fitting well with the ending of an antiphon, there is no need to doubt that it belongs to the authentic first mode; and so it is with the others.
