For recognizing this, the verses of nocturnal responsories, the psalms of the offices, and everything prescribed in the formulas of the modes are also extremely useful. If someone does not know these formulas, it is astonishing if he understands any part of what is being said. For in the formulas it is foreseen in which voices the chant of each mode begins more or less frequently and in which it scarcely begins.

In the plagal modes it is scarcely permitted to raise either the beginnings or the endings of distinctions to the fifth, since even reaching the fourth is very rare [Note: [Col. 0391D] It seems that one should read *soleant pervenire*, “they are usually able to reach.”].

In the authentic modes, except for the second, it is likewise scarcely permitted for those beginnings and endings of distinctions to rise to the sixth. The plagal first and third modes rise to the third; the plagal second and fourth rise to the fourth.

Remember also that, as the testimony of customary chants shows, the authentic modes scarcely descend more than one voice below their final. The authentic third mode appears to do this most rarely because of the semitone imperfection lying beneath it. The authentic modes rise to the octave and ninth, or even the tenth.

The plagal modes descend and rise to the fifth. Authority grants them the sixth or seventh for ascent, just as it grants the authentic modes the ninth and tenth. The plagal first, second, and third modes sometimes necessarily end on the acute a, [♮], or c.

The rules stated above must be observed especially in antiphons and responsories, whose chants need to be adapted to psalms and verses and therefore must be supported by common rules. Otherwise, you will find many chants in which gravity and acuteness are so confused that it cannot be discerned to which they belong more—the authentic or the plagal.

Moreover, when searching for unknown chants, we are greatly aided by adding the aforesaid neumes and accompanying passages. Through their suitability, we perceive the character of each sound by the power of the mode.

A trope is a kind of chant, which is also called a mode; we must say more about it.

# CHAPTER FOURTEEN. On the tropes and the power of music

Some people, through long practice with these tropes, recognize their characteristics and distinct appearances, so to speak, immediately upon hearing them. It is like an expert in peoples who, when many persons of different nations are set before him, can observe their appearance and say: “This one is Greek, that one Spanish, this one Latin, and that one German; this one, however, is Frankish.”

In the same way, the diversity of the tropes is adapted to the diversity of minds. One person delights in the broken leaps of the authentic second mode; another chooses the pleasure of the plagal third; one prefers the chatter of the authentic fourth; another approves the sweetness of the same plagal mode; and so it is with the rest.

Nor is it surprising that hearing is delighted by a variety of sounds, since sight rejoices in a variety of colors, smell is nourished by a variety of odors, and the tongue takes pleasure in changing flavors. Through the body’s window, the sweetness of delightful things thus enters wonderfully into the inner chambers of the heart.

Hence, just as health of both heart and body is diminished or increased by certain flavors, colors, odors, or even the sight of colors, so, as we read, a certain frenzied man was recalled from madness when the physician Asclepiades sang. Another man was so inflamed by the sweetness of the cithara that, driven mad, he sought to break into a girl’s chamber; but when the cithara player changed the mode, he was led to repentance and withdrew in confusion.

Likewise, David used the cithara to calm Saul’s demon and broke the demonic savagery with the powerful force and sweetness of this art. Yet the full extent of this power is revealed only by divine wisdom. Let us use in divine praises what we have perceived from it, as it were, in a riddle.

But since we have scarcely tasted a few elements of the power of this art, let us see what things are necessary for singing well.

# CHAPTER FIFTEEN. On composing a suitable modulation

Just as in meters there are letters and syllables, parts and feet, and verses, so in harmony there are *phthongi*, that is, sounds. One, two, or three of these are fitted together into syllables; the syllables, either singly or doubled, form a neume, that is, a part of the chant. One or more parts make a distinction, that is, a suitable place for breathing.

It should be noted that the whole part must be marked and expressed compactly, while the syllable must be expressed more compactly. The *tenor*, that is, the duration of the final voice, is somewhat longer in the syllable, longer still in the part, and longest in the distinction. It serves as a sign in these divisions.

Thus the chant must be beaten out, as it were, with metrical feet; some voices must have a pause twice as long as others, or twice as short, or a trembling duration—that is, a varied tenor. A long duration is sometimes indicated by a plain stroke placed beside the letter.

Great care must be taken that the neumes are distributed in such a way that, whether the neumes are formed by the repercussion of the same sound or by the joining of two or more sounds, they always correspond and answer one another either in the number of voices or in the proportion of tones: sometimes equal to equal, sometimes double or triple to simple, and sometimes in a sesquialteral or sesquitertian proportion.

[Col. 0393] [Col. 0395]

The musician should decide from these divisions how to make the chant proceed, just as the metrician decides with which feet to make a verse. The musician, however, is not bound by so strict a necessity of law, because in every respect this art alters the arrangement of the voices with a reasonable variety [Note: [Col. 0395C] Ottobonian manuscript: “permits them to be mixed.”].

Although we often do not comprehend this rationality, that which delights the mind, in which reason resides, is nevertheless believed to be rational. These matters, and others like them, are better demonstrated through conversation than through writing.

The distinctions should therefore, as in verses, be equal, and sometimes repeated identically or varied by some small alteration. When several have been doubled, they should have parts that are not excessively different and that are sometimes transformed into one another through the modes, or appear as similar ascending and descending forms [Note: [Col. 0395C] Another manuscript: “when they have been especially beautiful.”].

Likewise, a returning neume should return by the same route by which it came and retrace the same footsteps. Just as one line rises by leaping from the acute notes, another should oppose it from the grave notes with a corresponding inclination, as happens when, in a well, we look across at ourselves in our reflection.

Sometimes one syllable should have one or several neumes; sometimes one neume should be divided among several syllables. These neumes may all be varied: sometimes they may begin from the same voice, sometimes from different ones, according to the varying qualities of relaxation and acuteness.

Likewise, almost all distinctions should proceed toward the principal voice, that is, the final voice—or toward one of its related voices if that has been chosen in its place. Sometimes the same voice that ends all the neumes, or several distinctions, should also begin them, as anyone who investigates Ambrose may discover.

There are also chants that are almost prose-like and observe these principles less strictly. In them it does not matter if, in different places and without distinction, some parts and distinctions are larger and others smaller, in the manner of prose.

I call these “metrical chants” because we often sing in such a way that we seem to scan as if we were moving through verses by their feet, as happens when we sing actual meters. In these, care must be taken that excessive disyllabic neumes are not joined continuously without the admixture of trisyllabic and tetrasyllabic ones.

Just as lyric poets joined different feet now in one way and now in another, so those who compose chants arrange neumes that are reasonably distinct and varied. The distinction is reasonable if the variety of neumes and distinctions is so moderated that the neumes answer the neumes and the distinctions the distinctions in some constant similarity and consonance—that is, so that there is a dissimilar similarity, in the manner of the most pleasing Ambrose.

There is no small similarity between meters and chants, since neumes take the place of feet and distinctions the place of verses. You may see one neume proceeding in a dactylic meter, another in a spondaic, and another in an iambic meter; and you may see a distinction that is now tetrameter, now pentameter, and elsewhere almost hexameter. Many other arrangements also occur, so that ascent and descent are placed before, beneath, beside, or between one another, sometimes jointly, sometimes separately, and sometimes in combination, in the following manner.

Likewise, the parts and distinctions of the neumes and of the words should end together. There should not be a long tenor on certain short syllables or a short tenor on long ones, because this produces [Note: [Col. 0396C] Manuscript F: “dissonance.”] unseemliness, although it will rarely be necessary to attend to this.

The effect of the chant should imitate the events of the subject: in sad matters the neumes should be grave, in peaceful matters cheerful, in prosperous matters exultant, and so forth.

We often place a grave or acute accent over the voices, because we sometimes utter certain sounds with greater force and sometimes with less. Thus the repetition of the same voice may often appear to be an ascent or a descent.

Likewise, at the end of distinctions, the voices should approach the place of breathing more rarely, as if, like a tired horse, they arrived at rest with a heavy gait. The densely or sparsely composed notes can often indicate this matter, as appropriate.

In many places the voices become liquid, as letters do, so that the beginning of one mode passes clearly into another and seems not to come to an end. Over a liquid voice we place a dot, as though marking it, in this manner:

> Ad [G] te [DE] le [Ga] va [a] vi. [G.]

If you wish to pronounce it more fully, without making it liquid, there is no harm; indeed, it is often more pleasing. Everything we have said should be done neither too rarely nor too continuously, but with discernment.

# CHAPTER SIXTEEN. On the manifold variety of sounds and neumes
It should not seem surprising that so great a quantity [Col. 0397A] of such diverse chants has been formed from so few voices—voices which, as we have said, are joined to one another in only six ways, both by elevation and by descent. For although syllables are formed from a small number of letters, even if not very many, the number of syllables can be calculated; nevertheless, an infinite multiplicity of parts has grown from syllables. Likewise, from a few feet many kinds of metres are made, and a metre of one kind is found to differ through very many variations, as in the hexameter. Let the grammarians see how this happens, since to explain it belongs to another subject. Let us, if we can, consider by what methods we may construct neumes that differ from one another.

The movement of voices, which was said to occur harmoniously in six ways, takes place through arsis and thesis—that is, elevation and descent. Through this twofold movement, arsis and [Col. 0397B] thesis, every neume is formed, except repercussed or simple neumes. Arsis and thesis are then joined either to themselves—arsis to arsis and thesis to thesis—or one to the other, as arsis to thesis and thesis to arsis. The joining itself is sometimes made from similar elements and sometimes from dissimilar ones.

There is dissimilarity when, among the movements just mentioned—that is, tones, semitones, ditones, and the rest—one has more or fewer voices than another, or when the voices are more closely or more widely joined in different ways. Further, even when the movement has been joined in a similar manner, one movement may be placed before another, that is, above it; or beneath it; or beside it, when the end of one movement is the beginning of another on the same voice; or between it, when one movement is placed below another and is less grave and less acute; or in a mixed position, partly between and partly beneath, before, or beside it. These positions may again be distinguished according to the various qualities of relaxation and sharpness, increase and diminution, and of the modes themselves. Neumes too may be varied through the same forms of arsis and thesis, and sometimes distinctions as well. For this reason we have added a diagram, so that the way may be easier to follow with the eyes. [Col. 0397]

## CHAPTER XVII. That everything written can be reduced to song

[Col. 0399A]

Having briefly indicated these matters, I shall here give you another very clear argument, extremely useful in practice, although hitherto unheard of. When the cause of all melodies has become clear, you will be able to apply to your own use whatever you find advantageous, and nevertheless reject whatever seems discordant [Note: [Col. 0399D] F. “dissonant.”].

Consider, then, that just as everything spoken is written, so everything written is reduced to song. Everything spoken is therefore sung, while writing is represented by letters. But so that our rule may not become too lengthy, let us take only the five vowels from these six [Note: [Col. 0400D] Better, “from the same letters.”] letters. Without them no other letter, nor even a syllable, is thought capable of sounding. They are especially responsible for the formation of words whenever a sweet harmony is found in different parts, as we often see in verses whose lines are consonant and answer one another in metre, so that you may marvel at a kind of symphony of grammar. If a similar musical response is joined to it, you will take delight in a double modulation.

Let us therefore take these five vowels. Perhaps, since they contribute so much harmony to words, they will contribute no less to song and to neumes. Let them be placed in order beneath the letters of the monochord, and since there are only five, let them be repeated until a vowel has been assigned beneath every sound, as follows:

[Musical diagram]

In this diagram consider only this point: since all speech is moved by these five letters, it must also be admitted that the five voices move in relation to one another, as we have said. Since this is so, let us now take some passage of speech and sing its syllables by applying the sounds that the vowels written beneath those syllables indicate, as follows: [Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399] “Holy John, the abundance of your merits—not worthily to sing.” [Musical notation: C D; F C D; D E F G; G F G; F E C; D D F; E D; C D D.]

There can be no doubt that what has been done with this sentence can also be done with every other sentence. But so that no burdensome necessity may be imposed on you—for in this method scarcely any symphony contains five voices, and it is often impossible to go beyond those five as freely as one might wish—I add another verse of vowels, but make it different in such a way that it begins at the third position of the preceding one: [Col. 0400C]

[Musical diagram]

Here, since there are everywhere two accompanying sounds in which the five vowels are contained—one vowel being placed beneath each sound, while the other gives you considerably greater freedom—you have the liberty to vary and proceed according to your will, with a more extended or more contracted movement. Let us now see what kind of symphony its vowels have brought to this rhythm. [Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399D] “Restraining the tongue, let him temper it, lest the horror of quarrels resound; let him cover the sight by fostering it, lest he drink in vanities.” [Musical notation: G G; F a G; a a a; a; G; c; c d; e d; c d c; c a G; a; c c a; F G G.]

We have left this argument in the final section only so that we might make the melody conform to its tetrardus. Since a particular chant, through its own vowels alone, lays claim to a melody so appropriate to itself, there is no doubt that it will become especially suitable if, through extensive practice, you select from among many possibilities only those that are best and answer most appropriately to one another; if you fill out what gapes, resolve what is compressed, contract what is excessively prolonged, and extend what is overly contracted, so that you produce one carefully finished work.

[Col. 0401A] I also want you to know that, like pure silver, every chant becomes more highly polished the more it is used. What displeases at first is later praised, as though polished by use like a file. According to differences of peoples and minds, what displeases one person is embraced by another. One is pleased by consonance, another prefers diversity. One seeks continuity and softness according to the wantonness of his mind; another, being serious, is soothed by sober chants. Yet another, like a madman, feeds on elaborate compositions and winding complications. Each person pronounces most sonorously the chant that he approves according to the quality inherent in his own mind.

If you cling to all these matters through constant practice in the arguments already stated, you will not be able to remain ignorant of them. Indeed, the arguments must be used until we understand them in part, so that we may reach complete knowledge. But since the brevity we have undertaken does not permit us to pursue these matters at length—especially since much can be inferred from them—let this suffice concerning singing. Now let us briefly explain the rules of diaphonia.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On diaphonia, that is, the rule of organum

“Diaphonia” means a separation of voices, which we call organum, when voices separated from one another sound discordantly in harmony and harmoniously in dissonance. It is used in such a way that a fourth string always follows the singer, as D follows A. If the organum is doubled upward through high a, so that there are D and high a, A resounds to D as a diatessaron and to high a as a diapason; D, in turn, forms with each of A and a a diatessaron and a diapente, while high a forms with the lower notes a diapente and a diapason.

Since these three species combine with the organum in such a degree and sweetness that they have been shown above to produce the likeness of the symphonies of voices, they are appropriately called unions of voices, although “symphony” is said of every kind of singing. The following is an example of these diaphonias:

**Diapason:** c d e c d e d c c c a g c d e d d c.  
**Diapente:** F G a F G a G F F F E D C F G a G G F.  
“Have mercy on me, God.”

**Diatessaron:** C D E C D E D C C C B A Γ C D E D D C.

This clearly corrected figure contains the preceding notes of the antiphon *Have mercy on me, God*, organizing the following notes by a diatessaron, which is commonly called organum [Note: [Col. 0401D] Better, “beneath”] *below the voice*, that is, beneath them; it retains the preceding high notes organized by a diapente, which is called organum *above the voice*. This antiphon is in the tritus tone, that is, the sixth, and the organum descends in it as far as low C, to which the organum sometimes descends. For just as the grave voices descend, so the acute voices ascend. You may also double the chant with the organum, and the organum with the chant, through a diapason as much as you wish; wherever its concord occurs, the harmony of the symphonies described will not cease.

Since the doubling of voices has now been sufficiently explained, let us describe the lower accompaniment sung by the singer in the manner we use. The higher form of diaphonia is hard, whereas ours is soft. In ours we do not admit the semitone and diapente; we do admit the tone, ditone, and semiditone together with the diatessaron, but the semiditone has the lowest position among these, while the diatessaron has precedence.

The chant of the diaphonia follows these four concords [Note: [Col. 0402D] Read “the chant”]. Among the modes, some are suitable, others more suitable, and others most suitable. Suitable are those that produce organum only at the fourth, through a diatessaron, as the deuterus in B and E. More suitable are those that answer not only at the fourth but also, though rarely, at the third and second through a tone and semiditone, as the protus in A and D. Most suitable are those that do this most frequently and most sweetly, as the tetrardus and tritus in C, F, and G. For these obey the tone, ditone, and diatessaron.

Of these, when the tritus is reached—whether the end of a distinction has arrived there or it lies nearest to the final note—the accompanying voice must never descend below it unless the singer has admitted lower notes. The organum may never be lowered from the lowest tritus, or from the note immediately above the lowest. When the singer has admitted lower notes at an appropriate place and the organum has been lowered by a diatessaron, then, as soon as the gravity of the distinction is abandoned so that it is not expected to be repeated, the accompanying voice should resume the position it previously held. Thus, if it has arrived at the final voice, it should remain with it; if it lies above it, it should meet the final voice appropriately nearby. This meeting is better made at a tone, less well at a ditone, and never at a semiditone. A meeting at a diatessaron scarcely occurs, since a lower accompaniment is more pleasing in that place.

[Col. 0402C] Care must nevertheless be taken that this not occur in the final distinction of the symphony. Often, when the singer has admitted lower notes below the tritus, we hold the organum suspended on the tritus. In that case the singer must not make a distinction on the lower notes; rather, by returning to the waiting tritus amid rapidly moving notes, he should assist it and repel both his own and the organum’s conclusion by making the distinction above.

Likewise, when the meeting occurs at a tone, the final note is sustained for a long time, so that the organum partly follows it and partly sings together with it. When the meeting is at a ditone, it is sustained longer, often through an intervening note, so that although the response is brief, the meeting at the tone is not absent. Because this occurs, the harmony ends in the deuterus. Even if the chant is not expected to descend farther to the tritus, it will then be useful for the protus to take up the force of the organum, follow the succeeding notes, and meet the end appropriately at a tone.

Likewise, since it is not permissible to separate by more than a diatessaron, when the singer goes higher the accompanying voice must ascend, so that C follows F, D follows G, E follows a, and so forth. Finally, apart from the square note, a diatessaron lies beneath each individual voice. Therefore, in whatever distinctions it occurs, G will possess the force of the organum. This happens whether the chant descends to F, or the accompanying voice follows it, or the chant makes a distinction on G. At suitable places F follows G and a; but if the chant does not end on G, F admits the force of the organum together with the chant. When the soft b occurs in the chant, F will be the organal note.

Since the tritus thus holds precedence in diaphonia and occupies the most suitable place above the others, we see that Gregory rightly loved it more than the other voices. For he supplied many beginnings of melodies and very many repetitions, so that often, if the tritus E and c are removed from his chant, he may seem to have lost nearly half of it. The rules of diaphonia have now been given; if you test them by examples, you will understand them perfectly.

## CHAPTER XIX. The testing of the foregoing diaphonia by examples

We therefore do not lower the organum from the tritus, whether the chant ends on it or on the following notes, as follows:

[Col. 0403B] Here is the end of a distinction on the tritus C. We do not lower the organum from it because it has beneath it neither a tone nor a ditone, by which a meeting is made; it has a semiditone, but no meeting is made through a semiditone.

“Let me keep faith.”

Here is another distinction in the tritus F, in which we follow at the fourth, through a diatessaron, and a diatessaron accompaniment is more pleasing than a meeting:

“They themselves—me wholly [fragment].”

Here is another tritus of the same kind on F:

“I commit [it] concerning devotion.”

Here is another distinction in the protus D, in which a meeting at the tone is clearly made at the end.

Likewise:

“There was a man in Jerusalem,” or thus:

“Jerusalem.”

[Col. 0403D] Here is a distinction in the deuterus E, in which a meeting at the ditone, whether simple or interrupted, is pleasing:

“Come, to teach you the way of prudence.”

A distinction in the protus A. In this distinction lower tritus C, which lies immediately below the final D, has been admitted, and the former position has been resumed after the gravity had ended, where we said “the way of prudence.” Likewise here:

“At the sixth hour he sat beside the well.”

See how the organum ascends, taking care not to sing beneath the final distinction. [Col. 0404A]

“At the sixth hour he sat beside the well.”

See how, when the singer admits lower notes, we hold the organum suspended on the tritus:

“Victor ascended to heaven, from which he will descend.”

See how F follows G and a at the end. You will find the same practice used in the plagal tritus: just as it follows C and d, so F follows G and a, as follows:

“Come, let us adore.”

## CHAPTER XX. How music was discovered from the sound of hammers

[Col. 0404B]

As for the origin of the art of music, we kept silent about it at the beginning because we saw that the reader was inexperienced; we reserve it now for one who is more practiced and knowledgeable. In ancient times there were uncertain instruments and a multitude of singers, but they were blind: no human being could gather by any argument the differences among voices or the distinctions of symphony. Nor could anyone ever have learned anything certain about this art unless divine goodness had finally arranged what follows by its own will.

When a certain great philosopher, Pythagoras, happened to be travelling, he came to a workshop in which five hammers were striking one anvil. The philosopher, astonished by their sweet harmony, approached. At first he hoped that the power of the sound and its modulation arose from differences in the hands, so he exchanged the hammers; but after this was done, the proper force followed each one. Removing the hammer that was dissonant from the others, he weighed the remaining ones. In a remarkable way, by divine providence, the first weighed twelve, the second nine, the third eight, and the fourth six—by weights of some kind.

He therefore recognized that the science of music lies in the proportion and comparison of numbers. For that arrangement in the four hammers is the same as that now found in the four letters A, D, E, and a. If low A has twelve units and high a six, high a stands to low A in the proportion that is double in arithmetic, but in music is the consonance of the diapason.

Low D, which has nine, stands to low E, which has eight, in the proportion that is called *sesquioctava* in arithmetic, that is, *epogdous*, but in music is the consonance of the tone. Likewise, high a to low E, just as low D to low A, stands in the proportion called *sesquitertia* in arithmetic, but in music is the consonance of the diatessaron. High a to low D, just as low E to low A, stands in the proportion called *sesquialtera* in arithmetic, but in music is the consonance of the diapente.

If A has twelve and D nine, A will contain four ternary steps within twelve, while D contains three ternary steps within nine. Again, since A has twelve and D has nine [Note: [Col. 0403D] Read: “and E has eight”], A will have three quaternary steps, while E will have two, and the diapente is evident. Let twelve again be in A and six in the other a: six is half of twelve, just as high a is understood through half of the other A. Thus the diapason is present.

Therefore A to D produces a diatessaron, A to E a diapente, and A to the other high a a diapason. D likewise sounds a tone to E, and to either A or a a diatessaron or diapente. E also gives a tone to D and a diapente or diatessaron to either A or a. High a sounds a diapason with A, a diapente with D, and a diatessaron with E. The careful investigator will find all these relationships in the numbers stated above.

Beginning from this point, Boethius, the expositor of this art, demonstrated the many wonderful and most difficult harmonies of the art through numerical proportions. What more is there to say? Through the species mentioned above, that first Pythagoras constructed the monochord. Since in it the knowledge of the art is not wanton but carefully laid open, it pleased learned people in common, and up to the present day the art has gradually grown stronger, with that teacher always enlightening human darkness, whose supreme wisdom endures through all ages. Amen.

Here ends the *Micrologus*, that is, a brief discourse on music, composed by the most accomplished musician and venerable monk, Master Guido.

[Col. 0405]

## HERE BEGIN GUIDO’S VERSES ON THE EXPLANATION OF MUSIC AND THE ORDER OF HIS NAME

The hearts of men, softened by my songs, grow warm,

A single power has bestowed on me measured beats,

In heaven I pour forth songs most pleasing to the Highest,

Giving Christ’s court a gift with the voice of a teacher,

I wrote myself in order, the first who fashioned songs.

## HERE BEGIN ALSO GUIDO’S RHYTHMICAL RULES OF MUSIC

Delivered in the prologue to his antiphonary.

[Col. 0405B]

There is a great difference between musicians and singers:

The latter speak; the former know what Music composes.

For whoever does what he does not understand is defined as a beast.

But if they praise the sharpness of a thunderous voice,

A vocal she-ass will surpass the nightingale.

Therefore dialectic removes their claim to existence.

For this reason the immense multitude of rustics,

So long as it lives in vain, labours under astonishing madness,

While no antiphon is learned without a teacher.

Reject, then, those notes used by the common people,

With which one never advances without a guide, like a blind man,

And learn these seven notes through seven characters:

ut, re, mi, fa, ut, sol, re, la, mi, fa, sol, ut.

Γ, A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

[Col. 0405C] a, b, c, d, e, f, g, a, [a]

la, re, mi, fa, ut, sol, re, mi, la, fa, sol, la.

For the other set of seven that follows afterward

Is not another set, but repeats the same rule,

Because there is an equal seven-day week of voices, as of days.

If you wish to see with your eyes what you hear,

While your mouth remains silent, let the evidence of manual work

Be established through definite numbers [Note: [Col. 0405] V. “so that, plainly, the small pupils may see the things we call thus: the space—or spaces—of the first letters.”].

Some place the Greek gamma Γ before the first letter,

[Col. 0406B] From which the whole line is divided by nine steps.

Where the first step ends, there will be the first letter.

In the same way, let an equal number of steps be made from the first,

And the place of the second will be revealed in the order stated above:

This harmony of sounds musicians call a tone.

Again, divide the whole string of Gamma into four;

The third will immediately sound nearer to the second.

A diatessaron is slightly more than two tones.

The short interval itself is called a semitone;

A tone is what the measure of nine parts produces.

The diatessaron receives its name from four.

If a tone is added to it, a diapente arises,

A Greek name translated into Latin from the word for five.

[Col. 0406C] For if it makes three steps, it consists of five voices.

Thus the first gives the fourth an indication

Of four steps, and the second serves the fifth

By the same number.

The third leads to the sixth, and does not alter the calculation.

For the seventh from Gamma, make it the middle of the whole [text uncertain; Note: [Col. 0405C] A. “makes its”].

Then the eighth takes its proper place from the first.

Indeed, the first becomes the first again, without changing its number.

Thus the second gives the second, the third the third,

The fourth the fourth, the fifth the fifth, each its own letter.

[Col. 0407A] The acute is marked by the same letter as the grave,

From the first voice to the eighth, or to the same letter.

Musicians call this harmony of sounds a diapason,

Whose name is transferred to a letter from all the rest,

Because it contains all the voices, or because it divides the whole line

By two steps into the same letter,

And, doubled twice, brings the monochord to an end.

It contains five tones and two semitones.

It contains within itself a diapente and a diatessaron.

It is the greatest unity of symphonies and voices.

I am astonished that some have made four signs for the voices,

As though these were the same as the fifths, some of which are dissonant.

Some, although related, do not consonate perfectly.

### Also concerning divisions

[Col. 0407B]

Likewise, Gamma, through the nine steps we mentioned:

Just as the first step gives the first, so the third gives the fourth;

The fifth gives the first, the sixth the fourth, and the seventh again the first.

The first step of the first also establishes the second;

Likewise, the third terminates its end in the fifth.

The fifth again gives the second, and the sixth renews the fifth.

The first of the four steps of Gamma mentioned above

Shows the third, and likewise the second shows the seventh.

The third marks the same seventh in triplication.

By squaring the third we also produce the sixth.

Thus, immediately at the next step, we write the third again,

And by squaring it again complete the other sixth.

[Col. 0407C] There are some who add, among the acute notes beside the first letter,

A sign which Father Gregory did not approve, calling it wantonness.

Modern scholars do not even mention it.

Although among some people it is used as a little note,

Among many it is rightly called superfluous.

The other second is always authentic.

Take careful note: all tones are made through nine steps,

The diatessaron through four, as we said above,

The diapente always through three, and the diapason through two.

In this way the monochord is easily made.

But if cymbals are fashioned by the work of musicians,

These measurements must be observed especially in their weight.

By these measurements the sounding organs are also proportioned,

And all vessels properly made by musicians.

By these measurements the whole Church now sings to God.

[Col. 0407D] Every voice is joined to the second and to the third,

But to the fourth and fifth it is joined in no other way

Unless a diatessaron or diapente is present.

The second voice is joined by a tone or semitone;

The ditone and semiditone are also named.

But if a voice advances beyond the second to the third,

It is called a diatessaron when it proceeds to the fourth;

It is called a diapente when it is joined to the fifth.

No voice will move except through these six movements.

Since every song is formed through them,

I urge you, prudent singer, to learn them perfectly:

For whoever knows them fully has no uncertainty in song.

### Which voices may be raised or lowered

[Col. 0408A]

Therefore the first, third, fourth, fifth, and seventh

May be raised or lowered four times;

But the sixth and second have no such permission.

The second may not be lowered to the lower fourth,

Nor may it ever be raised above the fifth.

The sixth is not joined to the upper fourth or lower fifth.

### On the distinctions among voices

Because semitones and tones are fitted together differently

With seven sounds, there are seven distinctions,

So that the sound of no voice is identical with another.

Yet among the seven voices there is a certain concord.

Often, if not always, the same antiphon

Is sung at different pitches without changing its harmony.

### On the four modes of voices

There are, indeed, four modes among the seven little voices,

Which must be learned with the greatest care; the rule of the Greeks

Calls them protus, deuterus, tritus, and tetrardus:

Protus is first, and the second is called deuterus;

The third is called tritus, and the fourth tetrardus.

They are arranged in order among the voices in this way.

### On the proximity of voices through the four modes

The first voice and the fourth present the first mode;

The second gives the second, and likewise the fifth.

The third, compared with the sixth, often sings the same thing.

The singular seventh joins these to the fourth mode,

Yet in ascending it sounds like the third,

And in descending it offers itself as a little sister to the fourth.

### On the similarity of the first and fifth voices

Moreover, the fifth is very similar to the first,

[Col. 0408C] But only in descending; for if you mark

The semitones and tones, you will see this as you hear it.

The remaining voices differ greatly from one another;

Each makes its neume unlike the other,

Nor does it give the neume of another the place of its own position.

### Also on the four tropes divided into eight

For a curious ear it will be extremely useful

To observe and understand how the harmony

Is sung in four modes with transformed appearance.

From these four modes we subsequently make eight,

Because we distinguish grave and high chants,

Calling them, in the Greek manner, authentic and plagal.

### Also on authentics and plagals

High chants are authentic; the grave ones are called plagal,

And when both are counted in four tones,

They indicate eight formulas of tones or modes.

Protus is the first authentic, and the second is the plagal of protus.

Deuterus is the authentic, which we call the third.

The fourth, following in order, is its plagal.

The fifth is the authentic tritus, and the sixth is its plagal.

Then the authentic tetrardus is the one we call the seventh.

The plagal of tetrardus is the eighth, which follows the seventh.

Of these, two share one voice, as we said before,

Because in nature there are truly four voices,

And if you understand them, nothing in this art is more useful.

### On the final notes

Although a chant has all voices and modes,

It nevertheless belongs to the mode that its final note sounds.

For from that note it takes the rule of how it should proceed.

We have the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh voices as finals.

Many place endings everywhere without distinction, just as beginnings.

Each chant regularly reaches the octave

And can descend to the fifth from the final,

When there is no distinction between plagals and authentics.

But if it is necessary to distinguish plagals from authentics,

The plagals leap to the fifth and go no farther,

And, descending to the fifth, they find their proper limit.

But the authentics appropriately leap to the octave,

[Col. 0409B] and from the final descend by one tone, no farther.

When no tone lies below the tritus, it has the gravest final.

The beginning too ought to be consonant with the ending.

Therefore it should not exceed the fifth from the final.

The plagals should not extend their beginning beyond the fourth.

Among the others the second voice lies in an inferior position;

The third and sixth are used much more frequently against it.

Holy Gregory is my witness in this matter;

He did not wish it to be principal [Note: [Col. 0409D] A. “he wished it”].

The authentic deuterus took the third in its place,

Whose final, although it is the sixth, often begins with it.

Many things are used without being governed by the rule,

Because music has long since fallen out of practice through time,

While envy and sluggishness remove every subject of study.

The following, however, is widely evident concerning the voices:

They function like syllables and parts, cola and commas.

Verses often sing together through art, as in metre.

We have found it best to mark them with letters alone.

Nothing is easier for learning song,

If they are used constantly for at least three months.

“Blessed be the name of the Lord forever.” [d: name; c d c; d c c; c a a; a; G G G.]

“Our help is in the name of the Lord.” [F G a G F G; F F; F; c F F F; D c D D.]

Neumes are commonly made for the sake of abbreviation.

If they are made carefully, they are counted as letters,

Provided that the letters are arranged with lines in this way [Note: [Col. 0409D] Here the manuscript has blank lines, with only initial letters.].

Then, as study advances, between two lines

One voice may be inserted, as reason requires,

So that its position may vary according to different circumstances.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The material enclosed in parentheses is taken from the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

[Some place two voices between two lines,

Some place three, while some have no lines at all,

[Col. 0410A] And since their work is difficult, this is the gravest error.

But the simple method is quickly grasped:

The third and sixth tones are written most frequently,

And the mind soon recognizes them when they are often repercussed.

The use of letters and neumes should be constant.

The place of each sound is easily understood,

Even when only one letter is prefixed.]

So that the character of the sounds may be distinguished more clearly,

We mark certain lines with different colours,

So that the eye may immediately recognize the place of each tone.

In the order of the third voice a shining saffron radiates;

Its related sixth glows red with yellow vermilion:

The affinity of the colours indicates the rest.

But if neither a letter nor a colour is present for the neumes,

It will be like a well without a rope:

[Col. 0410B] Though its waters are abundant, they are of no use to those who see them.

That which I mentioned earlier will also be very useful:

If you take care to inspect neumes of similar shape,

Observe how differently they sound in different places and modes.

You will easily understand the suitability of the neumes,

And the place of each sound on the various lines,

If you practise frequently with the formulas of the modes.

A symphony sings together with symphonies of whatever kind;

Know that the symphony itself is of the same kind.

Therefore we append the eight melodies to all the antiphons,

[Note: [Col. 0410D] V. “with letters prefixed at the head of the lines.”]

A greater number of voices may be made brief; the mark becomes a limit in the space.

It is the sign of the following neume, indicating where it must be placed,

So that it may not be put in its proper place when necessity demands otherwise.

Although someone may sing a chant from memory,

[Col. 0410C] If he does not perceive from memory all its movements and sounds,

What they are and what kind they are, let him not claim to understand anything.

Up to this point we have brought the hidden Muses into the light,

And, to the honour of almighty God, by whom we exist and live,

We have offended the envious by offering this to the willing.

I shall briefly disclose the forms of the constitutions.

The conjunction of certain sounds is so called

When there is only an intensification, or conversely a relaxation.

The first constitution consists of two sounds,

The second of three, the third of four,

And the fourth of any five voices.

Of these, the first is simple, the second is doubled.

The third calls forth four varieties.

The fourth sounds in eight ways the consonant diapente.

If one voice is added to one constitution in all its modes,

There are as many modes.

If the second sounds are removed, there will again be as many.

Thus every constitution arises from another:

The first gives the second, and the second the third;

The third makes the fourth, as this page shows [Note: [Col. 0411B] Admont. “Victor [c c] ascending [d c a] to heaven [c], from which [c a] he had descended. [G F G G] See how F follows G and a at the end. The same practice is found in the plagal tritus, namely, that b follows C and D just as E follows G and A, in this way:

‘Come, to let us pray.’

].

[Col. 0411A] A sound is whatever has the concord of the rule,

Associating any forms of constitutions,

Until the space of the forms restrains the diapason.

For we rarely use spacious forms, especially empty ones,

In song; shorter forms, more closely connected,

Are approved by frequent practice.

And since larger forms are made from smaller ones,

There can be no doubt that whoever knows the smallest

Will have no uncertainty about the larger.

Again, there may be great variety in any large form:

At one time a voice sounds simply in the chant,

At another it doubles or triples itself through repercussion.

The related voices that the rule demonstrates

Are not rejected by the concord of these constitutions;

Rather, the same melody is always present in one and the other.

[Col. 0412A] I have made clear rules and delivered to singers

An antiphonary perfected according to rule,

Such as they have never had in former times.

I ask you, blessed brothers, for the sake of these great labours:

Pray to the merciful God for wretched me, Guido,

And for my helpers, that he may be favourable to us.

Help the writer of the work also with your prayers.

Pray for the teacher, whose assistance

The author and the scribe both require.

Glory be to the Lord. Amen.

Behold, a description of the voice has been set forth in every way.

The tone is in numbers, as nine exceeds eight;

The semitone, which derived its name from that name.

The ditone and half-ditone hold the whole diatessaron.

And this makes the whole known through a square distinction;

Add a tone above it, and you will see the diapente of sounds.

[Col. 0413A] And the tone divided into three will mark the same thing,

Joining both in the middle of the total diapason.

For it returns the double sound as the same single sound.

Add twice six, and you will see the known diatriton,

The ditone and half-ditone, because the other is called the ditone.

No musical movement will make its course without these movements.

Something has been represented by number as it modulates,

And this lies hidden as fixed, but becomes clear through tension and relaxation.

A mode is the comparison of one *phthongos* with another *phthongos*.

The compared differences of voices give one another their mode.

The voice that follows a tone and a semitone is called protus.

The neighbouring order knows what deuterus and tritus are.

And it has pleased tetrardus to differ from them by only a tone,

The ditone and half-ditone, whose rights immediately follow.

No musical voice among these exists without the law of the modes.

[Col. 0413B] The unruly common people perceive only the endings of these.

[Col. 0414A] The four authentics are doubled by acquiring their plagals,

Unless the fourth, being simple, establishes the seven distinctions;

Thus the poet sings: “seven distinctions of voices.”

The seventh attached itself to the eighth because it resembles it.

Through these the authentics acquired a grave distinction,

While the plagals desire thin and lower voices.

In these, however, the comparison differs only slightly.

If by chance you wish to write two of them for one voice,

The delta will hold primacy over the remaining four.

An *enthymeme* closes the sounds and marks those that are remote.

They agree through a bend, with the diatessaron added as a link;

A comparison of steps joins the intensifications through the diapente.

The diapason possesses the right of the space of both,

And one takes the place of the other when it assumes its functions,

Which then one takes from the other when it assumes its functions.

[Col. 0414B] Thus two places vary the sign whose form is the same.

[Col. 0413]

# Other Rules of Guido Concerning Unknown Chant

Repeatedly set forth in the prologue to his Antiphoner.

[Col. 0413B] In our times singers are foolish beyond all other people. For in every art we know far more by our own understanding than what we have learned from a teacher. After reading only the Psalter, little boys recognize the readings of all books, and uneducated countrymen suddenly understand the art of agriculture. Whoever has learned to prune one vine, graft one little tree, or load one donkey will not hesitate to do the same—or even better—with everything else. But wonderful singers and students of singers, even if they sing every day for a hundred years, will never by themselves, without a teacher, sing even one small antiphon, losing as much time in singing as they could have used to learn thoroughly both divine and secular [Col. 0413C] scripture.

And what is more dangerous than all these evils, many clerics and monks of religious orders neglect the psalms, sacred readings, and nightly vigils performed with purity, as well as the other works of piety by which we are summoned and led to everlasting glory, while they pursue with constant and utterly foolish labor a knowledge of singing which they can never attain.

Who would not also lament that there is such a serious error and such dangerous discord in the holy Church that, when we celebrate the divine office, we often seem not to be praising God but competing with one another? Scarcely does one person agree with another—not the student with the teacher, nor the student with his fellow students. Hence it has happened that there are no longer one or merely a few [Col. 0413D] antiphoners, but as many as there are teachers in the individual churches; and it is now commonly said that an antiphoner is not Gregory’s, but Leo’s or Albert’s or someone else’s. [Col. 0414B] Since learning one is extremely difficult, there is no doubt that learning many is impossible.

Since in this matter they themselves alter many things according to their own wishes, they ought to be little or not at all displeased with me if I depart from common usage in scarcely anything, so that every melody may return uniformly to the common rule of the art. Since all these evils and many others arise through the fault of those who make antiphoners, I strongly admonish and solemnly protest that no one should presume to provide an antiphoner with neumes unless he is able and sufficiently understands how to perfect the art itself according to the rules set out below. Otherwise, whoever has not first been a student of truth will certainly be a teacher of error.

[Col. 0414C] With God’s help, therefore, I have arranged to notate this antiphoner in such a way that from it any sensible and diligent person may henceforth learn chant easily. After he has properly learned one part of it from a teacher, he will undoubtedly recognize the rest by himself, without a teacher. If anyone thinks that I am lying about this, let him come, make the experiment, and see that little boys among us do this, although because of their ignorance of the psalms and of ordinary letters they still receive harsh beatings. They often do not know how to pronounce the words and syllables even of the antiphon which they can correctly sing by themselves without a teacher. With God’s help, any sensible and diligent person will be able to do this easily, if he takes care to understand with what diligence the neumes are arranged.

[Col. 0414D] The voices are arranged so that every sound, however often it is repeated in a chant, is always found in one particular order of its own. To enable you to distinguish these orders more easily, thick lines are drawn; some orders of voices are formed on the lines themselves, while others are [Col. 0415A] formed between the lines, in the middle of the interval or space between them.

Therefore, however many sounds there are on one line or in one space, they all sound alike. But so that you may also understand how many lines or spaces contain one sound, certain letters from the monochord are prefixed to any lines or spaces, and colors are likewise applied above them. From this it may be understood that throughout the entire antiphoner and in every chant, however many lines or spaces bear the same letter or the same color, they sound alike in every respect, as though all had been on a single line. For just as a line signifies the unity of sounds, so in every respect a letter or color signifies the unity of the lines and, consequently, of the sounds as well.

[Col. 0415B] If, then, everywhere you inspect the order of the sounds beginning from the letter or colored line, you will also clearly recognize that in all second orders there is the same unity of voices and neumes. Understand the same about the third or fourth order and the rest, whether you observe the higher or the lower orders.

It is therefore absolutely clear that all neumes or sounds placed in the lines of the same letter or color, or equally extended along a differently lettered or colored line, sound alike in every respect. But in different lines or spaces, even neumes made in the same way do not sound alike at all. Therefore, although the placement of the neumes may be complete, it is altogether blind and [Col. 0415C] worthless without the addition of letters or colors.

We use two colors, namely saffron-yellow and red, and through these colors I give you a very useful rule by which you will most suitably recognize, for every neume and every individual voice, what tone it belongs to and what letter of the monochord it belongs to—provided that, as is extremely advantageous, you keep the monochord and the formulas of the tones in frequent use.

There are seven letters of the monochord, as I shall show more fully below. Wherever, therefore, you see saffron-yellow, that is the third letter, C; and wherever you see vermilion, that is the sixth letter, F, whether [Col. 0415D] the colors are drawn on lines or between lines. Thus, in the third order beneath the saffron-yellow is the first letter, A, in which the first or second tone lies. Above this, beside the saffron-yellow, is the second letter, B, in which the third or fourth tone lies. Then in the saffron-yellow itself is the voice—that is, the third letter, C—in which the fifth and sixth tones lie. Next to and above the saffron-yellow, and third beneath the vermilion, is the fourth letter, D, in which the first or second tone lies. Near it is the fifth letter, E, by the vermilion, in which the third or fourth tone lies. In the vermilion itself is the sixth letter, F, in which the fifth or sixth tone lies. Beside and above the vermilion is the seventh, G, in which the seventh or eighth tone lies. Then the first letter, a, is repeated in the third order above the vermilion and the third beneath the saffron-yellow; in it lie the first or second tone, as stated. After this, all the other letters are repeated [Col. 0416A] differing in nothing from the earlier ones. All these matters will be taught you more fully by this diagram.

Although two tones always belong to one letter or voice, nevertheless the formulas of the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth tones fit individual neumes and sounds much better and more frequently. The formulas of the first, third, fifth, and seventh tones fit only when the chant descends from a high pitch and reaches a grave ending.

[Col. 0416C] Finally, understand that if you wish to progress in these notations, you must learn a number of chants by heart in such a way that through each individual neume you can recognize by memory all the modes or sounds—what they are and what their character is. To understand something by heart is very different from singing it by heart: the former belongs only to the wise, whereas the latter is often done by the uncomprehending. For simple people, these instructions are sufficient for recognizing neumes in a simple way. But how voices liquefy, and whether they sound connected or separate; which are lingering, trembling, or sudden; how a melody is divided by distinctions; and whether a following voice is lower, higher, or at the same pitch as the preceding one—all this is shown by an easy explanation in the figure of the neumes themselves, provided that they are deliberately composed as they ought to be.

# Epilogue: On the Formulas of the Modes and the Qualities of Chants

[Col. 0416D] The mode of voices, issued according to the wish of the ancients, separated from the true and proper kind of chant and reduced to chromatic softness because of a lack of rational principle, has now scarcely been restored to its former condition except through difficult labor. Indeed, because the system issued by its authors already lacked the gravity of proper regulation. This is no wonder: since some entrusted it to the judgment of the ears, while others, acting according to a stronger plan, assigned it to rational principles, both groups wrote different things in different ways, as their will dictated. Therefore, insofar as we can, let us follow the investigators of reason and discuss the matter briefly and concisely.

## Chapters

1. On the movement and pitch—or gravity—of the voice.
2. On integrity and diminution. [Col. 0417A]
3. On the consonance, or lesser agreement, of the voices with one another.
4. On the affinities of different voices; on what is proper or accidental to each; on the four kinds of modes and their division, with their differing distinctions; on the formulas of the differences and their properties.

## I

A voice is air struck in a way perceptible to hearing, insofar as it exists in itself. Every voice is either continuous or divided. It is continuous when the sequence of voices follows in such a way that the end of one and the beginning of another cannot easily be distinguished, as happens when we observe the arrangement of colors in the heavenly rainbow. For red is seen in such a way that its beginning or end nevertheless cannot be grasped. [Col. 0417B] The same is true of the other colors. A divided voice, however, is one produced separately, one by one.

No voice is produced unless motion comes first. When motion precedes, if it is swift it makes the voices denser and higher; but if it is slow or sparse, it makes them lower and fuller.

A musical voice is produced by motion, and motion contains duration in itself. It expresses the quantity of the motion, so that if the motion is short, its duration is also very small; if it is greater, it has greater duration. Musical motion is produced in only six ways: by the tone, semitone, semiditone or trihemitone, ditone, diatessaron, and diapente. It is therefore pleasing to observe that as the motion increases, so does the duration; for example, the ditone contains two tones and therefore has twice the duration. [Col. 0417C] Duration is the length of each individual voice, which grammarians mark above short and long syllables as they mark time.

## II

Of the motions mentioned above, some are complete—that is, they divide the monochord according to regular proportions—such as the tone and the others. Others fall short of completeness and cannot divide the monochord into equal proportions, such as the semiditone.

The tone, therefore, is a complete dimension, because it attains a regular division of the monochord through the sesquioctave proportion; the diatessaron through the sesquitertian proportion; and the diapente through the sesquialter proportion. Thus every tone is made in nine steps, the diatessaron in four, and the diapente in three. The diapason, however, is everywhere made in two steps, since the voices succeed one another reciprocally in the parts of the consonances. [Col. 0417D]

## III

[Col. 0417D] Every chant is completed by seven dissimilar voices, of which some are consonant and others dissonant. The first and fourth voices therefore have formulas that are very similar—three in descent and two in ascent. The second and fifth have four in descent and one in ascent. The third and sixth have four similar formulas from below, but not even one from above.

After these, the fourth is more widely separated from the seventh, and they retain no consonance of proportions with one another. Likewise, the first and fifth have similar formulas from above, but none from below. [Col. 0418A] The second and sixth rise by four similar formulas and descend by one; hence both are assigned to the protus. The third and seventh have three ascents and two descents, and exhibit the mode of the deuterus. The fourth and eighth, however, agree less in one ascent.

It should be noted that those voices are said to belong to one mode which agree more closely in ascent. Although they are said to belong to one mode because they have similar ascents and descents, nevertheless none of them agrees with another in an ascent corresponding to its descent, or in a descent corresponding to its ascent.

## IV

Each voice has something proper to itself, since their affinity does not agree entirely in pitch or gravity, and since they are always mingled with some likeness [Col. 0418B] to foreign voices—that is, with voices belonging to another mode. Thus D and A are affinities: although they are not both alike in the protus and therefore do not belong to one mode, each retains its own qualities. D descends by a tone and a semitone, and then rises by a tone, semitone, tritone, and semiditone up to another high d. A descends by a ditone and a semiditone, but rises by a tone, semitone, and ditone up to another high a. I think that the dissimilarity between affiliated voices has now been sufficiently demonstrated.

I shall now explain the similarity of similar voices. Although D is protus and G is tetrardus, both descend by a semitone and ditone; and the symphony contained in D, if it is descending, can then also be sung in G. This is clear from the example in the following antiphon: [Col. 0418C]

> Gracious Spirit [c], enlightener of all.

## V

[Col. 0418D] There are four modes of voices: protus, deuterus, tritus, and tetrardus. Each has an equal number of subjugal modes; the principal modes we call authentic, while the subjugal modes we call plagal. Their distinction is as follows.

When any chant rises through eight voices but descends through five, and when among all of them there are twelve, one of which is counted twice, all the grave voices, together with part of the high ones, are assigned to the plagals. The authentics, on the other hand, include all the high voices together with some of the grave ones.

It should be noted that there are three orders of voices: grave, middle, and high. Of these, the middle voices are always joined to both groups; the high voices belong with the authentics, and the grave voices with the plagals. Thus three voices from both groups are always proper to each of them.

## VI

The formulas of the distinctions of these modes are arranged according to the beginnings of the chants. Just as the final voice measures a particular mode, so the beginnings of the same chants rationally adapt formulas more suitable to themselves, so that the connection may be beautiful and may proceed according to its proper movements in each case.

We have said that there are six such movements. When these are combined with three adherences [Note: [Col. 0417D] F. *aderectiones*], they produce in each [Col. 0419A] mode formulas that are different and more extensive, or in some cases more restricted, according to the ways in which each movement can be joined to the adherences. No mode is permitted to have more extensive formulas unless they can be regularly generated from it itself. Thus the greatest caution is required in the patterns of voices when they have grown in qualities and quantities.

For this reason musical movement contains quality and quantity. If movement ceases to possess quality and quantity, it will no longer be musical movement. The quality of movement is whether it is protus, deuterus, or some other mode. Its quantity is whether it is double, sesquialter, or sesquitertian. Quality is prescribed in the species of the modes, and quantity in the magnitude of the movements.

Moreover, the different species of the modes also prevail greatly in quantity [Col. 0419B] [Col. 0420A] or quality, since one proceeds with a straightforward and tranquil course, like a narrative; another is sung in winding leaps; another appears talkative and fierce, raising the minds of the listeners aloft; while another is peaceful and expresses joy of character. This will be sufficiently evident to anyone prudent who takes care to understand it.

Each mode has different formulas, which we regularly derive from each mode in the following way. First let a musical movement be established, containing quality and quantity, from which a regular voice arises. From the quality of the mode and from its quantity the individual movements are produced. A voice is prefixed, suffixed, or subjoined. When these are mixed together, they produce regular and highly approved formulas in each mode. So that this may be more easily understood, we have added a figure, providing an easier path through the eyes. [Col. 0420B] [Col. 0419]

[Col. 0421A] The protus therefore has ten regular formulas: six prefixed, three suffixed, and one subjoined. The prefixed formulas are made by the tone, ditone, semiditone or trihemitone, and diapente. Suffixed formulas are those in which the beginning of the antiphon is placed on the same voice at which the formula ends. These are made in two ways: sometimes on the first voice, namely the voice that ends the formula; sometimes on affiliated voices, that is, on those which agree with the final voice through the six consonances mentioned above. Subjoined formulas are made by the semiditone. They are called subjoined because the endings of the formulas are led beneath the beginnings of the antiphons.

Since the protus appears to have two different formulas at one ending, it is useful to examine more fully by what distinctions the two can be recognized, [Col. 0421B] since one is authentic and the other plagal. And [Col. 0422A] whatever is established for the protus must also be maintained for the others.

We therefore place the formulas of the authentic protus in the fifth position from the final voice, and we do the same in the other authentic modes. We place the formulas of the corresponding plagal mode in the third position from the final voice. Hence it must be carefully observed that in the plagals the endings or beginnings of distinctions must in no way be placed above the formulas assigned to them. If this happens, the chant immediately passes into the authority of the authentic mode, since only the authentics are permitted to raise the endings or beginnings of distinctions to the fifths.

And just as it is unlawful for plagals to raise the summit of their distinctions above their own formulas, so it is not suitable for authentics to raise the summit of those same plagals unless they are transferred. Thus each loses its proper force while striving to assume the rank of the other. [Col. 0422B]

[Col. 0421]

> The protus is present with the bonds of ten formulas,  
> Which everywhere join together the entire authentic mode.  
> Let these be dear to you and continually held in your mouth.  
> I ask you, do not diminish them; if you can, take care to add to them.

[Col. 0423]

# Letter of Guido

[Note: [Col. 0423D] In Pez, vol. VI of the *Anecdota*, p. 223. Vienna manuscript. An epistolary recapitulation of the whole work of the same Guido [Col. 0424D] to the monk Michael.]

## To Michael the Monk, Concerning Unknown Chant

[Col. 0423A] To the most blessed and sweetest brother Michael, Guido, cast down and raised up through many winding turns. Either the times are harsh, or the obscure distinctions of divine providence are at work, since deceit often tramples truth and envy tramples charity—envy which scarcely abandons the fellowship of our order, by which the assembly of the Philistines punishes Israelite perversity. Otherwise, if everything immediately happened as we wished, an overly self-confident spirit would fall to destruction. For what we do is truly good only when we ascribe everything we can do to our Maker.

This is why you see me exiled within far-reaching boundaries, and yourself suffocated in the snares of the envious, unable even to breathe. In this matter I compare us to a certain craftsman who offered Augustus Caesar an [Col. 0423B] incomparable treasure, unheard-of through all the ages—namely, flexible glass. Because he had been able to accomplish something beyond all men, he therefore believed that he deserved something beyond all men. Instead, by a most evil fate, he was ordered to be killed, lest, if the marvelous glass could also be durable, the royal treasury, which was made from various metals, should immediately become worthless [Note: [Col. 0424D] F. *vitiabilis*. Correction: *mutabilis*, changeable.] through it. Thus from that time onward accursed envy, as it once deprived humanity of paradise, also took away this advantage from mortals. For because the craftsman’s envy would not teach anyone, the king’s envy was able to destroy both the craftsman and his art.

[Col. 0423C] Therefore, with God inspiring charity, I have bestowed upon you—and upon others also, whoever they might be—with the greatest haste and care the grace given to me, most unworthy as I am, by God. We have all previously learned the ecclesiastical chants only with great difficulty; may those who come after us learn them with the greatest ease, and may they wish eternal salvation for me, for you, and for my other assistants. May God’s mercy grant forgiveness for our sins, or at least a small prayer arising from such great charity.

[Col. 0423D] For if those who have so far been able to acquire from their teachers only an imperfect knowledge of singing after scarcely ten years intercede most devoutly with God for their teachers, what do you think will be done for us and our assistants, who make a perfect singer in the space of one year, or at most two? Or if the customary misery of human beings should prove ungrateful for such great benefits, will the just God not reward our labor? Or, because God does all this and we can do nothing without him, shall we receive nothing? [Col. 0424A] Far from it. For the Apostle too, although what happens is the grace of God, nevertheless sings: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me.”

Let us therefore confidently devote ourselves to work of such great usefulness, secure in the hope of reward. And since, after many storms, the long-desired calm has returned, we must sail happily.

But since your captivity doubts your freedom, I shall disclose the order of events. John of the highest apostolic see, who now governs the Roman Church, heard the fame of our school and how, through our antiphoners, boys learned unheard-of chants. He was greatly astonished and invited me to him through three messengers. I therefore went to Rome with Lord Grunvald, the most reverend abbot, and Lord Peter, provost of the canons of the church of Arezzo, a man exceptionally learned for our time.

[Col. 0424B] The pontiff greatly rejoiced at my arrival, conversing at length and asking about many different matters. He repeatedly examined our antiphoner as though it were some kind of prodigy, and pondered the rules set before it. He did not stop or leave the place where he was sitting until, fulfilling his wish, he had learned an unfamiliar verse, so that he might recognize in himself, and so quickly, what he scarcely believed possible in others.

What more need be said? Illness compelled me not to remain in Rome even briefly, since the summer heat threatened us with destruction in the maritime and marshy regions. At last we agreed that, when winter returned, I should go back there, [Col. 0424C] so that I might reveal this work to the aforesaid pontiff and his clergy.

A few days later, wishing to see your father and mine, Lord Guido, abbot of Pomposa—a man deservedly most dear to God and to human beings for his virtue and wisdom, and a part of my soul—I visited him. When that man of penetrating intelligence saw our antiphoner, he immediately approved and believed in it. He regretted having once agreed with our rivals, and asked me to come to Pomposa. He advised me that, for a monk, monasteries ought to be preferred to bishoprics, especially Pomposa, because of the study which, through God’s grace and the industry of the most reverend Guido, has now for the first time been discovered in Italy.

[Col. 0424D] Moved by the prayers of so great a father and obedient to his commands, I therefore wish, with God’s help, first to illuminate such a great and distinguished monastery through this work, and to make myself superior as a monk [Col. 0425A] among monks, especially since, with nearly all bishops now condemned for the Simoniac heresy, I fear being associated with one of them.

But since I cannot come at present, meanwhile I send you an excellent method for finding unknown chant, recently given to us by God and proven most useful. For the rest, I greet most warmly Lord Martin, prior of the holy congregation and our greatest assistant, and with many prayers commend this wretched man to his prayers. I also remind brother Peter to remember him who remembers him: nourished on our milk, he feeds, not without the greatest labor, on coarse barley, and after golden cups of wine he drinks muddled vinegar.

[Col. 0425B] To find unknown chant, therefore, most blessed brother, the first and ordinary rule is this: if you sound on the monochord the letters belonging to any neume, you may learn it by hearing it from the instrument as from a human teacher. But this is a rule for little boys: good for beginners, but very poor for those who persist. I have seen many highly acute philosophers who, out of devotion to this art, sought teachers not only among Italians but also among Gauls and Germans, and even among the Greeks themselves. But because they relied on this one rule alone, they were never able to become, I will not say musicians, but even singers, or to imitate our little psalmists.

We must not therefore always seek the voice of a person or of some instrument for unknown chant, as though we were blind and could never proceed without a guide. Instead, we must commit to deep memory the differences and properties of each [Col. 0425C] sound and of all descents and ascents. You will therefore have a very easy and reliable method for finding an unheard chant, provided that someone knows how to teach not merely through writing but, preferably, through familiar conversation according to our custom. For after I began to teach this method to the boys, within three days some of them were able to sing unknown chants easily—something that could not happen through other methods even in many weeks.

If, then, you wish to commit any voice or neume to memory so that wherever you wish, in any chant you know or do not know, it may immediately come to you and you may confidently utter it, you must [Col. 0425D] notate that voice or neume at the head of some very familiar symphony. For each voice that you wish to retain in memory, you should have such a symphony readily available, beginning from that same voice. For example, this is the symphony which I use first and last in teaching boys:

> May [C]  
> thy servants [D F]  
> with loosened [D E D]  
> vocal cords [D D C D]  
> resound [E E]  
> the wonders [E F G E]  
> of thy deeds. [D E C D]  
> O [F G a]  
> holy John, [G F E D D]  
> release [G a G F E]  
> the guilt [F G D]  
> of the polluted [a G a]  
> lip. [F G a a]  
> [G F E D]  
> [C E D.]

[Col. 0426A] You see, then, how this symphony begins its six parts from six different voices. If someone knows the beginning of each part through sufficient practice to start immediately and confidently whichever part he wishes, he will easily be able to pronounce those same six voices, wherever he sees them, according to their properties.

When you hear a neume without notation, consider which of these parts is best suited to its ending, so that the final voice of the neume and the first voice of the principal part are at the same pitch. Be certain that the neume ends on the voice from which the part suitable to it begins.

But if you have begun to sing an unfamiliar symphony that has been notated, you must be very careful to end each [Col. 0426B] neume in such a way that the ending of the neume is properly joined to the beginning of the part which starts from the same voice on which the neume ended. Thus, if you wish to utter unheard chants properly as soon as you see them written, or, when hearing unnotated chants, to distinguish quickly how they ought to be notated, this rule will help you greatly.

Next, I placed very short symphonies under each individual sound. When you carefully inspect their parts, you will be glad to find, in order within the beginnings of those parts, all the descents and ascents of each voice. If you can undertake to sing whichever parts you wish from one or another symphony, you will have learned the exceedingly difficult and manifold varieties of all neumes through a very short and easy rule. All these matters, although we scarcely indicate them adequately with letters, are laid bare through easy conversation alone.

[Col. 0426C] Just as in all writing we have twenty-four letters, so in all chant we have only seven voices. As there are seven days in the week, so there are seven voices in music. The others that are added above the seven are the same and sing alike in every respect, differing in nothing except that they sound twice as high. Therefore we call seven grave and seven high.

The seven letters are designated not in two ways but differently, as follows:

> Γ, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, a, c, d, e, f, g, a, [a], b, [b], c, [c], d, [d].

[Col. 0426D] Anyone who wishes to make a monochord and to distinguish the qualities and quantities, likenesses and differences, of sounds and tones should earnestly strive to understand the very few rules set out below.

On the monochord, these letters or measurements are arranged as follows [Note: [Col. 0425] This monochord is drawn in the music of Abbot Odo (*Patrologia Latina* CXXXIII)]. Place the Greek Γ—that is, the Latin G—at the head. From there, beginning at the whole line lying beneath the sounding string, divide it with the greatest care into nine parts. Where the first part ends, place the first letter, A, beside Gamma. Beginning from that first A, likewise divide to the end into nine parts, and where the first part ends, attach the second letter, B.

After this, returning to Γ, divide from it to the end into four parts, and place the third letter, C, at the end of the first part. Similarly, divide from the first A into four parts [Col. 0427A] and mark the fourth letter, D. In the same way, just as the fourth was found from the first, so with the second you will find the fifth, E; with the third, the sixth, F; and with the fourth, the seventh, G.

Then, returning to the first A, divide from it to the end at the midpoint and find another first letter, a.
