Likewise, with the second you will find another second letter, b; with the third, the third, c; and in the same way with the remaining letters, following the same pattern through the diapason.

To summarize much about the division of the monochord in a few words: all tones run through nine steps to the end. The diatessaron always takes four steps, the diapente three, and the diapason two, because we divide by only these four methods.

Next, note that between the second and third, and between the fifth and sixth, the spaces are extremely small; these are called semitones. Between the other voices the intervals are larger, and are called tones:

> A–B: tone  
> B–C: semitone  
> C–D: tone  
> D–E: tone  
> E–F: semitone  
> F–G: tone  
> G–a: tone.

[Col. 0427B] Voices are joined to one another in six ways: by the tone, semitone, ditone, semiditone, diatessaron, and diapente. We have discussed the tone and semitone above.

A ditone occurs when there are two tones between two voices, as between the third and fifth, and elsewhere.

A semiditone is so called because it is smaller than a ditone: between two voices there is one tone and one semitone, as in D–E–F.

The diatessaron is named from four, because between one voice and the fourth above it there are two tones and one semitone:

> D–E: tone;  
> E–F: semitone;  
> F–G: tone.

The diapente is named from five, because between one voice and the fifth above it there are three tones and one semitone:

> D–E: tone;  
> E–F: semitone;  
> F–G: tone;  
> G–a: tone.

[Col. 0427C] Voices joined or moved in relation to one another agree or proceed in no other than these six ways. These are therefore called the six movements of voices, through which voices agree or move in relation to one another.

The agreement between a grave letter and its corresponding high letter—for example, from the first to the first, or from the second to the second—is called the diapason, that is, “from all.” It contains all the voices, five tones with two semitones, namely a diatessaron and a diapente. The diapason makes the voices so consonant that we call them not merely similar but the same.

All voices are similar, and produce [Col. 0428A] similar sounds and consonant neumes, insofar as they rise or descend in the same way according to the descent of tones and semitones. Thus the first voice, A, and the fourth, D, are said to be similar and to belong to one mode because each descends by a tone and rises by a tone, a semitone, and two tones. This is the first similarity among the voices, that is, the first mode.

The second mode lies in the second voice, B, and the fifth, E. Each descends through two tones and rises through a semitone and two tones.

The third mode lies in the third voice, C, and the sixth, F. Both descend by a semitone and two tones, but rise by two tones.

The seventh voice alone forms the fourth mode. It descends through one tone, one semitone, and two tones, while it rises through two tones and a semitone.

[Col. 0428B] Those who are fully trained in this art can vary any symphony according to these four modes. For example, someone may begin one symphony first on the first voice, A, then on the second voice, and afterward on the third. According to the different arrangement of tones and semitones belonging to those voices, he may utter the same symphony in different ways, according to the property of each voice. This is both very useful and very easy, as follows:

[Col. 0428C]

> You [D]  
> of the Father [F G]  
> everlasting [G G G G]  
> are [a]  
> Son. [F E D]  
> You [E]  
> of the Father [G a]  
> everlasting [a a a a]  
> are []  
> Son. [G F E]  
> You [F]  
> of the Father [a]  
> everlasting []  
> are [c]  
> Son. [a G F]  
> You [G]  
> of the Father [c]  
> everlasting [c c c c]  
> are [d]  
> Son. [b a G]

Careful attention must therefore be given to every melody, according to the kind of property by which it sounds, whether at the beginning or at the end, although we customarily speak only of the ending.

Certain neumes have been found by whose suitability we customarily recognize this. For example: [Col. 0427] [Col. 0427D] when, after a chant has been completed, you see that this neume of it fits its ending well, you will immediately recognize that the chant has ended in the first mode and in the first or fourth sound, because in these two sounds the mode is first.

[Col. 0428D] We customarily distinguish the first tone by this neume alone, although the same thing can be done, and sometimes better, with any other symphony that begins on the same sound. A symphony is recognized as belonging to whatever mode fits it; thus you understand whether you pronounce a neume correctly when you see that it can properly be fitted to symphonies of the kind in which it has been notated.

Note also how we call those forms “modes” which are improperly, or abusively, called tones [Col. 0429A] in the formulas of the tones, since properly speaking they are called modes or *tropes*.

You should also recognize how, in all the modes, when a melody is low, it is fitted to low formulas or melodies; but when melodies are high, they accord better with high melodies or formulas. Therefore, in the formulas of the modes you have two formulas in each mode: the first and second formula belong to the first mode, the third and fourth to the second, the fifth and sixth to the third, and the seventh and eighth to the fourth. The reason, therefore, that eight tones are spoken of is that they have eight formulas. The first, third, fifth, and seventh formulas contain high chants belonging to the four modes; the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth contain the low or less-high chants of those same modes. Hence the Greeks express the first and second tones much better by saying authentic protus and plagal of protus; the third and fourth, authentic deuterus and plagal of deuterus; the fifth and sixth, authentic tritus and plagal of tritus; and the seventh and eighth, authentic tetrardus and plagal of tetrardus. What they call *protus*, *deuterus*, *tritus*, and *tetrardus*, we call first, second, third, and fourth. What they call *authentic*, we call “greater,” “high,” or “acute.” *Plagal* we may call in Latin “subjugalis,” “lesser,” or “low.”

Whoever wishes to possess skill in singing ought especially to know these eight formulas of the modes, so that he may be able to observe how any neume or voice sounds in the chants of each mode. Moreover, although I have said that the first, second, and third voices agree with the fourth, fifth, and sixth, they nevertheless differ in this respect, and do not all produce neumes in the same way. For example, after C they have three tones in descent and before them two tones in ascent; but D, E, and F have only one tone in descent and three tones in ascent. Therefore many chants belong to the same mode, but not to the same tone. Some, however, who do not fully perceive this distinction, add an acute voice between the first and second, so that there are two “seconds,” and so that two tones and one semitone come after D, E, and F, as they do after A and C in ascent. Again, the acute D, E, and F can be lowered by two tones, as A, B, and C can, so that there may be no difference between D, E, F and A, C, since what is sung on A and C can also be sung on D, E, and F.

But in order that each voice may retain its own property, it is better to observe the nature of the chants. When a chant appears to admit these three tones, this should be done on F, G, A. When, however, after two tones it takes nothing but a semitone, this should be done on C, D, E, F, especially since the addition of this voice gives rise to the greatest confusion for beginners. For if there are two “seconds” after the first, when the first is joined to one by a semitone and to the other by a tone, it is easy to see that the first itself, and consequently the other adjacent voices as well, have two tones. For example, if a semitone follows the first, the first passes from protus into deuterus; but if one voice may belong to two or more modes, this art will appear to be concluded by no end and confined by no fixed boundaries. No one is unaware how absurd this is, since wisdom always spontaneously rejects whatever is confused and infinite.

If someone should say that this voice ought to be added so that low F, the sixth, may ascend by a fifth as far as A, the super-fourth above the line, or that the same sixth may descend to the sub-fifth, he must also accept the addition of another voice between the sixth F and the seventh G, so that the natural low second B may be raised to the fifth and the same acute voice lowered to the fourth. Since no one has done this, no one should do that either.

[Col. 0430B] Thus, as nature itself demonstrates, and as divine authority through blessed Gregory affirms, there are seven voices, just as there are seven days. Hence even the most prudent of poets sang of “seven distinctions of voices”; and the philosophers themselves confirmed this judgment with equal agreement. Meanwhile, care must be taken that it be known in how many and what kinds of tones each neume can or cannot occur.

This can occur in the third, sixth, and seventh tones, because these three tones ascend by two whole tones alike, and the same *symphonia* is produced in only two ways.

Moreover, the seventh voice agrees with the third in ascent: both are raised by two tones and a semitone, and likewise by two tones. The same seventh also agrees with the fourth by one tone in ascent, and by a tone and a semitone in descent; and it is likewise sung by two tones in either direction.

The first also makes all descending neumes in common with the fifth, for it is lowered by two tones and a semitone. Thus these voices make similar neumes: the first with the fourth, the second with the fifth, the third with the sixth, and the seventh with the first or with the third. No voice has more than four ascents or descents, because it cannot be lowered or raised except to the second, third, fourth, or fifth, according to the six species mentioned above: tone, semitone, ditone, semiditone, diatessaron, and diapente. For when a voice moves to the second, the interval is either a tone or a semitone; when to the third, a ditone or semiditone. To the fourth or fifth, the movement is only by diatessaron or diapente.

Understand further that in the authentic modes a chant ascends from its final voice to the octave; but it descends only one tone below the final, except in tritus, which is not lowered from its final, because it has not a tone but a semitone beneath it. In the plagal modes we descend and ascend from the final voice to the fifth, unless the chant is more extensive and has a plagal descent together with an authentic ascent; this, however, occurs very rarely.

The beginnings of chants may likewise occur on all those voices which agree with the final voice by one of the six consonances mentioned above. If you find anything otherwise, you will recognize from its rarity that it has been assumed by authority; it is not distinguished by the firmness of a rule. Who does not understand that voices become, as it were, syllables, parts, distinctions, or verses? All these agree with one another in marvelous sweetness, and are often more concordant in proportion as they are more similar.

These few remarks, spoken rhythmically and in prose as a kind of preface to the *Antiphonary*, concerning the formulas of modes and neumes, briefly—and perhaps sufficiently—open the door of the musical art. Whoever is curious should seek our little book called the *Micrologus*; he should also read through the book *Enchiridion*, which the most reverend Abbot Oddo composed with great clarity. I have left an example of it only in the figures of the tones, because I have accommodated myself to children, not following Boethius in this, whose book is useful not to singers but only to philosophers.

**The letter ends.**

[Col. 0431]

# Guido’s Treatise [Note: [Col. 0431D] Although the manuscript witnesses present it as Guido’s, the interpolated character is nevertheless shown by the material inserted on col. 433 from Theoger.] Correcting Many Errors That Occur in Gregorian Chant in Many Places

From the Tegernsee manuscript, fourteenth or fifteenth century.

[Col. 0431B] Considering the error of many people, I have been compelled, with God’s help, to bring Gregory’s chant—which many have monstrously corrupted in many places—back to its true modes, namely, its finals. I thought with sorrow about the quarreling of different people in the choir: believing that they possessed the true path of chant, each unjustly and wrongly reproves the other for singing badly. They make claims about truth or falsity, and about the finals of the modes, which I see to be excessively corrupted, assigning them to one another in no way according to musical practice.

I have also often observed that chant is repeatedly corrupted through the ignorance of certain people. Thus we have many chants in corrupted form which, in truth, were not originally produced as they are now sung in churches by the authority of the composers; rather, the wrongful voices of people following the movement of their own minds have perverted what was correctly composed and brought what was perverted into an incorrigible custom, to such an extent that the worst custom is now observed in place of authority and preserved as such.

There are also many clerics or monks who neither know nor wish to know the art of the most delightful music. Worse still, although they know it, they reject and abhor it; and if some musician confronts them concerning a chant which they utter either incorrectly or without proper composition, they angrily and shamelessly shout him down, refuse to submit to the truth, and defend their errors with all their effort. I have therefore resolved, so far as I can, to aid the bestiality of such people, wishing to restore every chant corrupted by them to its mode by musical terms—not by Greek names in the manner of speculation, but by positive recitation.

For they call many modes or tropes “tones,” although Gregory rebukes this in his little book on music, saying that it is abusive to call tropes tones. He also shows that *trope* is derived from the Greek *tropos*, which is interpreted as “turn” or “turning,” because each trope turns away from the other tropes toward its own rules and its own figures or modes. He says that *tone* is derived from *tonare*, “to sound” or “to resound.” Thus, in the same proportion by which a greater number exceeds a lesser, or a lesser is exceeded by a greater in the gravity of the same voice, the earlier sound of the voice exceeds the later, or the later is exceeded by the earlier. This tone arises from the sesquioctave proportion, in which the greater number contains the lesser wholly within itself together with its eighth part, as nine contains eight.

Leaving aside such speculations for the present, as well as the names mentioned—namely, *proslambanomenos*, *hypate hypaton*, and the like—we will proceed by positive explanation as necessity requires. We will chiefly concern ourselves with the solemnities of the Mass, which Holy Church calls the Gradual, paying little attention to the subtraction or addition of certain notes. I will title certain chants which I am obliged to restore to their true finals or modes.

I ask singers and readers not to think me arrogant, but rather to understand that I am undertaking this correction and restoration so that the position of so great an author may not be completely obscured by corruptors.

It would be a lengthy task to eradicate the error from all the chants in the Gradual, for some have sinned against the rules of musicians at the beginning of a chant, others in the middle, others at the end, and others in the ascent and descent of the modes. Thus, in the Introit *Populus Sion*, most people raise the beginning by a diapente from the final; some take its beginning on acute C; and others sing the words “and he will make heard” in different modes. Through this error the said Introit has come into the great falsity of the seventh mode. According to the rules of musicians who labor in practical work, Theoger and the others, this Introit should begin on low G, leap by a diatessaron—that is, to acute C—and, proceeding properly and rationally by singing through the acute heptachord, should bring its seat to the final on low F. [Note: [Col. 0432D] Read M on low G.]

[Col. 0433A] **Gradual *Qui sedes*.** Many recognize that this chant has been corrupted, namely at the beginning and in the word *super*, which naturally belongs to authentic tetrardus. It must undoubtedly begin on low F and rise to acute C; the syllable *su* is to be assigned to acute C, visiting acute G stepwise, so that this syllable immediately visits its diapente by way of acute A, B, and C. By an artificial course it then seeks and receives low G as its final, as befits an authentic mode.

**Gradual *Tollite portas*.** The melody of this chant is known to have been greatly corrupted by ignorant people. Since this chant is plagal protus, they take its beginning on low G, as in the present Gradual *Tollite*, or on low E, as in the Gradual *In sole posuit*, when they ought rather to take it on low A or low D. Thus they end the same chant on acute A, placing the seat of plagal protus according to their own pleasure.

They have not yet read Theoger’s words concerning this melody:

> “In this mode the *synemmenon* in the low register seems to some to be less necessary, and there is an argument about it, as it appears. But in our chant, which we boast to be Gregorian, it cannot in any way be avoided, as in this chant *In sole posuit*, and in others sung with a melody of this kind, and in very many others; otherwise the chant will be changed for the most part, or will not be ended correctly. And because the voices in the species of the diapason are said to be the same, we therefore surely do not see why the *synemmenon* tetrachord should not have a place in the acute register between F and D, when it can and ought also to have a place in the low register between Γ and D.” [Note: [Col. 0433D] It is not absent in *Mel*.]

These are Theoger’s words exactly. Therefore this sort of melody should be restored to its true form according to his teaching. Since, as has been said, plagal protus should begin on low D—as *Tollite* does on low A, and *A summo coelo* on E—it follows that, by continuing according to such beginnings, both will have their ending in their proper final seat, which is low D.

In these, as in all the other Graduals sung with melodies of this kind, low B-flat liquefies from its proper sound while descending by a tone; the same thing also sometimes occurs in other places.

**Gradual *Ostende nobis*.** The error of this chant occurs at the words *misericordiam tuam*. If the word *tuam* repeats the final voice of *misericordiam* while ascending, the phrase ends irregularly, because the first semitone would end on low C, which is not the seat of plagal protus, whereas this chant is of the second mode.

To restore it artificially to its proper seat, it must begin on low G; the final voice of *misericordiam* will be low D; and the following word, *tuam*, must begin on low D. Proceeding in this way in the plagal manner, it will end on low E. The final voice of the words *tuum* and *avertisti* serves, by the reasoning stated above, the same function as in *Tollite* and in other melodies of this kind.

**Gradual *Salvum fac servum*.** Some begin this Gradual on low F and, monstrously—for it is authentic protus—end it on acute A. That final is contrary to all musicians—and I say “musicians” without hesitation, for there are countless people who call themselves musicians, knowing, or thinking that they know, only the distinctions of the voices, like those who assign signs or names to the voices, saying *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. Such people labor and glory in musical falsities; even after all these signs have been abolished, they still destroy the nature of the voices.

I take those to be musicians whom Boethius calls musicians in these words:

> “He is truly a musician who, after considering reason, has acquired the knowledge of singing not as a servant but under the command of theoretical understanding.”

Returning to the matter at hand, that final voice is the seat of protus, contrary to such musicians. Those people are and are called censors—that is, opponents—and are not worthy in relation to these matters. All musicians agree that every chant must end on one of these four low voices: D, E, F, or G. But according to its corruptors this chant will end on none of them. The reason why it should end only on these four is omitted for the sake of brevity.

This Gradual must begin on low C and be sung through tone, semiditone, semitone, semiditone, tone, tone, semiditone, semiditone, tone, tone, and tone—namely, the two words *salvum fac*—and thus it is artificially brought to its final.

**Introit *Deus in adjutorium*.** This Introit is rarely sung correctly, because of its differing beginnings. Some begin it on low G and immediately err monstrously in the words *Domine* and those that follow; they finally arrive at low D, which is not the seat of authentic tetrardus, the mode of this Introit. Others begin on acute C and proceed in that manner, ending on low G, but they begin perversely.

Using the authority of John the Englishman, who says:

> “The whole force of a chant looks to its finals, and however it is varied, it must always be assigned to the mode in whose final it has ceased,”

the same Introit should therefore be suitably restored to its mode, however falsified or varied it may be. I say that this Introit should be restored as follows: let it begin on low G; let the word *Domine* begin on low C and be sung upward through tone, tone, semitone, and semitone; let the word *ad* begin on acute D; let *adjuvandum* begin on acute D and be sung through tone, tone, tone, semitone, semiditone, and tone; and let the word *me* end on acute C, visiting acute F. Proceeding in this way, it is suitably restored to its mode, namely authentic tetrardus.

**Communion *Passer invenit*.** This Communion is very rarely sung correctly. The error lies in beginning it on low G and carrying it to acute C or acute D, and in the middle of the chant changing the property of protus into that of tritus. Since this is such a great error, it should be restored in the following way to the property of authentic protus.

Let the Communion just mentioned begin on low D, and let its first syllable be carried to low G. When the word *domum* has ended on low G, let the following word also receive low G. The next word, namely *turtur*, should be sung on low F and G. Likewise, let the following word, namely *nidum*, together with the words that follow, be sung in unison; and let the second syllable of the word *reponat* visit acute B-flat. Let the word *pullos* be sung on low G and F. Let the word *suos* be sung on low F, G, and D. Let the word *altaria* begin on low F and be sung upward through a tone and a semiditone. Proceed in this way to the end, and without doubt it will rarely remain on low D. [Note: [Col. 0435D] *Mel.*: “will regularly rest in its proper seat.”]

** *Aufer a me*.** Many begin this Communion on acute C and end it on acute A, although it is perfectly clear to all musicians that neither is the final of any mode. Thus, through ignorance, they have falsified this customary tone and countless others. Since this chant is of the tetrardus mode, it must begin on low G; at the beginning the same chant immediately visits its diapente, acute D, and proceeds to the final word, *est*, which is sung only through acute A and low G. In this way it will remain in the tetrardus mode.

**Gradual *Domine praevenisti*.** This Gradual too could not remain without corruption. The same is true of another Gradual, *Benedicta et venerabilis*, which has the same melody, although it is sung more frequently in churches. The corruption is evident in the word *pretioso*, which ought to end on low G, because the melody is of the protus mode, whereas countless people end it on low C. The Gradual verse immediately shows this to be false, because it ends on low D. All the properties of protus also occur in the same melody, by which the corruption of that melody is clearly recognized.

Therefore, in order that you may arrive at protus, sing the word *pretioso* through low G, D, F, E, F, D, E, D, D, and then from acute A through G, E, G, F, E, D, E, F, D, D. In this way it will end regularly.

**Sequence *Eia recolamus*.** The seat of this Sequence is low G. When the verse *Deus qui creavit* has ended on acute D, the following verse, *mirabilis*, should not begin on acute G, as the customary corruptors have made it do, but on acute D. The word *mirabilis* should be sung through D, C, E, and onward, according to the way this Sequence remains and ends in this book on low G. [Note: [Col. 0435D] Perhaps: “is indicated.”] [Note: [Col. 0436D] I would read: “and it is tetrardus.”]

**Sequence *Sancti Baptistae*.** This Sequence is recognized as corrupted in the verse *placatus*, and also in the verse *et agni*. Some begin the verse *placatus* in different ways and dispute how it should begin, just as they do concerning the verse *et agni*. But since this Sequence is authentic protus, the verse *placatus* should rightly begin on acute A. Its final word, or that of its companion verse, then remains on acute D, and is thus properly brought to its final, namely low D.

**Sequence *Laus tibi Christe*.** The customary singers have erred in this Sequence, especially in the verse *Aphorisco*: they begin it on acute C and, continuing in this way, also end it on acute C. Yet they ought to end it on low F, since it is authentic tritus. Abandon the customary wailing in this verse; begin it on low F, and by proceeding in this way you will rationally end the Sequence on low F. The same judgment applies to the Sequence *Psallite regi*, since it has the same melody.

[Col. 0436C] ** *Laus tibi Christe Patris*.** This Sequence too has been corrupted in the verse *Ut liceat*. Some begin that verse on acute A, although it ought to end on low D, because it is authentic protus. To restore the Sequence to its final, after the verse *nobis terrena* has ended on acute A, let the following verse, *ut liceat*, begin on low D and be sung as follows:

D G F C G A F G F E E E F G G F E D E D D F E E D D.

When this verse and its companion have ended, let the final verse be sung as follows:

D E F G F F E E G A G F E D F E C E F D D.

In this way it is regularly brought to its final.

[Col. 0435]

# How Music Proceeds from Arithmetic

The following little work is found in the manuscript of St. Emmeram after Guido’s *Micrologus*. I do not know whether it is by the same author or by another.

[Col. 0435D] There are five kinds of inequality in arithmetic. Music rejects the last three and admits only the first and second, namely the multiple and superparticular kinds.

A multiple relation exists when the greater number contains the lesser number wholly within itself, either twice, three times, four times, and so on, with nothing lacking and nothing exceeding. From the root of this kind arises the first and most perfect consonance, called the diapason, which is in a double proportion; and the bisdiapason, which is formed in a quadruple proportion.

A superparticular relation exists when the greater number contains the lesser wholly within itself together with one of its parts: either one half, as three to two, which is called the sesquialtera, sescupla, or hemiolic proportion; or one third, as four to three, which is called the sesquitertia or epitritic proportion; and so forth.

From the root of this kind arise the two consonances diapente and diatessaron. The diapente is called sesquialtera, whereas the diatessaron is called sesquitertia. The tone also proceeds from the same kind and is formed by the sesquioctave proportion.

The remaining kinds of inequality are rejected, because when the greater number exceeds the lesser not by one part but by several parts, it follows that the voices measured by them become confused and discordant.

Thus the multiple kind contains the double, triple, and quadruple proportions. The double produces the diapason, as four is to eight. The triple produces the diapason and diapente, as two is to six. The quadruple produces the bisdiapason, as four is to sixteen. [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Diapason and diapente.”]

The superparticular kind contains the sesquialtera, sesquitertia, and sesquioctave proportions. The sesquialtera produces the diapente, as six is to nine or eight to twelve. The sesquitertia produces the diatessaron, as six is to eight or nine to twelve. The combination of sesquialtera and sesquitertia produces the diapason.

The sesquioctave, as eight is to nine, produces the tone.

The multiple kind of inequality therefore generates the diapason through the double proportion, as one is to two; the diapente and diapason through the triple proportion, as one is to three; and the bisdiapason through the quadruple proportion, as one is to four.

The superparticular kind of inequality creates the diapente through the sesquialtera, the diatessaron through the sesquitertia, and the tone through the sesquioctave proportion.

# On the Seven Voices

There are seven different voices which, repeated like the days of the week, complete two diapasons. The monochord ought not to extend beyond these two diapasons, because every string in the lower diapason has a corresponding string in the upper diapason that sounds with it.

For this reason the same diatessaron cannot be fitted below the sesquitertian interval, because, since the diapason contains five tones and two semitones, the diapente three tones and one semitone, and the diatessaron two tones and one semitone, in the two diapasons the four modes are each found four times.

Some of these voices are partly proper: the low voices to the plagals, the high voices to the authentics. Others are partly common to both plagals and authentics: the finals and the upper voices, in which the plagals share the same diapente with their masters. [Note: [Col. 0438D] Read: “they have the same.”] This also applies to the *Saeculorum amen*: although not on the same strings, it has its endings in the same tetrachords, and the plagals receive the same endings as their masters.

# On the Tropes or Tones

The tropes which we abusively call tones are, according to the terminology of the nations, four by nature: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian. According to the arrangement of the monochord they are called Protus, Deuterus, Tritus, and Tetrardus; according to the order of the letters they are as follows:

Protus extends in this arrangement from A to D; Deuterus from B to E; Tritus from C to F; Tetrardus from D to G.

But since high and low would confuse one another, it was decided that each trope should be divided into two, so that low voices would accord with low voices and acute voices with acute voices. The acute modes are called authentic; the low modes are called in Greek plagals, and in Latin subjugales or lateral modes.

Of these, the first, hypodorian, is sung from A to a; the second, hypophrygian, from B to b; the third, hypolydian, from C to c; and the fourth, hypomixolydian, from D to d. Dorian, the authentic mode, extends from D to d; Phrygian from E to e; Lydian from F to f; and Mixolydian from G to g.

These four modes are naturally separated from one another, so that one does not give another a place in its own seat; one either never receives the other’s neume or transforms it. Such are the melodies in these Offertories: *Jubilate. Ipse est Deus*, and so forth; *Deo nostro*; *Filiae regum*; *Varietate*; *Justitiae Domini*; *Factus est*, and so forth; *In ea sanctificatione*, and so forth; *Filiorum*, and so forth.

Every species of diatessaron, diapente, or diapason therefore begins from whatever trope it belongs to and ends in the same trope. Consequently, those species which begin on one and end on another, although they have the regular arrangement of tones and semitones, are not entirely natural, such as D–G and E–A.

Other species, which do not end in the trope on which they begin and do not have the customary arrangement of the diatessaron—that is, two tones and a semitone—such as F–B, must be rejected altogether. Likewise, the diapente B–F, which does not have the arrangement of three tones and a semitone, is not to be admitted. Thus all regular species of the diatessaron arise from the low voices, whereas those of the diapente arise from the finals.

Tetrachords are formed in two ways on the monochord: according to measurement and according to the institution of the tropes. Those constructed according to measurement have the semitone at the end, for they are counted as tone, tone, semitone. They also have the conjunction of the tetrachords—which in Greek is called *synaphe*—on E. The separated tones, called in Greek *diezeusis*, occur between A and B.

Those constructed according to the institution of the tropes have the semitone in the middle, for they are counted as tone, semitone, tone. They also have *synaphe* on D and d, while *diezeusis* occurs at A and G and between a and g.

In this arrangement of the tetrachords, the first letter of each tetrachord belongs to protus, the second to deuterus, the third to tritus, the fourth either jointly to protus and tetrardus, as D and d, or specifically to tetrardus, as G and g.

Protus has the diatessaron A–D, a–d; deuterus B–E, b–e; tritus C–F, c–f; while tetrardus has D–G and d–g.

Dorian is authentic and hypodorian plagal; Phrygian is authentic and hypophrygian plagal; Lydian is authentic and hypolydian plagal; Mixolydian is authentic and hypomixolydian plagal.

[Col. 0439A] The fact, therefore, that the tropes are called protus, deuterus, tritus, and tetrardus—that is, first, second, third, and fourth—results from their position on the monochord, not from their dignity. Each of them is authentic in itself, that is, authoritative or masterly.

From A to D all the species of the diatessaron are constructed naturally, because the diatessaron is found in the fourth division of the entire monochord. The first species of the diatessaron belongs to protus, extending from A to D and consisting of tone, semitone, tone. The second belongs to deuterus, from B to E, consisting of semitone, tone, tone. The third belongs to tritus, from C to F, consisting of tone, tone, semitone. The fourth is common to protus and tetrardus, having the same form as the first, from D to G.

Protus uses it in ascent, as in *Fac mecum*. Tetrardus uses it in descent, as in *Dabo in Sion Judaea et Jerusalem*. If you find any other species of the diatessaron, since it has no place in this regular arrangement, it must be rejected, as in the species from F which consists of tone, tone, tone.

## How the Species of the Diapason Are Constructed

All the species of the diapason are constructed so that they begin in the first diapason and end in the second, because the diapason is found in the second division of the entire monochord.

It must be understood that every lawful ascent and descent of a chant is constructed through the diapason. The first species of the diapason is the plagal protus, from A to a, with D in the middle. The second is the plagal deuterus, from B to b, with E in the middle. The third is the plagal tritus, from C to c, with F in the middle. The fourth is common to plagal protus and plagal tetrardus, from D to d, with G in the middle. This is the legitimate ascent and descent of the plagals.

Likewise, for the ascent and descent of the authentics, four species of the diapason are counted. If the first species was said to be the fourth with respect to plagal tetrardus, then with respect to authentic protus it is the first: from D to d, with a in the middle. The second is authentic deuterus, from E to e, with b in the middle. The third is authentic tritus, from F to f, with c in the middle. The fourth is authentic tetrardus, from G to g, with d in the middle. This is the legitimate ascent and descent of the authentics. Additions of voices in either direction are made by permission or authority.

There are two diapasons. In each of them every trope has two letters. Protus has A and D in the first, and a and d in the second. Deuterus has B and E in the first, and b and e in the second. Tritus has C and F in the first, and c and f in the second. Tetrardus has D and G in the first, and d and g in the second.

The plagals begin on the low voices and are excluded from the high ones; they share the finals and upper voices. The low and upper voices are the finals of the plagals; the high voices are the boundaries of the authentics. The tetrachord of the low voices is the lowest descent of the chant. The tetrachord of the finals is the exit of the melody. The tetrachord of the upper voices gives the beginnings of the differentiae, that is, of the *Saeculorum amen*, except for the *Saeculorum amen* of the second tone. The tetrachord of the high voices is the highest ascent of the chant.

The authentics end on the finals, have their middle on the upper voices, and begin through the *Saeculorum amen*; they rise to the high voices. The plagals descend to the low voices, have their middle on the finals and end there, and rise to the upper voices.

Protus in its authentic form, extending from D to d, has a middle on a. Deuterus in its authentic form, extending from E to e, has a middle on b. Tritus in its authentic form, extending from F to f, has a middle on C. Tetrardus in its authentic form, extending from G to g, has a middle on d. In the plagals, the middle and the final are one and the same.

In the authentics, the middle voices and the *Saeculorum amen* are the same. Protus, considered indifferently, extending from A to d, has two middle voices, d and a. Deuterus, considered indifferently, extending from B to e, has two middle voices, E and b. Tritus, considered indifferently, extending from C to F, has two middle voices, F and c. Tetrardus, considered indifferently, extending from D to g, has two middle voices, G and d.

The plagals ascend from the low voices through the finals to the upper voices. The authentics climb from the finals through the upper voices to the high voices. The plagals have the diatessaron below and the diapente above; the authentics have the diapente below and the diatessaron above.

## On the Recognition of the Four Modes

The first mode of voices occurs wherever a voice can be lowered by a tone and raised by the first species of the diapente. It may be recognized on the principal strings A and D, a and d, of protus, as the Antiphon *Prophetae praedicaverunt* demonstrates.

The second mode is revealed when a voice is lowered by a ditone and raised by the second species of the diatessaron. It occurs on the principal strings B and E, b and e, of deuterus; this Antiphon displays it in the plagal form: *Gloria haec est*.

The third mode is lowered by the third species of the diatessaron and raised by a ditone, as the special strings C, F, c, and f of tritus declare. Its indication is found in this plagal Antiphon: *Modicum et non videbitis*.

The fourth mode, raised by a tone and lowered by the fourth species of the diapente, we assign to tetrardus, because its principal strings D and G, d and g, constitute it. This mode is recognized both authentically and plagally in the Antiphon *Si vere fratres. Multi veniunt*.

It should be noted that, since each trope has the *Saeculorum amen* on its own string—for example, protus on a, tritus on c, and tetrardus on d—only deuterus transfers its *Saeculorum amen* from a to c because of the imperfection of the semitone.

No plagal places its *Saeculorum amen* on the same letter as its master, but always lower: protus on a, while its plagal alone is on F; deuterus on c, while its plagal is on a; tritus on c, while its plagal is on a; and tetrardus alone on d, while its plagal is on c.

The question is asked concerning the species of the diapason, which extends from D to d. Since this range is common to both the protus and the tetrardus, why does it produce not one mode but two? The answer is as follows: the protus has its final in D and its median distinction in a; the tetrardus subjugalis has both its final and its median distinction in G. The protus, however, moving through the subordinate distinctions, the median distinctions, and the final around a or D, also frequently employs its own species of diatessaron and diapente. The subjugalis tetrardus, on the other hand, intent upon its own species through cola and commas, moving chiefly around G, produces entirely different modes [Col. 0441A]: the protus more often by ascending, the tetrardus more often by descending.

The single letter D is principal twice on the monochord. It is, in fact, the principal of the protus, whose diatessaron is bounded by a and d. The same D is also the final of the melody of that protus. The letter d itself is the principal of the tetrardus, for its diatessaron is bounded by it and by its special note g. Thus the same fourth species of the diatessaron belongs to the protus only in form, but properly belongs to the tetrardus, since it is enclosed by its principal strings d and g. The same D is common because it is the last of the grave notes and the first of the finals. It is both the final of the protus and the lowest D of the tetrardus by descending through a diatessaron. The letter d above is the highest point of the protus’s ascent and the *saeculorum amen* of the tetrardus; it is also the last of the upper notes and the first of the highest notes [Col. 0441B].

Every note, in relation to the note next to it below or above, is either a semitone or a tone. Every note, at a third from itself, is either a semiditone or a ditone [Col. 0442A]. Every note, at a fourth from itself, is a diatessaron, except for F and the square B. Every note, at a fifth from itself, is a diapente, except for B and F, and for b and f.

Every chant descending one or two notes below the final, and reaching one or all of its notes above the diapente, will be authentic. Every chant descending four or five notes below the final, and touching nothing above the diapente, will be subjugalis. Every chant having a fully plagal descent will be subjugalis if it reaches one or two notes above the diapente. Every chant having one note below the final, and not going above the diapente, will be subjugalis. Every chant confined to only five notes can be common, but it should be assigned to whichever mode is more frequently represented in it [Col. 0442B]. Every chant not reaching five notes will, because of its imperfection, be subjugalis.

[Col. 0441] **On the invention of the synemenon**

The synemenon requires the gravity of the notes as much as their acuteness;

This may be proved by a twofold argument.

It regards the octave, because every little note wishes

Also to sound its own diapason of the synemenon,

And each mode possesses its proper species of the diapente:

The authentic above, the lateral mode has its own below.

The protus wishes to consist of the first species,

The deutrus of the second,

The third of the third species,

And the fourth likewise of the fourth.

Behold the lateral modes of the protus and deutrus,

And likewise that of the tritus.

According to its custom, this would no longer occur

Except through the synemenon.

Many Gregorian chants will make this secure.

The protus rules over the principal strings in the tetrachords,

Namely A, D, G, which are also designated by a and d,

Standing in the first species of the diatessaron and diapente.

Thus the order of the modes has the notes of the tetrachords.

The deutrus stands as deutrus, because in notes and in species,

Just as each is given its own series, so it varies.

**On the species of the diatessaron**

As the diapente varies fourfold, so the diatessaron varies threefold;

Nature establishes three species of the diatessaron.

The first consists of a limma with a tone given on either side.

The second formula places the limma after two tones.

The third places the limma before two tones.

A–D is a diatessaron; B–E is a diatessaron; Γ–C is a diatessaron.

**On the species of the diapente**

The species borne by the diapente are distinguished as follows:

The first consists of a ditone, a limma, and a tone—for example, from Γ to D.

The second consists of a tritone and a limma [Note: [Col. 0442] for example, from F to c, with the intermediate note.]

The third is the reverse [Note: [Col. 0442] for example, from E to an endpoint missing in the source.]

The fourth consists of a tone, a limma, and a ditone [Note: [Col. 0442] for example, from low A to E.]

**On the properties of the modes**

The nobility of the first pleases, as does the winding course of the second;

The loquacity of the fourth is pleasing, and your pleasure, O tritus.

**Where the tetrachord and the diezeuxis occur**

From these the tetrachords D–G–d are marked on either side.

Between G and A the diezeuxis appears twice in one place.

**On the six symphonies**

There are three simple symphonies, and just as many joined ones.

The simple ones are the diapason, the diatessaron, and the diapente.

The joined ones are called the diapason with the diapente,

The diapente with the tone,

And the diatessaron with the diapason.

**On the kinship of the protus and the tetrardus**

If on either side you join a tone to the tetrachord,

Or a diapente of the first or fourth species,

The precedence of the protus and of the tetrardus becomes evident.

**AROUND THE SAME PERIOD. THE ANNALS OF HILDESHEIM, QUEDLINBURG, WEISSENBURG, AND LAMBERT. PART ONE.**

*(In D. Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. III, p. 18.)*

[Col. 0443]

**PRELIMINARY NOTICE**

[Col. 0443A] The monastery of Hersfeld, founded by Archbishop Lull in the early years of Charlemagne and endowed with very considerable resources, gave rise under the reign of Louis I to the Annals which, in their first part, down to the year 829, were built upon the chronicles of Isidore [Note: [Col. 0443B] *Origins*, book V, 39.] and Bede [Note: [Col. 0443B] At the end of the books *On Times* and *On the Reckoning of Time*], upon the Murbach Annals as they still survive today in the Lorsch [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare, for example, the years 717, 748, 781, 786–791, and 795.] and Nazarian Annals [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare, for example, the years 709, 710, 725, and 752.], upon the Lesser Lorsch Annals [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare the years 738, 746, 750, 753, 754, 755, 758, 765, 768, 772, 773, 774, 787, 795, 801, 802, 806, 807, 810, and 815.], as well as upon the Lorsch Annals [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare, for example, 774, 776, 778, 782, and 799; and in the Quedlinburg Annals, the years 775–780, 782–784, 788, 789, 793, 794, 798–800, and 805.] and those of Einhard [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare the years 792, 805, 813, 818 and following down to 829, and the Quedlinburg Annals for 790, 795, and others.]. From the year 830 onward they were continued by successive authors through the ninth and tenth centuries, down to the years 973 and 984.

Lappenberg has already observed in our Annals [Note: [Col. 0444B] Vol. VI, p. 638.] that some information taken from Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History* was inserted into the earlier part; only a few items appear to have been taken from the Fulda notes, and only one of these concerns the monastery of Hersfeld—and that was not drawn from an ancient source, but excerpted from a misunderstood passage in the *Life of Abbot Sturm of Fulda* [Note: [Col. 0444B] The year 736, from the *Life of Saint Sturm*, chapters 5–6.]. Thus it is easily understood that the authority of the first part depends wholly upon its sources; the second part, however, runs in genuine form through the greater part of the ninth and tenth centuries [Note: [Col. 0444B] The arguments advanced by learned men in favor of another view do not persuade me. I do not recognize either the continuator of Regino or the Corvey Annals among the sources of the Hersfeld Annals; and, to touch briefly upon the arguments produced, the dedication of the church at Trier, certainly famous throughout all Germany, and the arrival of the Hungarians as far as Fulda, matters of the greatest importance to the people of Hersfeld and certainly well known to them, are sufficient.].

Waitz observed that the earlier part was repeated, or rather excerpted, in the Fulda Annals which I examined in the library of the Dutch at Leiden, then in the Lobbes and Alsatian Monastery Annals, which derived from the Weissenburg Annals, and in Marianus Scotus [Note: [Col. 0444B] Compare our Annals, vol. VI.]. The entire work—or at least that part of it which deserves the greatest attention—was copied by the annalist of Halberstadt and by the annalist of Weissenburg.

The work of the latter, previously known only through excerpts published by Wurdtwein [Note: [Col. 0444B] *Subsidia diplomatica* XII, 134 ff.], I found complete in a manuscript formerly belonging to Weissenburg, brought in 1560 by Johann Aegolf von Knöringen to the library at Ingolstadt and, together with that library, now preserved in the library of the Royal University of Munich. I incorporated it into our materials. It follows the books of Eusebius and Prosper; on the margin of the nineteen-year cycles of Dionysius, beginning in 532, a supplement was added at the end of the eleventh century, around 1075 [Col. 0445A]. A second hand, around 1087, inserted some material which we have arranged to be printed in italics, omitting the names of the eastern emperors down to Basil and Constantine, crowned in 976 together with their grandfather Constantine and their father Romanus, as well as the Roman emperors taken from some catalogue and inserted here and there at will.

The final four leaves of the manuscript contain the Lesser Lorsch Annals [Note: [Col. 0445C] At 807 they add: “After him another Grimoald succeeded to the kingdom and attempted to invade other kingdoms without the king’s command”; at 814, as in the Reims version, the correct reading is “he appointed his sons as dukes, Pippin in Aquitaine and Hlothar in Bavaria,” where in vol. I, p. 122, a typographical error printed two instead of one. In the year 817 [Col. 0445D] it adds the following catalogue of the Frankish kings:

**NAMES OF THE FRANKISH KINGS**

Hlothar reigned 43 years.

Dagobert reigned 17 years.

Sigibert, 23 years.

Hildebert the Adopted, 1 year.

Grimoald, 6 years.

Childeric, 14 years.

Theuderic, 17 years.

Pippin, son of Ansegisus, mayor of the palace, 27 years.

Chlodovech, 4 years; he died in the fifth.

Hildebert, 17 years.

Dagobert, 4 years; he died in the fifth.

Charles, mayor of the palace, son of Pippin, 7 years.

Chilperic, 5 years.

Theuderic, 17 years.

Carloman and Pippin, 7 years.

Childeric, 9 years.

Pippin, 27½ years.

Charles, 46 years.

Louis, 26 years.

Hlothar, 16 years.]

of the Reims recension [Note: [Col. 0445D] In the years 744, 764, and 786 it nevertheless follows the Fulda manuscript; in 792 the word *Prumia* is missing; in 776 it reads *Lauresheim*; in 785, *semetipsum*.], beginning, after a leaf has been cut away at the year 716, with the word *Reginfridus*. That the Annals down to 984 derive from the Hersfeld manuscript, while the remainder was added at the monastery of Weissenburg, is clear from the notes themselves; the names of the bishops of Speyer were added at the end of the eleventh century [Col. 0445B].

The other writer who copied the Hersfeld Annals—the annalist of Halberstadt, as I believe—remains hidden up to this point, but he can be recognized in the older part of the Hildesheim and Quedlinburg Annals down to 993, in Thietmar, in the Saxon Annalist and Saxon Chronicler [Note: [Col. 0445D] Numerous passages occur in both works and in the monk of Sassaw which C. Lappenberg and Waitz judged should be attributed to the Quedlinburg Annals. But since the unique Dresden manuscript presents not only the complete sequence of years but, from 961 onward, material different from that found in the Chronicler, it is clear that the Annalist, the Chronicler, and the Sassaw writer drew from the source of the Quedlinburg Annals. The description of the dedication of the church of Halberstadt in 992 was transferred to the Quedlinburg Annals from the Halberstadt source [Col. 0446D], and it is found in a genuine and fuller form in the Halberstadt chronicle.], in the monk of Sassaw [Note: [Col. 0446D] Mencken, *Scriptores* III, p. 1775 ff.], and in the Halberstadt Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0446D] Leibniz, *Scriptores* II.] and that of Staindel [Note: [Col. 0446D] Oefele, *Scriptores* I.].

Among these are the Hildesheim Annals, surviving in an autograph manuscript now numbered 6114 in the Royal Library at Paris, formerly numbered 1031, 1125, and 5993: a parchment quarto manuscript from the end of the tenth century and from the eleventh and twelfth centuries. After a breviary of Rufus Festus it contains a book *On the Order of Times*, compiled from the Chronicle of Isidore of Seville [Col. 0445C], the Lesser Lorsch Annals, and the Hersfeld Annals down to 993, written in a tenth-century hand. Various continuations, written by different hands succeeding one another, follow down to the death of the emperor Lothar III.

The book was first published by Chesne in *Scriptores Francici*, vol. III, p. 540, and thereafter repeated by Leibniz in *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium* I, p. 711. I examined it again at Paris in 1827 and now present it cleansed of its errors.

Its first part, down to 993, was composed by a Hildesheim writer [Col. 0446A] and written at the time itself, later enlarged in several places by additions from another tenth-century writer [Note: [Col. 0446D] See, for example, the notice concerning the foundation of the city of Hildesheim, which is written throughout the manuscript in capital letters, and the years 872, 875, etc.]. It was to be printed only from 814 onward, since the method of our work did not require the reprinting here of Isidore or the Lesser Lorsch Annals. Its author is entirely unknown.

Nor do we know the authors of the continuations down to 1109: certainly Hildesheimers, but men whose names are obscured by an undeserved darkness. Perhaps one exception is Thangmar, librarian and notary of the church of Hildesheim, tutor, friend, and envoy of Bishop Bernward to Otto III and Pope Sylvester II. Since he began collecting Bernward’s deeds while Bernward was still alive, and since in his *Life of the Bishop* he relates many matters in exactly the words in which they are found in our Annals [Col. 0446B], it would be possible to regard him as the author of the Annals from 1000 to 1022, were it not that this portion of the Annals declares itself attached to the monastery of Saint Michael, although Thangmar never professed himself a monk of Saint Michael.

The autograph manuscript shows that the Annals are earlier than the *Life of Bernward*. In the same manner, the continuation of the Annals down to 1038 was copied by Wolfhere, author of the *Life of Saint Godehard*. The fact that the entire work down to 1040 was in the hands of Lambert of Aschaffenburg is shown by the excerpts taken from it in his work.

The years 1041–1101, written by a man favorable to the party of Henry IV, as was fitting for a cleric of Bishop Udo, agree with the Würzburg Annals in many passages literally [Col. 0446C] [Note: [Col. 0446D] It is no longer permissible to doubt that Ekkehard of Aura’s Chronicle was derived from this source, now that his autograph has been before our eyes and the true reading of the work has been established.]. They also rest in large part upon material excerpted from the Chronicle of Hermann the Lame and its continuations [Note: [Col. 0446D] That the Hildesheim Annals in this part did not derive from the Würzburg Annals is shown by the fact that the years 1041–1100 were written by one hand, while the year 1101 was written by another, the same hand that added the history of 1102–1109.].

The final part of the work—the annals of the years 1109–1137—was composed by an enemy of Henry IV and, as the history of 1133 shows, by a man from Paderborn. He also added to the earlier years notes hostile to Henry IV.

The Quedlinburg Annals survive in the paper manuscript of the Royal Dresden Archives, written first by Peter Albinus [Col. 0447A] and then corrected and enlarged with notes by various sixteenth- and seventeenth-century scribes. Leibniz first published them in *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. II, pp. 272 ff., under the title *Chronicle of the Quedlinburg Saxons*; Mencken then compared them with the Saxon Chronicler in *Scriptores rerum Saxonicarum*, vol. III, pp. 170 ff. They have now been examined with the greatest care for our purposes by the distinguished V. Cl. Mauritius Haupt.

The first part of the work, down to 993 and perhaps to 1000 [Note: [Col. 0447D] There the Halberstadt annals excerpted by the monk of Sassaw come to an end; and the distinguished Lappenberg proved from the words “the future king,” used of Henry II in 995, that this part of the Quedlinburg Annals was not written before 1002.], flowed from the Halberstadt Annals, Bede’s *On the Six Ages*, the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings*, and other unknown sources. It made occasional use of Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, the Saxon Poet [Note: [Col. 0447D] The years 802 and 803.], and the Alamannic Annals [Note: [Col. 0447D] Compare 829, 860, and 917.] and Reichenau Annals [Note: [Col. 0448D] For example, 829, 860, 872, and 910. Compare our Annals VI, p. 642.]. It also inserted genuine notices chiefly concerning the family of the Ottos, which, as Lappenberg has already suggested, the author received from the Quedlinburg abbesses Matilda and Adelheid [Col. 0447B] [Note: [Col. 0448D] See our Annals, vol. VI, pp. 643–644.].

These notices, together with the rest down to 1025, must be counted among the principal sources for the history of that period: the author was contemporary, present at the events, and skilled in writing. That the work was continued beyond 1025 is proved by what it records about the arrival of Beatrice and her progress through the successive stages of her life. The work ends in the middle of a sentence. Yet no trace either of its continuation or of its earlier part has been found in the Quedlinburg Chronicles preserved at Halle in Saxony or in the Royal Library.

The edition based on the Dresden manuscript was corrected with the aid of the authors who copied both the Halberstadt Annals and ours, as well as Thietmar, the Saxon Annalist, and the Saxon Chronicler.

[Col. 0447C] The first part of Lambert of Aschaffenburg’s Annals also belongs here. It was compiled from the Hersfeld and Hildesheim Annals [Note: [Col. 0448D] Wherever the Hersfeld Annals leave off in 973 and 984, he consistently copies them down to 1039.], and from other materials written in Bavaria, perhaps at Passau or Freising [Note: [Col. 0448D] The years 974–983.], which also occur in the Chronicle of Staindel and in Aventinus.

We present it after the earlier editions—namely:

a) the first edition, published from the manuscript of the Augustinian Canons at Tübingen by Caspar Churrer at Tübingen in 1525, in octavo, and furnished with a preface by Philipp Melanchthon;

b) the Tübingen edition of 1533, in octavo, corrected by Ludwig Schradin, as he himself states, from the same manuscript;

c) Simon Schard’s edition of 1566, in folio, among the four chroniclers of German affairs, and his historical work of 1374, vol. I;

d) Johann Pistorius’s edition in *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, 1583, in folio, “corrected in many places from a very old book”;

e) the Strasbourg edition of 1609, in folio;

f) and that of Burcard Gotthelf Struve, 1726, in folio, in Pistorius’s *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, vol. II—

with the assistance of the following:

1. Manuscript C, in the Royal Dresden Archives, first examined by me and later copied for our purposes by the distinguished Ludwig Hesse, archivist of the Most Serene Prince of Schwarzburg. It is a paper manuscript from the end of the fifteenth or beginning of the sixteenth century and agrees very closely with the first edition.

2. The first edition, copied by the distinguished Hesse.

[Col. 0448B] 3. A manuscript of the ducal library at Gotha, a parchment folio from the twelfth century, written around 1137. It contains the chronicle of Ekkehard of Aura enlarged from Lambert’s Annals. It was written in the monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt and, together with the other manuscripts originating from that monastery, contains certain additions foreign to Lambert’s authentic text. It was nevertheless necessary to mention them, especially because the book is separated from Lambert’s period by no more than fifty years. The manuscript was generously and courteously made available to me by the distinguished Friedrich Jacobs, whose kindness and humanity are well known. Closely related to it is:

4. Manuscript C of the university library at Göttingen, formerly belonging to Andreas Erasmus von Seidel and later to Salomon Semler, a man highly deserving of recognition for his work on local history. It is a paper folio from the end of the fifteenth century [Col. 0448C], generously made available to me by the distinguished Beneke, director of the extensive library.

5. Manuscript C of the university library at Würzburg, a paper folio from the end of the fifteenth or the sixteenth century, collated with the printed editions by the distinguished Hesse, who also

6. recorded the readings of the Pistorius edition of 1583.

The second part of Lambert must be placed among the writers of the eleventh century.

[Col. 0447]

**ANNALS OF HILDESHEIM, QUEDLINBURG, AND LAMBERT**

**ANNALS OF HILDESHEIM** [Note: [Col. 0447] The following annals should be read in parallel.]

[Col. 0447C] Here begins the book *On the Order of Times*. The first among our authors to give a brief account of time through generations and reigns was Julius Africanus, etc. [lacuna] and to place the line of years at the side. By its indication, the total of the elapsed times may be known.

[Col. 0447D] In six days God formed all created things: on the first day, etc.

Antoninus Caracalla [lacuna] Naples is founded.

Theodosius with his sons Arcadius and Honorius [lacuna] Augustine flourished.

[Col. 0448C] Anastasius [lacuna] Boethius, the consul, flourished.

Tiberius, 6 years. After the Romans had been expelled, the Lombards came into Italy. The Goths in Spain, divided into two groups, were ravaged by mutual slaughter. BENNOPOLIS IS FOUNDED; THE CITY OF HILDESHEIM.

[Col. 0448D] Maurice [lacuna] Gregory dies.

Heraclonus with his mother Martina [lacuna] the monastery of Fleury is founded.

Constantine, son of Heraclius, reigned 6 months.

Constantine, son of Constantine, reigned 27 years [Col. 0449A]. Pope Eugene began to flourish in the sixth year of Constantine, and he himself sat for 2 years, 9 months, and 24 days. Vitalian, etc.—Sergius sat for 13 years, 8 months, and 14 days. Thus far we have recounted the deeds of the Roman princes and the pontiffs of the Roman church [Col. 0450A]. Pippin the duke, son of Ansegisus, etc.

**ANNALS OF QUEDLINBURG**

[Col. 0449A]

[Note: [Col. 0449D] The first age—the beginning—from Bede, *On Times*, chapter 14.] The first age extends from Adam to Noah, comprising ten generations and 1,656 years. It was entirely destroyed by the Flood, just as forgetfulness usually drowns infancy.

The second age extends from Noah to Abraham, likewise comprising ten generations but 292 years. In this age the Hebrew language was discovered. For it is in childhood that a human being begins to know how to speak after infancy, which received its name from the fact that one cannot *fari*, that is, speak.

[Col. 0449B] The third age extends from Abraham to David, comprising fourteen generations and 942 years. And because a person begins to be able to beget children from adolescence, Matthew took the beginning of his genealogy from Abraham. He too was made the father of many nations, since he received a changed name [Note: [Col. 0449D] “Who … received”: from Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 64, concerning the six ages of the world.].

The fourth age [Note: [Col. 0449D] “The fourth … to be completed”: from Bede, *On Times*.] extends from David to the migration to Babylon, comprising, according to Matthew, fourteen generations and extending for 484 years. From this age the period of the kings began, for the age of youth is suited to kingship.

The fifth age then extends to the coming of the Savior in the flesh. It too comprises fourteen generations and extends for 586 years. In it, as though exhausted by the heavy burden of old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly frequent misfortunes.

The sixth age, which is now in progress, has no definite sequence of generations or times, but, like an age that has grown decrepit, is to be ended by the death of the whole world [Col. 0449C]. They are called ages because they follow one another [Note: [Col. 0449D] “The ages … called”: from Isidore, *Etymologies* V, 38–39.]. As one age departs, another succeeds it, and their course is recorded through generations and reigns in the following manner.

The first age at its beginning contains the creation of the world. On the first day God created the angels under the name of light. On the second he created the heavens under the name of the firmament. On the third he created the forms of the waters and the earth under the designation of separation. On the fourth, the lights of heaven. On the fifth, living creatures from the waters. On the sixth, living creatures from the earth and the human being, whom he called Adam.

Adam [Note: [Col. 0450D] The material that follows in both works is taken from Bede, *On Times*, and Isidore.] at the age of 130 begot Seth, who was born after Abel and from whom came the sons of God. Seth at 105 begot Enos, who began to call upon the name of the Lord. Enos at 90 begot Cainan. Cainan at 70 begot Mahalaleel, whose name is interpreted as “plantation of the Lord.” Mahalaleel at 62 begot Jared. Jared at 162 begot Enoch. We learn that this Enoch wrote certain divine works, as the apostle Jude bears witness [Note: [Col. 0450D] “This Enoch …”: as found in Bede, *On the Sixth Age*, which the author also consulted below.]. Enoch at 65 begot Methuselah; after whose birth he was translated by the Lord. Methuselah at 187 begot Lamech. Giants were born, and the sons of God desired the daughters of men. Lamech at [Col. 0451A] 182 begot Noah, who built the ark. In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood came. From Adam to the cataclysm there were 1,650 years.

The second age contains 2 years [lacuna].

[The space of one and a half pages is blank.]

[Col. 0451B] [lacuna] the Phoenicians first discovered [Note: [Col. 0451D] The material down to Nicostrata appears to have been taken from Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 3–4, by the Quedlinburg author.]. Then Cadmus, son of Agenor, first brought ten and seven Greek letters from Phoenicia into Greece. The nymph Carmentis first gave the Latin letters to the Italians. Carmentis was so called because she sang the future in songs; her proper name, however, was Nicostrata.

Jephthah, 6 years. Hercules threw himself into the flames. Abessa, 7 years. The ten-year Trojan War arose. Achialon, [Col. 0451C] 10 years. He is not found among the Seventy translators. Jabdo, 8 years. Troy was captured, and Aeneas came to Italy. Samson, 20 years. Ascanius founded the city of Alba. Eli the priest, 40 years. The ark of the covenant was captured. The kingdom of the Sicinians came to an end. Samuel and Saul, 32 years. The kingdom of the Lacedaemonians arose, and Homer is proved to have existed.

The fourth age contains 483 years. David, 40 years. Carthage was founded by Dido. Gath, Nathan, and Asaph prophesied. Solomon, 40 years. The temple was built at Jerusalem, when 480 years since the exodus of the Jews from Egypt had been completed. From this it appears that Samuel and Saul ruled for 32 years, not 40. Rehoboam, 17 years. The kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided. Abijah, 3 years. The high priest Abimelech was held in distinction. Asa, 40 years. Haggai, Amos, Joel, Jehu, and Azariah prophesied. Jehoshaphat, 25 years. Elijah, Elisha, Obadiah, and Micah prophesied [Col. 0451D]. Jehoram, 8 years. Edom withdrew from Judah and appointed a king for itself. Ahaziah, 1 year. Elijah was taken up. Athaliah, 7 years. Jonadab, son of Rechab, a priest, flourished. Joash, 40 years. Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, was stoned. Amaziah, 28 years. Amos the prophet was in Israel. Uzziah, 52 years. The kingdom of the Assyrians was transferred to the Medes; it had stood from the beginning of Belus for 1,305 years. The Olympic Games were also instituted by the Greeks. Jotham, 16 years. Hosea, Joel, and Isaiah prophesied, and Romulus was born. Ahaz, 16 years. Rome was founded, and Israel was transferred to the Medes. Hezekiah, 29 years. Romulus appointed one hundred senators [Col. 0453A].

In the time of Romulus [Note: [Col. 0453D] “In the time … suffered”: the Quedlinburg author inserted this material, taken from another source.] an eclipse of the sun occurred. The ignorant multitude, unaware that it had taken place according to the certain law of the sun’s course, attributed it to the merits of Romulus, as though, if that mourning had been the sun’s, he ought not for that reason to be believed to have been killed, and as though the crime itself had not been indicated by the withdrawal even of daylight. The same thing truly happened when the Lord was crucified through the cruelty and impiety of the Jews. That darkness was not caused by the regular course of the heavenly bodies is sufficiently shown by the fact that it was then the Passover of the Jews. For the full moon is solemnly observed at Passover, whereas a regular eclipse of the sun occurs only at the beginning of the lunar month.

It is evident, as other writers add, that through the sudden storm and the obscuration of the sun the secrecy of his murder and crime deserved a just death. In the death of Christ, however, it became clear that the eclipse of the sun itself was the mourning of the element, which rightly had reason to grieve for its Creator.

Manasseh, 55 years. Numa added two months, and the Sibyl flourished. Amon, 2 years. Tullius conducted the census in the republic. Josiah, 31 years [Note: [Col. 0453D] Addition: “He died by lightning.”]. Thales the physicist flourished. Jehoiakim, 11 years. In his third year Nebuchadnezzar, who [Note: [Col. 0453D] “Who … dwelt”: the Quedlinburg author added this.] lived insane among wild beasts for seven years, captured Judaea. Zedekiah, 11 years. The temple at Jerusalem was burned.

From the origin of the world to the end of the kingdom of Judah there are 3,363 years.

The fifth age contains 589 years. The captivity of the Hebrews lasted 70 years. The history of Judith was written under the second Nebuchadnezzar, who is called Cambyses by another name [Note: [Col. 0453D] “Under … lived for 25 years”: the Quedlinburg author added this, apparently taken from Bede, *On the Sixth Age* [Col. 0454D].]. For he was not the great Nebuchadnezzar who captured Jerusalem, since after the destruction of Jerusalem he lived no more than 25 years.

Darius, son of Hystaspes, 36 years. In his second year the temple at Jerusalem was built, when the 70 years of the Jewish captivity had been completed [Col. 0453C]. In the second year of Darius, among the Romans, the seventh king after Romulus, Tarquinius Superbus, was reigning. He reigned for 27 years, and afterward consuls administered the republic for 464 years, down to Julius Caesar [Note: [Col. 0454D] “In the second … administered”: the Quedlinburg author appears to have taken this from Bede, *On the Sixth Age*.].

Xerxes, 21 years. Herodotus is recognized as a historian. Artaxerxes, 40 years. Ezra renewed the burned law, and Nehemiah restored Jerusalem. Darius, also called Nothus, 19 years. This age had Plato. Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, 26 years. Demosthenes and Aristotle were celebrated. Xerxes, son of Ochus, 4 years. Xenocrates flourished. Darius, 6 years. Alexander captured Jerusalem. Up to this point, the kingdom of the Persians; thereafter, that of the Greeks.

Alexander of Macedon, son of Philip, held Asia for 12 years. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, 40 years. The First Book of the Maccabees begins. Philadelphus, 38 years. The Seventy translators flourished [Note: [Col. 0454D] It is evident from Lambert that more material has been lost here.]. [lacuna] Euergetes, 29 years. Brutus conquered Spain. Soter, 17 years. The Thracians were subjected to the Romans. Varro and Cicero were born. Alexander, 10 years. Syria was subjected to the Romans by Gabinius. Ptolemy, son of Cleopatra, S [uncertain] years. The historian Sallust was born. Dionysius, 30 years. Pompey captured Judaea. Cleopatra, 2 years. Egypt was subjected to the Romans. Up to this point, the kingdom of the Greeks; now that of the Romans.

[Col. 0455A] Julius Caesar, 5 years. He was the first to hold the monarchy, and from him the Caesars received their name. From the creation of the world to the founding of the city—that is, Rome—there are 4,484 years. From the founding of the city to the birth of Christ there are 715 years; their total is 5,199.

Octavian Augustus, 56 years. In his forty-second year the Lord was born, with 4,952 years completed from Adam, or, according to others, 5,199.

Tiberius, 23 years. In his seventeenth year the Lord was crucified.

Gaius, 4 years. Matthew wrote the Gospel.

Claudius, 14 years. Peter and Paul set out for Rome, and Mark for Alexandria.

Nero, almost 14 years. Peter and Paul were handed over to the cross and the sword.

Vespasian, 10 years. In his second year Titus overthrew Jerusalem and razed the temple to the ground, 1,089 years after its first construction and 71 years after the Lord’s incarnation. The Colossus was erected at Rome [Note: [Col. 0455D] In what follows the Quedlinburg author adds much from Bede, *On the Sixth Age*, and other sources; Lambert, however, appears to repeat the Hersfeld Annals.], having a height of 107 feet [Col. 0455B].

Titus, 2 years. He was eloquent and pious, and remarkable for every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called the love and delight of the human race.

Domitian, brother of Titus, 16 years. He sent John the Evangelist into boiling oil and afterward banished him into exile on the island of Patmos, where, through God’s revelation, he came to know the Apocalypse. The same Domitian built the Pantheon at Rome, which Pope Boniface later consecrated in honor of Saint Mary ever-virgin and of all the mothers of Christ.

Nerva, 1 year, 4 months, and 8 days. In his first edict he recalled all the exiles and, at the request and with the consent of the whole people, annulled whatever Domitian Nero, who had reigned before him, had decreed through the cruelty and insolence in which he had burned too fiercely.

Accordingly, the apostle John, freed by this general clemency, returned to Ephesus. Because, during his absence, he saw that the faith of the Church had been shaken by heretics, he immediately strengthened it with the eternity of the word of God set forth in his Gospel.

[Col. 0455C] Trajan, 19 years. The apostle John, 68 years after the Lord’s Passion and in the ninety-eighth year of his own age, rested at Ephesus in a peaceful death. Simon, son of Cleophas and bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified in the 126th year of his age.

Hadrian, 20 years. He finally subdued the Jews by slaughter and leveled Jerusalem, utterly destroyed, with plows, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Zion shall be plowed like a field.” Later, on the site of Calvary where Christ was crucified, he built a city and ordered it to be called Aelia after his own name, since he was called Aelius Hadrianus; but ancient usage prevailed.

Antoninus Pius with his sons Aurelius and Lucius, 22 years. He was kind toward the Christians. Valentinus and Marcion are known.

Marcus Antoninus Verus with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus, 16 years. These men first administered the empire under equal legal authority, since up to that time the Augusti had ruled singly [Col. 0455D].

Commodus the Younger, 13 years. After the head of the Colossus had been removed, he ordered the head of his own image to be placed upon it [Col. 0457A]. Theodotion is regarded as an interpreter.

Aelius [lacuna].

[lacuna] Pertinax, 18 years. Symmachus is regarded as an interpreter.

Antoninus Caracalla, 7 years. The fifth edition of the Jerusalem text is discovered.

Macrinus, 1 year. Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, 4 years. The sixth edition is found at Nicopolis, and the unfortunate Sabellius arises.

Aurelius Alexander, 13 years. Origen is held in renown at Alexandria and indeed throughout the whole world.

Maximinus, 3 years. He persecuted the Christians.

Gordian, 6 years. Fabian flourished as bishop of Rome.

[Col. 0457B] Philip with his son Philip, 8 years. He was the first Christian emperor, and his son likewise.

Decius, 3 years. After killing both Philips— the elder at Rome and the younger at Verona—he began a persecution against the Christians out of hatred for them. Antony the monk flourished in Egypt.

Gallus and Volusian, 2 years. The Novatian heresy arose.

Valerian with Gallienus, for 15 years. When Valerian had stirred up persecution against the Christians, he was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians. There, deprived of his eyesight, he grew old in wretched slavery; wherever he went, Sapor took him along, forced him to bow face-down to the ground as an insult to the Romans, and, trampling him underfoot, mounted his horse. Terrified by so clear a judgment of God, Gallienus therefore restored peace to the Christians.

Claudius, for 2 years. He defeated and expelled the Goths, who had already been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia for 15 years.

Aurelian, for 5 years. He too persecuted the Christians.

Tacitus, for 6 months. After he was killed in Pontus, Florian obtained the empire for 88 days, and was then killed at Tarsus.

Probus, for 6 years. The heresy of the Manichaeans arose.

Carus with his sons Carinus and Numerianus, for 2 years. He triumphed over the Persians.

Diocletian with Herculeus Maximian, whom he had formerly made his fellow soldier and partner in the empire, for 20 years. These men ordered the divine books to be burned, the churches to be devastated, and the Christians to be afflicted and killed. In the twentieth year of his reign Diocletian laid down the purple at Nicomedia, and Maximian at Milan, and they chose a private life. Nevertheless, the persecution once begun did not cease raging until the seventh year of Constantine.

Constantius, Constantine’s father, in the seventeenth year of his rule, a man of the greatest gentleness and courtesy, died at Eboracum in Britain. Since he had many Christians in his palace, he wished to test whether they were truly faithful to their God. He promised them that, if they abandoned the faith, he would give them many gifts, but that otherwise he would inflict punishments upon them.
