When he saw that some had defected from Christ and others had remained immovable, he rewarded those who remained steadfast and made them his friends and advisers. But he disgracefully expelled those who had defected from the palace, saying that he would never trust people who were unfaithful to their God.

At this time Galerius Maximian was made emperor with Constantius. After Constantius’s death, Maximinus and Severus were created Caesars by Galerius in the first year. In the fourth year of the persecution, Maxentius, son of Herculeus Maximian, was proclaimed Augustus at Rome. Licinius, husband of Constantia, Constantine’s sister, was made emperor at Carnuntum.

Constantine, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, was made emperor in Britain and reigned for 30 years and 10 months. After killing Maxentius and driving out Licinius, he alone held the monarchy. Having been converted from a persecutor into a Christian through the baptism administered by the blessed Silvester, he built in his palace a basilica for Jesus Christ and the holy baptist John, which they call the Constantinian Basilica after his name. He built another for the blessed Peter and Paul in the temple of Apollo, enclosing the bodies of both in bronze, five feet thick. He also built many other churches at Rome, as well as a baptistery constructed with marvelous workmanship. He gave the city itself to the holy Peter, together with countless other possessions, ordering that throughout the whole world all bishops should regard the Roman pontiff as their head, just as kings and the other authorities regard the emperor.

Then, crossing into the East, he built a city bearing his name in the region of Thrace and established it as the seat of the whole Roman empire and the capital of the entire East. Through his efforts the Council of Nicaea was also celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, with an assembly of 318 fathers, in the year 318 of the Lord’s incarnation.

After Constantine’s death, his three sons—Constantine, Constans, and Constantius—were made emperors. When the other two had died, Constantius alone obtained the monarchy, having impiously become an Arian. Maximinus of Trier was held to be a distinguished bishop. The monk Antony died in the desert in the 105th year of his life.

Julian, for 2 years and 8 months. Having been turned from a Christian into a pagan, he cruelly persecuted the Christians.

Jovian reigned for almost one year. He became a Christian with his entire army, but his pious and joyful beginnings were marred by an untimely death.

Valentinian with his brother Valens, for 2 years. While Valentinian remained faithfully in the Catholic faith, his brother Valens was rebaptized by the Arian bishop Eudoxius and persecuted the Christians, to such an extent that by a decree of his authority he ordered monks to serve in the army and those unwilling to do so to be killed with clubs.

At this time the people of the Huns, long shut off behind inaccessible mountains, suddenly burst forth in frenzied fury against the Goths and, scattering and throwing them into confusion, expelled them from their ancient settlements beyond the Danube. The Goths were received by the emperor Valens without surrendering their arms, but soon, because of his greed, they were compelled by hunger to rebel. After defeating the emperor’s army, they ranged through Thrace and laid everything waste with slaughter, fires, and plundering. Ambrose and Martin were distinguished bishops, and the Goths became heretics.

[Note: What follows derives from the Deeds of the Kings of the Franks.]

At that time the Alamanni, a wicked and most evil people, rebelled against the emperor Valentinian. Defeated by him, they fled across the Danube and entered the Maeotian marshes. The emperor said: “Whoever can enter these marshes and drive out this wicked people, I shall grant them exemption from tribute and gifts for ten years.”

When the Trojans heard this—they were the remnants of Antenor’s army, having fled from Troy but unable to follow him—12,000 of them entered the Maeotian marshes. Near the borders of Pannonia they built a city called Sicambria and lived there for many years, until they grew into a great people. Entering the marshes after the Alamanni in order to obtain the ten-year remission of tribute, they killed them.

Then the emperor Valentinian called those Trojans “Franks” in the Attic language, that is, “fierce,” because of the hardness or boldness of their hearts. Later, leaving Sicambria, they came to Germany near the Rhine, with two leaders over them, Priam and Antenor. When they rebelled against the Romans, they were defeated by Aristarchus, commander of the army, and subjected to tribute, while both of the aforementioned leaders were killed.

After the death of Sunno [Note: So I corrected it; the manuscript has Surmone.] son of Antenor, and Marchomir son of Priam, who had reigned over the Franks after the death of their fathers, they chose Faramund, son of Marchomir, and raised him over themselves as their long-haired king. From then on the Franks began to have long-haired kings, down to King Hilderic, whose Pippin—the father of the great Charles, who was called mayor of the palace—seized both the kingdom and its name.

After Faramund’s death, Chlodio reigned. After Chlodio, Meroingus [Note: So I corrected it here and below; the manuscript has Merongus.], from whom the Franks were called Merovingians. After Meroingus, his son Helderic, father of the renowned King Chlodoveus, reigned.

This Chlodoveus was the first of the Frankish kings to be baptized by the blessed Remigius, together with his entire army. He expelled the Roman consul Aegidius, killed his son Syagrius, and took from the emperor Martian everything that the Romans possessed between the Rhine and Loire rivers.

After Chlodoveus’s death, his four sons divided his kingdom equally among themselves: Chlodomir, Hildibert, Lothar, and Hugo Theodoricus, born of a concubine. The latter granted most of the land of the Thuringians to the Saxons who remained, and made the Thuringians tributary to the royal territories in pigs.

After Theodoric’s death, Theobert reigned; after him, Theobald. After Theobald’s death, Lothar reigned; after him, Chilperic; after him, Lothar, father of King Dagobert. This Lothar killed Berthold, duke of the Saxons, and, after traversing all their land, left alive in it no man taller than his sword, which they call a spatha.

After Dagobert’s death, his sons Sigibert and Chlodoveus reigned after him. After Chlodoveus, Lothar; after him, his brothers Theodoric and Hilderic. Hilderic himself was exceedingly frivolous. In his time Pippin, son of Ansegisus, was mayor of the palace. After him, his son Charles administered the palace. When Charles died, and Hilderic, the last of the Merovingians, had been removed from the kingdom, Pippin, son of Charles, was anointed king by decree of Pope Zacharias, from being count of the palace. He fathered Charles the Great.

After Valentinian, the emperor Gratian reigned for 6 years with his brother Valentinian.

Valentinian with Theodosius, for 9 years.

Theodosius with his son Arcadius, for 11 years. Jerome the presbyter distinguished himself at Bethlehem above all historiographers.

Arcadius, son of Theodosius, with his brother Honorius, for 13 years. Honorius with the younger Theodosius, son of his brother Arcadius, for 12 years. Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome. In the seventh year of Honorius’s reign, God revealed to the venerable presbyter Lucian the bodies of the saints: Stephen the protomartyr; Gamaliel, who had been the teacher of the apostle Paul; his son Abihon; and Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night. John, bishop of Jerusalem, transferred them with the greatest honor to the holy church of Zion.

Jerome the presbyter died at Bethlehem in the twelfth year of Honorius, in the ninety-first year of his life.

Theodosius the younger, son of Arcadius, for 26 years. Augustine, bishop of Hippo and eminent teacher of the holy Church, died. In the time of this Theodosius, the brothers Bleda and Attila reigned among the Huns and devastated Illyricum and Thrace.

Martian with Valentinian, son of Placidia, for 7 years. The Angles, abandoning the land now possessed by the Danes, came with their king Anglinus to Britain, at the invitation and under the command of King Vortigern, to fight against the Scots and Picts.

The Council of Chalcedon was held under Pope Leo, with 630 fathers in attendance. After Bleda’s death, his brother Attila devastated almost all Gaul until, with God’s favor, he was driven off by the patrician Aetius [Note: Read Aeticius, that is, Aetius.] and Thurismod, a Gothic leader of the city of Reims [Note: It seems that “of Toulouse” or “of Narbonne” should be read.].

At that time Ermanaric ruled over all the Goths. He was more cunning in deceit and more generous in giving. After the death of his only son Frideric, he hanged his cousins Embric and Fritla on the gallows, carrying out his own will [Note: Thus the manuscript. The Leipzig edition has “carried out.”]. He likewise, at the prompting of his cousin Odoacer, expelled his cousin Theodoric from Verona and forced him to go into exile with Attila.

The patrician Aetius, the great salvation of the Western state and also a terror to King Attila, was killed by the younger Valentinian. With him the Western kingdom fell, nor has it since been able to recover [Note: This seems to have been taken from a book written before the year 801.].

Leo the elder, for 17 years. The Egyptian error of Dioscorus barks.

Leo the younger, for 1 year.

Zeno, for 17 years. Odoacer, king of the Goths, took possession of Rome.

Anastasius, for 27 years. Bishop Fulgentius is praised. Ermanaric, king of the Goths, was disgracefully killed—as he deserved—by his brothers Hemido, Serila, and Adaccar, whose father he had killed, after they had cut off his hands and feet. He is called Amulung Theodoric; his great-grandfather was called Amul, who was considered the foremost of the Goths. This was the Theodoric of Verona, about whom peasants once sang.

Theodoric, restored to the Gothic kingdom with the aid of King Attila, defeated his cousin Odoacer in the city of Ravenna. Attila intervened so that Odoacer would not be killed, and Theodoric assigned him to exile, granting him a few estates near the confluence of the rivers Elbe and Saale.

The emperor Anastasius, however, favoring the heretics, died by a stroke of lightning.

Justin, for 9 years. Theodoric, having gained possession of Rome, held John, Roman pontiff, imprisoned at Ravenna until his death, and also killed the distinguished consuls Symmachus and Boethius. Theodoric himself died a sudden death on the ninety-eighth day after Pope John had died; his kingdom was taken over by his nephew Athalaric. At the same time the holy Benedict shone forth like the sun on Monte Cassino.

Justinian the emperor, for 39 years. In his sixth year the fifth synod was celebrated. The first cycle of Dionysius began in the year 532 of the Lord’s incarnation, and the Justinian Code of laws was promulgated to the Roman world.

In the same year Hugo Theodoricus, King Chlodoveus’s son by a concubine, having succeeded his father in the kingdom, honorably invited Irminfrid, king of the Thuringians, to his election. This Hugo Theodoricus is said to mean “Frank,” because formerly all the Franks were called Hugones after a certain leader of theirs named Hugo.

Although he was illegitimate, his father Chlodoveus loved him more than his other sons because of the wisdom and courage divinely granted to him. By his father’s command and with the consent of the whole people, he received an equal share of the kingdom among his noble brothers—namely, Chlodomir, Hildebert, and Lothar.

When Thuringia fell to his portion, Irminfrid, his son-in-law, rejected the king’s invitation at the urging of his wife Amelberga. He said that Theodoric, because of his wife—who was Theodoric’s sister—ought rather to be her servant than king or lord over him or anyone else.

“Let him come first,” he said to the messenger, “bringing with him a heap of money of many kinds, so that, by my command, he may buy from my wife, from both of us of noble parentage, a written grant of freedom.”

Moved to unanimous Frankish fury by this reply, Theodoric sent him this answer: “I shall come, as you have ordered. And if gold is not enough for me, I shall give you, in exchange for my freedom, Thuringian and Frankish heads beyond counting.” [Note: The manuscript reads “tibi”; the second hand corrected it to “tibi.”]

Immediately gathering an army, he came to the region called Maerstem [Note: A district in which the city of Hanover lies.]. There he defeated and routed Irminfrid, who had met him in battle, inflicting great slaughter upon his people. Pursuing him as far as the river Ovacra, near a village called Arhen [Note: The Annals have Orheim or Horheim; compare the year 780.], he overwhelmed him in a great battle. After Irminfrid had fled, Theodoric stopped pursuing him further because of the fall of his own men and the wounds of the survivors, and fortified himself in an established camp for the treatment of the suffering.

When Theodoric heard that the Saxons—whose courage was already being proclaimed through almost the whole world—had arrived at a place called Hadalaon, he summoned them to his aid. He promised them, with an oath sworn by himself and his twelve most noble men, that, if they defeated the Thuringians opposing him, he would give them all their land as far as the confluence of the rivers Saale and Unstrut.

They did not delay, but came to him. Pursuing Irminfrid, they fought against him above the river Unstrut and inflicted such a slaughter of the Thuringians there that the river itself, filled with their corpses, provided them with a bridge.

Irminfrid, however, with his wife, his children, and one soldier named Iring, barely escaped after the Saxons captured by night the city of Schidinga, in which he had shut himself up.

Then Theodoric, after taking counsel, gave the victorious Saxons the whole land of the Thuringians to possess without perpetual tribute, except for the territory enclosed by Louvia [Note: These seem to be the southern mountains of the Thuringians.] and the Harz [Col. 0465] forests. But he ordered the Thuringians who had survived the slaughter to pay the king’s tribute in pigs as their service.

After this, having given his word to Irminfrid, Theodoric deceitfully ordered him to be killed in the city of Zülpich.

Attila, king of the Huns and terror of all Europe, was pierced with a knife and died at the hands of a certain girl whom he had violently seized after killing her father.

The emperor Justin the younger reigned for 11 years. The Armenians accepted the faith of Christ.

Tiberius, for 6 years. The Lombards devastated Italy.

Maurice, for 11 years. Gregory the Great flourished at Rome. Distinguished by every adornment of virtue, he sent the bishop Augustine with monks to Britain to evangelize the word of God to the people of the Angles, in the year 596 of the Lord’s incarnation.

Phocas, for 8 years. The Angles and Saxons in Britain received the faith.

Heraclius, for 36 years. The Jews in Spain became Christians.

Heraclonas with his mother Martina, for 2 years. Pyrrhus, bishop of the imperial city, was condemned by Pope Theodore in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

Constantine, son of Constantine, for 17 years. He convened the Sixth Synod. At his request Pope Agatho sent his legates to the imperial city; among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward its bishop, for the purpose of bringing about the unity of God’s holy churches.

They were received most graciously by Constantine, the most reverend defender of the Catholic faith. They were ordered to set aside philosophical disputations and to seek the true faith through peaceful discussion, and they were given from the Constantinopolitan library all the books of the ancient fathers that they requested.

There were also 150 bishops, with George presiding as patriarch of the imperial city and Macarius as bishop of Antioch. Those who asserted that Christ had one will and one operation were convicted of having falsified very many statements of the Catholic fathers [Note: Added in a second hand in the margin.].

When the dispute had ended, George was corrected. Macarius, however, together with his followers and predecessors—Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter—was anathematized, and Theophanius, an abbot from Sicily, was made bishop of Antioch in his place.

Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, who was one of them, publicly celebrated Mass in Latin on the Sunday of the octave of Easter in the church of Holy Wisdom, before the emperor and patriarch.

This was the Sixth Synod, celebrated at Constantinople.

# THE ANNALS OF LAMBERT

[Col. 0450A]

[Note: The first section—its beginning is taken from Bede, *On the Times*, chapter 14.]

The first age, from Adam to Noah, contains ten generations and 1,656 years. It all perished in the Flood, just as forgetfulness usually drowns infancy.

The second age, from Noah to Abraham, likewise comprises ten generations but 292 years. In it the division of languages took place. For after infancy, when a person cannot speak—that is, cannot *fari*, “to speak”—a human being begins in childhood to become capable of speech; hence the name “infancy” was given to it [Note: A later hand adds “1. 4.”].

[Col. 0450B] The third age, from Abraham to David, contains fourteen generations and likewise 942 years. Since a person begins to be capable of begetting children from adolescence, Matthew took the beginning of his genealogy from Abraham [Note: A later hand adds “of Christ,” Gospel 4.].

[Note: The fourth section—its conclusion is to be supplied from Bede, *On the Times*.]

The fourth age, from David to the migration to Babylon, likewise contains fourteen generations according to Matthew and extends over 483 years. In it the times of the kings began, because youthful dignity is suitable for kingship [Note: “In which the times of the kings [began],” with an added qualification, “the dignity [of youth] is suitable.”].

The fifth age then extends to the coming of the Savior in the flesh, likewise through fourteen generations and over 588 years. In it, exhausted as if by oppressive old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly frequent evils.

The sixth age, which is now taking place, has no definite sequence of generations or times, but will end, like decrepit old age, with the death of the whole world. Ages consist of generations. They are called “ages” because they follow one another. As some pass away and others succeed them, their course is written through generations and kingdoms.

The first age contains the creation of the world. On the first day God created the angels under the name of light. On the second he created the heavens under the designation of the firmament. On the third, under the term “separation,” he made the forms of the waters and the earth. On the fourth, the lights of heaven. On the fifth, living creatures from the water. On the sixth, living creatures from the earth, and the first human being, Adam.

In his 130th year Adam fathered Seth, from whom came the sons of God. In his 105th year Seth fathered Enos, who began to call upon the name of the Lord. In his 90th year Enos fathered Cainan. In his 70th year Cainan fathered Mahalaleel, whose name means “planting of the Lord” [Col. 0450D]. In his 72nd year Mahalaleel fathered Jared. In his 162nd year Jared fathered Enoch. We learn, on the testimony of the apostle Jude, that Enoch wrote certain divine things [Note: “We have learned this from Bede, *On the Six Ages*, and he consulted the same source in what follows.].”

In his 65th year Enoch fathered Methuselah; after his birth Enoch was translated by God. In his 187th year Methuselah fathered Lamech. Giants were born. The sons of God—that is, of Seth—desired the daughters of men—that is, of Cain. In his 182nd year Lamech [Col. 0452A] fathered Noah, who built the ark. In Noah’s 600th year the Flood came. From Adam to the cataclysm, that is, the Flood, there were 1,656 years.

The second age contains 292 years. In the second year after the Flood, Shem fathered Arphaxad, from whom came the Chaldeans. In his 35th year Arphaxad fathered [Note: An addition reads: “Cainan. Cainan, in his 130th year, fathered …”] Shelah, from whom came the Samaritans and Indians. In his 30th year Shelah fathered Heber, from whom came the Hebrews [Note: The manuscript has 130; the number 4 and Isidore have 130, but Bede has 30.]. In his 34th year Heber fathered Peleg. The tower was being built. In his 30th year Peleg fathered Reu. Gods were first worshiped. In his 32nd year Reu fathered Serug [Note: Reu is elsewhere called Ragau.]. The kingdom of the Scythians began. In his 30th year Serug fathered Nahor. The kingdom of the Egyptians arose. In his 39th year Nahor fathered Terah. The kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians arose. In his 70th year Terah fathered Abraham. Semiramis founded Babylon, and Zoroaster discovered magic. From Adam to Abraham there were 1,947 years.

The third age contains 942 years. In his 75th year Abraham came into the land of Canaan at God’s command. In his 86th year Abraham fathered Ishmael, from whom came the Ishmaelites. In his 100th year Abraham fathered Isaac. In his 60th year Isaac fathered Jacob. In his 90th year Jacob fathered Joseph. Memphis was founded in Egypt. Joseph lived 110 years. Greece began to possess grain crops. The Hebrews were enslaved in Egypt for 147 years, and Cecrops founded Athens.

Moses ruled Israel for 40 years; under him the Hebrews began to possess writing. Joshua ruled Israel for 26 years. Erichthonius was the first in Greece to yoke a four-horse chariot. Judges ruled from Moses to Samuel for 305 years.

Othniel ruled for 40 years. Cadmus, king of the Thebans, discovered the Greek letters. Ehud ruled for 80 years. Amphion the musician flourished. Deborah, for 40 years. Picus was the first to reign over the Latins. Apollo also discovered medicine. Gideon, for 40 years. Orpheus and Linus, musicians, flourished. Abimelech, for 3 years. He killed his 70 brothers. Tola, for 30 years. Priam reigned in Troy. Jair, for 22 years. Carmentis discovered the Latin letters. Jephthah [Col. 0452C], for 6 years. Hercules threw himself into the flames. Abessa, for 7 years. The ten-year war of Troy began. Elon, for 10 years. He is not found in the Septuagint. Labdo, for 8 years. After Troy was captured, Aeneas came to Italy [Note: An addition reads: “Here he perished by lightning. On the Greek side 877 were killed; on the Trojan side, 686.”].

Samson, for 20 years. Ascanius founded Alba. Eli the priest, for 40 years. The Ark of the Covenant was captured, and the kingdom of the Sicyonians came to an end. Samuel and Saul, for 32 years. The kingdom of the Lacedaemonians arose, and Homer is shown to have existed.

The fourth age contains 473 years. David reigned for 40 years. Carthage was founded by Dido. Gath, Nathan, and Asaph prophesied. Solomon, for 40 years. The Temple was built at Jerusalem, when 480 years from the Exodus out of Egypt had been completed. From this it is clear that Samuel and Saul ruled for 32 years, not 40.

Rehoboam reigned for 17 years. The kingdom of Israel and Judah was divided. Abijah, for 3 years. The high priest Abimelech was renowned.

[Col. 0452D] Asa, for 41 years. Haggai, Amos, Joel, and Jehu prophesied, as did Azariah. Jehoshaphat, for 25 years. Elijah, Elisha, Obadiah, and Micah prophesied. Joram, for 8 years. Edom withdrew from Judah and appointed a king for itself. Ahaziah, for 1 year. Elijah was taken up. Athaliah, for 7 years. Jonadab, son of Rechab, was distinguished as a priest. Joash, for 40 years. Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, was stoned. Amaziah, for 28 years. The prophet Amos flourished in Israel. Uzziah, for 52 years. The first Olympic festival was established by the Greeks.

[Col. 0454A] Jotham, for 16 years. Isaiah, Hosea, and Joel prophesied, and Romulus was born. Ahaz, for 16 years. Rome was founded, and Israel was transferred to the Medes. Hezekiah, for 29 years. Romulus appointed 100 senators.

Manasseh, for 55 years. Numa added two months, and the Samian Sibyl flourished. Amon, for 2 years. Tullus carried out a census in the republic. Josiah, for 31 years. Thales the natural philosopher flourished. Jehoiakim, for 11 years. In his third year Nebuchadnezzar captured Judaea. Zedekiah, for 11 years. The Temple at Jerusalem was burned.

From the beginning of the world to the end of the Jewish kingdom there were 3,363 years.

The fifth age contains 588 years. The captivity of the Hebrews lasted 70 years. The history of Judith was written. Darius, for 36 years. In his second year the Temple at Jerusalem was built, when the 70 years of the Jewish captivity had been completed. Xerxes, for 21 years. The historiographer Herodotus is recognized. Artaxerxes, for 40 years. Ezra renewed the burned Law, and Nehemiah restored Jerusalem.

Darius, also called Nothus, for 19 years. This age had Plato. Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, for 26 years. Demosthenes and Aristotle are praised. Xerxes, son of Ochus, for 4 years. Xenocrates flourished. Darius, for 6 years.

Alexander of Macedon, for 12 years; he captured Jerusalem. Up to this point was the kingdom of the Persians; thereafter, that of the Greeks. In his fifth year Alexander obtained Asia.

Ptolemy, son of Lagus, for 40 years. The First Book of the Maccabees began. Philadelphus, for 38 years. The Seventy translators flourished. Euergetes, for 26 years. Jesus composed the Book of Wisdom. Philopator, for 17 years. The Second Book of the Maccabees began. Epiphanes, for 24 years. The Romans gained possession of the Greeks. Philometor, for 35 years. Antiochus defeated him and oppressed the Jews. Scipio also conquered Africa.

Euergetes, for 29 years. Brutus subdued Spain. Soter, for 17 years. The Thracians were subjected to the Romans. Varro and Cicero were born. Alexander, for 10 years. Syria was subjected to the Romans through Gabinius. Ptolemy, son of Cleopatra, for 8 years. The historiographer Sallust was born. Dionysius, for 30 years. Pompey captured Judaea. Cleopatra, for 2 years. Egypt was subjected to the Romans.

Up to this point was the kingdom of the Greeks; thereafter, that of the Romans.

Julius Caesar, for 5 years. He was the first to hold the monarchy, and from him the emperors were called Caesars.

Octavian, for 56 years. In his forty-second year our Lord Jesus Christ was born, when, according to Jerome, 5,199 years had been completed from Adam.

Tiberius Augustus, for 23 years. In his eighteenth year our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified.

Gaius, for 4 years. Matthew wrote the Gospel.

Claudius, for 14 years. Peter went to Rome and Mark to Alexandria.

Nero, for 14 years. Peter and Paul were delivered to the cross and the sword [Note: An addition reads: “Lucan and Josephus flourished. Galba and Piso, 7 months. Otho killed them, for 3 months; he killed himself. Vitellius, 8 months; Vespasian killed him.”].

Vespasian, for 10 years. In his second year Titus overthrew Jerusalem and leveled the Temple to the ground, 1,189 years after its first construction, in the 71st year of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Col. 0456B] Titus, for 2 years. He was eloquent and pious.

Domitian, for 16 years. The apostle John was exiled to Patmos.

Nerva, for 1 year. John returned to Ephesus and wrote the Gospel.

[Col. 0456C] Trajan, for 19 years. Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified, and the apostle John fell asleep.

Hadrian, for 21 years. Aquila the translator arose.

Antoninus Pius, for 24 years. Valentinian and Marcion were recognized as heretics.

Antoninus the younger, for 19 years. Montanus, author of the Cataphrygian heresy, arose.

[Col. 0456D] Commodus, for 13 years. Theodotion the translator appeared.

[Col. 0458A] Aelius Pertinax, for 1 year. He has nothing belonging to history.

Severus Pertinax, for 18 years. Symmachus the translator is recognized.

Antonius Caracalla, for 7 years. The fifth edition is found at Jerusalem.

Macrinus, for 1 year; or Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, for 4 years. The sixth edition is found at Nicopolis, and the unhappy Sabellius arose.

Alexander, for 13 years. Origen flourished at Alexandria.

Maximian or Maximus, for 3 years. He persecuted the Christians.

Gordian, for 7 years. Fabian flourished as bishop of Rome.

[Col. 0458B] Philip, for 7 years. He was the first Christian emperor.

Decius, for 1 year. Antony the monk arose.

Gallienus and his son Volusian, for 2 years. The Novatian heresy arose.

Valerian with Gallienus, for 5 years. Cyprian and Cornelius were crowned with martyrdom.

Claudius, for 2 years. He expelled the Goths from Illyricum.

Aurelian, for 5 years. He too persecuted the Christians.

Tacitus, for 1 year.

Probus, for 6 years. The Manichaean heresy arose.

Carus, for 2 years. He triumphed over the Persians.

Diocletian and Maximian, for 20 years. After burning the divine books, they ordered the churches to be devastated and the Christians to be afflicted and killed.

Maximinus, son of Maximian, Severus, and Galerius, for 1 year.

Constantine, for 31 years. In his sixteenth year the Council of Nicaea assembled, in the year 318 of the Lord’s incarnation.

Constantius and Constans, for 27 years. The relics of Saint Andrew and of Saint Luke the Evangelist were transferred to Constantinople, and the heresy of the anthropomorphites arose. At the same time Athanasius, Maximinus, archbishop of Trier, and Hilary were regarded as distinguished in doctrine and faith.

Julian, for 2 years. Having been made a pagan from a monk, he persecuted the Christians.

Jovian, for 1 year. He became a Christian with his entire army.

Valentinian, for 11 years; Julian had deprived him of military service because of his faith in Christ. The Goths also became heretics.

Gratian with his brother Valentinian, for 6 years. Ambrose and Martin were distinguished bishops.

Valentinian with Theodosius, for 9 years. Jerome flourished at Bethlehem and throughout the whole world.

Theodosius, for 11 years. Saint John the anchorite flourished.

[Col. 0460A] Arcadius with his brother Honorius, for 13 years [Note: An addition reads: “He transferred the sacred bones of the prophet Samuel from Judaea to Thrace.”]. John Chrysostom and Augustine flourished as bishops.

Honorius with the younger Theodosius, for 15 years. Cyril flourished as bishop of Alexandria.

Theodosius the younger, son of Arcadius, for 26 years. The Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorius and his Pelagian supporters under Pope Celestine.

Marcian, for 7 years. The Council of Chalcedon was held under Pope Leo, with 630 fathers.

Leo the elder with Leo the younger, for 17 years. Egypt was freed from the error of Dioscorus.

Zeno, for 17 years. The body of the apostle Barnabas was discovered, and the Acephali heresy arose.

Anastasius, for 26 years. Fulgentius flourished as a bishop.

[Col. 0460B] Justin the elder, for 9 years. The Acephali heresy was renounced.

Justinian, for 39 years. In his sixth year the first cycle of Dionysius began, in the year 532 of the Lord’s incarnation.

Justin the younger, for 2 years. The Armenians accepted the faith of Christ.

Tiberius, for 6 years. Erminigild, king of the Goths, was crowned with martyrdom.

Maurice, for 21 years. Pope Gregory sent Augustine the archbishop with monks to Britain to evangelize the word of God to the people of the Angles, in the year 596 of the Lord’s incarnation.

Phocas, for 8 years. The Anglo-Saxons accepted the faith of Christ.

[Col. 0460C] Heraclius, for 36 years. The Jews in Spain became Christians.

Heraclonas with his mother Martina, for 2 years. Pyrrhus, bishop of the imperial city, was condemned by Pope Theodore.

Constantine, son of Heraclius, for 6 months. Paul, Pyrrhus’s successor, was condemned for the same insane doctrine.

Constantine, son of Constantine, for 17 years. He convened the Sixth Synod. At his request Pope Agatho sent his legates to the imperial city; among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward a bishop, for the purpose of bringing about the unity of the holy Church.

This Sixth Synod was held at Constantinople. One hundred and fifty bishops were present, with George presiding as patriarch of the imperial city and Macarius as bishop of Antioch. Those who asserted that Christ had one will and one operation were convicted of having falsified very many statements of the Catholic fathers.

King Tagobert of the Franks built the monastery at Wissembourg in the year of the Lord 623, in the twenty-third year of his reign. Thus far Bede.

(For the continuation, see column 466.)

# FIRST PART: YEARS 702–829

[Col. 0465]

# THE ANNALS OF QUEDLINBURG

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD’S INCARNATION

702. 703. 704. 705.

706.

707.

708. King Conrad went from Britain to Rome. There he was tonsured and became a monk, and remained in fasts and prayers until his last day. In the same year Druogo died.

709. A harsh season and failing crops.

710. King Pippin went into Alamannia.

711. The waters overflowed greatly.

712. Death of Heribert, king of the Lombards.

713.

714. Death of King Pippin, who was the son of Ansegisus. After him his son Charles reigned.

715. Battle of the Franks, and the death of King Dagobert.

716. Charles fought against King Ratbod.

717. Charles fought against the Franks on the Sunday before Easter.

718. Charles devastated Saxony with a plague.

719. Slaughter of the Franks at the city of Soissons, and the death of King Ratbod.

720. Charles fought against the Saxons.

721.

722 (721). Great abundance occurred.

723.

724.

725 (724). The Saracens first entered Italy [Note: Not at all; rather, Burgundy.].

726.

727. Saint Egbert migrated to Christ.

728.

729. Comets appeared.

730.

731. Charles devastated the region beyond the Loire, and Ragenfrid died.

732. Charles fought against the Saracens on Saturday.

733. An eclipse of the sun occurred.

734. Charles went into Frisia.

[Col. 0469] 735. Charles devastated the Gascons. Bede, the noble presbyter and distinguished teacher, died.

736. Beginning of the monastery of Herolfesfeld. Bishop Audoin died.

737. Charles fought against the Saracens in Gaul.

738. Charles entered Saxony again and made the Saxons tributary.

739. Charles entered Provence as far as Marseille.

740. Peace without any hostility.

741. Charles, son of Pippin, died. After him his sons Carloman and Pippin reigned.

742.

743.

744. Beginning of the monastery of Fulda.

745.

746. Carloman entered Alamannia. Saint Burcard was ordained the first bishop in Würzburg. In the same year Saint Wigbert migrated to Christ.

747. Carloman, proceeding to Rome, was tonsured, leaving the kingdom to his brother.

748. Grifo fled into Saxony.

749. Grifo returned from Saxony.

750. By decree of Pope Zacharias, Pippin was proclaimed king through the anointing of Saint Boniface, archbishop; and Childeric, falsely called king, was tonsured and sent back to a monastery.

751. Landfrid died.

752. Grifo died.

[Col. 0471] 753. Pope Stephen came to Pippin in Francia and sought protection against King Haistulf.

754. Pope Stephen anointed Pippin’s two sons, Charles and Carloman, as kings.

755. Archbishop Boniface was crowned with martyrdom for the name of Christ; Lull succeeded him.

756.

757. Organs came to Francia.

758. After defeating the Saxons, Pippin imposed tribute on them, requiring them to pay 300 horses each year.

759.

760. Pippin came into Wasconia.

761. 762. 763.

764. A severe winter.

765.

766.

767.

768. King Pippin acquired the whole of Aquitaine, and Wifarius was killed. In the same year, King Pippin, returning from Aquitaine to Saint-Denis, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, leaving the kingdom to his sons Carloman and Charles, who is called “the Great.”

769.

770. In this year Bertrada, Charles’s mother, brought into Francia the daughter of Desiderius, king of Italy.

771. Charles’s brother Carloman died, leaving the kingdom to his brother Charles the Great.

772. In Saxony Charles stormed Heresburg and overthrew their shrine, which is called Irminsul.

773. Invited by Pope Hadrian, Charles entered Italy and besieged King Desiderius at Pavia.

774. Charles captured Pavia and led King Desiderius to Francia. In the same year the Saxons, filling with wood and fire the church at Frideslar which Saint Boniface had built and dedicated, wanted to burn it; but they were completely unable to do so.

775. Charles captured Siburg and defeated the Saxons in battle near Brunesberg; afterward they massacred the Franks in their camp near Lidbiki. But near Ovaccram, Hessi came humbly to meet the king with his men.

776. The Saxons, having become Christians, were subjected to Frankish rule. But first they captured Heresburg, killing the king’s soldiers who were inside.

777. Charles held a public assembly at Paderborn.

778. While Charles was fighting against the Saracens, the Saxons ravaged Longana and from there Duccia and Confluencia, committing many crimes in the churches of God and against nuns.

779. Charles fought and defeated the Saxons near Bocholt.

780. Charles ordered the Saxons to be baptized between the confluence of the Ara [Note: [Col. 0473] That is, the Ora.] and the Elbe.

781. Charles proceeded to Rome, and there his son Carloman was baptized; Pope Hadrian, changing his name, called him Pippin. There also his daughter Ruodrud was betrothed to the emperor Constantine. In the same year [Note: [Col. 0473] A.D. 780. Annals of Lorsch, p. 31.] Charles returned from Rome to Francia, divided the land of the Saxons among the bishops, and established the bishops’ boundaries. He also built a monastery for Saint Stephen the protomartyr at a place called Seligenstadt; it was later transferred to a place called Halberstadt, where the episcopal see now is. He entrusted it for correction and extension to Hildegrim, bishop of Châlons, who was the brother of Blessed Liudger the confessor. He established the boundaries of this bishopric as the rivers Elbe, Saale, and Unstrut; the ditch near Groningen; the height of the forest called the Harz; the Ocker, Schunter, Dasanek, Drichterbiki, Aller, the marsh of Isunna, which separates the Bardengau and the Hüttengau [Note: [Col. 0473] In which is Wittenberg.]; the Ara, Milda, Bima, and Precekinna, and again the Elbe.

782. Widukind, together with the Saxons, killed four of Charles’s prefects and his entire army, except for a few who escaped, at a place called Suntel.

783. Queen Hildegard died, and the king married Fastrada in her place. The king’s mother Bertrada died. (784.) Charles fought against the Saxons at Thiatmelli and again near the river Hase.

784 (785). Charles entered Saxony through Thuringia, ravaging those who rebelled against him as far as the estate called Scheninge; meanwhile his son Charles fought against the Westphalians in the district called Dreini.

785. Thereafter the king remained in Saxony with his army for the whole year and ordered the Saxons to supply the army with everything necessary. Then the king returned to Attigny and ordered Widukind, who until then had remained rebellious against him, and Abbo, together with their companions, to be baptized at the same royal estate after they had given hostages. When they had been baptized, all Saxony was subjected to Lord Charles. The conspiracy of Count Hardrad and the eastern Franks was wisely suppressed.

[Col. 0475] 786. Charles proceeded to Italy and from there to Rome. A solar eclipse occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, from the first hour of the day until the fifth hour. Many signs are also reported to have appeared at the same time. For the sign of the cross appeared on people’s garments. Archbishop Lull died, and Richolf succeeded him.

787. Charles brought almost all Calabria and Apulia under his authority.

788. Charles reached the borders of Bavaria through Alamannia, and Duke Tassilo of the Bavarians was expelled from his rule and tonsured for his infidelity; likewise his son Thiado. Both were made monks.

789. Charles subdued the people of the Wiltzi, who are called Lutici, after building two bridges over the river Elbe.

790. Fire consumed the palace at Worms.

791. Charles subdued the people of the Avars, that is, the Huns. Charles had four sons: first Charles, then Pippin, king of Italy; Louis, king of Aquitaine; and Drogo, bishop of the church of Metz. This Pippin who had conspired against him was his son by a mother of obscure origin, not the king Pippin.

792. Pippin’s conspiracy against his father Charles was made public through Fardulf. For this reason Pippin himself was tonsured and confined in a monastery, while all the others were punished: some were beheaded, others hanged on the gallows. Charles entrusted the monastery of Saint-Denis to Fardulf as a reward.

793. The Saxons rebelled again, abandoning the faith.

794. The Felician heresy was condemned at the synod held at Frankfurt. Queen Fastrada died, and the king married Liutgard in her place. His namesake also fought against the Saxons at Sinadevelde.

795. Charles came with his army to Bardenwick.

796. Pope Hadrian of Rome died, and Leo succeeded him. Charles also ravaged Saxony.

797. Charles again invaded Saxony with his army and spent the entire winter at Heristal.

798. Charles struck down with great slaughter the Nordalbingians [Note: [Col. 0475] Read “Nordlindos.”], the killers of his envoys.

799. Pope Leo, whose tongue had been cut out and who had been blinded by the Romans and expelled from the pontificate, came to Charles in Saxony, seeing and speaking, at the place called Paderborn. The king received him honorably, ordered him to be brought back to Rome, and commanded that all his possessions be restored to him. In the same year Gherald, the distinguished margrave of Bavaria, and Eric, duke of Friuli, were killed by the Huns.

800. When Charles had come to the city of Tours, his excellent wife Liutgard died there. Returning from there to Francia, he proceeded to Rome to avenge Pope Leo.

801. On Christmas Day, at Mass, Charles was crowned by Pope Leo and was called emperor and Augustus by the Romans, with the title of patrician removed.

802. Aaron, king of the Persians, subjected Jerusalem to Charles [Note: [Col. 0477] From Einhard’s Life of Charles and from the poet Saxo.] and sent him one elephant.

803. After holding an assembly at the palace of Salz, Charles restored the Saxons to their ancient freedom and, in order that they might preserve the Catholic faith, released them from every tribute, except that he ordered all of them, rich and poor alike, faithfully to render to Christ and his priests the tithes of all their cultivation and livelihood.

804. Pope Leo came again to Francia. Charles transferred the Transalbian Saxons and those who lived in the territory of Wimadi to Francia, and gave their districts to the Obodrites.

805. Charles, son of Charles, ravaged the Bohemians with the Franks and Saxons. After killing their king, named Lecho, he returned victorious to his father.

806. Charles divided the kingdom among his three sons, Pippin, Louis, and Charles.

807. A very great mortality occurred at Fulda.

808. Charles the Younger, having conquered the Lini and the Smeldingi, returned victorious to his father.

809. The commemoration (depositio) of Saint Liudger, bishop and confessor [Note: [Col. 0477] Q. Thus manuscript L; “confession” in manuscript 1.].

810. In this year the fortress of Haboki was built on the river Elbe, and Pippin, son of the emperor Charles and king of Italy, died on the eighth day before the Ides of July, leaving the kingdom to his son Bernard. Charles’s daughter Ruotrud also died.

811. Charles, son of the emperor Charles, the eldest and most favored of his father’s sons, died on the second day before the Nones of December.

812. There was a solar eclipse after midday.

813. A bridge near Mainz suddenly burned in a fire in May. Archbishop Richolf died, and Hastulf succeeded him. The emperor also made his son Louis his associate in the whole empire by placing a crown upon him.

814. The great emperor Charles and apostle of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0479] The poet Saxo.] died on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his reign, and the fourteenth of his empire. His son Louis, who is called the Pious, succeeded him in the kingdom.

[Col. 0480] 815. On the advice of the bishops, Louis ordered all monks to sing the cursus of Saint Benedict.

816. Emperor Louis held a great synod at Aachen, and there established the rule of the canons.

817. The conspiracy of Bernard, his cousin, against King Louis.

818. Emperor Louis ordered Bernard, king of Italy and son of his brother Pippin, to be blinded. Then, overcome with remorse, he performed public penance. His wife Irmingard also died on the fifth day before the Nones of October. A solar eclipse occurred on the eighth day before the Ides of July. The basilica at Fulda was dedicated.

819. Emperor Louis married Judith, daughter of Welf.

820. In this year an unhealthy condition of the air brought pestilence upon human beings and beasts and consumed nearly all the crops.

821.

822.

823. Emperor Louis appointed his brother Drogo bishop of the church of Metz. The monastery of New Corbie was begun.

824. In the territory of Toul, a girl of twelve years, after the Eucharist which she had received at Easter, abstained first from bread and then from all food and drink for a full three years [Note: [Col. 0479] From Einhard’s Annals, under the year 825.]. In Saxony, in the district of Virsedi, lightning consumed twenty-six estates. In the territory of Autun, an enormous fragment of ice fell together with hail; it is said to have been fifteen feet long, seven feet wide, and two feet thick.

825. Archbishop Haistolf died, and Othger succeeded him.

[Col. 0484] 826.

827. The elderly Bishop Hildegrim died [Note: [Col. 0484] Of Halberstadt.]. Thiatgrim succeeded him.

828.

829. The precious bodies of Saints Valens and Senesius came to the island of Reichenau on the fifth day before the Ides of April.

# Annals of Weissenburg

[Col. 0465]

## In the Year of the Lord’s Incarnation

702. 703. 704. 705.

706.

707. [Note: [Col. 0465] W. “Pippin, son of Ansegisus, mayor of the palace, for twenty-seven years,” added by a later hand that inserted the succession of kings.]

708. King Cunrad of Britain proceeded to Rome, where he was tonsured and made a monk; in fasts and prayers he reached his final day. In the same year Drogo died.

709. The crop was hard and failing.

710. King Pippin proceeded into Alamannia.

711. [Note: [Col. 0467] “Tiberius, also called Absimarus, for seven years,” by the same later hand.] The waters rose greatly.

712. Heribert, king of the Lombards, died.

713.

714. King Pippin died; after him his son Charles reigned for twenty-seven years.

715. King Dagobert died, and there was a battle of the Franks.

716. King Charles fought against King Ratbod.

Codex 3 has the following instead: “706. Tagebert, the most Christian king of the Franks, built a monastery at Erfurt, on the mountain anciently called Merwigisburg, after Merwigo, a pagan king of the Franks, who was the son of Merwig, prince of Thuringia, and the great-great-grandfather of that same [Col. 0466] King Tagebert. After erasing the pagan name of the city and mountain, he named it Saint Peter’s Mountain, and there established monastic life just as he had previously done at Selsenburg, at the request of Adeodatus the recluse, who in the time of that same king had been enclosed beside the church of Saint Blaise, which stood above the aforesaid city, by Rigibert, bishop of Mainz. # Annals of Hildesheim

[Col. 0479]

815. In the third year of Louis, a great council was held at Aachen in the month of August, and it was ordered that all the monks should sing the cursus of Saint Benedict according to the regular order. Two books were written that year, one concerning the life of clerics and the other concerning the life of nuns. In that year Pope Leo died, and Stephen was ordained in his place to the episcopate of the Roman Church. In the month of October he came to the emperor Louis at the city of Reims and returned in peace. Bicgo, one of the king’s friends, who had married the emperor’s daughter, named Elpheid, also died at that time.

816. In the fourth year Louis the emperor held his assembly with the Franks at the palace of Aachen in the month of June. After a fast had been proclaimed, his son Lothar was ordained emperor, so that he might become his father’s associate in the kingdom. In that year Pope Stephen died, and Paschal succeeded him in the pontificate.

817. Bernard also, king of Italy, raised a sedition against the emperor; and Louis Augustus proceeded into Italy with an army.

818. In the sixth year of Emperor Louis, that is, in the year 818 of the Lord’s Incarnation, he defeated King Mormannus in Britain.

819. In the seventh year of his reign the emperor married Judith, daughter of Welf; and the basilica of the monastery of Fulda was dedicated. After this he rested for four years, and nothing historical occurred.

820.

821.

822.

823.

824. In the twelfth year of the emperor’s reign, that is, in the year 824 of the Lord’s Incarnation, a second expedition was undertaken against King Wiomarcus, and he ravaged Britain.

825. In the thirteenth year of the emperor, Wiomarcus was killed in his own house by the men of Landbert; and Archbishop Heistolf died.

[Col. 0483] 826. In the fourteenth year of Louis, Abbot Hiltwin transferred the bones of Saint Sebastian to Gaul.

827. In the fifteenth year of the emperor and the year 827 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the Saracens ravaged the territories of Barcelona and Girona.

913. Otto, the foremost of the dukes, from whom, as from a most fruitful stock, that imperial line of the Ottos—destined to benefit the whole of Europe’s boundaries in no small measure—sprang, cast off the burden of his earthly clay. Lady Oda, namely his mother, died in the 107th year of her life. Otto, the future king and emperor, was born.

914.

915.

916. The Hungarians, after devastating Saxony and plundering everything around them, came as far as Fulda.

918. Bishop Einhardus [Note: [Col. 0496] Perhaps of Speyer.] was killed.

919. As King Conradus lay dying, he—commended above all others not by the claims of kinship but by the duties of unconquered loyalty and outstanding virtue—resolved that Heinricus should succeed him and happily possess the scepters and kingdom. Having duly arranged everything, he entered the way of all flesh.

920. After the death of King Conradus, the aforesaid Heinricus, son of the duke of Saxony and lord of Francia, was elected and anointed king with the common consent of the senate and the people. How greatly he later prospered in victory by land and sea, and with what industry he governed his subjects at home and in war, is stated beyond the power of words and writing to express.

921. 922.

923. Sigismundus, bishop of Halberstadt, died. Bernhardus succeeded him in the episcopate, and his successor Hildewardus was born.

929. King Otto brought Edith, daughter of the king of the English, to Saxony to be joined to him in marriage.

[Col. 0500] 930. A fierce battle was fought against the Slavs beside the Elbe, near Lunkini, in which the Saxons won most gloriously: 120,000 Slavs were struck down, while 800 were led into captivity. On their own side, they lost two counts named Luthari, together with a few others, and many were wounded.

931. King Heinricus set out with his army [Note: [Col. 0500] Perhaps by a later hand.] against the Abodrites [Note: [Col. 0500] “Abodrite” is by the first hand.], subjecting them to himself.

932.

933. The army of the Hungarians was defeated by King Heinricus.

934. King Heinricus set out into Wucronin [Note: [Col. 0500] Perhaps by a second hand.], subjecting them to himself.

935.

936 (935). A great synod was held at Erphesfurt. (937.) King Heinricus died on the sixth day before the Nones of July; his son Otto, the peaceful one and ornament of Saxony, was chosen by hereditary right to succeed to his father’s kingdoms. The illustrious Queen Mechtild, after the death of her husband, namely the aforesaid King Heinricus, began, with holy devotion, to build a monastery on Quedeling Mountain, as he himself had previously decreed. She wished this to be a kingdom for the peoples and fostered it with all her strength. Since she knew that those well-born rarely and with great difficulty degenerate, she gathered not women of low status but young women of the highest nobility, properly destined to serve the canonical religious life; and, until the end of this fleeting life, she did not cease to nourish them in a motherly fashion with spiritual and bodily benefits.

937. Everhardus, duke of the Franks, Wigmannus the Saxon, and the wicked Thancmer conspired against the king with an empty agreement. But by God’s grace quickly revealing it to the king, that wicked conspiracy was wisely suppressed. For Tancmer was pitifully killed, while the others were mutilated and hanged. Everhardus was deprived of his honor and degraded; but Wigmannus, by supplicating at the king’s feet, was reconciled. At the same time the Hungarians came, devastated Thuringia, and then entered Saxony, where they perished in the marshes and other difficulties. Another part of the accursed army returned in flight to its own land. In the same year Hildebertus, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Fridericus succeeded him.

938. Count Eburhardus seized Heinricus, son of King Heinricus, and threw him into chains.

939. In this year, while the king was in the upper regions of the Rhine River, Heinricus, the king’s brother, Eburhardus, duke of the Franks, and Gisilbrachtus, count of the Lotharingians, crossed the Rhine with a wicked army they had assembled and devastated the greater part of the kingdom. When they returned rejoicing, the king’s friend Udo was informed. He attacked them with his men as they were returning and killed Eburhardus on the riverbank in a hostile manner, as he deserved. Gisilbrecht, however, was submerged in a brief whirlpool of the river, and those who were with him perished with him. His brother Heinricus, having obtained helpers and supplicating the king, recovered the king’s favor.

940. The church of Gandersheim was dedicated.

941. After King Otto had escaped the ambush of the conspirators against him, he immediately ordered, at Easter in the city of Quedeling, certain men—whose names were Erik, Reinward, Varin, Ascheric, Bacco, and Hermon—to be killed, and others to be banished into exile.

942.

943.

944. The king of the Greeks sent gifts to King Otto [Note: [Col. 0500] By the second hand.].

[Col. 0504] 945.

946. Queen Edith, wife of the great King Otto, tasted the bitter cup of death, leaving behind her two children, Liudolfus and Liutgarde.

947. A privilege from Pope Agapetus was conveyed to the Quedlinburg community and to that of Saint Servatius [Note: [Col. 0503] By the second hand, the marriages of Liudolfus and Liutgarde [Col. 0504] in the year 949, and the birth of Mathild from the Continuation of Regino, were added.].

948. A synod was assembled at Eggilenheim, presided over by Marinus, the apostolic legate [Note: [Col. 0504] I have corrected “Maximus” of the first hand to “Marinus.”].

949. Duke Conradus took Liutgarde, daughter of King Otto and Edith, as his wife. In the same year, envoys of the Greeks came for a second time to King Otto with gifts.

950. A great war arose between the Bavarians and the Hungarians.

951. King Otto set out for Italy, accompanied by his son Liudolfus the Pious; by Conradus the Boldest, the king’s son-in-law; by Fridericus, archbishop of the church of Mainz; and by an innumerable multitude from his entire kingdom. There the most invincible King Otto acquired for marriage Queen Adelheid, beautiful in appearance, prudent in counsel, highly distinguished in every moral virtue, descended from the royal line of her ancestors and great-grandparents, and already widowed from her most illustrious husband, namely King Lotharius. With her counsel also, the kingdom of Lombardy, which had fallen to her by hereditary right, was brought under Otto’s dominion together with the tyrant Beringerus. In the same year Heinricus, son of Duke Heinricus, was born.

952.

953. A sufficiently bitter and exceedingly cruel dissension arose between Liudolfus, the king’s son, and his uncle Heinricus, with the king supporting his brother’s side. It continued for two years amid fires, killings, and devastations, and many perished, not only from the common people but also from the nobles. In this year Mainz was besieged, as was the fortress called Rosodal; and a great battle was fought in that place.

954. Fridericus, archbishop of the church of Mainz, died, a man of the greatest abstinence, approved in holy religion and learning; and Wilhelmus, the king’s son, succeeded him. Liutgarde, of royal descent, died.

955. King Otto, at great danger to himself and his men, struck down the Hungarians in a great and bloody slaughter. In that war, however, Duke Conradus was killed with many others. Heinricus, duke of the Bavarians and brother of King Otto, also died. The strong Duke Cono tasted death at the hands of the Hungarians. King Otto also engaged in an extremely dangerous battle against the Abodrites, whom Egbertus, his maternal uncle’s son, had gathered against him. Mechtild, a radiant jewel [Note: [Col. 0504] Q. Thus the second hand; the first has “perlucida,” “shining through.”], shone forth at her birth as the ornament of her people and the joy of all, from the midst of the imperial crown. Otwinus was ordained bishop.

956. Liudolfus, the king’s son, set out for Italy [Note: [Col. 0504] I have corrected the first hand’s “respexit” to “perrexit.”] and brought it under his rule.

[Col. 0508] 957. Liudolfus, son of King Otto, died in Italy; he was carried from there to Mainz and buried at Saint Alban.

958. The sign of the cross appeared on people’s garments. To those who held it in mockery, it brought death; to those who venerated it piously and religiously, it caused no harm.

959.

960. Envoys of the people of Rus came to King Otto and begged him to send one of his bishops to show them the way of truth. They declared that they wished to abandon paganism and accept the name and religion of Christianity. He agreed to their request and sent Bishop Adalbertus, a man of the Catholic faith. But they lied in every respect, as the outcome later proved, since even the aforesaid bishop did not escape deadly danger from their ambushes.

961. Envoys of Pope John came, summoning him to Rome.

962.

832. Ludowicus, son of the emperor, in the twentieth year of his reign, conspired against his father at Longobardonheim [Note: [Col. 0483] Lampertheim. SS. T. I. 425.].

845. In this year the monks of Herolfesfeld were reconciled with Bishop Otgarius; and in the same year Emperor Ludowicus came to that same monastery on the second day before the Kalends of November, granted privileges and immunities to the monks, and confirmed them with his seal [Note: [Col. 0483] Hludowicus should be read. This passage was thus corrupted when inserted into the twelfth-century Annals of Corvey.].

[Col. 0487] 846. Ludowicus, son of Ludowicus, conquered Pannonia and, returning home, devastated the Bohemians.

951. King Otto went to Italy, and with him his son Liudulf, Duke Conrad, and Frithuric, archbishop of the church of Mainz. There King Otto took Queen Adalheid into partnership with himself, and subdued Berengar, king of the Lombards, to himself.

952.

953. A sufficiently bitter and exceedingly cruel conflict arose between Liudulf, the king’s son, and his uncle Henry, while the king himself supported his brother’s party. It continued for two years amid burnings, killings, and devastations, and many perished, not only from the common people but also from the nobles. In this year Mainz was also besieged, as was the fortress called Rossadal [Note: [Col. 0503] Rossthal, in the district of Cadolzburg, in the Radenz district of Bavaria. See the distinguished Wedekind, Notes I, 28.]; and a great battle took place at that place.

954. Frithuric, archbishop of the church of Mainz, died—a man of the highest abstinence, approved in holy religion and learning—and Willihelmus, the king’s son, succeeded him in his office. Bishop Thiothard, of pious memory, died; Otwinus succeeded him.

955. King Otto, at great risk to himself and his men, struck down the Hungarians in a great and bloody slaughter. In that battle, however, Duke Conrad, the king’s son-in-law, was killed together with many others. And Duke Henry of Bavaria, King Otto’s brother, died. In the same year King Otto engaged the Abodrites in an extremely dangerous battle [Note: [Col. 0503] H. Thus the manuscript; that is, “with the Abodrites.”], whom his maternal cousin Egberht had gathered against him.

956. Ruodbert, archbishop of Trier, and Hadamar, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, died. Henry, the bishop, and Hatto, the abbot, succeeded them. In the same year Liudulf, the king’s son, went to Italy and subdued it.

[Col. 0507] 957. Liudulf died in Italy; from there he was transported to Mainz and buried at Saint Alban’s.

958. The sign of the cross appeared on people’s garments, bringing death to those who held it in mockery; but it inflicted no harm on those who venerated it piously and religiously.

959. Abbot Hagono relinquished control of his office.

960. Envoys of the Russian people came to King Otto and entreated him to send one of his bishops who would show them the way of truth. They professed that they wished to abandon pagan practice and accept the religion of Christianity. He consented to their request and sent Bishop Adalbert, a Catholic in faith; but they lied to him in every respect, as the outcome later proved.

961. In this year envoys came to King Otto and summoned him to Rome to aid Pope John, so that he might mitigate the severity which King Adalbert had exercised over the realm.

962 (961). The apostolic man received him gladly and seated him honorably upon the throne of imperial authority; he increased the imperial blessing over him, so that he might be called and be Emperor Augustus. (962.) Abbot Gunther died; Egillolfus succeeded him.

963. In this year a great synodal council was held at Rome in the church of Saint Peter. Emperor Otto Augustus presided there, with a great multitude of bishops, abbots, monks, and [Note: [Col. 0507] H. m. “provosts”; cl. Sazaw.] clerics. Pope Benedict was deposed from the apostolic see because he had unjustly claimed the dignity of the Roman Empire. He was entrusted to Archbishop Adaldag and taken to Saxony, where he ended his life. In that same year a severe mortality struck the emperor’s army, and in it Henry, archbishop of the city of Trier, and Duke Godefrid lost their lives, along with not a few others.

964. In this year King Berengar of the Lombards was besieged on Mount Saint Leo, captured there, and forcibly taken, together with his queen and consort Willa, to Bavaria, to the fortress of Bamberg, where he ended the final day of his present life [Note: [Col. 0508] In the year 966.].

965. Emperor Otto came from Lombardy to Frankfurt and remained that entire year in the Saxon kingdom. Meanwhile he gathered all his people together for peace and harmony. And Brun, archbishop of the city of Cologne and the emperor’s brother, ended his life in peace.

966. For the third time Emperor Otto went to Italy. From there he proceeded to the threshold of Saint Peter, and there, praying to God and Saint Peter and giving thanks, because everything concerning him was proceeding favorably.

967. In this year the emperor sent his envoys to Archbishop Willihelmus and to his other princes, so that they might advance Otto, his son and namesake, with all royal dignity to [Col. 0511] Italy. There Otto the elder received him and brought him with him to Rome. He commended him to the later apostolic John, so that he might receive from him the imperial blessing and be called Emperor Augustus by all who knew him, just as his father was.

968. Archbishop Willihelmus departed from this world. Egillulfus, abbot of Hersfeld, was sent from Italy on the emperor’s behalf so that the brothers of Fulda might elect Wirinharius as abbot. From there he went to Mainz, so that the clergy and the whole people might establish the venerable man Hatto as their lord in pontifical office. In the same year Adalbert was appointed archbishop of Magdeburg.

969. Archbishop Hatto died; Ruodbert succeeded him.

970. Abbot Egillulfus died; Gozbert succeeded him.

971. In this year the palace at Thornburg was burned.

972. The empress came from Constantinople to Rome to Otto the younger, the emperor, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, the octave of Easter. In the same year that same Otto the younger came from Italy with the elder.

973. The elder Emperor Otto came with the younger to Quedlinburg, and there they celebrated Easter on the tenth day before the Kalends of April. Envoys of the Greeks, Beneventans, Hungarians, Bulgarians, Danes, and Slavs came there to them with royal gifts. Not long afterward, the pious Emperor Otto the elder died on the Nones of May; Lord Otto succeeded him.

Up to this point the Annals of Hersfeld appear to have extended.

[Col. 0512]

## ANNALS OF QUEDLINBURG

974.

975.

976.

977.

978.

[Col. 0516] 979.

980.

981.

982.

983.

984. The emperor’s little son, namely Otto the third, was anointed king at Aachen on Christmas Day by John, archbishop of Ravenna. But afterward, when the emperor’s death became known, Henry, formerly duke, returning from exile, entered the city of Cologne with those who favored him. At first he pretended that, out of the right of kinship, he would faithfully support the party of the child king; he took possession of the king, and then, driven by the goads of increasing greed and enticed by the persuasion of certain men, he tyrannically invaded the kingdom. He went so far in his arrogance that he sought both to be called king and to be blessed as king. He achieved being called king by a few; but he did not deserve to be blessed as king, because God forbade it, and because the struggle of those of the faithful who did not consent to him, but rightly favored the elected and anointed king, prevented it [Note: [Col. 0515] “Although he kept the king in his own custody.” Chronicon Saxonicum. [Col. 0516] M.].

Meanwhile, approved envoys were sent [Col. 0515] to the king’s grandmother in Lombardy, namely to the august empress Adelheid. Those who had bound themselves by an oath firmly to persevere in aiding the king’s cause earnestly begged her, explaining the disturbance in due order, that, if she cared anything for the kingdom and her grandson, she should hasten to succor her own people by the aid of her arrival and counsel [Note: [Col. 0516] I have emended this thus; the first manuscript reads “with food.”] as quickly as possible.

Having first secured divine assistance for herself, she hastened her journey greatly, accompanied by her daughter-in-law, the empress Theophanu, the king’s mother; by her illustrious daughter, the abbess Machtilde, the aunt of that same child king; by her brother, King Conrad of Burgundy; and by the duke of the Franks, his namesake. The foremost men of all Italy, Gaul, Swabia, Francia, and Lotharingia accompanied them, as did the Saxons, Thuringians, and Slavs, together with all the nobles. With united efforts of spirit, they assembled at Roza [Note: [Col. 0519] “Rare” in Thietmar.], either prepared to die faithfully for the king or—as happened by God’s grace—to conquer [Note: [Col. 0519] “They assembled without delay, prepared to conquer bravely. Then, after a council had been held,” etc. Chr. S.].

After a very great council had been held there, a wondrous and memorable sign for posterity appeared: a brilliantly shining star radiated in the very midst of the conflict between the parties, at the center of the vault of heaven, in the middle of the day, contrary to custom, as though it were about to offer divine assistance to the captive king. All who were present saw it and marveled.

When it was seen, the unjust party immediately became terrified and withdrew. The aforementioned Henry, deprived by right of the usurped name and kingdom, was compelled to present the king to his grandmother, mother, and aunt. Through the intervention of his father-in-law, King Conrad, and the princes, he was granted some measure of favor; and he departed sadly for his homeland.

Having thus received their sole pledge, the imperial ladies went to Saxony. First they reached together the city rising upon the summit of the already-mentioned Quedlinburg hill. They were received with the greatest honor, amid the sweet-sounding melody of the praises of the clergy, the people, and the virgins serving Christ there, who came to meet them twice over, piously rejoicing in the arrival of their spiritual mother, for which they had longed, and in the king’s triumphant outcome. They passed over the remainder of the road with the highest honor [Note: [Col. 0520] Thus I have corrected it; the first manuscript reads “of life.”].

(Up to this point the continuation of the Annals of Hersfeld appears to have extended.)

985. The Saxons invaded Slavonia, and Misacho came to their aid with a great army. They devastated that entire land with fires and killings. Meanwhile, the aforementioned Henry, returning to himself through divine inspiration, repeatedly and anxiously reflecting upon what he had done, how far he had raised himself beyond what was right and honorable, and from how great a height he had fallen, saw himself humbled by his own exaltation, in accordance with the evangelical word of truth; he was stung by consciousness of his disgrace and tormented by repentance for his guilt.

When the child king Otto the Third came to Frankfurt, Henry himself also came there and humbled himself justly, in order to escape punishment for his unjust arrogance. In the presence of the imperial ladies who held the care of the kingdom—the king’s grandmother, mother, and aunt—he presented himself to the little king whom he had captured and deprived of his freedom, whose kingdom he had tyrannically invaded. Humbly in dress and humbly in conduct, before the sight of all the people, with both hands folded together, he did not blush to surrender himself as a soldier who would henceforth serve with true faith. He stipulated nothing except his life and asked for nothing except grace.

The ladies, whose care, as we have said, governed the kingdom and the king’s childhood, were exceedingly joyful at the submission of so great a man. For it is the custom of the pious not only not to return evil for good [Note: [Col. 0520] “Evil for evils,” Chr. Saxo.], but also to repay evil with good. They received him with fitting honor, granted him faithful favor, and likewise raised him to the dignity of duke. Thereafter, not only among their friends but even among their closest friends, as the right of kinship required, they honored him with the affection of due love.

The distinguished margraves Thidericus and Ricdach died.

986. King Otto, still a very small child, went with a great Saxon army into Slavonia. There Misacho came to him with a very large multitude and offered him a camel and many other gifts; he also submitted himself to Otto’s authority. Advancing together, they devastated that entire land with fires and widespread depredations.

[Col. 0521] In the same year, on the western Quedlinburg hill, the monastery in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, was most diligently built under the rule of Saint Benedict by Mechtilde, the imperial jewel and daughter, as a memorial to her only and beloved brother. Ida, the royal lady and wife of Liudolf, son of the great Emperor Otto, also died.

987. The Saxons invaded Slavonia again. Finally the Slavs themselves submitted to the king’s authority, and the fortresses beside the River Elbe were restored anew. In the following winter the waters flooded excessively, and a mighty wind laid many buildings low.

988. The fierce heat of summer consumed nearly all the crops. Soon a great mortality among human beings followed.

989. Comets appeared, followed by a great pestilence among people and animals, especially cattle. Bishop Osdag also died; Gerdagus succeeded him.

990. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, at the fifth hour of the day.

991. The empress Theophanu celebrated the Easter festival with imperial splendor at the city of Quedlinburg together with her son, the emperor Otto the Third. There also were present Hugh, margrave of Tuscany, and Misico, duke of the Slavs, along with the other leading men of Europe who had gathered there to pay the honor due to the emperor, bringing as gifts whatever each possessed that was most precious. Misico and many others among them, honorably rewarded, returned to their homeland.

Hugh, however, continued in attendance upon that same empress and her son wherever they traveled, whether advancing through or governing the kingdom, until they reached Nijmegen. There, having as it were gathered the whole empire together under her authority, the empress Theophanu, having completed the course of her life in good works, alas, a grievous thing to say, was carried off by an untimely death on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July. From there, accompanied by the emperor—namely, her son—and by the mournful procession of her other faithful servants, she was carried to the city of Cologne and, as she herself had ordained, was buried with the final lamenting honor in the church of the martyr Saint Pantaleon, surrounded by a company of bishops, monks, and virgins, with all the clergy and people also present.

In the same year Ercanbald [Note: [Col. 0523] E. “of Strasbourg,” Annalista Saxo.], Biligrimus, bishop, Frithuric, archbishop of Salzburg, and Emnild, the daughter of Bruno, died. Manogold also, a son of the noble mother of Swabia, died in Saxony. Because of the faithful service he had personally rendered to the empress Adelheid [Note: [Col. 0523] “Frequently,” Chr. Saxo.], he was brought to the city of Quedlinburg in her company and honorably buried there.

992. The most glorious and famous dedication of the church of holy Halberstadt took place on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, by its venerable guardian, Bishop Hildeward, in the twenty-fourth year of his ordination. Eleven bishops consecrated it with him, in the number twelve that signifies apostolic dignity: Willigisus, archbishop of Mainz; Gisilharius, archbishop of Magdeburg; Lievitzo, archbishop of Hamburg; Liudolf, bishop of Augsburg; Hildebold, bishop of Worms; Retharius, bishop of Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0523] Hilderic, bishop of Havelberg; Erp, etc., Chr. Halberstadense; certainly a name is missing.]; Erp, bishop of Verden; Ursus, bishop of Padua; Hug, bishop of Chur; and Raginbrat, bishop of Mecklenburg.

In addition, Agio, archbishop of Capua; Reinvard, bishop of Trent; Manso, abbot of Monte Cassino; Thiatmar, abbot of Corvey; Luzo [Note: [Col. 0523] That is, Liudericus.], abbot of Lüneburg; Othrad, abbot of Merseburg; and Lantbrecht Longhelus [Note: [Col. 0523] “Longensis,” Chr. Halb.] abbot, were present, together with the serene King Otto the Third, his illustrious grandmother Adelheid Augusta, and her daughter, the jewel and brilliant scion of the royal line [Note: [Col. 0523] Thus I correct it from the Chronicon Halberstadense; “brilliant” [Col. 0524] in the manuscript.], Machtilda [Note: [Col. 0524] Abbess of Quedlinburg.], and her venerable granddaughter Hadwi, abbess [Note: [Col. 0524] Of Gernrode; from the Chronicon Halberstadense.], as well as Duke Bernhard, Leidulf, count of Capua, many prefects and nobles, and an innumerable and incomparable multitude of clergy and people. They cried out in praise of God and assisted by prayer in dedicating the aforementioned church.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, the entire sky was seen to be red three times during the night. In this same year Gerdagus, bishop of Hildesheim, went to Rome for the sake of prayer and, on his return, died in Lombardy, together with his priest Suidebold, his deacon Bodo, his brother Hroprecht, and his chamberlain. Bishop Berward succeeded him.

993. On the night of the feast of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr—that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of January—we witnessed a miracle unheard of throughout the ages. Around the first cockcrow, such a light suddenly shone from the north that many said day was rising. It remained for one full hour; afterward, when the sky had reddened somewhat, it returned to its usual color.

Bishop Dodo [Note: [Col. 0524] Of Minden.] died; Suigerus, an illustrious man and a religious of the monastery of the holy church of Halberstadt, succeeded him. Egbert, archbishop of Trier, died.

[Col. 0527D] 994. Liuldolf was ordained bishop of the church of Trier. Erp, bishop of Verden, died; Bernhard succeeded him. A most severe winter began on the third day before the Nones of November and lasted until the third day before the Nones of May, interrupted by only a very few days. Then, with pestilential and cold winds blowing, winter cold fell on many nights instead of dew. Finally, on the Nones of July, a great frost occurred, and such a drought of the rivers and scarcity [Col. 0528D] of rain arose that in many ponds even the fish died, while on the land many trees completely withered, and crops and flax perished.

A great pestilence among people, pigs, cattle, and sheep also followed. In many places the meadows dried up as though they had been burned by fire. Moreover, all the Slavs except the Sorbs defected from the Saxons. Liutpold, the distinguished margrave of the Bavarian frontier, was unexpectedly wounded by an arrow through a window in his lodging in the city of Würzburg and died on the seventh day before the Nones of June.

Count Egbert, wiser than the wise and bolder than the brave, departed this life on the Nones of April. Henry, Sifridus, and Udo, brothers, fighting with their men in a naval battle against the Northmen, were defeated and captured. Among them, Udo and very many others were killed in battle; the rest were ransomed for seven thousand talents. A great famine also occurred this year in many places of Saxony.

995. A year worse than the previous one arose for the Saxons. For such a pestilence raged among those called Osterludi [Note: [Col. 0529D] That is, Ostfalahi.], that not only their houses but also many villages remained empty of their dead inhabitants.

Moreover, crushed by great hunger and worn out by the constant incursions of the Slavs, the prophetic saying seemed rightly to be spoken of them, as their sins deserved: “I will send upon them three most grievous judgments: pestilence, sword, and famine.”

King Otto the Third, invading the Abodrites and certain lands of the Wiltzow [Note: [Col. 0529D] That is, the Welatabri, the Wiltzi.] with a great army, ravaged them with many fires and plunderings, although he was in no way able to suppress their uprising.
