Finally, returning from that expedition, he was worthily received in the city of Quedlinburg by his aforementioned and ever-memorable aunt, the abbess Mechtilde, with royal praise.

There Adelheid, her sister—the namesake of her grandmother, the empress Adelheid—rejecting royal suitors and their envoys, as well as promises not only of treasures but even of mountains of gold and cities beyond all measure [Col. 0529C], dedicated herself to living canonically under the yoke of the rule, in the presence of her brother, the emperor Otto the Third, before the sight of the entire senate and people, to the service of Saints Dionysius and Servatius as a sacrifice for her homeland. At that same hour, as a pledge of the sacred veil, she was consecrated to Christ, her heavenly bridegroom, by Hildeward, the bishop of that church, while the other archbishops and bishops also stood present.

In this same year Duke Henry the Second of the Bavarian region died an untimely death. After the death of Emperor Otto the Second, he had been enticed to invade the kingdom by another’s will rather than his own, to the point that, after capturing the emperor’s son, he might himself be elected king. But before the consecration he was led to repentance and rejected the kingdom; and, humbly subject to the king, he was honorably endowed with the Bavarian kingdom. In bringing peace to it, he thereafter flourished beyond his predecessors, so that the inhabitants of that kingdom called Henry “the Peaceful” and “the Father of the Fatherland.”

After his death, his son Henry, the future king, received the duchy of Bavaria by the grant of King Otto the Third. The venerable Gebehard, bishop of the church of Constance, died; Landbert succeeded him. The venerable Bishop Hildeward built a monastery of twelve virgins in the city of Stitterlingheburg [Note: [Col. 0529D] Stoterlingeburg, between Oker and Ilsa.] on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

In the territory of the church of Halberstadt, at a place called Hordorpio, a child was born having no body from the buttocks downward: neither legs nor male or female member, but only half a human being. Its hindquarters were like those of a featherless bird; its right ear was larger than its left, and likewise its left eye was larger than its right. Its teeth were of a dreadful yellow color. Its left arm, without four fingers, was otherwise whole, with only the thumb; its right arm was entirely absent. Before baptism it stared and saw with its eyes, but after baptism [Note: [Col. 0529D] Thus L.; the first manuscript has “before.”] it never opened its eyes. On the fourth day after its birth, the unspeakable monster died.

[Col. 0530B] A common disaster, the pestilence among pigs and cattle, afflicted all Germany. Theodoric, count palatine, and his brother Sigibert, distinguished Saxons [Note: [Col. 0529D] Thus L. and Ann. Saxo.; the first manuscript reads “plundered.”], died.

996. Liudolph, the radiant light of the holy church of Augsburg, was taken from this world on the eighth day before the Kalends of August and numbered among the heavenly family. Gevehardus [Note: [Col. 0529D] Gebehard of Ellwangen, an outstanding abbot [Col. 0530D]—that is, Ann. Saxo.] was appointed bishop in his place, foremost among distinguished abbots.

As time advanced, when divine judgment was carrying many away from the sanctuary of the Lord, Hildeward, the jewel of priests and the golden glory of episcopal dignity, bishop of the venerable church of Halberstadt, was released from the vanity of this world on the seventh day before the Kalends of December and presented to the sight of true Love, which is Christ [Col. 0530C], having become a pious imitator of that humility and love upon which one may believe [Note: [Col. 0530D] P. “a true Israelite,” p. [lacuna] e. Chron. Saxo.; cf. Ann. Saxo.].

Arnolfus succeeded him, sprung from a very illustrious lineage but nobler in character and distinguished by sincere generosity. In the spring of this same year, the aforementioned King Otto, having established peace between the Saxons and the Slavs, went to Italy and celebrated the Lord’s Resurrection at Pavia according to the royal [Note: [Col. 0530D] “Regal,” Chr.] custom.

Thereafter, having firmly taken possession of the entire Italian kingdom, he came to Rome and found Pope John, of blessed memory, dead [Note: [Col. 0530D] I have supplied the word from the Annals and Chronicle of Saxony; it is absent from the manuscript.]. With pious consent he allowed his nephew Bruno, a very distinguished man, elected bishop by the unanimous vote not only of the clergy but of all the Roman citizens, to be installed in his place. The Romans called him Gregory, dropping the name Bruno.

After he had been enthroned in the apostolic see, this man, with Lord Otto—until then called king—acclaimed by the Roman people and by nearly all the peoples of Europe, consecrated him Emperor Augustus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, on the venerable feast of Christ’s Ascension, in the ninth indiction.

After properly arranging the Italian kingdom, Otto returned to Francia and celebrated the birthday of the supreme emperor in Cologne, with fitting [Col. 0531A] honor. Adalbert, bishop of the city of Prague, was crowned with glorious martyrdom by the Prussians on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. Bernhard [Note: [Col. 0531D] Read “Brunwardus.”], bishop of the church of Würzburg, sent on an imperial embassy to Constantinople, died in the province of Achaea. Henry, himself distinguished and the brother of the illustrious chancellor Heribert, was appointed bishop in his place.

997. The Slavs, moved by the treachery innate in them, broke the treaty of peace and gnawed away at the Saxon borders by secret raids. The emperor, aroused against them, invaded with a great army Ztodorania, commonly called Heveldum [Note: [Col. 0531D] By the Havel.], an excellent land among the Slavic regions. He defeated and plundered it and, victorious, entered in glory Magdeburg, the chief city of Saxony.

Meanwhile, while Emperor Augustus—namely Otto the Third [Col. 0531B]—was traversing the land of the Heveldi and devastating it, the assembled Wiltzi unexpectedly attacked the province of Bardengau with extensive plundering and fires. Seeing this, the Westphalians, whom the aforementioned emperor, as he set out on expedition, had left to guard the province, quickly and forcefully engaged the Lutici. Although they were few, they struck down an innumerable multitude of pagans in such a slaughter and seized such great booty from them that neither the number of the slain nor that of the booty can in any way be expressed in human language.

In this year the restoration of the holy metropolitan church at the castle of Quedlinburg was undertaken with every effort at the command of the imperial daughter, the abbess Machtildis. Seeing that the church built by her grandfather and grandmother—namely, by Kings Henry and Mathilda—was narrower than the right of so lofty a dignity required [Col. 0531C], because of the throng of people gathering there, she used the benevolence innate and deeply rooted in her to add a structure broader and higher, for the enlargement of the same church in honor of Saint Servatius, archbishop and confessor.

She had it dedicated on the sixth day before the Ides of March by Arnolfus, the recently ordained bishop of Halberstadt, together with other archbishops and bishops, whose names it would now be tedious to enumerate individually, in a manner appropriate to the adornment of God’s house, with the entire assembly of clergy and people.

Not long afterward, she honorably dedicated the Walbeck church, which had been built in a short time, on the anniversary of the day of her august father Otto, through the same Bishop Arnolfus, in that same year, on the Nones of May, amid the greatest rejoicing of clergy and people.

In this same year a certain Crescentius [Col. 0531D], deceived by diabolical fraud, invaded Rome while Pope Gregory was absent. He received with an honor unworthy of him a certain John of Calabria, whom Lord Emperor Otto had sent to Constantinople with Bishop Bernward to obtain the daughter of the Greek emperor in marriage and who was returning from there with Greek envoys. He established John not so much as pope as an apostate, and kept the imperial envoys under guard in Rome.

This John [Col. 0532A], Greek by nationality and a slave by condition, exceedingly clever in cunning, approached Otto the Second, Emperor Augustus of pious memory, in humble clothing. Through the intervention of his beloved consort, the empress Theophanu Augusta, he was first supported by royal provision. As time went on, by the foxlike craft in which he was highly skilled, he so ensnared the aforementioned emperor that, having received sufficient favor from him according to place and circumstance, he was regarded as distinguished, almost among the foremost, until the emperor’s death.

After Otto the Second Augustus had died, when his son Otto the Third was already reigning—whom divine mercy, following from his mother’s womb, had exalted to the Roman Empire—the aforementioned John was able to exercise his inborn cunning all the more securely because the child king and his leading men were left to negligence [Col. 0532B].

Moreover, when the bishop of the church of Piacenza had died, a man of good character was chosen for it. When he had been unworthily expelled, the aforementioned John, not a shepherd but a wolf, took over that same church, not to govern it but to devastate it. When he had held it for several years, drunk with the devil’s poison of avarice, he raised himself so high above himself that, having truly become—as was said above—a member of Antichrist, he would rather defecate upon the very see of the blessed apostle Peter at Rome by fornicating than sit upon it in veneration.

### 998

Having heard this, the lord emperor prepared a second expedition into Italy. The venerable Pope Gregory, coming to meet him at Pavia, recounted to him the most wicked deeds of John and Crescentius. Moved by divine zeal, he hastened with the apostolic lord to Rome as quickly as possible [Col. 0532C].

When the aforementioned ministers of Satan heard this, John indeed took flight, while Crescentius shut himself up with his men in the fortress that joins Old Rome to the Leonine citadel. Then certain men who were friends not only of the emperor but also of Christ pursued John and captured him [Note: [Col. 0531D] Two words have been erased.]. Fearing that, if they sent him to the Augustus, he might escape unpunished, they cut off his tongue and nose together and completely tore out his eyes.

After divine punishment had thus been inflicted upon him, Pope Gregory honorably recovered the apostolic see and occupied it freely until his death. The Augustus-emperor, therefore, arriving at Rome, celebrated there the most holy Resurrection of Christ. Immediately after the octave, with ladders and siege engines he vigorously assaulted the fortress that Crescentius had occupied—until then impregnable to all [Note: [Col. 0532D] “The house of Theoderic, where that perverse man was seated,” Annals of Saxony.]—and ordered that, once captured, Crescentius be beheaded and that his body, thrown down from the top of the fortress, be hung by the feet on a gallows.

In the month of July a terrifying earthquake occurred throughout Saxony, and two fiery stones fell from the thunder: one in the city of Magdeburg itself, the other beyond the River Elbe. Their unprecedented fall foretold, by threatening dreadful destruction to all the people; and we saw this very clearly revealed in what followed—namely, when this world, struck three times in the brain, so to speak, by the blows of an incurable plague, lost its very vital organs.

### 999

For Mechtild, the most illustrious jewel of the imperial offspring, daughter of the great Augustus Otto, whom we have often mentioned—born of scepter-bearing parents, she passed through the beginnings of her budding childhood under the becoming and honorable care of her nurses, as befitted the daughter of the crown [Note: [Col. 0533D] Thus L.; *filio*, “son,” in the codex.] [Note: [Col. 0533D] *Transcendit*, “she surpassed,” is preferable; Annals and Chronicle of Saxony.]—then, as the flourishing years of her uncertain youth advanced, maturing in body and understanding beyond the others of her age, leaving nothing entrusted to her outside the discipline of governance, she lived amiably, affably, devoutly, and more generously toward everyone than toward herself.

In the eleventh year of her birth, although unequal to such burdens, she was placed in charge of the metropolitan church that was her hereditary possession, for perpetual governance, by the deliberate counsel of the emperors and their fathers, by the common election, and by the blessing of the bishops [Col. 0533B].

When she reached the fork of the Pythagorean letter—that is, the choice between the two paths—she immediately seized the narrow way, grasping the hope that does not disappoint, and with all the diligence of her soul endeavored to transfer herself and all that belonged to her from non-being to true being.

When her cousin Otto the Generous was departing for Rome, she governed the kingdoms entrusted to her in the emperor’s place, not with feminine frivolity. By the skill of her mind, in the manner inherited from her grandfather and father, she rendered even the hardened heads of barbarian kings so peaceful and submissive that, after the devastation of so many provinces and the unbridled upheaval of barbarism, she laid the first foundations of the peace which the holy Church of God now partly enjoys. She did not do so by the sword, weapons, or any military instruments—although she was fully capable of directing such things—but by constant perseverance in vigils, prayers, and fasting, intent upon God alone, with his assistance teaching and strengthening her. By laying those foundations she built them, and she did not cease building until later kings could attain the height of that same peace all the more easily, since, not by laboring but by entering into her labors, they would succeed her, in proportion as she herself had more watchfully toiled at first in constructing its lowest foundations.

In the final days of her life, at a conference held at Parthenopolis, with the assembly of bishops and Duke Bernhard, with counts and the whole senate and populace gathered, and with envoys from every nation also converging there, she was surrounded on every side [Note: [Col. 0533D] I have corrected the text thus: *unde quos secus*, “whence those on either side,” in the codex.] [Col. 0533D]. What she was like, how irreproachable she showed herself, with what marvelous discernment she assigned to each person what was his, with what great reverence she treated the persons of bishops above all others, with what skill she admonished nobles, judges, and others entrusted with such responsibilities, for strengthening the commonwealth and also securing private interests, with what gentleness she encouraged the devout, with what strictness she terrified the guilty, and with what industry she preserved, assisted, and enlarged her country—I do not think this can be comprehended by signs or expressed in words by anyone.

Having arranged all these matters there with the greatest order, she revisited with maternal affection the little sheep entrusted to her singular care, who had been anxiously awaiting her arrival. Received by them with fitting honor, she survived only a few days afterward. Struck by a slight fever, she gave back to him who is, and what is, and who alone is his own, the little body that necessarily had to be dissolved because it had been compacted from what is dissoluble. On the seventh day before the Ides of February, in a death unexpected by all but long foreseen by herself—for she had wished continually to anticipate that day and hour by prayers [Note: [Col. 0533D] Thus L.; *probis*, “good,” in the codex.]—she joyfully gave back to him who is, what is, and the one thing that is his own, the little body necessarily to be dissolved because it had been compacted from what is dissoluble; in him she had participated so honorably.

She was buried in the middle of the basilica of Saint Peter and Saint Stephen, beside the tombs of the kings, her grandfather and grandmother, Heinricus and Mechtildis, amid the excessive wailing and lamentation of her people [Col. 0534B], where she would happily await the day of the future resurrection.

Who, then, even if inwardly hardened with adamantine severity, could have witnessed this pitiful spectacle with dry eyes? The small orphaned company of the holy bishops Dionysius and Servatius, as well as the maidservants of the holy Mother of God, especially those from the western mountain, and those of Saint Andrew from the monastery of Walbeck—for she herself, as we said above, had been their foundress from the beginning—together with the other women serving Saint Pusinna at Winathusen and Saint Wicbert in the plain beside the royal court, whom she had fostered with maternal care and every diligence until that time [Note: [Col. 0534D] Thus L.; “these,” in the codex.]—although she had by no means been their original builder, after succeeding by right of kinship to the inheritance of her grandmother Mechtild—then, I say, mourned as they enclosed in a sarcophagus and committed to the tomb the mother whom they had known only the day before as strong, alive, and ruling the peoples, suddenly taken from them, never to return to their eyes except in the eternal vision. In a kind of mad outcry they declared that they preferred to die with her rather than survive her.

What more is there to say? When these lamentations had at last been completed, the aforementioned holy women, meeting with the bishops whom divine mercy had arranged to be present unexpectedly at her funeral—Arnulf and Bernward [Note: [Col. 0534D] They are absent in C; Leibniz restored them from the Annals of Saxony.], as well as Duke Bernhard—seeing that the only remedy remaining for wounds inflicted upon them was to choose as their lady and mother Mechtild’s cousin Adelheid, whom she had adopted, whom she had loved uniquely, and whom she had tenderly raised as a daughter, unanimously elected her.

They immediately sent envoys with all speed: first to France, to the empress Adelheid, Mechtild’s mother, and then to the Roman emperor Otto, her cousin, who were to carry this news to Rome. The envoys hurried on and soon reached the Augusta. Although she had already foreseen in her prophetic mind that something intolerable would happen to her, the unhappy message wounded her to the core. Taking with them other envoys of that same empress, they reached Rome and found the Augustus-emperor deeply mournful over the recent death of his nephew, Pope Bruno, who in the Roman language is called Gregory. By adding a second and much heavier grief to the first, they made him most sorrowful over the death of his most illustrious aunt [Col. 0535A].

Thus not only did the Augustus-emperor and his followers mourn the bodily death of the illustrious Mechtild; wherever news of her death resounded—through alleys, streets, crossroads, and remote places—people beat their breasts, tore their hair, and, loving mourning more than joy, struck the very air with their tearful cries.

At last, recovering their strength of mind after such great confusion, the emperor sent innumerable thanks to the holy community for the services rendered to his venerable aunt and for the election of his sister [Col. 0535B] [Note: [Col. 0535D] In manuscript M, “in the margin, after *et*, is written *grates*”; but from the Annals of Saxony and for the sense, it should stand here.]. He decided that she should succeed to the honor and burden of spiritual mother—not by commanding as he was able, but by making a pious request, as he was taught to do.

By the ordering of divine mercy this was accomplished without delay. On the solemn feast of the archangel Michael, after the election had been repeated, she was blessed by Arnulf, bishop of that church, in the presence of the other bishops, the royal lady Sophia, her elder sister, and her illustrious niece Abbess Hathwiga, and all the leading men and women of the kingdom, before the altar of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Stephen, the protomartyr. She was raised to the throne of the lady mother and burdened—not a little—with the charge of the rule, in which she might learn to behold her own life and that of her subjects as in a mirror and to govern all things diligently [Col. 0535C]. Whatever span of time the mercy of the Almighty would afterward grant her, she was to pass in outstanding dignity and joy, though never without vigilant care.

After a short interval, Adelheid, Mechtild’s mother, the renowned Augusta, empress of the Romans, who had distinguished the condition of the empire conquered by her and her consort, the great and peaceful Augustus Otto, by land and sea no less through her merits and character than he had consolidated it through his outstanding strength and triumphs, after his death, herself dying completely to the world, as though she had not been born for herself but had been divinely appointed solely for the use of the needy. Whatever she could possess—especially the revenues of the kingdom, acquired throughout the entire tributary world by right of tribute or even by gift—she never ceased, with cheerful mind and countenance, to commend to the hands of the poor, to be carried into the heavenly treasuries, among her other marks of virtue [Col. 0535D].

We often saw her, though most secretly, girded up for this desirable work as peasant women are, so that even the length of her garments could cause her no delay. She used both hands as though they were her right hands [Note: [Col. 0535D] Thus L.; *usa*, “she used,” in the codex.] and persisted in this pious labor until, her gait wavering, she failed not in generosity but in bodily strength and necessarily reclined for a little while to rest [Col. 0536A]. Yet she kept this intention: that whether sitting, standing, or detained by any occupation whatsoever, she would never cease from the work of mercy that was most familiar to her.

Thus, setting aside those things that seem to exist—not because they truly exist [Note: [Col. 0535D] “Because they truly exist,” in the Chronicle of Saxony.] but because they appear to exist to us, who live according to the quality of our senses, since they pass away—she raised herself entirely, by that noble prerogative of humanity of which I spoke, toward the things that truly are, since they regard neither their own beginning nor their end. Always looking upward with her better eye, she finally, at a very advanced age, departed gloriously to him whom she had thirsted for to the depths of her marrow.

This occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, when she was to receive the hundredfold reward for her labors [Note: [Col. 0536D] I have corrected this from the Annals and Chronicle of Saxony and from the necrologies of Stavelot, beginning in the eleventh century, and of Muri; the codex has “the seventeenth.”]. Accompanied by a company of angels, she was honorably buried in the basilica at Seltz [Note: [Col. 0536D] Seltz in Alsace.], which she herself had built through pious labor in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0536B].

### 1000 [Note: [Col. 0536D] Here the codex continues, omitting the year number.]

When the emperor learned of her death shortly afterward, the Augustus was afflicted by an excess of grief beyond belief. Seeing the holy Church of God, which until then had stood unshaken, supported with marvelous strength, now shaken by the successive fall of three columns—the lord apostolic, his aforementioned grandmother the Augusta, and his aunt, the imperial abbess Mechtild—and leaning upon him alone because of their departures [Note: [Col. 0536D] Thus L., from the Chronicle of Saxony; the codex has *sibi ipsi anniti*, “to strive for itself.”], he was weighed down by the burden of his cares.

Nevertheless, after properly arranging the matters that had to be handled there, whether ecclesiastical or public, he decided to visit his desolated homeland at a rapid pace, as though to console it. He did so with the greatest haste, with not a few members of the Roman senate traveling with him.

After crossing the difficult Alps, as soon as he was able to set foot in these regions [Note: [Col. 0536D] “The parts of Gaul,” Chronicle of Saxony.], all Gaul, France, and Swabia rushed to meet him in organized cavalry and infantry formations. The imperial ladies, his sisters Sophia and Adelheid, together with the leading men and women of both Saxony and Thuringia, also came to meet him. As though receiving one uniquely beloved who deserved such love, they welcomed him with unanimous rejoicing, while the world itself, so to speak, smiled. They remained with him in due affection for as long as the haste of his appointed journey allowed.

He, however, mindful of the evangelical command that says, “Seek first the kingdom of God” [Col. 0536D], desiring, in the manner of his imperial ancestors, that all his affairs be ruled and improved by divine mercy, went with humble devotion to Sclavonia to visit Saint Adalbert, recently crowned with martyrdom for Christ, and earnestly sought his intercession.

There he was received with the greatest unanimity by the Sclavonian duke Bolizlav, and gifts of every kind, gathered with the utmost diligence from throughout the world, were presented to him as tokens of service [Col. 0537A]. At that time, however, he accepted nothing of these gifts, since he had come there not to seize or take but to give and pray.

He returned to his homeland and, intending to celebrate holy Easter in the city of Quedlinburg, celebrated the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and the night of the Lord’s Resurrection on the very mountain where the holy women regularly serve Christ according to canonical rule. He did this out of love for his beloved sister Adelheid, the abbess, with the services of due veneration.

Yet whether that can rightly be called a night which is known to shine throughout the whole world with the triumphant light of the Redeemer of all, in a marvelous and ineffable manner, is another question.

From there, during the very hours of the morning office, he returned to his court to satisfy the expectation of the entire senate and people [Col. 0537B]. He spent that week in royal duties, governing, pardoning, giving generously, and rewarding. On the octave of Easter he departed from there, leading his sister through Mainz, Cologne, and Aachen—cities which at that time he was striving to place above all others after Rome—with the highest veneration and brotherly affection. After rewarding Bolizlav, he rested there for a little while, making preparations that seemed appropriate for the journey he had begun.

But since he could neither postpone the continuation of his journey for long nor bear to lose the sister whom he loved most intimately, the aforementioned Adelheid, they finally made a firm mutual agreement that she would come to Rome after him. Their grief somewhat eased, and he departed to hasten into Italy on his final journey, alas!, as he had resolved, while she returned to the monastery over which she had particular charge. Both departed with the vain hope of seeing each other again in this light.

The Augustus-emperor, however, once more crossed the immense Alps and, having traversed Italy, remained for some time at Pavia.

### 1001

From there, setting out for Rome, he resolved to celebrate there the most holy feast of the Lord’s Resurrection with due veneration.

Meanwhile, the cunning author of wickedness and inventor of every deceit, equipped with a thousand arts of harming, once again put on the serpent-like garment that he had formerly fashioned for himself in order to deceive the first human beings. He crept among the hearts of the Romans and puffed poison into their forked tongues, persuading them to attempt, for his sake, to lay their wicked hands upon the emperor himself [Col. 0537D].

But when they saw that, by the shield of divine mercy set against them, they were being driven back from harming the emperor, they punished with bloody slaughter anyone they could find who favored the just cause. They could not in any way be calmed from that wicked sedition until the emperor, compelled by the raging tumult, gathered together the strength of his men and departed from the city that he had previously loved above all others but that he now detested above all [Col. 0538A].

Grieving, as they say, he flew to the fortifications of a certain castle and there, through continual consideration of how to avenge the injury, completed the year that was then in progress [Note: [Col. 0537D] I have restored this word from the Chronicle of Saxony.].

### 1002

But at the very beginning of the following year, having been removed from this fleeting life on the ninth day before the Kalends of February—an event destined to be read about by almost the whole world, both because of the charge of intended vengeance [Note: [Col. 0537D] Perhaps: “with vengeance assigned as a crime”?] and because of the sorrows of this transitory life—he was placed in the bosom of the great patriarch Abraham, to be crowned for the better and to reign more happily at the time of the future resurrection, carried there by angelic hands.

To prevent news of this misfortune from being revealed too quickly to the audacity of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0537D] Thus I have corrected the text; the codex has *infortunum*, “misfortune.”], those who were present concealed and kept it secret until, having summoned their companions who were wandering dispersed among the castles [Note: [Col. 0537D] “After forming a funeral procession, they proceeded,” etc., in the Annals and Chronicle of Saxony.], they carried out the body of their lord and suddenly broke through [Col. 0538B], though many were left behind there, alas, through lack of horses and without hope of survival.

When so great a matter could no longer remain hidden, the Roman enemies, having learned of it, stirred up wars that would be accursed for all time, with unwarranted boldness. Equipped with weapons as though they were about to fight for their lives and homeland, they shamelessly attempted to tear apart the dead emperor’s body and, by marvelous forms of injury, without delay to torture him in death, though they had been unable to harm him in life.

While he still breathed the air above, unaware of the enormity of the deceit that lay hidden, he had placed them before all peoples in a kind of privileged affection [Col. 0538D]. The Romans attacked with a foul warlike assault [Note: [Col. 0538D] Thus the codex; the Annals and Chronicle of Saxony read *terna*, “threefold.”]; but divine mercy permitted them to be repelled again and again and repeatedly punished by cruel death, so that scarcely a few escaped ingloriously by entrusting themselves to hiding places and flight [Col. 0538C].

Our men, however, enjoying victory everywhere, carried the treasure—the deposit of precious weight—across the snowy peaks of the Alps with faithful devotion, now at last secure.

When Duke Heinricus learned of this, he, to whom supreme authority in the empire belonged, came to meet the lamentable funeral procession with a great accompanying multitude, exceedingly sorrowful for the dead man and for all that deservedly had to be mourned. With many groans he finally brought the dead body to Aachen, the place for which he had thirsted while alive.

Without delay they went into the church, and with a great honor of this kind—mingled, so to speak, with unbearable grief—he was committed to the earth, his great consolation [Note: [Col. 0538D] Perhaps “the great consolation of many”; the Chronicle of Saxony reads: “the great consolation is enclosed by many.”]. But his spirit, as we believe, was received into the heavenly palace through the united prayer of all who were present.

Meanwhile, while many people held different opinions and each sought to seize the right to the empire for his own faction, Margrave Eghard was most wickedly killed at Palithi by Sigifrid and Udo, together with many of his men, on the second day before the Kalends of May.

Then, on the third day before the Kalends of July, the aforementioned Heinricus, the royal nephew, was elected king by the Franks and, without the knowledge of the Saxons, was anointed and crowned at Mainz by Willichisus.

Rumor flew about these events, saying that he would come to Merseburg as quickly as possible; and so it happened. Duke Bernhard and the leading men of the Saxons came to meet him with the appropriate dignity, were kindly received by him, and immediately chose him as their lord and king.

They also discovered that Bolizlav, duke of Poland, had come to meet him and had begged the king for his favor, promising a treaty of peace—though it later became clear that this treaty was not firm.

Departing from there, the king spent some time in the cities and places of the province, prudently arranging what had to be done as time and circumstances required. The imperial ladies, Sophia and Adelheid, imperial daughters, received the novelty of so great a name with honor and came to meet him with as much affection as they could. They rejoiced with the king, their nephew, because they had not been permitted to rejoice with their brother.

Taking them with him in due honor, while his wife Cunigunda accompanied him, he reached the city of Paderborn. There a dangerous rebellion arose between the Bavarians and Saxons, followed by the death of many [Col. 0539B].

On the feast of the birth of the holy martyr Lawrence, the crown of blessing was placed upon Queen Cunigunda. The blessing of the abbacy of Gandersheim was also given to Sophia, the emperor’s daughter [Note: [Col. 0539D] Thus L., from the Chronicle of Saxony; “of the emperor himself,” in the codex.].

When these matters had been completed and the king had crossed the Rhine, each returned to his own place. Duke Herimannus resisted the king with the Swabians, and a certain faction of the Franks also began to rebel, perpetrating many useless acts, burning holy places, and laying waste to others. The Lord, however, very quickly humbled them [Note: [Col. 0539D] Thus L. and the codex.].

### 1003

King Heinricus invaded the Milkian Slavs in winter and, devastating them with bloody slaughter, brought them under his rule [Note: [Col. 0539D] See the Saxon annalist concerning the capture of the city of Bautzen.]. Thangmarus was killed together with others [Note: [Col. 0539D] I have corrected this to *Thangmarus*; the codex has *Thonginarus*. Thammo in the Annals of Saxony.].

During Lent he came to Parthenopolis to celebrate Palm Sunday there. From there he proceeded as quickly as possible to the metropolitan city of Quedlinburg, in the manner of the earlier kings, his ancestors and forefathers, and celebrated the Easter festival with his nobles and the gathering of the people.

After a few days had passed, he was persuaded by the prayers of the lady and mother Adelheid. Returning again with the queen, he rejoiced to participate in the feast of Saint Servatius, and afterward went to the city of Halberstadt to celebrate holy Pentecost there. Duke Hermann reached the end of his life, and the conflict with the Swabians came to an end.

### 1004

King Heinricus came from France into Italy to celebrate holy Easter there. But, with his joy taken away, he ordered many thousands of rebels to be killed by the sword, while all the buildings of Pavia, which the illustrious industry of former generations had constructed, were burned at once.

Lightning and thunder appeared in the same year together with an excessive and terrifying whirlwind, while peoples everywhere were struck with fear. After returning from Italy, the king soon afterward entered Bohemia to fight against it, since Bolizlav of Poland had unjustly possessed it.

Yet, with God’s help, the entire people surrendered themselves and all that belonged to them to the king with peace, while that tyrant Bolizlav escaped in disgrace. The king, thanks be to God, departed victorious with his men.

The monastery of Herolfesfeld, deprived by the king of the ancient right of its fathers, suffered great loss: it was stripped of its goods and deprived of its sons. Those whom it had gathered and educated under Charles, son of Pippin, through 170 and nine cycles of years, it lost in these times, its sins demanding this.

### 1005

Meanwhile, with his anger against Bolizlav still persisting, the king repaired his army and hastened into Poland, pursuing the fugitive, as though to defend his own injury—but, alas, destined to lose many.

Bernhard and Isi, Thiedbern and Bernhard [Note: [Col. 0540D] Soldiers of Halberstadt.], were killed together with others. The king, although grieving, returned with his army after accepting an unfavorable peace, carrying the bodies of the dead with him.

Kiesut died.

### 1006

Balduin rose up in Gaul against the king, together with Landbert, at Valenciennes [Note: [Col. 0540D] Valenciennes.], a city that was not his own. The king, taking this badly, hastened there with a prepared force. His men remained there for a long time, expending much effort in vain [Note: [Col. 0540D] A word or passage is missing in the codex.], and he returned after a fabricated peace [Note: [Col. 0540D] Thus L.; the codex has “a defeated peace,” while the Chronicle has “a made peace.”].

### 1007

He reached the city of Regensburg and celebrated the Lord’s Resurrection there. At the same time, deeply affected by the recent slaughter of his men, he sent envoys to Bolizlav, declaring that he thirsted for war and ordering him to prepare for war against him.

But unfavorable news about Balduin again spread widely, and this prevented the matter from being carried out. Returning quickly from there, and aided by the prayers of the holy Church, he rejoiced to receive as a man of peace the enemy whom he had left behind, after his adversaries had been reconciled to him in peace.

Meanwhile, Duke Bolizlav, provoked by the Saxons’ incursion following the king’s embassy and elated by bold warfare, advanced toward Parthenopolis. He devastated the whole region of Sclavonia in that area, either handing its inhabitants over to death or ordering them to be bound as captives, until he reached the bank of the River Elbe.

There, boasting certain arrogant words, he was prevented by the army of the supreme King, Saint Maurice, from accomplishing his will and returned to his own land, taking with him in chains strong Saxon men: Liudolf, Tadilan, and Tadi.

Hearing this, the king was grieved in spirit and urged his men not to let it go unavenged. But, I do not know through what obstacle, no result has yet followed such an intention.

On the Kalends of June, Count Hermann, brother of Bishop Arnulf, died [Col. 0540D].

### 1008

Bertlalis [Note: [Col. 0540D] *Bertradis*, L.], humble handmaid of the handmaids of Saint Servatius, resolved to visit the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul. She set out for the absolution of herself and of the soul of the lady Mechtild, and for the salvation of her own people.

Thus, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, putting aside every hardship, she labored greatly in crossing rivers, traveling over steep mountains and through the valleys of the earth, provided only that she might succeed in seeing what she loved [Col. 0541A].

At last she reached Rome rejoicing. She approached, embraced, and kissed the tomb of Saint Peter. After tearfully pleading there for those on whose account she had come, and after greeting the patronages of the other saints, she gave thanks to God and returned safely with her companions to her homeland.

A paschal star was seen at midday on Monday of Easter week, on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

Liudolf, archbishop of Trier, died, and Magingoz succeeded him. Bishop Notger of Liège died [Note: [Col. 0541D] Liège.], and Baldricus, illustrious in character, succeeded him.

In the same year Atalpero, a cleric and brother of the queen, an adversary of the king, stirred up many abominations. Against every right and law, he seized Trier for himself and his men and then departed.

When the king learned of this, he immediately gathered his forces and arrived. He besieged the Lutharians who resisted him in the palace, keeping them there for sixteen weeks. At last, compelled by hunger, they falsely surrendered their right hands, caused the king and his men to return, and nevertheless continued in their treachery.

Bishop Hildericus of Havelberg died, and Ericus succeeded him.

### 1009

A sudden and unprecedented overflowing of waters occurred in our time on the third day before the Ides of January, a Monday, on the tenth day of the moon. It caused loss to many and persisted in its fury for seven days.

Bishop Retharius of Paderborn died, and Meginwerck succeeded him.

Saint Bruno, called Boniface, archbishop and monk, was beheaded by pagans in the eleventh year of his conversion, on the frontier of Russia and Lithuania. Together with eighteen of his companions, he sought the heavens on the seventh day before the Ides of March [Note: [Col. 0541D] “Twelfth,” in the Chronicle and Annals of Saxony.].

Bishop Wigbert of Merseburg died, and Thietmarus succeeded him [Col. 0541C].

On Palm Sunday, drops of blood also fell upon people’s garments in certain places. On the third day before the Kalends of May, a Friday, on the first day of the moon, the sun was transformed by a horrible mist and a wondrous color. To the astonishment of those who looked, it appeared blood-red and smaller than itself, striking terror into them. It displayed such threats for two days; on the third day it was scarcely clothed in its own light.

Pestilence and mortality followed severely. The king, again moved by great grief and anger together, returned to France, and much damage was inflicted in many places. After spending the summer there, he returned to Saxony without peace [Note: [Col. 0541D] I have corrected this from the Annals of Saxony; the codex has “Spain.”].

Count Dedit, while traveling, was unexpectedly and treacherously killed by Werinzo and Fridericus, his cousin [Note: [Col. 0541D] “By Margrave Werenharius.”] [Col. 0541D].

Many fires were set throughout the regions, so that people in a certain village were burned to death. An unclear notice follows concerning Count Fricherus [source: *Fecit Fricherum comes*; Note: [Col. 0541D] Thus I have emended it, following the annalist: *exusti*, “burned”; the codex has *interfecit*, “he killed.”].

Machtildis, daughter of the king’s sister, fell asleep in the Lord.

At Mainz a new basilica, together with all the adjoining buildings, was also miserably consumed by fire, with only the old church remaining, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, a Monday, on the sixth day of the moon [Col. 0542A].

Thunder and flashes of lightning frequently occurred during the winter.

### 1010

Bishop Ansfridus, illustrious in merits, first faithfully administering armed service to the earthly emperor and then humbly obeying the Creator, devoted himself to the divine commandments. Therefore he shone forth distinguished by virtues; having trampled earthly things underfoot, he now rejoices within the angelic choirs and enjoys eternal goods.

In the same year the king gathered his forces for an expedition, intending to seek the Polish region of Sclavonia. But he did not reach the place where he wished to go; when a serious illness came upon him, he turned back halfway with a few men. The others, remaining prepared for war, devastated many places and carried away much plunder.

The basilica at Ungerestorp [Note: [Col. 0541D] I have emended this to *Ungerestorp*; the codex has *Vongerestorp*.] [Note: [Col. 0542D] Wunstorf.] was destroyed by a terrible stroke of lightning [Col. 0542B].

Comets were also seen.

### 1011

Duke Bernhard, second only to the king, rich in many kinds of gifts of wisdom, knowledge, and piety, was carried into heaven, to be mourned by the holy Church for a long time. Count Liudger, his brother, followed him in death on the eighteenth day, a man worthy of lamentation.

Pestilence and mortality raged, devastating monasteries, castles, and towns throughout all nations with an unprecedented storm. An unusual winter, harsh with hoarfrost and inconveniently prolonged, retained ice that could not be dissolved by the sun’s heat for a long time and rendered many human bodies weak.

Archbishop Willigisus died. Erkenboldus, abbot of Fulda, was substituted in his place, rejoicing deservedly while retaining his father’s name and assuming the honor of the pastoral dignity.

The enclosed priest Asico died [Col. 0542C] [Note: [Col. 0542D] Thus the Annals of Saxony; the codex has *Etsico*.].

In the same year, on the third day before the Kalends of August, a Monday, on the twenty-sixth day of the moon, enormous and dreadful icy hail fell.

Abbot Thietdivus and [lacuna], a monk, and Adhela, enclosed at Rome, ascended into the secrets of heaven [Note: [Col. 0542D] Thus the Annals of Saxony; the codex has *Deddile*.].

That year also, the savage death of Duchess Hildegard brought forth pitiful lamentation, as she left behind what she grieved.

It also removed from the royal stock the jewel Machtild, abbess, daughter of Liudolf.

Bishop Suithgerus departed to Christ [Note: [Col. 0542D] *Suthgerus* in the codex; *Suicgerus*, bishop of Münster, in the Annals.], and Thietricus was substituted in his place.

A great wind suddenly overthrew many buildings in a whirlwind and caused much other damage.

In that same year the king came to Tribur and rightly mourned a fresh slaughter of his men. Among them, when the king’s adversaries—Heinricus and the others—had attacked as though under the pretext of peace, Duke Thiedricus, his cousin, was captured; some of the others perished by the sword, while others could scarcely escape [Col. 0542D].

## 1012

Bishop Erluinus of Cambrai [Note: “Cameracensis” in the Saxon Annals] died; Gerhard was ordained in his place. Hermannus, a boy and duke, the king’s cousin, died.

In the same year, during Lent, a wondrous vision was shown to a certain monk who had been carried away in ecstasy—a vision said to be as terrifying to the impious as it was praiseworthy to the pious.

At the castle of Bavanberg in Francia, the dedication of a church took place in the tenth year of King Heinricus’s reign, on 6 May, with thirty-six bishops appointed to perform the work. Also present, sharing in the royal joy, were the lady sisters and abbesses Sophia and Adelheida, an outstanding ornament of the imperial court. There was also an extraordinary gathering of clergy and people. Among them, the king granted pardon to many accused persons and promised forgiveness to others.

Archbishop Tagino of Parthenopolis died, illustrious in his merits. Walthardus succeeded him, shining with the light of wisdom and knowledge and second to none in piety. Bishop Vunger died [Note: “Wugerus, bishop of Poznań,” in the Saxon Annals]. The priest and monk Thietmer died.

In a certain village of Saxon Swabia called Cocstede [Note: Kochstedt], twin brothers were born with teeth. They had mouths like birds [Note: “Ancae,” in the Annals of Christ]; one of them also had only half of a right arm, like a bird’s wing [Note: “Ancae,” in the Annals of Christ]. They are said to have smiled at one another on the third day after their birth. By common agreement they happened to die, because everyone feared that they would live for a long time.

In the same year, in Francia, though not far from Cologne, a terrible punishment of miserable death was inflicted on a certain man. Invisibly gnawed by mice in an unbelievable manner, and frustrated by the treatments of many of his people, he reached his final extremity.

A great disaster of devastation was also inflicted by pirates in the northern regions, in a certain province [Note: “Unna,” in the Annals of Christ and the Saxon Annals], so that, after many had been killed and others miserably captured, and after the buildings of many had been burned together with their possessions, scarcely a few escaped, as if naked. Earthquakes occurred in various places.

In this same year, a disturbance of the air, with thunder, lightning, and such an abundance of rain, occurred on 10 August that, lasting for two days, it caused very extensive damage: it destroyed many houses with their furnishings and heaps of grain, and also endangered human beings.

Archbishop Waldhardus, having drawn the lot of death and destined to live more happily with Christ, lived after the death of Bishop Tagino for three times three weeks and one night. He occupied the episcopal see for seven weeks and two nights, preaching with his mouth the triune and one God, anointed by the Holy Spirit, and preparing peace among one another and throughout all the churches of God in love of God and neighbor.

After his death, Bolizlawo, having gathered many thousands of his men, occupied the borders of Dalmatia. He deceitfully stormed the newly rebuilt city of Coloci [Note: “Lobau, Libije, Lobije”; the annalist writes “Libuzuam,” the chronicler “Eoloci”]. After a great slaughter on both sides, he returned home with our captives.

Duke Conradus, of royal stock, paid the debt of human nature.

King Heinricus, coming to Confluence for the feast of Saint Martin, held a great synod to condemn Thiedricus, bishop of Metz, and the other rebels against him if they refused to convert, as well as to conduct many other affairs there. Fearing the king’s decree only slightly, they sent envoys concerning peace, asking pardon. The king, wounded by a recent injury, did not satisfy their request; nevertheless, at the counsel of his faithful men, he granted them permission to meet him at Mainz. Some of them neglected to come; others obeyed the king’s command, as was proper. They returned home carrying back not the joys of complete peace, but the expectation of further delays before it could be secured.

The Jews were expelled by the king from Mainz; and the madness of certain heretics was also rejected.

## 1013

Two burning lamps, withdrawn from the world, are stored in heaven: Lievitzo, archbishop of Hamburg, and Wonleph, priest and solitary monk.

When the bishop was seized by a fever and, as death already approached, hoped from God for the reward of his labor, he—being a man of extraordinary charity—wisely provided his people with a harbor of salvation. Among the clergy he had a certain vicar who was especially familiar to him, Odda, noble and faithful. Proclaiming him highly learned in divine and human law and supremely worthy of the episcopate, he himself first chose him for this office in sacred prayer. Then, perceiving the same desire in the unanimous acclamation of clergy and people, he joyfully fell asleep in Christ [Note: “Christ,” 2 February, in the Saxon Annals].

But the king’s spirit was harsh [Note: Here, as often elsewhere, the annalist wrote in verse], and the miserable thirst for possession rejected the supplications of those who pleaded, despising the voices of those who wept. Unwanus succeeded to this dignity as archbishop; but he is preserved by God’s grace for better places or times [Note: He died in 1018; this part of the Annals was therefore written earlier].

King Heinricus, entreated by Bolizlavo with many appeals, came to Parthenopolis. There Bolizlavo honorably sent his son to meet the king with various gifts. After peace had been established on both sides, he gladly received his son back, having been ordered to see the king himself as soon as possible.

From there the king turned aside to Werla and stayed there for some time, arranging many matters as was customary. He also decided to celebrate Holy Easter at Aachen. This was prevented by a sudden and serious illness, which so greatly instilled in him, by divine action, a fear of death that he restored to their former positions some whom he had stripped of their rank and restored to his favor others whom he had unjustly deprived of its sweetness.

When he recovered, necessity compelled him to celebrate the Easter festivities at the monastery of Paderborn, something previously unusual for kings.

A horrible darkness caused by a violent storm suddenly terrified people. It was followed by crashing and fire, and in certain places it overturned churches and caused much other damage, on 15 May, with the new moon, on a Friday.

At Holy Pentecost, Heinricus assembled at Merseburg amid the greatest gathering of people. There he encountered Bolizlavo with a great array of various gifts, surrendering all that he possessed, and himself, for the sake of peace. Receiving him kindly and allowing him to remain with him for a few days, the king, as befitted royal dignity, permitted him to return with conspicuous honor, though not without loss to his own kingdom.

Many envoys also came from Slavonia. Among them was Othelricus of Bohemia, who honored the king’s presence with gifts. Although anger still remained between him, his brother Geramir, and the aforementioned Bolizlavo, good fortune followed him: honor was granted to his homeland, while his brother was sent into exile.

The priest and monk Eguardus died in the cloister.

The wise King Heinricus, perhaps corrupted by the counsel of fools, miserably plundered the possessions of the monastery of Fulda because the life of the brothers displeased him. An opportunity for correction became an authority for destruction. The cenobites, bearing the yoke of Christ, scattered here and there as fugitives.

For 270 years, since the time of the first Charles, they had served God in that place; now, in our times, alas, they remain a spectacle to the world, a source of grief to themselves, and a cause of fear to others.

A violent disturbance of the air also occurred that year, so that buildings collapsed in many places and certain valuable objects struck by lightning perished. On Mount Lüneburg, a horrifying chasm opened in the earth, threatening the church itself with collapse and completely removing, for a time, the inhabitants’ hope of refuge, while they were terrified by fear.

After affairs in Saxony had been properly arranged, the king entered Italy for the second time. In the same year, an excessive flood occurred on 15 December, with the ninth day of the moon, on a Tuesday, bringing much damage. The king, making light of it, continued the journey he had begun and honorably celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Pavia.

Also in this year, 1013, a great dispute arose in the monastery of the great margrave Gero between Bishop Arnulfus and Count Gero, so that certain men on the bishop’s side scarcely escaped the danger of battle through the merits of Saint Cyriacus the martyr, whose feast they were attending in the presence of Abbess Hatewiga.

## 1014

A flood also came.

As the king hastened toward Ravenna, he held a synod. With the authority of the pope and the advice of the entire senate, he recalled his brother Arnoldus, who had previously been granted episcopal dignity but had been compelled by force to return, and established him as archbishop with due honor. After properly arranging other matters there, he departed and reached Rome.

The entire city went out to meet him. Although their acclamation was discordant, they nevertheless, as was proper, offered praise to their lord, exalting him to the stars. There he obtained for himself and his wife the imperial name.

After spending only a few days there, believing public affairs to have been properly arranged and having amassed immense sums of money everywhere, he hastened his journey back to his homeland, not without harm to many. Many hostages and others who had been handed over to Roman custody craftily began to flee as the emperor returned, violating the peace and again devising plans for war.

In this same year the sun, moon, and other stars gave rise to fear through mournful signs, which were soon followed by savage pestilence and sudden death.

Misico, the son of Bolizlavo, was also captured by Othelricus of Bohemia after his companions had been treacherously slaughtered. He was presented to the emperor and handed over to custody, thus renewing his father’s grief.

The abbess Hatwiga, of good memory [Note: Of Gernrode], died. Bernharius, bishop of Verden, also died; Wikkier, provost of Cologne, succeeded him.

That year the emperor came to Corvey to visit the brothers, whose life displeased him, and he wished to correct it by imperial authority. Thus many of them, defending the institutions of their fathers and raging more fiercely than was right against imperial law, miserably lost their reason. Though struck on the cheek, they did not offer the other, as monks should, but, without counsel, rebelliously prepared a disastrous fight. What happened afterward is more astonishing in our times than suitable for committing to writing. Nevertheless, seventeen of them were captured and handed over to custody; the rest followed the emperor’s commands.

In the same year the emperor’s charity entrusted to Lady Adelheida two sisters [Note: That is, two monasteries], together with their daughters and the possessions belonging to them: the monastery of the former margrave Gero [Note: Gernrode], which he had built for the remembrance of his own soul and that of his son, on 1 November, a Monday; and he placed his daughter-in-law, namely Hatuwiga, living a religious life, over the community of nuns. He also entrusted to her the noble community of Frethun on 2 November, a Tuesday.

Having received these communities, she nourished and embraced them nobly, as befitted so great a name, and cherished them. Instructed by the wisdom of her distinguished mother and aunt, through which she had formed herself, she diligently taught them with every devotion, so that in either merit or example they might not appear inferior to anyone in that way of life.

The emperor, persuaded by the appeals of certain people, returned Bolizlavo’s son to him unharmed.

In Bohemia, at Othelricus’s command, many innocent people were killed.

A most pitiable and astonishing event occurred in the western regions on 29 September, a Wednesday, in Walachria and Flanders. Horrible clouds appeared which, remaining immobile in a wondrous manner for three nights, presented threats to those who watched them. On the third day, an unheard-of crash of thunder arrived, disturbing the seas so that they swelled terrifyingly and, rising unbelievably high, clung to the clouds.

When the inhabitants, groaning, saw the misery of sudden disaster in the mass of such a great flood, and imagined that, as after the death of Julian the Apostate, ships might hang from the steep mountains or everything return to the ancient chaos, they were struck by fear of death and began to turn their backs. But, because sins stood in the way, many thousands of people suddenly perished in the waves, unable to escape the face of the angry Lord.

Emperor Heinricus celebrated the Easter feast at Merseburg. There Bolizlavo lost all the gifts he had sent him, together with the emperor’s favor, when he angered him by a proud embassy.

## 1015

Here too he celebrated Palm Sunday at Walbeck and bound envoys from Italy to himself by oaths. After departing from there, Duke Ernestus [Note: Of Alamannia] perished while hunting, carelessly killed by his own men.

A disturbance of the air and a stroke of lightning in the same year brought dangerous damage to certain parts of the monastery of Saint Mary on the western mountain.

Therefore, when the emperor again visited the brothers of Corvey, he changed by force certain privileges and customs of their predecessors, which they had possessed for 239 years through the grant of Louis the Pious. He removed the father of the monastery and brought in someone unknown—perhaps a good man for them—who, as though more learned, might correct their errors and teach those who had strayed to walk more cautiously along the path of the holy rule.

They, grieving excessively, lamented that their life, which had shone as an example to nearly all monks, was being treated as worthless, and encouraged one another to depart rather than submit to injury. Thus it happened that very few remained, while the others, miserably wandering, were occupied by the world. But when many were again converted by the grace of God, they were pleased to submit themselves to the rule rather than love vanity.

That year the emperor also sent an embassy to Bolizlavo for the restoration of the territories he had taken. He replied proudly, as he was accustomed to do, that he wished not only to retain what belonged to him, but rather preferred to seize what was not his.

The emperor, rightly angered by this, prepared for war and summoned thousands of strong men to arms. With them he soon reached the borders of Poland. At the first entry, divine assistance was present: the enemies turned their backs, nine hundred elsewhere fell by the sword, and Bolizlavo himself escaped from his presence at a distance.

The emperor therefore rejoiced in spirit, with his followers still safe, except for the distinguished young man Hodo, who, weak in strength but accompanied by a few brave men, laudably met an undaunted death. His body, as they report, was tearfully taken up by Misico, the son of Bolizlavo, provided carefully with everything necessary, and returned to his own men for burial.

The emperor, however, grieved that anyone for whom he had previously achieved triumph had perished. Therefore, warned by the counsel of his men, he ordered the army to return after gathering its forces [Note: “Having placed them,” in L.; “having stationed them,” in another witness].

Since they were unfamiliar with the roads, they made their way through a certain forest to a place scarcely capable of holding so great a multitude. Surrounded on every side by marshland and encircled by a crown of foliage, it offered brief rest to the weary.

The leaders and the rest of the young men assembled, boasting of victory through their own strength and vainly threatening those who were absent with a repetition of the slaughter. No one, as was proper, sought to exalt the God of heaven and King of kings with praises, to return worthy thanks to him for the benefits bestowed, or to pour out prayers concerning the future. Therefore [Note: “And therefore,” in E.] it happened that we had to mourn.

Meanwhile the assembled army was surrounded by sudden fear of battle. The enemies appeared from their hiding places, mindful of the wrongs done to their fellow citizens. They shut some approaches with swords and drove others back with darts and spears. A cry arose, and whatever joy there had been was confused with grief, while the two sides fought fiercely. The hostile side would have yielded if our sins had not called them back.

The baggage of a certain Fridericus was endangered. While he wished to come to the aid of his men, he was struck down before them all.

Then, with grief renewed, Count Gero, pitying the fate of his dying friend, is said to have plunged into the midst of the enemy. Now with his powerful right hand he struck these down to destruction; now he trampled others beneath his snorting horse. At length, exhausted by the excessive slaughter, he was the first among many to taste the cup of glorious death.

The others, seeing themselves hemmed in, groaning, begged God to be reconciled to them, recognizing that he was angry. But the sentence could not be withdrawn, since it is clear that they were to die for Christ. There was no place of escape and no hope of preserving life. Without doubt they devoted their mortal lives to him [Note: “Thus I have corrected it,” following the advice of the distinguished Haupt; another witness reads “they knew”], who alone can kill and make alive.

Then very many fought for their homeland and their brothers. In particular, the Maurician soldiers [Note: That is, the Magdeburgers], followers of the Lord, fell bravely, obeying him with steadfast courage, as they had agreed.

May Adelheid, Ira, Thietmer, Gera, Doda, and Volcmer, together with many others, live more happily in heaven.

Eido, bishop of Meissen, rendered his faithful deposit to heaven; Agilwardus succeeded him. Megingoz, archbishop of Trier, died; Poppo succeeded him.

## 1016

On 11 February, with the thirtieth day of the moon, a Saturday, resounding clashes of clouds, accompanied by frequent flashes of lightning and excessive rain, overthrew very many buildings.

The emperor properly celebrated the Easter festivities at Paderborn.

Count Heinricus, of good memory, died.

Wigman, count of western Saxony, after peace had been reconciled between himself and Count Baldricus, was treacherously killed on the road through the plots of evil men, at the persuasion of the latter’s crafty, faithless, and avaricious wife.

## 1017

That year Emperor Heinricus joyfully took part in the Easter celebrations at Ingelheim.

In the monastery of nuns [Note: Quedlinburg], on 22 February, the church of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin was dedicated. At Magdeburg, the church of Saint John the Baptist was burned together with the monastery and one monk.

That year the emperor again moved his camp against Bolizlavo, but, impeded by excessive pestilence and mortality among the people, returned home without accomplishing anything in war. Immediately he was informed that Gerhardus, in Francia, was stirring up much evil, with very many people killed by civil warfare. Disturbed by this, he prepared to go there.

There was a lunar eclipse on 7 November.

Thaetdeg, bishop of Prague, died; Eghardus, abbot of Nienburg, succeeded him.

## 1018

Emperor Heinricus celebrated the feast of the Nativity of the Lord at Frankfurt and Holy Easter at Nijmegen.

That year, peace having been restored through envoys, Bolizlavo received the emperor’s favor.

A comet was also seen for a long time that year. It announced to the wretched world grief from the immense devastation wrought by Thiadricus in the regions of Gaul, as well as pestilence and mortality.

Baldricus, bishop of Liège, died in this disaster; Fulmodo succeeded him.

Heinricus, bishop of Würzburg; Thiatmarus, bishop of Merseburg; Arnoldus, archbishop of Ravenna; Odda, the venerable priest of Magdeburg; Athilger, provost of Halberstadt; and very many other nobles of both sexes were taken from this light.

Thiatburg [Note: I moved this sentence here from its original position after “provost”], daughter of Margrave Bernhardus, cast off the burden of the world, turned piously to religion, and was placed in the heavenly air.

## 1019

After celebrating the Nativity of the Lord in the city of Pölde, the emperor passed the Lenten season at Goslar. From there he traveled to Walbeck, accompanied by the empress and his venerable niece Adelheida, abbess of Quedlinburg, together with bishops and the assembled household of God of both sexes. Zealous in alternating divine praises, he joyfully and solemnly celebrated Palm Sunday.

Then he reached Merseburg to celebrate the Easter festivities. There the wickedness of many was exposed and punished with deserved penalties.

In this same year Fridericus, brother of the empress Cunigunda, died.

The aforementioned Bolizlavo also subdued Rus’ with the help of the Saxons.

That year the emperor’s cousins, the sons of Count Hermannus, began to rebel together with Thiatmarus, son of Duke Bernhardus. They were nevertheless arrested and committed to custody. Meanwhile Thiatmarus [Note: “T.” should be read here] escaped by flight and returned to his homeland; but soon afterward, within a few days, all of them alike were pardoned through the emperor’s favor.

Thus this disturbance was quieted for a time.

## 1020

Bernhardus the Younger, duke and brother of Thiatmarus, gathered an army from the west in order to rebel against the emperor and entered Schalkesburg [Note: Hausberge on the Weser above Minden]. The same emperor besieged it with his men. But Bernhardus, yielding to justice, obtained the emperor’s favor through the intercession of the empress, together with his father’s benefice.

In the same year, a winter harsher and longer than usual grew fierce—so severe that many perished from the force of the cold itself. It was followed by an unprecedented plague and mortality that suddenly devastated almost the entire world. In a moment, in the blink of an eye, it carried away the healthy, those almost entirely confident in their safety, and those rejoicing amid their very banquets.

Amid these common and fearful losses, our metropolis, by the judgment of God—which is never unjust—was struck with a grievous wound to the very core of its being. Four sisters were taken away almost within a single hour: Emerita, one of them, called Sisu in the service of Christ; two others, Othellulda, daughter of Margrave Thiedricus, and Thiedan, who surpassed the distinction of their birth by the integrity of their conduct; and Hennikin, who, although youngest in age and rank, was nevertheless of excellent character.

Before them, at the very dawn of Holy Good Friday, Lucia, a devoted servant of the poor, having crossed the sea of this world, was conveyed by the grace of God to the harbor of blessed rest.

At this time, an event such as we know was never witnessed in any earlier age is said to have taken place: the apostolic pope celebrated the Lord’s Supper and the Easter feast at Babenberg with Emperor Heinricus Augustus, in fitting ceremonial service. There, after being honorably entertained for some time according to the due rite of service from the emperor and the princes, and endowed with abundant riches of many kinds, he gladly, wealthy and unharmed, returned to Rome, the mistress of the world, which had been entrusted to him by apostolic authority.

Then, on 18 July, a Monday, with the twenty-third day of the moon, beginning at the third hour of the day and lasting until after the sixth, a great circle appeared around the sun, possessing the color of a rainbow. Four other brighter circles embraced it at two places in the form of a cross. Although three of them gradually faded, two—the middle and the northern—remained for a very long time.

Meanwhile a certain Otto, born from the noble lineage of the Franks, had imprudently taken an unlawful marriage partner. Because Archbishop Arkanbaldus of the see of Mainz repeatedly rebuked him for this incest according to ecclesiastical custom, Otto, blinded and enraged by love, arranged ambushes everywhere and prepared to lay an impious hand upon this priest of Christ.

But, by the merciful prevention of God, he was frustrated when the bishop escaped. He attacked, captured, and handed over to custody the companions who followed the bishop by ship, treating them with many inhuman injuries. He was all the more ferocious because he grieved that the blood of the bishop, which he had thirsted for beyond right and law [Note: “Which he had avoided,” in L.], had been taken from him.

When this was reported by a swift embassy to Emperor Augustus, he deliberated with the bishops and the leading men of the entire kingdom. First through envoys, then through friends, and finally in person, he tried to recall Otto from this empty madness. Since Otto resisted and rebelled against all these efforts, they subdued him by common agreement with the penalty of anathema, so that, touched at least by fear of punishment, he might strive to restore the bishop to the citizens, the children of Mother Church, with worthy penitential lamentation.

Otto treated this with complete contempt. He gathered his forces and his wife into a certain fortress called Hammerstein, which, they say, was fortified by nature rather than by human art: walled on every side by rocky masses and so strongly protected by the encircling Rhine that it offered anyone a difficult approach, whether for besieging it or attacking it in any way.

Trusting in justice, Emperor Augustus therefore surrounded this place with every kind of siege operation, granting the rebels neither entrance nor exit. Celebrating the Nativity of the Lord there, he reduced them so greatly that those who had thought they would yield neither to arms nor to thousands of armed men were finally destroyed by the hardship of famine. On the approach of the celebrated feast of Stephen the protomartyr, they surrendered themselves and all their possessions to the emperor’s power, negotiating only for the breath of this life.

For it was worthy and just that he who on that same day had piously prayed for his enemies amid the bloody blows of those who stoned him should, through his intervention, reconcile peace to his friends, namely the children of Mother Church.

A wondrous event, unheard-of throughout all ages, is said to have occurred among the inhabitants of the northern region. The rivers Elbe and Weser, through an extraordinary mass of flooding, not only overflowed their channels but were violently torn, by I know not what immense force of winds, from their very bottom. Rising higher than the surrounding towns, fields, and all the neighboring territories, and even higher than the hills and mountains which nature had fortified with a certain exceptional elevation, they submerged everything.

What is more pitiable and more incredible to hear, they carried entire villages, with their inhabitants, from one bank to another and set them down in the same arrangement as before, without the buildings’ structure having been broken apart.

They also affirm that a certain church, formerly built through the pious diligence of the ancestors and properly enriched by the generous vows of the faithful who gathered there, was torn completely from its former position by the same force as the other things and transferred elsewhere.

The aforementioned rivers, the Weser and the Elbe, were seen to burn unnaturally at the surface with fiery, smoke-emitting vapors for three successive days and nights.

What should I say about the corpses? Their number, difficult for any human calculation, had gathered into several great heaps like mounds. As the flood subsided and the pious diligence of certain people sought to provide them with the due service of burial, they were found so entangled in enormous and tenacious coils of serpents, snakes, and every kind of pestilence of that sort that fearful human beings could find no way to loosen them, neither with iron nor with any instrument of human skill.

But concerning what happened, what is happening, or what will happen to these things, we leave the matter to Christ to examine—the Christ who had foretold that this same oppression of the nations would occur amid the bewildering roar of the sea and the waves.

### 1021

When these things had been accomplished, the august emperor, returning thanks to divine piety for the victory and prosperity granted to him, joyfully entered the regions of Saxony. Meanwhile, as time advanced and he hastened to revisit Saxony, to observe Palm Sunday at Walbeck once more in due order, and thereafter to celebrate the Easter festivities at Merseburg with due reverence, news reached the imperial ears during the journey that the venerable Archbishop Heribert had departed from human affairs. How constant that bishop of blessed memory had been in prayer, how sleepless in vigils, how solicitous in caring for the poor, and how diligent in every ecclesiastical observance cannot be adequately expressed by human eloquence; but the miracles divinely accomplished at his tomb bear witness to it. [Col. 0551D]

The emperor therefore completed the journey he had begun. With all, so to speak, the foremost men of Europe converging there, and envoys of various peoples hastening from every direction to serve him imperially, he celebrated the most holy joy of the Lord’s Resurrection, while the whole world already smiled, with extraordinary glory, as befitted such a man. When these Easter festivities had been completed with great rejoicing, he proceeded from there to Parthenopolis. There he celebrated the holy days of Pentecost with no less joy and worthy reverence at the residence of the most famous archbishop of that city, Gerō. [Col. 0552A]

Returning thereafter to the royal estate called Allstedt, and holding an assembly there amid the gathering of the entire senate and people, he soothed the pious with exceedingly sweet kindness, terrified the guilty with stern severity, and, with every exertion, fortified his homeland among the cities of this province [Note: [Col. 0551D] One word is missing.] Thus he successfully completed the whole year.

After this he approached the church of Halberstadt and celebrated, with the most fitting honor, the solemn festival of the holy martyrs of Thebes, while Bishop Arnulf officiated. Then, wishing to visit his niece, the noble lady Adelheid, and to attend the dedication of the basilica at Quedlinburg, he reached that metropolis, arranging the visit with great familiarity, although it had been unforeseen and unexpected and decided upon only shortly beforehand.

Who could describe the escort of nobles, both counts and bishops and abbots, when the august emperor arrived; or the care with which the royal offspring received him; or the procession of the rejoicing clergy and people; or how the priestly people advanced adorned with mystical and angelic ornaments; or the gathering of the virgins consecrated to God, free from deceit and gall and shining fully with dove-like simplicity? No one could explain by the service of the pen or by the living voice what their singing was like, how praiseworthy it was, how harmonious their assembly, what their dress and their very manner of walking were. [Col. 0552B]

And what should I say of the thanksgiving of the most victorious emperor? All the regions of the world serve him, bending their necks beneath him; and he rightly rejoices all the more over glory heaped upon glory, the more he is glad, by God’s gift, to be higher than the rest and pre-eminent among all.

But lest I prolong the hearing of my audience through the excessive length of my speech, I shall briefly touch upon how this most holy dedication was carried out at his command.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1021, the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, on a Sunday, with the moon thirteen days old, in the twentieth year of the reign of the lord Henry II and the eighth of his imperial rule, while he himself was present with his wife, namely the empress Cunigunda, and with the assembled bishops and nobles of the entire kingdom, this church and its high altar were dedicated by Arnulf, bishop of the church of Halberstadt, in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, and of holy Mary, mother of the Lord, and of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0552D] Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Saint Dionysius and his companions, and Saint Servatius the confessor.
