Contained here are relics of Saint Servatius the confessor, Saint Anastasius, Saint Vitalis, Saint Pantaleon, Saints Aquila and Priscilla, Saint Nicholas, a finger of Saint Mark the Evangelist, Saint Pancras, Saint Maurice and his companions, Saints Clement, Cornelius, and Cyprian, Saint Candidus, Saint Stephen pope and martyr, Saint Vitus martyr, Saint Justa virgin, Saint Valentine, Saint John martyr, Saint Alexander pope and martyr, and very many other saints. [Col. 0553A]

The altar in the middle of the church was dedicated by Gerō, archbishop of Magdeburg, in honor of the holy and most victorious Cross, and of the holy martyrs Laurence and Pergentinus, brothers, Saint Laurence and Vincent, Saint Blaise, Saint Christopher, Saint Erasmus martyr, Saints Cosmas and Damian, Saint Clement, and Saint Maurice and his companions.

In this altar is contained a piece of the wood of the holy Cross together with a thorn from the crown. Also contained in it are relics of the holy martyrs Laurentinus and Pergentinus, Saint Maurice and his companions, Saint Vitalis, Saint George, Saint Vincent, Saint Blaise, Saints Fabian and Sebastian, Saint Christopher, Saints Cosmas and Damian, Saint Eustace, Saint Quintin, and Saint Liborius the confessor. [Col. 0553B]

The southern altar was dedicated by Meinwerk, bishop of Paderborn, in honor of Saint Liborius, all the saints and elect of God, Victor, Candidus, Exsuperius and their other companions, Saint Maurice, Saint Hippolytus, Saint Pantaleon, Saint Cyriacus, Saint Adrian, and very many other saints.

The northern altar was dedicated by Eilward, bishop of Meissen, in honor of Saint Bartholomew the apostle and of all the apostles, evangelists, and disciples of the Lord. In this altar are contained relics of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, Saint Paul, Saint Andrew, Saint James, Saint Thomas, Saint Bartholomew, Saint Philip, Saint Matthew, Saints Simon and Jude, Saint Barnabas, Saint Vitus, and Saint Mark the Evangelist.

On the western side, the southern altar was dedicated in honor of Saint Remigius, Saint Cyriacus martyr and his companions, Saint Sixtus pope and martyr, Saints John and Paul, the Four Crowned Martyrs, Saint Boniface and his companions, Saint Kilian and his companions, Saint Donatus martyr, Saint Wenceslaus martyr, Saint Anastasius pope, Saint Innocent, Saint Magnus martyr, Saint Lambert martyr, Saint Magnus the confessor, Saint Odalric, Saint Sixtus, Saint Arnulf, Saint Meinulf [Note: [Col. 0553D] Thus in L.; C. has “Mumilf”], Saint Gundulf [Note: [Col. 0553D] Missing in C.], Saint Liutger, Saint Wigbert martyr, Saint Maximin, Saint Valerius, Saint Eucharius, Saint Louis, Saint Paulinus of Trier, Saint Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, who surrendered himself into slavery for the son of a widow, [Col. 0553D] Saint Ethelbert, Saint Martin the confessor, Saint Metron, and Saint Zeno.

In this same altar are contained relics of Saint Donatus martyr, Saint Quintin martyr, Saint Maternianus the confessor, Saint Adulfus the confessor, Saint Germanus the confessor, and holy virgins from Cologne.

On the western side, the northern altar was dedicated in honor of the holy virgins Saint Stephana, Laurentia, Justa, Pusinna, Saint Cecilia, Saint Petronilla, Saint Gertrude, Saint Walburga, Saint Agnes, Saint Agatha, Saint Thecla, Saint Barbara, Saint Afra, the holy virgins of Cologne, [Col. 0554A] Saint Mary Magdalene, Saint Mary of Zosima, Saint Felicitas and her seven sons, Saint Odilia, Saint Lucia, Saint Adeltrudis, Saint Margaret, and all the holy virgins.

In this altar are contained relics of the holy virgins Saint Laurentia, Saint Justa, Saint Agatha, Saint Walburga, Saint Margaret, Saint Lucia, Saint Juliana, Saint Columba, Saint Cecilia, Saint Sophia, Saint Felicitas, Saint Afra, Saint Praxedis, and Saint Gertrude.

Finally, this royal hall, venerably supported by precious relics [Note: [Col. 0554D] Thus in L.; C. has “supported” in the plural], was richly endowed by the distinguished emperor of the Romans, together with his wife the empress Cunigunda and the royal relative, namely the noble lady Adelheid, recognized as the glory of the nuns, and together with her sister Sophia, [Col. 0554B] while all the nobles of the kingdom stood present with the common consent of clergy and people. Eagerly desiring that apostolic promise: “He who sows with blessing will also reap blessings,” he honorably enriched this praiseworthy basilica with many gifts of gold and silk and with an hereditary endowment of the greatest extent.

Then, on the eighth day of this dedication, thirsting to the very depths of his being for the dedication of the church of Merseburg—“incorruptible things in place of corruptible, eternal things in place of temporal, things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him”—he rejoiced with no lesser glory.

When the joys of the dedications had thus been completed and brought to an end, as we have said, the august emperor set out by an accelerated route toward a certain place of the kingdom mentioned above, called Allstedt. Having summoned the leading men of Germany, as imperial judgment required, he held a great assembly there. Having wisely arranged royal affairs, as the skill of his keen intellect had taught him, he entrusted himself and all that belonged to him to the golden faith of the Saxons, who bore hearts of stone, in whom his fathers—the sceptered emperors—had fixed the firmest anchor of hope, ruling by victory and victoriously commanding by fruitful rule. [Col. 0554C]

He rejoiced in them as the pillars and distinguished protection of the kingdom, and as the illustrious, peace-bearing offspring of heroes, continuously clothed in the toga, which would never, or never too late, be torn. He had loved them with paternal affection, striving to place nothing above them except God and his kindred twofold crown.

When this had been done, and circumstances required it, while the nobles of the kingdom eagerly demanded it, he began to set out to cross the difficult Alpine passes. Having overcome their hardships, he traversed all the provinces of that region, conquering, ruling, and commanding, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the Italian regions with imperial custom, gloriously and with authority.

### 1022

After this, moving from place to place, he brought a military force against the walls of the exceedingly well-fortified city of Troy, whose inhabitants he had recognized as rebels against royal authority through a provincial embassy. Although after a long siege and with great exertion by his men he conquered it most victoriously, in the manner of his forefathers and ancestors, he either handed the inhabitants over to death or ordered those captured to be bound—those who had previously, with obstinate spirit, lamented their resistance to him. Thereafter, with God’s cooperation, he rejoiced that they had been subjected to his dominion [Note: [Col. 0555D] Thus I corrected it; C. has “to the lord”].

But he was not elated by these successes. Rather, endowed with the wisdom and knowledge of God, he attributed this victory not to himself but to divine mercy and apostolic merits, and hastened toward the summit of the Roman See, joyfully supplicating and worshipfully glorifying it.

After remaining there for a little while, and having bound the nobles of that kingdom to himself with peace and favor, he crossed the snowy peaks of the Alps at a swift pace. There followed such a mortality that it can scarcely, or not at all, be explained by gestures of the voice or even by the work of the pen. [Col. 0555B]

The august emperor, escaping it under heavenly protection, reached the German regions accompanied by only a few soldiers, apart from those whom Mother Europe had admitted to him as they came to meet him. Soon afterward he held a great synodal assembly in the western regions, bishops from various lands and very many other people converging from every direction.

When these matters had been completed as circumstances and time required, they reached a certain place called Grone. There, in the royal presence, between the two bishops Gerō and Arnulf, a wicked and detestable sedition arose, hateful to every pious person. I call it wicked because it was dangerous; dangerous because it would not perish, [Note: [Col. 0555D] I adopted this from N. P.’s Saxon Chronicle], but, as I fear, would destroy them; and, alas, the expectation of the death of both of them persisted.

Then it was announced that Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0555D] Thus I correct it; C. has “Bernhard”], had departed from human affairs [Note: [Col. 0555D] The word is appropriate, but the space allows only one word].

Erispa, a nun of blessed memory, having been removed from the world, was numbered among the palace of heaven. Liudulf the provost, released from the body, gave his spirit joyfully to God. Gerburg, the illustrious daughter of the margrave Ricdag, was her name. From the earliest flower of youth she had been ensnared in the most honorable exercise of the liberal studies and adorned with every kind of virtue’s insignia. On the third day before the Kalends of November she presented to the earth what belonged to it and to God what belonged to God.

### 1023

Oda, a most religious lady, firstborn of Margrave Theodoric, was stripped of humanity and restored to heaven. Burgareda, though tender in age, had nevertheless been excellently formed by the diligence of her teachers; distinguished both by moral uprightness and by the dignity of her lineage, she was overtaken by an untimely death.

The august emperor Henry, properly celebrating the albs and Easter festivities at Merseburg, while princes gathered there in companies from every direction, was rewarded with what seems rare or altogether unheard-of [Note: [Col. 0556D] The passage is defective; the word “altogether” is absent]: the dedication of the same church three times.

Gerburg, while holy religion still flourished, having been canonically nourished by her predecessors but now advanced in years, was removed from human affairs. [Col. 0556A]

Arnulf, bishop of Halberstadt, endowed with divine wisdom and eloquent in human learning, destined to be mourned throughout all ages, was placed in the palace of heaven. After his death, the entire clergy and people chose as their bishop’s vicar a certain Hermann, noble by birth but nobler still in the uprightness of his character and learning, their senior.

Above all, the leading men serving the blessed protomartyr Stephen in military dress, offering gifts of money multiplied a hundred times over, did not delay submitting their own hereditary estates to royal authority, so that their will—namely, the aforesaid election—might stand more firmly.

Since we do not know by what order this could not be accomplished—whether our sins hindered it because it was his heart’s desire to remain subject to his own parish, or whether divine mercy had reserved him, enlarged and perfected in virtues, for this work at another time—we leave the matter to divine judgment.

Frederick, the royal chamberlain, born from the noble stock of the lordly princes, … greatly enriched by imperial abundance, conducted himself nobly; formerly among the foremost household officials, … oppressed by the same illness that he had contracted in the Italian regions, he died in sleep beneath the burden of the muddy mass.

The emperor, struck by his death not a little, richly endowed the monasteries of this region with the greatest wealth, supporting the poverty of the poor … for the salvation of Frederick’s soul.

Archbishop Gerō, afflicted by many pains, leaving those who came after him not without … [Note: [Col. 0556D] Lacuna; L. supplies “grief”], died to the world but lived for Christ.

Bishop Ailward, sparing in worldly matters … [Note: [Col. 0556D] Lacuna; perhaps “human affairs”], and knowing how to preserve moderation in enjoyment, was overtaken by an unexpected death and lamented by his people with no small number of groans, as was fitting for such a man.

In the same year Bernhard, bishop of Mecklenburg, Eilhard, bishop of Prague, and very many other bishops died.

Thus, when so many and such great teachers of the holy Church had perished, the august emperor Henry, learning of so great a disaster, grieved not moderately but anxiously and sadly, and spent some time mourning in those regions.

Meanwhile, wishing to celebrate the festival of the Lord’s Nativity with worthy reverence, he traveled with a royal retinue, as was fitting, to Bamberg. There a desolate crowd of various bishops had gathered around him in companies, each wounded to the heart by the death of his shepherd. All remained suspended in trembling perplexity over their cares, wondering to whose governance they would be entrusted by imperial authority. [Col. 0556D]

But the emperor, having reached a decision with those whom he held highest in his counsels, resolved that Hunfrith should be made the vicar of Archbishop Gerō.

On the same day Brandagus, previously elevated from the abbey of Fulda and now successor to Bishop Arnulf, was confirmed as elevated to the dignity of the sacred order. Huprecht, a man of the highest ability, obtained the rights of the episcopate in the place of Bishop Ailward. Hiza, ordained to the priestly office, succeeded in the place of Eghard, bishop of the church of Prague. Very many others were also ordained to the same honor, by whom the holy Church remains supported with remarkable firmness; to name them individually would seem too lengthy.

### 1024

After this the emperor, tormented by various sufferings, prolonged his stay in the same place through frequent illness. At last, having recovered his strength after the burden of so great an affliction, he set out at a swift pace, intending to go to Parthenopolis if he could accomplish what he had held as his vow.

At length, after long deliberation and after overcoming the difficulties of the arduous journey, he celebrated Palm Sunday joyfully at a place called Allstedt. On the day of reconciliation, however, because of the severity of his illness, he dismissed the crowd that had gathered and, accompanied by only a few, celebrated the Lord’s Supper and Good Friday splendidly at Nienburg [Note: [Col. 0557D] Nienburch, according to Chr. S.].

On Holy Saturday, therefore, having convened the senate and accompanied by his wife Cunigunda, he reached Parthenopolis. To set out in orderly detail with what authority everything was properly arranged for the imperial reception would require a long account. But let us return to the matter.

After the joy of the Lord’s Resurrection had been celebrated with solemn honor, the august emperor, having received many gifts of gold and silk from the bishop of that place, hastened to the metropolitan church of Halberstadt.

Thus the athletes of Saint Stephen, leading choirs with the religious discipline of the canonical rule and singing every sweet-sounding thing in harmonious concert for the august emperor as he approached the royal palace, greeted him with an extraordinary and immense rejoicing. Moreover, the distinguished nobles serving the protomartyr Stephen according to military law attended the most victorious emperor Henry with every kind of wealth, serving him with what care; and the wonderful display of gold and gems in the gifts presented there with imperial dignity was such that it could neither be conceived in human minds nor comprehended in writing. [Note: [Col. 0557D] M. notes that the words are not lacking and, according to Leibniz, should be inserted.]

What more is there to say? Without delay he proceeded to Goslar. After spending ten days there, he hastened joyfully to a certain place called Grone, where he was wearied by a prolonged illness through the long course of time.

At last, made drunken by the cup of bitter death, which he had received as a gift from the supreme Archer, he laid aside humanity and was carried into the palace of heaven.

Then, accompanied by mournful lamentation and an incredible multitude, he was carried to the castle of Bamberg, according to what he himself had decreed. He who while alive had been a great consolation to the holy Church was laid in the earth with great honor, destined to be mourned forever, amid tears and sorrow.

Soon afterward, at a brief assembly of the entire senate, Conrad, born from the illustrious lineage of kings, was elected to the kingdom. He was anointed and crowned by Aribo, archbishop of the church of Mainz.

After a short interval of days, Gisila, already divinely predestined, came to Mainz at the king’s command and invitation, while he himself remained there. In the presence of the empress Cunigunda, who honorably administered everything pertaining to the occasion, she was blessed and crowned with royal honor by the aforesaid bishop, amid a great gathering of clergy and senate.

From there the king proceeded, accompanied by the queen, and they reached Nijmegen. After remaining there for some time, they traveled through the western regions and entered splendid Frethennia. There the imperial daughters and sisters, namely Sophia and Adelheid, joyfully met them and received them even more joyfully, as the law of kinship required.

From there they reached Dortmund, where the western bishops and leading men gathered. They spent some time there and then came to the city of Minden to celebrate the festival of the Lord’s Nativity.

### 1025

They spent the Epiphany of the Lord joyfully among the people of Paderborn; he arranged many matters. Then, setting aside all delay, he hastened rapidly to the metropolis of Quedlinburg, the distinguished glory of the nuns.

Departing from there, within the walls of the city of Parthenopolis, he observed the Purification of Saint Mary with the greatest diligence, and joyfully proceeded to Merseburg. From there, traveling through the cities and places of various provinces, he had subjugated by imperial rule the regions of the peoples under his authority.

A wondrous dew, exceedingly astonishing in our own times, occurred on 4 February. The sun, borne upon golden chariots, was pouring over the middle height of the sky with the marvelous brilliance of its radiance when it suddenly appeared to shine in a threefold form. This remarkable portent was afterward proved by the outcome of events. [Col. 0558C]

The king was preparing to celebrate the festival of the Lord’s Resurrection with solemn Easter joy in the city of Augsburg.

In the same year famine prevailed, and many places perished by fire.

When Bolizlavo, duke of Poland, learned of the death of the august emperor Henry, he was lifted up in spirit and filled to the depths with the poison of pride, to such a degree that he rashly presumed even to have a crown placed upon him. Divine vengeance soon followed this audacity of his presumption. For within a short time he was compelled to suffer the grim sentence of death.

After him his son Misuka, the elder by birth, swollen with no different pride, spread the poison of arrogance far and wide.

The king, having arranged the matters of state necessary in Saxony, entered Francia and celebrated Easter at Augsburg in royal fashion. Not long afterward, intending to go to Italy to obtain the imperial dignity and the kingdom of the Romans, he reached Tribur. There, amid a great gathering of people, he wisely arranged affairs and undertook the planned journey, accompanied by the queen.

They sent their only daughter, dearly loved, to be brought up by his beloved and adoptive sister, namely Adelheid, the abbess. Soon afterward, when the arrival of Lady Beatrice had been confirmed, the aforesaid imperial abbess came from Drubeck [Note: [Col. 0558D] Drubke, Drubeck, this side of Wernigerode] with her women to meet her and joyfully led her with them to the metropolitan church of Quedlinburg. [Col. 0559]

But with what honor, as befitted royal offspring, with what affection of charity, and with what care she was received and later [Col. 0560] brought up by the abbess herself, by the nuns residing in the aforementioned place, and by all subject to her; and with what disposition of character, words, and actions she progressed through each increase of age—no ability to know or eloquence to tell is sufficient.

For with what praise can I relate that among the first … . . . . .

[Col. 0559] (The remainder has been lost.)

## ANNALS OF WEISSENBURG

[Col. 0514]

### 974

The lord Otto the Younger, emperor, proceeded to the castle called Bossut [Note: [Col. 0513] Bossut, near Saint-Ghislain, east of Condé, not far from Chimay], burned it, seized its guards, and brought them away with him.

### 975

The lord Emperor Otto held a great assembly at Weimar. In the same year the emperor ravaged and burned Bohemia and, on his return, came to Hersfeld.

### 976

### 977

The lord Emperor Otto proceeded with a great army against Bohemia and burned the greater part of that land.

### 978

[Col. 0517]

### 979

### 980

The lord Emperor Otto proceeded to Italy.

### 981

Adalbert, archbishop of Magdeburg and abbot of Wissembourg, died; Sandrald succeeded him.

### 982

The bishopric of Merseburg was destroyed, and a building of extraordinary size collapsed at Magdeburg.

### 983

Branthoh was appointed abbot of Fulda; and Otto II, the emperor of pious memory, died [Note: [Col. 0518] W. supplied this thus: C. lacks “Otto II died”].

### 984

The boy Otto was again made king; he made the lord Abbot Bernhard abbot of the brothers of Hersfeld.

[Col. 0525A]

### 985

Otto, duke and son of Duke Conrad, invaded this monastery, namely Wissembourg, by force and distributed its estates.

### 986

Bishop Balderic died. Rupert was ordained bishop.

### 989

Abbot Gisilharius died; Gerric succeeded him.

### 993

A synod was held at Aachen under Dominicus, bishop of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0526D] W. This is in the third hand].

### 1000

The empress Adelheid died.

### 1001

Gerric relinquished the abbacy and elected Sigebodo.

### 1002

Emperor Otto III died; Henry succeeded him. Abbot Sigebodo died; Luithard succeeded him.

### 1004

Walter was ordained bishop. This monastery was burned. [Col. 0525B]

### 1007

Gerric, the pious abbot, died.

### 1009

Bishop Brun was crowned with martyrdom.

### 1014

Henry was called Caesar at Rome.

### 1024

Conrad II became king. Six days before the Ides of September.

### 1025

Emperor Henry died; Conrad succeeded him.

### 1026

The lord Brun, priest and monk, died.

### 1033

The oratory of Saint Peter at Wissembourg was dedicated by Reginbald, bishop of Speyer, and an eclipse occurred at the Nativity of the Apostles.

### 1038

A dispute concerning the Advent of the Lord was raised by William, bishop of Strasbourg.

[Col. 0525C]

### 1039

Emperor Conrad died; his son Henry succeeded him.

### 1042

The Hungarians expelled their king.

### 1043

The empress Gisila died. Abbot Folmar died; Arnold succeeded him. King Henry took Agnes as queen.

### 1044

King Henry invaded the Hungarians with an army and defeated them in battle; he restored their king to them. He himself was in that battle, together with Gebhard, bishop of Regensburg, Brun, bishop of Würzburg, and many others.

### 1045

Bishop Brun died [Note: [Col. 0526D] In a contemporary fourth hand].

### 1047

King Henry held a great assembly at Rome. There the pope was deposed, and Swidger, bishop of Bamberg, was placed in the apostolic see. By him the king himself was called august emperor, and Agnes was likewise called empress.

[Col. 0526A]

### 1048

Pope Swidger died; Bishop Poppo of Brixen succeeded him.

### 1050

The lord Brun, bishop of Toul, was raised to the apostolic see.

### 1052

A great synod was assembled at Mainz, presided over by Pope Leo and Emperor Henry.

### 1053

The lord Brun, who was also Pope Leo, fought against the Normans with a large force of Franks and Latins. But alas, for grief! Almost all his men fell in battle, and he himself was scarcely saved by the fortification of the cities [Note: [Col. 0526D] That is, by a fortified place].

### 1054

The lord Pope Leo IX died in Christ. Sigebodo, bishop of Speyer, died.

### 1055

A conspiracy of Welf, duke of Carinthia, against the emperor.

### 1056

The lord Pope Gebhard, who was also Victor, came to Goslar. There Henry III, august emperor of the Romans, died; his son Henry succeeded him.

### 1058

Henry, count palatine, seized by madness of mind, received the tonsure and monastic habit and entered the monastery of Gorze under the appearance of religious devotion. But he withdrew the foot he had placed upon the path of life when he entered, and, unsound in mind, threw himself back into the world he had despised. Moreover, alas, unhappy parricide, he killed Lady Matilda, daughter of Duke Gozelin, who had been joined to him in marriage. In the same year Archbishop Liutbold died.

### 1059

Count Henry, again moved to repentance, entered the monastery. [Col. 0526C]

### 1060

Conrad, bishop of Speyer, died; Einhard succeeded him.

### 1061

Conrad, duke of Carinthia, died. Agnes received the veil as a sign of testimony.

### 1062

Anno, bishop of Cologne, abducted King Henry from his mother and appointed himself his tutor. In the same year two popes were sent to Rome, the bishop of Parma and the bishop of Lucca; they fought among themselves even to the shedding of blood.

### 1065

On Easter Tuesday Henry IV girded on the sword at Worms, with Archbishop Eberhard of Trier giving the blessing.

### 1066

A comet appeared.

Adalbert, bishop of Bremen, a wicked man and counselor of King Henry, among the many evils he carried out, caused abbeys, provostships, and everything he could strip from the houses of the saints to be handed over by the king to supporters of his wickedness. In addition, he claimed for himself the two abbeys of Corvey and Lorsch.

The soldiers of the abbot of Lorsch, distressed by this, built fortifications to resist him [Note: [Col. 0527D] I supplied the word], placing guards in them.

Similarly, Sigifrid, bishop of Mainz, and the other bishops, dukes, and princes, together with all who followed justice, conspired at Tribur. They urged the king to annul whatever had been done on the bishop’s advice and to withdraw from him. This did not escape the bishop’s notice; for during the night he fled without anyone pursuing him.

Thus, by God’s grace, that sacred place of Saint Nazarius, together with the other places of equal law, was saved.

In the same year King Henry took Berta, daughter of Margrave Otto, as queen.

Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, of pious memory, died. Conrad, provost of Cologne, was elected in his place, but the people of Trier, indignant, refused to receive him. Instead, having gathered a large armed force, they attacked him by night and struck down all who resisted them. They took away with them the lord himself, the king’s envoy, Bishop Einhard of Speyer, all the leading men, and their possessions. Not long afterward they released the bishop of Speyer and his men, but they struck the aforesaid elder Conrad with pitiable torture—alas, unhappy men!

Count William, also called the Bastard, killed the English and their king and obtained the kingdom.

### 1067

At the tomb of the martyr Conrad, God began to perform many signs of his mercy.

Einhard, bishop of Speyer, died; Henry succeeded him.

Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, was sent to defend Rome, which was in danger and fearful of attacks by its enemies.

### 1068

The waters overflowed. A great and previously unheard-of failure of wine and fruit occurred.

### 1069

There was a severe and harsh winter. King Henry invaded with an army the barbarians established beyond the river Elbe, killed a great many people, destroyed cities, and burned temples together with their idols. He returned with a great captivity and victory.

In the same year Dedi, margrave of Saxony, raised his hand against the king and accomplished nothing.

Adelheid, wife of Duke Rudolf, was falsely accused of not having preserved her chastity and was deprived both of her husband and of her honor.

### 1070

Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, a man of extraordinary boldness, died on the Nativity of the Lord.

Likewise, the lord God revealed to the world the merits of his beloved Sebald through works of virtue.

### 1071

Rudolf, duke of the Swabians, again received his wife, whom he had rejected because of an evil reputation, after she had been cleared before Pope Alexander.

The monks and household of the monastery of Stavelot were freed from great dangers through the aid of their patron, Saint Remaclus.

A great synod was held at Mainz, presided over by King Henry and the archbishop, together with legates of the apostolic lord and bishops and abbots of various provinces.

There Charles, bishop of the Church of Constance, although not yet ordained, was accused and convicted of having entered the sheepfold not through the door but through the heresy of simony, that is, by money, and was expelled from the episcopate.

Otto, duke of Bavaria, was judged an enemy, as though he had conspired against King Henry, and his office was transferred to others.

### 1072

Sigifrid, archbishop of Mainz, led by the spirit, entered the monastery of Cluny. He was brought back by the citizens and did not persevere in his vow.

### 1073

Since King Henry had offended the princes of his kingdom in many ways, they hated him. Indeed, all Saxony, as though it were one man, withdrew from him and rebelled.

### 1074

King Henry, reduced to extreme straits, prayed earnestly to the Lord and promised repentance, and his kingdom was confirmed.

In the same year the castles that the king had built as an offense against Saxony were dismantled.

This is the King Henry who, after excluding the bishop, made a seat for himself at Worms.

### 1075

King Henry gathered the entire military force of his kingdom, namely a vast army, and brought battle against the Saxons beside the river Unstrut. After many thousands had been killed on both sides, the king finally emerged victorious.

Hermann, bishop of Bamberg, a lying man devoted to avarice, after sitting for ten years, was deposed under Pope Gregory with a condemnation he deserved.

Again King Henry entered Saxony with armed soldiers. He received the Saxons, who were asking for peace, but pursued them all with cruelty rather than favor.

### 1076–1086

1076, 1077, 1078, 1079, 1080, 1081, 1082, 1083, 1084, 1085, 1086.

### 1087

The empress Berta died. Conrad was made king at Aachen on the third day before the Kalends of June.

### 1088–1146

1088, 1089—1146.

[Col. 0528D] The final note was added at last by a twelfth-century hand:

### 1147

King Conrad took the cross for the expedition to Jerusalem.

## ANNALS OF LAMBERT

[Col. 0514]

974. Henry, duke of the Bavarians, and Bishop Abraham, together with Boleslav and Misicho, entered into a wicked plot against the emperor. But when the emperor learned of this abominable conspiracy, he summoned all his princes and asked their advice about what he should do. They advised him to send for Duke Henry, Bishop Boppo [Note: Würzburg], and Count Gebhard, and to invite them by proclamation to a formal assembly. Without delay, by God’s favor, he surrendered himself into the emperor’s power. In the same year the emperor marched against Harald in Schleswig.

975. Emperor Otto held a great assembly at Weimar [Note: Weimar]. In the same year the emperor ravaged and burned Bohemia [Note: “and burned,” etc.; four letters are missing].

976. Emperor Otto marched into Bavaria, expelled Duke Henry, and entrusted Bavaria to Duke Otto.

977. The emperor marched with a great army against Bohemia and burned the greater part of that land in a conflagration. Henry himself, together with another Henry, had also invaded Passau [Note: Passau]. When the emperor heard this, he hurriedly moved his army there, besieged the city, received Duke Henry back into his favor, and then marched into Francia.

978. Boleslav came to Emperor Otto at Easter [Col. 0518]. He was honorably received, loaded with great gifts [Col. 0517] by the emperor [Note: A. i. one letter is missing], and returned home. Henry was also present with another Henry; they were arrested and sent into exile. In the same year King Lothair suddenly invaded the palace at Aachen with a select force of soldiers and remained there for three days. But Otto the emperor hastily pursued Lothair with an army as far as the River Seine [Note: Seine] and the monastery of Saint Denis; he did not capture him, because Lothair escaped by flight.

979. Count Gero was accused by a certain Waldon after killing him in single combat, yet Gero himself was beheaded by the emperor.

980. Emperor Otto marched into Italy, and Abbot Gozbert built a church at Ordorf.

981. Adalbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, died, and Hicillarius succeeded him. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome.

982. The bishopric at Merseburg was destroyed, and a building of astonishing size collapsed at Magdeburg. In the same year Emperor Otto fought an extremely dangerous battle against the Saracens in Calabria. In that battle Henry, bishop of the church of Augsburg, was killed, together with many other bishops. In the same battle, on the Ides of July, the most valiant soldiers Udo, Gebhard, Gunther, and Berthold were killed, together with many others, as were Duke Otto and Abbot Werner of Fulda. The emperor himself barely escaped with his life [Note: “with life,” etc.; one letter is missing].

983. Emperor Otto II, returning to Rome after affairs had gone badly, died [6 Ides of December, manuscript 3] and was buried there. Duke Henry of Bavaria seized the kingdom, but was rejected by the princes.

984. The emperor’s son, Otto III, succeeded his father in the kingdom and was anointed king at Aachen by John, bishop of Ravenna.

[Col. 0520] 985. Gozbert restored the abbey [Hersfeld, manuscripts 5 and 6], and Bernhard succeeded him.

986. King Otto, still a child, ravaged the Bohemians but received Misicho, who came to meet him with gifts.

[Col. 0522] 987. The king entered Bohemia again and compelled it to surrender.

988. The heat of summer was excessive. Rupert, archbishop of Mainz [Note: “Rupert … succeeded,” from the Hildesheim Annals, year 975], died, and Willigis succeeded him.

989. The empress Theophanu went to Rome and subjected that entire region to the king? [Question mark in the source.]

990.

991. The empress Theophanu died. Fire rose from the Rhine and consumed the neighboring villages. The monk Godehard was made [a monk].

[Col. 0524] 992. King Otto besieged Brandenburg. Gerdag, bishop of Hildesheim, died [Note: O.; “Bernward succeeded him,” added in manuscript 2]; the lord Bernward, the royal chancellor, most skilled in divine and human affairs, succeeded him. He was ordained on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: So I corrected it; VIII in manuscript 1, III in manuscript 4, XV in manuscript 5. Manuscripts 5 and 6 add: “The sons of Count Henry—Henry, Udo, and Sigifrid—fight against pirates; one of them was killed and two were captured.” These matters are absent from the same manuscripts in 994].

993.

[Col. 0560] 994. Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg [Note: L.; missing in manuscripts 4 and 5], died, and Gebhard succeeded him. The sons of Count Henry—Henry, Udo, and Siegfried—fought against pirates; one of them was killed and two were captured.

995. Abbot Majolus died.

996. King Otto came to Rome against Crescentius, where he also appointed Bruno to the apostolic see; through Bruno, Otto himself was made emperor. Godehard was made abbot at Altaha [Note: L. f. e. i.; absent in manuscripts 5 and 6].

997. John, bishop of Piacenza, seized the apostolic see through the counsel of Crescentius. Bishop Adalbert was martyred.

998. Crescentius was beheaded by the emperor and hanged before the city with twelve of his followers. The false pope John was blinded.

999. Pope Bruno, also called Gregory, died, and Gerbert, also called Sylvester, succeeded him [Col. 0562]. The empress Adelheid died [Note: Manuscript A assigns this event to the year 998].

1000. The emperor discovered at Aachen the bones of Charlemagne, which many people had remained unaware of until then. Gaudentius, the brother of the martyr Adalbert, was appointed archbishop at Prague.

1001. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome.

1002. Emperor Otto III died, and Henry the Bavarian succeeded him. Margrave Eggihard, usurper of the kingdom, was killed at Pola.

1003. Most of the princes defected from the king, but after a short time they were corrected and received back into favor.

1004. A lamentable fire at Pavia. Brun, the king’s brother, who had resisted his election for some time, returned to his favor.

[Col. 0564] 1005. Bernhard, abbot of Hersfeld, died, and Godehard succeeded him.

1006. Gunther, a nobleman from Thuringia, became a monk at Hersfeld; later, at the advice of Abbot Godehard, he moved to Altaha. There was a severe famine.

1007.

1008. Nothger, bishop of Liège, died, and Baldric succeeded him. The monk Gunther sought the wilderness.

1009. The great church at Mainz, which Willigis had built, was burned on the very day of its consecration.

1010. Ansfrid, bishop of Utrecht, died, and Adelbold succeeded him.

1011. Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Erkenbald [Abbot of Fulda, manuscripts 4, 5, and 6] succeeded him. Brantho took up the abbey.

1012. The great church at Bamberg was consecrated by Eberhard, the first bishop of that see. Godehard left the abbey of Hersfeld, and Arnold succeeded him.

[Col. 0566] 1013.

1014. King Henry and Queen Cunigunda assumed the imperial title.

1015. The emperor departed with an army against the Poles [Note: Manuscript L reads “Poles”; manuscript 6 and edition II].

1016. There was a great hailstorm, and many people were burned by lightning.

1017. Megingoz, bishop of Trier, died, and Boppo succeeded him. The emperor again led an army against the Poles [Note: Poles, manuscript 6 and edition II].

1018.

[Col. 0568] 1019. The emperor received the pope as a guest at Bamberg.

1020. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, died, and Pilgrim succeeded him. Erkenbald, archbishop of Mainz [Note: Missing in manuscript 1], died, and Aribo succeeded him.

1021. A great earthquake occurred in Bavaria.

1022. [Note: Manuscript 2 has this as follows: “Godehard was made bishop of Hildesheim.”] The lord Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim, died [the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, manuscripts 4 and 5], and Godehard, abbot of Altaha, succeeded him [ordained on the fourth day before the Nones of December, manuscripts 4 and 6].

1023. Gero, bishop of Magdeburg, died, and Hunfrid succeeded him. Brantho, abbot of Fulda [Note: Missing in manuscript A], was made bishop of Halberstadt [Col. 0570]; Richard [Note: In manuscripts 5, r. f. e. a. f., these words are assigned to the year 1024; “succeeded” in manuscripts 2 and 6] became abbot of Fulda.

1024. King and Emperor Henry II died, and Conrad succeeded him.

1025.

1026.

1027. King Conrad was made emperor at Easter. Gebhard, the emperor’s brother, was compelled to become a cleric from a layman.

1028. Henry, the emperor’s son, was made king at Aachen by Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne.

[Col. 0572] 1029. Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, died, and Eppo succeeded him. Werner, bishop of Strasbourg, died, and William succeeded him.

1030. Emperor Conrad entered Hungary with an army.

1031. Arnold lost the abbey of Hersfeld, and Bardo succeeded him. But after half a year, when Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, had died, Bardo succeeded him; Rudolf, however, took up the abbey again [Note: Manuscript L reads “Hersfeld—undertook”; manuscript 1, “undertook the abbey of Hersfeld”].

[Col. 0574] 1032. Arnold, having lost the abbey of Hersfeld, died at Gellingin [Note: Gellingen, Gollingen: formerly a monastery, now a village on the Wipper near Frankenhausen, in the principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt. Hesse].

1033. The empress Cunigunda died. The emperor led an army into Burgundy against Odo.

1034. Albwin, provost of Hersfeld, was made abbot at Neuburg [Note: On the Saale].

[Col. 0576] 1035. Rudolf, abbot of Hersfeld, was ordained bishop of Paderborn, and Meginher, a venerable man, succeeded him.

1036. Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, died, and Hermann succeeded him. [In the same year the monastery of the Scots at Erfurt was built by the lord Walter of Glisberg; he was buried there, manuscripts 4 and 5.]

[Col. 0578] 1037. The monastery of Hersfeld was burned. Duke Gozelo killed Count Odo, and with him about six thousand [Note: Missing in manuscripts 2 and 6] men.

[Col. 0580] 1038. Godehard, bishop of Hildesheim, died, and Diotmar succeeded him.

1039. Emperor Conrad died at Utrecht [Note: Missing in manuscript 4] on the Monday of Pentecost, and Henry III, his son, succeeded him. Richard, abbot of Fulda, died, and Sigewart succeeded him. Regenbald, bishop of Speyer, died, and Sibicho succeeded him.

## Hildesheim Annals

[Col. 0511]

974. Henry, duke of the Bavarians, was captured and sent to Ingelheim.

975. The winter was long, severe, and dry, and on the Ides of May a great snowfall occurred. In the same year Archbishop Ruodbert died, and Willigis succeeded him.

976. Henry, duke of the Bavarians, having been deprived of his authority and excommunicated, lived among the Slavs.

977. The same Henry, with the counsel of the younger Henry, invaded the city of Passau. He was besieged there by the emperor and compelled to submit to him.

978. Henry, formerly duke, together with the younger Henry [Col. 0515] and Count Ekbert, was arrested by order of the emperor and assigned to exile. In the same year the emperor invaded and devastated Gaul with a great army.

979. Count Gero’s treachery was made public by Waldon. Consequently they fought each other outside the city of Magdeburg, in the field beside the Elbe, and killed one another. Finally, Count Gero, found guilty of treachery, was beheaded.

980. King Lothair, coming to the emperor with great gifts, submitted himself and his son to the emperor’s will. In the same year, after peace had been secured, the emperor entered Italy.

981. The emperor celebrated Easter at Rome.

982. Emperor Otto fought an extremely dangerous battle against the Saracens in the regions of Calabria, where not a few of the leading men fell. In the same year Otto, duke of the Bavarians, died.

983. The emperor held a formal assembly at Verona. There Henry the younger was brought back from exile and appointed duke of the Bavarians. In the same year the Slavs became rebels. Not long afterward, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, the most gracious Emperor Otto died, leaving the kingdoms to his son and namesake.

984. The emperor’s little son, namely Otto III, was anointed king at Aachen on the day of the Nativity of the Lord through the anointing of John, archbishop of Ravenna. But afterward, when the emperor’s murder became known, Henry, formerly duke, returned from exile, entered the city of Cologne with those who supported him, and detained the king. By invading the kingdom, he associated many Saxons with himself; at the following Easter they elected him king at Quedlinburg. Some of the leading men did not consent to this election, but, grieving more for the king’s cause, fought against it with considerable determination. They restored the king to his kingdom and again made Henry duke of the Bavarians. In the same year Otwin, a pious bishop of praiseworthy memory [Note: “Hildesheim”; a gloss in a later hand], ended his life.

[Col. 0519] 985. Osdag, a man of the highest charity and chastity, proven in holy religion, was promoted to episcopal dignity with the great consent of clergy and people. In the same year the Saxons invaded the Slavic lands. Misacho came to their aid with a great army, and they devastated the whole land with fires and much slaughter.

986. King Otto, still a very young child, came into the Slavic lands with a great Saxon army. Misacho came to him there with a very large multitude, offered him one camel and many other gifts, and also submitted himself to Otto’s power. They proceeded together and devastated the entire land with many fires and acts of plunder.

[Col. 0521] 987. The Saxons again ravaged the Slavic lands. Compelled by this, the inhabitants submitted themselves to the king’s rule, and the fortresses beside the Elbe were restored. The waters also overflowed; nevertheless, the wind overturned many buildings.

988. An excessive and sudden summer heat burned fiercely and monstrously from the Ides of July to the Ides of August and destroyed the crops. The king celebrated Easter at Ingelheim.

989. The empress Theophanu, the king’s mother, went to Rome, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there, and subjected the entire region to the king. In the same year Bishop Osdag died.

990. Gerdag was ordained bishop on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. In this year the Saxons ravaged the Abodrites twice in a great invasion. Many of them, including men of the highest distinction, were killed; others were drowned in the river. By God’s grace the Saxons returned in peace and victory. Misacho and Boleslav, Slavic dukes, had come into conflict with one another in grave hostility. In the same year an eclipse of the sun occurred, followed by no slight mortality among humans and animals, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

991. The empress Theophanu died. Fire, rising from the Rhine, burned the nearby villages. Pirates also ravaged Stavoren [Note: In Frisia] by plundering and destroyed other places along the coast. King Otto besieged and conquered Brandenburg with a great Saxon army and with Misacho’s reinforcements. When he had departed from there, a certain Saxon named Kizo, with the aid of the Liutizi, audaciously enough invaded the same city against the king’s command and unjustly subjected the aforementioned Slavs, in defiance of every human and divine right, to his own rule. He attempted frequent raids of banditry into Saxony beside the River Elbe; by God’s grace he did not prevail, but fled secretly like a fugitive robber.

[Col. 0523] 992. King Otto again approached Brandenburg with a strong force of his men. Henry, duke of the Bavarians, and Boleslav, prince of the Bohemians, came to him with a huge multitude to aid the king. Boleslav, however, Misacho’s son, was entirely unable to come in person to the lord king—for a great war against the Russians was threatening him—and he had sent his own soldiers [Note: The word is now erased; that is, “to Otto”] faithfully enough into the king’s service. But the lord king, trusting in the Slavs’ good promises and unwilling to resist his own princes, again granted them peace and returned from there to his homeland. They, however, lied in every respect as usual. In the same year Bishop Gerdag visited Rome and the threshold of Saint Peter for the sake of prayer; on his return he died at Cumae on the seventh day before the Ides of December. He had held the bishopric for two years, two months, and fourteen days. Misacho died, and his son Boleslav succeeded him.

993. Bernward, the royal chaplain, was ordained bishop of the holy church of Hildesheim on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. Kizo, who had previously been a rebel and an exile, repudiating the faith he had long before promised to the Slavs, submitted himself, his followers, and the aforesaid city of Brandenburg to the king’s rule. The king celebrated the holy day of Easter at Ingelheim [Col. 0525]. From the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist until the fifth day before the Ides of November, excessive drought and terrible heat prevailed through almost the whole summer and autumn, so that countless crops failed to reach their seasonal maturity because of the sun’s heat. This was followed by severe cold, a great snowfall, and at the same time a great pestilence and mortality among humans and animals. In that year the Saxons prepared an expedition against the Slavs three times but accomplished nothing; on the contrary, the Slavs harassed Saxony with frequent raids [Note: H. c. l. S. f.; written by a second hand in an erased place. The number DCCCCXCIIII was written by the first hand; what follows was written by different hands].

[Col. 0559] 994. The sons of Count Henry—Henry, Udo, and Siegfried—fought against the pirates by order of the emperor. Of these, one was killed and two were captured [Note: These words seem to have to be supplied, according to Lambert]. The fortress of Ilsenburg [Note: Ilsenburg east of Goslar] became a habitation for monks [Note: This was written by a third hand, which continues to the end of the year 997].

995. The king ravaged the Abodrites, demolished their cities and settlements. Boleslav, Misacho’s son, came to his aid with a great army, and the Bohemians also came with the son of the other Boleslav. The king withdrew into Saxony with his army intact. Baldric, bishop of Utrecht, died, and Ansfrid, a layman and count of good reputation and honorable life, succeeded him, as those among whom he had lived testified about him. John, bishop of Piacenza, and Bernward, bishop of Würzburg, were also sent to Constantinople [Note: “Constantinople” corrected from “ex late regis c.”] to seek a bride there for the king. Legates of the apostolic see, together with the unanimous Romans and Lombards, invited the king to Rome. The most powerful Henry, duke of the Bavarians, while visiting his sister, Lady Gerbirga, who had been afflicted by a prolonged illness, died at Gandersheim on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, amid the great grief of all. The Slavs ravaged Saxony with frequent raids. Bernward, bishop of Würzburg, also died amid the dangers of the sea, afflicted by a serious illness.

996. Indiction 9. Pope John died. Therefore the emperor, already in Italy, stirred by the report, sent ahead certain princes [Note: That is, “some”], and by public agreement and election had his nephew, the lord Bruno, son of Otto, who governed the Verona March, ordained to the apostolic see under the name Gregory. Through him, at the next solemn celebration of Pentecost, the emperor himself was consecrated emperor and patrician. After holding a formal assembly with the Romans, he decreed that a certain Crescentius, because he had often assailed the former pope with insults, should be carried into exile. But at the pleas of the new apostolic pope the emperor remitted everything. Not long afterward, when the emperor had left the city, Crescentius expelled the lord apostolic pope from Rome, stripped of all his possessions. The emperor wintered in Francia. The chapel of the Holy Cross [Note: Hildesheim; Life of Saint Bernward, chapter 10] was dedicated.

997. At Pavia, the pope, having assembled a council of several bishops, struck the aforementioned Crescentius with anathema. Meanwhile Bishop John of Piacenza, returning from Constantinople, was admitted to Rome and had seized the apostolic see through the faction of Crescentius. Therefore he was excommunicated by all the bishops of Italy, Germany, and Francia and Gaul. The emperor also marched into Italy to purge the Roman sewer, entrusting supreme authority to his aunt Matilda, abbess of Quedlinburg; in her, remarkable prudence shone forth beyond her sex.

998. The aforementioned usurper John was deposed by the emperor, blinded, and mutilated in the nose; Crescentius was beheaded and hanged before the city with twelve of his followers. In the same year a certain woman in Bavaria [Note: This portion had already been erased and was supplied with the help of the Saxon Annalist. John Staindel writes the following in his Chronicle: “A certain woman from the household of Saint Maurice at Altaha gave birth to five sons in a single delivery”] gave birth to five sons in a single delivery.

999. [Note: The slanted writing was supplied conjecturally.] Abbess Matilda, sister of Emperor Otto II [Col. 0561], died. Pope Gregory died, and Gerbert, also called Sylvester, succeeded him. The empress Adelheid also died [Note: From here another hand].

Under Otto III, in the year 1000, the growing thousandth year established the number of the reckoning, according to what is written: “The thousandth year surpasses and transcends every year.” Emperor Otto III entered the Slavic lands during Lent to pray to Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr. There, after assembling a synod, he established seven bishoprics and arranged for Gaudentius, brother of the blessed Adalbert, to be ordained archbishop in Prague, the principal city of the Slavs, with the permission of the Roman pontiff and at the request of Boleslav, duke of the Bohemians—out of love and honor especially for his venerable brother, the worthy pontiff and martyr. Returning from there, he celebrated Palm Sunday festively at Naples. He then devoutly celebrated Easter at Quedlinburg. He observed the feast of Pentecost with fitting devotion at Aachen. At that time, moved by wonder, he ordered the bones of the great emperor Charlemagne to be dug up from within the church, contrary to divine religious practice, and then found marvelous varieties of things hidden in the tomb. But, as later became clear, he incurred the vengeance of the eternal judge on account of this. For the aforesaid emperor appeared to him after the commission of so great a deed and foretold to him [Note: Added by a fifteenth-century hand: “that his death would come more quickly.”].

1001. Indiction 14. [Note: The years 1001–1022, middle portion, are written by another hand.] The emperor celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Rome. Bernward, the bishop, arrived there during the Epiphany and complained about the many attacks of Archbishop Willigis, especially concerning the synod that Willigis had held with foreign bishops in his own church, namely at Gandersheim. In the presence of Pope Gerbert [Col. 0561; now erased; a fifteenth-century hand reads “Sylvester”] and Emperor Otto III, he completely annulled by synodal authority the metropolitan’s unlawful usurpation. Gerbirga, abbess of Gandersheim, died on the Ides of November.

While Otto III was emperor, indiction 15, 1002. Emperor Otto celebrated the Nativity [Note: Namely, of the Lord] at Todi with the lord apostolic pope. Proceeding from there toward Rome, he visited the town of Salerno, but, gravely afflicted by fever and the Italian illness, he departed this life by an untimely death on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, amid the universal grief of all—alas, what sorrow! Henry, duke of the Norici, a man outstanding in every ecclesiastical perfection, succeeded him, being ordained by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz [Note: “And by Bishop Bernward” was added by a fifteenth-century hand, incorrectly understood from the Life of Saint Bernward, chapter 38]. In the same year the new King Henry celebrated the Nativity of Saint Lawrence at Paderborn [Note: The name seems formerly to have been written “Paderborn.”]. There Lady Cunigunda received the royal blessing and the imposition of the crown from the aforesaid metropolitan. Sophia, elected to govern Gandersheim, also obtained, through the intervention of the princes, Lord Bernward’s permission to receive the blessing there from the pallium-bearer [Note: That is, Archbishop Willigis].

In the second year of Henry’s reign, indiction 1, 1003. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Frankfurt and Easter at Quedlinburg. Hermann, duke of the Alemanni, resisted the king’s election for some time but submitted himself to royal authority and, through the intervention of the queen and the princes, remained in his position of honor. Henry, son of Count Berthold, Bruno, the king’s brother, and both Boleslavs—the Polish and the Bohemian—treacherously defected from the king as guilty of high treason. But Henry, coming and fleeing to the king, was committed to custody at Giebichenstein [Note: Giebichenstein on the Saale]. Stephen, king of Hungary, came with an army against his uncle, King Julius. When he had captured him with his wife and two sons, they compelled his kingdom by force to accept Christianity. The chapel of Saint Martin [Note: Hildesheim] was dedicated.

In the third year, indiction 2, 1004. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Pavia; there the bishop of Verona and certain other leading men of the Italian kingdom came to him with royal gifts. Bruno, the king’s brother, also obtained the king’s favor through the intervention of Lady Gisla, his mother. A lamentable fire occurred in the city of Pavia.

[Col. 0563] In the fourth year of the same king, the most glorious Henry, indiction 3, 1005. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Thornburg and remained in the regions of Saxony until Lent. He spent Lent at Thiele and Easter at Aachen. Bernhard, abbot of Hersfeld, died, and Godehard, a man of monastic life, highly proven in holy conduct, succeeded him.

In the fifth year of Henry’s reign, indiction 4, 1006. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Paderborn; he joyfully observed the celebration of Easter at Nijmegen. Gunther, moved by divine piety, renounced the world and its pomp and became a monk. There was a severe famine throughout almost the entire land.

Under Henry, in the sixth year, indiction 5, 1007. The king again celebrated the Nativity at Paderborn. He came to Gandersheim for the Epiphany and wisely settled, through prudent judgment, the hateful dispute between Archbishop Willigis and Bishop Bernward concerning that same church. The lord Bernward, in the presence of the king, the archbishop, and the other leading men of the kingdom, dedicated that church and exercised episcopal authority there without anyone’s opposition.

In the seventh year of Henry’s reign, indiction 6, 1008. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Paderborn, Easter at Merseburg, and Pentecost at Cologne. Liudolf, metropolitan of Trier, died, and Meinzoz, the king’s chief notary, succeeded him. Nothger, provost of the monastery of Saint Gall and bishop of Liège, departed to Christ. After him, Balderic, chamberlain of Regensburg, entered upon the office. Gunther, a monk proven in holy conduct at the monastery, became a hermit.

While he was not yet emperor, in the eighth year, indiction 7, 1009. The king celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Salzburg and Easter at Augsburg. Rethar, bishop of Paderborn, died on the second day before the Nones of March, and Meinwerk, the king’s chaplain, succeeded him. The monastery at Mainz, built by Willigis with the greatest splendor and dedicated to divine honor and the relics of Saint Martin in anticipation of its future consecration, perished in a lamentable fire on the third day before the Kalends of September.

In the ninth year of his reign, indiction 8, 1010. The king celebrated the Nativity at Paderborn and Easter at Regensburg. Ansfrid, bishop of the church of Utrecht, died, and Adelbold succeeded him.

In the tenth year of his reign, indiction 9, 1011. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Frankfurt and came to Corvey at the beginning of the fast. There pious Duke Bernhard died on the fifth day before the Ides of February. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Michael at Lüneburg with great lamentation at his funeral, a monastery that he himself had built from the foundations and in which he had gathered a community of monks. After him his son Bernhard [Note: “Bernhard”—is he a namesake? A fifteenth-century hand writes “Benno”; see below] obtained the duchy. At this time Willigis, metropolitan of Mainz, also departed to Christ; Erkanbald, abbot of Fulda, entered his place. Our bishop Bernward consecrated him on the Kalends of April.

In the eleventh year of Henry’s reign, indiction 10, 1012. The king celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Thornburg and Easter at Liège [Note: Liège]. From there he proceeded to Bamberg with the greatest royal reverence. There the venerable monastery, the noble and special project of the lord king himself, was consecrated on the second day before the Nones of May by Eberhard, the first bishop of that see, with the consent and assembly of all the bishops on this side of the Alps, to the praise and honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his most precious martyr George, and for the protection of all God’s saints. Dagano, archbishop of Naples, died, and Walthard, provost of that church, succeeded him. After he too died only seven weeks later, Gero, a man perfect in every ecclesiastical endeavor, succeeded him. Godehard, having left the abbey of Hersfeld, returned once more to Altaha.

[Col. 0565] Under Henry, in the twelfth year, indiction 11, 1013. The king celebrated the Incarnation of the Lord at Paderborn. Later, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, because of sins, while the devil lay in wait, the principal church of the Hildesheim church was set alight by fire during the night; but, through the aid of divine mercy alone, it was quickly extinguished, thanks be to God! Yet this remains for us to mourn—ah, ah!—because in that fire, together with the most precious ornament of the missal, an immeasurable and irrecoverable quantity of books perished. The king celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary at Naples. Coming from there to Werla, he was seized by a serious illness and lay ill for five weeks. Christian, bishop of Passau, died, and Beringer, dean of that place, succeeded him. Godescalc, priest and provost of our community, died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.

Under Henry, in the thirteenth year, indiction 12, 1014. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Pavia. From there, proceeding with royal retinue to Rome, he received the diadem of the imperial crown from Benedict, the vicar of Saint Peter, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, by the general election. His wife, Lady Cunigunda, also obtained the same honor, with God’s consent. Thus, made emperor by the grace of God, he returned to Pavia. There he celebrated holy Easter. Returning from there, he joyfully observed Pentecost at Bamberg. At that time he ordered the privileges containing the rights of that place to be written down [Note: “privileges” corrected from “privileia” by the same hand], confirmed by the seal [Note: “with a sign,” added, or “by the seal,” by the same hand] of his authority and strengthened by the apostolic authority of the Roman pontiff, so that they might be secured by their ban, while Christ, King of kings, reigns forever and beyond.

In the fourteenth year of his reign and the second year of his empire, indiction 13, 1015. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Paderborn. He arranged that the dukes Udalric of the Bohemians and Boleslav of the Poles would come to him at Merseburg for Easter. Udalric appeared on the appointed day to clear himself of the charge of the crime of which he was accused. Because Boleslav neglected to do so, the emperor entered Poland with a strong force of his men during that summer. Duke Ernest was unexpectedly struck by an arrow from his own soldier Adalberhd while hunting and died a lamentable death. Lambert the warrior fell. In this year, namely of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1015, while Henry had reigned twelve years [Note: Read “fourteen”], and had already ruled as emperor for two years by God’s grace, the crypt of our monastery [Note: Saint Michael’s at Hildesheim], indiction 13, was dedicated on the third day before the Kalends of October by Bernward, the most venerable bishop of that church, by Tiederic, the most worthy bishop of the church of Minden, and by Ekkihard, the venerable bishop of the city of Schleswig, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and of his Mother, the perpetual Virgin, and for the special protection of the blessed archangel Michael and the entire heavenly host.

In the fifteenth year of his reign and the third year of his empire, indiction 14, 1016. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Paderborn. Hail of great size fell, and many people perished, burned by lightning. Count Wigmann was killed on the second day before the Nones of October.

1017, indiction 15. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Paderborn. In the same year he again entered Poland with an army. Meingoz, bishop of Trier, died, and Boppo succeeded him. Aeid, bishop of Meissen, fell asleep; after him Hildivard entered the office. Priest Liudolf died on the fourth day before the Nones of August; Priest and dean Godescalc died on the ninth day before the Kalends of October.

In the fifth year of his empire, indiction 1, 1018. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Paderborn and Easter at Bamberg. Henry, margrave of the Bavarians, died, overtaken by sudden death. In that year, during Lent at Goslar, while the emperor was present with the bishops and the other leading men of the kingdom at a synod, the lord Bishop Bernward separated Godescalc, son of the governor Eggihard, and Gertrud, daughter of Count Egberhard. Priest Maccho died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0567] In the sixth year of his empire, under Henry, indiction 2, 1019. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Würzburg. Later he marched with an army against Duke Bernhard to the fortress of Schalksburg, and there, thanks be to God, settled everything peacefully. In that year, at Easter, he received the pope from Rome as a guest at Bamberg.

1020, indiction 3. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Hammerstein. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, exchanged mortal life for angelic life on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April; Pilgrim entered his place. Erkenbald, metropolitan of Mainz, was taken from this life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September; after him Aribo, a man highly proven in the holy church, was appointed. 

In the eighth year of Henry’s empire, indiction 4, 1021. The emperor celebrated the Incarnation of the Lord at Regensburg. A great earthquake occurred in the regions of Bavaria on the fourth day before the Ides of May, at the tenth hour of the day, on the sixth day of the week after the Ascension of the Lord.

In the ninth year of the Empire, indiction 5, 1022. The emperor spent Christmas at Thorneburg. Thiedricus, bishop of Mimigardivord, died on the tenth day before the Kalends of February; Sigifridus, abbot of Parthenopolis, succeeded him. Thiedricus, bishop of Minden, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March. After him Alberich, provost of that same place, was elected, but, overtaken by death, he neither received consecration nor reached the episcopal chair. Sigiberhdus, however, entered the bishopric. The venerable lord Bernward, bishop of the people of Hildesheim, migrated to Christ on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December:

> May God grant him the fellowship of the eternal kingdom,
>
> May he, living in the citadel of heaven, be Lazarus’s companion. Amen.

In his place the holy church beneficially appointed to itself and its people the lord Godehard, formerly abbot of Herfeld and of Altaha.

[Note: [Col. 0567] From here another hand.]

In this year—namely, 1022 according to the incarnation of the Word, but the twenty-first year of the reign of the emperor Heinrich, and the thirty-first year of the episcopate of the venerable lord Bernward, bishop of this church, in indiction 5—on the third day before the Kalends of October, the oratory of this monastery, situated outside the walls of the city of Hildesheim and constructed by the aforesaid bishop with the greatest care for the dignity and benefit of monastic life, was dedicated and, moreover, consecrated with every devotion proper to ecclesiastical religion. It was dedicated in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and of his Mother, ever-Virgin Mary; of the salutary wood, the venerable and life-giving cross; as the special protection of the holy archangel Michael and of the entire heavenly host; and to the praise and veneration of all God’s saints.

It was dedicated by Bernward, the venerable steward of that church; by the honorable Unewan, archbishop of the church of Hamburg; by Ekkihard, bishop of Schleswig; and also by Bernhard—[Note: [Col. 0567] “Be........” indeed: fifteenth-century hand, “Bennone quondam.”]—the most reverend bishop of the church of Aldenburg, for the safeguarding of ecclesiastical peace and for the salvation and defense of Christendom.

And the estates and possessions pertaining to that place were so firmly established under the ban of their authority that, if anyone should seize anything from them by force or voluntarily, he would be subject to perpetual damnation. Whoever should in any way be liable or hostile to this place was to be condemned by perpetual anathema and erased from the land of the living. Let it be so, let it be so, let it be so.

> May this truly come to pass, with Christ reigning forever.

But soon the dwelling of that same monastery was entrusted for governance to the abbatial office of Goderamnus, provost of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon.

> For as long as he lived in this world,
>
> he piously ruled it.

1023, indiction 6. The emperor solemnly celebrated Christ’s incarnation at Merseburg. Gero, archbishop of Parthenopolis, died. Hunfrithus, a man in every respect highly esteemed for the service of the holy church, succeeded him. Arnolfus, bishop of Halberstadt, died; Branthog, formerly abbot of Fulda, succeeded him. Bernhard, bishop of Aldenburg, was elevated; after him Reinoldus was appointed.

The lord Godehard, in the first summer after his ordination, honorably began to build, by generous expenditure, a beautiful monastery on the southern [Note: [Col. 0569] “O......t......ali”; fifteenth-century hand: “orientali.”] side of our principal church. Wolframnus, elected from the same congregation, succeeded the lord Godehard. Count Liudolf died.

1024, indiction 7. Emperor Heinrich honorably celebrated Christ’s nativity at Bamberg, Easter at Parthenopolis, and Pentecost at Goslar. He later came to Gruna, where he fell ill and took to his bed; amid the grief of the whole kingdom—ah, ah!—he laid down his human life on the third day before the Ides of July. He had reigned twenty-two years, five weeks, and one day. May his soul rest in peace.

> Grant rest to the soul, you who govern all things everywhere!

On the sixth day before the Ides of September, Cuonradus entered upon the kingdom in his place. Our elder Godehard built his court on the eastern side of our city, at a place called Sulza.

1025, indiction 8. King Cuonradus celebrated Christ’s nativity at Minden with immense glory and rejoicing. There he also encountered many who had not been present at his aforementioned election; he received them all into his favor as men devoted to him. He celebrated Easter at Regensburg.

The lord Godehard began to inhabit a beautiful mountain on the western side of our city, which he later dedicated under the title and name of Saint Maurice, his supreme patron.

1026, indiction 9. [Note: [Col. 0569] From here another hand.] King Cuonradus magnificently celebrated Christ’s nativity at Lindburg. Wolframmus, abbot of Altaha, died. Ratmundus was elected in his place and, by God’s grace, consecrated.

Father Godehard solemnly consecrated our aforesaid new monastery, on the western side of our principal church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, in honor of the passion, resurrection, and ascension of Christ. Ekkihard, bishop of Schleswig, died. Rodulfus, elected from the clergy of Cologne, succeeded him.

1027, indiction 10. At Easter, King Cuonradus was made emperor at Rome. His son Heinrich began to be duke of Bavaria.

A general synod of bishops was held at Frankfurt in the presence of Emperor Cuonradus. At it the lord Godehard canonically retained his diocese over the territory of Gandersheim, with the testimony of seven bishops: Bruno of Augsburg, Eberhard of Bamberg, Meginwrec of Paderborn, Meginhard of Würzburg, Hildiward of Zeitz, Sigiberht of Minden, and Bruno of Merseburg.

At this synod Gebehardus, the emperor’s young brother, was compelled to lay down his arms and received the clerical tonsure. Wiggerus, a priest of our congregation, died.

1028, indiction 11. The emperor celebrated the Lord’s incarnation at Regensburg. Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, held a general synod with his suffragan bishops at Geisleden [Note: [Col. 0570] Geisleden in the Eichsfeld region.]. Among other ecclesiastical matters, a certain free man was accused there of the murder of Count Sigefridus. He cleared himself by means of red-hot iron and, after being tested by synodal decree two nights later, appeared unharmed.

Misako, who for several years had tyrannically usurped the kingdom of the Slavs against the imperial majesty, violently invaded the eastern regions of Saxony with a powerful army of his men. After carrying out burnings and plundering, he slaughtered the men, took many women captive, and drenched an utterly innumerable multitude of children in a pitiful and unheard-of slaughter. Through himself and his men—indeed, the devil’s satellites—he exercised an excessive savagery of cruelty in the lands of Christians, while God looked on.

1029, indiction 12. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Ingelheim. Brun of the city of Augsburg, the emperor Heinrich’s brother, died. Eppo, the royal chaplain, succeeded him.

A general synod was held at Palithi, with the emperor presiding and eleven bishops present. There the archbishop of Mainz again began to trouble the lord Godehard concerning Gandersheim.

Werinherus, bishop of Strasbourg, departed from the world; after him Willehaelmus, the queen’s chief chaplain, entered the office. Envoys of the Liutizi came to the emperor at Palithi and asked his help against the tyrant Misako, promising that they would faithfully serve him. And wickedness deceived itself.

1030, indiction 13. Emperor Cuonradus was in Hungary with his army. Goderamnus, the first abbot of Hildesheim, died on the second day before the Kalends of July. Aedelberhdus, provost of the monastery of the mountain of Saint John the Baptist at Hersfeld [Note: [Col. 0571] Hersfeld.], a monk of upright conduct, succeeded him. He was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January by the lord Godehard at the principal altar of the church of Saint Hildesheim.

In this year the lord Godehard, bishop, and Aribo, metropolitan of Mainz, were reconciled with one another concerning Gandersheim. For the metropolitan himself privately met Father Godehard and confessed and announced that he had been in error concerning that same parish. He promised every fraternal satisfaction and perpetual silence concerning the former dispute, under the true testimony of Christ and the church; he humbly asked that his previous errors be forgiven him by God. This has therefore been truthfully recorded here because the lord Godehard himself repeatedly and publicly declared the same thing in his preaching, confirming that it was true.

Unewan, archbishop of Hamburg, died; his provost Liebizo succeeded him. He also founded a beautiful church at Holthunon [Note: [Col. 0571] Osterholz.], in honor of Saint Benedict the abbot, suitable for monastic life.

1031, indiction 14. Emperor Cuonradus celebrated Christmas at Paderborn and Easter at Nijmegen. In the same year the emperor’s son, King Heinrich, himself duke of Bavaria, and Stephen, king of Hungary, confirmed peace with one another by oath.

Heinrich, son of King Stephen and duke of the Rus’, was torn apart and killed by a boar during a hunt, dying lamentably. The emperor invaded the Slavs with a small Saxon army in the autumn. He compelled Mysacho, who had long resisted him, to restore the region of Lusatia, together with several towns and the booty that had been taken in Saxony in earlier years, and to confirm peace by oath.

But only after the space of a month was Mysacho driven out by a sudden attack from his brother Bezbriemo and forced to flee to Oudalricus in Bohemia. But Bezbriemo sent the emperor a crown and the other royal insignia that his brother had unjustly usurped, and promised through his envoys that he would submit himself humbly to the emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0571] From here another hand.]

Arnolfus, abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, outstanding in divine and human matters, was accused by certain brothers there of some crime and was pitifully deprived of his proper dignity. In his place Bardo, administrator of the monastery of Verdun, was installed through the influence of Empress Gisla. Geroldus, a monk of Fulda, succeeded this same Bardo.

Wiggerus, bishop of Verden, died; after him Thietmarus entered the office. In the same year Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, of pious and venerable memory, went to Rome for the sake of prayer. Departing from there, he died at Cumae on the eighth day before the Ides of April—ah, ah! Bardo, who had recently been appointed abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, obtained the primacy of his dignity.

But soon Roudolfus, a monk of Boppo and provost of the monastery of Stavelot, succeeded him in the abbatial dignity; by the emperor’s decree the monastic observance there was changed through him.

[Col. 0573] 1032, indiction 15. Emperor Chuonradus celebrated Christmas at Goslar and Easter at Seligenstadt. In this year Bezbriemo was killed by his own men because of the monstrous savagery of his tyranny, and not without the plotting of his brothers.

Miseko immediately returned home. Recognizing that, because of the immoderate insolence he had exercised in previous years, everything he had suffered had rightly befallen him, he sent envoys to the emperor and requested a time to present himself and make appropriate satisfaction. Later, with the emperor’s consent, he came to Merseburg and, on the Nones of July, humbly surrendered himself into the emperor’s power, having laid aside his crown and all royal adornment.

The emperor received him more mercifully than he himself had expected, and divided between him and a certain paternal cousin of his, Thiedricus, the kingdom which he had previously possessed alone. Nevertheless, he later usurped it again for himself alone.

Oudalricus, however, invited by the same royal command, refused to come. Later, when the emperor was seated at Werben [Note: [Col. 0573] Werben on the Elbe.] for the purpose of pacifying the kingdom against the Liutizi, Oudalricus came to him. After he had also been convicted by reason of the ambushes he had laid for the emperor—ambushes he confessed to having made two years earlier—the emperor sent him into exile.

Sigifrithus, bishop of the church of Mimigardivord, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of December; Herimannus, provost of Cologne, succeeded him. Liebizo, archbishop of Hamburg, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of September; Herimannus, provost of the monastery of Halberstadt, succeeded him.

Arnolfus, abbot of Hersfeld, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of January and was buried at Gellingen, where he had then lived by permission to remain. But after three days and as many nights he was taken from there, dug out of the earth, and, by order of his successor Roudolfus, buried at Hersfeld in the church of Saint Michael. Wiggerus, priest and provost, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 0573] From here another hand.]

1033, indiction 1. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Paderborn and Easter at Nijmegen.
