In the summer he hastened into Burgundy with his army and received as a submissive adversary Oudo, who had long resisted him and had tyrannically usurped that region for himself against the emperor’s will. After receiving oaths of peace and hostages from him, the emperor returned peacefully.

In the same year Count Liudgerus, Thiedof, and Wolveradus, together with forty others, were killed near the fortress of Werben. Empress Cunigund, of pious memory, died on the fifth day before the Nones of March.

A solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Kalends of July, a Friday, the feast of the birth of Saint Peter the Apostle, at the sixth hour of the day, while the emperor was conducting a council with the leading men of the kingdom in the city of Merseburg.

The monastery of the holy archangel Michael at Hildesheim was dedicated on the third day before the Kalends of October by Godehard, bishop of that place, with a very large gathering of people. The monastery of Altaha was destroyed by fire on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

1034, indiction 2. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Minden and Easter at Regensburg. On Christmas Day envoys of various peoples came to him with the finest and most varied gifts. There Hilderich, who had killed Altmannus, was granted security of life and restoration to his homeland through the intercession of the empress and the bishop of Halberstadt.

At the Easter festival Oudalricus, duke of the Bohemians, through the intervention of the empress and the leading men, deserved to return home from exile in favor and received half of his duchy, while his brother Germirus retained the other half.

Udo, the young son of Count Otto of Hamerstein, died. Again in this year the emperor entered Burgundy with a large army, drove out Oudo, who once more resisted him, and entrusted the region to his faithful men, who confirmed their loyalty to him by oath.

Meginhard, bishop of Würzburg, migrated to Christ; Bruno, the emperor’s cousin, entered in his place, given by God. [Note: [Col. 0573] In red letters: ADEODATUS.]

Warmundus, bishop of Constance, died; his brother Eppo, the royal chaplain, succeeded him. Numerous and unusual wars arose between the Liutizi and our people near the town of Werben, in which some of our men were killed and many wounded.

Also, because our sins—ah, ah!—deserved this before God, the praiseworthy and honorable labor of the venerable Bishop Bernward, namely the monastery of the holy archangel Michael, was burned by lightning on the Kalends of June, on the eve of Pentecost, toward evening, and was pitifully damaged.

Misacho, duke of the Poles, died an untimely death, and Christianity there, begun well by his predecessors and strengthened still better by him, lamentably—alas!—perished.

The aforementioned Oudalricus, duke of the Bohemians, after his return, having blinded his brother and driven out his son, again broke his oaths and persisted in treachery. At last, while seated at dinner, he choked on food and drink and died.

Since, therefore, he despised justice and right and, after so many oaths, again consented to his former plots, from the place where a salutary restoration is provided for Christ’s faithful, a just killing came upon him for his wicked merits.

In the same year Thietmarus, bishop of Verden, migrated to Christ on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

[Note: [Col. 0575] From here another hand.]

After him Bruno, brother of Count Fridericus, entered as abbot of Nienburg and Magdeburg. Albwinus, exceedingly learned in philosophical arts and provost at Hersfeld—formerly the most renowned teacher of the school there—succeeded that same Bruno at Nienburg. At Magdeburg Sidaec, elected from that same church, was appointed in his place.

In the same year Count Thiedricus of the Eastern regions was surrounded and treacherously killed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December by the soldiers of Margrave Aeggihardus in his own bedchamber, under the pretext of a greeting. His son Daedi obtained his honorable dignity; he later took Ouda, widow of Willihelmus, prefect of the Thuringians, in marriage.

Count Hezo the Palatine died a lamentable death, allegedly poisoned by his concubine Tiethburga in a cup of poison. He was transported to Augsburg and buried in the church of Saint Oudalricus on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. Count Ekberthus died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

1035, indiction 3. Emperor Chounradus celebrated Christmas at Goslar with a very distinguished gathering of his people. Envoys of various peoples assembled there with gifts for him; after being rewarded as imperial majesty required, they departed.

There, also, on the Kalends of January, he entrusted the dignity of the abbacy to the aforesaid lord Albwinus. He condemned Chuonradus, son of Alberich, to exile for treason against the majesty.

During Lent the city of Werben was captured by the Liutizi, and the garrison of Count Daedi was led away captive. The monastery of Tegernsee [Note: [Col. 0575] Tegernsee.] was destroyed by fire on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

The emperor celebrated Easter at Paderborn, the Ascension of the Lord at Seligenstadt, and Pentecost at Bamberg. From there he sent word concerning his expedition against the Liutizi.

There, too, Chnut, king of the Danes, betrothed his daughter by oaths to Heinrich, the emperor’s son. Otto of Schweinfurt likewise betrothed Mathild, daughter of Bolezlavus, duke of the Poles, to himself.

The emperor entered the region of the Liutizi with a very powerful army and devastated it far and wide with fire and plundering. In the same year Herimannus, metropolitan of Hamburg, departed from this life. Adelbrandus, the royal chaplain, entered in his place. [Note: [Col. 0576] “BEZELINUS”; in the manuscript the letters “BEZ” are cut off.]

With the greatest joy of his own people and of his fellow provincials, he honorably received from his suffragan bishops the dignity of the priesthood on the Saturday before Christmas, the eve of Saint Thomas the Apostle, and on the following day his episcopal elevation.

Opperthus, abbot of the people of Ellwangen, died; Rihhardus, a monk of Fulda, succeeded him. Maerksuit, abbess of the women of Wongerestorp, died on the second day before the Kalends of November. After her Alberad, formerly abbess of Molinbech, assumed the same administration through the machination of Bishop Sigiberht of Minden, while the entire congregation resisted exceedingly.

In winter Chnuht, king of the Danes and English, died, overtaken by an untimely death, and the Christian religion, faithfully cultivated by him, began to be endangered. But his younger son, named Haerdechunt, obtained his kingdom after him with the consent of the people of the region.

Outa, abbess of Kaufungen [Note: [Col. 0576] Kaufungen in Hesse.], of holy memory, died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October. Count Bruno died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

1036, indiction 4. The emperor magnificently celebrated Christmas at Strasbourg with the greatest gathering of his leading men. He celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary at Augsburg, where he also held a public assembly with all the leading men of the surrounding regions. At it he entrusted the duchy of Carinthia to his cousin Chuonradus.

He removed Adalbero, accused of treason against the majesty, in the preceding year. At this time that same Adalbero killed Count Willehelmus and afterward fled to the fortress of Eresburg to hide.

The emperor celebrated Easter at Ingelheim. Then, proceeding to Tribur, he presided there over a general synod, at which the brotherhood of the bishops restored the earlier decrees and also established certain measures necessary for strengthening the holy church.

There, too, the aforesaid Otto, compelled by the synod, renounced by oath the Mathild who had been betrothed to him.

The emperor celebrated the Ascension of the Lord at Paderborn; he celebrated Pentecost and the nativity of Saint John at Nijmegen. There the queen came to Heinrich, the emperor’s son: her name was Cunihild. There, on the feast of the Apostles, she received the royal crown and, her name being changed, was called Cunigund in the blessing.

In the summer the emperor also entered the region of the Liutizi with his army. But, by God’s grace, after arranging everything according to his will and receiving hostages and an innumerable amount of money, he returned in peace.

Meinwercus, bishop of Paderborn, died on the Nones of June. Ruodolfus, abbot of Hersfeld, succeeded him. But the lord Meginherus, dean of that same place, a monk imbued with a great zeal for usefulness and of holy conduct, obtained the primacy of that dignity at Hersfeld.

Bruno, bishop of Merseburg, was taken away on the Ides of August; after him Hunoldus, provost of Halberstadt, was appointed. Thiedricus from that same monastery was placed over it there.

Biligrinus, metropolitan of the holy church of Cologne, of venerable memory and exceedingly energetic in all divine and human matters, migrated to Christ on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. Herimannus, a young man of the noblest character, archdeacon of that same church, royal chaplain, and chancellor of the lands beyond the Alps, entered in his place amid the indescribable joy of all the devout.

Branthohus, bishop of Halberstadt, departed on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. Burghardus, the imperial chancellor, honorably succeeded him.

Sigeberhtus, bishop of Minden, breathed out his spirit on the sixth day before the Ides of October. After him Bruno, a young man of noble descent and royal chaplain, received that same episcopal office by heavenly blessing, amid the general rejoicing of all Christ’s faithful.

Gozmarus, bishop of Osnabrück, died on the fourth day before the Ides of December. Albericus, the royal successor, took his place.

The lord Godehard, bishop of Hildesheim, ordained Bruno, bishop of Minden, and Burghardus, bishop of Halberstadt, as priests at Halberstadt on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, the Saturday before Christmas.

1037, indiction 5. The emperor honorably celebrated Christmas at Verona. [Note: [Col. 0577] A word is missing.] The empress, together with the king her son and her daughter-in-law, celebrated those same days at Imbripoli.

On the feast of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, Bishop Burghardus of Halberstadt honorably received episcopal blessing at Heiligenstadt from Bardo, metropolitan of Mainz, and his suffragans.

After Christmas the emperor held a general assembly concerning the affairs of state at Salerno with the leading men of the lands beyond the Alps and of our own lands. At it the archbishop of Milan, who was opposed to the emperor, was arrested and entrusted to Boppo, patriarch of Aquileia, for safekeeping. Escaping from him, he began openly to rebel.

The emperor pursued him immediately with an army and besieged the city throughout the entire following year, at great risk to the whole army.

Bruno, bishop of Minden, received episcopal anointing on the holy day of Pentecost from Herimannus, metropolitan of Cologne, in a field near Milan, with the emperor and king present together with many of the kingdom’s leading men.

On that same day, a great clash of thunder and lightning arose there at the sixth hour of the day. It killed, as is said, no fewer than sixty men from the emperor’s army, together with an uncountable multitude of horses and cattle. On the following day, at the same hour, it also killed some others. Throughout that summer our army endured many varied and unusual events of difficult circumstances there.

The bishops of Piacenza, Cremona, Vercelli, and others—some accused of treason against the majesty because they had sided with the aforementioned archbishop and with Oudo, the frequently mentioned tyrant, against the emperor—were taken captive and exiled to various places.

The aforementioned Oudo, while the emperor was administering the affairs of Italy, tyrannically invaded Lotharingia near the march of Duke Gazelo and his son Godefridus. He seized the city called Bera [Note: [Col. 0577] Bar.] through an unjust presumption. Near that city he was intercepted by those same dukes and, when battle was joined, fell ingloriously among the foremost, paying the just penalties of divine vengeance after breaking his oaths.

Unknown to the very victors, he was found naked among the common people on the following day, stripped both of life and of the kingdom which he had coveted by usurping it.

Tadilo, dean of our church, died on the first day before the Kalends of February: a venerable father in Christ and always memorable to the devout. Hagano, deacon and royal chaplain, died on the tenth day before the Kalends of March and was buried at Hersfeld. Counts Sigifridus and Dangmarus died.

1038. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Parma with his most noble household. On the holy day of the Lord’s nativity, toward evening, the townsmen entered into a conflict for a trivial reason. Many from the army were killed in it, especially three of the king’s retainers: Chonon, Magnum, and Suiegerus.

Because of this rash insolence, at dawn on the following day they themselves, together with the city and all their possessions, perished by booty, fire, and sword.

The emperor celebrated Easter peacefully and without any disturbance in the fortress of Spella [Note: [Col. 0579] Spello, near Foligno.].

The aforementioned metropolitan of Milan, after repeated and just admonitions from the apostolic pontiff, was anathematized at Easter by common episcopal decree and separated from the assembly of the faithful. Nevertheless, he persisted in his obstinacy and did everything he could to hinder the emperor throughout the present and following year.

At that time our holy bishop Godehard, of venerable memory, was taken from this life on the third day before the Nones of May, namely on the Friday after the Ascension of the Lord, and migrated to live forever with Christ in eternity. By his departure he brought immense sadness upon us wretched people.

We do not doubt that he truly went before us to God. Yet we rightly and continually lament that we are now deprived of his holy admonition and fruitful example of virtues in our presence. For what merit he possessed, each person can recognize at his own end, because, as it is written, each person is known at his end.

It is also sufficiently evident that he possessed great praises of merit, since at his death God revealed such wondrous deeds of signs in a miracle. Although that fact is known to all Christ’s faithful, it is nevertheless recorded here through the true experience of reports, as testimony to his holiness. [Note: [Col. 0579] Four blank lines; then another hand begins.]

In his place the lord Thietmarus, royal chaplain, succeeded him, exceedingly energetic in every divine and human matter. He was consecrated at Lorsch on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September by Bardo, metropolitan of Mainz.

Count Liudolf, the emperor’s stepson, died an untimely death on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. His brother Herimannus, duke of Alemannia, overtaken by a sudden illness, was taken from this life, lamented by all the good, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

Our noble queen Gunhild also migrated from this world on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. Her untimely death saddened very many people of every rank throughout the Christian empire.

Sigifrithus, count palatine [Note: [Col. 0579] That is, count palatine.], brother of Bruno, bishop of Minden, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of May and was buried at Wimmelburg [Note: [Col. 0580] “Vuidaburch,” corrected in the manuscript to “Vuimilaburh.” It appears to be Wimmelburg, near Eisleben, formerly a monastery demolished in 1525.].

1039, indiction 7. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Goslar with the most reverent rejoicing of his leading men. There he received envoys from all the surrounding regions, with the required declarations of tribute, to increase his magnificence. He sent them back peacefully, rewarded—as imperial munificence required and as they wished—with gifts both for his sake and in abundance of possessions.

There, among other decrees of his administration, he ordered Alberada, abbess of Molinbach, to surrender the abbey of Wongerestorp against the will of Bishop Bruno. After Easter, however, that same bishop compelled her to withdraw from that dignity, whether willingly or unwillingly, through a public renunciation.

The emperor celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary at Alstedt. He then traveled by a short route through eastern Saxony, settling affairs peacefully, and proceeded to Nijmegen. There he remained during Lent, holy Easter, and the Ascension of the Lord, suffering from gout.

From there he came to Utrecht to celebrate Pentecost, and there he celebrated the holy day in the greatest joy, proceeding in the splendor of the royal diadem. But on the following day, Monday, at the sixth hour of the day, on the second day before the Nones of June, while seated for refreshment, he was seized by a sudden collapse and, scarcely had the sentence of confession been pronounced, lamentably expired.

O hidden judgments of divine dispensation, equally wondrous and fearful! On the preceding day he had gone forth crowned as king and emperor of the world amid the greatest celebration of worldly pomp; on the following day—ah, ah!—he entered upon the way of all flesh and departed, destined to become ash and worm, except that we truly hope that, whatever negligence he contracted in the flesh, the prayer of the church intervened on behalf of his soul.

But as someone said:

> O mortal hearts, knowing nothing of their own fate!
>
> Yet, to speak more truly—O hard, and, if I may speak peacefully, utterly senseless hearts of the human race! When the head and strength of almost the whole world fell in the person of this man, no one truly lamented his death, so sudden and so perilous.

> May the Lord, ruler of kings, comfort him forever;
>
> May he live with Abraham’s children and in repose.

But his son, the lord Heinrich, exceedingly energetic in every display of virtue, having previously been crowned as sole monarch of the kingdom through the general acclamation of clergy and people, has now, without any troublesome opposition and with the greatest concord of Christendom, been enthroned on his father’s seat—thanks be to God!

> May God preserve him properly to a venerable old age,
>
> And may he himself, in peace, be gracious to his gracious Lord.

Chonradus, duke of Carinthia and cousin of Emperor Chonradus, died an untimely death on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, after being long afflicted by the royal disease.

On that same day Rihhardus, abbot of Fulda, of venerable memory, died. Sigewardus, a young man regularly and wisely nurtured by him there in divine service, took his place.

At that time Radulfus, abbot of Deutz [Note: [Col. 0581] Deutz.], also died. Sophia, a lady venerable in Christ and of pious memory, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of February. Her sister Adalheiht, the lady of Quedlinburg, succeeded her at Gandersheim, and their niece Theophanu obtained the abbey of Essen [Note: [Col. 0581] Essen.].

[Note: [Col. 0581] From here another hand.]

After the death of the aforesaid lady Sophia, our elder Thietmarus, the bishop, ordered that the tithes from Gandersheim and the surrounding little villages—which she had held in benefice from our elders—be received into his vesture. Bezoca, the provost, resisted this with her supporters through a frivolous plot.

When the abbess arrived, he himself demanded those same tithes anew by episcopal authority. Through the hand of Christian, count and advocate, he received them into his own possession, with due satisfaction and without any prohibition, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the northern choir. Later he restored them to the same altar and to the abbess as a benefice for as long as he lived, in return for the rent which Bishop Bernward, of holy memory, had established there.

Witnesses: Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne, with his four clerics; Bodo, our dean; Aellio; Wolfherus; Volcawardus; Reinbertus; Wolferus; Liudierus; Merkbardus; Werinus; Rihdagus; Thietmarus; Imezi; Adeldagus; Liudierus; Warmund; Wolferus; and many other laymen; Counts Thietmarus, Uodo, and Tiedricus.

1040, indiction 8. Our new king fittingly celebrated the Lord’s incarnation at Regensburg. While staying at Augsburg for the Purification of Saint Mary, he held an assembly with the leading men of the lands beyond the Alps concerning the stability of the state.

[Note: [Col. 0581] From here another hand, on palimpsest parchment, as far as the end of 1100; the scribe takes the emperor’s side, the glossator the pontiff’s.]

1041, indiction 9. King Heinrich attacked Duke Fratislaus of Bohemia in war; but, with many magnates and soldiers killed or captured in the clearing of the forest on this side and beyond it, he was unable to accomplish anything worthy. Peter also, king of the Hungarians, sent aid against King Heinrich to that duke [Note: [Col. 0582] The manuscript has “duke.”].

1042, indiction 10. The Hungarians, choosing a certain Ovo as their king, expelled their king Peter. A fugitive and exile, he sought and found the favor of King Heinrich, against whom he had rebelled in the preceding year. King Heinrich entered Bohemia, devastated everything with fire and plunder, and compelled the rebellious duke to give hostages, then to come humbly after him to Regensburg to make submission and to confirm by oath his fidelity and service to him. Ovo, king of the Hungarians, because King Heinrich had received Peter, whom he had expelled, ravaged the borders of Bavaria with plundering and fires; but a great part of his army was destroyed by Margrave Atbelheron.

1043, indiction 11. King Heinrich entered Pannonia, destroyed two very populous cities, and brought several more under submission. But because the provincials would not receive King Peter, whom he had brought with him, he appointed for them another duke whom they requested; after Heinrich’s departure, Ovo drove him back into Bohemia. Empress Gisla, mother of King Heinrich, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March and was buried at Speyer.

### 1044, indiction 12

King Henry invaded Pannonia again and, after receiving satisfaction, hostages, gifts, and confirmation of peace by oath, withdrew. On his return he attended the synod of Constance, where he remitted all debts owed to him and, destroying every enmity, confirmed by royal decree an unprecedented peace, both throughout all Swabia and in the other provinces of his kingdom. Then, having Agnes, daughter of William, prince of Poitou, anointed queen at Mainz, he joined her to himself in a royal marriage at Ingelheim. From there he allowed an infinite multitude of actors and jesters to depart hungry, empty-handed, and grieving. Margrave Liupold, son of Adalbert, the great scourge of the Hungarians, died prematurely. Bishop Thietmar died; Azelin was elected.

[Note: These words were written at the beginning of the year in the margin, but have now been cut away so that only “...marus episcopus obiit ...nus eligitur” can be read.]

### 1045, indiction 13

King Henry, entering Pannonia angrily for the third time, was made victorious by God’s merciful favor and through the intercession of blessed Bishop Ulrich. He drove out Ovo, together with his wife, sons, and relatives who had a place where they could escape, restored Peter to the kingdom, and, having subjected the kingdom of the Hungarians to himself, returned with the highest honor.

### 1046, indiction 14

King Henry entered Italy and was received peacefully by the Romans. He deposed three improperly appointed popes in a synod and made Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, pope. On that same day he and his wife, Queen Agnes, were elevated by the imperial blessing.

### 1047, indiction 15

Peter, king of the Hungarians, was captured and blinded by a certain Pannonian tyrant; the man who had expelled him began to reign. Pope Suidger died in the same year in which he had been appointed, and Boppo was ordained in his place.

[Col. 0583D] Duke Otto of Swabia died; Otto of Schweinfurt arose in his place.

### 1048, indiction 1

Pope Boppo died in the year in which he had been appointed. Bruno, also called Leo, bishop of Toul, was appointed pope in his place. The emperor Henry was born.

### 1049, indiction 2

### 1050, indiction 3

Archbishop Bartho died; Liupold was ordained in his place.

### 1051, indiction 4

### 1052, indiction 5

[Col. 0584A] ### 1053, indiction 6

Pope Leo led an army through Apulia against the Normans. After an immense slaughter on both sides, he returned without victory and died on 30 June of that same year.

### 1054, indiction 7

Gebehard, also called Victor, succeeded Pope Leo. Margrave Athalbert died. There was a great famine. Duke Welf of Carinthia died. Conrad, formerly duke of the Noricans, expelled by the emperor, died miserably in exile in Pannonia. Count Hezil of Oberstenfeld died on 27 January. Bishop Azelin died; Hettelo was elected.

[Note: Only this much now remains in the margin: “...linus episcopus obiit ...telo eligitur.”]

### 1055, indiction 8

Archbishop Hermann of Cologne died; Lord Anno was ordained in his place.

### 1056, indiction 9

A great slaughter of Christians was carried out by the barbarians called the Liutici. Some perished by the sword, others while fleeing into the water; among them Margrave William was killed. At the same time many princes of various provinces perished. Famine afflicted many provinces. Want and poverty prevailed everywhere; many evils occurred at that time. Emperor Henry, pierced to the heart by these afflictions, began to grow ill. Having been brought close to death, yet following wise counsel, he sought forgiveness from everyone whom he could, restored to some the estates that he had taken away, and forgave all who had committed punishable offenses against him. By the election of the Roman pontiff and of the other bishops and princes, he made his son Henry king. Having arranged these and other matters well, insofar as the possibility of life allowed, he ended this present life in God on 3 October.

### In the year of the Lord 1057, indiction 9

Henry, son of Emperor Henry, began to reign while still a very young boy. Empress Agnes, Henry’s mother, assumed the duchy of Bavaria. Pope Victor, having arranged many matters well in Germany, returned to Rome and ended his life in the same year. Frederick, also called Stephen, brother of Duke Godfrey, who had already become a monk on Monte Cassino, was appointed pontiff by the Romans in his place. He too died in the same year. Bishop Adelbero of Bamberg and Duke Otto of Schweinfurt also died.

### 1058, indiction 10

### 1059, indiction 11

Archbishop Liupold of Mainz died; Sifrid of Fulda was appointed in his place. Saint Cuno, bishop of Trier, was martyred: he was thrown three times from a rocky mountain into a deserted place by Count Theodoric, because he had been appointed without an election, and was buried at Doleia. There the Lord performed many miracles through him at that time. The count himself later did penance and, traveling to Jerusalem, ended his life; all his accomplices perished by an evil death. Odo was appointed in his place.

[Col. 0585A] ### 1060, indiction 12

### 1061, indiction 13

### 1062, indiction 14

### 1063, indiction 15

### 1064, indiction 1

### 1065, indiction 2

Bishop Gunther of Bamberg died; Hermann was appointed in his place. Count Gozwin was killed by the soldiers of Bishop Adalbero because of the injury he had inflicted in the bishopric of Würzburg.

### 1066, indiction 3

A comet was seen, and England was subjected by the Normans.

### 1067, indiction 4

### 1068, indiction 5

### 1069, indiction 6

### 1070, indiction 7

Margrave Dedi rebelled against King Henry.

### 1071, indiction 8

Otto, duke of Bavaria, rebelled against King Henry.

### 1072, indiction 9

The princes of the kingdom conspired against King Henry.

### 1073, indiction 10

The Saxons destroyed Harzburg, where they violated the tomb of the king’s son and scattered his bones.

### 1074, indiction 11

Hildebrand succeeded Pope Alexander.

### 1075, indiction 12

A battle was fought near the Unstrut on 9 June against King Henry. Many powerful men on both sides fell, and the Saxons took flight.

### 1076, indiction 13

A council was convened at Worms, where Pope Hildebrand was deposed.

### 1077, indiction 14

Lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne, died on 4 December. He founded five communities from the ground up: two in Cologne, one in honor of Saint Mary and another in honor of Saint George the Martyr; outside the city, one at a place called Grascabf, another at a place called Salevelt, and one on the mountain called Siegburg, where he now rests happily. Hildolfus, bishop, was ordained in his place. Empress Agnes died. Rudolf was made king at a place called Forchheim and, in the middle of Lent, was anointed king at Mainz by Archbishop Sifrid. Discord between the pope and King Henry was renewed because of the king’s disobedience.

[Note: The oblique letter inserted by a twelfth-century hand has been represented in this way.]

### 1078, indiction 15

A battle was fought near Strowi. On 7 August Bishop Hildolf of Cologne died; Sigewin was ordained in his place.

### 1079, indiction 1

A battle was fought near Flarchheim on 28 January. Bishop Hettilo of Hildesheim died. He held the bishopric for 25 years, [lacuna] days, [lacuna]. Udo, his noble canon, succeeded him.

### 1080, indiction 2

At Brixen in Noricum, an assembly of thirty bishops and a large part of the kingdom’s leading men was held against Hildebrand. A battle was fought near the Elster on 15 October, in which King Rudolf, who was also duke, was killed.

### 1081, indiction 3

King Henry besieged Rome. A battle was fought between Margrave Liupold and Conrad, brother of the duke of Bohemia, on 12 May. There was also a battle between the Swabians and Bavarians near the Danube, at a place called Hohstetin, on 11 August.

[Note: “Hochstadt.”]

Henry, the younger son, was born.

[Note: Almost the entire word has been cut away.]

### 1082, indiction 4

Hermann invaded the kingdom and was ordained by Sifrid of Mainz.

### 1083, indiction 5

Rome was captured, and Pope Hildebrand was expelled by King Henry. A great pestilence occurred. Hermann, who had invaded the kingdom, entered eastern Francia in a hostile manner.

### 1084, indiction 6

Emperor Henry returned from Italy, and Augsburg was besieged and captured by him. Hermann, bishop of Bamberg, died; he had been expelled from the bishopric. Archbishop Sifrid died in Thuringia and was buried at Hasungen. Wezelin was appointed in his place.

### 1085, indiction 7

A synod was held at Mainz, at Saint Alban’s. Pope Gregory, also called Hildebrand, died, as did Thietmar, bishop of Worms, and Count Hermann of the Palatinate. King Henry devastated Saxony.

### 1086, indiction 8

The Saxons, together with the Swabians, besieged Würzburg. The emperor came with a large force to relieve it, and a battle was fought near Bleichefeld on 10 August. But when the king had been put to flight, the Saxons captured the city. Hermann laid down the royal title and soon thereafter died. Würzburg was captured by the Saxons and soon recovered by the emperor.

### 1087, indiction 9

Empress Bertha died. A pestilence occurred [lacuna].

[Note: These words, written by a corrector’s hand, have now been cut away: “...tus ...u” seems readable. I think that “Margrave Henry died,” from the Saxon Chronographer, or “The arrival of Saint Nicholas at Bari,” from the Annalist, should be restored.]

### 1088, indiction 10

Wezil, archbishop of Mainz, died. Bishop Bucco of Halberstadt was killed at Goslar.

### 1089, indiction 11

Margrave Ecgibert besieged Hildesheim, where he captured Bishop Udo after a long siege.

[Note: I restore the passage with the help of the Saxon Annalist. In the codex only this can be read: “...rchio ... ubi Udo ...u ob ...t.” A fifteenth-century hand inserted into the codex the words found in Chesnius and Leibniz: “The margrave of Brandenburg besieged Hildesheim and captured Bishop Udo there.”]

A battle was fought near the castle of Glicho, situated in Thuringia near Erfurt, between Emperor Henry and Margrave Ecgibert, on the Lord’s vigil, a Sunday. Bishop Burchard of Lausanne was killed there. The following bishops died: Sigewin of Cologne and Otto of Regensburg. The following were appointed bishops: Hermann of Cologne, Ruthard of Mainz, and Emhard of Würzburg, on 25 July.

### 1090, indiction 12

The emperor set out for Italy. Hermann, bishop of Metz, Duke Liudolf, and Duke Bertolf, son of Rudolf, died. Margrave Ecgibert was killed. Lord Adelbero, twentieth bishop of the holy church of Würzburg after blessed Burchard, was appointed on 29 June. He lived in the bishopric for 45 years, 3 months, and 7 days, and died on 6 October.

[Col. 0587A] ### 1091, indiction 13

Mathilda of Lombardy rebelled against King Henry. In many regions, exceedingly strange little worms were seen.

[Note: It seems that this should be restored as it is read in both of Ekkehard’s chronicles, the Annalist and the Saxon Chronographer. The traces in the codex are: “...st ...o ...mult: s ...it.”]

### 1092, indiction 14

Count Conrad was killed by the Frisians together with many others on 21 July. A great pestilence of human beings and animals also occurred.

[Note: The codex reads “pestilestia.”]

### 1093, indiction 15

Magnus, duke of the Saxons, subdued the rebellious Slavs after capturing fourteen towns. On 28 July, around evening, a solar eclipse occurred in the third hour of the day, and a dragon was seen. Vratislaus, duke of Bohemia, fell from his horse while hunting and died suddenly [lacuna] throughout [lacuna] the north [lacuna].

### 1094, indiction 1

A great pestilence occurred.

### 1095, indiction 2

Ladislaus, king of Pannonia, a man of pious memory, and likewise Margrave Liupold and Henry, count palatine, died.

### 1096, indiction 3

An innumerable people, nearly 12,000—perhaps 15,000—armed from various nations and led by a certain monk named Peter, set out for Jerusalem. They compelled Jews to be baptized and, when the Jews refused, slaughtered them in immense numbers. At Mainz, 1,014 Jews—men, women, and children—were killed, and most of the city was burned. Jews throughout various provinces became Christians and then again abandoned Christianity.

[Note: The codex reads “XII,” though perhaps “XV.”]

### 1097, indiction 4

The emperor returned from Italy, where he had already remained for seven years. Conrad rebelled against his father, Henry; because of this injury, Henry entrusted the kingdom to his younger son. In this year [lacuna] of the whole [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna].

### 1098, indiction 5

Count Conrad of Hohenburg rebelled against the king and was therefore expelled. When the Christian army departed from the captured city of Nicaea, numbering more than 300,000 armed men, God provided such an abundance of necessities for life that a ram could be bought for one coin and an ox for scarcely twelve.

[Note: I restored this as “C. v. n. D.” by conjecture, since the remaining traces of the writing seemed closer to Ekkehard’s reading than to that of the Saxon Chronographer.]

Thus they came to besiege Antioch. It was besieged and captured after nine months [lacuna] and his other fellow soldiers. Some time later they too were besieged inside by the pagans. But, afflicted by extreme hunger and thirst, many among the crusaders ate horses and donkeys, and some scarcely refrained from human flesh.

[Note: I took “horses and donkeys” from the Saxon Annalist; they cannot be read in the codex.] They cried out to the Lord not to hand the Christians over to the Gentiles [lacuna].

[Note: Several lines here cannot be read. Compare the Chronographer and the Saxon Annalist.]

[Col. 0588A] ### 1099, indiction 6

The emperor celebrated Easter at Regensburg. In those same days a great mortality occurred, in which Count Palatine Rabbodo died together with countless others. On the Wednesday of Easter, Conrad, bishop of Utrecht, was cruelly killed by a Frisian merchant. Bishops Ulrich of Eichstätt and Hermann of Cologne died; Frederick was appointed in Hermann’s place. Pope Urban, also called Otto, died; Paschal succeeded him. Jerusalem was captured by the Christians. With Duke Godfrey leading the army and in [lacuna], [lacuna] thousand Moors were killed, and the treasures of the king of Babylon were seized.

[Note: The words “they determined to enter battle with the enemies” and the rest, up to “blessing God,” seem to be missing; they are found in the Saxon Annalist.]

The emperor’s son Henry was raised to the kingship at Aachen, while King Conrad remained in Italy with his father’s enemies and consented to this.

[Note: I restored “was raised to the kingship” in the right-hand margin; the place is blank in the codex.]

[Col. 0588B] ### 1100, indiction 7

There was a harsh winter and a great famine. Margrave Udo and several Saxons invaded the barbarians also called Liutici and triumphed honorably. Margravine Adela, traveling toward Rome, died. Duke Godfrey died at Jerusalem and lies buried not far from the Holy Sepulchre; he had led the Christian army. His brother Baldwin was appointed in his place.

[Note: The same hand appears here and there, though it has now changed somewhat.]

### 1101, indiction 8

The emperor celebrated Christmas at Mainz. Many princes gathered there and gave the emperor counsel that he should send messengers to Rome for the sake of ecclesiastical unity and appoint a pope according to the election of the Romans and of all the churches. Count Henry obtained the emperor’s favor, and the emperor himself handed over to him the march of the Frisians. Henry immediately went there with his wife, but he was killed, while she scarcely escaped.

[Note: [lacuna] “chus,” abbot, [lacuna] in the margin.]

### 1102, indiction 9

The emperor celebrated Christmas at Mainz, where Count Henry of Limburg was made duke.

[Note: “Limburg.”]

### 1103, indiction 10

The emperor celebrated Christmas at Mainz, where the princes gathered. On the Epiphany of the Lord, Emehard, bishop of Würzburg, sang Mass at Saint Martin’s. During the solemnities of the Mass, when the bishop was exhorting the people, the emperor, as though pierced in heart, promised God that he would go to Jerusalem for his sins, and thus he deceived the leading men of the kingdom. Although the princes often gathered at his court, they did nothing concerning public affairs except consume their own resources there. For that reason they maintained a pretended loyalty toward him and conspired against him. Thus he deceived all the princes of the kingdom, so that he accomplished nothing truthful in public affairs, except that everything deteriorated during his reign. Many cities and strongholds were destroyed in his war, and he was a robber of God’s churches, distributing their estates ostensibly to reconcile the princes. Why say more? No one has ever found such things written in the ancient volumes as the unheard-of crimes he committed. Unless God’s remarkable mercy had endured him and delayed him for repentance, the earth would have swallowed him alive, as it did Dathan.

[Col. 0589B] ### 1104, indiction 9

[Note: Some words were once readable in the margin.]

The emperor’s court was at Regensburg for Christmas. There Count Sigehard unjustly pronounced a judgment against certain dependents, and for this reason he was killed by them. From this arose the greatest persecution against the emperor, carried out by Sigehard’s relatives and by all the princes of the kingdom, since he would certainly not have been killed if the emperor had wished to help him. When he realized that he therefore had not a few adversaries and was surrounded on every side by their ambushes, he began to seek a suitable place of escape. At last he departed and came to Mainz with his followers to celebrate holy Easter. After Easter had been solemnly celebrated there, he came to Liège.

Count Hermann and Hartwig, provost of the church of Magdeburg, son of Count Ecgibert, who was to be appointed bishop there, were supposed to come to Liège. While they were traveling together, Count Theodoric of Saxony took them and all their possessions captive and prevented them from reaching the court. When the emperor learned of this, he was greatly angered. Around the feast of Saint Andrew, he assembled an army, accompanied by his son, and came as far as Fritzlar, since from there he was to proceed into Saxony. There, one night, his son took with him certain members of his father’s household—Hermann and others—and secretly departed on 12 December, intending to go to Bavaria.

When Margrave Theobald learned of the son’s separation from his father—he was the nephew of the aforementioned Count Sigehard—he came joyfully with all the leading men of that region to meet him and received him honorably. He judged it best that they celebrate Christmas at Regensburg. After Christmas he sent messengers to Rome, seeking advice from the apostolic see concerning the oath he had sworn to his father, namely that he would never invade the kingdom without his father’s permission and consent.

When the apostolic representative heard of the quarrel between father and son, hoping that these events had come from God, he sent him the apostolic blessing through Gebehard, bishop of Constance. He promised him absolution at the future judgment for the deed he had undertaken, if he wished to be a just king and governor of the Church, which had long been cast down through his father’s negligence. As soon as he received the words of apostolic consolation and release from the ban from the aforesaid bishop, he besieged the castle called Nuremberg and subjected it to his authority.

But when the father learned in the morning that he had been deprived of his son, he was overcome by excessive grief and returned to celebrate Christmas at Mainz. Bishop John of Speyer died.

### 1105

King [Note: The word can no longer be read.] came to Halberstadt and restored to their places and possessions the canons whom Bishop Frederick had unjustly expelled. The other canons were released from the ban because they had supported the bishop of the excommunicated King Henry. From there the king went to Hildesheim. When he approached the city, Bishop Udo departed with a few men. The canons were released from the ban; those who had been ordained, as well as the ordaining bishop, were suspended from office. Later the bishop, recalled at the advice of the canons, returned and, released from the ban, obtained the king’s favor.

There [lacuna] at Nordhausen, with the young king presiding, Archbishop Ruthard of Mainz and Bishop Gebehard of Constance [lacuna], after many chapters had been read, judged that simoniacs must be expelled from the holy Church. The fast of the four seasons [lacuna].

[Note: Namely, the emperor.]

Immediately after the Epiphany he sent envoys to Bavaria—namely, the archbishops of Cologne and Trier, Duke Frederick, and Chancellor Erlolf—to see whether they could reconcile him with his son. The son replied that he could not in any way enter into communion with him unless he were first cleansed of the guilt of excommunication by which he had long been bound under the judgment of the apostolic see.

When the envoys had returned, he set out with a large company for Thuringia, to a place called Erfurt, where he was properly received by Ruthard, archbishop of the see of Mainz. There he celebrated Palm Sunday, and holy Easter at Quedlinburg. At that time the patriarch of Aquileia arrived, saying that he had come to reconcile them if possible. He stated that he did not dare to enter into communion with the king unless the king wished to acknowledge himself guilty before God, humble himself before the whole kingdom, and obey the Roman see in all things. For he feared that the king might deceive him with his cunning speeches, just as he had often previously deceived others.

The same patriarch celebrated holy Easter at Mainz and, after Easter, returned home with the gifts he had received from the king. After Easter the son came to Goslar, where he held a general conference with the princes of Saxony concerning how, with God’s help and their unanimous counsel, he ought to order his affairs, cleanse the Church, which had been violated in every way, and restore it from division to unity.

The aforementioned bishop of Constance was also present, the most faithful associate of the lord pope. He had released the king and all his followers from the bond of excommunication, and by apostolic authority had deposed a certain prelate named Widelo.

[Note: Of Minden, according to the Saxon Annalist.]

Widelo had been the foulest author of all the crimes and impurities committed by the father. The bishop appointed another in his place, whom the king and the clergy of that place had elected.

Meanwhile, it seemed good to Gebehard, the legate of the apostolic see, and to Ruthard, bishop of Mainz, to hold a council in Thuringia during the week before Pentecost, at a place called Nordhausen, and to restore the Church, insofar as they could, to its former condition and recite there the ancient rule of the fathers. That is, they were to depose alive invading bishops and those who had entered by simony, exhume those who had been buried, require those ordained by them to receive the imposition of hands from Catholics, and forbid married clerics to celebrate any divine office.

When these matters had been properly arranged by divine inspiration, the king, taking with him the Saxons and Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz—who had long been expelled by his father—reached the bank of the Rhine after the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. His father, who was then staying at Mainz with his followers, refused passage. He bribed all those whom he could, especially the count palatine, who had promised the son the means of crossing, and moved the fleet of ships to the port of Mainz. With soldiers and citizens he prevented the son from crossing.

When the son saw that his father’s power had forestalled him and that he could not cross, the archbishop of Mainz returned to Thuringia. The son himself went to Würzburg, deposed Bishop Erlolf, whom his father had appointed there, and made Rupert, provost of that monastery, bishop.

After he had stayed there for several days, he returned again to Regensburg. His father, having gathered an army, pursued him as far as the bonds of Saint Peter. He directed his march through Bavaria and devastated and burned all those whom he could, who were adhering to his son. Thus he hastened toward Regensburg, where he had learned that his son was staying.

When the son heard that his father was unexpectedly approaching the city, he barely managed to depart and crossed the river called the Regen with his followers. While both gradually gathered their forces and the duke of Bohemia came to the father’s aid, messengers were sent between them to see whether they could somehow be restored to peace. But since there was no hope of recovering peace or concord, since part of his own multitude did not dare to fight, and since he could in no way resist his son, the father secretly fled at night with a few most faithful companions. Passing through Bohemia and Saxony with great difficulty across forests and rivers, he returned to Mainz, hoping perhaps to prevent passage at the port as before.

The son immediately pursued his father with his followers and came to the Rhine at Speyer. He hired the prefect of Speyer and, on the vigil of All Saints, secured the necessary ships. He also obtained control of the soldiers so that no one could resist until he had crossed the port.

On All Saints’ Day he raised the abbot of Hirsau to the episcopate of Speyer.

[Note: Hirsau; of Hirsau.]

When it became known to the father that his son had come to the Rhine at Speyer, he immediately hurried there from Mainz, already hoping to prevent his crossing. But he was extremely astonished to hear that the son had crossed with his followers. Struck by excessive fear, he returned the same day, fasting and greatly fatigued, to Mainz.

On the following day he sent the abbot of Saint Alban’s, named Theodoric, to his son at Speyer, imploring him by God to remember that he was his father and not to wish so stubbornly to drive him from the kingdom. The son delayed hearing him, but sent back the message that he should leave the city quickly, lest he be seized by his enemies.

The father departed from the city as quickly as possible and came to the castle of Hammerstein, where he remained for some time. The son came to Mainz, sent envoys to Thuringia for the bishop, and restored him to the glorious holy Church from which his father had expelled him.

Afterward, when the father saw the multitude of princes from the entire kingdom flowing together to Mainz and knew that the envoys of the apostolic see were also to be present—and since he was certain that his son intended to hold a general conference there—he considered whether he might somehow interrupt their purpose. He sent ahead Count Palatine Sifrid and Count William, who had remained with him after being hired, to see whether they could prevent the son’s appointed assembly. He announced that he himself would secretly come after them.

When they reached the forest called San [Note: On the left bank of the Rhine, between Bingen and Bacharach, where Soneck Castle stands.] and found the son with a great army on the other side, they could not resist him and took flight in the middle of the night. The son pursued them and came to Confluence. There he found his father on the opposite bank of the river.

When the two came together there, the father sent messengers to his son, asking for what belonged to peace. The father crossed the river to his son, fell at his son’s feet, and urged him to remember that he was his son and his own blood.

[Note: “He wished ... urged him”; the first word has been erased.]

But the son, falling at his father’s knees, begged him to obey the apostolic see and the whole kingdom. He promised that, if his father would not wish to have God in heaven as his father, he would there and then wholly renounce him as his earthly father; but he did not fulfill this promise.

While he spoke all day about these and similar matters concerning the condition of the Church and the salvation of his soul, in the evening both returned to their lodgings. During the darkness of night the father tried to flee, but, surrounded on every side by enemies, he could not.

In the morning they took the father to the castle of Bingen, where they spent that night. On the following day they led him, as though unwilling, to the castle of Bekelenheim.

[Note: Gau-Bockelheim, or Bichelsheim on the Nahe?]

On the vigil of Christmas they entrusted him to the careful custody of the bishop of Speyer. Unwashed, unshorn, and deprived of every service of God, he remained there throughout all the holy days. Thus the son returned to Mainz to celebrate Christmas.

Emperor Henry, staying at Liège, saw a dream worthy of being told. He imagined that he was walking in a garden planted with tall trees. The tree that appeared tallest fell to the ground, crushing one of the trees and bringing it down with itself. Then the other trees gradually fell. The outcome of events later confirmed this dream.

For the emperor, after falling ill not long afterward, died on the ninth day after eight days of illness, and was buried in the church of Saint Lambert before the altar of Saint Mary. Five days later Count Theodoric of Embeke died at Aachen. Magnus, duke of the Saxons, died, and the duchy was entrusted to Liutger of Süpplingenburg.

[Note: I supplied “Emperor Henry up to ‘the more prominent’” from the Saxon Annalist; in the codex those words have now been erased.]

The ninety-sixth king of the Romans, Heinricus, having expelled his father, began to reign in the year 1106, indiction 13. The emperor, however, began to weep excessively and to be sorrowful that such things had happened to him because of his sins. Fearing much worse treatment from the princes, he asked that the bishop of Speyer be brought to him and promised that he would do everything according to the counsel of the bishop and the magnates of the realm: he would hand over to his son the royal estates and castles, the finest and most strongly fortified possessions he had, so that at least his son might provide him with estates sufficient for his needs.

The bishop came to Mainz on the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist. He and the bishop of Würzburg received the order of the sacred anointing from Archbishop Ruothard [Col. 0593C], and after the celebration of Mass he recounted to his son and to all the princes everything that he had heard from the father. When the princes of the realm heard this, they agreed to assemble at Ingelheim on 2 Kalends of January. There the emperor was brought before them. He handed the kingdom over to his son and, falling at everyone’s feet—especially those of the cardinal legate of the Apostolic See—begged for pardon and absolution from the ban [Note: This is how the manuscript punctuates the passage]. He confessed that he had long been excommunicated by Pope Hildebrand, that he had unjustly set Pope Wicbertus over him, and that during his reign the commonwealth had been excessively disturbed. He confessed everything of which they had accused him, except that he did not worship idols.

The cardinal, who had unexpectedly come together with the others for these proceedings, said that he could in no way receive so great a person, on account of whom so many evils had been perpetrated throughout the entire kingdom, unless the pope himself came [Col. 0593D]. After the father had been deposed, the son returned to Mainz with the princes of the realm. On account of the royal possessions he sent Count Werinher of Hamersten and the wicked Volcmar, who had been his father’s counselor and an accomplice in all his crimes. On the eve of Epiphany he brought the possessions, and Archbishop Ruothard, together with all the clergy and people, received them honorably. He handed them over to the son before the princes, saying:

“If he had not proved to be a just ruler of the kingdom and a defender of God’s churches, may what happened to his father have happened to him also.”

When the emperor saw that pardon had been denied him, he considered how he might stir up vengeance against the commonwealth. He came to Cologne with the few who had remained with him and tearfully recounted to the citizens everything that had happened to them. Then he came to Liège, where the bishop and citizens received and consoled him honorably. He summoned Duke Heinricus and many other nobles to him, fell at their feet, asked their assistance, and recounted to them everything that had happened to him. When they heard his complaint, they were moved by compassion, promised him faithful assistance, and considered it best that he celebrate the Lord’s Easter there with them [Col. 0594B] [Note: The earlier hand reads *caelebraret*; the other, *celebrarent*].

When the son heard this, he informed the princes of the realm that they should assemble there and that he would hold a hearing with his father. He raised a great army, came to Aachen, and sent some of his army ahead to the river called the Meuse to secure the bridge for him. When those who had promised assistance to the father heard this—namely, the duke’s son—they assembled on the opposite bank of the river. At the instigation of the devil, a great slaughter took place between them on the Lord’s Supper; many also perished by submersion in the river. When the king learned what had happened, he feared that his enemies might attack him. He withdrew from there and came to the castle of Bonn, where he celebrated Holy Easter as best he could.

Then it seemed good to him to hold a court at Pentecost in the city of Worms [Wangion]. There he deprived Duke Heinricus of his public offices [Col. 0594C]. The father, however, celebrated the Lord’s Easter with great joy at Liège together with his followers, and after Holy Easter returned once more to Cologne. The citizens promised him under oath that they would guard the city for him, and thereafter, as he had instructed them, began to fortify themselves very carefully within and without.

When the king saw his father’s cunning and that he was practicing his old malice against the commonwealth [Note: This is how the manuscript punctuates the passage], he gathered a great army from the whole kingdom. After the feast of Saints Peter and Paul he came to the region of Koblenz; there, having assembled the army, he came to Cologne and besieged it.

The people of Cologne, like good soldiers, stood undaunted, resisting him bravely and fighting with the greatest courage, in a manner such as had never before been seen. Among them was a certain kind of men called the Gelduni, whom Duke Heinricus had sent to assist them: warlike, brave men, and highly skilled in battle [Col. 0594D]. Many therefore fell wounded, and the king’s army could not prevail against them. When he had remained there for three weeks and had no hope of capturing the city, he moved the army to Aachen. For it was a very hot summer, and because of the excessive stench the army could no longer endure the hardship.

Meanwhile the emperor fell ill at Liège and, brought almost to the point of death, died on the first of August. He sent the sword and crown that he still had with him to his son by Erkenbald, his most faithful chamberlain, and by Bishop Burchard of Münster, whom he was then holding in chains. He instructed his son to grant and forgive all who had remained with him in his distress, and also asked him to bury him at Speyer beside his parents.

The king immediately summoned the princes of the realm and asked their advice about what he should do concerning his father’s funeral. He had been buried as befitted a king, if he had deserved it before God, at Saint Lambert’s in Liège, honorably, by the bishop who had always been faithful to him in all things.

Then the princes of the realm advised him to order that his father be dug up, lest, if he held any funeral rites for him, he should be under the same sentence as his father; that he should place him in an unconsecrated building; and that he should send messengers to Rome to seek from the pope, if possible, absolution from the ban.

And so it was done, as we have said. He was placed on an island in the Meuse, and no further divine office was performed over him, except that a certain Jerusalemite monk happened to come and sing psalms for him continually, day and night, for as long as he remained there.

Alas that such a person ever deserved to be treated in this way by his son and by the princes of the realm—and, had divine vengeance not intervened, that such a fate should have befallen him at the end of his life.

After this the king decided to carry his father to Speyer. He ordered certain members of his household, especially Erkanbald, who had always remained at his side in his distress, to provide him with service there. When he had been brought there on the third day before the Nones of September, he was received honorably, according to the customary funeral rites, by clergy and people, and carried into the basilica of Saint Mary, which he had built with the greatest care.

For this reason the bishop forbade the celebration of any divine office there until they had been cleansed of this deed. The body was therefore placed outside the monastery, in a chapel that had not yet been consecrated. This caused great disturbance and mourning among the people, because he had loved the place and its people above all others. For a long time afterward the unburied body was visited there by the inhabitants.

The bishop of Liège, together with the others who had rebelled against the king, seeing themselves deprived of their support by the emperor’s death, came to Aachen to surrender, except for Duke Heinricus, who remained in rebellion.

When these matters had been completed, the king returned to Cologne in great anger. He ordered an army to be gathered throughout all the cities adjoining the kingdom [Col. 0595D–0596A], so that they might come to his aid by ship and that he might take revenge upon those men.

When the people of Cologne heard this, they were greatly astonished and terrified. Hemmed in on every side by enemies and having no hope anywhere, they promised to give the king six thousand talents of silver. The king, grieving that many had fallen during the siege, refused for a long time; at last, inspired by God, he consented. Thus the army dispersed, and each man returned joyfully to his own home.

## 1107, indiction 14

The pope, in accordance with the decision of a synod held at Troyes, suspended Routhard, bishop of Mainz, from office because he had restored Udo of Hildesheim without the consent of the church and because he had ordained Reynhard to the church of Halberstadt contrary to the canons. A similar sentence was issued against Givehard of Constance [Col. 0596B] [Note: The letter *D* has already been cut away], because he consented to those who had intruded Godescalc into the church of Minden in place of its bishop and because he ordained Heynricus of Magdeburg. The pope restored to all the churches there the freedom to choose as their prelates those whom they judged worthy, in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons.

King Heinricus came to Regensburg to meet the pope, but since the pope did not come, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there. He celebrated Easter at Mainz, and from there went to meet the pope at the border of Lotharingia and France. After messengers had been sent to one another for three days, they departed without accomplishing the business for which they had come. The king was at Metz for Pentecost.

From there he came to Saxony and found there the duke of Bohemia, expelled from his homeland. He ordered him to be restored to the duchy through Count Wicbertus.

In those days, while the king was at Goslar, thunder came crashing down upon him as he slept and terrified him by awakening him in the night. The lightning that followed melted the boss of the shield placed at his head and part of the sword lying beside him, while he himself remained unharmed.

Then, around the feast of All Saints, he went with his army toward Flanders. After confirming an agreement with the count of that province, Roupertus, he came to Aachen and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there.

## 1108, indiction 15

The king of Hungary began to conspire against the law. When the king heard this, he gathered an army and attacked him in war around the feast of Saint Michael. In the same year King Heinricus shut Count Palatine Sifridus in custody.

## 1109, indiction 1

A solar eclipse occurred on the second day before the Kalends of June. Several people perished by lightning. King Heinricus celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz, and after Pentecost attacked the king of Poland [Note: The source reads *Boulena*; the note gives *Polonia*.] in war and pressed him very hard. In the same year he betrothed the daughter of the king of England. Archbishop Routhard died [Note: From this point another hand begins—the same hand that added the annotations printed in italics; Col. 0596D].

[Col. 0595D] 1109. Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Bruno, bishop of Trier; Chancellor Adelbertus; Count Herimannus of Winceburg; and other distinguished princes went to Rome with considerable pomp, intending to establish peace between the pope and the king. The pope promised that he would receive him with all fatherly affection and gentleness [Col. 0596D–0597A], provided that he presented himself to the Holy Roman See as a Catholic king, as a son and defender of the Church, and as a lover of justice.

## 1110, indiction 2

On the Nones of March a glorious synod was held in the Lateran church, with Pope Paschal presiding. The legates mentioned above came to Liège to the king, bringing the pope’s response. There the king received the daughter of the English king as his bride; at Easter he endowed her at Utrecht in royal fashion.

At Utrecht all the princes of the West warmly approved the expedition into Italy. Around the fifth day before the Nones of June, a bright star appeared at night, sending very long rays from itself toward the south. A lunar eclipse occurred on the second day before the Nones of May [Note: The rest of *Mai* has been cut away; *Maii* in the Saxon Annalist]. The Slavs invaded the region of the Elbe peoples and returned after killing and capturing many.

Thereupon Duke Liutgerus, provoked, invaded the land of the Slavs hostilely, traversed their territory plundering it, captured nine cities that were more strongly fortified and more prosperous than the others, and returned victorious after receiving hostages from them.

Around the Assumption of Saint Mary, the king entered Italy with royal magnificence. All the fortified cities and all the castles submitted to the king.

## 1111, indiction 3

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Florence. After this, on the second day before the Ides of February, he was received honorably at Rome by the pope. After hostages had been exchanged on both sides, they sat in the church of Saint Peter to discuss ecclesiastical affairs.

While these proceedings were taking place, a disturbance arose through the faction of certain people on the steps of the church. Many were wounded and some were killed. When the king heard this, the council was broken up; the pope and the cardinals were assigned to the king’s custody [Col. 0597C]. The Romans fled across the bridge to the far side of the Tiber.

That same night the entire Lateran district was shaken by the tumult of war. At dawn, after standards had been raised, the people of the Lateran unexpectedly attacked the king as one body. The king’s chamberlains seized their weapons and bravely resisted the multitude. The king, whose ranks had now increased, attacked the advancing enemy boldly, though previously his forces had been few; he cut down many who met him and put the rest to flight.

Having gained a complete victory, he took the pope and the cardinals with him and proceeded toward the city of Alba. He pitched camp in the fields adjoining the city and remained there throughout Lent.

After these events, certain of the king’s nobles, having taken counsel together, approached the pope, who was still being held in royal custody. They advised and begged him to deal more gently with the king’s case, to forget any injury he might have suffered from the king, and to make a treaty with him. They offered the king’s fidelity and obedience and urged him in every way to arrange matters of peace and concord with the leading men of the kingdom.

The king himself humbly threw himself at the pope’s feet, asked pardon, and promised obedience, provided that the pope allowed him to exercise, by right of his Catholic royal predecessors, the royal power that belonged to him. Thus he repeatedly tried to persuade the pope to moderate the severity of his mind.

At last the pope was overcome and yielded, and he was permitted to return honorably to Rome [Col. 0598A]. Then, together with the cardinals and the other persons suitable for such a matter, the pope discussed the king’s consecration. On the appointed day, namely the Ides of April, he consecrated the king emperor in the church of Saint Peter.

When the solemn Mass had been celebrated up to the point of Communion, the pope, having ordered silence, addressed the king as follows:

“May this body of our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary and having suffered for the salvation of the human race, be the confirmation of true peace and concord between me and you.”

After they had received Communion, they kissed one another. Thereafter the emperor presented the pope with royal gifts and was dismissed by him with a greeting as a son from his father. He celebrated Pentecost at Verona.

On the seventh day before the Ides of August, with a very large gathering of bishops and other princes present, he buried his father at Speyer in royal fashion [Col. 0598B].

At the Assumption of Saint Mary, at Mainz, Adelbertus—most renowned of all the chancellors who had previously served in the king’s court—was made archbishop of Mainz by the unanimous election of the church, with the emperor present and consenting. Count Palatine Sifridus was released and restored to his rank.

## 1112

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. Liutgerus and Margrave Roudolfus were at odds with the emperor; consequently, by the judgment of the princes, both were condemned. The duchy was entrusted to Otto of Ballenstedt and the march to Elperic.

The emperor besieged Saltwidele. They remained nearby with an army, intending to fight the emperor. But when the fury of war finally subsided, the princes mentioned above enjoyed the emperor’s favor [Col. 0598C]. Adelbertus, the elected archbishop of Mainz, was committed to royal custody.

## 1113

Bishop Reynhard of Halberstadt and Wicbertus were for the second time marked out before the emperor for infidelity. The emperor came to Halberstadt while the bishop was absent and besieged Horneburg.

The bishop, Count Palatine Sifridus, Wicbertus, and Count Lothowicus remained encamped not far away, intending to fight the emperor. But after the city had surrendered and a day had been appointed for the bishop himself to excuse himself, if he could, from the charges brought against him, that military tumult came to an end.

The emperor went toward the Rhine. While these things were happening, Wicbertus was captured by the emperor’s friends. Count Palatine Sifridus was killed. This event brought the emperor no small joy.

The emperor celebrated Easter at Worms. The bishop of Mainz was brought there; Trèves was restored to the emperor; and he was again committed to custody. After Easter the emperor returned to Goslar. Bishop Reynhard obtained the emperor’s favor through the intervention of the princes, and Horneburg was burned.

## 1114

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Bamberg. On the day after Epiphany, having gathered the princes of the entire kingdom, he solemnized the marriage of the king of England’s daughter with immense splendor—of a kind that no king before him had arranged for a very long time.

There Lothowicus, who thought that he stood well in the emperor’s favor, was arrested at the emperor’s command and committed to custody. This event stirred many of the princes against the king. Udo, bishop of Hildesheim, died.

## 1115

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. He summoned Duke Liutgerus, the bishop of Halberstadt, Count Palatine Frithericus, and Margrave Roudolfus to attend this court. They did not come; meanwhile they remained in the garrison at Walbeck.

The emperor occupied Brunswick and devastated Halberstadt. Orlamünde was surrounded by a siege by his friends. Against them Duke Liutgerus and the princes mentioned above advanced, joined by Count Frithericus of Westphalia, his brother Heynricus, Heinrich of Lindburg, and Herimannus of Cavelage.

The emperor met them at a place called Welpesholt [Col. 0599B] [Note: Near Mansfeld]. There, on the third day before the Ides of February, they engaged him fiercely and won a complete victory [Note: The remainder of *Plei* has been cut away; Col. 0599D].

At the Nativity of Saint Mary, Theodericus, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, came to Goslar with a large gathering of Saxon princes and discussed certain useful matters concerning the churches.

A few days later, before the feast of All Saints, they assembled at Fritzlar to discuss matters relating to the honor of the kingdom and the public good. At about the same time the emperor came to Mainz. Suddenly the household of that city—both nobles and ministerials—approached him and begged him, promising that from then on they would be utterly faithful to him in every service, provided that he returned to them the bishop whom he had held captive for three years [Col. 0599C].

At last, overcome by their prayers and also compelled, as it were, by force of circumstances, he returned the bishop to them.

## 1116

Cardinal Theodericus died and was buried at Cologne, with fourteen bishops present, together with Duke Liutgerus and many other princes.

On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, the elected archbishop of Mainz was ordained by Otto, the venerable bishop of Bamberg.

There was a great disturbance in the atmosphere. Around the Nativity of the Lord, while the moon was shining brightly, another moon rose in the west. After it had long confronted the natural moon, with both appearing now to attack and now to flee, they were finally covered by a very dark cloud. When the cloud withdrew, the natural moon alone shone. A similar conflict was also seen among the stars.

[Col. 0599D] 1117. On the octave of Saint John the Evangelist, the earth was shaken throughout the world by a terrible and hitherto unheard-of earthquake. The danger raged continuously for many days, especially in Italy, to such an extent that, through the collision and collapse of mountains, the course of the river Aedissa was blocked for several days [Note: The Etsch?].

The city of Verona, the most distinguished city of Italy, collapsed, its buildings shaken and many of its inhabitants buried beneath them. Likewise, at Parma, Venice, and other cities, towns, and castles, many thousands of people perished.

The river Unstrut, its riverbed split open in the depths, was completely swallowed by the earthquake [Col. 0600A]. After the chasm itself had been filled again, although only after many hours, it flowed in its customary course.

Abbot Erkembald of Corvey and many others from Saxony went to Jerusalem. A few days before the Nativity of the Lord, the sky shone broadly with a fiery color after sunset. Not long afterward something like a broad sunbeam flashed out, and the moon also displayed a portentous sign to those who watched.

## 1118

Pope Paschal happily departed to the Lord. John, previously his chancellor, was chosen as his successor and was also called Gelasius.

The emperor, however, set up another in his place, namely the bishop of Braga [Note: That is, Bracarensis], whom they called Gregory. When this had been done, John, the elected pope, withdrew to Benevento. He excommunicated the emperor and his idol—for this is the name by which the man whom the emperor had substituted was called [Col. 0600B]—as well as all who supported that party.

The soldiers of the archbishop of Mainz, together with Count Herimannus, destroyed and burned Duke Frederick’s garrison at Oppenheim, and many were consumed by the fire.

Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, died after many labors undertaken for the Christian faith and was buried beside his brother Godfrey. The people of Jerusalem appointed another Baldwin, his nephew, in his place.

## 1119

Pope Gelasius died at Cluny while preparing to hold a synod in France, and was buried there. He was succeeded by the archbishop of Vienne, a religious man named Calixtus.

The emperor and the princes of the realm assembled on the feast of Saint John the Baptist and returned to concord, but on the condition that every matter which had hitherto disturbed the Church and supplied fuel for discord between them should be deferred until the presence of Pope Calixtus.

Many people were devoured by wolves.

Pope Calixtus held a synod at Reims around the feast of Saint Luke. Adelbertus, archbishop of Mainz, and many bishops of Germany attended. The emperor remained nearby with his followers to hear the synodal decrees, but nothing relating to reconciliation was accomplished; indeed, the emperor was excommunicated.

## 1120

Duke Liutgerus, Count Palatine Fridericus, Roudolfus, and many others were reconciled with the emperor at Goslar [Col. 0600D]. There was a severe famine: a measure of rye sold for two solidi.

## 1121

Duke Liutgerus and Count Herimannus of Winceburg went to Münster with a large and powerful force to restore Bishop Theodericus. During that restoration, through carelessness, the nobly built church of Saint Paul was consumed by fire together with almost the entire city.

The duke carried away almost all the city’s defenders as captives, both nobles and ministerials. After these events he received the fortified city of Dulmen into surrender.

Around the feast of Saint Michael, the emperor and the princes of the entire realm assembled at the episcopal seat of Würzburg [Col. 0601A] and returned to concord, reserving the settlement of the emperor’s case for the judgment and counsel of Pope Calixtus.

## 1122

On the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, extremely violent storms of wind uprooted countless buildings and trees. A flood caused by the falling of rainwater also occurred, beyond what any mortal could believe. Many people were drowned, and for those who escaped it became the cause of prolonged grief.

Around the feast of Saint Mary, an assembly of princes took place at Speyer. There the bishop of Ostia, a religious man and legate of the Holy Roman Church, absolved the emperor from the ban, with Pope Calixtus’s advice.

To satisfy ecclesiastical justice, the emperor surrendered the investitures of ecclesiastical dignities to Saint Peter [Col. 0601B], but only on the condition that, after a free election had taken place and the authority of the canons had been preserved, imperial authority would not lose what belonged to its jurisdiction in appointing bishops, abbots, or abbesses. If disagreement arose in appointing these dignitaries, as often happens, imperial power would intervene with the counsel of the wise.

## 1123

Adelbero, canonically elected archbishop of Bremen, went to Rome to reclaim the dignity of the pallium. There he was honorably received by Pope Calixtus and consecrated archbishop by him. After a synod had been held according to canonical and judicial procedure, he obtained the pallium, which had been lost through the negligence of his two predecessors [Col. 0601C] and transferred to the Danes.

## 1124

A lunar eclipse occurred on the Kalends of February. Hailstones of enormous size fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of August. A solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Ides of August. There was a great famine. Pope Calixtus died, and Honorius succeeded him.

## 1125

The emperor died at Utrecht within the week of Pentecost; his body was carried to Speyer. On the feast of Saint Bartholomew, all the princes of the entire empire assembled at Mainz, unanimously electing Duke Liutgerus king.

## 1126

The new king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Strasbourg and thereafter returned to his homeland.

Bishop Rotgerus of Naples died, and Northbertus succeeded him.

The king advanced into Bohemia with a very small force to restore Otto, who complained that he had been unjustly deprived of the honor of that province—rashly, indeed. For he took with him no more than three thousand men, while the enemy numbered twenty thousand or more.
