Two hundred more mobile men went ahead of the king, assigned to cut paths through the forests that separate Bohemia from Saxony. While they struggled through the pathless and precipitous forest almost by crawling, exhausted both by the depth of the snow and by cutting the paths, they were unexpectedly surrounded by an ambush of the enemy [Col. 0602A]. Most of the best men of the land fell there: strong and noble men, distinguished both at home and in war.

The king launched an expedition against Duke Frederick of Swabia or Alsace. But when Frederick withdrew into the more strongly fortified parts of the country, the king returned without accomplishing his purpose.

At Trier, at Saint Eucharius, the body of the apostle Saint Matthias was discovered beneath the altar of John the Baptist [Note: This sentence was inserted by Chesnius from the Saxon Annals; the place has now been scraped away]. After it had been honorably placed there, it was thereafter venerated with the greatest devotion by the entire German people.

## 1127

The king pressed the extremely well-fortified city of Nuremberg with a siege. Nothing worth reporting was accomplished there, however, and he returned from the place without result and with losses among his men.

Bishop Heynricus of Paderborn died, and Bernhardus succeeded him.

## 1128

Around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, the king launched an expedition against Conrad, the brother of Duke Frederick, and besieged the city of Speyer. After receiving hostages, he departed around the feast of Saint Martin.

## 1129

After Pentecost the king again surrounded the city of Speyer with a siege because its people had broken the oath of loyalty that they had given in the preceding year.

## 1130

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in tents near the city of Speyer, with a large gathering of princes. At last, when the people of Speyer saw the king’s steadfastness and were compelled by hunger, they surrendered themselves and the city to the king on the feast of the Holy Innocents.

Pope Honorius died, and Innocent succeeded him.

Burkhard of Lucca [Note: Loccum] was killed. The king, therefore, saddened and angered, surrounded Winceburg, the castle of Count Herimannus, to whom the planning and ordering of this killing were attributed, with a siege.

[Col. 0602C] 1131. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Godersheim. Herimannus, following the counsel of the princes, surrendered himself and the aforementioned castle to the king’s power. The king committed him to custody and ordered that the castle be destroyed to its foundations.

## 1132

A very violent force of wind overturned countless buildings. A lunar eclipse occurred on the fifth day before the Nones of March [Note: *Ma ...... c.*]. The translation of Saint Godehard took place.

Around the Assumption of Saint Mary, the king set out for Italy so that the pope might consecrate him emperor at Rome. On this journey, when he reached the city of Augsburg, he entered it peacefully. But through the faction of certain citizens a revolt arose against the king’s men; and for this reason, through a sudden fire, as commonly happens in such a tumult, almost the entire city was burned [Col. 0602D], and many perished both by the sword and in the flames.

## 1133

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Lombardy, at a village called Medicina [Note: Monsa?]. Throughout Italy he captured most of the fortified places that resisted him.

At last, on the second day before the Kalends of May, he entered Rome with the greatest favor. There, on the second day before the Nones of June, which was then a Sunday, Pope Innocent consecrated him emperor at the Lateran, in the basilica of Saint John the Baptist.

Bernhardus, bishop of Paderborn [Col. 0603A], who was then with the king, obtained from Pope Innocent for himself and his successors in that bishopric the use of the *rationale* at celebrations of Mass, at appointed times, at the dedications of churches, and at the ordinations of ecclesiastical ranks.

After this, when the emperor and his followers [Note: The manuscript has *........ uis*; *cum suis* has been restored from the Saxon Annals] were returning and came to a certain place called Clus, almost “closed off” because of the narrowness of its situation [Note: Clausen on the river Eisack, below Brixen in Tyrol], with a very high mountain adjoining it on one side and a very deep flowing river on the other, and with a road in the middle broad enough for four or five travelers to pass together, the inhabitants denied the emperor passage.

By a marvelous event and the evident help of God, he quickly broke into the place. After putting the enemy to flight, he passed through with his followers [Col. 0603B]. He also captured by a sudden assault the city situated on the crest of that highest mountain and carried away its ruler as a prisoner.

Two circles, a larger and a smaller, appeared around the sun on the third day before the Kalends of July, around the third hour. The smaller circle, surrounding the principal church of the see of Paderborn, and the larger, encircling the city, appeared to those who were stationed there.

On that very day, at the ninth hour, that church and almost the entire city were destroyed by fire—alas! A solar eclipse occurred on the fourth day before the Nones of August, around the sixth hour, to such an extent that the stars appeared in the sky.

Great atmospheric disturbances and an inundation of rains followed throughout the entire harvest season.

The king of the Danes mutilated many Teutonic immigrants who had settled in his land [Col. 0603C]. For this reason the emperor intended to launch an expedition against him.

## 1134

The emperor celebrated Easter at Halberstadt. There the king of the Danes came and surrendered himself to the emperor’s power, gave hostages, and swore that neither he nor his successors would obtain the kingdom except with the permission of the emperor and his successors.

In a splendid spectacle such as had never been seen in earlier times, on the holy day of Easter the Danish king, crowned according to royal custom, carried the emperor’s sword before the emperor, who was himself crowned according to custom. Thus he returned to his homeland in the emperor’s favor.

Northbertus, archbishop of Magdeburg, died, and Conrad succeeded him.

[Col. 0603D] 1135. On the Sunday before mid-Lent, namely the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0604A], a large gathering of princes from almost the entire kingdom took place at Bamberg, with the emperor present.

There, by the inspiration of God’s grace, Duke Frederick of Swabia, accompanied by the princes, was reconciled and joined in concord with the emperor.

At Pentecost, at Magdeburg, the princes of the realm for the first time swore before the emperor a firm peace at home and abroad for ten years.

On the feast of Saint Michael, at a place called Mühlhausen, Conrad, the brother of Duke Frederick, was reconciled with the emperor.

## 1136

The Slavs invaded the regions of Saxony. Against them Margrave Adelbertus led an army, repeatedly invading and ravaging their land.

Around the Assumption of Saint Mary, the emperor set out on an expedition to Italy.

[Col. 0604B] 1137. The emperor celebrated both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter in Italy, but Pentecost at Bari, together with a general assembly of the Italian princes.

There Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, died; Hugo, dean of Saint Peter’s, succeeded him, but he too died there after a few days. Both lie buried there.

The prince of Apulia, named Rozir, whose insolence had been the chief reason why the emperor entered Italy, established a strongly fortified castle on the very side of the city of Bari. He placed in it a multitude of robbers who oppressed the surrounding regions by land and sea with unheard-of misery and calamity, taking whatever they could reach.

He had done the same throughout almost all Italy.

After celebrating Pentecost, the emperor surrounded the castle with his army. He captured it with great exertion, handed it over to the flames, and leveled it to the ground [Col. 0604C]. The robbers who had been captured were hanged around the burned tower, five hundred or more in number.

Overcome by this terror, every city and every fortified place surrendered to royal power. From there the emperor crossed into Calabria. There the envoys of the Greeks came to him magnificently; he received and dismissed them even more magnificently.

Adelbertus, archbishop of Mainz, died. After his death the city, together with its principal church, was burned by fire.

Margrave Adelbertus, having gathered a strong force, traversed the land of the Slavs in winter, plundering it.

The emperor, having settled affairs in Italy, died on the second day before the Nones of December during the return journey. His body was carried back to his homeland and buried in royal fashion in his paternal inheritance, at a place called Lutheron [Col. 0604D].

# In the Year of the Lord 1029

## Dudo, Dean of Saint-Quentin of Vermandois

[Col. 0605]

## Historical Notice

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores, volume IV, page 93, introduction to Dudo’s *History of the Normans*, edited by D. G. Waitz.)

[Col. 0605A] Dudo, canon and later dean of Saint-Quentin of Vermandois, explains in the preface addressed to Adalbero, bishop of Laon, how he was led to compose a history of the Normans.

The undertaking of writing this history, begun while Duke Richard I was still alive, was carried through after his death, which Dudo places in 1002, while others [Note: [Col. 0605C] Cf. Lappenberg, *History of England*, II, p. 34.] place it in 996; but he nowhere indicated in what year he completed the work. Nevertheless, it must have been done after 1015, since in that year Dudo was not yet dean [Note: [Col. 0605C] Mabillon, *Annals*, IV, 244.]. He arranged the work, which he also dedicated to Duke Richard, Count Rodulf, and Robert, archbishop of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0605C] See the prefaces and poems in Duchesne, *Ancient Writers of Norman History*, p. 51 ff.], in three books [Note: [Col. 0605C] Perhaps Richard’s history ought to constitute a fourth book, since new prefaces are prefixed to it.]: in the first he briefly touches upon the deeds of Hasting; in the second, those of Rollo; and in the third he sets forth at greater length the history of William [Col. 0605B] and Richard. He testifies that he received the matters he narrated chiefly from Count Rodulf [Note: [Col. 0605C] P. 59. Verses to Count Rodulf, the narrator of this work: “The things written down in this book, which I composed after hearing them from him, I set forth astonished, trembling, dull, anxious, and uncertain.”]; he names no written sources. It was therefore inevitable that he should commit many errors, confuse dates and persons, and disfigure his narrative with other faults. Moreover, since he inserted many speeches and seems often to have devised and embellished descriptions of events and persons in the poetic manner, some judged Dudo to be a writer of fables rather than of history and thought his book to possess no authority [Note: [Col. 0606C] Vossius, *On Latin History*, p. 356; Rivet, *Literary History*, VII, p. 237. Cf. Bouquet, VIII, p. XXIV, who, in a remarkable error, judged the epitome made by William of Jumièges preferable to the author’s work.]. Yet this was a very superficial judgment. For although these objections are not without reason, and although, moved by affection for his people, he seems often to magnify their deeds excessively, [Col. 0605C] and furthermore burdens and rather disfigures [Col. 0606A] than adorns his book with pompous and inflated language, empty, obscure, and sometimes excessively childish verses, it nevertheless contains much that is by no means to be despised. Dudo was a well-educated man who also possessed a knowledge of Greek and had read several poets of antiquity [Note: [Col. 0606C] He himself cites Virgil and Ovid.]; yet, perhaps from affected modesty, he always professed himself unequal to his task, excessively ignorant, weak, and inarticulate. He set forth Norman affairs with great fullness, nowhere strayed very far from the truth, and, as Lappenberg has recently shown [Note: [Col. 0606C] *History of England*, II, p. 373 and elsewhere previously.], generally agrees with other sources. Whatever bears the scent of fable should be thought to have been drawn partly from the ancient songs of the Normans and partly received from the mouth of Count Rodulf and other men who had taken part in the events; and in these as well as in other passages he clearly described and, as it were, painted in vivid colors the customs and appearance of the people. I therefore have no hesitation [Col. 0606B] in reckoning his book among the more valuable monuments of this age; indeed, I should have thought it worthy of being published entire in the *Monumenta*. Since, however, he touched upon German affairs only in a few places, we leave to the French the task of preparing a new edition from the manuscripts, while here we present the fragments that illuminate the deeds of Otto the Great [Note: [Col. 0606C] We give the entire text from Duchesne. [The printed *Tertum* is an apparent error for *Textum*.] EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.]. These too, although sprinkled with certain errors, contain much worthy of notice—for example, what is reported concerning the meeting of King Otto and Duke William, Hermann, duke of the Saxons, captured by the Danes, the siege of the city of Rouen, and other matters.

We have corrected the text published by Duchesne (*Ancient Writers of Norman History*, pp. 51–159) from two manuscripts, that of Sirmond, now preserved at Middlehill [Col. 0606C] [Note: [Col. 0606C] *Archiv*, VII, p. 99.], and that of F. Ambrosius, with the assistance of the Rouen manuscript [Note: [Col. 0606C] On the other manuscripts, see *Archiv*, VII, p. 419.], formerly belonging to Saint Peter of Jumièges, a parchment folio manuscript of the early twelfth century, written accurately and with ample spacing [Col. 0607A] [Note: [Col. 0607A] In the same volume, but in another thirteenth-century manuscript, are contained: William of Jumièges, Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, an abridgment of the deeds of the Frankish kings—1137, the *Translation of the Nail*, etc., the *Vision of Charlemagne*, and, in another hand, fragments of William of Jumièges concerning Richard II.], collated by the distinguished scholar L. Bethmann.

The narrative of Dudo, which William of Jumièges reduced to an epitome [Note: [Col. 0607A] Preface: “For I gathered the beginning of the narrative up to Richard II from the history of the learned man Dudo, who diligently investigated from Count Rudolph, brother of the first Richard, what he committed to writing for transmission to posterity.”], was followed by Orderic Vitalis [Col. 0608A] [Note: [Col. 0608A] Preface to Book III: “For Dudo, dean of Vermandois, eloquently narrated the warlike deeds of the three dukes, and, abounding in manifold words and meters, composed a panegyric upon them.” The French writer Benoît de Sainte-More also seems to have had Dudo before his eyes; cf. Lappenberg II, pp. 374–394.], and Saxo Grammaticus likewise consulted him [Note: [Col. 0608A] Book I, opening: “Although Dudo, the writer of Aquitanian affairs, records that the Danes were descended from and named after the Danaans”; cf. Stephani’s notes, p. 31, etc.], so that the author’s reputation had already crossed the boundaries of Normandy and France by the Middle Ages.

**G. Waitz**

# The Three Books of Dudo, Dean of the Congregation of Saint-Quentin, on the Customs and Deeds of the First Dukes of Normandy

(Duchesne, *Ancient Writers of Norman History*, explaining the deeds performed by them throughout Gaul, England, Apulia, the principality of Capua, Sicily, and the East, from the year of Christ 838 to 1220—Paris, 1619, folio.)

## Duchesne’s Notice

[Col. 0607B] Dudo, at first a cleric, “canon, as he says, of Christ’s precious martyr Quintin,” and sent under this title by Albert, count of Vermandois, to Richard, duke of the Normans, so that through his intervention he might reconcile Hugh, king of France, who was hostile to the count. Later he was appointed dean over the whole congregation of Saint-Quentin, as he himself notes above. He begins his writing with Hasting, duke of the Danes, who preceded Rollo; he ends it with the death of Richard I, duke of Normandy, whose grandfather was Rollo. He declares, in his letter to Adalbero, bishop of Laon, that he began the work not of his own spontaneous will, but in order to discharge his duty of service to that duke, on account of the countless benefits which he had deigned to bestow upon him without any merit on Dudo’s part. He had not yet reached the first [Col. 0607C] parts of the work when sorrowful news announced that Prince Richard had died. Then he wished to set everything else aside in grief for him, as he himself testifies, because of excessive weeping and intolerable lamentation. But through his son, Duke Richard, and the distinguished Count Rodulf of Ivry, the same matter was brought before him again. Both pressed him with entreaties to carry out what Duke Richard, the father, had commanded, and protested that he should not leave his undertaking unfinished [Col. 0608B]. He yielded to their commands and prayers, completed the work, and dedicated it to Adalbero, bishop of Laon, for confirmation by his authority.

William of Jumièges, the monk, calls him a learned man in his letter to William I, king of the English. Orderic, monk of Utica, or Saint-Evroul, speaks of him in a few words in the prologue to Book III of his *History*: “Dudo, dean of Vermandois, eloquently narrated the warlike deeds of the three dukes; and, abounding in manifold words and meters, composed a panegyric upon them and sent it to Richard Gunnor’s son, seeking his favor.” And again, near the end of Book VI: “Concerning the arrival of the Normans and their savage barbarity, Dudo, dean of Vermandois, wrote diligently and sent his account to Richard II, son of Gunnor, duke of the Normans.” In this edition I used two manuscripts, one belonging to the illustrious Mr. Francis Ambrosius, the other to Mr. Jacques Sirmond; the latter alone also contains various poems interwoven in a style more rustic than poetic. Yet I did not wish to omit them, lest I should seem to some to have diminished the reliability of the history.

# A Panegyrical and Apologetic Epistle, Set Forth in Outline

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609A] To the illustrious and devoutly venerable Adalbero, adorned by noble birth, ennobled by wisdom, seated upon the episcopal throne of the holy church of God at Laon, guide of the sheep entrusted to him before the sight of the divine Majesty: Dudo, dean over the congregation of Saint-Quentin.

No one who understands the words of the Lord spoken to Nicodemus, “The Spirit breathes where it wills,” is unaware that the widespread proclamation of your most glorious name, exalted above the highest summit of Lebanon and brighter than light, has been extended and broadcast farther through a lengthy interpolation of great length and through the far-reaching interval of the earth’s expanded breadth. For, being made manifest to human sight by a sign, you have become sufficient consolation to all and all things to all; you surpass the eminence of all prelates [Col. 0609B] both by the seed of your noble birth and by the nourishing excellence of your merit. Therefore you, the summit of the episcopate, illustrious exemplar of uprightness, incomparable form of a transparent life, priestly glory, indescribable light of the universal Church, distinguished summit of holiness, inflexible pillar of all goodness, are rightly confirmed by a truthful declaration according to your merits.

For divine Majesty’s right hand determined to raise you—whose great and eminent person is celebrated by outstanding deeds—to such an honor of distinction, because divine charity, together with her manifold offspring, possesses the recesses of your undefiled breast and the inmost chambers of your innocent heart. Whatever each servant of God obtains through the constant and watchful effort of the children of that same charity, as the divine Spirit inspires and enlightens minds [Col. 0609C], and whatever can be attained through their most holy service, seems divinely to reign in you; wonderfully the fountain of charity has placed the whole accumulation of those virtues in the dwelling of your breast.

It is indeed certain to all who possess reason, my father and lord, that from the cries of your earliest childhood you wholly sacrificed yourself, through inward contrition of heart, as a living offering to the eternal priest; that you consecrated your breast as a throne for the heavenly Spirit by the fullness of your virtues; and that you dwelt in heaven in your mind. For the remarkable purpose of your joyful spirit—and it remains evident to the present time—has never been seen to deviate from its beginning through any flood of dissipation or crookedness of vice.

Touched, therefore, by the nectar of the Holy Spirit, you appear heavenly in singular marvel and marvelous singularity: while, like a mystical lamp [Col. 0610A], you blaze among the bishops of the world with solar brightness. What heart could be so stony, or be so enveloped in a covering of darkness, that, after observing your marvelous deeds, it would not immediately turn from its wickedness to a celibate life?

Indeed, all who strive to withdraw themselves from the winding road of that most bitter path, on which many are harshly led to death, and toward which the wisdom of the deceiving world directs the way of those whose united purpose imitates the pleasures of bodily delight, are made participants in your religious life. For throughout many past and future ages you have certainly appeared neither to have an equal before you nor a successor like you.

Nor is it surprising, most reverend bishop, if this has been divinely granted to you, so that you may be for the whole world a pre-eminent model of good conduct [Col. 0610B]. For from your very cradle you have appeared to climb, by the steps of the virtues, the temples of the starry homeland and to possess, by the greatness of your rewards, the star-bearing seats.

Yet even such deeds introduce a certain wonder, O bishop worthy of marvelous admiration, so that you could not be accused by the wicked whispers of unjust sophists. Having embraced the precepts of that life which always strives toward difficult heights, you applied such care to your pursuits that, whenever you heard from natives or from the report of any person that some form of religion flourished anywhere in the world, you never allowed an hour to pass until you hastened to fulfill it as quickly as possible.

You will enter the joy of your Lord through little things—that is, through the faithful distribution of the gifts of five talents and the prudent apportionment of food—and, when the Lord comes, you will be placed over many things as a good and faithful servant. For, joined to the fellowship of heavenly virtues, you will possess joys destined to endure without end.

The mina entrusted to you will, through your sacred transactions, return ten minas to the treasury of the supreme Master of the household when the Lord returns. For, having gained yourself for God through the commandments of the Decalogue, carrying sheaves of justice in your right hand, you will bring to the table of the invisible and immortal Bridegroom the hundredfold fruit, worthy to be his guest, just as a mina is reckoned at one hundred drachmas.

You have rightly obtained the rank of apostolic merit, and by divine lot have been exalted at the summit of that rank, namely in the number twelve; for if the mysteries of that number are weighed [printed *muneri*, apparently for *numeri*], everything is assigned to your eminence. That number is truly called “oddly even” (*impariter par*), composed of even-even and even-odd. For just as this number possesses the same significance as the numbers from which it is formed and another significance which they do not possess, so you possess from God both the religious power which belongs to all bishops assigned to that number and another power besides.

And just as it is called odd on one side and even on the other, so you are found unequal and equal to others who are exalted by the height of that number: unequal in holiness, but equal in title. It is rightly declared excessive in relation to its parts, since, when its proper divisors are added together, they exceed the sum of its original quantity; so, when the signs of your holiness are gathered together, you are found higher in merit than others serving God in the same number.

What else is indicated by the same number in the musical reckoning of modes except the sublimity of so great a patron? What else does twelve accomplish than to complete, by the increase of its duplication, the consonance of the octave (*diapason*) in relation to six, which, by a certain demonstration of its own, customarily signifies the perfection of something, just as it is itself perfect? And what is declared through the ascending order of this number except the immense perfection accumulated in you through the doubled increase of duplication?

For when this same number retains the consonances of the fifth (*diapente*) and fourth (*diatessaron*) in the ratios of three to two with eight and four to three with nine, then, at the time when your advancement raised you to pastoral government, it increased the eight beatitudes of life and joined your name to the choirs of angels. And just as, through multiplication by two, twelve rises to the accumulation of twenty-four, so the twofold observance of the two commandments—love of God and of one’s neighbor—has joined you to the twenty-four heavenly elders. With them, crowned with an unfading wreath, you will sing a new song to the one seated upon the throne.

Among these, just as that number, with its half placed above it—namely six, which, as has been said, lacks deficiency and excess—grows to eighteen, so you will delight effectively in the sweet-sounding consonances that render the service of the whole harmonic modulation through a honeyed song, hearing nothing defective and nothing excessive, according to the five tetrachords joined by eighteen unequal strings [Col. 0611D].

To what does all this tend? This is the reason. Having traveled through every region of Gaul and surveyed all the boundaries of Christians on every side, I find no one to whom the gifts of every honor ought to be attributed with equal distinction as to you. Therefore, memorable Father, after the illustrious fame arising from your marvelous deeds burst upon my ears, it constantly supplied my mind with goads to turn toward you; for, as though from the very dissemination of your name, I learned that you would satisfy my desires everywhere and become a refreshment for my need.

This need I have suffered from the beginning until now: I could find no one to whom I might present for correction the contemptible and rejectable composition of so small a work, [Col. 0612A] except you, whose praise seems to touch the heavens and to whom, as was said above, all honor is due. Such an honor I turn over in my heart and consider in my mind, as fitting so great a patron: so that whatever appears obscure in this book through its own darkness may be brought by you into the light; and that you may acquire not the reputation of a poor and inglorious author, but the praise of an excellent corrector.

Although I deserve to be reckoned foolish for this, I take courage from these letters and assume the boldness of audacity as I approach the presence of your majesty. With head bowed in submission of heart and body, I join prayers to prayers—not once, nor twice, nor three times, but repeatedly—that every scruple of unjust ambiguity may be [Col. 0612B] utterly and radically cut away by your sharp double-edged axes, forged from the purest steel of all wisdom.

Nearly half of this work seems wholly unrelated to useful business unless, with you as reaper, the thistles of superfluity are hoed away. For, while I am weighed down by bodily weakness and hindered by the necessity of worldly affairs, the eye of my mind, of its own accord embracing blindness rather than light, is stifled, blinded by desires for bodily joys, and submerged in an immense whirlpool of darkness. That eye, which I say is deprived of the support of true light, I desire to have illuminated by you, who are occupied with the precepts of the sacred writings.

I wish to make it clear to you that you should not think I clung to this work willingly or began it of my own spontaneous will. Two years before his death [Col. 0612C], I was, in the customary manner of frequent visits, with the distinguished Duke Richard, son of Marquis William, wishing to discharge my duty of service to him on account of the countless benefits which he had deigned to grant me without my deserving them.

One day he approached me and began to embrace me in the arms of most holy love, to draw me on with his sweetest words, and to charm me with pleasant entreaties; indeed, in love he solemnly adjured me and swore that, if I could in any way do so, I should relieve the desires long cherished in his mind—namely, that I should describe the customs and deeds of the Norman land, and even the laws which his great-grandfather Rollo established in the kingdom.

I was astonished as if beside myself, and for several days refused him, rejecting his requests. At last, moved by so many entreaties and wearied by such prayers, I scarcely bent my mind to place [Col. 0612D] the weight of so great a burden upon my shoulders. And although I had judged what was being demanded to exceed my strength, I placed the yoke of so great a burden upon my neck, becoming an imitator of the command that bids us stand firm, act manfully, be strengthened, and do everything in charity (1 Cor. 16:13).

The stylus of our ignorance had scarcely reached the opening parts of the work when, alas, sorrowful news announced that Richard, the prince renowned throughout the world, had died. I would have set all these things aside in grief for that prince because of excessive weeping and intolerable lamentation—which shook and tormented not only my heart but also the limbs of my whole body—had not the same matter been brought before me by his most excellent son, the patrician Richard, who still survived, and by the distinguished [Col. 0613A] Count Rodulf.

They both pressed their entreaties upon me, that I should carry out what Duke Richard, memorable for his life, had commanded while making his request; and they protested that the undertaking which I had promised him should not appear, through the fault of double-tongued speech, to be stained by any taint of falsehood, but should stand strong in the innermost marrow of its whole meaning. Yielding to their commands and prayers, I carried it through, although it does not boast of dialectical syllogisms or rhetorical arguments.

[Col. 0614A] I resolved to send it to your majesty so that falsehoods might be cut away and, if it contained anything true, it might be confirmed by your authority. Thus may the wonderful giver of rewards, who placed the distinguished Marquis Richard in the glory of his paradise, just as he raised you as a column of his holy Church, establish you, adorned with an everlasting wreath, as a senator of the heavenly court among all the choirs of the saints.

# Address to the Book

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613A] Since you have been arranged in a very slender theme,  
lacking every rhetorical method of sweet expression,  
Book, when I search through you with my inward eye,  
my mind is distressed that you long to bring before the public  
the figures arranged fruitlessly by my pen,  

[Col. 0613B] and that you may be jeered at amid arrogant, crafty uproar.

If seals preserve you for modest studies,  
the weariness of seclusion threatens us with harm. [The transmitted construction is uncertain.]  
For scarcely did the bronze tower conceal Danaë  
from the golden rain,  
as Fulgentius recounts in his myth.

Either now fly on to the Norman schools,  
or remain shut up and linger in the Frankish schools.  
I fear that a sufficient ridiculous sneer may arise against us  
if, impatient, you reject the lock once the bar is removed,  
and … hasten into the mouths of the sharp-tongued crowd. [The source marks a gap before the corrupt *proprias*, apparently *properas*, “you hasten.”]

The Normans will shake the unwilling poet with their whip.  
Now, boldly and swiftly, you will come before the public.  
How much they despise you, you will be tossed about in such a great flood.  
One here will spit foully through gathered lips and mouth;  
another, drawing back his nostril, will accompany it with an unspeakable sound;  

[Col. 0613C] and this one will applaud excessively with profane hands.  
Here one will stamp the ground three times with raised feet [Note: [Col. 0613D] Read *iste*, “that man,” for *hic*, “this man,” to make the verse scan.];  
another, searching out warts, will mark them with his mouth.  
If no flaw appears anywhere,  
he will certainly know how to distort sound passages with false charges. [The intervening *cordibus explosis*, “with hearts driven out/derided,” is obscure.]

But if from this he becomes more ruined and profane,  
let the madman rage more fiercely against all these things,  
and, whether unwillingly or willingly, thus you will undergo *ἀντία* (“opposites”) and *ὤντα* (“things that are”),  
at last beneath sneering mockery and every …  
you will be thrust fruitlessly into a shop for saffron, narcissus,  
ginger, a little spikenard, costus, and pepper:  

[Col. 0614B] whatever you contain is wrapped in idle pages. [The marked gaps and faulty syntax obscure the details; the book appears destined to wrap shop goods.]

A warning voice will have opposed you from afar, without care to remedy matters;  
if, acting on your own counsel, you complain  
that ours has failed you, keep recalling this to yourself. [The syntax is damaged.]

At the head of the title, with your forehead wavering, let a sharp title be placed.  
First let reverence arise for mighty QUINTINUS,  
so that he might open the heavens—the path he made by his death.  
By these deeds, and by his merits, let him mark the beginning.

Perhaps you will be able to despise this defenseless crowd,  
or the thousand perils of the scourging populace;  
yet, before such great merits of a shining name,  
the swollen ranks will scarcely dare to despise you.

Their rage will soften [printed *Nitescet*, apparently for *Mitescet*], and under such a leader they will withhold their spittle.  
When the fever has been withdrawn,  
let them not grow savage with their bare teeth.  
Under the sevenfold-flowing Spirit, happy book, with your holy guide [printed *liberi*, probably *liber*, “book”],  
continually protected, fortified, and aided,  

[Col. 0614C] you will blunt* [the object is unstated] through the merits of the gracious martyr Quintin.  
Nor should you complain that you departed unwarned,  
for what remains to doubtful fates, with a suppliant companion *[uncertain]*,  
and would that better things might follow me according to my desired affection.

# Verses to Richard, Son of the Great Richard

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613C] O you magnanimous, devout, modest one!

O you outstanding, fearing God!

O you magnificent, upright, kind one!

O you marvelous, good, and just one!

O you peace-loving one, offspring of God!

O you generous, sacred, modest one!

O you exceedingly radiant, merciful Richard!

[Col. 0613D] O you long-suffering, prudent Richard!

[Col. 0614C] O you most renowned, gracious Richard!

O you law-abiding, gentle Richard!

O you deserving, sweet Richard!

Peoples of every kind speak of you fittingly.

Remember modestly in a book the things you see.

Feed your heart and breast upon these things,

so that you may be able to be joined to those whom you recount.

# Anxiety and Dissuasion Concerning the Future Subject Matter

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613D] My anxious mind, tossed by various whirlwinds,  
by countless misfortunes,  
by the reversals of things flying about at inopportune times,  
and by the slips and revolutions of an agitating fate,  
wavers, clinging amid excessive sobs;  
my heart too, dreadfully afraid, withers in its scorched fibers.

My spirit, numb with grief, sighs bitterly;  
my tongue, already amid the hoarse passages of my throat,  
delirious, shudders, stammers, babbles, and falters;  
in squalid neglect it scarcely mutters sounding words;  
my sluggish intellect and small understanding,  
my difficult perception—and, alas, my mind filled with folly—

By what means can I relate in polished speech  
[Col. 0614D] what is entrusted to me to accumulate,  
what has been done by divine power and by heavenly command?  
I cannot draw out with human lips what has been done  
either privately by chance or publicly, arranged as it was.

Whoever takes upon himself a heavy burden beyond his power,  
suffering great mockery and ridicule,  
exposes himself to the foolish chatter of a joke.  
Often, for the careless follower of the wild beast in the art of hunting,  
both his presumption and the trackless forest bring him to ruin.

Thus the novice carries a shield as a memorial of war,  
sweating with easy effort in playful practice,  
but he does not know how to fight in a forced single combat.

[Col. 0615A] A bird will never traverse the space allotted to it  
unless its mother has gone before it as guide. [The first line is corrupt: *nunquam vestra tatus spatulum sibi cessum*; “space” reads *spatulum* as *spatium*.]

He who enters the sea in a small boat,  
ignorant of the sailors’ knowledge and art,  
is tossed now here, now there, or is often swallowed up.

He who is accustomed to sit often upon an ass without trappings  
is thrown down when, having become a horseman, he rushes forward.

There is no need to go to the marketplace to weigh the interest on merchandise  
for one who does not know how to buy cautiously what he wants or to bid,  
destitute of every art, reason, and counsel.

Thus, through every misstep, the man who attempts to repeat  
what he cannot define moderately is torn in different directions,  
unless the teaching and favor of learned men assist him.

Therefore I am now pricked by the squalor of my ignorance,  
not knowing what I should do, what I should undertake, or what I should leave undone.

[Col. 0615B] Although my dull understanding may digest,  
through the natural chatter of its foolishness,  
something lukewarm, tasteless, and dishonorable concerning the theme,  
relying on the strength of no author,

I shall attempt and accomplish whatever I can,  
trusting in the Lord who rules the world by his dominion,  
doing whatever he wills in heaven, on earth, and in the sea.

He compelled the creature accustomed to braying to utter full words and to speak to its rider in another’s words;  
he restored Lazarus after his burial,  
and wished the dead man, after the funeral, to run alive.

Then he went beneath the banners of the cross and redeemed the world.

Receive the deeds of your great-grandfather, revered prelate,  
and receive the deeds of your wealthy grandfather.

And receive the deeds of your father, known for his merits beyond the heavens,  
and, through his merits, a sharer with Christ.

Feed your mind upon his kindly virtues;  
instruct yourself by exercising yourself in his virtues.

Recalling his marvelous deeds, repeat them in speech;  
recalling his marvelous words as well.

And remember, remember the causes worthy of remembrance;  
now remember, remember what he nobly accomplished.

Recall, with distinguished efforts, his character,  
and remember it with distinguished efforts.

Read again this legitimate work and gladly imitate it,  
and, studying it, investigate this legitimate work.

You know that he always loved the camp of God, recalling it;  
you know that he venerated and loved the camp of God.

He himself was a wall of his homeland, not fragile before the battering ram,  
[Col. 0616A] and a gate difficult for the battering ram, not fragile.

The orphan, exile, and needy person received help, and the widow too;  
he was a comfort to all—orphan, exile, needy person. [The printed *viduaequo* is apparently *viduaeque*, “and the widow.”]

He founded churches and made pagans believe;  
he built shrines and founded churches.

With his heart and strength he loved God the Lord,  
and his neighbor as himself—with his heart, God the Lord.

Bravely he subdued fierce peoples by violent warfare,  
and bravely he trampled down fierce peoples.

With a friendly word he held sway over kings and dukes [printed *Legibus*, “laws,” apparently for *Regibus*, “kings”; Note: [Col. 0615D] *Induperabat*, “held sway,” is also used by Ennius.];  
more gracious in his kingdom toward kings and dukes.

He enriched envoys with various gifts and honors,  
and likewise the humble with various gifts.

Distributing cloaks, gold, skins, and horses,  
generous in gifts, distributing cloaks.

[Col. 0616B] He soothed the untamed Danes with friendly words,  
and, pressing them severely, he subdued the untamed Danes.

Everywhere the glory of our rank and order,  
and the support of rank and order.

Renowned in conversation, rich in the image of virtues,  
gentle in speech, renowned in conversation.

His good deeds now exceed my powers as an advocate,  
and his resources surpass an advocate’s powers.

His true testimony of probity remains,  
and the signs still shine; the testimony remains.

Shall I say more, or keep silent about what appears to have been done?  
In time to come shall I speak, or remain silent?

Behold, my account will be able to babble whatever it can,  
and my treatise too will babble at the same time.

With a roaring voice I shall thunder, trembling as I recall with vehement heart  
[Col. 0616C] what he spoke while alive; with a roaring voice I shall thunder.

O revered, devout, memorable, venerable patron,  
Bishop Robert, O memorable and devout one.

Search out the father’s remembered and forgotten triumphs;  
investigate his deeds and the things forgotten concerning the father.

And present yourself to the father through reverent words,  
looking upon his deeds, present yourself to the father.

May the father’s present prayer continually come to our aid,  
and may his unceasing vows continually come to our aid.

O that you may be strong, flourish, and powerfully endure through the ages,  
reigning with Christ—O that you may flourish!

May you remain in the Elysian field with your revered father,  
in the Elysian homeland of heaven.

# Verses to Count Rodulf, Narrator of This Work

[Col. 0615]

[Col. 0615C] Virtue, fame, and power, everywhere proclaimed,  
grew throughout the fiery world of the kingdom; let those overcome  

[Col. 0615D] yield to the probity of Count Rodulf.

Under those consuls the Roman world grew wise;  
now the Norman summit is the height of Richard’s honor,  
the virtue, glory, and power of the whole kingdom,  
strengthened by your kindly character and merits, Rodulf.

Through the recompensing one he flourishes, is feared, and prevails while he survives,  
pre-eminent in gravity of spirit and depth of heart.

From your mouth you pour the salt of a tranquil, nourishing breast;  
as the wave of salt seasons foods, so you season things with understanding.

A root of fruitful counsel, a jar of rich nectar,  
alive in intellect, gentle in radiant speech.

[Col. 0616C] As the sun warms this world, so you refresh all things with *sirmate* [reading and sense uncertain].

[Col. 0616D] As the Nile restores Egypt, so you revive the hearts of your people.

The Norman land deserved you as its radiant light.

You shine everywhere, glowing with the lamp of your heart.

The ancient foremost fathers and the nobles of our own time,  
Scipio, Pompey, and Cato, the glory of Rome,  
magnificent honor, ruling empire, and flashing dominion—

O fortunate spirit, who takes thought for the deeds of your homeland,  
the kingdom’s aid, support, and glory,  
whose deeds, written in this book, I arranged from your report,  
astonished, trembling, dull, anxious, and uncertain.

May the highest honor be yours while Christ reigns forever.

And may your present and future life be with the saints.

# Also to Robert, Archbishop

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617A] Most distinguished and venerable prelate,

magnificent summit of the churches,

our highest honor and our nourisher,

light, distinguished glory, and worthy salvation

of our holy rank, author of our order:

receive what has been arranged by my understanding.

Touch with sacred hand what I, a suppliant, bring,

untouched by those learned in grammatical art [the source marks a gap];

and, reading, examine everything that has been accomplished,

which sweet love and supreme care for

the distinguished father, sweet and generous,

the great Patrician and reverend

Richard, renowned throughout the faltering world,

now rightfully powerful in his eternal homeland:

sweet love and care for him made me write, though very briefly.

[Col. 0617B] He flourished in goodness and piety,

was strong in simplicity and probity,

shining in judgment and justice,

more splendidly in this kingdom,

in the time of the great king Clothar

and of Hugh, first duke and afterward king.

With a discerning heart and prudent mind,

remember his expenditures, deeds, and words.

Thus you may rightly be compared,

in worthy and similar goodness,

to so worthy and renowned a count,

so just, good, and modest,

so holy, devout, and venerable,

and rightfully possess what he enjoys,

and go on the right hand into the company above,

a beautiful lamb with shining white fleece,

joined to heaven’s inhabitants in everlasting peace.

Pontifical summit and honor,

shining with the highest eminence,

[Col. 0618A] glory of bishops according to your merits,

excellent shepherd of the Lord’s flock,

burning with peaceful piety,

generous in holy duties,

palm, glory, faith, and salvation

of the Church’s rank and order,

head of the Christian people,

distinguished aid of the fatherland,

venerable man, sacred in merits,

of the outstanding warlike great-grandfather,

of the grandfather shining in martyrdom,

and of the most sweet and excellent father,

laid open by my intellect

in the order of a prose theme,

by my foolish-speaking, senseless, dull,

[Col. 0618B] ignorant, inept work—see and receive it.

Flowing with their subject matter,

sweet, generous, and foolish,

in speech and truthful address. [*Famine* is from poetic *famen*, “speech.”]

Read the deeds, repeating them at length,

and remember whatever good you find.

Feed your mind with the fruitful harvest

and instruct your heart with such banquets.

May you be able to run, equal in deeds,

with your lord,

with the father, with the sacred ancestor.

Glory, life, salvation, and probity,

with body and mind preserved,

may you possess for a long and countless time.

And after the mournful destruction of death,

may you flourish in the Elysian homeland,

sharing in the heaven-sent things (Greek, corrupt as printed: “ΘΗΩΘΗΝ ΩΥΡΑΝΥΚΑΜ,” apparently *θεόθεν οὐρανικά*).

[Col. 0617] Beloved prelate,

venerable,

memorable,

and awe-inspiring;

whose name

can contain,

redeemed,

should be absent

Of marvelous

Receive the deeds

of your father and grandfather,

and wails aloud

and converse,

with its manifold

is deemed sorrowful—

indeed, [like an order] of widows—
Wandering throngs,

Exiled, destitute,

Hungry,

Thirsty also,

Deprived of light,

Counsel,

And clothing, naked,

Pressed by cold,

And full of disease;

Rich in every

[Col. 0619] Kind of wealth,

A throng of good

And evil,

The summit of pontifical

Honor,

Kings, and nobles,

Greek and Indian,

The clergy dedicated

To their lord’s

Lot,

The venerable order,

Beautiful Easterners

And Westerners,

And the Sicambrian,

Warlike and fierce,

[Col. 0619] Wept bitterly.

Excellent prelate,

And highest peak,

[Col. 0619A] O threefold manifestation, three supreme things,* one virgin God,

Pre-eminent divine power, heavenly pillar;

Glory of causes and order, harmony of the world,

Without beginning and remaining without end.

And Nous and Logos, sustainer and mighty maker of the world,

The idea of the star-bearing terrestrial globe.

With humble prayer I ask, aspiring through the vows of my prayers,

That you may favor beginnings trembling in their ignorance.

The deeds and fortunes of events, the misfortunes, briefly

I shall unfold, if I can, in a prose theme:

[Col. 0620A] What frenzied barbarity wrought under Alstemo as leader,

And what it finally wrought under Rollo, the worshipper of Christ.

How his offspring William, likewise, in every

Law and under a calmed rule, benefited the empire,

And also how, deservedly, Richard, renowned above the heavens,

The supreme patrician and devout worshipper of Christ, benefited it.

The fertile land of the Northman people rested under rightful rule

With you, God, as its guarantor—you who see all things, salvation itself—

You reign, you live, and you remain without end.

# BOOK ONE. HASTINGUS.

[Col. 0619]

[Col. 0619A] After the whole mass of the world had been described, and the circuit and surface of the earth carefully measured, cosmographers, conceiving the entire land enclosed on every side by the perpetual boundary of Ocean and measuring it by the heavenly axis of the four-part sky, divided it into three parts, reckoning Asia, Europe, and Africa. Of these, Europe, intersected by the channels of very many rivers and distinguished by various provinces, is bounded by the borders of its native lands. One of these, extremely extensive and the most abundant of the others because of the countless multitude of its inhabitants, is called Germania. In it the river Ister, rising from the summit of Mount Hatnoen [Atnoe], increased in volume through all sixty [stages?] and, flowing turbulently from south to east, separates Germania and Scythia as far as the place where it is received by the sea; it is called the Danube.

Thus, in the broad interval from the Danube to the boundary of the Scythian sea, savage and barbarian peoples dwell spread abroad. They are said, in barbarian fashion, to have burst forth from the island of Canza [Scanzia], enclosed by Ocean on every side, in manifold diversity, like a swarm of bees from a basket or a sword from its sheath. For there is there a very extensive region of Alania, an exceedingly abundant territory [Col. 0620A] of Dacia, and a very widely extended tract of Getia. Dacia lies nearest the middle, fortified in the manner of a crown, like a city, by immense Alps.

The peoples who inhabit these wondrous bends of vast extent, with Mars warning them to be warlike, are the Getae, who are also Goths, the Sarmatians and Amaxobii, the Tragoditae and Alans, and very many peoples dwelling around the Maeotian marshes and cultivating them. These peoples, inflamed by exceedingly wanton luxury and sexually violating very many women with singular depravity, beget innumerable offspring there through the obscene mingling of unlawful unions.

When these have grown up, and have become numerous through fierce quarrels over possessions against their fathers and grandfathers, or more often among themselves, and are no longer able to inhabit the land in which they live, they gather by lot a multitude of young men and, according to an ancient custom, drive them out into the foreign kingdoms of other nations, so that by fighting they may acquire kingdoms in which they can live in perpetual peace. Thus did the Getae, who are also Goths, devastate nearly the whole of Europe as far as the place where they now dwell.

When their expulsions and departures were completed, they formerly sacrificed while worshipping [Col. 0621A] Thur, their god. They did not offer him any gift of cattle, sheep, Liber Pater, or Ceres, but slaughtered human blood, considering it the most precious of all holocausts. For, when a divining priest had predetermined it, the yokes of oxen were fiercely struck once upon the head, and the brain of each person chosen by lot was shattered with a single blow and cast upon the ground. They searched out the heart-fibre on the left, namely the vein; after draining its blood according to their custom and smearing their own heads with it, they quickly spread the sails of their ships to the winds. Believing that they had appeased them by such a rite, they quickly mounted the oars of their ships. But if they had gone forth with a larger force of horsemen, they raised the warlike standards of battle.

Thus, escaping from their own borders, they directed their purpose toward the deadly upheaval of nations. They are exiled from their fathers so that they may clash manfully with kings. They are sent away destitute by their own people so that they may purchase food from foreigners. They are deprived of their own estates so that they may occupy those of others in peace. They are driven out as exiles so that, while fighting, they may grow rich. They are thrust out by their own people so that they may share with foreigners. They are separated from their nation so that they may rejoice in the possessions of others. They are abandoned by their fathers, perhaps never to be seen by their mothers.

The harshness of the young is raised up for the destruction of nations. The homeland is freed of its inhabitants, cleansed of them. The other provinces grieve, wickedly poisoned by a most numerous enemy. Thus they lay waste everything that stands in their way. They sail near the shores of the sea so that they may claim the spoils of lands for themselves. What they seize from one kingdom they carry into another. They seek harbors under a negotiated peace [Col. 0621C] in order to lend out the plunder they have taken.

The Dacians, therefore, are called Danai, or Dani, by their own people, and boast that they are descended from Antenor, who, after Troy had been plundered and having escaped through the midst of the Achaeans, entered the Illyrian territories with his followers. These Dacians, once expelled by their own people according to the reported custom, violently landed in the region where far-stretching Francia extends its territories, with the leader Anstinuus [also Hastingus].

He was accursed, yet exceedingly savage, cruel, and ferocious;

Pestilential, hostile, grim, brutal, and criminal;

Pestilential and fickle, insolent, boastful, and lawless;

Death-dealing, relentless, cautious, and everywhere rebellious;

A traitor and instigator of evil, a two-faced deceiver;

Impious and swollen with pride, seductive, deceitful, and bold;

[Col. 0621D] A gallows-bird, incestuous, unbridled, and quarrelsome;

An increase of pestilential evil, an accumulation of deceit;

To be marked not with ink but with charcoal.

And so much more monstrous than all others in wickedness,

As he is suspected to rise toward the star-bearing Olympus.

Here and there he polluted the exiled peoples, and claimed their resources for himself and his own. He invaded the dominion of Gaul’s power and usurped the kingdom of Francia for himself. He violated the priesthood and trampled upon the sanctuary. By word and deed he harassed the king of the Franks, who was dwelling sadly with his people in the cities. He roared around the walls of the strongholds like a wolf around sheepfolds. He despised the Franks, who had taken refuge in their fortifications out of fear. He pursued them all like a lion pursuing stags. He slaughtered those he found, killing those whom he discovered withdrawn in hiding.

A slaughter was made; the sorrowful were cut down by the point of the sword. The clergy were punished and put to death with cruel death. The wicked put on the little tunics which they had plundered from sacred altars. They clothed themselves in the white garment dedicated to the office of the Mass. Whoever took up arms against them was cruelly killed. The rest of the people, unaccustomed to arms, were led away captive. Wives, violated by many men, were led away as foreign women in lamentation. The entire female population of young girls was shamefully deflowered by them. Old men were dragged far and wide into exile together with the young. Whatever animals there were, they reduced to money.

The frenzied rage grew, increased by many evils. The shrine of the famous witness Quintinus, renowned above the heavens for his merits, was burned—an edifice richly furnished with monastic possessions. All the other churches located in the territory of the Vermandois were also burned to ashes, including the monastery of Christ’s agonothete, Dionysius, when Vulcan prevailed.

[Col. 0622B] Enno [also Emmo], bishop of Noviomagus, was killed with his deacons on the fourth day before the Kalends of May—alas, what grief! The whole population was led away captive to the ships. The basilicas of Christ’s confessors Medard and Eligius were burned through by those wicked men. The sacred church of the holy virgin Genevieve, located at Paris, was burned by those impious men. The other churches located outside the fortifications and scattered throughout all Francia were almost all burned. As evil raged, Francia was laid waste and utterly emptied. It mourned, deprived of Liber and Ceres, with which it had once been exceedingly rich. It grieved to be stripped of its inhabitants and deprived of its farmers. It wailed, unploughed by the share and uncultivated by the blade. The land grew numb in idleness, not exercised by the labor of oxen. Paths were forgotten, not worn down by human footsteps. [Col. 0622C] As time passed, the fields became dense with forests, shrubs, and groves.

Safety was proclaimed lost, and confidence in life departed from human beings. The Dacians approached those waters by ship and, leaping out from them, ravaged the neighboring lands. By night they attacked the bodies of those lying down, buried in the rest of Lethean sleep. After everything that had seemed worth taking had been laid waste, and after finding nowhere in all Francia any engagement of battle, they returned, plundering everything, to the protection of their ships.

When everyone had been summoned to deliberate over what they should do about their undertaking, Alstignus, the most wicked of all, spoke for everyone:

“Favorable breezes are increasing for us, and following winds breathe an easy path for us. If it does not displease you, let us go to Rome [Col. 0622D] and, just as we subdued Francia, subject it to our rule.”

This counsel pleased everyone. The plunderers set their sails and turned their prows away from the shores of Francia. After crossing high waves far and wide and claiming the lands on either shore for themselves, they desired secretly to seize Rome, mistress of nations, and sailed against the city of Lunxe [Lux], which is called Luna.

The leaders of the city, terrified by the dreadful assault of so great a force, fortified the city with very many armed men. The blasphemous Alstignus, realizing that the city could not be taken by arms by everyone together, devised a deceitful plan of the most wicked fraud. He sent a messenger to the count of the city and to the bishop, to deliver the following words to them. Standing before them, the messenger spoke as follows:

[Col. 0623A] “Alstignus, leader of the Dacians, offers you faithful service, as do all his men, who were expelled together with him by lot from Dacia. It is not unknown to you that, expelled by lot from Dacia, we were carried through the wave-roaming sea around all the oceans, borne along by the whirlwinds of the sea’s marvelous surges, and transported to the kingdom of the Frankish people.

“We invaded this kingdom, which had been granted to us by the lot of the gods, and fought strenuously in many battles against the Frankish peoples. We brought the whole region under the authority of our lord. But when all our dominions had been subjected, and wishing to return to the land of our birth, first battered by hostile north winds, then beaten by the contrary West Wind and South Wind, we unwillingly and barely swam to your borders.

“We have not come to devastate your city with iron, nor to carry the spoils of your district to our ships. We have no such strength, exhausted as we are by so many dangers. We beg you to grant us a negotiated peace; let us be permitted to buy what is necessary. Our lord has fallen ill and is full of many pains. He wishes to be redeemed by you through a life-giving fountain and to become a Christian; and if he should be overtaken by death in this illness, he wishes, through your mercy and piety, to be buried in this city.”

When the bishop and count heard this, they answered the messenger:

“We make a pact of perpetual alliance with you, and we shall make your lord a Christian. Whatever you wish to buy, we grant by mutual agreement between our people and yours.”

The messenger deceitfully reported to his lord everything he had said to them and everything he had craftily heard from them. A negotiated peace having been granted [Col. 0623C], and many agreements, purchases, and reciprocal arrangements having been made, the treacherous pagans and the Christians dealt with one another in turn.

Meanwhile the bishop prepared a bath, which would not benefit the treacherous man. The waters drawn from the depth of the well were sanctified. Candles were lit for the sacred mystery of the washing. Alstignus, the evil inventor of the deceitful plan, was brought in as a trickster. The treacherous man entered the font, washing only his body. The wicked man received baptism, to the destruction of his soul. The bishop and count received him from the most holy baptism. He was led away as if he were ill, anointed with sacred chrism and oil. He was not sick, but an ailing and wretched man in the business of treachery. He was carried away as if ill to the ship’s quarters, his whole body whitened.

He immediately summoned all the most wicked men to deliberate over his fraudulent deceit. He disclosed to them the accursed secret conceived in his frenzied heart:

“As night approaches, announce to the bishop and count that I am dead, and ask them, weeping profusely, to bury me, a neophyte, in their city. Say that you will give them my swords, armlets, and whatever else is my property.”

They did as they had been ordered. Coming before the lords of the city, they said with lamentation:

“Our lord, and your little son in faith, alas, has died. We wretchedly beg you to have him buried in your monastery and to accept the very great gifts which, as he was dying, he ordered to be given to you.”

Deceived by such a sophism and as though blinded by the giving and receiving of gifts, the Christians promised that the body would be received and decently buried in the monastery. The messengers returned and reported what they had deceitfully and mournfully obtained.

Then the obstinate and pestilential man, rejoicing in their answer, ordered the chief man from each tribe to be summoned. When everyone had assembled, Alstignus, more wicked than the most wicked, said:

“Make me a bier now, lay me upon it as though I were dead, and place my weapons with me upon it. Stand around it lamenting; wail through the streets and compel your people to mourn for me. Let your voice resound throughout all our tents. Let the men who command the ships cry out with the other companies. Have armlets and belts of iron carried before the bier. Display axes and swords polished with gems and gold.”

The wretched man’s command was carried out more quickly than words could say.

[Col. 0624B] The clamor of wailing and the tumult of mourners were heard. The mountains echoed and rang with the voices of those who deceitfully lamented. The bishop summoned by bells the people scattered throughout the city. The clergy came dressed in monastic garments. Likewise came the leaders of that city, soon to be crowned with martyrdom. The female population poured forth, destined to be led into exile.

They proceeded as one against the monster placed upon the bier. Students carried candles and crosses, preceding their elders. Alstignus was brought by the pagans, alive and placed upon the bier. At the city’s exit, the Christians met the pagans. Both peoples carried him to the monastery where his tomb had been prepared.

The bishop prepared to celebrate Mass for his little son in faith. The clergy stood in the choir, accustomed to sing with the greatest devotion. The Christians, destined for slaughter, did not know the deceit of the deadly fraud. The Mass was solemnly celebrated. All the Christians shared in the mystical sacrifice of Jesus Christ.

When these solemnities of the Mass had been suitably completed, and the pagans had gradually assembled, the bishop ordered the body to be carried to burial. The pagans demanded the bier with a great outcry and said in turn that he should not be buried. The Christians therefore stood astonished at their answers.

Then Alstignus leapt from the bier and tore a shining sword from its sheath. The wretched man attacked the bishop, who was holding a book. He cut down the bishop and the count, and the unarmed clergy standing in the church. The pagans blocked the doors of the church so that no one could escape. Then the rage of the pagans slaughtered the unarmed Christians. All whom the enemy’s fury found were handed over to death.

They raged within the precincts of the shrine like wolves within sheepfolds. The women held back their groans in their hearts and poured forth useless tears. Young men and virgins were chained together with thongs. The final day of life came upon them all, a brief and irrecoverable span of life.

Fighting through the city's defenses, they struck down whomever they found; the more vigorous citizens were crushed amid the sufferings of raging Mars. The people who had been in command of the ships arrived through the gates, now lying open by force. A line of iron stood with flashing points, drawn and ready for slaughter. They joined those already fighting, contending on either side against one another. They cruelly killed all whom they found resisting with weapons.

At last the battle ended—alas!—with the company of Christians slain. The rest of the grieving multitude [Col. 0625A] was led to the ships. The rage of the furious Alstignus subsided after the city’s leaders had been struck down. Alstignus and his men rejoiced, believing that they had captured Rome, the head of the world.

He congratulated himself on holding the sovereignty of the whole empire through the city which he thought was Rome, the mistress of nations. When he learned that this was not Rome, he was stirred to anger and said:

“Plunder the entire province and burn this city. Carry as many captives and as much spoil as possible to the ships. Let the farmers of this land feel that we have been in their territories.”

What the foul man ordered, his servant gladly prepared. The entire province was invaded and overcome by the most wicked enemy. A vast slaughter was made, and captives were led to the ships. With sword and fire they devastated everything that had come within their reach. When this had been done, they loaded the ships with captives and spoils. Now they turned their prows to be carried to the kingdom of the Frankish people. They crossed the Mediterranean Sea, returning to the kingdom of Francia.

Francia, overcoming so many peoples already proud in death,

Devoted lavishly to pious and honorable duties,

But with a people wishing to scatter their hair over you,

And to pollute you with a vain effort,

Having acquired through your empire kingdoms twice three times three,

Strong, hard, savage, steadfast, robust, and cautious,

Law-bearing, distinguished, gentle, mild, and radiant,

Energetic, faithful, gracious, devoted to the affairs of war,

Victorious in all things, powerful, skillful in triumphs,

But weighed down by so great a burden of guilt,

And, with the king neglected, full of every defilement,

Despising the commands of the Lord who thunders above the stars—

[Col. 0625C] Now you lie prostrate, sitting upon your weapons, ashamed,

Utterly stunned and stupefied, dull, anxious, and sorrowful,

Trampled upon, harassed, rejected, and rebuked,

With hostile criminals—filthy, grim, and wicked—

Pestilential, swollen with pride, boastful, and criminal.

For, restored to your arms, rise quickly; press forward more swiftly;

Now seek sound counsel for yourself and for your people.

May you repent, be ashamed, be weary, and shudder

At the dreadful wickedness brought about by many errors.

Write the commands of your God, reciting them everywhere.

That other offspring, that one from Dacia,* is sent forth,

About to glide over the swelling waves with vigorous rowing.

He will wage many battles against you through the years,

Conducting martial conflicts with sturdy weapons.

[Col. 0625D] Fighting, he will crush the savage thousands of the Franks;

At last, when a pleasing treaty has been made and peace established,

He will make your empire and your name equal to Olympus.

The proud peoples who refuse to serve you

He will crush with the sword, soften, and bring under submission.

O fortunate one, O thrice, four times, and a thousand times blessed,

Hail, rejoicing, and fare well, reigning through the ages.

[Col. 0626A] Meanwhile, while Francia was regarded as deserted like a wilderness, and while the dreaded arrival of the Northmen was feared like the roaring secrets of thunderous rumbling, and while the king of the Franks had no means by which to resist the pagans’ boldness with arms, he devised a plan highly beneficial to himself and his people: he would make an alliance with the exceedingly wicked Alstignus, so that peace throughout the kingdom might be established between them once the storm of the invading devastations had been calmed.

Therefore, after summoning the dukes, together with the bishops and counts and the troops of his attendants, he expressed what he had conceived in his heart and declared it in these words:

“O elders and lords, summoned here because of the complaint that threatens us, investigate the kingdom by seeking counsel among yourselves.”

Then the Franks, moved by the king’s address, unanimously said that they should go to battle and fight against them. But the king dissuaded them and began as follows:

“It does not seem to me wise to begin a war against them. If you go out to fight them, either you will die, or they, slipping away in flight, will return very swiftly to their ships. Let peace with the impious be sought, so that the land may rest in our time.”

This counsel, spoken by the king, pleased everyone. Envoys were sent peacefully to the savage Alstignus. Then, soothed by the total of the taxes and tribute that had been weighed out and gradually appeased by the burden of the payment exacted from the Franks, he did not any longer reject the peace that was being requested, but granted it voluntarily.

With the peace of the bishops thus firmly established, he was led to the king and, through an unbreakable pact, made with him the gifts of peace at the Olympiad [Col. 0626C]. United by imperial agreements and mutual consent, they became harmonious and unanimously allied.

Francia, previously afflicted by manifold devastation, rested; freed from the hostile plague that had run its course, it was released from the destruction of the swelling pagans. Let no reader recoil, we warn, at these shameful adverse events, which befell the Franks not for destruction but for correction because of their accumulated crimes.

The Frankish people, excessively full of the filth of defilements, was crushed by Alstignus as its avenger. The treacherous and perjured were deservedly condemned; the unbelieving and faithless were justly punished.

For this reason, rather than pursue in an extended narrative all the labors of that time, we shall more quickly turn our pen to the purpose of our undertaking [Col. 0626D]. Let the pen, however sluggish, briefly illuminate and arrange in summary how the things accomplished by God’s will occurred. Let it express the truth of the matter, rejecting the error of sophistry. Let it refute the confusion of obscene events and suppress the business of the salvation that is to come.

# EPILOGUE.

[Col. 0625]

[Col. 0625D] Holding to a grim cycle and proceeding along slippery byways,

Hearing in vain the winding turns of unstable roads,

Now halt the journey you began, Book, I ask you for a while;

Tired, cease now from the work of your shifting subject.

If you are able to be led farther, look ahead with care.

Now the long, rough road, rocky and stony throughout,

[Col. 0626D] Grassy, wooded, full of groves, slippery, and harsh,

Feed your horses with grain, now so emaciated,

For they retain the will to go, but have little power.

Let the iron on their feet be kept frequently polished and cleaned,*

Fastened beneath with nails,

And adorn their backs with strong trappings;

[Col. 0627] Bind their jaws with stitched bits and reins.

Thus perhaps you will be able to traverse the bright road

Without wandering, plunging, stumbling, or perishing,

[Col. 0628] Unless God, who justly triumphs from on high, gives aid,

And blessed Quintinus, as witness, intercedes,

Together with the one whose deeds we now sing, rejoicing.

# BOOK TWO. ROLLO.

[Col. 0627]

## PREFACE IN HEROIC METER, FOLLOWED BY AN ELEGIAC POEM

[Col. 0627A] Created in ancient times, the island called . . . . . . stands,

Fertile, rich in fields, wealthy in resources and [“laum,” uncertain],

Encircled forever by the boundary of the immense sea,

Generous in merchandise and rich in manifold profit.

There are many harbors here and there on either side,

Filled with ships bearing various cargoes.

It gave birth to Daedalus, highly skilled in many arts,

Beyond what is sufficient in art and knowledge.

Once, fleeing the walls of Minos, he joined wax

To make wings for himself by a wondrous device,

Believing that by means of swift feathers he himself

Could travel through the empty air safely, like a bird.

Reckless light-mindedness took his son as companion,

Careless of the fragile bond and undertaking.

Icarus rose at his father’s side, upon his father’s wings,

[Col. 0627B] Wishing fearlessly to imitate his father in flight.

His energetic father Daedalus flew toward the cold North,

And here touched the earth with his feet.

At last he himself stood upon the Chalcidian heights,

Knowing how to moderate his course amid the right-hand cold.

He established and dedicated a noble shrine to Phoebus,

And soon removed his life-bringing wings.

Daedalus’ offspring, less prudent in the face of danger

To come, traveled higher and more carelessly.

He rose higher than was proper into the unclean climate;

Soon the liquid wax remained, dissolved from the wing.

Icarus himself gave his name to the sea he encountered,

Buried in the famous, wave-resounding deep.

These monsters seek you, and this tale has happened

For your mocking laughter and ridiculous jeers.

[Col. 0627C] You lead forth, at the beginning of your undertaking, the great deeds of Rollo

And likewise of the young people of Dacia, in the flower of youth.

You leave the lowest parts of the earth, striving for things too lofty,

As though swifter than Daedalus—or than Icarus.

While it happens that you foolishly stretch your wings toward heaven,

The lofty subject becomes immense.

If only your powers, increased, had made it possible,

In the mind of your heart, to do what your will desires.

If you had known the manifold harmonic species

That preserve distinction in three degrees,

You could have sung, with sweet sound, among the intervals

Especially in harmonic songs.

You could have sung each of the eight modes attached to tetrachords,

[Col. 0628A] Which the diatessaron and diapente favor,

And with mingled tones, which dissonances form by exacting refinement,

When weighed out according to the unequal numbers of the art.

For the sesquioctave proportion closes the tone,

And the epitrite concord binds the diatessaron.

The melody properly establishes the hemiolic diapente,

Preserving the law of the arithmetical art.

The diatessaron and diapente together form the diapason

By an established twofold number.

The diapason and diapente of triple form,

And twice the diapason, consolidate the quadruple.

Now I am stung by excessive bitterness and pricked again,

And, trembling with fear, I am goaded and shaken.

Ah! may the rash games of the crowd not subdue you;

Ah! may thunderbolts not shake you headlong.

[Col. 0628B] Freed from ambushes, so that you may rightly protect yourself,

Behold, receive this wholesome counsel.

Commit the purpose of your heart to the thundering Lord;

May he scatter the games and disperse the lightning.

May he gradually carry you beyond the fortified sea

On the nourishing wing of the sevenfold-flowing stream.

And may he set you upon rich and grain-bearing soil,

After the forest of shrub and stone has been torn away.

May he enrich your understanding with rhetorical nectar,

And likewise intoxicate it with an Armorican measure,

So that, having acquired the melodies of others with plectrum and strings,

You may be able to sing a melody with a hymning voice.

For the blind, through the patrician’s eye; for the lame, through a staff;

For the adornment of the Church, and for food to the poor;

For orphans and exiles, and for the needy and wandering widow,

[Col. 0628C] As supreme guardian of order and of the sacred.

Although we have reached this point with sandy feet,

Through mud and a difficult path,

We attempt to extend our step farther,

But the novelty of the subject tears us apart.

Indeed, we are not able to proceed or stand firm in our undertaking;

I foresee that we are exhausted by the burden.

It is exceedingly difficult for us to set down the bundle;*

There will be loquacity, and excessive ridicule.

O spirit able to give form powerfully to all shapeless things,

Distributing gifts of heavenly nectar,

Nourishing spirit, come—you who gave birth to words—

Kindle life in our dull senses.

[Col. 0629A] I beg you, breathe here, and pour back our scattered hopes,

Gradually illuminating the chambers of my breast,

So that I may be able to touch the summits of so great a mass,

And rise, abundantly flowing, to what the pen has not attempted.

In prose I shall briefly relate whatever may be told,

With you as collaborator, guide, and maker.

When the providence of the divine Trinity above, by whose will all things alternate through the changing succession of revolving times, mercifully saw the Church—redeemed by holy blood, abundantly cleansed by the water of sacred baptism, and nobly anointed with the liquid of oil and chrism—cruelly afflicted by the cases briefly described above, it did not cease, urged by the continual and humble prayers of Christians, to provide her with saving assistance from the savage ferocity [Col. 0629B] of the Dacian-born heathen.
