Thus, from the source by which she had been lamentably afflicted, she might be vigorously renewed; by those through whom she had fallen headlong, she might be exalted to heaven; by those through whose deeds she had been despised, she might be restored through their gifts; by whose multitude she had been trampled, she might be adorned with their gold and gems; by whose plunder she had been reduced to rags, she might be splendidly clothed through their donation.

When the bands of many young Dacian-born men had become joined through human unions and fornication, and when they frequently incited the fires of war among themselves, against their fathers, and against their uncles, all the Dacian-born elders and men of power came to the king and said unanimously:

“The commonwealth is cruelly oppressed by hostile invasion and is shaken by the destruction of our sons and grandsons. We have abandoned the established custom of our ancestors; therefore the people of the Dacian nation, having suffered very many evils, is being destroyed. Consult, then, O King, for the kingdom which you ought to govern by peaceful rule, according to the ancient custom. Let Dacia be cleansed of the pestilential disease of the worst enemies, so that we who remain may be able to live and rest in perpetual peace.”

The king listened closely to their counsels. He quickly sent throughout the land of his empire an edict of his command that the grandsons and sons whom the lot of expulsion might find should be enrolled, and he ordered the satraps of that land to appear before him at the appointed day and time.

The report of the royal embassies immediately struck the minds of the young men. Their hearts trembled with anxious thoughts, wavering amid uncertain futures and tossing upon the unknown. Their stupefied spirit clung to what their senses did not know [Col. 0629D]. Indeed, the inadequate concern for the truth wearied them, and uncertain hope tore apart those who were in doubt. It was uncertain for them to foresee what judgment was turning in the king’s heart.

In those days there was an old man in the regions of Dacia, exceedingly rich in the abundance of all things and surrounded on every side by an innumerable multitude of soldiers. He had never bent the neck of his head to any king, nor, by entrusting his hands to anyone’s hands as a token of service, had he commended himself to the favor of any person.

Possessing almost the whole kingdom of Dacia, he claimed for himself the neighboring lands of Dacia and Alania, and by force and power subjected many peoples to himself through very many battles. He was, indeed, the most powerful of all the Easterners in outstanding virtue and the most excellent of all through the accumulated abundance of every virtue.

When he died, his two sons survived him, vigorous in arms, trained in warfare, most handsome in body, and strongest in courage. The elder of them was called ROLLO, while the younger was called GURIM.

When the young men enrolled by royal command approached their destruction, they bent the knee, lowered their faces, and earnestly begged in humble voices. They said unanimously:

[Col. 0630A] “Bring us help; come to our aid. We shall remain under the protection of your guardianship and shall serve you without ceasing. Our king wishes to expel us from Dacia and deprive us entirely of our estates and benefices. Have pity, we beg you; have pity on us, deprived of every hope and salvation.”

Then the two brothers replied to those who were humbly entreating them:

“We shall give you the best assistance, make it safe for you to remain in Dacia despite the king’s threats, and ensure that you may quietly retain your property.”

When they heard this, they sought the feet of Rollo and Gurim with a kiss and immediately returned rejoicing at the princes’ words.

Meanwhile truthful rumor spread and reached the ears of the king of Dacia: the supremely powerful leader—the father, namely, of Rollo and Gurim—had died and they now enjoyed the highest position by lot.

Then the king, remembering the evils which that leader had inflicted upon him, summoned all the princes of his empire and said:

“You are not unaware that the father of Rollo and Gurim has died. I shall therefore attack their territories, seize their cities, castles, and most strongly fortified places, and avenge upon the sons the deeds of their father; by crushing them, I shall satisfy myself upon their misfortunes. I beg you to prepare yourselves and your men to complete such undertakings.”

When the date of departure had been announced, they returned with their men from wherever they had come.

Soon the fierce youth of Dacia, burning with the excessive heat of anxiety, prepared what was necessary, but to no effect. Some fashioned light shields and shining darts, finished by the art of the forge. Others sharpened weapons, swords, and axes upon whetstones. Some made safe coverings for their heads, namely helmets; others made triple-woven coats of mail, that is, cuirasses, from iron and gold. Moreover, they remelted the weapons of their homeland in furnaces and renewed them upon anvils.

The unexpected report of this matter reached the ears of Rollo and Gurim, and they were disturbed by the words of such a report. They summoned a large force and a fitting body of flourishing young men, and gathered a multitude of those in middle age, the old, and those enrolled for destruction. Then, raising their right hands, they ordered silence.

When the tumultuous murmur of the people had been completely stilled, and Rollo had been elevated upon the platform of a fitting seat, he began in honeyed speech:

“You whose youthful ardor grows hot, and who surpass these others in the flower of superior virtue, I address you. With diligent purpose, imitate your venerable fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers. Grow strong manfully, take courage, and do not disdain to meet them suitably in equal turns. For the king of this realm is plotting to overrun us, invade the sovereignty of our dominion, and destroy us all. Before he makes the hereditary land of our rule subject to himself, let us seize in advance the land of his government, and, resisting his arrival with hostility, confront him.”

Immediately, all, heartened by these words, invaded the royal territory with their armies gathered together, and devastated the whole land as a raging volcano might. When the king heard this, he marched to battle against Rollo and his brother, but after fighting for a long time he turned his back and fled to the protection of the cities. Then Rollo buried the dead of his own army, but left the king’s dead unburied.

When the conflict between the king and Rollo had continued for the space of one five-year period, the king sent him the following deceitful message in peaceful words:

“Nothing stands between you and me except the favor of kinship. So that the commonwealth may rest, I ask you to permit me patiently to possess what is my right and what my father held; and you, what is your right and what belongs to you. Let peace and harmony, joined by an unbreakable treaty, exist between you and me.”

Then Rollo and Gurim, their soldiers, and those designated for extermination, highly approved the peace. When the time for swearing friendship had therefore been fixed, each came to the appointed meeting; enriched by mutual gifts, they entered into an alliance.

At last, the treacherous king, brooding in his hostile heart over the deceit of the fraud he had conceived, summoned part of his army, marched against them by night, invaded their territory, concealed ambushes near the city walls, and began to attack. Then Rollo and Gurim, with those who were with them, sprang out of the city and pursued the king, who was turning his back and pretending to flee.

When Rollo had crossed beyond the place of the ambushes, one part of the enemy emerged from hiding and attacked the city. Finding it empty of armed men, it set it on fire and carried away the spoils of all its furnishings. Another part, however, followed Rollo as he drove the king away with hostile ferocity. When the king saw that the city had been burned and that the ambushes were prevailing, he turned back and fought against him.

After many on Rollo’s side had been slain, his brother Gurim fell in battle. Seeing himself between the two armies—one pretending to flee, the other having emerged from hiding—and seeing his brother dead, Rollo, scarcely able to escape after being torn by numerous wounds, withdrew from them with a few companions.

Then the king besieged and captured the cities, and subdued the people who were reproaching him. Rollo, however, unable to remain in Dacia because he distrusted the king, made for the island of Scanza with six ships. Then Dacia, deprived of its pious leader, its patrician, and its strongest defender, shaken by great wailing, began to mourn exceedingly.

## Apostrophe

Dacia, which sends your sons to the Gauls by fate,

Lacking the promised truth, though what the stars have given

Will be bestowed—the omen and the merit,

Unknowing of the reward to come—

Cheer yourself, though you discover grief within your heart.

This is not the fate of the soul, but harsh fortune has struck you.

This wicked adversity will always turn its course;

Prosperity, rich in wealth, will offer him every good,

Enriching him, it will make him wealthy and generous.

And fruitful France, from your blessed offspring,

Conceived from the seed of noble worshipers of Christ,

When Dacians and Franks have been so peacefully reconciled,

Will give birth, produce, cleanse, and bring forth great

Kings, pontiffs, dukes, counts, and nobles—

Under whom the rejoicing world will flourish under Christ the ruler,

And through whom the churches will everywhere become fruitful;

And in whose new, everlasting Christ they will rejoice;

For whom, purified in a threefold baptism, the heavenly host will already have been brought in place of the lost tenth order.

When he had remained sorrowfully for a long time on the island of Scanza, burning with the anxious thought of a troubled mind and planning how he might avenge himself upon his enemies, many of those whom the king’s savagery had driven from Dacia returned to him. His limbs, wearied by toil and oppressed by sleep, were overcome with slumber, and a divine voice sounded to him, saying:

“Rollo, rise quickly. Cross the sea hastily by ship and go to the Angles. There you will hear that you will return safely to your homeland and enjoy perpetual peace there without harm.”

When he had related this dream to a certain wise and Christian man, the latter interpreted it in these words:

“As the course of future time declines, you will be purified by holy baptism and will become eminently a worshiper of Christ. From the error of the wavering world you will reach the Angles—that is, the angels—and with them you will possess the peace of everlasting glory.”

Immediately he fitted sails to the ships, equipped them with oars, and loaded them with grain, wine, and hides. Crossing the sail-bearing sea swiftly, he approached the Angles, where he supposed that he would remain quietly for a long time.

When the peasants of that territory heard that Rollo the Dacian was arriving, they drew up a very large battle line against him and attempted to drive him from those borders. As was his custom, he met them in battle without hesitation, felled many of them, and wearied the backs of the rest as they turned to flee beneath his spear.

Finally, the peasants gathered forces more numerous than before and once again directed an extremely strong battle line against Rollo, attempting either to kill him or force him to flee. But he, trained by the practices of war and made extremely hard by the necessity of combat, wearing a helmet magnificently adorned with gold and clothed in a triple-woven cuirass, advanced swiftly and fearlessly against the armed bands that reviled him and marched against him. With victorious hand and rapid pursuit he savagely struck down thousands of them, chased the fugitives, captured many of their leaders, and returned to the battlefield. There he buried the bodies of the slain, carried away the rest who were covered with wounds, and bound the captives to the ships.

Then, tormented by a threefold uncertainty—whether he should return to Dacia, proceed to Francia, or afflict the English land with warfare and claim it for himself—he began to be extremely anxious and sad.

## Apostrophe to the same man

Rollo, why do you tremble in horror and fear while wavering?

Why do you torment your mind, filled with thoughts of destruction?

Why do you burn your heart, renewed by the filth of cares?

Why do you open your mind, and what do you now turn over in thought?

Why do you remain fixed, father, with your gaze fastened upon one thing?

Recalling the uncertain and obscure, what do you reconsider in your mind?

Why are you amazed at the evil fortune of the present lot?

By fatal order, after many dangers of war,

After the surges of the seething sea and the swelling waters,

As an everlasting worshiper of Christ, you will prosper as a patrician, more eminent in the Frankish court through your merits;

You will receive a crown with a fitting reward for your merit,

And in the highest good you will deserve to enjoy divinity.

While he remained anxiously troubled by such disturbances, and the people of that region submitted themselves to his authority through the bond and obligation of loyalty, one night, as sleep spread gently through his limbs with the Lethean peace of slumber, he seemed to see himself set apart upon a mountain of the Frankish dwelling, formerly more elevated than all others.

At the summit of that mountain was a clear and fragrant spring. He saw himself washing in it and being cleansed by it from the contamination of leprosy and from the itching with which he had been polluted.

Finally, around the base of that mountain, which still survives at its summit, and on every side, there were many thousands of birds of different kinds and varied colors, even having red left wings. He could not, with his keen but narrowed gaze, grasp the inexhaustible extent of their multitude, spread far and wide.

Moreover, with orderly movement and flight, he saw them yield to one another in turn and approach the mountain spring, washing themselves in it with the fitting swimming by which, as is their custom, they cleanse themselves at the time of future rains.

When all had been moistened by that wondrous infusion, they took their proper places without distinction of kind or species and, without any quarrelsome contention, ate together in turn from a mutual pasture, as though in friendship. Carrying away small branches, they built nests with hurried labor; indeed, they willingly submitted to the command of his vision.

Soon he awoke, and, recalling the vision he had seen, summoned the leading princes and the leaders captured in battle, who had been brought up with them. He related the entire sequence of the vision in an unsettled manner and asked them what mystical meaning they thought it contained.

When all were silent, one of the captives, imbued with faith in the Christian religion and touched by the foreknowledge of divine inspiration, explained the mystical meaning of the vision, saying:

“The mountain of Francia on which you seemed to stand signifies its Church. The spring that was at the summit of the mountain signifies the baptism of regeneration. By the leprosy and itching with which you were infected, recognize the crimes and sins you have committed. That you washed in it and were cleansed by it from the disease of leprosy and itching signifies that you will be regenerated by the washing of holy baptism and cleansed from all sins.

“By the birds of different kinds with red left wings, whose immeasurable extent you could not exhaust with your sight, understand people from different provinces bearing chequered arms, who will become your faithful followers and whose innumerable assembled multitude you will see.

“By the birds infused into the spring, washed there in turn, and eating in a common meal, understand a people polluted by the contagion of ancient deceit, to be washed in a symbolic baptism and filled with the nourishment of the most holy body and blood of Christ.

“By the nests they made around the mountain, understand that the walls of the devastated cities will be rebuilt. Birds of different kinds will obey you; people of different kingdoms, having submitted themselves to your service, will obey you.”

Rollo, cheered by these words interpreting the marvels, released the interpreter of his vision and the others whom he had captured in war from their bonds. Enriched with various and diverse gifts, he sent them joyfully back to their own people.

At that time the most Christian king of the Angles, named Alstemus, adorned with every title of goodness and eminently worthy to be the defender of the most holy Church, governed the kingdom of the Angles with the greatest piety.

Rollo immediately sent his envoys to him and first explained to them what they should say. When they came before the king, they spoke according to the feeling of their message, with lowered faces:

“Rollo, our lord, the most powerful patrician and most excellent duke of the Dacians, offers you faithful service and an unshakable gift of friendship.

“Great king, we have suffered misfortune in the kingdom of Dacia and, alas, have been treacherously driven out. The hostile East Wind, together with the swelling upheavals of storm waves, drove us to your borders, deprived of every hope and protection of safety.

“When we attempted to return to Dacia and avenge ourselves upon our enemies, icy winter obstructed and blocked us. Frost crusted the earth and afflicted the mournful crowns of the grasses and trees; the rivers, restrained by the dense mass of icy crusts, built a wall for us. The water did not offer us a favorable passage.

“Some soldiers who were staying near the border of our arrival heard of us and drew up a very large battle line against us. They attacked us while harassing us. We, unable to sail either beneath the ice or upon it, resisted their boldness, disarmed many of them in battle, and captured them.

“We will not devastate your kingdom, nor will we turn to our ships with plunder taken anywhere. We seek an undisturbed peace in which to buy and sell, because in the season of approaching spring we shall depart for Francia.”

The king, lowering a cheerful face, spoke after hearing this:

“No land produces men more distinguished and more skillfully trained in arms than Dacia. Many have reported to us the widespread noble lineage of your lord, your misfortunes and labors, and even the treacherous perfidy of the king of Dacia. No one is more righteous in deeds than your lord; no one is greater in arms.

“Set aside the cares of this affair. Remain secure from arms, free from the hardships of battle, and exempt from every evil. Let it be permitted for you to buy and sell anywhere in the lands under our authority.

“We ask you to urge your lord to deign to come to us in the integrity of our faith, for I desire to see him and to console him above his misfortunes.”

The envoys departed and reported to Rollo everything they had heard. At once Rollo went boldly and without hesitation to meet the king, who was coming toward him. They embraced one another and exchanged kisses; then, after the troops of both sides had withdrawn, they sat apart.

King Alstemus then addressed him first:

Powerful in lineage, shining with the light of deeds,

Superior to all in character and merit, let us be joined

By the pleasing bond of faith in a single treaty.

I ask you to be part of my soul and always my companion,

And I beg you to remain within our borders.

Thus may you be cleansed of defilement by saving baptism.

Behold, accept the extent of our dominion throughout the world.

Remember me; I shall always be mindful of you,

Even if you now wish to advance elsewhere for a time.

If a savage and fierce people should presently attack me,

Wicked, keeping no faith and holding fast to no pledge,

As you are able, bring aid, saving me with steadfast effort.

And I shall assist you in like manner,

And my shield shall protect you and yours in mutual struggle.

Then Rollo, delighted by the king’s words, is said to have replied:

“I return thanks to you, most excellent of all kings, for your voluntary benefits. Whatever you have proposed should be done between you and me, make it as I desire. I shall not remain long in your kingdom, but shall go to Francia as quickly as I can. Wherever I may be in the world, I shall remain your friend, joined to you by an unbreakable bond of affection.”

After these words they were joined in a thoroughly unbreakable alliance, wonderfully enriched by the mutual exchange of appropriate things, and each returned with his own people to his own place.

Throughout the entire winter, Rollo the duke carefully arranged for the preparation of the ships and provisions necessary for the journey. He also summoned the soldiers of the flourishing English youth who had become his men and were to travel with him.

When, at the beginning of summer, the abundance of softly gleaming flowers smiled upon them, and white, fragrant lilies flourished among purple blossoms, he, always mindful of the vision that had urged him to go to Francia, boarded a ship after the sails had been spread across the fleet.

When the voyage had begun amid gentle winds, and they had reached the middle of the sea, seeing nothing except the sky embracing the surface of the water, the envious spirits, knowing that they would be washed in the name of Christ’s baptism and would attain the glory they had lost, groaned and raised dangers against them. Winds rushed from their seats, and from the lowest depths they hurled enormous waves into the abyss, lifting them toward the stars.

The sky thundered with repeated flashes of lightning, and a black night of dense darkness settled upon them. The oars were broken, and the sails could not withstand the fury of the winds. Thus, their strength exhausted, they entrusted everything to the winds. The ships tossed here and there as though among mountains and valleys, threatening everyone with sudden death.

Then Rollo, stretching out his hands, fell prostrate upon the ship and poured forth these words in a humble voice:

## Rollo’s Prayer

O almighty God, filling the heavens with light,

Who hold heaven and earth throughout the ages,

Whose divine power embraces all things in an eternal circuit,

You who wish me, infected with the vices and filth of sin,

To become a worshiper of Christ through the gift of a vision,

As the brief course of future time unfolds:

Receive my vows willingly, and favor my prayers with kindness.

Restrain the savage waves in their destruction,

Rescuing us from these disasters and from toil.

Suppress, soothe, and calm

The sea, raging excessively in a violent storm.

When the prayers of this supplication had been completed, the sea soon grew calm. The storms cleared, and with a desired breeze they quickly unfolded the immense stretches of the sea. The ships, broken apart by the storm, scarcely reached the shores of the Uvalgi.

When the Uvalgians heard that a barbarian people, violently battered by the stormy sea, had been carried to their shores, they gathered a multitude of peasants and unexpectedly attacked the duke Rollo, who had barely escaped the stormy sea.

He advanced against them in battle with his customary speed, sent many of them slain down to the underworld, and either drove away or captured the survivors.

While he lingered for a very long time and devastated the Uvalgians,

[Note: “That is, making short delays.”]

King Alstemus of the Angles, the most Christian and most distinguished of all kings in virtue, remembered the friendship by which he and Rollo had bound themselves in an everlasting treaty. He sent the illustrious duke twelve ships loaded with grain, wine, and bacon, and twelve more filled with armed soldiers, to the Uvalgians.

Rollo, delighted by these gifts, sent envoys enriched with extremely valuable presents to the king with thanks, and through them declared that he would serve the king.

The Uvalgians, supposing that Rollo would remain among them for all time because of the grain that had been brought in abundance, summoned Raginer Long-Neck, duke of Hasbaye and Hainaut, and Radebod, prince of the region of Frisia. With an army gathered from other districts, they attacked Rollo.

As often before, he advanced fearlessly to battle, killed many thousands of them, and drove Raginer Long-Neck and Radebod the Frisian back to their camps. Then he devastated the entire land of the Uvalgians and burned it with fire.

Afterward, angered because of this affair, he quickly attacked the Frisians and began to devastate their land. The Frisians therefore hastily gathered a mass of many peoples and added to themselves a multitude of commoners living on the borders of Frisia. They attempted, in a swift assault and with many battle formations prepared, to attack Rollo, who was encamped by the river Almere.

But Rollo and those who were with him, kneeling and covered by the protection of their shields while the horror of arms descended and they were enclosed by the flashing points of a close-formed line, awaited the beginning of the battle.

The Frisians, thinking that their number was extremely small, entered a war that would not benefit them. But the Dacians sprang upon them and, looking upon them, struck them down to extermination. They captured many leaders and led an innumerable host to the ships.

The remaining Frisians, despairing of themselves, thereafter became tributaries and obeyed all Rollo’s commands. After the tribute of Frisia had been collected, increased, and delivered, he immediately set the sails of his ships to the heights and turned their prows toward the lands of Rainer of the Long Neck, wishing to avenge himself upon the man who had been present at the Uvalgians’ side with the Frisians, now defeated in battle.

After traversing the sea, he entered the channel of the Scheldt, devastating the land on both sides. Advancing against Rainer of the Long Neck, he came to a certain abbey called Condatum.

Rainer fought many battles against him, but Rollo emerged victorious and powerful from them all. The land of both armies was devastated and suffered grievously. A severe famine arose because the earth was not broken by the plow. The common people were afflicted by want, worn down by hunger and war. Everyone despaired of living, deprived of the means of survival.

One day, while Rainer secretly remained in a place of ambush, wishing to fall upon the Dacians, the Dacians encountered him from every side, surrounded him, and, although he fought fiercely, subdued him. They bound him and led him to Rollo.

On that very day, the people of Rainer, who were hiding in ambush in order to capture some Dacians, attacked twelve distinguished soldiers of Rollo and captured them through their steadfast courage.

Then Rainer’s wife, weeping and lamenting over him, summoned her leaders and sent to Rollo, asking him to return her lord in exchange for the twelve counts who had been captured.

Rollo immediately received the embassy and sent word back to her:

“Rainer will not be returned to you, but will be beheaded unless you first return my counts to me, and in addition give me whatever gold and silver belongs to his dukedom, with an oath according to the Christian religion, as well as the tribute of this region.”

At once Rainer’s wife, afflicted by this mournful embassy, sent the captured counts back to Rollo, together with all the gold and silver she had been able to find anywhere. She also sent what had been granted to the sacred altars, as well as the tribute of that dukedom, with an oath that she possessed no more metal and could obtain no more. In humble and beseeching words, she asked Rollo to return her husband.

Moved by compassion and by the voices of those who pleaded humbly, Rollo had Rainer of the Long Neck brought before him and addressed him in peaceful words:

“Rainer, duke and most hardened soldier, born from the proud blood of kings, dukes, and counts, what injury had I ever done you? Why did you fight against me with the Uvalgians and Frisians?

“If you are now able to rage, weapons and followers are lacking. If you wished to escape from us by flight, you cannot get away entangled in shackles. I have repaid you with the same measure, as I did to the Frisians, for the evils you inflicted upon me without cause.

“Your wife and your leaders have sent me whatever gold and silver they were able to recover. I shall return half of the accumulated gift to you and send you back to your wife. From now on, grow gentle and rest; let there be no discord, but everlasting peace and friendship between you and me.”

After these words, Rainer’s legs were released from their shackles. Immediately Rollo, having made him an ally and enriched him with extremely valuable gifts and presents, also returning half of the gifts sent by the embassy, sent Rainer joyfully back to his wife.

When these matters had thus been settled in peace, Rollo, mindful of the vision and always hoping that what he had seen in sleep would come to pass for him, diligently asked what he ought to do.

## Apostrophe

Rollo, why do you linger and wander in these lands,

When you have already avenged yourself sufficiently upon all your enemies?

Stop; spare yourself. This course is better,

Because in the age of approaching time

You will endure the harsh wars of the Frankish people

And be exhausted by the wars of Aquitaine.

Then you will enter the dew of the clear spring and the sacred water,

Anointed with chrism and renewed by the liquid of oil;

You will receive the rewards of everlasting life as your gift.

In the year 876 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the noble Rollo, acting on the counsel of his faithful men, spread his sails to the navigable winds. He left the channel of the Scheldt and, after crossing the sea, reached the place where the Seine, flowing in a blue current and with clear courses, enters the flood of the swelling sea, often driven back by the fuller tide according to the phases of the moon, while it licks the fragrant grasses of its distinguished banks.

Approaching Gimegias by ship, he saw the monastery of Saint Peter adorned with the buildings of monastic habitation. Considering it a holy place, he delayed staying there, but brought his ships across the river to the chapel of Saint Vedastus. He placed upon the altar of Saint Vedastus the body of a certain virgin named Hameltrudis, which he had brought with him, and from the virgin’s name the chapel received an enduring name. The inhabitants call that place Saint Hameltrude.

When the poor and needy merchants living at Rotomagus, and the inhabitants of that region, heard that a large multitude of Normans was present at Gimegias, they came unanimously to Franco, bishop of Rothomagus, to ask what they should do.

Franco immediately sent to Rollo, asking him to grant security to himself and to those living in the district. Rollo, discovering that neither in the city nor within its borders was there anyone except an unarmed populace, gave the bishop security under the terms of his faith.

Then, setting his course upon a voyage that would benefit him, he came to Rotomagus and moored his ships, crowded with many soldiers, at the gate to which the church of Saint Martin is attached.

Coming down from the fleet and surveying the city with swift steps, he saw its masses scattered, the stones of its temples torn away, the churches displaced from their foundations, the walls broken apart here and there, and only a small, unarmed force. He began to hesitate in mind and to fix his gaze upon the vision he had seen across the sea.

## Apostrophe

O powerful Duke Rollo, most excellent prince,

This city will flourish with you as its prince, Christ granting it;

with the kingdom calmed by peace, it will be rebuilt,

Once the Franks have been consumed by war and the people subdued.

Behold, soon there will be churches in which you saw yourself rejoicing;

Behold, here is the spring of the font in which you saw yourself cleansed of leprosy.

You will build this homeland for your people, renewed by the spring.

In this city you will give the peoples laws and treaties,

And laws together with the strict fear of punishment.

In the wondrous time soon to come, in the age of your descendants,

Harsh centuries will shine when wars have been set aside.

And Fury, impious, sitting upon weapons,

Its forces of wickedness spent, will challenge no one with its voice;

Rather, the fierce wolf and the sheep will graze together in the field.

Then he returned to the ships and, after summoning his leaders, sought with shrewd judgment the counsel of his men concerning what he ought to do.

Then his men, as though foreknowing the future and imbued with the foreknowledge of divine inspiration, said to Rollo with one voice:

“This land is fertile in the abundance of every crop, wooded with trees, marked by rivers filled with fish, and sufficiently rich in the hunting of various wild beasts, but empty of armed soldiers.

“We shall subject it to our power and claim it for our lot. Through warfare we shall acquire the towns, villages, forts, and cities of neighboring peoples, so that our forces, withdrawn behind us, may be able to rest. Perhaps the interpretation of your vision will be fulfilled in these borders.”

Rollo, therefore, delighted by his men’s answer, departed from Rotomagus by ship and traveled as far as Arches, which is called Asdans.

Immediately Fame, conscious of whatever was happening anywhere, passed through the crossroads of Francia and announced that the Normans had arrived, gathered in an innumerable multitude along the channel of the Seine.

The Franks, astonished by their arrival as though by the sound of sudden thunder, summoned Alstignus, formerly the ravager of Francia, gathered an immense army, and came to the course of the river Othura.

Then Ragnoldus, prince of all Francia, said to Alstignus, the instigator of every wickedness:

“You were born from this people; give us advice concerning these matters.”

Alstignus replied to Count Ragnoldus:

“If you had asked my advice three days earlier, I would have given you what I had discovered by reflection. Simply send envoys to them to ask what they have to say.”

Then Ragnoldus said:

“Go quickly, we ask, to discover what they intend.”

Alstignus replied:

“I shall not go alone.”

They sent two soldiers with him who were skilled in the Dacian language. When they came to the bank of the river, they stood there and said:

“The companions of royal power command you to say who you are, where you come from, and what you seek.”

They replied:

“We are Danes, brought here from Dacia. We have come to conquer Francia.”

The others asked:

“What title does your lord bear?”

They answered:

“None, because we are of equal authority.”

Then Alstignus, wishing to learn what they would say about him, asked:

“On account of whose reputation have you come here? Have you ever heard anything about a certain Alstignus, born in your homeland, who sailed here with many soldiers?”

They replied:

“We have heard. He began under a favorable omen and with a good beginning, but he met with a bad end and outcome.”

Again Alstignus asked:

“Do you wish to submit your necks to Charles, king of Francia, devote yourselves to his service, and receive very many benefits from him?”

They replied:

“We shall never subject ourselves to anyone, nor shall we ever attach ourselves to anyone’s service, nor accept benefits from anyone. The benefit that would please us best is the one we shall claim for ourselves by arms and the labor of battles.”

Then the Franks asked:

“What are you going to do?”

The Dacians replied:

“Withdraw as quickly as possible and do not remain any longer, for we do not care about your evasions, nor will we tell you what we are going to do.”

They departed and promptly reported to the army what they had heard.

Ragnoldus then turned to Alstignus and said:

“What do you think? Shall battle be begun? You are from their people; you are not ignorant of the art of fighting in the Dacian manner. Tell us what we should do.”

Then Alstignus, a beast of poison supported by foxlike cunning, addressed the army:

“This people is extremely strong in the flower of youthful age, trained in arms, and experienced in very many battles. If it is attacked, great danger will arise for us.”

Then a standard-bearer of the Frankish army named Rotlandus is said to have replied:

“What counsel are you giving here? A wolf will never be caught by a wolf, nor a fox by a fox.”

Stirred by these words, Alstignus said:

“From now on, war will not be denounced by me.”

Meanwhile Rollo and those who were with him made a defense for themselves, an obstacle in the manner of a fortress. They fortified themselves all around with an embankment of excavated earth, leaving at the site of the gate an opening of great width, which remains visible to this day.

At dawn the Franks came to the church of Saint Germanus, heard Mass there, and partook of the body and blood of Christ.

From there they rode along the riverbank. Seeing the ships and the Dacians in the fortification of excavated earth, they attacked only the broad entrance to the gate. The Dacians, however, lay down inside on both sides across the level ground of the fort and covered themselves with shields.

Rotlandus, the standard-bearer of Ragnoldus, with the army he led at the head of the battle line, violently rushed upon them through the broad entrance of extraordinary length and began to fight them.

But the Dacians rose up and killed Rotlandus and his followers in an instant. When Ragnoldus, Alstignus, and the other counts saw all those men dead there, they turned their backs and eagerly sought flight.

Immediately Rollo, summoning those who had returned from pursuing the enemy, said:

“What evil have we done against the Franks? Why did they attack us? Why did they prefer to kill us? The beginning of this evil belongs to them—the fault lies with the aggressor, not with the resister; it is the presumption of the one who wished to kill, not of the one who defended himself.

“Whatever evil we now do against them, we shall commit because of the offense caused by their actions. Come, let us seize their forts and towns. Let us repay their offenses with retaliation, heaping up evils against them.”

With Duke Rollo urging them on in this way, they abandoned the fortification of excavated earth, sailed swiftly, seized the inhabitants of Mellendis before they could prepare, killed the leaders, quickly overturned the place, and devastated the entire province.

Count Ragnoldus, however, gathered an army larger than the former one and again attempted to attack them. The Normans gathered close together and lay down so compactly that their number appeared extremely small.

Immediately Ragnoldus began a battle that would not benefit his cause. The Dacians advanced unshakably through Ragnoldus’s battle line and struck many down with hard blows.

When Ragnoldus saw his men failing, he began to flee at a swift pace. A certain fisherman of the Seine, attached to Rollo, met him, pierced him with a weapon, and killed him.

When the Ragnoldians saw their lord dead, they turned to flight in great disorder and sought their horses. Then Rollo pursued them, killed many, and led still more captives to the ships.

After summoning his faithful men, he said:

“Come, let us now sail to Paris and seek out the citizens who fled from battle.”

The Normans therefore pulled their ships away from the bank at Mellendis, surrounded Paris, and besieged it, turning the booty of that province toward the siege.

While Rollo remained for a long time in the siege of Paris, the booty taken from distant regions began to run out. Immediately the Normans attacked the district of Bayeux, seized all its plunder, and began to assault the city.

The citizens resisted them fiercely, lest they should die, and captured Bothon, the foremost count of the Northmen.

The Northmen, grieving over Bothon, sent messengers to the people of Bayeux to say:

“If you return Bothon to us, we shall give you security for one year.”

The people of Bayeux, guided by counsel, said to one another:

“It is better for us to rest for the space of one year than to conduct everything through battles for the sake of one count.”

After security had been given, they returned Bothon, a most hardened soldier.

When the year had passed, while the siege of Paris continued, Rollo attacked Bayeux. He captured it by force, utterly overthrew it, and claimed for himself the captives and the booty of the entire region.

He also brought back with him joyfully a certain virgin named Poppa, beautiful in appearance and descended from proud blood, the daughter of the powerful prince Berengarius. He took her as his wife and begot from her a son named William.

Finally, while remaining in the region around Paris, he sent an army against Évreux so that the city and its bishop might be captured. The army came, attacked the city, and seized many of the people and much booty. But the bishop, named Sebur, escaped by God’s favor.

The Normans immediately seized the booty of that district, devastated the entire land, and returned to Paris.

Thus, terrified by such events, many peoples of Francia paid tribute to Rollo, while many others resisted him.

[Col. 0641D] But when the English heard that Rollo had besieged the city of Paris and was being hindered by French affairs, and supposed that he would not come to the aid of his friend, King Alstemus, they rejected the bond of their sworn faith and began arrogantly to grow insolent, fighting fiercely against the king in unremitting wars. The English land was being devastated by the king’s army and by those resisting him; the commonwealth, afflicted by evils, was being brought to nothing. The king’s soldiers and the various forces opposing them were being overtaken by death in many forms.

Therefore King Alstemus, most Christian, since he had no means by which to resist the arrogance of the English, sent a certain count to Rollo, who was fighting near the walls of Paris. Coming to him with downcast face, the count said:

[Col. 0642A] “King Alstemus of the English sends you the gift of an unbreakable friendship, dear to him. Formerly, my lord, you and Alstemus, peaceful king of the English, made a pact of mutual aid: whichever of you should need assistance would be strengthened by the other’s support, and whichever of you was overthrown by adverse fortune, the other would come to his aid. Therefore, oppressed by the unexpected yoke of the treacherous English, he begs your outstanding power above all others to come quickly to his aid, because the English, knowing that you are occupied beforehand with the business of war against the French, do not think that you will come to the aid of my lord.”

Rollo gave the king’s envoy what was necessary and ordered him to wait three days. Then, summoning his princes, he began to inquire what he should do concerning this matter. At once he sent to the leaders of the city, ordering them either to surrender it to him, [Col. 0642B] or to give hostages, or to prepare themselves for defense. But the citizens refused to surrender the city to him or to give hostages; instead, they hurried to prepare themselves for the battle of the coming day.

At dawn Rollo rose after a night of unbroken conflict and entered into the day’s battle. He afflicted the citizens with fighting throughout the entire day. But when he saw that he could not capture the city, at nightfall he adorned his ships with sails, abandoned Paris, and reached the land of the English as quickly as he could, together with the envoy of King Alstemus.

Then King Alstemus, made happier by the envoy’s report, summoned an army of a great multitude and hastened to Duke Rollo. When they met, they embraced one another warmly and exchanged friendly kisses. Immediately Rollo began to address the king in a gracious voice:

[Col. 0642C] “I offer you worthy thanks, my lord king, because you sent me twelve ships filled with excellent soldiers and as many loaded with grain, wine, and bacon, to Walgres.”

Then the king said in a prophetic voice:

“I owe you the greatest thanks, because you abandoned for my sake the kingdom given to you by God, and hastened to come to my aid. You do not know the reason why I ordered you to help me. The kingdom over which I ought to preside and which I ought to benefit is being devastated, and the dignity of my rule is being destroyed, because the English, swollen with the insolence of their arrogance, haughty and perverse, refuse to obey my commands. Departing from me, they have conspired among themselves; repudiating me and my service, they hold me in contempt. Indeed, they seize for themselves the profits of my towns.

“Therefore I beg you to help me crush [Col. 0642D] and scatter them, to break and trample down their rebellious strength, so that, even against their will, they may be reduced to service and may pay harshly for what they deserve in punishment. I shall therefore give you half my kingdom, and I shall willingly grant you half of my possessions and household goods. Thus, bound together by the indissoluble bond of united friendship, let us hold the kingdom together and share in all its honors and advantages.”

Thus King Alstemus gave Rollo half the kingdom and half of his possessions.

Duke Rollo immediately replied to the king:

“It is yours, my lord king, to command; mine to obey. Those whom you wish, I shall crush; those whom he wishes, I shall scatter. I shall overthrow their cities and burn their villages and towns. I shall trample and scatter them; I shall subject them to you and kill them. I shall take captive their wives and offspring, and I shall devour their herds.”

When these matters had been settled between them, they proceeded as one against the English who resisted the king. Rollo fought many battles against the English and besieged their cities, many of which he devastated after burning them with fire.

When the English saw that they could not prevail against the king but were being afflicted by exhaustion, they came to Rollo and, falling on their knees, said:

“Most powerful of the Danes, let us make peace and agreement with King Alstemus, because we acted rashly against the king, breaking the bonds of loyalty that we had promised him. We shall give him hostages for the preservation of our faith, and from now on, submitting ourselves willingly to him, we shall serve him faithfully.”

When Rollo heard this, he went to King Alstemus and reported to him what the English had said. Then the king, moved by pity for those who had once been his own, said:

[Col. 0643B] “So that the commonwealth may not be scourged any longer, if you advise it, my friend, I shall receive them into our service once they have given hostages.”

Then Rollo said:

“You, lord, receive hostages who will remain faithful to you. I, however, a foreigner who does not know the customs of the English, shall receive hostages who will remain faithful to me.”

Immediately each offended English count, bearing the burdens of his offense and repentance, gave one hostage to the king and another to Rollo. Thus, chastened and reconciled through Rollo, they rested.

The king, however, supposing that Rollo would remain in the English land for all time, designated for him half the kingdom—namely its cities and fortresses, villages and towns, halls and palaces, and whatever household goods belonged to his possessions. He also begged Rollo to allow him to be redeemed through the holy font and cleansed from his offenses.

But Rollo, always mindful of the vision, did not consent to the king’s requests. Instead, leading before the king the hostages who belonged to his share, he said with a serene face:

[Col. 0643C] “My lord king, I have now repaid in kind the benefits you bestowed upon me at Walgres. The kingdom that you freely gave me I return to you by means of this sword, whose hilt contains twelve pounds of gold. Moreover, order the hostages who are mine by right and who stand here to be received, taking care lest the treachery of their fathers and grandfathers deceive you again when they reject you. I shall quickly return to France, and I shall afflict, crush, destroy, and overcome my enemies. I ask only that you do not prevent those who prefer to follow me from doing so.”

The king, amazed and giving thanks for these words, said:

“Most powerful duke, part of my soul, I shall go with you. I shall humble kings, dukes, and counts before you.”

Rollo replied:

“By no means, my lord, abandon the kingdom over which you ought to preside and which you ought continually to benefit by your aid.”

At once Rollo left the king amicably, gathered an immeasurable multitude of young men, crossed the channel, and came to the French kingdom. Immediately dividing the counts of his army, he sent some down the course of the Seine, others along the Loire, and others along the Garonne, to plunder the provinces lying between them, sailing swiftly. He himself came again to Paris, began to attack the city, and devastated the land against his enemies.

King Charles, hearing that Rollo had subdued the kingdom overseas, after wearing it down with ceaseless wars, and had subjected it to the king and to himself, asked the advice of the French and summoned Franco, bishop of Rouen, who had already been assigned to Rollo.

[Col. 0644A] When the French assembly had gathered to deliberate concerning such intolerable attacks by the pagans, and Archbishop Franco had been summoned, Charles, grieving over the poverty of his kingdom, said:

“The kingdom over which I ought to preside is being laid waste. The land is not cut by the plow. The commonwealth is both taken captive and killed. I cannot oppose Rollo, because every day I am deprived of my possessions. Therefore I ask and beg your holy fatherhood to obtain for us from Rollo a truce of three months; and if during those days he should perhaps wish to become a Christian, we shall give him the greatest benefits and reward him with great gifts.”

Franco, having heard this, returned to Rouen and said to Duke Rollo with the humblest entreaties:

“The king of the Franks orders you to grant them peace for three months; perhaps a wholesome agreement will be reached between you and him.”

Rollo, having heard this, followed the counsel of his men and granted the king a pact of three months. During this very brief period the land rested from the pagans.

But when the Burgundians—namely Richard and Ebalus, count of Poitiers—heard that the Franks, unarmed and cold in their arms, almost like women, had asked Rollo for security, they sent to the king and to the counts, saying:

“Why do you allow the land you hold to be devastated by pagans? Why do you not aid those over whom you ought to preside and whom you ought to benefit? Why do you not resist the people who have been driven out from their own borders? We shall aid you if you wish, and if war should perhaps break out against us, we shall willingly be present.”

The Franks, angered by these insulting words, began to rebel against the pagans when the period of security had ended.

At once Rollo, supposing that the Franks considered him contemptible because of the security he had granted, began ferociously and cruelly to devastate, tear apart, afflict, and destroy the provinces, laying waste the people.

His men, meanwhile, went toward Burgundy and sailed by way of the Yonne into the Saône. They devastated on every side the lands bordering the rivers as far as Montclar, invaded the province of Sens, and, after plundering everything, returned to Saint-Benedict against Rollo.

When Rollo saw the monastery of Saint-Benedict, he did not wish to defile it, nor did he allow that province to be plundered, out of reverence for Saint Benedict. He went, however, to Étampes and destroyed the entire neighboring land, taking very many captives. From there he came to Villemeux and plundered the surrounding lands; then he hastened to return to Paris.

But when the peasants saw that the strongest Frankish warriors and the fiercest Burgundian fighters had been utterly destroyed, they gathered a multitude beyond counting, carrying uselessly the weapons to which they were unaccustomed, and attempted to attack Rollo.

Rollo looked back and saw the air dusty and thickly darkened by the very dense movement of infantry. Summoning his leaders, he said:

“A people on foot—or perhaps cavalry—is following us. Let our infantry quickly take the road; let the cavalry remain with us, so that we may see what strength those who wish to destroy us possess.”

[Col. 0645A] While Rollo waited with the cavalry, the peasants approached, horsemen together with foot soldiers. Immediately Rollo rushed upon the commoners and struck them down with cruel slaughter until they were annihilated. He crushed them, and, after carrying out a great massacre, returned to his men.

Later Rollo, burning with an excessive heat of fury and thirsting for vengeance against his enemies, attacked the city of Chartres in a hostile manner. He devastated the counties of Dunois and Chartres and besieged the city with a great army.

A certain bishop named Guvaltelmus, a most religious man, was in charge of the city. Mourning and lamenting, and persisting in continual prayers, he sent to Richard, duke of the Burgundians, and to Ebalus, count of Poitiers, asking them to come to the aid of the city, which was threatened with death, for the love of God.

### THE LIBERATION OF CHARTRES

[Col. 0645B] He also sent messengers to the Franks with this mournful embassy. They quickly joined Count Richard and attacked Rollo, who was fighting near the walls of Chartres.

Rollo, as usual, rushed upon them steadfastly. The Franks and Burgundians, recovering their strength and taking courage once more, attacked Rollo, who was stubbornly resisting them. Many Christians and pagans having been killed, both armies stood in battle, exchanging life through alternating blows.

Suddenly Bishop Guvaltelmus, as though about to celebrate Mass, wearing his mitre and carrying a cross and the tunic of the most holy Virgin Mary in his hands, accompanied by the clergy and citizens, and surrounded by armed ranks, leapt from the city and struck the backs of the pagans with weapons and swords.

When Rollo saw that he stood between the two armies, that he could not prevail, and that his own men were diminishing, he passed through their midst and began to withdraw from them, lest he be overtaken by death.

### ADDRESS

Rollo, mighty, vigorous, and most formidable in arms,

Do not be ashamed if you are now considered a fugitive.

It is not Franco who puts you to flight, nor does the Burgundian strike you;

Nor the gathering of the two peoples, with its many kinds of ranks;

But the life-giving tunic of the Virgin, Mother of God,

Together with the relics, the sacred amulets, and the revered cross.

which the venerable bishop, worthy as he is, bears in his hands.

May your will always be able for you, as it was of old;

and now your will and your power will proceed lawfully,

and your power and human will will very soon know one another again.

[Col. 0645D] Your will will now regard its own power as a friend;

and its power will thus make available its own will.

With these two joined together and separated,

you will either accomplish, or fail to accomplish, whatever business the matter requires;

without them you will complete no important undertaking.

Often each violently gains its own friend.

Often each resists its friend with a swift obstacle.

While nature preserves due measure, because of which friend

the condition of the human creature is held to be sorrowful.

### ANOTHER ADDRESS TO ROLLO

Having endured many threats and excessive labors,

From which fortune has wearied you with complaints,

[Col. 0646A] From now on it will give you better things, with everlasting harvest.

So many hardships long endured will now be followed by joy.

From here, hereafter, you will reap long joys, sorrow having been subdued.

Labor has made you a craftsman of war up to this point;

After these sorrows you will have ample gifts of rest.

For many rewards grow out of grievous labor.

A certain body of pagans, escaping by chance the danger of battle, reached Leugas and climbed the heights of a mountain.

When such a great and fierce conflict of war had ended, Ebalus arrived in the evening with his men and bitterly reproached the Franks and Burgundians:

“You treated me as nothing when you began the battle without me. I shall be reviled by all the peoples who will hear of these events. Alas! I would rather have died with this people [Col. 0646B] than have been absent from the battle.”

Then the Franks and Burgundians said to Ebalus, who was complaining without reason:

“Some combat still awaits you, in which you can test yourself and your men. Look: the Northmen have been driven from the battle and have seized the summit of the mountain as a place of refuge. Therefore hurl them down from the mountain and crush their pride. Avenge the blood of the Franks and Burgundians who, alas, lie on this field. Let those who boast that they have escaped the danger of death now feel that you have arrived.”

After these words Ebalus attacked the Northmen, who were exceedingly terrified on the mountain. Ebalus climbed the mountain with his men, while the Danes resisted him with javelins. Ebalus hurled missiles at them, while the Danes wounded them with javelins. The sons of Ebalus attempted to climb to the summit of the mountain; the sons of Rollo hurled them down to its base.

The men of Ebalus carried to the mountain the hedges and walls that the Danes had made for the purpose of capturing the city. But the Danes took those same walls and hedges away from them, enclosing themselves with them as a defense.

The Frankish people awaited the end of the quarrel. Ebalus, seeing that the battle he had begun was not benefiting him, went to Richard, the duke, who was pitching camp on the field of battle.

Then the army surrounded the mountain so that no one could escape. When the Danes saw themselves surrounded by the multitude, they said to one another:

“If we wait for the coming day, perhaps we shall all be killed by the sword.”

A certain man born of the Frisian people, who had been accepted among them, said to those fearing death:

“I shall give you advice that will benefit you. In the silence of the dead of night, let some of our men secretly descend from the summit of the mountain and sound their horns outside around the tents. When they hear the blast of the trumpets, supposing that our duke Rollo is present, they will flee in terror, confusion, and fear, scattering here and there. We, descending from the mountain, shall rush upon the camp of the leaders and fight our way fiercely through their midst. Then let us hasten to attack our lord, and so escape the danger of death.”

They replied:

“You give us sound and wholesome advice, suited to the circumstances. It is better for us to act in this way—that is, either to escape or to die—than to remain here, be captured alive, and be afflicted with various punishments.”

Therefore, in the silence of the dark night, some descended from the mountain. Passing secretly through the tents and going beyond them, they began to sound their trumpets outside and to strike sudden terror into the enemy.

[Col. 0647A] The others, escaping quickly from the mountain amid great tumult and the great clatter of shields, attacked Richard, who was sleeping in his tents. Thus fighting fiercely and passing through the middle of the army, they took the road that Rollo had followed and went free with rapid steps. Coming to the Othura, they set their weary feet upon a high place surrounded by marshland.

The army, greatly terrified, began to waver here and there, thinking that Rollo was present. Ebalus, terrified by what had happened, sought the house of a certain fuller and hid there for a long time.

At dawn the army saw that the mountain was empty of enemies and pursued them as far as they had gone.

The Northmen immediately killed the countless animals they had brought with them. They seized and stripped half the hides of the animals and made a fortress for themselves out of the corpses. Placing one upon another, they stretched the bloody hides outward, so that frightened horses and astonished horsemen would not approach.

When the Franks and Burgundians had pursued them and arrived, and saw the enclosure made from the bodies of horses, oxen, donkeys, goats, and sheep, with the hides hanging outward, they said to one another:

“Who will attack these men? Let whoever wishes to lose his life approach the fleshly and wondrous fortress.”

After these words they each withdrew to their own places, while the Danes returned to their ships.

When Rollo saw his soldiers, he said to them joyfully:

[Col. 0647C] “O strongest of men, most formidable in arms! How did you escape the battles?”

Then they reported to Rollo everything that had happened.

Rollo, violently agitated and raging with the fiercest furies, began to devastate, destroy, and burn the entire land with fire. At once all safety was proclaimed lost, no confidence in survival could be found, the commonwealth was destroyed, and the churches were left deserted.

The Franks, unable to resist the pagans, and seeing all France coming to nothing, came unanimously to the king and said:

“Why do you not aid the kingdom over which, with your scepter, you ought to preside and which you ought to benefit? Why is peace not obtained through counsel, since we cannot attain it through wars or by any means of defense? Royal honor and power are being subjected, while the insolence of the pagans is rising. The land of the French region is like a desert, because its people are dying either of hunger or by the sword, or are perhaps being taken captive. Protect the kingdom, if not with arms, then at least with counsel.”

Then King Charles said to them furiously:

“Give me counsel that will be wholesome and appropriate for the kingdom and for us.”

Then the Franks said:

“We shall give you, if you trust us, counsel worthy and salutary for you and the kingdom, so that the people, afflicted by extreme want, may rest. Let the land from the River Andelle to the sea be given to the pagan peoples. Give your daughter in marriage to Rollo. By this means you can prevail greatly against the peoples resisting you, because Rollo is born of the proud blood of kings and dukes, most beautiful in body, ardent in arms, prudent in counsel, handsome in appearance, gentle toward his own, a faithful friend to those who trust him, and a fierce enemy to those who oppose him; a vassal of discerning mind, steadfast and mild as circumstances require in everything, instructed in speech, teachable in affairs, benevolent in action, honorable in eloquence, filled with manly virtue, humble in conduct, most prudent in worldly matters, just in judgment, extremely cautious in private matters, exceedingly rich in gold and silver, continually surrounded by a very large retinue of soldiers, and, indeed, endowed with every excellence.”

At once, having followed this counsel, Charles sent Franco, archbishop of Rouen, to Rollo, duke of the pagans. Coming to him, Franco began to address him in flattering words:

[Col. 0648B] “Most outstanding of all dukes and most excellent of all men, will you contend against the Franks throughout your entire life? Will you always fight against them? What will become of you if death overtakes you? Of what creation are you? Do you think you are a god? Fashioned from mud, are you not a human being? Are you not food for worms, and ash and dust? Remember what you are and what you will be, and by whose judgment you will be condemned. You enjoy Herebro [reading uncertain], as I think; do not provoke anyone further to battle.

“If you wish to become a Christian, you can enjoy present and future peace and remain exceedingly rich in this land. King Charles, the most patient of kings, guided by the counsel of his men, wishes to give you this maritime land, which has been devastated excessively by Anstignus and by you. Moreover, so that peace, concord, and a firm, stable, and lasting friendship may remain between you and him for all time, he will give you his daughter, named Gisla, as your wife. Through this union you will rejoice in offspring and hold the kingdom forever.”

When he heard this, Rollo summoned the leading men of the Danes and recounted in their hearing what the bishop had reported to him.

The Danes, remembering the interpretations of the dream, said to Rollo:

“This land, utterly desolate and deprived of soldiers, not worked by the plow, rich in good trees, divided by rivers full of fish of many kinds, abundant in game, not ignorant of vines, fertile in soil worked by the knife, surrounded on one side by the sea, which will provide an abundance of diverse things, and on the other side by waterways carrying every good by ship, almost like the kingdom of France—if it is inhabited by a multitude of people, it will be very fertile and exceedingly productive, and sufficient and suitable for us to inhabit.

“The daughter whom he promises you, born in due order from the seed of both families, of fittingly tall stature, most elegant in beauty, as we have heard, a completely chaste virgin, prudent in counsel, cautious in the business of worldly affairs, most easy in conduct, most gracious in conversation, highly skilled in the labor of her hands, and, indeed, preeminent among all virgins—she is fit to be joined to you in marital friendship.

“From this, the counsel appears to us to be more wholesome and likely to benefit us, and secure against the error of any quarrel: that you should have the king’s daughter in a marriage bond. Remember the interpretations of the dream and its mystical meanings. As we suppose, what it signified will turn to prosperity for us in these lands. We have fought enough and defeated the Franks; it seems fitting that we now rest and patiently enjoy the fruits of the land.

“Send the bishop back to the king, so that, if he gives you what he promised, he may declare that you are ready for his service. Send him word again concerning a truce of three months, and that, during the period of the truce, he should come, if he wishes, to meet with you at his pleasure and make you secure in every respect concerning his words and promises.”

At once Rollo informed the aforesaid bishop of this and sent him back to the king to report it.

When the bishop came to the king, he summoned an assembly of bishops, counts, and abbots and said:

“Rollo, duke of the Northmen, promises you love and unbreakable friendship, and also a pact of service. If you give him your daughter in marriage, as you told him you would, and grant him the maritime land in perpetual possession through generations of generations, he will submit his hands to you in fidelity and will perform your service without interruption. Through him you will be able to blunt the swelling pride of those who resist and quarrel with you, and, greatly strengthened, you will recover your power.”

When the bishop had reported these things, the Franks rejoiced and unanimously urged the king to give his daughter and the land to Rollo.

The king of the Franks, compelled by their request, gave his daughter to the bishop on Rollo’s behalf as a pledge, under the bond of an oath and sworn agreement.

When these arrangements had been made, defined, and confirmed at the appointed time and place, and a truce had been granted, each returned to his own place.

Franco, archbishop of Rouen, went to Rollo and explained to him in order everything that had been done. Rollo and his men, hearing this report, were greatly delighted and recalled the figurative meaning of the vision.

Duke Rotbert, hearing that King Charles was giving his daughter to Rollo and that they were being reconciled, with peace being established throughout the world, sent a messenger to Rollo with peaceful words to deliver the following message.

When the messenger arrived, he said to Rollo in supplicatory language:

[Col. 0649D] “Duke Rotbert of the Franks offers you faithful service. He has heard of the agreement between you and the king and rejoices greatly. He says that it is fitting for you and your men to rest, to rebuild the land that has been given to you, to restore the cities and walls, and to live in perpetual peace. You have waged enough battles and displayed enough manly arms. You have shown sufficiently what strength you possess; you have endured enough dangers; you have served enough as a veteran; you have been praised throughout the whole world.

“Indeed, the same duke, entreating you and bending the knees of his heart, orders you to allow him to receive you, marked in Christ’s name and washed in the saving font of baptism. From then on, if it pleases you, you will be inseparably faithful friends, and no one will be able to stand against you. He will continually perform your service and will make the king well disposed toward you at all times.”

After these words, and following the counsel of Bishop Franco and his counts, Rollo said:

“I wish to consent to the king and the Franks, so that he may come to the appointed meeting and redeem me by immersing me in the font. Let him be a father to me here, in paternal love; I shall be to him as a son, in the affection of a son. Let him come to my aid, if necessary, as a father to a son; I shall do the same for him as a son to a father. Let him rejoice in my prosperity and grieve in my adversity. Whatever things are in my power shall belong to his jurisdiction, and whatever belongs to my jurisdiction shall be in his power.”

The messenger therefore reported to Duke Rotbert what he had heard.

Accordingly, at the appointed time they came to the designated place called Saint-Clair. Rollo’s army sat on this side of the River Epte, while the king’s and Rotbert’s armies were on the opposite side.

At once Rollo sent the archbishop to the king of the Franks to deliver the following message:

“Rollo cannot make peace with you, because the land you wish to give him is uncultivated by the plow, entirely without flocks and herds, and deprived of human inhabitants. It contains nothing from which he can live except robbery and plunder. Give him some kingdom from which he may obtain food and clothing until the land you give him is filled with an abundance of wealth and produces seasonal provisions for human beings and animals.

“Moreover, he will not be reconciled with you unless you, together with the archbishops and bishops, counts and abbots of the entire kingdom, swear under the sacrament of the Christian religion that he and his successors shall hold the land you are going to give as a permanent estate and freehold, from the River Epte to the sea, forever.”

Then Duke Rotbert of the Franks and the counts and bishops who were present, together with the abbots, said to the king:

“You will not have a duke of such distinction unless you do what he desires. If you do not give it because of the service he has rendered to you, at least give it for the sake of Christian religious worship, so that such a great people, which is perishing through diabolical error, may be won for Christ. Otherwise the summit of your entire kingdom and the Church will be destroyed by the attack of the invading army, although, acting in Christ’s place, you ought to be their most steadfast king and protector.”

Then the king wished to give him the land of Flanders so that he might live from it, but Rollo refused to receive it because of the obstruction caused by its marshes. Therefore the king promised to give him Brittany, which lay on the border of the promised land.

Immediately Rotbert and Bishop Franco reported everything to Rollo and brought him, with the integrity of Christian faith and with hostages given, to King Charles.

The Franks, looking upon Rollo as the invader of all France, said to one another:

“This duke possesses great power, great strength, and great counsel and prudence—and also great endurance—for he has waged so many battles against the counts of this kingdom.”

At once, compelled by the words of the Franks, Rollo placed his hands between the hands of the king, something that neither his father, nor his grandfather, nor his great-grandfather had ever done for anyone.

Thus the king gave his daughter, named Gisla, as wife to that duke, and granted him the designated land as a freehold and estate, from the River Epte to the sea, together with all Brittany, from which he could live.

When Rollo refused to kiss the king’s foot, the bishops said to him:

“He who receives such a gift ought to seek it by kissing the king’s foot.”

But he said:

“I shall never bend my knees to anyone’s knees, nor shall I kiss anyone’s foot.”

Compelled by the entreaties of the Franks, he ordered a certain soldier to kiss the king’s foot. The soldier immediately seized the king’s foot, brought it to his mouth, and, remaining standing, fixed a kiss upon it, causing the king to fall backward.

Thus great laughter arose, and great tumult among the people.

For the rest, King Charles, Duke Rotbert, the counts and nobles, the prelates and abbots, swore by an oath of Catholic faith to the patrician Rollo his life, his limbs, and the honor of the entire kingdom, as well as the designated land, so that he might hold and possess it, hand it on to his heirs, and so that the succession of descendants through all generations might possess and cultivate it from generation to generation forever.

When these things had been completed as described, King Charles returned to his own lands. Rotbert and Franco remained with Rollo.

### ADDRESS TO ROLLO

[Col. 0651B]

Rollo, by your mystical understanding you will grasp what you have seen.

You will stand at the lofty summit of the mountain of the Church.

In the saving font you will be cleansed from the leprosy of sins.

Now men, carrying shields in place of birds,

Will climb the mountain of the Church and cleanse themselves in the font.

You will never see their end.

Freed from sins, they will taste the mystical sacred rites,

And they will make nest-dwellings around the mountain’s ridges.

They will build churches supported by diverse gifts.

Good duke, pious duke, ever-revered patrician,

All the things your spirit drew from sleep are present for you.

Preserve in holy baptism what you have now promised.

Abandon Satan’s unspeakable work, and his poisonous rites;

Seek the true God always with vows and humble prayer;

Observe the precepts of his commandments;

[Col. 0651C] Give laws to the people and enact statutes confirmed by the learned.

Enjoying peace, the people will rejoice for all time,

Always remaining and dwelling under your authority.

All will be protected from the plots of robbers and thieves.

Supreme guardian of the Church and helper of the poor,

Peaceful protector and defender of the kingdom,

Its defender, governor, ruler, and founder,

May you flourish forever through enduring merits.

In the year 912 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, Archbishop Franco baptized Rollo, instructing him in the Catholic faith of the most holy Trinity. Robert, duke of the Franks, received him from the font of the Savior, bestowed his own name upon him, and honorably enriched him with great gifts and presents. Robert—who was also called Rollo—had all his counts [Col. 0651D] and soldiers, indeed his entire army, baptized, and had them instructed through preaching in the faith of the Christian religion.

Thereafter he summoned Bishop Franco and asked which churches in his land were held in the greatest veneration, and which were said to be more powerful by reason of the merit and patronage of the saints. Then Franco said:

“Rothomagus, Bayeux, and Évreux each have a church dedicated in honor of the most holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ and Virgin. On the mountain amid the dangers of the sea stands a church bearing the name of the Archangel Michael, prefect of paradise. In the suburb of this city there is a monastery consecrated in the name of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles; in it the venerable archbishop of this city, Audenus by name, shone exceedingly with signs and miracles. Because he feared your arrival in Francia, he was carried away [Col. 0652A]. Gimegia, which you visited earlier, has a church of Saint Peter, the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, supported by his merits. There are many churches situated in your dominion, but these are the principal ones.”

Then Robert said:

“On the boundary of our power, which saint is considered more powerful in merit?”

Franco replied:

“Saint Dionysius, a Greek by nation, converted to the Catholic faith through Saint Paul and afterward sent by blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, to preach in Francia. He suffered many torments from the pagans and was long beaten; finally, for the love of God, his head was struck off with blunted axes.”

Then Robert said:

“Before the land is divided among my nobles, I desire to give a portion of it to God, to holy Mary, and to the saints named, so that they may deign to come to my aid.”

Franco replied:

“You are acting according to a counsel inspired by God, and it is fitting that you should do this during these seven days in which you are clothed in white garments of chrism and oil.”

Accordingly, on the first day after his baptism, Robert gave to God and to holy Mary the land of the church of Rothomagus, a very large tract, to be possessed perpetually by its canons. On the second day, he gave land to the church of holy Mary of Bayeux. On the third day, to the church of holy Mary of Évreux. On the fourth, to the church of the archangel Michael, which was at times surrounded by the flooding of the sea’s storms, according to the course of the moon and the arrangement of the waxing number seven. On the fifth, to the church of Saint Peter and Saint Audoin. On the sixth, [Col. 0652C] to Saint Peter and Saint Aicard of the church of Gimegia. On the seventh, he gave Brenneval with all its dependencies to Saint Dionysius.

On the eighth day of his purification, clothed in chrismal or baptismal garments, he began, in his own words, to measure out land for his counts and to distribute it to the faithful. Finally, after preparing a great nuptial celebration, he took Gisla, the king’s daughter, as his wife; through her he reconciled himself and made peace with the Franks. He granted security to all peoples who wished to remain in his land. He divided that land among his faithful by the measuring cord, rebuilt the whole region, long deserted, and refounded it, filling it with his soldiers and with immigrant peoples.

He imposed upon the people perpetual laws and statutes, sanctioned and decreed by the will of the nobles, and compelled them all to dwell together in peaceful conduct. He established churches that had been utterly ruined [Col. 0652D], restored the numerous temples of the pagans after their destruction, and repaired and enlarged the walls and fortifications of the cities.
