He subdued the rebellious Britons and fed his entire kingdom sufficiently from the provisions of the Britons.

Finally, in the land under his authority he issued a ban—that is, a prohibition—which forbade any thief or robber to exist there or anyone to give assent to an evil intention. He further prohibited anyone from carrying the tools of a plow home to the house; instead, they were to leave them in the field with the plow, and no one was to send a guard after the horse, donkey, or ox, lest it be lost.

Because of fear of this prohibition, a certain farmer living in the village of Longapetentis left the tools of his plow in the field and, as midday approached, came home to eat [Col. 0653A]. His wife began to rebuke him with harsh words and an obstinate heart for leaving the necessary implements of the plow and the things belonging to his work there. After troubling and scolding her husband for a long time, she gave him food.

Meanwhile, wishing to make her husband anxious about what had happened, so that he would not leave the implements there again, she secretly went to the field as quickly as she could and took away the straps of the yoke, the plowshare, and the knife. So that her husband would not see her carrying them off, she returned home as though she had come from somewhere else.

When her husband had eaten his fill, he rose and went to the field where he had been working, but did not find the tools of the plow. He returned home sadly and told his complaining wife. She began to abuse him, reproachfully and spitefully saying:

“You worthless man, go now to Robert [Col. 0653B] the duke, and he will quickly make you a plowman.”

He immediately ran to Robert and reported to the duke that the tools of his plow had been taken from him. At once Robert summoned a certain official and said to him:

“Give this farmer five shillings, with which he can buy what he has lost. Then go as quickly as possible to the village and investigate the author of the theft by trial with fire.”

The bailiff examined all the inhabitants of the village by fire, but, finding none of them guilty of the theft, reported back to Duke Rollo. Rollo summoned Archbishop Franco and said:

“The God of the Christians, in whose name I was baptized—if he knows the truth of these matters, it is strange to me that, when the accused thief was tested by fire in his name, he did not make the culprit known to us.”

Franco replied:

“The fire has not yet touched the guilty person.”

Then Robert said to the official:

“Go [Col. 0653C] again, and examine the inhabitants of the neighboring villages by the punishment of fire in the name of Jesus Christ.”

The official fulfilled the duke’s order and reported that he had found no one guilty. Robert immediately summoned the plowman and asked him to whom he had said that the plow tools had remained in the field. The farmer replied:

“To my wife.”

She was summoned and came, and the duke said to her:

“What did you do with your husband’s plowshare and knife?”

She denied that she had possessed them. She was beaten with brooms, and this compelled her to confess the theft before everyone.

Then Robert said to her husband:

“Did you know that your wife was a thief?”

He replied:

“I knew it.”

And Robert said:

“You will rightly die under two decrees: first, because you are the head of the woman and ought to have corrected her; second, because you consented to the theft and refused to reveal it.”

At once he had both of them hanged [Col. 0653D] and brought to an end by a cruel death. This judgment terrified the inhabitants of the land. No one afterward dared to steal or rob. Thus the land became quiet, empty of thieves and robbers, and silent, freed from every disturbance.

[Col. 0654A] The people rejoiced in uninterrupted peace and prolonged rest, dwelling securely under Robert’s rule. They were rich in every good thing and feared no hostile army.

For King Charles once sent two soldiers to his daughter Gisla, who was married to Duke Robert. When Gisla saw her father’s soldiers, she put them aside in a certain house so that her husband Robert would not see them. She gave them every good thing and made them remain there for a very long time.

Robert’s counts were astonished that the soldiers of King Charles were staying at Rothomagus and were not enjoying the presence of Duke Robert. They came to him and said:

“Why have you not informed us of what the messengers of Charles told you?”

Robert asked:

“Where are my father-in-law’s envoys?”

They replied:

“You are uxorious and effeminate, [Col. 0654B] because, while avoiding your presence, they are with your wife.”

They were saying that Robert had not known her according to the law of marriage. At once the duke, inflamed with anger, had the young men of his household seized from their hiding place and led to the market for the sale of goods, where, when the populace had gathered, he had them slaughtered.

When Robert, duke of the Franks, heard that, because of the killing of the two soldiers, the bonds of the peace joined between the king and Robert, duke of the Northmen, had been loosened and broken, he began to oppose Charles, to destroy him, and to lay waste his possessions.

He sent an envoy to Robert of Rothomagus, saying:

“With your counsel and supported by your aid, I wish to seize this kingdom from Charles and drive him from Francia.”

Then Robert of Rothomagus replied to the envoy of the Frankish duke:

“Now your lord wishes to ride too much and to act beyond the law. Let him destroy only what belongs to the king; I do not wish him to take up the government.”

Gisla, meanwhile, the king’s daughter, had already died. What happened between Charles and Robert will not be recorded here, because it is told elsewhere.

Robert, patrician of the Northmen, advanced in age and experienced through the immense labor of wars, summoned the nobles of the Danes and Britons. He gave all the land under his authority to William, son of Poppa. The nobles placed their hands in the hands of the young William and bound themselves to him by an oath of alliance.

After living for another five-year period, weakened by age and with his body exhausted of strength, unable to ride, yet holding a pacified, stable, and tranquil kingdom, he suffered the grievous loss of his earthly possessions and, full of days, passed to Christ, whom honor and glory belong through ages of ages. Amen.

# EPILOGUE

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653D]

An inexperienced sailor committed to the deep sea,  
I am carried in a small vessel, full of cracks and holes,  
With battered stern and prow broken by the swollen sea,  
With shattered rudders and oars destroyed,  
And all the sails torn apart by the violent whirlwind—  
Shipwrecked, stunned, stupefied, dull, anxious, uncertain.

[Col. 0654D]

Entangled in the sandbanks, I do not know what will now be done.  
Ah! Wretched as I am, no exit anywhere lies open  
To me, enclosed amid such mighty waves and surrounded by storms.  
Ah! For me the sky is everywhere, and everywhere the sea;  
I have scarcely swum this far across the middle of the waters.  
I would rather never have entered the sea than perish here.

[Col. 0655A]

Beneath the little vessel the sea murmurs through the broken reefs,  
While the hostile waves of the sea foam in the storm.  
The unfriendly waters now lap the keel in peace-destroying fashion,  
Threatening it with a deadly embrace and dreadful blasts.

I am held fast by the sea’s wrathful, predatory force,  
And the lifted wave strikes sharply against the curved hollows.  
Now, reckless judge, I cling to the trembling waters.

But you, whom they proclaim to possess a changing state and a stable motion,  
Since motion itself is also a state,  
Restrain the sea-wandering swellings of my mind;  
Break apart the deadly sandbanks of my wandering heart,  
And lift up the keel of my stormy intellect,

[Col. 0656A]

So that, with rudders, oars, and sails restored,  
Though my intellect, senses, and understanding are small,  
And though I am now traveling through the surging sea of this work,  
I may, as a sailor, climb into a tranquil harbor  
With the flowing blood of martyrdom, adorned with victory,  
And poured out, bright, and radiant with the blossom of every good.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0655]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0655B]

Once almighty God,  
Born and begotten of the holy Virgin mother,  
Whom our faith truly calls the Word made flesh (*Sarcalogon*),  
Commanded the disciples to climb aboard the vessel  
And depart across the sail-bearing, wave-wandering sea.

Soon he ordered innumerable crowds to sit,  
And, ascending the lofty summits of the mountain,  
He sought the divine power of the heavenly Father.

Soon the blue night began to break before them;  
The dark waters boiled terribly,  
With the swollen left wind of the whirlpool.  
Salvation was loudly invoked,  
And hope and confidence,  
Among all the very greatly trembling disciples,  
Resounded amid the deadly image of the pestilential air.

[Col. 0655C]

At the fourth watch, in the swelling darkness,  
Christ entered the wave-wandering sea  
With dry footprints and carried himself across the waters,  
Walking upon the liquid waves of the suffering sea,  
Presenting himself to the trembling disciples.

Then fear seized their trembling limbs;  
The disciples’ hearts, stunned, clung fast.  
They did not know what to do at the final crisis.  
A chilling terror struck their breasts intensely,  
And an immense cry beat against the stars of heaven.

After God made himself known to the disciples,  
Standing on the fluid sea with thoroughly dry feet,  
Peter soon addressed the Lord with ringing words,  
Taking courage and strength:

“O powerful Christ of heaven and sea,  
If your holy mercy has now come to us,  
And faith is secure and proven for everyone,  
Command me to go across the sea with you.”

The one who, by the command of his order, was invigorating and gracious toward them answered:

“Come.”

Trusting in the Lord, who has power over the sea,  
Peter quickly and immediately left the boat  
And placed his foot upon the waves of the sea.

A new event had struck his trembling mind  
When the sea stirred up dreadful dangers—  
For as long as he did not doubt.*

The swollen waters lifted Peter up,  
[Col. 0656B] and, losing confidence in himself, he deeply repented.  
Peter, submerged bodily in the middle of the sea,  
Cried:

“God, rescue me from these waves!”

The holy right hand of Christ immediately seized him,  
and he said:

“Why, you of little faith, do you now stagger and doubt  
As you waver in the strait?”

At once God and Peter climbed together into the boat,  
Amid the disciples saddened by the storm.  
The harmful winds immediately subsided.

Earlier we had penetrated the greatly swollen sea  
By the power of supreme Christ.  
We have now almost reached the middle of our course.  
The open sky is seen everywhere, everywhere,  
And on every side the threatening blue water.

Now fear draws more sadly upon my breast;  
The waters raise up the mass of my ignorance.  
I repent of what I began, and am weary and distressed by it.

[Col. 0656C]

Most high Christ, my God, I ask that you graciously  
Reveal your face to my knees.  
Look upon my fallen hopes with the support of your divine power.  
Extend your holy hand to me now trembling,  
So that I may climb toward radiant deeds,  
With you as supreme guide, with you leading the way,  
And toward however many grim dangers confront me.

Build my mind with the sevenfold nectar of the Spirit,  
My heart with the support of a rhetorical flood,  
And my tongue with a threefold mode of speech;  
Sprinkle me with the saving fountain of knowledge,  
So that the account may be brief yet credible,  
And so that from this there may arise, I know,  
An open account for humanity [Col. 0656D]  
Of this history which we shall disclose.

May brevity, distributed through speech, shine forth;  
May every explanation sparkle throughout.  
May scantiness likewise be joined to the nature  
Of the person, and may, from the facts given  
And from the matter itself, an appropriate rhetorical method be derived,  
With the seven elements now well understood,  
And with all disputes settled,  
By your gift, O God, born of the Virgin,  
With the unbegotten Father and the holy Spirit,  
You, God, reigning forever and seeing all things.

## PRAYER

[Col. 0657A]

Heavenly glory,  
Almighty support,  
Fountain of sensation,  
Powerful heavenly divinity,  
Origin of light,

Heavenly manifestation,  
Beginning and source of things,  
You who make the sequence of causes clear,  
First offspring,

And light of the unbegotten Father,  
Light from sacred light,  
And truly God from God.

O loving Father,  
Unbegotten God,  
[Col. 0657B] O begotten Son,  
O Spirit, God proceeding forth.

O one God,  
O strength of the Godhead.  
For there are not three gods.

We acknowledge you as one God.  
I ask suppliantly  
That you favor my prayers.

[Col. 0658A]

Though, at this undertaking, I am shaken by my mournful ignorance,  
Under your guidance, gracious martyr,  
I shall now recount  
Your radiant life.

Though my understanding be dull,  
May he whose work I recount himself grant assent,  
So that I may be able to set forth clearly  
The good deeds he performed in the world:

How the treachery of the dark Duke Arnulf  
Was slain by God’s pre-eminent witness.

Glory to the Father,  
[Col. 0658B] And equally to the Son,  
And to the Holy Spirit,  
To the one God simply and indivisibly,  
Now and always,  
Throughout perpetual time,  
Through joined and unbroken  
Ages of ages.

# DESCRIPTION OF THE LIFE OF DUKE WILLIAM

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657B]

Since it is the duty of the one who has granted victory’s reward in the present age and bestowed the benefit of unfading glory in the heavenly kingdom to arrange the radiant praises of the most glorious martyrs and to illuminate their deeds by proclaiming them with supreme force, therefore we shall weave together, in brief preliminary fashion, the life, deeds, and triumph of the most powerful Duke William—not loftily adorned with verbal colors or the ornament of elevated speech, but composed simply and in the modest language of natural expression.

Thus the history of his deeds, frequently recited, may stir the hearts of all, and especially of those descending from his line, toward the rewards of heavenly joys. May the foundation of our faith thereby be firmly strengthened; may the worship of our religion be diligently nourished; may contempt for the fleeting and deceptive world arise; may desire and love for heavenly things be more abundantly generated through the fruit of saving work; may the incentive to holiness increase; may the steps of advancement be raised; and may the gate of heavenly contemplation be entered by the saving path.

[Col. 0657D]

Therefore the most glorious and powerful duke and count William, the beloved champion of the eternal King, born from distinguished stock—his father being a Dane, namely Rollo, and his mother a woman of Francia, namely Poppa, as was recounted in the preceding book—was born in the city of Rothomagus.

His father, rich in an abundance of every possession and wealthy in every kind of treasure, entrusted him, washed in sacred baptism, to a certain exceedingly rich count named Botho for upbringing, and handed him over to be educated as was fitting.

Finally, the most beautiful boy, living familiarly among orthodox men of the most honorable life, and beginning to show himself a man of blessed memory and good character, devoted the period of his youth to Jesus Christ, strengthened especially by the abundant commerce of the fourfold virtue, and subjected and surrendered himself wholly to divine service.

Indeed, he was filled ever more abundantly with divine grace and enriched more fully with the wisdom of the sevenfold gift. Each day he increased more pleasingly through the abundance of his merits; he was richly instructed in divine teachings, strengthened abundantly by monastic observances, willingly distinguished by the administration of ecclesiastical religion, and abundantly suffused with the nectar of honeyed sweetness.

He was conspicuous in appearance, tall in stature, vigorous in mind, mature in the integrity of his character, and striving with all his strength to become a perfect man. He scorned the boasting of this age and bravely avoided the pomp of the world. His face was altogether joyful, his mind peaceful and serene, his speech most sweet, and his conduct in society most gentle.

He desired to leave this fleeting world and become a monk at Gimegia. He often repeated this intention in his mind and clung to it through repeated, deliberate thoughts. He diligently sought to know what Christ willed concerning this matter. He sought judgment about it, in case it might come to him from heaven. For this reason he devoted himself constantly to tears and harshly withheld food from his body. He persevered in all-night vigils and refreshed the poor with food. Inflamed by the heat of this zeal, he resolved to become a monk and abandon the world.

## ADDRESS TO WILLIAM

O holy William, rejoice in youthful well-being,  
Fragrant with the flower of youth and just entering adolescence,  
Why do you hasten the vow uttered in your present speech?  
Why do you wish, with a swift vow, to go to Christ’s refuge?  
Why does vigilant custody guard your tender years?  
Why does a rule now discipline your bodily habits?  
Why does the red rule bind you tightly to chaste companions?

[Col. 0659A]

Cease from your vows; you must enjoy yourself, for your sake and ours.  
For from your seed will be born a radiant duke,  
Adorned with heavenly gifts drawn from above.

Under whose marvelous hand Francia will change its appearance;  
He will lead, drive, move, bend, and swiftly summon it in triumph,  
After you have departed to Olympus through martyrdom.

An excellent judge, he will govern the noble reins of the kingdom;  
He will weigh complaints with an equal balance and scales.  
With a just judgment he will impose torments upon the guilty,  
And give the righteous the rewards of his lavish gift.

Acting everywhere through a mound of the four virtues,  
He will bear upon the summit of his holy head,  
As one distinguished by shining emeralds,  
A radiant diadem earned by merit.  
He will climb, worthy under Christ’s guidance, into the Elysian field.

When, however, through the grace of divinity going before him, he flourished according to the strength of his age, was honored for this goodness, and advanced abundantly in the pursuits of holiness, the counts and nobles of the Northmen and Britons gathered together unanimously and said to one another what they should decide and do:

“Our duke, namely Rollo, also called Robert, continually worn down by the immense labor of wars, exhausted by the many dangers of the surging sea, afflicted by the hardship of frequent voyages, weakened by countless nights spent without sleep, infirm from the bruises of many wounds, drained and exhausted because his strength had been emptied by weakness, and finally consumed by the long duration of advanced age, is no longer able to support or defend another’s kingdom, or to preside over and benefit both himself and us with confidence.

“Let us inquire whom he has chosen as his heir in the kingdom won through battles, and whom he has appointed as suitable for us. He has a son born from the noblest stock of the Franks, a man most distinguished in body, strengthened by vigorous health, and most skilled in understanding, formed by the study of many matters. With his father’s approval, let us make him our duke and place him before us as patrician and count.”

Once this plan had been reached—or rather, through the merciful dispensation of almighty God—the nobles came unanimously to Robert, who was advanced in years and wearied by old age in the see of Rothomagus. With gentle speech and lowered faces they said to him:

“Most powerful lord duke, you are weighed down by the inconvenience of old age and can no longer provide salutary help to yourself or to us. For this reason foreign peoples now afflict us and utterly seize our possessions. Division and civil conflict take place among us; the kingdom is not established as a united whole, and therefore the commonwealth is dissolved and ruined.

“Choose, therefore, we ask, one who may rule and benefit us, to whom we may carefully submit, so that he may be our advocate, duke, and patrician, while we serve him obediently and in person.”

Then Rollo, most humble, compelled by the words of his people, began his reply:

“Since you know that old age takes away all health, and you see that I am no longer strong enough or useful to you, let a duke be established for you by your counsel and judgment, one who will rule diligently and benefit you as I have done until now.

“I have a son sprung from the seed of the noblest Frankish lineage. Prince Botho, commander of our army, raised him as a son and sufficiently instructed him in character and the studies of war. I ask you to choose him as your duke and protector, patrician and count. Let him wisely aid you in counsel and steadfastly benefit you in battle. Let him protect you from your adversaries with hostile force and legally establish lasting peace among you.

“As I have been told, he wishes to devote himself to monastic affairs and, changing his clothing, to attach himself to contemplative studies.”

Then the counts, made joyful by the speech of this reply, answered:

“He will be our hereditary and suitable duke, and we will honorably obey his command. We will make the kingdom of the Frankish people inclined toward him.”

The duke, rejoicing that the words of his soldiers favored his wishes, ordered Botho, commander of the army, to bring to him [Col. 0660B] the hope of the people, namely the young William. Botho quickly brought William to his father, after summoning the nobles of the entire kingdom.

Then the kind father lovingly received his dearest son, embraced him tenderly as was right, and, with spiritual insight, foresaw that he would greatly surpass the years of childhood.

Both rejoiced: William in his father’s honor,  
And the distinguished father in William’s noble deeds.

The old man, bowed beneath age, rejoiced in the offspring of his virtue,  
And the radiant son rejoiced in the father of advanced years.

The father would soon climb to heaven, his son to be the future witness;  
The son would be reborn for the world through his blessed father.

Repeating sacred embraces in embraces,  
They continually exchanged kisses with honey-sweet mouths.

[Col. 0660C]

Father and son sat together, giving thanks.

Then Rollo, having summoned the nobles more privately, said to them in words of entreaty:

“Here is the one you seek; here is the heir of our possession; here is the one who will rule over you. With your favor, I hand over to him the kingdom acquired through the labor of struggles and the sweat of battles.

“He will rule this people in my place and will be a most worthy heir of our dominion. Imitate his virtue, and observe with prophetic insight what he will become. He will steadfastly support our laws and statutes, and, while he survives, our right and decree will not be erased. Nor will the land which I assigned to you by lot disappoint you; rather, he will enlarge and increase it further.

“Therefore, for the sake of preserving fidelity, give your hands into his hands. I ask you to bind yourselves to him by the oath of our faith, through continuous and unbreakable service and military duty.”

When he had spoken, Count Berenger and Alannus, together with the other Britons and the nobles of the Northmen, willingly submitted themselves unanimously to William. They bound themselves to him by an oath of sacred faith and gave their hands into his hands in place of their hearts. They vowed that they would serve as soldiers and fight against neighboring peoples.

After this, when a period of one five-year cycle had passed, Rollo died and, as we believe, was happily crowned in the heavenly throne. The Northmen and Britons gathered together once more and again confirmed the substance of their faith to William, their most excellent duke and patrician, by the firm pledge of their fidelity.

Having thus attained the summit of such honor and dignity, and being most worthily surrounded by fitting counts and soldiers, he vowed to Christ that he would support the kingdom and never inflict any injury upon anyone.

He was enriched with the honors of holiness and magnificence, illumined by the practices of prudence and caution, with the mercy of the Holy Spirit going before him. He regarded the earthly things of this age as of little worth, just as he had vowed in childhood. He governed the people vigorously by his father’s laws and condemned the guilty to punishments according to them.

He diligently observed the rule of an innocent life and administered the reins of ecclesiastical governance skillfully according to the lay order. He surpassed everyone in strength of mind and body and exceeded all in knowledge of legal and public affairs. He instructed everyone by the example of good will and compelled everyone by the teaching of patience and religion.

[Col. 0661B]

He was a steadfast defender in adversity and a most skillful reconciler in prosperity. Truth and glory were in his house; equity and justice were in his works. By truthful speech he rebuked offenders and by the severest correction reproved the negligent.

When he flourished more abundantly in such gifts of heavenly dispensation, and the fame of his good works spread widely and increasingly throughout almost the entire world, they wholly abandoned the pledge of faith they had promised and began to rebel against Duke William.

When the truth of this immeasurable report reached the most powerful duke, he sent his envoys to the Britons, urging them to recover their senses quickly and hasten to Rothomagus to serve him.

But they foolishly remained in their perseverance in unbelief and sent envoys back to Duke William, saying:

“We will no longer serve you as soldiers or attend you, because we have always lived under the authority of Frankish rule. Your father Rollo, having gathered together bands of barbarian newcomers, once invaded Francia and acquired for you as a peaceful kingdom the land that you now possess, by the gift of the king.

“But the land we hold was not given to him as a possession for his heirs. It was assigned to him only so long as he might live from it, until the land which he had received by the king’s gift, after it had been devastated, could be rebuilt.

“Nothing has been decided between us and you except friendship and concord, with equal wishes and equal counsel. Until now we have had a king and have not lacked a duke and protector. Britannia has never been subject to the service of any land except Francia, nor has it subjected itself to the rule of anyone.”

When Duke William of the Danes heard the message of this British embassy, he summoned the nobles of the Northmen to deliberate on the matter. After they had assembled, he repeated the sequence of this astonishing embassy in their hearing.

Then a certain Bernard, privy to Duke William’s secrets, and Botho, commander of his household, astonished by these messages, said to everyone:

“Strange, unheard-of, and astonishing to us is the answer contained in this message. When, long ago, with your father Rollo, we expelled the Danes and, scarcely having crossed the sea, attacked the borders of the English, they wished to rise up against us. By resisting them with hostile force, we defeated them and struck them down severely, even to destruction.

“When these matters had been peacefully settled with King Athelstan, and we had entered the land of the Welsh by the force of the winds, they themselves, having gathered an army, wished to resist us. We attacked them opportunely and subdued them in battle.

“Finally, we penetrated as far as Radebod the Frisian and then Rainer of Hasbain; we made them tributaries to us. With matters in this state, we came to Francia, seized it through war, and laid waste the whole land except for the fortified cities.

“While we were remaining in the siege around Paris, we returned to England for love of King Athelstan and subjected his injurious and faithless people to us by force and authority. After the English had been subjected to King Athelstan according to our will, we returned to Francia with an army greater than before and crushed it through many wars.

“When King Charles saw that he could not prevail against us, he sought peace and concord from us and gave his daughter in marriage to your father Rollo. He voluntarily handed this land over to us as a pledge of peace, for the perpetual possession of our heirs, and subjected the Britons to service and their land to our habitation.

“While your father was still alive, they submitted themselves to you by an oath of true faith and by service. After the grievous loss of your father, they renewed their faith and have served you until now.

“What shall we now do against the Britons who have rendered service and then rebelled, we who have fought so many and such great battles? They recognize us as weakened in strength and exhausted; therefore they have dared to send back such a message. They think that the food of this land, by which our bodies are sustained, has made us unarmed and has completely deprived us of strength.

“Let them feel that our power has not withered through our residence in this kingdom, and let them experience our strongest vigor. Let them be trapped by the plans they are devising; let them recover their senses in vain concerning their replies, which will bring about their destruction and correction. Let us destroy their arrogance by our strength and crush their pride by our power.”

## ADDRESS

O William, future witness of Christ Jesus,  
Be strengthened, grow strong, and labor in sacred endeavor.  
Awaken and be powerfully fortified,  
And restrain the barren, savage Britons by reason.  
Strike down their wicked pride with force.

Their counsel is foolish in speech  
And their malignity dull.

[Col. 0662D]

For they are torn by wars, crushed by plague and famine.  
Showing indulgence, pity, and mercy, and forgiving what was neglected,  
You will bend them through the steadfast force of an oath,  
And, coming to their senses, they will serve you reverently.

At the words of this exhortation, William was terribly moved and incited. He hastily assembled the armies of his entire realm and went toward the river Couesnon, intending to subdue the Bretons. Terrified by his arrival and unwilling to serve William, the Bretons concealed themselves in the refuge of their cities. William then occupied all the land of the Bretons with his army and overturned many fortified places. When William had returned from Brittany to the city of Rouen, the Bretons followed him, invaded, and ravaged the district of Bayeux. William therefore recalled his entire army, anticipated their return, and fought valiantly against them. After many Breton princes had been slain, he gained a triumph over his enemies. He then devastated their land, afflicting them with hunger and want and crushing them with immense slaughter.

When Berenger, Alan, and the other Bretons saw that they were not sufficient and could not prevail against William, they sent him an envoy with supplicatory words:

“While your father obeyed, we served him, and we desire to serve you as well. We beg you not to despise us or in any way reject our service, but to look upon us as a merciful Lord looks upon offended servants. Blinded by the counsels of the wicked, we neglected the commands of your authority. Let your anger be turned away from your servants, and grant us complete peace and happiness. Bend the kindly ear of your magnificent compassion toward these wicked servants guilty of scandal and offense. For what we promised you by the sacrament of the Christian faith, we have hitherto denied by our evil conduct against you. We repent of having gone astray against you and abandoned your service.”

Taking advantage of this embassy concerning their neglected military service and obedience, and their proclaimed humility, the mighty duke William consulted the Danish princes about these matters. He received Berenger, duke of the Bretons, burdened with guilt for the offense and neglected service and with the plea for mercy, through gratuitous compassion, and bound him to himself by an oath of enduring fidelity and service.

But Alan, who had been the author and instigator of this quarrel and dispute, he rejected and cast off; he expelled him and his followers from Brittany. Alan himself could not remain in Brittany, nor anywhere in France, for fear of Duke William; as an exile, he sought the aid of Alstem, king of the English.

William then vigorously governed the peoples of both realms and began to flourish abundantly in power and valor. The fame of his goodness spread through the regions of the world; his chaste continence was proclaimed ever more widely, and he did not devote himself to the pleasures that produce offspring. His counts therefore pressed him—not because of the urgency of human sexual weakness, but lest an heir to so great a lineage, honor, and dukedom should fail or be lacking—to enter into a lawful marital union for the preservation of succession with a most noble virgin, of exquisite beauty, exceptionally prudent in counsel, extremely cautious in worldly affairs, most fitting in her conduct, wisely eloquent in conversation, and elegantly and skillfully accomplished in womanly pursuits.

## APOSTROPHA

Burning with zeal for innocent causes, martyr Clionee,

Blooming in radiant foreknowledge of abundant reward,

Shining with the increase of divine prosperity,

Resplendent in the fitting goodness of future glory,

And perpetually atoning by the light of your widespread goodness.

Indeed, more radiant than all in worthy merits,

Do not tremble, fear, or dread a few things [the reading is uncertain],

Nor dread the lawful right by which you made

The covenants of the marriage bed.

For this mingling of sacred pleasure,

Neither violated untouched faith nor suffered a stain upon chastity,

Nor did desire profane the merit of your sacred heart.

For from your seed will succeed a radiant duke,

Strengthened by the gift of virtues and glittering with merits,

Who, in the manner of his father, will subdue the people by strong authority.

He will rule as sovereign and rightly exalt his governance,

Devoting all his efforts to Christ;

He will govern the many-streaming nation with just reins.

Under whose hand there will be peace—peace, concord, peace, peace.

Resplendent in the foregoing writings and in other such things, the most blessed athlete of Christ was made known throughout all the ends of the earth, the fame of his goodness going before him. He was sufficiently enriched by an abundance of fleeting possessions and lavishly endowed by the grace of divine increase. [Col. 0664B] He was beloved by all inhabitants of the earth, and still more beloved by God and the citizens of heaven.

At that time, by mutual will and suitable agreement, he joined himself in a friendship with Duke Hugh, though the bond would not endure forever. Thereafter he was joined by a fragile pact of friendship to the magnate Heribert.

A certain Riulf, filled terribly with the wickedness of treachery, saw that Duke William, his lord, was greatly strengthened and prospering through the protection of his friends. He summoned many of the princes of the Northmen and said deceitfully:

“Our lord William, born from the noblest seed of the Frankish race, is acquiring Frankish friends for himself, excluding us from his counsel and examining us with hostility because of our distress. He is trying to drive us entirely from the kingdom and to crush the necks of those who remain beneath the yoke of servitude. The land we possess he will give to his relatives as the possession of their heirs, and he will enrich them abundantly with our gifts.

“Let us therefore wisely seek sound counsel against what he is plotting. Let us make among ourselves a pact of everlasting alliance and hold it unshaken by the anchor of steadfast will. Let each of us aid any one of our number whom he sees oppressed, and protect him with continual assistance as he would himself. Indeed, if he should wish to destroy all of us together, let us resist his audacity as enemies.

“What that treacherous man constantly plots to do to us by crafty deceit, let us do to him unexpectedly and as soon as we can. Let us send him an intermediary to say that, if he wishes to have us ready to serve him, he should grant us land as far as the river Risle. If he grants it, we shall be enriched by the frequent presence of soldiers. Deprived of soldiers, he will be rendered powerless and will no longer attempt to extend the force of his indignation against us. Then we shall be more powerful than he in fortune and valor, while he will have only the name of power.”

When this fraudulent plan had been devised, they sent messengers to William to communicate their wicked inventions. When the intermediary stood before William and had completed the business of the embassy, William was astonished at the word of such extraordinary presumption. He summoned his princes to consult them about these commands and sent an envoy back to Riulf with peaceful words, instructing him to say:

“I cannot grant you the land you request from me, but I shall gladly give you all the equipment I possess: namely, arm-rings, belts, coats of mail, helmets, and cambisators [the reading is uncertain], horses, axes, and excellent swords wonderfully adorned with gold. If you willingly devote yourselves to my service, you shall enjoy my continual favor and the palm of military success in my household. I shall place the counsel of my authority in your mouths, and whatever you wish shall be carried out at your command. Whomever you wish to oppress, I shall harshly oppress; whomever you wish to cast off, I shall utterly cast off. Whatever you order to be exalted, I shall powerfully exalt; whomever you wish humbled, I shall terribly humble. This country shall be governed and ruled by your counsel, and therefore your power shall be exalted in everything. Henceforth my life and my judgment shall be in your power.”

When the messenger of this humility reached Riulf, the author of the entire presumption, and reported to him the embassy of such humility and gentleness, Riulf was enticed by the arrogance of his own rashness. He made light of the commands of Duke William’s most humble plea, summoned the princes who followed his presumptuous will, and repeated what he had heard from the speaking envoy in words of fraudulent cunning.

Then, suffused with the poison of treachery and swollen with a defiant mind, he foolishly chattered these words into the ears of the princes:

“The language of such humility as you have heard foretells that he intends us to yield and fall asleep; and thus, by the delay of so much postponement, he is trying to gather together against us the Frankish kindred of his nobility, the princes he has bound by oath, and the allies he has summoned. Let us therefore take care not to be deceived or crushed by the Frankish peoples. Let him not continue to trample us down through the cunning of his argument; rather, let us promptly meet him with a massed army at the city of Rouen, so that he and his advisers may be handed over to Rouen. Then, with greater hope and confidence, we shall be secure and free from revolt without restraint.”

## APOSTROPHA TO RIULF

Ah, Riulf, through harmful strength and wicked designs,

What bitter plague of treachery and envy defiles you?

With the crime of vice now growing gross, proud Riulf,

Why do you rage in vain, why do you rage treacherously?

Infected with vices, riding in the ornamented chariot of your mind,

Why do you boast of strength when goodness has been exhausted?

Why do you take pride in swollen arrogance, displaying excessive pomp?

Why do you strive, laboring in an empty effort,

To oppose the will of the Lord who remains above the stars?

Tell me, enemy of God, where will you hasten?

Where will you carry your camp, and where will you quicken your step?

Where do you urge the whole misled army to go

By your crafty sophistry, raging with bitter madness?

Having suffered countless falls and misfortunes,

Struck by the judgment of God, that mighty pestilence,

I fear that you are hastening with swollen steps

Toward a fluid destruction and a headlong Charybdis.

For it is characteristic of the proud to raise themselves very high,

And then to be tormented excessively by sudden disaster.

The lofty brow is worn down, its empty arrogance destroyed;

But the humble bear a shining crown encircling them.

At the word of this pestilential exhortation, they massed their army, secretly crossed the bed of the Seine, and pitched their camp in a certain meadow beside the city of Rouen.

Fearing the sudden attack of this perverse multitude, William sent them an envoy with the most humble words, who was to say what you will now hear:

“Our lord William, radiant in the flower of youthful age, wishes to be peaceful and well disposed toward you in every respect. He commands you to share with him the honor of the entire country and, as the first and greatest in his council, to surpass all others. The land you ask to be given you he will gladly grant not only as far as the Risle, but even as far as the Seine. For he trusts that he will be protected by your aid; and you should not doubt that you will be fostered and fortified by his protection. Whatever you desire, have; whatever possessions you want, possess without delay. Come humbly and peacefully to him, as he requests, and, falling into friendly conversation with him, dwell with him.”

Then Riulf, the most wicked instigator of this evil, raging in the furies of diabolical deceit, said above all to the envoy:

“Return more quickly and tell William and all his people to leave the walls of this city and hasten to seek their Frankish kinsmen. He shall no longer be heir of this land, nor shall he rule us any longer, because he is unsuitable and subject to us. The land he promises us will not be given as his gift, because what one does not possess cannot be given. If he prefers not to abandon the city, we shall continually attack it; once it has been captured, we shall crush William and his people with the sword.”

When the intermediary had hurriedly reported to Duke William what he had heard, William stiffened in astonishment at the novelty of the matter. He summoned his princes, assembled his army, left the city, and climbed the slope of the mountain overlooking the city, wishing to observe the army of his enemies, in case he might be able to fight them.

Seeing that the army of his enemies was larger and more numerous than his own, he said to Bernard the Dane:

“I shall go to Bernard of Senlis, my maternal uncle, and remain with him until he provides us some assistance. By his counsel and aid I shall recover this land and crush all these armies of the Franks as enemies. I shall wipe them out, and their plan, entirely from the face of the earth; none of these lineages shall remain anywhere in the world.”

Then Bernard the Dane is said to have replied:

“We shall hasten with you as far as the little river Epte, but we shall not enter France. In former times, together with your father, we often invaded it in war and struck down many at the beginning of the battle. Moreover, we have either killed or captured the grandfathers and uncles, fathers and paternal uncles, maternal aunts and paternal aunts, cousins and kinsmen who are still alive. How shall we be able to withstand the presence of so many enemies? Would you rather live on a worthless and useless foreign crust than rule and protect a kingdom? I and my companions will not follow you, nor will we go wherever you wish. We shall return by ship to Denmark, the land of our birth, because we lack a leader and defender. You are no longer able to command us, weakened as you are, because you fear death threatening these enemies.”

Incited by these harshest words, William said to Bernard the Dane before the other princes:

“You have shamefully assailed me with harsh and obscene words when you called me effeminate, cold in arms, and even worthless. Behold, I shall go first as standard-bearer, hastening into battle, and I shall steadfastly crush the army of my enemies. My sword shall devour the flesh of the perjured, and I shall break apart and scatter their camp. Do not remain any longer sluggish and fearful; follow me quickly, and let us attack them like wolves attacking lambs.”

When Bernard saw the courage and manly steadfastness of Duke William, he said to him with the most humble words:

“Most powerful lord duke, do not be angry at our speech, for what you command us to do is proper and useful. Let us merely discover who will go with you into battle and who will come to your aid.”

When Bernard inquired, three hundred men were found ready to fight and die with William. They came before him with one accord, performed the Danish rite of forming a judgment of alliance, faith, and assistance, and struck their weapons together in a pact of mutual will. The rest of the people, cold in arms, withdrew in swift flight to the city’s refuge.

## APOSTROPHA

Famous in conduct and merits, patrician William,

Do not tremble in fear or shrink in shame

From quarrels, words, threats, disputes, separations, brawls,

Wars, arrogance, frauds, duels, and weapons.

This people, filled with the filth of treachery,

Rages against you without cause:

Sullen, fierce, boastful, insolent, reckless, rebellious,

Inconstant and at odds with itself through its love of novelty;

Wasteful of words, but not wasteful of deeds;

Perverse, proud, malicious, wicked, criminal,

Death-dealing, guilty, pestilential, criminal, profane,

Pouring forth many poisons of a viperous man,

Weary of the stable course of peaceful tranquility.

Jerubbaal—Gideon—crushed them by shaking them,

Warned by the divine command and heavenly direction,

Having selected three times four times twenty-five illustrious armed men,

Tried and approved at the command of the heavenly Judge.

So, with God’s aid, this host will likewise be destroyed,

Worthy reward for your merits, while you rejoice with three hundred men.

Then William, clad in iron together with the three hundred, suddenly rushed upon the hostile camp of the rash multitude, crushing and tearing them apart with swords and spears. He broke into the tents of the princes and set fire to the huts of their soldiers. Those whom he found he struck down with the sword and sent those who resisted him to the realm of Orcus.

When William had triumphed over his enemies, Riulf vanished in flight. The part of the army that pursued him could not capture him, because he concealed himself in the dense forest. The Seine swallowed many of them, while the forest covered many others who had been torn apart.

William then surveyed the field of corpses and, finding none of his own dead, glorified God with his men, because God had come to the aid of those who trusted in him. The place where this remarkable battle occurred has to the present day been called Pratum-Belli, “Meadow of Battle.”

As William was returning from the battle, a certain soldier from Fécamp met him and announced that a son had been born to him by his beloved wife. William was therefore happier after the battle had been completed, and happiest because of his son. He sent Heiric, bishop of the church of Bayeux, holiest of all bishops, and Bothon, most distinguished of all soldiers, to cause the son to be reborn and renewed through the sacred baptismal water, oil, and chrism.

## APOSTROPHA

Behold, a worthy heir for you, patrician William,

Who will vigorously govern the people with just reins.

As a reward for your blood, a worthy crown will be given you.

His praiseworthy name will be recognized by the setting sun,

Once his goodness has been proclaimed, and by the rising sun;

And the north and the south will likewise equal you in merits.

Then William, exalted sublimely by such slaughter and ruin, securely obtained both kingdoms, that of the Bretons and that of the Northmen, and no one dared contend against him. The princes of the Frankish people and the counts of the Burgundians served him. The Danes, Flemings, English, and Irish obeyed him. The other peoples dwelling within the sphere of his kingdom obeyed his rule with one accord.

At the time of the most worthy hunt, when servants, driven by wanton luxury, gather together for the hinds that are about to conceive their young according to the law of nature, he ordered spacious pavilions to be prepared for him at a place called Leons.

When Count Heribert heard this, and Hugh, duke and prince of the entire kingdom, as well as Count William of Poitiers, they hastened to him there. William, rejoicing at their arrival, received them respectfully with great ceremony and had them remain with him for the long and delightful season of the hunt, feasting splendidly in royal luxury.

One day William of Poitiers said to William of Rouen:

“Lord duke, do you know why we have come here?”

He replied, “I do not know.”

The other said:

“Unwilling to send envoys to you, so worthy a count, I preferred to perform the business of an embassy myself. I have come so that you may give me your sister as a wife and so that we may be joined to one another by an indissoluble bond of friendship and affection.”

Then William of Rouen is said to have replied jokingly:

“Men of Poitiers are always timid, cold in arms, and greedy. It is not fitting that such a girl should belong to them.”

When William of Poitiers remained fixed in a single glance, irritated by these words, William of Rouen continued:

“Tomorrow, do not be troubled; after consulting my faithful men, I shall give you an answer concerning both matters.”

The following day, after consulting Hugh the Great, the energetic Heribert, and his faithful men, he gave his sister to Duke William of Poitiers. He honorably adorned her with an abundance of bridal possessions, carried her in female horses laden with trappings and artistically girded with gold and amber, and escorted her respectfully to the Poitevin court amid a vast and innumerable multitude of slaves of both sexes and many chests filled and weighed down with silk garments woven with gold.

When Heribert saw William of Rouen strengthened and prospering, striving sufficiently in Christ through strength of mind and body and through his outstanding deeds, he gave him his daughter on the advice of Duke Hugh the Great. William led her magnificently into the strongholds of the city of Rouen, splendidly supported by marvelous wedding songs, furnishings, and unheard-of adornments of indescribable honor and dignity, and surrounded on every side by an immeasurable multitude of horsemen.

Holiness and prudence shone forth in him; equity and justice continually excelled. He severely crushed the proud and malicious, and reverently exalted the humble and benevolent. By gifts and words he led pagans and unbelievers to the worship of the true faith, and urged believers to praise Christ. He governed not only the monarchy he held but also, through vigorous counsel, the neighboring kingdoms. The English obeyed his commands, the Franks and Burgundians his words. Wherever his name was heard throughout the earth, everyone praised it magnificently.

When Alstem, the peaceful king of the English, heard that William surpassed all the Frankish nation in valor and power, he sent his envoys to him with immense gifts and presents. He begged William to recall to the kingdom of France his nephew Louis, the son of the captive King Charles, who had already been overtaken by death in captivity, and to establish the kingdom for him, raising him to perpetual rule with the counsel of the Franks; and, moved by compassion for love of Alstem, to receive Alan, who had been expelled because of the offense in Brittany and deprived of Alstem’s affection.

Immediately, on the advice of Duke William, Hugh the Great, the most powerful duke of the Franks, and Heribert, the magnate of the princes, summoned Louis back, together with the bishops and with the counsel of the metropolitans, and anointed him king of the peoples dwelling in France and Burgundy. William received Alan, who returned with Louis, for love of King Alstem, and restored to him whatever he possessed in Brittany. Thereafter Alan continually adhered to William’s commands.

Five years after the king’s anointing had passed, the Franks began to quarrel with Louis and oppress him in many ways; indeed, they attempted to drive him from the kingdom. When the king saw that he was being abandoned and considered worthless by the Franks, he sent envoys to Henry, king beyond the Rhine, requesting his aid and seeking to bind him to himself in perpetual friendship.

The response was that Henry would not enter into an alliance with the king of the Franks except through Duke William of the Northmen. When this was reported, King Louis, worn down by the insults of many tribulations and afflicted by the calamities of countless troubles, came to Mount Balon against Duke William of the Northmen. He begged William to aid and defend him against the rebellious Franks and to obtain for him the friendship and assistance of Henry, king beyond the Rhine.

Moved by compassion for the king’s affliction, William brought him to the dwelling of the city of Rouen and honorably kept him there many times with all his people. The king remained in the house of Duke William as a house-servant and underling, humbly awaiting his assistance.

## APOSTROPHA

A margrave powerful by right, shining forth worthily in merits,

Every nation now freely submits to you;

It loves you, serves you, attends upon you, and clings to you.

Indeed, the king humbly and prostrate in prayer

Begs for your assistance, that he may be protected by your valor.

Bishops, dukes, counts, and nobles revere you,

As do clergy and common people alike on every side,

As a bearer of peace and a forerunner of salvation;

By arms and prayer they ask you to aid them.

At once William sent a certain Tetger, a young nobleman of his household, to Henry, king beyond the Rhine, so that he would not delay in doing by his own hand what King Louis requested of him. Henry the king and Duke William were joined by a pact of indissoluble friendship and had long been bound to one another by mutual agreements of good will.

King Henry received Tetger honorably and had him remain with him for a long time. Later, after enriching him with various gifts and diverse presents, he sent him back to Duke William, together with Duke Cono, the confidant of his secrets.

William received Cono with a magnificent display of immeasurable reverence and asked why a duke of such dignity and honor had come to him. Cono replied:

“You sent to our king Henry, who is joyful in the prosperity of your resources, so that he and Louis, king of France, might be joined to one another through your prudent counsel, and so that whichever of them was pressed by necessity might be fortified by the assistance of the other. Since the king judged this counsel salutary for himself and his people, and all the more stable and secure through your agency, he sent me to you so that you might bring the king to the appointed meeting. He also commanded me to remain as a hostage wherever you wished until you returned and brought back the king secure from every adversity.”

When William heard the command of this astonishing and immeasurable embassy, he sent to King Louis and announced that he was pleased with the business of such an embassy.

On the appointed day of departure, after an innumerable multitude of troops had been assembled, William said to Duke Cono of the Saxons, wishing to discover whether anything hidden lay in his heart:

“Prepare yourself for the journey and quickly equip yourself with greaves, because I shall send you to the city of Bayeux until, as you said, we return unharmed.”

Then Cono said, “Send me wherever you wish, even among the Danes subject to your rule.”

William replied, “You shall go with me to the appointed meeting, for I do not distrust you.”

Cono answered:

“If I go to the city of Bayeux, I shall unquestionably remain your faithful man. But if, as I do not believe will happen, I set out with you, I shall remain your faithful armor-bearer and constant guardian of your life against the plots of your enemies.”

After these words, they went with one accord and a great army to meet King Louis, whom Duke Hugh the Great and Count Heribert were awaiting in the district of Laon. When Hugh the duke and Count Heribert saw the legions of such an immense multitude, surpassing the armies of the Bretons and Northmen in soldiers, they were astonished and said to one another:

“What comparison is there between our army and this one? If a quarrel should arise between us and them, they will devour us like wolves devour lambs.”

Thereafter Hugh the Great and Count Heribert ordered their men to ride apart and forbade William’s army to mix with any of their own.

King Henry was with an innumerable multitude of armies at a place on the Meuse called Vensegus (Vouziers on the Aisne). As King Louis approached the appointed place of meeting, William went ahead with five hundred soldiers. At his instruction Duke Cono preceded him and announced his arrival to the king in these words:

“William, margrave and duke of the Northmen and Bretons, faithfully serves you in Christ. Unwilling to retain me as a hostage, he has come to you under the guarantee of your sacred faith and wishes to inquire what ought to be done between you and King Louis.”

Then King Henry asked:

“Of what power, dignity, honor, and goodness is this William, who is joined to me by the grace of friendship?”

He replied:

“He is a man of great patience and justice, great power and sufficiency, and great and unheard-of honor and prudence. No king except you, and no duke or count, is as magnificent as William. Surrounded by a constant multitude of princes and young nobles, he feasts splendidly from golden vessels and cups, encircled by a great variety of noble attendants and servants, and diligently exercises the laws and decrees of the orthodox Fathers. No one is more just in deeds, no one holier in words, no one more powerful in arms. No one dares inflict prejudice upon another in his kingdom; no one commits theft or sacrilege. The inhabitants of his land live together in concord under its laws and dwell as one people, restrained by the decrees of the holy Fathers.”

While they spoke to one another in alternating conversation, William arrived with five hundred soldiers. When Duke Cono heard of his arrival, he quickly sprang up, received his sword faithfully, and led him respectfully to King Henry.

King Henry immediately rose and went to meet Duke William. After they had exchanged a kiss, each sat down. Then William said:

“King Louis sends you a gift of inward affection and love. You sent Duke Cono to me so that I might come to you as though I were a pledge and hostage. But, because I do not distrust you, behold, I have come with him. You said that you would not be joined to King Louis by the bond and tie of friendship and assistance unless I were the agent of this business. Report to the king what has been determined for you concerning this matter.”

Then King Henry replied:

“Let King Louis come tomorrow under your leadership, and through your vigorous intervention everything that has been desired and beneficially decreed by our faithful men and yours will be completed.”

Meanwhile the Lotharingians and Saxons began to address Cono insultingly and mockingly, saying:

“What an astonishingly capable and powerful duke of the Northmen and Bretons, who has come here adorned and decked out in gold with five hundred soldiers!”

William, understanding through the Danish language what they were saying in mockery, overheard it. Somewhat angered, he withdrew and reported to the king everything he had heard while the king was speaking.

The next day, as King Louis proceeded to the appointed meeting with an incredible and innumerable army, William anticipated his arrival. The Willelmids who went ahead began to break down the walls and doors of the house where King Henry was staying, to tear and wrench them apart, and to occupy the interior by force and power.

Fearing their attack, King Henry fled to another house. He said to Cono, the confidant of his secrets:

“This meeting, as I think, is neither effective nor suitable for us; rather, it will turn to our ruin and destruction, indeed to unheard-of disgrace. Go and tell William, the richest of all dukes, that, out of the faith we hold between us, he should restrain his angry army, lest they continue to break down the walls and crush the doors of our dwelling, and lest a quarrel arise among peoples differing in language, dress, and weapons.”

Cono immediately sprang out and met Duke William, who was coming to the meeting. He reported what William’s men who had gone ahead had done.

Then William said to Duke Cono:

“Go and tell them, by my command, to depart.”

But when Cono arrived and asked them to leave, they not only rejected his command but also attacked the other houses outside, which stood there, destroying them with great violence and uproar.

Therefore Cono immediately sought Duke William again in rapid and swift flight. William was approaching the meeting with the remaining legions. Cono said:

“Most powerful Duke William, your men would not leave the houses at my command; rather, they are hastening to destroy the others. I beg you, bending to the ground, do not allow such things to happen, lest unheard-of slaughter arise among the people.”

Then William gave Cono a sword whose hilt, gold plates, and bosses were artistically and marvelously fashioned from six pounds of gold, so that Cono might carry it as a signal for them to leave and show it to the army occupying and still destroying the houses.

When Cono hurried back to meet them and displayed the sword of Duke William, shining with gold and gems, they did not immediately comply. But, with downcast faces inclined toward the sword, they left the houses, crushing one another excessively as they departed, and returned silently to their duke.

William then came to King Henry and said that King Louis was present. At once, at William’s urging, King Henry went to meet him. After they exchanged a kiss and clasped hands, they entered the house and sat down.

Enriched by many suitable agreements and varied gifts and presents, they were joined and allied to one another by an unbreakable bond of friendship, assistance, and mutual support, through the counsel of Duke William, the most distinguished of all dukes. Hugh, duke of the Franks, was present, but was not the author of a sworn affection; Heribert, the chief of the magnates, was unwilling to take part.

While the kings were speaking more privately, Duke Hermann of the Saxons began to address Duke William in the Danish language. Then William, duke of the Northmen, said to Hermann, duke of the Saxons:

“Who taught you the Danish language, which is unfamiliar to the Saxons?”

He replied:

“The warlike and outstanding people of your weapon-bearing lineage taught me the Danish language against my will.”

William asked, “How against your will?”

Hermann answered:

“Because, invading many camps of my dukedom again and again, he waged innumerable battles against me, captured me in battle, and dragged me away with him; therefore I learned it unwillingly.”

Meanwhile Duke Cono said to the Saxons mockingly:

“What do you think of William, duke of the Northmen and Bretons? Is he not a duke of remarkable power, resources, and an immeasurable multitude? Except for our king, who is more powerful, richer, or better than he?”

The Saxons replied:

“We did not know his abundance of resources, and therefore earlier we unjustly disparaged him with words based on a false opinion.”

As Duke Cono recounted William’s remarkable deeds and abundant resources, the Saxons and the other bystanders began together to magnify him in their words with eternal praise.

Having thus rationally defined and completed these matters, as King Louis was returning to Laon with Duke William and the other princes, an embassy bearing worthy rejoicing met him and announced that a son had been born to him by his beloved wife, named Gerberga. On hearing this, he became more cheerful and said to Duke William, in the presence of the aforementioned princes:

“Until now, you have generously assisted me, though I was wickedly beset by many insults and grievously burdened by many difficulties; you have appropriately come to my aid. Indeed, by nourishing me with the richest fare from your resources and protecting me from the gathering of the malicious, you have cherished me. Therefore I beg you to receive my son, born yesterday, from the sacred baptismal font as one regenerated, giving him and publicly confirming the name Lothair, so that, bound together by a stronger bond of affection and by broader ties of love, we may enjoy what is mine as yours and what is yours as mine, according to our mutual needs, as one in mind.”

Duke William, favorably disposed toward the king’s fitting request, is said to have replied:

“Now, and for as long as I remain alive, I shall carefully fulfill whatever you command. You shall rule the kingdom of France and the other kingdoms over which your father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and even your great-great-grandfather held dominion, with me as your leader, me as your supporter, and me preceding you in all things. We shall subject to you the necks of the arrogant rebels and disarm those who refuse to serve you, while I stand beside you. Those whom you prefer to raise up, I shall exalt; those whom you wish to cast down, I shall trample to the ground. Indeed, whatever you wish, know that it shall be done by me.”

When both had thus concluded their speeches, the princes, moved by anger in their hearts though not in their faces, were astonished at this concerning the Frankish people. From then on, with deceitful hearts, fraudulent intentions, and sophistical speech, they began to treat William, a poisonous omen, wickedly.

William, leaving the king and his army in the district of Laon, hastened to Laon the Fortified, also called Bibrax, preceded by a choir of bishops of the Frankish people. The entire clergy of the see of Laon and the whole population, together with an imposing monastic display and the most powerful bishops, received him reverently. They brought forth from the font the child who had been given the name Lothair, renewed and purified with holy water, oil, and chrism. Then, after enriching him with exceedingly great gifts and outstanding presents, William left him at Laon with his mother Gerberga.

He himself quickly returned to the king with his companions and reported to him everything honorable that had taken place. The king wished fittingly to honor William for all his benefactions, but William accepted none of these things; rather, with thanksgiving, he returned everything to the king.

## APOSTROPHA

Duke, noble and excellent standard of your people,  
Bound to kings by a pleasing covenant and a firm bond,  
Having sown peaceful peace along the paths of the world,  
And having received an adoptive child from the nurturing one,  
Exalting him through the wave of saving baptism,

Turn your steps, hasten, and spur your horses,  
Return swiftly to the borders of your native soil,  
Where the people under your sacred rule  
Continually behold the consolations of worthy protection.  
For without you, every affair might well totter.

When these matters had thus been duly arranged, with the king [lacuna], and with them kissing and embracing one another amid excessive rejoicing, the king set out for Laon and William began to proceed more swiftly toward the region under his rule.

## APOSTROPHA

O Rouen, behold, your renowned duke has come to you,  
And governs the kingdoms of the Gauls with just reins.  
He will abundantly scatter the seeds of justice among the Northmen  
And walk the path of judgment with vigorous merits,  
Until, crowned with the reward of worthy martyrdom,  
He ascends to the Elysian field, endowed with a crown,  
And merits the enjoyment of divinity in the highest good.

Now he protects you everywhere by the power of arms;  
Then he will protect you by worthy prayers and gracious merits.

When swift rumor suddenly struck the minds of the inhabitants of the Northman territories concerning the desired return of Duke William and announced beforehand that their duke, so magnificent, was present, the whole city of Rouen, stirred by immense joy, suddenly rushed forth to meet him. It searched out various side-roads so that it might see him. Women stood upon the walls and fortifications; the common people of old age stood at the crossroads; and the populace of young and middle age ran out to meet him. The clergy, awaiting him at the city gate, joyfully received him with the reverence proper to monastic discipline.

At once he began to enforce the laws and judgments, as well as the paternal decrees that had been neglected in his absence. Defining and settling disputes and complaints by law, he reconciled everyone either through legal judgment or concord.

Then he built at Jumièges—a marvelous thing to say—a temple of monastic religion, of remarkable design, abundantly supported by clergy. There was a certain most holy abbot, Martin, who governed the monks of that monastery under the discipline of a strict rule of contemplative practice.

One day, having gone to Jumièges for the sake of prayer, William pondered in his mind what he had conceived in the first flowering of his heart and spoke to the most holy abbot Martin:

“Why does the Christian religion attend the church in a threefold order? Will those who differ in the duties of Christian religion have one reward and one prize?”

The abbot replied:

“Each person will receive his own reward according to his labor. But to you, who are wavering about such matters, I shall disclose them more clearly. The whole of Christian religion consists in a threefold order: it is carried out through the generous labor of laymen, canons, and monks, and through the articles of faith it expresses the Trinity in persons and the one God in substance. Their service, when happily perfected, advances toward heaven with equal steps.

“And although there are three orders, the way toward exalting the worship of the true faith is a twofold path along a road with two directions, in the sure hope of true belief. One of these, called *praktikē* [πρακτική], travels more broadly and has deserved to be called canonical; under its authority the lay order remains and lives. The other, called *theōrētikē* [θεωρητική], brought within limits compressed on either side, does not travel across level ground but, fixed in seclusion and rejoicing in perpetual secrecy, always strives toward the heights. This has been called apostolic; we sinners endeavor to carry it out and struggle with it through the continual efforts of inward devotion.”

Hearing this, William replied to the abbot:

“In the flower of my early age I wished to pursue the freer and broader way; but I desired above all to imitate the way confined and narrowed by boundaries. Yet my father and his princes appointed me, against my will, as their duke. But since I am now my own master and possess authority over myself, I wish to attain the gymnasium of the contemplative life, more narrowly bounded on either side, by leaving the world and changing my habit.”

When the most excellent abbot Martin heard the purpose of this astonishing intention, he suddenly sighed and, drawing the words from the depths of his breast, said:

“Defender of this homeland, why have you examined such a course and resolved to undertake it? Who will care for the clergy and the people? Who will withstand the army of the pagans advancing against us? Who will vigorously govern the people by the paternal laws? To whom will you entrust and commend the flock? To whom will you grant the command of Britain and the Northman region? The providence of divine will will not agree with your plan, nor will you complete what you are preparing to do; nor, with my support, will it in any way be undertaken.

“But if you prefer, by the force of your authority, to become a professor of this monastery and of the path of theoretical (*theōrētikēs*, θεωρητικῆς) discipline, abandoning the world and applying yourself to it, then, if you seek me, you will nowhere be able to find me in my own territory.”

Against these efforts of excuse and contradiction, Duke William is said to have replied:

“My beloved son Richard, still enveloped in the ignorance of childhood, will be duke in my place, most powerful in this region, with my princes willingly supporting him; and what I have vowed to God will be fulfilled as soon as I can.”

As William was leaving the temple entrance with Abbot Martin, the small phalanx of monks fell at his feet, begging him to accept, in the charity of God, daily provisions—namely, food for the body. Moved in spirit by the abbot’s objections, he refused their petitions and would not accept their charity for food in any way; instead, he sought the city of Rouen more swiftly.

## APOSTROPHA

God alone foreknows and predestines every good;  
God foreknows every evil but does not predestine it.  
He foreknows your happy will and predestines it, but does not—  
He who remains the highest Trinity, one power—

He foreknows your happy will through his anticipatory knowledge;  
As your merit increases, you will receive the palm of martyrdom.

That same night, when the red bile was seething together with the other humors, he began to be tormented by exceedingly severe pains. He considered that this evil had befallen him because he had neglected the charity of food and drink which he had refused when the monks begged him to accept it.

Therefore, after summoning the princes of the Northmen and Britons and bringing with them a boy named Richard, of exceptionally elegant appearance, he disclosed to them in secret the remarkable secret of his mind, which he had earlier related to Abbot Martin.

When the most noble princes of the Breton and Northman regions learned of Duke William’s unprecedented and almost monstrous plan, they were overcome with astonishment and ecstasy and said to him, lamenting greatly:

“Why, after examining such matters in the mind of your heart, have you resolved upon them? And if, by thinking, you have decided upon something that will never happen, why did you tell us? Who will defend us from the attack of the destructive savagery of the approaching pagans, and who will protect us from the plots of the Frankish people? Let what will never be fulfilled be considered no further.”

Then William, moved by their obstacle of resistance and dissuasion, is said to have replied:

“It will be considered, and with God’s favor it will be fulfilled. But since you must not resist the will of almighty God or reject my plan, I beg you to support my counsels. Whatever may befall human affairs, choose my son Richard as your duke while I am alive, and, with the intention of preserving loyalty and military service, place your hands in his hands.”

Immediately the Northmen and Britons replied to William:

“We agree to this counsel, and we shall faithfully do what you ask.”

Accordingly, the Northmen and Britons at once commended themselves unanimously to Richard, binding themselves to him by an oath of true faith.

William, however, when his humors had been calmed and his strength had been restored from weakness, began to recover and daily to carry out whatever good he could with diligent care.

The princes of France bore the weight of envy and hatred against William, but they did not dare to reveal the malevolent purpose of their thoughts. Nevertheless, the instigator and inciter of crimes poured the poison of his cunning through the hearts of evil men, rejoicing that the human race was sinking ever further into evil and could not return to the garden of delights.

For this reason he aroused hatreds, stirring up the fires of quarrels, and disturbed the covenants of the Church’s peace, its foundation shaken whenever fear was impressed upon it. In the madness of greed he inflamed the hearts of many, so that they would neither remember the judgments of God nor perceive them in their minds.

When this poison had thus been heavily disseminated through the members of the devil, while hostile rage advanced ever more cruelly and the wickedness of evil men prevailed more disastrously, the justice of the entire kingdom was profaned. Many were expelled from the rank of due honor and deprived of their possessions.

Therefore a certain prince named Arnulf, the most famous margrave of the region of Flanders, infected to an extraordinary degree by the filth of this poison, took from Count Herluin the castle called Montreuil. Deprived of the castle and of so great an honor, Herluin sought the aid of Hugh, Duke of the Franks, with the utmost haste, so that he might come to his assistance, since he was Hugh’s count and a soldier ready for every service.

Duke Hugh did not receive him reverently, as he was accustomed to do, but negligently kept him on an equal footing with his own recruits. Herluin, filled with the need of great necessity, pursued Hugh, Duke of the Franks, every day, begging him repeatedly to come to his aid.

But, despairing of that assistance and seeing himself abandoned to the protection of his aid, he approached William, Duke of the Northmen and Britons, on account of the affair described above, and fell at his feet so that William might help him.

William ordered him to be lodged with honorable ceremony and to be supplied with whatever was necessary, with great refinement. On the following day Herluin came before Duke William and humbly sought his aid in many petitions.

Duke William comforted him and is said to have replied:

“Why does Hugh, your senior, the Duke of the Franks, not console you as he should? And why does he not provide what is necessary for your disastrous ruin? Return to him quickly, and if he is ever willing to help you, test him with many entreaties; and if anyone comes to your aid, let him bear it with displeasure.”

Herluin immediately returned to Duke Hugh and humbly asked, through many appeals, whether he would help him. To his urgent request Duke Hugh replied:

“I and Arnulf, bound by the entangling bond of a sworn friendship, do not wish, on your account, to break the ties of concord, affection, and our mutual agreement.”

Changed in spirit by this hopeless reply, Herluin said to Duke Hugh:

“Since you are in no way eager to come to my aid in my necessity, as would have been proper, it is fitting that, if anyone helps me, you should not take it badly.”

Then Duke Hugh, supposing that Herluin had been deprived of every protection and consolation, said:

“Whoever provides you assistance will not wrong me.”

After this statement of desolation had been completed, Herluin returned to Duke William. Falling at his feet, he carefully reported to William everything he had heard.
