Immediately William summoned the entire army of Britain and Normandy and, on account of the wrong done by Arnulf, Duke of Flanders, hastened to assist Herluin.

When he was near the castle of Montreuil and had seen it from above, he summoned the men of Coutances and said to them:

“If you wish to enjoy, by my favor, the first reward of military service, a greater honor, and preeminence in my household, do not delay bringing me the stakes from the enclosure of the castle of Montreuil, and bring me captured those who oppose us and hold the castle.”

At once, at these words of encouragement, the men of Coutances attacked the castle unanimously like wolves attacking lambs. They plundered and destroyed the castle, carrying the stakes of the wall before William and bringing the captives with them.

After the castle of Montreuil had been captured and the murmur of the destructive rebellion quieted, William ordered a meal to be prepared for himself within the castle and to be served honorably to Herluin, who was supplying the royal treasures.

While Duke William was dining in the castle, he said to Count Herluin, who was serving the meal:

“Behold, I return to you the castle which the Duke of Flanders unjustly took from you.”

Herluin replied:

“My lord, I shall not accept this castle, because I cannot guard it or defend it against Duke Arnulf.”

Then, moved by compassion, Duke William said to Herluin:

“By assisting you I shall protect you; by helping and guarding you I shall defend you. I shall restore and rebuild this castle for you. I shall fortify it with an impregnable defense of towers and fill it with such strength of ditch and rampart that it cannot be captured or destroyed. I shall fill it abundantly with grain and wine and completely fortify it for you by rebuilding it.

“Whichever of my princes you choose shall remain with you, surrounded by a multitude of his faithful men. If war should break out against you from Arnulf, I shall quickly come to your aid with a multitude of my armies. But if he seeks a truce of peace, we shall grant it to him on the counsel of our faithful men. If, meanwhile, he wishes to come against us to a formal judgment, making use of judgment, justice, and law, we shall come against him on your behalf to judge him according to the decision of our counselors.

“If, with stubborn heart, he devastates the estates of your inheritance, we shall burn all his territory with the assembled army of his dominion. I shall be your willing and benevolent helper, your defender against your adversaries, an attentive hearer of your complaints, a watchful consoler in your misfortune, and indeed a true giver of the goods appropriate to you.”

On hearing this, Herluin immediately fell with his faithful men at William’s feet.

After the castle had been firmly refortified, more abundantly filled with grain, wine, and an ample supply of hides, and sufficiently honored with a very large number of soldiers, William returned with his men by swift cavalry to the walls of the city of Rouen.

That duke was truthful in speech, prompt and just in judgment, most gentle in conversation, and most humble in conduct. Moreover, he shone with the titles of every virtue and vigorously adorned the property of the churches.

When he flourished through increased devotion to every goodness and the widely proclaimed fame of so great a man spread throughout France and the other kingdoms, while he diligently exercised the laws and decrees of orthodox authorities and of his father, the aforementioned Arnulf, Duke of the Flemings, wickedly filled with the poison of viperous cunning and fatally enticed by the heat of diabolical fraud, cruelly urged on by the deceitful counsel and malice of certain princes of the Frankish people, began to devise and plan the sorrowful death of William.

Inflamed by the envy of this poisonous evil, he sent messengers on the most fraudulent of missions to Duke William, who were to say, under the guise of the most wicked deceit, whether he would accept the hands of faithful service and friendship.

When they arrived before William, they began to address him humbly with downcast faces and subdued voices, speaking peaceful words:

“Our lord Arnulf sends you faithful service in Christ. Not wishing to begin a quarrel against you, he asks with the utmost humility for a period of truce. Meanwhile, he asks you to come against him to the appointed judgment and, for love of you, wishes to abandon to Herluin whatever has offended him, and, if it pleases you, to bind himself to you by an indissoluble bond of friendship.

“Afflicted by gout and other illnesses, he no longer seeks to quarrel with anyone. He wishes his people to be restrained by law or concord, and he hastens to maintain peace, as long as he lives, between the dominion of your authority and his own. Since they are joined by a continuous and neighboring boundary, it is fitting that peace and concord exist between us and your people, so that your inhabitants may rejoice in such princes, and so that none of your people may wrong any of ours, nor any of ours inflict harm on any of yours by force and power.

“Let those who are neighbors in the kinship of the land be harmonious and united under the law. A duke of such goodness and gentleness ought not to reject a necessary and timely request; rather, he should favor it with all his strength, lest the commonwealth, weakened by such plundering and burnings, should sink disastrously into worse ruin.

“While a sufficiently evil dispute presses upon us, many other evils have now accumulated and, compelled by wickedness, will prevail for the worse. Judge what is better: to investigate and accomplish what is good, or shamefully to cling to and complete that which is not a created thing but the absence of goodness, in the most heinous deed.”

Deceived by the detestable fraud of these messengers, the powerful Duke William said secretly to Count Herluin:

“What do you think of the meaning of this proposal and embassy?”

Herluin replied:

“My spirit fears that we may be deceived and that we may be ensnared by the most humble petitions of these men, by whose treachery we have been deceived so many times.”

William summoned the other princes and said:

“Since you know that, as the course of my active life declines, I wish to be confined within the cloister of the contemplative life, construct peace with me throughout the earth as quickly as you can, because no holocaust or sacrifice is so acceptable to God as the increase of peace.”

To Herluin he said:

“Do not fear or be troubled, for you will never be deprived of the protection of my consolation or that of my people.”

Accordingly, after consulting his faithful men, Duke William granted Count Arnulf a truce of three months and ordered him to come to the appointed judgment.

When the time of the impending judgment had been fixed, William, the most powerful of all dukes, summoned the army of the Northmen and Britons and set out as far as the district of Amiens.

## APOSTROPHA

Duke, sprung from a name poured forth by Christ,  
Guardian and author, aided by no one unworthy, except by Christ,  
Most worthy of the reward of heavenly gifts,

You will leave behind the mournful death toward which you hasten,  
Finding a life worthy of everlasting peace,  
While the palm of martyrdom bears the crown of triumph.

Arnulf, infected by the envy of wicked deceit, came with all his men to the stream of Corbie. He sent a messenger to Duke William, asking him to come against him as far as Pinchinac, so that the waters of the Somme might serve as a barrier between the two armies, lest, if he carried out the treachery that the unhappy man was planning, he should be prevented by the arrival of the Northman army.

Duke William, however, believed the embassy of perverse deceit and, favoring its fraudulent entreaties, compelled the army of his legions to go there.

Arnulf, delighted and cheerful at the report he had received, settled with his men on the bank of the river Somme, on this side, where William was to be martyred; the deceitful and treacherous man settled on the farther side. There is an island there, surrounded on both sides by the seething whirlpool of the Somme. Arnulf approached it by boat with four treacherous men, pretending that he wished to be reconciled with the most holy Duke William.

He sent to Duke William, using deceitful and peaceful words, asking him to come there with twelve of his soldiers.

When William crossed over by boat with his twelve men, Arnulf came to meet him limping and supported by two of his men. He began to speak to him, pretending and deceiving him with the most humble proposals:

“I come to you as a suppliant, so that you may reconcile my people and yours and thus be my helper against my faithless men, since, overcome by humility, I am unable to rule and oppress the rebels of this land.

“For by a salutary counsel you rule the monarchy of all Gaul. Therefore I desire that you be regarded as duke and margrave over me and mine. Be my defender and advocate against King Louis, Prince Heribert, and the most powerful Duke Hugh.

“As long as I live, I shall be your tributary, and my people shall serve you as a servant serves his lord. After my death, you shall possess the kingdom of my dominion. I shall willingly abandon to your Count Herluin whatever has offended me, and I shall remain peaceful and well disposed toward him at all times.”

Duke William, thinking that Arnulf was speaking with a benevolent and sincere heart and with complete faith rather than treachery, reconciled Herluin with the treacherous Arnulf and all his men.

Almost the whole day was spent in tedious circumlocutions. After peace had been agreed between the two princes—William in good faith, Arnulf and the other princes with treacherous hearts—William returned with his twelve men. After giving Arnulf a kiss, he entered the ship alone with the rower, while the twelve companions went ahead in another boat.

Then the treacherous Eiricus, Balzo, Robert, and Ridulf began to address Duke William in deceitful and alternating voices:

“My lord, my lord, forgetting better counsel, please turn the boat back for a moment, because we wish to speak with you privately. Our lord can no longer attack you, for you know that he is being held by the illness of gout; but he sends you a remarkable message, which he has forgotten.”

Then William, wholly steadfast in faith, repeatedly urged on by the entreaties of the treacherous men, quickly turned the boat and came to the riverbank, secure from weapons and without his men, in order to speak with them.

But those four men, already concealed beneath coverings, swiftly drew their swords. In the mad fury of their monstrous wickedness, they were quickly carried across in their boat, joined their army, and gained possession of their escape by swift cavalry.

The Northmen and Britons, however, deeply mourning the death of their lord William and eager to avenge it, found no ford anywhere, though they ran swiftly here and there.

Thus the precious Margrave William, most glorious witness of Christ, was consecrated by a blessed martyrdom. In this way he attained the kingdom of heaven, which he had long desired, and was happily crowned while living in Christ.

The blessed man’s body lay lifeless, drenched in the dew of his own blood. But his soul, led into heaven by angels, was placed immeasurably among the choirs of angels.

Immediately a certain phalanx of the deceived and martyred William’s men ran to him and carried him by boat across the river Somme with great lamentation. Searching with immense sighs of the heart and abundant tears of the eyes for his bruises, and turning over his bloodstained garments while weeping, they found a very small silver key hanging from the band around his waist.

When they asked many of his household servants why that key had been hung from his belt, a certain chamberlain, who knew his secrets, replied:

“Our lord William vowed to leave this fleeting world and, after this sorrowful judgment, to become a monk at Jumièges. This key guards a certain chest and locks up the monastic habit, namely the hood and the woolen undergarment.”

The sacred body was immediately placed in a bier and carried swiftly, amid great lamentation, to the city of Rouen, where they honorably buried it in the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God.

Almost the entire province also assembled, mourning with ineffable sorrow and sending deep sighs up to heaven, bringing with it his son Richard in grief.

Before the body was placed in the tomb, Berengar and Alan, the other Britons, and the princes of the Northmen saw Richard and said, lamenting greatly:

“Alas, we have lost our lord; let us unanimously make this one our lord.”

Immediately they enthroned the boy Richard, of holy memory, and, willingly becoming his faithful men, unanimously made him their duke.

Thus the most sacred Duke William, the most glorious martyr of Christ, completed the course of his struggle in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 943, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], while King Louis held the kingdom of France and the living and true God reigned in the fullness of the Trinity and the majesty of unity.

## APOSTROPHA

Released from the swelling heat of the sea,  
From harmful sandbanks and from Charybdis, which swallowed all alike,  
From the mass of a manyfold and spreading whirlwind,  
And from winds mingled together with rolling sand,

I, a fragile potter’s vessel bearing matter—alas!—  
Have been carried to a harbor deprived by the storm.  
What path, what life, what salvation, what summit of merit, what hope of faith,  
And what crown grants the honorable reward of labor,  
By which those worthy are enriched with heavenly gifts,  
And the births of the eighth order are renewed?

But because these are worthless, muddy vessels of clay,  
I think I shall be unable to give them to anyone or put them up for sale.  
Rather, crushed upon the shores of the sea, they will lie.

There is, however, another harbor, filled with diverse merchandise,  
Where the worthy purchase their expenses with varied profit.  
There the reward of the contest is granted;  
There lifeless limbs are given life in Christ.  
To this harbor I shall proceed with a ship full of varied merchandise.

Let what has long been accidental now be arranged; they will be received,  
Lest I, the potter, suffer ridicule so ridiculous [reading uncertain],  
And the loss of the work and of our labor.

## EXHORTATION TO THE MUSES, THAT THEY SING OF RICHARD

Flowering Muses, accustomed to clear-sounding songs,  
To play the many-stringed lyre with measured ringing:  
Clio, Melpomene, Polyhymnia, Erato, Thalia,  
Terpsichore, Euterpe, Calliope, Urania [reading uncertain],

Offer the distinguished gift of the lyre, resounding with blessedness,  
Sweet-sounding songs and a high-flying voice,  
For the renowned patrician, and the revered count and duke,  
Who strove duly to please God supreme.

I ask each of you to sing your sweet song individually,  
In alternating meter with a varied train.

## CLIO I

If our foolish thoughts had not brought forth  
Sluggish silence and dumb muteness,  
And if an interpreter of sacred history  
Had not arranged its mysteries in plain order,

It would have been my pleasure to sing what  
Richard, the vigorous count and margrave,  
The worthy duke and honored patrician,  
Desires to have sung.

Because, in the credible order belonging to me,  
I must render histories of events to posterity,  
I shall now give this typological deed  
In dissonant verse to the learned sisters.

## II

I delight to resound in lyric meter,  
What kind of man the revered count was  
And with how great blessedness he flourished.

Let the renowned phalanx of sisters be present  
And recount his merit with me.  
I shall confess that, for his merits of blessedness,  
This good and kindly servant of Christ  
Is joined to the angelic ranks,

When the Judge rewards his servants,  
Destroying the guilty in evil punishments.

## III

Let us now reconcile this man, already placed among the ranks  
Of the chief fathers, on account of his merits,  
His wonders, his flourishing deeds,  
His marvelous works, and his monastic practices,  
Which shine worthily and still endure,

With the honey-tongued leaders, while he remains bodily whole.  
For while he flourished in the world,  
He performed everything contained in the sacred decrees of the fathers.  
With a pious heart he loved the Lord God,  
And worthily joined himself to him in a near covenant.

## IV

If our will were effective and capable  
Of writing how he lived, flourished, and acted,  
Although my understanding is unskilled,  
As is fitting for poets to record him,  
I would write of the just margrave and patrician,  
The holy duke and revered count.

For what the prophets related in mystical words  
With prophetic and typological hearts,  
He diligently believed, recited,  
And heard and remembered in his mind as sacred.

## V

Although I am pleased to recall and speak of what is fitting,  
I shall speak to the sisters, though I may now be more foolish,  
Of the perennial fruits of our salvation,  
By which faith, hope, and glory grew in this world,  
Shining among the assemblies of the apostles.

I would dare to join Richard,  
The great, holy, pious, just, and upright duke,  
To their number—not, indeed, in rank  
Or according to any reckoning,  
But in wondrous merit; for holy Peter  
Does not begrudge merits equally pious.

## VI

If you find someone like the count,  
Friendly reader, reveal him to me.  
Who is there now, born of earth,  
Who has brought good to the people  
And endured as many crosses, insults, and torments  
As he did, through the divine power of faith?

He rightly restrained the untamed,  
And fiercely resisted the Danes.  
As a companion of the martyrs in merit,  
He enjoys perpetual rest.

## VII

Instructed by wisdom,  
And delighting in religion,  
Behold how greatly he adorned  
The sacred chairs of bishops—  
This duke, patrician, and count.

For how many such men do you still see?  
It is not permitted to say many,  
For he was inferior to no one  
But proved superior.

Added to the confessors,  
A holy duke and margrave.

Although he had already entered  
Into the covenant of a chaste bed,  
Sincere and lawful,  
For the sake of posterity,  
Who now would attempt to deprive him  
Of a virginal crown?

His conscience, aware of righteousness,  
Did not suffer a stain of shame;  
Rather, he remained chaste.

## VIII

Now, reader, having been led by reason,  
Extend your attentive mind in due order  
Through all the saints with an inclined spirit.

If anywhere you find one corresponding to our father  
In deeds, merits, and service  
To the divine worship of the passing world,  
With fitting devotion,  
Behold any patrician you may find.

For all these qualities appropriate to our father  
Remain constant in all his actions.

And when the world is summoned in a great host  
Before the face of the radiant Judge,  
And when that apostolic senate  
Has sat upon the judgment seat,

Richard himself, supported by merits and conduct  
Upon a radiant throne,  
Will bring forth judgments and laws  
For the great world.

And when Christ, judging wisely, assigns  
The strong rewards to the holy martyrs,  
He will bear a rose-colored crown,  
For which he endured along the proper path.

And when the priests, receiving a glowing reward  
For the subjugation of the flesh and the profit of their gain,  
Enter in due order, according to their merit,  
The innermost chamber of the heavenly kingdom,

Behold, with victorious palm—[lacuna]

“Well done,” it will be said, “receive it, servant;  
For great things in place of small things—well done, faithful one.”

## IX

The threefold fruitful earth blesses  
The nurturing cultivator with abundant fertility.  
Thus the true sower taught,  
Sending the seeds of the nurturing Word into the world.

When others bring forth, shining,  
Their polished sheaves above the stars,  
Each reclaiming the rewards of his labor  
And contending for his own portion,

You will see Richard radiating  
With three crowns on high.

He advanced to the sixtieth,  
From thirty by divine power;  
From the left he led his footsteps  
To the right, always resplendent,

Happy beneath a virginal diadem.  
He will be given as a companion to virgins;  
He will follow the most beautiful Lamb  
And proceed wherever he has gone.

He will sing what is fitting for the pure,  
A song of birth with heavenly sweetness,  
Resounding in five tetrachords:

“So great are the gifts that exist for you, Christ,  
You who surpass all that is above,  
And for whom nothing upright is established at its limit,  
And with whom all things are upright.”

## PREFACE TO BISHOP ROBERT

Although you are considered inexperienced in speech  
And deprived of eloquence,  
Remaining without knowledge, dying, and existing  
Without rhetorical flavor,  
And dull, thoughtless, and inactive,

Prepare, O Muse, ornaments for our little book,  
Though small.

Tongueless and foolish  
In all reasoning,

Reveal in writing  
The splendid deeds  
Of the sacred duke,  
The just patrician,  
And the gracious margrave.

Since you are powerful in knowledge,  
Recall with warm truth  
The good things he himself accomplished  
And performed while he lived.

For it is fitting throughout  
To offer the sacred count Richard,  
The just, pious, and modest,  
The highest songs of praise.

Let us all pray that there may be for him  
Throughout every age  
Rest, salvation, honor,  
And increase of glory,

By the divinity of the Trinity  
That governs everything  
Which exists, is powerful,  
And flourishes.

## ANOTHER PREFACE

No Muse sings at all  
For one whose power of speech  
Is either babbling and shrill  
Or absent, as is usual in a little boy.

Ignorant, thoughtless, dull,  
And more foolish than everyone,  
Although I am frivolous  
And chatter clumsily,

You see how I have arranged the deeds  
Of the renowned, good, and just man  
In an unpolished utterance.

Of the valiant marquis,

A little poet among speakers.

Now I am driven onward, and what must be said—

These things move the untutored poet;

Those compel me to write.

Yet stay here with me,

Wherever I may have gone.

Though you are unpolished,

Go, I pray, healthfully.

Astonishment strikes me, behold,

And many things terrify me;

New figures arise

[Col. 0685D] Which it is not lawful to keep silent.

My mind flees, greatly amazed;

My breast is constrained by the burden.

Traversing the Christian armies,

I went around them,

And found no one such,

Though all were previously known,

As Richard the marquis,

To whom so many qualities converge.

We shall call him thrice blessed,

And four times ten thousand times;

Him benign, him modest.

The page shall resound.

Him pious, just, and holy,

Approved and supreme.

[Col. 0686A] Normandy is witness

To this his beneficence,

And France also is witness

To this his generosity;

Burgundy confirms

His courage.

Kingdoms, deeds, holy words—

Indeed, they and all else marvel:

In thought, deed, and speech

No one has shone greater.

In the highest goodness may rest be granted him,

Everlasting glory.

## PRAYER

The lofty deeds of the Danes, once a lowly theme,

Now rise before me as I run,

A grim mass.

For by their own weight, since in our ancient age

Such things were neither heard

Nor seen as worthy of praise,

They are therefore known to none,

Nor believed, and attempted by few.

Holy Spirit, come, I beg you suppliantly,

Radiating nectar through your sevenfold streams.

But whatever power you have granted this

To be accomplished,

Grant me also the ability to speak of it.

## PREFACE TO BISHOP ROBERT

Ruler of the heavenly element, governor of earthly hell,

Mind [ΝΟΥΣ] of the whole world, its glory and dominion.

Sidereal pillar, exemplar, strength, and heavenly power,

Uranian divinity, eternally holding all things.

Sequence of causes, movements through created things,

Compactor of human beings, glory of the divine ones.

Although all things offer you every duty of praise

With varied song and differing procession,

In this ode we have sung you as king of all,

With unceasing vows and suppliant prayers.

You are called the fruitful Trinity and the simple Monad;

Whether, as the Greeks [ΕΛΛΗΝΑΣ] divide you,

They distribute you into hypostases [ΥΠΟΣΤΑΣΕΙΣ],

Yet one single essence [ΟΥΣΙΑΝ ΜΙΑΝ] into three,

Or as the wider world proclaims:

One true hypostasis [ΥΠΟΣΤΑΣΙΝ ΜΙΑΝ], namely three persons [ΤΡΙΑ ΠΡΟΣΩΠΑ];

You are always present, always the same, and remain yourself.

You are the unbegotten Father, believed to be the one who begets;

Thus Wisdom, rejoicing, applauds the begotten Son.

The Spirit, truly living, flowing from both as Paraclete.

In these three we worship one Godhead [ΘΕΟΤΗΝ] (thus written).

It is pleasing that this is so called because, seeing, it runs into everything,

And nowhere can anything be present outside itself.

When stable movement and movable stability exist,

The truthful Catholic faith proclaims this.

The substantial Being [ΟΝ], the pattern [ΤΥΠΟΣ] of things, the idea of the world,

By itself remains and flourishes as goodness.

This is not, nor is that: all that exists is the true God [ΘΕΟΣ];

Not here, not there, but wholly powerful for everything.

The Unoriginate [ΑΝΑΡΧΟΣ] testifies that it is Length and Greatness and Smallness [ΜΗΚΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΓΑΛΟΣ ΜΙΚΡΟΣ]:

Length [ΜΗΚΟΣ], while it continually governs every inward thing;

Smallness [ΜΙΚΡΟΣ], while it grants help and salvation to the smallest things;

Greatness [ΜΕΓΑΛΟΣ], while in great things it gives life to the greatest.

Thus it always presides over great, middle-sized, and small things,

Itself indivisible, remaining wholly everywhere.

Being [ΩΝ], beginning [ΑΡΧΗ], middle [ΜΕΣΟΝ], end [ΤΕΛΟΣ], … and of all things [ΠΑΝΤΩΝ],

Since from him all things whatsoever flourish.

Let the very Archetype [ΠΡΩΤΟΤΥΠΟΝ]—the nothing [nihilum; the printed text is uncertain]—protect him,

So that you may marvel, reader, remembering this Catholic doctrine.

The incomprehensible nature, which flourishes in everything,

Clearly surpasses both the intellect [ΝΟΕΡΟΣ] and the Word [ΛΟΓΟΣ].

While it is grasped by no one, it is itself called nothing.

But whenever it appears, behold … the God-manifest [ΘΕΟΦΑΝΗΣ].

It is said always to grow from nothing into something;

They write that all created things together arose from this nothing.

Hence he is called and spoken of as darkness:

For thus the holy Psalmist [ΨΑΛΜΙΣΤΗΣ] resounded.

[Col. 0687B] As are his darknesses, so also is his light;

To the reprobate he is darkness, and to the upright he is light.

When the ordered streams of truth are thus arranged,

You must of your own accord conceive what follows.

Let us not, proud through any [thoughts?; the reading aminis is uncertain] or any elegance,

Presume to define before God the Judge what is proper,

Nor is it ready, fitting, or lawful for anyone to reveal

Who, what kind, and how great the Lord [ΚΥΡΙΟΣ] remains.

It is more worthy of prayer, better and nearer,

To bind him to the mind while remaining pure oneself.

He wishes to be prayed to with devoted and peaceful words;

He is present, ready to grant generously and to yield readily.

With these measures, trustworthy and worthy of belief,

I embrace him with vows and unceasing prayers.

I make known the truly unbegotten Father,

The begotten Offspring,

And the Spirit flowing from both as from a source.

To whom all things that exist rightly confess with joy,

And who rules by his own authority everything that is.

Whom thrice three companies in heaven always praise together,

Whom they sing in remembrance and worship in reverence;

Whom the assembly of the patriarchs, sounding together,

Sings joyful songs without stint;

To whom truthful prophets bring forth praises in procession,

Sacred utterances that they sang and that remain powerful;

Whom the twelvefold phalanx, remembering …, venerates,

Despising all things and worshiping him by following;

Whom the innumerable host of witnesses eternally sings in hymns,

And rejoices in thanksgiving, disregarding blows;

The summit of virginity, from whom, taking beauty,

It modulates conspicuously and echoes wondrously;

Whom heaven praises above and earth below,

And whom all the elements serve and worship in reverence.

Whatever remains, and whatever approaches, O gracious Creator,

Look upon with favor, I beg, kindly hearing prayers.

Taking pity on our present works, set them in order, we pray,

And fill our senses and make our mouths fruitful.

The material urges and love constrains me

To compose for Richard a title of lofty praise,

He who flourished for you through the ages as a wondrous servant,

Trampling every evil and lifting up every good.

For it is pointless to keep silent about the imitable struggle of outstanding leaders, long ago exercised through many deeds with the benevolent purpose of a most holy intention, and about their insignia and, especially, the works in every respect most worthy of those diligently devoted to good intentions, without setting them down and explaining them as far as possible: so that, clarified in written records for the memory of those who come after, they may shape and instruct their minds toward what is better by salutary fruit, and so that from the example of this contemplation they may happily acquire eternal blessedness. Therefore let us undertake the life of the most kindly leader Richard, although in a dull style; he flourished in the meadow of the holy Church through deeds of exceptional worth, shining like a star in the sky. May it also be granted to us, through his merits, reverently to make his life known—he who was the Church’s supreme reverence and supreme adornment. Thus, since on earth we healthfully enjoyed the protection of his guardianship and benefaction, may we through his prayers

[Col. 0688B] and merits be defensibly protected from every affliction.

Accordingly, the venerable duke Richard, a man of outstanding memory and supreme power, the most radiant patrician of holy remembrance, and the most famous marquis of memorable kindness, sprang from the most illustrious seed of a bright and noble lineage. His native origin blessed with the sacred beginning of his birth the Calcensis district, bordering the sea, the walls of the fortress of Fécamp, and the ancestral fields extending through the furthest reaches of Belgic France. His mother, whom his father, Duke William, most glorious martyr, had found pregnant with this happiest pledge and fruitful in the birth of an adopted and illustrious offspring, he had caused to be conveyed by splendid and fitting carriage to the court of the see of Fécamp, so that, if Riulfus, the most savage of all beasts,

[Col. 0688C] should claim the monarchy of Normandy with his accomplices, as was believed, she might cross more quickly to the English and he might not seize her.

On the day when, as has been related, battle took place between Duke William, already distinguished, and Riulfus, blasphemous and perjured in many ways, the venerable matron gave birth to a boy of blessed memory. She sent a certain young man named Fulcard to announce to Duke William the desired event of the birth.

William, who had gained victory over his enemies with three hundred men and was riding across the field of battle, stained with warm blood, observing thousands upon thousands of corpses lying dead, and gratefully offering supreme thanks to the King of kings, was met by a messenger announcing the joy of the newborn child.

## APOSTROPHE

O parents ever deserving of such offspring,

At whose birth many citizens, both heavenly beings

And earthborn people alike, breathed forth immense joys.

The heavenly order rejoices at such a future fellow citizen;

Humanity, approved by the holy Judge, gives thanks.

Under whose governance the world, ever joyful,

Will enjoy the most worthy gift of tranquil peace.

Then the most renowned duke, deservedly joyful and happy after accomplishing a marvelous triumph, and made still happier by the birth of an heir and successor, sent Henry, the highly revered bishop of Bayeux, and Bothon, greater and foremost in the military service of his household, so that they might receive the boy, renewed with the life-giving liquid of holy oil and chrism and washed in the typological bath and fountain of regeneration,

[Col. 0689A] calling him Richard.

They gladly undertook the commission of this expedition, and, approaching the walls of Fécamp at swift pace, were received by clergy and people, with the monastic arrangements reverently prepared.

On the following day, when the clergy of the entire province and people of both sexes came from every side to celebrate the baptism of the newborn child, the boy was regenerated by Henry, the most reverend bishop of Bayeux, together with the other bishops of that land, in the blessed fountain of mystical washing, by a saving threefold immersion. Marked with the nectar of sacred chrism and in the name of the divine Trinity, cleansed of the squalor of the old man, the aforesaid bishop, together with Count Bothon, received the boy Richard from the purification of the holy bath.

When these things had been performed with great reverence, and the clergy were praising God together over the birth of the duke’s son, the crowds of people returned, and the bishop with Bothon reported to Duke William what had been done concerning the boy.

## APOSTROPHE

Happy, O worthy destiny,

Of the celebrated sacred infant,

Born of a distinguished father and mother,

And also named Richard.

His purification,

And his renewal,

Were performed in the name

Of the Father, Lord, and God,

And of this Son of God,

And of the Holy Spirit and God—

Yet of one God,

In the everlasting name of the true one.

They were performed most fittingly

In your noble fortress, O Fécamp,

Which flourishes near the shores of the sea.

May it know—or, in the variant ciat or ciet, “may summon”—all clergy,

Common folk, and peoples from every side,

So that it may offer sacred jubilations

To the Father and to the Word-bearing God,

Born through virgin birth,

Together with the sacred Spirit …

After an interval of two hours, when the infant Richard had grown abundantly through wondrous increases, Duke William began to deliberate prudently about the welfare of the kingdom and, desiring to fulfill what he had turned over in his heart concerning the successor to his dukedom, began to consider where and by whom the child could be healthfully nourished and educated.

Long and intensely troubled by these reflections, and eagerly desiring to observe carefully what health and soundness the child possessed, and, as his age increased, what appearance and stature his desired son Richard would have, he sent household servants who knew his secret to carry the child secretly to the village called Chevillei.

When the infant had been brought to the place of the aforesaid village, and he had taken with him three trusted confidants, Bernard, Bothon, and Anslec, the duke went to him. After examining him closely, touching the structure of his limbs with his hands, recognizing that he was handsome for his age,

[Col. 0690A] and observing that he was surpassing the ordinary growth of infancy in a vigorous way, he embraced him affectionately and kissed him tenderly. Then he began to tell the three companions mentioned above what he had long examined in his heart:

“Until now I have ruled this kingdom vigorously by your counsel,” he said. “I have defeated in war the Britons who rebelled against me; I have rebuked the pagans who invaded our borders; I have boldly subdued the Flemings and the other peoples whom I considered to be within the sphere of our power. Indeed, if I have accomplished anything good, I performed it gently and mildly, compelled by your most benevolent exhortation.

“Now, concerning what I am planning to do, give me your assent. For every kingdom lacking an hereditary lord is desolated and divided, and very many seditions, quarrels, and unheard-of complaints are generated in manifold ways. Therefore, with your favor, let this little boy be established as my heir and successor in the governance of our duchy.

“I wish and earnestly entreat you that, having become faithful to him through the faith of our mutual trust, you make this kingdom secure for this infant, because we do not know what the future time of uncertainty may bring forth.”

Then they replied to the elder, who was speaking so graciously:

“We have obeyed your commands throughout the course of our lives, and as long as we survive, this boy will be our fitting companion and hereditary duke and patrician; we shall obey his command in all things. This counsel will please all who dwell under your protection.”

Then, fulfilling the orders of the most noble marquis, securing the kingdom for the most beautiful boy Richard, and voluntarily giving their hands in an oath of true faith over sacred relics,

[Col. 0690C] they commended themselves to him.

## APOSTROPHE

O powerful, upright, and pious Richard,

Future duke and martyr.

This vigorous boy, born of a sacred mother,

Will be heir of a just lineage;

He will not be unwelcome to God,

Nor to clergy or people.

Rather, he will be a fitting and suitable father,

Just and patrician.

A holy marquis, a steadfast and good count,

A duke of Christian worshipers.

Shining and sacred, he will propagate

True faith

And laws. As a pious ruler he will distribute

Just reins to the people.

And, as a father governing the common people,

He will justly pacify them.

To that boy be glory, peace, and honor,

And the grace of Jesus Christ.

When this business of the counsel had been completed—indeed, by the disposition of almighty God—his father began with sagacious mind to consider in what place and by what people the boy could be healthfully nourished and educated.

Engaged in these deliberations, he said to the three men previously named:

“Since the city of Rouen uses Roman eloquence rather than Dacian, while Bayeux more frequently enjoys the Dacian language than the Roman, I wish him to be nourished and educated under your

[Col. 0691A] care, with great diligence, becoming fervent in Dacian speech and learning it with such tenacious memory that one day he may speak abundantly against the Dacians.”

Then Bothon, consenting to the elder’s voluntary request and accepting the distinguished infant for the care of educating him, quickly brought him to the city of Bayeux and guarded him as the apple of his eye.

For love of his beloved son, Duke William celebrated Easter of that year at Bayeux, having gathered the nobles of the British and Norman regions. He remained there until the festive days of the sacred solemnity of Pentecost had passed.

Desiring the infant Richard to be confirmed and exalted in the kingdom by the oath and sworn pledge of his faithful men, he took seven nobles of greater power and disclosed to them, together with the three written above, the secret of his will:

“Since the fortune of events is always turning through innumerable accidents, and the outcome of causes is certain to scarcely anyone, I therefore wish, with your favor, that while I am alive my son Richard be established by you as heir of my dominion; that you grant your hands to his hands in place of his heart; that the pledged fidelity of your true faith be firmly secured by oath; and that by your most useful counsel the whole country itself be prudently governed.”

The seven nobles replied joyfully:

“If you are not troubled in mind by what you have proposed, after examining, considering, and indeed foreseeing it, it would be entirely fitting and proper for us to have you do this at our request and through our careful exhortation, because this matter is necessary, and especially so for us.”

After giving their hands to the infant Richard, making an oath of obedient service and military allegiance over the most sacred relics, they promised and vowed to him that they would be faithful to him in all things.

## APOSTROPHE

Noble boy, of sacred rank and order,

And of distinguished degrees, of gracious character,

Born of a splendid father,

From the radiant and freeborn lineage of your mother.

This country and region is deservedly subjected to you,

The land in which you were born.

For you will be a good duke and gracious count

To the native people dwelling here;

You will also be the adornment of the churches,

Sacred glory, hope worthy of remembrance.

The wanderer, orphan, exile, and needy person,

Receiving help from you,

Will depart joyfully and satisfied.

When these matters had been settled by sagacious, prudent, and salutary counsel, and many affairs of the holy Church and the commonwealth had been beneficially arranged, each man returned home joyful and happy.

Meanwhile the well-disposed infant Richard, renowned for the grace of his first flower, was being formed year by year. The grace of the Holy Spirit enlarged the chambers of his heart and, by the abundant gift of ardent study and sagacious intellect, heaped up in him what was sufficient for both.

Wisdom was building a house supported by columns within the structure of his heart. He himself, according to the strength of his age, accomplished whatever good he could through excellent deeds. As he grew vigorously through human development, so he was happily enriched by the merits of his life.

Whatever good he heard, he retained by recalling it faithfully; but he rejected and despised evil. Whatever was hidden beneath the obscurities of the law, he unraveled completely by opening it up more clearly.

After his father William, as has been related, had been martyred through the stain of treachery and crowned happily in the starry kingdom, before his body was buried in the tomb, those who remained in the kingdom and had not gone with him to the mournful assembly brought the boy Richard.

Then, seeing a boy of such beauty and dignity, the Normans and Britons, sobbing in mournful and lamenting voices and uttering deep sighs amid the howling of many, said with one accord:

“Behold whom we are to serve; behold for whom we are to fight; behold to whom, while his father lived, we pledged our faith.”

Then Beringer, the foremost count of the British region, spoke first for them all, lamenting and grieving:

“O elders and lords, deceived treacherously by Arnulf’s faithlessness, mourning and grieving over the pitiable death of our most pious marquis, before the lamentable body is laid in the tomb, let us make this boy our lord. This boy must be substituted in his father’s seat, so that he may be our duke and patrician.

“Let this boy be established as prince of this kingdom, lest foreign peoples invade us and, deliberating to rule over us through this unheard-of act of treachery, claim for themselves the Norman and British territories.

“Restoring the lost shield of his father to his shield and restoring it to his offspring, let us resist those who wish to rule over us.”

After these words, they all praised the counsel together. The counts, with a great multitude of nobles, advanced amid the stirred-up rush and murmuring howls of the crowd toward the boy Richard, who was held in immense reverence.

When the murmur of the tumultuous peoples had been calmed and silence had scarcely been obtained, Beringer and Alannus, together with the other counts of Normandy and Brittany, gave their hands to Richard and willingly submitted themselves to him, as they had once promised his living father.

Having brought forward pledges consisting of precious relics of the saints, they sanctioned for him the terms of their unimpaired fidelity and military service, by the death-bound oath of Christian conspiracy.

When these mournful rites had been completed and many had returned to their own places, Richard, a boy of expected nobility and renowned for courage,

[Col. 0692D] remained at Rouen with the young men and his father’s household servants.

## APOSTROPHE

Rouen, spread along the banks of the Seine,

A city fertile in every good thing and in fierce soldiers,

Always teeming with [laon, uncertain], rich in wealth and full of gifts,

Joyful in the hunt, sufficient and most prosperous,

Rich in many kinds and species, and richer in fish,

In tall birds and in the two-edged hawk skilled in hunting.

Indeed, better than every city, indeed more excellent,

More powerful than the port that flourishes among the Belgians,

The Celts, and the English.

Rejoice, dance, make merry, and be glad, because

A perfect lord and lawgiving master has been given to you.

When his father has died, Duke, patrician, and marquis

Will be held to be the celebrated Richard,

Just, gracious, pious, innocent,

Holy, religious, benevolent, sacred, and upright,

Solemn, renowned for his merits, worthy, and lovable,

Beloved, revered, venerable, and memorable,

Strong by right through the ages, powerful by right in every respect.

He will one day govern you, protect you, and assist you,

And through his continual merits, throughout every age,

You will be made splendidly rich and generously endowed.

His goodness, piety, and reverence

Will finally compel you to ascend the Elysian fields.

When the king of France, Louis, heard that Duke William of the Normans had been martyred because of the cunning of Arnulf, count of Flanders, for the stability of the holy Church and of holy faith and peace, and for his fidelity to the king, he grieved greatly. Excepting those who had plotted his death, he hastened to Rouen with the nobles of the kingdom and his counts, to deliberate about what had occurred through the wicked craft of Count Arnulf.

The people of Rouen, however, gladly welcomed King Louis when he arrived, thinking that he would ride against the Flemings and wished to inflict on them bitter and deadly vengeance for the unheard-of crime they had committed.

King Louis then summoned Richard, a boy of such great beauty, to come to him. Weeping with deceitful and fraudulent affection, he received and kissed him, and, retaining him, began to eat and recline with him.

On the following day, when the boy’s fosterer wished to take him to another house so that he might bathe and guard him, the king forbade it and kept him with himself. On the second and third days likewise, when the fosterer was eager to do the same, the king refused, forbidding it with obstinate heart.

When the fosterer perceived that a boy of such sweetness had been captured, he afterward attempted to take him nowhere.

The report of this matter then stirred up the whole city, and rumor of the boy’s capture was spread and scattered throughout the entire town.

At last the suburban inhabitants gathered together with the citizens and, rushing in popular fashion to the house of the city’s princes, began to curse them, uttering enormous groans and saying in loud voices:

“Through our negligence we have lost Duke William, our foremost advocate. Yet by your treacherous counsel this exile will not be driven out here. We shall rightly kill all the perjurers and the king, and we shall free Richard, a boy of such great dominion, so that he does not remain in exile.”

Many of the nobles, driven to fury by the citizens’ harsh words, quickly clothed themselves in iron and arms and joined the armed crowd.

Many peasants, however, fearing the people’s rage, remained in their houses, firmly barring their doors.

Immediately the common people, together with the armed soldiers, hastened with burning zeal and rapid steps to attack the king and his counts.

When the king heard the murmur of the tumultuous uproar, he began to ask the cause of the disturbance. He was told:

“The princes of this city, because you are holding Richard, a boy of such great hope, in captivity, are eager to attack you quickly. You will scarcely escape the danger that threatens; you will scarcely be freed from the citizens and their armed crowds.”

Then the king, seized by icy fear and trembling and shaken by the prospect of imminent ruin, at last came to himself and sent to Bernard, the prince of the Norman army, asking him to come quickly to his aid for the love of God.

Bernard promptly sent back to him these words:

“I shall free neither myself nor him; but when this sedition has arisen, I think I shall perish.”

Then the king again sent to ask him to give counsel by which he might be freed.

Bernard, fearing that both he and the king might be killed, sent word back that the king should take Richard, the boy of exalted aid, in his arms and come suppliantly to seek the mercy of the soldiers and citizens.

The king, distrustful of himself and fearing the destruction and slaughter of his men, took Richard, the boy of such great promise of deliverance, into his arms and carried him before the armed crowd. In a suppliant voice he begged the mercy of those who wished to kill him and his men:

“Behold, I and your lord. Do quickly whatever you wish with me, only I humbly beg you not to kill me and my men. Your lord has not remained with me as a captive to be held, but so that he might be instructed in royal knowledge and palatine eloquence.”

But they received Richard, the boy of such great courage, and permitted the king, full of the deepest entreaty, to return to the hall of his dwelling and to his own men.

King Louis, however, anxious about these troubles and uncertain and wavering about what would come, following the salutary advice of his bishops and counts, sent for the leading men of that city—namely Rodulfus, Anslec, and Bernard—to hasten to him.

When they had been summoned and brought before him, the king said sadly to the princes:

“Warned sharply by fear of death concerning your lord, and intending to console you over his death, I came here. But I encountered a sorrow more grievous than my former grief, because your suburban inhabitants with the citizens, and the soldiers with the gathering of peasants, wished to crush and tear me and my men apart in sudden destruction.

“But, freed by your counsel, Bernard, from the deadly enemy of such a great sedition, tell me what I am to do.”

Bernard replied:

“Your spirit bears with excessive bitterness what the peasants together with the citizens have done against you. Therefore you must be saved from the fraud of the wickedness that has been exposed.

“Since our lord Duke William was in every way your fortunate ally, it is fitting that you authorize, by an oath of sacred faith and with your hands placed upon the most holy relics, that the land be possessed by Richard, the boy of great posterity, by hereditary right. You must also guarantee that from this time onward you will remain harmless toward him and will be his helper and defender against all earthborn enemies.

“Thus you will be able to rejoice in our service and military allegiance, while we enjoy your protection and governance. If anyone quarrels with you, we shall crush him; and if anyone rises up against us, we shall cast him down to the ground by the strength of your power.”

Then the king deceitfully replied to Bernard:

“Whatever you have said, I shall do, and I shall willingly or unwillingly compel my men to do it for the present.”

Immediately he granted Richard, the boy of outstanding innocence, the land to be possessed by hereditary right from his grandfather and father. When the relics of the saints had been brought forward and his hands placed upon them, he first invoked God and swore that he would aid Richard against everyone; he also compelled his bishops and counts to do the same.

When these matters had been settled and completed in this way, the king fraudulently said to the Norman princes:

“Since by the promise of a truthful oath I have given your lord and you a faith of unimpaired substance, let me have your steadfast confidence in my aid, and let none of you waver in seeking help and comfort.

“But allow your lord to remain with me, so that, instructed through conversation rich in eloquence, he may learn to define and determine words concerning difficult matters. He will learn knowledge of many things better in my palace than while staying in his own house.

“Wherever I go, he will go with me; wherever I remain, he will remain. By the effective aid of his father I hold the governance of all France and Burgundy; therefore I shall be his helper and comforter as long as I survive. Since his father was taken by death on my behalf, I would be more savage than a beast if I did not aid him.”

Deceived by these fraudulent speeches of the king, who was pretending goodness, the princes of the Normans surrendered Richard, the boy of their desired hope, to King Louis for education.

The king then departed with the boy to the walls of the city of Évreux and arranged the laws of the commonwealth. In word and deed he pretended to offer good-willed assistance, but in his heart he bore a plan of evil intent.

After remaining for a long time at Évreux and deceitfully compelling the citizens to swear allegiance to the boy, he returned to the palaces of Rouen.

On the following day, having summoned the city’s princes, he delivered these fraudulent and deceitful words:

“I intend to hasten against the author of our loss and grief. I shall return to Laon, taking with me Richard, the boy entrusted to you; then, having gathered the Burgundians and assembled the Franks, I shall besiege Arras until I capture him.

“I shall overthrow all the fortifications of the Flemings and hostilely scatter their possessions. Wherever I learn Arnulf to be, I shall quickly extend the advance of my army there. If I find him anywhere, I shall give him the vengeance he deserves.

“But you must be prepared to recover your lord with me.”

Blinded by the pretenses of such sophistries, they allowed the boy, their future aid, to be taken away by him.

## APOSTROPHE

Rouen, your boy now,

A marquis powerful by right, has been given to you;

He is captive—weep and tremble,

For he is led away, alas for grief,

By the king and Frankish satraps,

Like a stranger to foolish Dacian nobles.

Count Arnulf, stained by the unheard-of corruption of fraudulent murder, and fearing the future arrival of the king should he act rightly, sent envoys to him with very great gifts, to say the following:

“Most pious lord king, our lord, overcome by a severe illness, sends you faithful service, if you are willing to receive it. You have heard through the false opinion of an exposed rumor that our lord Arnulf favored the unjust death of Duke William. He wishes to expiate and amend this before you, at the judgment of your men, even by fire.

“As for the soldiers who inflicted many evils upon William and brought him to death, he will denounce them from now on, if by such actions he can earn your favor.

“In order that you may benevolently assent to his requests, he sends you ten pounds twice over—twenty pounds—of the purest gold. Moreover, as long as he lives, he will voluntarily pay you the tribute of his entire region every year. His men will perform your service in all things, and wherever you go in war, they will go.

“He himself cannot come to you, because, as you know, he is afflicted by gout. May our prayers encourage the indulgence of your mercy toward one afflicted by such a wound of illness and accused without cause of such a crime. May fitting compassion forestall your anger, so that you do not abandon your servant, hated by you without cause.

“The power is yours, and the kingdom is yours; do not destroy what has been entrusted to you. You can more easily destroy all the Flemings than shatter glass vessels with a hammer.”

Then the king’s counselors, blinded by the gifts, said to him:

“You ought not to wrong anyone who strives to justify himself before you. He declares himself free of deceitful crime and intends either to justify his men or to exterminate them.

“For the sake of failing to recover what you need, you ought not to destroy the man whom you hold, nor in any way allow yourself to be deprived of him. It is not your right to avenge all those who will be killed, but to pacify the survivors who quarrel over their deaths.

“Remember the evils and disgrace that the Normans inflicted upon you at Rouen, and beware lest, by bringing worse things upon you, they take the Norman kingdom from you.”

Then the Flemings said:

“Besides these things, our lord sends you the greatest counsel concerning this matter: keep Richard his son forever, and the usufruct of the kingdom forever. Oppress the inhabitants of that land with the harsh yoke of law and servitude, and compel them to serve you obediently.”

Deceived and blinded by this wicked counsel and by the gifts, the king retained Richard, the boy of such great worth, and left Arnulf in possession of what had fraudulently been taken from William because of him.

## APOSTROPHE

O Louis,

If you would keep in a good heart

The vows you made,

And all that you swore,

Revered king,

When, ruling well,

You exercised authority;

With the assistance

And salutary protection

Given by so great an avenger,

The father of Richard,

Religious,

Innocent,

A martyr of Christ,

Endowed with simplicity

And uprightness,

And generosity.

Why do you now cast away

What Belgic,

Celtic,

And Aquitanian

Gaul extends

In multiplied

Territories everywhere?

Why, loosened

From the law,

Savage and wicked,

And betrayed by cunning gifts,

Do you withdraw

From the honorable

Term of your faith,

Now that the bond

Of trust has been torn away?

Why do you detain

The offspring of that gracious man,

Bound by the cord

Of impiety,

By wicked fuel,

Alas, to be nourished

By a dark desire,

Held outside the law

By a fate he desired?

Cease from wickedness;

Disdain to hold

Whatever is impious.

[Col. 0698] Release Richard,

I beg you, the young man,

So that he may fulfill

His gracious rights.

By whatever means you capture him,

You yourself will be captured,

And in fitting recompense

You will return.

[Col. 0697A] There was a certain young man named Hosmund, the educator and exceptionally shrewd guardian of Richard, the boy of outstanding renown. One day, while the king was absent, he had the boy—who had been taken into custody undeservedly—ride out hawking, so that he might learn to catch birds with his hawk. When the king returned, and learned from the words of Queen Gerberga that Richard, intent on the delight of boyhood, was accustomed to go outside Laon in pursuit of this memorable skill, he summoned Hosmund, his tutor, to him.

When Hosmund stood before him, the king raged with savage fury. Pointing out that the secret of the boy’s wicked imprisonment had long been concealed, he began: “Wicked beyond all others, where did you take your master the day before yesterday? Once your master’s kneecaps have been burned, I shall deprive you of your eyes if you ever take him anywhere again.”

Then he entrusted the boy jointly to other young men, commanding them to guard him carefully and to ensure that he could not escape by flight. But when Hosmund realized that Richard, a boy of such sweetness, had been captured, he sent someone to the men of Rouen to announce the blasphemous affair of so great a deception.

The people of Rouen, astonished at the wicked king’s altered purpose, humbly implored aid from God for so grave a matter. They therefore sent throughout the whole Church of the Norman and Breton regions, asking the priests to celebrate Masses devoutly for him, the clergy to devote themselves to psalmody, and the people to fast barefoot and clothed in sackcloth.

When the Norman and Breton bishops heard the report of this sorrowful embassy, they proclaimed a three-day fast in every month for the people and prayed to the Lord God with poured-out supplications and alms given to the poor, asking humbly that he return to them Richard, the boy so greatly desired. The clergy of monks and canons sang psalms for him in supplication, while the devout people visited the churches and uttered groans of prayer.

Meanwhile Richard, a boy of such beauty, distinguished in lineage and renowned for his uprightness, was being adequately instructed in every kind of knowledge concerning the hunt. He spent a substantial part of that age endowed with strength, and was useful and serviceable to everyone, as though mature in years. In accordance with the powers of his age, he reproved whatever was illicit; he treated as worthless whatever stimulated the soul to evil. With lively wit he richly armed his tongue and adorned it with the speech of eloquent abundance.

He pursued through study whatever he did not know and reconsidered it; nothing obscure was hidden from him. He consecrated the tender age of his boyhood to Jesus Christ and, although still of tender years, devoted himself entirely to the divine commandments.

For this happened by divine permission: the boy, conspicuous in form and more radiant than the rest, was raised only in the king’s palace. In many ways they gladly distinguished him by their conversation and instructed him with the honey-sweet savor of courtly speech.

[Col. 0698A] In the course of time, the King and Lord, appeased by the continual prayers of the Normans and Bretons and by the fasts devoutly practiced each month, rescued Richard, the boy of immeasurable promise, from the king’s hands in the following manner.

The aforementioned young man Hosmund, his most upright guardian, seeing that his master was being detained for so long and was being surrounded alternately day and night lest he be taken away from the young men, began to consider how he might rescue him from so many guards. Accordingly, one day he compelled the boy to take to his bed by feigning weakness for this purpose; and, as though his bodily health had been concealed, he caused him to grow weaker by making him utter frequent cries of pain.

The report of this false condition filled the city, and the pretense was spread abroad as truth by the announcement of rumor. On the third day, the guards, supposing that the boy, who had been watched with such care, was already overcome by death, went here and there to attend to their own affairs and departed.

Thus, while the king and the citizens were dining and the streets were empty of people, the boy, clothed in a gray cloak, left Laon swiftly with Hosmund on swift horses. With rapid riding he reached the castle of Coucy. There he entrusted the boy to the castellans, men of abundant integrity, and that very night set out for Count Bernard, his uncle, who was staying within the walls of Senlis.

## Apostrophe

Now, bishops of Normandy,

and princes, triumphant in every war

of the kingdom, together with the clergy

of every order, and the sorrowing people—

boys, old men, and maidens,

young men and all women,

and the common crowd rushing into the streets—

send forth mournful cries

in sorrowful tones and refrain.

For joy has been given to you:

Richard, the noble, innocent,

wise, most holy boy,

beautifully handsome and radiant,

has been released from royal bonds

and escaped from his guards.

Freed from the stubborn fetter,

he will be your mighty leader.

Now render thanks to God

for the child who has been set free.

[Col. 0698D] In the silence of the dark night, Bernard saw Hosmund and, astonished, said to him: “What news have you, Hosmund? Nothing good concerning my nephew?”

He replied:

[Col. 0699A] “My lord, if I rescue him from the hand of the savage king, what will you do with him?”

Bernard answered: “I shall raise you to high rank, enriching you with many honors; I shall exalt you greatly, making you rich in benefices. As for my nephew, I shall restore him to the hereditary kingdom of his father and compel the princes of the Normans and Bretons to serve him.”

To this Hosmund replied: “Late in the day I secretly took your nephew from Laon and entrusted him to the castellans of Coucy to guard.”

At once Bernard rose, happier than usual, and hastened at a swift ride to Paris, to Hugh the Great, duke. When Hugh the Great saw him, he said: “Why have you hurried to us so suddenly and so early?”

Bernard replied: “Because King Louis guards my nephew more strictly and more carefully, I have come to you so that you might give me some counsel concerning him. And if someone should rescue him from the king’s hands, what assistance will your clemency grant him?”

Then Hugh the Great said: “Everyone is astonished at what King Louis is doing. The boy’s father was deceived and killed because of his loyalty to the king, and the king himself holds his son captive. Would that someone rescue him from the king’s chains and bring him to me!”

Bernard said: “My lord, what will you do if what you have said comes to pass?”

Hugh the Great answered: “I shall subjugate the Normans and Bretons for him and make him possess everything that his father held. I shall aid him against the king and bravely assist him against Arnulf and all his enemies.”

Then Count Bernard, adding prayers to prayers and falling humbly at his feet, said: “Most powerful duke, do not be angry if I repeat what I wish from you. So that I may openly prove myself trusting in your promises, by your own request give me the fullest assurance of the words you have pledged. For I have at Coucy the boy, whom Hosmund rescued from the captivity of the treacherous king out of such love.”

The Great Duke, rejoicing over the boy’s rescue, said to Count Bernard: “So that you may be more confidently assured of my proposal’s purpose, I shall do for you and for him what you humbly request.”

When relics had been brought and his hands placed upon them, he swore by an oath of true faith that he would aid the boy against everyone.

## Apostrophe

Through the honeyed power of your goodness,

[Col. 0699D] Hugh, powerful, strong, and vigorous,

great, illustrious, and deserving,

great-hearted, good, life-giving,

wondrous, upright, excellent—

behold, remember your aid,

and remember the work

of outstanding goodness that you undertake.

Help the deserving boy,

protect him, save him, sustain him;

let him hold what his father held,

and rejoice in recovering it;

let him possess and have it,

doing what he has always striven to do.

After these and similar things had been accomplished, Count Bernard hastened by rapid horse to Coucy. He kissed the boy, so carefully guarded, and, rejoicing in the embraces he had long desired, led him with a large army to the city of Senlis.

King Louis, having experienced a double grief—because he had captured the boy and because the boy himself had escaped—sent an envoy to Hugh the Great, ordering him to compel Count Bernard to return the boy. Hugh the Great sent the king the following reply:

“I shall not take from Bernard Senlis, Coucy, Torcy, or the castle of Créteil; nor can I compel him by any efforts to return Richard, his most beloved nephew.”

Meanwhile Count Bernard of Senlis sent to Bernard of Rouen and the other Normans to announce swiftly the desired outcome. The Normans and Bretons, exceedingly joyful at the rescue of the boy they desired, offered vows and thanks to almighty God on his behalf.

For this reason Count Bernard of Senlis set out to meet Bernard of Rouen and Bernard the Dane, in order to consult them about what should be done with the boy. When they had enjoyed mutual and highly confidential conversation and had long deliberated on restoring the boy to his kingdom, Count Bernard said to Bernard the Dane:

“Lest King Louis notice the purpose of our intention, I shall not come here to you again for a meeting. But believe what I send you by a messenger, marked by a sign agreed between us; and devise, by ingenious effort, how to make King Louis act the fool, because he wishes to destroy all of us—both you and us—cruelly.”

After cautiously discussing several matters, each returned as quickly as possible to his own place.

Meanwhile King Louis, anxious about the boy’s rightful rescue and exceedingly sad and mournful because Hugh had sent him a reply expressing distrust, sent for Count Arnulf of the Flemish people, so that he might give great assistance in this matter, and summoned him to come quickly to meet him.

They met swiftly in the district of Vermandois, at a village called Restibulis, and began to consider what they should do. Arnulf, fearing the vengeance due for his deserved destruction and angered by crafty deceit, said to King Louis:

“I am terrified by the fear of immense danger, and I tremble to the innermost marrow of my bones over what is to come, lest perhaps the Normans and Bretons, joining Duke Hugh, who is violently quarreling with you, and seeking military aid, rise up against us with one accord and bring about our ruin.

“Nevertheless, I shall give you advice concerning this, so that we do not incur the danger of the harm to come. Blind Hugh’s eyes with gifts and benefices, so that he may be unable by right to oppose what you have done. Grant him Normandy from the Seine to the sea, so that you may be able to hold peacefully what lies this side of it. The Normans, divided in this way, will be left desolate and will no longer be stirred to battle against us. Thus you will reduce and disarm the power of men who no longer serve one lord alone.

## Apostrophe

Inventor of crime, of counsel and evil,

utterly of what is forbidden, of fraud and impiety—

[Col. 0701A] why do you strive, by your treacherous counsel,

to crush and thwart God’s foreknowledge?

Alas, alas, through your treachery he fell—

the already worthy father of this offspring;

that he might be purer in the sight of the Lord,

strengthened by martyrdom, he shines forth as a witness.

Your wickedness will torment and tear this child in a similar way,

yet will not defile him.

Here he will truly sit, a more splendid duke,

a prudent, peaceful, deserving count,

holy, religious, good, and pious,

a supreme patrician, a provident margrave,

defender of his country and of the man in need of help [the printed *at indigus opis* is faulty, apparently for *ac indigi opis*],

comforter of the wretched,

and likewise of widows and orphans.

For all, every good and prosperous gain,

[Col. 0701B] he will bring about by fitting governance,

guiding them with moderation and correcting them by law,

to the heavenly pastures of the starry field.

King Louis, using the wicked cunning of deceit, sent bishops of great dignity to Hugh more quickly, asking him to come to him promptly in the faith by which lord and vassal are bound together.

Thus Hugh the Great, compelled by the very frequent entreaties of the bishops, set out to meet the king at a village in the district near Compiègne called La Croix. He said to the king:

“For what matter have you compelled me by your pledges and distinguished envoys to hasten here?”

The king replied: “So that you may return Richard, whom Hosmund stole and brought to Count Bernard.”

Great Hugh answered:

[Col. 0701C] “Unless I take by force the castles over which Bernard presides, I cannot in any way comply with your prayers and desire.”

Then the king said: “So that you may find me not injurious to my need but a source of consolation, I shall grant you the counties of Évreux and Bayeux, and indeed everything from the Seine to the sea, for you to possess. I shall hold what lies this side of the Seine and accomplish from it whatever accords with my will.

“Let us be harmonious and of one mind in every affair, as is fitting for a king and a duke forever. I shall proceed on this side of the Seine and besiege Rouen; you, enclosing Bayeux with military force, shall conquer it. Thus let us crush the Normans, these newcomers and proud men, and subject them to our rule. In this way they will either be softened and subjugated,

[Col. 0701D] or, exterminated, they will quickly return to Denmark.”

But Hugh the Great, forgetting the oath he had made to Bernard for Richard’s assistance, and moreover dazzled by benefices and cities, made this treaty with the king. Once the appointed time for carrying it out had been determined, each returned to his own domain.

When Count Bernard learned of this agreement, he went more quickly to Duke Hugh. Coming into his presence, he said with troubled heart and face:

“Great and most faithful duke, you surpass everyone until now in merit and in the constancy of your faith. But I am astonished that you have lied concerning an innocent boy, although of your own accord you promised it by the faith of a Christian oath. You ought to preserve inviolate the faith you promised and not pollute it with gifts or benefices of any kind.

“The Normans and Bretons know what you pledged to the boy, and the princes of France have rejoiced over this plan. What is more disgraceful than this infamy? What is more liable to blame than such blasphemy? The report of so great a treachery and the wickedness of so evil a duke is spread throughout the walls of the cities of France; everyone whispers about so great a duke and protector, telling how he was deceived and made to lie by gifts and benefices.”

Against the force of this reproach Hugh the Great replied, breathing sighs from the depths of his heart:

“What you have said, you have reported in true and pure words, for I have forgotten the oath by which I freely promised to be the boy’s defender and helper. I have accepted from the king, as a gift, the land from the Seine to the sea, which he is to possess by hereditary right; and I gave him the assurance of wholly reliable faith, promising under oath to be his helper from that land which lies this side of the Seine, provided that he never opposed the land he gave me.

“But since you are a count of remarkable intelligence, immense resourcefulness, and cunning, and shrewd in every affair, I beg you to rescue me by some sophism from the disgrace of this report. Sixteen days from now, the king and I shall hasten into Normandy. He himself will besiege the city of Rouen, while I, as sworn, will besiege Bayeux. Thus we shall afflict the Normans and Bretons and reduce them to humble servitude. Whoever is stubborn and rebellious against us shall be exterminated; whoever dares to take up arms shall be killed. If you possess any prudence and ingenuity, I beg you to free me from the guilt of this perjury.”

When Bernard saw that Hugh the Great had opened his heart, he said to him:

“Because you are the most kindly of lords, and because that boy is my most beloved nephew, I shall reason as best I can, if perhaps I can disrupt what you two have planned.”

At once Count Bernard learned the king’s and his own lord’s plans and the appointed time of the campaign against the Normans. Recalling the benevolence of his lord, he returned more joyful to Senlis and quickly sent to Bernard of Rouen and Bernard the Dane, secretly reporting what he had heard from Hugh the Great and also Hugh’s intention.

He further instructed them not to defend the city in hostility to the king; instead, with a choir of canons and monks prepared, they should receive him cheerfully, as though rejoicing at his arrival, and by pursuing many arguments should compel the king to oppose the land that he had given Duke Hugh the Great.

Bernard of Rouen, made happier by the embassy and by the secret counsel he heard from the messenger, disclosed it to the Norman princes whom he summoned. Since the Normans knew that Bernard had never deceived any of them, and also knew the secret of Hugh the Great, they praised his plan together.

When the appointed time for the sworn expedition arrived, the king came with a military force of Frenchmen gathered from every direction into the district called Calais, and began to harass the people and estates with fires. Duke Hugh the Great, drawn into this conspiracy, set out for the county of Bayeux with a large army.

Count Bernard of Rouen, therefore, not forgetting the counsel of Bernard of Senlis, sent a deceitful message to King Louis in peaceful words, asking him to hasten with his bishops and princes to the city of Rouen and no longer devastate with such ferocity what belonged to him.

The king, pleased by the command of this embassy and congratulating himself on increasing the advancement of his rule and honor, entered the city of Rouen with the nobles of France after subduing the city and its princes. He forbade the rest of the armies to ravage the land under his authority any further.

Bernard, the other princes, and the clergy of the entire city came out to meet him before the Beauvais Gate and received him with bold cunning.

At dawn the following day Bernard came into the presence of King Louis and began deceitfully to address him in the humblest words:

[Col. 0703B] “Most invincible lord king, from long ago until now you have been steadfast and unwavering in faith and praiseworthy in all your deeds. We lost our duke and protector through Arnulf’s treachery, but by God’s grace we have recovered you as king and protector.

“We do not care about the offspring whom Hosmund stole and took away from you; nor will we ever serve him or fight in his service, because it is better for us to be royal men and courtiers than to be the followers and servants of such a count.

“Yet we have heard something astonishing, beyond belief and more than sufficiently marvelous, from those who told us that you have granted to Duke Hugh, who is always quarreling against you most stubbornly, an extensive land from the Seine to the sea’s end, and that he is still attacking the land of Bayeux and occupying it with a great army.

“Sweetest king, the little worth and slight military service that you have reserved for yourself! You have strengthened your enemy with twenty thousand armed men. Who has seen men stronger in war or wiser in counsel than those of Coutances and Bayeux?

“If you had held a military force like William, you could have dominated all these peoples by their counsel and arms. Did not William, relying on half of this army, accompanied by Hugh and Herbert, travel separately and safely to King Henry?

“Who will protect and defend, benefit and rule this city that you have retained? The men of Bayeux and Coutances guarded this city, prominent in the Frankish and English port. The abundance of all the good things of that land was available to us, and we were wealthy through the resources of that territory.

“Take back the city, then, because we have no resources by which we can live in it; and give it to Hugh, so that he may rebel against you with greater security. We shall return to Denmark with all our people by swift sailing and later devastate this place with a still larger military force, as Rollo once did. Afterwards it will belong neither to you nor to Hugh.”

The king, provoked by these deceptive complaints, asked Bernard to give him counsel concerning these matters.

Then Bernard said: “Send a messenger to Duke Hugh the Great to oppose the fields of Bayeux to him, and to say that he may not possess them for more than three nights and that he no longer holds them, because he has acted on bad advice.”

At once the king sent to Hugh to deliver this message. When the envoy stood before Duke Hugh and announced these words to him, he was astonished and, fixed in a single gaze, said:

“The cunning of two princes has compelled the king to send such a proposal.”

Because of this contradiction, Hugh the Duke returned to Paris and sent to King Louis, saying:

“Why has what you freely gave me been taken away?”
