The king replied: “The land of Normandy must never be governed by the protection of more than one lord. What ought to be continuous must not be divided. Rollo, driven out from the borders of Denmark, claimed this land entirely for himself, and thereafter it was never divided by anyone.”

The Danish people do not know how to serve any lord except one alone.

The envoy carefully reported to Duke Hugh what he had heard from the king. Meanwhile Bernard of Senlis, hearing of the unexpected and extremely rapid return of his lord Duke Hugh, came to him at a gallop.

He said: “Duke of steadfast trust, since you have been released from the fetter of your harmful oath, remember the oath by which you pledged yourself Richard’s helper.”

Hugh replied: “I shall not be able to help him, because the entire Norman people is subject to the king.”

Bernard answered: “Wait attentively for the outcome of the matter, and see what the days to come will bring forth for him.”

## Apostrophe

[Col. 0704C] O king, why do you not remember yourself

and that father of his who benefited you,

by whose continual protection you now hold kingdoms,

and who accomplished many things

for you, and who fell as a sacrificial victim

of the heavenly King, and whatever things of his lie hidden [the text is uncertain after the asterisk].

And now, although his own father,

powerful in enduring truthful speech,

surpassing others in arms,

and although his grandfather held [what was held] by sacred right,

you inflict prejudice

upon this still innocent and upright boy,

Richard, nobly born of a celebrated lineage.

With the stain of this crime,

countless disasters will hinder you;

because of it, in the end,

they will seize you and destroy you

at the final limit.

Meanwhile King Louis lingered within the walls of Rouen, arranging the affairs of Normandy as its lord. Through the deceptive intention of a false belief, supposing himself to be king and protector of the Normans, he passed his time there in unstable leisure.

One day a certain young man of the French people asked the king to grant him the sufficient abundance of all the possessions of Bernard the Dane, as well as his wife, who was exceptionally beautiful.

When the other young men heard the report of this request in secret, they came to the king and said:

“Lord king, we serve you constantly and always, and we are enriched by the abundance of no possessions except food and drink. Expel and exterminate these foreign Normans from here, we beg you, and grant us their benefices together with their wives.

“We shall govern this city in service to your loyalty, and you will never be able to waver over the faithlessness of any of us.”

Bernard and the Danes learned of this wicked plan; nevertheless, after consulting among themselves, they committed it to silence.

When King Louis had returned to Laon, the Normans, exceedingly wearied by the zeal of stepmotherly hatred and deeply troubled by the ambitious and disgraceful request of the young men, unanimously began to devise the king’s destruction.

To deceive the king by some crafty effort, the Norman leaders sent soldiers of the nobler and wealthier Danish power as envoys to Haigrold, king of Denmark, asking him to hasten to aid his kinsman Richard, son of the great Duke William. For the king of the French people was claiming the sovereignty of all Normandy for himself and removing every honor from Richard, whom his uncles had rescued.

King Haigrold of Denmark, great-hearted, received the Norman envoys honorably out of love for his kinsman Richard. He built ships, filled them with provisions and soldiers, and came more swiftly than he could have been expected to do to the salt shores of Corbon, where the Dive pours itself into the stormy sea with rapid course, accompanied by an incredible multitude of young men.

When the men of Coutances and Bayeux heard that King Haigrold had arrived for love of the boy Richard, they came to serve him. At once the report spread rapidly through the regions of France, announcing that pagans of immeasurable numbers were present on the Norman shores.

Bernard and the other men of Rouen, while pretending in words to be loyal to King Louis, sent to him deceitfully, saying:

“Since pagans of innumerable and abundant multitude, radiant in the flower of their first youth, have been brought to our borders, we beg you to summon a military force and come quickly to our aid, if you prefer to enjoy authority over the region of Normandy.”

The king said to the envoy: “I have heard by the report of rumor that what you say is true.”

Therefore, warned by the report of this destructive embassy, King Louis came suddenly to Rouen with an army of the French people, bringing with him Count Herluin and his brother Lambert.

When King Haigrold heard of the arrival of the king of France, he sent him a deceitful invitation through the Normans, asking him to come meet him.

As King Louis, confident in the multitude of his armies, prepared to go to this meeting that would bring about his destruction, Bernard of Rouen, pretending to be loyal to the Franks, said to him:

“The people against whom you are going to negotiate remember with inward love that they loved our count William, and they hate exceedingly, from the depths of their hearts, the man for whose sake he was martyred. Because of Count Herluin’s quarrel, the Normans, deprived of such a leader, will engage him with the intention of killing him if they should see him.

“Therefore do not take him with you, lest, when they recognize him, a quarrel arise between the two armies.”

Then, as the story goes, one of the young men replied to Bernard:

“On your account and that of the other foreigners, is such a count as Herluin to be hidden away in any hiding place?”

Bernard silently observed what was being done and suppressed in his heart the pain caused by this reproach.

King Louis, admonishing the Frankish army, took Count Herluin with him and pitched his camp on this side of the course of the Dive. The men of Coutances and Bayeux, with King Haigrold, fixed their tents beyond the waters of the Dive.

Bernard rose early and came to King Louis, saying:

“Lord king, rise more quickly and secretly examine with your men what must be done. This people is of a different character from the Franks and is exceedingly full of ingenious cunning.”

Then, with the king’s approval, someone lying inside replied to Bernard, who was standing outside:

“Go to sleep at once; we do not care about such things.”

Angered by these words, Bernard quickly returned to the camp at Rouen.

When the sun was hot, at the third hour of the day, the forces of the men of Coutances and Bayeux began to cross the bed of the Dive. Seeing this, Bernard again sought the king and said:

“King, continue sleeping more than enough, for the Danish people has crossed the river Dive and is standing mounted on the shore. I do not know with what bold intention.”

Awakened by threatening words, the king rose quickly, surrounded by a crowd of counts and soldiers, and hastened to meet his own destruction.

Calling Bernard, he said to him:

“I do not know what my spirit forebodes; it is not content with peaceful rest. It anxiously urges me to encounter either battle or something new.”

To this Bernard replied:

“Did I not warn you repeatedly that Count Herluin should not be brought here?”

Having said this, he came to the place where the meeting had been arranged.

There stood King Haigrold with the men of Coutances and Bayeux, while King Louis stood nearby on the other side with the Franks. There also stood the chosen youth of the Danes, leaning on their spears and holding shields in their hands, seeking an opportunity by which they might kill the Franks and the king.

As King Louis and Haigrold, king of Denmark, engaged in conversation by mutual agreement, with the Franks and Danes—and likewise the men of Coutances and Bayeux—armed all around them and looking on [a word is missing after the source asterisk], Count Herluin said to a soldier whom he had once known:

“Of what health, what prosperity, or what means are you,

[Col. 0706D] you and the origin of your family?”

The man replied:

“I am of sound health, wealthy happiness, and sufficient abundance.”

The men of Coutances and Bayeux began to ask the man who had been questioned who it was that was inquiring so familiarly about the advantages of his prosperity.

He replied to those asking:

“Herluin, distinguished count of the castle of Monasteriol.”

Then the men of Coutances said to the men of Bayeux:

“Is this not the man through whose quarrel, or on whose account, our lord William, the most honorable margrave and duke, was deceived and martyred? Shall this hostile man be rescued from our hands?”

At these words, an uncontrollable murmur arose. All the Danes, angered by fury, twisted their weapons; raging with bitterness over the death of so great a lord, they seized the opportunity, attacked Count Herluin, and killed him without fear.

The Franks, eager to avenge Count Herluin and defend themselves with weapons, boldly rose against them. By the deceit of this opportunity, a savage battle began. Their arrows and lances broken in combat, the Franks fought fiercely with drawn swords.

At last, surrounded on every side by the numerous and destructive crowd of the men of Coutances and Bayeux, as well as the pagans, they were slaughtered and torn apart like sheep by wolves.

Thus, having engaged in battle with deadly force, eighteen most noble counts were overtaken by death, scattered by raging Mars on King Louis’s side. There was no hope of life or escape for those who remained.

King Louis, seeing himself abandoned by the protection of the Franks and having experienced the danger of battle, sought the aid of delayed flight. When King Haigrold saw that King Louis was absent, he cut through the center of the army on a swift horse and pursued him at speed.

King Louis fled here and there, since the bridle had slipped from the horse’s head and he held only the reins in his hands. King Haigrold quickly pursued Louis, thus impeded; holding a gleaming sword by its hilt, he drew it from the hollow scabbard at his side and entrusted the king to his own soldiers so that he would neither escape nor be killed.

Rejoicing that he had captured the king, he himself hurried back to the battlefield and continued to strike down to the point of annihilation the Franks who were still defending themselves with weapons. He drove the Franks, torn by wounds, down into the underworld.

The Normans, having gained victory, weapons, and spoils, and traversing the battlefield in safety, carried away the lifeless members of their own people for burial.

## Apostrophe

Worthy of the merits of the future duke,

the celebrated, good, and just Richard,

the radiant boy of sacred character;

and worthy of your fidelity,

by which you now hold this homeland

through battle—

O Norman nobles, mighty enough

in the struggle of battle and in triumph,

cautious, wise in counsel, and upright in all things,

preserving peace with steadfast purpose,

[Col. 0707D] and the petition of sacred faith—

now be greeted, fare well, and be welcomed forever.

And may you, your offspring, and your holy descendants,

every generation of the consecrated stock,

after the sorrowful dissolution of your limbs,

obtain a suitable place of sevenfold rest.

Renewed in the highest good

of a new destiny, may you, gathered together with the saints,

receive its blessings—prosperous, twice twofold, of the eighth and twice—,

you who hold the kingdom of this homeland

by the strength and power

of mighty and tenacious Richard the boy’s fidelity.

Meanwhile King Louis escaped from the hands of the guards, deceived by their greed for plunder, and fled here and there, wandering aimlessly at the speed of a swift-footed horse. A soldier from Rouen, seeing him unarmed and moving restlessly from place to place, attacked him; addressing him by name, he spoke harshly:

“Where are you going, King Louis? Where are you directing your desolate journey? You shall not escape from our lands, into which you foolishly crept while unjustly invading them.”

With these words he turned his warhorse, rushed upon King Louis, seized him by the bridle, and compelled him by force to ride with him. But the king, deprived of all his weapons and unable to free himself from the man’s grasp, said to him in the deepest distress:

“Who are you, and where are you forcing me to go?”

The man from Rouen replied:

“I will lead you there, and from now on you will in no way remain your own master.”

The king, despairing of himself and saddened by the necessity of the impending danger, said to his violent captor:

“Have mercy, I beg you, have mercy on me, and through your compassion rescue me from the hands of those who seek my life and lie in wait for me. Restore me to Laon, so that I may be able to glory and rejoice in Frankish rule. Without you I shall obtain no glory; and whatever authority and honor shall be mine will be yours. If you wish, I shall make you king over me; if not, I shall grant you half the kingdom. Let there be the greatest trust in word and deed between you and me, bound by the oath of Christian alliance.”

Repeating these words again and again and pleading with tears, the king fell from his horse at the feet of the man who was leading him. Then the soldier, moved by the king’s sorrowful lament and compelled by his many entreaties, spoke with tears rising in his eyes:

“Give me assurance of your promises, and I shall escort you safely and unharmed to Laon.”

After they had voluntarily made this pact and given their word, the soldier began to lead the king, leaving the straight road. Meanwhile Bernard of Rouen, deeply grieved at the king’s rescue, hastily sent messengers to prevent King Louis from crossing at any of the ports of the Seine. He himself, outstripping the slow-moving king, went ahead as quickly as he could and hurried with his soldiers to Rouen on swift horses. He sent highly trustworthy scouts to search for the king.

The soldier who was trying to free the king did not wish to keep him at home, lest he be found there by chance, but at night placed him on an island in the Seine, intending to conduct him to Laon once the exhausted scouts had departed and returned.

The scouts, therefore, knowing that King Louis was being held by that soldier, came to his house. They seized his wife, sons, and daughters, his horses and mares, sheep and oxen, and all his household goods, and brought everything to Rouen, reaching Bernard before him.

When the soldier realized that he could no longer conceal the king, he came as quickly as possible to Bernard of Rouen. Throwing himself at his feet, he begged him, once he had received the king, to return his wife to him. Bernard, now happier than usual, received the sorrowful and captive king and returned the soldier’s wife to him.

Then he sent word to Bernard of Senlis and informed him of the king’s desired recovery. The count Bernard, joyful and glad, rose immediately during the night and went to Hugh, the great duke, at Paris. Hugh said to him:

“Have you heard, my lord, as rumor spreads, of some new event?”

He replied:

“Nothing.”

And the other said:

“Know for certain that Haigrold, king of the Danes, because of Richard my nephew and his own kinsman, has fought against King Louis; that in this very conflict four times four counts were killed, together with Herluin, count of the little monastery-fortress, and his brother Lambert; that, moreover, in a most grievous slaughter of the Franks, their king was put to flight and captured; and that he is still held under guard in Rouen by the Dane Bernard.”

The great duke Hugh, astonished at what was being reported, said:

“Now the king has suffered what he deserved, and Count Herluin what was rightly fitting; and the other counselors have endured what they ought to have suffered. For William, duke of the Northmen, died as a martyr for loyalty to the king and the Franks, and because he restored to Herluin the monastery-fortress that had previously been taken from him. Yet the king, who ought to have avenged that execrable and unheard-of crime, kept his son in custody at the advice of the perfidious Herluin and Arnulf, and unjustly claimed his hereditary land for himself. By the judgment of the heavenly King, King Louis is suffering a fitting retaliation for Duke William’s son, your nephew, whom he held captive, and for the land that he usurped. The Northmen, who have subdued King Louis by such persistent cunning, possess greater counsel than the other peoples.”

Then Bernard said:

“My lord, remember what you promised to me and to my nephew; and, as is fitting for you, help and support him.”

The duke replied:

“Before King Louis is released from the impediment of captivity and restored to the kingdom of Frankish rule, the land of the Northmen will be held peaceful and secure, confirmed by an oath of true faith to your nephew Richard and authoritatively secured by the bishops, counts, and abbots.”

Meanwhile a sorrowful report reached the ears of Queen Gerberga: it was explained that the king had been captured, twice nine counts had been killed, and the rest put to flight. The queen, continually lamenting the disastrous fate of her husband the king and of her people, and cruelly tormenting her heart with anxiety over so great a calamity, could find no sound counsel anywhere in all France. She sent to her father, King Henry of the Transrhenan lands, and to her brother Otto, radiant in the flower of youth, reporting the grievous affair of her misfortune and asking them to assemble an army and besiege Rouen, so that by force and power they might ransom her lord, King Louis.

But King Henry sent word to his daughter, Queen Gerberga, that he would not come to besiege Rouen, because King Louis was deservedly and rightly suffering this misfortune as divine punishment for the injustice he had acquired: he had kept captive the son of Duke William, who had died because of Arnulf’s treachery, and had unjustly claimed for himself the entire region of the Northmen, which Duke William’s grandfather had acquired by warfare.

Meanwhile King Haigrold was strengthening all the Northmen and the pagan inhabitants in turn in their loyalty to the boy Richard. He compelled them in every respect to observe the rights, laws, and statutes of Duke Rollo. He worked diligently to fortify the cities and castles, lest fortune should perhaps turn their circumstances adversely.

### Apostrophe

O pious, prudent, good, and temperate;

Brave, steadfast, wise, and just,

Rich, distinguished, wealthy, and capable—

King Haigrold.

Although you are not anointed with chrism,

Nor reborn through holy baptism,

Now farewell, hail, and ever be greeted

In divinity.

You who, by protecting the celebrated Richard,

After capturing the king and laying the Franks low,

With your avenging right hand

And the battle of combat brought to completion,

Now powerfully guide the reins of the kingdom,

And bind all men by the bond of faith,

So that all may serve

In obedience to Richard,

The innocent boy who stands near you,

Born of noble lineage,

And flourishing in merits and in age,

Abundant and nurturing.

Queen Gerberga, utterly deprived of her father’s and brother’s protection, suffering the loss caused by such great anxiety and supported by no hope of consolation, even fearing the loss of her kingdoms, sought the aid of the great duke Hugh on the advice of the bishops. The great duke Hugh reverently received her and the bishops accompanying her; honorably providing what was necessary, he kept them with him for many days.

Meanwhile he sent Count Bernard of Senlis to Bernard, the soldier of Rouen, instructing him to summon the leading men of the Northmen’s council and hasten with them to the holy clergy. They fulfilled the command more quickly than words can say and came against the great duke Hugh, with Bernard leading them, hastening to the appointed place.

Then the great duke and the bishops said to the Northmen:

“Give us back our elder, King Louis.”

But they replied:

“He will not be returned; rather, he will be held.”

Then the great Hugh said:

“But we shall give you his son and two bishops, and as many young attendants of his household as you wish in his place, so that the Frankish prelates, counts, princes, and abbots may come against you at the appointed meeting, and by an oath of complete and true faith may authorize, strengthen, and confirm the land of the Northmen to Richard and his descendants forever.”

The princes of the Northmen praised this counsel and, placing complete confidence in the great duke Hugh’s faith, returned the king. In exchange they received his son, two bishops—Hildier of Beauvais and Guy of Soissons—and a very large number of soldiers.

The great Hugh then led the king to his own people, so that he might rejoice with them and with his wife.

When the appointed time of the agreed term had arrived, the king came with a military force and with the prelates of France to the river Epte against the Northmen, together with the great duke Hugh. Although his son, whom he had given in his place, had died in Rouen, with his hands placed upon reliquary-cases containing relics, he personally guaranteed, in his own words, the security of the kingdom that his grandfather Rollo had acquired for himself by force and power, arms and warfare.

He and all the bishops, counts, venerable abbots, and princes of the kingdom of France guaranteed the kingdom to the innocent boy Richard, so that he might hold and possess it, and so that neither he nor his succession might render service to anyone except God; and if anyone should wish to attack him through a quarrel of perverse invasion, or to invade the kingdom through any outbreak of conflict, they would in every way prove themselves his most faithful helpers in every necessity of adverse circumstance.

When these matters had been determined by the eloquence of lawful definition, with King Louis present and the great duke Hugh and his men beside him, the leaders of the Bretons and the nobles of the Northmen, with willing hearts and hands extended on behalf of the boy Richard, a youth of ineffable excellence, again pledged by an oath of most faithful Christian security their military service, aid, and obedience.

Then the Northmen and the Bretons brought Richard, a boy of such great honor, dignity, and beauty, to Rouen, rejoicing exceedingly.

When the old men and young men of both sexes, boys and infants dwelling in the city and throughout the territory of that district, learned that Richard, the boy whose sight they had long desired, was approaching, the crowd roared everywhere with joy. The people rushed upon the people in overflowing numbers, pressing fiercely together as countless throngs piled upon one another, and they hurried to run out to meet the boy of life-giving and honey-sweet innocence, though impeded by the obstacle of their mutual and accumulated crush and unable to proceed.

The clergy of the entire region, having prepared the monastic treasures, scarcely burst beyond the suburbs of Rouen because of the force of the tumultuous multitude. Praising God with a renewed festival of rejoicing over the return of the child and carrying the bodies of the saints on biers, they led him all the way to the altar of the holy Mother of God.

### Apostrophe

O radiant city, gleaming with sacred soldiery,

Richly full of every good,

Peacefully resting, fierce port of refuge,

O Rouen, receive with everlasting joy

The one returning, filled with divine nectar,

The patrician duke, powerful by right.

For this wondrous and life-giving,

Honey-sweet duke, count, and

Patrician will be a steadfast margrave for you.

And he whose once-fragrant fame

Is worthy to be greatly increased by his abundant virtues—

The four regions of the cosmos will acknowledge him;

No one will have been more holy than he,

In deed, in speech, or even in thought.

For in these three things

The supreme importance of his conduct is found.

Immediately, surrounded by very prudent and distinguished attendants, he began to shine with deeds divinely accomplished and worthy of the greatest honor. As a rival of virtue, he lavishly offered rewards to all, and compelled monks, clerics, and laymen to devote themselves to divine service. He shone splendidly in character and in rich merits, and vigorously governed the clergy and people with these reins. He was a severe avenger of crimes and a generous distributor of good things.

For an abundant supply of various wild beasts provided him with food from the forests, since after the proper examination and administration of judgment and justice, he gave himself over to hunting. The young man, strengthened by merit, grew through success, abolishing vices by the increase of flourishing virtues. Skillfully and persistently he strove toward the summit of goodness and perfection, so that he might rejoice with the saints in the time of future rest.

At that time there was a certain Rodulf, surnamed Torta, who after William’s death claimed for himself the honor of all Normandy more arrogantly than his other peers and indecently usurped the possessions belonging to the lord. Every day he distributed to the worthy boy Richard and his young attendants a daily allowance of eighteen denarii. His household servants were oppressed, wickedly constrained by poverty and hunger.

Therefore Richard, a youth of industrious understanding, summoned the princes of the region of Normandy and asked them what he should do about the insufficient distribution. The princes, bound to him by an oath of true faith and, some of them, enriched by his benefactions, reported to Rodulf, surnamed Torta, the anger of the offended lord.

Rodulf sent his companions back to Richard, the boy of most discerning excellence, begging permission to come before him and make amends for the offenses he had committed against him.

Then the thoughtful boy, having considered their request, is said to have replied:

“You know that my grandfather claimed this city for himself by warfare.”

They answered:

“We know.”

And he said:

“Did my father hold this city by hereditary right? After the death of my grandfather and father, ought I not to possess it by hereditary right? See whether his father, grandfather, or great-grandfather held this city as he holds it, and investigate whose claim is prejudiced—mine or his.”

While they were astonished at such remarkable words, he is cautiously said to have added:

“If he wishes in any way to earn our favor, let he and his entire household leave the city as quickly as possible and stay in a village a mile away from the city, until he sends his messengers to me and hears what I shall send back to him. But if he treats the counsel of our command as worthless, we shall renounce him completely and send to the Franks, so that they may give us sound advice in this matter.”

They reported to Rodulf Torta what they had heard. Thinking that his departure, together with that of his people, would appease his lord—and also fearing that a Frankish army might arrive—he left the city with his entire household and stayed in the peasants’ meadows.

Meanwhile Richard, the boy of such great ability, bound to himself by an oath of true faith the soldiers who had strayed from the right path, and also confirmed the citizens of the entire city by the bond of loyalty.

On the following day Rodulf Torta sent several of his companions to the boy of such great moderation, asking him to permit Rodulf to come before him for judgment and justification and to receive the pledge required as compensation for his offense.

Then the boy, stirred by the force of a sharp mind and prudent caution, said:

“You know that he once inflicted an unheard-of wrong upon me.”

They replied:

“We know.”

“Does he not still do so through the rashness of his audacity? He shears the meadows of my peasants with scythes, grazes them with horses, tramples them with hooves, and kills and eats cows, rams, bulls, and pigs. If he does not depart from our borders and is not expelled, he will swiftly incur the penalty he deserves. What you have advised him until now you are still advising him; but it will be of no benefit to him.”

They, astonished at such words, fell on their faces and said:

“Lord, we beg you, do not become angry, and do not let your fury rage against us; for we are entirely faithful to you and will never adhere to him.”

After they departed, they reported to Rodulf Torta what they had heard. He, losing confidence in himself, quickly abandoned the meadows and came with his entire household in haste to Paris.

When his son, who was bishop of the city of Paris, saw his sudden arrival, he was struck with terror. Drawing sighs from his breast, he said:

“Why, father, have you hastened here with your entire household of both sexes?”

Rodulf reported to the bishop the calamity of his misfortune and the disastrous danger of his situation. The bishop and his father sent messengers back and forth to the boy of such great strength, but their efforts did not prosper.

When the elders of Normandy saw that he had expelled so prudently the leader of the soldiery, they feared him greatly.

When he shone with such distinguished and numerous signs of present and future good works, and the fame of the youth’s great intelligence struck the minds of those dwelling in Gaul; when, radiant with the abundant increase of the fourfold virtues, he ruled the kingdom of Normandy as king, subject to no one but God, and governed it by the judgment of just rule—the great duke Hugh, seeing him strengthened and outstanding in all his deeds, commanded Count Bernard, who was living in the city of Senlis, to come to him, summoning Bernard of Rouen as well.

He said to them:

“I have received messengers from many plotters against the young Count Richard, who are reconsidering their plans and attempting to invade the land of the Northmen through hostile conflict. Richard serves neither king nor duke, and renders obedience to no one except God. He holds the monarchy of Normandy like a king, yet has no friends bound to him by an unbreakable treaty of assistance and alliance.

“His father fell through the treachery of Count Arnulf. See to it that he is not deceived by the perfidious envy of that same cunning. The king, not forgetting his former injuries, still broods over the anger caused by his misfortune and captivity; seeking your destruction, he is associating many men with himself through the deceit of this affair.

“Seek, therefore, sound counsel for yourselves, so that, secure from ambushes and deceptions, you may not fear the fatal outcome of worldly change.”

The great duke Hugh offered this proposal with cautious purpose, wishing and desiring to join his daughter to Duke Richard in the bond of marriage.

Then both Bernards said:

“We do not know, my lord, how to investigate a plan concerning this matter, but by your goodness give us favorable assistance in this undertaking. Until now, following your prosperous counsel, we have walked along the path of righteousness; from this point onward, rejecting completely the byways of a crooked path, with you as our leader and adviser, we shall proceed—while preserving the faith that we gave to Count Richard.”

Hugh began to reveal his well-disposed plan:

“Have you yet sought for Duke Richard of the Northmen a wife suitable to his generous humanity and dignity, and fit for him?”

They replied:

“Not at all.”

And he said:

“Where will you turn the purpose of your counsel, or whose daughter will you claim and subject to him?”

Bernard of Senlis, moved by the affectionate presentation of these proposals and perceiving the intention of his lord, replied with an argument carefully reasoned:

“My lord, we do not know whose daughter, except yours.”

When the great Hugh understood that both men had perceived the inclination of his will, he is said to have replied, revealing the intention of his heart:

“It is not the custom of France for any prince or duke, though surrounded by abundant soldiery, to remain every day in such a position of dominion and authority without either willingly serving according to his own inclination or, compelled by force and power, submitting more humbly to an emperor, king, or duke. And if he should persist in the rashness of his audacity and refuse to serve anyone willingly from the abundant resources of his wealth, quarrels, dissensions, and innumerable misfortunes regularly befall him.

“Therefore, if your nephew Duke Richard should be willing to bend himself so as to serve me, I would gladly join my daughter to him in marriage according to your most salutary counsel, and I would stand continually as defender and advocate of him and of the land he possesses by hereditary right, against everyone.”

Then Count Bernard of Senlis is said to have replied:

“Since King Louis previously held Richard, the young duke and my nephew, captive, and since he sought to destroy all the Northmen through treachery, I would prefer that you give your daughter as wife to Richard, so that he may serve you, rather than to the deceitful king.”

Thus the great duke Hugh gave his daughter to Richard, the most noble young man, with the security of an oath—not, however, according to the established law of a Fescennine marriage-purchase, but according to a specified and sworn term of marital union.

When the report of this truthful arrangement struck the ears and heart of King Louis, and disturbed Count Arnulf, who deeply feared the destruction of a future vengeance; when he learned that Richard, duke of the Northmen, was joining himself to the daughter of the great duke Hugh in marital union for the sake of descendants and succession, and that, serving him for her sake and for the assistance of every consolation, he was binding himself to him through the appropriate service of a united friendship and an indissoluble alliance—they were terrified by excessive fear lest they be crushed and subjugated by the forces of so many soldiers belonging to the two great dukes.

After the embassy of each side had been carried out and reported, they met one another in the district of Vermandois and began to consider what they should do concerning the destructive alliance of the two dukes, joined in a sworn conspiracy.

Count Arnulf said to King Louis, desiring with all his strength to destroy and annihilate the young Duke Richard in the flower of his youth:

“The father of the great duke Hugh, Robert, with the support of Rollo, the grandfather of Duke Richard, unjustly seized the scepter of this government from your father Charles and wickedly subjected nearly all France to himself.

“When an immense quarrel arising from such a severe dispute grew, and France, devastated by the destructive conflict of two kings, mournfully endured the execrable strife of an accidental calamity, your father Charles, deprived entirely of the hope of Frankish assistance and in every respect lacking supporting aid, quickly sought King Henry of the Transrhenan lands. He promised him the kingdom of Lotharingia if Henry would strike against King Robert, who had been set over him through the execrable audacity of the Franks, and, gathering an army, come with him into France and boldly wage war against Robert.

“What happened in that conflict in the course of those times is known to none of our people as an untested matter. Robert deservedly perished in battle, and your father, King Charles, rightly obtained the reins of the kingdom.

“But Hugh, Robert’s son, infected with the poison of that same presumptuous rashness, is attempting to seize the scepter of this kingdom over you and to destroy both you and me, your faithful servant, entirely, having won the duke of the Northmen to his side. It is therefore fitting, most powerful king, to consider how you may preserve and govern the kingdom of France. For the princes of this land obediently adhere to Hugh and willingly serve him.”

Against these words King Louis replied to Count Arnulf:

“Give me counsel by which I may resist the arrogant insolence of Hugh, protect myself, and defend my kingdom.”

The deceitful Count Arnulf, wishing to destroy and annihilate Duke Richard with all his people, so that he might not avenge his father’s undeserved death in days to come, began to encourage the king with fraudulent words:

“I shall give you sound and favorable counsel, by which you will be able to crush and overthrow Hugh and Richard. Give Otto, your wife’s brother, the kingdom of Lotharingia, which your father promised to his father, the king of the Transrhenan lands, so that, laying waste to Hugh’s land, which resists you as far as Paris, he may besiege and capture Rouen for you.

“Once enriched with the abundant resources of that land, surrounded by a great multitude of nobles, and remarkably strengthened by the defenses of such cities, you will be able to wage war against Duke Hugh without fear.

“For the land of Normandy is more abundantly filled than all others with every kind of resource. It is richly supplied with hunting of boars, deer, bears, and roebuck; it is stocked with many kinds of young from every sort of wild and domesticated bird; it is fertile in fish of various species; and it is generous in all the good things its inhabitant needs.

“You ought to possess a land of such abundance, since your grandfather, great-grandfather, and other ancestors held it on account of these very things. Remember the evils and injuries that the Northmen deceitfully inflicted upon you. You will easily be able to wipe out their multitude from that land, because they are timid foreigners and accustomed to practice piracy at sea. The land of Normandy is greater in value, strength, and abundance than the land of Lotharingia.”

Persuaded by these and similar arguments, King Louis is said to have replied to Count Arnulf:

“A count of such nobility and a prince of such cunning and prudence ought faithfully to accomplish what he wisely advises his lord. Therefore, since you are better known to all my people, more credible, and more powerful than the others, I beg you to convey to King Otto what you have devised as an honorable counsel for the sake of its execution.

“Through your vigorous intervention, let him assemble all the warlike forces under his authority and come; laying waste to Hugh’s possessions up to the walls of Paris, let him compel Hugh, by the destruction caused by that disastrous overthrow, to recover his senses; let him utterly crush him with many acts of plunder and burning; acquire for us, in exchange for the kingdom of Lotharingia, the kingdom of the Northmen; drive its rebellious inhabitants out beyond its borders; let the Saxon strength test the land of Normandy, and, if it is able to struggle against it, let it prove its power; let it besiege and capture Rouen for us, and, capturing Richard, the youth of such great arrogance, treat him as worthless.”

Count Arnulf, eagerly desiring utterly to destroy Richard—described in the text as “of sacred memory” [anomalous]—lest he avenge his father’s innocent blood, hastened to King Otto of the Transrhenan lands. Coming before him, he addressed him in the most humble words:

“King Louis of the Franks offers you the gift of a dear and unbreakable friendship. Unable to endure the destructive contention and rashness of Duke Hugh and Richard, count of the Northmen, he sends me to you so that, through your compassion, you may provide him some assistance.

“Hugh is joining his daughter to the young Richard in marital alliance and marriage. Richard, having become Hugh’s man, obeys him in everything as his lord out of love for him. Encouraged by Hugh and by a thousand soldiers, he is preparing to invade the kingdom of France and hastening to possess its reins and scepters, just as his father once did.

“We beg you, blunt the arrogance of their presumptuous will by your strength and destroy the boastfulness of their perverse pride by your power. If you fulfill the wish of our petition, and if by besieging Rouen you acquire the kingdom of the Northmen for us, we shall give you forever the kingdom of Lotharingia, which had been promised to your father in return for the battle magnificently fought on the field of Soissons.”

Otto rejoiced at the message of the desired embassy. He assembled and united a very large force from the eastern lands, made an agreement concerning the kingdom, and came swiftly, laying waste to everything, while King Louis met him with a great army near Paris.

When all Hugh’s possessions had been consumed and devastated, Count Arnulf said to King Otto:

“This city, girded on every side by the everlasting ribbon of the Seine, stands impregnable against every people that might attack it. We therefore beg you to turn the army of so many legions toward the district of Rouen, for before you reach the borders of the Northmen’s countryside, the keys of that city will be brought to you.”

### Apostrophe to Arnulf

Why do you desire harsh, stubborn, wicked, arrogant, and evil kings to check the power and will of God, who knows all things, whose work endures and whose heat reaches all things?

Although your sword struck the worthy duke—alas, the father of this holy boy—so that he might become a holier, life-giving witness of God, your frivolous vows will not foresee the outcome you desire.

But behold: a more life-giving count, a wealthier margrave, and a duke holier than all—noble, renowned, pious, just, life-giving, upright, holy, harmless, and good—will now establish every good and crush every evil.

King Otto, compelled by the persuasive arguments of many kinds of petitions, moved the army of such great multitude and, protected by King Louis, encamped above the stream of the Epte, which by a boundary of separation limits the kingdoms of France and Normandy.

Then Otto summoned Arnulf, the instigator of all the evil, and demanded the keys of Rouen, which Arnulf had promised would be brought to him.

Arnulf, with the cunning purpose of his mind, began to address King Otto:

“My lord king, no one from Rouen dares to attack you, because from here all the way to Rouen there is a wooded land, and bands of robbers live in its forests and groves, practicing brigandage. There is another watercourse nearby, called the Andelle, richly supplied with meadows and every kind of resource. We ask you to pitch your tents there tomorrow; then the nobles of Rouen will come there, bringing you the keys of the city and gifts of precious honor.”

King Otto, compelled by these pleading words, withdrew from that place and settled in the meadows beside the little river Andelle.

At dawn the count of deceitful cunning stood before King Otto, who was surrounded and resplendent with an assembly of bishops, dukes, and nobles. Wishing to punish the youth of Richard’s radiant adolescence and to lead the kings to Rouen, he said to Otto:

“Confused by the shame of future mockery, the people of Rouen are ashamed to send you the keys unless they are overwhelmed by the force of an enemy. Therefore, surrounded by the armies of two kings and so many dukes and nobles, they will not delay in surrendering the city to you.

“My lord King Louis earnestly begs you, therefore, to set out in the morning for Rouen. Send before your presence a very powerful legion to seize the city by hostile attack and, if it finds anyone standing outside for the sake of battle, to drive them fiercely back into the city. Then you may safely pitch your tents from here by the Beauvais Gate.

“When you have drawn near, your army and that of my lord will make them anxious, and in the first preparation for battle and in the ensuing clash we shall be able to observe what strength and courage this city possesses.”

Then a certain nephew of King Otto spoke with boastful words:

“My lord king, if you permit it, I shall go ahead and measure out your camp. If battles should break out against me, I shall crush their thousands with my sword. I shall test what kind of appearance, strength, and courage they possess in battle, and what caution, foresight, and prudence they display in war.

“I have often fought against Danes, Alans, Goths, and Huns, but I have never entered combat against the Northmen. Once the battle lines are prepared, I shall provoke them, storm the city, and scatter and disperse the people of this foreign nation.”

He spoke thus in youthful boasting, unaware of the varied and accidental outcome of battle. Immediately King Otto, compelled by the most humble royal entreaties and admonitions, advanced with his army at speed, sending before him his nephew of perverse arrogance with the legions drawn up.

### Apostrophe

Great King Otto, worthy of remembrance,

Why do you seek, with hostile assembly,

To tear apart and stain with malign effort

Richard, the celebrated and sacred,

Noble, just, upright, temperate,

A holy patrician margrave,

Now a duke, magnanimous and brave?

Why do you not, by powerful thought,

Resist the command of the highest King?

No one can resist the Most High,

Nor can anyone now turn back His celestial will.

This highest count, duke, and patrician,

This holy, celebrated, temperate margrave,

Will govern the people by laws of mercy;

Astute, he will torture the wretched accused,

And give worthy rewards to the just.

Shining with holy character and merits,

Thus he will climb to the gleaming stars of heaven.

But you, powerful and vigorous king,

Will be crushed by everlasting divine power;

You will lie beneath ridiculous mockery.

Thus, rejected by the Northmen,

You will go in shame to the court

Of your own seat.

When the nephew of King Otto approached the city gate called the Beauvais Gate, and with flashing cavalry and blazing arrogance attacked the Northmen in hostile battle with his lines drawn up, the Northmen, experienced in such struggles, pretended to flee and, as though defeated by their enemies, hurried back toward the city’s defenses.

The Saxons, delighted by the apparent flight and enamored of the outcome of such an encounter, pursued them in hostility. At last, when the king’s nephew had engaged them upon the bridge of the Beauvais Gate, he thought he would storm the city walls.

But the Northmen, armed and advancing against them from every side, leapt upon them like lions upon sheep. They began to tear them apart, throwing them down and killing them with flashing spears and swords, and cutting them to pieces with axes like wolves [the printed word bidentes is uncertain].

After many Saxons had been killed and many more crushed and wounded, the king’s nephew died upon the bridge beneath swords and lances. Finally, having won the victory, the Northmen captured many of the nobles in the deadly clash of battle.

When the remaining Saxons saw the king’s nephew lying dead upon the bridge, they seized him with great force and in a hard struggle, and, while the Northmen led many of their men captive to the city walls, they carried the dead man to the other battle lines.

When the quarrel of the hard and prolonged battle had been divided in this manner, the Saxons and Franks stood on one side and the Northmen on the other; the people of the Transrhenan lands no longer wished to mingle with them.

Meanwhile, the report of the deadly event struck King Otto, announcing the cruel death of his nephew; and the whole army was thrown into confusion by the news of so great a loss. Immediately, by common agreement, they attacked the city as enemies, wishing to avenge the blood of the young man held in such reverence. But the Saxons and Franks, accomplishing nothing around the city and lamenting excessively because so many of their soldiers had been killed, [Col. 0719C] returned to the camp, carrying away the corpses of the dead.

King Otto, saddened by the death of his nephew and by these misfortunes, and seeing the inhabitants of that land approaching the city from the opposite side, said to his nobles: “Can this city be encircled by our army, so that those who cross by ship may not pass beyond?” They replied: “By no means, because the single and undivided Seine, with its storms, washes the walls of the city; indeed, swollen and driven back by the waves of the sea, according to the appointed course of the waxing and waning moon, with the increase of the number seven, when the tide rises, it reaches the gates and walls of the city before us.”

Then King Otto sent to Richard, asking permission to go and pray at the shrine of Saint Audoen. Permission to pray having been granted, the king [Col. 0719D], with the bishops and commanders, laid aside his arms and went to the monastery situated in the suburb of the city, dedicated in honor and worship to Saint Peter and Saint Audoen. He himself and his men bestowed many gifts there. Then, remaining in the monastery, he summoned the nobles and said:

“Decide in your minds what ought to be done for us, and let each man state what seems right to him in this affair. Deceived by the request of King Louis and by the deceitful sophistry of Count Arnulf, we came here, where, instead of recovering honor, we are shamefully suffering loss, disgrace, and confusion of our honor. We have not been able to prevail against the Northmen by any hostile effort, because everything favorable is supplied to them through the channel of the Seine. I am therefore tormented by unbearable sadness and pierced by excessive anxiety; [Col. 0720A] for I cannot foresee what ought to be done amid the ruin of such disastrous events and misfortunes.

“You, who are older in age and understanding, and whose counsel I consult about the matters to be carried out, all of you carefully examine with the thought of inward reflection what ought honorably to be undertaken. If it pleases you, I could seize the wicked sophist Arnulf, bind him with chains, and send him to Count Richard, so that he might avenge upon him his father, because he deceitfully compelled both us and King Louis to hasten here, wishing to kill Duke Richard as he once did his father.”

Then the bishops and nobles answered King Otto, saying:

“It will be execrable and disgraceful in the eyes of all if he is captured and sent to Richard for punishment. The shame, dishonor, and disgraceful confusion and loss that you are suffering as a fitting return for your deserts will not be erased, because your army, oppressing Richard and his men by an unjust siege, remains here unjustly. Instead, give careful thought to a prudent departure and return from here, and observe with the greatest attention that nothing worse or more shameful befalls you.

“You have justly lost your nephew, your companions, your attendants, and very many soldiers in the quarrel of this siege, because you unjustly invaded and besieged this city. For, without deliberation, you hastened here at the suggestion of the crafty Arnulf; take care that you do not return without deliberation. From the sea as far as the Seine all the inhabitants are gathering, and after two years they are eager to attack you with their battle lines prepared.

“It is beyond our strength, counsel, and resources to remain here for a long period of time. King Louis greatly regrets having come here, because in prolonging this siege he knows that he is accomplishing nothing. Arnulf, entangled in many winding sophistries, having revealed the ingenuity of his falsehood, hides here and there and no longer wishes to speak with you.

“Therefore, weighing the matter again in the thought of inward reflection, consider what we Transrhenans ought to do in this siege. The city will not be captured, hostages will not be given, but an unconquerable loss will rapidly increase for us. Would that each of us, by the command of your order, were at the place where he first sought the land of his birth! But since our wishes are still of no avail, we beg you: turn your steps toward a favorable return, so that we may again seek the land of our birth.”

Thus, warned by these words [Col. 0720D], and fearing the destructive events of future danger, King Otto, as though restored to a proper state of mind, pondered for a long time and said to the nobles:

“Lest we suffer worse misfortunes by chance than those already endured, and lest our enemies rejoice any longer in the success of our loss, let us, if you wish, resume tomorrow the road by which we shall return.”

The Transrhenans approved this counsel in every respect. After prayers had been offered in the basilica of Saint Peter and Saint Audoen, they happily returned to their tents.

Count Arnulf, however, having learned from the report of certain men that he should take precautions lest he be captured, awakened his army in the silence of the dark night. He folded up the camps and tents, secretly and with all the equipment loaded onto horses and wagons, and set out at night, silently, cautiously, and secretly, making his way with all speed back to the fields of Flanders.

## APOSTROPHE

Otto, rise more swiftly, and flee now, quickly;

Seek the soil of your birth!

For the heavenly Avenger terrifies your ranks.

Rise now quickly—yield!

Your treacherous commander has vanished; behold, in flight,

Save yourself now, swift-footed!

Why do you still lie down against the will of God? Flee—

Go now, flee now, now, now.

When the Northmen’s army hinders you,

Alas, alas! You will go more shamefully.

Seek your step now, flee now, take up the road now;

Force the faithful to withdraw! [Col. 0721B]

Now, king, lest you perish, flee, yield, melt away;

Slip away, surrounded by the crowd!

The young Richard, noble, pious, and good,

Is already urging on a mighty host,

The supreme margrave, duke, patrician, and count,

And he longs to make you withdraw.

This ruler of the earth, wealthy, good, and wise—

Whether you wish it or not—stands forth.

He will distribute to the people the reins

Of laws and ordinances as a just judge.

After the mournful, deserved grief of loss,

He will worthily ascend Olympus.

## APOSTROPHE TO KING LOUIS

You whom royal splendor, a scepter flashing everywhere,

Displays as eminent; [Col. 0721C]

You whom royal offspring, issuing from either line,

Raises up through royal descent;

You whom it befits to exalt with the greatest effort,

If you perform royal deeds;

You whose great-grandfathers are said to have brought

Eighteen kingdoms into alliance with themselves—

Why do you desire so repeatedly to overthrow Richard,

That highly renowned young man?

Devoted to treachery, you will strive in vain

At all these things, and more than enough.

Now flee instead; this course is the better one,

On a swift and winged horse.

Once you wished to wage war against the Northmen—

What memory of that still touches you?

For, captured in the conflict of war,

You fell beneath countless misfortunes.

Now flee, yield, withdraw, take the road with rapid step,

If you wish to live!

Do not renew your quarrels against him

Whom the right hand of the heavenly Judge has sanctioned,

Whom the judgment of almighty God has predestined

By his character and merits,

Raising churches to lofty summits, so that he may

Build and establish them,

Protect and exalt the people, and, strengthened

By the sevenfold nectar of the heavenly Spirit,

Fortify, raise up, defend, and assist them,

And rescue them from their enemies; [Col. 0721D]

So that he may complete, adorn, tighten, and enlarge

The order and rank of monastic life,

And, compelling them to live by the established rule,

Force them into the service of the Most High;

And thus, gaining the fellowship of the heavenly crown,

He will live in the citadel of heaven.

## APOSTROPHE TO RICHARD

Richard, good, worthy of remembrance,

Worthy of reverence, worthy of love,

And gracious margrave, duke, and count—

For when you make the excessively fearful afraid,

Behold, fear falls upon them,

The fear of the Lord, the almighty King—

Do not now be anxiously afraid;

For, struck already in spirit

By God’s swift arrow, they will flee,

Many will be captured by your hands,

Many will die by the sword.

Thus they will scarcely return to their homeland.

You will tame the minds of peoples

As judge by laws.

But, by establishing churches,

You will urge their servants on

Through practical and theoretical work;

This threefold host of the order,

By the divinity of the sacred Trinity,

You will compel, drive, and constrain.

## APOSTROPHE

Delivered over to ambushes and gaping oars,

And to every evil,

Hated exceedingly, like rotten cattle,

A loathsome disaster, detestable,

Pestilential and harmful, indeed treacherous,

Injurious, a plague to all,

In word and deed and intention,

Guilty and subject to all—

Do not renew your quarrels any longer;

You will summon no one to lawsuits.

Cease opposing the young Richard,

A good man already predestined by God.

Margrave, patrician, duke, and count,

Chosen, gracious, and mighty,

Excellent, just, pious, and good,

Holy, temperate, and innocent,

Renowned as the summit of sacred religion,

And eminent as the pattern of the rule,

The supreme “idea” [Greek: ἰδέα] of this bright good,

He cherishes the Northmen’s people.

Thus the kings, terrified by the tumult of the common people during this nocturnal uproar and by the clatter of hoofed animals, and struck by excessive fear, supposed in the darkness of the night that Richard had arrived with his men for battle. Suddenly everyone shouted for safety, and confidence in life and hope of survival withdrew from them all. For they did not know what to do, wavering as to where their flight should turn. Their minds trembled amid their troubled circumstances, and their frightened hearts, unworthy of truth, wavered here and there.

One, clutching his sword, fled about like a madman; another, tearing away shields, wandered in a frenzy as though through hiding places. Some threw down tents and camps to the ground; others adorned their horses with harness. One ran here and there without knowing where; another, stupefied and trembling, remained fixed in a single stare. One searched for his superior amid the wavering and trembling crowd; another, unarmed among the mixed-up throng, felt his way about, shouting for his soldier. One sought flight on foot with rapid steps; others, urging their horses on with spurs, fled unarmed.

Some secretly concealed their triple-woven corselets and helmets decorated with gold; others claimed the royal ornaments and the remaining valuables for themselves. The great murmur of the terrified armies resounded loudly; and the inarticulate voice of the tumult and the clamor of the howls rang out in confusion [Col. 0723B].

For this reason, awakened by the tumultuous and plebeian clanging of this confused and high-soaring outcry, the people of Rouen, fearing that they might suddenly be forestalled at the dawn of the coming day [sic; perhaps “of the day”], fortified the city with armed guards. They themselves remained constantly awake, awaiting the sad outcome of the battle they desired.

But when dawn, flashing forth in a crimson garment, dried up the darkness of the shadowy night, and the appearance and perception of things returned, the Transrhenans began to set fire to their huts and to resume the road of their desired return, wandering fearfully here and there because they did not know the roads.

Duke Richard, however, a magnanimous leader, handsome with the flowering down of fitting youth, joyful and glad at the outcome of this affair, wished to attack them with all his men and battle lines prepared. But the people of Rouen, trying to dissuade the duke from his intention of an imminent engagement, said unanimously and gently:

“Most powerful lord duke, you are still in the tender years of youth, and you are the hope of our safety and confidence. We fear that, if you go, you may be overtaken by death. We believe that they are deceiving us by this pretense, and that, if we rush out of the city in this way, they intend to seize it. It is not our counsel that you engage with us in the battle of this conflict. Rather, whatever the outcome of this matter may be, guard the city manfully with the greater number of men. We will cautiously pursue them and try to harass them with arms.”

Richard, a young man of eminent nobility, was scarcely won over by this flattering persuasion and remained in the city with many men. The remaining troops of attendants and recruits pursued the royal armies, throwing many down and killing them [Col. 0723D].

At last, a certain division of the people of Rouen joined battle with them at the forest called Maliforaminis, and, with God’s help, defeated the enemy and won the triumph. Another group of Rouennais, waiting at the exits of the forests for the army of the two kings, overthrew and killed many of the enemy and drove the rest as far as the district of Amiens.

The Rouennais, having gained victory over their enemies and returning to the defenses of the city, reported to Richard everything that had happened. Then Richard, the margrave of memorable renown and most excellent duke and patrician, gave the greatest thanks to the King of the ages, with all the clergy and people, in the greatest gentleness. He joyfully distributed many benefits and gifts to the holy Church [Col. 0724A].

When these matters had been completed by divine direction, he began to be regarded as preeminent throughout all the land of the Northmen, Britons, Franks, and Burgundians. He shone because of the nobility of his lineage; he flourished with the ornament of virtues. He was illustrious in character and higher than the stars in merit. He gleamed in appearance and was second to none in compassion. The honey-tongued Ruler adorned the condition of the commonwealth, and he was known beyond the heavens for the reputation of every virtue.

By continual deeds, pursuits, examples, and teachings, he skillfully displayed all the advantages of goodness worthy of imitation. He was distinguished in countenance and still more distinguished than all others in every action. He shone sweetly in speech and was more agreeable than all in dress and gait. Bright of face, with honeyed speech, he was always serene and possessed the most joyful heart.

He burned with faith, hope, and charity, and with the twofold love of God and neighbor. He shone with prudent simplicity and flashed with simple prudence. He firmly settled quarrels, disputes, and conflicts, and ruled the people amicably, as a father rules his sons.

He overflowed with the benefits of goodness and instructed many by examples of virtue. In his household truth and glory dwelt; in his works equity and justice shone. The deeds of the Frankish and Burgundian nobles were directed by his foresight, and the useful affairs of the commonwealth were managed by his wisdom.

The tested reputation of his holiness, dignity, and abundance spread far and wide. The Flemings and the peoples of the East obeyed his command. But since a lamp placed upon a heavenly lampstand cannot remain hidden beneath the shadow of a bushel, he began to be regarded as preeminent among his own people, whom Christ the Lord had arranged to be revealed by wondrous signs [Col. 0724C].

A magnificent clergy and people obeyed the commands of so great a leader. Through the merciful assistance of almighty God and the diligent administration of their leader Richard, in those days the Church of Christ was beautiful and exceedingly lovely. At his instruction it was ordered according to sacred customs and illuminated by the insignia of virtues, having neither stain through crime nor wrinkle through duplicity.

It shone with the beauty of the sun in the exalted dignity of its prelates, and with the brightness of the moon in the humility of its subjects. He himself retained the state of an innocent life with the kindest disposition, and, with a most serene heart, adorned the governance of ecclesiastical administration, although he belonged to the lay order [Col. 0724D]. In deed, word, and prosperous thought he excelled all through the brightness of his merits and flashed with the splendor of his character.

Indeed, he was enriched more abundantly by the grace of the Holy Spirit and filled more fully with the wisdom of the sevenfold gift. Each day he grew more worthy through the abundance of merits and every good thing. With diligent and subtle inquiry he investigated everything that he could learn through lay understanding.

He was enriched with the honors of holiness and illuminated by the workings of magnificence, with the grace of the Holy Spirit going before him. He longed for heavenly things, thought little of vices, and increased the inhabitants of the Northmen’s land through law. He was a gentle young man, filled with every virtue, mature in the goodness of his character, and founded by Christ upon the steps of humility.

By word and deed he showed with what intention of mind he had been introduced to the salvation of the whole governance of his homeland [Col. 0725A]. He was the honeyed sweetness of the strong, the strength of the weak, the defender of orphans, the comforter of the wretched, the staff of the blind, the restorer of churches, the true light of the blind, the summit of clerics, the salvation of those who labor, the crown of nobles, the glory of bishops, the salvation of widows, the peak of priests, the lover of treaties, the cultivator of virtues, and the greatest hope of all.

He was the compassion of the sorrowful, the memorable pledge of friendships, the palm of the despairing, the protection of priests, the seat of laws, the ruler of peoples, the shepherd of the poor, the model of the good, the weapon of soldiers, the judgment of accusers and accused, the balance of legal questions, the appeaser of quarrels, the father of exiles, the receiver of refugees, the distributor of good things, the sweet love [Col. 0725B] of household servants, and the example of all.

He was the punishment of thieves, the loss of robbers, the corrector of confessors, the work of compassion, the wall of regions, the light of all, the pattern of holiness, the sweet head of consuls, the helper of kings, and the protector of all peoples.

## APOSTROPHE TO RICHARD

O Censor, whom the fame of renown raises from the western setting to the eastern dawn and to the sevenfold northern constellation—

Richard, patrician, count, duke, margrave, prince.

Burning with religion, flourishing with the ornament of virtues,

Gentle in address, renowned for the reward of goodness,

Preserving the path of judgment under the moderation of law.

Your great deeds surpass the little advocate,

Overwhelmed by the mass of manifold affairs.

Nor can he carry out what he always longs to write,

For the force of your eminent deeds has overcome his sluggishness,

Though he may be undeserving of whatever he strives to write.

Alas! May you flourish as God’s champion on the summit of the divine height.

May you possess joys with the saints through the pastures of peace.

When the celebrated margrave Richard, plainly Christ’s dove, without the gall of bitterness, shone with the titles of every virtue, and held the kingdom of the Northmen’s and Britons’ lands quiet and secure against its enemies, so that no people dared to make war against the descendants of Richard, Hugo, a great and remarkable duke, compelled by the weakness of his body, gathered his soldiers together and, lying at the point of death, said:

“I have entrusted my daughter, although she is still of tender age, to the most powerful duke of the Northmen, Richard, for a future marriage and union, under your oath and counsel. When she is of suitable age and fit for a husband, do not delay at all in giving her to him. Let him be the advocate of my wife and my son while my son is of that age; and willingly adhere to his most salutary counsels and commands.”

After Hugh, duke of the Franks, died, all came unanimously to Richard, the margrave of such great power, and committed themselves to the protection of his counsel and guardianship. They willingly devoted themselves to his service and gladly served him as their own lord.

He enriched them with exceedingly great gifts and wondrous presents and increased them with the most generous benefits. They loved him with the whole affection of their minds and honored him with the highest reverence. They humbly obeyed his commands and words and obediently followed his orders [Col. 0726A].

He ruled them gently, as a master of a household rules servants, and nourished them sweetly with the most kindly support, as a father nourishes his sons. By his counsel the useful affairs of the more hidden order, laboring in the arena of the theoretical life, were administered; and by his care the useful works of the order leading a more active life were adorned. That is, while it struggled in the contest of practical life, he compelled the governing authorities to rule the commonwealth firmly, gently, and mildly, and he threatened and demanded that they wrong no one.

While Duke Richard, wise and just in the moderation of the laws, governed almost the whole land of Gaul beneficially, the citizens of heaven rejoiced and offered immeasurable praises to the undivided Trinity. All the earth rejoiced, singing to the Lord with gladness [Col. 0726B]. All clapped their hands in the heights and gave thanks to the Almighty, who had granted them a patrician and duke renowned for such an increase of good things.

The Northmen, rejoicing in so great a censor and advocate, and wishing not only to enjoy him while he was present but also thinking about the future, so that the glory of offspring might not be lacking to the man and that the succession of generations might not leave the people without the man’s descendants, came to him and said:

“In every matter whose settlement is determined among orthodox people by the oath of true faith, it is worthwhile that the agreement be fulfilled within the indefinite span of the appointed time. Therefore, the daughter of Hugh, the great duke of the Franks, whom, while he was alive, you confirmed by oath as bound to you in marriage, ought, before the appointed limit of the established time, to be joined to you in a marriage worthy of the marital law, if she is suitable, capable, and marriageable.

“She is, as we have heard, a maiden of exceptionally elegant appearance and beauty, fit for the joining of a marriage and pleasing for the embrace of a suitable sexual union; she does not shrink from yielding to the strength of male seed.”

Richard, it is said, replied to his men with the power of virile abundance: “What has been confirmed by faith is bound to be fulfilled; consequently, it must be carried out.”

Immediately the resources for the wedding expenses were prepared, and the marriage gifts of wondrous arrangement were adorned. Thus, having summoned the nobles of the Northmen’s and Britons’ lands and prepared everything necessary for the fescennine celebration, he led her decently and honorably, amid an uncountable gathering of princes, to the palace of the city of Rouen.

## APOSTROPHE

O Northmen nobles, eager for the prosperity

Of the desired offspring, yet ever greedy and unworthy,

And warlike, burning with the fire of lively mind:

From this maiden who is being conveyed no offspring

Will be born to rule the people as heir.

But, by divine will and heavenly design, a maiden

Will one day arise from the Dacian stock,

Noble, gracious, beautiful, highly renowned, and revered,

Worthy, specially chosen, and worthy of remembrance,

Cautious in counsel, provident, and wise.

Richard, the just duke and margrave,

Will choose her alone from among many for himself,

Joining her to himself in marriage, bond, and covenant;

And, as time advances, an heir worthy

Of the gracious stock will be born.

When he was rejoicing in the fitting companionship of a wife of such nobility, bringing tranquility by salutary justice to the peoples of the Britons’ and Northmen’s homeland, and throughout almost all Gaul and Burgundy restraining by the authority of worthy power the sudden disturbances of evils that were rising up through salutary counsel, a certain satrap named Tetboldus, rich in possessions and abundantly supplied with soldiers, inflamed by stepmotherly furies and burning with jealousy and hatred, began to plot against him with many mockeries, to quarrel against him, and to attack his land without success.

When he decided that he was accomplishing nothing against him [Col. 0727B], he went to Queen Gerberga and her son, Lothair, king of the Franks, who were staying at Laon. By many entreaties he began to urge them to deceive Richard and remove him from such great honor.

Infected with the poison of jealousy, he said to the king and his mother:

“It is astonishing to me and to everyone that Count Richard, holding the kingdom of the Northmen and Britons, remains at peace, yet, lifted up over the Franks with presumptuous audacity, rules arrogantly above all others. He serves neither God nor anyone else; rather, in the boastfulness of his presumption, with an irreverent mind and an unbridled heart, he trusts in himself.

“He thinks nothing of any one of our people, and, like a king, rules and governs the Franks with proud dominion. By his counsel all the things that are harmful to the people of Francia are administered. It is not to your honor or ours that such a count should rule over us.

“It is a disgrace to your authority that he commands the Burgundians, rebukes and censures the Aquitanians, rules and governs the Britons and Northmen, threatens and devastates the Flemings, and joins the Danes and Lotharingians to himself and brings them into alliance. The English too submit obediently to him; the Scots and Irish are governed under his protection.

“All the peoples of all the kingdoms serve and obey him. There is no one except you who can resist his insolent boldness and that of his soldiers. More and more, and beyond measure, he grows stronger and prevails, and, trusting in his overflowing mass of soldiers, he does not come to his senses.

“See to it that he does not attempt to invade the kingdom inherited by you, and drive you out and expel you from it. If you held what he unjustly holds, you could claim all the kingdoms for yourself.”

After hearing these words of deceitful circumlocution, the saddened and agitated queen continued, addressing Tetboldus:

“You are privy to our secret and the faithful secretary and counselor of our more hidden counsel. Give us counsel concerning these matters. Supported by the strength of no assistance except God’s, we beg you, moved by compassion, to come mercifully to our aid in this affair. We are surrounded and oppressed on every side, and nowhere is trustworthy faith to be found.”

Count Tetboldus, desiring to destroy by deceit Richard, a patrician of such virtue, then offered the queen this counsel.

## APOSTROPHE

“Alas, why do you still rage, burning, O Arnulf, with hatred and treachery,

Overwhelmed and torn apart by the torches of jealousy?

Cease plotting against the will and power of heaven.

The labor you now turn over in your heart is utterly empty.

He cannot be captured whom God’s right hand sanctions and protects.

For the just, good, harmless, holy, and highly renowned

Richard, margrave, patrician, count, duke, and gracious lord,

Endowed with the shining store of fourfold virtue,

Corrects, increases, protects, assists, saves, and cherishes

The people entrusted to him, like a father.”

“If your son, King Lothair, sets out against his most strongly fortified cities with the military force of all Gaul and Burgundy, he will fight against Richard if he chooses to resist. If not, Richard will establish himself in the strongest defenses of the safest cities.

“Finally, gathering together an army of Christians and pagans, Richard will ravage everything and attack his cities; and if he should happen to capture them, he will securely hold the kingdoms of the Franks and Burgundians.

“It is wiser and more suitable to capture him by some deceit than to devastate his realm and besiege his cities, because we shall accomplish nothing on this expedition. He will observe the purpose of our intention and thus guard himself more cautiously.

“Instead, send an envoy to your brother Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, namely the eminent duke of Lotharingia, so that he may come to you on account of this affair of error and deceive Richard, a man of such exaltation, by some cunning sophistry.”

Immediately the queen sent to Bruno and conveyed to him the whole course of this deception. Bruno at once set out for Francia, and, coming to the district of Vermandois, sent a certain bishop to tell Richard deceitfully:

“Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, though unworthy, offers you the gift of his faithful prayers. Since our lord well knows what the Gospel says when it reports, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God,’ he earnestly asks you to come quickly against him in the district of Amiens.

“For he has heard of the quarrels rising up against you, and with burning heart he wishes, for love of you, to calm their swelling. He will reconcile you and his nephew the king in an unbreakable bond; he will make peace between you, Tetboldus, and the other ill-wishers, removing their destructive intention.

“He intends to restrain and pacify by the law of proper authority all the kingdoms of his nephew’s dominion and to tear apart and crush every quarrel. He desires to bind everyone to the loyalty of his nephew, and thus, after calming the storms of quarrels and establishing peace among all, to return to his own lands.”

Then Richard, the most gracious margrave, deceived by these treacherous words, began to go against Bruno with his faithful men. When he had reached the district of Beauvais, while Bruno was at Amiens, on the day appointed for their meeting, two men of Tetboldus came to him, saying, as though inspired by divine will:

“Duke, we wish to speak with you in secret.”

When Richard withdrew with them, they said:

“Duke, is it better to be duke of the Northmen than, outside your own land, to be a shepherd of sheep and goats?”

Count Richard remained fixed in a single gaze and astonishingly motionless, giving them no word of reply; and they were greatly astonished. When he examined what the proposition meant, and, as though withdrawn into himself, he said to the two men:

“From where are you, or whose faithful men are you?”

They answered: “What do you mean, ‘whose’? Are we not yours?”

Richard, perceiving that they were his faithful men but that they did not wish to reveal whose men they were, thanked them and bade them farewell, honoring them privately and especially. To one he gave a sword with a shining golden hilt worth four pounds [Col. 0729B]; to the other he gave a bracelet made of the same amount of pure gold.

When they had departed, he reported what they had told him to his nobles. They reconsidered and interpreted the proposition, with its great denunciation and comparison, and compelled him to return within the walls of Rouen and to send an envoy to Bruno to announce that he would not come to the appointed meeting.

When the envoy announced to Archbishop Bruno that Richard would not come to the meeting, Bruno was astonished and supposed that Richard had perceived the plan of such a great deception. He said to the envoy:
