“Go quickly and tell the great Duke Richard to come at least to the little river Epte, if he wishes to have rest and an increase of peace from his enemies; and I will set out there for love of him, to bring him comfort.”

Then the envoy replied: “He will not come against you to the meeting, either because of me or because of any of your men at present.”

Blocked by this answer, and with the treachery of such a great betrayal entirely exposed, Bruno returned to his own people in shame.

## APOSTROPHE

Behold, many are plotting,

O gracious Richard,

Great duke and patrician,

And gracious count to all,

To subjugate you by force

Through crafty cunning;

Each man turns over deceit,

By which to destroy you unjustly.

Therefore strive bravely;

Fight with hope and faith;

Strive with shining strength,

With merits and just reward,

So that you may always flourish

In diligent virtue,

And hold the balance and path

Of what is just and right.

You will enjoy such a destiny

That you will never be captured;

Rather, you will flourish through the ages,

Now and throughout all time.

Then throughout all Francia, Burgundy, and the other kingdoms, the report of such a betrayal and such deceit was made public, and Bruno, Tetboldus, and the other agents of such a plan and cunning were condemned by everyone [Col. 0730A].

But Duke Richard, the most holy of men, rescued from the snares of such deception and cunning, gave more devout thanks each day to the King of kings, who mercifully delivered him from the danger of death and captivity.

Thus he was always subject to Christ the Lord in all his works, armed with every strength of devotion and gentleness. Preeminent in character and merits, worthy to be the advocate of the holy Northmen’s Church, full of faith, most steadfast in hope, and most generous in charity, he obeyed God’s commands and trusted in the divine promises.

Rich in the abundance of possessions and virtues, he was diligent in divine worship and worldly affairs. Teachable in action, long-suffering in hope, wise in conversation, and prudent in counsel, he was constant and vigorous in correction, ardent in love of God and neighbor, patient in adversity, and strong in dangers. In divine and secular disciplines he was gentle and most generous in almsgiving.

Constant in the study of good works and anxious through fear of death, he was eminent in fear of God and magnificent in his lay order and manner of life. At the funeral rites of all he was most devout, in mercy and compassion glorious, endowed with outstanding intelligence and vigorous in every work.

Distinguished in judgment and justice, he was terrifying in severity toward the guilty and gentle in kindness toward the good. He was ready to extend favor according to merits and prepared to forgive those who offended him. Supreme in the steps of humility, he was preeminent in every service of hospitality.

He was a nourisher of monks and canons and a most compassionate and provident advocate of his flocks [Col. 0730C]. He was a faithful steward of the talent entrusted to him and an eminent moderator of quarrels. He sang of his own fault while punishing another’s severely. He cherished the people as a father cherishes his children, faithfully fulfilling Christ’s commands.

For your sake he sometimes conquered by arms and sometimes by patience; he subjected pagans to the lightest and sweetest yoke of Christ. He was the strongest defender of his homeland and the most holy comforter of widows.

Prudent, magnanimous, good, and temperate, he increased the peoples under established laws. He was an outstanding father to exiles and the needy, an incomparable comforter of orphans and minors, and he supplied abundant food to the poor. He shone as a constant restorer of churches.

He honored the sacred orders and ranks of the Churches above all others with wondrous reverence, and adorned all things monastic [Col. 0730D]. Attentive, benevolent, and teachable in every work, he examined and weighed the complaints of accusers and accused with an equal balance.

In judgment he did not regard the persons of poor or powerful people with any form of reverence. Rather, after removing the uncertainty of a scrupulous matter, he reviewed and judged the complaints of those who contended. In every affair he surpassed all in merits and deeds, and he was wondrous to everyone through the consideration of his goodness and honor.

He despised the arrogant and wicked, punished the rebellious and guilty, exalted the humble and benevolent, and trampled down robbers and unjust men. He encouraged the recruits of his household to serve by rewards and gifts, and enriched the older men abundantly with benefits.

Hardly anyone dared to inflict injury in his kingdom, and no one dared to steal anything from anyone [Col. 0731A]. Everyone lived securely under his rule, and all hastened diligently to perform every duty assigned to them.

## APOSTROPHE

With poured-out prayers, I, your suppliant reader, speak to you,

You who know and are well able in the sevenfold art.

My eloquence fails: I cannot raise him up

With as many praises as would be fitting.

The evils he has calmed and the goods he has bestowed

Cannot be compressed into verse or yield to words.

If anyone were a chief judge and governor of affairs,

He could write truthfully whatever he wished of this illustrious guardian

And defender of his homeland, this good duke,

Count, margrave, and patrician.

But I, foolish and dull, lacking every kind of reason,

[Col. 0731B] am unable to write or say what I desire—

the virtues of this man, recorded in a book of such distinction,

who sits upon his starry throne.

As these and many other acts of courage were scattered here and there, and as his abundant generosity in diverse matters was proclaimed ever more widely, Count Tetbold was consumed by tormenting envy and fury. Filled with the poison of malice and treachery, he daily urged King Lothar to deceive Richard, a man of such great dignity, by guile, and to hold Normandy beneath the yoke of his authority.

At last King Lothar, blinded by the count’s sophistical suggestions, sent a messenger to Richard to address him with deceitful words:

“Until when shall I await some sign of your repentance and reconsideration, while you so often regard me as a man of no account among any people?” Supported by the assistance of your enemies, could I not besiege and capture—apart from those of your friends—the cities of your fortifications? Will you never submit to anyone? Do you not know that I am king of the Franks? Could I not wrong you if, having gathered the forces that are mine by right, I hastened resolutely against you?

“If I believe your envious men, and you in turn favor my perjured and faithless enemies in your mind and heart, we shall never be reconciled by an agreeable treaty. Cease examining such matters, and let it please you to rejoice and celebrate with me. Let us therefore bind ourselves together by suitable agreements of mutual goodwill, so that none of our men may possess anything by his own arbitrary power. If anyone engages in quarrel or strife against you or me, let me crush and destroy your adversary, and you mine.

“Let us be of one heart, one mind, and one will; let us crush, scatter, and subjugate Tetbold and his followers. As for the Flemings and the other peoples who rebel against us, let us afflict them with the yoke of a dreadful law, and compel them to serve us and submit to our power. Therefore hasten to come against me swiftly at the appointed meeting, so that, bound together by an indissoluble agreement of friendship, we may rejoice as one, secure from enemies and adversaries.”

**Apostrophe**

Lothar, merciful, pious, just, and holy king,

upright, modest, noble, the kindly light of the world:

why do you plot deception, infected with filthy envy,

against Richard, the holy and just duke?

[Col. 0732A] Soon you will be ashamed to have conceived this perverse

and inglorious desire—alas, to have wished it.

Yet your wicked desire will not attain its power.

Thus Richard, the most excellent duke and count, deceived by the false embassies of these flatteries and threats, set out with a military force against King Lothar for the appointed meeting.

But the king secretly gathered Richard’s enemies around him: Tetbold of Chartres, Gozfrid of Anjou, and Count Baldwin of Flanders. Having covertly assembled a large army of Richard’s enemies, he remained by the little river Helnae with treacherous intent.

On the day appointed for the meeting, when it had deceitfully been arranged that they should enter into alliance, the great Duke Richard sent scouts to report to him what was being done at the king’s camp, to discover who was with the king, and whether any deception lay hidden in the proceedings of the meeting.

When they arrived there, they found Tetbold and the other enemies of Duke Richard in the king’s presence. At this they were exceedingly astonished, since they were awaiting the king’s orders.

While they remained for a short time before the king, behold, the mailed and helmeted armies of Counts Tetbold, Gozfrid, and Baldwin came upon the scene, advancing from every side with swift cavalry and eager, as they had been ordered, to attack Richard and his men in hostile combat.

When the scouts saw this, each signaled to the others that they should quickly report to Count Richard what they had seen. Then one of them, mounted upon the back of a swift horse, hastened back to the most worthy Count Richard, outstripping all the troops and crying out with great lamentation:

“Lord, lord, most mighty duke, save yourself lest you perish through the savagery of the enemy! For all your enemies have joined the king and are eager either to capture you and your men or to kill you.”

When he heard this, the fearless Duke Richard rose and, summoning his faithful men, said:

“Behold, our meal is prepared. Before we depart, let us taste it in the name of the Lord. Thus fortified by the banner of the most holy Cross, let us await the enemy’s battalions without fear. Their wickedness and treachery will deservedly wear them down, while the uprightness of pure faith and hope will rescue us.

“Do not let the attack of their perverse multitude terrify you; rather, let the memory of your robust predecessors in every adversity make you strong.”

While he sat at the meal and uttered these and many other exhortations, and while many of his faithful men were absent, another messenger came to report that the enemy’s lines were present.

When the most holy Duke Richard asked how many thousands of men the king had, and whether the king himself was present for the hostile encounter, a third messenger arrived, his horse driven on by spurs. He said to him:

“Lord duke, behold, the king and his army, armed in iron and drawn up in battle formation, are hastening to engage you.”

As he recounted this in a trembling voice, armed men appeared, rushing forth in battle array on every side. Then the incomparable duke and count Richard, seeing the danger now close at hand, rose immediately, abandoned his meal, withdrew from them, and crossed beyond the channel of the Dieppe, where he awaited the army of his reinforcements.

But the king’s army seized the fords of the Dieppe so that his forces could not come to him. Some of Richard’s enemies pursued the duke and attacked him in the middle of the ford.

While they were struggling there in combat, Duke Richard recognized one of his own huntsmen, named Walter. Fearlessly he ran there with his household men, rescued Walter, and put the other enemies to flight or death. He then stood against the entire royal army at the outlet of the little river Dieppe.

As the army of the king and his enemies converged from every side, the elders who were defending the approaches to the ford said to Duke Richard:

“Magnanimous lord duke, by God’s favor the fraud of this treachery and the deceit of this wicked deception have been exposed. Therefore, we beg you, do not let yourself be overtaken by death or captured; withdraw, and hasten on horseback to the city of Rouen, lest your enemies reach it before us by a faster route and claim it for themselves when they find it empty of soldiers.”

But Duke Richard rejected their counsel and wished to attack the approaching ranks with his recruits. When the elders saw that he persisted in his purpose and would not heed their words of salutary advice, they seized him by the reins of his bridle and urged him to withdraw.

At last, compelled with difficulty by the pleas of the older soldiers, he withdrew and hastened toward Rouen lest he be captured.

As soon as the rumor of the detestable, conspiratorial deception of the meeting became known, all the people of that region quickly flocked to the great Duke Richard, pressing him incessantly with repeated and varied admonitions [Col. 0733C] to repay King Lothar and Count Tetbold in kind for the deception they had contrived, by invading their kingdom.

He himself daily gave devout thanks to the King of kings, who had rescued him from the destruction of death or captivity. For this reason he honored churches more fully with hangings and monastic furnishings, and with a generous hand supplied the poor more abundantly with food and drink, devoting himself diligently to the service of God.

He weighed judgments more justly in the balance of righteous examination; restraining quarrels, lawsuits, and dissensions, he governed the people with moderation. He carried out every good work with greater skill and became more perfect in all his deeds through submission to God.

He supported orphans, foster-children, and exiles more gently, like a father supporting his sons, and more graciously comforted widows and refugees. He urged monks, canons, and laymen to serve God more strictly; rejecting pagans and criminals, he wisely nourished the people under his protection with the encouragement of security.

**Apostrophe to the City**

O city made more fertile by so many things,

by the fruitfulness of goodness and by sacred soldiers!

Behold your prudent, pious, holy, and good duke,

rescued from the plots of so many nobles,

performing the works of God and those fitting for you

along the straight path of judgment in all things.

But since I was not once your inhabitant,

I do not know how to relate what he strove to accomplish.

Would that you possessed loquacious poets

[Col. 0734A] who could labor to set forth the good things he undertook!

Your lack of rulers is the fault of your poets.

Now train countless boys in the arts,

so that whatever the successor of the great father accomplishes

they may know how to elaborate in many-voiced song.

Meanwhile, the goodness of so great a patron and duke was proclaimed more widely throughout all Europe. Tetbold, infected with the poisonous envy of treachery, again sought King Lothar and said to him with deceitful intent:

“Will you endure the presumption of rebellious Richard’s quarrel and allow his arrogance to persist in your kingdom? Will he hold the kingdom of Normandy without your grant of authority? How will you now be called king by right if you cannot rule the kingdom of the Franks?

“Moreover, perhaps, having summoned the Danish race, he is resolved to invade the kingdom under your authority with the arrogance of his pride, just as his grandfather Rollo once did against your grandfather Charles. Against the schemes of this presumptuous cunning I will give you counsel for successful and salutary assistance.

“Invade, besiege, and capture the city of Évreux for me; I shall claim the whole region of Normandy for you.”

The king, delighted and pleased by these promises, sent to all his faithful men that they should come to him for hostile combat. Having suddenly assembled the princes of all France and Burgundy, he advanced, besieged Évreux, and captured it in a sudden assault; then, as a voluntary gift in accordance with the agreement, he gave it to Tetbold.

**Apostrophe**

Renowned, nobly worthy, and exalted,

greatest marquis and revered duke,

guardian and defender of clergy and people,

ruler of the people, just and nourishing,

unfailing protector of orphan and exile,

kind comforter of the widow,

through these unexpected reversals of fortune

your modest purpose will not diminish.

Nor should you be lifted up by doubt;

misfortunes increase for themselves.

Now the one whom he honors tears him cruelly,

like Pyrrhus, eternal, restoring him,

like a father sweetly reviving his offspring.

What you now accomplish, always accomplish;

what you now perform, continue to perform.

The city secretly taken from you

will be returned to you by the supreme judge.

Thus the most powerful Duke Richard, saddened and grieved by the sudden turn of these events, summoned the strongest legions of the Norman army. Relying upon an innumerable military force, he marched against Tetbold, ravaged and burned the regions of Chartres and Dunois, and returned without fear.

After the armies of the great Duke Richard had dispersed and returned to their own places, Count Tetbold secretly gathered his army and slipped into Norman territory.

When the great Duke Richard learned from certain informants that Tetbold was approaching and attacking Norman territory, he sent a certain Richard to report swiftly what size army he had.

Richard, advancing by rapid horseback to the place where Tetbold was staying, found some of Tetbold’s men separated from the army and killed them. Covered in the blood of the slain, he reported to Duke Richard that Count Tetbold was present.

When the great Duke Richard saw him bloodstained, with his weapons soaked in blood, he said to those standing nearby:

“This man was indeed present with his followers in the battle.”

Then he asked him: “How many thousands of his army are there, and on which side of the Seine is he attacking our borders?”

He replied: “Three thousand, and on the left bank of the Seine, which is the Évreux side; he is advancing against us in hostility.”

The great duke said to him:

“If he wished to fight against us or to besiege the city of Rouen, he would hasten to attack us from the opposite side, where the city rises. But because the deep waters of the Seine stand as an obstacle between us and them, and he lacks ships by which to cross, he is not attempting to challenge us in war at all. Rather, he intends, with cruel disgrace to us, to ravage and burn the country under our authority.

“But we have ships. Let us take our nobles and cross over to them, and let us discover between us what may please God.”

After saying this, he sought the church of the holy Mother of God, placed a pallium as a precious gift upon her altar, and took refuge in the aid of efficacious prayer.

But God, who resists the proud and exalts and raises up the humble, heard the most humble request of his devout prayer.

Count Tetbold, however, continued wickedly to pursue his malicious purpose in the land of Normandy. Advancing with a densely packed, iron-clad battle line, he came as far as the houses of the estate of Hermentrude, situated at the river-port on the opposite side of the Seine from Rouen.

The most valiant Marquis Richard sought a vessel at the other port. Crossing the channel of the Seine throughout the night, he fell upon Tetbold at dawn and entered battle against him with only a few men.

In the first encounter of the battle they fought with shortened darts and lances; in the second, with flashing swords.

Then the powerful hand of the Normans, joining and interlocking their shields with one another, advanced in a flashing line of swords, attacked the armed Franks who stood in opposition, and, tearing them apart on right and left, overthrowing them and breaking their ranks, cut through the enemy’s formations. Riding over the corpses of the slain, they turned the battle against the dense ranks that remained on every side.

Here and there the slaughter of the Franks arose; many different hands were punished and killed. The warlike and savage Norman people swept through the dangers of battle like wolves through sheepfolds, fiercely killing and overthrowing the enemy’s ranks.

When Richard’s men cried out with one accord that the field of battle belonged to the great Duke Richard, the confidence to fight withdrew from all Tetbold’s men, and the cry for their lives was raised.

Each man did not know where to turn in order to save himself, or where to hide himself in concealment. Some concealed themselves amid the dense thickets where light was blocked out; others hid in marshes thickly rooted with alders, poplars, and other trees, lest they be killed by the Normans.

**Apostrophe**

You would have seen forests and open fields seething with fresh slaughter,

corpses of the dead lying everywhere, and mutilated bodies,

which the savage country people stripped of their clothing,

while the foaming streams reddened with sacred blood;

you would have seen each man devising various forms of death for himself,

and blood smoking upon the warm grass,

and Duke Richard rejoicing after the slaughter was completed,

with his joyful soldiers—if only you had been there.

At last Count Tetbold, deprived of his faithful men, who had been routed, overthrown, and killed, sought the aid of flight with a few companions and hastened away. Spurring their horses, they did not turn toward Évreux, which his men held.

That day he deservedly experienced the misfortune of the fourfold loss suffered by the blessed Marquis Richard: he saw his faithful men overthrown in battle; he himself was routed and wounded; one of his sons was overtaken by death and perished; and the city of Chartres and its stronghold were utterly consumed by fire and collapsed.

Richard, the marquis most famous for his goodness, weary from the battle and the long pursuit of the enemy, returned to Rouen in the evening.

Rising at dawn, he went out to the field of battle. Finding six hundred and forty dead, he grieved compassionately at the burial of so many and ordered them to be buried. Those who were still alive he had gently carried on litters to Rouen and treated.

Moreover, he ordered the woods and marshes to be searched, and found many dead and wounded, to whom he rendered the same compassionate service.

**Apostrophe**

Through the blue depths flows the Seine, its swelling river,

and its wandering current stirs immense expanses,

gently licking the fragrant banks where the grass blooms,

washing softly the tresses of the herbs with its swift wave;

when the returning sea twists back its current,

driven backward by the waves of the threatening waters,

the sevenfold [text uncertain] changes its courses or suffers its growth.

The hills, clothed in shadow and shining vine branches,

surround the delightful fields and noble vineyards.

The meadows gleam sufficiently under the irrigating courses of the waters;

there the city now called Rouen shines in great renown,

beside the flowing river, rich in pleasant uses,

through which it can arrange various kinds of commerce.

[Col. 0736D] But it is fortified still more brightly by the merits

and everywhere just conduct of the illustrious patrician Richard,

who, filled with the nourishing strength of unconquerable virtue,

protects you, exalts you, governs you, and cherishes and guards you.

More steadfast than gold, he drives away, withstands, and rebukes enemies—

marquis and duke, a count wondrous and astonishing in his deeds,

most worthy, upright, holy, pious, good, and modest.

After the great duke had triumphantly accomplished these and similar deeds, he quickly sent distinguished envoys from his household to Denmark, so that the most powerful people of the Danes might hasten to his aid.

The Danes, delighted by these embassies, promptly prepared and loaded their ships and hastened to Rouen. The most steadfast duke, seeing the leaders of so great a multitude [Col. 0737A] and eager to avenge the malice of his indignation and anger, ordered them to proceed to the Givold ditch and lay waste to the possessions of Tetbold and the king.

The Danes departed from there and, engaging the king and Tetbold, indiscriminately ravaged whatever they found. After devastating all the peasants’ villages, they burned the suburbs and overthrew many fortresses to the ground. They cruelly killed those who resisted them, and sorrowfully carried the rest of their force back to the ships.

The entire land of the king and Count Tetbold was desolated and wickedly afflicted by such enemies. Famine arose, because nowhere was the earth broken by the plow. Roads and paths became impassable and unknown, because no one’s footsteps wore them down [text uncertain]. Safety, hope, and confidence were cried out for by those who remained, because they were afflicted by the disgrace of every calamity.

But the land of the great Duke Richard was firm and peaceful, afflicted by no plague of misfortune, but cultivated everywhere by the labor of free choice. Every peasant freely did what he wished, having received the ability to act according to his will.

After Normandy had been afflicted for almost a period of five years by so much conflict, so great a disaster, and such plunder, by day and night and through countless misfortunes, it could no longer endure the dangers of such adversity.

Almost all France, subject to Tetbold’s rule, was therefore abandoned by its inhabitants, and the churches, deprived by these calamities, were frequented by no Christian.

The bishops of all France, having suffered the savagery of the pagan Normans, summoned a holy synod to investigate what they should do, since the Christians subject to them were harassed by countless misfortunes, innumerable fires, thefts, and enormous acts of plunder.

Tetbold, however, with the deceitful intent of his treachery, falsely suggested to the bishops and nobles that he was provoking quarrels with Richard and the pagans for the sake of the commonwealth and the king’s loyalty.

But when the bishops learned and heard of the goodness of the most holy Duke Richard, they marveled at the words of Count Tetbold.

For this reason, after consultation, they asked the bishop of Chartres to inquire what the great Duke Richard intended concerning the disgrace of this pestilential poverty and calamity.

Compelled by the admonitions of his fellow bishops, he sent a monk to Duke Richard, who delivered the message of the embassy:

“The bishop of Chartres offers you the faithful gift of his prayers. He desires to approach you and speak with you face to face; therefore he asks that a duke and guide for his journey be given to him, and a traveler to accompany him, lest your devils and wolves devour and consume him.”

When the most serene Duke Richard heard this, he smiled and sent someone to escort the bishop safely and unharmed to him.

When the bishop arrived, he began speaking to the great Duke Richard:

“The metropolitans, together with the bishops of the Frankish people, offer you unfailing gifts of prayer. We marvel in astonishment that, although you are renowned throughout the world as a principal worshiper of God and a Christian, you nevertheless permit pagans to rage so fiercely against Christians.

“While passing through the protection of your authority, I found the peasants of this land secure from the terror of hostile tyranny; they feared no sudden misfortune of adversity. I saw the shrines and churches reverently visited by the inhabitants, and the mystery of divine worship solemnly celebrated. I saw everything belonging to the worship of the true faith continuously performed and the faith of the Christian name increased.

“We, however, are worn down by plunder and fires, and even by sudden deaths at night; yet we do not know with what intention this detestable crime is being committed against us. Therefore we earnestly beg you, with the knees of body and mind bent, to explain to us in a truthful speech for what reason this execrable ruin is being inflicted upon the Frankish people, since we have approached you on this account.”

Then Duke Richard, truthful and just, said:

“Do you remember and recall my former misfortunes, the things I suffered and the wrongs I repaid? Did not Duke Bruno of Lotharingia, at the deceitful suggestion of Count Tetbold, attempt to deceive me? Was not King Lothar deceived by that same count’s crafty and false evasions, and did he not plot to capture or kill me, from which God rescued me by his abundant mercy?

“Did not that same count promise King Lothar the Norman territory if he would give him the city of Évreux, which he now holds? Moreover, did he not, after gathering a savage force, provoke me by ravaging and burning as far as the port of Rouen?”

Then the bishop said:

“You ought not to repay him in kind for the insult of that provocation. But the count claims that he is fighting and resisting you for the sake of the condition of the holy Church and the commonwealth. Whatever position the wicked king may take in this matter, we beg you to obtain the growth of peace, so that you may be able to rejoice with the bishops and King Lothar, and so that he himself may rejoice in you as such a duke and most Christian patron.”

But the most powerful Richard, recognizing that no holocaust or sacrifice is so acceptable to God as the growth of peace, and desiring to bring peace to the Frankish and Norman kingdoms, yet unwilling to reveal his disposition because of Tetbold, said to the bishop, envoy of his fellow bishops:

“I do not know whether I shall be able to obtain the happiness of peace from the pagans who have come here against me; because of this matter I waver and hesitate. Therefore, take with you some of your fellow bishops and nobles and approach me when the sun reaches the middle of the month of May. In the meantime I shall try, by soothing words, to restrain the fierce arrogance of the stubborn pagans.”

When the bishop reported to the king and his fellow bishops what he had heard from the great Duke Richard, Count Tetbold immediately noticed and understood that the desired peace had been sought without his counsel.

At once he sent a monk to the great Duke Richard to deliver the following words:

“Count Tetbold offers you faithful service. He regrets having been deceived by the wicked counsel of certain Franks, having quarreled and fought against you without cause, and having done what evil he did; he declares that he will do no further harm.

“If it pleases you, he desires to speak with you privately as a servant to his lord, and he will return to you Évreux, which the king took from you, for the sake of your love.

“His land, subject to his authority, is being ravaged by hostile tyranny through plunder and fires, and he cannot resist the savagery of so great a multitude, nor appease it with the accumulated wealth of the whole kingdom, except through you, who are the master of this matter.

“He begs, with the knees of body and soul bent, that you forgive the holy Church and the desolated people, and that you regard him as your faithful servant, restraining the pestilential attacks of the Danish ferocity.”

When Duke Richard heard this, he secretly gave thanks to God in his heart and said to the monk:

“If what you say can truly be so, is it true?”

The monk replied:

“It is true. He desires to earn no other favor than to return the city of Évreux to you, provided that your inward affection remains steadfast, so that peace and the concord of an indissoluble treaty may remain between you for all the days of your lives.

“He will come at night with his confidants, whenever you wish, to the walls of the city of Rouen, and will confirm by an oath of true faith what I have reported to you.”

Then Richard said:

“By the faith of God by which we live and are sustained, and by the firm foundation of our steadfast purpose, we praise and approve his coming to us, if he wishes, after six days have passed. Let us bind treaties that no circumstance can dissolve, but that are to be preserved by perpetual and inextricable laws.”

The monk reported to Count Tetbold what he had heard. Tetbold, delighted and cheerful at this message, came to Rouen by night with his confidants after six days had passed.

When each of them saw the other, each ran to meet him. They embraced one another, exchanged kisses, and sat down.

Then Tetbold was the first to speak:

“I come suppliant to your ineffable mercy, for I need everything through your compassion and God’s favor. Everywhere, the lands I possess have been burned, and the territory under my authority has become like a desert.

“Therefore I am gladly prepared to carry out what the monk reported to you. I shall make amends to you for every wrong arising from my counsel and action. For this reason, serving you as though in return for a favor, I shall serve as your soldier. I voluntarily return the fortress of Évreux to you, and I humbly ask to earn the pardon and forgiveness of your mercy for having held it against you.”

Moved in his heart by the devotion of this humility, the great Duke Richard mercifully answered Count Tetbold with the greatest humility:

“You have come here without hostage or oath of my faith, trusting without hesitation. Whatever you ask, you shall obtain. You shall have the happiness of continual peace; none of my men shall henceforth be hostile or harmful to you or yours.

“From now on I shall be yours, as you are mine; and through the intervention of mutual assistance we shall confidently comfort one another in turn. Let there be abundant peace, joyful rest, tranquil serenity, and stable and perfect concord between us, established by unbreakable decrees.”

Then, after the relics of the saints had been brought, they entered into alliance. Likewise, the counselors of both counts confirmed these same arrangements by an oath of true faith.

Then the most generous Marquis Richard honored him abundantly with very great gifts and presents. Tetbold, enjoying the desired kiss and longed-for embrace, departed and returned secretly to Chartres that same night.

On that very day, Tetbold’s men left the city of Évreux with all its possessions, as they had been ordered, and sent to Duke Richard for him to receive it. He received it, strongly fortified it with soldiers, and enriched and adorned it with an abundance of every good thing.

**Apostrophe**

Although the rustic style of our ignorance [for “ignorance”]

adorns this work with diverse meters of various kinds,

it is exceedingly empty, lacking in resources and deficient in art,

deprived of the sweet nectar of eloquent rhetoric;

it ought rather to flourish in heroic meter,

because these strong deeds of men are celebrated here.

For here was a strong man, steadfast and robust in arms,

[Col. 0740B] peaceful, good, upright, pious, and modest;

magnificent, deserving, exalted, noble, and nourishing;

illustrious, excellent, admirable, and comely;

greatest, outstanding, pre-eminent, and magnanimous;

distinguished, just, holy, humble, and graceful;

favorable, gentle, mild, meek, and severe;

long-suffering, renowned, solemn, lovable,

merciful, forgiving, compassionate, and punishing crimes;

protector, censor, guardian, and giver of honors;

prudent and wise, industrious, knowledgeable, and extraordinary;

learned in languages and in the various regions;

attentive, teachable, eager for and thirsting after good things;

wondrous, steadfast, gracious, faithful, and trustworthy;

tranquil, peaceful, joyful, cloudless, and serene;

[Col. 0740C] cheerful, sweet, kind, and approachable to all;

witty, fortunate, frugal, and skilled in law;

handsome, rich, wealthy, and generous;

the sweet head of the people, the hope and confidence of the poor;

tall, handsome, elegant, and beautiful in form;

a foot for the lame, an eye for the blind, and a staff for the faltering;

abundant drink sufficient for every thirsty person;

most generous food and varied nourishment for the hungry;

an extraordinary refuge for the poor, exile, and needy;

a protector of the widow, like a husband and spouse;

a comforter of kings, dukes, nobles, and counts.

While he flourished in the world, he became all things to all people;

he harmed no one and strove to benefit everyone.

Having completed these matters secretly and cautiously, Richard, the celebrated margrave and duke, ordered a stage of extraordinary breadth and length to be erected on the bank of the Givold ditch [Col. 0740D], for the arrival of the palatine nobles and bishops of the Frankish nation. When the appointed time came, on the Ides of May—that is, when the Twins were inflamed by the scorching sun—the palatines came there with the bishops to Richard the great duke, seeking to obtain peace. He ordered them to be received becomingly and reverently, and, having had tents made beside the splendid stage, to be lodged there.

On the following day they came before Duke Richard, presented him on behalf of the Franks with gifts of loyal service and prayers, and said:

“Duke of unheard-of power, sufficiency, and valor: the nobles of the entire kingdom of France, unanimously praying on bended knees with their hearts bowed to the ground, ask you to show mercy to the most holy Church and to the ringed people (annulata gens). The king, we, the rest of the Franks, and all the clergy of the whole kingdom wish you every good, present and future, if you restrain the savagery of the pagans and rescue France from their pestilential invasion. Whatever the king has done against you, he did at the urging of Count Tetbold’s deceitful counsel; and, remembering the good things your father inflicted upon his father, he is weary of his own deed. Just as King Louis, his father, flourished after being established in the kingdom with your father’s assistance, so he desires, with the great aid of your power, to hold his kingdoms and rule over the proud.

“May you agree through common prayers of mutual suitability, and may each of you, trusting in the other’s assistance, remain united. The king himself and the nobles of the whole kingdom of France will confirm by oath, with their own hands, the kingdom of Northmannia to you and your heirs forever; afterward none of them will in any way seek to inflict any harm or adversity upon you.” [Col. 0741B]

When they had delivered the terms of this embassy, the most excellent margrave and duke replied:

“O reverend prelates, richly endowed beyond measure with an abundance of every virtue, and nobles richly furnished with an overflowing wealth of all good and worldly things: I shall not hesitate to confess to you openly the purpose of my continual intention and will. Therefore, learn with confidence that I most earnestly wish to establish and carry out the good fortune of peace, rather than undertake any work of prosperity or honor. This has always been my highest and particular concern.

“But because of your importunities and quarrels I could not maintain it without being disgraced. For nothing is more grievously troubling in any matter than for someone either not to see what he desires or to see what he will lose. In either case the mind, burdened by the greatest weight of anxiety, wavers: it wishes both to possess what it has long watched for anxiously and not to lose what it has begun to possess.

“Therefore recall and remember the ambushes and evils I have suffered at his hands, and consider and observe to whom they have proved prejudicial, whether to us or to you. You are not unaware that Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and likewise duke of Lorraine, at the instigation of Count Tetbold, wished to deceive me. You are not unaware that your elder king Lothar, incited by that same man’s deceitful cunning, wished to capture or kill me. What shall I say of Évreux, which he returned to me, by God? [Col. 0741D]

“Moved by these and similar matters, and by many other importunities which it is tiresome to recount, I sent to the Danes so that they might come to my aid more quickly. When they attacked my enemies in haste, I ordered them to exercise against you the tyranny of this destruction, because, unless the matter were weighed seriously, the fool would not recover his senses. If, then, what you have told me is true, establish with me the opportunity for the peace that is necessary.”

Then the most famous margrave Richard, having summoned all the Northmen together, began to soothe and cheer them with the gentlest words:

“O fathers worthy of the highest reverence, wonderfully fragrant with the dignity of old age, maturity, and youth: I owe you continual thanks, and even abundant gifts, because, abandoning the land of your birth on account of the wrong unjustly inflicted upon me, you have until now quarrelled and fought against foreign peoples for love of me. The kings, dukes, and counts of those peoples, afflicted continually and hostilely by your devastations, humbly ask that a period of suspended peace be granted them. If it pleases you, it shall be granted; if not, it must be rejected. Decide the matter they have requested by common counsel, and take care to answer concerning it.” [Col. 0742A]

Then the Northmen, who were also Danes, replied unanimously to Duke Richard:

“By no means shall continuous peace, nor peace interrupted by periods of time, be granted. Rather, all France, once its leaders have been expelled or killed, shall be acquired for you by force and power. Alas, alas! What will the other Danes and Northmen do or say, those who, with ships prepared and loaded to assist in this undertaking, will attack together with us with savage hostility? What of the Irish, what of the Alans, what of the many other peoples? The purpose of your will, which you have disclosed to us, shall not be fulfilled while we live. But if you wish, we shall avenge for you the France we have invaded. If, however, you dislike this, it shall fall to us by lot. Therefore choose which of the two you prefer—for yourself or for us.”

When he heard this, the mighty Duke Richard pressed them with repeated appeals and, for eight days, earnestly begged them to make a treaty with the Franks on the basis of peace. The prelates and nobles of the Frankish nation therefore stood there each day in astonishment and watched the struggle over this peace-making. At last, since the great duke Richard could not calm such savagery by any efforts of entreaty, he said privately to his faithful nobles:

“This is a harsh and powerful people. When approached all together, they will not yield to our entreaties. Let the elders and the more powerful men be summoned secretly, in the silence of the coming night, and let us blind them with exceedingly great gifts and abundant benefaction, if perhaps they will favor our prayers and our wish.”

The leaders of the Franks considered this counsel sound and promising, and thought that it would benefit themselves. Accordingly, at twilight on the following night, when the elders of Northmannic descent and greater power had been secretly summoned, he disclosed what he was turning over in his heart through honeyed speech and said:

“O fathers rightly worthy of reverence, striving excessively for temporal benefits, for which you will be deprived of eternal life and deservedly enjoy Phlegethon: listen obediently to the opening of my speech. Although the whole human race was created by the Lord at its beginning and without an end, so that the ruin of the angels might be repaired, errant deviation draws it away along a varied and diverse path, preventing it from returning to its Creator.

“You think that your souls perish together with your bodies, and therefore you do not shrink from doing every evil. There is, in fact, another life beyond this one, of which you are ignorant; and whatever you do in this life will certainly be presented to you in that one.” [Col. 0742D]

Then they said:

“Tell us, we beg you, the secret of this proposition, and explain to us as quickly as possible the account of our condition.” [Col. 0743A]

Then the most prudent count, soothing them with gentle words, said:

“Our reasoning concerning our condition is recognized by the orthodox as true. When the tenfold order of heavenly citizens had been created, and the tenth had fallen through the quarrel and course of his stubborn arrogance and boastfulness, after the whole structure of the world and its wondrous adornment had been completed, God joined two elements—namely, the living and the mortal—and formed man as one being. He made him immortal from clay, crowned him with glory and honor, and placed him over the works of his hands, so that at some time he might pass without the death of the flesh into the heavenly glory of the angels, which the arrogant one had lost.

“He made him immortal in such a way that, if he bound himself by the bonds of love to obedience to his Creator, he would not have been subject to the laws of death. But, alas for grief! Deceitfully entangled by the treacherous craft of the ancient enemy, enticed by the allurements of desire, negligently scorning the commands of the Maker and thereby striving toward death, and driven from the delights of paradise, he was assigned to the world’s hardships. Nor did he alone receive the sentence of condemnation: he brought the entire succession of the human race with him into accursed wrongdoing and the bitterness of death. Hence the ancient enemy deceitfully held dominion over all human beings and wickedly subjected them to himself.

“But since I have briefly related the sequence of the creation and fall of the first man, to whom we cling with heart and mind, I wish to evangelize you concerning the faith of our belief. We worship one God in substance, and venerate a Trinity in persons. Although the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, nevertheless only one God is believed in.

“We call the Father the Begetter; we confess the Son to be begotten; we believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. In these three persons—the Begetter, the Only-Begotten, and the One Proceeding from both—we profess one divinity, equal glory, and equal majesty.

“This God suspended heaven through its subtlety, founded the earth by its mass, bound the seas with pebbles, and by his word made in them all things whatsoever he willed, establishing them by his spirit. He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light. With him there is no change or shadow caused by alteration. His being is always eternal [Col. 0743D] and immutable. Without changing himself, he orders mutable things; without becoming diverse, he performs diverse acts; without any change of thought, he forms unlike things.

“He is everywhere and wholly without place, because he is himself the God beneath, within, and outside all creatures: superior in governing, inferior in bearing, interior in filling, exterior in encompassing. Within the omnipotence of his judgment all things are confined, and his power is surpassed by no created nature. For the loftiness of his divinity neither began nor ceases to exist; it is neither born through a beginning nor restricted by an end.

“This God, the Word who was in the beginning with him and whom he begot without time, ordained to become incarnate for our redemption. At the angel’s announcement he proceeded from the flesh of the most holy Virgin into flesh, humbled even to the shame of human origin, the filth of swaddling clothes, and the lowliness of a manger. We can marvel at this birth, but we cannot fully behold it.

“For who can worthily explain how the coeternal One was born from the Eternal? How the One existing before the ages begot one equal to himself? How the One born is not later than the Begetter? What the Father is, that he begot: God from God, light from light, immeasurable from immeasurable, incomprehensible from incomprehensible, omnipotent from omnipotent—one with himself, coeternal, and equal to himself.

“Born from the Father without time, he deigned to be born from his mother in time; and, like electrum, he was one in and from both natures. He remained God with the Father and, for our redemption, became mortal man from his mother, so that by his abundant compassion he might rescue the human race, fashioned in his likeness and image, from the monstrous power of the fallen angels, its enemies. [Col. 0744B]

“Proceeding humanly through the course of passing times and wondrously performing various miracles, he gave movement to the lame, hearing to the deaf, sight to the blind, and former health to paralytics; he bestowed clean, pleasing, and delightful skin and flesh upon lepers; he made the swelling waves of the sea passable for himself and Peter; and he commanded the sea and the winds. He raised the dead, including Lazarus after four days in the tomb, and did everything he wished in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all the depths.

“Finally he came to the spectacle of voluntary death. Enduring it while affixed to the cross, and bringing forth water and blood from his side, he presented to himself the virgin and spotless Church, redeemed by blood and cleansed by water, so that she might have neither stain through crime nor wrinkle through duplicity. Having celebrated the mystery of death and despoiled hell, he rose on the third day. Showing himself openly to his faithful and conversing with them, on the fortieth day after his resurrection he raised to heaven, in the sight of the apostles, the flesh he had taken from the Virgin.

“He prepared this death—which the ancient enemy had inflicted upon the first man and his descendants—to be abolished for his servants, and showed them the inviolate path by which they might ascend from the place where they had fallen, when he carried our flesh with him to the stars.

“Therefore, if the human being—the union of the two elements—serves God while he lives and obeys his commands with every effort of his strength, the living and more powerful part, which drew its origin from the ether, will carry back with it to the ether the guestly inward parts of its body, once the enemy’s contaminations have been rejected.

“If, however, an earthly will has the taste of clay and pursues what is weighty and wicked, and if, through the excessive accumulation of vices and the rejection of the promises made in baptism, it has oppressed the powers of the soul beneath the weight of sins, then it will drag the soul with it and torture it in the underworld.

“For this reason Christians take the greatest care over graves, and entrust bodies to them as not wholly dead but given over to sleep [leg., ‘sleep’ for the transmitted reading]. For the ages will come when the soul’s companion heat will revisit the bones, and, animated by living blood, will bear its former dwelling places—namely, the corpses rotted in the tombs. They will be carried into the former airs, accompanied by the souls they once possessed, because the destruction of this death is the restoration of a better life.

“For even if decaying age should dissolve the whole body, so that only a tiny particle of it remained, and wandering winds and breezes should carry that ash through the empty void, it will not be permissible to say that the human being has perished. Rather, he will be rewarded with the one with whom he exercised the virtues of his soul, or punished with the one with whom he sinned. And so, with Christ the Son of God as judge, the wicked will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life.

“This is the catholic faith. Unless each person believes it faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved. This is the foundation of our saving belief; this is the symbol of the faith and salvation that will profit us.”

When the Danes heard this, they were astonished and, drawing their voices up from their breasts, said:

“Woe to us, ignorant of every good and unacquainted with the Scriptures, who know nothing of God’s power, since we differ in no way from beasts or the birds of heaven! They seek only to live for the present and preserve nothing acquired for themselves. We, too, seek continually to live in the same way by plundering; but we differ from them in this, that whatever exceeds our food and drink we store up for the future by hoarding it as treasure.

“Give us saving counsel, we ask, so that we may be able to live both now and forever.”

Then the duke said:

“If you wish to adhere to our counsels, I shall first have you baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Then you shall be instructed more fully by the bishops through abundant preaching of the complete faith. Afterward you shall be enriched with very generous gifts and extensive benefits, through which you may live and not perish forever. You shall enjoy without end both the comfort of the present life and the reward of future recompense, if you do not reject the happiness of the complete peace that I seek.”

They replied:

“We promise you both the security of peace and the continuance of the holy faith, and no errant delusion will ever drive us away from your counsel.”

When peace had thus been agreed upon secretly at night and the tranquility of the treaty sworn, Richard, soothing them with honeyed speech, said:

“Return secretly to your ships, parts of my strength and my soul, taking care that no one sees you and that no one learns that you have come here. At dawn I shall summon you again, together with the turbulent people of the dreadful neck, and I shall demand by many kinds of prayers that mercy be shown to you and to them, that peace be increased and an alliance of quiet be granted.

“Reject my words at first and quarrel with them; then, when the long hostility has scarcely come to an end, yield to my wishes.”

Having secretly concluded these words, each returned to his own place.

At first light the great duke rose quickly, summoned countless legions of Danes, and said confidently:

“Having until now endured the malicious evasions of your perverse intention, I shall once again and again reproach the excess of your stubborn heart. Give us, I beg, the opportunity for peace that you have so often rejected.”

Then the Northmen, divided in their will, replied to Richard together:

“He labors in vain who casts seed upon a rock. You pour out the labor of your words uselessly, speaking idly and needlessly. The peace and concord to which you strive in vain to make us submit shall never exist between us and the Franks. They shall be expelled, destroyed, and their entire nation utterly wiped out. Whoever is found unworthy shall be subjected to our dominion [variant: ‘condition’]. Did not your grandfather claim by arms the land over which you rule, after laying waste to the kingdom of France?”

Then all, from the least to the greatest, said in alternating voices:

“Either we shall die, or it shall be avenged.”

But the great Duke Richard joined entreaty to entreaty and earnestly urged them to grant peace. Their minds, however, did not yield to his prayers. Then those who had promised peace during the night said to the others:

“Since we came here for his assistance and defense, it follows that we should obey his prayers. It is fitting to do what he desires in his eagerness and willingly grant his wishes. Whose counsel shall we follow, if not his? Whose entreaties shall we heed, if not those of the man whose benefaction we enjoy every day, and not sparingly?” [Col. 0746B]

When those who knew nothing of the nocturnal counsel heard this, they were violently disturbed. They began to quarrel more fiercely, shouting their objections, and said:

“As we judge it, you are supporters—or rather flatterers—of this proposal, and therefore you are inflicting such wickedness upon us. It will not happen according to the pleasure of your plan, nor will any of us grant the peace that is sought. You have gaping mouths through which you have disclosed to us an intention suited to your will, and it will boldly resist us who survive. We shall not obey what the duke commands and requests because of your intervention; rather, France will be ravaged with arms more fiercely, even to destruction.” [Col. 0746C]

Then those who had already gained the advantage through the agreement of the nocturnal counsel, raging with the sharpest fury, said:

“Peace will not be granted because of our intervention; rather, whether you wish it or not, we shall grant it to the great duke. What have we to do with you, or you with us? Are we not older than you, nobler in ancestry, and stronger in arms? We ought to have been called not intercessors but grantors of peace.”

When Richard heard this, he withdrew and said to his leaders:

“Let them quarrel fiercely among themselves, and let us see which of them proves more powerful and stronger.”

After this conflict had been prolonged for three times three days, while the Franks and Richard’s men looked on in amazement, the opponents of peace said to the satraps whom they had acquired by prudent counsel during the night:

“You are more powerful by age, ancestry, and arms; therefore, willingly or unwillingly, we shall agree with you. If Duke Richard grants us the most generous expenses for our journey, and provides us with means to live and conquer a kingdom, we shall spare the kingdom of France as you request. Otherwise, under his direction, we shall subject the France we have invaded to harsher devastation through wars, fire, and plunder.”

The nobles of the pagans were pleased by these answers and reported them to Duke Richard. When the embassy had been completed, the mighty duke, joyful at the future peace, began:

“I shall supply abundant provisions, very many and well-protected travelers, and the most generous honors; I shall also provide them with the means to reach a fertile land.”

When the matter of this most generous promise had been reported, and Duke Richard was seated with his men while the Franks stood nearby, they came together and made a pledge of peace to him with bowed faces. Richard then sent the king’s envoys, enriched with exceedingly great gifts, back to King Lothar.

When the day and place of the peaceful assembly had been appointed and the desired truce granted, he kept the pagans with him so that the Franks would not rebel against them. When the appointed time of the desired assembly had passed, King Lothar came to the little river Epte with the Franks and pledged to Duke Richard a firm and unbreakable peace. He himself and the nobles of the kingdom swore to him and his descendants the kingdom of Northmannia, so that neither he nor anyone at his urging would inflict any harm upon that government.

When the assembly at which the desired peace had been obtained was finished, and the king and Duke Richard had been joined in treaty, each richly enriched by gifts exchanged between them, everyone returned to his own place in a prosperous journey. The duke of magnificent piety returned to the city of overflowing abundance and compelled the Northmen of monstrous ferocity to appear before him. He said to them:

“Do not waver in confidence concerning my promise. Behold, I am ready to carry out what I once pledged to you. I shall cause you to be reborn through the sacred font, and, with your ships loaded with grain and provisions, I shall provide you with travel supplies for the voyage.”

Then the great margrave received them from the prepared font of most holy regeneration, after they had been anointed with oil and chrism, granting them the most extensive benefits so that they might dwell in peace. Those, however, who wished to continue wandering in pagan rites, he had transported to Spain by travelers from Constantinople. [Col. 0747C]

During that expedition they conquered twice nine cities and claimed for themselves whatever they found in them. Plundering here and there and attacking Spain with hostility, they began to afflict it severely with fire and pillage. At last the Spaniards, after engaging the rustic peoples in battle, gathered an army and confronted the Northmen.

When Mars was raging, the Spaniards turned their backs to the foreigners, and a very great slaughter took place. On the third day the Northmen returned to the battlefield and, turning over the dead in order to strip them of their armor, found parts of the bodies of black Ethiopians that lay nearest to and against the earth, whiter than snow, while the rest of each body retained its former color.

But I wonder what the dialecticians will characterize concerning this, since they categorize accident and Ethiopian-ness as inseparable, yet here they see it changed. We do not wish to disclose more about this, but let us turn the style of our presumption back to the purpose of our intention. For these are the known good works of him who knows all that is done. He who is able will gladly elucidate them, but will not be able to set forth everything necessary to the account.

## APOSTROPHA

Thus far, borne through the great affairs of watery fate,

made and transformed in turn by varied whirlwinds,

and through Fortune’s twofold changes, both favorable and harsh,

carried upon the sea-sounding wave as the storm arose,

beneath your * I sang with our shrill hemlock-pipe.

[Col. 0748A]

Having left a stable harbor, quiet from the winds,

I plowed the exceedingly deep seas with a very small oar.

There are eight blessings of the sacred life, scattered everywhere,

through which the supreme good is bought by the sincere heart.

But my mind, meditating with a slender reed,

tries to grasp some gift of the good,

drawn from the profit of a small and modest payment.

Once France had been purified, as has been related, from the poison of pestilential hostility, and once the complaints and losses of the threatening evils had been rejected, and the welfare of the commonwealth throughout France had been arranged and established, the triumph of the desired peace led the way. The fame of the most blessed Duke Richard, illuminated by the merits that had been made known, increased and shone to immense proportions, and the report of his blessedness was spread more widely throughout the other kingdoms. [Col. 0748B]

During that period his wife, the daughter of Hugh the great duke, died. Grieved by the loss and desolation, he sent to Hugh, the brother of his deceased wife, asking him to send some household servants who would distribute to the Holy Church and to the poor whatever his sister had possessed by woman’s right.

Duke Hugh, however, sent word back to Richard the duke and patrician that he should freely do whatever his will supplied from all those possessions. Then Richard, the most powerful duke of overflowing generosity, distributed the gifts of so great a treasure among all the churches throughout France and Northmannia. Moreover, he abundantly gave to the poor many things that belonged to him, for the sake of his wife’s soul.

Finally, overcome by the weakness of pleasurable human nature, he fathered two sons and an equal number of daughters by concubines; one was named Geoffrey, the other William.

At last he joined himself by a friendly bond of forbidden union to a virgin of splendid majesty, born from the most renowned noble lineage of the Danes, the fairest of all the Northmannic virgins, extremely cautious amid the changing outcomes of civic and worldly affairs, instructed in the skill of feminine ingenuity, modestly distinguished by eloquence of abundant speech, richly endowed with a capacious treasury of memory and recollection, and fortified by an abundance of every good quality.

The nobles of the Northmen, knowing that she had sprung from the seed of a most noble lineage and thinking deeply about a successor, heir, and beneficial posterity for the people, said privately to the most powerful Duke Richard, with lowered voices and inclined faces:

“Since, my most powerful lord duke, you are, through the penetrating scrutiny of wise reflection, by far the most prudent of all the Franks, Northmen, and Burgundians, and of all kingdoms, we greatly wonder that you do not consider who will rule the people now subjected to your most powerful dominion after your grievous and destined departure. Fearing the unforeseen collapse of future loss, we are afraid that, after the mournful loss of your removal, foreign peoples may trample us when they find us without an advocate and heir.”

Then Richard said:

“Until now I have governed the commonwealth according to your most salutary counsel, and have helped it as I was able. Now explain clearly what you have determined in your hearts and for what reason.” [Col. 0749A]

They replied:

“We believe that the providence of the highest divinity has joined this Danish woman, whom you now cherish, to you for this purpose: that an heir, Danish on both his father’s and mother’s side, may be born as heir of this land and stand as its strongest defender and advocate. She is born of a proud lineage, beautiful in appearance, cautious and provident in counsel, devoted in mind, submissive in heart, modest in speech, gentle in conduct, and industrious and shrewd in every matter.

“Join her to yourself at once through the inviolable privilege of a marital bond, so that through her life-giving offspring this land of your rule may, when the death of your final destiny approaches, be governed safely and firmly.”

The most holy Duke Richard therefore gladly favored this counsel. Having summoned bishops with the clergy, nobles with the people, he betrothed her to himself according to the law of marriage. In the course of time she bore him five male children and three female.

He therefore walked along the straight paths of good works and vigorously governed the people with the just reins of law. Rebuilding the churches of Northmannia at his own expense, he adorned them with monastic furnishings; and from the treasury of his own resources he magnificently constructed very many churches throughout the land of the Franks.

In the city of Rouen he enlarged, in honor of the Mother of God, a remarkable monastery, honorably expanded in length, breadth, and height. On a maritime mountain, surrounded on every side by the flood of the returning tide according to the moon’s course, he built a sanctuary of extraordinary size and spacious walls for monastic habitation. There he compelled monks, bound under the arduous discipline of contemplative life by the regular statutes of their celebrated course, to serve Christ.

Since he abounded in countless increases of overflowing goodness, one day he approached the walls of the see of Fécamp. Standing on the platform at the entrance of his house, he saw that house itself higher and more capacious than the basilica dedicated in honor of the divine Trinity. Calling for a stoneworker skilled in architectural art, he said:

“It is fitting and necessary that the house of God and of prayer, adorned with the summit of extraordinary and distinctive beauty and height, should be higher than all the walls of the city. The Maker and Redeemer of the human race chose it for himself through gratuitous mercy, and it stands as the mother of wondrous regeneration through the symbolic washing of purification. In it we must hear the words of divine instruction and mourn our sins.

“This hall is called, and truly is, the gate of heaven, inhabited and governed by the citizens of heaven. The Psalmist says of this house: ‘The mountain of God is a fertile mountain, the mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell; for the Lord will dwell there forever.’ This is the mountain on which my grandfather sees himself standing and being washed, according to the oracle of divine vision, on the saving mountain, and sees himself cleansed from the leprosy of vices with which he had dreamed that he was infected.

“Therefore, since he grants that the house of God should surpass our dwelling in the design of a higher and more spacious summit, find out whether you can perhaps discover on the slopes of the neighboring mountains and hills some material of stone from which you may build the temple of God higher than the house of our residence.” [Col. 0750A]

The craftsman immediately took a mattock, approached the slopes of the nearest hills, and tore up their foundations with hoes. Finding no suitable stone material for the intended work, he sought the mountain slopes lying between two little streams near Fécamp. There he found a mass of gypsum, shaped and cut one gypsum stone, and brought it before Duke Richard.

Then the great Duke Richard said:

“Will you be able to find enough of such material?”

He replied:

“Enough, my lord.”

The duke said:

“Put this stone in a safe place, and send very many laborers to cut stones and build many kilns for quicklime. Once everything necessary has been prepared, I shall place this stone at the beginning of the foundation as the first stone in the erection of the house of God.”

Finally, the most famous margrave, having prepared the lime, cut and piled the stones, and skillfully arranged the bricks, built, in a form marvelous to speak of and behold, a sanctuary in honor of the holy Trinity, of wondrous design. It was fortified on every side with towers, arched in two tiers with remarkable artistry, and roofed with bricks skillfully joined together.

On the outside he whitewashed it; within, he painted it with scenes from history. He adorned the altars with gold and gems acquired at great expense, fashioned crosses of extraordinary size from the purest gold, added chalices of great weight and value in gold, and set golden candelabra before the sanctuary, surpassing human nature. He supplied censers of unheard-of size and value made of gold, and vestments smoothed by the Phrygian comb, dyed more than once in Tyrian purple; he also applied thicker gold and emeralds sewn above them, and entrusted to the church white and purple byssus woven with gold and silken cloth of wondrous workmanship.

He compelled a numerous clergy, receiving generous daily provisions each day and laboring beneath the discipline of practical life, to serve Christ.

When that temple had been filled with the abundance of monastic resources and most dutifully dedicated with episcopal blessing, he repaired at his own expense all the ruined churches situated throughout the lands of Northmannia and France. He shone through marvelous, just, and good deeds, and the fame of his integrity spread abundantly through distant regions. [Col. 0750D]

His appearance, crowned with the adornment of wondrous beauty, poured forth radiance from his face like the brightness of the sun. He possessed the highest honor wherever his name was heard, and all Gaul marveled at his overflowing goodness. A lover of piety and an energetic cultivator of justice, he shone forth; he anxiously stored the causes of all people within his breast and upheld pious laws for the people’s rest.

Very handsome in appearance, filled with brilliantly white hair, flashing in his eyebrows and the sharpness of his eyes, radiant in his nose and cheeks, honored by a long, white beard, tall in stature, learned in speech, full of strength of mind and body, overflowing with goodness, exceedingly shrewd in mind, fortified by the grace of God, he was altogether the salvation of all.

He raised up his friends and trampled down his haughty enemies. Cherishing his subjects, he crushed the fierce and rebellious. No storm of anger or discord penetrated his heart with any tumult of dissension, because the anchor of his exceedingly keen mind was fixed in the saving stability of justice and judgment, and in the hope of charity and faith.

The tumult of adversity did not toss his steadfast spirit like a breeze, nor did the abundance of his manifold and copious prosperity lift his mind into pride. Whenever causes of sedition arose in his kingdom amid varied murmuring, he calmed them by the decrees of the laws and by salutary authority.

His faith was held by so strong a root of truth that a mountain would fail or move before his words fell. Matters promised by him remained true and were subject to no penalty through any act; once promised, they remained perpetuated.

## APOSTROPHA

The immense fullness of this patrician’s goodness,

you see, beloved bishop.

The tokens of goodness which he rightly increases eightfold,

you see, beloved bishop.

What the Evangelist twice writes to the blessed widower,

you see, beloved bishop.

And what your father fulfilled through rich deeds.

Praesul, beloved, you see.

In speech, certainly, no one ever existed better than he,

Praesul, beloved, you see.

In deed, assuredly, no one was more powerful than he,

[Col. 0751C] Praesul, beloved, you see.

Nor is there any man more holy in his meditation,

Praesul, beloved, you see.

To this dull and worthless writing we have descended,

Praesul, beloved, you see.

The arrangement of the words and the subject matter are exceedingly beautiful,

Praesul, beloved, you see.

The presentation of the theme is frivolous, rustic, and worthless,

Praesul, beloved, you see.

Now, now, take these sweet deeds from a worthless endowment,

Praesul, beloved, farewell.

Therefore, deservedly, justly, and with good reason, after briefly reviewing his deeds, we call Richard, duke of the Norman region, blessed and holy; [Col. 0751D] for in him all the gifts of the evangelical beatitudes are found to have been bestowed in abundant measure.

The first of these is: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” This beatitude clearly shines forth in this confessor, who, although he retained the monarchy of the Norman region—not for the sake of this passing honor, but so that the condition of the holy Church might not be endangered by the attacks of pagans—devoted himself with all the exertions of his heart and the whole affection of his mind to the poverty of Christ, worthy of imitation. What the condition of worldly men considers precious, he regarded in his mind as dangerous. What it considers great, he regarded in his heart as fleeting. What it considers pleasurable, he regarded as not everlasting. Truly abandoning these things in his mind and utterly despising them in his heart, he attained, through Christ’s generosity, the kingdom of heaven, which he had long desired. Since he chose to belong to the kingdom of heaven as one poor in spirit, we believe that this was granted to him. [Col. 0752A]

The Gospel next brings forth what follows: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” Whoever reads the brief account of his life and learns something of how gentle, how meek, how loving, and how kind he was will be able to recognize something of his gentleness. He restrained Count Theobald, at one time by devotion and at another by arms. He conquered King Lothair through humility. He curbed the Danes through the sweetness of his words and by gifts. By addressing the Franks and other peoples with the humblest words and gifts, he won them over and joined them to himself. With the greatest devotion he protected the inhabitants of the Norman region. Like a devoted father of a household, he cherished his own people. He was loving in every undertaking; in every matter his words and deeds rang with gentleness. [Col. 0752B] He deserved to possess the land of the living, because he guarded the earth of his own body with meek kindness.

The third beatitude follows, in which it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Since he had indeed been rich in wealth and gifts, soldiers and household servants, he mourned that he was entangled and ensnared in worldly affairs. He mourned the depravity of monks whom misguided error, abandoning the narrow path, led away into the detestable precipice by the deceptive affairs of the deceiving world. He mourned the errors of canons who were falling away from monastic observances. He mourned the ignorance and sins of his youth; and, prostrate upon the earth, he moistened it with the excessive tears of his eyes.

It follows: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” [Col. 0752C] No one who carefully weighs the peaceful actions of Duke Richard doubts that he possessed this hunger and thirst. Because he burned with zeal for justice, he continually sought the path of judgment. He oppressed those who neglected justice with the dreadful yoke of the law; by the word of severity he corrected those who rejected it. While he survived, mercy and truth, as the Psalmist says, met one another in his kingdom; righteousness and peace kissed one another. He hungered and thirsted to win himself and his people for Christ, so that he might share eternally in God on the day of judgment. His most urgent and continual desire, his enduring hunger and unfailing thirst, was to make everyone a gain for Christ.

It follows: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” [Col. 0752D] Who doubts that the heart of so great a duke, patrician, and confessor was a sanctuary of the Lord and a palace of the eternal King? The purity of his heart shone far and wide, and his most serene countenance clearly revealed the cleanness of his mind. As a layman, he carried the precepts of the divine law in a pure heart; with a benevolent mind he nourished the rich, the middling, and the poor. What was the disposition of his heart, mind, and will is apparent in the churches of the Norman region, magnificently adorned with monastic possessions.

It follows: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God.” The reward of peacemakers is that they should be called—and should be—the sons of God. They should be sons in perfect charity; they should be called sons by dignity. This duke flourished through the gift of this blessing, because he made peace among all as far as he could. On Sundays and the festivals of the saints [Col. 0753A] he practiced this especially fully; he gently and kindly reconciled rebels and those at odds.

The Flemish count Arnulf by name refused at that time to serve and perform military duty for King Lothair. King Lothair, therefore, angered by this matter, summoned a hostile force of Franks and Burgundians, besieged and captured Arras, and subjected the other strongholds as far as the River Lys. Distressed by this misfortune, Count Arnulf humbly and devotedly appealed to Duke Richard to reconcile him with the king and the Frankish princes. Richard, endowed with his customary benevolent disposition toward reconciliation, undertook this matter against the king for the sake of peace; he reconciled Count Arnulf with the king and, with the utmost solicitude, compelled Arras to be restored to him.

[Col. 0753B] Nor should it be passed over that, after King Lothair’s death, Duke Hugh, enthroned in the kingdom, wished to march against Count Albert with a gathered army. Albert, fearing the arrival of the furious king, sent a certain cleric named Dudon, a canon of the precious martyr of Christ, Quintinus, to Richard, the patrician of supreme patience, asking him to intervene energetically on his behalf with the king, whose mind was full of deadly hostility, lest the territory of the Vermandois be devastated by the enemy’s savagery. Duke Richard received the cleric with the greatest reverence and went against the king, who intended to march with a hostile army against Albert. By restraining the angry king through petitions of many kinds, he made peace between Albert and the king, giving hostages. [Col. 0753C]

This duke therefore flourished most abundantly through the distinction of this beatitude, because he made peace among those whom he heard to be at odds, either in person or through envoys.
