He made peace between the Franks and the Lotharingians, the Burgundians and the Flemings, the English and the Irish, the Normans and the Bretons. For he knew that no sacrifice or burnt offering was as acceptable to God as the increase of peace.

This duke is therefore honorably numbered among those who are called the sons of God through faith and imitation, because with every exertion of faith he fulfilled what he understood to be fitting for so great a dignity, knowing that God does not forbid that very many should become gods through participation in divinity.

Let us therefore consider the continuation of the Gospel, which says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for [Col. 0753D] righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” If the cause of this duke’s persecution is sought, none other is undoubtedly found than the righteousness of Christ—Christ whom he loved with his whole heart, his whole soul, and all his strength; whom he worshiped and adored with complete faith and supreme devotion; for whom he built churches for monks and canons and distributed whatever was necessary. He compelled people to maintain religious worship, urged pagans to believe in Christ, and endured their attacks lest they devastate France.

Persecuted like an evildoer by King Lothair and Count Theobald, while zealously attending to monastic concerns, he did not cease praising Christ. Persecuted in many ways, he entered, as we believe, the kingdom of heaven that he had sought. Strengthened by the saying of our Savior: [Col. 0754A] “Blessed are you when they curse you and persecute you and say every evil thing against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is abundant in heaven.”

No one among us can enumerate how many and how great were the curses and blasphemies this duke endured for attaining the kingdom of heaven. He endured curses for the Catholic faith, for the protection of the kingdom, for the most severe destruction of the pagans, for the holiest correction of monks who neglected the rule, for concord among canons who were at odds with one another, and for the restoration of peace among laymen. Christ was indeed the cause of this duke’s suffering; therefore the threat of evildoers did not prevail against him. [Col. 0754B] He rejoiced in the heavenly reward that had been promised and exulted when the wickedness of all his envious enemies had been overthrown.

## APOSTROPHA

When, through the wondrous and magnificent deeds,

Famous among all worshipers of Christ,

Of Richard, count, patrician,

Illustrious duke, and worthy of remembrance,

I free myself from the humble themes of poetry,

The better part of his deeds appears concealed,

And now the brilliant series grows numb,

Which will bring sharp destruction

To the foolish—ah, to me—because it has not been disclosed,

The fruit of a gift exceedingly great;

You, excellent reader, will be defrauded,

Because the Muse has not touched the highest labor.

Alas, alas! Most mournfully and funereally,

[Col. 0754C] my mind, foreseeing death and grief,

recoils in horror from defining

the modes of a sorrowful event worthy of silence.

O sorrowful event, full of grief!

Although it is sad and threatening to speak,

And lamentable, querulous, and portentous to all,

Although it is grievous to write, I shall write.

I shall write what I grieve over, what I mournfully weep,

How this duke, patrician, and supreme margrave

Entered into life through the appointed

Thresholds of death for the flesh,

United with the Lord, Christ everlasting,

And—so that you may be even more astonished—

his passage into God was ΘΕΩΣΙΣ, that is, deification.

[Col. 0754D] Since, as has been briefly worked out in a dull style, he was fragrant with the lamp of so many beatitudes, he ordered a sarcophagus to be cut for him and placed inside the church called Fécamp, consecrated to the divine Trinity, before the place of his station; and every Friday he ordered that as much grain as it could contain and five solidi should be distributed to the poor.

Finally, after enduring with equanimity many adversities arising from innumerable kinds of misfortune, and many labors, for the love of God; after conducting the offices of temporal life well; after giving works of abundant and manifold mercy; after granting examples of life worthy of imitation by rulers; after redeeming innumerable ranks of captives; after restoring monasteries of monks and canons; and after lavishly distributing an immense quantity of various goods [Col. 0755A] to the needy, he began to suffer anxiety, to fall ill, and to fail in strength. He withdrew from the district of Bayeux to the palace of the see of Fécamp, lest, when he died there, the people should find the transfer burdensome.

When he was present at the palace of Fécamp, Count Rodulf, his brother, humbly said to him before the other faithful:

“Lord, most pious duke, we sorrowfully mourn to see you weighed down by illness. But tell us, we beg you, which of your sons will be heir in the kingdom under your authority?”

Then he said:

“He who, with the authority of your counsel, bears my name as duke and count shall be heir to my inheritance.”

Then Count Rodulf said:

“What of the others, my lord?”

He replied:

“When those sons of mine have been made faithful to my son Richard by an oath of true faith, and their hands have been placed in his hands as a pledge of their hearts, he shall grant them the land that I shall show you, so that they may live honorably.”

[Col. 0755B] Thereupon, as the illness grew worse, the cities of Normandy began to tremble with fear, to strike heaven with unrestrained mourning, and a dreadful terror began to run through the uncertain minds of the Normans lest he should die. Weeping, they sought the palace of the see of Fécamp with excessive howling and lamentation.

The great Duke Richard, weighed down by the oppressive force of his illness, clothed in sackcloth and barefoot, sought the shrine of the divine Trinity. Sending various gifts and precious offerings upon the altar, his face drenched by a shower of tears, humble, devoted, and lamenting, he received the symbolic provision of the saving viaticum—that is, the aids for the journey.

Then Count Rodulf said to him more privately:

“My lord, in what place of the church shall the tomb for your rest be prepared?”

[Col. 0755C] He replied:

“The corpse of so great a sinner will not rest within the entrance of this church, but at this doorway, under the eaves of the monastery.”

The following night his most holy limbs began to be seized by a gentle pain, and a penetrating, deadly flame attacked his delicate marrow with greater violence. Now his feet, now his soft legs, grew numb; his eyes grew dim in his dying body; all his limbs faltered. But his mind saw God and desired the eternal ages.

The cheeks and faces of all were filled with tears, and an unbearable sob occupied every voice. Tongues clinging to the palate were shaken by agitated entrails, and speech could scarcely break through the immense trembling groans.

But he, with suppliant eyes raised toward heaven and hands [Col. 0755D] lifted up, silently pouring forth vows and prayers, scarcely breaking into speech, said:

“Into your hands, Christ, I commend my spirit.”

Immediately, amid such a prayer, he breathed out his most holy spirit.

His holy soul, snatched away from the burden of the flesh, freed from earthly pressures, and joyfully migrated to its Creator, while the mourning of his servants resounded in heaven.

At once the report of this mournful loss grew throughout the cities of the Norman region, and every age and both sexes ran, howling and weeping, to attend the funeral. According to custom, after the body had been prepared and carried to the church he had founded, the entire populace in turn kept watch; the clergy passed the sleepless night in psalmody, and the people in lamentation.

O how immense was the weeping, how great the mourning [Col. 0756A] of the Normans, how many lamentations resounded through all the streets! The choir, shaken by sobs and tears, sang the Psalms, while the crowd of common people sent mournful voices through the air. The town of the see of Fécamp was shaken by the immense groans of the people, and the wailing of the howls touched the summit of Olympus.

The harmonies of the antiphons resounded in the choir, mingled with mourning, and the lamentation of the Normans echoed in heaven. The clergy poured forth funeral chants throughout the streets, and unbearable howling filled every house. The population of the Norman region stood lamenting at the crossroads and filled the wandering air with sorrowful voices.

Surrounded by such a multitude and enclosed by such a procession, the body was carried to the tomb, with the singing choirs preceding it. [Col. 0756B] The crowd of common people continued its howling; confused and inarticulate voices of the people resounded. No one could distinguish what the clergy or the populace were crying out amid the voices of the howls.

Who could have so iron, foolish, or stony a breast as not to break into tears, when the bier was held back by the people’s pressure, restrained by the longing of desire, and drawn backward by the affection of love? The counts beat their hands while weeping; the governors sang mournful Psalms amid their howling. Virgins, widows, and wives tore their hair while crying. Household servants of both sexes beat their breasts with their fists in grief. Soldiers tore themselves apart in lamentation. The clergy poured forth the laments of excessive weeping together with the Psalms. The crowd of peasants and country people bit the earth with their teeth. The assembly of the poor, deprived of the assistance of so great a consolation, howled bitterly; and the people, oppressing one another cruelly, gave voice to various forms of grief.

The different and varied cries of so many people, which scorched heaven, scarcely came to an end when the people had at last been broken apart, dispersed, and drawn away by the bishops; they placed the bier [Col. 0756C] with the body upon the tomb, poured incense over it together with blessed water, and, amid excessive groans, committed it to the sarcophagus. They hastily covered it with stone, preserving it in great honor.

On the following day Count Rodulf came with the bishops to the tomb. When he removed the cover of the sarcophagus, a sweeter fragrance, the scent of terebinth and balsam, flowed forth and filled their sense of smell. Finally they built above the tomb [Col. 0756D] a chapel of wondrous beauty, magnificently joined to a basilica of extended breadth. There he is honored, marvelously surrounded by columns and by the tomb, awaiting resurrection with Christ in glory.

Having completed the course of this fragile life, the great Duke Richard died in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand and two.

O Fécamp, ever fertile in sacred ashes,

Preserving in the bosom of your already consecrated earth

the ashes of saints, shining with the flower of their merits,

You shine forth, richly endowed with the threefold gift of salvation.

Once you shone with a sacred virginal crown,

When you preserved Leodegarius deprived of light,

And the holy speechless man, beaten with many blows,

By Duke Ebroin, filled with the jealousy of crimes.

[Col. 0757A] Hence, rendered acceptable to Christ by the favoring abundance of speech,

the sacred people continually serving Christ,

with the rubric of sacred Gildeberta yielding—“Lust” is corrupt or uncertain in the source—

and the virginal lineage removed through diverse distinction,

There grew up in you a manly, practical order,

Laboring for Jesus Christ over a long period.

Now you shine deservedly, exalted in life and name,

Constrained here and there within narrow limits,

And it does not travel across level ground; it always strives toward heights.

This is both apostolic and exclusively ΘΕΩΡΙΚΑ—contemplative—

rejoicing in secret withdrawal, happy in perpetual joy.

Rightly supported by these three blessed orders,

You lead forward the most holy Σῶμα, the body, of the gracious Richard,

By whose prayers you will be purified from every stain,

And by whose worthy merits you will migrate to the heavens,

[Col. 0757B] Behold, you hold what has been shaken off; by whose command you flourished,

And by whose patronage you were supported,

By whose lavish gift, supported, you will flourish.

## APOSTROPHA

O you who arrange all things under a neighboring dominion,

Binding the elements by a law and a pleasing covenant,

So that crackling cold is joined to heat,

And under alternating law gives way to water and air,

We now consecrate to you thanks and deserved honors,

To the Father, together with the Begotten Son and the Spirit alike.

You who allot manifold gifts to your servants,

So that each may bring forth his talents at the interest of rewards,

The one who retained the commerce of five talents

Diligently exercises what was given to him.

[Col. 0757C] Here, having gained two talents through active dealings,

He rejoices that he has now returned twice as much.

He will be counted a debtor of one talent,

The man who buries it in muddy caves.

When you examine the distinctions of all,

This man will return the rewards of the price already earned—

The man whom money buried in the ground condemns for theft and fraud.

He will pay, alas, thrust down into the deepest Stygian fires,

Lamenting under punishment the neglected profits,

Cast out from the walls of the peaceful palace.

Fearing that the punishment of Gehenna might condemn me,

I remained anxious and hesitating, wondering what I should do.

The Norman land suddenly urges me, within its walls,

[Col. 0757D] to write, Christ, the struggle of your soldier.

Many things frightened me as I hesitated before such matters:

The weight of the subject and the appearance of the work,

My foolish heart, the excessive barrenness of my dry tongue,

My worthless person, unskilled in art and inert in ability,

And the fact that the praise of God would be unadorned upon sinful lips,

And that I could not produce what I desired.

[Col. 0758A] And that he would depart without praise in these verses,

He who, for foolish me, bestowed every good.

But your present trust, Christ, came to me,

So that you might easily give life to my mouth.

Relying upon you, I forced myself into this foolish work,

With you as giver, you as guide, you as craftsman.

Therefore, King, I humbly beg you with heart and voice,

With strength joined to it and a suppliant mind alike,

That it may please you to let me gladly attain what has pleased you to grant,

Flowing into my prayers while my sins recoil.

Oppressed by the many-sided mass of various crimes,

My disposition, foolish and stained with blemishes,

Has kept me wretched and unwilling for five decades,

And fear of Stygian punishment weighs me down.

For I remember that I have done scarcely anything good,

[Col. 0758B] And that in so long a span of time I have done nothing useful.

These things do not spur me on; they gnaw at the depths of my mind,

They afflict, torment, tear apart, and lacerate me.

But you, Almighty One, true hope of our salvation,

Order of all things, whatever flourish and whatever lie hidden,

Raise me up, who have fallen; cleanse me from the filth and stain of vice,

And strip me of present blemish and past guilt.

Make me free from future guilt, King of kings,

so that, made pure, I may proclaim you God.

Your whole creation, joined at the loins, celebrates you,

Whatever the earth carries, whatever the heavens bear and have borne,

Whatever the sea’s deep whirlpool nourishes for diverse uses,

And the flying air, winged and feathered [f. alite].

When you shall be judge in the divine power of the Father,

[Col. 0758C] Giving punishment to the rejected and rewards to the good,

And when from afar you shall see me bound outside the fragrant dwelling,

for here, alas, my memorials promise me this:

That he may very soon transfer me, white, among the lambs,

The right-hand fellow-lamb of that life-giving fleece,

Known deservedly above the heavens through the merits of Quintinus,

Whose useless little servant and attendant I am.

[lacuna]

May you live, Fécamp, always through prosperous years;

Rejoice, Fécamp, because you are most worthy of praise.

You Fécampois gird yourselves with the swords of virtues;

You strike down the shadowy enemies at the doors of the Church.

Happy Fécamp, with John’s star shining,

Who through vigilant care deserves the future kingdoms.

He sows in mourning and will reap fruits in his own joys.

[Col. 0758D] His flock is safe, having followed the Lord’s commands.

For, wishing to benefit himself, he gives both things that are necessary:

It is expedient that he endure, and that he care for ecclesiastical matters,

Under whom Bernard is Christ’s sweetest nard,

An enemy to distress, who breathes forth the holy fragrance.

## In the year of the Lord 1027. Gauzlin, archbishop of the Church of Bourges.

[Col. 0759]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. II, p. 39.)*

[Col. 0759A] Gauzlin, the illegitimate son of Hugh Capet, king of the Gauls, made great progress in letters under Abbo, his teacher, in the monastery of Fleury, and especially in the practice of every virtue. Therefore he was first ordained abbot of Fleury, at the wish of his brother King Robert; yet he did not obtain this dignity easily, because he had not been born of a legitimate marriage.

Later, when he was promoted to the see of Bourges, more serious disturbances arose on that account. On this matter we should hear the contemporary writer Ademar of Chabannes in his Chronicle:

“King Robert appointed Gauzlin abbot in place of the deceased Abbo, abbot of Fleury, who had been killed by the Gascons, although the monks resisted, unwilling to have the son of a prostitute rule over them. For he himself was the son of the most noble prince of the Franks [Col. 0759B]—Hugh Capet—a bastard, brought up from childhood in the monastery of Saint Benedict. The aforementioned king later also made him archbishop for the people of Bourges, after Archbishop Dagbert had died. But the people of Bourges themselves, carrying on a rebellion for five years, refused to receive him within the city, crying out with one voice: ‘It is not fitting for the son of a prostitute to rule the Church.’ Later, through the mediation of Abbot Odilo, the king’s will prevailed, and by God’s will Gauzlin was received into the see.”

Below, when the same writer speaks of the ordination of Gerald to the see of Limoges—whom he says was ordained in the episcopal rank by Seguino, the archbishop of Bordeaux—he adds:

“For Gauzlin, archbishop of Bourges, could not be present, because [Col. 0759C] he had not yet been received in the see of Bourges.”

Once admitted into his own city, he confirmed this year the charter of the foundation of the church of Saint Austregesilus at Graciacum. Gauzlin attended the synod of Airy, in the district of Auxerre, in the year 1020.

From the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, volume II of the *Spicilegium*, we also infer that he sat in the Council of Orléans in 1022, at which certain heretics were condemned and later committed to the flames, because he subscribed to a certain decree of King Robert, publicly issued at Orléans for Micy, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1022, when the heretics were condemned at Orléans.

In 1025 he blessed his monk Felix, returning from Britain, as abbot, at the urging of Hadegogis, countess of the Bretons, so that he might govern the monasteries of Saint-Gildas and Moriac in the district of Vannes, which she had restored, after returning there. This is read in the *Life of Saint Gildas* in the first Benedictine century.

[Col. 0760A] There was a serious controversy between Gauzlin and Jordan, bishop of Limoges. Jordan had been consecrated by Seguino, archbishop of Bordeaux, as we have already reported from Ademar of Chabannes. Later, however, retracting what he had previously said, Ademar testifies that Jordan was consecrated by Islo, bishop of Saintes, who was coadjutor to the archbishop of Bordeaux. He had earlier given the reason why Jordan was consecrated by someone other than the archbishop: Gauzlin had not yet been received in the see of Bourges. But shortly afterward he offers another reason: because, he says, Gauzlin demanded money for the imposition of hands, he was despised. [Col. 0760B]

Labbe notes that these words are absent from the manuscripts of the Thuane and Clermont College collections. But there was a sufficient cause for the dispute: Jordan had been consecrated without the authority of his metropolitan. Thus a synod was held in France before King Robert, where seven archbishops were present on Pentecost, together with their suffragan bishops. It excommunicated the entire Limousin region except the place of Saint Martial [lacuna] and forbade Jordan from exercising his episcopal office.

Jordan could have purged himself before the pope, as Ademar observes, but he preferred to promote peace and offer an example of humility. For, making satisfaction barefoot, with one hundred clerics and monks, all likewise barefoot, he went to the see of Bourges. There the archbishop came out with the clergy to meet them; leading them honorably inside, he released what he had bound.

[Col. 0760C] Helgaud, a monk of Fleury, is the authority in his abridgement of the *Life of Robert* that Gauzlin, together with other bishops of Gaul, raised the body of Blessed Anianus and transferred it, in the year 1029, to the new church founded by King Robert himself in the city of Orléans and solemnly blessed. That is also said to be the year in which Gauzlin died, although others defer his death to the following year. His epitaph, given by the distinguished Baluze in volume IV of the *Miscellany*, assigns the day of his death to the eighth day before the Ides of March. We have omitted publishing that epitaph here because it is barbarously written and tells us little about Gauzlin—namely, that he completely renewed the monastery of Fleury, where he lies, after it had first been consumed by flames.

[Col. 0761A] There exists a letter of this archbishop to King Robert, numbered 96 among the letters of Fulbert of Chartres, concerning the causes of the rain of blood, in which he replies to a question posed to him by the king. As is related in an old fragment of history preserved by Pithou, in the region of Aquitaine near the coast, three days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, blood rained down. When it fell upon human flesh, clothing, or stone, it could not be washed away—that is, removed by washing—but if it fell upon wood, it was easily washed away.

[Col. 0761B] Count William had written this to King Robert and consulted Gauzlin about the portent, asking whether anything similar had ever occurred and what it might portend and signify. The king’s letter is number 39 among the letters of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, in volume IV of Quercetanus’s *Collection of the History of France*.

Gauzlin replied that bloody rain foretold war, especially civil war. He adduces the testimony of Valerius Rufus in the book of *Memorable Deeds*, where he teaches that similar prodigies, during the consulships of Gaius Volumnius and Servilius Sulpicius, [Col. 0762A] preceded the beginnings of the civil war under which the Roman state suffered for so long. In Sicily, shields sweated blood; among the people of Metz, bloody ears of grain fell into a basket; and at the town of Caere, waters mixed with blood flowed.

Afterward he lists many examples from the history of Eusebius and others, especially the signs that preceded, under the emperor Justinian, that bubonic plague in which people died within three days. We omit the rest of this letter, which, considering the time when it was written, contains a considerable amount of learning. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, also replied to the same question, and, taking the circumstances of those times into account, not without learning.

[Col. 0762B] Aimoin dedicated to Gauzlin a book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*. In the Chronicle of an unknown author, reported in volume IV of Quercetanus’s *Collection*, Gauzlin is praised in these words:

“During these times the excellent abbot Gauzlin flourished at Fleury. Because of the probity of his character and the freedom of his spirit, he obtained from King Robert the episcopate of Bourges together with the abbacy of Fleury.”

[Col. 0761]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

[Col. 0761C] Gauzlin, or Gauslin, or even Gaucelin, was regarded as one of the great philosophers of his age and a prelate of great authority, “a man of universal knowledge and weighty authority” [Note: [Col. 0761D] Dom Pierre de Saint-Romuald, a Feuillant, in his *Chronological and Historical Treasury*, volume II, [Col. 0762D] p. 639, makes Gauslin the natural brother of Hugh Capet, contrary to the authority of contemporary authors.] (MAB. *Acta*, vol. VIII, p. 31, no. 3).

He was the natural son of Hugh Capet, later king of France (ADEM. *Chronicle*, p. 172), who had him raised from his earliest youth in the monastery of Fleury. There Gauzlin found excellent teachers for the time (HELG. *Life of Robert*, p. 75); and, with a fine intellect, he acquired a substantial knowledge of sacred and secular literature.

He benefited so well from the instruction of the learned Abbo in particular that, having deeply engraved it in his heart, it passed naturally into his speeches. He made no less progress in piety than in letters, and succeeded so well in joining the two that those who knew him best did not praise his learning without also praising his virtue (FULB. letters 40, 44). In this way Gauzlin prepared himself to become one day, as a contemporary author puts it, the support of orthodox faith and the pillar of Christian piety.

So many fine qualities, even more than his closeness of blood, helped make him dear to King Robert. Once the prince had recognized his worth, he placed such confidence in his counsel that he undertook almost nothing important without his advice.

[Col. 0762C] At Abbo’s death, which occurred on the thirteenth of November 1004, Robert gave Gauzlin the abbey of Fleury (ADEM. ibid.). The monks strongly resisted receiving him because of the defect of his birth, but the king’s will prevailed.

Hardly had Gauzlin become secure in possession of this dignity when he found himself in conflict with Fulk, bishop of Orléans, concerning the dependence of his monastery—a dispute that had already divided Abbo, his predecessor, and Bishop Arnulf II. Fulbert of Chartres, Gauzlin’s friend, nevertheless advised him to give the prelate the satisfaction that he believed was owed to him. Apparently the matter was settled in this way.

[Col. 0762D] The abbey of Fleury had long been famous, but it acquired new distinction under Gauzlin’s government through the arrival of several eminent persons from both Spain and France. Renouncing their wealth, the honors of the world, and even ecclesiastical dignities, they withdrew into this pious refuge to end their days there (MAB. ibid., vol. VI, p. 423). The monk Aimoin, who was one of its greatest ornaments, wished to honor the early years of the new abbot—whose fellow student he had been under Abbo—by dedicating one of his works to him.

[Col. 0763A] The king had conferred this abbey on Gauzlin eight or nine years earlier when, in 1013, the Church of Bourges became vacant through the death of Dagbert. He then gave Gauzlin that archbishopric as well (MAB. *Annals*, book LIII, nos. 11, 91; ADEM. ibid.; DU CHES. vol. IV, p. 96).

The citizens of Bourges, struck, like the monks of Fleury, by Gauzlin’s defective birth, protested against his promotion and refused to recognize him as their pastor. This refusal compelled Gauzlin to travel to Rome. There he was honorably received by Pope Benedict VIII and won the esteem of all the Romans who came to know him.

After making his eloquence admired in a public speech that he had occasion to deliver, he returned with a papal rescript to Geoffrey, count of Bourges. By means of this document he was enthroned in his see and remained its peaceful [Col. 0763B] possessor.

In 1020 he attended the great Council of Airy (Conc. vol. IX, p. 842), convened to restore peace and tranquility in Burgundy. Two years later, when King Robert assembled another council at Orléans to judge a kind of offshoot of the ancient Manicheans who were disturbing the Church of France, our prelate was also present and played a prominent role there.

He acted there both as bishop and as abbot, a title he retained for the rest of his life by keeping the abbey of Fleury. As abbot, he presented to the council the profession of faith of his brothers. In it, recalling the teaching of the six general councils that the Church accepted, they declared that they held no other beliefs concerning religion.

[Col. 0763C] It was apparently as a consequence of what Gauzlin then did against these heretics, who were confuted, that Ademar of Chabannes regarded him as a defender of the Catholic faith and a pillar of Christian piety (MAB. *Acta*, vol. VIII, p. 31, no. 3).

A disastrous fire having reduced the monastery of Fleury to ashes on 30 July 1026, the generous abbot undertook to rebuild it and completed the work within two years (BAL. Misc. vol. II, p. 307; DU CHES. ibid.). In 1029, he was present, together with two other metropolitans (HELG. ibid., p. 73) and several bishops, at the celebrated dedication of the church of Saint-Aignan at Orléans, which King Robert caused to be carried out in his presence and that of his entire court. Gauzlin died [Col. 0763D] that same year, on 2 September (MAB. An. book LVI, no. 60; BAL. ibid.), while making the rounds of his diocese. His body was carried to Fleury and buried in the principal church, as he had arranged during his lifetime. André, one of his monks, composed his Life almost immediately afterward; it is still preserved in manuscript. Others composed epitaphs in his memory. [Col. 0764A] Three different ones remain, almost equally barbarous. We select the least bad, reported by Dom Mabillon, who wisely removed several verses. M. Baluze published another (BAL. ibid., vol. IV, p. 555), and the third has never been printed.

## EPITAPH

Here beneath this mournful marble lies the sweet glory of the kingdom;

Here beneath the earth’s dust lies the great honor of his homeland.

Here, Gauzlin, is your rest and the end of your labor,

Until the Lord comes to give fitting rewards to the pious and punishments to the wicked.

Holy Peter, Father Benedict, holy Virgin Mary,

Endow your faithful servant with manifold interest.

[lacuna]

At the eighth hour [Note: [Col. 0763D] The words *Octavas Martis* have misled a great many writers, both medieval and from more recent centuries (MAB. An. book LVI, no. 60; BAL. ibid., vol. II, p. 307), who understood them to mean the eighth of March, on which date they place Gauzlin’s death. In that case, it would have to be assigned to the year 1030, because, according to them, this eighth day fell before Easter in 1029. But the words of the epitaph signify only the eighth hour of Tuesday, which was 2 September; [Col. 0764D] on that day the Fleury Necrology records this death. Since the short chronicle of the same place assigns it to the year 1029, we must adhere to that date, which is confirmed by the historian of our prelate, who says that he died in the twenty-fifth year since he had become abbot of Fleury. If he had died only in 1030, it would have been the twenty-sixth year (Marca, *Hisp.*, appendix, pp. 1025–1026).]

At the eighth hour of Tuesday Apollo was passing beyond the windows,

[Col. 0764B] when savage death snatched these joys from his grieving servants.

For his sake, whoever reads through this inscription, pour forth [a prayer].

However learned Gauzlin may have been, so far as we know he left no substantial products of his learning. The author of his Life does indeed mention a public speech that he delivered at Rome and that brought him universal applause, but he does not tell us whether it deserved to be handed down to posterity, either because of the subject it treated or because of the manner in which the orator handled it. The same writer also speaks of a profession of faith that Gauzlin presented in 1022 at the Council of Orléans, but he does not say whether the writing went into sufficient detail or had sufficient length [Col. 0764C] for it to be regarded as a theological treatise.

It is also known that Gauzlin wrote a great many letters concerning various affairs that affected him personally or in which he was obliged to become involved. Such, among others, was his dispute with Foulques, bishop of Orléans; and such was the deposition of Tedfroi, abbot of Bonneval, who, having withdrawn to our prelate’s vicinity, induced him to take up his interests. Fulbert of Chartres wrote Gauzlin four letters concerning these two affairs (FULB. ep. 39, 40, 44, 73), which presuppose at least as many letters on Gauzlin’s part. They even mention a fifth letter that he wrote to Arnoul, abbot of Saint-Père-en-Vallée. He also had occasion to write [Col. 0764D] concerning the resistance offered to his promotion to the archbishopric of Bourges, and in reply to Hadvise, duchess of Brittany, to the princes Alain and Eudes, her sons, and to the bishop of Vannes, concerning Félix, a monk of Fleury, whom they requested as abbot of Saint-Gildas of Rhuys (MAB. An. book LV, no. 53). [Col. 0765A] None of these letters now remains, though they would give us further information about all these events.

Nevertheless, we possess two other letters by our prelate on two other subjects. One is addressed to Oliba, bishop of Vic in Catalonia. Gauzlin speaks there more as an abbot than as an archbishop, although he assumes both titles. It is a letter of condolence on the death of Bernard, count of Besalú and Oliba’s brother, in reply to the circular letter by which Oliba had announced this death to his friends.

The other surviving letter of Gauzlin is more interesting. It is a reply to King Robert (FULB. ep. 95), who had written to our prelate [Col. 0765B] and to several other learned men in his kingdom concerning a kind of rain of blood that had fallen on one of the maritime coasts of Aquitaine. The prince urged them to tell him whether antiquity supplied any example of a similar phenomenon and what unfortunate event had followed it. Gauzlin showed the king, from the collection of Valerius Maximus, the Chronicle of Eusebius, the History of the Lombards, and other ancient monuments, that phenomena resembling the one in question had indeed been seen in former times and had been followed by public calamities, of which they are almost always portents. As for the different nature of the stains produced by this bloody rain, he answers only [Col. 0766A] with mystical and moral reasoning. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, who had also been consulted about the same phenomenon (ep. 97), gave an almost similar answer. Such was the spirit of the age.

The acts of the Council of Limoges (Conc. vol. IX, pp. 872–873), held in 1031, include a fairly long speech that Gauzlin had formerly delivered at court, in the presence of King Robert, against those who, refusing to recognize Saint Martial as an apostle, placed him among the confessors. Among the arguments used there by our archbishop, one notices some taken from the false acts of the saint. Those of Gauzlin’s own composition have scarcely more force than the others. It seems that Odolric, abbot of Saint-Martial and a great partisan of Martial’s apostolate, who produced this speech at the council’s assembly while praising its author highly, possessed it in written form.

Gauzlin gave his abbey of Fleury a fragment of Our Lord’s shroud, enclosed in a gold reliquary shaped like an arm. On it he had engraved these four short verses, apparently of his own composition (DU CHES. vol. IV, p. 96):

Joyful gladness

This hand bears,

Radiantly filled

With Christ’s shroud.

[Col. 0765]

# GAUZLIN’S LETTERS

## FIRST LETTER. TO KING ROBERT  
### Concerning the causes of the rain of blood

[Col. 0765C]

(See below under King Robert.)

## LETTER II. TO OLIBA, BISHOP OF AUSONA  
### Concerning the death of Bernard, count of Besalú, Oliba’s brother

(FLOBEZ, *España sagrada* XXVIII, 274.)

G., archbishop and abbot by the mercy of almighty God, sends abundant greetings to the lord O., raised by grace to the same dignity.

Hearing that the proclamation of your holiness, filled with the fragrance of spiritual spices, grows greater and greater each day, we extol God with joyful voices of praise, praying that his merciful right hand may govern you for a long time in this life. But while we always desire to hear prosperous and joyful things from the love of your fellowship with the ear of our heart, in turn we learn of matters that infect the mind and affect it with an evil report. For we grieve deeply when we learn that B., your brother in goodness, the light of his homeland and the relief of the afflicted, has died; and we grieve still more when we feel that you are endangered by excessive sorrow at his death.

Therefore we urge you to read our letter and seek a harbor of consolation, that you may find it. Let not the departure of your brother make you sorrowful, since you know that this irrevocable hour has been appointed for mortals. We also make known to your fatherhood that we have already offered prayers to God for his soul, as for our brother and your friend. We send your blessedness consolation from the blessing of Saint Benedict; receive it with the same charity with which it is sent. May our poured-out prayer also gently console his brother Wifrid, his wife and son, and his friends.

[Col. 0767]

# GAUZLIN’S SERMON ON SAINT MARTIAL

(See the Acts of the Council of Limoges II, held in 1031, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLII, col. 1356.)

# YEAR OF THE LORD 1030. ADALBERO, BISHOP OF LAON

[Col. 0767]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia christiana nova*, vol. IX, p. 521.)

[Col. 0767A] Adalbero, also called Azelinus, a cleric from the kingdom of Lothair, of which he was notary in 974, was made bishop at a very young age with Lothair’s support. On Palm Sunday, the Kalends of April, he was consecrated at Reims in 977 by Archbishop Adalbero, according to the continuator of Flodoard. His name is found subscribed to two documents from the years 972 and 974; but our Mabillon has already observed that both subscriptions were added later. In 980 he subscribed the charter of Herbert, count of Troyes, for the monks of Dervy; and about the same year he gave the church of Pierre-Pont to monks restored in the abbey of Saint-Vincent. In 986 he subscribed the donation of certain churches by Notrannus, bishop of Nevers, to the chapter of the major church of Nevers. [Col. 0767B] About the same year he was accused of adultery with Queen Emma; on this matter Pagius should be consulted, vol. IV, p. 53. In 987 he obtained from Hugh Capet a diploma confirming the possessions of Saint-Vincent of Laon; he also subscribed the same king’s decree for the monks of Corbie. In 989 he subscribed the privilege of Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, concerning the immunity and donation of the borough of Saint-Remi. In 991, when Charles, duke of Lorraine, had invaded Laon and was staying there with Arnulf of Reims, Adalbero surrendered the city to King Hugh. Hence Pope Sylvester accused him of treachery; and Guibert speaks of him as follows, book III:

“Ascelinus, who is also called Adalbero, born of Lorraine, rich in wealth and opulent in possessions, after transferring enormous sums, having sold everything, to the see over which he presided, adorned his church with truly exceptional ornaments and increased the possessions of the clergy and the episcopate; but he stained all those benefactions with a most eminent wickedness: he betrayed his lord the king, an innocent child, to whom he had sworn the oath of fidelity.”

In that same year, 991, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, Adalbero was present at the assembly of bishops convened at Saint-Basle against that same Arnulf. About 994 he attended another synod of the province of Reims. In 998 he subscribed a charter of King Robert for the monks of Saint-Denis, to whom he dedicated a poem—or rather, if one prefers, a satire—which Adrien Valesius illustrated with notes in 1663. In 1008 he subscribed another charter of King Robert for the monks of Saint-Denis at the council of Chelles. In 1015 he attended the Council of Reims and subscribed, under the name Azelinus, another diploma of the same Robert for the monastery of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon. Since he wielded great authority in the kingdom, through his agency Ebalus was appointed to replace Archbishop Arnulf in 1021. We discuss the disturbances that he caused in the Church of Soissons at about the same time [Col. 0768B] under Harduin, bishop of Noyon. In 1027 he attended the coronation of King Henry I, celebrated at Reims on Pentecost itself, and subscribed King Robert’s privilege for the monks of Dervy. In the same year he subscribed another charter of the same Robert for the monastery of Jumièges; he survived until 1030.

Before his death he had considered providing himself with a successor, Wido, nephew of Berold, bishop of Soissons. Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, strongly disapproved, writing to Adalbero himself and to Archbishop Ebalus and denouncing that detestable innovation—namely, that one church should have two bishops. Gerard’s zeal broke Adalbero’s plan and brought it about that Gebuinus, not Wido, [Col. 0768C] succeeded him. A letter of Fulbert to Adalbero survives. Dudo, dean of Saint-Quentin in the Vermandois, dedicated to Adalbero three books on the affairs of the Normans, which Quercetanus published with other Norman historians.

He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, according to the Saint-Vincent necrology, and was buried with the other prelates of his see [Col. 0769A] in the basilica of the monastery of Saint-Vincent, to which he had contributed much, as his epitaph, transcribed by the Sammarthani, teaches in these words:

Here, full of years, Bishop Adalbero died,

He who during life once founded much for this place.

Here he built the altar’s glory, here the glory of the Crucified,

And brightened the shrines of the saints; here also the church

He made wholly honorable and restored all that was old.

On the right he set up a tower and treasuries,

[Col. 0770A] And gave ornaments, making them excellent.

He constructed a pontifical vestment, completed with marvelous skill,

And gave three copes, many dorsal cloths and carpets.

For the honor of this church he accomplished many other things as well;

He also gave the brothers episcopal gold.

To the saints’ reliquary chests he presented altars,

Confirming this in writing, so that no one might ever undo it.

May worthy remembrance of him therefore be granted each year,

And may the Lord, in mercy, grant him everlasting rest.

[Col. 0769]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, VII, 293.)

[Col. 0769B] Adalbero left a satirical poem of four hundred and thirty hexameter verses, dedicated to King Robert. It is a kind of dialogue between that prince, who was still young, and our bishop, already advanced in age. The author treats, ironically and almost always allegorically, what was happening in the kingdom and what seemed to him contrary to good order. He took the opportunity to make his ill humor felt against those whom he disliked. Gerbert, who had reproached him for his treachery toward Prince Charles, was among them (MAB. *Act.* vol. VII, preliminary matter, no. 137). He is the person whom Adalbero designates under the name Neptanabus. All these circumstances show that the poem was composed before the end of the tenth century.

Adalbero treats the king’s affection for the monks as a kind of crime, from which, he says, there was no hope that he would ever withdraw. What shows that the poet exceeded the bounds of fair criticism, whether in what he says against the monks or in his other censures, is that he does not even spare Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, who was venerated by popes, emperors, kings, the holiest bishops, and the whole Church.

Another satirical poet, a contemporary of Adalbero (*Analecta*, vol. III, p. 534), thought himself entitled in turn to criticize the man who had criticized so many others. This is how he speaks of him concerning [Col. 0770B] Landry, lord of Dunois, whom he represents under the name Architophel and other allegorical names:

Adalbero does not understand why Architophel laughs:

He carries a fox in his breast and does not know how to spare his own.

The allegorical and at once ironic style that Adalbero employed in his poem, together with its poor versification, has cast great obscurity over it. Nevertheless, several historical features can be discerned, especially concerning the birth, handsome appearance, intellectual qualities, weaknesses, and virtues of King Robert; the power, greatness, and preeminence of the kingdom of France; and finally certain customs of the French, little known to [Col. 0770C] everyone.

This led the new editors of the *Historians of France* to prepare an edition of the poem with learned notes, which they will include in their fine collection. The celebrated Adrien Valesius deserves credit for the first edition that appeared. Having unearthed the work, together with several other ancient monuments, in a manuscript of Paul Petau’s (Bibliothèque de Saint-Germain-des-Prés), he published it after the panegyric, also in verse, of the emperor Berengar. The volume is in octavo and was printed in Paris by Cramoisy in 1663.

[Col. 0769]

# NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULUM

(Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. X.)

[Col. 0769] Adrian Valesius extracted this little work from a manuscript codex of Paul Petau and published it with notes in 1663, at the end of the poem *On the Praises of Berengar Augustus*. In it Adalbero converses with King Robert and sets forth, now allegorically and now ironically, what seemed to him to be badly administered in the kingdom of the Franks. Valesius discusses the value of this poem, as well as matters concerning its author, with sufficient accuracy in his notes. Nevertheless, he says that Adalbero, or Azelinus, was loved by William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, from whom he often received letters; we observe that this assertion greatly needs new testimony.

Moreover, the most learned man does not mention the suspicion of adultery into which Adalbero fell with Emma, the wife of King Lothair. Concerning this, he writes as follows [Col. 0771] to Adelaide, his mother, through Gerbert’s agency:

“My grief has been aggravated, O my lady, O sweet name of mother: when I lost my wife, my hope rested in my son (he became an enemy, at the instigation of Duke Charles, who accused her, together with certain others, before Louis). And from my shame and that of my entire family my once sweetest friends have withdrawn. They have brought a most abominable charge against the bishop of Laon. They persecute him and strive to strip him of his own dignity, so that everlasting disgrace may be inflicted upon me, as though it were the most just cause for my losing my honor, etc. (GERBERT, letter 50).”

As for the precise time when Adalbero composed his poem, it is useful to note the following. It certainly seems to have been written after Hugh’s death, since it makes no mention of that king. It is also probable that it was not written during the period of adversity that he suffered under King Robert while Pope Sylvester governed the Church. Sylvester occupied the papal see from 999 to 1003. From this one may conjecture that Adalbero’s poem should be assigned to about 1006, when Robert could be called young and Adalbero old, or advanced in years. Adalbero was then perhaps sixty years old, since he had been made bishop in 977. In any case, that same prelate was still alive in 1027, for he then subscribed a judgment held by King Robert for the monks of Jumièges. This proves, at any rate, that he could not have been called advanced in age before 1006. But these matters are not important enough to detain us longer. Let us hear Adalbero himself speaking with the king. As Valesius notes, the letter P placed before a verse indicates the prelate; R indicates the king as interlocutor. We retain Valesius’s extensive notes; anything we add is marked with an asterisk.

[Col. 0771]

# ADALBERO’S POEM TO ROBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS

(Dom Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens*, vol. X.)

## THE PRELATE

Thus I, the prelate Adalbero, write to King Robert (1),

A prelate advanced in age. The Laonese order of brothers (2),

The flower of the young and the fruit of the old, greets you in mind.

Write down on the tablets of your heart, point by point,

[5.] How much God has granted you and what things he has sent.

Examine, weighing the truth, whether all this is deserved.

For your fathers, O king, were emperors long ago (3).

An imperial nurse gives you milk as you suck (4);

While you are still a boy, the whole world measures out its lord, and everyone (5)

[10.] Rejoices with him, claps his hands, delights, and hopes (6),

Then with united voice crowns him king.

It awaits the coming of the times of peace.

The slippery age of adolescence has now passed:

Your image already shines with the bloom of youth (7).

[15.] Your appearance seems beautiful to us above all others (8);

You appear weak in no part of your limbs.

Although heavy in mass, you are nevertheless light with strength.

The common people rejoice, and the wise also are glad.

You have yoked beneath your feet many powerful kingdoms (9).

[20.] What do you complain of? What has he defrauded you of? What do you mutter to say?

No will at all cuts off the lineage bestowed by birth;

The pedigrees of nobles descend from the blood of kings.

## THE KING

Good praise and noble birth belong to kings and dukes.

You have spoken enough about appearance and virtue.

[25.] The virtue of the soul is more important than any virtue of the body.

## THE PRELATE

We ask for room to speak now; do not answer anything.

With your peace, pious king, we beg you to hear what must be said.

Do not despise me, since my innermost being trembles.

My grieving heart pours forth many tears; my trembling mouth utters sighs;

[30.] My contorted face cannot endure to speak.

Here is the expression of the body, with no moderation of voice.

In a few verses I shall attempt so great a sorrow.

The writings sent by the famous men of Croton are on display (10).

Above them is written a title, an ancient law:

[35.] “Let what is denied voluntarily be compelled by force:

As the command wishes, so let the order transform itself.”

Let that lazy, deformed, and altogether ugly rustic

Be adorned with a beautiful crown set with a thousand gems.

The guardians of the law compel men to wear cowls (12).

[40.] Let them pray, bow, remain silent, and compose their faces.

Let naked pontiffs follow the plow without end (13),

Singing verses with the goad of the first father.

And if by chance a place among the prelates should be vacant,

Let shepherds of sheep, sailors—whoever he may be—be enthroned (14).

[45.] Yet this must be sung with very subtle reasoning.

Let no one skilled in divine law attempt the episcopal office,

One emptied of the sacred Scriptures,

And whom not even one day’s study has disciplined (15);

Let him know the alphabet only, counting merely on his fingers (16).

[50.] These are the leaders; let the world adore them as teachers (17),

And let it aid them, so that they may be famous, without even excluding kings.

They give commands openly, but secretly whisper with deceit.

If this fixed divine rule remains established (18),

Discipline, vigor, virtue, and soon every adornment

[55.] Of the Church’s splendor will wither in a short time.

The commonwealth, governed in this way—yes, in this way—

Will lie buried in peace when its laws have been extinguished (19).

Luxury and incest, theft—then crimes will stand forth.

The freedom to commit offenses—then crimes will stand forth.

[60.] Those whom knowledge alone accompanies are excluded (20),

The fellow servants of Christ and those whom wisdom nourishes,

And those in whose backs the scar reveals the rudiments

Of sound doctrine.

If a great error of sacred faith should arise,

[65.] Let those involved be strangers to every censure.

At the king’s command let these be cut off from every [office] (so in the text);

Once all have left, let them guard the chamber behind closed doors (21).

This alone is written in gleaming gold as a command:

That the king’s steward, administering worldly affairs (22),

[70.] Be lazy, cowardly, and filled with little virtue.

Let him seek what belongs to others and reclaim his own while giving nothing,

And continually remain separated from the marital lot (23),

Unless hope stands firm for him as a claimant to the king’s inheritance (24).

It is the ancient will of the fathers, handed down as customary,

[75.] That the guardians of the chambers be chaste and sober.

Let the man who does not know how to grind be dearer to the king:

The description of great Caesar commands greater things of them (25).

Let that sacred monastic order deviate from its seat:

Let them take beautiful wives and attempt battles.

[80.] Terrified by the edicts, wondering where I might turn,

“Let the governors of my affairs be summoned,” [I thought] (26).

I reviewed everything, my throat shaken by sobbing,

Believing it wholly removed from the laws of our fathers,

Because it had never been heard of in ancient times,

[85.] Except for arrangements suited to stewards.

They soon propose to send a master to investigate;

Gaul produces monks whom the rule of the Fathers nourishes.

[Col. 0775] Let a monk be sent to the monks [lacuna].

Here is a wise man, here is a clever man, faithful in speech;

[90.] He is always accustomed to observe the laws of the fathers

And prudently knows how to bend the bold toward piety.

Cautious counsel is followed by action without delay.

He sets out in the evening and returns to us in the morning,

And swiftly leaves behind the foaming neck of his horse.

[95.] Where, where, where is the prelate? The good nurse? Hey, boy, wife?

He is disordered, having now put aside his former clothing.

A tall cap of Libyan bear hide (27);

His garment is shortened to the length of his legs (28),

Split in front, and sparing nothing behind.

[100.] His hips are tightly girded with a decorated baldric (29).

Many varied objects hang from the belts:

A bow with quiver, pincers and hammer, a sword,

A firestone, iron for striking, and oak together.

The bones tighten the surface, spread downward (30).

[105.] He walks with leaps—the spurs prick the ground (31);

He began to stretch the tops of his feet with twisted beaks (32).

He enters, whom the familiar brothers labor to recognize (33).

The citizens rush together and fill the spacious halls.

Thus the deformed man is set before the pontiff.

[110.] “Are you my monk, the one I sent?” [lacuna]

He lowers his fists and stretches his elbows upward;

He raises an eyebrow, twisting his neck with his gaze.

“Now I shall remain a soldier, a monk in another fashion” (34).

“I am not a monk; by the king’s command I serve as a soldier.

[115.] For my lord is King Oydelo of Cluny.”

## THE KING

Then are you pondering the cause of what is being kept silent? (35)

In my studies I remember learning the figures of forms.

## THE PRELATE

May your burning indignation not hinder what I say (36).

With your permission, let me report the Lord’s command:

[120.] The very wanton people of Sarra, in the manner of their filthy ways (37),

Have subdued the kingdom of the Franks with their hands and sword

And consume whatever Gaul nourishes.

Everywhere the earth is red, soaked with a rosy liquid.

Torrents of blood overflow from excessive slaughter;

[125.] The labor of the Church, every inward adornment consecrated,

The bodies of the saints fly scattered through the air.

There are already alliances of birds, and alliances of wolves (38).

It ravages the episcopal see of Tours with slaughter (39).

Martin weeps and himself cries out for a protector (40).

[130.] Oydelo has compassion, being bound by a similar law.

He went to Rome to pray for the monks’ salvation (41).

The Cluniacs raise their voices and make a din (42):

They cry out and warn: “Make ready at once, master,

To take up arms for your men and the things they must place first—

[135.] What belongs outside and what belongs within.

Your lunar shield must first hang before you (43);

Moreover, put on a triple coat of mail.

Let slippery belts support the helmet around your loins (44);

With straps binding your head, crown it with a sword.

[140.] Keep the darts behind your back, then hold the sword in your teeth,

And compel the sluggish young men to mount carts (45);

He ordered the troop of old men to mount horses,

Let two mount an ass, and finally a camel (46);

If these are insufficient, mount the buffalo three at a time.”

[145.] [Col. 0777] A thousand thousand men advance before the citizens (47).

The matter is carried on with the sword for three days (48).

As standard-bearer, eager, I began not to sleep (49);

With my jaws split open, I threw back my breath while fighting.

By the gods above, I do not know how many thousands I struck down—

Jupiter counts him double with the better pebble.

That third [day] is not rightly assigned to the god Mars.

Driven by a spear from my horse, I abandoned the shameful standard.

Fleeing with the others, I sought my native kingdoms.

Know that these things were accomplished at first light in December (50).

This same undertaking will be attempted before the Kalends of March.

[155.] The commander of the army, Oydelo, sends us to you (51).

The military order of the monks greets you as its lord.

The line summons and urges you to adorn the wars,

Surrounded by the marching column; hasten to fulfill the command (52).

[160.] It is fitting for you to die in arms rather than cultivate the fields.

To send forth more men than Asia promises leaves (53),

More than black Africa, more than the shore of the sea drinks in sand—

The third part of the world, Europe, boasts no fewer.

What do you want, madness, most worthy of gloomy cloisters? (54)

[165.] Drive your nails through the body, lest the pale flesh escape.

## THE KING

Believe me, your threatening words do not frighten me (55).

That teacher Neptanabus taught me very many things (56)

(The splendid hall slips along its gilded roofs and gleams).

## THE PRELATE

They tear apart the garment each person had been holding (57).

Afterward I observed neither truth nor falsehood concerning these things.

This, then, is the transformation of the kingdom’s order (58).

Everyone can join one thing to other things;

Wisdom shows what nature denies.

The hope of the young, the coming day, those who refuse to learn (59),

[175.] The cause of the old: to lament the childish courses of life without hope.

If I were diligent and knew everything in all matters—

Alas, wretched fool that I am, what now presses upon me with regret.

I do not know rakes, nor have I seen grim battles.

A bad situation: what I know they defend; what I do not know they surrender (60).

[180.] If this should happen, empty, I shall blow upon ashes:

Either the king’s ashes or those of my Muses I shall blow upon (61).

## THE KING

“If you are a famous Muse,” let the priest of the Muses cry out (62).

## THE PRELATE

Persius, in indignation, will then bring forth the one-eyed priest (63),

Who reads and understands the Muse’s office without the Muses.

To desire the good, yet eagerly long to delight in sacred speech,

I shall always be found mindful of these things and similar to the just;

This is what I always judge: I choose to know God,

And to prefer that knowledge above all things.

If prosperity is yours, do not be weary of remembering this (64),

[190.] O king, with how great an honor the King of kings has enriched you.

He first granted gifts better than all these,

For he gave a portion of himself—and that portion is true wisdom (65)—

Through which you can always know the things that are heavenly.

You must know what heavenly Jerusalem is,

[195.] What its stones, walls, gates, and structure are,

And for which citizens it has been built to endure.

It is governed in ordered distinction, not by a small number of soldiers,

But a differentiated authority prefers some to others.

It would take too long to unfold each point, because of the tediousness.

## THE KING

[200.] To know is nothing of mine, but always belongs to the beneficent God.

[Col. 0779] The human mind always seems close to God.

He cannot know himself who does not wish to know what is above him.

That Jerusalem is powerful, I think: it is the vision of peace.

The King of kings governs it, and the Lord rules over it.

[205.] When it divides its parts among themselves, it remains one and the same.

No shining gate is closed by any metal.

Here are walls without stones, stones without wal—

They are living stones; the gold of the streets lives.

It is believed to shine more brightly with refined gold,

[210.] With angelic citizens, and also with companies of human beings (66).

One part reigns; another part hopes.

This alone I know, but concerning these things I seek greater knowledge.

## THE PRELATE

The diligent reader greatly desires to know many things for himself,

But, sluggish and slow, he is accustomed to forget what came before.

[215.] Dear king, turn over the books of Augustine (67):

He is proved to have described what the lofty city of God is.

## THE KING

Come, I beg you, prelate, tell me who are there at the side (68):

Peers of princes, and whether there are any who stand in the order—[uncertain reading: *patus*].

## THE PRELATE

Seek Dionysius, who is called the Areopagite (69):

[220.] That prelate labors over two books concerning these things,

And the holy Gregory speaks about them as well (70),

In the *Moralia*, examining Job, a work of great faith.

The same man, completing his discourse, explains it openly (71);

And here, at the end, he plainly treats Ezekiel’s matters.

[225.] These are the writings that Gaul received when he gave them,

But such precedence is not visible to human eyes.

We shall say what our mystical intention is after this:

A distinct heavenly order is arranged (72),

After whose model the earthly order is said to be established.

[230.] God instituted ministers for the ancient people of the Church under the Law (73)

—an institution called “Synagogue” by a functional name—

And through Moses he set them in place and governed them,

As the sacred histories tell us they were established.

The order of the Church is called the kingdom of heaven (74),

[235.] In which God himself arranged pure ministers.

There the new law is observed under Christ the prince (75),

And the faithful judgment of the pontiffs established this as well (76):

How, by whom, and what sort of persons are to be appointed there.

From this the Church’s condition enjoys tranquil peace;

It must adapt itself to two laws (77):

The divine and the human, whose distinction shapes it.

The divine law divides none of its parts (78).

It forms them all under equal condition,

Although nature or rank produces them unequal.

[245.] The offspring of a craftsman is no less [worthy] than that of a king.

This pious law separates them from every worldly stain (79).

They do not split the earth, nor stand behind oxen.

They scarcely sully themselves with vines, trees, or gardens.

They are not executioners, innkeepers, or even swineherds (80),

[250.] Nor goatherds, nor shepherds,

Nor do they sift Ceres’ grain; the greased cauldron does not cook them.

They do not force their backs to crawl over the backs of oxen (81).

They are not washermen; they disdain boiling clothes (82).

But they must cleanse their minds and bodies (83):

[255.] Adorned with good character, they are guardians of others.

Thus God’s eternal law commands the pure to be,

And judges them free from servile condition.

God chose these as his servants; he himself judges them so:

He calls out from heaven that they must be chaste and sober.

[260.] He subjected every kind of human being to their command (84);

No prince is excepted, since he says “every kind.”

He commands them to teach the observance of the faithful sect

And thus to plunge the instructed into the sacred bath of washing (85).

He appointed physicians when wounds have festered (86),

[265.] Through whom the cauteries of words are to be applied.

He commanded that the sacrament of his body and blood (87)

Be handled properly by the priest alone.

He entrusted the greatest things to those whom he asked to handle him (88),

Things promised by the voice of God and not denied (89).

[270.] We believe and know this, unless their own crimes drive them away.

They ought to ascend to the foremost seats in heaven (90).

They must keep watch and spare themselves many foods (91),

And pray continually for the calamities of the people and for their own.

I have said little about the clergy, but have left much more unsaid (92).

[275.] Therefore all are equal in condition (93),

If one law encloses the one house of the Lord.

The matter of faith is simple; the order of the status is threefold.

Human law imposes two conditions (94):

The noble and the servant are not bound by the same law.

[280.] For the first [orders] are two: one rules, the other commands (95);

At whose command the commonwealth appears secure.

There are others whom no power constrains (96),

If they flee the crimes that royal scepters restrain.

These are the warriors, protectors of the Churches;

[285.] They defend the great and the small among the common people,

And likewise protect everyone and themselves.

Another division of servants by condition (97).

R. This afflicted class possesses nothing without labor.

Who could unravel, by counting the marks of an abacus,

[290.] The industry of servants, their journeys, and such great labors?

P. Treasure and clothing are sustenance for all servants.

For no free man can live without servants.

When labor arises, they desire both expense and possessions,

And king and bishops appear to serve their servants.

[295.] The master is fed by the servant whom he hopes will feed him,

R. The servants’ tears and groans have no end (98).

P. Thus God’s house, which is believed to be one, is threefold (99).

Now some pray, others fight, and still others labor:

These three exist together and do not permit division.

[300.] They stand through the duty of one; the work of two

Provides comfort to all in alternating turns.

Thus such a threefold connection is simple:

So the law prevailed, so the world rested in peace.

The laws are wasting away, and all peace is now ebbing.

[305.] Human customs change, and the order changes too.

King, then you rightly hold the scales, then you protect the world,

When you restrain those inclined toward wrongdoing with the reins of the laws.

R. Now, look: your white head already imitates a swan (100).

This is evidently what the nature of old age has said.

[310.] Such a nature has compelled belief that is not sound (101).

P. Another nature spurs me on; that one does not fail through old age (102).

R. How many natures are given to a human being? Tell me!

P. I suppose two (103).

R. Yet, of these two—which you know to be manifold—assign, from what she says, whose words they are (104).

[315.] A mere grammarian, much less a beguiling dialectician (105),

You remember very little of your earlier studies.

P. Whoever remembers a little does not forget everything (106).

R. You do not know how to remember the one who spurs you on, because of old age (107).

P. You press me too hard by provoking me to say what I would not wish to say.

[320.] This is the voice that resounds; madness does not torment me (108).

If nature compels the old, I do not sharply blame them (109);

Those skilled in art do not establish an end for nature (110).

Some say that fire is the artificer, wisely.

For others, nature is the splendid will of God.

[325.] For God is the nature of God; it is not so with human beings.

If he is truly God, he is the same and unchangeable.

That which is his own does not cease to be what it is by changing it.

The nature of the highest Father: each created thing

Receives a nature as soon as it first receives its origin.

[330.] Things joined to bodies undergo sensation;

There are some others that do not undergo it.

And if the body is changed, that too is changed:

It perishes along with what perishes, and remains when that remains.

These are joined to incorporeal things, but another kind to other things.

[335.] Those that are not joined to a body do not perish.

Human nature renders the human being twofold, duplicated.

One part is joined to the human body, but, when separated,

One is joined to this, while another is joined to that.

Whatever is contrary will be approved by neither this nor that.

[340.] Terrified, avoiding nature, the little she-ass speaks (111).

Neither passion nor any bodily nature understands.

That which revolves around the knowledge

Of the body, nature never perceives as something else;

But what she does not know is said to be known by her.

[345.] These matters must be grasped through intellectual perception:

There is an understanding by which both are known.

I call necessary what each of these requires;

These arguments too are necessarily so called.

R. Do all things derive their arguments from necessities?

P. [350.] Another hammer is present, and here it is a probable cause.

I have found what I set out to find, not forgetting these matters.

I speak of the present, and what I declare is true.

R. What is not true may not be called true;

A fable does not resemble truth, nor is it called true (112).

P. Behold, I have spoken the truth. You know that I do not exceed the truth.

No song of mourning or fable charms my love (113).

Do not suppose that these things happened thus, but that all could have happened:

I should like to set everything forth; although under a true theme,

There is nevertheless here a digression outside the subject.

[360.] It concerns the subject, yet it is called outside the subject;

It does not seem alien to its proper meaning.

It has the flavor of an ending and a purpose: it is not a fable, but a fact.

[lacuna] preceded; let joined persuasion come.

Now let the wise and moderate, contending in every way for the law of God the Father,

[365.] seek rewards or punishments by salutary right (114);

By powerful reasoning let them accept what is just, or what the unjust suffer;

Let them dispute doubtful matters without doubting what is certain;

And let them defend evils: these come from outside (115).

[370.] You possess, O king, the authority granted to an orator (116).

Now you demonstrate; then the order of the powerful deliberates,

Examining matters affirmatively with religious judgments,

From which they may be able to refute opposing claims.

R. [Col. 0785] A twofold judgment follows a threefold correction.

[375.] First, what sort of matters are at issue for us, transference, and end (117),

And the conjectures by which these ought to be distinguished.

P. A cause is not individual, but particular.

You will not find the four things you seek here (118),

But there is one arrangement of laws, taking up contrary things.

[380.] And I think that both the cause and its portion are above,

I have properly set down my feet; the other rises while it is fixed (119).

I estimate what I have touched; I have not departed from reason.

Nature, which does not die, compelled us to disclose these things (120).

I am blamed without deserving it, because I am forced by violence to say these things.

[385.] What have I done wrong against you? I have fulfilled the laws of nature.

You grieve worthily, since you, a king, are ordered to serve (121),

You, first among the Franks, a servant in the order of kings.

The one who does not guard his own words is badly disturbed here.

The kingdom of the Franks subjugates kings in the time of the fathers (122),

[390.] And always possesses the highest honor.

The scepters of the fathers’ kings restrain no one’s scepters (123);

Each man rules, rejoicing in his virtues, and commands equally (124).

We know that dominion has now fled from kings (125).

R. Thanks now to the Most High, through whom I desire to reign (126).

[395.] I do not claim it on account of my merits; rather, by everlasting praise,

May glory, praise, honor, and power belong to him who rules all;

With bended knees I always adore him as a suppliant,

So that we may be permitted to preserve the laws of our fathers (127).

P. The divine law forbids what corrects the two alternatives (128);

[400.] One permits, the other commands; and they are the lesser matters.

I judge that which is handed down later to be the greater:

Whatever is useful seems necessary to compare (129).

Let us always honorably hold to that which pertains to more matters (130),

and to whatever is stronger and most weighty.

R. [405.] Let the Almighty judge; may that divine judgment be with me.

P. Good peace on every side after struggles and labors (131),

And may the condition of the Church maintain its own laws by itself.

May the commonwealth possess the laws described, and no others (132).

Let Basil and Benedict observe their own kingdoms (133);

[410.] Let them hold whatever their kingdoms command.

May bishops henceforth never celebrate in the countryside (134).

Thus they maintain their own laws, if they do not concern themselves with rural matters.

May our order not dare to abandon the governance of justice (135),

But always apply itself with all its strength:

[415.] May it appoint just rulers, not men capable merely of enforcing the law (136),

Rulers of the poor and likewise of the wretched widows.

Let no one go to church except at night-time (137),

To go once; let everyone be permitted to pray during the day (138).

Let him judge and regard those present and those to come (139).

[420.] Let all receive a benefit according to their merits (140)

—may I alone be excepted, with your permission—faithful men.

Let them be permitted to utter seven praises through the hours (141),

And an offering with vows (142).

R. May this be the Father’s permission (143),

When the Loire attempts to lick the Calabrian fields

[425.] And the raging Tigris seizes the Spanish lands,

When Mount Etna produces roses or lilies in its lake.

If such things come to pass, then fear that these things will come to pass.

May the grace of Christ confirm you, Bishop Adalbero;

And likewise our own grace: deservedly worthy of a royal gift,

[430.] Not because you rave, but because you allegorize for us (144).

[Col. 0787]

## NOTES OF ADRIEN VALESIUS ON THE POEM OF ADALBERO

[Col. 0787A] Some years ago I came upon a small old manuscript, marked with the name and handwriting of Paulus of Padua, a man of consular rank. It contained, among other works, the poem of Adalbero, bishop of Laon, addressed to Robert, king of the Franks; the Chartulary of the monastery of Lérins; the Life of Abbot Suger; the letter of Count Stephen to his wife Adela; the Judgment of Varennes—or, as it is commonly called, the hearing of Queen Ermengardis and of the leading men of Louis, son of Boso—in the year 898, in the eighth indiction; and also the inquiry or election of bishops, clergy, and peoples for the consecration of a king, together with the queen’s ordination.

Of these works, the Life of Suger, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, was published some time ago, unless I am mistaken, by François Chesne; the Judgment of Queen Ermengardis, daughter of Louis the Younger Augustus and wife of King Boso, was recently published; and I arranged for the letter of Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, to his wife Adela and their children concerning the siege of Antioch to be published by Luc d’Achery in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, in the year 1661.

Among the other works that have not yet appeared in print, the poem of Adalbero stands out above all. In it the bishop converses with King Robert and exposes, now allegorically and now ironically, the abuses committed in the kingdom of the Franks both by people of every profession, especially monks, and by the king himself.

This poem seems considerably obscured both by the conversation between king and bishop, by its crude and trivial verses—that is, through the fault of the writer, or rather of the age—and by its almost continual allegory or irony. Nevertheless, it contains many things worthy of remembrance, both concerning King Robert’s lineage, appearance, and virtues, and concerning the greatness, power, and autocephaly of the Frankish kingdom; it also contains certain rites and customs of the Franks of his own age that are not known to everyone. Thus, if not for the weight of its words, then certainly for the weight of its subject matter, the name of its author, and its age of more than six centuries, it ought to be valued and treated as a treasure.

Therefore, when my brother urged me to publish this dialogue, I readily agreed and did not allow Adalbero’s work to remain any longer among my papers. I have therefore appended to a poem composed 740 years ago a poem of 650 years’ antiquity, adding to the praises of Berengarius Augustus, a Frank by nation, the praises of Robert, king of the Franks, and placing them beneath it. I shall also try to illuminate these praises with brief notes.

I have designated Adalbero the bishop as speaking with the letter P, and Robert the king with the letter R.

### (1) Thus Bishop Adalbero writes to King Robert:

In the old age of the bishop.

[Col. 0788A] Adalbero—whom Guibert, abbot of Nogent, affirms in Book III of his *Life* to have also been called Ascelinus or Azolinus—was born in the kingdom of Lothair, that is, he was a Lotharingian Frank. Through the favor of Lothair, king of the Franks, on Easter Day in the year 977 he succeeded Rorico, while still a young man, in the bishopric of the Church of Laon. Since he was a wealthy and well-funded man, he bestowed many substantial gifts upon his Church and the clergy of Laon; but he stained his generosity, learning, and other qualities by conspicuous treachery.

For on the day of the Lord’s Supper, in the year 990, after the gates of Laon had been opened at night, he handed over to Hugh, king of the Franks, Charles, duke of Lotharingia, who was in his thirty-seventh or thirty-eighth year—Guibert calls him a king and an innocent youth—and whose counselor he was and to whom he had sworn allegiance. In this way he made Hugh master of his wishes and of the kingdom. Hence some historians call him the aged traitor and false bishop of Laon.

In the year of Christ 991, in the reign of the Lord Hugh Augustus and of the most excellent King Robert V, in the fourth indiction, he took part in and subscribed to the pseudo-synod held in the territory of Rheims.
