There, together with his fellow priests, he condemned Arnulf, the natural son of King Lothair and archbishop of Rheims, whom he himself had previously reconciled alone, and deprived him of his archiepiscopal dignity.

Dudo, dean of the clergy of Saint-Quentin, dedicated to the same Adalbero, by an epistle, three books on the deeds of the Normans, carried down to the death of Richard the Elder, duke of the Normans—that is, to the year of Christ 996 or, if Dudo is to be believed, 1002. In it he praises Adalbero’s lineage, wisdom, and virtues, especially his goodness and holiness. From this it appears that Adalbero, or Ascelinus, continued to live after 1002—he was still alive in 1027, for he subscribes to a hearing held that year by King Robert [BOUQ.]—and remained bishop of Laon.

Sylvester the Younger, bishop of Rome, who began to sit in 998 [999], says that Azelinus or Adalbero, bishop of Laon, was accused of public crimes by a letter of King Robert—remarkably—and of the bishops, and was summoned to Rome to plead his case. Adalbero himself complains that he had been excluded from his own see by royal force through the faction of certain people, though he had not been deprived of his episcopal office.

Nevertheless, he successfully weathered all these storms and soon recovered the prince’s favor. He was the king’s friend and even his intimate, as this poem shows. The learned bishop, as the times permitted, composed it in old age for a king educated in letters and fond of learned men, as Glaber Rodulfus and Aimoinus testify. He speaks of himself as follows:

Thus Bishop Adalbero writes to King Robert,

In the old age of the bishop.

Thus he speaks of Robert, king of the Franks:

“The image of your youth now shines forth in bloom.”

And Robert speaks of himself:

“Now this white head of yours imitates a swan.”

Since Adalbero says that he is writing to King Robert, addresses King Robert everywhere, and nowhere mentions Hugh, it appears that he composed this poem after the year of Christ 998, that is, after the death of Hugh, King Robert’s father. Odilo was then ruling Cluny; Adalbero mentions this abbot, who is known to have succeeded Maiolus after Maiolus died on 11 May 994, in the eleventh year of Otto III’s reign.

Furthermore, Azelinus counted among his closest friends Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, who in Letter 45 calls him the illustrious bishop of Laon and a great Father. Fulbert asks him—God had given him an incomparable ability to persuade well—to urge the king to avenge the murder of his subdean. Adalbero was also loved by William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, from whom he frequently received letters.

### (2) The Laon order of brothers,

The flower of the young and the fruit of the old greets you in spirit.

That is, the clergy of the Church of Laon, both the greater and the lesser, who are my brothers in Christ, greet you not with their tongues but with heartfelt prayers. The older, or more honored, clergy were called priests and deacons; the younger clergy were subdeacons and those of the lower orders. Gregory, in chapter 44 of Book V of his *History*, calls the former “greater clergy” and the latter “lesser clergy.” Fortunatus, in Poem X of Book II, similarly designates both groups in his address to the clergy of Paris, using the terms “old” and “young”:

“In the midst stands Germanus, bishop in honor,

Who rules the young on one side and raises up the old on the other.”

Nor does Adalbero compare the young to flowers and the old to fruits absurdly; spring belongs to the young, autumn to the elders.

### (3) For your fathers, O king, were emperors long ago.

Adalbero did not say this falsely. Robert had Hugh as his father, Robert as his great-grandfather, and Odo, the brother of his great-grandfather, as kings of the Franks; his great-aunt Emma was also queen of the Franks, wife of King Rudolf.

Through his grandmother Hadewidis or Hawidis, he was related to her father Henry the Saxon, surnamed the Fowler, king of the people beyond the Rhine, or of the Eastern Franks; to her brother; and to her brother’s son and grandson, the emperors Otto. For Hugh, Robert’s father and king of the Franks, was a first cousin of the emperor Otto II; the emperor Otto I had as his maternal uncle and grandfather Henry, king beyond the Rhine; and the emperor Otto III and our Robert were the sons of first cousins.

Moreover, since Hadewidis was the sister of Gerberga, who by her second husband Louis, king of the Franks, was mother of Lothair, king of the Franks, and grandmother of Louis, Robert’s father Hugh was a first cousin both of Lothair, king of the Franks, and of Otto II Augustus. Robert himself and Louis, son of Lothair—the last of the Carolingians to reign among the Franks—were children of first cousins, or sons of the children of first cousins. Therefore Adalbero rightly adds:

“The genealogies of nobles descend through the blood of kings.”

### (4) The empress-nurse gives you milk as you suck.

Adelaidis, wife of Hugh, king of the Franks, and mother of our Robert, is perhaps improperly called “empress” by Adalbero, just as her husband Hugh was called “Lord Hugh Augustus” instead of king in the synod held in the basilica of Saint-Basle in 991.

The Acts of that synod begin as follows: “In the fifth year of the reign, from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, of Hugh Augustus and of the most excellent King Robert, a synod was assembled in the territory of Rheims.”

Thus Helgaldus, in chapter 13, calls our Robert, the son of both, “emperor of the Franks,” and calls his threats imperial and his command imperial. Thus Gerbert calls Lothair, the son of Louis by Gerberga, king of the Franks, “Caesar” in the verses written on his tomb.

It is difficult to know who Robert’s mother Adelaidis was, since Helgaldus merely says that her illustrious lineage originated in Italy, without naming her father or mother. Some very recent writers falsely believe that Adelaidis, who was Robert’s mother by Hugh, was the daughter of Lothair, king of Italy, and the sister of Emma, wife of Lothair, king of the Franks.

For Adelaidis, by her first husband Otto, Lothair, king of Italy, bore a daughter, namely Emma, wife of Lothair, king of the Franks, and mother of Louis, as Odilo writes in the *Life of Adelaidis Augusta*. By her later husband, Otto Augustus, she bore a daughter bearing her own name, Adelaidis, and three sons, as Witichindus teaches.

Since, therefore, Lothair, king of the Lombards, had by his wife Adelaide only one daughter, named Emma, Adelaidis, mother of our Robert by Hugh, clearly cannot be regarded as the daughter of Lothair, king of the Lombards.

It should also be noted that at that time it was customary for illustrious women to nurse their children with their own milk. Adelaidis, although she was the wife not yet of Hugh the king but certainly of Hugh, duke of the Franks and count of Paris, gave her son Robert her breasts and did not wish to employ any nurses for the infant, so that she might be her son’s entire and undivided mother:

“The empress-nurse gives you milk as you suck.”

### (5) While still a child, the whole world measures you as its lord,

And rejoices with you, and so forth.

The whole world measures you as its lord while you are still a child, and rejoices with you.

### (6) It applauds with its hands, rejoices, and wishes

You as its king; soon, with united voice, it crowns you.

Those who elected the king—the Frankish, Saxon, and Lombard bishops and counts—all, according to their ancestral or Germanic custom, honored the future prince with clapping of hands and accompanied him with acclamations. Then they approved him, or, as the common expression was, praised him together; after the oath of allegiance had been promised by each in order, they blessed and crowned the king; they placed the crowned king on the royal throne; and, after he had been raised to the royal seat, they honored him with the appropriate congratulations and ceremonial observance.

With Adalbero, “rejoicing” refers to the acclamations, while “wishing him as king” refers to collective praise or confirmation. Gregory mentions the clapping of hands in Book II, chapter 42 of his *History*, where the Franks of Cologne, clapping both with their palms and with their voices, raise Clovis on a shield and establish him as their king; although in the Julian manuscripts I find *parmis* written instead.

In the *Life of Henry of Bavaria*, the first of that name among the emperors and the second among the kings, believed to have been written by Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht and a contemporary author, the following is found under the year 1004:

“King Henry there, at Pavia, is received by the noble Lombards who had gathered to welcome him with worthy applause, and is led amid the rejoicing of the entire city to the church of Saint Michael. There the clergy, there the assembly of nobles, there the common people of both sexes—all with one accord acclaim Henry as king with one voice, praise him together, and designate him by raising their hands. Thus, having been praised together, he is crowned; once crowned, he is honored by all as duty requires; then he is led to the palace with complete joy.”

In the year of Christ 997, when his father associated him with himself in the kingdom, Robert was still a boy, as Adalbero says—about sixteen years old, since he died in 1031 and Helgaldus says that he died at the age of sixty.

### (7) The image of your youth now shines forth in bloom.

Robert was a young man, or at the beginning of youth; having passed through adolescence, he was about twenty-seven years old in 998, when he lost his father. Therefore the contemporary author Glaber Rodulfus writes of both of them in Book II, chapter 1:

“King Hugh, having established his kingdom in peace, died happily. For at that time King Robert was young, prudent and learned, sweet in speech, and distinguished for his piety.”

[* From the youthfulness of Robert noted here, some infer that Adalbero composed his poem immediately after the death of Hugh Capet; but his words do not seem to be accepted so scrupulously, as is clear from what was said in the Preface. Robert could indeed be called young in 998; but it is not likely that Adalbero, who was still alive in 1027, was called old in 998. BOUQ.]

### (8) His appearance seems beautiful to us beyond all others.

Helgaldus says that Robert was tall in stature, with smooth or straight hair, a long and open nose, raised shoulders, and, finally, a distinguished and truly royal appearance. Gerbert mentions King Robert’s bright face and cheerful expression in one of his letters.

Nevertheless, he was stout, perhaps with a somewhat prominent belly, though in such a way that his stoutness did not impede the strength or agility of his body, if Adalbero’s words are to be trusted:

“Although heavy in mass, you are nevertheless light with strength.”

[Col. 0792A] William of Nangis, a monk, certainly also calls Robert a robust and agile young man.

### (9) He has yoked beneath your feet many mighty kingdoms.

This verse refers back to the fifth verse:

“How many and how powerful kingdoms God has granted or sent to you.”

To you, Robert, God subjected powerful kingdoms: France, Burgundy, and Aquitaine. Just as, when the Merovingians ruled in France, there had been three kingdoms of the Franks—Neustria, Austrasia, and Burgundy—so, after the death of Louis the Pious Augustus, when the provinces of Frankish territory were divided among several rulers, our kings began to be called kings of the Western Franks. Nevertheless, three kingdoms were assigned to them: Western France, or Neustria; Burgundy, though greatly diminished; and Aquitaine.

Thus Abbo writes in Book II that King Odo subjected France, or Neustria, Burgundy, and Aquitaine to himself, and calls that threefold or triple kingdom:

“Thus the triple kingdom rejoices in a single ovation.”

And in the consecration of King Louis the Transmarine, performed at Laon, which I possess in writing, I find the following:

“Almighty and everlasting God, multiply the gifts of your blessings upon this servant of yours, whom with humble devotion we have likewise chosen for kingship, so that, and so forth; so that he may not abandon the royal throne, namely that of the Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanians, nor the scepters of these peoples, but, with your help, may restore their minds to the harmony of their former faith and peace.”

In Flodoard, under the year 969:

“Lothair, still a boy and son of Louis, was consecrated king, with the support of Prince Hugh and the other bishops and nobles of France, Burgundy, and Aquitaine.”

Glaber Rodulfus, in Book II, chapter 1, says that, after the leading men of the kingdoms of the Franks and Burgundians had been gathered in the royal city of Orléans, Robert was established as king by his father while his father was still alive. He omitted the Aquitanians because they were then in rebellion.

In an old chronicle I find that in 1059 Philip was consecrated king by order of his father Henry, in the presence of the archbishops of France, Burgundy, and Aquitaine and twenty-two bishops.

### (10) The celebrated writings sent by the people of Croton are openly displayed.

[* Here Valesius is at a loss. It is well known that the people of Croton were very famous athletes, but not writers; perhaps writers are meant here. BOUQ.]

### (11) That rustic, lazy, deformed, and ugly in every respect

Is adorned with a beautiful crown glittering with a thousand jewels.

[Col. 0792D] If I am not mistaken, Adalbero complains that obscure and ignoble men, idle, deformed, and vicious in body and mind, were made abbots and wore a gemmed episcopal mitre, which he ironically calls a crown.

At that time certain abbots already enjoyed this privilege; Pope Urban II later granted the right to wear the mitre to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1088. Valesius understands this as an abbatial mitre, which he supposes was worn by abbots chosen from the ignoble—that is, from the lowest class of the people.

But the most learned man is mistaken. No abbot is found to have been granted the use of the mitre before Egelsinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine near Canterbury, to whom Alexander II granted that privilege on account of the dignity of that Roman alumnus and apostle of the English. This practice only began to become common under Pope Urban II, who bestowed the same privilege upon Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, and Hugh, abbot of Cluny. See Mabillon, *Preface to Part I of the Sixth Century of the Benedictine Annals*, section IV.

### (12) The guardians of justice compel them to wear cowls:

Let them pray, bow, keep silent, and lower their faces.

A cowl, prayer, the inclination of the head and body while wearing it, or prostration on the ground to receive a blessing, silence, and the lowering of the eyes and of the whole face are characteristic of cloisters and appropriate to monks.

Adalbero therefore indignantly attacks the Frankish nobles, and even the guardians of justice—that is, the governors of cities, whom our historians indiscriminately call, according to their twofold duty of fighting and judging, sometimes counts and sometimes judges—for being made monks by abbots through ambition and greed [* Others will say, “through zeal for the salvation of souls,” and will turn it into praise. BOUQ.], and for compelling pious and simple men to change their way of life and dress.

Under Robert’s reign we have notable examples of this change in Arnold, count of Angoulême, and Burchard, count of Corbeil and Melun, who became monks after having been counts.

Earlier, William, surnamed “Stupe’s Head,” duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, had professed the monastic life in the monastery of Saint Cyprian at Poitiers and later transferred to the monastery of Saint-Maixent, where he is said to have died about the year 963.

### (13) Let naked bishops follow the plow without end,

Singing the songs of the first parent with the goad.

[Col. 0793C] Let naked bishops follow the plow and oxen with a goad, singing the songs of the first parent expelled from paradise.

With these words Adalbero attacks the abbots, who claimed for themselves nearly all the insignia and rights of bishops and had cast bishops down from part of their honor and prosperity, reducing them to a humbler condition.

[* Is there anywhere a record that bishops were stripped by abbots of both property and honor, as the annotator assumes here? But he sees those whom he dislikes in the worst possible light. BOUQ.]

### (14) And if the place of a bishop should happen to be vacant, let them enthrone

Shepherds of sheep, sailors, whoever he may be.

Adalbero is indeed mocking, but nothing prevents truth from being spoken through mockery. He is indignant that men entirely ignoble, born of shameful and utterly base parents, ignorant of divine law and sacred books, altogether ἀγραμμάτους καὶ ἀναλφαβήτους—“unlettered and illiterate”—were raised by King Robert to the episcopal rank.

Glaber Rodulfus, a monk of Cluny, writes that Robert was accustomed to do this, and judges the king on that account to be highly deserving of praise. These are Rodulfus’s words about Robert, king of the Franks, in Book III, chapter 2 of his *Histories*:

“This king, therefore, as a most wise worshiper of God, was always a lover of the humble and, as far as he could, a hater of the proud. If any episcopal see in his kingdom became vacant of its proper bishop, he took the greatest care that a useful shepherd, even if lowborn—Valesius adds, ‘ignorant of divine law and sacred books’—should be restored to the Church rather than a noble person devoted to worldly pomp.”

In this matter he imitates Christ the Lord, who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27). For this reason he also found the leading men of the kingdom exceedingly resistant: despising humble men, they chose proud men like themselves.

Adalbero, therefore, was not alone in criticizing and condemning this in Robert; many of the nobles of the Frankish kingdom did so as well. Certainly our ancient historians, the Lives of holy bishops, and the old *Formulas of Marculf* show that our kings considered not only moral integrity and prudence but also nobility when choosing bishops.

For no other reason does Thegan the Frank, a noble man, grieve and complain that in his own age men of the lowest servants, sons of goatherds freed into liberty, were made supreme bishops. “All are one in Christ Jesus. There is neither slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28). Therefore, in sacred matters, the one who excels in virtue and learning should be preferred. Nobility should be preferred only when all other things are equal.

### (15) And whom not a single day’s study has constrained.

That is, who has not studied even for one day.

### (16) May he know the alphabet only well enough to count on his fingers.

Let holy Adalbero understand this to mean that he knows only how to count letters on his fingers, just as the author of the *Panegyric on the Praises of Berengarius Augustus* and many others, including older writers, used “to know” for “to understand,” and “wise” for “learned.” Even today we say *savoir*, “to know,” from *sapere*, and call a learned person *savant*, that is, “wise,” and rightly so. For learning does not belong anywhere except in the wise.

[Whether this assertion of Valesius is true, let others judge. BOUQ.]

### (17) Let these men be nobles; let the world honor them as teachers,

And let it assist them as the celebrated, with not even kings excepted.

[Col. 0794C] Let such bishops—so ignoble and so unlearned—be nobles of the kingdom; let them sit first among the Frankish optimates in the place due to bishops. Let everyone regard and greet them as teachers; let even celebrated kings not be excepted—that is, let you yourself also, Robert, who chose them as bishops, worship and honor them.

### (18) If this rule of the divine ones should remain established,

Discipline, vigor, and so forth.

“Rule of the divine ones”: the rule of kings, the rule of the prince Robert. Adalbero means: if the king persists in observing this pernicious rule, this custom of choosing unworthy bishops, it will greatly harm both the churches and the commonwealth, or kingdom, of the Franks.

### (19) When the laws have been extinguished, it will rest buried in peace.

This was written as follows: “It will be led to the utmost limits of death,” instead of “it will rest buried in peace.” Many such readings, written above the text in Adalbero’s own hand, are found in this poem. I shall report each in its proper place, if they are worth so much attention.

### (20) And those too are excluded whom knowledge alone accompanies,

Christ’s fellow servants and those whom wisdom nourishes, and so forth.

In these eight verses Adalbero indicates that learned, good, and wise men, devoted to Catholic and holy teaching, are removed far from bishoprics, from assemblies or synods convened to oppose heresies, and from the king’s council.

### (21) When everyone has gone out, let them guard the bedchamber behind the doors.

Perhaps *ingressis*, “when they have entered,” should be read.

### (22) So that the king’s administrator, managing worldly affairs,

May be lazy, idle, and so forth.

I cannot guess whom Adalbero designates by the name “the king’s administrator,” any more than I can determine what is written above concerning the people of Croton, or what is inscribed as the most ancient law. “Managing worldly affairs” means “administering property.”

### (23) And let him remain perpetually separated by the lot of marriage.

That is, let the king’s administrator not take a wife, but remain celibate forever.

### (24) So that no hope of profit may stand for the king’s heir-seeker.

Let the king’s administrator have no hope of profit except when the king claims some inheritance, or vindicates some property for his treasury as ownerless. If this is the true meaning of Adalbero’s words, as it seems to be, then the king’s administrator here will be the administrator of the treasury, like the chamber guards and chamberlains below.

### (25) The great Caesar’s decree commands these greater things:

Let that sacred monastic order depart from its seat;

Let them take beautiful wives and attempt battles.

The emperor Valens, after issuing a law that monks should serve as soldiers, ordered those who refused to be killed with clubs by tribunes and soldiers, as the priest Jerome writes in his *Chronicle*. The law of Valens is preserved in the *Theodosian Code*.

Shortly before this, the emperor Julian had prohibited by law soldiers from becoming monks before completing their military service. Valens indeed ordered monks to serve in the army; Constantine Copronymus, son of Leo, commanded or compelled those same monks to take wives and wear white garments, as Theophanes, translated by Anastasius, and others have handed down.

Adalbero, however, seems to have been misled by the name and to have falsely attributed to Constantine the Great what was done by Constantine Copronymus. Above he calls him “the great Caesar” and calls his law “the decree of the great Caesar.” The title “great Caesar” does not suit Constantine Copronymus, that very evil and impious opponent of images, any more than it suits the Arian emperor Valens.

But why does Adalbero say these things about monks of his own age, or what similar practice was taking place among our monks at that time?

### (26) It pleases me to summon the governors of my affairs.

[Col. 0795D] Since this verse disrupts the sense, it is either superfluous or has been placed in the wrong position.

### (27) A high cap made from the hide of a Libyan bear.

Adalbero condemns and ridicules the monastic habit: monks, having forgotten their profession, wore caps made from bearskin, garments shortened to the length of the legs and open in front and behind, decorated belts, swords, bows, and spurs, and rode about on horseback. Orderic Vitalis, reporting events of the year 1089, says: “Now nearly all common people cover their heads with a band or cap. Scarcely any soldier comes out in public with his head uncovered and properly tonsured, according to the Apostle’s command.” Previously, that is, the Gauls and Franks, following Roman and German custom, were accustomed to have their heads uncovered and bare [Col. 0796A]. Moreover, this half-line is Virgil’s, from Book V of the *Aeneid*.

[lacuna] With the hide of a Libyan bear.

(28) And the garment is shortened to the length of the legs:

It is split in front, nor does it spare the rear.

Adalbero altered the latter part of the first line in order to correct the error, and wrote above it, instead of *curtata talaris* (“the ankle-length garment is shortened”), *talaris adempta* (“the ankle-length garment removed”). Glaber Rodulfus lived during the reign of Robert and narrated the life of William, abbot of Dijon, or of the monastery of Saint Benignus. In chapter 24 he introduces William preaching at the consecration of the basilica of Saint Benignus, in chapter 16, as follows: “Do you not see these most savage slits and mutilations of garments? These shavings of the hair along men’s necks, and so forth? For all these things, recent and newly spreading, have arisen from the fury of diabolical superstition” [Col. 0796B]. The same author speaks of the matter at the end of Book III of his *Histories* and ridicules the Frankish men for their truncated clothing.

According to Glaber, William, abbot of the monks, condemned these recent practices among laymen; nevertheless, the monks imitated them when riding and travelling, cutting and shortening their ankle-length, hanging garments so severely that they scarcely reached the knees. Although these garments ought to have been closed on every side, they opened them in front and behind, so as to be more agile when mounting a horse. In these mutilations and shortenings—and also in the slits made in clothing—we are still utterly mad today.

(29) He girds his loins with the most tightly fastened, ornamented baldric.

Adalbero calls the belt a *baldringum*, a word I have not encountered elsewhere; what we commonly call a *baudrier* derives from *baldringum* [Col. 0796C]. He calls it an ornamented baldric because it was embroidered with a needle. Among the Germans, *ring* means “belt,” as Cangius shows under *rinca*; *bald*, however, means “a bold man.” Thus, according to the etymology of the word, *baldring* would have been the belt of a military man, a man vigorous in arms.

It should be noted that in the following verses a pair of pincers, a hammer, and oak are assigned to a monk on horseback: pincers for pulling nails from soles and from the horse’s hooves; a hammer for shoeing the horse, or for driving the nails into its hooves; and oak, or oak leaves, for receiving and preserving the fire struck from flint by iron.

(30) The hose, spread downward, clings closely to the body.

Paul the Lombard in Book IV calls these *osas*, the monk of Saint Gall in Book II calls them *hossas*, and others call them [Col. 0796D] leg-bindings, gaiters, or boots; Matthew of Paris calls them military footwear, commonly known as *housses*. The Germans still call such coverings for the lower legs *hosen*, while we call them *housses*. But it should be considered whether here Adalbero, by *ossae* spread downward and tightening the surface, may instead be designating a cloak which the monk, about to ride, had taken up and thrown over all his clothing and arms against the rain.

[* Medieval writers consistently understand leg-bindings under the name *osae*, as you can see in Cangius’s *Glossary*, s.v. BOUQ.]

(31) Walking in leaps—the spurs prick the ground—

That is, the monk moves in a leaping fashion after dismounting from his horse, and with his spurs now pricks not the horse’s flanks [Col. 0797A] but the ground. Adalbero also altered this line, being somewhat dissatisfied with it, and wrote above it:

The spurs prick the ground impressed by leaps.

(32) [lacuna] the spurs prick the ground.

He began to stretch the tips of his feet with twisted beaks.

The monk proceeds by leaps and pricks the ground with his spurs when he begins to extend the tips of his feet and twist the beaks, since because of his enormous shoes he cannot advance in any other way. Orderic Vitalis, in his account of the events of 1089, describes shoes of this kind in these words: “Shoemakers make on footwear things like scorpion tails, which are commonly called *pigacia*.” Again: “Courtly men attach to the joints of their feet the likeness of serpent tails.” Thus these things, resembling the tails of serpents and [Col. 0797B] terrestrial scorpions and commonly called *pigacia*, were attached to the joints of the feet, or to the tops of the feet—that is, they were sewn onto the front or forward part of the shoes.

Therefore Adalbero says:

He began to stretch the tips of his feet with twisted beaks.

He calls these serpent tails and shoe-*pigacia* “beaks,” because they resembled the beaks of birds or ships. John Dubravius likewise calls such footwear beaked shoes. In Book XX of his *Bohemian History*, concerning John, king of Bohemia, who imitated French customs, he reports the following concerning the year around 1328: “He had an exotic appearance in the cultivation of his hair, in the wearing of beaked shoes on his feet, and in clothing his body with little cloaks scarcely covering half his buttocks.”

In the chronicles containing the deeds of Charles VI, king of France, composed by a learned monk and preserved in the Thuane Library, I find the following concerning the French, especially the nobles, who besieged Nicopolis in 1396: “They wore excessively fringed and sleeved garments, and always beaked shoes two feet long, and sometimes longer; this reprehensible extravagance prevailed among the nobles, especially those of France.” The author then added concerning these same Frenchmen, when they were preparing to fight Bayezid, whom he calls Basatus and Basita: “And so that they might walk more easily on foot, they cut off the long and excessive beaks of their shoes, which—shamefully—this reprehensible and vain curiosity had until then maintained among the nobles; and at that time it came to an end.”

(33) He enters, whom the brothers known to us strive to recognize.

The citizens converge and fill the spacious palaces.

[Col. 0797D] Thus, disfigured, he is set before the bishop.

The monks, the brothers known to Adalbero, and the citizens hurry up and set before their abbot a monk who, having removed his monastic habit, is dressed in secular clothing, armed, and so disfigured that he can scarcely be recognized by them. Adalbero calls the abbot by the envious name “bishop,” that is, “overseer,” as though he were the overseer of the monastery’s precincts and palaces; below he ironically calls Odilo “king.”

(34) Now I shall remain a soldier, a monk according to a different custom.

I am not a monk, but by the king’s command I serve as a soldier;

For my lord is Odilo of Cluny.

When the abbot does not recognize the monk as a soldier and asks whether he is the monk whom he sent somewhere the previous day, the man replies: “At present I am a soldier, at present a monk: when I travel, a soldier; when I remain in the monastery, a monk. Why do you question me? Properly speaking, I am not a monk, but by command of my lord Odilo, abbot of Cluny, who is my king, I serve as a soldier.” What could be imagined more amusing?

This monk, then, belonged to one of the many monasteries governed by Odilo throughout Gaul, as Jotsaldus the monk teaches. Jotsaldus composed three books on the life and virtues of Saint Odilo, abbot, for Stephen, bishop and Odilo’s nephew. I recently found these books in the Thuane Codex, namely in the lectionary of the Church of Lyon; they deserve to be read throughout. Peter Damian says that he condensed them into an epitome, without naming their author.

[* You have the Life of Saint Odilo written by Jotsaldus in Mabillon, *Saeculum VI Benedictinum*, Part I [Col. 0798B], p. 679 and following. BOUQ.]

(35) Are you then meditating, according to the unspoken implication, on the cause?

In my studies I remember learning the figures of rhetoric.

King Robert, who is called by Helgaud the father and nurturer of monks, and who loved Odilo greatly, as Jotsaldus, Glaber Rodulfus, and others relate—Robert, I say, hearing that the monks he loved so greatly, and also his friend Odilo, were being attacked and ridiculed by Adalbero, cannot restrain himself from breaking his silence. “And you,” he says, “bishop, *κατὰ τὸ σιωπώμενον*—according to what is left unspoken—are meditating on the cause? Did you intend that I should make no reply and give you no answer, so that, while you attacked and ridiculed the monks and my singular friend Odilo, I might seem by my silence to agree with you, and that by my silence, or rather by my *ἀποσιώπησις*—my keeping silent—and my reticence, I should abandon, betray, and leave undefended good men, using a figure long familiar to me as a boy in school?”

Adalbero depicts Robert as angry with him, or at least as appearing agitated, because he thought and wrote badly of the monks. Hence he adds:

(36) May your heated indignation not obstruct us.

May I report the Lord’s command in peace.

“May your indignation, I beg you, pious king, not interrupt my speech; may your anger not harm me. With your permission, may I report the Lord’s commandments.”

(37) A most insolent race of Saracens, according to its custom,

Occupies the kingdom of the Franks, subdued by hands and the sword,

And devours whatever Gaul nourishes, and so forth.

The Saracens, says Adalbero, a very insolent people, occupy and plunder the kingdom of the Franks, subdued by force and arms; they flood Gaul with blood, scatter the relics of the saints and expose them to birds and lions—if there were still any lions in Gaul at that time—and above all devastate the bishopric of Tours. Moved by this injury to blessed Martin, and also to you, Odilo, and to your people, he went to Rome to pray for the safety of the monks.

Adalbero writes these things as pure riddles. Who were those Saracens who at that time devastated the kingdom of the Franks, and especially the bishopric of Tours, in this way? The Saracens of Fraxinetum had previously occupied the Alpine heights and captured Maiolus, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, Odilo’s predecessor, together with all his companions, as he was returning from Italy and the city of Rome; he had to be redeemed for scarcely a thousand pounds of silver. Shortly afterward, however, all these plunderers of the province and of Italy were killed by William, count of Arles, as Glaber Rodulfus and Odilo himself relate in the little book on the life of Abbot Maiolus [Col. 0799A].

In the year 994 or 997, the fortress of Saint Martin and his basilica, together with twenty-two churches, were burned on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, as the Thuane Chronicle—which ends in the year 1137—and a monk of the Greater Monastery teach. But that fire was entirely accidental, since no author is named; nor should it be attributed to any people hostile to the Christian religion, still less to Saracens, who at that time may have harassed the coast of Narbonne Gaul with brigandage and secret plundering but could not penetrate into the interior Celtic regions around Tours.

Around the year 1000, the Norwegians, or Norsemen, were summoned by Richard the Younger, leader of the Normans, against Odo, count of Chartres and Blois, who also held the city of Tours. After first defeating the Bretons in battle, capturing and burning their fortress by treachery, and slaughtering its inhabitants, they went by ship toward Rouen. I do not think that Adalbero designated these idolatrous peoples by the name “Saracens,” because, after peace was soon made between Richard and Odo by Robert, king of the Franks, the auxiliaries were dismissed, and in the following year they returned home from Normandy—or, as others prefer, to the island of England or Britain from which they had come—so that they had no time to devastate Gaul or lay waste the territory of Tours.

There were also many wars between this Odo and Fulk, count of Anjou, which caused the destruction of the interior of Gaul and of the territory of Tours. Fulk held Amboise and Loches in the district of Tours; Tours obeyed Odo. Fulk, threatening that city, set against it the fortress of Montboyau, and in 1016 defeated Odo in battle at Pontlevoy. But these events occurred long after this poem was composed by Adalbero, and perhaps even after Adalbero himself had died, when King Robert no longer shone with the vigor of youth—not with beginning youth, but with declining youth.

(38) They have become the companions of birds, and now of wolves.

That is, the bodies of the saints. Adalbero altered this line, but less successfully:

The fellow citizens of birds and now the companions of lions—

namely, the saints, or their ashes and relics.

(39) He devastates the bishopric of Tours with slaughter.

[Col. 0799D] That is, the race of the Saracens.

(40) Martin weeps and likewise calls for a protector.

Odilo sympathizes, being bound by a similar right.

Did Adalbero perhaps intend, under the designation “Saracens,” the princes of France—namely the counts, marquises, and dukes who were then tearing apart the kingdom of the Franks, occupying cities and castles, fighting among themselves with arms, and plundering sacred and secular possessions in the manner of Saracens? Above all, did he mean Fulk, count of Anjou, the devastator of the bishopric of Tours and of the possessions of blessed Martin?

Certainly, in Book II, chapter 4 of Glaber Rodulfus’s *Histories*, Hugh, archbishop of Tours, says and complains that Fulk had taken from the mother Church of the see entrusted to him many estates and dependents [Col. 0800A]. Fulbert likewise writes in Letter 99 that Count Fulk had invaded and taken away Church property, and that he had urged the archbishop of Tours and his fellow bishops to excommunicate him. Elsewhere we read that, during Robert’s reign, certain nobles laid hands on the goods and possessions of Cluny, and that Odilo complained about them before Pope Benedict VIII through his representatives, in the presence of Robert, king of the Franks, and his princes, nobles, and officials, who had come to the threshold of the apostles. Thus Odilo could easily sympathize with Martin, since he himself was bound by a similar right—that is, since he had himself suffered the same injury at the hands of others.

(41) He went to Rome to pray for the monks’ salvation.

Neither Jotsaldus nor Peter Damian, who made an epitome from Jotsaldus, helps us here. These are Jotsaldus’s words about Odilo: “The city of Rome also rejoiced, the mistress of the world, often visited by the companionship of so great a man, through love and longing for the holy apostles.” The same author also says: “When King Henry was hastening to the citadel of the Roman Empire in order to be advanced to the imperial dignity, Odilo accompanied him.”

Our author says that Odilo came to Rome for his own affairs, or to reclaim the property of his monasteries and churches; and this may nevertheless be true.

(42) The Cluniacensians raise their voices and give a din:

They shout and advise: “Quickly arrange, master,

For your men to take up arms, and what they ought to put on,” and so forth.

The jocular old man describes Odilo’s entourage as he travels to Rome. Here the Cluniacensians call him “master,” just as above:

“They intend to send someone, soon to inspect the master.”

As earlier in his description of Odilo travelling as a monk, so now in his description of Odilo’s entourage travelling to Rome, Adalbero indulges in mockery. Clearly, as is often fitting in the case of bishops and monks, Adalbero was not a friend of the monks—especially the then flourishing Cluniacensians—or of the very illustrious and powerful abbot Odilo.

Adalbero represents the Cluniacensians asking Odilo what clothing they should wear if they are all to go to Rome, how he wishes them to be equipped and armed, and what they ought to take above, below, outside and openly, and inside:

And what they ought to put on,

[Col. 0800D] What is external, and what is internal.

Someone may say: Are voices, din, and shouting appropriate for monks speaking to their abbot? They are plainly not appropriate, unless they were abusing their abbot’s patience; and it is likely that the Cluniacensians were doing this at that time, although Valesius appears not to remember how great their reverence was toward their most holy abbot.

For Odilo was such a gentle man, and forgave those who failed to follow discipline so readily, that many reproached his excessive clemency and mercy toward offenders, as Jotsaldus, Peter Damian, and Sigebertus write. By this gentleness of their abbot, by his frequent absence, and by the great resources of his monastery, the Cluniacensians could easily become overbearing, so that they shouted and made a din in the abbot’s presence and, forgetful of monastic silence, raised an outcry unbecoming even to laymen.

(43) First your lunar shield must hang there.

In addition, put on a triple-woven coat of mail.

Odilo prescribes for his monks, who are to become companions on the Roman journey, the clothing and equipment proper to each one, ordering all sorts of ridiculous things that ought neither to be done nor commanded. First he orders each to put on a coat of mail over the shield hanging from a strap thrown around the neck. Adalbero calls the crescent shield a “lunar” shield: an Amazonian buckler, or very short shield, shaped like half a moon and emitting two horns.

(44) Let slippery straps support the helmet at your loins;

With a sword, crown your head bound tightly by straps.

[Col. 0801B] Odilo continues and orders that helmets no longer be placed on the brothers’ heads but hung from their waist-belts; and—something that belonged properly to the leg-bindings—that their heads be bound with very long straps in the shape of a crown, shaved around with razors, or at least that their caps be held on their heads by straps tied beneath the chin. He orders the darts, or weapons, to be thrown behind the back and swords to be held clenched between bare teeth, just as Ranimirus II, king of Aragon, is said to have held the reins of his horse while armed:

Hold the darts behind your back, and then the sword between your teeth.

Adalbero properly says “crown the head.” Monks, and also clerics, were tonsured in the shape of a crown. For this reason both groups still call this tonsure a “crown,” using the old name.

(45) And he forces the sluggish young men to mount wagons,

And orders the crowd of old men to mount horses.

[Col. 0801C]

Of the monks who are to follow him into Italy, Odilo puts the younger men into wagons and the old men on horses, whereas the younger ought to travel on horses and the old men in wagons, carts, or carriages. From this it is clear what credence should be given to Adalbero’s jokes, leaving aside what follows.

(46) Let two mount each donkey, and finally mount a camel;

If these do not suffice, mount the buffalo three at a time.

Since there are not enough horses, Odilo orders two of his companions—both servants and monks—to sit on each donkey, three on each buffalo, and ten on each camel. These things are certainly ridiculous and invented; nevertheless, from them we understand that Odilo’s entourage travelling to Rome was enormous. For when a crowd of old men is said to have followed him, who does not see and understand [Col. 0801D] that a much larger multitude of young men accompanied him? Hence Adalbero adds:

A thousand thousand men proceed before the Roman citizens.

Indeed, wherever he lived and wherever he went, such a great crowd of brothers followed Odilo that you would think him no longer a commander or prince, but truly the archangel of monks, as Jotsaldus records in his life of him.

[* He names the holy man thus to demonstrate reverence, not to describe his retinue. Fulbert of Chartres greets him as “archangel” among other things because of his exceptional holiness. BOUQ.]

That commander and prince of monks—or rather king, as he is called above—commanded not only monks but also abbots. Jotsaldus records fourteen monasteries subject to Odilo throughout Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Provence, as well as the monastery of Nantuad, which Count Gislebert had entrusted to him for reform.

William, duke of Aquitaine, also attracted Odilo to himself with many great gifts and entrusted several monasteries under his authority to Odilo’s governance, especially Ingeriacum and the monastery of Saint Cyprian located in the suburb of Poitiers. Odilo was likewise honored by the friendship, services, and gifts of Robert, king of the Franks; of the empress Adelaide, mother of both Ottos; of Henry, emperor of the Romans, who gave Cluny a scepter, orb, and imperial crown of gold; and also of the emperors Conrad and his son Henry. From Stephen, king of Hungary, and Sancho, king of the Cantabrians [Col. 0802B] and Navarre, he was likewise accustomed to receive letters together with benefits and gifts.

He built some monasteries partly from their foundations; others, half-ruined or threatening to collapse, he restored, enlarged with estates and distinguished ornaments, and filled with monks. He was sometimes received as an honored guest not only by abbots but also by dutiful bishops. Among the Gallic abbots of that time—happy, rich, and powerful, to the envy even of bishops—Odilo stood out most prominently and, as it were, reigned. He was powerful over Cluny, the wealthiest monastery, and over so many great monasteries spread throughout Gaul and also Lombardy; he was almost equally the friend of emperors and kings.

(47) A thousand thousand men proceed before the Roman citizens.

[Col. 0802C] Accompanied by very many monks, Odilo came to Rome and displayed the spectacle of his splendid entrance into Rome.

(48) The matter is carried on by the sword, extended over three days.

It is read elsewhere: “The matter is carried on by the sword and extended over three days.” What Adalbero describes in this line and the following nine, or what he intends, is not easy to say. He recalls a matter carried on by the sword for three days, a battle fought on the Kalends of December, and a standard-bearer who, thrown from his horse by a lance, disgracefully abandoned the banner and returned home in flight with the others. He is certainly indicating some laughable event that happened at Rome to Odilo and his companions, and an unfortunate outcome of the pilgrimage.

(49) As standard-bearer in the midst, hurrying, I began not to snore:

Having parted my buttocks, I expelled wind while fighting.

[Col. 0802D]

This standard-bearer, positioned in the middle of the column, whom Adalbero represents as speaking about himself, is Odilo himself. He confesses that he expelled intestinal wind while fighting—that is, *βδέσμα*—and that he fled with his men toward Gaul:

Fleeing with the others, I sought my native kingdom.

What is even more astonishing is that these words were written while Odilo was alive. He died in 1048, at the age of eighty-seven, long after Adalbero himself.

(50) Know that these things were done on the first day of December;

This same thing will be attempted again before the Kalends of March.

Adalbero indicates that something happened to Odilo at Rome on the Kalends of December, and that he would attempt the same thing there again on the next Kalends of March [Col. 0803A]. By these words he attacks the frequent Roman journeys of abbots, especially Odilo—journeys burdensome to monasteries and hostile even to discipline. For the monks who accompany a travelling abbot cannot observe most of their rules; and those who remain in the monastery do not take care to observe them in the abbot’s absence.

(51) Odilo, the commander of the army, sends us to you.

The warlike order greets you as lord of the monks.

He urges you, summoning the ranks, to array them for war.

Surrounded by the column, execute the command quickly, and so forth.

Here Adalbero introduces a monk as though he were an envoy sent to Robert, king of the Franks, by Odilo. In the name of his abbot, he greets the king and urges him to make war swiftly upon the sacrilegious nobles who have seized his possessions [Col. 0803B].

The words of the Cluniacensian monk, the envoy, deserve attention: he calls his abbot Odilo “commander of the army,” calls the monastic order a “warlike order,” and earnestly insists that the king quickly summon soldiers, gather troops, prepare for war, and carry out his abbot’s orders as soon as possible.

Fulbert, bishop of the Church of Chartres, calls Odilo “the archangel of monks,” and “our,” that is, his own, archangel in Letter 66. Jotsaldus, following him, likewise calls him “the archangel of monks.” From this he seems commonly to have received the name “archangel” [Col. 0803C].

It is established that the Greeks often called the archangel Michael, by *κατ’ ἀντωνομασίαν*—“by antonomasia”—*Ἀρχιστράτηγος*, that is, “commander of the army,” “commander of the heavenly soldiers,” or “leader of the angelic army.” If, therefore, Odilo could be called an archangel after the manner of Michael, he could also, by the same name, be called “commander of the army,” though specifically of the monastic army.

Odilo’s envoy—or rather Adalbero—calls the monks’ order a warlike order because at that time, whenever monks travelled, they rode on horseback girded with swords, equipped with quivers, wearing truncated clothing—that is, military cloaks—and using spurs, after the manner of soldiers.

Glaber Rodulfus is the authority for this in Book II, chapter 9 of his *Histories*. During Robert’s reign among the Franks, when the Saracen king of Córdoba, Almanzor, was devastating Galicia, Navarre, and Castile with continuous raids, capturing Christian cities, and winning battles, the monks of that region were compelled by a shortage of soldiers to take up arms and wage war. At that time also, because of the scarcity of armies, the monks of that region were compelled to take up military weapons. Thus at least among the monks of Spain there was then genuinely a military order.

In the same author, Book III, chapter 4, I find that certain clerics or canons of the monastery of blessed Martin at Tours then put on arms and served as soldiers, and that some of them fell in battle.

(52) Surrounded by the column, execute the command quickly.

It is more fitting for you to die in arms than while cultivating the fields.

These are the words of Odilo’s envoy to Robert, king of the Franks: “Arm yourself with your men and carry out as soon as possible the command of Odilo, commander of the army; attack the enemies and plunderers of our monastery. For you, lord king, it is more fitting to fall gloriously while fighting than to perish through a slow and sluggish death while cultivating fields, or farming and idling.”

By these words Adalbero accuses the monks of arrogance, since they would command the king, and accuses the king himself, for whom he composed the poem, of inactivity and laziness. Yet the king is certainly said to have been a man of more than monastic simplicity.

(53) Europe, the third part of the world, boasts of sending more men than there are leaves in Asia and Africa, or thirsty sands on the seashore.

The envoy continues to explain Odilo’s commands and to leave no room for doubt about waging war. “King,” he says, “know and be convinced that Europe, which is no less than a third part of the world’s lands, will send and add to your aid more monkish comrades-in-arms than there are leaves in Asia and Africa, or sands on the seashore. Europe boasts of this.”

By these words Adalbero indicates that there was an excessive multitude of monks in Europe in his own time. What would he say if he were alive now?

(54) What do you want, madness, most worthy of the gloomy cloisters?

Fix your claws through the body, lest the livid man escape.

“What do you want, madness, worthy now of being confined not in monasteries but in prison cells?” This is an exclamation by Adalbero, bishop of Laon, against the monks who were urging, compelling, and, so to speak, singing a war song to the king in order to make him avenge their injury by arms. He does not hesitate to call them mad and most deserving of a gloomy prison, with the greatest bitterness and hostility, and with a manner scarcely episcopal.

The second line may refer to Robert, ordering that claws be driven into Adalbero’s body lest he escape, livid and envious of the monks’ wealth and glory.

(55) Believe me, your threatening words do not frighten me;

That teacher Neptanabus taught me very many things.

When King Robert saw that the monks were not only being ridiculed but also called mad and worthy of imprisonment by Adalbero the bishop, he broke his patience. He denied that he was moved by Adalbero’s threatening words or deterred by his statements and jokes from loving the monks. He said that he had had a monk as his teacher, from whom he had learned many, very great, and most useful things; that, after God, he attributed to him whatever he knew; and that he both owed and deferred greatly to him as the author of his learning.

For it is established that Gerbert, Robert’s teacher, born of obscure parentage in Aquitaine, grew up as a monk from childhood in the monastery of Aurillac; afterward he governed the school of Reims, or the Church of Reims. Hence, in the subscriptions to his letters, he often calls himself “Gerbert, formerly headmaster” and “Gerbert, abbot of the school,” that is, head of the school.

His pupils included Robert, son of Hugh, and Otto III, son of Otto II Augustus. Robert became king of the Franks; Otto, after his father’s death, became emperor; Leotheric later became archbishop of Sens; Ingo became abbot; and Fulbert became bishop of Chartres.

“Robert, having been entrusted by his mother to the school of Reims, was given to Lord Gerbert for instruction; and while he taught him the liberal disciplines …,” as Helgaud writes.

William, a monk of Malmesbury, is the authority in Book II of his *Deeds of the English* that Gerbert learned astrology, the abacus, and the other mathematical arts from the Saracens of Spain, and opened public schools in Gaul. His pupil Otto calls him in writing “most skilled in philosophy and crowned in the three branches of philosophy.”

Others have more plausibly reported that he was commended to Marquis Borrell by the abbot of Aurillac and taught mathematics by Haito, bishop of Spain. They call this Borrell now duke of Citerior Spain, now count of Barcelona.

(56) That teacher Neptanabus taught me very many things;

The hall is collapsing beneath its domes, where it shines splendidly with golden roofs.

Nectanabis was a king of Egypt, a contemporary of Agesilaus, king of the Spartans. Plutarch of Chaeronea mentions this Nectanabis, or Nectanabides, more than once in his *Life of Agesilaus*; Diodorus Siculus also mentions him, calling him now Nectanebis, Νεκτανεβίς, and now Nectanebos, Νεκτανεβός. Pliny, in Book XXXVI, chapter 9, has “Nectabis” corruptly for Nectanabis.

That Nectanabis, or rather Nectanabus, is the man whom Adalbero, corruptly, calls Neptanabus. King Robert of the Franks ironically calls his teacher Gerbert “Neptanabus,” or rather “Nectanabus,” the name of an ancient king of Egypt, because Gerbert excelled in astrology and mathematics in the manner of the Egyptians.

The Egyptians are thought to have discovered and mastered astrology through prolonged observation of the stars, as Cicero teaches in Book I of *On Divination*, Pliny in Book VII, chapter 56, and others.

This is the most certain and successful interpretation of Adalbero’s line. I could never have reached it without the added designation “teacher.” Robert therefore says that he learned many things from his teacher:

“The hall is collapsing, where it gleams splendidly with golden domes.”

Here, “the hall is collapsing, where it gleams splendidly with golden domes”: that is, the school at Reims, near the Major Church of the city, which shines with a gilded dome but, because of its age, is collapsing or threatening to collapse.

A dome is the center of a vaulted roof, like a shield in the middle of a church, where all the beams meet; or, in the middle of a temple or church ceiling, it is the place from which gifts or votive offerings hang.

(57) In pieces they tear apart the garment each was holding.

These words seem to have been written by Adalbero about the Cluniacensian monks sent by Odilo to Robert, king of the Franks, to seek counsel and assistance. After the leader of the embassy had finished speaking, they each tore their own garments in order to display their grief and move the king.

[Col. 0806A] (58) Therefore this transformation of the kingdom is a transformation of the order.

This transformation among the Franks of the clerical or priestly order, and especially of the monastic order, is therefore a transformation of the kingdom itself. Thus Adalbero concludes and brings his speech against the monks to an end. At the beginning he had said in this line:

As it pleases the empire, so let the order transform itself,

and likewise:

Let that sacred monastic order deviate from its seat.

Certainly, the Gallican, or Frankish, monks of that time were by no means free from disorder and had departed from discipline. This is shown not only by all those verses of Adalbero, but also by many monasteries in the Frankish kingdom that were especially renowned and wealthy: above all, the Parisian monastery of Saints Vincent and Germanus [Col. 0806B]; the monastery of Saint Dionysius, famous for the martyr’s tomb; the monastery of Fossat; and several others mentioned by Glaber Rodulfus and the rest. Since their monks were leading an almost secular life, they had to be compelled by royal authority and by the intervention and efforts of better men to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Odo, in the *Life of Count Burchard*, says that Magonard, abbot of Fossat, a nobleman, delighted in bird-catching, dogs, and hunting; and that whenever he went anywhere, he used to remove his monastic garments, put on costly furs, and place a *calamaucum* or *camelaucium*, a kind of cap, on his head instead of a hood. He then adds: “All his subjects likewise followed the same practices as far as they were able. This custom was practiced by all the monks of that kingdom” [Col. 0806C].

Willelmus, who was made abbot of the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon in the year 990 by Bruno, bishop of the Church of Langres, restored to its former condition by correction the discipline of regular life, which had already nearly collapsed through the negligence of earlier generations, just as blessed Benedict had arranged it. Through many monasteries in various parts of the world that had strayed from the regular path, both personally and through those whom he appointed abbots, he subjected them to the monastic order, as is found written in the *Chronicle of Benignus*. The author of this chronicle adds that the monasteries of Jumièges, Bèze, Rouen—Saint-Ouen—, Saint Michael the Archangel on the Mount, Saint Germanus at Paris, Saint Faro at Meaux, Saint Arnulf at Metz, Gorzia, and the monastery of Saint Aper at Toul, along with others, were entrusted to him for correction and restoration to order [Col. 0806D].

Glaber Rodulfus writes as follows of the bishops, abbots, clerics, and monks of his age in Book II, chapter 6: “Whenever the religious spirit of the bishops has failed, the strictness of the abbots’ rule has withered, and the vigor of monastic discipline has grown lukewarm, then, following their example, the rest of the people have become transgressors of God’s commandments. What else is happening than that the whole human race together is once more slipping into the ancient chaos of the abyss?”

The same author, in his book on the life of William, abbot and priest, relates that William governed and restored to a better condition and order of life the monastery of Saint Saturninus on the Rhône; the monasteries of Vézelay, Fécamp, Reims, Melun, and the site of Saint Michael the Archangel near the fortress of Ternodore [Col. 0807A]; and about forty other cells.

### (59) The hope of the young: the coming day, for those who do not wish to learn.

The cause of the old: without hope, they lament their youthful course.

Adalbero now turns to maxims that are only loosely connected. “Young men,” he says, “being lazy and idle and not eager to learn, postpone literary studies to the future because they hope to live for a long time. But old men, whose youth has been spent without study, since they can no longer hope for a long life, regret with groans the youth they passed badly and carelessly, and vainly wish to call it back, though it will never return.”

### (60) An evil thing: what I know they defend; what I do not know, they yield.

What I know is commonly prohibited and forbidden; what I do not know is permitted, is regarded as permitted, and is practiced. Thus, even today, we commonly say *defendre*—“to defend”—for “to forbid” and “to restrain.”

The manuscript had a superscript in the same sense:

> An evil thing: what I know they despise; what I do not know, they seek.

### (61) Either the king’s ashes or I shall breathe forth my Muses.

I would most gladly emend this to “I shall breathe forth our Muses,” if the following did not occur: “if the celebrated Muses.”

### (62) If you celebrate the Muses, let the priest be called “musard.”

The king is speaking and says that if Bishop Adalbero cultivates the Muses, or literature, ignorant people who despise learning will insult him by calling him a “musard priest.” Even today we call an idle and inactive person a *musard*; likewise *muser*, just as the Germans say *musen*, means “to idle.”

### (63) Persius, indignant, will then bring forth the one-eyed priestess.

In Persius’s fifth satire the verse reads:

> Hence the great Gauls, and, with her rattle, the one-eyed priestess, etc.

Adalbero had read Persius attentively, for the preceding verse—

> That Jupiter counts with the better pebble—

and another—

> With cheeks parted, I rejected my breath while fighting—

are each half taken from Persius. The first is from Satire 2, addressed to Macrinus on the good mind:

> Count this day, Macrinus, with the better pebble.

The second is from Satire 3, which rebukes laziness:

> He yawns at yesterday, with his cheeks parted on every side.

Likewise, below, at verse 200, “My knowing is nothing” is a hemistich from Persius.

### (64) If things prosper for you, do not be reluctant to remember this.

Adalbero had written above it, unsuccessfully resisting the obstinate short syllable: “May it not displease you to remember this?”

### (65) For a part of himself, which part is true wisdom.

Adalbero had written above it:

> Giving understanding of what true wisdom is.

### (66) For angelic citizens, a structure is also built for human throngs.

One part reigns; another part hopes.

This heavenly Jerusalem was constructed by God so that it might be inhabited by angels and human beings alike [Col. 0808A]. One part of them already reigns there; the other hopes to reign there after death, or after sins have been expiated by fire. If the reigning part referred to the angels and the hoping part to all mortals, it would have to be said that Adalbero believed that the gate of heaven is not open to Christian and Catholic human beings until after Judgment Day. Many others also believed this, but wrongly.

### (67) Read through the books of Augustine, beloved king.

He is shown to have said what the lofty city of God is.

Beloved king, read Augustine’s books *On the City of God*.

### (68) “Tell me, I beg you, bishop, who are the inhabitants there,

Peers in principality, and, if any, those in the order.”

The king asks Adalbero who the inhabitants and the peers in principality are, and who are so called, in the city of God, in the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0808B]. Adalbero playfully enjoys tmesis here, as above:

> Sarra, a race of banqueters, exceedingly wanton by custom.

### (69) Seek Dionysius, who is called the Areopagite:

He labors to write two books about these matters.

Dionysius, who is called the Areopagite by most people—but falsely—composed one book of fifteen chapters *On the Celestial Hierarchy* and another of thirteen chapters *On the Divine Names*. These are the two books Adalbero indicates, and he says that they were written by Dionysius. By adding that he is called the Areopagite, he reports a popular opinion that had already been gaining strength for one hundred and sixty years, rather than accepting or believing it as true [Col. 0808C].

### (70) The bishop, that holy man Gregory, also speaks of this,

Examining the morals of the great king Job in his faith.

The thirty-five books of Pope Gregory—commonly called Gregory the Great, and the first of that name to preside over the Roman Church—are the *Morals on the Book of Blessed Job*, addressed to Leander, bishop of Seville. I see that Adalbero and many others call this moral exposition the *Morals*. Gregory also wrote twenty-two books of *Homilies on the Prophet Ezekiel*, addressed to Martinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

In both works, Adalbero says, Pope Gregory wrote about the City of God, or heavenly Jerusalem, and about its inhabitants and principalities. “Gregory speaks from there,” that is, Gregory wrote about that matter: *Saint Grégoire en parle*. We still commonly speak in this way today.

### (71) Completing his discourse, he explains it openly—

Here also, at the end, he clearly speaks of Ezekiel:

> These writings Gaul received when he himself gave them.

[Col. 0808D]

Adalbero says that Gregory himself sent and gave these two books of *Homilies on Ezekiel* to the bishops of Gaul. I have not read this elsewhere.

### (72) . . . . The upper order is arranged in distinct ranks,

By whose model the earthly order is said to be established.

The manuscript had the following superscript:

> The earthly order is said to be distinguished according to its likeness.

It should be observed that the word *order* is mentioned very frequently in this poem, in the second verse:

> . . . . . The Laon order of brothers.

[Col. 0809A]

Likewise:

> As the empire wishes, so let the order transform itself.

> Let that sacred monastic order deviate from its seat.

> The warlike order of monks salutes you as lord.

> This, then, is the transformation of the kingdom’s order.

And concerning the heavenly or supreme Jerusalem:

> It is governed in distinct order, though not by a small soldiery.

> Peers of princes, and if there are any also in the learned order.

> . . . . The upper order is arranged in distinct ranks,

> By whose model the earthly order is said to be established.

> Ministers of the ancient Church’s people under the Law,

> Whom God instituted through Moses and governed in order.

> The order of the kingdom of heaven is called the Church.

> The faith is simple; but its status is threefold in order.

> Human morals change, and the order also changes.

[Col. 0809B]

> Now you demonstrate; then the order of the powerful deliberates,

> Examining, etc.

> Let our order not dare to abandon

> The governance of justice.

> First among the Franks, you are a servant in the order of kings.

Thus this poem may be entitled *On Order*, because Adalbero teaches in it that just as heaven, or the supreme Jerusalem, is governed according to order and has orders distinct from one another, so human beings on earth have different orders and different laws that ought to be observed.

### (73) Ministers of the ancient Church’s people under the Law,

Which is called “Synagogue” by an ordinary designation.

God instituted through Moses those whom he governed in order.

In the manuscript, the second of these three verses had been deleted [Col. 0809C]. In it Adalbero says that the ancient Church, consisting of the people established under the Law, that is, the Jews, was called “Synagogue” by an ordinary designation.

### (74) The order of the Church is called the kingdom of heaven.

The order of the Church is called the kingdom of heaven.

### (75) And there the new law is honored, under Christ as prince.

Adalbero also emended this verse in the following form:

> And there the new law is enjoyed, which is called grace.

### (76) The faithful judgment of bishops also established this:

How, by whom, and what sort of men are to be appointed there.

The canons decreed by bishops gathered in synods determined what sort of men the ministers of the Church should be, by whom they should be appointed, and according to what procedure. These canons, I say, are called by Adalbero the judgment of the bishops [Col. 0809D].

### (77) It is necessary to adapt it to two laws,

The divine and the human, which discernment fashions.

It is necessary to adapt the condition of the Church to two laws, the divine and the human, which discernment fashions. Adalbero changed the second verse as follows:

> Of the virtues which the mother, discernment, distributes;

that is, the two laws which discernment, the mother of virtues, distributes.

### (78) No one divides the divine law among its own members.

That is, among its own ministers, or the ministers of its Church. Although they are different in birth, God wished them all to be of equal condition.

### (79) The devout law separates these men from every worldly stain.

[Col. 0810A]

The laws of pious rulers forbade clerics, or the ministers of the Church, to occupy themselves with sordid services and lowly trades, and, granting them complete immunity, devoted them exclusively to the altars.

### (80) They are not executioners, innkeepers, or swineherds.

Executioners were already then called what antiquity had called *laniones*, “butchers.” Adalbero therefore says that altar ministers, or clerics, reject sordid occupations: they are not farmers, cowherds, or winegrowers; they scarcely plant trees or cultivate gardens; nor are they butchers, or meat sellers, innkeepers, or swineherds—he says *necne* instead of *nec*, “nor”—nor goatherds, shepherds, or keepers of sheep.

They do not separate the flour of wheat or the flower of rye from bran with a sieve; nor do they concern themselves with the kettles placed over the fire in which meat is cooked—that is, they are not cooks—however much Adalbero expresses this in the verse:

> Nor do they sift Ceres; the greased kettle does not cook for them.

Here *lebeta* is used for *lebes*, “kettle.” Adalbero says all this in order to accuse King Robert of elevating shepherds and sailors—as he says above—that is, peasants and the lowest and most humble people, to the episcopate.

### (81) They do not make their backs crawl over the backs of oxen.

That is, clerics do not place pigs, tied by their feet, on oxen in order to drive them into the city for sale.

### (82) They are not washers; they disdain boiling garments.

They do not wash linen or linen cloths, and they disdain boiling linen garments in lye. For here *fervere*, “to boil,” is used for *fervefacere*, “to make boil.”

Or perhaps Adalbero is referring in this verse to fullers, who customarily washed, scoured, and polished woolen clothing.

### (83) But they ought to cleanse their minds and bodies, etc.

Adalbero asserts that clerics, especially priests and bishops, ought to be clean, chaste, and sober not only in soul but also in body, adorned with good morals and free from servile status. Certainly slaves could not attain the clerical office unless they had first been granted freedom. The ministers of Christ and of the altar ought not to be subject to human slavery, as we read in the *Life of the Emperor Louis the Pious*.

### (84) He subjected every human class to their commandment;

No prince is excepted, since he says “everyone.”

God wished all human beings, whatever their profession or rank—even princes, kings, and emperors—to be subject to priests and bishops in spiritual matters; to be taught the Catholic faith by them; and, once instructed by them, to be immersed in the sacred font.

### (85) And thus those instructed are plunged into the sacred bath of the font.

From this it is understood that even then those who were baptized as adults were customarily plunged into the sacred font, rather than having water merely poured over their heads.

### (86) He appointed physicians when wounds have become putrid,

Through whom the cauteries of words are to be applied.

God gave us priests as physicians, so that they might heal the wounds and putrid ulcers of our souls—that is, more serious sins—with certain cauteries, as it were, made from their words, or from health-giving precepts, exhortations, and counsels. If I am not mistaken, this should be understood of laypeople confessing their sins and receiving penance from a priest.

### (87) The sacrament of his body and blood

He commanded that the priest alone should properly administer it.

Christ commanded that the priest alone—*solus sacerdos*, or presbyter—should properly administer the sacrament of his body and blood. The manuscript has *quo* for *ut*, “so that.”

### (88) He entrusted the greatest things to those whom he asked to handle him.

Christ entrusted the greatest things to those whom he commanded to handle him; that is, he entrusted the supreme mysteries to the faith of priests, by whose hands he wished and commanded his most holy body to be touched and handled.

At that time they used “to ask” instead of “to command,” as a milder word. Jonas, who flourished 350 years before our Adalbero, during the reign of Chlodoveus the Younger, reports in his book *On the Life of Abbot Columbanus* that Brunichild, raging against her captive grandson King Theudebert, “asked that Theudebert be made a cleric, and not many days later, after his clerical ordination, impiously ordered him to be killed”—that is, she ordered him to become a cleric and shortly afterward to be killed.

Many others speak in this way, not ineptly, because the requests of the powerful are to be regarded as commands; and whoever is able to compel, when he asks, must be regarded as commanding, ordering, and directing.

Since Jonas has been mentioned, I should add that in Book XVIII of the *Frankish History* I showed that he was not a Scot, as is commonly believed, nor an abbot, but an Italian by birth and a monk of Bobbio. It is useful to know what his homeland was.

Recently I found in an old manuscript the life of blessed Attalus, abbot of Bobbio—thus he is always called there, and more correctly, since he is commonly called Attalas or Attala. In it Jonas himself writes, concerning a visit to his mother after nine years and concerning two companions on his journey:

> “With the priest Blidulf and the deacon Ermenoald as companions, in the month of February we reached the appointed place. It was the distinguished city of Segusio, once a colony of the Taurini, one hundred and forty miles from the monastery [of Bobbio]. When we arrived there, we were received gladly by our mother after so long an interval of years.”

From these words it is understood that Jonas was a native of Segusio, since both his mother and his brother lived there. Segusio, or Segusium, is called a town by Pliny and Ammianus, a city by Gregory and others, and by some a *civitas*. It lies one hundred and forty—or rather one hundred and sixty—thousand paces from the monastery of Bobbio [Col. 0811D]. The town is situated at the foot of the Alps and is regarded as the boundary of Gaul and the beginning of Italy. Certainly Italy begins at that place, which everyone also assigns to Italy.

### (89) We believe and know that what was promised by God’s voice was not denied,

Except to those whom their own crimes drive away.

We believe and know with certainty that the sacrament of his body, promised and given by Christ to his disciples and to the Church, was denied to no one except those who, because of very grave sins, had been removed from communion.

### (90) They ought to ascend to the foremost seats in heaven.

Priests, and especially bishops, ought while they live to strive and take care that, once dead, they may deserve to attain the foremost seats in heaven. It is certain that these are owed not to rank but to merit.

### (91) It is fitting that these men keep watch and abstain from much food,

And always pray for the ruin of the people and of themselves.

It is fitting that priests and bishops care for the people entrusted to them and, like shepherds of flocks, watch over each of their charges; that they be content with little food; and that they always pray and plead with God for the sins of the people and for their own.

Adalbero said above that they ought to be chaste and sober. Thus Ammianus Marcellinus writes in Book XXVII that provincial bishops are commended for moderation in eating and drinking and even for the plainness of their clothing. Bishop Gregory of Nazianzus relates the same thing in his *Poems*, page 11.

### (92) I have said little about clerics, but have left more unsaid.

[Col. 0812B]

I have said little about clerics, but omitted much that I could have said. Adalbero changed this verse and substituted a more polished one:

> I have said little about the clergy, little about the order.

### (93) Therefore all are equal in condition,

If one house of the Lord is enclosed by one law.

The first verse refers to what Adalbero wrote above about the ministers of the Church, or clerics:

> It forms them all in equal condition.

In place of the second verse Adalbero supplied this:

> Thus one house of the Lord is governed by one law.

### (94) Human law imposes two conditions:

Noble and slave are not bound by the same law.

[Col. 0812C]

Adalbero says that all people, at least among the Franks, are divided into two orders: one class consists of nobles, the other of slaves. By “nobles” he designates the honored, the warriors, and all freeborn persons who live from the income of their patrimony; by “slaves” he designates everyone else—namely, merchants, artisans, farmers, and others who support themselves by their trade—the people whom the Latins call the *plebs*; finally, household servants and bondmen.

Adalbero also calls the freeborn noble, at verse 293:

> For no freeborn man can live without slaves.

He likewise calls slaves the common people, at verse 285:

> The greater and lesser members of the common people defend [them].

Thus Gregory, in Book X, chapter 4, calls the envoys of Childebert, king of the Franks, “very freeborn by birth,” and in chapter 29 calls the parents of Aredius “very freeborn,” meaning noble [Col. 0812D].

### (95) For there are two foremost men: one rules, the other commands.

They belong to the class of nobles, and among them two stand out and hold the chief position: the king and the emperor. The commonwealth stands and is supported by their counsels and arrangements. From this class also come counts, marquises, and dukes.

### (96) There are others whom no power constrains;

If they flee the crimes that royal scepters restrain.
