These five verses describe the nobles, or freeborn, who serve as warriors and defend themselves, as well as the Churches and clergy, and the greater and lesser people—the *plebs* or common people whom Adalbero above called slaves—from injury by force of arms.

### (97) The other division of conditions is that of slaves.

This afflicted class possesses nothing without labor.

Adalbero now speaks of slaves, meaning not only household servants and bondmen, but also those who support themselves through trade, any craft, or labor. This class of people is extremely hardworking, and seems to have been born and made for the use and service of others. Hence Adalbero denies that they possess anything except what has been acquired through labor, and below, at verse 296, says that it is altogether impossible to recount

> The zeal of slaves and such immense labors.

[Col. 0813B]

In the following verse he also designates them by the name “laborers”:

> Now some pray, some fight, and others labor.

Adalbero adds that nobles or freeborn men are clothed by slaves; that even masters are fed by slaves; that everyone acquires wealth through them; and that no one can live or possess the necessities of life without them. Finally, whenever the king himself, or bishops and nobles, need the labor of slaves, they seem in a certain sense to serve them.

### (98) The tears of slaves, their groans, have no end.

The singular number is used for the plural: that is, there is no end or limit to the tears and groans of slaves.

### (99) Therefore the house of God is threefold, though believed to be one;

Now some pray, some fight, and others labor;

These three exist together and do not suffer division.

[Col. 0813C]

The house of God, which is believed to be one and which Adalbero has mentioned above as one—that is, the Church—is divided into three parts and into three classes of people. Among Christians, some pray, others fight, and others labor: clerics pray, soldiers fight, and the rest labor, namely, the people or commoners.

This is the threefold condition that Adalbero expressed in the verse:

> The faith is simple; but its condition is threefold in order.

This threefold condition, threefold order, and threefold profession of human beings is also called by Adalbero a threefold yet simple connection:

> Thus such a threefold connection is simple.

[Col. 0813D]

This is because these three orders, or these three classes of people, are members and limbs of one body, namely, the Catholic Church. They need one another, cling to one another, and are neither capable of nor able to endure division or discord.

### (100) Now behold, your white head resembles a swan;

Nature is shown to have made you say this through old age.

Adalbero had said that laws were already wasting away and peace was slipping away; that human morals were changing and the order was changing as well. Accordingly, King Robert mocks the bishop, who had complained about the condition of his times, by saying that he was raving and had poured forth such words through the defect of old age.

Adalbero’s head was completely white—what should rather have been called *canens*, “whitening,” than *candens*, “shining white.” The king says that it resembles a swan, or is like one, just as even today we commonly say that someone whose head and beard are entirely white is an old man white like a swan: *Il est blanc comme un cygne*.

Adalbero altered the second verse in the following form, though less successfully:

> Nature has shown that you, an old man, said such things.

### (101) Such nature has compelled me to believe that you are not sane.

That is, old age, whose nature is deranged, compels me to believe that you are not of sound mind. The manuscript had this superscript:

> Such nature has compelled you also to be unsound.

The sense is: the nature of old age has compelled you to be unsound, compelled you to rave, and to speak these foolish things to me.

### (102) Let another nature spur me; that one does not fail through old age.

Another nature, which does not fail through old age, has spurred and compelled me [to say] these things to you—namely, the rational and immortal soul, upon which old age does not fall. Adalbero speaks to the king in this way to deny that he himself is raving.

### (103) R. “Tell me how many natures are given to a human being.” P. “I think two.”

Namely, the mind or soul, and the body.

### (104) “From what speaks, state whose words they are.”

Of these two human natures, tell me which one is speaking, whose words they are, and to which one the voice and speech belong.

### (105) A mere grammarian, let alone an unlicensed dialectician,

You remember very little of your former studies.

[Col. 0814C]

You, Adalbero, who are only a grammarian and do not know the laws of dialectic, remember very little of what you once learned in school. Adalbero corrected the second verse as follows:

> Now I know what little of my former studies you recall.

A *simplex grammaticus*, “a mere grammarian”—*un simple grammairien*—is even today commonly said of someone skilled only in grammar, who knows nothing beyond grammar. An *illex dialecticus* is the same as *exlex*, Greek ἄνομος, “without law”: one who does not know the laws or rules of dialectic.

### (106) Whoever remembers a little does not forget everything.

These are Adalbero’s words, asserting that he has not forgotten all his studies, since, as the king himself bears witness, he still remembers something, even if very little.

At that time *parvi*, “small ones,” was used to mean “few.” Thus in the preface to the Salic Law the Frankish people are said to have been few in number; and Virgil likewise calls those few in number *exigui*, “small.” Everyone knows that *exiguus* and *parvus* have the same meaning.

The later Greeks likewise used μικροῖς for ὀλίγοις, “few.” Pyrrhus, who surrendered Antioch to our men, complained that he had only a few Franks available to carry out the task and said:

> Μικροὺς Φρανκοὺς εἴχομεν  
> “We had few Franks.”

In Gregory, Book VIII, chapter 30:

> “For it is better that a few obstinate men perish than that God’s anger hang over the whole innocent region.”

And in Book IV, chapter 30:

> “There were then great men from the Arverni,”

that is, “few obstinate men, many men,” as it is read in the published *History* of Gregory [Col. 0815A].

Julian, archbishop of Toledo, introduces Argabard, bishop of the Church of Narbonne, speaking to Wamba, king of the Goths, as follows:

> “We have indeed escaped the sword in very small numbers; but we beg pardon for the few.”

### (107) You do not know, through old age, how to remember the one who spurs you.

Through old age, bishop, you do not know how to remember the one who spurs you; because of your age you cannot remember my words, by which you have been pierced like an ox by a goad, when I called you unsound, a mere grammarian, and an unlicensed dialectician, and said that you remembered very little of your earlier studies.

### (108) This spirit resounds; madness does not torment me.

[Col. 0815B]

Within this body of mine there is, and dwells with me, a rational soul, through whose benefit and agency I speak to you, king. I mean a soul that indicates and testifies to its own nature even by its name. For *anima* means spirit and wind.

Nor has old age made me delirious, unsound in mind, or demented, as you said above.

### (109) If the nature of old men compels it, do not sharply blame me.

If, as you said, king, the nature of extreme old age is such that it compels us to become insane or at least delirious, you wrongly and groundlessly charge me with a fault that belongs not to the person but to age, and that I, as an old man, cannot avoid, however much I may wish and desire to do so.

### (110) Those skilled in art set down a definition of nature;

Some wise men call fire an artificer.

Some experts in art, or wise men—that is, philosophers, or *sophi*—define nature as an artificing fire; others define it as the will of God. What follows consists of philosophical divisions concerning natures, and likewise concerning every argument, whether necessary or probable, and concerning truth and other matters. These require neither our work nor exposition.

### (111) Terrified, the little she-ass speaks, fleeing nature.

The she-ass, terrified at the sight of the angel brandishing a drawn sword, spoke to her master Balaam in an unheard-of prodigy.

### (112) A fable does not resemble the truth, nor is it said to be true.

A fable does not resemble truth, nor is it called or regarded as true. Thus in Ardo’s *Life of Benedict, Abbot of Aniane*, *similare* is often used for “to resemble”:

> The mares whom you imitate.

From *similare* we derived *sembler* and *ressembler*.

### (113) No fable or nursery tale soothes my love.

I hate nursery tales, that is, nonsense and fables.

### (114) Let the wise and temperate seek,

By saving justice, rewards or punishments;

Let the powerful in reason receive them, whether the just or the unjust suffer.

Adalbero partly altered these two verses as follows:

> Taught by the laws, let the wise and temperate seek  
> Rewards or punishments; with faithful reason, etc.

### (115) And let them defend evil; those evils come from outside.

[Col. 0816A]

And let them prohibit and forbid evils, as above at verse 179:

> What I know they defend; what I do not know, they yield.

Adalbero also altered this verse as follows:

> Let them dissolve the evils that have been enacted from outside.

### (116) You possess, king, the faculty granted to an orator.

Now you demonstrate; then the order of the powerful deliberates,

Examining with religious judgments

The one by whom matters may be declared invalid.

Adalbero designates three kinds of speech: demonstrative, which includes praise and blame; deliberative; and judicial. He says that Robert, king of the Franks, who knows the art of oratory, demonstrates at assemblies of the people what he approves and judges ought to be done; then the nobles deliberate about these matters.

The “order of the powerful” consists of bishops, abbots, and secular princes or nobles—namely, dukes, marquises, and counts. After the final verse, three verses had been erased from the manuscript and are missing [Col. 0816B].

### (117) Beforehand, the qualities of matters, their interpretation, their end,

And their conjectures must be distinguished by us.

Beforehand, the quality, translation, end, and conjectures of matters must be distinguished by us.

### (118) You will not find these four, which you seek here.

Quality, translation, end, and conjectures.

### (119) I placed my feet properly; while one is fixed, the other rises.

One foot rises while the other is fixed.

### (120) This nature did not compel us, dying, to disclose these things.

It was not this aged, near-death old age [and] delirious nature that compelled us to explain them. This verse of Adalbero answers the king’s earlier verse about Adalbero:

> Nature is shown to have made you say this through old age.

### (121) You are rightly saddened, since you, a king, are ordered to serve.

This verse of Adalbero refers to another preceding verse of his:

> Kings and bishops seem to serve servants.

### (122) The Frankish kingdom subdues kings in the time of its forefathers,

And ever prevails in exalted honor.

Clovis, king of the Franks, overthrew and subjected to his rule the kingdom of the Alamanni in part of Germany and the kingdom of the Visigoths in Aquitaine. His sons, above all others, occupied the kingdoms of the Burgundians and Thuringians after killing their kings.

Charlemagne obtained the kingdom of the Lombards in Italy after capturing King Desiderius; he subdued the kingdom of the Huns and Avars in Pannonia, the Saxons, the strongest and largest people of Germany, the rebellious Bavarians, and several peoples of the Slavs or Wends [Col. 0816D].

### (123) The scepters of kings, subject to no ancestral scepter.

The kings of the Franks have never been subject to any scepter, or to any other king or emperor. This is true and worthy of remembrance and observation.

For this matter, the words of Fulk, archbishop of Reims, to Arnulf, king beyond the Rhine, recorded by Frodoard in Book IV, chapter 5, deserve attention:

> “Concerning the fact that they presumed to act without Arnulf’s counsel—that is, to make Charles king—he asserts that they followed the custom of the Frankish people, whose custom had always been that, when a king died, they chose another from the king’s family or succession, without regard for or consultation with any greater or more powerful king.”

### (124) Whoever rules it, rejoicing in virtues, governs with equal justice.

And whoever rules that Frankish kingdom is endowed with many great virtues and governs well and justly. Adalbero says this about Robert himself, king of the Franks.

### (125) We know that the empire has already been put to flight by kings.

We know that emperors have been driven into flight by the kings of the Franks and expelled from their territories.

In the year 978, namely, Lothair, king of the Franks, after recovering Metz, suddenly arrived with a large army and forced the emperor Otto the Younger to flee from the palace at Aachen together with his wife. In the same year Otto entered France with sixty thousand soldiers, ravaged the lands of Reims, Laon, and Soissons, and dared to burn the suburb of Paris. Relying on Count Hugh of Paris, Duke Henry of Burgundy, and enormous forces, the king compelled him to flee. He pursued the emperor not only as far as the Aisne at Soissons, where many were overwhelmed by the force of the river and perished, but also for three days and three nights as far as the Meuse and the borders of the Frankish kingdom, as Hermann, Sigebert, William of Nangis, and the other chroniclers relate [Col. 0817B].

Likewise, in the year 1006, Robert himself, king of the Franks, accompanied by Richard II, duke of Normandy, drove the emperor Henry from the siege of Valenciennes. This castle, situated on the border of the Franks and Lotharingians, had been attacked by Baldwin, count of Flanders [Col. 0817C].

### (126) Now I give thanks to the Most High, through whom I greatly desire to reign;

I do not attribute it to my merits, etc.

I give thanks to God, who made me king, through whom I live and through whom I reign. I do not attribute so much to my merits—which are nonexistent or insignificant—as to think that I owe my kingdom to them.

These are the words of the most devout and profoundly humble king Robert, who is therefore called by Helgaud “the humble king,” and sometimes “the most humble.” For this reason he forbids Adalbero above to say more about his appearance and virtue:

> You have spoken enough about appearance and virtue.

This manner of speaking remains in use among our Gallo-Franks today: *C’est assez parlé de cela*, “Enough has been said about that.”

He also says:

> My knowing is nothing; it is always [the work] of the gracious divine power.

### (127) So that we may be permitted to preserve our fathers’ laws.

With knees bent, I humbly pray always to God that I may be able to preserve the ancestral laws, and that I may ensure that they are preserved by all subject to my authority; nor will I ever depart from them, or permit them to be abandoned, says the king. Gregory, Book IX, chapter 30, records: “The people of Tours gave King Charibert an oath; likewise, he promised under oath that he would not impose new laws or customs upon the people, nor any new ordinance relating to confiscation.” Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, likewise reproved Childeric, monarch of the Franks, because he had so suddenly altered the ancestral laws and customs that he had ordered to be preserved. In 869, too, when Charles the Bald was to be crowned at Metz in the church of Saint Stephen, he declared to all the Lotharingians who were present that he would preserve law and justice for each of his faithful subjects in his own order, according to the laws applicable to him, both ecclesiastical and secular. In 877, when his son Louis was to be crowned at the palace of Compiègne, the promise made to the bishops was as follows: “I promise and pledge to you that I shall preserve for each one of you, and for the churches entrusted to you, canonical privilege and the due law and justice, and that, with the Lord’s help, I shall provide protection insofar as I am able.” I found the same response of our kings to the bishops in three ancient manuscripts. The profession of Philip, then seven years old and soon to become king of the Franks, made in 1059 in the major church of Reims, is composed in the same words and with the same meaning. He also adds that, for the people entrusted to him, he would by his own authority grant the administration of the laws as established in their proper jurisdiction—that is, as the designated king Boso says, he would preserve and provide everyone with law, justice, and proper protection.

**(128) Divine law forbids what corrects between the two.**

Elsewhere the superscription reads: “There is one law that forbids”; less satisfactorily.

**(129) Whatever is useful seems necessary to bring together:**

[Col. 0818C]

Whatever seems useful and necessary to bring together.

**(130) Let whatever concerns many matters, which are always honorable,**

**And whatever is stronger and most weighty, let us always uphold it honorably:**

Let us always honorably uphold that law which concerns many matters and is stronger and more weighty.

**(131) May good peace come everywhere after conflicts and after labors:**

And may the condition of the Church maintain its own rights by itself.

Adalbero desires peace for the kingdom of the Franks after the civil wars and battles, so that the Church may flourish there and be able to preserve its own rights.

**(132) Let the commonwealth possess its laws,**

**Set down, and no others . . .**

[Col. 0818D]

Let the Franks have their laws set down for themselves, and let them observe these and no others. The written or recorded laws are the Roman Law—this was the name given to the Theodosian Code—the Salic Law together with the Capitularies of Charlemagne and of his son and grandson Charles, and the Burgundian Law in the western kingdom of the Franks, which at that time included Aquitaine and part of Burgundy. The Church was governed above all by Roman Law, or the Theodosian Code; the Gauls and the lay Franks likewise used the Salic Law and the Capitularies added to it by our emperors; the Burgundians used their own laws, or the laws of Gundobad. Other laws, that is, unwritten ones, are called by Adalbero customs. It is clear that these had then become established in various parts of France, under various counts and dukes, in differing forms, and were later committed to writing and treated as laws. This is now called customary law and is still opposed to written law, that is, to Roman law—not because it is not written, but because it was set down much more recently and many centuries after the Roman laws, and also after the Frankish and Burgundian laws.

**(133) . . . let Basil and Benedict**

**Observe their own kingdoms: let them hold whatever their kingdoms command.**

Let the monks of Basil and Benedict observe their own rules; let them also retain their possessions and obtain whatever their rules command or permit. Adalbero calls the rules of the Basilian and Benedictine monks “kingdoms” ironically, just as above a certain monk calls Lord Odilo, abbot of Cluny, his king and professes that he is his subject:

“For my lord is King Odilo of Cluny.”

For some time already, the rule of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, introduced into Gaul, had been observed by certain monks. Aredius, abbot of Attane in the Limousin, who died in 591, founded a monastery in which not only the rules of Cassian but also those of Basil and the other abbots who established the monastic life were honored, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, reports in Book X, chapter 29, of his *History*. In the *Lives* of the holy abbots Eugendus of the Jura and Philibert of Jumièges, mention is made of the rule of Saint Basil. Philibert continually devoted himself, through assiduous and most diligent reading, to the charisms of Saint Basil, the rule of Macarius, the decrees of Benedict, and the institutions of Columbanus. Ardo, a monk of Aniane and a disciple of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, who flourished under the emperors Charles and Louis, wrote that Benedict had attempted to ascend to the sayings of blessed Basil and also to the rule of Saint Pachomius. The monk Hugh asserts that Basil’s rule consists of his statutes, which Rufinus translated and which I found in a very ancient manuscript of the Paris monastery of Saint-Germain; they are divided into 203 questions and answers. In any event, Adalbero says this in order to show what he has already sufficiently demonstrated above: that the monks of Basil and especially of Benedict in Gaul often departed from their own laws.

**(134) Let bishops henceforth never frequent the countryside,**

**If they wish to maintain their own rights, let them not concern themselves with rural matters.**

[Col. 0819D]

Let bishops henceforth not ordinarily live in the countryside, nor frequently linger there, or often idle away their time in fields and pleasant villas, since each of them ought to devote himself to the care of his own city or of the people entrusted to him. Let each bishop sit in his own see, ultimately preserving his own rights inviolate and becoming an object of universal veneration, if he neglects the countryside, does not give himself over to his pleasures, does not prefer retreats to cities, and does not personally concern himself with his estates and suburban revenues.

**(135) Let our order not dare to abandon the administration of justice,**

**But let it always apply itself to this with all its strength:**

[Col. 0820A]

Let the episcopal order—or each bishop—be most observant of equity and the good, and never dare to depart from law; rather, let him always accommodate himself with all his strength to justice. By “the administration of justice,” Adalbero means the rule of justice or law. At that time, bishops had their own court, as they had had in earlier times; this is explained more clearly below.

**(136) Let it appoint just and capable governors, not according to custom,**

**Governors of the poor, and likewise of the wretched widows.**

Let our order, that is, the episcopal order, appoint just and capable governors of the poor, widows, and orphans, such as were by no means customarily appointed. “Not according to law,” that is, not according to custom. Perhaps, however, one should read “and not predatory according to law,” so that the meaning is: Let it appoint just governors of widows, and not governors who are predatory according to custom—that is, not avaricious by habitual practice. Those governors of the poor, wretched widows, and orphans were undoubtedly deacons, guardians and dispensers of sacred money to be distributed to the needy.

**(137) Let no one go to church during the night except once,**

**Let it be permitted to all to pray during the days.**

Let no one go to church at night more than once. This should be understood of clerics, whom Adalbero wishes to visit the church no more than once each night, or to join the Matins and Lauds in continuous and uninterrupted chanting. He teaches us, above all in the *Life of blessed Leodegarius*, concerning the killing of Ebroin, master of the royal household, that laypeople were accustomed to attend these Matins once each week, namely on Sunday night. Or perhaps Adalbero wishes or desires all night vigils and nocturnal Masses—observances that were held or celebrated in various ways by different people not only on the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, and at Pentecost, but also in honor of various martyrs and confessors—to be abolished except for one, because much obscene behavior was then carried on in churches by laypeople, encouraged by the darkness. The ancient Fathers also complained about this matter. Hence arose the proverb that young men who attend all-night vigils and nocturnal Masses are said to seek God by groping and handling. I think that Adalbero exempts the night of the Nativity of the Lord rather than the night of Easter or Pentecost, because throughout the Christian world even today, after almost all other vigils have been abolished, it is celebrated with an all-night vigil and Mass.

**(138) . . . let it be permitted to all to pray during the days:**

Let churches be open to laypeople throughout the day; let them be permitted to pray openly to God there all day, without any suspicion of disgrace.

**(139) Let him judge, and consider those present and those to come.**

Let our order, or the bishops, judge in such a way that in their judgments they take account not only of those living in the present but also of posterity, of each one’s reputation, and of the commandments of their Lord. Bishops, especially after Constantine the Great became a Christian, undoubtedly had their own special court and always judged all the clerics and monks subject to their church, as well as ecclesiastical matters. In Gregory’s *History of the Franks*, Book V, chapter 5, Peter the deacon, his brother, “after a court had been held in the presence of Saint Nicetius, bishop and maternal uncle of his, went to Lyon; and there, with Bishop Syagrius standing by and other priests present, together with many secular nobles, he cleared himself under oath that he had never been involved in Sylvester’s death.” In Book VIII, chapter 39, Bishop Baudegisilus of Le Mans is said to have discussed cases daily with the judges. In Book IX, chapter 6, concerning Ragnemodus, bishop of Paris, punishing a certain impostor, Gregory reports: “Having taken the cross away from him, he ordered him to be expelled from the boundary of the city of Paris. But after making another cross, he began again to practice what he had done; and when he was captured by the archdeacon and bound in chains, he was ordered to be kept in custody.” In Book V, chapter 48, I find Leudast, count of Tours—there is no doubt that the other counts did the same—sitting in judgment with elders, both lay and clerical, that is, with clerics and laymen. Gregory’s account of Nicetius, bishop of Lyon and his maternal great-uncle, in the book of his life, contains these words: “At a certain time he sent Basil the priest to Count Armentarius, who in those days governed the city of Lyon with judicial authority, and said to him: ‘Our bishop has brought this case, which is being brought again, to an end by his judgment; therefore he warns you not to presume to reopen it.’ In a fury he replied to the priest: ‘Go and tell him that many cases have been brought before me which will have to be ended by another judgment.’” Here one sees that there was a dispute over jurisdiction between the bishop and the count of Lyon.

**(140) Let all the faithful receive a benefit according to their merits**

**“Except that I alone, with your permission, shall be excluded.”**

Let all who are faithful to you receive from you, O king, each according to his merits, benefits—except for me alone, with your permission. Adalbero is joking and, in these words, reproaches Robert as though he were generous toward everyone except himself, to whom, I mean, Robert owed so many and such great things. For Adalbero seemed to have bestowed Laon and Charles upon Hugh and Robert, and the kingdom upon both together. Robert, acknowledging this, soon orders him to enjoy his favor and says that he is most deserving of royal gifts:

“May Christ’s grace, Adalbero, bishop, confirm you,

And ours as well; you are deservedly worthy of a royal gift.”

**(141) Let it be permitted to utter the seven praises at the appointed hours:**

The seven praises to be uttered at appointed hours and offered to God by clerics in the Church are Matins, or the Matins; Prime, or daybreak; Terce; Sext; None; Vespers, or the lighting of the lamps; and the beginning of the night, or Compline.

**(142) . . . a sacrifice with vows.**

Let the heart sacrifice itself to God with prayers and be offered like a victim. For “the sacrifice for God is a troubled spirit and a broken heart” (Psalm 50). Or perhaps Adalbero means that laypeople should offer their gifts at the altar as victims and join almsgiving to their prayers, because “prayer is good together with fasting and almsgiving.”

**(143) . . . Let this be the father’s permission,**

**When the Loire shall attempt to lick the Calabrian fields:**

“These things will happen which the father, or Bishop Adalbero, wishes and commands to happen,” says the king, “when the Loire—called the Loire of Adalbero through scribal error—will leave Aquitaine and attempt to flow through Calabria, and when the rushing Tigris, named for its speed like an arrow, will flood Spain instead of Mesopotamia, and when Mount Etna, marvelous in its fires, will produce a lake of roses and lilies.” That is: these things will occur or happen no more, no sooner, and no more easily than the things desired by Adalbero. Therefore the king adds:

“If such things come to pass, then fear that these things too will come to pass.”

From this it is understood that at that time in the kingdom of the Franks neither the rights of the Church were wholly preserved, nor were the monks everywhere observing the laws of Saint Benedict; that evil customs contrary to written laws had become established in France and ought to be abolished; that the bishops of France had lived more frequently and for longer periods in the countryside than in their respective cities, either idling in softness or rusticating sordidly like farm managers, and caring more for their estates than for the people entrusted to them; that they had often departed from equity and justice in their judgments and had entrusted the care of the poor and widows to unjust and predatory deacons; and finally, that the seven canonical hours were not then everywhere and by all clerics in western France duly observed for praising God and singing psalms and hymns. Robert calls Adalbero’s wishes “the father’s permission” because Adalbero had twice wished that these things be permitted to all and made lawful:

“Let it be permitted to all to pray during the days.”

Likewise:

“Let it be permitted to utter the seven praises at the appointed hours.”

**(144) Not because you are raving, but because you speak to us in allegory.**

[Col. 0822D]

The meaning of the words is: “Bishop Adalbero, may Christ’s grace and ours together confirm you. You are worthy of a royal gift because you are not raving but speaking to us in allegory”—that is, because through allegories you teach us what should be done and warn us what should be avoided. Thus the king excuses himself, since earlier he had called Adalbero unsound.

# In the Year of the Lord 1030. William V, Duke of Aquitaine

[Col. 0823]

## Historical Notice on William V

(*Literary History of France*, VII, 284.)

[Col. 0823A] William’s father was William IV, surnamed Fier-à-bras, count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine, whom he succeeded as early as 990. His mother, Emma, was the daughter of Thibauld and sister of Odo, both of whom successively became counts of Champagne (Malleac., *Chronicle*, pp. 203–204; Ademar, *Chronicle*, pp. 16, 173; Mabillon, *Annals*, Book I, no. 37). Born with every fortunate disposition of heart, mind, and body, he knew how to combine these with learning uncommon in his time, singular piety, and all the other excellent qualities that make great princes (Ademar, ibid., pp. 172–173, 177 and following). He therefore deserved to bear the surname “the Great” as a title of distinction. It is no small subject of praise for the schools of the tenth century that they formed so accomplished a pupil.

[Col. 0823B] Having been successfully instructed in letters from childhood, he developed such a taste for them that he later made them one of his more ordinary occupations (ibid., p. 177). In this way he became skilled at wielding the pen as well as the sword, and thus revived in his own person the conduct of the ancient emperors, who knew how to unite the tumultuous labors of Mars with the gentle exercises of Minerva. His taste for books was so well known to his friends, even those farthest away, that they believed they could give him no more agreeable present. With this purpose in mind, Canute, king of Denmark and England, sent him an ancient manuscript written in letters of gold and enriched with images separately representing a great number of saints (Councils, vol. IX, p. 882). William’s love of letters extended to those who cultivated them (Ademar, ibid., p. 173). It was enough to be learned to be assured of sharing in his favor and benefactions. For this reason he summoned the learned Fulbert from Chartres to Poitiers, overwhelmed him with honors, and gave him the treasury of Saint-Hilaire. For the same reason he conferred the abbey of Saint-Maixent upon Rainald, surnamed Plato, who was regarded as one of the learned men of his time.

William’s piety was still greater than his learning. It made him the defender of the poor, the father of monks, the protector of churches, and the beloved friend of bishops, several of whom he almost always had near his person (pp. 172–173). [Col. 0824A] He also took pleasure in having abbots and regular monks around him and willingly made use of their advice in governing his territories. Our purpose does not allow us to enter into detail about everything he did for their benefit. We shall say only that in 1010 he refounded the abbey of Maillezais, which was later erected into a bishopric and subsequently transferred to La Rochelle. He also founded the abbey of Bourgueil on land of his own and reformed several other monasteries, particularly those of Charroux and Saint-Jean-d’Angély. The abbeys of Cluny, Saint-Martial of Limoges, Saint-Michel-en-l’Herm, and many others likewise benefited from the generosity of this devout and magnificent prince. His piety set itself still broader aims. [Col. 0824B] Distressed by the corruption of morals, the eagerness with which ecclesiastical property and the property of the poor were plundered, and the contempt shown toward clerics, and also fearing the harmful consequences of the doctrine of the new Manichaeans, who were beginning to disturb Aquitaine, William convoked various councils, both at Charroux and at Poitiers, in order to bring some remedy to so many evils (Ademar, ibid.; Councils, ibid., pp. 733, 780–782).

From his youth he adopted the custom of going to Rome every year to visit the tomb of the apostles; and if he missed making this pilgrimage in any year, he made up for it by going to Saint James in Galicia (Ademar, ibid.). A misfortune that befell the city of Poitiers gave our generous count an opportunity to display both his magnificence and his piety (ibid., p. 180). After the city had been reduced to ashes by an unforeseen fire, William undertook to rebuild its cathedral and other churches, together with his palace, and made these buildings much more beautiful than they had been before. With the same generosity, for at least three years, he also supplied the almost immense expenses of rebuilding the cathedral of Chartres, on which his friend Bishop Fulbert was working (Fulbert, letters 16, 80, 104).

Such expenditures did not prevent him from maintaining his dignity with royal pomp and magnificence (Ademar, ibid., p. 172). Whether traveling or holding court, he appeared a king rather than a [Col. 0824D] duke. Yet all this splendor of greatness was free from [Col. 0825A] ostentation and pride. However elevated our count appeared in glory, he was no less affable or obliging toward everyone. A prince is always powerful when he possesses the hearts of his subjects. It was perhaps even more by this means than by any other that William became absolute throughout Aquitaine. The Emperor Saint Henry, Robert king of France, Alfonso of Castile, Sancho of Navarre, and Canute of Denmark and England all considered it an honor to be bound in friendship with so accomplished a prince. The popes and the entire Roman people valued him no less; and whenever he went to Rome, they received him with the same honors as if he had been their sovereign (Ademar, *Chronicle*, p. 173).

It was not the fault of the lords of Lombardy that he did not [Col. 0825B] actually become one (ibid., p. 182; Fulbert, letters 119, 123–126). Upon the death of the Emperor Saint Henry, they looked to our count to replace him. After deliberating among themselves, they sent envoys to Poitiers to offer him the crown of Italy, which would have been followed by the imperial scepter. A more ambitious and less prudent prince would have accepted offers so flattering with a kind of eagerness. But William, who did nothing without deliberation and moderation, first wished to determine for himself whether a project of this kind possessed as much solidity and advantage as it possessed brilliance. He traveled to Italy, and after holding several conferences with the nobles of the country, he understood that there was no safety in trusting people of [Col. 0825C] their character. He therefore despised their offers and caused their plan to fail. He even condemned it with abhorrence when he learned that one of the conditions required him to depose the bishops and substitute others in their place (Fulbert, letter 126). Thus this occasion served only to display more clearly the religious principle and wise policy of our pious and prudent count. Since the Italians had been unable to obtain the father as their king, they asked for his son. William did not appear disinclined to this and even took some steps toward it. Nevertheless, the matter did not succeed, apparently for the same reasons that had prevented its success in the case of the father (letters 15, 118).

The piety that animated all the other actions of [Col. 0825D] our prince also directed his studies. They were neither vain nor motivated by mere curiosity. The knowledge of religion was their principal object. He devoted particular attention to the study of the Holy Scriptures, of which he acquired a fairly extensive understanding (Ademar, ibid., p. 177). Indeed, one can see that he cites them appropriately in his letters. His connections with men of letters also reveal other features of his studies. Wishing to know what had been the end of Solomon, he persuaded Hildegar, Fulbert’s agent at Poitiers, to ask the learned prelate what the ancients had thought about it (Fulbert, letter 80). Fulbert satisfied him and, at his request, explained in another letter what [Col. 0826A] the oath of fidelity contained, as well as the reciprocal duties of vassal and lord (letter 101).

This great prince died at Maillezais, clothed in the monastic habit, on the last day of January 1030, after governing his territories with admirable wisdom, most vigorously, for thirty-nine years (Malleac., *Chronicle*, p. 207; Ademar, ibid., p. 150). He was then seventy-one. William successively contracted three legitimate marriages (Ademar, ibid., pp. 170–172; Malleac., ibid., p. 206): the first with Adalmode, widow of Aldebert, count of Périgord, by whom he had a son named William; the second with Brisque, sister of Sancho, duke of Gascony, who made him the father of two other sons, Odo and Thibauld, who died as a child. [Col. 0826B] Finally, after Brisque’s death, our prince married Agnes, who gave him two more sons, Peter Aigret, or “the Very Lively,” and Geoffrey, surnamed Guy, together with a daughter bearing the same name as her mother. The four brothers who survived their father succeeded one another in his territories, which is rare. The last two abandoned their own names and took that of their father, William. Agnes, their sister, married the Emperor Henry the Black and, through her learning, piety, and skill in the art of ruling, became an ornament to her sex. Agnes, their mother, William’s widow, contracted a second marriage with Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou (Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova*, vol. IV, p. 350).

Ademar (*Chronicle*, p. 177) informs us that Count William, in imitation of certain Roman emperors, knew how to wield the pen as well as the sword; but he does not tell us whether he left any writings other than simple letters. Of all those he had occasion to write, which would have formed a considerable and valuable collection for history, only six remain. They were printed without order among the letters of Fulbert of Chartres and form part of those that du Chesne selected to join to his other monuments relating to the history of France (Du Chesne, vol. IV, pp. 191–194). They are also found among the proofs of Besly’s *History of the Counts of Poitiers*. They are much more correct in these two later collections than in the first. M. du Boulay, who places our prince among his illustrious academicians and takes the opportunity to speak of his letters, says that they contain some elegance, *satis elegantes* (Egas du Boulay, vol. I, p. 597).

Three of them are particularly interesting in relation to the plan the Italians had of transferring the kingdom of Italy, together with the government of the empire, to William or his son. In addition to several circumstances concerning this famous event, the author left in them important observations on politics—not the art of manipulating and deceiving men, but the enlightened prudence needed to avoid being deceived by them. One of these letters is written to Maginfred, marquis of Susa, and to the marchioness Bertha, his [Col. 0827A] wife. While praising the good faith of this Italian lord and that of Bishop Alric, his brother, William admits that he was far from finding the same disposition in the nation as a whole, and that this was one of the reasons why he rejected their offers.

The other two letters are addressed to Leo, bishop of Vercelli, a particular friend of our count, who had worked hardest to bring about the projected plan just mentioned. The first shows that William was not unwilling to accept the Italians’ offer on behalf of his son. The other, which is the longest of them all and the best written, concerns various matters. It contains both humor and seriousness. After pleasantly and courteously joking about a mule from Poitou that the bishop of Vercelli had asked him for, the author turns to serious matters and succeeds in giving us striking evidence of his piety, his religion, his fairness toward his friends, and his esteem and respect for bishops. It is in this letter that he tells us that, if he had agreed to depose the bishops of Italy, the kingdom would have been his. It is easy to understand that this is only the smallest part of the letters he wrote concerning this great affair.

Only one of all the letters he had occasion to write to Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, remains to us; Fulbert wrote to him often in turn, as appears from his collection of letters. [Col. 0827C] Our prince’s letter, which is numbered 128, bears unequivocal witness to his esteem and [Col. 0828A] attachment for that great prelate. In it William briefly touches upon King Robert’s plan to have the prince his son crowned, apparently Hugh, and freely states what he thought of it.

He also wrote several letters to Aribert, abbot of Saint-Savin in Poitou, in order to obtain monks from him for the reform of the abbey of Charroux. But only one has come down to us, the misfortune of the times having deprived us of the others. The surviving letter contains highly edifying evidence of its author’s zeal for good order, the esteem in which he held regular monks, and the fruitfulness of his study of Scripture.

Among the other lost letters of Count William, one is known by name: the letter in which he described to King Robert a kind of rain of blood, mentioned earlier, and the effects that followed from it, asking him to consult the philosophers of his kingdom on the matter. It is also known that he wrote another to Azelin, bishop of Paris, in which he spoke of the king in a manner that greatly displeased him when it was communicated to him.

Finally, the sixth letter of our prince that remains is a reply to one of Hildegar’s letters. Hildegar was Fulbert’s agent at Poitiers and scholasticus of Saint-Hilaire. If one stopped at the inscription it bears in Fulbert’s collection of letters, one would take it to be by Hildegar rather than by Count William, so coarse are the errors that have crept into this edition. It reads *Hildegarius* instead of *Hildegario*.

[Col. 0827]

# Letters of William, Duke

*(In du Chesne, Historians of France, vol. IV, p. 193.)*

## First Letter of William to Maginfred, Marquis, and His Wife

[Col. 0827D]

To the most illustrious Marquis Maginfred and his most prudent wife B., William, by the grace of God duke of the Aquitanians, wishes perpetual prosperity.

What has been undertaken concerning my son does not seem to me to be sound, useful, or honorable. Your people are faithless; serious plots will arise against us. If we cannot either avoid or overcome them, the kingdom will be of no benefit to us and our reputation will be endangered. In our own regions, too, various people are already beginning various undertakings, stirred up by innovations; they see us occupied with this matter at present and think that we will be more tightly engaged in it in the future. You yourselves judge it disgraceful and useless that these things should occur and not be restrained while we are occupied elsewhere. Therefore, by the faith and friendship that exists between us, we implore you to work out how we may withdraw from what has been begun without disgrace to either you or us, taking care that my son, or anyone else, does not learn of this until we speak with one another privately. But if, by God’s arrangement, it cannot be abandoned and must be carried out, see to it that it proceeds with the agreement of the archbishop of Milan, the bishop of Vercelli, and the others concerned. Farewell.

## Second Letter of William to Leo, Bishop of Vercelli

William, by the grace of God duke of Aquitaine, sends greetings to Lord Leo, bishop of the Vercellians.

The Italians urged me and my son to involve ourselves in the kingdom of Italy, making us, with all the good faith they could muster, an oath concerning the acquisition both of that kingdom and of the Roman Empire. Therefore I write to you and ask your favor: help us in this matter as you know and are able best to do. Let it now become apparent whether what you have always told me is true—namely, that you are my friend and would take care of my affairs if necessary. Know this: if you favor our side, you have never seen days as good as those in which you will send us to that honor. For without a doubt everything we possess will be yours. Write back to me how confidently I may rely upon your affection and assistance. Farewell.

## Third Letter of Leo, Bishop of Vercelli, to Duke William

To Lord William, duke, brother Leo sends service.

Do not grieve, dearest friend, if the Lombards have deceived you. I shall certainly give you excellent advice if you are willing to trust me. Be a brave man; do not concern yourself with the past, but beware of the future. Send me word through your most faithful man what you wish to do, and I shall give you excellent advice. Send me a remarkable mule, a costly bridle, and a splendid carpet, which I asked you for six years ago. I tell you in truth: you will not lose your reward, and I shall give you whatever you wish. Farewell.

## Fourth Letter of William to Leo, Bishop of Vercelli

To Lord Leo, bishop of the Vercellians, William of Poitiers, his most illustrious friend, sends greetings and service.

[The supplied source ends here, at the end of the salutation.]

I am not at all saddened, dearest friend, by the deception of the Lombards. For they did not deceive me, since I would by no means have placed confidence in their promises. I do not concern myself with their past deceptions; by God’s grace I shall guard against their future ones. Yet I am not a little surprised at you, since you both have a long memory for the past and boast of possessing no less foresight regarding the future, because you consented to the cause of that Cuno, who neither ever gave you anything in his own land nor, it is said, is able to give anything, nor can he take anything away in the kingdom of Italy. But although in this matter you seem not to have given yourself sound advice, and although you offered no support to me when I tested my friends, I shall nevertheless await that excellent advice which you promise to give me, if I am willing to trust you.

Write to me, therefore, explaining how you wish me to trust you, and what benefits will come to me through your counsel from the gift of that Cuno, if I cease seeking the kingdom of Italy, which is promised to me and which I could obtain, God willing, if I cared greatly to pursue it. The mule which you requested I cannot presently send you, because I do not have one of the sort I would wish for your purposes; nor is there to be found in our regions a mule with horns, or one having three tails, or five feet, or anything else of that kind, so that you could properly call it “marvelous.” I shall, however, send you as soon as I can one of the very best among those I can find in our country, together with a costly bridle.

As for the carpet, I could send it to you, had I not forgotten how long and wide a carpet you requested some time ago. Remind me, I beg you, how long and wide you want it to be, and it shall be sent to you if I can find one. If not, I shall order one to be made for you as you wish, [Col. 0830A] provided that such a thing is customarily woven among our people.

Nor do I seek the reward which you promise—that you will give me whatever I wish—for this cannot be done. I ask, however, that even if I give you nothing, you remember me in your prayers and pray for me, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the Lord’s will and be protected by his holy temple. And do not delay that excellent counsel which you promise me.

Your promises stir me to place great confidence in you, because it is my part to trust a friend and not doubt his promises; and it is my part either never to promise or to fulfill what I have promised. Earlier in our conversation we jested with you, lord Leo, dearest brother; now we shall speak seriously.

I do not accuse the Lombards of deception, although they intended to practice it upon me insofar as they were able. The kingdom of Italy was within my grasp, if I had been willing to do one thing which I judged impious: namely, to depose, at their pleasure, the bishops who were in Italy and to raise others again according to their will. But far be it from me to do such a thing—to dishonor without fault the shepherds of the Church, whom my fathers always honored and whom I myself have always exalted as far as I was able.

Under this condition certain leading men of Italy wanted to make either me or my son king. The prudent margrave Meginfridus did not approve this disgraceful condition for me, nor did his brother Alricus, a good bishop; I have never regretted making use of the very sound counsel of these men. I consider them superior to all the Italians in intelligence, loyalty, and goodness.

If any of my possessions should truly please you and I am able or ought to send it, your hope will not be disappointed. I ask you to repay me with an equal return, so that you too may not make yourself unequal to my wishes. I desire to see your letter on the next approaching feast of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in which the secrets of your heart may be disclosed to your most faithful friend.

May you live in Christ, and may you prosper—living and prospering.

## EPISTLE V OF WILLIAM TO FULBERT, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

To the lord Fulbert, venerable bishop of the people of Chartres, William, by the grace of God duke of Aquitaine, sends greetings and affectionate friendship.

[Col. 0830D] When you first deigned to come to us at Poitiers, excellent prelate, and agreed to our request that you take charge of the church of Saint Hilary, our joy was great. But this joy is accompanied by much sorrow because you are reluctant to return to us. We therefore ask your graciousness not to fail to come, if possible during the octave of Pentecost. Otherwise, we guarantee you a safe journey, traveling with your clerics and household, at least eight days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. You will have enough soldiers with us.

If you remain with us no more than three days, you will greatly refresh us during that brief time. O, if you had come during the Rogation days just past, what consolation and joy you would have brought to us, our bishops, and our nobles!

If you wished to return to Chartres in time for the feast of Pentecost, or if you wished to withdraw so as not to go to the court of the lord king, you would have a sufficiently honorable reason. At present I am refraining from going to him, thinking that I shall incur less hostility on account of my absence than if I were with the lord king or queen, since I would not consent to a king being appointed without my brother Count Odo. Whoever he himself wishes to become king, you may know for certain that I too wish him to become king.

Whatever you hear about his agreement with the lord king, and where he is, if you know, I ask you to write back; also tell me whether the new king will be consecrated or not, and by whom. Farewell.

## EPISTLE VI OF WILLIAM TO ARIBERT, ABBOT

To the lord Aribert, holy and venerable abbot, William, by the grace of God duke of Aquitaine, sends every prosperity.

I have already appealed twice to your charity, asking you to send to the monastery of Carroficius some of your monks who are fervent in observing the Rule of Saint Benedict, whose holy way of life might provide a good example to the brothers of that place and relieve their abbot of the burden of government. Since you have not yet granted my request, I now knock a third time at the door of your charity, like that evangelical petitioner who earnestly asks a friend: if not for friendship, then at least because of my persistence, lend me as many men as I need.

I therefore beg you, in the name of the Holy Trinity, which is one God, to send me at least ten brothers from the fellowship of your angelic order, remembering at last the apostolic saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” Farewell, together with all your people.

## EPISTLE VII OF WILLIAM TO HILDEGARIUS

To Hildegarius, William sends wishes for the attainment of good things.

Your prudent simplicity has found such favor with me that what you asked of me to be done is no more [desired] by you than it is willed by me. But since at present I do not have the means, my heart fears that you may suspect me of intending to deceive you with words. I beg you, by the faith that exists between us, to believe that this is not my intention and to endure a little longer until, released from the very serious duties by which I am hindered, I can give you my assistance.

If, however, impatient of delay, you come to me soon, and I respond less fully to your wishes, once you have been fully informed of the reason, you will by no means rightly be angry with me. Farewell now and always.

R. Turonensis (R. of Tours)

[Col. 0831]

## DIPLOMA OF DUKE WILLIAM

By which he grants the village of Saint Macarius, where this saint rests, to the church of the Holy Cross of Bordeaux. (Year 1026.)

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. II, Instruments, p. 268.)*

[Col. 0831C] I, William, in the name of God, by God’s gift duke of Aquitaine, and my wife Aremberga, consider the gravity [or: grievousness] of my sins [and recall the goodness of God, who says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you”]. Therefore I grant to the basilica of the Holy Cross of Bordeaux the protection of that place and the free allod, exempt from every evil exaction and every act of plunder; and the village of Saint Macarius, where the body of blessed Macarius himself lies buried and rests, together with the tithe and all its possessions, rights over land and sea, and the right of blood [and over all possessions], together with the toll; and another protection belonging to Saint Mary of Macha [or Machao], with its tithe and every right and custom, together with the island adjoining it, and with the *paduensa* on land and sea; and another village of Saint Hilary of Ortellano [or Ortillano], with its tithe [and with the *paduensa*, of waters, woods, and lands]; and another village called Solaco, with the oratory of Saint Mary the Mother, together with its tithes, fresh waters, and lands, from the sea of Salissa as far as the sea of Girauda, and from Ubre of Syort as far as Grava, together with marshland, mountains, pine forest, fishing rights, and all the meadows belonging to Salvicina; together with male and female slaves.

Behold, all these villages, with their rights of blood and over all possessions, with their churches and all their customs and rights, with the customary payment of three *modii* of salt, and with the *pojadas* and the *fromentada*, and with all their appurtenances in meadows, customs, woods, vineyards, roads, and paths, I give, transfer, and convey to the most holy church situated at Bordeaux, and to its congregation serving God there. I hand them over as provisions and suitable support for the monks dwelling there, and I grant them the power and lordship to hold and possess them freely and to do collectively whatever they wish, with no one contradicting them.

But if henceforth anyone should arise under a false title—a count, bishop, or any tyrant of this world—who dares to appropriate the possessions listed above for his own use and takes anything away by force, let him first incur the wrath of almighty God, be excluded from the fellowship of Christians, and be swallowed alive by the earth together with Dathan and Abiram. May he never appear with the just at the holy resurrection, but may he be tormented with perpetual punishment in the snares of Cocytus. And if any adversary should arise and violate these protections, let him be compelled to pay the brothers one thousand pounds of gold.

[Col. 0834A] This donation was made in the year 1027 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the presence of Fulco-Gaufridus, the baron Truncardus, Combaudus of Ostend, William the provost, Edward and Guilbert, knights, and others; with the assistance of the monasteries, first of the Holy Cross, Saint Mary of Solaco, and Saint Macarius, and of the other churches, under Abbot Gombaud and Godefred, archbishop of the church of Bordeaux.

[Note: [Col. 0833A]]

Henry III, king of England, testified that he had seen this document himself, and he reports it in his letters, from which we have collected many variant readings. At the end of his letters the king adds:

> “Therefore, so that every suspicion of false Latinity, by which the aforesaid charter appears defective, may be utterly removed from the present and future generations, and so that no prejudice or burden may in any way arise on this account for the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Cross of Bordeaux, or for the abbot and monks serving God there, whom we embrace with sincere charity in the Lord, we ratify the same charter, notwithstanding this defect. We hold the aforesaid grants and donations to be valid and acceptable, and we freely grant and confirm them on behalf of ourselves and our heirs to the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 0834A] just as they are contained more fully in the aforesaid charter of the aforementioned duke, and as the confirmations of William, formerly duke of Aquitaine, and of our uncle King Richard, then count of Poitiers, and of Queen Eleanor, his mother and formerly queen of England, reasonably attest. These men are witnesses: the venerable Fathers A., archbishop of Embrun, and P., bishop of Hereford; John, son of Geoffrey; Philip Basset; Ralph, son of Nachat; John of Lexenthon; John Mannifest; Guy of Roussillon; and many others.
>
> “Given by our hand at Bordeaux on the twenty-third day of the month of August, in the twenty-seventh year of our reign.”

.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1031: BLESSED WILLIAM I, ABBOT OF SAINT-GERMAIN-DES-PRÉS

[Col. 0833]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. VII, p. 435.)*

[Col. 0833B] Blessed William I, noble by birth but far nobler in religion, was first a monk of Luciacum or Lucedium in Italy, then a monk of Cluny, afterward prior of Saint Saturninus of the Port on the Rhône, in the diocese of Uzès, commonly called Le Pont-Saint-Esprit, and later abbot of Saint Benignus at Dijon. From there he was frequently summoned to restore the vigor of regular discipline in various places and governed many monasteries.

Among these was Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which he undertook at the command of King Robert and Queen Constance and instructed in holier observances. Concerning this, the continuator of Aimoinus says in Book V, chapter 47:

> “While the monks of the aforesaid monastery, under Abbot Ingo, were living according to secular custom, the most devout King Robert, together with his wife, namely Queen Constance, after Ingo’s death summoned William, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, and gave him the abbey of Saint-Germain. He organized it according to the Rule and died in the year of the Lord 1030.”

Yet he was no less provident in temporal affairs. At the judgment of King Robert he obtained the removal of the evil customs which a certain deputy or advocate of his, named Pipinellus Garini, was exacting in the village of Antoniacum and its dependencies (in the year 1027).

He was likewise concerned for the deceased brothers. He renewed an old statute of his predecessors requiring their names to be pronounced in the chapter on every anniversary and five psalms to be sung daily at the conclusion of chapter. To another statute—namely, that every day one portion of bread and wine should be given for the dead—he added that, from his days until the end of the world, a full thirty-day observance should be held in the church for brothers who died, and likewise in the refectory on their anniversaries, with their names pronounced in chapter. This was done in the year 1028 with the counsel and testimony of Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil.

Shortly afterward William seems, with the king’s consent, to have resigned the abbacy to Adrald. Certainly, he relinquished the government before his death, which occurred in the year 1031, on the Kalends of January, in the monastery of Fécamp, where he was also buried. On that day the necrology of Prés records: “On the Kalends of January died lord Abbot William, exceedingly zealous in religion.”

[Col. 0835]

## LETTER OR CHARTER OF BLESSED WILLIAM TO THE BROTHERS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-GERMAIN-DES-PRÉS

*(Year 1028.)*

*(Dom Félibien, History of the Abbey of Saint-Germain, Documents, p. XXIV.)*

[Col. 0835A] Let those professed in the Church of Saint-Germain of Paris know that lord William, the first abbot, with the consent of the entire chapter, established that on every anniversary the names of the deceased brothers should be pronounced in chapter and that every day five psalms—namely, “Hear my words”—should be sung at the conclusion of chapter.

This custom had been corrupted for certain reasons. His predecessors, the abbots, had established—and he did not wish to change—that every day one portion of bread and wine should be given for the dead. He nevertheless added that, from his days until the end of the world, a full thirty-day observance should be held in the refectory and in the church for brothers who died, and likewise in the refectory on their anniversaries, with their names pronounced in chapter. Whoever corrupts this constitution, let it rebound upon his own head.

This was done with the counsel and testimony of Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1031: SAINT WILLIAM, ABBOT OF SAINT-BENIGNE OF DIJON

[Col. 0835]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT WILLIAM

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Sixth Century, Part I, p. 320.)*

[Col. 0835B] 1. It is clearly inferred from Rodulfus Glaber’s little book on the Life of William that William’s death must be assigned to the year 1031, since Glaber explicitly states that he died in that year at the age of seventy. That he spent almost his entire life in the exercises of monastic life is shown by the fact that, scarcely having passed his seventh year, he assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Luciacum. From there, out of a desire for stricter discipline, he went to the monastery of Saint Michael and soon afterward withdrew with Saint Majolus to Cluny in Gaul.

Luciacum—or, as others call it, Lucedium or Locedium, commonly Di Locedia—is an ancient monastery of our order, originally called Saint Michael’s and later Saint Januarius’, because the relics of that saint were transferred there. The neighboring town likewise took the name Saint Januarius. It lies not far from the city of Vercelli, to whose diocese it once belonged. Today it is subject to the bishopric of Casale, in the territory of Montferrat. It first passed from the Benedictine order to the Cistercians and, after various fortunes, finally fell away to secular clerics, as Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia observes in his *History of Piedmont*, chapter 33.

2. In the twenty-ninth year of his age—that is, in 990, in the third indiction—William was ordained abbot of Saint Benignus by lord Bruno, bishop of Langres, says the Benignian chronicler. In addition to the privilege of Pope Benedict—whom some believe to have been Benedict VII—granted to the same William, this opinion appears to be opposed by a certain fragment of the manuscript history of the monastery of Saint Benignus, in which it is said that the church of Saint Benignus was begun by William in 982 and completely restored in 986.

These matters, however, are not so weighty that we should readily depart from the authority of a serious and contemporary writer, especially since Rodulfus Glaber and the Chronicle edited by Labbe agree with the Benignian chronicler. It is also established that the privilege of Pope Benedict must be assigned not to Benedict VII but to Benedict VIII, since Ughelli, in volume II of *Sacred Italy*, column 996, records that it was issued in the year 1015.

3. “The aforementioned William,” says Glaber in Book III of his *Histories*, chapter 5, “was keen in intellect and distinguished in prudence; for this reason he held the highest position in the palaces of kings and other princes.”

Blessed Odilo, his fellow student under Saint Majolus, encompasses his praise in a few words, but words superior to many books, in his little work on the deeds of Saint Majolus, where he says:

> “And, with the leave of the spiritual craftsmen laboring in the same workshop, let me say that one in particular shone forth: he who recently departed from human affairs and who labored more than all of us, namely lord Abbot William. Of his most illustrious deeds, praiseworthy life, and wondrous conduct, our smallness is not sufficient to relate fully what it perceives.”

Jotsaldus, in his lament on the death of the same blessed Odilo, celebrates William and Odilo together in the same verses, which we shall present below in the Eulogy of Odilo.

The old author of the Chronicle of Fécamp likewise writes that William was thoroughly educated in the liberal arts and, in ecclesiastical disciplines and all spiritual offices [lacuna], imbued and enlightened by the grace of the virtues.

Hence there was scarcely any monastery in the Roman Empire that was not entrusted to William’s care. He himself presided over some of them or placed his disciples over them; as for the rest, he brought the abbots who already governed them, by his examples and admonitions, to the careful practice of regular discipline.

“Of blessed memory,” says the same author, “Abbot William illumined all the regions of the Roman Empire by the abundance of his religious devotion, and by the image of his fervor reformed and kindled the lukewarm spirits of many abbots.”

Sigebert, under the year 1027, lists him among the notable abbots through whose work ecclesiastical religion flourished in the eleventh century: “In France and Burgundy [lacuna] through William of Dijon, venerable for his strictness.”

Finally, as Glaber says in the passage cited, whenever any monastery was deprived of its own shepherd, William was immediately compelled by kings or counts, as well as by bishops, to undertake its government in order to improve it.

The same author asserts that William was placed over nearly forty monasteries. The Benignian chronicler lists most of them: apart from Saint Benignus, which he is discussing, they were Verzey, Bèze, Reomay, Tonnerre, Melun, Saint Arnulf of Metz, Saint Aprus of Toul, Gorze, Fécamp, Jumièges, Saint-Ouen of Rouen, Saint Michael on Mount Tomb, Saint Faro of Meaux, Saint-Germain of Paris, Fruttuaria, Saint Amator near Langres, and Saint Mary near Saxonicus-Fons. Glaber adds the monastery of Saint Saturninus on the Rhône, which has now been reduced to a priory and subjected to the monastery of Ambronay.

There is no time to discuss all these separately. But concerning Fruttuaria, which this holy man founded on his paternal estate, and Fécamp, where he died, we shall add some material from the monuments of those places. As for Saint Benignus and Bèze, the chroniclers of those monasteries have written especially about them; we shall present their excerpts below.

[Col. 0838A] 4. Although, so far as we know, Saint William was honored among the ancients by no public cult, Arnold Wion and Hugh Menard nevertheless inserted him among the saints in the Benedictine Menology and Martyrology on his natal day in January. All later writers, following them, have likewise bestowed upon him the title of saint—and not without reason, since so many arguments are available to demonstrate his sanctity that scarcely any more certain evidence can be found for any saint of this age: foreknowledge of death, the performance of miracles, and above all an utterly blameless life and singular observance of the monastic rule.

For this reason Glaber, the writer of his Life, a serious man of great authority, calls Saint William’s death, in the final chapter, a passage “to the holy, divine light,” and observes—something most worthy of note—that the miracles he had performed while still alive continued after his death at his tomb.

He must be heard in Book IV of the *Histories*, chapter 4:

> “One thing remains which I know is not contained there”—that is, in the Life of Saint William. “For the aforesaid Father departed from the world to the rest of the blessed in the regions of Neustria, namely in the monastery of Fécamp [lacuna] and was buried, as befitted so great a man, in the finest place of that church.
>
> “After several days had passed, it happened that a boy of about ten years, exhausted by a severe illness, was brought to his tomb in the hope of recovering his health. There, after being left alone by his parents, he lay down. Suddenly he looked up and saw a little bird sitting upon the tomb, having the form of a dove. He gazed at it for a long time and fell asleep. Then, waking after a gentle sleep had refreshed him, he found himself healthy, as though he had never felt the severity of his illness. His joyful parents therefore took him back, and the joy became common to all.”

5. “The body of Saint William,” says the author of his Life, “was buried in the greater basilica of Fécamp, in the sight of the brothers going and returning”—that is, before the altar of Saint Taurinus, bishop of Évreux, which today is called the altar of Saint Benedict.

From that place it was later transferred to the chapel dedicated to blessed Mary Magdalene—at what time and for what reason is unknown—and placed on the Gospel side. There it is still preserved in a stone sarcophagus, three feet long and nine inches wide, enclosed within a chamber in the wall toward the north, bearing the following inscription on a sheet of lead, discovered in 1638:

> Reader, recognize that Abbot William, full of days,  
> An old man, lies here.  
>   
> He had shone as the first shepherd of this place,  
> Where, by God’s gift, he established many monks.  
>   
> The first day of January shone anew for his soul,  
> Whom the whole New Jerusalem came to meet.

[Col. 0837]

## ON THE MONASTERY OF FRUTTUARIA, FOUNDED BY BLESSED WILLIAM

[Col. 0837D] 1. Since scarcely anything is found about the monastery of Fruttuaria either in the Life of William written by Glaber or in the Benignian chronicler, it seemed appropriate to discuss it here at somewhat greater length. Among all the other monasteries governed by our William, it possesses the special distinction of having been founded by him on the estate of his own paternal inheritance; hence knowledge of its beginnings will be especially useful for illuminating the deeds of this blessed man.

It was situated between the two rivers Orco and Malone in Cisalpine Gaul, within the boundaries of the diocese of Ivrea. It was first founded and endowed through the generosity of the brothers of blessed William and of his other kinsmen; it was then increased by various donations from others and finally strengthened and fortified by diplomas and privileges of princes and supreme pontiffs. In both nobility and abundance of wealth, it yielded to scarcely any monastery in all Italy.

An old author expresses its origins in a few verses, which Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia, copied from the ancient Chronicle of the monastery, inserted into his *History of Piedmont*:

> If anyone wishes to know in advance when  
> The work of the Fruttuaria monastery was rightly begun:  
>   
> It was then the lofty thousand and third year  
> Since the birth of the heavenly Prince born of the Virgin.  
>   
> The seventh Kalends of March and the first indiction  
> Both run their appointed course.  
>   
> King Ardoin, weakened in the rule of his scepter,  
> Reigns in the West and presses on into Ausonia.  
>   
> The Lord himself aids the place and enriches it with his gift;  
> He has provided for the brothers in their continual labors.  
>   
> Bishop Ottobianus consecrated it by the authority of his office;  
> Abbot William builds this place for the Lord.

2. But no one explains the origins of his monastery better than William himself. For this reason we reproduce below the charter reported by the author mentioned above from the archive of Fruttuaria.

3. I do not know in what year this document was drawn up. William himself may not have expressed the date, or the person who copied it from the original may have omitted it. The copyist also seems, whether through ignorance of reading or for some other reason unknown to me, to have covered this precious monument with so many errors.

Nevertheless, from various charters reported by Guichenon in the *Bibliotheca Sebusiana* and by Ughelli in volume IV of *Sacred Italy*, in the section on the bishops of Ivrea, it is clear that Abbot William omitted nothing that could firmly establish the freedom of the monastery of Fruttuaria, both in temporal and in spiritual matters, so that it could not easily be shaken in later times.

First, he arranged for Emperor Henry to confirm everything that had been given to the monastery either by his relatives or by other pious men. A diploma of that Henry exists concerning this matter, issued in the year 1014. From it we learn not only many things about the various possessions that the monastery of Fruttuaria already held at that time, but also the noble lineage of our William and the names of several other distinguished men who, having rejected the allurements of the world, were then living the monastic life in that place. Moreover, the judgment or charter of Gonthardus, praised above in William’s document, is confirmed by Henry.

“Lord Abbot William,” it says, “approached our clemency, asking that a certain monastery, situated in a place called Fruttuaria, be strengthened by our authority. It was built in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Benignus the martyr, from the personal inheritance of his brothers Gotfred, Nitard, and Robert, as is contained in the charter of judgment issued by Gonthardus the deacon. Having received his petitions, we first confirmed it by royal decree,” and so forth.

Among the other benefactors of the monastery he lists Ottho William, a kinsman of our William, as we have said above. Several charters of his exist, issued in favor both of the monastery of Saint Benignus and of the monastery of Fruttuaria.

> “Let him have and hold in quiet right the fortress of the Lombards with all its appurtenances, and all those estates and courts which Ottho, also called William, count, son of Adalbert and grandson of King Berengar, gave to that place within the boundaries of Lombardy from the inheritance of his parents and relatives.
>
> “We further establish by the firmness of this decree of ours that all those lands which the aforesaid monastery ought to possess from the inheritance of Robert, formerly a most noble man and the father of the aforesaid Abbot William, shall be held by it in perpetuity . . .
>
> “We confirm all that inheritance and those possessions which by paternal and maternal right were owed to Otbert, son of Gerard and grandson of Count Otbert. This Otbert made the holy church of Fruttuaria his heir when he and his father abandoned the world, giving themselves and all that they possessed to God and becoming monks . . .”

Toward the end he lists the cells, or priories, which at that time depended upon that monastery: “the cell of Asti, the cell of Naviglio, the cell at Quaranta, the cell at Cavaglià, the cell at Paderno,” and so forth.

4. In the year 1023 William obtained another privilege from the same emperor. By it the monastery of Fruttuaria was received under the emperor’s special protection, “as is contained in the charter of judgment issued by Gunthardus the deacon,” and the privilege of Benedict VIII was confirmed.

“Then,” it says, “so that it may remain more firmly established, we strengthen it by imperial authority and receive it under our protection on the condition that no duke, margrave, or anyone else . . . We also establish and confirm by the authority of God and of ourselves that the aforesaid place shall retain the liberty mentioned above in all respects, and that whatever has been established concerning its liberty and stability, the election and consecration of its abbot, by Lord Pope Benedict and by many bishops in privileges and synodal decrees, shall be preserved at all times, valid and supported by unshaken firmness.”

Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, observes in the *Chronicle of Verdun* that our William, whom he calls “a vigorous ruler and outstanding in religious devotion,” was especially beloved by blessed Henry. A little farther below he says that the same William “was said to be above the Rule because of the rigor of his more fervent purpose.”

5. After the death of Henry Augustus, his successor Conrad, at the request of blessed William, likewise strengthened the liberty of the monastery of Fruttuaria by his own authority, using almost the same words as Henry, as is clear from his charter reported by the same Guichenon.
