In it John, abbot of that place, is mentioned; in the Benignian Chronicle he is called Joannetinus; Henry and his imperial successors are said to have been admitted “into the fellowship of the brothers.”

> “We have judged it fitting to confirm the monastery of Fruttuaria by written decrees, at the request of lord William, abbot of Dijon. He built the aforesaid monastery from its foundations out of the estates and alms of his relatives and of the other faithful of Christ, and gathered there many men serving God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.
>
> “Desiring that we and our successors forever should share in all the benefits of his benefactors, just as he had associated our predecessor Henry of blessed memory with his own fellowship and that of the brothers, he caused the first abbot of the same monastery, named John, to be consecrated in his presence, and entrusted both him and the entire place to his imperial protection, chiefly so that he might preserve for it in all respects the same liberty which the monastery of Cluny is known to possess.
>
> “We, therefore, providing for our salvation,” and so forth.

He also confirms the privileges and synodal decrees of Pope Benedict and the other bishops in the same words as those cited above from Henry’s diploma. Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia observes that this was also done by other emperors and even by the Roman pontiffs in his *Catalogue of the Abbots of Fruttuaria*, chapter 27 of his *Chronological History of Piedmont*. There he says that the Abbot John mentioned here was the son of Count Guido of Saint Martin and grandson of Ardoin, king of Italy.

6. King Robert of the Franks was no less devoted to the monastery of Fruttuaria than the emperors, although it lay outside his own dominion. Accordingly, when William requested confirmation of certain possessions that had been granted to his monastery in France, the most devout king willingly granted his assent and, by a general decree, affirmed for the monastery of Fruttuaria everything that had already been given to it or might afterward be granted to it within the boundaries of his kingdom. (See above, under King Robert, among his ecclesiastical decrees.)

7. We must now present the charter of Lambert, bishop of Langres, who confirmed the exemption of the monastery of Fruttuaria from subjection to the monastery of Dijon, which William had obtained from Bruno. No public document of Bruno existed, however, because death overtook him before he could complete the matter.

This charter is, as it were, a summary of all the other documents which [sic] we have presented above for asserting the freedom of that monastery. It is found in the second century, no. 79, copied from the royal archive at Turin.

I, Lambert, bishop of the holy Church of Langres, have resolved to make known to those now living and to those yet to come that a certain beloved among the beloved—namely, Abbot William—approached our fatherhood with just petitions, so that, by synodal decree, a certain testament which the benevolence of our predecessor Bruno, of blessed memory, had been unable to complete because death intervened might be brought to fulfillment by the authority of our goodwill. He ought rightly to obtain this all the more easily, since it is recognized that zeal for God requires it altogether.

For one of his blood relatives, named Godefred, upon coming to holy conversion, devoutly offered to God everything whatsoever he possessed, chiefly with the intention that a monastery should be built from his own property. So that it might not become subject to any episcopal see or monastery, careful deliberation determined that it should be built in a certain place anciently called Fructuaria. By a legal charter, this property was handed over by Nithard and Rotbert, Godefred’s brothers, to a certain levite named Guntard, so that he might make a testamentary disposition concerning it under wholly unrestricted conditions. This was indeed done, though not without the assistance of many people, especially King Arduino and his wife Berta. Through their prudent efforts, the testamentary gifts were legally confirmed, and ornaments of no small value were evidently presented to the holy monastery of Dijon: namely, one Gospel book wonderfully adorned with gold, gems, and precious stones; one chasuble decorated with gold; two gilded stoles with their maniples; one belt; and four similarly gilded amices.

They took care to do this both so that the place from which Fructuaria had taken its beginning might be honored by these benefits, and so that those who remembered this in later times would have no occasion by an evil intention to construct a scandal from it. We, therefore, weighing the rights of equity and consulting the gain of souls rather than the desires of the wicked, and also fulfilling the promises of our holy predecessor, neither differing from the apostolic privileges and decrees, nor from the imperial and royal commands, proclaim that the monastery of Fructuaria, with all the possessions which it appears to hold, movable as well as immovable, is subject to no subjection and to no jurisdiction belonging to our bishopric or to anyone else. Rather, under its own pastor, so that it may enjoy in all respects the complete liberty granted to it by the Roman See, and so that, once such a bond of subjection has been removed, it may be recognized as independent, we both will and decree, under synodal authority, that no monk, nor any successor of the aforesaid lord Abbot W., shall bring any complaint or accusation against the aforesaid place, or demand any property or subjection from it.

[Col. 0842D] Therefore, so that this place, called Fructuaria, may also by our authority remain free and absolutely released through an unshaken stipulation, immune from every complaint, and always fit, with Christ as its guide, for sacred increase in the bringing of souls to fruitfulness, we have signed this with our subscription, with witnesses admitted from our clergy.

The sign of Lambert, bishop of the see of Langres.  
The sign of Berald, archdeacon.  
The sign of Berald, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, and others.

Enacted publicly at Dijon, on the third Ides of January, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1017, in the fifteenth indiction, while Robert was reigning as king of the Franks. I, Oddo the chancellor, have recognized and subscribed this testament, completed and praised and confirmed by the entire synod of the holy Church of Langres.

[Col. 0843A] **8.** Many, attracted by the renown of the monastery of Fructuaria, gave to it not only their possessions but also themselves. Among them was the celebrated Arduino, king of Italy, who, after affairs had gone badly for him against the Emperor Henry, renounced the world and withdrew to the aforesaid monastery, where he died and was buried; some have honored him with the title of Blessed. He is distinguished by this title in Bucelinus’s Benedictine Menology, where he is recorded as having died on 2 March 1018.

This reputation for holiness, by which Fructuaria was then commended, was transmitted also to later generations, as can easily be gathered from various charters reported by Guichenon. Agnes the empress, mother of Henry Augustus, especially cherished this place. Through her intervention, and that of Blessed Anno, archbishop of Cologne, Pope Alexander II confirmed the privileges of the same monastery in a charter of his own in the year 1070.

Certainly, when Blessed Anno, as Lambert of Schafnaburg, a contemporary author, reports, while staying in Italy turned aside to the monastery of Fructuaria for the sake of prayer, “there he admired the monks’ extremely strict way of life according to the institutions of the Rule, and, on his return, took away with him some of them, highly approved in the work of God.” He established them in the monastery of Siegburg, which he himself had founded. This, the same author says, was the occasion for regular observance to be restored in the other monasteries as well.

**9.** The Augusta Agnes herself, having renounced the vanity of the world, stayed at Fructuaria before she established her residence at Rome. How greatly she venerated the monks of that place can be inferred from her letter, which she wrote shortly before withdrawing among them. It runs as follows in Guichenon, *Centuria* II, no. 77, copied from the Fructuarian Chartulary:

> A., empress and sinner, to A. [Andrew], good Father, and to the brothers gathered at Fructuaria, in the name of the Lord.
>
> My conscience, the servitude of a handmaid whose eyes are in the hands of her mistress, terrifies me more than every specter and every image. Therefore I flee through the places of the saints, seeking a hiding-place from the face of this fear. I have no small desire to come to you, since I have learned that your intercession is certain salvation; but our journeys are in God’s hand and not in our own will.
>
> Meanwhile, in spirit I adore at your feet, asking you, with a compassion like Gregory’s toward Trajan, to seek pardon for me from the Lord. For if that one man obtained a pagan’s release from the prison-houses of hell, you will easily save one Christian woman. If you decide to do this, I ask that, as a sign of your compassion, you send me word of your fellowship and brotherhood, and send it to me as soon as possible.
>
> I also ask that you deign to accept the small gift which I am sending as a sign of admonition, so that I may believe that you have begun to care for me. Farewell; and you, good Father, commend me carefully to the more spiritual brothers in the monasteries and cells, so that they may make me a participant in their prayers, fasts, and all their good works.

**10.** Through the intervention of the same Augusta, her son, the Emperor Henry, gave the whole of Rivus, with all its appurtenances, in the county of Aix, to the monastery of Fructuaria, as is certain from his charter, which is cited in *Centuria* XI, no. 76. At the beginning of the following century, the patriarch of Jerusalem entered into an association with the brothers of the monastery of Fructuaria; a letter concerning this matter is found in the same work, no. 73.

Peter Damian devotes all of booklet 18, chapter 3, addressed to Countess Adelaide, to praising the monastery of Fructuaria, where he states that he was received as a guest for ten days. This celebrated monastery still endures, enjoying both spiritual and temporal jurisdiction of the widest extent. In it, Mauricius, son of the duke of Savoy, who presided over the place at the beginning of the present century, established a college of secular canons.

[Col. 0843]

## ON THE MONASTERY OF FÉCAMP

[Col. 0843D] **1.** Although, as Glaber records, Blessed William presided under the title of abbot over nearly forty monasteries, and although, because he restored regular discipline and bestowed other benefits, very many monasteries of Gaul and Italy eagerly claim him for themselves, the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Fécamp nevertheless possesses a special and very celebrated distinction: after nearly thirty years of his governance, it was honored by his tomb.

That he assumed the governance of the monastery of Fécamp in the year 1001 is expressly stated in two Chronicles preserved by Labbe in volume I of the *New Library*. One of them is there called the Rouen Chronicle, the other the Fécamp Chronicle. The author of the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne agrees with them. No one can call into question that he died in 1031.

Fécamp—commonly called Fescan—is a town within the boundaries of the diocese of Rouen, although entirely exempt from it. It lies in the Pays de Caux, overlooking the sea. In that place Waningus, a nobleman, built a monastery for women in the seventh century. After it was destroyed by the Northmen, another monastery for men arose at the beginning of this century through the generosity of the dukes of Normandy; it still surpasses the other monasteries of the province in wealth and nobility, under our congregation of Saint Maur.

We presented the Life of Waningus, its first founder—or rather, fragments of that Life, mutilated and drawn from uncertain authors—in the second century. Besides this Life, we have before us, from a manuscript codex of the same monastery, a book entitled *On the Revelation, Building, and Authority of the Monastery of Fécamp*. In it the beginnings of the place, the disasters and ravages inflicted by the Northmen, and finally its restoration are explained at greater length.

From this book we learn that Saint Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, was invited by Richard I, duke of the Northmen, to send Cluniac monks to Fécamp, to replace the canons who then occupied that church. When the holy man refused to do this, later, in the time of Richard the Younger, our William, already abbot of Saint-Bénigne, was placed over the same establishment, where he restored the monastic life.

That Richard loved William above all the pious men who flourished in Normandy at that time is testified by Hugh of Flavigny in the *Chronicle of Verdun*. After first praising Richard, who, having expelled the canons, established monks at Fécamp under William’s direction, he concludes as follows:

> In his time Normandy flourished with religious men, who flocked to him like bees to their hives. Among them he honored this blessed man, William the abbot, with especially devoted reverence, loving him so greatly with a particular affection that he rejoiced to obey his commands and comply with his counsels.

William had acquired this authority through the holiness of his own life and that of his monks. We have already learned from the Chronographer of Saint-Bénigne by what method monastic life was established there under his governance; but it will become clearer from the celebrated little book. We had originally decided to publish the book in its entirety, since it contains much worthy of knowing about the monastery of Fécamp and is dedicated to William, abbot of Fécamp, whether the second or the third of that name. But since nearly the whole work has already been published by Arthur du Monstier in *Neustria Pia*, it seemed sufficient to present what bears more particularly upon our purpose.

First, however, a few words must be said about the illustrious men who flourished at that time in the monastery of Fécamp.

**2.** The illustrious men who flourished under Abbot William in the monastery of Fécamp are listed in the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne. We gave the complete passage above. There were also several princes descended from the most noble blood of the dukes of Normandy who at the same time put on the monastic cowl there. Among them, William of Jumièges, in book V, chapter 13, mentions William, son of Richard II, who in his youth assumed the monastic wool at Fécamp.

A short time afterward, Nicholas, son of Richard III, also embraced the monastic life there under Abbot John, compelled by his own uncle Robert, who obtained the duchy of Normandy in his place. Nicholas later became abbot of Saint-Ouen at Rouen and was distinguished by many virtues, as Orderic Vitalis reports in book VIII, where he describes his praises at length.

Some include among these men Malger, who was eventually raised to the see of Rouen; but his deeds obscured the glory of his birth.

**3.** In a few words, Orderic praises the first three abbots of Fécamp after its restoration, in book IV; from him one may gather how great the reputation of that monastery was at that time:

> The monastery of Fécamp, situated overlooking the sea, and so forth, was governed after William of Dijon, a wise man and most fervent in religion, by John, a venerable abbot, for fifty-one years. After him William of Roz, a cleric of Bayeux but a monk of Caen, held it for nearly twenty-seven years. Like mystical nard, he breathed forth charity in the house of the Lord, together with generosity and manifold goodness. The works which he diligently performed openly, or offered to almighty God in secret before a few witnesses, testify what spirit dwelt in him; possessing him entirely, it led him to the throne of the Lord of hosts, there to be crowned.

The same author has more to say about William II in book XI, where, among other things, he presents his epitaph, composed by Hildebert of Le Mans.

But, leaving these matters aside, since they have already been published, we shall present from a manuscript codex of Fécamp a fragment of “the letter of Bishop Balderic to the people of Fécamp, as reported by Adelino, who had been appointed his guardian and servant in the hospital.” The fragment is as follows:

**4.** William shone among his predecessors and among his fellow provincials as the sun shines more brilliantly and more prominently than all the other lights. For this man, endowed with great knowledge of letters, first archdeacon of Bayeux, afterward a monk of Caen, and finally abbot of Fécamp, a venerable and hoary-headed person, a certain majesty of religion, elevated this house by the discipline of his morals, enlarged it in its walls, and—what was especially remarkable in him—enriched the community of the brothers.

Many noble laymen and clerics, attracted by the fragrance of his religion, were aroused to conversion, voluntarily put on the monastic habit, and were instructed in his holy institutions. I myself, who speak with you, heard, while living far away, a good report of our William. Drawn by it, and with the permission of our abbot—for I had and still have another abbot—I came to Fécamp in order to attach myself to him, and was gladly received, although I was a man of no account.

Nearly all whom you see he himself gathered. Yet we were more numerous than we are now, because after his passing some of our number gradually followed their leader. The vigor of the order sustained us; by words and examples he instructed us; with paternal affection he made us all part of himself. For, to speak the truth, on account of God he became all things to all people.

Therefore our tears follow him, and for that reason our sighs accompany him. On that day he was our leader: no one was more abundant in tears. In his little bed he struggled with himself in sighs; amid the crowd he was calm with us; in a corner of the church, or in the solitude of his pallet, he was wholly troubled. He argued with himself over our transgressions and mercilessly crucified himself.

If anything occurred through the guilt of the brothers, what excess did he not make his own by compassion? As often as anyone sinned—or I, wretched man, sinned—so often did he sacrifice himself. He frequently kept vigil through the night in prayer, and, groaning most quietly, troubled God; he contended with Him without offense, and through that friendly contention reconciled Him both to himself and to us, like another Solomon. He redeemed us with alms, because whatever was entrusted to him he faithfully distributed.

What poor person ever felt that his hand was barren? What church did not possess his generosity? He went around the corners and streets of the lepers and, entering their little huts to speak familiarly with them, often even kissed their elephantine hands, so that he might attend to everyone’s needs, so that the distress of any poor wretch might make itself known to him. The holiness of his good conduct cannot be fully expressed in words.

The same abbot is said to have been called *Puellam*, commonly *la Pucelle* (“the Maiden”), because of the elegance of his appearance. He built several churches in the town of Fécamp and established a universal almsgiving to be distributed daily to the poor. He governed the monastery for twenty-nine years and was buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary the Elder, opposite the altar.

His death is recorded in the cited Necrology in these words:

> 25 March: the deposition of lord William, third abbot of Fécamp.

For praises of the monastery of Fécamp, see Dudo, dean of Saint-Quentin, who closes the final book of *On the Customs and Deeds of the Normans* with an encomium of the monastery of Fécamp. It is enough to extract a few verses:

> O Fécamp, ever fruitful in sacred embers,
>
> preserving in the bosom of your now-consecrated earth
>
> the ashes of the saints, shining with the flower of their merits,
>
> resplendent with the abundant gift of salvation from the Trinity,
>
> once you shone with a sacred virginal crown,
>
> when you preserved Leodegarius deprived of light.
>
> May you live, Fécamp, always through happy years;
>
> rejoice, Fécamp, for you are most worthy of praise.
>
> You, people of Fécamp, gird the swords of virtues;
>
> you guard the doors of the Church and strike down the misty enemies.

But now it is time to present the fragments of the book which we promised above.

[Col. 0847]

## EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK ON THE REVELATION, BUILDING, AND AUTHORITY OF THE MONASTERY OF FÉCAMP

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0847B]

I have composed a little book on the revelation, building, and authority of the monastery of Fécamp, illustrious Father William, and I have sent the completed work to be corrected and confirmed by the sincere judgment of your affection, so that the assent of your exalted person may both command that the little book be published and grant weight and authority to the work once published.

Indeed, illustrious Father, I would rather have concealed my ignorance under cautious silence than reveal it publicly through the presumptuous evidence of some writing. But by the persistent command of our brothers, and by an insistence that commands, our spirit is compelled to exceed its abilities and unexpectedly expose its ignorance to the eyes of many people.

Our spirit, I say, is compelled to ignore its own ignorance and to display obedience to the entreating command of our brothers. Yet the judgment of our mind in no way consents to this obedience, and the shame of our purpose wholly resists it. Nevertheless, since holy obedience excuses no work as difficult or impossible, nor ought to excuse one, after long hesitation and pretending the delays of many procrastinations, under the pressure of the continuous command of fraternal love I finally took up the burden imposed upon me and, in a rustic and undistinguished style, disclosed and set forth the beginnings of the monastery of Fécamp in the following little book.

In this book I have inserted nothing false or deceptive. Rather, I have written the sacred histories of the men of old, known through faithful narration and preserved in the tenacious memory of their descendants, as they were handed down to our own times through the diligent reports of later men; and I have published what I wrote for the authority of the Church of Fécamp and for the benefit of the brothers who read it, and so forth.

### From chapter XV

Meanwhile it happened that the canons of Fécamp began to imitate the ways of other canons, to enter the broad roads of destruction, and to pursue luxuries and slothful pleasures in temporal matters. When the most prudent duke Richard heard and came to know of this wretched life and impending misery of the canons, he grieved greatly. Horrified by the ways and conduct of wicked men, he hurriedly sent envoys to Cluny and summoned Saint Maiolus to Fécamp with prayers of great humility, begging him to arrange and order the new church according to the Rule and constitution of Saint Benedict.

Saint Maiolus said to him:

> I shall undertake the magnitude of this labor, dearest son Richard, on this condition: that you give to God throughout your entire duchy the custom commonly called *pasnagium* [Note: [Col. 0847D] *Pasnagium*, also called *pastionaticum* or *pastinaticum*, commonly *panage*, is a payment or tax for the gathering of acorns and the right to pasture pigs or other animals in the lord’s forest.], and decree that no prince under your authority shall ever again exact it.

But Duke Richard, not because of the disease of avarice, but because hidden divine providence had arranged matters and had transferred to Saint Abbot William the glory of organizing the holy church, listened to the counsel of his men and did not heed Saint Maiolus’s request. Thus it happened that Saint Maiolus returned to Cluny, and the correction or expulsion of the canons was delayed for some time, and so forth.

### From chapter XXI

[Col. 0849A]

Meanwhile he carefully investigated, and by investigating sought to determine, to whom above all, according to the Rule and institution of Saint Benedict, he should entrust and commit the Church of the Holy and Undivided Trinity to be arranged and governed.

At that time William, abbot of blessed memory, was illuminating every region of the Roman Empire by the abundance of his religious life, and was instructing and kindling the lukewarm minds of many abbots by the image of his fervor. Saint Maiolus had appointed and established him as abbot and master of the Church of Dijon; he was exceedingly well educated in the liberal arts and imbued and enlightened by ecclesiastical disciplines, all spiritual offices, and nearly every virtue.

Therefore the illustrious duke Richard sent his envoys to so great and such a man. He disclosed the intention of his purpose and begged him, with prayers of great humility, to arrange and instruct the Church of Fécamp according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

William, abbot of blessed memory, is said first to have answered them:

> Dearest sons, we have heard that the Norman dukes, barbarous and savage men, overthrow rather than build holy temples, destroy and drive away rather than gather or nourish holy communities of spiritual men. Therefore return to your duke and tell him that we are wholly unprepared for this matter, since we lack horses for ourselves and the brothers who must be brought there, and lack pack animals for the expenses of the brothers who must be transported.

When the illustrious duke learned this through the report of the returning envoys, he was alarmed. He hurriedly prepared many horses and pack animals, which, when the envoys returned, he humbly sent to Abbot William of blessed memory.

### From chapter XXII

Then the blessed abbot, observing the duke’s persistence and perseverance, and weighing against that persistence and perseverance his good will and holy devotion, gathered a very large multitude of spiritual brothers, set out on the journey, and after a few days presented himself and many of the brothers to the desire of the eager duke.

The excellent duke received him with complete sincerity of heart and with the love of complete sincerity. As though he had received Christ, he dismissed the other servants and served him with his own hands. After a brief interval he led him to Fécamp, gave and handed over to him the church of the Holy Trinity, and begged that, once given and handed over, it be arranged and ordered according to the Rule and institution of Saint Benedict.

The excellent duke Richard, I say, gave and handed over the Church of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp to Abbot William of blessed memory and expelled the enormous multitude of carnal canons. He retained and restored to the church all their possessions, and, after expelling the canons who refused to convert, restored to the abbot an appropriate compensation.

### From chapter XXIII

On the night before the day on which the Church of Fécamp received the spiritual monks and expelled the carnal canons, the entire roof of the church seemed to the canons themselves to be covered with eagles. These eagles appropriately signified the procession of the entering monks, their spiritual flight, and thereafter the descent and dwelling of the protecting angels.

### From chapter XXIV

Accordingly, the blessed and glorious Abbot William began to govern and administer the Church he had received, to arrange and correct it according to the institution of Saint Benedict, and to summon faithful men from various provinces and unite and strengthen them in heavenly service.

Thus, by a sudden conversion, the Church of Fécamp burned and blazed with the zeal of heavenly men, and surpassed and eclipsed the surrounding churches in the glory of its great reputation. By its instantaneous transformation, the Church of Fécamp attained such a summit of exaltation that it surpassed all the churches of Gaul in deed and in the appearance of supreme religion, just as it surpassed them in name and in the special privilege of its designation.

The Church of Fécamp shone greatly in frugality and chastity, and in the abundance of voluntary poverty. The evident display of its virtues revealed the remaining beauty hidden in its form, and by the evidence of its manifest virtues it kindled and urged the minds of those who looked upon it to undertake and imitate the plan of its way of life.

At that time the Church of Fécamp knew nothing of individual ownership of property, but recognized only the unifying love of community. Distributing different portions according to the various needs of the needy, this love renewed and represented the primitive image of the holy apostles.

Because of the eminent perseverance in these good works, Duke Richard became wholly attached to the Church of Fécamp, and devoted himself with complete providential care to its interests. He loved the regular life and true religion of the illustrious men of the Church of Fécamp and frequently visited them with such devotion that he served the heavenly congregation with the collected wealth—or, so to speak, the richness—of his entire duchy. He himself often served the brothers who were dining, according to the custom of servants; and, after completing this service of such humility, he would sit last of all the brothers and rejoice to be refreshed by the delightful nourishment of regular meals.

### From chapter XXV

[Col. 0850D] Meanwhile the illustrious duke perceived the criticisms and slanders of certain clerics, and foresaw future adversities of a certain kind. Because of the duke’s excessive love and the great religious devotion of the holy church, the disease of envy had infected them and tormented those who were infected with the cruel anguish of inward hatred.

When the duke learned of the malevolence of these slanderers and recognized the proud presumption and presumptuous arrogance of the clerics, he hastily summoned to Fécamp all the bishops and nobles of Normandy. He rescued and freed the Church of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp from the yoke and customary claims of all the bishops, whether just or unjust.

Robert, archbishop of Rouen, enacted and desired this freedom. Because of the memory of his father and the command and wish of his present brother, he also released and freed twelve other churches from every episcopal custom and exaction. The archbishop and the other bishops strengthened the charter of the granted freedom by their signs and consent, and entrusted it for confirmation to the attestation of noblemen.

Thus the prudent duke, wishing by every means to free the holy church and by every means to confirm and preserve the freedom that had been established, summoned King Robert and many nobles of Gaul to Fécamp. By royal charter and authority, and with the consent and attestation of his peers, he rescued and freed the Church of Fécamp from the yoke and customary claims of all the bishops. He ratified and strengthened his own charter and arrangement and that of his nobles.

[Col. 0851B] Rejoicing, therefore, in the established freedom of the Church of Fécamp, and considering with lively intelligence how it might endure forever, Duke Richard compelled Abbot William of blessed memory and sent him, charged with the duty of his embassy and laden with many gifts, to the apostolic authority of the Roman See.

After completing the journey, Abbot William reached Rome. He explained to Pope Benedict of pious memory the purpose of his arrival and the will of the duke who had sent him. With a prayer of great humility, he appropriately requested confirmation of the charter and the authority of an apostolic privilege.

Pope Benedict, admiring the duke’s diligence and rejoicing with the greatest exultation at the presence of the friend he had received, confirmed the charters offered to him with the seal of his excellence and willingly delivered the privileges that had been requested. He released and rescued the Church of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp from the yoke, subjection, and customary claims of all the bishops and established and received it under the governance and protection of the Roman Church alone.

He established, I say, that the Church of Fécamp should be subject only to the Roman Church, and that, exempt, released, and wholly free from the power of all other churches, it should remain in the form of the monastery of Cluny.

Having received the carefully sought privileges of apostolic authority, Abbot William of blessed memory returned swiftly to Normandy. He explained in detail that the desire of Duke Richard had achieved its intended result and that the duty of the embassy entrusted to him had been successfully completed.

The duke, therefore, filled with inexpressible joy, gave thanks with the fervor of his whole intention to the triune and one God, who by the hidden counsel of divine providence, through the agreement of so many persons, released and freed from the yoke and authority of all men the church which his father Richard had founded and which he himself, at his father Richard’s request and command, had completed and arranged.

Thereafter he honored his most beloved abbot William with great gifts and sent him back, honored, to the Church of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp, earnestly entreating him again and again to guard the Church entrusted to him according to the religious observance of the order he had begun, and by guarding it to complete and confirm it.

The blessed abbot, receiving his holy prayers and the excessive humility of his holy prayers as divine oracles, entered Fécamp and governed the Church of Fécamp through the turning of many years, until Duke Robert’s journey to Jerusalem. By word and example he kindled and reformed those subject to him, in the image and likeness, honor and glory of almighty God, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0851]

## THE LIFE OF SAINT WILLIAM, BY GLABER RODULF

(See *Patrologia*, volume CXLII, column 697.)

[Col. 0851]

## A SECOND LIFE: EXCERPTED FROM THE CHRONICLE OF SAINT-BÉNIGNE OF DIJON

(*Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* VIII, 335.)

[Col. 0851D] **1.** In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 980, in the eighth indiction, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of King Lothair [Note: [Col. 0851D] Read “27.”], that same king gave to Bruno, a cleric of the Church of Reims and his own relative, related to him by blood [Note: [Col. 0851D] The author of this Chronicle frequently records the distinguished deeds of this Bruno. His eulogy is found in the old Martyrology of the monastery of Saint-Bénigne in volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, p. 657. He was the sister’s son of King Lothair, born namely from Aldrada, daughter of Louis I and wife of Reginald, count of Roceium.], the bishopric of the city of Langres.

This Bruno was ordained bishop by the hands of Burchard, archbishop of Lyon, in the church of Saint Stephen, at the age of twenty-four. In that same year, namely 981 from Christ’s Incarnation, he was received by the clergy of the city of Langres.

After obtaining the bishopric, he strove with every effort at his disposal to follow the example of the good shepherd. Observing that the monasteries belonging to his diocese were almost entirely ruined in their spiritual religion and in the administration of the temporal necessities, he began to seek how, by God’s disposing providence, he might restore them to their proper condition.

Therefore, removing Abbot Manasses from the authority which he had not used well, he appointed in his place a certain man named Azo from the monastery of Derventum. He was Aquitanian by birth and adorned with good morals and religious conduct.

After completing two years in office, Azo returned to his own monastery, relinquishing the governance of this place, and once again Abbot Manasses resumed his office.

**2.** When Lord Bishop Bruno saw that the condition of the place remained uncertain, he humbly approached Lord Maiolus, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and earnestly begged that with his assistance he might restore its inner religious life and its external possessions to a better condition.

Moved by his prayers, the reverend Abbot Maiolus gave him twelve monks, chosen from the entire community, instructed in the disciplines of holy religion, learned in divine and human wisdom, and distinguished by noble birth.

When they arrived, the bishop arranged matters as follows: on the day of the translation of Saint Bénigne, while the monks together with the clerics subject to them were performing the nocturnal office before the tomb of the aforementioned martyr in the crypt, these men were to begin the morning synaxis in the upper choir before the principal altar of Saint Maurice.

This was fittingly done, so that those who had come to display the light of religion might enter as daylight approached. Accordingly, while those men proceeded here and there, the ones living at the place began to shine through holy conduct; and the place, which previously appeared to everyone to be confused by wicked acts and unspeakable negligence, now seemed, through the blessed exercise of every virtue, to be flourishing.

3. But since the activity of the aforesaid Father was directed toward other places as well, and this place could not remain without an abbot, he was again moved by the prayers of Lord Bishop Bruno and appointed over the flock of this monastery a certain brother named William: a most fervent executor of his order, shining forth as a lamp of every nobility, laudably rooted and founded in true humility, the charity of fraternal love, and the excellence of the highest discretion—which is recognized as the mother of all virtues. He established him as spiritual father for the sons who asked for one.

He was originally from Italy, born of sufficiently high lineage and noble ancestry. The aforesaid Lord Maiolus, coming from Rome, found him in the monastery called Laucéio, where he had been brought up from childhood. Taking him with him at the young man’s own request, he brought him to Cluny, where he was flourishing in youthful age.

4. He was therefore ordained abbot by Lord Bruno, [Col. 0854A] the bishop, in the year 990, in the third indiction. Having assumed the office of abbot, he began to exercise himself in divine virtues. For he was chaste in body, devout in mind, gracious in speech, endowed with prudence, distinguished by temperance, firm in inward strength, steadfast in the judgment of justice, constant in patience, vigorous in endurance, gentle in humility, full of the grace of good works, and indeed overflowing with the innermost affections of charity.

He was always solicitous for the poor, loving Christ with all his heart; and although, like Martha, he was unable to serve him bodily, he refreshed him daily in the needy. He offered everyone the most generous hospitality; no one was excluded, and no one suffered rejection. He delighted in the words of the divine commandments, because through them he was instructed both to shape his own conduct and to teach and correct those entrusted to him.

He presented himself to all as an example of virtuous living. And just as he was first in rank, so he strove to be first in action, in accordance with the evangelist’s words: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). He rebuked sinners before everyone, out of the zeal of holy love, so that the others might have fear. The words he uttered in reprimand, censuring what was to be censured, seemed hard and harsh, like goads, so that they were almost feared more than blows, according to the saying: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. 12:11).

Some he addressed with flatteries, others with admonitions, others with threats; and thus, following the Apostle, he proclaimed the word and insisted “in season and out of season,” reproving, pleading, and rebuking “with all patience and [Col. 0854C] teaching” (2 Tim. 4:2). He was affected by the misfortunes of the wretched as though he himself were suffering. His mouth was so filled from the abundance of his heart that almost nothing other than the divine law resounded from it. And because Scripture says, “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17), he therefore drew away from the wickedness of the world as many people as he could by persuasion.

Just as he himself yearned with all his strength, through heavenly desire, for the kingdom above, so he wished all people to journey there with him, if that were possible. Nor was the desire conceived in him by true love frustrated in any way. For he who is charity, and who fulfills the will of those who fear him, brought the fervent longing of the man of God to fulfillment.

At his exhortations, many abandoned what they possessed, submitted themselves to the discipline of the Rule, and, following the footsteps of blessed Benedict, denying themselves, served the true King with all their strength. From different regions, an innumerable multitude therefore flocked to his monastery. Though diverse in nationality, they were united in mind, so that the saying read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the beginning of the nascent Church seemed literally fulfilled in them: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

5. As zeal for religion increased within, the provision of external resources also began to abound considerably, according to the Lord’s promise to his own in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:23). Lord Bishop Bruno, greatly gladdened in heart by their virtuous way of life, devoted every effort to supplying what was necessary for their use.

He therefore restored to Saint Benignus and his monks the church situated at Saciacum, etc. Thus, investigating everywhere, he restored what had been taken away, and willingly granted from his own rights whatever might be necessary and useful to them. While Lord Bishop Bruno and the venerable Abbot William zealously contended with one another in restoring this place, it began to grow and, as it were, to flourish anew, etc.

6. Duke Henry himself—brother of Hugh, king of the Franks—having heard of the reputation for holiness of the excellent Father William, entrusted to him the abbey of Versiacum, [Note: [Col. 0855D] Another reading has Vezeliacum. Some people wish our William also to have presided over that monastery, perhaps on the basis of this passage. It was an abbey of our order, commonly called Vézelay, now converted into a college of canons. Vergiacum continues under the title of a priory, commonly called Saint-Vivant, after Saint Viventius, who rests there, near the town of Saint-Jean-de-Latone.] which had been reduced almost to nothing, so that he might restore it to its former condition; and he did so with God’s help.

Lord Bishop Bruno, observing that Father William was so fervent in religion and monastic discipline, and that the places entrusted to him were progressing daily toward improvement, committed to his care all the monasteries in his episcopate: namely, the abbey of Bèze, [Note: [Col. 0855D] We shall discuss this monastery in detail below. It has continued until now under our congregation of Saint Maur, commonly called Bèze, as have the three following monasteries: Reomaus, [Col. 0856D] commonly Moutiers-Saint-Jean; Tornodorum; and Molundum, commonly Molôme, which was transferred into a priory of Saint Martin that obeyed only itself.] dedicated in honor of the Apostles Peter and Paul; the monastery of Saint John, called Reomaus; the church of Saint Michael the Archangel near the fortress of Tornodorum; and the abbey of Molundum, where Saint Valerius [Note: [Col. 0856D] He was an archdeacon of Langres, killed during the invasion of the Vandals.] the archdeacon and martyr rests.

He governed all of these so vigorously that after him, when they were distributed among individual abbots, none of them could equal the condition in which he had maintained them at that time.

7. In the sixth year after his ordination, Abbot William journeyed to Rome to the thresholds of the Apostles, seeking their patronage with devout prayer. From there he went to Mount Garganus, to Saint Michael. But on arriving at Beneventum, he was seized by the chains of a very serious illness.

Afflicted for a long time by the weakness of this illness, and already regarded by his own people as unlikely to recover, one night he was carried away in spirit and brought before the tribunal of the fearsome Judge. There, while he was being rebuked for certain excesses, especially for indiscriminate severity, and feared that for these faults he would be condemned to the eternal punishments of Gehenna, Saint Pope Gregory, as it seemed to him, received him into his protection, on the condition that he would thereafter live with more vigilant care and correct his former errors by works of piety and mercy [Col. 0855D].

After the vision, returning to himself, he began to recover from the illness that very day, and exchanged his former austerity for the greatest compassion. From then on, throughout his life, he honored Saint Gregory with special love.

At last many people from his native land—that is, Italy—began to gather to him: some well trained in letters, others instructed in the mastery of various crafts, and others skilled in agriculture; their art and ingenuity proved extremely beneficial to this place. The number of monks living under his direction therefore increased daily, so that in this congregation there were ordinarily seventy or eighty brothers each day, apart from those who were in other monasteries.

8. Among the many good things that Lord Bishop Bruno accomplished in this place—for it would take too long to enumerate each of his deeds—we can say this briefly: everything formerly bestowed on this place by the ancients, and afterward seized by evil men or divided up by wicked rectors, was restored by Bishop Bruno. Although those men do not lose the reward of their almsgiving, this man is nevertheless no less deserving of thanksgiving.

From the ashes of the dead, this place was raised through him to a more excellent condition than it had ever possessed before. This abbey, founded by Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres, established and enriched by King Guntramnus, restored by the emperor Charles, called the Bald, and by Lord Bishop Isaac, [Note: [Col. 0856D] Charles’s diploma concerning this matter, which Isaac obtained for the benefit of the monastery of Benignus, was published by Perard, as was another diploma of King Rodulfus, at the request of Gautzelin, bishop of Langres. In it Isaac, the restorer of the place, is called a bishop of extraordinary holiness.] was renewed by the honored Bishop Bruno and the venerable Abbot William, not only in other matters but also through the construction of a new church.

In the marvelous work of this basilica, the lord bishop supplied the expenses and brought marble and stone columns from every direction, while the reverend abbot hired the craftsmen and directed the work. By their labor they built a temple worthy of divine worship. The form and refinement of this skillfully wrought structure are not meaninglessly displayed in writing to those less learned, since many things in it appear to have been made with a mystical meaning and ought to be attributed more to divine inspiration than to the skill of any individual craftsman.

9. This temple was founded in the year 1001 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. Its length was approximately two hundred cubits, its width fifty-three; its height will appropriately be stated below.

The lower house of prayer, in which the most sacred body of Saint Benignus the martyr is venerated, having almost the same dimensions, is supported by 104 columns. Built in the form of the letter T, it extends equally in length and width in four rows of twelve columns each. It rises to a height of ten cubits and has concealed vestibules on both sides.

It contains five altars: the first consecrated in honor of Saint Benignus himself; the second in memory of Saint Nicholas and all confessors; the third in veneration of Saint Pascasia the virgin, who rests there, and of all virgins; the fourth in honor of Saint Irenaeus and all martyrs; and the fifth under the names of the holy confessors and abbots Saint John and Saint Sequanus, and Saint Eustadius the priest, who rests there.

10. In this place, then, the blessed limbs of the aforesaid witnesses of Christ surround the resting bodies of the saints; their names were recorded at the beginning of this book. [Note: [Col. 0857D] The chronographer discusses these saints at length at the beginning of his work. If you wish, consult the first volume of the *Spicilegium*, p. 353. Urbanus and Gregory were bishops of Langres and founders of this monastery, which had almost collapsed into nothingness until Isaac, Bruno’s predecessor, restored it. Argrimus was discussed in the previous *Saeculum*.]

The bodies of the holy confessors and bishops Urbanus and Gregory were originally buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist; after a long period, they were raised from there. Half of Saint Gregory’s body was deposited in the church of Saint Benignus when, out of fear of the pagans, the body of that same holy martyr was exhumed and brought to the city of Langres; at that time the other half of the aforesaid confessor’s body was retained there.

Finally, when Saint Urbanus’s body was raised and placed in a coffin, the Lord gladdened the hearts of his servants living in this place through it with many signs of miracles. When the body of the venerable Bishop Isaac was being transferred elsewhere by certain priests, because the construction of the temple required it, it was reportedly found largely intact, together with the head, still wearing clerical clothing. Likewise, the priestly garments of Lord Bishop Argrimus, together with his hood and even his inner hair shirt, were found incorrupt as testimony to his holiness.

Nearby, Saint Radegundis was also found, with a plaque of lead bearing her name at her head. Her bones were discovered wrapped in linen coated with wax and placed in a wooden chest buried in the ground.

Moreover, blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours, mentions the other saints whose bodies are known to have been buried here, describing some of their miracles [Note: [Col. 0858D] In Book 1, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 50, and in the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 42 and following]: namely, Benignus the martyr, our special patron; Tranquillus the confessor; Hilary the senator and his wife, Saint Florida, a religious woman; and Pascasia, virgin and martyr.

Pascasia, taught and baptized by Saint Benignus, was seized by the cruelty of the pagans and led to punishment after his martyrdom. When she remained steadfast in the faith of Christ, she was first afflicted by the squalor of prison and afterward, for her confession of the Godhead, condemned to death—as a certain ancient glass painting, surviving to our own times, showed in an elegant depiction.

This church, of which we are now speaking, was therefore enriched in no small degree by the venerable bodies of so many saints, apart from the relics of other saints, whom it seems superfluous to enumerate.

11. Joined to the lower crypt described above is an oratory facing the rising sun, built in a circular form and illuminated by six windows. It is thirty-seven cubits in diameter and ten cubits high. This oratory is surrounded by three circular rows of columns—forty-eight in all—arranged according to geometric proportion. Above it, the roof, raised to a lofty peak, is elegantly crossed by a three-part structure consisting of twenty-four columns and thirty-two arches, arranged in equal numbers.

This oratory is consecrated in honor of Saint John the Baptist, whose altar is illuminated by the light of three windows. From this church, thirty-seven steps on the right and left, sufficiently lit by frequent windows, lead by a spiral stairway without obstruction to the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God.

That church is supported by sixty-eight columns and has almost the same proportions and form in diameter and height as the lower church; it is illuminated by eleven glass windows. The marble altar of the perpetual Virgin is approached by four sets of three steps. Beside them are altars on either side: on the right, one in honor of John the Evangelist and his brother James, and of Saint Thomas the Apostle; on the left, one in honor of Saints Matthew, James, and Philip the Apostles.

12. From this church, thirty steps on either side, corresponding to one another and sufficiently bright, provide a continuous ascent by spiral stairways to the church of the Holy and Undivided Trinity. Built in the form of a crown and resting on thirty-six columns, it gleams with extraordinary brightness, windows everywhere and the open sky above pouring in light. It resembles the lower house in breadth but is twenty cubits high.

The altar of the Holy Trinity is placed so that it can be seen by those entering from every direction and by those standing anywhere in the church. From there, an ascent to the highest level opens by four stairways made on both sides. Two of them, arranged in the same manner, extend for fifteen steps to the oratory of Saint Michael. That oratory is thirty-three cubits long and ten cubits high, constructed on a *vili* [sic; perhaps “plain”] plan, and has seven windows. The other two stairways lead upward for fifty steps.

At the bottom of these stairways, two covered walkways have been constructed along the wall. Extending at equal intervals from the eastern side to the western, one below the temple through arched passageways and the other above the roof along a wall approximately three cubits high running around it, they protect those walking from falling.

Beginning, however, on the right or left side of the temple, they lead inward and beneath its wings by certain concealed entrances, directing the passage to the upper roof. Along the level path mentioned above, they proceed inward on every side until, reaching the lintel of the western doors, they descend by matching stairways of twenty steps into the portico of the greater church.

Built in the form of a cross, that church is 128 cubits long and, as stated above, fifty-three cubits wide. Its height is thirty-one enormous cubits in every direction, and forty cubits in the middle. It is illuminated by seventy glass windows and supported by 121 columns. Some of these stand quadrangularly beside the capitals of the strongest pillars, forty in number, and appear to be crowned together as though by a single crown, although the form of all of them is not of one size.

On both sides it has twin porticoes, crossed by double vaults, containing four altars each. On the northern side, one is in honor of the holy Apostles Peter and Andrew, and the other in honor of Saint Bartholomew and the Apostles Simon and Thaddaeus.

The altar of Saint Paul is in the upper church, before the altar of the Holy Trinity, because he was caught up to the third heaven and saw the secrets of God.

On the southern side are two altars: one in honor of the holy Apostles Matthew and Barnabas and Luke the Evangelist; the other in honor of the holy martyrs Stephen, Laurence, and Vincent.

There is another altar on the western side of the church, on the same southern side, in honor of the holy martyrs Mammeas, Desiderius, Leodegarius, Sebastian, and Gengulfus. On the opposite side are the holy martyrs Polycarp, Andochius, Thyrsus, Andeolus, Symphorianus, George, and Christopher, and the holy confessors Urbanus and Gregory, whose bodies adorn the present house.

The principal altar is consecrated in honor of Saints Maurice and Benignus, and of All the Saints. The altar to its right is in honor of Saint Raphael the Archangel and all blessed spirits; the one to the left is in honor of Saint Mark the Evangelist. In the middle of the church is the altar of the Holy Cross and of All the Saints.

Before this altar is the triple entrance to the crypt, from which one ascends by fifteen steps to the upper church.

13. The tomb of the holy and glorious martyr was constructed as follows. It is a tomb built of squared stones, eight cubits long and five cubits wide. Its stone summit is supported by four columns; in ancient times, four marble columns were placed above it.

Formerly, above the stone arches that supported it, there was a wooden apse six cubits long, three cubits wide, and seven and a half cubits high. Clad on every side in gold and silver, it displayed the history of the Lord’s nativity and passion in projecting relief work and very fine painting.

This most fitting ornament of which we are speaking was, however, dismantled by Lord Abbot William to provide relief for the poor during a famine. Together with it, a golden chest magnificently adorned with gems, three silver panels, two silver censers, crosses, and every ornament made of gold and silver were sold.

Before these events, splendid ornaments—gems, costly cloths, chests, panels, crowns, ecclesiastical vessels, and also candelabra fashioned from gold and silver—together with an image of our Lord the Savior made of gold by casting, had been carried away by the deception of thieves during the feast of the saint himself, after the guards had been killed.

These ornaments had been bestowed upon this place in ancient times by Guntramnus and the other kings, in reverence and honor of God and Saint Benignus the martyr. But after they were taken away in former times by the sacrilegious hand of the worst men, no prince afterward appeared who was able to recover so great a treasure.

These matters have been stated briefly to make known the antiquity and glory of the place at Dijon. Finally, it should be noted that the building of this temple contains 371 columns, apart from those in the towers and at the altars; 120 windows fitted or to be fitted with glass; eight towers; three doors; and twenty-four entrances.

14. Let us now turn our pen to explain the deeds of Father William that we had omitted. When he visited the palaces of emperors or kings, he did not seek what was his own in them, but what belonged to Jesus Christ. Through familiar conversation with them, he would intervene on behalf of the oppressed; or else he would win people from the secular or clerical state for God, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they might abandon their possessions and, setting aside worldly concerns, strive to serve God in tranquillity.

As we have said, many people therefore gathered to him. Though diverse in nationality, they were united in mind. The shepherd rejoiced in the growth of his flock, and rejoiced still more that all were devoted to the work undertaken.

Because he watched over the flock entrusted to him with vigilant care, he deserved through divine grace to rejoice in this life over the fruit of his labors. For he restored to its former condition, by correction, the discipline of regular life, which had almost collapsed through the negligence of earlier generations, according to the form established by blessed Benedict. Throughout various regions of the world, he also subjected to the monastic order many monasteries that had strayed from the regular path, both personally and through those whom he had appointed as abbots.

He rejoiced and gave thanks to God especially because he saw that many of those whom he had brought up under his care were suitable to govern the monastic order. We have judged it worthwhile to insert some of them into this book, so that posterity may know how vigorous the monks were who emerged from this congregation and so that their memory may endure in praise.

15. When the venerable William first assumed the office of abbot, there was among the monks living in this place a certain young man named Hunaldus. Seeing that he possessed an energetic intelligence, the aforesaid Father retained him while the others departed. He especially imbued him with every kind of learning and established him in the house of God as a chosen vessel.

The skill of this brother assisted him in everything he needed. Finally, he entrusted him with the care of this sacred enclosure. Hunaldus pursued that responsibility with such care that almost all the ornaments in this basilica were assembled through his efforts.

At last, after the death of the aforesaid Father, he obtained the abbey of Tornodorum and rested there, having spent twenty-seven years in its governance.

Another citizen of this fortress of Dijon, a man of noble birth named Rodulfus and surnamed Albus, came to conversion at the very beginning of William’s new administration. Through his money the poverty of the aforesaid Father was relieved, and through his counsel and assistance the burden of governing this place and the monastery of Bèze was lightened—for William still had only a small number of monks. This brother assisted him so greatly in external concerns that he alone seemed to provide an abundance of support. But, against William’s wishes, the shortness of his days took this consolation away from him.

Another man was also attached to the aforesaid Father, named Theoderic, a citizen of this region. After a long period of instruction, William appointed him prior of the monastery of Fécamp and finally placed him in charge as abbot of the community of Cemmeticum.

Another, a knight from the fortress called Beaune, named Ledbaldus and surnamed Sapiens because of his devotion to study, was attached to Father William. Instructed by him in spiritual learning, Ledbaldus served for a time as archimandrite at Tornodorum.

16. Stirred by the reputation for holiness of the excellent Father William, a certain cleric from Metz, born of a noble family and named Benedict, joined his discipleship. In a short time, by striving to imitate him, he attained perfection in monastic life through learning and conduct.

Through Benedict’s report, Lord Adelbero, bishop of Metz, learned of Father William’s religious way of life. He summoned William humbly and entrusted to him the abbey of Saint Arnulf, where William appointed Benedict himself as Father. Benedict devoted many years to holy works there and, at his death, was distinguished by many virtues.

So that the reverend Abbot William would not return from so great a bishop without a gift, he received from that prelate a stole woven with gold and two purple copes decorated with a golden border. The aforesaid Benedict, once ordained abbot, also offered him a chasuble suitably ornamented with gold and other vestments as a blessing. The aforesaid Father distributed these as he wished between this place and Fruttuaria, which he had recently begun.

After the death of the aforementioned abbot, William governed the aforesaid abbey of Saint Arnulf for many years.

17. A certain man also came to him from the clergy of Toul, named Arnulfus, highly educated in letters and trained in every kind of worldly wisdom. Within a short time he attained instruction in the more perfect life. Lord Father William entrusted to him the care not only of this place but also of all the places under his administration.

We shall relate later how many good things he accomplished in this place, etc.

Lord Bertoldus, bishop of the Leuci, whose city is called Toul, sought a conversation with the aforesaid Abbot William through the complaint of a cleric who had fallen away from him. Observing in William’s words an unshaken and unflattered constancy of mind, and admiring the other notable virtues shining forth in his conduct and deeds, Bertoldus urged him with persistent prayers to accept the abbey of Saint Aper and undertake to reform it according to the institution of Saint Benignus.

Granting his request, William changed that monastery into a regular condition within a few years. He found vigorous monks there, among whom he later appointed one named Widricus, after not many years, as Father of the monks in that monastery.

As the teachable disciple of an excellent master, Widricus strove to imitate him in everything so closely that Father William seemed somehow to be represented in all his words and deeds. Instructing many in holy conduct, he produced from his own congregation several Fathers of the monks of other monasteries.

18. Many priests and abbots, therefore, abandoning responsibility for the places or churches entrusted to them, flocked to the teaching of Father William.

A certain bishop of the city of Albenga, which lies near the city of Genoa on the sea in Italy, abandoned his episcopal see and submitted himself to the authority of the aforesaid Father.

Another bishop, named Barnabas and Greek by nationality, lived in this monastery under William’s direction for many years. Yet another bishop, named Benignus, came here from Rome and remained with him for several years, subject and obedient. [Note: [Col. 0861D] In the Benignian Necrology other bishops of the same place are likewise listed as monks: namely, John, archbishop of Corinth, on the Ides of December, and Pibo, bishop of Toul, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.]

Many abbots also came voluntarily from different regions and submitted themselves to him, ready to obey. Among them were Abbot John, called the Capuan; another John, abbot of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Ravenna; Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Saint Severus in the city of Classis; Anastasius; Marcus; and many other abbots, whom it would take too long to enumerate.

The number of monks who came from those regions cannot be counted. A certain Milanese archdeacon named Gotefredus also came, nobly arriving as befitted a nobleman and bringing many treasures. Among them was an onyx altar, suitably adorned with gold and silver, as well as everything belonging to a chapel, namely ecclesiastical furnishings.

He remained a monk in this monastery for many years. Later, with Abbot William’s consent, he was recalled to his homeland and appointed abbot at Milan.

19. Finally, those holy men, fathers and teachers of hermits, whose reputation for holiness was known far and wide—namely Romualdus, [Note: [Col. 0861D] Romuald, Father of the Camaldolese; William, his disciple, praised by Peter Damian in his *Life* of Romuald, no. 31; and perhaps Martinus, or Marinus, under whose direction Romuald first learned the principles of the eremitical life.] William, and Martin, whom the city of Ravenna held in great veneration, as well as the other men whom Italy contains within itself, sought the companionship of Father William, because the union of saints is pleasing and joyful and necessary to the Church, whereas the companionship of the wicked is an impediment to the good.

Those devotees of the desert, abandoning the quiet of solitude, rejoiced to associate with the coenobites under his direction. Two of their number, John and Paul, both learned in letters, were therefore attached to him; their wisdom benefited many souls unto salvation.

Both of them were exceedingly fervent in monastic religion and worthy of imitation by the others in coenobitic conduct. In the contemplative life they devoted themselves constantly to reading and prayer, and before those who saw them they were at once examples and objects of admiration.

Paul, of revered memory, rested in peace among us. [Note: Is this the Paul designated in the Necrology of Saint-Germain as “Paul, solitary of Saint Benignus,” on 6 Kalends of June? That they were recluses there is also inferred from the Benignian Necrology itself, where John is listed as a recluse on the Ides of July.] John, [Note: [Col. 0864D] We shall discuss the monastery of Fruttuaria separately below, where a charter mentions John as the first abbot of that place.] a man of God, was summoned by Lord Father William on account of his holy way of life and appointed abbot of the monastery of Fruttuaria.

Since the opportunity has presented itself, it seems appropriate to state briefly how that place was founded.

20. The aforesaid Abbot William had two brothers of the same parents: one was named Nithardus, the other Gothefredus. The first was distinguished by the honor of the countship; the other was content with the pay of military service. By frequent admonition, the aforesaid Father drew both of them away from the allurements of the world and converted them to Christ.

Coming together to this monastery at Dijon, they gave our holy protector Benignus, among other things, a certain estate belonging to their rights, called Wlpianum, as a kind of foreknowledge of things to come.

In that place Lord William founded a church in honor of Saint Benignus, so that knowledge and honor of that saint might increase in that region; so that he might build for God something received from the inheritance of his parents; and so that their offering might contribute to the gain of souls. He also intended that the fruits of the good works performed there might be for himself and for them an abolition of sins and a worthy recompense of rewards in eternal life.

For this reason that place was called Fruttuaria. Within a short time it became a noble monastery, to which both spiritual and temporal resources were brought from this place: many relics, including the bodies of saints; volumes of books; all kinds of ecclesiastical furnishings; and many monks likewise went there.

The place was also magnified in possessions and riches by resources from other places subject to his authority and by offerings brought from every direction, so that during his lifetime the congregation of that place numbered one hundred monks, apart from the dependent cell-monasteries, of which there are nearly thirty.

Having summoned the bishops of the region, King Arduino—who later rested there with his wife—and many nobles of that kingdom, he caused that place to be consecrated in honor of Holy Mary, Mother of God, Saint Benignus, and all the saints.

He also founded other monasteries in that same region. With monks assigned and abbots appointed, the monastic order still flourishes there. He established a monastery for religious women as well.

21. Having heard of the fame of the man of God, the most noble Richard, count of the Normans, sent to him, reverently asking that he come to him. At last, willingly proceeding as he had been asked, he came to him; and Richard received him honorably, as was fitting, and by many entreaties prevailed upon him to accept and adorn with a college of monks the church dedicated to the name and honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, formerly constructed in a place called Fécamp and suitably restored by Richard to a more ample condition. Granting his requests, he adorned the aforesaid place with every form of religious devotion and with all other abundance of good things, so that, above all the places of that province, it might always flourish with happy growth.

Many noble men gathered at that place, both clerics and laymen, desiring to be instructed by his teaching. Among them was Bishop Osmund, who became a monk distinguished for holy and religious living. Two clerics also, highly learned in the liberal arts, setting aside the king’s court, sought Father William with devoted minds. One of them was called Jocelin, the other Beringerius: the former afterward became abbot, while the latter ended his life in the same place.

From overseas regions as well—that is, from the land of the English—a certain nobleman, distinguished by royal descent and named Clement, left behind the pomps of the world and came to the same monastery, wishing there to serve God. But since people arriving from his homeland frequently visited him, and since he preferred to serve God in quiet rather than hear the world’s vanities continually, he sought the monastery at Dijon, where he completed the course of a praiseworthy life. Thus, in accordance with the etymology of his name, he was gentle in spirit and adorned with every virtue, especially humility, by which he declared himself so abject and worthless that, although he held the rank of priest, throughout his entire life he presumed to approach that ministry only once.

22. After William had ruled the monastery at Fécamp for almost thirty years, when he was already weighed down by both old age and illness and had chosen the place of Fruttuaria as his dwelling, desiring to rest in his native soil, Robert, prince of the kingdom, who after the death of his father and brother held primacy among the Normans, considered that the condition of the place could not otherwise remain without damage. He therefore asked, through envoys, that same Father to appoint an abbot in his place.

In response to his request, William appointed as abbot a monk whom he greatly loved, the prior of that place, named John, although he would have preferred to place him in charge elsewhere. This man, born in Ravenna in the regions of Italy, learned in letters and instructed in the medical art at the command of that Father, proved above all others an assiduous imitator of his religious way of life, his teaching, and all his virtues.

Because of his smallness of body he was called Joannelinus, a diminutive form of John; but such grace shone forth in him in humility, wisdom, discretion, and the remaining virtues that—as Saint Gregory recounts in the first book of the *Dialogues*, concerning the priest Constantius (book I, chapter 5)—it was a marvel to observers that such great gifts of God’s grace should abound in so small a body. But since he still inhabits an earthly house, it is enough to have said this much. For Scripture says: “Do not praise a man during his lifetime” (*Ecclesiasticus* 11).

23. The aforementioned Count Richard also entrusted other places to the aforesaid Abbot William: Gemmeticum, as we have already said; the monastery of Saint Audoen; and the Mount of Saint Michael the Archangel. At the latter place, after the death of the aforesaid Father, Abbot John appointed as its father a certain monk of the aforementioned Father William.

This brother was called Subpo, born in the land of the Romans and educated in all holiness by the instruction of the master just mentioned. After certain difficulties had arisen, he abandoned that place and governed the abbey of Fruttuaria for many years.

[Note: Arturus, in *Neustria pia*, records that Subpo gave several sacred vessels to the church of Saint Michael. He writes that Subpo withdrew to the same Fruttuaria in 1048 and died there in 1061.]

King Robert also entreated the aforesaid Father to accept the abbey of Saint-Germain at Paris and organize it according to regular discipline. This he did. Count Odo likewise, with equal devotion, entrusted to the same venerable Father the church of Saint Faro in the city of Meaux.

The honorable bishop of the Church of Metz, Theodoric, also commended the abbey of Gorze to him with the same zeal for God, after the abbot of that place had died. While governing the aforesaid place, he drew from the clergy of Metz a certain well-educated cleric named Sigifredus into the monastic order. After his death, Sigifredus governed the same community.

24. Lord Arnulf, the prior of this place, as we have already said, was urged by the prayers of Father William and of the aforesaid bishop to undertake the care of that place and the office of abbot. But he, a lover of humility, refused in every way, preferring to be subject rather than to preside. He asked Father William only for the care and lordship of a certain small place.

That place is situated on the boundary of the dioceses of Toul and Langres, in a place called Brittiniaca Curtis.

[Note: In the year 1005, Bishop Berthold of Toul gave this place two altars, so that it might be distinguished by William through monastic religion. Perardus possesses the charter of the donation. Bruno, later Pope Leo IX, dedicated and endowed the church of the same place.]

How, however, it was given to Saint Benignus, the patron of this place, we shall now relate.

Jacob, bishop of the city of Toul, was returning from Rome. Moved by the fame of the miracles that God’s mercy worked in this place through the merits of that saint, he came to the tomb of the martyr of Christ, desiring to obtain forgiveness of his sins from God through the intercession of this glorious martyr. While he remained for several days at his tomb, penetrating the innermost regions of heaven, he was called by the Lord to the heavenly kingdoms. Aided by the prayers of Saint Benignus, he received glory with him in heaven and, on earth, a worthy burial beside his tomb.

His sister, named Liliosa, came to the threshold of Saint Benignus and gave her aforesaid estate to Saint Benignus the martyr for the burial of her brother. At that place they built a church in honor of Saint Benignus, etc.

Accordingly, the aforementioned Lord Arnulf chose this place and diligently labored to enlarge it. Constructing there a large first basilica, together with workshops and the other dwellings useful to monks, he established a noble monastery and worked to increase it with possessions and lands.

The author adds much concerning various donations made to the monastery of Benignus at that time, which it did not seem worthwhile to reproduce here. He also lists numerous cells—or, as they are commonly called, priories—that were either newly built at the same time or assigned to the monastery of Saint Benignus.

Among these are Wulnonisvilla in the county of Troyes, and Albiniacum in the county of Perthois. Arnulf, mentioned above, adorned the church of the latter with books, providing the expenses, while Lord Girbertus did the writing. This Girbertus is said to have been among the first whom Lord Abbot William nurtured there, and he was called “the Scribe” from his office.

In the year 1005 the cell of Saint Stephen near Beaune was restored and endowed with new estates, and was entrusted to William’s care. In the year 1023 the cell of Blessed Mary at Salmacia was given to the same monastery, so that monks might be sent there, etc.

Several charters concerning these matters are preserved by Perardus. There, too, Lethaldus the knight gives, in the year 1006, the church of Saint Peter in a place called Puteoli, so that monks might be established there; and Haimo, by the counsel of Bishop Lambert, subjected the place of Saint Flavian to William in the year 1030, so that he might restore the monastic order there.

Imbertus, then archdeacon of Langres and later bishop of Paris, offered to Saint Benignus, with the gift and approval of Bishop Lambert, the abbey of Saint Amator near Langres, so that monks might be established there to serve God day and night with hymns and praises.

With the approval of the same Lambert, Count Aymo gave William an abbey consecrated in honor of the holy Mother of God, Mary, situated before his castle called Saxonis Fons, so that the monastic order formerly established there might be restored through William’s efforts.

We omit the other donations. But we must not pass over the encomium of the distinguished bishop Bruno, which the chronicler presents in these words:

25.
