Since it would be lengthy to recount all that was bestowed upon this monastery during the time of Lord Bishop Bruno, and all that was increased through him or on his account by the goods of others, let us come to the end of his life, which must always be mourned and lamented by the inhabitants of this house of God.

But first we shall briefly describe what his manner of life was. He was generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devoted in prayer, perfect in charity, lavish in kindness, ready in speech, and most holy in conduct. To the irreverent he was terrifying in appearance, fearsome in severity, worthy of respect in his bearing, and venerable in his goodness.

The gentleness of humility tempered the severity of his authority. In each person he considered not the power of the individual but the elegance of his conduct, and he honored each one more highly in proportion as he had learned to live more holily.

He was a father to clerics and monks, to holy women, widows, and orphans. He stood so evenly between rich and poor that the poor looked upon him as a father, while the rich feared him as a superior rich man.

Throughout his life he protected and defended Burgundy by his patronage—not with shield and lance but through prudent counsel, by which he had bound all the princes of the country to himself. Thus, when King Robert of the Franks repeatedly entered this land with a very large army, devastating many places with fires and plunder, he could retain nothing in it as long as Bishop Bruno lived.

And because he could not harm Bruno, he inflicted the violence of this misfortune upon Lord Abbot William, taking from him the abbey of the monastery of Saint John at Réomé, because William favored the cause of his own bishop, as was just.

Finally, at a certain time the aforementioned king came with a large army to the fortress of Dijon, devastating and ravaging the surrounding region. Fearing his anger, the aforesaid Abbot William ordered all the monks to withdraw from this place into other monasteries. He caused some, together with the books and all the ornaments of the church, to reside inside the fortress of Dijon and in the church of Saint Vincent, which the monks of this place then possessed by peaceful right.

He left only a few brothers in this place, with Lord Abbot Odilo, to guard the site and serve Saint Benignus. He had summoned Odilo for this purpose, so that, if the king should perhaps devise some evil against the place, he might be moved by Odilo’s prayers to abandon it.

When the king, who was kindly disposed by nature, learned that the monks had been dispersed because of him, he was deeply grieved. After a few days had passed, he returned to Francia without accomplishing anything.

In that same year, which was 1016 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Bishop Bruno died on the second day before the Kalends of February, after completing thirty-five years in the episcopate, etc.

26. Since we are approaching the end of the book, we shall relate the death of Father William. After laboring for forty-two years as a diligent cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard, continually cultivating, propagating, and enlarging it, when he was already greatly weighed down by old age and many illnesses and desired to be released and to be with Christ, wishing to bring his labors to a good completion, he went around all the monasteries that had been under his governance.

Beginning in Italy, he visited them and exhorted the brothers to retain in their minds what they had learned from him and to strive to fulfill it in their actions. His teaching was that, in accordance with what the Rule of Saint Benedict commands, they should always display humility to those who saw them—in speech, in every action, and in the quality of their clothing—and that, anticipating one another in honor, they should show love without pretense.

He also trained them, intent upon these and other works of virtue, in the disciplined practice of reading and chanting.

After visiting the other monasteries while teaching these things, he reached the monastery called Fécamp. There, more heavily burdened than usual by illness and sensing that the final day of his calling was approaching, he summoned the brothers, exhorted them for eight days, and commended them to God through absolution and prayer. On the eighth day, the Nativity of the Lord, having received the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, he gave his spirit back to God.

His body was embalmed with spices by the physicians who were present there and was honorably committed to burial in the same monastery, before the altar of Saint Taurinus the confessor.

After his death, Lord Halinardus undertook the care of governing souls. The aforesaid Father had chosen him as his successor with the counsel and approval of the brothers and had sent him the pastoral staff.

[Note: Halinardus, who later became archbishop of Lyon, had a Life written from this author of the Benignian Chronicle; we shall give it under the year 1052, when he departed this life.]

The aforesaid Father William died in the year 1031 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

It seemed worthwhile to add here two matters specifically concerning the monastery at Dijon. The first is a notable example of William’s charity toward the poor, which he displayed in the monastery of Saint Benignus itself, taken from the *Chronicle of Verdun* in volume I of Labbe’s Library. The second is a letter of Pope Benedict VIII to the same William concerning the monastery of Benignus, in which mention is made of Bishop Benignus, discussed above on page 340; we have it transcribed from the manuscript history of that place.

Thus Hugo relates it in the *Chronicle*, near the end of Part I, chapter 27:

27. Nor should the memorable deed of William *Supraregula* be left unmentioned. When he had returned from the monastery of Fruttuaria, which belonged by right to the church of Dijon, and had been received at Dijon as was fitting, he inquired in the chapter how the brothers were doing and whether they lacked necessities.

When he heard that everything was plentiful and that there was no place of need that could not be closed with a slight barrier, he asked about almsgiving. He learned that, although the customary alms were given, they did not assist the poor according to what they were able and possessed.

Inflamed by the zeal that consumes the flesh of the saints, he rebuked their hardness and rose swiftly from his seat in deep indignation. Having begun the antiphon prescribed for the Mandatum, “Where is charity?”, and not proceeding beyond it but constantly repeating its opening, he came to the storeroom.

Seizing whatever weapon happened to meet the hands of Phinehas, while “Where is charity?” was always in his mouth and heart, he smashed the vessels in which grain, barley, and wine were stored. Calling the poor, he filled their little vessels, continually uttering from heart and mouth: “Where is charity?”—and testifying to it through the display of his deed.

They could scarcely ever appease the indignation of his spirit sufficiently for the accumulated goods to be distributed, since “Where is charity?” was continually repeated, and the monks themselves were reproached as “fattened, made sleek, and enlarged.”

Nor did he cease until all that store had been given to the poor. Then, returning to Italy, after having awaited his departure from this world for two years, he was at last compelled to return. Passing through Dijon, he visited the places entrusted to him; afterward he went to Fécamp, where, as the year 1021 of the Lord’s Incarnation was approaching [read: 1031], in the fourteenth indiction, he died on the Kalends of January.

At his tomb a ten-year-old boy was healed of a very serious illness.

Here we may remove the scruple of the distinguished Daniel Papebrochius, who, in his notes on this passage in the *Life of Saint Richard*, Bollandists, June 14, p. 997, says that he would gladly learn in what place the Ritual books contain this antiphon.

We answer him briefly that it is still sung in monasteries on Thursday of Holy Week, at the Mandatum. By this name, both then and in William’s time, the washing of the feet is understood; it is performed on that very day not only in monasteries but also in most colleges of canons.

The same antiphon is found in the monastic Processional and in the booklets of the offices of Holy Week, which during that week are commonly used not only by clerics but also by all the faithful.

The letter of Pope Benedict should now be presented.

28. Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, venerable abbot and beloved son in Christ: eternal greeting with Apostolic blessing.

Having heard of the vigilant care with which you watch over the sons entrusted to you, we give thanks to almighty God. Finally, we have learned that for a long time you have been suffering the frequent attacks of your enemies, and that your Church has now almost been stripped bare by plunderers. We grieve with you over the misfortunes that you suffer from outside.

For the long-suffering patience that you have shown your adversaries up to now deserves our rejoicing, and your goodness deserves our praise. But let it suffice that you have shown this patience hitherto; the Church’s goods must not be reduced with impunity entirely to nothing, nor must the order of monastic religion—which is known to flourish powerfully under you—be weakened through the privation of want.

You have with you our son Benignus, bishop, who has become a monk, thanks be to God. We admonish him to conduct himself honorably and religiously, to observe his profession of obedience in conduct and action, and to remain in the vocation to which he has been called.

Moreover, we command him with full authority to pursue the enemies of the holy martyr Benignus with every zeal for justice and, by divine authority, to strike them with anathema. We also command you not to withdraw your support from him in this matter. Just as we grant him authority to strike down your invaders, so we order and command you—and by true obedience we instruct you—not to hinder or prohibit him from restraining those evildoers with the sword of the Lord’s word.

Thus our authority may be properly strengthened: those whom he binds shall be bound by Apostolic authority and ours, and those whom he absolves shall likewise be absolved by our absolution.

We also give him the power to ordain and, whenever he is lawfully requested, to ordain in the holy Church—nevertheless at your command.

---

## Two Letters of Saint William, Abbot of Saint Benignus, to Pope John XIX

*(See below under John XIX.)*

## Letter of Saint William, Abbot of Saint Benignus, to Odilo, Abbot of Cluny

Concerning the death of William, count of Burgundy; the death of Richard, count of the Normans; and matters chiefly concerning the monastery of Vézelay.

*(Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. IV, p. 333.)*

To Lord Father O., sweeter than honeycomb and honey, Brother W., with the other brothers, sends the gift of highest happiness.

Desiring with burning eagerness to know with certainty everything that concerns you, we have sent you this little letter as an account of what is happening among us.

Within, by divine grace and with your merits assisting us, we are well; outwardly, however, we are sorely wearied by certain misfortunes.

You have already heard, as we believe, that Count William has departed from human affairs and been buried at Dijon. We have received no report of the death of Count Richard and have learned nothing except what we have heard from those who speak of it.

Moreover, we inform your fatherhood that the monastery of Vézelay, after Landricus the count had shamefully expelled its monks together with their abbot, was taken over by Lord Odo without consulting the bishop of Autun.

For this reason he has been stirred to such great anger against you, us, and our place that he not only threatens to inflict upon us whatever evils he can by himself and through his men—namely, by taking away the monastery of Magerbrense and excommunicating all the altars that we possess in his episcopate—but also by stirring up against us all the bishops, clerics, and laymen whom he can, of whatever order or dignity.

He has also excommunicated the brothers of our congregation, so that no one may inhabit the aforesaid place, enter the church, or presume to celebrate any divine service in it.

They themselves, however, trusting in the Apostolic privileges by which the liberty of that place had been secured by earlier pontiffs, counted his sentence as nothing and took care to abandon none of the prohibitions. Instead, despising the letters he sent concerning this matter, they threw them onto the ground to be trampled underfoot.

Consequently, not only was he inflamed with still greater anger, but a great accusation against us also arose among all who heard of these things far and wide. Everyone who hears them—not only enemies but even those who had previously seemed friendly—supports his injustice against us and accuses us of unheard-of presumption and even of dreadful greed in the eyes of secular people.

They say that it is not lawful to remove any abbot from his own dignity for any reason without canonical examination and the judgment of the bishop to whose diocese he is known to belong.

Hearing many such things not only from our rivals but also from those who agree with us, and being unable to obtain from the bishop the lifting of the bond of anathema with which he had bound the brothers—unless they first abandoned the place and returned to you with all their possessions—we could find no sounder counsel than to send them word on your behalf that they should return to you as quickly as possible, lest someone, overtaken by sudden death, should fall under the danger of excommunication.

Whether Count Landricus will permit this, or whether they themselves will be willing to do it, remains uncertain to us.

We have therefore taken care to make all these matters known to you, desiring to learn as soon as possible, through your letter, your will and command concerning them all.

Farewell.

---

## Privilege of Saint William, Abbot of Saint Benignus, for the Monastery of Fruttuaria

*(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of Benedict*, sixth century, p. 347.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

We wish it to be known to our brothers, both present and future, and to all the sons of the holy Church, of whatever order, honor, or dignity, that the monastery newly constructed in the place formerly called Fruttuaria shall remain entirely free and completely exempt from every subjection owed to any diocese or monastery.

We wish to explain and make known the reasons for this, lest the turmoil of an evil and ill-considered opportunity steal upon anyone.

A certain brother of ours by blood, named Gottofredus, while still wearing secular dress and living freely upon his paternal inheritance, chose to abandon the world completely and follow God. Accordingly, seeking the holy monastery at Dijon, he there, by God’s will, received the monastic habit.

All the brothers of that place who were present and saw this with their own eyes know, and can know, that the same Lord Gottofredus made no lawful donation from his own patrimony, which he had left behind, because his brother Nitardus had succeeded to it by hereditary right. Not long afterward, Nitardus followed his brother into the aforesaid monastery at Dijon.

Robert, the only one of their brothers who remained a layman, together with his aforementioned brother Nitardus, among the other gifts of their possessions, handed over specifically the place called Fruttuaria, which they had given to the Lord for the construction of a monastery, in the quiet and secure condition in which they possessed it, to Gontardus, a venerable man and archdeacon of Turin, so that he might draw up a lawful testament from it, called a *Judicatus* [or *Indicatus*].

This was done on the understanding that, after the possession of the aforesaid brothers had passed into the possession of the Lord, it should in no way lose its first and ancient dignity of liberty.

Therefore, since Christ was made heir of the inheritance of our blood relatives through the hands of our aforesaid two brothers, at last, just as the undertaking began with a just intention, so it was fittingly completed with God’s help.

Meanwhile, it was confirmed and firmly established, solidly and immovably, that it should be subject to no bishopric, monastery, or secular dominion. It was strengthened by imperial, royal, and episcopal decrees and privileges.

Moreover, it was supported by an Apostolic document from the supreme pontiffs of the universal Church: first from Lord Pope John, and afterward from his successor, Lord Pope Benedict. When Benedict was seated in the Lateran basilica, surrounded on every side by a full synod, forty bishops were present, apart from abbots and the other faithful of various orders and dignities, together with the Cardinals of Saint Peter.

All of them afterward confirmed and signed the testament that Lord Pope Benedict made for that place, and together condemned it with the weapon of excommunication and malediction.

No one should stir up, as a pretext against a sanction of such great authority, any of our brothers or anyone wishing to plot against the place by unjust conspiracies, so that they may seek grounds for impugning this liberty from the fact that I was appointed abbot in the monastery where the brothers named above received the habit of holy life, and that I set my hand to the construction of the monastery at Fruttuaria.

For a just cause defends me, as has been shown above, and the place itself is protected by that restoration. It has been given to God free from the old liberty of freeborn possessions; and because the poverty of those same brothers and our kinsmen was insufficient to establish it, it was founded through the ministry of many men, especially King Ardoin and his wife Berta.

Moreover, Nitardus, having become its successor through a lawful testament, afterward gave the patrimony left by Gottofredus completely to Fruttuaria by a legitimate transfer.

But lest any just occasion should give rise to a seed of detraction through an evil reception, with the goodwill of Lord Bishop Bruno, who did not differ from our intention concerning all the matters mentioned above, and with the more distinguished ornaments obtained from both parties’ brothers and friends and sent from that monastery to Dijon in his memory and for his consolation—namely, one book-cover wonderfully adorned with gold, gems, and precious stones; one chasuble decorated with gold; two gilded stoles with their maniples; one belt; and four gilded amices—

Since the reasons for this document have been set forth, it remains for what follows to be confirmed by suitable witnesses and certain testimonies.

For this confirmation, etc., I, Brother William, called abbot, testify with truthful affection, as though speaking in his presence, that for love of God I have faithfully labored over the matters stated above. Now, confirming this testament with my own subscription, I admit all who subscribe to an equal reward for this return, according to their wishes and ability, and I earnestly ask many witnesses, present and absent, to subscribe.

Leoterius, by the mercy of God archbishop of Sens, subscribing; I asked our suffragans to subscribe.

Goslinus, archbishop of Bourges and abbot of Saint Benedict, I have confirmed.

Fulco of Amiens, I have confirmed.

Fulbertus, bishop of Chartres, I have confirmed.

Odilo [or Odo], abbot of Cluny, I have confirmed.

Everardus, abbot of Saint Martin, I have confirmed.

Gosbertus, abbot of Saint Julian at Tours, I have confirmed.

I, Brother Arnulf, prior, etc.

Theodertus [probably Theodebertus], abbot.

Osmundus, bishop; Ecmonus, etc.

I, Robert, by the grace of God king of Francia, asked that my name and that of my son, King Hugh, be written.

I, Robert the king, have confirmed with my own hand.

I, Hugh the king, have confirmed.

I, Erveus, archiclavis of Saint Martin at Tours, have confirmed.

I, Hugh, archbishop of Tours, have confirmed.

I, Robert, archbishop of Rouen, confirm with full authority.

I, Hugh, bishop of the church of Bayeux, have confirmed.

I, Hugh, bishop of Coutances, have confirmed.

I, Hugh, bishop of Évreux, have confirmed.

I, Norgaudus, bishop of Avranches, have confirmed.

I, Rotgerius, bishop of Lisieux, have confirmed.

Siefredus, bishop of Sées, has confirmed.

# Appendix to Saint William

## Annals of Saint Benignus of Dijon

Edited by G. Waitz, Ph.D.

*(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores, vol. V, p. 37.)*

The brief annals, written in one and the same hand up to the year 957 from the Cologne codex, where a continuation was afterward added by various hands, were published in *Monumenta*, Scriptores I, p. 97.

We find the same annals transcribed, but enlarged with many notes, a large part of which concerns affairs of Toul.

[Note: Years 895, 906, 921, 934, 962, 963, 994, 996, 1000.]

These notes occur in the *Annals of Saint Benignus of Dijon*. One codex of them is still preserved in the library of the University of Dijon and bears the number 269. I transcribed it in 1837.

It seems to have been written at the beginning of the twelfth century. Besides other material, it contains, on folios 44–57, a table of cycles carried down to the year 1064, continued on the final folios to the year 1215.

[Note: Compare *Archiv*, VII, p. 445.]

On its margins someone in the twelfth century added, up to the year 1000, those notes which, as I have said, partly agree with the Cologne Annals and partly explain affairs of Toul. Thus he appears to have had before his eyes in this city a copy of those annals, reproduced and enlarged.

The same hand, or one from the same period, transcribed the Lyon Annals for the year 840. Another hand followed the annals down to the year 1063, and another continued them to the year 1124.

Both these and other writers added, for the earlier years, matters concerning Langres and Dijon.

[Note: Langres: years 838, 856, 880, 922, 981, etc.]

[Note: Dijon: years 871, 912, etc.]

Others added matters concerning Verdun.

[Note: Verdun: years 564, 753 [760], 868, 882, 915, 923, 925, 939, 940, 951, 973, 1005, 1046, 1060.]

Finally, others collected various notes, drawn partly from sources unknown to us and partly from their own knowledge of events. All of them, however, seem to have been engaged in this work at the beginning of the twelfth century.

From the year 1125 onward, many successive authors appear, generally contemporary with the events they narrate and well informed about them. Yet the earlier material must often be considered no less authoritative, since most of it was copied from older codices.

To make this more readily apparent, I have arranged in italic type everything that seems to have been taken from the Toul codex. I have distinguished it so that passages closely approaching the Cologne Annals are indicated by more compact type, while the remainder is set more widely.

The other material is printed in ordinary type; but I have noted as accurately as possible which hand is responsible for each portion.

No one who sees that the notes written there by different hands have here been reproduced by a single pen will deny that the Annals of Besançon were copied from these annals.

[Note: The Annals of Saint Benignus did not derive from the Annals of Besançon. Nor was the monastery of Saint Benignus founded in 1002, but already in the sixth century.]

The writer of the Besançon annals frequently confused the years, for example, assigning events belonging to 828 to 855, and placing the events of 888 and 899, written by one hand in the Dijon codex, under the years 891 and 892.

[Note: The Besançon writer often badly confused the years; for example, he assigned to 855 events belonging to 828, and placed under 891 and 892 events of 888 and 899 that were written by one hand in the Dijon codex.]

Nor do the Besançon annals follow the traces of these beyond the year 1118.

[Note: Years 600, 652, 731, 830, 879, 883, 888, 933 [1033], 1052 [1087], 1088, 1101, 1103–1107. In 1117 they add certain matters, mostly concerning the history of the monastery. The note for 888 agrees word for word with what I published from this codex in *Archiv*, VII, p. 448; there, perhaps, 888 should be read instead of 869.]

This is approximately the period when, as I said above, the earlier Dijon writers cease. Since some of the earlier material was also omitted—for example, all the Verdun notes—I suppose that these were inserted into the Dijon codex only later.

The Besançon Annals were continued in that monastery from 1119 to 1174; the Annals of Saint Benignus of Dijon were continued in this book by various hands to the year 1214.

But there is another one.

2. Montpellier Codex no. 48, folio, formerly C. Bouhier B. 48 and once kept in the same monastery of Saint Benignus. Written in the thirteenth century, it contains on folios 11 and following chronological cycles extending from the year 1 to 1595, written in three columns; in their margin are annals which closely approach those mentioned above. Up to the twelfth century only a few entries survive, and these are partly drawn from elsewhere; from the year 1108 onward, however, more numerous entries occur, which, although not attributable to a single writer, can readily be understood to have often been taken from Codex 1 [Note: [Col. 0876D] See what I noted under the years 1110 and 1121.]. Perhaps at times the same person entered a similar note in both codices; one seems to have preferred this source, another that one. After the year 1214, however, this codex alone received what was handed down in the monastery’s memory, and it was continued with such material up to the year 1285. I transcribed all this in 1837.

Labbe published a large part of the Annals from Codex 1 (*Bibl. mss.* I, p. 293); from it, the continuators of Bouquet received fragments (XI, p. 345; XII, p. 310; XVII, p. 741). What is found in Codex 2 has, so far as I know, remained unpublished.

G. WAITZ.

# ANNALS OF SAINT BENIGNUS OF DIJON

[Col. 0875]

[Col. 0875C] (564.) During the time of this [Note: [Col. 0875] I have taken over from the preceding years this single entry, written by hand β. I have omitted the rest down to the year 752. Codex 2.] Childebert II, Saint Agericus, bishop of Verdun, was renowned for miracles; the poet Fortunatus also does not leave this unmentioned [Note: [Col. 0876D] See Bertarius, *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, chap. 6, *Mon. SS.* IV, p. 42.].

753. [Note: [Col. 0875] 752 corrected to 753; codex.] There, King Pippin was blessed by Pope Stephen at Paris, together with his sons Charles and Carloman and his daughter Gisela, amid the solemn rites of the masses, at the command of Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and blessed Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0875] First hand. This was copied in the Annals of Besançon.].

The ordination of Lord Madelucus, bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0875] By hand β.].

(760.) In the time of King Pippin, Saint Madelucus, bishop of Verdun, flourished [Note: [Col. 0875] By hand γ.] [Col. 0876C]; his body, buried in the crypt of Saint Vitonus, was found incorrupt after forty years.

768. King Pippin died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0876D] I would think that the annals for 768–772 also belong to the annals copied in the Cologne materials, although those begin only with the year 773. The sources of these annals are indicated in *Mon. SS.* I, p. 96.].

769. The beginning of the reign of King Charles.

770. (Or 771.) Carloman died on the second day before the Nones of December.

772. Adrian became pope.

776. The conversion of the Saxons.

778. Charles entered Spain.

[Col. 0877A] 779. Charles came to Saxony.

780. Saxony was captured.

781. Charles went to Rome.

786. The sign of the cross appeared on garments. Charles also proceeded to Rome, then to Saint Benedict and Capua.

788. Charles came through Alemannia to the borders of Bavaria.

790. Duke Tassilo came to Francia, and Bavaria was captured.

791. Charles advanced against the Slavs called the Wilti.

793. King Charles ravaged the kingdom of the Hungarians.

796. Pope Adrian died; Pope Leo succeeded him.

800. Lord Charles, king, was made emperor and was called Augustus by the Romans.

809. The death of Saint Liudger, bishop and confessor, Charles’s chaplain.

814. Emperor Charles died. The beginning of the reign of Louis, his son, Charles the Great.

816. Pope Leo died [Note: [Col. 0877] By a different hand.].

817. Stephen succeeded him and died that same year; Paschal succeeded him.

822. A severe famine.

823. The vision of Wetti.

824. [Note: [Col. 0877D] More correctly, 823.] Charles, son of Louis, was born at Frankfurt on the Ides of June [Note: [Col. 0877] Written in different ink and repeated in the Annals of Besançon.]. That year the emperor wintered in the new palace there; and at Rome, on Easter Day, he was crowned and proclaimed emperor by Pope Paschal [Lothair [Note: [Col. 0877] Absent from the codex and the Annals of Besançon.]]. Drogo was ordained priest at Frankfurt on the day before the Ides of June [Col. 0877C], and the bishopric of Metz was also given to him [Note: [Col. 0877] “Became” corrected to “was ordained”; codex.]. Pope Paschal died. Eugenius succeeded him.

827. Valentinus succeeded as pope, and Gregory succeeded him.

835. The twenty-second year of Louis’s reign.

838. Alberic, bishop of Langres, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0877] By hand δ; the Annals of Besançon place this under 855.].

840. Emperor Louis died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the third day before the Nones of May [Note: [Col. 0877] By another hand.].

An eclipse of the sun occurred during the Rogation days, on the third day before the Nones of May, a Wednesday, around the eighth hour of the day, and lasted nearly half an hour. It was so dark that the stars appeared with great clarity in the sky [Note: [Col. 0877D] From the Annals of Lyon I, p. 110.]. That year Agobard, bishop of Lyon, of holy memory, died on the eighth day before the Ides of June. Emperor Louis also died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, and a memorable and remarkable work called the Old Forum at Lyon collapsed on the very day autumn began; it had stood from the time of Emperor Trajan for nearly seven hundred years [Note: [Col. 0877] “Work” corrected from “of a work”; “itself” corrected from “he himself.”].

[Col. 0878A] Amolo, deacon of the aforesaid bishop, was ordained bishop at Lyon on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0877D] This belongs under the year 841; see the Annals of Lyon.]; and a tearful war took place between the sons of Emperor Louis not far from the city of Auxerre. In it, the Christian people on both sides cast one another down in mutual slaughter on the seventh day before the Kalends of July. At the beginning of that same year, during the night, a great light issued from the north and spread far and wide; by a deadly portent it seemed almost to turn night into day.

841. War between the three brothers, namely Louis, Lothair, and Charles, the sons of Emperor Louis.

843. Sergius succeeded as pope.

846. Leo succeeded as pope.

855. Benedict succeeded as pope. King Lothair, son of Louis, died on the fourth day before the Kalends of October. Thus we entered [Note: [Col. 0877] In the same hand as the preceding entries; this may belong either to this year or to 857.].

856. Bishop Teutbald died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0877] By hand δ.] [Note: [Col. 0877D] Bishop of Langres.].

[Col. 0878B] 857. Nicholas succeeded as pope.

867. Adrian succeeded as pope.

868. A severe famine. Hatto, bishop of Verdun, died [Note: [Col. 0877] By an uncertain hand, β or γ. Now scarcely legible.]; Bernard succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0877] Now scarcely legible.].

869. There was again a severe famine, together with mortality among human beings and a pestilence among animals. King Lothair died [Note: [Col. 0877] By hand ε.].

871. A violent wind. The monastery of Dijon was begun [Note: [Col. 0877] By hand ε.] [Note: [Col. 0878D] Restored; see the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, in Dachery, *Spicilegium*, second edition, II, p. 376.]. Pope John succeeded.

873. The arrival of locusts.

877. On the day before the Nones of October, Emperor Charles and Queen Hilmentrudis died. Charles again entered Italy, while Carloman entered the same land by another route. Charles, terrified, fled and died on that very journey.

878. On the fourth day before the Kalends of November, an eclipse of the sun occurred on a Wednesday around the eighth hour of the day and lasted nearly half an hour; it was so dark that the brightest stars appeared [Note: [Col. 0877] “Eclipse” corrected from “eclipse of the sun.”].

879. King Louis of the Saxons, while his brother Carloman was still alive, entered Bavaria. The death of King Louis occurred on the fourth day before the Ides of April [Note: [Col. 0877] Perhaps III; corrected from IIII in the codex.].

880. Bishop Isaac died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0877] By hand δ (?)]. [Note: [Col. 0878D] Bishop of Langres.].

881. On the third day before the Nones of August, in the fourteenth indiction, on the day of Mars [Tuesday], with the sixth concurrent, the Franks entered battle against the pagans. Louis, son of King Louis, was the first to go forth to battle, and, by God’s gift, they gained the victory; an immeasurable and very large part of the pagans fell [Note: [Col. 0877] The codex has *inierunt*; the Annals of Besançon have *incoaverunt*.].

882. Bernard, bishop of Verdun, died; Dado succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0877] In a scraped place, by hand β or γ?].

884. The seat of the Northmen was at Duisburg. King Carloman died on the Nones of December.

885. Charles was made emperor of the Franks.

887. Burgundy was ravaged by the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0877] By another hand. The Annals of Besançon place this under 891.].

[Col. 0879A] 888. Emperor Charles died. Arnulf became king.

889. Odo, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0879] By another hand, ζ.].

893. The beginning of the reign of Charles the Child. His soldier was Hagano.

(895.) The city of Toul was burned on the second day before the Nones of April [Note: [Col. 0879] Perhaps this too belongs under 893.].

895. Arnulf was made Caesar at Rome [Note: [Col. 0879C] The Annals of Cologne place this under 896.]; the misery of famine and mortality was reported, as well as that of a Christian man eating the flesh of another. The Hungarians entered Italy and did much [Note: [Col. 0879C] The Annals of Cologne place this under 899.]; and Emperor Arnulf died, while Louis was raised to the kingship.

899. Count Richard of Burgundy fought the Northmen at the estate of Argenteuil and killed them on the fifth day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0879] Same hand as under 887; the Annals of Besançon place this under 892.]. King Odo died [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand ζ.].

900. King Zundebald killed Arnulf’s son [Note: [Col. 0879] Read, from the Annals of Cologne: “Arnulf’s son was killed.”].

[Col. 0879B] 901. King Zendaebald died [Note: [Col. 0879] Added by another hand, or by the same hand at a later time.].

902. Petronilla died.

904. War between Conrad and Adalbert, the Franks, in which Conrad fell [Note: [Col. 0879] The codex has *Adalbcum*.].

905. Adalbert was beheaded.

906. Bishop Ludelmus died on the third day before the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 0879] Perhaps *Hidelmus*; codex.] [Note: [Col. 0879C] Bishop of Toul.].

909. The Hungarians ravaged Saxony and Thuringia.

911. Louis, son of Arnulf, died. Duke Burchard was killed. Conrad, son of Conrad, was raised to the kingship.

912. Comets were seen. Then Bishop Warner of Langres made a privilege concerning the church of Saint Vincent [Note: [Col. 0879] By another hand, δ?] [Note: [Col. 0879C] See the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*, cited above, p. 380.].

915. The principal church of Saint Mary of Verdun was set ablaze [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand γ.] [Col. 0879C] [Note: [Col. 0880C] See *Mon. SS.* IV, pp. 36, 40.].

916. The twenty-fourth year of Charles.

920. King Conrad died, and Henry succeeded him.

921. The ordination of Lord Gauzlin, prelate of Toul, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0880C].] Count Richard died on the second day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand δ.].

922. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, Charles fought Robert, and Robert was killed. Bishop Warner died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand δ.].

923. Dado, bishop of Verdun, died [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand γ.].

925. Bernuinus succeeded [Note: [Col. 0879] Written in ink different from the entry for 923.].

929. Pope John died; John succeeded him.

934. The conversion of the monks of Saint Aper.

935. The great King Henry died, and Otto succeeded him.

[Col. 0880A] 936. John died. Pope Leo succeeded him, and Stephen succeeded Leo; Marinus succeeded Stephen.

939. Bernuinus died [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand γ (?).] [Note: [Col. 0879] Added by another hand: “In nineteen years there are 235 lunations.”].

940. Berengarius succeeded [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand γ (?).].

946. Pope Marinus died. Agapitus succeeded him.

951. King Otto entered Italy and subjected it to himself. From the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus, the clerics were expelled by Berengarius, bishop and monk; monks were substituted for them, and Humbert, the first abbot, was placed over them [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand γ (?).].

953. The conspiracy of Liudolf and Duke Conrad against King Otto.

954. Pope Agapitus died. Octavian succeeded him.

957. Liudolf, son of King Otto, died there after subjecting Italy to himself. Crosses appeared on garments.

[Col. 0880B] 961. Otto, still a boy, was raised to the kingship in the palace at Aachen. An eclipse of the sun occurred.

962. The death of Lord Gauzlin, prelate, on the seventh day before the Ides of September.

963. The ordination of Lord Girard, pontiff, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

965. Pope Octavian left Rome. John was substituted in his place.

966. Octavian died.

972. The great Otto, emperor, died.

973. The death of Lord Humbert, abbot, on the second day before the Nones of December, the first abbot of the monastery of Saint Vitonus [Note: [Col. 0879] The remainder was added by hand γ.].

981. Bruno was ordained bishop through the hands of Burchard, archbishop of Lyon [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand δ.] [Note: [Col. 0880C] Bishop of Langres.].

[Col. 0880C] 983. The younger Otto, emperor, died.

989. In the month of August, in the evening hour, comets were seen in the west. King Robert began to reign [Note: [Col. 0879] By another hand.].

990. The death of the pious father, Lord Abbot Robert, on the Nones of August [Note: [Col. 0879] “Who this Abbot Robert was is uncertain,” Mabillon, *Annals* IV, p. 62.]. The ordination of the lord and distinguished father William, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, by the hands of the memorable Bruno, bishop of the city of Langres, to the office of abbot and priest [Note: [Col. 0879] “Of Besançon” has been erased in the codex and the Annals of Besançon. “M. M.” was written in a scraped place.].

994. The death of Lord Gerard, bishop, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

996. Bishop Bertold entered Toul on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

997. The ordination of the same man [Note: [Col. 0879] Perhaps this should be joined to the preceding entry: “On the fifth day before the Ides of October, the ordination of the same man,” although the final words appear to have been written under 997 by another hand.].

1000. The death of Bishop Stephen on the fourth day before the Ides of March.

1002. Otto III died [Note: [Col. 0879] By hand ε. Here the first hand ends.]. That year the foundations of the new monastery of Dijon were begun on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, a Tuesday [Note: [Col. 0879] By another hand.].

1003. In the month of February, comets were seen in the morning in the eastern part of the sky.

1005. Abbot Fingenius died [Note: [Col. 0881] By hand γ.] [Note: [Col. 0881C] Of Saint Vitonus of Verdun.]. Richard, most pious, succeeded him; by him the foundations of the monastery of Verdun were also begun.

1015. The death of Lord Warner, abbot [Note: [Col. 0879] By another hand.].

1016. That year Bruno, distinguished bishop of the church of Langres and protector and defender of Christ’s poor, died [lacuna].

1017. Lambert succeeded [Note: [Col. 0881] In the same hand as the entry for 1015.].

1018. That year the church of Saint Mary in the monastery of Dijon, together with the entire courtyard of that place, was dedicated by the hands of Bishop Lambert on a Tuesday of the Rogation days (May 13) [Note: [Col. 0879] By another hand.].

1024. Emperor Henry died. Because he had administered the governance of the kingdom vigorously, he acquired eternal remembrance for himself; Cono succeeded him in the kingdom.

1026. That year Otto, count of Burgundy, died.

[Col. 0882A] 1027. Arnulf, prior, died.

1030. Lambert, bishop of Langres, died; Richard succeeded him. Richard was expelled from the bishopric by Girard the archdeacon and, going to Flanders, died there; Hugh succeeded him in the episcopate.

1031. The death of the distinguished father William.

1033. That year an eclipse of the sun occurred on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul (June 29), on a Friday during the midday hours, and a bright star was seen [Note: [Col. 0881C] This is explained more fully in the Annals of Besançon.].

1046. Richard, the most pious abbot, died [Note: [Col. 0881] “Abbot” is absent from Codex 1.] [Note: [Col. 0881C] Of Verdun.]; Walerannus, brother of Hugh, bishop of Langres, succeeded him. Richard, bishop of Verdun, also died; Theoderic succeeded him. Halinard, archbishop of Lyon, was ordained abbot at a place called Erbrestino, before Henry Caesar, son of Cono [Note: [Col. 0881] By hand γ.] [Note: [Col. 0881C] See the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, in Dachery, second edition, p. 393. Perhaps Herbrechtingen in the duchy of Württemberg.].

1049. That year Saint Pope Leo came to Gaul, and at the Council of Reims Hugh, bishop of Langres, was deposed; Harduinus succeeded him.

Codex 1 [Note: [Col. 0881B] The following sections are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0881B]

1052. That year Lord Halinard, archbishop of Lyon and abbot of this church, died at Rome; John, abbot of Fécamp and a monk of this place, succeeded him in the archbishopric and abbacy; after the abbacy was resigned in its third year, we remained without an abbot for two years.

1056. Adalbero was ordained abbot of Dijon by Harduinus, bishop of Langres, on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

1057. That year the church of Saint Mary at Saxios m[... ]s [uncertain] was dedicated by the aforesaid Bishop Harduinus, and the charter of the donation made by Count Aprimo and his sons was confirmed [Note: [Col. 0881] By hand γ.] [Note: [Col. 0882C] Saxonum Fontes, in the diocese of Langres, was transferred by Armo to the church of Saint Benignus; see Bishop Lambert’s charter, *Gallia Christiana* IV, p. 142.].

1060. Abbot Walerannus died [Note: [Col. 0881] By another hand, which also wrote the entries for 1049–1057.] [Note: [Col. 0882C] Of Saint Vitonus of Verdun.]; Grimoldus succeeded him.

[Col. 0883A] 1061. King Henry died; his son Philip reigned, assisted by his brother Hugh the Great, who distinguished himself as a powerful man in the army of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0883] By hand γ?].

1063. Pope Alexander II died [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.].

1064. [Note: [Col. 0883D] More correctly, 1066.] A comet appeared; and Harold, king of the English, was killed, with William the Norman succeeding to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0883] A single hand wrote a large part of the notes from the continuation of the cycles on the final folios of the codex up to 1123.].

1065. Harduinus of Langres died; Raynardus, surnamed Hugh, succeeded him.

1074. Pope Gregory VII [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.].

1075. Robert, duke of Burgundy, died; Hugh, the son of his son Henry, succeeded him.

1077. Adalbero, abbot of Dijon, died, and that same year, at the Council of Autun, Lord Jarento, prior of La Chaise-Dieu, was ordained on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. Rainardus, bishop of Langres, died [Col. 0883B] [Note: [Col. 0883] By hand ε.]. Robert succeeded him.

1078. That year great thunder and lightning occurred in January and February, and the moon appeared black and blood-red on the third day before the Kalends of February. War took place in Saxony, in which King Rudolf was killed [Note: [Col. 0883] By a later hand.]. Wicbertus seized the apostolic see.

1085. Rudolf, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vitonus, having left it and suffered persecution on behalf of the Roman Church, came to Dijon [Note: [Col. 0883] By a later hand.].

1087. Pope Victor III [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.]. A comet appeared [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.], and William, king of England, died.

1089. Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.].

1095. The Council of Autun of thirty-six bishops, where the journey to Jerusalem was first sworn.

[Col. 0883C] 1096. A council was held at Clermont by Pope Urban. That year a tower fell and crushed four monks and four servants [Note: [Col. 0883] Not entirely clear.]; an immeasurable army went to Jerusalem, and Antioch was captured [Note: [Col. 0883] Not entirely clear.]. Pope Urban died; Paschal II succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0883] Not entirely clear.].

1098. The Cistercian order began [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.]. Jerusalem was besieged and captured by the Franks.

1100. Rudolf, abbot of Verdun. That year Jerusalem was captured.

1104. After his father Philip, King Louis was crowned [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.].

1106. A comet appeared [Note: [Col. 0883] Perhaps by another hand through 1118.]. Henry Augustus also died. Henry, his son, succeeded him.

[Col. 0883D] 1107. That year Pope Paschal came to Gaul, and the church of Saint Maurice at Dijon was dedicated by that pope on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0884D] Of Dijon.]. A council was also held by him at Troyes on the Ides of May.

[Col. 0885A] 1110. Robert, bishop of Langres, died. Joceranus succeeded him after two years.

1111. Here Pope Paschal was captured by Henry, king of the Germans [Note: [Col. 0885] “Here … pope” was written by another hand in a scraped place.].

1112. Jofredus, prior of Dijon, died.

1113. Lord Jarento, abbot, died. Ademarus succeeded him.

1116. Abbot Ademarus died. Henricus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0885] Thus in the codex.].

1117. Great earthquakes occurred in various places, and lightning killed many people.

1118. Pope Paschal died. Gelasius succeeded him.

1119. Pope Gelasius died. Calixtus succeeded him.

[Col. 0885B] 1123. A council was held at Rome by Pope Calixtus, and peace was made between Henry Augustus and Pope Calixtus. Abbot Henry left his abbacy. Hugh, a Cluniac monk, succeeded him. That same year it also seemed that the very numerous stars had fallen from heaven, and a great mortality occurred among persons of rank.

1124. Lord Pope Calixtus died; Honorius succeeded him. Five months later Emperor Henry died, and [lacuna] succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0885] Thus in the codex. With this hand ending, various entries of equal date follow one another.].

1125. That year, on the feast of Saint Mammes, Bishop Joceranus resigned the bishopric, and Guilencus succeeded him on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0885] *Mammentis* in the codex.].

1129. Hugh resigned the abbacy. Peter succeeded him. Louis had his son Philip crowned at Reims. Pope Honorius died.

[Col. 0885C] 1130. Pope Honorius died; Innocent II succeeded him.

1131. A council was held at Reims by Pope Innocent. Philip, the young king, died [Note: [Col. 0885] The entry is cut off.]; his father, the king, had his brother crowned at the same council.

1134. Henry, king of the English, died.

1136. Wilencus, bishop of Langres, died.

1136 (?). That year William of Sabran, a Cluniac monk, was ordained bishop of Langres, and sat there for two months. In the following year Gottfridus, a monk of Clairvaux, was ordained bishop of the same see.

1137 (?). That year this church was burned by fire, together with the entire castle and its churches, on a Wednesday, the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0885D] [Note: [Col. 0885D] The vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul fell on a Wednesday only in 1139.]. Many powerful men also died that year, namely Emperor Lothair and King Louis, father of the king of France. Peter Leo also died, the man who had seized the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0885] I have supplied *apostolic* from the incomplete form *postol*.].

[Col. 0887A]

1140. That year Lord Robert, son of Duke Hugh of Burgundy, was ordained bishop of Autun [Note: [Col. 0887D] Of Burgundy.], and died that same year on the fifteenth day before the Nones of August.

1142. Hugh, the peaceful duke of Burgundy, died. Here Abbot Peter resigned his abbacy [Note: [Col. 0887] The word is cut off after *uām*.].

1143. Pope Innocent died. Celestine succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0887] More has been erased.].

1145. Peter of Beaune resigned the abbacy. Philip succeeded him.

1147. That year Pope Eugenius and King Louis were both at Dijon on the Sunday in the middle of Lent, and on the following day, namely Monday, the church of Dijon was consecrated by that same pope. King Louis of the Franks [and emperor [Note: [Col. 0887] “And emperor” was added by another hand.] ], with an immeasurable army, undertook the journey to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0887B] 1151 (or 1152). That year there was a great famine. Many princes perished [Note: [Col. 0887] The words are cut off after *ipes, mes*.]. Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0887] The codex has this instead of Conradus.], Count Geoffrey of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0887] The words are cut off after *ii, ni*.] [Note: [Col. 0887D] Geoffrey.], Count Theobald of Chartres and Blois [Note: [Col. 0888D] ], and others [Note: [Col. 0887] The words are cut off after *ii, ni*.] died. That year there was also a great shortage of wine [Note: [Col. 0887] The words are cut off after *ii, ni*.].

1153. That year Pope Eugenius and Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux died.

1154. That year, eight days before Christmas, Pope Anastasius died, and Adrian succeeded him.

1155. That year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, there was a great earthquake, and on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, on a Sunday, around the third hour [Note: [Col. 0887] The reading is scarcely clear. The sixteenth day of October was a Sunday.].

1159. That year a severe winter came, with frost and snow, on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

1161. That year, on the second day before the Ides of February, after midnight, the moon was darkened and turned blood-red; it remained so until daylight.

1162. That year, in the month of September, Odo, duke of Burgundy, died, leaving a son, Hugh.

1163. That year Godefridus resigned the bishopric, and Galnerus, son of Duke Hugh, became bishop.

1167. [lacuna: a line and a half erased] The emperor also had himself crowned at Saint Peter’s in Rome with his wife [Note: [Col. 0887] The erased portion is a line and a half; the word following *cum* is cut off.].

1171. Saint Thomas was martyred.

1175. Philip resigned the abbacy on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0887] The reading is not entirely clear.]. John succeeded him.

1177. That year a severe famine prevailed [Note: [Col. 0887] The reading of *prevailed* is not entirely clear.]. [lacuna] carried the large silver panel of the high altar to the poor [lacuna].

[Col. 0887D] 1178. That year at Venice peace was restored between Lord Alexander and Emperor Frederick, and the schism was brought to an end. That same year this church ceased to lie under the interdict imposed by Lord Pope Alexander because of the claims of the house of Morey, which we had refused to relinquish to the monks of Clairvaux [Col. 0889A]. The interdict had lasted from the middle Sunday of Lent, which then fell on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, until the third Sunday after Easter of the following year, which fell on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May; then, at a general council, it was lifted by that same pope. That same year the sun was darkened on the Ides of September around the ninth hour [Note: [Col. 0889] A different hand continues Codex 1.]. That very year, on Holy Saturday, the entire population saw three doves descend from above onto the tower of the Most Blessed Mary at the hour of Compline and carry with them, as it were, burning candles.

1179. That year a general council was celebrated at Rome by Lord Pope Alexander III. That year King Philip of the Franks was crowned at Reims on the feast of All Saints. Bishop Walter of Langres died on the sixth day before the Ides of January [Col. 0889B]. Manasses succeeded him.

1181. Pope Alexander III died. Lucius III succeeded him.

1182. John resigned the abbacy on the second day before the Kalends of July. Aymo succeeded him.

1183. Hugh, duke of Burgundy, took Beatrice, daughter of the count of Albon, as his wife at Saint-Gilles.

1185. That year Hugh, duke of Burgundy, besieged Vergy and accomplished absolutely nothing there; indeed, King Philip of Gaul subjected him to his authority. Pope Lucius died. Urban III succeeded him.

[Col. 0889C] 1186. That year the same king captured and burned Châtillon. That year discord arose between the pope and the emperor, and Henry, the emperor’s son, took as his wife at Milan the aunt of William, king of Apulia, and subjected Tuscany to himself.

1188. That year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, Lord Aymo, abbot of this place, died; on the same day Lord Peter was elected, and five days afterward he was consecrated at Troyes by Lord Manasses, bishop of Langres, in the presence of another Manasses, bishop of Troyes.

[Col. 0889D] 1190. That year the lord emperor, King Philip of the Franks, and the King of England took the cross in order to depart for Jerusalem, wishing to confront Saladin, who was devastating the entire land; many other noble and powerful men also departed with them.

1192. That year a comet appeared.

[Col. 0891A] 1200. That year a council was convened at Dijon in this church by Lord Peter of Capua, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See. The archbishops of Lyon, Reims, Besançon, and Vienne were present, together with eighteen bishops and the lords abbots of Cluny, Vézelay [Note: [Col. 0891D] In the diocese of Autun.], Saint-Remi of Reims, Saint-Denis of Paris, and many others, whose number we have not specified. The council lasted from the feast of Saint Nicholas, which is in September, for seven days. A few days later, the aforesaid cardinal recalled the council as a particular council at Vienne, where he promulgated the sentence issued by Pope Innocent throughout the entire land subject to and obedient to the King of the Franks: no divine office was to be celebrated in the churches except the baptism of infants and the penitence of the dying [Col. 0891B]. The interdict among us lasted from the third day after the Purification of Blessed Mary until the vigil of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. That same year Lord Varnerius, bishop of Langres, resigned the bishopric into the hands of Lord Pope Innocent. Hilduinus, then dean of that church, succeeded him.

1204. That year, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, Constantinople was captured by the Franks. That same year Lord Peter of Grancey resigned this abbacy, and Lord Nivardus succeeded him; we received him on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

1206. That year Lord Nivardus resigned; Lord Walter of Paris succeeded him.

1207. That year Lord Walter was made abbot of Vézelay [Note: [Col. 0891] Codex 1 has an incomplete form, *...z...acensis*.], and Lord Adam became abbot of this place.

1209. That year Bishop Roderic died [Col. 0891D]. William of Joinville succeeded him.

1210. That year Bédais and Carcassonne, cities of the Albi [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0891] It seems that not “of the Albigensians” but *albit...lium* or something similar was written.], and the greater part of their land were conquered by the Franks.

[Col. 0893A] 1212. The army of the Christians went into Spain against the Saracens.

1213. That year Lord Louis was crowned at Reims by William, the archbishop, in the presence of the King of Jerusalem, on the feast of Saint Sixtus; in the following year he captured Jarochale, Thoar, Mior, and Bordaul. That same year King John of Jerusalem was received in this church on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

1214. In the year of the Lord 1214, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, on the sixteenth lunar day, the King of France and the Duke of Burgundy fought against Emperor Otto at Cambrai and defeated him [Col. 0893B]. Emperor Otto was put to flight, and the greater part of his higher barons were captured and led away in chains to Paris.

The following is written on the next page:

In the year 1243, on the last Sunday oct[...], of Saint Apollinaris, stars were seen falling from heaven [Note: [Col. 0893] *gerie*, *limo*, and certain other words in this year are not entirely legible. The bishop of Autun was Walter.].

## Codex 2

[Note: [Col. 0881]

What precedes this year agrees partly with Codex 1 (the years 404, 407, 512, 526, 575, and 1020), and is partly taken from elsewhere (the years 486, 802, 814, 910, 939, 969, and 1000). It is useful to present the following from the ninth century onward:]

802. That year Charles, son of Pippin, was made emperor of the Romans. At the request of Pope Adrian, he was summoned, besieged the Lombards at Pavia, captured King Desiderius and his wife, and granted good privileges to the lord pope.

814. That year Charles the Great, emperor, departed from this world.

910. That year William the Pious, duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne, having no heir, built the monastery of Cluny on his own estate, which is in Burgundy in the district of Mâcon; placing Berno over that place as abbot, he granted the aforesaid place great revenues from his possessions by hereditary right. That same year he began to build the monastery of Déols.

939. The first darkness occurred.

969. The second darkness occurred. [This was written by a later hand.]

1000. [Pope Sylvester died,] formerly called Gilbertus; at this time the thousandth year from the Incarnation of the Lord was completed. [This was written in the fourteenth or fifteenth century.]

1020. That year the church of Saint Mary in the monastery of Dijon was dedicated, with loving devotion, through the hands of Lambert, bishop of Langres. (See above, under 1018.)]

.

[Col. 0882B]

1052 [Note: [Col. 0881] 1050 corrected to 1052; Codex 2. *Allinardus* corrected to *Allinardus*.]. That year Lord Halinard, archbishop of Lyon and abbot of this church, died; John, abbot of Fécamp and a monk of this place, succeeded him. He later resigned the abbacy, and we remained without an abbot for three years.

1056. That year Adalbero was ordained abbot of Dijon by Harduinus, bishop of Langres, on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

[Col. 0884A] 1077. That year Adalbero died. Gerento, prior of La Chaise-Dieu, succeeded him and administered the office well there. Regnardus, bishop of Langres, died; Robert, bishop, succeeded him [Col. 0884B].

1085. That year the monks of Verdun came to our church [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand. Nearly the same words—“That year the monks … of Verdun came to this church”—had been written under 1135 and have now been erased.].

[Col. 0884C] 1096. That year Antioch was captured by the Franks [Note: [Col. 0883] By another hand.].

1098. That year the Cistercian order began. Jerusalem was besieged and captured by the Franks.

1100. That year the tower of the choir fell and crushed four monks and four servants.

[Col. 0884D] **1107.** In this year Pope Paschal came to Gaul, and this church was dedicated by the pope himself; he also held a council at Troyes on the Ides of May. This pope was captured by Henry, the Teutonic emperor. [Note: [Col. 0883] Various contemporary hands succeed one another; they nevertheless copied most of their material from manuscript 1.] [Col. 0886A] In that same year [Note: [Col. 0885] Rather, in 1110. But in manuscript 1 it is written in such a way that it could be referred to this year.] Robert, bishop of Langres, died [Note: [Col. 0885] “died” is cut away.]. Jocerannus succeeded him after two years.

**1113.** Jarento, the abbot, died; Ademarus succeeded him.

**1116.** In this year Ademarus died. Henry succeeded him.

[Col. 0886B] **1124.** In this year, through Pope Callistus, Henry resigned this abbacy; Hugo, a Cluniac monk, succeeded him.

**1121.** [Note: In manuscript 1 these words are written opposite the year 1121, but by a sign they are referred to 1125; this led the scribe of manuscript 2 into error.] In this year, on the feast of Saint Mammès, Jocerannus resigned the bishopric, and Wilencus succeeded him.

**1129.** In this year Hugo resigned this abbey; Petrus of Geneva succeeded him.

[Col. 0886C] **1136.** In this year this church was burned by fire, together with the entire castle and the churches [lacuna] [Note: From the other manuscript it is clear how the lacuna is to be supplied.] on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul.

**1137.** In this year Wilencus, bishop of Langres, died; Willelmus [lacuna] [Note: From the other manuscript it is clear how the lacuna is to be supplied.] Cluniacensis (“of Cluny”) [Note: “Thus I seem to have read it.”] [Col. 0886D] and held the see [lacuna; Note: From the other manuscript it is clear how the lacuna is to be supplied.].

[Col. 0888A] **1141.** [Note: In the manuscript the years 1180–1215 precede the years 1140–1187.] In this year Petrus of Geneva resigned this abbacy. He had administered it faithfully and in his days acquired Ulmetum. Petrus Berne succeeded him.

**1144.** In this year Petrus Berne resigned his abbacy. Philippus succeeded him.

**1146.** In this year Pope Eugenius and Louis, king of France, were together at Dijon on the Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* (“Rejoice, Jerusalem”) is sung, and the lord pope consecrated this church on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March [Note: Another hand corrected this to [lacuna] May; a more recent hand wrote April.].

[Col. 0888B] **1153.** Pope Eugenius died.

[Col. 0888C] **1163.** In this year Cottfredus resigned the bishopric; Warnerius, son of Hugh the duke, succeeded him.

**1166.** In this year Philippus, king, was born to that queen who was the daughter of Theobald, count of Champagne.

**1171.** In this year blessed Thomas, bishop of Canterbury, was martyred.

**1175.** In this year Philippus resigned this abbacy. Johannes Lumbus succeeded him.

**1177.** In this year [lacuna] for which [lacuna] that [lacuna] from the greater altar [lacuna] disbursement for the poor.

[Col. 0888D] **1178.** In this year peace between the lord Pope Alexander and the emperor Frederick was restored at Venice, and the schism was brought to an end. In this same year this church, which had been placed under interdict by the lord Pope Alexander because of the claims of the house of Morey [Note: Perhaps *Moremis* in manuscript 2? The letter *d* is cut away in manuscript 2.]—claims which we were unwilling to surrender to the monks of Clairvaux—ceased to be bound. The interdict lasted from the middle of Lent, which was then the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, until the third Sunday after Easter in the following year, which was the eleventh day before the Kalends of May; and then, at a general council, it was lifted by the same pope [Note: “a” corrected; later manuscript 2 reads “by.”]. In this same year the sun was darkened on the Ides of September, around the ninth hour. In that very year, on Holy Saturday [Note: Thus manuscript 2.], the entire populace saw three doves descend from on high upon the tower of the Most Blessed Mary at the hour of Compline, bringing with them what appeared to be burning candles.

**1179.** In this year a general council was celebrated at Rome by the lord Pope Alexander III. In the same year Philippus, king of the Franks, was crowned at Reims on the feast of All Saints. Galterus, [Col. 0890B] bishop of Langres, died on the sixth day before the Ides of January. Manasses succeeded him.

**1181.** Pope Alexander died. Pope Lucius III succeeded him.

**1182.** Johannes Lombardus of Fruttuaria resigned the abbacy on the second day before the Kalends of July. Aymo succeeded him; he was then abbot of Saint-Seine [Note: In the diocese of Langres], a monk of this church. He remained there for sixteen years and administered it well.

**1183.** In this year Hugh, duke of Burgundy, married Beatrice, daughter of the dauphin, count of Albon.

**1184.** In this year Hugh, duke of Burgundy, besieged Vergy [Note: Perhaps *Vergein*? manuscript 2], but accomplished absolutely nothing there; indeed, Philippus, king of France, brought him under his dominion [Note: Thus manuscript 2.].

**1185.** In this year Pope Lucius died. Urban III succeeded him.

**1186.** In this year the same king captured and burned Châtillon. In that same year discord arose between Pope Urban and the emperor Frederick; and Henry, the emperor’s son, took to wife at Milan the aunt of William, king of Apulia [Note: Some words have been erased in manuscript 2.] [lacuna]. In this year Jerusalem was captured by Saladin.

**1187.** In this year Louis, son of Philippus, king, was born to Queen Elisabeth, who was sister of Baldwin, count of Flanders.

**1190.** [Note: In manuscript 2 the year and the word “died” have been cut away.] The lord Aymo, abbot of this place, died; the lord Petrus was appointed in his place. In that same year the emperor went to Jerusalem [lacuna]. The king of the Franks, Philippus, and the king of England, Richard, went to Jerusalem [with them Hugh, duke of Burgundy, son of the daughter of Theobald, count of Champagne; he remained there after the king’s departure and died there, and in the following year the king of England was captured by the Teutons; Note: These words were added afterward by another hand in manuscript 2]. The queen of the Franks, Helizabez, died [Note: “Fran—” is cut off in manuscript 2].

[Col. 0892A] **1195.** Manasses, bishop of Langres, died; Warnerius, abbot of Clairvaux, succeeded him.

**1200.** In this year a council was convened in this church by Lord Peter of Capua, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. The archbishops of Lyon, Reims, Besançon, and Vienne, with their suffragans [Note: Thus manuscript 2], attended, as did nearly all the abbots of the kingdom. The council lasted from the feast of Saint Nicholas, which is in September, for seven days. In this year a monk of Cluny, the brother of the count of Auvergne, came wishing to govern this abbey over Lord Petrus, but he did not prevail.

In this year Lord Garnerius was expelled from the bishopric of Langres; Holduinus succeeded him [Note: Thus manuscript 2].

[Col. 0892B] **1203.** In this year Holdoinus, bishop of Langres, died; Grobertus succeeded him.

**1204.** In this year Constantinople was captured by the Franks. In that same year Lord Petrus of Grancey resigned this abbacy, and Nivardus succeeded him [abbot of Saint-Seine [Note: What follows was written by a later hand in an erased place. The surviving words “Lord Nivardus resigned” show that the earlier readings agreed with manuscript 1. The designation is not entirely certain], who was abbot for one year and five months; Walterius, a monk of Saint-Germain [Col. 0892C] of Paris, succeeded him. He was abbot for two years less one month; afterward he became abbot of the abbey of Vézelay [Note: Perhaps *Verlizivensis*? manuscript 2]. After him Adam succeeded, and was abbot for five years and three months; Gilebertus succeeded him [Note: “suc—” is cut off.]].

**1207.** In this year Adam became abbot, a monk of this church and prior of Saint-Apollinaris. While he was governing this abbey, the ornaments of our church were sold—namely, silk copes, pallia, golden crosses, a twelve-mark golden cup (*calips*), several silver chalices, basins [Note: The reading *ci* is not entirely certain], silver phials, and many other things—as well as many possessions. Perhaps not through his fault, but by divine vengeance, he and the others who consented were expelled from the abbey.

**1209.** In this year Grobertus, bishop of Langres, died. Willelmus of Joinville succeeded him.

**1210.** In this year Odo, duke of Burgundy and count of Nevers, and many other barons went to fight the Albigensians. They devastated Béziers and Carcassonne, and an immense slaughter of Albigensians took place. After this the count of Montfort remained there to conquer the entire land.

[Col. 0894A] **1212.** In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1212, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, a Friday, before midnight, in a leap year, Hugh, son of Odo the duke, was born to the lady of Vergy [Note: *gerie*, *limo*, and certain other words in this year are not clearly legible. The bishop of Autun was Galterius.]. He was baptized by Goslimus [Note: *gerie*, *limo*, and certain other words in this year are not clearly legible. The bishop of Autun was Galterius.], bishop of Autun, in summertime, on the day of the [lacuna] apostle [Note: It appears to read this in manuscript 2. The feast of the apostle Andrew was 30 November.], in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

**1213.** In this year Adam resigned. Gelebertus, prior of Saxifont [Note: In the diocese of Langres], succeeded him.

**1214.** In this year Philippus, king of France, went into Flanders against the excommunicated emperor Otto. The king defeated him and captured two hundred and sixty knights [Col. 0894B], except for the count of Flanders, the count of Boulogne, and several others from the Teutonic land. Of the princes named, only the duke of Burgundy, called Odo, was there. This took place on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, that is, three days after the feast of Saints James and Christopher, and it was a Sunday.

[Col. 0893] **1215.** In this year Pope Innocent III convened a general council in the Lateran church, where almost the whole body of the universal Church was present.

**1216.** In this year the lord Pope Innocent III died at Perugia on the tenth day before the Kalends of August and was buried in the church of Saint Herculanus; Pope Honorius III succeeded him. In the same year Louis, son of the king of the Franks, Philippus, entered England to conquer it with the aid and counsel of the barons of England; and in the same year the king of England, who was called John Lackland, died. In the same year the emperor of Constantinople, Henry of Flanders, died. Petrus, count of Auxerre, succeeded him. In the same year Thomas, the venerable bishop of Lismore [Note: In Ireland], while staying in the church of Saint Benignus, consecrated the altar of Saint Blaise on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October. In this year the lord Airardus of Brienne came from overseas and brought with him the daughter of Henry, count of Champagne, whom he had married. In the same year Oto, son of the lord of Saxifont, who was prior of that place and a monk of Saint Benignus, was elected abbot of Luxeuil. He remained there for five months; afterward he became a monk of Clairvaux, stayed there for four months, and then died [Note: The remainder was added by another hand.].

**1217.** In this year there was a great wind throughout the world. Mortality among human beings and failure of the crops.

**1218.** In this year Odo, duke of Burgundy, who had taken the cross and was the son of the duchess of Lorraine, died. In the same year Simon, count of Montfort, who was harassing the Albigensians, died. In this year Damietta was besieged by the Christians at the beginning of July. They remained before it for one year, four months, and five days [Note: Perhaps *eum*?], and it was captured by them, through the action of the Lord.

**1220.** In this year Willelmus, bishop of Langres, was advanced to the archbishopric of Reims; Hugo of Mont-Royal succeeded him [Note: The manuscript reads *successi*].

**1223.** In this year John, king of Jerusalem, came to Gaul and was received by Philippus, king of the Franks, and by all the princes of his kingdom with great joy and honor. Later in the same year the aforesaid glorious king of the Franks, Philippus, died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, amid the great mourning and sorrow of the entire people of his kingdom, with the aforesaid John, king of Jerusalem, present. Also in the same year Louis, son of the aforesaid Philippus, was crowned in the city of Reims by Willelmus, then archbishop of that city, in the presence of the aforesaid king, amid great joy and peace among all the people of Gaul, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

**1226.** [Note: In the manuscript this appears to have been assigned to 1227.] In this year Louis, king of the Franks, besieged Avignon with an innumerable army on Pentecost and remained there for nearly four months. There the count of Saint-Pol and many other nobles and commoners were killed; afterward the city was surrendered to him, and he overturned all the city’s walls and its entire fortification, and subjected all the other land to himself as far as Toulouse. As he was returning from the aforesaid city, he died at the city of Pancier [Note: Montpensier], and was buried in the monastery of Saint Denis after his father [Note: The passage from “and all the other land” through “after his father” is cut off in manuscript 2]. His son Louis was crowned at Reims on the vigil of [lacuna] [Note: Supply: the feast of Saint Andrew.].

**1231.** In this year Hugo, bishop of Langres, died on the Tuesday before *Laetare Jerusalem* (“Rejoice, Jerusalem”). Robert of Toreta succeeded him.

**1236.** In this year a son of Hugh, duke of Burgundy, was born.

**1239.** In this year the Tartars came out of their land and destroyed Russia, Poland, and Hungary.

**1240.** In this year the barons of France were defeated [Note: This is how I seem to have read it. The princes set out for the Holy Land and were defeated there; compare William of Nangis in Bouquet XX, p. 328]—the king of Navarre and the duke of Burgundy. The count of Bar died, as did the counts of Montfort and Nevers, and many other nobles.

**1241.** In this year the lord abbot Raymundus of that church, of blessed memory, died. He built a grange [lacuna] within this abbey, and acquired this church at our expense [lacuna] he made. The lord Stephanus [Note: Thus I have supplied it], born at Loix, succeeded him, aged twelve and a half years [as printed; the reading is anomalous]. In this year Gregory IX died. In his time there was discord between him and Frederick the emperor, which lasted for [lacuna] years [Note: The manuscript leaves a space here], and the Holy See was vacant for two months. Two legates and many prelates—archbishops, bishops, and abbots—were captured, and the archbishop of Besançon perished at sea. Celestine succeeded him and lasted for fifteen days; the see was then vacant for a year and more. Innocent IV succeeded him; he immediately left Rome and came to Lyon [Note: The manuscript reads *ludum*], where he celebrated a council in the second year of his pontificate.

**1244.** In this year the king and queen were at Dijon. In this year the Babylonians destroyed the Promised Land and the Lord’s Sepulchre as far as the cities of Tyre and Acre [Note: Or *Adcor*? Perhaps Acre].

**1249.** In this year the lord Hugo, bishop of Langres and formerly abbot of Cluny, died overseas, having taken the cross. In the following year Guido of Rochefort, a canon of the same church, succeeded him. In this year King Louis, with his wife and his two brothers Charles and Robert, went overseas to fight against the pagans. On his first arrival he captured Damietta and held it for nearly half a year, but by God’s permission a misfortune befell him. For at Eastertide, when he went out from Damietta with many thousands of foot soldiers and knights, he fought with the pagans. He was captured in that same battle, along with many barons; his brother Robert was killed. He was then ransomed, together with all those who were with him, for 100,000 gold marks, on the condition that Damietta be surrendered. Once it had been surrendered, the pagans utterly destroyed it [Note: The manuscript reads *destuxerunt*], saying that because of it they had always been harassed.

**1252.** In this year the shepherds went out with many people joining them, wishing to cross the sea. They said that the Lord, at his birth, had chosen to reveal himself through an angel to shepherds, and therefore they wished to go to the place where he had been born and overcome his enemies. But that undertaking was reduced to nothing.

**1254.** In this year the lord [Note: *Dps*; perhaps *Stps*, that is, Stephanus] of Loix, abbot of this church, a most prudent and faithful man, died—namely, at the beginning of the fast, which was then the fifth day before the Kalends of March. Fifteen days earlier, having been placed in danger of death, he had resigned the abbacy into the hands of the bishop of Langres, and had administered it well. On the day after his deposition, Lord Petrus of Fosseto was elected.

**1255.** In this year Pope Innocent IV died; Pope Alexander IV, who was bishop of Ostia, succeeded him [Note: Written twice on two lines].

**1259.** In this year there was sickness and mortality among human beings throughout the whole world, so that scarcely any household could be found in which someone healthy remained. This mortality began in Holy Week before Easter and lasted approximately one month.

**1260.** In this year, almost throughout the Christian world, laymen, together with many clerics, began to scourge themselves with whips, dressed in white garments with their shoulders uncovered.

**1261.** In this year the lord Pope Alexander IV died, namely on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

**1266.** [Note: The passage from “In this year” through “with many” was written in an erased place by a hand other than that of the remainder.] In this year the vigorous prince Charles, brother of Louis, the most glorious and Christian king of France, went honorably with his wife and children, and with many thousands of Frenchmen, to Apulia to attack Manfred the apostate. He defeated and killed him without serious loss. For the aforesaid Manfred had changed his arms in his army, and, having been killed by chance, it was unknown who had killed him. After he was killed, and his wife and sons and very many counts and barons had been captured, Charles became king of Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria.
