[Col. 0897] **1267.** [Note: The words from “In this year” through “example” were written in an erased place by the same hand that wrote the beginning of the entry for 1266.] In this year Odo, the firstborn of the duke of Burgundy, a good, prudent, and Catholic knight, died overseas. In his death he showed us all a supreme example of humility. For eight days before he died, he had himself carried to the hospital of the poor outside the walls of the city of Acre [Note: Thus manuscript 2]. There, after removing all the royal ornaments of purple and gray, he had himself placed on a poor little bed without a mattress, covered only with a certain band, and ordered his knights, under oath, that at his death no solemnity should be performed except the divine office, and that only a single candle should burn at his death and burial [Note: Perhaps “except that”?].

**1271.** In this year the tower of the choir fell and crushed no one; the other walls of the church, however, *evincl.* … *indutibus* [lacuna; these surviving readings are materially uncertain], by the will of the monks and the craftsman [lacuna].

**1285.** In this year Philippus, king of France, rose against Peter, formerly king of Aragon, condemned by the lord Pope Martin IV, with many barons of France and a strong army of warriors. In this campaign the king himself gained the outcome [Note: *itum*, *titus*; the reading is not entirely certain] with an immense multitude of his men. That apostate also ended his life in the same year by divine will. After Philippus, king of France, died, his son, named Philippus, succeeded him in the kingdom. He was very handsome in appearance and was in his twenty-second year; he was also king of Navarre and count of Champagne, and possessed many other lands [Note: Supplied from what is no longer legible]. In this same year Pope Martin IV died, and Honorius succeeded him.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1031. ROBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS.

[Col. 0897]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Magnoald Ziegelbauer, *Conspectus rei litterariae Ordinis S. Benedicti*, part I, p. 323.)

[Col. 0897A] At the time when Gerbert—formerly a monk of Aurillac, then abbot, afterward bishop of Reims, then of Ravenna, and finally pope of Rome—was directing the schools at Reims under Adalbero, archbishop, he educated Robert, the son of King Hugh, in every form of humane learning and cultivated knowledge. Concerning this royal pupil, the monk Helgaud of Fleury relates the following:

“Robert was entrusted by his father to the school at Reims and given to Lord Gerbert for instruction; Gerbert adequately trained him in the liberal disciplines.”

The same is recorded by the *Chronicle of an Unknown Author*, which begins in the year of Christ 988 and ends in 1015:

“In his place, that of Arnulf, the king of Gaul had Lord Gerbert, the philosopher-monk, consecrated. This Gerbert was the teacher of King Robert, son of that Hugh, and of Lord Leotheric, archbishop of Sens, [Col. 0897B] successor of Sevinus.”

But it is better to hear a fragment of the *History of the Franks*, from Louis the Pious down to King Robert, in which both this king’s education and Gerbert’s ecclesiastical dignities are described:

“Robert was a gentle man, and not moderately learned and religious. For he had as his teacher the wise Gerbert, who afterward, by the same king, deserved the bishopric of Reims; and from there, on account of his learning and wisdom, he was taken up by Otto of the region beyond the Rhine and obtained the episcopate of Ravenna. Behold what sort of prince he had as his pupil among the Gauls, and what honors he obtained in the Church.”

[Col. 0898A] Since this king’s virtue, no less than his distinguished learning, belongs to the glory of Benedictine discipline, we shall here bring forward something about both. To speak first of his pursuit of virtue: Robert was a most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith. When Lisojus and Stephanus, the new Manichaeans, had corrupted its integrity, he condemned them and those implicated with them in heretical depravity to the fire at Orléans. He gave outstanding examples of Christian gentleness and charity. Twelve men convicted of conspiring against his sacred person, three days before Easter, he ordered on the very day of the holy Lord’s Resurrection to be endowed with communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0898B] and refreshed at the royal feast. On the following day, after an inquiry had been held, they were condemned to death. But the most gentle king absolved them, saying:

“Those who had been fortified with heavenly food and drink ought not to be condemned.”

The most Christian Robert was nowhere without the poor. He had twelve poor household dependents who, wherever he went, preceded him riding on little asses. This was the holy king’s retinue. In the royal cities and fortresses—namely, Paris, Senlis, Orléans, Dijon, Auxerre, Avallon, Melun, and Étampes—he maintained one thousand poor people. [Col. 0899A] During Lent he arranged for bread, fish, and wine to be supplied daily to two hundred of them. On Maundy Thursday, kneeling, he distributed with his own hand bread, vegetables, fish, and money individually to three hundred. At the sixth hour he gave a more generous alms to one hundred selected poor clerics. When he had risen from the table, he laid aside his royal clothing, put on a hair shirt, and with admirable compassion and humility washed the feet of the poor. He founded a great number of sacred buildings and monasteries from their foundations; Helgaud’s *Life* should be consulted concerning them. He was constant in the praises of God.

By his wife Constance Robert had four sons—Hugh, Henry, Odo, and Robert—and also a daughter named Adelaide. Hugh, whom he had admitted to a share in the kingdom and who inspired [Col. 0899B] such great hopes for himself that he was already called “the Great,” died in 1025 and was buried at Compiègne at Saint-Corneille. When the king and queen were overcome with the deepest grief at his death, our holy William, abbot of Saint Benignus, consoled them with these words, as Rodulfus Glaber reports in his *Life*:

“You ought not to consider yourselves unfortunate because you have lost such a man; rather, very fortunate, because you deserved to have such a man. From no class of human beings do I think so very few will be saved as from that of kings.”

When they replied in astonishment, “Why do you say this, Father?” he answered:

“Have you not heard how the sacred Canon relates that scarcely three out of thirty kings have proved good? Therefore, I ask you, cease weeping for this young man as dead; instead, rejoice with him, since he has been granted rest and freed from evils.”

[Col. 0899C] King Robert’s learning and education were no less than his piety. On this subject Trithemius must be heard in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* [Note: See also his *Annals of Hirsau*, year 995]:

“Rupertus—Robert among the Germans, as among the Gauls—was a noble, strong, just, learned, and religious king of France, and rightly deserves a place among ecclesiastical writers, since he composed chants and responsories in a sweet and regular melody for the honor of the Catholic Church. He was exceedingly learned in humane letters, especially in music; and so religious that he sang the canonical hours in church with the clerics, while outside he recited them at home with his household. He was so pious and compassionate toward the poor that at times he stripped off his own garments and covered their nakedness with them. A book never left his hands, so that even when sitting on the tribunal amid the tumult of judgments and cases, he kept an open Psalter in his lap.

“Thus, after his death, he is said to have shone with miracles. His is the well-known sequence sung on the days of Pentecost concerning the Holy Spirit, *Veni, sancte Spiritus* (“Come, Holy Spirit”); the responsory concerning Saint Peter, *Cornelius centurio* (“Cornelius the centurion”); the one for the Nativity of the Lord, *Judaea et Jerusalem* (“Judaea and Jerusalem”); and that Alleluia, *Eripe me de inimicis* (“Deliver me from my enemies”), along with many others of which I am unaware.

“When the responsory *Cornelius centurio* was offered with great devotion at Rome, [Col. 0900A] while the supreme pontiff was celebrating Mass and Saint Peter was at the altar, the ministers of the altar, rushing forward, thought that the wealthy king had offered a great quantity of gold. But when they found a written and marked slip, they marveled and praised the prince’s ingenuity and devotion. Therefore, at the clerics’ request, the pope decreed, in memory of the most holy king, that this responsory should henceforth be sung in honor of Saint Peter.”

Although these words are somewhat lengthy, they are in reality brief if applied to the glory of so great a prince.

Moreover, because King Robert was excessively devoted to letters, some called him a priest of the Muses, or a *Musard*. For, says Bulaeus [Note: *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 351], this word of ours, [Col. 0900B] the Gallo-Roman *muser*, by which we mean leisure, is undoubtedly derived from the Muses. Those who devote themselves to the Muses seek leisure and retirement and do not involve themselves in affairs. Thus, implying that it is difficult to please everyone, he replies to Adalbero in a poem that if anyone embraces the Muses, he is immediately called a *Musard* by the foolish and unlearned:

> If you celebrate the Muses, they cry: “Priest Musard!”

Robert, renowned for holiness and miracles, died in the year of Christ 1031. At his funeral his subjects cried out:

“While Robert ruled and governed, we lived in safety and feared no one. To the Pious Father, Father of the senate, Father of all good things: a blessed soul and salvation, a blessed ascent to the realms above, a blessed dwelling with Christ, King of kings, forever.”

Helgaud also adorns him with this same eulogy:

[Col. 0900C] “To him the ecclesiastical order clung unceasingly, and the monastic order was always dear to him [lacuna]. When he spoke, who was not gladdened with great joy? Whoever desired peace, in his presence, did not turn away from anger? Looking upon the presence of his face, who did not forget deceit? Through his prayers, which monk did not find rest, and was not loved, cherished, and revered? By his most holy admonition, which cleric did not become a lover of chastity? His friendly words—what were they not as medicines? His looks—how did they not benefit the foolish like a rod? Looking upon his humble eyes, who did not meditate on heavenly things? What poor and hungry person left his table without being satisfied? Did widows and the poor not display the garments he had given them, after the example of the good Dorcas? [Col. 0900D] Did not the entire multitude of the wretched call him father and nourisher? After holy David, no king on earth was like him in holy virtues, humility, mercy, piety, and charity, because he always clung to the Lord and did not depart from his commandments with a perfect heart?”

Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, calls King Robert “holy Father” in Letter 87; likewise, William, duke of Aquitaine, calls him “Theosophus” in a charter for the monastery of Bourgueil.

[Col. 0901]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 329.)

[Col. 0901A] William of Malmesbury (*De regibus Anglorum*, p. 65), along with many other writers, agrees in praising King Robert’s learning highly. He made scarcely any other use of it, however, than to compose hymns, sequences, responsories, and other pieces of the same kind, in order to enrich the Offices of the Church. This is why he was given the title “Theologian,” *Theosophus*, in a charter of William V, count of Poitiers (Du Cange, *New Glossary*, vol. VI, p. 1126).

**1.** Of all the hymns composed by our pious monarch, only one is known by name: that which begins with the words *Chorus novae Hierusalem* (“Choir of the New Jerusalem”) (Clichtove, *Elucidatorium*, p. 37). It is in iambic dimeter verse, and the author exhorts the faithful [Col. 0901B] to praise the Savior for the glory of the Resurrection, by which he took his captives from hell and brought them into heaven. Guillaume Durand, book IX, chapter 21, no. 23, assigns it without hesitation to King Robert, although Josse Clichtove, who published and paraphrased it, transfers the honor to Saint Ambrose. It is claimed (Mezeray, *History of France*, vol. I, p. 382) that our prince’s devotion to the Blessed Virgin led him to compose other hymns in her honor. But none is identified specifically.

**2.** Robert also composed several sequences that were formerly sung at Mass in certain churches. One is the sequence for the Ascension of the Savior, which begins *Rex omnipotens die hodierna* (“Almighty King, on this day”) and is found in Clichtove’s collection, together with the explanation supplied by that editor (Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. V, p. 994; Alberic, *Chronicle*, part II, p. 35; Clichtove, ibid., p. 206). Another is the sequence for Pentecost, which begins with the words *Sancti Spiritus assit nobis gratia* (“May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us”). M. Baillet attributes it to Notker the Stammerer; but William of Malmesbury, Clichtove—who printed and commented on it—and various other writers regard it as a work of King Robert. Perhaps because he confused it with the other famous sequence for Pentecost, *Veni, sancte Spiritus, et emitte* (“Come, Holy Spirit, and send forth”), Durand, Trithemius (*Chronicle of Hirsau*, vol. I, p. 141), Cardinal Bona, Archon, and several other authors wished to honor this latter work by assigning it to the same prince. It is commonly believed, however, to be by Pope Innocent III.

[Col. 0901D] **3.** The responsories and antiphons with which the pious king enriched the Offices of the Church are numerous. One of the most famous is that still sung today in several churches on Christmas Eve: *Judaea et Jerusalem, nolite timere* (“Judaea and Jerusalem, do not fear”) (William of Malmesbury, ibid.; Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 117).

[Col. 0902A] There are three for the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, which Favyn included in his *History of Navarre* and Clichtove in his *Elucidatorium* (Favyn, *History of Navarre*, book III, p. 141; Clichtove, ibid., pp. 117–118). Each of these responsories consists of three hexameter verses. The first begins with the words *Solem justitiae* (“Sun of righteousness”); the second with *Stirps Jesse* (“Stock of Jesse”); and the third with *Ad nutum Domini* (“At the Lord’s command”).

Robert had a particular devotion to the Blessed Virgin, whom he customarily called the Star of his kingdom (Favyn, ibid.). He invoked her very frequently, almost always having these two verses on his lips, which are believed to be his own composition:

> Kindly mother of the Redeemer, source of the world’s salvation,  
> Shining Star of the sea, more splendid than all the stars.

[Col. 0902B] The oratory or chapel that he had dedicated in his palace at Paris under the invocation of Our Lady of the Star led one of our historians (Favyn) to believe that this prince had instituted the order of knighthood that bore the same name. Consequently, he attributes to him the form of prayer that the knights were required to recite daily. But this institution is more than three hundred years later than Robert and belongs to King John.

Another famous responsory among those composed by our religious prince is the one beginning with the words *Cornelius centurio*, for the feast of Saint Peter. It is said that Robert, while at Rome, personally presented it at the altar of the prince of the apostles, where it was highly appreciated and applauded (Trithemius, ibid.; Martène, [Col. 0902C] ibid.; Alberic, ibid.).

He composed several others in honor of the holy martyrs, one of which begins as follows: *Concede nobis, Domine, quaesumus* (“Grant us, Lord, we beseech you”) (MART., ibid., pp. 568–569; CLICH., ibid., p. 121; *Belg. Chr. mag.*, pp. 92–93). But the most famous of all is this one: *O constantia martyrum* (“O steadfastness of the martyrs”), which is still sung at Saint-Denis in France and is found in some Processionals among the Common of Martyrs, although it was composed specifically for Saint Denis and his companions. Various historians maintain that Robert began it in this way in order to put an end to the importunities of Queen Constance, who was pressing him to compose some chant in her praise.

[Col. 0902D] Robert composed one on Saint Martin: *O quam admirabilis* (“O how marvelous”). He is also credited with the responsories or antiphons *Eripe me de inimicis meis, Deus* (“Deliver me, O God, from my enemies”), *Pro fidei meritis* (“For the merits of faith”), etc.; *Cunctipotens genitor* (“Almighty Father”) (MART., *amp. Coll.*, ibid.; ALB., ibid.; *Belg. Chr.*, ibid.). To all these individual pieces, our zealous prince is said to have added several others that possessed merit, “many other beautiful [pieces]” (*alia multa pulchra*) (MALM., ibid.; MART., *Anec.*, ibid.). But [Col. 0903A] they are not made known to us in detail; and although their beauty is praised, one must nevertheless look in them less for delicacy of thought, choice, nobility, and arrangement of expression than for sentiments of piety. Perhaps the melodies to which the author, who was skilled in ecclesiastical chant, set them gave them beauties not found in the text.

M. Hubert, in his *Antiquities of the Royal Church of Saint-Aignan of Orléans*, p. 39, says that King Robert also composed a ten-line poem in honor of the relics of this saint, beginning with the words *In virtutem tumuli* (“Into the power of the tomb”).

### 4

Whatever the other productions of King Robert’s pen may have been, only two short letters have been preserved for us. One is the ninety-fifth among the letters of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and concerns that kind of rain of blood of which mention has been made more than once. Although it is expressly addressed to Gauzlin, archbishop of Bourges, it appears to have been circular. At the request of William the Great, count of Poitiers, Robert there urges the learned men of his territories to inform him whether prodigies resembling this rain had ever occurred.

The other letter of this prince, which Helgaud inserted almost in its entirety in his *Life* and which Baronius reports from Helgaud, was written to Leutheric, archbishop of Sens, in order to correct him for two errors into which he had fallen. Mézerai (ibid., p. 383) and several other writers, who take this letter as an opportunity to praise Robert’s doctrine and eloquence, assume that Leutheric held the same error concerning the Eucharist as Bérenger of Tours later did. But the issue was only the abuse that this prelate sometimes made of the Eucharist in order to test the guilty (HELG., ibid.). His other error consisted in attributing to the divine nature the sufferings [Col. 0904B] that had fallen only upon the human nature. The letter of our generous prince, which breathes a zeal entirely aflame for the purity of religion, had its effect and corrected the archbishop. It shows that the formula used in administering the Eucharist was then somewhat different from that now in use.

[Col. 0903]

## HELGAUD, OR HELGALD, MONK OF FLEURY: EPITOME OF THE LIFE OF KING ROBERT, FROM THE WRITINGS OF ANOTHER MONK

[Note: [Col. 0903C] See what the authors of *Gallia litteraria* discuss concerning this title and the testament prefixed to Leodebodus’s *Life*, [Col. 0904C] in our next volume, col. 1266 of the edition.]

(DUCHESNE, *Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 59, from the edition of Pierre Pithou, corrected on the authority of an old manuscript codex preserved in the library of the distinguished man Alexandre Petau, senator of Paris.)

## PROEM

[Col. 0903C] The man of God, the most holy Anianus, among the other possessions that he received from God in this world, had distinguished and diligent Fathers to govern his holy place of God. Among them one flourished most benignly, named Leodebodus, powerful in holiness, learning, wealth, and glory. He lived in the time of Clotaire, king of the Franks and father of the elder Dagobert, and in Clotaire’s days he was elected father of the monastery of Saint Anianus.

After Clotaire and his son Dagobert had died, the illustrious Clovis succeeded him in the kingdom, clothed in the adornment of justice and piety. The abbot mentioned above approached him and, by deed and word, obtained from him the village of Fleury to be prepared for the monks’ use, giving in exchange the small estate of Attigny, with all that adjoined it, situated on the river Aisne. Therefore, mindful of himself, he drew up a charter concerning these matters, secured it by royal authority, and had it kept in the archive of the monastery of Saint Peter, which he later built himself. In it he made the brothers of Fleury heirs of the entire royal fisc of Fleury, just as he had acquired it from the king with a devoted heart. The following letter declares what and how much he subjected to the royal authority of Jesus Christ, the lord Peter, Saint Anianus, and the Frankish king Clovis.

[Col. 0903] **THE PROEM ENDS.**

## THE TESTAMENT OF LEODEBODUS, ABBOT, BEGINS

[Col. 0903]

[Col. 0903C] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

In the second year of the reign of our lord Clovis, most glorious king, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, strength and firm power are acquired so that testimony may support both the rustic and the learned mind. And since this is so, under the protection of God’s right hand, I, Leodebodus, write these things, though an unworthy and sinful abbot.

Since divine mercy raised me to the honor of abbot of the basilica of the lord Anianus, where that lord himself rests in the body, and appointed me guardian of the same place, I deemed it fitting—and my will most fully consented in devotion—that from my own property, both in that basilica and in the basilica of the Lady Mary, which John of Fleury once built anew, where the venerable man Fulcaldus is known to preside as abbot and guardian, and also in the estate of Fleury, which I appear to have exchanged from my own possessions with the glorious and exalted lord King Clovis and his glorious wife, the Lady Queen Bathilde, where I intend to build a monastery in honor of Saint Peter, to pray for the royal welfare and for the whole [Col. 0905B] people, in which the aforementioned man of God, namely the holy bishop Anianus, lies honorably buried, and in which monks are to live according to the rule of the most holy Benedict and the lord Columbanus, I should specially bestow upon Christ the bishop a portion of my own property.

Therefore, for the lord of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Anianus and for the monks serving there, where by God’s favor they presently discharge their office, and from my right into the right of the aforesaid basilica, from this present day I transfer portions of land situated within the estate of Nogrometus, in the territory of Bourges, called Litmaro and Mariniacum, which I appear to have received from the women Aviana and Prosperiana by written charters, with houses, buildings, slaves who have not been freed by me, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, with all their rights and appurtenances, and with every kind of livestock residing there, as I have declared; likewise my portion situated within the estate of Littidum in Sologne, which I appear to have purchased from a woman named Agana for a stated price by a deed of sale, with houses, buildings, slaves, except those whom I shall set free, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, and all its appurtenances, as I have possessed it; likewise my portion at Vetula Casa, which I purchased from Abbo and his son Fraternus for a stated price by a deed of sale and which came to me through letters of donation, with manses, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, and every kind of livestock and its appurtenances, as I have possessed it; likewise my portion in the estate of Frieto in Sologne, as I have possessed it, with manses, tenant settlers, woods, meadows, fields, and pastures in their entirety, with its boundary and every kind of livestock residing there; and also the lands or meadows that I appear to have purchased from Albuna in the district of Étampes, as I have possessed them in their entirety.

In the same way I donate silver vessels, *anacleta*, weighing eight pounds and two ounces; two sandals for Mass, and cloths for the table together with capes and all the equipment, and two embroidered veils. I establish with complete devotion that all these things shall remain perpetually in the power and ownership of that monastery and of the monks serving God there. Likewise, in the district of Bourges, called Mont, which is near the village of Carbrias, I donate the portion of land that I appear to have purchased from Domolus and his wife Ingara, or from several other people, and whatever came to me there by a letter of donation or by any other contract.

Also, what I possess in Bria, which is above the river Flironte, which I appear to have purchased from several people and which is joined to that mountain, with houses, buildings, slaves who have not been freed by me, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, with all their rights and boundaries and every kind of livestock, as I have possessed it, I donate. Likewise I donate the estate of Camberon, which is near the boundary of Clariacum or the village of Ucellus, which I appear to have purchased from the heirs of Mummolus for a stated price by a deed of sale, with houses, buildings, slaves who have not been freed by me, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, every kind of livestock, and all the rights, appurtenances, and boundaries belonging to it, as I have possessed it, to Saint Peter of Fleury.

Likewise, concerning the estate of Rausedon, which is in the district of Meung and which I purchased from the heirs of Waginus for a stated price, I decree that the aforesaid portion shall belong perpetually, by right and ownership, to the basilica of the lord Peter of Fleury, so that it may possess it in its entirety with full freedom of will.

Likewise I assign perpetually for possession to the aforesaid basilica of the Lady Mary my portion situated near the village of Columnae, the fourth part of that estate of Colomnum, with manses, tenant settlers, cultivated and uncultivated fields, and every kind of livestock in its entirety, as I have possessed it.

Likewise, in Simpliciacum, which is in Sologne, the portion that I appear to have purchased from a certain man named Aregisilus and from others, for a stated price by a deed of sale, with manses, woods, meadows, fields, pastures, every kind of livestock, and its appurtenances, as I have possessed it, I grant to the basilica of the Lady Mary, and I desire with complete freedom of will that it possess it forever.

In the same way, to the aforementioned monastery, which I intend to build in honor of the lord Peter in the estate of Fleury, as has been said, where monks are to live according to the rule, I donate from the present day the fisc of Fleury, with houses, buildings, slaves, except those whom I shall not free from the yoke of servitude, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, vineyards, waters and watercourses, with its additions and appurtenances and every kind of livestock, with all its rights and boundaries, as it was possessed by the fisc at that time or came to us.

Likewise I grant Melliacum, which I appear to have purchased by a deed of sale, with houses, buildings, slaves who have not been freed by me, cultivated and uncultivated fields, and also the mill workshop that appears to be in Malva in that territory, in its entirety with its boundary and every kind of livestock, as I have possessed it.

Also, what I appear to have purchased from the heirs of Paulonus, formerly a merchant—namely, plots within the town of the city of Orléans, with the houses built upon them, with tenant settlers residing there, and vineyards belonging to the town of that city, and also the little estates called Curun, Canavarias, Simpliciacum, and Caliacum beyond the river Loire, which I appear to have purchased for a stated price at an earlier time.

Accordingly, in a court before the apostolic man, the lord Bishop Audoenus, and the illustrious man Chrannulfus, a nobleman, together with the other abbots, it was agreed that, of all these things, both lands and slaves and vineyards, one half should be retained by the portion of the basilica of the Lady Mary, while I should receive the other half in its entirety under my own right. I appear to have received that half by their judgment. I now assign it in its entirety to the aforementioned monastery of Saint Peter built at Fleury, to be possessed perpetually.

Likewise, the estate of Asinarias, which is in the valley and which came to me, as its documents declare, from the property of the illustrious man Trodoveus by letters of exchange, while, in return, I appeared to have given him that portion situated at Suncantum and Warentias, which I had formerly purchased from a woman named Machilde for a stated price by a deed of sale, in exchange for the aforesaid Trodoveus, in that same estate of Asinarias: the portion of the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter built at Fleury shall receive and possess it in its entirety, without anyone’s hindrance, with all its rights and boundaries, as I have possessed it, and every kind of livestock residing there.

The plots within the walls of Orléans which I appear to have purchased from the cleric Cronulfus for a stated price by a deed of sale, where Leobastus the tenant settler appears to reside, I decree that I give with complete freedom of will to the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter and to the monks dwelling there.

Likewise, thirty good horses, ten herds of horses with their breeding stallions, twenty herds of oxen, five cows, and ten herds of cattle.

I have thought it necessary to insert, by the force of this document, the silver that I donate to that monastery of the lord Peter and to the monks serving there: ten pounds of pure, stamped, overseas silver *bacchoaicha*, one of which has a golden cross in the middle. I also donate a dish that has, in the middle, an image of a man’s head, likewise in gold; and likewise two smaller gilded Massilian dishes, which have nielloed crosses in the middle. I wish these silver objects to remain perpetually under the right and ownership of the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter.

As for the clothing that I appear to possess in my poverty, apart from what I assigned above to the basilica of the lord Anianus, the remainder that is left over shall be received for possession by the portion of the lord Peter of Fleury.

I do not expect, nor do I believe it possible in any way, that any of my heirs or any other person will attempt to act against this present letter. But if anyone does so and attempts to violate my act, first let him incur the anger of the heavenly Trinity; and, in addition, let him restore to the basilica of the lord Anianus, to the basilica of the Lady Mary, and to the monastery of Saint Peter built at Fleury double what I have given to those basilicas, according to the degree to which the properties themselves shall have been improved, to the abbots or monks serving there; and let him be liable to the rights of the fisc for three pounds of gold and twenty pounds of silver.

To make this donation more secure, I have decided to attach it to the municipal records, and I have caused two letters of identical wording to be written concerning the property named above: one, to remain in the archive of the lord Anianus; the other, to be received and preserved for future times by the portion of the monastery of the lord Peter, so that the monks serving God there may be able to defend what I have given them by that document.

Moreover, let this donation made by me remain firm and inviolate at all times, with a stipulation included in every respect. Done publicly at Orléans.

It should also be added that which we ought to have stated above: whatever we have assigned to the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter of Fleury, which we built anew, and whatever shall hereafter be assigned to it by God-fearing men, whatever the abbot who presides there may wish to do with it for the use or advantage of that monastery, or for the profit of his soul or the necessity of the brothers, let him have free power, without detriment to or impediment of the frequently mentioned monastery.

Leodebodus, sinful abbot; a letter made by me.

Audoenus, sinful bishop: at the request of the venerable man Abbot Leodebodus, I reread and subscribed this letter.

Leodegarius, though an unworthy bishop: at the request of Abbot Leodebodus, I confirmed this letter of his devotion in the name of Christ.

Beccelenus, abbot. Ado, abbot. Salomon, abbot. Leotsindus, abbot. Burgulfus, priest. Higecius, deacon and deputy steward. Martinus, deacon. Boso, deacon. Agneramnus. Dagobertus. Mummolenus. Vapingus. Sigirigus. Framesindus. Autbertus. Salomon, or Boso. Pappolus. Sisobaldus, or Saxo. Amnegisilus, witness. Manasses. Authacarius. Nonno. Hildulfus. Grimoldus. Segonius.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 623, issued in the month of June, in the second year of the lord Clovis, king of the Franks, son of the elder Dagobert, the marvelous builder of the place of Saint Denis and his companions.

This distinguished abbot Leodebodus’s love for the place of Fleury can be recognized from certain of his acts. For in the estates of Camberon and Rosdon, which he gave to Saint Peter, he himself established and left to the brothers of Fleury the following custom: that whoever possessed the churches in whose parishes those estates lay should cause one half of the tithe of the fields and vineyards of those estates to come, in some places, to the brothers’ ownership, and in others the whole of it. This usage is still observed to the present day.

Nor should it be omitted that a further indication of how wealthy he was is that he purchased the inheritance of Thomas, a citizen of Paris, for one thousand six hundred solidi of refined gold. This is attested by the charter of the aforementioned seller, made out to the lord Leodebodus and kept in our archives, although it has been consumed by age.

Of this inheritance, situated in the territory of Orléans, one half was bestowed by him upon this sacred place, while the other half remained with the monastery of Saint Mary, which a certain John, as written above, had built from its foundations, and of which that same servant of God, Leodebodus [Col. 0910A] the abbot, was abbot, having under him Fulchaldus, a nobleman.

He also purchased from the woman Machilde the fourth part of Suncantum and the estate of Warentiarias for three hundred tested gold solidi, and Rosdon from Auderan for two hundred solidi of the same metal.

He himself continued until the eighteenth year of the aforesaid King Clovis and thereafter brought the course of his praiseworthy life to its conclusion by a holy death. From the Lord’s Incarnation, no more than 620 years are found to have passed before the construction of this sacred monastery was begun by the lord Leodebodus, with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns.

The testament of Leodebodus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anianus, which was made under Clovis, king of the Franks, son of the elder Dagobert, ends. Amen. Amen.

## THE EPITOME OF THE LIFE OF KING ROBERT THE PIOUS BEGINS

## PREFACE

[Col. 0909]

[Col. 0909B] The dignity of the heavenly empire, against which the power of the spirit of pride wished to make itself equal, chose in this world rulers powerful enough to govern the scepters of this age. And just as the holy Church, which is our mother, obtained for herself, to govern the people of God, pontiffs, abbots, and the other ministers of the sacred order, so also in this world it chose emperors, kings, and princes “for the punishment of wrongdoers” and for restraining the insolence of the wicked, so that God might be praised for ever and ever.

And since the account began with the fathers of the monastery of the lord Anianus, it is necessary and useful that one more distinguished father be taken as an example for all, so that the whole world may receive relief from him, because the mercy of Christ the Lord chose him as a good man and divine majesty “set him over his household.” [Col. 0909C] Let us say why we have brought these things forward.

Therefore, by the will of the omnipotence of almighty God and with the assistance of blessed Anianus, we commemorated the lord and venerable Leodebodus, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Anianus, through the testament by which he bestowed his own property upon Saint Peter of Orléans, the Lady Mary, and Saint Peter of Fleury. Now we have taken care to add to this writing that, as the sound of the piety and goodness of Robert, the most gentle and pious king of the Franks, son of King Hugh, went forth into all lands, he adorned, loved, and cultivated this holy place as far as he was able.

With his favor, we wish to undertake the life of this most excellent king, so that it may be imitated by present and future generations. For here those whose souls are sick will perceive the worth of works of charity, humility, and mercy, without which no one can reach the heavenly kingdoms. In these virtues he shone so brightly that, after the most holy king and prophet David, no one equaled him, especially in holy humility, which always brings its lovers close to God and joins them to God in body and spirit. [Col. 0910C]

At the beginning of this description, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, where he wishes, and how and to whom he wishes, breathes forth his innate goodness, we shall openly set forth all the appearance of his face and the beauty of his body, as we ourselves observed them.

**THE PREFACE ENDS.**

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0909]

[Col. 0909D] At the time when God looked upon the sons of men to see whether there was anyone understanding or seeking God, there was a king of the Franks named Robert, born of the noblest lineage, his father the illustrious Hugh and his mother named Adelaide, who proved worthy of the distinction of having such a son and was greatly praised for it.

His renowned ancestry, as he himself asserted in his holy and humble words, had descended from the regions of Ausonia. Adorned with honorable deeds, he grew daily in the light of his merits, he who was marked by the perfection of all knowledge.

His bodily stature was lofty; his hair was very smooth and well arranged; his eyes humble; his nose long and open; his mouth pleasant and sweet for giving the kiss of holy peace; his beard quite dignified; his shoulders extended high. The crown placed upon his head declared that he had proceeded from a royal line through ancestors and forefathers.

Seated upon a royal horse—marvelous to say—the toes of his feet almost touched the heel, and to those who saw it in this world this was a wonder. In him there was constant and frequent prayer to God; his kneelings were certainly innumerable; and, to speak in the words of Aurelius Victorinus, as an example of human conduct, he was a man advanced to the highest things through every kind of labor. When standing in the council chamber, he most willingly confessed himself to be a servant.

He was never led to vengeance by an injury received. He loved simplicity and presented himself in ordinary conversation, at table, and in his manner of walking. He devoted himself so fully to eloquence that no day passed without his reading the Psalter and beseeching God Most High with holy David. He was gentle, agreeable, civil in spirit, and gracious, more beneficent than flattering.

This king was also exceedingly learned in letters; in his most prudent heart were implanted by God the gifts of perfect knowledge. For his most pious mother sent him to the school at Reims, where he was entrusted to the lord Gerbert for instruction. Gerbert was to train him sufficiently in the liberal disciplines, so that in all things he might please almighty God [Col. 0911B] through noble virtues. And so it happened.

That Gerbert, on account of the great merit of his wisdom, with which he shone throughout the world, obtained the pontificate at Reims through a gift from King Hugh and adorned it splendidly for several years with those things that were necessary for the holy Church. After leaving it, he was made rector of Ravenna by Otto III. From there, ascending swiftly to the apostleship of the most holy apostle Peter, he performed many distinguished works of virtue, especially in holy almsgiving, which he firmly maintained while he lived faithfully.

Among other things, joyfully playing with the letter R, he wrote of himself:

> Gerbert ascends from R[heims] to R[avenna]; afterward, as pope, he flourishes at R[ome].

This plainly demonstrated that the honors of three bishoprics, which he received, governed, and held after becoming a monk under the profession of the regular life of our father Benedict, were indicated at the head by the sign of this letter R.

In learning the arts, this most humble man of God had the lord Ingo as his companion. Rewarded with the abbacy of Saint Martin of Micy, and later made illustrious to the world by the abbacy of Saint-Germain of Paris, Ingo was thereby honored as befitted so great a man. How greatly the growth of these virtues flourished in him, we have taken care to record briefly in a few words, since we aim at brevity.

At one time, when this man of mercy and piety was staying at the palace of Compiègne, he performed there, in one instance, an act that has remained evident to every age and left an example of piety and mercy for all to imitate.

As the beloved king was about to celebrate Holy Easter in that place, on the day of the Lord’s Supper, twelve leaders of an evil conspiracy swore that he would die: his life would be taken and his royal honor removed. The most merciful king ordered them to be seized and brought before him. After questioning them, he commanded that they be kept in the house of Charles the Bald, lavishly refreshed with royal food, and notably fortified on the day of the holy Resurrection by receiving the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On the following Saturday they were brought forth, judged, and condemned, with as many sentences pronounced against them as there were men. The prince of God, pious and prudent, hearing and understanding this, absolved them for the sake of the gracious Jesus, saying that those who had been fortified by heavenly food and drink ought not to be condemned. But, so that they would not do such things again against anyone, he instructed them in his holy words and thus ordered them to return unharmed to their own homes.

With respect to robberies inflicted upon him by poor clerics and laypeople—concerning things that certainly consisted of gold or silver and very costly ornaments—he was entirely compliant. When people wished to investigate them, he threatened them with his authority, swearing by the faith of the Lord that they should not lose what they had carried away.

At Étampes, Queen Constance had built a noble palace together with an oratory. Pleased with it, the king sat down to dine there with his companions and ordered the house to be filled with holy poor people. Among them, one placed himself at his feet and was satisfied by him beneath the table. Not forgetting an ornament that hung from the knees and weighed six ounces of gold, which in rustic language we call a *labellum*, he tore it away with a knife while the king was watching and immediately prepared to leave.

Once the house had been emptied of the crowd of poor people, the king ordered those who had already been satisfied with meat and drink to be driven far from him. As they were rising from the table, the queen saw that her lord had been robbed of his ornament. Disturbed, and without constancy toward the holy man of God, she uttered these words:

> “Alas, good lord! Which of God’s enemies has disfigured you with an honorable garment of gold?”

He replied:

> “No one has disfigured me; rather, the man who took it, since it was more necessary to him than to us, will, God willing, profit from it.”

When these words had been calmed, the king withdrew into the oratory, rejoicing by God’s gift over what he had lost and over his wife’s remark, while the lord William, abbot of Dijon, Count Odo, and not a few leading men of the Franks stood by.

There are still some notable acts of his piety to relate. To a certain prelate [Leutheric, archbishop of Sens] who held wrong views about the Lord and sought proof for certain matters in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, the king, lover of goodness, took strong exception and wrote to him in these words:

> “Although you bear the name of knowledge, and the light of wisdom does not shine in you, I wonder for what reason you would seek, for your most wicked commands and for the bitter hatred that you bear toward God’s servants, an examination in the body and blood of the Lord. Since what the priest who gives it says is: ‘May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation to you in soul and body,’ why do you, with rash and polluted mouth, say: ‘If you are worthy, receive it,’ when there is no one who can be considered worthy? Why do you attribute bodily sufferings to the divinity, and connect the pain of human infirmity with the divine nature? I swear by the faith of the Lord,” said the prince of God, “you will be deprived of the honor of the episcopate unless you turn back from these things, and you will be condemned with those who said to the Lord, ‘Depart from us’; nor will you share with those to whom it is said, ‘Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.’”

By these words, the prelate, poorly instructed but wisely taught by the pious and good king, came to rest, fell silent, and ceased from the perverse doctrine that was contrary to all goodness and was already growing in the world.

Placed in the bosom of Mother Church, this servant of God became the most steadfast guardian of the body and blood of the Lord and of their vessels. He ordered everything so exactly that God seemed to be received not in another’s glory, but in the proper glory of his holy majesty. [Col. 0913A]

This was his devotion; this was his strong provision: that God should be sacrificed with a pure heart and in a white garment for the offense of the whole world. While placed on earth, he rejoiced in this service as though already in heaven.

He took delight in the relics of the saints, in garments well adorned by him with gold and silver, in white vestments, priestly clothing, precious crosses, chalices fashioned from good gold, censers emitting choice incense, and silver vessels for the cleansing of the priest’s hands—he who at that hour stood pouring out prayers to God for the sins of the whole people.

And what of this? A silver wine vessel, called a *canthara*, had been stolen by one of his clerics, which made him exceedingly sad. Yet not in such a way as to trouble the cleric, who afterward became precious to him. Threatening that the theft would be investigated, the king compelled the cleric, whether willing or unwilling, as the perpetrator of the evil deed, to seek out the vessel, ransom it, and restore it to its place.

In this matter the king, the friend of God, joking with the cleric, said:

> “It is better to bring something into one’s own house than to carry it out, lest one become like Judas, who was a thief and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it” (John 12:6).

Afterward he kept this man close to his service and worthy of his good counsel. This most pious man knew, by God’s power, how to care for his own wounds and those of others, in accordance with the commands of Father Benedict: not to expose or make them public. Therefore, we pray that God, in his mercy, may erase the sins of this man on account of such an act, so that, with all the saints interceding, he may possess the joys promised to the righteous.

It is exceedingly pleasing to bring this also to the ears of the faithful, since it is altogether worthy of being recounted. The memory of this generous and most serene king, and his worthy deed, will summon us, lovers of God, when the trumpet has sounded in the hearts of the faithful and the unfaithful—not that trumpet made of bronze, but the one that proceeds from the heavenly treasury and, opening its mouth, says: “Store up almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will itself intercede for you” (Ecclesiasticus 29:15).

When we think of such a man, many things occur to us in thought, hearing, and speech—more than can be recorded because of their multitude. God alone, in his powerful wisdom and knowledge, his ingenuity and skill, knew them, and they cannot be comprehended by the capacity of wretched humanity.

And because we love the world, we delight in the works of this most excellent king, in which, as we believe, God is praised—the glorious King whose kingdom will be the perpetual inheritance of the man who was conspicuous for the integrity of mind and body. Let the whole world believe that, if the Son of God slain for sinners had willed it, the world would still be enjoying his pleasant and delightful life.

Once, as he was going to church and prostrated in prayer before God, the gentle king, humble of heart, suffered a certain indignity concerning fur ornaments hanging from his holy neck. While he poured forth prayers to God, the thief Rapaton stood nearby—not that most powerful leader of thieves who holds first place in the reading of the Book of Kings. For, taking half of the end of the king’s cloak, he received from him these most gentle commands, sweeter than all honey:

> “Go away from here, go away. Let what you have taken be enough for you, because what remains will also be necessary for someone else.”

The thief, confounded, withdrew at the command of the holy man, who, according to his custom, consented for the love of God to the needs of the endangered and utterly poor, so that he might have as intercessors before God those whom he knew already to have become citizens of God.

The royal residence called Poissy, situated above the Seine, is very suitable for the kings of the Franks. In it, we have learned from ancient men, three monasteries were built: one in honor of Saint Mary, another of Saint John, and a third of Saint Martin the Confessor. Of these, the good king took over the one dedicated to Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, and rebuilt it from the foundations. He made it sufficiently honorable in its furnishings and clergy, with gold and silver [Col. 0914B]. He never ceased praising God there. Moreover, while remaining devoted to God in prayer there, when he returned to the place where his most humble body rested, after pouring out the accustomed showers of tears in prayer, he found there his lance, well furnished with silver by his glorious wife.

Considering it, he looked outside to see whether he might find someone for whom this silver would be necessary. Finding a very poor man, he cautiously asked whether he had some kind of iron tool with which the silver could be removed. Without knowing why he was asking this, the poor man was told by the servant of God to look for one as quickly as possible. Meanwhile the king continued in prayer. The man who had been sent returned and offered a tool quite suitable for the task. The doors of the house were shut, and the king, removing the silver from the lance together with the poor man, gave it to the pauper [Col. 0914C], doing him good; with his own holy hands he put it into the man’s sack and instructed him, as was his custom, to take care on his return journey that his wife should not see him.

The poor man obeyed the king’s commands. When this had been done, the queen arrived, wondering what had happened to the lance, which had been so dismantled, although she had hoped that her lord would be greatly delighted by its splendid appearance. Thereupon the king, swearing by the faith of the Lord, jokingly declared that he knew nothing of the deed. A friendly dispute then arose between them, by which the distribution of alms had benefited—and would benefit, by God’s doing—the dead of this world and the living before God. More things concerning his very great piety must still be related.

A certain poor little cleric, departing from the kingdom of Lothair and coming to this servant of God of whom we speak [Col. 0914D], was received by him. This cleric was called Oggerius. The king welcomed him with extraordinary goodness, associated him with his college of holy clerics, and adequately supplied him with what he needed, hoping that he would remain with him for many days and years. Yet he was found to be otherwise than the king had wished to foresee. For the words spoken of him by the prophet David were deservedly spoken of this man:

“The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. He refused to understand, so as to act well. He devised iniquity upon his bed. He stood upon every evil way, but he did not hate wickedness” (Psalm 35:4–5).

For in him shone the likeness of Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, who, having the money-box, carried away what was put into it. Once, as the hour of day was growing late [Col. 0915A], after supper had been taken with his household and night had already begun to fall, while he was considering the completion of the things that had to be rendered to God, he proceeded according to custom to the house of God. Clerics carrying candles of no small weight went before him. After they had set them down, the humble king indicated that they should not approach the high places. The king stood in a corner and, with a silent heart, rendered joyful vows to his God.

While meditating in the presence of the Lord, he saw the aforementioned Oggerius approach the altar, place the candle on the ground, and conceal the candlestick in his robe. The clerics, who ought to have guarded against this theft, were thrown into confusion. They questioned the lord king about the theft, and he replied that he knew nothing about it in any way. This reached the ears of his wife, Queen Constance, concerning whose name someone once made this jest:

“Steadfast and strong—she is not the Constance who plays tricks.”

Inflamed with fury, she swore by the soul of her father William that she would inflict punishments on the guards, deprive them of their eyes, and disfigure them with other torments unless they returned what had been taken from the treasury of the holy and just man. When the king, in whom piety found its resting place, heard this, he summoned the little thief and spoke to him as follows:

“Friend Oggerius, go away from here now, lest my wife, inconstant Constance, consume you. What you have is sufficient until you enter the land of your birth. May the Lord be with you wherever you go.”

When the thief heard this, he fell at the feet of the most merciful king and rolled about, crying: “Help me, lord, help me.” The king, wishing to rescue him, said: “Go on, go on; do not remain here” [Col. 0915C], giving him also other things along with what he had carried away, so that he would not lack provisions on the road.

After several days, the same servant of God, believing that the man could by then have reached his native soil, turned to his attendants and said, most playfully and cheerfully:

“O good Theudo”—for this man was familiar to him—“why are you working so hard to look for the candlestick, when almighty God has assigned it to his little pauper? For you and yours should know that it was more necessary to him than to us, since God has granted us sinners everything that is on earth so that we may assist the poor, orphans, widows, and the whole people of God.”

His officials had built at Paris a magnificent palace at his command. Wishing to ennoble it by his presence on the holy day of Easter, he ordered the table to be prepared in royal fashion [Col. 0915D]. While he had water ready for washing his hands, a certain blind man appeared among the crowd of poor standing before him, who were his continual memorial. The man humbly offered a prayer that the king might throw water into his face. The king, taking the poor man’s request as a joke, immediately threw the water into his face when he first received it in his hands.

At once, before all the nobles who stood by, the man’s blindness disappeared with the sprinkling of the water. Everyone rejoiced in the Lord, and the man sat down to the meal among the banqueters, happier than before. The whole day, those reclining at table discussed this event, to the praise of almighty God. Their words would perhaps have been empty and idle had they not been illumined by so great a light on that day [Col. 0916A]. Nor can it rightly be considered undeserving that this palace should be honored by frequent royal assemblies, since divine power adorned it with such a miracle and consecrated it with the rejoicing of the people, when the most devout king wished to eat there on the first day.

The same most serene king, vigorous in the strength of justice, took care that his mouth should not persist in falsehood, but that he should utter truth in heart and speech, continually swearing by the faith of the Lord God. Accordingly, wishing to justify his own men from whom he received oaths, just as he justified himself, he had a wholly crystal phylactery made, adorned around its circumference with pure gold, without any relic of a saint enclosed within it. His chief men, unaware of this pious deception, swore upon it. He also ordered another to be prepared in silver, in which he placed the egg of a bird called a *grippis*; upon this he required lesser officials and peasants to swear [Col. 0916B].

How well and fittingly the words of that holy prophet agree with this holy man:

“He shall dwell in the tent of the Most High who speaks truth in his heart, who has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbor, nor accepted reproach against his neighbor” (Psalm 14:3).

It is entirely certain that he clung to this good with the whole intention of his heart, so that he might deserve to be a co-heir in the heavenly inheritance of the blessed.

How great the virtue of humility was in him must be stated in a few words. The humble king was conversing with the bishops of his kingdom. During the conversation, as he looked at each one, he saw that one of them was weighed down by the mass of his body [Col. 0916C], with his feet dangling above the ground. Moved by compassion, he searched from a distance and found a footstool. Taking it up with hands dear to God and to men, he did not refuse to offer it to so great a bishop, nor did he disdain to place it beneath his feet.

This bishop was Lambert of Langres, a man distinguished in knowledge, religion, and goodness. All the bishops and princes were often greatly astonished at the deed of the aforementioned Robert, the most humble and renowned king.

That king Robert, beloved by God, always remembered the holy law, because he was mindful of God’s work in all his ways. For he knew what was written: “Knowledge is virtue; the guardian of virtue is holy humility.” He had also read the saying of blessed Pope Gregory:

“Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.”

He had read what one of the Fathers had said:

“All labor without humility is vain; the sign of humility gives the kingdom of heaven.”

Let us therefore pray to almighty God that this elect man, who, having laid aside every swelling of pride, was joined to Christ God by the virtue of holy humility, may be joined to him in the world to come in such a way that, separated from the left side at the judgment, Jesus Christ may find in him nothing to condemn to punishment, but rather something that, through manifold mercy, he may advance toward the crown that he promised to those who love him, for glory.

For this man of God, so great and of such quality, loved, desired, and believed in God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, the sure hope of the faithful.

[Col. 0917A] Rejecting the boastfulness of a proud mind, the humble king Robert, who must be named with manifold piety, always strove to please by good virtues the One who dwells on high. Avoiding the exalted, he received as many humble people as he could, who at appointed times would render true praises to God.

In this he also took an example from Ambrose, the venerable bishop of the city of Milan. Ambrose subjected two clerics of the Church over which he presided to severe reproaches because of their proud bearing, until, after trampling down the swelling of pride, they learned to proceed in humility; they had been corrected by the rod of priestly discipline.

That same blessed bishop, in his treatise *On the Flood and the Ark of Noah*, took care to describe arrogant people in this way, namely those whom Isaiah describes as the daughters of Judah, flashing with the gestures of their eyes and [Col. 0917B] carrying themselves with raised necks. Such people raise their eyebrows, are puffed up in heart, swollen in breast, and hold their necks thrown back. They barely brush the ground with the soles of their feet, while balancing their whole body and lifting themselves upon an empty covering. They advance with their steps directed forward, leaning the crown of their heads backward; they gaze at heaven and disdain the earth, as though fixed by pain in the neck so that they cannot incline it.

Therefore God erased them from the book of life, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11). Nor does he cause them, through their contrivances [or: meritorious deeds], to cleave to the heavenly realms among the merits of the saints. We have said this so that all may know what contempt for the world existed in so great an emperor of the Franks, who through holy humility possessed the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 0917C] The grandfather of this renowned king, Hugh, called “the Great” on account of his piety, goodness, and courage, built splendidly, together with his son, the monastery of Saint Maglorius, confessor of Christ, in the city of Paris. There he placed monks prepared to live under the rule of Father Benedict. He endowed that place with gold and silver, as well as other ornaments, for his own salvation, that of his son, and that of his future descendants.

His mother also, the aforementioned Adelaida, a queen greatly to be admired for her holy devotion, built the monastery of Saint Frambaldus in the city of Senlis, where she placed twelve clerics to serve the Lord and abundantly supplied them with the means of life. She also built a monastery in the Parisian territory, at a village called Argenteuil, where she gathered a considerable number of women servants of God, prepared to live according to the rule of Saint Benedict. She wished it to be dedicated and consecrated to almighty God for the praise and glory of the Inspirer of all good things, under the honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin.

She likewise made for Saint Martin the pontiff an excellent chasuble worked in gold, containing between the shoulders the majesty of the true pontiff, as well as Cherubim and Seraphim bowing their necks before the Ruler of all. On the breast she placed the Lamb of God, the victim of our redemption, and in the four directions she fixed the four living creatures adoring the Lord of glory.

She also made for the same blessed confessor one cope woven with gold, and two of silver. For her special friend after the Lord, namely blessed Dionysius, she likewise presented a chasuble made with marvelous workmanship. For him she also wove another ornament, as befitted so great a woman, called “the orb of the world,” very unlike that of Charles the Bald.

For the faithful queen hoped to have a portion with him to whom God had promised that he would obtain whatever he asked in a word that was not empty. Indeed, all her descendants proclaimed themselves servants of so great a martyr in every work, rendering to their Lord the obedience owed by servants.

For this family had as its special friends Saint Mary; the father and leader of monks, Saint Benedict; Saint Martin; Saint Anianus; and the victorious martyrs of Christ, Cornelius and Cyprian; and, most desired of all, the glorious martyr [Col. 0918B] Dionysius and the renowned blessed virgin Geneviève.

The good father is said to have spoken as he was dying:

“O excellent son, I adjure you by the holy and undivided Trinity: never let your mind be stolen away into consenting to the counsels of flatterers, or into allowing them, through poisoned gifts and presents, to lead you toward their wicked desires from these abbeys that, after God, I entrust to you perpetually. Nor, led by levity of mind, should you in any way sell off, plunder, or, when anger is aroused, scatter them.

“Above all, I impress this upon you: under no circumstances allow the leader of all, I mean Father Benedict, to be separated from you. He is the entrance to salvation before the common Judge, the harbor of tranquility, and, after the death of the flesh, the refuge of security.”

It is pleasing to record briefly what good works this servant of God, the mother of the most prudent [Col. 0918C] king Robert, performed. When he was still young, he suffered from a severe bodily illness, which placed his father and mother in fearful danger. On his behalf, in the elder church of the city of Orléans, which Saint Euvertius founded by the right hand of God and blessed according to ecclesiastical custom in honor of the holy and life-giving Cross, she made an image of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ hanging on the cross, fashioned from pure gold, so that he might be freed from the danger of death—he whom almighty God had already decreed would reign with him over the world. And by its power he was indeed delivered.

His father had also given, for his only son, to the place of the holy Cross a silver vessel weighing sixty pounds, which remained in the holy house of God down to our own times.

As he grew in age and became a man of strength, this man of God, who pleased God almighty by praise and word, grew sorrowful in spirit and returned as a gift, for the place of the saving Cross to be celebrated through the ages, the entire territory of the holy Cross that Bishop Fulk had given to the powerful Hugh of Beauvais as assistance [Col. 0918D]. He always loved this place, namely the see of Orléans, with particular affection, because he was born and grew up there; and afterward, having been regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit, he received there the solemn blessing of his elevation as king.

The lord Theodoric, bishop of that city, whose voice poured forth the praise of the Lord worthily and laudably, wishing the memory of his name to be preserved in the monastery of the holy Cross, ordered a vessel to be made from one hundred solidi of the finest gold, in which the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ would be consecrated. The king had joined himself to this great bishop with a humble mind. Touched by heavenly love, he had made for that holy chalice a paten on which to prepare the body of the Redeemer of the world, so that it might be for him a sign of the cross as an aid, and the holy Passion a true redemption of soul and body.

He also honored the lord Bishop Odolric in priestly vestments in such a way that, standing at the Lord’s sacrifice, he appeared entirely surrounded by gold and purple. He presented to that same place of the holy Cross an onyx vessel, which the wealthiest king had purchased for sixty pounds, together with another silver vessel and a maniple.

He also gave three precious hangings for the adornment of the church, for the salvation of himself and his sons, and many other things that cannot be recorded in writing or comprehended by number [Col. 0919B]. For the bodies of the precious martyrs Savinian and Potentian, who suffered most fiercely in the city of Sens, he clothed with gold, silver, and gems, so that the whole world might delight in them—men whom the king had honored on earth in a manner worthy of praise.

Furthermore, to Father Benedict and his monks, to whom he had always clung with his whole heart, he most kindly granted the fishery of the Loire River, confirmed it in writing, and asked from them nothing other than the support of their intercession. He also confirmed by royal authority the privilege concerning the immunity of the place of Fleury, or concerning the rights belonging to the monastery, and marked it with his seal as a good and wise man.

In honoring Father Benedict with ecclesiastical ornaments, he made completely clear how greatly he loved him. For he covered the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God, with a most precious pallium after the fire that had been the immense calamity of our holy place. He also richly ennobled this holy place with a thurible everywhere wonderfully raised high in gold and gems.

This thurible was entirely suitable for the golden censer made by Abbot Gauzlin, a marvelous craftsman. Its work shines above everything that we who write these things have seen in the place of Fleury.

He rebuilt from the foundations the monastery of Saint Cassian, the supreme confessor, in the city of Autun, also called Augustodunum, which had been utterly ruined by excessive age. There he placed ministers of God and reestablished the abbey as before, providing expenses for those who served God there [Col. 0919D]. This was his devotion; this was always his will in the work of God.

A loss befell the king at the palace of Compiègne through a noble theft. The day of Pentecost was then approaching, when the Holy Spirit, filling souls, cleanses the hearts of the faithful so that they may please the Father and the Son, with whom the Holy Spirit possesses an equal share. On that day, the glorious father-king wished to establish his son Hugh as king, a young man of the most vigorous nobility. Because the immense goodness of father and son had been proclaimed throughout the whole world, everyone hastened to have him made king, for they delighted in such a man.

This good young man was of the highest integrity: he embraced everyone, loved everyone, despised no one, and was beloved and always loved by all [Col. 0920A]. On the first day, after the marvelous blessing had been completed, the father rejoiced in his son and exulted with immense joy. The father’s admonition to his good son on that day was as follows:

“See, my son, always remember God, who today has made you a participant in his kingdom, so that you may delight in the paths of equity and justice. May God grant this to me, I ask, that I may see it, and to you, that you may act according to his will, which is always present to all who desire it.”

During these festive solemnities, one of the clerics, who had conceived perversity in his mad heart, hastened to carry out his plans. The man of God possessed in his treasury an image of a stag made of pure silver, in which he took delight at solemn festivals. He had received this gift from Richard, duke of the Normans, for human uses, and, gracious in speech and gracious in heart, he did not delay in dedicating it to God [Col. 0920B]. Attached to this ornament was a horn cup, in which wine was carried for the celebration of the sacrifice.

A certain pestilential and wicked cleric, seeing these things, seized them and hid them in his leggings. Going here and there, he found no one to whom he could sell them, nor any way by which he could destroy the image of the stag. Everyone should believe that these objects were preserved through the merits of the pious king, who was faithful to God with his whole heart.

For on the third Saturday, while he was conversing in the oratory of the Tower of Charles with someone closely attached to him in perfect friendship, behold, the thief came and positioned himself before the altar. He scattered useless prayers, drew out long sighs, and covered the image with a large altar-cloth, together with the cup; then he went away shamefaced, poor man, not knowing whose eyes were fixed upon him.

The king ended his conversation, went lightly to the altar with his true friend, took back his possessions, and happily returned them to the minister. He charged his companion that, as long as he lived, he should not make the man’s name known in the world or bring shame upon so great a man.

But because the intention of certain perverse minds opposes our narrative—people who envy others every good they themselves cannot attain and, with the goad of malice, do not blush to suppress it as far as they can; who, if any human excess has been committed, bark with a dog’s tooth at all the succeeding shoots of good works so that they may be suffocated; and who do not fear to tear apart this most holy man—they say:

“These works that have been brought forward as good deeds will not benefit his soul unto salvation, since he did not shrink from the crime of an illicit union, when he took as his wife a woman who was his *commater* and bound to him by a tie of consanguinity.”

It is pleasing to refute their irrationality by the evident testimony of holy Scripture. Yet, lest they perhaps claim that the opportunity for speaking has been closed to them, let them provide us with someone who has not fallen into sin. Who, indeed, will boast that he has a pure heart, when Scripture’s testimony proves that not even an infant of one day is clean?

I have said this to restrain the inertia of foolish people, not to conceal the fault of a man who voluntarily repented. Just as holy David, although forbidden by the law, unlawfully desired and seized Bathsheba, so this man, acting against the laws of the sacred faith, wickedly joined the aforementioned woman to himself as wife. It was not enough for David merely to sin against the woman; by plotting the death of an innocent man [Col. 0921A], he incurred a double sin. This man, for his part, preferred to offend God rather than preserve an undefiled marriage-bed with a woman forbidden to him by a double law.

But the true Physician, by the gracious ordering of the human race, healed the wound of each sin: David through his prophet Nathan, when, after the parable of a poor man’s one little ewe-lamb and a rich man’s abundant flock had been presented to him, he acknowledged himself guilty and said that he had sinned; and this man likewise through the lord and venerable Abbo, the abbot of Fleury, chosen by God—now, by the favor of Christ’s grace, shining with miracles—who rebuked him harshly, privately and publicly, without fear of death.

The rebuke of this holy man continued until the most gentle king acknowledged his guilt, completely abandoned the woman whom he had wrongly joined to himself [Col. 0921B], and washed away the stain of his sin through an acceptable satisfaction before God.

Thus both kings were pleasing to God, since they had been crowned by him. Nature gave birth to them naked for the world, but God’s holy providence wished them to be glorious and renowned in the age. And because, as Scripture says, God permits what he does not will to happen, gracious dispensation allowed them to fall into sin in such a way that they might recognize themselves as equal in human frailty to their subjects, spend the rest of their lives in vigils and prayers, and endure various sufferings of the body. Thus the testimony of holy Scripture might be fulfilled in them, which says: “God chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

Both sinned, as kings are accustomed to do; but, visited by God, they repented, wept, and groaned, which kings are not accustomed to do. Following the example of blessed David, our lord Robert confessed his fault, begged forgiveness, lamented his misery, fasted, prayed, and transmitted the testimony of his confession to all ages through publicly proclaimed grief.

What private persons do not blush to do, the king did not blush to confess. Those who are held by laws dare to deny their sin; they disdain to ask forgiveness, although the man who was bound by no human laws sought it. What he did in sin belonged to his condition; what he did in supplication belonged to his correction. The fall was common, but the confession was distinctive. To incur guilt belongs to nature; to wash it away belongs to virtue.

For this reason he did not disdain to do these things, since he knew that God must be feared by the small and the great, and that every powerful person is admonished by divine Scripture: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God.”

Thus this humble king, freed from legal bonds, was nevertheless guilty before his own conscience. Wishing to subdue himself by these bonds, he prayed for divine assistance, so that he might be cleansed from every stain of crime.

And indeed, since the gentle and meek-hearted holy king had always possessed outstanding marks of his gentleness and piety, frequently forgiving his adversaries and considering it necessary to abstain from killing them, it is not surprising that he should grieve so deeply that a harmful sin had crept upon him. Therefore he asked to be freed from mortal sins, praised the Lord his God, proclaimed the Lord’s justice, and his tongue rejoiced in the justice of the One who looks down from heaven [Col. 0922A], which proceeded from the womb of the untouched Virgin.

I have judged it worthy to insert into this account one deed accomplished by the father of this renowned and God-elected king. In it, truthful priests, abbots, and monks who are not ignorant of holy discipline will find a model of virtue that they can not only imitate but also admire. Above all, they will find marks of piety and mercy deserving every praise.

Once, while solemnly celebrating the holy day of Easter in the city of Paris, he returned joyfully on the second Saturday to his house at Saint-Denis and spent the solemn days there. When the third Saturday arrived, at the hour when God is praised throughout all ages [Col. 0922B], he rose from bed and prepared to go to church.

Looking around, he saw two men lying opposite one another in a corner, engaged in a wicked act. Pitying their frailty, he removed from his neck an ornament of skins, which was extremely valuable, and with a kindly heart threw it over the sinners. Having done this, he entered the church of the saints to pray to almighty God, where he prayed for those sinners, lest they perish.

After prolonging his prayer and hoping that the sinners, now dead to the world and alive to God through repentance, had already gone away, he summoned the guardian of his body and, in the humblest words, ordered him to bring another ornament of the same kind. He imposed this command with imperial threats, ordering that the matter should never be disclosed either to his glorious wife or to anyone else.

O how perfect was the man who thus protected sinners with his own garment! How holy a priest, how pious an abbot, how religious a monk, how straight a norm of virtue and perfection upon which anyone desiring the paths of justice may rely! For the father and leader of monks commands that sins be confessed in such a way because he knew how to care for his own wounds and those of others, not to expose and publicize them.
