O blessed piety and mercy, made participants in God, which flourished in so great and such a man! Our Robert himself possessed them as though they had been left to him by his father as an inheritance.

Ingo, a man of the highest nobility and goodness, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain located in the city of Paris, sent two brothers of good reputation to this servant of God at Orléans, for his own benefit and that of the brethren. When he saw them, he honored them with the kiss of peace, as was his custom, and most kindly asked them why they had hastened to him.

Their proper names were Herbert, the one, and Gauzfred, the other; they were men of no low rank in the monastic order. In pious fashion he commanded them to attend his presence after the matutinal hymns and to have an audience concerning whatever they wished.

While they were observing his orders, it happened that, in the very church where they were seated, a candle went out before their eyes. After it had gone out, he summoned from his bed the religious man Theudo, his close companion, handed him a candle, and sent him to seek a light as quickly as possible.

Meanwhile the most devout king was occupied with psalms and prayers. When the man who had been sent returned, he saw the man of God holding a burning candle in his hands—he who held charity in his conduct. Amazed by this and wishing to praise God with hymnic voices, he was forbidden by the king in every way, so that, freeing himself completely from the boastfulness of a proud mind and praising God’s power in all things, he might say with David:

“I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:7).

And again:

“I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word” (Psalm 118:107).

We read in the divine Books that to serve God is to reign. This was certainly known by the one who admonished us, saying: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Psalm 2:11). Our blessed man, of whom we are speaking, fulfilled this to the extent of his ability and will.

And just as Moses, the servant of God, overthrew Amalek by his most humble prayers and extended hands [Col. 0923B], so this true friend of God, having conquered his enemies through the power of the Holy Spirit, always had God as his helper, he who is the salvation of all.

A sweetness of spirit shone in him, by which he won every person to himself. He possessed saving wisdom, with which he delighted in the company of his people. He taught some through readings, others through hymns and praises; always exhorting them to such things, he became, according to the Apostle, “all things to all people, that he might win all” (1 Corinthians 9:22).

Moreover, what the bishops and abbots themselves were reluctant to do, although it is their duty to correct those who err and to call good people to better things by their example, this true friend of God dared to do. From the treasury of his heart proceeded the voice of rejoicing and salvation, in which he delighted with all the saints, crucifying his flesh, according to the Apostle, “with its vices and desires” of this world (Galatians 5:24), and always preparing himself as a temple pleasing to the divinity.

He was first at the divine office and diligent in praising God. Wherever he had to go, a vehicle was prepared to carry the tent of the divine ministry. When it had been fixed upon the ground, the sacred objects were set down there, so that, since according to the Psalmist “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Psalm 23:1), he might show himself a devoted servant, offering devout praises to God in whatever place he might be.

The words of the most blessed Anthony were fixed and firmly planted in the heart of the most gentle king, who loved God well:

“Always desire Jesus Christ, for in every place established upon earth are the kingdoms of heaven.”

He spent the holy nights—that is, the nights of the Lord’s Nativity, holy Easter, and Pentecost—entirely without sleep until the very morning. Neither sitting nor standing did he take sleep, until he received the saving reception of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he awaited and desired.

This fact about him was proven and made known throughout the whole age. On the solemnity of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, he kept the custom that he observed at the Nativity of the Lord: after the praise of the Lord contained in the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, Mass was celebrated devoutly at the first hour of the morning. This was established by the holy authority of Gregory the Great and others in the Mass, and again by the teaching of Amalarius, which he took from the sayings of the holy Fathers [Col. 0924A].

We must not omit what his custom was in giving alms at the seats of his kingdom. In the cities of Paris, Senlis, Orléans, Dijon, Auxerre, Avalon, Melun, and Étampes, at each of these residences, an abundance of bread and wine was given to three hundred—or, more accurately, one thousand—poor people. This was done especially in the year in which he passed to God, the year 1032 of the Lord’s incarnation.

Besides this, wherever he went during holy Lent, he ordered bread, fish, and wine to be given daily to one hundred or two hundred poor people. On the day of the Lord’s Supper, a number that seemed incredible to those who did not see it, but most remarkable to those who saw it and served in the undertaking, no fewer than three hundred were gathered through his provision. Kneeling on the ground, each received from his holy hand vegetables, fish, bread, and one denarius [Col. 0924B].

This took place at the third hour of the day, and likewise at the sixth hour. He also provided one hundred poor clerics with a portion of bread, fish, and wine, honoring each of them with twelve denarii, while continually singing David’s psalms in heart and voice.

After the meal, the humble king prepared himself for God’s service. He removed his clothing and put on a hair shirt. Then, joined by a company of clerics numbering one hundred sixty or more, he washed their feet according to the example of their Lord and wiped them with the hair of his head. At the Lord’s command, he rewarded each of them with two solidi, while the clergy were present and a deacon stood by to read the passage according to John concerning what was said and done at the Lord’s Supper.

With such deeds the king, glorious in merits, occupied himself. Throughout the entire holy day of Good Friday he visited the places of the saints and adored the Lord’s cross, until the vigil of the holy Resurrection. At that vigil he immediately undertook the sacrifice of praise, which never departed from his mouth throughout all ages.

By these merits of virtue and by such displays of good works, the glorious and world-renowned king Robert showed himself marvelous to the world and left himself as an example for all posterity.

[Col. 0924D]

This, moreover, after God, was the special glory of kings: in honor of the sacred number of the holy apostles, whom he always loved with a benevolent heart and whose solemn festivals he anticipated with a vowed fast, he took twelve poor men with him, whom he loved especially. To them he himself was true rest after their labors. For, likening these holy poor men to the strongest young donkeys, he sent them before him wherever he went, rejoicing, praising God, and blessing his soul. In refreshing these men and countless other poor people, he never had any unwillingness, but always willingness. For those who were dying, provision was made so that no one should be lost from their number; there was a succession of the living for them, and their offering before God of so great a king. This was his constant concern, this was always his good will, to which he had always clung through participation in the supreme Good. It was true goodness, in which the most distinguished versifier delighted in these verses:

[Col. 0925A]

> The greater care of goodness is to lighten brothers’ labors,  
> and to become desired aid for the sad;  
>   
> to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, release  
> the bound, reconcile those who are at odds;  
>   
> and whatever comforts wretched people seek,  
> to bring these forth, as far as possible, with a pious heart;  
>   
> so that, rightly and truly eager, truly benevolent,  
> he may flee what is evil and do what is good.

Everyone in the world recognized that all these things existed in so great a man, because God always loved him.

Moreover, he rebuilt from the foundations in the city of Orléans the monastery of Saint Aignan, his singular advocate before God. No one can declare how pious a love of holy devotion he had toward him, because he always wanted to have him, after God, as his helper, protector, and defender, wherever his steps might be able to go. For one day, when he was asked by a certain special friend of his own friends why he exalted such and so great a bishop, and not other saints, with praises of this kind, he is said to have replied in a most humble and devout voice:

“Who is Aignan? Aignan—Aignan certainly is the true consolation of our people, the strength of those who labor, the protection of kings, the defense of princes, the joy of bishops, and the outstanding and indescribable support of clerics, monks, orphans, and widows.”

And, joking with the boys standing around, he said: “Is not this man of whom we are speaking, Arianus—[or: ‘Arianus’]—a frequent and true, proven deliverance for you boys from the punishment of rods?”

Burning with honor for so great a bishop, this fragrant flower and ornament of the holy Church, and moved by God’s grace and the desire to place him in a higher position, he began to build the house of the Lord over him in better form and, with God cooperating and Saint Aignan providing assistance, brought it to completion. The building itself is forty-two measures in length, twelve in width, ten in height, and has one hundred twenty-three windows.

He also made nineteen altars in that monastery, to the praise of the saints, whose memory we have taken care to record here: the principal altar, in honor of the apostle Peter, to whom the aforesaid king joined the co-apostle Paul in the blessing, since previously only Saint Peter had been venerated there; one at the head of Saint Aignan; another at his feet; another in honor of Saint Benedict; the rest in honor of those whose names are inscribed, namely Saint Evurtius, Saint Lawrence, Saint George and All the Saints, and also Saint Martin, Saint Maurice, Saint Stephen, Saint Antony, Saint Vincent, Saint Mary, Saint John, the Holy Savior, Saint Mamertus, Saint Nicholas, and Saint Michael.

He made the head of the monastery with marvelous workmanship, in the likeness of the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, and of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, established at Clermont. He overlaid the bier of Saint Aignan at its front with fine and excellent gold, precious stones, and pure silver. He entirely covered with fine gold the altar panel of Saint Peter, in whose honor the place stands. After the death of her most holy husband, Constance, the noble queen and his glorious wife, assigned to God and Saint Aignan a sum—namely seven pounds of that metal—to improve the roofs of the monastery he had built; when these were opened from the bottom to the top, the sky could be seen more clearly than the earth. In it there was a quantity of fifteen pounds of tested gold. He distributed what remained where it ought to be distributed, because he was concerned for the churches of God, in accordance with the useful will of his lord.

After all this, the glorious King Robert, eager for holy blessing, in the thirty-sixth year of his ordination, blessing, and accession as king, summoned, by imperial command, the archbishop Gauzlin of Bourges and the abbot of Fleury, Leotheric of Sens, and also Arnulf of Tours. Their presence was followed by the bishops Odolric of Orléans, Theodoric of Chartres, Bernerius of Meaux, Guarinus of Beauvais, and Rodulf of Senlis. Nor was the presence lacking of the lord and venerable Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and of other good men of no small merit, with whom he always desired to converse.

By these men, certainly, and by other ministers of God, the noble body of God’s friend, the most holy Aignan, was lifted from the tomb together with the bodies of the saints Euspi­cius, Monitor, and Flosculus, confessors; Baudelus and Scubilius, martyrs; and Agia, mother of Saint Lupus the confessor. It was guarded, praised, and celebrated in hymns and praises in the church of Saint Martin by the glorious king himself and by the others whom the document has already mentioned, who had come for such a task, until the useful and necessary things for the holy blessing had been prepared.

[Col. 0926C]

When everything had been prepared, he solemnly caused that place to be blessed and consecrated by those holy priests, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1029, in the twelfth indiction. Then, on the shoulders of the illustrious king, amid peoples rejoicing and exulting together, the body was carried with praises into the new church that the illustrious Robert himself had built. They praised the Lord and Saint Aignan with tambourine and choir, with strings and organ, and placed him in the holy place for the honor, glory, and praise of Jesus Christ our Lord and of his servant Aignan, adorned with special glory.

When the solemn blessing and everything pertaining to the dedication of the holy church had been completed, Robert, the father of his country, worthy now to be named with reverence, went before the altar of the most holy Peter and the beloved lord Aignan, in the sight of all the people. Removing his purple garment, which in the rustic language is called a *rocus*, and fixing both knees upon the ground, he poured forth a prayer of supplication to God with all his heart in these words:

“I give thanks to you, good God, who today have brought my desire to fulfillment through the merits of Saint Aignan, gladdening my soul with the bodies of the saints who triumph with him on this day. Therefore, Lord, through these your saints, grant forgiveness of sins to the living, and life and everlasting rest to all the dead. Look favorably upon our times; rule, order, and guard your kingdom, which by your kindness, mercy, and goodness has been given to us, for the praise and glory of your name, through the wondrous power of Saint Aignan, who has wondrously liberated the father of his country from enemies.”

When the prayer had been completed, each person returned joyfully to his own affairs, and on that very day the place was splendidly ennobled by his gifts: four exceedingly precious hangings, a silver pitcher, and a chapel, which after his death he assigned to almighty God and to the most holy confessor Aignan.

The chapel of this most pious, prudent, and powerful king Robert was as follows: eighteen good, excellent, and well-prepared copes; two golden Gospel books, two silver ones, and two other small books, together with one overseas missal, well prepared with ivory and silver; twelve golden reliquaries; one altar wonderfully furnished with gold and silver, containing in its middle a precious stone called *onychinus* [onyx]; three golden crosses. The largest of these contained seven pounds of pure gold. Five bells. One of these was quite remarkable: it contained two thousand six hundred pounds of metal, and upon it he ordered the sign of baptism made with oil and chrism to be impressed, as ecclesiastical order requires, and that it should be called “Robert,” to the attribution of the Holy Spirit.

He also gave this saint two churches, Sentilly and Rutinay, with their villages and everything pertaining to them; he confirmed them by royal decree and ordered them to be strengthened. He also obtained from the lord Theodoric, venerable bishop of Orléans, the altars of those churches, together with the episcopal privilege concerning them, made by the bishop himself, which he bestowed upon Saint Aignan and the illustrious king who had always loved him with a good heart and with a voice of rejoicing.

The noble Walter built the castle called Crépy in the territory of Soissons. The nobleman made the abbey of Saint Arnulf, which he had founded, noble and illustrious throughout the ages. In our own time he appointed there an abbot named Lezcelin, a man of good reputation and a monk professing the regular life, who came each year to this man of God. He was received by him as a servant of God; and after they had conversed about heavenly things, on his return he was splendidly honored with honorable gifts, which were joined to heavenly things through the virtue of perfect charity.

On one occasion during holy Lent, as he was traveling customarily from Poissy to the king, they partook together of both temporal and spiritual food. Then, joining themselves to one another through ancestral goodness, the good abbot offered the king the charity of God, for the relief of his most humble body, so that he might have some easing of his food and, by knocking through prayers at the gates of heaven, might become a companion of the saints.

The man of piety refused this and, throwing himself upon the ground, begged in every way that the abbot not oppress him by force, because by obeying such a command he had not yet offered God any vow of fasting. Hearing this, the abbot assumed the bonds of silence. Reflecting in his heart on what would be perfect in virtue for the observance of the king’s fast, he received him into a varied and unnumbered celebration of Masses, so that God might grant him firm devotion through them.

Rejoicing in the gifts received from the holy man, the king gave thanks to God and immediately observed a holy fast, awaiting the resurrection of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. It was also customary for this lover of good things, as a religious practice for the cleansing of his sins, that from Septuagesima until Easter, he often used no mattress but received the strongest earth as a place to lie, stretching himself continually toward heaven.

May this brief prayer, subscribed here for these and his other deeds, benefit his soul: May God wipe away the stains of his former actions, consign them to perpetual oblivion, and grant him a share in the first resurrection—he who is the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ, living and reigning forever and ever.

What can be joined to my heart that is sweeter or more delightful than that I should praise my teacher and helper in all the works of God? I return, I return, and, as I used to do in the days when we looked upon one another together, I recover his lovable and most desired goodness for myself. I also delight in it and experience what benefit it brought me. In it, as far as I remember, I receive and feel nothing except what a good son receives from a good father, a friend from a friend, a beloved man from one who loves him.

Yet I blush deeply in recounting the good works of this admirable man, since in him there always flourished the things fixed in the heights of heaven, for the gain of souls and bodies. Whenever he saw anyone laboring in God’s work, he encouraged him with his voice, secretly lifting him up with a gift: his gift was very poor in promises, but exceedingly great when given.

On an estate of the monastery of Fleury, by the paternal command of my admirable abbot Gauzlin, I began to build a church, modest indeed but festive. People flocked to it in love, for it was to be consecrated with a fitting blessing. Although it was incomplete and made of wood, the king, a man desirous of heavenly things, set out from the castle of Vitry, wishing to see it with his most holy eyes.

It had already been blessed by the venerable archbishop Gauzlin of Bourges, at the command of the lord and beloved bishop Odolric, who had given to that church the surrounding land in full measure and to its great advantage. Entering it and praying, the king placed upon the altar a cloak worth four pounds. Since it had been consecrated in honor of the saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, it undoubtedly took such firm hold of his heart that, when I later came to him at Paris, he splendidly adorned it with relics of those holy martyrs—namely Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—and enriched it through their intercessions.

These were the gifts of their protection: a portion of the chasuble of Saint Dionysius, of the dalmatic of Saint Rusticus, and of the chasuble of Saint Eleutherius; garments sprinkled with their blood; some of the dust of their flesh; and the triple cord with which Dionysius, the precious martyr of the Lord, had been bound.

With these and other relics of the saints, the place was nobly distinguished by the king who loved God. The most precious relics of the saints mentioned above were received at the monastery of Fleury by the lord Gauzlin, abbot, a man most honorable in giving and receiving, on the day of the Kalends of October, on which the solemnity of the saints Germanus, Remigius, and Vedastus, confessors, is celebrated throughout all ages.

But when that church had been burned after sins had occurred, I, wretched man, rebuilt it with the assisting hand of the Lord: through the merits of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, of Father Benedict, and of those same saints, what had been made of wood became stone. The glorious bishop Odolric, a man of great goodness, wished to have it dedicated and consecrated to the Lord God and his saints by his own hand, not by another’s, as before.

He acted as befitted such a man. For throughout the whole time he lived, he protected me with every kind of love, through the power of God at work, so that in everything I ever desired I never encountered his unwillingness, but always what was honorable and useful. May the supreme Pontiff, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, deign to grant him the inheritance of the holy priests, which this illustrious priest always desired to attain here through the honor of the episcopate. May the Redeemer and Creator, the gentlest liberator of holy souls, destroy his sins, place him among the heavenly beings, and join him to the citizens of heaven.

Those entering this church see before their eyes the verses written below, preserving the memory of Saint Dionysius and of the founder of the place. They recognize them divided into two parts, beside the altars consecrated in their honor. On the left side of the altar of Saint Dionysius are these:

> Saint Dionysius, entering these thresholds,  
> join us to the Lord by holy aid.  
>   
> Whoever you are who seek the Lord, entreat the thundering Lord  
> that he may preserve Helgaudus in his love.  
>   
> For his love of Christ built this venerable temple  
> for the Lord and for Dionysius.

Likewise, on the right:

> This house is dedicated forever to God on high,  
> through the effort and good counsel of Helgaudus.  
>   
> From here the gate of the paradisal kingdom is struck:  
> from here the devout people rejoice together with the Lord on high.  
>   
> As you enter together, may Christ Jesus preserve you.  
> Say, all of you, with faithful voice throughout every age:  
>   
> So be it: Amen, amen, amen.

In the days of this man, whose deeds we describe with God’s assistance, the splendid abbot Gauzlin shone in the monastery of Fleury, a celebrated place, illustrious before the world through his merits and joined to God by holy works, powerful in spiritual as well as human knowledge.

In his heart were the good flowers of sacred Scripture brought forth by the teacher Abbo. Having been most honorably imbued with them, he poured them forth for everyone, so that people could delight in heavenly things. In holy almsgiving he was so generous that, while he himself was exposed to the fiercest cold, he removed his fur garments and clothed Christ’s poor, so that he might receive a reward from the remunerator of good deeds, from whom he would hear:

“I was naked, and you clothed me. Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me. Come, blessed ones of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34–38).

The perfect king fixed this man firmly in his sight. Since he loved him more than others and bound him to himself especially through his counsels, he always regarded the advice received from him as proper; nevertheless, he never regarded it as unjust.

Honoring him with the honors of this world, he bestowed upon him no minor dignities: the abbey of Saint Benedict, which is the head of the entire monastic order, and the bishopric of Bourges, of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, which holds primacy throughout Aquitaine and was and is the honor and ornament of France. Whatever sins he committed in these offices, true charity and almsgiving, which flourished in him with great strength, will consign to perpetual oblivion through the operation of the blessed good that he possessed by participation in the supreme Good.

During the days of Septuagesima, while the illustrious king was residing in Paris, the humble abbot, as was customary, sent men to him for the benefit of the most sacred place. Those who were sent were called by these names: Alberic, one man adorned with the glory of the priesthood, a man of overflowing charity; joined to him by God’s gift and by the command of the most excellent father Gauzlin was a brother named Helgaudus, whom that prince loved with fatherly affection; and a third, named Hisembert, who labored with them in fraternal service and had been made a monk worthy of his conversion.

Since he was going to celebrate the days of holy Lent at Poissy, he hastened the journey, while we traveled with him at his imperial command, to give an account of the matters concerning which we had approached him. But when we came to the bank of the Seine called Carolivenna—that is, “the fishing-place”—which was difficult to cross, by his holy command we alone entered the little boat, while he watched and considered what outcome would befall us, expecting us to come to him safely and cheerfully.

Through the intercession of this king, help came to us wretched men from God, who is everywhere praised, blessed, and adored. As we sailed and led our horses by their reins alongside the boat, it happened that one hoofed animal, untamed and never before having done such a thing, placed its two forefeet into the boat amid the waves. Through its violent frenzy the boat was endangered, dragging us already into the depths.

Calling upon the Most High King, after God, together with his companions and the powers of heaven, the king sent immense cries toward heaven on account of our danger. In a loud voice he ordered us to let go of the reins and drive the horses far from the boat. At his beloved command, when we released the reins as he had ordered and the horses’ feet were thrown out of the boat, we began to be carried toward the shore.

He himself also invoked Saint Dionysius, Saint Benedict, and all the saints of God for our assistance, his eyes filled with tears. The One who is blessed forever heard his prayer. It happened as he wished, and when the boat had been brought to land, by God’s grace he received us unharmed; together with him, we praised the wondrous God.

From that event onward, almighty God made us his praisers for all time. We remained with that man of God in that place for three days, delighted by his sweet conversation as well as by his pleasing appearance. May he, who redeemed that most holy soul with his precious blood, place it, we pray, in his kingdom.

Still, it pleases us to set foot in a greater subject than that which we entered, hastening in our account toward his glorious departure. We shall dare to commend him to our Lord with truthful and not false praises, open and not feigned, marked with the seal of the Holy Trinity, so that through the power of the Holy Spirit he may deserve to escape the day of final vengeance.

But since we have written certain further things about his wondrous activity, joined to true humility, things that benefit and will benefit many toward salvation, it remains, once these have been made known, that his most holy death—which by God’s gift was praiseworthy and glorious—should not leave us idle.

Having the desire to die to the world and live for Christ God, the most vigorous king, wishing to see the One to whom everything belongs and to whom we attribute everything we write, wanted to have on earth as his companion one whom heaven cannot contain. When, during a certain Lent, he was traveling to the saints joined to him in God’s service, he visited, prayed to, and honored them, striking their ears with humble and salutary prayers so that he might be found worthy, together with them and all the saints, in God’s praises.

He labored in this with the strength of body and spirit, seeking to overcome through God’s power. Entering the territory of Bourges, Saint Stephen the protomartyr received him together with Saint Maiolus, pre-eminent in merits; Saint Mary, together with the renowned and supreme martyr Julian; and again that most devout virgin of virgins, Mary, together with the great confessor Saint Giles.

The illustrious Saturninus, together with the strong Vincent; the worthy Antoninus, together with the martyr Fidus; and Saint Gerald of the Lord made him, as he was already returning home, safe once more through the glorious Saint Stephen. Spending with him a joyful Palm Sunday on earth, he hurried to Orléans, where at Easter he would receive the Author of our salvation.

On this journey many gifts were given by him to the saints, while his hand was never empty toward the poor. For that land contained many sick people, especially lepers; the man of God did not shrink from them, because he had read in the holy Scriptures that the Lord Christ had often been received as a guest in the appearance of lepers.

Hurrying to them with eager mind and entering among them, he personally gave them sums of money and, placing kisses with his own mouth upon their hands, praised God together with them in all things, remembering the words of the Lord who said: “Remember that you are dust and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19 [the printed citation reads “Gen. XIII, 19”]).

For the others he sent gifts devoutly, for love of almighty God, who works great things wherever he is. Divine power granted this perfect man such great grace in healing bodies that, when he touched the place of a wound with his most devout hand and impressed upon them the sign of the holy cross, he removed from them all the pain of their illness.

The servant of God, not forgetful of complete charity, considered the noble deed of the monk Martyrius, who bound a leper in his own garment and lifted him onto his shoulder. When he wished to perform the duties of service for him, he suddenly returned to heaven; and Christ, who had been received in the appearance of a leper, ascended and said to him:

“Martyrius, you were not ashamed of me on earth; I will not be ashamed of you in heaven.”

May this man of whom we speak, by God’s favor, have a share with Saint Martyrius, since through these and other good works he hastened to join himself to Christ God.

[Col. 0932A]

In the building of the churches of God, this king, anointed with both temporal and spiritual oil, desiring by the gift of holy blessing to fulfill his power and will and longing to attain the palm of eternal blessedness, began among other things to consider—and after considering, to bring to completion—how the saints of God should be honored and exalted with praise, according to their dignity and merit. He was never weary of speaking of them or praising them throughout all his days.

Indeed, this will appear in the things appended below, written down and joined to the preceding material: everything was always a concern for him—whatever is modest, chaste, holy, and whatever holy Church, truly a virgin and mother, possesses. Yet God was never forgotten by him.

In that same city of Orléans he built, as we have said, a monastery in honor of Saint Aignan; likewise another in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Hilary, the supreme confessor; also one of Saint Mary, Mother of God, surnamed “Fabricata.”

There he also built a monastery of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ; the monastery of Saint Paul the apostle at the village of Cantogilo; the monastery of Saint Medard at the castle of Vitry; the monastery of Saint Leodegarius in the Aquiline Forest; a monastery of Saint Mary at the castle of Melun, together with another church; the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Regulus in the city of Senlis; a monastery of Saint Mary at the castle of Étampes; likewise, in that same castle, one church in the palace; in the city of Paris, a church in the palace in honor of Saint Nicholas the bishop; the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre; a church of Saint Michael in the forest called Bieria; likewise the monastery of Saint Germanus of Paris, together with the church of Saint Vincent, in the forest called Ledia; in the village called Gomedus, a church in honor of Saint Aignan; likewise in the village of Faida, a church in honor of Saint Aignan; the monastery of Saint Mary at Poissy; and the monastery of Saint Cassian at Autun.

For all these things, and for the countless others that he accomplished through the power of the Lord, let each of us pray, let us all pray, and let us say:

“God, who made your servant Robert flourish among the most holy kings in royal dignity, grant, we ask, that, through the intercession of the glorious Mother of God Mary with all the saints, he whom he temporarily represented on earth may also rejoice in their perpetual fellowship in heaven. Through the same Lord of ours.”

Before his most holy death—which occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, the day of the passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul—the sun appeared throughout the whole world, darkened as though it were the fourth moon, its rays withdrawn; at the sixth hour of the day it grew pale over humanity. It so obscured the sight of people that no one recognized anyone else until a certain interval for recognition had passed.

What it portended soon became clear, when it left us wretched people nothing but intolerable grief over his death. For from the day of Saint Peter to the day of his most holy departure, twenty-one days are counted. During those days he meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, singing the holy songs of David, so that without doubt this could be applied to him, which was said especially of the most holy Father Benedict:

> Constant in singing, he never gave rest to the plectrum;  
> singing sacred things, he died constant in song.

This blessed soldier had recognized that peace was free and rest tranquil for God’s servants when, withdrawn from the storms of this world, they entered the seat and security of the eternal harbor and, death swallowed up, came to immortality.

For he hastened through the virtues named above to pass from present sadness to perpetual joy. He said that perfect joy belonged to the one who labored so that he might see Christ God. Prepared to depart from this world, he always invoked the Lord Jesus, the teacher of his salvation and welfare.

To see the unconquerable power of the eternal King, he ceaselessly prayed in voice and with signs that angels, archangels, and all the saints of God would come to his aid. He continually fortified himself on his forehead and eyes, nostrils and lips, throat and ears with the sign of the holy cross, commemorating the Lord’s incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, ascension, and the grace of the Holy Spirit. He maintained this custom throughout life, and holy water was never lacking to him when he wished it.

Filled with these and other good virtues, at sixty years of age, as we believe, he awaited death fearlessly. When the weakness of a severe fever grew stronger, he requested the saving and health-giving viaticum of the life-giving body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Having received it, and after a brief interval, he departed to the King of kings and Lord of lords and happily attained the happy kingdoms.

As we have said, he fell asleep in the Lord on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, at the dawning of the “third day of the Sabbath” (*diei tertiae Sabbati*; the printed wording is uncertain), at the castle of Melun. He was carried to Paris and buried at Saint-Denis beside his father, before the altar of the Holy Trinity.

There was immense mourning there and intolerable grief. The crowd of monks lamented the absence of so great a father; the innumerable multitude of clerics, grieving over their own sorrows, which had been piously relieved by that holy man; and the countless number of widows and orphans, lamenting the benefits they had received from him, raised immense cries to heaven.

There was, certainly, one voice from all:

“Great king, good God, why are you killing us, when you take away our good father and join him to yourself?”

Striking their breasts with their fists, they went and returned to the saint’s tomb, repeating the verse of the speech already mentioned and adding a prayer that God might have mercy on him, through the prayers of all the saints, forever and ever.

At his death—alas, what grief!—they cried out repeatedly:

“While Robert ruled and governed, we lived securely and feared no one. To the pious father, father of the senate, father of all good people: happy is his soul and his salvation; happy his ascent to heaven; happy his dwelling with Christ, the King of kings, forever.”

The portion of this wondrous king, therefore, in the heavenly kingdom was the Lord God. Indeed, this must be recounted. Raised to the lofty height of royal power, this most humble man of God cast away from himself the boastfulness of a dishonorable mind, the exaltation of honors and the glory of the world, and, placing his treasure in heaven, for this reason God became his portion.

Great before God was his treasure, an excellent heap of holy riches, an everlasting bed of holy rest, whose propitiation is God, who was the liberation of the whole world.

Among other things, one matter causes us grief: such a great man lies without an inscribed stone, without a name, without letters, although his glory and memory throughout the whole world are in blessing. Therefore, the example of this most serene king, who continually clung to the ecclesiastical order and to the monastic order, always beloved by him, has benefited and will benefit every age. Christ God had given him as a good father to everyone.

Nevertheless, at the end of this work it pleases me briefly to record the innumerable goodness of this wondrous king. Who conversing with him was not made joyful with great joy? Who, desiring peace, did not put away anger in his presence? Who, looking upon the presence of his face, did not forget deceit? Which monk did not find rest through his prayers and was not loved, cherished, and honored?

Which cleric, through his most holy admonition, did not become a lover of chastity? For whom were his friendly words not medicines? For whom did the sight of him not benefit the foolish like a rod? Who, looking upon his humble eyes, did not meditate on heavenly things? What poor or hungry person departed from his table without being satisfied?

What dead person, at the end of his life, was not clothed in his garment? Who dull of understanding was not made wise by him? Did not widows and poor people, following the example of the good Dorcas, show the garments given to them by him? (Acts 9:39.) Did not the whole multitude of the wretched call him father and nourisher? Did anyone fall into sin without receiving the help of his holy consolation? Did anyone drowsing from weariness fail to be awakened from sleep by him? Did anyone praising God not have him as an example?

Did anyone wishing to give alms fail to take him as an imitator, like another John? I mean John, the patriarch of Alexandria, who, because of his immense mercy—which he showed toward the wretched and the poor—deserved in his life and throughout the whole world to be called and to be merciful.

Indeed, after holy David there was no king on earth like him in holy virtues, humility, mercy, piety, and charity, which is above all and without which no one will see God, because he always clung to the Lord and did not depart from his commandments with a perfect heart.

We leave the remaining matters concerning the military affairs of the world—the enemies he conquered and the honors he acquired through virtue and skill—to be written by historians. If such men exist and write these things, they will find in them a father and sons renowned in war and glorious with distinguished fame.

And now, from the monks, clerics, widows, orphans, and all Christ’s poor, receive in part an everlasting farewell, our heart’s love, Robert. Bring forth prayers for the servant who is reconciled to Christ God, whom you pleased by your praiseworthy life and service and through the merits of holy virtues deserved to attain the heavenly kingdoms.

May almighty God grant this—he who justifies the ungodly, gives life to the dead, and adorns heaven with the most holy kings—whose kingdom and rule endure forever and ever.

[Col. 0935]

## Epitaph of Hugh the Great, son of King Robert

Composed by Gerard of Orléans. From an old manuscript of the most illustrious Alexander Petavius, senator of Paris.

[Col. 0935B]

> France, mourn the young man taken from you,  
> mourn the losses of you whose head had risen high.  
>   
> Strip off whatever you have; hasten to tear your garments,  
> tearing your hair and scattering ashes upon your head.  
>   
> Hugh, who could make the untamed enemy obedient,  
> the ancestral glory, the flower of young men, has fallen.  
>   
> Loved with wondrous affection because of his exceptional character,  
> now there are mourning and immeasurable grief.  
>   
> The Celtiberians weep; Rome sought you as king,  
> pitiable boy! Yet here you are buried.  
>   
> Handsome in appearance, merciful to the conquered, fierce toward enemies:  
> if you could have become a man, Babylon would have trembled before you.  
>   
> The Parthian, because of you, would have put away his weapons in his quiver,  
> and the world, appearing lesser, would have yielded its honor.  
>   
> Therefore may there be peace for you, which knows no bounds by enclosure.  
> We ask the reader to bend toward this and repeat it.

[Col. 0935]

# Letters of King Robert of the Franks

## First Letter: Robert to Leotheric, Archbishop of Sens

[Col. 0935C]

“Since your name is Knowledge, etc.” It appears above in the Life of Robert, column 912.

## Letter II: Robert to Gauzlin, Archbishop of Bourges

Around the year 1022.

ROBERT, by the will of God king of the Franks, sends greetings to GAUZLIN, bishop of Bourges.

I wish you to know how my mind is affected—just as can sometimes happen when the human mind is stirred, if something extraordinary and unexpected is heard. When, therefore, on Saturday, the day already spent, I was sitting at supper, a certain letter was brought to me [Col. 0935D] from Count William concerning a portent marvelous to hear of: namely, that three days before the solemnity of John the Baptist, in certain parts of my kingdom—specifically in the regions of Aquitaine, near the coastal district—blood of such a nature rained from heaven that, when by chance it fell upon human flesh, or upon clothing, or upon stone, it could not be removed by washing. If, however, it fell upon wood, then it could be washed away thoroughly.

Indeed, through the same letter Count William asked me to inquire of the wise men of my kingdom what this portent might signify. I therefore wish and ask you to search through certain histories to see whether anything similar has ever happened, and what event followed such a portent. Write back to me through this same messenger [Col. 0936C] how the matter occurred and in which history it may be found. I beg you, nevertheless, not to delay writing back to me, for I shall retain the messenger bearing this portent until you have answered me. Farewell.

## EPISTLE III. GAUZLIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, TO KING ROBERT  
*(Around the year 1022.)*

To the most excellent lord Robert, king of the Franks, humble Gauzlin sends fellowship with the eternal King.

What you were pleased to ask us concerning the prodigy that occurred is plainly revealed to us from the histories. That blood upon a sword portends either civil war or nation rising against nation, Valerius Rufus reports in the fourth chapter, “On Prodigies,” of his book *Memorable Deeds*:

> “In the consulship of Gaius Volumnius and Servilius Sulpicius, this prodigy portended the beginnings and outbreaks of civil wars in the city of Rome. Pieces of flesh, scattered in the form of a cloud, fell down. Birds flying overhead carried off the greater number of them; the remainder lay upon the ground for several days, altered neither by foul odor nor by a deformed appearance. In Sicily, two shields were seen to sweat blood; and bloody ears of grain fell into baskets for the reapers. At the town of Caere, waters mixed with blood flowed forth.”

Eusebius’s *Chronicle* reports the following concerning prodigies:

> “During the reign of Valentinian, after sunset, the sky in the north became like fire or blood. The invasion of the Huns into Gaul followed, after the peace had been broken.”

Likewise, in the seventh year of the Emperor Leo, blood burst forth from the earth in the middle of the city of Toulouse [Col. 0937A] and flowed throughout the entire day, signifying that the rule of the Goths had been overthrown.

Likewise, in Book III, chapter 6, of the *History of the Lombards*:

> “In the time of Theudebert, king of the Franks, a bloody sign appeared in the sky, resembling a bloody spear. At that time Theudebert himself, waging war against his uncle Lothar, severely afflicted Lothar’s army.”

Likewise, in the same history:

> “In the time of Justinian, a very great pestilence arose especially in the province of Liguria. Suddenly certain marks appeared on houses, doors, vessels, or clothing. If anyone wished to wash them away, they appeared more and more strongly. After a full year had passed, glands began to arise in the groins of human beings or in other weaker parts, in the form of a nut or a date; these were soon followed by an intolerable fever, so that a person died within three days. If, however, anyone survived three days, he had hope of living.

> “Everywhere there was fear, everywhere mourning, everywhere tears. For, as popular rumor reported the flight of the calamity from life, houses were abandoned by their inhabitants, with only puppies guarding them. Only the livestock remained, in the pastures with no shepherd present. You could see villas or fortresses previously filled with crowds of people become, on the following day, utterly silent, as everyone fled. Sons fled, leaving their parents’ corpses unburied. Parents, forgetting affection for their own flesh, abandoned their children in the fever. If some person was moved by ancient piety and wished to bury a neighbor, he himself remained unburied; and while performing the burial service, he was killed. While he rendered service to the dead, his own funeral remained without service.

> “You would have seen the world reduced to its ancient silence: no voice in the countryside, no whistle, no ambushes of wild beasts against the livestock, no damage to domestic birds. The crops, having passed the time for harvesting, awaited the reaper untouched. The vineyard, its shining leaves gone but its grapes still radiant, remained unharmed as winter approached. During the night or day, a crowd of combatants seemed to resound; many heard something like the murmur of an army. There were no tracks of travelers, no assailant could be seen; yet the number of corpses surpassed what the eye could take in. Pastoral places had been turned into burial grounds for human beings, and human dwellings had become refuges for beasts.” [Col. 0937D]

We have briefly recorded these few matters from the histories.

As for the fact that it fell upon stone and could not be washed away, this seems to signify the holy Church, which, founded upon the rock—that is, Christ—will suffer tribulation. That it fell upon human flesh and clothing and could be washed away may appropriately be understood as follows: by flesh, the people; by clothing, the substance granted to us for the support of this life.

By wood, moreover, the life-giving wood of the holy cross and baptism, by which we have been regenerated to life, are to be understood. Wood grows green through the moisture of water. And when the Jewish people thirsted in the wilderness and could not drink the waters because of their bitterness, Moses, at the Lord’s command, cast wood into the water, and the bitterness was changed into sweetness, and the people were refreshed. You are not ignorant of what Noah’s ark, built of wood, signifies.

In all these matters, the Lord worked nothing but his mercy through wood. Since, therefore, blood was washed away from wood, it is believed that through repentance, almsgiving, and the other fruits of mercy practiced within the bosom of Mother Church, the severity and indignation of God, the just Judge—which is deservedly owed to sinners—may be turned toward mercy.

For the Lord is merciful, as the Psalmist says, so merciful that he saves not only human beings but also animals.

May almighty God enlarge your rule, may his right hand always protect you, may he grant you a long life for the peace of holy Church, and may he adorn you with his blessing in all things.

## EPISTLE IV. FULCO, COUNT OF ANJOU, TO KING ROBERT  
*(Around the year 1022.)*

To his lord Robert, king, Fulco, count of Anjou, sends greetings and faithful service.

Count William of Poitiers, my lord, spoke to me recently and said that, after the Italians had departed from you, distrusting the prospect of having you as king, they asked that his son be made king. Although unwilling and compelled, he finally replied that he would yield to their will if all the margraves of Italy, the bishops, and the other leading men consented to it. They promised that they would bring all these men to consent in good faith, if they could.

He therefore now sends you word, humbly asking your favor, that you retain the men of [Col. 0938C] Lorraine, Duke Frederick, and as many others as you can, so that they do not come to an agreement with King Conrad, bending them as far as you can toward giving him assistance. For this business he will give you one thousand pounds of coin and one hundred cloaks, and to Lady Queen Constance five hundred pounds of money.

He asks you to greet her and your son the king on his behalf. I also ask that you inform me by letter or messenger what your mind is concerning this request he makes of you, so that I may report it to him. Farewell.

## EPISTLE V. COUNT ODO TO KING ROBERT  
*(In the year 1024.)*

To his lord King Robert, Count Odo.

[Col. 0938D] My lord, I wish to say a few things to you, if you will deign to hear them.

Count Richard, your faithful man, advised me to come to justice or to an agreement concerning the complaints he had against me. I placed the entire matter in his hands. Then, with your consent, he appointed a hearing for me, specifying when and where the matter could be settled.

But when the appointed time was approaching and I was prepared to undertake the matter, he ordered me not to weary myself by coming to the appointed hearing, because you were unwilling to accept any other justification or agreement than this alone: that you should maintain against me that I was unworthy to hold any benefice from you. He also said that it was not proper for him to present me for such a judgment without the assembly of his peers.

This is why I did not appear before you at the hearing. But I am greatly astonished at you, my lord, who judged me unworthy of your benefice so hastily, without the matter having been examined. For if regard is paid to the condition of my lineage, God’s grace would show that I am entitled to inherit. If regard is paid to the character of the benefice you gave me, it is clear that it does not come from your treasury, but from those possessions that, by your grace, come to me by hereditary right from my ancestors.

If regard is paid to the merit of my service, you yourself surely know how I served you—at home, in war, and abroad—so long as I possessed your favor. But after you turned your favor away from me and attempted to take from me the honor you had granted, if, in defending myself and my honor, I committed anything displeasing to you, I did so after being provoked by injuries and compelled by necessity.

For how can I surrender and not defend my honor? I call God and my soul to witness that I would choose to die honored rather than live dishonored. But if you cease wishing to dishonor me, there is nothing in the world that I desire more than either to possess or to earn your favor.

For your hostility is extremely painful to me; yet, my lord, it also removes from you the root and fruit of your office: I mean justice and peace. Therefore I humbly beseech that clemency which is naturally yours, unless evil counsel has taken it away, that at last you cease persecuting me and allow me to be reconciled to you either through your household or through the hands of leading men. Farewell.

# HYMNS AND RESPONSES ATTRIBUTED TO KING ROBERT

*(We publish the hymn on the Holy Spirit from Daniel, *Thesaurus hymnologicus*, vol. II, p. 35; the others were supplied by Clichtoveus, *Elucidatorium ecclesiasticum*, Paris, 1521, folio, vol. II, pp. 37, 206, 207, 217, 230, 141, 121. See the literary notice above.)*

## I. Hymn on the Holy Spirit

*[Note: All lovers of sacred songs, whoever and however many they were, considered the royal poet, singing the Lord’s name in the likeness of David, worthy to be exalted with the highest praises. Clichtoveus says very well: “This prayer, in my judgment, cannot be commended enough, for it surpasses every commendation. I would readily believe that the author—whoever he may have been—when he composed it was inwardly suffused with a certain heavenly sweetness, through which, with the Holy Spirit as his author, he poured forth such sweetness in his concise words.” Hence it is hardly surprising that the Sequence printed above was used in many churches, especially on the Monday of Pentecost. For in the Sunday liturgy the chant “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us,” which bore the mark of greater antiquity, established its place almost everywhere. As matters now stand, since from the universal destruction of Sequences that took place in the sixteenth century only Robert, together with three other poets, escaped unharmed, this hymn is sung on the solemnity of Pentecost “and is said every day through the following Saturday, inclusively.” Nor did our poem fall silent in Luther’s Church; it is nevertheless regrettable that no one rendered the Sequence elegantly and sweetly into German. For an older translation, see *Altd. Bl.* IV, p. 379.

—2. Matthew 5:3, “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

—4. *Aug.*, “and in weeping.”

—6. *Pm. Torr.*, “in light.” All the editors of the poem thought that its verses ended in *homoioteleuton* [similarity of ending]. The sixth stanza is praised in the Augsburg Confession.

—7. *M. 12*, “heal”—*riga* [“water”].

—8. *Pr.*, “restore what.”

—9. *M. 12, 17. Fr. Es.*, “with sacred sevenfold [gifts].” These books make the ninth stanza very closely connected with the tenth.

—Finally, do not overlook the artistic structure of the entire poem. The poet asks only that the Holy Spirit come and give his gifts to the faithful. He therefore begins: “Come,” and again requests the holy gift by repeating the word “Come” three times. In a similar fashion, stanza nine presents the word “Give” in its first position; after two intervening verses, it is pronounced three times in stanza ten.]*

[1.] Come, Holy Spirit,

and send forth from heaven

the ray of your light.

[2.] Come, Father of the poor,

come, giver of gifts,

come, light of hearts.

[3.] Best of consolers,

sweet guest of the soul,

sweet refreshment.

[4.] Rest in toil,

relief in the heat,

comfort in weeping.

[5.] O most blessed light,

fill the innermost depths

of the hearts of your faithful.

[6.] Without your divine power

nothing is in a human being,

nothing is innocent.

[7.] Wash what is dirty,

water what is dry,

heal what is wounded.

[8.] Bend what is rigid,

warm what is cold,

guide what has gone astray.

[9.] Give your faithful,

who trust in you,

the sacred sevenfold gift.

[10.] Give the merit of virtue,

give the outcome of salvation,

give everlasting joy.

## II. Hymn for Eastertide

May the choir of the new Jerusalem,

with the new sweetness of honey,

bring forth its song, celebrating

the Paschal feast with sober joys.

When Christ, the unconquered lion,

rising after the dragon had been crushed,

resounds with a living voice,

he raises the dead to life.

The wicked underworld restores the prey

that it had devoured;

freed from captivity,

the hosts follow Jesus.

He triumphs magnificently

and, worthy of greatness,

makes the realm of the sun and sky

one commonwealth.

Let us, his suppliant soldiers,

pleading in song, beseech the King

to place us in his

most glorious palace.

Through ages that know no end,

glory to the supreme Father;

and honor be to the Son

and to the Spirit, the Paraclete.

Amen.

## III. Another hymn for Eastertide

Let the songs of these assemblies,

which you have filled with grace

through the power of the Resurrection,

resound to you, author of light.

This day signifies to us

that the final day will come,

on which it will be permitted

for the dead to rise and be restored to life.

The first octave is restored,

when death is taken away from the waters,

when we are circumcised in mind,

and at last are born anew.

When we see our morning

return after the enemies have been defeated,

we reject the world’s luxury

and take the bread of salvation.

May this be a life-giving solemnity;

may this festival be bright;

may this day, restored from the underworld,

be given over to rejoicing.

Amen.

## IV. Prose for the Ascension of the Lord

The almighty King, on this day,

after the world had been redeemed

by his triumphant power,

ascended into the heavens from which he had descended.

For, after he had risen, forty

sacred days having passed, he strengthened

the hearts of the apostles, leaving them

the dear kisses of peace.

To them he also gave the power

to release sins,

and sent them into the world

to baptize all souls,

in the mercy of the Father,

the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

And while eating with them,

he commanded them not to depart

from Jerusalem, but to await

the promised gifts.

“For after not many days

I shall send you the Paraclete Spirit

on earth.

[Col. 0942A] And you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, and Samaria.”

And when he had said this, while they watched, he was lifted up, and a bright cloud received him from their eyes, as they gazed into the air.

Behold, two men clothed in white garments stood beside them, saying:

“Why are you amazed at the heights of heaven?

For this Jesus, who has been taken up from you to the right hand of the Father,

will come in the same way as he ascended,

seeking the profits of the talent entrusted to you.”

O God of sea, sky, and field,

you created the human being;

the enemy, by crafty deception,

drove him from paradise

and dragged him captive with himself [Col. 0942B] to the underworld.

With your own blood you redeemed him, O God;

there you lead him back,

from where he had previously fallen from the glory of paradise.

Judge, when you come to judge the ages,

grant us, we ask, everlasting joys

in the homeland of the saints,

where we may all sing alleluia to you.

Amen.

## V. Prose for Pentecost

May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us,

which makes our hearts its dwelling,

after all spiritual vices have been expelled from them.

Nourishing Spirit, enlightener of human beings,

cleanse the dreadful darkness of our mind . . .

Holy lover of pure thoughts,

mercifully pour your anointing into our senses.

Spirit, purifier of all offenses,

purify the eye of our inner person,

so that the supreme Father may be seen by us,

whom only the eyes of a pure heart can behold.

You inspired the prophets

to proclaim beforehand the illustrious praises of Christ;

you strengthened the apostles

so that they might carry Christ’s trophy throughout the world.

When God made, through his Word,

the structure of heaven, earth, and the seas,

you spread out your divine power over the waters,

to nurture them.

You make the waters fruitful

for the giving of life to souls.

By your breathing you make human beings spiritual.

You, Lord, united the world,

divided by languages and rites;

you call idolaters back to the worship of God,

best of teachers.

Therefore hear us, your suppliants,

in your mercy, Holy Spirit,

without whom all prayers are believed to be empty

and unworthy of God’s ears.

You, Spirit, who have taught the saints of all ages, by the prompting of your divine power, to embrace [it],

today, by granting Christ’s apostles

a gift extraordinary and unheard-of

through all the ages,

have made this day glorious.

Amen.

## VI. Response

As the Lord entered the holy city, the children of the Hebrews, proclaiming the resurrection of life, cried “Hosanna in the highest” with branches of palm.

—Verse: When the people heard that Jesus had come to Jerusalem, they went out to meet him with branches, etc.

—Antiphon: Hail, our King, Son of David, Redeemer of the world, whom the prophets foretold would come as Savior to the house of Israel. For the Father sent you into the world as a saving victim; all the saints from the beginning of the world were awaiting you. And now: Hosanna to the Son of David.

## VII. On the same feast, another response

At the Lord’s command, who enriches our honor: just as the thorn produced the rose, Judea gave birth to Mary.

—Verse: So that grace might cover fault and virtue might cover vice. Just as the thorn produced the rose, etc.

## VIII. On Septuagesima

My sins, Lord, have been fixed in me like arrows. But before they produce wounds in me, heal me, Lord God, with the medicine of repentance.

—Verse: For I know my iniquity, and my offense is always before me; against you alone I have sinned. But before they produce wounds, etc.

## IX. In Lent

Let us amend for the better what we have sinned through ignorance, lest, suddenly overtaken on the day of death, we seek time for repentance and be unable to find it.

Attend, Lord, and have mercy, for we have sinned against you.

—Verse: We sinned with our fathers; we acted unjustly; we committed iniquity. Attend, etc.

### Sunday in Passiontide

Lying men surrounded me; without cause they struck me with blows. But you, Lord, my defender, avenge me.

—Verse: For tribulation is near, and there is no one to help. But you, Lord, etc.

## X. In Eastertide

Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him. For what he lives, he lives for God. Alleluia, alleluia.

—Verse: Let the Jews now say how the soldiers guarding the tomb lost the King when the stone was set in place. Why did they not guard the Rock of justice? Let them either return him buried, or worship him with us as risen, saying: For what he lives, etc.

## XI. On the day of the Lord’s Ascension

After his passion, he appeared to them for forty days, speaking about the kingdom of God. Alleluia. And while they watched, he was lifted up. Alleluia. And a cloud received him from their eyes. Alleluia.

—Verse: And while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the Father’s promise. And while they watched, etc.

## XII. On Pentecost

When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together, saying: Alleluia. And suddenly a sound came from heaven, alleluia. Like a rushing wind, it filled the whole house, alleluia, alleluia.

—Verse: They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak. Like a rushing wind, etc.

## XIII. On the feast of the Sacrament of the Eucharist

A certain man made a great supper and sent his servant at supper time to tell those who had been invited to come, [Col. 0944B] because everything was ready.

—Verse: Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you. Because everything was ready, etc.

### On the same feast, another response

Elijah looked toward his head and saw a cake baked under the ashes. He rose, ate, and drank, and walked in the strength of that food as far as the mountain of God.

—Verse: If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And he walked, etc.

### On the same feast, another response

Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.

—Verse: What other nation is so great that it has gods who draw near to it, as our God is present with us? He remains in me, etc.

## XIV. At the Dedication of a Church

Bless, Lord, this house that I have built for your name; hear, from the lofty throne of your glory, the prayers of those who come to this place.

—Verse: Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you. Hear the prayers from the lofty throne.

### On the same feast, another response

Terrible is this place. This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven. Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.

—Verse: When Jacob awoke as though from a deep sleep, he said: Truly, etc.

## XV. Of several martyrs

O praiseworthy steadfastness of the martyrs! O undying charity! O unconquerable patience!

Although, amid the pressures of persecutors, it may appear contemptible, it will be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the time of recompense.

—Verse: Therefore we ask that it come to our aid through its holy merits, honored by the Father who is in heaven. It will be found to result in praise, etc.

## XVI. Response for Advent

“Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign and be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice on the earth. And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteous one.”

—Verse: In those days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name.

## XVII. Response for the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

Judea and Jerusalem, do not fear. Tomorrow you shall go forth, and the Lord will be with you.

—Verse: Stand firm; you shall see the Lord’s help over you. Tomorrow you shall go forth.

## XVIII. Response for the Nativity of the Lord — Of the Blessed Virgin

Holy and immaculate virginity, with what praises I should exalt you I do not know, because you carried in your womb him whom the heavens could not contain.

—Verse: Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb, because, etc.

### At the Purification of Blessed Mary

Rejoice, Virgin Mary: you alone have destroyed all heresies, you who believed the words of the archangel Gabriel.

While remaining a Virgin, you gave birth to God and man.

And after giving birth you remained an inviolate Virgin.

—Verse: We know that the archangel Gabriel spoke to you by divine command.

[Col. 0946A] We believe that your womb was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit.

Let the unhappy Jew be ashamed, who says that Christ was born from Joseph’s seed.

While remaining a Virgin, etc.

## XIX. In commemoration of the Blessed Virgin

For you are happy indeed, holy Virgin Mary, and most worthy of all praise,

because from you has arisen the sun of justice, Christ our God.

—Verse: Pray for the people; intervene for the clergy; intercede for the devout female sex.

Let all who celebrate your commemoration experience your help.

Because from you, etc.

## XX. On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin

The star of the sea, Mary, has come forth today

to give birth to the sun of justice,

the supreme King.

—Verse:

Faithful ones, rejoice to behold the divine light.

Star of the sea, etc.

# DIPLOMAS OF ROBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS

## I. Diploma of Kings Hugh and Robert concerning the election of abbots and the church of Saint Leodegar at Campellis  
*(In the year 994.)*

*[Note: The monastery at Campellis mentioned here was situated in the diocese of Langres, not far from Bèze. It was entirely different from the collegiate church at Campellis in the diocese of Paris, in the region of Brie, which is mentioned in the Life of Saint Medericus, included in the Benedictine *Saeculum tertium*, part 1. It is also called the monastery of the blessed martyr Leodegar known as Campellis, at the beginning of Book V of Glaber, who spent some time there as a monk.]*

[Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Book VI, p. 598, from the cartulary of Saint-Germain of Auxerre.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Hugh and Robert, illustrious kings by the grace of God.

The benevolence and excellence of kings ought not merely to strengthen the wishes of all our military men devoted to our service, insofar as these wishes are fitting for good men, but also to supply them with magnificent assistance, to encourage them with kindly favor, and indeed to advance them with every power of goodwill. For let the king know that he becomes a participant in great and eternal reward when, in whatever manner, he involves himself in the things of God. Moreover, he will not be deprived of the magnificence of the most benign Jesus, the author, provider, and supporter of virtue, when he assists on his behalf what is undertaken according to God’s will. For he himself, with the greatest kindness, is the rewarder of all things done through love of almighty God.

Therefore the benevolence of kings, by whose authority the things that are bestowed upon the houses of God ought to remain fixed and undisturbed, trusting in the most merciful compassion of Jesus, awaits the just rewards of eternal life.

Accordingly, rejoicing in the holy will of the great and most honorable Duke of Burgundy, named Henry, we authorize, confirm, and establish forever, without disturbance, the matters that he has brought to our attention through the venerable abbot named Hilderic—for all these requests of his are worthy.

That abbot, a man full of God, petitioning on his part for the things upheld by the religion of Saint Benedict, indeed by the inviolable authority of the canons, asks that the place of his abbey, established in the territory of Auxerre under the honor of Saint Germanus, should have a permanent election of abbots according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

Therefore, agreeing with the will of this duke—our brother, whose wish is just—and with the abbot’s embassy, because it is right, we exhort by petition and command by royal authority that no one be appointed there as abbot except one whom the united company of all the brothers has elected in the fear of God.

We place the protection of this abbey under the hand of the kings, or perhaps of the dukes of his kingdom, so that none of the nobles may dare to invade it or even seek to do so.

We remove hostile customs from it in such a way that from this time into eternity it suffers no adversity, but serves God freely, free from every injury.

Because the duke loves this place—choosing that same patron, Saint Germanus, as his special patron in heaven before God—he enlarged it by constructing from his own patrimony a small abbey in honor of the holy martyr Leodegar, called Campellis, and likewise restored to it the estate of Magniacum.

This was done so that there should always be eight monks in the aforesaid small abbey, subject to the abbot presiding over the place of Saint Germanus. These monks may neither withdraw their allegiance from the place of Saint Germanus nor place anyone above themselves except the abbot of Saint Germanus.

If that abbot should enlarge the little place, through his own efforts or through the generosity of good men, beyond eight monks, may he merit the favor of the Almighty here and in heaven for the reward of this benefit.

Therefore, so that we may deserve to share in this good deed, we have irrevocably strengthened this decree of our authority with our seal, and we wish it to be observed lawfully throughout all ages.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the eighth year of the reigns of Kings Hugh and Robert. Issued, in God’s name, successfully [at the monastery] of Saint-Denis.

## II. Robert’s decree confirming the possessions which Count Burchard and Bishop Rainald gave to the monastery of Fosses  
*(In the year 998.)*

[Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Book VI, p. 598, from the Fosses cartulary.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, by the merciful providence of God, king of the Franks.

If, for love of God and of the benefits of those who serve him in places devoted to divine worship, we generously bestow useful gifts, we do not doubt that the reward of eternal recompense will be paid to us by the Lord.

Therefore let the discernment and diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that a certain venerable bishop of the holy Church of Paris, named Rainald, and his father, the God-beloved Count Burchard, approached our serenity, humbly requesting that we graciously grant and confirm by a decree of our authority the possessions that they had given to the monastery of Fosses, dedicated in honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and blessed Maurus, a disciple of Father Benedict, who rests in that same place.

They had given these possessions to the abbot of that place, named Teuto, and to the brothers serving God there, for the reward of eternal life, for the absolution of their souls, and for the soul of Countess Elisabeth.

At the urging and intercession of our beloved ones—namely, our sweetest mother Adelaide and our wife Berta—we gladly favor their requests and confirm, by a decree of our munificence, the gift made to the aforesaid abbot [editorial addition: and] to the remaining monks of the aforesaid church.

By this decree we prescribe and command that from this day forward the aforesaid abbot and the other monks of the aforesaid monastery may freely possess those possessions that are in the county of Paris: namely, the estate called Nobiliacus, with its advocacy and vicariate, with its church and altar, free from synod and *circada*, with woods, vineyards, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and all its appurtenances.

Likewise, in the same county, they gave a church situated in the village called Nosiacus, through the intercession of Goscelin [or Roscelin?], viscount of Melun, who held it from their benefice.

Likewise, in the same county, in the estate called Licias, the holding of Algardis, with vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and everything belonging to it; and in the county of Melun, one allod called Curciacus, with advocacy and vicariate, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and everything pertaining to it.

And in the county of Gâtinais, another allod called Seia, with advocacy and church, with water and a fishery, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, they shall suitably hold and possess without any authority of the vicars.

For this reason we also command that no king, no bishop, no count, and no power whatsoever presume to dispose of these possessions or to decide or delegate any of them under his authority. Rather, they shall remain in perpetuity, with secure stability, in the power of the aforesaid brothers to dispose of them or do with them whatever they choose.

And so that this decree of our prescription and confirmation may retain inviolable and firm force throughout all ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the tenth year, while the glorious King Robert was reigning. Publicly issued in the city of Paris, in the year 998 of the Incarnation of the Word.

## III. Decree of King Robert by which he confirms the grants made to the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre by earlier kings and others  
*(Around the year 1002.)*

[Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Book VI, p. 600, from the cartulary of Saint-Germain of Auxerre.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, by the favoring mercy of the Divinity, king.

[Col. 0948D] It belongs to royal dignity to extend itself toward the worship of religion with piety and justice, and to listen with willing hearts to the devout petitions of God’s servants. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of God’s holy Church know that the venerable abbot Heldric of the monastery of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, accompanied by the community of monks of that place, brought before our majesty a certain charter of royal munificence obtained and granted to the aforesaid monastery by our grandfather Hugh the Great, and humbly requested that it be renewed by our authority and transmitted to posterity. Thus we might grant, by this testimony of our sanction, the privileges of the apostles and all the charters of our predecessors—namely, the kings—which had been inserted into that charter; [Col. 0949A] so that, in accordance with their authenticity and the contents of their grants, they might remain perpetual and unshaken and endure inviolate.

We readily assented to their petition, especially out of regard for the memory of our glorious uncle, Lord Henry, duke of Burgundy, and of his brother Otto, who devoted themselves in a particular way to that place under the protection of blessed Germanus, so that they might also be committed to burial there. We too therefore commit, entrust, and exalt that place to sacred reverence rather than to any form of subjection. We again confirm all the charters and authorities by an edict of our assent; and we wish the community itself to remain quiet and free under our fullest protection. We decree that everything belonging to that monastery, or seeming in any way to pertain to it, [Col. 0949B] shall remain inviolate by our authority, and we receive it under the governance of our protection. Thus, under our protection, they may live peacefully and, by living, remain at peace.

No bishop, nor any of the episcopal officials, shall presume to exercise judgment there; and no public judge, no collector of judicial authority, no one of our faithful, nor any person, great or small, shall dare to enter upon any matters subject to that place in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, constrain the men of that monastery—whether slaves or free men—who dwell upon the land of the same monastery, or seek unlawful pretexts in our time or in the future. [Col. 0949C] Rather, let the monks of the aforesaid monastery be permitted to possess peacefully, under a single charter of immunity, the properties assigned to their support.

Therefore we order that neither the monks themselves, nor their merchants, nor the men who seem to place their hopes in that house of God, be compelled to pay toll in cities, villages, or estates, at markets, harbors, or gates, as is contained in the charter of the most glorious Emperor Charles.
