We command by ordering, and confirm by commanding, that no abbot of that place, nor any other person, be permitted to divert or apply any of all the aforesaid properties to uses other than those we have established, or to grant any of them to someone else to possess. Nor may anyone presume in any way to demand from them rent, honor-payment, gifts of any kind, [Col. 0949D] or the feeding of dogs or horses on their estates, or any services received from those servants of God, except according to religious custom for the sake of hospitality. Rather, whatever can be done from those properties shall, in accordance with what has been prescribed, be held at all times, by regular administration, for their uses and advantages, with God as its author.

Meanwhile, we wish and confirm that whatever those who come from the world to that monastery to pursue a regular way of life, with God’s favor, offer or transfer from their possessions, or whatever other people may give, shall always remain and endure inviolate, without alteration, according as their intention and gift are shown to have been made.

We also grant that community permission to elect an abbot for itself [Col. 0950A] according to regular institution when another has died. And lest they ever be reduced under the domination of any bishop, and lest any bishop presume to demand that abbey from the royal majesty or to trouble or disturb the monks, we prohibit all such actions absolutely by this charter of our authority.

If anyone should attempt to become a rash violator or despiser of this authority of ours, let him not obtain what he seeks; moreover, for contempt of royal majesty, let him be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of refined gold, half to our treasury and half to the monks themselves. As for the other provisions of the aforesaid immunity, let punishment be exacted from those who despise them.

And so that this confirmation or charter of our high authority may always possess stronger validity, we have subscribed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Done publicly in the city of Auxerre.

## IV. Diploma of King Robert of the Franks for the monastery of Saint-Magloire at Paris (c. 1002)

[Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 107, from the autograph document of Marmoutier.]

In the name of the supreme and incomprehensible Trinity, existing in the unity of the Godhead, Robert, august king of the Franks, by the disposition of the clemency of the aforesaid Godhead, with the queens Adelaide, his venerable mother, and his most noble wife Berta by name intervening, we wish it to be clearly known to all living under our authority, of whatever order.

While we live, move, and exist subject to God and his saints, it is fitting that we should be moved by the flood of error affecting us and our people, and beseech the merits of the saints and ceaselessly implore them, so that through their intercession we may be able to live in peace and, after the end of this fleeting age, contemplate the God of gods in holy Zion. Therefore, considering it the proper course that what is reckoned to us for the profit of the talent entrusted to us, and what is granted to the Lord and his faithful, should remain inviolate and undefiled, and moved also by mercy toward the poor and by the entreaty of the aforesaid honorable queens, [Col. 0950D] with the assent of our nobles, we have issued a charter of permanence concerning the properties which our father, King Hugh of blessed memory, and we ourselves piously granted to the monks serving Christ and the most holy Magloire, who rests in the city of Paris. There we also founded a monastery for the aforesaid outstanding confessor and the other saints assigned there, on account of their bodies, which, as strangers, had been lodging across the lands of others.

First, there is the land on which the monastery itself stands, and the estate which we gave on the day of the translation of the saints, called Villaris, with the entirety of what belongs to it, and the chapel consecrated there in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. Likewise, there are the other properties previously given, of which the first is the little church in the Parisian suburb, not far from the walls, [Col. 0951A] dedicated in honor of Saint Magloire, with the land adjoining it, in which the burial place of those monks is situated. There is also the enclosed vineyard situated beside Saveias, which our grandfather Hugh of divine memory, the son of our namesake King Robert, gave.

Likewise, there is part of the land beside Montmartre which Count Fulk gave. There is also the small estate which William granted near the aforesaid mountain. There is also the estate in the county of Melun called Grandis Campus, and the estate called Alodus in the county of Paris beside Fontenay.

There are also churches in the county of Poissy: first, one in the estate of Madrie, dedicated in honor of Saint Denis, with the chapel situated at Marolles, founded in honor of Saint Martin. Another church at Vernoil, dedicated to Saint Stephen, and in the same village a chapel [Col. 0951B] consecrated to Saint Hilary. Finally, there is the little church in the village called Saint-Leodegarius, which is known to be blessed in his name.

There are also three manses which Riculfus held in benefice from the aforesaid estate of Madrie, in the bishopric and county of Paris. There is a church sanctified in the name of Saint Mary, and in the same county, in the estate of Issy, nineteen arpents of vineyards and meadows. Likewise, at Vigneux, five arpents of vineyard. In the estate of Châtrons, one mansus of arable land with a productive vineyard; and in the aforesaid county, in the village called Montium, one mansus of arable land with an abundant vineyard.

In the same territory, above the river Vigenne, there is half a small estate called Murcinctus, with an abundance of meadows. Nearby there is another small estate called Sienis-Villere, with a chapel built there in honor of Saint Genevieve. In the county of Orléans there is the estate called Cilliniacus with everything adjoining it. There is also one mill at Paris on the river Seine. Likewise, in the county of Orléans, a church in the village called Gimminiacus.

We confirm by our authority all the aforesaid properties, and whatever thereafter may be offered to that church by Catholic men out of love for God and reverence for those saints, so that they may remain strengthened forever under our fullest protection and the safeguard of immunity. Thus, from this time forward, no one shall dare to enter upon them in our time or in the future in order to hear cases or exact fines or taxes, demand lodging [Col. 0951D] or provisions, take sureties, unjustly constrain the men of that church—whether free or enslaved—who dwell upon their land, or seek any restitutions or unlawful pretexts; nor shall anyone presume to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the properties of the aforesaid monastery peacefully under the protection of our immunity, for the support of the monks serving God there, and let them prosper in increase throughout perpetual ages.

We also wish the assent of all our bishops and counts to agree on this point: that the same place shall always have an abbot from its own community, who will care for and administer that house of God and the monks living there [Col. 0952A] with the proper honor. Likewise, no metropolitan, nor any subordinate of his—not even the bishop of Paris—shall presume to enter there on account of any ordination, unless he comes when summoned, whether to celebrate holy Mass, consecrate churches, or perform the blessings of clerics; and whoever has been summoned must not refuse the duty owed.

And since they are known to be pilgrims and foreigners, they must always be treated and protected kindly, mercifully, and piously by benevolent and Catholic men for the sake of Christ, from whom all of us likewise wander as pilgrims in the world.

We have also decreed by the authority of our charter that no one shall exercise power over those servants of God or attempt to impose anyone among them against their will. Rather, everything within and outside shall remain in their own disposition, administration, and election, so that the servants of God who serve him there may safely and worthily pour out prayers to the Lord for us, for the stability of the whole kingdom granted to us by God, and for the remedy of the souls of those who, out of love for God and the saints, have offered their gifts there, as well as of those who in future will give their rewards.

And so that this authority may be regarded as firmer in the name of God, and may be more diligently preserved by the faithful of holy God’s Church and by our own people, we have subscribed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Place of the monogram.

The chancellor Rotgerius wrote this.

[Col. 0952C] Place of the seal.

## V. Privilege of King Robert for the monastery of Fécamp

It confirms the restoration of the monks of Fécamp made by Count Richard and the donations made by him to that place (1006).

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, IV, 185.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, king by the favor of divine clemency.

Since we are counted among those who are designated by the royal name, it would be exceedingly impious, if we cannot devoutly fulfill in every respect the duty of that name, to pass over everything ineffectively. Therefore, the just cause of the church of Fécamp, which we visited for the sake of prayer and by which we are petitioned, we both kindly receive and gratefully fulfill. Let it therefore be known to those present and those to come that we have been entreated by the pious petition of our beloved and faithful Count Richard to confirm by our charter the properties which he gave to this place, consecrated in honor of the consubstantial and undivided holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and secured by a written testament.

Having gladly heard his prayers, as was just, we willingly undertook to fulfill them. For the intention of the pious Richard the elder led him to build this place so that a community of monks might live there under the rule of Saint Benedict and serve the praises of God. Since death intervened and prevented him from fulfilling that desire, his pious son Richard, his namesake, undertook to fulfill it; and, having found Lord Abbot William by divine providence, he appointed him master and rector of the monastic observance that is seen there.

Under him, as the number of monks increased, this younger Count Richard strove to enlarge its temporal resources. In the county of Caux, in the village of Fécamp itself, a third part of the hospites, whom they call settlers, [lacuna] one part of the forest, bounded from the public road to the sea; to it he also gave, in the city of Rouen, the church of Saint Paternus with one mansus, where it is situated, etc.

These properties, and everything given by the count himself or by his father, everything granted by our generosity, and whatever any faithful person may thereafter confer upon this place, we sanction and confirm, etc.

In the election, appointment, or consecration of the abbot, let the custom be followed among them which has until now been most illustriously preserved in the monastery of Cluny, from which the source of holy monastic religion has already flowed far and wide through many places, and from which, by God’s favor, it has flowed even to this place.

We leave nothing to any bitter usurper by which the service of God there could be impeded. Rather, whatever our predecessors have granted by royal authority to any monastery for the preservation of secure peace, we most willingly assent to here, in this place dedicated to the honor of the holy Trinity, even if these things are not fully recorded in writing. May the holy observance which, with the Lord’s assistance, now flourishes there in a worthy manner of religious life not fail, but advance more and more for the benefit both of our souls [Col. 0953C] and of the souls of all the faithful.

Just as we have decreed that we shall leave the right of dominion over this place to no order, dignity, power, or hereditary succession—not even to our own majesty—so we deny no one who wishes to earn a worthy reward from Christ the authority to restore its inhabitants to their former condition if, God forbid, they should at some time depart from the upright purpose so well begun.

And so that the authority of our confirmation may possess inviolate and unshaken permanence, we have decreed that it be marked with the sign of our ring and monogram.

Done at Fécamp in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1006, indiction four, on the third day before the Kalends of June, the fifth feria, in the most celebrated joy of the Lord’s Ascension, [Col. 0953D] successfully.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] The chronological notices agree very closely.]

## VI. Diploma of King Robert confirming the foundation of the nunnery of Beaumont near Tours (1007)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 696.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, king by the mercy of God.

If we appear to assent to the petitions of God’s servants who appeal to us concerning any ecclesiastical needs, and extend assistance so that service in the divine host may be rendered more abundantly in places dedicated to God, we are confident that this will undoubtedly prove advantageous to us both for passing through the present life in temporal prosperity and for happily attaining the future life.

Therefore we wish it to be thoroughly known to all Christ’s faithful and our own, both present and future, that Hervé, levite and chief key-bearer of blessed Martin, approached the serene height of our majesty, humbly begging and, in his begging, earnestly requesting that by the authority of our charter we should issue a charter for him concerning the church of Blessed Mary of Beaumont, situated not far from the castle of Father Martin, together with all the properties belonging to it, namely vineyards and meadows, for which he had given his faithful man Eblon land in exchange, land no less valuable for producing revenue than the church named above; and concerning a certain fishpond called Malamorta.

He also petitioned concerning the estate of Soriniacus and the church founded in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with everything belonging to it—vineyards, meadows, woods, and waters, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands—as well as concerning twenty arpents of vineyards which seem to lie near the suburb of the aforesaid town of the confessor of Christ, situated between the channels of the Loire and the Cher.

When we had carefully asked him what work he intended to undertake with the aforesaid properties, he replied that he was greatly saddened that there was no monastery in the county of Tours where holy women might devote the service of their devotion to Christ, as was found in many regions of the earth. For this reason, and for no other, he sought to have the document made, on the condition that every year, on the autumn feast of the aforesaid Father Martin, the said holy women would pay twenty solidi from all the properties listed above as rent into the treasury, for the purchase of incense or oil.

Moreover, not forgetting himself, he added that the virgins who would serve God there should daily pour out prayers to the Lord, first for me and my successors, then for himself and for the welfare of his whole community and of his advocate Martin.

Thus, having presented these matters, Hervé approached the excellence of our rule with humble prayer and requested that we likewise strengthen by the assertion of our authority whatever he himself might give in the future, or whatever other faithful men of Christ might give [reading: “other faithful men”], for the redemption of their souls [Col. 0954D].

We were pleased to assent to this most salutary petition, beneficial both to him and, according to the emendation, to us, for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents, and to confirm in the form of a written charter everything mentioned above. That is: the church of Blessed Mary of Beaumont, with everything adjoining it, namely vineyards, meadows, and the fishpond called Malamorta, for the food of the aforesaid handmaids of God; the church of Soriniacus, with its church and everything adjoining it—that is, vineyards, meadows, woods, waters, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands—and with all the tenant farmers of that estate; [Col. 0955A] also twenty arpents of vineyards between the Loire and the Cher; and the estate of Liura, with its churches and everything belonging to it, with the consent of Count Odo and his brother Landric, from whose benefice it appeared to derive, four miles distant from the castle called Île; and also the village of Quiciacus with everything belonging to it, which the aforesaid Hervé himself appeared to hold.

Therefore, ordering, we command, and commanding, we order that no public judge or administrator of the commonwealth, of either higher or lower rank, presume to enter these aforesaid properties of Saint Mary—whether churches, villages, or any possessions which the basilica of Saint Mary now or in former times justly holds in any provinces or territories of our kingdom, or which divine mercy may thereafter wish to increase in the right of that basilica—in order to hear cases according to judicial custom.

Nor shall anyone so rashly dare to exact fines, taxes, lodging, provisions, or toll from any transactions, as is contained, as we have said, in the charters of many kings; nor take sureties, constrain men—whether free or enslaved—dwelling upon the land of that basilica, or seek any public services, restitutions, or unlawful pretexts.

If anyone should dare to burst forth into such audacity as to presume to violate this charter of our authority and high dignity, let him know that, as is contained in the other charters of our royal and imperial predecessors and ancestors, he will not only fall under the displeasure of Christ and ourselves, but will also be punished by a fine of two hundred solidi of fully refined gold.

And so that the authority of this charter of ours may achieve an inviolate effect, and that it may more truly be believed by all the faithful of holy God’s Church and by our royal successors to have been made by us, and may be preserved with inviolate diligence, we have marked it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lord Hugh, archbishop.

Sign of Bishop Avesgaud. Whoever presumes to violate this charter knows himself bound by their excommunication, unless he quickly repents and comes to make amends.

Count Odo, etc.

Odolgerius, dean; Hervé, chief treasurer; Walter, precentor; etc. [Col. 0955D]

Done in the forest of Boulogne, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1007, indiction five. The levite Theodoricus, acting in place of Francon, chief chancellor, reviewed this charter. I, Hervé, and my fellow canons of Saint Martin confirmed it in full chapter.

## VII. Diploma of King Robert of the Franks for the monastery of Corbie

It restrains the unjust customs and oppressions of Elfredi of Encre, advocate of Corbie (1016).

[D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 379, from the autograph document.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, R[obert], by the grace of God king of the Franks.

[Col. 0956A] I wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church, both present and future, that in our times the malignity of perverse men has prevailed, so that the condition and justice of holy mother Church seemed daily to diminish, especially at the hands of those who ought to be the advocates and defenders of holy places but instead become their plunderers and robbers.

For this reason, since I was often petitioned by the venerable Herbert, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, who frequently experiences this pernicious evil from the wicked and malignant Efredus, his soldier and the aforesaid monastery’s advocate, I have learned that, whenever he is summoned to a royal expedition, he demands that the expenses of his journey be prepared for him by the men of that monastery. Or, if he is returning from some journey and night overtakes him, he orders lodging in the abbey and service for himself to be provided by the men of the village where he lodges. If any offense of whatever kind occurs among the men under his advocacy, he demands to have the full legal justice.

If something needs to be repaired in his castle at Encre, he compels the men of the aforesaid monastery to go to that work.

It has therefore been established by our judgment and that of our nobles that, although he holds his benefice from the abbey itself on account of his advocacy, he ought not to exercise the aforesaid customs against that monastery, except if the abbot of the place should have to go on a royal expedition and order him to go with him, or command him to go on his own with his soldiers. Then he may demand his expenses from the advocacy, but not without reason. [Col. 0956C]

Nor shall he have any other legal jurisdiction in the abbey, unless the abbot’s mayor, his provost, or the abbot himself is unable to exact justice from him when he has committed an offence against him; and from that legal jurisdiction he shall receive one-third.

Nor shall the advocate’s castle be built or repaired by compulsion of the abbot’s men. Nor shall he eat in any village of the abbey unless the abbot has invited him, or the provost of the village has done so for his own advantage. Nor shall he compel any man of the abbey to appear at his court on any pretext, nor demand from him a cause of contempt.

Therefore, if Efredus himself or his successors should presume to violate this sanction of ours and of our nobles, let them incur the penalty for our contempt, the condemnation of the dread judgment, and perpetual excommunication. [Col. 0956D]

This constitution was enacted in the village called Pont-Sainte-Maxence, while the glorious King Robert was reigning, in the twentieth year, indiction fourteen.

+ Sign of Robert, glorious king.

## VIII. Charter of King Robert by which he grants the chapel of Saint John the Evangelist, situated in the city of Autun, to the monks of Flavigny at the request of Abbot Amadeus (1018)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, p. 257.]

In the name of the supreme Trinity and undivided Unity, I, Robert, king by the grace and kindness of Jesus the Redeemer.

[Col. 0957A] We wish it to be made known to the diligence of all the faithful of holy mother Church, of the present as well as of the future age, that a certain Amadeus, abbot of the monastery of Flavigny, founded in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the venerable martyr and bishop Praejectus, came into our presence requesting that a certain chapel belonging to us, situated within the walls of the city of the Aedui and dedicated in honor of blessed John the Evangelist, be given to the aforesaid place, namely Flavigny. It was so necessary to the brothers of that place that they sought it for the purpose of lodging.

His petition appeared neither unacceptable nor unjust. For if all reasonable petitions deserve favor, how much more those whose reward is known to be more abundant on the day of judgment? Therefore, since we have often heard that something similar was undertaken and carried out by our predecessors, we gladly granted effect to his petition, so that the often-mentioned place, namely Flavigny, and the monks dwelling and serving the divine majesty there, might henceforth possess perpetually, without anyone disturbing them, the aforesaid chapel consecrated, as we have said, in honor of Saint John the Evangelist, together with everything that appears to belong to it.

And so that they might henceforth possess a firmer guarantee of holding it, we ordered this document to be made for them and commanded it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Done at Autun in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1018, indiction one, in the thirtieth year of the reign of the most glorious King Robert, on the third day before the Kalends of March.

I, Walter, bishop of the see of the city of Autun, assented in the name of Christ [Col. 0957C] and confirmed it with my own hand.

Sign of Hugh, bishop [Note: [Col. 0957D] of Auxerre.]

I, Baldwin, bishop of the holy see of Thérouanne, assented in the name of the wood of the Cross.

I, Theodoricus, bishop of the city of Orléans, confirmed it with my own hand.

I, Robert, duke of the Burgundians [Note: [Col. 0958D] Son of King Robert], confirmed it with my own hand.

## VIII (again). Charter of Robert, king of the Franks, concerning the castles built at Montbazon and Mirebeau, and prohibiting any harm from being inflicted on the monks of Cormery (1018)

[Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 137, from the archives of the monastery of Cormery.]

[Col. 0957D] In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Robert, king of the Franks by the ordering of divine providence.

If we care for God’s servants, especially those who, leaving all their possessions, are known to follow Christ, and extend assistance for more genuine service to divine power in places dedicated to God, we are confident that this will undoubtedly prove beneficial to us both for successfully conducting our mortal life and for happily attaining eternal life.

Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church, and especially to the nobles of the entire kingdom, that Count Fulk approached the royal sovereignty of our majesty concerning the advantages and interests of a certain monastery called Cormery, built in honor of almighty God and Saint Paul the apostle, which he wished to establish and strengthen by our authority. Count Fulk himself had built, in his time, in the county of Tours, a castle called Montbazon on the land of that monastery; and he had built another castle in the county of Poitiers, called Mirebeau, near the land of that monastery.

The monks of the aforesaid monastery feared that these castles might in the future become harmful and hostile to them or to their properties. Therefore the noble and religious abbot of that place, named Theobald, came with his monks to the aforesaid Count Fulk, asking him to use his force and power, as far as he could, to take care and prevent those castles from ever becoming violent toward the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0958B] or any of its properties.

Then the aforesaid abbot and his monks suggested to Fulk that he approach our royal excellence, so that what they were requesting from him he might request from our serenity, and so that he might confirm permanently by a written charter and charter of our authority what he had promised.

Count Fulk, bound by the greatest love both to the aforesaid abbot and to his monks, as men especially religious, and even more so for the remedy and salvation of his soul, promised that he would always be ready and prepared to comply with and assist their prayers in this matter.

Therefore he approached our magnificence and diligently brought to our ears the matters we have just described. We, gladly and effectively assenting to the suggestion of Fulk, who was especially faithful to us—and indeed so that we might merit the greater grace of almighty God and rejoice in the lasting stability and peace of our kingdom—by this writing and charter of our authority forbid and prohibit that there ever be anyone, whether a soldier, any man, or any person whatsoever, from the two castles named above or from any other castles belonging to Count Fulk, who dares or presumes to inflict upon the aforesaid monastery of Saint Paul the apostle, or upon any of its properties, any contrary usage, custom, violence, or domination, except as was done in the times of our predecessors: namely, Lothair, king of the Franks, and our father Hugh, likewise king of the Franks, and also in the times of Count Fulk and Count Geoffrey, the grandfather and father of the aforesaid Count Fulk.

We establish, command, vehemently threaten, and warn that no one who succeeds them, whatever his power or condition, should ever dare to violate this statute of our authority in any respect, lest his impiety and arrogant rashness pay the avenging penalties before Christ the judge.

And so that the authority of this statute and charter of ours may possess firm and inviolate force, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with our ring.

Sign of Robert, most glorious king.

[Col. 0959A] Gotfridus the monk wrote this, acting in place of Francon the chancellor; and Francon himself subscribed with his own hand.

## IX. Privilege of King Robert for the monastery of Cormery (1018)

[Dom Martène, same work, p. 138.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Robert, king of the Franks by the ordering of divine providence.

If we care for the servants of God, and especially for those who, abandoning all that is theirs, are known to follow Christ, and if we extend aid so that they may serve divine power more faithfully in places dedicated to God, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly prove beneficial to us for conducting our mortal life prosperously and attaining the eternal life happily.

Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, and especially to the leading men of our entire kingdom, that Count Fulk came before the royal majesty of our sovereign power, seeking by our authority to establish and strengthen the welfare and advancement of the [lacuna] monastery called Cormaric, established in honor of almighty God and the holy apostle Paul, founded long ago and faithfully administered by abbots obedient to God—namely, in honor of Saint Martin, our holy and particular patron [lacuna], and of Paul, the supreme and deservedly venerated theologian—built, endowed with the greatest abundance of goods and resources, and occupied by a numerous company of monks serving Christ. This place, moreover, had been held in due honor by our predecessors, parents of good and worthy memory, and had been imperially secured by a privilege; and they had decreed, under royal attestation and with every deliberate consideration, that the possessions granted to it from every direction should be assigned in every respect to the aforesaid monastery.

I too, lending a pious ear to just and devout counsels and assenting with the greatest willingness to salutary petitions, having learned of the pious and faithful request of the aforesaid count, took care to grant my assent. For this place had anciently been seen to be under the special lordship of kings. But because of the harassment of many wicked citizens, who, like a ship upon the wave-tossed currents of the sea, continually persecute the Church of God, the abbot of that place and the monks were compelled to approach the royal serenity, considering that its protector should be restored by royal provision against excessive disturbance, and its defender against those who opposed it through harassment.

The royal majesty, assenting to their wish, appointed as its protector, or advocate, that same Count Fulk—namely, the great-grandfather of the present Fulk—who at that time appeared to be the nearest and most powerful person after the king. His descendants thereafter brought that abbey under their own dominion.

The aforesaid count, therefore, fearing the exaltation of his lineage, or perhaps fearing that one of his own family, or he himself, overcome by love of money at Satan’s prompting, might in the future sell it to some outsider or subject it as a benefice to anyone, was earnestly urged by the venerable lord Richard, abbot of the aforesaid place, and by the monks subject to him, to ask me to forbid and prohibit this by a charter of privilege. This we now do.

By royal authority I command and order, and I adjure all by the divine name of the holy and undivided Trinity, that no one presume by rash undertaking to transfer that same abbey into the dominion of any person; rather, let it remain in the safe custody and protection of Count Fulk and his successors. If anyone attempts such an act, let him not obtain at all what he desires, and let the same place return to our protection and dominion, or to that of our successors; thereafter let it be subject to no dominion except the royal one.

If anyone—and we do not believe this will happen—should boldly attempt to ravage this royal written command and then wish cowardly to abandon it, may he have his portion with Dathan and Abiram, and with those who said to the Lord God, “Depart from us; we do not wish to know your ways”; with Herod, the slayer of the infants; with Nero, the killer of the apostles Peter and Paul and of many martyrs; with Aurelian, the most impious executioner; and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord. May he be anathema maranatha and exist eternally burning in the punishments of hell.

And so that this benefit of our authority may be more truly believed by all through the succession of years and more attentively observed, we ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring and caused the monogram of our name to be suitably written.

**The sign of Robert, the most glorious king.**

### X. Diploma of Robert, king of the Franks, for the restoration of the monastery of Lagny. (Year 1018.)

*[Mabillon, On Diplomatics, book VI, p. 601, from the cartulary of Lagny.]*

Robert, by the ordering of God’s clemency king of the Franks.

If we willingly grant assent to the just petitions of our faithful, and if we take care, out of goodwill and without any ill will, to accomplish what they reasonably request, we believe that this makes them more loyal to us and confirms the stability of our kingdom under divine protection—especially if the matter concerns what belongs to the honor of the holy Church of God.

Let it therefore be known to the common body of the Church and to our faithful, both present and future, that one of the nobles of our kingdom, named Stephen, a count most distinguished in nobility and power and also our most beloved nephew, humbly approached the magnificence of our highness and devoutly explained to our serene ears how his father, Count Herbert, had restored a certain abbey whose monastery was founded in the county of Paris, in a place called Lagny. Once renowned for its broad expanses of land and extensive possessions, it had later been destroyed and entirely abandoned through pagan persecution. His father had restored it and, after compensating his own faithful through exchanges, had restored for the most part the abbey’s own land.

The aforesaid Count Stephen therefore humbly requested that, by a command of our authority, we confirm that the land which his father had returned or donated there, or which he himself might still give, or which any other Christians and faithful members of the Church might give by donation, could be securely held and possessed by that abbey forever.

Granting a more generous assent to his prayers, and with the counsel of our nobles and the leading men of our kingdom, he deserved effectively to obtain what he had humbly requested. We therefore ordered this command of our highness to be made, by which we command and confirm that whatever the aforesaid abbey is known presently to hold, and whatever thereafter is donated by the faithful of Christ for it to possess, it shall hold and possess by the firmest right.

And so that this command of our authority might obtain firmer force in God’s name, we ordered it to be sealed beneath with the impression of our ring.

Done publicly in the city of Sens, in the year 1018 of the Incarnation of the Lord, in the thirty-second year of the reign of the most serene King Robert, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

The sign of King Robert. The sign of King Hugh. The sign of Henry. The sign of Robert. The sign of Letricus, archbishop.

Baldwin, subchancellor, acting in the place of Arnulf, archbishop and first chancellor, examined and confirmed this.

**Note:** The year 1018 recorded here was the first year of Hugh, son of King Robert, who had been crowned in the preceding year, but it was not yet the thirty-second year of Robert himself. Perhaps this should instead be referred, according to the new reckoning, to the following year, 1019, which could be considered the thirty-first year of Robert, counting from the time when he began to reign jointly with his father. Count Herbert, mentioned here, was buried in the monastery of Lagny. In my presence his bones were transferred from the old basilica to the new one, together with part of his epitaph, carved into stone.

### XI. Privilege of King Robert for the monastery of Micy. (Year 1022.)

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 706, from the archive of Micy.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

By the duty imposed upon us by royal dignity, we are bound to provide for the monasteries established in our kingdom in such a way that we may liberally confirm everything freely granted to them by others, and everything they are known to possess, so that they may in the future suffer no disturbance concerning these matters.

Let everyone therefore know that the venerable Bishop Odalric and Albert, abbot of Saint Maximin at Micy, together with certain brothers, having appeared in our presence, humbly requested our serenity to renew for them certain privileges granted to the monastery of Micy by our royal predecessors, namely Clovis, the most Christian first king of the Franks, and the emperor Charles. The seals of these privileges, as we ourselves saw, had been entirely broken and worn away through excessive antiquity.

Favorably granting their petition, for the salvation of my own soul—that is, of me, King Robert—and of my wife Constance, and of our sons, King Hugh and Henry, and also Robert and Odo, we issued this command of our royal dignity for the protection of the aforesaid monastery of Micy, so that a saving benefit might come to the brothers serving God there without any disadvantage, and so that our perpetual memorial might be preserved among them.

Having considered the substance of the aforesaid privileges, we have decided that the possessions contained in them and in other royal privileges should be confirmed and recorded in this charter, possessions which, at the present time, the brothers of that monastery securely and peacefully possess by God’s grace.

First is the estate of Micy with its dependencies, together with the river Loire and the Ligeret. In the city of Orléans they possess, in allodial tenure, the cloister of Saint Maximin, free from every exaction and customary due; a chapel consecrated in honor of that confessor; and a perpetual prebend of the Holy Cross. In the borough of Dun they possess one oven in allodial tenure; beside Saint Aignan, the abbey of Saint Maximin and its borough; and in the borough of Saint Aignan, one-half oven held in fixed tenure, which pays a rent of four denarii and an obol at the Mass of the Holy Cross in the month of May.

Beside Saint Donatian they possess one allodial holding. Outside the city, opposite the cloister of Saint Maximin, they possess a portion of allodial land belonging to that cloister, and the prebend of Saint Aignan.

They also possess the church of Saint Denis in allodial tenure, with all the cultivated and uncultivated lands belonging to it, meadows, pastures, vineyards, male and female servants, and villages—namely Bruyères, Caventon, Albures, Asnières, and another estate called Nemours; Masny and Boschellum in fixed tenure; and the estate of Dreux in allodial tenure, located in the county of Gâtinais.

In the county of Orléans they possess the village of Ulmer with everything belonging to it, and the estates of Audoeniputei (Empuis), Bitry, Mount Cuichet, Piray, Sarcin, Grangiolles, Vignay, Haia-Corbi, and Nociment. King Clotaire, son of the elder Clovis, granted these estates to the aforesaid place.

Besides these, they possess the chapel of Saint Maximin situated on the Loire, free from every customary due and from the authority of our officials; also the valley and Cergy with the land and forest belonging to it; everything belonging to that same village; all of Spedes and Montigny; Vacherie; and all of Ronedus [elsewhere, Rollenum], as far as the land of Saint Lifard extends; Alenay and Bonneville; one casaria in the village of Sumon; and all of Silvestre’s village. King Childebert bestowed these possessions on the aforesaid place.

They also possess in the county of Chartres Fraxinetum, Saumaricum, the village of Clessa with everything belonging to it, certain land in a village called Vonnas, and Maissy and Lincomis. King Dagobert granted these possessions to the aforesaid place.

In the county of Dun they have a cell at a place called Mont-Létard, with the river Coneda, mills, forest, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, vineyards, dependants, and servants. King Theuderic granted this cell to the place of Micy from the inheritance of Lupus, the most wicked duke.

They also possess Cambiacum, given by the elder Clovis, with its church and everything belonging to it; likewise Prunay, Berelle, Espine, Toscham-Rotundam, Brueil, the Wood of Saint Agilus, and certain clearings beside our forest called the Forest, where boundary markers have been set.

They further possess, by gift of King Pippin, Fontaines and Malveries, held both in allodial and fixed tenure; Fauvanes and the village of Marcellus; and Chandre with everything belonging to it, cultivated and uncultivated lands, male and female servants.

By gift of Emperor Louis and his son Lothair they have the right to travel with three ships along various rivers of the empire—namely the Loire, Cher, Seine, Marne, Vienne, Sarthe, Mayenne, and Sidil—for whatever needs of the monastery may arise, so that they may go and return securely and freely and pay neither toll nor customary due nor any other levy.

Moreover, no collector of the fisc is to demand or receive any customary due whatsoever from carts, wagons, pack animals, or any vehicle traveling by land or water, or from any commerce belonging to the aforesaid place. Nor is any judicial authority to presume to exact anything, impose or collect any legal charge or customary due, or inflict any disturbance concerning any business conducted in the villages or lands, forests or waters of the aforesaid monastery.

The monks themselves, however, may establish whatever customary dues they wish on their lands or waters. These include a salt toll and tolls on other goods transported by land or water; and they may collect in their lands the other legal payments, namely blood-money, abduction, homicide, arson, and the other customary fines.

By gift of Charles the Bald they also possess Gauday with its church and everything belonging to it, cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, male and female servants, and certain villages—namely Mont-Belleri, Pacy, Mauselan, the wood called the King’s Wood, Gilfred’s Wood, the Wood of Saint Marcellus, and certain clearings between Mount Bellenus and the public road, where boundary markers have been set.

In Secalonia they possess the estate of Vennes with its church and everything belonging to it; Macheries, Mesum, and Brueil; the Cosdrena forest with its adjacent clearings; and, in the parish of Litigny, a stone mill. They have these possessions by gift of Lothair, son of Emperor Louis.

By gift of King Clodomir they possess Fontenelles with everything belonging to it—cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, forest, clearings, male and female servants. They also have this communal right by gift of Alberic, viscount of Orléans: throughout the entire forest adjoining the aforesaid estate of Fontenelles, wherever boundary markers have been placed between their own forest and the forests of our barons and knights, they may at all times keep two hundred pigs feeding on acorns without any pannage or other service.

The same monastery also possesses many holdings which, because they are expressly named in the privileges of preceding kings and in authentic documents of the pontiffs, we have not wished to record in this present charter.

But so that we may not appear inferior in generosity to the aforesaid kings, we grant as a benefit to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery two mills held for rent below the Loire, above Saint Hilary, together with all the water which Hugh the knight gave them; they are to pay three solidi in rent at the Mass of the Holy Cross in May. Opposite Saint Martin, on the Loire, we grant and confirm to them forever, from our own right, two mills with the water belonging to them.

We also grant that all our free and servile men who reside or have houses on their lands shall forever pay every customary due and the tallage under that name, exactly as their own men do.

And just as our father, King Hugh, of pious memory, had granted them, once each week, on whatever day and night they wished, the freedom to fish throughout the whole stretch of the Loire river’s water belonging to our jurisdiction, by whatever method of fishing they choose, so we grant and confirm this to them forever.

Because our officials of Orléans and our knights, together with the servants of Landric, knight of Balgency, and certain others—as has often reached our ears—are daily ravaging the lands of the aforesaid monastery and inflicting many injuries upon the people dwelling there, by this command of our royal authority we now prohibit all such conduct in every respect.

Landric, knight of Balgency, and his sons Landric, John, and Hervé have agreed to this and have openly confessed before us and our faithful that, up to the present, they have had, or ought by right to have, absolutely no right, customary due, or service whatsoever in all the lands of Saint Maximin or over its people.

We therefore prohibit and strictly command by royal authority that in the village of Micy, in the estate of Saint Denis, in the chapel of Saint Maximin across the Loire, in Cambiacum, in Gauday, Mont-Belleri, Malveries, Canaries, Fontaines, Villa-Marcellus, Rosaries, Asnières, and Mesum, and in all the dependencies known to belong to these villages, as well as in other villages, lands, or among their people, none of our officials—neither count, envoy, judge, steward, nor anyone invested with public authority—shall presume thereafter to exact any legal payment, customary due, or service, or to cause any disturbance or opposition, or to take anything away or inflict any harassment.

Rather, let the aforesaid brothers be permitted to possess peacefully and freely, under our fullest protection, in our times and in those to come, as God disposes, the possessions mentioned above and everything they have acquired forever through the gifts of kings, princes, or any other faithful persons.

And so that this authority of ours may be believed with greater certainty and, with God’s consent, better preserved by the faithful in our times and in those to come, we ordered it to be strengthened below with the mark of our seal.

The sign of King Robert. The sign of Hugh, son of Robert. The sign of Henry, son of King Robert. The sign of Robert, son of King Robert.

Names of the witnesses: The sign of Tetduin the cleric, son of Regina, the woman whose benefice it was. The sign of Leuteric, archbishop of Sens. The sign of Gostin, archbishop of Bourges. The sign of Odalric, bishop of Orléans. The sign of Guarin, bishop of Beauvais. The sign of Franco, bishop of Paris. The sign of Count Ivo of Beaumont. The sign of Ebo the knight. The sign of Guarin, knight of Paris. The sign of Amalric, knight of Montfort.

I, Baldwin, chancellor, have read and subscribed.

Done publicly at Orléans, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1022, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of King Robert and in the fifth indiction, when Stephen, the arch-heresiarch, and his accomplices were condemned and burned at Orléans [elsewhere: when the heretics were condemned at Orléans].

### XII. Privilege of King Robert for the church of Saint Martin, at the request of Saint William, abbot of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon. (Year 1023.)

*[Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictine Saints, sixth century, p. 467.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Robert, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

Let the knowledge of all the faithful of holy mother Church, both present and future, know that one of our counts, named William, came into the presence of our serenity, asking and earnestly requesting that we permit him to entrust to me a certain church consecrated in honor of Saint Martin, situated in the suburb of the fortress of Beaune, formerly an abbey but now entirely destroyed, which he also possessed by right of our benefice. The agreement was that we should transfer that same church for perpetual possession to a certain congregation serving God according to the rule at Fruttuaria, near the Alps.

I willingly wished to yield to his reasonable and devout petition, since I had previously granted to that monastery, by the firmness of a royal command, a certain abbey of Saint Mary situated in the suburb of Chalon, together with the church of Buxy and the allodial estate of Cassiniacum with the church of that village.

I gave all these things at the urging and request of Lord William, the devout founder of that place at Fruttuaria, with Gosfred, bishop of Chalon, intervening and subscribing, together with the other bishops who had taken part in the council recently held at Airy.

I therefore make known to all that Count William returned the aforesaid church of Beaune to me, and that I gave it to the monastery of Fruttuaria. Toward that place we express such an affection of goodwill that whoever throughout the whole kingdom under our dominion wishes to contribute anything there for the redemption of his sins shall have the assent of our authority. Just as we have confirmed the gift by the authority of our command, so we decree that it may also lawfully be given and held in the future without objection. We mark this agreement concerning these matters with the impression of our ring.

Done at Avallon, in the year 1023 of the Incarnate Word, in the thirty-seventh year of Robert’s reign.

I, Baldwin, chancellor, have read and subscribed.

### XIII. Command of King Robert for the monastery of Bellimont near Tours. (Year 1022.)

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 708, from the archive of Saint Martin.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Robert, by the mercy of God king.

If we willingly assent to the petitions of the servants of God who knock at our ears concerning various ecclesiastical needs, and if we extend assistance more abundantly to those serving in places dedicated to the Lord for the worship of the divine army, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly benefit us both in passing through the present life in time and in happily attaining the future life.

We therefore wish it to be known to all our faithful and the faithful of Christ, present and future, that the subdeacon Sulpicius, archclaviger of Saint Martin, approached the serenity of our highness, humbly imploring and earnestly begging that by the authority of our command we order a charter to be made concerning those matters for which we had already ordered a charter to be made on a previous occasion, at the request of Hervé, levite and archclaviger of Saint Martin, our faithful predecessor and the predecessor of this same Sulpicius.

The matter concerned the church of Blessed Mary of Bellimont, in which the aforesaid holy man Hervé established the rule of nuns, situated not far from the fortress of our father Martin, together with everything belonging to it, namely vineyards and meadows; also a certain fishpond called Malamorta; and various arpents of vineyards situated in different places near the suburb of the town of the aforesaid confessor of Christ, Martin, between the channels of the Loire and the Cher.

That is, four arpents of vineyards from the treasury, not far from the town of Saint Martin on the side of the Cher river. They are bounded on two sides by the estate itself, on the third by the land of Saint Andrew, and on the fourth by the public road. They pay a rent of sixteen denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, four arpents of vineyards from the treasury in the suburb of the castle of Saint Martin on the southern side, in the place called Beyond Bera. They are bounded on one side by the land of Saint Venantius, on two sides by the common land of the brothers, and on the fourth by the public road. They pay a rent of sixteen denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, one arpent of vineyards from the treasury in the suburb of the castle of Saint Martin on the western side. They are bounded on two sides by land belonging to the estate itself, on the third by the land of Saint John and Saint Paul, and on the fourth by the public road. They pay a rent of four denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, one arpent of vineyards from the treasury in the suburb of the castle of Saint Martin on the western side. They are bounded on one side by the public road, on two sides by land belonging to the estate itself, and on the fourth by the land of Saint Paul. They pay a rent of four denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, three arpents of vineyards from the treasury in the suburb of the castle of Saint Martin at the wall of Curaecium. They are bounded on two sides by public roads and on the remaining sides by the land of the Holy Cross and the meadow of Saint Venantius. They pay a rent at the Mass of Saint Martin **[lacuna]** on the western side. They are bounded on one side by the land of Saint Martin of Portaria, on the other by Portaria itself and the land of Saint Sulpicius, and on the fourth by the public road. They pay a rent of three denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, three quartarii of vineyards from the treasury in the suburb of the castle of Blessed Martin on the eastern side. They are bounded on one front by the road leading into the city, on one side by the road whose end reaches the gate of Saint Julian, on the other side by the land of Saint Paul, and on the other front by the allodial land of Ademarus. They pay a rent of seven denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, four arpents of vineyards at Portaria, not far from the castle of Blessed Martin on the southern side. They are bounded on two sides by land belonging to the estate itself, on the third by the land of Saint Venantius, and on the fourth by that of Saint Denis. They pay a rent of sixteen denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Likewise, one-half arpent of vineyards at Portaria in the suburb of the castle of Blessed Martin on the western side. They are bounded on one front by the land of Saint Mary, on one side by the land of Saint Monegundis, and on the other side and end by public roads. They pay a rent of two denarii at the winter Mass of Saint Martin.

Concerning all these vineyards, which we have listed here together with their boundaries, we had already confirmed a certain document which the same Lord Sulpicius had ordered to be made concerning them, with the assent of Roger the dean and the other brothers.

The aforesaid faithful of ours, Lord Sulpicius, archclaviger, also begs that a certain altar be inserted into this command—an altar situated in the middle of the church of the most blessed Martin, in honor of the holy cross and Saint Peter, where Lord Hervé, archclaviger, of holy memory, lies buried. He himself, mindful of his soul, has already granted this altar in perpetuity to that place, namely Saint Mary of Bellimont.

It belongs to the treasury of Saint Martin, on the condition and under the agreement that the nuns serving the Lord shall henceforth and forever restore, as far as they are able, the capes and other ornaments of Saint Martin without payment.

Considering his petition sufficiently reasonable, we willingly granted assent to his wishes and ordered this command to be made both concerning the altar itself and concerning all the matters written above.

If anyone should presume to violate this command of our authority, let him know that he has not only fallen into offense against Christ and against us, but is also liable to a penalty of **[amount uncertain in the source: “denariorum solidorum excocti auri”]** in refined gold.

And so that this authority of ours may obtain inviolable effect, we confirmed it with our own hand and marked it with the impression of our ring.

Robert.

I, Baldwin, chancellor, have reread and subscribed.

### XIV. Charter of King Robert and Queen Constance concerning the donation of an estate near Verberie, made to the abbey of Compiègne. (Year 1029.)

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. IV, p. 602, from the original document.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I, Robert, by the grace of God king of the Franks, and Constance, by divine will queen.

If the first fruits of charity, adorned by the devout expenditure of religious generosity, are effective and suitable for strengthening the condition of any dignity and then presenting the fullness of future recompense, it is most fitting that royal dignity should repay and abundantly increase them—through those by whom the greatness of its dignity may be raised by exaltation and exalted by elevation—and finally should await eternal things through a blessed exchange and possess what it awaits in certain hope.

We exercise this kind of generosity in part as a duty when we do not refuse to confer temporal goods upon holy places and communities of the faithful, so that the cultivators of the Christian religion and of the ecclesiastical order may serve the divine commands with greater freedom, the more fully they have been released from every hindrance of necessity.

Let it therefore be known to the whole body of the faithful of holy mother Church, both present and future, that I and my wife Constance, especially dear to me in our happy companionship and sufficiently useful and energetic in administering the affairs belonging to her, have humbly given and devoutly transferred, by praetorian and forensic right, for our safety and for the salvation of our souls and of our son Hugh—who, before his death, had already been raised to the throne of the kingdom and, alas, was buried there in our own days—the estate adjoining our royal seat at Verberie, which my aforesaid wife had purchased with gold brought from her father’s gift, to the church of Saint Mary of Compiègne. She embraced the worship of that church above that of the other saints, and the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian rest there.

The things belonging to the aforesaid estate are these: two churches with four mills, fifty-three inhabitants or tenants, together with forty-four arpents of vineyards and forty and a half arpents of meadows. Finally, from the tenants and other lawful exactions, it will pay each year, under the name of rent, two pounds of denarii and eight solidi.

We further record the things we have conferred with the estate: one forest situated above the church of Saint Germanus, and another at High Monticel; then as much cultivated land belonging to the allodial estate as two plough-teams can scarcely cultivate throughout all the seasons of each year.

We also grant two manses adjoining the same allodial estate, one in the village of Mohericourt and the other in the village of Venette.

We have confirmed all these things, lawfully given and transferred by forensic and praetorian right to the church of Compiègne, by a command of our authority, and we decree that they remain confirmed in the future. We order them to be marked with our seal, as is written below.

Done publicly at Orléans, in the year 1029 of the Incarnate Word, in the forty-third year of the reign of King Robert.

I, Baldwin, chancellor, have read and subscribed, and by subscribing have read.

**Note:** Two things are to be observed in this diploma: first, that King Robert uses the pronoun “I” at the beginning of the text; concerning this, see Book II, chapter 3, no. 21. Second, Constance begins the diploma together with him, contrary to custom, namely because she herself makes the donation from her own property jointly with the king.

## Before the year 1033. Meginfred, master and provost of Magdeburg.

### Notice concerning Meginfred

*(In Canisius, Ancient Readings, Basnage edition, vol. III, p. 86.)*

Meginfred corrected and renewed the earlier biographer who had already committed the Life of Emmeram to writing. Either that author’s records had been corrupted, or, more probably, they had been written in an inept and barbarous style; Meginfred felt compelled to apply his hand anew to the writing of this Life. That earlier writer was called Cyrinus and Heres.

He appears to be known only by the name Meginfred. Surius believed that he had been bishop of Regensburg, perhaps misled by subscriptions appended to the synod of Dingolfing in the year 774, where Heres signed. But he was not bishop of Regensburg, since at that time Scripertus held that see. Later, however, Arnulf calls him bishop of the Church of Freising.

The period in which he lived is uncertain. Vossius believed the name Cyrinus to be fictitious, because no bishop of Freising is recorded under that name, nor indeed any bishop of Regensburg. But that man lived in the year 760 and died in the year 783. He was a Benedictine monk, then abbot, and finally the fourth bishop of Freising.

Meginfred was much better known, for he was among the more learned men of his age: a monk of Fulda at the beginning of the tenth century, and afterward elevated to the direction of Parthenopolis, or made provost of Magdeburg. Canisius once conjectured precisely this. His words are:

“Is this Meginfred the man whom Trithemius, in the Chronicle of Hirsau, under the year 1010, calls a celebrated monk of Fulda and distinguished chronicler, and whose labors he says assisted him greatly? Certainly the year 1010 suggests the same man, and it could have happened that he was summoned from Fulda to Magdeburg for the provostship.”

He had written twenty-four books of Chronicles, often praised by Trithemius. He then turned to correcting the Life of Emmeram. That brief work contains scarcely anything beyond Emmeram’s bloody death, inflicted by Lantpert because of an accusation that rape had been committed against his sister.

Meginfred lived during the times of Otto II and Otto III, and afterward also under the reign of the emperor Henry II.

Emmeram, as they say, was a bishop of Poitiers among the Gauls. Abandoning the episcopal see and the flock entrusted to him, he wished to travel to Pannonia so that he might bring the idolaters there to Christ. You may read the rest in Meginfred. It is sufficient to observe that he himself sought Bavaria in the year 697, under Duke Theodo IV; therefore the men who committed his Life to writing here lived many times and years after him.

## One book by Meginfred on the Life and Virtues of Blessed Emmeram

*(Canisius, Basnage edition, Ancient Readings, vol. III, p. 87.)*

### To the procurator of Saint Emmeram, concerning what he owes to him and to reason, P. A. [Purchard, abbot].

[Col. 0969B] To Lord Purchard, not slow to pursue every excellence, revered for his fatherly dignity and cherished for his manifold [Col. 0970B] virtue, Arnoldus [Note: [Col. 0969] Arnolfus, count of Cham and Vochburg, monk of St. Emmeram, provost and master.] pre-eminently subject to him as abbot, and consequently deservedly subject to the others, [Col. 0971A] yet placed in charge of the monastery’s affairs—whatever a faithful servant is to his lord, or a disciple to his master. [Col. 0972A] See below, at the beginning of ARNOLDUS, *On the Miracles of St. Emmeram*.

## HERE BEGINS THE LETTER AND PROLOGUE OF MEGINFRED, MASTER AND PROVOST OF PARTENOPOLIS, TO ARNOLDUS, MONK OF ST. EMMERAM, AND ALSO HIS PROVOST AND MASTER.

[Col. 0971]

To his dearest A. M. [Master Arnoldus], greetings in Christ.

[Col. 0971B] The sayings of the saints, though they appear simple, are fruitful with life-giving spirit and religious through the weight of truth; they are not pompous through the artifice of alluring composition. Since they are signs of immutable virtues, neither favor nourishes their merit nor indignation diminishes it. As their dignity flowed, as it were, from holiness, so their integrity proceeds from the reality of things; and just as their composition is spiritual, so their power is wondrous. Through the same members of speech, they unite the womb of faith to the generation of the image of God, and through the bosom of faith they make it firm.

From this I can infer, brother, how true a religion is owed to holiness, and how holy a confession to truth—lest I seem either presumptuous against the Spirit or an impostor concerning simplicity. But since your affection has imposed this burden upon me, which I have willingly undertaken for love of the blessed martyr and bishop Emmeram, I ask pardon both from his holiness and from the writer of his holiness, so that reverence for the former may deem me a worshiper, and wisdom in the latter may deign to make me an imitator. Indeed, if we cannot imitate the deeds of the saints, at least we may meditate upon them; we may admire what we desire, so that one day we may be permitted to desire what we admire. For divine mercy is not circumscribed: it helps even where there are no merits.

Therefore I beg you to come to the aid of my prayer, lest either my profession, weakened, should fail, or, through the excuse of ignorance, pious goodwill should sharpen the teeth of envy—whence it also desires to remain hidden with you, lest it blush in public.

[Col. 0971] The letter ends.

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0971]

[Col. 0971C] Although Christ’s warfare is conducted by various modes of combat and crowned with diverse glory of triumph, the discipline is nevertheless equal, the devotion similar, and the form the same. As those who bear the imprint of their king, stamped with the seal of patience, breathe toward him with restless spirits and restore their likeness to one face—that of the first piety—so the patriarchs and prophets, bearers of the law and conquerors of kings, blessingly greeting the Church of the New Testament, which was to be united into one body through the mediator Jesus Christ, salute from afar the succession of holy offspring by the oracle of the Holy Spirit and the instrument of true confession. Through various displays either of words or of deeds, they portray those whom they foresaw would one day be united with themselves in conduct.

Among these, some also describe the holy martyrs by the example of those who came before, [Col. 0971D] so that it may shine more brightly than the sun that there was one spirit in them all. Therefore, through contempt for the pain of kinship [Col. 0972C] and for bitter death, they aspire more familiarly to the throne of eternal charity. Amid torments, the free contemplation of hope, because of the harshness of their condition, advanced to the height of glory.

If they received so much veneration from those who honored them while they did not yet exist, what veneration will they receive from us, who, instructed by their teachings and examples, are daily cherished by their intercessions? Among these was the blessed bishop Emmeram, who left behind in the world a golden reputation, for he shed his precious blood for his brother. And so that the authority of his piety might be doubled, he laid another’s crime upon his own innocence, in order to free from bodily death the one whom he had previously rescued from the destruction of the mind. Concerning his character, struggle, triumph, and merits, whatever could reach us through writings and recent [Col. 0972D] memory, we provide for future generations.

[Col. 0971] The prologue ends.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS.

[Col. 0971D] **Chapter I.** How blessed Emmeram was brought up at Pictavis, educated in letters, and made beloved by all.

[Col. 0972D] **Chapter II.** How, after the flowers of childhood and the good fragrances of adolescence, he was raised to the dignity of the episcopate on account of the maturity of his character.

[Col. 0973A] **Chapter III.** How he exercised himself in the training-ground of virtues and showed himself an example of these virtues to his subjects and to others.

**Chapter IV.** How, not content with caring for the sheep entrusted to him, he led others into the Lord’s fold and, moreover, desired to travel as a pilgrim for the name of Christ.

**Chapter V.** How, after a noble debate of the spirit, he came as an exile into Bavaria and entered Ratisbon.

**Chapter VI.** How he asked the prince for permission to go to Pannonia, and, not obtaining it, submitted his mind to the divine disposition.

**Chapter VII.** How he cultivated Noricum, still a novice in the faith, and, after laboring there for three years, resolved to go to Rome.

**Chapter VIII.** How, following the example of the Lord’s love, he took upon himself the burdens of others and, through the spirit of prophecy, foretold ecclesiastical events; and so directed his journey toward Rome.

**Chapter IX.** How the duke’s daughter was publicly exposed in her crime, and how Lambertus persecuted the man of God and, for his disobedience, was punished by a severe sentence.

[Col. 0974A] **Chapter X.** How the gracious bishop sang hymns and strengthened his disciples with speech.

**Chapter XI.** How the tyrant, bitterly receiving the holy man of God, handed him over to his men for punishment, and concerning the flight of his companions.

**Chapter XII.** How the man of God was cut limb from limb, and how two of the executioners and the priest Vitalis were saved through a repentant heart.

**Chapter XIII.** Concerning the miracle performed in the limbs of the man of God, the departure of his holy soul, his burial at Ascheim, and the alteration of the nature of the world.

**Chapter XIV.** How, through revelations in wondrous order, he was transferred to Hiatoscopolis, that is, Ratisbon, and there honorably buried, and how the peace of the heavens returned.

**Chapter XV.** How the three executioners perished, what punishment seized their lord, and by what misery his posterity was afflicted.

**Chapter XVI.** Concerning the miracles of the places of his mutilation and calling.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK ON THE LIFE AND VIRTUES OF BLESSED EMMERAM.

[Col. 0973]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0973B]

### Emmeram’s homeland

In the regions of Aquitaine there is a city exceedingly renowned for the titles of its illustrious men, named Pictavis. There blessed Emmeram was brought up in the bosom of Christian parents and handed over to the schools to learn the letters of sacred instruction. How teachable he was, the dignity associated with virtue at the end of his education revealed. Even in the simplicity of childhood, his instruction so lifted his mind toward the heights of the Scriptures that everyone’s judgment foretold what he would become: everyone’s eyes perceived it, and the affection of all loved him.

Although he had been brought from his homeland, he prudently received the favor shown him and increased it once received, so that neither humility diminished his glory nor dignity aroused envy.

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0973C]

### He becomes a bishop

A happy adolescence therefore followed in so perceptive a boy, and the growth of his years blossomed together with the growth of his virtues. The maturity of his character preceded his manhood, for the wisdom that had grown up with his tender years easily persuaded the young man, by the weight of reason, how light every transitory thing was.

Thus it came about that he did not turn his eyes toward the hope and joys of the world, nor did he regard sadness or fear as worth consideration. Therefore, in correcting his friends, his spirit was free, his exhortation gentle, and his speech measured. Moreover, the beauty of his body commended the worth of his heart, and wisdom offered its sweetest gifts from a most honorable vessel.

Distinguished by these adornments, [Col. 0973D] the man of God ascended through the ecclesiastical ranks and, after winning love, earned reverence, until, by the Lord’s arrangement and with the agreement of all, he was ordained bishop, guardian of good conduct and example of life.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0974B]

### His virtues

Once the lamp had been set upon high, what rays it gave forth and with what serenity it illuminated its homeland would furnish material for every discourse. Let us therefore speak of what kind of man he was toward himself, then toward his subjects and toward others.

He arranged a double guard for the body and a double guard for the mind. To prevent the law of the body from weakening the law of the mind, and full pleasure from exhausting the abundance of the heart, he continually took precautions through the discipline of fasting and vigils. Moreover, by the alternating succession of reading and prayer, he both restrained the wanderings of his expansive mind and excluded the warfare of hostile suggestion. In every activity, the solemn work of psalmody was always dear to him as the fitting material for both purposes.

He was truly a singular treasure for the poor, a father to orphans, a refreshment for the aged, the sole support of widows, the hope of the despairing, the medicine of the sick, and a refuge for the wretched. He was so hospitable that neither did an exhausted household withdraw its hand from giving, nor did the constant arrivals wrinkle his brow; for those who came he supplied abundantly both the delights of the soul and what nature required.

Vigilantly watchful over the flock entrusted to him, he so barricaded the entrance of grim rapacity with pastoral weapons that, through the lanes and individual homes of the faithful, the heavenly course of the star beat back the darkness and error.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### He converts many to the faith

There was no place so insignificant, no person so humble, that he would not turn toward it for the salvation of souls, redeeming the time lest he should return empty to the Lord’s granary. This would have been enough for some, and not unreasonably, if they had diligently confined themselves to the territory assigned to them for priestly cultivation. [Col. 0974D] But such zeal for the Lord’s harvest burned in him that he drew the neighboring provinces of the Gauls and of other peoples to the shore of steadfast conduct with Peter’s hook.

Therefore many persons, both devout and indifferent, frequented his seat; the fragrance of his virtues brought them from distant places. To each, the faithful steward wisely distributed his deposit according to that person’s measure, so that what was said of him no less than of the other apostolic men might be said: “Your flashes have illumined the world” (Ps. LXXVI).

While the glowing fire of heavenly love did not see, in gathering individual souls, the smallness of its harvest grow to match the greatness of its desire, and while indignation at considering that his labor had been valued at nothing troubled him, it came to him amid the struggles of a debating conscience that the Avars—whom we call by other names Huns and Hungarians—lay stagnant in the old decay of idolatry in their Pannonian dwelling, and that, amid the light of so many peoples in those regions, this one alone did not possess the day of truth.

Hearing this, and moved by such a great loss of souls, he sometimes relieved the grief of his heart with hope of recovering the nation; at other times the difficulties of the roads, the foreign customs of the places, affection for those whom he was about to leave, and consideration of human weakness drew his foot back somewhat from his undertaking. Yet when the opportunity was offered him, he thought it neither possible nor right to neglect it, as he eagerly wielded the hoe of faith in breaking up the soil of deceived paganism—especially since he himself had often desired to undergo danger for the love of brotherhood and of God.

## CHAPTER FIVE

[Col. 0975C]

### He seeks Bavaria

The better judgment therefore prevailed: the difficult road and the superior cause. Having appointed a man of tested character to represent him, he himself, a vigorous soldier, girded himself for new campaigns. Among the other companions of his necessity he enlisted a certain priest, Vitalis, as interpreter, since he did not know the Germanic language, and he set out—to establish discipline amid barbarism, a homeland in exile, and kinship among savages.

Although he had previously possessed all these things in abundance, he left them behind even better; and what could have been enjoyed pleasantly without desire, he renounced with its enjoyment and permission, lest the present abundance of possessions should burden the treasury of blessed recompense. The rich man, made poor, displayed poor riches.

[Col. 0975D] From there, so that no idleness might make the restless farmer sluggish, he boldly undertook the journey. He himself strove to make both Gaul, through which his road led, and the regions adjoining the Rhine River flourish with the shoots of God’s word, and to make the grafted bud of the new man put forth leaves from the dead stock of the first-created man. But the outcome of the work proved Christ to be the giver of growth, since, when knowledge of God was added to merits, he brought forth offspring of regeneration.

In this way the faithful man reached the borders of the Bavarians. To the south they extend to the Alps, to the east to the Hungarians, and to the north the boundary of Germany stretches toward the Hercynian forest. [Col. 0976A] He was not frightened by this boundary. Following the authority of the descending Danube, he arrived at the city of Ratisbon.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] The following had been written in another hand in the margin: “This is the city which the Teutons formerly called, from *Germanus* or *Germanicus*, *Germanisheim*. In modern times our language Germanizes its name as *Reganisbure* [Col. 0976D]; Roman antiquity, as some testify in their writings, called it *Tiburnia*.”]

That city, once the metropolis of all Germany both in name and in the dignity of its princes, and still the chief city of that people, the head of an ancient lineage, he adorned by the arrival of the most blessed priest. The splendors and insignia conceived in the triumph of a victorious people were transformed for the better by the new proclamation of peace, and he increased them with the spoils of faith and the adornment of holy religion.

## CHAPTER SIX

### He seeks Pannonia

#### The borders between the Hungarians and the Bavarians are deserted

The duke of the province, Theodo, who then possessed its sovereignty, learned of the holy bishop’s arrival and, having summoned him into his presence, asked him, among other things, [Col. 0976B] what was the cause of his exile.
