After explaining his name and nation, Emmeram stated that he had left the dwelling of his native boundary for this reason: to reconcile to Christ the Creator the peoples of Pannonia, who still raged with the savagery of paganism, and that he had bound his resolve by this oath—that either, having obtained what he desired, he would end his life’s profession in fruitful peace, or, through devoted struggle, shed his blood as a martyr.

The duke, forewarned by divine counsel, replied that he opposed nothing to so pious a zeal and resisted nothing so great a virtue, except that a certain impossibility blocked the opportunity to travel there: namely, the discord and long-standing dispute of wars between himself and the Avars. The borders on both sides were deserted, so that around the river Anesim cities and places once most densely inhabited [Col. 0976C] bristled with such savage beasts that no passage lay open for travelers to cross.

He advised and rather begged him to deign to remain with him and his people. It was not right to pass by those who were so crude and imperfect in the faith—especially since these people desired what was necessary, while Emmeram perhaps rejected what was superfluous. He should take care lest indiscriminate piety lose its reward by offering annoyance to the unwilling, when it could bring assistance to the willing, and lest he love the impious in such a way as to neglect the pious.

But the man of God, fixed in his resolve, could not be turned by any gesture to desire anything other than what he had begun, unless perhaps contradiction itself should oppose heavenly judgment.

When the duke’s wisdom and the multitude of the people perceived that his exhortations supplied food to the minds of those who heard them, both through teachableness and through sweetness, they obtained their salvation by force, since they could not obtain it by supplication, fulfilling the Savior’s words: “The kingdom of heaven has suffered violence” (Matt. XI).

They had prevented him from leaving the province, so that no opportunity might arise for the blessed man; and human presumption prevailed to good effect, since the condition of his salvation arose from that very source. But the holy Father, troubled by the injury of the road from which he had been barred, began to consider what this difficulty placed before his righteous will might signify, [Col. 0977A] especially since, from the bosom of truth, the fulfillment he ardently desired had been promised as attainable, and he himself pursued it with no weak faith.

As he pondered these things, the example of the apostles came to him: heavenly governance sometimes sent them to certain peoples through responses or difficulties, and at other times prohibited them from going to certain peoples. He therefore rejoiced, submitted his mind to the heavenly disposition, and gave his consent to the zeal of the people. About to offer God the counsel of salvation upon the altar of obedience, he bound himself to the people by mutual love, and brought the struggle of his ministry to its conclusion even at the risk of his life.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### He wishes to go to Rome

The inhabitants of the city and of the entire region were indeed distinguished by the abundance of worldly happiness, but, having only recently been brought to the faith, they had not yet uprooted the thickets of their deceived antiquity from the roots, and ignorance had nourished a custom that clung tenaciously.

For this work the vigorous cultivator girded on all the tools of Christian religion. Having cut away the useless shoots of paganism, he raised up the sacrament of faith, distinguishing it with every flower of righteousness. Since he was intensely diligent in perfecting God’s people, he supplied a rule of life through the brightest example of his conduct and instructed them through the most gracious manner of speech.

It was not enough for such a burning lamp merely to offer the ordinary rule of preaching: he observed everyone’s conduct and examined everyone’s abilities. Laying aside not authority but severity, he humbled episcopal dignity in order to enter the home of each private person. In the Church he arranged what was common; among individuals he debated their particular offenses. Like the good shepherd, he preferred both to know his own and to be known by his own, lest silence grant assent to vices and hasten destruction.

Thus none of his subjects failed to draw a line of uprightness either from the deeds or from the words of their teacher. Accordingly, his celebrated contest was sobriety with the sober, self-restraint with the humble, and generosity with everyone. But against the stubborn he rose with magnanimous effort and extended the rod of authority against arrogant insolence, setting hope before their desires, so that through varied contests in this arena of struggle he might eventually arrive at the palm of victory.

For three years he traveled through the Bavarian territories engaged in these and similar works. As one destined to approach no small portion of the praise of the heavenly homeland, through the Spirit who speaks to the heart of Jerusalem he sensed that his days were already inclining toward the shore of eternal rest. So that he might open more quickly to the Judge who knocked, he awaited the treacherous time with vigilant watchfulness, lest, while the bridegroom delayed, human frailty should fall asleep.

Since he knew that the spirit is made more alert by the body’s fatigue, and that the sleep of sluggishness less easily steals in amid the business of honorable concern, and also so that hostile deceit might not strike him, shod and watchful, on the heel along the road of good intention, he asked permission from both the duke and the people to be allowed to go to Rome, to the thresholds of the blessed apostles, in order to petition the gatekeeper of the heavenly court to admit his knocking [or, supplication].

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### His predictions

At this same time, the hostile party, about to engage in a final battle all the more dangerously because it was to be defeated all the more gloriously, found a deceitful opportunity and devised a kind of combat in which either the bowels of charity had to be closed, or the disgrace of the sacred order had to be exploded as a scandal to the Church.

For the daughter of the aforementioned prince, named Uta, had been violated by Sigibald, the son of a certain judge. As the stain of her customary shame grew heavy in her womb, she weighed its disclosure not only as the loss of her noble status but also as a matter of life and death. What were they to do? [Col. 0978B] What counsel were they to take? The time of childbirth was pressing, and guilt threatened destruction.

Their only remaining refuge was trust in the piety of blessed Emmeram and counsel in his holiness. Pale despair rolled itself to this place; his feet were kissed and caressed; the crime was disclosed; pardon was begged. Finally, his fatherly piety was consulted about a remedy for her life. The manner of the complainants was all the more tearful because the expectation of punishment for the deed was more immediate.

When the blessed Father heard their groans, he began inwardly to sympathize with them. Although he travailed with a spirit of grief, he nevertheless set the face of rebuke firmly against their offenses. He explained that the wounded modesty of noble regeneration was more shameful and that the eternal judgment of the just Judge was to be feared more vehemently—especially since the punishments of the present age [Col. 0978C] differ from eternal punishments not only in magnitude but also in kind.

As is customary, he therefore showed the penitent the way of reconciliation. He himself, through a profound counsel of love, was about to take upon himself the burdens of others, and he secretly instructed them to transfer this stain onto him, so that they might more easily escape the duke’s fury, whom he knew to be inexorable when disgrace added to his grief.

But lest foresight be lacking in his piety, and mute innocence should offer faith and an example to guilt, if, by laying his shoulders beneath another’s crime, he remained silent to his own injury, he summoned more familiarly a certain priest named Wolflaicus, a man of attested truth and sound judgment. To him he cautiously disclosed his secret, insofar as he knew it through divine revelation.

For he said that, because of another’s crime, he would depart from this present life amid various torments and suffer punishment for a certain fictitious guilt. He asked the priest, after his death, to announce this to all the ranks of the Church, so that no one would presume to believe this infamy concerning him, or, by imitating his example, stumble into an offense. While he was alive, he urged him to persuade everyone that this matter was to be concealed.

The same priest faithfully kept silent testimony to his innocence for as long as he ought, and openly proclaimed it when it was fitting.

After this, worthy of God, Emmeram received permission from the prince and the people and seized the journey he desired. As was fitting, he was escorted with righteous affection. From the entire city a multitude of both sexes poured forth, following the departing man with prayers and tears, and in every way measuring the price of the love they had received against the measure of their grief.

The common people of lesser fortune either mourned the loss of his fatherly presence or doubled their prayers for his return. From one source of love, a twofold flood of tears poured forth, and their mourning was compounded by both the uncertain hope of his return and the present sorrow of his departure.

As the pious shepherd knew how to do, he soothed them with an ample course of commendation. After greeting everyone, he set out on the road.

## CHAPTER NINE

### The duke’s daughter is violated

As he proceeded farther, the daughter of the aforementioned duke was exposed for the crime she had committed and brought before her father’s tribunal. She was questioned about the perpetrator of so grave an offense.

For a long time, as her spirit grew numb with feminine fear and her tongue faltered between fear and love, she was pressed by the force of her accusers and cast her disgrace upon the person of the innocent bishop.

When her father heard this, he blazed with indignation all the more vehemently as he swelled with the pride of his exalted dignity. Taking up a sword, he rushed to extinguish his own offspring and would have completed the deed had not the hands of those present snatched the girl from the danger hanging over her.

But a savage sentence pursued such fury. He disinherited her and banished her to distant Ausonia, to be punished by perpetual exile; paternal pity never recalled her, because the grief that deep shame had nurtured is inconsolable.

Lambertus, the girl’s brother, was present at this judgment. Great sorrow seized him on account of his sister’s disgrace. As is familiar to youth, reckless fury took hold of him on the basis of false belief. After raging like a beast in mingled grief, madness entered his anger; abandoning tears, he leapt to vengeance. Taking with him a considerable company, he hurried to pursue the man of God.

## CHAPTER TEN

### Emmeram sings hymns

Meanwhile the Father of holy memory completed a three-day journey and, in a certain village called Helphandorf, where a spring flowed with clear waters, wove reasons for delay for his companions, having found an opportunity to act.

His mind illumined by divine love, whenever it found the field of battle, prepared weapons of faith and steadfastness and the works of hope and prayer for the coming hour, so that the disciples were overcome with astonishment at the fact that anything could weigh upon the bishop.

Around the third hour of the day, while he was singing the canonical hymns and fulfilling the appointed office in the presence of the holy relics, the young man mentioned above arrived. In the mad tumult of his heart he displayed the recklessness of his purpose. The clashing weapons of the multitude made a threatening demand for the bishop’s name and struck great terror into his companions.

As commonly happens, they hurried in trembling to the doorway of the house. After recognizing the appearance of fury and the crowd, they fearfully announced to him that this enemy was directing such violence against him.

He answered their fear from the hidden source of firm hope, saying that their arrival brought him no fear, since through it his troubles would end and joys without end would follow. The pain of the body, which passes in a moment, is brief, and the punishment that brings eternal life is light.

“The danger is small,” he said, “the hour of this death, which the breast of good faith patiently receives and leaps beyond through desire for eternity. Therefore we must see to it that fear does not strangle us before the cause of fear arrives. If one gives fear free rein, it punishes more dangerously than the executioner.

“For fear is driven out, grim and most shameful, by the opposing force; whoever it captures dies before being punished. He dies, I say, not only shamefully but unhappily, because he is taken away both willingly and without hope. Whoever distrusts the possibility of suffering contrary things for the sake of justice dies without faith and is punished without end.”

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

[Col. 0980B]

### The young duke orders him to be punished

As he continued speaking, the deadly young man burst in. As though a stone had been thrown into that house, he leaned upon his staff and stood over it, violently demanding that blessed Emmeram be brought to him.

When Emmeram had been brought forward, the young man received him with burning eyes and spirits, mocked him bitterly, and called him son-in-law. When the priest of God rightly rejected this, the young man continued. His anger foamed into defiance, and he hurled fiery insults. Finally he said:

“We have raised up the ruin of our house; we have advanced our calamity; we have cherished in our bosom the fire of our glory. Why, then, did you defile a daughter for her father and my sister for me? The royal virgin, filled with your lusts, has exposed the disgrace of her lineage and the damage to her modesty. The laughter of our enemies, the sorrow of her father, and the grief of her brother: a noble pledge is condemned as a whore.

“Is this what it means to be a bishop? Is this what it means to be a friend? Is this evidence of religion? Is this a sign of your piety? Is this how you repay our merits—when we, taking you in as a stranger and pauper, built you up in our wealth for the reverence of the whole people?”

Then the soldier of Christ said: “No, my son; your merits and our will seek another grace, and one far different. Therefore you ought to have good hope and a good faith, for that suspicion is not proved which derives no faith from the past and has no cause in a person’s merits. Why should I harm those who have merited well, when I have often helped even those who merited ill?

“Therefore you, whom I neither fear because of your threats nor admonish because of fear, lay aside your obstinacy, set aside the temper of suspicion, and return to the testing of truth, lest through your rashness you fall into destruction.

“I have resolved to go to Rome, to the thresholds of the holy apostles, where Peter had his chair; Truth itself established him in its Church as the examiner of truth. Just as his vicar draws honor from that place and order, so he holds authority from the same source, and his judgment does not err, because it is established by Christ its author.

“There, either through you or through a messenger, it will be possible to test the weight of canonical examination concerning the charges brought against me, so that I may be found either bound or absolved.”

But when he had received this utterance of gentleness, the tyrant’s blind presumption, steeped in fury, unleashed its vehement rage. He drove into the breast of so great a father the staff he carried in his hand, and, not revering the temple of the Lord, he dared to lay murderous hands upon him. He incited his companions with wicked shouts to drag him away in bonds and disgrace.

And so it happened, as flattery always makes the tyrant’s downward impulse more precipitous: immediately surrounded by soldiers and stripped of his religious garments, he was bound with ropes in their lodging over a ladder.

Terrified by so criminal an assault, the companions of the holy man fled, fulfilling, through the greater image of the example, the prophetic foretelling that says: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matt. XXVI).

The precious martyr of Christ, perceiving that his devoted soul was about to be offered to God, recognized that he had to fight in a more perilous struggle. Accordingly, with more attentive care he turned to Christ, the leader of his victory, armed outwardly with patience and inwardly with prayers. In every spirit he clung to him whose love soothed his soul while cruel punishment tore his body.

## CHAPTER TWELVE

[Col. 0981B]

### Emmeram’s body is cut apart

Meanwhile, five executioners were chosen to cut the body of so great a priest limb by limb and joint by joint, so that they might feed the tyrant’s bestial spirit with repeated wounds. The executioners’ judgment was divided.

Two of them, detesting so cruel a duty, asked pardon, lest justice punish them for a deed to which not their will but their lord’s savagery compelled them. The others, judging vain things to be true, said: “Hands indecently laid upon women must be cut off to deter incestuous crimes.”

Thus they counted the joints of his fingers by their wounds, and severed the digits joined by birth, delaying death so that it might come more bitterly through torment.

But why should eloquence linger here, where the place belongs to a voice blocked by sighs, not depicted by the art of composition? Therefore, after his feet and hands had been cut off, his eyes gouged out, his ears severed, and his nose mutilated, at last the martyr’s chastity was attacked, and the private organs of modesty were cut away by a detestable blade.

Amid all this, a voice, though faint, exercised David’s melody in praise of the Creator. Envious of this, they tore out his tongue by the roots and cut it off. Then they withdrew, leaving behind the man who had been so repeatedly mutilated.

But the warrior of God was wrapped in blood on the same field of victory until the companions of the blessed man emerged from hiding places and corners, accompanied by neighboring women summoned for the sake of human compassion.

When he realized that they were present, he asked for water to refresh his breast.

The aforementioned priest Vitalis said to him: “I cannot marvel enough that, with nearly all your limbs lost and about to cross the very threshold of light, you should desire some drink—as though you would enjoy a little more time of life amid your mangled remains—when, exhausted by so many torments, you ought to desire an end to your pains rather than an extension of them.”

At this, the athlete of God, as great in overthrowing vices among his subjects as he was unconquered in enduring torments, gathered his spirit and raised the courageous power of reason with the little bodily effort he could make, judging the testing of his mind more grievous than the cutting of his limbs.

“It is the mark of impatience,” he said, “when someone, compelled by pain, wishes to burst beyond the limits of the present life and despises the saving offering of the penance granted to him, whereas it is a sign of great obedience to await the sentence of the Judge.

“But how burdensome it is to your sluggishness to render us the service of human compassion and provide refreshment to a breast exhausted by torments! May this demand torment your days, so that whenever you take a drink of any kind, you may suffer derangement of mind. You will bring danger to no one, but through this example you will become a type of disobedience.”

The force of this sentence was experienced by that same Vitalis for the many years he lived afterward. Whenever he tasted any drink, he immediately became mentally deranged, running through the streets of the city, across rocky places and the tombs of the dead, making a terrifying uproar. Nevertheless, in such stupidity he was dangerous to no one.

Often, too, he wandered so far that he ran across the summits of towers [Col. 0982B] and suffered no harm from falling.

For the rest, this same man walked rightly along the path of pious conduct. By diligently carrying out the offices of the Mass and the other ecclesiastical duties, he fulfilled all the obligations of charity to the extent of his ability. This one thing alone he endured until the end of his life, as we are permitted to judge, both as an example and as a safeguard of humility.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN
Emmeram’s Burial.—Meanwhile, the inhabitants of the region, moved by human compassion for the martyr’s precious remains, gathered them together in a tree called White Thorn while they were burying them. Before they had withdrawn far after completing the burial, two exceedingly handsome men, previously unseen, rode along the royal road and, ploughing from either side, came together at the place where the blessed bishop’s remains had been deposited. When the tree mentioned above was pointed out to them, they reached it in the sight of everyone, but suddenly disappeared. At this disappearance all who had been present were astonished; hastening at once to the tree, they did not find the remains that had just been placed there. Nearly all the inhabitants of that same place became witnesses of this event, both because of its evidence and because of its novelty: divine providence had provided for those precious remains, since even among the saints it does not allow a hair of the head to be lost (Luke 21).

While this was happening, those who had been with God’s holy servant lifted him from the field of combat and placed him on a cart, intending to take him to the village of Ascheim, which was twelve miles distant; there was a church there dedicated to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that such a great and eminent person might not perish in the poor huts of peasants. Accordingly, women gathered from the neighboring area, together with approximately two hundred men, followed the venerable funeral procession and gave free rein to the faithful’s prayers of compassion.

Having already covered a large part of the journey, they reached a certain grassy field three miles from the village of Ascheim. And behold, as the blessed bishop was about to depart for heaven, he began to wail with whatever voice he possessed, indicating that the hour of his calling had arrived. One of the travelers, discerning this carefully, warned his companions to lift Christ’s martyr from the cart and lay him upon the earth. Immediately, in a sunny grassy place, the martyr began to yield up his life amid trembling reverence.

At the departure of that holy soul from the Egypt of this world, everyone standing nearby saw a light, like an immense lamp, proceed from the holy man’s mouth and penetrate heaven itself. The brightness was so intense that it struck back against the eyes of those looking upon it as though with lightning, and terror shook their limbs with trembling, so that they scarcely dared to place the blessed man’s body back on the cart.

Thus they conveyed him from there to the aforesaid Ascheim with a reverence worthy of a father, and buried him in the church of blessed Peter the apostle with due honor, while the people of the place gathered together. But since the most blessed bishop was unwilling to await the day of his resurrection, justice required that he should also protect with the relics of his sacred body those whom he had nourished in the bosom of the faith. The order of nature therefore began to be disturbed, and the violence of the elements proclaimed the will of so great a priest. For suddenly a storm of winds arose; the bright region of the sky was covered with clouds, and the face of heaven was darkened by thunder’s roar and flashes of lightning that terrified mortal hearts, while the air dissolved into rain and flowing streams for forty continuous days.

## CHAPTER XIV

His Translation.—Then, as the human race always turns its attention to unfamiliar things in times of distress and seeks answers concerning dangers, divine power was consulted and divine mercy entreated, until it was revealed in a nocturnal vision that the fortunate relics ought to be transferred without delay from there to the city of Regensburg.

Accordingly, the leading men of that place assembled, removed the venerable body from its tomb, and placed it on a boat on the river Isar, lighting candles in accordance with religious custom. As they followed the downstream course, with the river flowing in its natural direction, they entered the Danube through its mouths. From there, as they struggled upstream against the current—a thing that nature does not permit without great labor—the immobile object was propelled against the moving water with such speed through the merits of the martyr that it seemed as if the wind were stretching a sail behind the river.

A very remarkable event, yet one comparable with the holy man’s character, increased the wonder of the company. Just as he had lived in this world amid the storms of raging folly without losing either the fire of heavenly love or the light of truth, so the candles lit beside his sacred body looked down upon the blasts of the storms and the torrents of rain in perpetual serenity. Both riverbanks greeted so bright a sign and joined in shared rejoicing.

Entering the aforesaid city amid this joyful celebration, they encountered the sacred ranks of the clergy, the religious banners leading the way, and the rest of the customary procession, together with Prince Theodo of the province and the nobles. The entire region had poured forth to welcome its patron, and the earth itself seemed shaken by their hymn-singing voices.

Thus, when solemn celebration had been arranged in the church of blessed Gregory [George] the martyr, which he himself had once frequently visited because of his familiarity with prayer, the ferocity of the raging air grew calm, and the peace of the atmosphere and the command of light returned. It is handed down and confirmed by firm assertion that along that road, as he was carried from the boat to the church, divine mercy glorified him with thirty signs.

## CHAPTER XV

The Punishment of the Executioners.—Since the preceding narrative has woven together what was known and believed concerning the bishop’s struggle and triumph, it seems appropriate to relate what end immediately befell his persecutors, so that this knowledge may both restrain the wicked and protect the good: the former, because they will not dare to do what they wish; the latter, because they will not suffer what they ought not.

As we said above, five men were chosen to torture him. Of these, two were frightened by the crime; but in the case of the other three, their master’s command, from outside, drove them both to dare and to perpetrate the crime, while the iniquity implanted in their very marrow sharpened their resolve. Thus those two timid men, while the holy martyr prayed for them, were granted pardon and spent their lives in peace. The others, however, were delivered to the spirit whom they had served in this world within seven days; horribly and for a long time tormented, they finally rushed, in the deep silence of one night, into the wilderness. There, raving through rugged and inaccessible places, they perished; afterward they appeared nowhere, either alive or dead. They were crushed by a double calamity, as the prophet says (Jeremiah 17).

Their lord Lambert also, when an occasion arising from his crimes rose up against him, was condemned to perpetual exile and disappeared far from his own people, deservedly despised. He left to his descendants this inheritance of punishment: within a few years, cut down prematurely by the sickle of death, and with nearly all their life painfully torn away, they were themselves torn apart in payment for the blood of the innocent martyr. Those who could survive, or who still survive, testify by the same form of misfortune to their wretched lineage, and owe their miserable shortness of life more to the sighs of weakness than to any useful purpose.

And what wonder is this? If innocent blood touched his relatives by blood, while even his buildings suffered the losses of his impiety in accordance with the prophetic saying, “Let his habitation be made desolate, and let there be no one dwelling in his tent” (Psalm 68), so that, collapsing in ruinous disfigurement as shrubs and nettles climbed over them, they became unfit for human habitation and, by the neglected appearance even of inanimate things, proclaimed him a damnable and detestable man.

## CHAPTER XVI

Miracles.—We have spoken of the dwelling places of that senseless man and of the buildings of the place itself, since their visible desolation bears witness to his invisible destruction. Next we shall say, by contrast, how greatly the field of the blessed man’s struggle and the place of his calling shine with glory, so that, while the reverence due to those places is proclaimed, one may infer in what dwelling the martyr’s soul rejoices.

Therefore, where the blessed priest was struck down, this solemnity honors that place and this protection covers it: namely, that, rising by its own growth to the height of one cubit, it promises assurance of hoped-for pardon to those who seek it there in faith. Moreover, it knows nothing of the laws of the raging wind; it does not shine white with snow, nor wither in autumn; it does not freeze in winter and is not scorched by heat. It offers only the beauty of spring and ever-green grass as a pleasant turf.

For this reason, too, the neighboring Christian people built a church there in honor of the martyr who triumphs in that place, because of the frequent arrival of votive congregations. The place where his spirit entered the starry realm, long abandoned to neglect and almost worn away by oblivion, vindicated its dignity in the following manner.

In winter, as is natural in Germany, when an immense quantity of snow covered the entire surface of the earth, the small plot containing the body alone remained free from it. As it impressed upon passersby here and there the wonder of its miracle, it simultaneously taught the cause of its greenness and recalled the death of the blessed martyr. Therefore faith also established a basilica there, so that hope might be encouraged more effectively; and hope flourished in both places through the fruits of prayers to such an extent that, if they had to be counted, they would overwhelm the diligence of the person counting them.

# BEFORE THE MIDDLE OF THE ELEVENTH CENTURY

Arnold, descended from the Count of Vohburg, monk and dean of Emmeram.

## Notice Concerning Arnold: His Age, Homeland, Birth, Deeds, and Writings

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores IV, 543.)*

Arnold, born of a noble family—for he himself says that his maternal grandfather was the margrave Berhtold and his paternal grandfather the nobleman Arnold [Note: I. 13. The family of the counts of Cham and Vohburg is traced back to Berhtold; consequently many also assigned Arnold to this family. Arnold himself, in I. 13, mentions a niece who had married the nobleman Adalram.]—was educated in the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg and professed as a monk. At first he devoted himself to reading the writers of Roman antiquity; later, like Othlon, he passed from secular literature to sacred studies.

Trained in these studies and “delighted by graceful speech,” he regretted that the Life of his patron Emmeram had been written in an uncultivated and rustic style of expression, and he resolved to revise it. But the brothers, judging it sacrilegious that a man intent, as they thought, on innovations should touch venerable antiquity, petitioned the abbot that Arnold be sent into exile.

Accordingly, he went to Saxony and at Magdeburg formed a friendship with Meginfred, the master of the school [Note: They thought this was the same man whom Trithemius says was a teacher at Fulda and wrote the Fulda Chronicle and many other works (Chronicon Hirsaugiense, year 986, I, p. 128), as did Canisius (II, Preface), Vossius (De historicis Latinis II, 42), and others. But C. Suysken (Acta Sanctorum, September VI, p. 456) rightly observes that according to Trithemius’s calculations (p. 153), this man had already died in 1010. In the Fulda Necrology, however, no Meginfred appears between 1000 and 1050. I do not know whether Trithemius invented him from his own imagination.], and moved him by his prayers to rewrite that Life. This happened in the final years of Henry II [Note: Arnold’s letter to Burchard.].

After three years he returned to the monastery [Note: Arnold’s letter to Burchard.] and left the work unfinished; he finally received it only in 1030, when Burchard had become abbot [Note: I think the words of the letter must be understood in this way. Arnold could not have said that the work had been completed in three years, since he received it only in 1030, whereas it had been undertaken in the time of Henry II, that is, before 1024.]. Yet he does not seem to have immediately shared it with others [Note: “At your arrival—the little book came”: he writes this to Burchard. Burchard, however, came from the monastery of Reichenau to become abbot of Regensburg in 1036; see the Annals of Saint Emmeram, minor, Monumenta Germaniae historica I, p. 94, and Hermann the Lame, under the year 1030.].

For he had long before vowed that he would write the saint’s miracles [Note: II, 52.], and he decided to append to that Life some miracles partly narrated in the ancient Life and partly performed later at Regensburg. We see him occupied in composing these in 1035 or 1036 [Note: In the preface to the second book, written in 1036 or 1037, he says: “the little book on miracles which I had composed in the preceding year.”]. When this was finished, he dedicated both books to Abbot Burchard.

But soon he undertook a new labor [Note: Letter to Burchard.] and proposed, as a demonstration of his devotion to the saint, to celebrate his worshipers. First, therefore, he narrated the deeds of Bishop Wolfgang and Abbot Ramuold and committed to memory the affairs of Regensburg that had come to his knowledge. Later, after giving this book the form of a dialogue, he ranged more widely. Admonished by that Ammonicius whom he invented as speaking with him, he collected from every source various matters and diverse, manifold histories, so as to live up to the name of Collector assigned to him [Note: Chapter 35: “Now it remains, O Collector, according to your name, that what must henceforth be collected be carefully set down”; compare chapter 69.]. He proceeded according to no fixed order [Note: Chapter 50: “the little work . . . however far it may have wandered through the variety of its judgments”], recording now this, now that, on his tablets.

He seems to have been occupied with this for some time. For he himself indicates that the work progressed gradually and slowly [Note: Chapters 7 and II, 61.]. Having begun it under Abbot Burchard, he wrote the second part under Udalric, who succeeded Burchard in 1037 [Note: Annals of Saint Emmeram, minor, cited above.] [Note: Chapter 48.]. He wrote some portions during the summer [Note: Chapter 21.] and others as the feast of Saint Emmeram on September 22 approached [Note: Chapter 49.]. After a certain matter had already been recorded, Bishop Engilmar of Parenzo, who is known to have visited Germany in 1037, arrived and confirmed what had been written [Note: Chapter 53.].

He therefore collected many matters highly worthy of notice. Born of a noble family and experienced in journeys undertaken to Saxony and Pannonia [Note: Preface to Book II; chapter 22.], he had seen some things himself [Note: I, 5, 12; II, 22, 46 (“We ourselves saw this sign and touched it with our own hands”), 47, 52, 56, 57. He had personally known the hermit Gunthar, whom he discusses from chapter 61 onward; chapter 68.] and had learned others from friends and various people [Note: I, 7, 8, 13, 17; II, 12, 23, 28, 34, 45 (“The faithful brothers of our congregation, who happened then to be present, customarily bear witness to this event”), 53, 61, 68, 75.].

In the first book, besides Aribo, he also copied the Life of Saint Boniface [Note: I, 1.] and used various charters of the monastery [Note: I, 5, 7.], chronicles [Note: II, 24. Perhaps he means the Minor Annals of Saint Emmeram.] and other writings [Note: I, 1: “written scraps,” from which we extracted these passages; compare chapter 5.]. He used these sources in such a way that he must be counted among the most important sources for the history of Bavaria.

But, what we regret, he advanced by circumlocutions and used language that was excessively expansive [Note: He himself criticizes his youthful verbosity in II, 51. But he says: “Nor did I intend to describe these matters otherwise than so that they might benefit the edification of the faithful”; chapter 17; compare chapter 56 and elsewhere.]. He enlarged the book so greatly and covered those precious narratives with so many lengthy speeches and discussions—things that contribute nothing to the clarification of history—that no one here would wish to read the entire work.

The other works Arnold wrote are not of great importance [Note: The Anonymous of Melk, On the Saints of the Church, chapter 62, cites only the dialogue.]. While he was staying in Pannonia, he composed antiphons and responsories in honor of Saint Emmeram [Note: Letter to Burchard; preface to Book II, edited in Acta Sanctorum, September VI, p. 512.].

In 1031, under his direction, since he had been appointed provost, an inventory was made of the properties belonging to Saint Emmeram [Note: Pez I, 3, p. 67: “In the year 1031 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fourteenth indiction, this present inventory of the property of the monastery of Saint Emmeram was made under Abbot Burchard, by his order, with Provost Arnold likewise investigating it, and with the community of the brothers and the household approving.” “Reichenau sent us this abbot; may heavenly grace preserve him and increase all that has been entrusted to him.”].

Furthermore, a homily On the Eight Beatitudes and on Saint Emmeram is also attributed to him [Note: Pez IV, 2, p. 29. At the end these verses are read:

“Abbot Arnold treats the discourse which he had called ‘one’;

Giving the eight blessed ones a single reward freely.”

But Suysken had already observed in the work cited above, p. 457, that Arnold was not an abbot.], but it seems more correct to assign it to another writer of that name [Note: The work praised by Aventinus as Arnold’s On the Saints of the Church is the work edited here; Pez already thought so in IV, Preface, p. VI. For in his letter to Burchard he says: “Then I collected which ecclesiastical writers there had been,” and subsequently reviews them. Arnulf the monk, whom Sigebert mentions in On the Saints of the Church, chapter 157 (“Arnulf the monk, selecting from the Proverbs of Solomon more suitable sayings, wrote and arranged both their literal and allegorical senses with metrical elegance”), was undoubtedly someone else.].

Arnold died before the middle of the eleventh century, although, when he was writing his books, he flourished in youthful age [Note: Letter to Burchard, II, 51.]. Othlon, who had already entered the monastery and after several years wrote the Life of Wolfgang, makes no mention of Arnold as still living; indeed, he plainly identifies him as dead [Note: The preface above, p. 525. A letter to Abbot Leginward, appointed in 1048, prefixed to the book On the Translation of Saint Dionysius, relates that the abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims came to Regensburg and there learned many things about the situation of that city from Arnold’s own account; but it does not indicate when this occurred. The story, which in no way can be counted among the genuine sources of history, will be discussed elsewhere.].

Arnold’s book seems never to have crossed the walls of the monastery; certainly, apart from Othlon, no medieval writer, so far as I know, used it. In the sixteenth century, however, Aventinus [Note: Compare note 29.] and Laurentius Hochwart [Note: Oefele, Scriptores rerum Boicarum I, pp. 161 ff., 176, and elsewhere.] drew extensively from it.

In 1602 Canisius brought the work to light from a manuscript which, unless I am greatly mistaken, was the autograph [Antiquae lectiones II, p. 1; reprinted by Basnage III, 1, p. 88]. After him, only fragments were published by Mabillon [Acta VI, 1, pp. 5 and 476] and Suysken [Acta Sanctorum, September VI, p. 486] [Note: Others in June III, pp. 415, 420.], and these were corrected from a manuscript of Saint Emmeram under the direction of Abbot Frobenius.

1. That codex, preserved among the Munich manuscripts [Emmeram O 3], has been transcribed for our use by the distinguished Foringer. The fact that this membranous book of the eleventh century is Arnold’s autograph is clearly shown by the corrections very frequently introduced into the text in the same hand and by additions made in the margin.

On folio 9 it presents Arnold’s Office of Saint Emmeram; on folio 16, a short poem by Arnold [Note: Pez published this in IV, 2, p. 37; J. B. Kraus presented it engraved in copperplate in his work On the Translation, plate XIII.], followed by a letter addressed to Burchard.

On folio 21 follows Meginfred’s Life of Saint Emmeram; on folio 35 verso, Arnold’s first book, whose final words were added by a later hand, from the fifteenth century, at the bottom of folio 58. For the leaf that completed the quire was cut away together with these lines; the fact that this had already happened in the fifteenth century is shown by the page numbers written at that time [Note: Folio 58 is marked 77, followed by 78, now folio 60, on which begins the Treatise of the Venerable Priest Constantinus on the Passion and Glory of the Blessed Martyr Emmeram (Pez IV, 2, p. 23); Arnold’s homily mentioned above follows on folio 66. Folios 59, 64, 65, and the remaining leaves were added in the fifteenth century; see Archiv VIII.].

Whether the second book was ever included in this volume I would question. Certainly Canisius, who also possessed its autograph, must have found it elsewhere. By the middle of the eighteenth century no copy of it existed in the monastery of Saint Emmeram [Note: See Ratisbona monastica, fourth edition (1752), p. 112. Codices Saint Emmeram O 4 and O 5, which contain the first book, were copied from the autograph in the fifteenth century. Codex Saint Emmeram Y 4, a paper manuscript of the seventeenth century, contains some excerpts from Canisius’s edition.].

Since this is so, and since the parchment eleventh-century codices of Admont likewise present only the first book [Note: Archiv VI, pp. 172, 174.], I had the second reproduced from Canisius’s edition.

**G. Waitz**

# TWO BOOKS BY ARNOLD ON THE MIRACLES AND MEMORY OF THE BLESSED EMMERAM, EDITED BY G. WAITZ, PH.D.

[Note: Several passages of the first book that Pertz abbreviated as being of lesser importance have been restored from Canisius [Antiquae lectiones, Basnage edition III, 105]. Editor of the Patrology.]

## Acrostic Poem on Blessed Emmeram

E — Emmeram, deign to be present to your servant;  
M — By these prayers cleanse minds, together with the heart, from defilement;  
M — Apply strong remedies to distorted morals;  
E — In mercy rescue the monks from the harsh cares of the world;  
R — Thus you are able to subject kings to the king’s law, and us as well;  
A — I learn the courtly things that ancient times do not touch;  
M — Hence at last Christ’s name gives an omen to many;  
M — By a perfect gift, surely bestowing his ages;  
V — Kindly power of the cross, which marks light with the light of light;  
S — Under it, whoever seeks the greatest goods shall be safe;  
M — Great father among the great, and most humble brother among the least;  
A — Bestowing golden sacred gifts, forgive all sins;  
R — Under right guidance, make us not to be without fruit;  
T — Martyr Emmeram, kindly bishop, be mindful of us;  
I — May he render his servants pleasing to you; grant us benefits;  
R — Count ten rightly, add six, and thus you grasp these things.

[Note: That is, Θεός Πατήρ, “God the Father.”]

A — The matters previously written and most truly recounted at once adorn the substance of this book;  
L — Meginfred, learned and aptly named a Saxon, is an ornamenter in words and a subtle cultivator of meaning;  
M — If anyone seeks me by name, then, O provost, let him know Arnold;  
V — May relief be his. Amen.

[Note: διοικητής, “steward” or “provost.”]

[Note: In the four corners of this poem are painted monograms: “Emmeram martyr,” “Arnold,” “the martyrs’ palm,” and a fourth which seems to be read as “Gebehard.” Besides certain mystical explanations, these verses are also written beside them:

“In praise of blessed Heimram, the sinner Arnold published these books, who m[lacuna] a cultivator.”

“Abbot Burchard and Bishop Gebehard designate the time in which this most beautiful work was used.”

Finally, at the bottom on the right are these words: “rie re (?) composed this here and fashioned the monograms.”]

# TO THE PROVOST OF SAINT EMMERAM: WHAT HE OWES HIM AND TO THE COMMUNITY

[Col. 0991]

To Lord Burchard, never slow in all that is best, revered for paternal dignity and cherished for his manifold goodness, Arnold—although, as is fitting, deservedly subordinate to him, the abbot, above all others, yet provost over the monastery’s affairs—sends whatever a faithful servant owes his lord, or a disciple his teacher.

First of all, since through the patronage of the most blessed martyr Emmeram not I alone, but also the whole community of monks belonging to him together with me, gives thanks to God—who previously bestowed his mercy upon our littleness in many ways, and now has manifested his customary clemency toward us more clearly than before—in this undoubtedly, that he has sent you to us from such a place, where until now, by his gift and with the assistance of the most holy Virgin Mary, there abound fathers and brothers, very noble and praiseworthy both before God [Col. 0991B] and before the world, who know how to manage both their own affairs and those of others with understanding. Therefore I, the least disciple of true understanding, have taken from this an opportunity and confidence, under your rule, which is to be approved, to write the present letter. Although it may seem partly to contain the history of my ignorance, nevertheless, in the poor outline of our aforesaid and often-to-be-mentioned patron, it serves wholly the sweetest memory of him.

Accordingly, in reading and understanding the divine books, because of my sins, I was exceedingly sluggish; and, to speak the truth, I am still not free from this fault. Although I could have had examples from my elders for correcting this vice, as well as the others, the obstacle was unwillingness, and that abusive practice which they call neglect. One day, however, it happened that one of the brothers, my fellow student and classmate, died in my presence by the sting of death. What he saw at the very moment of death he revealed to those standing by, even though he did not speak. For when we had lifted him from the bed and laid him on the ground, he first struggled with his arms as if against someone; then, turning his gaze sharply to the left, he so recoiled from the face of the enemy that, by the rolling of his eyes, the turning away and thrusting of his head—so that I may express the gesture—he nearly pushed away those standing near him as though with a deathblow. And, to make clear [Note: [Col. 0991] *patefaceret* corrected to *patesceret* in manuscript 1.] how much the faith of Christ avails where it possesses merit, and how much is lacking where it is dead, he stretched out his right hand as far as he could, wishing to make the sign of salvation; but, being quite unable to form it, he trembled in a sudden convulsion, and, covered with pallor, grew rigid [Col. 0991D]; thus he breathed his last.

But we all together, our psalmody interrupted by sobs, were turned to mourning. For who would not have wept there, where each person, reminded within his conscience of his own weakness, could scarcely speak through his tears? I myself, too, after several years, with Christ as my witness, have written and committed these things to memory not without groaning and tears.

For a flourishing young man, also a brother of my own age and my companion in youthful frivolity, upon whom I had leaned, became for me a reed staff transformed into a serpent, so that I fled. Frightened away by this, I withdrew from the pagan books to which until then I had clung for the sake of worldly glory, and I became involved in divine books with sounder judgment. Then for the first time I began to discern the difference between light and darkness, between the Lord and Belial. At that time, having returned somewhat to myself, I gathered, in part, who the ecclesiastical writers had been.

Among their most beautiful variety I carefully noted the most blessed confessor of Christ, Hilary, a man of lofty mind, and how far he stands above the reading of simpler brothers; Ambrose, how eloquent and orthodox he is; John of Constantinople, how delightful and golden; Gregory of Nazianzus, how marvelous and *anastasificus*—that is, life-giving—as a teacher [Note: [Col. 0991] *quam* supplied above the line in manuscript 1.]; Jerome, how concise and upright; [Col. 0992B] Augustine, how eloquent and profound; Pope Gregory of Rome, how sweet and clear; Isidore of Spain, how concise and well ordered.

These men, and their highly venerable and useful predecessors or successors [Note: [Col. 0991] *sequaces* supplied above the line; *precessores vel successores* in manuscript 1.], had already drunk abundantly from the fountains of the Savior and offered their drink to us with the sweetest charity [Note: [Col. 0991] These words added later in manuscript 1.]. When I read their works—which seemed credible to the most learned but, according to my own capacity, even marvelous to me [Note: [Col. 0991] These words added later in manuscript 1.]—I delighted alike in the authority and in the sweetness of their elegant language.

But, by contrast, I was greatly embittered by the domestic deeds, so to speak, of our most illustrious patron, the martyr Emmeram [Note: [Col. 0991] “E.” in manuscript 1, more often.], which had long before been written, as I think correctly, by a certain bishop of the church of Freising who calls himself Cirinus—that is, “heir” [Note: [Col. 0991] These words added later in manuscript 1.]—but which, before our time, had been corrupted through the negligence of our elders [Col. 0992C].

When, with the abbot permitting it, I wished to correct them with a simple intention, and did not want them to remain longer uncorrected as a disgrace to our place, the minds of certain brothers rose up against me, saying that it was not right for me to add or subtract anything from the words of antiquity, especially since more learned men had left these matters untouched. To them my answer seems proper if I moderate it in this way: Why those men did this—or rather, why they did not do what was useful in this respect [Note: [Col. 0991] *in* supplied later in manuscript 1.]—is rash to investigate in view of my insignificance. I shall say only this, with their peace and that of all good men: not only are later people permitted to alter ancient things, but they may also utterly discard them if they are disordered; if, however, they are orderly but less useful, they may bury them with reverence. For by divine dispensation many things are left by those who preceded us to those who follow, so that the latter may have an opportunity to merit either the admission or the remission of some sin.

Even country people warn us against this kind of simplicity—or, to speak more truly, stupidity. They think those people sin who cut down trees in which pagans used to practice augury. What more need I say? Yielding for a time to my rivals, by order of the abbot I withdrew into exile in Saxony [Col. 0993A], carrying with me in his little book the holy Emmeram, who wished me to be his servant.

There, by pretending to know what I did not know, I made Meginfred, a master of Parthenopolis, my friend through a few small services. As I frequently heard him disputing wisely, I admired his intellect; through this he also came to recognize my devotion. In familiar conversation, recognizing his style and holding firmly to my fixed purpose, I asked him, as a pledge of friendship, not to be reluctant to forge a new book for our patron. When he refused, as though it were beyond his ability, and I responded by invoking the duty of charity, while he maintained, with a still stronger excuse, that this task was better suited to our people, I replied in turn that it was almost natural for fellow citizens to envy one another [Col. 0993B]. At last, overcome, he submitted his mind to my will—or rather to that of blessed Emmeram.

When I urged him to hasten, he replied with a cheerful face that what was to be tested within the household with the utmost diligence before it was presented beyond the walls to the eyes of many. For this reason, as I think, the work dearest to me remained unfinished for three years, although it had been begun during the reign of the most august Emperor Henry.

Thus, when I returned from Saxony to the monastery, I brought with me a hymn of the most blessed martyr, which the aforesaid master composed for me in Sapphic meter when I had asked him for at least a verse as a pledge of the book. Finally, when Conrad was emperor, and his son Henry nevertheless reigning, while Gebehard II governed the church of Regensburg, at your arrival the little book—so often desired and long awaited—came.

Let its entirety be assigned to blessed Emmeram, its material to Cirinus, its renewal to Meginfred, its completion to the sinner Arnold, its use to those who have no eye of envy [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.], and its reward in life to all who cultivate the memory of that martyr beloved of God.

For his worship, through my small service [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.], though my obligation to him is immense, I shall briefly relate what happened to me and what kind of consolation came to me.

There was a certain necessity for which my abbot had sent me to Pannonia. As I was often endangered in the deep channels of the Danube, at the Charybdis of Pogica [Note: [Col. 0993D] “At Pogen.”], where there seems to be a dwelling-place of death, I experienced the greatest danger. There the sailors, seizing the great oars and as though intending by their own strength to carry the ship out of the river’s precipice [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.], fell into such despair that, looking at one another and unable even to speak, they became completely drenched with fear of death [Col. 0993D].

Then, having kissed the little cross that hung from my neck and contained relics of the martyr from the *cambota*, I began to turn such thoughts over within me: “Do you suppose that the patron known throughout the world will today be proved to be my salvation here?” Immediately the ship, shaken as though by some threatening force [Col. 0994A], and cast out of the pit of destruction, began to float again, with no one guiding it—rather, with the Lord guiding it. Then, after a favorable journey, on the third day I was carried to the soil of Pannonia.

There Archbishop Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0993D] Of Strigonium, also called Austricus; see Mabillon, *Acta* VI, I, pp. 72 ff.] received me more humanely than the others and addressed me with greater familiarity. When he read that old and corrupted book of blessed Emmeram, he approved its material [Note: [Col. 0993] *p. c. s. et veste r. e.*, corrected in manuscript 1, with other letters erased.] together with its sense, but criticized the sequence of these matters together with its style, as hanging upon a thread of reasoning.

While I remained with him for six weeks, I composed several antiphons with responsories in memory of the most holy patron [Note: [Col. 0994D] See *Acta SS.*, September VI, p. 512.], relying not so much on my own talent as on a mind devoted to the martyr’s praises. The aforesaid bishop had his monks and clerics learn them and celebrate them publicly in the church on the day of the martyr’s nativity, in accordance with what is written [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.]: “Let the old things depart [Col. 0994B] from your mouth” [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.], setting aside the old chant of that man, which our people sing more from ancient custom than from any boldness grounded in authority.

After these events had taken place in Pannonia, and after I had completed the mission for which I had been sent, I returned to Noricum. When I revisited Regensburg, I was received with great charity by the brothers; may the Lord repay them for this.

Here, while I was seeking with the greatest desire to hear or see something sweet or glorious about Saint Emmeram, I received the following vision in sleep. Blessed Emmeram, as though covered with a green cloak, seemed to me to be lying on a well and decently adorned bed on the southern side before the church doors. When the brothers, wishing to enter the church, saw him, they withdrew in terror.

I alone remained behind, and was so curious [Col. 0994C] that, kneeling at the steps beside three arches, I gazed at him until he uncovered his face and said in Latin [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.]: “You are permitted to see my face because you have labored in my praises.” When I saw that his face was exceedingly bright and radiant, I cannot at all express how great a jubilation there was in my heart [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.]. I silently reflected to myself only this: “Perhaps on the last day he will say on my behalf to Christ: ‘Lord, give me this sinner.’”

At that point I awoke; and even now, to tell the truth, being wicked and not upright, I desire through your prayers and through the constant prayer of the fathers and brothers to obtain from him—whose mercy is better than lives—that my sins may not obstruct the joys of that delightful vision.

[Col. 0994D] For the rest, since what remains calls for a conclusion to the letter, I do not want you to be unaware that the ancient author of this work ends his book at the point where, in the volume concerning the miracles of the most blessed martyr, this material, together with the preceding three sections that I have set out more fully through my diligence, was assigned as the fourth chapter [Note: [Col. 0993] *antiqus* in manuscript 1.]. What follows I have added in a humble style, to be defended by your authority against my rivals [Note: [Col. 0993] *us* corrected in manuscript 1.], inserting it in a single reversed order [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.] because of the similarity of the subject [Note: [Col. 0993] Added later in manuscript 1.], for the memory of myself and of those who with me in the monastery were able to remember the signs performed on account of Christ’s martyr.

For the preservation and propagation of these and of his other praises, may your life flourish, your dignity prevail, and your fatherhood prosper, by the Lord’s gift. Amen.

[Col. 0995] [Note: [Col. 0995D] We append the letter of Meginfred: “THE LETTER OR PROLOGUE OF MEGINFRED, MASTER AND PROVOST OF PARTHENOPOLIS, TO ARNOLD, MONK OF SAINT EMMERAM, ALSO PROVOST AND MASTER. To his dearest A. M., greetings in Christ. The sayings of the saints…” The remainder is to be found under MEGENFRED above.] Here ends the epistolary defense concerning method, or the alteration of ancient works.

# Table of Contents of Book One [Note: [Col. 0995] This heading is absent in manuscript 1.]

[Col. 0995A] 1. [Note: [Col. 0995] The numbers are absent in manuscript 1.] Concerning the bishops or dukes of Paguaria, and the heretics expelled from it by Saint Boniface; also concerning the miracles frequently performed at the tomb of blessed Emmeram, and his second translation. 2. Concerning the adulterous woman who could in no way enter the martyr’s church until she had purified herself through confession and repentance. 3. Concerning the man captured by robbers and sold twice, who, after returning to his homeland following a three-year exile, presented himself to blessed Emmeram with a great miracle. 4. Concerning the girl who remained fasting for an entire year and was restored to ordinary life at the martyr’s memorial. 5. Concerning the benefactions of princes, counts, and judges bestowed upon Saint Emmeram, and concerning the marvelous triumph that Emperor Arnulf obtained through the most evident assistance of that same witness. 6. Concerning Bishop Tuto, endowed with the spirit of prophecy, and King Conrad, who was afflicted by illness at Saint Emmeram’s because of an imprudent command. 7. Concerning the man who, at a prince’s banquet, refused the martyr’s charity and was struck by a terrifying blow. 8. Concerning a monk of Saint Emmeram who, in the dangers of the sea, sensed the saint’s presence through the benefits of his deliverance. [Col. 0995C] 9. Concerning an apostate monk who was twice seized by a demon and as many times liberated through the prayers and merits of blessed Emmeram. [Col. 0996A] 10. Concerning a certain demoniac miserably possessed by a legion, to whom the Savior’s grace wondrously restored health at the memorial of Christ’s martyr. 11. Concerning a descendant of the tyrant Lantpert, who was prevented from entering the church of Christ’s martyr by a double blindness occurring within one hour. 12. Concerning the miseries by which men of tyrannical descent are afflicted even to the present, and concerning the conversion and humble offering of certain members of that same lineage, as well as the hardness of Adalram, miraculously softened by the martyr’s power. 13. Concerning twelve men who had sworn unlawfully against the martyr’s altar and were consumed by manifold punishment. 14. Concerning what happened to a certain little woman who was punished with paralysis for the theft of a chalice and marvelously healed at Saint Emmeram’s. 15. Concerning what even the Jews do not at all deny: the miracles very frequently performed in the church of Saint Emmeram. 16. Concerning a paralytic healed at Saint Emmeram’s. [Col. 0996C] 17. Concerning the death of Bishop Michael and the sign of the bell.

# Prologue to Book I: Concerning the Miracles of Blessed Emmeram

[Col. 0995]

[Col. 0995C] The merits of the saints live in the churches, and they themselves exist more powerfully, although removed from our eyes, than they were thought to do while living among us. Although we firmly hold this as a matter of faith, miracles nevertheless support us in it and expose the ignorance of brutish unbelief: at the lifeless relics of the saints, the impossible returns to the sick as possibility, and what was not returns as being—while all secular powers are defrauded concerning this pivotal matter.

For if either royal power, which surpasses all others, or any skill of craftsmanship—which sometimes repairs what is gaping—were to exert itself, how could it restore a bodily condition to a blind man? Since these things are established, none of the conclusions of prudent faith remain hidden.

Therefore, since we are writing to you, in whom the life-giving Spirit has planted a living faith, heir to his gifts of grace, we shall relate a few of the many miracles that divine mercy granted to its witness Emmeram—or repeat what has been related by others. For to you he makes an experiment concerning invisible things, and even concerning things not yet done, through the substance of past events and the evidence of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1).

[Col. 0995] Here ends the prologue.

# Here Begins Book One

[Col. 0995D] 1. When the sacred body of Christ’s martyr Emmeram had been honorably buried at Regensburg, and those who sought the protection of divine mercy at his tomb had by no means been deprived of the reward of their faith, at length, after much time had passed amid such benefits, a venerable man named Gaubaldus undertook the governance of the bishopric of that same church [Col. 0997A].

Before him, not only this church—the very one of which we are now speaking—but also the other churches in Bavaria had remained without definite bishops after Roman times [Note: [Col. 0997] I have consistently marked with the letter “a” the passages added later by Arnold in the manuscript. Nevertheless, it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are owed to Arnold himself.]. For the Noricans had only recently received Christianity, and heretics had insinuated themselves among them; as they were accustomed to do in other regions, they had confused right and wrong there.

Some of these men [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Some of these men”—“deceived” is drawn from the *Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 9.] claimed to be bishops, others priests, and others clerics of various orders. By certain contrivances they embellished their inventions, and so for many years they deceived the people together with their princes. This error, hated by all good people but vigorously pursued by the wicked, grew especially strong under the dukes, whose names we partly do not know and partly omit out of deliberate caution.

At the time when remedies were being prepared for so great a plague, these dukes were ruling: namely, Dioto, an illustrious man, whose sons did not succeed him in the kingdom. Then another Theodo, a vigorous and energetic man, under whom the most renowned confessor of Christ, Routpertus, together with other servants of God, came to Juvavium and there completed the course of his present life [Note: [Col. 0997] *Christi* was entered in a scraped-out place and written in the margin, as Foringer observed.] [Note: [Col. 0997] *stipulante* corrected to *asstipulante* in manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] *stipulante* corrected to *asstipulante* in manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997D] Compare the anonymous *On the Conversion of the Carantanians*, beginning.] Under him Saint Corbinianus came to Freising [Note: [Col. 0997D] See the *Life of Saint Corbinianus*, chapter 10.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.] [Note: [Col. 0997] The passages marked “a” were added later by Arnold; it is not entirely certain whether the words “p. R. t.” are Arnold’s.]

That duke had sons as successors to the kingdom, namely Diotpertus and Grimaldus. After them, Hucbertus provided this people with a duke. He had given to Saint George and Saint Emmeram, under a certain itinerant bishop named Ratharius, an estate called in the charters from which we have taken this material Pirchinwanch [Note: [Col. 0997D] Purckwang near Wildenberg; see Ried I, p. 54. I have found nothing elsewhere concerning Hucbert’s donation.].

In the time of this duke [Col. 0997C], the most blessed bishop Boniface, because of the greatest care he had for the Lord’s sheep, entered Bavaria and expelled some of the heretics from it; but he could not, as he wished, eliminate them all [Note: [Col. 0998D] From the *Life of Boniface*, chapter 8.]. After Boniface had returned to Francia and the aforesaid duke had died, Udilo obtained the dukedom of this people under Prince Pepin.

He [Note: [Col. 0998D] From the *Life of Boniface*, chapter 9.] sent envoys to Italy and asked Saint Boniface, who was returning from Rome (in the year 739), to deign once again to visit the Norican peoples living under his rule. The bishop, filled with God, willingly agreeing both to this embassy and to the request, hastened his journey into Bavaria, hoping to correct what he had previously been unable to correct.

Here, with the Lord cooperating and the aforesaid duke supporting him [Note: [Col. 0997] *stipulante* corrected to *asstipulante* in manuscript 1.], he decreed ecclesiastical laws, utterly uprooted the heretics, [Col. 0997D] and drove out all the schismatics. He divided the province into parishes and appointed bishops to them by canonical ordination. Among these he placed the aforesaid Gaubaldus over the see of Hiatospolis [Note: [Col. 0998D] Hiatospolis, as though from Greek ἄδος πόλις, “city of Hades,” is Regensburg, from ὅω.].

While Gaubaldus was tending and enlarging the sheepfolds entrusted to him, among the other things that he arranged and ordered well, he took counsel with the clergy about opening the tomb of blessed Emmeram [Note: [Col. 0998D] What follows is drawn from Aribo’s *Life of Saint Emmeram* (*Acta Sanctorum*, September VI, p. 481.)]. Since frequent miracles loudly proclaimed that this ought to be done, the common agreement of all approved it.

What more need be said? On the appointed day of the translation and elevation, everyone’s wishes converged. An innumerable crowd of both sexes had gathered for the praises of the martyr, who had rested for so long among mortals in neglect. All hastened to see more clearly the benefits of the martyr that they had so often heard about; everyone hurried to take part in the new rejoicing.

At last, the chosen priests, together with the deacons and the others necessary for opening the tomb, drove the people outside the church and secured the doors from within with bolts. When, with trembling reverence, they had loosened the earth from the tomb and moved the stone laid over it from the right to the left by only about a palm and a half, fear fell upon everyone, so that the hands of those laboring slipped from the stone because of their excessive terror.

Struck by this fear and deprived of their strength, they fell to the ground. But one of them, who had been standing on the right, placing his chest beneath the stone, supported it alone for as long as it was necessary, though it was enormous and his own strength was insufficient, until the others recovered their ability and, coming to his aid, applied their hands again to the undertaking. Then they removed it with such speed and confidence as though it had no weight of gravity at all.

What is signified by this threefold miracle except what is proclaimed by the prophetic mouth: “God is wonderful in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give strength and power” (Psalm 67:36)? Out of reverence for his martyr, the power of the Most High struck these men down terribly, but for his praises it marvelously restored them to their former strength. Thirdly, to one man serving the sacred ashes he granted the gift of strength, to the glory of his name, who is three and one.

For this threefold sign, the venerable priests gave thanks to the benevolent Trinity. Amid the great rejoicing of clergy and people, they removed the incomparable treasure of the purple-clad body from the tomb where it had until then been hidden and transferred it to a venerable new monument, which they had already prepared with sufficient care. In it the princes had gold plates affixed with the most beautiful silverwork and had them distinguished by a varied arrangement of jewels.

May the Lord, through the intercessions of his illustrious witness Emmeram, deign to be merciful both to their spirits and to us sinners!

## 2

A certain man in the bishopric of Freising, because his wife had been deprived of the use of her eyes, dismissed her and took another woman in violation of God’s command [Note: [Col. 0999D] This has been taken from Aribo.]. The bishop, in whose diocese this had occurred, took action against the adulterer and the woman he had taken, and, after convicting him, punished him with the canonical penance [Col. 0999A].

But, at the instigation of her persuader, the obstinate woman could not be separated from the illicit embraces. When a gathering was to take place at the church of blessed Emmeram and this woman hurried there together with those traveling to it, at a place called Vivarius, from which she caught sight of the church, about two hundred paces from the city, the awareness of her notorious crime began to torment her.

She began to be shaken by a terrible trembling and, weakened, collapsed upon the ground. When her companions raised her up, if she wished to go forward, she could not proceed; if she tried to return, she had no ability to go back.

In this distress, a priest who happened to arrive found her and asked what crime had ensnared her and caused her to suffer such things. When she had related the matter as it was, the same priest advised her to return to her bishop. When she did so, poured out her wound in tears, and promised satisfaction from a pure heart, she received the medicine prescribed by the Church. Then she proceeded to her physician, blessed Emmeram, free from the wound of the soul and secure from bodily pain.

From this matter it is easily understood how far those who are uncertain are separated from the kingdom of God—those who are thus held back from entering the dwellings of his elect. May the strongest medicine of Christ prevent this from happening to us.

### 3.

As blessed Emmerammus, seasoning the peoples with the fragrances of his virtues, drew them to himself from every direction, it happened that a certain faithful man, who—as the outcome proved—with good intention was travelling there alone, was attacked by robbers at a place called Verroniwaida, which the Latin expression renders as “Distant Pastures.” They detained and stripped him, then sold him to the Eastern Franks. Thus he became a purchased slave elsewhere, though he wished to become a newcomer at the martyr’s shrine.

A certain man who acquired him after he had been sold on transferred him by a commercial sale to a certain Thuringian in the territory of the Parathani, at that time savage pagans.

[Note: This and the following material of this chapter are from Aribo.]

When the Christian realized that he was among gentiles and worshippers of idols, he began, with every effort he could make, to display faithful and willing service to his temporal master, whether present or absent. He was skilled in working with wood; by this craft he used to construct mills along watercourses. Because of this skill, and because of the attractive arrangement of buildings, the slave became especially dear to his master.

Therefore, wishing to secure him to himself by certain bonds, the master attempted to join him in marriage with a young widow, beautiful according to the corruption of this flesh, whom one of the slave’s fellow servants had left without children. Refusing her, the captive replied—not by his will but by the lot that had befallen him:

“I left a lawful wife in my homeland, when I was brought here on account of my innumerable sins.”

[Col. 1000A] “How, then, while she is alive, can I take another wife?”

Provoked by these words, the master launched into the fiercest threats, saying:

“May the Lord do this to me, and add this also, unless you take her in marriage: I shall hand you over to the Saxon people, who serve so many demons through their filthy idolatry. For I know, and have learned by experience, that if you do not wish to take a wife here, you would rather flee than remain with me in these regions, so that, disgraced by your flight, I may nevertheless afterward remain defrauded of the price paid for you.”

While the master, on account of sin, and the slave, on account of justice, argued continually in such terms, the man—already elderly in age and conduct—recognized that he could not otherwise avoid his master’s command without being handed over to a people ignorant of God, whose way of life he feared as death itself. At last he admitted that he was willing to join himself to her.

Then the master, delighted, took the woman’s hand, wrapped it in his cloak, and, as is customary in weddings, granted her in marriage to the old man before witnesses; then he departed.

The religious old man, having received the woman, proceeded to the house of the detested inheritance. They entered the bedroom and, taking food according to the custom of newlyweds, climbed into the bed she had prepared, though with very different intentions.

The old man said to her:

“Take care, dearest daughter, lest by this joining in the marriage chamber we offend the supreme Craftsman, since the joys of temporal life fail after a few days but give birth to eternal losses for souls. Enjoy, then, the work of my craft in the pleasures of life, and grant me only this: do not plunge me beneath the yoke of this union into destruction while my wife is alive.”

But she, overcome by carnal pleasure, would not at all consent to her husband’s request. Indeed, she threatened to denounce to her master what he had said in her ear.

When the old man saw that this kind of exhortation was accomplishing little, he softened his companion’s wantonness and her provoked spirit with flattering words:

“We must take care, dearest sister, that although we are Christians we do not enter marriage according to the rite of the gentiles, but rather abstain for three days, beseeching the Lord to grant us the begetting of children, since a woman is to be taken not for lust but in hope of offspring.”

When the woman heard this, she despised it, turned toward the wall, and immersed herself in sluggish sleep.

But the religious old man, with tears and inward devotion, implored the mercy of the Almighty, asking that through the merits and intercessions of his beloved martyr Emmerammus he might deign to aid him.

Because divine compassion heard his prayer, it most mercifully revealed this at that very moment. For when he too had fallen asleep from grief, a very handsome man stood before the bed of the sleeping man. Carrying a staff in his hand, he struck him in the side and said:

“Rise and go to the church of the most blessed martyr Emmerammus, to whom you have again dedicated yourself.”

The old man replied:
