“How shall I travel through so many unknown expanses of land without food?”

The man who stood there answered him:

“Rise; do not hesitate. Take the bread placed in the upper dining room; it will itself suffice as food for you until you complete your journey.”

After this vision, the man awoke. For some time he searched the hidden recesses of his spirit, uncertain whether he had received the admonition while asleep or awake. Nevertheless, he rose according to the command of the watchful figure and found in the upper dining room bread so white and so flavorful as he had never before seen or eaten.

Taking it with him and leaving behind the other household belongings, he carried only a single garment and the double-bladed axe he was accustomed to bear in his hand.

Hastening back toward the solitude, he poured out tearful prayers to the Lord, asking that through the merits of the renowned martyr Emmerammus He might deign to prosper his journey.

He completed the journey, as he desired, through pathless regions and deserts with uninterrupted success for almost fourteen days. Finally, on the fifteenth day, at about the third hour, he reached a mountain lying opposite Regensburg between the waters of the Danube and the Imbris. From its lookout, adjoining the planting of vineyards, he saw the martyr’s church—the dwelling of his great works—and gave immense thanks to God.

Then he descended from the mountain and, after crossing the river by boat with the other groups who were going in crowds and yet competing with one another to reach the martyr’s shrine, he too hurried forward with every possible speed, rejoicing.

When he had entered the long-desired church, he clung to the pavement and fulfilled his three-year vow with tears and prayers. When the solemnity of the Mass had been completed, as was fitting, on the Lord’s Day the religious old man went outside the entrance of the church. He displayed the bread by which he had been nourished for so many days, truthfully related the story of his exile and return, and divided the two portions that remained from the food among the poor before the eyes of the entire people. He proclaimed that the benefits of so great a patron ought to remain in eternal memory.

What more should be said or written about this except what the Psalmist calls an everlasting memorial:

“Great is the glory in your salvation, Lord” (Psalm XX);

“You have placed glory and great beauty upon him.”

O gracious Jesus, this alone may be said to you under his patronage: just as you have given him to many as a powerful patron, so through his intercessions be gracious to us here and forever.

### 4.

There was a girl living in the diocese of the church of Freising. As was her custom, she went out at first light to undertake the work of pastoral care, namely, to lead her father’s animals to pasture.

[Note: This chapter too is from Aribo.]

It happened that, by a hidden judgment of God, she suddenly received such a change of spirit that she no longer wished to take any food at all for the use of life.

When her parents saw this, and her relatives learned of it, they gathered around her in astonishment. First they entreated her, then rebuked her, and finally compelled her by every kind of effort to take nourishment. But she obstinately refused everything that could be eaten or drunk, confessing that she had no pleasure whatever in food or drink.

The girl’s relatives tried pouring water mixed with milk by force into her mouth, to see whether she might perhaps swallow even a small quantity of liquid. When she unwillingly sipped its taste, she immediately vomited it back up, her neck raised, mixed with blood.

Then, not knowing what else they could do, her parents took counsel and decided to present her to Joseph, bishop of Freising, hoping that by his authority he might restore the girl to ordinary life.

While he attempted to satisfy their hopes, he rebuked the girl sternly and compelled her to eat. But she rejected food and drink as though they were refuse. Not only did she remain without eating that day; she also completed an entire year fasting, though not without the work of her hands.

Her face was exceedingly pale and drained of blood.

This seems very strange to us, and indeed incredible to the minds of human beings—or altogether to those brutish people who gaze less clearly into the mirror of the heavenly oracle. For no word is impossible with the Lord (Luke I). And again:

“Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm CXXXIV).

He alone knows why a man was born blind, and why he brought about so great a matter in a little woman. He knew by whose merits he wished to grant her salvation, and to whom he wished to reveal it through nightly visions: for the girl, long regarded by mortals as a portent, was to be brought to the shrine of the martyr Emmerammus.

When this became known to her parents, they quickly and eagerly took up their daughter. They wished to travel to the city that enclosed his holy body, but, distrustful of undertaking the journey because of its length, they took her with them to the place where the faithful witness had received the purple triumph of martyrdom.

There, humbled to the ground, she prayed as best she could and knew how. When she rose, she asked for bread. When it was brought, she stood up healed—and was healed.

The Christians who were present, seeing Christ’s wonders, praised him, perhaps shouting aloud even then. We, however, now praise him together in silence, recalling these things or reading them in the office of proclamation.

But you, holy martyr Emmerammus, worthy of veneration, for whose honor the living Bread performed this miracle in bread, obtain for us from him that we may eat and drink this Bread in his kingdom at his table with the righteous.

### 5.

The honor, reverence, and devotion with which princes honored blessed Emmerammus are demonstrated, among the other estates and precious gifts bestowed upon him by them, by the following: to the east of this province lies Lunaelacus, rich in excellent live fish, from which comes royal food; to the west lies the wine-bearing soil of Spalt, from which comes royal drink.

[Note: Lunaelacus: Monsee, granted in 831 by Louis the German and his wife Hemma; see Ried, *Codex diplomaticus*, vol. I, p. 29.]

[Note: Perhaps Spalt is the market town or settlement that occurs in Ried I, pp. 526, 656.]

The territory of Regensburg also bears witness, as does the royal estate which Charlemagne granted to blessed Emmerammus and his monks under an imperial charter, extending from the summit of the southern mountain between the public roads as far as the monastery walls themselves.

[Note: See Charlemagne’s charter in Ried I, p. 8.]

Among the other matters which he established and ordered in royal fashion and with imperial power, he deprived Duke Tassilo of his kingdom and compelled him, together with his son Dioto, to become a monk. He also restored to the Church, under Bishop Simpert, the see of the bishop of Regensburg, which earlier dukes had transferred outside the city, and established it at the basilica of the martyr Saint Emmerammus, situated within the walls of that same city and dedicated to the blessed apostle Peter.

He honored the martyr’s place with royal generosity as a protection for himself, placing it under the one who had been enthroned there in the episcopal see.

The charters and testaments of the dukes who governed the duchy of Bavaria under the Frankish kings before this prince, preserved among us, sufficiently indicate what goods they bestowed upon blessed Emmerammus.

His son, the emperor Louis of blessed memory, and those who succeeded him in the kingdom, as well as counts, nobles, and many officials of judicial rank, enriched the aforesaid place with possessions of such extent and character that this is testified not merely by the greater part of the bishopric of the city of Regensburg, but also by its better part.

Among all those who reverently worshipped or reverently loved Christ’s martyr, I think it right to single out Arnulf of blessed memory, son of Carloman: first duke of Bavaria, then king of Francia, and finally emperor at Rome on account of the defense of blessed Peter, after remarkable victories (887–899).

[Note: In the manuscript some material has been erased. In its place—according to Föringer, and reportedly written in the blank space in the Emmeram library; see Ried I, p. 5—a seventeenth-century hand added the following fable: “Among the other matters which he established and ordered in royal fashion and with imperial power, depriving Duke Tassilo of his kingdom, he compelled him, together with his son Dioto, to become a monk. He also restored to the Church, under Bishop Simpert, the see of the bishop of Regensburg, transferred by earlier dukes outside the city to the basilica of the martyr Saint Emmerammus, situated within the walls of that same city and dedicated to the blessed apostle Peter. He honored the martyr’s place with royal generosity as a protection for himself, placing it under the one who had been enthroned there in the episcopal see.”]

[Note: “Peter” is added afterward.]

Under this prince, as though laying a foundation for the writing of the martyr’s miracles, I wish to set down the following, because beginning here—with one known and especially devoted to this same martyr of God—I shall be able to make a fitting procession through the other princes to be recorded.

For Arnulf, hoping that God would thus be gracious to him, chose blessed Emmerammus as patron of his life and kingdom. He adhered to him so closely that near the monastery he built a great palace suited to royal worship.

Since he had experienced his patronage sufficiently in difficult affairs and in many battles, he perceived it more clearly when he took part in the battle of Marah.

[Note: In 893?]

There, as I remember reading, at the first clash, when the spears were rattling, those who belonged to the tyrant’s party saw the emperor’s battle lines being defended by unknown and beautiful men. As was revealed to those worthy of knowing it, these were saints whose patronage Arnulf had earnestly commended himself to before setting out.

At the sight of these men the enemy formations were terrified, and the battle on the opposing side began to slacken.

One of the tyrant’s soldiers, angered by this, seized a shield and carried the chief standard before the legions. He addressed and encouraged them arrogantly, urging them to recover their courage for battle by his example.

As he rushed forward at full speed and nearly attacked the prince himself, he encountered an old man venerable with white hair but terrifying in appearance. The old man declared to him that Emmerammus was resisting him, thrust his hand into the shield-boss, and tormented him as he struggled in vain until all those who had been emboldened by his prompting became fugitives.

[Note: Added afterward.]

[Note: Added afterward.]

The man who had seen and endured these things later confessed and disclosed in humility that they had truly happened and been spoken, not fabricated.

Thus the glorious prince, greatly rejoicing in such a victory, returned to Regensburg. There he was received by the harmonious ringing of the bells of all the churches, and the triumph, together with the miracle, was proclaimed and celebrated.

Then, using wise counsel and pondering the saying:

“On the day of good things, do not be unmindful of evil things” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 27),

and because he was displeased that nine had failed to glorify the One whose name is eternally blessed, he sent gifts of thanksgiving throughout all the monasteries of Noricum.

To his special patron Emmerammus, as an offering of thanksgiving, he gave the entire decoration of his palace.

There was a square ciborium, whose roof was covered with gold and whose summit was encircled by a garland of jewels. The body, displaying the likeness of both the upper and lower parts as a sign of the twofold love, was supported by eight golden columns. These too represented the likeness of so many virtues or beatitudes.

[Note: See Mabillon, *Iter Germanicum* (Annales edition, vol. 2, p. 10), who describes this as a small portable altar.]

It also contained complete books of the Gospels, covered with gold and gems, written, painted, and ornamented in every manner.

One of them was a cubit in size, of such workmanship, value, and weight that it would not easily find an equal.

[Note: Compare Eccard, *Francia Orientalis* II, p. 563; Mabillon, cited work, book I, p. 9; *Ratisbona monastica*, fourth edition, p. 106; and the dissertation on this book written by Sanftl in 1786, quarto.]

On its right-hand side the arrangement of the gems even completed the number one hundred. Some of them were so large that four of them covered sixteen cups, arranged in the form of the holy cross, four in each of the four sections of the middle row.

The innermost, narrower row held thirty-two cups, each covered with smaller gems. The outermost row corresponded beautifully to them: it was adorned with larger gems arranged in turrets and with pearls inserted into the battlements, in the most delightful fashion.

Yet, since these things by no means sufficed for the devotion of the generous prince toward so great a patron, he added as a gift a silver grating to be placed beneath the aforesaid ciborium.

He also added pairs of cloaks of various colors and kinds, among which one, woven in a single piece, measured thirty cubits in length.

But why linger over these things any longer? Finally, at Saint Emmerammus, he ordered a mausoleum to be prepared for himself, so that, when he was to meet death, he might have in heaven as a more gracious advocate the one whom, while living and in good health on earth, he had wished—and indeed caused—to be powerful for himself and his people.

Come to the aid of the soul of this your servant, and of the multitude that still serves you, with a powerful prayer before the Almighty, blessed Emmerammus!

### 6.

Under the aforesaid prince, Tuto, a monk of Saint Emmerammus, presided over the church of Regensburg. He remained in this life from the seventh year of that emperor’s reign until the twelfth year of the reign of Henry the Saxon (894–930).

His predecessor, King Conrad, came to the city of Regensburg because public affairs required it (918). After settling the matters for which he had come, he approached, according to the ancient custom of kings and having been forewarned, the church of blessed Emmerammus, as though to receive permission to return to Francia.

There, while visiting the tombs of the princes—namely, those of the emperor Arnulf and of Louis, who had died prematurely in childhood—the chaplains suggested to him improperly that, by royal right and power, he should claim for himself, as the successor of his ancestors, the aforementioned book of great value.

[Note: “n. h. q. p. i. m. e. m.; successit” corrected to “excessit” in an erased place, 1.]

When the bishop named above was ordered to surrender the book, but, because of fear of the martyr, had no courage at all to do so, threats finally brought matters to the point that he unwillingly displayed the book on the altar before the prince.

Nevertheless, he pronounced this curse:

“Let him be the debtor of blessed Emmerammus on the day of judgment who removes this from his service.”

The king was soon to learn how powerful this was.

[Note: Added afterward.]

He ordered the book to be rashly taken away and carried off. But when he had mounted his horse, he was struck near the monastery by an attack of dysentery.

Terrified by this, and recognizing through his torments the connection between the deed and its consequence, he restored the book to blessed Emmerammus at that very moment. He carried the illness with him and finally closed his last day in Francia (23 December).

Then the venerable bishop Tuto, clinging to Christ in his martyr, added as much as he could to the crowns of the princes Charles, Carloman, and Arnulf. For blessed Emmerammus he prepared a golden altar, decorated it in the most beautiful form, and adorned it with a thousand gems.

Though blinded in body, he was illuminated in mind. He transformed the necessity of his chastened infirmity into the noble virtue of the spirit. Since he did not greatly lament the deprivation of a light that he shared with the flies, he possessed such spiritual consolation that through him he foresaw future events and openly declared things in which he himself had little interest.

While staying at Lunaelacus, situated about thirty rastas from Regensburg, he announced to his people one day that a great fire had occurred there.

[Note: In 906? See *Annales Ratisbonenses*, MGH SS I, p. 94.]

Having borne witness not only to this event but also to the whole of his piety there, he departed from this world—as our good hope tells us—and migrated to the heavenly dwellings, where he would always see Emmerammus, his patron, whom he had loved here.

May his favorable intercession obtain for servants, before the true Light, the illumination of our eyes, so that we may never sleep the sleep of death at the gates!

### 7.

After the monastery of the most blessed martyr Emmerammus, which had previously stood outside the city, came to be within the walls of the city of Regensburg—walls that Duke Arnulf had quickly built under King Henry, dividing the work among the nobles—his son Otto, the first emperor from the Saxon people, thought fit to come to this same city (954?).

After carrying out and celebrating the matters belonging to imperial jurisdiction, he had given blessed Emmerammus a royal estate which the German language calls Halfandorf and which the Roman tongue renders as “Village of Help.”

[Note: See the charters of 940 and 950 in Ried I, pp. 96–97. They were not, however, issued at Regensburg, where the king apparently did not arrive before 954.]

At that time Bishop Michael of Hiatospolis prepared a banquet for the emperor in one of the monastery’s palaces and made the prince recline there with the leading men.

When they had nearly been strengthened by the custom of banqueters and made merry with wine, the emperor, speaking in Saxon with a cheerful voice, said:

“Whoever drinks whose beer should also sing that person’s song.”

“We have eaten and drunk the goods of blessed Emmerammus. Therefore it seems right to me that the banquet should be concluded with his *caritas*.”

[Note: He was the one who killed Saint Emmerammus; his descendants are also discussed in chapter 12.]

At once the cupbearers appeared, offering each person, at the emperor’s command, the martyr’s *caritas*. Out of reverence for him, as everyone kissed one another and encouraged one another to drink the cup of *caritas*, one man arrogantly refused it, saying:

“Heilram [perhaps: ‘this *caritas*’] has no place in my belly, because food and drink have already occupied it.”

His tongue was still trembling from the utterance of the words when he received from the wall, against which he was leaning with his back supported by a hanging cloth, such a powerful slap that he was thrown from his seat and fell headlong into the middle of the palace. At the same time fear and deep astonishment seized everyone.

Then the religious monarch entered the church hastily with the bishops and nobles. As the bells rang together, praises and litanies were celebrated to God and the martyr in thanksgiving.

But lest this seem incredible to anyone, let every faithful person know that I did not invent it in any way. I received it, as I have written, from a certain faithful and elderly man named Sigibald, who testified by the faith of Christ that he had been present at this banquet and had likewise spoken the truth.

But you, holy Emmerammus, whom the Almighty wished to honor by this sign as by the others, pour out prayers to him for us sinners, so that through true *caritas* we may be able to turn aside the angel of Satan who strikes us with blows!

### 8.

Under the bishop mentioned above, whose name was angelic, there was a monk of blessed Emmerammus, and also the church’s custodian and sacristan, named Adalpertus.

He undertook a pilgrimage overseas out of desire for holy places. As he sought Jerusalem and examined the sanctuaries of the heavenly treasure in the other places, he was worn down by a thousand adversities and tested by land and sea. He was repeatedly proved to have been rescued from the very jaws of death through the prayers of his patron.

A report by him, inserted here, reveals how once this happened through an especially evident sign:

“One day we undertook a sea journey. The density of the clouds, the collision of the waves, and the blasts of the storms produced for us a gloomy night. As we were tossed here and there by winds and waves, and dangers threatened death, matters reached the point that the sailors cried out repeatedly: ‘Lord, there is no [hope].’ And the helmsman said trembling: ‘It is failing.’

“Then I, wretched man, pondering the depths and believing that all hope of life had been exhausted, fell asleep from grief.

“In sleep I seemed to see the pastoral staff of my lord the martyr Emmerammus hanging before my eyes—the staff commonly called a *cambota* or crook. Since its hook was turned toward my face, and I sensed that the benefits of my often-tested patron were near me, I tried to insert my hand into it, so that he might deign to pull me after him, clinging to him, out of the depths of the sea.

“Then, at the very moment when I extended my hand—which I was raising as though awake—I awoke and saw night changed into day, sorrow into joy, and the stormy sky into serenity.

“Rejoicing at the sight, I marveled, together with those who were marveling, at so sudden and rapid a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

“The sailors, recovering their strength, gave thanks to God for our safety and for the greatness of the miracle.

“But I, giving thanks to the fountain of every good, attributed to the patronage of the most blessed martyr Emmerammus what could in no way have happened through our merits.

“Through him may he who neither sleeps nor slumbers render dreams and waking hours harmless for us, and grant us the ability to remain awake for good works.”

### 9.

In the preceding chapter I wrote what was a consolation to the hooded man and monk. In this one I wish to connect it with what is a source of fear to the perverse and likewise of terror to apostates.

There was at Regensburg a certain man named Sigibertus, free according to human law or worldly condition, but lacking and sick in true Christian freedom.

I learned that he was so greatly afflicted by fantastic illusions that, whether asleep or awake, he could have no rest at all unless he had made himself a hooded monk at Saint Emmerammus.

When this had been done, the harassment of the demons ceased, and the various obstacles caused by the evil spirit were quieted through the martyr’s prayer.

But after several days, that wretched and unhappy man, forgetting his defender, consented to the secret suggestions of the one who had unwillingly lost his dominion over him.

Complaining about the “pots of meat left behind in Egypt” and regretting that in the monastery he suffered want of certain things whose small abundance he had falsely abandoned in the world, he removed the monastic habit, with the mockery that the common people now have in a proverb:

“Away, away with the hood; you will burden my neck no longer. Because of the monks’ poverty, I must quickly return to the tanner’s block.”

He said this because he had previously been a leatherworker, or a deceitful maker of footwear.

But he did not long rejoice that he had thus mocked the monks. Not long afterward he was handed over to the evil spirit.

Driven by it into extreme madness, he was dragged, already chained, to Saint Emmerammus and bound to a column in the choir. When the brothers had gathered and prayed for him tearfully, he sometimes leapt about, terrifying those standing nearby with his shouts; at other times he lay on his back.

Finally, the devil held him suspended in the air until the majesty of divine compassion came to his aid through the prayers of the faithful, and especially through the patronage of blessed Emmerammus.

Then, falling back onto the pavement, he began, with his neck thrust forward by the demon’s violence, to vomit blood mixed with pus.

When this had horribly polluted the pavement, the prince of filth suddenly removed all the filth from it, carried it with him to the glass window, shattered the window as a sign of his departure, and thus vanished among the spiritual powers of wickedness.

That man afterward spent many years in severe penance, practicing barefoot walking in the utmost poverty.

Holy Emmerammus, honored by the Holy Trinity through a threefold miracle, intercede for our negligence before the One whose mercy no sins of mortals can overcome.

### 10.

Among the innumerable misfortunes of human circumstances, it seems—and truly is—very pitiable and even more grievous that the enemy of the human race should enter as though into their own dwellings those human beings of whom God ought to be the possessor.

Yet this really occurs by the hidden and just judgment of God. For such people are sometimes handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord’s coming.

One of these, named Gestiliub, was handed over to the worst of guests. Noble by birth but wretched everywhere, he was bound within by a multitude of demons and outwardly by an iron chain. He was taken through many holy places to be cleansed, but was brought back without having been freed.

Finally, by divine mercy, which directed matters according to its will, he came to Saint Emmerammus, the magnificent liberator of such people through a heavenly gift.

There, bound by two chains, he was so bestial and savage that three men, divided into equal numbers on his right and left, could scarcely restrain him from destroying himself and others.

After prayers had long been offered for him, and while he was a source of horror and an example to many, before the confession of the most blessed martyr the shaggy and dreadful guest confessed the name of the legion and was expelled from the host who had formerly been dear to it, but had then become exceedingly bitter through the martyr’s prayers.

Then, if you had been present, you would have seen a remarkable thing: a man who shortly before had been stretched in bones and sinews by alien strength was suddenly content with an ordinary movement of the body, stripped of those powers and restored to himself at one and the same moment.

Through the charity of the saints whom he had sought in order to be relieved of his misery, he was presented to blessed Emmerammus; through that sweetest patron he gave thanks to God, and at the same time all the people of Hiatospolis rejoiced together with him.

For this and for the other miracles of your power, Lord of lords, the present and future generations will praise your works. They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, recount your wonders, and declare the power of your fearful deeds.

With them we too say humbly and supplicantly:

“Grant to Emmerammus, your faithful witness, the salvation of us all.”

### 11.

How great the merits of blessed Emmerammus the martyr are in the presence of the Almighty is testified by the wretched lineage of the tyrant Lampertus, now for more than three hundred years.

One man from his stock was seeking the church of our patron one day with others. When they attempted to enter, he was suddenly struck blind in the very middle of the atrium adjoining it.

As he wandered there, feeling his way with his hands and stumbling with his feet, passersby asked who he was and what he was suffering. When he confessed, together with his misfortune, his unhappy lineage, he left the atrium by their advice and guidance.

Soon recovering his sight, he did not sufficiently examine himself regarding what had happened to him. Thinking himself released from some burden, he joined the crowd of those entering. Then, as one wonder followed another, he was struck blind again at the very entrance of the doors.

Therefore the people, giving honor to God, immediately expelled him outside. By this most evident sign everyone inferred that he was an enemy of the martyr.

Carrying with him the testimony of this event, together with public shame, and greatly amazed that he had twice been blinded and illuminated, he returned home. The following saying then circulated among his companions and relatives:

“Let everyone know that no one from the posterity of Lampertus will be granted access to Saint Emmerammus unless it has been obtained with great humility and through a prayer of very great power.”

But you, magnificent Light of the world, through the intercessions of your martyr illuminate the darkness of our hearts, so that we may not be exiles from the heavenly kingdom but may be admitted to the wedding of the Lamb.

12. Certain noble men, known to us by kinship and by the time in which they lived—we shall suppress their names, since every neighbor is ashamed, through fear and distress alike, of the disastrous plague that for a long time and with great violence raged among men of tyrannical posterity—sent offerings of their possessions, together with the prayers of priests and the supplications of other servants of God, to blessed Emmerammus, so that they might be permitted to enter the dwelling-place of his repose without public disgrace. When this seemed to have been obtained, word was brought to them that they might come with good hope. They came and were admitted with humility and trembling, and were not received fruitlessly. For, reverently placing their heads and hands upon the altar, they declared themselves perpetual censual tenants of the martyr.

Some gave servants, male and female, that they might find favor in the presence of so great a patron. Others bestowed landed estates, so that they might no longer remain among the guilty. One left behind a three-year illness; another laid down a two-year infirmity; another overcame the continual harassment of an evil spirit. Finally refreshed by these and similar benefits—for previously they had been afflicted by innumerable evils—they returned to their homes.

But one of that same stock, stiff-necked Adalrammus by name, did what blessed Emmerammus had not wished. He had unjustly claimed for himself a portion of the estates that his nephew had assigned by witnessed deed as an inheritance to the martyr. Summoned on this account by the leading men and challenged by the advocates, he utterly refused to render justice because of the hardness of his heart. Blessed Emmerammus, however, the best defender of his own, afflicted him so severely for his rashness and wickedness that for several weeks his illness was both punishment and terror to himself, and an inconsolable grief to his friends.

It therefore happened that he often wished for death, but death, though desired, did not come. At last, undoubtedly learning the truth from the very appearance of events—that he had offended the one whose most holy martyr he had dishonored—and grieving that he lived most miserably while nevertheless being unable to end such a life even by death, he adopted a late but nevertheless good counsel. He hurriedly sent his wife with their little son to the martyr; that is, he made my niece go there with her nephew to restore the estates.

They arrived on the night of the martyr’s vigils and, in the morning, explained the circumstances to me. After receiving from me the counsel necessary for the boy’s salvation, at about the second hour of the day of the most blessed martyr’s nativity she approached the altar almost as a mother. First she caused the first of her sons to pay the due to Saint Emmerammus; then, with his hands drawn forward in the Bavarian manner and before witnesses, she restored the estates just as they had previously been conveyed, and returned home.

Afterward a messenger came to me who swore by blessed Emmerammus that the aforementioned Adalrammus had died at that very hour in peaceful repose, at the same hour in which this restoration had been made at Regensburg. Therefore, all of us who are worshipers of so great a patron, let us sing grateful praises to God and to him!

13. The mighty works of God must be considered with the greatest attention, and the anger or patience of the saints must be feared exceedingly. For when these saints act as our protectors, the Most High enthroned will be merciful to us; but when they are offended and despised, he will not leave the offense unavenged, whether after a long or a short time, nor will he regard it as a trivial matter.

What happened at the church of Saint Emmerammus under Bishop Michahel was sufficiently demonstrated by what our elders—who remembered that time—reported to us. For the bishop, having taken defenders on behalf of the martyr’s property, engaged in a great conflict with Margrave Pertoldus.

**[Note: [Col. 1009D] Concerning him, see Thietmar II, 14; III, 7.]**

After the struggle had long continued on both sides, the parties finally reached an equal settlement: by the oath of twelve noblemen, as the prefect demanded, the matter was to be removed from blessed Emmerammus. With the *cambota* of the martyr himself placed upon his altar, men of the prescribed number came forward and swore.

**[Note: [Col. 1011D] It was a staff on which the lame leaned. Thus Peter the Deacon says: “They hung the *cambuttas* of the same lame man before the church doors.” But the word is taken for a pastoral staff; for bishops and abbots alike carried it, and it was sent to those who were absent, who thereby received the governance of the Church as though by this sign. Thus Orderic Vitalis, Book III: “Through the *cambuta* of Ivo, bishop of Sées, he transferred the external authority of the abbey.” They also used the *cambuta* in giving faith and making an oath, and an example of this is found here. Finally, it was hung at the tombs of the dead; thus one reads in the *Life of Desiderius, Bishop of Cahors*, chapter 19: “While the staff of the blessed man, which the Gauls call *Cambucca*, was carefully hanging at the head of his tomb.” *Cambuca*, *cambuta*, and *cambota* are therefore the same thing. BASN.]**

But struck by divine vengeance, they departed carrying a great evil with them. My grandfather on my father’s side, Arnoldus, was afflicted by the same retribution: at that very moment his right arm was weakened, and a few years later, alone in the river Nab, though his companions survived, he ended his life by a sudden death.

What the others who had sworn together suffered I shall briefly relate. One was blinded; another strangled; another deprived of his senses; another released by paralysis; another disemboweled; another burned by lightning; another consumed in the fire of his own house; another became one-handed and one-eyed; another was struck by cancer; another was disfigured by the plague of elephantiasis; another was burdened by dropsical swelling. They ended a wretched life by a wretched death.

For this reason my maternal grandfather, namely the aforementioned Count Peratholdus, touched by a terrifying warning, donated to blessed Emmerammus the suburban estate called Isininga through the arrangement of the venerable, pious abbot Ramuoldus [lacuna] of that same estate.

**[Notes: [Col. 1011] Added later in manuscript 1.]**

**[Note: [Col. 1011] The reading of this word is uncertain; Föringer noted that it may perhaps be read *addicens*.]**

**[Notes: [Col. 1011] Added later in manuscript 1.]**

He assigned its service, to be rendered twelve times, to the charitable use of the monks and also to the twelvefold refreshment of Christ’s almsgivers.

**[Note: [Col. 1012D] See the charters in Pez I, 3, pp. 92, 99.]**

But you, most holy martyr Emmerammus, glorified by the miracle of twelve, pour out abundant prayers for us sinners, who until now have abused twelve irreligious practices, before the one who had dedicated this number to the apostolic choir!

14. Although the Christian faith holds this most certainly—that those who are generous to the poor in the Lord’s name ought to be, and truly are in every respect, rich in God—and although he himself is rich toward all and can give sufficient things to everyone, nevertheless, so that there may never be lacking in the world those in whom human frailty can redeem its sins, he daily bears the burden of poverty in his least members (Ephesians II).

For the sake of relieving these people, who travel through the houses and lodgings of the faithful, the stinginess and wickedness of certain persons become so hardened that, under the pressure of hunger and cold, they are forced to fall into the bitter hovels of death. Under this pretext, the multitude of false brothers violently dictates its judgment, so that it may consume as many as possible in misery.

These men are not humble in spirit but poor in possessions and vices. Through secret and open robberies they obstruct Christ’s poor, preventing them from sometimes receiving relief even from good believers, by whom good and wicked poor alike cannot easily be distinguished. As sons of the devil, allied with perverse and criminal men, some of them commit exceedingly cruel acts of banditry in forests and villages; others undertake utterly wicked deeds in sacred places.

Some who appear more holy than the rest, frequenting churches under the guise of hypocrisy and coveting sacrilegious little profits there, willingly or unwillingly reveal publicly how empty they are of true riches. What more need be said? We have often seen such men apprehended in holy places, not without a miracle; their thefts and other crimes made it sufficiently clear that they had not come as true worshipers to adore God in spirit and truth, but as fraudulent or deceitful flatterers (John IV).

Some of these, granted mercy, were saved in the spirit of gentleness. Others, who appeared harder of heart, were corrected by public punishments, lest impunity make them worse. A hidden portion was reserved for the patience of the saints, because the mortals who were ignorant of the deed also remained ignorant of who and what sort of men they were—except those who were conscious of having committed such acts.

Among their number was a certain woman, a native of the city of Regensburg, who one day approached the shrine (*confessio*) of Christ’s martyr Emmerammus, called “of the feet,” as though to worship. There, by furtively snatching a chalice which she found upon the altar of Blessed John, and seeing as she looked about that she was alone, she did grave harm to her own salvation.

After hiding it at home, exchanging its silver for lead, and abusing it for her own purposes, she was, by a manifest judgment of God, struck down by paralysis. Burdened by this affliction for two years, and finally stretched out under continuous pains, she learned whom she had offended in the martyr’s place. Because she had despised his confession, she now plainly bore the mark of confusion in her own body.

Returning to herself, and striving through a penitent heart to attend to her sufferings, she arranged, with the small sum that she was able to collect through the assistance of her neighbors, to have a new chalice made. Then, after confessing her offense to the priests, she was carried in a basket to Saint Emmerammus, since she had lost the use of her limbs.

When she had restored the chalice with her own hand, though supported from above, and had poured out her innermost prayers with tears, she suddenly sprang from the basket and bed restored to health, loudly giving thanks to God and blessed Emmerammus. And because she was now gladly free of the basket that she had brought—or rather by which she had been brought—with her sufferings, she left it joyfully beside the base of the altar.

The faithful immediately hung it outside the church as a memorial and, with the greatest joy, added it to the multitude of signs hanging in that place.

But since so great a miracle had been provided from heaven, the merit of so great a martyr must be carefully considered. He willed that the woman, deprived of the service of her feet, should come to the altar of his repose by a route opposite to that taken by those who walked—namely, so that where previously, blinded by impiety, she had silently concealed her offense, there afterward, under the light of pious confession and the recovery of health, she might herself, together with the others, learn what is written: “The Lord preserves the feet of his saints.” And also the saying of the prophet Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Isaiah LII).

May he deign to make us participants in these blessings through the prayers of his most beloved martyr, he who, seated above the Cherubim, looks upon the abysses (Daniel III). Amen.

15. Since divine benefits are, until the end of the world, the resurrection and ruin of many, the omnipotence of the Creator is declared daily. It directs the hearts of the faithful along the path of his commandments, saves the humble people, and humbles the eyes of the proud.

He therefore chastises the children of the sacred faith mercifully, so that he may correct them; but the unbelieving and impious, because of their hard and impenitent hearts, he condemns by a just judgment. Hence the Christian people rejoice in the grace of almighty God, separated from the hand of foreign sons, whose sons are like young plantings, whose daughters are adorned on every side, whose storehouses are full and overflowing from one thing into another, whose sheep are fat, and whose oxen are heavy. “There is no breach in their wall, no exile, and no outcry in their streets” (Psalm CXLIII).

Ensnared, therefore, by this false prosperity, the pagans and Jews commonly reproach Christians, saying that while Christians are worn down and burdened by many kinds of oppression, they themselves, by contrast, possess consolation and relief in all their affairs. Pestilence and famine afflict our people as though they were poor and destitute, while an excess of possessions refreshes—or rather stretches to the point of bursting—them, in whom lies the source of every evil.

Against their empty boasting, spiritual abundance fully consoles us, if we are worthy. From its fullness David, overflowing in speech and consoling the heart humbled by afflictions, says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from them all” (Psalm XXXIII). “The death of sinners is most grievous” (Psalm LXXII), for pride held them captive, since “they shall not be scourged with men.”

When we say to them, “Why do you not believe in the Lord, whose yoke of faith the whole world now rejoices to have taken upon itself?” they reply that the practice of true faith must be tested equally in prosperity and adversity, and that it must be determined who in the world appears to lie under a curse.

We, however, respond that the world’s curse will be changed into heavenly blessing, hunger into satiety, and mourning into joy; therefore we must patiently endure the adversities of the world.

“You,” they say, “as usual, always regard uncertain things as certain; and so, with a certain ease, you try to lead us to these beliefs.”

Desiring to win them by some means for the Lord’s name, we teach them in words such as these:

“It is established that Christians have been greatly confirmed in the faith by the deeds of their ancestors and by their words. Among the other evidences of truth, miracles also strongly support it—miracles manifested from heaven at the memorials of the saints. Because of their greatness and frequency, we do not think that even the enemies of this name and religion can remain unaware of them.”

When these words had been spoken on our side, the Jews, attempting to oppose them with the hardness of a stony heart, shout and cry out:

“We know very well where your conclusion is heading. In the church of your martyr Emmerammus, because it is known to all who live in Regensburg that the lame have been restored and those afflicted by other ailments have been cured by the true physician, we do not deny this. But by the Messiah whom you call Christ, and by the one whom you say is your patron, we never admit that any such thing has been done.

“For the Almighty, in every place of his dominion, does whatever he wills as God. He can also grant health to the sick in the streets and perform in synagogues or in our schools such things as you boast have been done in your churches.”

Then, as though their mouths were suspended toward the vault of heaven and their insolent tongues were passing over the earth, we silenced them with a speech of this kind:

“When our Lord Jesus Christ lived bodily among men and magnificently bestowed the gifts of his goodness upon your fathers both inside and outside the synagogue, you not only proved ungrateful toward him, but, killing yourselves by the most wretched madness, heaped this also upon your iniquities for your own harm: you reviled in him the head of all good things, as well as his chosen members, from whom you ought to have drawn the salvation freely offered.

“Behold, we turn to the nations, which have learned to praise the Lord faithfully in his saints. Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of God’s grace and, by your negative refusal, have rejected every good thing from your salvation until this day, we fruitfully offer these pearls to those who know how to receive them with honor.

“But for you there will be eternal confusion, as Christ testifies in his Gospel: ‘The sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness and punished without end’ (Matthew VIII).”

But, to return to the purpose of our humility, O readers and hearers who confess the true faith: whatever seemed doubtful to the Jews concerning the grace of Christ and the glory of the saints, we advise your love that it is not doubtful but must always remain certain—that the door of God, which is closed to some, will be opened to others by the just judgment of God.

Before him, and in him, we must pray from the heart that we may not be condemned with this world but saved by the powerful grace of the Redeemer. In his love, together with faith, we must place our hope, lest he permit us to perish from the company of the righteous, for whom he deigned to undergo the death of the cross.

16. There was a certain freeborn man, a vassal of Burchard, margrave-count **[Note: [Col. 1013D] Of the Eastern March; he appears to have been the son of Berthold mentioned in chapter 13, whom Thietmar, V. 21, calls Buccho. Nevertheless, above, p. 415, note 66, I incorrectly identified him as the son-in-law of Duke Arnulf and the father of Bishop Henry of Augsburg. This man was certainly of advanced age; and since Widukind calls him (III, 36) a soldier of moderate means, he cannot be assigned to this noble family of counts.]** and prefect of Regensburg.

Divine scourges chastised him, so that, with his sinews contracted, he was deprived of the use of almost all his limbs. After he had long been worn down by such a punishment, he was finally carried to Saint Emmerammus, in a hope that would not disappoint, so that God’s work might be manifested in him, in a cradle more suitable until then for infants than for men.

When the vehicle had reached the altar of the martyr and prayer had been offered there for a while, he who had clung to the cradle like a little child was suddenly raised up strong and stood upright like a man. Those present then saw, in the martyr’s new miracle, his full and lofty stature, like an image of the general resurrection.

In the church of that same martyr they offered God the sacrifice of a shout of praise, according to what David says: “The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Psalm CXVII).

Together with them, our sweetest patron—granted an eternal homeland in place of a brief exile, awarded a reward in place of the immeasurable burden of his labors, and having acquired a precious death through an extraordinary kind of martyrdom—glories in your kingdom, Christ, with the crown whose radiance is increased by the jewel of your special and intimate love.

May we also, according to our measure, be found humbly marked by that jewel at the hour of our calling, through your mercy, which does not permit the good things in the hearts of truly faithful people to fall asleep, but brings their works to completion with the full fruit of perseverance.

17. The glory of the saints reigning together with Christ, fathers and brothers, is greatly to be revered; their anger must be avoided in every way, and their patience must be feared by every sex and order. For to them the Lord says: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zechariah II, 8); and in the Gospel: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

These thunderclaps, proceeding from the very throne of heaven and resounding fearfully over mortals, are so scorned—alas!—by the badly deaf hardness of worldly people that, coveting the property of churches or of the poor, they seize the Lord’s inheritance and make it their own; or rather, they make themselves and their possessions part of the devil’s portion.

Against them the curse is pronounced through the prophetic saying: “Woe to those who unjustly join field to field” (Isaiah V, 8).

Among them are some who appear more honorable and more self-controlled in carrying out such deeds. When they see others inclined to perpetrate the acts I have briefly mentioned, they cunningly incite them; and, so that they may cling more tenaciously to these little affairs, they repeat their encouragements, stubbornly promising to be their helpers before judges and, if necessity requires, their fellow swearers.

Then, as though in a way returning to themselves—or rather turning backward by winding paths into the hiding places of wickedness—they abandon for a time those to whom they gave the counsel of iniquity and slyly betake themselves to the men whose property they have exposed to plunder or robbery. In exchange for silence about their falsehood or for a saleable testimony to the truth, they fill the hands of the unwary with gifts, and by such a stratagem extort from simpler people whatever they appear to possess.

To this great evil, thickened in the common crowd by a thousand devices, the prefects and counts, who ought and are able to cure it, refuse not only to oppose and resist it, but even add to it themselves. They also dishonor, as far as lies within them, every beauty of justice, so that they may fill the insatiable pit of avarice not merely wickedly but disgracefully.

For the swift overthrow of their insolence the prophet cries out—or rather, through him the person unjustly oppressed demands vengeance: “Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts” (Psalm XCIII, 2).

This cause, which ought to be called not a cause but a plague—that is, the mingling of demonic things with human affairs and, nevertheless, the preference of human things to divine—some people pursue so eagerly for earthly gain that, through the flattering strokes and enticements of other wicked counsel in which they abound, they even try to infect the shepherds of the Church and endeavor to turn the rams of the Lord’s flock into wolves.

Whoever fails to observe their poisonous agreements—

**[Note: [Col. 1015D] That is, pacts and agreements.]**

—undoubtedly incurs danger to his life. Michahel, bishop of the city of Reginum (972), learned this sufficiently through his own experience.

When he had decided to seek a position at the palace in order to petition the emperor for an episcopate for one of his nephews, and had prepared gifts with which he hoped to obtain this, those who wanted ecclesiastical dignities to be for sale before princes persuaded him to adorn the petition he intended to make with the treasures of God’s beloved martyr Emmerammus.

He, agreeing with guilty and perverse advisers, removed these treasures shortly before the martyr’s birthday in September and took them with him to the episcopal estate called Berabartashusun.

**[Note: [Col. 1015D] Beratzhausen, on the river Laber.]**

On that same day his deadly retinue gathered there. Then, suddenly struck by a bodily affliction, he began to be driven toward death in his final hour.

When he felt it approaching, troubled and bitter, and had already despaired of being able to remain longer within the bounds of this life, he summoned the *vicedominus*, called in soldiers as witnesses, and addressed certain attendants who had more affection than fear for him, and on whose intimacy he had habitually relied, in these words:

“It once happened that I took part in a serious battle beside the river Lech, under the first Saxon emperor, Otto.

**[Note: [Col. 1016D] In the year 955.]**

“When the fiercest fighting had taken place between our men and the pagans, and, by Christ’s favor, the Christians had triumphed, the Hungarians cut off my ear and, with swords and spears, struck me down among the others and leveled me with the earth. There, unexpectedly carried away, I perceived that the merciful patron was present with his benefits for my salvation; now I fear him, angry because of my sinful rashness.

“Come, I beg you, faithfully do what I command. Take from here—would that never again for the evil I intended to do—my twenty whole cloaks, marked with a definite number, and offer them, though small in comparison with the greatness of my sins, to the great and blessed martyr of Christ, Emmerammus, for him to aid whomever he wishes.

“Reverently return to him a portion of his own treasures, which, foolish and insufficiently cautious, I removed in dishonor of his honor and service.

“Also place upon and around his altar the golden chalice that I made for that most renowned martyr, in a work and form sufficiently decent, as I think, and with it everything that I have described in words. Thus, as the message of my humility, you shall say:

“‘That sinful man Michahel, although by right of sacred order he shared in the name of the angels within the holy Church, nevertheless judging himself undeserving and far unequal to the ministries of so great an office, and having become your adopted servant, blessed Emmerammus, even beneath the pontifical insignia, now placed at the point of death and devoted to reverence for you, has sent and returned these things to you. As he draws his last breath, he has also entrusted his soul together with his body to your patronage.’”

When these actions and words had met with and alarmed not a few people, because of the neglect of the saints commonly and abusively practiced among mortals, a certain bell of modest size, displayed in the basilica of our patron by the bishop’s envoys together with the other objects, proclaimed a great miracle through the mouths of those who spoke of it.

When the emperor Otto II once heard at Saint Emmerammus its singular ringing, louder than that of the others, he is said to have remarked that he wanted to have that bell, or one like it. Taking this as his opportunity, the aforementioned bishop ordered the same little bell to be removed and transported with him on the road, thinking that by offering the prince the desired object he would be doing enough.

After it had been carried out of the martyr’s church, as we learned from the report of a certain priest, by the will of almighty God it became mute through a change in its sound. No craft could restore its function of producing harmonious sound until the day and hour when it was returned to the house of God’s beloved martyr. Then, although insensible, it made human senses perceive that it felt the presence of its lord, and it rang sweetly.

Truly these are your works, Christ, who are believed to be, and are, the Wisdom of the eternal Father. David, rejoicing in heart, cries out to you:

“How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Psalm XXX, 20).

And again:

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice” (Psalm L, 10).

Delighting in the desire for you, and urging those who believe in your name toward perfect praise at the end of the Psalms, he says:

“Praise the Lord with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation” (Psalm CL, 5).

Behold, O lover of human salvation, Maker and Restorer of our race, who are also kind toward the ungrateful and wicked: through small and insensible things you accomplish great and wondrous works, making people of understanding fit for your blessing.

Those who receive this with the ear of the heart and persevere in obeying it to the end will not fear greatly on the last day, nor will their ears ring at the hearing of evil, when the enemy, exulting over the destruction of the wicked, boasts, saying:

“I have prevailed against them” (Psalm XII, 5).

O good Jesus, what shall we sinners say there, where scarcely even the righteous will be saved? We have no other hope than the one declared by your chosen psalmist, who was both king and prophet and who cried out to you from his whole heart with every modulation:

“You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Psalm CXLI, 6).

We have learned through evangelical teaching that this hope must be requested from the Father in your name while the time of mercy lasts. For your Gospel, O Truth, says:

“Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you”; and again: “While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light” (John XII, 35–36).

We must also heed most carefully that statement which excludes every human excuse, and strive toward it with our inmost sighs:

“Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XV, 16).

Therefore, turning to you, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, we ask that, in the name of that same Only-Begotten Son, whose charity your martyr blessed Emmerammus uniquely imitated among many witnesses—

**[Note: [Col. 1017] The remainder is written in a first hand of the fifteenth century on the following folio, together with the ancient ending of this book, which has been cut away.]**

**[Note: [Col. 1017] The remainder is written in a first hand of the fifteenth century on the following folio, together with the ancient ending of this book, which has been cut away.]**

**[Note: [Col. 1017] The remainder is written in a first hand of the fifteenth century on the following folio, together with the ancient ending of this book, which has been cut away.]**

**[Note: [Col. 1017] The remainder is written in a first hand of the fifteenth century on the following folio, together with the ancient ending of this book, which has been cut away.]**

—in ineffable and customary mercy toward sinners, forgive those who confess and have confessed the wickedness of their hearts; pour into them the anointing of your richest consolation; and confirm in us the works of divine mercy.

Grant that what appears sweet and delightful in this world may grow bitter through reverent consideration of your fear, and that what is bitter may grow sweet through the most gentle contemplation of your love.

Thus, while the world itself turns, may we rise, with you raising us up, from the fall into and love of sin, lest at the end of the ages, when all human beings have risen with their bodies, we be eternally put to shame and punished. Instead, having now been made, by your grace, worthy purchased slaves together with fellow servants, may we then be assigned with your friends to joys that endure forever, and may we safely behold the Lord Jesus, your Son, the Liberator and Bishop of our souls and bodies, the just Judge of the living and the dead, living with you and reigning in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

# Prologue to the Book Concerning the Memory of Blessed Emmerammus and His Devotees

Among the other sacramental mysteries of heaven, the writings of the Old Law testify that, for the building of the tabernacle, the leaders of the tribes and all the wealthier people of God offered precious gifts at the divine command (Exodus XXXV). The poorer people, likewise moved by the same command, added even goat hair as tokens of devoted minds (ibid.).

But what does the New Law contain concerning this matter, and in what way does it correspond with the ancient Law? Christ makes this clear in his Gospel: he preferred the two small coins of the poor widow to what the rich displayed or put into the treasury (Mark XII; Luke XXI).

A certain man, apostolic in office and merit, explained this briefly and excellently, as though thundering from heaven, when he said: “The kingdom of heaven is worth as much as you possess.” This judgment agrees with what sacred Scripture elsewhere cries out: “From the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be demanded” (Luke XII).

Therefore, the one who possesses much must carefully heed the Apostle’s words: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians I). But the one who has received less must not regard it as something to be neglected; rather, according to his ability and knowledge, he should strive to accomplish something useful from it.

Whoever diligently carries this out and shows reverence for the divine gift pays the debt demanded by Scripture, which says:

“Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him” (Psalm LXXV).

For whatever we piously and worthily offer to him, or whatever vow we are able to fulfill, we have received from his gifts, since he is the Giver of all good things.

Hence the apostle James, commending the procession of these same gifts, says:

“Every good gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I).

The Psalmist urges us to draw near to his illumination, saying:

“Draw near to the Lord and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded” (Psalm XXXIII).

Truly, those who have drawn near to him have been illuminated by his gift. Through deeds and words devoted to the Church’s sacraments, they have merited that glory of the face which the Sun of Justice, by his vision, prepared eternally for his elect.

Through the example and teaching of such people, while the wheel of this world turns, Christ will find acceptable fruit in his trees. Since I do not have such fruit in my own tree, being like a useless shoot, I greatly fear for myself that the master of the household, offended by the barrenness of my wickedness, may say:

“Why does he occupy the ground? Cut him down and cast him into the fire” (Luke XIII).

This punishment, terribly prepared for the reprobate and, alas, often compared with my sins, comes before my mind as I am tossed amid the waves of my thoughts. If I am to escape it, I see this as the best remedy: that I should not cease seeking the protection of the saints, diligently clinging to their praises, so that they may deign to obtain pardon for my offenses from the most merciful Lord.

But perhaps someone will say: “What is it to you?” Could it be fitted for the function of harmonious sound until the day and hour when, returned to the dwelling of God’s beloved martyr, although insensible it indicated to human senses that it felt the presence of its lord, and rang sweetly.

Truly these are your works, Christ, who are believed to be, and are, the Wisdom of the eternal Father. To him David cries out, rejoicing in his heart:

> “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Psalm XXX).

And again:

> “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice” (Psalm L).

Delighted by the desire for him, and urging those who believe in your name toward the praises of perfection at the end of the Psalms, he says:

> “Praise the Lord with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation” (Psalm CL).

Behold the Lover of human salvation, the Maker and Restorer of our race—who is also kind even toward the ungrateful and wicked—working great and indeed wondrous things through small and insensible means, so that he may make people of understanding fitted by his blessing. Those who have perceived this with the ear of their heart and persevered to the end in obeying it will not at all be afraid on the last day, nor will their ears ring from hearing evil (Psalm III), when the enemy, rejoicing over the destruction of the wicked, will boast, saying:

> “I have prevailed against them” (Psalm XII).

O good Jesus, what will we sinners say there, where scarcely the righteous will be saved? We have no other hope than that which your chosen Psalmist, who was both king and prophet, defines, crying out to you with all the marrow of his heart:

> “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Psalm CXLI).

We have learned through evangelical teaching that this hope is to be requested in your name from the Father while the time of mercy lasts. For your Gospel, O Truth, says:

> “Walk while you have the day, lest darkness overtake you. While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light” (John XII).

And that saying, which excludes every human excuse, must be attended to with the utmost diligence and pursued with inward sighs:

> “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (Matthew XXI; John XV).

Therefore, turning to you, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, we ask that, in the name of that same Only-Begotten Son of yours, whose singular imitator in love was your blessed martyr Emmerammus, you may, with the ineffable and customary clemency that you show toward sinners, forgive those who confess and have confessed the wickedness of their hearts; pour into them the anointing of your most abundant consolation; and confirm in us the works of divine mercy. Grant that what appears sweet and delightful in this world may grow bitter through reverent consideration of your fear, and that what is bitter may become sweet through the most gentle contemplation of your love.

Thus, while the world itself is turning, may we rise—resurrected by you—from the fall into and the love of sins, lest at the end of the ages, when all human beings have risen with their bodies, we be eternally put to shame and punished. Rather, having now been made purchased servants, worthy through your grace, may we then also be assigned to your joys, which will endure forever with your friends; and may we safely behold the Lord Jesus, your Son, the liberator and bishop of our souls and bodies, the just judge of the living and the dead, living with you and reigning in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] See the following page.]

[Note: [Col. 1021] [ [Col. 1021] This note appears at the foot of column 1021, but the callout number, 23, is not printed in the text.] The canon adds at this point:

**THE BISHOP HERIBERTUS GIVES THESE FOUR VERSES:**

> In various hours I read writings of labor devoted to praise;  
> I read, reread, and repeatedly read them again;  
> And I found nothing in them that could be regarded as a fault.  
> This alone I say: you and your work please your friend.

And afterward:

> In the year of the Lord MCCCICV [as printed], the reverend father in Christ, lord Ludovicus, venerable abbot of this church, M . . . ., father of the poor, crown of the monks, and the venerable lord . . . . . succeeded as abbot.]

## BOOK II BEGINS: ON THE MEMORY OF THE BLESSED EMMERAMMUS AND HIS DEVOTEES

[Col. 1021]

[Col. 1021A] After he had been taken from human affairs (in the year 972), as we described at the end of the preceding book, the mercy of almighty God revealed, through circumstances of this kind, how it had watched over the clergy and people of this church, whom the Prince of Shepherds had willed to preside over his sheep, and whom, in his secret counsel—to which every heart is open—he had chosen for pastoral care.

There was a man of free birth, vigorous in virtue, an Alamannian by nation, named Wolfgangus. He himself ordered the interpretation of his name to be written in a certain place as *Lupambulus* (“wolf-walker”). At first he had led a praiseworthy and chaste life among the canons or clerics; then, desiring to be bound by stricter rules, he professed himself a monk in Swabia among the coenobites who are called Solitaries [Note: [Col. 1021C] In the monastery of Einsiedeln.].

As he trained himself not only to resist vices firmly but also to devote himself freely and persistently to the practice of virtues, he sharpened the eye of his mind more intensely upon the mirror of the twofold love. He seemed to himself to appear almost empty before the Lord, with his single and hidden talent, unless, after bringing it forth and doubling it, he also took thought for the salvation of others. For this reason he left the monastery, though not the monastic life [Note: [Col. 1021] Witness 2 lacks this; I supplied it from Othlo’s *Life of Wolfgangus*.]; indeed, desiring, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1021C] 1 Corinthians XII, 31.], to strive after greater gifts, he came through Alamannia as an exile into Noricum.

Proceeding toward its eastern region with a humble retinue, he sought the borders of Pannonia for the sake of preaching. From there he was summoned by Piligrinus, bishop of Passau, who received and fostered him, as was fitting, with the office of pious hospitality. At the bishop’s request and command he also remained for several days, thoughtfully considering among other things why he had been prevented from bringing the people of Pannonia to God.

During this period of residence the same bishop made excellent use of him. He was exceptionally learned and of very noble birth, and, in accordance with what the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1022C] 1 John IV, 1], “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God,” he tested sufficiently, through the secret and public observance of divine service and continual searching of sacred Scripture, that this stranger whom he had received was not a vagrant monk but a settled member of the household of the true faith.

Therefore he spoke familiarly to some of his own people on Wolfgangus’s behalf, saying:

> “O how fortunate the church that, by God’s will, will be given this priest! It therefore seems to me exceedingly necessary and useful to request for this servant of God the administration of the bishopric of Regensburg. For wherever good will abounds, it is most fitting that a well-placed opportunity should enable it to proceed also to good works. The good that this man wished to sow in the prepared [Note: [Col. 1021] *duratis* in Othlo.] hearts of the pagans for the service of salvation [Note: [Col. 1021] *et* in Othlo.], which their blindness rejected, may perhaps one day, when this same man cultivates the Lord’s field, yield its fruit among Christian peoples.”

In response some said:

> “How can it happen that this poor and unknown man should attain the honor of so great a bishopric, when certain persons of noble blood have already attempted to acquire it for themselves from the emperor by compensating him with estates and money?”

He answered them with weighty words, though not at excessive length:

> “Divine and human judgments are proved to differ greatly from one another. From the beginning of the world, the searcher of hearts and reins has chosen contemptible and ignoble things in order to confound the strong [Note: [Col. 1022C] 1 Corinthians I, 28]; and, conversely, the world proudly raises what belongs to it for a moment, only to cast it down shortly afterward in disgrace. Therefore I consider it worthwhile to send to the margrave, by whose counsel the emperor is accustomed to do many things, so that he may advise him not to allow anyone to receive episcopal dignity through ambition or the heresy of simony. Rather, whoever he finds to be humble, modest, and learned, and proves to be suited to ecclesiastical duties, let him promote him to the summit of the Church, whatever his station or lineage may be, for the sake of eternal recompense.”

What more is needed? The emperor, instructed by the bishop’s embassy and the counselor’s advice concerning his own and the Church’s interests—or, more truly, moved by the nod of God, in whose hand is the king’s heart—changed his mind. The good prince Otto II turned away all who were laboring to obtain the same bishopric and devoted himself entirely to the election of the venerable Wolfgangus. Thus he quickly sent messengers after him.

When they proceeded as they had been ordered, they found him still staying with the aforementioned bishop, though he was already planning to return to his homeland. He was unaware of the embassy and of the other actions undertaken on his behalf and was therefore directing his mind elsewhere.

When the messengers informed him why they had come, he first withdrew into the secret chamber of his heart, commending himself and his affairs inwardly to God. Then, explaining his situation to the bishop, by whose affection he had been detained there, he lightened what oppressed him through a combination of dove-like simplicity and serpentine prudence, speaking as follows:

> “This new proposal that has come to me through the prince’s messengers has been brought about by your affection, for which, without doubt, you will receive the reward of good will. But it inspires fear in my smallness, because I do not know whether it is God’s will, and because the world, under the appearance of religion, draws many toward vices.”

The bishop replied:

> “What you say you fear is the mark of a prudent mind. Yet the Psalmist raises this toward good hope when he says [Note: [Col. 1023D] Psalms CX, 10; XVIII, 10]: ‘The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord’; and again: ‘The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.’ The Apostle also commends it, saying [Note: [Col. 1023D] Romans XI, 20]: ‘Do not be high-minded, but fear.’ Elsewhere, speaking of the desire for a bishopric, he says [Note: [Col. 1024D] 1 Timothy III, 1]: ‘Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work.’

> “Therefore, if, together with your own salvation, you desire to benefit others and wish a good work to be present in every place, do not refuse to enter the episcopal order when you are called to it under fear and humility. Otherwise you seem to fall into what David says: ‘Because he did not desire blessing, it shall be far from him’ (Psalm CVIII, 18).

> “Guarding against this in every way, strive to be numbered among those of whom it is written: ‘Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars forever and ever’ (Daniel XII, 3). Through the fulfillment of this office you will attain the point at which, in the recompense of the righteous, the ruler of all will say to you: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matthew XXV, 23).”

While the bishop was speaking thus, the venerable man, perceiving through contemplation of his mind the governance of divine providence, replied:

> “Behold the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I, 38).

Then he set out with those who had been sent by the prince and traveled toward the western regions of Bavaria. When they had reached the city of Regensburg, the clergy and people, having unanimously elected him bishop according to ecclesiastical custom, sent him to the emperor with a general embassy.

The emperor received the embassy graciously, and, after the bishops had approved the blessed man and he had wisely delivered a speech in their presence, imperial authority raised him up and bestowed on him pontifical honor by means of the pastoral staff [Note: [Col. 1024D] That is, *pedum*, “staff.”]. As soon as the emperor had entrusted him with his see and the Lord’s flock, he sent him back to Regensburg with a considerable retinue.

[Col. 1024A] There, when he was received by the faithful and favorable welcome of many, he first presented himself humbly to blessed Emmerammus; then he sought the intercession of the saints in each of Regensburg’s monasteries; finally, after solemn preparation and procession, he approached the church of Saint Peter.

When he had been led into it with songs of joy and a voice of rejoicing, and had been enthroned beside the altar according to the custom of bishops, he was commended by the clergy and people to the supreme Shepherd. After several days, he was consecrated there as an apostolic priest by Archbishop Fridericus and his suffragans.

Unwilling to carry this consecration about with him as an empty title, he cultivated the episcopal office most diligently by day and night, so that under this order he might possess more abundantly the grace of the Holy Spirit as a guest in his heart. Touched gently by its inspiration and made cautious and prudent in all things, he by no means wished to change his monastic habit because of his episcopal dignity, as though he were ashamed to be a monk, which he had been. Rather, he displayed outwardly through good examples and moderate clothing the humility of mind that he possessed within.

Mindful also of Solomon’s admonition, which says, “They have appointed you ruler; do not become exalted, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus XXXII, 1), he did not seek to rule over the clergy. Instead, he strove to be a model to the Lord’s flock morning and evening, wisely observing—or, rather, more wisely turning away from himself—that saying which, through the prophet Ezekiel, is directed against wicked shepherds, with the Lord saying:

> “Woe to the shepherds who fed themselves and not my flocks” [Col. 1024C] (Ezekiel XXXIV, 2).

Therefore, wholly devoted to the divine law, among the other ministries of pastoral care, by the sermon he customarily delivered to the people during the solemn celebration of Mass, he accustomed the people to frequent the churches so much that on feast days the custodians of household affairs scarcely seemed to remain at home.

At the exceedingly sweet exhortation of so great a bishop, a crowd of both sexes flocked together in rivalry. The fragrance of heavenly spices drew them there, as he who had given those spices himself wafted them abroad—like bees, which the scent of honey and nectar seems to draw behind it. Since the pious father most earnestly desired to be useful and suited to them, when discussing the kingdom of God and the trampling underfoot of the vanities of this world, he did not use obscure and sophistical arguments. Rather, he tempered the sweetness of his honeyed mouth with a certain severity that I cannot explain in words, so that he seemed, through a simple and excellent manner of speaking, to touch the innermost thoughts of each person. By such skill he drew tears from the eyes of some, as signs of the heart.

He had indeed received from the Holy Spirit such a powerful grace that those who attended his preaching and listened to him intently rarely or never departed from it without an outpouring of tears.
