Through this great good, granted to humanity by the giver of all good things, the enemy of human salvation, wounded by his own malice and attempting to oppose it, exercised with all his strength the envy that he had always possessed.

For one day, when the aforementioned bishop Wolfgangus, of blessed memory, was preaching to the people from the pulpit or ambo in his customary manner, the devil, finding nothing else and prevented by the Lord from opposing him, suddenly stirred up a whirlwind, and with the whirlwind a tumultuous disturbance. With the disturbance he raised a confused murmur and shouting, as well as a tremendous crash above the roof of the church; and, scattering dust and mist within the church’s enclosures, he cast a dark gloom over the sight of some.

When the people unexpectedly saw and heard these things, they were terrified—indeed, what was worse, almost deprived of their senses—and began rushing together and apart, uncertain in the midst of universal confusion and disturbance in which direction they could turn more safely and appropriately.

Meanwhile voices could be heard saying on one side, “A great fire is raging in the city”; and on the other side others were shouting, “Look! A sedition has broken out, and the throats of many are being cut by swords.”

Although sensible people labored greatly, but in vain, to calm such shouting, at last those who had been deceived by the enemy’s schemes burst from the church in such a violent rush by companies that, from so great a multitude, scarcely a few seemed to have remained inside.

Then the bishop, whom such a commotion of storm might, in accordance with human frailty, have driven even from his place if he had not been Christ’s servant—for he had his house founded firmly upon the rock—did not move his step. Remaining steadfast and immovable, he cried out with great faith:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, extending your customary grace to your faithful, grant that today they may see the glory of your name and the confusion of the devil.”

These words were followed by calm weather, and after the calm the return of the people to the church. Then the venerable bishop poured out upon them the spices and ointments of sacred teaching. On that day, with God infusing heavenly sweetness into his speech, he benefited them so greatly that he clearly overcame or put to flight the enemy who, through the excess of the disturbance, had nearly harmed everyone.

Afterward the devotion of the faithful began to regard it as a custom and a law that they should go out in companies to meet and follow the bishop at the stations, and embrace with the utmost affection the distribution of his preaching, as the good fragrance of an apostle.

Through this means the same venerable father strove to draw the Lord’s sheep more and more each day toward exercises of piety, after the manner of the animal called the panther. Physiologists say that the panther is friendly toward all animals except the dragon and serpents; by emitting a good odor, it usually draws to itself all living creatures that are nearby and instills its love in them in a wondrous way.

## THE DIALOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 1025]

[Col. 1025C] While I am writing these things and anxiously preparing my mind to write other matters, my companion, brother Ammonitius, the most faithful associate of my affairs, comes to me and addresses me courteously as follows:

> “Where is the dialogue that you pledged to write in the name of the Lord about the miracles of blessed Emmerammus and the governance of his monastery? You are indeed bound by your promise—or by a strong excuse.”

Then I replied:

> “I do not at all deny that I am bound by it. But I postponed it because I was not certain under whose person I could most suitably compose the dialogue, since very many people have often discussed with me the praises of our patron and other useful matters, and have joined themselves to my smallness by a bond of necessity.”

He replied:

> “According to Solomon, let one be your counselor out of a thousand [Note: [Col. 1025D] Ecclesiasticus VI.], and he will make you secure in this matter. For, if you wish, you can appropriately use the person of Ammonitius for any brother who reminds or exhorts you toward good. None of your friends will say that he has been despised or be indignant that another has been preferred to him in this matter.

> “Therefore, without further postponement, take up the dialogue; and, as you proposed, weave into the praises of the martyr the memory of Christ’s confessors. Add to it whatever your mind rightly or appropriately dictates to you, or whatever reason suggests for writing.”

“I am ready,” I said, “to do what you urge. But first I think the reader should be humbly asked not to seek in my little works an artificial composition of words, but, if he wishes, to attend to the work of a simple and humble style. I have preferred to labor in this way for myself and my fellow brothers rather than be found idle without the work of my hands.”

With this confidence and intention the work begun proceeds.

Accordingly, Wolfgangus of Regensburg, bishop of blessed memory, having examined and understood the affairs of the bishopric entrusted to him by divine providence, took more seriously than anything else the fact that the monks of the most blessed martyr Emmerammus had been without an abbot for so long and had been like sheep wandering without a shepherd. For this reason he sent to the monastery at Trier, where blessed Maximinus rests in body, and summoned from there the venerable old man Ramvoldus, who had once been his chaplain under Archbishop Henricus.

“Why,” said Ammonitius, “had they been without an abbot for so long, if they were monks? And if they were monks, under whose rule did they live? Reason itself demands that this also be explained.”

“This,” I replied, “you can learn through a brief account. It was an ancient custom in the Church of Regensburg that those who were bishops were also abbots. Some retained the title for temporal advantages, not the offices. They feared that, if they placed an abbot over the monastery—since everything is to be expected from the father of the monastery—the service compelled from them would be diminished.

“For this reason they allowed the monks to obtain elsewhere whatever they could for food and clothing, because they themselves abused for their own service the goods belonging to the monks’ provisions.” [Col. 1027A]

After these words, the brother with whom I had begun to weave the dialogue, using his own name, warned me in my ear:

> “Speak cautiously, and write still more cautiously. For if the bishops hear or see these statements written, perhaps they will say that you wish to accuse them of robbery and injustice; and they will attribute your freedom to arrogance, as though you had rashly attempted to criticize those for whose defense Scripture cries out—or rather, the Lord commands through Scripture—saying: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones’ [Note: [Col. 1027D] 1 Chronicles XVI.]. And again: ‘Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye’ [Note: [Col. 1028D] Zechariah II.].”

I answered him with tongue and pen:

> “If they are bishops in the sense in which they are called bishops, they do not harm us but greatly benefit us. May the Prince of shepherds, in whom is the fullness of all good things, bring this about. But since this pleases you—or rather, since it is just—let us keep peace with them and be subject to them.

> “I want you to know, however, that I do not regret having spoken the truth, since good people use not only good things but also bad things for good. But now the time and your desire demand that I return to the remnants of my narrative.

> “There is also another reason why abbots were not appointed in the aforementioned monastery. From the time when bishops were first ordained in Bavaria by blessed Boniface, the vicar of the Apostolic See, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, monks and canons succeeded one another in this bishopric by turns: if the predecessor was a canon, the successor became a monk, and a canon in turn succeeded that predecessor. This custom continued down to our own times.

> “The episcopal see, however, was at Saint Emmerammus until the time of Prince Charles, who restored it to the city where it had previously been.

> “As for your question concerning the rule under which they lived, I will settle it briefly. First, they made their profession according to the rule of Saint Benedict before the bishop, who acted in place of the abbot. Then the bishop gave them permission to give and receive because of the poverty of the place.

> “The elders who could obtain them used linen shirts; the rest were clothed in wool because of the scarcity of hair-cloth garments. After the bishop, the provost and dean governed the monastery. Those who were older had cells or chambers; the younger men were divided among themselves for purposes of custody. They had a poor common ration and ate birds. They did the rest according to the customs that, at that time, existed in royal monasteries.”

Because these arrangements displeased the aforementioned man, the reverend bishop Wolfgangus, as we have said, took Ramvoldus, mature in years and conduct, for the work of divine ministry and appointed him first provost and then abbot of the monastery.

Some of the bishop’s fellow priests and counselors, displeased by this, said:

> “Why are you wasting there, on your priests, the goods belonging to Saint Emmerammus? Many praise you, but in this matter they do not praise you; rather, they condemn you. Therefore use the office of bishop and abbot, as your predecessors have been accustomed to do until now, so that they may not lack the profit of certain things. Such folly too must be seasoned with the salt of wisdom.”

He answered them prudently:

> “I am not ashamed to be called foolish and stupid for God’s sake. But I want you to know that I will never impose upon myself a burden that I cannot carry by claiming for myself both the name of bishop and that of abbot.

> “For, as blessed Gregory testifies [Note: [Col. 1028D] Gregory, *Register*, Book III, Letter 11], it is exceedingly unfitting that, when someone cannot properly fulfill one of these offices because of its magnitude, he should be judged capable of both.

> “It is enough for a bishop to devote himself with the greatest vigilance to pastoral office. For an abbot, it is sufficiently laborious, though greatly fruitful, to provide for the salvation of the brothers and to manage the affairs of his monastery well in every respect.

> “Therefore he himself must also distribute offices among the brothers, so that in them he may considerably lighten his burdens, recalling the words and writings of the prudent man whom we mentioned. They contain this principle: just as it is indecorous that, in the human body, one limb perform the function of another, so it is plainly harmful and exceedingly shameful if the individual ministries of affairs are not assigned to corresponding persons.

> “As for what you have proposed, I do not wish to squander the goods of Saint Emmerammus, of which you accuse me of being the destroyer. Rather, I wish in every way to preserve them for the one to whom they were entrusted, for the use of the servants of God, and for our see.

> “But matters of this kind are quite different from what you imagine. We shall scarcely be able to escape punishment, since we have assigned to our own service the goods of the saints—goods greater not only in quantity but also better in quality—and, compelled or overcome by justice, have left smaller portions to those who were closer to him, because they visited him more frequently and clung to Christ more familiarly day and night, praising him among his holy elect.”

Those who had raised the question replied:

> “You have sung mercy and judgment to the Lord; you have rightly preferred divine matters to human ones; you have usefully changed ancient arrangements. What remains on our part except that we too say: ‘Thanks be to God. Amen. May it prosper happily’?”

---

“This conclusion to your statement,” said Ammonitius, “seems to me sufficiently appropriate. But perhaps some people dislike the fact that you write and dictate so slowly, almost as though you were sleeping. Therefore command your pen to run swiftly.”

I replied to him:

> “At times I am hindered by weakness and the variety of my occupations, so that I do not quickly produce what must be written. But since I know that this delay has not satisfied you, I wish first, out of affection for you and the others whom impatience makes the passage of time seem long, to remind you of the words of blessed Jerome if something is postponed for a while that they desire to see and hear; afterward I will add whatever little statement I am able to find.

> “This true gatherer of verbal fragments, in a certain letter that he wrote to blessed Augustine, uses solid brevity to say: ‘Often what is rash turns into disaster’ [Note: [Col. 1029D] Jerome, Letter LXXXIX.].

> “Applying the brevity of this little verse to my own advantage, I wish, by proceeding or writing slowly, to avoid the snares of heresies, into which many have fallen headlong because they neglected caution and trusted in their own opinions.

> “As for what you said about my dictating as though I were sleeping, it reminds me not to be more sleepy, but to become more vigilant through liberal study. Would that I might and could follow this, so that I might gain my own soul.”

The companion in the dialogue replied:

> “Do not think my little admonition an insult. Rather, explain the excellent praises of Christ’s confessors that you have begun to narrate.”

“Although,” I replied, “you press me as an importunate exactor, so that you seem even to burden me, nevertheless, since charity commands it, I will try to satisfy you as best I can.”

The venerable bishop Wolfgangus, a man of great authority among bishops, observant of the rule among canons, singular in piety among monks, exalted in humility, and universal in charity, having become, according to the Apostle, “all things to all people” [Note: [Col. 1029D] 1 Corinthians IX], excelled especially in generosity toward almsgiving.

Through the praiseworthy ministry of almsgiving, and through the offering of his other virtues, it pleased God to make his goodness evident by many signs while he was still in this present world. I learned one of these from the account of a certain faithful old man. His story was as follows:

> “I had a soldier under my command who, one day, was present with others [Note: [Col. 1029D] These words are written in another hand in the manuscript.] in the basilica of Saint Paul, where blessed Bishop Wolfgangus was celebrating Mass.

> “When he first saw him dressed in humble clothing, as befitted a monk, and then saw him wearing the vestments of a priest, he despised him with the dullness of the common people and, murmuring in the speech of his heart, said: ‘The emperor was exceedingly foolish at the time when he preferred this ragged and contemptible man in episcopal promotion to powerful persons who abound in the regions under his rule.’

> “He who knows human thoughts rebuked this murmuring at that very moment and clearly exposed it for the correction of the fault. For just as he answered thoughts in the Gospel, so he concealed this man’s inward murmuring for a time, so that the man might be corrected in the present and others might avoid the evil of murmuring in the future.

> “For he was suddenly seized by such great terror that he could scarcely remain seated without the support of those standing nearby. When I saw him trembling and pale, I immediately ran to him and asked what was wrong and what he was suffering. Then, after priests had been summoned, he confessed that he had thought wickedly against the man of God and that he had therefore been struck by dangerous fear.

> “I sufficiently established how great a terror or affliction had seized him by keeping him at my house for several days. After caring for him and seeking his health in many ways, and when the priests who were laboring on his behalf could not restore him to health even with their prayers, I took him back to the city of Hiatospolis (Regensburg), where this evil turned into good for him.

> “There, humbling myself at the feet of the bishop, I wished to explain the man’s distress and my own. But the man of God, before anyone announced to him the reason for which I had come, anticipated what I wanted to say and said: ‘Rise, be silent; I know what you want.’

> “Then he turned to the chamberlain and said: ‘Brother Tagino, take holy water from beside my bed and sprinkle it over the man standing before the door of the chamber.’

> “Meanwhile he drew a cross with his hand against the door and murmured something. The man was healed at that very hour.”

[Col. 1030B] “Truly,” said Ammonitius, “evil has been turned into good. For not only was the bishop’s insult avenged through the soldier’s rebuke, but the merit of so great a priest was also revealed to many through the marvel of the soldier’s healing and the magnificent revelation of the spirit.

> “I greatly wonder that the aforementioned chamberlain was loved so dearly by him, since, as I have heard, he was irascible and excessively severe and for that reason hated by nearly everyone who was in the bishopric. The bishop, on the other hand, was gentle and pious.”

“Certainly,” I replied, “he too was not without severity; otherwise he would have observed less fully what the Apostle says: ‘Reprove, entreat, rebuke’ [Note: [Col. 1030D] 2 Timothy IV].

“But the man you say was hated by many because of his severity, I understand to have been energetic and clever. For that reason he was dear to the venerable bishop: he was very necessary, and the bishop had recognized through a revelation of the spirit that, if he was blameworthy in anything, he could be improved through the changing of the right hand of the Most High.

“After the death of blessed Bishop Wolfgangus, to whom he had clung faithfully, this man served the emperor Henricus among his most faithful ministers. By the emperor’s command he was made archbishop at Parthenopolis. Although he possessed many virtues, he became more distinguished through the pious lavishness of his almsgiving, as well as through humble chastity of body and praiseworthy moderation in clothing.

“He did not sweep the earth with tunics and fur garments, as many are accustomed to do, garments acquired at great price. Rather—a rarity in worldly practice—he was content, with firm strength of mind, with the clothing of sheep, and took care to celebrate Mass daily. He also never ceased most devoutly to render the entire office of psalmody.

“In the seventh year after his death, his body was found intact. The glory of the resurrection shone so brightly in it that those standing around and looking at it marveled greatly at its radiance and incorruption, especially when they saw that, although the garments of his successor had also been consumed, only the bare bones remained.

“Truly the Lord remembered his words, by which he consoles his faithful, saying: ‘Not a hair of your head will perish’ [Note: [Col. 1030D] Luke XII].

“Behold, he who has done all things well now reveals in part, through certain of his servants, what will be completely accomplished in all at the general resurrection—when, without doubt, each of the elect will rise, attaining the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ [Note: [Col. 1031D] Ephesians IV].”

“I confess,” said the companion in the dialogue, “that what displeased me now pleases me; and where Truth displays such things, no one who thinks soundly is offended through unbelief. But it is now time for you to return to the point from which you digressed. If I am not mistaken, the order of the narrative requires you to relate more fully in what follows the life of the venerable abbot, which you touched upon only briefly earlier.”

“You have me ready to obey,” I replied, “but we must earnestly implore the help of him who says in the Gospel: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ [Note: [Col. 1031D] John XV].

“Therefore, with his grace going before and accompanying us, our speech and work alike proceed well. However small it may be, it desires to prosper appropriately in the name of the Lord.”

“Thus the venerable Father Ramuoldus, having been entrusted with the governance of the monastery, sufficiently demonstrated in that administration what sort of man he had been before. For, first exercising himself in the spiritual arena, and thereafter accustoming his subjects to labor at the virtues, he strove in every way to do and teach what he knew to be just, holy, devout, and honorable. Hence many even of noble birth, prompted by his pious deeds, abandoned the world and humbly submitted themselves to his instruction. Among them and together with them—what gravity was his, what self-restraint, what purity, what generosity in almsgiving, [Col. 1031C] what guardianship of humility, what expenditure of intelligence—it is beyond my ability to recount fully and to praise as it deserves. Indeed, I would judge that the whole weight and dignity of this subject should be left to the most learned and eloquent men, unless I knew that the devotion of the poor is not despicable to God. By this hope my spirit is lifted up, and although my style and pen are slight and rustic, they nevertheless run confidently, writing the deeds of the saints, because the kingdom of God is not in speech, nor in the splendor of eloquence, but in work and truth [Note: [Col. 1031D] 1 Cor. IV.].

As I began to say, that same man of God possessed glorious and magnificent virtues in a praiseworthy manner, and cultivated them manfully. He set before all his people, with such natural ease, the norm and mother of the virtues—that is, discernment—that it seemed to have been granted to him from above as something uniquely bestowed. Supported by this virtue, he so employed the four principal virtues that, through prudence, having cast away the sluggishness of dullness, cunning could never creep up against him. He likewise retained justice in all things, insofar as this is possible for mortals, so that he neither exceeded the proper measure by excess nor long succumbed through deficiency. Through temperance he so restrained his susceptibility to passion that he did not fall into folly through insensibility. He so used the weapons of fortitude that, by overcoming the enemy through it and driving away fear, he nowhere broke out into the audacity of insolence.

Directed by these and similar virtues into the way of justice, and led into the path of God’s commandments, as he himself desired, the venerable Father revered with all his strength the gifts of the Holy Spirit, poured into and distributed among vessels of virtue sevenfold. He was also careful, both for himself and for others, prudently to observe in all things, according to the Gregorian teaching, that wisdom should not puff him up; that understanding, while running subtly, should not go astray; that counsel, while multiplying itself, should not become confused; that fortitude, while providing confidence, should not precipitate him; that knowledge, while knowing and not loving, should not press forward; that piety, while inclining beyond rectitude, should not distort; and that fear, while trembling more than was just, should not plunge him into the pit of despair.

These matters I have set forth briefly, [Col. 1032B] O Ammonicius, as the greater charisms with which the man of God was endowed. Now I shall take up other matters and explain somewhat more fully certain lesser virtues—lesser, yet sufficiently great for imitation—by whose advancement he was trained. Though small in stature, he was great in knowledge and piety, and through ascending the tree of virtues he daily merited to see Jesus. Of him he could say with the Psalmist: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he himself will draw my feet out of the snare” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Ps. XXIV.].”

Ammonicius replied:

“I am greatly delighted by the opening remarks that have been gracefully spoken about the man of God. Behold, I hear of a Zacchaeus, and not of a publican, although Jesus also ate with publicans and sinners [Note: [Col. 1032D] Matt. IX.]. I hear of a spiritual father; I hear of a man of great deeds. Although there are few who imitate these deeds perfectly, there are nevertheless very many who venerate his Lord in the saints. Therefore, be swift in dictating and writing, and imitate the Psalmist who says: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” [Note: [Col. 1032D] Ps. XLIV.]. For I desire to hear the deeds of one whom, while he was in the body, I was not worthy to see.”

“Be patient,” I replied, “and discerning. I shall endeavor to satisfy your desire. Indeed, as I indicated in part above, the most venerable abbot Ramuoldus was a member of Christ, and the inhabitant of his heart—namely, the gracious Spirit—made his members, even in extreme old age, so joyful and comely, and worthy of a certain reverence, that they seemed, almost contrary to nature, to display the agility and purity of a seven-year-old boy. [Col. 1032D] If something unusual of this kind should at some time occur in any mortal on some occasion, it ought to be noted by the faithful only in saints and elect persons. For Satan transforms himself into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 1032D] 2 Cor. XXI.], whom even the perfect will scarcely be able to avoid or overcome.

Against him the man of God bravely waged Christian warfare. Among his other offices of good conduct, after frequent and useful silence, he possessed a gentle eloquence. In divine matters his speech was abundant; in human matters it was brief but not idle. His clothing too was moderate and monastic, without pretense. [Col. 1033A] His food was so scant that it did not exceed what was necessary but could suffice for nourishment. In this he was often sparing toward himself, but toward others generous and liberal. After the food necessary to sustain the body, at the time when words commonly abound, he exercised himself in psalmody or reading instead of taking a walk of a thousand paces.

He took the greatest care of Christ’s poor. Thus, at the daily meal, he practiced mercy toward fifty poor persons, apart from the twelve and the three whom the brothers served; by cultivating mercy in that number, he strove to merit a remission consecrated in the same number, with the fountain of mercy himself, who says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Matt. V.]. This man was exceedingly eager to fulfill in deed what is written: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Luke XI.].

What had been ordered to be prepared somewhat more delicately for him, as an old and infirm man, to refresh his little body, he frequently converted to the use of the poor. Sometimes, out of humility and necessity alike, he himself tasted a little of it, and distributed the rest among the poor and sick who, hindered by weakness and severe illness, could not come to the church where they ought to receive alms. He entrusted this work to a certain familiar and faithful servant, granting him a special benefit for that purpose: he was to travel diligently throughout the entire city and seek out those in whom Christ might be clothed and fed.

According to the rule of Benedict, his table was always shared with guests and pilgrims. O praiseworthy man, who, wholly poured out into the bowels of mercy, took care to gather, feed, and clothe Christ in his least ones! He never grew weary of these works or ceased from them. He also permitted clothing and food to be given to the poor at times by the hands of others whom he had entrusted with this task. He himself, however, carried a purse with him, from which, at the proper time, he distributed coins and small change to the needy and to pilgrims; he was not ashamed to be and to be called their almoner, certain that Christ too, according to his promise, would not be ashamed of him before the angels of God.

Thus the provisions that ought to have been given to those arriving at the monastery gate, after being reduced and diminished before his time, he so improved and enlarged in his own time that, [Col. 1033D] for the performance of works of humanity, there is there even to this day, on one side, a fairly substantial hospice for strangers, and on the other, a venerable hospital for the unfortunate. Hence, because of the multitude of poor who received consolation from him daily, he was called the Father of pilgrims, widows, and orphans.

For his benevolent reception of them, and also because of the many revelations, who could doubt that this venerable old man should be placed among the sheep at the right hand? To them the King, seated upon the throne of his majesty, will say: [Col. 1034A] “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you gathered me in; naked, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Matt. XXIII.].

In order to become a participant in these things, this man of God, in accordance with the Apostle, who commands us to pray without ceasing [Note: [Col. 1033D] 1 Thess. V.], prayed unceasingly with the Psalmist, saying: “Make me a participant, O God, with all those who fear you and keep your commandments” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Ps. CXVIII.].”

After I had said and written these things, Ammonicius raised a question, saying:

“The testimony taken from the Apostle, which commands that one should pray without ceasing, although credible, as being supported by apostolic authority, nevertheless seems to many impossible and beyond human capacity. For they say: Who among mortals, leaving aside all the other things that must be done, could pray without ceasing?”

“What wonder,” I replied, “if the blindness of ignorance has covered those who do not wish to attend to the light of divine speech, which exhorts us: ‘Search the Scriptures’ [Note: [Col. 1034D] John V.], and you will find in them? Of these Scriptures it is said elsewhere: ‘Not all receive the word, but those to whom it has been given’ [Note: [Col. 1034D] Matt. XIX.].

“In sacred Scripture, the simpler people, if they sought, would find things sufficient to nourish them; but the more discerning find in it things to admire and in which to exercise themselves. The Psalmist designates such people when he says: ‘They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep’ [Note: [Col. 1034D] Ps. CVI.]. Hence, through a certain wise man [Note: [Col. 1034D] St. Gregory, letter on Job, book IV.], the same Scripture is very suitably compared to a river in which the lamb walks and the elephant swims.

“Whoever receives from the streams of this river—that is, from the teachings of sound doctrine—a threefold measure with unity, and learns from the one fountain the mysteries of sacred faith and the other gifts of salvation distributed in manifold ways among the first, middle, and final things, will perceive that what seems impossible to human weakness is possible through divine assistance. Otherwise, if it is not possible, it will not be believed either, and we shall be forced to accuse the Apostle, since he commanded the faithful to do what he himself did not do and what could in no way be done. May the entanglement or deception of this error therefore be far from us and from all Christians.

“Let us say, then, what Christian faith accepts: whatever a person serving God rightly does shall be counted as prayer. For example, when you necessarily care for your body, almsgiving or the just administration of other things will pray for you; but if you have nothing from which to give, good will is sufficient.

“Whom, then, do you think prayed for Paul, O Ammonicius, when, preaching the kingdom of God all day, he prolonged his discourse almost until midnight [Note: [Col. 1034D] Acts XX.]?”

Ammonicius replied: “Justice and mercy.”

And I said: “You have judged rightly. For thus works of justice and mercy are shown to pray without ceasing for the faithful, in accordance with what the same Apostle elsewhere testifies, saying: ‘The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings’ [Note: [Col. 1035D] Rom. VIII.]. I do not mean that this should be understood as though the Spirit himself groans, but because he makes those whom he causes to pray also to groan.”

“I confess,” said Ammonicius, “that I have been satisfied by the resolution of the question proposed. But my desire to hear the illustrious and useful things that brooks no delay demands that you quickly bring forth whatever you still have to say about the man of God, and then proceed energetically and safely to other matters, with me as your companion.”

“Let it be done,” I replied, “if it is possible, that what you so greatly desire may be written swiftly by me. Rather, may the will of almighty God be done, so that human frailty, casting aside the things that fade away, may desire and be able to pursue what is truly called good and truly is good.” [Col. 1035B]

“Eagerly yearning for these exceedingly necessary affections, the most venerable abbot Ramuoldus, in his own time, showed himself, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, not only a spiritual father to the worshipers of Christ in interior matters, but also a most prudent steward in exterior matters. Through the adornment of the church and monastery, through the provision of necessary furnishings and the administration of many diverse things, he made his old age somehow grow young; and from the treasury of wisdom he brought forth new things together with old [Note: [Col. 1035D] Matt. XIII.].

“Since the whole of the present life is full of temptations, he was often tempted and tested in many ways. At last he fell into so grave a temptation under the affliction of phlegm or [Note: [Col. 1035D] In the manuscript, in another hand.] scotoma that, while the other members of his body continued to perform their functions quite vigorously, he completely lost the sight of his eyes.

“How patiently the man of God endured this sad deprivation and the harshness of this affliction he made known in words of this kind when certain persons, standing in his presence, questioned him about it and wept:

“‘Let a person cease lamenting over the loss of defective sight, which always retains the certainty of remaining in hope, according to the truthful promise of the Savior. We are not blind, for we already possess eyes enlightened through faith [Note: [Col. 1035D] Matt. XIII; John VIII, XII.]. But the blind person is the one who lacks the faith that enlightens and remains in darkness.

“‘Hence, for those who walk by faith it seems exceedingly unworthy to place a high value on the use of the present light, which they share with flies and the vilest creatures, even with serpents. Therefore, it is fitting to direct all our strength toward him who says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” [Note: [Col. 1035D] John VIII.].

“‘If it pleases him, he can easily restore and present the light of the body that he gave and took away. But if he does not wish to do so, he must be blessed without complaint, feared always as the King of justice [Note: [Col. 1036D] Dan. III.], and loved with the whole mind and strength as the Father of mercies and of all consolation [Note: [Col. 1036D] 2 Cor. I].’”

After these words had been spoken and heard, tears began to flow—not of the kind that had flowed shortly before, but of another kind—much more abundant and much more useful. For they remembered, both from Paul’s teaching and from the man of God’s commendable patience, that in weakness strength is most certainly perfected [Note: [Col. 1036D] 2 Cor. XII.]. Divine power later deigned to declare this in the venerable old man, both mercifully and powerfully.

For after he had spent nearly two years blind under the stroke of blindness, one night, as he had been accustomed to do, he was moving among the altars as a frequent worshipper (*venipeta*, alternatively *vaenipeta*), diligently applying himself to sacred work. He did not wish to spare his decrepit age before he recognized that the grace of God was present through the Spirit.

Then, prostrate before the holy cross and sufficiently humbled by tears and prayer, when the weariness of his body seemed to demand rest—or rather, when the Lord, who neither sleeps nor slumbers [Note: [Col. 1036D] Isa. V.], willed to glorify his work—he suddenly fell asleep in body, though not in mind.

And behold, the image of our Lord Jesus Christ crucified appeared to him to descend from the cross and come toward him. Standing before him, it took with both hands, as it seemed to him, burning candles from a candelabrum placed close by upon the steps, and violently pressed them into the old man’s eyes.

At first, because of the Lord’s descent in the image, he endured no small weight of agony. Then, perceiving through the fire that something glorious was being signified, and sensing through the light that darkness was being driven away, he rose covered with tears and sweat. Immediately turning his eyes back to their former use, he began to wonder within himself and, with his inner man, to search more deeply what it meant that, after so long a time during which many had despaired of it, he had received his sight.

When, in a short while, reason had satisfied the man concerning this matter, and the man had satisfied reason, then, with the service of his mouth rejoicing together with the dwelling-place of his heart, he gave magnificent thanks to God. God had deigned to visit his servant in such a way that bodily chastisement became correction for him, while the restoration of his eyes stirred many to affection for holy and honorable things.

In order that this event might be held more tenaciously in the memory, the man of God ordered that, among the other signs or indications of miracles, ocular circles be hung in the church. This church, endowed with the sacred body and merits of the blessed martyr Emmeram and furnished also with the patronage of other saints, is accustomed to provide mortals with very many benefits sent down from the heavenly watchtower. Because of the healing benefits bestowed there and the frequent circulation of the fame arising from it, this place rejoices to receive the multitude of those who come.

Among them, some who are burdened by various illnesses, having been visited by the bowels of the mercy of our God, are revealed; others, while they are heard concerning other needs, are consoled by the same mercy. In voice and heart they cry out thanks to the Author of salvation for the common benefit of all.

Therefore we too, who write and read these things, and who often discuss such matters among ourselves in reasoned conversation, should give praise to God with a common voice not only for those things that are here before our eyes and hands, but also for all his gifts and benefits.” [Col. 1037A]

## Ammonicius

“We know that it is fitting for the creature to serve the Creator and, according to the Apostle, to give thanks in all things [Note: [Col. 1037D] 1 Thess. V.]. We willingly embrace this as far as our ability permits, first by obeying the Lord’s and the Apostles’ commands, and then by assenting to the sound exhortations of your charity and of others.

“But this disturbs the minds of certain faithful people, because there are many mortals who scarcely praise God in prosperity, but in contrary and adverse circumstances not only fail to praise him, [Col. 1037B] but—what is worse—criticize or blaspheme him, saying that whatever happens against their wishes is the work of the devil.”

## Collectitius

“Because many people speak many things carelessly and falsely, they become dangerously entangled in various snares of error. Those who wish to avoid their entanglements must, with Paul, wisely endure the foolish [Note: [Col. 1037D] 2 Cor. XII.], until the multitude of the reprobate, diminishing nothing of the glory of the children of God, is brought to nothing—that is, thrust into hell—and the small number of the elect, written by name in heaven, is placed there to rejoice eternally with the multitude of angels and always to behold Christ in his kingdom. This will occur when, through them, the number of the angelic order that fell is completed—the order whose archangel apostatized through pride together with his followers.” [Col. 1037C]

## Ammonicius

“While I was asking about the disturbance caused by the mad rashness of the foolish, you have explained in a brief verse not only how they are to be endured, but have also introduced the terrible sentence of the final judgment and magnificently recalled the glory of the saints. Thus you have made this same verse weightier through the authority of divine speech than tedious through length.

“Now, therefore, it is appropriate that, setting aside those who, because of the hardness of their own stupidity, are usually more a burden than a benefit to us, you turn your style toward those who strove with all their strength to walk in good ways [Col. 1037D] and knew very well how to praise the Creator in all his works.

“Since their deeds, by which they wore smooth the road of the present world, have already in part been commended to memory through your dictation, charity and the usefulness of your labor demand that you now proceed without reluctance, forging your way through the account of where, when, and how they departed this life, in what places their bodies were laid, and what signs of their holiness shone forth after death.”

## Collectitius

“What I have written thus far, and what I am still going to write, concerning holy men and their marvelous virtues [Col. 1038A] inspires no small fear in my lowliness. For I know myself to be a sinner, and it seems exceedingly unworthy that a sinner or unjust man should claim for himself, by writing about a holy and just matter, the subject of an arduous work.

“Under this circumstance, the mercy of him who died for our sins, the just one for the unjust, offers consolation to my timidity. In a certain sense, whoever spreads and proclaims the memory of his servants for the praise and glory of his name ministers to him. Therefore, encouraged and armed against the torpor of idleness, I confidently order my pen to plow the proposals of your charity.”

## Ammonicius

“He who gives the work of love himself rewards it. [Col. 1038B] Therefore, placing your hope bravely in the help of divine compassion, proceed cheerfully along the path of the requested narrative.”

## Collectitius

“I shall proceed willingly, desiring in every way that he himself be present to me.

“Thus, after many works of piety and equity by which he strove to serve God and by which he governed the Church entrusted to him, the venerable bishop Wolfgangus—often named and destined to be named still more often—being established at Regensburg, was preparing to undertake a journey into the eastern region of this province, since the necessary change of circumstances demanded it. He began to suffer from fever.

“The man of God not only made this bodily affliction profitable for his soul through vigils and prayers, [Col. 1038C] but also, increasing the work and adornment of good will through almsgiving, sent everything he was able to possess into Christ’s treasury through the hands of the poor. Thus, intending to proceed toward the eastern regions, he commended the course of his life by diligent prayers to him who knows no setting.

“When, traveling downstream on the Danube, they had reached by boat the place called Puppinga [Note: [Col. 1038D] Pupping, not far from Efferding in Austria, Waitz.], he was unable to proceed farther, because the time of his dissolution was approaching. There, as heavenly grace visited him, he learned that what had long before been revealed to him in a vision would soon be fulfilled.”

## Ammonicius

“Tell me what revelation he received, and where, when, or through whom he learned it. Do not suppress it in silence, but explain it clearly for fraternal charity.” [Col. 1038D]

## Collectitius

“I shall say or write this briefly, though not lightly, because the summer heat makes me ill.

“Once, when the man of God was staying in Alamannia and wished to set out on a pilgrimage, he saw in a dream the most blessed confessor of Christ, Otmarus, to whom he very frequently commended himself and his affairs, standing before him. When he was commanded to look attentively, he received from him words of this kind:

“‘Because, when asked by you, I asked the Lord on your behalf, and I have been heard, I now plainly declare to you what is to come. Poor and needy you will leave this province, but in another, in which you will live in exile for the love of the Lord, you will by divine predestination receive a bishopric sufficiently wealthy in perishable goods.

“‘If, in its administration, you show yourself faithful and sow good things without weariness, according to what is written, “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” [Note: [Col. 1039D] Gal. VI.], after completing twenty-two years you will depart from this transitory life and enter the eternal one.

“‘And this I wish you to know without doubt: you will return your soul to the Creator in the place where, under Christ’s name, my memory is honored and worshiped by Christians. I hope to come there at the hour of your departure from Egypt, this world, together with the others whom, through good merits, you will summon and prepare from the army of the Lord to assist at your death against the aerial powers and spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places [Note: [Col. 1039D] Eph. VI].’”

After these and similar words had been spoken, the spirit that had appeared vanished in the night vision, leaving the venerable Wolfgangus partly joyful and partly sad. I should say that he was joyful not because of the little glory of this world, which is merely colored by the dignity of an episcopal rank, but because of the joyful promise of the eternal kingdom. I should say that the man of God was sad not because of the brevity of the years granted to this life, but because of the lamentable prolongation of his earthly dwelling, in accordance with the Psalmist’s verse: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged” [Note: [Col. 1039D] Ps. CIX.].”

## Ammonicius

“It is commonly asked what the aerial powers are, and how spiritual wickedness can be in the heavenly places, since no wickedness has ever inhabited the heavenly realm. Therefore, this ought to be explained.” [Col. 1039C]

## Collectitius

“These words about which the question has been raised are not mine but those of the blessed Apostle Paul. Therefore, those who do not know that the expanses of the air are called heavenly places, and who are ignorant that apostate angels move about in them, and who for that reason are accustomed to doubt the Apostle’s statements, I refer to the Second Epistle of the blessed Peter. There, concerning the expanses of the air, which are called heavens, destroyed in the first flood and destined to be destroyed in the second, he teaches the faithful as follows:

“‘This is hidden from scoffers: that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth, standing out of water and through water, by the word of God; through these the world that then existed, flooded with water, perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire until the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people’ [Note: [Col. 1040D] 2 Peter III.]. And shortly afterward:

“‘The burning heavens will be dissolved, and the elements will melt in the heat of fire. But we await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells’ [Note: [Col. 1040D] Ibid.].

“Concerning the fallen angels also, who wander in the heavens destined to perish by fire, whom the Apostle calls aerial powers and spiritual wickedness: their multitude in the air—that is, in the lower heavens—is so great that, as was revealed to a certain holy man, if they had bodies equal in size to our bodily forms, they would block the sunlight from mortals.

“Jude the Apostle, in the Epistle that is counted among the canonical writings, presents the following judgment concerning them: ‘The angels who did not preserve their principality but abandoned their dwelling, the Lord has kept in everlasting chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day.’

“Since the proposed question has thus been suitably resolved by apostolic testimonies, I do not know whether anyone can remain in doubt. I do not doubt; rather, I know and am certain that the devil and his attendants have been condemned in hell and in the air. I am the more certain because, when I was in Pannonia some years ago, one day from the third hour until the sixth I saw a devil or dragon hanging in the air.

“Its size was incredible, and its length so great that it seemed to be stretched out over nearly a mile. Its crested head was raised like a mountain; its body, in accordance with what the Lord says to blessed Job about Leviathan [Note: [Col. 1040D] Job XLI.], was compacted with horrible scales and covered as if with shields or iron-armored bucklers. Along its sides and back a sooty blackness disfigured it; its belly, by contrast, and likewise the part of its body on which it was accustomed to lie upon the ground, were discolored by a pale bluish hue, resembling a sulphurous hearth.

“Its enormous movements, curves, and extensions, and finally the movements of its entire body, both in parts and as a whole—in short, all the efforts of the dragon at that time—were harmful to mortals insofar as God permitted, and all the more harmful the nearer they were. For, since it was summer, specifically the Friday of the second week after Pentecost, the frost that is more natural to a dragon than to other animals so altered the air that fever attacked many people and cold consumed no small number of the beasts of burden.

“It had no wings or legs or feet, nor did it appear to have any, since its scales and ribs sufficed for locomotion. The thickness of its breast equaled the thickness of its head. From there it gradually diminished toward the end of its tail, whose extremity nearly matched the height of great fir trees.

“Unwilling that so immense an enemy, whether the devil or a friend of the devil, should terrify the faithful people any longer, the Lord suddenly caused it to be moved from the north and mixed with the dense clouds in a great rush. We saw it pass over us at tremendous speed, and we heard its hiss together with the shrill sound of pipes, not without fear. Immediately the clouds, which from morning until that hour had seemed almost motionless, were so shaken and driven about that throughout that entire day and night the thunder and flashes did not cease; indeed, they continued until evening of the following day.” [Col. 1040D]

## Ammonicius

“Did you remember anything at that time of what blessed John writes in his Apocalypse concerning the dragon and the beast?” [Col. 1041A]

## Collectitius

“Indeed, these things came to mind. Above all, I was pressed by the recollection of the passage in that same Apocalypse, which says: ‘Woe to you, for the Dragon has come to you with great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time’ [Note: [Col. 1041D] Rev. XII.].

“Although I knew that the Antichrist and the devil were signified by the beast and the dragon, and that the day of universal judgment was certainly not then approaching, nevertheless, disturbed by the extraordinary spectacle, I thought about many things and anxiously sighed over my own death or that of the others who were witnessing these terrifying events with me.

“Then, restored by the regard of divine mercy to the hope of continued life, I first gave thanks to almighty God, [Col. 1041B] who had delivered us from the power of the devil. Thereafter I began to turn over in my mind and consider whether, at any time while reading and searching the Scriptures, I had found anything like what I had happened to see on that day.

“Among the other things through which my mind passed, there returned to my memory the words and writings of the blessed bishop Isidore [Note: [Col. 1041D] Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4.]. In his book of *Etymologies*, he writes about the nature of the dragon as follows:

“‘The dragon is the greatest of all serpents, or of all animals upon the earth; the Greeks call it *draconta*. From this the Latin word was derived, so that it is called *draco*. It is often said to be dragged from caves into the air, and the air is stirred because of it.

“‘It is crested, with a small mouth and narrow tubes through which it draws breath and extends its tongue. Its power is not in its teeth but in its tail, and it harms by striking with the tail rather than by a bite [reading: *rictu*, “with the mouth,” rather than *ictu*, “by a blow”]. It is harmless with respect to poisons.

“‘Poisons are said not to be necessary for it to cause death for this reason: if it binds someone, it kills him. Not even the elephant is safe from it because of the elephant’s great size. For, lurking near the paths along which elephants customarily walk, it ties up their legs with its coils and kills them by suffocation.

“‘It is born especially in Ethiopia and India, in the very heat of perpetual summer.’”

## Ammonicius

“I believe that what you yourself saw or what others have said about the nature of the dragon, or about the beast friendly to the ancient enemy, is sufficient. Now, therefore, you must return to where you digressed.”

## Collectitius
[Col. 1041D] “Since both the time and the subject demand this, it will be my own will to follow your admonition, and, if the great Lord wills it, not without humility [Note: [Col. 1041D] These words were written in the manuscript in a different, smaller hand.]. Therefore, as I began to relate a little earlier in dictation, the venerable bishop, greatly beloved by the good and faithful, mindful of the admonition he had once received through a revelation of Christ’s confessor, and also knowing for certain that the prince of this world would come against him and fight him together with the powers of the air, yet hoping in the Lord’s mercy—for he had nothing against him—that through the intercessions of the saints his soul would overcome the enemy of the human race, ordered, in his final agony, that he be carried by the faithful into the oratory and laid before the altar of Saint Otmar.

When this had been done, he recovered somewhat from his illness and sat down; then, taking the stole, he first purified himself through confession. Next, he earnestly and clearly admonished those present, and all who had been entrusted to him, concerning faith, hope, and charity; at the same time, with deepest sighs, he commended his death to God and his saints. Having received the viaticum, he humbled himself to the ground.

Then the attendants, or chamberlains, attempted to drive everyone from the church except those familiars who customarily remained there. But the man of God forbade them, saying: ‘Open the doors; allow all who wish to remain here to be present at our dissolution. For we mortals ought not to be ashamed of anything except evil works, when we have necessarily paid the debt of death, since Christ, who owed nothing to death, was not ashamed to die almost naked upon the cross for the salvation of the human race. Let each person see in our death what he fears and does not guard against in his own. May God deign to have mercy on me, a wretched sinner now suffering death, and on everyone who looks upon it with fear and humility.’

When he had said this, he reverently breathed his last.

Soon afterward arrived Hartwig, archbishop [Note: [Col. 1042D] Of Salzburg. WAITZ.], of blessed memory, and a certain Count Arbo, one of the most faithful among the faithful and, among the laity, especially dear to the man of God. The venerable Bishop Wolfgang, having been forewarned by the spirit on the preceding night that these men would also come, made this known to certain people [Col. 1042C] after a long silence and when the distress of his body had been relieved. He frightened those standing nearby and suddenly said: ‘Clean the house, sweep the courtyards; good guests are coming to us today. And so that you may believe me when I say what is true, this shall be a sign to you from my mouth: the ship carrying the possessions of my lord Archbishop Hartwig and of the excellent Count Arbo has suffered shipwreck and loss on the Danube; but by God’s mercy the men have been saved, and those same lords will soon come to you after my death.’

Why say more? When what had been foretold by blessed Wolfgang had been fulfilled, his body, accompanied by the archbishop and a great multitude of the faithful, was reverently transferred, and on the seventh day after his death it was brought to the city of Regensburg [Col. 1042D]. There, when the blessed bishop had been received at Saint Peter’s and commended to God, whom he had served, through the celebration of vigils and Masses, he was clothed in the pontifical vestments in which he had been consecrated, in the basilica of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, as he had ordered while alive, according to what is written: ‘I will clothe you with changing garments’ [Note: [Col. 1042D] Zechariah III.].

There, as I heard from an elderly and devout priest who clothed him in the vestments, to reveal the merit of so great a bishop, not only was an evil odor absent, but a good one was also present, in accordance with what the Apostle says [Col. 1043A]: ‘We are a sweet odor to God in every place, to some unto life, to others unto death’ [Note: [Col. 1043D] II Corinthians II.].

Then, lifting the blessed man’s body with great reverence, they carried it to the church of Christ’s martyr Emmeram, whose honor he had cherished during his life with deepest affection and the utmost devotion. When the solemnities of the Mass and the rites of burial had been properly completed [Note: [Col. 1043D] In another hand at the margin.], on the eighth day, reckoned from the day before the Kalends of November on which he had departed this life, he was magnificently and honorably buried on the southern side of the basilica of Saint Emmeram, twelfth in the order of bishops—a number quite fittingly assigned as sacred to such a man. In him the Lord afterward powerfully manifested by miracles and signs that ‘he has placed him with the princes of his people’ [Note: [Col. 1043D] Psalm CXII.].

### Ammonicius

[Col. 1043B]

“Now, since you have placed the man of God among the bishops by the number twelve, as seems appropriate to me, it is fitting that you should recount by name those who governed this Church before him and append briefly to this work those whom he had as successors. Some people take delight in reading such things.”

### Collectitius

“It is not known for certain who was the first planter of divine plantations in that place [Note: [Col. 1043D] Who the first bishop of Regensburg was is unknown. BASN.]. Nevertheless, I shall obey your affection as best I can. Thus, as the written records of ecclesiastical donations and transfers attest, this see had, during the times of the Romans, the venerable man Primus [Note: [Col. 1043D] All this was written in a smaller hand in the margin. BASN.], together with a considerable number of other bishops whose definite episcopal administrations we read about, though we have been unable to discover their names. Then, under the kings of the Franks and also the dukes of Noricum, there was a certain religious minister of the Church named Lupus, and his successor, called Ratharius, before that ordination of blessed Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, which he carried out or arranged in Noricum by the authority of the apostolic see, according to the provisions of the canons.

[Note: [Col. 1043D] The authors disagree about the antiquity of the Church of Regensburg. Those who list many bishops in that city under the Romans, giving their names, resort to fables; nor do those who make Paulinus the first bishop of this city, succeeded, according to Arnulf, by Lupus, provide anything more certain. Others wish Rudbert, afterward Emmeram and Erhard, to have governed this Church; yet they had no fixed sees there, but rather stayed there from time to time in order to lead the people to the faith. Even if Rudbert had been bishop there, this would add nothing to the antiquity of the Church of Regensburg, since he lived in the eighth century, as we shall prove in his Life. It is much clearer that Gaubald was the first bishop of Regensburg; he received his orders from Boniface of Mainz. After him Sentpertus is counted, who subscribed to the Bavarian assembly held at Dingolfing in the year 772. BASN.]

“Afterward the following men presided, whose names are given below. First of all, Lord Gaubaldus, a holy and devout man, presided. Under him the body of blessed Emmeram, true martyr and bishop, was transferred from the place where it had been laid when it was brought here from Ascheim. After him Sintpertus received the episcopal chair together with ecclesiastical government. He built and adorned for blessed Emmeram a new basilica with more spacious dimensions and greater expense. In due order he was followed by Adalvinus, Baturicus, and Erchanfridus; Embricho succeeded them, a man venerable in age and merit, as we have learned from a truthful chronicle.

Then the bishopric of Regensburg came to Asperto, who was succeeded by a man of great gentleness and piety named Tuto, distinguished for his intelligence. His successors were Isangrimus, Gunthar, and Michael. After this blessed Wolfgang governed the Church. He was followed, in succession, by Gebhard and another Gebhard; Orno succeeded them, and then the third Gebhard, the emperor’s brother, outstanding both in the nobility of his lineage and in the dignity of pontifical honor.

From that man who, named Lupus, shepherded the Christian sheep in his pastoral office under the duke called Dieto, down to the one who now governs the Church, there have been seventeen bishops of this see [Col. 1044B]. May the pious Prince of shepherds deign to place these men in the kingdom of heaven, and in the multitude of his mercies may he not disdain to make us sinners sharers in eternal salvation.”

### Ammonicius

“Amen. Now it is time for you to turn your pen to the miracles which the grace of the Almighty has deigned to perform at the tomb of blessed Wolfgang, bishop and confessor, who is always glorious and wondrous in his saints. You ought to write these things also, especially because there are some who do not believe that certain chosen men belong to the number of the saints unless they have seen wonders and signs at their tombs.”

### Collectitius

[Col. 1044C]

“I know and understand that, by obeying you, I am serving the customs of many; therefore I am prepared to follow your preceding admonition with the present account.

“A certain man afflicted with blindness, and greatly saddened on that account, approached the tomb of blessed Wolfgang. There, having shed tears and poured out prayers, he recovered his sight, rejoiced that he had been heard, and, greatly gladdened, gave thanks to God and the holy bishop. Thus, accompanied by restored health, he returned to his own home.

“On another occasion a certain little woman was carried by her family, in the hope of recovering her health, to the church of blessed Emmeram, martyr and bishop. There, while she earnestly implored the saints’ intercession before the altars, she eventually became exhausted by the effort or by her illness and sat down on the ground beside the tomb of Christ’s confessor Wolfgang. As the poor woman, bowed down in body [Col. 1045A] and mind, desired to be aided by the venerable bishop’s prayers and merits, suddenly the contraction of her side and the knotted binding of her other limbs were released, and they were torn apart so violently that blood poured out onto the pavement.

“Then the woman, terrified at first, began to cry out from fear; afterward she leapt up and gave thanks to the saving power of the holy Trinity and to the merciful power that had obtained healing through the saints. Restored to herself, she returned from the church’s healing dwelling to her own home. Afterward those responsible for this matter hung above the church doors the little bench on which the poor woman had been accustomed to support herself with all her strength and crawl rather than walk, for the glory of the divine name and in memory of so great a sign.

[Col. 1045B] “One day [al., ‘On Sunday’] a poor little man—and, as I learned from a truthful report, the almoner of the bishop of Ravenna—came to the church of blessed Emmeram to pray. While he repeatedly asked to be freed, through the merits of the saints, from the weakness of his limbs that had long clung to him, he finally lay down in the place which had been endowed and enriched by the sacred body of blessed Wolfgang.

“There, having fallen into a blessed sleep, he saw standing beside him a tall man, venerable with white hair, who said to him: ‘Why are you here, or for what reason have you come here?’ He replied: ‘Lord, I, a wretched man, have come here for this reason: that I might be healed of the illnesses by which I have suffered and been afflicted for several years.’

“Then the venerable hero, touching the sick man with the pastoral staff that he appeared to carry in his hand, and who was pitifully deprived of the functions of his limbs, said: ‘Behold, you will be healed in the name of the holy Trinity.’ Then he who had lain there as though dead was roused from the sleep of illness through the merits of the revered bishop. He suddenly leapt up and, shouting in amazement or rejoicing, praised God and his saints as much as he could and urged others to praise them also.

“These three chapters, therefore, written in the name of the holy Trinity in memory of the venerable bishop, I believe suffice as the testimony of two or three witnesses for those who do not attempt, with proud eyes and an insatiable heart, to oppose the triune and equally divine name. Moreover, I hope that the merit of this same holy man will, through the revelation and also the cooperation of heavenly grace, be declared still more clearly [Col. 1045D] and abundantly, and that it will be praised more fully by us or by others in the Lord.”

### Ammonicius

“The hope of all the faithful is placed and fixed not merely justly but necessarily in the omnipotent Lord, who pours out the ointments of his mercy so abundantly that he does not wish to withhold his benefits even from the ungrateful. His praise in the memory of the saints ought to receive ever fuller increase until the end of the age, according to what the Psalmist says in the one hundred forty-fourth Psalm: ‘Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you’ [Col. 1046A]. ‘They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they shall tell of your power.’

“Therefore, take up the dialogue manfully between the two of us, and, once you have written about blessed Wolfgang, write also about the venerable man Ramuold, commending him with the highest devotion to faithful memory: how the praiseworthy duality of so great a bishop and abbot, accompanied by love of God and neighbor, together with faith and charity, reached that place where the holy Trinity rules forever and the undivided unity of the Godhead reigns eternally with the saints and the elect.”

### Collectitius

“Amen. May the Lord’s will be done for the salvation of the human race and in the humble account of this little work. Thus may the pen perform its office, so that through it an acceptable sacrifice of obedience may be prepared for God.

[Col. 1046B] “After the death of blessed Bishop Wolfgang, the servant of the omnipotent God, Ramuold, an abbot of distinguished memory, suffered many adversities amid various trials in the governance of the monastery and the administration of the coenobium. These grew to such an extent that, under Gebhard, the first bishop of this see [Note: [Col. 1045D] In another hand in the margin.], the servant of God was defamed before the emperor Otto III through the slanders and accusations of certain people.

“Matters came to the point that the prince, believing what he ought not to have believed, became doubtful and uncertain about the man of God’s religious character. When he came to Saint Emmeram’s, as emperors customarily did, he was so embittered in spirit that he would neither speak to him nor turn his eyes toward him. While prayers were being offered by him in the altar sacristy, before him who made the fabric of heaven, earth, and sea [Col. 1046C], a certain associate of his, named Heribert—at that time perhaps a chaplain, but afterward bishop of Cologne—approached him. Deliberately he said to him: ‘My lord, you ought not to be angry with the man of God.’

“To this the emperor replied: ‘Since it is written, “You shall not curse the prince of your people” [Note: [Col. 1046D] Exodus XXII; Acts XXIII.], I know that it is not right for a man of God to slander or curse me, especially since I have never done anything to him that deserved a curse.’

“Then Lord Heribert, a good and faithful counselor, replied: ‘If imperial authority is eager—as it ought to be in your presence—to examine the venerable abbot, question him about this matter before the holy congregation, and let it be determined whether the charges brought against him are true [Col. 1046D] or false. I believe in God and hope that neither the maturity of so venerable an old man, nor the wisdom and humility granted him by God, would ever have permitted him to say the things which his enemies have said about him, whether true or fabricated.’

“Then the emperor, restoring his composure to the will of divine providence, entered the cloister, taking with him a few beloved companions [reading uncertain: ‘of peace’]. There, seeing the venerable Father prostrate on the ground with the brothers, he was astonished and said: ‘He has done me great harm who, reporting these things as a message from Bishop Gebhard, planted them in my ears and thereby stirred me, unwary as I was, against this abbot and the holy college entrusted to him. I know indeed that for this careless credulity in believing falsehood I must do no small penance in my life. Now, because my sins have exposed the feet of your holiness, I beg you to put your shoes back on and return to us.’

“Having done this quickly, the venerable hero Ramuoldus went out with the brothers and confidently addressed the prince, saying: ‘We know, of course, that the imperial authority you possess was given and established from above, and that whoever God blesses is blessed. Since we have not been wholly foolish in this matter, but are still to some extent knowledgeable, where did such presumption come from in my littleness, that I, a worthless little man, completely forgetting my proper measure, should dare to curse your exaltedness, which the King of kings and Lord of lords has already deemed worthy of his blessing? [Col. 1047B]

“‘Whatever judgment may please your majesty, I am ready to clear myself of the charge brought against me, and also to satisfy all those present by the testimony of truth concerning this matter.’

“The emperor, after considering his reply, spoke these words: ‘Just as we delight in truth, so, on the contrary, we are angered by falsehoods. Therefore we judge that God’s judgment must be exalted above the judgment of mortals, who easily deceive and are deceived. I prefer to believe good things about good men rather than evil things about the corrupt. Nor is it fitting for anyone rashly to believe anything from anyone. Thus your verbal defense of the charge, expressed by your own mouth, is a very great satisfaction to me from so great a man. Now, equally appeased by this judgment, evident in a different way, I desire, O elder beloved by God, to meet with you in some private place for spiritual conversation and admonition, and also to be consoled by you. I desire that the burden of the kingdom, which I have received though unworthy, be lightened through him who says in the prophet Isaiah: “The yoke shall rot because of the oil” [Note: [Col. 1047D] Isaiah XXIII.].’”

### Ammonicius

“This is what is said through the prophet: ‘Be ashamed, Sidon, said the sea’ [Note: [Col. 1047D] Isaiah XXIII.]. Behold, we who by right ought in all things to humble ourselves before our superiors are often provoked to anger by the goads of pride because of words of fraternal admonition, and we customarily become indecently and excessively agitated against fathers and brothers. Conversely, a secular person, not only honorably established in office but also exalted to the imperial height of rule, by assuming the form of humility, puts to shame pride, the overthrower of the archangel and the mother of the devil.

“What does this good will accomplish through such humility except that our pride may be reproved, that justice may in some way confront us, and that it may bring words of this kind into our hearts? ‘Be ashamed, Sidon,’ said the sea—that is, ‘Be confounded, negligent monk or nun,’ says the faithful person, though secular: you have cast aside the supreme virtue of monks, namely humility, and stubbornly appropriated to yourself the greatest vice, namely pride. Whoever strives to fulfill what the Apostle says will carefully avoid or overcome this most wicked and most biting hold of all sins: ‘Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation’ [Note: [Col. 1047D] I Peter V.].”

### Collectitius

“To this testimony of sacred reading most fittingly applies what the Truth says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted’ [Note: [Col. 1047D] Matthew XXIII.]. These truthful words, being holy and evangelical, teach that exaltation should be feared by some and humility rejoiced in by others.

“But since we all offend in many ways [Note: [Col. 1048D] James III.], the proud must be tolerated and continually visited through fraternal admonitions, so that what they do wrong in pride may be corrected by a change to humility [Col. 1048B]. It is exceedingly dangerous for pride to sit in a human heart as though in its own nest. Therefore the faithful should humbly ask that the mercy of almighty God deign to turn so pestilential a mistress away from us and from all Christians.”

### Ammonicius

“May it be so, may it be so, according to your word, so that this pestilential vice may fall throughout the whole world.”

### Collectitius

“Now, therefore, let us appease those whom your sharp little admonition has marked out for negligence and the vice of vices with what follows. The aforesaid and often-to-be-named glorious Emperor Otto III, religious in many respects, entered with the venerable abbot the church of Saint Benedict, devoted in many ways to divine service. There, greatly humbled and cast down through the medicine of confession, he was placed between two altars established under the figure of a twofold love and consecrated in honor of the same most venerable Father and of Christ’s illustrious martyr Kilian. At the spiritual father’s command, he sat before him like a most worthless little servant on a low three-legged stool, accompanied by humility, that best of mothers.

“There he heard many things that customarily destroy foolish deeds, as well as many others which the hearts of the stupid refuse to receive with their stiff necks. Finally, changed into another man through this encounter and inwardly touched by the admonition of the man of God, he felt God’s grace present with him. It bestowed on him the greatest compunction, through which the outer man not only most subtly agreed with the inner man [Note: [Col. 1048D] In the manuscript, in another hand.], but also did so most beneficially [Note: [Col. 1048D] In the manuscript, in another hand.].

“When he had thus made satisfaction for human frailty to that point in time, he went outside and said to his attendants: ‘Truly, the Holy Spirit has spoken through this man’s mouth. Today, in his speech, I have proved the truth of Solomon’s saying: “The words of the wise are like nails driven firmly in place” [Note: [Col. 1048D] Ecclesiastes XII.].’

“The divine command most certainly gives a free spirit to those who observe it [Note: [Col. 1048D] In another hand.]. When the emperor’s attendants looked carefully at him, they marveled at the change in his face and said: ‘My lord, what has happened to you, that you are so drenched both in tears and in sweat?’

“He replied: ‘Do not wonder that I am wet with sweat; wonder rather that I am alive from fear. May I never fall into such a trial except for the salvation of my soul. In this holy elder I have clearly discovered how great an honor must be shown to God’s chosen servants.’

“After this he ordered the bishop of Regensburg to be summoned before him. Standing before the altar of Saint Emmeram, he said to him under threat of punishment: ‘Beware lest, while I live, you do anything further against the abbot of this monastery and the brothers who serve God and Saint Emmeram here. Let what rightfully belongs to you as bishop remain yours; let the monks’ possessions remain securely protected under the guardianship of all good men. Therefore, on whatever day you transgress in the matters you have now heard with your own ears, know beyond doubt that, whether by divine or human agency, you will be harshly and bitterly dealt with for the evil of so great a crime.’

“Then the emperor turned to the abbot and brothers and, with his customary compassion, bade them farewell, saying: ‘May the merciful and compassionate Lord deign to preserve you inwardly and outwardly, so that in your prayers you may remember not only us but also the whole Christian people.’

“Having been commended to the Lord with psalms and hymns, the most devout Augustus, preceded as customary by the holy imperial lance bearing the cross, departed from this city to seek Italy and also to visit the most powerful city of Rome, which some customarily call the mistress of the world or the greatest of cities.”

### Ammonicius

“How can this earthly city be called the greatest of cities, when the most magnificent city of God, which he himself began to build from the beginning of the world through living and chosen stones [Note: [Col. 1049D] I Peter II.], may rightly be called the mistress of the world or the greatest of cities? For the truth of this matter, so that no one in his frailty may doubt, Wisdom, crying out from her sanctuary through Solomon and proclaiming her omnipotence, says: ‘I held primacy among every people; by my own power I trampled the necks of the proud and exalted’ [Note: [Col. 1049D] Ecclesiasticus XXIV.].

“It seems necessary, therefore, that the present dialogue should satisfy fraternal simplicity with evident reasoning on this question.”

### Collectitius

“I thought everyone had been satisfied by that most famous work of blessed Augustine in which he discusses, with the greatest abundance, *The City of God*.
