Opposed to it is the city of the devil, which the King of kings daily casts down and diminishes through pride, while, conversely, through the spirit of humility he exalts his own city, begun among the good and to be completed among the good, according to what is written: ‘The Lord shall establish peace within its borders’ [Note: [Col. 1049D] Psalm CXLVII.], giving also to the children of men the power to become children of God, who are born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God [Note: [Col. 1049D] John I.].

“But since I see that your affection eagerly desires that something about this should be discussed in this little work through my small ability, I shall do so according to my measure—not as I wish, perhaps, but as I can.

“From the creation of the world, therefore, the city of God has been in conflict with the city of the devil. A considerable part of the latter was that Babylon, once renowned among the nations [Note: [Col. 1049D] Isaiah XIII; Jeremiah LI.], in which the language of the whole earth was once confused [Note: [Col. 1049D] Genesis XI.] because of pride; it had been raised to a height of more than one hundred and twenty cubits. Christ most clearly overthrew it in his city, that is, in Jerusalem, ‘whose participation is in unity’ [Col. 1050B] [Note: [Col. 1050D] Psalm CXXI.], on the day of Pentecost. For the Holy Spirit, coming upon the disciples with a sudden sound and appearing visibly to them in fiery tongues, granted the company of one hundred and twenty brothers gathered in one upper room under the love of gracious Jesus the unity of languages [Note: [Col. 1050D] Acts II.], so that they might preach throughout the whole world and bear witness to the Lord’s triumph. Through it the devil, defeated and bound in the chains of his own wickedness, groans and howls throughout the whole world over the apostate city—once raised up by its pride, now cast down through the humility of Christ’s disciples—or rather, over the entire Christian people, protected, as it were, by the shield of divine defense [Col. 1050C].

“From this it will be proved with complete certainty that the city of God is always growing and the city of the devil eternally diminishing.

“Thus, in ancient times, a not insignificant portion of this city belonging to the devil was Rome, possessed by the devil through idolatry. Before it confessed Christ and suffered many martyrdoms under his name—a wondrous statement, but truly credible—it was transformed by him who is powerful enough to raise up children of Abraham from stones [Note: [Col. 1050D] Matthew III.] and was joined to the heavenly hierarchy. Though previously devoted beyond measure to the worship of idols, it now rejoices that it has been endowed with the faith of Christ and with manifold veneration of the saints.

“Truly, the faithful in this city see fulfilled what the Apostle says: ‘Where sin abounded, grace shall abound still more’ [Col. 1050D] [Note: [Col. 1050D] Romans V.].

“Behold that ancient Babylon, which, persuaded by pride, once thought it could obtain dominion over the whole world, lying desolate, filled with dragons and evil beasts. But this city—Rome—because it too once followed diabolical error and the confusion of every evil, received, as blessed Peter testifies, the name Babylon [Note: [Col. 1050D] I Peter V.], and because of the power of its empire was then called the mistress of the world. Later, however, through that same Apostle and his successors, it was humbled under the power of Christ and, from being the city of the devil, became the city of God [Col. 1051A]. It grew so greatly in divine worship that, in place of the ruins of its walls and ancient temples, countless buildings of churches and monasteries rise every day.

“Of their incredible number, as I heard from an old man who said he had been raised in that same city, twenty are possessed by nuns, forty by monks, and sixty by canons, apart from those outside the city and the other churches and chapels that abound in the City.

“Come now, brother, you who are angered by those who call Rome the greatest of cities. Consider, if you can, what dignity came to it from the day when Peter saw Christ meet him outside the gate of the Roman city. There he also worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, where are you going?’ And the Lord said: ‘I am going to Rome to be crucified again’ [Col. 1051B].

“That place where Christ was crucified in Peter, or Peter for Christ, and where Paul was beheaded for the supreme Head, is worthy of every kind of veneration, under the love of him who, for the salvation of the faithful, established such things by his ineffable mercy. Why, then, is it surprising that this city should be called the greatest of cities, when the Creator of all things himself deigned to visit it in such a way that he wished to glorify his chief members there through a most glorious passion?

“Behold, we who, by God’s gift, have one most blessed martyr, Emmeram, as our patron rejoice and are glad in the memory of the saints. How much more should those rejoice whom God, who is rich toward all [Note: [Col. 1051D] Ephesians II.], has enriched with the bodies of so many martyrs and, so to speak, with the most precious and glorious pledges of heaven [Col. 1051C]!

“Why say more? Thanks be to God, for Babylon has fallen [Note: [Col. 1051D] Isaiah XXI.] in Rome. In that city, as a new people rises under confession of Christ’s name, marveling greatly at its own transformation, it says with the Psalmist: ‘This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High’ [Note: [Col. 1051D] Psalm LXXVI.].

“Looking upon this city from every direction, the many peoples gathered there take up the words of sacred Scripture and say: ‘O almighty Rome, glorious things have been spoken of you, because you have become the city of God’ [Note: [Col. 1051D] Psalm LXXXVI.]. Through the Head of all good things, who reigns forever, Christ, under the preaching of the apostles and the testimony of the martyrs, the heads of the Dragon have been broken in you, and he has been given as food to many peoples, according to what the Psalmist, praising the Lord in the assembly of the saints, says: ‘You have broken the heads of the Dragon; you have given him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia’ [Note: [Col. 1052D] Psalm LXXIII.].”

### Ammonicius

“Since you have answered with clear reasoning the question I raised in the person of a preacher, it remains now, O Collectitius, that, in accordance with your name, you carefully append what must be gathered afterward. The benefit of readers demands that the Psalmist’s verse which you have proposed be explained. For it seems almost unbelievable to everyone that human beings can and ought to eat the Dragon.”

### Collectitius

[Col. 1052A]

“It is the custom of sacred Scripture to arrange its statements through figures and various forms. One of these is called metaphor, that is, transformation. Through it divine speech says that the Dragon is to be eaten by human beings; but this eating is understood as nothing other than destruction and annihilation. For just as food and nourishment are ground and crushed by the teeth and thus reduced to nothing, so too the Dragon—that is, the devil—is crushed by Christ’s power and trampled down forcefully by his churches, or annihilated, as the Savior himself says to his disciples in his Gospel: ‘Behold, I have given you power to trample upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy’ [Note: [Col. 1052D] Luke X.].”

### Ammonicius

[Col. 1052B] “Thanks be to God, because you have accommodated yourself to my weakness—or rather, to fraternal necessity—in resolving this question as well. Indeed, the time and the subject now require that, having left these matters in their proper place, you return to the history of Ramuold, the venerable abbot and most beloved Father.”

### Collectitius
Five years after the imperial departure from the city of Hiatospolis, whose inhabitants we are, the blessed abbot Ramuoldus, weakened by a lingering illness, began to be deprived of bodily strength, while spiritually rejoicing that the inner man was being disciplined through this sickness, according to the Apostle’s saying: “When I am weak, then I am strong and powerful” [Note: [Col. 1052D] 2 Cor. 12]. Through this bodily weakness he was brought to the final light of the present life. On that day the venerable hero, rising from the bed which for fourteen consecutive days he had been unable to leave because of his illness, clothed in the tunic of his holy calling and somewhat relieved of his fever by spiritual medicine, took a stole, gathered the company of the brothers, sat down in their midst, and spoke with powerful eloquence as follows:

“God the Father, out of great love and by a great plan, sent his Only-Begotten Son to save the human race. Hence through the Prophet he was also called the Angel of Great Counsel [Note: [Col. 1052D] Isa. 9]. Although by divine power he could have snatched us from the power of the devil, he did not wish to use that power alone for the redemption of the human race, because of the justice especially proper to the Holy Trinity. Rather, through his ineffable mercy, he offered to the Father the human being whom, together with a soul, he had assumed in becoming incarnate from the Virgin; suspended upon the cross, he reconciled the world to God through his most holy blood, and also set him forth against the ancient enemy in the form of humility—the enemy whom, through the most wicked murder of pride, he boasted that he had overcome. For Christ, upon the wood of the cross, became obedient unto death to the Father’s will, whereas the disobedience of the first man had brought about the wound leading to death.

“Brothers, love with the greatest devotion, pursue, and cherish this virtue—obedience—by which Christ accomplished the beautiful wholeness of human redemption. Praise the Holy Trinity, which created us in its own image and likeness, with intellect, memory, and will, in the most diligent reverence of fear and love. Therefore, with devoted mind, emulate, according to the Apostle, the greater gifts [Note: [Col. 1053D] 1 Cor. 12], and meditate in your hearts upon Solomon’s saying: ‘Fear God and observe his commandments; for this is the whole human being’ [Note: [Col. 1053D] Eccles. 12].

“Behold, I am advanced in age, Catholic in faith, and, to speak truthfully, very deficient in the virtue which ought to support that faith. With the day of my summons at hand, I am entering upon the way of all flesh, hoping to come to the joys of the heavenly homeland through him who is the wondrous Liberator in his many mercies. But you, my very heart in Christ, love this Father, whose fatherhood is able to place your souls among the number of God’s children together with their bodies. And accept this sign of things to come, though it is unworthy that I should announce it: after my departure you will suffer many adversities in this place, and you will be so embittered by them that you will even be compelled to leave it. Yet the agitation of so great a storm will quickly be calmed by divine consolation. Therefore I advise each of you to hasten to return here, to the place of your profession, where you may continually hear or [Note: [Col. 1053D] another reading] practice the harmony of spiritual voices.

“As for the rest, I now bring this conclusion of my fraternal admonition to an end: strive to possess the serpent’s prudence, which is lesser among the virtues, so that through carelessness you do not lose the golden humility of dove-like simplicity, which is the greater. Above all, take up what Christ commanded his disciples in his Gospel, saying: ‘Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves’ [Note: [Col. 1053D] Matt. 10].”

Then, with the greatest humility between the abbot and the brothers, a mutual confession having taken place, together with the very necessary forgiveness of sins sought and implored from heaven, and with inner sighs that seemed to touch heaven, the venerable hero first commended the flock entrusted to him to the Supreme Shepherd. Then, bidding farewell to the brothers, who because of tears and sobs could scarcely speak, he said:

“Go, dearest brothers, and prepare yourselves to celebrate the divine office; hasten together with the greatest speed to complete the sacred order according to custom. And hold this final memorial of the old man as a blessing: ‘In the name of the Lord, the salvation of us all.’”

When they had all said “Amen” together and went out sorrowfully, seeking consolation from the Holy Spirit, truly the Paraclete [Note: [Col. 1054D] another reading], the man of God, foreseeing in spirit that his soul would soon be released from the body, ordered those present to carry him to the oratory adjoining his cell and to lay him down between two altars: his head turned toward the altar of Saint Benedict, the holy Father, and his feet toward the altar of Saint Kilian, martyr of Christ. Placing his hope most firmly in the name of the latter, as in an omen of the salvation of all, he ordered Masses to be celebrated there and the memory of the Lord’s Passion to be enacted with the greatest devotion.

When this had been completed and the time of Communion had come, as soon as the man of God received the Eucharist of the Lord’s body and blood, he sent his soul from the prison of the flesh to the eternal homeland. In his final agony he held his hands extended beside his head, just as he had been accustomed to do in prayer.

Then the religious elders—namely, Gotahardus, abbot of the monastery of Altaha, and Adalpertus, Father of the monastery of Seeon—came running with the other brothers. With devout minds they offered hymns and praises to God and endeavored to commend the spirit of the pious Father to the mercies of the grace of the Almighty. When these rites had been duly and reverently completed, those whose hearts divine inspiration had deigned to visit more than the others raised their voices in faith and said:

“Lord, as we hope, this man of yours did not complete in vain so many years of life granted to him in the present age. Today, made a centenarian by your summons, we marvel more at his removal from our midst than we grieve over it.

“Certainly the law of numerical calculation instructs the skilled practitioner first to place upon the left hand, by the number thirty, the lawful kiss of legitimate marriage. Then it suggests that upon the same left hand he take up, by the number sixty, the clear burden of widowhood. Third, when seeking the conclusion or perfection of the hundred, he must pass to the right hand and there paint a crown, which signifies the inestimable glory of virginity and the eternal laurel of the heavenly kingdom.

“He is by no means unworthy of the sublimity of this number, being pierced through by the subtlety of Solomon’s admonition, which must be carefully examined and which designates the fool by saying: ‘Cursed is the child of a hundred years’ [Note: [Col. 1054D] Isa. 65]. Your beloved servant, however, carefully avoiding this in every way—whose dead little body we, standing around his bier, are now attending with funeral rites—longed throughout all the days of his life to be found among those whom that distinguished verse of your Psalmist marks out: ‘With the holy man you will be holy, and with the elect you will be elect’ [Note: [Col. 1054D] Ps. 17]. Therefore, as your faithful believe, from you, who are rich toward all, he has now received, in exchange for his perfection of a hundred years, the heavenly blessing in your presence.

“Let us therefore, your little servants, struck down in mourning by the recent death of this beloved elder, rest for a little while in the confession and consolation of your holy name, so that the weakness of human frailty may be relieved. Nevertheless, in the fervor of praise of the nourishing Trinity, it pleases us to warm the outer man together with the inner through words such as these:

“Glory to you, Trinity, one equal Godhead, before all ages, now, and forever.”

Ammonicius.

“Amen. It is clearly established that the man of God, following the example of his predecessors, led a life filled with virtues in this age; and that among mortals he so reverently put off the earthly man [χοϊκόν, *choïkon*]. From this I also judge that, because during his life he took care, as far as he could, to avoid the little glory of this world, by dying—or by stripping off the earthly man [Note: [Col. 1055D] 1 Cor. 15]—he entered the ineffable joy of that glory which always remains, of which the Apostle says: ‘Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what the Lord has prepared for those who love him’ [Note: [Col. 1055D] 1 Cor. 2].

“To this clear testimony of the greatest consolation faithful David agrees, saying to the Lord: ‘How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you’ [Note: [Col. 1055D] Ps. 30]. And shortly afterward: ‘You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men’ [Note: [Col. 1055D] ibid.]. Therefore you too, O Collectitius, protected from the contradiction of tongues in the Lord’s tabernacle, continue along the royal way as you began, writing out the most illustrious life of the man of God.”

Collectitius.

“I am pleased, I confess, O Ammonicius, that you encourage me to write the life of the man of God after his death. For both the Law and the hope of Christian faith firmly maintain that the saints—that is, the elect—when they have died carnally to the world, truly and spiritually begin to live for God. Hence miracles multiply even at their dead bones, and countless benefits are bestowed upon mortals through their pious intercessions.

“I shall briefly relate shortly how splendidly such benefits were supplied from heaven at the tomb of this confessor of whom we are speaking, so that I may not unduly prolong the fraternal charity which is eager to receive these and other things.

“When news flew abroad that the man of God had died, the belief that he had lived with God moved many people to hurry to the funeral of so great a Father with the greatest devotion of heart. Among them was Henry, then holding the rank of *hypatos* and ruling over the Noric and Carinthian peoples [Note: [Col. 1055D] another reading], who a few years later was to become king not only of Germany or Gaul but also emperor of all Italy and Augustus Caesar of the Roman city.

“He brought with him Bishop Godehard, who had previously been somewhat opposed to the holy man but now came with his mind changed, as the fountain of his tears testified. In humbly serving the servant of God at his burial, he presented himself as a servant to the supreme and humble Lord of lords.

“When nearly all who served God at Regensburg had gathered together and were singing reverently at the funeral of the pious abbot, the prince himself was not ashamed to carry the bier upon his own shoulders and to prepare the burial with especial care. Finally, he entered the grave and himself closed the coffin, which had already received the body of the man of God. He chose its little key as a most precious pledge for himself and, afterward, when established in the royal insignia, always kept or retained it with him as though it were a sign of triumph.”

Ammonicius.

“With some astonishment I may ask whether these things were done at the command and by the will of the man of God, or whether they happened so by chance. For I have rarely heard of anyone who, after being entrusted to burial, was enclosed in a coffin secured with locks.”

Collectitius.

“It is no wonder if a simple man marvels at such trifles, since King and prophet David, to whom the hidden things of wisdom were divinely revealed, marveled at the power of the heavenly sacraments, saying: ‘Wondrous is God in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give strength’ [Note: [Col. 1055D] Ps. 67].

“Having become a participant in this great strength by the gift of the Supreme Giver, the blessed Father Ramuoldus, firm in Catholic faith and knowing Christ to be the Rock who saved the world through wood, ordered a wooden chest—or sepulchral [Note: [Col. 1056D] another reading in the manuscript] box—to be placed within a stone sarcophagus. It was covered with red leather in memory of the Lord’s Passion, so that after his death it might receive his little body. His hope was that the one whom, while he lived in the present age, he had daily fed and clothed from that same chest among the flock of the poor would not disdain, by his almighty mercy, to raise him among the elect and place him in the bosom of eternal blessedness.

“If by these few words, O Ammonicius, you think your wonder and inquiry have not been sufficiently satisfied, I ask you to return to what Scripture says: ‘Nothing happens on earth without a cause’ [Note: [Col. 1056D] Job 5]. This must especially be observed in the deeds of the saints, and it can most truly be proved.

“For the reason why the most blessed abbot Ramuoldus was compelled for a time to leave the monastery at Regensburg and return to Trier was the civil war that existed between Duke Henry and Margrave Berchtold, and among the other nobles of Prince Otto, who was then besieging the city of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 1056D] another reading in the manuscript]. When the conflict had been settled, and as though the blessed Emmerammus were indicating that he should return through the administrator of his place [Note: [Col. 1056D] another reading], the venerable elder returned from the city of Trier to Hiatospolis, bringing with him many relics of saints from Lorraine.

“Their salutary arrival also became the reason for the crypt built at Saint Emmerammus. Its construction, arranged with considerable skill by the man of God, presents to those who look upon it a threefold and also a fourfold form. Since the author of this work loved the Holy Trinity and firmly held the faith of the four Gospels, it offers a kind of credible testimony to that fact.

“The columns that support the same crypt church beautifully join together, by their duality, the twofold love—namely, of God and of neighbor. The five altars, in which as many reliquary boxes were placed with the relics that the aforementioned hero brought from Lorraine, remind us to retain in memory the chief observance of the five books of Moses and urge us always to possess fivefold prudence in the five senses of the body. The sixth altar, called ‘at the feet,’ declares by the perfection of the number six that all things are brought to completion.

“In this basilica, therefore, so rich in typological meaning, dedicated by the blessed Wolfgang in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity and of all the saints, the most venerable Father Ramuoldus was laid in the tomb that he had prepared for himself fifteen years earlier, on the southern side of the same crypt beside the altar of Blessed Pope Gregory, and was buried magnificently. The order of the clergy stood by and sang psalms, the company of monks also sang together, and three assemblies of virgins, or holy women, commended the soul of so great a Father to the Supreme Father.

“After this, O Ammonicius, to temper the wonder concerning the lock of the cloister—or concerning the little key seized by the prince because of humility, or taken away because of religious devotion—I wish, as a satisfaction to your charity, to append one verse from Sacred Scripture. For the Lord says to one of his elect: ‘On that day I will receive you as my servant and set you like a signet in my presence, because I have chosen you’ [Note: [Col. 1057D] Hag. 2].”

Ammonicius.

“When pigments are ground, they are changed into a more pleasing appearance; so you too, when challenged by a question, will become more useful to yourself and to your neighbor in dictation and writing. Behold, while attempting to resolve a small question, you have not only advanced a great proposition but, through the agility divinely granted to you, have made it so lively that you have in a manner compelled stones to become articulate.

“Therefore what remains must now be undertaken energetically, and this path of charity must be walked by your own feet [Note: [Col. 1057D] another reading], namely, so that miracles and signs may follow the miracle which you have brought forward to the prophetic signet, proving after the man’s death the life of the man of God” [Note: [Col. 1057D] another reading].

Collectitius.

“I am ready, with the Lord’s permission, to do as you request, since I know that I previously promised you as much.

“A certain man came to Saint Emmerammus seeking the aid of the saints. Because he was possessed by a demon, he suffered greatly in the presence of everyone. Then the brothers, remembering what kind of Father they had recently buried, had the man led—or rather dragged—into the crypt endowed with the body of the man of God.

“There, after he had long been rolled about and had been more than grievously torn by the possessor, he began to shriek and cry out amid growling [Note: [Col. 1058D] another reading], and to make a din with insults and curses [Note: [Col. 1058D] another reading], saying:

“‘Woe to you, Rantolt, because you did many evil things to my lord and through you he lost much of what was his by right. For this reason you labored day and night to injure him and to gather for your God as many people as you could. And now, on top of all this, you set me on fire and inflict great force upon me.’

“When the demon, amid such torments, pressed the poor man’s head against the pavement with such violence that it nearly forced him to die, those present ran up, lifted him, and dragged him to the tomb of Christ’s confessor. There, when they had scarcely compelled him—while the powers of the devil resisted dangerously—to incline his head and place it upon the tomb, he was freed by the grace of God. Rejoicing at this sign, those who had previously been saddened by compassion gave magnificent thanks to the Redeemer, not only because the man had been rescued from the power of the devil, but even more because through this present great miracle it had been revealed what merit belonged to the Father who had recently been buried there.

“As usual, pilgrims and citizens came from every direction to the festival of Saint Emmerammus. Among the others who hurried there was a certain little woman deprived of the light of her eyes. She entered the blessed crypt during the night, worshiped at the tomb of Christ’s confessor Ramuoldus, and poured out prayers with tears. Then almighty Lord, wishing through his ineffable power to glorify his servant among mortals, restored light to the woman who had been blind.

“The woman rose and called her husband to her ear, saying: ‘Master, thanks be to God, for I have recovered my sight.’ Since he did not believe her, and she, on the contrary, displayed sure signs, he began: ‘You must suppress this event in silence. You must act secretly and arrange for us to leave the city before daylight; for I am a cleric, and therefore I am ashamed to remain with you amid such a crowd.’

“When the woman, newly illuminated, agreed to this counsel of darkness and was returning home carelessly with the cleric, she was immediately struck by a very grievous ailment and became blind again.”

Ammonicius.

“This event recalls what the Lord himself says in the Gospel concerning the ten lepers cleansed by him, and the tenth who returned to give thanks: ‘Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?’ The Evangelist immediately adds: ‘And he was a Samaritan’ [Note: [Col. 1058D] Luke 17].

“From this it is plainly evident that whoever guards his soul and hates iniquity will not be without the duty signified by the Samaritan name. Therefore, O Collectitius, since after sorrow you introduced joy and then again added sorrow to it, it is fitting that, if the Lord has at that time supplied some remedy for so grievous a misfortune, your charity should explain it more quickly, in accordance with the form of our dialogue.”

Collectitius.

“The grace of our Redeemer knows no lack of remedies. Trusting in its fullness, the woman mentioned above came again to Regensburg in the hope of receiving light. Approaching the place of the tomb where she had previously experienced great benefits, she first purified herself before the priests through confession and plainly reported what had happened to her. Then, prostrate on the ground and humbled in mind, and swiftly aided by the prayers of God’s beloved confessor, she deserved to receive from the source of all good the sight of her eyes, wrongly lost.

“Then both she and all the others who had heard and seen these things gave immense thanks to God. Thus each person returned joyfully to his own home, carrying with him a threefold miracle by which the Holy Trinity deigned to declare that the pious abbot Ramuoldus had been its most faithful servant, since he had loved the true Lord.

“On another occasion, two women came to Saint Emmerammus, summoned by the report of miracles. Both were afflicted by demonic harassment. It became most clearly evident that their cleansing or liberation had been granted by divine mercy through the charity of the saints to the venerable Father Ramuoldus, because these same little women had previously been brought to the memorials of other saints without being delivered. Later, entering the famous crypt not at one and the same time but at different times [Note: [Col. 1059D] another reading], and being exorcised at the tomb of the blessed man by one and the same Lord, they were mercifully freed from the worst invader.

“The faithful brothers of our congregation who happened to be present at the time usually bear witness to this event. And, wondrous to say, they saw the unclean spirit leave one woman through a foul mist and another through the loathsome deformity of a beetle.

“What more is there to say? It must be spoken with our own mouth—or rather, held most firmly in our hearts [Note: [Col. 1059D] another reading in the manuscript]—‘Thanks be to God.’ For by these and similar signs, through the clear merits of the elect, the Lord is blessed by his own, while the devil is deservedly confounded and driven away by those who are not his, as Scripture testifies, saying: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’ [Note: [Col. 1060D] 2 Tim. 2].

“Once, when Christian people were coming together to the church of Saint Emmerammus the martyr not only from the city of Regensburg itself but also from its surrounding places, a certain woman came among the others who had gathered, carrying a recent token of a miracle. A spindle had attached itself to her hand, entangled with a twisting of threads. Since she could not tear it away from her palm in any way, nor drive so great an evil from herself by any means, she finally came anxiously to the tomb of the most venerable Father Ramuoldus.

“When she worshiped there and poured out prayers with tears, placing her trembling hand upon the blessed man’s tomb in the hope of salvation, she immediately lifted her hand away from it sound and whole through the power of the Lord’s hand. Then those who happened to be present at this event, together with the custodians who had run up, gave thanks to God and the blessed man and hung the same spindle in a small silver crown suspended above the tomb, so that it might be displayed to later generations as a great miracle.

“We ourselves saw this sign and touched it with our own hands. We know that our testimony in this matter is true, and we are not unaware that through this recent miracle, as through the other benefits of healing, the almighty Lord wished to glorify his saint.”

Ammonicius.

“I confess that I am pleased with the threads of your charity, which you have woven not only truthfully but also gracefully from the warp of your propositions and the weft of signs concerning the life of the saints. It is now appropriate for you to fasten various matters, rationally gathered from every direction and suited to the benefit of readers, with the threads of grammar.

“For the agility of your intellect and the exercise of study—or rather, the splendid variety of this whole fabric—can, as it seems to me, lighten or lessen the many burdens of your task. In addition, I admonish your fraternity that, in enlarging this little work, you should set forth the succession of abbots, explaining which Fathers and how many presided over the monastery of this most holy patron of ours [Note: [Col. 1060D] another reading], in which the highest service is owed to the Lord.”

Collectitius.

“First I want you to know, O Ammonicius, that I myself experienced the benefits of healing which I noted above at the tomb of the blessed Ramuoldus, confessor of Christ, when my own illness was taken away. For when I was a boy and had heard that many had been restored to health at the resting-place of the blessed man, I was suffering severely from fever. To obtain relief from it, I had myself thrown down upon the pavement and, persuaded by the advice of a certain priest who had been a familiar companion of that pious Father while he lived, I tried to give myself over to sleep there.

“When I had slept for a short while, I saw in a dream the revered Father dressed in monastic habit, as though seated at the right hand of Saint Emmerammus the martyr. Looking upon his venerable white hair, I marveled at the beauty of his face and at the whiteness of his other limbs. Greatly gladdened by this vision, I who had previously been exhausted rose up healthy, giving thanks to God because I felt the relief of his healing hand.”

Ammonicius.

“Your childhood, O Collectitius, rightly consoled by divine power, preserved this benefit more tenaciously in its memory, so that as a young man you would have reason to give thanks to so great a Father by now devoutly writing his deeds—he who then helped you and still diligently helps you by praying.

“From this point onward, the order of events requires that you describe the succession of the Fathers requested above in an appropriate sequence of words.”

Collectitius.

“I am ready, through charity, to follow the will or love of my neighbor, which, if it proceeds along the straight path, will bring eternal happiness to every Christian [Note: [Col. 1061D] 1 Cor. 13]. The Apostle confirms this by saying: ‘Love of neighbor does no evil; therefore love is the fullness of the law’ [Note: [Col. 1061D] Rom. 13].

“Accordingly, after the revered Father Ramuoldus, a man of great memory, the government of this monastery was assumed by the abbot Wolframmus, himself a servant of God in gentleness and the other virtues. He had as his successor an abbot elected from the college of the brothers, named Rihboldus. Lord Hartwicus, a friend of great virtue, succeeded him; he voluntarily abandoned the leadership of the monastery and left the abbacy to Lord Burchardus to govern.

“After Burchardus had died, divine providence, as we hope, appointed for our needs a venerable and likewise lovable man, Lord Udalricus, previously distinguished by manifold goodness in the canonical life and now regularly appointed over this monastic congregation.

“Thus the blessed Ramuoldus, who most excellently revealed his desire for the Lord through the name of the willing ram [or: *arietem*, ‘ram’ according to another reading], that is, one desiring Christ, was the first administrator of this place according to the Rule. He shows that the man who now administers the government of the monastery with us is sixth from him in number and deservedly second in succession. Under him we hope to be permitted to celebrate the sacrament of the number six for a long time, and likewise to exercise, in divine confession, our other pursuits of piety in deed and word.”

Ammonicius.

“Your composition, which you have made gradually by writing and which has crept along to this point [Col. 1061C], must henceforth be made to run, so that you may timely collect or compose something to offer at the festival of Saint Emmerammus, which is already preparing its appearance and is, as it were, smiling upon its own new offering—especially to your particular patron, or rather to the common helper of all who seek the Lord.”

Collectitius.

“I know myself to be very unworthy to claim for myself the particular patronage of so great a patron, since I am a sinner. Therefore, humbled, I desire that at least this much be granted to my smallness through his prayers: that with the other faithful I may be able to embrace blessed communion.

“Under the impulse of this desire, then, I shall undertake to forge what follows.

“In the annual course of the year, when the natal day of this often-mentioned and even more often-to-be-mentioned patron of ours returned, a considerable crowd had gathered there because of his customary benefits. When the sacrifices of praise had been offered there to God and the saints through the divine offices, and the solemn rites had been duly completed, not without signs and miracles, everyone returned home with joy.

“Then it happened that a certain poor man, who had decided to go with the others to such great rejoicing but had been unable to arrive, could only finally be brought by his companions to the desired place on the seventh day. For he was paralyzed and, so to speak, more than lame [Note: [Col. 1061D] another reading]. Therefore they had transported him with difficulty in a cart from a distant place.

“At the first hour of the eighth day, by nods and signs as best he could, he asked his friends to lead him into the church of Saint Emmerammus. Supported by the hands and arms of his companions, he stood on the western side of the blessed basilica, beside a column which customarily has consecrated water in a stone vessel, and, turning toward the east, he prayed in silence with his head slightly bowed, since he could not speak.

“Behold, he saw opposite the altar of the most blessed martyr, as though it were surrounded by fire and great light, and he perceived rays like those of the sun being sent from it into his face. Then, terrified and trembling because of the extraordinary vision and drenched in excessive sweat, he gradually recovered and began to speak, saying:

“‘Thanks be to God. What a great thing I see! Truly the Lord is in this place, who through the prayers of his beloved witness bestows here excellent remedies or consolations upon the sick and sorrowful.’

“When these things had been seen and heard, people came running from throughout the church. As the people watched and marveled at the same miracle, the Kyrie eleison was sung [Note: [Col. 1062D] another reading]. When the shouting could scarcely be endured by the ears and meanwhile greatly frightened us who were singing at the front, the same man, surrounded by a crowd of those who had happened to flock there because of the novelty of the event, was brought into the choir.

“After he had prayed there for a while before the altar of Saint Emmerammus, he rose from the assembly of the brothers who had approached when the prayer was completed. The prior ordered him to sit on the steps and to recount his story before everyone. He immediately obeyed and briefly explained what he had suffered since childhood. He stated that for eight years, up to that day, he had been afflicted by paralysis, deprived of the use of his hands, and entirely without the ability to walk with his feet.

“Then, having asked for and received a staff, since he needed another’s support because of his unsteady gait, he took up a cross for the love and hope of the Redeemer, for whom the blood of the martyrs was shed. Through the cross, we believe and know that the light of faith was given to the human race.

“Thus, going before the crowd as its leader, he proceeded to Saint Peter, presenting himself with his new health at the episcopal see, so that more people might share in the common joy and he might appear to fulfill what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests’ [Note: [Col. 1062D] Luke 17].

“There, having received counsel from the *Matricularii* not to prove ungrateful like the nine, but to return to the place where he had received the gifts of healing and, with the tenth—that is, the Samaritan—to give great thanks, he returned to Saint Emmerammus accompanied by almost the entire city.

“On that day, throughout the streets—indeed, throughout every part of the city of Regensburg—the Kyrie eleison resounded. The Christe eleison echoed. ‘Thanks be to God’ was gratefully spoken, now by some, now by others, and in this way the journey of faith was trodden by all.

“In the church there was such exultation among those praising God and comparing the eight years with the eight beatitudes of the eighth day that, through the exceedingly necessary good of confession and contrition for the faithful, the devil was forced to groan that he had suffered harm in many ways and to complain that he had incurred a great loss because of the gathering at the martyr’s shrine [Note: [Col. 1063D] another reading].

“What more is there to say? After the solemn visitation, the clergy, the choir of monks, and likewise the people of both sexes had paid vows to the nourishing Trinity with threefold prayers, permission was finally given to all to depart with a blessing and to return home with the rejoicing of a threefold miracle.”

Ammonicius.

“This threefold miracle which you have written was manifested in one man in the name of the Holy Trinity. It is, as it were, your own greeting to the approaching festival, for the solemnity of our most blessed patron, Saint Emmerammus, the martyr of Christ, is threefold.

“The passion-day natal feast of the blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, precedes it; then follows the very celebrated dedication of this church, happily endowed with the purple bones of the same witness, the most illustrious virgin Thecla [Note: [Col. 1063D] another reading]. That intervening festival, especially important to our people, powerfully holds its own middle place between the preceding and the following one [Note: [Col. 1063D] another reading], like a kind of royal dignity.

“Therefore it is no wonder that you try to turn your little work, wherever it may wander through the variety of its propositions, back toward the praise of the Holy Trinity. Now, since you have proposed a miracle concerning Saint Emmerammus marked by one and the same threefold sign, it follows that you should take up something enriched by numerical meaning which requires a third element, so that in your customary manner you may bring the conclusion to the honor of the Holy Trinity.”

Collectitius.

“Since a human being possesses the Trinity within himself, it is necessary that the creature be subject to the Creator, whose love must be preferred to nothing. Since all human beings together, pooling their vows into one, would scarcely suffice to render the tribute due to the supreme Lover, how much less I, a wretch, who until now have done nothing worthy of my order? Therefore, weighing deeply in my heart how much danger the neglect of that trinity within me—namely, understanding, memory, and will—both generates and bears, I scarcely at last commanded my laziness, for the remedy of evils [Note: [Col. 1063D] Another reading.], so that what curiosity had once gathered in childhood from useful matters, youthful verbosity might now simply bring forth. Thus, although I cannot serve by deeds, at least I may appear to serve by words the honor of the omnipotent and only Trinity. With this intention also, in accordance with your admonition, I shall undertake what I am about to write.

“Among the other scourges by which the grace of almighty God has deigned to visit the people of this, our native province, at one time many were suffering greatly from pain in their eyes [Col. 1064A]. When at last the plague had ceased for everyone, it suddenly attacked me with such force that, while my left eye was moderately painful, I was entirely deprived of the use of my right eye by excessive swelling. For a most severe pestilence had so occupied it that it appeared as though a fist had been set against it. Because of this, when I came by night to the church and prayed more privately beside the confession of blessed Emmeram, I rose after shortening my prayer; and because I was severely burdened by the pain, I sat there sadly in a corner. Then I began to turn various thoughts over within myself concerning what had happened to me. With humbled heart [Note: [Col. 1064D] Another reading.], I was compelled to say: ‘Lord, if you will, you can save me’ [Latin: *Domine, si vis, potes me salvare*; Note: [Col. 1064D] Matthew VIII.], and through the prayers of my patron—namely, your beloved martyr—you can easily drive away even this great evil.

“But I know myself to be less suitable for you, Wisdom of the supreme Father, to display in me the pitiable work of your mercies, since for many years it has occupied my mind to write your wonders at some time, to praise your omnipotence in them, and likewise to hand down in writing to posterity the words and deeds of the elect. If what I have desired, and still desire, pleases your goodness in this matter, I give thanks; but if you prefer to chastise me with blindness, I am ready—as one who owes you everything—to bear patiently whatever your judgment imposes. Having thought and spoken these things secretly, I did what the faith of Christ, through an inner inspiration, suggested that my humility should do: I moistened the tip of my thumb slightly with saliva, and, where I felt the greater pain, I impressed the sign of salvation three times [Col. 1064C]. Meanwhile, I meditated in my heart and nevertheless pronounced with my mouth that Gospel saying: ‘The Lord made clay from spittle and anointed my eyes; and I went and washed, and I saw’ [Latin: *Lutum fecit exsputo Dominus, et linivit oculos meos: et abii et lavi, et vidi*; Note: [Col. 1064D] John IX.], and I believed in God.

“At that very moment so sudden a change was wrought in me by the right hand of the Most High that, with incredible speed, the pains were driven from my head—indeed, the pernicious pestilence was removed from my entire body. Carefully considering this event within myself, I could scarcely wonder enough at who I had been and who I was. Then, wishing as though out of curiosity to satisfy myself concerning the sudden miracle, I felt the afflicted place with both hands; and I rejoiced to find there not even a trace of pain or swelling. Accordingly, I rose and hurried to the place where I had previously prayed, and there I gave thanks to God and to Saint Emmeram. [Col. 1064D] When I approached a candle and tried to read in a book that through age was nearly worn out, I proved that I had recovered clearer sight than I had possessed before.

“Now, lest anything seem lacking to this great solemnity, which pours out the nectar of joy in full measure for the benefit of our brothers, the following account of a miracle must furnish the feast abundantly, so that its concluding third part may faithfully serve what the holy Trinity accomplished in it. There was a certain cleric, born of noble lineage, who at a particular time, when necessity demanded—or rather charity commanded—was received for the sake of hospitality into a lodging adjoining the monastery of Saint Emmeram. When he began to fall ill, after a few days he was brought by the severity of his illness to such a state that his life was entirely despaired of. Then, in the middle of the night, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, he said: ‘If only someone would bring me water to refresh my soul from the fountain of Saint Emmeram, which is in the cloister of the brothers who serve God and him!’ One of those standing by, who at that time was serving him and wished quickly to fulfill this request [Note: [Col. 1065D] Another reading.], ran to the church and, as is customary in such circumstances, knocked rudely at the door. Immediately admitted by the keepers, and, because he was a familiar person, allowed to go to the fountain, he drew water without delay [Col. 1065B] and brought it with certainty to the man who had sent him.

“When the sick man had tasted a little of it, he was immediately restored completely by the improvement in his condition and said: ‘In the name of the Lord, I have drunk excellent wine instead of the water you brought. Blessed Emmeram received from the excellent Physician what he has just provided for me.’ The man who had brought the water replied: ‘I do not know whether the water has been changed into wine; this alone I know for certain: I drew the liquid from the well with the pump.’ The men and women who were present followed up his words, saying: ‘It is widely known that the force of the fever from which you suffer not only consumes the body’s strength, but also alters the taste of the palate and throat, so that you cannot taste properly.’ He held out to them the cup from which he had been drinking and said: ‘Drink, you too, and test whether I have been deceived or whether what I said is true.’ When they had drunk and truly perceived the taste of wine, they raised their voices in faith and said: ‘Thanks be to God, for in all our lives it has never happened to us to drink such good and noble wine.’

“That this great miracle was not contrived by a human being but was performed by supreme Truth on account of the martyr’s merit is attested by Bishop Engilmar, who still remains in this life. Once, while he was residing at Regensburg, he saw, read, and approved writings of my insignificance at Saint Emmeram. One day, standing beside the well or fountain by which he remembered that his forehead had once been restored to health, he called me and, taking the occasion from that same fountain, declared what I have written. Calling Christ as witness [Col. 1065D], he affirmed that this was true, and that he had learned the same great miracle not from another but in his own person, through an experiment both truthful and effective.”

Ammonicius.

“A faithful saying, worthy of all acceptance [Latin: *Fidelis sermo et omni acceptione dignus*; Note: [Col. 1065D] 1 Timothy I.], because the true vine, who is Christ [Note: [Col. 1066D] John XV.], in order to reveal the merits of his branches—that is, the apostles, martyrs, and other elect—makes, as it were, new wedding-feasts every day through these and similar miracles. Behold, the memory of the most blessed martyr Emmeram rightly supplied wine instead of water, together with health. By this life-giving deed it would undoubtedly be proved that he once labored excellently in the Lord’s vineyard [Col. 1066A] and bore abundant fruit in it. O what joy, as the report flies, is poured forth from such events among the children of the Church, when they hear that these things have been solemnly celebrated far and wide concerning their mother! For this reason, to enlarge your little work, bring with the greatest diligence into the Lord’s granary whatever reasonably occurs to your mind. Thus the things done by the holy Trinity in the fourfold region of the world will somehow also have a place in your account.”

Collectitius.

“Since you briefly noted the four regions of the world, whose distinguishing emblem is divided either into four times three or three times four, because of the most sweet memory of our patron, I am pleased to append here to the preceding three miracles one that is also the fourth. The intention is that unity should adhere to the Trinity in such a way that a credible quaternity, made firm by the equal length of its sides, should preserve throughout the faith of the four Gospels.

“There was a certain very poor man who, together with another equally needy person, was seeking holy places. He was not supported by a staff but leaned upon little stools, so that he crawled along the road more than he walked. When, around the hour of dinner, they reached a certain spring of clear water, the man with the little stools said to his companion on the journey: ‘Come, my friend, here we shall take our meal in the name of the Lord, and when we have been refreshed, we shall depart with thanksgiving.’ His companion agreeing and sitting down on the ground at the edge of the spring for the eating of bread, the little-stool man, drawing water from that abundant and pure mirror [Col. 1066C], invoked the Lord, known everywhere to the faithful, before bringing the drink to his mouth:

“‘Lord Jesus Christ, who are accustomed to hear the desire of the poor, glorify in me today the merits of your martyr Emmeram, since, by his charity and with your blessing, I now long to quench my thirst.’

“And behold, while he was drinking, before he had withdrawn his hand from his mouth, the One whose grace knows no slow delay loosed the restraints of all his limbs. Immediately leaping up and running here and there, he gave thanks to God and to the holy martyr Emmeram. Then the inhabitants, summoned by the novelty of the event, built a church there in honor of the martyr, in memory of so outstanding a miracle.

“I learned that this happened in the regions of Italy from the report of a certain brother who had been converted from the laity. While still a boy, he had been an exceedingly curious listener to such matters [Col. 1066D]. He confessed that, through confidence in and consolation from this benefit, he had been moved to abandon the brigandage he had cruelly practiced for many years, and likewise, at Saint Emmeram’s, to lay aside his wolfish rapacity, so that, from a wolf becoming a sheep, he might be pastured with Christ’s sheep in the Lord’s fold.”

Ammonicius.

“Since by dictating you have arranged, as best you could, the benefits of Christ, so that the memory of his saints might be propagated everywhere and embraced uniquely by all good people, the recent diminution of the goods of Saint Emmeram, together with the complaint uttered by some concerning it, seems to me reasonably to demand that something be inserted into this little work in lively diction. In this way those who seize ecclesiastical property may be admonished—if they wish to follow sound advice—to repent; and those who have been troubled or saddened by the wrongfulness of this affair may confidently expect to receive some consolation from the righteousness and mercy of the eternal King.”

Collectitius.

“Since all who abuse the wisdom of the saints will undoubtedly be punished either here or in the future, the immoderate murmuring must be restrained—whether it consists of people secretly voicing complaints or of those who openly and plainly say: ‘Saint Emmeram is now asleep, since he allows his goods, as though they were not his, to be taken from him and his own.’ To such people sensible and prudent men should suggest and say: ‘Behold, he who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps’ [Latin: *Ecce non dormitat qui custodit Israel*; Note: [Col. 1067D] Psalm CXX.].

“Moreover, we should add this ourselves: the goods of Saint Emmeram, which are truly good, cannot in any way be taken from him or diminished for his companions. As for those things called goods according to the world, however small they may be, we have heard, read, and seen that they have never been outside the care and protection of the supreme Shepherd and Guardian, nor outside the providence of his beloved martyr. From ancient times this has been declared not only miraculously but also powerfully by countless acts of virtue [Col. 1067C]. Of these I shall now endeavor to insert one great miracle, necessary for the present time and widely spread because of its magnitude among both nobles and commoners, thereby serving the benefit of readers and at the same time satisfying your requests.

“In the time of Henry the Pious, Augustus and illustrious emperor, when many things had been lost through negligence from the bishopric of Regensburg, and many goods from the abbey of Saint Emmeram had been ruined and dispersed because of a dispute between the bishop and the abbot, it happened that Lord Bruno, the emperor’s own brother, attempted under pretext of hereditary right to claim for himself the possession and estate commonly called Enterhof—that is, ‘the court and estate of poison.’ But according to those of deeper understanding, who investigate each matter more ingeniously, it may not improperly be called ‘the hope of the ether,’ that is, of heaven, in accordance with the way the Saxon language customarily renders things into German. For the Saxons are accustomed to call hope, in the sense of expectation, by a closely related word [Note: [Col. 1067D] In the manuscript, another reading.].

“Since he did not dare publicly to use force against ecclesiastical property contrary to the emperor’s edict, it finally came about by deliberate arrangement that at a place called Aetinga a hearing or judicial conference would be held concerning this matter. There, after all the judges or scabini who were in that county had been corrupted by money, and others from elsewhere had been hired for the same purpose, the craft and cunning of all the advocates were so confounded from heaven that, by common agreement, a certain judge named Otpolt—introduced or suborned by the opposing party—was unable and did not know how to judge anything that could injure the cause of Saint Emmeram or our own. At that time many people entrusted much to his loquacity.

“Accordingly, publicly marked by our defender as a liar and falsifier, he caused many to marvel, and to fear as well. Yet, lest the aforementioned Bishop Bruno appear to succumb to such disgraceful confusion together with his supporters, at his request a palatine assembly was held at Regensburg, as though the miracle that had occurred there might be annulled. But the matter had a very different outcome, when the entire council assembled there, willingly or unwillingly, obeyed the divine will.

“For in the judicial hall, with Duke Henry presiding together with the empress Cunigunda, his sister, and with men of consular rank or counts seated on the benches, as courtly custom required, throughout the entire court one could hear the voice of those supporting the bishop’s party against Saint Emmeram, while also saying that no one could resist Bruno, such a great and powerful person, and prevent the aforesaid estate from coming into his control that day by the judgment of all. His grandmother, named Judita, duchess of the Noric kingdom, had handed it over to Saint Emmeram for herself and her sons Hulduwic and Henry as a royal fisc, on the condition that if a bishop or any powerful person should usurp the same estate or withdraw it from the monks’ uses, it would immediately revert to the right of her heirs.

“The judges and nobles also placed this opinion first, affirming that the agreement concerning the gift had been violated by Gebehard, bishop of Freising [Imbripolitanus]. Then, with the prince’s consent, Bruno summoned from outside the court leading men endowed with great eloquence, as well as other judges and advocates versed in law, to support his cause. They were equipped or prepared outside with every kind of cunning and craft, so that they might, as he supposed, recite within the court arguments in defense of his party, paying no attention to what is written: ‘There is no counsel against the Lord, who knows the hearts of men’ [Latin: *Non est consilium contra Dominum, qui novit corda hominum*; Note: [Col. 1068D] Proverbs XXI.].

“When everyone had entered and they had reached the place and time at which the falsehood and malice of the forensic judgment had to be excused and the triumphal dignity of the palace, as it were, secured, not only was the man previously accused of falsehood convicted of being guilty of the same repudiation, but the mouths of all who favored the opposing party were so closed and changed by heavenly power that none of so many people skilled in cleverness could say either what he had resolved while deliberating with himself or what he had learned to say from others whispering it into his ear.

“Then the entire senate, which had gathered in great numbers, was moved by the evident miracle to praise Christ. Throughout the court a humble and truly praiseworthy cry of thanksgiving to God resounded [Col. 1069A], while from the other side a pleasing murmur exalting the praises of the most blessed martyr Emmeram echoed in the ears of the multitude. Among them, a certain famous count, a man distinguished in Christian religion, named Eberhard, is said to have declared: ‘Behold, the King of kings plainly destroys the rights of worldly laws. He who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble has done and does all things well, now and forever.’

“Then Lord Bruno was seized by immense fear; indeed, by the force of heavenly power he was so inwardly overcome that not only did he, humbled before princes and people, grow cold, sweat, and turn pale that day, but he also spent the following night sleepless within his household walls, at great risk to his life. On the next day, when the sun had already illuminated the world, he drove away through penitence and tears the darkness of the error by which he had been deceived [Col. 1069B]. With an offering he presented himself to blessed Emmeram, humbly confessing his offense to the brothers. Then, walking barefoot among the memorials of the saints, he underwent so arduous an exercise that he did not pass by any of all the altars that abound among us without placing a gift upon it with his own hand.

“Finally, before the altar of our renowned patron, he swore that he would never again do anything harmful to him or to his people, nor use any force against the church’s property; he also confirmed this before witnesses. The wine that he had promised to give at a banquet to the supporters of his party he gave to us out of charity, and he most earnestly commended his life to the brothers’ prayers.”

Ammonicius.

[Col. 1069C]

“I cannot sufficiently marvel at how great a hardness of heart there is in the aversion of mortals who see and hear such great miracles and others like them, so that they dare to take away the goods of the saints. The obstinacy of people today appears to my insignificance comparable to the Jews’ deep-rooted stupidity, which during Christ’s Passion did not allow them to believe in the Son of God, even when they saw the rocks split, the veil torn, and the sky darkened. Indeed, they saw the whole world in many ways subjected and serving the Stone whom they rejected and the King whom, through the judgment of their wicked tongue, they stubbornly not only renounced but also condemned to the most shameful death.”

Collectitius.

[Col. 1069D] “O Ammonici, there is no reason for you to marvel greatly at this endurance of earthly or transitory goods being dominated or taken away, since the Author himself of all goods, when he was tempted by the devil for our salvation, carried by him to an exceedingly high mountain, and likewise transferred by him to the pinnacle of the temple, finally endured patiently from that enemy’s members spittle, blows, scourges, and the other things belonging to the disgrace of the cross.

“You should also remember that verse which the Psalmist inserts in his writings for the consolation of those who are under affliction, saying: ‘My soul has waited for the word of the Lord; my soul has hoped in him’ [Latin: *Sustinuit anima mea in verbo Domini, speravit anima mea in ipso*; Note: [Col. 1069D] Psalm CXXIX.]. The Savior himself confirms this consolation in the Gospel, saying providently to the disciples: ‘In your patience you shall possess your souls’ [Latin: *In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras*; Note: [Col. 1069D] Luke XXI.].

“Do you suppose that the Lord does not take account of the deeds of mortals, when throughout nearly the whole world the goods of Christians have been proscribed? Far from it! Believe me: neither the person who gives or has given goods to the saints nor the person who has taken them away or will take them away will lack his reward. Judas has already unhappily received the reward of the Lord’s betrayal and will possess it still more unhappily forever. The thief, on the other hand, through the exchange of his confession, has already received his most welcome remedial reward and will possess it most happily forever.”

Ammonicius.

“I do not deny that I and those others have been fully satisfied both by the account of the great miracle and by the resolution of the murmured complaint. Indeed, I plainly confess this for the very reason that I know with certainty that the King of kings can in no way be changed, corrupted, or deceived: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay’ [Latin: *Mihi vindictam et ego retribuam*; Note: [Col. 1070D] Romans XII.].”

Collectitius.

“We must advance somewhat farther in this line of thought. For we who are called Christians and ought to be Christians must not only say with our mouths but also extend such a benefit to our neighbors in our hearts that whoever curses us or does us any evil may, so far as we are concerned, not be subjected to the curse. Rather, aided by the blessing and prayer of fraternal charity, may he revive from the death of sins and be restored by divine power to the path of salvation. For this reason, I am pleased to insert here one example from the life of the Fathers for those who do not disdain to read the writings of my insignificance, so that the essential good of patience may be demonstrated and, by contrast, the detestable evil of impatience condemned.” [Col. 1070C]

Ammonicius.

“We learned even as children by experience that it is very useful for someone to be summoned or converted to goodness through holy examples, or turned away from evil. Therefore we are ready and willing to hear—or, with profitable curiosity, to read—something of this kind.”

Collectitius.

“A certain brother in ancient times came to one of the Fathers, perhaps named Abraham, who was already renowned among the servants of God for the perfection of his virtues [Col. 1070D]. Among his other anxieties of temptation, this brother complained to him, saying: ‘The spirit of impatience and pride attacks me so fiercely that I cannot resist such a perverse plague in any way. If anyone does me an injury, I shall repay him in word or deed, because of our malicious and foolish fellowship.’

“The elder replied: ‘The Apostle commands the faithful—indeed, Christ through the Apostle: “If someone strikes you in the face, if someone devours you, if someone takes away your worldly substance, endure it patiently, for the sake of him who loved us” [Latin: *Si quis vos in faciem caedit, si quis vos devorat, si quis mundi substantiam tollit, patienter sufferte, propter eum qui dilexit nos*; Note: [Col. 1070D] 2 Corinthians XI.]. And again: “Be patient toward all, for patience produces testing, and testing produces hope, while hope does not disappoint” [Latin: *Patientes estote ad omnes, nam patientia parit probationem, probatio vero spem, spes autem non confundit*; Note: [Col. 1071D] Romans V.].’

“Then, when the brother insisted through his hardened heart that he could in no way follow the Apostle’s words through patience, the elder said: ‘We must pray most earnestly that the Lord may deign to remove this hardness of heart.’ When the elder had prayed, he said most humbly to the Lord, with the brother listening: ‘Lord, we are not in need of you. Behold, we human beings, unwilling to resist the fault of impatience, suppose that we can do everything in our own power without you.’

“At these words, by God’s gift, the brother was suddenly so changed and contrite that he not only made satisfaction before the elder through penitence, humbled by his unusual obstinacy of mind, but, after all the disturbance of his temptations had been calmed, departed a better man.”

Ammonicius.

[Col. 1071B]

“Thanks be to God, because, through heavenly medicine, the patience of the man of God remedied the impatience of the weak brother. Now, since you have mentioned the temptations of ancient times, it is fitting that you draw your agility from the sweetest inner chamber of charity, if in these times anyone from among the faithful serving the King of kings anywhere has encountered an equally powerful and grievous temptation.”

Collectitius.

“There is no doubt that the devil still possesses the same arts that he possessed in ancient times. Indeed, we must believe with absolute certainty that the merciful Jesus, defending his elect by resisting the deceptions of the ancient enemy, exercises his customary clemency toward his own until the end of the age. For this reason none of the faithful should doubt that the servants of God are now tempted by the devil in many ways, just as at the beginning, and that they are likewise, as then, always and everywhere defended by the Restorer of the human race amid the various storms of temptation. So that this may be recognized more clearly, O Ammonici, and so that the truth may be conveyed by the following narrative to others who do not despise such matters, listen.

“There is, as I believe, an elderly religious man still in this life, a convert from the laity, named Guntharius. Once, in the world, swollen with an abundance of possessions and vain because of the nobility of his lineage, he had been a son of pride [Col. 1071D]. But afterward, through God’s mercy, he became so humble a monk that I cannot and should not rightly compare any hooded monk of our time with him who has been converted from worldly vanity.

“He was first tested under Gothehard, abbot of Altach, in all patience and obedience, and began to desire to walk the path of a higher life. Therefore, having received permission from the father of the monastery, he undertook a solitary life. To carry it out with divine assistance, and to test himself with spiritual [Col. 1072A] caution and prepare his mind through exercises of virtue, he sought a certain mountain, which the Germanic language now calls Rancinga and which is situated almost one *rasta* from the aforesaid monastery.

“[Note: [Col. 1071D] ‘A mile,’ says Scriverius in his notes on the manuscript; nevertheless, I observe that this word had a different usage, since in Jerome’s time it meant a mile. Thus he comments on Joel: ‘The Latins call it a thousand paces, the Gauls leagues, the Persians parasangs, and the whole of Germany rastas.’ But the usage of the word or the measurement of distances has changed, since Bede asserts that two leagues, or three miles, make a rasta, and elsewhere: six leagues are three rastas. BASN.]

“Remaining there for nearly three years, he was content with meager food, the humblest clothing, and a small cell. When some people marveled at his arduous life, they came with gifts, visiting and honoring Christ—who for our sake became humble—in his servant. Then, fearing that the crowd and the little glory of the world might under the appearance of religion steal or diminish something of his true goods, he fled from there and withdrew into the wilderness called the Northern Forest, intending to fight a solitary battle there courageously against the devil.

“As soon as he had settled there, the servant of God consecrated his eremitical life to *ruchatica* [“rustic”?] or spiritual warfare [Col. 1072B] and endured many different, numerous, and severe temptations. Of these I shall now attempt to set down one that has come to the knowledge of my insignificance through a truthful report, for the benefit of readers; after a short interval, with his life continuing, I shall record another more severe.

“In winter, when the Noric land is covered beyond the usual extent by the immensity or density of the snow, something like an athletic trial befell the aforesaid servant of God—indeed, a true and venerable seasoning of tested patience. For when, because of the excessive snow, bread could not be brought to him from the monastery for nine continuous days according to custom, nor could any human being send anything there from elsewhere, and he himself, hindered by the recent novelty of his dwelling, had not yet labored there to produce anything from which he could obtain food, he suffered three days of hunger. On the fourth day, unwilling to tempt the Lord, he began to dig up and pull out wild herbs from the icy depth of snow, which had already grown higher than the height of an average man, and put them into a pot to be cooked.

“When they had been softened somewhat by fire and water that day, he postponed his meal until the fifth day. Then, awaiting the canonical hour of refreshment, he set before himself, for food, the pottage he had prepared the previous day and cooked again. But when he tasted it, he could not eat it. Rebuking himself, he said: ‘O Guntharius, your pride does not allow you to be refreshed by this humble food. Where now is the steaming or most delicate flour? Where now are boar’s shoulders, or bear’s and pork meat, seasoned with pepper at the cooks’ invention [Col. 1072D]? Where now are the peacocks that remain unspoiled after cooking, or the pheasant birds flavored with the enticing tastes of many kinds of seasoning? Where now is the tested wine brought to you daily from the storeroom, at your pleasure, until you were satisfied? Therefore, instead of the more delicate food and drink to which you were once wholly devoted amid the riches of the world, be content now with the breakfast of a poor man’s meal, in the name of Jesus Christ, the Redeemer of all, who, though he was rich [Col. 1073A], became poor for your sake, so that you might become a participant in his riches.’

“What more is there to say? Finally, on the sixth day, giving full thanks to God, who does not disdain to feed even the young ravens from the abundance of his goods, he received nourishment from the aforesaid wild herb, now cooked for the third time and thus scarcely softened, though necessary to the body, yet very disagreeable to it, together with beech leaves, which he laboriously gathered after scraping them free of snow. Thus, amid great turmoil and controversy among various thoughts, and the manifest assault of diabolical temptations, he awaited the consolation of divine mercy.

“Then, as commonly happens in disturbances of this kind, when waves of thoughts succeeded and drove one another from opposite sides, a certain thought gently crept in from the right and, as though coming from Christ’s side, faithfully declared to the man of God: ‘Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord’ [Latin: *Exspecta Dominum, viriliter age et confortetur cor tuum, et sustine Dominum*; Note: [Col. 1073D] Joshua II.].

“Opposite it—that is, from the left—the devil’s persuasion, through whose envy death entered the world, broke in and protested importunately, composing words and deceits of this kind: ‘Since it is written, “Do not seek higher things” [Latin: *Altiora ne quaesieris*; Note: [Col. 1073D] Ecclesiasticus III.], and since, being a frail human being, you sought the wilderness, you acted not only foolishly but also with great insolence in bringing yourself here, intending to offer blasphemy to your Christ, like a starving dog, and to die here most miserably without his support.’

“But in opposition, the good thought and cautious concern replied: ‘Since Christ, who is Lord of all, himself struck down the tempter devil with the spear of the Gospel word [Col. 1073C], saying, “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” [Latin: *Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo Dei*; Note: [Col. 1073D] Matthew IV.], let distrust not steal upon you, O poor man of the world, rich man in Christ. Rather, place your hope most firmly in him of whom the Psalmist sang: “The Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvation of his anointed” [Latin: *Dominus fortitudo plebis suae, et protector salvationum Christi sui est*; Note: [Col. 1073D] Psalm XXVII.].’

“Again, when the enemy of human salvation suggested something sinister and deceitfully insinuated that in such misery and labor the weakness of the flesh could not persist, the man of God replied: ‘If my Christ wishes me to live without eating, he can easily accomplish it, according to what is written: “No word is impossible with God” [Latin: *Non est impossibile apud Deum omne verbum*; Note: [Col. 1073D] Luke VII.]. And again: “All things are possible to one who believes” [Latin: *Omnia possibilia credenti*; Note: [Col. 1074D] Mark IX.]. But if he does not wish to do this, either he will mercifully provide me with food, according to what he himself says in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you; for your Father knows that you need all these things” [Latin: *Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et haec omnia adjicientur vobis; scit enim Pater vester quia his omnibus indigetis*; Note: [Col. 1074D] Luke XII.], or else, without murmuring, his will—which cannot be unjust—must be accepted with unblemished faith.’

“Divine mercy’s consolation followed this faith and exercise of faith. Through certain men it sent him enough bread [Col. 1074A]. They, walking with semicircular [or crescent-shaped] devices over the mountainous mass of snow, could scarcely reach the man of God by crawling on the tenth day. Then, giving great thanks to God, who did not abandon those who hope in him, Guntharius became better acquainted with God through the test of patience and, through the generosity of the Source of all good, became more useful thereafter to others as an example of humility and perseverance.

“Thus it happened that some clerics and monks, as well as faithful laymen, prompted by him and through him—or rather drawn by divine inspiration—began, under the fellowship of his prayers and labors, to serve the King of kings in the same wilderness, whose inhabitant he had chosen to be for the love of Christ. There, while many were setting the ascent of their hearts within the valley of tears and advancing daily from virtue to virtue [Note: [Col. 1074D] Psalm LXXXIII.], it happened that a certain priest born of the Saxon people, also called Tammo by his household, approached in the manner of newcomers and attempted, under the appearance of a praiseworthy residence, to join himself to the community of the man of God and his fellow soldiers.

“When the man of God, with the teacher Experience going before him in part, had presented him to the abbot of Altach, and he had promised obedience according to the rule of Saint Benedict, he was immediately, under the terms of the obedience he had promised to the abbot, returned—or entrusted under the strictest supervision—to the aforesaid elder, as the other hermits who remain in that place were accustomed then, and still are accustomed, to do. He therefore returned with him to the retreat of the wilderness.”

«While he, together with the other brothers, served the Most High in the deepest humility [Col. 1074C], and spent some time in the cell allotted to him according to the institutions of the Fathers, with humility accompanying him, he was suddenly so burdened, through the insidious onset of vainglory, by the mass of pride that he not only disparaged the venerable old man in secret mutterings, whispering into the ears of certain admonishers, but even dared openly to break out into slander against so great a man, saying: “What and who is Gunthar? A layman and an ignoramus, whose life is rightly despised.”
