The servants of God who happened to be present and had heard this replied: “As it seems to us, humility—the guardian of the virtues—has withdrawn far from your mind, and the monster of pride has plainly invaded you. It was pride that once arrogantly persuaded the sons of perverse confidence to build the Babylonian tower [Col. 1074D], and it has now suggested such abominations to you concerning a man of God. Without doubt, he first brought the banners of Christ’s cross into this wilderness, he who says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ [Note: [Col. 1074D] Luke IX]. This man is also one of great authority, who has now reached old age and extreme old age by obeying the divine commandments most faithfully.”

He answered them arrogantly: “His authority, too, is of no account to me, because he is entirely worthless. I shall remain apart in a special cell and serve Christ—who has granted us knowledge and ability—with a free mind, not under Gunthar’s authority.”

What more? After this priest had been separated for several days from those whom he had despised, the subverter showed him certain visions—or rather fantasies—administered by the tempter. His heart was so elevated by them that he would seek nothing with a humble and simple desire. Thus it happened that, in the dead of night on which Christians celebrate the feast of Saint Agnes, while he was giving some attention to prayer, he first heard a delightful voice and shortly afterward a mournful one, and saw a vision with his eyes.

At first, therefore, he heard a harmony, as though two choirs of men and women were singing from afar and, in alternating response, answering one another most beautifully. Gradually, as the song grew louder and the flashing light increased, they came toward him. Then the enemy of the human race, who, as the Apostle Paul testifies, “also transforms himself into an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 1075D] II Corinthians XIII], presented himself to him with such brilliance that he seemed to be anything rather than the devil.

When the priest had gazed at him for some time and marveled at his beauty, the apparition said to him: “Do you see that I am Christ? Why do you not adore me? Do not doubt it: I have come for this purpose, to tell you what you ought to do.”

But the priest, whom the devil’s illusions had already deceived, said: “If you are the son of Mary, behold, I adore you.” Falling down, he adored him, [Col. 1075C] completely forgetting the answer which, as he read in the *Life of the Fathers*, a most cautious old man had given concerning such a temptation.

For it is written there—as I now recall—that an old man was similarly tempted by the devil. But, because divine mercy surrounded and protected its servant, the tempter was soon exposed by a few words. For when the wicked one said perversely to the old man, who remained silent for a long time and was inwardly considering who the apparition might be, “I am Christ; why do you delay adoring me?”, he received this answer: “Whom have I adored from my infancy until now, if not Christ, the Son of the living God? If you were Christ, you would in no way ask me to render you this service, which I have always humbly offered, insofar as I have been able, to Christ the Lord, my true Lord.”

Then the enemy of the human race, struck and confounded by the old man’s firm faith, vanished, leaving there clear signs of his presence—that is, a stench.»

**Ammonicius.**

«O Collectitius, what you have written is full of horror, and this statement of yours is exceedingly harsh: if these things truly happened in this way, who, then, can escape the enemy’s snares?»

**Collectitius.**

«Your question, O Ammonicius, ought to answer this doubt, at once perverse and exceedingly dangerous. It ought to be answered by the voice that once came from heaven to Antony, who was lamenting the enemy’s snares stretched throughout the world and nevertheless weeping. It said: “Humility clinging to Christ will pass beyond all these snares.”

For the rest, believe me: if the humility of Christ had reigned in the brother mentioned above, he would never, having fallen into the devil’s pride, have adored him. This will become most evident in what follows.

After he had most wickedly adored him, the ancient enemy inflicted another wound upon him and said: “The Antichrist now reigns in Judaea, and Elijah and Enoch are preaching there. You too, together with them—who are to be killed by the Antichrist for confessing my name—will in the present year be crowned with martyrdom.

“But before you travel there, you must correct everything in the monasteries of this province that deserves correction, and preach the word of truth to many.” [Col. 1076B]

The priest, eager for novelties, began: “What sign will you give me by which I may become certain that I shall do what you have said?”

The deceiver replied: “You will be given not one sign for your certainty, but three. Today, before the third hour, you will perform one in Gunthar’s left eye, which he has almost lost because of illness; another in the brother who has been sick for many days and is blind, whose name is Remigius; and a third in the man called Razo, whom his enemies have blinded and made lame.

“Moreover, regard as a sign of certainty the sandals which you will soon find placed beneath a certain hollow tree. I command you to use them thereafter in celebrating the solemnities of the Mass.”

What more? After these things had been impressed upon the proud man by diabolical deceit, and after he had been shown, among the bushes planted around the dwelling in which he lived as a wanderer, a kind of ascent and descent together with other inexplicable phantasmal marvels, at the very twilight of dawn the priest mentioned above abandoned his own private cell and, under the vain hope of the devil’s promise, sought Lord Gunthar’s hut.

When the venerable hero saw him, he was astonished and amazed at his sudden arrival, since the priest had been separated from him under the rule of pride and had maliciously deprived him—like a man who did not know letters—of the assistance of his own learning. Wishing to say nothing, he remained silent.

Then the man who had arrived swollen with empty glory said to the reverend old man under the appearance of religion: “We do not fail to know that, according to the institutions of the Fathers, we ought not to leave our cell and come here unless summoned. But our arrival, prompted by humility and commanded by our Lord Jesus Christ, is very necessary for you and for the others.”

The old man, protected by the defense of the Spirit, said: “Where did you get this, or when did the Lord Christ give your fraternity new commands?”

He replied: “This night.”

The old man said: “What commands?”

The priest replied: “That I should correct and renew the regular observances in the monasteries of Noricum, preach the word of God widely to the peoples, and, after healing the illness of two brothers—namely, Razo and Remigius—restore their sight, and return the brightness of vision to your eye, which has been troubled by pain for many years.”

When the old man heard these words spoken through Tammo’s mouth, he confronted his boastfulness, saying: “Believe me, Gunthar would rather lack both eyes than see through the concession of the one who deceitfully promised you these things. Nothing is truer than that you have been surrounded by diabolical art and utterly deceived.”

The priest who had come added a frivolous statement to this judgment: “If I do not do what I have said before the third hour of this coming day, do not believe me.”

The man of God said: “The Truth in whom we believe will reveal to you and to all of us today that the father of lies has deceived your arrogance.”

Then the priest withdrew from the old man’s sight, persisting in the obstinacy of his bound mind. He took the blind brother with him into the church, as though he intended to pray for him so that he might receive his sight from the Lord. But although he prayed for a long time and the light he requested was not granted, he prolonged his vain attempt at empty glory almost until the sixth hour.

Then, surrounded on every side by horror and terror and thrown into confusion not without great shame, he hurried to Lord Gunthar. Falling on his face before him, he said to him with tears: “Unless your prayers, venerable Father, have greatly helped me, and the prayers of the other servants of God have snatched me from the pit of destruction, I know with complete certainty that, because my sins have caused it, I have ceased to be Christ’s servant. From now on, the one whom I adored as Lord of lords—alas, alas, miserable that I am!—will claim and possess me as his own servant, for I adored the minister of every wickedness in place of the Lord of lords.”

To this Lord Gunthar, girded with spiritual weapons, replied: “Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom Truth himself said, ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Note: [Col. 1077D] Matthew XVIII], denied Christ, the excellent Master, three times. But after the Lord looked upon him and he wept bitterly [Note: [Col. 1077D] Luke XXII], he received forgiveness from the one who alone knows how to sympathize with our weaknesses, according to his great and abundant mercies.

“Therefore, you ought not, because of your fall, give the devil complete joy by falling into despair. Rather, seek humbly the mercy of almighty God, whom no offenses of mortals can overcome.”

After the old man’s admonition, the priest remained shaken by grief over his recent fall. When he came near the hour of divine service and attempted to join the assembly of the brothers gathered there, and served with them for a while in the singing of psalms, the ancient enemy began to assail him fiercely and to trouble him openly, saying:

“What you read and sing—my writings are about me [Note: [Col. 1078D] Another reading]. Whether you wish it or not, from now on you will remain mine, because you have been wholly reduced under the power of my will. Do not be deceived or misled by Gunthar’s vain and false suggestion; no one will snatch you from my hand.”»

**Ammonicius.**

«Behold, once again it comes to mind—or rather, it now presses itself more tenaciously upon my mind—that what the excellent versifier wrote about this most wicked tempter, when mentioning the Lord’s temptation, reads as follows:»

> When with the Lord he seeks the mountain heights, and showed  
> All the riches of kingdoms throughout the world: “All these,” he said,  
> “You shall possess through my gift, if you adore me, prostrate.”  
> As perverse as he was, so perversely did he speak.

**Collectitius.**

«For the moment you ought to be silent, O Ammonicius, until you hear in a truthful narrative to what end so great a temptation came, and then join me in offering praises to God.

From that day onward, the priest mentioned above, weighed down by the burden of his dangers, although he devoted himself to the strictest penance, was in no way able to repel the new and ancient enemy, who continued to harass him exceedingly at every hour.

Thus it happened that Lord Gunthar summoned the man of good counsel, namely Ratmund, abbot of Altach; Ratmund, taking the bishop of Passau with him, came to conduct an inquiry concerning this matter.

When the bishop, speaking privately with the abbot and Lord Gunthar, heard of the priest’s fall and recognized that he had been deceived by diabolical illusion, he carefully considered how this great evil had occurred and said:

“Behold, what we read beforehand in the evangelical truth has happened in this brother. For the Lord says in his Gospel: ‘Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted’ [Note: [Col. 1078D] Matthew XXIII].

“Therefore provision must be made so that the destructive exaltation which, through diabolical persuasion, has brought the wretched man down may, by the medicinal humility of Christ, be wondrously healed, raised up into the strength of faith, and thus directed onto the way of eternal salvation.”

Then the bishop, on the authority of the sacred canons, ordered the fallen brother to cease from priestly office until he had made satisfaction and until a beneficial judgment had been determined.

What more? Afterward, while diabolical harassment greatly confounded this same monk and deterred him from the service of God through prolonged nocturnal disturbances and cries, word was sent everywhere to the Fathers and brothers that they should ask the most merciful Lord, by common prayer and by the singular and healing secret offering of the sacrifice of salvation, to forgive the fall of their sick brother.

When some had prayed kindly for him, and especially when Lord Gunthar had labored for him before the presence of the divine majesty—he who at every hour had extended the hand of consolation to the wavering and tottering man and had most certainly promised him that the gracious Jesus would have mercy on him—at last, after six months had passed, he who had been attacked by the most wicked assailant felt relief and received a remedy.

By this urgently needed nourishment, through divine mercy, the same brother was refreshed and renewed inwardly and outwardly. He is now completing his eighth year in the practice of the greatest humility, obedience, and abstinence, striving to draw near to the one from whom he had departed and gone astray through pride, who also says through the prophet:

“Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you. And if your sins are red like scarlet, they will be made white like snow” [Note: [Col. 1079D] Isaiah I].»

**Ammonicius.**

«O how great and how profound is the judgment of divine dispensation! For the sake of more provident caution, it permitted the brother about whom you have spoken to be afflicted by the most wicked enemy so severely that he would have fallen completely into despair, unless this humble old man, the servant of almighty God, Lord Gunthar, as we hope, had raised him through constant exhortation into the hope of recovering salvation and strengthened him with manifold examples of the saints drawn from the divine fountain!»

**Collectitius.**

«Because you interrupted the discourse of my humility by crying out in praise of God, I am grateful. But please allow me to bring to its conclusion what I began to narrate.

For this is surely the most wondrous thing of all such matters, which I myself heard with my own ears from the old man’s mouth and scarcely drew from him in a familiar conversation about sacred reading.

When the priest mentioned above, placed in the anguish of the greatest temptation, repeatedly ran to and from the old man and cried out in a plaintive voice, “I cannot stand; I cannot endure; pray for me, man of God,” the old man said:

“I trust in gracious Jesus that he will deliver you. Only be patient and steadfast, and do not doubt his almighty grace, with whom no word is impossible [Note: [Col. 1079D] Luke I].

“What you are now enduring is, in general, horrifying and fearful to human frailty throughout all the kingdoms of the earth. But because of this, the faithful must not despair of the Lord’s mercy, with which the earth is filled. For he who is able to raise up children of Abraham from stones [Note: [Col. 1079D] Matthew III] can also deliver you from your present temptation and make you worthy of his calling.”

The tempted man added: “Would that it might happen to me according to your word! But I greatly fear the danger of the temptation that has come upon me, miserable as I am, beyond human measure. For at the very hour of prayer, when I open my mouth in praise of God, the adversary seems to thrust his rapacity inward into my belly and onward to my heart, to take away the heart’s strength, to draw out my senses completely, and to make me alien to myself. Above all this, he boasts that he knows everything that I know, will, and am able to do.”

The old man replied: “Do not hesitate in faith concerning the divine aid that will be sent in due time from above. Although it is delayed for a time, it is not taken away. The devil has absolutely no power to harm or weary you unless he is permitted by God. God would never permit these things to happen unless he wished to humble you.

“Sometimes the Lover of humankind pretends not to know what we suffer, yet he frequently provides something that causes us wonder. Do not fail, brother, but, according to the Apostle, ‘stand firm in the faith, act courageously’ [Note: [Col. 1079D] I Corinthians XVI], and [Col. 1080A] ‘be strengthened’ [Note: [Col. 1079D] II Timothy II] in the name of the one who alone knows how to heal human frailty.

“As for your complaint that the devil boasted of knowing your will and ability: he himself—you know this well—is sufficient for you in this struggle; that is what drives the devil toward destruction.”

After these words Satan immediately appeared in the old man’s presence, disturbing the tempted brother and saying: “Gunthar has not only spoken a lie now, but often lies and tries to deceive you. Moreover, he carefully seeks out and loves a thin and delicate fur garment.”

As he attacked and insulted the old man, the old man feared that the devil’s insolence might cast the brother’s mind into despair of the good of salvation. He burst out and said:

“O enemy of God and of humankind, may your pride and your lie remain with you in eternal perdition. But we, who use not only sheep- and goatskins but also enjoy the simplicity and humility signified by them, will easily overcome you, the worst of wolves, through him who loved us, and by the power of Christ we trample upon your power.

“Believe Gunthar the sinner: that the brother whom, by permission of the living God—who came into this world, the Son of Man, to seek and save what had perished [Note: [Col. 1079D] Matthew X]—” [Col. 1080D] [Editorial note: “Here, in order that the sense may be complete and the suspended period, so to speak, concluded, something is missing—for example: ‘whom you now torment in every way with temptations will soon escape your snares.’ EDIT. PATROL.]

After these and similar struggles, and after many other arrows of his wickedness had been hurled uselessly against the tempted brother, the devil was so driven away by divine mercy that, departing amid disastrous cries and plaintive lamentations, he unwillingly made it plain how deeply he grieved and would continue to grieve that he, the conqueror of a human being, had been conquered by a human being.» [Col. 1080C]

**Ammonicius.**

«Thanks be to God, whose mercy is without number, and who, having already done all things well, also wondrously brought this about: that the man who had fallen most dangerously might, through mercy, be raised again into the state of faith. This confirms the testimony of the Psalmist, which he places in the one hundred and fourth psalm [Note: [Col. 1080D] Correct to Psalm 144], saying: “The Lord lifts up all who fall, and raises up all the needy.”

Therefore, dearest brother, as it seems to me, you have aptly taken the name Collectitius, both to veil the nakedness of the Teutonic language and to commend the collected usefulness of what you have said and will say. For this reason I also think it right that, fulfilling the designation you have assumed, you should proceed by enlarging the work you have begun, gathering what is useful as you continue, intending to dictate and take up these things in the name of the one who says:

“Whoever does not gather with me scatters, and whoever is not with me is against me” [Note: [Col. 1080D] Luke XI].

Thus you will serve him who is, and who was, and who is to come.»

**Collectitius.**

Amen. Would that I be found among those who gather with Christ, and not be condemned with those of whom it is written:

“Let them become like the grass of the housetops, which withers before it is plucked up; with which the reaper does not fill his hand, nor the one who gathers sheaves his bosom” [Note: [Col. 1081D] Psalm CXXVIII].

In this manner, too, may it come to pass. I shall again undertake to narrate what the Lord, with his inspiration going before and his assistance following after, will deign to give or bestow.

«In the same bishopric in which the events mentioned above had occurred, another remarkable event also took place, one which ought to be noteworthy to everyone and likewise to be avoided.

There was a certain sacristan of the church of Passau, whose name was said to be Wilibert. One day, as part of his customary diligence and the duty entrusted to him, he was going around and inspecting the various places of the church when, in a hidden spot, he came upon a certain cleric—his own disciple—who had fallen ruinously into a certain wicked deed [Col. 1081B] [read: pernicialiter, “perniciously.” E. P.].

The disciple, immediately fearing human beings more than God and his elect, begged his master not to tell anyone about the evil he had seen. But the master, horrified by the crime, said:

“I call upon the Lord and his saints as witnesses that, for fear of the salvation of my soul, I dare not conceal what you have done from my first superior, and then from the other spiritual men who may apply the remedy of repentance to your deadly wound and offer the exhortation of life-giving counsel.”

The disciple then added this empty talk: “Since you reject my request with your severity, there is no doubt that you wish to hand me over to punishment.”

The teacher replied: “God forbid that I should treat you wickedly or wish you to be handed over to punishment!”

After these words, master and disciple departed from one another, possessing very different intentions.

For the disciple turned what the master had said well into his own evil and deception. Darker than night, during the night he not only strangled his master but also hung him by his own cords and bands from the beams of the bedroom in which, as I suppose, he usually slept alone to preserve chastity.

Eager to hide this wicked deed in the crypts of malice, he left the door shut inside. Then, having separated the roof and ceiling by a fissure, the most wicked thief went out and replaced the tiles in such a way that, except for the man who had been hanged, it would remain entirely hidden from human eyes that anyone had entered.

Thus it happened that a very grave scandal spread throughout the entire Church, and it especially raged among the laity, who hurled public slanders and said:

“Behold the holiness of the clerics! Behold the merits of those who unworthily preside over the churches! Behold the priest who, on the very day on which he celebrated Mass twice, imitating Judas, hanged himself by a noose.”

At this, the bishop of Passau was greatly disturbed. Since it was not lawful for his own murderer to be buried, he ordered—by some authority of which I know nothing—that the body be burned in the fire, unless perhaps he commanded this so that animals would not be contaminated by touching or eating the corpse [Note: [Col. 1081D] Matthew XXVII], as people would judge, by an inhuman act; or, as I consider more likely, this happened by divine dispensation, as will become clear below.

For when the whole body had already been consumed by the flames, in the sight of everyone who was present the heart, as though unwilling to burn, emerged from the midst of the flames. At this, the people were astonished. As often as they threw the same heart into the fire to burn it, they saw it emerge unburned.

Finally, when those present held the heart in the fire with all their strength by means of poles and sticks, and still it did not seem to be consumed, the corpse-bearers withdrew, carrying away with them a great miracle.» [Col. 1082A]

**Ammonicius.**

«A very wondrous event, and one not only for us but also for all who read it! Therefore I urge your charity to draw from it more diligently something that may edify those who hear and likewise those who read these things.»

**Collectitius.**

«Although I am not worthy to speak and write such things, or various matters of this kind concerning the wondrous works of great men, I nevertheless consider that in this matter I must not withdraw from the obligation of obedience, nor from the seasoning of fraternal love, insofar as God may deign to grant it.

For I did not propose to describe these things in any other way than so that they might benefit the edification of the faithful.

Some think that the priest’s heart could not be consumed by fire because, while he lived, he had no conscience guilty of the fire of Gehenna, apart from the common frailty of the human race. Others say that the sinner was saved according to the Apostle, yet in such a way as though “through fire” [Note: [Col. 1081D] I Corinthians III].

But I would affirm that, if what I heard about him is true, and if what I once diligently read in the words of blessed Jerome is true, all sins are certainly erased by martyrdom.»

**Ammonicius.**

«Since you have mentioned martyrdom, and since some people think that those are martyrs who are punished by any kind of penalty and driven toward death, while others, on the contrary, assert that those perish utterly whom it happens to die suddenly in the manner of mortals—through strangulation, drowning in water, fire, or destruction of another kind—I would like to learn from your account what the true and certain kind of martyrdom is.»

**Collectitius.**

[Col. 1082D] «I think the testimonies of Sacred Scripture satisfy this inquiry. One of them is: “The righteous person, by whatever death he is overtaken, will be in refreshment” [Note: [Col. 1081D] Wisdom IV]. Another is: “It is not the punishment that makes a martyr, but the cause” [Note: [Col. 1082D] Saint Gregory, Book II, Indiction 10, Letter 37, from Cyprian, *On Twofold Martyrdom*, to Fortunatus].

From this you can also gather that the true and certain kind of martyrdom is for a person to be killed, not by himself but by others, on account of righteousness. For evangelical truth affirms this and cries into the ears of the faithful:

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” [Note: [Col. 1082D] Matthew V].»

**Ammonicius.**

[Col. 1083A] «You have responded forcefully enough, O Collectitius, to the solution of the question I rashly advanced. Nevertheless, you have served us well with the testimonies you produced, and not without gratitude.

Now, therefore, it is fitting that you explain how the aforementioned matter reached the point at which the person guilty of so great a deed came publicly to light.»

**Collectitius.**

«You will find me pliable as wax if what has been sown by a sinful man can proceed toward good fruit.

There was a certain culpable and criminal charge, concerning which the cleric who had committed the sacrilege and homicide mentioned above and had most wickedly concealed it was required to clear himself by oath. But he could not accomplish this at all.

For he had been unable to establish his innocence either by water or by fire before the clerics who had wished to swear with him concerning the alleged crime. Then the wretched man, entirely intent on rushing headlong into destruction, finally broke out into such madness of an obstinate mind that, under the most perilous presumption, he desired to avert the suspicion of the crime from himself by receiving the Lord’s Body.

The bishop wisely confronted this most dangerous risk. For, having learned through the more reliable report of the brothers that the cleric was not of such character that he ought to be permitted to undergo so great a judgment, he ordered him to be confined meanwhile under strict guard, while he considered with sound counsel what ought to be done with him.

Then, surrounded on every side by anguish, he brought out from the hiding place of his guilty conscience the crime he had badly concealed. He confessed that, out of fear of the accusation, he had strangled and also hanged the priest mentioned above, and that for this reason he had been unable to clear himself of the charge.

When the bishop heard this, he removed him from the clergy and deprived him of sacred orders. By pastoral authority he commanded him to practice penance with all his strength and thus withdraw himself from the devil’s snares.»

**Ammonicius.**

«First, we must all together give thanks and praise to God, because he did not permit the disgrace of the sacred order—which, bursting forth improperly from the death of the priest mentioned above, had cast no small shadows of ignorance or horror over the minds of some—to remain hidden for long beneath the disguise of falsehood.

Then, because of so great a crime, with grief piercing our inmost being, we are compelled to cry out in lamentation:

“Alas! What a great evil is wrought by hatred of righteousness! Under the devil’s persuasion it flared up so fiercely in the person mentioned above that the perverse disciple not only wickedly persecuted his teacher but also most evilly killed the priest. Worse and more grievous than all the malign schemes of the crafty one, through the hanging of the lifeless body he even deceitfully pretended that the man who had been hanged had, like Judas, been his own murderer!

“Behold, what Sacred Scripture reveals about the sins hidden away has come into the open:

‘I hid my sins as gold, and concealed my iniquity in my bosom’ [Note: [Col. 1083D] Job XXXI].

“Burdened with such anger and hatred, it is accustomed not only to grow dangerously thick with time but also to harden most perniciously, as sacred speech bears witness and says:

‘Long-standing anger produces hatred, but hatred kills.’

“If people could bodily see these poisons and from whom they are customarily poured out, they would undoubtedly recoil from them exceedingly.

“If this has happened to anyone, I would like your charity to insert the account here.»

**Collectitius.**

«Just as charity covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 1084D] I Peter IV; Proverbs X], so, conversely, anger and envy, forgetting love, maliciously consuming natural goodness, and accumulating dissensions and offenses through various occasions, drag hatred all the way to homicide.

No one should doubt that this most grievous evil of all is always secretly suggested by diabolical instigation among the other schemes of its arts. At times, however, the most wicked sower is accustomed to scatter discord and other evils so openly among human beings, and to such an extent, that many even perish through them unless someone, by God’s gift, turns back and comes to his senses and, flying by repentance from Satan’s snare, scarcely manages to withdraw himself from that tenacious glue.

There are many who, though not all, are aware of these things.

For the rest, so that I may satisfy your love, I shall present a fitting example concerning this matter in the present chapter, and shall humbly set down what follows by gathering it together.»
«There was a certain soldier of Pavia, whose name, pious faith hopes, is now written in heaven. As I learned from the report of Lord Ardericus, bishop of Vercelli [Col. 1084C], after he had, in the *manus* (“hand”; sic) of youth, according to human custom been detained and bound by worldly entanglements, and after he had for many years trained himself quite vigorously in military arms among his fellow soldiers and had already fathered sons, at last he came to himself and turned away from worldly vanity. He laid down the belt of worldly warfare at Saint Peter’s in that same city, and, desiring under the monastic habit to bear the marks of the cross, began to serve Christ, the King of kings.

His son, himself also a vigorous soldier, had been left at home as heir to his father’s property. Through a certain Aginulf, namely the blood brother of the palatine count, he was subjected to such great hostility and ambushes that he did not dare to leave the threshold of his own house [Col. 1084D]. For this reason, the same man who, after his military service, had become a monk—full of compassion and, with the permission of the abbot under whose direction he lived—sent a messenger to the aforementioned man, asking him to come to him out of reverence for Saint Peter.

Although Aginulf was somewhat fearful of the man’s religious standing, he nevertheless came not humbly but arrogantly. When the man of God had prostrated himself before him in the form of a cross and had been lifted up by him, not without astonishment, he said to him with the greatest humility:

“Good elder, what benefit is it to you to have my son’s blood shed, whom you so eagerly desire to have killed by your men? I am a poor servant of God’s servants and of yours. I beg you, by the mercy of our Lord Jesus, to withdraw your spirit from what you have begun, and deign to spare the wretched man who cannot resist your dignity.”

But Aginulf, raised up by the resentment of pride and provoked by the goads of the enemy, affirmed under oath that he wished no more willingly to preserve his own life than to accomplish, either by himself or through his men, the taking and extinguishing of the life of the man for whom the man of God was so earnestly pleading.

Then the humble monk, shedding tears, said—more for Aginulf than for his son:

“Ah, ah, Lord Aginulf, how willingly and necessarily I would wish, if I dared to ask the Lord concerning my sins, that you might see him whose bitterness, through the suggestion of homicide, has been so sweetened for you that you do not wish to be restrained from so great an evil either by God’s mercy [Col. 1085B] or by reverence for blessed Peter. I trust in the Lord that, if you saw him, you would change your mind without delay.”

After hearing these and similar words, the man who had come when summoned departed, carrying with him the burden of an obstinate mind.

But on the following night he perceived, through the prince of darkness and minister of death, how disastrous was the deed he had insolently resolved to undertake. During the first watch of the night, while Aginulf himself lay in bed with his wife, while the young female attendants were already lying in the chamber, and while they kept watch before the bedchamber doors, an Ethiopian suddenly appeared standing beside the little furnace. He rekindled the fire by blowing upon the logs that had been placed on the partly extinguished embers, and terribly struck those present with terror and astonishment [Col. 1085C]. He so weakened and shattered the strength of nearly everyone who saw these things that, although they wished to speak as necessity required and to sign themselves with the sign of the cross or the protection of faith, they could not do this effectively, nor could they even utter a sound. Instead, throughout the whole night they howled miserably and continually gnashed their teeth.

Then the master of the house, Aginulf himself, seeing the devil standing close by and, as it were, warming himself at the fire, was greatly afraid that this black, shaggy, dreadful guest, who had arrived unexpectedly and had been given power from above, might carry him away from within his domestic walls and make him, most unhappily, a household member with the sons of Gehenna.

What was he to do? What counsel could he take? Entangled in the greatest anxieties, he could not even utter what he had seen, dreadful as it was [Col. 1085D]. All the persons under his patronage trembled and grieved together; under threat of death, they all suffered one and the same punishment.

At last, when the inner man recalled the secret of the holy faith, he began to sing psalms inwardly. He had already learned the psalms—not bringing forth words by the service of his mouth that night, but turning the whole power of body and soul silently toward God until daylight.

When he had thus read through the Psalter, not with outward but with inward singing, from beginning to end, he scarcely deserved, by the clemency of him who takes away the sins of the world, to be freed with his household from the demonic infestation and to have the Christian understanding restored by great and powerful grace.

When the sun’s radiance was illuminating the earth, he heard from his wife’s words that a great danger of nocturnal terror had fallen upon those who remained there, and said:

“I do not fail to understand that this evil happened because of my sins, since so many people endured the hardship of seeing it together throughout the whole night. Therefore I know that today I must humbly return to the man of God whom yesterday I contemptuously scorned.”

Immediately he went where he had resolved to go. Having summoned the man of God’s son, he prostrated himself face down before him, did penance for having been so inexorable the previous day, and willingly offered him peace, although earlier, when asked, he had refused to grant it.

Because of this, the man of God rejoiced and gave magnificent thanks to the Almighty. Likewise, when all the people heard what had happened, they praised the one who softens human hardness.»

Ammonicius

[Col. 1086B]

«I admit that I am pleased by the judgment you set down in the preceding chapter, both to expose and to guard against the malice of diabolical suggestion. It can, as it seems to my insignificance, properly be called a living vision, because through it the enemy was prevented from killing his neighbor, and the living man was vigorously restored to the grace of common humanity together with the living man.

For the rest, concerning what occupies my mind, I give your Affection this advice: close the book of the present dialogue, lest perhaps it exceed the reasonable size of a single volume.»

Collectitius

«Although I do not consider it a great matter to be judged by a human being or by a human day, nevertheless it seems fitting to my own judgment that I should consent to your Affection. Proceeding in the steps of the narrative toward Gaul, I shall first touch upon something that happened there which may be useful to readers and hearers; then I shall move toward the end of the volume, so that there the ardor of dictating and writing may rest for a time or grow faint—just as the sun, turning daily toward its setting, ceases, by its absence, in some manner to burn or shine upon mortals as it pours the darkness of night upon the world.

“There was a certain nobleman living in the kingdom of Gaul. He regularly occupied himself, among other pursuits, with hunting, and one day prolonged the return home that he considered necessary until the twilight of day and night. At that point his dogs, as usual pursuing a little fox, entered a certain cave of the mountain.

The lord and master, grieving greatly over the loss of the dogs because they could neither be seen nor heard, sent some of his soldiers and companions to bring him fire with a light from the neighboring villages. He also sent ropes with long lines, by which they could descend into the mountain and enter its hollow.

When one of those who had been sent with the fire and ropes entered through the opening and wandered inside for a very long time, at last, scarcely finding his way back by following the sound of the trumpeter’s horn, which meanwhile was sounding outside, he returned to his lord and said:

“‘My lord, these mountains are entirely hollow, and their interiors appear like a deserted region. Unless you give me helpers of your own who will draw the ropes with their lines and will not shrink from supporting them over the rough rocks [Col. 1087A], and who, divided at fixed intervals, will wait for me with the most vigilant guard while preceding me with a light, you will never see the man you send again, and yet you will lose the dogs forever. For I do not hope to return from so many winding passages unless, God permitting, it should happen that my insignificance exchanges safety for continual contact with the ropes.’

“What more need be said? At that very moment the man entered again with those whose assistance he had requested. For some time he proceeded under the guidance of the ropes, enduring delays that were hateful, though, as the outcome proved, not fruitless.

When, carrying the light and making the arrangements absolutely necessary at that time, he came upon a certain dreadful and dark corner, he saw two men standing close by and horribly flogging stones with iron threshing instruments [Col. 1087B].

The investigator of the dogs, terrified by the unfamiliar sight and, in the manner of human weakness, almost collapsing to the ground, prepared to flee. But one of the threshers stopped him, saying:

“‘Do not flee or be afraid, for, through the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, you have been sent here so that I may tell you who I am and why I have stood here in such tribulation through the passage of so many years.’

“When the man who a little earlier had been fearful through weakness heard Christ’s name, he became strong and courageous. He asked, speaking in these words:

“‘Why are you here? Or why have you, such a great man, whom I knew in the world as a judge and court official and whom I recently saw in good health in your own home, been assigned to the bakery and hovel of this place [Col. 1087C]? I know the place where you lived in the world, and I often enjoyed a good banquet from your property and estate. I also knew the inheritance of your birth, and I commended your wife and children to my memory well enough. If you are that man whose person I believe I recognize clearly, tell me.’

“When he had spoken the name he had received in baptism and added the names of the estates in which he had lived, the one who had been questioned replied, as one taken from this life:

“‘I myself was once the man you have just said that I was. But because of my sins I was assigned here to the fire of purgation many years ago. What you see is not flesh but spirit. I am greatly amazed whether any of my people still live, or whether anyone can survive in the world, where everything grows old and fails.’

“The other man, who had been mentioned as his companion in conversation, replied:

“‘I too cannot help wondering why you have spoken of years, when today is the seventh day since your death and tomorrow will dawn as the eighth. Your wife is alive, and your sons remain in good health. I do not say this falsely but truthfully, because I saw them the day before yesterday.’

“But the dead man answered:

“‘The seven or eight days since the moment of my death do not seem to me to have passed until now. Rather, I believe that the painful danger of eighty years has raged against me. Therefore I ask you in the name of Jesus Christ, Savior of all, not to despise my misery [Col. 1088A], but to tell and announce as quickly as possible to my people, as my messenger, that, if they wish me to be redeemed, they must return the estate to its rightful heirs which I once took from weaker men through the perverse judgment of the *scabini* (judges).

“‘If they do not do this, I know for certain that I shall not escape these punishments until the day of judgment. But if my request is fulfilled, I hope that my bonds will not be held long, but that I shall immediately be released.

“‘And this will be the surest sign of my redemption for them and for you: if you return here and do not find me, then you may return safely to your own people. There is also another sign at hand, which will be shown to you without delay in the dogs. You will have them with you; they would have returned at first, unless, at the Lord’s command, they were remaining in this place.’

“At that very hour, when the dogs arrived, the man returned. Having appeased his lord by the presence of the dogs, he hurried to the widow and sons of the man to whom he had just spoken—the deceased—and told them what he had heard and seen in the hidden recesses of the mountain [Col. 1088B].

They immediately wept over the evil that had been done, did penance, and hastened to redeem the soul by almsgiving, returning the estate to those from whom the man who was suffering punishment had said he had taken it.

Then, at everyone’s request, the man returned to the mountain where he had received the promise of the hoped-for release. Through the fountain of immense mercy, and so that solitude and darkness would not be terror and horror to him, he entered with companions carrying a light. He found one man released according to the promised sign, and he not only saw but also envied the other, who had been left behind in punishment.

After leaving that place, he took care to proclaim among the faithful thanksgiving to God.»

Ammonicius

«What does it mean that iron threshing instruments were seen in the punishment of purgatory, and that stone scourges were displayed, and that of the two companions one was left there while the other was taken away through release? This question and wonder concerning such matters rightly awaits clear signs of release.»

Collectitius

«If you wished, O Ammonicius, to be content with what was written, read, and said long ago concerning such matters, which has been published about these things, I believe that the explanation blessed Gregory once set down in the book of the Dialogues, answering Peter’s questions and expounding such visions in plain speech, would be sufficient for you [Col. 1088D].

But since I cannot otherwise turn aside your persistence, I shall briefly say what seems to me concerning these things.

The threshing instruments were rightly and fittingly seen, according to what the prophet testifies when he says: “The strong man shall be afflicted there” [Note: [Col. 1087D] Zeph. I.].

That the sinners were seen laboring under the scourges of stones most clearly rebukes the hardness of human perversity. The Psalmist threatens it, saying: “Many are the scourges of the sinner” [Note: [Col. 1088D] Ps. XXXI.].

But that one was taken up through grace while the other was left in punishment through the justice of the judge agrees perfectly with the evangelical saying by which a threefold class of human beings is indicated, when the Lord says:

“‘There shall be two in one bed: one shall be taken and the other shall be left. There shall be two women grinding together: one shall be taken and the other shall be left. There shall be two in the field: one shall be taken and the other shall be left’” [Note: [Col. 1089D] Luke XVII].»

Ammonicius

«The solution of the threefold question pleases my understanding greatly, both because of its brevity and because of its usefulness» [Col. 1090A].

Collectitius

«And it pleases my humility to close the book in the name of the Holy Trinity, because the sun is already seeking its setting at the end of the short little day.»

Ammonicius

«Happily. Amen.»

[Col. 1089]

ARNOLD, COUNT OF VOHBURG, MONK AND DEAN OF EMMERAMM, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT: HOMILY ON THE EIGHT BEATITUDES AND SAINT EMMERAMM

(From P. R. Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, part II, p. 29, from a manuscript codex of the library of Emmeramm.)

[Col. 1089B] Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew: “At that time, when [he …] the mountain,” and so forth.

HOMILY ON THE SAME READING

Jesus Christ our Lord, Creator and Redeemer of the human race, invites all people without distinction of persons to the gift of his kindness, saying generally: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Hence the apostle Peter also says: “In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.”

This thirst must not be understood as belonging to the outward man but to the inward man, who surpasses the outward in such beauty and nobility, like a precious gem, that rightly, both in ourselves and in others, he is loved more than the outward man [Col. 1089C], because the outward man receives life from the inward man.

For just as the thirst of the outward man is extinguished by various kinds of liquid, so the thirst of the inward man is refreshed by the various sayings of the divine word. If any of us suffer from invisible dryness, let them come in faith to the Savior; let them drink by obeying his commandments; and by drinking—that is, by living well—let them live eternally.

The Lord himself shows by an evangelical utterance what reward the taste of this drink attains: “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The belly from which living waters go forth is the perceptive understanding of the soul. A river of living water flows from this belly when we humbly strive to minister to our neighbors the spiritual gift that we receive from God [Col. 1089D].

Therefore Solomon also says to each believer: “Drink water from your cistern and the streams of your well; let your springs flow out, and divide your waters in the streets. Keep them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share them with you.”

Each believer drinks water from his own cistern and the streams of his own well when he first pours the gift of spiritual understanding into himself, fulfilling through works those things which he understands himself to possess by divine favor. Then his springs flow outward when he externally supplies the grace of divine gifts to others. His waters are divided in the streets when, according to the quality and capacity of each listener, he makes the way of truth widely known through words and examples.

He then keeps them for himself alone, and strangers—that is, demons—do not share them, when he strives, as far as he can, to offer the drink of spiritual grace outwardly to others, not through the vice of malicious exaltation but through the spirit of true humility.

[Col. 1090C] The Lord Jesus offered this drink of salvation to his disciples so that they might drink and living waters might flow from their breast, when he deigned to make known to them the grace of the eight beatitudes. These open the free entrance of the heavenly kingdom to those running the course of life. For he says:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

The affliction of poverty is therefore an indifferent matter in this world, which will be judged blessed or not blessed in the future according to the character and choice of those who endure it. There are many whom the misery of poverty constrains, but the promise of heavenly reward will not enrich them, because they do not know how to hold the hardship of want in check with the bridle of patience. What they cannot obtain by possessing it, they desire inwardly through the evil of greed [Col. 1090D].

The poor in spirit are those who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, submit themselves to voluntary poverty. Therefore, according to the Savior’s judgment, that poverty is praiseworthy which either does not desire to possess or, if it possesses, leaves it by distributing it for God’s sake [Col. 1091A].

“Because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Although those who despise this world are still burdened by bodily weight, nevertheless, already through the grace of faith and hope, they will possess the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

“Blessed are the meek.”

The meek are the gentle, who strive to imitate the Lord of gentleness, who says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart.” Just as he grants to all people alike the gift of his freely given compassion, so the meek, as far as they can, strive to benefit everyone without the gall of bitterness.

“Because they shall possess the earth.”

Not the earth that appears to our visible eyes and produces the varied substance of trees and grasses, but the earth that the Psalmist spiritually contemplated as invisible, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

Therefore the land of the blessed is called eternal rest, because just as earth surpasses all the elements in solidity, so heavenly blessedness will remain solid and perpetual. Indeed, the meek possess the earth when, on the day of judgment, they rise bodily, so that, just as they have observed the divine commandments in body and soul, they may be crowned eternally with the double robe of body and soul [Col. 1091B].

“Blessed are those who mourn.”

Not through the ordinary course of worldly grief, but through the prompting of repentance for the loss of their own good works and those of others. There are four kinds of tears, distinguished in these ways. They are moist, salty and bitter, warm, and pure.

They are moist so that they may wash away the filth of sins and restore the fall of sacred baptism to the rank of worthy reconciliation. Hence Isaiah says: “Wash yourselves and be clean.” Just as visible water washes the impurity of the flesh, so the soul is spiritually washed by an abundance of tears [Col. 1091C].

They are salty and bitter because, through hope of pardon and fear of the fire of Gehenna, they restrain the mind of each believer from the guilt of carnal lust, as the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded”; and the Apostle says: “Without peace and chastity no one will see God.”

They are warm, to repel the cold of unbelief and kindle the fervor of charity. As a lamp is without oil, so faith is without the lamp of charity.

They are pure when someone, through the continual practice of weeping, has hoped for pardon for his sin and begins to weep no longer from fear of the fire of Gehenna but in expectation of eternal blessedness, singing daily with the Psalmist in prayer:

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion.”

Such people deserve the joys of divine consolation, as follows: “because they shall be comforted”—namely, with that consolation which will be given to the saints after this life in eternal rest.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.”

To hunger and thirst for righteousness is to hear the Lord’s commandments with a willing mind and to fulfill them with complete eagerness in one’s works.

In this passage righteousness is to be understood in two ways. Righteousness signifies the Lord Christ, of whom the apostle Paul says: “He was made our justification and sanctification.” We may also understand as righteousness the just commandments of God, which are believed to justify those who observe them.

Those who endure such hunger for righteousness rightly deserve to hear the words of blessed satiety: “because they shall be filled”—not with that fullness which hunger later follows, but with the fullness for which the Psalmist sighed while he still remained in the land:

“But I shall appear before your sight in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” [Col. 1092A].

“Blessed are the merciful.”

One is called merciful who feels compassion for the needs of others. Whoever desires to attain the good of true mercy must show mercy: first to himself, lest, by consenting to evil works, he commit something that will open for him the bosom of torment in the future; and then he must extend mercy to others according to his strength, having first learned it in himself through the performance of good works.

“Because they shall obtain mercy”—not that mercy which can increase or diminish according to the changing times [Col. 1092B], but that which will suffer no loss in the contemplation of God forever.

“Blessed are the pure in heart.”

That is a pure heart which will have been cleansed from every filth of vice and which is polluted neither by an evil conscience nor by the constant presence of wicked thoughts. Concerning this purity of heart the Psalmist prayed to the Lord, saying: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”

“Because they shall see God.”

For God is spirit. No one can behold God except through the spiritual eyes of a pure heart. He will be seen here through a special grace, but in the future face to face, as John says: “When he appears, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is.”

[Col. 1092C] “Blessed are the peacemakers.”

Peacemakers are those who strive to make peace, first within themselves, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires.” Then they summon the hearts of those who are at odds to concord with the grace of gentleness. Hence the Psalmist says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful.”

“Because they shall be called sons of God.”

Therefore the peacemakers will rightly be called sons of God, since they strive to imitate the Lord of peace. For the Son of God came into the world for this purpose: to reconcile the human race to God his Father and, through the grace of his passion, to open the door of the heavenly kingdom.

When the Savior was born, a multitude of angels sang peace to this world, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men” [Col. 1092D]. And the Savior himself, about to depart from the world, commended the same peace to his disciples, saying: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace.”

Brothers, in the name of peace he took care to leave nothing other than himself, as Paul says: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one.” Therefore we must love peace with complete devotion if we wish to have the God of peace reconciled to us.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness.”

Many endure persecutions—murderers, thieves, and adulterers—yet they will not be comforted by heavenly blessedness. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an adulterer, or a rapacious person.”

But those who suffer persecution [Col. 1093A] for Christ—“theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore the Lord also says elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” This is the freely given mercy of the Savior: to make his followers heirs of the heavenly kingdom, so that those who have despised temporal goods for his sake may possess everlasting joys without end.

These eight beatitudes, spoken by the Lord, pertain through a general calling to the election of the saints. They justify those who observe them and lead them to the joys of eternal happiness.

The ninth beatitude that follows is ascribed particularly to the holy apostles and martyrs, as follows:

“Blessed are you when they curse you and persecute you.”

The blessed apostles and martyrs therefore endured from those present not only prisons and chains, but also, from those absent, the insults of curses and slander [Col. 1093B]:

“and say every evil thing against you, lying.”

For the cunning of the persecutors fabricated lies against the preachers because it found no trace of wickedness in them. The Lord himself added the reason why they would presume to do such things: “because of me,” as if he were saying: “They bring all these things upon you not out of hatred for you, but because of my name.”

“Rejoice and exult,” since you will receive the grace of everlasting reward for the labor of your struggle.

“Because your reward is great in heaven.”

The reward of the saints is rightly called great, since the Lord will repay them a hundredfold in heaven according to the quality of their merits, and they will possess the joys of everlasting life in divine contemplation.

[Col. 1093C] The glorious martyr of Christ, Emmerammus, thirsted in his burning mind from childhood for a taste of these eight beatitudes, and also of the ninth—which, as we have said, applies only to martyrs—while living under the diligent care of teachers, until he had ascended the fork of the Pythagorean letter [Note: [Col. 1093C] That is, Y]. This letter, through branches swelling to the right and left, distinguishes the way of life from the way of death [Col. 1094A].

After ascending to the fork of this letter and looking with spiritual eyes to the right and left, he abandoned with complete eagerness the left-hand way, which the Lord’s voice calls broad and spacious, and seized the right-hand way, called narrow and constricted, with the fitting grace of determination, as the conduct of his life later proved.

Once he had resolved to live well, he progressed from virtue to virtue day and night. Through the united acclamation of all, he was raised to the primacy of episcopal dignity, having first ascended through the degrees of the clerical order according to the decrees of ecclesiastical law [Col. 1094B].

Since he excelled in the highest virtues, at the summit of his office he began to turn over in his mind the evangelical saying: “To whom more is entrusted, from him more is required.” He feared that he might return to Christ with the talent entrusted to him without profit. With a noble company of clergy he had destined himself to be a preacher to the nation of the Huns, which at that time, blinded to the light of truth, devotedly submitted to various forms of idol worship.

When, prevented from doing this by the divine will, he scattered the seeds of faith through Noricum for three years and converted many there to the light that is Christ, he departed to the Lord with the palm of a most wondrously consummated martyrdom. To him be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1094C] Arnold the abbot treats the *Logos* (“Word”), whom he had called *ōn* (“the One Who Is”).

Freely giving the Monad as a reward to the eight blessed ones.

APPENDIX TO ARNOLD

[Col. 1093]

I. DESCRIPTION OF THE TAXES, REVENUES, AND PRODUCE FROM THE ESTATES OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT EMMERAMM, IN THE TIME OF ABBOT BURCHARD (1031), WHEN ARNOLD WAS SERVING AS PROVOST

(From R. P. Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, III, col. 67.)

[Col. 1093D] In the year 1031 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fourteenth indiction, the present description of the property of the monastery of Saint Emmeramm was made under Abbot Burchard, at his command, with Arnold the provost investigating it, and with the approval of the community of brothers and the household [Col. 1094D]. This abbot was sent to us by Augia; may heavenly grace, preserving him, increase all that has been entrusted to him.

From this city: three and a half hides of Salic land. The servitors hold three hides; the steward holds twelve acres; the Salic serfs, fifteen acres; nine manses: each pays thirty denarii and nine loads of wood; 132 garden plots. In this city payments are made.

From Hartinga: three hides and twenty-two acres of Salic land. Senior Sicco holds two hides; junior Sicco holds one hide. The mounted man holds one hide. The Salic serfs hold twenty-six acres. There are six manses: they pay twenty-five jars of beer, and three others must give four piglets. Each gives a sheep worth a tremissis, two chickens, twelve eggs, and six denarii for scarlet dye. Three people make, twice a year, a linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide. One male and five female taxpayers.

From Skira: five and a half hides of Salic land, and the tithe from the village itself. Ten manses. Each pays annually a sheep worth a tremissis and six denarii for scarlet dye [Col. 1095B]. Of these, five owe twenty-five jars of beer each; the other five owe four piglets, one *mala* with two wheels [a vehicle; uncertain], and an oak wood. The steward holds one hide. Two foresters hold one hide and twenty-three acres. They owe seven woolen cloths, nine cubits long and four wide; five linen cloths, twelve cubits long and four wide. Two male and seven female taxpayers.

From Alpurc: seven hides of Salic land, less six acres. The steward holds one hide. Four manses owe the same tax as is paid at Eiterhof. One mill with a single wheel; two woolen cloths.

From Eiterhova: eight hides of Salic land. The steward holds four hides. The mounted men hold twenty-five hides. The Parscalci hold two hides. There are seventeen and a half manses; altogether, sixty and a half. They pay one sheep and one pig worth a tremissis, four piglets, two chickens, twelve eggs, two measures of hops, and twelve handfuls of rushes. Two manses make one woolen cloth seven cubits long and four wide.

The mounted men pay ten and seven pigs worth tremisses, one whole solidus and the other half a tremissis. Two make one shirt ten cubits long and four wide. Some of them give five cartloads of beer; seven ride and pay the aforesaid tax.

The Parscalci pay one sheep fewer than twenty, and fifty measures of oats. Six mills. From the mills and the woodland: nine hundred [units]. Four male and twenty-four female taxpayers. The servitors hold twelve hides without tax.

From Matinga: four hides of Salic land; four manses; two woolen cloths; the same tax as is paid at Eiterhof [Col. 1095D].

At Ascahc: eight vineyards. The vine-dressers hold eighteen acres.

At Rota: half a hide of vineyard.

At Heridios: the tithe of everything that is paid there. On the southern side of the Danube, in the woodland belonging to Ostoronhof, the tithe of everything that is paid from it.

At Vuimdibere: the tithe of everything paid from the forest and from the other things belonging to the use of that same mountain. At Reinanbach: two hides. From these are paid six measures of rye and nine measures of oats. Phrisginga pays five denarii and twenty coins.

At Inlaraspach: two hides. At Vodalprethisperga: five hides. At Rudilinga: three and a half hides. The steward holds one hide [Col. 1096A]. From half a hide, fifteen measures of rye are paid. At Hetinpach: one hide pays ten measures of oats, twenty coins, and a sheep worth five denarii; another hide pays sixty denarii.

At Tanna: one hide pays ten measures of oats and one measure of rye. Five manses. The manses each pay a sheep and a pig worth a tremissis, thirty jars of beer, three smaller measures of wheat, one woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide, and the tithe from the village itself. One mill with two wheels.

From Perga: three hides of Salic land and one mansus, with the same tax as is paid at Giginhova. One mill with two wheels; one-third of the tithe. The cleric holds one hide. Ten male taxpayers and nine female taxpayers [Col. 1096B]. Foresters, vine-dressers, and others: fifty acres and one [uncertain].

At Haganpuoch: three hides; from these one hundred coins are paid.

From Ufhusa: three hides of Salic land and the tithe. The cleric holds one hide; the steward holds one hide. Ten manses. Of these, one pays five jars of honey, another pays four measures. They pay a pig worth half a solidus, a sheep worth a tremissis, four piglets, three chickens, twelve eggs, and fifty-four denarii for scarlet dye. Two make one woolen cloth seven cubits long and four wide, and one linen cloth ten cubits long and four wide. The Salic serfs hold thirty acres. Five male taxpayers and thirty-nine female taxpayers.

From Hachalstat: six hides of Salic land, seven manses. The steward holds one hide and twelve acres, and the tithe from the village itself [Col. 1096C]. Each gives twenty-five jars of beer, a sheep worth a tremissis, two chickens, and twelve eggs. Two make one linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide; three make, twice a year, one woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide, and forty-two denarii for scarlet dye. Three female taxpayers. The forester and others hold thirty-three acres.

De Tuncilinga: six hides of salic land and a tithe. The steward has four hides, Richere two hides, Reginpato one hide, and Heizo one hide. Eight manses. Each pays twenty-five vessels of beer. Hungelt: one sheep worth a tremissis and two chickens, twelve eggs; together they make four woolen cloths, nine cubits long and four wide, and two six cubits long and four wide. Each pays five denarii for vermilion. Three mills, with five wheels. Ten pelt-workers. They themselves provide thirty piglets, each worth five denarii. Their women pay six denarii in winter. Foresters and others hold sixty acres. One male and nine female tenants.

De Erchanpiunt: three hides of salic land. The steward and others hold two hides. At Erilinga there are ten hides. Each pays twenty-five vessels of beer, a pig worth thirty denarii, a sheep worth a tremissis, one modius of wheat, and twelve denarii for the work of the wife. The Parschalci hold two hides, from which they pay two sheep, each worth a tremissis, ten modii of oats, and one parafredus.

De Pisinga: six hides of salic land and twenty-one acres; a tithe from two churches, from the estate itself, and from four other places. The priest has five acres and one hide. The steward has two hides and nine acres. Ten manses: each pays twenty-five vessels of beer, three modii of oats, twelve eggs, and two chickens; two make linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide; three make woolen cloth twice a year, nine cubits long and four wide; and six denarii for vermilion. Two mills with three wheels. The salic servants hold twenty-seven acres. Two female tenants.

De Sahsinperc: two hides of salic land and twenty-seven acres. Three cellarii pay three solidi. At Ruit, one hide of salic land and three acres.

De Tanna: seven hides of salic land, with a tithe from twelve churches. The steward has five and a half hides. The priest has two hides. The servants hold three hides. Ten manses. Each pays twenty-two vessels of beer, two chickens, twelve eggs, Hungelt, one sheep worth a tremissis, six and a half woolen cloths nine cubits long and four wide, five linen cloths twelve cubits long and four wide, and forty denarii for vermilion. Three mills with five wheels. Two censual hides provide twelve modii of malt, measured by heaped modii. Ten cellarii. Of these, four provide twenty vessels of beer. Two provide thirty denarii, and two others thirty denarii. Two are without census. Foresters and others hold three hides. One male and eleven female tenants.

De Sippinhowa: two hides of salic land, two manses. These provide twenty-five vessels of beer, two chickens, twelve eggs, and work as at Tanna.

De Niwnhusa: seven hides of salic land, ten manses. They pay a pig worth one solidus, three modii of wheat, thirty vessels of beer, three chickens, and twelve eggs; three make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide; two make linen cloth fifteen cubits long and four wide. At Vualda, two hides provide ten modii of oats, five modii of rye, and one modius of wheat. One hide likewise pays a pig worth a tremissis, twenty vessels of beer, and modii of wheat; from another, five modii of oats and three modii of wheat.

At Habachstal they provide seven modii of oats, a pig worth a tremissis, and one heaped modius. At Wiuari, two hides provide four solidi and twenty denarii. At Orto, one hide provides three vessels of honey. Likewise, from one farm, one vessel of *menis* [uncertain]. The priest has one hide. A tithe from eight villages and from the estate itself. One mill. The steward has two hides. The servants have one and a half hides. The salic servants have one hide. Two female tenants.

De Engildiesdorf: five hides and twenty-four acres of salic land; a tithe from the estate itself. The steward has one hide. Four manses: each pays thirty vessels of beer, raises four piglets, a sheep worth a tremissis, two modii of wheat flour, and four chickens. Three make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide. Two make linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide. Three female tenants and one male. At N., half a hide. From this, three vessels of honey are paid; from the other part of the hide, five modii of oats and one modius of rye are given. At Husterin, half a hide. The same census is paid from it. At Starcholvesdorf, two hides provide forty vessels of beer and four piglets; in one year they make woolen cloth nine cubits long and nine wide, and in the next year linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide.

De Inninga: six hides of salic land, eight and a half manses. Each pays two pigs, worth one tremissis, four piglets, raises two chickens, twelve eggs, and provides linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide, half of which is worked from his own materials. Three make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide. Two mills with four wheels. The steward has three hides; the salic servants hold fifteen acres. The servants hold two hides. At Keltingon, four and a half hides of salic land. At Emheringun, two hides. From these they provide two pigs, worth two tremisses, twenty modii of oats, and two modii of rye.

At Plioningun, two hides. From these are given two sheep worth five tremisses, two cartloads of beer, and two modii of wheat flour.

At Gisalpachc, one hide pays ten modii of oats, one modius of rye, and a pig worth a tremissis. At Stenihart, one hide pays ten modii of oats, one modius of rye, and a sheep worth five denarii. Twelve female tenants and three males.

De Ruiti: four hides of salic land. At Chesinpurun, five hides of salic land; tithes from the estate itself and from twenty hides. The Parschalci hold seventy-six and a half hides. Skafuuar has one hide. The herald has one hide. Two foresters have one hide. Fishermen hold three hides. Eleven horsemen: each provides a full souma of wine, six modii of oats, one modius of rye, and one heaped modius. Sixteen of the Parschalci each provide one souma of wine, six modii of oats, one modius of rye, one smaller modius of wheat, half a measure of flax, as much honey as can be held in the hand, a sheep worth a tremissis, a vessel full of beans, another of flax, and parafredi. In addition, fifty men each provide one souma of wine, six modii of oats, and a sheep worth a tremissis.

At Vuollincheim, half a hide provides one cartload of salt, three modii of oats, and a sheep worth five denarii. At Sechtaha, one hide provides one smaller modius of rye and one smaller modius of wheat. At Puoch, one hide provides one modius of rye. At Chesinpurun, the salic servants hold half a hide and twenty-eight and a half manses. Each pays six modii of oats, one souma of wine, two chickens, twelve eggs, two modii of the heaped measure, and a sheep worth a tremissis. Two make one woolen cloth seven cubits long and three wide, and linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide. Six mills with twelve wheels. One complete ford, and another half a ford elsewhere. The steward has one and a half hides. Two mills with four wheels. The priest has one hide; Adalhart has two hides; Razi has half a hide. He pays a sheep worth four scoti and four modii of oats. The salic servants hold one hide and two acres. The number of modii of oats here is reckoned at thirty-four. From all that is provided from Ruit, ninety-four soumae of wine are collected. At Hal, four frying pans; at Chizeinisloch, two hides.

De Lutranpach: ten hides of salic land, with a tithe from five churches. The priest has one hide, the steward two hides, and eighteen manses. Each pays two pigs worth tremisses, five chickens, and twelve eggs. Each makes from his own resources linen cloth six cubits long and four wide, and three [of them] make woolen cloth twice a year, nine cubits long and four wide. Four Hungeli. Three censual hides, from which fourteen vessels of honey are paid. The servants hold four hides. Two cells with three hides of salic land. Six cellarii. Each gives three modii of rye and fifteen vessels of beer; four give forty vessels of beer and eight modii of rye. The salic servants hold four hides and eight acres. From an outer farm, half a hide, from which thirty denarii are paid; from another farm, ten denarii.

At Racholveshouun, three hides, from which thirty vessels of beer, ten modii of rye, five modii of wheat, and sixty denarii are paid. At Sigonhouun, five modii of oats and three modii of rye. Six mills with ten wheels. Six male tenants: each pays thirty denarii; five pay fifty denarii. Thirty-six women: each gives ten denarii. Twelve salic women give sixty denarii. Thirty-two pigs and sixteen sheep remain.

De Pheringa: three hides of salic land, with a tithe from the estate itself and from three villages. The priest has two hides and three acres. Eight manses. Each raises four piglets and gives two chickens, twelve eggs, a sheep worth a tremissis, and eighteen denarii for vermilion. They pay one Hungelt and make four linen cloths, ten cubits long and three wide; woolen cloth six cubits long and four wide. Of the three, one is paid in the length of six cubits and width of four. The steward has half a hide. The salic servants hold thirty-three acres. Ten female tenants pay one hundred denarii.

De Hartheim: four hides of salic land, five manses. Each pays a sheep worth a tremissis, and pigs of equal value, raises four piglets, and pays six denarii for vermilion, two chickens, and twelve eggs; three make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide; three make linen cloth ten cubits long and four wide. The salic servants hold thirty acres. Two male tenants and eleven female tenants pay ten denarii and four solidi.

De Perchusa: six hides of salic land, with a tithe from the estate itself and from twenty churches. The priest has one hide; the steward has seven hides. Ten manses. Each pays twenty vessels of beer, one sheep worth a tremissis, one modius of wheat, three piglets, two chickens, and twelve eggs. Two make two woolen cloths seven cubits long and four wide. Two make linen cloth ten cubits long and four wide.

At Scafasholi, four hides. Each pays twenty-five vessels of beer and a sheep worth a tremissis. Five mills with five wheels. One Hungelt. At Fihohus, four hides. Each pays fifteen vessels of beer. At Suinesdorf, one hide, paying twenty vessels of beer. At Gundolvingun, thirty modii of oats, five larger modii of wheat, and eighty denarii are paid from four hides. Richperat has three; Sindolt, one hide; Suithart, one hide; the salic servants, three hides. Twenty-seven male and sixty-seven female tenants.

De Husa: four hides of salic land, four manses. Each gives a pig worth two tremisses, a sheep worth a tremissis, four chickens, twelve eggs, and a vessel of vermilion. Two make linen cloth ten cubits long and four wide. The steward has one hide; the foresters and other salic servants have one hide. One tavern. One mill.

De Truthmuotehem: seven hides of salic land, with a tithe from the estate itself. The priest has one hide. The steward has two hides and two acres. Ten manses: each pays a pig worth one solidus, thirty vessels of beer, one modius of wheat, and two chickens. Three make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide. Two make linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide. One tavern, one mill. The servants and the remaining salic servants hold four and a half hides. Forty male and female tenants. At Gundolvesheim, five acres provide tremisses.

De Lucilinaha: eight hides of salic land, with a tithe from the estate itself. The priest has one hide; the steward, five hides. Twelve manses. Each pays thirty vessels of beer, a pig worth a tremissis, one modius of rye, and two chickens. Three make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide. At Iterpurgarivit, five hides provide twenty vessels of beer and a pig worth a tremissis.

At Tanloch, one hide pays twenty vessels of beer, a pig worth a tremissis, and one modius of rye. Five men from Lucilinaha pay a pig worth five denarii and ten vessels of beer. At Vuilda, four hides provide a pig worth five denarii and ten vessels of beer; one hide pays twenty vessels of beer and a sheep worth a tremissis. Four mills. The salic servants hold two hides. Adalpero has one hide. At Vuilda, one of Ruita provides vessels of honey. At Tiorohartasperga, half a hide.

De Emihova: three hides of salic land. The steward has twelve acres. Four manses. From two hides are paid two pigs worth half a solidus each and forty vessels of beer; from another two hides, two sheep worth tremisses and forty vessels of beer; one hide pays twenty vessels of beer.
