Two make woolen cloth nine cubits long and four wide. Two mills with four wheels. The salic servants hold twenty acres and one hide.

De Isiniga: four hides of salic land and nine acres. A tithe from the estate itself. The steward has two hides and five acres. Junior Perman has thirteen acres and his brother Liuzi ten acres. Vine-growers hold forty-eight acres. The salic servants hold fifteen acres. Seven manses. Each pays thirty vessels of beer, a sheep worth a tremissis, two chickens, and twelve eggs; three make woolen cloth twice a year, nine cubits long and four wide; two make linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide. Five male and eleven female tenants. At Skiosdorf, the hides provide four solidi.

De Stabilwis: five hides and nine acres of salic land, with a tithe from the estate itself and another place. The steward has two acres; four salic servants hold forty acres. Nine manses. Three make woolen cloth twice a year, nine cubits long and four wide. Two make linen cloth twelve cubits long and four wide.

De Orilinhem: fourteen hides. Each pays fifteen vessels of beer, a pig worth fifteen denarii, one modius of wheat, and one modius of oats; together they provide fifteen solidi for labor. The steward has eleven acres and one hide. The forester has six acres. At Alaraspach, one mill with three wheels. The miller has fifteen acres.

At Hegilinhoven there are five hides and seven acres. From these are given forty denarii and sixteen modii of oats. At Horsconoshovan there are fifteen hides. From these fifteen solidi in iron are paid. At Etmatesdorf there are seven farms. From each, forty-five denarii are given. At Suainicandorf there are two hides. They pay seventy denarii. At Priempere there are thirteen hides. Each pays thirty vessels and thirty denarii. At Mantalha, eight hides. From these, payments are made. At Duomantala, six farms provide nine solidi. At Fiscpac, two hides, from which forty denarii are given. At Sunit, three vessels of honey are given. At Puolonsuant, there are nine farms. From seven, one talent is paid, and the cidalarius holds one. At Erilinpach, there are four farms. From these, four solidi are given. At Furdona, ten farms. From these, ten solidi are paid. At Proualasdorf, three farms. Four solidi are given from them. At Urpach, three farms. From these, three solidi are given. At Hwilinan, two farms. From these, forty denarii are given. From Maganaspach, twelve solidi. From Abbatiswinidun, four solidi and ten denarii. From Harda, one talent and ten denarii.

At the monastery gate: one hide of salic land, which the minister holds as a benefice; one tithe from the principal estate and from sixteen others. Four small estates, two granted as benefices and two censual, from which fifty-eight denarii are returned. A censual household, reckoned by heads—that is, twelve men and fifteen women—belonging to the aforesaid gate, must annually pay from the towns and suburbs, as well as from the small estates and the farms lying outside them, three pounds and six solidi in denarii.

The following places render service in full: from the estate at Egilisprunna, a church with the tithe of that place and of thirteen others. Four and a half hides of salic land. The salic servants hold twelve acres. Eight mansores, each of whom returns seventeen vessels of beer, one sheep worth a tremissis, and one and a half modii of flour; in alternate years he returns Hungelt. They plow three days a week and work three days a week; one boat. Their women provide three lodiles, while two provide one camisile. Two mills. One house.

From Cheringozashova, eighty denarii. From Talahova, seventy denarii, seventeen vessels of beer, one sheep worth a tremissis, seven modii of oats, four cartloads of firewood, one chicken, five eggs, and one fattened pig. They work in [lacuna], likewise in autumn; they plow three days a week, weed, mow, bring in one cartload, cut hay, and bring it in.

From Scerhanhova, forty vessels of beer; they plow eighteen acres per year. From Frianvelt, thirty modii of beer and two of rye. Each year they plow six acres. From Marchunashusa, they return twelve masses to be made. From Entihova, eleven denarii.

The priest has one hide. The steward has one hide and eight acres. One equitarius has one hide and one tithe. He rides wherever he is ordered.

From Dechtapeta, a church with the tithe of only one place. Five hides of salic land. The salic servants hold twenty-seven acres and one vineyard with a vine-grower. At Roccashova, two hides, from which twenty vessels of beer and thirty denarii are returned, together with one modius of wheat. Two mills.

At Gebrihinga, a church with the tithe of that place and of four other places. Twenty-three hides of salic land and two acres. The salic servants hold twelve [acres]. Six day-work tenants (*jurnales mansores*), each of whom owes seventeen vessels of beer, one sheep worth a tremissis, and one and a half modii of flour; in alternate years he returns one boat as Hungelt. They plow two acres a week and work four days a week. Their women, in groups of three, provide one *ludilo* [a textile term; uncertain]; two provide one small shirt (*camisile*). They return two cups of vermilion.

At Tegandorf, nine censual hides, which together return five cartloads of beer, twenty-two and a half modii of flour, and six solidi in denarii. At Essislidorf, half a hide; from it they pay forty denarii and two modii. From Sinzinga, sixty denarii. From Altasvelt, fifty denarii. At Matinga, a church with the tithe of that place; four censual hides, which together return three cartloads of beer and forty denarii. Two mills.

These are the benefices of Poppo at Geltolvinge, with which he was enfeoffed by Saint Emmeram, together with Ulric, his son. At Geltolvinge, four courts; at Maurlinge, one court; at Lintach, a forest and a court. At Harthusen, two courts; at Wolferchoven, two courts; at Rudelinge, one and a half courts.

These, however, are held by others who received benefices from him: at Hakhelstat, one hide; at Aitterhoven, two hides and a third of the tithe; at Rudelinge, half a hide; at Chessawe, two hides; at Much, near Ronige, one hide; at Niderspach, two hides; at Swinsbach, two courts; at Gailspach, one court and one hide.

### Burchard, abbot of Saint Emmeram, makes an agreement with the people of Ruit

In the name of the Lord. Let it be known to the faithful, not to the unfaithful, how the abbot Burchard, of blessed memory, among the other measures he undertook or arranged for the benefit of the property of Blessed Emmeram and of those serving him, with the consent of the entire community of brothers and with the participation of his advocate, the most excellent count Kadalhob, made this concise agreement with the people of Ruit.

Of the household belonging to Ruit—that is, the manses, or the hiltiscalci—freed from the fiscal salt tax, increased in part by the amount they had previously paid each year, they were to pay from each hide one souma of wine, drawn from no other source than their own produce. This wine—whether the aforesaid servants bought it here or went to Pauzona to buy it—was to be of such quality that, at Skafward’s discretion, under oath, it would be entirely approved and then stored in the cellar.

They declared this increase of the census on the condition that, as colonists or cultivators, they should not be transferred elsewhere, but should be permitted, together with their descendants, to live, remain, and serve in these places and lands known to belong to the aforesaid estate under the name of Ruite. The salic servants were also to make salt vessels and other necessities, receiving clothing and provisions from the aforesaid estate granted to them.

The witnesses of this agreement—many of them summoned according to Bavarian custom by the ears—whose names are written below, were: Williham, Aceli, Adalbreht, Pabo, Arnolt, Haitfolc, Ledunc, Engilhere, Heizo, another Heizo, Rutpreth, and Engelhere.

### Otto, bishop of Regensburg, remits to the monastery of Saint Emmeram ten talents which his predecessor Gebehard had customarily exacted from the abbot each year on the feast of Saint Emmeram

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Otto, bishop of Regensburg by the grace of God. We wish it to be known to all lovers of truth, present and future, and especially to our successors, how, out of love for God and for our salvation, and for the remedy of the soul of our predecessor Gebehard, of pious memory, we desired to relieve the service which that predecessor had imprudently caused the abbot of that place to pay him each year on the feast of Saint Emmeram—twenty talents—and which he left, transferred to our own time, as though it were owed by customary law.

We therefore gave, at the request of Abbot Eberhard, half of that amount, namely ten talents, decreeing that each of our successors should either dine there in the customary manner while celebrating the public Mass at the monastery on the birthday of the aforesaid martyr of Christ, or, if he could not attend the feast, should receive ten talents of silver in commemoration of his lawful station. Let him know without doubt that if he should attempt to add anything to this sum, fixed by us in a salutary decision, he will store up for himself the greatest wrath on the day of wrath.

The witnesses of this act are the religious clerics Peruuart, Sigbreht, Cumpo, Hartuic, Sigihart, Sigepolt, Cumpo, and Odalrih. These laymen of the people are also witnesses: Count Heinricus, his brother Pabo, Udalrih of Praeginza, Roh, Aribo, Adalhoh, Mahtin, Prun, and Cotescalk.

### Heinrich, duke of Austria, grants to the monastery of Saint Emmeram a certain right formerly held by Wernher of Winchelsaezze by benefice

Heinrich, duke of Austria by the grace of God, sends greetings in Christ to all Christian faithful, both of the present age and of the future.

Since the petition of Christ’s servants is to be granted for God’s sake and in God, we make known to the judgment of all good men that, at the petition of our beloved abbot Adelbert, we have granted and transferred to the church of Saint Emmeram our right which Wernher of Winchelsaezze appears to have held from us by benefice. The grant is made on the condition that the aforesaid abbot and all his successors may hold and possess it peacefully and without injury from us, from our son Liupold, and from all our successors, for the use of the brothers serving God there.

So that our action might be more firmly impressed upon the memory of all, future as well as present, we ordered this charter to be written concerning it and the attending witnesses to be recorded: Count Liutolf, Count Sifrid, the steward WVerinhard, Udalricus, Albero of Burkartesdorf, Heinrich of Mistelbach, and Albero of Kunringen. Their total is as follows: from Ufhusen, one solidus; from Skure, two solidi; from Egilsbrunne, two solidi; from Lanne, two solidi; from Bisingen, one solidus; from Bentelingen, one solidus; from Gebrichingen, one solidus; from Ysiningen, one solidus—making twelve solidi annually.

## II. The Annals of Saint Emmeram of Regensburg

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores I, p. 91.)*

### Notice

The greater Regensburg annals were first printed by Mabillon from the manuscript of Saint Emmeram *(Analecta*, vol. IV). We now owe a much better and most carefully prepared copy of the same authentic manuscript to the scholarly labors of the distinguished Bernhard Docen, custodian of the royal Munich library and a most deserving associate in our undertaking. Attached to a letter which he sent to the directors of the Society in November 1823 was a description of the manuscript, from which we report what is relevant here.

The manuscript is numbered E. 79 among the manuscripts of Saint Emmeram. It was written at the beginning of the ninth century—or, more accurately, in the fourth year of our lord Louis, in the tenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May—as the learned man reasonably infers from the final words of the erased sentence on the first page. It contains a work on computation, an astronomical calendar, nineteen-year cycles for the years 779 and 873, and, beginning with folio 80 and extending over the final six leaves, these annals, written by one and the same hand.

The same hand added the numbers 824 and 849; another hand continued the sequence from the year 850 to 941, without adding any notes, so that the entire work of the annals appears to have been written in the year 823. Since this is so, and since the words lacking meaning under the year 805 reveal not the author but an incompetent scribe, I accept the opinion of the distinguished Docen, who holds that these entries were copied from a somewhat older manuscript—which I suppose to have contained the nineteen-year cycles of the abbey of Saint Emmeram. The same is suggested by the plan of the work, by the many years without notes, and by a similar work preceding it in the same manuscript. Some annotations agree with the Salzburg annals.

Andreas Felix Oefelius published the lesser Annals of Saint Emmeram in volume I of his *Scriptores rerum Boicarum*, p. 46, from a parchment manuscript brought to the Munich library by Hartmann Schedel. Together with Bede’s book *On the Reckoning of Time*, it contains nineteen-year cycles from the birth of Christ to the year 1063. According to Oefelius, the annotations are due to two scribes, whose hands he distinguished by upright and slanting letters. We, however, have thought that not two but several men added notes, however brief, over the course of the centuries, and that some passages were copied less accurately by Oefelius. We therefore sent a letter on the matter to our Docen, but regret that his inquiries have so far failed to reach the manuscript.

Andreas of Regensburg may perhaps have used it in his chronicle of the bishops of Regensburg. Although his reckoning of the years generally does not agree at all with our annals, he nevertheless says, in assigning the beginning of Saint Wolfgang’s episcopate to the year 962: “or, as it is read in a sufficiently authoritative chronicle.” He also names Gaubald as the first bishop of Regensburg, although the more correct form is Gausbald or Gauzbald, since he is also called Gauzebald in the Metz annals under the year 743.

## The Year of Our Lord 1031. Aribo, Archbishop of Mainz

### Historical Notice

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis I, p. 134.)*

Aribo, from the family of the counts of the Summuntarians—of Hohenwart—was archbishop of Mainz from 1021 to 1031. He presided over the Council of Mainz in 1023 and over those of Seligenstadt in 1024 and 1026. Besides letters to Abbot Berno, cited by Trithemius in chapter 309, he wrote a Commentary on the Gradual Psalms, which Sigebert mentions in chapter 140. More about this Aribo may be found in Georg Christian Joannis’s notes on book V of Nicolaus Serarius, volume I of the *Rerum Moguntiacarum*, p. 463 and following.

[Column 1109]

> **Privilege apparatus, retained at its source clauses.** At **Cols. 1117B–C**, *a fluvio Tiberis* means “from the River Tiber,” while the parenthetical *flumine Tiberino* is “the Tiberine river.” At **1118A**, *monasterium Sanctae Agnetis* is “the monastery of Saint Agnes,” while *Aguntii* is the variant place/name form. At **1118B**, *positum infra fluvium* means “situated below the river,” against *constitutum inter flumen Tiberis*, “established between the River Tiber [and …].”

> At **1118D**, *pergentem* (“proceeding”) is paired with *pergit* (“proceeds”), and *revolventem* (“turning back”) with *revolvit se* (“turns itself back”). At **1119A**, the alternative Greater Lake boundary forms are retained as alternate boundary readings rather than silently made into one route. At **1119D–1120B**, *atque* means “and”; the corrupt expanded inheritance reading *haeredem ita ut episcopus qui per ipsam in jam* is preserved as a defective alternative; *castaldatu* is the variant form of “castaldaticum/office of the castaldus”; and *mandatariis* means “agents/mandataries.”

> At **1119D**, *regione Transtiberim* means “the Transtiberine district.” At **1120C–D**, *in loco qui Maliana dicitur* and *in praedicto loco qui vocatur Malliana* mean respectively “in the place called Maliana” and “in the aforesaid place called Malliana”; *cum turre et oratorio infra eamdem curtem cum* means “with a tower and an oratory within the same court/estate, with …” and remains an incomplete alternative reading. At **1121B**, *alia vero vobis vestrisque* means “but the other [things] to you and yours” in the Trastevere ordination clause. The full alternative boundary readings at **1121C–D** remain source readings with their respective territorial clauses, rather than a generalized statement that the passage is corrupt.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1032. EBALUS, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Column 1109]

### HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IX, p. 64.)

[Column 1109A] Ebalus, count of Roucy, originally a layman, had married Beatrice of Hainaut, daughter of Count Rainerius and of Harwidis, sister of Robert, king of the Franks. The *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book III, chapter 25, relates his election as follows:

“After Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, had died, Azelinus—that is, Bishop Adalbero of Laon—hailed a certain layman named Ebalus, formerly his secretary and privy to his cunning; and he obtained from the king, through his flatteries, that the man should be appointed. He was truly a man of no discipline, knowing nothing of letters except a few arguments of syllogisms, by which he was accustomed to mock even uneducated and simple people. Under the appearance of learning, however, he had long before been reaching toward the summit of so great an honor, and was accumulating his hope through much money, which he had shamefully amassed by usury. Azelinus had sought this very thing long before, and was now laboring especially so that through him he might exercise his cunning more freely.”

[Column 1109B] Against this testimony, however, he has Fulbert of Chartres, who plainly contradicts it. In letter 38 to his fellow bishop Guido, Fulbert shows that nothing was to be feared from Ebalus’s ordination as archbishop of Reims:

“If he is, as is said, a Christian from infancy, sound in judgment, instructed in the sacred Scriptures, sober, chaste, a lover of peace and charity, disturbed by no crime and by no mark of disgrace, and finally elected by the clergy and people of his city—for great men, he says, Ambrose of Milan and Germanus of Auxerre and several others, because they existed in such a condition while still in lay dress, suddenly became holy prelates for us—”

Moreover, when, because of certain losses [Column 1110B] inflicted upon the Church of Reims by Odo, count of Champagne, Ebalus, becoming more faint-hearted, was considering withdrawing from office, Fulbert urged him not to abandon the care of the Lord’s flock:

“I have heard,” he says, “that you are so afflicted by grief that you wish to abandon the care of the Lord’s flock; and I rebuke this sharply but amicably, bearing witness that, if you do this, you have not been a shepherd.”

Finally, you will find in the same author another letter bearing even more splendid testimony, which begins: “To Ebalus, the glorious father and archbishop, worthy of glory and honor”; and ends:

“Farewell forever,

O angel of great counsel, with Christ as your adviser.”

Ebalus was seated in 1022, according to the *Chronicle of Centula*; but we have shown, in the case of his predecessor Arnulf, that the beginning of his pontificate must be assigned to the year 1021. In 1026 he restored to the monastery of Mouzon the church of Douzy, which it had possessed from ancient times. In 1027 he crowned Henry I king, while his father Robert was still alive, on Pentecost. In 1032 he arranged for the restoration of the monastery of Épernay. According to the Reims Necrology, he died on 11 May; according to the *Chronicle of Mouzon*, in 1033 his body lay buried beside the steps of the choir toward the gallery, beneath a stone bearing only his name: “Ebalus, archbishop.” He is said to have given his canons the church of Bethana Court for his anniversary.

[Column 1111]

## CHARTER OF EBALUS, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, FOR THE MONASTERY OF MOUZON

(Year 1024)

(*Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, vol. II, p. 7.)

[Column 1111B] In the name of the supreme and undivided Trinity. I, EBALUS, by the favor of heavenly grace, although unworthy, chief bishop of the holy Church of Reims,

wish it to be known to all religious men, clergy, and faithful laypeople that the venerable abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Mouzon, named Boso, came into the presence of our lowliness and humbly requested that I restore, for the love of God, because of the poverty of the place, and for the remedy of my soul and those of my predecessors, the church situated in the village called Douzy. This church had anciently been subject to the church entrusted to him by God’s will, but had for some time been withdrawn through the negligence and carelessness of his predecessors, so that it might supplement the food of the brothers serving there under the rule of Saint Benedict.

Moved by compassion for the poverty of the place, I granted his humble petition [Column 1111C] and, in the presence of several faithful standing by, returned the church to the aforesaid place, just as I had already determined by vow. By the authority of almighty God, of holy Mary his mother, and of all the saints, and by the decree of our pontifical authority, I forbid anyone among our successors to withdraw this same church in any way from the aforesaid place or to inflict prejudice upon it. And so that this donation may remain firm and unshaken through the course of succeeding times, quiet and free from all contradiction by wicked men, we have confirmed it with our own hand and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of our faithful.

The sign of Ebalus, chief bishop of Reims. The sign of Bishop Adalbero. The sign of Hugh, archdeacon. The sign of Hardwin, archdeacon. The sign of Alulf [Column 1112C], archdeacon.

[Column 1111]

## LETTER OF THE CLERGY OF NOYON AND TOURNAI TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF REIMS, CONCERNING THE ELECTION OF A BISHOP

(Year 1030)

(*Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, II, 48.)

[Column 1111D] To the lord Ebalus, most glorious archbishop of Reims, and to the other bishops of the metropolitan diocese—namely, Adalbero, bishop of Laon; Rotger, of Châlons; Gerard, of Cambrai; Varinus, of Beauvais; Wido, of Senlis; Fulco, of Amiens; Drogon, of Thérouanne—the clergy and people of the Church of Noyon [Column 1112D] and Tournai, specially devoted to this holy see, send greetings.

Since, according to canonical institution, no Church deprived of pastoral governance may lawfully seek the appointment of a prelate except through the authority of the metropolitan and diocesan bishops, we, compelled by necessity, approach the excellence of your holiness, most blessed fathers, and direct our eyes, as it were, toward the mountains of God. Through them, with God’s favor, we trust that help will come to us.

For you are rightly called lofty mountains: by the dignity of your summit you surpass the height of the cedars of Lebanon. In you the dwelling of the living God, divinely established, is recognized. Made nearer to heaven, you are nearer to the true sun, who is called and is the Father of lights, from whom the source of all light proceeds. Enlightened by his power, you illuminate even those below through their participation in the light conveyed to them, and, by the heavenly dew flowing down from above, you make the lowly into those who follow after you.

Therefore, fleeing more confidently beneath the shadow of your summit, we ask to be protected by your defense, so that, compassionating us in a fatherly manner because of the long lament of our grief [Column 1113B], you may offer us the help of consolation and not delay bringing the hope of the joy we have begun to its fulfillment.

We grieve and, wailing, are exhausted by tears, being utterly desolate at the death of our most devout father, namely Bishop Hardwin, whom—alas!—the common fate of human existence suddenly snatched away from us. Yet we have begun to be consoled in our tribulation by the compassion of the most serene King Robert. Through his immeasurable piety, at the petition of the whole Church, we asked for a ruler: namely, Lord Hugh, provost of our Church of Tournai and archdeacon of Cambrai. By common vote we elect him as shepherd, request him as ruler, and proclaim him as bishop.

We therefore choose him as one whom apostolic and canonical authority requires to be Catholic in faith, prudent by nature, [Column 1114A] teachable, patient, temperate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, humble, affable, merciful, learned, instructed in the law of God, cautious in understanding the Scriptures, practiced in ecclesiastical doctrines, and, according to the path of Scripture, orthodox tradition, and the canons, decrees, and constitutions of the apostolic see, one who understands ecclesiastical rules with sound judgment and teaches and preserves them with sound speech.

He embraces the faithful word that accords with doctrine, corrects with modesty those who resist it, and is strong in resisting and reproving those who oppose sound doctrine. He is hospitable and modest, manages his own household well, is not a recent convert, and has a good reputation [Column 1114B]. In each degree, according to ecclesiastical tradition, he ministers for every good work and gives an answer to everyone who asks for an account.

Since he is endowed most fully with these and other virtues, we earnestly ask that, as soon as possible, you consecrate him bishop for us by your blessing, so that, with God as author, the people who have long lacked episcopal governance may, under so great a pontiff, be turned to the shepherd and bishop of their souls and be able to serve their Lord. For, as Scripture bears witness, the integrity of those who preside is the salvation of their subjects; and where obedience is safe, there the form of doctrine is sound. Since, however, we cannot all be present either by horseback or on foot, we unanimously give our assent to this document.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1033. POPE JOHN XIX

[Column 1113]

### HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Ciaconius, *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 288.)

[Column 1113C] John XIX was a Roman, from the counts of Tusculum—who are also called the counts of Segni—the son of Gregory and full brother of Benedict VIII, his predecessor. This occurred as an exceedingly rare example, once previously in Stephen II and his successor Paul, who were brothers, and again now in John and Benedict VIII; no other such case is found to have occurred.

John was bishop of Porto under the emperors Henry and Conrad the Younger, the Augusti. He sat for eight years, nine months, and nine days. Guido and Theoderic, ancient authorities, report that he had been a monk of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Saint Anastasia at Rome. He was created pope on the day before the Kalends of March, having been substituted by the faction of the Tusculan counts [Column 1114C].

Platina calls this John XXI, because he wrongly includes the fictitious female pope John in the number of pontiffs, as well as John XVIII, who usurped the papal see against Gregory V, the legitimate pontiff. Nevertheless, in his own charters, of which many copies survive today, he calls himself XIX.

When the illness from which Emperor Henry had been bedridden grew worse, and since he had no sons, he advised that Conrad, duke of Franconia, be chosen as his successor. He declared his wife Cunigund a virgin; and he himself died a virgin on 13 July 1024, leaving among men the greatest reputation for his purity [Column 1115A]. His memory is commemorated among the blessed on 14 July.

Emperor Conrad II was crowned at Rome, in the Vatican basilica, on Easter Day, 26 March, by Pope John XIX, in the year 1027. He terrified the Romans who were harassing Pope John with threats and also threatened them with destruction unless they ceased troubling the pontiff.

Basil the Younger Augustus died at Constantinople around the Kalends of October.

Emperor Constantine X Augustus ruled alone for two years and eleven months.

In the year 1028, Guido of Arezzo, a man highly skilled in the art of music, is said to have published the new system of bending the voice, which is observed to this day, by assigning letters and syllables to the movements of the fingers of the left hand [Column 1115B]. He also composed other works, which Trithemius mentions.

Emperor Constantine X Augustus died around the Kalends of September in the year 1029.

Emperor Romanus IV Argyrus Augustus ruled for five years and six months.

Under John XIX, in the year of our Lord 1030, the third congregation of Saint Benedict, called Vallombrosa, had its origin. In that year its first assembly was held, at which its author and founder, Blessed John Gualbert, a Florentine and most holy man, was made general abbot.

While still young, as he was seeking to avenge the murder of his brother with a large armed force [Column 1115C], he happened by chance to encounter his enemy in the town of Miniatis. Terrified by fear, the man immediately became a suppliant to John and, falling at his knees [Column 1116A], asked pardon through the grace of Christ. When John allowed him to depart unharmed, he immediately entered the nearest church. The Crucified One, whose image he was praying before, was then clearly seen by him and by all who were present to incline his head and thank John for his deed.

Struck with amazement by this prodigy, John abandoned everything, chose the monastic life, and withdrew to the place called Vallombrosa, beside the Apennine. There he instituted discipline under the rule of Saint Benedict, with a garment of Venetian color. Alexander II and Gregory VII confirmed this institution.

He died in the year of our Lord 1074, in the monastery of Passignano, on 12 July, renowned for miracles, and was buried there. True report says that Gregory VII declared him among the saints; Celestine III likewise confirmed this with certainty. His successors, excellent men [Column 1116B], promoted the institution. This is transmitted in the chronicles of the monk Bernard and of Saint Antoninus.

In the year 1031, Blessed Dominic, a performer of wondrous deeds and founder of many monasteries, died at Sora, already nearly eighty years old, and was buried in the monastery that later received its name from him. Peter Damian calls him “the armored one” (*Loricatus*), because he used a cuirass of harsh material worn beneath his garment to mortify the flesh.

Three councils were held during John’s pontificate: the council of Gerbicum and the council of Frankfurt in 1024, and the council of Auburium in 1030.

John, whose life is greatly praised, died in the eighth year, ninth month, and tenth day of his pontificate, on 8 November 1032, and was buried at Saint Peter’s. The see was vacant for two days. The authorities are Glaber Radulfus and Leo of Marsica in the *History of Cassino*.

[Column 1115]

### DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

(Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 357.)

The bulls of John XIX were written by the hand of John Sergius, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church (1, 10, 18); John Roger, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church (1, 10, 18) (2); John George, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church (1, 10, 18) (4, 5, 9, 19); and John John, cardinal and chancellor, acting in place of Peter the deacon (7). Compare the bull in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, V, 1110.

Issued through the hand of Benedict, bishop of Porto, acting in place of Peregrine, archbishop of Cologne, librarian of the Holy Apostolic See (4).

Issued through the hand of Boso, bishop of the Church of Tivoli and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See (4, 5, 7).

Issued through the hand of Peter, bishop of the Church of Palestrina and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See (6).

## LETTERS AND CHARTERS OF POPE JOHN XIX

### I. Privilege of Pope John XIX for the Church of Porto

(Year 1025)

[Marini, *Diplomatic Papyri*, I, 70.]

[Column 1115D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, Benedict, bishop of the holy Church of Porto, and to his successors forever.

Since what the faithful reasonably request must always be granted, it is fitting that in granting privileges we extend our benevolence [Column 1116D] and generosity. And because, hindered by secular affairs, we are very far from the summit of perfection, we chiefly trust that we shall earn pardon and obtain grace from almighty God if we provide defense and our protection to those who hold to the standard of righteousness and excel in evangelical conduct.

Therefore, because your devotion has humbly asked our sublimity to grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the aforesaid bishopric with its appurtenances, yielding to your prayers, by the tenor of this decree we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the aforesaid episcopate, namely the Church of Porto, which appears to be situated outside the aforesaid city [Column 1117A] of Porto, bearing the name of Saint Hippolytus, with the vineyards and gardens surrounding the same church; likewise one enclosure, an enclosure of a vineyard, and one vineyard in its entirety situated at Cardeto; and at Finilia, two enclosures with their vineyards and the lands within them.

All these are situated on the greater island, as well as the church of Saint Mary, a small one, and likewise the church of Saint Laurence with the bishop’s residence, cells, gardens, and vineyards; five enclosures: in one there is the church of Saint Peter, Saint George, and Saint Theodore; in another there is the church of Saint Vitus, bounded by the wall and by the river—the Tiber—and by its surrounding boundaries; a third is above the riverbank [Column 1117B]; a fourth is beside Saint Laurence and extends as far as the Trajan estate.

Also an enclosure of a vineyard in the place called Scarajo, and another parcel called Clusura; one parcel of vineyard at the Tower of Cucuzuta (Cucuzina), and another at Monton.

Likewise one estate in its entirety called Bacatu (Bacani), with its appendage called Scriptula (Criptulis), in which there are ancient cisterns situated beside the same city of Porto. Its boundary begins on the first side at a tree called Tramarice (Tumarice), proceeds to the Colunnella, which appears to stand in the field at the second mile from that city, and then continues by a straight road along the Salaria as far as the fishermen’s hut. From there it returns to the sea through Buccina and follows the seashore around as far as Saint Nympha, and as far as the mouth of Miccina [Column 1117C], with the places called Juncera (Jonceta), as far as the baths, and as far as the place called Trajan’s Port, and as far as the palace called Progesta, and as far as the ancient city itself with Trajan’s Lake.

Also another smaller castle in its entirety with everything belonging to it; and in the Constantinian city, everything that the aforesaid bishopric is known to possess there, together with the ruined Church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, with the crypts where the animals belonging to that church appear to remain. From there it extends to Saint Mary, which is situated in the arch, with its crypt, house, and cistern, and as far as the house called the Bath of Venus, and as far as [Column 1118A] the public road within the same castle, and the reed-filled land of that city—namely, the monastery of Saint Agnes—with the saltworks and vineyards which it appears to possess within its lands.

Moreover, an estate in its entirety called Palmis, with houses, vineyards, lands, and pastures, extending as far as the ancient oven, which belongs to the aforesaid bishopric; and in the same estate an ancient tomb, situated on the Porto road approximately ten miles from the city of Rome.

Likewise the smaller island in its entirety, with vineyards, houses, and lands, with the place called Scarajo, which was formerly Trajan’s Port, adjoining the same Bacani estate, and with everything belonging to it.

Also an estate in its entirety called Judaeorum, and an estate called Gualdus (Galdus), with all their appurtenances, situated beside the aforesaid ancient city; and also one complete saltwork, situated in seven salt pans.

Likewise at Bacani and at Generula (Genestula), nine salt pans, all the salt pans known to belong to your bishopric; and also an estate in its entirety called Greater Gualdus, with the church of Saint Aurea and its tomb, and the arable land called Planura, in which cisterns appear to be situated, [Column 1118B] lying between the Tiber River and the conduit called Arcioni.

We also confirm to you the entire court called Galeria. There is in it the church of Saint Mary with chambers or small gardens (or dining rooms), and various rooms [Column 1118C], and all its buildings known to exist within and around it, with all its boundaries, termini, and limits; with farm lands, woods, and marshes (Pantonis), with the bridge and the stream itself called Galeria, as far as the river; together with fields, meadows, pastures, willows, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, perpetual waters, places for constructing watermills, and everything belonging to the aforesaid court called Galeria.

Likewise a cultivated and cleared meadow in its entirety, situated in the field called Merul. It runs across the mountain formerly held by John of Miccina and the heirs of the late Stephen the money-changer; from there it is led [Column 1118D] beyond the road through the estate formerly held by John of Sergius; it crosses another carriage road and comes to the estate held by the heirs of the Trastevere family, as marked by marble boundary stones.

From there it goes to the estate of the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and continues along an ancient ditch which, in springtime, carries water into the Galeria stream; then it continues through the middle of the Galeria stream toward the mill of Silva and turns back along the carriage road as far as the middle valley of the mountain called Zunul. It continues as far as the Staffile, which stands at Lintiscino, and as far as the head of the valley—[the valley of Stabla, and through the ditch of that valley it continues from the foot of the salt pans]—enclosing the entire field as far as the parcel called Ticli (Ticoli), and the Galiarda fishpond, which encloses that parcel [Column 1119A], where there are thirty salt pans. It continues beside the salt pans belonging to the monastery of Miranda as far as the Greater Lake; and [along the bank of the Greater Lake and along its bank’s third part] along the bank of the Lake as far as Bordunaria; and from the [foot of the ancient] salt pans as far as Bacani; and as far as the land of the aforesaid bishopric; and as far as the conduit called Arcion; and along that conduit as far as the stream called Galeria; and beyond Galeria, along the conduit, as far as the aforesaid first boundary of Prata Caraci.

Within these boundaries, the following places and names are included: Caesarius, Palmis, Sorbilianus, Greater Pantanum, Old Clusa (the old court of Galeria, Greater Panianum [Column 1119B]), Meodian (Rugnosus, Mount of Canaparia, high Longeria), Rugnosus Mountain, Cannoparius, Celza, Greater Boundary (the greater public field), Accursed Stagnellum, Ticeli, Galiarda Fishpond, Olibastrum, and the foreign Stagnellum, with all their appurtenances.

We also confirm to you and to your successors forever four principal *untiae* (twelfth-shares) in full, constituting a third part of the entire Greater Lake of Porto.

Likewise we grant and confirm to you and to your successors the tower in its entirety called the White Tower, with houses, vineyards, gardens, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, marshes, and streams, cultivated and uncultivated, vacant and occupied, and with everything generally and entirely belonging to the aforesaid tower and the Gualdus of Longeria, just as its boundaries indicate: on the first side, the stream called Galeria; on the second, the river called the Tiber; on the third, Pulverinula; and on the fourth, the conduit called Arction.

We also grant to the people who from time to time will dwell in the aforesaid tower that they shall be subject to no one’s power or jurisdiction, serve no man, and render military service to no one except the bishop who is then in the aforesaid bishopric.

We also confirm to you and to your successors forever all the property and resources, movable and immovable, of those people who die without an heir and intestate, suddenly carried off by judgment—or, [Column 1119C] as the variant has it, by the judgment of God—and who cannot themselves dispose of their resources, throughout the city of Porto, or in Trastevere, or on the island of Licaonia, or wherever the rights of your bishopric are seen to exist.

We establish the holy mother Church of Porto as heir, and thus confirm that the bishop who has been appointed in that bishopric at any time shall have the authority to order and dispose of the inheritance as he wishes, so that these things may not perish forever but may always assist him, insofar as they can, through his prayers [or, according to the variant, his necessities].

Furthermore, from the right of our sacred Lateran palace, which belongs to our public authority, we grant to you and to your successors forever the whole *castaldaticum* of Porto, in its entirety—that is, whatever our castaldiones have hitherto possessed from the whole city of Porto, from its gates or ships, and likewise from the whole Bordunaria, or whatever belonged to them anywhere outside or within.

We grant you and your successors possession of this office forever, so that it shall be in your power to appoint as castald or agent whatever person you wish to install there. Whatever he acquires or may possess from that office shall be transferred to you and to your successors, for you to do with it whatever you wish, provided that, if our count or our successors wish it, he swears fidelity concerning what belongs to our palace.

Those counts who from time to time are there—whether appointed by us or by our successors—shall in no way dare to appoint or install another castald or agent except those whom you or your successors appoint or install [Column 1120A]. If they do so, or forcibly remove anything from the aforesaid castaldaticum, or wish to violate or oppose what has been handed over by us to you and to your successors, each shall pay four pounds of gold: half to the bishopric and half to our palace. Whatever they have appointed in the castaldship—our castald, or an agent—shall be removed.

If he remains obstinate, he shall be excommunicated until he has made true satisfaction [variant: your satisfaction].

Likewise we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever, from the city of Porto, two fishermen and two curiales, of whatever sort you or your successors wish to choose from among the men who are or may be found there.

We therefore grant and confirm all these things forever to your religious authority. We further decree that those two fishermen and two curiales shall henceforth render no payment or service, nor be summoned to court by anyone who at any time holds dominion in that city of Porto. We subject them to your authority and that of your successors.

We also confirm to you and to your successors an estate in its entirety called Genisianum [in the place called Maliana], and Malian, together with a small island beyond the stream situated in that place [Column 1120B], with everything belonging to it, situated on the Porto road [in the aforesaid place called Malliana], beside Malian, belonging to the monastery of Saint Pancratius.

We also confirm to you and to your successors forever the entire island called Licaonia. In it are the church of Blessed John the Baptist [with a tower and oratory within the same court], and the church of Saint Adelbert, with houses and oratories within the same court, with gardens and watermills and their appurtenances.

It is situated within the city of Rome and extends, as [the variant says, from the Plantone bridge], from one end of the island to the other, where the river divides. Below that point it extends as far as the boundary of your bishopric and, below the aforementioned bridge, thirty feet farther downstream, through water and dry land.

Likewise we grant and confirm to you [Column 1121A] the Hand of Saint Mary and of Saint John the Baptist, with its vine-planted garden, just as the documents of acquisition or offering preserved in the bundle of the priest Leo of blessed memory appear to contain it: namely, houses, dining rooms, and ruined buildings, together with a gate and a well of fresh water, as well as sheds, and gardens with all kinds of fruit trees and olive trees. It is situated in the seventh region of Rome, in the place called Proba, beside the monastery of Saint Agatha on the Subura; its boundaries on both sides are public roads.

Moreover, we confirm to you and to your successors in the same church gardens, onion beds, or olive groves, together with arable land situated on Mount Albinus; and another complete piece of arable land with ruined buildings and all its appurtenances [Column 1121B], situated outside the Salarian Gate at the Cucumber Slope.

In the same way, we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the entire episcopal power of appointment—whether of priests, deacons, deaconesses, or subdeacons, or of churches and altars—which it may be necessary to exercise throughout Trastevere, except perhaps when a cardinal priest, cardinal deacon, subdeacon, or acolyte of the sacred Lateran palace is to be appointed [the text is corrupt here]. But we grant you and your successors, or the bishops whom you invite, full authority to ordain, bless, and consecrate all such persons and things.

And lest your diocese be encroached upon by any bishop, we take care by this apostolic privilege to set forth and confirm its boundaries to your church, beginning [Column 1121C] at the first boundary, the broken bridge where the water divides [the variant reads: “called Antonina, where the water is led”], namely along the wall of the city of Trastevere, through the Septimian Gate and the Gate of Saint Pancratius; then along the paved road of that gate as far as the marble bridge over the Arrone; then along that paved road as far as Paritori; from there turning through the marshes as far as the sea; then along the sea as far as two miles beyond the Lighthouse, and as far as the greater spring [or mouth]; from there returning through the middle of the greater river, it comes as far as [Rome in the middle of] the branch of the broken bridge beside the Marmorata; from there to the middle of the bridge of Saint Mary, and to the middle of the bridge where the Jews are seen [or formerly were accustomed] to dwell [Column 1121D]; and it returns through the middle of the aforesaid broken bridge, where we have already spoken of the Antonine water. This is the first boundary, excluding the Catholic churches of Trastevere—namely Saint Mary in Trastevere, Saint Chrysogonus, and Saint Cecilia—and the monastery of Saint Pancratius and of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Nevertheless, in those churches and monasteries, whatever it may be necessary for the bishops of Porto, or for bishops invited by them, to do, we grant them authority to perform.

Likewise we grant and confirm within the aforesaid bishopric the parish churches of Saint Mary and Saint Apollinaris at the Broken Mill, the parish church of Saint Stephen at Pauzi, and the parish church of Saint Mary at Apruniana (Aproniana), as well as all small or large churches of whatever name that are or may be within the aforesaid boundaries [Column 1122A], except those situated in Trastevere which we have already mentioned.

Meanwhile, we decree and command, just as our predecessors commanded, that in the entire river flowing beside the city of Porto no one may dare to establish mills or a bridge in any way without your command or that of your successor bishops, according to the ancient custom. Once a mill or bridge has been established—or restored, or made—by you or by others whom you have instructed to do so, it shall be administered at your discretion.

As for the bridge of that city [the variant reads: “as for the crossing, through the bridge of that city”], no one may dare to cross it in either direction with a wagon loaded with wine or provisions [Column 1122B].

Again we decree and command that no presbyter [the manuscript breaks off: “presb . . .”], or any cleric of whatever order, may be summoned to court by anyone from the whole aforesaid bishopric, compelled to settle a dispute [or, according to the variant, to create a dispute], or required to perform any service, except by the bishops of Porto, in whose parish they are.

Whoever, whether duke, count, viscount, chamberlain, or someone sent by our apostolic see, or any other authority that has held dominion over that city of Porto—of whatever rank he may be—wishes to remove or diminish from the right, power, or jurisdiction of the aforesaid bishopric any of the aforesaid immovable properties, or the aforementioned castaldaticum, or the two fishermen and two curiales, or all the aforesaid clergy; or attempts to violate the diocese; or recalls the people living in the aforesaid tower, or anywhere where the property of this bishopric has been mentioned, to public service—let him know that he shall pay to the bishop himself, whoever he may be at the time, twenty pounds of the purest gold, and shall moreover be subject to anathema.

Therefore, establishing by apostolic censure, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under adjuration by the divine judgment and by the prohibitions of anathema, that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever dare to oppose, transgress in any respect, or diminish anything that we have established for the praise of God and for the stability or increase of the aforesaid bishopric; but, just as it has been established or granted above by us, so shall he permit it to remain perpetually and for all time, without any diminution, to the very end. If anyone, however—which we do not desire—should presume with rash audacity to act against this our privilege, or in any respect to contravene it, and should fail to allow it to remain firmly established as we have prescribed above, and should not observe it in all things, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, who exercise his vicariate, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and destined to be wholly consumed in the fire together with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all his pomps. But whoever, with pious regard, proves in all things to be the guardian and observer of this our apostolic privilege, may he deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and eternal life from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and from all his saints, for ever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the eighth indiction.

## II. John XIX grants the pallium to Archbishop Bisantius of Canusium [that is, Bari] and confirms his rights. (Year 1025.) [UGHELLI, *Italia sacra* VII, 601.]

**JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother and our spiritual son BISANTIUS, consecrated by us archbishop of the holy Church of Canusium, for all the days of your life.**

[Col. 1123B]

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For from this the greatest profit—and above all the first reward—is prescribed by the Creator of all things, God, in the heavenly courts: namely, when distinguished and venerable places have undoubtedly been brought into a better condition.

Therefore, because you asked us, out of regard for your dignity and loving fraternity, to grant and confirm to you for all the days of your life the aforesaid archbishopric of the holy Church of Canusium, with all its adjacent and appurtenant territories—namely, twelve bishoprics, as former times, that is, our predecessors of holy memory, had decreed, so that the archbishop should ordain twelve bishops under himself—we now rightly favor the wishes of those who ask. Accordingly, we consecrate you, the aforesaid Bisantius Angelicus, as archbishop in the aforesaid holy Church of Canusium, with all its cities and castles, namely: Canusium, Bari, Modugno, Gioia? [Juvenacium], Molfetta, Ruvo, Trani, Canne, Minervino, Acquatecta, Monte Melioris, Labellotatum, Cisterna, Bitetto, Salpi, Conversano, Polignano, and Catera, together with the other cities and castles adjacent to them or situated there far and wide, until the twelfth bishopric is completed.

[Col. 1123C]

Therefore we confirm to you all estates and farmsteads, together with houses and vineyards, male and female slaves, together with estates and agricultural holdings, and mills; shores with harbors; mountains, hills, plains, and meadows; and likewise parish churches or churches with all their titles, as well as their chapels. We further confirm monasteries of men and women, both Greek and Latin, with all ecclesiastical orders—deacons, subdeacons, readers, and priests—and all estates and possessions, cultivated or uncultivated, together with everything that is generally accustomed to be called and named rural property, in its entirety and with all appurtenances, within the boundary of Apulia.

Moreover, with the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the others whose vicariate we likewise exercise, we grant you permission to use the pallium throughout all the days of your life and to consecrate bishops with all humility and reverence. For to undertake so great a pastoral office, if it is considered without inward vigilance, is more a burden than an honor, since one cannot sufficiently care for one’s own affairs unless one also manages those of others in a salutary manner.

Having briefly set these matters forth, now, benevolent and most beloved in Christ, be an example of every goodness; be an example to all who see or hear you; imitate the footsteps of your predecessors on earth, so that you may deserve to be their companions in heaven.

We grant and confirm to you, from this eighth indiction and for all the days of your life, the aforesaid archbishopric of Canusium with all its appurtenances, and the consecration by your hands of the bishops themselves, together with the use of the pallium by apostolic authority, to hold and govern, and to rule and administer with complete fear of God. Thus no patrician, catapan, excubitus, or any person of imperial rank, honor, or dignity shall dare or presume to judge, molest, or trouble you in any matter; nor shall any cleric, layman, or other person of any kind dare or presume to do there anything troublesome or contrary.

[Col. 1124B]

We decree, therefore, by apostolic censure, under adjuration by the divine judgment and the prohibitions of anathema, that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor any king, emperor, or person of great or small power, shall dare to prohibit or violate what has been established and ordered by us. If anyone, however—which we do not believe—should with rash audacity set himself against this our instrument and apostolic privilege, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the others, he is bound by the bond of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God; and let him be a companion in hell with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the impious. But whoever, out of regard for this our apostolic privilege, proves to be its guardian and observer, may he deserve to receive from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life for ever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Roger, regional notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the eighth indiction. Farewell.

## III. Bull of Pope John XIX to all kings, bishops, dukes, counts, and others. (About the year 1025.) [*Mémoires et Documents historiques de la Suisse*, vol. III, p. 429. Lausanne 1838. 8vo.]

[Col. 1124D]

**JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all kings, bishops, dukes, counts, and all princes in whose power the Roman monastery is understood to possess any churches or lands, greetings from God and apostolic blessing.**

I ask all your fraternity together that, for the love of God and of holy Peter and of us, you take care to protect the aforesaid Roman monastery and everything belonging to it, and that in all things you guard and defend it.

[Col. 1125A]

If, however, there should be anyone within your jurisdictions or lands who attempts to inflict any injury or trouble upon the aforesaid place or upon the lands belonging to it, I ask all your fraternity together to see that justice and a proper judgment are rendered to the aforesaid place. But if they despise this and wish to persist in their wickedness, let them know that by our apostolic authority they are to be excommunicated and cursed, barred from the thresholds of the holy Church, separated from the fellowship of all Christians, and plunged into hell with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive, unless they quickly come to make restitution to Saint Peter’s Roman monastery.

Let them be excommunicated and anathematized on behalf of Saint Peter the apostle, who received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing—those who unjustly hold the lands of that same Saint Peter and refuse to return them; and likewise those who conceal them and refuse to point them out or disclose them to the ministers of the holy Peter.

[Col. 1125B]

Let those wretched men be condemned in hell with Judas, who handed our Lord over to the impious Jews; with Pilate, who ordered that Lord himself to be crucified; and with Herod, who killed himself. Let all those who unjustly hold or conceal the lands of Saint Peter’s Roman monastery be condemned with them.

May the Lord hand them over, falling before their enemies: may they go out against them by one road and flee from them by seven, and be scattered throughout all the kingdoms of the earth. May their corpses become food for all the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, with none to drive them away. May the Lord strike them with madness, blindness, and fury of mind; may they grope at midday as a blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness, and may they not direct their ways. May they suffer accusation at all times and be oppressed by violence, with no one to free them. May they take wives and let another sleep with them while they look on. May they build houses and not dwell in them. May they plant vineyards and not harvest them.

May all these curses, and many others, come upon all the men who unjustly hold the lands of Saint Peter’s Roman monastery, or who conceal them, unless they quickly come to make restitution.

## IV. John XIX confirms the possessions of the Church of Silva Candida at the request of Bishop Peter. (Year 1026.) [UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, I, 93]

[Col. 1125D]

**JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Silva Candida, and through you to that venerable bishopric and to your successors, the bishops, forever.**

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For from this we shall gain the greatest reward before the Creator of all things, God, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have undoubtedly been brought into a better condition.

Therefore, because your filial affection requested that we grant and confirm to you and to your venerable bishopric those possessions which our predecessor pontiffs granted and confirmed to the aforesaid use of your bishopric, for the restoration and renewal of that sacred place and for the remedy of their souls and those of their successors, we, likewise moved by clemency and inclined by your prayers, by the tenor of this our apostolic privilege grant and confirm to you, the aforesaid beloved son Bishop Peter, your aforesaid bishopric in its entirety, with all its full possessions: with all parishes, titles, clergy, chapels, estates, courts, lands and farmsteads, villages, vineyards, lands, and everything that is known to be adjacent or belonging under the jurisdiction and dominion of that same bishopric.

[Col. 1126A]

First, namely, the estate in its entirety called Caesarea, with its lands and tenants, called Furculae, Tondiliani, and Martiniani. Likewise the colony of Salaro, and that of Cortina and Gradulsi; the colony of Valle, and of Fontana and Sanctus; the colony of Coriliano and of Lauro; likewise the colony of Casa Nova; the colony of Tribuno and of Masopane; the colony of Castanea Cupa and of Cobelli; the colony of Caesarius—or by whatever other names they are now called—with all their vineyards, farmsteads, and appurtenances; with all their boundaries and termini, that is, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, perennial waters, buildings, ruined structures, sandpits, and their attached and adjoining properties.

[Col. 1126B]

Also the church of Saint Andrew the apostle, built within that estate, together with the tenants and agricultural workers, taxpayers and compulsory laborers, male and female, sons, daughters, and grandchildren residing there or descended from them, wherever they may be found, and with all the census payments, gifts, dues, and compulsory services belonging to it, situated in the territory of Nepi, twenty miles more or less from the city of Rome, from the body of the patrimony of Tuscia belonging to our holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we govern.

Its boundaries are: on one side, the land of the monastery of Saint Stephen the Minor, from Saint Peter; on the second side, the wood and land belonging to John the grammarian; on the third side, the pastureland of Donicus; and on the fourth side, the estate of Claudiana.

Likewise we grant and confirm to you the estate in its entirety called Buxus, in which the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda appears to have been built; and the estate in its entirety called Artronum; and Mount Jordan, with houses, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, together with the male and female slaves and tenants of every sex and age residing there, and with all that belongs to them, situated in the territory of Silva Candida.

Its boundaries are: on the first side, the aforesaid land of the holy bishopric; on the second side, the stream called Galeria; on the third side, Bibarus; and on the fourth side, Criptula.

[Col. 1126C]

Also the estate in its entirety called Mons Aureus, with all its appurtenances: on one side, the mountain called Jordan; on the second side, Criptula; on the third side, the farmstead called Palmira; on the fourth side, the estate called Lauret; and on the fifth side, the land and monastery of Saint Martin.

Likewise the estate called Mons Grundul, with everything belonging to it. Its boundaries are: on one side, the estate of Aquilin; on the second side, the estate of Palmi; on the third side, the estate of Mons Aureus; and on the fourth side, the estate of Criptula.

And Bibariola, together with the estate called Oripo, with everything belonging to it. Its boundaries are: on one side, the property of the monastery of Saint Martin; on the second side, the estate called Insula Sancta; on the third side, the court of Saint Peter and the estate of Mons Grundul; and on the fourth side, the island belonging to the court of Saint Peter.

[Col. 1127A]

Also the estate called Criptulus and Palmis, with all their appurtenances: on one side, the estate of Fulisanus; on the second side, the estate of Lauret; on the third side, the land of Saint Martin; and on the fourth side, the estate of Serianus.

At the bottom, the estate of Isidore, with all its appurtenances: on one side, the land of the monastery of Saint Martin; on the second side, Castagnetol; and on the third side, Insula Sancta.

Finally, the estate itself of Insula Sancta, with everything belonging to it: on one side, the farmstead called Bruce; on the second side, Donicus; on the third side, Musanus; and on the fourth side, Saint Laurence of Panti.

Likewise the estate of Saint Basil, with everything belonging to it: on one side, the farmstead of Saint Peter, called Pauli; on the second side, the valley called Intensonosa; on the third side, Barbarol; and on the fourth side, the monastery of Saint Stephen.

[Col. 1127B]

Moreover, the estate of Panori, with everything belonging to it: on one side, the estate of Aprunianus; on the second side, Silva Candida; on the third side, Musanellus; on the fourth side, Camiliar; and on the fifth side, the tower of Aurelian.

Also the flint-stone property of Saint Stephen, with the saltworks; and the estate of Lauret: on one side, the land of Saint Peter; on the second side, the land of Saint Martin; on the third side, the mountain of Iliodorus; and on the fourth side, the estate of Oripo, or the farmstead called Pauli.

And the estate of Serianus, with all their appurtenances: on one side, the land of Saint Martin; on the second side, Silva Candida; on the third side, Insula Sancta; and on the fourth side, the wood of Saint Peter.

Also the farmstead called Castagnolum: on one side, the property of the Four Holy Brothers; on the second side, the estate of Orbanula; on the third side, Mussan; and on the fourth side, Massanellus.

And the wood called Magia, with all its appurtenances: on one side, the stream of Galesia; and on the second side, the monastery of Venus, called Huppla Ancilla Dei.

[Col. 1127C]

All those estates and farmsteads, with lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, cultivated and uncultivated places, are situated in the territory of Silva Candida, twelve miles more or less from the city of Rome.

Also an entire water-mill in the village called Galeria, with everything belonging to it; and the land of Simitaritia, called Pastina, situated far off. Its boundaries are: on one side, Gualdus Donicus; on the second side, the land of Saint Peter called Campus Massanus; on the third side, Mount Actionus; and on the fourth side, Mount Pauninus, situated beside the aforesaid bishopric.

Likewise, another water-mill on the same stream, with everything belonging to it, belonging by right to that bishopric.

[Col. 1128A]

We also grant and confirm to you all parishes, churches, and parishes’ territories, with all their appurtenances and adjacent properties, namely: the parish church of Saint Mary at Silva Candida with its titles; the title of Saints John and Paul at Lutino; the title of Saint Angelus at Musano; the title of Saint Donatus at Majorata; and the parish church of Saint Gregory in that place; the title of Saint Anastasius at Musano; and the parish church of Saint Angelus at Ruscindum with its lands.

Likewise the parish church of Saint John at the Ninth Mile, with its lands and titles; the title of Saint Martianus in that village, with its lands; the title of Saint Andrew with its titles; also the title of Saint Mary with its lands; the title of Saint Nicholas, which is in the castle of Mount Depinus; the title of Saint Mary called Insirigus, with its lands; the title of Saint Pancratius with its lands and titles; Saint Mary on the Island, with its lands; the parish church of Saint Mary Lutia, with its lands; the island of Saint John with its title and land; and the title of Saint Gregory in that place.

Likewise the parish church of Saint Paul at Formello, with its lands, vineyards, gardens, olive groves, and titles; the title of Saint Sylvester at Columna, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Angelus at Mubiano, with its lands and gardens; the title of Saint Martin, with its lands; the title of Saint Genesius in Dalmatia, with its lands; the title of Saint Laurence at Formello, with its lands and gardens; the title of Saint John in that place, with its land; the title of Saint Peter, with its land; the title of Saint Angelus at Lauret; the title of Saint Valentine at Criptulus; and likewise the parish church of Saint Cornelius at Craparium.

[Col. 1128B]

And by the page of this our privilege and decree, we confirm forever to the aforesaid holy bishopric of Silva Candida, with its lands, vineyards, olive groves, and titles: the title of Saint Pancratius, with its lands; the title of Saint Mary, with its lands and meadow; the title of Saint Valentine, with its lands, olive grove, and meadow; the title of Saint Donatus, with its lands; the title of Saint Mary, with its lands; the title of Saint Laurence, with its lands; the title of Saint Anastasius at Cannetalo, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Vitus, with its lands; the parish church of Saint Paul, with its lands, vineyards, and rights; the title of Saint Sylvester and Saint Angelus, with their lands, vineyards, olive groves, and rights; the title of Saint Mary, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Christiana, with its lands, vineyards, and woods; the title of Saint George; the title of Saint Martin, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Cassianus, with its lands and vineyards, and three households; the title of Saint Anastasius, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Justina, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Angelus, with its lands; and the title of Saint Gregory, with its lands and vineyards.

[Col. 1128C]

Likewise the parish church of Saint Marcellus at the Fourteenth Mile, with its lands, vineyards, larger olive grove, and titles; the title of Saint Mary at Scrofano, with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Stephen at Matera; the title of Saint Mary at Matera; the title of Saint Blaise at Scrofano; the title of Saint John at Scrofano itself; and Saint Eugenia, with its lands and vineyards.

Likewise the parish church of Saint Mary at Molmula, with its lands, vineyards, and title; and Saint Angelus, with its lands and vineyards.

We also confirm to you the farmsteads and colonies, and the castle in its entirety, called Dalmachia, Balneo, Stabla, and Massaviliana, or by whatever other names they are called, together with the households, male and female, or tenants belonging to each place, with houses, vineyards, lands, woods and meadows, perennial waters, and everything belonging to the aforesaid farmsteads, colonies, and castle.

[Col. 1129A]

It is situated in the territory of Nepi, twenty miles more or less from the city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on one side, the road between the military station of the tower of Crapacorius and the land of the pasture of Saint Peter; on the other side, the land of Mount Arsitium and Focapran, which is called Columella, and the land of the tower of Crapacorius, which is called Matera; and on the fourth side, the land of Saint Laurence, which is called Salicara, and the stream that runs through Bussetum and Malcan.

Likewise we grant and confirm to you forever the church of Saints Rufina and Secunda, situated at Rome beside our palace, with everything belonging to it.

We also grant and confirm to you forever the church of Saint Mary, with all its appurtenances, within this Roman city, not far from the mountain called Augustus.

In the same way, we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever, just as they were granted and confirmed by the most holy pope mentioned above or by certain of our predecessor pontiffs: namely, the five monasteries of Saint Stephen the Greater and the Lesser, of Saints John and Paul, of blessed Martin, and of blessed Thecla, situated beside the great church of Saint Peter, with all their appurtenances; and all the consecrations that take place there, whether in that holy church of Saint Peter or in the other churches situated throughout the entire Leonine City.

[Col. 1129B]

If it should be necessary to consecrate them, no other bishop shall presume to undertake such ministry or consecration, except you and your successors, the bishops of the Church of Silva Candida, forever.

We also grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the holy Saturday for celebrating the sacrament of baptism and performing the entire office in the church of blessed Peter the apostle. Whatever gold, silver, cloth, wax, or other things have been placed, offered, or cast upon the great altar, or in the confession, or have been offered to you, from the third hour of the day—that is, from the hour when we wish you to enter the church to ordain and perform the divine office—until you have completed the Mass of the holy Sunday, shall, through your stewards, come into the possession of you and your successors, without any opposition.

[Col. 1129C]

And because, up to our time, Palm Sunday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, and Good Friday were celebrated in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, from which nearly all churches received instruction as from their mother and mistress, with such irreverence that no procession with palms was held there on Palm Sunday, nor was *Gloria in excelsis Deo* said on the day of the Lord’s Supper, and on Good Friday the office was not performed there with the reverence that was fitting, we grieved and, desiring to improve this through you and your successors, decree that every year on Palm Sunday you shall go out in procession from the church of Saint Mary in the Tower, and, coming to the great altar of Saint Peter, celebrate Mass.

Likewise, every year on the day of the Lord’s Supper, we wish you and your successors to celebrate Mass upon that same altar of Saint Peter, say *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, prepare the holy chrism, and perform whatever pertains to a bishop. And every year on Good Friday we wish you and your successors to perform the entire office reverently, as is fitting, upon that same great altar of Saint Peter.

[Col. 1130A]

In these three Masses—namely, the Palm Sunday Mass, the Mass of the Lord’s Supper, and the Good Friday office—whatever gold, silver, cloth, wax, or other things are placed or cast upon the aforesaid sacred altar of Saint Peter or in the confession, or offered to you, from the hour at which that Mass or office begins until it is completed, shall, through our custodians, likewise come into the possession of you and your successors, without any opposition.

On these five days, if it seems useful to you and your successors to have one of our deacons minister, we wish you to request this as an honor to Saint Peter.

[Col. 1130B]

We grant and confirm to you and to your successors the authority over that church of Saint Peter and its aforesaid monasteries, and all their ecclesiastical judgments, as well as those of the entire Leonine City. Likewise, for the anointing and consecration of the emperor, we summon first your fraternity and that of your successor bishops, so that the emperor may first be blessed by those to whom the governance of the whole Church of Saint Peter and of the Leonine City has been entrusted.

Furthermore, all sacred offices and rites that we and our successors ought to perform, if we are unable to perform them because of illness or some other obligation, we decree by apostolic authority shall be performed by you and your successors, both in the aforesaid Church of Saint Peter and its monasteries and throughout the entire Leonine City.

[Col. 1130C]

The consecration of the altars of the Church of Saint Peter and of the other monasteries, as well as the consecration of the churches, altars, priests, deacons, and deaconesses of the entire Leonine City, we grant and confirm forever to you and your successors, as has been stated above.

Moreover, for the Church of Saints Rufina and Secunda, over which by God’s authority you preside, we grant and confirm forever to you and your successors also the church of Saint Adalbert and Paulinus, together with the church of Saint Benedict, with all its entirety and appurtenances. Just as you hold them today under your authority, they are situated within this Roman city, on the island of Lycaonia, so that they may be, whenever you wish, an episcopal residence, a suitable refuge, and a convenient dwelling for you and your successors, just as Saint John between the two bridges appears to belong to the Church of Porto.

[Col. 1130D]

The priests and clerics who from time to time serve in the same church of Adalbert, Paulinus, and Benedict we wish to be subject to you as proper sons of your church. We withdraw them from every other jurisdiction, entrusting them nevertheless to your fatherly care, so that they may await only your judgment, serve your dominion, and in all things obey your reasonable commands. Thus, as seems good to you, it shall be permitted by our apostolic authority forever for you to ordain, govern, instruct, and correct them as is fitting.

All the aforesaid places and households, with everything belonging to them, just as they have been listed above, we give, bestow, grant, confirm, and establish forever, from this tenth indiction, to you and to your successors in the same venerable bishopric, for the use and benefit of that venerable bishopric and of the bishops who from time to time hold that church.

[Col. 1131A]

We decree, therefore, by apostolic censure, under adjuration by the divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor anyone who has exercised public offices, nor any other person, great or small, shall dare or presume to act against this our pontifical privilege with respect to anything contained above, or to alienate or take away anything. Rather, we decree that all these things shall remain firm and stable for all time, just as they have been established and confirmed by us.

If anyone, however—which we do not desire—should with rash audacity presume to become in any respect a transgressor against this our apostolic privilege, or dare to break it, and should refuse to be obedient and observant in all things, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God and of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, whose vicariate we exercise, though unworthy, by God’s favor, he is bound by the bond of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God; and let him be a companion in hell with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the impious.

[Col. 1131B]
