But whoever, out of regard for this our apostolic privilege, proves to be its guardian and observer, may he, through the merits and prayers of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, deserve to receive in the heavenly courts rewards, the grace of blessing and mercy from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and eternal life, and may he find them for ever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of George, regional notary and scribe of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December and in the tenth indiction stated above.

Theobald, bishop of the Church of Bell. tren. [as abbreviated]; Theobald, bishop of the holy Church of Albano; Dominic, bishop of the Church of Lavicanum; Peter, bishop of the Church of Praeneste; Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia; Stephen, priest of the title of Saint Cecilia; Benedict, archdeacon; Hugh, deacon; Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Damasus.

[Col. 1132A]

Crescentius, deacon; John, subdeacon; John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark; John, deacon by the grace of God; John, subdeacon of Mira; John, priest of the title of Saint Calixtus in Trastevere; Crescentius, deacon; Rodolphus, unworthy priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Laurence situated at Clausura; John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; Franco, deacon; Raynerius, deacon.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, through the hand of Benedict, bishop of Porto, and in the place of Peregrinus of Cologne, archbishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the nineteenth of that name, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the apostle; in the third month, December, in the tenth indiction.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person shall rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, or take away its possessions, or retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with unjust vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact for those whose governance and support they were granted, so that they may be useful in every respect, without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see.

[Col. 1132B]

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical, secular, or other person, knowingly and rashly attempts to act against this page of our constitution, then, after being warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge before the divine Judge that he is guilty of the iniquity committed. Let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment let him be subjected strictly to punishment.

But for all who preserve the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

## V. John XIX, at a council, invests Peter, bishop of Silva Candida, with the entire land of all the churches of Galeria, after receiving the staff. (Year 1026.) [UGHELLI, *ibid.*, p. 98.]

[Col. 1132D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, John, by divine providence the nineteenth Roman pope, knowing that almost everything is consigned to oblivion because of human frailty, have commanded to be committed to writing the things done in former times for the honor and benefit of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, so that those who come after may know the devotion shown toward our places, and so that, if any have been rebellious, they may waste away and be ashamed.

When Gregory, bishop of the aforesaid martyrs Rufina and Secunda, had died, we consecrated Peter bishop. After his consecration, before three years had elapsed, the priests of Saint Nicholas of Galeria began to bring a complaint before that bishop concerning the priests of Saint Andrew. The priests of Saint Andrew, however, asked the bishop to go there and build altars in the aforesaid church of Saint Andrew. The bishop replied that he ought not to consecrate altars there, since the priest of Saint Nicholas was bringing a lawsuit concerning that very church: “Let both parties first come before us, let the matter be settled according to law, and then, if I can do so canonically, I shall gladly go to perform the service of Holy Church.”

After hearing this, they returned and reported it to the archpriest and the other priests. Summoned canonically again and again, at last both parties came before their bishop. Wishing to settle their case in such a way that no further dispute might ever arise from it, the aforesaid Bishop Peter brought them before our presence. We were seated in the church of Saint Sylvester, which is within the Lateran palace, together with Theobald of Velletri, Peter of Palestrina, Benedict of Porto, Theobald of Albano, Peter of Ostia, Dominic of Labico, Benedict the archdeacon, Crescentius and Raynerius the deacons, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Damasus, Franco, cardinal-priest of Saint Sixtus, Tuidiscus, cardinal-priest of Saint Marcellus, and many other priests and clerics. Present also were Benedict the primicerius, another Benedict the secundicerius, Crescentius the nomenclator, Peter the first defensor, Stephen the protoscriniarius, John Deubaldus the dative judge, our brother Lord Alberic, count of the palace, and John Tocco, count of Galeria.

We caused the aforesaid priests of both churches to enter with a few laymen from Galeria, namely John son of Rudolph and Baldo. Then the bishop came to our feet and began to explain how, in what manner, and for what reason he had summoned them. We began to inquire into the case that was disturbing them, and to consider and settle it with a tranquil mind.

When the matter was prolonged, as I believe by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, it came to my mind that the bishop of Saint Rufina must receive much revenue from so many priests and from so large a population of Galeria. Thinking this privately and wishing to learn the amount of the revenue of the aforesaid Galeria, I questioned the bishop as follows:

“I believe that the bishop of Saint Rufina receives a great deal of revenue from so many priests and from so large a population of Galeria.”

The bishop replied: “From the priests of Saint Nicholas the bishop receives fourteen solidi per year, and from the priests of Saint Andrew thirty denarii—nothing more.”

When we heard this, we were overcome with the greatest sadness. Abandoning the case that we had been considering, we all turned with one spirit and one mind, compelled by so great an impiety, to address this matter. Then we summoned the archpriest of Saint Nicholas with his associates and the syndic of Saint Andrew with his associates. Since the archpriest was absent because of illness, we addressed them as follows:

“Tell us why you give so little to the bishop, and why you do not give him even a third, as other places do.”

They replied: “It has been our custom.”

We answered: “Do you have anything written about this by any bishop?”

They replied in every respect: “No, lord.”

Then, while the bishops, priests, deacons, and judges were seated, we asked what ought to be done about this. The aforesaid bishop came forward to our feet and began as follows:

“Lord, if it pleases you, return to the case for which we came here; reserve this matter for a suitable time.”

Then, moved and greatly angered against him because he did not want us to bring forward what he himself ought to have investigated, we said:

“I am astonished that, although you are prudent and powerful, you do not raise up your church but rather oppress it. Why did you not say this throughout all these days? Why do you not demand from them that custom which all churches possess? I shall not be held accountable for what is in that Church: I gave it to you. If you do not wish to demand a third from them, I shall demand it, so that the Church entrusted to you may not diminish during my time and yours.”

Corrected by these words, Bishop Peter replied:

“Lord, I am prepared to accept whatever you and this holy council judge.”

Then the entire council defined and judged that, setting everything else aside, the church of Saint Rufina and its bishop should first be honored, and that the bishop should receive from me the third of all Galeria. The priests renounced their claim to it and promised to give the whole amount to him and to his successors forever. Then they were to return to the case already begun; and so it was done.

For I, having taken the staff, invested Bishop Peter with the whole third of all the churches of Galeria, together with the customary payment, on behalf of himself and his successors. The priests of both churches consented, rejected their former claim, and promised to give it, saying that they would previously have given it voluntarily. [Col. 1134C]

It was judged again that this should be placed under the prohibition of anathema and confirmed. And it was done. For, at our command and that of all the aforesaid priests, bishops, and deacons, Benedict, bishop of Porto, having taken up the stole, said:

“By the authority of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle; by the authority of our lord Pope John, who presides over this holy council; and by the authority of this holy council, we curse, excommunicate, and bind with the perpetual bond of anathema anyone among the priests, clerics, or laymen, or any person whatsoever among mortals, who should presume in any way to contest the third of all the churches of Galeria with Bishop Peter and his successors, or should intend in any way to defraud them of it.

“We also decree and establish, by apostolic authority, that what we have judged concerning Galeria shall be observed by everyone, in all the places of the aforesaid bishopric of Saint Rufina, by all priests, clerics, and laymen, and by every person, under a similar anathema. After the aforesaid third has been demanded three times by Bishop Peter or his successors, and all have acclaimed it, they said: ‘Let it be done, let it be done. Amen, amen.’

“And so that it may be observed more diligently and known more clearly, we commanded Gregory, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, to write out the entire matter in order, and we wished it to be confirmed by the signatures of all who were present.”

Benedict the archdeacon was present, and I judge it valid forever.

Peter of Palestrina, bishop, was present, and I judge it valid forever.

I, Benedict, bishop of Porto, was present, and I judge it valid forever.

Issued on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, through the hands of Boso, bishop of the Holy Tiburtine Church and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See. I was present and judge it valid forever.

Raynerius, deacon of the deaconry of Saint George, was present.

Leo, bishop of the Church of Ostia, was present and judge it valid forever.

Gregory of Saint Lucia was present and judge it valid forever.

Benedict, bishop of the Church of Anagni, was present.

John, bishop of the Church of Blera, was present and judge it valid forever.

Benedict, bishop of Cerveteri, judge this decree firm and valid forever.

Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, was present.

Raynerius, bishop of the Church of Nepi, judges this decree firm and destined to remain forever.

Amasus, bishop and chaplain of the lord pope.

Franco, cardinal-priest of Saint Sixtus.

Benedict, by the grace of God secundicerius of the Holy Apostolic See.

John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.

Crescentius, by the grace of God nomenclator of the Holy Apostolic See.

I, Stephen, by the grace of God scribe of the Holy Apostolic See, wrote this, and so forth.

## VI. Pope John XIX’s Privilege for the Monastery of Cluny

He declares that he confirms all the monasteries and places belonging to the monastery of Cluny and previously granted to it by certain faithful Christians, kings, bishops, dukes, or princes. He also forbids any bishop or priest to come to Cluny for an ordination, the consecration of a church, priests, or deacons, or the celebration of Masses, unless invited by the abbot of Cluny. The monks of Cluny are instead permitted to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever their abbot pleases. Likewise, he forbids any bishop or priest to excommunicate the Cluniac brothers wherever they may be located. He further decrees that the monastery of Cluny shall be a bosom of mercy for all who flee to it for salvation, and establishes that, if anyone bound by anathema should seek that monastery, whether for burial of the body or for the sake of some other benefit or salvation, he is to be kindly received and tended with the oil of the healing remedy. Finally, he determines that the election of the abbot of Cluny belongs to the congregation of that place. (Year 1027.) [Bullarium Cluniacense, p. 8.]

[Col. 1135C]

[Col. 1135D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Odilo, abbot of the monastery called Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the county of Mâcon, and through you to all your successors, the abbots, forever.

Since the grace of apostolic charity ought to assist the petitions and needs of all the faithful, the clemency of its favor must be bestowed still more generously upon those whom holy Roman Mother Church rejoices to possess as her own and especially as her sons. She does so for the sake of her own benefit and by the distinguished authority of the Fathers who preceded us. The sublimity of apostolic authority ought all the more fully to comply with their desires and wishes insofar as it is more certain that they desire and seek nothing except what contributes to the propriety of holy devotion and the usefulness of true religion.

Whenever they humbly seek our assent and the protection of the accustomed apostolic authority in matters concerning their needs and welfare, it is fitting that we should freely assist them out of a regard for kindness and properly strengthen them in complete security, so that from this the highest reward may also be granted to us by God, the creator of all, in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, because you asked us to fortify the aforesaid monastery through a document of apostolic authority, to confirm that all its possessions should remain there inviolably by perpetual right, and to establish them securely through the document of our privilege without the yoke or rule of any person whatsoever, we, moved by your prayers and at the intervention of the most invincible and pious lord Henry, august emperor, and for the remedy of his soul, establish and decree through this privilege of our authority that you should possess, with complete security and without anyone’s opposition, all the places and monasteries belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny that were granted to that place by various most faithful Christians, kings, bishops, dukes, or princes, and acquired by your predecessors in the abbacy—namely Berno, Odo, Aymard, and your predecessor, Saint Mayeul of blessed memory—or whatever else appears to belong to the same place. You and all your successors shall possess these things forever.

Moreover, strengthening this decree under the proclamation and confirmation of divine judgment and under the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no bishop or any priest whatsoever may presume to come to this venerable monastery to perform any ordination, the consecration of a church, priests, or deacons, or the celebration of Masses, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that place. The monks of that place shall instead be permitted to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever it may please you and your successors.

We prohibit, under a similar proclamation of anathema, that the same place be burdened by the title of interdict or by the bond of excommunication or anathema imposed by any bishop or priest whatsoever. The authority of the holy apostolic see does not permit the generous liberty granted to anyone by that see to be cut down by the obligation imposed by any person whatsoever. Nor shall the brothers of that place, wherever they may be, be held bound by the curse or excommunication of any bishop.

For it appears dishonorable to us that, without our judgment, a son of the holy apostolic see should be anathematized by anyone as though he were the disciple of some subordinate church. If, however, a suitable reason should move anyone against them, and the matter could not otherwise be determined or decided, let the apostolic judgment be patiently awaited and humbly requested; that judgment permits no one to suffer prejudice from it.

We also decree, and by the authority of him whose office we exercise, however unworthily, we establish that the same place shall be a bosom of mercy, a harbor of complete piety and salvation, for all who flee to it for salvation. Let the righteous find a place there, and let the wicked who wishes to repent not be rejected. Let mutual fraternal charity be offered to the innocent, and let those who have given offense not be denied hope of salvation and the indulgence of mercy.

If anyone bound by anathema should seek the same place, whether for the burial of his body or for the sake of some other benefit or salvation, let him by no means be excluded from pardon and the mercy he desires; rather, let him be kindly received and tended with the oil of the healing remedy. For it is just that, in a house of mercy, the love of holy brotherhood should be offered even to the righteous, and that the sinner who flees for pardon should not be denied the remedy of indulgence and salvation.

Let it be for all who come there a cause of salvation, here and forever, a refuge of divine compassion and mercy, and a protection of apostolic blessing.

We further decree and establish without qualification that, when the abbot of the aforesaid place dies, no other person is to be appointed there through the violence of anyone. Rather, the congregation of the place shall choose, according to the fear of God and the rule of the legislator Benedict, the father who is to preside over it; and, for his ordination, let whatever bishop the congregation wishes be summoned.

Whatever lands you now hold, and whatever lands you and your successors may be able to acquire, we grant to you to possess forever.

If anyone, however—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt by reckless audacity to act or proceed against the tenor of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him know that he is to be bound by the bond of the anathema of our Lord and of the prince of the apostles, Peter, and that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most atrocious pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Let him likewise be cast into the abyss and Tartarean chaos, there to perish with the impious.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours, may he obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life, and so forth. Amen.

## VII. Letter of John XIX to Poppo, Patriarch of Aquileia

(Year 1027.) [UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 49.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Poppo, patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia: perpetual salvation.

Since the care of watching over all the Churches of God and pious places presses upon us with great concern, lest they suffer any loss in their necessities but rather receive the resources of their proper benefit, it is fitting that we should devote ourselves with the eagerness of our whole mind especially to the stability and integrity of those ancient places, and diligently gather their benefits and supports there. Thus what we confirm for the ancient places from our resources, for the honor, praise, and glory of the holy name of our almighty God and of his divine majesty, may be acceptable to him, and may a worthy recompense for such pious love be conferred upon us by his most abundant mercy in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, because you ask us to confer upon you the patriarchate of the holy Church of Aquileia, with all its honor and possessions, as a single whole, just as it was formerly decreed by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by Eugene, Gregory, and our other predecessors, bishops of this apostolic see, we, yielding to your prayers, grant it by apostolic authority and confirm through this document of our privilege that the patriarchate of the holy Church of Aquileia shall be the head and metropolitan see over all the Churches of Italy, since we know that it was established before all the others and founded in the faith of Christ.

We also wish holy Aquileia to be, in all matters of faith, special, vicarial, and second after this holy Roman see, just as it appears formerly to have been granted by blessed Peter the apostle.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we grant to you and your successors the pallium, which we wish you to use when celebrating the solemnities of Mass: at the Nativity of the Lord, at the solemnity of the Epiphany, at the four feasts of Saint Mary, at the dedication of the same church, on the day of its anniversary, on Maundy Thursday, on Holy Easter, at the Ascension of the Lord, on the day of holy Pentecost, at the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, at the feasts of all the apostles, at the feast of All Saints, and at all the other principal feasts, as well as at the consecration of bishops.

We also command that you use the *rationale* at the other feasts in the same manner as the pallium.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to you and your successors all the bishops belonging to the holy Church of Aquileia, as well as the monasteries … and all the parishes belonging to the same patriarchate, together with all their plebes, titles, churches, chapels, castles, villages, cultivated and uncultivated lands, or their tithes, with their produce and revenues, with all their equipment and appurtenances, whether already acquired or yet to be acquired, whatever can be said or named.

We also confirm to you and your successors the island called Grado, with all its possessions, which had been taken away from the same Church of Aquileia by a barbarous attack and falsely used the patriarchal name. Concerning this island many of your predecessors, in the time of my predecessors and of many emperors, issued complaints through many synods. Your rival was summoned to these synods many times by synodal sentence and imperial command, but refused to come.

For this reason, and also at the intervention and request of our beloved son Conrad, august emperor, we convened a synod at which many bishops from our own region, as well as Lombard and Teutonic bishops, and abbots were present. He himself, although canonically summoned to it, delayed coming.

Therefore, by the judgment of all the bishops who were present, the same island was restored there with all its possessions, so that it might be lawful for you to govern it according to God and according to your desire, together with everything that is known to lie under or belong to the jurisdiction and dominion of the aforesaid patriarchate, just as blessed Peter the apostle formerly entrusted it to his disciple Mark the Evangelist and to his successor, the distinguished man Hermagoras.

Therefore, establishing this by apostolic censure under the adjuration of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we forbid that any pontiff who succeeds us, any bishop, or any person great or small should ever presume to perform any ordination throughout the boundaries of your patriarchate or within the dominion belonging to your bishops without your consent and that of your successors, so that, with God’s help, the orders of the Churches may diligently increase.

If anyone, however—which we do not desire—should by reckless audacity become a transgressor of this apostolic privilege of ours, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God, of Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and of us, who exercise their office, he is bound by the bond of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God.

But whoever observes in all things the institution of this letter of ours may deserve to obtain from God, who lives and reigns forever and ever, the grace of blessing, eternal life, and absolution from all his sins. Amen.

Written by the hand of John, cardinal and chancellor, in the place of Peter the deacon, in the month of September, in the tenth indiction.

[Col. 1139D]

[Note: Here, in place of “the tenth indiction,” the eleventh indiction must be restored. For Ughellus, in volume I, quotes another privilege granted to the bishop of Silva Candida, written by the hand of George, regional notary and scribe of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December, indiction ten. After the subscription of the twenty prelates named in it, it reads: “Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January through the hands of Benedict, bishop of Porto, and in the place of Peregrinus, etc., in the third year of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the nineteenth, [Col. 1140D] in the most holy see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the month of December, indiction ten”—that is, in the year of Christ 1026.

Since in that year of Christ he reached the third year of his pontificate on 17 December, in the preceding subscription the eleventh indiction must be restored in place of the tenth; otherwise he would count the fourth year of his pontificate in September 1026 and the third year in December of that same year. Pagi, *Annales Baronii*, vol. IV, p. 123.]

Issued by the hand of Boso, bishop and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the month and indiction written above, in the most holy see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the fourth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the nineteenth.

## VIII. John XIX Confirms the Property and Rights of the Church of Tibur at the Request of Bishop Benedict

(Fragment—year 1029.) [UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1307.]

To our beloved son in Christ and spiritual son, Benedict, consecrated by us bishop of the holy Tiburtine Church … We also confirm the churches that your predecessor, Bishop Boso, consecrated in the present year, namely those of Saint John and blessed Juvenal.

In the name of … In the seventh year of the pontificate of our lord John XIX in the most holy see, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth day of the month of January, John, bishop of the holy Tiburtine Church, with the consent of the entire congregation of the bishopric of Saint Lawrence, martyr of Christ, grants to all the venerable clergy and priests the entire half of the deceased persons of the city of Tibur belonging to him, under oath by the priests, with the penalty above of three ounces of refined gold [the reading *obritiae* is uncertain]. Tedemandus, citizen and notary, wrote this.

[Col. 1140A]

+ John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, of the holy Tiburtine Church.

## IX. At a Synod, John XIX Restores the Patriarchate of Grado to Urso, Its Patriarch, after It Had Been Reduced under the Authority of Poppo, Patriarch of Aquileia, Contrary to Law and Right

(Year 1029.) [MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 491.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

If mortals were not inevitably threatened, through the fault of their first parent, with the accident of perishing, no reason at all would compel them to commend to future ages, in indelible writing, the deeds of those people—good as examples or evil as warnings; nor would it be less fitting to examine the authors who are present and follow the written acts.

But because, as has been stated above, through the offense of our first parent the condition of all subsequent generations began to decline, human prudence wisely found that its own deeds ought to be recorded, lest they perish with it, whether for the instruction of future ages or for the avoidance of what might be obscure. Thus the record itself, outlasting forgetful generations, might indicate what had been useful and what had been uselessly done, and might, through clear investigation, distinguish truth from falsehood at the proper time.

If it has been decreed that this be observed in secular affairs, it must be observed with still greater care and diligence in ecclesiastical matters. Those who are devoted to eternal tranquility fear the storm of the world all the more; they flee the unrest of mortals all the more because they desire to please the living God alone throughout the ages.

For this reason we wish it to be known to all the sons of the holy Church of God what, in our times, through the devil’s agitation—alas!—was stirred up between Urso, patriarch of Grado, and Poppo, patriarch of Forojulium, and to what outcome it was brought.

When the people of Venice conspired against their lord, the doge, and against the aforesaid patriarch, his brother, each of them, setting aside the dignities and concerns that belonged to him, withdrew elsewhere until, once the secular disturbances had been quieted, they could return to their own places, as the subsequent outcome of events demonstrated.

Meanwhile, inflamed by his ancient zeal, the enemy, Poppo, patriarch of Forojulium, went to the city of Grado. He asked the citizens to receive him as the helper of his fellow patriarch of Grado and of his friend the doge. When they were unwilling to agree, he confirmed by an oath to God and to eight of his men—as we learned from the report of Patriarch Urso, from many Venetian nobles, and from the bishops of the province—that he would enter the city in order to preserve it safely for the doge and for his brother, the patriarch.

After he had entered, however, he forgot his oaths. In the manner of the pagans, as we have learned concerning secular affairs, everything found in the church was plundered with a hooked hand. The nuns of two monasteries were raped and violated by his men, and he spared neither the monks.

Moreover, removing the bodies of the dead, which desired rest, from their own tombs, he transported them dishonored to his own city. He likewise carried away the relics with him, though fewer than he desired. He broke the altars and carried off the treasures. He left the city of Grado fortified by his men, although deprived of certain patrons.

Not satisfied with this, he added iniquities to iniquities (Psalm 68:28). He sent his envoys to us, asking that we confirm all his places for him, and specifically the island of Grado.

When I replied that it did not justly or canonically belong to him, and that ancient privileges did not assign it to him, they said:

“Our lord does not ask that it be confirmed to him in any other way than as it was confirmed to his predecessors and to his Church through the privileges of your predecessors; it appears to belong to him justly and canonically, and he can prove this and promises to do so.”

After hearing this, we did not think that he would dare to mock the apostolic see, especially since we knew that for this very reason Patriarch Urso had been summoned to Rome by Pope Benedict of good memory, and had admitted that he could not come under the pretext of fear of the emperor. Although he sent his envoys, we yielded to his requests and instructed our son Peter the deacon and chancellor to give him a privilege.

We also ordered that the matter of the island of Grado be inserted, as you will hear:

“Moreover, we confirm to you the island of Grado with its possessions, as it is known justly and canonically to belong to you and to your Church through ancient privileges, and as you yourself can justly prove at any time and promise to do so, so that it may be lawful for you to govern it according to God.”

The whole matter turned out to be the opposite of this. For it was not proved that the island justly belonged to him. When he was summoned to give satisfaction to the patriarch of Grado concerning this, as he had promised, he delayed coming. Nor did he govern the island according to God, nor did he demonstrate, as he had promised, that it belonged to him through ancient privileges.

The privilege, written under the aforesaid condition and confirmed by our hand, was sent through his messengers.

Less than three days after their return, a messenger of the patriarch of Grado arrived, presenting us with a mournful letter. When we had read it, we were overcome by great sorrow. But, recovering hope from the fact that he had promised that he could prove at any time that he possessed justice, we sent our messenger Gregory, a man proven in faith and distinguished by every eloquence, to both parties, with letters fatherly summoning them to our synod.

When Poppo saw the letters, he was angered … As Gregory reported, he did not even bow his head, but rather denied the tenor of the privilege. He complained that he had lost the island of Grado and declared that he could not come to our synod for any reason whatsoever. But concerning the wording of the privilege, he was shown in that very place to be a liar, because Gregory produced the copy.

As Gregory was returning, Patriarch Urso joined him and came to us, having been summoned. When Poppo, patriarch of Forojulium, learned this, he sent a certain monk as his envoy to us, equipped with neither a credible argument nor the just defense that he had promised. When I wished to retain him after hearing of the arrival of Patriarch Urso, he took flight.

The patriarch of Grado came before us and complained tearfully for three days. Afterwards, a synod was convened in the church of blessed Sylvester within our palace. The venerable bishops Peter of Piperno, Benedict of Porto, Dominic of Labico, Boso of Tibur, Reginerius of Nepi, Benedict of Cerveteri, Dodo of Nocera, Peter of Palestrina, John of Blera, John of Orte, Azo, Amatus or Benedict were seated with us, as were the deacons Benedict the archdeacon, Crescentius, Peter the archdeacon and chancellor, Crescentius and Raynerius, deacons and cardinals, Stephen, Peter, John and another John, and many other bishops, priests, and deacons, whose signatures are seen below.

All the events were reported in order, and the privileges of our predecessors were produced—namely those of the most holy Pelagius, Gregory and Honorius, Stephen and Gregory, Leo, Sergius and Leo, Benedict, Adrian, Boniface, Romanus, Theodore, Anastasius, John, Sylvester, and Sergius. Following their example, and taking into account the many provisions established concerning the same See of Grado, the synod reached the following decision: by the judgment of our bishops, we were to make a privilege of confirmation for Urso and his successors concerning the perpetual stability of that see.

And so we did. Establishing this by apostolic censure under the adjuration of divine judgment, we decreed that no one at any time should presume to disturb or molest the aforesaid Patriarch Urso or his successors concerning the aforesaid patriarchate of Grado or its property and possessions.

Rather, the frequently named patriarch of Grado and his successors were to possess it in its entirety, peacefully and without any opposition, forever. Moreover, no one was to be permitted to elect his suffragan bishops without the voluntary consent of him and his successors.

Whatever he or his successors should issue according to canonical rule for the care of the Church entrusted to them, we command that it be observed both by their suffragan bishops and by the clergy and people.

But whoever should presume to violate or transgress in any respect these provisions promulgated by us out of pious concern, let him incur the anger of almighty God and perish, pierced by our anathema; let him also be condemned forever with the devil and lament.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours may deserve the grace of the holy Trinity, enjoy our blessing, and rejoice throughout the ages of ages.

Written by the hand of George, scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the eighth indiction. + Farewell in health.

I, Benedict, bishop of Porto, was present and subscribed.

I, Boso, bishop of the holy Tiburtine Church, subscribed.

[Col. 1143A]

## X. Letter of Pope John XIX to Peter, Bishop of Gerona, Concerning the Privilege of the Pallium

(Year 1030.) [FLOREZ, *España Sagrada*, XLIII, 430.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Gerona and beloved son in Christ: perpetual salvation in the Lord and apostolic blessing.

Because we do something for the sake of your love, we trust that we please God all the more devoutly because we know that your way of life is glorified by both evangelical and apostolic [Col. 1143D] testimonies. For it is referred to his praise that which is said: “He who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him.” If, therefore, through charity we remain in God and God in us, and without it we cannot please God, we ought to place it first in all our works without interruption.

And because, urged by the pastoral concern with which we seem to have been divinely endowed, we asked you, when you came to the threshold of the apostles, whether we might redeem certain captives from the Spaniards, you replied that you wished and were able to redeem thirty captives and grant them freedom for the remedy of our soul, if we would grant you the use of the pallium twelve times a year. Therefore, inflamed with zeal for God, who redeemed them with his own blood, [Col. 1144A] we have granted your request and conceded to you the right to wear the pallium only twelve times a year: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, at the Epiphany, at the Lord’s Supper, at the Resurrection of the Lord, on the Monday of the Resurrection, at the Ascension of the Lord, at Pentecost, on the feast of All Saints, at the Assumption of holy Mary, at the feast of Saint Saturninus, and at one council of your diocese.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by the modest vigor of your conduct, we urge you to make it correspond with the adornments of your character, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be conspicuous in both respects. Therefore, let your life be a rule for your sons. If any crookedness has been introduced into them, let them be straightened by it; in it let them see what they should imitate; by continually considering it, [Col. 1144B] let them advance, so that, after God, their having lived well may appear to be due to you.

Therefore, let neither temporal prosperity, which flatters, exalt the heart, nor adversity cast it down; but whatever it may be, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience. Let hatred find no place with you, nor undiscerning favor; let the wicked recognize strictness, let evil suggestion not make the innocent guilty in your eyes, and let favor not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself indulgent toward offenders, lest you permit what you have not punished to be committed. Let there be in you both the sweetness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of a judge: the one to cherish those who live innocently, the other to restrain the disorderly from wickedness by striking them when they must be struck.

But since sometimes the zeal of superiors, when it wishes to be a strict avenger of the wicked, [Col. 1144C] allows correction to pass into cruelty, restrain anger by judgment, and examine the discipline of censure in such a way that you both strike down faults and do not withdraw your affection from the persons whom you correct. Show yourself merciful to the poor, insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let modest correction oppose those who oppress. Do not accept anyone’s person against justice, and do not despise anyone seeking justice.

Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither a rich man’s power may persuade you to hear anything concerning him outside the path of reason, nor a poor man’s humility make him despair of his own cause. Thus, by God’s mercy, you may be such as sacred reading commands, saying: “It is necessary that a bishop be irreproachable.” But you will be able to use all these virtues beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows it never departs from the right path.

[Col. 1144D] Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you carefully preserve them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly. May the Holy Trinity surround your brotherhood with the protection of its grace, and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to attain eternal sweetness.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## XI. Letter of Pope John XIX to Robert, King of the Franks, concerning the immunity of the monastery of Cluny. (A.D. 1024–1031.) [Bullarium Cluniacense, p. 7.]

[Col. 1145A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Robert, king of the Franks: most beloved greetings with apostolic blessing.

Since, O most devout king, now that the charity of many has grown cold and iniquity has abounded, the condition of the Church is being thrown into confusion in many places, not only by outsiders but also by those who are called sons in name only; the order of sacred religion is despised, piety and the form of justice are dishonored, and apostolic privileges, or even royal commands, are irreverently annulled in substance through their presumption: your sublimity ought to keep watch, so that, in the kingdom entrusted to you by God’s authority, the rule of the Catholic faith may retain its vigor, holiness and religion may splendidly hold the trophy of victory against the enemies of truth, and the sacred rite of the preceding Fathers may remain inviolate. Through these things, both your faith may receive the fullness of blessings, and the devotion of your subjects may thereby advance more and more toward an increase of virtues.

[Col. 1145B] For the responsibility of this matter is demanded not only from us, to whom pastoral care has been entrusted, but also from you, to whom it has been entrusted with the greatest accountability, to be rendered with the full dignity and power of kingship. For—and we cannot say this without profound grief—certain men of yours, introduced into the priesthood by an accursed transaction, are not satisfied with dissipating, after neglecting the order of religion, what they unjustly acquired in the pursuit of earthly luxury; they also attempt, to the accumulation of their own condemnation, to claim for themselves and misuse for their own purposes those places which the faithful, having built them from their own possessions and resources, entrusted by testamentary authority to the power of the Roman Church.

[Col. 1145C] Such men clearly desire to tear apart the very head, when they seek to separate the members from it, and do not cease to harass with injuries and insults those whom it regards as its own dependents. Miserable men, they are ignorant that the decrees of this holy see must be received and venerated by the sons of Mother Church with such pious faith that they accept them without hesitation as rules of the canons, since it has the right to judge concerning the whole Church; no one may quarrel with its decree or sit in judgment upon its judgment. The sentence of this judgment should all the less be annulled by anyone, since it is more certain that it is established by the firmness and authority of the apostle Peter.

[Col. 1145D] For the venerable Pope Leo, admirable teacher of holy doctrine, says in one place: “It is no small madness to mutter against him who has the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom as his protector and patron; all the more so if many words of an inflated spirit are let loose here, lest Peter’s vengeance perhaps be reserved for the future.”

[Col. 1146A] Therefore, desiring to drive the rage and insolent arrogance of such men far from our places, and especially and particularly from the monastery of Cluny, which is our own possession, we have wished to grant this privilege by apostolic authority to our dearest son Odilo and to his successors in perpetuity. We are sending it to your nobility with these letters so that it may be read aloud in the hearing of you, your priests, and your nobles, and confirmed, strengthened, and authorized by royal command and authority. Thus no priest or prince whatsoever may ever dare to quarrel or mutter against this decree of apostolic authority, lest, struck by apostolic anathema, he suffer the penalties of strict vengeance and, as a transgressor of the royal command, be deprived even of temporal goods, in addition to the punishments of hell.

## XII. Letter of Pope John XIX to Gauslenus, Bishop of Mâcon, in defense of the liberty and immunity of the monastery of Cluny from all episcopal jurisdiction. (A.D. 1024–1031.) [Bullarium Cluniacense, p. 8.]

[Col. 1146B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gauslenus, bishop of Mâcon: most beloved greetings with apostolic blessing.

The holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority presides over the remaining Churches as their head and hinge, suffers whatever dishonor is inflicted upon it all the more intolerably in proportion as the person by whom it was inflicted appears closer to its unity. Since you were raised to episcopal glory, you have appeared as a son and disciple of the Roman Church, and from now on you have been counted as such by us and by our predecessors.

[Col. 1146C] But now, we do not know by what novel presumption you have been enticed and inflamed with an unquenchable desire, so that you oppose your mother and raise your heel against us—your master through the merits of the apostle Peter. You disturb the monastery of Cluny, which shines forth in holiness before nearly all nations, is supported by apostolic privileges, withdrawn from everyone’s authority, and reserved to the judgment of the prince of the apostles and his vicars. You irreverently attack the venerable Father, Lord Odilo, abbot, even before unbelievers; you harass the brothers living there, who desire transient rest in order to obtain perpetual rest; and you strive to annul apostolic privileges.

[Col. 1146D] We regard this as though you were eagerly seeking to tear apart our own limbs—and as something that cannot occur without your ruin. Take care, carefully warned as you are, for the sake of your soul, and leave our singular monastery to us. Otherwise, while you desire to become its accomplice against us, you will by apostolic authority be made an outsider to our order.

If some suitable reason moves you against him, confidently seek our judgment, under which alone he remains. We, who protect him both from you and from everyone, do not permit anyone to claim prejudice against him.

## XIII. Letter of Pope John XIX to Bochard, Archbishop of Lyon, concerning the immunity of the monastery of Cluny. (A.D. 1024–1031.) [Bullarium Cluniacense, p. 9.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bochard, [Col. 1147A] archbishop of Lyon: most beloved greetings with apostolic blessing.

We are deeply grieved that Gauslenus, your suffragan of Mâcon, eagerly seeks to usurp, against apostolic privileges, the ordination and consecration of our monastery of Cluny; and we grieve all the more because he has become guilty of so many apostolic excommunications through sheer greed.

[Col. 1147B] Since we have understood that, for love of Saint Peter, whose singular monastery it is, you have favored and continue to favor his cause, we return thanks to you, increased by apostolic blessings, and ask you to continue doing so. We also ask you to forbid that bishop, as we have done in our letters, to seek consecration, ordination, or any right in our monastery, lest, while he unjustly seeks this, he be deprived by apostolic authority, because of his disobedience and upon the repeated complaint of so many Fathers, of that which is lawfully permitted to him.

## XIV. John XIX confirms the privileges of the monastery of Fulda at the request of Abbot Richard. (A.D. 1031.) [Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 351.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Richard, abbot of the venerable monastery of our Savior Jesus Christ and of the holy martyr Boniface, situated in the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fulda, and through you to all your successors.

It accords with apostolic governance to assist those endowed with devout religion through [Col. 1147C] kindly compassion and to grant the minds of petitioners their request with eager devotion. Therefore, since you asked me, dearest son, that the aforesaid monastery of Fulda be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the apostolic see, so that, specially established under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church, we favoring your pious desires commit to effect by this authority of ours what you have requested.

We therefore commend to your faith and discretion the aforesaid monastery, with all its movable and immovable possessions belonging to it, which it now has or, with God’s help, will have in the future. We also grant and give you the monastery of Saint Andrew, called Exailum, situated beside the basilica of [Col. 1147D] Saint Mary at the Manger (*ad Praesepe*), with all its dwellings.

We therefore confirm by the command of our privilege the monastery of Fulda, which the holy martyr of Christ Boniface first built, enriched with many ornaments and estates, and fortified with the defenses of kings and princes, together with all its cells, churches, courts, and everything belonging to it. We command and establish that no future abbot shall presume to receive consecration anywhere except from this apostolic see.

[Col. 1148A] For this reason we specially appoint and consecrate him, and wish him to be distinguished by the privileges of the Roman and apostolic see, so that the other Churches may know that the Church of Fulda is a special daughter of the holy Roman Church. To you, therefore, dearest son, we grant primacy among all the abbots of Gaul and Germany, in sitting and judging, and in holding council with the other abbots.

No bishop, archbishop, or patriarch may rashly celebrate the solemnities of Mass upon the altar of your patronage unless he has received permission from you. No person of princely rank may dare to subject either all or part of the possessions of this monastery to any mortal or grant them as a benefice, except the abbot alone, who is entitled to grant lawful benefices to his men and officials. But the Church of Fulda, as the special daughter of the Roman Church, shall serve it freely and securely.

[Col. 1148B] If, God forbid, any abbot of your monastery should become infamous through some crime, we command that he not suffer the judgment of summons until he has been heard by our apostolic see. It is also permitted to you, dearest son, and to your successors, the abbots of this monastery, following the custom of bishops, to appeal to the apostolic see for the defense of yourself and your Church, and to defend yourselves against all your rivals with the shield of Roman majesty.

Moreover, for love and reverence of the venerable Church of Fulda, we grant to you, dearest brother, and to your successors, the abbots, the use of the dalmatic and sandals in the celebration of Mass, so that in this too you may appear specially distinguished above others by the privilege of our love.

We have also decided, after deliberation, that at suitable times it should be reported to our concern for you how monastic religion is directed according to the rule and how the concord of the brothers is preserved through devotion to ecclesiastical [Col. 1148C] profession, lest, God forbid, under the pretext of this privilege, the disposition and conduct of your rectitude should in any way be turned aside from the norm of justice.

We also forbid, in accordance with the petition of Saint Boniface and the decree of our predecessor Zachary, that any woman enter the same venerable monastery. We further command and earnestly admonish that no human being remove anything from the revenues and estates, tithes, and other offerings of the faithful, or from the households belonging to the hospital of the poor or to the guesthouse entrance, or presume to receive anything from them as a benefice. Rather, as the most blessed martyr of Christ Boniface established, let everything remain valid and ordered, both what appears to belong to the uses of the brothers [Col. 1148D] and what pertains to the various functions of service.

Above all these things, we establish by the page of this decree that whoever—a prelate of any Church or a person endowed with any dignity—attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema; incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniarius of the Holy Roman See, in the month of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

## XV. Letter of John XIX to Jordan, Bishop of Limoges, and the other bishops of Gaul, concerning the apostolate of Saint Martial. (A.D. 1031.) [Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 417.]

[Col. 1149A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Jordan, bishop, and his clergy, and to all the bishops of Gaul: most beloved greetings with apostolic blessing.

It belongs to pastoral concern, whenever some controversy arises in the Church, to eradicate it at the root with the sickle of a severe tongue before it gains strength, and to sow in its place both divine and most holy examples that may make God’s harvest and [Col. 1149B] gladden it. Why we have undertaken such things, what follows will make clear.

The most blessed Martial, as we find in his deeds, was baptized by Peter, prince of the apostles, when Christ was teaching and commanding in the world. He was so inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit that, abandoning his parents, he chose to serve the Son of God alone; and, with the apostle Peter confirming it, he desired Christ as his Teacher and Lord, by whose blood he had been begotten. And so it happened.

For he was present at the raising of Lazarus; he was present at the Supper; he ministered at the washing of the feet. After the Passion, when they thought they were seeing a spirit, he saw Thomas touch the hands and side. When it was said to the apostles, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in [Col. 1149C] the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28), and so forth, and, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20), he heard these words.

He saw Christ ascending into heaven; he both saw and received the Holy Spirit descending in fiery tongues, and he used all languages. Then he adhered to the prince of the apostles, being related to him by flesh and his son by baptism. From Peter, at Christ’s command, he was sent to preach in the provinces of Gaul. There, removing an innumerable people from the worship of idols, he dedicated them to Christ by his teaching, confirming this holy and pious teaching by the gravity and piety of his conduct, by raising the dead, restoring the lame, giving sight to the blind, and performing every kind of wonder.

[Col. 1149D] Now, as we have heard, certain men among you presume to disparage him, as though he had nothing in common with the apostles but only with confessors. They seem not to speak but to rave, since, weighed down by bundles of sins, they attempt to judge in heaven.

We call our Peter, to whom the keys of heaven were entrusted, a confessor because he confessed Christ, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). We call him an apostle because he was sent by the Lord himself to preach. We call him a martyr because, preaching Christ, he ended his life by martyrdom. We believe him to be the prince of the apostles because he established apostles, such as Mark, his son by baptism, and Matthias, chosen by lot, Luke, disciple [Col. 1150A] of the apostle Paul, and Barnabas, and very many others.

Or do they perhaps refuse to admit these among the apostles because they were chosen and sent by apostles, while they do not wish Martial to appear distinguished by apostolic dignity because he was not one of the Twelve?

They think that there are no other apostles except those Twelve. But what of what the apostle Paul says to the Philippians? “I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, but your apostle and minister of my need” (Philippians 2). We also find Silas and Judas called apostles by the apostles.

[Col. 1150B] The Church of the English, even to this day, calls the most blessed Gregory, whom we call a confessor, its own apostle. Roman pontiffs are called apostolic because they act in the place of an apostle. Since, therefore, the name “apostle” is not a matter of number but of commission, whoever, with God revealing it, is sent to preach and by his pious exhortation and example frees the people divinely entrusted to him from the power of the devil may rightly be called an apostle, because “apostle” means “one who is sent.”

[Col. 1150C] We, however, built upon the firm rock, declare that Martial, of whom we speak, may be called an apostle, whether Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to whom he was bodily joined and whose glory he saw and whose blessing he received, counts him among confessors or among apostles. We also judge that apostolic offices may equally be performed for him in the divine mysteries. Nor do we believe that anyone can doubt his blessedness when one enviously strives to deprive of apostolic dignity him whose name corresponds to his sacred deeds.

So that the reverence and celebration of so great an apostle might be more exaltedly remembered throughout the whole world, we have built and dedicated in his honor a most beautiful altar in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter at Rome, on the southern side of the church, on the third day before the Ides of May. There the memory of that holy man is devoutly venerated every day, and especially on the day of his birth, which is the day before the Kalends of July, is remembered more sweetly each year.

## XVI. Letter of John XIX to Saint Odilo, Abbot of Cluny—rebuking him because he refused the archbishopric of Lyon. (A.D. 1031.) [Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 418.]

[Col. 1150D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odilo, abbot: most beloved greetings with apostolic blessing.

According to the teaching of the most blessed Gregory, many things appear good and are not. Nevertheless, since it is said, “If you ask, you will hear,” we judge that all the things of yours which appeared good are not good.

For what is holier in a monk than obedience? What is more acceptable in a Christian? Is not obedience better than sacrifice, according to the prophetic judgment? And the Lord’s voice says, “I desire obedience, and not sacrifice.” How greatly blessed Benedict extols it in his praises is not worth inserting here, since it is not unknown to you.

[Col. 1151A] We therefore perceive an injury to the holy Church of Lyon, which sought you in marriage because you were suitable for her; you even spat in her face. We pass over the injury to the holy people, whose governance you refused and still refuse, sparing only your life. We are silent about the fact that you disregarded the authority of so many prelates who admonished and entreated you to approach episcopal dignity, that you made yourself disobedient to the holy Roman Church and to us.

[Col. 1151B] We neither ought nor can leave this unpunished, unless perhaps obedience should wash away what disobedience stained and satisfaction cleanse what transgression defiled—that is, unless you obediently accept the governance of the aforesaid Church, which through disobedience you have despised until now; otherwise you will learn what bitterness or severity the Roman Church knows how to impose upon the deserving.

For just as this sacred governance must not be rashly usurped by anyone, so, when the Church requests it, it must not be avoided by anyone like you. Otherwise you will be guilty of the loss of as many people as you could have benefited by example and teaching for their salvation.

We speak plainly, and about matters which we confidently believe you fully know. Therefore let the written page now be silent, and let the tongue speak—that of Bishop Gaudfrid, to whom we have entrusted the disclosure of my will, as clearly as daylight, both to you and to your brothers and to the whole Church. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 1151D] What Hugh of Flavigny says—that Odilo was appointed archbishop of Lyon by Gregory VI—is adequately refuted by this letter of John. It is also certain that this honor was offered to Odilo after Archbishop Burchard, who died in 1033. John was still seated at that time. Glaber, in Book V, chapter 4, and Hugh in his *Chronicle*, relate the matter. Both attest that the supreme pontiff sent Odilo the pallium and ring, and that the holy man refused the honor; but that he accepted the pallium and ring so that he might reserve them for the future archbishop. Hugh adds that they were preserved at Cluny until his own time.]

## XVII. Letter of absolution granted by John XIX to Hugh, Bishop of Auxerre. (A.D. 1032.) [Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 419.]

[Col. 1151C]

John, by the grace of God bishop of the Roman see, to all the sons of the Church throughout the world.

There can be no greater sacrilege in the Catholic Church than to suppose that any stain of crime, especially in one who is penitent, cannot be dissolved by the key granted by the Lord to Peter. We must recall before the eyes of the mind the fall of that first shepherd himself: when he denied the Teacher, as soon as he repented he not only did not lose the rank or dignity of the apostolic summit, but Christ later entrusted him more clearly with the guardianship of his flock. This, we believe, was nothing other than a remedy for those who have fallen.

Therefore, to our brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, who confesses his sins to God and to us [Col. 1151D] and declares himself guilty, we promise that he will obtain from God, who makes the promise, the forgiveness of full indulgence, according to the assurance of the same one who said: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9). For this reason he ought to become especially dear to us: corrected by fear of God, he appears most humble, and in such persons God finds rest.

[Note: [Col. 1152D] As far as we can understand from the deeds of the bishops of Auxerre, our Hugh wished to be absolved by the supreme pontiff for this reason: although he was bishop of Auxerre and count of Chalon, he had undertaken and carried out wars ever since he had been ordained bishop.]

## XVIII. Letter of Pope John XIX to Bardo, Archbishop of Mainz. (A.D. 1032.) [Gudeni, *Codex diplomaticus*, I, 15.]

[Col. 1152A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother and fellow bishop Bardo, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Although it is fitting for all Christians to follow the charity of Christ, from whom they derive their name—for he loved us so greatly that by his own blood he freed us from the power of the devil—we, especially those who exercise priestly dignity, ought to follow charity in every respect, so that, according to divine speech, we may show that we love our neighbor as ourselves.

[Col. 1152B] Following this principle, our most holy predecessors, who by divine providence presided uniquely in the see of the blessed apostle Peter, devised the most sacred ornament: the pallium, to be worn during the solemnities of Mass as a sign of dignity and holiness. It seemed proper to grant it, as a means for cultivating every honorable moral practice, on certain feast days to other fellow bishops whom their benevolent works had made more distinguished than others.

Since your brotherhood has requested this and follows the example of your predecessors in wearing it, we grant it to you on the following feast days, namely: on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at the Epiphany, on the day of the Lord’s Supper, on holy Easter, at the Ascension [Col. 1152C] of the Lord, on holy Pentecost, on the feasts of holy Mary, on the birthdays of the apostles, on the feast of Saint Martin and of Saints Lambert, Alban, Sergius, Bacchus, Aureus, and Justina, at the ordination of your suffragan bishops and clergy, on the day of your birth, and at the dedication of your church.

We grant your brotherhood permission to have a cross carried before you, and we grant you permission to ride on horseback at festive stations. If anything should occur in your Church or in those of your suffragans that properly requires an apostolic judgment or the presence of an apostolic legate, and such necessity presses you that you cannot wait by any means, we judge by apostolic authority that you may settle it in our place, [Col. 1152D] provided that in this and in the matters written above you observe the measure which you know your predecessors used according to the privileges of our most holy predecessors.

The honor of these dignities must be preserved by the modest vigor of your conduct. Nevertheless, we urge you to make all the adornments of your character [Col. 1153A] correspond to them, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be conspicuous in both respects.

Therefore, let your life be a rule for your sons. If any crookedness has been introduced into them, let them be straightened by it; in it let them see what they should imitate; by continually considering it, let them advance, so that, after God, their having lived well may appear to be due to you.

Therefore, let neither temporal prosperity, which flatters, exalt the heart, nor adversity cast it down; but whatever it may be, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience.

Restrain anger by judgment, and use the measure of discipline in such a way that you both strike down faults and do not withdraw your affection from the persons whom you correct. Show yourself merciful to the poor, insofar as virtue permits; let your defense assist the oppressed; let modest correction [Col. 1153B] oppose those who oppress. You shall not accept anyone’s person against justice, and you shall not despise anyone seeking what is just. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither a rich man’s power may persuade you to hear anything concerning him outside the path of reason, nor a poor man’s humility make him despair of his own cause. Thus, by God’s mercy, you may be such as sacred reading commands, saying: “It is necessary that a bishop be irreproachable.” But you will be able to use all these virtues beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows it never departs from the right path.

Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood, these are the duties of the pallium and of the aforementioned virtues. If you carefully preserve them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly. May the Holy Trinity surround your brotherhood [Col. 1153C] with the protection of its grace, and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to attain eternal sweetness.

Written by the hand of Sergius, regional notary and scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

## XIX. John XIX confirms the transfer of the episcopal see from Ciza to Naumburg at the request of Bishop Hildiward. A.D. 1032. [Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, col. 481.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Hildiward, bishop of the holy Church of Naumburg, and to all your successors [Col. 1153D]: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

It accords with apostolic governance to assist those who make pious requests with benevolent cooperation and to grant the minds of petitioners their request with eager devotion. For from this we shall undoubtedly earn the greatest reward from God, creator of all, if venerable places are suitably ordered and brought by you into a better condition.

Therefore, dearest son, when you were absent, at the request of our most Christian son, the emperor Conrad, and of our brother Hunfred, archbishop of Magdeburg, as well as of those who bestowed their inheritance upon the Church—namely, Margrave Hermann and his brother Ekkihard—and especially for the great usefulness and security [Col. 1154A] of your Church, with the advice of our bishops and clergy, we granted permission to transfer the episcopal see from Ciza to Naumburg.

Now, since you are present with your clergy, the more distinguished members of the people, and the messengers of the aforesaid emperor and archbishop, we approve what has been done with the advice of those same archbishops and clergy, and confirm it with perpetual stability both to you and to all your successors. For what we read was often done out of necessity according to the canons, we do not forbid to be done in our own times.

Since, therefore, the transfer of your see was carried out canonically and by the common consent of all to whom it pertained, let all your successors be elected without contradiction by the clergy and people of Naumburg and be regularly consecrated to the same title. [Col. 1154B] Let them be subject with every devotion of piety to the archbishops of Magdeburg, their metropolitans, whose diocese the transfer does not exceed.

With the council likewise consulted, we are pleased to add that the Church of Ciza, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, must not be entirely neglected. Instead, monks or canons shall be substituted in the place of the clergy who have moved to Naumburg, so that they may serve God there more fully from the revenues of that Church and, as sons of peace, may always devoutly obey their mother, the Church of Naumburg, in the Lord.

[Col. 1154C] If anyone, which we strongly do not believe, should presume through rash presumption to oppose this apostolic privilege of ours, or in any way contradict it, or become its violator, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, and of ourselves, he is bound by the chain of anathema, alien from the kingdom of God, and destined to share hell with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ; let him also be subject to excommunication until, repenting, he returns to satisfaction and suitable correction.

But whoever, out of regard for it, proves to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours may deserve to receive from the Lord the grace of blessing, eternal life, and the joys of the eternal kingdom, world without end. Amen.

## XX. Letter of John XIX on behalf of the monastery of Saint John at Angeriacum. (A.D. 1024–1033.) [*Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 466.]

[Col. 1154D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, vicar in the city of Rome of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to all the archbishops and bishops residing in Gaul, together with William, the devout duke of Aquitaine; Geoffrey, count residing in the city of Angoulême; also Elias, count residing in the city of Périgueux; likewise to the sons of Hugh residing at the castle of Leziniac; and also to William of Paterniac, and another William of Talamont; likewise to William, viscount, son of Kalon of Castello-Oniac; Aimeric of Taleburg; William of Surgeries; Albuin; and all the greater and lesser nobles residing in the regions of Aquitaine: most blessed greetings with apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1155A] We ask all of you, the aforesaid elders, and those who are not listed here by name, you and your successors forever, to observe the terms of this our decree—namely, that from this present day, the Kalends of May, you defend and kindly treat the monastery of the most holy and blessed forerunner and martyr of Christ, John, and of Reverentius, confessor of the Lord, situated in the place called Angeriacum, together with the religious lord Aymericus, father of that place, and the entire company of monks entrusted to him by God; and that you venerate it in every respect as is fitting, especially because we have heard that the rule of the most holy Father Benedict is being observed there inviolate.

Therefore we earnestly ask, and by command we command, that from this hour onward, throughout the ages of ages, no one dare violate any property [Col. 1155B] of the aforesaid monastery, nor—God forbid—presume to take anything from it, except solely with the consent of the father of that place and of all the brothers. But whoever wishes to observe this declaration of ours, let him have blessing from the Son of Saint Mary and from the forerunner of that same Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be absolved by the blessed apostle Peter and by me, the vicar of that same shepherd, from every bond of sins, etc. But fare well and pray for me.

## XXI. Letter 19 of Pope John to Count William (around 1030)

[Histoire générale du Languedoc, vol. II, Documents, p. 185, from the manuscript Chronicle of Amymericus de Peyrat, Colbert Library.]

[Col. 1155C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends his most beloved greeting and apostolic blessing to the lord William, glorious count.

We send to your kindness, as to a most beloved son, that you may heed our exhortation and do good to the monastery of Saint Peter of Moissac, so that blessed Peter himself, who is the shepherd and nourisher of all the faithful, may do good to you when you have been removed from this present life.

Arnaldus Oddo, viscount of Gascony and your knight, unjustly possesses two churches belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter. One is built in honor of Saint Martin, in the place called Orriolo; the other, of Saint Saturninus, is in Flamalinges. Command Arnaldus to restore to Saint Peter the two churches [Col. 1155D] with all their appurtenances, so that the brothers dwelling in the aforesaid monastery may receive from those churches what is rightfully theirs, and may daily beseech the Lord’s mercy on your behalf, so that when by divine summons you are carried from this light [Col. 1156A] by holy angels, you may have eternal rest.

But if you do not carry this out according to what we have sent you through the present letter, know by the authority of the apostle Peter that you are excommunicated, so that you may neither enter a church nor receive communion. Farewell.

## XXII. Letter 19 of John in which he urges all “doers of good” to undertake the restoration of the Church of Maguelone

(1024–1033) [Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, col. 570.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends his most beloved greeting, together with apostolic blessing and absolution, to all the doers of good in the Church of Maguelone, dedicated and to be dedicated to the honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, teacher of the nations. [Col. 1156B]

We have heard that the aforesaid Church of Maguelone, because of the demands of sins, has been reduced to nothing; and we grieve greatly, because the desolation of churches is recognized as a loss to Christians. For this reason we wish to urge both the Christians of the aforesaid Church and all those living round about to labor for the restoration of this church. By apostolic authority we promise that whoever strives to restore the aforesaid church—whether by offering from his own inheritance or possessions, or by returning benefices—will merit forgiveness and remission of his sins from the just Judge.

For he who offers his own property [Col. 1156C] and he who returns ecclesiastical benefices for the common good will receive one and the same reward, and will likewise enjoy apostolic blessing and absolution. But if any bishop, or anyone possessing an honor of whatever rank, wishes through evil intent to alienate, usurp, or sell what has been taken away there, let him be struck by the curse of anathema and be regarded as a stranger to the fellowship of Christians and to the kingdom of God.

We wish this decree to be confirmed by all the bishops whom Arnaldus will invite, as they will recognize below that we have done. Fare well.

Aldericus, bishop of Vercelli by the grace of God.

Reynaldus, bishop of Pavia by the grace of God.

Peter, who is called bishop of Santa Rufina, subscribed and confirmed.

Ismundus, archbishop of Embrun, confirmed.

Oldericus, bishop of the Church of Orléans +.

Raymundus, [Col. 1156D] bishop of Riez.

Deodatus, bishop of Luni, confirmed.

Alcuinus of Asti confirmed.

Vaudinus of Turin confirmed.

Bernardus of Agen confirmed.

Deodatus, bishop of Toulon, confirmed.

Peter, bishop of Marseille, confirmed.

# Letters of Various Persons to John

## I. Letter of Saint William, abbot of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, to John XIX

He warns him not to allow the Church of Constantinople to claim for itself the title “Universal.” (Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, VIII, 335.)

[Col. 1155D]

To Pope John, who by the grace of God and reverence for blessed Peter has obtained the most excellent seat in the world [Col. 1156D], William, servant of the cross of Christ, sends the seat of judgment with the apostles and the crown of the kingdom.

We are instructed by the words of the teacher of the nations that an elder must not be rebuked. Yet the same man says elsewhere: “I have become foolish; you compelled me.” Therefore, out of the diligence of filial affection, we urge your common fatherhood to imitate in one matter the Lord and Savior, who sees through the thoughts of human beings, and to say to someone united with you in mind, as he himself said to Peter: “What do people say about me?”

If his answer is given in faith, observe how it sounds. If it is clear, take care that it not be obscured; but if it is obscure, the Light of the World must be entreated that you may shine in such a way as to provide light for all who are established in the bosom of the Church, so that they may walk along the way of God’s commandments.

But there is a report of something that recently happened among you, concerning which anyone who hears it and is not scandalized should recognize that he is far removed from heavenly love. For although the power of the Roman Empire, which once ruled as a monarchy throughout the world, is now governed by countless scepters in different regions of the earth, the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth rests with the teaching office of Peter.

We have said this so that you may understand that the Greeks obtained what, as we have heard, they sought among you through no other means than vain glory—*cenodoxia*.
