In all other matters also, we wish you, as befits a universal prelate, to grow more vigorous in correction and discipline within the holy and apostolic Church, and to remain eternally and happily strong in Christ.

## II. The same author to the same person

He inveighs against the Simoniacs. (Mabillon, ibid., p. 330.)

Spare, I beg you, spare—you who are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Let it be enough that Christ was once sold for the common salvation of all. [Col. 1157C]

Now, renegades from the true light, shepherds in name alone, look behind you and see where the sheepfold of Christ—or rather, his members—are going. If the stream is lukewarm near its source, there is no doubt that it will stink when it flows far away. Therefore, care is sold to certain people for their own destruction.

I wish all of you shepherds and bishops together to remember the axe of the Judge, who stands before the door.

## III. Letter of Halinardus, abbot of Saint-Bénigne, to Pope John XIX

(Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, IV, Appendix, 728.)

To the holy lord, teacher of the whole world, namely John, universal pope: from the humble abbot of the house of Saint-Bénigne, together with the whole congregation, the service of faithful prayers.

[Col. 1157D] It is known throughout the world that the shepherd of the Roman Church exercises the apostolic office in such a way that whatever he establishes in the ecclesiastical order remains ratified, stable, and inviolate forever.

It is therefore fitting that the ruler of citizens should always have with him the philosophy of virtues—namely, discernment—lest he to whom authority over churches has been given establish something ignorantly because of whisperers, something which, once he has come to know the true antiquity, he would not hesitate to destroy.

This is clear; and for that reason we anticipate your judgment and say that it has been fully brought to our notice that our neighboring canons, longing to seize monastic honor, [Col. 1158A] intend to seek your authority and highness, so that, having received permission from you, they may transfer our cemetery to their castle.

You know, however, that those who wish to alter the ancient constitution of the Fathers seek not the things of God but their own. We therefore ask, for God’s sake, that you do not grant this; and we shall fittingly preserve the memory of your service.

## IV. Letter of Jordan, bishop of Limoges, to Pope Benedict VIII, concerning not placing Saint Martial among the apostles

[Note: [Col. 1157] In the meantime, after Pope Benedict had died, John XIX replied to Jordan’s letter.]

(Gallia Christiana, II, Appendix, p. 161.)

To our lord and venerable pope Benedict, beloved by God and human beings, Robert, king of the Franks by the grace of God; William, duke of Aquitaine; the archbishop of Bourges; the archbishop of Bordeaux; the archbishop of Tours; all their suffragans; and also Isambert of Poitiers, Arnaldus of Périgueux; Jesolo, Roo, and their other fellow brethren; Jordan, bishop of Limoges, who ordered this charter to be written—all send greeting and affection to the apostolic lord.

We know and believe that our Lord Jesus Christ chose twelve apostles for himself, to whom he gave the power of binding and loosing. One of these, Judas by name, fell; in his place the other apostles chose another, Matthias by name, in order to restore the number twelve.

To their company the Lord chose seventy-two others, whom he also called disciples. From among these, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, chose one named Martial, who was with him in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ; at the supper, and wherever our Lord displayed some miracle to his apostles, blessed Martial was present with Saint Peter.

After the Lord’s holy resurrection and ascension, blessed Martial, who had been one of the seventy-two disciples, remained attached to blessed Peter. Blessed Peter sent this Martial, together with two priests, Alpinianus and Austriclinianus, to preach to the Gallic people.

As they journeyed, they came to Els. There Austriclinianus, one of the priests, died. Immediately blessed Martial returned to Rome and announced to the holy apostle that one of his companions had died. The apostle said to him: “Take this staff for yourself, and when you reach the body, touch it with this staff of mine and say: ‘In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, rise, Austriclinianus; God will be the companion of your journey.’”

Blessed Martial carried out the holy apostle’s command, touched the body of Austriclinianus, and he was immediately restored to health. Then they set out and came to the city of Limoges.

There they found Duke Stephen worshiping idols with his entire household. Martial immediately preached to him in evangelical words, converted him to Christianity, and baptized him together with his whole household.

In the temple where the duke had previously worshiped vain and deaf idols, blessed Martial, with his two priests Alpinianus and Austriclinianus and with the assistance of Duke Stephen, built a basilica and dedicated it in honor of blessed Stephen, the first martyr. There he celebrated the divine mysteries, admonished and taught, until he brought the whole people of Aquitaine from the way of error to the true life, which is Christ.

He continued celebrating the solemn rites of Mass there until he died before the very altar of the protomartyr Stephen and, with great reverence from the angels, returned his soul to God. Duke Stephen buried his body outside the city with great honor, in the place where Saint Martial himself had built a church in honor of Saint Peter, his teacher.

Saint Aurelianus was his successor. Saint Martial himself had drawn him from the underworld. After him came Ebulus, Alicus, Ermogevianus, and other successors, thirty-six in all. I am the seventh, called Jordan, the least of them all.

All these regarded him as a most holy confessor; likewise all the abbots who have lived in his monastery down to the present day.

The abbot who is now in office, deceived by novelty and lifted up by pride, came to me—though I am inferior to my predecessors—and begged me to place the most holy confessor among the apostles in my council and at the synod. I refused to do so.

Persisting in his assertions, he, together with twelve monks of that monastery, pledged me his loyalty, promising that he would defend me with authority in every council. He could not do this at the council of William, duke of Aquitaine, in the presence of the archbishop of Bourges, Isambert of Poitiers, and their other suffragans.

All the bishops of the Franks, Auvergne, Gascony, and Aquitaine with whom I have spoken approve and confirm that the most holy confessor Martial ought not to be removed from the place in which the holy Fathers and our predecessors placed him, and that there is no apostolate unless it is confirmed by authority.

They offer this argument: “If I place Saint Martial, who was one of the seventy-two, among the apostles, they will place all those seventy-two among the apostles, and hold that wherever their bodies are buried, that very place possesses apostolic status.”

To you, then, I, Jordan, send this letter on behalf of the aforesaid persons: namely, King Robert, William duke of Aquitaine, all the archbishops—catholic men, that is—who oppose my placing Saint Martial [Col. 1160B] among the apostles.

But if you dare to do what your holy predecessors Gregory, Clement, Boniface, and many others did not do—to place confessors among the apostles—then, if it is a sin, let it be yours. I shall be free from guilt; it will be neither my iniquity nor my sin.

I shall show you the will of all the people of Aquitaine, because that deceptive abbot does this for no other reason than that he wishes to destroy the episcopal see of the first martyr and to debase the apostolate of Saint Peter.

Send me your letter by the bearer of this charter, and communicate your will to me in every respect. For the present I shall not be able to speak with you, but as soon as I am able I shall visit the threshold of Saint Peter.

[Col. 1160C] Fare courageously; carry out the commands of the Fathers; do not transgress.

# In the Year of the Lord 1038: Saint Godehard, Bishop of Hildesheim

## Life of Saint Godehard

By Wolferus, his contemporary and disciple, canon of the same church.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, VIII, 395, from the manuscript of Compiègne.)

## Preliminary Observations

### 1.

Besides Saint Bernward, whose Life we gave above under the year 1023, we have in this century another light of the German Church, supplied to us by the Church of Hildesheim. He is Godehard, whose acts were printed by Surius, Brouwerus, and finally the Bollandists, written by a serious author and a contemporary.

No one doubts the authority of this Life, although there is not complete agreement about the author’s name. Brouwerus and Surius attribute it to a certain Arnoldus, on the authority of several manuscript codices, from which they testify that they transcribed it. The Bollandists and the other more recent scholars, however, maintain that Wolferus was the first author of the Life, on the basis of an older manuscript of the abbey of Graecia.

Furthermore, in volume VII of May, in the Appendix, they cite another codex, namely the Bamberg manuscript, in which Wolferus is explicitly identified as the author of the Life.

We readily accept this latter opinion, provided it is granted that this Life, first written by Wolferus, was later reread by Arnoldus, who added several miracles lacking in the earlier Life. Wolferus dedicated his work to his teacher Albuinus, while Arnoldus likewise addressed it to Menghardus.

As a result, in some copies it is found dedicated by Wolferus to Albuinus, while in others—and indeed in most of them, although they are more recent—it is found dedicated by Arnoldus to Menghardus.

### 2.

This difficulty, however, ought to cause no problem, since everyone agrees that the first author of this work was a contemporary of Saint Godehard and had often, indeed intimately, associated with him. This is evident from the whole composition of the work, from which the same author’s sincerity in dedicating it and his discernment in distinguishing facts are also apparent.

It may be inferred that he was a canon because he reports that he heard Abbot Gunther preaching to his brothers in chapter, although he himself was outside the chapter with others; for monastic law permitted no one wearing the canonical habit to enter the chapter.

At other points, however, he seems to suggest that he had embraced the monastic life, since he declares that he was educated in the monastery of Altach and calls Athelbert his abbot.

For the rest, we conjecture that this Life was somewhat enlarged by a later author, since in certain manuscripts it is somewhat longer than in the others. Here we present it in full, but with those passages that not all the manuscripts contain enclosed in brackets, so that anyone may easily distinguish what is found in all the manuscripts from what appears only in some.

### 3.

After the Life we append the history of the translation of this same holy man, which was also written by an eyewitness. We could not omit a monument of such value, from which much can be extracted to illuminate ecclesiastical history.

From it we learn that Saint Godehard’s canonization took place at the Council of Reims under Pope Innocent II, who presided there, and that the decree itself is reported. These matters had been lacking in all editions of the councils.

It is also clear from this that the synod held at Liège under the same pontiff preceded the Council of Reims, although the editors of the councils assigned Reims the first place, heedlessly following the author of the Life of Saint Bernard in this matter, as Brouwerus observed.

Moreover, Bishop Bernard, chiefly through whose efforts Saint Godehard was entered into the catalogue of the saints, founded a notable monastery in honor of that most holy prelate. He laid its first stone in 1133, calling Benedictine monks from the monastery of Fulda, who had been formed there under Abbot Frederick and who, with God’s favor, continue there to this day.

Nearly all writers place Saint Godehard’s death on 4 May; some place it on the following day. We have preferred the former opinion, which appears more certain than the latter; but there is greater difficulty concerning the year.

Brouwerus assigned his death to the year 1037; with Henschenius, we assign it to the following year, as can be proved from the acts reported here. The same date is explicitly given in the manuscript Saxon Chronicle and in the Hildesheim Chronicle, which Franciscus Quercetanus published in volume III of the writers of Frankish history.

The memory of Saint Godehard is celebrated by nearly all the writers of Germany; his name appears frequently in the sacred calendars of the churches, although it is absent from the Roman Martyrology. In the Benedictine calendar he is commemorated on 4 May.

His sacred body is preserved in an underground crypt beneath the choir of the cathedral church. This does not prevent other—and indeed many—churches from boasting that they possess some portions of the relics of the same saint.

[Col. 1161]

# [Life of Saint Godehard]

## Letter of Wolfredus to Albuinus

[Col. 1161A] To my venerable lord and teacher Albuinus, adorned with the highest reverence and always to be honored with the fullest devotion, Wolferus, small in spirit and body, offers whatever is properly owed in return for the manifold debt of subjection.

[Note: [Col. 1161B] Brouwerus and others read “Menghardus,” and below “Arnoldus,” as stated in the preliminary observations. Some manuscripts give only the first letter of each name: M. A.]

As I was about to write the history of the life and formation of our blessed-father-and-shepherd Godehard, bishop, I hesitated anxiously for a long time, deliberating between hope and fear, because I knew that I was unequal and insufficient for so difficult and distinguished a work.

For in proportion as I was summoned by delight and hope in the virtues that the Lord displayed through him, I was frightened and held back by the manifold consciousness and fear of my own negligence. At length, however, obedient partly willingly and partly unwillingly to the commands of my teachers and brothers, and especially of the blessed man and true worshiper of God, our abbot Athelbert, [Col. 1161B] I attempted to reach such a height, and judged that I ought to offer the work more privately to your clemency, O noble teacher. With you there would be an easy opportunity for pardon of errors, a ready and impartial kindness in removing or adding material, or at least a prompt and unopposed speed of eternal silence.

Nor should you, venerable Father, disdain in astonishment or be astonished with disdain that you alone, from the general college of bishops, abbots, and teachers, are specially chosen, as it were, to inspect my trifling work. The prudent diligence of the aforesaid adviser and instigator of mine provided for this, especially because, through the merit of your faith and affection, the Life of our same Father has always shone before all others for you, both before and after his promotion to the episcopate.

He himself also opened to you, more privately and familiarly than to anyone else, the secrets of his heart, following the example of Christ and the disciple whom he loved.

For this reason, as I have said, he urged me—unequal and insufficient for such a work—especially because during the years of my adolescence I traveled back and forth between the monasteries of Herveld and Altach, after the manner of Orosius, [Note: [Col. 1161B] The presbyter Orosius undertook various journeys for the sake of learning. [Col. 1162B] Thus he was sent by Augustine to Jerome.] and because I frequently heard from Christ’s faithful people about his earliest deeds and, despite the small capacity of my still youthful intellect, gladly retained them.

I therefore call God to witness—he who examines the secrets of hearts—that I shall write nothing in praise of his memory except what I myself saw and heard, or learned from people who were truly truthful and also trustworthy.

This was especially so when I was away from Altach for the sake of study. I often enjoyed the companionship and conversation of a certain elderly priest named Reginoldus, [Note: [Col. 1162B] Two manuscripts, in Bollandus, read “Ratmundus”; two others, “Rumoldus.”] whom you knew better than I did; and, if God sometimes deigned to grant it, I was instructed in this very matter by his truthful account.

He had certainly remained attached to Godehard from infancy in faithful service, had first instructed him in the letters of sacred learning, and knew better than anyone all his words and deeds up to his monastic profession and even his promotion to the episcopate.

### 2.

I, too, in accordance with the customary manner of ancient obedience, have decided first to offer to your discernment whatever I may perhaps have been able to compile, whether suitable or unsuitable, so that through you errors may certainly be corrected, gaps filled, superfluities removed, necessities supplied, and, wherever I have gone astray—as I confess happens easily—my stupidity may obtain pardon.

Thus it may also be fortified against the mockery of those who attack it by the defense of so great an authority. Yet, with God as my witness, I am not greatly troubled if some puffed-up person mocks me for such things or reproaches me for having composed something overly verbose and inelegant, provided that I have constructed for serious students and God-fearing people a simple statement of the truth, and have set forth a reliable order of events and times for those who, perhaps with the inspiration and favor of the Lord’s Spirit, will later know and wish to adorn the Acts and Life of the aforesaid bishop with fitting reverence, once the cloud of envy has passed away and been extinguished.

I openly profess that I am willing to labor in the manner of a cleverer dog which, released at the hunter’s nod or sign, works throughout the day without interruption and almost without weariness—not to seize prey for itself alone, something it does not even presume to do, but to fulfill the playful will of its commanding master by capturing something rare and unusual.

In this way not only may the master rejoice more festively with his household, but the pleasure of a more sumptuous dinner may also be reserved for friends who might arrive later. In this manner, I say, I gladly profess that I labor—not to acquire praise for myself, which I neither deserve nor deem myself worthy to receive in this matter, but to offer, for the present and for posterity, as I have said, the everlasting memory of a just man, however unskillfully composed.

Why, then, should I be ashamed to be compared with dogs, which, I think, by the gift of the Creator possess greater and more excellent understanding among brute animals, since even that Canaanite woman of the Gospel was not ashamed—indeed, she rejoiced—to be compared by the Lord with dogs, and Lazarus, despised by the rich man, did not shrink from being comforted by their licking?

For in proportion as they are superior to brute creatures, they are nearer to rational beings.

Nor should any of the faithful be disturbed by what those aforementioned mockers object to my foolishness: that it is unfitting to publicize the allegedly lowly lineage of so distinguished and renowned a man [Note: [Col. 1163D] Bollandus reads this way, and more correctly according to the author’s meaning, who here is speaking of the obscurity of Saint Godehard’s family. Brouwerus and our codex, however, read [Col. 1164D] “intimate.” From this passage the opinion of Crantzius and certain others is rejected, namely, that Godehard was descended from the family of the princes of Bavaria.], and that it would be better, as they think, to conceal it by silence in his praise.

For anyone of sound judgment does not pay such attention to the empty boasting of noble birth as to the more useful privilege of divine inspiration. To such people no one appears noble except one who is proven to have been ennobled by virtue, since it is written: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3).

And the prophet says: “The Lord makes poor and enriches; he raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to seat him with princes and grant him the throne of glory” (1 Samuel 2).

We describe this as having been truly fulfilled in him, with the whole holy Church as witness, because we saw him led by the Lord along straight paths, made great in the sight of kings, seated gloriously among princes, speaking wisdom among princes, and happily holding the throne of glory.

Hence none of the faithful doubts that he now rejoices, undoubtedly, among the order of holy priests before Christ.

If, therefore, the statement of my frivolous loquacity has gone beyond what is permitted or pleasing in its prolonged speech—a result certainly caused by timidity, which fears everything, even what is safe—you, distinguished Father and teacher, who are believed both to owe this to the memory of the aforesaid bishop and to desire it for our ignorance: you, I say, in whom lies both the skill to approve and the power to reject, wisely provide, disregarding the criticism of anyone, that what is inept and useless be buried in eternal silence, while what is beneficial, by the Lord’s gift, be brought forth without the taint of flattery.

For if anything departs from the truth, it will be attributed not to my incompetence but to your negligence. But if anything should prove more suitable, it will be your part, not mine, as a certain man said while humbling himself:

“If anything pleases when spoken, the praise will belong to the adviser.”

# Prologue

[Col. 1163]

[Col. 1163D] Because the evangelical voice of Truth commands that a lit lamp be placed not under a bushel but on a lampstand for the illumination of the faithful (Matthew 5), and because we are commanded to conceal the secrets of kings, whereas the works of God are rightly to be revealed and magnified (Tobit 12), we have therefore judged it worthy and even glorious to present the Life of our blessed and venerable Father Godehard, bishop, insofar as divine clemency permits, as an example to the present and future generations, and to set forth for those who fear God the credible teaching of his deeds. [Col. 1164D]

We truly fear that we are not free from the guilt of negligence if we allow, beneath the silence, those things that we both saw and heard in him and that are worthy of praise. For Bavaria, once cultivated from the beginning by the plow of God’s word and sufficiently made fertile by the seed of the sacred faith, sent him to us, through Christ’s permission, as a true teacher of religion and as a physician for us, who needed one.

We Saxons—or rather, Saxon-born people—and, as is thrown at us in mockery and derision, long untamed by the word of God, are not free from danger if, through the hardening of domestic indolence, we neglect his glory by silence. [Col. 1165A]

# Here Begins the Life

[Col. 1165]

### 4.

[Col. 1165A] In the seven hundred and forty-first year of the Lord’s Incarnation, when Charles I [Note: [Col. 1165C] Here the author calls Charles Martel “Charles I.” Although he did not use the title of king, everything was nevertheless in his power, so that he left the kingdom to his sons to administer in the same manner. Finally, after Childeric had been deposed, Pippin assumed the title of king, which he already possessed in fact.]—son of the first Pippin, son of Ansegisus, son of Arnulf—departed this life and left the kingdom to his sons Carloman and Pippin; and in the following year this Pippin fathered Charlemagne, the monastery of Altach was wisely begun by worshipers of Christ and happily completed in the religious discipline of monastic life [Note: [Col. 1165D] The printed editions read: “was happily completed about fifteen years before the division of the bishoprics,” which took place after the following year in Bavaria through Saint Boniface the archbishop. [Col. 1166C] The manuscript of Graecia, however, in Bollandus’s notes, reads as follows: “Wisely begun by Saint Pirminius and the lord Odilo, duke of Bavaria, together with other worshipers of Christ, and happily completed in the religious monastic institution, before the division of the bishoprics, which took place ten years later in Bavaria through Saint Boniface,” etc.], before the division of the bishoprics that was carried out ten years later in Bavaria by Saint Boniface the archbishop, by decree of Pope Zachary and with the consent of King Pippin.

This occurred after his brother Carloman, three years earlier, had been tonsured and made a monk at Rome and had relinquished to Pippin his hereditary share of the kingdom and property. At that time Eichstätt was entrusted to Willebald, Salzburg to John, Freising to Erembert, and Regensburg to Gaibald [Garibald], and the Christian religion was there worthily strengthened for God.

In the aforesaid monastery, the service of Christ prospered happily from the beginning and advanced laudably for nearly a hundred years in the monastic way of life, until that detestable dissension began between the emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, and his sons Louis, Lothar, and Charles; and afterward, when the emperor had died, it continued for many years among the brothers themselves, as the chronicles testify.

In that period, many churches were stripped of their possessions and monasteries thrown into disorder. Among them, the property of the same Church of Altach, which had been bestowed there by the faithful and had until then remained undisturbed, was plundered [Col. 1165C] and divided among those serving this crime, according to the will of the rioters, as a benefice—or rather, a malefice.

Because of this necessity, the monastic observance there came to an end. Nevertheless, under the rule of canons the same place continued for a hundred years, until the time of Duke Henry, of blessed memory, whom we later saw become emperor. [Note: [Col. 1166D] This is Henry, duke of Bavaria and emperor, renowned for his holiness.]

The pious king Otto, son of King Henry the Saxon, often resolved to restore it in certain places, but he could not accomplish this because of widespread misfortune and, above all, because the schemes of his brother, Duke Henry of Bavaria, obstructed him.

Indeed, at the first royal appointment, in the presence of their father and the princes, Henry resisted him, boasting in a sort of playful indignation that he was nobler. He always persisted in that vain purpose, privately and secretly against his brother the king, and publicly against the king’s son Louis [others read “Ludolfus”], as Bavaria still testifies.

### 5

Therefore, a boy of outstanding character, named Godehard, was happily born and brought up near the monastery of Altach, in the village of Rithenbach in the diocese of Passau, by truly Christian, devout, and honorable parents. While still a very young child, he devoted himself to the study of letters, in a manner somewhat contrary to his parents’ intention.

[These were the schools he attended, near the monastery of Altach, across the river Danube. **Note:** This miracle is absent from our manuscript codex, as are many other passages that are enclosed in brackets at their proper places. When the holy boy rose in the morning and came near the Danube to visit the schools, since there was no bridge there by which he could cross the river, God providing, whether going to the schools or returning from them, he found someone who supplied him with a safe and unharmed passage across the river.]

In that same monastery the boy in question was faithfully offered by his parents and devoutly received by the brothers. By the Lord’s gift, he commendably drank in the draught of literary knowledge and willingly received an understanding of divine law, insofar as his still childish intellect allowed, in accordance with the saying: “Learning is easiest where the Spirit of God is present as teacher.”

[For from the earliest flower of his childhood, or rather of his youth, the holy boy began to shun vanities and avoid frivolities. He preferred to take up God’s yoke and pursue the paths of the virtues rather than follow the vanities of this world, as that age is always accustomed to do. He began to advance without slackness from good to better, and from better to best. For this reason he was always wearing away the thresholds of the church, so that there he might drink in the streams of sacred law and thereby intoxicate his thirsty mind. The fear of God was with him, drawing him back from every childish wantonness. Thus he presented himself to everyone in such a way that he most clearly appeared to be an instrument of the Holy Spirit. Hence it also happened that, although he remained among religious men in secular clothing, he plainly attracted many of the religious to holiness of life.]

### 6

When he had spent several years in the said monastery of Altach living this praiseworthy life of good and honorable conduct, had reached the years of adolescence, and the reputation of his holy life had spread throughout Bavaria,

[Col. 1167A]

at that time the blessed man Christian,

[**Note:** Bollandus has “Frederick of Juvavum,” that is, the archbishop of Salzburg, and considers this more correct. Hundius, in volume II of *The Salzburg Metropolitan Church*, where he discusses the lower monastery of Altach, reports that Godehard was ordained acolyte and then subdeacon by Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg, who at that time held Altach as a benefice, and that he was also made provost of the canons. He thinks that everything said here about Christian does not fit well, since Christian himself was elected bishop of Passau in 991, at which time Erchambert was already administering the monastery of Altach; according to the same Hundius, at the place cited, Erchambert is said to have begun governing the monastery in 990.]

bishop of Passau, governed that same monastery as a benefice during the time of the elder Duke Henry. The brothers assembled there for divine service, after recognizing the boy’s praiseworthy character in the fear of God,

[they informed the bishop of Passau, who at that time governed the same monastery as a benefice, by commending the boy to him.

**Note:** So the Bodec manuscript in Bollandus’s Appendix; the others read: “they made him known to the bishop.”]

When he heard this, being certainly a most prudent man, he gave thanks to God and, having taken the boy away from there, received him into his household. When he recognized that, through Christ’s grace, the boy was ascending from virtue to virtue, he loved him even more, rejoicing in the ability divinely bestowed upon him,

[and entrusted to him the office of chancellor,

[Col. 1167B]

in which office he conducted himself in such a way that he showed himself to everyone to be an instrument of divine wisdom,]

and for three years he took him with him on various difficult journeys of military expeditions and other travels, as though for the purpose of testing him, and instructed him more devotedly in the catechism of the sacred faith and religion.

[But the holy young man Godehard feared that, amid the many affairs by which he was encumbered, something vain might slip into his mind. Therefore he asked permission to withdraw from the aforesaid bishop; having obtained it only with difficulty, he]

sent him back, adorned with the rank of subdeacon, when the brothers of the same monastery earnestly requested him as a supplement to the divine service. There, throughout the period of his adolescence, he watched over the pursuit of holy conduct more keenly from day to day, and devoted himself more fervently to the common advantage and benefit of the brothers: he anticipated his elders in honor, according to the Apostle (Rom. 12:10); encouraged his peers by upright examples; and frequently urged his subjects toward better things with sacred admonitions. Thus, with divine mercy accompanying him, he soon attained the discipline of true religion in its fullness, was raised to the dignity of deacon, and—God having predestined it, as later became clear—was appointed provost of that same monastery.

### 7

Then, in the year 988 after the Virgin’s childbirth,

[**Note:** “Eighty-third” should be read; in that year Otto II died.]

when the emperor Otto II had been removed from this life after the exceedingly dangerous and also most disastrous war in Calabria, still notorious throughout the world for its devastation and disgrace, and had been buried at Rome with the profound grief of all Christendom, though with sufficient honor; after the rash destruction of the bishopric of Merseburg,

[**Note:** Dithmar gives a fuller account of the destruction of the church of Merseburg in Book III. Its possessions were distributed among various parties, and the see itself, deprived of its episcopal seat, was subjected to the church of Halberstadt; the abbey was erected in place of the cathedral church. This continued until the year 1005. For then, as Dithmar relates in Book VI, King Henry, wishing to correct the blemish of his predecessors, restored the bishopric of Merseburg and gave it to his chaplain Wigbert, whom he subsequently enriched with many possessions.]

and after the death of Count Gero, innocent, according to the voice of the people, the aforementioned Henry, duke of Bavaria and father of the emperor Henry, had been removed from office by his cousin the emperor seven years earlier because of the disloyalty and tyranny that he had exercised against him in the manner of a father. Then, on the pretext of seeking justice,

[Boll.: “of justice”]

and hoping to gain the kingdom, he was vainly exalted by the madness of arrogance. At the instigation of his seducer, he attempted to crush the lordly son, the heir to the kingdom worthy by God’s ordinance, and to raise himself to rule the kingdom as monarch. Yet his foolish plot was peacefully suppressed by the kingdom’s leading men who truly feared God, especially Willegis, metropolitan of Mainz, and Bernard, duke of Saxony. After many things, appropriate and inappropriate, which are better left silent here because they are more fully contained in the Chronicles, his former dukedom was restored to him.

On the approaching day of the Nativity of the Lord, the boy Otto honorably received the crown of the kingdom from the aforementioned metropolitan and began happily to grow, in the manner of his ancestors, in every ecclesiastical perfection. The initial indication of his praiseworthy ability was that, in the seventh year of his accession, he caused the aforementioned monastery of Altach, with the counsel of the bishops and finally with the assistance of the aforesaid duke, to be restored to its former state of monastic religion.

### 8

A certain venerable man named Erchembert was appointed abbot there. With the Lord’s help, through him the divine service was devoutly organized according to the rule of Saint Benedict. At once, in response to his most salutary admonition, the young Godehard, converted in heart and mind from the vanity of the world, became a monk together with several brothers of that place, in the thirty-first year of his age, as he himself often told us. Several brothers from that same monastery, however, subsequently departed, as memory later made known; among them was a certain T.

[**Note:** Thus the Compend manuscript; Brouverus and Henschenius, in the Bollandists under 4 May, have “Thietmarus.” Henschenius suspected that something was missing from the text and inserted dots, together with the words *sed non*—words found neither in Brouverus nor in our copy—reading: “of the church . . . but not the bishop.” He also cites the Graz manuscript, which gives the passage as follows: “a certain Dietrich, whom …,” but rejects this reading because, as it seemed to him, no bishop of Minden bearing that name is known from that period. Nevertheless, I consider this reading more probably genuine, for in the Saxon Chronicle manuscript in our possession, under the year 1022, it says: “Theoderic, bishop of Minden, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March”; he is undoubtedly the man mentioned here. For no one is unaware that Dietrich and Theoderic are the same name.]

whom we later saw as bishop of the church of Minden. But the newly adopted novice of the new religion, trained in a better life, aspired with all the affection of his heart and mind to the heavenly court, just as he had done in his earlier purpose. Thus the new teacher, having considered his worthiness—something certainly unusual in such matters—entrusted the entire care of the divine fold completely to him after himself, and chose him especially as his son in spiritual discipline.

[For he was fervent in charity, energetic in labor, devoted in prayer, profound in meditation, elevated in contemplation, honorable in body, pure in heart, strict toward himself, compassionate toward the faults of others, outstanding in humility, joyful in poverty, and radiant in true chastity.]

Yet after three years the aforesaid abbot, either because of illness

[Col. 1169B]

or because he was weary of secular administration, abandoned that office and resolved to devote himself, in the sight of the inner Judge, to the solitude of a more secluded life.

### 9

In those same days the aforementioned duke of Bavaria died. His place was taken by his pious son Henry, who followed not his father’s insolence but the beginning of wisdom, the fear of the Lord, in its fullness; for he was especially trained in every literary discipline and was wholly Catholic in faith and conduct.

Immediately inflamed with devotion to divine service, he grieved that the aforementioned monastery had again been deprived of a spiritual shepherd and wished to appoint the same Godehard, then a priest, as its abbot. For two years Godehard resisted him with sufficiently justifiable excuses, since, while his pastor was still alive, he ought not to usurp his seat and place. But after the abbot, summoned by the brothers and also by the bishops, refused to return and instructed them to appoint whomever they wished in his place, Godehard was finally overcome by episcopal authority and the unanimity of the brothers and accepted that office according to the duke’s decree.

At once, at the beginning of his promotion, he devoted himself wholly and watchfully to Christ. He anxiously took care to enter, together with the brothers associated with him, upon a stricter path of regular life, and for eight years he exercised himself there unceasingly in this pursuit. In addition, through manual labor he obtained abundant produce and necessary resources.

There, too, on a certain mountain called Helingersberg,

[**Note:** Jacob Gretser, at the end of the *Life of Saint Henry*, in his book *On the Bamberg Possessions*, published various charters in favor of the monastery of Altach, which Saint Godehard then governed. The fifth concerns the village of Helingersberg and was issued in 1009 at Merseburg.]

he built a strong fortress and within it a most beautiful church in honor of the holy mother of Christ, Mary, whose special service he was destined to undertake, together with a suitable building. All around, especially in the Bohemian Forest, which lies close to that province, he and the brothers, following the apostolic example, cleared thirty manses and more from forests and thickets by the labor of their hands and converted them to useful purposes for those serving God there.

Meanwhile, in the year 1002 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the noble emperor Otto III departed this life by an untimely death, and the aforementioned Duke Henry, distinguished by every form of piety, succeeded him in the kingdom.

### 10

At that time, in the monastery of Hersfeld,

[**Note:** Hersfeld was a very celebrated monastery of our order in Hesse, where the body of Saint Wigbert was laid.]

there was a venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Wigbert, B.

[**Note:** Our codex gives the name of this abbot in this form; Brouverus and Bollandus call him Berthold; the Graz codex, as Henschenius notes, gives Bernhard, which appears to be the genuine reading. Indeed, the Saxon Chronicle manuscript, repeating the appointment of Godehard to govern the monastery of Hersfeld in the very words of this Life, calls the abbot Bernhari. The Bodec manuscript in Bollandus’s Appendix has Berinherius.]

a man remarkable in birth and dignity. Yet, to speak without prejudice to peace, he had, in human fashion, become more intent than the order of his profession allowed upon the praise of popular reputation. Perhaps for this reason he sometimes indulged the brothers of the same monastery more generously than their proper way of life permitted, so that, following the custom of canons, they claimed possessions for themselves both in private buildings and in horses, as well as in many more elegant garments and other displays of worldly glory.

They also arrogated to themselves the license to give and receive, together with illicit and excessive banquets and other practices of that kind. When this abbot had been ill for two years before the end of his life, and was staying beyond the river Fulda on a mountain where he himself had built a monastery in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle, enjoying the comfort of the company of soldiers and his other familiars, the brothers, moved by indignation and feeling almost despised by their father, repeatedly sent various complaints to the king, both personally and through letters and messengers. They complained that the necessities of food and clothing were being denied to them, while, with the other poor of Christ starving, ecclesiastical resources were being utterly squandered on empty and useless things.

The wise king understood their complaint more deeply than they supposed, but, since he also knew their way of life,

[Col. 1170C]

he postponed responding by concealing the matter for some time. At last, overcome by their persistence, he replied in measured words that, if their father recovered by God’s gift, he would gladly admonish him about such matters; but if he died, he would provide, both for them and for himself, through the counsel of wise men and in accordance with the fear of the Lord, by appointing a shepherd over spiritual and temporal affairs.

### 11

When the aforementioned abbot died shortly afterward, he appointed the aforesaid Godehard as their father and governor, on the advice of the bishops. He also earnestly warned him to provide for them in all things according to the fear of the Lord and monastic religion.

Godehard was brought there by Archbishop Willegis, who also wisely instructed him in doing good, as he well knew how to give thanks to God.

[Col. 1170D]

At his first arrival, he gave thanks to divine mercy and diligently sought its direction in past, present, and future matters. First, in accordance with the precept of the Rule, he laid before them commands that were harder and more severe, and, at the metropolitan’s request, granted them permission either to celebrate these observances with him or to depart wherever they wished.

They immediately formed a unanimous conspiracy and all went out together, except for a few elders and little boys who remained, and they were scattered in various ways among different places. Later, however, with wiser counsel and with the help of those who had remained—who understood his ability and gentleness—he recalled almost all of them to the fold, some sooner and others later, and, with the Lord governing, easily reunited them under Christ’s light yoke.

He immediately purged the city itself and the cloistered residences of many superfluous and unsuitable buildings, honestly restoring them to a form appropriate to monastic necessities. Together with the brothers whom he found there and acquired elsewhere, he served God worthily and men commendably in that monastery for seven years.

Two other monasteries were also entrusted to him, Degarense and Cremense,

[**Note:** Bollandus has “Tegerense and Chremsense.” Both still exist and belong to the Benedictine order. The first is Tegernsee, commonly so called from the nearby lake, in Upper Bavaria; its abbot held a place among the princes of the Empire, as is clear from a privilege granted by Louis IV in 1321. The other, in Upper Austria, is called Kremsmünster and is extremely famous for the magnificence of its buildings and other features. The emperor Saint Henry gave two manses to the monastery of Saint Quirinus, situated in the place called Tegrinse, at the request of his wife Cunigunde and Abbot Godehard; Gretser published the charter, dated 1019, at the end of the *Life of Saint Henry*.]

which he likewise governed with equal diligence in the service of Christ.

### 12

At the same time there was in the regions of Thuringia a certain nobleman, illustrious in rank and merits, named Gunther.

[**Note:** Gunther will be discussed below under the year 1045, where we shall present his Life.]

Lamenting the sins of his youth, carefully considering the character of his actions, and going before the face of the Lord in confession, yet mistrusting his own bodily and spiritual weakness,

[he came penitently to Hersfeld to the new abbot, as later became clear, and completely opened to him the secret of his heart and will. The abbot, rightly fearing God, received him as a penitent with gentle consolation and suitable provision, and, with the Lord’s cooperation, converted him by his most salutary admonition all the way to the profession of monastic life. He immediately]

assigned irrevocably to Saint Wigbert, with the consent of his heirs and by a firm conveyance, the many private properties of his inheritance that he had received from his ancestors, in order to renounce completely whatever belongs to the world. First, however, he arranged by testament before witnesses that, once he had become a monk, he himself would possess the monastery called Gelinge for the sake of food and clothing, and that from it he would provide the necessities for the brothers serving Christ there with him.

But the abbot, after prudent consideration, judged that such an agreement would pose the greatest danger to this newly converted man on the way of God’s commandments, and that it would produce a daily loss to his soul greater than, as he thought, the support it offered to his body. In the meantime, therefore, with prudent purpose he suspended him from his undertaking and brought him with him to the monastery of Altach, while he still wore lay clothing.

There the man in question, pierced in heart,

[Col. 1172A]

asked the abbot whether, before his profession, he might travel to Rome and seek the intercession of Christ’s apostles and the other saints for the deviations of his former life and for his entrance into a new life. With the abbot’s permission he went and returned; then, before the altar of Saint Maurice,

[**Note:** So Bollandus, supported by the *Life of Saint Gunther*. Our codex, however, together with Brouverus and other manuscripts, reads “of Saint Mary.”]

he laid down his belt, shaved his head and beard, and, after making the customary petition, was received and tested for some time according to the Rule. From that same shepherd he then received the habit of monastic life.

### 13

After his vow of profession, however, he did not forget the agreement mentioned above. He approached the abbot and asked permission to return to his homeland and occupy, according to the agreement, the place he had contracted for. The pious Father consented for the time being, unwilling by stubborn opposition to prevent him from pursuing an affection, though wrongful, until by reason’s prompting he could gradually calm his unlawful desire.

When he came to the place called Gelinge and began arranging what was necessary for those living there, many and various difficulties arose for him from the hidden snares of the tempter, God permitting them, as we certainly believe, as an example like that of blessed Job. Since he, previously unaccustomed to poverty and labor, repeatedly fled to the abbot in complaint and anxiously sought his counsel and help in such matters, the concerned Father deeply perceived the instability of his mind and greatly feared that a change of heart might follow. Sometimes he mitigated his sadness with gentle consolation and sweet-spoken admonition; at other times, according to the Apostle, by reproving, pleading, and rebuking him, “in season and out of season,” he chastised his wavering mind (2 Tim. 4:2) and endeavored to bring him back to the way of salvation. Yet this produced only slight progress.

But when they had often struggled with one another in this dispute, and both had repeatedly become exhausted by such distress, one day, when Gunther again presented his complaint about his anxiety, the man of God, moved by the proper zeal for justice, replied with an inflamed spirit, as they say: either he should serve God more devotedly in the steadfast obedience he had promised, or else, once again entangled in Satan’s snares, he should abandon the habit and return to the world’s customary vanity.

At these words the astonished hearer trembled in shock, and, at last recoiling from the enormity of his error, lamented.

[**Note:** The Bodec codex in Bollandus’s May Appendix adds: “The abbot also secretly reported this entire matter in due order to the pious emperor Henry,” and so forth. These words occur in the *Life of Gunther* itself, published by the same Wolferus, the author of this *Life of Godehard*, which appears below under the year 1045.]

Having inwardly forgotten the entire agreement mentioned above and erased every complaint about whatever hardship he had suffered, he went to the monastery of Altach, where at that time, to speak for the benefit of all, a singular zeal for divine worship was flourishing under the care of that same Father. There he humbly subjected himself to the brothers and, in a short time, was fully instructed by the infusion of divine dew in the rigor of sacred religion. He even afflicted himself beyond the requirements of the Rule, to the amazement of his superiors.

### 14

In the third year after his conversion, he sought a hermitage in the aforementioned Bohemian Forest. There he lived for thirty-seven years

[**Note:** The same codex and the Bamberg manuscript have “almost thirty-six years.”]

with those dwelling alongside him, in the practice of holy religion and in the utmost rigor of voluntary poverty.

Their food was simple and scant. With diligent effort it was procured from the Hungarian king, from Bohemia and Poland, and also from various other provinces, together with clothing.

[**Note:** So the same manuscripts; others read: “It was varied, obtained by varied effort.” Brouverus and the Compend manuscript below have: “from Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, and the rest.”]

As for drink, as everyone knows, they had absolutely nothing there except water; and even that was given to guests in sufficient quantity but to the brothers by measure.

For that brother learned no letters at all except the Psalms. Nevertheless, through the brothers’ frequent reports and through listening with still greater eagerness to the word of God, he wonderfully acquired the whole meaning and understanding of the Gospel, the Law, the Prophets, and also the histories. Thus he very often set forth the more obscure matters of mystical interpretation, sometimes in jest and sometimes in admonition, before astonished listeners.

[**Note:** The Bamberg manuscript reads: “so that at times he might present the more obscure matters.”]

We, who knew him more intimately, often heard this, especially when we attended his sermon on the feast of his great solemnity, namely the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, his special patron. On that day, in a chapter conference, he admonished his brothers while instructing them about the life and conduct of that Father, his food and even his clothing, and his works, so that they might patiently endure their poverty in a manner pleasing to the Lord God.

I speak the truth, and I do not lie before God: almost all who were present at that sermon were moved by God’s gift to pour out abundant tears. The venerable abbot Ratmund of Altach sat there with many brothers of his monastery and also many other guests. We were absent, because our religious observance forbade us to enter there in canonical dress; nevertheless, the familiarity of the brothers and especially the abbot’s permission secretly placed us around the windows, unbeknownst to the preacher.

For he was, as is said of Saint Benedict, whom he followed in life and conduct after God, “knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned” (Saint Gregory I, *Dialogues* II, chapter 1).

### 15

Blessed Godehard, now wearied by old age and labor and also filled with weariness of secular administration, entrusted, with the consent of the king, the governance of Hersfeld to the distinguished man Arnold, previously his provost there, and that of Dagar to Berthold,

[**Note:** The Graz codex has: “Purchard.” In our copy only the first letter of this name, B, was present, just as above in the case of Arnold, A.]

his equally venerable chief officer. Thus he returned to Altach, where, if it should please God, he resolved to persevere to the end of his life in the proper practice of the religion he had begun.

He devoted himself with every form of dedication to adorning that same monastery, as is still evident there today, with books and the most precious missals, vestments, and various other useful ecclesiastical ornaments. Above all—and this is also universally known—he raised many brothers in that monastery who were distinguished in learning and conduct; later, at the request of kings and bishops, he distributed them among various monasteries as fathers and teachers.

But when he had already rested for ten years in that laborious yet agreeable solitude, engaged in such pursuits, and when with his whole heart he longed, through sighs by day and night, to please the Lord in the land of the living, he finally saw a remarkable dream, as he often told us. After that vision he had no doubt that he would depart from this world whenever God commanded.

[**Note:** The Bamberg manuscript reads: “Because of this, he thought with the greatest certainty through the vision that he would pass from this world.”]

### 16

One night, as he had now been accustomed to do for thirty years, he entered the church after only the first period of the night’s rest and spent the night intent on psalmody and the other offices of that kind. After Matins he continued in the resolve he had begun. When dawn was already shining, he entered his room, drowsing slightly, and, merely leaning over a bench, saw the following dream.

An olive tree of beautiful size stood in the cloister court. He thought that he was sitting beneath that tree, engaged in reading, when certain grave and unknown persons approached him. They claimed that they had been sent by that king to dig up the same olive tree and bring it to him for royal service.

Without delay, as it seemed to him, they seized axes and digging tools and attempted to uproot it with the greatest haste. But the deeper they dug, the denser the tenacity of its roots they encountered. Seeing this, and wishing to hurry, they brought axes against the roots, cut them through, and, carrying away the uprooted tree with them, departed.

Immediately, as he thought, countless and beautiful shoots grew from the dense mass of roots that had been left behind. They filled the entire court through their multiplication, so that people of different sexes and ages also came and, pulling up many young plants from those groves, spread them throughout the fields and along the roads.

When he awoke, he immediately entered the church and, casting his thoughts upon the Lord, commended himself more attentively to divine mercy, for he judged with greater certainty after that dream that he would soon depart.

[**Note:** The Bamberg manuscript reads: “because, in accordance with that dream, he thought that he would depart from there sooner.”]

Yet every wise person plainly understands that this signifies something else: anyone who carefully considers the abundance of his teaching will recognize that it had been left behind in the practice of the earlier religion and was afterward healthfully dispersed everywhere, in various doctrines watered by divine dew.

### 17

Since, by the favor of divine mercy, I have described the Life of the blessed man from its beginning until now—not by my own knowledge, which certainly amounts to nothing, but by that mercy’s aid—through many praiseworthy events, I return fitting thanks to the same mercy for having enabled me to know. And I implore your help, venerable Father, whom I have chosen from beginning to end as my teacher, defender, and corrector in all things, especially in this undertaking. I appeal, I say, to your help and that of those like you, and I beseech God’s aid, so that from now on, under his direction, I may truthfully and appropriately describe greater and more praiseworthy things without the taint of falsehood.

In the year 1022 after the mystery of the Incarnate Word of God, in the twenty-first year of the reign of our lord Henry, and the ninth of his empire, the venerable Bernward, bishop of our Church, of blessed memory,

[**Note:** We presented the *Life of Saint Bernward* above under the year 1023, in which year he died and Godehard succeeded him, a conclusion that seems more probable to us.]

departed from this life

[Col. 1175B]

to everlasting life. His death certainly grieved the whole region profoundly.

For, to pass rapidly over the entire history of his life, he was justly fervent in every holy devotion to divine service, wisely provident in every matter of worldly usefulness, lawfully severe toward rebels and the obstinate, properly gentle toward the obedient and moderate, compassionate and generous in almsgiving and mercy, and appropriately devoted to vigils, fasts, and prayers.

He fittingly enriched our monastery,

[**Note:** He calls the cathedral church a monastery.]

with books, silk, gold, silver, gems, paintings, and many other ecclesiastical ornaments, and, with God’s help, raised many clerics who were also useful in divine service.

He consecrated to God in monastic religion the venerable church of Saint Michael, built by his own labor and adequately endowed from his inheritance and acquisitions. He built very strong and honorable towers, together with an adjoining wall, on the eastern and western sides of our city, for the protection of the citizens. He built many churches, together with various useful buildings, throughout the estates of the bishopric, and diligently watched over everything belonging to episcopal provision, both spiritual and temporal, with complete propriety.

### 18

At that time the emperor was at Gruona, and, in his customary manner of piety, always kept the aforementioned abbot with him. When the messenger arrived with this mournful report, the emperor bewailed Christ’s faithful servant and his own friend with fitting grief and commended his pious soul to God and God’s holy angels with due remembrance.

Then he spoke privately with the abbot and disclosed to him, in a confidential conversation, the secret of his will concerning the episcopate of that same see. The abbot immediately resisted him to his face and replied that he was unworthy of such an important and distinguished office and honor.

Again and again the emperor admonished him with greater devotion, speaking from the abundance of his heart. But the abbot firmly persisted in the excuse he had begun, saying that he had rejected greater burdens of wealth for this very reason: so that he might devote himself more freely to God alone and await the end of his fragile life more securely in the poverty he had always loved.

The emperor attempted through the bishops to soften the hardness of his heart and asked them to speak with him about the matter. In their conversation he resisted with his customary confidence, and finally replied that, if they considered him worthy of the title, he would rather continue waiting until the see of Regensburg or Passau became vacant, where he could benefit not himself but only his people.

Thus the matter was discussed among them there throughout the entire week, but he always resisted with the same steadfastness of opinion.

### 19

Finally, on the Vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle, which at that time fell on the Thursday before Advent, he again saw a dream that he often afterward recounted, first only to the emperor and later to us also, with rejoicing and even tears.

After his customary night vigils and morning prayers, he saw in a vision—or so it seemed to him—the courtyard of the same church in which, three days later, he was to be consecrated. An enormous crowd was in tumult, earnestly disputing about the bishopric of Hildesheim.

Then, in the midst of the crowd, a venerable matron approached him with a beautiful company of young girls. She was wondrous in face and clothing. Taking him by the hand, she led him away from the thronging crowds into that same church. Then, extending her right hand, she merely signaled to him that he should come before the Crucified One to ask forgiveness.

[**Note:** That is, he was to incline his body and show reverence.]

As soon as he bowed himself to prayer, she and those standing around began to sing this hymn to God in a clear voice:

“Merciful one, pour your anointing into our senses.”

At that voice he awoke from sleep, moved by the mystery of the vision, entered the church, prostrated himself before the Lord’s altar, and commended himself and his vision to divine mercy.

When day came, he went privately to the emperor. Having laid aside the stubbornness of his mind, he revealed the sequence of the vision and finally pledged that he would submit to divine predestination and also to the emperor’s counsel and will.

Without delay, at dawn on that same day, our clergy and the military arrived. When the emperor disclosed to them his secret—or rather, the divine decree—their unanimous agreement joyfully received it with praise of God, although at first, and not without reason, some were frightened and feared such an outcome, either because his life was unknown to them or because they had once heard of the excesses of his youth.

On the following day, the feast of the Apostle, the pastoral charge was entrusted to him amid the greatest rejoicing of clergy and people. On the next Sunday, the First Sunday of Advent, he was worthily consecrated to God by Aribo, metropolitan of Mainz.

20. Yet at the very beginning of that same dignity—or, as he himself regarded it, burden—a trial, justly predestined by God, as we truly believe, was not lacking. For on that very day, before the solemn celebration of Mass, his consecrator, Aribo, secretly met with him and the bishops and, by imposing his ban, prohibited him from exercising any pontifical office in Gandersheim [Col. 1177A] and the surrounding territory. [Note: [Col. 1177D] How great were the disturbances already aroused over jurisdiction in the Gandersheim monastery, which the archbishop of Mainz arrogated to himself against the rights of the bishop of Hildesheim, is clear from the Life of Saint Bernward, where the right of the bishop of Hildesheim is also properly established and this entire controversy is explained at greater length.] He, in accordance with his customary simplicity, neither approved nor retained that ban, but immediately fled to the emperor, seeking from him alone protection in such matters. The emperor promptly summoned the archbishop with his brothers in a friendly manner and, concealing the displeasure in his heart, wisely and peacefully settled this new conflict by removing the ban. And so, after the aforesaid consecration had been festively celebrated, they spent that day rejoicing in the fear of God [Col. 1177B] and happily brought their assembly to an end in peace.

21. Therefore, readers, let it not seem inconvenient or tedious to you if, for the sake of necessity, the beginning of this conflict—certainly necessary for you in what follows—is recalled at greater length. A certain Saxon duke named Luitolf, together with his wife Oda [elsewhere, Yda], went to Rome with the counsel and permission of Saint Altfrid, the fourth bishop of our Church, [Note: [Col. 1177D] Altfrid succeeded Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, in the bishopric of Hildesheim. Ebbo, expelled from the see of Reims because of his conspiracy against Louis the Pious, governed this church for some time. Altfrid died in 975; we published his Eulogy in Part II of the fourth century.] and brought home relics of the holy bishops Anastasius and Innocent, obtained from Pope Saint Sergius. In their honor he first built a monastery and convent of virgins at Brunesteshusen, and then, four years later, at Gandersheim. He granted these estates, with the adjoining territory and all his inheritance, for the use [Col. 1177C] of those serving Christ there, and appointed his daughter Hathamuda [elsewhere, Hademuta] as the first abbess, with that same bishop ordaining her.

Thus the entire territory belonged from the beginning, continuously, to the bishops of Hildesheim for two hundred and forty [Note: [Col. 1177D] Without doubt one should read “one hundred and forty,” for no more years intervened between the year 856, when the Gandersheim monastery was built by Altfrid, and the time of Willegis.] years, and no prelate of Mainz claimed anything from it either for himself or for his Church, until Willegis, the twelfth metropolitan after Rabanus, occupied the see of Mainz. He was certainly a man distinguished in every aspect of Catholic piety, but in this one matter dangerously rash. At the urging—to speak the truth without fear—of Lady Sophia, sister of the emperor Otto III, who, lifted up by youthful ostentation and the dignity of her lineage, eagerly desired to receive the veil from Palligerus [Note: [Col. 1178D] That is, from the archbishop. The Bamberg manuscript, however, reads “from Adalgerus alone,” who was only a bishop.], he attempted to usurp that same place for himself.

Nevertheless, this scheme [Col. 1177D] perished in the presence of the king and the princes when Osdagus, the eighth bishop of our Church after Altfrid, opposed him with the voice of truth and justice [Col. 1178A]. Only with difficulty, and through the intervention of the king and his mother, did he obtain from that bishop permission for the archbishop to celebrate Mass there on the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist and to perform Sophia’s veiling together with him; as for the other virgins to be veiled, our prelate would make the arrangements by his own right.

Soon afterward the aforesaid Bishop Osdagus died, and Gerdagus was elected for us. When two years had passed, Lord Bernward, the royal chaplain, obtained the same see. That archbishop consecrated him, but remained completely silent about the earlier claim until the venerable Lady Gerberga [Note: [Col. 1178D] Gerberga, in the Bamberg manuscript Gerbirga, and in another Bamberg witness Gerburc, was the sister of Otto II; Sophia, however, was his daughter and the sister of Otto III.] wished the new monastery that she had built after the fire to be consecrated [Col. 1178B]. Since illness prevented her from making the necessary arrangements, she entrusted this task to the aforesaid Sophia, certainly her spiritual daughter and also her niece. Sophia immediately, in her customary manner, disregarded her own bishop and honorably invited the archbishop for such matters. He once again, forgetting the law because of this prompting, hastened to invade the place, but, warned by a letter from our prelate, postponed his action.

He was invited again, and again rejected by right of authority. At the third invitation the archbishop came there, intending, as he supposed, to dedicate the church. But Eggiardus, bishop of Schleswig, a truly faithful son of our Church, sent there with the clergy by our lord, prevented him by the authority of Scripture. After many and varied debates of this kind, the matter was finally adjourned by the neighboring bishops until the presence of the Roman pontiff [Col. 1178C]. [Note: [Col. 1178D] The printed editions add *and of the emperor* after the word “pontiff,” and this is correct according to the Life of Saint Bernward.]

22. But at that time the pious emperor Otto III departed to Christ. In his place, as has been stated above, Henry entered upon the kingship. He immediately celebrated the feast of Saint Lawrence at Paderborn, where Lady Cunigund received the royal crown. The aforesaid Gerberga, abbess of Gandersheim, having also been taken from this world, Sophia succeeded her and, once again in the customary manner, obtained, through the intervention of the princes, Lord Bernward’s permission to be blessed by Palligerus.

Then the new king began the first year of his reign on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity at Palithi. There, in his presence, the dispute between the bishops—so often mentioned—was recited, and he grieved inwardly. To settle it, he resolved to celebrate the long-postponed dedication of the Gandersheim church on the vigil of the Epiphany of the Lord, after gathering a number of bishops.

On the appointed day they arrived there and began the office of dedication. After the sacred rite had been completed inside, the king, together with the bishops and nobles, went out before the doors to the people. There, [when the metropolitan of Mainz had arrived with the other bishops and had completed the office of dedication,] Archbishop Willegisus [Note: [Col. 1179D] The words enclosed in parentheses are found only in the Bamberg manuscript.] publicly acknowledged his guilt, in his own judgment, and renounced his right and claim to that same place [in the presence of the king and many of his nobles]. As testimony to this renunciation, he handed his episcopal staff to Lord Bernward before the clergy and people, as later became clear at the council of Frankfurt.

After this dispute had been settled, the archbishop loved our prelate with every honor and affection for the rest of his life. Having honorably acquired fraternity in our monastery, he showed the greatest affection both to the place and to the brethren. Five years later, full of days and good works, he departed to Christ. His successor, Erkambald, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fulda, was consecrated at Mainz by Lord Bernward on the Kalends of April. Presiding there for nine years, he honored his ordainer, who was also related to him by blood, with due devotion, and remained completely silent concerning the dispute mentioned above.

Aribo, the royal chaplain, succeeded him. Bernward, in the customary royal manner, marked him out by the gift of the imperial ring and ordained him priest at the principal altar of the aforesaid Gandersheim church. In the presence of the emperor and the bishops, and by the authority of the Word of God and the ban of Saint Peter, he publicly prohibited him from usurping, invading, or claiming that altar, the place itself, or the surrounding territory. In retaliation for this ban, Aribo inflicted the aforesaid trial upon our Father.

Yet, to conceal nothing of the truth, that same archbishop was genuinely worthy of praise in lineage, dignity, and the commendable gravity of his conduct, but he was partly culpable toward us only in this rashness. This, then, is why a brief account of this conflict is recorded here: so that the truth and rationale of the subsequent dispute concerning the same Gandersheim territory may be understood more clearly.

23. Thus blessed Godehard, adorned with the insignia of the pontificate, arrived at Hildesheim on the Nones of December and found everyone rejoicing at his arrival. As soon as he recognized that the discipline of our monastery had, by God’s grace, been reasonably preserved until then, he immediately rendered worthy praises to divine mercy and strove to enlarge it with every effort of devotion and to adorn it through the practice of divine worship.

In external matters, he diligently watched over the general governance of clergy and people with episcopal vigilance. For this he continually entreated God day and night, throughout his entire life, with unceasing groaning [Col. 1180A]. He not only carefully preserved himself in his accustomed holiness and in the perseverance in good works that he had begun, but also religiously increased it day by day. Strengthened by the Holy Spirit, he persevered to the end in vigils and prayers, in the continual—and scarcely credible—frequency of fasts, in the most generous outpouring of alms, and, in short, in the profound gravity of every fear of God.

Thus, not to omit any encomium of his virtue, he was both a source of fear and an object of honor to kings and nobles; to others, each according to his station, he was likewise both feared and loved. He was rightly solicitous for all, becoming all things to all in Christ, while remaining severe and frugal toward himself alone.

He wisely governed his monastery with pastoral care [Col. 1180B] and frequently increased the brothers’ provisions of food and clothing and the other necessities of human need. By admonishing and exhorting them, and by instructing them in many ways, he led them to observe sacred religion. The young men and boys whom he found there to be of good character and intelligence he distributed among various schools in different places. Later, through their service, he obtained manifold and varied usefulness for his Church in reading, writing, and painting, as well as in the many more honorable disciplines of clerical office.

He also enlarged, with both propriety and usefulness, the ecclesiastical treasury, which he found well supplied there. Whatever he found ruined or dilapidated in the ecclesiastical buildings—not only in his principal city but also in the other places under his care—he hastened with the greatest speed to pull down, renew, and improve.

Among these works, he demolished the baptismal church that our tenth bishop, Otuinus of blessed memory, had built in the southern part of our church in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Epiphanius the bishop, whom, by God’s gift, he had brought to us as our patron from the city of Pavia [Col. 1180C]. [Note: [Col. 1179D] This refers to the translation of his body from Pavia to Hildesheim, carried out through Otuinus’s efforts in the year 963. Brouwerus published a History of this translation [Col. 1180D]. See also the Bollandists, 21 January. Even today the relics of this holy man are preserved at Hildesheim, but in the cathedral church. The monastery mentioned here is occupied by the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, as Brouwerus and Henschenius note.]

Because of age and neglect, he tore down that church and, on the same site, founded a worthy monastery in the aforementioned honor during the first year of his episcopal ordination. He completed it in the fourth year and gathered there a canonical community of considerably greater honor and usefulness in the fear of God. By acquiring an exchange of property, he adequately clothed and fed it and endowed it there for the future with abundant resources sufficient for such purposes [Col. 1180D].

24. I think, therefore, that the first miracle performed through him by Christ’s grace in that first year of his ordination should properly be inserted here, for the hope and joy of readers. I do not lie, with the Truth itself, which is God, as my witness: the miracle was entirely concealed by him from that time until the end, but was spread abroad by the clergy and people who were present.

In that same year Archbishop Aribo invited the emperor to Mainz for Pentecost [Col. 1181A], where he assembled a general council. In it, with the advice of the bishops, he corrected many things that had gone astray. Above all, however, he resolved to separate Count Otto of Hammerstein and Irmengard, who were living together unlawfully. Yet he could not carry this through completely, because the man corrected himself to some extent, partly out of royal fear and partly through episcopal admonition; the woman, however, publicly violating the ban, completely lost her right and law there, as is clear even today.

Our prelate, summoned to that council by both imperial and pontifical command, was hastening there, accompanied—though unwillingly—by a splendid multitude of clergy and soldiers. One day he was traveling through a district called Longingaha, near the aforesaid castle of Gruona, where by God’s grace he had both been elected and consecrated.

It happened there that a certain woman was tormented by an unclean spirit and was being carried by her parents or relatives around to churches, seeking the protection of the saints. When they learned that the new bishop was approaching, they hurried toward him with the sick woman, trusting in his holy reputation.

But the unclean spirit, frightened by their very haste, asked through the afflicted woman’s anxious cries where she was being taken. When they answered that she was being dragged to meet Bishop Godehard, it immediately began to resist miserably with a dreadful bellowing and howling. To the amazement and fear of those who were leading her, it struggled against them so that she would not come to the bishop, wailing and shouting that she neither heard nor could see Godehard.

While the afflicted woman was being dragged along by the faithful, who were truly burning with faith and hope, and the evil spirit resisted with all its force, at last, thanks be to God, the demon was driven out and the woman was freed. She was brought sound in mind and body to the man of God, who had sat down under a tree for refreshment.

When he learned what had happened, he was pierced by fear and joy alike. He rightly gave thanks to divine mercy, prostrating himself face down in tears. Then he laid his hands upon her, strengthened her in faith with blessing and prayer, and sent her away restored—and indeed rejoicing—with the rejoicing citizens and friends. Thus he continued the journey he had begun.

Accordingly, all who accompanied him loved and feared him even more, since they recognized such merit before God. Nevertheless, he imposed strict silence concerning this event [on both the girl’s parents and those who were with him] [Col. 1181D]. But neither the woman who had suffered it nor the crowd that had witnessed the healing miracle kept silent.

25. There was also, on the eastern side of our city, a dreadful marsh, wholly detested by those living around it because of the widespread fear it inspired. For they thought that there they either heard or saw, both at midday and during the night, certain horrible apparitions. The place was called Sulza, after the salt spring that bubbled there in the middle [Col. 1182A].

After seeing the marsh and hearing of the fantastic apparition by which the foolish populace was terrified, he invaded the same marsh in the second year after his arrival, carrying a cross and relics of the saints.
