He established his dwelling there and, in the midst of the danger, founded an oratory in honor of the holy apostle Bartholomew [Note: [Col. 1181D] Later, at the beginning of the twelfth century, this place passed to the Premonstratensians through the beneficence of Bishop Bruningi, according to Brouwerus.].

When the oratory had been completed and dedicated in the following year, he utterly eradicated every demonic apparition from the place and made it pleasant for all who lived there or came there, rendering it habitable without any temptation. There he built a hospice of Christ for the reception of the poor. Since it abounded in every provision for human need, he entrusted it to a faithful priest of his, Bernward, whose name is rightly inserted here because of his merit in faith [Col. 1182B].

In the name of Christ he repeatedly adjured him with terrible solemnity to provide not only for those living there but also for all who might happen to arrive, furnishing food and clothing as appropriately as he would have to render an account to God for this very stewardship. [Note: [Col. 1181D] The Bamberg manuscript reads: “So that he might labor diligently in the care of the poor, just as he would have to render an account to God for this very administration” [Col. 1182D]. In this passage he wished to benefit all who sought help, but especially those whom he knew were not wanderers and deceivers.]

26. There was, however, one class of such people—namely, those who wander through regions and kingdoms in monastic, canonical, or even Greek dress—whom he mockingly called, after the manner of Plato, “Peripatetics.” These men, I say, he utterly detested, reproaching them as though they were accursed. Nevertheless, because they professed the name of Christ, he consoled them with the necessary support for two days, or at most three. After providing them with shoes or clothing, he urged them to depart, lest they forget their customary wandering.

When some wished to remain with him longer, he ironically brought forward that saying of Gregory in the *Dialogues* (Book II, chapter 13): how an enemy deceived a foolish traveler hastening toward holy places through his traveling companion, through the pleasantness of a spring or meadow, or even through the sweetness of food.

Sometimes, when his close companions reminded him—which did not displease him—that true friends of God were often found among such people, he immediately added that jest of Jerome: “Liars cause the truthful to be scarcely believed.”

Yet if he recognized any of them as steadfast in the worship or fear of God, he loved them in matters pertaining to God, privately rather than publicly, which they themselves also preferred. [Note: [Col. 1182D] The same manuscript adds: “Cherishing them with every affection, he kept them with him publicly and privately.”]

He was also remarkably gentle and forgiving toward offenders and wrongdoers. If any such people fled to him for confession and penance, he immediately pardoned their offenses with ready clemency. With vigilant care, he [corrected them through prudent counsel so that thereafter they would not fall into such things out of necessity, and] provided them with every sufficient means for the future [Col. 1182D].

In this he followed the example of his holy patron, Bishop Nicholas, who, with the gold of his alms, removed the incestuous disgrace of the virgins, their father’s poverty, and the shameful dishonor of the whole household, and by his merciful clemency relieved the need of every poor person who in any way came under his care [Col. 1183A]. Following this example, our prelate strove always and everywhere to console the needy. He also took pleasure in speaking with such people, enjoying himself with them in jest and even at table.

27. In that same year—namely, 1024 from the Nativity of the Lord—Emperor Henry of blessed memory, in the twenty-third year of his reign, departed to Christ. His death sorrowfully disturbed all the joy of Christendom that had flourished under him.

He was succeeded by the noble and energetic Conrad, who began the first year of his prosperity at Minden on the Nativity of the Lord. After the Epiphany he came to Hildesheim. There the aforesaid Archbishop Aribo, who for two years during the emperor’s lifetime had remained silent, again found an opportunity to begin troubling blessed Godehard over Gandersheim. The new king, however, settled his scheme through the counsel of the nobles.

The king then traversed Saxony by a short route, proceeded through Thuringia and Francia [Bod.: Franconia] during Lent into Bavaria, and honorably celebrated Holy Easter at Regensburg (Remersburg). That summer he passed through Bavaria, Swabia, and the lands of the Carinthians, together with the boundaries of the surrounding provinces, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Liège. At the Purification of Saint Mary he remained at Augsburg; from there he directed his journey toward Italy, and successfully celebrated the following Easter at Vercelli. Thus he visited and traversed the neighboring regions all around in the renewed splendor of kingship [Col. 1183C].

In his third year [Note: [Col. 1183D] The Bamberg manuscript reads: “in the third year of his reign.”] our prelate began to inhabit the Beautiful Mount on the western side of the city. Five years later he dedicated it, in title and name, to Saint Maurice, his supreme patron. He also dedicated a beautiful church at Holthusen, suitable for monastic life, in honor of Saint Benedict the abbot [Note: [Col. 1183D] Although the monastery has been destroyed, the place has retained its name on the Weser River, about eleven German miles west of the city of Hildesheim.]. Throughout the territory of his bishopric he either diligently built many basilicas himself or gratefully consecrated to God those constructed by other faithful Christians.

28. At that time the aforesaid Archbishop Aribo convened a general council of twelve bishops at Seligenstadt on the feast of the holy apostle Matthew [Note: [Col. 1183D] This is the well-known monastery on the Main between Hanau and Aschaffenburg.]. There he publicly brought our prelate to trial over the aforesaid Gandersheim territory, but the unanimity of the brethren adjourned that synod until the following year.

The king began the feast of the Nativity of the Lord at Ivrea [Note: [Col. 1183D] Ivrea, or Eporedia, now called Ivrea, is an episcopal city in the territory of the Salassi, under the metropolitan see of Turin, on the Dora River.]. From there, heading toward the thresholds of the apostles [Col. 1184A], he entered Rome joyfully and prosperously on the Tuesday before the Lord’s Supper. On the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection he gloriously received the crown of imperial dignity from blessed John, the vicar of the apostles.

Returning on the following Sunday, and having forcibly occupied the surrounding region by authority, he returned home in peace. He celebrated the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist at Imbripoli [Note: [Col. 1183D] It is remarkable how much this place has troubled the ingenuity of writers. In the old edition Surius restored the reading “Herbipoli.” The manuscripts, however, vary: Imbrolis, Imbripolis, and in Bripoli. There can be no doubt that the reading should be Imbripoli, as one word. Brouwerus thinks that this city was Verla, a town of Saxony; Bollandus, however, asserts that it was the famous city of Regensburg, saying that among the ancient Teutons the word *Regen* meant rain. Although our Adolphus Overham rejects this etymology in his notes on the Life of Saint Meinwerc, he nevertheless proves beyond question that Regensburg was often called Imbripolis.].

There, when Duke Henry of Bavaria died in a good old age, he entrusted the same duchy to his son, Lord Henry, by the choice of the princes.

29. In that same year Aribo of Mainz convened a synodal council at Frankfurt, with the emperor presiding together with twenty-three bishops. There, once again, according to his custom, he troubled the blessed man Godehard over the matter so often brought forward [Col. 1184B].

At last our prelate, through the mercy and assistance of the supreme Truth, which is God, canonically retained the proprietary right of his bishopric over the entire Gandersheim territory, with the testimony of seven bishops who had both heard and seen the aforesaid agreement at Gandersheim: namely, with Bruno of Augsburg delivering the declaration, Wernher of Strasbourg pronouncing the decision, and the metropolitan himself—truly unwillingly—affirming it by the ban of the Word of God.

These were the bishops who provided our elder with their testimony, as they had heard and seen it: Bruno, bishop of Augsburg; Everhard [Ebehard], bishop of Bamberg; Meinhard, bishop of Würzburg; Meinwerc, bishop of Paderborn; Sigebert, bishop of Minden; Hildeward, bishop of Zeitz [Note: [Col. 1184D] Under him the episcopal seat was transferred to Naumburg.]; and Bruno, bishop of Merseburg.

30. The royal and episcopal assembly there was indeed splendid and properly arranged. On the eastern side, before the altar, Archbishop Aribo sat with his suffragans: Wernher of Strasbourg, Bruno of Augsburg, Meinwerc of Paderborn, Everhard of Bamberg, Meinhard of Würzburg, Godehard of Hildesheim, Branthop of Halberstadt, Wigger of Verden, and Hazecon of Worms.

On the western side sat the emperor. At his right were Archbishop Piligrinus of Cologne, with his subordinates Sigebert of Minden, Sigifrid of Münster, and Benno of Utrecht. At his left was Archbishop Hunfrid of Magdeburg, with his bishops Hildeward of Zeitz, Bruno of Merseburg, Luizone of Havelberg, and Theoderic of Meissen [Col. 1185A].

In the southern region sat Bishop Rambrecht of Verdun, Rodulf of Schleswig, and Hildolf of Mantua [Note: [Col. 1185D] He alone of the Italians attended this council, as he also did the council of Frankfurt in 1007, where the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg was confirmed by the bishops of Germany. In Ughellus, volume I of *Italia Sacra*, he is called Isolphus. A German by birth, he administered the Church of Mantua from 1007 to 1044, introduced Benedictine monks into the church of Saint Andrew, and enriched the monastery with many possessions.], together with Reinoldus [Reginoldus] of Aldenberg.

In the northern region were the abbots Richard of Fulda, Reimboldus [Regimboldus] of Lorsch, Arnolf of Hersfeld, and Gerbert of Mainz, along with seven others of the same order [Note: [Col. 1185D] All the printed editions have “six.”].

The following feast of the Nativity of the Lord the emperor celebrated at Liège; Easter he solemnly kept at Aachen, where his son Henry honorably received the crown of royal dignity from Archbishop Piligrinus, by the election of the clergy and people.

That year Aribo again convened his synod at Geislingen and summoned our elder Godehard, through envoys and letters, to trouble him once more. Declining to go, he instead sent the venerable Tadilo, dean of our monastery, with some brothers to meet him. Tadilo greeted him honorably on behalf of his elder and reminded him of the decision of the previous synod. By presenting a great number of authorities on both sides and with the assistance of the bishops, he restrained him, at least for that time, from renewing the claim [Col. 1185B].

31. In the following year as well, while the emperor was seated at Palithi, the aforesaid archbishop held a synod there and began a complaint against the blessed man in the emperor’s presence. After many and varied discussions, however, he finally desisted, scarcely persuaded by the bishops.

That year Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, died, and Eppo succeeded him. Wernher, bishop of Strasbourg, was also taken from this life, after which Willehelmus was appointed.

In the following year the emperor celebrated Pentecost at Merseburg. There the aforesaid Archbishop Aribo and our elder Godehard were reconciled with one another over their long dispute. For the metropolitan himself secretly met Father Godehard in the presence of the bishops, confessed and declared that he had been mistaken concerning this parish, promised, under the true testimony of Christ and the Church, every fraternal satisfaction and perpetual silence concerning the former dispute, and humbly begged that his earlier errors be forgiven him for God’s sake.

This account is therefore truthfully recorded here because it is confirmed by Lord Godehard himself, who repeatedly testified publicly in his preaching that it was true. [Note: [Col. 1185D] The Bamberg manuscript reads: “When the term of this postponement had finally arrived, Archbishop Erbo—for it always calls Aribo by this form—warned, as we truly believe, by God’s will, secretly met our elder, blessed Gotehard, and confessed and declared that he had been mistaken concerning the aforesaid matter; and so, before the bishops, he promised every fraternal …,” and so forth.]

That year Unwan, archbishop of Hamburg, died, and Liebizo succeeded him. Then the emperor celebrated Christmas at Paderborn. On the holy day, during the solemn celebration of Mass, Archbishop Aribo delivered a public sermon in which he asked the emperor and his brothers for permission to go to Rome and requested that clergy and people obtain God’s pardon for him.

Thus, after the Purification of Saint Mary, he set out and went to Rome. From there, however, he departed and died on the eighth day before the Ides of April—alas, alas!—in the eleventh year of his ordination. His death was rightly mourned by all Catholics, for in every aspect of ecclesiastical religion he was truly praiseworthy.

A simple and upright man, Bardo, abbot of Hersfeld, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1186D] We shall discuss him under the year 1051.]. With God visibly advancing him, he happily rose within a short time to the summit of the highest perfection. His pious life and deeds are not recorded here more fully because, thanks be to God, at Mainz he is honorably celebrated among the apostolic priests for his merits in holiness.

I shall mention one privilege of his perfection, however, which sound-minded clerics in our neighboring regions offered him as a mark of honor: because he shared a name with blessed John the bishop, and because of the sweet-sounding melody of his preaching, he was to be called Bardo-Chrysostom.

32. On one occasion, when our blessed prelate Godehard was traveling around the boundaries of his parish in episcopal fashion to visit the people entrusted to him, he went to his estate at Hirgenhusim [Huginhusen or Engelhusen] to spend the night [there] and to refresh the poor with the generosity of alms in which he surpassed all others.

A poor widow from that same household presented her little son before him, a very poor child weakened by an exceedingly miserable disease. He was afflicted partly by paralysis and partly by leprosy; his limbs’ sinews were twisted, and his entire body was deprived of the usefulness of its natural formation [Col. 1186C]. His hands and arms, knees, feet, and shins flowed with putrid swelling and running pus, so that he could not move even a step in any way, or at least crawl anywhere.

He received the child with a cheerful face and heart, gratefully, as though he were truly a gift from God, and ordered that he be taken along after commending him carefully to his chamberlains. “God is powerful,” he said, “who from the beginning did not disdain to assist the wretched and sinners through various remedies of his mercy. He can also gladden us concerning this poor child in his customary manner of mercy.”

The child was brought with the bishop to our principal church and was supported there for several weeks, not without great labor on the part of the boys who cared for him. At last, after four [Col. 1186D] or five months, he gradually began—plainly through the merits and prayers of the blessed man—to recover. As the flow of swelling and pus partially subsided, he sometimes rose up and sometimes crawled forward, as though exercising the sinews of his limbs for walking.

The pious prelate recognized this and, often weeping for joy, gave due thanks to divine mercy. He did not cease to pray earnestly to God, as later, by God’s gift, truly became evident. [Note: [Col. 1186D] The Bamberg manuscript adds: “This boy, I say, was named Werin; the holy bishop …”]

Within the space of a year, as is certainly known to everyone among us, the boy recovered into better health: the multitude of diseases was driven away and the contraction of his sinews relaxed. Day by day he grew stronger for every kind of service.

This same man, named Werin, has now served unharmed for twenty years and more in the episcopal chapel. He does, however, display to all who see him, as though in testimony to God’s power, the actual distortions of his limbs—and, so to speak, certain humps—in his legs and hands.

### 33.

To many others also, suffering under various conditions of human frailty—some, indeed, and this is the most serious matter, weighed down by the burden of sins, while others were afflicted by different illnesses—who fled to him, he extended the aid of his intercession. Through the tireless persistence of his holy prayers, he both freed them from the danger threatening them and, with God’s help, guarded them thereafter from such things. I could truthfully recount many things about them, widely known to many people, if at that time I had not passed over them in silence, concealing them at his command, chiefly so that I might not either impose excessive weariness upon readers or increase the sin of unbelief in those who are sluggish regarding such matters.

I shall nevertheless relate one event which, as if in comic mockery, occurred at Goslar, when, toward the end of his life, he built a church there in the royal residence at the command and request of the empress Gisela.

[Note: Goslar is a free city of Lower Saxony. The church that Saint Godehard built there was dedicated by Pope Leo IX around the year 1049.]

There was there a certain married woman living a lay life but devoted to the fear of God, named Hatteha (Hathzeca). The bishop himself received her son from the sacred font as godfather, because he perceived in her a religious faith. It happened that at one time she was afflicted by a very severe pain in her eyes and suffered for several days so intensely that she could neither take food nor drink nor obtain any bodily rest. At last, compelled by the anguish of the most grievous pain, she sent her godson to the bishop with blessed gifts, informing him of the extremity of her illness and seeking from his compassion some help of healing.

When the bishop heard this, he smiled with joyful cheerfulness. At that very moment a poor man had happened to bring him some reddish flowers from a tree called in the German language *Spinnelbum*; the bishop fortified them with the sign of the cross and gave them to the boy, saying:

“Take,” he said, “these little flowers to my friend, your mother, so that she may keep them in memory of me and ask God for remedies of health.”

Without delay, as she often afterwards told us under oath, when she brought the flowers near her diseased eyes, she perceived that all the pain of her entire illness immediately fled from her head with miraculous speed. At once, when the doors or windows of her room—which for several days had been kept carefully closed because of her illness—were opened, she began to see more clearly and felt no further suffering of this kind.

The next day she came to the bishop and, rejoicing and weeping at once, humbly offered due thanks to God’s mercy and to his visitation. He received her kindly, comforted her, and instructed her to place firm hope in the Lord and to do good without ceasing. He also ordered a priest to anoint her eyes with the sacred oil called that of the sick. This anointing, together with his devout prayer, completely healed her from that same pain until the end of her life.

[Note: Codex Bodec.: “from a tree which in the Belgian language is called *fusarius*”; indeed, they say that this tree is suitable for making spindles.]

### 34.

I shall also set forth as an example and as a warning to the faithful, and as a source of fear and dread to the negligent, what happened to him in the third-to-last year of his present life.

There was in our congregation a certain priest, born of the household of the Church, almost ignorant of literary learning—so that, as the truth may proceed in peace—but subtly and excessively skilled in worldly cleverness. To the astonishment of everyone, he rose from the lowest poverty to the greatest wealth.

First he was happily raised up by Bishop Bernward; then, for certain reasons better left unmentioned now, he was humbled by Emperor Henry. Again this blessed man raised him up through compassionate kindness, because he seemed useful to him in the affairs of the Church; nevertheless, he was often treated in various ways amid adversity and prosperity.

At last, by his cunning, he so won the favor of so great a bishop that he alienated many who had previously served the bishop faithfully, depriving them both of their master’s favor—which was certainly displeasing to him—and of their dignity and the benefit of their property. But no one should find this surprising, since, as blessed Gregory testifies, it often happens that a mind occupied with many matters, and especially with divine things, is easily stolen away by flatterers.

Eventually that man was publicly cursed by everyone, and even at times sensible people reproached the bishop for such insolence. In the end, however, he was restored to favor by those whom he had innocently alienated.

### 35.

After several years, the pious bishop became more clearly informed about such matters and at times humbled himself to seek pardon from those who had been unjustly injured. One day he ordered the provost of our congregation, the dean with several brothers, and his other leading men to assemble at Holthusen, where he happened then to be staying. The venerable man Rathmund, his sister’s son and abbot of the monastery of Altaich, was also present. In the presence of that priest, he gave all who claimed to have been injured by him permission to speak freely.

Immediately, without delay, several kinds of complaints were brought forward, both by the abbot himself and his attendants who were present as guests, and by our own men. Everyone publicly spoke against him as if with one voice.

All together they charged him, first, with the general scandal brought upon the Church and episcopal honor; then the citizens and guests each brought forward their particular injuries and losses. When he heard them, he smiled as though mocking them—for he was exceedingly clever—and, as if astonished, asked what all this meant. Then, by the fabrications of his worldly wisdom, with which he was entirely filled, though before God it is reckoned folly, as became manifest in his case, he eloquently refuted each accusation and wonderfully reduced all who opposed him to seeming dumbness and speechlessness.

### 36.

At last the pious bishop, truly pierced by the Holy Spirit and additionally moved by a remarkable zeal, considering at once the evident truth of the matters and the man’s presumptuous confidence of heart, immediately silenced every voice. Then, speaking in a measured manner, he began, to the amazement of all:

“Hildewin”—for that was his name—“look: all those standing around you, as you suppose, you have defeated. Look: by your subtlety you have shown them all to be liars, while God examines the truth. Now turn to me and, adjured by Christ, answer the truth to me alone.

“I confront you,” he said, “with an evangelical sentence. Since you do not fully understand the evangelical meaning, I address you in the German tongue. Hildewin,” he said, “do you love me?”

At once he replied confidently: “Truly, I love you.”

Again the bishop said: “Hildewin, do you love me?”

He answered: “Certainly, I love you.”

The bishop asked him a third time: “Hildewin, do you love me?”

At last the wretched man, astonished by that evangelical example—but, alas, not rightly pierced by it, replied in an angry and tearful voice:

“God,” he said, “who knows all things, knows that I truly love you.”

Then the bishop said:

“See: if you speak the truth, you have satisfied me; but if you are foolish, you have miserably bound yourself. Yet if you love me faithfully, as you say, feed my sheep—that is, love my brothers and friends, including my guests and poor people; love your fellow servants and those of your household.

“Therefore I admonish you before God: if you have truly sworn this, preserve yourself in truth; if not, repent worthily. Under this condition, return home now and, if God wills it, enjoy in my favor both your dignity and your benefice and property.”

Thus he dismissed the assembly, while everyone marveled and trembled.

### 37.

Nevertheless, he ordered them all there to receive an expression of charity from one another and thus depart in peace. Among them, Hildewin sat down to dinner cheerful and happy, as though exulting in his victory, and returned home unharmed.

In the evening he sat pleasantly at home with his own people, feasting and making merry, and uttering insults and threats against those of whom he complained that they had injured him. He then went to bed and rested, apparently in good health.

At dawn he rose vigorously to attend to his duties and quickly put on his shoes. But when he rose hurriedly to put on his tunics, he suddenly collapsed and, overtaken with miraculous speed, miserably breathed his last.

He left behind many and very extensive possessions: property of his own, innumerable and costly garments, other money, and livestock. Yet the blessed bishop, grieving over his death beyond what can be believed, ordered all of it to be distributed to the poor for the remedy of his soul. From his heart, though late, he granted him remission of sins and did not cease laboring frequently with fasts and entreaties for the deliverance of his soul.

Therefore, since we have now reproved him beyond what was required, more from a concern for necessary truth than from envy or hatred, and perhaps exposed our own negligence in many matters as less serious than his, we beg you, readers, in your charity: when you read these things, pray the Lord to grant him indulgence and remission of sins—for your own [*our own*, edition] blessedness. Thus this reproach may perhaps become for him, before the mercy of the Judge, a pardon that can be forgiven.

### 38.

There was also in our congregation a man of venerable life, rightly praiseworthy in every observance of the canonical rule, named Tadilo. I have already briefly mentioned him above. At first, under Lord Bernward, he was *vicedominus* on account of his faithfulness and industry; but this blessed bishop appointed him for the benefit of the Church to the deanship and the office of schoolmaster. Because he pleased him in his heart by his merit in religion and charity [Bol.: piety and chastity], he adopted him as his fellow canon and fellow servant in the service of God.

The whole Church that knew him bore witness that he was elderly and experienced, distinguished for humility and love, but moderately severe in governing and admonishing the brothers, and diligent before God in every exercise of virtue. In his admonitions he often used that amusing proverb:

“Let people love,” he would say, “but hate vices.”

Several years earlier [Note: The printed editions read “months.” The Bamberg codex reads somewhat differently: “The bishop, as he had learned from the Holy Spirit, often foretold the day of his death, namely, that he would precede the passing of our blessed Father Godehard by one year and six months.”], the blessed bishop often told him, as it seemed to us in jest, that he would depart this life either together with him or shortly before him.

Most recently, when Tadilo was lying ill at the point of death, the bishop sent his nephew, the abbot mentioned above, to visit him in his place and seriously instructed Tadilo to receive the sacred anointing with oil, truly repenting and confessing his sins, with complete faith; and, fortified by the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, to depart fearlessly. He truthfully promised him that, while still alive, he would continually implore God’s grace for the remedy of his soul and would follow him in the peace of Christ within the coming year.

The abbot anointed our beloved and rightfully ever-memorable master with sacred oil, together with the brothers standing by, and by the authority and command of the bishop granted him full remission. Two days later he departed, truly blessed, to Christ. His death nevertheless grieved us bitterly, because it deprived our congregation [rather, our entire Church] of the patronage, counsel, and teaching of so great a man.

Yet we declare, with clergy and people as witnesses, that we have never seen—and shall never see—a man of that order more honorable in every ecclesiastical virtue. We ought rightly to retain his memory in our hearts, and we do not hesitate to remember him truly before the presence of the saints.

Thus God clearly fulfilled the prophecy of the blessed bishop, taking Godehard happily from this life only one year and three months after Tadilo.

[Note: Bamberg: “who preceded him by one year and six months.”]

### 39.

As the end of the blessed Father Godehard’s life now approached more visibly, he always strove from virtue to virtue through increasing works of goodness, so that he might merit to see the God of gods in Zion. Since the practical exercise of many duties had now ceased, he devoted himself without interruption to the sole exercise of contemplation. From the general practice of his life he retained only three things in particular: the psalter, almsgiving, and, above all, abstinence, which he constantly kept as his companion and friend.

Indeed, if on rare occasions during more festive seasons, compelled by the obedience of the brothers, he took food of a richer kind or drink stronger than his stomach was accustomed to, it brought more discomfort to his body than nourishment.

Thus, at the final Christmas of his present life, in the year 1036 [Note: Henschenius substituted the year 1038. Emperor Conrad, however, was in Italy that year and celebrated Christmas at Parma. Hence the learned man conjectures that our author confused what happened in 1039 with what had taken place in the preceding year. The Grecian codex has the year 1039.], while the emperor was staying at Goslar, he himself devoutly celebrated the feast at Holthusen. He rendered, according to the Gospel, to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s: in the prescribed manner offering himself as a spiritual sacrifice to Christ, while also, according to his strength and in accordance with custom and duty, rejoicing with his clergy and people in both divine and human matters.

He eagerly awaited the most sacred days of Lent—which, as he often proclaimed in jest, were most health-giving—with the greatest joy of heart and mind. Passing through them bodily as though outside the body, with his nerves scarcely holding together, he reached holy Easter.

Nevertheless, he completed Palm Sunday, the Lord’s Supper, and the feast of Christ’s Resurrection with the proper episcopal office, gathering strength beyond his capacity. Thus he visited the stations in the surrounding places during the Easter days, admonishing the faithful according to his customary devotion. During those days he often publicly announced that he was now rejoicing with them in the final happiness of bodily fellowship and that, at the Lord’s Ascension, he would be summoned to whatever place God should command.

[Note: Bamberg: “Especially, however, in the final year of his present life, chastising himself throughout the whole of Lent, he scarcely completed Palm Sunday with the episcopal office proper, having gathered his strength only with difficulty.”]

We, however, hearing these things, almost mocked them, because we had already heard him threatening us so often that he would soon return to his ancient homeland, namely Bavaria.

[Note: Bamberg: “because it was necessary for him to depart to another place at the Ascension of the Lord.”]

### 40.

After the Sunday called *in Albis* [Note: This is generally what they call the Sunday *in Albis*, because on that day the newly baptized would put off their white garments], he departed from us and went with his aforementioned nephew, the abbot Radmund, to Adenstad [another reading: Eistat], where he was striving to complete a church that had recently been begun. Unable to resist his illness any longer, he lay down as his flesh failed.

When the sorrowful news became known, the aforementioned abbot Rathmund [Note: Bodec.: “Abbot Adelbert”; Boll.: “the aforementioned abbot”], a man wholly devoted in heart and mind to divine service, and our provost and dean with the priors came to visit him. They found him, however, concealing his weakness, seated according to his customary ecclesiastical labor and supported by the hands of those around him.

He received them joyfully with the sole cheerfulness of charity. As though forgetting his suffering, he asked with apparent wonder the reason for their arrival and ordered himself to be carried back to his chamber.

There, after the clergy had been admitted and assembled, he first diligently admonished each one regarding the administration of his obedience. Then he instructed all of them generally, both wholesomely and terribly, by exhorting and reproving them concerning the observance of the sacred faith and religious life.

Next he commended himself to their prayers against the snares and deceptions of the cunning tempter. He clearly foretold to them, almost as if in jest, the day and time of his death, the order of his funeral rites, and even the manner of his burial, as later happened.

“Go,” he said, “and prepare yourselves for the coming joy of the Lord’s Ascension, each according to the quality of his obedience and also the measure of his spiritual distinction. Await my arrival joyfully, as though you were truly going to rejoice with me here and in the future.

“For on the vigil of the Ascension I shall come to the mountain to my holy patron Maurice, and there I shall spend the holy day and night. I shall nevertheless send you an abbot who will perform the procession and the solemnities of the Mass in my place.”

Then, raising his eyes and sighing deeply, though seeming still to smile, he said:

“After those things have been completed as Christ wills, I shall come at dawn on Friday to Saint Michael, to spend the night with the abbot and brothers; from there, on Saturday, I shall go to Saint Andrew to pray; and from there I shall come to you, remaining entirely with you.

“On Sunday let us solemnly celebrate the day with the brothers and friends summoned together, and so bring to a complete end the joy of our entire feast.”

After saying this, he gave them his blessing and dismissed us, all of us marveling and filled with astonishment.

### 41.

The blessed Father also had in his private service a certain distinguished young man, the son of a widow, an artisan skilled in painting, who cared for his plain clothing and footwear. His name was Buno [Note: It is written *Bunonem* everywhere; Surius’s first edition, however, has *Brunonem*]. From the beginning of that same year the bishop often instructed him that he would be traveling with him to his homeland, Bavaria.

For, as we have said, long beforehand he had often seriously promised that he would revisit his homeland. When many people of every rank voluntarily offered themselves and wished to travel with him, he thanked them for their devotion but chose Buno alone to accompany him.

On that same day, before the arrival of the clergy, while the bishop was changing his clothing in seclusion as usual, he ordered Buno to put on the very garments that he himself had removed and to come quickly to him.

The young man contemptuously disregarded these words as delirious or mocking. But the bishop, apparently displeased, said to his chamberlains:

“Go, put the garments I removed on him and bring him to me.”

They immediately dragged him behind the chamber curtain, dressed him, and led him before the bishop as though in mockery. After gazing at him for a long time, the bishop said:

“Know for certain that in that same garment you will find a *rumor* [fluid; rheum].”

[Note: Bollandus thinks that the word denotes *rheuma*; perhaps *humorem* should be read.]

After these words the boy went out. At that very moment an intolerable chill seized him, and at the same hour he fell sick and collapsed into bed.

When the bishop asked about him after the brothers’ departure, he was told that the boy was ill. He immediately summoned the steward and instructed him:

“See that the boy is carefully and without distress taken to his mother, so that he may be ready to meet me and travel with me.”

He was taken away at once, and as his strength declined day by day, he was prepared for death.

[Note: Bamberg: “to travel with me. From that day our bishop, as his strength declined day by day, was prepared for death, and from the aforesaid village was brought to Holthusen, and so forth.”]

### 42.

Then, as his fever grew worse, our bishop was brought to Holthusen, where there was an abundance of buildings sufficient for the multitude who customarily gathered according to ecclesiastical practice to visit so great a man.

There, amid the great attendance of clergy and people, the venerable Lady Sophia of Gandersheim arrived. At last, speaking peacefully, she laid aside her former obstinacy and turned herself with complete faith and devotion to the friendship of the blessed man.

Having found an opportunity and the crowd having been removed, with the clergy standing by, she began by speaking of a certain frivolous obstinacy that had arisen among the clerics of her church against the blessed man, and began promising due satisfaction.

At her words he replied angrily, partly compelled by his illness and partly, as it seemed to us, moved by indignation, and asked that such matters be postponed for the future.

She, however, concealing his agitation and fearing that his death might come more quickly, persisted again and again in her offer of satisfaction, even weeping, and begged him to deign to accept it.

But he said:

“Lady, for God’s sake be silent for a little while and postpone these matters until we meet on the feast of Saint Mary.”

She, understanding—as everyone thought—that his end was approaching more quickly, yet greatly fearing his words, said:

“Would that your life, O beloved Father, might remain with us until that time arrives!”

But he, strongly gathering his strength, opening his eyes and looking around at everyone for a long time, said:

“Our life and our death truly rest in the power of God. Nevertheless, in the Truth, who is God, I tell you that on the feast of Saint Mary, wherever God wills, we shall certainly be together, and there, before the true witness, we shall discuss both these matters and the other things about which we disagree.”

After saying this, he closed his eyes and fell silent.

Struck with great astonishment, she silently said to those standing around:

“Alas, wretched me! Am I perhaps going to die and soon follow him?”

She nevertheless did not dare disturb him further, but humbly asked him both pardon and permission to depart.

Then, opening his eyes, he briefly—but beneficially—admonished her regarding the observance of sacred religion, reproved her for her manifold administration of the obedience entrusted to her, and, raising his right hand, fortified her with a blessing. Granting her remission for the time being, he dismissed her, not without great fear, as she herself confessed.

### 43.

After a week had passed, the blessed Father, his body now completely failing, was anointed according to ecclesiastical custom by the abbot and the other brothers with the liquid of sacred oil. As he had foretold, on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension he was carried to the mountain of Saint Maurice.

[Note: Regarding this mountain, the Saxon Chronicle manuscript says under the year 1025: “He began to inhabit the beautiful mountain on the western side of his city, which he later dedicated to the title and name of Saint Maurice, his supreme patron.”]

There the brothers immediately came to him weeping, together with an innumerable multitude of other faithful people, and could no longer conceal the bitterness of the grief with which they were afflicted in their hearts. An equally countless multitude of the faithful also gathered, and an equal bitterness afflicted them over the death of their most beloved shepherd.

Although his tongue was already almost failing, he dismissed them kindly with words of consolation and ordered them to return at dawn.

When they had departed and spent that holy night in great sorrow, the blessed Father, according to his custom, continually turned over the psalms in his mind as though they were sweet nourishment. Completing his course in such meditation, he commended his soul attentively to God.

[Note: Thus Bamberg; other copies read: “completing his course, he kept vigil through the night.”]

At earliest dawn the clergy returned after Matins had been completed. He then gave them his final address, brief but salutary, admonishing them concerning observance of sacred religion and obedience. After reciting the verse of confession together with them, he dismissed them with a final farewell to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass with the abbot.

The merciful bishop, not forgetting his promise, anxiously asked about his aforementioned chamberlain Buno. When he learned that the boy was physically beyond hope, he sent him a message:

“Take courage, my boy, in the Lord, and be strong, because the time is now near when you must truly arrive with me at the homeland of eternal blessedness.”

The boy heard these words joyfully. No longer thinking about his present life, on that very holy day of the Lord’s Ascension he asked for the saving viaticum. Having received it, he awaited the blessed bishop’s promise with joy.

### 44.

After the celebration of Mass had been completed among us and the festive meal had been taken in haste [*festively*, variant], the brothers returned to their beloved bishop at about the tenth hour of the day. They found him almost unable to speak with his tongue, but, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 14), singing with spirit and mind, and laboriously turning over the psalms in his breast alone.

After taking counsel, they stationed four choirboys on either side of his little bed and had them recite the psalter aloud and distinctly from the beginning.

When the blessed Father heard them, he seemed to take pleasure in the melody and rested somewhat; at times he also desired to sing the psalms together with them. Yet those principal verses that especially pertained to supplication to the Lord he recited more loudly, with his eyes open and raised.

At midnight, when the psalter had been completed and his end was now becoming more clearly imminent, they began the office of Matins. When they reached the psalm *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel*, the blessed man, struggling in his final agony and scarcely able to keep his eyes open, heard the clergy singing, “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.” He said:

“To guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1).

At this word, while the clergy were singing the *Gloria Patri* with the antiphon “I ascend to my Father and your Father,” he was lifted from the bed by those standing near him. Thus that truly blessed soul, while the body seemed to fall asleep, was released from its bodily prison.

The bells immediately rang together. The brothers in the monasteries, who had been awaiting his blessed death with vigilant care, devotedly recited the prayers for the dead for the salvation of so beloved a soul.

### 45.

I do not think, therefore, that the first sign of his merit, declared at his blessed death with God as witness, should now be passed over in silence.

The aforementioned boy Buno was lying in his mother’s house beside the church of Saint Michael. His limbs were already dead, with only his final breath fluttering in his breast, and he was regarded as beyond hope. When the bells immediately began to sound, he awoke as though from sleep and asked in astonishment what this was.

His mother, concealing the truth, told him that the beginning of Matins was being announced. But he, as though indignant at the deceit of his mother and those standing around, said:

“Why are you deceiving me? Why are you hiding the truth? Truly, at this signal my beloved Lord has ascended to heaven and, alas, forgetful of his promises, has left me wretched. Rise,” he said, “and, lifting up your hands and hearts, commend his beloved soul to divine mercy, and beg that he remember me now.”

Raising his eyes to heaven with whatever effort he could make, he said:

“O holy bishop, O most merciful Father, by the one to whom you are going I adjure you: remember me now, and do not leave me behind in the flesh after you, since you often promised that I would go with you to the homeland.”

They were astonished and grieving at once. While they obeyed his command, they scarcely had time, with their eyes turned back, to see him immediately lifeless. They laid him down at once and, abandoning their weeping, rejoiced that he had obtained what he desired.

### 46.

After the brothers in the monasteries had completed the proper funeral and Matins offices, celebrated Masses, and frequently recited psalms, they commended their shepherd to divine mercy with all the greater devotion because they trusted more confidently that they themselves would be commended by him.

When Bruno, bishop of the Church of Minden, whose blessed Father had adopted him as a spiritual son, arrived—he had also, after learning of his illness, been staying near our borders—at the third hour of that same day the entire clergy proceeded to the mountain where our special treasure was kept. They were accompanied by the people, soldiers, household, a great multitude of citizens and inhabitants of the surrounding region, and especially the poor. They carried him to the monastery of Saint Michael, as he himself had determined while alive.

As they approached, the funeral bier of the deceased young man was brought out before the gates of the courtyard, accompanied by a considerable crowd of relatives and citizens. It was also carried by the attendants around the churches that had been arranged, before the feet of the bishop.

Our powers of eloquence are certainly insufficient to recount how great were the weeping and lamentation there, whether of clergy, people, or even the poor. In the mind or voice of each person, mourning and joy sounded together: the hearts of the faithful bore sorrow for the present and joy for the future, because, as is sung of Saint Martin, it was pious to weep and pious to rejoice.

We therefore wept deservedly, because we had lost such a shepherd; but we also rejoiced rightly, because we had sent such an intercessor ahead of us.

### 47.

After vigils had been duly performed there according to our ability, the blessed body was honorably carried in the morning to Saint Andrew. After sacrifices had been offered there, it was then placed with due veneration in our principal church.

On the following day, as Sunday dawned, brothers and sisters from various monasteries throughout Saxony gathered to perform the service of so great a patron. They lamented with fitting grief the abandonment of the clergy, the desolation of the people, and the general loss suffered by all Christianity.

After the bishop had most devoutly completed the Mass, the sacred body of the blessed man was buried according to ecclesiastical custom in the midst of our choir. There, up to the present day, it has been visited with fitting reverence by Christ’s faithful, insofar as human frailty permits.

The little body of the aforementioned boy was first buried by the same bishop before the western entrance of the church.

Lady Sophia, whom we also mentioned above, now increasingly troubled by the warning she had received, sent her sisters and priests there with offerings and humbly commended herself to the merits and prayers of the blessed man. Thus she awaited in fear both the approaching Assumption and the Nativity of the blessed Mother of Christ.

At the beginning of the following year, however, three days before the Purification of Saint Mary, she departed this life. In this too God clearly revealed the prophecy of the blessed Father.

We also, insofar as God permits, ought rightly and frequently to commend the soul of that abbess to divine mercy. During her life she always cherished our congregation with complete affection and left to posterity a sure testimony of that same love.

### 48.

Regarding the miracles that divine kindness mercifully displayed for the salvation of believers through the merits of the blessed Father after the dissolution of his body, we have judged that it is better to write a few than many. We do not wish either to burden the diligent or the sluggish with weariness, or to bring upon unbelievers the danger of unbelief through the length of the narrative.

Above all, however, we do this because of certain persons of vain mind who, according to the customary practice of our homeland, wander through holy places and rashly pretend to be blind, crippled, speechless, or possessed. Before the altars or tombs of the saints they roll themselves about in the presence of the people, beat themselves with their fists, and immediately proclaim that they have been healed. Their only motive is the insane pleasure of receiving from the common people a larger alms or profit.

Thus it happens—as we have already said that the blessed man often remarked regarding such people—that “liars cause the truthful scarcely to be believed.”

When such persons are clearly caught in this kind of deception, even the true powers of the saints are driven by this doubt into dangerous despair. Indeed, those who are truly healed are sometimes believed to be deceiving people, not only by the faithless but occasionally even by the faithful, as plainly happened to us in the case of a certain little woman.

### 49.

In the first year of the aforementioned bishop Helizo [another reading: Hetelo], on our special feast, namely the Assumption of Saint Mary, a certain old woman unknown to us, with her head veiled and her face clouded, threw herself before the tomb of the blessed man. There she rolled about for a long time in the manner described above, customary among the deranged. At last she leapt up and proclaimed that, although she had been blind for many years, she had there and then been restored to sight.

[Note: He was taken from the provostship of Goslar and appointed bishop of Hildesheim after the death of Azelin in 1054. He held that see for twenty-five years and was buried in the church of Saint Maurice on the mountain, which he had first founded for nuns and later for canons. Henschenius further notes that the Grecian codex contains here some material concerning the three immediate successors of Saint Godehard—namely Thietmar, Akelin, and Helizo or Hetelo.]

As soon as the report had spread, clergy and people rushed together, and the bishop himself also arrived. When they were already hastening to give public thanks to God, the woman’s fellow citizens came—people who had known her previously and had often caught her in this kind of falsehood. They truthfully declared that she had lied both on this occasion and many times before.

When the people, rightly angered, began to rise against her in order to mistreat her, the clergy nevertheless defended her out of reverence for the blessed bishop. Confounded, she departed and never again appeared among us.

Having therefore avoided such deceptions thereafter through careful discernment, and having passed over with doubt the statements of many unknown persons, although those statements might in fact have been true, we direct the course of our narrative only to those things that we ourselves saw in the presence of the truth of God, or that we certainly heard from people whom we knew to be truthful in the fear of the Lord.

[Col. 1198A] **50.** The first [miracle] was this—and it was and is known to everyone. One of the workers of our church, named Luidger, was placing timbers in the church courtyard when a rather heavy beam fell and terribly crushed his thigh, shin, and foot, leaving him completely disabled. Because the blessed Father had previously recognized him as faithful and useful, he ordered him to sit daily before his table with the poor for alms. Miserable man that he was, in addition to the pain of his disability he often afflicted himself with even deeper grief, because he could no longer be useful for the work to which he had been assigned. Nevertheless, whatever he could do either sitting or crawling, he diligently undertook as a voluntary service; nor did he allow any time to pass—except when he was sleeping or eating—without seeming always to be useful in some way.

It was customary for our beloved bishop to have boys, and sometimes stronger poor men, go repeatedly through streets or dug-out hollows among the rocks; they would bring him small stones of snowy, black, red, or occasionally variegated color. He would grind and polish these, and by various striking or rubbing transform them into the likeness of precious stones, placing them decorously on altars, in books, or in reliquaries. The poor man mentioned above devoted himself particularly to this work, usefully anticipating the industry of the others; and the bishop was thoroughly pleased with him on account of this kind of resourcefulness. At times he also joined the painters and those who fitted glass into windows, and among them too he proved usefully industrious.

[Col. 1198C] **51.** After the blessed bishop had been taken from this life, he himself was tonsured and dressed in wool, abstaining from meat and other more sumptuous food. He went to the bishop’s tomb and served there, with all the fidelity he could muster, both the custodians and the other faithful. Finally, with the masters’ consent, he took over the entire guardianship of the tomb. He performed this service while scarcely able to support his weakened leg with a piece of wood and lifting the rest of his body with a staff. Yet the devotion of obedience supplied the strength that infirmity denied him.

He did not know the psalms, but the words he learned through the faithful’s recitation or instruction he carefully repeated, keeping more devout watch and frequently lying prostrate in the manner of the faithful seeking pardon. As he persisted more firmly in this diligence and strove to advance as far as he could, one Saturday toward evening, while the evening praise was being sung in the choir, he prostrated himself beside the bishop’s tomb. There he remained for a long time, held almost motionless either by sleep or by ecstasy; and, as he later admitted, he was invisibly tormented by an intolerable stretching or contraction of his limbs and nerves.

When the praise had ended, he rose as if drowsy and, appearing more ill than usual, scarcely returned to his lodging. Immediately he lay down on his bed and struggled painfully throughout the night with that severe stretching of his limbs. At last, shortly before matins, he fell asleep and saw a dream in which he was ordered to rise and hurry to the church to give thanks to God. Quickly awakened, he arose, then removed the support from his thigh and cast aside his staff. At the hour of matins he entered the church, openly praised God before everyone, and afterward, healthy for the rest of his life, served with ever greater devotion the longer he lived.

**52.** There was also a woman named Mersvid, very well known to all who lived with us, who had wandered about blind for many years. On the day after the Assumption of Saint Mary, she was given sight at the same tomb of the blessed bishop, before the clergy and people.

[Col. 1199B] **53.** A certain peasant from the district belonging to the church called Holthlaon, named Emko [Deniko], miserably worn down by a long illness, had for many years been deprived of the use of his legs because of a contraction of the loins. At last, scarcely crawling with the support of staffs, he reached the holy man’s memorial; there, on the anniversary of the holy man’s death, he recovered complete health before the clergy and people, while all of us looked on.

**54.** A certain noblewoman, not unknown, from the bishopric of Minden, named Siuve, was raising her brother’s daughter, whom she had adopted as a daughter and loved deeply. Struck by a very serious illness, the girl began to be in danger and lay lifeless for two days, as though already dead. While relatives, household members, and townspeople sat around her, weeping in deep compassion over the girl’s great beauty, an old woman who served the church spoke of the memory of our bishop and explained how, through divine mercy, the sick were healed at his tomb.

Moved by this exhortation, the lady herself entered the church at the hour of matins. Prostrate before the altar and shedding abundant tears, she vowed with heartfelt devotion offerings to God, to Saint Mary, and also to the soul of the blessed bishop on behalf of her niece. Immediately, as she herself swore to us with tears, she returned and found the girl seeing and speaking. The girl asked for food, received it, and, with Christ granting this through the merits of the holy man, recovered complete health.

On the fifth day afterward, her aunt brought her to the altar of Saint Mary and to the bishop’s tomb with the promised offerings, and before a multitude, with sufficient testimony from the townspeople and her fellow countrymen, demonstrated how she had been healed.

**55.** Our brother Volcward [variant: Folchardus], a priest of memorable reputation, at that time steward, later our provost, and finally the blessed bishop of the Church of Brandenburg, had—as everyone knows—served our Father faithfully and pleased him deeply. After the bishop’s death, while he was making his customary rounds of the episcopal estates, he came to a village called Eckershuson [variant: Aschgereshusen]. Turning aside to a certain house for a meal, he found a little boy afflicted by a miserable wasting illness. For several weeks the boy had lain deprived of the use of all his limbs and, as everyone thought, was approaching death day by day.

The priest, who was always compassionate toward such cases, gazed at him for a long time with tears and asked the household about the duration and course of the illness. When he learned the facts, he persuaded the weeping mother to promise candles at the holy bishop’s tomb, each candle equal in length to the boy. She immediately did so most willingly. But since the poor woman had no wax for such a purpose, he ordered a light to be prepared from flax [lychnum], had the boy measured limb by limb so that he could carry the exact measure with him, and, providing the wax himself, offered candles for the sick boy at the holy man’s memorial.

After this they sat down to eat and, as if they had forgotten the boy, began to talk among themselves about other matters. Meanwhile the boy, with astonishing speed, came back to life as if from death. To everyone’s amazement he sat up in bed, called his mother, crawled out from his bedding, asked for food, and received it at once. Thereafter he remained healthy through the merits of the holy man.

**56.** There was also in our congregation a certain young man named Desiderius, converted from the laity, tonsured into the clergy at the command of the same blessed man, and advanced as far as the diaconate. Since he could not regularly perform the full office of singing and reading with the brothers, the holy man ordered him to serve with the church custodians so that he would not be entirely idle.

In the time of our bishop Azelin [Note: [Col. 1199D] Bamberg: our revered bishop Wecelin.], after the wretched burning of our monastery, this brother of ours was sitting one evening during the Christmas holidays in the schools, conversing with the boys, when he was suddenly and miserably struck by blindness and fell. When another illness developed, he remained bedridden for a long time.

During Lent, while the blindness continued, he recovered from the other illness. He regularly attended the church according to custom and repeatedly prostrated himself at the bishop’s tomb, hoping to be healed. It happened on a weekday before Easter—certainly on the Kalends of April—[Col. 1200D] when we celebrate the arrival of the relics of the holy martyrs of Cantius [Note: [Col. 1199D] They are so called: they were Saints Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilius, who are said to have suffered with their tutor Proto at Aquileia on the day before the Kalends of June. Their Passion is attributed to Saint Ambrose in Mombritius. Another version, from an ancient manuscript of C. V. Ulrich Obrecht, was published in the Appendix to the Gallican Liturgy.]—that while he was prostrate there at matins, his right eye suddenly seemed to itch. When he rubbed it rather forcefully with his hand, a considerable amount of blood burst forth, and immediately he regained sight in that eye. For this divine clemency everyone together praised God, while awaiting the Lord’s customary power of mercy for the remaining eye.

After Easter, on the anniversary of our holy Father, when the bishop had celebrated a Mass for the dead in his memory, he collapsed as if overcome by illness during the offering, before the clergy and people. Immediately blood burst from his eyes, nostrils, and ears, and, when the eye opened, he clearly received his sight. At the conclusion of the missal service, the bishop addressed the clergy and people, exhorting them to offer due praises to God; and, with all shedding abundant tears in unison, he too praised God.

At that very moment [variant: on that day], thanks be to God, the brother recovered completely and thereafter remained faithful to his promised profession until the end.

**57.** We therefore pass over many praises of our blessed shepherd, for the reason stated above, although by divine clemency we often perceive them being gloriously accomplished from the beginning until now. Nevertheless, we will not conceal this, which we know to be true with the testimony of the entire holy Church: many people frequently come joyfully to his tomb with offerings and publicly report that they and their loved ones have been freed by the merits of his powers, through swift assistance, from various troubles or illnesses.

For whenever any inconvenience or distress befalls someone, as soon as that person turns to the memory of this holy Father—or, while absent, makes a vow of an offering to him wherever he may be—he undoubtedly begs in true faith, hoping for some consolation at that very moment; and, with his merits interceding, obtains it more quickly, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who works all things in all, and who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# TEN MIRACLES PERFORMED BY SAINT GODEHARD WHILE HE WAS STILL ABBOT

[Col. 1201]

## I. Concerning a man suffering from fever whom he healed in Bavaria

[Col. 1201B]

**58.** A certain citizen of Passau named John was afflicted by fever for a long time. It happened that the holy Father Godehard, still abbot of his monastery at Altach, came to Passau on business concerning that monastery. When the sick man learned of his arrival, he sent his brother to him, asking that he deign to visit him for God’s sake; and the holy man did so.

When he saw the fevers in which the man lay, he groaned and said:

> “O Father Adam, who blinded you so quickly that you opposed the commands of your Creator and subjected us all to so many evils through your sin? Behold: after the temporal sufferings we endure here, unless we keep his commands, we fear that we shall suffer eternally; and this temporal evil will be for us the beginning of eternal evils.”

After saying this, he took a cup, poured wine into it, blessed it after marking it with the sign of the cross, and handed it to the sick man, saying:

> “Drink, brother, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be strengthened in him.”

The man drank, trusting in God’s mercy and the holy man’s merits. Immediately he rose, completely freed from every trouble of the fever, and went to the church of Saint Stephen praising God.

## II. Concerning a monk whom he freed from a severe fever by his prayers

**59.** The holy man Godehard took a certain monk from his monastery at Altach with him to the monastery at Herfeld. After arriving there, the monk lay ill with the distress of fever. The holy Father frequently visited him for his consolation.

On one occasion he said to the sick man:

> “My brother, how are you?”

The sick man replied:

> “See, Father, the distress of fever torments me so greatly that life now seems almost absent from me.”

The holy man said to him:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ suffered greater things for us than the troubles of your fever can be.”

The man lying there replied:

> “I know, my Father, I know that he endured far heavier torments for us, even to the bitterness of death.”

Saint Godehard said:

> “In the name of Jesus Christ, who endured heavier things for us, rise; and, singing among your brothers, bless him who washed and redeemed you with his blood.”

The sick man replied:

> “I shall rise in the name of Jesus Christ, go to my father, who is also the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, and say to him: ‘I am no longer worthy to be called your son’ (Matthew 15:19), ‘but show me your mercy, as to your servant’ (Psalm 118:124), though one who has strayed from your way; and mercifully receive me as I return to you.”

While he was saying these words, he rose and went to the choir. To everyone’s amazement, he praised God and sang with those standing there, and blessed him.

## III. Concerning a young girl freed from the distress of fever

**60.** In the town of Teckendorff, in Bavarian territory, a certain young girl was weighed down severely by fever. Some respectable women were attending her and told her how the man previously mentioned had been freed at Passau from the rigor of fever through the merits of the blessed Godehard after drinking wine blessed by him.

When she heard this, the sick girl said to her father:

> “O my beloved father, I beg you, through Jesus Christ, to send to the holy man Godehard and ask him to bless a little wine in his cup or chalice and send it to me, so that I may drink from it and be relieved from the feverish heat by which I am continually afflicted and burned.”

When the father heard this, he sent as she requested and received blessed wine from Saint Godehard. The sick girl drank it in the name of Jesus Christ and was suddenly healed. She rose praising God, who through the merits of Saint Godehard had mercifully freed her from the violence of the fever.

## IV. Concerning a schoolboy healed from a similar fever

**61.** The servant of God Godehard, being merciful from the heart and carrying a compassionate concern for the afflicted, always visited the homes of the sick and bedridden, either personally or through others.

It happened once, while he was still presiding over the abbey at Altach, that a certain schoolboy belonging to a poor widow was seriously ill with fever. The holy man repeatedly visited him with his customary compassion and at one point said:

> “Son, act manfully, bearing the Lord’s chastisements, and let your heart be strengthened in him. For he is the one who strikes, heals, and restores, chastising his chosen ones so that they may not be handed over to eternal death.”

The young man replied:

> “What strength do I have to endure and bear these grievous things patiently?”

The holy Father said:

> “Have confidence, son, knowing that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us (Romans 8:18); and willingly choose, with the Apostle, to glory in your infirmities, so that Christ’s power may dwell in you as it did in him, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).”

The sick man replied:

> “I ask you, holy Father, to entreat God earnestly for me in my misery.”

The holy Father had an apple in his hand, which he had perhaps brought with him or found beside the sick man’s bed. He blessed it and gave it to the sick man, saying:

> “Take this, son, and eat the apple in the name of Jesus Christ. If it is his will, rise healthy from your bed; but if not, let this illness remain with you, and bear it patiently, so that you may deserve from God the reward of eternal life, in which there is eternal health.”

The boy ate it and rose healthy, praising God.

## V. Concerning a young man drowned and restored to life through the merits of Saint Godehard

**62.** A certain young man from the castle of Stauwenborch in Bavaria, wishing to cross the Danube, was drowned when storms overturned the boat. He remained there undiscovered for more than three hours. At last his lifeless body was cast onto the bank, and he was carried dead to his parents’ house.

Relatives wept and members of the household mourned the sudden death of so famous a young man. The holy abbot Godehard happened to pass through the place and, hearing the voices of those wailing, said:

> “O death, how bitter is your memory to a human being! (Ecclesiasticus 41:1.) How suddenly and unexpectedly you extinguish life! You are most terrible to sinners, but for the righteous you are greatly desired and precious.”

While he was saying these and similar things, the young man’s wretched mother came and fell at the holy man’s feet, saying:

> “Lord, if you have any power with God, have mercy on me and raise my son.”

The holy Father replied:

> “Believe me, woman: as truth is and daily experience teaches, we are all subject to the power of death; therefore blessed are the dead who die in the Lord (Revelation 14:13). Death strikes all who live in the world, not in one way but in almost a thousand. Blessed is the one who keeps watch (Revelation 16:15) and is prepared in advance for his coming.”

Again the woman said in a tearful voice:

> “Behold, my only and beloved son has suddenly perished, suffocated in the river. I fear his damnation, because he was excessively worldly. Therefore, merciful Father, I beg you: if you have any power with God, raise my son, so that he may confess his sins and be fortified with the holy sacraments of the Church; afterward, if it pleases God, let him rest happily in peace.”

The holy man, using the Savior’s words, replied:

> “O woman, great is your faith (Matthew 15:28); let it be done for you as you have asked.”

He went with her to the corpse lying on the bier, took the young man’s hand, and said:

> “Young man, I say to you, arise.”

The young man rose unharmed and healthy. He asked the holy man, for God’s sake, to hear his confession and impose a saving penance upon him for his sins. The holy Father granted his request; after hearing his confession, he fortified him with the sacred sacraments of the Church.

When this had been done, the young man said:

> “Holy Father, command me now to rest again in peace. I greatly loathe the world, which sends its lovers into hell, the grievous punishment of which I have partly experienced.”

The man of God said:

> “Sleep, my son, and rest happily in the peace of Jesus Christ.”

He replied:

> “Amen.”

He bowed his head and happily fell asleep in God’s grace. His mother, made joyful by what she heard and learned and entirely free from grief, gladly entrusted her son’s body to burial according to ecclesiastical custom and, with as much devotion as she could, joyfully commended his soul to God.

## VI. Concerning a woman in labor who was freed from the pains of childbirth by the saint’s prayers

**63.** While the holy Father Godehard was sitting in his cell after the matins vigil for the sake of prayer, it happened that a woman living near the monastery was suffering in labor. The holy man took pity on her, fell to the ground, and devoted himself to prayer, saying:

> “O Lord God almighty, help your creature; have mercy on Eve’s daughter laboring under her mother’s curse.”

At once, in an unexpected manner, the woman became silent, because she had given birth to a son. Later, when she fell asleep, it was revealed to her that she had been freed from the pains of childbirth through the prayers of Saint Godehard.

She gave thanks to God, who had visited her so mercifully through the holy man’s merits. She had her son called Godehard and, while he was still a child, entrusted him to the holy man to be instructed in the discipline of the religious life. For this reason the women of that region became accustomed to invoke the patronage of Saint Godehard during the pain of childbirth, and many of them found the fulfillment of their requests.

## VII. Concerning a companion whom he had on the road, who fell and broke his leg, but whom the holy man immediately healed

[Col. 1204D]

**64.** When Saint Godehard was perhaps going to the Roman curia on business concerning his monastery, he had several of his monks with him in his company. One of them, older than the others, named Erkenfrid, was proceeding carelessly. As he climbed the mountain called Godehard’s Mountain, the horse fell with him and completely broke his right leg.

Groaning with tears, he murmured against the holy man of God:

> “Why, Father, did you lead me to the precipice of this mountain, so that you might kill me?”

The holy Father replied:

> “I know, my beloved son, that you began this journey with me unwillingly and inwardly disparaged me by murmuring. Therefore your reward was then returned to you. Repent, therefore, and pray God to forgive you this offense, so that you may be healed.”

He replied:

> “Help my infirmity, Father, and forgive me what I have done against you; and let God’s scourge torment me as much as it pleases.”

When the man of God heard his devotion, he touched the broken bone of his leg and said:

> “The Lord Jesus Christ heals you, brother; now rise in his name, so that we may walk.”

The man rose completely healed and continued the journey with him. Later he followed him to Hildesheim and remained with him until the day of his death.

## VIII. Concerning a blind woman whom he illuminated with God’s help

**65.** It happened once that Saint Godehard was passing through the town of Strawigen [variant: Stravubingen] in the diocese of Regensburg. A certain blind woman, a beggar going from door to door asking for bread, met him. Perhaps she was trying to avoid the noise of horses; she struck her foot against a stone and fell very heavily.

When Saint Godehard saw this, he immediately dismounted from his horse, ran to her, embraced her, and raised her up. As carefully as he could, he wiped the filth of the mud from the poor woman’s cloak and said:

> “Why did you fall, mother?”

She replied:

> “I am blind, friend, and therefore I cannot see the obstacles in the roads or avoid them.”

The holy Father, feeling compassion for her from his heart, said:

> “O my God, how many insults and burdens there are on earth for your creature! Well, then, it is said: ‘Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth!’ (Revelation 8:13).”

After saying this, he mixed mud with spittle, following the example of our Savior (John 9:6), and smeared it on her eyes, saying:

> “O Lord Jesus Christ, who in the sight of your disciples made mud from spittle and smeared the eyes of a certain blind man, and he saw: illuminate also the eyes of this poor woman of yours, so that she may confess your name and glory in your most worthy praise (Psalm 105:47).”

After these actions and words, the woman began to look at the holy man. She fell at his feet and said:

> “My eyes have seen the salvation of God.”

She lay prostrate and kissed his feet, then went home praising God for the powers and merits of the holy man.

## IX. Concerning a possessed woman healed through the merits of Saint Godehard

**66.** At a certain time Saint Godehard was staying in the city of Regensburg, perhaps on business concerning his monastery. A woman possessed by a demon was brought to him to be healed.

The man of God looked at her and said:

> “Answer me, unclean spirit, concerning what I ask you. What are you doing here in God’s creature?”

The demon replied:

> “Her soul is mine by full right, because she is a sorceress, and through her I have won many souls.”

The holy man said:

> “Why is she yours because of sorcery?”

The demon replied:

> “Have you not read that the Lord commanded pythonic spirits, diviners, and sorcerers to be exterminated? For what do such people do except serve me and my princes? They are idolaters. We can scarcely possess anyone with as great a right as those ensnared in such vices. Do you not know that among a thousand sorceresses or diviners scarcely one is found who wishes to confess this vice? Thus we close their mouths, so that in no way can they speak about such things.”

The holy man said:

> “I know that your wickedness and that of those like you is great. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that God’s goodness and mercy are greater. Therefore, unclean spirit, give honor to God and depart from his creature, so that she may return to the grace that you took away from her.”

The demon replied:

> “Why are you using such violence against me? What have I done to you, or what charge do you have against me?”

He replied:

> “Listen, insolent and unclean spirit. In that eternal homeland from which you fell through pride, my joy in the common good will be as great as my joy in my own good—indeed, much greater. Therefore here it is fitting to grieve over another’s evil much more intensely than over one’s own. Through this I shall deserve eternal life. I therefore have a just charge against you, because you unjustly possess and punish my sister, the creature of your Creator God.

> “I am not, as you claim, using violence against you. For the glory of God and the love of his creature—for whom his Only-Begotten Son, pouring out his blood, endured the death he loved so greatly—I do not fight against you as a mere combatant but as a glorious victor [decerto, ‘I contend’]. Therefore I command you, proud and unclean spirit: in the name of Jesus Christ, depart from her, and do not presume henceforth to trouble God’s creature.”

Thus the evil spirit departed, and the woman fell as if dead. The holy man immediately raised her up. Once standing, she publicly confessed with tears the vice of sorcery, which she had practiced many times before. The holy man absolved her by the power of the passion of Jesus Christ.

## X. Concerning a very dull boy whom he made teachable by his prayer

**67.** In the city of Passau there was a very wealthy citizen who had a son whom he loved most tenderly. The boy was so dull that in three years he had been unable to learn even the alphabet.

Therefore his father approached Saint Godehard, reported the hardness of his son’s heart, and urgently asked him to pray earnestly for the boy, so that almighty God might deign to enlighten him.
