Saint Godehard summoned the boy and read over him the following words:

> “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclesiasticus 1:1);

together with the collect:

> “O God, who through your coeternal Wisdom created human beings when they did not yet exist,” etc.

He added:

> “Go, son; may that best of teachers, who suddenly taught the apostles, instruct you and lead you along the right way to clearer knowledge.”

The boy was so transformed that within a short time he surpassed all his relatives and all his contemporaries—and even those older and more learned than himself—in the fullness of wisdom. Later, because of the depth of his understanding and wisdom, he was elected and ordained bishop of Passau. He then labored most zealously for the salvation of souls, both his own and those entrusted to him.

# The following miracle occurred when he was bishop

## Concerning the dead who rose from their tombs at the holy bishop’s command and left the church, because they had been excommunicated, whereas the living had refused to do so

**68.** It happened that the holy bishop Godehard excommunicated certain of his subjects for their rebellion, after the customary warnings. Some of them, stirred up by the poison of their wickedness, arrogantly and insolently entered the church while he was celebrating.

When he learned of this, he turned away from the altar and said:

> “I command all of you who are excommunicated, by the power of the Holy Spirit and of holy obedience, to leave the church.”

But the rebels and excommunicates paid no attention to this command and remained in the church.

Then certain dead people who had rested for many years in their tombs rose and left the church. They had perhaps been buried under excommunication, unknown to those who had buried them [Note: [Col. 1207C] Saint Gregory recounts a similar story in Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 23: nuns excommunicated by Blessed Father Benedict were seen leaving the church in which they had been buried whenever the deacon proclaimed during Mass, “If anyone does not communicate, let him withdraw.” But at last they were released through the offering of the holy Father.].

When the rebels saw this, they were ashamed and left after the dead. When the holy bishop had finished Mass, he went out to them and said:

> “Listen, rebels and unbelievers, and behold God’s just judgment against you. See: the dead obey God in his vicar, but you, filled with a proud spirit, have despised obedience. These dead, therefore, will rise against you in judgment and will bring a sentence of condemnation against you, unless you perform full and fitting penance.”

After saying this, he turned to the dead and said:

> “Brothers, I absolve you by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ from the sentence of excommunication with which you have been bound until now, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Go; return to your places and rest in peace while awaiting the coming of the Judge.”

The dead bowed their heads and joined their hands, as if giving thanks, then returned to their places and rested.

# CANONIZATION AND TRANSLATION OF SAINT GODEHARD  
## How the blessed Godehard was enrolled among the saints, and concerning the subsequent miracles

[Col. 1207]

[Col. 1207B] **1.** Glory to the supreme Creator and restorer of the human race, who, not because of our merits but through his immense goodness, deigned to reveal his confessor, the blessed bishop Godehard, to the people of our time for the salvation of all believers; and who wished to make known among the nations of various lands the man who, because of the passage of time, had already been obscured by a certain cloud of forgetfulness, so that at last he might be venerated by the inhabitants of our Church. He wished his glory to reach not only those belonging to the household of faith but also to spread among foreign nations.

I undertake to describe how and in what order the translation of this confessor of ours took place—not in inflated language or strutting in the grand cothurnus, but in a simple style. I do not trust the small spark of my own talent, but rather that evangelical saying:

> “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80);

and again:

> “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

Through writings, past events—which in a short time would otherwise be handed over to oblivion—are recalled to memory. And through deeds virtuously performed in the Church, the faithful are inflamed when they are read, and the torpor of their minds is shaken off.

**2.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1128 [Note: [Col. 1207D] This passage also proves that the blessed Godehard died in the year 1038. For if you add ninety years to 1038, you will find the year 1128, which the author assigns here.], the ninetieth year after the death of the blessed Godehard, the venerable Berthold [Note: [Col. 1208D] Berthold held this see for fifteen years and died in 1130. He founded the monastery of Bertholdirod for regular canons not far from the city of Hildesheim; it later passed to the Cistercians.], a man distinguished in every ecclesiastical discipline, highly learned in literary knowledge and greatly adorned by the uprightness of his morals, presided over the cathedral of our church.

By governing it wisely and gathering religious men to himself from every side and from various churches, he raised it to such eminence that during his tenure he built various cells and strengthened them in a spiritual way of life through gentle exhortation.

While he was seated in the common assembly of the clergy entrusted to him and, as was his custom, continually discussing the welfare of the people of our Church, God brought it about—as later events showed—that a discussion unexpectedly arose concerning our patron, the blessed Godehard. Again and again several people repeated the matter, complaining and grieving that they possessed so merciful a patron but did not offer him honor worthy of him in the Church of God.

For how great a mercy and how manifest a grace the aforementioned confessor had obtained for our brothers through his merits before God was made known by all the authoritative men present at that assembly. As a result, the minds of all who were seated there were not merely gladdened; they were also unanimously inflamed to multiply his praises in the Church of God.

3. For the aforementioned bishop Berthold, our bishop, disclosed to all who were present the private favor granted to him by our patron, and, not without contrition of heart, recounted to our brothers how he had come to know him as a merciful intercessor before God. For, in the time of his youth, when he was occupied with youthful diversions among the other adolescents, it happened [Col. 1209A] that in the suburb of our city he unintentionally pierced a certain layman with a lance and struck him to the ground as though dead. The man, apparently half-alive, was carried home, confined to bed, and remained in danger of death. But our aforesaid bishop, grieving and mourning, was thrown into various anxieties: he was distressed that he would have to be rejected from sacred orders as a homicide, and thus his mind was drawn into diverse thoughts. At length, wavering like a ship caught in the waves of the sea, he turned to our patron, blessed Godehard, as to a safe harbor; he fixed his hope in him like an anchor in firm ground, and with contrite heart and humbled spirit begged that he might rescue him from the anxiety that threatened.

But while the wounded man already lay in the throes of death, [Col. 1209B] firm in faith, he prostrated himself at the tomb of our holy patron, spent the entire night in prayer, and implored mercy more by the groaning of his heart than by the utterance of his voice. At last, near the end of the night, exhausted by his vigils and disturbed by pain, he was compelled to enter into sleep. In that sleep, the stature and appearance of our patron were most certainly manifested to him in a vision, as he had seen them in this life. For, while he was still between wakefulness and fully developed sleep, the person of our patron appeared to him in a vision and carefully instructed him to have the solemn rites of Mass celebrated for him; and he immediately added that the office should be sung: “Do not be afraid, Zachariah; your prayer has been heard” (Luke 1:13). When he had seen these things, he awoke [Col. 1209C] and began to continue his prayers with ever greater persistence. But on the road he received a messenger who most certainly announced that the sick man had escaped death. Hearing this, he rejoiced in heart and spirit and blessed the God of heaven, who had preserved such a patron for us in our church.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Bollandus has: “whom, however, he had never seen”; whether this is more correct is uncertain. For if Berthold died at the age of eighty or ninety, he could have seen Saint Godehard while the latter was still alive.]

4. At that time there was in our community a certain religious priest named Adelbert, who lived according to the rule in the cell of Saint Bartholomew, situated in the eastern part of our city. When he heard what our bishop had related, he saw that the occasion was suitable and likewise disclosed to everyone the favor that had been bestowed upon him by the Lord through our patron. For one night, while he was going around the altars of our church imploring the protection of the saints, he finally prostrated himself beside the tomb of the blessed confessor. But when he rose, he indiscreetly grasped the sarcophagus to lift himself up; immediately his thumb withered at its own joint. Seeing that his hand had now been disabled, he prostrated himself on the ground, suppliant and lamenting, and asked blessed Godehard for pardon and mercy. At once, without delay or injury, his thumb sprang back into its proper place. [Col. 1209D]

5. Hearing this, a certain master from Mount Saint Maurice named Reinard, a man of advanced age, [Col. 1210A] who himself had experienced the manifest favor of our patron, saw that the opportunity was appropriate and did not keep it silent, but clearly revealed it to all who were present in our community, saying:

“There was a certain boy committed to his custody, to be instructed in the clerical discipline. He was so afflicted by the epileptic illness, which in the common tongue they call ‘the falling sickness,’ that he was thrown to the ground at least six times every day and was endangered by excessive exhaustion almost to the point of death. One day he was brought to the protection of our blessed confessor, but on the way he fell to the ground twice. Prayers were poured out for him at the tomb; alms were distributed to the poor; and he returned completely healed to his own home.”

6. When these three signs had been recited in the common assembly by authoritative [Col. 1210B] men, all received them with joyful minds and urged our bishop to undertake by every means how he might canonize our blessed bishop Godehard among the other saints of God—something he was willing to do of his own accord. But since divine assistance must be invoked in small matters, and still more in great ones, in which we await a happy outcome, it pleased everyone that special prayers should everywhere be offered to God in our church for this cause, lest we begin anything vain or ill-advised against the Lord’s will that we would be unable to bring to a good result.

Accordingly, it was decreed that all, both great and small, after the hour of Matins had ended, should assemble at the tomb of that blessed patron of ours, Godehard, [Col. 1210C] prostrate themselves humbly upon the ground, and sing to the Lord with contrite and humbled hearts the psalm, “You have blessed your land, O Lord” (Psalm 84:2). It was also decreed that in every monastery situated within the territory of our church special prayers and distributions of alms should be made for him, since it is impossible that the voices of so many prayers should not be heard.

7. After these things had been carried out for some time, our church was shaken by a new tribulation. For our aforesaid father, alas, was taken from us in this life, and our whole church was thrown into confusion, deprived of so great a shepherd. But God, who comforts the afflicted in their tribulation, did not permit his church to drift long upon the waves of this world without a governor, knowing that “where there is no governor, the people will fall.” For our whole church, assembled together, elected as spiritual shepherd Bernard, [Col. 1210D] the high provost, a man learned in every clerical discipline and adorned with excellent morals, by the common consent of the clergy and the enthusiasm of the people. He protested, resisted in every way, and loudly declared himself unworthy, yet they brought him to the chair of the high priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Bernard presided over the Church of Hildesheim from 1130 to 1157. Although he had become blind nine years before his death, he had Bruno, the dean of his church, as his coadjutor; Bruno later succeeded him in the episcopate. How greatly he benefited the Church of Hildesheim and our order can easily be judged from the translation of Saint Godehard and the establishment of the monastery of Saint Godehard.]

When this had been done, the cause of our patron, which because of our tribulations had already declined somewhat, was renewed, and everyone labored to bring it to completion in the proper order.

8. But since canonical regulation, on account of the deceptions of demons that have frequently occurred in such matters in the Church of God, has decreed that no one may be canonized without apostolic authority and the approval of his life by authoritative men—a requirement that had greatly delayed our cause previously, both because of its difficulty and because of the length of the journey—it happened, with God’s assent, that what previously could not be brought to completion without great expense and the utmost labor was unexpectedly brought to us as if to our very door.

For a curia was summoned to the city of Liège, where Pope Innocent, with the Roman Church and a large part of Gaul, together with King Lothair and nearly all the bishops of the German region, assembled to deliberate concerning the violence perpetrated against the Roman Church by Peter Leonis, who at that time had violently usurped the papacy, and to devise how they might destroy that idol placed in the temple of the Lord. It therefore happened that on Laetare Sunday, “Jerusalem,” many Catholic men assembled in the aforesaid city, some with the apostolic pontiff and others with the king, and deliberated concerning the common condition of the Church. Among them our bishop Bernard, attending with the leaders of our church, saw the opportunity granted to him and approached the apostolic pontiff together with the entire Roman curia. The life of our shepherd was recounted before them, and prayers were most devoutly offered that he might be canonized by the apostolic pontiff in the Church of God.

9. But since it is the custom of the Roman Church to canonize the saints of God in a general council, and since such a council had at that time been summoned to the city of Reims for the feast of Saint Luke, after taking counsel he postponed our church’s petition until that place and promised most certainly to decide it there. Having done this, our bishop, encouraged by the apostolic promise, returned joyfully and was devoutly received by all; he reported what answer had been given him.

Then, hearing what had been promised by the apostolic pontiff, all rejoiced unanimously and most devoutly offered prayers to our bishop, asking him not to withdraw from so great a promise, but, even though it would be laborious, to present himself together with the leaders of our church at the appointed synod. The day had now arrived on which a synod of the entire Church on this side of the Alps had been summoned. Then our aforesaid bishop Bernard, together with Norbert, the metropolitan of Magdeburg, [Col. 1211D] who at that time was a man of great renown in the Church of God, and with the leaders of our church, set out for the aforesaid synod. With God’s assent, he arrived at Reims with great success and in good time.

[Note: [Col. 1211D] This is the celebrated Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian order.]

There they were honorably received. After the synod had already been held for several days, our bishop Bernard [Col. 1212A] met with the apostolic pontiff Innocent and his cardinals and most devoutly reminded him of the cause of our blessed patron, which had been delayed until then. But, with God’s assent and through his action, he found everyone unanimous and in agreement with his petition, as subsequent events made clear.

10. For on the following day, while the apostolic pontiff was presiding in the general synod, no one prompting him but God bringing it about, he delivered a clear speech to all, in which he eloquently set forth our church’s petition concerning our patron and most devoutly asked them to give their assent.

When this had been done, the bishop of Tarragona, [Col. 1212D] a religious man learned in literary knowledge, explained the manner in which the translation should be carried out: namely, if our church should establish through legitimate witnesses and an oath the things being said about our patron. At these words the apostolic pontiff intervened and declared that he had been so thoroughly informed about the matter by the princes of our land in the Church of Liège that it was unnecessary to testify to it a second time—something that could be proved more brightly than by the sun itself.

[Note: [Col. 1212D] Henschenius calls him Michael in his notes on this passage.]

When all had heard what the apostolic pontiff said, everyone unanimously gave assent that he should be canonized. They urged that praises be offered to the Lord, who deigns to rescue his servants from the weakness of this flesh and place them among his saints and elect. Immediately the *Te Deum laudamus* was sung; praise was offered to almighty God; and thus at last the assembled synod came to an end.

Our bishop then, equipped with the apostolic letters, returned all the way to us and was kindly received by clergy and people. The apostolic letters were opened, and when they had been read aloud, praises were offered to God. The text of the apostolic concession follows in these words:

11. INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Hildesheim: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Bernard, your bishop, came to us in the plenary synod that by God’s grace had been assembled at Reims. With the testimony of our brother bishops, abbots, and others who had come with him, he declared that Godehard, your bishop, of holy memory, had lived commendably in the world and had shone forth with many miracles both during his life and after his death.

Therefore, giving thanks to almighty God with our brothers, and having taken their counsel and commendation, because we believe that the same man has been crowned in heaven with the saints, we decree that he be honored among the saints. We command you to establish a solemnity for that blessed man in your church and to take care to assemble for it every year.

Given at Reims, the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

12. But because winter was then approaching and he could not make arrangements for so great an undertaking, it seemed appropriate that what had been granted by the apostolic pontiff should be announced to Catholic and religious men, and that the translation itself [Col. 1213A] should be postponed until the fourth day before the Nones of May.

The time had now arrived when so famous a report—namely, of the translation of so great a patron—was gathering in our city many religious people as well as men and women of every condition. Seeing this, a council was held in the common assembly concerning how he might be transferred carefully and without disturbance, lest any scandal should arise for our church from it.

For there were certain highly religious men who greatly feared that, because of the length of time, either the body would not be found or no indication of sanctity would be discovered. But after many discussions, all finally agreed that, once the crowd had been dismissed, everyone should assemble before Matins and open the tomb in which he had been placed with complete devotion.

At midnight, therefore, our bishop [Col. 1213B], together with the religious men assembled with him—both monks and regular clergy—entered the crypt of our church with great fear and trembling and ordered the sarcophagus in which our patron had been placed to be opened. Meanwhile, he and the other faithful devoted themselves most earnestly to prayer.

But where the greatest labor had previously seemed necessary to break open the sarcophagus, now, by God’s action, it immediately opened and offered the easiest access to the body. When the sarcophagus had been opened, who could express either in speech or in writing how many tears one would have seen among those standing there, what sobs one would have heard, or how spiritual the condition of the body appeared?

What more is there to say? A certain divine and unknown fragrance spread forth. It refreshed some of those standing there with a kind of spiritual sweetness and strengthened them in perfect faith in his sanctity. Then one would have seen everyone humbly excusing himself and declaring himself unworthy to touch the body of so great a patron, since they knew that their own lives were far removed from his holiness.

At length, while all hesitated and caused a long delay, our brother Provost Berthold lifted the body and, because of the multitude of people who had assembled to see so great an event, carried it into the seclusion of our sacristy. [Col. 1213C]

13. Let what has been said thus far suffice concerning how blessed Godehard was translated. It remains now to make known to your charity how through him the world was illuminated and how his fame was exalted even among the most distant and most pagan peoples.

For, because of the passage of time, the merits of his life had almost been erased and were known only to a few; through the translation of his body, however, they were made most clearly manifest to everyone. The Lord performed so many miracles through him that neither tongue can express them nor writing record them.

I shall undertake to describe those that are better known and more evident, so that in them posterity may be able to place its confidence in the protection of so great a Father.

On the very day of the translation, while the body was being carried with great reverence by clergy and people as far as Mount Saint Maurice, it happened that a certain man fell into the river [Col. 1213D] that flows past our city and, remaining under the waters for a long time, completely expired.

[Note: [Col. 1213D] The inhabitants call it the Ingra; about three leagues below Hildesheim it joins the Leine.]

When the body of our patron approached him, he was restored to his former life and, with the Lord’s help, was lifted from the ground sound and unharmed. Afterward he appeared for a long time in the service of our patron and did not prove ungrateful to God for the life restored to him. [Col. 1214A]

14. Having heard this, our church did not immediately and indiscriminately accept it, but humbly awaited another miracle that would be more certain and manifest. The following day, when the anniversary of our patron dawned, after Mass and the appointed hours had ended, a certain mute woman who had a son deprived of sight was suddenly, as if [Col. 1214B] in ecstasy, thrown down and rolled upon the ground for a short while.

After some time had passed, the mother’s tongue was released and the boy’s sight was restored; and it was confirmed to everyone that the event was a manifest miracle. For at that time there were in our city certain authoritative men from Corbie, [Col. 1213D] fellow countrymen of that woman, who had known her and most truthfully reported that she had long been mute and that her son had been deprived of sight.

[Note: [Col. 1213D] An illustrious monastery of Saxony, which owes its origin to Saint Adalard, as is related in his Life in the ninth-century volume.]

When this was heard, clergy and people assembled together in our church, and praises were offered to the Creator, who knows how to free his elect from all uncertainty and establish them in perfect faith. For signs are given to unbelievers, not to believers, so that through miracles and unusual events they may be confirmed in matters removed from our senses and memory.

15. The praises for the aforesaid miracle had scarcely been offered to God when a certain lame man, who had long been crippled, suddenly raised himself up and planted his foot firmly upon the ground. Thus it happened that on the very anniversary of our patron five miracles occurred within our basilica, which appeared manifest to all: the blind man saw; his mother spoke; and three lame men received the power to walk.

When this had happened, the report and fame of our patron, because of the multitude that had gathered for the translation of so great a man, became increasingly known and spread throughout all the neighboring lands. Consequently such a multitude of people imploring the protection of our shepherd flowed into our city [Col. 1214D] as no human being had ever before seen in our church, nor, I think, will see afterward.

For everyone brought to the protection of our shepherd those who were sick, feeble, lame, deaf, and mute, as well as those possessed by demons or afflicted by any other illness, seeking the recovery of health.

16. Around the same time, certain authoritative men from Thuringia [Col. 1215A] arrived, bringing with them their shepherd, whose one hand was disabled.

[Note: [Col. 1214D] Thuringia was once a very extensive region, which even bore the title of a kingdom under the first dynasty of our kings. It is now greatly reduced and is a province of Germany in Upper Saxony, subject to various princes.]

When they implored the protection of blessed Godehard, he immediately recovered his health and raised his disabled hand. After this, all unanimously gave praise to God and, as a sign of the truth, compared one hand with the other. For they found the hand with which he had previously held his pastoral staff wrinkled and hardened, while the other, with which he had not worked, was white and soft.

17. After this had happened, certain matrons from the same land came all the way to us, bringing with them a mute man who had long been unable to speak. While they persisted in prayer and implored the protection of blessed Godehard for him, suddenly the bond of his tongue was broken and its function was restored through the mercy [Col. 1215B] of God.

18. At that time there was at Erfurt [Col. 1215D] a vicedominus who, out of God’s mercy, supported a lame man who was weak in almost all his limbs and dependent upon his alms.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] A principal city of Thuringia, possessing a celebrated university.]

Having heard of the miracles performed through our patron, he sent the man to our church to seek his protection. And just as he believed, so, through God’s mercy, he received. For the man whom he sent to us weak and altogether unable to walk, he received back, with God’s help, sound and unharmed.

19. At that time there was in the cell of Saint Paulina [Col. 1215D] a certain lame man, long known and conspicuous to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] A monastery of Thuringia founded by Countess Paulina during the reign of Emperor Henry IV, with monks summoned from the monastery of Hirsau. On this consult Trithemius’s *Chronicon Hirsaugiense* under the year 1107, where the first abbot is said to have been Gerung, a monk of Hirsau. [Col. 1216D]]

A powerful man from Thuringia [Col. 1215C], with the abbot’s permission, took him into his care and, through the Lord’s mercy, provided him with what his body required. The man came to the protection of blessed Godehard and received bodily wholeness.

20. At that time there was also in Thuringia a certain hunchbacked girl, greatly bent over in the back. Coming to the protection of blessed Godehard, she was straightened through God’s mercy and, something that rarely happens, was entirely freed from her hump. A man born in the same land was likewise freed from the same illness through the mercy of the Lord and blessed Godehard.

21. At the same time there was a certain matron from Hesse [Col. 1215D], known to all her fellow provincials and afflicted by the greatest illnesses for many years.

[Note: [Col. 1216D] Hesse is a province of Germany belonging to the Rhenish circle, whose princes are called landgraves.]

When she no longer hoped for anything except death, she finally humbly implored the protection of blessed Godehard and prostrated herself upon the ground; in a marvelous manner she received health. For in her groin, where previously there had been healthy flesh, an opening suddenly appeared, and she abruptly expelled two stones of such size as no one had previously seen in a human body. After this, she carried one of them with her to our church, to the protection of blessed Godehard, as a sign of the miracle; the other she kept at home as a sign of God’s power.

22. Around the same time a notable miracle occurred in Thuringia, worthy of being handed down to memory. Two men, joined—alas!—in an evil partnership, committed a theft and stole some hides from a certain man. It happened that both were captured and dragged to judgment.

But when both, having been convicted, were being handed over to the gallows, one of them groaned with his whole heart and, doing the only thing he could, implored the protection of blessed Godehard with contrite and humbled heart. The other, as if despairing, made no petition and uttered no word of remorse.

It therefore happened that they were bound with one rope and hanged from one branch. After this, one immediately gave up his spirit; but the other, who had implored the protection of blessed Godehard, hung without injury or distress.

After a considerable number of hours had passed, the man whose hides had been stolen drew nearer and, seeing that one had expired, addressed the other, whom he thought still alive. He asked whether he was alive or had been able to retain life. The latter, hoping that help had arrived for him, confessed both that he was alive and that he felt no pain.

Hearing this, the man who had ordered him to be hanged inflicted great inhumanity upon him. He twisted the rope by which he had been suspended, pressed the body down toward the ground with a firm effort, and hoped in this way to break the vertebrae of his neck. Having done this, he immediately departed and had no doubt that he had now fulfilled his entire intention.

After they had gone, however, a long time passed, and the aforesaid man loosened his hands, which had been tied behind his back, tore apart the cloth tied before his eyes, and at last broke the rope by which he had been suspended. Having fallen to the ground and seeing that he had suffered no injury, he took flight and hurried into the nearby forest.

Some men who had not gone far saw this, followed him in amazement, and urged him to leave the forest and to expect nothing but good from them. At length, strengthened by their encouragement, he left the forest and, glorifying and magnifying the Lord with them, reached the church.

Later he came to the protection of blessed Godehard and related to all of us what had happened to him through the mercy of God and blessed Godehard, with his fellow citizens—many of whom had come with him—bearing witness to it.

How many men whom God has delivered from hanging and from the very point of death through the merits of blessed Godehard would be a long matter to describe individually, especially since the ropes by which they had been suspended can be shown to everyone who comes to our church.

23. At that time two women came from far away to the protection of blessed Godehard, and they most devoutly related to all of us the favor granted to them by him.

One, after an immense illness, lost all appetite for food and drink, to such a degree that for two months she took neither food nor drink. Seeing that she could not preserve her life in this way for long, she implored the mercy of blessed Godehard and recovered her former condition.

The other, who had long been deprived of sight, was given sight on the road along which she was traveling to the protection of blessed Godehard. [Col. 1217A]

24. At the same time there was in the bishopric of Minden a certain man possessed by a demon to such a degree that several people could scarcely restrain him from killing himself and delivering others to death.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] Minden is a Hanseatic city of Westphalia, formerly under the rule of its own bishop; by the Peace of Münster it was given to the Elector of Brandenburg.]

At last, with his hands bound behind his back and his feet shackled, he was brought by his parents to the protection of blessed Godehard, and everyone humbly implored his help.

His master, named Hezelin, seeing the extremity of his torment and his greatest tribulation, took pity on him, set him free, and gave him as a servant to blessed Godehard. After this, he immediately recovered his health and, his bonds removed, returned home sound and unharmed with his parents. [Col. 1217B]

25. At the same time a certain man of great penitence and austerity came to our church. For many years he had subdued his flesh by vigils and fasts, to such a degree that he even wore an iron cuirass against his flesh.

While he was devoutly persisting in prayer before our patron, in the sight of many people, through the grace of God the cuirass burst apart like spider’s web and fell down to the ground. O man most worthy of all praise, through whose merits the bonds of sins are broken and iron fetters dissolved!

26. At that time the abbess of Wunstorf [Col. 1217D] had a certain very weak lame man who had entirely lost the bone in his knee and could twist his leg in whatever direction he wished, as if it had no joint.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] A monastery in the diocese of Minden founded by Theoderic, [Col. 1218D] bishop of that city.]

When the abbess perceived that so many miracles were being performed through our patron, she brought the aforesaid lame man with her to the threshold of our patron and, through God’s action, brought him back sound and unharmed.

But as she returned to the church entrusted to her, she brought him back with hymns and praises, giving thanks to God for every gift bestowed upon her. Seeing this, a certain woman who was less religious and did not fear the Lord burst out with these words: she would never seek the protection of blessed Godehard unless she saw a certain boy, then crawling in the street with all his limbs disabled, walking with an upright stride.

It therefore happened that a few days later the boy’s parents brought him to the protection of blessed Godehard. After prayers had been said for him, they received him back sound and able to walk. When the aforesaid woman saw this, she repented with contrite and humbled heart of the rash words she had spoken and vowed to the Lord that she would visit our patron.

After this she sighed from the depths of her heart, considering that she lacked the necessities for the journey and the means by which she might provide at home for the children born to her. While she was thus anxious, it happened [Col. 1218A] that her little son went out of the house without her knowledge, carrying a little cloth that he had found in the street. In it the mother found nine coins, as though the child did not know what he was doing.

After these things she offered praise to God and blessed Godehard, who had both rescued her from anxiety and eradicated all doubt from her heart.

27. Around the same time there was in the bishopric of Minden, in a village called Lancesberg, a lame boy who was crippled in a marvelous manner. Although poor, his parents brought him to the protection of blessed Godehard and most devoutly implored his mercy for the boy’s recovery.

But when they had remained there for a while without seeing any improvement in the boy, they prepared to return to their own dwelling [Col. 1218B], because they no longer hoped to be heard. When they had come near the village called Runeburg and had decided to rest in a certain meadow, they broke into tearful words, complaining that they had come to the protection of blessed Godehard amid great tribulation but had received no favor for their child.

While they were speaking thus, the boy suddenly extended the limbs that had previously been bent and sprang joyfully and triumphantly from the cart in which he was being carried. When the neighboring people saw this, they immediately praised the Lord together and devoutly led the healed boy to the nearest church.

But lest so great a miracle be consigned to oblivion, the people of the region erected a small hut at the aforesaid place, where, long afterward, faithful passersby brought offerings in reverence for this miracle. [Col. 1218C]

28. At that time there was also in Goslar a certain lame man known to everyone, who had likewise gone to blessed Godehard for the recovery of his health and, with the Lord’s help, received it. He left in our church the stools on which he had previously crawled, as if as a memorial, and himself walked upright.

Several religious men of that city confidently affirmed this to everyone; they had known him as a lame man for many years.

[Note: [Col. 1218D] Goslar is an autonomous city of Lower Saxony, at the sources of the River Oker in the Duchy of Brunswick, not far from Hildesheim.]

29. At that time, in a place belonging to the territory of our church called Aulica, there was a man suffering from such a serious illness—one called a fistula [Col. 1218D]—that he had completely despaired of life. For he had lost the femoral node formerly situated at the joint and feared that he would soon lose the remaining part as well.

He ordered himself to be carried to the protection of blessed Godehard and, through God’s action, received bodily health. Afterward, as a sign of the miracle and of the gift granted to him by the Lord, he ordered the node that he had previously carried in his hand to be hung in the church; then he returned home joyful and lively.

30. Around the same time there was a certain matron born in the region of Herford [Col. 1219A], who was completely paralyzed and whose limbs were all relaxed. No limb performed its proper function, nor had any been able to do so for many days.

[Note: [Col. 1219D] Herford is an imperial and Hanseatic city of Westphalia, not far from the city of Münster, under the Elector of Brandenburg.]

She had spent most of her property on physicians, but through them she could not recover bodily health. Hearing of the great favor granted by the Lord to people through the merits of blessed Godehard, she rejected external physicians, commended herself entirely to the mercy of the Lord, and ordered herself to be carried to the protection of blessed Godehard.

After she had remained for some time in our church, she was restored to health both through the prayers of the faithful and through the protection of blessed Godehard, and all her limbs were restored to their former strength. Thereafter she frequently came to the threshold of blessed Godehard [Col. 1219B] and offered the Lord no small thanks for the gift bestowed upon her.

31. Not long afterward a certain man came to our church, bringing a much-loved daughter who was suffering from a grave illness and was already approaching death. For a bone of immense size, sharply pointed on both sides, had adhered to her throat for six days, and no one could extract it by any skill.

The man first went around to the physicians then residing in our city and asked them what he should do about his daughter, but he found no sound advice. Deprived of every external counsel, he came with his daughter to the protection of blessed Godehard and implored him for her with the deepest devotion.

It therefore happened that on that very day [Col. 1219C] the girl expelled the bone without injury and recovered complete health. Not long afterward another man suffered from the same illness for seven days, and death was already certainly threatening him. He came to the protection of blessed Godehard, was immediately freed, and was restored to his former condition.

32. It happened at about the same time that a certain Eckehard of Wigeleve forcibly and unlawfully seized one of his kinsmen and imprisoned him contrary to right and justice. While he was being held in captivity for some time, it happened on the very night of Pentecost, while the morning offices were being celebrated, that he prostrated himself on the ground and implored the protection of blessed Godehard for his liberation. At length, rising from prayer, he approached an opening so narrow that a three-year-old boy [could] not have passed through it; but when he applied his head, the opening, as it seemed to him, widened, and he passed through unharmed and safe. When this had happened, it quickly became known to everyone that the captive had broken out of prison and escaped. Immediately they all pursued him together, fortified the roads by which he might escape with guards, and made every effort to seize him; but, with the Lord and blessed Godehard assisting, it happened that he passed through all their ambushes, and, though he recognized them, was recognized by no one. He immediately betook himself to the protection of blessed Godehard and gave thanks to the Lord in our church for his deliverance.

33. At that time there was a certain man in captivity in the March of Hungary, fettered with exceedingly strong chains. He hoped for nothing except either to lose everything he possessed or to suffer death. The fame of blessed Godehard resounded in his ears, and he learned how much the Lord worked for love of him. At once he prostrated himself on the ground and most devoutly implored his protection. It happened, therefore, that on that very night the chain with which he was bound broke apart, and, with God’s help, he escaped from captivity. Everyone in our church saw him and learned with certainty that this had happened to him.

[Col. 1220B] 34. At the same time, a certain pagan from the farther regions of Slavia was captured and imprisoned in the city of Havelberg. [Note: Havelberg is an episcopal city under the metropolitan see of Magdeburg, on the River Havel, from which it took its name; it is subject to the dominion of the Elector of Brandenburg.] He had learned through report about our patron and, as a pagan, had in some way grasped how much the Lord worked for love of him. One night, compelled by fear of death and wavering between hope and fear, he addressed a prayer from the depths of his heart to blessed Godehard and most devoutly begged him to have mercy on him. After this, while the great and strong wooden trunk in which he had been enclosed remained intact, he drew out his feet without injury, as though from liquid matter, and did not know how this had happened to him; nor did he attempt to flee in any way. When day dawned, the guards came and found him, not without great astonishment. [Col. 1220C] They questioned him about how this had happened to him through invoking the name of blessed Godehard; they were amazed, reported it to their lord, and asked what they should do next. Their lord, however, moved by so great a miracle, granted him mercy and ordered the captive to depart unharmed. How many prisoners, and how many who were fettered with the greatest chains, the Lord released from the deepest tribulation through the protection of blessed Godehard, it would be tedious to enumerate in writing, since the actual instruments of torture hanging in our church make it possible to know. Therefore we have not thought it superfluous to pass over in writing many of these matters, which would make a lengthy account, and to proceed to make other events known.

[Col. 1220D] 35. Not long after the events we have related, there was a certain man who had an only son, greatly loved by him. The boy, playing in childish fashion by running about the fields, happened by chance to come to a ditch, when a great mass of earth suddenly collapsed upon him. His father, unaware of this and not finding the boy at home, searched everywhere but could not find him in any way. Then someone said that he had seen the boy playing near the ditch, but that afterward he had not appeared. On hearing this, the father hurried to the place where, as the man had said, he had last seen the boy, and saw that a great mass of earth had recently fallen. When he saw this, he gathered many people to him, quickly removed the earth, and found the boy showing no sign of life. Since he had heard that our patron, blessed Godehard, was a patron of great mercy, he immediately directed most devout prayers to him, adding that, if the Lord through Godehard’s merits restored the boy’s former life, he would offer the boy to him as a perpetual servant. After this, the boy was restored to his former life and returned home together with his father. We later saw him with his father in our church and learned with complete certainty from the father himself that this was what had happened to the boy.

36. At that time there was a certain man in a place called Minden, so afflicted with dropsy that he had suffered from it for about a year and now expected nothing but death. After hearing the name of blessed Godehard, he humbly invoked him for help in his illness and meekly begged him to assist him in his distress. It happened not long afterward that someone whom he had never seen before and never saw afterward entered to him; making an incision, he caused such an abundance of water to flow out of him that scarcely could anyone have carried it in a tub. After doing this, he applied treatment and departed, never appearing again. We later saw the man perfectly healed and learned truthfully from his own account that this was what had happened to him.

37. At about the same time, through blessed Godehard, a notable miracle occurred, worthy of remembrance. Certain pilgrims traveling from Rus’ [Note: The Bollandists think that *Prussia* should be read, since the whole of Poland lies between Saxony and Russia.] were coming to the protection of blessed Godehard and entered a certain wilderness on Palm Sunday. While they were trying to perform divine worship in Christian fashion, a multitude of pagans suddenly attacked them and put to death as many as they could. It happened that the priest who had been with them fell and passed to the Lord through suffering. The others, seeing that they too were about to be killed, prepared to resist them, although unarmed; but they most devoutly implored the protection of blessed Godehard. After this, although a larger number of armed men engaged the unarmed pilgrims, the pagans, through the Lord’s action, turned in flight and threw down their weapons here and there. The pilgrims, seeing this, struck them with the staffs used by pilgrims, killed about six of them, and, having become victorious, took the weapons the robbers had thrown away. They brought both a shield and a sword into our church as signs of victory.

38. Not long afterward, it happened that a certain fisherman wished to cross the Weser with his boy and was attending, as usual, to his livelihood. But when he had reached almost the middle of the water, such a storm arose that he doubted whether he could escape with his life. Seeing the wind rising more and more, the master [Col. 1222A] loudly called upon the help of the people; but the boy directed a prayer to blessed Godehard. It happened that the master, who knew how to swim, trusting in the people’s help, was submerged, while the boy, who did not know how to swim, was rescued through the intercession of blessed Godehard.

39. At that time a certain poor woman also came to our city, born in the region of Speyer. [Note: Speyer, formerly called Nemetes, is an episcopal city under the metropolitan see of Mainz, in the Lower Palatinate, under the authority of its own bishop.] She brought with her a little girl whose limbs were all weakened and who was entirely unable to walk. After remaining about a month in our city without obtaining any grace for her daughter, she sadly decided to return to her own land, since she now thought herself unworthy of being heard. But when she reached the bank of the Weser at a place called Münden, had sent the donkey to pasture, and had lifted her daughter from the cart, the girl, who had previously been weak, suddenly rose up while her mother was at a distance and burst into these words. For she cried out that she was truly receiving the grace of blessed Godehard and that he was staying there with her. When she had said this, all her limbs, which had previously been weak, were restored to their natural condition, and she was completely healed. We all saw her healed in our church and gave praise to the Lord for the gift bestowed upon her.

40. Near the beginning of the translation of blessed Godehard, there was a certain Slav who had long been deprived of sight and was living among pagans. Hearing of the wonders that God worked in honor of blessed Godehard, he reached his shrine and humbly implored his protection. But while common prayers were being offered for him in our church—for he had recently abandoned the error of paganism and come to the sacrament of baptism—it happened, because our sins demanded it, that he did not recover his health. Deprived of every hope, he returned home after some time. His fellow tribesmen, however, who remained in their paganism and saw that he had not regained his sight, immediately subjected him to insult and ridicule, saying that he had abandoned his god and had found no salvation in another. While they reproached him with these and similar things, the man was overwhelmed with shame and tried to take his own life. But, O man most worthy of all praise, who both preserved his temporal life and freed him from eternal death! While he still remained intent on killing himself, he was given sight through the merits of blessed Godehard. He reproached those from whom he had previously received insults, saying that their gods were deaf and mute, and most truthfully declared that he would never receive any good from them. Many later saw him in our church and learned with complete certainty that he had been given sight.

41. Not long afterward, it happened that a certain man from Poland came to the protection of blessed Godehard. But as he was trying to enter the doorway of our church, he was suddenly seized by an evil spirit and thrown horribly to the ground. When he was forcibly carried into the church and brought to the tomb of blessed Godehard, he began to rage with such fury that anyone could have marveled. At length the body of blessed Godehard was brought to him, and he was blessed with the sign of the holy cross; immediately he was freed, with evidence of a great stench.

42. At that time there was a certain man in the diocese of Utrecht devoted to the merchant’s trade. He frequently crossed the sea and sought out whatever things he needed. Once, in the middle of the sea, he was caught in a tremendous storm. Everyone cried out, and nothing was feared except the final end of life. At length, after some time had passed and they had regained strength of spirit, they implored the help of blessed Godehard and vowed that, if they escaped, they would bring a silver ship. We later saw them bringing a silver ship into our church and learned with complete certainty that this was what had happened to them.

43. It also happened at that time in Holland that, on one occasion, the sea flowed inland in a flood and submerged an immeasurable multitude of people. Some who perceived this took refuge in a certain basilica dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, where they hoped to escape death. But when the sea continued to rise and was already striking the very wall of the basilica, they saw that they could not escape and implored the help of blessed Godehard; they immediately experienced it visibly. For at once the sea flowed back to its accustomed place and was divinely restrained from spreading over the land again. Thus the Lord our God showed us the protection of blessed Godehard not only on land but also most certainly made it manifest at sea. For how many ships caught in great storms the Lord has rescued through him is still testified by the wax ships hanging in our church.

44. At about the same time the emperor Lothair of the Romans was sending his legates to the emperor of Constantinople—namely, Eilbert, provost of Goslar and our brother—and was restoring between them the ancient treaty of the emperors, which had already been almost neglected. While this man was crossing the sea and proceeding on a favorable course, it happened that one of his servants fell backward from the stern and, remaining beneath the waves for a long time, was seen by no one. As he was swallowed up by the sea and every voice was drowned out, he implored the protection of blessed Godehard with the only intention of which he was capable and most devoutly begged him to free him from the danger of death. While he was thinking this, a man with a white-haired face appeared to him, drew him to the surface of the sea, and taught him to swim, something he had not known before. Those who were in the ship, seeing this, loosened the sail and reached him in the smaller boat that accompanied them. Thus the aforesaid servant, almost swallowed by death, was rescued and restored to life in a wondrous manner. We all later saw him in our church and learned from truthful testimony that this was what had happened to him.

45. Not long afterward, a miracle occurred in the regions of Hungary, worthy of remembrance. A certain count of that region had a son in whom he had placed all his temporal hope and confidence. The boy fell ill and was already in danger of death. While everyone anxiously watched over him night and day and wavered between hope and fear, it happened that the boy drew near to death and one day, around the first hour, breathed his last. When this had happened, while everyone redoubled their mourning and lamentation and prepared what was necessary for the funeral, a certain man from the Bavarian region happened to arrive; he had himself lifted the boy from the sacred font. Seeing the father’s and mother’s incomparable grief, he took pity on them and began to make known to them the name of blessed Godehard, devoutly announcing how great a grace the Lord grants to the faithful who hope in him. On hearing this, the father and mother, without hesitation, prostrated themselves on the ground with firm faith, most devoutly implored the mercy of blessed Godehard, and vowed that, with their offerings, they would undertake a journey to his shrine if through his protection they could recover their son and restore him to his former life. When they had finished, evening had already arrived, when, unexpectedly, the boy returned to life and, wondrous to say, rose from the bed of his illness without any sign of injury. The vow that his father and mother had made they fulfilled without delay, and with substantial offerings they visited the shrine of our blessed patron Godehard. We received them honorably in our church and learned from their truthful report that this was what had happened to them.

46. At about the same time, while so many miracles were flourishing through blessed Godehard, it happened that two men, bloated from excessive drinking, left our city and wished to cross to the neighboring village. While they were standing in the middle of a field, one of them happened by chance to find a bone, which he picked up and carried with him for about an hour. Seeing that the bone was of great beauty and whiteness, he said that he wanted to travel through the land and announce to everyone that he was carrying a relic of our patron, so as to obtain temporal profit like the others. After saying this, he was immediately seized with madness, taken home speaking incoherently, and delivered to an evil death the following night. When this was heard, great terror was instilled in the people, and if any doubt about our patron had crept into their hearts, it was entirely expelled.

47. In those times there was a baker of the brothers named Adelwardus. Certain pilgrims turned aside to his lodging and, in the manner of hospitality, stayed with him overnight. When they led their horses to water, they placed his young son, still of tender age, on a horse and took him away without the father’s knowledge. While they were watering the horses, the terrified child accidentally fell from the horse, was immediately carried beneath the waters, and no one knew where he might be sought. The pilgrims, unable to find the boy, returned sadly to the house and told his father what had happened to his son. On hearing this, the father rose quickly, went sadly to the water, and searched for the boat that had been drawn far away; since he could not find his son alive, he tried at least to find him dead. After searching for a long time in the place where the boy had fallen and not finding him, he returned to land and sought a hook. Once he had found one, after a long interval he found the boy. When this had happened, he turned aside into the nearest house and laid down the dead boy, who showed no sign of life, carefully seeking only what was necessary for the funeral. While these things were taking place, the boy’s mother, together with the other women, a great number of whom had entered the house, implored the mercy of the Lord and blessed Godehard; she most devoutly begged that he not withhold from her the customary kindness he had bestowed upon everyone. What more is there to say? After a short time, the boy emitted a sob; the water he had swallowed flowed out with great force, and at length he regained his former life.

48. At about the same time there was a man devoted to the merchant’s trade, who traveled through various lands in conducting business and with difficulty obtained a livelihood for himself and his family. Once, for the sake of commerce, he was traveling with several others among pagans and was carrying a considerable amount of property. As they proceeded on their journey in prosperity, they happened to enter a vast wilderness, where they encountered a considerable multitude of pagans. Seeing this, they ran to arms and prepared defenses for themselves on every side, but they were unable to resist their numbers. The pagans then killed some of them, mutilated others, took others captive, and plundered their goods. Among the captives, the aforesaid man was captured together with a young boy, his brother’s son, and was taken into the most remote regions of the pagans. There he was detained on a certain island of the Ocean, [Note: Henschenius would prefer to read “an island of the Baltic Sea,” probably Rügen, the last of the lands held by the Slavs.] where he labored long at servile work and had no means of escape, since the sea surrounded it on every side and he could find no place by which to flee. At length he vowed that he would go to the protection of our patron, blessed Godehard, if he would show him some way to escape their hands.

After this, one day, as he walked anxiously along the seashore and devoted himself to prayer, he found a small boat in a hidden place on the shore, in which he hoped, with God’s help, to cross the sea. But because the sea was great and wide, he was afraid to attempt such a danger, and commended himself to the prayers of blessed Godehard, asking him to inspire his mind and prepare suitable means by which he might escape such great tribulation. When he had finished, night had already come, and he prepared for flight with fixed resolve. Taking two small spears and a piece of cloth torn from a mattress, he went to the boy, his brother’s son, who was staying in another village, and took him away with him. When he reached the little boat, he made a sail from the spears and the cloth he had brought with him, and thus commended himself to the mercy of the Lord and blessed Godehard. Those who lived on the island, seeing this, immediately pursued him; but, with God’s help, they could not catch him and rowed home without accomplishing their purpose. The aforesaid man, not forgetting what he had vowed to God, immediately came to the protection of blessed Godehard and asked that the spears and the cloth from which he had made the sail be hung in our church in memory of so great a miracle.

[Col. 1225]

## APPENDIX

[Col. 1225C] 49. Meanwhile, while these things were taking place and the memory of blessed Godehard was being greatly celebrated, it happened that the archbishop of Cologne, named Henry, [Note: Henry I, count of Molenarck, succeeded Saint Engelbert in 1225 and held the office for twelve years. He seems to be intended here rather than Henry II of Wirnemberg, ordained in 1306. The miracle related below, in no. 51, took place during the lifetime of Caesarius of Heisterbach.] passed through our city with a considerable company of clergy and people and learned of the miracles mentioned above that were being performed through him. He therefore came to the convent of our brothers and devoutly asked for admission to our fraternity. To confirm this fraternity, he humbly requested that some relics of our blessed patron be given to him, promising that he would ensure that the saint was celebrated throughout his entire diocese and that fitting honor would be shown to so great a man. But because we postponed his request on account of the absence of our shepherd and promised that we would satisfy his wishes when the shepherd was present, not long afterward our lord, having learned these matters in our convent, agreed to the archbishop’s request and ordered that what he had asked for be given to him. At once the abbot of blessed Godehard was sent to him with a portion of the relics, which he received most devoutly.

The archbishop sent this portion to his native land, namely Swabia, and there established a church in his honor. As many people flocked to it and recovered with complete certainty the salvation of soul and body, it happened one day that a certain man’s hand was cut off, so completely that not even the smallest part remained joined to his body. Seeing that he had become one-handed, he took up the hand, and, with his faith strengthened, placed it against the stump; then he traveled to the same church, to the protection of blessed Godehard. As he most devoutly implored his mercy, the celebrated miracle occurred: the hand was joined to the stump and restored to its former condition.

50. There was a certain honorable man named Theodoricus, a citizen of Hildesheim. Moved by singular devotion, he established a fraternity of Saint Godehard and brought men and women into it, giving a sufficiently generous alms from his own resources to the poor on the feast of the said bishop Godehard. While he was lying ill with a certain disease called consumption, the physicians abandoned him, having despaired of his life. One night, which he passed almost entirely without sleep, Saint Godehard appeared to him in pontifical vestments and said to him:

“Why are you suffering, brother? Why do you lie prostrate in bed?”

Theodoricus replied: “Burdened by a serious illness, I can do nothing but lie prostrate; but I beg you, Saint Godehard, pray for me.”

The holy man said to him: “Rise in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, go to the church, show yourself to your fellow members, and say to them: ‘The Lord Jesus has healed you through my merits, because you promoted my honor in this illness.’ Moreover, tell them to persevere in what they have begun. I shall be their brother and defender against the evil enemy and against everything that can harm their honor, life, or reputation, and I shall always be their intercessor with God.”

The sick man rose and did what had been told him. All who heard the message blessed God, who had given them such a patron and intercessor. The aforesaid Theodoricus, now healthy and cheerful, lived many years afterward, devoutly commending himself to God and Saint Godehard.

51. Master John, dean of Aachen, [Note: The same miracle is related by Caesarius in Book VIII of his *Miracles*, chapter 77.] when he was a student, was once so gravely ill that, after confession and anointing, he seemed to have nothing left but death. When the disease’s matter had rushed into his brain, he lay alone and fell into a trance. He saw unknown men enter, placing before him scale-pans that they carried in their hands, together with short, square wooden weights. While they stood on one side of the bed, he saw three illustrious confessors enter and surround him on the other side: Saint Martin of Tours, Saint Godehard, bishop of Hildesheim, and blessed Bernward. In their presence the boy John was placed on one dish, and pieces of wood on the other. When the balance was raised, the sick youth was found to be lighter. The aforesaid confessors placed a small and destitute beggar-boy in his lap; immediately, when they raised the opposite dish as well, they appeared heavier than the pieces of wood. John, who related this vision to me, immediately broke into a sweat, underwent a crisis, and quickly recovered from that illness.

The final miracle of the Leipzig edition, of the shorter life.

[Col. 1227]

[Col. 1227C] 52. In the year of the Lord 1338, the city of Passau, surrounded and tightly besieged by the bishop of Passau with a large force of armed men, was so hard-pressed that the people within it, despairing of safety, wished to surrender to their enemies. One among them, however, who placed particular trust in Saint Godehard and was sitting among the leading men of the city, said:

“We have heard of many notable works of mercy and no small increase of saving assistance: how Saint Godehard, who arose from our own land—indeed, from our own diocese—stood by many who were afflicted, and how they received consolation from him, as is well known to many. It is therefore fitting that we too should implore his help, humbly asking that he mercifully assist us and turn away from us the anger of God, by which we have deserved this calamity.”

The old man’s words pleased everyone, and all supported his encouragement. They unanimously made a vow to send some of the citizens with offerings, asking that he come quickly to their aid in their necessities. Once this vow had been made, they found themselves consoled with marvelous speed. For the noble prince, the duke of Bavaria, [Note: In Henschenius’s view, this was Louis, son of Louis the Bavarian. While his father was pursuing the imperial dignity, he could have earned the title of duke of Bavaria; he was also called margrave of Brandenburg.] came and intervened in the matter, establishing a friendly truce between the bishop of Passau and the citizens of the city besieged by him. Thus the bishop departed, and the city rejoiced in an unexpected peace. Meanwhile the said duke of Bavaria confirmed the peace begun between the bishop and the city and granted consolation to people of both sexes. The citizens of the said city sent their representatives, as they had vowed, to the tomb of Saint Godehard with votive offerings, telling everyone there how they had suddenly been freed from the greatest tribulation through the intercession of Saint Godehard.

[Col. 1227]

## SECOND APPENDIX  
### Miracles performed in foreign provinces to which the relics of Saint Godehard were carried

[Col. 1227D] For those who wish to know what and how great works the Lord deigned to perform through the merits of blessed Godehard, when we were in the diocese of Utrecht and in other places, carrying with us his venerable relics, we have taken care to record briefly certain events. We clearly witnessed the honorable abbot in Dokkinge being healed of the flow of blood from which he had suffered severely and for a long time. Through his intercession God also powerfully and visibly freed a certain matron, who had asked that the same relics be brought to her with good hope, from a double illness—dropsy and gout—from which she had long suffered. Moreover, when the belts of many people were applied to the same relics and then placed upon the limbs of the sick, both secular and enclosed, they are known to have immediately recovered their health: namely, those suffering from daily or tertian fever, headaches, pain of the eyes, teeth, and other limbs.

54. When a certain woman absented herself from her fellow citizens while we were granting them the confraternity in the customary manner, blessed Godehard admonished her in a vision, asking why she wished to deprive herself of so great a benefit. She replied that she had nothing to offer and heard that, when she rose in the morning, she should offer whatever she found with her. Finding two coins of heavier currency in her purse, she offered them, and publicly declared that this had happened.

[Col. 1230A] 55. A certain important man, who was very hostile to us and was trying to turn the people away from us and obstruct our work in every way, began to suffer such danger from swelling of the throat and entire head that he seemed almost to be failing, until, coming to his senses and repenting in his heart, he was freed through the intercession of blessed Godehard from the jaws of death itself and corrected his error with devotion and humility.

56. A certain woman gave birth to twins, delivering one before our arrival, but then began to be in danger for three days with the other. When we arrived, however, she was immediately delivered through the touch of a belt to which the holy relics had been applied.

57. Moreover, when the principal church of Utrecht had long been deeply troubled by the suspension of divine worship, it resumed the divine offices because of the arrival of the relics of blessed Godehard [Note: This miracle seems to belong to the beginning of the fifteenth century, when, according to Heda, the abbot of the Island of Saint Mary excommunicated the people of Utrecht by authority of the Roman pontiff because they had rejected Bishop Sueder. This lasted until the year 1437, when, through the agency of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, Walrarius yielded to Rudolf, who was elected after Sueder.] and granted immense joy to the entire people at the dedication of the church itself.

[Col. 1229]

# THE LETTERS OF SAINT GODEHARD

(Mabillon, *New Edition of the Analecta*, p. 435.)

## LETTER I. OF GODEHARD, ABBOT OF TEGERNSEE, TO THE BROTHERS OF NIEDERALTAH

He announces how he was received by the people of Tegernsee and wishes that there may be a mutual communion of prayers between both communities.

[Col. 1229C]

Godehard, abbot, although unworthy, to W. and the other brothers: whatever is owed to beloved sons in Christ.

Although, compelled by nature, we rightly suffer inwardly and outwardly while laboring under the law of our frailty, nevertheless, on this journey which we undertook at the command of our lord the duke, we still rejoice that we are prospering through your prayers. For we have been received honorably and charitably by all the brothers, and they devoutly do whatever we regularly command them.

Moreover, we ask that from now on we may be joined to your brotherhood and prayer, and, together with me, we commend to you our brothers whom we have sent to you, so that you may show them every charity and kindness, as our holy Father Benedict commands. Send us Horace’s book and Cicero’s letters.

## LETTER II. OF THE SAME GODEHARD TO THE BISHOP THEODULUS

[Note: This is Goteschalk, bishop of Freising, who appears in the catalogue of the bishops of Freising. *Gotscalch* in the Germanic language means “servant of God,” and in Greek, Θεόδουλος (*Theodoulos*), “God’s servant.”]

He explains that he undertook the governance of the monastery of Tegernsee not out of greed or ambition, but in obedience owed to the prince.

To the lord Theodulus, the most clear mirror of pontifical priests, Godehard, who shamefully pretends to be a monk before God and himself, sends what is owed to the Lord.

The further course of the blameworthy invective devised against us by a sparkling pen and a seething spirit appears exceedingly remarkable. If my own conscience had ever reproached me in the case of even one such wicked accusation, with what shameful face and repentant mind I would willingly have separated myself from the communion of all Christianity! May deceitful greed be far from me, by which I might so impiously desire what belongs to another, although I could in no way live without your possessions.

May Venus—or rather, the enchantress of greed—be so completely put to sleep in me that I should dare jealously to look with a lustful eye upon one joined to another’s marriage. We renounced our little possessions without any disguise or pretense—well done! But afterward we did not advance as we ought, because, as is more truly known, not all Christians are Christians, nor are all men men, nor are all monks monks. Yet these are Christians and monks; we wish to reverse these things, but cannot; we strive, but grow weak.

If someone is marked by some coloring or sprinkling of Christianity, and is catholically excused from committing crimes of such great destructiveness, when and how is one praised who is accused of being subject to so many vices? As for your saying that I secretly burst into the Lord’s sheepfold, the faithful testimony of the court and the countless ranks of the Christian people proves otherwise, because I presumed to claim for myself nothing from the jurisdiction of your authority or that of anyone else, except what I received today from the authoritative hand of the supreme Prince—whether I wished it or not, I do not say.

I have not found any such prohibition of obedience written in the Rule of Benedictine life, although the Rule has often and repeatedly been worn here and there by our hands. Whatever fault I feel I have committed in these matters through the heat of such a peril, I firmly hold, with the conscience of many as witness, that I can emerge from it without any difficulty. Farewell.

## LETTER III. OF THE SAME TO AZELINUS, ABBOT OF LUNELAKE

That he should present himself as soon as possible to the bishop of Passau.

[Col. 1231B]

G., your most devoted brother in all things, sends many greetings in the Lord to A., abbot of the brothers of Lunelake.

We know that your prosperity in all things is a source of joy to us; and if it is otherwise, we gladly share your sufferings in the same way. At the most recent feast of the apostles, we attended the solemn office of Mass celebrated by the Christian bishop (of Passau). Although we resisted with the greatest earnestness, he nevertheless summoned you episcopally and firmly decreed that, unless you came to him within fourteen nights, you were to be excommunicated. Therefore we advise you to come to him with the permission of your bishop G., and in his presence hear for yourselves how the outcome of this matter is to be determined. If you need anything from us [Col. 1231C] for the conduct of this affair, we are ready, in whatever way you wish, to support you. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. THE SAME AUTHOR TO A CERTAIN ABBESS

Abbot G., the least of all who preside, offers to Lady Abbess T. or A. devoted service and the dedication of diligent prayer in Christ.

We ask you to remember that we have always loved you in the Lord, and have wished you to become Christ’s beloved little lamb; indeed, we chose you for ourselves as a most beloved sister in a special sense. This sister of ours came to us before Christmas, complaining to us of the misery of her many needs. We would most willingly have allowed her to remain with us and, insofar as we were able, would have ordered that what she needed be provided for her, if the nature of her sex permitted women to live together with a monastery of brothers. For, as holy men attest, stubble, straw, and fire are never reconciled with one another unless one is quickly consumed to the detriment of the other.

Therefore we ask you not to allow her, to the disgrace of our profession or of the monastic habit in which this sister is clothed, to wander any longer through various places. Rather, for the love of God and for the sake of our future defense before God, deign to associate her with the works of your handmaids and to bestow upon her whatever necessities your alms permit you to provide. Farewell.

## LETTER V. THE MONKS OF TEGERNSEE TO GODEHARD, BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM

They indicate that, after Albinus, they have elected Ellinger again as abbot.

[Col. 1232A]

To Lord G., adorned with the bishop’s mitre, divinely exalted above all others of that name in this age in accordance with his merits and the office befitting them, the brothers of Tegernsee, serving under the protection of Saint Quirinus, offer whatever sons owe to a beloved father and servants to their lord.

That your holiness, reverend Father, may long flourish and remain strong in all things with a happy and prosperous outcome, let it certainly be known to your fatherhood [Col. 1232B] that with attentive devotion we continually beseech God day and night, and humbly commend the same prayers to our holy patron Quirinus, so that he may carry them to God on your behalf. As long as our place is able to endure, there will never be forgetfulness of the benefits bestowed upon us by your kindness. For the sons who will be born and rise up, proclaiming the same things to their descendants, will say: “As a father has mercy on his children, so he has always mercifully treated his servants without charge.” Even if human speech were to remain silent about this recompense, it will be certain for you before God and Saint Quirinus.

Therefore, beloved Father, never from the very beginning of your aid and consolation have we been in greater need than we are now, as necessity presses upon us. For tribulation and distress have long since, so to speak, made their beds among us. To drive away these evils, the help of your holiness is invoked before God. To you, therefore, after God, we say with tearful voices: “Remember your congregation, which you willingly possessed from the beginning; be a helper in the tribulations that have found us in great measure.”

Our elder A. [Albinus], overcome by the force of illness, resigned his priorship and left us bereft. Therefore, having assembled, we chose Ellinger as our father and elected to receive him, if it pleases God. Whether we can obtain this election depends upon the machinations of our enemies. For we complain to your fatherhood that, through the effort of the aforesaid A., we were almost handed over, without our knowledge, to the rule of an alien and unknown authority [Col. 1232D]. We fear that this may still happen unless God looks upon us with the eyes of his mercy.
