We therefore earnestly beseech your kindness to deign, as is customary, to labor on our behalf, so that, although absent, we may rejoice in the preservation of your fatherhood; that our election may also be granted to us; and that the emperor may not carry away our possessions—a prospect which we fear almost daily before our eyes. No one would dare doubt that you have great influence with the heavenly Emperor; and, because of those merits, you are able to obtain anything from the earthly emperor as well.

## APPENDIX TO SAINT GODEHARD

[Col. 1233]

## CHRONICLE OF HILDESHEIM

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Writers, vol. VII, p. 845.)

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE

[Col. 1233A] The Church of Hildesheim possessed Annals carried down to the year 1040, together with Thancmar’s book and both works of Wolfher, when, as the eleventh century was drawing to a close, the Chronicle began to be written. It was brought from the beginning of the episcopate down to the death of Bishop Ettilo, who died in 1079, and filled only a few pages. The author’s name is concealed; if he is nevertheless to be sought among the scholars of the Church of Hildesheim, one might perhaps call him Godefrid, whom we read to have died under Udo.

Whoever he was, in recording events that preceded his own time he copied the Hildesheim Annals, the Life of Bernward, and the Life of Godehard, and was able to use the books and charters preserved in the church treasury. The genuine portion of the little book, however, comprises the Life of Ettilo, and seems to have been completed immediately after his death.

This first edition of the book, which the Saxon Annalist copied at the end of the twelfth century [Note: [Col. 1233D] Down to the year 1079; see the notes in the margin of our edition, vol. SS. VI.], appears to have formed part of a pontifical book prepared by Bishop Udo for the use of his Church [Col. 1233B]. In it were read a calendar, a martyrology, the canonical order, and other matters relating to the affairs of the Church. Today only a copy made in the twelfth century survives.

The parchment codex, in what is called large quarto format, now belongs to the library of His Serene Highness the Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg at Wolfenbüttel, and formerly belonged to Hildesheim. Written toward the end of the twelfth century, it contains, after its first eight leaves—whose earlier writing was erased in the fourteenth century and which now display the order “This is the manner of the refectory”—on folio 9 a listing of the kitchen services for the year from the greater provostship; on folios 10–15, the calendar of the Church of Hildesheim; on folios 16–24, sayings of the Fathers by which the clerical order is instructed to live well; on folio 34 and folio 35, the names of our brothers who were archbishops and bishops; then, after folios 35, 35, and 36 had been erased, on folios 36–128 it presents the Martyrology and Necrology.

Folios 129–130 contain the names of the churches that expect from us, as brothers and sisters in Christ, our prayers in the daily sacrifices, and that owe us theirs [Col. 1233C], and so forth; then the names of the bishops of the Church of Hildesheim, followed by those of the priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, and scholars who died from the year 1078 onward under Bishop Udo. Folio 131 contains the names of kings and emperors from Pippin, son of Ansegisus, through the death of Henry IV in 1106. Folios 131–162 contain the Chronicle of Hildesheim. Folios 164–173, written in a fourteenth-century hand, contain foundations and charters; folios 179–188 contain foundations and obediences written in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. These are followed, on folios 162 and 189–204, by notices and charters of the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries inserted into the book. Thus it is clear that the book was not only written for the use of the church but was continually used and enlarged for three centuries.

Accordingly, it is permissible to conclude that Udo’s book, our source, was enlarged both while Udo was alive and after his death, just as we have established that various codices of the book of censuses, praised under the name of Censius the chamberlain, were used and enlarged in the Roman Church [Col. 1234A] [Note: [Col. 1233D] *Archivum*, vol. V.].

In Udo’s own codex, the Chronicle was enlarged by the Lives of the bishops who succeeded Ettilo from 1079 onward—Udo, Brun­ing, and Berthold, and perhaps also Bernhard and Bruno, who died in 1153 and 1162—by different scribes and was inserted into our codex toward the end of the twelfth century. In the same hand, the Life of Hermann was added and carried down to the beginning of Adelog’s episcopate in 1171.

Whoever the writer was, he inserted the names of Bishops Bernhard, Bruno, Hermann, and Adelog into the episcopal catalogue in red letters; he must therefore be considered to have flourished under them. Perhaps he was none other than Berno, the celebrated scholar of that period, whom we know to have occupied the Hildesheim see after Adelog.

The Life of Adelog, written by a hand of the early thirteenth century, together with the Lives of Berno, Conrad, Herbert, and Sifrid, his successors down to 1227 [Col. 1234B], was erased in the fourteenth century and written again in the same place. Thus today only the beginning, written by the author’s own hand, survives; the remainder bears the hand of the fourteenth century. Why this happened is unknown.

By contrast, the Life of Sifrid’s successor, Bishop Conrad, who died in 1249, remained intact and displays a mid-thirteenth-century script. The Life of Henry, who died in 1257, appears twice: once on folio 146, written by another hand of the same period, and again on folios 147, 147, and 148, written by a fourteenth-century hand. The Lives of John and Otto, who died in 1261 and 1279, were written by fourteenth-century hands; these perhaps later added the Lives of Sifrid and Henry, who died in 1310 and 1318. The final lines of Henry’s Life belong to another fourteenth-century scribe.

The remaining portion of the work—the Lives of Otto, Henry, John, Gerard, John, and Magnus, covering more than a hundred years—is owed to a single fifteenth-century scribe, who brought the book to an end in 1433.

The work, therefore, composed from the end of the eleventh century through the fifteenth century by successive Hildesheim canons and written, as it were, in the name of the Church [Col. 1234C] [Note: [Col. 1234D] The beginnings of the Lives, customarily read on the anniversaries of the dead, are shown on pp. 859, 860, and 863], commands considerable confidence in matters concerning the Church and contributes to the illumination of Saxon history.

Leibniz published the book in *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. I, pp. 742–772, under the following titles: “Chronicle of the Bishops of Hildesheim”; “Extracts from the Ancient Necrology of the Church of Hildesheim”; “Lists of the confraternities and bishops of the Church of Hildesheim”; “Names of the archbishops and bishops who were first canons in the Church of Hildesheim”; “A few extracts from the book of donations made to the Church of Hildesheim”; and “A fragment concerning certain relics of the cathedral church of Hildesheim”—in an incorrect order, though using the same Wolfenbüttel codex, which I number as follows:

[Col. 1235A] 1. I made it the foundation of our edition. I reproduced the book literally, but from the twelfth century through Bishop Berno, the principal bishop, I considered it necessary to restore the spelling, insofar as concerns the diphthong *ae* and the letter *t*, in those passages where an older text is repeated by a scribe of a later age. I reserved the more extensive Necrology and other material less appropriate to the plan of this volume for another place.

For the same purpose, two other codices preserved in the Wolfenbüttel library among the *Extravagantes* also had to be examined:

2. Codex no. 115, in folio; and

3. Codex no. 227, in quarto.

Both are paper manuscripts. The latter, being copied from the former, is of no importance. The former, after excerpts from Engelhus’s Chronicle, contains several historical extracts, including material from Jordanes on Gothic affairs and other matters; finally, on folios 188–196, it presents a Chronicle of the Bishops of the Diocese of Hildesheim as well as of the abbots of the monastery of Saint Michael. This derives, like codex 1, either directly from Udo’s book or from another copy of it and for that reason offers in some places a better reading, which I did not hesitate to adopt in the text [Col. 1235B].

Since it also contained certain information about the tombs of the bishops and other matters known to a writer living in the middle of the fifteenth century, I arranged, with the assistance of our Wattenbach, for these to be noted and for some information about the bishops of that century to be appended [Col. 1236A]. The Chronicle of the abbots of Saint Michael, however, will have to be assigned to the later writers.

The greater part of the book was written in the middle of the fifteenth century; the remainder around 1458, with additions by entirely different hands in 1471, 1472, and subsequent years. Leibniz used our book in editing the Chronicle of the Bishops of Hildesheim and the Abbots of the Monastery of Saint Michael, vol. II, pp. 784 ff.

The older part of the Chronicle was known to the Saxon Annalist; the entire work was known to Conrad Bothon and Henry Bodon, who incorporated much of it into the *Pictorial Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1235D] Leibniz, *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, III, p. 277.] and the Gandersheim compilation.

In the notes we owe much to the distinguished scholar of Hildesheim affairs, the most illustrious Hermann Adolf Luntzel. Through his kindness I readily obtained material from his rich store of learning with which to illuminate the time and place of our native history.

As for the catalogue of the bishops of Hildesheim [Col. 1236B], which Leibniz says he took from the chronicles of Abbot Eggehard of Wurzen for Abbot Egbert of Corvey and inserted in volume II, p. 772, of his collection [Note: [Col. 1236D] Ibid., II, p. 332], I judged that this excerpt, being of no value, should be omitted.

(Folio 129) Names of the churches that, as brothers and sisters in Christ, expect our prayers from us in the daily sacrifices and owe us theirs, for the living and the dead, as we received from our elders.

[Col. 1237]

[Col. 1237B] The Church of Reims, which was the mother of the Church of Hildesheim in its canonical establishment. The Church of Paris in France. Saint Gereon’s in Cologne. Bamberg. Münster. Paderborn. Halberstadt. Fulda. Hersfeld. Corvey. Helmwardeshausen. Herse. Gandersheim. Goslar. Ringelheim. Brunswick. Prague. Monte Cassino. Tours. Quedlinburg. Magdeburg. Osnabrück. Altach. Tegernsee, whose members gave us here a missal together with a Gospel book and lectionary as a sign of brotherhood.

All these churches must announce to us by letters and messengers the names and deaths of their deceased, and we must do the same for them, so that common prayers may be offered for thirty days. On anniversaries, at Masses and other commemorations of the dead, and in autumn during the three days of remembrance of the brothers, the names of the aforesaid churches must be recited in the public assembly. At public Masses, for both the living and the dead, the memory of our brothers and sisters must be celebrated during these three days with offerings and alms [Col. 1238B].

These are the names of the bishops of the Church of Hildesheim from the time of Charlemagne, who founded this church.

## [LIST]

[Col. 1239A] Pippin, son of Ansegisus, reigned for twenty-five years. His son Charles reigned for twenty-five years. Pippin reigned for twenty-seven years. Charlemagne reigned for forty-seven years. Pope Leo III, who is called “the Blinded,” placed the imperial crown upon him at Rome and instituted the singing of the acclamations “Christ conquers” for the pope, kings, and princes on the day of his ordination.

His son Louis reigned for twenty-six years. Louis reigned for thirty-five years. Louis reigned for thirty-five years. Louis reigned for six years. Charles reigned for thirteen years. Arnulf reigned for twelve years. [Col. 1240A] Louis reigned for seven years. Conrad reigned for twenty years. Henry reigned for thirty-six years. Otto reigned for eleven years. He established the bishopric of Magdeburg with its five suffragan sees. Otto reigned for eighteen years. Otto reigned for twenty-three years. Henry reigned for fourteen years. He established the bishopric of Bamberg. Conrad reigned for seventeen years and six months. Henry [Note: [Col. 1239] “Henry, seventeen years and four months” is absent from the codex, but seemed to require supplementation.] reigned for seventeen years and four months. He built the community of Goslar at his own expense.

Henry, son of Henry, called the fourth king of that name, excommunicated by four Roman pontiffs—Gregory VII, Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II—died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1107, in the fifty-third year of his ordination [Col. 1241A] [Note: [Col. 1241] Thus I emend; the codex has “three.”] [Note: [Col. 1241] The word is absent in the codex]. He had reigned for fifty-one years after the death of his father, the Emperor Henry of blessed memory.

On the vigil of the Epiphany of the Lord, at the royal court in Ingelheim, in the presence of his son, King Henry V, and in the hearing of many princes of the realm who had withdrawn from him on account of his excommunication and had chosen his son as king, he sought absolution from the Roman legates Richard of Albano and Gebhard of Constance, but did not receive it. There he returned the crown and the other royal insignia to the princes. In the same year, on the seventh day before the Ides of August, he died at Liège without having been absolved [Note: [Col. 1241] The second section begins here].

## 1

The great Emperor Charles, who at the end of his life finally compelled the Saxons to the faith of Christ through diverse and varied conflicts in the twelfth war, and with God’s help and the counsel of the bishops strengthened the Christian religion among them—having caused churches to be built at Paderborn, Corvey, Minden, Hildesheim, Herstelle, and other places, and having established in advance the bishoprics that were to exist there—departed to Christ in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 814, in the seventy-second year of his age, the forty-third of his reign, and the fourteenth of his empire. His son Louis succeeded him.

Louis, in accordance with his father’s decree, likewise established these same bishoprics, and himself caused GUNTHARIUS to be ordained the first bishop in Hildesheim. At the beginning of his episcopal ordination, this bishop built a chapel in the cemetery [Col. 1241C], in which he was later buried and rested with his successors [Note: [Col. 1241] “which he himself built,” p. 2] (+ year 834? July 5).

## 2

REINBERTUS, the second bishop, succeeded him. After Reinbertus died, this occurred in the year 835 of the aforementioned incarnation of the Lord (February 12).

## 3

EBO, archbishop of Reims, was deposed and, by the emperor’s clemency, confined at Hildesheim. He presided over the church for twelve years and exercised the episcopal office as he himself understood it (+ year 851, March 20).

## 4

Then, in the year 847 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1241] 848, in the second source], ALTF RIDUS, the fourth bishop, was ordained (before August 15). By governing the church according to the rule, he reasonably annulled, by the decree of the canons, whatever his predecessor had rashly usurped from the sacred orders.

The same prelate began our monastery in the fear of the Lord and, at the very beginning of its foundation, consecrated the eastern crypt in honor of the holy Virgin Mary [Col. 1241D]. He also donated to our church two estates belonging to him, Saleghenstad [Note: [Col. 1241] *halegenstad* and *asvede*, in the second source] [Note: [Col. 1241D] Osterwieck?] and Asnede [Note: [Col. 1241D] Essen]. In them he established the monasteries: Salegenstad for monks and Asnede for virgins. (Compare the *Life of Godehard*.)

In the year 852 of the aforementioned incarnation of the Lord, this same bishop, together with Liudolf, began a convent first at Brunesteshusen and, four years later, at Gandersheim [Note: [Col. 1241] *gandeschem*, in the second source], as has been stated. He also began to build a church there and appointed Hathamoda, daughter of that duke, as its first abbess. He granted tithes from the property of his church there as a benefice, for the provision of his service and revenue, and with paternal devotion provided from his own resources whatever else might benefit those serving Christ there.

Eighteen years later, when Hathamoda had died, he appointed her sister Gerberga abbess. (Compare the Hildesheim Annals.)

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 872, the twenty-sixth of his own ordination, he completed the monastery of Hildesheim, which he had begun, thanks be to God, and devotedly dedicated it to the divine Majesty in honor of Saint Mary, under the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, Tiburtius and Valerian, and the holy virgin Cecilia, on the Kalends of November.

Three years later, in the twenty-ninth year of his ordination, full of days and truly full of good works, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 1241] “the first” is absent] (874), namely on the Assumption of Saint Mary, he was truly taken into the company of the saints and departed. He was buried and came to rest at Asnede, in its church, which he himself had begun and completed and dedicated. To this day, as those who live in that place truthfully affirm, he is made known to all through many distinguished signs of healing miracles.

In that same year—that is, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 875—Emperor Louis, son of Louis, died.

(Hildesheim Annals) After Alfrid, a certain monk of Corvey, Liudolf, was designated, but he was carried off by sudden death before taking office.

## 5 (Hildesheim Annals)

MARCQUARDUS, the fifth bishop, succeeded next. He also laid the beams of the church at Gandersheim. In the fourth year of his ordination he was killed by the Slavs [Note: [Col. 1241] “and buried at Ebbekersdorf,” in the second source] (+ Annals, 880, February 2). According to the report of the elders, he himself negligently lost the aforementioned abbeys of Salegenstad and Asnide.

## 6 (Hildesheim Annals)

Then, in the year 880 of the Lord’s incarnation, WICBERTUS was elected bishop. In his time he was highly skilled in the medical art [Note: [Col. 1241] Absent in the second source], and with his own hand produced the Bible [Note: [Col. 1242D] That is, the Bible], which is still preserved in the monastery, and provided extensively for the benefit of his church.

Also, looking to the welfare of the brothers, he distributed the entire substance of the church’s property with subtle skill among villages, estates, households, and tithes. He decided to establish one-third of it for the brothers’ provision, but, overtaken by death, left the same provision to be completed by his successor. (Life of Godehard.)

In the year 883 of the Lord’s incarnation, the fourth of his own ordination, he also dedicated the completed church at Gandersheim. When Abbess Gerberga died, he appointed her sister Christina [Note: [Col. 1241] *Christiana*, in the codex] there (+ year 903, November 1).

## 7

[Col. 1243A] WALBERTUS, the seventh bishop, succeeded him. He faithfully established the provostship and provision of the brothers, as his predecessor had prescribed, and acquired for both the reward of eternal recompense before God. (Life of Godehard.) After Christina [Note: [Col. 1243] *Christiana*, in the codex] died, he appointed Roswitha abbess (+ year 919, November 3).

## 8 (Hildesheim Annals)

After Walbert, SEHARDUS, the eighth bishop, was placed in office. In the year 926 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1243] 923, in the second source], he dedicated the western tower at Gandersheim; and after Roswitha died, he appointed Wendelgard abbess.

In our monastery he also honorably covered the altar of the Holy Cross, the walls, and the Gospel lecterns with silver (+ year 928, October 10).

## 9 (Hildesheim Annals)

Then, in the year 928, after Sehard had died, THIETHARDUS, abbot of Hersfeld, was ordained our ninth bishop [Note: [Col. 1243] *novus*, “new,” in sources 1 and 2]. Among the many signs of his piety, he adorned the panel of the principal altar with the purest gold, gems, and precious stones, as it appears today. In Gandersheim, in the year 939 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1243] 938, in the second source], he also consecrated a new church for the nuns in honor of Saint Mary.

## 10

(He died in the twenty-seventh year of his ordination; compare the Hildesheim Annals. + year 954, September 13.)

OTWINUS, abbot of the Parthenopolitan see, was ordained the tenth bishop [Note: [Col. 1243] Before his abbatial dignity he had first been a monk of Augsburg, in the second source, second hand]. For thirty years he provided extensively for the benefit of his church. In particular, he acquired the estate of Giesenheim [Note: [Col. 1243D] Geisenheim, rich in wine] for the benefit of the brothers [Note: [Col. 1243] Absent in source 1]. He also established that wine should be provided to the brothers for sixteen days during the principal festivals.

He gathered precious gold, gems, stones, and pearls for the construction of a chalice and paten; but, overtaken by illness, he reserved them for his successor under seal and in the faith of Christ. In the thirtieth year of his ordination he happily departed to Christ. (Life of Godehard.)

After Wendelgarda died, he also appointed Gerberga [Note: [Col. 1243] *gergham*, in source 1] abbess at Gandersheim (984, December 1).

## 11

OSDAGHUS, the eleventh bishop, succeeded Bishop Otwin in the twenty-ninth year [Note: [Col. 1243] “After Otwin had died,” in the second source] (985). From his inheritance and acquisitions he established the estate of greater Algermissen [Note: [Col. 1243D] Algermissen], together with thirty hides, for the benefit of the brothers (989, November 8).

## 12

After Osdag died in the fourth year of his ordination [Col. 1243D] (990), GERDAGUS, the twelfth bishop, succeeded him. From his own property and acquisitions he also gave the brothers the estate of lesser Algermissen and Sighebrectheshusen [Note: [Col. 1243] *sighebretthehusen*, in source 1] [Note: [Col. 1244D] Sievershausen? Sibbesse?], amounting to forty hides. (Hildesheim Annals.)

In the third year of his ordination he went to Rome, and on his return he departed to Christ on the seventh day before the Ides of December (992, December 7).

[Col. 1244A] **13.** *(Thangmar, Life of Bernward.)* Then, in the year 993 of the Lord’s incarnation (January 15), BERNWARD, the royal chaplain, was appointed the thirteenth bishop of our church. From the beginning of his promotion, whatever he could acquire he wisely and faithfully distributed for the benefit of his church [Note: [Col. 1243] “for the benefit” instead of “for the use,” 2.]. For the gold and precious stones which Othwin of blessed memory, as was stated above, had reserved, Bernward fashioned into a chalice and paten of great beauty and, as it now appears, considerable size [Note: [Col. 1243] “and,” 2.]; and he gave many furnishings to his church, as is recorded among the works of his life.

He also built and partly dedicated the monastery of Saint Michael [Note: [Col. 1243] “the monastery ... he donated” is absent, and much more is read below, 2.], in which he established an abbey and a community of monks. For their benefit he donated estates, manors, and dependent households amounting to three hundred hides [Col. 1244B]. He also generously increased the provision and clothing allowance of the brothers, assigning to fulfill these obligations the manor of Hemethesdoron [Note: [Col. 1243] “the manor of Greater Hemethesdorn,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 1243] “Hemelesderen,” gloss, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1244D] Himmelsthür.] with its possessions in households and tithes [Note: [Col. 1243] “tithe,” 2.]. (1022, October 30.)

At Gandersheim also, as previously noted, after being wearied by various vexations from Archbishop Willigis and also from Aribo, he finally obtained victory when justice prevailed; and, in the presence of King Henry and Archbishop Willigis, he worthily consecrated there a new monastery in the year 1007 of the Lord’s incarnation and in the fifteenth year of his ordination (1022, November 20).

**14.** *(Wolfher, Life of Godehard.)* In the year 1022 of the Lord’s incarnation (December 2), in the thirtieth year of his ordination, blessed Bishop Bernward departed to Christ [Col. 1244C], and the venerable Godehard, abbot of Altaich, succeeded him. He persevered to the end as an example of justice and humility to all, in every form of holy religious life.

At the beginning of his promotion he was accused by Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, concerning the church of Gandersheim, and for several years was harassed by various vexations. At last [Note: [Col. 1243] “done” erased, 1.], in the year 1027 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fourth year of King Conrad’s reign [Note: [Col. 1243] “in the reign,” 1.], but the first of his empire [Note: [Col. 1243] “nra” has been erased, 1.], when a general synod had assembled at Frankfurt, with the emperor himself presiding together with twenty-two bishops, he canonically retained the diocese and authority over the territory of Gandersheim by synodal decree, with the testimony of seven bishops.

He also generously increased the brothers’ provision and clothing allowance. [Col. 1244D] At his manor of Hildesheim, when the old church which Bishop Othwin had built there had fallen into ruin, he constructed a beautiful monastery in honor of Christ’s Ascension. In it he gathered several clerics who were usefully accomplished in various branches of scriptural study and painting. He supplied them sufficiently with the necessities of food and clothing from his acquisitions [Note: [Col. 1243] “necessities,” c.].

But because of the guilt of sins, the same monastery was consumed by fire, the community dispersed, and the resources assigned there were scattered in different directions.

**15.** *(Compare Life of Godehard, chapter 33, and Annals of Hildesheim, for 1038.)* When he died in the sixteenth year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1245] The second manuscript reads: “He was buried in the crypt of our principal church.”] (1038, May 5), THIETMAR, the royal chaplain, succeeded him (1038, August 20). He resolved, through benevolent love, to enlarge the benefit of his church and its brothers in many ways, but, hindered by our sins, he did not fulfill this. Nevertheless, he increased the brothers’ daily provision and donated to them an estate in the village called Wengarde, acquired from the priest Walbert [Note: [Col. 1245C] Wennerde, formerly situated near Sarstedt.]. (Annals of Hildesheim, for 1039.)

In the first year of his episcopate, when Sophia, abbess of Gandersheim, had died and his sister [Note: [Col. 1245] “sister” partly erased, 1.] Adelaide had been appointed in her place, he introduced her by royal command into the same church before the altar. When she promised him obedience and submission, he entrusted her to perpetual care; he also reclaimed, by the authority of his ban [Note: [Col. 1245] “te” erased, 1.], the tithes which his predecessors had granted there as a benefice [Note: [Col. 1245] “predecessors” is partly erased, 1.], and received them when Count Christian, the advocate of that church, returned them. By the authority of his ban he confirmed them as his own property and that of his church, while Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, stood present with an innumerable multitude of clergy and people.

Nevertheless, at the archbishop’s request and with the counsel of his clergy and people, he restored those same tithes there to the altar and the abbess, for the same service and census [Note: [Col. 1245] “namely,” 2.] which blessed Bishop Bernward, his predecessor, had instituted there [Note: [Col. 1245] This passage reads: “This Thietmar ruled for six years or thereabouts and was troublesome to the monastery of Saint Michael, removing certain goods—namely, the tithes at Lafferde, Eggensen, Nettlingen, Savingen, and Beddingen [ [Col. 1245C] Lafferde, Hoheneggelsen, Nettlingen, Savingen, Beddingen.]—and goods at Wenthusen, through the persuasion of certain wicked men, in the same manner as Hildewin, who led blessed Godehard into similar actions, though he did not prevail. For the holy man, perceiving his wickedness [corrected by the second hand from “his wickedness”] and the envy of certain others, did not agree with them. After blessed Godehard’s death they did not cease; rather, by fox-like cunning they eventually induced the devoted Bishop Thietmar to remove from the monastery the same goods which blessed Bernward had bought from Otto III’s treasury and granted to the aforesaid monastery. Nevertheless, after the pitiable death of certain envious men, moved to repentance, he restored everything to the monastery. Yet afterward, I do not know by whom, these same goods, together with certain others—namely, the tithe at Berberch [ [Col. 1246C] Bierbergen.]—were taken from the monastery [thus corrected by the second hand; the first hand reads “received”] and granted to other churches, without fearing the curse of blessed Bishop Bernward, as is explained more clearly in his Life. When he was overtaken by sudden death [the second hand adds: “and buried beside the wall toward the sacristy”], in the year 1044, Azelinus [2].]

[Col. 1245C] **16.** *(Compare Life of Godehard, chapter 33; Annals of Hildesheim, for 1044.)* When Thietmar had been overtaken by sudden death (1044, November 14), AZELIN, the royal chaplain, succeeded him. He brought considerable benefit to his church through various acquisitions; nevertheless, as we fear, he stood guilty before God because he imprudently demolished our monastery after it had been consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 1245] “the larger church,” second hand.].

He also often resolved to increase the brothers’ advantages, but, hindered by various occupations and finally overtaken by sudden death, he did not fulfill this. Nevertheless, he gave a pontifical ring [Col. 1246A] and a good dorsal inscribed with his name, together with a bell called Cantabona. He also gave a crown radiant with gold and silver, hanging before the principal altar [Note: [Col. 1245C] A fifteenth-century gloss calls it “Lüttike Krone” (“little crown”).] [Note: [Col. 1245] This passage reads: “In the year of the Lord 1054 Azelin departed to Christ and was buried in the principal church beside the column of All Saints on the southern side; in his place Ethilo was appointed,” and so forth.]

**17.** After his death (1054, March 8), ETHYLO [Note: [Col. 1246C] King Henry IV calls him “Hezilo” in a charter of 1057.], provost of Goslar, was appointed to our church. He was distinguished both by literary learning and by discretion, the mother of virtues. He joined, with marvelous skill, a new body of moderate design to the ancient head of the church which Lord Altfrid had founded in that place by divine revelation. This was the work begun by his predecessor in the western part of our city, whose size exceeded the narrowness of our resources.

As time went on, he enriched it with estates acquired by himself, with pallia, chalices, and a crown representing the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, as well as with other ecclesiastical ornaments; moreover, he adorned it with a more precious treasury of books, gold, and gems [Col. 1246B].

He also reduced the brothers’ provisions, which had not been included within a fixed number, to a definite number—namely, fifty—and, by the authority of his ban, established that an equal portion should be given to all according to the regular institution, something our custom had not possessed until that time.

He was diligent in honoring the clerical name and most zealous in advancing boys and young men to the spiritual arms of the clerical militia. In them he set himself as an example of how one ought to become what he taught by word.

The poor themselves still testify how generous he was in almsgiving [Col. 1246C]. Yet he supplied their poverty with such discretion that he entirely eradicated the mother of vices, idleness, from those who were at least able to work a little.

Nevertheless, in him the divine judgment has, as we fear, something with which to strike: he changed the institution of our order in the abbreviation of the divine office, in excessive clothing, and in relaxing the strictness of the regular life—or rather, I should not say that he changed it, but he did not oppose those who were changing it. For one is held equally guilty for consenting to error and for failing to prohibit unlawful things when one can.

Then, as the resources of the church increased [Col. 1247A], he sought to enlarge the number of those serving God. In honor of Saint Maurice, in the monastery which Bishop Godehard of blessed memory had built [Note: [Col. 1247] “G.”, 1.], he established nuns. Considering both the suitability of the place and the nature of this sex, more prone to sin, he expelled them and placed twenty canons in the new monastery. He supplied them with the necessities of food and clothing and placed over them Cono, his near kinsman, later bishop of Brixen.

When the evening of his life was already approaching, and he was about to offer the evening sacrifice, he first transformed a house of war into a house of peace in the eastern part of our city, adding a new structure. He established fifteen canons there, provided them abundantly with necessities, and entrusted them for governance to Provost Adelold, a man of holy memory [Col. 1247B].

But because illness prevented him from consecrating that monastery, he entrusted its consecration, under the title of the Holy Cross and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt, a very powerful soldier of the church in war.

When he had been thoroughly purified by the fire of illness, at the exhortation of the aforesaid bishop, he repented from the heart before our brothers and returned whatever he had taken away—namely, the tithes and manors of Wangarde, Eymbrike [Note: [Col. 1247D] Emmerke.], and Poppenburg [Note: [Col. 1247D] Poppenburg on the Leine.]. Whatever he had accumulated over a long period, he sent ahead, like a prudent animal, through the hands of the poor to be offered to the Lord.

For he considered it impossible that the prayers of many should not be heard, and therefore he did not pass over any community in all Saxony without honoring it with some gift, however small, of charity.

He also confessed the change made in our order, received a penance, and admonished our brothers who stood present, both by invoking the fear of God and by advising and commanding them, that the order be restored to its former state.

It is also pleasing to add this to the sum of his virtues: when nearly all Italian and German bishops had subscribed to the unheard-of condemnation of Pope Gregory VII, one not found in the entire series of canons, he too subscribed through fear of death; but, being a man of exceptionally keen intelligence, he condemned what he had written by placing an obelus beneath it.

Because we in our own time have suffered most grievously the penalty of that subscription and the excommunication which followed it for this disobedience [Note: [Col. 1247D] For example, in the year 1080, when Saxony was devastated.], it seemed a mark of negligence to pass over in silence the great acumen of so great a man, by which he absolved himself from this before God.

When King Henry IV was devastating almost all Saxony by plunder and fire, Ethylo, after giving an immense sum of money, managed to ensure that not a single house in our entire episcopate was burned.

If anyone objects that one ought not to pray for a man whom we have said was bound by the penalty of excommunication, let him know with absolute certainty that Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, absolved him at Corvey together with Bishop Eilbert of Minden by apostolic authority. Afterward Ethylo never communicated bodily with excommunicated persons, and never did so in spirit.

Lord Bishop Hettylo of blessed memory died in the year 1079 of the Lord’s incarnation (August 5), in the twenty-sixth year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1247] “XVII, XXVI,” second hand.], and rests in the monastery of Saint Maurice, in the place which he had himself prepared by digging his grave. Since many of his benefactions still live on in our community, his new and celebrated memory also lives perpetually among us.

**18.** UDO succeeded him as the eighteenth bishop and ruled our church for thirty-three years. To speak with everyone’s agreement, because he indulged too much in the pleasures of temporal life [Col. 1248B], he paid the fitting penalties for his frivolity by God’s just judgment.

When Margrave Ecbert was savagely attacking our episcopate with fires and plunder and was hemming in the city walls with a most severe siege, the same bishop was compelled, for his own protection and the defense of the church [Note: [Col. 1247] “for protection,” second hand.], to distribute to the soldiers the tithes, almost all of which were vacant for him, and other possessions of the church. What is more harmful, he relaxed for the people under his authority the fines—that is, the monetary penalties established for criminal offenses.

At the end of his life, however, having sincerely corrected his conduct, he transferred some estates of his own property, together with their servants, to episcopal right. The properties which he possessed at Bocholt [Note: [Col. 1247D] Buchholz north of Hanover, or Bokholt in the district of Bodenteich.] by hereditary title, and what he had acquired at Witisleve [Note: [Col. 1248D] Wetzleben near Wolfenbüttel.] from a certain Godescalc by purchase, he assigned for the use of the brothers.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 1247] “thus,” 2; a word is lacking, 1.], he arranged that the venerable [Note: [Col. 1247] “venerable” (singular), 1.] abbesses Elika and Athelheidis, daughters of his brother [Note: [Col. 1247] “Elika and Aelheidis,” second hand; “Athelhedis,” first hand.], should donate to our church their estate at Hevenhusen [Note: [Col. 1248D] Hevensen near Hardegsen.] [Note: [Col. 1247] “Heneshusen,” second hand.] with all its appurtenances (1114, October 19).

After him BRUNIGGUS, dean of Goslar, mature in age and distinguished in ability, was appointed to our church (1115). He governed our episcopate for four years; but, because he refused to receive consecration from Adelbert of Mainz, he resigned the episcopate. He transferred himself to the church of Saint Bartholomew, to which he had donated some episcopal goods and some property of his own, and there, devoted to God, awaited the day of his death [Note: [Col. 1247] “where he was also buried,” second hand.] (1120, March 3).

**19.** Thereafter BERTOLD, our venerable provost, was placed at the head of our church with the consent of clergy and people (1119, between June 5 and October 31). Exceptionally learned in ecclesiastical office and distinguished by his zeal for religious conduct, he strove by every means to attach all religious persons to his church [Col. 1249A].

He was the first in our episcopate to enclose holy virgins [Note: [Col. 1249] In place of the following, the second manuscript has: “He also renewed the monastery called Vessingerade, now called Marienrode, placed there brothers of the Cistercian order, and settled the nuns who had formerly lived there at Iserenhagen.”], and he introduced clerics called regulars. He established a provostship of that order at Banchenrothe [Note: [Col. 1249D] Now Marienrode.] from his own goods and from episcopal possessions.

At the head of the sanctuary of the principal church he also built a work of elegant construction (1130, March 14).

**20.** Bishop BERNHARD succeeded him (1130, between March 28 and June 12). First a master of the schools and then provost of the principal church, he was elected bishop against his will, with equal desire on the part of clergy and people.

As a man distinguished by learning, discretion, and every excellence of virtue, once elected he took care to gather what was scattered, preserve what was gathered [Col. 1249B], and increase what he possessed in suitable ways.

King Conrad, with the consent of the princes, granted him the abbey of Ringelheim [Note: [Col. 1249D] Ringelheim on the Innerste.], formerly royal but now episcopal, in perpetuity for himself and his successors (1151, July 30). At Alsburg [Note: [Col. 1250D] Oelsburg.], since he had not previously possessed the whole provostship, Duke Henry transferred his share to him, and he united it entirely with the proprietary goods of our church.

In honor of our blessed Bishop and confessor Godehard—deservedly and not inappropriately entered into the catalogue of the saints, whose translation Bernhard himself had solemnly celebrated by the authority of Pope Innocent and with the cooperation of the Council of Reims (1132)—he built, dedicated, and endowed a monastery on the southern side of our city. He established there brothers who were to serve God in the monastic profession and placed Frederick over them as their first abbot (1146).

Piously attentive to the brothers’ welfare, he gave them part of the estate he possessed at Waleshusen [Note: [Col. 1250D] Wallshausen.] to increase their provisions.

The estates which the venerable abbesses Adelaide and Elika had donated to the church he distributed among the brothers with this arrangement: the manors and dependent peasants were to serve the brothers’ use, while the ministerials were to serve the episcopal court in the manner of household officials; nevertheless, the goods or benefices of ministerials who died without an heir were always to be added to the brothers’ possessions.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that he diligently sought out our manor at Embreke, which we had lacked for a long time, and restored it to the brothers. From it he arranged that four services should be provided by the brothers’ decision: two for the brothers of Saint Maurice and the Holy Cross, on Ascension and Pentecost, with us in the refectory; one on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul; and the fourth on the anniversary of that good Count Thietmar who had given us these goods.

To show the brothers in every way his affection of fraternal love, he distributed to them, with the intervention of Lord Hermann, a venerable priest of Thuringia, half the offerings of the altar of blessed Mary, a third part of what was offered to blessed Godehard, and also the offerings of the tomb, in their entirety (1146).

And, so that they would not be forced to experience a shortage of necessary goods, he established that, when absent with permission, they should receive the full portion of their provisions for fifteen days, except for wine. When wine was lacking, he ordered ten pennies to be given in place of wine, whereas previously seven had been given.

He also obtained from Emperor Lothair permission to rebuild the completely ruined castle of Winzenburg as a safeguard for the church. He rebuilt it and asked that its freedom—for the church, for himself and his successors, and without anyone’s encroachment—be confirmed by the bans of the two Roman pontiffs, Innocent and Eugenius, great men in Christ (1135, November 25) [Col. 1250B].

He also removed a wooden tower ruined by age and replaced it at no small expense. When he surrendered Imbrike to the brothers, he gave them, as a testimonial, a silver vessel for chrism and a very good dorsal (1149, May 27).

He purchased for the church from his own resources episcopal vestments decently adorned with gold embroidery, and offered blessed Mary two pontifical rings inscribed with his name: one surrounded by topaz and other gems with pearls, the other quadrangular and radiant with excellent jacinth.

How he also adorned our monastery with bells and paintings is evident to everyone.

Finally, throughout his life he peacefully possessed the prerogative of episcopal office which his predecessors, namely the bishops of Hildesheim, had held in the church of Gandersheim. For, after Lady Liutgard had died, he personally consecrated Lady Adelaide, canonically appointed in her place, at Goslar, in the imperial court of Lothair, in the church of the blessed apostles Simon and Jude, after she had promised him the obedience owed to him.

When she died, he arranged for Lady Adelaide, duly substituted for her, to be consecrated in the monastery of Gandersheim through the hand of Lord Bernhard, bishop of Paderborn, because he himself was hindered by blindness; she personally promised him obedience.

He died in the year 1153 of the Lord’s incarnation (July 20), in the twenty-third year of his ordination, and rests in the monastery of blessed Godehard.

[Col. 1250D] **21.** After the death of Lord Bernhard, BRUNO, the dean, a good and prudent man, was placed at the head of our church. For the ten years during which he presided, he devoted himself entirely to preserving and improving the church’s possessions.

With an expenditure of nearly fifty marks he had the roof and pavement of the principal church improved. He repaired the dilapidated workshops of the episcopal household and court. At considerable expense he also fortified the castle of Winzenburg with a very strong tower [Col. 1251A].

For its library he contributed the entire New and Old Testament, both glossed, commentaries and histories, treatises on the divine books, books of physics, and many others marked with his name.

He increased the church’s ornamentation by giving a chasuble decorated with gold embroidery and made of samite, a dorsal made of pallium cloth, a mitre, gloves, new sandals, and other customary items, as well as a reliquary and the foot of a cross.

He further offered for the brothers’ provision three and a half hides and two plots at Eilstringe [Note: [Col. 1251D] Eilstringe, deserted, near Rosenthal], three hides and three plots at Solesze [Note: [Col. 1251D] Solschen.] with eight dependent persons, and a silver cup purchased for seven marks [Note: [Col. 1251] Up to this point the first scribe wrote.].

**22.** [Note: [Col. 1251] The number is missing.] When Bishop Bruno had died [Note: [Col. 1251] In manuscript 2, Bruno’s death is said to have occurred around the years 1163 or 1164, or thereabouts.] (1162, October 18), HERMANN, provost of the Holy Cross, was unanimously elected by all. From the faithful of the church, but only after first consulting the emperor, who was then staying in Italy, he received the oath of fidelity. Having freely administered all his affairs and interests concerning episcopal revenues, he followed the emperor into Italy with his military force and obtained the investiture of the regalia at Pavia [Note: [Col. 1251D] According to Lüntzel, Hermann was consecrated after December 21, 1164.].

Once established in the episcopate, he governed his subjects with humility always joined to the fear of God and every gentleness. He showed such benevolence toward the brothers that, near the beginning of his promotion, he granted them a third part of the offering at the choir of Saint Godehard.

For the commemoration of all faithful departed souls, which he was the first to make solemn in our church, he assigned to the brothers three hides at Sutherem [Note: [Col. 1251D] Sottrum.] and a mill from his patrimony.

He solemnly dedicated the church of Gandersheim, disfigured by fire but restored through the efforts of Abbess Adelaide, with the cooperation of Hartwig, the venerable archbishop of the church of Bremen, and many other bishops.

Nor did he ever suffer any trouble from opposition in the church of Goslar. Indeed, at a solemn court held at Goslar, when he was still a deacon and several bishops—such as Conrad of Mainz and Reinald of Cologne—were likewise in the diaconate and possessed only the simple honor of election, the elected bishop of Hildesheim was compelled to undertake the burden and labor of receiving the emperor in procession and addressing the people, although this belonged to the office of their dignity.

Several years after his promotion, certain of his own dependents, because he did not wish to be subject in every respect to their desires, devastated the episcopate with such plunder and fires that scarcely a third of the episcopate remained untouched by this calamity [Col. 1252A].

When the disturbance had been somewhat quieted by the counsel of the emperor and his princes, Lord Bishop Hermann set out for the Lord’s Sepulchre. During this journey, besides other hardships, he suffered shipwreck and fell into such poverty that a prince so great, illustrious in birth and dignity, was reduced to public begging.

He was nevertheless piously received, kindly treated, and honorably sent away by the patriarch of Jerusalem and the other religious men of that land. He hastened his return to his homeland. Reaching Italy in good health, he began to fall ill there and, full of faith, died at Susa [Note: [Col. 1251D] Susa.], where he was also buried [Note: [Col. 1251] “Here the first hand ends; the second hand of the thirteenth century begins.] (1170, July 10).

[Col. 1252B] **23.** [Note: [Col. 1251] The number is missing.] After Bishop Hermann’s death, ADELOGUS [Note: [Col. 1251] “Delogus,” c.] the provost of Goslar was elected by all (1171).

As is contained in his privileges, he piously cared for the brothers’ interests in many ways. When he recovered the castle of Honburg [Note: [Col. 1252D] Homburg.], which Duke Henry had alienated from the church, with the cooperation of Lord Emperor Frederick and by paying money (1181), he ordered that two hides at Waltrinkehusen [Note: [Col. 1252D] Waltringhausen, principality of Schaumburg.] and Westenhem, paying ten shillings, should be provided by two brothers, namely Ludolph and Adolph, who had received part of that castle as a benefice, and by two other brothers, Bodo and Bertold, who had likewise received their share feudally from the bishop; and that ten marks should be given for the purchase of an estate for the brothers’ use (1183).

He also acquired for our church the estate of Count Otto of Asle [Note: [Col. 1252D] Asle, Asselburg near Burgdorf, not far from the Innerste.], purchased with much labor and great expense from the count’s widow, Lady Salome, to whom it had passed by lawful succession, with the consent of her daughter and the lawful consent of her other heirs. Lord Emperor Frederick facilitated the transaction and confirmed the episcopal act in every way (1186).

He assigned seven hides and eight acres at Stenem, belonging to that same estate and at that time unoccupied, for the brothers’ use, with this condition: only after the church’s goods and pledges, which had been pledged for the purchase of those estates, had been redeemed were they to have free use of them.

He further lent sixty marks of silver to the two brothers Ludolph and Wilbrand when they were setting out for Jerusalem with the emperor. He received as security the church’s castle of Halremunt [Note: [Col. 1252D] Near Springe.], which they held from the bishop as a benefice [Note: [Col. 1251] “They held in fief,” second hand.], together with certain of his ministerials, and stipulated that, once the pledges had been redeemed, the same marks were to come from the heirs of the aforesaid brothers for the use of the church [Col. 1253A] [Note: [Col. 1253] A fourteenth-century hand begins.].

He also committed to writing certain customs and certain rights of the church which, before his time, we had not possessed in specifically written form, so that they could not later be overturned by the wickedness of malicious persons; and by his merciful goodness he added certain other provisions not previously held (1179).

Specifically, he established that neither he nor any of his episcopal successors should presume, without the counsel of the prudent brothers, either to decide important matters, lease major benefices, or, if necessity should arise, pledge or in any way alienate the revenues of his table.

He also decreed that the communities should suffer no loss in their provisions through the debasement of the coinage, and confirmed by his ban that twenty-four tested silver shillings should always equal one mark.

He also confirmed the synodals of the archdeacons [Note: [Col. 1253] “S., which concern,” c.] from their churches or chapels which were under their authority, after the death of the priests who had held those churches or chapels from the bishop.

He granted in perpetuity the brothers’ testaments, whether made by the brothers themselves or bequeathed to them through the testaments of others, and secured them by the authority of his ban.

He also established that neither he nor any of his episcopal successors should grant or donate a ban or any church established in our episcopate to another church for perpetual possession without the consent and counsel of the brothers.

The brothers had received from their former bishops the privilege of choosing an advocate whom they considered suitable to protect the goods of their obediences; that advocate, however, was not to approach those goods for the resolution of lawsuits unless summoned.

But our aforesaid father and bishop, granting us a still greater gift of benevolence, with the consent of Lord Emperor Frederick, completely freed the aforesaid brothers’ goods from advocates and transferred every right of deciding cases, whether personally or through his friends, to the obedience-holders [Note: [Col. 1253] I correct thus; the manuscript has “of the obediences.”].

He also permanently freed the farms of our provostship—namely, Hisnem [Note: [Col. 1253D] Itzum, Hasede, Losebeck, now the New City of Hildesheim.] and those of Hasen and Lusbike—from the intolerable yoke of advocates and entrusted them to the provost for governance.

He also gave the church a very good bell [Note: [Col. 1253D] “Zadtt klokke” in a seventeenth-century marginal hand.] and two long candlesticks, and spent nearly twenty marks on repairing the roof of the principal church.

[Col. 1254A] Throughout his life he freely exercised episcopal office in every respect in the church of Gandersheim. For, after Lady Liutgard had died, he consecrated Lady Adelaide, canonically substituted for her, in the same monastery; and whenever he wished, he celebrated the synod and the consecration of chrism there [Note: [Col. 1253] “Here he built the tower of the monastery of Saint Godehard,” second hand.].

He died in the year 1190 of the Lord’s incarnation (September 20) and was buried in the middle of the crypt of the principal church.

**BERNO.**
### 24. Berno, bishop

Berno the bishop succeeded him. He had first been master of the schools and thereafter dean of our church; by the unanimous election of the clergy and the consent of the whole people, he was appointed head of our church. Having been elected as a prudent and provident man, endowed with literary learning, he took care during his tenure of the bishopric to administer it in such a way [Col. 1254B] that he devoted himself in every possible manner both to the honorable acquisition of property and to its suitable preservation.

For, in addition to the many expenses incurred in imperial service [Note: [Col. 1253] *deest* (“is missing”) in one witness], during the short time in which he presided over our church, he spent 600 marks and more on freeing the revenues of the episcopal mensa, on redeeming the goods held in the name of the bishopric as fiefs, and on redeeming the large paten of the chalice [Note: [Col. 1253] Under this bishop Saint Bernward was canonized by Pope Celestine III, through the efforts of the aforesaid Bishop Berno and Theoderic, abbot of our monastery (corrected by a second hand in S. Michahelis to “his monastery”), who was in every respect a provident man and ruled commendably. Spiritual matters, however, partly began to grow lukewarm because of excessive wealth. He bestowed many precious objects, in the form of vestments and copes, on our monastery (corrected to “his monastery”) for the increase of divine worship, and obtained the mitre, sandals, and other privileges in the year of the Lord 1195. Afterward, having died as bishop in the Lord, he rests in the middle of the greater church near the steps of the baptistery. Inserted by witness 2.].

He was no less attentive to the usefulness and advantages of the brethren: at his own considerable expense he freed four hides at Olem [Note: [Col. 1253D] Ohlum.] from lay control and, with the bishop’s consent, assigned them to the prebends of the brethren; he also established that bread from these should be provided in the refectory for three weeks each year, as is customary.

He likewise gave a third part of the money for redeeming the tithe at Hoctenem [Note: [Col. 1254D] Hottelem. In 1196, on 6 March, Conrad of Hildesheim, the imperial court’s elected chancellor, appears in a charter of Henry VI granted to the church of Utrecht.]; he arranged that three talents should be given from it annually, and from these he assigned nine denarii to each prebend on the day of his anniversary. On that same day he ordered that an honorable candle be placed at his tomb and twenty shillings be distributed as a greater alms.

Moreover, when the castle of Halremunt fell vacant to him, he promoted its infeudation with great maturity of counsel, since he prudently judged that it should be enfeoffed for many reasons; thus considerable possessions that the bishopric did not previously have would accrue to it, and revenues of thirty shillings would be added to the prebends of the brethren [Note: [Col. 1253] *prebendi* (“of the prebend”) in one witness.].

He also bestowed on the church books of the Old and New Testaments, glossed and produced with great scholarly diligence. This too should be added to his praises: all [Note: [Col. 1253] “revenues” or something similar is omitted, according to Leibniz.] the provostship’s estates of Saint Peter’s Mountain in Goslar, which for a long time had been pitifully occupied by laymen through the negligence of the provosts [Note: [Col. 1253] *mirabiliter* (“miraculously”) in one witness.], he completely freed through many labors [Col. 1254D] and innumerable expenses, as a prudent and vigorous man, [Col. 1255A] and had them secured by apostolic authority so that they might not thereafter be pledged.

How beneficent he was toward the brethren of that place is attested by his praiseworthy deeds; among them he lives in a celebrated and deservedly lauded memory (+ year 1194, October 28).

### CONRADUS

#### 25. Conrad

Conrad, our brother and chancellor (1194–1198; † in 1202), was first bishop of our church and afterward transferred to the bishopric of Würzburg. He was killed in that city on account of justice.

He suitably increased the adornment of our church. For he gave three chasubles: one of red figured silk, another of white silk, and a third of violet-purple silk, all ornamented with gold embroidery; two dalmatics, one [Note: [Col. 1255] “of silk” is missing.] of red figured silk, the other of white silk; a good white alb [Col. 1255B] of white silk; three altar cloths, two of red purple, one encircled with gold and another starred, and a third for daily use at the altar; a good curtain, customarily hung on the northern side of the sanctuary; one shaggy purple cloth; six copes, three of red figured silk and three of white; two beautiful reliquary chests of gold and gems; two portions of the relics of Saint Stephen and Saint Lawrence; and a little balsam.

Furthermore, he redeemed the advocacy of our city at no small cost. He gave the brethren a share of the advocacy over the estate … [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 1255D] Lede, a deserted village near Gronau.] (1198).

### HARBERTUS, 26th

[Note: [Col. 1255] Thereafter Harbert, the twenty-sixth, flourished as bishop through the unanimous esteem of the clergy. He rests before the altar of Saint Catherine, on the north side. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1204.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1216 [Note: [Col. 1255] “1200” (*MCC*) in witness 1. A seventeenth-century hand wrote in the margin: “Here, through the copyist’s error, there is a mistake in the number. For Harbert was still alive in 1206, when he consecrated three altars in the crypt, as follows in this same book.” I indicated the year 1216, guided by what D. Zeppenfeldt noted in *Beiträge zur Hildesheimschen Geschichte*, vol. I, p. 73.] (March 21), Harbert, of blessed memory, the twenty-sixth bishop of our church, died. He had first been cantor and thereafter provost of the greater church [Col. 1255C] of ours. Throughout his administration he usefully and faithfully distributed the prebends of the brethren, and he demonstrated by the actual performance of his works the great and sincere affection that he had always held for our church.

When Lord Conrad, chancellor of the imperial court and the twenty-fifth bishop of our church, transferred to the bishopric of Würzburg during the gravest dissension in the Empire, in the time of the blessed-memory Philipp and Otto (1198), and when Pope Innocent III of that name repeatedly and emphatically urged that our abandoned church should obtain its rightful shepherd, Harbert was elected bishop by the common and canonical consent of the entire chapter and clergy, while all the laymen were wholly opposed [Note: [Col. 1255] Reading: “*o. l. omnibus o. c. c.*”].

Because of this, our church endured many [Note: [Col. 1255] Witness c reads *multas* (“many,” feminine) instead of *multos* (“many,” masculine).] grave labors, expenses, dangers, losses affecting both common and private property, and alienations of episcopal possessions.

At last, when God’s mercy awakened on our behalf, after he had been consecrated bishop and had returned to our episcopal residence, from which he had been expelled for a year and more, and after affairs had been brought into reasonably good order, he diligently strove to gather what had been scattered, rebuild what had been burned and destroyed, recall what had been alienated [Note: [Col. 1255] Corrected from *alienanata*.], and reform in every respect, both internally and externally, the church that had been shaken by the long storm of its tribulations.

For six estates—Orsleve, Wackensleve [Note: [Col. 1255D] Oschersleben and Wackersleben in the principality of Halberstadt.], Stockem [Note: [Col. 1255D] Stöckheim.], Otfredesem [Note: [Col. 1255D] Otfresen, Uppen, and Ringelheim.], Upum, and Rengelem—which the aforesaid chancellor had pledged for more than five hundred marks to Count Siefrid of Blankenburg, he completely freed from every claim by that count, giving him two hundred marks of silver and assigning him certain other revenues and vacant benefices [Col. 1256B].

He also freed a portion of those same goods from certain knights and servants by giving thirty marks; he freed the estate at Mallerten [Note: [Col. 1255D] Malerten.] by giving sixteen marks; and he likewise freed the estate at Stockem, which the brethren of Wulflebuthe later held by force, by paying ninety marks.

He recovered the episcopal allod at Afdendorp [Note: [Col. 1256D] “The old village,” near Hildesheim.] and the mill in the city, pledged to a certain Gerhard for eighty marks, as well as the estate at Vorstede [Note: [Col. 1256D] Förste.], pledged during the chancellor’s time to Theoderic of Alten for sixty marks, by paying 140 marks.

He spent 300 marks for the church of Gandersheim and sixty marks in the case of the abbey of Ringelheim. In compensation for the damage inflicted by Lippold of Escherde on the mill and other property of the church, he spent ninety marks of his own money and gave the brethren the estate and advocacy of Monestede [Note: [Col. 1256D] Münstedt.]; he redeemed them for sixteen marks from Heinrich and his sons, who held them.

Acquiring for four marks sixteen shillings’ revenue in the same village from a certain Exzo of Eilstringe, he assigned it annually for bread for the schoolboys in the refectory. He also redeemed the advocacy of the obediency at Wittenburg and another advocacy over twelve acres with the brethren’s money. Likewise, he assigned the advocacy of the goods of the greater provostship at Idagesem [Note: [Col. 1256D] Perhaps Itzum?] and the tithe of the same village for the benefit of the brethren, so that his memory might be celebrated; and, to prevent any of his successors from alienating them, he confirmed them by the authority of his ban [Col. 1256D].

He also donated to our church the *cura* at Vorstede, purchased for 107 marks from Bruno the custodian [Note: [Col. 1255] Perhaps read *curiam*, “court.”]. For the property at Repenarde [Note: [Col. 1256D] Reppener.], which the brethren purchased for themselves from the church of Saint Martin at Minden [Note: [Col. 1257] Read “which they purchased.”], 500 marks from his own resources were expended [Col. 1257A]. He also donated two tithes at Dunhusen [Note: [Col. 1257D] Dunsen, prefecture of Lavenstein?] to the church.

How much he spent on the roofs of the principal church and on the buildings of the episcopal court, which he found ruined both through age and through negligence [Note: [Col. 1257] *tamen* (“nevertheless”) in one witness.], is evident to all [Note: [Col. 1257] *elucessit* (“was evident”) in one witness.].

### SIFRIDUS, 27th

[Note: [Col. 1257] He rests before the altar of Saint Peter.]

The anniversary of Siefrid, the twenty-seventh bishop of our church and a most gentle man. He gave the church the advocacy at Hemedesdore over all the goods of that estate, wherever they might be situated, purchasing it from the brethren Hugo and Eustace for 100 marks, on the condition that, if anything beneficial and advantageous should arise in time [Col. 1257B] [Note: [Col. 1257] Witness c reads *commodum* (“advantageous”).], the chapter should be free to make arrangements concerning it.

He gave our church the advocacy at Wittenburg over the allod and twelve acres, purchased from Arnold the layman, and, in his own time, the tithe of one hide and twelve acres in the same village, reasonably acquired. Furthermore, he made one of his own acres beside the gate of Saint Peter, which had previously been held by feudal right, into a cloister holding and added it to the cantor’s court.

He also assigned two acres in the new city to the greater provost, while the provostship was vacant, for the use of certain lights; and he gave us the site of a fishpond that had been less useful, near our dormitory.

He also gave a small acre and its advocacy, purchased from Heinrich the chamberlain and his sons, for the permanent vicarages. Wishing also to provide for the church with pious goodwill, with the consent and counsel of the chapter [Col. 1257C] he decreed that no successor of his, nor anyone else, should alienate the advocacies of the greater provostship that the provost now holds and that might later be freed from laymen.

He died after his resignation in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1227, on the day before the Ides of November. May his soul, through the mercy of God, rest in peace. Amen. [Note: [Col. 1257] After this, folio 145 verso follows, written by a thirteenth-century hand.]

### CONRADUS, 28th

[Note: [Col. 1257] The word is missing in one witness.] [Note: [Col. 1257] “The twenty-eighth bishop was an outstanding doctor of theology.”]

The anniversary of the venerable Lord Conrad, the twenty-eighth bishop of our church. After he had commendably taught sacred Scripture at Paris and preached the crusade against the Avians [Note: [Col. 1257D] That is, the Albigensians.], he was appointed to govern our church. Since this venerable man was guided by the Spirit of God, he took great care of spiritual matters, [Col. 1257D] yet for that reason he did not neglect the administration of temporal affairs.

In his time the Dominican and Franciscan friars were received, as were the penitential sisters of Saint Mary Magdalene. He generously assisted them in building their churches and conventual buildings, and purchased nearly all their lands at his own expense. The convents of Wülfinghausen [Note: [Col. 1257D] Wülfinghausen, south of Hanover.] and Fraukenberg [Note: [Col. 1257D] In Goslar.] were also built in his time, as was Winhusen [Note: [Col. 1257D] Near Celle.], to whose community he assigned the parish church of that village. He provided and spent many resources for other religious communities as well, while taking care that no defect should arise in conventual or parish churches through which the dignity of the Church might be diminished.

As a provident shepherd and diligent steward, he enriched our church and bishopric through the purchase of goods and the redemption of advocacies. For he generously and unconditionally gave the chapter’s redeemed advocacies of the estates at Barum [Note: [Col. 1258D] Barum, Beddingen, Eggelsen, Bültum, and Addelum.], Beddigen, Eckelsem, Bultem, and Addenem to the brethren as prebends [Col. 1258B].

Likewise, he gave to the church of Saint Maurice’s Mountain, for God’s sake, the advocacy redeemed from Lord Berthold of the Old Market. Moreover, he redeemed from the chamberlain the advocacy in the city and over certain acres situated behind the city, together with certain offices of the brewers; and he redeemed the advocacy at Malerten from Count Bernard of Spiegelberg, paying money.

He also redeemed the advocacy at Honhamelen from Lord Theoderic the free man for 170 marks of refined silver, and from him he purchased, for sixty marks of weighed denarii, ownership of the castle of Depenow [Note: [Col. 1258D] Depenau, in the parish of Stenwede.].

With the assistance of the peasants, he acquired the advocacy of the estate at Hardeshem [Note: [Col. 1258D] Harsum.] from Lord Conrad of Piscina for 550 pounds of Hildesheim denarii [Col. 1258C].

He also bought half the advocacy at Aulica [Note: [Col. 1258D] Elze.] from Lord Lippold of Escherte for sixty-five pounds. He paid him forty pounds and, for the remaining thirty-five, pledged one farm at Rodem [Note: [Col. 1258D] Kirchrode, near Anderten.] and one farm at Anderten; he departed leaving them pledged.

He also bought the office of steward from Ernest the steward for 170 marks, especially since he had suffered many inconveniences from him in the provision of food. With the cooperation of our provost and chapter and the abbot of Saint Godehard, he bought the mill of the cupbearer for 180 pounds. The rent accruing to his mill from this purchase—namely, one wagonload of wheat, one wagonload of rye, and one wagonload [Col. 1258D] of barley—he permanently assigned and donated for the consolation of the poor schoolboys serving in the choir of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

He also solemnly instituted the celebration of the Conversion of Saint Paul, and ordered that on that day a charitable meal with venison from the tithe at Giften [Note: [Col. 1259D] Giften.] be given to the brethren.

In temporal matters he acted so prudently that he removed harmful things, recovered alienated property, and built useful structures. He also recovered the tower in the upper castle of Winzenburg from Lord Theoderic of Stockem, raised it into a single dwelling, and improved the bishop’s residence with fine buildings, as is evident.

He also freed the Bavarians’ Mountain in the same castle, the advocacy of Hildesheim, and the estate at Clauen [Note: [Col. 1259D] Clauen.] from those of Escherte, who were occupying them unjustly.

He built and fortified the castle and city of Rosendal [Note: [Col. 1259D] Rosenthal.]. For its purchase, construction, and relief from siege, and also for the siege of the city of Peine [Note: [Col. 1259D] Peina.], he spent 8,000 talents of Hildesheim currency.

He completely demolished and destroyed a tower at Sarstedt [Note: [Col. 1259D] Sarstedt.] that had been unjustly built on his property [Col. 1259B]. Besieging Emna [Note: [Col. 1260D] Today Gronau; see below under Bishop Siefrid.], he captured and destroyed it. Likewise, he stormed and destroyed the castle called the Island [Note: [Col. 1260D] Werder, where there was a Carthusian monastery in 1660.], situated near our city, into which violators of the peace had retreated.

Seeing the burdens and oppressions of the free men of the lesser county near Nortwolt, he bought it from Count Conrad of Lauenrode [Note: [Col. 1260D] The castle of Lauenrode, opposite Hanover.] for 380 pounds of Hildesheim currency.

Finally, considering in his last days the danger and burden faced by travelers at Poppenburg, he bought part of that castle for 220 pounds and the smaller tower for ten pounds. There he built a residence with its buildings, costing nearly 100 pounds, and he did not allow new tolls to be instituted, by which travelers are accustomed to be unlawfully harassed.

Moreover, he bought half the advocacy at Sarstedt [Note: [Col. 1260D] Sarstedt.] for 650 pounds and built a castle there at great expense and cost. For these expenses he pledged certain goods belonging to the episcopal mensa and left them pledged [Note: [Col. 1259] These matters have already been read above.].

In the case of the church of Goslar, he also spent 200 marks of refined silver and, in the form of a judicial proceeding, established by lawful proofs that that church was subject in spiritual matters to the bishop of Hildesheim.

In addition to all this, he prudently freed our diocese from the jurisdiction of the duchy. Lord Otto, duke of Brunswick, had intended to usurp this jurisdiction for himself before the lord emperor and the princes in a solemn court at Mainz (perhaps 1235). There he publicly protested before everyone that the bishopric of Hildesheim was subject to the domination of no one and to no duchy, but only to the bishop himself; and this was approved by all the princes.

As bishop on four occasions in the affairs of the crusade, the Roman Church, and his own church, he crossed the Alps, undertaking great labors and expenses. Through his initiative our monastery was also restored with new beams, rafters, and roof tiles, and, through the alms of the faithful who cooperated, roofed with copper. He also had the Hildesheim episcopal house, which had been damaged by leaking water, covered with good boards.

After all these things had been successfully completed, judging himself inadequate to govern the church, both because of old age and because of the schism that existed between the apostolic see and the Empire, he asked for and obtained his resignation from the elected bishop of Ferrara, then legate of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1259] “Thus it is read”; not as Leibniz writes, “not at all.”]. He resigned the position, not the dignity.

After staying for some time with the Dominican friars, he left our city because of the discord that had arisen in our church at the time of the election and departed for Schonowia, where, passing to the Lord, he rests happily. He governed our church for twenty-seven years and died, in the third year after his resignation, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord 1249 [Note: [Col. 1259] 1248. A second hand, from the middle of the thirteenth century, follows.].

### HEINRICUS, 29th

[Note: [Col. 1259] “Heinrich” is a fourteenth-century heading.]

After the resignation of the venerable father and lord Bishop Conrad, Lord Heinrich, provost of the Hildesheim church, was elected our bishop. But the petition made on behalf of Lord Hermann, provost of Saint Cyriacus in Brunswick, disturbed his election in many ways, so that, although invested by the king and confirmed by the archbishop, he could not obtain peaceful possession of our city. Since all the castles and towns of the church, except Winzenburg, had been occupied by his adversary, he went to Pope Innocent IV, who was then residing at Lyons, to redress the injuries inflicted on him and his followers.

Because of the respect due to his mature person, and because of the urgent petitions of Siefrid, archbishop of Mainz, although at the beginning of his arrival the lord pope and the whole curia had been favorably disposed toward him, nevertheless, through the various suggestions of many noble friends of the aforesaid petitioner, the case of the said bishop remained suspended for a year and more.

At last, after obtaining the venerable father and lord, the bishop of the church of Strasbourg, as executor, and after receiving many favors granted to him by the apostolic see, he was honorably dismissed by the lord pope. The bishop of Strasbourg, acting as he had been instructed, ordered that all and each of the bishop’s rights should be restored to the aforesaid bishop [Col. 1260D], restraining opponents and rebels by the ban of his judgments.

When the adversaries appealed from his judgments, they arranged for the parties to be summoned before the lord pope. There, when the petitioner appeared in person and the procurators of the frequently mentioned bishop were also present, the aforesaid petitioner received from the mouth of the lord pope, after silence had been imposed on him, a contrary judgment concerning the church of Hildesheim [Col. 1261A].

Although the said bishop was occupied by many conflicts during his time, because of which he left many goods belonging to the episcopal mensa pledged, nevertheless he took care to provide for the church’s interests wherever he could.

For he freed the advocacy of the estate at Hardessehem, which Lord Conrad, bishop of our church, had redeemed for our church from Conrad of Piscina, a ministerial of the church, but which was afterward long obstructed by Count Meinhard of Schladen, from whom the aforesaid man of Piscina had held it as a fief.

He also redeemed from the noble brothers Ludolf and Adolf of Dassel half the castle at Honburg, which they held as a fief from the church, for 300 pounds, and donated it to our church.

He likewise obtained half the ownership of Empna [Col. 1261B] from Lord Conrad, formerly provost of the Mountain and the true heir, so that it might be enfeoffed to the church’s ministerials. They afterward, with the consent of the aforesaid provost, pledged that same fief to our church for 1,000 pounds.

The aforesaid bishop received the remaining half, which had been pledged in the name of the church, from Count Hermann of Woldenberg [Note: [Col. 1261D] That is, Woldenberg.] for sixty-five marks and five shillings, and left it to the church as security for the money.

He also purchased from the men of Lutterberg [Note: [Col. 1261D] Perhaps the counts of Lutterberg.] the county situated beside the Leine [Note: [Col. 1261D] The Leine is a river.], which had become vacant to them through the death of Berthold the advocate. From the advocate’s widow and daughter he obtained for himself and his successors five pounds of annual revenue in Damme from the yearly rent of the acres, on condition that he should defend her against those who molested her.
