He also gave the tithe of newly cultivated land at Vorholz [Note: [Col. 1261D] The Vorholz, near Heersum.] as a prebend for the brethren. He freed the advocacy at Damme [Note: [Col. 1261D] The Dammstadt, between Hildesheim and the village of the Mountain.], which the counts of Woldenberg held as a fief, from everyone, and left it entirely free to the church.

He died in the year of the Lord 1257, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1261] Here a hand of the fifteenth century begins again.].

### JOHANNES, 30th bishop

After the death of our venerable father and lord Heinrich, John, provost of Saint Maurice, was elected bishop of our church by equal vote and unanimous consent. In his outward conduct he behaved in such a way as to draw to himself the affection of both the great and the small. Attentive to the peace and welfare of the church, he strove, as far as his strength and ability permitted, to recover what had fallen away and been alienated.

First, he purchased for our church from Lippold and Basil, brothers of Escherde, the advocacy of the estate at Cherstede [Note: [Col. 1261] Sarstedt.] for 100 pounds of Hildesheim denarii.

Likewise, from Lippold of the Old Market, he purchased the advocacy of that same place for 34 talents.

From Lippold [Col. 1262A] of Escherde, he purchased a part of the castle of Depenow for seventy of Bremen silver.

From Egbert, he purchased the castle of Lutter [Note: [Col. 1262D] Lutter am Barenberge.] for 500 marks of refined silver, less twenty marks, and twenty-five hides.

In the same village, from John the chamberlain, he purchased two hides for thirteen talents.

In the same village, from Count Heinrich of Woldenberg, he acquired seventeen freed hides and seven enfeoffed hides for seven marks of refined silver.

From Count Burchard and Count Heinrich, brothers of Woldenberg, he purchased the village, its ministerials, and certain appurtenant goods for 400 marks of refined silver [Note: [Col. 1261] *Itemite* is a scribal error for *item* (“likewise”).].

For the acquisition of the castle called Peine and the payment of the debts of Gunzelin, son of Burchard of Wulflebuthe, he spent 1,010 talents of Hildesheim denarii.

He redeemed for 940 talents of Hildesheim denarii the episcopal goods pledged by his predecessor [Col. 1262B]; for these he left certain episcopal goods pledged.

He bought four hides from the men of Ringelheim. From these he established that, on the day of his anniversary, eight denarii should be given to each prebend; one shilling to the chamberlains and bell-ringers [Note: [Col. 1261] Witness c reads *campenariis* twice.]; five shillings to the schoolboys; and a candle of one pound of wax to the altar of Our Lady.

He also bestowed on our chapter seven hides at Ochtersem, which had fallen vacant through the death of Heinrich, son of Lippold Craz, so that the feast of John before the Latin Gate might be celebrated solemnly. From those same goods he arranged that each of the lords should receive one shilling; that the altar servers and those presiding over the choir should receive a double portion; that the two boys who would sing the *Alleluia* should receive one shilling; that poor schoolboys should receive ten shillings [Col. 1262C]; that the chamberlains and bell-ringers [Note: [Col. 1261] Witness c reads *campenariis* twice.] should receive one shilling; that two pounds of wax should be used to light candles around the choir; and that on that same day a charitable meal of two courses of chickens, with bread and wine, should be given.

He presided over our church for three and a half years. He died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1261 [Note: [Col. 1261] He was buried south of the steps of the baptistery.], on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the fourth year of his ordination.

### OTTO, 31st
### Anniversary of Lord Otto, the 31st bishop of our church

This lord was born to that once-noble Otto, duke of Brunswick. [Note: Otto died in 1252; Albert first ruled alone, then in 1267 received the Brunswick lands, leaving the Lüneburg lands to John.] When his brothers Albert and John succeeded to their paternal inheritance, he was first elected a canon of our church; then, when our church became vacant through the death of the venerable father Bishop John, of pious memory, while he was in his fourteenth year, he was postulated as bishop of our church. While this postulation on his behalf remained pending until his fifth year, he was confirmed by Pope Urban IV. Thus, through him, our church was governed for many years in the order of the subdeaconate, both in spiritual and temporal matters.

When Pope Gregory X summoned a council at Lyon, and he had then for the first time been promoted to the orders of deacon and priest, he journeyed to the council with the other bishops (in the year 1274). There, because of the renown of his lineage, he was graciously received by the pope, and by papal mandate he was consecrated bishop by the reverend father Werner, archbishop of Mainz. Returning successfully, he carried out the pontifical office as well as he could amid his various occupations.

From the time when he assumed the governance of our church until the end of his life, he retained a zeal for God and for the church and strove to exalt it to the best of his ability. He freed certain episcopal properties that his predecessors had pledged, and acquired certain other properties for himself and his successors, namely:

Before the castle of Poppenborch, ten hides for 150 talents; three parts of the advocacy at Chyerstede from the men of Escherde, two parts for eighty talents; a certain county jurisdiction beside Cherstede, comprising the villages of Hottenem, Luppenstede [Note: A deserted place.], little Lobeke [Note: Kleinen Lopke.] and certain other surrounding villages, from Bruno of Gustede for fifty talents; the advocacy at Clowen [Col. 1263: “dowen” in witness 1.] from Sifrid of Rutenberge for fifty talents; the advocacy at Borchdorpe toward Mirica [Note: Mirica, merica, and erica all mean the same thing as *Heide* in our March, signifying a forest.], from Lippold of Escherde for forty talents; a fishery on the Layna near Ruthe, from Lord John of Adenoys for fourteen talents; the castle of Hudhe with five hides, a meadow with a mill, and two fisheries, from Hillemar of Oberge for two hundred marks. He rebuilt this castle almost entirely from its foundations at great expense.

The county jurisdiction of Nowen [Note: “Rowen” in the edition.] [Note: Compare H. A. Lüntzel, *Die ältere Diöcese Hildesheim*, p. 165.] from Count Henry of Woldenberg for 120 marks; the advocacies at Ringelem, Uppem, and Solide [Note: Söhlde.], and the county jurisdictions at Soltga and Ris [Note: Bereler Ris.], as well as ownership of the castle of Werdere [Note: Werder on the Nette.], its mill [Note: “i” in witness c.] and fishery, and nine adjacent hides, from Count Ludolf of Woldenberg for 450 marks. He also obtained the same castle as a free [Note: “libro” in witness c.] castle for the church, so that the said count and his heirs would hold it by the same right by which the counts of Halremunt and Sladem and the lord of Honburg are known to hold their castles from the church. It was further stipulated that the said castle could not be alienated by the count or his heirs “under any cloak whatsoever” [Note: That is, under any pretext.]; rather, at the appointed time, the castle together with the mill, fishery, and the aforesaid nine hides would remain with the church for a fixed and agreed price, namely 350 marks, of which fifty marks have already been paid by the bishop.

He also recovered the allod of Veteris villa, which had been alienated before Hildesheim for eighty talents. He acquired the castle of Woldenberg, together with only the castle’s enclosure, from the counts of Woldenberg for 1,500 marks, and also partly walled it on its southern side at great expense. He acquired an allod at Rod near Woldenberg and a meadow adjoining the castle for seventy marks. He redeemed the estate of Holle, which he found pledged, for 150 marks.

He acquired the advocacy at Holle, the county jurisdiction there, and the *Gografschaft* over fifteen villages from Count Ludolf of Woldenberg for 144 marks; and the advocacy at Badekenstede [Note: Baddekenstedt.] from the same man for twenty-six talents. He also acquired the greater county jurisdiction beginning at Scirbeke near Harlessem and extending along the Hever to the spring of Sebbettessen on the side of Gandersheim, and as far as the bridge of Olkessen [Note: Schirbeck and Harlessem, deserted villages near Hildesheim; the Hever near Bilderlah; Sebexen; Gandersheim; Olxheim. Compare Lüntzel, p. 155.], together with one-fourth of the county jurisdiction over Amberga [Note: In which, for example, Bockenem lies.], from Count Hermann of Woldenberg for four hundred marks.

He acquired the advocacy at Sibbethtessen from the properties of the custodianship, from Hugh of Holthusen, for twenty marks. He acquired a pond near Eddessen and the mill of Berge with its fishery. He freed from obligations, for a large sum of money, a forest in the Harz [Note: Harz.] called Wrochterewolt from many *Echtwardi* [the term is uncertain in the source], and obtained it for the church.

At Tyderingerod he acquired fifty *Echtwardi* from Lippold of Vreden for twenty-four marks. He retained for himself and his successors a tithe at Hemmendorpe that had fallen vacant. He repaired the episcopal residence at Hildesheim, which was almost ruined, with walls, beams, and a stone roof, and restored it with other buildings.

He roofed the dining hall at Poppenburch and the small adjacent tower with stone. He walled the castle of Wincenburg from Beyerberg to the gate. Before the castle of Peine he built a stone gate and roofed it with stone; he likewise roofed the vaulted structure in the castle with stone and renewed almost all the other buildings there.

He also freed the fief of the castle-town and county jurisdiction of Peine from Count Widekind of Poppenborch, who freely resigned it into his hands. He freed the advocacy at Lapidibus from John and Conrad Acken.

He obtained from Lord Henry of Honborch, in judicial proceedings, that it would be lawful for the church to redeem the castle of Honburg every year, always between Easter and the feast of Walburga, for three hundred pounds in Hildesheim denarii.

Furthermore, the chamberlain, marshal, cupbearer, and other officials [Col. 1265A] of the bishop had in fact taken possession of certain furnishings belonging to some of their predecessors, the bishops; the bishop abolished this entirely.

What more need be said? Indeed, the church would have received a far greater increase through him if persecution from within and from his brothers had not existed. Thus, through wicked counsel, Duke John proceeded with armed force against the bishop and the church, inflicting severe damage not only on lay possessions but also on the possessions of the churches.

At last peace was established between the bishop and that duke, and they were firmly reconciled to one another. But behold, Duke Albert the Elder—more savage than the others—stirred by the spur of envy against his brother the bishop, resolved to humble him and the church, and carried out his purpose. Not content that he had deceived the church in many matters, including the five villages belonging by ancient right to the county jurisdiction of Soltga, which Margrave Otto of Brandenburg unjustly adjudicated to that duke despite the bishop’s opposition and protest, he also stirred up adversaries against the church. These men had free and safe passage through the duke’s territory to injure the church by plunder and arson, and to return safely to their fortifications.

Therefore, on the bishop’s advice, help was sought from Duke John. Since, despite the various legal proceedings maintained on both sides, brother could not prevail with brother through the brother, John took pity on his brother and promised assistance. At his initiative, moreover, the archbishop of Bremen, the lower lords, and also Margraves Otto and Albert of Brandenburg were strongly encouraged to support the bishop against the duke.

But behold: Duke John died first (in the year 1277, December 13), and Duke Albert was appointed guardian. Thus, through the death of the one and fear of the other, the assistance promised to the church almost perished.

Nevertheless, trusting in the assistance of the church of Magdeburg and of the margraves, the bishop reluctantly opposed his brother on behalf of the church. At first he acted manfully against his brother, but when those who had promised assistance grew sluggish in bringing it, the church’s fortifications of Cherstede and Empne were captured by fire missiles, and the church’s more important ministerials were taken captive there (in the year 1279).

From this great ruin of the church there arose immense grief throughout the land. But the bishop, whom the sorrow afflicted more deeply, grieved even more; and the grief became so powerful in him that, as is believed, it caused his death.

Struck inwardly by vehement sorrow, and seemingly conscious of his approaching death, on the Friday before the day on which, in the year of the Lord 1279, the feast of Saint Ulrich fell—a Tuesday—he paid the debt of the flesh [Note: Buried before the altar of the Holy Cross. Witness 2.]. With the brothers summoned in chapter, he drew up his testament before them concerning the newly cleared land at Emberke, which he had caused to be brought under cultivation with the consent of all concerned. He offered it, together with its ownership, tithe, and every right, as he himself had held it, upon the relics of the Blessed Virgin, leaving the chapter free, after his death, to dispose of those properties as they should judge beneficial according to God for the salvation of his soul.

Accordingly, by order of the chapter, a common charity will be given from that newly cleared land on his anniversary: to all the brothers and vicars, chickens with bread and wine; to each brother, twenty denarii; to each vicar, ten; to the three bell-ringers, one solidus; to the three chamberlains, one solidus, since they will assist the bell-ringers in ringing; and to the poor scholars, twelve solidi.

The bishop also bestowed certain ownership-rights in properties upon the poor scholars, from which the provisions for his anniversary night will be procured out of those twelve solidi. Two candles, made from three pounds of wax, will be placed: one at the altar of the Blessed Virgin in the choir, the other at the bishop’s tomb. They will burn from one vespers to the next.

The aforesaid bishop, also looking to the welfare of persons and of the church, at the very hour [Note: Thus I have corrected it; witness c reads “properties.”] when he drew up his testament, at the chapter’s devout request, granted the chapter the year of grace concerning the benefices held from the bishop. The provost John likewise granted it concerning his benefices, and the chapter concerning its obediences, in this manner: whoever among the brothers dies before the feast of Saint James will receive the new revenues of the following year, as is fully contained in the letters of that bishop and of the chapter.

As the bishop died on the day of Saint Ulrich, which then fell on a Tuesday, as has been said, behold, something marvelous but not impossible for God followed: within six weeks, on the same day of the week on which the bishop had died, Duke Albert died thereafter (in the year 1279, August 15), as though summoned by God’s judgment.

Bishop Otto governed our church for nineteen years, counting the period of his postulation, and exactly seven months [Note: Thus witness c; yet he seems to have sat only eighteen years.].

### SIFRID, the 32nd

[Note: The heading is missing.]

When our venerable father and lord Bishop Otto died, Sifrid, dean of the church of Magdeburg, descended from the noble house of Querenvorde—a man in every respect great-hearted, learned in letters, upright in conduct, and endowed with many virtues—was canonically elected as our bishop. The venerable Bernard, elect of the holy church of Magdeburg, and the illustrious Albert, margrave of Brandenburg, gave their advice and assistance toward this election. At that same time they were staying in the city of Hildesheim with a large army, bravely defending our widowed church against Duke Albert of Brunswick, who was attacking it.

After receiving confirmation and consecration from the archbishop of Mainz, and the investiture of the regalia from the most serene Roman king Rudolf, he endeavored with all his strength to restore our church, which he found gravely troubled because the fortifications of Tzerstede and Empna had been completely destroyed by the aforementioned duke and not a few of the church’s ministerials and vassals had been captured.

For after that duke died a few days later, Sifrid freed the captives by paying a considerable sum of money. In the course of time he restored the destroyed fortifications, namely Empna [Note: “Emna” in witness c.] and Tzerstede. He relocated Empna to a safer site and, changing its name, called it Gronowe.

But behold: after Duke Albert, as mentioned above, had been removed from this life, his sons, Dukes Henry [Note: Duke in Grubenhagen.], Albert [Note: Duke in Göttingen.], and William [Note: Duke of Wolfenbüttel.]—following in their father’s footsteps—rose ferociously against the bishop and the church.

When the bishop vigorously resisted them, an unfortunate event occurred. Of the church’s principal ministerials and vassals who had withdrawn to Castle Campe [Note: Not far from Brunswick.] for the sake of protection, approximately seventy were captured after the dukes had surrounded the castle in a tight siege for some time and finally stormed it.

As a result, the church was placed in such danger and cast down so far that scarcely any hope of recovery or revival remained. Yet the bishop, trusting in the Lord and setting himself as a wall of defense for the church, did not despair.

When discord arose between the brothers, that is, the dukes themselves, he entered into an alliance with two of them, namely William and Albert. From them he obtained Castle Stouphemborch [Note: Staufenburg near Osterode.] as a pledge for a specified sum of money in the name of military pay, so that he and the church might be defended against the third.

After various assaults and conflicts had taken place on both sides, the bishop captured several soldiers and servants of the opposing party. Through them he freed many of his own men from captivity and once again fortified himself for the defense of the church.

After these events, Dukes Albert and William, with the assistance of the bishop, besieged the town of their brother, Duke Henry, called Helmstedt. The citizens, pressed by the siege, exchanged truces on both sides and requested that a number of the more important soldiers, both from the bishop’s side and from the dukes’ side, be sent into the town, supposedly to negotiate peace and concord.

When these men had entered and had already been received into lodgings, suspecting no evil, the faithless citizens—carrying words of peace in their mouths but not in their hearts—closed the town gates and cruelly killed them inside [Note: Here it is reported that three noble knights of our diocese, namely Stenberch and Saldar and others, had been treacherously killed. Witness 2.].

This mournful deed gave the whole land cause for lamentation.

Afterward, by command of the aforesaid Roman king, peace was sworn among the princes and nobles of Saxony. Duke Henry of the castle of Harlingeberch [Note: Herlingsberg near Goslar.] inflicted various harms on all his neighbors. Therefore the said princes—including the bishop—and the nobles of Saxony rose against that duke, as a general violator of the peace, at the king’s command, and besieged Castle Harlingeberch.

When the same duke hastened to relieve the castle, he was defeated in a great battle with the princes and nobles, and Castle Harlingeberch was captured.

Through this capture the bishop recovered by occupation the jurisdiction at Bocla [Note: Buchloden.], which Duke Albert and his son Henry had long unjustly retained (in the year 1291). In his presence, as the secular judge of that place, he had the castle publicly proscribed and, after judgment had been delivered, caused it to be utterly demolished.

As time passed, he built Castle Levenborch [Note: Liebenburg.] at a site not far away, at great expense. Through it he recalled to the church many properties and rights that had been taken away and alienated.

Dukes Henry and Albert, grieved both by the construction of the castle and by the recovery of the church’s rights and properties, besieged Castle Levenborch with a large army while it was still a new foundation. But when they saw the bishop preparing himself courageously to repel them, and recognized his greatness of spirit and steadfastness in his holy purpose, they withdrew, leaving behind in the field the siege engines and other weapons that they had brought to storm the castle.

In the same year, however, those dukes gathered a large army, erected a castle highly prejudicial to the church above the river Fusenna [Note: Fuse.] near the castle of Olesborch, and, giving it the name Lowendal, occupied it.

To prevent them from having free and frequent access from that castle for attacking the church, the bishop erected another castle, named Papenborch, at a place little more than a bowshot away, and supplied it with many armed men. Through this castle, those holding Lowendal were so hemmed in and constrained that those who had previously besieged others were themselves besieged: from besiegers they became the besieged.

At last, when those in Castle Lowendal began to run short of supplies, while those in Castle Papenborch prospered, Lowendal was captured, and both castles were utterly demolished.

What more need be said? The illustrious Otto, duke of Lüneburg, built Castle Calenborch [Note: Calenberg.] on the river Leine. Because this threatened the church with the greatest harm, the bishop could neither tolerate nor willingly endure it; he rose against the duke and attacked him by every means available.

Duke Otto, having conspired against the church with Dukes Henry and Albert of Brunswick, and being supported by Margraves Otto and Hermann of Brandenburg and several other princes and nobles, gathered a large army and invaded the church’s territory. They captured two stone towers, Stederdorp and Oberge, which were the residences of certain knights faithful to the church, fortified them strongly, and from these and their other fortifications attacked the land and the church with the utmost severity.

The bishop, however, great-hearted in adversity, unaccustomed to despair or to be cast down, but trusting in the Lord his God, hired innumerable men-at-arms and mercenaries and repelled force with force, sometimes with restraint and sometimes without restraint.

During that same war he captured and destroyed certain fortifications of the dukes, namely Uslere, Everborch, Geveldehusen, and Echte [Note: Uslar, Gieboldehausen, Echte; Everburg is unknown.]. In many conflicts, by the grant of the Lord God, from whom all victory comes, he triumphed. In this same war he gained so much that he paid many debts by which he had previously been bound.

At last, after Castle Oberge and Stedemdorp had first been destroyed, a settlement was arranged between the bishop on one side and Dukes Otto of Lüneburg and Albert of Brunswick on the other, with Duke Henry excluded.

When Duke Otto included Castle Calemberch in the *sona* [Note: That is, in the reconciliation.], the bishop excluded from that same reconciliation the bridge before the castle over the river Leine.

Duke Henry, however, continuing to attack the church, built a castle called Mosborch within the bounds of the county jurisdiction of Bocla. The bishop and others, who regarded such a construction as improper, immediately surrounded it and utterly destroyed it.

Although that duke nevertheless persisted in persecuting the church, and the noble men, the counts of Werdere and Sladen, supported him, the bishop besieged Castle Werdere [Note: In the district of Ambergau.] for some time, captured it, and destroyed it.

Castle Walmoden, to restrain the attacks launched by the aforementioned Duke Henry from Castle Luttere, was purchased for the church for 950 marks of pure silver. Castle Sladem was heavily besieged.

At last, after a settlement had been arranged between the duke and the bishop, the bishop no longer endured severe attacks and wars; rather, he enjoyed a measure of peace, though only for a short time before the end of his life.

During the events described above, he also built Castle Rutam [Note: Ruthe.] at the place where the Leine and the Indistria meet, at great expense. Because of it he suffered severe attacks and wars from Otto, duke of Lüneburg, for a long time.

After peace had been made between them (in the year 1283, December 16), the bishop obtained in legal proceedings that the duke grant to him and to the church ownership of Castle Lowenrode and the town of Hanover. The same duke, however, received these from the bishop as a fief, giving only one hundred marks in return. [Col. 1269D] This was done for the bishop and the church as compensation for Castle Huden, which the aforesaid duke had destroyed.

He also freed a certain part of Castle Popenborch from the claim of Count Gerard of Scowenborch by paying money. He purchased Castle Herste [Note: Harste.] near Göttingen, which was later captured by treachery and destroyed.

He also purchased Castle Westerhove [Note: Westerhof.], highly useful to our church, together with its county jurisdiction, for 1,020 marks of pure silver, for himself and his successors. He freed the advocacy in the city from Ludolf the chamberlain. He acquired the advocacy at Hasikenhusen [Note: Compare Lüntzel, cited work, p. 240.] from Lippold of Dalem, a knight.

He improved the episcopal palace with many buildings and constructed a chapel there anew. In it he instituted four canons, for whom he ordained that forty pounds of Hildesheim denarii be provided annually from the offerings and revenues of the church of Saint Andrew; and that twelve pounds be given to the provost of that church, or to the city archdeacon.

He also added three hides at Reden, which had fallen vacant to him, for the aforesaid canons.

During his final days, when he was enjoying a certain degree of peace, as stated above, he purchased Castle Hundestruge and the town of Dasle [Note: Hunnesrück and Dassel in the Solling forest.], together with the adjoining county jurisdiction, for 1,900 marks, by right of purchase, leaving them for the most part to be paid off by his successors (in the year 1310).

Although the said bishop was surrounded for almost the entire time in which he governed our church by the harsh persecutions of powerful princes and others, and was occupied by the tumults of serious wars, and afflicted by the tribulation and sorrow of evils, nevertheless he did not neglect to look after the welfare of our church in spiritual as well as temporal matters. Rather, in both respects, so to speak, he exalted it amid pressures and enlarged it amid straits.

And, so that what has been said above about temporal matters may suffice, in spiritual matters he was as follows.

Although he was occupied with temporal affairs and did not fear the authority of adversaries and princes, he loved Christ the King with all his inmost being. For he gladly listened to the divine office, having Mass sung before him every day according to the chant, unless some great necessity prevented him. Whenever a feast with nine lessons was celebrated, he not only had Mass sung but also the offices of matins and vespers, with his clerics, according to the tones, with pauses and great attentiveness.

On the greater feasts, at the ordinations of clerics, at the veiling of holy virgins, and at other pontifical offices, when he himself celebrated the solemn rites of Mass, the Lord granted him such strength and devotion that he burst into tears and moistened his face with a rain of tears. He was so devoted that he could scarcely say or utter what had to be sung or spoken; rather, he had to interrupt his words with sobs [Note: *Prorumpere* corrected to *interrumpere* in witness c.].

He also diligently exercised for many years the office of sacred visitation, which had been neglected by his predecessors, uprooting and dispersing harmful things, building and planting what was beneficial, correcting and reforming, both in head and in members, whatever he knew required the discipline of correction and reform. He did not seek what was his own, but what belonged to the Lord Jesus Christ, and above all showed in his own person, through life and conduct, word likewise [Note: Added.], and example, how subordinates ought laudably to conduct themselves in the house of the Lord.

This glorious bishop accomplished many other things belonging to contemplation and active life, but they are not written in this book, lest they cause weariness to its readers or hearers. These matters have been written so that it may be known that he was powerful in every respect and renowned for many virtues.

He governed our church for thirty years and ten months [Note: Added.]. For in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1310, in the thirty-first year of his pontificate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, he paid the debt of the flesh and departed to the Lord [Note: Buried in the middle of the church beneath the crown. Witness 2.], leaving the church improved in honor and power, but, to speak truthfully, weighed down by many burdens of debt.

### HENRY, the 33rd

[Note: The heading is missing, as it is in all those that follow.]

He was succeeded by the venerable man Henry, dean of our church, descended from the illustrious line of the counts of Woldenberg [Note: Because he was a gentle man, some called him Aleke. Witness 2.].

From the most serene Henry of Lützelburg, then Roman king and afterward emperor, he obtained that Castle Hundesruge and the town of Dasle, together with the adjoining county jurisdiction, should be perpetually united to our church, and that he and his successors should receive them as a fief among the other regalia that our church holds from the Empire (in the year 1310, September 6).

As time passed, he paid for this castle, town, and county jurisdiction, since they had not yet been paid for by his predecessor, who had purchased them.

At the beginning of his promotion, he found the burgesses and citizens of our city in such a great and stubborn rebellion that they refused to render him the homage of fidelity. They had seized properties in the city of Hildesheim that had become vacant through the resignation of his vassals, and had resisted him in many other matters concerning the liberty of our church. He restrained them with appropriate moderation.

After gathering a large army and besieging the city, he built Castle Sturewold [Note: Steverwald.] [Note: He also called it Alekenburg. Witness 2.], and so constricted them by withdrawing the use of mills and pastures that within a few days they reached an agreement with him, surrendered to him, rendered the homage of fidelity, and left secure the liberties of the church that they had invaded.

Among the articles of this settlement it was expressly stipulated that the gate behind the city, through which one goes to Saint Paul’s, having been continuously closed for many years, would henceforth remain open.

To cut off every future cause of dissension between the clergy on one side and the burgesses on the other, and to block, as far as possible, the path to the expense of litigation, it was established by perpetual statute and privilege that, if any dispute should arise between the clergy and the burgesses concerning the liberties or immunities of the church or any other matter, whatever the canons of our church wished to affirm under oath as just would remain permanently secure to them, without anyone’s contradiction.

Every year, when new consuls have been appointed, those same consuls, when summoned by the bishop or chapter, will come into their presence and, touching the relics of the saints, swear that they will faithfully hold and guard all the city gates, and that they will open especially the gates of Saint Pantaleon and the gate behind the city for the bishop or chapter, day or night, whenever they have need.

Also every year, on the Monday at the beginning of Advent [Note: “Of the fast,” written by a later hand.], the said consuls will swear in the general chapter that they will faithfully defend, insofar as they can, all the liberties and immunities of the church.

When these matters had been settled, he powerfully besieged Castle Hoinboke [Note: Hohenbüchen.] together with the lord of Homborch, with the assistance, to some extent, of certain other princes. He captured it after the siege and caused it to be utterly demolished.

He purchased the town of Bockenem for the church for 1,100 marks (in the year 1314, March 8).

He had serious wars with the illustrious Otto, duke of Lüneburg, who had held the town of Hanover and Castle Lowenrode, together with certain counties and other properties, from the church as a fief and whom he arranged to receive them from himself. He fought several battles, being defeated in some and victorious in many.

At last, after a settlement had been made, the same duke received the aforesaid properties as a fief from the bishop and acknowledged himself a vassal of the church.

The same bishop greatly restrained the abyss of usury, which devours souls and drains resources and had become deeply rooted among the citizens of Hildesheim.

He led a chaste life and performed the pontifical office devoutly and with great diligence, like a good, simple, and upright man, departing from evil and possessing zeal for God and his neighbor [Note: The word was added by a more recent hand.].

But in his final days, his rivals arranged for an apostolic mandate, burdensome to him and intolerable to his subjects, to be directed against him—not out of love of justice, but as fuel for hatred and out of the spite of vengeance.

Therefore, foreseeing such great evil, he arose like the good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep, and went to the Apostolic See to lay before the supreme pontiff the fraud and deceit involved.

There, while pursuing his right, he was struck by fever and died for his flock. He was honorably buried in the monastery of Saint Clare at Avignon in the year of the Lord 1318, on the third day before the Ides of July, in the ninth year of his pontificate [Note: Here a different hand of the fourteenth century begins.].

On his anniversary, from the tithe at Solide, each brother present will receive seven denarii and half a *stoup* of wine; the vicar, four denarii and a quarter of wine; likewise the master of the school, the subcustodian, and the succentor; a candle of one pound of wax; for the scholars, five solidi; and for the chamberlains and bell-ringers, three solidi [Note: Again, a different hand of the fifteenth century begins.].

### OTTO, the 34th
To the venerable father, our lord Henry of Woldenberg, our bishop, who died happily at Avignon and about whom sufficient writing is found above, succeeded his uncle, our lord Otto of Woldenberg, provost of Saint Maurice’s Mount, unanimously elected as our bishop. At the beginning of his entry into office he had a conflict with certain oppressors of our land, namely those of Engelbostel and Münchhausen [Note: Engelbostel and Münchhausen], near the village of Oesselse [Note: Oesselse, in the district of Ruthe]. With God granting victory to our men, the enemies were overcome—some captured, some killed, and some put to flight [Col. 1273B]. From their captivity our lord bishop extorted a large sum of money, by which he and his people were enriched.

But he, like a faithful and good steward, converting the monies that came to him in this way to the benefit of our church, recovered and redeemed the castles and episcopal possessions that his predecessors had pawned or alienated. He bought the castle of Luttere, the office at Berka, and the advocacy at Calefeld [Note: Berka and Calefeld, in the principalities of Göttingen and Grubenhagen, in the diocese of Mainz] from the dukes of Brunswick for three thousand and sixty marks. He also paid in full the money still owing for which his predecessor, our lord Bishop Siegfried, had purchased the castle of Lindau [Note: Lindau] from the nobles of Plessen, and in that castle he built an impregnable palace with a high wall.

[Col. 1273C] He constructed the castle of Sturwold almost entirely with solemn and impregnable buildings, as is evident, apart from the old palace which his immediate predecessor and uncle, our lord Bishop Henry, had built, at great expense. He also arranged for many buildings in the other castles of our church that had fallen into ruin to be rebuilt—buildings that it would be difficult to describe individually.

While he was still provost of the Mount, for the praise and honor of almighty God and of his glorious mother, the virgin Mary, he established the singing in our church every year, by all the clergy, both religious and secular, of a certain Mass commonly called the Golden Mass, on the Saturday immediately following the festival of the Communes [Note: The Communes, “the holy common week” (*die heilige gemeinwoche*), were the days commemorating the Saxons’ victory over the Thuringians, celebrated in the week after Saint Michael’s Day; see Haltaus, *Jahrzeitbuch der Deutschen des Mittelalters*, 1797, pp. 142–143] (5 February 1315). For this purpose he assigned a large and suitable provision from the tithe at Zolde, to be distributed during the same Mass to those present [Col. 1273D].

He also ordered two torches to be lit and kept burning every year throughout Advent, out of reverence for the hymn [Note: That is, the hymn] *Veni Redemptor*, in our choir before the lectern at Compline; and he ordered that every schoolboy present at that Compline, even if he had come from elsewhere, should be given a loaf by our provost. Moreover, he established the feast of blessed Elizabeth, with solemn singing and celebrations, to be observed in our church as a double feast, and endowed it with revenues.

He arranged, with proper provision, for the anniversaries of our lords Bishops Siegfried and Henry, his predecessors, and his own anniversary to be celebrated solemnly every year in our church. He governed our church in complete and tranquil peace, so that he and all his subjects became greatly enriched [Col. 1274B]. Indeed, by God’s disposition and with the favor and friendship of the noble princes, Dukes Otto of Lüneburg and Otto of Brunswick, sons of peace and justice, the peasant women in many villages of his territory could be seen walking about in good garments and cloaks lined with vair.

When, therefore, all that the said lord Bishop Otto had laudably and successfully completed for the advantage and benefit of our church, like a good and faithful shepherd, he paid the debt owed by human condition in the sixteenth year of his ordination [Note: Concerning the year of his death, see *Beiträge*, vol. I, pp. 90–94, and the charters in Lüntzel, *Dioecesis Hildesiensis*, pp. 423–424] [22 August 1331], and rests in our church before the altar of All Saints [Note: He died in the year of Our Lord 1331, in the fifteenth year of his ordination. The numerals have been corrected]. May his memory and [Note: Thus in the correction] his blessing be eternal. Amen.

## HENRY, 35th

[Col. 1274C] He was succeeded [Note: An excerpt from the bishop’s oath is printed in *Deductio jurisdictionis meyerdingicae ecclesiae cathedralis Hildesheim*, by the provost and chapter of Hildesheim, 1758, folio, p. 70] [28 August] by the venerable father, our lord Henry, son of the illustrious [Note: That is, “and elegant,” in witness 2] Duke Albert [Note: That is, Albert of Göttingen] of Brunswick. At his election a detestable schism arose. For some of our lords adhered to his election, while others adhered to Lord Eric of Schauenburg, provided by the Apostolic See; the citizens of Hildesheim also supported Eric, partly because of the power of Lord Henry himself, and partly because of the debasement of our coin, which they had perhaps caused. Certain members of the Hildesheim council who favored the said Lord Henry had been expelled from the city.

Those who remained and gave assistance to the said Lord Eric invaded our diocese fiercely, with great wars. They captured the town of Dam, which adhered to Lord Henry, and destroyed it utterly, apparently with the cooperation of certain vassals of our church [Col. 1275A] [Note: In the year of Our Lord 1332, on Christmas night].

Lord Henry, wishing to divert the course of the Indistria from the episcopal mill, engaged in a conflict with the inhabitants of the city near the city; they prevailed, and some of his men, put to flight, fell. Some of these were killed, while others were taken captive. The said Lord Eric, wishing to enter the city with armed men, encountered many people from the city near the village of Hasede [Note: Hasede], who wished to introduce him. Lord Henry and his men attacked and defeated them, gaining the victory.

After this, truces were made for ten years (1333). When they expired, a greater war arose than before and lasted almost three years. During it, many castles and episcopal possessions of our church, as well as possessions of certain monasteries [Col. 1275B] and collegiate churches, were pawned, and some were completely alienated.

When Lord Henry was failing and almost despairing in this war, almighty God, through the merits of the glorious virgin Mary, his mother, in whom Henry had placed full and firm confidence, granted him victory over his enemies in the meadow between Sturwold and the city. Many of the enemy were drowned and very many were carried away captive. By this victory he was so enriched, and his adversaries so thoroughly subdued—even though Lord Eric himself had meanwhile died—that from then onward he prospered in all his undertakings. The citizens, seeing themselves weakened, submitted to the grace of the said Lord Henry, so that they were reconciled and made peace with one another in friendship (1346).

As compensation for this dispute, the said citizens paid twelve talents of Hildesheim pennies every week toward the payment of masons, carpenters, and other laborers engaged in building the castle of Marienburg, which Lord Henry then erected and constructed, until the castle was completed [Col. 1275C] [Note: Even today, the *vronetynf* belonging to that castle is paid from each house, except for certain feudal possessions held by the lords bishops, the monastery of Saint Michael, and a few vassals. The reason for compelling them to build the aforesaid castle was this: the bishop defeated them near the mill called “the mill” (*de Lamolen*) in the city meadow, where many were captured and drowned. Added by a second hand].

Afterward, with the Lord God’s help, the said Lord Henry returned to the bosom of mother Church. He had been bound by sentences of excommunication imposed by the apostolic lords Clement and Innocent because he had opposed the provision made by the Apostolic See for the said Lord Eric. Innocent absolved him [Note: In the year of Our Lord 1347, added by a second hand], and Henry was again provided to our church (1353).

Thus reconciled, with the aforesaid wars and tribulations ending and tranquil peace following, he recovered, to the best of his ability, the pawned castles of the church and the goods of the episcopal table. He purchased the castles of Woldenstein, Schladen, and Wiedelah [Note: Wiedelah] for a large sum of money for our church. He constructed the castle of Marienburg anew; he bought Woldenstein from the noble Siegfried of Homburg, Schladen from Meynekone, count there (1342), and Wiedelah from the men of Gowisch; and he ordered those castles repaired wherever they had fallen into ruin (1341).

He solemnly established the feast of the glorious Body of Christ in our church and in the other collegiate churches, together with the annual celebration of his anniversary. He also left his successors ten castles that were not pawned but free and unencumbered, namely Sturwold, Marienburg, Ruthe, Peine, Lebenburg, Schladen, Wiedelah, Luttere, Woldenstein, and Winzenburg [Note: Winzenburg, correction], along with many possessions of the episcopal table. He also destroyed the castles of Grensleben and Hildeshausen in the county of Dassel.

He governed our church for thirty-two and a half years [Note: He died in the year of Our Lord 1362, correction]. He was buried before the altar of blessed Katherine the virgin (6 February 1362). May his soul rest in everlasting peace. Amen.

## JOHN SCHADELANT, 36th

After the death of Lord Henry of Brunswick, the pope provided the bishopric of Hildesheim to a certain venerable and good man of the Order of Preachers, a doctor of sacred theology, whom people commonly called Bishop John Schadelant. At the beginning of his entry into office he asked for the theological and legal books of his predecessors. Then the officials of the court showed him coats of mail, shields, and helmets, saying that such had been the books of his predecessors. Because the customs of the country did not suit him, he therefore resigned the bishopric into the hands of the lord pope, from whom he had received it [Col. 1276C] (1364), and perhaps remained in the bishopric for two years [Note: Buried at Mainz among the Preachers, correction].

## GHERARDUS, 37th

After him, the venerable father, our lord Gherardus, of the family of the barons of Monte near Minden, then bishop of Verden and formerly cantor and later dean of our church, was transferred to the church of Hildesheim by Pope Urban V. He was an eloquent, prudent, and magnanimous man.

In the first year of his entry into office he captured sixty armed Westphalian raiders who were attacking the town of Eltze. But, considering that he might not be able to keep them without compromising his honor, he released them all, free and unharmed.

Then, in his third year [Note: That is, 1367, added by a second hand], around the feast of the Nativity of Mary (1367), when our bishopric was being invaded hostilely by Duke Magnus of Brunswick and the Bishop of Halberstadt, with the assistance of the Bishop of Magdeburg, Bishop Kogelwyt, as well as men from Anhalt and Hadmersleben, together with many other barons [Note: That is, barons] and a very large multitude of armed men, Lord Gherardus, bishop, met them near the village of Farmsen [Note: Farmsen, east of the city; the Chronicle of Saint Giles and Botho write “Gheimessem” and “Dinklar”]. After a very long battle had been fought, with God and his mother assisting, our men won a glorious victory. Very many of the enemy were killed [Note: “And,” added by a corrector], and the aforesaid duke and the Bishop of Halberstadt, Albert, were captured with a great multitude of their men.

Our lord bishop could have extorted a very large sum of money from them, but, fearing the tyranny of the Archbishop of Magdeburg, who at that time enjoyed great authority with Emperor Charles IV, and also fearing the power of the younger Duke Magnus, who had then been elevated to the duchies of Brunswick and Lüneburg, he accepted from the aforesaid captives only thirteen thousand marks of silver, and that solely as a gesture of friendship [Note: With this money he built, endowed, and founded the Charterhouse near Hildesheim].

After this, discord arose between our lord bishop and, on the other side, Dukes Otto [Note: Of Salzderhelden] and Albert [Note: Of Göttingen] of Brunswick. Certain vassals and ministerials of the church of Hildesheim rebelled against our bishop and went over to the said dukes. Lord Bishop Gherardus besieged them powerfully in the castle of Walmoden (1368). By a remarkable feat of engineering, he caused the castle to be flooded and completely destroyed by diverting a watercourse and carrying an embankment to it, as the present appearance demonstrates.

Yet, with an unfavorable outcome, while these disputes were continuing, the aforesaid dukes captured Alfeld, a town of our church, plundered it, and erected a new castle there (1370). But the Lord God and his pious mother [Col. 1277C], not forgetting their mercy and not wholly abandoning our church, afterward poured out some consolation by arranging that the officials of our lord bishop, having attacked the enemy near the castle of Woldenstein, captured twenty-four prominent armed men from the retinue of the said dukes; Duke Otto himself barely escaped by flight.

From then on, after legal proceedings had intervened, truces were made. Finally, Alfeld and its new castle were restored to us, and the dukes’ captives were released.

Throughout his entire tenure, the same lord bishop suffered many and various adversities—plunder, burnings, and rebellions by his subjects—from all the surrounding dukes, nobles, and oppressors who attacked him. Nevertheless, with the help of God and his mother Mary [Col. 1277D], in whom he placed complete confidence, he prevailed laudably in every matter.

He besieged the castle of Calenberg and diverted the river Leine, though with great labor and expense, as is evident. He acquired the castle of Coldingen for our church [Note: Pawned by Duke Magnus] and retained it through many expenditures in wars and labors. He bought the castle of Vienenburg from Count Conrad of Wernigerode for a large sum of money. He captured the castle of Blankenburg with the assistance of Count Dietrich of Wernigerode; nevertheless, after receiving a certain sum of money in a legal settlement, he restored it to Count Burchard of Regenstein [Note: Thus in the correction]. He began constructing the castle of Steinbrück.

At the saltworks of Salzgitter [Note: Salzgitter] he bought certain revenues called *bokpennige* from the men of Kniestedt. He purchased the village of Misburg [Note: Misburg near Hanover] and the adjoining forest from the men of Roden for a fixed sum of money, namely seven hundred marks [Note: Seven hundred, correction]. He arranged for a stone house or palace to be built at Poppenburg. He gave more than one hundred marks for new organs to adorn our church. He purchased the village of Peine near Kirchwehren for one hundred marks. Moreover, he gave our church a chalice adorned with pure gold and precious gems. He solemnly established his anniversary to be celebrated in our church. He arranged for the episcopal hall, almost ruined and consumed by age, to be rebuilt. He founded the Carthusian cloister with the assistance of good men and endowed it with revenues.

He governed our church for thirty-three years. He was very approachable and kind to his subjects, especially to the clergy; he was sufficiently learned and therefore a patron of clerics. He also composed and dictated many prayers and writings, both in prose and in verse.

When he had reached decrepit old age, his subjects, and especially the vassals of the church, stirred up serious tumults and wars among themselves. In these conflicts our church was placed in the greatest danger and suffered severe oppression and injuries. Since the bishop, weakened by old age and unable to restrain their rebellion, could not cope with them, the following arrangement was made: Lord John, son of the Count of Hoya, then bishop or elected bishop of Paderborn, was appointed coadjutor to the Bishop of Hildesheim. He curbed the previously existing insolence, at least to some extent.

After John had been transferred to the bishopric of Hildesheim, Lord Gherardus survived only a short time [Note: He therefore died in the year of Our Lord 1398, correction]. He died on 15 November 1398 and was buried among the Hildesheim Carthusians. May he rest happily in Christ. Amen, and so forth.

## JOHN, 38th

The aforementioned John, having been promoted to the bishopric of Hildesheim [Col. 1278D], accomplished several things with considerable vigor at the beginning of his tenure. He restrained and suppressed Duke Frederick of Brunswick, who was oppressing the land of Hildesheim. He also stormed and utterly destroyed the castle of Vreden [Note: On the Leine, not far from Gandersheim], which was highly prejudicial to the church of Hildesheim, with the cooperation of Duke Henry [Col. 1279A]. In this way he governed the church of Hildesheim for about twenty years, according to his ability, in a reasonably suitable and peaceful condition.

Meanwhile, however, it happened that the venerable Lord Eghard of Hanenzee, provost of the church of Hildesheim, a man of great learning and industry, was violently dragged and carried away from the city’s immunity, as though he had violated the peace of the land, then commonly called the *Landfrieden*. He was imprisoned in the tower of Sturwold and held there for almost two years, finally meeting his death there.

When a rumor arose that he had been killed in that same tower, the aforesaid lord bishop made a public protest before the assembled clergy and people of the city of Hildesheim and before his vassals (1405), declaring that he was innocent and free from responsibility for the killing or death of the said provost, and offering to clear himself publicly before everyone. But after a discussion among those who were present at the time, the oath was remitted to the lord bishop.

Nevertheless, to speak with complete frankness, the same lord bishop allowed the reins of extravagance and association with women to slacken beyond measure and more than was fitting. Consequently, all the castles and possessions of the church, as well as the goods belonging to the episcopal table, were left by him either pawned or alienated. And because, as became evident, he conducted himself too much like a layman, many excesses and improprieties followed. For these reasons, and also for many others, as the almighty God is reasonably to be feared, he afflicted us, our entire land, and our people most severely with repeated scourges [Note: “Scourges,” correction].

In particular, during the final period of his life—namely, five years before the death of the said bishop—an intolerable storm of wars and battles rose against us. The Archbishop of Cologne, the Archbishop of Magdeburg, the Bishop of Halberstadt, all the dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg, and the Duke of Schleswig [Note: “Of Schleswig,” correction], together with very many counts and barons from many lands and all their cities and vassals, formed a fierce alliance against the bishopric of Hildesheim alone, as though they intended to destroy it completely. They ravaged it on every side with plundering, burnings, killings, captures, devastation, and the burning of churches [Col. 1280A], in the most hostile manner.

These wars and enmities lasted for nearly three continuous years. During them our men also suffered disastrous defeats in two battles, one near Osterwieck and the other near Grone [Note: 1421, Chronicle of Saint Giles; 1422, Botho]. In the latter, alas, the lord son of the Duke of Saxony, our fellow canon and provost of Saint Maurice’s Mount, was killed (1421).

It is not easy to describe the nature and extent of the losses that the church and our entire land suffered as a result. The present burdens of debt and other certain indications clearly reveal them. Thus it happened that the aforesaid lord bishop, overwhelmed by both old age and poverty [Note: “Poverty more than old age,” added by a second hand], accepted as his coadjutor Lord Magnus, son of the illustrious Duke of Saxony [Note: A word omitted in witness c.], then Bishop of Kammin [Col. 1280B]. With the consent and unanimous election of the chapter of Hildesheim, as well as the acquiescence of the clergy, the vassals, and all concerned, he obtained from Pope Martin V that Magnus be substituted for him as bishop of Hildesheim.

When Lord Magnus was promoted to be our bishop, the entire clergy and people rejoiced. After a short interval, Bishop John died and was buried in the middle of our church [Note: In the year of Our Lord 1424]. He governed our church for twenty-five years, more or less, and left it burdened with enormous debts and stripped of all its possessions. He left his successor no place at all free, and no revenues—or only very few—on which to rely. May almighty God pardon him for all these things [Col. 1280C].

## MAGNUS, 39th

When the same Lord Magnus found the bishopric of Hildesheim in such extreme poverty, he brought as much as he could from his own funds, by means of which he has lived and persevered to this day. The same Lord Magnus received the castle of Greene [Note: Not far from Gandersheim], with its appurtenances, into his possession from the Duchess of Brunswick.

He also purchased the stronghold of Dachtmissen [Note: Near Burgdorf] from Ludolf of Esscharte. Soon afterward he restored it to Duke Otto of Lüneburg under certain agreements, in exchange for the acquisition and purchase of several castles in the lordship of Homburg. For these he also paid the same Duke Otto a large sum of money, namely more than ten thousand Rhenish gold florins in ready cash [Col. 1280D].

## SUPPLEMENT IN MANUSCRIPT 2

[Col. 1279]

[Col. 1279D] Lord Magnus governed temporal affairs quite laudably and bought many castles under contracts of redemption. He died in the year of Our Lord 1452, on 21 September, and was buried in the middle of the church.

It also happened [Note: Another hand begins] that Lord Magnus, weighed down by old age, chose as his son the illustrious prince Lord Bernard, Duke of Brunswick, who governed as administrator for seven years.

Afterward [Note: Another hand] Ernest, Count of Schaumburg [Note: Schaumburg], was elected in 1458. Once confirmed, he governed for thirteen years [Col. 1281A]. He was a kind and approachable man, but alas, he was not devoted to spiritual matters. It was also said that he died dangerously without the sacraments [Note: “And it is true,” in another ink in the margin]. In other respects he governed well. He died in the year of Our Lord 1471, on 22 July, and was buried near the treasury of our church.

In the year of Our Lord 1468 there was a war between Duke William and his sons Frederick and William on one side, and the cities commonly called the Hanseatic cities on the other; both sides inflicted many losses upon one another. But from the year of Our Lord 1471 there was a particularly serious war between the aforesaid dukes of Brunswick and Ernest, Bishop of Hildesheim, and it was reported that the same bishop died at that time from excessive grief [Col. 1282A].

In the following year, namely 1472, a grave dispute arose between the city of Hildesheim and Bishop Henning on one side, and the vassals of the diocese, certain canons, and the towns of the land on the other. They refused to receive the same Lord Henning as bishop. God knows how it will end, but already many villages have been laid waste, alas! [Note: In another ink.]

In the same year a comet was seen. Erfurt was largely consumed by fire: the Merchants’ Bridge, almost all the houses of the priests, and the principal churches—namely, those of the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint Severus—together with twelve other churches.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1038: CATWALLONUS, ABBOT OF REDON

[Col. 1281]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING CATWALLONUS

(*Mabillon, Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, book LV, p. 321)

At about the same time (1026), the noble Breton Simon, son of Bernard, from whom Roca-Bernardi received its name and who was lord of that place, built the monastery of Saint Gildas in the Forest, in a place in the county of Nantes then called Lampidric. There he appointed Helgot, a holy man and monk of Redon, as abbot.

At that time Abbot Catwallonus presided over the monastery of Saint Savior at Redon. He is praised in the writings of the aforementioned Simon for the construction of the monastery; in those writings the chronological indications are inconsistent, since the monastery is said to have been founded in the year when Henry was ruling the kingdom of France.

But it is certain from other evidence that Catwallonus was abbot of the monastery of Redon at precisely this time. He had succeeded Mainard, a man of exceptional holiness, who obtained Belle-Île, commonly called Guedel, from Geoffrey, duke of Brittany. At Geoffrey’s command, Catwallonus—said to have been Geoffrey’s own brother, and himself a man of great religious devotion—introduced a community of monks onto Belle-Île.

After Mainard’s death, Catwallonus was recalled to govern the monastery of Redon and undertook to restore it, since it was nearly ruined. We possess testimony to this in a letter of Catwallonus himself, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Sergius at Angers, written to Hildegard, duchess of Angers and wife of Fulk Nerra, at the time when her husband was waging war against Alan, duke of Brittany. We present this letter below.

The same Catwallonus also wrote another letter to a certain abbess whose name began with the letter L. I believe her to have been Letgard, abbess of Saint Mary of Charity at Angers.

The same abbot is said to have met a certain worthy but rustic man named Gurkius, a Norman by birth, who lived on the island of Saint Gudwalus, and to have urged him to grant the aforesaid island to Saint Savior. But, being as savage as he was, and accustomed to dress in white woolen garments, he rebuked the petitioner harshly and drove him away. At last, however, he was softened and surrendered himself and all that he possessed to the Savior.

## LETTER OF CATWALLONUS TO HILDEGARD, DUCHESS OF ANGERS, WIFE OF FULK NERRA

(*Mabillon, Annales Benedictini*, IV, 321)

[Col. 1281B] Abbot Catwallonus of the monastery of Redon, with the flock entrusted to him, sends the gift of salutary prayers to Hildegard, queen of Angers.

We give thanks that you have not disdained to visit our humility through frequent messengers and letters, asking us to remember you in our prayers. Therefore, if you trust that God may in some measure be moved to mercy toward you through us, know that, although we are sinners and insufficient for ourselves, we remember you every day before the Lord.

For a long time it has not been unknown to us how sincerely you offer the worship of religion to God and service to God’s servants. Even if rumor concealed this in silence, the clarity of your works would not be silent. We urge you above all to strive to advance more ardently in goodness.

Since, therefore, we intend, if the Divinity consents, to restore our monastery next March, which through its age is almost on the verge of ruin, we are sending you this brother to purchase wine from the vineyards granted by God’s munificence. We are concerned, not without reason, that because of the discord being waged between your lord and the prince of Brittany, someone may obstruct him or cause him to suffer harm.

We therefore entrust him to your protection and ask that, for the honor of the Savior whom we serve, you not neglect to assist him in whatever matter may require your help. We also ask that you allow him to depart free from tolls at every place and port subject to your authority, as we trust in you. Farewell.

## LETTER OF CATWALLONUS TO LETGARD, ABBESS OF SAINT MARY OF CHARITY

Catwallonus gives thanks for the letters sent to him by the same abbess, who had asked him for the assistance of his prayers.

(*Mabillon, Annales Benedictini*, IV, Appendix, p. 732, from the manuscript of Saint Sergius at Angers)

[Col. 1283B] To the most reverend mother L. . . . , Catwallonus, the least of abbots, sends the prize of eternity.

I received the letters of your devotion with the greatest gratitude, and I give many thanks for the gift you offered. Yet I cannot cease to wonder that it occurred to your mind to drink muddy water while abandoning a clear spring—that is, neglecting the Fathers, who are twice as good as I am—to ask from me, in greater confidence, the absolution of your sin.

Therefore I fear, and in my narrowness I fear even more, lest what is a remedy for you become shipwreck for me, since from childhood I have covered myself with such stains of crime that I surpass the drops of the sea and the grains of sand, and in my miserable wickedness the bright stars of heaven. For that reason I am unfit to be of use to your prayers.

But because you ask a dusty little man to pray to God—and this is urged by that very thing which is God, namely charity—and because we are admonished by the apostolic oracle that we should mutually bear one another’s burdens, I implore the undivided essence of the Trinity that, once the tumult of sins has been calmed in you from heaven, you may receive what Mary of the Gospel received, and hear what she heard in the sweetest voice of God.

“O little woman,” he said, “fervent in love, accept this as your reward: because you trust in me, the physician, forgiveness of sins shall immediately be granted to you!”

So that our prayer may obtain this more easily, I shall arrange for the solemn sacrifice to be offered three times in both communities of the brothers: those who live on the Island and those in the monastery called Redon.

Above all, I urge you to strive to be a model worthy of imitation by those subject to you. If you have been so until now, be so henceforth with greater attention; indeed, I say, with greater fervor. Farewell, and do not forget me in your prayers.

## BEFORE THE YEAR 1040: FROUMUNDUS, MONK OF TEGERNSEE

[Col. 1283]

## LETTERS OF FROUMUNDUS

(Edited by R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus*, V, I, 158, from the Tegernsee autograph)

### I. To Gozpert, abbot of Tegernsee

He writes that he had not foreseen his departure from the monastery of Saint Magnus and asks for parchment on which to write.

[Col. 1283C]

To G., filled to fullness by heavenly favor with the dignity of merits, F. sends the most devoted pledge of due submission [Col. 1284C].

I testify before God that my departure from the monastery of Saint Magnus and my sudden separation from your brotherhood were not foreseen by me. I would never have wished to act so inhumanely as to leave without your knowledge. Although at times I was absent from you in bodily space and separated from you in physical conversation, I was never separated from you in the love of my mind, after I had first begun ardently to cling to you through the bond of charity.

I humbly ask your piety to remember me in your prayer in the holy place, for the abolition of my offenses. For when do we forget you, and when do we fail to remember ourselves? May both possibilities be absent.

But because we do not wish to be deprived, if you deem us worthy, of your spiritual consolation, we ask that some parchment be given to us for the benefit of our spiritual and temporal exercise. For, as you know, I gladly devote myself at times to the study of writing. But now, since my parchment has run out, I have no means of writing unless your hand supplies it through generosity. Farewell.

### II. To the same

He swears that he did not take away a certain book.

To his elder G., worthy of all veneration, F., Cucullio in name alone.

Until now, my elder, I was exceedingly confident in my heart of the security of your favor. But now everything is otherwise because of my sins. I am very sad about the theft of the book mentioned above as belonging to you. But I wish to clear myself of such a crime, in whatever way pleases your fatherly authority.

What more is there to say? I declare with my own mouth and, secure in conscience, subscribe with my own hand, saying: If I, F., stole that book of yours, M., which you mention, or received it from someone who had stolen it, or possess it in any way, or know where it is or who possesses it, may the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—which I receive frequently, though unworthy—become for me condemnation and not redemption.

### III. To Ruotker, abbot of Würzburg

He defends himself against his sharper letter.

To Abbot R., most learned among doctors, from humble F., endowed with no merit.

The letter headed with your name had greatly saddened our hearts. At first sight it had seemed to present itself as though it had been composed by the wit of your dictation. But when I reread it with a restored and attentive mind, I remembered that you had never composed any words in such an uncultivated [Col. 1285D] style. For the indecorous writing raged into such insults that it was not content merely to tear me apart, but even flared up in anger against our senior. If I did not fear honoring Ruotker’s person, perhaps I would use words so foul and shameful that no worse insults would remain.

You rebuked me for neglecting a caution of which I knew nothing; I neither committed it with my own hand nor ever received it from those who brought it. They brought a certain Hezilin, utterly unknown to me—just as I had never seen him—asking, I do not know what, on behalf of some mixed herd. After I had removed this matter through a spirit of single combat, I had possessed it in no way. With an uneven arrangement of numbers he also asserts that I detest study, the best part of a human being, although all wise men know that the greater part of a human being is the soul [Col. 1286A], and reason seems to be occupied wholly in study. Finally, an appended gloss claimed that by the discoloration of the sun I would attain grace, whereas the truthful orthodox judgment testifies that the sun’s discoloration signifies the heat of persecution.

But if I provoked so great a fury that, in the manner of irritated men, your speech or dictation suffered an eclipse, forgive such an offense, venerable abbot. If the childish mind of any other of your people has flared up in this way [cod., “had flared up”], we leave the matter to your judgment.

### IV. Letter of the monk Reginbald, perhaps of Saint Emmeram, to Froumund, in which he returns Persius and gives thanks for various kindnesses

[Col. 1286B]

To his kinsman F., of exceptional affection, REGINBALDUS, in most faithful service to you both.

We ask you not to take offense that we have most recently failed to return your little book to you. For when we received your welcome message, our messenger departed without our knowledge, before we could send you through our little literary compositions whatever private matters were necessary for us and for you. Since we endured this with great displeasure, through this messenger, more faithful both to us and to you, we have sent you the aforesaid codex, returning worthy thanks because you were willing to lend it to us for so long. But through the same bearer of this note we ask that our book entitled *Persius* be sent back to us.

Moreover, since at that time we had no opportunity to give thanks for your gift of parchment [Col. 1286C], we offer you the greatest thanks. For the promise and consolation concerning our journey that you yourself gave us, it is not within our power to reward you with the gratitude you have deserved and, with God’s permission, will deserve. We earnestly desire that rewards worthy of eternal recompense may be rendered to you. Farewell.

### V. The same to the same. He asks him to indicate what he wants concerning a certain journey. He requests parchment, etc.

To F., the dearest of his friends, REGINBALDUS, liable to the spittle of all, offering whatever more festive greeting can be devised.

Although, my dear, I often sigh, greatly troubled by your absence [Col. 1286D], nevertheless, if matters are going prosperously for you, the mist of sorrow is wiped from my heart and my heart smiles. But concerning those matters of which our last little conversation was concerned, when you departed from me—fixing their memory mentally in my heart—tell me whether you wish to undertake that journey with me; or, if this cannot be done, what and how much you are able to do for me as I proceed, by means of the little composition of a letter, as you said.

Moreover, however much parchment you may have for copying the little books that you know are suited to me, nevertheless, if you have no further need of those seven skins found there, send them to me. Greet on my behalf your senior who is staying with you in every respect, and both of you, as far as you are able, be diligent in satisfying our senior in the little task entrusted to you [Col. 1287A], since he has very great confidence in your fidelity. Farewell.

### VI. The same to the same and to others. Why he has not visited them; concerning certain little books, etc.

To his lords and brothers in Christ, W., P., M., and F. [f., WIGONI, PABONI, MEGINHELMO, FROUMUNDO], REGINBALDUS, most negligent in the profession of letters, offering whatever more festive greeting can be devised.

Although my outward self has been deprived of your sight for a long interval, my inward self, in the contemplation of intimate affection, never ceases to remember you. Know that the reason I did not visit you during the days that have passed, as I promised, was the presence of my senior. Moreover, it did not seem especially suitable to me to undertake that journey by my route at this season, since fodder was expensive everywhere and the weather was uncertain; nor would you have had a place or leisure to listen to me and give me gentle counsel concerning the matters I would have whispered into the chambers of your ears.

As soon as the waiting for the Paschal festival has passed, when the loosened earth sends forth its grasses, I promise to come to you, as long as life remains. To you, most loving brother Froumund, I have sent through this parchment-bearer the remainder of the little book that you requested, ordering you to copy it as quickly as possible so that you may return it immediately, because I have sufficiently satisfied the owner of that book—I do not know whether at your own requests.

But to you, lord and master Meginhelm [Col. 1287C], I have been unable at this time to satisfy. The book you wanted is kept in our library, but I doubt whether it is corrected or not. If I discover that it will be useful to you, I shall arrange to carry it away with me. Farewell, and grant me, miserable—I mean truly miserable—to your prayers.

### VII. Froumund to the monk Pabo, concerning clothing with which he may protect himself from the cold

To the lord Pabo, brother Froumund, whatever charity there is in the Lord.

The pressure of the approaching winter compels me to say what we need. Relying too much on your customary kindness toward me, I ask you to send me two shaggy mittens, of pigskin, beaver fur, or fox fur, so that when I wear them I may avoid the danger of cold in my hands. May our beloved brothers Liutold and Wuirunt also be well. After greeting them by name on my behalf, ask them to give some wax generously. Farewell.

### VIII. To R. [f. REGINBALD], a monk. He urges perseverance in the monastic state and asks to be aided by the prayers of the monks of Cluny

To R., my most beloved brother, from F., wholly faithful to you in mind.

You did well to inform us through a known messenger where you had crushed beneath your heel the cares of the sorrowful world. For throughout all regions we sought you with grieving minds. But we rejoice exceedingly to hear that you are resting in monastic quiet, with every worldly tribulation lulled and defeated. Rejoice, most beloved brother, that you have found what you always sought with a sighing spirit.

I ask you not to let any deceiver or seductress tear you away from the path of truth. Do not look back in order to loosen the knot by which you have thrust yourself forward; henceforth devote yourself to perpetual charity. When fleeing from the world, if you look back in your mind, you will marvel that you escaped so many and such hostile dangers of the world in safety.

Why say more? From the time I, an unworthy man, was ordained priest, I have not forgotten you; indeed, thereafter, whenever I remember myself or my own people, I never fail to remember you. For we hope and desire in spirit that one day you may come to places nearer to us, with the praiseworthy permission of your most worthy abbot [Col. 1288B]. I trust in the Lord Jesus Christ that, satisfying my wish, he may lead me to the place where the holy signs of our redemption have been found. And if this happens, I wish to see you and commend myself to the holy prayer of the seniors of the monastery of Cluny, if they deign to receive me. Farewell.

### IX. Froumund to the same. He asks him to send a copy of the poet Horace

To R., my most beloved fellow brother, your faithful F., although worthless, sends diligent prayer from the heart.

If you still have the book of Horace in your hands, I ask you to send it to me so that I may copy the portion of that same book that is still lacking for us; and if you do not have it, we ask that another book which you know to be useful to us be sent. Our book, which you have, is also very necessary to us. Therefore we ask you to send it by the present messenger. Whenever you wish, I shall immediately return it to you, if that is necessary. When, with your help, I copy the book of Horace, I shall not delay coming to you at once.

### X. To the same. He asks that his blind nephew be brought before the altar of the holy bishop to receive sight. He complains that his book has been badly treated, etc.

To R., half the consolation of my life, from F., whatever joy there is in Christ.

I ask you to bring this boy, the son of my niece, a good woman, who is almost deprived of the light of his eyes, before the altar of the holy bishop [f. Saint Emmeram], and pray before God for his health [Col. 1288D]. And if you know of any remedy for this kind of infirmity, or can inquire about one, we ask you to provide it for him for the love of Christ.

If I had possessed anything dearer to me than you, I might perhaps burden this little page with reproachful words, because I received our book entirely wrinkled, muddy, and partly torn. But may it be far from me to grieve you with even one word. At the head of that same book were inserted two leaves. On one was a circle containing a description of the four regions of the world; on the other was a letter of the kind they call *formata*. I ask you, embracing your knees, to send these back to me.

### XI. To the same. He asks that the poems of Statius be sent to him

[Col. 1289A]

To the lord R., whose wisdom flows like rain, from F., his servant, as many greetings as a wandering wolf knows the different paths.

I do not wish you to doubt in any way that I am bound to you in my heart by the bond of complete charity. Therefore I ask you to arrange for me to see the book of Statius. It can now be carried to me, and immediately returned to you without any wrinkle or damage, through messengers who travel back and forth with empty baggage. But if charity between us has completely grown cold—which may that never happen!—send our book to us. Farewell.

### XII. To Gozpert, abbot of Tegernsee. In what condition did he find the monastery’s estates when he inspected them?

[Col. 1289B]
