To G., his senior, from F., the last of your servants, no one else and nothing other than what I was long ago.

I have gone around, by observation, the places of the obedience entrusted to us, insofar as I have so far been able, and I find that only a very small part has been left to us. Something so great must be accomplished that, in this administration, we owe a due share to the poor, the household members, and the foreign guests.

In the region of the Danube I recovered grain that they took away in the previous year, and the office that belonged to the greater man who had been there in the preceding year was also taken away, yet no one gave me any answer at all about this. For the entire tithe has been divided here and there among our own people and outsiders [Col. 1289C]. If you do not prohibit this, what outsiders possess will be wholly withdrawn from the house of God.

I ask your fatherhood to grant us the whole tithe in the present year for burning into lime. For there is a church in our obedience called Holzchiricha, supported on every side by forked props and ruined in its walls; unless it is helped quickly, it will collapse entirely.

### XIII. To Master Meginhelm. He urges him to bring forth the powers of his talent

To my lord and master M., remarkable in character and wonderfully endowed with a spotted nose, from F., your faithful servant, frequently preparing faithful service.

Remember me, in the manner of a masterly and wondrous medicine, to preserve in what follows the vigorous and health-giving restraint of blood [Col. 1289D]. Subscribe with a sacred style, just as a foolish servant provokes you with foolish words; but write wisely, following the sacred Scriptures. Do not scorn to preserve in a handkerchief whatever salutary thing you know. Scatter seeds; I, your dry servant, will make wisdom grow.

### XIV. To his abbot Peringer. He asks leave and permission to fulfill his vows in the city of Augsburg

To his ever-venerable senior P., from F., unworthy of any veneration but nevertheless wholly devoted to you in mind.

[Col. 1290A]

I ask your fatherhood to receive my messenger with the ears of your customary piety, as though he were speaking with you in person about necessary matters. For he does not speak himself: this inanimate thing is sent by an animal on behalf of an animal to an animal. Therefore we speak to you not jokingly but as though we were physically present.

Your kindly compassion knows at last how, once, when I had fallen ill in the city of Augsburg, I was sick in despair of my life. Following the advice of those who cared for me, I bound myself by a vow that, if I recovered from this illness, I would come every year to the tombs and patronage of those saints who rest there. I have utterly neglected this, sinner that I am, but every year I said: “Tomorrow, tomorrow”; I ask permission to go immediately.

Therefore, my father, I ask nothing great or burdensome, but only one horse for me to ride and one man to ride with me. For provisions I ask nothing else except the portion of food that would be given to me while I was here at home; and, in addition, whatever your grace deigns to give, I neither reject nor refuse. Who would not fear having lied to such a patroness, whose feast has been read to us today? Therefore, if you wish to have any concern for my life, may I, with your help, remain in the city of Augsburg at the Nativity of Saint Mary. Farewell.

### XV. To the same. Concerning the administration of the church entrusted to him

[Col. 1290C]

To Father P., whom I am to love perpetually in Christ, from F.

In a brief verse I pray for every prosperity, dear one.

Because you entrusted to me the affairs of this holy Church to guard, I have therefore served in all these matters, laboring until now as far as I was able. But now it seems to me that, because of the worthlessness of my [uncertain reading: *naucitatis*], certain matters which my predecessors had in their hands . . .

The rest is absent from the codex.

### XVI. To the same, perhaps, concerning certain books returned by him

To P., lover of manifold goodness, from F., his most humble brother, greetings.

[Col. 1290D]

I return thanks, kneeling fully to the ground, because I so often see you laboring on my behalf in pious love. In your brief note you asked me to lend you the book of Boethius. I copied two of its books with my own hand and, as I think, fully adorned them with a glossed transcription. I kept one of them with me and left the other at Augsburg, together with the book of Juvenal and Persius, in exchange for Boethius’s *Arithmetic*, in which you yourself wrote a considerable amount for my sake, and for the book of Cicero’s *Invectives against Sallust*.

By returning the books that were lent to me and receiving back our own, I willingly satisfy your command. Farewell.

# Poems of Froumund

*(R. P. Pezius, cited above.)*

### I. On an image of the Crucified

[Col. 1291A]

This vine adorns the branches of the eternal offspring,

from which new cups are given to the world from a fountain;

the victorious right hand and unconquered arms of Christ

have snatched them in a pious embrace from the enemy’s jaws.

The livid serpent sees the Tartarus destined to perish,

and licks its sluggish head, muddy and earthy.

[lacuna]

Light is always present to me, yet I cannot see the book’s light;

nor does any reader’s understanding suffice.

### II. To Pabo

Hail, fellow brother, always sweet to me in love.

You are sweeter to me than the taste of honey in the mouth.

The liquid does not know how to love, but love grows sweet and enters the heart,

and joins one breast to another by a bond.

With all others excluded, may you be dearer to me than these.

Conversely, when they are cast aside, may you be more eager for them in this way.

I follow you, as the world’s course is carried around in song.

Nowhere am I torn away; never am I driven from you in my heart.

This splendid day is rightly called so, and surpasses all festivals,

because it has made me see you and you see me.

Let one rejoice in the other when he sees the other safe.

I esteem you, noble boy, because you are greater in lineage;

therefore I am ready to be your servant above all.

### III. For shaggy leggings, however worthless, to the abbot

The lofty mountains are already concealing their crags beneath snow;

the winds persist in blowing over the plain, and the cold breathes.

Everywhere your storm buffets your servant with its whirl.

But every assault is driven away by furs.

On one side I am covered; on the other the cold shakes me;

above all, the cold creeps through the veins of my shins.

My little legs stiffen and harden like stony icicles.

You can mend this, Father. If a shaggy hide

is given, or an old one, or a newly sewn covering,

whatever it is that you give is a venerable gift.

### IV. For the sick Pacho

Should I admonish our brothers for Pacho’s sake in verses or in words,

concerning what you wish to give back to our sick brothers?

Now the seasons demand that the rough grasses be rubbed with oil.

Consider this in your mind, Father: behold, the strength of the two is alike weakened,

their cups and their table are shared.

Whatever belongs to them, they enjoy by a common lot.

Whatever one suffers, let that same thing be made common to both.

When one ham has been consumed, let another portion be supplied.

While one rejoices, let neither utter complaints.

We sin ourselves if we are not one for everyone.

And the greatest reward is to add care for the sick.

### V. Against those who were pressing Froumund to receive the priestly order

[Note: [Col. 1291D] See Mabil., volume IV of the *Analecta*, p. 357.]

There are those who say to me: “Why now, Froumund, last of all,

when you are not the last excluded, nor rejected by your father,

does time and age now demand that you become a priest?

Why do you delay going with the others? Receive the bright,

whitish garments that celebrate the sacred mysteries,

which the bishop celebrates with his hands. If Christ scatters chrism,

it is poured also upon these anointed ones whom he touches with his thumb.

Thus grace has often flowed through blessed peoples,

when the right hand of the Most High had blessed the blessed

and made them his priests, servants in sacred order.”

They strive, I admit, to compel me, as though I were a wise man.

Fools do this, nourished by a windy breath,

not because they desire virtues, but because they applaud deception.

Let us remain humble; let us remain unlearned before all.

Their hearts are never nourished by such speeches;

rather, more and more, Lord, I shall extend the zeal of my mind toward that place where he has commanded the righteous to set their hope in matters to be undertaken, together with my hands

and all my deeds, or with whatever efforts and skill I recover,

so that whatever follows may wholly become his—

whatever belongs to him in words or actions.

We shall return the bold endeavors of the body to his praises.

But to those who discuss such matters we respond:

“The tongue of fools is easy and ready with words.

For whoever speaks first, others recognize him more clearly,

because pride rules in his mind,

while inwardly his heart remains empty of understanding.

These concerns do not bite us. Let God deal with them also.

I cannot occupy so exalted an office,

pressed down everywhere beneath the weight of sin.

I have something to say, and I shall unfold it all in order.

First, it pleases me to be devoted to a single field of study.

I say everything as it is and pursue no frivolity.

I have resolved to learn books and to teach others.

May almighty God grant that in this time, under your rule,

I may grow in Christ, as it flowed in ancient time,

and may I not be torn away into hard labor:

so that, however poor I may be, I can be a fellow-worker.

There is reward for all, because you yourself weigh the labors

of the servants who burn sweetly in service to you.”

### VI. Against Gerhard, who struck a boy savagely with a stone

[Col. 1293A]

We make Gertrud a witness that Gerhard is rightly hated by the brothers,

because he had dared deeds hateful to everyone,

unworthy for you to endure.

For, cursing our boy and perhaps drawing blood,

he then seized a great stone and hurled it at him

with an unsteady run; the boy barely escaped the blow.

But the stone missile, carelessly released from his hands,

was carried into the air with the harsh, hoarse sound of hissing.

The air, not stopping the wounds and scorning the blows of the thrower,

lets the stone that causes wounds fly onward.

Stones collide and much fire is struck out.

The wall built from a stone embankment is shaken.

We marvel that the sun has been darkened by dust.

[Col. 1293B]

The sky is disturbed; Tartarus below is shaken.

So a wolf, tearing the unlucky grass with its feet,

whips up into the wind a dense cloud mixed with spray,

darkening the shepherd’s eye, stuffed with dust,

so that the guardian of the flock may not notice the mad creature’s evil deeds.

No differently do we accuse the innocent, defenseless boy,

than if a lamb were seized among scattered sheep,

when the shepherd has withdrawn, his courage failing.

Thus we, false shepherds, retain our pupils.

Then I, worthless under the name of a false shepherd,

leave the tender lamb, soon to be held by the enemy.

Who could imagine such a thing happening—

that an evil beast should be in the cloister, in a lair blocked with stone, while the monastic flock suffers upon the earth?

Here the hated wolf has come, fallen from the opening

through which thieves enter, slaughter, and destroy everything.

Thus, placed in the safe valley of the willow grove,

we drive away the flock’s offspring with secure bows.

Thus the stretched-out wolf meditates on stripping away the fleece;

it presses its bloody jaws, lest its breath disturb the straw.

The fleeces shudder if the stench breathes upon them.

Let us all seize stones; let the enemy also be stoned.

Driven from the borders by biting, fierce dogs,

driven farther away, exhausted, let him suffer wounds.

After condemning him in this way, let us return to the city.

Let us close the gates and secure the halls with bars,

so that hereafter no bear may break through from the bones,

and let every kind, both sheep and wolf, depart far away.

May Christ God himself, the merciful one, reign among us,

the Son of the Father, who drove away the wounds of death.

[Col. 1293D]

May the Spirit of them both preserve the roofs of the houses.

### VII. To Liutold, bishop of Augsburg

Brother Froumund sends Liutold a thousand greetings,

and as many as all the little flowers now rise from the earth.

### VIII. Epitaph of Ilisa or Elisa, his mother

In this stone tomb lies Ilisa, having completed her bodily life.

Envious death seized that which had been her life.

If the letter that Greece calls *sigma* [σ] were absent,

her name would be *Ilia*, as her lineage has shown.

After many years, her son Froumund the monk

performs the funeral service for her.

Dulichium gave birth to fathers, and Troy to earlier ancestors;

this small place now covers this body.

No people made her beauty second to another’s;

thus she was set above all the rest upon earth.

The inscription that you see asks that you remember in your prayers

the body and soul, so that peace may remain with them.

Consider also in your mind that you, a stranger and exile,

will lie in these lands, expelled from your own.

Therefore I ask you, brother, to ask equally with prayer

that he now grant her a perpetual homeland.

And may he lead us with similar forgiveness to the stars—

he who conquers death and prepares all good things.

On the third day before the Kalends of October

he took her from the world and restored her to the heavenly ones.

### IX. On the arrival of Duke Henry of Bavaria

[Col. 1294B]

Sweet-born one, offspring of ancient scepter-bearing rulers,

hail, illustrious prince, perpetual peace of your fatherland.

Sweet.

God from on high, look down now from your heavens upon your own,

Sweet.

and deign to be the duke of a duke; crown him with triumphs.

May there come to you, holy Quirinus, a renowned offspring,

born from the noble stock of patricians.

Sweet.

Behold pious Duke Henry, serene prince,

foremost defender and founder of the people and the nation.

Sweet.

Receive kindly him who reveres you, venerable one,

who seeks you and believes that you will grant him forgiveness.

Sweet-born one.

O young men, children, and all who are swift,

run competitively; hasten here in a race.

Sweet.

Let us resound sweet songs in praise, brothers:

you will be a blessed duke throughout the ages, glorious in triumphs.

Sweet.

Let the trembling, stooping old men run here,

if not immediately, then gradually toward the spectacle.

Sweet.

Let every people run, whoever possesses the use of speech;

let them praise in wonder the one whom they had never seen there.

Sweet.

Let children hang their small bodies on the hedges,

or climb the roofs, so that they may see such things.

Sweet.

Let antlered stags come from every direction into these mountains,

and let every kind of wild beast look out from the rocky crags.

Sweet.

Citizens born from tree trunks, loosen your mossy garments.

Purple must be carried into these woods by the toga-clad offspring.

Sweet.

Wood-dwellers, scatter unfamiliar thyrsi for him;

who can bring forth odes in his honor as he might deserve?

Sweet.

Say: “May you be safe, duke and strongest of the nation.

May health, restored to your life, remain with you for many years.”

Flying among you, my little winged creature buzzes breathlessly,

and the tiny fly gives my murmurs of love.

### X. To the same. He prays for a prosperous journey and return

The people dwelling in the Alps send you greetings, lord,

especially Froumund, who desires to be yours.

How tearful are the times that press upon your servants!

You depart from your fatherland—what are your kingdoms?

When you pass from here like a father, every boy becomes an orphan.

May you be, I pray, a generous duke in your kingdom.

My life is worth nothing if it does not always adopt you;

when your head is absent, then I shall be a trunk.

If you can, I can; if not, I too am utterly nothing.

To prevent evils from occurring, my life seeks you.

But rather I pray that you proceed, now look down upon your cares.

All prosperity will come to your peoples.

[Col. 1295B]

Go forth wisely to the nations, man of virtues:

you pass forth joyfully and return from there more joyful.

And may God, author of honors, grant that you bring back from there

a glorious name over the empire.

And may those not yet born recount your entire fame

through posterity and remember your merit.

Say, accompanying him with harmonious voices, little peoples:

“Lead the duke safely, nourishing God.”

Holy angelic citizens, lead Henry

along every road that he himself undertakes.

May you be safe, and may your young men and all your ranks be safe,

those who together with you choose the sweet journey.

Proceed, salvation of our nation, return safely;

be ruler of kingdoms and destroyer of evils.

[Col. 1295C]

Be a terror to plots and a peace enduring for your people.

For may a golden path lead your life,

may peace leap through your limbs and joys inhabit your hearts.

May hostile encounters and evil meetings be far away.

### XI. To the same, of nearly the same subject

I would always sing of you, if I could sing very well,

nor would honey be so sweet to my lips.

I would draw out long joys, because I would sing sweet songs;

while I remain in the body, I sing always out of love.

Leaning down, I kiss the footprints where you will walk,

if only you were going out on foot: for that would be rest.

I shall climb the mountains and traverse all the remote places,

watching in every direction for your return to the fatherland.

Now again and again may you be well, kindly patron;

the entire holy Church asks the Lord on your behalf.

For you are beautiful in face, and likewise in character and conduct;

you are also the life of your servants, good duke.

### XII. To Saint Henry and his brother Bruno. He rejoices at their return to their fatherland and asks him to receive the people of Tegernsee back into favor

People of the Augusti, hail, prince of peoples,

son of the Church, himself beautiful and a father.

Duke, glory of the fatherland, peace and father of the Church.

You will always be safe, and your entire army safe.

Hail with the people accompanying you.

And may you, prince Bruno, be safe with your brother,

beautiful in face and noble in birth.

[Col. 1296A]

Hail, Duke Henry, beloved by your peoples;

you are the offspring of kings, and you too hold the scepters.

No earthly king will ever surpass you.

A companion in strength, noble and pious,

gentle in character, you also excel in every deed.

May the Lord bring this about, so that you may be his own.

Let praise be given to the reigning Lord for our prince:

he has led him safely to his own seat.

Let each strive with his own song to assemble beautifully [the surviving word is incomplete: *pulc-*]; let all love be in hearts, and honor be borne in the voice.

May the longer day surpass the nights in light,

so that every season may sing of him in musical melodies.

May you lead [and] sing praises, night and day:

let human words sound, let instruments strike their sounds.

The greatest mass of the earth trembles at the sound

made by the peoples and charming choirs.

There is a great gathering of peoples everywhere with the dukes,

who rejoice that you have returned to your fatherland.

The Frankish citizens look upon you with gentle hearts,

bold in strength, for they are your offspring.

But the treacherous enemy has withdrawn from our borders:

like a wolf, he goes into the woods and abandons his ambushes.

You subdue barbarian peoples; no one fears.

The farmers sing and do what pleases them.

Weapons lie idle and shields are silent; with you as prince, there is peace.

No one attacks us with hostile plots.

We also desire to see from you a sweet-born offspring,

a hope for us and a strong flight from the barbarian people.

May your offspring, with you as prince, be our prince,

possessor of the throne and ruler of the empire.

[Col. 1296C]

Thus far, my lord duke, I was singing of you in joy;

we played with songs and studies of every kind.

Behold, suddenly a thunderbolt rushes down as though sent from heaven,

a hasty messenger bearing dreadful news.

He said that you were violently angry with us,

as the outcome proves. Alas, what shall I do?

For my trembling hand has been struck by the anger of lightning;

it terrified the children and struck the old men themselves.

We are burned excessively by the fire of your fury;

who could count these things in words?

It has scorched the wretched people touched by their own crime,

searching out the fault of body and spirit.

We, weak ones, are touched by the breath of a very great crime—

not by the blowing of winds, but by the evil force of men.

[Col. 1296D]

But what was so great the fault of your servants

that no one was permitted to see whom he wished?

It is wicked to excuse the offense; perhaps even one person could have been excused.

Why does the whole countless flock fall into wrongdoing together?

But at last have mercy on your own; now spare the poor wretches.

Have mercy on your unworthy servants.

### XIII. A votive poem concerning the same

Hail, Caesar, illustrious hope of noble fathers,

who, arriving, bring a joyful day upon your face.

Receive him, immense Father; receive him, exalted Son,

and Holy Spirit, three and one, amen.

Receive your rejoicing servant, most chaste Mother,

Church, and joyfully receive your son.

Behold, Caesar returns from the summit of famous Rome

[Col. 1297A]

to you, holy Peter, bearing great joys.

He wishes you to flourish as patron in both places;

be his help in both places.

Let him rejoice that he has sought to possess perpetual heirs,

and that he has bestowed estates upon the holy Church.

Let the pious praise of the brothers not be silent in his service;

let the temple be adorned for his service.

Do not fail as a gracious companion of Christ, Saint George;

if you can, add our prayer to the heavenly prayer.

By your prayer, Kilian—if we ask worthily—

bring our prayer to Christ’s ear, Kilian.

May you be a Caesar worthy of the saints and a beloved pledge

to the King of heaven; come, beloved Caesar.

The beloved Caesar is here; let every hostile fraud fall.

Now all fear is absent; the beloved Caesar is here.

[Col. 1297B]

Let all peoples carry their gifts with joy,

appropriate offerings for you, beloved Caesar.

We bring you gifts to Christ according to our small measure;

from our little heart we bring you gifts according to our measure.

Be the comfort of the weeping and the light of those lacking light,

a staff for the lame and the one salvation of the needy.

A woman deprived of her husband calls you for help,

and the orphan likewise calls you to his aid.

O exceedingly strong one, whom no enemy terrifies,

whose empire no boundary restrains.

Through your years bring stable peace to the Church,

and stable praise of God to the Church.

Let there be no lack of abundance in affairs or peace in days.

May the right hand of Christ grant long times to your reign,

and lengthen the time according to your vow.

May prosperity be given to the peoples and multiplied for you;

may you be quick-hearted toward the commands of God.

May Christ’s grace be with you in manifold gift,

and may he fill you with his manifold gift.

May he give you Samson’s arms and Solomon’s mouth,

Absalom’s face, and Job’s and Daniel’s faith.

Glory and praise to God, with the triumph of the Son accompanying it.

[lacuna]

### XIV. On the twelve apostles of the Lord

Blessed Peter provides the foundations of the Church.

Paul carried seed to unknown lands.

Andrew brought the little banner of the cross to Patras.

Thomas, by touching, wiped away the wounds of the scars.

Through James, Jerusalem is saved.

Behold the welcome grace of God above all in John.

And Philip shines by his word like a lamp in the darkness.

You see India growing dark through the merits of Bartholomew.

You seek the highest, Matthew, when you abandon earthly profits.

Simon, you overthrow Arfaxan and Zaroes in Persia.

With the same [power], Thaddeus restrains malicious hearts and their deceits.

By sacred lot Matthias is numbered among the Church.

The choir of the prudent enters; that of the foolish remains behind.

Gate of life, receive Christ’s sweet brides.

Have mercy on your suppliant peoples, King Christ.

### XV. On the Nativity of the Lord and baptism

O companions—ho, ho! Citizens, all come running together;

let the small and the people be present, a great chorus.

Let there be no delay: let the old men hasten their steps here,

so that together, of one mind, we may hurry along the road.

Hasten now from the house to the brother who perhaps lies there snoring in dreams,

with a sweet-sounding song.

Now everything that exists awakens, because God is present, born.

Brother, why do you alone lie indoors?

The heavenly little band has already come to meet us as a witness,

and now every human race sings of him among the peoples.

Rise quickly, brother; brother, sleep is also death.

Proceed with your companions, and let us hurry to the waters.

Run, boy, now run, boy, now to be dipped in the waters:

Tegernsee itself rouses you from sleep.

Bury the deceits of cold sleep beneath the whirlpool of the deep,

and the wickedness that drags you into darkness is washed away.

[Col. 1298B]

The Lethean, infernal baptisms seek Christ [the syntax is corrupt or uncertain]; whoever suffers this sickness does not follow the Lord.

### XVI. To Saint Godehard, abbot of Tegernsee, with whom he offers good wishes for the other brothers

I would rejoice nobly if I knew how to compose a song;

I would wish to send greetings in every way to the brothers,

of a kind that singers and readers alike would marvel at.

Behold, my abbot, and also yours, Godehard,

sends every good thing of love to those dear to him.

As a father he is gentle, and as a brother he is flattering;

he sharply urges my fellow companions when they swell.

Brother Froumund, although not worthy to be called so,

sends ten times a hundred, and a thousand times a thousand greetings

[Col. 1298C]

to those beloved of the Lord and likewise of holy Quirinus.

May the sower of the joys of the present life and of the future

increase peace in you and grant quiet.

By his holy power may he drive away all sadness,

although we are shaken by the weight of many evils.

Of these things let us entreat Christ, the Lord above, with prayer,

that almighty God may drive away evils and restore prosperity.

To you, venerable hand, and to old age worn down by years,

I send greetings to all the priests in a single verse:

Wigo, Perngerus, Gundroh, and dear Otherus.

May they be strong and well, and enjoy a long life.

And Gotafrid too is here for me to write—bald,

whiter than swans. May length of years nourish you,

[Col. 1298D] leading you through the ages and at last presenting you to the heavenly powers;

and may you, a troop of youths like me, be able likewise—

you who are mine, and whom we grieve to be few.

Ah, ah! Death has snatched away some, while life has blessed others.

I ask that these may prosper here; but may those others rest in peace.

Hail, boys, holy servants and attendants of Quirinus;

now, illustrious company, I kiss you above and below.

May I be a son to you all, or rather a servant.

Bowing my face, but not with a proud mind,

I commend myself to your prayers, holy congregation.

### XVII. On the son of the widow of Nain, raised from death to life by Christ

When the Lord had performed very many signs throughout the world,

wishing to hasten to that city which the people there

[Col. 1299A] call by the name of Nain,

it happened that, as he came, he encountered a widow.

The sacred writings relate this: the widow and a large crowd

were carrying on a bier her only son,

who had died; the grieving mother followed.

She did not recognize the Lord standing beside her in his kindness.

Taking pity, he said: “Woman, stop weeping for the boy.”

Then, in his mercy, he approached and touched him with hands of compassion,

crying out more loudly: “I say to you, O dead man, arise.”

He rose and sat up, and he spoke. Glory to you, Christ!

Then the mother received her son, born again.

Great fear seized those standing by, and the crowds everywhere

glorified God, saying: “This greatest of prophets

has arisen among us and has performed wonders,

[Col. 1299B] through whom God himself has visited us and his peoples.”

Most high God, raise me, Froumund, buried beneath death;

raise me again, Christ, in your splendid mercy.

Let not perish what your right hand has planted, Christ.

### XVIII. On the man with dropsy, healed by Christ on the Sabbath

When the Pharisees recognized that the Lord Christ was reclining at dinner

with the ruler, the Pharisaic group was present, lying in wait

to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath.

He wants to count as evil the one who knows no crimes;

he wants to trap by ambush the one who absolves the crimes of death.

[Col. 1299C] A man with dropsy was before him, and Christ, taking hold of him,

healed him completely, removing the swelling from his entire body.

The Pharisaic group muttered furiously, angered by the ulcer

of envy and struck by its own weapons,

because he healed worthy bodies on the Sabbath,

although they themselves release an ass or an ox for the sake of their profits.

“Which of you, I ask, would not lead his witless animal to water,

and, if it fell into a well, hurry to pull it out?”

He had spoken, and, overcome by the blow of his word, they fell silent.

### XIX. On Christ healing the paralytic

The Lord has now crossed the waters and come to his own city:

[Col. 1299D] behold, men are carrying a man lying on a bed.

When the Lord saw the trusting hearts of those who hurried forward,

he said to the sick man: “Have confidence: your sins are forgiven.”

The wretched scribes, scorched by the flame of envy, said:

“This man blasphemes, because he does not even forgive sins.”

Jesus the Lord answered them in this way:

“What is easier for this man: for sins to be forgiven, or for him to walk?”

That power has indeed been given to the Son of Man

to forgive sins and at the same time to grant the power of walking—

you and all the people who are present together, see this.

He said to the sick man: “Now rise and take up your bed,

with body and heart made sound.” Thus Christ most fittingly acts.

[Col. 1300A] Repay now the service that he has performed for you:

carry the one who carried you; do good, since he feels no evil

when he walks.” Then all the people raised songs to Christ.

### XX. To Peringer, abbot of Tegernsee

Alone, I shall speak a farewell to everyone in little verses.

First I address him who is father to the others:

Father Pernger, worthy of the name of shepherd,

hail, worthy parent, bearer of an honorable name,

who rebukes children, young men, and us elders,

and especially me alone together with the other boys,

because we have never properly given you a little verse.

Therefore I shall make songs in little verses.

[Col. 1300B] Now compose verses, whoever among you knows how to write,

so that his anger may now be driven from his mind.

I shall approach first and offer him a thousand greetings;

if this pleases him, I wish to make still more resound.

We brothers shall speak of games and praises in song,

so that the boys may please him with worthy measure.

A hundred times, and beyond that a thousand, I offer greetings

to the fathers and to all the brothers in the Lord.

I admonish the lazy boys with these words

and call them back to my bosom with a trembling voice.

Those whom I once taught deserved to be congratulated,

and I wished to renew myself through the offspring of study.

As far as I could, I also gave examples of conduct;

now I often weep and groan over those who are empty.

[Col. 1300C] Those whom I begot I now reject, since I am also distressed by their deeds,

overturned in their understanding and improper in their morals.

They neither recognize me nor examine themselves inwardly,

so as to say together: “This is my Father.”

I speak, and you do not recognize your own parent?

Stand still; recognize me: I am the Father in person.

Often I instructed you, nourishing you with writings and words;

I am biting in speech, but in my heart I love you.

Is this labor of mine rendered void, wholly lost,

while you look at me with grim eyes?

If I were to make tails hanging from my belts

and gesticulate with my hands, standing slipperily on my feet;

if I were a wolf or a bear—but I should like to pretend to be a fox—

if I made masks with forked hands;

if I could compose sweet or deceptive stories,

like Orpheus singing and calling back Eurydice;

if I sang many songs with sweet melody,

with frightened feet running from every side;

the one who happened to be nearer and came to see me would rejoice,

and the ridiculous performance would shake all the boys.

If my sweet pipe had worn down my lips,

I would fashion kisses amid laughter and games.

Truth-speaking is less dear to you than a lying little tongue;

you love jokes more than metrical compositions.

For I have decided that playing through songs is better,

since such songs make the mind and intelligence grow.

Again I call you back with a very celebrated summons:

come together here, boys; learn what I have desired.

Not everyone hates those who speak harsh little words,

nor does everyone love the one who speaks elegantly.

[Col. 1301A] Now with sweet songs I gather you all together,

and I cry out vigorously while I perform the melody.

To my dear little sons, Froumund gives whatever love he has—

you who are devoted to study in our time.

I place you first, my beloved brother Georgi,

who came here for the sake of study from his homeland.

Dear little sons, now learn study gladly.

I love you in spirit and teach you with my heart as well.

If I could know that you took pleasure in my words,

I would rejoice to make progress toward those places of rest.

Come, fellow brothers, let us compete in metrical song:

let one who surpasses this be better than the rest.

With a grieving heart I groan and speak on your account at last.

Now sing psalms, all of you, I ask, little sons.

May the Lord, appearing as one to be revered throughout the world,

[Col. 1301B] now in his clemency join you to the heavenly kingdom.

May Christ preserve all the fathers, brothers, and elders together,

and be gracious to his servants.

Let us say to Father Pernger with kindly hearts:

“Abbot, remain safe, abiding through long years.”

And may we all rejoice with him forever,

through what the Lord grants, he who governs all that exists.

When you read this again, Father, I address you yourself,

more learned in words and higher in merits.

### XXI. That rewards are to be expected for good deeds and punishment for evil deeds

If we delay, our times do not delay.

Everything that exists beneath the curved vault of heaven fails.

[Col. 1301C] But the breath of man endures forever.

Whether our bodies now perform evil or good,

whatever each person does, he receives without the passage of time’s age.

If we wish to obtain good rewards, let us do what is right.

### XXII. To Meginhelm, against the proud

You raise your tower-like head above all the heavens;

higher than the fir trees, you trample the stars with your heels.

You appear higher than lofty mountains,

but in your blind breast you are stupider than a cuckoo.

The bird itself flies on wings, but you do not even know how to crawl.

It possesses time itself, but you possess no proper times.

What in the world beneath heaven, I ask, resembles you?

You are more foolish than all empty bellows.

The bellows draws back its breath whenever it has blown it out;

[Col. 1301D] you are wind completely empty of breath.

You will be great to yourself, but you seem small to me;

and to me, Meginhelm, you will always be the one you once were.

Begin now to set your humble foot upon the earth;

you will not be able to overcome the bodily measure.

If you can, do you wish to climb the lofty heaven?

No: I ask you, stand upon the earth, lest you be seized by evils.

### XXIII. To Christ, Savior of the world, concerning the slaughter of the Holy Innocents

Innocents of the Lord, come to our aid, holy ones.

Free us from grievous sins through Christ’s name.

Receive us, you who rule; receive us in your voice.

Have mercy also on all your own, whom you redeemed

by your blood poured out, shining in the prison with light.

You drew your own from death; death, slain, sleeps.

By your death you opened the joys of life.

Herod, pourer of blood and savage enemy,

is destroyed by you, defeated, most powerful David.

The enemy was swifter, flying through every wind,

biting like a roaring lion and desiring to destroy Christ.

He was laying harmless children low to bodily death,

yet the demon did not enclose the slain in Tartarus.

The grace of the Most High carried them instead into heaven’s embrace.

They bear their names upon their foreheads, and also the Father’s name,

all of them, and they cry out while singing a beautiful song.

With a booming sound [Bombo; wording uncertain], laments are wept with Jacob’s wife.

Above, she mourns for the children taken away, as a mother mourns,

[Col. 1302B] but she does not wish to cease lamenting in excessive grief.

They exist, but they have no sad return,

so that they may come again into the world—a lament useless for that purpose.

All worldly things remain, their sorrows wiped away, until the Almighty,

coming, gathers us all together there.

My moist eyelid calls you, holy ones, with its weeping.

I ask you always to bend the Ruler of the world by your prayers.

Strong King Jesus, who rules, have mercy, we pray.

Take away the sin which Fromundus committed impiously in the body—

the sin from me, whom Christ has dyed with his blood.

“Eudochias osoplon stephanosas, Kyrie Christe”—

“Lord Christ, having crowned [them] with the weapon of good will” [Greek transliteration; wording partly uncertain].

The innocent saints, who sing songs of praise,

sing beautiful songs before the Lord’s throne.

Avenge our blood, *haima* [Note: [Col. 1301] Greek Ἇιμα, “blood”], shining with the light of light.

The number of the brothers has been spoken; rest until—

[Col. 1302C] there is still a little time, when the strongest King stands near.

Innocents of the Lord, come to our aid, holy ones.

### XXIV. Epitaph of Rihker

Rihker’s bodily remains rest in this tomb;

he is buried in the tomb, he who pleased the people.

We sing songs, but bathe our faces with tears;

we perform the duty of funeral and prayers.

We mourn in vain, while the remains return to the grave.

Why do you groan over what this is, and from where you carry the body?

Death remains in life, since it is enclosed within the body.

We carry dust, and are food for worms;

when our flesh has dissolved into worms, we become dust for the winds.

[Col. 1302D] Life never remains, unless death comes with it.

Here consider that there is more reason to rejoice in blessed death:

why do you groan, guest, at having reached your own lodgings?

While bodies perish, souls are then blessed by death;

then souls increase while little bones perish.

On the fifth Ides of June he completed the course of his age.

May the troop of brothers pray that his spirit may be well.

### XXV. Verses on a book of compositions [Note: [Col. 1301] It is contained in that codex which I have hitherto cited under Froumund’s name], collected for himself

What Christ’s grace granted me as I composed—in verses or on pages—

I have resolved to turn into a written corpus,

whenever I can fittingly undertake it,

so that at last, dead, I may add it to the praises of the Lord.

When the tongue no longer sounds, let the remaining letter compose it.

Even if they are weak, they should not be scorned by the reader,

[When no speech withdraws itself from gracious Christ,

he will give to all, as he himself wills, and he does not look upon bodies,

filling small things with great ones and scorning the strong in lofty places.

For this reason I have decided to spare no words,

so that whatever is not sent into the fire

or carried swiftly by a messenger’s course throughout the world may be written.]

### XXVI. Udalpert’s verses in a book of Psalms [Note: [Col. 1303D] They exist in the same codex]

I, Udalpertus, labored to write out this book of Psalms,

so that here you too, Heilwih, might feed your soul.

I adorned it as I could; thus it was fitting to ennoble

the lady of the Psalter, whom I also honored as a noblewoman.

Through these writings you make the burdens of cares lighter,

[Col. 1303B] and meditate upon the joys that remain in heaven.

May you desire to devote yourself to these more than to women’s amusements.

May you meditate on these again and again forever.

Certain joys remain, whatever these hearts may ponder.

By these means you can overcome the powers that follow, hostile to you.

### XXVII. Apologia [Note: [Col. 1303D] From Froumund’s codex, although, because of the difference in the hand—which is nevertheless very ancient—it is not entirely certain to whom this poem should be attributed] for the school of Würzburg and its master, against a certain slanderer

As this city bears the name of useful herbs,

with which those who are imbued restore their limbs to health,

so it is the mother of perfected students.

For it produces learning, the medicine of fools.

Through its proper name it divinely displays an omen:

that its fruit can drive away the grief of vice,

[Col. 1303C] since the growth of roots produced by the village is hostile,

driving away the force of disease while benefiting the whole world.

Those swollen with filth and tormented by folly,

like lepers or those who live viciously,

are brought here because they are renewed more effectively

by learned words than their bodies are by health-giving herbs.

To acquire feasts from the highest archives of the woods,

and also to search out the *dindima* [*dindyma*] of the perfected school.

Wangia, why do you languish while preserving foolish ranks?

May your foolish youth hate our assemblies.

How much our rector’s rules, like gold refined and tested by fire,

are of no mean honor—

him whom we see to be the chief column of the Church.

To him proceeds whoever wishes to please by teaching.

[Col. 1303D] Primate of primates, who reveals the hidden things of poets,

he surpasses the summit of all the world’s honors.

For in merits the world bears no little man comparable to him.

He himself shines as the glory of poets of every kind.

By Christ’s authority he governs the scepters of a master.

Beyond the study of Scripture nothing concerns him;

he remains a cultivator of virtue and eternal salvation.

He possesses such strength of mind as a gift of the Omnipotent;

a living stream of learning flows from his breast.

The eternal Godhead gives him a river of words.

This instruction of his is an ornament to us,

[Col. 1304A] for whom honors continually grow like spring flowers.

When he brings light to the unlearned or sharpness of mind,

he teaches the grammatical parts and all the arts.

By night, and in the daytime as well, he refuses to cease,

drawing forth the statements of learned orthographers.

No writings are ever a labor to so great a shepherd;

like the light of the sun, every volume lies open to him,

and by his intelligence he makes the round world bloom like spring.

Energetic and just, laden with twin virtues,

he gives generously, like sleepless Argus, the provisions of instruction.

With subtle care he keeps watch over his own flock.

His school may be attended without payment.

On account of the capable, he never despises the incapable.

He strengthens the prudent while rebuking the foolish.

By common agreement we all join ourselves to him alone.

[Col. 1304B] He equals Samson’s strength and Solomon’s learning.

Free from deceit, he proceeds according to the law of teaching.

But our company, made happy by such a prince,

skillful, sleepless, and alert, will all revere him.

He never grows sluggish, though the one who rightly belongs to him rests.

Such a teacher’s word brings the joys of life,

on account of whom diverse peoples come here;

not only neighbors, but pilgrims seeking him.

Crowds hasten to the walls of this city.

They long to have him as their guide or admonisher.

When the offspring of nobles seeks his affection,

the reading of the pupil will not become a disgrace to him.

Let anyone attend him; by advancing himself, he becomes like a father.

No mortal possesses such skill.

Let none of the eight virtues be lacking to the highly learned man.

[Col. 1304C] With these ornaments, the glory of his humble mind stands firm.

May he live unharmed, with enduring prosperity,

full of virtues and serene in success.

May no event remain for him that can cause harm.

Freed from sorrows, may he rejoice and be safe everywhere.

May the joys of true peace be most celebrated for him.

May his life advance through the highest limits of its course,

and may gifts of salvation be his in old age.

Worthy, through wondrous virtue, to enter heavenly things,

may he visit eternal light and heavenly rest.

When the Savior of the world, the ruler of heaven,

shall break the bonds of death at every gate

and, through the divine voice, strip away Death,

commanding the people to proceed before his seat,

[Col. 1304D] then, for the merits of a life adorned by learning,

he will shine here, or carry joys with him,

together with all the disciples who have lived under his governance,

whose pupils then follow the supreme bishop.

For them he shines like the stars and rests.

Rejoicing in such increase from the five talents

now entrusted to him and then returned to the Lord,

O distinguished boy, who kindle us like fire,

you who first assailed this man with fabricated curses,

babbling that you held yourself to be a teacher superior to him,

when you said this, you showed great folly,

placing learned Plato after Labeo.

[Col. 1305A] If only you had been mute when you uttered that.

When you reproach him before everyone,

you show that you have provoked a mad dog, while yourself being faulty.

bearing in your unsound mind an enraged Diana,

or that you have broken a mother’s neck,

or a father’s.

You, worshiper of the furnace, keep the lot of the silent one;

unclean in morals, filthy with vices, raging,

ugly, blasphemous, full of the dung of vices,

empty in understanding, so that you are disturbed while falsely sane.

You are unworthy to be held among the clergy,

or perhaps to be a thief—I do not care to say.

But this is what they said who saw your writings:

that such things came upon you because of your own fate and guilt,

so that you may be under punishment for such a poem.

[Col. 1305B] He reproves this blemish, which wears everything down through the ages.

All who support him are superior to this man.

You, sower of anger and destroyer of friendships,

show yourself: why do you force us to lay aside our robes,

being harsh to us and sending messages of litigation?

Do you not know that here we lead a honey-sweet life,

peaceful on every side and overcome by no one?

None of our bitter words would disturb you

if you had ceased, and had not asked for such things.

I know that we, unwilling, have been challenged to fight from the ground up.

Therefore do not bark from quarrels, but give thanks,

because I speak these things not by quarrelling, but by giving counsel.

It is dangerous for you to approach our threshold,

and the place of the school with your frivolous mark of words.

Why do you strive for this, so that you still groan in tears?

You will lament forever if you move us to fight.

[Col. 1305C] Do you wish, through conflict, to give your back to war and defeat,

or, after the battle array, to surrender yourself bound in handcuffs?

Give up the encounter of war, fledgling of an ass,

who, in the place of a robber, are prey for a lion’s cub.

If you persist in entreaty, we shall rejoice in these parts,

so that you may see war stripping the wretchedness from you,

and you may lie helpless at our feet like a worm.

You are crowned with peace; may you pursue it in speech,

you who have understood with me the noble teaching of the master,

who instructs us and adorns us with reason and wit.

Because you praised him, you made me exceedingly happy.

Let grievous discord flee from anger between us.

Let us be free from war, twins in love:

you shall enter with me David’s covenant and Jonathan’s.

Let nothing savage disturb us now or ever.

Many marvel, those who observe such things.

There are those who, with quarrels fixed against us as a pledge,

will conquer everyone, and you will appear to them as a lynx,

although you are a subtle judge, a flower of youthful age,

scorning falsehoods, and falsehoods beyond measure,

holding this as certain: to surpass all in eloquence—

our protection, honor, and speech.

Say, why do you rage against us, threatening wars?

Despising peace, while raging with love of Mars,

are you a composer of meter because of hideous lies?

You will disturb the woodland Muse with discordant pedestrian reasoning,

deceiving the Muse and driving Arethusa away,

because a mute syllable, spoken according to rule,

[Col. 1306A] shows that it should be placed legitimately.

You do not know that in poetry there is rhythm;

I see that, as a poet, you abandon the bounds of grammar.

A poor frog once began an empty lawsuit,

saying that it carried divine medicine for wild creatures.

But the fox’s cunning rebukes it for these faults:

“You do not deceive me, since you imagine yourself a physician.

I know that you are defective through your spotted skin;

I testify that the greatest plague afflicts you.

First offer yourself some comfort or medicine;

hereafter apply to us the aid of the art of Paeon.”

Thus you are an emender, and thus an accomplice of vice.

With monstrous voices, wholly empty of learning,

you will blame a crime, but soon provide an example of it,

for Scripture reveals what the heart does not conceal.

With false verses offered, unmetrical and unmodulated,

[Col. 1306B] you would not have shown yourself foolish if you had kept silent,

but now the mark of your speech shows you to be an idiot.

You do not distress us while supplying weapons for battle,

threatening us with wars like a great tyrant,

and rejoicing to turn over what you do not dare to dictate.

Let us ask that divine help be first for us.

Christ, deem worthy to protect the troop of your clergy.

May the sanctifying sign of the cross drive every evil from here,

the sign which King Constantine first experienced in battle.

May the aid of Michael also be from heaven.

May Gabriel’s protection be a defense for our safeguards.

May Raphael’s hand rescue us from corruption.

All angelic citizens, give us strength.

With the gifts of assistance, let us venerate the sacred John.

[Col. 1306C] In the battle of meter we ask Peter for defenses.

Paul, companion of the heavenly court, protect us.

May the grace of the Levite Stephen give the joys of life,

and may Saint Kilian extend a hand of help.

With the palm of peace, may he defend his own sacred image.

May Quirinus, divine witness, be our protection.

Stand by, Ambrose, patron of generous battle.

Holy Jerome, who governs the spears, we ask you to stand by.

Let Augustine, the excellent rhetorician, defend us.

Doctor Gregory, grant that battles may not be a grief.

Let unconquered Benedict protect us in battle.

Let us seek Burchard’s tomb without being slow in prayer.

And may the teachers’ eloquence here be wondrously effective.

Whether saints or all of them together, come to our aid,

providing our camp with protection from the stars.

[Col. 1306D] Let us sing these things; we regard Mars as nothing.

Thus armored, we stand ready to fight.

Even if you admit a thousand arrows against us,

you may come against us like hail in your attack.

Yet the Saxon sword, with its strength fully extended, pierces your parasites worn out by fighting,

and the Noric and Swabian peoples desire to join alliance.

They do not follow you, but aid us—

those who do not fear to butcher you by defeating you.

You will never believe this until you see it in combat.

You do not know that Latins are first in this kingdom,

nor will you be surprised that we are equal companions

here, whether learning or coming against you.

And may you grant us, all around, the regions

[Col. 1307A] whose handsome young men are noble here.

You, on the contrary, seek spiritual monsters.

You stand without skill, trusting in these quarrels of Mars.

Because you trust in them, you will leave the battle defeated.

Now you recognize that you cannot defeat us.

When peoples give protection to those who worship images,

fleeing like beasts from the rule of instruction,

when you count the living as fugitives from the encounter,

why would you wish to bring back infernal gods,

whom the law of Pluto condemned to the dragon’s jaws?

When the lyre does not resound to soothe his anger,

whatever he accepts from these, may no prayer now restore.

Rising from the tomb, the shadow of Hercules does not protect you.

I know that this demigod cannot provide such a trophy for you.

Again the worship of wicked gods increases.

[Col. 1307B] If you believe that, you will utterly lack reason:

a soldier of Christ would wish to join pagans to himself.

David will never fight with a companion’s united effort.

Do not join Herculean battles to him in any prayers.

Let the arrogant servants flee Christ-worshippers in the contest,

having embraced the worship of black demons.

While they lived, they were never free from quarrels,

nor can they be joined as companions or serve in a troop.

I know that these lots of war cannot unite their cohorts.

If you recruit them, you give the duties of light to darkness.

Offended by such things, or rebuked by the heavenly inhabitants,

they do not follow you, but accompany us.

They are our protectors, whom you do not know how to seek.

But you follow deceivers, so that afterward you may weep,

if the dead are joined to the living in battle.

[Col. 1307C] I know that this armor will not harm us.

Now it will act contrary to nature, unless its own laws depart.

But why do you wish to abandon your own posts to enemies?

Here you, utterly worthless, crazed, frivolous, and skilled in nothing, will be overcome by our spears.

If your words proceed and your insults wound us,

you will be able to see brave athletes and poets.

Never yielding, while you flee with your dependents,

you will perish with your belly split by our spear,

*sarissa* [cod. *sarisa*].

[Col. 1308A] Swift as the wind, all the youth will put you to flight,

when whoever stands beside you is cut down.

Pierced through the ribs, dying, you will be defeated, enemy;

you will fall upon the earth, spilling your entrails from your loins

[or: “opening your entrails,” *f. reserando*].

Finally, exhausted and pressed by a whirlwind of weapons,

our captive, do not afterward become a fugitive,

hostile to us and troublesome without cause.

You will be led away, bound by bridles or chains,

shut in prison, lamenting, or thrust into fetters.

Now provoke us, so that your life may perish in this way.

Cease now to suffer the losses of your anger or of ours.

You recognize the advantage if you ask for the gifts of peace.

Do not come in duplicity; quickly surrender your hands as a suppliant.

Receiving the commandments of our king’s law,

[Col. 1308B] when all manly strength is utterly absent from your heart

to protect yourself or ever overcome us,

captured by folly and reduced to nothing,

we wish you here to take a drink

from the stream of our innocent fountain,

without bile, with the excessive sweetness of honey.

If you learn from this place, you immediately recover your senses.

You will drink the teaching of right living and of speaking rightly.

If you despise these things or reproach our people,

the hydra growing with a Herculean fiber will dry up,

and then it will be your honor to die on our account.

You will not defeat us, even if the prince of hell

leaves hell for you and approaches as your helper.

You compel us to destroy you; by fighting, you drive us back.

Therefore cease from this; resist us in no way.

[Col. 1308C] This was spoken in prescribed metrical melody,

when I pray for his help and also his venerable name,

from whose gifts I perform the measure of reason,

believing the teaching of Scripture, which speaks in this way.

Mark everything you do with the Lord’s name.

While I ask for leaders of the word of the Creator,

planting the divine field first with seed.

(The rest appears to be missing.)

## BEFORE THE MIDDLE OF THE CENTURY. EBERHARD, ABBOT OF TEGERNSEE

[Col. 1307]

### LETTERS OF EBERHARD

(Edited by R. P. Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus*, V, I, 135.)

### I. To his brother, whom he rejoices to know is still alive and invites to him

[Col. 1307D]

Eberhard, servant of Christ’s servants, to his most beloved brother.

[Col. 1308D] Just as Jacob revived when he heard that Joseph was alive, so our life, after the falsely reported news of your death, grows cheerful with great joy. As we once promised, we still remain steadfastly and without doubt in our affection for you, and we greatly desire to see you in the place where we now dwell. Therefore we ask that, if you do not wish to come to us without the consent of your brothers, you seek permission from all the brothers in our name, so that you may stay with us for a little while, and so that we may rejoice in your being alive as much as we were saddened when we heard that you had died in Italy.

### II. To Count Udalric. He asks him not to take it badly that, without consulting him, he had chosen Sigihard as advocate of his monastery, etc.

Eberhard, the most worthless servant of God’s servants, offers to Lord Count O. [ODALRIC, or UDALRIC] devoted service and constant persistence in prayers in Christ.

[Col. 1309B] Since we have nowhere else so firm a refuge as in you, we persistently appeal to you, calling upon you now at a suitable time, now at an unsuitable one. At the command of our lord the duke, with the counsel of the monastic congregation and at the petition of the whole household subject to us, we appointed Sigihard as our advocate. Since you were not with the duke, nor in such a neighboring place that we could seek your permission, we ask you not to be angry with us over this matter, but to grant us your favor. We also ask through your clemency that you order your soldier Pennon to return to us the servants and maidservants of Saint Quirinus who belong to us. If he says that we hold any of his benefice, we shall gladly return it to him. You ordered your soldier Wolfold to return to us the tithe at Ismanninga, but he has still refused [Col. 1309C] to do so. Therefore we ask again and again that you send your messenger together with our present messenger, so that he may firmly order him in your name to return the tithe to us. Farewell.

### III. To Godchard, apparently abbot of Niederaltaich, to whom he commends his brother Egino

To Abbot G., most learned guardian of the monastic life, E., your devoted servant, and the brothers subject to him, offer whatever sons owe to their most beloved Father.

Our fellow brother Egino, whom for a short time we were nourishing in the lap of our humility in your place, as best we could, we now return to your fatherhood at his request. From the least to the greatest, we all prostrate ourselves at your feet and ask, entreat, that you receive him charitably—that is, half of our heart—in the place of true sonship, and that you do not otherwise deal outwardly with one whom you never cease daily to make obedient inwardly to Christ God. If he has committed any offense against you in word or deed, as we frail men do every day, we ask that it be wholly forgiven by God and by us; and, if we are in no way worthy to obtain for him what we ask, we will gladly receive him back into our brotherhood with your permission.

### IV. To Henry, duke of Bavaria. He explains that bodily illness prevents him from traveling to him, and asks him to appoint Count Udalric as advocate of his monastery, etc.

To our senior, Lord Duke H., Abbot E. offers, from himself and the whole [Col. 1310A] congregation, whatever prayer and service we can provide.

We would gladly have come to you before you departed from this region for another, so that we might see and speak with our most beloved lord, as we rightly ought. But at present we have nothing at hand that would be honorable for us to offer you or fruitful for us. Frequent bodily illness also hinders me, as does the unexpected preparation of riders or horses for that sudden journey.

We now ask that, with your authoritative hand, you give us Count Udalric as advocate of the monastery. I am ashamed to tell them openly how great a scarcity the brothers suffer. For I fear to disclose everything to you as it is. But in these matters we await help from God alone and your fatherly consolation.

### V. To Count Theomon or Diemon, asking him to protect and defend the monastery’s estates situated at Halla from unjust invaders

To the venerable Count Theomon, E., an unworthy abbot, greetings in the Lord.

We ask, my lord, that we may have the support of your kindness in all our affairs. We especially need that support in the places where you possess authority. For whatever we have at Halla in household members or in other property will quickly be destroyed and taken away by enemies unless, for God’s sake and Saint Quirinus’s, you defend and oppose this. We ask you to do so wherever you can. Farewell.

### VI. To the same person, asking him either to reward the bearer of this letter with some honorable service or not to begrudge him permission to seek another lord

E., called a monk in name alone, to Count D., his most beloved kinsman, greetings in Christ.

This friend of ours and your devoted servant has come to us, complaining that he has never labored worthily in your service or that of your predecessors, and therefore says that he still lacks a benefice. He admits that he would rather serve you than any other man, if you would show him even a little mercy. We ask you to give him some assistance, whether through a benefice or in some necessary business. [Col. 1310D] But if you do not wish to do so, we advise and ask you to allow him, with your gracious permission, to seek another lord.

### VII. To H. He returns a certain brother to him and urges him to care for him diligently

To H., whose reputation for universal goodness is spread everywhere, E. and the brothers subject to him, greetings in Christ.

We have sent you the brother whom you entrusted to us—not because we are weary of laboring for him or of providing, as far as we are able, what he needs. For we have already proved that he is diligent and capable of learning. Therefore we advise you to deal with him faithfully, just as you received him into your trust, lest your labor—and indeed ours—be consumed uselessly, or the hope of those who sent him be frustrated. If we can fulfill any of your wishes concerning him, we shall continue to labor for him tirelessly and gladly, as we began. We have no other services at hand; although unworthy, we nevertheless constantly remember you in our prayers. Farewell in Christ.

### VIII. To Engelbert, bishop of Freising [Note: [Col. 1311] This is indeed my conjecture, although Hund’s *Catalogue of the Frisian Letters and of the Abbots of Tegernsee* does not sufficiently support it], concerning the death of the monk Otpert; he asks that he be aided by prayers

To our senior bishop E., whatever a subject owes to his beloved lord.

Our brother O., priest and monk, died on the eighth day before the Ides of April. For his repose, command prayers to be offered through the holy places of your episcopate, as we trust in your kindness.

### IX. To Judith, an illustrious woman, whom he asks not to begrudge consulting a remedy for his afflicted health

To the worthy lady Judith, deserving of every reverence and to be embraced with holiness, Eberhard offers the marks of most faithful service together with devout prayer.

Your piety’s grace rejoices in knowing that I am sound and whole in my progress; my mouth delights in a taste sweeter than honey and more nourishing than milk. When I extend the anchor of my hope toward you as though under a protective bulwark, I seem to be in that most firm and inextinguishable tower of Babylon, from whose every hostile assault I believe myself guarded.

Because of dangerous infirmities—for I am continually troubled in body [Col. 1311C]—I beg you to send some medicinal preparation, together with nourishing coriofolium [an uncertain plant] and other spices necessary for this purpose. Write down how the potion itself is to be taken and with what precautions, and whether it is to be expelled upward or downward. If I am restored to health, know that thereafter I shall be, as it were, especially your own man. Please also deign to send venison kidney-fat, or something similar containing fat, because the hardness of my emaciated flesh in the bite of my teeth, even when they have been ground down, is nothing but a source of distress. I beg you, if it can be done, to arrange that the medicinal preparation arrive before Lent. Farewell.

## X. To Wigo, dean of Phyuhtwang, from whom he asks assistance through prayers and other acts of charity that Wigo had undertaken for him when he departed

[Col. 1311D]

To the lord and venerable WIGO, dean, distinguished by every virtue, and to all his most beloved fellow brothers: E., alas, straying in every respect, sends the unbroken bond of undefiled love.

Since every undertaking is weak in itself and needs the support of another, I therefore, not unaware of your customary piety, earnestly beg you to remember the consolation which, before I departed from you, I promised myself and which I now humbly ask you to deign to fulfill. For I am greatly afraid when I reflect with myself what I ought to do in return for the vow which long ago I promised to keep in all things, though under compulsion, lest, having behaved weakly and negligently in so great a work, I somehow incur divine displeasure.

For this reason I ought now to labor to appease divine clemency: because the things which, as you know, I ought to have asked for eagerly and without ceasing, I rejected with the greatest—alas!—delay and resistance [Col. 1312B]. Therefore I have great need of your support and prayers, as well as of those of others who equally fear God, lest what Holy Scripture cries out should happen to me: “Because you are neither hot nor cold, but are judged merely lukewarm, therefore you shall be vomited out of my mouth.” Farewell.

## XI. To King Henry. He implores his aid against certain men who are trying to take for themselves a particular site beside Lake Tegernsee

To H., most worthy of the royal throne, E., abbot of the monastery of Tegernsee [Col. 1312C], appointed by your grace: whatever a servant [owes] in royal administrations.

Since we are hemmed in on every side by the persecutions of our enemies, after God we hope for no refuge in all these matters except in you. Therefore we labor and fail in everything, because we have no one from whom we may see the Church’s property faithfully defended. Oh, how great is royal power! It says only, “Let it be,” and the thing is perpetual. May this force of your imperial authority, we beg, extend even to us.

There is a site situated on the shore of Lake Tegernsee which Poppo and his brother Piligrim, together with their mother, are unjustly attempting to take away from the house of God for their hereditary use. But we beg you to forbid this by your imperial command [Col. 1312D], lest the site be taken from the house of God by false or bribed judges before it has been judged in your presence.

# BEFORE THE MIDDLE OF THE CENTURY. PERINGER, ABBOT OF TEGERNSEE

[Col. 1313]

## THE LETTERS OF PERINGER

(Edited by R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus*, V, I, 141, from a Tegernsee manuscript.)

### I. To Count Diemo: he is ready to receive Wezilin, provided that he restores certain things recently taken from him

[Col. 1313A]

To the venerable lord D., count, P., servant of Saint Quirinus, and the other brothers send devoted service and diligent prayer in Christ.

As you promised us concerning our friend Wezilin, we are ready to receive him at Egilinga on the appointed day, namely the Friday that is now next. He says that two horses were returned to him in exchange for his one, and we acknowledge this; but each of the two was as valuable as his own. But we say nothing about those horses, nor about the other things excessively and unreasonably dispersed here and there in money, clothing, oxen, sheep, and much grain, together with livestock of many kinds [Col. 1313B].

We demand none of these things, but we bear the loss, and we ask you, for the love of God and Saint Quirinus, to deal with all this according to your nobility and our necessity, and to order that other horses be returned to us—horses which, in addition to those two, he has taken away from here.

Moreover, after he departed from here, three horses belonging to our servants were stolen. Some of our men, and also the provincial clerics, suspect that he and his associate Pezilin were involved. We ask you also to order that these horses be returned to us, or that he deny under proper judgment that he has or took them.

### II. To Abbess V., to whom he excuses himself for not having sent the horses requested, and sends certain small gifts

[Col. 1313C]

To the venerable ladies in Christ, Abbess V. and B., Christ’s little lamb, P. sends whatever a very small man can offer to such worthy persons.

We are deeply sorry that we have nothing with which we can fulfill the wish of your request—or rather, of your command—for no horse was found in our possession when this place was entrusted to us, except a very few, and those themselves unsteady and slow-footed. Nevertheless, by these small gifts we indicate, as quickly as we can, that we are fulfilling your wish.

The diligence of our prayer accompanies your journey, insofar as God deigns to hear us, until we hear that you have returned peacefully to your own home [Col. 1314A].

### III. To Archpriest A. He asks him to compel Tagininus to restore the tithes at Ezinhus

P., unworthy of the name of abbot, to the lord Archpriest A.: whatever charity there is in Christ.

You have often been told about the tithe of our monastery at Ezinhus, which Tagininus took from us for two years. This year he denied before us and our advocate that he would henceforth claim it for himself. But he deceived us, and now he has taken it for a third year.

Therefore we ask your piety to correct this, as you know that it is necessary for him before God and useful to us for the ministry of the poor [Col. 1314B]. Farewell.

### IV. To Abbess R. Why has he not yet sent the requested glass?

P., wholly unworthy of his own name, sends to the most worthy lady Abbess R. the diligence of his most devoted prayer.

The fact that we have not yet given you the glass, as you requested, was not due to the stinginess of our disposition, but because we had not yet prepared any. For now we attend to that work every day, and when we complete it, immediately after the feast of Saint Andrew, we shall send it to you by our messengers.

If you wish to provide us with some assistance for our food, in grain or another kind of cereal, we are in great need. Farewell.

### V. To King Henry. That he free him from the injuries and persecution of Count Diemo

[Col. 1314C]

To his lord H., most noble leader of the Christian army, P., wholly unworthy of the title of abbot, together with the congregation entrusted to him, sends the most devoted duties of diligent prayer.

Under the hand of your protection, and because of your almsgiving, we have hitherto lived very peacefully. But those who now persecute us against you and against God we can no longer conceal.

Lord Count Diemo persecutes us with hostility. In the end, he has taken away our boat, by which we were supposed to transport wine, vegetables, and other necessities to our brothers. He has also taken many nets from us, as well as offerings and grain which our men ought to have sown in the field [Col. 1315A]. In addition, breaking into the little houses of the servants, he violently strips them of everything they possess. They have no personal property which he does not order to be searched out and taken.

Why say more? Unless your protecting hand is extended over us and our property, and he, terrified by you, is forbidden to commit such a crime, he alone will bring the holy place of the body of Saint Quirinus to destruction. We beg you to set a day for him on which he must return to us both the boat and the nets.

### VI. To the same, complaining bitterly about the persecution and harassment of Count P. and other adversaries

To his lord H., victorious king, P., the least of your servants, together with the brothers subject to him.

We continually devote ourselves to the most earnest prayers for you [Col. 1315B]. While you labor, as is fitting, in your extensive kingdom, we, your little servants, have no rest in your embrace, enclosed within the narrow cloister of the monastery.

For we see all the buildings miserably collapsed and consumed by age, because Count P. takes the labor-services each year from the Wormsgau—the very services which your blessed father granted to this place each year for its renovation. This continued until Abbot E. [Eberhard]. We complained to our lord duke about these same services, and he ordered P. not to claim them for himself thereafter, but this was of no benefit at all.

In addition, we suffer excessive persecution from our fellow citizens, namely the former advocates [Col. 1315C], who, moved by the greatest anger and hatred against us because they have been entirely deprived of the monastery’s property, strive with everyone they can to accuse us of the worst crime. They do this before bishops and princes, so that this same infamy may reach you.

We beg you, by God’s mercy and for the sake of your almsgiving, not to satisfy their wishes by bringing any sudden accusation against us, but to reserve the matter for your judgment—or that of your faithful bishops or abbots—so that the truth of the case may be examined in our regard. Farewell.

### VII. To Duke H. of Bavaria. He asks that a hide belonging to the estate of Sciphusa be returned to his monastery

[Col. 1315D]

To the lord H., most noble leader of the Christian army, P., your servant, together with the brothers.

Day and night we continually entreat God for your salvation. We asked our senior, the most august King H., to grant us a certain estate called Sciphusa from the abbey of our monastery. He kindly received this request and ordered us diligently to discover with messengers what and how much it was that we had requested.

When we had done this, we reported the truth to the king. It seemed little to him, but much to us. In addition we said: “A servant of your mother has one hide from the same estate as a benefice. What do you command concerning it?” He replied: “After the death of my mother, let it remain and serve the household and the servants of Saint Quirinus.”

Since that blessed woman has now died, and we cannot presently approach the king, let it suffice for us, we beg, that you exercise royal authority in this region in the king’s place. Let the royal promise be confirmed by you, and order that the aforesaid hide be returned to us, as the king had decreed.

### VIII. To Bishop Gotschalk of Frising. He will send the requested glass after Easter

To G., most worthy bishop, P., devoted to you and therefore rightly your own.

My venerable lord, we do not presently have ready the glass which you requested—or rather, as is proper, commanded. But although we are pressed by want of food, immediately after Easter we shall order our glassmakers to devote themselves to this work, and whatever is made from it we shall not delay to report to you through our messenger as quickly as we can [Col. 1316B]. Farewell.

### IX. To Count F. That he postpone the assembly at Pipurch for a short time

To the most venerable lord Count F., P. and the entire congregation of Saint Quirinus send diligent prayer and devoted service.

All together, prostrate at your feet, we ask your pious fatherliness to postpone for three days the council which you wish to hold at Pipurch concerning the common land, and to let it wait until we have spoken with you. Farewell in Christ.

### X. To Bishop Egilbert of Frising. Concerning certain brothers to be initiated into sacred orders

[Col. 1316C]

To his lord E., clothed from heaven with the episcopal mitre, P., wholly unworthy of the name of abbot, sends whatever a servant owes his lord.

If it pleases you, my lord, we need to ordain certain of our brothers for the ministry of the Lord at the altar of our holy father Quirinus—namely those whose lives we are confident of, as far as human judgment can establish. For the earlier brothers, worn out by excessive age, are already growing weary and weak.

If you command it, I wish to speak with you about where and when, because various necessities, within and outside the monastery, are pressing upon us.

### XI. To Count Udalric. For the restoration of the property from which Penno stripped his servants

[Col. 1316D]

To the most noble lord Count V., P. and all the brothers send devoted prayers.

What you ordered concerning our servants, whom Penno stripped of their own possessions, has helped us not at all. Instead, by various evasions, he now brings one excuse against us and now another. We are greatly ashamed and weary that we so often cry out to you about this, because he neither fears God in our regard nor respects any human being in our regard enough to do what you ordered him.

Again and again we beg you, beloved lord: command him concerning this matter, because we dishonor you greatly and show contempt if we bring a complaint about your men to the lord duke. Farewell.

### XII. To Abbot R., whom he asks to be permitted to retain his servant with him for a longer time

[Col. 1317A]

To the lord Abbot R., P., an unworthy abbot, sends whatever a devoted servant of yours can offer.

A messenger sent by you came to one of our servants [Col. 1318A], through whom he had commanded us, in exaggerated terms, that R., your servant, should come to you as quickly as possible. But we beg you not to take him away from us in our great need, because if he now abandons the work he has begun, we shall have completely lost all the work of the present year. Farewell.

# BEFORE THE MIDDLE OF THE CENTURY. ELLINGER, ABBOT OF TEGERNSEE

[Col. 1317]

## THE LETTERS OF ELLINGER

(Edited by R. P. Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus*, V, I, 151, from a Tegernsee manuscript.)
