### I. To Froumund, a monk of Tegernsee. Concerning his excellent disposition toward him, and the priestly order, for which he congratulates Froumund

[Col. 1317B]

To COMARCH FROUMUND, worthy in all things of the splendor of a rose, ELLINGER, the least of all men, sends whatever can be offered most joyfully in Christ.

When, therefore, beloved master, I was meditating with the innermost affection of my heart on composing some irreproachable words for your benevolence, and ignorance once and again obstructed what would have pleased my will, then at last, trusting and comforted by the staff of your secrecy, I hoped that, although they deserved criticism, you would nevertheless not disclose them, since they are signs not of presumption [Col. 1317C] but of affection.

But so that no doubt may arise that the love of you which occupies the innermost chamber of my heart is always burning within me and rejoicing exceedingly in your prosperity, I earnestly beg this of you in every way.

Recently, however, I learned something that stirred me with indescribable affection: namely, that you have been promoted to the order of the priesthood. On this account, bending my knee, I earnestly ask that the memory of your least servant remain with you, so that yours may remain more firmly with me. For these things greatly rejoice me, echoing the prophetic words: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.” Farewell.

### II. To Egilbert, apparently bishop of Frising. He asks him to protect a certain shepherd against the injuries and snares of his sheep

Because our knowledge makes known to us that your excellence and holiness hate every path of iniquity, we have thought it useful to lay before you the errors which clearly await the judgment of your governance [Col. 1317D].

This shepherd, the bearer of the present letter, poured out before us the complaint of his misfortunes. He grieved that certain sheep from the flock entrusted to your lordship were utterly kicking away the pastures and safeguards of divine law, wandering through the byways of vice [Col. 1318B].

Moreover, while he strives to bring them back to the sheepfold of Mother Church through the medicines of repentance, they burn with such savage fury and tear him apart with the teeth of envy that he despairs of being able to escape such ambushes of misery and death unless you deign to place him as soon as possible under your protection.

Since we are separated by so many intervening places and cannot provide him with any assistance, we commend both him and this matter into the hands of your power, so that you may mercifully receive his complaints and defend him with episcopal authority for the name of Christ. Do not, by consenting to the sin of the wicked, bring upon your holiness any danger of offense.

### III. To Bishop D. He complains about an estate ravaged and unjustly alienated by the bishop’s subjects

[Col. 1318C]

To the lord D., adorning the episcopal throne with virtues, E., together with his subjects, sends perpetual fellowship with those chosen by the Lord.

When we learned, most reverend of bishops, that you had been appointed ruler of this province, we hoped—and our hope remains fixed—that by divine providence you had been given to orphans as a father and helper no less than, because of the excellence of your piety, as a refuge and defender of monks.

Yet the estate which Emperor Henry granted to our monastery by a royal charter of donation and confirmation, as we have learned from certain people—though scarcely able to believe it—has been devastated and alienated from us under your authority [Col. 1318D].

The arbitrators testify that nothing has been usurped by us on this estate except what, by the emperor’s command, was pointed out to our monastery by them with its boundary and was lawfully confirmed in the presence of you and your advocate.

Therefore we earnestly implore you, for the name of the Lord and the love of Saint Quirinus, and also for the salvation of your soul and that of your parents [Col. 1319A], not to order any harm to be done to our monastery.

### IV. To N., apparently an archbishop, whose estranged disposition he strives beyond hope to recover

+ To the excellence of the venerable dignity of bishops, exalted by the sublimity of holiness, + the last in the order of abbots sends greetings to the senate of the heavenly court.

Although I had always striven to obey, most reverend patriarch, the commands of your benevolence in all things, just as long ago I obeyed the orders of your mother, of blessed memory, at the king’s court, when I asked your fatherliness for permission to depart and for your blessing [Col. 1319B], I am astonished that you have dismissed me with such great indignation.

My household members—both secular men and those of the monastery—have reproached me for precisely this: how, after having hitherto experienced the assistance and regard of your piety, I could have deserved such contempt from you.

For I know that the abundance of every kind of knowledge is stored in the sanctuary of your breast, and that the words of Scripture, “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things,” leave no room there for negligence. From this I am confident that, because of the greatness of your majesty, the lowliness of my poverty will not be reduced to nothing.

For the future, if my service has been acceptable, deign before the presence of your lordship to reveal to me the shame of so great a confusion, specifically by making known the source and cause of the contempt mentioned above [Col. 1319C].

This, moreover, gives clear evidence that I make these assertions without falsehood: when I prostrated my prayers before your holiness, because of the grievous need of this burned-out monastery, I obtained from you no favor or charity of assistance.

### V. To N., a bishop, perhaps Nitker of Frising. He excuses himself before him for grain not granted

To the sanctuary of merits worthy of embrace, duly appointed vicar of Christ, + entrusted by Christ’s grace with the care of the guardian, sends the joys of the heavenly dwelling.

We confess that, for as long as we live, it is fitting that all our efforts should be devoted to you with every possible expression of devotion that can be offered to the affection of any friend, since the excellence of your generosity is entirely worthy of every service, inward and outward, being constantly rendered [Col. 1319D].

Yet these letters, presented to the sight of your affection, bring us the blush of confusion. We confess that the greatness of your benefaction cannot be matched by any constancy of our service. In this matter we invoke the testimony of him who searches out the secrets of all hearts, since in the place designated by you no capacity for offering service is available.

If we had learned of your notification concerning this affair before we ordered all the grain to be taken away from there, we would have striven to fulfill your request no otherwise than if we had provided the means of sustaining our own life [Col. 1320A].

But someone might say that, by making a request of our household, we could obtain for you in that place the service you seek. It is therefore useful to respond truthfully to this point: during the most recent Easter season, despite our earnest embassy, we were unable to obtain from our servants any supplement for the restoration of our monastery.

Furthermore, we sent our messenger there to order our provost to prepare lodging for you and to provide you with every service he could. Farewell.

### VI. To the same, perhaps Bishop Nitker of Frising. He commends to him someone who is in danger of losing his benefice

+ To the lord N., a desirable sanctuary of merits [Col. 1320B], worthy vicar of the apostles, E. sends, after dwelling in this exile, greetings to the senate of the heavenly homeland.

Hoping that the bearer of this letter might have some influence before your lordship and that my request might accomplish something, he has not ceased earnestly to beg that, through my embassy, he might be commended to your fatherliness.

Therefore I earnestly implore you, for the love of Christ and because of the devotion of my service, to deign to hear his complaint and to set your powerful patronage against the power of his lord, in aid of his distress.

A benefice, conferred upon him by paternal right—if it is lawful to say so—or acquired from earlier bishops through continual gifts, he fears will be completely alienated from him unless your assistance comes to his aid.

The sagacity infused into you from heaven [Col. 1320C] will be able quickly to examine whether he is asking anything in this matter contrary to the rule of justice.

### VII. To Abbot V., from whom he recalls the brothers, angered against him by hostile reports on the arrival of the bishop of Frising

To V., adorning the sublimity of abbots through every capacity for virtue, E., the last of Christians, sends the joys of the heavenly citizens.

Since it was our wish to satisfy your desire, the sudden arrival of our bishop, announced throughout our monastery, compels us to ask that our brothers, devoted to your service, be released to the poverty of our congregation before what was promised to your charity is carried out [Col. 1320D].

As we have learned, false accusations by flattering tongues were reported concerning this monastery, and by deceitfully fabricating them they stirred up certain indignations of the same bishop against us.

Therefore we earnestly implore you, since we place particular hope in your kindness, to ensure through letters of recommendation to him, or through embassies, that this may be accomplished when, on his first entry, this residence is presently honored by his arrival, so that it may not be defamed or shaken by the storm of his terror.

Moreover, we wish your kinship to advise him to imitate the shepherd who laid down his life for his flock, and to protect, through his patronage, the flock gathered into the refuge of the sanctuary, lest it suffer any hostile division or scandal [Col. 1321A]. Thus it may clearly appear how valuable your kinship is to him.

For it is fitting that the episcopal excellence divinely bestowed upon him should be crowned through the clemency of compassion [Col. 1322A].

[Col. 1321]

# EPITAPH OF ABBOT ELLINGER

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 437.)

[Col. 1321B]

Here, it is known, lie the limbs of Ellinger,

who rejected vices by righteousness.

Adorning the rule of abbots

with holy conduct,

he presided over the monks

with a father’s piety.

With ever-watchful care

he removed what would harm his followers;

by making the good rejoice,

he corrected the wicked.

He instructs all more by examples

than by teachings:

difficult for the depraved,

but gentle and approachable to the mild.

He despised the world

while he bore the weight of the flesh;

trampling only upon the flesh,

in mind he sought the heavens.

Washing himself continually

in the fountain of many tears,

he soon overflowed toward the people

with joyful eyes.

He despised riches . . . as things washed away,

although his wealth had made the poor rejoice.

His fasts had worn down his life,

and had made him exceedingly generous

with gifts to the poor.

[Col. 1322B]

They never lacked such a minister

for Christ,

though what was hidden from the people

was known to the Lord.

Because they loved him

more than they feared him,

he was gentle with disciples

and likewise with servants.

He condemned no one

whom he had overcome by judgment;

skilled in counsel,

helpful in assistance.

While he lived in the world,

he crucified himself for the Lord,

bearing the weapons of the cross

through love of such a leader.

A living stream of teaching,

wise in heart,

he made those near him

well watered by it.

He who ordered a crypt

to be decorated with paintings,

and built a church beside it,

mindful above all of the end,

investigated every matter;

thus, while his body remained strong,

he subdued crimes.

Ask, readers, with humble prayers,

that his spirit,

crowned with peace,

may rest in heaven.

# BEFORE THE MIDDLE OF THE CENTURY. UDALRIC, ABBOT OF TEGERNSEE

[Col. 1321]

## THE LETTERS OF UDALRIC

(Edited by R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus*, V, I, 228.)

### I. To Bishop P. [read perhaps N., Nitker, bishop of Frising]. He reports to him the cleric Raher, guilty of many crimes, and asks that Canon G. be supplied for the parish office

[Col. 1321C]

To P., who crowns all the bishops of our age with the maturest and wisest piety, V., the least of abbots, sends greetings to the senate of the heavenly court.

We have discovered that the cleric Raher assigned to our jurisdiction is stained by many crimes, and is no less detestable for the crime of sorcery than blameworthy for the infamy of adultery.

From this we certainly do not fail to recognize that he contributes nothing to the flock entrusted to him through the edification of his example; rather, through the tangled paths of his errors, he does great harm. He deprives the people, through his own faults, of the whole law of Christianity and the grace of baptism, and even of the celebration of Masses [Col. 1322C].

For it is reported—something pitiable and tearful—that many of this same people have departed from this world without confession of sins and without communion of the viaticum, and have also been buried without commendation of their souls.

Since not only those who commit wrongdoing are guilty, but also those who consent to the wrongdoers, and since whatever is done by disciples reflects upon the teacher, we grieve that an increase of sins is being accumulated against us through such negligence, and we fear that your holiness may consequently suffer some injury to the soul.

Therefore, most beloved Father, we earnestly and humbly implore you to entrust this ecclesiastical care temporarily to your canon G., together with our household, until you gladden our presence by a conversation in your living voice, or until, in your synodal decree, you judge what definite decision you establish concerning this affair [Col. 1322D].

Know that in all these matters we obey, as is proper, the institutions of your most venerable fatherliness, according to the rule of justice [Col. 1323A].

### II. To Archpriest G., apparently of Frising, that he remove and depose the same Raher

+ To G., appointed by the grace of Christ alone as guardian of the Lord’s flock over which he presides, adorning the dignity of the archpriesthood with the highest wisdom: the excellence of complete devotion.

Through the report of our faithful I have learned that our cleric Raher, subject to your governance [manuscript: “our cleric, subject”], is scattering and tearing apart like a ravening wolf the flock entrusted to him, which he ought to have nourished and refreshed with paternal love, but which he does not fear to destroy.

Therefore I implore your charity, through divine love, for the sake of Saint Quirinus, and also for the sake of our service, to set without delay a suitable day on which, after examining his crimes according to the law of Christianity, you may depose him from the governance of the people entrusted to him [Col. 1323B].

But lest the practice of Christianity there suffer any harm meanwhile, I ask you to entrust the church and all the things belonging to it to our cleric who is near you, until, by summoning us in person, you bring this affair to a lawful conclusion.

For not only those who commit the crime are guilty, but also those who consent to the one committing it. Because of this criminal and the offense he causes, we fear that we shall incur danger to our souls.

Although gifts blind the eyes of the wise, nevertheless he offers us no service so acceptable that we would wish, for its sake, to pay an infernal penalty [Col. 1323C].

### III. To the same, concerning the same matter

As much shameful embarrassment does this matter bring openly upon us as sorrow afflicts the secrets of our heart, because for such a matter I am compelled, through letters of our embassy, so frequently to disturb the tranquility of your lordship.

The cleric under our jurisdiction, who has often caused us no small scruple of offense, but who has always been protected by the refuge of your defense and has never suffered any punishment, now performs before the supreme tribunal of the emperor the duties of informer and accuser against us [Col. 1324A].

It is fitting that, through your wisdom, you investigate how harmful a negligence he maintains toward the people entrusted to him, lest, as is said, some soul of yours should hereafter incur a magnitude of danger [sic] on this account, since not only those who act are guilty, but also those who consent to the agents.

As for the fact that, while his wife was still alive, he took another wife: even if our notification on this matter were silent, it would nevertheless not be hidden from your prudence as you investigate it, how greatly he has destroyed the people entrusted to him.

Although our monastery suffers many temporal losses because of him, we put all these aside, since we fear much more an increase of eternal calamity.

Therefore we earnestly ask that your benevolence assist our desire and that a worthy successor be appointed to the church which he has repudiated [Col. 1324B].

### IV. To the same, concerning the same cleric, whom he complains he was unable in any way to bring back to better conduct

After receiving permission from your lordship, when I wished to examine our cleric Raher according to canonical propriety, he showed himself rebellious and arrogant, although he perceived that I was assisting him with paternal love.

By oath I promised him immunity from everything he had done against me in any way, provided only that he abandon the iniquity he had undertaken against Christian religion.

But how great his stubbornness was in these matters, the bearer of this letter—who was present at our conversation—will reveal truthfully, if you command it. I fear to trouble your old age if I undertake to explain the intricacies of his controversy to your fatherliness in writing [Col. 1324C].

In the matter mentioned above, because I refuse to overlook your cleric, I suppose that you are partly aware of it already: if he did not wish to return gently to the path of justice after straying, at least he should be compelled by severity.

In addition, know that I humbly implore you to deign to entrust the church he abandoned to the cleric whom I am sending to you.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1039. THE SEQUENCES OF GODESCHALK

(Daniel, *Thesaurus Hymnologicus* II, 3)

[Col. 1323]

## SEQUENCES

### I. On the Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

1. The first verse is found word for word in Psalm 67:23; that prophecy is said to have been fulfilled in the conversion of Saint Paul. Ad.: God the Father foretold through the prophet David: “I shall convert Paul from Bashan”—that is, from his evil faith, for Bashan was a region of the Gentiles and is interpreted as “dryness” or “barrenness”—“I shall convert him,” I say, “to the depth of the sea,” that is, to knowledge of the true faith [Col. 1325B–C].

It may also be understood in another way: “I shall convert Paul into the depth of God’s secrets,” since he was caught up into the third heaven, and so forth. Concerning these matters, read the treatise of Marsilio Ficino inserted in his letters. For the Church sings of him:

Placed upon the earth,

you sought the secrets of heaven;

which are not permitted to a human being
You have perceived [him] speaking. Whatever the case may be, the word “convert” certainly attracted Godeschalk, and he repeatedly inserts it into what follows as the primary subject of the poem and, so to speak, the underlying thread of its entire texture.

—2. Augustine: “Struck down by the voice of Christ from heaven”—he fell upon his face, first to be prostrated, afterward to be raised up. It is said that Paul’s name was changed on the anniversary of his conversion; consequently, his festival and its name-feast are celebrated together on 25 January. But the people of the Middle Ages made a second and disgraceful mistake concerning the Apostle’s name. [Col. 1325D] They were thinking least of all about the word, but labored over the sound: “Just as the fox deceives other animals, so the saint took letters from kings, so that he might persecute Christians.”

—3. M. 11: “This Word.”

—4. M. 10: “assailing.”

—5. “They act with us”: the manuscripts M. 10 and 11. In the Missals everywhere: “I am Jesus,” as in Acts 9:5. E. s. I.: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

—6. Psalm 17:8–9: “The earth was shaken and trembled; fire rose from his face.” Godeschalk thought that an earthquake had occurred when that heavenly light surrounded the Apostle.

—7. Pr.: “Saul”; Ad., Torr.: “Saul”; Pr., Nb., Md., Torr., Lud.: “fellow-Christians.”

—8. Al.: “hence.” Psalm 67:24: “the tongue of your dogs, from the enemies, from him.” Dogs elsewhere signify filthy and insolent people, but here the dogs of God are priests (cf. strophe 12), whose task is to bark by preaching against unbelievers and to keep wolves away from Christ’s sheep. Paul is by far the most eloquent of these dogs. [Col. 1326B]

—9. Lud.: “with.” Cf. Acts 9:22.

—11. M. 11: “is witness.”

—12–14. M. 11 and Nb.: “here.” M. 11 and Pr.: “of dogs.” M. 11: “in these he crushed.” Pr., Nb., Lud.: “scraped together.” Imagine the sense of the strophes to be this: That divine dog had two molar teeth, the Law and the Gospel; for he teaches and inculcates both in his preaching and in his letters. With these teeth he crushed the forms of all medicines, and he was not alien to the habit of dogs, which everyone knows lick wounds in order to heal or soothe them.

—16–17. In each book the order of the strophes is disturbed; Ludecus omits them. Pr., Md., Torr., Ad.: “turned toward us.” Nb.: “converted”; “the converted.” “Chosen vessel,” Acts 9:15; H. 90:11.

—18. Psalm 114:3: “The sea saw it and fled; Jordan turned back.” Ludecus: “By the sea the Gentiles, and by the Jordan the Jews, are understood allegorically; many of them were converted through Paul.”

—17. Thus in the manuscripts; in the Missals: “having left the …” Here Og should be understood as the devil, who tries to oppress and delay the nations redeemed from the depths of vices, just as Og did the Israelites in the desert. Similarly Augustine, *On the Trinity* IV.15: “Just as Amalek resisted the children of Israel so that they might not enter the promised land, so the devil resists us; but he is conquered when Moses extends his hands in the form of a cross, that is, Christ upon the cross.”

[Col. 1323D]

1. The Lord said: “From Bashan I will turn, I will turn into the depths of the sea.”

[Col. 1324D] 2. He both said it and did it: when he struck Saul down, he established Paul.

3. Through his incarnate Word, through whom he made the ages as well.

[Col. 1325A] 4. While he was attacking him, he heard: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

5. “I am Christ: it is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

6. At the face of the Lord the earth was moved, and immediately it trembled and became still,

7. When he came to know and believed in the Lord, Paul ceased persecuting Christians.

8. “This man is the tongue of your dogs, returning to you from the enemies, O God,

9. When Paul, in the mouth of all the priests, lays down the laws of the commandments,

10. Teaching that there is no other crucified one except Christ God,

11. Who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, whose witness Paul is.” [Col. 1325B]

12. Hence the tongue of the priests, licking in the manner of a dog, crushed with these two molars—the Law and the Gospel—

13. He scraped together all the forms of medicines by which the wounded are healed and those requiring nourishment are restored.

14. Through him, converted toward us, may you give life to sinners, O Christ;

15. You who, for the sake of converting those who must be converted, converted Paul, the chosen vessel.

16. When he taught this, the sea saw God and fled; Jordan turned back.

[Col. 1326A] 17. For the multitude of the Gentiles, returning from the depths of vices, with King Og of Bashan confounded,

18. Worships you alone, Christ the Creator, whom it also recognizes as having come in the flesh as Redeemer.

## II. On Blessed Mary Magdalene

[Col. 1326D]

Just as in the preceding sequence Godeschalk celebrated the great Apostle converted from Saul into Paul, so in this distinguished poem, notable for both simplicity and sublimity, he now sings another illustrious example of confession, a most sweet subject for angelic rejoicing. Indeed, the story of Magdalene—whom Francis de Sales calls the queen of repentant sinners—both holds and moves the heart with such sweetness that we are not surprised that she has so often been praised and celebrated in sacred poems by poets of nearly every age. Her name is also found written two or three times in the calendar of festivals. Besides her principal feast, 22 July—which in some calendars is furnished with an octave and which alone is found in the Roman Breviary—in older books the festival of the Conversion of Blessed Mary Magdalene is quite frequent (on 1, 10, or 11 March, or on the Thursday after *Judica*, because of the Gospel of the day); occasionally the feast of her Translation also occurs (4 November). In the Lutheran Church the festival of Mary Magdalene was observed in some regions. In Ludecus we read an Office of the Mass and Hours, in which only the Collect has been altered, and that not inappropriately. After this, her memory—which, by Christ’s command, is to be preserved wherever the Gospel is preached—gradually fell more and more into disuse.

—1–3. The poet proclaims the majesty and divinity of Jesus Christ, who nevertheless did not disdain to come into the world under the appearance of sin in order to save sinners; 1 Timothy 1:15. M. 6: “creator, redeemer.”

—3. Br., Cl.: “and Lord.”

—6. She was a Canaanite sinner because she was a Gentile.

—7. Matthew 15:27: “But she said: ‘Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.’” Ad.: “The Lord fed her with the crumbs of his table, as she requested; but he fed Mary with cups and tears of the innermost heart”—that is, he gave her the gift of repentance and tears. But the strophe is understood less artfully in this way: The Canaanite received crumbs, that is, an earthly gift, the healing of her daughter; Mary received a supernatural gift, the remission of sins.

—8. These signified eternal blessedness.

—11. M. 6: “to be wiped.” M. 11, Mg.: “to be washed, wiped.” Gregory: “Kiss Christ like Magdalene, not like Judas.” “She goes around with kisses,” perhaps from the Epistle: “I will rise and go around the city.”

—13. M. 5: “from a virgin,” as in the Apostles’ Creed. Pr., Ad., Torr., Lud., Rbch.: “from sin.” For Christ’s food is to convert sinners, strengthen the righteous, and restore the lost tenth drachma.

—16. Thus M. 5 and 11; the others: “cleansing.” M. 11, Br., Cl., Torr., Nb., Md.: “the sevenfold Spirit.”

—17. Pr., Ad., Torr.: “you give the risen one to all to see.” Nb. [Col. 1328C], Md.: “the one rising from the dead.” All the poems composed in her praise mention that Christ first appeared after the Resurrection to Magdalene.

—18. Nb., Md., Torr.: “signing this”; Mg.: “signing her.” The proselyte Church, gathered from the Gentiles. Torr.: “By this Mary is signified the Church converted from the Gentiles to the faith, which heretics and other wicked people harass just as the Pharisee harassed Mary—and the leprosy of vices, which is always heretical.”

—19. Br., Cl., Nb., Md.: “the Pharisee.” Lud.: “having become [one].” In the margin: “the leprosy which.” Ad.: “Christ was invited by Simon to the banquet of the Law; Magdalene’s contrition and repentance prepared for him the banquet of grace.” The Pharisee’s arrogance is despised, as in our author:

“For the love that let tears flow as balm
at the feet of your divinely transfigured Son,
despite the Pharisee’s scorn.”

—21. Rbch.: “you were present.” I do not know where V. D. found this reading.

—22. “Wipe away the filth of sins, as Magdalene wiped your feet with her hair.”

1. Praise to you, O Christ, who are the Creator (and Redeemer, likewise Savior)

2. of heaven, earth, sea, angels, and human beings,

3. whom alone we confess as God and man.

4. You came to save sinners,

5. assuming the form of sin without sin,

6. and visited Mary Magdalene from the same flock as the Canaanite woman.

[Col. 1326B] 7. At the same table of the divine Word, refreshing one with crumbs and the other with cups,

8. reclining at the banquets in the house of Simon the leper, in symbolic form.

9. The Pharisee murmurs when the woman conscious of her guilt weeps.

10. The sinner despises a fellow-sinner; you, who know no sin, hear the penitent, cleanse the defiled, and love her so as to make her beautiful.

11. She embraces the Lord’s feet, washes them with tears, wipes them with her hair, anoints them with ointment while washing and wiping, and goes around them with kisses.

[Col. 1327A] 12. These are the banquets that please you, O Wisdom of the Father.

13. Born of a Virgin, you do not disdain to be touched by a sinful woman;

14. You were invited by a Pharisee and filled with Mary’s dishes.

15. You forgive much to one who loves much and afterward repeats no crime.

16. You cleanse her of seven demons, O sevenfold Spirit.

17. You give yourself, risen from the dead, to be seen first by all.

18. Through this woman, O Christ, you mark the proselyte Church, which you call, though foreign-born, to the table of the children.

19. Amid the banquets of the Law and of grace, the Pharisee’s arrogance despises her, and heretical leprosy afflicts her.

20. You know what she is: she touches you because she is a sinner, because she seeks pardon.

21. What would the sick woman have had if she had not received it, if the physician had not been present?

22. King of kings, rich toward all, save us, wiping away all the crimes of sinners, hope and glory of the saints.

## III. On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 1328D]

In this sequence also the poet, as usual, uses wholly biblical language, and we find many things of every kind expressed by him subtly and wittily, so that in some passages it is not easy to perceive what he means. The poem was recited on 29 August, though rarely on the principal feast of Saint John himself. Other hymns, of which there are many, and other sequences of Saint John should be compared with the poem’s subject. For here there is a great difference between the rite of the ancient and that of the more recent Church. In the former, John enjoyed almost the highest honor of Christian antiquity, and he had several festivals: besides the Nativity and the Beheading, the Conception of John is also found on 24 September, for example in the Brandenburg Calendar, and many sermons were delivered on the Lord’s Forerunner. Today, in the Roman Church, John’s principal feast is kept as a first-class double feast with an octave, and his Beheading as a greater double feast, but in many dioceses it is no longer a public or popular holiday. Protestants, moreover, disregarded Luther’s own words: “The feast of Saint John the Baptist, on which the New Testament began, should be retained.” (*Walch* XXII, 1510.) Thus in very many churches the devout memory of John lies buried.

—1. Psalm 46:6–7: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises. For God is King of all the earth; sing praises wisely.” Ad.: The poet urges the people to sing praises: first once, in praise and glory of the divine nature with respect to essence, and then three times with respect to the persons. This has been stated more subtly than can be proved. Because of the number of syllables, the word “sing praises” should be read only twice in this clause.

—2. Fr.: “with the cithara.” M. 10: “and with the cithara.” With this psaltery or cithara of song—that is, with his tongue—the offspring of a barren mother, born of a Virgin, sang in the Church to his Lord.

—6. Torr. omits. Colossians 3:5: “Put to death therefore the members which are upon the earth.”

—9. Fr., Ad.: “resists.”

—10. “Be still”—cease from sin.

—11. Psalm 57:4–5: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the enchanters.” Torr. explains admirably: The asp is a species of serpent which, when it hears the enchanter, closes one ear by pressing it against the ground and twists its tail into the other.

—Fr., Pr.: “prison.” The poet indicates either a pretended royal dignity or cowardice.

—12. “Of light” may refer either to a lamp or to the Almighty. Lud. in the margin: “a shining lamp,” as in John 5:35. H. 179:3–4: “the lamp of Christ and the evangelist of everlasting light.”

—15. John was Christ’s friend; Herod was the devil’s, whose pleasures he pursued. Cf. John 17:12.

—14. Pr.: “the girl pleads.” Torr.: This verse contains the rhetorical figure called *dissolution*. It also contains another figure, brevity, since the entire story of John’s beheading is narrated as briefly as possible.

—15. Fr.: “before he becomes”; Lud.: “he is.” In the poet’s view, the words “dance” and “sanctity” are wholly opposed. For, as Chrysostom wishes, “where there is dancing, there is the devil.” Augustine’s judgment of dancers does not differ from this: he regards every movement or leap of wantonness as a leap into the depths of hell. Nor does William of Lyons maintain this conception of dancing ineptly: a dance is a circle whose center is the devil.

—16–17. Torr.: “might be.” Isaiah 57:1: “The righteous perishes, and no one considers it in his heart.” Fr.: “while he is.” Psalm 115:5: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” Many poets and preachers lament the execution of Saint John, whose author was a deceitful prostitute. Luther attacks it with his customary ferocity:

“Thus it ends; thus it comes to pass with that great and distinguished man, so magnificently praised by human beings and angels, indeed by his own Lord: he is made to suffer so shameful a death because of a wicked, desperate harlot, and his head is brought into the harlot’s chamber on a platter, so that she may take pleasure in seeing it. It would be no wonder if the fire of hell had struck into it.”

—18. M. 10, Fr.: “such and so great is.” Md.: “such and of such greatness.” Ad., Br.: “and how great.” Lud. in the margin: “nearer by nativity.” Claudius: “John the Baptist stands in the visible world immediately and directly before him, and therefore first draws the gaze toward himself.”

—19. M. 10: “by death condemns”; Nb., Lud.: “condemns.” Matthew 10:24: “The disciple is not above his master,” etc. John himself calls Christ the Bridegroom in John 3:29.

—20. M. 10: “led forth,” which suits the rhythm. Others: “led.” “Holy angels.” Pr.: “the angels of heaven.” Nb.: “the angels of heaven.” In this clause Godeschalk is very far from the doctrines of the scholastics: according to them, John descended to limbo and announced Christ to the Fathers, after which he was freed by the Redeemer together with the others.

1. Sing praises to our King, sing praises wisely,

2. for the psaltery is pleasing together with the cithara,

3. to the Virgin’s Son, singing to whom the son of the barren woman

4. struck the cithara of the flesh in the house of the Lord.

5. While teaching by living what he proclaimed by crying out,

[Col. 1327C] 6. mortifying the members that are upon the earth and teaching this to others:

[Col. 1328A] 7. John, the voice of one crying in the wilderness, preparing for Christ a perfect people.

8. But this voice does not correct the impious Herod whom it rebukes.

9. Nevertheless he did not remain silent, but resisted the crime even to the shedding of blood.

10. “It is not lawful,” he said, “for you to have your brother’s wife, whom you have taken for yourself: you have sinned; be still”—thus the Lord commanded the penitent.

11. Herod, like a deaf asp, wisely rejects the voice of the enchanter; he fears John as just and holy, whom he has bound in prison.

12. The lamp, the friend of almighty light, sits in darkness,

13. while the son of perdition devotes himself to the pleasures of the prince of the world.

[Col. 1328B] 14. The harlot persuades, the girl dances, the king commands, and the saint is beheaded.

15. The king gives John’s head to the dancer—John, who was holy before he was born.

16. Behold how the righteous perishes, as though he were not beloved by God,

17. although his death is precious in the sight of the Lord.

18. We have perceived in our hearts what and how great he is, since he is made near to Christ in dignity and in death.

19. For the Bridegroom’s bridegroom is condemned to a most shameful death, and they rightly condemn the friend to a most shameful death.

20. Led forth from the prison of the flesh, he is borne with singing by the angels to heaven as an angel.

[Col. 1328C] 21. And make us also sing praises to you on earth, O Christ, in memory of the Baptist.

[Col. 1329A] 22. With Herod’s table rejected, while we receive you yourself at the table of your altar, may we sing praises to you on high.

## IV. On the Division of the Apostles

[Col. 1330D]

Although the sacred day of the Division of the Apostles is not celebrated, nor is the people publicly instructed about it in a sermon, nevertheless, since it is a feast of the Church and the songs breathe something of ancient and more genuine antiquity, I could not refrain from appending them. Without doubt the poem above was intended to be understood as praise of these men; nor do I judge it unfairly, although it is more lengthy and verbose than it ought to be.

That festival of the Division—or, as it is more rarely called, the Dismissal and Dispersion of the Apostles (among our people, *Aposteltheilung*, *Apostelscheidung*, *Aller Aposteln Tag*, *der zwölf Boten Tag, als sie versandt wurden*: “the division of the Apostles,” “the separation of the Apostles,” “All the Apostles’ Day,” “the day of the twelve messengers, when they were sent out”)—either celebrates Christ himself initiating his apostles into their office and commanding them to go into the whole world, Matthew 10:28; or it was instituted in honor of a sufficiently uncertain tradition. For they say that, before dispersing throughout the whole world, the apostles jointly established a rule for preaching and a summary of Christian doctrine, and assigned by lot the provinces in which each would teach especially.

This solemnity is wholly unknown to Roman, Italian, and Mozarabic books, but was adopted by the Germans, French, Hungarians, and other peoples. Almost everywhere the festival’s proper date is 15 July, as in the Calendars of Brandenburg, Havelberg, Magdeburg, Halberstadt, Meissen, Minden, Nuremberg, and others, as well as in the Linz Calendar, etc. Among others, however, such as the Mainz and Salzburg churches, it is 17 July; in the Paderborn Calendar as it now stands, it is 16 July.

—1. Just as the heavens and the firmament declare the glory of God, so the apostles, illuminated by heavenly doctrine, preach nothing other than the glory of Christ; hence they are rightly called “heavens” (strophes 1, 20, 21, 24), although previously they were of the earth, that is, they burned with earthly desires. The image is taken from Psalm 19, which was recited on all the feasts of the apostles.

—2. The apostles, through whose proclamation the incarnate Word becomes known to the world, are superior to the prophets and the other teachers of the Law.

—3. Isaiah 9:6.

—4. Add. Torr.: “that.” Ad.: For it was unknown even to the angels, who, admiring him at his Ascension, said: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” It was also hidden from the devil.

—5–6. Thus Chrysostom calls the Apostle Paul an earthly angel.

—5. Thus M. 11 and Md.; cf. Galatians 4:4. M. 10, Pr., Nb., Md., Br., Cl., Lud., Ad.: “born.” Torr.: “a man born of a woman.”

—7. Acts 1:3, 8, 9. The poet has woven together passages from Scripture: John 20:19–21; Mark 16:15; Matthew 10:16, 18.

—10. M. 10 and 11: “leaders”; others: “princes.”

—11. Ad., Torr.: “Matthias and Matthew”; in the manuscripts and the other books, the name of Matthias is omitted. The same occurs in the prose: in “Bright are the saints,” the Apostle’s name has been omitted. We cannot avoid admitting that the Fathers of the ancient Church were somewhat troubled by the number twelve attributed to the apostles. Nor is this surprising. For they seemed to do a grave injustice to Paul, whom the Church’s office proclaims to be worthy of the twelfth throne, if anyone wished to deny him apostolic dignity. On the other hand, they seemed to disregard the exceptionally weighty testimony of history if anyone wished to reject as illegitimate the election of the Apostle Matthias, to whom the Acts of the Apostles assigns no slight praise.

To resolve this difficulty, the ancient Church, guided—indeed, I might say captivated—by the illustrious name of Paul, appears not to have rejected Matthias the Apostle, but in a certain sense to have neglected him. Certainly it is clear that Matthias obtained his feast day much later than the other apostles. I am not unaware that his day is already mentioned in Gregory’s Sacramentary; but the manuscript books prevent me from attaching great importance to this, since the best of them contain nothing about that day. Moreover, in the Canon of the Mass Matthias is found listed not among the apostles but among the martyrs.

Finally, a sacred sermon preserved in Pelbartus makes it sufficiently clear that preachers, lest the name of the Apostle Matthias should become dishonored among the Christian people, deliberately celebrated him with praises. A certain soldier, wishing out of devotion to choose one of the apostles as his patron, as is customary, encountered the name Matthias once, twice, and a third time among the names of the apostles that had been written down. Angered, he threw it away, saying: “What have I to do with him, if I could not have one of the greater apostles as my patron?”

Some time afterward, when the soldier wished to visit the holy places associated with Christ’s Passion, his ship was driven by enormous storms at sea, so that the desperate men, compelled by lot, had to cast one of them into the sea. The lot fell upon the soldier. When he had been exposed on a bare plank to the waves and was already near death, behold, he saw a splendid man dressed in costly clothing, who said: “Would you be willing to render service to the one who would free you from these dangers?” The soldier replied: “As long as I live, I promise to serve him.” But the other said: “I am the Apostle Matthias, whom you scorned to have as your patron.” Extending his hand, he rescued him.

The present rite of the Roman Church vindicates the Apostle Matthias, as it were, from the insult of earlier centuries. For he is ranked with the other apostles in the same place and number; he has his own feast day and his own honors, and, so far as I know, differs in nothing except that in a leap year the honors due to him are rendered on the following day.

“The twelve judges,” Matthew 19:28. H. 232:5: “you judges of the just age.” M. 11: “in unity.” The apostles were sent not to separate themselves from the faith, which is one, or from God, who is one, but so that all might strive toward one and the same goal, gathering all people into one.

—14. Psalm 19:4–5.

—16. M. 11, Br., Lud.: “the Gospel of peace”; Pr.: “good things.” Nb., Md., Br.: “the good.” Romans 10:15; Isaiah 52:7.

—18. Br.: “Christ”; M. 11: “grace.”

—19. Isaiah 45:8.

—20. Jeremiah 23:5: “Behold, the days are coming, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch.” Pr., Nb.: “he raises up.” Others join the words “righteous branch” to the preceding strophe.

—21. Luke 8:15: “They bear fruit with patience.”

—22. Ad., Cl., Torr.: “These are the heavens.” John 15:15.

—23. At the festival of the Division, which is celebrated today. Md., Br.: “one of peace.” John 17:23.

—24. Nb., Md., Br., Lud.: “you dwell, O King.”

1. The heavens declare the glory of God the Son, the incarnate Word, made heavens from the earth.

2. For this glory belongs properly to the Lord alone,

3. whose name is “Angel of Great Counsel.”

4. This counsel is an ancient, profound, and true help for fallen humanity, known only to the saints.

5. When this angel, made man from a woman, made the immortal from the mortal, heaven from earth, and an angel from a human being,

[Col. 1329B] 6. this is the Lord of hosts, God whose angels sent to earth are the apostles:

7. To them he showed himself alive after rising, in many proofs, announcing peace as victor over death.

8. “Peace be with you; I am he,” he said. “Do not fear any longer. Preach the Word of God to every creature before kings and rulers.

9. As the Father sent me, so I send you into the world. Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”

10. Hence Peter, prince of the apostles, went to Rome; Paul taught grace everywhere in Greece; these leaders, three times four, preached the Three and the One in the four quarters of the earth.

[Col. 1330A] 11. Andrew, both Jameses, Philip, Bartholomew, Simon, Thaddeus, John, Thomas, and Matthew—the twelve judges, divided not from one but into one—gather into one those divided throughout the world:

12. Their sound has gone out into all the earth,

13. and their words to the ends of the world.

14. How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize good things and preach peace,

15. saying to those redeemed by Christ’s blood: “Zion, your God will reign,”

16. who made the ages by the Word, the Word who at the end of the ages was made flesh for us.

17. This Word whom we preach is Christ crucified, who lives and reigns as God in heaven.

[Col. 1330B] 18. These are the heavens in which you dwell, O Christ; in their words you thunder, flash through signs, and shower grace.

19. To them you said: “Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the righteous one; let the earth open and bring forth.”

20. Raise up a righteous branch—you who, sowing our earth with apostolic words, make it germinate.

21. By their words, holding fast the Word of the Father, make us bear fruit for you in patience, O Lord.

22. These are the heavens in which you dwell, Angel of Great Counsel; you called them not servants but friends, and made known to them everything that you heard from the Father.

[Col. 1331A] 23. At their division, guard the gathered flock undivided and bound in the bond of peace, so that we may be one in you, just as you are one in the Father.

24. Have mercy on us, you who dwell in the heavens.

## V. On One Virgin

[Col. 1332D]

This sequence is to be sung on the festivals of virgins, and its subject concerns virginal chastity. In it the author proceeds as though he were speaking of only one virgin, although it can be applied to several. The sequence is divided into three parts. In the first, he urges every faithful soul to rejoice in virginal steadfastness. In the second, he praises every virgin for resisting carnal temptations. In the third, he describes her glory and reward in heaven.

This is Adelphus. Nevertheless, you see that the poem fits well the legend of Saint Margaret, Virgin and Martyr. The ancients relate that she subdued the devil, who appeared to her in prison in the form of a most monstrous beast, by placing her foot upon him, and, after subduing him, drove him away. Therefore, if the poet did not pursue this virgin with singular praise, you may easily believe that her martyrdom itself was vividly before his eyes.

—Psalm 149:2: “Let the daughters of Zion rejoice in their King.” We are astonished that any marriage-bed should be defiled by the crime of sin; this accords with that Augustinian decree concerning concupiscence.

—4. Ad.: “there are merits.”

—5. Ad.: He touches upon the words of Genesis, where God cursed the serpent: “You shall lie in wait for his heel, and she shall crush your head.” These words were a prophecy of all virgins who wage war in chastity, and principally of the glorious Virgin Mary. Md., Ad.: “who harms.”

—10. Md. omits “in.”

—11. Ad.: “those who are tempted”—“let them resist.”

—12. [Col. 1334A] Md., Ad.: “drew near.” Md.: “to the Lord.”

—13. Pt.: “now among.” Md., Nb.: “led away”; but he follows the traces of the Psalmist, Psalm 45: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her.”

—14. M. 10: “will follow.” Jerome: “Marriage fills the earth; virginity fills paradise.” The Teutonic poet rendered the passage in more concentrated colors (Wackernagel, p. 620): “Then Jesus led the dance with the whole host of maidens.”

—15. Ad., Md., Nb.: “whose.” Pt.: “you us.”

1. Let the daughters of Zion rejoice in their King,

2. knowing nothing of a marriage-bed defiled by the crime of sin,

3. of whom you, O Christ, bridegroom of virgins, are the Son of a Virgin.

[Col. 1332A] 4. By whose grace wondrous works have been accomplished in your saints,

5. so that you may grant us to see them in this virgin whose feasts are celebrated today:

6. who, though of fragile female sex, manfully subdued the right of the flesh,

7. and here led an angelic life in the flesh, while living beyond the flesh.

8. The ancient serpent marvels at this; cunningly he watched her heel:

[Col. 1333A] 9. while plotting how to harm it, his head is crushed beneath the woman’s feet.

10. You taught this woman, O Christ, to overcome the enemy’s ambush at the first encounter,

11. when she did not consent but resisted him; he who is accustomed to conquer the tempted, if they do not resist,

12. was made by this resisting virgin to flee from her; when he had been put to flight, she drew near to you, O Lord.

[Col. 1334A] 13. For, brought among the virgins after her who is the undefiled mother, she is worthy to be the attendant of the Virgin of virgins, Mary.

14. In a white robe she now follows you, the spotless Lamb, Son of the Virgin, wherever the flower of virgins may go.

15. Through her intercession protect us.

# In the Year of the Lord 1060. Leduinus, Abbot of Saint Vedast of Arras

[Col. 1333]

## Historical Notice

*(From the new edition of* Gallia Christiana, *vol. III, p. 379.)*

[Col. 1333B] Leduinus, or Lieduinus, formerly a layman and a monk of devout observance, summoned by Balderic, was placed over the monastery of Vedast by Blessed Richard—not, indeed, in 1018, as Locrius writes, unless perhaps as provost, but certainly he was already in charge in 1023, on the first day of May. On that date he was present at the general assembly convened at Compiègne by order of King Robert and entered into a fraternal association between the Church of Beauvais and his own, as is clear from the charter concerning the matter transcribed by Chesne (*Preuves de l’Histoire de Montmorency*, p. 12) and by Miraeus (*Notitia ecclesiastica*, p. 148).

There is scarcely another abbot in this series whose memory is more blessed, for he devoted himself extensively to restoring and securing moral discipline, both within and outside the monastery, and labored no less diligently to preserve and increase its material resources. He restored the monastery from its foundations; and, according to Book III, chapter 59, of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Gerard the bishop consecrated it in 1031, as Gazaeus reports.

He established the provostship of Bercloën on its own allod under the auspices of Saint Vedast; he acquired Haspry by exchange from the monks of Gennete in 1044, and afterward redeemed Angilcuria by paying a price in exchange for Haspry. A letter of Gerard the bishop to this same Leduinus survives, in which Gerard thanks him for having sympathized with the mother Church of Arras, which had been burned by fire falling from heaven on 30 July.

Likewise, through the agency of the abbots Leduinus and Rotricus of Sithiu, Bishop Gerard finally yielded to the counsel of certain bishops of Belgium. Following the judgment of the bishops of Burgundy, they required both themselves and all people to bind themselves by oath to observe peace and justice; the Franks called it the truce, as it were the way of God (*treviam Dei*).

Around 1028, after the nuns had been expelled from the monastery of Marchiennes by order of Count Baldwin and monks had been substituted in their place, Leduinus introduced a new colony there as abbot; he is said to have presided over it for nine years. In the meantime he subjected Harmaticum to the monastery of Marchiennes; it remains its cell to this day.

He is named in 1036 in a charter concerning the rights of the toll of Arras, once granted to his church by King Theodoric; in 1038 in connection with the advocacy of the abbey of Marchiennes; and again in 1041 in the donation of Ermentrude for the burial of her husband, Gatterius, castellan of Cambrai, at Elnone. Therefore he did not die in 1040, as Locrius asserts.

[Col. 1335]

# Constitution of Leduinus, Abbot of Saint Vedast of Arras, Concerning the General Court

*(Marten, *Amplissima Collectio* I, 381.)*

[Col. 1335A] I. A man belonging to the general court must attend three courts each year: one on the Friday after Epiphany, another on the Friday after the octave of Easter, and the third on the Friday after the feast of Saint John the Baptist. No external authority may come to these courts or preside there in judgment—neither a count nor any advocate—but only the abbot or provost.

II. If someone of greater power, or someone who does not belong to the jurisdiction of this general court, has a case and wishes to bring a complaint before the court, he may come and lodge his complaint, and his case shall be judged correctly according to the law of the court. He shall then depart, while the court remains in its freedom.

III. In this general court, therefore, with the abbot or provost presiding and the assessors also seated around him, [Col. 1335B] if anyone has a complaint against another, he shall stand and lawfully make his complaint against him. His complaint shall be heard and carefully examined, and the matter between the two shall be judged according to the law of the court.

IV. Whoever has taken an oath shall have an interval of twenty nights.

V. Whoever has given a surety of five solidi according to the law shall pay thirty denarii as the peace-fine; two parts of this peace-fine shall belong to the provost, while the greater officer of the court shall have the third part. But if the claim is that of the abbot or provost, the greater officer of the court shall have the entire peace-fine.

If, however, anyone who has grounds for a complaint delays making it at the present court, he may not make the complaint at all until the day of the next court. But the abbot or provost, if he has grounds on which he wishes to make a complaint, may at any time in his own chamber acquit a man of the court, raise a complaint against him concerning his own chattel, and enforce the law; and the judgment made in the abbot’s chamber must follow the custom of the court. But in response to another person’s complaint, as has been said, he must judge no one except at the court.

VI. A man belonging to the general court pays no head-tax, nor does he pay or owe any advocacy payment, because he is free from this exaction without harassment. If he takes a wife according to his own law, the man and woman shall pay five solidi as *comedo*, that is, a license payment. If he takes a wife outside his own law, he has acted unlawfully and shall pay as much as can be obtained from him by entreaty. If he marries a free woman, he shall pay nothing, because he has converted his wife’s freedom to his own law.

VII. If a man dies, he shall pay five solidi as the mortuary due. When a woman dies, she shall pay nothing, because she leaves her offspring as her inheritance. Of these five solidi, both the marriage payment and the mortuary due, the greater officer of the court shall have the tenth denarius.

VIII. A man of the general court may not sell or pledge the court’s allod, nor give it to another church, except with the permission of the abbot or provost. But if, compelled by some necessity, he wishes to sell or pledge it, he shall come and offer it to the abbot. If the abbot wishes to redeem it, he must be allowed to have it at a lower price than anyone else; if he does not wish, or is unable, to redeem it, he shall grant him permission to sell it—not to an outsider, but to a near kinsman or to someone subject to the same law—so that the allod of the court may not appear to be disinherited. But if he does this without the abbot or provost’s knowledge, and the abbot, upon learning of it, wishes to pursue the matter, neither shall the property remain with the buyer nor shall it return to the seller; rather, the church shall rightfully claim its allod for itself.

IX. I, Leduinus, abbot of the church of Blessed Vedastus, wished to make known by committing to writing this account, or constitution, of the general court, so that it might remain ratified and unshaken in its freedom at all times, for both future and present sons and faithful members of the Church. This was done with the consent and arrangement of the advocates and other faithful members of the Church at that time, whose names are these: Robert, Pasciculus, and Helgotus, advocates, gave their assent. Stephanus Bechez, who was the chief officer of this court, and his brothers Rainboldus and Gontrannus; Varnerus Malnis; Wlago of Walenscurt and his brother Johannes; Albricus the castellan; Gerricus of Herchingehen.

[Note: This Leduinus was also abbot of Marcianus after the restoration of the monastery.]

This was enacted in the time of Count Baldwin “Fair-Beard.”

[Note: Baldwin, called Fair-Beard or Bearded, died in 1036, after having ruled Flanders for forty-eight years.]

## In the Year of the Lord 1040. Othelbodus, Thirty-Sixth Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Bavo of Ghent

[Col. 1337]

## Historical Notice

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. V, p. 179.)*

Othelbodus governed from the year 1019 until 1034. Mabillon mentions, in the Second Benedictine Century, in his Observations on the Life of Saint Bavo, p. 396, a letter that this abbot wrote to Otgiva, countess of Flanders, in which he enumerates the bodies of the saints preserved in the church of Saint Bavo. You will find this letter in Miraeus’s new edition, p. 348.

[Col. 1337]

## Letter of Abbot Othelbodus to Otgiva, Countess of Flanders  
*(Around the year 1030.)*

It lists the saints and possessions of the monastery of Saint Bavo.

*(Edited by Miraeus, Donat. Belg., p. 348.)*

[Col. 1337A] To our most serene lady, Otgiva, countess, Othelbodus, by the grace of God abbot, and the other brothers of the Ghent monastery, offer the due services of obedience and prayer.

Your most excellent piety commanded us to write down the names of the saints whose bodies, by God’s favor, are venerated among us. Obeying your commands, we have briefly recorded and presented them to you, so that their memory might remain continually with you in the present, and so that you might merit to have a share with them in the future. Their names are these:

The first and foremost patron of our homeland is Saint Alewinus, surnamed Bavo.

[Note: Concerning Saints Bavo and Landoaldus and the others whose bodies once rested in the monastery of Bavo, see our Belgian Fasti.]

He was the most noble and wealthy count of the Hasbaye district, cousin of the most blessed virgin Gertrude. Converted with complete devotion of mind through the preaching of the blessed bishop Amandus—or rather, through the inspiration of almighty God—he abandoned his kindred and homeland, followed Christ and that same consul of Ghent, and, while striving to leave earthly things behind, merited to obtain heavenly ones. But the book of his Life relates these matters more fully.

[Col. 1338A] The second is Saint Landoaldus.

[Note: Concerning Saints Bavo and Landoaldus and the others whose bodies once rested in the monastery of Bavo, see our Belgian Fasti.]

Ordained bishop at Rome and summoned by the aforementioned bishop Amandus so that he might enlarge the Lord’s flock of the faithful in Gaul through holy preaching with him, after converting a large multitude to the Lord, he governed the bishopric of Trajectum for nine years. From childhood he formed Saint Lambert in heavenly studies. After many distinguished good works, he was buried in that same episcopal city.

The third is the blessed Amantius, archdeacon of that same bishop Saint Landoaldus; he was placed with him in the same chest.

The fourth is Adrianus the martyr, his envoy to King Childeric, who was killed by a robber while on that embassy and was buried together with him.

[Col. 1338B] The fifth is Saint Vinciana, a virgin and sister of that same Saint Landoaldus.

The sixth is the blessed Landrada, abbess of Belisia, who instructed the blessed Amalberga.

These saints came together with the blessed Landoaldus from Rome, sharing everywhere in his labor and preaching; they were buried together with him and, by God’s favor, brought all the way to us. But the book written about their deeds bears clearer witness to all these matters.

The seventh is Pharaildis, a virgin long ago laid to rest among us.

The eighth is Saint Livinus, a bishop who came from Scotland for the sake of prayer. He was killed by wicked men near a certain estate belonging by inheritance to Saint Bavo, and received from Christ the martyr’s palm.

The ninth is Macarius, of blessed memory, archbishop—as he himself testified—of the see of Antioch.

[Note: “As we ourselves saw.” Note the age of the writer, Abbot Athelbaldi. Macarius, however, died in 1012.]

As we ourselves saw, he was distinguished for wisdom and uprightness of conduct. After many hardships of pilgrimage, the Lord deigned to send him to us; having freed him from the troubles of this present life and exalted him to eternal glory, He wonderfully honored him with frequent signs of miracles.

[Col. 1339B] Furthermore, no one who has not seen with his own eyes how many relics of very many saints are preserved among us—namely, those of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, deposited here from the very beginning of Christianity—will readily believe either one who tells of them or one who writes about them. The greatest and most precious of these is a large portion of the saving wood, most clearly drenched with the blood of our Redeemer and most fittingly set in gold and precious gems.

Now, therefore, our sweetest lady, since you have been sufficiently informed about the bodies and relics of the saints, let your piety, if it pleases you, take notice of what sort and size this place once was, and into what poverty it has now fallen. Yet it was the head of the region, holding primacy over the other cities, and was called by the ancients the fortress of Ghent. There the holy bishop Amandus, after converting the pagans, built a temple for the Lord in honor of the blessed apostle Peter, incorporating great relics, and, establishing a community of monks there, most worthily strengthened it with apostolic privileges and royal decrees. There, too, the illustrious Father Bavo, most perfectly accomplished in every virtue, was sublimely exalted by almighty God.

As that place increased and grew daily through his merits and the signs of his virtues, and through the offerings of the faithful, after the passage of many years, because the sins of Christians demanded it, the Northmen came to the place, devastated it, burned it, and plundered everything, except for the bodies of the saints, which, chiefly through the labor of the faithful, were carried away in flight to the royal mount of Laon.

When they remained there for a long time because of fear of those Danes, who had occupied everything, their inheritance passed to others, and householders and outsiders alike plundered it. Moreover, the great Arnulf, the great-grandfather of our present lord, taking away very large portions from there, distributed them among his retainers according to what adjoined each of them.

[Col. 1340A] In the district of Courtrai: the estate of Elisachia, with its church and thirty-eight manses; likewise the estate of Sidenghem; and, in the estate of Holthem, fourteen manses; and in the district of Metelent, in the estate of Siclinis, four manses, with two mills and two brewing-houses; and in the district of Tournai, the estate called Fontaneia, with all its appurtenances; and in the district of Troyes, the estate called Columna, and another estate called Niola; and in the district of Brabant, the estate of Meren, with its church and seventy-seven manses; likewise the estate of Crainham, with its church and thirty manses; likewise Bellavium, with its church and all its appurtenances; likewise the estate of Brugecine, with all its revenues; likewise the estate of Milinia, with its church and all its dependencies; likewise the estate of Mershem, with its church, meadows, pastures, woods, and all its dependencies; likewise the estate of Singem, with its church and the other things belonging to it; likewise the estate of Badengem, with its church and the remaining revenues; likewise the estate of Mortesela, with its church and appurtenances; and in Masmine, five manses with a church.

In the district of Flanders: Bettingem, with its church and everything belonging to it; likewise Holtasma, with its church; the church of Ottold; and the church of Adingem. In the district of Mempiscus: the estate of Guntrengem, with its church. And in the district of Ghent, these estates: Hemthorp, Hufoine, Bergine, and Was monastery, with all their appurtenances, and the church situated at Merendra.

The counts of the provinces and the bishops also each obtained their portions, every one in his own places, until the time of our predecessor of pious memory, namely the lord abbot Odwinus. He approached the most pious emperor Otto and obtained from him certain estates adjoining his imperial domain. Some of these, having been unjustly seized there, remained so because of his death. Of them, the bishop of Liège retained two royal estates, Calmund and Meldrada.

[Note: Meldrada, commonly called Meldert, is a village in the diocese of Mechelen, under the deanery of Tienen, near Hoegaarden. The cult of Saint Ermelindis the virgin is celebrated there; see Molanus, *Natalibus SS. Belgii*, and our Fasti for 29 October.]

[Col. 1340D] With their appurtenances, as did Count Renoldus of Soissons, who retained the estate called Vasleia; Widmarus, the estate of Letbeca, with its church and all its appurtenances; Countess Uda, the estate of Warminia.

[Col. 1340D] With fifteen dwellings and its appurtenances; Count Renerus.

[Note: Renerus, or Raginerius, count of Hainaut.]

The estate of Letha, with its church and revenues; likewise Sconarda; and Robert, the estate of Grenberga; and many others, which it would be tedious to enumerate.

Meanwhile, we have briefly touched upon what was once unjustly or violently taken from this holy place. Now, if it pleases your piety to hear it, let us return to what remained for the saints, or what was later recovered after their return from the aforementioned mountain through the laborious toil of our parents.

[Note: Rodenborch, today Ardenbourg, is a fortified town of Flanders, now under the control of Catholic Holland. There was once a chapter there dedicated to Blessed Mary and Saint Bavo. The foundation charter is found in the supplement to Miraeus’s Diplomas.]

In the district of Flanders, that is, at Rodenborch, there are two churches, together with certain additional portions of land subsequently donated through the devotion of the faithful. Likewise at Baltreshanda, at Lappescura, and in the estate of Velhem, five measures or manses; and in the district of Mempiscus, in the estate of Cunengem, one church.

In the district of Ghent, in the estate of Merendre, five M.; in Wilda, five M.; and at Winderholt, one church; and between Marca and Ekkergem, sixteen M. with a church; and between Siedrengem and Singengem, and Achtine, ten M.; likewise in another estate called Singengem, on the river Scheldt, five M. with a church; likewise in Guddengem, five M.; and in Sualmis, an estate with churches and twenty M.

[Note: Sualmis, today Municx-Swolmen, is a village in the county of Aalst and the diocese of Mechelen, under the deanery of Ronse. Its patronage still belongs to the bishop of Ghent, as successor of the abbot of Bavo. The tithe belongs to the cathedral chapter of Ghent, which arose after the secularization of the abbey of Saint Bavo in 1536.]

[Col. 1341B] And in Papengem, an estate with a church and thirty M.; and in Kothem and Gisensela, six M. with a church and a half.

[Note: Papenghem, today Papinghem, is a village under the parish of Ulierzele, in the county of Aalst, the diocese of Mechelen, and the deanery of Oordegem; the bishop of Ghent likewise holds its patronage.]

[Note: Gisensela, today Gyseele, is a parish under the same deanery of Oordegem and the same patronage.]

These are a few of the many earlier properties that came into the possession of the saints.

And these are the properties that the aforementioned lord abbot Odwinus later obtained through the clemency of the pious emperor Otto: in the district of Tournai, the estate of Waterlos, with its church and all its dependencies; and in the county of Antwerp, the estate of Buchost, with its church and revenues.

[Note: Waterlos is a patrimony of Saint Bavo, a parish of French Flanders in the bishopric of Tournai and the deanery of Helchin. Its patronage still belongs to the bishop of Ghent.]

[Note: Buchoult, today Bouchout, is a parish in the diocese of Antwerp, not far from Antwerp, formerly called Bacwalde—mentioned in the testament of Saint Willibrord, *Cod. Donat. Piar.*, chapter 8—and hence under the patronage of the abbot of Saint Bavo of Ghent, but now under that of the bishop of Ghent.]

[Col. 1342A] He also graciously granted us precinct rights and tolls throughout his entire kingdom.

The kindness of our most benevolent lord Baldwin also came to the aid of our misery and poverty. From his own property, in the district of Flanders, at a place called Ruga, he donated two hundred measures of land suitable for sheep pastures; and in the district of Ghent, in the estate of Stota, seven measures; and in the district of Brabant, the estate of Selleca, with its church and ten measures; and in our estate of Waterlos, seven measures.

[Note: Selleca, today Zellich, is a parish in the diocese of Mechelen, between Brussels and Aalst; its patronage is the same as above.]

Thus, after diligently examining all these matters with our officials, we were scarcely able to reckon 1,200 M. serving the use of the brothers.

Behold, our most merciful lady, we have disclosed to you everything that formerly belonged to us, what came afterward, and what belongs to us now. Henceforth, look upon our place and have pity on us, so that our Lord almighty may, through the intercession of all His saints and through our humble prayers, look upon and govern our lord Baldwin, your children, and your kingdom. May He grant you a quiet and tranquil life in the present, and an eternal kingdom and rest in the future. Amen.

## In the Years of the Lord 1033–1048. Pope Benedict IX

[Col. 1341]

## Historical Notice

*(Ciaconius, De Vitis Romanorum Pontificum, p. 289.)*

[Col. 1341D] Benedict VIII, called IX, a Tusculan from the counts of Tusculum, previously named Theophylact, son of Alberic, brother of Benedict VIII and John XIX, a cardinal deacon, sat under the emperors Conrad the Salian and Henry III Augustus for twelve years, four months, and twenty days. He was created on 11 November and removed from the pontificate on 22 January 1045, in the twelfth year of his priesthood, first month, twelfth day.

Sylvester III, a Roman, son of John Laurence, bishop of Sabina, was created in schism against Benedict IX. He sat for one month and twenty-nine days.

[Col. 1342D] He was created on 22 January and was removed from the pontificate by Benedict IX on 11 March 1045.

Benedict VIII, called IX, after Sylvester III was expelled, sat again for one month and twenty-one days, from 10 March until 1 May of that year, on which day he voluntarily abdicated.

Benedict IX, with the support of the counts of Tusculum, was appointed in succession to his deceased uncle John. Since he harassed the Romans from day to day, now one way and now another, at length, after a conspiracy had been formed by many, he was driven from his see in the year of the Lord 1045, after twelve years of prolonged endurance. In his place they installed John, bishop of Sabina, on 22 January, and called him Sylvester III. The Tusculan nobles could not endure this insult. Therefore, making an assault with soldiers and aided by a gathered multitude of countrymen, they expelled Sylvester on 11 March and drove him from the Lateran patriarchate, restoring Benedict. Meanwhile, a certain third John, a Roman archpriest, invaded the same see and brought even greater deformity upon the Church; thus three pontiffs simultaneously disturbed the Roman see. But when Benedict saw that he was held in hatred and contempt by everyone and lacked sufficient strength to withstand so great a storm, he voluntarily abdicated his dignity. The man was John Gratianus, son of Peter Leo, a man of outstanding nobility in the City, who, after his consecration, was given the name Gregory VI.

Sylvester III, a Roman by birth, previously called John, formerly bishop of Sabina, was created during the schism through the efforts of certain Romans after Benedict had been expelled. He sat for one month and twenty-nine days without interruption. Holding the Lateran patriarchate, he was expelled by Benedict; he occupied the basilica and palace of Saint Peter and held them by force for some time, while nevertheless exercising the rights of the pontificate.

[Col. 1344A] That Benedict IX was the nephew of Benedict VIII is attested by Cardinal Peter Damian, who for that reason calls him Benedict the Younger. Hermannus Contractus, a distinguished writer of history, reports that he had previously been called Theophylact. Glaber, a monk of Cluny, states that he attained the pontificate before reaching puberty. Therefore, if there was any wrongdoing in corrupting the election, it is thought to be attributable not to him but to his friends and relatives.

During the pontificate of Benedict IX, the king of the English came to Rome out of devotion and in fulfillment of a vow. Having fulfilled his vow, he returned to his homeland. Some write that at this time Gerard the Venetian, bishop of the Hungarians, an excellent and highly learned man, endured martyrdom with the greatest equanimity at the hands of the enemies of the Christian faith. For he was tied to a cart, cast headlong from a very high mountain, and torn to pieces.

[Col. 1344B] Bruno of Würzburg, a theologian, and Hermannus Contractus, historian and mathematician, flourished in the year 1040.

The emperor Romanus IV in the East was killed around 1 March in the year 1035.

The emperor Michael IV the Paphlagonian, Augustus, ruled with his wife, the empress Zoe, for six years and six months.

The emperor Conrad died on 4 June in the year 1040.

The emperor Henry III the Black, Augustus VI, from Germany, emperor of the West, ruled the empire for seventeen years, four months, and twenty-two days.

The eastern emperor Michael IV abdicated in August of the year 1040.

The emperor Michael V Calaphates, Augustus, ruled with his wife Zoe Augusta for four months and five days.

The emperor Flavius Constantine XI Monomachus, Augustus, ruled with the empresses Zoe and Theodora for thirteen years, beginning in the year 1042.

[Col. 1343]

## Diplomatic Notice

*(Jaffé, Regesta Romanorum Pontificum, no. 359.)*

The bulls of Benedict IX were written by the hand of Sergius, scribe [or chief scribe] and notary of our sacred Lateran palace (1, 3, 4, 7, 8). By whose hands they were dated has not been recorded.

[Col. 1343]

## Letters and Diplomas of Pope Benedict IX

### I. Privilege Granted by Benedict IX to Gumbaldus, Abbot of Saint Croix of Bordeaux, in Favor of the Cell of Blessed Mary of Soulac  
*(Year 1036.)*

*[Marten, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, I, 156.]*

[Col. 1343D] Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gumbaldus, abbot, and the monks of Saint Croix of Bordeaux, and to his monks living in his monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, called Soulac: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist with benevolent compassion those distinguished by pious religion and to grant with eager devotion the requests of petitioners. For from this we undoubtedly earn the chief reward of profit from God, the creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition. Therefore, because you asked us to fortify the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary by the authority of the Apostolic See, to confirm inviolably and by perpetual right everything belonging to it, and to establish and strengthen by the page of our privilege that it should remain free from every yoke under the authority of any person whatsoever except the abbot of Saint Croix and his monks, for this reason, moved by your prayers, through this privilege of our authority we decree that all cultivated and uncultivated lands, slaves and female slaves, and everything else that can be said or named as belonging to the same monastery, as well as whatever in the future may be donated or offered there by kings, dukes, or any of the faithful, shall by our authority remain free from every outsider.

Therefore we wish that no viscount, no count, no archbishop, no bishop, and no person great or small exercise power over the things mentioned or presume to use force against them, nor dare to inflict any adversity contrary to this privilege. By apostolic authority we prohibit all archbishops and bishops, and all other clergy, from exercising any jurisdiction over the aforesaid monastery or over any of its dependencies.

We grant absolution so that, if any excommunicated person comes to the Mother of Christ from whatever region, from sunrise to sunset, he shall be absolved on God’s behalf and ours from every excommunication—whether imposed by an archbishop or a bishop—except that of the abbot of Saint Croix and his monks living in the aforesaid place, for as long as he remains under the power of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God. To them we grant the power of binding and loosing against all evil Christians who may wish to do anything harmful to the aforesaid monastery or to its inhabitants.

We order that the church of Saint Croix, founded by the counsel and command of the Roman Church, together with its monks and all its dependencies, be free from the excommunication or harassment of every person. Likewise, we wish that no bishop in whose parish the same monastery is situated dare excommunicate your lord and abbot, or any of your clergy serving in the monastery of Saint Mary, or summon them to a synod. By apostolic authority, under the observance of our judgment and divine judgment, we establish the prohibition of anathema.
