We establish that when the abbot of the monastery of Saint Croix dies, no count, archbishop, bishop, prince, or any person whatsoever shall, for any reason of greed, elect or consecrate an abbot in the monastery of Saint Croix. Rather, he shall be elected by the entire congregation living there and in the other churches subject to it, together with the faithful and elders of that place, and shall be consecrated by us and our pontifical successors by common counsel, if the archbishop in whose diocese it is situated should refuse to consecrate him.

We also grant permission to you and to your brothers living in the monastery of Saint Mary of Soulac to have all the sacred vessels consecrated by whatever bishop you wish, to have your clergy ordained, and to receive chrism.

But if any person of whatever rank should presume to act against this privilege of apostolic confirmation, or should attempt to bring a lawsuit against the aforesaid monastery with all its dependencies, or should be disobedient to our commands in any of the matters written here, then, by the authority of God and of us, let him be not only anathema maranatha—that is, bound forever in chains as one lost—but also excluded from the kingdom of God. Whoever, however, supports and observes this privilege with pious generosity shall merit to obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Sergius, chief scribe of our sacred palace, in the month of October, in the fifth indiction.

### II. Letter of Benedict IX to Rolandus, Provost, and the Other Canons of the Church of Saint Florence  
*(Year 1036.)*

*[Ughelli, Italia Sacra, III, 56.]*

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved in Christ Rolandus, provost of the Church of Saint Florence, and to the other canons, your fellow brothers, and your successors forever.

If we satisfy the just petitions of the servants of God, we undoubtedly observe the apostolic commands. Therefore, moved by your prayers, dearest son, we confirm and strengthen for you and your canonical successors everything that we granted in the document, and it is established that the confirmation which your bishop appears to have made for you in our presence was written down. The rule that is now preserved in your canonry is thus to be maintained, for through the same document the bishop appears to have entrusted and subjected the canonry to the protection and defense of our apostolic authority and that of our successors, so that you may be able to preserve it securely and free from every injury.

Therefore, moved by this petition of yours, we have declared that we receive you as provost, and your successors, who will lead the canonical life, under the protection of our apostolic defense. We likewise receive all the possessions, estates, and lands that your canonry possesses and will possess: namely, near the city of Florence, the King’s Meadow with all the manses and territories that your aforesaid canonry now possesses and holds in the Florentine estate; the estate of Saint Andrew with everything belonging to it; the entire estate of Quinto; the entire estate of Cintoria, as you yourselves appear to hold and possess it; and that portion which Petrus the primicerius appears to have usurped contrary to canonical statutes; the parish of Exinea, with its estate, manses, and all the territories and tithes that appear to belong to that parish or estate.

Moreover, everything that Theuzo, son of Lepistus, donated for the salvation of his soul in the church of Saint John or to the same canonry; the land of Saint Proculus in the aforesaid parish; the estate situated within the parish of Saint Peter called Valea, with all its dependencies and appurtenances; and whatever, anywhere in the same diocese, the canonry then possessed or appeared to retain; and whatever Gerard the archpriest held as a benefice from the Church of Florence, both in tithes and in manses and estates; and whatever Abbot Stephanus held as a benefice.

Likewise, whatever benefices belonged to the primicerius; and the parish of Saint Hippolytus situated at the Elsa; and the field and garden beside the church of Saint Reparata.

All these things, just as they have already been granted and confirmed to you by Gerard, your bishop, so we confirm and establish them in perpetuity for you and your successors, together with all your movable and self-moving property that you now possess or that belongs to you anywhere, and whatever you may hereafter justly and lawfully acquire from the bishop of that city or from other public or private persons.

Therefore, commanding, we order and confirm by apostolic authority that neither the bishop of that city nor any person, great or small, shall have the power to dispossess, trouble, harass, or inflict any diminution upon you in regard to your property that justly and lawfully belongs to you, so long as you live canonically. But if any rash person should dare to do so and does not make amends within forty days, let him be bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God until he offers worthy satisfaction. Whoever proves himself the guardian of our decree, however, shall have the blessing and grace of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us.

+ Farewell in good health, and so forth.

### III. Benedict IX Confirms the Property and Episcopal Rights of the Church of Silva Candida  
*(Year 1037.)*

*[Ughelli, Italia Sacra, I, 100.]*

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable bishop of the Church of Saint Silva Candida, and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist with benevolent compassion those distinguished by pious religion and to grant with eager devotion the requests of petitioners. For from this we shall obtain the chief reward of profit from God, the creator of all, since venerable places, suitably ordered, will undoubtedly be brought to a better condition.

Therefore, because your prudence asked us to grant and confirm to you the aforesaid bishopric with all its dependencies, which appear to lie in various places or which are known to have been unjustly retained or seized by certain persons, moved by your pious prayers, first, as you value most highly, we grant you the episcopal dignity, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, and confirm it by apostolic authority in every way we can. In honor of Jesus Christ our Lord, we confirm to you and your successors the entire estate called Buxus, in which the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda appears to have been built as an episcopal see. You have also fortified and enclosed it through your own efforts with a wall and moat, and have filled it adequately with people and priests.

We likewise subject all these things to your power and that of your successors, so that no one among our pontifical successors, or any other person, may dare to constrain them by reason of the glandaticum, herbaticum, or any other fodrum, levy, court, payment, or device, or in any way compel them to give anything. Thus, as we have said, it shall remain forever in your power and that of your successors, without contradiction from any person, and you and your successors may build or construct the same church as you see fit, just as you have done.

Likewise, we grant and confirm the entire estate called Avion, and Mount Jordan, with houses, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, and with the slaves, female slaves, and tenant farmers of both sexes and every age living there, together with all their appurtenances, situated in the territory of Silva Candida, bounded as follows: on the first side by the land of the aforesaid bishopric; on the second side by the stream called Galeria; on the third side by Ulbasol; and on the fourth side by Criptule.

Also the estate called Mons Aureus, with all its appurtenances: on one side, the mountain called Jordan; on another side, Criptule; on the third side, the estate called Palmi; on the fourth side, the estate of Laureta; and on the fifth side, the land of the monastery of Saint Martin.

Likewise, the estate called Mons Grunduli, with everything belonging to it, bounded as follows: on one side, the estate of Mons Aureus; on another side, the estate of Criptule and Ulbarolo; on the third side, the estate of Palmi and the estate called Oripo.

The estate called Oripo, with all its appurtenances, is bounded as follows: on one side, the land of the monastery of Saint Martin; on another side, the estate called Insula Sancta; on the third side, the estate of Saint Peter and the estate of Mons Grunduli; and on the fourth side, the land of the estate of Saint Peter.

Likewise, the estates called Scriptule and Palmi, with all their appurtenances, bounded as follows: on the first side, the estate of Fulisan; on the second side, the estate of Laurete; on the third side, the land of Saint Martin; and on the fourth side, the estate of Sevonum.

Entirely likewise, the estate of Isidore, with all its appurtenances: on one side, the land of Saint Martin; on another side, Castrangotol; on the third side, the Holy Table; and finally, the estate called the Holy Table itself, with everything belonging to it, bounded on one side by the estate called Bucce; on the second side by the mountain called Dompnico; on the third side by Musana; and on the fourth side by Saint Lawrence of Panti.

In the same way, the estate of Saint Basilides, with everything belonging to it, bounded on one side by the estate of Saints Peter and Paul; on another side by the valley called Intentionara; on the third side by Vivarolus; and on the fourth side by the monastery of Saint Stephen.

Furthermore, the estate of Panzius, with all its appurtenances: on one side, the estate of Apronianum; on another side, Silva Candida; on the third side, Musanellum; on the fourth side, Canullanum; and on the fifth side, the land of Aureliana.

And the wood of Saint Stephen, with the Salarian Way; likewise the estate of Lauretum, with everything belonging to it, bounded on one side by the land of Saint Peter; on another side by the land of Saint Martin; on the third side by the mountain of Iliodorus; and on the fourth side by the estate of Oripo, or the estate of Paul.

And the estate of Serianus, with all its appurtenances, bounded on one side by the land of Saint Martin; on the second side by Silva Candida; on the third side by the Holy Table; and on the fourth side by the wood of Saint Peter.

Also the estate called Castagnetolum, bounded on one side by the Four Holy Brothers; on the second side by the estate of Orbanula; on the third side by Musana; and on the fourth side by Massanellus.

And the wood called Mag, with everything belonging to it, bounded on one side by the stream of Galera and on the other side by the mountain called “the handmaid of God.”

All the estates named above and the farmsteads, with their lands, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated woods, situated in the territory of Silva Candida approximately twelve miles from the city of Rome, together with the water mill operating on the stream called Galeria and everything belonging to it, and the land of Semitarisia called Pastinum Longum, bounded on one side by Gualdsidincus; on another side by the land of Saint Peter called Campo Mastali; on the third side by the estate of Mons Arcionis; and on the fourth side by Mount Paurum, are established beside the same bishopric.

Likewise, another water mill on that same stream, with everything belonging to it, shall belong to the jurisdiction of the same bishopric.

[Col. 1349C] Moreover, following our predecessors, we grant and confirm to you the estate called Cesana, together with its holdings and its tenants, who are called Furculo, Tandilianus, and Martinianus. Likewise, the colonies of Solarium, Cortina, and Gradolfum; the colony of Vallis, of Fontana, and of Sanctus; the colony of Castagna Cupa and of Calbellus; the colony of Besanus, or by whatever other names they are called, together with all their houses, vineyards, farmsteads, and appurtenances. Also all these together with their boundaries, termini, and limits; lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, fruit trees—fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing—of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, perennial waters, buildings, ruined structures, underground chambers, sandpits, and their adjoining properties; together with the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle, built within that estate [Col. 1349D], along with the male and female tenants, household dependants, and laborers, their sons and daughters, and their grandchildren residing there or otherwise belonging to it, wherever they may be found, with every census and payment, levy, and compulsory service, and whatever ought to be paid in full from that estate called Cesana to our Holy Roman Church according to customary practice; and with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid estate of Cesana, situated in the territory of Nepi, twenty miles, more or less, from the city of Rome, from the body of the patrimony of Tuscia, belonging to our holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve. Its boundaries are: on one side, the land of the monastery of Saint Stephen the Lesser at Saint Peter; on another side, [Col. 1350A] the wood and land that belonged to John the Grammarian; on the third side, the pastureland called Dompmea; and on the fourth side, the estate of Claudiana.

We also confirm to you, in full, the farmsteads, colonies, and castle called Dalmachia, with its holdings and farmsteads, namely Attici, Dalmachia Balneo, Stabbla, Massa Juliana, or by whatever other names they are called, together with the male and female households and the tenants belonging to each place, with houses, vineyards, lands, woods, meadows, and watercourses, and with everything belonging to the aforesaid farmsteads, colony, and castle, situated in the territory of Nepi, twenty miles, more or less, from the city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on one side, the road that runs between the military estate of Curte de Capracorio and the land of the pasture of [Col. 1350B] Saint Peter; on another side, the land of Monte Arsitia and Focazan, which is called Columnella; on the third side, the land of Curte Capracorio, which is called Matera; and on the fourth side, the land of Saint Lawrence, which is called Silicara, and the stream that runs through Buxetum and Madulanum.

Furthermore, we grant and confirm to you, and through you in perpetuity to your episcopal see, the lands and vineyards in full whose names are Campomastali, or the wood of Campo Monti, and Lacusello, together with all their boundaries, termini, and limits; vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, buildings, ruined structures, attached and adjoining properties, and everything generally and wholly belonging to them [Col. 1350C], all situated in the territory of Silva Candida. Their boundaries are: on one side, the land of the aforesaid episcopal see; on another side, the land of Gratianus, which is called Mons Arioni, or Majoratu, as far as the stream of Campo Monti; on the third side, beginning at that stream, as far as the valley of Arenula, and Buxetum, and from there through Novelletum as far as the ancient road on which a marble pillar lies, and as far as Cesa de Calariculo; and on the fourth side, from Cava de Castagneto as far as the stream called Galera, and as far as the wood of your episcopal see.

We also grant and confirm to you and to your successors all that land and wood which Calolidus had once seized and had renounced in writing to your predecessor, Bishop Guido. Their names are these: the valley of John Ecco, and [Col. 1350D] Mons Vespuleti, the valley of Giusule, and the mountain called Puzali. Their boundaries are: on one side, Galeria; on the second side, the ford called de Perenna, and from there by the road and along the boundary as far as the three wells situated on the ridge of the mountain called Puzal; and along that mountain ridge and the boundary as far as the public ancient Silicina road, and the ditch that lies beside that same road; and from there along the boundary and road, and by the lucernaria situated on the same boundary, and along that boundary as far as the limits where the wood of the aforesaid episcopal see ends, and the wood of the monastery of Saint Martin extends as far as Saint Peter; and the farmstead called Rusina, and at that same place the Columnella appears to stand fixed; on the third side, the greater boundary and the public road that leads as far as the estate called Mensa [Col. 1351A] Sanctarum, which belongs to the aforesaid episcopal see; and on the fourth side, the mountain and wood called Ballaria, held by your own bishopric, situated beside Buccege and beside the farmstead called Rusina.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to you in full the estate called Maurorum, with all its boundaries and limits, situated in the territory of Silva Candida, on the Cornelian Way, twelve miles, more or less, from the city. Its boundaries are: on one side, the road leading to Mensa Sancta; on another side, the mountain called Ovea and Caput Poncinum; on the third side, the road leading to the saltworks; and on the fourth side, beside that road, Castagnetulum and Mons Armatus, together with Ficarola, all belonging to the aforesaid episcopal see.

Likewise, the estate called Campus Trojanus, the estate called [Col. 1351B] Bursicella, the estate of Gradilia, and the estate called Mons de Sorbo, all in full with their boundaries and appurtenances, situated on the Aurelian Way, twelve miles, more or less, from the city of Rome.

Likewise, six full portions of the estate called Atticianus, and the mountain called Dominicus, with all their appurtenances, situated on the Aurelian Way, thirteen miles, more or less, from the city of Rome. Its boundaries are: on one side, Massa Margarita and Casandria, belonging to Saints Basilides, Tripodis, and Magdalene, which is the property of your aforesaid episcopal see; on the second side, the estate and the estate called Agellus, which belong to that same bishopric; on the third side, the estate of Verecundus, which belongs to the monastery of Saint Martin at Saint Peter; and on the fourth side, the other six portions of the aforesaid estate Atticianus.

[Col. 1351C] Likewise, eight estates—Lapmianus, Pathinus, Margaritus, their Greek [names], Casanellus, Casapupulis, and Savinulus, which is also called Sambuculus—adjoining one another, situated on the same Aurelian Way, twelve miles, more or less, from the city of Rome, in the territory of Saint Basilides. Their boundaries are: on one side, the estate of Atticianus; on another side, the estate of Casandrus; on the third side, the estate called Patriciorum, or whatever other neighboring properties there may be.

Also the estate called Judaeorum in full, with its boundaries and limits and everything belonging to it, situated in the aforesaid territory of Silva Candida.

Furthermore, we grant and confirm to you in full one farmstead called Urbanum, or by whatever other names it is called, in [Col. 1351D] which there are lands, fields, meadows, pastures, and everything belonging to it, situated in the territory of Sutri. Its boundaries are as they are or were from the beginning.

Likewise, we confirm to you and to the Church over which you preside the estate situated on the Appian Way in the territory of Velletri, namely the estate of Urbana, with Capuanus and Caesarianus, together with the holdings belonging to that same estate, with every right, equipment, and instrument, and with its boundaries and termini. The church of Saint Felix is situated there, as is recorded in your documents and as is also read in full on the stone tablets that appear to be set into the wall before the doors of the basilica of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda.

Furthermore, we grant and confirm to you, within this city of Rome, the land where the great house once stood, together with everything belonging to it, situated in the place called Diburum. [Col. 1352A] Its boundaries are: on one side, the land where the house of Marcezia, wife of Stephen the Seneschal, stood; on another side, the land where the house of Butius, son of Simeon, stood; on the third side, the public road; and on the fourth side, the greater ancestral property and the road leading to the monastery of Saint Cyriacus.

Moreover, without doing anything new—namely, since we know that our predecessors did the same for the most holy churches of Albano, Ostia, and Porto, and for other churches—we establish by this page of our apostolic decree, beginning with the present sixth indiction, and confirm by the authority of the chief of the apostles, that priests, deacons, monks, mansionarii, clerics of whatever order or dignity, nuns [Col. 1352B], and deaconesses shall all be exempt from lay service, jurisdiction, and public payment in Galeria, whether within the castle or living outside it. Thus, if the emperor, marquis, their envoys, or our successors should come there, no expense shall in any way be collected from the aforesaid persons by public officials, nor shall any injury be inflicted upon them in any way.

Rather, for love of the Most High God, from whose lot clerics take their name, let them be suitably honored. Let them render an account only to you, your successors the bishops, your vicedomini, or our officials, and await your judgment, so that God may be honored and you and your successors may not be deprived of the service and obedience of your sacred orders. Let them remain under your judgment [Col. 1352C] and jurisdiction, according to the tenor of this our apostolic decree, all contradiction by anyone being removed. Thus, no count, viscount, castaldus, chamberlain, or any other person shall dare to lead them into service or compulsory labor, summon them to jurisdiction or a court, lodge in their dwellings, invade them, or presume to defraud them. Rather, only by your command and with their willing consent shall their affairs be regulated, arranged, judged, and settled as is fitting.

Moreover, if any Christian should die there without an heir or testament, we decree by apostolic authority that the Church over which, by God’s authority, you preside, together with you and your successors, shall succeed to his property according to law. We decree that a third [part or payment] be rendered to you and your successors by all the churches, priests, and clerics of Galeria, without any diminution.

[Col. 1352D] In like manner, we grant and confirm to you the lands and houses where the officials used to live, with all their appurtenances, situated in Galeria beside the church of the blessed Nicholas, confessor of Christ, which you yourself consecrated before the garden of the castle. That house, moreover, appears more suitable for the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas and for you and your clerics, although lay and secular persons remain in it to commit lust and secular crimes. For it is not right that a house of prostitution and dishonest profit should be attached to a church. We also caused you to be invested with that house through Benedict the oblationarius.

[Col. 1353A] Likewise, we grant and confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity the church of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, situated beside our palace, and the place called Cellarium or Lardirium, in full, with its various underground chambers, walls, and buildings, as well as vineyards, gardens with olive trees and other fruit trees, various enclosures, ruined structures, and lands, as they appear to be delimited. The boundary begins beside our palace called Scuta, and from there runs straight behind the vestiarum to your aforesaid basilica Ulpia; from there beside the wall of our scriniarius, across the land where columns appear to lie, straight to the road; and along that road descending to the boundary that lies in your land and in the land of the priests of the monastery of Saint Pancratius [Col. 1353B]. The boundary then turns along the aforesaid *ellium* [reading uncertain] and wall beside the land of those priests, where olive trees appear to stand, straight to the small tower in the wall of this revered city of Rome, together with that small tower and wall, or the Saracen tower, with the underground chambers and ruined structures beneath and beside it, as well as the other towers extending along one side beside your land; and the marsh, with the whole of that marsh, reaching the public road that leads to the church of Saint John the Baptist or to our palace. From there it turns back beside the land that belonged to Elperinus and Azo, brothers, and the vineyard of the church of Saint Nicholas, or the land of the heirs of Maio Capuanus, or the little garden that once belonged to Angelus [Col. 1353C], or the earthen house situated beside another public road leading to our aforesaid Lateran palace.

Likewise, we confirm to you the church of Saint Martina with all its property and appurtenances, situated at Rome near the mountain called Augustus.

[Col. 1353D] Also the church of the holy Adalbert and Paulinus, together with the church of Saint Benedict and all their property and appurtenances, as you hold them today, situated within this city of Rome on the island of Lycaonia, so that they may serve you and your successors, whenever you wish, as an episcopal residence, a suitable refuge, and a convenient dwelling, as the church of Porto has the church of Saint John between the two bridges. The priests and clerics who from time to time serve in the same church of Saints Adalbert, Paulinus, and Benedict we wish to be subject to you as proper daughters of your Church. We withdraw them from every other jurisdiction and entrust them to your fatherhood alone, so that they may await your judgment alone, serve under your authority, and in all things obey your reasonable commands. Thus, with our apostolic authority, it shall be perpetually lawful for you to order, govern according to God, instruct, and correct them in whatever manner pleases you.

At the same time, we grant and confirm to you all the parishes and parish churches, with their appurtenances and adjacent properties, namely: the parish of Saint Mary at Silva Candida with its titles; the title of Saints John and Paul at Lucanum; the title of Saint Angelus at Musanum; the title of Saint Donatus at Majorata; and the parish of Saint Gregory at [Col. 1354A] Galeria with its titles; the title of Saint Gregory in that place; the title of Saint Anastasius at Musanum; and the parish of Saint Angelus at Duscitulum with its lands; likewise the parish of Saint John at Nono with its lands and titles; the title of Saint Marcianus in that village with its lands; the title of Saint Andrew with its titles; also the title of Saint Mary; the title of Saint Nicholas, which is in the castle of Monte Destini; the title of Saint Mary with its lands; furthermore the parish of Saint Pancratius with its lands and titles; the title of Saint Mary on the island with its lands; the parish of Saint Lucia on the island with its lands; likewise the parish of Saint John on the island with its title and territory; the title of Saint Gregory in that place; and the parish of Saint Paul at Formello with its lands, vineyards, gardens, olive groves, and titles; the title of Saint Sylvester at [Col. 1354B] Columna with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Angelus at Olibanum with its lands and gardens; the title of Saint Marcianus with its lands; the title of Saint Genesius at Dalmachia with its lands; the title of Saint Lawrence at Formello with its titles and gardens; the title of Saint Mary with its territory; the title of the Savior with its lands; the title of Saint John in that place with its territory; the title of Saint Peter with its land; the title of Saint Angelus at Laureto; the title of Saint Valentine at Cryptula; and likewise the parish of Saint Cornelius at Capricornus.

By the page of this privilege and decree of yours, we perpetually confirm to the aforesaid episcopal see, with its lands, vineyards, olive groves, and titles: the title of Saint Pancratius with its lands; the title of Saint Mary with its lands and meadow [Col. 1354C]; the title of Saint Valentine with its lands, olive grove, and meadow; the title of Saint Donatus with its lands; the title of Saint Mary with its lands; the title of Saint Lawrence with its lands; the title of Saint Anastasius with its lands and vineyards; the parish of Saint Titus, not far from Civitella, with its vineyards, lands, and titles; the parish of Saint Paul at Formella with its vineyards, lands, and titles; the title of Saint Sylvester and Saint Angelus with their lands and vineyards; and the parish of Saint Donatus at Collina with its lands, vineyards, olive groves, and titles; the title of Saint Mary with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Christina with its lands, vineyards, and woods; the title of Saint Gregory with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Martin with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Cassianus with its lands, vineyards, and three households; the title of Saint Anastasius with its lands and vineyards; and the title of Saint Justina with its lands and vineyards; [Col. 1354D] the title of Saint Angelus with its lands; the title of Saint Gregory with its lands and vineyards; likewise the parish of Saint Marcellus at the Fourteenth Mile with its lands, vineyards, olive grove, titles, and all its appurtenances; the title of Saint Angelus with its lands and vineyards; finally, the parish of Saint Peter at Beczano with its lands, vineyards, larger olive grove, and woods; and the titles of Saint John, Saint Stephen, and Saint Mary at Pentpertusa; the title of Saint Mary at Sepefane with its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Stephen at Matera; the title of Saint Mary at Matera; the title of Saint Blaise at Scrofano; the title of Saint John at Scrofano itself; and that of Saint Eugenia at Matera; the title of Saint Lawrence at Scrofano with all its lands and vineyards; the title of Saint Eugenia with its lands and vineyards; likewise the parish of Saint Mary at [Col. 1355A] Olibula with its lands, vineyards, and title, and Saint Angelus with its lands and vineyards.

We likewise grant and confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity, just as they were granted and confirmed by the most holy Pope Sergius and by our other predecessors, the five monasteries—Saint Stephen the Greater and the Lesser, Saints John and Paul, the blessed Martin, and Thecla—situated beside the great church of Saint Peter, or in the other churches established throughout the entire Leonine City. If it should be necessary to consecrate them, no other bishop shall presume to undertake such ministry or consecration, except you and your successors, the bishops of the Church of Silva Candida, forever.

[Col. 1355B] We grant and confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity Holy Saturday for celebrating the sacrament of baptism and performing the entire office in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, and upon the great altar. Whatever gold or silver, cloth, wax, or other things may be placed, offered, or cast upon that venerable altar or at the confession, or offered to you, from the third hour of the day—that is, from the hour at which we wish you to enter the church to arrange and perform the said office—until you have completed the Mass of the holy Lord’s Day, shall come, without any contradiction, into the possession of you and your successors through your custodians.

And because, in the time of our predecessor Lord John, Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday, and Good Friday were irreverently celebrated in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, from which almost all the churches received their teaching as from a mother and mistress—so that on Palm Sunday no procession with palms was held there, on Maundy Thursday “Glory to God in the highest” was not sung, and on Good Friday the office was not performed there with the reverence it deserved—we were grieved. Desiring to improve this through you and your successors, we establish, as was established, granted, and confirmed to you by that same predecessor, that every year on Palm Sunday you shall depart in procession from the church of Saint Mary in Thermis, and, coming to the great altar of Saint Peter, celebrate Mass.

Likewise, every year on Maundy Thursday, [Col. 1355D] we wish you and your successors to celebrate Mass upon the altar of Saint Peter, sing “Glory to God in the highest,” prepare the holy chrism, and perform whatever pertains to a bishop. Also, every year on Good Friday, you and your successors shall reverently perform the entire office upon that same great altar of Saint Peter, as befits you.

In these three Masses—the first, the Mass of Palm Sunday; the second, the Mass of Maundy Thursday; and the third, the office of Good Friday—whatever gold or silver, cloth, wax, or other things shall have been placed or cast upon the aforesaid altar of Saint Peter or at the confession, or offered to you from the hour at which those Masses and offices begin until they are completed, shall likewise come, without any contradiction, into the possession of you and your successors through your custodians [Col. 1356A].

During these five days, if it should seem useful to you and your successors to have one of our deacons minister in honor of Saint Peter and out of reverence for you, we wish you to request this.

We grant and confirm to you and your successors the authority of that same church of Saint Peter, its aforesaid monasteries, all its mansionarii and dwellings, and the entire Leonine City, to enthrone and install the Roman pontiff in the apostolic see. To you, who are daily engaged in the service of Saint Peter, we entrust this. We also specially summon you, together with the others, for the blessing. Likewise, when the emperor is to be anointed and consecrated, we first summon your fraternity and that of your successors, the bishops [Col. 1356B], so that those to whom the governance of the whole Church of Saint Peter and of the Leonine City has been entrusted may first bless him.

Moreover, all the sacred offices and ministries that we and our successors ought to perform, if we are unable to perform them because of illness or some other concern, we decree by apostolic authority shall be performed by you and your successors, both in the aforesaid venerable church of Saint Peter and its monasteries and throughout the entire Leonine City.

The consecration of the altars of Saint Peter and its monasteries, as well as the consecration of the churches, altars, priests, clerics, and deaconesses of the entire Leonine City, we grant and confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity, as stated [Col. 1356C] above.

Whatever customary payments are due to you from the officials of the great altar, we confirm to you and your successors by this document. Likewise, on Holy Saturday, for the meal, twelve solidi in denarii of whatever currency is current at the time; five on each Ember Saturday; and two, together with a candle of oil and candles, for each feast on which you are required to spend the night there. Likewise, on the feast of Saint Peter and during its octave, on Gaudete Sunday, on the feasts of Saint Andrew, Epiphany, Ascension, Pentecost, and Saint Rufina, thirty pounds of wax; two measures of oil; and two pounds of frankincense. As for hanging candles with their fixtures and lamps, let there be enough, as has always been customary [Col. 1356D].

On Easter Monday, according to the ancient custom, at Staffile, where we dismount from our horse, you receive us and our successors. We grant you the gloves, which we are also accustomed to use at Mass, as a memorial of our service. Because you have always served the Holy Roman Church faithfully and purely, we decree by apostolic authority that you, and not only you but all your successors as bishops, shall perpetually be librarians of our see—and rightly so, since you labor in the apostolic Church and always stand as faithful witnesses in apostolic writings.

All the aforesaid things, as stated above, beginning with the aforesaid sixth indiction, together with six portions of saltworks situated in the New Field and adjoining one another, beside the saltworks of the heirs of John We and of Peter the cardinal [Col. 1357A], we give, bestow, grant, confirm, and establish in perpetuity for you, your successors the bishops, and also your church of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, for the use and benefit of that venerable episcopal see and all its bishops who shall hold the aforesaid Church in their time.

We establish, by apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that none of our successors who are pontiffs, nor anyone who has held public office, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever dare or presume to act against this pontifical privilege of ours concerning anything contained above, or to alienate, remove, or diminish it. Rather, we decree that everything remain firm and secure for all time, just as it has been established and confirmed by us [Col. 1357B].

If anyone, which we do not desire, should presume with reckless boldness to oppose any part of this our apostolic privilege, or to violate it, or dare to break it, and should refuse to be obedient and observant in all things, let him know that, by the authority of God Almighty our Lord and of Peter, chief of the apostles, whose place we occupy, unworthy though we are, yet by God’s favor, he is bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God. Let him be assigned to burn with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the ungodly, as their companion in hell.

But whoever, with devout regard, proves to be the guardian and observant keeper of this our apostolic privilege, may, through the merits and prayers of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, [Col. 1357C] and of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, deserve to receive in the heavenly citadels rewards, the grace of blessing, and mercy from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and may deserve to obtain and find eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniarius and notary of our sacred palace, in the month of November, in the aforesaid sixth indiction. Farewell.

Benedict, bishop of Fallarita and Castellum. I, Gregory, designated by the Holy Roman Church for the governance of the Church of Todi. I, Leo, deacon of the Holy Roman Church. Benedict, oblationarius. Benedict, cardinal of the title of Equitius. Bonizo, priest and vicedominus of Saint Rufina, and, by the grace of God, designated bishop of Tuscania. I, Crescentius, subdeacon of John the Roman. [Col. 1357D] Therefore we decree, etc. If, then, anything, etc. But to all, etc. Amen.

### IV. Benedict IX confirms the rights and possessions of the monastery of Cassino, “whose abbot’s consecration,” he says, “we recently received through the gift of the most pious emperors Henry and Conrad of the Romans.” (The clause appended to the published copies of this bull, from the word “written” through “twenty-ninth,” belongs, as Gattula notes in *Hist. Casin.* 119 from Peter’s Register, no. 18, to the document of Benedict VIII [above, Benedict VIII, no. 29]. According to him, this charter of Benedict IX ends with these words: “Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniarius and notary of our sacred palace, on the Kalends of July, in the fourth indiction. Farewell.”) (Year 1038.)

[Margarini, *Bullar. Casin.*, II, 79.]

[Col. 1358A]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ to our most beloved son Richerius, venerable and religious abbot, consecrated and ordained by us, of the most sacred monastery of the blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, situated on the mountain called the Castle of Cassino, and to his holy congregation.

If, compelled by the ministry with which we appear to be entrusted, we ought to grant the requested apostolic assistance to all churches, those that look especially to our apostolate alone ought to obtain it all the more swiftly and fully, the more opportunely we recognize that they need it, so that no injury may come to venerable places received under apostolic protection which is not averted by the resistance of our arm. Finally, we believe God to be the rewarder of these our cares [Col. 1358B], whom we desire to be praised peacefully in those same places. For the praises and prayers of those dwelling there will be acceptable in proportion as their minds, with our assistance, have been removed from every disturbance.

Therefore, because you asked us to fortify by privilege, after the manner of our predecessors, the monastery of Saint Benedict situated on Mount Cassino—whose abbot’s consecration we recently received through the gift of the most pious Henry and Conrad, emperors of the Romans—and to defend and confirm its properties under threat of anathema, we have yielded to your prayers. We grant and confirm the aforesaid monastery to you, consecrated by us, and to your successors, [Col. 1358C] who are to be consecrated by us and our successors in perpetuity, without any Simoniacal corruption intervening, together with all its churches, cells, castles, etc.

After your death, let no one appoint an abbot there except one whom the convent and the common will of the brothers shall have chosen from that congregation itself. Let the elected abbot come freely and without payment to us or our successors for consecration. But if he should come from elsewhere, or should prefer to be consecrated by some other archbishop or bishop, then let both the consecrator and the consecrated be anathema.

And below. Furthermore, by apostolic censure and invocation of the divine judgment, we command that no bishop presume to excommunicate a priest in the aforesaid monastery or in the churches subject to it, or to summon him to a synod, etc.

But if anyone, which we do not desire, should presume with criminal boldness to oppose or in any way transgress these provisions established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the chains of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God; and that he has been assigned to burn with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in eternal fires and punishments [Col. 1358D].

But whoever, with devout regard, proves to be the guardian and in all things the keeper of this apostolic ordinance and of the matters pertaining to the worship of God, may, through the intercession of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and of the blessed confessor Benedict, obtain in abundance the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written [Col. 1359A] by the hand of Stephen, chief scriniarius of the holy apostolic see, in the month of June, in the sixth indiction.

Farewell.

Given on the Kalends of July through the hands of Boso, bishop of the holy Church of Tivoli and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year 1038 from the incarnation of the Lord; in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Benedict VIII; in the twelfth year of the reign of Lord Conrad, emperor of the Romans; in the sixth indiction, on the twenty-ninth day of June.

### V. Benedict IX sends an assistant to Poppo, archbishop of Trier; he announces that Simeon has been enrolled among the saints. (Year 1041.)

[Hontheim, *Hist. Trevir. diplom.*, vol. I, p. 376.]

[Col. 1359B]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Poppo, archbishop of Trier, distinguished not so much by his own merits as by the divine gift.

Having received your letter of reverence, and having read and reread it, we have laid its force in the depths of our heart, so that, when you asked, we might grant what you desired. For we ought, insofar as we can, to imitate the rule of that Master who was not obstinate toward those who asked rightly; who did not delay those seeking him in truth; and who was not slow to open to those persistently knocking at his doors.

Although we have responded later than we wished, nevertheless, at the sound of your page, we answer in affection. For we do not act when we wish to act, but when we receive from God the ability to act, and when the heavenly dispensation has harmonized all things with their appointed times. Since, therefore, you have remembered that the apostolic see, over which by divine favor we preside, is the refuge of all ecclesiastical pastoral care, and have sought refuge in it with your petitions, we have granted these very things with a willing embrace. For it is the source and foundation of the churches, the Lord having thus rewarded Peter’s confession: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” It plainly seems fitting that all Christian fidelity should hasten to it, and that it should itself extend a hand of consolation to all.

But since you are engaged in combating the iniquities of wicked men and punishing them with a special sword, you asked us to send you, as an assisting bishop in the matters divinely entrusted to your care, one who might act in our place. We are sending him.

[Col. 1359D] [Note: “Whom indeed both uprightness of character, as his name indicates, etc.” The name and status of this man, sent by the supreme pontiff to assist the archbishop of Trier, are nowhere explicitly recorded. Nevertheless, Papebroch’s conjecture in the *Acta Sanctorum*, June, vol. I, p. 97, letter A, is prudent and supported by various considerations: namely, that he was Gratian, archpriest, a man of the highest commendation. He later prudently diverted Benedict and Sylvester, who were contending for the pontificate, from usurping it; and, having been elected pope, he himself was called Gregory VI, although he later yielded the pontificate because he was willing to do so.]

This man is adorned both with uprightness of character, as his name indicates, and with the discerning beauty of a wise mind. We have judged him especially suitable for this task; we have recognized him as God’s faithful and prudent servant, possessing both the serpent’s cleverness and the dove’s simplicity. From his lips, as it were, honey flows, filled, according to the capacity of his hearers, with heavenly ambrosia. We have separated him from our body like a right arm, praying for his health and joy.

We are therefore sending him to console you in your necessities, both in the work of consecration and also in the anointing of confirmation, and, with God’s favor, in whatever other necessities he may be able to assist according to the will of your holy fraternity. You should not refuse or neglect to treat him as is fitting. We believe that you need no admonition in this matter, since your kindness is more abundant precisely because it is holier.

[Note: That is, both in the work of consecration and in the anointing of confirmation. Toward the middle of the thirteenth century, the archbishops and bishops of Germany gradually adopted titular suffragans, and those suffragans became ordinary assistants. The Lateran Council had recently permitted this, for serious reasons, so that, where public affairs, ill health, hostile incursions, or lack of letters and learning stood in the way, bishops might associate an assistant with themselves in sharing their duties. Accordingly, Theodoric II, archbishop of Trier, was, so far as is known, the first of all to employ, around the year 1241, Henry, bishop of Ösel, as a suffragan. Thus what the Roman pontiff had now sent to the archbishop of Trier in the eleventh century—a titular bishop to assist him in consecration, confirmation, and other necessities—is not an ordinary example.]

As for that man Simeon, whom you show to be shining with innumerable miracles and resplendent with divine virtues: it is clear from this that he bore within his fragile body a treasure of spiritual grace, so that he not only provided for his own salvation but also brought manifold healing to others.

Since, therefore, he is believed to have attained that eternal perpetuity of supreme blessedness and heavenly fellowship, as is more frequently revealed by the working of signs, our apostolic authority, following the judgment of the divine Arbiter and supported by the agreement of many of our brethren, decrees that this man of God, Simeon, must henceforth and forever be called a saint, and that his feast day, like those of the other saints, must be celebrated each year with the greatest reverence.

For the one who commends himself is not approved, but the one whom the Lord commends, as the Apostle says. Let his name glory, be praised, flourish, please, be celebrated, loved, and venerated; and let it be inserted into the Martyrology. May he intercede before the most merciful majesty of the divine power for our sins and negligences and for those of the persons entrusted to us, so that the wonders which he visibly displays upon the bodies of the sick he may graciously display in our souls by an unseen power.

Farewell.

## VI. Bull of the canonization of Saint Simeon, the recluse of Trier. (Year 1041.)

[HONTHEIM, in the work cited above, p. 277.]

[Col. 1360D]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, priests, and [Col. 1361A] the entire clergy, and to all peoples both of the Teutonic kingdom and of every nation and language: most beloved greeting, with apostolic blessing.

The ineffable authority of the divine majesty, which is ever accomplishing ineffable things, is proclaimed wonderful in its saints and is likewise manifested in its works, granting them the power and strength to heal every disease and every infirmity. God himself, distributor and author of spiritual gifts, granted this gift to his innumerable soldiers even in this mortal body, while they lived in the world, so that they, possessing the faithful pledge of the Holy Spirit in hope of future reward, might rely upon it with greater confidence and strength; and so that the nations, contemplating the divine mysteries, might put aside every superstition and turn from the depths of their hearts to the way of Christian truth.

He likewise bestowed and magnified others, whose number is similarly incomprehensible, with works of virtue after they had cast off the bonds of the flesh, so that, when their bodily remains had been placed in the tomb and their limbs dissolved into ashes and embers, faith might be impressed and increased in those who perceived and witnessed these wonders: namely, that they live happily there where true and eternal life exists. No one may approach that life unless, hating the pleasures of temporal life, he always longs for it with the whole intention of his mind, should he at some time deserve to be recalled from pilgrimage to his homeland and from exile to restoration.

Therefore, since by frequent reports from messengers and by repeated written communications a great cry and resounding rumor has flown from the region of Trier to us at Rome, and now even farther, namely, that there lies there the wondrous body of a certain man, Simeon, shining with signs and prodigies, virtues and miracles, like the sun at midday under a clear sky, we kissed the earth more closely and blessed the Lord with our whole heart, mind, and strength. He has graciously, in our own times, kindled within the holy body of his Church this distinguished member with divine light, so that he may be a burning lamp placed upon a lampstand, shining for all who are in the house of the Lord.

[Note: Thus, having been summoned and urged by our most beloved brother, the lord Poppo. For many centuries canonization, or enrollment in the catalogue of the saints, was carried out solely by episcopal authority. The canonization of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg—the diploma of which appears in the *Bullar. Mag. Rom.*, vol. I, p. 22, Luxembourg edition—is believed to have been the first among those requested from the Roman see and solemnly decreed by Pope John XV in the year 993. See Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Annales Benedictini*, book I, no. 77, p. 82. This present canonization of Saint Simeon followed as the second. See Papebroch, *Acta Sanctorum*, June, vol. I, p. 96, letter B.]

Thus, having been summoned and urged by our most beloved brother, Lord Poppo, archbishop of Trier, so that we might determine and decree by a salutary definition of our apostolic authority what seemed to us appropriate concerning the celebration of this most holy man, we make known by these letters to all whom we named above in the greeting what we have judged concerning this matter.

For, [Note: Having gathered the splendid fraternity of our Roman clergy. When canonizations were first carried out by the Roman pontiffs, they were customarily decreed only with the approval of a general synod, as Christian Lupus relates in the *Scholia*, vol. III, p. 569. This continued until Eugene III, the first to canonize without a council, in his consistory alone, Saint Henry the Emperor, by the fullness of his power. He used the reasoning that the authority of the Roman Church is the foundation of all councils. See the bull of canonization in the *Bull. M. Rom.*, cited above, p. 31. From that time the pontiffs reserved this authority exclusively to themselves; eventually this papal reservation was generally and universally accepted by all the churches, chiefly through the authority of a decretal of Gregory IX, in chapter 1, *X, De reliquiis et veneratione sanctorum*.]

having gathered the splendid fraternity of our Roman clergy, while the annual return of the Nativity of the Most Holy Virgin was shining throughout the world, we determined by unanimous deliberation and grounded our decision upon the firm foundation of a solemn decree: namely, that this same man of God, Simeon, whom the Lord commends and approves, filled with holiness and grace, as the manifestation of so many virtues shows, must without doubt be called a saint by all peoples, tribes, and languages; that his recurring feast day must everywhere be solemnly observed each year, celebrated and venerated as a festival; and that his name must be inserted in its proper place in the Martyrology together with the names of his companions.

[Note: Thus in the autograph.]

To this sentence we also added the following: whoever proves to be a rash despiser and stiff-necked opponent of this our constitution should first know that he gravely offends the Lord; next, that he must not hope in any way for the protection of that saint—or indeed of all the saints in whose fellowship he rejoices—or for our apostolic blessing hereafter. May these blessings be multiplied upon its protectors, forever and ever. Amen, amen, amen.

## VII. Benedict IX confirms the integrity and freedom of the patriarchate of Grado in synod, at the request of Patriarch Ursus, Dominico Contarini, and the Venetian people through their legates. (Year 1044.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 605.]

[Col. 1362C]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to URSUS, patriarch of Grado: perpetual salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Just as we rejoice greatly in the Lord and glory in the gift of his grace when the holy Church grows magnificently and expands most widely through good works, so we are exceedingly afflicted and troubled by her oppression, concerning which a repeated account of lamentation has reached us. She ought not to have been shaken by such great oppressions by those from whom she should have received support and honor. Therefore, when the evasions of such men have been removed—for by poisonous malice goodness and truth are usually concealed and obscured—substantial assistance must justly be offered to those who lament, and the apostolic see must support those whom, by divine grace, it is worthy to assist with the help of Christ.

We must ensure that an imprudent intention does not advance amid the disturbance of the whole Church, and that things once prohibited by our holy predecessors and by the other saints do not revive again. Consideration of our see compels us not to neglect, for God’s sake, those matters which have come to our notice as requiring correction, but to amend them with worthy correction.

And if secular offices have their proper order, and the discipline handed down by our ancestors must be preserved, who could tolerate ecclesiastical orders being violated and confused by presumption? Or who could tolerate their being so neglected that what requires correction is postponed because no assistance is given?

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the sons of the holy Church of God that, in the time of our predecessor Pope John, an abominable crime was committed against Ursus, patriarch of the Church of Grado in New Aquileia, by Poppo, bishop of Cividale, at the devil’s persuasion.

[Col. 1363B] The aforesaid Poppo, coming deceitfully to the city of Grado, invaded it and, after invading it, devastated it in the manner of the pagans; he violated the churches, broke the altars, carried off the treasures, destroyed the monasteries, and, not being ashamed of such great crimes, further petitioned this apostolic see through his false pretenses. Through his messengers he asked that a privilege be issued to him specifically concerning the island of Grado, which he had promised to demonstrate belonged to him justly and canonically, and by ancient privileges. Accordingly, he obtained a privilege in the following terms: if any dispute should ever arise concerning it, he would prove that it belonged to him justly and without any impediment, exactly as he had promised.

The result was entirely contrary to this. When Ursus, patriarch of the Church of Grado, first through his messengers and then in person, came to this apostolic see to complain about the invasion of his see, the same Poppo was summoned to give satisfaction, as he had promised. He not only delayed coming, but was wholly unable to demonstrate that the aforesaid island belonged to him justly and according to God’s law, by ancient privileges, as he had promised. Indeed, he denied the terms of the privilege.

Since he was able to demonstrate nothing of what he had promised, the privilege he had obtained under the aforesaid condition was justly voided according to its own terms and regularly reduced to nothing.

For this reason our predecessor Pope John gathered a holy synod in the church of Saint Sylvester. Before its presence came Ursus, patriarch of the Church of Grado, and displayed many privileges granted by our predecessors to his see concerning the status of his metropolitan church and its dependencies: namely, by the most holy Pelagius, Gregory, Honorius, Stephen, another Gregory, Leo, Sergius, another Leo, Benedict, Hadrian, Boniface, Romanus, Theodore, Anastasius, John, Sylvester, and Sergius.

Our predecessor carefully considered all these documents and, confirming the ancient rights by synodal judgment under invocation of the divine judgment, constructed a new privilege in the following terms: no one at any time should presume to disturb or molest the aforesaid patriarch Ursus or his successors in the aforesaid patriarchate of Grado, as though it were his property and possessions. Rather, Ursus and his successors, in full possession and free from everyone’s opposition, should hold that same patriarchal see with all its dependencies in perpetuity.

He also sent a letter to Poppo ordering him, under oath by three persons, to restore everything that had been taken from the patriarch of Grado. Poppo not only failed to fulfill this, but, with certain dishonorable supporters aiding him, deceitfully obtained a privilege against divine law concerning the security of his own church and the subjection of the patriarchate of Grado.

Adding iniquity to iniquity, and thereby increasing his condemnation, even in our own time he again secretly entered the city of Grado and committed every abominable crime there: he burned the entire city together with its churches, smashed the altars, carried off the treasures, and took away with him whatever the fire had spared, according to the custom of the pagans.

Finally, because of this repeated sacrilege, the patriarch of Grado sent a complaint to the apostolic see in a letter, through the same invading perpetrator. But before we could restrain him for so great an outrage, he was removed from this life by divine judgment without confession or viaticum.

At last Ursus, patriarch of Grado, together with our beloved son Dominico Contarini, duke of the Venetians or Dalmatians, and the people of Venice, petitioned us through their legates: Benedict, venerable abbot of the monasteries of the Holy Trinity and Saint Michael the Archangel at Brondolo; John Stornatus; and Gregory the cleric. They asked that everything subject to him and to his see be restored by our authority, and that we annul the privilege Poppo had acquired concerning the subjection of the Church of Grado contrary to divine authority.

They further asked that we openly renew and confirm the privileges of our predecessors concerning the status of his church, both with regard to the property and possessions of his patriarchate and with regard to those known to lie within the territory of Venice or the Italian kingdom, or in the county of Istria—namely, all that his predecessors appeared to have held and possessed at Rialto, Malamocco, Jesolo, Pineto, Cittanova, in the borderland of the aforesaid city of Grado, at Ursiano or Gaiazzo, in Zemuli, partly in the territory of Aquileia and along the maritime boundary; in Istria, at Trieste, Koper, and Piran; likewise at Cittanova and Poreč; [lacuna]; at Pola and at the Castle of Saint George; and in all the other places, both within and beyond these territories, including Bologna, Romagna, Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, and whatever places in the Italian kingdom or in Venice their predecessors were seen to hold and possess. They asked that Ursus and his successors be able to retain and possess all these things without anyone’s opposition or resistance.

Gladly assenting to their petitions, warmed by zeal for the house of God, and judging their request just, we gathered a holy synod in the Roman Church. With us sat our venerable bishops, priests, deacons, cardinals, subdeacons, abbots, and others, some of whose names are these:

John, bishop of Lavicanum, our nephew.  
Tedald, bishop of Albano.  
John, bishop of Porto.  
John, bishop of Praeneste.  
[Col. 1365A] Benedict, bishop of Ostia.  
Amatus, bishop of Velletri.  
Bonizo, bishop of Tusculum.  
Honestus, bishop of Foropopoli.  
Adam, bishop of Fossombrone.  
Crescentius, bishop of the Church of Saint Rufina.  
Vido, bishop of Humana.  
Andrew, bishop of Perugia.  
Ubertus, bishop of the Church of Sassena.  
Arduin, bishop of Ferentino.  
Theudald, bishop of Saint Marianus.  
John, bishop of the Church of Saint Sabina.  
Theuderic of Urbino.  
Theudald. Ubertus.  
[Col. 1365B] Benedict, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and vicedominus.  
Hugh.  
Peter, our chancellor.  
Leo, Romanus, Crescentius, and Peter, also called Mancio, our deacons.  
John, arch-canon and archpriest of the canonical church of Saint John before the Latin Gate.  
John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia.  
John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin.  
John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Damasus.  
Ubertus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
Martin, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina.  
Theudald, primicerius.  
[Col. 1365C] Benedict, offertory officer of the Holy Roman Church.  
Benedict, priest and cardinal of the title of Saint Sylvester.  
Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus.  
The subdeacons were John, Adelmarius, Etrozo, and Sico.  
Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory called Clivus Scauri.  
Bartholomew, venerable abbot of Saint Mary of Grottaferrata.  
Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary called Saint Peter ad Vincula.  
Leo, abbot of Saint Paul the Apostle.  
George, abbot of Saint Lawrence outside the Walls.  
[Col. 1365D] John, abbot of Saint Sabas.  
Peter, abbot of Saint Mary on the Aventine.  
John, abbot of Saint Rophillus of Foropopoli.  
Bonizzo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Perugia.  
Felix, abbot of Saint Blaise.  
Simeon, abbot of Saint Mary in Pallara.

And the other members of the Holy Roman Church residing with us, by whose deliberation we decreed that this privilege of our apostolate should be issued to you, our venerable brother Ursus, patriarch of the Holy Church of Grado. To you in particular we now address our speech, because we clearly know that you and your Church seek justice.

Therefore, by the authority of the prince of the apostles Peter and of ourselves, whose place we hold, imitating the privileges of our predecessors, we decree that the aforesaid Church of Grado be a patriarchate established in perpetual stability. To you who preside there, and to your successors, we grant the freedom to exercise the entire office of metropolitan and patriarch.

Concerning all your possessions we command and forbid that any patriarch, archbishop, provost, dean, vicedominus, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or collector of anything, nor any public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority, presume to inflict any force or invasion, or in any way to cause trouble, upon you, Ursus the patriarch, or your successors, whether in the churches and parishes belonging to your church, or in the monasteries, households, tenant farmers, servants, slaves, or bondsmen, or in the other things that remain upon the lands of that same church.

Rather, everything we have mentioned shall be freely retained and possessed in perpetuity, according to every right and title of the Holy Church of Grado, by the patriarchs who now and hereafter preside there, without anyone’s disturbance.

As for the privilege which Poppo, bishop of Cividale, deceitfully obtained from this see concerning the subjection of the patriarchate of Grado: since we determine that it is supported by no canonical authority, by the authoritative judgment of our venerable brothers residing with us we utterly corrupt and annul it, reducing it completely to nothing.

If, therefore, any of our successors or any other person should presume to act against this privilege of our concession and confirmation, or should consent to those who presume to do so, or should become their supporter, and should not instead strive to observe it in its entirety, let him know that he is bound by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and by the bond of our anathema; that he is alienated from the kingdom of God; and that, together with the devil, as a transgressor of the holy Fathers, he is condemned without end.

But whoever proves to be a guardian and observer of this our privilege may deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the just Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, both here and forever.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scrivener and notary of our sacred Lateran palace, in the month of April, indiction XII.

Farewell.

## VIII. Letter of Pope Benedict VI to Obertus, abbot of Saint Miniatus. (Year 1044.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 62.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son OBERTUS, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Miniatus of Florence, and to his successors: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

It seems very good that, when pious places request protection from our apostolic see, we should grant it willingly. But you, dearest son, requested that we provide, in our customary kindness and by our command, apostolic protection and defense for the monastery of Saint Miniatus, which you have deserved to govern.

We judge this holy and pious; therefore we ought not to refuse it, but to grant it with the greatest readiness. Accordingly, yielding to your prayers, we grant apostolic protection both to you and to your successors. We adjudge all persons who oppose that monastery or inflict injury or violence upon its property—[fol. something is missing]—its resources, or the precedence of acts from earlier times, so that no king, no emperor, no bishop, no duke, no margrave, no count, no viscount, and no person, however insignificant, may dare to presume anything of this kind.

This applies specifically to the property granted to the monastery by the bishops of Florence—namely, Hildebrand, Lambert, and Atho—or given to it by other persons for the sake of their souls, as well as to what you yourself have acquired there and may acquire from now on.

By apostolic censure we establish that, if any public or private person, great or small, should attempt to molest or disturb you or your successors concerning all those possessions, movable or immovable, or to seize them from your hands, that person shall be bound by the bond of anathema and condemned by our apostolic curse until he makes satisfaction for such offenses.

Whoever, however, proves to be a guardian of the strengthening, protection, and confirmation of this our protection may deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the just Judge, our Lord God.

Written by the hand of Sergius, notary of our sacred palace, in the month of April, indiction XII.

Farewell.

## IX. Letter of Benedict IX to Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg. (Years 1012–1024.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 71.]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy ADELBERT, bishop of the holy Church of Hamburg: apostolic blessing.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost day and night in guarding their flock, and keep watch with ever-vigilant eyes lest any of the sheep perish by wandering or be carried off, torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much exertion and care ought we to remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls?

Let us attend to our charge and not cease to fulfill our duty toward the guardianship of the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the guilt of negligence torture us before the supreme Shepherd because of our sloth.

For this reason we are now judged, among others, to possess a higher dignity of honor. Therefore we grant to you and to all your successors, in perpetuity, the legation and archiepiscopal authority over all the northern kingdoms: namely, the kingdoms of the Danes, Swedes, Norwegians, Icelanders, and all the islands adjacent to these kingdoms.

We also send to your holiness the pallium, according to custom, for the celebration of the solemnities of Mass, which is not [lacuna] another thing that restrains the unruly from depravity by striking them. May your defense assist widows and orphans who are unjustly oppressed.

Behold, dearest brother: among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you diligently preserve them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.

May the Holy Trinity graciously preserve your fraternity safe and sound for a long time, and, after the bitterness of this age, lead you to everlasting blessedness.

Given by the hand of Leo, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March, indiction III.

## X. Letter of Poppo, archbishop of Trier, to Benedict IX, supreme pontiff, seeking the canonization of blessed Simeon the recluse at Trier.

[Col. 1368D]

To the most reverend Father of fathers, BENEDICT, venerable in grace and name, POPPO, though unworthy, yet by the clemency of God’s generosity minister of the holy Church of Trier, offers due submission with the whole affection of his love.

Some time ago, when, with the consent of the lord John of venerable memory, your predecessor in this holy apostolic see, I had gone as a pilgrim to Jerusalem out of love for seeing the tomb of the God-man Jesus Christ, the wickedness of evil men increased greatly in our region. It increased so much that even now they cannot withdraw their hands from the wickedness they began, plundering and devastating everything around them.

Concerning this I repeatedly implored the presence of my lord the king, asking him to extend to me the hand of his correction, but I achieved nothing. I also often pleaded for the same matter with your aforesaid predecessor, but so far I have obtained no consolation.

For this reason I desire that your God-loving fatherhood may now at least console me, and send me one of your more honorable and prudent men who may assist me in my necessities with both advice and help: help, I say, concerning the adversities; advice concerning matters which I do not believe are hidden from the ears of your holiness.

But if these things have until now been hidden from you, I now beg you to grant a favorable hearing to my letters. A man of praiseworthy holiness of life recently departed from this life among us. If we ought to believe the signs and virtues that the Lord performs through him, we have no doubt that he enjoys fellowship with the saints in eternal blessedness.

Yet it is not so much the signs, which are common to the faithful and the unfaithful, as the power of faith—which separates the faithful from the unfaithful and which flourished greatly in him while he still remained in the body—that makes us certain of his holiness.

Therefore both the clergy and the people of our Church summoned us and earnestly requested that, together with the life and miracles of this holy man, we send our letters to this apostolic see over which, by God’s appointment, you preside. We were to ask for what we believe worthy of petition: that, if it should seem prudent to you, once your apostolic decree has been given to us, we might be permitted to inscribe his name among the names of the saints and to render to him the other honors owed to the saints.

Therefore, whatever consolation and advice your wisdom determines that I should seek concerning the alleviation of the anxieties that have arisen on every side, may you graciously make known to me without lengthy delay.

[Col. 1370B] May your honor and merit increase before God and men.

## In the year of the Lord 1042. Heribert, bishop of Eichstätt.

[Col. 1369]

# Hymns of Heribert, edited by Heinrich Denzinger, professor of theology at the University of Würzburg

[Note]

Heribert, the fifteenth bishop of Eichstätt, governed the Church for twenty-one years. He was elected in 1021 and died in 1042, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August. Eichstätt tradition reports that he was born among the Franconian counts of Rothenburg.

Concerning him, the anonymous Hasenried author, who in 1075 sent a letter to a canon of Würzburg concerning the bishops of Eichstätt, writes [Note: In Gretser’s historical *Catalogue of All the Bishops of Eichstätt*, vol. VIII of his works]:

“Heribert, noble by birth and nobler in character, an elegantly learned man, kinsman and namesake of that holy Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, became bishop by the favor of divine grace. He was brought up and educated at Würzburg, and so excelled in the distinguished sweetness of his style of composition that at that time he had no equal in this art.

Inspired by the Holy Spirit, he composed six most beautiful hymns: one on the holy cross, *Hail, holy cross*; another on Saint Willibald, *Sea, fountain, gate*; a third on Saint Walburga, *Hail, flower of virgins*; a fourth on the finding of Saint Stephen, *God of gods, Lord*; a fifth on Saint Lawrence, *May the voice ascend to the stars*; and a sixth on all the saints, *All you heavenly orders*.

He also composed five intimate prayers to Saint Mary, all of which commonly begin, *Hail, Mary, full of grace*. He also composed these two introductory chants: *Attend, all peoples*, and *Sinners, women and men who once sinned*.”

We print below the hymns from the Eichstätt Breviary, which was first printed, except for the hymn on Saint Stephen, which we found in Daniel’s *Hymnological Treasury*, Halle, 1841, p. 289.

For more concerning Heribert’s life, see Gretser, in the work cited, and Andrew Straus, in his work *On Men Distinguished by Their Writings, Learning, and Piety Whom Eichstätt Either Produced or Nurtured*, Eichstätt, 1709, p. 172.

# Hymns of Heribert

## I. On the Holy Cross

[Col. 1369]

Hail, holy cross,  
hail, glory of the world,  
our true hope,  
bringing true joys,  
sign of salvation,  
salvation in dangers,  
life-giving wood,  
bearing the life of all.

We always praise you  
as worthy of worship,  
you life-giving cross;  
in you, the redeemed,  
we always sing to you  
the sweet glory of the age.

Through the wood we were servants;  
through you, the wood, we are free.

[Col. 1370]

You who slay original sin  
upon the cross,  
cleanse us, O Christ,  
from our personal stains.

Taking pity on fragile humanity,  
through the holy cross  
grant forgiveness to those who have fallen.

Protect, save,  
bless, sanctify  
the whole people  
through the sign of the cross.

Drive away sickness  
of body and soul;  
before this sign  
let no danger remain.

Praise to God the Father  
in the cross of the Son;  
equal praise  
to the Holy Spirit.

May joy be granted  
to the highest citizens, the angels;  
may honor in the world  
be granted to the discovery [exaltation] of the cross.

Amen.

## II. On Saint Willibald

Sea, fountain, gate  
and source of the lands,  
God, you are the head  
of all good things.

From you good things flow;  
to you they return.

Far from the islands,  
the good portion of the sea  
has returned to the fountain  
and seeks you,  
Jesus, fountain  
of living waters.

God is the fountain of the sea;  
Willibald is its portion,  
and from distant native shores  
he thirsts for him.

Like a stag,  
he hastens toward his drink.

O blessed fosterling  
of the islands of the angels,  
make us worthy,  
through earnest prayer,  
of the water  
which whoever drinks  
will never afterward know thirst.

Though cleansed by baptism,  
wicked deceptions  
always defile us  
and plunge us evilly  
through the pool of sin  
into punishment and death.

But by your prayers

we all beseech you

to rescue us from

the savage peril of Charybdis,

as we touch, with tears,

the harbor of salvation.

Praise to you, Trinity,

praise and power;

the rivers praise you,

heaven and earth;

from sea to sea

[Col. 1372] let there be praise this day. Amen.

## III. On Saint Walburga

Hail, flower of virgins,

sister of the great

brothers Willibald

and Wunebald;

hail, bride

of virginal beauty.

Among the countless

saints whom she sent forth,

England, a joyful mother,

joyfully gave birth to you

and joyfully sent you forth,

angelic flower.

The Mother of the Lord,

both mother and virgin,

joined you, a virgin,

to the choirs of virgins,

and dedicated you,

a bride, to her Son,

when you entered the bridal chamber

of the King of heaven.

You hear the joyful

angelic song:

“Enter, virgin,

into the joy

of your Bridegroom.”

Praise to you, Trinity,

praise and power;

the five wise virgins

praise you;

may the virgin Walburga

pray to you for us. Amen.

## IV. On Saint Lawrence

[Col. 1371A]

May the voice and song

of all who praise you together,

O God, mount even to the stars

and strike the inmost heavens.

For the festival is here,

the venerable day

on which Lawrence entered heaven

by reason of his merits.

Having overcome the fires

and the impious torturers,
