having conquered savage enemies,

he now rejoices among the heavenly ones.

May he himself deign

to beseech the most merciful Lord

[Col. 1371B] to save us

from eternal fires

and from demons.

To God the Father be glory,

and to his only Son,

with the Spirit, the Paraclete,

now and forever. Amen.

## V. On All the Saints

All the heavenly orders,

to whom this day is dedicated,

a thousand thousand thousandfold,

hear your suppliants.

[Col. 1372A] First, fiery powers,

then, filled with knowledge,

thereafter, help us by your prayer,

O thrones of the Lord.

Then, consecrated to the powers,

and you, terrible in silent gestures

(or perhaps nods: *nutibus*?),

and radiant in your faces,

favor the peoples of Christ.

You, Father Abraham, be present,

bearing a glorious lineage;

together with these,

obtain for us by prayer

the forgiveness we need.

Holy key-bearer, be present,

and lawgiver of the new peace,

and every cross-bearer of Christ:

[Col. 1372B] cleanse our deeds together.

To God the Father be glory,

and to his only Son,

with the Spirit, the Paraclete,

now and forever. Amen.

## VI. On the Finding of Saint Stephen

God of gods, Lord,

King of everlasting glory,

King of unconquered soldiers,

hear the song of your suppliants.

The earth, covering the hidden

[Col. 1373A] treasure of the sweet prize,

now, with the protomartyr found,

restores to the world the hope of grace.

All you devoted martyrs,

praise the protomartyr;

he is worthy of your praises,

your leader and champion going before you.

He is the first to be granted the laurel

in the Lord’s battle-line;

when cast down beneath the stones,

he was received by the Son of God.

Now, protomartyr Stephen,

receive our devout prayers,

by which, through you, we beseech

[Col. 1374A] that we may be reconciled to God in heaven.

The Lord heard him

when he prayed for his persecutors,

and in mercy he will hear him

when he prays for your suppliants.

And you, Gamaliel and Abibon,

joined with Nicodemus,

do not cease your prayers

for the transgressions of the people.

Glory to the Most High Father,

the greatest praise to the Son,

with the holy Spirit,

now and throughout every age. Amen.

# Works of Emma, Queen of the English

[Col. 1373]

## In the Year of Our Lord 1045: An Encomium of Emma, Queen of the English, Daughter of Richard I, Duke of the Normans, by an Unknown but Contemporary Author

(Edited by Duchesne, *Ancient Writers of the History of the Normans*, p. 163.)

## Preliminary Notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 574.)

A writer known to us only by his status as a monk of Saint-Bertin has left us a work entitled *Praise of Emma, Queen of England, Daughter of Richard I, Duke of Normandy*—a title as grandiose as it is inadequate to express the nature of the work and give a proper idea of it. In fact, it is less the praise of this princess than the history of Canute the Great, king of Denmark and England, whom she married in a second marriage, and of Harold, that king’s son and successor.

It is divided into two books. The first, which is very short, contains an abbreviated history of Sweyn, king of Denmark and Canute’s father, and the beginnings of Canute’s own history. The second book, which is more extensive, is devoted to describing Canute’s reign and the revolutions that followed it in England under Harold and after his death, when Edward, son of King Æthelred and Queen Emma, came to the throne.

This event took place in 1042, and our author did not carry his history any further. At the end, he describes the good understanding and union that prevailed between this prince and Canute II, his maternal half-brother, king of Denmark. This shows that the historian undertook to write only some time after the period just mentioned. But it is certain that he completed the work before the year 1052, the date of Emma’s death. The work is dedicated to her in a separate letter, followed by a notice or summary of the whole history.

This work, which Duchesne made public from a manuscript in the Cottonian Library, appears to have been little known, since it has still received only this one edition. It certainly deserved a place in the collections of the historians of England and Denmark that have been printed during approximately the last century. Besides the many details that illuminate the history of these two kingdoms, its contents must be regarded as highly trustworthy. It is the production of an author who was not only a contemporary, but who also held historical truth in especially high regard, as he explains himself. Moreover, the style is very good for the century in which the work was composed. In several places it is even ornate and animated to the point of retaining something of poetic style.

## Prologue

[Col. 1373B] May salvation be yours from the Lord Jesus Christ, O queen, who surpass all those of your sex in refinement of character. I, your servant, cannot offer your nobility anything worthy through my deeds, nor do I know how I might please you at least through words. For your excellence shines more brightly than the radiance of the sun itself, surpassing the virtue of every skilled and eloquent person, in all who know you.

I therefore esteem you, who have deserved so greatly of me, to such a degree that I would meet death without fear if I believed it would benefit you. For this reason, as you command, I eagerly desire to entrust to posterity in writing the memory of accomplished deeds—deeds, I mean, pertaining to your honor and that of your own people. But I doubt whether I can be sufficient for myself in undertaking this.

For this is properly required of history: that it deviate from the straight path of truth by no detour of error. Whenever someone writing the deeds of another inserts something false into the truth, whether through mistake or—as often happens—for the sake of embellishment, the listener surely regards the whole account as tainted by the admixture of even a single known falsehood. Therefore, I think historians must take the greatest care lest, by opposing truth through the insertion of certain falsehoods, they also lose the name that their office seems to give them. Facts lend credibility to truth, and truth likewise lends credibility to facts.

As I reflect on this and other matters of the kind, shame greatly torments my spirit, [Col. 1376A] when I consider how badly human custom conducts itself in such matters. For if someone sees a person using generous language to express the truth of a matter, he sharply reproves him as excessively talkative; but of another, whom I have said avoids slander and is more restrained than is fair in narration, when he ought to uncover what is hidden, he says that he has concealed what was open.

Surrounded, therefore, by such anxiety, I fear that those who envy me will call me talkative if, in writing the history, I use an extended narrative and neglect the elegance of composition. Yet since I see that I cannot escape writing, I think one of the alternatives I have proposed must be chosen: either to submit to the various judgments of men, or, by neglecting what you, my lady queen, have commanded me, to remain silent rather than carry out those commands.

[Col. 1376B] I therefore prefer to be reproved by some for talkativeness rather than have the truth of a most memorable matter concealed from everyone through me. Accordingly, valuing highly the lady who commands me, I have chosen this course, setting aside henceforth excuses that might be offered, and from this point I shall weave together the narrative.

## Argument

[Col. 1375]

[Col. 1375C] Perhaps, O reader, you will wonder and reproach me as a writer for error or ignorance: why, at the beginning of this little book, have I proclaimed the deeds and praises of the most serene King Sweyn, when in the letter written above I promised to make this little book a praise of this lady? You yourself will admit that this is so, and you will nowhere find me departing from her praises, if you compare the beginning with the middle and the ending with the beginning, in a discerning manner.

And so that no cloud of error may prevent you from seeing this, take as your theorem the following example drawn from comparable and entirely true matters. Who could deny that the *Aeneid*, written by Virgil, answers everywhere to the praises of Octavian, although scarcely anything—or certainly very little—of his name seems to have been expressly inserted? Observe, therefore, that praise attributed to one’s lineage ennobles the glory of the person’s own dignity and distinction in every respect.

Who, then, could deny that this book answers throughout to the praises of the queen, when it is written not only to her glory but also appears to possess the greatest share of her glory? If this does not seem plausible to you, let it be confirmed by the evident sign of another matter.

You know that wherever you turn a circle, you will undoubtedly make the point its beginning; and when the circle has been continuously revolved, its circumference returns to its beginning, by which return the circuit of its figure is completed. In the same way, therefore, the queen’s praise shines at the beginning, flourishes in the middle, and is found at the end, embracing absolutely the whole substance of the book.

Since you perceive this with me, draw the conclusion as follows. Sweyn, king of the Danes, powerful in virtue, arms, and counsel, subjected the English kingdom to his rule by force; and, when he died, he appointed his son Canute as successor to that same kingdom. Later, when those same English opposed him and fiercely resisted force with force, he fought many battles; and perhaps the fighting would scarcely ever, or never, have ended, had he not at last obtained the marriage-bond with this most noble queen, through the favor of the Savior’s grace.

While he was still alive, he handed over all that lay under his authority to the son born to him by this same queen—namely, Hardecanute. After his father’s death, Hardecanute was absent from the English, for he had gone to administer the kingdom of the Danes. This absence gave an unjust usurper an opportunity to invade the borders of his realm. After seizing the kingdom, the usurper killed the king’s brother by a most wicked act of treachery. But divine vengeance followed, struck down the impious man, and restored the kingdom to the one to whom it belonged.

Thus Hardecanute, having recovered the kingdom and obeying his mother’s counsels in every respect, ruled it imperially, increasing its wealth. He also, in accordance with the nobility expected of him, used remarkable generosity toward his brother, sharing with him the honor and riches of the kingdom.

Having observed these things, O reader, and having examined the text with a vigilant—or rather, penetrating—eye of the mind, understand that the entire sequence of this little book answers to the praises of Queen Emma.

## Book One

[Col. 1375]

[Col. 1375D] I have learned from a truthful account that Sweyn, king of the Danes, was by far the most fortunate of nearly all the kings of his time, so much so that—something that rarely happens—a most fortunate outcome followed his fortunate beginnings, in accordance with God and the world.

He derived his origin from the noblest people, which is the first distinction among human beings, and he acquired for himself great honor, according to worldly standards, through the administration of the government he held. Divine power then granted him such favor that, even as a little boy, he was loved by everyone with deep affection. His own father, however, hated him intensely—not because of any childish fault deserving this, but solely because of envy.

When he became a young man, he grew daily in the people’s love; consequently, his father’s envy increased more and more, until he wished to expel him from his homeland no longer secretly but openly, asserting under oath that he would not reign after him.

Therefore the army, grieving, abandoned the father, clung to the son, and diligently defended him. For this reason they met in battle. In that battle the wounded and defeated father fled to the Slavs, where he died not long afterward, and Sweyn peacefully occupied his throne.

I would like briefly to recall how energetically and wisely he meanwhile arranged worldly affairs, so that, by inserting these matters, it may be easier to descend gradually through them to what follows.

When he was enjoying peace in safety, without trembling at any enemy invasion, he nevertheless lived in camp as though always fearing imminent danger. For, if enemies should appear, he might perhaps be unable to resist them at all; and he allowed nothing to be neglected in preparing for his men whatever would be necessary for war, specifically so that, through leisure, as commonly happens, their manly spirits might not grow soft.

Yet he could find no task so difficult that he would force unwilling soldiers to undertake it. Through great and generous munificence he had made them devoted and faithful to him. And, so that you may know how great was the affection for him in the hearts of his men, I can affirm with certainty that none would avoid danger through fear of death, and that, for loyalty to him, any one of them would fearlessly confront innumerable armed enemies with bare hands, provided only that the royal standard were shown to those advancing.

But lest anyone think that I am inventing these things falsely out of affection for someone, it will become clear to a careful observer in what follows whether I have spoken the truth or not.

For it is undoubtedly clear to everyone that human custom is such that often, when matters turn out successfully, the minds of some people are stirred beyond measure by a flood of thoughts; and, through excessive freedom in a time of leisure, some undertake what they would scarcely dare to imagine, much less do, when placed in adversity.

So it happened also to the soldiers of the aforementioned king. When everything had gone favorably during a long and undisturbed peace, and they relied firmly on their lord’s steadfastness in rewarding good service, they decided to pursue the same undertaking as he did: to invade the English land and add it, by the fortune of war, to the borders of his dominion.

“Turkill, the commander of your army, my lord king,” they said, “has departed with your permission to avenge his brother, who was killed there. Taking a large part of your army with him, he rejoices in having conquered; and now, as victor, he holds the southern part of the province. He prefers to live there in exile, having become a friend of the English whom he defeated by your hand, and to glory in this, rather than to bring back the army, submit to you, and have the victory attributed to you.

“And now we are deprived of our companions and of the forty ships that he took with him, loaded with the foremost Danish warriors. Let our lord not endure such a serious loss. Let him go, take with him the army that wishes to go, and we shall acquire Turkill, rebellious as he is, together with his followers, as well as the English allied with them and all their possessions.

“For we know that they cannot long resist, since our countrymen will easily come over to us. If they should choose to do so, the king, sparing his leader and the Danes, will increase them in honors. But if he should refuse, they will feel the power of the one whom they despised. Deprived of this land and that, they will pay the penalty among the king’s foremost enemies.”

When the king heard this exhortation, he first began to wonder greatly to himself, because what had occurred to him while he had long concealed and disguised it had likewise taken root in the minds of his soldiers, who knew nothing of his own thought.

He therefore summoned his elder son Canute and began to ask what he thought about this matter. Questioned by his father, and fearing that he would be reproved if he opposed his father’s desire through a trick of indolence, Canute approved not only the necessity of going to the land but also urged and encouraged his father not to allow any delay to hold back what had been begun.

Thus, strengthened by the counsel of his nobles and relying on the goodwill of his soldiers, the king ordered a large fleet to be prepared and the entire Danish army everywhere to be notified, so that it would appear armed on the appointed day and, hearing the king’s decision, would most devotedly carry out whatever was commanded.

Immediately, at their lord’s command, messengers traversed the whole province and roused even the peaceful people, [Col. 1378C] lest anyone from so great an army be absent. Every warrior in the land would either incur the king’s anger or hasten to obey his command.

What happened, then? Without opposition they assembled, and, equipped with weapons of war, presented themselves in groups before their king, displaying that they were prepared for danger and death, if only they could accomplish their lord’s will.

But when the king saw the countless people, he ordered his will to be proclaimed by a herald’s voice: namely, that he wished to arm a fleet against the English and to subject this entire country to his dominion by sword or stratagem.

When everyone judged this worthy of approval, he first chose those who were to guard his kingdom, lest, while he rashly sought another’s, he lose what he securely held and, intent upon both, rule neither.

For he had two sons of good character. Of these, he joined the elder to his retinue, but placed the younger in charge of the rule of the entire kingdom, assigning him a military force and a few leading men who would wisely instruct the boy and stand as a wall for him by their counsel and arms.

When everything had thus been properly arranged, he reviewed the companions of the expedition. Leaving his younger son in his seat of authority, he boarded the ship surrounded by armed soldiers.

Without delay they hastened from every direction to the shores, and everywhere a harvest of weapons of many kinds was displayed. At last, assembled together, they boarded the high-sterned ships; the bronze-beaked vessels distinguished the individual commanders.

Here one could see lions cast in gold upon the ships; there birds approaching on the tops of the masts, marking the southern winds with their own verses; elsewhere various dragons threatening flames from their nostrils. On one side were men glittering with solid gold or silver, in a way scarcely inferior to living men; on the other, bulls with necks raised upward and legs extended, imitating at once the lowing and running of living creatures.

You would also see dolphins cast in electrum, and centaurs of the same metal recalling the ancient story. I could tell you of many other emblems of the same workmanship if the names of the monsters carved there did not escape me.

But why should I now describe the sides of the hulls, painted not only with decorative colors but also rough with golden and silver figures? The royal ship surpassed the others in the beauty of its appearance as greatly as the king surpassed his soldiers in the honor of his dignity. Of that ship, it is better for me to remain silent than to say little about something so magnificent.

Trusting in such a fleet, they suddenly departed joyfully at the given signal. As they had been ordered, some in front and some behind, but with their beaks aligned, they circled around the royal ship.

There you would see the blue sea foaming broadly, struck by frequent oars, while the sun’s radiance, reflected from the metal, extended doubled rays into the air.

What more need be said? At last they approached the borders toward which their minds were directed, when the inhabitants of the neighboring coastal country were alarmed by the ill tidings.

Without delay, as soon as the royal fleet cast anchor, the inhabitants of that place hurried to the gate, prepared—but in vain—to defend their entrance against a more powerful enemy.

Finally, leaving the ships behind, the royal soldiers came ashore and fearlessly prepared themselves for battle on foot. At first the enemies fought back stubbornly, but afterward, overcome by fear of danger, they turned to flight and offered those pursuing them the opportunity to wound and kill them.

Thus the king, encouraged by the outcome of his first battle, invaded the neighboring region, routing and putting the enemy to flight. Then, made bolder by such success, he returned to the ships and invaded in the same manner the remaining harbors, which enclosed that land in great number.

At last he conquered the whole country with such labor that, if anyone wished to go through his entire history in full, he would greatly fatigue his listeners and wrong himself, since he would scarcely be able to touch on everything as he wished.

But I leave the narration of these matters to another. I am eager to pass over them briefly and hasten to other things, directing my style toward Sweyn’s death, so that I may illuminate the beginning of the reign of the fortunate king Canute.

For when the aforementioned king had already been enthroned throughout the whole country of the English, and when scarcely anyone still resisted him, he lived only a short while longer, though that little time was glorious.

Foreseeing that the dissolution of his body was near, he summoned his son Canute, whom he had with him, and announced to him that he must enter the way of all flesh. After giving him much advice about governing the kingdom and exhorting him greatly to devotion to Christianity, and giving thanks to God, he entrusted the royal scepter to that man, most worthy among men.

The Danes in particular, who were his rightful subjects, strongly supported this action and rejoiced that Canute was established as their king while his father was still alive.

When this had been done, the father asked his son that, if he ever returned to the land of his birth, he should take his father’s body with him and not allow him to be buried as a foreigner in foreign lands. For he knew that those peoples hated him because he had invaded their kingdom.

Not long afterward, he paid nature’s final debt, sending his soul back to heaven and returning his limbs to the earth.

## Book Two

[Col. 1379]

[Col. 1379C] After his father’s death, Canute prepared to retain the scepter of the kingdom, but he could not accomplish this, because he lacked a sufficient number of loyal men. The English, remembering that his father had unjustly invaded their borders, gathered all the forces of the kingdom alike to drive him out, since he was still young.

When the king learned this, he secretly obtained through faithful friends a plan suited to his honor and ordered a fleet to be prepared—not because he fled in fear of the harsh outcomes of war, but in order to consult his brother Harold, king of the Danes, about this matter.

Thus, having taken back his father’s fleet and renewed the rowing crews, he entrusted his royal sails to the winds and sea. Yet he did not bring back with him the entire army that had entered the country with his father and with him.

For Turkill, whom we mentioned earlier as commander of the army, having observed that the land was excellent, preferred to spend his life in that fertile country, after making peace with its inhabitants, rather than return to his own country as though expelled.

And, as some say, he did not do this out of contempt for his lord, but so that, when he returned with renewed strength and the assistance of his brother to subdue the kingdom, he might either bend the kingdom’s nobles to surrender through his advice or, if that achieved little, strike the enemies fighting against his lord from behind while they were off their guard.

The truth of this is evident from the fact that he retained the greater part of the soldiers with him, and that the king allowed no more than sixty ships to depart with him.

The king therefore reached the confines of his native land with a favorable voyage [pervenit. ED. P.], while all who had formerly been loyal to his father as king wondered at his solitary return.

Flying rumor suddenly filled the palaces of King Harold with news that his elder brother, Canute, had arrived at his shores. The king and the whole army alike were astonished, and, still unaware of what awaited him, they anticipated harsh fortunes for him.

Accordingly, chosen soldiers were dispatched from the king’s side, and horses prepared for his reception were sent out to meet him. Brotherly affection moved the brother to serve his honor.

When at last Canute entered his brother’s dwelling in a manner befitting a king, his brother himself met him at the first entrance. Their bodies pressed together in mutual embrace, they repeatedly planted loving kisses upon one another.

Tears, shed partly from affection and partly on account of their father’s death, moistened the necks of both. When these had scarcely been dried, they were refreshed by much conversation.

As each inquired about his brother’s fortune and disclosed his own, Canute, who was the elder by birth, addressed his brother Harold as follows:

“Brother, I have come partly because of my love for you, but partly also to avoid the unexpected rashness of barbaric fury. I do not fear the wars that I shall undertake again for my glory; rather, I have come so that, instructed by your counsel and supported by your aid, I may return assured of victory.

“First, if you do not begrudge me my glory, do this for me: divide with me the kingdom of the Danes—my inheritance, which you alone hold—and then the kingdom of the English, if by united effort we can add it to our inheritance.

“Whichever of these two you choose, hold it happily, and I shall likewise hold the other. For this purpose I shall winter with you, so that there may be enough time for your counsel, and so that, as necessary, the ships and army may be restored, lest supplies fail when the time for battle arrives.

“Our Turkill, by abandoning us as he did our father, remained in the land and retained a large part of our ships. I think he will be our enemy, but he will not prevail.”

King Harold, hearing what he did not wish to hear, received his brother with these words:

“I rejoice, brother, at your arrival, and I thank you for visiting me. But what you say about dividing the kingdom is difficult to hear. I govern the inheritance that our father entrusted to me, with your approval. If you have lost this greater inheritance, I grieve for you; but, though ready to help you, I cannot consent to divide my kingdom.”

Hearing this and silently recognizing that his brother had spoken rightly, Canute said: “Let us be silent about this for the present. Perhaps God alone has arranged it more rightly.”

Conversing in these and other diverse ways, and dining at royal banquets, they remained together for some time. They improved their ships and restored the army. They also went together to Slavonia and brought back their mother, who had been staying there.

Meanwhile, one of the English matrons had a ship prepared for herself. Taking the body of King Sweyn, buried in his own country, embalming it with spices and covering it with cloaks, she went to sea and, sailing favorably, reached the ports of Denmark.

She then sent a messenger to both brothers, announcing that their father’s body was present, so that they might hasten to receive it and place it in the tomb he had prepared for himself.

They came joyfully, received the body with honor, and with even greater honor placed it in a monastery built by that same king in honor of the Holy Trinity, in the tomb he had prepared for himself.

When this had been completed, and summer was already approaching, Canute hastened to return, with his army restored, and avenge his wrongs.

As he was walking near the shores, a few sails suddenly appeared in the middle of the sea. Turkill, remembering what he had done to Sweyn and that he had then remained rashly in the English land without the permission of his lord Canute, sought out his lord with nine ships and their army, in order to make clear to him that he had not remained behind against his safety when he departed.

When he arrived, he did not dare enter the shore without orders. Instead, he cast anchor, sent messengers ahead, and asked permission to enter the harbor.

When this was granted, he came ashore, sought his lord’s mercy, and, reconciled to him with much effort, gave an oath of loyalty that he would henceforth serve him faithfully.

He stayed with him for more than a full month and urged him to return to the English, saying that he could easily overcome them, since their borders were well known to both of them far and wide.

In particular, he said that he had left thirty ships in the English land with a most faithful army, and that they would receive them honorably when they arrived and would illuminate the borders of the whole country.

Then the king bade farewell to his mother and brother, returned to the boundaries of the curving shore, and went to the place where he had already assembled the splendid spectacle of two hundred ships.

There was such an abundance of weapons that one of those ships, if all the rest had failed, would have possessed more than enough arms. There were also so many kinds of shields that one might have thought the armies of all peoples were present.

Such beauty was found in the ships that, to eyes dulled by looking at them, they seemed to distant observers more flame-coloured than fiery. Whenever the sun mingled its radiance with them, the gleam of the weapons shone on one side, while on the other the flame of the hanging shields glittered.

Gold burned on the beaks, and silver shone in the ships’ various forms. The fleet was so magnificently equipped that, if the Lord wished to conquer any people with it, the ships alone would terrify the enemy before their warriors undertook any battle.

For who among the enemy, seeing on the ships lions terrifying in the gleam of gold, metallic [*metallicos*?] men threatening with golden faces, dragons blazing with refined gold, and bulls threatening death with horns radiant with gold, would not fear the king and such a great force?

Moreover, in so great an expedition there was no slave, no freedman born from slavery, no ignoble man, and no one weakened by old age. All were noble; all possessed the strength of full maturity; all were fit for any battle; and all were so swift that the speed of mounted men seemed contemptible to them.

Thus this army, having boarded its proud ships, entered the open sea. The anchors and ropes were released from the shore, and it swept across the waves with such force that one might have thought the winged ships were flying above the waters, scarcely restrained by the ropes in so vast a sea.

The royal ship, however, was the honor and focus of the others, because they had no other aim than to enlarge the majesty of their king with every effort.

In an ordered and expectant formation, with a favorable wind, they reached Sandwich, the most famous of all English ports. After casting anchor, the scouts made their way to the shore on poles; having very quickly explored the neighboring land, they returned to the familiar ships and announced to the king that thousands of opponents were ready to resist.

For the inhabitants, burning with fierce rebellion against the king and the Danes, had gathered the phalanxes they believed sufficient for the struggle. They flew forward, massed together in one body and conspiring as one, destined to die by the right hands of nobles.

Then Turkill, recognizing that the moment had arrived in which he could demonstrate his loyalty to his lord, said:

“I shall undertake to overcome this battle for my lord with my men, and I shall not allow my king, who is extremely ardent because of his youth, to take part in this battle. If I am victorious, I shall win a triumph for the king himself; but if I fall or turn my back, it will not bring such glory to the English, because the king will survive, and he will renew the battle and perhaps avenge my wrongs.”

When this statement seemed wise to everyone, the king consenting, Turkill went ashore with his men and drew up his line against the attack of the English, who had then assembled at a place called Scorastan.

The Danish army that went ashore numbered forty ships and more, but this number was still nowhere near half the enemy’s forces. The commander, however, trusting more in courage than in numbers, broke through every delay, sounded the trumpet, advanced at the front, and, always imploring God’s help in his mind, cut down everything before him with the edge of his sword.

At first the English, stronger in the opening encounter, slaughtered the Danes terribly, so that they almost achieved victory and forced their opponents to flee, had not the commander held them back by his exhortation and, mindful of their courage, made them ashamed to flee.

For he reminded them that there was no escape: the enemy was on land, while their ships lay far from the shore. Therefore, if they did not conquer, they must all perish together.

Thus made more courageous, they immediately demonstrated in battle how dangerous despair can be. Indeed, despairing of flight as a refuge, they raged against the enemy with such madness that one could see not only the bodies of the dead falling, but also those of the living dodging blows.

At last, having obtained the desired victory, they buried the bodies of their own men whom they were able to find. After plundering spoils from the enemy as well, they returned and prepared to invade the prostrate region.

Turkill increased Canute’s military glory by this first achievement and later earned a large part of the country for this service.

At that time he returned to his lord and reported to him and his companions what had happened, making them more eager for battle by the spoils he had brought, rejoicing in the booty and in the success of victory.

Encouraged by this example, a certain Eric, a duke and prince of the province called Norway—for he too belonged to the officials of King Cnut, had long been subject to him, was a vigorous warrior, and worthy of every honor—obtained permission, went out with his men, attacked part of the country, seized the spoils, destroyed villages by invading them, subdued the enemies who encountered him, captured many of them, and at last returned victorious to his companions with the booty. When he had returned, the king, sparing the country, forbade any further plundering of it, but ordered the city of London, the metropolis of the land, to be held under siege, since the nobles, part of the army, and the immense multitude—for it is very populous—had taken refuge there.

And because foot soldiers and cavalry could not accomplish this—for on every side the city was enclosed, as it were, by water, though not by an equal current—he had it hemmed in with ships furnished with towers and held it under the firmest blockade. Thus God, who wishes to save all human beings rather than destroy them, seeing these peoples struggling amid such danger, removed from the body the prince who presided within the city and joined him to everlasting rest. Once he was dead, the way was open for Cnut to enter freely, and both peoples were granted the opportunity to breathe for a little while after peace had been concluded.

And this was done. For the citizens, having honorably buried their prince and having taken salutary counsel, chose to send envoys and convey to the king their wishes: namely, that he extend his right hand to them and receive the city peacefully. When this proposal seemed sufficiently acceptable to Cnut, a treaty was confirmed, and a day was appointed for his entry.

But part of the army within the city rejected the citizens’ decision. Secretly, on the night before the day on which the king was to enter, they went out of the city with the dead prince’s son, intending to test once more, with an innumerable force gathered together, whether they might perhaps keep the king from entering within their borders. Nor did they rest until almost all the English had joined them, being still more favorably disposed toward them than toward Cnut.

Cnut entered the city and took his seat upon the royal throne, but he still did not believe that the Londoners were loyal to him. Therefore, during that summer, he had the fleet’s equipment restored, lest, if the army of his adversaries should attack the city, he might be handed over by the enemies within to those outside and perish. Taking precautions against this, he once again, for a time, withdrew prudently; boarding his boats and leaving the city, he went with his men to the island called Sheppey, where he spent the winter and peacefully awaited the outcome.

Edmund—for that was the name given to the young man who had gathered the army—entered the city in grand procession after Cnut’s departure, bringing with him a considerable, indeed innumerable, crowd. Immediately everyone followed, obeyed, and supported him, urging him to become a brave man and saying that they would choose him rather than the Danish prince.

The chief earl on his side was also Edric, powerful in counsel but changeable and deceitful in his treachery; Edmund had placed him at his ear in all affairs. It is said that at that time the young man offered King Cnut, as he was departing, single combat. But the wise king is said to have replied:

“I shall await the proper time for the contest, when I am no longer apprehensive of chance but certain of victory. You, however, who desire battle in winter, take care lest you fail even at a more suitable time.”

Thus the king wintered as best he could on Sheppey, which in Latin is called “Island of Sheep.” Edmund, meanwhile, dismissed his army and spent the last part of the winter in London.

When winter was passing, he again assembled an army throughout Lent. Soon after Easter he prepared to drive the king and the Danes from English territory, and, coming with an innumerable multitude, he suddenly resolved to attack them.

But the report did not escape the Danes. Leaving their ships behind, they made for dry land and prepared themselves to meet whatever came against them. They had with them a banner of marvelous portent. Although I believe it may seem incredible to the reader, nevertheless, since it is true, I shall insert it in my truthful narrative.

Although it was woven of the simplest and whitest silk, with no image of any kind worked into it, during battle a raven always appeared upon it as though woven there. When its people were victorious, the raven seemed to gape with its beak, flap its wings, and stand unsteadily upon its feet; but when its own people had been defeated, it became completely still, with its entire body hanging downward.

Thurkill, the author of the first battle, asked about this and said: “Let us fight bravely, companions, for there will be no danger for us. The unsteady raven of the prophetic banner bears witness to this.”

When they heard this, the horses grew bolder, and, hardened by their iron coverings, they advanced against the English at a place called Ashingdon, which we Latins may interpret as “Mountain of Ash Trees.”

Before the engagement had yet begun, Edric, whom we have called Edmund’s foremost earl, addressed his men as follows:

“Let us flee, companions, and withdraw our lives from imminent death; otherwise we shall perish at once. For I know the Danes’ toughness.”

Then, concealing the banner that he carried in his right hand and turning his back upon the enemy, he deprived the battle of a large part of the soldiers. Some say that he did not do this out of fear but through treachery, as later became clear, because the testimony of many asserts that he had secretly promised this to the Danes in exchange for some benefit—I do not know what.

When Edmund saw this and was surrounded on every side, he said:

“O Englishmen, either you will fight today, or all of you together will submit. Fight, then, brave men, for freedom and country. Those who are fleeing, being cowardly, would have been a hindrance to the army had they remained.”

Saying this, he entered the midst of the enemy, slaughtering the Danes on every side and, by this example, making his nobles more eager to fight.

A most grievous infantry battle therefore began. Although fewer in number, the Danes, unwilling to yield, preferred destruction to the danger of flight. They resisted bravely and continued the battle from the ninth hour of the day until evening, not willingly exposing themselves to the swords, but more forcefully pressing their opponents with the points of their own swords. Armed men fell on both sides, but more from the side that was greater in number.

When the hours of night were already approaching with evening, the love of victory overcame the disadvantages of darkness. They did not shudder at the darkness, since a greater concern pressed upon them, nor did they consider it fitting to yield to night while they burned to prevail over the enemy. And if the bright moon had not revealed the enemy himself, each man would have struck his fellow soldier as though he were a resisting foe, and no one from either side would have survived except those whom flight saved.

Meanwhile the English began to grow weary and gradually to consider flight, as they observed that the Danes were united in the resolve either to conquer or to perish altogether, to the very last man. They seemed to the English then more numerous and, in such a prolonged struggle, stronger. The English rightly suspected them of being stronger, for, already goaded by the blows of iron and thrown into confusion by the fall of their comrades, they seemed to rage rather than fight.

Accordingly, the English turned their backs and fled here and there without delay, continually falling before their adversary. They added glory to Cnut and victory to his cause, while Edmund, their prince, was forced to flee.

Although he was defeated and withdrew, yielding to stronger opponents, he did not yet despair completely. He entrusted himself to safe places so that, after gathering a stronger multitude, he might test once more whether something favorable might perhaps befall him.

**[Col. 1386A]** The Danes did not pursue the fugitives far, because, being unfamiliar with the places (or perhaps, *incognitis*, “by unfamiliar places,” ED. P.), they were held back by the darkness of night. The English, however, knowing the area, quickly escaped from the hands of the enemy, leaving them to the spoils and giving themselves over to dishonorable refuges.

Then the victors, rejoicing in their victory, spent the remainder of the night among the corpses of the dead, more than half the night having already passed. They did not divide the spoils during the night; meanwhile they searched for their own men and gathered together so that they might be more secure, and all remained together in one place.

When morning dawned, they recognized that many of their own had fallen in battle, and they buried their corpses as best they could. From the bodies of the adversaries they also stripped away the spoils, leaving their corpses to beasts and birds. Then they returned to their ships and made for London again, seeking sounder counsel for themselves.

The English likewise took counsel with their prince and sought God’s help in this matter, so that those who had so often been defeated by arms might at least be able, through some counsel, to remain supported.

Now Edric too, who had earlier withdrawn from the battle as a fugitive, returned to his lord and companions and was received, since he was a man of good counsel. Rising in the midst of the army, he addressed them all in these words:

“Although almost all of you hate me because I withdrew from the battle, nevertheless, if you were willing in your hearts to obey the words of my advice, you could become more victorious through my counsel than if you resisted these men with the arms of the whole country. For, having sufficiently experienced the Danes’ victories, I know that it is entirely useless for us to resist them. This is why I withdrew from the battle, so that afterward I might help you with counsel—not, as you suppose, because I was overcome by any fear.

“When I knew that I would necessarily have to flee, what was better: to withdraw wounded or unharmed? Without doubt, flight sometimes wrests a certain victory from a stronger enemy whom arms cannot resist. All of us who are here fled, alas! But lest such a misfortune happen to you again, let us extend our right hands to the Danes, so that, having them as allies, we may at least avoid flight and the danger of war.

“Yet this cannot be done except by dividing our kingdom. I judge it better that our king should possess half the kingdom in peace than that he should unwillingly lose the whole of it alike.”

The nobles approved his speech, and Edmund, though unwilling, nevertheless consented. He chose envoys and sent them ahead to Cnut’s ships, so that they might extend their right hands to the Danes and receive theirs in return.

When the Danes first saw them approaching, they suspected that they were scouts. But after they saw them drawing nearer, they summoned them and began asking what they wanted. When they learned from them that they had come to establish peace, they gladly brought them into the king’s presence.

For the Danes were earnestly desirous of peace, already weary of war and of the continual voyage. Then the envoys, having greeted the king peacefully, said:

“Our prince and the multitude of our nobles have sent us to you, O king, that you may agree to peace with them. Give us your right hands and receive hostages from us, and likewise give hostages to us, together with half the kingdom. Rule peacefully in the northern part; on the other side, let our Edmund be in the territories of the southern region.

“For this reason we have come to you as envoys. Do well and consent to the proposal. Otherwise, although we have been driven from you by war once and again, we shall still be strengthened with greater force to fight against you.”

The king did not answer them rashly. After sending them away, he sought counsel from his own men, and afterward peacefully consented to their proposal. For he had heard from his men that many of their number had fallen and that there was no one to replace those who died, since they were far removed from their native land. Although very many of the English were being killed, their number was not diminished so greatly, because, being stationed in their own country, they always had someone available to restore the place of the deceased.

The envoys were therefore recalled, and the king said:

“I consent to your embassy, young men, and, as you have said, half the kingdom shall be freely mine. Nevertheless, your king, whoever he may be, shall also pay tribute from his part to my army. I am owed this from him, and therefore I do not approve any other agreement.”

The treaty was therefore confirmed, and hostages were given by both sides. Thus the armies, released from the burdens of war, joyfully obtained the peace they desired.

Nevertheless, God, mindful of his ancient teaching—that every kingdom divided against itself cannot long endure—soon afterward removed Edmund from the body, taking pity on the English kingdom. For perhaps, if both had survived, neither would have ruled securely, and the kingdom would have been gradually destroyed by renewed conflict.

The dead royal youth was buried in a royal tomb, and the people of his homeland mourned him for a long time and greatly. May God grant him every joy in the heavenly throne.

The reason God had ordered him to die soon became clear, because the entire kingdom immediately chose Cnut as its king. The man whom it had previously resisted with every effort, it then willingly subjected itself and all that belonged to it to him.

Thus, by divine mercy, the vigorous man Cnut assumed the monarchy of the kingdom. He nobly appointed his dukes and earls and thereafter held the kingdom of the English peacefully to the end. He was still flourishing in the first bloom of youth, yet he possessed incomparable prudence.

Consequently, he loved those whom he had previously heard serving Edmund faithfully and without deceit, while he hated those whom he knew to be treacherous and who, during the war, had wavered deceitfully between the two sides. So much so that one day he ordered many of the princes to be killed on account of such treachery.

Among them was Edric, who had fled from the battle. When he asked the king for rewards on this very account, as though he had done it for the king’s victory, the king, somewhat sorrowfully, said:

“You who deceived your lord through treachery—could you be faithful to me? I shall repay you with rewards worthy of you, but take care that you do not henceforth rejoice in such deceit.”

Then he summoned his own duke, Eric, and said: “Pay him what we owe him—namely, kill him, so that he may not deceive us.”

Eric did not delay. He raised a double-headed axe and severed Edric’s head with a powerful blow, so that by this example soldiers might learn to be faithful, not faithless, to their kings.

When everything had thus been properly arranged, nothing was lacking to the king except a most noble wife. He ordered her to be sought everywhere, so that, once found, he might lawfully acquire her and make her, when obtained, partner in his rule.

Accordingly, the kingdoms and cities were searched, and a royal bride was sought. After a long search far and wide, one worthy of him was scarcely found. This imperial bride was discovered on the borders of Gaul, especially in the region of Normandy. She was exceedingly rich in lineage and wealth, yet, in the charm of her beauty and prudence, she surpassed all the women of her time, being a celebrated queen.

Because of these distinctions the king desired her greatly, and especially because she was descended from the victorious people who had claimed a portion of Gaul for themselves, despite the opposition of the Franks and their prince.

Why delay over the details? Suitors were sent to the lady, royal gifts were sent, and words of entreaty were also sent. But she refused ever to become Cnut’s bride unless he affirmed under oath that he would never allow the son of another wife to reign after him, but only her son, if God should grant him a son through her.

For it was said that the king had sons by another woman. She therefore prudently looked after her own interests and, with shrewd intelligence, knew how to arrange in advance what would benefit her.

The king was pleased by the virgin’s condition, and, once the oath had been sworn, the virgin was pleased by the king’s wish. Thus, thanks be to God, the noblewoman Emma, most distinguished of women, became the wife of the mighty King Cnut.

Gaul rejoiced, and the land of the English also rejoiced, as so great an honor was carried across the sea. Gaul, I say, rejoiced that it had brought forth so great a woman worthy of so great a king. The land of the English rejoiced that it had received such a woman into its cities.

O event prepared by a thousand times a thousand prayers, scarcely at last accomplished under the auspices of the Savior’s grace! This was what the armies on both sides had long and intensely desired: that so great a woman, worthy of so great a man, should be joined to him in a worthy marital bond and calm their warlike disturbances.

For what greater or more desirable object could there be among their wishes than that their destructive and thankless labors of war should end in the peaceful tranquility of peace, when equals met equals in bodily strength and courage of spirit, and now these, now those, with the fortune of war alternating, conquered one another at great cost to themselves?

But when, by divine dispensation and after many envoys had for a long time passed between them, they at last agreed to unite themselves in marital union, it is difficult to believe how great a joy suddenly arose in each of them concerning the other.

The king rejoiced that he had unexpectedly entered such a noble bridal chamber. She, on the one hand, was inflamed by the outstanding virtue of her husband and, on the other, by joyful hope of future offspring.

Both armies also rejoiced beyond estimation, hoping that their resources would be increased by their common strength, as the outcome later proved. For many peoples subdued in war, and many nations far distant from one another in life, customs, and even language, were compelled forever to pay annual tribute to the king and to the king’s descendants.

But is it surprising that such a great and eminent king should defeat those who resisted him in battle, when he brought very many of them voluntarily under his rule, partly through generous gifts and partly through the favor of his protection? Certainly not. For divine grace breathes where the balance of justice and uprightness is held evenly.

But why delay over the details? I have said that there was great joy in the marriage of these two eminent persons; I say that there was much greater joy when the opportunity for male offspring was received.

Not long afterward, by the favor of the Savior’s grace, the most noble queen gave birth to a son. Since both parents rejoiced in him with deep and, so to speak, singular affection, they sent their other sons to Normandy to be raised, while retaining this one here as their future heir to the kingdom.

Accordingly, as is customary among Catholics, they washed their dearly loved pledge in the sacred font of baptism and gave him a name that in some way conveyed an indication of his future virtue. He was called Hardecnute, a name referring to his father with an addition.

If its etymology is sought in the Teutonic language, one can recognize what kind of man he would be and how great. For *harde* means “swift” or “strong,” and both qualities—and much more than these—could be recognized in that one man, since he surpassed all the men of his time in excellence of every virtue.

I cannot enumerate all his virtues. Therefore, lest I stray too far from my subject, I shall return to what has gone before and follow the order of the history.

When the boy of whom we are speaking had grown to maturity, his father, still living in complete prosperity, bound the whole kingdom subject to his authority by an oath of allegiance. He afterward sent him with chosen soldiers to obtain the monarchy of the kingdom of the Danes.

Since King Cnut first held sole rule over the Danes and, having secured dominion over five kingdoms—Denmark, England, Britain, Scotland, and Norway—became an emperor, he also became a friend and intimate of ecclesiastical men. To bishops he seemed a fellow bishop in the display of complete religious devotion; to monks, not a secular man but a coenobitic one, in the restraint of his most humble devotion.

He diligently defended wards and widows, supported orphans and strangers, suppressed unjust laws and those who followed them, exalted and cultivated justice and equity, built and honored churches, increased the dignities of priests and clergy, and imposed equality and unanimity upon all his subjects. Of him one could say the verse of Maro, if it did not lie outside the Catholic faith:

> All night it rained; in the morning the spectacles return.

Caesar shares a divided empire with Jupiter.

He strove to please God in every way. Therefore, whatever good he had learned ought to be done, he entrusted not to negligence but to action. For what church does not still rejoice in his benefactions?

But, to say nothing of what he did among those who lived in his kingdom, Italy blesses his soul each day; Gaul prays that he may enjoy good things; and Flanders, more than all the others, prays that he may rejoice with Christ in heaven.

Passing through these provinces, he made for Rome. As many can testify, he displayed such great works of mercy on this journey that, if anyone wished to record them all, even if he produced countless volumes from them, he would eventually confess, exhausted, that he had scarcely run through even the smallest portion.

I shall say nothing of what he did in every individual place. Nevertheless, so that what I assert may become more credible, I shall give as an example what he did in the city of Saint-Omer, which I remember having seen with my own eyes.

When he entered the monasteries and was received with great honor, he walked humbly, fixing his eyes upon the ground with marvelous reverence and pouring forth, so to speak, rivers of tears. With complete devotion he sought the intercession of the saints.

But when the time came for him to enrich the sacred altars with royal offerings—ah! how often he first pressed tearful kisses upon the pavement! How often he struck that venerable breast with his own blows! What sighs he uttered! How often he prayed that heavenly mercy would not be angry with him!

At last, by his attendants, an offering of no ordinary size was presented to him as he approached (*imminenti*; variant *immerenti*, “to him, unworthy”)—not something enclosed in a purse, but something immense, carried in the outspread lap of a cloth. The king himself placed it upon the altar, a cheerful giver in obedience to the apostolic command.

Why do I say “upon the altar,” when I remember seeing him go around all the corners of the monasteries and pass no altar, however small, without giving it gifts and imprinting upon it sweet kisses?

Then the poor appeared, and they too were immediately given gifts, each one individually.

These and other deeds still more marvelous I myself, your little servant, saw performed by the lord Cnut, Saint-Omer and Saint Bertin, when they took place in your monasteries. For these good deeds, obtain for so great a king that he may live in the heavenly dwellings, so that your canonical servants and monks may be praying for him in their daily prayers.

Let kings and princes therefore learn to imitate the actions of this lord. To be able to ascend to lofty places, he humbled himself in the lowest; and, so that he might attain heavenly things, he cheerfully gave away earthly ones.

He had not forgotten his own condition: that he would die in this world and leave behind everything that can be desired in the age. For these riches, which he could not take away with him when he died, he distributed honorably during his life to God and to his holy places, lest, if he devoted himself to avarice, he should live hated by all, with no one to pray for anything good on behalf of his soul, and another should succeed him who would live more generously in his kingdom and resent his predecessor’s parsimony.

He took sufficient care that this should not happen and left his descendants a good example of generosity and every kind of goodness. They too, thanks be to God, still preserve it excellently, being powerful in the administration of the kingdom and in the splendor of their virtues.

When so great a king had returned from Rome and had remained for a short time in his own land, after arranging everything well, he passed to the Lord, to be crowned at the right hand by the Lord himself, the author of all things.

All who heard of his death were thrown into confusion, especially those who had served his throne. Most of them would have wished to die with him, if that did not displease the divine dispensation (with *non*, “not,” supplied by ED. P.).

Queen Emma mourned with her relatives; the poor howled together with the powerful; bishops and clerics wept with monks and nuns.

But as much as he was mourned in the world, so much may he rejoice in the palace of heaven. These mourned what they had lost; those may rejoice over his soul, which they receive. These buried his lifeless body; those may lead his spirit upward to rejoice in eternal rest.

For his passing, earthly people alone wept; but for his spirit, let the citizens of heaven intervene together with earthly people. Let us earnestly pray to God that his glory may increase each day. And because he deserved this through his goodness, let us cry out daily:

> May the soul of Cnut rest in peace. Amen.

When King Cnut had died and had been honorably buried in the monastery built in honor of Saint Peter, Queen Emma alone remained in the kingdom, grieving bitterly over her lord’s death and anxious because of the absence of her sons.

One of them, Hardecnute, whom his father had appointed king of the Danes, was living in his own kingdom. The other two had been entrusted for upbringing in the territories of Normandy and were living with their relative Robert.

It therefore happened that certain Englishmen, having forgotten the piety of their now-dead king, preferred to disgrace rather than adorn his kingdom. They abandoned the noble sons of the illustrious Queen Emma and chose as their king a certain Harold, who is falsely claimed to have been the son of a concubine of King Cnut.

The assertion of many, however, maintains that this same Harold had secretly been taken from a serving woman who was giving birth and placed in the chamber of the concubine while she lay ill. This account may be believed more credibly.

After being chosen, and fearing what might come, he immediately summoned Archbishop Aelnot, a man endowed with every virtue and wisdom. He commanded and begged him to bless him as king, to entrust to him with the crown the royal scepter committed to his keeping, and to lead him by the same authority to the lofty throne of the kingdom, since it was not lawful for anyone else to do so.

The archbishop refused, asserting under oath that he would praise or bless no one else as king while the sons of Queen Emma were alive.

“Cnut entrusted them to my faith. I owe them fidelity, and I shall preserve my loyalty to them. I place the scepter and crown upon the sacred altar. I neither deny them to you nor hand them over to you; but by apostolic authority I forbid all bishops, lest any of them take them away or hand them to you or bless you.

“If you dare, invade what I have committed to God and to his table.”

The wretched man did not know what he should do or where he should turn. He threatened, but achieved nothing. He offered gifts, but gained nothing and grieved, because the apostolic man could neither be overthrown by threats nor bent by gifts.

At last, in despair, he withdrew. He despised episcopal blessing so thoroughly that he not only hated the blessing itself but also fled from the whole Christian religion.

While others entered the church in Christian fashion to hear Mass, he either surrounded himself with hunting dogs in the woods or occupied himself with any other base pursuits, so that he might avoid what he hated.

The English saw this and grieved, but because they had chosen him as their king, they were ashamed to depose him. They therefore resolved that he should remain their king to the end.

Queen Emma, meanwhile, awaited the outcome and, troubled for a while, prayed daily for God’s help.

He secretly—for he did not yet dare to act openly—plotted against the queen, but no one allowed him to harm her. Therefore, with his men and through a wicked plan, he wanted to kill the sons of his lady, so that he could thereafter reign securely while living in sin.

Yet he could not accomplish this in any way unless, aided by the deceit of treacherous men, he devised what we shall now relate. Having discovered this stratagem, he caused a letter to be composed in the queen’s name to her sons, who were staying in Normandy. We do not hesitate to append a copy of it.

> Emma, queen in name only, sends maternal greetings to her sons Edward and Alfred.
>
> While we mourn separately the death of our lord the king, dearest sons, and while day by day you are increasingly deprived of the kingdom that is your inheritance, I wonder what counsel you are pursuing, although you know that, through the delay of your absence, the power of your usurper is daily becoming more secure.
>
> He constantly travels through villages and cities and makes the princes his friends by gifts, threats, and entreaties. Yet they would rather have one of you reign over them than remain under the rule of this man who does not command them.
>
> Therefore, I beg one of you to come quickly and privately to me, so that you may receive sound counsel from me and learn how the matter I wish to be accomplished ought to be carried out. Through the present messenger, also send me word about what you intend to do concerning these matters.
>
> Farewell, entrails of my heart.

This fraud, composed at the command of the tyrant Harold, was sent to the royal youths by deceitful messengers. It was presented to them in the name of their unsuspecting mother, and they received it honorably as a gift from their parent.

Unaware of his treachery and, alas, too credulous toward the falsehood, they imprudently sent word back to their mother that one of them would come to her. They appointed a day, time, and place for him.

The messengers returned and reported to the enemies of God what answer they had received from the most noble youths. They then awaited his arrival and devised, to their own ruin, what they would do to him.

When the appointed day came, Alfred, the younger brother, with the approval of his brother, chose companions in arms and set out, arriving in the territories of Flanders. He stayed there briefly with Count Baldwin, who urged him to take some of his army with him because of the enemy’s ambushes.

But he took only a few men from Boulogne and crossed the sea in the usual way aboard ships. When he came close to the shore, he was immediately recognized by the adversaries. They hastened toward him, intending to attack him, but as soon as he realized who they were, he ordered the ships to be pushed away from that shore.

Then, boarding another vessel at anchor, he prepared to visit his mother, believing that he had escaped every danger of ambush. But when he was already nearby, Earl Godwin came to meet him. Alfred placed himself under his protection, and Godwin immediately became his sworn man, affirming this by oath.

Godwin diverted him from London and led him to a village called Sildefordia. There he distributed Alfred’s soldiers in groups of twenty, twelve, and ten among the various lodgings, leaving only a few with the young man who were to attend upon him.

He supplied them abundantly with food and drink and then withdrew to his own lodging, intending to return in the morning to serve his lord with due honor.

But after they had eaten and drunk and, being tired, had gladly gone to bed, behold, the accomplices of the unspeakable tyrant Harold arrived. They invaded each lodging, secretly removed the arms of the innocent men, bound them with iron manacles and fetters, and kept them for torture on the following day.

When morning came, the innocent men were brought into the midst of the assembly and wickedly condemned without being heard. After they had all been disarmed and their hands bound behind their backs, they were handed over to the most savage executioners. These had also been ordered to spare no one except the tenth man whom chance might select.

Then the torturers made the prisoners sit in an ordered line and, insulting them greatly and beyond measure, imitated the example of the executioner of the Theban Legion, who decimated innocent men far more mercifully than this.

That pagan king spared nine Christians and killed the tenth. Although he was a pagan and slaughtered Christians, he nevertheless ordered them, like glorious soldiers, to be beheaded openly in the field, without being entangled in bonds.

But these men, Christian in name yet utterly pagan in deed, slaughtered chained heroes like swine, even though they deserved no blows from their spears.

Therefore all ages rightly call such torturers worse than dogs: not through the violence of warfare but through their own treacherous ambushes they condemned the honorable bodies of so many soldiers.

Some, as has been said, they killed; others they consigned to slavery. Others, seized by blind greed, they sold. Some they kept bound in chains for greater mockery.

But divine mercy did not abandon the innocent who stood in such danger. We ourselves saw many whom heaven rescued from that mockery, without human aid, breaking through the barriers of their manacles and fetters.

Since we have passed swiftly over the sufferings of the soldiers, it remains for us to abbreviate the course of our narrative by recounting the martyrdom of their prince, the glorious Alfred. For if we wished to touch upon everything that was done to him individually, we might multiply everywhere, and especially for the lady queen, the pain of it.

In this matter, I beg you, lady, not to seek more than what we shall briefly tell you out of consideration for your grief. Much could be said if we were not sparing your sorrow. There is no pain greater for a mother than to see or hear of the death of her beloved son.

The royal youth was therefore captured, secretly led out from his lodging, and taken to the island called Ely. First he was mocked by a most wicked soldier. Then men still more contemptible were chosen, so that the lamentable youth might be judged according to their madness.

Once appointed judges, they decreed that first each of his eyes should be torn out as an insult (*oculi utrique*; variant *oculos utrosque*, “both eyes”). When they prepared to carry this out, two men were placed upon his arms to hold them, while one was placed upon his chest and another upon his legs, so that the punishment might be inflicted upon him more easily.

Why should I dwell upon this agony? Even as I write, my pen trembles while I shudder at what the most blessed youth endured.

I shall therefore pass more briefly over the misery of such calamity and touch upon the end of this martyrdom. He was held by the impious, and, after his eyes had been most impiously gouged out, he was killed.

When the murder had been completed, they left his lifeless body there. But the faithful monks of Christ, namely those of the same island of Ely, took it and buried it honorably.

Many miracles are performed at the place of his burial, as certain people say—people who also repeatedly claim that they have seen them. And rightly so: he was martyred innocently, and therefore it is fitting that through him the power of the innocent should be exercised.

Let Queen Emma therefore rejoice in so great an intercessor, for the one whom she had as a son on earth she now has as a patron in heaven.

[Col. 1394B] But the queen, shaken by the unprecedented nature of so great a crime, silently considers what ought to be done. Her mind is therefore driven this way and that, and she hesitates to believe that such treachery could have occurred—especially since she was overwhelmed by inconsolable grief at the death of her son, yet was all the more consoled by her certainty that he was resting in blessedness. Thus, as we have said, she was distressed for two reasons: by the pitiable sorrow over her son’s death, and by her distrust concerning the dignity of the rest of her life.

But perhaps someone will cry out at me here—someone whom envy makes hostile and burdensome to this lady: “Why did she refuse to die by the same death, when she had no doubt that the son slain through this treachery was enjoying eternal rest?” To refute this, I think the following answer should be given: If a persecutor of Christian [Col. 1394C] religion and faith had been present, she would not have fled from risking her life. Otherwise, it would have seemed wicked and abhorrent to all orthodox people if a woman of such reputation had been deprived of life through ambition for earthly power; nor, indeed, would death have been regarded as an honorable end for a lady of such resources. [Note: [Col. 1393] Here the author imitates the words of Adherbal in Sallust, *Jugurthine War*.]

Keeping these and similar considerations before her eyes, and judging that authentic command of the Lord’s exhortation conducive to the preservation of her fortunes—by which, evidently, he instructs the chosen: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another”—she makes every reasonable effort to preserve the dignity that remained to her, in accordance with her circumstances, and at last makes prudent use of the favor of heavenly providence. She believes it useful to seek foreign nations, and by shrewd planning carries this through to its conclusion. Yet she discovered that those to whom she went were not foreign to her; [Col. 1394D] while staying among them, she was honored with the utmost courtesy, no less than if they had been her own people.

Accordingly, in proportion to the circumstances and the time, she gathers around herself as many loyal nobles as she can, and, with them present, lays bare the secrets of her heart. After they had approved their lady’s plan, preparations were made for the ships’ provisions for her exile. Thus, taking advantage of favorable winds, they cross the sea and make their way to a certain anchorage not far from the castle of Bruges.

This castle is inhabited by Flemish settlers and is considered highly renowned both for the throng of merchants and for the abundance of everything that mortals value most. Here, in fact, she is honorably received, as was fitting, by Baldwin, margrave of that province, son of the great and unconquered prince, and by his wife Athala—which name is interpreted as “most noble”—the daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, and of Queen Constance. They also grant the queen a house in the aforesaid town suitable for royal expenditure, and generously provide her with provisions. Some of these she accepts with thanks, while in part she shows, in a certain way, that she has no need of them.

Having thus been placed in such complete security, she sends envoys to her son Edward, asking him not to delay coming to her. He obeys them, mounts a horse, and reaches his mother. But when they were granted the opportunity to speak with one another, the son tells her that he pities her fortunes but can in no way help her, since the English nobles had sworn him no oath; [Col. 1395B] this circumstance indicated that assistance should be sought from his brother.

When these matters had been settled, Edward returned to Normandy, while the queen’s mind still hesitated over what she ought to do. After his departure she sent messengers to her son Hardecnut, who at that time held the government of the Danes. Through them she disclosed the unprecedented nature of her suffering and asked him to hasten to come to her as quickly as possible.

When the horror of so great a crime struck his ears, his mind at first, overcome by intolerable grief, faltered in deliberation. For his heart burned to avenge his brother’s wrongs, indeed even to obey his mother’s embassy. Foreseeing both possibilities, he prepared as large forces [ED. P.] of ships and soldiers as he could, placing the greater number of them in a certain inlet of the sea, so that, if the opportunity—or even the necessity—of fighting or resisting arose during his journey, they might come to his aid. Meanwhile, accompanied by no more than ten ships, he set out for his mother, who was being worn down by no small anxiety of grief.

While they devoted themselves to a favorable voyage, not only did they drive the salt foam through the air in rivalry [Note: [Col. 1395] Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 39], but they also raised the topsails under the favorable winds, so that the face of the sea, never stable but always rendered doubtful and treacherous by the shifting of the winds, suddenly saw a foul storm of winds and clouds massing behind them, and the surface of the sea was thrown into confusion as the south winds came upon it.

Therefore, as ordinarily happens in so grave a situation, anchors were cast from the prows and fastened in the sands of the seabed. Although this event was then troublesome for them, it is nevertheless believed to have happened by the will of God, who orders all things, as the outcome of the matter later proved, when the limbs of everyone surrendered to peaceful, restful sleep.

For on the following night, while Hardecnut himself was resting in bed, a divine vision was shown to him. It strengthened and comforted him and commanded him to be courageous. It further urged him not to desist from what he had begun, because within a few days the unjust usurper of the kingdom—namely Harald—would be killed, and the kingdom, conquered by his father’s forces, would return unharmed to its rightful heir by the most just succession.

When the dreamer awoke, he was made more certain by these indications, gave thanks to almighty God for so great a consolation, and had no doubt whatever about the future that the vision had foretold to him. At last, when the sea’s anger had abated and every storm had subsided, he spread the folds of the sails under favorable winds. Thus, making a successful voyage, he reached the harbor of Bruges.

There, after securing the ships with anchors and cables and assigning sailors to guard them, he proceeded directly by road with his chosen men to his mother’s lodging. No page will ever be able to explain what grief and what joy arose at his arrival. There was no small sorrow when the mother, by a kind of mental image, contemplated in his face the features of her slain son. Yet she also rejoiced with great joy when she saw that the survivor had arrived safe and sound. Hence she knew that the entrails of divine mercy were looking upon her, since she had not been deprived of such consolation.

Not long afterward, while the son remained with his mother and awaited the promises of the vision already mentioned, messengers arrived bearing joyful news. They announced that Harald was dead, and they also reported that the English princes did not wish to oppose him but instead rejoiced with him in many celebrations. Therefore, they urged him not to disdain reclaiming the kingdom owed to him by hereditary right, and to provide jointly for the preservation of his own dignity and their safety.

Encouraged by this, Hardecnut and his mother decided to return to the shores of their ancestral kingdom. As soon as the report of this moved the ears of the people, one could immediately see everything filled with grief and mourning. The rich grieved at her departure, because they had always enjoyed her gracious conversation. The poor grieved at her departure, because her long-continued generosity had defended them from the burden of poverty. Widows and orphans grieved, those whom she had drawn from the sacred font of baptism and enriched with no small gifts. I do not know with what praises I should extol her, since she was never absent from those who were being reborn in Christ. Here her faith is plainly worthy of praise; here her goodness is to be celebrated in every respect. If I were to speak of each of her benefactions in equal detail, I believe that time would abandon me before the subject did. Therefore I hasten to return to the course of my narrative.

While preparations were being made for the return of the queen and her son, the entire shore was thrown into confusion by lamentation and groaning, and all hands were raised angrily toward heaven. They wept because she was departing from them, although throughout the whole period of her exile they had regarded her as one of their own citizens.
