She had been a burdensome guest to none of the rich and oppressive to none of the poor. You might have thought that everyone was changing his native land and that all wished to seek foreign regions with her.

Thus the whole shore mourned, [Col. 1396D] and thus the entire assembled people wept. Although in some measure they rejoiced with her that she was returning to her former rank and dignity, they could not send away such a noblewoman with dry eyes. At last love of her homeland prevailed, and, after kissing everyone individually and bidding them a tearful farewell, she went out onto the deep sea with her son and her household, not without a great abundance of tears poured forth on both sides.

The English princes, confident that their embassy had preceded them by only a little, came to meet them before they crossed over, judging it best both to satisfy the king and queen and to submit themselves as devoted subjects to their rule. Once Hardecnut had been reassured by this, he and his mother finally reached the harbor of the overseas shore and were received most gloriously by all the inhabitants of that land. Thus, by the grace of the divine gift, the kingdom owed to him was restored.

When these matters had been completed and all his affairs had been settled in the tranquility of peace, he was seized by brotherly love and sent messengers to Edward, asking him to come and hold the kingdom with him. Edward obeyed his brother’s command and crossed to England, and the mother and both sons enjoyed the advantages prepared for the kingdom without any dispute arising between them. Here faith was maintained among the partners in the kingdom; here the inviolable pact of maternal and fraternal love flourished. Jesus Christ, Lord of all, who makes those of one mind dwell together in a household, granted them all these things. To him, who remains in the Trinity, an unfading empire flourishes. Amen.

## From the Chronicles of Thomas Rudburn, concerning Queen Emma

[Col. 1397]

She married Æthelred, and afterward Cnut.

She bore holy Edward and Hardecnut.

She saw these four kings bearing the scepters.

Thus she was both mother and wife of the kings of the English.

[Col. 1397]

## Letter of Queen Emma to her sons Edward and Alfred

(See above, col. 1392.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1045: Poppo, Archbishop of Trier

[Col. 1397]

### Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, XIII, 406.)

[Col. 1397B] Poppo, son of Leopold, margrave of Austria, and of the most noble woman Richarda, and paternal uncle of Ernest II, duke of Swabia, whose guardianship he undertook, was exceptionally cultivated in literary and virtuous studies. Having been provost of the Church of Bamberg, he was appointed by the emperor Henry II to replace Megingaud, in order to suppress the madness of Adalbero, who nevertheless yielded to Poppo.

At the end of the year 1016 he was brought by the emperor to Trier and, by the unanimous votes and suffrages of the clergy and people, was requested as bishop. He was consecrated by Erchenbald, archbishop of Mainz, whom the emperor had summoned to Trier for this purpose, amid the immense joy of the entire people, in the year 1017, on the Kalends of January.

Among the bishops who attended Poppo’s sacred anointing was Theodoric of Metz, who repeatedly and fruitlessly asserted that the metropolitan consecration belonged to him. Hardly had Poppo been declared bishop when he took care to have the immunities and privileges of his Church protected by imperial authority. Not long after his consecration, he went to Rome and received the use of the pallium from Benedict VIII by a bull dated 8 April of that same year.

When he returned to his diocese, he found it torn apart and afflicted by various devastations of brigands. To heal the wounds of his Church, as Browerus says in Book XI of his *Annals*, he immediately arranged to seek remedies everywhere, and to attach to himself by benefices and feudal grants men especially distinguished for their military glory, to whom he could entrust the task of pacifying and defending the province. By their diligence and tireless use of arms, he expelled the brigands everywhere from the castles they had occupied for their own security, and kept the others who desired revolution faithful and obedient to their duty.

Since one Adelbert alone refused to carry out the commands, and from the castle of Saint Crucis—formerly dedicated to the saint and situated on a nearby hill south of the city—continually harassed the bishop’s court, servants, and all supplies by frequent raids, Poppo finally suppressed the rebellious enemy’s spirit and defeated him by the skill of Siko, a man outstanding in hand and counsel.

Siko, who had offered Poppo his labor and counsel for this purpose, went alone from the city to the castle gate at a suitable time. Pleading thirst, he asked Adelbert the tyrant, in accordance with the custom of their former friendship, to give him a drink. When Adelbert readily offered it through a servant, Siko, after drinking as much as he needed, ordered the master to be told that he gave him very great thanks and that before long he would see this benefit of having quenched his thirst repaid with grateful remembrance and, indeed, with an equal return of thanks.

After saying this, Siko departed and began to unfold the tricks that he had long ago devised in his mind for Adelbert’s deception. He equipped thirty wine casks, placing one armed man in each. Having reinforced the casks with bars and handles, he entrusted each to two exceptionally strong men, who were disguised in peasant clothing in order to deceive the enemy; their weapons were hidden inside the casks. Finally, to conceal the deception, he covered the vessels with blankets and much cloth.

When everything had been arranged, Siko looked for a time suitable for carrying out what he had begun. As soon as he found one, full of good hope, he secretly left the city with the carriers. He himself, knocking at the castle gate with only a few attendants, ordered it to be opened and heard the customary question: “Who are you, where are you from, and what do you want?” He answered only that Siko had arrived with wine for a formal gift, in order to discharge the favor he had promised long before.

When Adelbert received this message, ignorant of the trick, he opened the doors. Then Siko ordered the coverings and cloths to be removed. After commending the gift in a brief speech in Adelbert’s presence, he gave his men the signal to attack. At the first signal, with a tumult (sic), they leapt from the vessels, rushed upon everyone they encountered, and stained everything with slaughter and carnage; before all the others, they attacked Adelbert himself.

After the brigands had thus been killed, overpowered, and destroyed, the fortification was leveled with the ground and reduced to desolation. Siko, besides receiving the honor of restored peace and of having freed the city from Adelbert the raider, received distinguished feudal grants and benefices from Poppo. At almost the same time, Adelbert’s castle at Skiva, by the River Saar—later called Montis Clari—was overthrown and utterly destroyed at Poppo’s command.

When Adalbero saw that Poppo’s power and fortune had been firmly established to an extraordinary degree, he became much more humble than before. He handed over to Poppo not only the palace and the fortresses of the Church that he had occupied, but also the castles of Sericum, Rutichium, Sarburg, and Bern, reserving for himself a title to one of them. He then returned to the monastery of Saint Paulinus, of which we have already noted that he had been provost, and, abandoning every thought of honors, withdrew to a salutary retirement.

Poppo, having received all of Adalbero’s fortifications into his allegiance through his surrender, found Bern Castle resisting for some time, fiercely defended by brigands. But at last it was captured, its defenses having been scattered and demolished, and was utterly destroyed.

[Col. 1399D] Moreover, throughout the entire period in which Megingaud held the bishopric, the Church of Trier suffered a notable loss and ruin of every kind through Adalbero’s faction. Indeed, they report that the cathedral had been reduced to such utter desolation that, since no one required its roof and walls to be repaired, the clergy were forced by fear of collapse to abandon the church and suspend divine worship. The monasteries likewise fell into a shortage of necessary things during that same period.

To bring a remedy to these evils, Poppo devoted himself with exceptional diligence to restoring and adorning the churches, and enriched with estates and possessions the monasteries that internal sedition had exhausted. He restored the monks to the church of the Virgin Mother of God at the Martyrs, expelling the canons who had occupied the place after forcibly excluding the Benedictines.

In the first year of his episcopate, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fifteenth indiction, he also petitioned the emperor Henry II to grant his assent to the foundation of the collegiate church of Prüm. In the year 1018 he caused the outstanding gift of royal generosity—namely, Koblenz—and the abbey in the district of Trier, with all its appurtenances and rights, to be assigned to his Church. At approximately the same time he obtained the estate of Puzenvelt from Count Kaledo and his wife Irmingard by way of a precarious grant.

In the year 1022 the emperor Henry II was in Italy, intending to defeat the Greeks and Saracens who were ravaging Apulia and Campania. Poppo led eleven thousand armed men from his own people through the region of the Marsi to join him. He attended the Council of Aachen in the year 1023.

While he was turning all his care toward preserving the dignity of his diocese, he undertook on this occasion to reform the morals of the nuns of the monastery of Palatiolum, which had been softened by wantonness and luxury. It happened that he had given one of them, according to custom, a seam of his pallium from which she was to weave episcopal stockings. She returned the garment impregnated with a love potion in order to seize the bishop’s love.

As soon as Poppo put on the shoes, he immediately experienced the power of the potion in an extraordinary way and began to burn with all his mind and thought for love of the wicked woman. Astonished at the unusual tyranny of lustful flesh, and having made a similar experiment in others as well, he had no doubt that the woman was the author of the most shameful crime. Once the matter had been investigated and proven, everyone unanimously agreed that the most wicked enchantress should be expelled from that community and that the others should be brought back under stricter monastic rules.

When the majority, clinging to a more relaxed way of life, utterly rejected this, the archbishop decided that the community should be completely dissolved, while the others were given permission to transfer to other monasteries.

Nevertheless, entrusting the care of his Church to Theodoric of Metz for the sake of a pious pilgrimage, Poppo went to Jerusalem with leading members of the clergy. He was accompanied by Simeon, a Sinaitic monk, who had been sent from the East into Gaul by his abbot to receive substantial alms from Richard, duke of Normandy.

After the alms had been delivered by his companions to the monastery, Simeon remained for some time at Rouen and then decided to go to Trier; from there he accompanied Poppo, who was setting out for the Holy Land. Poppo remained on this journey for three full years. When he returned to the city in November 1028 and learned that Simeon, seeking a more tranquil life, desired to withdraw and therefore wished to be enclosed, he offered him the choice of establishing his dwelling in the territory of Trier.

Simeon asked that a place be assigned to him in the ancient structure called the Black Gate. On the feast of Saint Andrew, while a great multitude of people and clergy gathered to watch, the archbishop enclosed him in a narrow corner of that structure. There he spent seven years in constant prayer and great austerity of life.

[Col. 1401A] At approximately the same time, Poppo’s sister Christiana, following Simeon’s example, was enclosed somewhere within sacred walls and lived alone for herself and Christ.

In the year 1031, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, Poppo, invited by Abbot Humbert, consecrated the restored church of Echternach and transferred the bones of Saint Willibrord, after raising them, to a more honored tomb.

Around the year 1033 he reached an agreement with his neighbors concerning the boundaries of the Kilwald forest and recovered various estates alienated from his Church. Around the year 1035 he took part in two exchanges concluded between different monasteries. In the year 1036 he received twelve hides and the same number of serfs from Thiefrid, advocate of Trier, who had married his kinswoman Luitgard, and he granted the two spouses permission to live together.

In that same year and the following one, he approved various gifts given by Adalbero, provost of Saint Paulinus, to the monastery of Saint Matthias. He held a synod on the sixth day before the Ides of June 1037, at which Adelbert, margrave of Lorraine, and his wife Judith, appearing before him, granted the village of Momendorff to that monastery.

It is said that by this year he had introduced canons into the Palatiolum nunnery in place of the nuns. In the year 1039, on the Ides of September, he obtained from Henry III perpetual possession of the county of Marvelis, which the emperor Conrad had granted to the Church of Trier.

He sent a letter to Benedict IX, asking him to send a prudent man who might support him in his needs with both counsel and assistance. He also informed the pope of the death of Simeon the hermit and urged [Col. 1401C] that he be enrolled among the saints.

Acceding to Poppo’s prayers, Benedict sent him a bishop as coadjutor. Papebrochius conjectures that this was Gratian, an archpriest and prudent man. He also decreed that the man of God Simeon ought to be called a saint, and that his feast day, like those of the other saints, should be celebrated every year with the greatest reverence, as is clear from the pope’s letters and from the bull of canonization issued in the year 1042.

In that same year Poppo built a church in honor of Saint Simeon at the gate formerly consecrated to Mars among the pagans, namely, amid the ancient ruins of the old structure in which Saint Simeon had lived while he was still alive. He installed brothers, or canons, there to serve God and granted them estates and annual revenues.

In the year 1045 he obtained from the emperor Henry III a notable privilege confirming the possessions of the greater church.

He died on 16 June 1047 and was buried in the church that he had built for Saint Simeon. A lead tablet was placed upon his chest with this inscription: “Poppo, archbishop of Trier, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.” The following epitaph was engraved in bronze:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1057, in the seventeenth year of Henry II as king, but the first as emperor, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, Poppo, the archbishop beloved of God of this see of Trier, died.”

It is worth noting here that he had nothing in common with that Poppo who converted the Danes to the Christian faith. Although his tomb was once visited by those peoples, he is nevertheless entirely different from that man.

[Col. 1401]

## Letter of Poppo to Pope Benedict IX

(See above, among the letters of Benedict IX.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1045: Venerable Angelrannus, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Richarius at Centula

[Col. 1401]

### Historical Notice

(From *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. X, p. 1249.)

[Col. 1401D] Angelrannus, surnamed “the Wise,” was born at Centula to respectable parents. As a young man he entered the cloister of Saint Richarius. He was sent by Abbot Ingelard to investigate the schools located far away, and obtained Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, as teacher and instructor.

Meanwhile, after accompanying King Robert on his journey to Rome and receiving priestly ordination, he returned to Centula. When Ingelard died, the brothers elected him unanimously. But what modesty the man possessed! He secretly fled from the monastery and hid himself in the retreats of the forest of Olnodiol.

Soon, after being sought at the king’s command and finally discovered, he was compelled, against his will, to undertake the burden imposed upon him. The king therefore entered the church basilica with joy and, while a crowd of nobles and commoners looked on, transferred to him the rule of the entire place by means of ropes hanging from the standards, ordering that his blessing be expedited as quickly as possible.

Angelrannus immediately applied himself to the work. He built walls, clad altars in gold and silver, enlarged the sacred vessels, renewed the agreement previously made with Notker, bishop of Liège, and concluded with Durandus in 1022, acquired Scabellivilla from Richard, duke of Normandy, acquired Comitis-Villa from Angelrannus, count of Ponthieu, recovered Noguerias in 1035, and acquired the mill of Montignac in 1044.

At the urging of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, he composed in heroic verse the Life of Saint Richarius, together with his miracles and the account of his translation to the monastery of Centula, as well as the Passion of Saint Vincent the martyr and the Life of Saint Austreberta the virgin. He also composed fitting songs in honor of Saints Wulfram, archbishop, and Walaric, abbot.

The fame of his name spread so widely everywhere that many nobles entrusted themselves to him for instruction in letters. Two of them were especially distinguished: Guido, later bishop of Amiens, and Drogo, later bishop of Thérouanne.

Toward the end of his life he was so afflicted by paralysis that Fulco, a monk of that place, obtained the abbacy through the intervention of his father, Count Angelrannus, from King Henry, who happened at that time to have come to Ponthieu. When Angelrannus learned of this, he cursed the military men whom Fulco had summoned to a festive banquet on this matter, and declared that, as long as he lived, Fulco would not even become abbot of another place.

To restrain his ambition more easily, Angelrannus met the king in his carriage, severely rebuked him, and brought him to repent of what he had done. Shortly afterward, after the king had appointed another successor, the pastoral charge was restored to Angelrannus.

Angelrannus did not long survive this. Tested by prolonged paralysis, he finally reached the end and migrated to his heavenly homeland on the fifth day before the Ides of December 1045. His body was buried in the basilica of Saint Richarius at the altar of Saint Lawrence. A paralytic woman is said to have been healed at his tomb. Nevertheless, he has so far received no public cult and has not been entered in the catalogue of the saints.

[Col. 1403]

## Life of the Venerable Angelrannus, Abbot of Centula

(Edited by Dom Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, Sixth Century, Part I, p. 494, from Hariulf, a near-contemporary writer of the *Chronicle of Centula*, in Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, and collated with the autograph manuscript codex.)

### Preliminary Observations

1. The monastery of Centula, which we said had been built by Saint Richarius around the year 625, was destroyed by barbarians toward the end of the ninth century and remained almost uncultivated until the beginning of the eleventh century. Its restorer was Ingelard, formerly a monk of Corbie, who became abbot of Centula. Our Angelrannus, or, as others write it, Ingelrannus, succeeded him. He was a man endowed not only with learning for his time but also distinguished by excellent deeds and piety; hence he received the surname “the Wise.”

We have copied his Life from Book IV of the *Chronicle of Centula*, omitting, however, those things that did not contribute to our subject. The author of this Chronicle is Hariulf, who lived in the monastery of Centula shortly after Angelrannus. He himself attests this more than once, especially at the end of Book IV, where he reports that he was made a monk by Gervinus II, the successor of Angelrannus through Gervinus I.

From his epitaph, published in volume I of the *Analecta*, we learn that he, formerly a monk of Centula, became the third abbot of Aldenburg.

2. Angelrannus deserves a place among ecclesiastical writers on account of certain short works published by him. Four books *On the Life, Miracles, and Translation of Saint Richarius* survive in a manuscript codex at Centula. He composed them at the urging of Fulbert, formerly his teacher, as he himself testifies in the dedicatory letter addressed to Fulbert.

Angelrannus also composed other short works in verse, which the author of the Chronicle discusses below in section 15. Moreover, the name “Scholar,” which Angelrannus himself applied to himself, and the books that he acquired for the library of Centula, clearly demonstrate his great inclination toward learning. The same is proved by the numerous pupils whom he had at the monastery of Centula. All these matters are explained more fully in his Life.

Finally, Blessed Gerald, later abbot of Silva Major, testifies in the Book of the Miracles of Saint Adalard, which he published while he was still living at Corbie, that Ingelrannus was present at one of Saint Adalard’s miracles. On that occasion he praises his learning in these words:

“Abbot Ingelrannus was present at Matins. At that time he philosophized more deeply than the others; nor had chance sent him to witness this sign, but Saint Richarius, whose flock he was pastor, had sent him.”

3. There is no difficulty concerning the year or day of Angelrannus’s death. Hariulf expressly gives the year of his death as 1045. The day is assigned in the monastery’s obituary in these words: “On the fifth day before the Ides of December, Angelrannus the abbot died.”

4. Under Abbot Angelrannus, Odelgerus was prior of the monastery. His name, with the title “saint,” appears in the catalogue of the brothers enrolled at Centula, under the fifth day of February, in these words: “On the Nones of February, that holy Odelgerus, monk and prior, died.”

He himself, however, like Angelrannus, is celebrated by no public cult; indeed, it is entirely unknown where their bodies lie. It was therefore sufficient to grant both the title “Venerable.”

Nevertheless, we infer that Angelrannus’s feast was once celebrated among our Centulans from an old catalogue added to Hariulf’s Chronicle by another but ancient hand, where these words are read:

“These are the solemnities properly belonging to Centula: the Kalends of January, the Dedication of the Church; the fifth day before the Nones of March, of Abbot Gervinus; the fifth day before the Ides of December, the Deposit of Saint Angelrannus, our abbot.”

Let this suffice as an indication; his deeds must now be set forth, among which the praise of Odelgerus will also appear.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 1405A] 1. Since the whole world rejoices that it has been redeemed by the descent of the Only-Begotten Son of God through the assumption of flesh, and since there is universal exultation and a common deliverance, nevertheless the joy of certain places is recognized as their particular possession: that they have had men such that, by the distinction of their holiness and learning, they may deservedly be called fathers and shepherds.

The sweet province of Ponthieu, distinguished by its location and name, has often possessed this privilege and rejoiced in the birth of outstanding men. Finally, it once produced that most radiant star, the blessed Richarius, whose patronage and bodily presence make Centula rejoice in its blessedness. It is also known to have produced, after those whom we have read above that it deserved to have, the man of glorious memory, Angelrannus. Since he surpasses every praise of his time, the memory of his name extends everywhere.

2. Angelrannus was born to God-fearing parents who, according to the pomp of the world, were not especially noble, although entirely freeborn, and who were exceptionally distinguished by fear of God. Before his birth, it was divinely revealed what reputation and what good fragrance he would one day possess.

For one night, while asleep, his mother saw what seemed to be a wreath gently proceeding from her, encircling the walls of all Centula and causing everyone’s mouths to open in his praise and admiration. When she disclosed this to her religious husband, he, inspired by the grace of the heavenly gift, said with certainty that this would be a forewarning of the excellent offspring whom they were shortly to receive by the Lord’s gift, one who would fill everyone with the fragrance of good works.

Thus, beginning to show a good disposition and vigorous with the sharpness of profound understanding, he was found, while still within the age of childhood, burning most ardently with a desire to learn letters. Even then, as God inspired him, the boy displayed by a kind of prophetic sign what he would become. Since it is written, “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom,” and Wisdom is Christ, the Wisdom of God, he showed beforehand that he would become a temple of supreme Wisdom, since he could not be satisfied with knowledge of letters.

And because he preferred not to embrace the world’s wantonness but to be perpetually devoted to the service of God, he was clothed in the monastic robe within the cloister of the monastery of Saint Richarius. Then, as divine gifts increased with his age, he adorned the habit that he preferred before human eyes with the qualities of manifold holiness.

Humility, the mother and nurse of the virtues, was present in him. The ineffable quality of obedience prevailed in him. He preserved that charity which knows not how to hate anyone.

3. Indeed, because, as has been said above, he was greatly eager for learning, after receiving permission from the abbot of the place, Ingelard—who was worthy of no small reverence—he investigated the teaching of distant schools, like the most prudent bee that circles the orchards of different flowers in order to fill its receptacles with the sweetness of honey.

Finally, he obtained as master and instructor Fulbert, the venerable bishop of the city of Chartres, a man proved by the experience of many and most richly adorned with the liberal studies, and one to be named with great honor. Fulbert was his adviser and his instructor both in morals and in letters.

The venerable bishop rejoiced in the consolation of so great a disciple, and was strengthened by the diligence and talent of so capable a pupil. At last, after Angelrannus had been thoroughly instructed in grammar, music, and dialectic, Fulbert sent him back to Centula, a most beloved novice, already adorned with the priesthood. The devout community of the Centulans received him as if he were a great treasure.

Then the foremost pearl of great knowledge, which had been sought with immense zeal, was brought forth. Books were repaired; books not yet written were copied; boys were educated; treasures of wisdom were distributed to very many; the homeland was enlightened; and Centula, which had been foretold as destined to be blessed by such a father, was called fortunate by everyone throughout the surrounding region.

The will and desire of the people, who ardently desired that this should happen, were happily fulfilled.

### 4

At that time King Robert, distinguished by the light of prudence, was being glorified by the scepters of the kingdom of the Franks after his father Hugh. By divine prompting, as we believe, the aforesaid man was brought to his notice in the following manner. While he was still being detained in the regions of France by his scholarly studies, the aforementioned king was compelled by devout good will to go to Rome. While, on his orders, men thoroughly instructed in the offices of divine service were being sought in various places, Angelrannus was proclaimed by everyone to be effective in this matter. Thus, when the journey had been prepared, the king set out upon the road, and Angelrannus joined him as a companion of most honorable life.

Meanwhile, as they traveled, riches that had until then been hidden were more widely revealed; words of preaching came forth and poured themselves into the hearts of those who passed by. The king marveled at his speech, delighted in the purity of his continent life, and everyone was astonished at the brilliance of his tongue and reverenced the purity of his spirit. Indeed, what was reported to have occurred on that journey seems worthy of insertion into the history: for it was indicated by manifold testimony that throughout the entire road he served God and the king in divine service in such a way that he never needed the aid of books. Whether this could have happened, let the sluggish not judge, but let the diligent examine it. Thus they reached Rome and returned from there successfully.

[Note: An old Chronicle, praised by Besly, recalls Robert’s Roman journey; some assign it to the year 1026. But from the History of the Translation of Saints Savinianus and others, which we published above, it is clear that Robert undertook that journey much earlier. For there, in chapter 26, Queen Constance is said to have remained with her little son Hugh Tillo, anxious lest Bertha supplant her, and to have been comforted by Saint Savinianus. Since she did not know who Savinianus was, she learned this from Theoderic, who later became bishop of Orléans. Theoderic died, as we stated in his Life, in January 1022.]

### 5

As a result of this journey, the man of God Angelrannus came to the king’s attention; therefore the king did not wish, even in his heart, to leave him among the lowest. Meanwhile, while the king was considering with what honor he might support him, the ever-venerable Angelrannus continually exalted Centula by his residence there. And, by God’s ordering, it came about that the abbey of Centula was deprived of paternal care.

Thus Angelrannus was compelled, by the unanimous election of the brothers of sounder counsel, to undertake that office; he had been prepared for it by the foreknowledge of the Lord before all ages. Then the king, rejoicing that he had found, as he had desired, a place to honor, came swiftly to the aforesaid Centula for this purpose.

But the speed of the report, striking Angelrannus’s ears, filled his inmost heart with salutary fear more quickly than words can say. He could not discover what he should do. The unanimous election of the brothers, despite the very slight opposition of certain men puffed up by their own nobility, compelled him to assume the pastoral office, and royal authority was also close at hand to drive him to it. But he, who preferred to be subject rather than to preside, judged himself wholly unworthy to receive this charge.

Taking courage, therefore, he sought out the forest thickets and concealed himself there in certain hidden places, so that he might not be found. When the king arrived and asked for the man, the crowd of monks declared that he had secretly withdrawn. The king marveled at his purpose, praised his humility, and ordered that they proceed more quickly and bring back to him the Lord’s chosen man.

The soldiers therefore went out, seeking the illustrious soldier of God. They asked everyone they met whether they had seen the most renowned man anywhere. At last, after much searching, he was recognized as hiding in the forest of Olnodiolum. They hurried there, searched for him, found him, brought him back, and presented him to King Robert.

The king, rejoicing, entered the basilica of the church and, while every noble and common person looked on, delegated to him the rule of the entire place by means of the ropes hanging from the bells. Then the king himself ordered that the worthy consecration of his blessing be hastened as quickly as possible.

Truly, this man was a member of the heavenly Head: remembering that his Lord, when the peoples wished to make him king, had fled into the mountain, he preferred to enter a cave rather than be lifted up by the pride of preeminence.

### 6

Now that he had undertaken the office of abbot, who could adequately explain his good works? His constant endeavor was to keep his own life free from blemishes, always to provide what was good before God and human beings, to cut away what was unsuitable in those entrusted to him, to increase their good qualities by example as well as by word, always to pursue whatever was good, and always to avoid whatever was wicked.

Nor was it enough for his benevolence to obtain the salvation of souls; he also took care to honor the place entrusted to him with earthly buildings. In the end, he built walls, clothed the sacred altars with gold and silver, and enlarged the holy vessels of Christ as far as he could. His holy spirit clearly delighted in good works, and his devout mind was nourished by holy exercise.

Meanwhile Notker, bishop of Liège, to whom certain estates of Saint Richarius had been pledged by Lord Abbot Ingelard, had died, and after two others Durandus had assumed the episcopate of that see. Abbot Angelrannus therefore approached him and begged him to renew, so that it might not be invalidated, the agreement that his predecessor and Angelrannus’s predecessor had made.

The bishop yielded to the prayers of the venerable man—for he had also been asked to do the same by Lord Ebalus, bishop of Reims—and issued the following renewed charter:

[Note: Ebalus held the Church of Reims from 1024 until 1033, when he died. He was buried in his own church near the choir steps. Several letters of Fulbert of Chartres to him are extant.]

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, etc. These things were enacted publicly at Liège, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1022, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Henry, etc.

With this agreement thus advantageously restored, he returned to the monastery.

### 7

On another occasion he also went to Neustria and, having spoken with Marquis Richard, asked that same duke to grant something to Saint Richarius for the salvation of his soul. Knowing that the man was prudent and a lover of the monastic way, Richard readily complied, presenting through Angelrannus’s hand to Saint Richarius a chasuble of precious purple and the church of Scabelliville. Concerning this donation he drew up the following document:

[Note: Richard II, son of Richard I and Gunnor, had a brother named Robert, archbishop of Rouen, concerning whom more will be said shortly below.]

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Richard, by the grace of God duke of the Normans, wish it to be known to the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God that Abbot Angelrannus of the monastery of Centula, where the venerable confessor Saint Richarius rests, sought our clemency so that we might confer something upon that holy man from the gift of our almsgiving.
>
> Therefore, on the advice and at the suggestion of our faithful men, we have decreed that we permanently hand over to the aforesaid saint and his servants the church situated in Scabelliville. The aforesaid abbot and brothers, under the testimony of this present charter, promised that, for the love of our father, of ourselves, and of our mother, wife, and offspring, the number of persons of that congregation would be increased by one monk, on the condition that, when he dies from this world, another succession should follow through the ages.
>
> They further promised that, from this day forward, we and our sons, who are called associates of the aforesaid congregation, should be considered participants in all the good things that may be done there. Therefore, so that this donation may remain firm in future times, we ordered it to be confirmed under a grave anathema pronounced by the archbishop in my presence, or by certain bishops with their priests who happened at that time to be attending our court. We also ordered this charter to be drawn up and wished it to be marked with the sign of our own hand.

> Sign of Richard, marquis. Sign of Robert, archbishop. Sign of Gunnor, their mother. Sign of Judith. Sign of Richard, the boy. Sign of Robert, the boy. Sign of William, the boy. Sign of Malger.

> Done at Rouen, on the second day before the Ides of March.

Robert himself, archbishop of Rouen, also, knowing Lord Angelrannus to be a good man, gave him a fine hanging, with which our church is still adorned today.

[Note: Robert governed the Church of Rouen for forty-eight years, from 989 until 1037, when he died. Orderic Vitalis discusses him, and Fulbert of Chartres wrote several letters to him.]

### 8

Since we have now entered Normandy, it is pleasant to pause briefly in order to explain something necessary. We reported that, under Lord Ingelard, the honorable body of blessed Vigor the bishop was transferred from Neustria to Centula. Since we were deemed worthy of this, let us render heartfelt thanks to almighty God.

Confident, therefore, in God’s gift, in the blessing conferred upon us through the holy body, let us now deal with those who try to obscure so great a good of ours. Something has been brought to our attention which, with God’s help, will be cleansed by abundant reasoning—provided that an oblique listener, moved by envy, is not present.

We attack no one individually; we answer everyone at once. Whenever it happens that one of our people discusses the holy body with Neustrians or Silvanectians, they say, “He was our bishop; he rests with us”; while the others likewise report that they possess him, our treasure given to us by God seems, as it were, to be obscured amid uncertainty.

Therefore we now provide this explanation, by which we may truthfully prove that he is with us. If anyone defends his possession of him by the miracles that have become famous, we too have experienced the same miracles in a much more magnificent manner. Truly Christian faith declares that all those joined to God can display divine power not only in the place where they are bodily held, but wherever they are faithfully invoked.

Let our discourse now proceed in the name of the Lord toward its appointed goal, and let us confirm that we possess this saint, even if he appears elsewhere to perform great works. Christ, the Truth, supports us; the soul of the holy man, blessed forever in its heavenly inheritance, will bear witness; indeed, testimony to our words will be made from his own words.

The Neustrians, who are also Normans, nevertheless seemed blameworthy for not having guarded their bishop well. But the following saying pricks the mind: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

Leaving them to deal with other matters, let us proceed, since it is evident that they have been sufficiently punished by the loss both of the treasures once possessed and of those now lost. As for the citizens of Silvanectum, who foolishly pride themselves on the holy body, let us now close their mouths.

At the first time, therefore, when Centula was blessed by the arrival of the holy body, it remained for some time without any supporting accounts of his deeds. The informer had reported his name, rank, and episcopal city, but had kept silent about the rest.

When this venerable Angelrannus, surnamed the Wise, had succeeded Abbot Ingelard, he found it necessary to go to Normandy, as explained above. After completing and settling the matters for which he had gone, he began asking the clergy of that province and the monks of Saint-Ouen whether they knew any saint named Vigor.

They knew him very well, but were astonished only that the abbot himself did not know so great a confessor. They related his origin, his life, and his dignity.

Then the abbot asked them to show him the written Life and to grant him permission to copy it. When they agreed, they were struck by the following words from him:

> “The body of this saint is held in the monastery of my lord Saint Richarius, in the monastery of Centula.”

Then the monks of Saint-Ouen said to him:

> “Honored Father, know that you truly possess him if, when you inspect the bones themselves, you do not find the chin with you. You will not find it there for this reason: thanks be to God, we have it here.”

When he returned to our country with the little book of his Life, he took care to test the information immediately. He examined the holy limbs and, finding the entire heap of bones, discovered that the chin was missing.

But since the reading of the Life taught on what day the saint had departed from the world, he hesitated briefly about what to do, because the festival of All Saints, according to the modern institution of the Fathers, claimed that day.

[Note: Yet the festival of All Saints had already been received in the ninth century. Louis the Pious, at the urging of Pope Gregory IV, ordered it to be celebrated in Gaul and Germany. See Thomassin, *On Festivals*, book II, chapter 21. Even today our Centulan monks assert that the body of Saint Vigor is kept with them.]

He decided that the saint’s own feast should be presented again on the following day. And so it happened, but not in a manner entirely fitting for so great a confessor.

Having profitably inserted these matters, as we hope, let us proceed to the Life of Lord Angelrannus. Elsewhere we shall give more certain proofs concerning Saint Vigor, proofs that cannot be challenged.

[Note: Namely, in chapter 20 of the fourth book of this Centulan Chronicle, in the Deeds of Blessed Gervinus, which we shall publish in another volume of this century.]

### 9

With great effort and ingenuity, this venerable man always strove to restore to the use of the monastery whatever had been taken away by some fraud, whether during the period of desolation or under the rule of his predecessor.

The constancy of inner strength that dwelt in his mind subdued the great arrogance of powerful men, because, protected by the confidence of his sanctity, he feared the power of no one.

In the end, Count Angelrannus of Ponthieu, son of Hugh the advocate, had become his fellow godparent, having experienced his holiness, and was also moved by great fear toward him, since he knew that no perversity of human ingenuity could succeed with him.

An ancient custom had been preserved: on the feast of Saint Richarius, the entire military force of Ponthieu would come to Centula and, as though to the lord of their homeland and the guardian and advocate of their salvation, hold a solemn court for him.

Whenever the aforesaid count inevitably entered the monastery on the feast of the holy Father, or on any other day, the venerable abbot immediately accused him, with such authority of denunciation, if he had taken anything from the place, that you would think—not from the manner of the circumstances but from the manner of the rebuke—that a servant was being rebuked by his lord, not a count by a monk.

If he ever failed to obey the one correcting him, the abbot, a lover of the place, who could say, “Zeal for God’s house has consumed me,” immediately intensified his words, called him faithless and a robber, and excommunicated him unless he promised to make amends.

This strength of spirit accomplished much and ensured that nothing was taken from the place during his time. We have learned this for the following reason: since in our own age there are no donors, it seemed that matters were going well for us if we did not suffer the most hostile plunderers.

Yet the venerable Angelrannus achieved not only that nothing should be taken from him, but also that much should be given and restored to him by God’s grace.

Thus Count Angelrannus, encouraged by his admonitions, assigned a certain village to Saint Richarius. Drawing up a charter concerning its surrender, he wished it to be confirmed by royal authority, as follows:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Angelrannus, wish it to be known to the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God that, while the most excellent King Robert was staying at the palace of Compiègne, I presented before him, for confirmation, the charter of donation that I had made to Saint Richarius.
>
> For I had handed over to that saint, in the county of Ponthieu, a village called Counts’ Village, under this agreement: that I myself, as long as I lived, and after me one heir whom I should designate while alive, should hold it, and should pay twelve denarii as rent on the feast of Saint Richarius, which is celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of October.
>
> If the heir designated by me should neglect to pay, let him either make legal amends or lose it. I presented this grant in the presence of the king and the nobles of the kingdom and judged that it should be confirmed by royal authority.

[Note: Namely, his first translation from the ancient original site at Centula; his Nativity is celebrated on April 26, while his translation is celebrated on June 2.]

> Sign of King Robert. Sign of Queen Constance. Sign of Duke Henry. Sign of Robert. Sign of Odo. Sign of Count Angelrannus.
>
> Done at the palace of Compiègne, on the Nones of April.

### 10

A certain soldier named Hucbertus, who was bound by oath to serve our abbot as a beneficiary, proved on several occasions to be a source of trial for the venerable Angelrannus.

Some of Hucbertus’s relatives had held, for a fixed term under an arrangement, a village of Saint Richarius called Noguerias, and on that occasion he claimed it for himself as an inheritance.

When the abbot contradicted him and Hucbertus became enraged, the venerable Angelrannus had to endure many harsh things through his intrusion. How strongly he was bound by the bond of love toward his own people became clear when he did not cease to contend, by the authority of both divine and human laws, against Hucbertus and against all who attempted to seize the possessions of the brothers.

Instructed by the example of God and our Lord, and inflamed by the love of him who laid down his life for his sheep, he too did not fear enduring many dangers and many snares of the wicked for the villages and estates of the Church of Centula. Certainly, he would have laid down his life for those entrusted to him, if it had been necessary; and, when necessary, he did not refuse to be afflicted by many injuries for the sake of their temporal property.

To save the souls of his subjects, he was never known to have spared his own temporal safety. For the cruelty of the tyrants had not grown so far that they destroyed bodies in order to drive away souls; rather, their greed had advanced to the point that, by stripping people of their possessions, they made them miserable. Since that magnificent man was their constant opponent in the face of their savagery, he suffered much from them and even endured a blow from a sword as a lover of God.

But because we may truly say that the righteous person trusts like a lion, he, relying upon a good conscience, feared no suffering on behalf of those entrusted to him. Charity held the first place in him and certainly drove fear outward.

Thus he persisted against Hucbertus until, by the judgment of the nobles in the presence of the king, he established the lawful title to the village mentioned above.

### 11

But what human hearts does greed not harass, if an opportunity is present? King Henry, enticed by desire, after it had been determined that Hucbertus should not possess the village as his own property, took it and enjoyed its revenues for five years.

When the abbot repeatedly rebuked him, however, Henry was finally compelled by fear of God’s judgments and broken by the venerable Angelrannus’s continual threats. He yielded it to us and drew up a charter concerning its return, which we also usefully record here:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to all the sons of the Catholic Church who have care of soul and body.
>
> We wish it to be known to all present and future what sort of return we have permitted to Saint Richarius for the sake of our souls and those of our successors.
>
> A certain soldier named Hucbertus held Noguenaria with its dependencies, a village of Saint Richarius, through the wrongful violence of his seizure. All his predecessors who had held it had taken it from Saint Richarius under the pretext of a payment. But Hucbertus, wishing to seize it as his own, was somewhat repelled by the protest of the abbot and brothers. After he had been completely repelled, the judgment of our court transferred it, by our command, into our possession. I held it solidly and peacefully for five years.
>
> Afterward, mindful of my soul, and although thinking only a little about its redemption, I was also inclined by the abbot and the community of monks, and I handed it over to Saint Richarius.
>
> Count Angelrannus, the advocate of that place, also added his petition, to which I agreed on the condition that he should never receive any customary payment from it.
>
> So that none of my successors may dare to violate this, I have struck with the anathema of Hezelin, bishop of Paris, and of all the Franks who were with me—not excepting the abbot himself—anyone who might hand it over to another under any pretext, lest some fresh error of ours bring our soul into danger.
>
> We therefore prohibit, again and again, by our authority and by the threats of all our bishops, that any evildoer should dare to usurp it in any way, lest I be placed in that rejection where my merits could not help me.
>
> So that no one may doubt the command, let him see in writing the edict of the one who commands.

> This was enacted in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1035, while King Henry reigned, in the third year of his reign. Abbot Angelrannus subscribed; the monk Rollandus subscribed; Gualterus subscribed; Algisus subscribed; and others.
>
> These are also witnesses to the excommunication of all the bishops, especially Hezelin of Paris. Whoever thereafter violates these things, let him be anathema *maranatha* with Dathan and Abiron. Amen.
>
> Here we omit the restoration of the mill made to the same monastery by the soldier Raginere.

### 12

Although the abbot Angelrannus’s provident care was always directed toward this holy place in every matter, his benevolence was not lacking in relieving the needs of the poor.

Piety was therefore his inseparable companion, through which, with the grace of God assisting him, he shone as an exceptional comforter of the wretched. Many times he went out from the cloister so that he might somehow find an opportunity to show mercy. When he was thought to be going out to arrange some useful matter, he, hungry for justice, desired to be filled by acts of mercy.

Indeed, the pious “thief” sometimes carried a purse filled with the treasures of mercy. Whenever he saw some poor person approaching from one direction or another, before the person reached him he would throw the denarii he had taken onto the ground. Then the merciful Father would call the person who wished to pass by over to him and, as though unaware, would ask what the object lying on the ground might be.

The person, not knowing what had been done, would say, “Lord, I see coins lying on the ground.” Then that kindly deceiver and pious trickster would order him to go and pick them up for himself, saying that they had been prepared for him by the Lord.

O man truly worthy of God! O soul continually to be raised by every praise! So that he might not remain without the fruits of life, he constantly persisted in acts of piety; and, so that passing praise might not disturb him, he concealed those very pious acts.

It is pleasant briefly to contemplate our own depravity and the crookedness of our minds. When we do not perform good deeds, we wish to be praised; and if we happen to do even a little good, we wish to be proclaimed by everyone. We shine neither in action nor in any virtue, yet we extort honor as though we were holier merely because of our habit.

Utterly condemnable misery: not to be holy, yet to demand the due of holiness!

Thus Angelrannus, a true worshiper of God, remained illuminated by exercises in good works, a devoted lover of hospitality, a constant guardian of humility, and an eternal hostage of charity.

### 13

I consider it a most impious error not to mention his acute intelligence. For, at the command of his venerable former teacher, namely Lord Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, he made the Life of the life-giving confessor of Christ, Richarius, which had been briefly written by the ancients, more pleasing in heroic verse. He added almost nothing from outside, but represented the same meaning in every respect.

He also gathered into one little book the miracles that our Lord and Savior displayed in his own time through the merits of that same saint and joined them to his ancient miracles.

[Note: See the preliminary observations, no. 2.]

At the beginning of these, he subsequently began to speak as follows concerning what he had woven above:

> Now I shall set forth what my own eye has seen.

Afterward he inserted that translation of Saint Richarius which we explained more fully in the preceding little book.

[Note: In the manuscript the title of chapter 9 is given as follows: “Concerning the miracles of Saint Richarius that occurred in his own time.” But the chapter itself is missing; perhaps it was nothing other than the little book concerning the account of that same Saint Richarius.]

### 14

The excellent life of this man, so dear to God, had kindled many people’s zeal for the love of heavenly things. Therefore we now judge it most fitting to show, in the deeds of his disciples, how greatly God’s grace flourished in him. Having already shown that he was truly holy and therefore close to God, we may thereby make his goodness shine more brightly, since he is proved magnificent not only by his own progress but also by that of those entrusted to him.

There was therefore in this holy monastery a man of venerable life named Odelgerus. He displayed, by God’s grace, a great light of religion through extraordinary abstinence, supreme obedience, and vigilant custody of his mouth. From childhood he had indeed been trained in sacred disciplines under Lord Abbot Ingelard, but under the most reverend Angelrannus he held the ministry of dean or prior.

He devoted himself constantly to reading and prayer, and also strove for simplicity and purity of mind; he was powerful in the disciplines of a great life. In administering external matters as well, he proved sufficiently upright and very capable.

He had the continual custom that, whenever the brothers, because of the indulgence of a more relaxed life, were talking together about something worldly or even irreligious, he would withdraw into the church. There, intent upon psalmody and compunction, he diligently joined himself to the Lord.

Moreover, so that he might not be hindered by any impulse or by anyone’s arrival, he would take care to climb to the upper parts of the church. There, free and secluded, as though close at hand and nearby, he offered sacrifices of praise and prayer before the divine eyes.

After spending a long life in the holy vocation, he came to his end. When he was close to death and was surrounded by the brothers and the servants of the church, he suddenly cried out and said:

> “Behold, the choir of angels is present.”

For almighty and merciful God wished to show how devotedly he had served him, and therefore sent the ministers of his divinity to the dying man, so that in their sight and presence he might depart from the body without grave fear or pain.

On this occasion, while everyone present was astonished, he suddenly added:

> “Behold, the choir of prophets.”

After a brief silence he continued:

> “Behold, the choir of apostles.”

Then he said:

> “Behold, the choir of martyrs.”

When he had been silent for a little while:

> “Behold,” he said, “the choir of confessors.”

Finally, after announcing:

> “Behold, the choir of virgins,”

he gave up his spirit at that very moment.

Because he had seen that the citizens of the heavenly homeland had come to receive him, he testified to it by following them. The most reverend Abbot Angelrannus therefore buried him, as was fitting, with honor in the little church of Saint Vincent the martyr, which stood adjacent to the cloister. Over his tomb he composed this epitaph:

> He was a worshiper of justice and a lover of goodness,  
> Odelgerus, who rests in this tomb.  
> The light of February, the ninth, removed him from life  
> And, as is hoped, sent him to the heavenly kingdom.

### 15

Among the monuments of his great wisdom, the venerable Angelrannus composed, in honor of Saint Richarius, certain chants with a sweeter melody, although ancient ones were abundant. He also fitted particular chants to the honor of Saints Walaricus the abbot and Wlfrannus the archbishop. He composed metrically the Passion of the blessed martyr Vincent and subjected the Life of the holy virgin Austreberta to verse.

Since so great a brilliance of knowledge could not easily remain hidden, many nobles submitted themselves to his teaching. Among them were two distinguished men: Guido, bishop of Amiens, and Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne.

[Note: Guido, after Fulco his brother—who was deposed at the synod of Reims under Pope Leo IX—ascended the throne of Amiens. According to the Centulan Chronicle, he died in 1074. Below, no. 22, he is called archdeacon.]

[Note: Drogo held this see from 1031 to 1078. He took part in the council of Reims under Leo IX and in the elevation of the body of Saint Bertin. He has already been discussed more than once.]

These men called themselves his disciples; throughout their lives they always rejoiced that they had been enlightened by his prudence. His goodness in teaching had spread so far that everywhere and by everyone Angelrannus was specially and deservedly called “the Wise.”

### 16

Since he possessed, in wondrous fashion, such and so many reputations for goodness, and the apostolic saying was fulfilled in him—“We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:15)—the examiner of hearts, seeing that this servant of his desired with tireless longing to be joined to him, decided to polish him further in the file of temptation and to test him upon the anvil of bodily infirmity with the hammer of his own blows, so that he might receive him one day in a purer state—or rather, so that he might heap up for him an abundance of merits.

In the end, paralysis struck him with such severity that afterward he could neither bring his hand to his mouth nor move himself in bed. His innocent hands were bound by the chain of heavenly discipline; those hands, which had always exercised themselves in good works and had taken the greatest care to avoid evil, were restrained from touching this or that, whether good or evil.

He therefore always returned thanks to the Creator. To the one to whom he had previously shown himself devoted in every good work, he now, pressed by illness, offered the sacrifice of praise with heart and tongue. Although he was so bound by this disease that he was wholly incapable of acting for himself, his authority was nevertheless feared everywhere and his name reverenced everywhere.

Often he would sit somewhere and weep copiously. When those attending him asked the reason for his tears, he replied that he was thinking with fear of the punishments of sins, which, with the devil as their minister, were suffered within the confines of hell; for that reason, he said, he could not refrain from weeping.

Likewise, when at other times he showed himself exceedingly joyful and the servants asked what made him appear so cheerful, he said that this exultation had flowed to him from the joys of the heavenly angels and the everlasting happiness of the saints.

### 17

As he grew old, when it seemed useful to many that a successor should be appointed for him, a certain man noble according to the flesh—namely Fulco, son of Angelrannus, count of Ponthieu, and a foster-son of that same place—attempted, with the assistance of his relatives, to seize for himself the rule of the aforesaid place of Centula.

When King Henry of the Franks came to Ponthieu through some chance circumstance unknown to me, Fulco, with his father the aforesaid count intervening, wished to obtain from that king dominion over the entire place. This was done, entirely without the knowledge of Lord Abbot Angelrannus.

Fulco, believing from the royal grant that he was about to become abbot, then took an impudent liberty. He provided an opulent banquet for certain soldiers in the brothers’ refectory, in a manner plainly unsuitable, so that he might make them more loyal to him and more ready to acquire honor for him.

When this was reported to Father Angelrannus, he summoned the attendants and immediately ordered himself to be carried there. The servants therefore carried him in their hands as far as the door of the refectory. There he planted his feet and, by the authority of almighty God, anathematized those who had gathered.

From that moment their entire faction began to fall apart. You could see the better among them—those in whom at least a little fear remained—trembling before the face of the just man as though guilty before a judge, and being wonderfully terrified by the fire of excommunication he had pronounced.

The man of God then withdrew from there, summoned Fulco, and asked him in threatening words whether he wished to become abbot. When Fulco, out of shame, gave no answer, Angelrannus pronounced sentence, saying that he could not become abbot so long as Angelrannus himself remained in the body.

Although that same Fulco had also received from his father the gift of another abbey, he was nevertheless never able to become abbot of any place while the blessed man lived, because the word of the man of God prevailed.

In this matter it is observed that the holy man acted through a prophetic spirit, since he had foretold—not without divine prompting—that Fulco could not become abbot so long as Angelrannus remained in the body.

Indeed, after the venerable Father Angelrannus withdrew to the heavenly dwellings, Fulco was given the office of abbot on the first day after his burial and was placed over the monastery of Forest, which, as is clearly shown in this work, had anciently been a cell of the brothers of Saint Richarius. But shortly before this it had been taken away by the counts of Ponthieu and claimed for itself the name of a little abbey.

## 18

And since we have reached this point, it is fitting to relate, so that posterity may know the facts, how that place was taken from us. From the day on which the blessed and holy Father Richarius received the end of his mortal life there [Col. 1417B], and thereafter until the time of Abbot Ingelard, it remained under the authority of our community. But Hugh, first duke and later king, at the time when, to guard against barbarian incursions, he took Abbatis-villa from us and made it into a fortress, appointing the knight Hugh over it, also snatched the cell of Forestis from our jurisdiction and handed it over to that Hugh to possess permanently, since he had married the duke’s daughter, named Gela.

Previously, therefore, clerics had served the Lord in that same cell; but at Hugh’s request some monks from our community were installed there. They also obtained as abbot, in the same manner, a monk of our community named Guido, the brother of Lord Angelrannus. When he had ministered there for some years in the governance of souls, he had as his successor in office a monk of our community named Hucbertus. Although that place was being taken from us, it was nevertheless decreed, out of love and honor for the blessed Richarius, that its abbots should always be monks from our community.

After Hucbertus had died, this Fulco assumed the governance of the place—the man whom we have noted as having wished to usurp for himself the dominion of our monastery. It is fitting, however, to speak of Lord Guido the abbot. Though he shone with distinguished conduct pleasing to God, he was deprived of the light of his eyes, like the holy Tobias; nevertheless, the brightness of divine contemplation continued wholly undiminished in his mind. As soon as he had received this scourge from God the loving Father with thanksgiving, he asked that another be appointed in his place; and, returning to Centula, he spent the remainder [Col. 1417D] of his life in holy service there.

He also entered into his rest on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

[Note: [Col. 1417D] The Centula Necrology assigns this very day in these words: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of May, Guido the abbot died; he was the brother of Abbot Angelrannus.”]

He was buried by his venerable brother Angelrannus beside the body of that holy monk Odelgerus, and the following inscription was placed above him:

> This carved stone, marked with little letters, shows  
>   
> that here lies Guido, a father rightly to be remembered.  
>   
> The distinguished grace of life raised him from the world;  
>   
> may the world raise this exalted man through its prayers.

It is also pleasing to report that the Hugh mentioned above was called not a count but an advocate. This title was distinguished in his case because King Hugh appointed him defender of the church of Saint Richarius. His son Angelrannus, the father of this Fulco, was likewise content with that title until, by God’s permission, he killed the count of Boulogne in battle and married his most noble widow, named Adelwia. Because he had taken a countess as his wife, he thereafter received the title of count; and this title has since been customarily and permanently retained by his successors.

## 19

But let us return to our Angelrannus and begin to relate how the good man obtained a worthy successor. When, as stated above, he learned that Fulco had wished, through the intercession of his parents and the payment of a price, to seize the administration of the office, he wished to approach the royal majesty and plead that the care of souls should not be sold. Since he could not do so otherwise because of his illness, he accomplished it by being carried in a cart; and, addressing the king with sufficiently severe words, he threatened that the king would undergo the torments of hell for having sold the benefice.

The king, who was considered a man of good sense, repented; and, having asked pardon for his guilt, he promised that he would make amends. Not many days had passed after this when, as we hold, by divine will, Richard, the abbot of Verdun, appeared at the royal hearing. He had with him as chaplain Gervinus, a most reverend monk and uniquely beloved for the merit of his goodness.

Since this is the Gervinus whose succession after Angelrannus brought joy to Centula, we consider it most appropriate to relate from the beginning who he was, so that [Col. 1418C] the more fully the man is known, the more fully he may be loved.

[Note: [Col. 1418D] He has much to say here about Gervinus, which we shall present in its proper place under the year 1074.]

## 20

The God who created all things, therefore, had already determined to soothe his servant’s longing with the delight of the heavenly kingdom. He had made him fit for himself through the purification of a very long illness; yet, by the inward counsel of his wisdom—by which he chastises every son whom he receives—he made the health of that same servant more grievous than usual. To the man for whom he was soon to provide incomparable sweetness, he multiplied the intensity of long-endured pain.

But, to show that this correction had proceeded not from anger but from the highest mercy, he displayed over him signs of unmistakable goodness. For although that most blessed man had always been wholly devoted to the study of Sacred Scripture, and although he was now oppressed by a most serious illness, his affection and will could never be restrained from divine works. At one time he persisted tirelessly in psalmody; at another he lingered over the sacred meditations of the divine commandments; at another, reclining on his bed as though he were standing at the altar, he sang the solemn rites of the Mass with his own voice.

Hence it happened that some people wondered that a man known to possess such wisdom seemed to be performing the work of a madman. But he judged all those whom he heard expressing such wonder to be foolish and ignorant of every good thing.

It happened, then, that once, after he had sung Mass while reclining in bed with his hands extended, and when almighty God wished to reveal to the ignorant what was being done with him, he indicated after the Mass had ended that he was suffering from thirst. He therefore ordered a servant to bring him a cup of wine. The servant quickly brought wine, but the saint indicated that he did not wish to drink that wine. The servant returned and brought another, but at the first taste the blessed man rejected this one as well.

When the servant saw that he had refused wine once and twice, and the old man indicated that he wanted another, the servant pleaded that he had no other wines. Then the holy man—and his very words must be given—said: “Bring me some of that which I had at Mass just now.”

When they heard this, those standing around him froze with fear and answered the sweetest Father with tears: “Father, you shall have no more of that unless the one who gave it to you before gives it to you again.” For while he was believed to be celebrating Mass outside himself, when he came to that point at which the sacred communion of the Lord’s body is customarily administered, he was being refreshed by heavenly food sent as a gift from above.

Recognizing, therefore, that his attendants had learned the hidden secret, and wishing in every way to conceal the goodness God had worked in him, he ordered them, as though angered, to withdraw more quickly. Holy men have this characteristic: when they do good works, they wish them to remain concealed, lest, by receiving the applause of passing praise, they diminish before God the reward of their work.

## 21

While these things were taking place, and the blessed man already seemed about to be released from the body because of the great severity of his illness, and for that reason was being carefully watched by those whom he had nurtured [Col. 1419C], an urgent matter arose which made it necessary to send someone to the royal court.

Lord Gervinus, who by then held the governance of the place, ordered one of the brothers to carry out this business. But the monk, who wished to be present at the departure of the best Father, to be enlightened by it, and to take part in the funeral rites, replied that he would not do so, offering every possible excuse.

Then the venerable Gervinus, compelled by this reply, went to the holy man of God, Angelrannus, where he lay, and informed him of the monk’s disobedience. Angelrannus had the same monk summoned to him and asked why he had not fulfilled the command; then he ordered him to fulfill it.

When the monk still refused, the holy abbot, enlightened by the grace of a prophetic spirit, promised, saying: “Go and do what you are commanded, and know that this body will not enter the earth until you return.”

Encouraged by this promise, the brother set out and presented most effectively before the king’s ears the matters for which he had been sent. When the heavenly summons came, however, by which Angelrannus, seeking the things of heaven, was to abandon earthly things, that holy soul, to be presented by the ministry of angels before God’s sight, left the prison of the flesh on the fifth day before the Ides of December.

Now the stone that had been polished by many-sided workmanship is placed in the heavenly building; now the lily flower that had grown in the valley of humility watered by heavenly dew adorns the heavenly garland; now the gem that had shone amid diverse cuttings completes the divine diadem. [Col. 1420A]

The monk, having completed the tasks for which he had been sent, was returning when suddenly, in the city of Amiens, where he had turned aside to lodge, a dreadful announcement of the Father’s death struck him. It was evening, and preparations were being made for the evening meal; but he left the lodging and the food, mounted his horse with all haste, and returned to Centula. There he found the holy body, already lifeless, placed in the monastery and honorably surrounded by the watch of the brothers, soon to be committed to burial.

He was therefore present and assisted; and, when his desire had been fulfilled, the Father’s prophecy was also fulfilled: he had promised that his body would not enter the earth until that same monk returned from the king’s court.

The body of the holy man was buried within the venerable church of the most holy soldier of Christ, Richarius, at the place where the martyrdom of blessed Laurentius is venerated. His venerable successor, Abbot Gervinus, bestowed such adornment upon the burial that it might be thought that the honor of so great a tomb would suffice for the holiness of any of the ancient Fathers. He rightly judged that the bodily remains of one who, crowned with an unfading laurel, hymns praises to Christ eternally with the heavenly beings should be preserved with fitting honor.

Amen.

These events took place in the year 1045 of the incarnation of the Son of God, indiction XII.

## 22

But Christ the Lord, whom this blessed man had faithfully served, deigned to make known to mortals by clear signs how highly his service was valued and by what great reward he would be exalted from heaven.

In the district of Vimeu there was a woman who had a daughter afflicted by paralysis. Unable to perform any task, she was kept lying on a bed as though dying. When the woman learned of the holiness of the blessed Abbot Angelrannus, and was inflamed with fervor of faith and eager for her daughter’s healing, she led the girl with a candle to his tomb.

After the sick girl had devoutly offered the candle at the tomb of the man of God, she sat beside the tomb and yielded for a little while to sleep. Then she awoke completely healed. In the presence of the monastery’s brothers, who praised God, she returned joyfully and eagerly to her own home in the village from which she had come, called Filcharias.

[Note: [Col. 1419D] Feuquières.]

She announced to everyone how great a favor God had done for her through the blessed Abbot Angelrannus.

Guido, then archdeacon of the church of Amiens and later bishop of that same see [Col. 1420D], who had been Angelrannus’s student in literary studies, adorned his tomb with the following epitaph:

> He whom this tomb covers, the excellent Angelrannus,  
>   
> was pastor and abbot of this monastery.  
>   
> Leader of the Church’s flock, the glorious hope of monastic life,  
>   
> he lived—and in the world was pure, and in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1419D] They assert that this bishop was especially devoted to the poetic art: William of Jumièges, *History*, book VII [Col. 1420D], chapter 44, and Orderic Vitalis, book III, where they say that he produced a book in heroic verse, *On William the Conqueror’s Expedition to England*.]

## 23

Whoever wishes to know, therefore, how great was the usefulness of this holy place should look at the following verses, which were written about it so that posterity might know and imitate it:

> What Abbot Angelrannus contributed to our little dwelling,  
>   
> this inscribed stone, seen here in white, preserves in writing.  
>   
> He built the church of Saint Vincent, and likewise that of Saint Benedict;  
>   
> he constructed a cell and prepared one for the sick.  
>   
> From the foundations he restored the paradise.  
>   
> He had the panel of Peter’s altar made,  
>   
> and had two censers cast from silver.  
>   
> He adorned with pure silver the Gospel book  
>   
> and the Life of Saint Richarius.  
>   
> There is also a book of Epistles and Gospels,  
>   
> which his industry prepared entirely in silver.  
>   
> His splendid chalice too is seen to be held in honor,  
>   
> together with a fitting paten joined to it;  
>   
> and besides this, another chalice which he always used at Masses;  
>   
> one dorsal and three precious chasubles.  
>   
> He preserved and redeemed lands that had been overrun,  
>   
> such as Nogueria, Gaspannia, and Drusiacum,  
>   
> the church of Guibrent, Frocort, and Mont-Rochon,  
>   
> the church of Sacricamp, amid dreadful danger,  
>   
> while many strove to make the opposing party prevail,  
>   
> contending against many and suffering many wrongs.  
>   
> What I have related above, and many more things besides,  
>   
> he accomplished; the knowledge of the Lord knows how it happened.  
>   
> The books that he himself renewed exceed all number;  
>   
> moreover, those that he himself repaired exceed all number.  
>   
> Through such things and others he earned, as we hope,  
>   
> the rewards of the heavenly kingdom; reader, we affirm that he was able to attain them.  
>   
> This was the final end of his studies:  
>   
> by dying he restored the church of holy Mary.  
>   
> May her intercessions with the Lord benefit us.  
>   
> Therefore may the rewards of life belong to the one who recalls these things;  
>   
> may he be condemned through whose neglect these things perish.

## 24

That same honorable man, concerned for posterity, wrote a rhythmic catalogue of the Fathers of this holy place. He did not identify all of them, but mentioned only those whose names seemed to be indicated either by charters or by some scraps of writing, or whom the Life of Saint Richarius specifically identified. This, then, is the honorable Angelrannus.
