# LIFE OF SAINT RICHARIUS, FIRST ABBOT OF CENTULA

Written in verse by INGELRAMNUS, a scholar and monk of that saint.

*(Edited by Dom Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, II, 261.)*

## Notice

After Alcuin’s *Life of Saint Richarius*—see among Alcuin’s works, *Patrologia Latina*, vol. CI, col. 681—we present Ingelramnus, or Angelramnus, previously unpublished. He was first a monk and then abbot of Centula at the beginning of the eleventh century. At the command of his venerable former teacher, namely Lord Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, as Hariulfus says in *Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 8, he made more pleasing in heroic verse the Life of the blessed confessor of Christ, Richarius, which had been briefly written by ancient authors. He added almost nothing from outside, but reproduced the same meaning throughout.

Ingelramnus divided his poem into four books. In the first he presented Alcuin in almost pure form—except for the metrical arrangement—as will be evident to anyone who compares chapter with chapter. But why would he have passed over Ratbertus, if Ratbertus had perhaps written about Richarius? In the second and third books he rendered in verse the Miracles of Saint Richarius written by an ancient author; in the fourth he rendered in verse the Account of Saint Richarius.

Besides Wandalbertus, Usuardus commemorates Saint Richarius on the sixth day before the Kalends of May in these words: “In the district of Ponthieu, Saint Richarius, priest and confessor.” The region of Ponthieu, commonly called *le Ponthieu*, is a tract of Picardy lying within the boundaries of the Amiens, Morini, and Neustrian peoples. Its chief town is Abbavilla, Abbeville; two leagues east of it lies Centula, or Centulum, a small town where the monastery of Centula stands. Both places are now distinguished by the name of Saint Richarius—Saint-Riquier—beside the stream called Scarduon, which the inhabitants commonly call *la rivière aux Cardons*.

The dignity of that monastery was once great, especially from the time of Saint Angilbert, its abbot. In his monastery he established three hundred monks, one hundred boys to be educated there, and Perpetual Praise.

[HARIULFUS, *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 11.]

There flourished there abbots of outstanding dignity and religious excellence: Saint Angilbert, son-in-law of Charlemagne, who consecrated three churches in his monastery for Perpetual Praise—the first in honor of the Holy Savior and Saint Richarius, the second of Saint Mary, and the third in honor of Saint Benedict [Hariulfus, *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 8]; Nithardus, Angilbert’s son and successor—or, if we believe Petavius in his *Syntagma* of Nithardus, the son and successor of Louis; Helizachor, after Helricus, a most holy abbot; after Ribbodo, Louis, descended from royal stock; Hruodolfus, uncle of the most glorious King Charles, namely Charles the Bald; and, not to mention Heligaudus, a count who became a monk and abbot, and Guelfo, a most holy abbot, Karlomannus, son of that same most glorious King Charles.

Shortly afterward, during Karlomannus’s rule, the monastery was destroyed by barbarians. After it had been restored, Ingelramnus, a monk of Corbie, presided over it after Ingelard. He was distinguished by pious and illustrious deeds, indeed also by the gift of prophecy; and he had as his successor Gervinus, a man of exceptional holiness.

[Hariulfus, book III, chapter 22.]

We pass over the others, as well as monks distinguished for piety, among them Ansegisus, sent by Charles the Bald as envoy to Pope Nicholas [Hariulfus, *Chronicle*, book III, chapters 14 and 20]; Hieremias, who later became bishop of Sens; and the monk Odelgerus, whom Hariulfus greatly commends in book IV, chapter 10.

Even today the monastery of Saint Richarius at Centula, inhabited and cultivated by our people, is not without distinction. We believe that its beginnings were laid by Blessed Richarius around the year 625. That the Rule of Saint Benedict was in force there from the beginning, or certainly not long afterward, is clear from the fact that Coschinus, abbot of the monastery of Jumièges, presided over the monastery of Centula in the third place; and the Acts of Saints Philibert and Aicadri, abbots, make it evident that the monastery of Jumièges had adhered to the Benedictine institution from its origin.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 1423]

> The life of the holy Father Richarius, written in verse,  
>   
> was composed for him by his servant,  
>   
> Abbot Ingelramnus; and many miracles  
>   
> which the Lord performed through him were also recorded.  
>   
> Careful reader, although they are in a poor style,  
>   
> do not disdain to read our little verses.  
>   
> You will consider many things worthy of correction;  
>   
> nevertheless, you will find something useful in them.  
>   
> When you recognize a fault, remember to correct yourself;  
>   
> attend to what is useful, so that you yourself may become useful.  
>   
> To the unbegotten Father, to the begotten Son, be glory;  
>   
> glory also to the Holy Spirit of them both.

## INGELRAMNUS THE SCHOLAR TO BISHOP FULBERT

To Fulbert, sufficiently and soberly filled with the gift of every kind of wisdom, divine and human, his instructor and lord; Ingelramnus, the least worthy monk among his scholars, offers himself for the knowledge of the Divinity to which we are called.

Who should rejoice more than you in our progress, since you never cease, with fatherly affection, to devote yourself to urging us to undertake great things? Yet we, given over to laziness, can scarcely bring forth anything that we understand to be useful. Thus, because we are unwilling to expend the talent so that it may gain profit, we deserve not to hear the delightful “Well done,” but rather, with the useless servant, to suffer the loss of the buried money.

Our faults deserve the result that you, hindered by many affairs, present yourself less often to our sight. In this respect, although the constancy of your holiness is not diminished, our negligence is justly punished: those things which we ought to bring forth remain hidden, and we are deprived of the things we need to know.

Fearing to fall into this fault of silence, I have placed upon myself a burden of no small magnitude: namely, to write metrically the Life of Saint Richarius. Since it had been published carefully and clearly in rhetorical style, I resolved neither to add nor to subtract anything from it, but merely to render the author’s words in meter.

I did this not because an inability to invent new material constrained me, but because I was persuaded by the imitation of the poems of certain venerable singers of divine things. Avoiding new inventions, they reproduced the meaning of Sacred Scripture simply. In my judgment, their labor should not be regarded as a building erected upon another’s foundation, but rather as a most dutiful recitation of divine miracles.

At the beginning of each of the four books that I composed, I inserted a prologue, solely to ask forgiveness from you for me, a new poet, since many faults might be noticed in them. Because I composed this little work through the assistance of your labor, I have devoted it to your correction; nor did I allow it to be brought forth publicly until your favorable clemency deigned to approve it.

Therefore do not refuse to accept the gift offered; do not decline to lend pious ears to an unprofitable poem, so that in this too the fullness of your praise may increase, when a future age knows that you had pupils capable of being of some use. If I deserve to obtain this, entrust the task to our fellow scholars. Some of them are indeed worthy to receive credence for their authority.

## PROLOGUE OF THE PROPOSITION

[Col. 1423]

> Whenever the devotion of Christ’s worshipers considers  
>   
> the praises of the saints, who is praised except Christ?  
>   
> For whatever is done through his gift is attributed to him.  
>   
> Therefore ecclesiastical praise ought to continue,  
>   
> and unceasing song should be made in hymns,  
>   
> not only with the voice but also with the melody of the heart.  
>   
> This is certainly shown to please the Lord and the saints.  
>   
> Moreover, it is useful to write the deeds of the saints.  
>   
> For when the life of the blessed passes through bodily ears,  
>   
> the mind burns with divine love  
>   
> and longs, once it has laid aside the covering of the flesh,  
>   
> to share the company of those whose radiant deeds it admires.  
>   
> Therefore I undertake to write the Life of holy Richarius in meter,  
>   
> so that those who delight in poetry may have this work;  
>   
> while those who prefer prose may have  
>   
> the version that our predecessors once composed.  
>   
> Nor shall I write only the wonders that he performed while alive.  
>   
> For after he cast off the burdens of the flesh,  
>   
> the saint lacked for a long period the cloister of writers;  
>   
> although he performed very many deeds,  
>   
> they were entirely silenced, as though they had never occurred.  
>   
> But after the spark of our talent shone again,  
>   
> through the grace kindled by the almighty Lord,  
>   
> I took care, insofar as I could, to commit to writing  
>   
> whatever miracles the aforementioned shepherd performed.  
>   
> And, to make our little books more substantial,  
>   
> I joined to them what ancient industry had recorded.  
>   
> I did not begin this work out of a desire for praise—  
>   
> my conscience is witness—but wishing future generations to know  
>   
> that our shepherd had clients of such a kind  
>   
> who, even if imperfectly, knew how to play with verse.  
>   
> But since there are three books in the ancient codex,  
>   
> our meter has attempted to reproduce that number.  
>   
> I have decided to give the same boundaries  
>   
> that those books themselves are known to possess,  
>   
> in the works that I am going to write.  
>   
> In addition, mentioning only a few miracles out of many,  
>   
> miracles performed in our days through the merits of the saint,  
>   
> I undertake to add a fourth book to the others.  
>   
> Let no one perhaps mark them as poorly composed.  
>   
> I confess that when I began to fashion them in study,  
>   
> I had not yet completed three weeks of years.

[Note: [Col. 1425] That is, he had not yet completed three weeks of years, or, if we interpret correctly, twenty-one years.]

[Col. 1425]

>   
> you, unbegotten, who begot for yourself the eternal Son,

## I. How Holy Parents Gave Him Birth

> If anyone has diligently examined the deeds of the Franks’ ancestors,  
>   
> he will learn that, by fighting, they often overcame  
>   
> the barbarian kings’ armies.  
>   
> Thus Dagobert held his kingdom in peace,  
>   
> so that he could be called a peaceful Solomon, a second Solomon.  
>   
> With generous hand he offered the peoples popular gifts  
>   
> and rendered fitting service to Christ’s servants.  
>   
> Then, in many places throughout the land, settlers began  
>   
> to establish sacred buildings, and the religious people  
>   
> of the Lord increased. At that time, shining  
>   
> like the morning star in the star-bearing skies,  
>   
> Richarius, born of illustrious parents,  
>   
> shone in the village that had been called Centula  
>   
> because it had a hundred hearths. He was dear and beloved by all.  
>   
> In him the nobility of his lineage did not alone shine forth;  
>   
> ultimately he remained steadfast in holy conduct,  
>   
> so that, though a layman, he displayed the signs of a holy life.

## II. By Whose Instruction He Took the Narrow Path

> At that time the district of Ponthieu also deserved to shine,  
>   
> radiant with the splendor of two priests.  
>   
> The name of the greater of them was CAIDOCUS;  
>   
> Ireland sent us these men, distinguished by their merits.  
>   
> The people, refusing to hear salvation from them,  
>   
> neither received them worthily nor treated them with due honor,  
>   
> but rather began to drive them from their own territory.  
>   
> Their cruel violence moved holy Richarius,  
>   
> and, rescuing the righteous men from the savage populace,  
>   
> he gave them lodging, kept them, and kindly cared for them,  
>   
> as God ordained, so that both might be saved.  
>   
> The lamp, long kindled by divine light,  
>   
> could not be shut in but extended its rays widely.  
>   
> After he had received the strangers into his house,  
>   
> he generously supplied their bodily needs from his own means,  
>   
> carefully gaining the profit of a holy life.  
>   
> Nor did the barren earth fail to receive the seeds of the word.  
>   
> He planted in the mind what it had received through the bodily ear,  
>   
> and carried many grains of Christ to the granaries.

## III. How He Lamented the Sins of His Former Life

> Thus also the holy man, eloquent in speech,  
>   
> touched at once by holy reason and heavenly inspiration,  
>   
> disclosed in a pious mind the sins of his own life.  
>   
> Whatever sinful pleasure had brought guilt to his youth,  
>   
> he cleansed with a stream of tears.  
>   
> Because he had offered hospitality to God  
>   
> under the appearance of servants, he was received  
>   
> by God’s own mercy.  
>   
> From then on he took up the beginnings of religion;  
>   
> and, following apostolic custom, wisely set aside later things  
>   
> and hastened toward what lay before him.  
>   
> He remembered the Psalmist’s prophetic verse,  
>   
> which says that the elect pass  
>   
> from virtue to virtue, so that they may approach  
>   
> the Lord, the God of gods.

## IV. How He, Possessing Many Virtues, Became a Priest

> Thereafter he restrained himself from bodily food  
>

>

## IX. How Steadfast He Was When Returning from the Britons

> After he had supplied the rural people with the pasture of his teaching,

## X. How, by Praying, He Overthrew the Enemy Who Tested Him

> Finally, he endured the shame inflicted by the enemy,  
>   
> which the Lord’s mercy turned into an honor of praise.  
>   
> Seeing a matron supported by the assistance of a horse,  
>   
> chaste under holy religious observance,  
>   
> into whose holy heart he had poured the teachings of life,  
>   
> he then resolved, as it happened, to return.

But the woman, carrying the child’s tiny limbs,  
follows the holy man, so that he might bless him,  
the child whom he had already received from the sacred water of the font.

[Col. 1429B] And when the holy man of God had scarcely received the infant,  
as the ancient enemy was exercising his age-old snares,  
the horse gnashed its teeth; with its feet loosened,  
it turned rabid, running, leaping, and rushing about.

Seeing this, the mother turned away her terrified eyes,  
lest she should see the child’s destruction as he fell.  
But the crowd of servants, fearing harm to both,  
does not cease emitting cries, lamentation, and mourning.

But the right hand of Christ—which had taken Peter as he hesitated in the waves—preserved the child as he fell.  
For after the man of God had raised his prayers  
and offered them on high, the child suddenly came  
unharmed and safe to the ground; the rider was given rest,  
and the mother embraces her offspring joyfully in her arms.

[Col. 1429C] Thus, for the honor of his servant, the Lord transferred  
the enemy’s deceits, and the proud wing became a humble teacher.  
After this he wished never again to mount  
the back of a fierce horse, but rather that of a gentle ass:  
for, while Life hastened to undergo death,  
it was carried by this lowly conveyance.

Thus, while he traveled through many places for the sake of instruction,  
the diligent ass was sufficient to carry the holy man.  
And wherever the traces of his steps turned,  
either he sounded forth psalms to holy Christ in harmonious song,  
or the word of his teaching was heard from his mouth.

Nor is it surprising if he himself preached Christ with his tongue,  
since he had scarcely ever withdrawn from him in sober mind:  
through him he consulted for the wretched, and toward the proud  
he proved stern, mercifully consoling their anguish;

[Col. 1429D] and, rebuking them severely, he restrained their conduct.

### XI. How King Dagobert, moved by his fame, visited him

At a certain time, compelled by the holy man’s reputation  
and by the suggestion of one of his soldiers, Giselemar,  
the aforementioned King Dagobert came into those regions.  
He visited the servant of the Lord, wishing to entrust himself  
to the prayers of so great a man.

The holy and exceptional man honored him in two ways:  
with the holy sign of his right hand he strengthened him;  
then boldly corrected him for timidly allowing himself to remain ignorant,  
urging him to despise worldly pomp completely  
and, in faith, to learn not to be deceitful in speech.

He urged him not to rejoice in the steps of passing honors,  
but rather to fear the power of the Eternal One,  
and to keep the praise of that One always upon his lips:

[Col. 1430A] to hold firmly that no power in the world exists  
which, while it flourishes in greatness, is not emptied like a frail shadow;  
that it slips away like the small foam  
which rivers produce, if the breath of temptation blows for a short while.

Rather, let him undertake to endure great torments courageously;  
for from whomever much is given, much will be required.  
If one scarcely suffices to render an account before God for himself,  
how will he be able to bear an account for many?

Therefore everyone ought to fear being placed over others  
rather than being subject to them. For one who is regarded as subordinate  
will bear the burden of judgment only for himself;  
but he who is raised to the honor of kingship  
will be weighed down before God by his own burden  
and by the burden of many others.

This sober correction penetrated the king’s mind,  
and he asked the priest to become his guest.

[Col. 1430B] Relying upon Christ’s rule, the priest did not reject  
the banquets of the world, so that an opportunity for teaching  
might arise from this. He came to the royal court,  
and occupied the entire day and the following night,  
offering the banqueters the food of heavenly life.

His steadfastness so greatly pleased the king  
that he granted him something from his own revenues,  
from which a lamp might shine in the temple of God.  
For he considered it entirely just that,  
just as he had been illuminated by divine light through that man,  
so he himself should illuminate the Lord’s temple  
with a visible gift.

### XII. How, wishing to avoid people, he sought the desert

Because the man of God was honored by many peoples,  
he thereafter wished to avoid the sight of human beings,

[Col. 1430C] so that, cautiously shunning earthly honors,  
he might contemplate heavenly things alone within himself.

He abandoned the world, and desired the desert,  
where he could be free for the worship of the Lord  
and gather the fruits of contemplation,  
while he did not neglect active works, to which he eagerly aspired.  
He reflected that the Lord had praised Mary’s portion  
as the better one, because it would not be taken away from her.

Remembering this, he strove to enter a secluded life,  
where he might frequently investigate heavenly things alone.  
He entrusted the church which he himself had built  
to be held under the care of another administrator.

Giselmar, a lover of divine law, and Maurontus,  
sprung from a distinguished lineage, were empowered by the king—  
being then charged with guarding the lands and woods—  
to grant him a little dwelling in the forest of devout Chrisciacum,  
where he might remain.

[Col. 1430D] Maurontus, afterward led by divine love,  
laid aside his arms and assumed the monastic habit.

### XIII. How he built a church in the dwelling granted to him

In the place where the aforementioned men  
had prepared a small dwelling for the saint,  
the saint laid the foundations of a church.  
Then, accompanied by only one servant,  
he entered a cell made of exceedingly humble construction,  
suitably fashioned as a dwelling for a holy life.

He despised the world, judging it proud  
if someone appeared to possess the world’s pleasures.  
There he mortified himself severely,  
praying, keeping vigil, and performing frequent fasts,

[Col. 1431A] until his bones scarcely clung together at their joints,  
and he could move his trembling steps only with difficulty,  
supported by a staff. Climbing the world by the effort of his spirit,  
he always contemplated heavenly things alone with a devout mind.

He was alien to this age and close to Christ.  
He fought against and overcame him  
who had once rejoiced that he had conquered Adam;  
treading upon the asp and basilisk, he continually  
crushed the head of the ancient enemy.

Despising the earth, he sighed for the court of heaven,  
and continually climbed toward it by Jacob’s ladder.  
Along the narrow path that leads to the heavens  
he fortified the venerable road with unceasing prayers.

The harshness of the desert did not confine the column of his light;  
rather, he shone forth, radiant with abundant splendor.

[Col. 1431B] Therefore, driven by many kinds of suffering,  
many people gathered around the holy man.  
He received them kindly and strove to heal them  
with the remedies of prayer.  
Whatever illness afflicted each person,  
he approached the holy man and returned home cured.

### XIV. How the holy man spoke with his servant about his approaching death

But I have decided not to set forth all his miracles,  
only the outstanding features of his holy life,  
lest, while I am judged too slow in speech,  
the fame of the many signs he performed should grow cold.

It is enough now to say how he left this present age,  
leaving these matters themselves to the learned.  
For, knowing the day on which he ought to lay aside  
the garment of the flesh and receive the reward of long labor,  
he summoned to himself a servant named Sinobardus,

[Col. 1431C] and, soothing him in a fatherly voice, addressed him thus:

“My son, I clearly see that my own flesh must soon be laid down,  
and I shall approach the sight of the King,  
whom I have long desired to behold.

Go and prepare a vessel in which my body may be placed,  
not with excessive ornament, but as the use of the flesh requires,  
until that time when it will be preserved there,  
until all corruption shall receive incorruption.

And prepare yourself always, brother, with all your strength,  
so that, when the hour that now approaches me comes for you,  
you may lay down this fragile body without fear.

I am myself walking the road which the whole earth will occupy.  
May the mercy of Christ alone now come to my aid,  
and may he rescue me from the jaws of the grim lion,  
who once by his own death withdrew me from that place.

[Col. 1431D] And may he who granted the consolations of this present life  
generously grant me the gifts of the life to come.”

Thus spoke the Father. But bitter tears released the servant;  
nevertheless, with pious willingness he followed the master’s commands.  
Having found wood, he split it, hollowed it, and prepared it,  
and did his utmost to fit it to the father’s limbs.

He watered the work he had made with mournful tears,  
almost filling it with tears before it was filled  
with the Father’s body.

Meanwhile, while the servant was carrying out the holy man’s orders,  
a more severe anguish of illness had weakened the saint,  
and scarcely did breath remain in his cold body.  
Nevertheless, he did not restrain his mouth from the prayers of Christ  
or from praise.

While he was receiving the life-giving food of the divine body  
and pouring forth continual prayers in words,  
on the sixth day before the Kalends of May,  
when Phoebus looked upon the world,

[Col. 1432A] the holy man passed into heaven.  
The servant placed him where he himself had ordered while alive.

But, astonishing to tell, while the disciple was performing  
the Father’s funeral rites, he was suddenly overcome by sleep.  
He dreamed as though he were being led into a radiant palace,  
and in his vision he saw a beautiful place of extraordinary splendor,  
whose brilliance even surpassed the rays of the shining sun.

There he saw Richarius dwelling in blessedness  
and heard him say these words:

“Behold, brother, the kind of dwelling Christ has given me:  
precious in place of poverty, shining in place of darkness,  
flashing with such great radiance in place of smoke-filled gloom.”

After he awoke from that sleep,  
he completed the service of the funeral rites more joyfully,  
God so disposing that such great and immense anguish  
might be consoled in the servant  
and the saint’s glory revealed.

[Col. 1432B] As I have related, the holy man was buried by his servant,  
in the place where he had served the wishes of Christ the King most fully.

Nor was it long afterward that Ocioaldus,  
abbot of the monks whom the estate of Centula contained,  
a man of no small religious devotion, came there.  
On the Ides of October he carried away the body of the holy man Richarius and placed it where it now rests.

In that place, through God’s granting, marvelous things often occur,  
so that the holy faith of those who pray may be made evident,  
the merits of the one who was sacred there may be recognized,  
and, as the Psalmist sings, Christ may be praised in him.

### XV. How a cripple was healed by the holy man at his cave

A certain man crippled in his limbs but strong in the power of faith  
often came to the holy man’s cave, praying.  
Suddenly he departed from that place healed,  
glorifying the Lord because he had gone away thus strengthened.

Nor did he alone deserve to experience this assistance;  
many others whom grace visited received similar benefits.

### XVI. How the bonds of prisoners were broken through the merits of the holy man

Some men bound and fettered in chains  
were being led along a path near Richarius’s church.  
As soon as they were able to see it from a distance,  
they cried out: “Priest of Christ, release us!”

Then, through the merits of the holy man,  
the iron bonds were broken.

### XVII. A brother is saved while many others perished from pestilence

But what one of the brothers of Saint Richarius suffered  
must now be related in due order.

A cruel disaster was once destroying many  
of the inhabitants of the land; finally,  
one of Saint Richarius’s brothers was struck by that dreadful calamity.

Although he feared the destruction of death because of the plague,  
he learned to hope for life under so great a patron.  
Therefore, accompanied by a crowd of his brothers,  
he fled to the saint’s mausoleum  
as to a sure source of consolation.

While the prayers of all were poured forth there,  
the man who had suffered rejoiced to depart healed.

### XVIII. A final exhortation is joined to the end of the little book

Let the hearer understand what our faith is worth  
if we seek an intercessor for ourselves,  
one who has so quickly been accustomed to drive away  
bodily illnesses from us.

For the miracles performed display the saint’s merit,  
and what follows is seen to confirm his former life:  
the virtue that appears after his funeral rites  
declares what the holy man had been.

[Col. 1433A] Behold the poor man of Christ; consider,  
company of brothers: he has become a companion  
of the riches of Christ.  
He who wished to be despised before human eyes  
now rejoices to have the companies of Angles [Angels] as companions.  
He who avoided honors in the present world  
rejoices that he has deserved heaven by an everlasting right.

He therefore appears worthy of everyone’s honor,  
because he always clung gently to the Lord of all.  
It benefits us also to venerate him above all,  
since we are seen to be close to his members,  
so that those whom he nourished with the seed of the divine Word  
may know that they succeed him as worthy heirs.

Our praise is not so much beneficial to that holy man  
[Col. 1433B] as his imitation is beneficial to us.  
Indeed, he rejoices more if someone good imitates him  
than if someone empty praises him with a loud voice.

[Col. 1434A] Therefore, holy Fathers, brothers,  
and faithful company, who have come in devotion  
to the feast of so great a Father,  
strive to undertake the labor  
that, at your request and through his prayers,  
your petitions may ascend to the heights  
of the throne of the supreme King.

Adorn yourselves with spiritual beauty;  
let a twofold love always flourish within you,  
and let the lamp of hope and faith remain continually alight.  
Follow the rule that the holy Fathers taught,  
so that in heaven you may be joined to them.

And, as Paul commands, reject what harms the world;  
live in this age content with what is just,  
awaiting the Lord’s coming and the blessed hope—  
the Lord who redeemed us from the bonds of death by dying,  
so that, stripped of guilt, he might make us a people pleasing to himself,

[Col. 1434B] to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit,  
glory is equally due.

Let it be enough to have brought forth these few things  
about the saint’s life.  
Now the labor demands that the first little book be brought to an end.

It contains nothing distinctive; the following is said about the writer of the miracles.

[Col. 1433B]

Because the rhetorical writer saw that these matters were numerous,  
he took care to make two little books from them.

1. A remarkable account of something at the estate of Sidrudis.  
2. What happened to a certain linden tree at that estate.  
3. A spring burst forth there through the merits of the holy man.  
4. A woman of Burgundy is healed by the holy man through wine.  
5. A certain prostitute becomes crippled and is herself healed.  
6. The most grievous fishing expedition of a wretched thief.  
7. A woman with contracted hands is healed in both hands.  
8. A certain man who was not a thief is held as a thief.

[Col. 1434B] Here, in Anonymus, the healing of the crippled woman is inserted.

9. A blind girl is healed from her mother’s womb.  
10. Brothers from Denmark remove the holy man through fear.  
11. While the holy man is being carried back, one sick man is healed.  
12. Likewise, a man suffering from dropsy is saved on his return.  
13. The weakened body of a certain child is restored.  
14. Concerning a certain blind man who was crippled throughout his body.  
15. A certain blind woman receives sight.  
16. The iron chains of a certain prisoner are broken.  
17. A certain deceiver is mocked when he comes to us.  
18. A crippled girl is raised up on the feast of the holy man.  
19. A certain girl suffering from an equal pestilence is healed.
