2. The holy man rebukes and scourges a certain thief.  
3. On the feast of the holy man, a little woman dies while weaving.  
4. A certain wretchedly crippled girl is raised up.  
5. A blind man brought to the holy man receives light.  
6. A certain man crippled throughout his body becomes well.  
7. A certain man is saved from a miserable affliction of the eyes.  
8. A terrible contraction of one man is loosened.  
9. A certain man is healed in all the limbs of his body.  
10. A man whose left side had been condemned by paralysis becomes well.  
11. The contracted left side of a certain girl is raised up.  
12. A certain little woman rejoices, her right side healed.  
13. The weakened body of a crippled child is healed.  
14. A mute from his earliest years receives speech.  
15. A crippled child in a cradle is saved, and another as well.  
16. A proud Dane is corrected by divine justice.

[Col. 1433] We omit here the miracles indicated in the preceding chapters and described by Ingelramnus, since, apart from their metrical form, they contain nothing different from those narrated by the primary author (in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century II, p. 222). Ingelramnus added a fourth book concerning the transfer of the body of Saint Richarius and the miracles that followed from it; we immediately present that book from the fifth Benedictine century.

# BOOK FOUR, OR THE ACCOUNT OF SAINT RICHARIUS, ABBOT, FROM THE MONASTERY OF SITHIU TO CENTULA

(From the Centula manuscript and the April volume of the Bollandists.)

[Col. 1433]

### I. A metrical account of Saint Richarius

[Col. 1433D]

Thus far the ancient page of the book retains  
the miracles of the holy man, which I sang in verse  
as best I could.

[Col. 1434D] From this point I shall embrace more particularly  
those which my own eye saw.

Arnulfus, strong in talent and also supported by great wealth,  
possessed our homeland as margrave.

[Col. 1435A] Having acquired it by fraud, as he often did in many matters,  
he transferred the holy man from there, desiring to possess  
so noble a treasure together with certain saints of his own region.

Now, already advanced in age, laying aside the garment of the flesh,  
he ordered his son to be made his heir,  
the son who bore the grandfather’s own name.  
At that time he held the authority of the kingdom second only to the king.

Humble toward all, pious and kind toward all,  
he was the son of Hugh the Great, the illustrious duke Hugh,  
who afterward, raised to royal honor,  
ruled the kingdom of the Franks with remarkable moderation.

Bearing heavily the fraud mentioned above,  
he restored to the homeland whatever had been taken away.

To make the saint’s return more celebrated,  
[Note: [Col. 1435D] In the *Chronicle of Centula* manuscript, it is stated at the margin: “In the year of the Lord 952 the body was taken away and brought into the monastery of Saint Bertin on the fourth day before the Kalends of September—namely, into Centula under Abbot Fulcheric, with the clergy who were present there—as in Hariulfus, book III, chapter 12.”]

[Col. 1435B] he ordered an immense crowd of people to gather.  
And not only did an assembly from our own land come together;  
a gathering was also made from many Franks.

Afterward he ordered the saint’s relics to be returned to him.  
The aforementioned boy, receiving his commands—

[Note: [Col. 1435D] The younger Arnulfus.]

—became sad at being deprived of so valuable a possession.  
But, considering that it would not be safe to refuse,  
he returned it unwillingly, fearing that he might otherwise be compelled.

At last the glorious day had dawned for the world  
on which so welcome a reception of the saint was to take place.  
The two parties came forth, rejoicing and weeping.  
The former handed over what they had always wished to possess;  
the latter received that without which they could not bear to live.

[Col. 1435C] Afterward the leading men of the people were asked to swear  
that absolutely nothing was missing from the saint’s body.  
When this had been done, our people hastened to return.

O memorable day! O light worthy of devoted celebration,  
on which the saint deigned to behold his native boundaries!

[Note: [Col. 1436D] In the manuscript of the *Chronicle of Centula* there is a charter of King Lothair, granted at the request of Hugh the Duke and Abbot, by which the villages assigned by him to the monks in the district of Ternois are confirmed—namely, Botritium and Rolleni-curtis. It was enacted at the palace of Compiègne in the twenty-first year of Lothair. Adalbero, the king’s notary, acting in the place of Adalbero, archbishop of Reims and chief chancellor, authenticated it.]

No one will be able to recount adequately the joy of that day,  
nor the immense rejoicing that the saint’s arrival  
stirred everywhere.

For wherever the procession came to any village,  
the entire crowd of peasants came out to meet it,  
and in their joy they cast their groans toward the stars.

Before they had reached the church, when they were still  
almost a league away, the aforementioned duke  
dismounted from his horse and began to walk  
with bare feet,

[Col. 1435D] carrying the bier on his own shoulders,  
together with those of the people who appeared more noble than the others.

He carried it for so long, drenched in tears,  
until he joyfully placed it upon his own altar.

[Col. 1436A] But let the reader consider what had been accomplished  
by divine power.

This return of the saint, which I mentioned above,  
took place when the fields were yellow with full ears of grain.  
But because there were not enough buildings  
to accommodate so many soldiers,  
they spread themselves throughout the fields.

Who could say how thoroughly the harvest was destroyed,  
when one part was trampled beneath horses’ feet,  
another part devoured by their mouths?  
A further part was burned,  
the standing grain being set alight in many places  
and the grass consumed to its roots.

At last they departed, leaving the land bare.

I shall tell of something marvelous:  
after scarcely a few days had passed,  
behold, an incredible harvest began to grow again,  
fruitful; and when the season and hour of reaping approached,  
you could see the entire countryside yellow with grain,  
as if the region had suffered no damage at all.

Seeing that this had been accomplished through Richarius’s merits,  
the entire people turned to the praises of the Lord.

### II. How a man and woman who fell into a well survived

Among the marvels and virtues of the holy man  
there was also this: while a great crowd of people  
had assembled for his feast,  
there happened to be, near the entrance of the church, a well  
whose water had long since completely dried up.  
Its mouth had been closed with old wickerwork.

A man and a woman, unaware of it,  
while walking over it, fell into its great depth.

Who could doubt that they had suffered mortal danger?

[Col. 1436C] Yet they were seen to be brought out  
from the hollow of the well, not only alive  
but sound in their entire bodies.

### III. How a certain man, while eating fish, swallowed a fishbone

The people of the Lord were celebrating Palm Sunday  
according to custom, triumphantly carrying palms.

[Note: [Col. 1436D] Hariulfus: “Palm Sunday, which the common people call Flowering Easter, was celebrated according to ecclesiastical tradition; on that very day a certain cleric …”]

A certain cleric, eating with the monks,  
a man born of parents not without distinction,  
carelessly swallowed a fishbone with a piece of food.

Feeling the pain, when evening came  
he tried to expel it by vomiting, if he could.  
But because he could not, his condition became worse  
on the following day.

The third day brought still more serious symptoms,  
and finally, on the fourth, he began to contemplate death,  
also arranging whatever seemed appropriate.

He sent word asking the abbot and the brothers to come and see him.  
When they entered, he spoke to them at length about his death  
and asked that he might deserve to be buried with the monks.

On the venerable Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, however,  
the crowd of his relatives led him to the saint’s church

[Col. 1437A] while the brothers were celebrating the solemnities of Mass.  
Supported by two men, one on his right and one on his left,  
and already almost breathing his last,  
he climbed to the holy altar.

After he had placed some books there as an offering,  
he tried as best he could to turn back.  
But scarcely had he turned around  
when, touched by a heavenly sign,  
he felt warm water pour over his entire body  
and cried out that he no longer felt any pain.

From that moment we too rejoiced,  
as though he had been brought back from death,  
offering high praises to the Lord.

### IV. Concerning the church-workman who fell from a high roof

Ingelvinus was a cutter of wood among us,  
accustomed to repair the church’s collapsing roofs  
and bold enough to climb still higher places.

[Col. 1437B] During the Easter celebrations he climbed the church tower,  
having been asked to fasten again the broken rope of the bell.  
After properly completing the duty assigned to him,  
he tried to close a hole in the roof.

But deceived by the confidence with which he believed  
that he could hold himself securely,  
he slipped from the lofty roof of the church  
and would have suffered a terrible death  
had divine power not carried him toward part of the wall.

The stones projecting there happened to be arranged  
so that one could walk around the church by them  
more safely and, using them, fix one’s steps.  
Above them there was an attached protection of parapets, and so forth.

### V. How a mad girl lived after climbing the church

The mind of a certain girl had been turned to madness;  
driven by distorted perception, she wandered everywhere.

[Col. 1437C] After traversing the streets of the village at night,  
while we were keeping the morning vigils with hymns,  
she saw the doors of the church open, as was customary.  
She entered, shouting and grinding out dreadful words.

Turning her steps toward the sound of our voice,  
she encountered the staircase that led upward.  
Unable to climb by its steps, she began nevertheless to ascend.  
But once she had begun to reach its summit,  
she proceeded, running over the breaks  
in the projecting stones, as a mad person does.

[Col. 1438A] Who could doubt that she had fallen into mortal ruin?  
And yet, although she did fall, she suffered no harm from death.

Indeed, continuing on and wandering about as she ran,  
she came to the entrance of the spiral staircase  
by which the heights of the church were reached,  
and climbed it as far as it extended.

What she did afterward can scarcely be adequately described  
by anyone’s tongue. She did not cease uttering terrifying cries  
and running around the church.

No one will fully understand from how great a danger  
she was saved, unless he has seen those places himself.

But we, stupefied and troubled by fear  
that the church might be polluted by her fall,  
since the time and occasion had not yet come  
to explain the matter to the crowd standing there,  
began urgently to signal that they should climb up, seize her,  
and bring her down with them.

[Col. 1438B] But no sane person dared to touch the madwoman.  
At last, of her own accord, she retraced her steps  
by the same route.

### VI. How the holy man’s servants were spontaneously released from their bonds

[Note: [Col. 1437C] These four miracles, which contain nothing distinctive, may be found in the April volume of the Bollandists.]

### VII. A brother is healed by the holy man at the request of his brother

### VIII. How the rain stopped on the feast of the holy man

### IX. How thieves of the holy man were unable to light a piece of wood

In the district of Amiens there is a place called  
Mons Desiderii, with a village beneath it.

[Note: [Col. 1438C] Mondidier.]

There is a church there dedicated under the patronage  
of a certain holy man.

The men of Roye began war against this fortress.  
After plundering many villages, they approached the village  
which, as I have said, contained the saint’s church.

The thieves, inflamed by fury, attacked it,  
being profane men who did not hesitate to violate the church.

By chance a candle stood near the church’s altar.  
Assuming that they could steal it,  
they carried it away when they departed.

But after they were able to return to their own homes,  
they tried to light the wax which they had carried with them.  
Yet the fire placed against it was utterly repelled,  
as though the material had been turned into stone.

They tried again, and again labored in vain.  
They regretted having violated the saint’s sacred things in this way  
and quickly returned what they had taken from the church.

Some report that these things happened in this manner,  
although that place was outside our own region.

# Around the middle of the century: Papias the Grammarian

[Col. 1437]

## NOTICE

(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers and Ecclesiastical Writings*, II, 621.)

[Col. 1437D] Papias the grammarian flourished around the year 1050,  
as stated in the manuscript of Alberic’s *Chronicle*,  
not in the year 1200, as Trithemius incorrectly writes  
in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Alberic’s words are these:

“In the year 1053, the thirteenth year of the emperor Henry, son of Conrad, Papias published his book, namely the *Elementarium doctrinae erudimentum* [*Elementary Instruction in Learning*]. This is proved by the number of years, where he discusses the ages of the world in the first letter and, by counting, reaches this year.”

That he spent ten years composing it is confirmed by verses  
added to Papias in the Aquicinctian copy and transcribed  
by the very learned man and my most intimate friend,  
John Mabillon. I shall set them down here.  
They mention a certain Rainaldus, by whom this codex  
was copied in the year of Christ 1173.

If the world never grew dark during the day,  
no lamp would be needed for human eyes.  
Thus, whoever sees everything clearly in Scripture  
has no need of this book’s assistance.

But since no one exists who knows everything,  
this book must be embraced by all.

Like a bee’s honey gathered through ten years of labor,  
Papias gave this work to all as something to be read.

But, so that our food might be richer  
and more abundant from its wealth,  
Rainaldus added these riches to us.

So that our table might not lack such sweetness,  
his helpful hand was active in this work.

Accept this pleasing gift, Savior,  
and may this labor obtain perpetual rest for him.

May your flock, Aquicinctum, love this book,  
read it again, take delight in it,  
and preserve it with every effort.

The time when it was written is given  
by the years that join Jesus to it:  
one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

[Col. 1439C] As you read these things, know that,  
as the reward for his labor, the scribe asks not for gold  
but for a prayer.

Therefore return a prayer, since, more precious than gold,  
devout prayer wins God’s favor.

This *Elementarium* of Papias is preserved on parchment,  
folio by folio, in our library at Leiden,  
among the Latin manuscript codices, number 14,  
as stated in the catalogue of the books of this library,  
published in quarto at Leiden in 1674 by Frederik Spanheim,  
page 400, which may be consulted.

John Trithemius, in the place cited, also states  
that Papias wrote a book of letters to various persons.

Moreover, Elias Putschius published, among the ancient grammarians,  
*Explanations of Ancient Abbreviations from the Glossary of Papias*;  
Charles du Cange did not notice them in the manuscripts  
that he had the opportunity to examine.

His *Glossary* is in fact extant in print,  
edited by the care of Boninus Mombritius,  
whose two volumes *On the Lives of the Saints*  
were published at Venice in 1490, on April 19.

Certainly Papias himself seems to suggest in the preface  
that he did not so much compose a Glossary anew  
as enlarge and develop one previously arranged  
in some fashion. He writes:

“Now, concerning the name of this art, it seems necessary not to omit the following point: although formerly, because it retained the interpretation of a word or simply of one expression or another, it was called a *Glossary*, now, with definitions, explanations according to rules, statements, and many additions of this kind, it may more fully and appropriately be called the *Elementarium doctrinae erudimentum*.”

Thus writes Charles du Fresne, lord du Cange,  
in the preface to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*,  
section or number 44, page 36. In section or number 46, page 37,  
he adds the following:

“Papias is followed by Ugutio of Pisa, who produced a much fuller work, enriched by many additions of vocabulary and *etymōn* [etymologies], whether it is called a Glossary or a Dictionary. It is commonly found in libraries in manuscript. I do not think it was printed, because, when the art of printing was invented, it was still being used in the schools; the work compiled from Papias and Ugutio by John of Genoa was the one then in use.

“We do not learn from the preface to that work who this Ugutio was or in which century he lived; but we learn it from a manuscript chronicle. We shall transcribe its words here:

“‘At this time’—around the year 1192—‘Agno Ugutio, a Pisan by nationality and bishop of Ferrara, who had been appointed by the Apostolic See as coadjutor to the abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, a prodigal man, composed the book of *Derivations* from the book of Papias, which is there.’

“In the preface, however, he discloses the purpose of the work and his own name as follows:

“‘Therefore, with God’s gracious favor, we resolved to compose a work in which, above all, there would be found the meanings of words, the distinctions among meanings, the origins of derivations, the assignments of etymologies, and explanations of interpretations. Through ignorance of these matters, the Latin language, naturally needy because of a certain indolence among learned men, is considerably restricted.

“‘We shall strive to accomplish this not merely so that we may gain the fragile glass of empty reputation, but rather so that a common benefit may blossom from it for all who devote themselves to the knowledge of letters.

“‘Nor should it escape our minds that, in this work, we have applied perfection only gradually, since nothing among human things is found polished to the utmost, although, in comparison with others who have treated this same subject, we may not unjustly appear to excel by a certain singular perfection.

“‘Here the child will take greater pleasure; here the adult will be nourished more abundantly; here the mature scholar will delight more richly. Here are the gymnosophists of the trivium, here the teachers of the quadrivium, here the professors of law, here the investigators of theology; here the governors of churches will make progress.

“‘Here will be supplied whatever has hitherto been omitted through lack of knowledge; here will be polished whatever has long been wrongly used.

“‘If anyone asks who was the author of this work, the answer must be: God. If anyone asks what instrument produced this work, the answer must be: a Pisan by nationality, named Hugutio, as though from *Eugetius*, that is, “good earth,” not only for those now living but also for those to come; or Hugutio, as though from *Vigetius*, that is, “verdant earth,” not only for himself but also for others.’”

Ughellus places his death around the year 1212,  
among the bishops of Ferrara; these matters concerning Ugutio  
were unknown to him.”

These are the exact words of Charles du Fresne,  
lord du Cange, in the places cited.

Cornelius a Beughem also mentions Papias the grammarian  
in his little work *On the Incunabula of Printing*,  
under the entry “Papias,” page 103.  
He says that his *Vocabulary* was printed formerly  
at Milan in 1476 in folio, and at Venice in 1487, 1491,  
and 1496 in folio.

He writes that Papias, Lombard by nationality  
and a grammarian by profession, flourished—incorrectly,  
with Trithemius—in the year of Christ 1200.

# In the year of the Lord 1045: Robert, Bishop of London

[Col. 1441]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, volume IV, p. 461.)

Robert, abbot of Jumièges, was substituted for Bishop Alwoldus—  
whom William calls Elfevordus—on the London see in 1044,  
through the agency of King Edward, by whom he had been summoned  
to England. He later became primate of Canterbury.

While governing the bishopric of London,  
he remembered his monastery and gave it many ornaments,  
including a Sacramentary, at the end of which  
he wrote the charter that we present below.

[Col. 1441]

## CHARTER OF ROBERT

[Col. 1441A] Let it be known to all the faithful, both present and future  
through succeeding generations, that I, Robert, formerly abbot  
of the monks of Jumièges and afterward made bishop  
of the holy see of London, have given this book  
to Saint Mary in this monastery of the monks of Saint Peter  
entrusted to me, in honor of the saints mentioned here  
and for the remembrance of me, so that it may be kept here forever.

[Col. 1442A] If anyone removes it from this place by force, fraud,  
or in any manner whatsoever, may he suffer damage to his soul  
because of what he has done, and may he be blotted out  
from the book of the living and not be written with the just.

And may he be condemned with the severest excommunication—  
whoever removes even one of the vestments  
that I have given to this place, or any other ornaments,  
silver candlesticks, or gold from the altar panel. Amen.

# In the year of the Lord 1045: Garcia, Monk of Saint Michael of Cuxa

[Col. 1441]

## ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

(*Literary History of France*, VII, 345.)

Baluze, in his appendix to the *Marca Hispanica* (pp. 1072–1082), gave us a document that deserves to be known, although it is written in a diffuse and obscure style and is full of grammatical errors. It is the work of Garcias, a monk of Saint-Michel de Cuxa, or Cusan, in the diocese of Elne—today Perpignan in Roussillon—who had had as his teacher a certain Arnol, apparently a monk of the same place, and who was writing in 1040. This rather prolix work is addressed to Oliva, bishop of Vic and at the same time abbot of Cuxa. Garcias undertook to describe the origin of his monastery and to make known to posterity the ceremony of the dedication of its church and the great number of relics then preserved there. The enumeration he made of them is accompanied by a reasonably accurate notice of the saints to whom they were believed to belong. He added a fine description of the high altar that Oliva had constructed. After this comes an exhortation that the author delivered to his brothers on the feast of the dedication. Thus his work consists of two parts, one historical and the other moral.

[Col. 1443]

## LETTER OF GARCIA, MONK OF CUXA, TO OLIVA, BISHOP OF AUSONA

On the beginnings of the monastery of Cuxa and the sacred relics kept there.  
(About the year 1040.)

(Edited by Baluze in the Appendix to the *Marca Hispanica*, p. 1072, from the cartulary of the monastery of Cuxa.)

[Col. 1443A] [Note: [Col. 1443] The text suffers in more than one place from incurable corruption.]

To the most glorious and, among pious bishops, most merciful Father Oliva, the least of good monks, but the servant of your holiness, and, as long as I live, the attendant of your grace and authority, Garcias: the service of due obedience and the incomparable reward of eternal rest.

When almighty God was creating the substances of visible and invisible things and considering the causes and operations of events, he chose, before the foundation of the world, for the praise and glory of his own power, a man desirous of being the imitator of heavenly graces, who would necessarily exercise authority over the work of the world and over all living creatures. To the grace and likeness of this man he gave you to be compared with the whole human race, joining you to the fellowship of bodily frailty [Col. 1443B] and granting you, in accordance with the breadth of your heart, an intellect incapable of being filled or satisfied with every kind of knowledge. First, indeed, he compelled you, from the disciplines of your flourishing youth, through exercises and great diligence, to labor as time advanced; and thus, for the merits of justice, he piously placed you at the head of the administration of every affair through hereditary succession, so that the continual performance of commendable actions might be joined to the acquisition of sublime thoughts.

But deservedly the dispensation of the Father’s will, having rejected the honors of the world, once more gave you to his Church as its ruler, so that I, imprudent and exceedingly unlearned, might everywhere under your hand and blessing possess the security of secret counsel and the fullest protection of greater gain. I myself have learned this through abundant and secure experience [Col. 1443C], while, as the refuge of my beloved teacher and, in every respect, your intimate associate Arnallus, and as a memorable guide—namely, in the instruction and exaltation of Christ and his saints, in the enclosing of their relics, in the dedication of our altar, and also in the destruction by fire, as well as in the restoration accomplished by your laborious work and again in the blessing of the glorious valley, even after the incursion of its destroyers—I performed, as ordered, the service of your sincere love and experienced the assistance of my lord Michael. If I have assigned colors of propitiation and figures of the Evangelists, I hope, Christ permitting, that in your salvation all these things may be brought to greater perfection. Meanwhile [Col. 1444A] I beg you not to blame, as a rival, what I have put forward in uncultivated speech, but, as a kindly man, to vindicate your own shining intellect.

I therefore found certain things written among the documents, and from them I resolved, with willing purpose, to preserve for the benefit of many whatever I was able to find more clearly, as follows.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of October was celebrated the dedication of the monastery of Cuxa to the holy archangel Michael. The dedication was performed by Vuarinus, the religious abbot of that estate, a man highly prudent in worldly affairs, fully capable of teaching the people extemporaneously, and shining with great ease in learned studies, under the guidance of the divine hand. Together with Sunierus, bishop of that diocese, who assisted with his authority and knowledge, and with bishops from various sees—seven men in all, outstanding in nobility and [Col. 1444B] prudence—he dedicated it amid an infinite multitude of nobles powerful in authority, and an eminent assembly of clerics and laypeople of both sexes and of various ranks and dignities. They enriched it jointly with double gifts, restored abundance to royal dignity through offerings and crowns, and established it in unshakable perpetuity of law, free from the execution of any servile obligation, so that, with its own resources, it might always remain mistress in the extension of its boundaries. The more holy among them adorned this church with a large portion of venerable saints; the greatest of the people and the powerful, richly endowed through the generosity of their gifts and raised almost to the summit by every good thing, consecrated to the Lord this sacred temple for both parties.

For this reason, from that church and dedication there gradually comes to those who love remembrance an agreeable recollection, to be known in its entirety and in complete truth. First, in a few words, he should proclaim how gloriously God made the place and temple his own, how readily the merciful kindness of our Redeemer attends the prayers of those who supplicate him, and in what manner that place shines among the foremost places of the whole world in fullness and veneration. Indeed, it is worthy of praise and testimony to hand down more ancient matters to the memory of posterity.

Accordingly, after the apostolic weapons of vengeance and the restoration of the most sacred monastery of Saint Andrew the apostle—things that appear before us and are read—and after the divine providence that acted through the most holy bishop Germanus, the illustrious Pontius, a man of exceptional nobility and a commendable life, administered the community of that ruling monastery. Under Seniofred, count of blessed memory, who had already placed his hope in good fruits and who was more powerful in strength and authority, he was prudently supported by the arms of patience and was held, above the others, to possess a singular share of his favor. One day he raised him up with pious words, saying:

“We greatly offend the Creator of all in the place over which we preside and in which we exercise, through the duty of paternal vigilance, the care of administration, because we prefer to be distracted by ambition for worldly affairs rather than to fight, in the oversight of temporal [spiritual] matters, for what pleases God, in order to repair the war of twofold hostility and the disturbances of savage rebellion. Indeed, after the dangers of the entire place—or, so to speak, after the rod of God’s wrath—we have hastened, for unforeseen reasons, to the uses of all people, happier through inept offices than through virtue or religion; and without the sweat of our own hands we are praised by everyone as more exalted in power. Finally, as you know, he inflicted great slaughter through the waters and, miserably overcome because of the merit of his fault, perished. Thus, having been sworn to and restored by venerable men through kindness, and strengthened by royal commands and privileges, I consider it my duty, at the command of our serenity, to provide a supplement to the interrupted work, so that it may withstand the violence of the flood [Col. 1445C] or the blows of thunderbolts, and may be able to turn the inundations of rain into a hope of joy.”

To him the other replied:

“From where shall I obtain a name and an offering of praise, or joy for my soul?”

“There is,” he said, “a very small building—not, I will not say, a church, but a little oratory before the church of Saint Germanus—dedicated under the title of the archangel Michael, which at times remains excluded from the attendance of everyone. Therefore, according to your judgment and wisdom, let us raise up the entire church, together with its inhabitants, as a fitting hall in revenge upon the fatherland, for the advantage of perpetual warfare, and against unfruitful wickedness.”

Then the prince, as though hastening to grant a compassion already conceived, said:

“It shall be permitted to pursue this with glorious prayers, so that it may be reduced under no one’s authority, and so that the house of the Lord may be built for religion and praise, through the power of Christ and the honor of the supreme Michael. Through that same archangel, may the wretched enemies be driven away and pursued rather than admitted as participants. And, to speak fittingly, it is appropriate that the first of all the saints and victor over the proud Dragon should possess his sacred church, possess power, and receive the portion of a crown; that he, the lofty warrior, should be salvation for the present age and for all the posterity of our people, a leader, defender, and triumphant victor in the new battle, and that he should be found a kindly defender of those who obey him.”

Thus, with the worthy man placing everything most diligently into a single human discourse, and perhaps strengthened by angelic consolation, he laid the foundation with common stones and blocks used by the people, most splendidly. When he had raised its material higher—to a length of thirty-three cubits and a width of nearly forty palms—he finally brought it down with great elegance into the height of the arch, although Fortune begrudged success; for, as someone says, happiness is always subject to adversity, and many will pass through it, and knowledge will be manifold.

In that place, as was fitting, the angel or heavenly man Vuarinus was taken up, repeatedly building the basilica. With compact workmanship he raised the walls high, in the magnificent construction, with marvelous wonder; and he covered the roof’s gables most beautifully with the height of its timbers and the brilliance of its ornaments. [Col. 1446B] He also made the first building, the Holy of Holies, which is called the presbytery, as well as the level pavement, with pleasing workmanship. Above it he set up the altar of the great prince Michael upon four very beautiful columns made from *agonoscema* [uncertain term], with fitting honor.

The entire outer surface of those columns was smoothed by the craftsman’s skill, while their interiors were hollowed out. In them he placed an altar of considerable thickness, thirteen half-feet long, so to speak, and nine wide, with an entrance toward it through all the columns. Inside and out there was nothing that the mind or eyes might admire less, because of the excessive whiteness. In the middle of the altar he enclosed the form of the life-giving cross; in a deeper and more hidden place he appeared to begin [a repository] containing gifts which he himself had once acquired at great prices in Jerusalem, Rome, and certain other places. On the higher level he buried, with the full gaze of the mind and the full devotion of the heart, many relics of the saints by which that place was distinguished, and relics given by religious men, blessing the mercy of our God.

Finally, the chorus of venerable bishops mentioned above, an innumerable assembly of invited persons, built the altar and, having anointed it with the mystical gifts of spiritual sanctifications and with the unctions of the sacred charism, raised it for the offering of our Redeemer’s sacrifice, invoking him and praising the whole order with great praises. Meanwhile, in the altars of the church they placed relics according to each altar’s name and handed them down perpetually, for use in the Church, to those who would follow, so that they might always be praised, both for the stability of the earthly kingdom and for the ease of the heavenly kingdom.

They committed the following to memory concerning the relics of the greater altar.

In this venerable altar there are, first of all, relics of that saving cross upon which the King of heaven, our Lord the Son of God, completed the sacrament of the passion of the whole world and endured the offering of remission for the life of mortals.

There are relics of the veil and cloths with which, having assumed the Incarnation, he remained clothed in a child’s body, both human and divine.

There are relics of the Lord’s head-cloth, in which the labor of his passion is separated from the majesty of his divinity, and the weakness of our understanding is represented through the labor of his torments.

There are relics of the linen cloth with which God and Man wrapped his limbs and, humbly washing the feet of his disciples, wiped them.

There are relics from the tomb where the Lord’s flesh, according to its nature, rested, and from which he rose from the dead, giving life to our death.

There are relics from the manger in which the pious Mother laid the infant limbs of God the Lord according to the form of a servant.

There are relics from the fragments of that bread with which Christ satisfied five thousand men in the desert from five loaves and two fish.

There are relics of the garment of the most blessed virgin Mary, who enclosed outwardly the mystery of the divine incarnation and conceived and bore in her womb the life-giving Word of God.

There are relics of that glorious archangel Michael, namely, from his cloak, in his holy memory.

There are relics of the hairs of the blessed precursor and Baptist John, who, because he forbade the violation of a brother’s marriage, was imprisoned and bound by Herod, and, at the request of women, was beheaded in testimony to our Redeemer.

There are relics of the beard and of the corporal cloth, and also of the cross, of Saint Peter the apostle, who, in confessing the only-begotten Son of God, received primacy as the foundation of the house of the Lord and became the first occupant of the priestly chair of the city of Rome. Under the emperor Nero he was crucified with his head turned downward, as he himself wished; he was crowned by martyrdom and buried there with fitting honor.

There are relics of the apostle Paul, who merited the dignity of apostleship among the apostles and was appointed teacher of the nations in the true religion. For the truth of Christ he was beheaded by Nero, and in the city of Rome he is venerated with equal remembrance [Col. 1447C] with Saint Peter.

There are relics of Saint Andrew the apostle, who held Scythia and Achaea for the sake of preaching. In the city of Patras, under the proconsul Aegeas, with his hands and feet bound and his whole body stretched out with ropes upon a cross, he survived there for two days and died a blessed death.

There are relics of the blessed apostle James, who was beheaded by Herod at Jerusalem. His bones were transferred to Spain and are honored with the most renowned veneration at its farthest boundaries, namely, facing the British Sea.

There are relics of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, who, preaching Christ’s Gospel in India, showed the light of knowledge to the peoples until the time of his passion and, struck down by the sword for the integrity of the faith, died. From there he was transferred to Benevento, where he is celebrated through the pious veneration of the faithful.

There are relics of Saint Mark the evangelist, who first occupied the chair of Alexandria and founded the Church of Egypt through his faith and diligence. Finally seized by pagans, with a rope thrown around his neck, he was summoned as a martyr to the heavenly kingdoms and was assigned by religious men to the island of Venice.

There are relics of Stephen the protomartyr, who was ordained deacon by the apostles and, stoned by the Jews and the chief priests in Jerusalem, fell asleep in the Lord as a martyr.

There are relics of Saint Ignatius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, who was third after the apostle Peter in that same Church. At the instigation of the emperor Trajan he was condemned to the beasts, suffered many kinds of torments under that ruler, and lies in the same city.

There are relics of the blessed Clement, who governed the Roman Church fourth after Peter. During the persecution of Trajan he was exiled beyond the Pontus Sea, into the desert adjoining the city of Cherson. An anchor was tied around his neck and he was thrown into the middle of the sea; his memory is preserved there to this day.

There are relics of Saint Apollinaris, bishop and martyr, who followed the apostle Peter from Antioch and was sent by that apostle from Rome to Ravenna. Under the emperor Vespasian he completed his martyrdom.

There are relics of the blessed Sebastian, who, under the persecution of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, after holding the command of the first cohort and rejecting the blandishments of the fugitive world, was pierced with arrows by soldiers and beaten with clubs, and as a martyr reached Christ at Rome.

There are relics of Saint Vincent, martyr and deacon, who, together with his bishop Valerius, was severely tormented by many imprisonments in the city of Caesaraugusta, Valentia, and under Dacian gave back to Christ, as a martyr, his unconquered spirit.

There are relics of Saint Maurice, who was first standard-bearer of that legion which, under Maximian, was gloriously crowned for Christ in the city of Sedunum, at the place called Agaunum.

There are relics of the blessed Victor, who, at Marseille, was most cruelly beaten and hanged, tormented with oxen, and thrown into a millstone, thus completing his martyrdom.

There are relics of Saint Saturninus, who, at Toulouse in the time of Decius, was seized by pagans in the Capitol of that city, tied with ropes to a bull prepared for sacrifice, and thrown from the summit of the Capitol down all the steps; thus he breathed out a soul worthy of Christ and rests there.

There are relics of Saint Marcellus, who, suspended on the *equuleus* and tormented with clubs, suffered martyrdom at Spoleto.

There are relics of the blessed Julian, who was seized by pursuing persecutors and killed by having his throat cut, a horrible death, in the territory of Brioude.

There are relics of Saint Lawrence the archdeacon, who, after many slashings and beatings, was stretched upon an iron grate, tortured after a long and manifold punishment, and then exposed upon a bed of burning coals. Under Decius Valerian, illustrious Rome retains him in pious memory.

There are relics of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, who was beheaded at Rome, in his own see, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

There are relics of Saint Hippolytus, who, following the example of the martyr Lawrence, was stretched out and long beaten with clubs and hooks; then, with his feet bound to the necks of untamed horses, he was dragged through thistles and thorns, and at Rome gave up his blessed spirit.

There are relics of Saint Apuleius, who, abandoning Simon Magus, devoted himself to the teaching of the apostle Peter and at Rome, under the consul Aurelian, completed the crown of martyrdom.

There are relics of Saint Vitalis, who at Ravenna, after excessive torments, received the palm of capital martyrdom.

There are relics of the blessed Agapitus, who was struck down by the sword at the city of Praeneste.

There are relics of Saint Mercury, who, while serving in the armies of this world, became a true and spiritual soldier and, at the death of Julian, that most impious Augustus, proved a most illustrious champion, as is read in the *Acts of Basil the Bishop*.

There are relics of the blessed Lantbert, who, at the public estate of Tongeren, was unexpectedly crowned with martyrdom inside a church by most wicked men.

There are relics of Saint Fabius the martyr, who, when he refused to carry the standards of the governor, was condemned to death at Caesarea by a furious judge.

There are relics of the blessed Projectus, martyr and bishop of Auvergne.

There are relics of Saint Fortunatus, who suffered martyrdom at Aquileia.

There are relics of the blessed Nazarius, whom Anolinus, after he had long been tormented and afflicted amid the fury of persecution, ordered to be struck with the sword at Milan.

There are relics of the blessed Longinus, a soldier and martyr, who opened the side of the Lord hanging upon the cross with a lance.

There are relics of Saint Protasius, who completed his martyrdom by decapitation at Milan.

There are relics of Saint Priscus the martyr, who rests at Capua.

There are relics of the blessed Antoninus, who, illustrious through the dignity of the Lord’s honor, endured martyrdom at Apamea.

There are relics of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, who, under the proconsul Galerius, in Africa, at Carthage, inspired by love of Christ and struck with the sword, departed to the Lord as a martyr.

There are relics of Saint Lucius, who in Africa, under Decius and Valerian, when the fury of persecution arose, completed the contest of confession together with many others.

There are relics of the blessed Dionysius, who faithfully carried out his holy work at Paris and, seized by the prefect Fescennius Sisinnius, endured martyrdom.

There are relics of Saint Alexander, who, fastened to the cross at Lyon, breathed out his lifeless spirit.

There are relics of the blessed Orontius the martyr, who, despising bodily death at the city of Embrun, attained the crown of life.

There are relics of Saint Tiberius, who, tortured by various torments in the time of Diocletian, completed his martyrdom in the territory of Agde.

There are relics of the holy Savior, shining in the memories of the pious in the kingdom of Christ.

There are relics of the blessed Genesius the martyr, who was apprehended at Arles by officers and beheaded on the bank of the river Rhône.

There are relics of Saint Felix, who at Girona was bound with heavy chains, dragged through all the streets by untamed mules with his hands tied behind his back, and drowned in the depths of the sea, thus accomplishing a glorious martyrdom.

There are relics of the blessed Cucuphas the martyr, who, cruelly tortured and bound with chains, was stretched upon a gridiron and suffered at Barcelona under Galerius, Maximian, and Rufinus.

There are relics of the holy martyrs of Massa Candida, who, confessing Christ the Son of God in the time of Valerian and Gallienus, were cast into the fire at Carthage.

There are relics of the blessed Cosmas and Damian, who, after enduring beatings, the *equuleus*, fires, and blows from arrows, were put to death by the sword at Aegeae under the governor Lysias.

There are relics of the holy Justus and Pastor, who, while still boys being instructed in letters, threw down their school tablets and ran willingly to martyrdom; hence they were slaughtered by executioners in a field outside the city of Complutum.

There are relics of Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours, a man supreme and incomprehensible [Col. 1450A].

There are relics of the blessed Brictius, a man of admirable holiness in the city of Tours.

There are relics of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, whose flowers of eloquence spread their fragrance throughout the entire Church of the world.

There are relics of the blessed Gregory the Dialogist, who, ordained pope at Rome, led a celibate life.

There are relics of Saint Syrus, bishop, who rests with a glorious end at Pavia, where the Church founded through the faith of believing peoples stands.

There are relics of the blessed Gunterand, king of the Franks, who was distinguished by spiritual works and remains famous for miracles at the city of Chalon.

There are relics of Saint Paul, bishop, who diligently fulfilled the ministry of preaching at the city of Narbonne and rests there famous for miracles.

There are relics of the blessed Trophimus, who performed countless miracles at the city of Arles in Gaul and there fell asleep in peace.

There are relics of the blessed Severus, a priest who converted a great multitude of pagans to the faith of Christ at the city of Vienne.

There are relics of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, illustrious by birth and miracles.

There are relics of Saint Felix, priest of the city of Nola, honorably buried at Pincis.

There are relics of Saint Medard, bishop and confessor of the city of Soissons.

There are relics of the blessed Martial, a man of admirable holiness and religion at the city of Limoges.

There are relics of Saint Maximin, glorious bishop at the city of Trier.

There are relics of the hair of the blessed Salvius, who rests at Albi, distinguished by virtues and miracles.

There are relics of the hair of Saint Caesarius the deacon, buried near the city of Terracina.

There are relics of the blessed Paulinus, bishop, distinguished at Nola in Campania by learning and abundant holiness of life.

There are relics of Saint Germanus, glorious at Paris for virtues and miracles.

There are relics of Saint Hilary, bishop of Carcassonne, a man of great virtue.

There are relics of the blessed Lupus, who fortified Troyes through prayer.

There are relics of Saint Eusebius, bishop of the city of Vercelli.

There are relics of the blessed Philibert, abbot in the territory of Rouen, illustrious in all purity and in the virtues of his spirit.

There are relics of Saint Giles, abbot in the territory of Nîmes, most renowned for signs and holiness.

There are relics of Saint Ugbert, a king, a man endowed with great virtues and excellent pursuits in Italy [Col. 1450D].

There are relics of the blessed Leodegarius, bishop of Autun.

There are relics of Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, adorned with words and virtues.

There are relics of the blessed Gerald, who performed many works in the habit of Christian religion.

There are relics of Saint Firminus, commendable at Uzès for holiness, patience, and faith.

There are relics of Saint Agnes, who was thrown into the fire and struck with the sword at Rome under Symphronius.

There are relics of Saint Agatha the virgin, who, after slaps and imprisonment, after the *equuleus* and tortures, after the cutting off of her breasts, after being rolled upon potsherds and coals, completed her life in prison.

There are relics of Saint Segolina, an excellent woman and glorified by wondrous works.

There are relics of Saint Eulalia, who, after suffering many torments at the command of the governor Dacian, was finally hung upon the *equuleus* and torn with claws; with flaming torches placed on both sides, she gave up her spirit after inhaling the fire, at Mérida in Spain.

There are relics of Saint Leocadia the virgin, who at Toledo, under the dreadful custody of a prison, with her knees placed in prayer, delivered her undefiled spirit to Christ.

There are relics of Saint Eulalia the martyr, who suffered under Dacian in the city of Barcelona.

After the passage of eighty-seven years from its construction, and from the Nativity of the Lord Jesus Christ in the year 1040, this church was governed by Oliva, illustrious in the praise of our age, dear to all through the integrity of his life and morals, and most eminent in the education of his sons and in grace. He held firmly to the soundness of holy faith in truth and embraced it in sincere devotion of heart. [Col. 1451B] He wished the pledge of the humanity of our Lord and of so many of his faithful to be weighed by bodily eyes; therefore, like blessed Moses, he constructed a propitiatory over the altar through the mastery of craftsmanship, having attained prosperity. He arranged it, as was fitting, with such great beauty for the contemplation of God in his entirety that the eyes of those who looked upon its appearance could scarcely be satisfied.

I mean that he placed four bases, one man’s stride apart, at a distance from the foot of the altar, and upon them, with willing strength, he raised an equal number of columns of reddish marble, each made from a single stone, seven feet high. Explicitly, in the sanctuary, he represented the figures of the Cherubim overshadowing the glory of sacred veneration, and in the columns he foreshadowed the glory of the martyrs. They, reddened by the suffering of the body and made white by the purity of the spirit, came through the water of baptism or of their own blood [Col. 1451C] to the growth of the fruits of God’s justice; and the company of teachers, who through steadfast courage and zeal for righteousness support the people joined to the supreme Head in the unity of faith.

Upon the tops of the columns, in order to impress the brightness of ecclesiastical chastity and, through the merits of those making progress, to remove empty fears by the flowers of spiritual graces, he set capitals of white marble, with leafy bodies and patterns of various flowers.

Above these, as the arrangement required, he placed, on both sides of the propitiatory, columns facing one another, made of cut wood and extending three half-cubits, with arches. Within the joints, through cut and sawn wood, he joined together the virtues of the saints, so that, facing one another like windows, each might raise the other into the stability of a fruitful tree, as it were, producing useful fruits.

Between the joints of the arches and the ascent toward the crown, he laid out windows, varied with paintings of every kind and with a multitude of forms and workmanship executed with the greatest care. He also carved, in a square circuit so that they faced one another face to face, four images of the Evangelists in worked wood. Beneath them he placed figures in the form of the upper structure and beneath the curve of the lower arch, so that their gaze might correspond, through the grace of the Gospel, to the four quarters of the world, while at a higher level they looked upon the Lamb.

Along the inner circuit, not for the pomp and splendor of the common people but for the praise of the twelve apostles and the virtue of their good Master, the most wealthy bishop affixed thirteen rows of precious wood. Thus the apostles, among the paths of the just, might from within illuminate the Son of Man in the spirit of his glory; and the holy living creatures might outwardly proclaim the Lamb of God, standing through all ages under one dominion; and, within and without, they might familiarly adorn the tribunal and throne of the eternal King with revelations of the mystery, and, offering pious gifts, become one body in Christ.

He caused all the material, within and without, to rise to a lofty height, and adorned the surfaces and corners with the hands of craftsmen in such a way that nowhere did a joint appear among the panels.

He himself had already embraced, for a long time, the space that lay behind the altar of the venerable Michael, through singular design and munificence. He arranged it for the holy work of the Lord and, outside, above the revered bodies of the martyrs Valentinus and Flamidianus and of the confessor Nazarius—whose bodies are now venerated there with fitting honor—he built, with beautiful and ornamented workmanship, a church of the blessed mother Mary and of the archangels of God in the crypt called the Manger.

Thus, on either side of the Virgin, the angels of the Most High God proclaim by praises and merits the glory of so great a Mother of God, in service of the new salutation: on her right Gabriel announces the conception and birth, while on her left the radiant Raphael affirms the fullness of virginal glory. At her feet, or in her bosom, he enclosed them for service and buried martyrs here and there, who might speak of themselves or of the salvation of the sick: “Behold, this is God, our strength.”

Before the face of the Queen, terrible and divine as he is, Michael, as though for the protection of the Son born before the ages, assigned him to the faithful and to all who came to him, saying: “You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger” (Luke 2:12). Thus, so that the house might possess, in the confession of the true faith, what was fitting for the Most High—the motherliness of the birth—and, in its proper order, might place the glory of the saints in a lower position, as though in the service of the Virgin, he made, in the likeness of a royal throne, not up to the highest pinnacle of the temple but according to the measure of the space, an upper chamber of the greatest and most wonderful workmanship. It was to divide the sanctuary from the front part of the church. There, before many pious witnesses, he dedicated with devout hands a bright altar of the blessed and indivisible Trinity, so that Mother and Son might be proclaimed every day and adored by mortals in continual praise.

For both works, in order to give sanctification of penitence to those who confessed, he placed, in good order, small doors leading inward to the relics of the saints, protected within, so that all might be united in the one thing that is manifested to God alone through splendid rewards. Accordingly, to provide access to the altar of the Holy Trinity within the Holy of Holies, he suitably placed steps, so that those who attempted to ascend or descend might pass easily.

A monk of good reputation therefore assisted him in everything, following the path of the master, like that Oliba; he was a man of the greatest patience and gentleness and, under him, guarded the house with the utmost vigilance in its various activities.

Dearest brothers, we have wished to say these few things from among many about the construction of the church, for the joy of our present feast, so that the wonderful building of the house of the Lord might delight the hearing, and the city beloved by God might fit immense roofs within the structure of faith. Passing from the sacred visible altar to the inner altar of life in due order, let us kindle the incense of goodwill, mercy, justice, kindness, gentleness, and sobriety. In the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father, let the anointed stone be exalted with the adornment of pure confession.

Let the heart of each one of us be an altar; let purity and chastity be living stones; let the fear of the Lord be an ever-watchful guardian, and faith a priest, so that nothing foul may be found inside the Lord’s tabernacle and nothing unworthy admitted.

Let the devil depart with his passions and adversities, and let Christ enter with the blessings and riches of fullness. Within, let us contemplate the Lord’s subtle judgment, and in this our city—or rather, God’s city—which God has shown to be humble through the blow of fire and the judgment of justice, let us recall, in due season, the virtues.

This place had not yet received a fitting form and appearance when it was greatly adorned, at their own expense and through their gifts, by the men mentioned above, within the boundaries of Gaul and Spain, between the gulf and, to speak plainly, the sight of the celebrated and renowned mountain of Canigou, in the valley stretched out beside the most pleasant little river Llitera. It was visited wondrously by the word of God’s protection and magnanimously distinguished by the varied members of its construction and adornment.

This is approved by God, since it is seen everywhere adorned with the marks of beauty, with trees and orchards, and with wooded groves, so that the angelic citizens dwelling there may be believed to be blessed spirits who remove the danger of the evil that came before.

It is also a valley where neither winter’s cold nor summer’s sun is accustomed to harm excessively, because spiritual grace overshadows it, together with the abundant gift of generosity and the overflowing of peace; and, to express it in merciful words, it is a season for its inhabitants of full maturity, so that they may come to the maturity of perfection.

For they delight in the gentleness of prudence, the brightness of faith, the beauty of confession, the loveliness of justice, and the abundance of mercy, so that each may turn the defenses of souls toward God.

All, I say, love one another with devoted affection, cherish one another, and, like a single body with diverse members, sustain one another in due fraternity. Indeed, [Col. 1453D] amid adverse circumstances, or when provoked by opposing forces, they ask divine assistance until, with the utmost strength and determination, they confound their enemies before God and human beings, protected by their earnest supplication and by the archangel’s kindness.

For those whom the presence of the archangels makes more religious are worthy of praise, as are those whom the testimonies of their fellow countrymen, proclaiming their evil persuasion, prove guilty. All deceive themselves when the House of the Lord is dishonorably damaged or defaced by them; they enjoy the world’s honey-sweet and abundant glory, yet do nothing resembling their fathers’ virtue or piety. Instead, they pluck and swallow good and excellent things amid their pleasures—all vain, swollen with pride, and frenzied, devoted to wickedness. Among them there is no one who listens to or understands God, nor anyone who [Col. 1454A] applies himself to goodness, or bends and leads another in the fear of the Lord.

All savor what is earthly, undisciplinedly craving an excess of overflowing abundance. The fathers who lived there contended in complete justice and in every fear of the Lord. Hence everyone joyfully called them blessed:

“You are the blessed flock of Christ; you are the sons of the elect; you are the beloved of God and of your neighbor; you are pillars beneath heaven, standing temporarily like angels upon the earth. You bear a human body, but perform the work of angels.”

Woe, however, to every person who, in return, speaks with altered faith according to his downfall and does not observe that God, the source of every virtue, always joins the ends of those who came before to the beginnings of those who follow. For example, so that he might display neither group with praiseworthy splendor, [Col. 1454B] on the vigil of Christ’s apparition the disaster of a fire melted the whole area outside the church hall. Although those who saw the fire around them might have helped or extinguished it, no one attempted to do so, preserve whatever remained safe, or raise it toward the commendable good of the living.

By God’s judgment and the mercy of blessed Michael, that most admirable structure—which a fire had long ago destroyed—has now been built with extraordinary splendor, both in its manner of construction and its size, as well as in the munificence and glory of each feature, inside and out.

Truly, the island is desirable by its privilege: a portion of land that is an ornament, an enrichment in many respects to the whole country, and a salutary aid to its own region for the wise and the unlearned, the small and the great, and even the rustic. [Col. 1454C] According to the quality of their merits, it possesses the highest summit of honor. The island is renowned for pure and honorable precepts and for the sweetness of blessing; it is sincerely devoted to the dignity and uprightness that command the reverence of its citizens. The island, compacted for the protection of all with caves and conduits, springs and gold-bearing streams, grainfields and vineyards, is eminently glorious. Unless it has been violated by the merits of those standing upon it, it is preserved by the strength of its nobility for God, anointed with the oil of peace.

Although it is narrower in breadth for those who contend, its recesses remain broader in immeasurable length as a reward for those who conquer.

Come, then: celebrate the festive day, faithful crowd; clothe yourselves with strength in joyful hearts, and exult with jubilant rejoicing, because your sorrows have been changed into joy and [Col. 1454D] your sad garment turned into a robe of gladness. The wall of discord that the devil had built he has excavated; he did not move the rock. He shook the foundations of the Church, but did not overthrow the immovable tower. He cast down the stones, but did not uproot the roots. He saw the anointing and immediately abandoned the temple’s strength.

Let the ancient plunderer mourn and blush at having lost his spoil, since we see fulfilled what we heard the prophet foretell: “Indeed,” he says, “captivity shall be taken from the strong, and what had been seized shall be rescued from the mighty.”

Let us all rightly say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Let us, too, awaken completely—those who by habit and appearance have merited this angelic way of life—and in no way turn away from the mercy we hope for, since each of us is able to contemplate day by day the [Col. 1455A] chief angel and the first among Christ’s wonders. From him let each person seek the rewards of our entire faith for a single benefit; and, in the defeat of every quest, let us unanimously desire that he restore the proper vigor, or rather the proper order and the great observance of honor, in all things living and nonliving, immovable and capable of movement, serving in body or appearance, form or kind; and that peace and truth preserve everywhere the angelic dignity and human devotion.

Let us raise up all that we are able and must offer in his praise and wonder. Let us not turn the sight of our bodies or the recesses of our minds here and there, so that the diversity of worldly things may recognize that the wills and agreements of all [Col. 1455B] endure in our chosen unity—especially today, when the King of kings has invited us to the wedding of his Son.

“The wedding is ready,” he says, “and our fattened beasts have been sacrificed.” [Col. 1456A] The Bridegroom sits in the bridal chamber with glory and magnificence, and receives with joy those who enter. Before the doors are closed, let us hasten with swift feet to our Prince, lest we be left outside.

Let us gladly glorify in his saints the splendor of glory and the figure of his substance; and, for the sake of restoration, let us partake in divine love of the bread and wine mixed with water, to be received in their original form. With every desire, let us love him in whom all things exist, by whose passion those whom we daily venerate for their presence were sacrificed and crowned.

Let us bring the solemn festival of the temple’s anniversary, and, in ordered choirs, raise a beautiful voice in praise of the saints, with resounding hymns and lamps kindled, and lift our minds to him who, with the [Col. 1456B] Father and the Holy Spirit, the triune and one God, lives and reigns forever and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Around the Middle of the Century. Dominic, Patriarch of Grado and Aquileia in Venetian Territory

[Col. 1455]

## Letter of Dominic to Peter, Patriarch of Antioch

(Edited by Cotelier, *Monuments of the Greek Church*, II, 108.)

[Col. 1455C] To the most excellent and holy presiding authority of the Church of the Antiochenes, the eminent patriarch, a great and apostolic man: Dominic, by the grace of God patriarch of the Church of Grado and Aquileia.

### 1

With every desire and reverent devotion, and with the intention of most faithful service, we urge that your Church be honored and cherished by our reverence and friendship. It is known to be the sister of our mother, the Roman Church, and is proclaimed second after its founder’s merits—namely, those of Peter, prince of the apostles.

Leaving these matters aside, the fame of your piety, proclaiming everywhere that it is complete in faith and deed, compels us to render humble reverence to you, and, since you walk along the way of the Lord, to follow in your footsteps.

### 2

Although we are separated in the northern region by the longest intervals of land and sea, we are joined in the love of our hearts. We desire to be attached to the knowledge of your holiness, returning to us a share in mutual love.

Therefore we inform you that our Church took its origin from the proclamation of blessed Mark the Evangelist; that, with blessed Peter establishing it, it possessed the honor of the patriarchal name within Italy alone; and that, in the Roman assembly, it obtained the right hand of the ecumenical pope.

We shall show you the order of this matter more fully at a future time, after we have mutually clarified, through an exchange of letters, those things that pertain to the faith. At present, captivated only by love for your goodness, we hasten to reach your knowledge alone, so that we may establish perfect charity between us, upon which we shall henceforth build the things of God more exaltedly.

### 3

Nevertheless, we cannot keep from your fatherhood the fact that we have heard the holy Roman Church being disparaged by the clergy of Constantinople. They criticize the most sacred unleavened bread which we consecrate and receive as the body of Christ. They assert that we are excluded from that body and judge us separated from the unity of the Church, because we celebrate the Eucharistic sacrifice without the mixture of leaven.

Yet, desiring to preserve the unity of the Catholic Church without any schism, we retain the custom of unleavened bread not only according to apostolic tradition but according to that of the Lord himself. Nevertheless, because the sacred mixture of leavened bread is believed to have been accepted by the most holy and orthodox Fathers of the Eastern Churches, let us faithfully understand both customs as legitimate and confirm them salutarily by spiritual understanding.

For the mixture of leaven and flour used by the Churches of the East declares the substance of the incarnate Word; whereas the simple mass of unleavened bread maintained by the Roman Church unquestionably represents the purity of human flesh, which it pleased the divinity to unite to itself.

### 4

Therefore, those who so shamelessly contradict the sacred and apostolic decrees ought to be rebuked by your fatherhood. In what they imagine they are building, they not only destroy what has been built but also excavate the very foundation.

For blessed Peter and Paul preached in Italy in vain if the Western Church is deprived of the blessedness of eternal life. No one will attain it unless he has become a participant in the body and blood of Christ, as he himself testified: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:53).

If, then, the offering of unleavened bread is not the body of Christ, we are all deprived of life in some way. Therefore, having briefly understood these matters through your holiness, and in accordance with the signs of our love, we ask that the evidence of your own mind be sent back to us in reply.

VI.—Privilege of Pope John XIX for the monastery of Cluny. He declares that he confirms all monasteries and places belonging to the monastery of Cluny, together with whatever had previously been granted to it by faithful Christians—kings, bishops, dukes, or princes. He also forbids any bishop or priest to come to Cluny for any ordination or consecration of a church, priests, or deacons, or for the celebration of Masses, unless invited by the abbot of Cluny; but he permits the monks of Cluny to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever their abbot pleases. Likewise, he forbids any bishop or priest to excommunicate Cluniac monks wherever they may be. Moreover, he decrees that the monastery of Cluny shall be a bosom of mercy for all who flee to it for salvation; and establishes that if anyone bound by another’s anathema should seek that monastery, whether for burial of the body or for some other benefit and for the sake of salvation, he should be kindly received and tended with the oil of saving medicine. Finally, he declares that the election of the abbot of Cluny belongs to the congregation of that place, 1135.
